**[THE COMPLETE WORKS OF PETER OF BLOIS]**

## Prolegomena to the Paris Edition, edited by Peter de Gussanville, priest of Chartres

(*The complete works of Peter of Blois, archdeacon of Bath in England, corrected according to manuscript codices, etc.* Paris: at the expense of Simeon Piget, Rue Saint-Jacques, under the sign of Prudence, 1667, folio, with royal privilege.)

[Col. IX]

## Dedicatory Letter

To the Most Illustrious and Most Reverend Lord Louis de Bassompierre, Bishop of Saintes, Peter de Gussanville, priest of Chartres, greetings.

What I had long desired with ardent prayers, most illustrious Prelate—that there might be some public memorial of my gratitude and devotion toward you—I have at length obtained through God’s supreme and singular kindness. The very distinguished Peter of Blois has provided an apt occasion for happily carrying out this purpose. For, as I was about to publish his works for the third time, I had to seek a patron under whose illustrious name they might retain the authority and reputation which they have possessed among learned men for more than four hundred years. And whom else could or ought I seek as patron of Peter’s works but you, most excellent sir? I am bound to you by so many and such great obligations that, even if I devoted all that is in me—which I know to be very little—to your affairs and advantage, I should seem unable to repay even the smallest part of your benefits to me. Indeed, as I attentively ponder the extraordinary kindness and goodwill which you showed me when I formerly lived with you, and which you still show me, unworthy though I am, I recognize that only voice and pen remain to me by which I may proclaim your beneficent nature and your disposition so ready to win men by kindness.

Allow, therefore, my gratitude to be made public, while, under your glorious auspices and through my care, the works of Peter of Blois are made available to the public. In this third edition they required patronage such as yours, so great and so distinguished. For since James Merlin, their first editor, sought the protection of Michael, bishop of Langres; and John Busaeus, their second editor, that of Wolfgang, archbishop of Mainz, Elector and Chancellor of the Holy Roman Empire; surely, when they were to be published for the third time, a patron had to be called upon who was not inferior to Michael and Wolfgang in nobility of birth, splendid achievements, virtues, and dignity. Thus, fully restored to their splendour and integrity, they might come into the hands of learned men, who had preserved in their libraries only mutilated and imperfect copies. Besides carefully correcting in many places the works already brought to light once and twice, and arranging them in a better order, I have also added many other things, both from unpublished works of Peter of Blois himself and from writings of other authors which in some manner concerned the full and complete elucidation of these works.

But there is another reason why, in dedicating Peter’s works, I invoke the aid of your authority. I observe in you the virtues which our archdeacon of Bath declares necessary in bishops, in his letters and especially in his book *On the Appointment of a Bishop*. Thus no one, on learning from the beginning of the book that Peter’s works are inscribed to you, will fail immediately to see, at the very threshold, a living image of what Peter of Blois taught. You did not ascend to the highest ranks of the episcopate through unworthy flatteries of a nobleman, constant visits, importunate petitions, or empty display of merits or learning, but through virtues alone, as though by steps. Having therefore obtained a bishopric which you neither sought nor asked for nor even desired, you have always rendered faithfulness, sincere and holy, first to God and then to the king. You devote care, labour, and money to rebuilding the bishop’s residence, restoring your cathedral church, long ago destroyed by Calvinists, and feeding the poor. Especially mindful that our Lord, shortly before his death, declared that he gave his own peace to the apostles and disciples and left peace with them, you labour to recall the divided to concord. Not only clerics, but secular persons also, even powerful men of your diocese—heretics themselves, trusting in your integrity and drawn by your gentleness and humanity—resort to you. They make you judge and arbiter of their disputes; they debate their controversies before you and comply more readily with your decisions than with decrees of the senate. These are truly episcopal duties, through which you have very often converted heretics to the Catholic faith.

I could and would recount here many other, indeed very great, things concerning you which I myself have seen and witnessed, had you not imposed perpetual silence upon me by the authority which you exercise over me. It will be sufficient if you receive with a serene and open countenance the dedication of Peter of Blois’s works, and regard it as an immortal proof of my devotion toward you and testimony of my respect. This I readily promise myself from your kindness. Farewell, most illustrious bishop.

Given at Paris, the fourth day before the Kalends of April [29 March], in the year of the Lord 1667.

[Col. XI]

## Life of Peter of Blois

Compiled principally from his own letters and contemporary writers.

[Col. XIA] Our Peter, whose name has long been most famous throughout the world, was French by nation and a native of Blois. Although in Letters 20 and 46 he himself calls himself English, it is nevertheless clear from the headings of his letters and treatises that he was French and born in the most noble French city of Blois, for everywhere in them he calls himself Peter of Blois. Nor is he called English for any reason other than that he spent twenty-six years in England. Thus, in Letter 93 he expressly declares himself French: “Brother, we are in sweet France,” etc. “It is enough for me if I live and die where I was born and reared.” Thus he calls his brother William “of Blois” in Letters 90 and 93. Thus in Letters 76 and 77 he calls a certain Peter, one of his compatriots, “of Blois.” Finally, weary of English exile—for he calls himself an exile—in Letter 160, written from England to Odo of Sully, bishop of Paris, he confesses that he is held by the most ardent longing for his native country:

> Alas for me, because my sojourn has been prolonged [Col. XIB] for so long, and there is no one to pity the exile; there is no one to be moved by Joseph’s affliction. Shall I always be a wanderer and fugitive upon the earth? Will no one put an end to my pilgrimage, so that at least once before my final breath I may be allowed to breathe in my native air?

His parents belonged to the leading men of Lesser Brittany, distinguished by virtue and sufficiently wealthy; their resources were ample even for the needs of the poor (Letter 41). I cannot affirm that he had brothers other than William of Blois, whom he says was an abbot in Sicily (Letter 93) and who, at his exhortation, chose, after leaving the abbacy, to be numbered among monks of the lowest rank. This I know: from Letter 36, that he had a nun as a sister, named Christina; and from Letters 131 and 132, that he had one nephew, or perhaps two, though he does not state whether they were through a brother or a sister.

As a young man he diligently applied himself at Paris to the liberal arts and refined literature, to which people gathered from every quarter as to the most celebrated [Col. XIC] market-place of learning; above all, however, he devoted himself to poetry and rhetoric. Of poetry, indeed, he gives this indication in Letter 76: “For I too once devoted myself to trifles and love-songs; but through the grace of him who set me apart from my mother’s womb, I rejected all these things from the first light of youth.” Of rhetoric, the following words of Letter 26 offer clear proof: “Secular law, luxuriating in the glorious furniture of words, charm, and elegance of speech, had powerfully attracted me and intoxicated my mind.” Accordingly, in Letter 8 he writes that, when he was at Bologna among the Italians, he frequently delivered short addresses to students of jurisprudence at the request of his fellow students. This also indicates that he was not ignorant of either law: pontifical law, namely, and imperial law.

Letter 43 shows how far he advanced in medicine. The aforementioned Letter 8 likewise plainly declares how much he knew in mathematics.

[Col. XID] But, leaving Bologna and returning to Paris, he bade farewell to all these disciplines, in order to devote himself wholly to the study of theology alone (Letter 26). Since he possessed outstanding natural ability, he advanced so far in this divine science in a short time that he was thought to have devoured it rather than learned it. He deserves, therefore, to be numbered among the most distinguished theologians of his age, especially for his profound knowledge of Holy Scripture, as his writings demonstrate.

Indeed, perhaps the single most certain proof of his intellectual excellence is what he says in Letter 92: while writing one letter, he dictated three others, most different from one another, to as many men:

> I say this truthfully, not boastfully. The lord of Canterbury has sometimes seen, and you yourselves with him, as have many others, that I dictate on three different subjects to three scribes and keep pace with the hurrying pen of each; and, as is written of Julius Caesar alone, dictate and write a fourth letter. If this seems doubtful to anyone, I ask that the experience of the deed establish the credibility of the statement.

What need is there to mention here our man of Blois’s outstanding love for God? [Col. XIIB] His very many letters written to monks, nuns, and other persons outstanding in the praise of virtue testify to it. In them a certain most sweet fragrance of Christian piety affects readers’ minds so that they feel themselves wholly penetrated and kindled by I know not what sparks. Nor was that piety useful and fruitful only to himself, but, when occasion offered, it also spread to others, especially when ecclesiastical discipline and observance of the sacred canons were at issue. Then he spared neither labour nor vigils. Then, forgetting his own advantage and concerns, he vigorously defended God’s cause even against great men and bishops. Thus he sternly reproved Richard, archbishop of Canterbury, whose intimate and member of household he was (Letter 5); and likewise certain courtly bishops who, neglecting the flocks entrusted to their faith, lingered too long at the court of the Sicilian king. This is observed by Rocco Pirro, Sicilian abbot, in his *Description of Sicily*, in these words:

> Peter of Blois wrote a commentary *On the Appointment of a Bishop* against Sicilian prelates who, in service of the king and neglecting their own flock, spent their time at court.

For these men, if Richard, archbishop of Canterbury, speaks truth in a letter written through Peter of Blois to Alexander III, did not leave the court for seven or even ten years.

[Col. XIIC] Our Peter showed more than sufficiently how devoted he was to the Roman See when he stood with unconquered spirit on Alexander III’s side against Octavian, the antipope. On his way to Rome he was seized and robbed by Octavian’s adherents, as he himself says (Letter 48), after he had completed the course of his studies at Paris, when he was perhaps travelling to Bologna and before he departed for Sicily—namely, in the year of the Lord 1163, since Octavian died in 1164. He also saw to the payment of St Peter’s penny, as it was called—that is, the alms long established by English kings for the English school in the city of Rome. He finally persuaded Henry II, who strongly resisted this, lest the pious prince seem to have deprived the poor of alms bequeathed to them by his forefathers. On this matter Peter himself should be heard, in his *Invective against the Corruptor of His Works*:

> King Henry of good memory had at one time become implacably and irreconcilably enraged against two priors of your order concerning St Peter’s penny. No one dared to oppose him; I stood in the breach for them, and in the time of wrath I became reconciliation.

[Col. XIIIA] He acknowledges one teacher and master, John of Salisbury, later bishop of Chartres, a man cultivated in every kind of learning. His *Polycraticus*, which he published on the frivolities of courtiers, transmits to the everlasting memory of humankind praises of John worthy of cedar and obelisk.

With so illustrious a teacher, our man of Blois ascended to the lofty summit of learning. Consequently he was most welcome to many great men and was honoured by them with the highest dignities. Sent to Sicily about the year of the Lord 1167 by Rotrou, archbishop of Rouen, of the family of the counts of Perche and uncle of the queen of Sicily, he was appointed tutor to William II, king of Sicily, set over the sealing of his letters and diplomas, and possessed great influence among the Sicilians. He testifies to this in Letter 131, addressed to his nephew, prior of a small monastery:

> You have often been able to learn, from the testimony of the pope who now sits, from many of his cardinals who exercised legations in my time, from my brother, from the abbot of St Denis, and from other magnates in the land, that when I was chancellor and teacher of King William II in Sicily—then a boy—and after the queen and the elect of Palermo the administration of the kingdom depended very much upon my judgment, etc.

Shortly after his return to France, Henry II summoned him to England and sent him to the king of the French on important business. Peter remained at Henry’s court until, inflamed with desire for a quieter life, [Col. XIIIC] he went to Richard, archbishop of Canterbury, whose chancellor he calls himself in Letters 38 and 130. In this archbishop’s name he was also sent as envoy to Henry II to transact matters of greatest importance concerning the Church. Finally, after Henry II’s death, he lived at the court of Eleanor, queen of the English, and wrote many letters on her behalf to various persons.

Apart from the embassy which he undertook to Henry II at the instigation of Richard, archbishop of Canterbury, he discharged two other especially distinguished missions. The first was in 1176, to Alexander III, Roman pontiff, in order to plead before him Richard’s case against Roger, the designated abbot of St Augustine’s, Canterbury. Roger claimed that he ought to be consecrated in the church of his monastery by the archbishop of Canterbury; Richard maintained that this should instead take place in the mother church at Canterbury. But the affair turned out as Abbot Roger wished, as William Thorn relates in the *Chronicles of England*, under the year of Christ 1176. The second was in 1187, on the occasion of the lawsuit which Baldwin, likewise archbishop of Canterbury, brought against the monks of his cathedral church. Baldwin wished, namely, to establish a collegiate church of secular canons to the detriment of the monks, who were canons of this church. When the matter was reported to Urban III through our Peter, the archbishop of Canterbury lost his case, as may be seen in Gervase of Canterbury’s account of Henry II, under the year 1178.

[Col. XIIID] Nor, indeed, were the weightiest affairs entrusted to our man of Blois without good reason, nor were the great titles of honour and dignity conferred on him by eminent men undeserved. His uprightness of life and holiness of conduct were such that he seemed to direct himself and all his possessions to the glory of God alone and the benefit of the Catholic Church. What else does he do when, in Letter 130, he sternly rebukes William, king of Sicily, for invading the rights of the Church and selecting bishops according to his own whim and judgment? What else when, in Letter 123, he awaits an appropriate opportunity either for exile or for martyrdom? What else does that supreme patience which he showed in illnesses and hardships, of which he speaks in Letter 31, demonstrate? What else when he left the court of Henry II, king of the English, in order to care more securely for his salvation? “Led,” he says at the beginning of Letter 147, “by a certain spirit of ambition, I had immersed my whole self in civil waves; forgetting the things behind, I stretched forth toward those ahead, but not in the manner of the Apostle. Yet the Lord chastened me severely and did not hand me over to death. Fastening me to a bed of pain, he poured out the spirit of his indignation upon a small, abject, and miserable body. I was distressed unto death, and the separation of soul and body already most certainly threatened; but the Father of mercies, understanding that affliction would give me understanding, remembered mercy in his anger, restrained the spirit of his wrath, and blew the spirit of ambition away from me. Thus I resolved to leave and cast aside the cloak with Joseph, the tax-office with Matthew, the burial cloth with John, and the water-jar of covetousness with the Samaritan woman.” [Col. XIVB] “The Lord helped me; and the dew of divine compassion extinguished the blaze of ambition which torrents of gold and silver had previously been unable to temper within me.” Finally, what else does that Christian humility show, by which he refused to permit himself to be advanced to the sacred order of priesthood except at a very advanced age (Letters 127 and 139)? He refused the archbishopric of Naples, a bishopric offered to him once and again in these regions, and, measuring honour by its burden, as he himself says in Letter 131, confined ambitious impulses within the sober limits of moderation.

Although from some passages of his letters he may seem to have sought riches and served his own interests too much, nevertheless Letter 58 sufficiently shows with what zeal he cultivated poverty. And indeed, how could one be thought to have sought wealth and pursued his own advantage who relinquished a deanery in favour of Cistercian monks [Col. XIVC] (Letter 152), because he could not reform the corrupt morals of his canons for the better? Who, in Letter 5, attacks in rather sharp words Richard, archbishop of Canterbury, whose chancellor he was, because he did not govern the flock entrusted to him with due solicitude? Who, content with a single prebend of the Church of Chartres, desired to be received into the household of William, archbishop of Sens? Who, finally, worn out by old age, came to such poverty that, although he had received many benefices from Henry II and had formerly been chancellor to two archbishops of Canterbury, he was driven from the archdeaconry of Bath by the faction of certain envious and ill-disposed men? Later granted the archdeaconry of London, to which much honour but little income was in fact attached, he wrote to Innocent III, Roman pontiff (Letter 151), asking him to provide an income by which he could worthily maintain the office of archdeacon of London.

[Col. XIVD] At last his virtue—as commonly happens to the greatest and best men—was exposed to the weapons of envy. Thus in his *Invective against the Detractor* he found it necessary to defend his reputation against the slanders of a malicious man; and in Letter 149 he complains that the rank of archdeacon had been taken from him in his old age through certain impostures. But to crown all his misfortunes, after being assailed by every kind of calamity and hardship, he ended the last day of his life in a foreign land—which he calls exile in Letter 160—and not in his own country, as he most earnestly wished. For when, in extreme old age, he wrote to Odo, bishop of Paris, begging him to free him from exile, he ends the letter thus: “If I am not allowed to live in my own country, may I at least be allowed to be buried there.”

He died in England, if historians are to be believed, in the year of restored human salvation 1200. For although we possess nothing certain or fully established concerning the year of his death, the time when he died may nevertheless be inferred to some degree from Letter 151, addressed to Innocent III [Col. XVA] about the year 1199.

How highly he was regarded not only by his own countrymen but also by foreigners, especially the English, Nicholas Harpsfield, an English author, teaches in chapter 20 of his *History of England*, where he speaks of him as follows:

> Peter of Blois’s abundant gifts do not permit me to dismiss him with a bare and simple naming. For he was a man highly cultivated in every kind of learning for his time—not an Englishman, to be sure, but a Frenchman—whom Henry II greatly valued for his learning and prudence. He often employed his services in embassies to foreign peoples. Sent to Rome by the king and Baldwin, he also vigorously defended Baldwin’s cause against the monks. In this matter Gervase attacks him rather bitterly as architect and leader of all those disturbances. He seems to have been a man of frank and rather liberal spirit in rebuking the faults not only of friends and ordinary people, but also of great men. He did not refrain from admonishing a certain friend who had abandoned the discipline of the Carthusians, to which he had committed himself; Richard [Col. XVB] of Salisbury, archdeacon, and the bishop of Rochester, who were excessively devoted to hunting and hawking; and also Richard [variant: Richards], bishops of Bath and Canterbury, concerning their duty. He complained even to the king about the wrongs inflicted upon the people by sheriffs and by those entrusted with the keeping of the royal forests. He carefully clears the king of responsibility for the murder of St Thomas, and shows how much help, in all his difficulties, he placed in the prayers and protection of the deceased. He seems to have been secretary to Richard of Canterbury and to have cultivated among his chief friends John of Chartres, to whom various letters are addressed. King Henry valued the reading of these so highly that he urged everyone to collect Peter’s letters, saying that he was held by a great desire to read them. He was archdeacon of Bath, then of London, and finally of Canterbury. They say that he was honoured with priesthood. Yet, so far as I have read, I find that he calls himself a deacon, not a priest. Among many other works which he composed, he wrote the *Life* of Archbishop Wilfrid and of Guthlac the Confessor, [Col. XVIB] and he lived down to the times of King Richard.

[Col. XV]

## Preface to the Reader

[Col. XVB] We have said more than enough concerning Peter of Blois in his *Life*. Now, kindly Reader, I wish briefly to give you some notice of his works. One hundred and fifty years ago—that is, in 1519—James Merlin, doctor of theology at Paris, a man of singular learning and piety, brought together and made public Peter of Blois’s works in one body. He was penitentiary of the cathedral church and archpriest of the church of St Mary Magdalene in the city; he also collected the general councils into one volume and published many other works.

This man, the first editor, was grieved that Peter of Blois, who had once shone so brightly in the Church, was almost hidden in darkness. He therefore saw to his publication with the utmost labour, although he left this edition insufficiently corrected and defective in many respects because of the scarcity of copies.

> **[Note: Col. XVD]** Before this, however, Peter of Blois’s *Letters* had appeared without indication of place or time—at Brussels, however, at the press of the Brethren of the Common Life, about 1480—in folio. This edition contains one hundred and seven letters, and Peter de Gussanville did not know it. **Editor of the Patrology.** [Col. XVID]

Eighty years later, namely in 1600, John Busaeus, a man as learned as he was pious and sufficiently known through his writings, followed him, fired by the same zeal, and again brought Peter of Blois into the light. Yet, because he had not seen Merlin’s edition, he omitted certain works published there: namely, the *Sermons*, the treatise *On the Perfidy of the Jews*, and the greater part of the treatise *On Christian Friendship*. Five years later, however, after finding new manuscript codices, he published these latter two treatises in a volume entitled *Paralipomena of Peter of Blois*—“Supplementary Matters.”

We owe great gratitude to both men, since they deserved well of the Christian commonwealth of letters. But because copies of both editions had long been unavailable and were urgently sought with the greatest zeal by learned men, while no one undertook this work, I, though the least of scholars, most willingly accepted this labour at the advice of friends, seeing that it would redound to the benefit of the Church, for whose advantage alone I have undertaken to labour. Kindly Reader, learn briefly what I have accomplished in this edition. From the two earlier editions I have made one, supplying from the other what was lacking in either. In our edition we have followed Busaeus’s copy as the more reliable, but have corrected it as carefully as possible in many passages with the help of manuscript codices gathered from every quarter. We have retained the summaries of the letters, variant [Col. XVIB] readings with notes, lists, indexes, and marginal notes, as well as the two brief indexes of proverbs and barbarous words which he published. We have restored Peter of Blois’s genuine sermons, already published by Merlin. We could not produce a more corrected text of these, because despite every diligence and inquiry we were unable to find any manuscript copies of them; we only added marginal notes and passages of Scripture which had been lacking. We added an outstanding sermon, namely Sermon 75, on two verses of Psalm 93, through the work of the Reverend Father Lord Simon Guillemot, subprior of the monastery of Saint-Ghislain in Hainaut. He kindly sent it to us after having it copied, not without labour, from a manuscript codex of the abbey of Cambron. We also added many things anew: having learned that many works of Blois still lay hidden in libraries, we spared neither labour nor expense in order to recover them.

At last, after a long and anxious wait caused by the disasters of war, we received from the Oxford library two notable treatises: *On the Usefulness of Tribulation* and *What Sort They Are*. For this benefit we are indebted to the exceptional kindness of the very distinguished Henry Justel, son of Christopher. These two treatises were sent to him, after correction involving no little labour, by the most learned Mr Wallis, Savilian Professor of Geometry at the University of Oxford.

I shall say nothing about the usefulness of Peter of Blois’s works. To offer my own judgment after so many and such great men who have praised them for nearly five hundred years would be great rashness. Hardly any celebrated author can be found who has not made honourable mention of him, in matters concerning history, morals, and also the sound doctrine of the Church. Thus some seem not without reason to number him among the later Fathers of the Church. [Col. XVID]

These are the general remarks which we have had to make concerning Peter of Blois’s works, friendly Reader. Now the individual works must be examined one by one. But first a catalogue of all the works must be set out.

[Col. XVII]

## Catalogues of the Works of Peter of Blois

### I. Drawn from the Author Himself

[Col. XVIIA]

Peter of Blois, in the little work which he entitled *Invective against the Corruptor of His Works*, writes as follows concerning some works which he had already published:

> That I am not accustomed to flatter great men in their vices, or praise the sinner in the desires of his soul, is apparent:
>
> In my *Compendium on Job*; in my *Letters*; in my book of *Exhortations*; in my *Dialogue addressed to King Henry*; in my *Treatise on the Jerusalem Pilgrimage*; in my book *On the Tricks of Fortune*; in my recent work *On the Defence of the Faith*; in my book *Against the Perfidy of the Jews*; in my book *On Confession and Penance*; in the work entitled *The Episcopal Canon*; and in very many other writings of mine, etc.

[Col. XVIIB] Thus far he. What those “very many other writings” were, he nowhere stated. Only at the beginning of the *Compendium on Job* are two treatises cited:

- *Treatise on the Transfiguration of the Lord.*
- *Treatise on the Conversion of Saint Paul the Apostle.*

And at the end of Letter 14, addressed to the chaplains of Henry II, king of the English, there is cited:

- *Book on the Deeds of Henry II, King of the English.*

### II. From John Trithemius, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*

Peter of Blois, archdeacon of Bath, intimate friend of John, bishop of Chartres, to whom he dictated several letters; a diligent and learned student of the divine Scriptures and exceptionally learned in secular letters; acute and vigorous in intellect; a man who knew not how to flatter, but to rebuke, the faults of princes and prelates; held in esteem by kings, princes, and bishops for his learning and uprightness of life; wrote many little works, of which the following are reported. [Col. XVIIC]

*On Christian Friendship*, book I: “Because they are diminished.” *On Salutary Penance*, book I: “You asked me that for you.” *On Hastening the Passage*, book I: “Who will give to my head.” *On the Quality of Penance*, book I: “The excess of your severity.” *On the Study of Wisdom*, book I: “You are divided, and your heart.” *Against the Corrupter*, book I: “Your little exhortation.” *Exhortation to an Abbot*, book I: “You were chosen by your own.” *On the Office of a Bishop*, book I: “You ask more urgently.” *On the Peril of Prelates*, book I: “Whenever I recall the words.” *On the Life of Court Clerics*, book I: “I give thanks to grace.” *Letters*, 194 in number, book I: “Having been asked by you.” [Col. XVIID] *On the Deceptions of Fortune*, book I. He also wrote many other works. He flourished under Emperor Frederick I in the year of the Lord 1160.

## III. FROM THE THIRTEENTH CENTURY OF WRITERS OF BRITAIN, CHAPTER I, AND FROM THE BIBLIOTHECA OF C. GESNER, ENLARGED IN ITS LATEST EDITION

*On Christian Friendship*, book I. *On Salutary Penance*, book I. *On Hastening the Passage*, book I. *On the Quality of Penance*, book I. *Sermons on Fasting*, book I. *On the Study of Wisdom*, book I. *Against the Corrupter*, book I. [Col. XVIIIA] *Exhortations to an Abbot*, book I. *On the Office of a Bishop*, book I. *On the Deceptions of Fortune*, book I. *On the Peril of Prelates*, book I. *On the Life of Court Clerics*, book I. *Letters*, 194 in number, book I. *On the Holding of Synods*, book I. *The Episcopal Canon*, book I. *The Life of Patient Job*, book I. *The Life of Archbishop Wilfrid*, book I. *The Life of Guthlac the Confessor*, book I. *Dialogue of a King and an Abbot*, book I. *On the Pilgrimage to Jerusalem*, book I. *Sermons for Feast Days*, book I. *On the Conversion of St Paul*, book I. *On the Transfiguration of the Lord*, book I. *On the Affirmation of Faith*, book I. *Testimonies to the Catholic Faith*, book I. *On the Perfidy of the Jews*, book I. [Col. XVIIIB] *The Gathered Bouquet of Flowers*, book I. *The Deeds of Henry II*, book I. *Pious Exhortations*, book I.

Gerard Johann Vossius, in book III of *On Latin Historians*, mentions a certain little work of Peter of Blois in these words: “The same Peter of Blois, at the request of the abbot and convent of Crowland, added an appendix to Ingulph’s *History*, by which he carried that history down to his own times, as Brian Twyne noted in book I of *On the Antiquity of Oxford University*, where he also adduces from that appendix a notable *abridgement* [Greek: *peritomē*].” This passage is read in the same words in the appendix joined to Ingulph both in the English and in the German edition. But the inscription in each is: “Appendix to Ingulph by an uncertain author.” Therefore, that we know its author’s name is owing to Brian, whom I readily persuade myself to have found it in manuscripts.

## IV. FROM OUR EDITION

[Col. XVIIIC] Letters, 183 in number. Sermons, 65. Shorter works, namely: *Treatise on the Transfiguration of the Lord*; *Treatise on the Conversion of St Paul*; *Compendium on Job*; *Treatise on the Pilgrimage to Jerusalem*; *Instruction in the Faith for the Sultan of Iconium*; *Book on Sacramental Confession*; *Book on Penance, or Satisfaction*; *The Episcopal Canon, or Treatise on the Instruction of a Bishop*; *Invective against the Corrupter*; *Book against the Perfidy of the Jews*; the twofold *Treatise on Christian Friendship*; *Treatise on the Usefulness of Tribulations*; the treatise *What Sort They Are*; *Fragment of a Letter on the Observance of Silence*; *Fragment of a Book on the Deceptions of Fortune*; [Col. XVIIID] *Treatise on the Division and Writers of the Sacred Books*; *Treatise on the Most Holy Eucharist in Verse*. A few words must be said about all of these.

### Letters

The Letters stand first, as the most brilliant among the works of Blois. Concerning their excellence, it will suffice to say that learned men flourishing during the last four centuries have praised them, especially Baronius, who enriched the latter part of his *Annals* with much testimony drawn from these letters themselves and drew from their sources many observations most worthy of notice and knowledge. It is therefore no wonder that so many manuscript copies of them have been scattered throughout the world, so that more than twenty are found in Paris alone [Col. XIXA]. Their number is uncertain, since some manuscripts contain more and others fewer letters. All agree on 160; the rest are of doubtful authenticity, since they are absent from most manuscripts and differ greatly from Blois’s style. Yet it is clear even from reading the surviving copies that Peter of Blois wrote many other letters, in which he himself mentions many that no longer survive.

Moreover, the order of the letters is altogether perverse. Busaeus could easily have reformed it for the better, but did not. Yet because it has long since been universally accepted by learned men, particularly Baronius and other writers of ecclesiastical history, we considered it a scruple of conscience to alter it. In the notes, however, we have indicated, so far as conjecture permitted, in what year each letter was written. Nor should it be omitted that, following Busaeus’s example, we removed several items from the number of letters and placed them among the shorter works, [Col. XIXB] although almost all manuscripts place them among the letters: such as the *Treatises on the Transfiguration* and *on the Conversion of St Paul*; the *Instruction in the Faith for the Sultan of Iconium*; the books *On Confession* and *On Penance*; the *Instruction of a Bishop*; and others which are more truly shorter works than letters.

### Sermons

The Sermons follow. We have taken them from Merlin’s edition, and it must be believed on unquestionable authority that they are genuine and authentic sermons of Blois: first, because they were long ago published by Merlin himself, who possessed the autograph; and also because Bale, a man devoted to antiquarian study, in his catalogue of Peter of Blois’s works, *Century* XIII, chapter 31, reported the first sermon in the same manner as Merlin. Moreover, Busaeus himself—who five years earlier had published sermons of Peter Comestor under the name of Peter of Blois—says at the end of his preface to the *Paralipomena of Peter of Blois*:

> Furthermore, certain other sermons of Blois, differing from mine, have recently been discovered by scholars of Ingolstadt [Col. XIXC]. But the most distinguished Henry Canisius, professor of the University of Ingolstadt, will arrange for them to be printed at the next fair, either at Mainz or elsewhere, together with certain other little works of ancient authors.

These are Busaeus’s words about Canisius, who presumably, prevented by death, left those sermons—undoubtedly similar to ours—unpublished. Finally, these sermons wholly savour of the style of our Peter, as will be clearer to anyone well versed in reading him. I pass over the many turns of phrase found in the letters and in these sermons alike, to which I refer the reader for brevity’s sake. I also pass over the frequent, almost continuous citations of Holy Scripture with which Peter of Blois’s works are sprinkled, since this feature belongs not to him alone but to every writer of his age, as appears from the writings of St Bernard, Peter the Chanter, Lombard, Maurice, Peter Comestor, and others.

That the sermons published by Busaeus under the name of Peter [Col. XIXD] of Blois are by Peter Comestor, or Manducator, is clearer than daylight. Yet Busaeus, otherwise a most learned man, deserves pardon. Knowing that certain sermons had been composed by Peter of Blois, and having no copy of them available, he eventually obtained a single copy sent to him from Louvain, bearing the title *Sermons of Master Peter*, and supposed these to be sermons of Peter of Blois. But that they are not his, but Peter Manducator’s, is shown most clearly by very many manuscripts found in various libraries. We shall produce five or six manuscript codices which we have seen and collated.

The first is the Mentelian manuscript, that is, the manuscript of Jacques Mentel, doctor of medicine at Paris. This ancient codex restores these sermons to their legitimate author, Peter Manducator, and bears this inscription: “Order of the Sermons of Master Peter Manducator through the course of the year.” At the end of the codex occur these words: “Here end the Sermons of Master Peter Manducator.”

The second codex is from Marmoutier, of excellent and ancient authority, being copied about the time of Comestor himself [Col. XXA], as appears from these words written at the end of the codex in precisely the same hand as the rest of the work: “This book belongs to St Martin, etc. The book was made in the time of William the Armarius, in the eighth year of Abbot Hervé.” This Hervé, as appears from the list of abbots of Marmoutier found in the notes to Guibert of Nogent, held pastoral office from the year of Christ 1178 to 1186. The beginning of the codex is as follows: “Here begin the chapters of the Sermons of Master Peter Manducator contained in this volume, etc.”

The third is a Corbie manuscript codex of no mean authority, in which there is no title. Yet the sermons are the same as in the former manuscript. The fourth is a Carthusian manuscript from the monastery of Val-Dieu in the district of Perche. This codex, written nearly 500 years ago, has on its opening page: “Order of the Sermons of Master Peter Manducator through the course of the year in the synod, etc.” Finally, we saw three distinguished codices of these sermons in the library of the monastery of St Victor at Paris, in whose church Peter Comestor was buried. [Col. XXB] In them the same title occurs, namely, “Sermons of Master Peter Manducator”; and besides those published by Busaeus, there are found several other sermons by the same Peter Manducator which have not yet come to light.

### Treatise on the Transfiguration

The *Treatise on the Transfiguration of the Lord*, which in very many manuscripts stood among the Letters, we have placed among the Shorter Works, following Busaeus’s method, as also the treatise on the conversion of St Paul and certain others. We corrected this treatise with the aid of Merlin’s printed copy and the manuscript of Henri Valois.

### On the Conversion of St Paul

Likewise, we collated the treatise on the conversion of St Paul with Merlin’s printed edition and the Mazarin and Valois manuscripts.

### Compendium on Job

The *Compendium on Job* contains the life, sufferings, and death of the holy prophet Job, as Henry II, king of [Col. XXC] England, had asked Peter of Blois to provide, as Peter himself states in the preface to this work. It was corrected from the Merlin, Mazarin, and Valois copies.

### On the Pilgrimage to Jerusalem

For the occasion on which the *Treatise on the Pilgrimage to Jerusalem* was written, see the notes. In correcting it we used the manuscripts Hard., Sorb. 2, Ful., and Vall.

### Instruction in the Faith

The *Treatise on Instruction in the Faith* was corrected with the aid of the manuscripts For., Hard., Laun., Ful., Sorb. 1 and 2. This treatise is also found in Matthew Paris under the year 1169. It appears to be the same work which Blois himself calls the *Affirmation of Faith* in the *Invective*, and elsewhere the *Book on Faith*. This *Instruction* was sent, in the name of Pope Alexander III, to the most powerful prince, the Sultan of Iconium. For it, one should consult writers of this century, especially Baronius, *Annals*, vol. XII.

### On Confession

The *Book on Sacramental Confession* was corrected with the aid of the manuscripts Vall., Camus., Vici. [Col. XXD] 3, and Merlin’s printed edition. Here Blois treats confession as the third part of the sacrament of penance, and shows that each and every mortal sin, even the most hidden and shameful, must be disclosed in confession.

### On Satisfaction, or Penance

The *Book on Satisfaction and Penance* was likewise corrected with the aid of the manuscripts mentioned above. In it our Peter attacks a certain abbot who customarily imposed upon his monks, after confession, penances harsher than those which he wished imposed upon himself.

### The Episcopal Canon

The *Episcopal Canon*, or *Instruction of a Bishop*, which Trithemius calls the *Book on the Office of a Bishop*, is found in Val., Sorb. 1, Maz. 1, Vict. 3, and Merlin; these we used to correct it. It is a most learned treatise and exceedingly necessary for bishops.

### Invective against the Corrupter

The *Invective against the Corrupter* was written against a certain regular canon who had written against our Peter and criticized his writings. We corrected this treatise by means of Sorb. 1, Vall., Boer., Maz. 1, Vict. 3, and Merlin. [Col. XXIA]

### Against the Perfidy of the Jews

The *Book against the Perfidy of the Jews* was written to refute Jews, especially concerning the coming of the Messiah; it proves this elegantly from various passages of Scripture. We collated it with the Camus manuscript and Merlin’s printed edition.

### On Christian Friendship

The *Treatise on Christian Friendship*, already published by Merlin, was first issued incomplete by Busaeus, who had not seen Merlin’s edition, and then complete five years later. We used that copy; the Camus manuscript and Merlin’s printed edition assisted us in correcting it. It is divided into two books, and the books into several chapters. It appears to be Peter of Blois’s latest little work, since at its beginning he himself acknowledges that he wrote it when already old, with his strength broken and near to death.

### On the Usefulness of Tribulations, and *What Sort They Are*

[Col. XXIB] With regard to those two new little works, namely the *Treatise on the Usefulness of Tribulation* and the treatise *What Sort They Are*, we received them, as stated above, from the most learned Mr Wallis. Since he had little confidence in copyists, he wished to correct them only with immense care and tireless labour, especially because the copies he used were extremely difficult to read and full of abbreviations. Anyone not thoroughly accustomed to ancient handwriting and ancient abbreviations would be liable to stumble over almost every word, although the handwriting of the autograph is very old and, for its time, fairly beautifully written. These are the words of that learned man, which may serve me in place of an admonition to the reader.

He says further that, in addition to the Oxford codex which he used, he corrected much by means of two other manuscript codices from the library of Merton College, Oxford, and another Bodleian codex, from which he supplied many things either missing or corrupt in his own copy.

### On Observing Silence

[Col. XXIC] We obtained the fragment of a letter on observing silence from manuscripts in the library of Merton College, Oxford, through the kindness of the same Mr Wallis, who graciously sent it to us with the two preceding treatises, until the complete letter may be found.

### On the Deceptions of Fortune

We drew the fragment of the *Book on the Deceptions of Fortune* [Note: [Col. XXI] It is chapter 12 of book I of John of Salisbury’s *Polycraticus*, *Patrologia*, vol. CXCIX.] from the library of St Victor at Paris, where it lay hidden in a volume of Peter of Blois’s letters. The very courteous and most friendly François le Tonnelier, librarian of that same library, very graciously communicated it to me, as he did many other things, after first discovering it himself. Since this book *On the Deceptions of Fortune* is distinguished, and is often cited by its author in the letters, especially in Letter 19, we shall owe great thanks to English scholars—to whom we are already especially indebted for the above-mentioned treatises of Peter of Blois communicated to us, and to whom we offer all the gratitude we can [Col. XXID] for this—if they will deign to seek out that treatise, together with some other little works by the same author, in their very rich libraries and send them to us.

### Division and Writers of the Sacred Books

We have added the small treatise on the division and writers of the sacred books from Merlin’s edition, although we have found it in no other copy.

### On the Eucharist

Finally, we have published the treatise on the Eucharist, composed in verse, from Busaeus’s edition, although neither Blois himself nor any other author makes any mention of it.

It is now worth while to give the reader a warning concerning the notes. We offer you, kindly reader, not long commentaries but notes as brief as possible, pertaining either to textual criticism or drawn from history [Col. XXIIA], so that whatever might hinder or delay the reader even a little may be removed from his path, and a smooth and open road to understanding the whole work may be opened. We composed these notes not upon the shorter works themselves, save incidentally and rarely, but chiefly upon the letters: both because the letters hold the chief place among Blois’s works, and because the printers, hurrying on an undertaking long desired by the most learned men, pressed us exceedingly hard.

After Busaeus’s notes had been published, we found in France many manuscript codices which Busaeus himself had not had the opportunity to see. Moreover, many things certainly escaped a foreigner, a German and thus rather unfamiliar with our history, which have in our age happily been brought out of darkness and made public property. Hence, I think, there is no one who does not see most clearly how much light can be cast upon the history of Peter of Blois and the more difficult passages of his writings. As for the manuscript codices which we used, [Col. XXIIB] they were supplied to us by men eminent in every kind of learning. Although nothing can be added to their praise and distinction by my words, it is nevertheless pleasant to set out their names individually here, so that posterity may know through whose help and assistance Peter of Blois, as though the grime and squalor of antiquity had been wiped away, now emerges into the light more elegantly and splendidly adorned.

First, John Launoy, Parisian theologian, generously gave us a manuscript codex which is both the oldest and of the best authority. Another of no less value came into our hands through Raymond Formentin, canon of the Church of Orléans. Two further codices were supplied from the distinguished library of the most eminent Cardinal Mazarin. Three other manuscripts came from the most ancient and, among scholars, most renowned library of the Parisian monastery of St-Germain-des-Prés. One came from that same library, another from Bec, and a third from Marmoutier. Dom Luc [Col. XXIIC] d’Achéry, the most worthy prefect of that library, gave these to me because of our longstanding friendship. By his singular kindness he is known and dear to everyone; while he appears, almost incidentally, to gather only the lesser ears of grain from ancient manuscripts, he furnishes students of antiquity with a most abundant harvest.

Moreover, Charles le Tonnelier, the ever-watchful librarian, generously supplied me with three manuscripts from the library of St Victor, renowned throughout the world. Although I should greatly wish to return thanks worthy of his kindness toward me, I cannot; for he has also given me access to other manuscript codices, from which I have drawn many things hitherto unpublished, as will be noted in their proper place. Others came from various libraries: those of Mr Boyer, senator of Dijon; Mr Hardy, senator in the Parisian prefecture; Mr Hautin, likewise senator in the Parisian prefecture; the convent of the Friars Preachers of St James at Paris; the Parisian Fathers of Feuillants; Mr Vallin, canon of Nantes; and likewise two from the Sorbonne library. [Col. XXIID] The papers of the most illustrious and celebrated Pierre de Marca, formerly Archbishop of Paris, also aided us greatly. They were lent to us by the learned Étienne Baluze, and in them that most learned man had noted variant readings which he had collected from two manuscript copies of Peter of Blois’s letters.

The manuscript codex of Henri Valois, royal historiographer, was also of great use in correcting the shorter works; it contains the *Treatise on Job*, *On the Transfiguration of the Lord*, and *On the Conversion of St Paul*. There also came into our hands a manuscript codex of Nicolas Camusat, formerly canon of the Church of Troyes, now preserved in the library of the Jesuit College of Clermont at Paris. By its aid we corrected the shorter works *On Confession*, *On Penance or Satisfaction*, [Col. XXIIIA] the *Episcopal Canon*, *Against the Perfidy of the Jews*, and *On Christian Friendship*. I omit the previously published copies, which I also consulted where needed: namely, the one prepared by Jacques Merlin, doctor of Paris; and the Mainz edition, in which only the Letters were published.

So that the reader may more easily recognize the sigla of the codices which we have used, here are the signs which we have thought should be appended.

Laun. denotes the manuscript codex of John Launoy. For., the manuscript codex of Raymond Formentin. Maz. 1 and 2, the first and second manuscript codices of Cardinal Mazarin. Sang., the manuscript codex of St-Germain-des-Prés. Bec., the manuscript codex of the monastery of Bec. Major., the manuscript codex of Marmoutier. Vict. 1, 2, and 3, the first, second, and third manuscript codices of St Victor at Paris. Boer., the manuscript codex of Mr Boyer. Hard., the manuscript codex of Mr Hardy. [Col. XXIIIB] Haut., the manuscript codex of Mr Hautin. Dom., the manuscript codex of the Parisian Dominicans. [Col. XXIVA] Ful., the manuscript codex of the Parisian Feuillants. Vall., the manuscript codex of Mr Vallin. Sorb. 1 and 2, the first and second manuscript codices of the Sorbonne. Marc., the papers of Mr de Marca. Vales., the manuscript codex of Henri Valois. Cam., the manuscript codex of Nicolas Camusat. Merl., the edition prepared by Jacques Merlin. Mog., the edition of the Letters published at Mainz.

I would also have you know, excellent reader, that our notes were enriched by many important papers [Note: [Col. XXIIIB] See the Appendix.], the greater part of which the distinguished Mr de Vion d’Herouval, who has deserved supremely well of all scholars and whose kindness and lavish generosity toward all learned men will be celebrated by learning as long as it flourishes, graciously supplied us—either drawn from his own storehouse or collected from his friends with tireless study and labour. Certain other most distinguished and courteous men likewise generously gave us some papers, whose names we shall place at the head of the papers as a mark of honour. [Col. XXIVB]

[Col. XXIII]

## EXTRACTS FROM THE PREFACES TO THE OXFORD EDITION, PREPARED BY THE REV. J. A. GILES, LL.D., PRIEST OF THE CHURCH OF ENGLAND AND FORMER FELLOW OF CORPUS CHRISTI COLLEGE, OXFORD  
(Oxford and London, 1846)

We publish the writings of Peter of Blois in the following order:

## I.—LETTERS

1. The 183 letters made public by Peter de Goussainville; 2. letters rejected by him as being, as it were, of no authority; 3. certain unpublished letters.

The Letters of Peter of Blois first appeared, without date or place, in folio. Whether any other copy of this first edition, now exceedingly rare, survives besides that preserved in the Bodleian Library at Oxford is unknown to us.

My principal assistance in editing the letters of Peter of Blois came from three manuscript books: one preserved at New College, Oxford, and the others in the library of Sidney Sussex College, Cambridge. In the *Catalogue of Manuscripts of England and Ireland*, the latter two are marked Δ, 5, 7 and Δ, 5, 13. I read through the former of them in its entirety; yet it is not especially old, for scarcely two hundred years had passed since it was copied from a Durham codex which, I fear, has now perished. The other, bearing the siglum Δ, 5, 13, belongs to the fourteenth century or the beginning of the fifteenth, and is the more valuable because it contains almost all those letters which Goussainville rejected. These codices are numbered 33 and 34 in this Catalogue.

1. First edition, without year or place. 2. Merlin’s edition, 1519. 3. Busaeus’s edition, quarto, Mainz, 1600. 4. Goussainville’s edition, Paris, folio, 1667. 5. MS, Cambridge University Library, I i, 6, 27. 6. MS, Gray’s Inn, London. 7. Lambeth MS. 8. MS, Royal Library, Paris, 2604. [Col. XXV] 9. MS, British Museum, Royal 15 B iv. 10. MS, British Museum, Royal 14 C iv. 11. MS, British Museum, Royal 8 F XVII. 12. MS, British Museum, Harley 3709. 13. MS, British Museum, Harley 3672. 14. MS, British Museum, Harley 3684. 15. MS, British Museum, Cotton Vespasian E XI. 16. MS, British Museum, Burney 303. 17. MS, British Museum, Arundel 227. 18. MS, Oriel College, Oxford. 19. MS, Exeter College, Oxford. 20 and 21. MS, New College, Oxford, 127, and MS, British Museum, Royal 10 A XVIII; for the order in those codices is the same, except that the Royal codex is imperfect after Letter 139. 22. MS, Bodleian Library, 426 [2327 in the *Catalogue of All English Manuscripts*]. 23. MS, Bodleian Library, 759 [2671]. 24. MS, Bodleian Library, 570 [2017]. 25. MS, Bodleian Library, 303 [2089]. 26. MS, Bodleian Library, Laud 650 [643]. 27. MS, Municipal Library of Arras. 28. MS, Corpus Christi College, Cambridge, 425. 29. MS, Corpus Christi College, Cambridge, 366. 30. MS, Trinity College, Cambridge, B. l. 18. 31. MS, Cambridge University Library, Ff. 5, 46. 32. MS, Corpus Christi College, Cambridge, 266. 33. MS, Sidney Sussex College, Cambridge, Δ, 5, 7. 34. MS, Sidney Sussex College, Cambridge, Δ, 5, 13.

Besides these codices, nearly thirty others are preserved in the Royal Library at Paris, the greater part of which I have examined. But, as I think, these contain three or four fragments of letters which you would look for in vain in this edition. If I subsequently ascertain this with certainty, I shall not fail to publish them in an Appendix together with an unpublished letter of Bede and a few others which came into my hands too late.

Letters 1–183 are the same as those contained in Goussainville’s edition. The others have been added from elsewhere: namely, 183 through 208, found in the old editions but omitted in Goussainville’s edition, now claim a place among the genuine letters on the testimony of the Sidney Sussex manuscript. All those that follow, 209 through 243 [except 219, published by Bouquet, vol. XVII, p. 473], are now printed for the first time from manuscript codices. Among these new letters, many are so marred by bad handwriting and even corrupt that they can scarcely be read. One of them, no. 239, found in the New College, Oxford, manuscript, is wholly obscure to me; reluctantly, I leave it for others to clarify.

## II.—SHORTER WORKS

[Col. XXV]

Two shorter works, hitherto unpublished, are now printed for the first time in this edition; and they are certainly most worthy of publication. The first, entitled *The Passion of Reginald, Former Prince of Antioch*, was supplied by a manuscript codex preserved in New College, Oxford, and collated with two other British Museum manuscripts. The New College codex can scarcely be read through the fault of an incompetent scribe; the others are mutilated. Only with great and arduous labour do we commit the transcribed work to print.

The other bears the title *Dialogue between Henry II and the Abbot of Bonneval*. Only one Lambeth codex contains this little work. It contains many things worthy of notice concerning that most eminent king who united the Anglo-Saxon and Norman peoples into one.

We did not consider it worthwhile to reprint the fragment of the *Book on the Deceptions of Fortune*, published in Goussainville’s edition, because it is read word for word in chapter 12 of book I of John of Salisbury’s *Polycraticus* [Note: [Col. XXV] See *Patrologia*, vol. CLXXIX.].

## III.—SERMONS

Two manuscript codices preserved in the British Museum contain some of Peter of Blois’s sermons. With their aid, we gathered into one three fragments of homilies scattered here and there and more than once corrected the text of Goussainville’s edition. Apart from the codices mentioned above, I have been unable to find, either in England or in the overseas libraries which I visited, other codices containing sermons of Peter of Blois.

## IV.—POEMS

The homilies are followed by poems, among which the following are now published for the first time:

1. A poem on penance. It is found in Lambeth manuscript no. 36, fol. 95, and Brussels manuscript no. 1968.  
2. Verses in praise of wine.  
3. A reply to someone against beer. Both are supplied by a Cambridge codex (Mori 131, Cambridge G. g. 6, 42, art. 3).  
4. A headless poem. Taken from a Bodleian manuscript [perhaps Laud 650], where it occurs without a title at the end of Letter 111.

The metrical little works *On the Struggle of Flesh and Spirit* and *On the Blameworthy Life of Clerics*, ending in rhyming syllables, are printed in the Paris edition as one and the same undivided poem at the end of Letter 57. But, following the agreement of the Sidney Sussex manuscript (Δ 5, 18) and the Brussels manuscript (9608), in which the second part, or second poem, bears a distinct title, we have made two works out of one. In these poems, the sense is often extracted with the greatest difficulty, as usually happens in writings of this kind, because the author is constrained by strict rules of rhyme; while he labours at the troublesome selection and arrangement of rhymes, he very frequently draws words away from their natural meaning. [Col. XXVII]

Busaeus was the first to make public the *Treatise on the Holy Eucharist*, copied, as he says, “from a most ancient codex in the library at Tervuren of the most serene and illustrious prince Charles, Cardinal of Lorraine and Bishop of Metz and Strasbourg,” in which it is ascribed to Anselm, Archbishop of Canterbury. From the verses of the *Invocation to the Father*:

> . . . Peter,  
> Mark beforehand, form, etc.

and from certain repeatedly occurring expressions which savour of Peter of Blois’s mode of speech, Busaeus judged that this poem should be ascribed to him rather than to Anselm. It is absent from the manuscripts we have seen.

I do not admit into this edition the book entitled *Remediary of Sins*, compiled by Peter from a work of Gregory, since it contains nothing new. It survives at Arras in France, but is imperfect through a shameful mutilation; it also survives at Cambridge and at Oxford in the library of Merton College. The little work *On the Art of Letter-Writing*, compiled from Bernard, is preserved in manuscript in the Cambridge library.

In certain manuscript catalogues, a book entitled *Basiligerunticon* is ascribed to Peter of Blois; it is none other than the *Compendium on Job*.

A manuscript little work entitled *Breviloquium* survives in the library of Gray’s Inn, London; catalogue compilers ascribe it to Peter of Blois, but omit to state on what authority they rely. This little book, a fragment of ill-digested theological miscellany, as it seems, certainly has nothing to do with the Archdeacon of Bath.

It is now agreed among learned persons that the continuation of Ingulph was falsely ascribed to Peter of Blois.

[Col. 0001]

# THE LETTERS OF PETER OF BLOIS

(*The Complete Works of Peter of Blois, Archdeacon of Bath; now for the first time edited in England with the aid of manuscript codices and the best editions by J. A. Giles, LL.D., priest of the Church of England and former fellow of Corpus Christi College, Oxford. Vols. I–II: Letters. Oxford and London, 1847, octavo.*)

## FIRST LETTER. PROLOGUE, TO HENRY II  
[Written before A.D. 1200.]

[Col. 0001A]

**SUBJECT.**—This letter serves as a preface, as the author noted at the end of the letter. In it he explains to Henry II, king of England, why he allowed this collection of letters to be published, although it was little polished and elaborated in style.

To HENRY [Note: [Col. 0001C] Who and what sort of man this Henry was, we shall explain fully at Letter 66.], by the grace of God most illustrious king of the English, duke of Normandy and Aquitaine, and count of Anjou: his own PETER of Blois, Archdeacon of Bath, greeting in Him through whom kings reign.

At your request that I collect the letters which I have sent abroad to various persons, and carry together, as it were, diverse kinds into a single bundle, I am swept into uncertain [Col. 0001B] feelings. For amid various occupations and the stormy waves of court life, it is hard for me to write anything, and far harder to oppose the command of your majesty. Indeed, I call your requests a command, because, as one of my masters writes quite elegantly [Note: [Col. 0001C] Some think this is John of Salisbury, because Peter of Blois regularly calls him his master. Yet where these verses, cited here by Peter of Blois, are to be found is quite uncertain, unless we say that he published many little works which have not reached [Col. 0002C] our hands, but still lie hidden in certain libraries, especially those of England.]:

> The prayer of rulers is a compelling form of command,  
> And the powerful man pleads as though his sword were drawn.

You should know for certain that, if I had formerly foreseen that my letters would receive an audience of such dignity, a more careful file and more exacting vigilance would have corrected whatever in them might offend delicate ears. But now, in the native roughness in which they were composed, they present themselves, though fearfully, to your eyes, awaiting censure rather than seeking favor; and they place the highest reward in this: that they are not rejected, not spat out, but at last obtain—for this is greatest to them—indulgence.

You know indeed that the vein of talent does not always answer to the will; and sometimes more commendable sayings offer themselves to one writing by chance which cannot be found through the intensity of study and the searching of laborious meditation. Your eminence also, I think, carefully observes that nearly all my letters depended upon another’s decision; and that now because of the urgency of pressing needs I had to write more uncouthly, now more briefly because of the slightness of the subject, now more plainly, diffusely, or simply because of the inadequacy of the persons to whom I wrote or who were writing. Let your eyes therefore behold and forgive my imperfection; and, if you find anything conducive to salvation, let it be inscribed in the book of remembrance. For the Lord sometimes reveals to little ones what is hidden from the wise [Note: [Col. 0001] Luke 10]. Lepers announced salvation to Samaria, and Balaam’s beast of burden recalled its master from an unlawful path [Note: [Col. 0001] IV Kings 7]. If, for the sake of public instruction, some things from the books of the Gentiles have been inserted, let them not turn to disgust in you. For David made a diadem for himself from the diadem of Melchom, the idol of the Ammonites [Note: [Col. 0001] II Chronicles 20]; and the Apostle Paul once elegantly adapted poetic verses to reproach the Cretans [Note: [Col. 0001] Jerome, Epistle 84, to Magnus].

[Note: [Col. 0002C] That many things from the books of the Gentiles may usefully be employed by ecclesiastical writers is argued more fully in Epistle 8; we refer the reader to it and to our notes there.]

And, I pray, let it not be burdensome to your magnificence if in some of my letters the style of devoted correction has extended even to your own person. For affection dictated all of this: “I am jealous over you with God’s jealousy” [Note: [Col. 0001] II Corinthians 11], zealously desiring and thirsting for your salvation in the bowels of Christ [Col. 0002C] and in unfeigned charity. I do not recall having written anything flattering to you, nor am I a seller of oil. And I know that, while the salt of correction is accepted by the Lord in every sacrifice, honey is rejected in every sacrifice. Solomon also testifies: “Those who say to the wicked, ‘You are righteous,’ shall be cursed by peoples; but blessing shall come upon those who rebuke them” [Note: [Col. 0003] Proverbs 24]. I close the first letter; for since it is, as it were, a preface to the others, it will be reckoned a fault if it runs to excessive length. Farewell.

## LETTER II. TO THE SAME KING HENRY. [A.D. 1182.]

**Summary.**—He consoles King Henry the father, who grieves excessively at the death of his son Henry III; and shows that although the custom of mourning those departed from life is pious if it is moderate, there is no cause for bewailing the son’s death so bitterly, since he had exacted from himself such great penalties for the sins of his past life that there can be no doubt that he exchanged this life for eternal life.

To HENRY, by the grace of God illustrious King of the English, Duke of [Col. 0004A] Normandy and Aquitaine, Count of Anjou: PETER of Blois, his own Peter, Archdeacon of Bath, greeting, and a spirit of fortitude in adversity.

“I heard, and my belly was troubled; at the sound my lips trembled” [Note: [Col. 0003] Habakkuk 3]. For I learned from the report of your household that that greatness of soul of yours, hitherto distinguished by public renown, has been crushed by the death of your son:

[Note: [Col. 0003B] This Henry was the firstborn of the sons of Henry, King of the English, and of his wife Eleanor, although before him there had been another, named William, who died almost as a boy, when his father was not yet king but only Duke of Normandy and Count of Anjou. This Henry, by his father’s will, was anointed king in the fifteenth year of his age, having already taken as wife Margaret, daughter of Louis the Younger, King of the French.

This consecration was indeed disastrous and the cause of many evils. First, it was the true occasion of the murder of St Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury. After peace had been made between Henry, King of the English, and Archbishop Thomas through the efforts of Pope Alexander III and Louis the Younger, Thomas returned to England and publicly excommunicated the Archbishop of York together with the other bishops who had consecrated the younger Henry, and all the magnates and others who had attended the consecration. The father king, inflamed with anger, uttered somewhat harsher words against St Thomas; from these the wicked parricides rashly seized an occasion to kill the holy bishop.

Secondly, the younger Henry was a king without a kingdom, or at least without royal power. Gervase rightly says in his Chronicle: “He died in the thirteenth year of his reign, though he did not hold the reins of rule even for half an hour.” And although while he lived he was called Henry III, because he did not outlive his father Henry II, he was not counted among the kings of England. Thus afterward the son of King John was called Henry III.

Thirdly, that coronation became the material cause of great dissension between father and son. The new king grieved that he was king without a kingdom and royal authority and, urged by evil counsel, made war once and again upon his father. At first he was prompted by his mother Eleanor and his brothers, and assisted by the forces of his father-in-law Louis the Younger. Later, by his own impulse and indignation—because his father had made Richard Duke of Aquitaine and Geoffrey Duke of Brittany, while leaving him only the hope of reigning after himself—he joined his brother Geoffrey and certain Aquitanian nobles and provoked his father with military disturbances.

When the father could not recall his rebellious sons by gentle commands, he entered Aquitaine with an army to oppose their evil attempts. While he was detained in the siege of the city of Limoges, [Col. 0004B] the younger king was seized by a sudden fever. As the disease worsened and physicians despaired of him, he sent to his father, humbly confessing his offense and begging as a final favor from paternal kindness that he might deign to visit him as he lay dying. On hearing this, the father’s heart was moved toward his son; but friends argued that it was unsafe to trust himself to the wicked conspirators around the son. Therefore he did not go to his son, but, as a token of clemency and forgiveness granted, sent his familiar ring and pardoned him all things. Receiving the ring and kissing it, he immediately closed his final day.

These things are almost word for word from Brompton, William of Newburgh, and others.

Ralph de Diceto, Matthew Paris, and Thomas Walsingham, however, assign another cause for this final war. They say that the younger Henry declared that war not against his father but rather by his father’s command or urging against his brothers, because Richard of Aquitaine and Geoffrey of Brittany would not render obedience—or, as they call it, homage—to their brother Henry himself [Col. 0004C]. Shortly afterward, however, Geoffrey, having understood his father’s will, obeyed; Richard refused, thinking it unworthy that brothers should subject themselves to a brother while their father lived. This obstinacy displeased the father, and so he impelled Henry to take arms against his brother Richard.

Nevertheless, this does not seem probable, since the son, at his end, sent to beg his father’s pardon for his treachery, and the father, fearing the plots of the conspirators, refused to go to his son. Add that William the Breton, a contemporary writer, briefly sums the matter up thus in the *Philippid*, Book II:

> But King Henry the Younger, illustrious offspring  
> Of the King of the English, while he made war upon his father  
> And upon his own brothers, at that same time paid  
> The debt of nature. [Col. 0004D]

Whatever the case, he died truly repentant at Château-Martel, not far from Limoges; wrapped in the cloth with which he had been anointed with chrism at his consecration, he was carried to Rouen, as he himself had directed, and buried in the cathedral church beside the altar of St Mary. Gervase narrates the matter thus in his Chronicle:

> “When the father king heard that his son had ended his life, suspecting treachery, he ordered the body to be brought to Rouen, though he himself did not wish to be present. As it was being borne toward Rouen amid the mourning and tears of all, and was laid overnight in the church at Le Mans for the sake of resting on the journey, the bishop and citizens of Le Mans forcibly had it buried there in the church [Col. 0005C]. But after the army had dispersed, the king, more fully informed of his son’s death, came with Richard, Archbishop of Canterbury, to the church at Le Mans; having taken up the body of his son, the younger king, he reached Rouen and ordered it buried there.”]

—and, degenerating through a certain womanish softness, gives itself over to groans and tears; laying aside the dignity of majesty, it wastes away childishly in needless grief. I do not blame in you the feeling of sorrow, but the excess of mourning. I know that it is pious to weep for the dead and that the law of nature enjoins such mournful feelings. Job, on hearing of his sons’ deaths, expressed the force of his grief by tearing his garments and sprinkling dust [Note: [Col. 0003] Job 1]. When Sarah died, Abraham came to weep and mourn for her [Note: [Col. 0003] Genesis 33]. Jacob, thinking his son Joseph [Col. 0005A] devoured by a beast, continued mourning for many days [Note: [Col. 0005] Genesis 37]. Joseph also, carrying his dead father with his brothers and all the elders of Pharaoh’s household, came to the threshing-floor of Atad beyond the Jordan, where they completed seven days in weeping and lamentation over Jacob’s death [Note: [Col. 0005] Genesis 50].

When King Josiah died, it is likewise written [Note: [Col. 0005] II Chronicles 31] that all Judah and Jerusalem mourned him, and above all King Hadadrimmon; so that it became proverbial and people commonly said, “His lamentation is like the lamentation of Hadadrimmon” [Note: [Col. 0005] Zechariah 12]. In Ecclesiasticus we also read [Note: [Col. 0005] Chapter 22] that mourning for the dead is lawfully observed for seven days, and there occur these words: “My son, shed tears for the dead” [Note: [Col. 0005] Ecclesiasticus 38]. Christ shed tears for Lazarus [Note: [Col. 0005] John 11]. Therefore I do not wonder if you offer tears of piety for so lamentable [Col. 0005B] a funeral. For you are not among those of whom the Lord said through the prophet: “He struck them, and they did not grieve” [Note: [Col. 0005] Jeremiah 5]. And, to use Job’s words [Note: [Col. 0005] Chapter 6], “Your strength is not the strength of stone, nor is your flesh bronze.”

But, I pray, let there be a limit here to mourning, lest grief carry you beyond measure. Your occasion of grieving for your dead son should be more restrained, because he departed most Christianly—indeed, I should say not “died,” but “went away”—and by grieving as a penitent escaped eternal sorrows. For, while we weep, he now says most securely: “Do not weep over me, but weep over yourselves” [Note: [Col. 0005] Luke 23]. David wept for his parricidal son: “Absalom, my son, my son Absalom!” [Note: [Col. 0005] II Kings 19]. He wept over Saul and Jonathan, lamenting the end of those whom the dominion of death had enveloped without end [Note: [Col. 0005] II Kings 1].

Yet if it is pious to weep for your son, it is also pious to rejoice. For if the Apostle Peter [Note: [Col. 0005] Matthew 26] and Magdalene mourned their own falls [Note: [Col. 0005] Luke 7], this man, though young and among inciters to wickedness and, so to speak, “like a lily among thorns” [Note: [Col. 0005] Song of Songs 2], cast himself down into every humility of penitence:

[Note: [Col. 0005C] Historians recount remarkable and incredible things about the repentance of the younger Henry. They say that when no hope of life remained, he first confessed his sins and received absolution before prelates, and then publicly; afterward, clothed in haircloth and with a rope tied around his neck, he burst out before the bishops and religious men who were present in these words:

> “I hand myself over, a sinner, unworthy, guilty, and liable, by this rope to you, ministers of God, asking that our Lord Jesus Christ, who forgave sins to the thief confessing upon the cross, may through your prayers and through His ineffable mercy have pity on my most unhappy soul.”

And all replied, “Amen.” He then said to them: “Draw me from [Col. 0005D] this bed by this rope and place me upon that bed”—that is, the bed of ashes which he had prepared for himself. They did as he commanded and placed two enormous square stones at his head and feet. Thereafter, fortified by the most sacred provision of the Lord’s Body and Blood, he yielded up his spirit in the fear of the Lord.

These are almost word for word from Roger of Howden and Robert of Torigni, writers of the same century. They agree with what Peter of Blois writes at the end of this letter: “No one,” he says, “was humbler in confession, more contrite in accusing himself, more devout in amendment, harsher in afflicting his own flesh, more fervent in every act of satisfaction.” And a little later: “For he judged himself, lest he should afterward be judged.”]

turning the world’s joys into mourning and pleasures into grief. [Col. 0006B] “His mourning was turned into joy” [Note: [Col. 0005] Psalm 29]; let yours also be turned. Let it contribute to the fullness of your joys that such a son proceeded from your loins, one into whom all nature’s gifts had flowed:

[Note: [Col. 0006B] The historians of this period describe the outstanding disposition and eminent virtues of this prince. Above all, Gervase of Canterbury and Robert of Torigni. The former speaks of him thus:

> “He was lovable to all, handsome in appearance, and especially renowned for military glory, so that he seemed second to none; he was humble, teachable, and gracious. Thus both those near at hand and those far away loved him warmly.”

The latter, in the Appendix to Sigebert, under the year 1182:

> “In the year 1182 Henry III, our most beloved lord, the young king, son of Henry II, most excellent and most illustrious King of the English, died at Château-Martel: a man to be mourned in every respect. He was exceedingly handsome in face, upright in manners, more generous in gifts than all whom we have seen in our age, though no land had yet been assigned to him, although his father gave him fifteen thousand pounds of Angevin money each year and more besides. But this was too little to satisfy the breadth of his heart. In military service he was so great that he had no equal; princes, counts, and even kings feared him. Approaching his end, because through the counsel of evil men he had offended God, His holy Church, and his father by war for almost a year, he received penance from a most holy bishop and many others; and at his end he directed by letters to his father that he should make amends on his behalf for what he had offended against God and the holy Church. Before his death he had arranged that his body should be buried in the church of Blessed Mary at Rouen, where his first ancestors Rollo and William Longsword lie,” etc.

He then recounts what occurred at the funeral in nearly the same manner as Gervase above.

An anonymous poet of the same age also sang the praise of Henry the Younger in the following verse in Brompton:

> The honor of every honor, the beauty and glory of city and world,  
> The splendor, glory, light, and summit of knighthood;  
> [Col. 0007D] Julius in genius, Hector in virtues, Achilles  
> In strength, Augustus in character, Paris in face.

Nor should William of Newburgh be heard, *History of English Affairs*, Book III, chapter 7, where he speaks so maliciously of him:

> “That restless boy, born indeed for the destruction of many, came to this end; yet he was so pleasing and favored by men—because ‘the number of fools is infinite’ (Ecclesiastes 1)—that splendid things were said even of him after his death.
