Finally, after his death, certain men, out of a desire for lying and with the most shameless vanity, spread abroad the report that cures of the sick occurred at his tomb, evidently in order that it might be believed either that he had had a just cause against his father or that by final penitence he had eminently pleased God.”

It is evident that William wrote this from an unfair hostility toward him, in order to gain the favor of Richard, then King of the English [Col. 0008D], because Henry his brother had taken arms against him; whereas nearly all historians—and especially Peter of Blois, who was nowhere a flatterer of kings or magnates—praise him as a prince of many virtues.]

He was one whom the most distant nations feared, and whom even an enemy and an envious man was obliged to respect and love.

Having attained above all mortals the glory and preeminence [Col. 0007A] of worldly knighthood, he finally became and died a soldier of Christ in the abasement of temporal things and the humility of penitence. He gave you an example, that you too might follow the footsteps of the penitent [Note: [Col. 0007] I Peter 2]. No one was humbler in confession, more contrite in accusing himself, more devout in amendment, harsher in afflicting his own flesh, more fervent in every act of satisfaction. For by the counsel and suggestion of a treacherous faction:

[Note: [Col. 0008D] He means that impious conspiracy of the wife and sons against Henry the father, joined by the forces of the King of France and the magnates of Normandy. All historians of this period recount that its outcome was disastrous.

I judge that this letter was written in the year 1182, when King Henry the Younger died.]

he had rashly raised and aimed his bow against you; but the Lord stretched His bow against him and prepared in it weapons of death [Note: [Col. 0007] Psalm 7], wishing to give in him a sign to you and others, that you might flee from before the bow and that His beloved might be delivered [Note: [Col. 0007] Psalm 59]. Therefore, since we have the most certain hope of his salvation—for “blessed are those who [Col. 0007B] die in the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0007] Revelation 16]—to use the Apostle’s words: “Do not grieve over one who sleeps, as do those who have no hope” [Note: [Col. 0007] I Thessalonians 4]. He has now escaped every judgment, for he judged himself lest he be judged afterward.

Would that, dearest prince, while this age endures—or rather, while this age flows away—we might judge ourselves. For this world is deceitful, life brief, the end uncertain, the departure terrible, the Judge fearful, and punishment without end. Therefore turn the tears you expend upon the dead into the weapons of penitence; so that, just as your son preceded you to death by the troubled ordering of fate, you may, by the well-ordered course of this mortal life, precede others unto life.

## LETTER III. TO G., A NOBLEMAN.

[Col. 0007C]

**Summary.**—He severely rebukes a man noble by birth who had reproached his chaplain for the lowliness of his family. He shows that poverty is to be valued more highly than splendor of birth devoid of virtue; humility is to be pursued and pride avoided.

To his dearest lord and friend G., PETER of Blois, Archdeacon of Bath, greeting, and knowledge of yourself.

Your chaplain reported to me, with sobbing and anxious weeping, the grievous and excessive injuries of reproach with which, as he declares, you treated him most uncivilly, though he had not deserved them, [Col. 0008A]. I know that Moab is proud [Note: [Col. 0007] Isaiah 14], and that this very rebuke of mine, proceeding from sincere friendship, will make you my enemy. I remember having read: “Rebuke a wise man, and he will love you; rebuke a fool, and he will become more pestilent” [Note: [Col. 0007] Proverbs 9]. Therefore I do not place a title at the head of this present letter, wishing to test what private and secret correction can accomplish in you; I shall apply the cutting iron if you do not feel the poultices.

What glory, I ask, has accrued to you because you reproached this honorable and commendable man with the lowliness of his birth? Why do you boast of your lineage? “Whom do you make yourself?” [Note: [Col. 0007] John 8]. Human descent is wandering and uncertain; and sometimes one thought to be the son of a prince is the son of a kitchen-player, as the poet testifies:

> [Col. 0008B] Though your ancestral wax masks adorn  
> Your halls on every side, virtue alone and unique is nobility.

[Note: [Col. 0008D] These are Juvenal’s genuine words, *Satires*, 5; but the Marcian manuscript has: “Nobility alone is that which adorns the mind with virtues.”]

“The sons of men are deceitful in the scales, that they may deceive together in vanity.” They regard themselves as great who are either small or altogether nothing. Why do you consider yourself greater in your own estimation than common human opinion considers you? Weigh yourself more secretly; do not sell yourself as greater than the balance of truth weighs you. It is the Lord’s word: “A weight and a weight are an abomination to me” [Note: [Col. 0007] Proverbs 20]. He is in heaven who searches hearts and reins [Note: [Col. 0007] Psalm 7]. See that you mix in no deceit, but make yourself reasonably balanced before God and men. “He acted deceitfully,” it says, “that his iniquity might be found unto hatred” [Note: [Col. 0007] Psalm 35].

What profit was it to you, wretch, to magnify the boastfulness of fictitious nobility and cast upon a poor friend [Col. 0008C] the stigma, as it were, of criminal poverty? Certainly, with poor Christ the title of poverty is precious. Christ was poor and the son of a poor Virgin; He chose the poor as apostles [Note: [Col. 0007] James 2]. Nor did He deign to enter the house of a petty king, lest He seem to honor riches [Note: [Col. 0007] John 4]. Nebuzaradan, leaving only the poor in the land of promise, carried all the rich into captivity [Note: [Col. 0007] IV Kings 25].

In pride and in the misuse of your forebears, you ascribe to yourself a virtue for glory; yet you stain their reputation with shameful repute, and, degenerating from the dignity or goodness of your lineage, dishonor the famous memory [Col. 0009A] of your ancestors by a shameful manner of life. Why do you praise the stock of a nobility now extinguished? A branch indeed commonly commends its root, and fruit its stock. What use is there in an old trunk if it has already withered, if no commendable fruit has come from it? Hear, wretch:

[Note: [Col. 0009C] A striking description of human baseness. Innocent III gives such descriptions repeatedly in his books *On Contempt for the World*.]

hear, successor of ancient Adam: fragile potsherd, dissolvable clay, dead skin, vessel of decay, tinder for moths, food for worms. What have you to do with your forefathers? Just as an innocent son shall not bear his father’s iniquity [Note: [Col. 0009] Ezekiel 18], so neither is a reprobate son fit to glory in his father’s deeds. What proofs do you present to us that you are the son of him whose pompous memory you magnify and exalt?

Certainly, this is why the Lord willed Abraham to receive offspring by Sarah and Hagar [Note: [Col. 0009] Genesis 16], and Jacob by two wives and also two maidservants [Col. 0009B] [Note: [Col. 0009] Genesis 29]: that the succession of the human race, uncertain and ignorant of its parents’ condition—whether it descends from a free woman or a slave—might not exalt itself in the ambiguous glory of nobility. For the titles of Sarah or Rachel, which wandering and vulgar opinion sometimes ascribes to itself, are proscribed and erased by wickedness in morals and bondage in sins; so that those who are puffed up by another’s virtue, which they do not know within themselves, may by their conduct show themselves to be children of handmaids.

Moreover, in Jacob’s house bastards together with legitimate children received a share in the cord of inheritance [Note: [Col. 0009] Genesis 49], and jointly issued the judgment for dividing the family estate:

[Note: [Col. 0009D] *Hercisco* is an ancient word meaning “I divide an inheritance.” It is derived from the Greek ἕρκιον, meaning “an enclosure.” Thus *herciscere* properly refers to that division by which houses and fields are partitioned, and ownership is distinguished for each person. So Martini in his Lexicon. Calvin likewise says in his legal lexicon: “*Herctum* is division”; whence Cicero, *On the Orator*, Book I: “He who does not know by what words an inheritance ought to be divided cannot plead an action for dividing a family estate.” And in Digest Book X the second title is *On Dividing a Family Estate*. Therefore an action for dividing a family estate is a civil action concerning an inheritance to be divided among co-heirs, says Busaeus on Epistle 8. Thus, although in law the word “family” often refers to property and persons, in this place it means things pertaining to the substance of an estate.]

Why do you make changing distinctions among human kindreds? We all, each and every one, descend from one father. [Col. 0009C] Christ Jesus, certainly, “fair in beauty beyond the sons of men” [Note: [Col. 0009] Psalm 44], of whom it is written that “He is noble in his gates” [Note: [Col. 0009] Proverbs 31], whose nobility and generation the prophet cannot sufficiently declare [Note: [Col. 0009] Isaiah 53], and who alone is the author of our nobility [Note: [Col. 0009] Matthew 1], took flesh from righteous and unrighteous, [Col. 0010A] from great and lowly alike.

For the paschal lamb [Note: [Col. 0009] Exodus 12], according to the Septuagint translators:

[Note: [Col. 0009D] The passage in Exodus among the Septuagint translators reads thus: “Πρόβατον τέλειον, ἄρσεν, ἐνιαύσιον ἔσται ὑμῖν· ἀπὸ τῶν ἀρνῶν καὶ τῶν ἐρίφων λήψεσθε ὑμῖν.” “A sheep—that is, a lamb—shall be perfect, male, one year old for you; you shall take it from lambs and kids.” In some manuscripts, after ἄρσεν (“male”), ἄμωμον (“without blemish”) is added, which St Cyprian translated *sine vitio*, “without fault.” The Chaldean paraphrast renders: “You shall take [it] from lambs and the young of goats.” Pagninus: “You shall take [it] from sheep and goats.” St Ambrose likewise: “A lamb without blemish, clean, mature, male, one year old.”

Theodoret aptly says on this passage: “Κελεύει οὐ μόνον ἐκ τῶν προβάτων ἄρνας ἐνιαυσίους, ἀλλὰ καὶ ἐκ τῶν αἰγῶν ἐρίφους, οὐχ ἵνα κατὰ ταὐτὸν τοῦτον κἀκεῖνον θύσωσιν, ἀλλ᾽ ἵνα ὁ μὲν πρόβατον ἔχων θύσῃ τοῦτο, ὁ δὲ σπανίζων προβάτου τὸν ἔριφον.” That is: “God commands them to take not only year-old lambs from the sheep, but also kids from the goats; not in order that they should sacrifice both together, but so that the person who has a sheep may sacrifice it, while the one who lacks a sheep may sacrifice the kid.” Busaeus added certain matters on this passage, to which we refer the reader.]

was taken from sheep and goats; in this you see most clearly that with Christ every fortune and every condition is accepted. Why, then, do you commend yourself by another’s virtue and glory in the exaltation of your lineage against a poor man? “Let him who boasts boast in the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0009] I Corinthians 1]; for it is not one who commends himself who is approved, but one whom God commends [Note: [Col. 0009] II Corinthians 10]. “The Lord will destroy all deceitful lips and the boastful tongue” [Note: [Col. 0009] Psalm 11].

You would do better to think more humbly. In the Blessed Virgin, although she herself derived her origin from priestly and royal stock, the Son of God chose not nobility but humility. “He has regarded the humility of His handmaid” [Note: [Col. 0009] Luke 1]. It is written [Col. 0010B] that “God gives grace to the humble” [Note: [Col. 0009] I Peter 5], and “His conversation is with the humble” [Note: [Col. 0009] Proverbs 3]. “Upon whom,” He says, “shall My spirit rest, except upon the humble and meek?” [Note: [Col. 0009] Isaiah 11].

What have you to do with the poor chaplain, proud and foolish man? You abase and trample down the eminence of your lineage by your wickedness; he shines forth among his own by holy and honorable conduct. I know that you take it ill that I instruct you, that

> … I tear your ancient grandmothers from your lungs [Note: [Col. 0009] Persius, *Satires* 5],

but your salvation troubles me. For I fear that pride may roll you down into ruin and a precipice. For it is written: “Before ruin the heart shall be exalted” [Note: [Col. 0009] Proverbs 16]. He who dwells on high and looks upon lowly things [Note: [Col. 0009] Psalm 112] detests pride above all things.

This is that bloodthirsty [Col. 0010C] harlot who gives men, from Babylon’s golden cup, the spirit of dizziness to drink [Note: [Col. 0009] Jeremiah 51]. This is that Athaliah who almost exterminated the entire royal race [Note: [Col. 0009] IV Kings 11]. This is the leprosy of a scar in an ulcer [Note: [Col. 0009] Leviticus 13]. This is the beast of the forest that devours Absalom’s army [Note: [Col. 0009] II Kings 18]. This is [Col. 0011A] rust and moth which, by corrupting, consumes every ornament of the mind [Note: [Col. 0011] James 5]. This is the tower in Siloam that kills its builders [Note: [Col. 0011] Luke 13]. This is the elephant in the Book of Maccabees that killed Eleazar by its bulk [Note: [Col. 0011] Maccabees 5]. This is that assassin in Prudentius’ *Psychomachia*, whom one of the virtues killed:

[Note: [Col. 0011D] Busaeus rightly observed that, in the contrary sense, this should be read: “which one of the virtues killed.” The passage from Prudentius occurs in the *Psychomachia*, section 5, “The Battle of Pride and Humility.”]

Descend, therefore, into your conscience and see whether there is any matter for glory there. For “this is our glory: the testimony of our conscience” [Note: [Col. 0011] II Corinthians 1]. Do not believe flatterers who nurse you. Certainly, “the people who call you blessed lead you into error” [Note: [Col. 0011] Isaiah 9]. Let those who say to you, “Well done, well done!” immediately bear their confusion [Note: [Col. 0011] Psalm 39]. “A man’s enemies are those of his own household” [Note: [Col. 0011] Micah 7]. These are those of whom Jeremiah speaks to Zedekiah [Note: [Col. 0011] Chapter 38]: “Your men of peace have deceived you”; “their words are smoother [Col. 0011B] than oil, yet they are darts” [Note: [Col. 0011] Psalm 54]. Thus Joab killed Abner [Note: [Col. 0011] II Kings 3] and Amasa [Note: [Col. 0011] II Kings 20] with a gently fashioned sword—that is, with the word of treacherous flattery.

Cultivate, therefore, your conscience. For this is the field which the Lord has blessed [Note: [Col. 0011] Genesis 27], of which it is written: “The beauty of the field is with me” [Note: [Col. 0011] Psalm 49]. Plant and sow there the seed of virtues, the fruits of life, and let the fragrance of holy reputation burst forth. For according to the precept of the divine law: “If you give of your seed to the idol Moloch,” that is, to the king of pride, “you shall die” [Note: [Col. 0011] Leviticus 20]. Nor can you exalt your lineage more honorably than by casting off the arrogance of pride and conforming yourself to the humble. Farewell.

## LETTER IV. TO R., A CISTERCIAN PRIOR. [Circa A.D. 1195.]

[Col. 0011C]

**Summary.**—He congratulates a monk on his progress in the religious life, laments his own lot as one living in the world, commends himself to the monk’s prayers and sacrifices, and then resolves a certain doubt.

To his dearest companion and intimate friend R., Cistercian prior, P. of Blois, Archdeacon of Bath, greeting and continual progress in Christ.

I rejoiced at the things that were said to me [Note: [Col. 0011] Ps. 121]. For from the trustworthy report of travellers I learned that, advancing day by day and from strength to strength [Note: [Col. 0011] Ps. 88], you have earned the prize of the cloistered warfare. You have ascended the mountain of sacrifice; but I still linger in the muddy valley and wait with the ass [Note: [Col. 0011] Gen. 12]. Taking up the wings of contemplation, you rise above these worldly things; [Col. 0011D] the glue of an earthly dwelling has so fastened me down that I cannot fly. Alas for me, because my sojourning far from God has been prolonged [Note: [Col. 0011] Ps. 119]. And who will give me wings like a dove’s, that I may fly away and be at rest? [Col. 0012A] [Note: [Col. 0011] Ps. 54]. In all things I sought rest [Note: [Col. 0011] Ecclus. 24], and in all things I found pain and labour. There is no rest except in the inheritance of the saints, concerning which it is written: “This is my rest for ever and ever” [Note: [Col. 0011] Ps. 131]. But I, a carnal man and sold under sin [Note: [Col. 0011] Rom. 7], am fixed in the mire of the deep [Note: [Col. 0011] Ps. 68], and cannot breathe freely into the liberty of the children of God.

Help me by your prayers, dearest friend; for my days have passed away [Note: [Col. 0011] Job 17], and, according to Job’s saying, I shall not return by the path on which I go. I am not far from that common goal appointed to all flesh. My wrinkles bear witness against me [Note: [Col. 0011] Job 16]; we have already put on grey hairs, heralds of the final hour. Yet, according to the Apostle’s testimony, everything that grows old and becomes obsolete is near to destruction [Note: [Col. 0011] Heb. 8]. Pray, therefore, brother, lest the crisis of utmost necessity overtake me [Col. 0012B] unprepared. Amid your more private tears, offer remembrance of me there where the Son is sacrificed to the Father. I know that the persevering prayer of a righteous man avails much [Note: [Col. 0011] Jas. 5], and that, when a person’s own petitions sometimes obtain nothing, another’s intercession accomplishes it.

I received and read devoutly the letters of the lord abbot and your own. Yet I wonder that you should be moved to astonishment and perplexity because in the book which I composed, *On the Deceptions of Fortune*, I frequently used the following explanation: “It happened,” that is, “it could have happened”; “it will at some time occur,” that is, “it will at some time come to pass.” Nevertheless, in matters dependent upon Fortune’s snares and admitting either alternative, receiving uncertain outcomes, I safely introduced this kind of explanation, since this form of speech is also frequently found in matters which have definite and, as it were, [Col. 0012C] necessary outcomes.

For in Leviticus it is read [Note: [Col. 0011] ch. 7]: “If anyone shall eat of the sacrifices of peace offerings on the third day, the offering shall not profit him.” “Shall eat,” he says—that is, “shall wish to eat.” And it must be understood thus; for since the third day signifies the life to come, in which it is not permitted to work, this eating must signify not the deed but the will to do it. You have a similar instance in Job [Note: [Col. 0011] ch. 9]: “Who has resisted God and had peace?” “Resisted,” that is, “wished to resist.” For you recall having read of Pharaoh’s magicians: “The magicians also did as Moses did, in order to bring forth gnats, but they could not” [Note: [Col. 0011] Exod. 8]. “They did,” it says—that is, “they wished to do.” Therefore, if in matters that are contingent I have sometimes admitted this mode of expression as though positively and by way of example, do not [Col. 0012D] be troubled. For this manner of speaking may frequently be found also in matters which convey a certain necessity of truth.

Again I ask that prayers may be offered for me. Burdened with sins, weighed down by the mass of my body, entangled in cares, infected with unclean desires, weak, anxious, and wretched, [Col. 0013A] I shall not lift myself above myself [Note: [Col. 0013] Lam. 3], except through him who raises up the fallen and heals the broken-hearted [Note: [Col. 0013] Ps. 146]. Farewell.

## LETTER V. TO RICHARD, ARCHBISHOP OF CANTERBURY

[Note: [Col. 0013C]

After the death of St Thomas, when the see of Canterbury had been vacant for two years and five months, Roger, abbot of Bec, was elected. Yet neither the bishops of the province, nor the monks of Canterbury, who had the right of electing the archbishop, nor the papal legates then present [Col. 0013D] in Normandy, nor King Henry himself, who had joyfully ratified the election, could induce him to consent to his election. Richard, a native of Normandy, was therefore appointed in his place. From his earliest age he had worn the monastic habit in the church of Canterbury; afterwards, having become chaplain to Theobald, archbishop of Canterbury, he had diligently served him together with Blessed Thomas. Finally, when he was prior of the Benedictine monastery at Dover, he was raised to the archbishopric of Canterbury. After the customary election, when his consecration was hindered by the envy and faction of the retainers of the younger King Henry, he went to Alexander III and, after various calumnies by his opponents, was at length consecrated by him. Richard therefore returned as archbishop, primate of all England, and papal legate according to the custom of [Col. 0014C] his predecessors, and was honourably received into his see at Canterbury.

These are Gervase’s words; and he adds the following concerning Richard’s character: “By the good manners and affability with which he was endowed, he became so agreeable that he pleased the eyes of everyone except the envious.” Godwin’s words about him agree with this: “A man of remarkable prudence, exceptionally generous, kind, courteous, and affable.”

He governed the church of Canterbury for nearly eleven years. Gervase relates the following remarkable event before his death, though scarcely consistent with the “good manners” attributed to him: “While Richard, archbishop of Canterbury, sober by night had given his limbs to sleep upon his bed, a terrible and majestic figure appeared to him in a night vision, saying to him once and again: ‘Who are you?’ Since the archbishop, overcome by fear, answered not a word, that figure added: ‘You are he who has dissipated the goods of the Church entrusted to you, and I will dissipate you from the earth.’ Having said this, the figure disappeared,” etc. The archbishop himself died shortly afterward, as the same writer relates. William Thorne and Knyghton, canon of Leicester, report the same story.]

[About A.D. 1176.]

### SUBJECT

He freely rebukes Richard, who had come from a monastery to the archbishopric of Canterbury immediately after St Thomas the martyr, and who devoted himself to accumulating wealth and to secular rather than spiritual concerns. He also sets forth the complaints then made against him both by the people and by King Henry II.

To the reverend father and lord RICHARD, by God’s grace archbishop of Canterbury, primate of all England, [Col. 0013B] and papal legate, PETER of Blois, archdeacon, greeting, and awakening to better things.

I desired to return to you in haste, but royal authority does not permit it. A thousand times I have sought leave to depart; yet I have neither suffered a refusal nor obtained permission. Whenever I complain of the delay I make and allege the urgency of your recall, his sole and daily answer is: “You will leave tomorrow.” Throughout all the days of the year I have not been able to find that “tomorrow”: while it is sought, it remains hidden; and perhaps, when it is not sought, it will appear.

Meanwhile my soul has been greatly troubled, and you have caused me to waste away like a spider, because my enemies who trouble me reproached me, saying every day: “Where is your lord?” [Note: [Col. 0013] Ps. 26, 14]. Where is he hiding? Where is he sleeping? How long [Col. 0013C] does the sluggard sleep? Let him who sleeps arise, and let him rise from the dead [Note: [Col. 0013] Eph. 5]. It is already time to rise from sleep [Note: [Col. 0013] Rom. 13], to watch over the flock entrusted to him, and to consider what predecessor he had. Did he receive the grace of God in vain, so as to nullify both the grace bestowed on himself and the glory of his predecessor? He has already nullified it in [Col. 0014A] part; nor do we see when he will restore what he has lost or redeem what he has put at risk.

They charge you, therefore, with this: that the ark of the Lord is captured by foreigners [Note: [Col. 0013] 1 Sam. 4]; that the Church of God is trampled by laymen; that rust consumes Peter’s sword [Note: [Col. 0013] John 18]; that Christ’s sacraments are held cheap; that God’s terrible name is taken in vain; that lawful marriages are dissolved under the pretext of perjury. They charge you with this: that Malchus stretches sacrilegious hands against Christ, Pashhur against Jeremiah [Note: [Col. 0013] ch. 20], and Belshazzar against the vessels of the Lord [Note: [Col. 0013] Dan. 5]. Yet whenever I extol in you the grace of innocence and humility, they say: “It is not enough for a man of so great a prelacy not to do evil, unless he also adds the doing of good. For not only the tree that bears bad fruit, but also the tree that bears no good fruit, [Col. 0014B] will be cut down and cast into the fire” [Note: [Col. 0013] Luke 3].

“Your archbishop,” they say, “found the Church in an excellent condition, but he has forsaken and cast it down. The dignity of the Church of Canterbury, which the glorious martyr had reddened with his own blood and, as though by an eternal testament, confirmed by his death and the shedding of his brains, has been nullified by Richard’s faintheartedness. He has brought it back into the reproach of its former slavery, though it had raised itself into the grace of full liberty. Why,” they say, “does he occupy the land? When will he die and his name perish?” [Note: [Col. 0013] Ps. 40]. Why does he not at least awake? “Will not he who sleeps rise again?” [Note: [Col. 0013] ibid.].

In all these things my shame is before me all day, and confusion has covered my face at the voice of the reproacher and slanderer [Note: [Col. 0013] Ps. 45]. Therefore my tears are my bread day and night [Note: [Col. 0013] Ps. 41]; and where, beneath [Col. 0014C] the shadow of your name, I had hoped to be magnified and exalted, there reproach and misery awaited my heart [Note: [Col. 0013] Ps. 68]. For you have become a byword in men’s mouths, and the almost universal occupation is to let loose insolent tongues against you in hateful whispering. If I wish to commend your diligence in improving [Col. 0015A] buildings, cultivating estates, and administering such outward matters as human necessity continually demands, they distort everything. “What glory is it,” they say, “that he makes fishponds and encloses wild beasts with a fence, if clerics utter curses and the doors are thrown open to every dissolution of religious cloisters?”

What advantage is there in enriching arable land with dung and marl [Note: [Col. 0015D] There is a method of cultivating and manuring fields which we French call *fumer et marner*, “dunging and marling.”], if in cultivating the Lord’s harvest neither thorn is plucked out nor thistle uprooted, nor is the word of the Lord sown? [Note: [Col. 0015] 1 Cor. 9]. Is God concerned for oxen and asses, that he should be so busily occupied with oxen and asses? Why does he not discharge the office of the legation entrusted to him? He is bound rather than a legate.

“They say that the Lord commanded the prophet to whom he had entrusted a mission [Col. 0015B] to pluck up and destroy, to scatter and overthrow, to build and plant” [Note: [Col. 0015] Jer. 1]. Your lord [Note: [Col. 0015D] He calls Richard, archbishop of Canterbury, his lord because Peter of Blois was at that time his household official and chancellor. It is also evident that when he wrote this he was at the court of the king of England, for whom he was performing a mission on Richard’s behalf.] has turned the understanding of a spiritual office into the letter—or, more truly, into a blotting-out.

This further heightens my sorrow: the lord king, who loves you with all his heart, whose affection for you I continually read in the book of experience, and who opposes himself as an impregnable wall against those who trouble you in the Roman curia, himself frequently rebukes your negligence and idleness, though with private and moderate correction. He often stirs you by letters and messengers, taking it most gravely that, by the licence of impunity, you provoke the evildoers of his realm to monstrous crimes. How kindly he very recently wrote and sent to you, I believe you have fixed firmly in memory. Among these words, I, who was privy to the secrets, confidently bring into common knowledge this memorable saying: “Let the lord archbishop know that if my son the elect, or any bishop of the realm, or earl, or any distinguished person, should presume to oppose his will or ordinance, or should hinder him from fulfilling the duty of the legation entrusted to him, he will find in me the persecutor and avenger of this contempt, as though he had treacherously offended against my crown.”

I know, Father, that the lord king has long desired, and still desires, that by your counsel and assistance “rebukes may be made among the peoples” [Note: [Col. 0015] Ps. 149], that [Col. 0015D] your hand may seize judgment [Note: [Col. 0015] Deut. 32], and rebuke on behalf of the meek of the earth [Note: [Col. 0015] Isa. 11].

I have indeed reported harsh things to you, most loving [Col. 0016A] Father; and perhaps someone will impute it to rashness that I do not flatter, that I do not fawn, that I do not anoint the venerable head of a bishop with the oil of a sinner [Note: [Col. 0015] Ps. 140]. Whatever the foulest swine may grunt, I admonish and shall admonish you in the bowels of Christ and in unceasing memory of your benefits, that you may fulfil the episcopal office with such diligence that your ministry may not be blamed. For you have read: “Cursed is the man who does the work of the Lord negligently” [Note: [Col. 0016D] The Hebrew version reads “deceitfully”; the Syriac, “with deceit”; the Chaldee paraphrase, “in fraud”; but the version of the Septuagint translators: “Cursed is he who performs the works of the Lord negligently.”].

God chose you from cloistered and spiritual warfare as a priest for himself. Take heed lest, having begun in the Spirit, you be perfected in the flesh [Note: [Col. 0015] Gal. 3]; and lest that saying be understood of you: “My Spirit shall not remain in man for ever, because he is flesh” [Note: [Col. 0015] Gen. 6; Ps. 9]. Do you suppose that, concerning the souls entrusted to you, you will not be required to render an account in the strict examination? [Col. 0016B] Because of this the wicked man provoked God; for he said in his heart: “He will not require it” [Note: [Col. 0015] Ps. 9]. But he surely will require it, most exactly, to the last farthing; and I fear that it may happen more promptly or more severely than we are willing to believe or fear.

Would that you were willing to recall the threats of the Most High, by which in the clearest vision he disclosed to us the dreadful sentence of his wrath. “It is dreadful to fall into the hands of the living God” [Note: [Col. 0015] Heb. 10]. For “a fire has been kindled in his anger” [Note: [Col. 0015] Jer. 15], which you have sometimes seen spiritually, but may you never experience sensibly [Note: [Col. 0016D] In the manuscript of St Mark it is written: “And may you never, I pray, sensibly experience him whom you have seen spiritually.” So Mazarin manuscript I and Vall.].

## LETTER VI. TO RALPH OF BEAUVAIS

[About A.D. 1155.]

[Col. 0016C]

### SUBJECT

He replies to the invective of a certain master who bitterly attacks the life of clerics living in bishops’ courts; and he sharply rebukes him in turn because he has spent his whole life in secular letters. He urges him at least to spend his final old age in meditation upon his last things.

To Master Ralph of Beauvais, PETER of Blois, archdeacon of Bath, greeting, and that at least in old age you may be an old man.

I received your letter, though highly invective, with complete equanimity and thanksgiving. Your rebuke of me is affection; and therefore your blows are more welcome to me than the breasts of those who feed me. Would that the righteous man might always correct me [Col. 0016D] in mercy and rebuke me, but that the oil of the sinner might not fatten my head [Note: [Col. 0015] Ps. 140].

You judge the life of court clerics to be utterly condemnable, and in condemning it you employ nearly the whole of Juvenal’s satire:

> “If you are not yet ashamed of your purpose …”  
> [Note: [Col. 0017D] This is Satire 5, beginning “If you are not ashamed of your purpose,” etc., from which is taken the half-line “to live from another’s dish,” cited in this letter.]

Good master, if you retain by memory the trifles of childish derivations in which you have grown old, then, although *curia* (“court”) is said to derive from *cruor* (“blood”), clerics who associate with prelates of the Church are not “courtly”; for among them no judgment of blood is exercised [Note: [Col. 0017D] Since the Church abhors blood, clerics were from ancient times forbidden to participate in judgments of blood and criminal causes, especially by the Eleventh Council of Toledo, ch. 6: “Those by whom the sacraments of the Lord must be handled may not conduct a judgment of blood,” etc. Many canons concerning this matter are cited by Antonio Agustín, *De actionibus et judiciis*, title 20, ch. 7.].

And although canonical institution forbids court clerics [Note: [Col. 0017D] Thus in all printed editions. But in all manuscripts the word “clerics” is absent, and rightly so.] to be promoted, the Lord has more frequently chosen the clerics of bishops as priests for himself. You reproach us because we always live from another’s dish. If bishops summon us to share their care, so that we may labour together in the cultivation of the divine harvest and in threshing the Lord’s threshing-floor, [Col. 0017B] what injustice is it if we also share in their goods? According to the sentence of divine law, “No one muzzles an ox while it treads out the grain” [Note: [Col. 0017] Deut. 25; 1 Tim. 5; 1 Cor. 9]; and, as Paul testifies, “No one serves as a soldier at his own expense” [Note: [Col. 0017] 1 Cor. 9]. Since he who serves the altar ought to live by the altar, it is not absurd that I, or another who ministers to a bishop at the Lord’s table, should become his fellow diner at food.

You complain that I squander my days uselessly when I could bear very abundant fruit in the camp of the schools. Good master, these in which we dwell are the camps of God [Note: [Col. 0017] Gen. 52]; and know that this is none other than the house of God and the gate of heaven [Note: [Col. 0017] Gen. 28]. In the household of my lord the archbishop of Canterbury are men most learned, among whom is found every [Col. 0017C] rectitude of justice, every prudence of foresight, every pattern of teaching. After prayer and before their meal, they continually exercise themselves in reading, disputation, and deciding cases. Every difficult and knotty question of the kingdom is referred to us; when these are brought into common hearing among our companions, each one, according to his rank, sharpens his mind for sound speech without quarrelling or detraction, and draws from a subtler vein what seems to him more prudent and sound. If God reveals what is superior to one of lesser rank, the whole body assents to his judgment without any envy or distortion.

But you, disputing endlessly over trifles amid tumultuous uproar and sailors’ shouting, beat the air to no purpose. You are still exercising your mind over letter and syllable and such elementary rudiments of learning. And, if it may be said, you—a boy of a hundred years and an old man at the alphabet—teach wisdom [Note: [Col. 0017D]

The two words “teach wisdom” are absent from For., Ful., Boer., Bec. Dom., Hard., [Col. 0018D] Sorbonne manuscripts 1 and 2, Vict. 1 and 3, and from the Mainz and Merlin editions, as also from Busaeus’s manuscripts except the single Cartb. manuscript. But in Laun., Maz. 1, and Vall. the text reads: “You, a boy of a hundred years and an old man at the alphabet, to use Job’s phrase (ch. 32), I had hoped that greater age and a multitude of years would teach wisdom. But, as I see, there is a spirit in men, and the inspiration of the Almighty gives understanding.”

An “old man at the alphabet” means one who learns the elements among boys, says Lipsius on these words of Seneca, Letter 36: “An old man at the alphabet is a shameful and ridiculous thing.”

I judge this letter to have been written about A.D. 1177, when Peter was with the archbishop of Canterbury.]

Indeed, it is sufficiently shameful and burdensome to me that all your contemporaries have ascended the mountain of higher learning, while you have remained in the mud of coarser understanding with the ass. Priscian and Tully, Lucan and Persius—these are your gods [Note: [Col. 0017] Gen. 21]. I fear that at the crisis of final necessity it may be said to you in reproach: “Where are your gods in whom [Col. 0018B] you trusted? Let them arise and help you, and protect you in your necessity” [Note: [Col. 0017] Exod. 32]. You are always circling Mount Seir [Note: [Col. 0017] Deut. 2], and cannot come to the land of promise.

Master, for you and your imitators the Lord has turned rivers into blood [Note: [Col. 0017] Ps. 104], so that they may not drink. He also gives you a brazen heaven and an iron earth, when the Lord turns your carnal learning, in which you have stubbornly hardened yourselves, into sin [Note: [Col. 0017] 2 Sam. 2]. Master, do not speak lofty things in boasting; let old things depart from your mouth, for the Lord, the God of knowledges, abhors the error of pagan philosophy, of which you are still an idolater. In every Christian he accepts purity of conscience. For the Apostle condemns things [Col. 0018C] which indeed have an appearance of wisdom [Note: [Col. 0017] Col. 2], according to the commandments and teachings of men, if they do not build up toward salvation.

Would that, master, you were wise and understood and foresaw your last things [Note: [Col. 0017] Deut. 32]. At your now-decrepit age, that philosophy would be most necessary to you which is frequently described in schools but still more often prescribed: namely, continual thought of death. The prophet says: “Lord, make known to me my end” [Note: [Col. 0017] Ps. 38]. And Solomon: “My son, remember your last things, and you will never sin” [Note: [Col. 0017] Ecclus. 7]. That lamenting prophet Jeremiah [Col. 0019A] mourns the sinful soul, forgetful of its end: “Her filthiness,” he says, “is in her feet, and she did not remember her end” [Note: [Col. 0019] Lam. 1]. And he adds: “She has been cast down exceedingly, having no comforter” [Note: [Col. 0019] ibid.].

Let the day of death be your meditation, master. For death, which lies in ambush for the young, stands at the door for you elderly men; it watches your heel and will not cease until a pit is dug for the sinner [Note: [Col. 0019] Ps. 93]. Therefore I beg and truly counsel you in charity: you who have hitherto served the changing fortunes of this world, serve God at least for a little while; and offer to the Most High the dregs of your old age, you who spent the flower of your youth and adolescence on trifling things.

## LETTER VII. TO MASTER A.

[Col. 0019B]

### SUBJECT

He tries, by testimonies of Holy Scripture, to recall from devotion to drunkenness a certain master who, from a most acute disputant, had become an excellent drinker.

To Master A., PETER of Blois, archdeacon of Bath, greeting, and a continual remembrance of honour.

As I was recently leaving your house and table, Master P. met me as I went along the public road, cheerful, and much more cheerful than was fitting. He was evidently out of his senses; for he had drunk at your house a spirit of dizziness and fury, and all his brain burned with wine or ale. He seized the bridle of my horse and, nearly throwing both horse and rider headlong to the ground, turned me aside from my route. I drew away [Col. 0019C] his hands, and our servants sharply rebuked him; but in a rash and confused tongue, with demonic shouting, he thundered: “He will certainly come, he will come; he will come, willing or unwilling, and my most beloved master will drink of the Son of God.” Grieved, [Col. 0020A] I followed him and was dragged unwillingly along.

When my servants, who had been sparing toward his rashness, had with much insistence removed his hands from my bridle, and he saw us turn the horses’ heads back toward the road from which he had led us, he pursued us for a long time with stones and clods and assailed me with unheard-of obscenity of speech.

Certainly I had always considered him an industrious, discerning, and modest man; but on that occasion he had drunk with you, at whose house, as is publicly said, there is neither reason nor measure in drinking. And what glory is it to you, friend, so to affect a man with drink that he unlearns being a man and passes utterly into bestial folly? It is no great occasion for praise that you pour and keep pouring wine into your friends, and by pouring [Col. 0020B] them full bring them into confusion.

It is written in Habakkuk [Note: [Col. 0019] ch. 2]: “Woe to him who gives drink to his friend, making him drunk, that he may look upon his nakedness!” By the testimony of sacred speech, those who sit down to drain cups and devote themselves to continual drunkenness incur a manifold sentence of curse. The Lord says through Isaiah the prophet [Note: [Col. 0019] ch. 5]: “Woe to you who are mighty to drink wine, and strong men at mixing drunkenness!” Solomon concisely and elegantly enumerates the subsequent evils of drunkenness, saying: “For whom is woe? For whose father is woe?” [Note: [Col. 0019C]

The Hebrew version reads thus: “For whom is woe? For whom sorrow? For whom contentions or quarrels? For whom speech? For whom wounds without cause? For whom redness of eyes? Is it not for those who linger over wine, who go seeking mixed wine?” In precisely the same manner the Septuagint, approaching more closely to the Hebrew truth:

> “For whom is woe? For whom turmoil? For whom judgments? For whom vexation and chatter? For whom needless bruises? Whose eyes are darkened? Is it not those who linger over wines? Is it not those who track down where drinking parties are held?”

That is: “For whom is woe? For whom tumult? For whom lawsuits? For whom [Col. 0019D] troubles and vexations? For whom needless bruises? Whose eyes are livid? Is it not for those who linger over wines? Is it not for those who seek out where drinking bouts take place?”

The sense is: no people are more wretched than those who spend a long time day and night over wine. For at one moment their head aches, at another their stomach is tortured, at another their limbs are paralysed; now they break out into quarrels, now wounds are inflicted upon them without cause, and now through habitual drinking they fall into dimness and blindness of the eyes, which not infrequently results from excessive wine. Thus the wise man’s purpose in this exclamation is to draw his son away from the vices to which youth is especially liable, and to restore him to sound sense and wisdom. If any refuse to do this for love of virtue, let them at least learn through fear of punishment and the shamefulness of their sins to abstain from shameful vices: namely, fleshly luxury, drunken excess, and lust, which produce endless evils [Col. 0020C] and torments.

But when he says, “For whom quarrels? For whom wounds?”—in the Vulgate, “For whom wounds without cause?”—he means that amid drinking there arise disputes, shameless speeches, and harmful reproaches, from which fights and sometimes wounds among friends follow over a worthless matter.]

For whom are wounds? For whom are quarrels? For whom is *suffosio* (“digging-under”) of the eyes? [Note: [Col. 0020C] Thus it is read in ancient editions before the Sixtine Bible, although all manuscripts have *suffusio*, as does the present Vulgate; Bede reads it likewise. [Col. 0020D] Lucas of Bruges agrees in the Roman corrections, saying that *suffusio* should be read, from *suffundo* (“to suffuse”), not *suffossio*, from *suffodio* (“to dig underneath”). The Chaldee paraphrase, conforming to the Hebrew, translates “redness” or “red colour”; the Syriac, “livid eyes”; the Arabic, “discoloured eyes,” which is the same as livid.] Is it not for those who linger over wine and apply themselves [Note: [Col. 0020D] The Victorine manuscripts read: “Who sit down to cups and devote themselves to drunkenness.” The Hebrew version cited above is clearer: “those lingering over wine,” etc.—that is, those who consume their time in drinking and go to seek mixed, or rather tempered, wine; or those who seek the place where wines are mixed, that is, where banquets are held; and, according to the Septuagint, those who seek not only to drink much wine but to spend as much time as possible in drinking.] to draining cups?

Surely, according to the saying of the Wise Man, “This drink will turn to vomiting, and this pleasure to nausea” [Col. 0020C] [Note: [Col. 0019] Ecclus. 31]. “Awake, you drunkards,” says the prophet, “and weep; and howl, all you who drink wine in sweetness” [Note: [Col. 0019] Joel 1]. The Apostle also forbids drunkenness in many ways [Note: [Col. 0019] Rom. 13]. Canonical censure, moreover, pronounces sentence of deposition upon clerics who become accustomed to drunkenness. For where drunkenness reigns, reason is banished, understanding is blunted, counsels go astray, and judgments are overthrown [Note: [Col. 0021] 1 Cor. 5, 6].

If, according to the Apostle, it is good not to drink wine [Note: [Col. 0021] Rom. 14], I do not see how its contrary can be good. Therefore that prudent woman, instructing her son in a vision, said: “Do not give wine to kings, O Lemuel, lest perhaps they forget the judgments of God and overthrow the justice of the people. Nor is any secret safe where drunkenness reigns” [Note: [Col. 0021] Prov. 31]. Lot, whom Sodom had not conquered, was conquered by wines [Note: [Col. 0021] Gen. 19]. The vineyard planted by Noah [Note: [Col. 0021] Gen. 9] likewise spared not its own author, and from the father’s offence the stain of servitude is passed down to his descendants even to this day.

It also added greatly to the commendation of the titles of Blessed John the Baptist that he drank neither wine nor strong drink, nor anything that could intoxicate [Col. 0021B] [Note: [Col. 0021] Luke 1]. The Lord commanded Aaron and his sons, when they were about to enter the tabernacle, to abstain from wine and every intoxicating thing [Note: [Col. 0021] Lev. 10]. Because the Rechabites, according to the command of Jonadab son of Rechab, abstained from every drink [Note: [Col. 0021] Jer. 35] which could occasion drunkenness, they remained free when all the tribes were carried captive.

You who once set disciplinary warfare and books before everything else have now, as I hear, transferred books to cups. You have changed writing into drinking; and, to my grievous sorrow, you are now proclaimed an excellent drinker, whereas you were formerly a most celebrated disputant. I add one thing to what has been said: either show yourself more corrigible in this respect, or I shall vomit you from my heart; and, breaking the bond of our friendly association, I shall nullify the favour of our former intimacy. Farewell.

## LETTER VIII. TO A CERTAIN PRIOR

[Note: [Col. 0021C] In the Mainz and Merlin editions and in almost all manuscripts, the title here is: “Peter of Blois’s reply to a certain prior who did not admit the words of secular learning into sacred discourse.”]

### SUBJECT

He explains that the Church of God, like the moon, has had various conditions; and that sayings of pagan philosophers and even of jurists may properly be employed in imparting sacred doctrine.

You complain and vehemently accuse me because, while recently speaking [Col. 0022A] in chapter to your brethren about the varied raiment of the bride [Note: [Col. 0021] Song 6], I inserted certain matters which, as you claim, savoured more of a pagan and heathen philosopher than of a professed Christian faith. I firmly maintain what I said, and this has not escaped your memory; in it you will find nothing except what is Catholic, unless you distort straightforward statements by a sinister interpretation or a perverse recollection.

In recounting the varied conditions of the Church militant, since in sacred discourse the present Church is frequently understood by the moon, I adapted to the Church certain properties of the moon’s course. For just as, in Martianus’s astronomy, the moon in its newness is called *menoeides* (“crescent-shaped”); when waxing and already grown to the middle, *diatomos* (“bisected”); when it approaches a circle, *amphicyrtos* (“gibbous”); and when at its full it is wholly bright, *panselenos* (“full-mooned”): so the Church of God, which after the lunar pattern borrows its light from the sun of righteousness, might tolerably be called *menoeides* in Abel and the patriarchs; *diatomos* in the time of the prophets; *amphicyrtos* in Christ’s advent; and *panselenos* in his resurrection and the confirmation of the faith.

For that the Church was then at last perfect and perfectly ordered, when Christ ascended into heaven, the prophet declares quite expressly by a similar example: “The sun,” he says, “was lifted up, and the moon stood in its order” [Note: [Col. 0021] Josh. 10]; that is, Christ ascended and through the apostles established the Church in the order of holiness.

Indeed, if the Holy Scriptures [Note: [Col. 0021D]

The holy Fathers maintain that books of the pagans can usefully be read by churchmen. Basil the Great accordingly composed a rather extensive treatise on reading pagan books, in which he also proves at length from the Scriptures themselves that great benefit results from reading pagan authors. His examples are Moses, who, instructed in Egyptian learning, came to the contemplation of the true God; and Daniel, who, after being trained in Chaldean learning, later attained divine doctrines. He then teaches the manner in which such books should be read—or rather selected—by the example of bees, which make sweetest honey from flowers gathered everywhere:

> “Thus those who are diligent in reading do not pursue only what is sweet and pleasant in such writings, but strive to store up from them some benefit for the soul.”

> “In the same way, those who pursue not merely the sweet and pleasing quality [Col. 0022C] of such writings may lay up some benefit from them for the soul.”

Finally he concludes thus:

> “And since by virtue we must be brought to our true life, and virtue is celebrated greatly by poets, greatly by historians, and still more greatly by philosophers, we must give the greatest attention to such portions of their writings.”

That is: “Since through virtue one ascends to this true life, and virtue itself is greatly commended by poets, historians, and still more by philosophers, we must devote ourselves especially to such passages in their writings.”

Gregory of Nazianzus does likewise in the oration which he delivered at the funeral of Basil the Great. His words are somewhat lengthy, but because they bear in a remarkable manner upon our subject, it will not be tiresome to quote them:

I think it would be agreed by all who have sound minds that education holds the first place among the good things available to us—not only this nobler education of our own, which, despising every elegance and ambitious ornament of discourse, cleaves solely to salvation and to the beauty of things apprehended by the mind, but also the external learning which most Christians, through faulty understanding, reject as treacherous, dangerous, and leading far away from God [Col. 0023C–D].

Afterwards he draws a comparison from all created things, each of which is by its nature either useful or harmful according as one uses it well or badly; for even from venomous animals beneficial medicines, such as theriac, are usefully made. Finally he draws this conclusion:

> Therefore education is not to be despised because some people think so; rather, those who hold such an opinion must be regarded as uncouth and uneducated—people who would have everyone be like themselves, so that their private ignorance may be concealed in the general mass and they may escape the exposures of their lack of education.

St Jerome frequently and splendidly developed this divine teaching of his master, but especially in Letter 84 to Magnus. There he shows that Moses, the prophets, the books of Solomon, and even the apostle Paul borrowed certain things from pagan books. St Augustine too, in the second book of *On Christian Doctrine*, chapter 18, maintains that we should not shun anything from the pagans if we can seize from it something useful for understanding the sacred Scriptures; rather, we should claim everything from them for our own use, as from unjust possessors [Col. 0024C–D]. Finally he concludes: “Whoever is a good and true Christian should understand that, wherever he finds truth, it belongs to his Lord.” Theodoret also writes elegantly on this subject in his treatise *On Greek Affections*, to which, for brevity’s sake, we refer the reader.

But, to add something concerning persons of our own time and to stop the mouths of certain half-learned and over-scrupulous people, the testimony of St Charles Borromeo will suffice. Lipsius speaks of him thus: “Jerome’s opinion is that the Stoics agree in many respects with our doctrine,” etc. “I hear that that great Charles Borromeo—most illustrious by birth, sacred purple, and virtue, and, I would add, by holiness—often confessed that through the books of Epictetus he had been moved and admonished toward contempt of human things and love of divine things.”

If you attend carefully to these matters, you will not judge it absurd that expressions drawn from philosophy or civil law should sometimes be admitted into Christian teaching, especially where reason requires it [Col. 0022C]. Hear what Job says of the Lord: “He commands the sun, and it does not rise; and he seals up the stars as under a seal. He makes Arcturus, Orion, the Hyades, and the inner regions of the South” [Note: [Col. 0021] Job 9.].

The prophet Jeremiah seems to have been trained, as it were, in civil law. He describes with the technical elegance of certain legal terms the purchase of his cousin’s field which he had concluded: “I bought the field from Hanameel, the son of my uncle, who is at Anathoth; and I weighed out for him silver, seven staters and ten silver pieces. And I wrote it in a document, sealed it, summoned witnesses, and weighed the silver in scales. And I received the sealed deed of possession, the stipulations, the ratifications, and the external marks” [Note: [Col. 0023] Jer. 32.].

Indeed, as you read in Deuteronomy [Note: [Col. 0023] Chap. 21.], a foreign woman captured in war, if her beauty pleases you, may lawfully be taken as wife after her nails and hair have been cut and her garment of captivity laid aside. Thus, if there is any writing of the pagans that pleases me amid the conflict of studies, after removing the superfluity of words I may appropriate it for myself, so that spiritual children may be begotten from it in faith. For the law commands that, if in a field or tree you find a bird sitting upon its eggs or young, you must take the eggs or young but let the mother go [Note: [Col. 0023] Deut. 22.]. Nor should one be concerned with the letter where fruitful meanings are found [Col. 0023A–B].

You rebuke me because, in exhortations which I sometimes delivered at Bologna at the request of our fellow students, I used expressions that had the flavor of civil law. But civil law is holy and honorable, and approved by the enactments of the orthodox Fathers. In those aforementioned exhortations I was speaking to lawyers about the terrible sentence of strict and final judgment, and I said that it could not be challenged either by the remedy of appeal, by the aid of a petition, by a subsidiary *actio in factum*, or by any benefit of restitution [Col. 0023B–C].

I said that the Ancient of Days, among the children of the kingdom [Note: [Col. 0023] Dan. 7.], whom he will summon, as though by a measuring-line of distribution [Note: [Col. 0023] Ps. 77.], to the eternal inheritance according to the measure of their merits, would pronounce a judgment for the division of the family estate. I said that those who delayed confession of their sins through shame or contempt would be punished by a double penalty [Note: [Col. 0023] Jer. 17.]; for in civil law an action was doubled through denial [Note: [Col. 0024D] Among jurists, *inficiari* means to deny a debt or deposit. See Brissonius, book *On the Meaning of Words*.].

Know one thing: I shall never raise a question concerning the source discipline from which words are taken, provided that they build up toward salvation. For neither do we ask in what soil, or by the care and cultivation of what gardener, herbs have grown, provided that they possess healing power.

## LETTER IX. TO A CERTAIN DESERTER FROM THE SCHOOL OF LETTERS

### SUBJECT

He attacks a certain pupil of his [Col. 0024B] who, having completed the course of liberal arts, intended not to devote himself to theology until he had spent two years in idleness; and he argues at length that every kind of idleness is destructive.

Having taken leave in a manner neither lawful nor honorable, you have abandoned the camp of scholarly service like a fugitive and deserter; from the most restful labor you have transferred yourself into the most laborious idleness. I had instructed you as a pupil and advised you as a friend, that by unbroken persistence in study you might bring your incompleteness to fulfillment and rise from pupil to master.

You reply that you have labored long enough in the liberal disciplines, and that your intention is to take breath for two years before you storm the difficulties of theology. Would that you had prescribed twenty or thirty years for this desire—or rather, this sloth and failure! [Col. 0024C]. I call it failure, for “your soul has failed for your salvation” [Note: [Col. 0023] Ps. 118.]; and it would seem better to me that a man walking on the path of condemned opinion should entirely abandon the undertaking of virtue than postpone it [Col. 0025A]. Delay in a holy and honorable purpose is a great ruin.

Though you are teachable now, at a more advanced age you will not be capable of learning. Therefore, at the present moment, what is postponed is taken away. The prophet’s words are: “This people says: The time has not yet come for building the house of the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0025] Hag. 1.]. Most wretched man, why do you defer a commendable work for two years? Perhaps tomorrow you will not exist. The wise man says: “Whatever your hand is able to do, do with diligence” [Note: [Col. 0025] Eccl. 9.]:

> He who is not ready today will be less ready tomorrow.  
> [Note: [Col. 0025] Ovid, *Remedies for Love*, book I.]

In your letter I read: “I shall devote myself to myself and to my books, and in my chamber I shall be my own pupil and master. I have never rested; I have always labored. Now I shall turn labor into idleness and repose.” Brother, would that you had wisdom and understanding and could distinguish idleness from repose! [Col. 0025B] You have heard of the Lord’s repose: “He rested from all the work which he had completed” [Note: [Col. 0025] Gen. 2.]; yet you have not read of his idleness.

We read [Note: [Col. 0025] Ecclus. 33.] that idleness is the enemy of the soul. For a mind given over to leisure is gnawed by empty anxieties; and, by Solomon’s testimony, desires gnaw at the sluggard [Note: [Col. 0025] Prov. 21.]. The same teacher says [Note: [Col. 0025] Ecclus. 22.] that a lazy person deserves to be stoned with ox dung—that is, with disgraceful rebuke.

> See how leisure corrupts an inactive body,  
> And how waters grow foul if they are not stirred.  
> [Note: [Col. 0025] Ovid, *Letters from Pontus*, I, elegy 5.]

Flaccus says:

> Unless you ask for a book and light before daybreak, unless  
> You direct your mind toward studies and honorable pursuits,  
> Envy or love will keep you wakeful and torment you.  
> [Note: [Col. 0025] Horace, book I, epistle 2.]

Or do you seek proof of this?

> The question is asked why Aegisthus became an adulterer.  
> The cause is obvious: he was idle.  
> [Note: [Col. 0025] Ovid, *Remedies for Love*, book I.]

According to Jerome’s testimony [Note: [Col. 0025] Book II against Jovinian.], the sin of the Sodomites was fullness and abundance of bread [Note: [Col. 0025] Ezek. 16.]. The law too commands concerning sacrifices that an ox be offered at the entrance of the tabernacle [Note: [Col. 0025] Lev. 1.], because those who labor in the field of the Lord’s cultivation may freely enter the heavenly tabernacle.

Why do you complain of the labor of study and sigh with all your heart for idleness? Scholarly labor is leisure, but busy leisure—leisure that makes the mind attentive to honorable things. Hence it is written [Note: [Col. 0025] Ecclus. 38.]: “Write wisdom in leisure, and one who is less occupied by activity will find it” [Col. 0025C–D]. Thus the hungry disciples rubbed ears of grain on the Sabbath [Note: [Col. 0025] Luke 6.]; this signifies the threshing out of useful meanings, which is undertaken more diligently by a tranquil mind.

Thus a man enters the grave in abundance [Note: [Col. 0025] Job 3.], because, hidden from the disturbance of men [Note: [Col. 0025] Ps. 30.], he indeed diminishes outwardly, but inwardly is refreshed and enriched beyond measure by the fruit of spiritual study. Thus in Ezekiel [Note: [Col. 0025] Chap. 46.]: “The gate of the inner court which faces east is shut during the six days in which work is done, but on the Sabbath day it is opened” [Col. 0026A]. Those who are free from earthly things attain knowledge of spiritual things more easily. “Be still,” he says, “and see that I am God” [Note: [Col. 0025] Ps. 45.].

Thus Martha is troubled about many things [Note: [Col. 0025] Luke 10.]. Leah’s eye is impeded by bleary weakness, but Mary with Rachel has chosen the best part [Note: [Col. 0025] Gen. 29.]. And when Jacob rests at Bethel, he comprehends heavenly mysteries [Note: [Col. 0025] Gen. 18.]. This is holy leisure, studious leisure.

But what you call leisure is not keeping watch, not reading, devoting yourself to revelry, yielding to the enticements of the flesh, languishing in sleep, and indulging in drink. You should have feared the Lord’s voice, angry at such leisure: “I will not endure your new moons and Sabbaths. My soul has hated your idlenesses, appointed days, and feasts” [Note: [Col. 0025] Isa. 1.]. The prophet also laments over the idle soul, saying: “Her enemies saw her and mocked at her Sabbaths” [Note: [Col. 0025] Lam. 1; Col. 0026B].

Jerome’s saying is [Note: [Col. 0025] Seneca, epistle 83.]: “Leisure without letters is death and the burial of a living man.” Wretched man, whatever you have learned in a long course of time, two years’ idleness will blow away; and that windy verbosity of logic in which you swell will fly away like a night vision and a dream [Note: [Col. 0025] Job 20.].

Do you suppose that peace of mind consists in the body’s peace and quiet? Perhaps you will have peace, but a most bitter peace. You imagine, I know, that you possess peace: solitude in the dwelling-place, indulgence in the body’s demands; and behold, “in your peace there is most bitter bitterness” [Note: [Col. 0025] Isa. 38.]. Whoever gives care to the flesh for its pleasures [Note: [Col. 0025] Rom. 13.] suffers the torments of an accusing conscience and always carries an enemy of the household within himself [Col. 0026C].

As the wise man says: “The solitude you desire is the overthrow of virtues. Woe to one alone, because if he falls, he has no one to raise him” [Note: [Col. 0025] Eccl. 4.]. Solitude provoked Amnon, the brother of Tamar, to incestuous intercourse with his sister [Note: [Col. 0025] II Kings 13.]. Solitude is what plunges a strong man most forcefully into guilt. Through it, virtue yields its weapons to unchastity; the resolution of a holier life degenerates; and the glory of a fragrant reputation shamefully vanishes.

While you were pursuing study at Paris, people said publicly that in this human life you presented yourself as an angel. I fear that you, who had passed from being a man into an angel, may return from an angel into a man. For according to the saying of Truth [Note: [Col. 0025] Matt. 12.], the unclean spirit, wandering through desert and dry places and finding no rest—yet finding rest with one resting in idleness—takes seven spirits more wicked than itself; it finds the house empty and cleansed by the brooms of discipline, occupies it while empty, and changes the latter state of that man for the worse [Col. 0026D].

For a long time I invited you to scholarly service; for a long time I cried out and labored in crying out, lest you recoil from this labor—I have truly labored. For to persuade and not succeed in persuading: that is labor before me. Yet you ought not to recoil from the labor and difficulty of theology [Col. 0027A]. The labor of the scholar is not in deeds but in words; and, to use Solomon’s expression: “All the labor of such a man is in his mouth” [Note: [Col. 0027] Eccl. 6.].

Certainly the Lord wishes his commandments both to be known and observed with labor; for he himself is the one “who devises labor in the commandment” [Note: [Col. 0027] Ps. 93.]. Hence the righteous man, desiring to know and keep the words and commands which proceeded from the lips of the Most High, says with the prophet: “Because of the words of your lips I have kept hard ways” [Note: [Col. 0027] Ps. 16.].

Again I beg you: do not fear or postpone this labor. To become effeminate through leisure and torpid through sloth is nothing other than to suffocate virtue, nourish pride, and build a road to Gehenna. Of such people it is said: “They are not in the labor of men, nor are they scourged with men; therefore pride has taken hold of them,” etc. [Note: [Col. 0027] Ps. 72.]. Without doubt, those who are not scourged temporally with men will be scourged eternally with demons; and those who do not labor with men will labor with demons [Col. 0027B]. Farewell.

## LETTER X. TO G., CHAPLAIN OF THE KING OF SICILY

### SUBJECT

He bitterly complains that the young king of Sicily has raised an utterly unsuitable man to the bishopric of the Church of Agrigento. At the same time, he shows that it is the duty of the chaplain to whom he writes seriously to admonish the king of this error, not merely once but a second and third time.

For some time a report has sounded abroad and is now publicly becoming widespread: your lord, the king of Sicily [Note: [Col. 0027C]

Certainly some rash person perversely diverted this letter to the king of France, as Busaeus learnedly observes. For all the printed editions and the greater part of the manuscript codices read “king of Sicily,” or “Sicilian king,” as Sorb. 1 and 2; Vict. 1 and 2; For., Ful., Vall., Hard., etc.; so too does the Vatican manuscript copy and others in the possession of Busaeus himself. To be sure, some witnesses, such as Laun. and Maz. 1, have: “King of the Franks,” etc., “conspired with the count of Clermont to ruin the Church of Bourges.” But it is perfectly clear that they followed ignorantly and foolishly the error of that first copyist.

For how could these things apply to the king of France, where he says that the young king preferred the treacherous counsels of ignoble men to the lord of Salerno and the count of Avellino, his uncles? Could this have referred to Louis VII, king of France, who was already an old man and knew neither the archbishop of Salerno nor the count of Avellino? All these things, however, are said by the historians of the period about William II, king of Sicily.

The Sicilian author, Abbot Rocco Pirro, explains the matter more clearly, having described the affairs of his native land accurately. In his account of the Church of Agrigento, he states that Gentile, bishop of Agrigento, had stirred up many courtiers against Richard, bishop-elect of Syracuse, who himself sought the archbishopric of Palermo; when Stephen of Perche, a kinsman of the king, was elected archbishop, Gentile himself was thrown into chains with several courtiers. At that time King William especially worked to have the brother of the count of Loricello, the king’s cousin, intruded into the Church of Agrigento. But shortly afterwards, when Stephen resigned his dignity and left Sicily, Gentile was released from prison after matters had been settled, restored to his former rank, and, with several others, appointed among the king’s household officers and the councillors of the court.

Moreover, it should be noted that the same Rocco Pirro erred when he said that this letter was written to Richard, bishop-elect of Syracuse, whereas in all printed and manuscript copies the heading of this letter is “To G., chaplain.”]

has forgotten his salvation and his father’s tradition and, together with the count of Loricello [Note: [Col. 0028D] Robert, a kinsman of King William II, concerning whom Fazellus says: “At that time, among the nobles were Robert, count of Loricello, the king’s cousin,” etc. I think this is the person whom Rocco Pirro names among the constables of Sicily as follows: “The count of Loricello, nephew of King Roger or of William II through Beltran.”], has conspired for the ruin and desolation of the Church of Agrigento [Col. 0027C]. He intends to make the count’s brother bishop and violently intrudes him, though the chapter protests.

Yet you know him to be a statue and a useless block of wood. I am astonished that you do not go up to oppose it and set yourself in opposition for the house of Israel [Note: [Col. 0027] Ezek. 13; Col. 0028A]. Unhappy man that I am, why do I not have access to that count, so that I might persuade this inhuman man of something? I would announce his wickedness to the wicked man, and, even if I did not gain him for God, at least I would fully perform the duty of one who preaches the Gospel.

“O God, zeal for your house has consumed me. Zeal for you has made me waste away, because your enemies have forgotten your words” [Note: [Col. 0027] Pss. 68, 118.]. Truly they have forgotten them. For your word is, Lord: “My house shall be called a house of prayer, not of intrusion” [Note: [Col. 0027] Isa. 6; Matt. 21.]. “Holiness becomes your house, O Lord” [Note: [Col. 0027] Ps. 92.], not intrusion. “Look upon the face of your covenant, O Lord” [Note: [Col. 0027] Ps. 73.]. Be zealous for the honor and beauty of your house and for the place where your glory dwells [Note: [Col. 0027] Ps. 25]; let no unclean and uncircumcised person rush into it [Note: [Col. 0027] Isa. 25].

Console the Church, which has been delivered over to trampling [Col. 0028B], and say to her: “Do not fear, daughter Zion” [Note: [Col. 0027] John 12]; “city of Jerusalem, do not weep” [Note: [Col. 0027] Luke 7]. “Glorious things have been spoken of you, city of God” [Note: [Col. 0027] Ps. 6]. “I shall humble the glory of those who humble and disgrace you; I shall make you the pride of ages” [Note: [Col. 0027] Isa. 60.].

O detestable deed! O youth to be lamented! Why does a son of the Church rise against his mother? Why has he cast away the counsel of piety and gone in the counsel of the ungodly? [Note: [Col. 0027] Ps. 1.] “In one day their thoughts shall perish” [Note: [Col. 0027] Ps. 145.], but “the counsel of the Lord remains forever” [Note: [Col. 0027] Ps. 32.].

“Woe to the land whose king is a child” [Note: [Col. 0027] Eccl. 10.]. I grieve that, among the first acts of his rule and in the freshness of royal anointing, he ventures on this. Would that the power of consecration had restrained him from such violence! Great indeed is the efficacy of this sacrament [Col. 0028C]. For Scripture testifies of David that, after he was anointed by Samuel, “the Spirit of the Lord was directed upon David from that day onward” [Note: [Col. 0027] I Kings 16.].

Saul too, on the day when he was sprinkled by Samuel with the little vessel of oil [Col. 0029A; Note: [Col. 0029] I Kings 10.], was changed into another man; and when the Spirit of the Lord rushed upon him and he came to the company of prophets, he began to prophesy with them. Caiaphas, who pronounced the judgment in that council where the Lord’s death was being discussed, saying, “It is expedient that one man should die for the people,” did not say this from himself, as the Evangelist says [Note: [Col. 0029] John 11.], but, being high priest that year, he prophesied.

Yet neither the power of anointing, nor the frequent exhortation of religious men, nor fear of God, nor reverence for the Church, nor loss of reputation, nor the example of his father’s gentleness [Note: [Col. 0029C] I do not see what our Peter means by that “fatherly gentleness.” For no historian of this period fails to condemn the wicked character of William I, king of Sicily, the father of this William; and they state that he was therefore called “the Bad,” while his son was called “the Good.” Thus Fazellus, after Falco, a contemporary writer, says of him: “William I was keen-minded and vigorous in war, but in greed, avarice, and credulity he was second to none.” Rocco Pirro, in his *Chronology of the Kings of Sicily*, says of him: “His character gave him the surname ‘the Bad.’” Unless perhaps we say that, after his death, when affairs in the kingdom were in disorder, he was missed by his subjects, who, as often happens, had forgotten his vices—as Fazellus himself testifies.] turns him back from his obstinacy.

You have named to me two persons who are his familiars and intimates. Though they are ignoble in mind and birth, he has accepted their friendship most gratefully [Col. 0029B]; they incite and inflame him toward this rash act. But certainly “a man’s enemies are those of his own household” [Note: [Col. 0029] Mic. 7.]. This utterly ill-advised young man has preferred their treacherous counsels to the lord of Salerno [Note: [Col. 0029D]

This is Romuald, archbishop of Salerno, nobly born, a learned man distinguished for prudence, who is numbered by historians among the leading counsellors and administrators of William II’s kingdom. Rocco Pirro says of him, while listing the regents of the kings of Sicily: “Romuald Guarna, archbishop of Salerno, together with Queen Margaret, during the childhood of William II.” He is also reckoned among the learned writers of his age. Baronius frequently cites Romuald’s *Chronicle*, from the very beginning of the world down to his own times, in the *Annals*.

He subscribed the First General Lateran Council [Col. 0030C] under Alexander III in the year 1180. Alexander III also wrote several letters to him, preserved among the decretals. He died in 1182, after presiding over the Church of Salerno for twenty-seven years.]

and to the count of Avellino [Note: [Col. 0030C] This was Roger, a kinsman of William I, says Fazellus, Decade 2, book VII, chapter 4, following Falco. Falco, recounting the conspiracy made by nobles against King William I, among whom was this same Roger, says concerning events after the conspiracy was discovered: “Nearly all the others were led out to the galleys and left the borders of the kingdom. But the king spared his kinsman Roger, count of Avellino. What he judged a most heinous crime in others, he thought should in Roger, because of the instability of youth, be called an error rather than a deed; he was also moved by the entreaties and tears of his cousin Adelicia, grandmother of the same count, who, having no other surviving heir, loved her grandson most tenderly.” After the death of William I, however, Queen Margaret, mother of the infant William II, admitted him among the chief counsellors of the realm.], his uncles, whose fidelity and prudence the necessities of the king have often tested—men who would redeem the boy’s disgrace with their death and would not consent to the humiliation of the kingdom, even to bloodshed and perpetual exile.

But because the sins of the people demand it, he has removed friends and kinsmen far from himself; and, walking in Rehoboam’s path, he has rejected the counsel of venerable maturity [Note: [Col. 0029] III Kings 12.]. Yet the Lord will be zealous for the honor of his bride, and, destroying the wicked wickedly, will abundantly repay those who act proudly [Note: [Col. 0029] Ps. 30.].

And because that wretched youth, at the prompting of evil men, has laid rapacious hands upon the treasures of the Church [Col. 0029C–0030A], I fear that the Lord may burn in anger against him and that what Job says may happen: “The treasures which the wicked man swallowed he shall vomit out, and God shall draw them from his belly. He shall pay for all that he has done, and yet shall not be consumed” [Note: [Col. 0029] Job 20.].

It did not become him to stretch lay hands toward sacred things. You ought often to have impressed on him how Uzzah was struck by the Lord because he stretched out his hand toward the ark of the Lord—devoutly indeed, but unworthily [Note: [Col. 0029] II Kings 6.]. You ought to have explained how, in Jason’s time, that perpetual fire which had endured from Jeremiah’s time to Nehemiah’s was extinguished because Antiochus, on Jason’s occasion, laid hands upon priestly matters [Note: [Col. 0029] II Macc. 1.]. You ought to have explained how Belshazzar’s kingdom was seized and devastated by the Persians, by the sign of the avenging and writing hand: “Mene, Tekel, Peres” [Col. 0030B; Note: [Col. 0029] Dan. 5.], because he had profaned the vessels of the Lord at a banquet.

You ought to have deterred him by these and similar examples. But the word of the Lord is bound in your mouth [Note: [Col. 0030D] The proverb “a dog before a morsel” can be applied to court clergy who conceal the sins of princes and great men. Of them Scripture says: “Dumb dogs, unable to bark” (Isa. 56), because they love gifts and pursue rewards.], and you are not moved by Joseph’s affliction. You fear man, and neither zeal for the Lord nor the Church’s suffering touches you.

But according to Job’s testimony, “upon one who fears frost, snow shall come” [Note: [Col. 0029] Job 6.]. It is glorious for any Christian to suffer affliction, provided that the cause is not shameful but commendable in Christ. “Let none,” says the apostle Peter, “suffer as a thief” [Note: [Col. 0029] I Pet. 4.]; but if you endure while doing good and blessing, this is grace before God. Therefore the apostles went away rejoicing from the presence of the council because they were counted worthy to suffer insult for Christ’s name [Note: [Col. 0029] Acts 5.].

If he holds your exhortation in contempt, that contempt itself will turn to your glory. Job says: “A lamp despised in the thoughts of princes [Col. 0030C] will be ready for the appointed time” [Col. 0031A; Note: [Col. 0031] Job 12.]. And what is that time but the time of which it is said: “When I receive the appointed time, I shall judge justices” [Note: [Col. 0031] Ps. 74.]?

Know one thing: if you do not announce his wickedness to the wicked man, he will die in his wickedness, and his soul will be required from your hands [Note: [Col. 0031] Ezek. 3.].
