He is your sheep, and you have undertaken his care at your own peril. See that you do not imitate those who seek milk and wool from sheep, not salvation. It is dangerous for you if you turn pastoral ministry into a shearer’s office.

Absalom shears his sheep and kills his brother [Note: [Col. 0031] II Kings 13.]; so a prelate kills his neighbor’s soul when, while that man sins outrageously, he either keeps silent, conceals it, or consents, so as to gain temporal profit from it. I know without doubt that, if you had prayed more earnestly, pleaded your case, and turned the man away from this inhuman tyranny, you would have succeeded [Col. 0031B]. For “grace is poured upon your lips” [Note: [Col. 0031] Ps. 44.], and your word—or rather, the Lord’s word—is living and effective, sharper than every two-edged sword [Note: [Col. 0031] Heb. 4.].

It is that ploughshare with which Shamgar killed six hundred Philistines [Note: [Col. 0031] Judg. 3]; the jawbone of an ass with which Samson killed a thousand of his enemies [Note: [Col. 0031] Judg. 15]; Jael’s nail [Note: [Col. 0031] Judg. 4]; Phinehas’s dagger [Note: [Col. 0031] Num. 25]; Gideon’s sword [Note: [Col. 0031] Judg. 7.]. If you pursued Christ’s cause from the heart, he in whose hand are the hearts of kings [Note: [Col. 0031] Prov. 21.] would give your voice a voice of power, make the voluntary offerings of your mouth pleasing, and turn the king’s heart to your will.

For, as the Lord says, “It is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you” [Note: [Col. 0031] Matt. 10.]. He gives the word to those who proclaim the Gospel with great power [Col. 0031C]. He would stand by you at the fitting moment, if you were urgent out of season and frequent in your urgency.

Your letter says that at first you approached him gently and amicably. But he answered that he was not at fault, but the count of Loricello was. When you approached him again, he considered you mad, as you assert; therefore you put silence upon your mouth and left him to his own judgment. I attribute your first use of gentleness to prudence, for princes should not be exasperated by quarrels but corrected more moderately, as the apostle Paul writes to Timothy: “The servant of the Lord must not quarrel, but be gentle toward all, patient, correcting with meekness those who resist the truth” [Col. 0031C–D; Note: [Col. 0031] II Tim. 2.].

But having offered the word of exhortation once and a second time, you ought to have given that same exhortation a third utterance [Col. 0032A; Note: [Col. 0031D] That is, to admonish a third time. See Columella.]. Perhaps the number three would have added something to its effectiveness. Goliath was struck down by the third stone [Note: [Col. 0031] I Kings 17.]. Moses overcame Pharaoh’s magicians by the third sign [Note: [Col. 0031] Exod. 8.].

I grieve that, in making excuses for sins, he transfers his guilt to another when he ought humbly to confess it and devoutly correct it. God is grievously offended when someone conceals his own wickedness and carries it out through another’s agency; for it is written: “The wicked man, hand joined to hand, shall not be innocent” [Note: [Col. 0031] Prov. 11.].

[Note: [Col. 0031D] I have restored this final word as *malus* (“wicked”), for previously the text had *manus* (“hand”), doubtless through a scribal fault. All copies read thus, and the Vulgate reading agrees. The Hebrew version also has: “Hand to hand, the wicked man shall not go unpunished.” More clearly, the Chaldee says: “He who stretches out his hand against his fellow shall not be innocent of evil” [Col. 0032D]. The Syriac likewise reads thus. But the Septuagint has: *cheiri cheiras embalōn adikōs ouk atimōrētos estai*—“One who lays hand upon hand unjustly shall not be unpunished.” Jerome agrees with this in book III against Rufinus: “One who lays a hand unjustly shall not be unpunished.”]

So Saul said of David: “Let not my hand be upon him; rather, let the hand of the Philistines be upon him” [Note: [Col. 0031] I Kings 18.]. So the Jews, crucifying the Lord with their tongues, yet saying, “It is not lawful for us to kill anyone” [Note: [Col. 0031] John 18.], handed him over to soldiers to be killed, so that the blame might be transferred from themselves to others [Col. 0032B].

Do not wonder that he considers you mad. It is no wonder if a mad person thinks others mad. Certainly, when one of the sons of the prophets came and anointed Jehu king, the others asked, “Why did this madman come to you?” [Note: [Col. 0031] IV Kings 9.] Thus among those whose inner eyes are blinded by ambition or envy, the Lord’s discourse is cheapened and life-giving, edifying words are called madness.

I know what your lord dreams of and what he seeks in this raising up of his Dagon, in this tyrannical intrusion. Would that he gained wisdom and understanding sooner; would that he distinguished more prudently between spiritual and worldly things. For it is fatal in a ruler either to catch the scent of gifts or to seek favor for persons. For the prophet testifies: “In whose hands are iniquities, their right hand is filled with gifts” [Col. 0032C; Note: [Col. 0031] Ps. 25.]. Yet iniquities will pass into punishment and gifts into sorrow, because Job testifies: “Fire shall devour the tabernacle of those who gladly receive gifts” [Note: [Col. 0031] Job 15.].

Blessed, however, be the Lord, who has hitherto preserved King Henry of England unharmed by such things. For he has shaken his hands free of every gift; nor, in promoting prelates of the Church, has either the offer of a gift or personal favor ever been able to turn him aside. Therefore the Lord has magnified him in the sight of kings [Note: [Col. 0031] Ecclus. 45.] and, in accordance with the name of the great ones who are upon the earth, has stored up glory and honor upon him [Note: [Col. 0031] Ecclus. 15.].

Fare well, dearest friend, and diligently persist in the correction you have begun, until your lord returns from the trackless way of his error [Col. 0032D] to the way of righteousness.

## LETTER XI. TO R., A CLERIC NOW ADVANCED IN AGE

[Col. 0033A]

### SUBJECT

He urges a certain cleric, who had promised God that he would enter religious life, to fulfill his vow and not allow either the severity of religious discipline or the complaints of parents and friends to call him back from his purpose, unless he wishes to go to ruin.

Peter of Blois, archdeacon of Bath, to his most beloved companion and friend R.: greeting, and steadfastness in keeping the right way.

You had resolved to break with all the pomp of the world and the enticements of worldly life, so that, poor yourself, following the poor Christ, you might gain the riches of eternity. Yet the unconsidered impulse of the flesh, treacherously flattering and deceptively friendly, turns you aside from the path, while, troubled by faintness of spirit, you shrink from [Col. 0033B] the first beginnings of religious life and the entrance into holiness. Because until now you have wholly immersed yourself in the pleasures of the world, a change of food, rough clothing, the yoke of obedience, the restraint of silence, regularity of conduct, and the austerity of discipline seem altogether unbearable to you. Truth, which cannot lie, cries aloud: “My yoke is sweet and my burden light” [Note: [Col. 0033] Matt. 11]. If you believe Christ, or believe in Christ, why do you consider burdensome what he himself judges light? If you are opposed to Christ, you grievously burden yourself: “You have set me,” he says, “as one opposed to you, and I have become a burden to myself” [Note: [Col. 0033] Job 7]. A pagan says:

> What you bear badly, accustom yourself to bear, and you will bear it.  
> [Note: [Col. 0033] Ovid, *Art of Love*, book II.]

And you, if you are willing to grow accustomed to the Lord’s yoke, becoming like [Col. 0033C] Ephraim, “a heifer trained to love threshing” [Note: [Col. 0033] Hos. 10], will seek what you fear and desire what you dread. One who emerges from darkness exposes himself to public daylight with eyelids half closed and weaker sight; if he becomes accustomed to the light even a little, what had formerly tormented his eyes will be transformed into delight.

The willing, indeed, is present with you, as you say, but you do not find the power to accomplish it [Note: [Col. 0033] Rom. 7]. For if you wish to cast off the burden of ingrained old habits, that task lies before you. Follow him whom you had vowed to follow, and he himself will mercifully and effectually breathe favour upon your vows. “Come to me, all you who labour and are burdened, and I will refresh you,” says the Lord [Note: [Col. 0033] Matt. 11]. Begin, I beg you, and the Lord will prosper your beginning:

> He who has begun well has half the work done.  
> [Note: [Col. 0033] Horace, *Epistles* I.2.40.]

[Col. 0033D] If that terror of the night, which is accustomed to steal in during the first stages of holy living, should tempt you, the Lord will provide you, even with the temptation, a way of escape [Note: [Col. 0033] 1 Cor. 10]. “The life of man upon earth is temptation” [Note: [Col. 0033] Job 7, according to the LXX]; and therefore, if you intend to serve him for whom service is kingship, you will not be wholly exempt from temptation. For Wisdom says: “My son, when you come to the service of God, stand in righteousness and fear, and prepare your soul for temptation.” Yet as fire tests gold, so temptation tests a man. Temptation, when God’s grace goes before it, will make you stronger in adversity and watchful in dangers.

Therefore, brother, I beg you, undertake and enter upon the way of life, you who until now have walked by the way of death. You see that there is nothing but crushing sorrow and misery in our ways, and that everything under the sun is labour and affliction of spirit. The course of this present life is smoke and vapour appearing for a little while [Note: [Col. 0033] Jas. 4]. I know that your parents draw you back from the better purpose. Let not the treacherous and seductive affection of kinship delay, I beg you, or frustrate the purpose of your conversion. Do not love against Christ those whom you are bound to hate for Christ’s sake. Many have lost their souls for the sake of their parents; through them the world, which had withered within them, grows green again, and they seek for others the riches and other hindrances to salvation from which they had unburdened themselves, as though they believed beneficial to others what they had certainly learned to be harmful to themselves. Is what is damnable for one wholesome for another? Are the pleasures of the living comforts to the dead?

[Col. 0034B] He is impious who is cruel to his own soul for the sake of his parents; and no one has greater rashness than one who thus perilously lays down his soul for his friends [Note: [Col. 0033] John 15]. You who chose to dwell humbly and to be lowly in the house of the Lord, how do you again glory in things tending to the prejudice of everlasting shame? The glory of the world, false and deceiving, misleads its lovers. Whatever it promises for the future or displays in the present will all come to nothing, like running water. Do not yield to foolish flesh, which drags both itself and you into the lake of Gehenna, [Col. 0034C] as is read of Zimri, who gave both himself and the royal house to burning and to be consumed by fire.

We carry our enemy about with us; and, in Solomon’s words: “Guard the gates of your mouth from her who sleeps in your bosom” [Note: [Col. 0033] Mic. 7]. No plague is more effective in doing harm than a familiar and domestic enemy. This is fire in the lap, a serpent in the bosom; this is a contentious man’s wife—our own most wretched flesh. Although it is tormented by pains, filled with delusions, stained with filth, afflicted with infirmities, subject to passions, worn down by scourges, beaten with blows, and finally appointed to death, yet it still bristles with the stings of resistance: rebellious, proud, murmuring, complaining, obstinate, restless; it conspires for its own destruction and that of the soul. Nor does it think itself satisfied until it has hurled itself and the soul [Col. 0034D] into the abyss of eternal damnation.

Why does most unhappy flesh not consider what noble and necessary guest it possesses, by whose benefits it is sustained, governed, and honoured? Whatever it hears, sees, feels, understands, says, or does, it owes entirely to its guest. Deprived of that guest’s aid, it would become like earth without water: an unclean corpse, food for worms, corruption of the air. “Its iniquity was found unto hatred” [Note: [Col. 0033] Ps. 35], since it wickedly hates that which it ought to have loved with all its inward being. It hates, I say; for “he who loves iniquity hates [Col. 0035A] his own soul” [Note: [Col. 0035] Ps. 10].

Return to your heart, I beg you, dearest friend, and do not follow where foolish flesh has dragged you. It is blind, and if it leads you, it will roll you down with itself into the pit of death. You know what you have done; for, to use Solomon’s words: “You have struck your hand with a stranger; you are ensnared by the words of your mouth and caught by your own sayings” [Note: [Col. 0035] Prov. 6]. You are angry with me because I so insistently invite you onto the stricter way of life—a way which, as you maintain, I myself stubbornly flee and avoid. Certainly my situation differs: I have never bound myself by the obligation of any vow. I judge yours otherwise, since you have solemnly made a vow of a holier purpose. For it is written: “Make vows and fulfil them” [Note: [Col. 0035] Ps. 75]. You have turned your free choice into necessity, and you can no longer reject or delay your conversion without danger to your soul and injury to your reputation.

[Col. 0035B] For he demands what has been offered, though he did not demand that it be offered. To postpone a vow is nothing other than to indulge oneself wantonly against Christ. The Lord does not accept the promise except for the sake of its fulfilment. Act more quickly, then, lest unexpected death forestall the execution of your vow. Leave the world before you are left by the world. Go forth from the land of unlikeness; from the midst of a crooked and perverse generation; from darkness into light; from misery into joy; from toil into rest; from exile into your homeland; from death into life. I beg you, be readier to provide for your salvation, lest you only begin to wish to fear when you are unable to do so. He who abandons opportunity is fled by opportunity. Perhaps your wrinkles already bear testimony against you.

[Col. 0035C] The eleventh hour presses upon you, and the Lord invites you to work. If you do not wish to work while you can, then by God’s just judgement you will not be able when you wish to. See how, in this valley of tears, a dark cloud envelops almost all of us, where we have become a sad and tearful spectacle to God and his angels [Note: [Col. 0035] 1 Cor. 4]. Some, led by a spirit of dizziness, walk stumbling and collide with others wandering astray [lacuna].

Others grasp at clouds and vanities. Some wallow voluptuously in muddy and foul places. Others, in the desires of their souls, choose death for themselves. Others swallow the wind. Others gather into a pierced sack. Others devour most greedily whatever they seize. Others gather burning coals into their bosom. Others are submerged in the deep, [Col. 0035D] “whose end is destruction.” Others, emerging from the mist, breathe freely in the pleasant air, saying with jubilation: “Blessed be God, who has not given us into the pit of destruction” [Note: [Col. 0035] Ps. 54], “who brought us out of the pit of misery and the mire of dregs” [Note: [Col. 0035] Ps. 39].

Go forth, I beg you, from darkness into light, from labour into rest, from perdition into salvation. Take up the weapons of holiness, the exercise of divine soldiery, the pursuit of discipline, the most peaceable fruit of righteousness, and the first-fruits of eternal blessedness. Your days have passed, and it is dreadful to fall [Col. 0036A] into the hands of the living God [Note: [Col. 0035] Heb. 10], to lose life that does not fail, and knowingly to entangle yourself in everlasting pains.

## LETTER XII. TO A CERTAIN NEPHEW OF HIS

**SUMMARY.**—He consoles his nephew, who is grieving excessively over his uncle’s death, the burning of his house, and an injury to his foot; and he argues that the afflictions of this life are signs of God’s love toward us, and that the world is so vain that one who has departed from it through death ought least of all to be mourned.

I share with sympathetic feeling the misfortune that you lament; for it is right that I, who was your friend in prosperity, should profess friendship in adversity. Sudden death has snatched away your uncle from us. If he could be redeemed by tears, almost all Orléans [Col. 0036B] would dissolve into tears. Yet, since the loss caused by death admits no benefit of restoration, apply at least that consolation which both propriety requires and affection dictates. I loved your uncle most intimately; I appoint you heir to that intimacy and affection. Death has taken your uncle from you; but love is strong as death [Note: [Col. 0035] Song 8], and in me has restored an uncle to you. If opportunity offers me material for your advancement, love shall be stronger with me than death, and favour than nature.

Yet I cannot bear calmly that you grieve inconsolably, and that, in addition to the pain of your wounds, you complain that the Lord has added [Note: [Col. 0035] Ps. 68] the accidental twisting of your foot and the burning of your house. In these matters divine mercy has given you proof of its most certain love. For “whom God loves he corrects; and he scourges every son whom he receives” [Note: [Col. 0035] Heb. 12]. The blows of the just and merciful God are sweeter than the words of a flatterer. “Let the righteous man correct me,” says the prophet, “in mercy, and rebuke me; but let not the oil of the sinner anoint my head” [Note: [Col. 0035] Ps. 140].

If the Lord has struck and bruised your foot, he is the one “who raises up those cast down” [Note: [Col. 0035] Ps. 144], who heals all their wounds [Note: [Col. 0035] Ps. 146]. Since we are all children of wrath [Note: [Col. 0035] Eph. 2], why do you complain of the scourge of mercy in Christ? “When his wrath has blazed briefly” [Note: [Col. 0035] Ps. 2], who knows whether God may turn and forgive, and leave a blessing behind him? [Note: [Col. 0035] Joel 2]. God does not forget to show mercy [Note: [Col. 0035] Ps. 93], but even in anger [Col. 0036D] remembers mercy [Note: [Col. 0035] Hab. 3]. If you bear his scourge with equanimity, wrath will pass into grace, and “according to the multitude of sorrows in your heart, his consolations will gladden your soul” [Note: [Col. 0035] Ps. 93].

Perhaps he punishes you in time so that a temporal punishment may redeem you from the fires of eternal death. In the building of the Temple all stones were first struck with hammers, so that no sound of hammer might be heard when they were put in place [Note: [Col. 0035] 1 Kgs. 6]. So too living stones, which are to be set in that heavenly Jerusalem, “built as a city” [Note: [Col. 0035] Ps. 121], [Col. 0037A] are first polished by the varied hammerings of misfortune [Note: [Col. 0037] A most fitting allegory. Thus in the hymn for the feast of the Dedication of a Church: “Stones polished by hammerings and pressures,” etc.] before they are placed in the structure of the heavenly dwelling. Nor is grain stored in the Lord’s granary until it has been beaten out by flails or the feet of threshers.

But concerning your uncle’s death, you should have great cause for consolation: he lived with the greatest innocence, did nothing in the world in a worldly manner, and exchanged transient days for eternal ones. He “entered into the powers of the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0037] Ps. 70] and into the treasuries of imperishable glory; “his place has been made in peace” [Note: [Col. 0037] Ps. 75]. We, dragging out a wretched life in toil and misery, have been made a reproach and derision to those who dwell in the city of the Lord of hosts [Note: [Col. 0037] Ps. 47].

Have we not become a spectacle to those citizens of Jerusalem, “whose participation is in the same” [Col. 0037B] [Note: [Col. 0037] Ps. 121], whose communion is in the bond of love and unanimity in virtues, while our whole manner of life tends now in one direction, now another, and in all its actions disagrees wholly not only with our neighbours but even with itself? Consider each person’s judgments, pursuits, vows, counsels, duties, sayings, and deserts, and you will see everything confused in a kind of variegated and conflicting diversity.

Some who could live without any danger or labour embrace certain dangers of death and unbearable labours in order to live. Some, in Tantalus-like fashion, thirst amid waters, while amid abundance they afflict themselves with hunger. Some have bound themselves by a vow of continence and, as the prophet says, neigh after other men’s wives like stallions let loose [Note: [Col. 0037] Jer. 5]. Some, after gathering infinite wealth, think they have gathered nothing. Some anxiously seek, yet cannot discover how the small property they possess may be spent. Some pursue honours but cannot attain them. Some flee honours and are dragged to them unwillingly. Some despise human praise and are praiseworthy in this. Some hunt after worldly fame at all times and are infamous at all times. Some seek rest through labours. Some cannot find rest even in rest. Some are honourable in others’ eyes but become contemptible in their own. Some trust a flattering tongue more than their own conscience. Some magnify themselves through tyrannical usurpation. Some make themselves low through their kindness.

[Col. 0037D] Some tremble where there is no fear [Note: [Col. 0037] Ps. 13]. Some are secure amid the most certain danger of death. Some do not rest until they obtain the thing they have desired; once they have it, they judge it cheap and contemptible. Some, having obtained what they did not desire, conceive in it an inestimable pleasure. Some live simply and prosper in everything. Some deal in deceits, and everything opposes them. Some live as they please and are always vigorous. Some do not depart from the rules of Hippocrates and are continually ill. Some feign folly wisely. Some, by excessive wisdom, become foolish. Some spring from the bosom of philosophy to arms. Some, leaving cloistered or scholarly repose, wear themselves out with daily bodily toil. Some glory in disputes and contradictions. Some are tortured if they must dispute. Some are exceedingly cautious in trivial matters, but in difficult and serious affairs requiring mature counsel are utterly unadvised. Some are burdensome to their friends and household, yet humbly honour their enemies. Some who profess the truest friendship persecute their enemies with the greatest severity. Some humble themselves proudly. Some exalt themselves humbly.

[Col. 0038B] Some are pleasing in their lies. Some always labour to be most truthful and are thought most deceitful. Some always postpone what it is not expedient to postpone, and rush headlong precisely where a matter needed sounder counsel. Some, conspiring toward the ruin of their souls, make their bodies the object of luxurious care. Some, zealously seeking the soul’s salvation, spare not their miserable and afflicted bodies. Some never think of tomorrow. Some direct the eyes of providence toward the future in all things. Some increase Christ’s patrimony from their own. Some follow Christ in poverty in order to store up Christ’s patrimony for their nephews. Some are inwardly simple and outwardly stern, thereby fostering a social bond among brothers. Some are outwardly gentle but inwardly murmur, thereby unsewing the unity of brotherly fellowship. Some, when angry, rage for an hour. Some cover and hide injuries for a time beneath a dissembling expression. Some weep under pretended laughter. Some rejoice under the hypocrisy of mourning. Ambition leads some to ruinous honours. Some count honours as nothing without profit. Some prefer always to give to the ungrateful. Some prefer to lend to debtors who will never repay a loan. Some turn over every book and learn nothing; and some promise everything but do not fulfil their promises. Some do everything imprudently, and it succeeds for them as they wish. Some arrange everything prudently, [Col. 0038D] and it always turns out contrary for them.

Some are magnified by their nobility; others are humbled by it. Sometimes a fool is more acceptable to princes because he is low-born than a nobleman because he is wise. Some shake off all care entirely. Some involve themselves inadequately not only in their own affairs but also in those of others. Some order everything by another’s counsel. Some follow the judgement of their own will in all things. Difficult affairs never trouble some; others anxiously torment themselves even over trifles. Some empty themselves in order to spare others expense. Some are lavish with another’s goods but miserly with their own. Some, though quite poor, make and sew many garments. Others, worse still, begin many buildings and do not finish them. Some eat in order to fast. Some fast in order to eat.

And why should I range over everything? “Though I speak with the tongues of men or of angels” [Note: [Col. 0039] 1 Cor. 13], I cannot recount the discordances of those dwelling in this land of unlikeness, since each person not only disagrees with his neighbours but is at variance with himself. Rejoice, then, that your uncle has been snatched away from this evil world, lest wickedness should change his understanding [Note: [Col. 0039] Wis. 1]. He has been brought out of the world, [Col. 0039B] of whom the world was not worthy [Note: [Col. 0039] Phil. 2]. He has been taken from the midst of a crooked and perverse generation, that he may dwell in the splendours of the saints, where the harmony of virtues brings all things into peace and concord, where the condition of life is unchanging and joy everlasting.

Do not murmur, then, over the burning of your house or the twisting of your foot. For if you imitate the gifts of soul in which your uncle excelled, your foot “will stand in a straight place” [Note: [Col. 0039] Ps. 25], and the Lord will be “a lamp to your feet” [Note: [Col. 0039] Ps. 118]. Thus he will lead you upon the paths of righteousness [Note: [Col. 0039] 2 Cor. 5], so that in exchange for a fragile house you may have in heaven a house not made with hands: wholesome, pleasant, incomparably beautiful, and eternal. Send me the verses and light pieces which I wrote at Tours; and know that, once they have been copied out here, you will receive the same again without any delay.

## LETTER XIII. TO A NOVICE MONK

**SUMMARY.**—He rebukes a novice monk who, before the proper time, desires a priory—that is, freedom to leave the monastery and authority to preach God’s word. He warns that a novice monk ought rather to be taught than to teach, to be subject rather than to preside, and to remain hidden rather than appear in public.

I had set a guard and watch over my mouth, but I am compelled to relax it into words of bitterness, since you, a novice and cloistered monk, desire a priory. You say that in the parish of the priory which you seek, you would win many people for God. I am doubtful about your gain, but certain of your ruin. For what is it for a cloistered monk to return to the world except for an inhabitant of heaven [Col. 0039D] to fall into hell? You wish to preside before you have learned to be subject or to live with others, and you anticipate office before discipline.

This order is perverse: before you teach, it is fitting that you be taught. The Apostle, instructing Timothy what kind of person he ought to choose for the ministry of God’s word, says: “Not a novice, lest perhaps, suddenly lifted up, he fall into pride and into the temptation of the devil” [Note: [Col. 0039] 1 Tim. 3]. It is dangerous for novices, not yet firm in holy religion, to go out in public and usurp the offices of the perfect. For that son of the Shunammite woman, because while still [Col. 0040A] tender and little he went out to the reapers, returned to his mother crying, “My head aches,” and died [Note: [Col. 0039] 2 Kgs. 4]. Dinah, Jacob’s daughter, would have escaped the violence of Shechem, her ravisher, if she had not gone out in public [Note: [Col. 0039] Gen. 34]. It is counted among Jacob’s gentleness that he stayed at home, while Esau, fierce and hairy, hunted abroad [Note: [Col. 0039] Gen. 25].

Would that your desire were to grow accustomed to the Lord’s yoke and to sit in the cloister, especially while youth is still in its course! For Wisdom testifies: “It is good for a man when he has borne the Lord’s yoke from his youth. He shall sit alone and keep silence; for he shall raise himself above himself” [Note: [Col. 0039] Lam. 3]. But the impulses of man, as Scripture says [Note: [Col. 0039] Gen. 8], incline toward evil from youth. Embrace, therefore, the Lord’s yoke and delight in his bonds: for the Lord’s yoke [Col. 0040B] is sweet and his burden light [Note: [Col. 0039] Matt. 11]. Of Wisdom it is written: “Put your foot into her fetters, and do not be weary of her chains” [Note: [Col. 0039] Sir. 6].

Having once entered the cloister, you have shut yourself in and bound yourself in Christ’s bonds. You have indeed shut and bound yourself by the yoke of obedience, the enclosure of the order, observance of discipline, and the bond of fear and reverence. That enclosure had been cast aside by the man of whom Solomon sings reproachfully, saying: “I passed by the field of a slothful man and by the vineyard of a fool, and nettles and thorns had filled it all, and its stone wall was destroyed” [Note: [Col. 0039] Prov. 24]. I know, indeed, that you are a scholar and brought some scholarly learning with you into the cloister. Yet do not suppose that you possess God’s Spirit until Moses’ dragon [Col. 0040C] devours Pharaoh’s dragons [Note: [Col. 0039] Exod. 7], until the knowledge of charity empties out the knowledge of vanity.

You are still a novice and do not know how you ought to labour in the Lord’s husbandry. For it is written in the law of the Lord: “You shall not plough with the firstborn of an ox” [Note: [Col. 0039] Deut. 15]. You read in Leviticus [Note: [Col. 0039] ch. 2]: “If you offer to the Lord a gift of the first-fruits of your crops, from ears still green, you shall roast them with fire and crush them after the manner of meal.” In this the life of novices is plainly represented: their minds, still burdened and swollen with the moisture of fleshly desires, are not accepted in the Lord’s sacrifice until first roasted by the fire of tribulation; nor do they lay aside the chaff of former impulses unless they are crushed by labour and abstinence.

The saying of Ecclesiasticus is [Note: [Col. 0039] ch. 4]: “Do not thrust yourself into the crowd, nor bind upon yourself [Col. 0040D] double sins.” This is what some do who assume the office of teacher without sufficient merit. As you assert, charity compels you toward teaching; whom do you think you are deceiving? The Apostle, speaking to the Corinthians, says: “Charity is not ambitious; it does not act wrongly” [Note: [Col. 0039] 1 Cor. 13]. But we know that you act wrongly, and blind ambition drives you to this. “If a serpent strikes the enchanter, who will heal him?” [Note: [Col. 0039] Sir. 12]. The keys of the kingdom of heaven were not entrusted to the Prince of the Apostles [Note: [Col. 0039] Matt. 16] until he had been tested by a threefold confession of faith.

Would that the Lord might stir your spirit, [Col. 0041A] he who stirred the spirit of the younger boy for Susanna’s deliverance [Note: [Col. 0041] Dan. 13]. He is also said to have stirred the spirit of Othniel [Note: [Col. 0041] Judg. 3], the spirit of Deborah [Note: [Col. 0041] Judg. 4], the spirit of Gideon [Note: [Col. 0041] Judg. 6], and of all the others through whose ministry he effected his people’s deliverance. I do not know whether perhaps you say with the Apostle that you learned the Gospel not from man but from God alone. Would that you knew that “he who takes the sword shall perish by the sword” [Note: [Col. 0041] Matt. 26]! For one who unworthily presumes upon the word of preaching kills himself.

Imperial law does not admit a person under twenty-five years of age to the office of guardian. Nor are the heavens opened to Ezekiel [Note: [Col. 0041] ch. 1] until he completes his thirtieth year, so that he may understand the visions of God; nor is Moses [Note: [Col. 0041] Exod. 7] sent to deliver the people from Egypt until he has passed seventy years. I am grieved that you desire a priory; [Col. 0041B] yet you would obtain a priory easily if you desired to be last. He who alone raises the poor from the dust teaches us, in the school of evangelical discipline, not to seek prelacy. You burn with the desire to shine for others: would that you burned with a burning desire not to shine! “John,” says Christ, “was a burning and shining lamp” [Note: [Col. 0041] John 5]. Let it suffice you to burn in the cloister. For if you wish to shine before men, I fear lest the light that is in you be darkness [Note: [Col. 0041] Luke 11]. For those who please men “have been put to shame, because God has despised them” [Note: [Col. 0041] Ps. 52]. It is good to burn, but with the fire of charity, not vanity. “I came,” says the Lord, “to cast fire upon the earth; and what do I wish but that it should burn?” [Note: [Col. 0041] Luke 12]. He indeed burned and shone of whom, by Truth’s testimony, no one greater among those born of women had arisen [Note: [Col. 0041] Luke 7].

But you, [Col. 0041C] so long as you are under the bushel, can burn and shine, but for few; to shine publicly, however, is not granted you until you are set upon the lampstand. Therefore wait meanwhile, and burn wisely. For the reprobate also burns, but like fire among thorns [Note: [Col. 0041] Ps. 117]. And the wicked, as is read, “burned in their lusts” [Note: [Col. 0041] Dan. 13]. If you wish to leave the cloister in order to gain freedom, you stray and wander from the way: for in withdrawing from the cloister, you move far from God. Nor can I see you freer than if, for Christ’s sake, you undertake and fulfil cloistered servitude. You make yourself most free if you serve from the heart him for whom service is kingship.

You say that if you had a priory, or at least free permission to go out and preach, you would produce timely fruit in God’s Church. You would indeed—were it not that the world has already sold you by Judas’s [Col. 0041D] treacherous kiss; and while it enticed you with a deceitful kiss, it said to Satan’s angels: “Whomever I shall kiss, that is he; seize him” [Note: [Col. 0041] Matt. 26]. For they now hold you in their grasp and compel you to desire what you voluntarily renounced. I fear that, having begun in the Spirit, you may be brought to completion in the flesh [Note: [Col. 0041] Gal. 3].

You renounced the world [Col. 0042A] and its pomps, and spiritually overthrew Jericho within yourself. You know that Joshua’s curse still endures: “Cursed is he who rebuilds Jericho” [Note: [Col. 0041] Josh. 6]. It does not befit a professed member of the monastic order to return to the world. If you desire to preach and teach, first be taught what you ought to teach. You still have the office of one who mourns, not of one who teaches. Moreover, certain persons have gone out from your house under the pretext of instructing others and converting them to a purpose of holier life, and through them your house has been scandalized. The Lord flatters no one. “Woe to the man through whom scandal comes” [Note: [Col. 0041] Matt. 18]. “Woe to you,” says Christ, “who traverse sea and land to make one proselyte” [Note: [Col. 0041] Matt. 23]. “These are they,” says the Apostle, “who enter houses and lead captive little women burdened with sins” [Note: [Col. 0041] 2 Tim. 3].

Certainly, in the cloister you can [Col. 0042B] read, write, and teach. Wisdom says: “Write wisdom in leisure, and he whose activity is diminished shall receive it” [Note: [Col. 0041] Sir. 38]. Paul too wrote while in chains and built others up toward salvation [Note: [Col. 0041] Eph. 6]. Jeremiah, shut in prison, writes and commands Baruch to read the Lord’s threats [Note: [Col. 0041] Jer. 38]. Love the cloister, I beg you, and cut from your mind the desire to go out. For in my considered judgment, if paradise exists in this present life, it is either in the cloister or in the schools. Whatever lies outside these two is full of anxiety, restlessness, bitterness, fear, care, and pain.

But you have dreamed, I do not know what sweetness of the world within the cloister; if perhaps through folly you obtain it, it will fly away like a dream, and amid the frivolous blessednesses for which you sigh you will find [Col. 0042C] yourself deceived. That false and seductive pleasure of roaming abroad will consume the fruits of cloistered innocence; and what you now consider honourable and profitable will turn into injury to your reputation and danger to your soul.

## LETTER XIV  
[Note: [Col. 0041] This letter, though elegant, is absent from certain manuscript codices.]

### TO THE COURT CHAPLAINS OF THE KING OF ENGLAND

**SUMMARY.**—He acknowledges that, through the benefit of a severe illness, he came to recognize the perils of courtly life. He describes at length its many vanities and troubles. He says that more learned clerics are inexcusable before God if they pursue courts, and exhorts the chaplains to whom he writes to abandon them by his example.

To his beloved lords and all his clerical friends of the chapel of the lord king: Peter of Blois, archdeacon of Bath [Col. 0042D], greeting in the true source of salvation.

I thank your graciousness as much as I can, because, for as long as I lived among you, you treated me with brotherly affection; and grace did no less for me among you than, among others, either the long-standing condition of being nursed or nature itself. Whenever we rode, you were a lamp to my feet; you served me as a conveyance on the road [Col. 0043A]. But when our beasts were granted a Sabbath—for I have not seen men keeping Sabbath at court, and therefore in that respect the beasts are better off—that weariness which often afflicts courtiers was stolen away from me by your most delightful conversations. You were my comfort and rejoicing on the road, in the chamber, and in the chapel.

Led, indeed, by a certain spirit of ambition, I had plunged my whole self into the waves of secular affairs; casting God, his Church, and my own order behind my back, I anxiously considered not how great were the things the Lord had done for me, but how great the riches I might amass for myself. Forgetting, therefore, the things behind, I stretched myself toward those ahead—but not in the Apostle’s manner [Note: [Col. 0043] Phil. 3]. Yet the Lord chastened me sorely, but did not give me over to death [Note: [Col. 0043] Ps. 117]: afflicting me upon a bed of pain, he poured the spirit of his indignation into a small, abject, and wretched body [Col. 0043B]. I was distressed unto death, and the separation of body and soul was now most certainly imminent. But the Father of mercies, understanding that affliction would give me understanding, remembered mercy in anger [Note: [Col. 0043] Hab. 3]; and at once restrained the spirit of his wrath and breathed the spirit of ambition out of me.

Certainly, I had often read Solomon’s saying: “To go from lodging to lodging is a most wretched life” [Note: [Col. 0043] Ecclus. 29]; and I knew that courtly life is death to the soul. I recalled that it is blameworthy for a cleric to entangle himself in courtly or secular business. Nor had that saying of Ecclesiasticus, which ought to have drawn me and men like me away from courtly anxieties, slipped from my memory: “Do not seek guidance from a man, nor a seat of honour from a king; do not parade yourself as wise before the king. Do not seek to become a judge unless you are strong enough to break through the iniquities of the people. Do not thrust yourself into the multitude of the city, nor bind double sins upon yourself” [Note: [Col. 0043] Ecclus. 7].

Yet ambition had so intoxicated me, and the flattering promises of the prince had so overthrown me, that, knowingly and deliberately, I seemed stubbornly to have conspired toward every danger to my soul and ruin to my body. Nevertheless, recognizing in the Lord’s scourge the grace of paternal correction, I meditated by night with my heart; I exercised myself and searched my spirit [Note: [Col. 0043] Ps. 76]. Thus I resolved to leave and renounce the cloak with Joseph [Note: [Col. 0043] Gen. 39], the tax-office with Matthew [Note: [Col. 0043] Matt. 9], the linen cloth with John [Note: [Col. 0043] Mark 14], and the water-jar of desire with the Samaritan woman [Note: [Col. 0043] John 4] [Col. 0043D]. The Lord heard me, and the dew of divine mercy extinguished the ardour of ambition which torrents of gold and silver had previously been unable to moderate within me. “Confirm, O God, what you have wrought in me” [Note: [Col. 0043] Ps. 67]; do not allow me to return to my vomit, nor ever to rebuild Jericho, which I have destroyed [Note: [Col. 0043] Josh. 6].

I, most rotten dust, soon to be scattered upon the winds by a slight breath—why did I gasp after greater riches? My little belly [Col. 0044A] is satisfied each day with one small loaf; and the Lord had given me means by which, every day, with cheerfulness of mind and bodily repose, I could feed many bellies. Was I, miserable man, bound to hunt and go hungry in camps, to the destruction of my soul and body, in order to feed a multitude of beasts and men? Is it a man’s glory to feed both men and beasts, while fasting from God’s word and the food of the soul? “Food is for the belly, and the belly for foods,” says the Apostle; “but God will destroy both it and them” [Note: [Col. 0043] 1 Cor. 6]. But the bread of life will endure for ever [Note: [Col. 0043] John 6].

Indeed, the retainers, in whose numerous multitude great men especially boast, are the hunters and fowlers of their own lords: they follow prey, not men. This is very clearly shown by the fact that [Col. 0044B] the great number of retainers did not follow those whom kinder fortune raised to riches and honours while they were still poor, nor would follow them now if they fell again into like poverty. For this utterly vain vanity our courtiers now serve amid toil and misery, in many watchings, in great perils—perils of sea, perils of rivers, perils of bridges, perils of mountains, perils among false brethren [Note: [Col. 0043] 2 Cor. 11]—frequently at the risk of death, amid bodily breaking and weariness, and in other dangers of life. In these they would deserve the glory of martyrdom if they endured them for Christ’s name. But now they are martyrs of the age, professors of the world, disciples of the court, soldiers of Herlewin.

“For through many tribulations the righteous enter the kingdom of heaven” [Note: [Col. 0043] Acts 14]; but these, through many tribulations, earn hell. “Woe to you who draw the yoke of iniquity,” as the prophet recalls, “with cords of vanity” [Note: [Col. 0043] Isa. 5]. “What does it profit a man if he gain the whole world, yet suffer loss of his soul?” [Note: [Col. 0043] Matt. 16]. It would be far better to be righteous than rich, for, in Solomon’s testimony [Note: [Col. 0043] Prov. 11], “Riches will not profit in the time of vengeance”; for when the rich man perishes, he will not take everything with him, and the glory of his house will not descend with him [Note: [Col. 0043] Ps. 48]; but righteousness will deliver from death [Note: [Col. 0043] Prov. 11].

Most wretched men, when shall we enjoy in peace and gladness the goods which the grace of divine mercy has bestowed upon us beyond all the measure of our merits? We would gladly enjoy them; but Lady Ambition does not permit it [Col. 0044D], since she urges us toward greater acquisition of riches and ever opens wider gulfs. Yet, according to Solomon, “The miser will not be filled with money, and he who loves riches will not receive fruit from them” [Note: [Col. 0043] Eccl. 5]. The title of poverty is indeed lowly among men, but glorious before God and his angels.

I know that those who dwell—or rather die—at the court of the lord king are often exhilarated by hope of royal generosity, which sometimes pours itself out magnificently and lavishly upon many [Col. 0045A]. Everyone hopes that what he sees happen to many others will happen to himself. Under the comfort of this sweet and uncertain expectation, tedious things delight, burdens are lightened, bitter things become sweet; and our martyrs do not feel their labours, though weak, nor their expenses, though avaricious.

> Thus, lest he lose, the gambler never ceases from losing;  
> And flattering dice call back his eager hands.  
> [Note: [Col. 0045] Ovid, *Art of Love*, book 1.]

They seem to me, in their words and desires, to rehearse that little verse of Persius [Note: [Col. 0045] *Satires*, 2]:

> “Now it will be given—now, now!”—until, deceived and without hope,  
> No coin sighs any longer from the bottom of the purse.

Moreover, according to the wise man [Note: [Col. 0045] Seneca, *Epistle* 1], “Economy at the bottom of the purse comes too late.”

At court this is detestable: those who love more are loved less [Col. 0045B]. The unskilled and altogether useless are also enlarged by more splendid benefices; riches are piled upon the rich, and there is no one who looks to the poor and needy. Elisha filled the empty vessels, and when the empty vessels failed, the oil stopped [Note: [Col. 0045] 4 Kgs. 4]. But at court empty vessels are despised and full ones filled; wood is carried into forests and water into seas.

For my own part, I would lament the losses arising from enormous expenses, and above all the loss of wasted time, unless I counted it the greatest fruit of my labour that, through God’s grace and his own, I have always had our prince favourable, gentle, approachable, and kind. I never presented him with petitions which he did not generously receive; indeed, in many respects his benefits of kindness sometimes anticipated even the preparation of my heart [Col. 0045C]. I loved him, love him, and shall always love him with affection; nor may God love me if I desist from loving him. For his grace has perpetually claimed me as its own; and his shall always be whatever I think, whatever I write, whatever I am, whatever strength or ability I have.

For this reason, as long as I enjoyed your companionship, every day on which I did not enjoy conversation with the lord king seemed to me a sad and cloudy day; but a day on which he deigned to speak with me was wholly spent in joy, like a wedding-day. I say with the greatest confidence, and have the greater part of the world as witness, that in this respect, since the time of Charles, there has been no prince so kind, prudent, generous, and vigorous. I have touched briefly upon these things in his praise [Col. 0045D], because in these four qualities all the virtues of princes are effectively comprised.

You should also know that, for the glory and magnificence of the lord king, I have already composed in large part a book concerning his deeds, which must be communicated to your brotherhood. But the hand of the craftsman is still correcting and polishing that work, so that when it comes before the public it may not fear either the tongues of detractors or the venomous bites of envy.

Moreover, although we owe service and reverence to princes, and especially to the king, as to one who excels, according to the Apostle [Note: [Col. 0045] 1 Pet. 2], nevertheless men of our profession could serve princes more effectively in churches than in camps [Col. 0046A]. I do not consider it absurd if simpler men, less trained in Holy Scripture, purpose to serve in the service of royal majesty.

But a man established in sacred orders and strong in sacred eloquence—who is now bound to send his springs forth abroad and return to the Lord with profit the talent entrusted to him by the Lord—is altogether inexcusable if he involves himself in secular business and entangles himself in courtly bonds. Hear what the Lord says of such men through the prophet: “I gave them,” he says, [Col. 0046B] “my silver and gold; but they made Baal from my gold and silver” [Note: [Col. 0045] Hos. 2]. Do not those for whom God has given wisdom and eloquence in order to give knowledge of salvation to his people [Note: [Col. 0045] Luke 1] fashion Baal out of the Lord’s gold and silver? Yet they bury the Lord’s talent in the earth and construct Baal, while for the profit of temporal things they stake life and soul as if in a throw of dice.

These establish the ark of the Lord at Ashdod [Note: [Col. 0045] 1 Sam. 5], which is interpreted “the fire of desire,” because through ambitious desire they make void the glory of our profession. The Lord turns their rivers into blood, so that they cannot drink; and gives them iron earth and brazen heaven, so that, deprived of heavenly rain, they may produce no fruit of life [Note: [Col. 0045] Deut. 28]. They perish knowingly and deliberately, because the Lord has mingled among them [Col. 0046C] a spirit of dizziness [Note: [Col. 0045] Isa. 19]; and the wise king, the winnower of the ungodly, brings the wheel of evils upon them.

Men of ruined life torment themselves with labours, torture themselves with cares, disembowel themselves with expenses. Do they not bear the image of the spider, which weaves a web from its own entrails in order to catch a most worthless fly? What is the empty glory they hunt but a most worthless fly—buzzing, filthy, and stinging? Some, pleading an excuse in sins and putting forward the loincloths of the old Adam [Note: [Col. 0045] Gen. 3], when asked why they follow the court—which they do not doubt is opposed to God and their salvation—introduce examples from ancient times to colour and defend their ambition. “They were sent,” they say, “for the correction and instruction of kings: Moses to Pharaoh [Note: [Col. 0045] Exod. 3], Jeremiah to Zedekiah [Note: [Col. 0045] Jer. 33], Elijah to Ahab [Note: [Col. 0045] 3 Kgs. 18], Jehoiada to Josiah.”

O courtly cleric, did the Lord send you to the king? Did he send you into his service, or rather did ambition force its way in? Certainly, after the signs in the bush, the serpent, and the leprous hand [Note: [Col. 0045] Exod. 3], Moses excuses himself from the commission laid upon him [Note: [Col. 0045] Exod. 4]. If even an impossible mission is laid upon you by the king, you offer yourself freely, boast great things, and promise greater. Nothing seems burdensome to a willing mind, nothing difficult to the ambitious. Therefore [Col. 0047A] ambition is a kind of ape of charity. For charity is patient [Note: [Col. 0047] 1 Cor. 13] for eternal things; ambition endures everything for perishable things. Charity is kind to the poor; ambition, to the rich. Charity bears all things for truth; ambition, for vanity. Both believe all things and hope all things, but in vastly different ways: the latter for the glory of this life, the former for glory without end. For glowing gold behaves one way in fire, smoking straw another. Charity never fails; ambition never rises. For ambition itself is wickedness upon a talent of lead. This is the eye of all courtiers, as Zechariah says [Note: [Col. 0047] ch. 5]. This is their eye throughout the whole earth—not the right eye, but the left.

For all who serve in the camp of ambition have been captured by Nahash the Ammonite and have lost their right eyes [Col. 0047B] [Note: [Col. 0047] 1 Sam. 1]. They are sharp-sighted in acquiring temporal things, but do not consider the loss of the life that is passing, or the imminent punishments of eternal death. They are blind to good, but clear-sighted in evil. “They are wise,” says the prophet, “to do evil; but they do not know how to do good” [Note: [Col. 0047] Jer. 4]. They themselves, however, are scattered like stones of the sanctuary at the head of every street [Note: [Col. 0047] Lam. 4]. They devote all that they know, say, and do to acquiring temporal things.

I especially wonder about one thing: how can a courtier endure such troubles when he has long been accustomed to scholarly service and the camps of discipline? I return to courtiers: among them there is no order, reason, or measure in eating, riding, and watching [Col. 0047C]. A cleric or knight at court is served bread that is neither properly worked nor leavened, made from beer dregs: leaden bread, weedy and raw; while the wine is spoiled either by sourness or mould, cloudy, greasy, rancid, pitch-flavoured, and flat. I have sometimes seen wine set before magnates so full of dregs that it had to be strained rather than drunk, and then only with eyes shut, teeth clenched, horror, and grimacing. The beer drunk at court is horrible to taste and abominable to behold.

At court, because of the crowds, animals both healthy and diseased are indiscriminately sold, as are fish already four days old [Col. 0047D]; yet rot or stench does not reduce the price at all [Col. 0048A]. For the servants do not care about the death or illness of their unhappy guests, provided their lords’ tables are served with fuller dishes. Bellies are filled with carrion and become the tombs of many dead things eaten at table. Many would also die more often from the corruption of such foods, were not the hungry greed of the belly and the Scylla-like gulf of that destructive abyss to consume everything with the help of strenuous exercise. Hence, if they are allowed to remain for any length of time in one town, some of them always lie near death.

I cannot bear to relate the other hardships, especially those of the marshals.

[Note: [Col. 0047D] *Mareschallus* is an extremely common word, especially among writers on English affairs. William Somner thus explains it in his *Glossary*: “*Mareschallus* is derived from the old word *mare*, which means ‘horse,’ and *schal*, that is, ‘servant.’ For, they say, it was once the name of a low office, meaning the keeper or servant of horses. Afterwards it became the title of an eminent dignity. For thus they called the person whom the Latins otherwise called *comes stabuli*, master or prefect of the horses, in Greek πρωτοστράτωρ, ‘chief master of the horse.’ See Cassiodorus, book 6 of the *Variae*; P. Gregory, book 6 of the *Syntagma*, ch. 8; Hotman, commentary on *De verbis feudalibus*; and Gerard Vossius.”]

These men are the most flattering of flatterers, the worst slanderers, the most shameless extortioners. They are most importunate until they receive something [Col. 0048B]; once they have received it, they are ungrateful; and unless the giver keeps extending his hand, they become enemies. I have seen very many who had dealt generously with marshals, but who, after seeking lodging with great labour following the exhaustion of a long journey, were shamefully expelled by marshals arriving in arrogance and abuse. While their meals were still half-cooked, or perhaps when they had already sat down to table, or even when they were asleep in their beds, the marshals cut the horses’ halters and flung their baggage outside indiscriminately, and not without loss. Having lost everything they had brought for the comfort of night-time repose, these wretched though wealthy men had nowhere to lay their heads that night.

To the miseries of courtiers I add this: if the king promises to stay somewhere for the next day, especially if a royal proclamation has publicly announced his will, know most certainly that the king will set out very early in the morning and frustrate every man’s plan by an unexpected suddenness. Therefore it often happens that those who let blood at court [Note: [Col. 0047D] The word *sanguinem*, “blood,” is absent from Sorb. I, [Col. 0048D] Vict. II, and Vict. 3, and not improperly so; for *minuere*, “to diminish,” alone means to open a vein, φλεβοτομεῖν, “to perform bloodletting,” as appears in the ancient customs of the monastery of Cluny, compiled by St Udalric, book 2, ch. 21, where he sometimes uses only the word *minutio*, “bloodletting.” He flourished in 1080; these customs are found in the *Spicilegium* of D’Achery. Lanfranc, Archbishop of Canterbury, speaks in the same way in his *Decrees for the Order of St Benedict*, ch. 12. The usage is also frequently found in the statutes of the Carthusians.], or take medicine, neglect bodily care and follow the prince. They stake their lives as if on a throw of dice; lest they lose what they neither possess nor ever will possess, they do not fear to lose themselves. You may see men running out as if mad, pressing pack-horses [Note: [Col. 0048D] Thus Sorb. 1, Dom., and the three Victorine manuscripts read, as does the Würzburg manuscript cited by Busaeus; others have *saumarios*, as does Busaeus’s Confluentine manuscript. Nor is this wrong, although Busaeus, following Gerard [Col. 0049D] Vossius, rejected this word and proposed *sagmarios*. Nor do I see why Vossius, with Busaeus’s approval, wished to emend the word in St Bernard, book 3 of *On Consideration*, ch. 3, where it reads: “Pack-horses, not relieved of their burdens, nevertheless return home laden, even against their will,” and advised reading *sagmarii*, when all St Bernard manuscripts read *summarii*, as the most learned Dom Jean Mabillon, Benedictine, assured me; in his latest edition of St Bernard’s works he fittingly restored *summarii*. We certainly know with Vossius that σάγμα means a burden or pack-saddle to which loads are fitted, whence σαγμάριοι, “pack-carriers” or “bearers of burdens.” But we also know that *summarii* is an ancient, though non-classical, word, exceedingly common in Bernard’s age among authors who wrote especially about French and English affairs [Col. 0050D]: Matthew Paris, Ralph de Diceto, John Brompton, Gervase of Dover, and others. Nor do I deny that this word derives from Greek σάγμα, whence Latin *sauma*, later *summa*, French *une somme*; whence *saumarius* and *summarius*, French *sommier*, English *sumpter*.], and seeing four-horse carts charge against four-horse carts; everyone is thrown into tumult against everyone else, so that from the very confusion of things the appearance of hell is most plainly portrayed for you.

[Col. 0049A] But if the prince says beforehand that he will depart early tomorrow for a definite place, the plan will without doubt be changed; therefore know that he will sleep until midday. You will see pack-horses waiting under their loads, carts standing silent, outriders drowsing, court merchants anxious, and everyone muttering among themselves. Men run to court prostitutes and tavern-keepers to ask them where the prince is going. For this class of courtiers often knows the secrets of the palace. The king’s court is continually followed by entertainers, washerwomen, gamblers, confectioners, innkeepers, tricksters, mimes, barbers,

“Worthless fellows” [Note: [Col. 0050D] Busaeus says that he restored *balatrones*, because it is a Latin word used by good authors for men of no value. Yet none of our copies reads *balatrones*, but *baratrones*, which is also admitted by recent authors, such as Spelman, who says: “*Balatro* or *baratro*: ‘a scoundrel,’ says Lydius, from M. Goldast.” And Laurence of Lucca states in his *Onomasticon*, from Festus: “*Balatrones* were once called *baratrones*, as though worthy of the *barathrum*, the abyss.”]—the whole tribe of them.

We have often seen, while the king slept and all things kept [Col. 0049B] the middle silence, that “a word came from the royal seats” [Note: [Col. 0049] Wis. 18]—not an all-powerful word, but one that set everyone in motion—and named the city or town to which they were to go. After the long weariness of uncertain waiting, it was granted us as a consolation to lodge where a supply of lodgings and provisions was expected. So great, confused, and tumultuous was the rushing about of horsemen and footmen that you would think an abyss had been overturned and an eruption made from hell.

But when our outriders had already completed that day’s march, or all or nearly all of it, the king, changing his will, turned aside elsewhere, where perhaps he had a single house and an adequate supply of provisions which he shared with no one. And, if I dare say it [Col. 0049C], I believe that he increased his pleasures by means of our straits.

Thus, wandering three or four miles through unknown woods and often in darkness, we thought our wish had been fulfilled if we happened upon a dirty and worthless hut. There was very often among the courtiers a harsh and bitter quarrel over hovels; men attacked one another with swords for lodging for which it would be unworthy to contend even among pigs. I do not believe that any of you is uncertain how matters stood that night for us or our mounts. But I and my household were divided, and scarcely within three days [Col. 0050A] could I gather together those who had been scattered.

Most high almighty God, you who are King of kings and Lord of lords [Note: [Col. 0049] 1 Tim. 6], who are terrible among the kings of the earth, who take away the spirit of princes [Note: [Col. 0049] Ps. 75], who give salvation to kings [Note: [Col. 0049] Ps. 143], in whose hand is the heart of the king and who turn it wherever you will [Note: [Col. 0049] Prov. 21], turn and convert this king’s heart from this pestilential custom, so that he may know that he is one man, and may learn and become accustomed to show the grace of royal generosity and the feeling of human compassion to the men whom not ambition but necessity draws after him.

Allow me, I pray, still to bewail my sorrow a little, lest I return to the laborious court, covered with the darkness of death, where there is the shadow of death and no order [Note: [Col. 0049] Job 10]. For, to return to the court’s servants: with the outer gatekeepers a man may perhaps earn a two-day favour by manifold service [Col. 0050B], but it will not last until the third day unless it is redeemed by continuing gifts and services. They will lie that the king is asleep, ill, or in council; if you are honourable or religious, because you gave them nothing yesterday, they will compel you to stand outside for a very long time in mud and rain. And, so that they may wound your heart more unjustly with anger and more cruelly torment you, they will allow ash-stained scullions and gallows-birds to enter freely at their first word.

May the Most High confound the chamber-door keepers. They do not fear to cover the face of any worthy man with manifold confusion and shame. You have escaped terrible rods; yet if you give nothing to the doorkeeper, nothing has been achieved:

> “If you bring nothing, Homer, you will go outside.”  
> [Note: [Col. 0049] Ovid, *Art of Love*, book 2.]

After the first Cerberus, another remains for you, more horrible than Cerberus, more terrible than Briareus, more wicked than Pygmalion, more cruel than the Minotaur. Whatever necessity of death or danger of disinheritance hangs over you, you will not enter to the king. Rather, as more often happens, to distress you more severely and, so to speak,

> “that Codrus’s guts may burst”  
> [Note: [Col. 0049] Virgil, *Eclogues*, 7],

your adversary will be introduced while you are excluded.

Lord Jesus Christ, if this is how life is lived, and if such is the life and spirit of those who follow the camps, may I, I pray, never return to camps. For the loss of the years [Col. 0051A] which I spent in trifles about the court cannot be measured. I greet you and your service—lest I call it courtly wickedness. There is another service to which the Apostle, writing to Timothy, invites me: “Fight the good fight, holding faith and a pure conscience” [Note: [Col. 0051] 1 Tim. 1]. When he says “the good fight,” he plainly excludes courtly service as self-condemned, dishonourable, reprobate, ruined, and damned.

You also, dearest friends, should sometime reflect in the bitterness of your souls upon the days you have wasted in court. “It is now the hour for us to rise from sleep” [Note: [Col. 0051] Rom. 13]. “Rise after you have sat” [Note: [Col. 0051] Ps. 126], lest you “sleep in death” [Note: [Col. 0051] Ps. 12]. Life flees from us; death presses near; the enemy lies in wait to seize us, and there is no one to rescue us. Indeed, I am jealous for you with God’s jealousy [Note: [Col. 0051] 2 Cor. 11], [Col. 0051B] zealously desiring and thirsting for your salvation in the bowels of Jesus Christ. You see that the court is full of snares of death; inevitable and uncertain death, and a terrible judge, await us. It is dreadful to fall into the hands of the living God [Note: [Col. 0051] Heb. 10] and incur those torments that have neither interruption nor end.

I know that I have overthrown the spiritual Jericho, and I remember that Joshua, Moses’ successor, said: “Cursed is he who rebuilds Jericho” [Note: [Col. 0051] Josh. 6]. For I have advanced in my days, and, to use Job’s words, “My wrinkles bear witness against me” [Note: [Col. 0051] Job 16]. And again: “My short years pass away, and by the path on which I go I shall not return” [Note: [Col. 0051] ibid.]. I shall therefore reflect upon lost days in bitterness of soul, and shall devote the remainder of my years [Col. 0051C] to study and peace.

May our companions and friends fare well, and may every one of them know that I am theirs.

## LETTER XV. TO COUNT RAINALD

[Note: [Col. 0051D] Raynald—or, according to others, Reginald—of Monçon, was the son of Reginald, Count of Monçon, otherwise of Bar, and Agnes, daughter of Theobald the Great, Count of Champagne. When he was treasurer of the church of St Martin at Tours and provost of the Church of Chartres, he succeeded, about the year 1187, Peter of Celle, abbot, as bishop of Chartres, according to Souchet in his manuscript history of that same church; not John of Salisbury, as Busaeus wrote. For all agree that Peter of Celle was John of Salisbury’s successor. Thus Stephen of Tournai, writing to our Rainald and congratulating him upon his promotion to the episcopate, mentions [Col. 0052D] John and Peter as his predecessors. All historians agree, as does the Chartres necrology, which speaks thus of his virtues:

> “On the eighth day before the Kalends of August died Reginald, illustrious Count of Monçon. For his soul Reginald his son, venerable bishop of the Church of Chartres, granted to the chapter of Chartres, to possess by full right in perpetuity, the chapel of Saints Sergius and Bacchus, situated in the court of the episcopal houses, with the freedom and immunity in which he possessed it. In return for this gift it was established that the anniversaries of his father and mother, of Count Henry, and of the bishop himself when he dies, should be celebrated, and that the income of the said chapel should be distributed among the canons [Col. 0053D] who were present.”

Later, in the same source:

> “On the sixth day before the Ides of December died, in the year 1217, the venerable father of pious memory Reginald, revered bishop of this holy see, son of the illustrious Count of Monçon, most noble by the renowned lineage of the princes of France and by royal [Col. 0054D] kinship, but far nobler in generosity of spirit, and humble and kindly in heart.”]

ELECTED BISHOP OF CHARTRES. [A.D. 1178.]

### ARGUMENT

He instructs the son of Count R., elected bishop of Chartres, concerning the virtues with which a bishop ought to be adorned and the vices from which he ought to recoil.

The noble Church of Chartres has called you from subject to prelate, from son to father, from disciple to teacher. If you wish to be what you are called, so that you may be reckoned among the Lord’s elect—he who sends roots [Col. 0051D] among his chosen [Note: [Col. 0051] Ecclus. 24], and whom he chose, them he also predestined [Note: [Col. 0051] Rom. 8]—turn away from your former way of life. Putting on the new man, put off all the oldness of your former life [Col. 0052A]. When you were a child, you thought and spoke as a child; but now, because you have entered the fullness of manhood, the things of childhood must be put away [Note: [Col. 0051] 1 Cor. 13], so that your actions may have nothing childish or immature about them, but in all things you may present yourself as a man perfect in Christ.

Above all, embrace humility, so that nothing haughty may appear in you, whether in word, face, or gesture. “Your brethren have made you their leader,” says Wisdom; “be among them as one of them” [Note: [Col. 0051] Ecclus. 32]. Display no singularity; exercise no lordship. “Be not,” says the blessed Apostle Peter, “lords over the clergy, but examples made to the flock among the people” [Note: [Col. 0051] 1 Pet. 5]. He who calls those things [Col. 0052B] which are not as though they were [Note: [Col. 0051] Rom. 4] has called you to exercise priestly service for him, so that in the house of his mother you may be a faithful and prudent steward—not a master but a servant, the guardian of his possessions and advocate of his people.

The Lord has placed you to correct princes, instruct peoples, comfort the afflicted, inspire fear in wrongdoers, free clerics, humble the proud, and protect the humble. Recognize, I pray, your calling [Note: [Col. 0051] 2 Cor. 1]. For the Lord has not called you again to uncleanness, so that you may spend your days in pleasures and make provision for the flesh in its desires [Note: [Col. 0051] Rom. 13]. All such things must be banished from the mind of a future bishop, for it is written [Note: [Col. 0051] Ecclus. 43]: “The hand which washes another’s filth must be clean” [Col. 0052C].

Indeed, in Exodus we read [Note: [Col. 0051] ch. 29] that, when Moses at the Lord’s command proposed to consecrate Aaron as high priest, he first carefully washed him, clothed him with a linen tunic, and girded him with a belt. This shows that one to be consecrated bishop is first washed, so that, reformed from his former way of life into new innocence, he may receive the growth of virtues. The linen tunic signifies purity of life; it is bound with a belt so that chastity may be nourished under stricter guardianship. A hyacinth-blue robe is also put on him, so that his conduct may be heavenly [Note: [Col. 0051] Exod. 28], so that he may now speak no human words and know nothing except Christ.

The breastpiece is added upon the shoulder-garment [Note: [Col. 0051] ibid.], in which were doctrine and truth, so that he may be a scribe [Col. 0052D] learned in the kingdom of God and, when the occasion requires, [Col. 0053A] bring forth from his treasury things new and old [Note: [Col. 0053] Matt. 13]. These things are most strictly required by the office of your administration: in every respect humility that is not contemptible, dignity that is not presumptuous, must be present in you.

Today, in the promotion of some men, the first question is what the total of the revenues may be, not what the way of life of those subject to them may be. Yet God is not mocked. He called you to honour because of burdens, not to multiply the number of your household or horses; not to grant dignities to relatives, but to give knowledge of salvation to his people. There is greater joy for God and his angels if, through the office of a prelate, a sinner is converted from his evil way [Note: [Col. 0053] Luke 15], than if, through that prelate’s activity, the pomp of episcopal eminence is increased in mounts and retainers. There is no joy of angels [Col. 0053B] in that which overthrows the houses of the poor, from whom you exact burdensome procurations. They complain and say: “You have multiplied the nation, and not increased the joy” [Note: [Col. 0053] Isa. 9].

If you profess yourself a disciple of him who came to serve, not to be served [Note: [Col. 0053] Matt. 20], you will so serve the poor that your ministry is not blamed [Note: [Col. 0053] 2 Cor. 6], and that the patrimony of Christ and of his poor, entrusted to you for the necessities of the needy, is not spent on extraordinary uses.

The Lord is the guardian of this patrimony and will demand from you a most exact account [Note: [Col. 0053] Matt. 18.]; he will exact everything, down to the last farthing [Note: [Col. 0053] Matt. 5.]. Indeed, for this reason the wicked man has provoked God; for he said in his heart, “He will not require it” [Note: [Col. 0053] Ps. 9.]. Yet he certainly will require it. Nor can the eminence of your birth and the number of your retainers make you excusable [Col. 0053C]. If, because you are the son of a count or cousin of a king [Note: [Col. 0054D] Namely, Philip Augustus, king of France, whose father Louis the Younger had married Adela, sister of Agnes, the mother of Renaud himself.], you are obliged to spend with a more lavish hand, this necessity does not touch Christ’s patrimony. Episcopal moderation ought to restrain in ecclesiastical matters the expenses which, perhaps enormous because of your rank, you would otherwise have incurred from worldly resources.

You were chosen by Christ as bishop in order to exercise the priesthood for him: to render the people acceptable to the Lord, zealous for good works, instructing them by word and example [Note: [Col. 0053] Titus 2.]. Therefore, having cast off every old vanity, strive to fulfil the bishop’s office in your conduct; and, that you may offer the Holy of Holies the service of devoted worship, put on holiness. [Col. 0053D] Be, I beg you, well ordered in character; ardent in love; gentle in fellowship; steadfast in promise; strong in endurance; inclined to concord; stern in correction. Be upright in judgments, modest in speech, discerning in giving, industrious in administration [Col. 0054A], vigorous in action, diligent in assistance, trustworthy in counsel, circumspect in answers. Show yourself devoted to your superiors, kind to inferiors, gentle to equals, stern to the proud, gracious to the humble, merciful to penitents, inflexible toward the obstinate. Show yourself a John to the incestuous [Note: [Col. 0053] Matt. 14.], a Jehu and a Mattathias to apostates [Note: [Col. 0053] 4 Kings 9; 1 Macc. 2.], a Phinehas to fornicators [Note: [Col. 0053] Num. 25.], an Elijah to idolaters [Note: [Col. 0053] 3 Kings 18.], a Peter to liars [Note: [Col. 0053] Acts 5.], a Paul to blasphemers [Note: [Col. 0053] 1 Tim. 1.], and Christ to merchants [Note: [Col. 0053] John 2.].

The course of this temporal life is exceedingly brief, but its end is dreadful and uncertain. The more illustrious the title of your nobility, the more gloriously it increases your praise if, in holiness in Christ’s service, you surpass those whom you outstrip in birth. [Col. 0054B] In the episcopal state there is no middle course: either your way of life will be worldly and shameful, or holy and glorious alike before God and men. Nothing so swiftly darkens or illuminates a man’s life as pontifical authority. One quickly becomes either a pleasing fragrance to God or a public scandal.

Some gems shine more brightly in darkness than in light. Certain men were quite commendable before they obtained rank; but, placed upon the Church’s lampstand, they turned light into darkness and reputation into disgrace.

It is commonly said that honours change character, though seldom for the better. For many it would have been better still to remain hidden beneath the bushel and beneath the shadow of an honourable reputation [Col. 0054C], rather than to climb the lampstand amid disgrace. Their ugliness would still have lain hidden in poverty’s obscurity, had not rank publicized it. Honour grew, and disgrace grew with it; for, as the satirist says:

> Every vice of the mind is accounted a crime so much the more conspicuous,  
> as the man who sins is reckoned greater.  
> [Note: [Col. 0053] Juvenal, *Satires* 8.]

A private sinner is often spared; but if a prelate sins, every tongue is sharpened to spread his disgrace. Many, persuaded by others, believe that their sin is altogether hidden; but they are dangerously deceived. Let every prelate know that in some respect he is always disreputable unless he demonstrates true holiness by his works. It is written that “the voice of the people is the voice of God” [Note: [Col. 0053] Isa. 66.]. In my judgment, moreover, common opinion would not lightly exalt [Col. 0054D] any prelate unless the results of his works and continual experience had commended him.

If, therefore, you delight in possessing the titles of public approval, seek to please Christ and men—not in an abundance of riches, but of graces; not [Col. 0055A] in the adornment of clothing, but in virtues. Consider detestable the lives of those bishops whose dress is ostentatious, whose gait is marked by an uplifted neck, whose face is grim, whose eyes are fierce, whose threats are terrible; who lord it over the clergy, rather than becoming examples to the flock among the people [Note: [Col. 0055] 1 Pet. 5.]; whose god is their belly [Note: [Col. 0055] Phil. 3.]; whose life is buried in death—liars, babblers, and proud men, companions of thieves; colleagues not of Peter but of Simon, disciples not of Christ but of Nero.

While they rob the poor, burden monasteries, extort from the clergy, turn God’s justice to profit and offer it for sale, and conduct the trade of Gehazi [Note: [Col. 0055] 4 Kings 4.], they heap up for themselves a treasure of wrath and death along with their treasure of money. Christ, whom they do not fear as judge, they shall have as avenger. Hold most firmly [Col. 0055B] that if a prelate once extends his hand to such monstrous deeds,

> A dog will not be frightened away from a greased hide.  
> [Note: [Col. 0055] Horace, *Satires* II.5.]

Rather, once glued fast by the stickiness of wickedness, he will thereafter be unable to draw breath freely; nor, except through the manifold severity of penitence, will he return to innocence.

For a prelate is very rarely found who does not have flatterers at his side, men who feed and caress him, who make his head fat with the oil of the sinner. “The sinner is praised in the desires of his soul, and the wicked man is blessed” [Note: [Col. 0055] Ps. 10.]. These are the men who, when they see their lord’s mind wavering amid temptations, though they could instruct him with a word of exhortation, tear him away from sin, and raise him toward virtue, instead extinguish within him the spirit of virtue with honeyed speeches [Col. 0055C], although it is written [Col. 0056A], “Do not quench the Spirit” [Note: [Col. 0055] 1 Thess. 5.]. They nullify and overthrow the still feeble efforts of a holier purpose.

If he vows continence, if he disposes himself toward abstinence, they say: “Be kind to yourself, lord. You are young; fasting is troublesome to the head; excessive affliction of the flesh produces illnesses. You must stretch the string so that it does not break. All this ought to be deferred until mature years. We are no better than our fathers. Woman was created for man’s consolation. To man and woman it was said: ‘Increase and multiply, and fill the earth’ [Note: [Col. 0055] Gen. 1.]. Your strength is not the strength of stone, nor is your flesh bronze [Note: [Col. 0055] Job 6.].
