The Lord does not take account of the sins and ignorances of youth [Note: [Col. 0055] Ps. 24.]. Sleep, recreation, and the laying aside of cares are nature’s closest friends. He guards the fortress well who [Col. 0056B] diligently preserves his body” [Note: [Col. 0055] Bernard, Sermon 2, on the Assumption of the Blessed Virgin.].

“It is rash to afflict oneself without necessity. Religion in the young rarely has commendable outcomes; older age will sufficiently redeem the slipperiness of youth. Penitence is timely enough if it comes before the day of death. The thief repented on the cross [Note: [Col. 0055] Luke 23.]; no one repented too late whom death found repentant. It belongs to your lineage to follow youthful impulses, to indulge more freely for a time in looser desires, and then at the time of maturity to give forth the fragrance of sweetness” [Note: [Col. 0055] Jerome, Epistles 7 to Laeta and 47 to Sabinianus.].

By these and other means the enemy sows weeds over the field [Note: [Col. 0055] Matt. 13.]; but iniquity has lied to itself [Note: [Col. 0055] Ps. 26.]. For, to answer its last words first, that great Count Theobald [Note: [Col. 0055C] Renaud’s grandfather through his daughter Agnes, who bore Renaud. Theobald was Count of Champagne, a man most renowned for the nobility of his lineage, his holiness, his deeds, and his power. John of Saint-Victor, in the *Memorial of History*, preserved in manuscript in the library of Saint-Victor at Paris, writes of him under the year 1137:

> “At this time Count Theobald of Champagne flourished: father of orphans, judge of widows, eye of the blind, foot of the lame; exceptionally generous in supporting the poor, in building monasteries, and toward all religious persons with incomparable liberality. He had four sons who were counts: Henry of Champagne; Theobald of Blois and Chartres; Stephen; and William, archbishop of Reims. He also had several daughters, one of whom, named Adela, King Louis VII of France took as wife, and by her Philip Augustus was begotten.”

Here it should be noted [Col. 0055D] that it is falsely said that Stephen was Count of Chartres. No author attributes this to him; all agree that he was Count of Sancerre, or Sacro-Caesarea, and that after his wife’s death he became a Carthusian.

Alberic, monk of Trois-Fontaines of the Cistercian order in the diocese of Liège, a contemporary author, writes thus in his manuscript *Chronicle* concerning the great Theobald:

> “In the year 1152 Theobald, Count of Champagne, died on the sixth Ides of January and was buried at Lagny. He had four sons: Henry, Count Palatine of Troyes, famed for generosity and liberality; Theobald, Count of Blois, who held Chartres; Stephen, Count of Sancerre, which is called Sacrum Caesaris; and William, Archbishop of Sens and afterwards of Reims, to whom Master Peter Comestor wrote the *Scholastic History*. He also had six daughters. The first was Maria, Duchess of Burgundy; the second Agnes, Countess of Bar-le-Duc; the third, a certain duchess in distant parts—afterward William of Goët, in the diocese of Chartres, married her; the fourth, Matilda, Countess of Perche; the fifth, a nun of Fontevraud; and the sixth, Adela, Queen of the Franks.”

How pious and holy Theobald was appears from the fact that he was joined in intimate friendship with Saint Bernard and wholly depended upon him in matters pertaining to God. The countless churches, [Col. 0056D] monasteries, and hospitals founded and enriched with gifts by him also demonstrate it; Burgundy and Champagne especially are filled with them. I would recount more about him, if I were not consulting brevity, and if a certain hope had not dawned upon me that some distinguished writer of our age will undertake this work and give us the history or genealogy of the illustrious Counts of Champagne, interrupted by the death of the learned Pithou.], and many other of your forebears [Col. 0056C], shone with the titles of great virtues even before entering youth [Col. 0057A]. Your uncle also, Archbishop of Reims [Note: [Col. 0057C] This is William, surnamed White-Hands, son of Theobald the Great. “Having indeed been educated under the rod of Bernard of Clairvaux, he became most religious,” says Tavellus in his *Life of the Archbishop of Sens*. “Accordingly, from youth he put on the gravity of old age,” says Peter of Blois here. First a canon of Saint Quiriacus, or Cyriacus, at Provins, he was elected bishop of Chartres but was not consecrated. After some time he was consecrated Archbishop of Sens, then of Reims, and finally was created Cardinal-Priest of the title of Santa Sabina by Alexander III at the Lateran Council in 1179. He was renowned not only for illustrious but for royal birth; not only for talent and the glory of his deeds, but also for exceptional piety toward God.

Alexander III sent him, while already Archbishop of Sens, as legate to England to investigate the death of Saint Thomas; there he acted so prudently and courageously that he brought King Henry of England to penitence. How highly his nephew Philip Augustus, King of France, valued him is made clear by the fact that he made him supreme administrator of the realm, and kept him constantly at his own side. Thus, when Pope Lucius III, ardently desiring to see him, wrote to the king requesting that he send the cardinal, Augustus replied to Lucius:

> “Our dearest uncle William surpasses all our friends and faithful men: in our counsels he is a watchful eye; in affairs, our right hand. For him to leave us even temporarily would be to give way to our enemies. We have kept him as a thorn in our enemies’ eyes and a spear in their sides, judging that nothing can be done without him, whether peace or war must be discussed with our enemies.”

He died in 1202. Historians mention much else about him in various places.] put on the gravity of old age from adolescence; from then on he set the ascents in his heart and, through the growth of virtues, ascended to the eminence of a more perfect life.

Certainly, the people who flatter you lead you into error. Believe Paul, teacher of the Gentiles, not the flatterer, most dear friend. “Abstain,” he says, “from fleshly desires, which wage war against the soul” [Note: [Col. 0057] 1 Pet. 2.]; “for if you live according to the flesh, you shall die” [Note: [Col. 0057] Rom. 8.]—that is, with the death which neither dies nor ends. The wisdom of the flesh, which counsels you toward unlawful things, is hostile to God [Note: [Col. 0057] Jas. 4.]. Attend to the suggestions of those who flatter you, and see what fruit you attain by their counsel. For in pleasures of the flesh, what delights passes quickly, while what torments remains without end [Col. 0057B]. “What fruit had you,” says the Apostle, “in those things of which you are now ashamed?” [Note: [Col. 0057] Rom. 6.] These are what accompany the works of the flesh: cravings of anxiety and madness, acts of abomination and uncleanness, and outcomes of repentance and shame. Of all the things in which we offend God, nothing remains except a conscience that bears witness to uncleanness and tortures itself by recollection of sin. In the Apostle’s testimony, the fruit of sin is death; but the fruit of righteousness is hope and joy in the Holy Spirit [Note: [Col. 0057] Gal. 5.].

You became a disciple not of Epicurus but of Christ: to bear Christ’s cross in your body, not to make provision for the flesh in its desires [Note: [Col. 0057] Rom. 13.]. If you have undertaken Christ’s ministry, show yourself in all things as God’s minister, so that God’s name may not be blasphemed because of you [Note: [Col. 0057] 1 Tim. 6:3]. [Col. 0057C] He whom you propose to serve is holy, innocent, undefiled, made higher than the heavens [Note: [Col. 0057] Heb. 7.]. “Be holy,” he says, “because I am holy” [Note: [Col. 0057] Lev. 11.]. “This,” says the Apostle, “is the will of God: your sanctification” [Note: [Col. 0057] 1 Thess. 4.]. And he adds: “That you abstain from fornication; that each one may know how to possess his vessel in sanctification and honour” [Col. 0058A] [Note: [Col. 0057] ibid.]. Let a man regard you as a minister of Christ and a steward of God’s mysteries [Note: [Col. 0057] 1 Cor. 4.].

You administer well [Note: [Col. 0058D] Blesensis took this saying from Saint Bernard, Sermon 1 on Saints Peter and Paul.] if you live orderly, sociably, and humbly: orderly toward yourself, sociably toward your neighbour, humbly toward God. If entering upon the better life seems burdensome to you, its progress will be more welcome; and the more certain expectation of reward will lighten the very severity of a holy resolve. The prophet says: “Because of the words of your lips, I have kept hard ways” [Note: [Col. 0057] Ps. 16.]. “The light and momentary affliction which is ours,” says the Apostle, “works in us an immeasurable weight of glory” [Note: [Col. 0057] 2 Cor. 4.]. Hope will pass into possession, labour into reward, continence into glory, abstinence into a crown: what is brief into perpetuity; what is changeable into eternity.

Among other things, I humbly and earnestly beg you, as my lord and friend [Col. 0058B], that you receive this exhortation of mine, which proceeds from the heart, patiently; and that you do not take it ill that I write “you” in the singular—*tu*, *tibi*, and *te*. For plural speech, by which we lie while addressing one person, is the speech of flattery, utterly foreign to sacred discourse.

[In the Harleian manuscript [3672], after the letter there occurs the following.

This letter is continuous with the preceding one and has neither a rubric nor even a letter-number.—Let it not shame you that you have played, but do not let play become habitual; and you who have played rashly, let reason—the teacher of conduct—teach you to direct yourself toward the fruitfulness of life, so that you may worthily exercise the priesthood, the divine gift of the pontifical office, to the praise of Christ’s name. Be pious, just, sober, prudent, chaste, [Col. 0058C] humble, teachable in God’s law, and do not be a barren tree. Govern yourself more fittingly in your office; and, having driven vice far away, be clean from the stain of sin, so that you may minister at the altar of the pure Virgin while pure yourself.

Drive far from you the ministers of impurity: a wicked companion more powerfully corrupts the life of the good and afflicts it with the loss of reputation. Thus [Col. 0059A] presumption draws strength from association with like persons. A prelate’s life is cheapened by companionship with the base. As a pious protector of the poor, give to everyone who asks; rebuke evildoers forcefully; and wash your sacred hands from the contaminating touch of a filthy gift. Let no one flatter you with a reward; freely bestow the favours sought, but grant benefices to those worthy of them. Do not give to ministers of crimes; do not, under a show of compassion, impiously abuse for your own purposes rather than the Church’s the assistance of the poor entrusted to you. Let no actor carry anything away from you; nor entice infamous friendships at the expense of Christ’s patrimony.

Administer the Lord’s goods cautiously; speak little, but speak truthfully. Confirm words by deeds, for it is unfitting that a priest’s mouth should casually be polluted by falsehood. Do not disdain to benefit from the counsel of the prudent, nor let wholesome exhortation disturb you adversely. You are bound to abstain from every appearance of evil [Col. 0059B]; under the bridle of temperance, flourish in sobriety, the teacher of chastity. Do not bend toward enticements through varied and wandering desire, but cleanse the darkness of the blinded mind with virtue’s ray.

## LETTER XVI. TO A CERTAIN BISHOP, NOW ADVANCED IN YEARS

**Subject.**—He earnestly exhorts a bishop distracted by many affairs and occupations to adopt a calmer way of life, for the sake of securing his own salvation and that of others; and to consider that it is not enough to be conscious of no serious fault unless he joins many good works to an innocent life.

When I came and found you entangled in so many affairs, surrounded by so many crowds of people, distracted by so many occupations in such different directions, I grieved for you [Col. 0059C], and my inmost being was shaken with the pious feeling of compassion. For who could patiently endure that so noble a soul, imbued with spiritual teachings, should, under a certain veil of freedom, degenerate into servile work? A soul entangled in so many labyrinths must necessarily be more often in bondage; for not only does its earthly dwelling weigh it down, but it itself also diffuses itself into the unrest of earthly things, so that with Jeremiah [Note: [Col. 0059] Ch. 31.] it says, “My inward parts are poured out upon the ground.” And with Ezekiel [Note: [Col. 0059] Ch. 41.], “The ground reached to the windows, and the windows were closed.” Thus heaven is changed into earth, gold into dross, spirit into flesh. The carnal man weighs down the spiritual, and Pharaoh’s dragons swallow Moses’ dragon [Note: [Col. 0059] Exod. 7.].

I shall speak, therefore, because if I keep silent, my own mouth will condemn me. I shall ask you as a lord [Col. 0059D], admonish you as a father; and if I cannot otherwise recall your soul to knowledge of its condition, I shall use the song of love and say: “O fair one, if you do not know yourself, go forth after the flock of your companions” [Note: [Col. 0059] Song 1.]. For no one knows himself until he reviews his days, following in recollection after the flock and multitude committed to his charge. Therefore I shall speak, and either diminish something of your unbearable burden of cares, or extinguish it altogether, and infuse some instruction and edification [Col. 0060A]. For upon the tabernacle’s lampstand are vessels for pouring, extinguishers, and snuffers [Note: [Col. 0059] Num. 4.].

But I should be a transgressor of the Lord’s law if I tolerated a grove growing beside the altar of the Lord—that is, if a multitude of anxieties were allowed to run wild around the Church’s ruler. What is put in certain peril is greater than every treasure. What is exposed, as though to the cast of a die, to eternal destruction is priceless and beyond every valuation. These theatrical little harlots must utterly be driven away: sirens sweet unto ruin; flies destroying the fragrance of ointment [Note: [Col. 0059] Eccles. 10.]; mice bursting forth from the earth to gnaw the entrails of those who place the ark of the Lord—that is, ecclesiastical administration—beside Dagon [Note: [Col. 0059] 1 Kings 5.], who administer temporal matters no less, and perhaps more diligently [Col. 0060B], than spiritual ones.

The prophet says of such men: “You made my soul waste away like a spider” [Note: [Col. 0059] Ps. 38.]. For a spider weaves a web from its own entrails and wastes away in weaving it, in order to catch a most insignificant fly. What else does the man do who disembowels himself in expenditures and cares, in order to acquire a fly—or rather the new wine—of fragrant reputation and the favour of a harlot’s tongue? Upon men of this sort the Lord sends a spirit of dizziness and makes them wander in a trackless place rather than a road [Note: [Col. 0059] Ps. 106.]. Thus the children of Israel spent forty years on a journey of three days about Mount Seir, and did not enter the promised land [Note: [Col. 0059] Deut. 2.].

These are lunatics, offered to the Lord for healing [Note: [Col. 0059] Matt. 17.]: now falling into the water of cares, now into the fire of greed [Col. 0060C], hatred, anger, or some extraordinary pleasure. I can scarcely believe that in such a disturbance of soul anyone can find, in prayer, the dew of devotion or the streams of grace. For the storm is violent, and the surges of the sea in the heart are wondrous. These are those to whom the Lord promised an iron heaven, so that they may be deprived of heavenly rain or grace; and a bronze earth, so that, inwardly hardened around earthly matters, they may bear no fruit of life [Note: [Col. 0059] Lev. 26.].

Far be it—far be it, most loving Father—that I should insinuate or presume anything unfavourable against your innocence! Yet the charity through which I bear you in my heart makes me afraid; may it make you afraid as well! “Blessed is the man who is always afraid” [Note: [Col. 0059] Prov. 28.]. It belongs to a prudent man to regard every work of his as suspect. “I feared all my works,” says Job [Note: [Col. 0059] Ch. 9.]. When we have done all things well, we ought to say that we are useless servants [Note: [Col. 0059] Luke 17.]. A man’s days are short [Note: [Col. 0059] Job 14.]. We do not know what he who is terrible in his counsels over the children of men has determined concerning us [Note: [Col. 0059] Ps. 65.]; we do not know what tomorrow may bring forth [Note: [Col. 0059] Prov. 27.]. This is the prophet’s word: “Behold, you have made my days measurable; for man passes by in an image” [Note: [Col. 0059] Ps. 38.]. “My days have passed,” says Job, “and by the way by which I go I shall not return” [Note: [Col. 0059] Job 16.].

[Col. 0061A]

> The passing years plunder each of us.  
> He who is not [fit] today will be less fit tomorrow.  
> [Note: [Col. 0061] Ovid, *Remedies for Love*.]

I shall not say that a great part of your life, but rather a great part of your death, has already passed. The clepsydra [Note: [Col. 0061D] From Philelphus, book V, epistle 6: “A clepsydra was once a glass vessel which showed the hours marked out in equal divisions; at its bottom was an opening through which it emitted water, and thus, by the diminution of the water, one could see how many hours there were.” Therefore it is called a *clepsydra* because it conceals or steals water. Caelius Rhodiginus, *Antique Readings*, book XVIII, chapter 39, calls the clepsydra an astronomical or horological instrument measuring hours [Col. 0062D]. Cleomedes calls it *hydrologia* (ὑδρολογία, “water-measurement”); hence the person who kept the clepsydra equal was called *erydor* (ἐρύδωρ) [reading uncertain]. Since the Romans divided military watches equally into four periods, the *primipilus* distinguished them by clepsydras. Hence Vegetius: “The watches are divided into four parts by the clepsydra.” And Caesar, speaking of the island of Britain, says: “We observed that the nights were shorter than on the Continent, by definite measurements of water.”] exhausts not merely its final drop, but all that has already flowed out; nor is death only in the last part of your life, but in all that has preceded of it.

Noah laboured for a hundred years in building the ark to save himself and his own [Note: [Col. 0061] Gen. 6–7.]; but how much have we laboured, whose individual days are momentary, passing, and final? We must greatly fear lest our flight occur in winter or on the Sabbath, when work is not permitted [Note: [Col. 0061] Matt. 24.]. Therefore the *gomor* was to be gathered on the sixth day [Note: [Col. 0061] Exod. 16.], because in this sixth age we must work so that in that seventh we may rest, when it will be said: “Let them rest from their labours” [Note: [Col. 0061] Rev. 14.].

Perhaps in [Col. 0061B] your heart you say with the Apostle, “I am conscious of nothing against myself” [Note: [Col. 0061] 1 Cor. 4.]; and with blessed Job, “My heart does not rebuke me in my life” [Note: [Col. 0061] Job 27.]. But, most kindly Father, a clean conscience without work does not suffice for salvation. The prophet says: “Turn away from evil and do good” [Note: [Col. 0061] Ps. 33.]. Each is incomplete without the other. In the Gospel, the Lord condemns the servant not only when he acts wickedly, but when he languishes from good work [Note: [Col. 0061] Luke 12.]. For not only the tree which bears bad fruit, but also that which bears no good fruit, will be cut down and thrown into the fire [Note: [Col. 0061] Matt. 3.].

Keep always in your heart the horror of this fire, most beloved Father, so that fear of eternal death and desire for endless life may continually press and grind you. These are the millstones with which the Christian soul is ground; one of them, without the other, ought not, according to the Lord’s command [Col. 0061C], to pass as a pledge. For we have all sinned [Note: [Col. 0061] Rom. 3.]. See, Father, how much satisfaction you have made for yourself, so that you may know what is lacking to you. Not to speak of your own soul, see how many souls you have drawn from the lion’s mouth and from the jaws of hell; how much profit from the talent entrusted to you you have gained by work, word, and example; how regularly you have fulfilled the six works of mercy which the Lord will set forth at judgment [Note: [Col. 0061] Matt. 25.]; how diligently you have cleansed your flesh by fasts and disciplines; and how strongly you have gone up against opposition for the house of the Lord. By your profession you are bound to all these things, and all these, Father, will be required from you most exactly.

Perhaps it will be reckoned rashness and presumption that I admonish you [Col. 0061D], but charity compels me. I know that on the day of dreadful judgment we shall render an account even for idle words [Note: [Col. 0061] Matt. 12.]. No royal command [Col. 0062A], nor any temporal advantage to men, will there excuse transgressions. But someone will say: “Whatever sins we have committed may be abolished by the benefit of confession.” Yet no one is secure about long life; Scripture testifies: “When they say, ‘Peace and security,’ then sudden destruction will come upon them” [Note: [Col. 0061] 1 Thess. 5.]. Sudden and uncertain death [Note: [Col. 0061] Augustine on Ps. 50.] often forestalls the remedy of penitence; and illnesses, which are very often severe and growing worse, extinguish the spirit of devotion through bodily anguish. It is wholly certain that what man does not punish, God will punish. It is dreadful to fall into the hands of the living God [Note: [Col. 0061] Heb. 10.]. For who can dwell with devouring fire, or who can stand with everlasting burnings? [Note: [Col. 0061] Isa. 33.]

These considerations move me to admonish you, Father, that henceforth [Col. 0062B], as far as you can, you keep sabbath from the turmoil of worldly affairs. Have mercy on your soul by pleasing God [Note: [Col. 0061] Ecclus. 30.]. If you do not possess yourself, you possess nothing. May the peace of God, which surpasses every understanding [Note: [Col. 0061] Phil. 4.], make you free from every sensual and worldly concern; this crowd of occupations is death to the soul. Therefore Solomon says: “My son, let your activities be few” [Note: [Col. 0061] Ecclus. 11.]. And behold, one greater than Solomon teaches us to be anxious not merely about few things, but only about one: “But,” he says [Note: [Col. 0061] Luke 10.], “one thing is necessary”—namely, to love God, which cannot be attained without purity of heart. No one does good until he comes to this one thing. It is written: “One thing have I asked of the Lord, and this will I seek” [Note: [Col. 0061] Ps. 26.]. For the ark was completed in one cubit [Note: [Col. 0061] Gen. 6.].

The commandment [Col. 0062C] of charity is the perfection of highest peace. Therefore the prophet says: “I have seen an end to every perfection; your commandment is exceedingly broad” [Note: [Col. 0061] Ps. 118.]. Yet because “the mouth speaks from the abundance of the heart” [Note: [Col. 0061] Matt. 12.], I fear that the filial affection and zeal which I have conceived for your salvation may extend this letter without limit. Therefore, lest I offend delicate ears by excessive speech, I close the letter with the words of the teacher of the Gentiles: “Grace be to you and peace from the Lord Jesus Christ” [Note: [Col. 0061] 1 Cor. 1; Gal. 6; Eph. 6; etc.].

## LETTER XVII. TO A CLERIC WHO IS A MERCHANT

**Subject.**—He shows that a cleric engaged in trade differs in no respect from a usurer, and that every endeavour to amass wealth is vain and ruinous.

[Col. 0062D] PETER OF BLOIS, Archdeacon of Bath, to his beloved companion and friend G., greeting and remembrance of eternal salvation.

If you considered the rank of your profession and the grace of the divine calling, you would occupy yourself with reading rather than trade, with the liberal arts rather than merchandise. For it is dangerous in a layman, but ruinous in a cleric, to increase one’s private means through commerce and, by the ambitious sale of goods, to expose oneself for sale to the devil. The cleric who buys at a lower price in order to sell at a higher is a son of avarice, an idolater of money, a servant of Mammon, and “sold under sin” [Note: [Col. 0063] Rom. 7.]. Since a form of usury is to give one’s neighbour less and receive more from him, I do not see how the cleric who seeks profit for himself at another’s loss can be free either from the crime of usury or from its criminal name. Indeed, the moneylender, while openly despoiling his neighbour, is worse than a thief or a robber. You give wine for grain, a horse for wine; and thus, under the appearance of exchange or the pretext of delay, you receive an increase in your purse and a loss in your soul. You are far worse than the Jews: they lend at interest only to a stranger, but you to both stranger and neighbour [Note: [Col. 0063] Ecclus. 29.]. You will gather riches and in the end will not rejoice; and what the Lord says figuratively through Jeremiah will happen to you: “The partridge has brooded over what she did not lay; he has made riches, and not by judgement: in the midst of his days they shall leave him, and at his end he shall be found a fool” [Note: [Col. 0063] Jer. 17.]. For the moneylender will have the most wretched end to this life: his end is destruction [Note: [Col. 0063] Phil. 3.], his death detestable, his condemnation without end.

Yet you soften the charge of trading, and, devising excuses for sins, propose that what you receive in excess is the fruit of your labour and prudence, since you bought the thing while it was selling more cheaply. You say that it is by no means absurd to turn labour into gain and risk into profit. Whatever argument you put forward, I announce this one thing to you: you have turned trade into a danger to your salvation. The sacred canons abhor a cleric who is a trader. Since blessed is the man “who has compassion and lends” [Note: [Col. 0063] Ps. 111], and who “has not given his money at usury” [Note: [Col. 0063] Ps. 14], we may judge him excluded from eternal blessedness who does not give as he has received [Col. 0064A], who does not observe, in accordance with the counsel of Holy Scripture, the grace of giving and receiving [Note: [Col. 0063] Matt. 10]. Moreover, you credit to your glory what adds to the sum of your condemnation, because in commercial affairs you publicly boast that you are shrewd—though would that you had never learned an office condemnable to you!

The Prophet says: “Because I have not known trading, I will enter into the powers of the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0063] Ps. 70].

[Note: [Col. 0063C] This is the version of the Seventy Interpreters, except that they have “trades,” Greek πραγματείας (*pragmateias*, “commercial dealings”). Thus the Old and Roman Psalters read, and Arnobius, Chrysostom, and Augustine follow them; likewise the Ethiopic version. The Hebrew has “numbers”; the Chaldaic version, “their number”—perhaps, “of your benefits”; the Syriac and Arabic read “writing.” Theodoric, following Symmachus, has: οὐ γὰρ οἶδα ἐξαριθμῆσαι, “For I do not know how to count out.” The Vulgate, however, reads “learning,” with which agrees Jerome’s version according to the Hebrew truth, where “branches of learning” occurs; for in certain Greek manuscripts πραγματείας is read. Augustine also follows this elsewhere. What follows, “I will enter into the powers of the Lord,” is in Hebrew “into strengths.” The sense of this verse according to the Hebrew version is: Since I have not known the number, or cannot count your benefits toward me, I shall daily proclaim your power—that is, your mighty deeds—and righteousness. But if the word *Sephoroth*, “numbers,” is taken to mean the art of calculation employed by merchants, and especially connected with trade—since nearly all commerce is conducted by counting and drawing up accounts [Col. 0064D]—the sense will be: Since I have not known the business of the world, I shall approach to celebrate your righteousness and mercy, and the very great benefits I have received from you. According to the Vulgate version, the sense here is: Since I am not educated in branches of knowledge, whether sacred or secular, it will suffice me to meditate on the wonders of God and to recall and commemorate his power. Thus Genebrard and others.]

He knew how great the danger in commerce was. For Job also, who awaited a sure entrance into the powers of the Lord, said: “Two kinds of men have appeared difficult and dangerous to me: a merchant is hardly stripped of neglect of God, and an innkeeper shall not be justified from the sin of the tongue” [Note: [Col. 0064D] It should first be known that this sentence is not found in the book of Job, but is taken from Ecclesiasticus, chapter 26, verse 37. Further, in the original text these two words, “of God” and “of the tongue,” are absent; Blesensis adds them for greater intelligibility. Thus the Septuagint reads: μόλις ἐξαιρεῖται ἔμπορος ἀπὸ πλημμελείας, καὶ οὐ δικαιωθήσεται κάπηλος ἀπὸ ἁμαρτίας, that is: “A merchant is hardly freed from wrongdoing, and an innkeeper shall not be justified from sin.”]. Indeed, you lose reputation and soul in order to acquire things that must be lost. Christ’s judgement is that the whole world is not to be gained by anyone at the cost of suffering loss to his soul [Col. 0064B; Note: [Col. 0063] Matt. 16]. You judge the contrary, caring nothing for your own perdition and preferring the money of ruin to the salvation of your soul. You reckon it the height of happiness to possess immense and superfluous wealth, a tenth part of which you will not spend in your entire lifetime. Would that this money had never existed, which has taken from you not only God but also your neighbour—and yourself! Indeed, if blessedness were conferred through riches, the Lord would not compare them to thorns [Note: [Col. 0063] Matt. 13], nor would he proclaim the blessedness of poverty [Note: [Col. 0063] Matt. 5]. If riches were commendable before God, they would more often fall to the lot of the righteous and God-fearing.

But now, behold, sinners, abounding in this world, have obtained riches [Note: [Col. 0063] Ps. 72]. Usurers and violent persecutors of the Church [Col. 0064C] are those who today heap up the amplest wealth. Esau, whom the Lord had rejected, went forward with four hundred men, while Jacob crossed the Jordan with his staff [Note: [Col. 0063] Gen. 32]. Do you fear, wretch, that what you have prepared will not suffice you? Surely your life will fail before your provisions do. Not to say of you: avarice causes many to be needy amid riches. For it is God’s judgement that a man be punished in the very thing in which he has sinned [Col. 0065A], so that he who always fears want may always be in want. As it is written: “He who fears frost, snow shall come upon him” [Note: [Col. 0065] Job 6]. One thing I know: you gather everything into a pierced bag, and it will not profit you on the day of vengeance. For when you perish, you will not take everything away, nor will the glory of your house descend with you [Note: [Col. 0065] Ps. 48]. Perhaps an enemy will succeed you; he who today plans the day of your death will enter into your labours, and, scattering with a more lavish hand the temporal goods which you hoarded after the manner of Tantalus, will reap the fruit of pleasure. But you will sleep—and would that it be with your fathers—and your tomb will be your house for ever.

It would suffice me if it sufficed you, if you would rid yourself of the vice of commerce: “Having food,” says the Apostle, “and wherewith to be covered, [Col. 0065B] let us be content with these. For those who desire to become rich fall into temptations and the snare of the devil” [Note: [Col. 0065] 1 Tim. 6]. Moreover, if you gather wealth in order more abundantly to have the necessities of this life, you deceive yourself; for an increased abundance of temporal possessions increases poverty. “The rich,” says the Prophet, “have lacked and suffered hunger; but those who seek the Lord shall not be deprived of any good thing” [Note: [Col. 0065] Ps. 33]. In the poet’s words:

> The love of money grows as money itself grows.  
> [Note: [Col. 0065] Juvenal, *Satires* 14.]

Therefore I beg you, and counsel you in true charity, that, content with the lawful acquisition of goods, you cease from excessive gains, lest hereafter you dishonour the reverence due to your order by the crime of trade. But if [Col. 0065C] you do not comply with a friend’s counsel, know that “the axe is laid to your root” [Note: [Col. 0065] Matt. 3]. For those “who execute vengeance among the nations, rebukes among the peoples” [Note: [Col. 0065] Ps. 149] have already scented in you the crime of trade and usury. And unless I had humbly pleaded for you, they would have cut you down as a tree bearing most condemned fruit. If eternal punishments do not move you to amendment, let at least the disgrace of this life and temporal losses concern you.

## LETTER XVIII. TO A CERTAIN MASTER, HIS FRIEND

**Subject.**—He most severely censures the character, disposition, and utterly wicked life of a certain bishop, to whose court he was invited by his friend.

Master Peter of Blois, Archdeacon of Bath, to his dearest companion and friend, Master N., greetings.

[Col. 0065D] I know that it proceeds from sincere affection that, by messengers and letters, you repeatedly urge me to return to your lord, who desires to have me as a familiar counsellor and a member of his household table. Once his table was made for me “a snare, a recompense, and a stumbling-block” [Note: [Col. 0065] Ps. 68]; therefore I do not return. For my many services, by which I thought I had wholly earned and purchased him, I received not a benefit but an injury; not gratitude but wrong. Therefore I do not return. He received the keys of the kingdom of heaven not [Col. 0066A] to take away revenues, but to correct transgressions. Yet in everything he thinks, deliberates, does, or says, he seeks gain and aims at profit, rashly presuming that everything possessed by his subjects is his own.

Indeed, in the Apostle’s testimony, parents store up for their children, not children for their parents [Note: [Col. 0065] 2 Cor. 12]—if this man is a father rather than a stepfather. For he is a harsh persecutor of his own people, a shameless exacter,

> a grim Procrustes.  
> [Note: [Col. 0065] Ovid, *Metamorphoses*, book VII.]

He hates honourable men, oppresses the prudent, lays snares for the unwary, despoils the rich, burdens the poor, benefits no one, and harms everyone. On every pretext, by right and wrong, he collects money; he delights in what he has collected. Nor does he fear loss to his own or another’s soul, [Col. 0066B] provided that by any means whatever he can obtain temporal advantage. He is far unlike the Doctor of the Gentiles, who desired in his subjects fruit for his soul, not gifts or payments, and therefore said: “I seek not the gift, but the fruit” [Note: [Col. 0065] Phil. 4].

Whenever someone comes to him, he observes not the visitor’s face but his hand, as though he were always expecting gifts. He has a hardened brow in begging; ungrateful when he has received; inhuman when he has not received. Intolerant of another’s speech, a most shameless exacter of another’s property, a most miserly giver of his own, merciless to the afflicted, gentle toward the cruel, unstable, intractable, incorrigible, tolerable to none, hateful to all; an enemy of peace, despiser of faith, adversary of unity, faithless in [Col. 0066C] counsel, negligent in action, furious in anger, slow to show mercy, unrestrained in speech, gluttonous, talkative, and drunken at banquets, swollen in prosperity, timid in adversity.

Your lord does nothing according to reason, but everything according to whim; and as though he had degenerated into a brutish mind, casting off from himself all counsel and discriminating judgement, he follows his own appetite. “Man, though in honour, did not understand; he was compared to senseless beasts and made like them” [Note: [Col. 0065] Ps. 48]. In accordance with the word of Nathan the prophet [Note: [Col. 0065] 2 Sam. 12], he bears the image of the man who, though he possessed countless sheep, coveted the one little ewe of a poor man. Nor is he unlike Ahab [Note: [Col. 0065] 1 Kgs. 21], who, though he possessed an abundance of every kind of wealth, cast his eyes upon Naboth’s little garden and obtained by the owner’s death the vineyard that he desired [Col. 0066D]. Would that he were wise and understood [Note: [Col. 0065] Deut. 32]! But “he would not understand, that he might do well” [Note: [Col. 0065] Ps. 35]; for he has hardened himself in his wickedness, and by constant sinning has fallen into contempt. The abyss of vices has swallowed him; therefore he does not recognize his offences or feel the sickness of his wounded and endangered soul. It is certain that a limb which has become numb is more dangerously diseased; and he who conceals or does not know his own transgressions is far from salvation.

Compunction never rends your lord’s heart; affection does not move it; pity does not soften it. He is not softened [Col. 0067A] by services, is ungrateful for benefits, deaf to prayers, savage in judgements, unfaithful in counsel, shameless in disgraceful matters, rash in divine things, secure amid danger to his soul, faint-hearted at temporal loss, ready for quarrels, inhuman in hatreds. He does not remember favour shown him; for the memory and vengeance of injuries alone, he turns about every craft of his turbulent mind. It is written: “A monkey on a roof, a foolish king sitting on a throne” [Note: [Col. 0067] A proverb used by St Bernard, *On Consideration*, book 2]. “Honour to a fool is a sword in the hand of a madman” [Note: [Col. 0067] Prov. 26]. And he who gives honour to a fool is like one who throws a stone into Mercury’s heap.

He has ascended to the eminence of the pastoral chair, not called by the Lord as Aaron was [Note: [Col. 0067] Heb. 5]. For his ascent pleases neither God nor men. The prophets and apostles—whose likeness he wears [Col. 0067B], or rather whose monkey he is, as a degenerate successor and rejected heir—were strong in battle [Note: [Col. 0067] Heb. 11], not soft in silk, not given to gluttony, not proud, not envious, not rapacious, not enervated by lust. It is ridiculous for a prelate to be eminent over peoples while subject to vices: to be grandiloquent in speech but faint-hearted, lax, and weak in deed; to walk in pomp and with an arrogant countenance, while possessing no testimony of an unblemished conscience.

> Boastfulness of lineage and the disgrace of the common people  
> do not agree well, nor do they dwell in one seat;  
> [Note: [Col. 0067] Ovid, *Metamorphoses* 2.]

nor do haughty eyes and foulness of character, baseness of life and the authority of honour. The unhappy man pays no attention to the testimony of his own conscience; he falsely represents himself as greater than he is, [Col. 0067C] thinks rank to be virtue, and, though wholly unworthy of every honour, believes that he has obtained by merits what the Lord allowed him to be elevated to: a place of downfall, an occasion of eternal condemnation, and a disgrace in this present life. Dangerous is that height which brings danger. Too late is the complaint: “Because in lifting me up, you dashed me down” [Note: [Col. 0067] Ps. 101]. It would have been better for him not to have ascended the step of eminence than soon, with shame, to hold the lowest place [Note: [Col. 0067] Luke 14]. For I know that this will happen, and presumptuous exaltation will not escape the danger of a fall: “the axe is laid to the root” [Note: [Col. 0067] Matt. 3].

Moreover, if he considered these loincloths of the ancient curse, the shadowy glory of painted and fleeting honour, and the disgraceful beginnings of his origin, he would find himself more wretched than all men [Col. 0067D], since from his earliest age he has learned nothing but shameful things and has grown up in vices by practice. From his youthful years he has presumptuously committed shameful deeds; and when elevated to the chair of pestilence, he has not ceased from oppressing his subjects, from injuries and exactions. He escapes from himself and, seeking himself outside himself, walks in things great and wonderful above himself. Thus he presides over many in order to benefit none; thus he rules, that every injustice may rule him. His rule furnishes an example of pride and a pattern [Col. 0068A] of wickedness, whereas the Prince of the Apostles writes and says, “Not lording it over the clergy, but being made an example of the flock to the people” [Note: [Col. 0067] 1 Pet. 5].

Look at him speaking; look also at him walking:

> What threats he bears upon his face, with how great a haughtiness he crushes all things!  
> [Note: [Col. 0067] Statius, *Thebaid* 1.]

He always walks about, casting his eyes around haughtily, with uplifted neck and tossing shoulders,

> recalling greatly the reclining Maecenas.  
> [Note: [Col. 0067] Juvenal, *Satires* 3.]

All his effort, all his honour, all his glory, indeed all and only the substance of his usurped dignity, consists in this: the thrusting out of his breast, elevation of neck, pompous gait, rolling eyes, arrogant countenance, and thunderous threats. And, to include much in few words: with him all is given over to pride; nothing to holiness, nothing to chastity, nothing to friendship, and finally nothing remains for honourableness.

[Col. 0068B] Before he ascended to this height of ruinous power, there was in him a shadowed appearance of liberality, a display of hypocritical humility contrived with the colouring of pretence; but honours change characters. What is written happened in his case: “Every man first sets out good wine, and when they have become drunk, then that which is worse” [Note: [Col. 0067] John 2]. Once made bishop, he immediately turned into open hatred the grudges which, while he was a private man, he cloaked under the false appearance of benevolence. For, in Scripture’s testimony, “There is one who humbles himself wickedly, and his inward parts are full of deceit” [Note: [Col. 0067] Ecclus. 19].

He permits no one to live about him except emasculated and effeminate men, who flatter him and permit him to pursue the passions of his desire; [Col. 0068C] for “every animal loves its like” [Note: [Col. 0067] Ecclus. 13]. These are they who call the wretch blessed and fatten the sinner’s head with the oil of flattery [Note: [Col. 0067] Ps. 22]. “The sinner is praised in the desires of his soul, and the wicked man is blessed” [Note: [Col. 0067] Ps. 10]. For if an honourable man approaches him to instruct and form him, to exhort him more intimately toward the fruit of a better life, he becomes angry, burns, and is distressed. It will go very well for the man who corrects him if he escapes unharmed,

> if he may be permitted to return from there with a few teeth.  
> [Note: [Col. 0067] Juvenal, *Satires* 3.]

You urgently call me back to your bishop’s house and his execrable table. I do not value your bishop so highly that I should perish for his sake. I know that “he who touches pitch shall be defiled by it” [Note: [Col. 0067] Ecclus. 13]; and a serpent in the bosom, fire in the lap, and a mouse in the wallet repay their guests badly. Holiness befits the house of a bishop; [Col. 0068D] but, to include the lord as well as the household, nothing in this house is more damnable in merit, more seditious in company, more dishonourable in morals, more filthy in conscience, more blameworthy in reputation, or more ruinous in example.

“Lift up your hands, O Lord, against his pride” [Note: [Col. 0067] Ps. 73], and break the horns of the sinner. Remove from your house the idol Moloch [Note: [Col. 0067] Lev. 18]; fulfil what you promised prophetically: “He who practises pride shall not dwell in the midst of my house” [Col. 0069A; Note: [Col. 0069] Ps. 100]. “Moab is proud, and his arrogance is greater than his strength” [Note: [Col. 0069] Isa. 16]; therefore I have sworn and resolved to turn aside and keep far from him. For I cannot endure a son of pride, an idol of abomination, lofty eyes [Note: [Col. 0069] Prov. 6], lying lips, and a boastful tongue [Note: [Col. 0069] Ps. 11]. Therefore I flee and keep far from him, that I may fulfil in myself the Prophet’s word: “With a proud eye and an insatiable heart, I did not eat with him” [Note: [Col. 0069] Ps. 100].

## LETTER XIX. TO R., A FRIEND AND STUDENT OF CANON LAW

**Subject.**—He resolves two questions proposed to him. The first is whether a woman who, believing her husband dead, has professed the monastic life may, upon his return, reclaim her husband on her own authority. The second is whether, after that husband has died, she is bound to resume the monastic life.

[Col. 0069B] Peter of Blois, Archdeacon of Bath, to his beloved companion and friend R., greetings, and whatever is better than health.

Recently, in a scholastic disputation, certain questions brought forward, as you say, held your mind in suspense and doubt. You put them to me and urgently seek their solution. Yet since you are in the schools while I am in the camp, and since you have now spent two years on laws and decrees, I fear that you do this as a test, so that you may cunningly catch me in my simplicity. I might have told you what that prudent woman is recorded to have answered Joab when he sought the head of Sheba: “It is a proverb,” she said, “that those who inquire should inquire in Abel” [Note: [Col. 0069D] That is: when people are in doubt and wish to ask about their doubt, they should go to ask in Abel, a city of Palestine, and there an answer will be given them—because this is the city in which are wise men who answer in Israel concerning all doubts. Thus Tostatus on this passage. The Hebrews offer another interpretation, but all interpreters agree that it is especially obscure. This interpretation better accords with the letter and history, and Peter of Blois followed it in comparing Abel with Paris, whence wise men are consulted from the whole world.].

Let those who inquire inquire at Paris, where the most intricate knots of difficult questions are untied. You will be able to find more easily, among those who practise such matters, the solution to the questions you propose. For my part, I do not begrudge you what I know. May God grant you the freewill offerings of my mouth [Note: [Col. 0069] Ps. 118], so that the questions you propose may be solved, if not according to reason, at least according to the person! I think it enough for myself if I establish the solution I shall give by the authority of one law or canon.

You ask concerning a woman who, believing on the plausible report of good men that her husband, gone abroad, had departed this life, entered a monastery [Col. 0070A] and took the veil: when her husband returns and does not reclaim her, can she leave on her own authority and reclaim her husband?

You ask also whether, if, after professing a purpose of holiness, she is to be restored to her husband, she must, after his subsequent death, be compelled to observe her vow—for the cause which seemed for a time to suspend her vow has been removed.

I answer the first question: the vow of continence which she made without her husband’s authority and permission could not bind her. This is most clearly evident from the eighth synod, the synod of Pope Eugenius, Gregory’s letter to Urbicus, Nicholas’s letter, and the statements of Augustine. Jerome too, in his commentary on the Epistle to Titus, firmly affirms this same point; [Col. 0070B] Ambrose likewise, in the book *Questions on the New and Old Testaments*, disapproves a woman’s vow unless the consent of her husband, vowing with her, is present. Augustine clearly declares the same in the *Questions on Numbers*.

Although it may appear from the council held at Compiègne [Note: [Col. 0070D] These are the words of the council: “If a woman, without the leave of her husband, has put a veil upon her head, if it pleases the husband, let him receive her again into marriage.” For *commeatu* (“leave”), some manuscripts have *comiato*, as in the *Capitularies*, book V, chapter 6; in Burchard’s *Decrees*, book IX, chapter 47. In Ivo, part VIII, chapter 185, it reads “without *commeatu*”; while in part IX, chapter 124, “without permission.” Thus our people derived *comiatum*, and from *comiatum*, *congé* (“leave”).] that, unless the husband calls her back, she cannot leave, you should understand that she cannot leave if the husband wishes to vow continence. Otherwise, if the husband refuses likewise to convert or neglects to reclaim his wife, he must be compelled by the Church either to reclaim his wife or to bind himself by the bond of chastity. Augustine testifies to this in his exposition of Psalm 149.

But if you object that it was in her own power [Col. 0070C] never to demand the marital debt from her husband, and that she could bind herself in this respect, I answer that, since the Apostle says that “the husband has not power over his own body, but the wife” [Note: [Col. 0069] 1 Cor. 7], and conversely, she could not without her husband’s permission impose the law of chastity upon her body, which was not in her own power. You have this expressly in the letter of Alexander II to Landulf. Further, since she made the vow of chastity under the influence of error, this vow does not appear binding; indeed, to tell the truth, she did not consent to it. For by the principle of civil law, nothing impedes consent more than an error that reveals ignorance. Therefore, if she desires to be a mother, let her go out in the name of the Lord and resume marital embraces, if her husband either refuses to convert together with her or neglects to reclaim his wife.

[Col. 0071A] But if the husband thereafter truly pays the debt of death, she, freed from the law of her husband, may marry whom she wishes, in the Lord [Note: [Col. 0071D] Two supreme pontiffs, Celestine III—as found in the Decretal *Placet*, *On the Conversion of Married Persons*—and before him Alexander III, chapter *Quidam*, under the same title, both in the very century of Blesensis, decided that she cannot marry. This is because by entering the monastery she promised not to demand the marital debt, which was within her own power; that promise was not dissolved by her husband’s death. They add that it is advisable for her to return to the monastery, though she is not to be compelled to do so. To the analogy here adduced by Blesensis concerning the servant [Col. 0072D], I answer that the reasoning is entirely parallel. For the servant, after the death of his lord who had withdrawn him from the monastery, cannot indeed be compelled, by reason of a vow or profession made against his lord’s will, to resume the purpose of monastic life; yet he can be compelled to keep his promise not to demand the marital debt, and therefore not to contract marriage.]: nor should she be compelled to observe a vow which was invalid from the beginning. For, to state the analogy plainly, a servant whom his master has withdrawn from a monastery, if he later obtains the benefit of freedom and there is now nothing to hinder his vow, nevertheless shall not be compelled to resume the stricter purpose of life.

I communicate these things to your inquiry as God in his sweetness supplies for the poor [Note: [Col. 0071] Ps. 67]. If something more elegant is given you from above, do not begrudge it me; for I am ready to be taught by my disciple as by my master. For most blameworthy is that shame which does not receive the benefit of instruction from one inferior as well as from one superior.

[Col. 0071B] You cannot yet have my book *On the Deceptions of Fortune*, which you ask for. Before it goes out into public, it will first undergo the judgement of a more corrective file, lest anything unshapely or uncouth remain in it to offend the reader’s eyes or ears. As for what you wish to know, both by letter and through your cleric, why this new little work of mine is entitled *On the Deceptions of Fortune*, when nothing is read in it that has not been taken from the New or Old Testament, understand that the reason is this. The first book sufficiently explains that fortune is nothing, and fairly plausibly refutes the opinion of those who measure the events of temporal affairs by a certain deceptive variability of fortune, whereas the very mutability of those events is wrought immutably in itself by God’s providence. Therefore at the head of the book is written: *On the Deceptions of Fortune*—not because fortune or its deceptions are anything, but because in the exaltation or humiliation of men, which many regard as fortuitous and uncertain, all things are shown to proceed from divine dispensation.

And that you may know this with the faith of your own eyes, I send you five quires of this new work, that you may read them, not copy them, and send them back to me by the bearer of this letter with all speed. Fare well, dearest friend in Christ.

## LETTER XX. TO LORD CRISPIN AND MASTER PAGANUS. [A.D. 1188.]

[Col. 0071D] **Subject.**—He complains that the ill will of courtiers excludes him from the promised court and society of Renaud, Bishop of Chartres [Col. 0072A]; he praises that bishop’s humanity and liberality, and urges him fearlessly to undertake the defence of ecclesiastical liberty against royal exactions.

To his dearest friends, Lord Crispin and Master Paganus, Master Peter of Blois, Archdeacon of Bath, greetings in the author of salvation.

Your lord [Note: [Col. 0072D] That is, Renaud, Bishop of Chartres, concerning whom we have spoken in connection with Letter 15.] had promised me that he would put an end to my exile and honourably call me back to the land of my birth. Would that with him there were not “Yes and No” [Note: [Col. 0071] 2 Cor. 1], and that pastoral gravity did not degenerate in him! I know that detractors, as the Apostle says, “hateful to God” [Note: [Col. 0071] Rom. 1], have magnified their supplanting of me [Note: [Col. 0071] Ps. 40]. For in the houses of bishops and kings dwell pestilent frogs, [Col. 0072B] dog-flies and gnats, Egypt’s most grievous fly [Note: [Col. 0071] Exod. 8]: talkative, chattering, lying flatterers. Of such men it is written: “Their land brought forth frogs in the inner chambers of their kings” [Note: [Col. 0071] Ps. 104]; “their teeth are weapons and arrows, and a sword is in their lips” [Note: [Col. 0071] Ps. 56]. Thus the flattery of a prostituted tongue and the envy of a detractor have grossly poisoned for me the favour of your lord.

This is that pestilent air and corrupting breeze which today generally infects courtiers, so that it tears men of proven integrity away from the sides of magnates. For the plague of envy does not weigh the merits of virtues, but endures the torments of conscience, while headlong ambition and the desire for self-exaltation blind it. But blessed be God, who has brought me back to such moderation of estate that my own means suffice for the fulfilment of my wish [Col. 0072C]. No one will henceforth cast in my teeth: “I have enriched Abraham” [Note: [Col. 0071] Gen. 14]. I shall no longer drink from the well of Samaria, from which the more one drinks, the more one thirsts. I prefer to possess little with purity of conscience rather than innumerable dignities with the worm that does not die. Now, by God’s grace, that treacherous and deceitful affection for relatives will not be able to call me back, which so often set me, as it were, upon the throw of a die and so often compelled me to cross the sea under peril of my life. I have chosen a hiding-place, that I may not see the evils of my people, because, to use Job’s words, “the earth has been given into the hand of the wicked” [Note: [Col. 0071] Job 9].

Believe me: he who has lain hidden has lived well; and within
Each man ought to await his own fortune. [Note: [Col. 0071] Ovid, *Tristia*, elegy 4.] To Abraham it was said: “Go out from your land and from your kindred.” [Note: [Col. 0071] Gen. 12.] And why should I not go out, or [Col. 0073A] why should I return to my parents, among whom I found nothing but the hands of harpies, the counsels of Achitophel, [Note: [Col. 0073] II Kings 15.] the wiles of foxes, and the stings of scorpions? Although I owe my parents natural affection, I do not owe them this: that I should ruin myself for their sake, or turn aside from the course of honour for them.

For the cows which bore the ark of the Lord to Beth-shemesh [Note: [Col. 0073] I Kings 6.], though they were drawn by a certain natural attachment to their calves, nevertheless did not turn their necks back toward them. Many have lost their souls for the sake of their parents, because, loving flesh more than spirit in them, they rashly and cruelly laid down their souls for their friends. I am a Levite—indeed, an arch-Levite. It is written in the law of the Lord that no one is to be admitted to the priestly or Levitical order unless he first [Col. 0073B] says to his father and mother, “Farewell!” [Note: [Col. 0073] Deut. 35.]—that is, unless affection for his family is utterly extinguished in him.

I return to your lord, whose companionship and most delightful retinue I regret having lost. I hoped that he would become more diligent through my association with him, since his noble intellect and rich memory would, through my counsels, raise themselves to the summit of virtues and produce timely fruit in the Church of God. Dearest friends, make up for my absence now, and do not cease to urge your lord with wholesome counsels, that, having laid aside youthful frivolity, he may put on pontifical gravity. For zeal and concern for that noble soul trouble me.

For I have not found a bishop so sociable, so open, [Col. 0073C] so lavish toward all in generosity and liberality. He gives to everyone who asks; for from tender childhood he has given promise of generosity. Mercy grew up with him, so that with blessed Job he may confidently say: “From my childhood a generous disposition grew up with me, and it came forth with me from my mother’s womb.” [Note: [Col. 0073] Job 31.] Yet I wish that reason prescribed a measure to his generosity, and that moderation set bounds to the gifts he makes to soldiers or actors. The measure of benefits bestowed upon the poor ought indeed to be without measure.

But insofar as, through flattery aided by his gifts, his reputation increases toward empty boasting, so much does the title of his beneficence vanish among the good and serious, as though into vapour and smoke. He is bound to distribute the patrimony of the Crucified, not to soldiers but to the poor—[Col. 0073D] a patrimony of which he is not lord [Col. 0074A] but guardian—so that he may show mercy and lend for the needs of the needy, as an executor administering a testament.

I have sometimes seen him so drained by extraordinary acts of generosity that necessity compelled him, unwilling and grieving, to engage in exactions and plunder. Would that he had remembered and effectually observed Paul’s words in the Second Epistle to the Corinthians: “I do not say,” he says, “that your generosity should mean relief for others but hardship for you; rather, that your abundance should supply their want, so that there may be equality, as it is written: ‘He who had much did not have too much, and he who had little did not have too little.’” [Note: [Col. 0073] II Cor. 8.]

I beg you, press him at a fitting time not to obscure the glory of the noble Church of Chartres, but to sustain it by assistance, raise it by counsel, and adorn it by the merits of holy conduct. [Col. 0074B] If he wishes to serve wholesomely Him whom to serve is to reign, and to have praise in His name, let him go up against the adversary and set himself as a wall for the house of the Lord. [Note: [Col. 0073] Ezek. 13.] For no title to illustrious reputation can belong more fittingly to a prelate than that he should courageously defend the condition of ecclesiastical liberty.

If he has done anything wrongly, if anything has at any time darkened his life, zeal for your house, O God, and love of justice will wholly restore and redeem it. These two things cause a man’s dead reputation to live again; and one who was formerly exposed to accusing tongues may afterwards, in the freedom of public favour, pour forth a fragrance of sweetness.

Indeed, as we have heard, an edict has gone forth from King Philip [Col. 0074C] [Note: [Col. 0073D] He means Philip Augustus, king of the Franks, who, in order to conquer Saladin, the most powerful prince of the Saracens, and to assist the Holy Land, demanded a tenth of all goods from laymen and clerics alike. This tenth was called the Saladin Tithe because it was collected to expel Saladin from the Holy Land.] that the realm of France should be registered and the Church burdened with repeated tithes. Thus the tithe will gradually pass into customary practice, [Note: [Col. 0073D]

Blesensis had rightly foreseen this. For although that overseas expedition was undertaken with such great preparation and zeal, it was nevertheless delayed for two years, while the tithes were exacted and paid. Nor, when the war ceased, did the exaction cease, as Choppinus indicates in book III of *De Domanio*, title 23:

> “The plan of holy expeditions having been neglected, the revenues of benefices are nevertheless tithed, and the tithes are retained in the annual accounts of the treasury as though they were patrimonial property.”

Written in the year 1188, when the kings of France and England, many magnates, and an innumerable multitude of others took the cross to assist the land of Jerusalem.]

and an abuse once presumed will impose shameful servitude upon the Church. A heaven-sent opportunity for triumphant grace is offered to our lord. It is in his choice either shamefully to submit a degenerate and dejected spirit to servitude, and impose an unbearable yoke upon his successors, or to obtain the eminence of an unfading crown.

I beg him not to fear an outburst of royal indignation. Since he is equal to the king in birth, [Note: [Col. 0074D] Because Rainald was a blood-relative of the king. See the notes to Letter 15.] he is not inferior to him in dignity. It is said through the prophet to the minister of God: “Kings shall be your foster-fathers, and you shall suck at the breasts of kings.” [Note: [Col. 0073] Isa. 49.] But in this cause God, who is greater than all, is the final [Col. 0074D] cause.

A good bishop, however, sows in persecution [Col. 0075A] what he will reap in joy. [Note: [Col. 0075] Ps. 125.] “His seed shall be mighty upon the earth”; [Note: [Col. 0075] Ps. 111.] for pressure will bring forth liberty, affliction delight, and bitterness sweetness. If he exposes himself to shame and confusion for Christ’s Church, it is written: “Because of double shame and reproach, they shall possess double in their land.” [Note: [Col. 0075] Isa. 61.]

What should a Christian doubt, for whom “to live is Christ and to die is gain”? [Note: [Col. 0075] Phil. 1.] Whatever happens to him, if he loves Christ, “his life is hidden with Christ in God.” [Note: [Col. 0075] Col. 3.] I beg that neither the favour of a flattering breeze move him nor a stormy whirlwind bend him. A whirlwind was once stirred up so that Elijah might be carried into heaven. [Note: [Col. 0075] IV Kings 2.] He is certain that he will die, but uncertain when he will die. He is nature’s debtor and must pay it death’s tribute. “We do not know what the coming day will bring forth,” [Note: [Col. 0075] Prov. 27.] [Col. 0075B] and who is secure of the present day? Who knows whether an ignominious, shameful, or sudden death may seize him, with none to rescue him?

When a man’s life is sweetest and most pleasant to him, then bitter death separates him from it. [Note: [Col. 0075] I Kings 15.] Scripture testifies: “When they say, ‘Peace and security,’ then sudden destruction and anguish will come upon them, as upon a woman with child, and they shall not escape.” [Note: [Col. 0075] I Thess. 5.] Job also says: “They spend their days in prosperity, and in a moment they descend to the underworld.” [Note: [Col. 0075] Job 21.] “It is dreadful to fall into the hands of the living God.” [Note: [Col. 0075] Heb. 10.]

Holy and salutary, therefore, is the thought of willingly exposing oneself to danger of life or reputation for Him who is the author of life and the rewarder of glory. It is safer for a man to lose his soul for Christ in order to keep it, than to keep it in order to lose it. The sum of this exhortation is that [Col. 0075C] your lord should look carefully to himself: that loss of earthly goods may not frighten him; that the favour of princes may not entice him; that ambition may not weaken him; and that the deceitful and treacherous hope of a longer life may not seduce him with its flatteries.

## LETTER XXI. TO H., A CANON, FORMERLY A FRIEND

**Argument.**—He describes and attacks the notable pride and arrogance of H., a canon formerly his friend.

PETER OF BLOIS, archdeacon of Bath, to H., his once beloved son and friend: greeting, and a more humble spirit.

Searching carefully and examining diligently everything which you possess by the benefit of nature or grace, [Col. 0075D] I cannot sufficiently wonder from what source an occasion for pride can have crept into you. For, because several causes concur in you, you ought to have been humble and lowly in your own eyes.

When recently I found you at Rouen and entered into conversation concerning our mutual association and friendship, I could not wring from you even one little word of gentleness or affection. I proposed whatever humility or modesty can suggest to the human heart, in order to draw from you some word of gentleness and humility. But you, in pride [Col. 0076A] and insolence, rolling your lofty and unbridled eyes in haughtiness, looking down upon everything with a certain pompous and supercilious expression, and conducting all things as though by sovereign command, scarcely—and even then most indignantly—looked at, and looked down upon, a friend to whom you can never be of necessary service and whose aid you always need.

For you looked at me only in order to despise me, and in order to turn your face away with a certain haughty lifting of the eyes from one who loved you sincerely. I know no reason for this except that you wished to appear great in your own eyes, though perhaps in the eyes of others you are judged most contemptible. I consider it the height of madness if a man bereft of reason judges himself wise; and I judge it no lesser insanity if one who is low-born and imprudent swells with arrogant pride.

Certainly, the arrogance you display would be intolerable enough in a king’s son; yet it is publicly known that you are not a king’s son, though he who begot you was crowned. I wonder whence the foot of pride has come to you; whence you have conceived matter for self-exaltation, unless it is because you are attached to foresters, so as to put into writing the tyrannical exactions by which the poor are oppressed. But those whom you enter upon the pages of condemnation before the foresters write you down and proscribe you before the Lord in the book of death.

When you were wholly ignorant of the literary art, you know that the letters of your friends, which you corrupted, made you a canon; and through those same letters you could easily be excommunicated, if they informed the supreme pontiff, together with your other enormities, of the office of condemned usurpation which you exercise.

Moreover, it was said to Daniel: “Daniel, [Col. 0076C] shut up the words and seal the book until the appointed time.” [Note: [Col. 0075] Chap. 12.] So I too shall endure patiently and will not pour out against you the spirit of my conceived indignation, until I learn what familiar and friendly correction may be able to accomplish in you.

Indeed, I ascribe it to foolishness that I instruct a fool and proud man. Solomon says: “He who rebukes the wicked brings a stain upon himself,” [Note: [Col. 0075] Prov. 9.] and “he who teaches a fool is like one who glues together a potsherd.” [Note: [Col. 0075] Ecclus. 22.] Correction is superfluous in one whom his obstinacy makes incorrigible, according to Solomon’s testimony: “Though you crush a fool in a mortar like groats, pounding him with a pestle, his folly will not depart from him.” [Note: [Col. 0075] Prov. 27.]

Descend, I beg you, into yourself, and dig through the wall of your conscience. You will see the kinds of abominations by which you may judge yourself unhappy. [Col. 0076D] For thus the Lord says to Ezekiel: “Son of man, dig through the wall”; [Note: [Col. 0075] Chap. 8.] and when he had dug through it, behold a multitude of creeping things and abominations. Another prophet had dug through this wall and, considering the misery of his own condition, said: “I am the man who sees my poverty.” [Note: [Col. 0075] Lam. 3.]

Nevertheless, you cannot be wisely humble, because you walk in things great and wonderful beyond you; conceiving the wind of great self-exaltation, you stretch yourself toward clouds and impossibilities. “The Lord will destroy deceitful lips and the tongue that speaks great things.” [Note: [Col. 0075] Ps. 11.] [Col. 0077A] “Do not give me loftiness of eyes, O God.” [Note: [Col. 0077] Ecclus. 23.] Take care, I beg you, lest the magnificence of your heart become an occasion of ruin to you. For it is written: “Before ruin the heart is exalted.” [Note: [Col. 0077] Prov. 16.] “I saw the wicked greatly exalted and lifted up,” [Note: [Col. 0077] Ps. 36.] he says, and adds: “I passed by, and behold, he was no more.” [Note: [Col. 0077] Ibid.]

Know one thing: with this pride of yours you can be pleasing neither to God nor to man. For even a bird is not accepted in the Lord’s sacrifice unless its feathers and the pouch of its lungs are removed. [Note: [Col. 0077] Lev. 1.]

## LETTER XXII. TO MASTER JOHN OF SALISBURY. [A.D. 1170.]

**Argument.**—He consoles John of Salisbury, living in exile with St Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury, with hope of future recompense. He urges [Col. 0077B] him to continue steadfastly to contend for the defence of ecclesiastical liberty, while putting away every desire for vengeance. He does not doubt that this struggle will at last have a glorious outcome in Thomas.

To his dearest friend Master JOHN OF SALISBURY, PETER OF BLOIS, archdeacon of Bath. [Note: [Col. 0077C]

Only the Merlin and Sorbonne manuscript 1 copies have “archdeacon of Bath” here in the title; it is not read in all the others, and rightly so, since Peter of Blois does not seem yet to have been in England when he wrote this. See his *Life*, prefixed by us to his works.—“To John of Salisbury.” This is John of Salisbury, the most learned among the scholars of his age, as his various works attest. Some of them have been printed; others, preserved chiefly in English libraries, await the assisting hand of scholars.

Born of modest parents and slender means, he remained for some time at first with Peter of Celle, who supported him kindly and generously. Hence Peter often calls him his clerk. John himself testifies in Letter 8 how much he was indebted to Peter. He then went to Paris, the citadel of learning, for study; under the care of Theobald the Great, Count of Champagne, a most generous man, he was educated in the schools.

Afterwards he went to Rome to visit Pope Adrian IV, his countryman. Adrian received him so warmly and liberally that he admitted him to further intimacy, frequently had him as a table-companion, and disclosed to him the more secret recesses of his conscience, as John himself testifies in his *Metalogicon*, book IV, chapter 42. John also plainly declares in the *Polycraticus*, book VI, chapter 24, how freely he spoke before Adrian at the supreme pontiff’s own command.

Having returned to Paris, he served for some time as a teacher in the university there; among his pupils of great name was Peter of Blois, who therefore often calls him his master. Then, after returning to his native country, he was first a familiar of Theobald, Archbishop of Canterbury, and afterwards the inseparable companion, until death, of St Thomas, Theobald’s successor. Thus Peter of Celle, book VII, Letter 8, says that he was “sprinkled with the precious blood of blessed Thomas the martyr.”

Four or five years after the death of St Thomas—namely, in the year of Christ 1176 according to Ralph and Gervase, or 1177 according to the Monk of Auxerre and Robert of Torigni—through the agency of William, son of Theobald the Great, who had been transferred from the see of Chartres to the archbishopric of Sens, and at the request of Louis the Younger, king of the Franks, John was elected bishop by the chapter of Chartres. Accordingly the dean, the cantor, and several members of the clergy of the Church of Chartres came to Canterbury with letters from the chapter, the king, and the Archbishop of Sens. They were introduced into the chapter of Canterbury and produced letters attesting the good faith and authority of their petition, as Gervase and Ralph relate.

After the letters had been publicly read, the elect was brought to the church amid the highest joy of all, with hymns and songs. He was then conducted into France by the men of Chartres and consecrated at Sens by Maurice, bishop of Paris. He governed the Church of Chartres for six or seven years. For he died in 1182 [Col. 0078D] and was buried in the abbey of Josaphat near Chartres.

He used to attribute his advancement to the merits of the glorious martyr, St Thomas, his master, and therefore very frequently wrote in his letters or charters: “John, by divine mercy and through the merits of St Thomas the martyr, humble minister of the Church of Chartres.” The Necrology of Chartres extols his piety and holiness wonderfully, and records among other things that, following his master’s example, he habitually wore haircloth from neck to feet; thus John Baptist Souchet relates in his manuscript history of the Church of Chartres, book IV, chapter 22.

Among the many benefits he conferred upon the Church of Chartres was found a precious vessel in which the blood of St Thomas was preserved: blood which he had collected, after the holy man’s death, when it had been shed upon the pavement of the church. Gervase says of it: “That most holy blood was collected together with the brain and fragments, carefully stored away, and shortly thereafter was to be offered to the whole world.”]

Greeting in the author of salvation.

Whenever I carefully consider the common afflictions of the English Church [Note: [Col. 0078D] The writers of that age, and especially the *Process of St Thomas*, compiled from the *Four-Part History* or *Quadrilogue*, relate at length the history of the calamities which arose in the English Church from the conflict between King Henry and Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury. [See *Patrologia*, vol. 190, edition.]] and the exile of your lord Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury, [Col. 0078A] it brings me very great consolation that he sets himself as a wall for God’s justice and for the liberty of the Church, and that through this persecution he will deserve a glorious end.

I see that you have been placed between hammer and anvil, and that sinners continually forge upon your backs. [Note: [Col. 0077] Ps. 123.] Yet if you fight in Christ and for Christ, He will not allow you to be tempted beyond what you are able to bear, but will make with the temptation a way of escape; [Note: [Col. 0077] I Cor. 10.] and the Lord will take the rod of sinners away from above the lot of the righteous, lest the righteous stretch out their hands to iniquity. [Note: [Col. 0077] Ps. 124.]

If truth does not lie, the outcome of your persecution will be unending blessedness. “Blessed,” He says, “are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake.” [Note: [Col. 0077] Matt. 5.] The Apostle Peter says: “Let none of you suffer as a murderer, [Col. 0078B] or thief, or slanderer, or one who covets what belongs to another.” [Note: [Col. 0077] I Pet. 4.] “For it is not the punishment but the cause that makes martyrdom.” [Note: [Col. 0077] Aug., Letter 147.] And, as the Apostle also says: “If you suffer anything for righteousness’ sake, blessed are you.” [Note: [Col. 0077] I Pet. 3.]

It is indeed God’s gift to believe in Him, but it is also an excellent gift to bear insults for Christ. “To you,” says the Apostle, “it has been granted for Christ, not only to believe in Him but also to suffer for His sake.” [Note: [Col. 0077] Phil. 1.] Therefore [Col. 0079A] I rejoice with you because you have turned justice into judgment, because you restrain the rebellion and obstinacy of certain persons by the punishment of suspension, [Note: [Col. 0079D] He seems to speak of the excommunication which St Thomas had pronounced against those who unjustly held property occupied from the Church of Canterbury, and likewise against the Archbishop of York, other bishops, and magnates who had attended the coronation of the younger King Henry. See the *Process*, book II, chapter 29; Gervase and Ralph.] provided that you do this from a movement of reason and justice, not through zeal for revenge or desire to avenge another’s injury.

I beg you, do nothing from resentment or hatred, but let all your actions be done in charity. For you will not gather sheaves of salvation from this persecution unless your entire intention proceeds from the inmost heart of charity. Since in Holy Scripture an oven signifies anger or persecution, we are taught in Leviticus that the sacrifice which is to be baked in an oven [Note: [Col. 0079] Lev. 2.] must first be sprinkled with the oil of charity, lest it be burned. The mind of one preparing himself to endure persecution must first be softened with the oil of charity, so that he may neither fall away from charity in adversities [Col. 0079B] nor burn against his brother with zeal for vengeance or hatred.

It is therefore meritorious for you, and praiseworthy before God and men, if you restrain the disobedience of subjects through justice as intermediary. “Blessed are those who keep judgment and do justice at all times.” [Note: [Col. 0079] Ps. 105.] In carrying out justice there ought to be no respect of persons or selection. Whether the person is a brother or son, prelate or subject, the fruit of justice must always be sought; those who judge the world must always judge justly.

For when the Levites, in killing their brothers and sons, had avenged the sin of idolatry, Moses said to them: “Today each of you has consecrated his hands in his son and in his brother, that a blessing may be given to you.” [Note: [Col. 0079] Exod. 32.] Solomon likewise says: “Those who rebuke shall be praised, and [Col. 0079C] a blessing shall come upon them.” [Note: [Col. 0079] Prov. 24.]

It is greatly praiseworthy in your lord that he has so gone up alone against the adversary, that he sets himself as a wall for the house of Israel and pleads for the gentle of the earth.
