[Note: [Col. 0079] Isa. 1.] Today we have him, singular and unique among the sons of the shaken. “A son has been born to us in place of our fathers,” [Note: [Col. 0079] Ps. 126.] who, after the example of the Apostles, alone today “executes vengeance among the nations and rebukes among the peoples.” [Note: [Col. 0079] Ps. 149.]

And just as those princes of peoples, who are now gathered with the God of Abraham [Note: [Col. 0079] Ps. 46.] for Christ’s justice, [Col. 0080A] have been exceedingly raised up as the mighty gods of the earth, [Note: [Col. 0079] Ibid.] so his honour also, if he perseveres in administering justice, shall be raised without measure.

That he is now in exile, that many things are attempted to his disgrace—by the benefit of patience all this will be turned to his glory. “Our light and momentary tribulation,” says the Apostle, “works in us an immeasurable weight of glory.” [Note: [Col. 0079] II Cor. 4.] “Show yourselves as ministers of God in much patience.” [Note: [Col. 0079] II Cor. 6.]

> For virtue is a widow when patience does not make it firm.  
> [Note: [Col. 0079] See Newburgh, book II, chapter 25, and Polydore, book III of *English History*.]

And who has triumphed from the earliest cradle of the Church without patience? Indeed, although your lord has much of the spirit of fortitude, it is said that, because of the coronation of the new king of the English [Note: [Col. 0079D] This was the true and only cause or occasion of St Thomas’s death. For, through the mediation of the supreme pontiff, the king of the Franks, and the Archbishop of Sens, Thomas had been reconciled to King Henry, though Henry had retained hostility for a very long time and persistently. The harmful decrees which had caused so disastrous a conflict between king and archbishop were withdrawn and abolished, and the archbishop himself was permitted to return to possession of his church and all its goods. But because he would allow no diminishment of its rights, he excommunicated, in the name of the supreme pontiff, the Archbishop of York, who had consecrated the younger king, several bishops and magnates, and all others who had attended the coronation. To avoid appearing to avenge an injury done to his own person, he had previously obtained the sentence of excommunication from the supreme pontiff. This so inflamed Henry’s anger that he burst out into certain harsh words against the archbishop, from which wicked men took occasion to murder the holy man.] [Col. 0080B] carried out by the Archbishop of York, and because of certain privileges, as they say, fraudulently obtained against him, he was so troubled that from faintness of spirit and tempest “his feet were almost moved, his steps almost poured out.” [Note: [Col. 0079] Ps. 72.]

Nevertheless, you who are the archbishop’s hand and eye, strengthen with your holy exhortations the feeble hands and make firm the weak knees. It is no wonder that he is disturbed by tribulations and pressures. Yet if he leans wholly upon and clings to Him who sends forth roots in His chosen ones, he will safely meet every wind of temptation and whirlwind. [Note: [Col. 0079] Ecclus. 24.]

Certainly the ancient fathers, when they were at times under severe constraints, were often overcome by weariness. Thus that strong endurance of sufferings, by which they burned in the Lord, seemed for a time to grow lukewarm and numb, [Col. 0080C] until, clothed from on high with power through the grace of divine consolation, they rose again in a spirit of fortitude.

Elijah, fleeing from Jezebel’s face and made weary of this life, cast himself beneath a juniper tree and asked for his soul that he might die. “It is enough for me,” he said; “take away my soul.” [Note: [Col. 0079] III Kings 19.] The Apostle too, wasting away with a similar weariness, said: “We were burdened beyond measure, so that we were weary even of life.” [Note: [Col. 0079] II Cor. 1.] The prophet, frequently experiencing these wearinesses, says: “Through the strength of Your hand I failed, and You made my soul waste away like a spider.” [Col. 0081A] [Note: [Col. 0081] Ps. 38.]

But charity grew stronger in them out of weariness, and from weakness itself strength increased—a thing which might perhaps seem incredible to someone, unless the Apostle, who had often read these things in the book of experience, bore testimony to it: “For when I am weak,” he says, “then I am stronger”; and it was also said to him: “Power is made perfect in weakness.” [Note: [Col. 0081] II Cor. 12.]

If, therefore, because of the onset of evils which your lord endures, or because of the desolation of his own people, or because of the length of this exile, you see numbness of mind creeping over him, be a comfort to him, lest he despair or waver. For the time of his visitation is near. If the swellings of the sea are wonderful, wonderful also is the Lord on high, [Note: [Col. 0081] Ps. 92.] who turns the storm [Col. 0081B] into a breeze and the king’s indignation into favour.

Through the legates of the Apostolic See [Note: [Col. 0081C] Several legates were sent at various times by Alexander III to establish peace between King Henry and St Thomas. But who these men were, sent after the coronation of the younger Henry and mentioned here by Blesensis, is wholly uncertain, since not a word concerning that legation is found in the authors of the time, nor even in Baronius, who described the entire affair with the greatest care. Unless perhaps we identify them with the cardinals Gratian and Vivian, whom historians relate were last sent by the supreme pontiff for this cause in the preceding year, 1169. See *Process*, book II, chapter 27; Gervase, Ralph, and after them Baronius, vol. XII, under the year 1169.—This letter seems to have been written in 1170, since it mentions the coronation of the younger Henry, which took place that year. At the beginning of the following year, 1171, St Thomas was crowned with martyrdom.] with whom I came from the Roman curia as far as Bologna, he will either be most firmly reconciled with the king of the English in the near future or be transferred to the eminence of a greater patriarchate.

But however the Lord may choose to dispose of his affair, if he perseveres as he is today, let him confidently await the outcome of this struggle. Therefore let him not heed the voices of flatterers, but follow the Spirit of God which is in him; and wherever the Spirit goes, let the wheels also move together. [Note: [Col. 0081] Ezek. 10.] For I know that the course of his contest will be glorious if only he perseveres in the course of fortitude and constancy [Col. 0082A] which he has begun. “For he who has contended lawfully shall be crowned”; [Note: [Col. 0081] II Tim. 2.] and although all virtues run toward the prize, perseverance alone is crowned.

I beg you, as my lord and master, to inform me more frequently of your own condition and his. For, since I can do nothing else, I continually pray for you, that, through the preventing grace of the Most High, you may obtain the favour of the king of the English and free administration of your affairs.

I have read your book *On the Trifles of Courtiers*, and it refreshed me wonderfully. For it contains an excellent model of learning, and, because of the artful variety of its thoughts, an inestimable source of delight. Fare well.

## LETTER XXIII. TO OCTAVIAN, [Note: [Col. 0081C]

This is Octavian, a noble Roman. First apostolic subdeacon under Alexander III, then cardinal-deacon of SS. Sergius and Bacchus, afterwards made cardinal-bishop of Ostia by Lucius III, and vicar of the city by Clement III, Ciaconius says in the *Lives of the Popes*. As to the legation in which he was engaged when Blesensis “wrote him this letter, full of complaints concerning the wrongs committed in the Church of God,” Baronius, under the year 1187, says that he “was sent by Urban III to England with Hugh de Nunant, bishop-elect of Chester, otherwise Coventry. He entrusted them with a legation to Ireland, to crown there John, son of King Henry II. But the king postponed the coronation and took the said legates with him into Normandy,” etc.

[Col. 0082C] “This is the Octavian to whom Richard, king of the English, when setting out for the holy war, spoke many shameful things on meeting him at the mouth of the Tiber—for he was bishop of Ostia—reproaching the Romans with simony: namely, that they had received 700 marks for the consecration of the bishop of Le Mans, 1,500 marks for the legation of the bishop of Ely, and a great sum so that the Archbishop of Bordeaux, accused by his own clergy of a crime, might not be deposed.” Baronius reports the same from Roger.

He is also the man whom, Baronius says, Celestine III sent in 1192 with Jordan, cardinal of Fossanova, into Normandy, to settle the dispute between William, bishop of Ely and chancellor of the kingdom of England, and Walter, Archbishop of Rouen—a matter of which we shall speak below in its place. But they departed without accomplishing anything.

How highly he stood in Innocent III’s esteem appears especially from this: the supreme [Col. 0082D] pontiff ordered the castle of Monte Santa Maria destroyed, where, in his predecessor’s time, Conrad Musca had detained Octavian, bishop of Ostia, as he was returning from France, “so that this demolition might be a memorial for all time,” says Ciaconius in the same place. Innocent also instructed him, whom he had made his vicar in the city, to dedicate certain altars of St Peter’s Basilica with solemn rite. Moreover, he twice sent him as legate from his side: once to Sicily, to the Empress Constance, to exact in his own name and that of her son Frederick II an oath of fealty, and to grant her, by benefice-right and in the name of the Apostolic See, the titles of the kingdom according to ancestral custom. Again he was sent into France to Philip Augustus, so that he might declare void the lawful [Col. 0083D] marriage which Philip had contracted with his wife Ismberga or Engelberga, and the adulterous union which he had entered, against law and right, with Agnes, otherwise Maria, daughter of the Duke of Merania in Istria. Raynaldus, under the year 1200.

It should further be noted that all the copies call Octavian “cardinal-priest” in the heading, although Baronius says that the man sent by Urban into England was only a cardinal-deacon. [Note: [Col. 0083D] Roger’s text reads “subdeacon,” but “deacon” is rightly supplied in the margin.] Ciaconius above likewise says that he was made cardinal-bishop only by Clement III.]

CARDINAL OF THE ROMAN CHURCH. A.D. 1187.]

[Col. 0082B]

**Argument.**—He complains sorrowfully that persons everywhere unworthy—whether one considers learning, virtue, or age—rush through the height of ambition into bishoprics and other dignities. He earnestly entreats Octavian, legate of the Apostolic See, to employ his authority to keep all ambitious persons and simoniacs away from the helm of the Church.

To his dearest lord and friend Octavian, cardinal-priest of the Holy Roman Church and legate of the Apostolic See, Master Peter of Blois, archdeacon of Bath: greeting.

O cares of humankind—O how much emptiness there is in things! [Note: [Col. 0081] Persius, *Satires* 1.] O vain glory! O blind ambition! O [Col. 0083A] insatiable hunger for earthly honor! O moth of hearts, overthrow of souls, desire for offices! Whence has this plague crept in? Whence has this accursed presumption grown strong—that the unworthy should seek dignities, and that, the less they have deserved to rise to honors, the more importunately they thrust themselves upon honors?

Today, through right and wrong alike, these wretches run, at the peril of soul and body, to the pastoral chair; nor do they consider that it is for them a seat of pestilence, while for themselves and others it becomes an occasion of ruin. Among flocks and herds, Jerome testifies, the ram and bull that excel the others in body and spirit go before them [Note: [Col. 0083] Jerome, *Letter to Fabiola* and on Isaiah 34.]; but man, more beastly than all beasts, presumes to rule his betters all the more indiscreetly and boldly as he has less confidence in titles of virtue or purity of conscience. [Note: [Col. 0083] Seneca, *Letters* 90.]

[Col. 0083B] Would that they were wise, understood, and foresaw their latter end [Note: [Col. 0083] Deut. 32], and did not add the sins of the people to their own transgressions! The words are those of Ecclesiasticus [Note: [Col. 0083] Ch. 7]: “Do not seek from a man a position of leadership, nor from a king a seat of honor. Do not seek to become a judge unless you have strength to break through the iniquities of the people. Do not thrust yourself into the people, nor bind double sins to yourself.”

He who has learned nothing becomes another’s teacher and, like sounding brass or a tinkling cymbal [Note: [Col. 0083] 1 Cor. 13.], usurps the office of preacher, though he is a useless log and a mute idol. Among the ancients, the condition of the wise was held inestimably venerable; today prudence is trampled underfoot as cheap and contemptible, while, by an abominable reversal, folly is set on high. This is what Ecclesiastes mournfully [Col. 0083C] laments: “I saw,” he says, “an evil under the sun: a fool set in lofty dignity, and wise men sitting below.” [Note: [Col. 0083] Ch. 10.]

Those wholly ignorant of Holy Scripture usurp the unbearable burden of dignity, presuming upon knowledge belonging to others rather than their own. Different was the Apostle’s judgment when instructing his disciple: “To you,” he says, “I entrust, son Timothy, the governance of the Church of God, because I know that you possess knowledge of the sacred writings.” [Note: [Col. 0083] 1 Tim. 1; 2 Tim. 3.] For spiritual knowledge is a sword in the hand of a mighty man. It is the bag in which David put three most clear stones, with which he overthrew Goliath. [Note: [Col. 0083] 1 Sam. 17.] It is the ass’s jawbone with which Samson made a slaughter of a thousand enemies. [Note: [Col. 0083] Judg. 15.] It is that ploughshare with which Shamgar killed six hundred Philistines. [Note: [Col. 0083] Judg. 3.] An unlettered bishop is a mute herald.

[Col. 0084A] It belongs to a prelate to instruct those subject to him, to render the people acceptable to God by opening the mysteries of the Scriptures. For Peter and his successors are commanded to put out the net into the deep [Note: [Col. 0083] Luke 5]: that is, to disclose for the catching of human beings the profound understanding of Holy Scripture. Yet today, “as the people, so the priest” [Note: [Col. 0083] Isa. 24]; as is his darkness, so also is his light. “Be ashamed, Sidon,” says the sea [Note: [Col. 0083] Isa. 23]; let the prelate be ashamed and grieve that he rules the people without benefiting them, that he has assumed the office of teacher yet is mute in the instruction of the people.

It is the utterance of the lamenting prophet: “My people have become a lost flock; their shepherds have led them astray” [Note: [Col. 0083] Isa. 50]; “mute dogs, unable to bark.” [Note: [Col. 0083] Isa. 56.] They ought to have driven wolves away from their flocks, but they themselves are wolves toward their own people; caring neither for their own salvation nor for that of those entrusted to them, they hurl themselves with their flocks [Col. 0084B] into the pit of eternal death.

Today mere boys and effeminate men are promoted to the episcopal dignity. Thus Joseph is sold to Potiphar the eunuch [Note: [Col. 0083] Gen. 39], when a fruitless and effeminate bishop presumptuously usurps, to his own condemnation, Christ’s teaching and the stewardship of God’s sacraments. But when the Lord sends Jeremiah to instruct the people—Jeremiah whom he had sanctified from his mother’s womb—the prophet, considering his own incompleteness, as one still elementary and unformed in the shaping of words, replied: “Ah, ah, ah, Lord God, I do not know how to speak.” [Note: [Col. 0083] Jer. 1.]

Moses also, when he was sent by the Lord to free the people of Israel from Egypt, said: “I beseech you, Lord, send whom you will send; from yesterday and the day before yesterday, since you spoke to your servant, I have become slow of tongue.” [Note: [Col. 0083] Exod. 4.] And who today excuses himself from the pontifical burden? Who today pleads his insufficiency? Who today is dragged unwillingly to it, or protests? Where today can one find another like Ammonius? [Note: [Col. 0083] Palladius, *Lausiac History*, ch. 11; Socrates, bk. IV, ch. 18.] When clergy and people had elected him bishop, he utterly refused to consent to the election. As they prevailed and dragged him unwillingly forward, he cut off his left ear at its root before them all, saying: “Divine law permits no man with a severed ear to be made bishop.”

When Timothy the patriarch judged him worthy of the episcopate even if his nose and ears were cut off, provided that he excelled in knowledge and virtues, and they again seized and dragged Ammonius unwillingly along, Ammonius said: “Unless you release me swiftly, I shall cut off my tongue, because of which I please you.” [Col. 0085A] For the appetite for dignity is heavenly in its origin: in heaven it “conceived and brought forth iniquity.” [Note: [Col. 0085] Ps. 7.] By means of it, he who had not yet labored so as to sit wished to sit on the sides of the north. [Note: [Col. 0085] Isa. 14.] But these men too have not yet labored in order to sit—to ascend the eminence of the pastoral chair. They have not yet undertaken the purpose of perfection. They have not yet, with Peter, left the net; with John, the sheet; with Matthew, the tax-office; with Joseph, the cloak; with the man of the Gospel, the burial of their father; with the Samaritan woman, the water-jar—that is, the desire of the world.

Because of the sin of such men, as of the sons of Eli, the ark—that is, the glory of the Lord—has today been transferred from Israel to Ashdod [Note: [Col. 0085] 1 Sam. 3], that is, to the fire of concupiscence. Yet this fire does not kindle, [Col. 0085B] but fills with smoke; it does not illuminate, but blinds, as it is written: “Fire fell upon them, and they did not see the sun.” [Note: [Col. 0085] Ps. 57.] From Ashdod it is transferred into the temple of Dagon [Note: [Col. 0085] 1 Sam. 5], that is, of sadness or desolation. Is not an unlearned and foolish prelate an idol of sadness and mourning—one elected in God’s wrath and in the desolation of the people, and set up like an idol [Note: [Col. 0085] Isa. 57]—so that what is read in Matthew may come to pass: “When you see the abomination of desolation standing in the holy place,” that is, in the Church of God, “then woe to those who are pregnant and nursing”? [Note: [Col. 0085] Matt. 24.]

For those who had conceived the spirit of salvation are suffocated by the example of such men. Those who sought the nourishment of heavenly life are sustained by no pasture of the divine word. “The little ones,” says the prophet, “asked for bread, and there was no one to break it [Col. 0085C] for them.” [Note: [Col. 0085] Lam. 4.]

Therefore you, most beloved Father, who have been sent from the side of the supreme pontiff to serve as Christ’s legate, arise for the uprooting of this most accursed plague. Behold, the Lord has set you over nations and kingdoms, “to pluck up and to destroy, to scatter and to dissipate, and to build and to plant.” [Note: [Col. 0085] Jer. 1.] Let the zeal of your authority be kindled and burn against the evil of ambition; scatter and uproot wicked plantings. Build and plant in the Church of God such men as humility, innocence, a more approved life, and learning commend—[Col. 0086A] men who teach their subjects; who do not flatter the rich or burden the poor; who do not fear the threats of the powerful; who correct crimes and do not squeeze purses; whose speech is teaching, whose conduct is justice, whose authority lies not in dress or ostentation but in learning and the defense of faith; whose life is publicly commendable and whose memory is in blessing.

At the arrival of you and your colleague [Note: [Col. 0085C]

Hugh, bishop-elect of Chester, mentioned above.

This letter was written in the year 1187, in which, according to Baronius, Octavian was sent into Ireland.]

I pray that the Church of Christ may rejoice, so that, oppressed by simoniacs and the ambitious, she may breathe again under your consolation. May the clergy rejoice and the peoples exult that today in you they have received fellow citizens of the apostles and members of God’s household, bearing peace and enlightening their country, seeking for us and for others the rewards of eternal life, so that from the labor and solicitude of your [Col. 0086B] legation you may carry back unfading sheaves of righteousness.

## LETTER XXIV. TO THE HOUSEHOLD OF THOMAS, ARCHBISHOP OF CANTERBURY

[Note: [Col. 0085C] The title of this letter varies. In some copies it is thus: “A letter of excuse”; in others, “An exhortation that R. be reconciled to blessed Thomas”; in others it is otherwise. But in none is the name of Peter of Blois found—something also found in many other cases. Yet no one has doubted that it is his.]  
[A.D. 1169–70.]

**SUMMARY.**—Reginald, archdeacon of Salisbury, had incurred the displeasure of Thomas, the exiled archbishop. Peter wishes him, being ready to make satisfaction and be reconciled, to be restored to friendship and, through that friendship, to partnership in the persecution.

You grieve and complain because I went to the archdeacon of Salisbury. [Note: [Col. 0085D] This is Reginald, who later became bishop of Bath. Saint Thomas was deeply offended with him, as is evident from the letter which he wrote to his messengers whom he had sent to Rome, in Baronius, vol. II, under the year 1168, in these words:

> “Take precaution and maintain continual vigilance against our adversaries, and especially against that bastard, fornicator, and enemy of the Church’s peace—the son of a priest, Reginald of Salisbury—who, insofar as he can, everywhere slanders and [Col. 0086C] maligns our person, saying that we are traitors and that we gave him our word that we would not harm his father in any respect, etc. He also says that, if the lord pope should die, he would have us erased from the book of life, boasting that the Roman court is so venal that, through gifts, he can obtain whatever he wishes. [Col. 0086D] He likewise urged the king of England to make requests of this sort to the lord pope: that authority be committed to some bishop in England to crown the king’s son and consecrate bishops, in order thus to deceive the lord pope. When the king answered that he believed he could not obtain those requests from the lord pope, Reginald replied: ‘The lord pope acts like a stupid and foolish man if he [Note: This does not seem to be an addition.] grants your requests.’”

These allegations seem to have been wrongly suggested to Saint Thomas by certain ill-wishers, if the things Peter of Blois writes of the same Reginald in this letter are true. More concerning the same Reginald occurs at Letter 30.] But if it is a fault to have gone to him, necessity excuses me. In the word of the Lord I tell you that I neither knew nor [Col. 0086C] had heard that your lord had conceived any resentment or hatred against him.

Even now I know with complete certainty that he desires with all his heart to be reconciled to your lord; and already, unless an enemy had obstructed him, he would in every respect have made satisfaction and humbly cast himself at his feet. I still daily hope for his correction and conversion, and I apply diligent effort toward it. But there are some with him who sow tares and strictly forbid him to be reconciled to your lord, if he desires the welfare and peace of his father, whom he loves above all things, [Col. 0087A] and of his whole family.

You know indeed that he is a prudent and capable man and could be most useful to you and your lord if he stood with you and took upon himself a share in your persecution. I know also that even the slightest exhortation from the lord of Canterbury would effectively incline him to this. I beg you, take pains that a letter on this matter be sent to him from your lord. If you do not do so for the sake of your own advantage, do it at least for the prospect of his conversion and salvation.

Certainly Moses, wishing to turn Hobab away from the error of paganism and to retain him as necessary, said: “We are setting out for the place which the Lord will give us. Come with us, and we shall do you good, because the Lord has promised good things to Israel. Do not [Col. 0087B] leave us, for you know in what places we ought to pitch camp, and you will be our guide.” [Note: [Col. 0087] Num. 10.] If Moses asked a pagan to become his guide, let an archdeacon, inferior to Moses, not be ashamed, I pray, to associate with himself an archdeacon as a partner in sufferings and labors. For this is precisely what the archdeacon desires: that he may find labor and suffering for him and with him.

Recently we were reading in the Book of Kings and encountered the words of Ittai the Gittite to David, who was leaving Jerusalem barefoot before Absalom, when David told him to return. He answered: “As the Lord lives, I shall not leave you, neither in life nor in death.” The archdeacon therefore sighed and said: “May the Lord do so to me and add this also, before I die, [Note: [Col. 0087] 2 Sam. 15] [Col. 0087C] that I may be able thus to say this from my heart to the lord of Canterbury, and fulfill it in deed.”

I beg you, suggest to the lord archbishop that he not provoke his cleric with words or embitter him with threats, lest, while wood is being cut with a neighbor in the forest, the iron slip from the axe-handle [Note: [Col. 0087] Deut. 19] and kill the neighbor. For, Gregory testifies, we cut wood when through rebuke we cut down the sins of our neighbor; but the axe-head slips and kills the neighbor when an insulting correction turns the neighbor’s conscience, wounded away from the spirit of love, into deadly hatred. [Note: [Col. 0087] *Morals*, bk. X, ch. 9.]

Certainly, no admonition is acceptable in the eyes of the Most High unless it is made from the depth of charity and in a spirit of gentleness. This is clearly evident from Elijah’s words: “Behold, a spirit of the Lord overturning mountains and shattering rocks—and the Lord was not in the spirit; and after the spirit an earthquake—and the Lord was not in the earthquake; and after [Col. 0088A] the earthquake a fire—and the Lord was not in the fire; and after the fire the whisper of a gentle breeze—and the Lord was in the whisper.” [Note: [Col. 0087] 3 Kings 19.]

For, just as terrifying rebuke is expressed by the foregoing things, so gentle and friendly exhortation is signified by the whisper of a gentle breeze. The latter is made in silence; the former in anger and tumult, as it is written: “The waters of Siloam run in silence, but the waters of Rezin pass in tumult.” [Note: [Col. 0087] Isa. 8.]

Moreover, the lord of Canterbury, who, as it seems to me, has now undertaken the purpose of a stricter and loftier life, [Note: [Col. 0087D] He speaks of Saint Thomas, who went to Pontigny and put on the monastic habit blessed and sent to him by Alexander III, then staying at Sens; from the *Proceedings*, bk. II, ch. 12; Baronius, vol. XII, under the year 1164. From the foregoing it might be inferred that this letter was written about 1164, when Saint Thomas withdrew to Pontigny after returning from Pope Alexander, who was then at Sens. But the letter seems to have been written [Col. 0088D] at Paris, before Peter went to Sicily. Yet because he says at the beginning of the letter that he went to the archdeacon of Salisbury, it seems more probable that this letter was written only around 1170, when Saint Thomas had already long been in exile. For it is established that Peter of Blois returned from Sicily in 1168 and remained for some time at Paris, until he was summoned to England by Henry II around 1170.] has received not the spirit of this world but the Spirit who is from God. Therefore let the love of God, which has been poured into his heart, [Note: [Col. 0087] Rom. 5.] extend even to his neighbor, as befits a holy man.

Thus, if the archdeacon of Salisbury persists in the satisfaction and obedience that he promises, the bowels of charity should be opened to him. I myself consider it a great gain to win so great a man, who, if he clings to the footsteps of the lord of Canterbury, will bear fruit in due season in the Church of God. If some occasion of suspicion against the archdeacon still remains in his mind, let him test his faith by deeds before admitting him into the sanctuary of his intimacy. Joshua did not receive the angel as a friend before learning that he was a friend: he first asked whether he was on his side or that of his adversaries. [Note: [Col. 0087] Josh. 5.]

I assert confidently that, if he should seek to bring about his conversion, he will find Paul in him in whom he finds Saul. For anxious concern for the archdeacon’s conversion and salvation [Col. 0088C] touches me; I cannot but love one who often anticipates me in his blessings.

## LETTER XXV. TO THE OFFICIAL OF THE BISHOP OF CHARTRES

**SUMMARY.**—He exhorts the official to abandon the office he has assumed, because of the grave and numerous abuses joined to it; accordingly, he describes at length the frauds and devices of officials.

Master Peter of Blois, archdeacon of Bath, to G., official of the bishop of Chartres: greeting and salutary counsel.

Because I love you most affectionately in the bowels of Jesus Christ, I have resolved to exhort you by wholesome admonitions to depart in good time from Ur of the Chaldeans [Note: [Col. 0087] Gen. 15] and from the midst of Babylon, and to abandon the ministry of this most damnable stewardship. I know that greed for gifts overturned [Col. 0088D] your heart so that you became the bishop’s official. You had at one time read, but perhaps neglected, that saying of blessed [Col. 0089A] Job: “Fire shall devour the bodies of those who gladly receive gifts.” [Note: [Col. 0089] Ch. 15.] Therefore blessed is he “who shakes his hands free from every gift.” [Note: [Col. 0089] Isa. 33.]

I believe such officials derive their name not from *officium* (“service”) but from the verb *officit* (“it harms”):

> For this race of men is called **Officiperdi**:  
> *Officit* is a word excessively cruel and bitter;  
> a term full of evils—hence he is called an *officialis*.

The entire purpose of officials is to shear, squeeze dry, and flay, on behalf of the bishops, the most wretched sheep entrusted to their jurisdiction, as though acting in the bishops’ place. For these are the bishops’ leeches, vomiting up the blood of others which they have drunk. For Scripture testifies: “The riches which the wicked man gathered he shall vomit up, and God shall draw them from his throat.” [Note: [Col. 0089] Job 20.]

These men [Col. 0089B] are like a sponge in the hand of one pressing it, and like filters, channeling riches to their masters while retaining for themselves from their accursed gains nothing but the filth and dregs of sin. What they collect by oppressing the poor becomes luxury for bishops but torment for officials.

> Thus you bees make honey—not for yourselves. [Note: [Col. 0089] Virgil, *Life*.]  
> Thus you heap up wealth—not for yourselves.

These are those secret little doors through which the ministers of Bel secretly carried away the sacrifices placed on the table by the king. [Note: [Col. 0089] Dan. 14.] Thus the bishop, as if by a long hand, seizes another’s goods; removing from himself the stigma of the crime, he thrusts the danger of guilt and infamy upon his officials.

Therefore, as though beneath the bishop’s shadow [Col. 0089C] and under the pretext of cloaked justice, they oppress subjects, burden churches, and violently invade the revenues of others. Their eyes are fixed on gifts; they pay no heed to orphan or widow. These are the words of Jesus son of Sirach: “The lust of a eunuch deflowers a maiden; so also does one who by force renders an unjust judgment.” [Note: [Col. 0089] Ecclus. 10.]

A eunuch oppresses a virgin and, seeking no offspring from the oppression but serving only his own lust, corrupts but does not beget. Thus a prelate who satisfies his anger or avarice and seeks no fruit of justice corrupts but does not correct; he exasperates but does not amend. For what is done under the pretext of counterfeit religion or feigned justice bears no fruit unto life and builds nothing for salvation.

Saul spares the best flocks of Amalek as though to sacrifice them to God, [Col. 0089D] and incurs the divine displeasure. Gideon makes an ephod from the spoil of the Midianites, [Note: [Col. 0089] Judg. 8.] and it turns to ruin for him and his house. I could bear more patiently this administration which you have damnably usurped, if you did not excel in knowledge of sacred letters. The causes and judgments into which you recklessly—indeed, I might say shamelessly—thrust yourself are decided more by customary and secular law than by ecclesiastical law. It did not become a learned ecclesiastic to entangle himself thus in secular affairs. [Col. 0090A] [Note: [Col. 0089] 2 Tim. 2.]

Writing to the Corinthians, the Apostle says: “If you have secular disputes, appoint as judges in the Church those who are least esteemed among you.” [Note: [Col. 0089] 1 Cor. 6.] The office of officials, among whose number you have enrolled yourself, today consists in confusing laws, stirring up suits, undoing settlements, contriving delays, suppressing truth, fostering falsehood, pursuing profit, selling equity, gaping after exactions, and devising tricks. They burden their hosts with excessive transportation and a multitude of retainers. They demand delicate and superfluous foods, though it is written: “Eat and drink what is set before you.” [Note: [Col. 0089] Luke 10.]

Prodigal with what belongs to others, they are miserly with their own; they lie in wait for words and hunt syllables. They set traps and nets [Col. 0090B] to catch money; they interpret laws as they please and, according to their own will, now reject them, now admit them. They pervert sound statements and overturn prudent legal arguments; they break covenants, nurture quarrels, conceal fornications, dissolve marriages, encourage adulteries, enter houses, and lead captive “little women laden with sins”; [Note: [Col. 0089] 2 Tim. 3.] they defame the innocent and acquit the guilty. And, to comprise much in few words: while these sons of avarice and servants of Mammon transact everything for sale, they put themselves up for sale to the devil.

The Lord says in the Gospel: “Freely you received; freely give”; [Note: [Col. 0089] Matt. 10.] and Solomon in Proverbs: “Buy truth, and do not sell wisdom and instruction.” [Note: [Col. 0089] Prov. 23.] I fear that the spirit of pride and the desire to rule may carry you away into false vanities and insanities. [Note: [Col. 0089] Ps. 39.] Would that you attended to the words of Wisdom, threatening such men: “O you who delight in multitudes, power was given you by God, who will examine your works and your thoughts, because, although you were ministers of his kingdom, you did not judge rightly. But the Lord will appear terribly, and a most severe judgment shall befall those who preside; [Col. 0090C] a stronger torment presses upon the stronger.” [Note: [Col. 0089] Wis. 6.]

Friend, you fight most perilously in the arena of this world: death follows you; life flees; the flesh flatters; the world entices; the roaring lion, seeking whom he may devour, runs about. [Note: [Col. 0089] 1 Pet. 5.] For everyone who contends in the contest abstains from all things. [Note: [Col. 0089] 1 Cor. 9.] Would that you abstained from such harmful men, [Col. 0090D] so that the prince of this world might have nothing in you that is his, and so that the adversary might have nothing in the arena in which one runs for the prize by which to catch or hold you, or delay you from the prize.

If you believe me—indeed, if you believe in God—leave promptly the office of official: that ministry of condemnation, wheel of evils, and spirit of dizziness that whirls you around toward emptiness. Have pity on your soul by pleasing God, [Note: [Col. 0089] Ecclus. 30.] whom you cannot please without the destruction of your office.

## LETTER XXVI. TO A CERTAIN COMPANION OF HIS

[Col. 0091A]

**SUMMARY.**—He writes that, having abandoned the study of civil law, he is applying himself to theology at Paris; that the study and practice of civil law do not suit clerics because of the very great abuses of advocates.

To his lord B. and his most beloved companion, Peter of Blois, archdeacon of Bath [Note: [Col. 0091D] “Archdeacon of Bath” is wrongly given in the title. Peter of Blois had not yet departed for England when he wrote this, but was still applying himself to theology at Paris, as he himself admits in the letter. Yet that title occurs thus in Sorb. 1; Maz. 1, 2, and Merl., but not in the other manuscripts.]: greeting.

Our devotion would have been more fervent in this epistolary greeting, were it not opposed by either the envious distance of places or the scarcity of travelers. Therefore let present and never-interrupted affection supply greetings sent by proxy. Since civil possession does not require bodily presence, you have me nearer even though remote, and possess me more strongly in absence; [Col. 0091B] nor does local interval, bodily distance, or the passage of time weaken the strength of affection.

And if you attend to the first law concerning verbal obligations:

> “An interval of intervening time does not invalidate an obligation.”  
> [Note: [Col. 0091] *Digest* bk. 45, law 1, from Ulpian.]

Being yours and most devoted to you, I apply myself to theology at Paris, often sighing for the camp of Bologna’s warfare—a camp I loved intensely and abandoned too soon and prematurely. Yet we read concerning a legacy of use and usufruct that a usufructuary may anticipate the ripeness of fruits; and from olives a more abundant supply of oil commonly flows before the time of ripeness. [Note: [Col. 0091] *Digest* bk. VII, tit. 1, law 27.]

Running, therefore, to the oil which Aaron is commanded to offer with cakes, [Note: [Col. 0091] Exod.] I take leave of the laws of the world for a time, lest the oil of the sinner make me fat. [Note: [Col. 0091] Ps. 22.] For the law of the Lord [Col. 0091C] is an unspotted law, converting souls. [Note: [Col. 0091] Ps. 18.] And I should make myself a transgressor of the divine law, unless, with such theology as I possess, I offered incense with a handful of fine flour. [Note: [Col. 0091] Lev. 6.]

Certainly secular law, luxuriating in the splendid furnishings of words and the graceful urbanity of eloquence, had powerfully attracted and intoxicated my mind. But the prophet abhors Babylon’s golden cup, [Note: [Col. 0091] Jer. 51.] in which is signified eloquence’s charm, building toward Gehenna. Yet because I have not yet enlarged my steps in the law of the Lord, [Note: [Col. 0091] Ps. 17.] I often devote free time to reading the *Code* and the *Digest* for solace, not for practice.

The practice of law is a matter full of danger for clerics: it claims the whole person so completely that it deprives him of care for his household, suspends him from spiritual things, and tears him away from divine things. Therefore John Chrysostom, as the Tripartite History relates, [Note: [Col. 0091] Bk. X, ch. 3.] although he excelled in civil learning and eloquence, nevertheless refused at the urging of his friends to undertake the office of advocate. It is dangerous to be so entangled in human laws [Col. 0092A] that the mind should fast, even for an hour, from meditation upon the divine law. No one can at once pray and plead, petition and prosecute, exercise Christ’s ministry and the office of advocate, lest, hastening in both, he perform neither well.

I do not deny or gainsay it: it is good to know laws, but not for gain, not for an unjust shortcut through law, but for the investigation of truth and the equity of judgment—if perhaps it should sometime be necessary for me or another to be a judge or assessor to a judge. Today the patrons of causes serve avarice alone; and that once venerable name and glorious profession of advocate are cheapened by notorious venality, while a wretched and ruined man sells his tongue, buys lawsuits, dissolves lawful marriages, breaks friendships, revives the ashes of settled [Col. 0092B] disputes, violates agreements, disparages settlements, breaks privileges, and—stretching traps and nets to catch money—overturns every law.

Therefore an imperial constitution removes purchasers of lawsuits from the office of pleading. By praetorian law and the law of interpreters, extraordinary penalties are imposed upon those who betray their clients or otherwise offend. An advocate ought to give freely what he has freely received; [Note: [Col. 0091] Matt. 10.] to plead for orphan and widow, for the public good, and for the Church’s liberty; to demand nothing, accepting what is freely offered; to rescue the needy from the hand of the stronger and the destitute and poor from their despoilers. [Note: [Col. 0091] Ps. 34.]

A modest and honorable fee would be more profitable to him than to stretch without limit the bosom of insatiable avarice through right and wrong alike; for “better is a little to the righteous than the many riches of sinners.” [Col. 0092C] [Note: [Col. 0091] Ps. 36.] If he freely and willingly expends the talent of knowledge entrusted to him by the Lord, the Lord’s hand is not shortened, so that he cannot reward him according to his merit and confer even greater things. Let him therefore safely entrust this to the Father of orphans and Judge of widows; [Note: [Col. 0091] Ps. 67.] for he is a magnificent promiser and a generous rewarder.

## LETTER XXVII. TO THE CANONS OF BEAUVAIS

[A.D. 1171.]

**SUMMARY.**—He teaches that the death of Saint Thomas the Martyr, Archbishop of Canterbury, should not be lamented, since he exchanged earthly life for heavenly, and a wretched life for a glorious one. He carefully describes Thomas’s virtues; he rebukes his cathedral monks because, secretly and in contempt of the common election by bishops and abbots, they elected a successor; finally, he wishes that the supreme pontiff may restrain the ambition both of clerics and of monks.

To his most beloved brothers and friends, the canons of [Col. 0093A] Beauvais, Master Peter of Blois, archdeacon of Bath: greeting and love.

The shepherd of our souls has departed.

[Note: He means St Thomas, concerning whose wicked and cruel murder all the historians of that century, especially the English, have written at length. Among them, the book entitled *The Process, Life, and Death of St Thomas* has described everything accurately.]

I had resolved to weep for his death; but he has withdrawn, not died; he has gone away, not perished. For the death by which the Lord has glorified His saint is not death but sleep: the harbour of death and the gate of life, an entrance into the delights of the heavenly homeland, into the powers of the Lord, into the abyss of eternal brightness. For, intending to travel abroad, he took a purse of money with him, intending to return at the full moon; for his soul, rich in merits, when it leaves the body, will return at the general and full resurrection to its former lodging.

When, about to depart for the heavenly fair, he had gathered many virtues, as various wares, into a single bundle, [Col. 0093B] old age, that is, the death of this world—an unworthy old woman, quarrelsome, complaining, importunate, envious, hostile, and deceitful—began to turn over his little packages and to investigate more scrupulously whether there was anything in that wrapping of merits which belonged to her dominion. But he, like a cautious and prudent man, was unwilling to suffer the loss of his life. For he had long desired “to depart and be with Christ” [Note: [Col. 0093] Phil. 1], and at that time he especially longed to leave the body of this death.

Accordingly, he threw a little dust into the old woman’s mouth, as though by way of tribute and toll. Then that false report began to circulate among the people and spread everywhere: “A most savage beast has devoured Joseph” [Note: [Col. 0093] Gen. 36]. For the garment of which he was stripped was a deceitful [Col. 0093C] messenger of death. But Joseph lives and rules throughout all the land of Egypt. His blessed soul, unburdened of its corruptible spoils, flew freely from the dust of this earthly existence into heaven. He was received by Him who says: “I go to prepare a place for you; and I shall come again and receive you unto myself” [Note: [Col. 0093] John 14]. “Made perfect in a short time, he fulfilled many years; he was taken away lest wickedness should alter his understanding” [Note: [Col. 0093] Wis. 4]. He was called into that heaven of which the world was not worthy. This lamp has not been extinguished; rather, it has been struck by a passing blast so that it may shine more brightly, and, no longer hidden beneath a bushel, may give light to all who are in the house. “He seemed in the eyes of the foolish to die” [Note: [Col. 0093] Wis. 3], but his life is hidden with Christ in God. Death seemed to have conquered and swallowed him, but “death has been swallowed up [Col. 0093D] in victory” [Note: [Col. 0093] Col. 3]. “You have granted him the desire of his heart, O Lord” [Note: [Col. 0093] 1 Cor. 15]; for he had long served you, “because of the words of your lips guarding hard ways” [Note: [Col. 0093] Ps. 16].

Indeed, from the earliest habits of his youth, he began to grow old in maturity of character, and to restrain the itching impulses of carnal insolence by vigils, fasts, disciplines, haircloth, and the constant girdle of continence. Thus he was called by the Lord, like Aaron [Note: [Col. 0093] Heb. 5], to impart [Col. 0094A] to His people the knowledge of salvation, so that he might render the people acceptable to the Lord, zealous for good works [Note: [Col. 0093] Titus 2], and prepare for the Lord a perfect people [Note: [Col. 0093] Luke 44; probably an erroneous citation]. The Lord chose him as priest for Himself, that he might be among His people a leader and teacher, a mirror of life, a pattern of penitence, and an example of holiness.

The Lord, the God of knowledge, had given him a learned tongue and had abundantly poured into him the spirit of wisdom and understanding, so that among the learned he was more learned, among the wise wiser, among the excellent better, among the humble a companion, among the great greater. He was a herald of the divine word, a trumpet of the Gospel, friend of the Bridegroom, pillar of the clergy, eye of the blind, tongue of the dumb, foot of the lame, salt of the earth, light of his country, minister of the Most High, vicar of Christ, the Lord’s anointed.

His whole manner of life was [Col. 0094B] a school of uprightness, an edification of morals, and a structure of salvation. He was upright in judgment, diligent in administration, discerning in command, modest in speech, prudent in counsel; exceedingly sparing in taking food, most generous in giving; peaceful in anger, an angel in the flesh, gentle amid injuries, fearful in prosperity, altogether secure in adversity, lavish in almsgiving, wholly devoted to mercies. He was the glory of religious persons, the delight of the people, the terror of princes, a god to Pharaoh.

Of him we may confidently say and sing that “he did not go after gold, nor hope in treasures of money” [Note: [Col. 0093] Ecclus. 31], for he neither accepted gifts nor deigned to show favouritism. Others, when raised to the summit [Col. 0094C] of cathedral eminence, immediately devote themselves more eagerly to bodily care, regulate their diet more carefully, fear bodily illness no less than hell, and in all things desire a longer span of life. But from the first moment of his elevation, he ardently desired the end of life—or rather, to speak more truly, the beginning of living. For, as Solomon says: “When a man has finished, then he begins” [Note: [Col. 0093] Ecclus. 18]. For departure from this passing life was his entrance into that life which neither passes nor ends.

Beginning in his tenderer years, through every age, as though through every hour of the day, he laboured like a diligent and vigorous worker in the vineyard of the Lord of Hosts; and thus, in the consummation of the saints, he closed the course of his transient life. Indeed, having long lived a heavenly manner of life and being away from the body, [Col. 0094D] he yearned to pass by the brief course of temporal life into those heavenly delights.

Therefore, taking up the purpose and sign of pilgrimage, “he drank from the brook in the way; therefore his name has been exalted in his homeland” [Note: [Col. 0093] Ps. 109]. Thus our lords and brothers, the cathedral monks, have been made orphans without a father. But may God, “who brought again from the dead the great shepherd of the sheep, in the blood of the eternal covenant, our Lord [Col. 0095A] Jesus Christ” [Note: [Col. 0095] Heb. 13], Himself, to use the words of Moses [Note: [Col. 0095] Num. 27], provide a man to be over this multitude.

Moreover, very many complain and endure with the greatest impatience that Christ’s seamless garment [Note: [Col. 0095] John 19] has been torn between them and the bishops of the land.

[Note: That is, the monks of Canterbury claimed that the right of electing the archbishop belonged to them. The suffragan bishops, on the contrary, said that it belonged to themselves. The dispute was settled in this way: two monks having been proposed to the king of England, one was elected at his pleasure by the chapter of Canterbury and confirmed by the bishops. Gervase and Ralph relate the whole matter very fully. Moreover, Innocent III, in the ninth year of his pontificate, A.D. 1206, declared by solemn decree that the right to elect the archbishop of Canterbury belonged to the cathedral monks alone; see Matthew Paris, *History of England*, under King John. Innocent’s ruling begins: “The greater causes of the Church,” etc.]

Not only the cow and the ram, but the turtle-dove and the dove have been divided and separated from one another [Note: [Col. 0095] Gen. 15]. That presumptuous mistress of discord, fuel of hatred and occasion of scandals—namely, the usurpation of electing separately and privately—has dared to break in even upon professors of religion, so that, with the common deliberation of bishops and abbots despised and cast aside, there might be a secret and furtive election, contrary to custom, hostile to laws, condemned by decrees, and rejected by established practice.

[Col. 0095B] All the others who now regard themselves as injured and slighted would willingly and unanimously, without any division or scandal, have bestowed their votes upon the person whom the monks have elected. But now I fear—may God avert it!—that this election may prove to be his downfall, and that this acquisition of shadowy liberty may turn into a source of servitude for the Church of Christ.

Indeed, this plague and countless others now infect and corrupt the body of the universal Church. Laymen rush into the Holy of Holies, while “the stones of the sanctuary are scattered at the head of every street” [Note: [Col. 0095] Lam. 4]. Cloisters are now turned into camps and marketplaces; religious persons into pagans, shepherds into wolves, lilies into thorns, gold into dross, wheat into tares, wine into vinegar, oil into lees. May the Lord look upon the face [Col. 0095C] of His covenant [Note: [Col. 0095] Ps. 73], and not give over to trampling the vineyard which His right hand planted, the Church which He acquired with His own blood.

May He raise up the spirit of Moses and exalt the horn of that unicorn, that uniquely supreme and singularly universal bishop, so that [Col. 0096A] his hand may seize judgment: that with his horn he may winnow Syria, thunder against Edom, hurl lightning against the calves of Bethel [Note: [Col. 0095] 3 Kings 12], against the idols of Egypt, against the fat cows of Samaria [Note: [Col. 0095] 3 Kings 22], against the priests of Baal, against shepherds who feed themselves, against judges who enact unjust laws, against mute dogs unable to bark [Note: [Col. 0095] Isa. 56], against Zechariah’s jar [Note: [Col. 0095] ch. 6], against the implements of the foolish shepherd, against the ambition of Simon Magus, against the tyranny of the world and the ambition of the cloister, against transgressors, against the arrogant, against oppressors of the poor, against disturbers of ecclesiastical peace and overthrowers of the faith.

## LETTER XXVIII. FROM ROTRO, BISHOP, TO WILLIAM, ARCHBISHOP OF SENS

[Note: On William of Sens, later archbishop of Reims and cardinal, see what we have said on Letter 15.]

[A.D. 1172.]

[Col. 0096B]

**SUMMARY.**—Rotro, archbishop of Rouen, implores the assistance of the archbishop of Sens, that by his exertions he may avert the ruin threatening the Church of Rouen and its most noble town of Andely, arising from the war between the kings of England and France.

To William, archbishop of Sens and legate of the Apostolic See, R. of Rouen—

[Note: That is, Rotro or Rotrou, an Englishman, son of the earl of Warwick and Margaret of Perche. First archdeacon of Rouen, then bishop of Évreux, and finally archbishop of Rouen in [Col. 0096C] 1165. With the bishop of Nevers he was sent as legate to Henry II in 1170 to establish peace with St Thomas. That peace was confirmed through the intervention of the same legates, in the presence of Louis, king of the French. The same Rotro later, in 1172, presided over the council of Avranches, held by Cardinals Theodinus and Albert and many other bishops for the second absolution of the king of England from responsibility for St Thomas’s death; at that council the king of England was absolved of the tragic death of St Thomas. The extent of his loyalty to his king is shown by the more forceful Letters 33 and 154 of Peter of Blois, which he wrote to Queen Eleanor and Henry III, the king’s son, urging them immediately to cease their war against the king. Nor without result: the fighting ceased, and the sons returned to the favour of their royal father. He was also the man who, somewhat later, crowned Henry the Younger King again in [Col. 0096D] England with his wife Margaret, daughter of the king of France. Nor without result: the fighting ceased, and the sons returned to the favour of their royal father. Rotro died in the year of Christ 1183.]

Greeting, and a spirit of compassion for the afflicted.

If the beginnings of the nascent Church are recalled, then, just as among believers there was unity in faith, spirit, and baptism, so, with their resources pooled into one, all had one desire: to relieve [Col. 0096C] the needs of the poor and to regard the necessities of all as their own. For the Lord’s garment is one and undivided; the Bride of Christ has never suffered division, nor endured the insults of an alien concubine. Her bridegroom testifies to her unity in the Song of Songs [Note: [Col. 0095] ch. 6], saying: “My dove, my beloved, is one” [Col. 0097A]. He did not wish her to be reckoned by a multitude of numbers.

For although there are many Churches, they are nevertheless united into the frame of one body, so that, just as through the injury of one member all the members of the body suffer by a certain participation in compassion, so the desolation of one Church should be turned into a common groaning. Therefore, since in the bond of charity singularity has no place, but whatever is endured by individuals redounds to a common loss, and since from the present discord of kings we see a destructive ruin threatening the Church of Rouen, we fly to your favour, in whose affection and prudence we place fuller confidence in Christ.

For you are he in whose counsel and aid [Col. 0097B] the little boat of blessed Peter placed the chief anchor of its safety when it was raging more dangerously amid the waves of schismatic persecution. God granted you, in youth, understanding beyond the aged, and enabled you to anticipate the future grey hairs of nature by a more mature old age of character. Reason, that mistress, restrained in you the unstable impulses of youth; and so, once every liberty of wantonness had been cut off, neither beauty, nor nobility, nor abundance of wealth, nor power, nor the other things by which chastity is assailed, could overturn your purpose of chastity. Rather, your modest conduct in all things displayed more of an angel than of a man.

We pass over in silence your other virtues, in which you shine miraculously. You do not need to beg for our praises, since report has most widely proclaimed your integrity and prudence.

[Col. 0097C] We return to the troubles of ourselves and our Church, with which hostility surrounds us. For you know how all France has conspired for the destruction of the Normans.

[Note: He means the war between Louis VII, king of the French, and Henry II, king of England. All who have written the histories of the French, English, and Normans deal with it.]

The Church of Rouen will not escape the loss of the impending ruin unless it is supported by the aid and counsel of your highness. If, therefore, you look to the aforesaid unity of the Church, it is yours to avert what we fear; it is yours, with every precaution, to forestall our necessities, so that sincere charity and friendly compassion may devote itself to [Col. 0098A] another’s concerns just as it would show itself in its own.

May the lord king of France remember that the Church of Rouen is his own, for it constantly intercedes for him especially as for its one and particular king, and acknowledges all its possessions to be subject to his jurisdiction. It does not befit royal majesty to lay waste what is its own, or to attack those Churches of which it is guardian and patron. If another were assaulting us, we should seek a remedy from him, not elsewhere.

Accordingly, we commit Andely—

[Note: Also called Andeleium and Andelcia. It is a town of Normandy on an island of the same name. William the Breton describes it elegantly in Book VII of the *Philippid*:

> There is a place called Andely, which now gives its name to an island,  
> Where the fruitful Seine divides itself into twin channels;  
> Then, flowing back not far away, it returns into itself and makes one stream,  
> And everywhere encloses within itself a tract of land.  
> So great a swelling raises its plain on high  
> That it does not fear to be covered by the surrounding waters.  
> The water’s surface, rounded on every side  
> In a circular embrace, does not bend aside  
> Into any diverging wedge, but limits itself  
> Within its own bounds, so that no angle breaks its circuit.

It was formerly the patrimony of St Mary and of the archbishop of Rouen, as William of Newburgh says, Book V, chapter 33. Hence Rotro himself, below, in Letter 33, calls it the sole support of his life. Walter, his successor, writing to his friend Ralph, dean of London, says: “The king has occupied the sole and only patrimony of the Church of Rouen, namely Andely,” etc.; “Certainly, if he wished to pity us and spare our life, he would have spared Andely.” How it came into the hands of the king of England—or rather, of the duke of Normandy—will be explained at Letter 138.]

—and our other possessions to his and your protection and guardianship. Indeed, since the whole disposition of the kingdom of France depends on your discernment and counsel, since the hearts of kings are in your hand and peoples incline according to the decision of your direction, it is incumbent upon you to seek those things which belong to peace; or, if this disagreement cannot be restored to peace, at least to free from the incursions of war the ecclesiastical properties entrusted to your protection. And since Andely is the sole means of livelihood for us and our household, spare our town if you wish to spare our lives.

## LETTER XXIX. TO THE ABBOT AND CONVENT OF ST ALBANS

[Note: The monastery of St Albans, in Hertfordshire, England, was founded by Offa, king of the Mercians, in A.D. 794. Monks were established there, for whom he obtained many notable privileges from Adrian IV. Particularly commendable among these was the privilege that its abbot should rank first among all the abbots of England. This occurred at the Council of Tours, presided over by Alexander III, where Robert, abbot of St Albans, sat before the other abbots of England; see Matthew Paris, *Life of Offa, King of the Mercians*.]

**SUMMARY.**—He complains of the inhospitality of the prior of Wallingford and adduces many points in praise of hospitality, adding that in ancient times monks and monasteries were especially commended for it.

To the reverend fathers and friends, the abbot and convent of St Albans, Master Peter of Blois, archdeacon of Bath, [Col. 0098C] greeting in Him who is truly salvation.

Recently I was returning from a visitation of my archdeaconry. I sent my servants ahead to Wallingford to prepare lodging for me. When they asked the prior of that place to lend them vacant houses for my use for one night, and had already brought there everything necessary for ourselves and our beasts of burden, the prior answered them with much arrogance and abuse, and, almost going so far as the outrage of blows, assailed them with the shameful foulness [Col. 0099A] of insulting words.

Your house, indeed, once very famous for its observance of religion and order, was accustomed also, in its exercise of hospitality, to diffuse far and wide the sweet odour and fragrance of glorious renown. But now, to the injury of the head, the corruption of a lower member is reflected back; and from a particular corruption the defect of the whole body is judged.

The Apostle’s word to the Hebrews is: “Do not forget hospitality, for by it some have pleased angels received as guests” [Note: [Col. 0099] Heb. 13]. Where, I ask, is that grace of hospitality which your predecessors once exercised in Scetis? Mutius, Apollonius, Paphnutius, Macarius, Antony, Paul—among whom there was a long contest of pious rivalry as to which should break bread for the other, when the Lord, through the grace of hospitality, [Col. 0099B] doubled their daily allowance of provisions [Note: [Col. 0099] Jerome, *Life of Paul the Hermit*].

The decree of the prince of the apostles is: “Be hospitable to one another without murmuring” [Note: [Col. 0099] 1 Pet. 4]. The Prince of princes also will say to some at the dreadful judgment: “I was a stranger, and you did not receive me” [Note: [Col. 0099] Matt. 25]. It was the merit of hospitality that the two disciples journeying to Emmaus, once *akrisia* (ἀκρισία) had been removed—

[Note: ἀκρισία means confusion, or a disordered state of affairs; as though he meant that the darkness was lifted from the disciples’ eyes, which had previously prevented them from recognizing Christ.]

—recognized the Lord in the breaking of bread [Note: [Col. 0099] Luke 24]. Many also believe that blessed Gregory was that householder who, in the exposition of this same Gospel, is said to have received the Lord in a leper [Note: [Col. 0099] John the Deacon, *Life of Gregory*, Book 2, ch. 22].

The royal line of England, because one of its ancestors bestowed the grace of courteous humanity upon a leper whom he had received as a guest, rose from the office [Col. 0099C] of forester to the height of royal dignity [Note: [Col. 0099] Gregory, Homily 23 on the Gospels]. By the grace of hospitality Abraham received from Sarah, old and barren, a son in whom the Lord promised the blessing of all nations [Note: [Col. 0099] Gen. 18]. Angelic guests delivered Lot from the overthrow and burning of Sodom [Note: [Col. 0099] Gen. 22]. Rahab obtained, from her guests Caleb and Joshua, the salvation of her household at the destruction of Jericho [Note: [Col. 0099] Josh. 6]. The hospitality of the Shunammite gave her a son through Elisha’s prayers and raised that same son when dead [Note: [Col. 0099] 4 Kings 4]. For the poor widow who received Elijah as a guest and fed him, by the infusion of heavenly grace, neither oil nor flour thereafter failed.

The analogy is plain: while [Col. 0100A] hospitality flourished in monasteries, the princes of the earth everywhere, and in rivalry with one another, enlarged religious houses with great resources; but when the vessels failed, the oil stopped. Since the time when hospitable liberality began to fail in monasteries, the generosity of magnates has stopped and ceased. I fear that the sons of the poor widow, whom the prophet had delivered, may again be seized by creditors as slaves.

For holy religion, the mother of monks, is today given over to trampling; her possessions are dragged off for plunder and spoil; and what the devout generosity of former princes bestowed, the avarice of modern men presumes to reclaim and take away, not without great loss through usury. Defective hospitality, indeed, separates many from the friendship and favour of the great. Thus, when the arm is broken, [Col. 0100B] the shoulder falls from its joint. While the once-revered authority of religion becomes worthless, trodden beneath the oppression of princes, Job’s imprecation is fulfilled:

“If I ate my morsel alone [Note: [Col. 0099] 3 Kings 17], for compassion grew up with me from my childhood and came forth with me from my mother’s womb; if a stranger stood outside, if my door was not open to the traveller, let my shoulder fall from its joint, and my arm be broken with its bones” [Note: [Col. 0099] Job 31].

Indeed, the aforementioned prior was once severely punished for this same offence. I thought that affliction had given him understanding, but his hand is still stretched out, and he will not cease from dishonouring your house until the shoulder is cut from its joint, the diseased sheep from the flock, and the rotten member from the [Col. 0100C] body.

## LETTER XXX. TO R., BISHOP-ELECT OF BATH

[Note: He is Reginald, son of Jocelin the Lombard, bishop of Salisbury, to whom his father had given the archdeaconry of that Church. When Henry II, king of England, at the request of Cardinals Albert and Theodinus, legates, had granted that free elections should be made in vacant churches, Reginald was elected to the bishopric of Bath. But when Henry the Young King opposed his election and those of others, Reginald went to Rome with Richard, archbishop-elect of Canterbury, to secure confirmation of his own election and those of the others [Col. 0100D]. Soon afterwards, he sent to Henry II letters concerning confirmation of his own election and those of the other elect, and concerning Richard’s consecration by Alexander III as archbishop of Canterbury; the letters are found in Roger of Howden’s *Annals*, Part II.

When they were returning from Rome, Richard, fearing that Henry the Younger might devise some evil against the elect, consecrated Reginald bishop of Bath within the valleys of Maurienne, in the church of St John; the archbishop of Tarentaise also laid hands upon him. Reginald had first made a purgation that he had knowingly procured the death of blessed Thomas neither by word, deed, nor writing. Others also swore that, as they believed, he had been conceived [Col. 0101B] before his father Jocelin had been advanced to the order of priesthood. This was done in 1174. He held the bishopric for sixteen and a half years, until 1192, when the monks of Canterbury elected him archbishop. Yet about fifty days after his nomination he died, [Col. 0101C] and was buried at Bath.

Moreover, the *Four-Part History*, in Book V of the *Process*, includes him among St Thomas’s household in these words: “Reginald, English by nationality but Lombard by education and surname, [ [Col. 0101D] Note that his father Jocelin is called ‘the Lombard.’] prudent and energetic beyond his years, spirited and effective in affairs, who, by the merit of his own industry and integrity, was promoted to the bishopric of Bath.”

Baronius agrees, writing thus in Volume XII under the year 1172: “Reginald the Englishman, surnamed Lombard, raised to the bishopric of Bath, is numbered among St Thomas’s household; Peter of Blois wrote an apology for him,” namely Letter 45. Yet I am surprised that this Reginald is numbered among St Thomas’s household, since he was sent to Rome by King Henry against St Thomas, and St Thomas himself attacks him sharply in a letter written to his household, who were then at the Roman curia on behalf of his cause, as Baronius records [Col. 0101D] under the year 1168. But since no other bishop of Bath named Reginald is listed by any author, it must be said that he incurred St Thomas’s displeasure unwillingly and for some reason. How earnestly and lovingly he strove to be reconciled with St Thomas, with what lamentations and what penitence he tried to return to his favour, is clear from Letter 24 of Peter of Blois.]

[A.D. 1175.]

**SUMMARY.**—Peter had seen, once, twice, and a third time in a dream, his friend to whom he writes adorned with episcopal insignia. He discloses the vision to him and wishes, whatever its ultimate origin, that it may attain its fulfilment.

To his dearest lord and friend R., bishop-elect of Bath, Peter of Blois, archdeacon of Bath, greeting and prosperous success according to your desires.

Since the state of human life is varied by manifold change, I find nothing among temporal things, except one thing, which represents an image of heavenly life. Love alone is not altered by a chance event; bodily separation does not divide it; the length of time does not efface it; nor does it yield to failure. Love alone enables us to see, speak with, and embrace absent lords and friends. With a certain angelic swiftness and imaginary intercourse it flies across and returns, so that it complains neither of the burden of bodily mass nor of the injury of local distance.

Therefore days continually offer me your presence in imaginations and nights in visions. But now I behold in you the previously unseen insignia of a new dignity; and perhaps my anxious mind, concerning your advancement, either already senses what has occurred [Col. 0101B] or, by a more certain wish, foreknows what is about to happen. God and my conscience are witnesses to what I say.

On that Sunday when is sung, “I am the good shepherd” [Note: [Col. 0101D] John 10], I seemed in sleep to see you being adorned in pontifical vestments by a certain very large and most venerable person, who in stature resembled the bishop of Évreux, but in age the archbishop of Rouen. While I stood by that work joyfully and devoutly, I saw your feet in stockings and your hand distinguished by no ring. I silently asked what this meant. The venerable man replied: “For a time he will not have a golden ring, but a stone one”—that is, one made continuous by a single gem set in a circle. “But at last his mother will give him more precious sandals and a greater ring, through the cunning of a young man to whom a crown will be promised by a priest. Yet each will be disappointed in his expectation. The former will soon pass to his fathers; the latter, after opposing and then returning, will make use of gifts. Know one thing: when you have received the silver pieces, you will wrest away both sandals.”

While I was engaged in these dreams and enjoying the empty delights [Col. 0102B] of the vision, the bell was rung for Matins; the importunate bells took away what blessed sleep was bestowing. The following night repeated this vision a second and third time, with the same sequence of events.

And concerning lots of human curiosity—

[Note: A lot is something indifferent in itself, that is, something which may be either good or bad. Augustine, on Psalm 30: “When we hear the name of lots, we ought not to seek out diviners. For a lot is not something evil, but a thing which, in human uncertainty, indicates the divine will. The apostles too cast lots when Judas, after betraying the Lord, perished. And just as it is written of [Col. 0102B] him: ‘He went to his own place’ (Acts XII), they began to ask who should be ordained in his place. Two were chosen by human judgment, and one of the two was chosen by divine judgment. God was consulted concerning which of the two He wished, and the lot fell upon Matthias.”

To distinguish good lots from bad, three things must be considered: first, the source from which they flow; second, the manner in which they are used; third, their end. The good source of lots is God, and likewise anyone who is guided by God’s testimony; the evil source is the devil, and likewise anyone who occupies himself with lots apart from God’s testimony. Under this distinction, lots are properly divided into divine, diabolical, and human.

The good manner of using lots is one employed according to God, without fraud against piety and justice; the bad manner is the contrary. Thus lot-casting is either religious or irreligious; and the latter has many forms: vain, rash, superstitious, and so forth. The end of lots is either that something be allotted to someone, that it be decided what must be done, or, finally, that the future may be known. Thus lots are distributive, consultative, or divinatory. St Thomas rightly says, *Summa Theologiae*, II–II, question 95, article 8: ‘Lots are properly so called when something is done so that, upon considering its outcome, something hidden may become known. If by the judgment of lots one asks what is to be assigned to a person—whether a possession, an honour, a dignity, a punishment, or some action—it is called a distributive lot; if one asks what ought to be done, it is called a consultative lot; but if one asks what will happen, it is called a divinatory lot.’ See also the same author, Opuscule 25.]

—and the turning of the Psalter—

[Note: The Psalter may be opened or turned over (and the same may be said of the Gospel or any other book of Holy Scripture) for various purposes: sometimes for consolation. Thus Gregory of Tours, Book V of the *History of the Franks*, ch. 47: “Hearing this, while I sat sorrowful and troubled in the house of the church, I entered the oratory and took up the book of Davidic song, so that when opened it might give some verse of consolation. In it this was found: ‘He led them forth in hope, and the sea covered their enemies’” [Col. 0103A] (Ps. 77).

Sometimes it is opened for instruction and correction of conduct. Thus Augustine, *Confessions*, Book VIII, final chapter: “I hurried back to the place where Alypius was sitting. For I had placed there the book of the Apostle when I rose from it. I seized it, opened it, and silently read the chapter upon which my eyes first fell: ‘Not in revelries and drunkenness, not in beds and impurities, but put on the Lord Jesus Christ, and make no provision for the flesh in its desires’ (Rom. 13). I did not wish to read further, nor was there any need; for immediately at the end of this sentence, as though a light of security had been poured into my heart, all the darkness of doubt fled away.”

Sometimes it is opened to discover the future; and this occurs in two ways: either through divine inspiration, which belongs to few, or through human judgment—either judgment which assumes that the meaning which it will derive from the opening of the book is certain, or [Col. 0103B] uncertain.

Francis was guided by divine inspiration, as St. Bonaventure relates in his Life, chapter 13:

> “It was therefore communicated to his mind by a divine oracle that, in the opening of the book of the Gospels, Christ would reveal to him what would be most pleasing to God in him and concerning him. After prayer had first been offered with much devotion, he caused the sacred book of the Gospels, taken from the altar, to be opened in the name of the Holy Trinity by his companion, a man indeed devout toward God and holy. And since, in the threefold opening of the book, the Lord’s Passion always occurred, the man full of God understood that, as he had imitated Christ in the deeds of his life, so he ought to be conformed to him in the afflictions and sufferings of the Passion before he passed from this world.”

Chramnus too seems to have acted under the same spirit. Gregory of Tours, Book IV, chapter 16, says:

> “Chramnus, pursuing them with an army, came as far as the city of Chalon and, laying siege to it, took it. From there he advanced as far as the fortress of Dijon; and when he arrived there on the Lord’s Day, I shall tell what was done. St. Tetricus the bishop was then there. Having placed three books upon the altar—that is, the Prophets, the Apostle, and the Gospels—the clerics prayed to the Lord that he might show what would happen to Chramnus: whether success would attend him, or whether he could indeed reign, as divine power might declare. They also agreed together that whatever each first opened in the book he should read at Mass. Therefore, opening first the book of all the prophets, they found: ‘I will remove its hedge, and it shall become a desolation; because it ought to have produced grapes, but produced wild grapes’ (Isa. 5). Opening the book of the Apostle, they found: ‘For you yourselves know well, brethren, that the day of the Lord will come like a thief in the night. When they say, “Peace and security,” then sudden destruction will come upon them, like the pains of a woman in labor; and they shall not escape’ (1 Thess. 5). But the Lord says through the Gospel [Col. 0103D]: ‘Whoever does not hear my words shall be likened to a foolish man who built his house upon sand: the rain fell, the floods came, the winds blew, and rushed upon that house; and it fell, and its fall was great’ (Matt. 7).”

To this may also be referred what the same Gregory says of Merovech, son of Chilperic, king of the Franks at Soissons, Book V, chapter 14:

> “Merovech, however, not trusting the pythoness, placed three books upon the tomb of St. Martin: the Psalter, the Books of Kings, and the Gospels. Keeping vigil throughout the night, he asked that the blessed confessor might show him what would happen to him, and that, with the Lord revealing it, he might know whether he could obtain the kingdom or not. Thereafter, having continued for three days in fasting, vigils, and prayers, [Col. 0104A] he again approached the blessed tomb and opened the book that was Kings. The first verse of the page which he opened was this: ‘Because you have forsaken the Lord your God and have walked after strange gods, and have not done what is right before his sight, therefore the Lord your God has delivered you into the hands of your enemies’ (3 Kings 9). In the Psalter this verse was found: ‘Yet because of their deceitfulness you have set evils before them; you cast them down while they were being raised up. How they became a desolation! Suddenly they failed; they perished because of their iniquities’ (Ps. 72). And in the Gospels this was found: ‘You know that after two days the Passover will take place, and the Son of Man will be delivered up to be crucified’ (Matt. 26). In these responses he was confounded,” etc.

All these divinatory lots are harmless.
