But there is another kind of opening of the Psalter or another book of Scripture, done by human judgment: if faith is placed in it [Col. 0104B], this practice is improperly called “the lot of the saints,” and is deservedly condemned by councils as diabolical.

The Council of Vannes, canon 16:

> “And lest that perhaps seem omitted which most especially attacks the faith of the Catholic religion: since certain clerics devote themselves to auguries and, under the name of a feigned religion, profess knowledge of divination through those practices which they call the lots of the saints, or promise future events through the inspection of any writings whatever—any cleric found either to consult or to teach such things is to be held outside the Church.”

The Council of Agde, chapter 42, uses the same words, except that it extends the censure of the canon of Vannes to laypeople as well. The First Council of Orléans, canon 30:

> “If any cleric, monk, or layperson believes that divination, auguries, or the lots which they falsely claim to be those of the saints should be observed or disclosed to anyone they think fit, let them, together with those who believe them, be expelled from communion with the Church.”

The Council of Auxerre, canon 4:

> “It is not permitted to consult diviners or auguries [Col. 0104C], nor coragii, nor to look to the lots called those of the saints, or those made from wood or bread; rather, whatever a person wishes to do, let him do all things in the name of the Lord.”

In the Capitularies of Charlemagne, in Sirmond, vol. II of the Councils of Gaul, p. 157:

> “Inquiry is to be made concerning books or tablets, and no one is to presume to cast lots in the Psalter, the Gospel, or other things, nor to observe any divinations.”

Finally, chapter 11 of the work *On Remedies for Sins*, circulated under Bede’s name, in Antonius Augustinus at the end of the *Epitome of Ancient Pontifical Law* and in vol. I of the Councils of England:

> “To observe auguries, or lots falsely called those of the saints, or divinations, or to promise future events by inspection of any writings whatever,” etc.

Finally, one who opens sacred books in order to seek in them the future, while judging uncertain the knowledge he will obtain from them, is not free from all fault. This is divinatory lot-casting by human judgment [Col. 0104D], and it is of this that Blesensis speaks here. Busaeus therefore wrongly supposed that the discourse here concerns consultative lots, whereas it deals with divinatory ones.

Consultative lots are concerned with in chapter 20 of Augustine’s Letter 119, as also in what Cedrenus relates concerning the younger Heraclius, in the royal edition, p. 412, and concerning the elder Andronicus in Nicephorus Gregoras, Book VIII. St. Thomas teaches in the passage cited above when consultative lots are lawful.

Finally, divisory lots are concerned with in the same Augustine’s Letter 180. These ought not to be employed except in necessities, religiously and reverently.

---

…that I might investigate the outcome of this vision more carefully [Col. 0103A] [Note: Not, however, as though he had placed no faith whatever in these things; the words of the letter itself plainly declare otherwise.], the first verse that met my eyes was: “Moses and Aaron among his priests” [Col. 0104A] [Note: Psalm 98.]. I indeed do not know what the nocturnal revelation portends. Yet, because I saw that no equal return was being made to your fidelity and devotion [Col. 0105A]—which experience of royal necessity has tested through so many labors and so many dangers—I was continually tormented by the long expectation of my desire; and I believe that, from the remnants of thoughts which uncertain hope had long prolonged, the soul of the sleeper formed for itself the images of the vision already mentioned.

May the Lord deal with you according to my heart; and, making my desires marvelous in you, may he not disappoint with its fulfillment the affection of one who loves you.

## LETTER XXXI. TO RALPH, ABBOT OF FONTANES

[Note: This Ralph is the man whose praise H., a monk of the same monastery, trained under the same rule, briefly describes in vol. II of the *Monasticon Anglicanum*, fol. 733: “A man worthy of every praise; a mirror of religion, flower of the order, model of discipline. His memory is as a composition of fragrance, the work of a perfumer—of him, indeed, who has gathered the encomia of virtues into a fragile vessel.”

Moreover, the monastery of Fontaines was founded in the time of St. Bernard, namely in the year 1132, by Cistercian monks from the monastery of York, brought there by Archbishop Thurstan.]

### TO THE ABBOT OF FONTANES

**SUMMARY.**—He gives thanks both to Abbot R. because he pitied him in his severe illness, and above all to God because he mercifully scourged him. At length, from Holy Scripture, he shows that illnesses and the other afflictions of this life are salutary, useful, and sweet, and are to be numbered among God’s singular gifts.

To the reverend father and lord R., by God’s grace abbot of Fontaines, P., his own, archdeacon of Bath, greetings in him without whom there is no salvation.

I have heard with what devout kindness you grieve over my sufferings, sharing the evils I endure by a certain participation in endurance and by the affection of deepest compassion. I give thanks to the Giver of grace because he has mercifully scourged me. For when I walked in things great and wonderful beyond me, and continuous prosperity had, as it were, lifted me above myself, the Lord, lifting me up, dashed me down [Note: Psalm 101.], and humbled me—he who is before the ages. Through my hardness and impenitent heart [Col. 0105C] I was storing up wrath for myself on the day of dreadful judgment [Note: Rom. 2.]. Christ changed wrath into grace for me, wishing me to be weak lest I should be more grievously weak. I was careless and forgetful of my salvation; but the multiplication of illnesses spurred me—sluggish and growing slow upon the Lord’s way—into running. The Prophet’s words are: “Their infirmities were multiplied; afterward they hastened” [Note: Ps. 15].

Yet I am still grievously afflicted. Would that I might endure patiently what I suffer; for every affliction of heart or body is without merit and without the fruit of salvation unless seasoned with patience. Virtues themselves, unless they have patience as their foundation, lose both the name and office of virtue:

> For that virtue is widowed which patience does not strengthen.

[Note: This verse is taken from Prudentius’s *Psychomachia*, “The Conflict of Patience and Anger,” section 4, last verse.]

Some are strong in prosperity, confessing the Lord [Col. 0105D] when he does them good, but in miseries they do not stand firm [Note: Ps. 48.]. Certainly patience is very often endangered when injuries provoke it. For human strength is not bronze so as to endure; rather, one’s endurance advances or fails, diminishes or grows, according to the dispensation of divine grace.

Who would not count misery and illness among God’s gifts, when Christ says to the Apostle: “My grace is sufficient for you, for strength is perfected in weakness” [Note: 2 Cor. 12]? Therefore the same Apostle, taught in the school of experience what the Master had once foretold, says: “When I am weak, then I am stronger and powerful” [Note: ibid.]. What appears to the wisdom of this world—which is foolishness with God—to be affliction, is consolation [Note: See Peter of Blois’s treatise *On the Usefulness of Tribulations*.] to those upright in heart. Hence the Apostle says: “For my part, I will glory in nothing except my weaknesses” [Note: 2 Cor. 11.].

Job, punished by bodily affliction and the loss of temporal substance [Col. 0106B], says: “He who is afflicted shall be in glory” [Note: Job 22.]; and what impatience counts as punishment becomes consolation to one who endures humbly. For when he weighs the fruit of patience more carefully, the burden is lightened and affliction becomes sweet, while amid the very pressure of grievous burdens he already tastes beforehand the firstfruits of the future consolation.

Therefore Job says: “Let him withdraw his hand and cut me down; and let this be my consolation: that in afflicting me with pain he does not spare me” [Note: Job 6.]. Habakkuk likewise sang in his canticle: “Let rottenness enter into my bones, and let it bubble beneath me, that I may rest in the day of tribulation and rise up to our armed people” [Note: Hab. 3.]. He knew that the vintage would follow threshing, joy would follow affliction, and bodily disgrace would yield [Col. 0106C] to a crown.

Writing to the Corinthians, the Apostle says: “As the sufferings of Christ abound in us, so through Christ our consolation also abounds” [Note: 2 Cor. 1]. And to the Hebrews: “Having been made a spectacle through reproaches and troubles, we received the plundering of our goods with joy, knowing that we have a better and lasting substance” [Note: Heb. 10]. James too, knowing how great is the abundance of God’s sweetness in his scourges, says: “Count it all joy, brethren, when you fall into various temptations” [Note: Jas. 1]. For the Lord scourges every son whom he receives [Note: Heb. 12]. He visits him at dawn and suddenly tests him; he visits and tests him so as thus to guard his spirit against the evil spirit [Note: Job 9]. “And your visitation,” says a certain sick man, “has preserved my spirit” [Note: Job 10].

By the Lord’s scourge [Col. 0106D] the dust which habitual sin has gathered for the disfigurement of the soul is shaken out, and through an outward wound the inward wound is healed. For, according to Solomon’s testimony, “the bruise of a wound wipes away evils, and the stroke reaches the innermost parts of the belly” [Note: The Septuagint reads: *hypōpsia kai syntrimmata synanta kakoīs, plēgai de eis tamieia koilias*—“Bruises and crushings meet evils, but wounds penetrate into the secret chambers of the belly.” Aquila and Theodotion have *mōlōpes traumátōn*, “bruises of wounds.” The Hebrew version reads: “The cleansing of evil is by the bruise of a wound, and by strokes in the inner parts of the belly.” The Chaldee: “Terrors and blows meet evil, and strokes reach the inward parts of the belly.” The Syriac: “Breaking and punishment have met the wicked, and a blow reaches the inmost parts of their belly.” The Arabic: “Reproaches and fractures will meet the perverse, and disturbances in the chambers of the belly.” The sense, therefore, is this: just as wounds in the outer and inner skin are healed painfully, so the evil person is purified and healed by afflictions and distresses. The metaphor is drawn [Col. 0108D] from the body to the soul. It is as though he said: what we see happen in bodily wounds must be understood likewise of wounds of the mind. As wounds on the outer skin and strokes driven more deeply, even to the inward parts and entrails, are healed with pain and suffering, so an evil person never becomes wise except through his own hurt, nor is he corrected except by pain and distress. *Livores* properly denotes congealed blood in Hebrew.].

Thus the Lord is angry in order to make gentle; he afflicts in order to spare; he casts down in order to raise up. “And who, O Lord, knows the power of your wrath?” [Note: Ps. 89.] For the wrath of God is full of mercies; and the signs of your chastisement, which you exercise especially upon your own people, are sure signs of loving-kindness. For “the souls of the righteous are in the hand of God” [Note: Wis. 3]. Therefore, amid delights and pains, amid the Lord’s wrath and mercy, the wise recognize something special in scourges: “The daughters of Judah rejoiced,” he says, “because of your judgments, O Lord” [Note: Ps. 96.]. All discipline is exceedingly bitter at present, but in the future it will yield the most peaceable fruit [Note: Heb. 12].

Indeed, those who are not in the labor of human beings and are not scourged with them [Col. 0107B] will be scourged with demons. It is therefore better for the righteous person to be cut here and burned here, so that temporal suffering may swallow up eternal torments. “We passed through fire and water,” says one, “and you brought us out into refreshment” [Note: Ps. 85.]. For the righteous person, according to blessed Job’s testimony, “shall forget his misery and shall not remember it, as waters that have passed away” [Note: Job 11]. “At evening he shall rise like the noonday brightness, and when he thinks himself consumed, he shall rise like the morning star” [Note: Job 6].

Plainly, I am still afflicted anxiously; the Lord’s arrows are still in me, and their indignation drinks up my spirit. Yet I know that the punishment is less than the sin which preceded it. It is God’s gift that I am ill; God’s grace that I am afflicted [Col. 0107C]. A physician does not always administer sweet things to the sick person, but often offers bitter draughts. Bile caused by excessively delicate food is often purged by wormwood; abscesses which have grown through idleness and gluttony are healed by cautery and cleansed by incision. To me the alternation of fever, heat, and cold is a purgatory.

[Note: This is the common opinion of theologians after the Council of Trent, session 14, chapter 9: illnesses, afflictions, and scourges by which we are punished by God in this life, if borne patiently, are satisfactory and lessen the punishments of purgatory. Thus Sylvius, *Supplement*, question 15, article 2.]

But I hope in him who is our hope that “a second tribulation shall not arise”; nor will the Lord judge me twice for the same thing [Note: Nah. 1]. If I endure patiently and with equanimity the present sufferings of the flesh, a momentary punishment will redeem me from endless death, and temporal affliction will pass away together with eternal punishment.

I suffer, indeed, for my sins. Would that it had been granted me from above to suffer for righteousness: for “blessed [Col. 0108A] are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake” [Note: Matt. 5]. “Let none,” says the Apostle Peter, “suffer as a thief, or murderer, or covetous person, or one who covets another’s possessions; but if, while doing good, you endure, this is grace before God.” We often read that illustrious men, venerable old men, noble boys, and even delicate virgins endured for Christ scourges, fires, swords, beasts, and other kinds of punishments. They were tortured for righteousness; I am afflicted for my iniquity. Christ’s grace is sufficient for my endurance, so that I may have examples of his patience and my weak flesh, so often scourged, may not fail through faintness of spirit and tempest [Note: 1 Pet. 4].

## LETTER XXXII. TO THE PRIOR OF CANTERBURY

[Col. 0108B]

**SUMMARY.** Trusting in the friendship and charity of the Prior of Canterbury, he commends to him a certain matter concerning the convent of Canterbury.

To his dearest kinsman William, Prior of Canterbury, P. of Blois, Archdeacon of Bath, greetings, and whatever is more precious than health.

Such is the law of friendship and the condition of charity: friends should pursue the inward affections they hold in common in the outward result of deeds amid mutual necessities. We have indeed recently formed our friendship; and overflowing, fervent affection fully established within a shorter space a favor which frequent services could not have extorted, nor the familiarity of long time have secured.

Thus a momentary conversation and brief acquaintance united me to you in the bond [Col. 0108C] of charity, so that I regard myself as wholly yours. Indeed, I should count you as another self, if there could be as great an identity of bodies as there is a singular unity of wills. Perhaps I deceive myself, and you do not answer my affection in equal measure. Yet it would be ungenerous for you to falter in friendship when your words, works, face, gait, and every other thing promise an effective and steadfast friend.

I send and entrust to your love H., the bearer of this letter, and the business he has with the convent of Canterbury, humbly asking that in his case I may experience how you are willing to respond to the mutual bond of friendship. Whatever he obtains through your favor, I shall regard as bestowed on me; and service rendered to an absent and new friend will oblige me to fuller thanks. Farewell.

## LETTER XXXIII. TO HENRY III, KING OF ENGLAND

[Note: He was the eldest son of Henry II, king of the English, whom his father had wished to have anointed king. Later, after entering into a conspiracy with his mother and brothers, he took up arms against his father. His unfortunate coronation, this conflict, and the death of the younger Henry are discussed at length in the notes to Letter 3.]

**SUMMARY.**—R. [Note: Rotrou. See the notes to Letter 28.] Archbishop of Rouen endeavors to call Henry III, king of the English, back from his undertaking of war against his father Henry II, and commends Les Andelys [Note: See the same place.] to his protection.

To Henry III, by God’s grace illustrious king of the English, the Archbishop of Rouen sends greetings in him who gives salvation to kings.

Since the office of administration entrusted to us obliges us to take care of souls, for which the strict Judge will demand from us the most exact account in the terrible examination, we ask that it may not burden your Excellency [Col. 0109B] if we beseech you as lord, exhort you as king, and instruct you as son. For the word of the Lord is not bound in our mouth; but in the spirit of freedom we speak what may bring salvation to souls, peace to peoples, liberty to the Church, honor to God, and deliverance to the fatherland, and may lead you back from the trackless way of error to the path of truth and justice.

You do not consider, dearest son, what you have undertaken; nor do you measure the outcome of the work you have begun. You hasten to satisfy the desires of those who hate you, and you summon an enemy against your own head. You are not attacking barbarian nations, but your own household and intimates; you are not invading foreign regions or hostile strongholds, but your own. You afflict a people subject to you, not rebellious; [Col. 0109C] you pursue not an enemy but a father—indeed, you do not pursue your father but yourself.

For your father, setting aside care for his own body and soul, exposed himself to every labor and danger in order to make yours what you now seek to make yours; or, more truly, what you intend to make not yours. By fighting you will not make more yours what paternal cession, the general desire of the people, the oaths of princes, and hereditary succession had bestowed on you. What you peacefully possessed as king and prince, you now usurp as a tyrant and invader, by despoiling churches, oppressing the poor, arson and homicide, and finally parricide.

Those who rise armed against their parents are deemed parricides; both the laws of the world condemn them and the canons exclude them from the benefit of succession. [Col. 0109D] You have turned your right into wrong, intending to extort through injustice what equity offered you. I would call this childish, were it not that it exceeds the malice of mature age. If you come into conflict with your father, it is doubtful whether it benefits you to be defeated or [Col. 0110A] to conquer. If piety dwelt on earth, you would more gloriously maintain that you should yield to your father than triumph over him.

To yield and submit to one’s father is commanded by the law of Moses, the law of the Gospel, the authority of the canons, the institution of the apostles, imperial laws, the very condition of humankind, and natural law. You make yourself an enemy of God and justice and a transgressor of every law if you do not obey your father, to whom you owe all that you are: from whose flesh and blood, by the benefit of your seed-origin and nature, you received flesh and blood.

Who gave you the material of existence? Your father. Who brought you up? Your father. Who trained you in military arms? Your father. Who emptied himself to make you king? Your father. Who labored in all things so that you might peacefully possess all things? [Col. 0110B] Your father.

You find nothing to blame in your father except that he earned your extravagant favor and devotion—which perhaps less lavish generosity might have gained—by kindness and liberality alone, generously and abundantly bestowed. Accordingly, the French peoples have obtained what they wished. For Normandy, pressing upon their necks, which they had always found defended and impregnable, they now weaken on every side through your agency, so that thereafter it can neither raise its head against them nor withstand hostile attacks.

O lamentable frivolity of youth! Yet it is no wonder. If God grants you a longer course of life, when older you will weep for what you now commit while immature; nor then will there be room for repentance, when affairs have come to such desolation [Col. 0110C] that they cannot be restored. Dearest son, though I speak bitterly to you, I speak thus out of love; for I cannot calmly endure the ill-considered impulses of your mind. Would that death, which you compel me to desire, had forestalled these days in which I see you as persecutor of father and fatherland; in which I behold you friend to your enemies and enemy to your friends; in which I see you in such a condition as though you had fixed a sword to your own throat.

Further, know that Les Andelys is the sole support of our life. I entrust it to your protection. If you expose Les Andelys to robbers and incendiaries, you will take from me the means of living, while giving me the will to die. Farewell.

## LETTER XXXIV. TO P., BISHOP OF PÉRIGUEUX

[Note: He is Peter Minet, a native of Blois, as may be inferred from his being a cousin of Peter of Blois. With Bertrand, metropolitan of Bordeaux, he went to Alfonso, king of Castile, in 1170, with other magnates of Aquitaine, to escort Eleanor, daughter of Henry II, king of the English, to be joined to the same Alfonso in marriage. He was also present at the dedication of the church of St. Amand of Buxières in the district of Angoulême. He died in 1177.]

[c. A.D. 1172.]

[Col. 0110D]

**SUMMARY.**—He excuses himself before the bishop of Périgueux, who had invited him to his court, explaining that the promises of his former lord so entice him that he cannot now meet the bishop’s expectations.

To the most reverend lord and father Peter, bishop of Périgueux [Col. 0111A], P. of Blois, the least of his kinsmen—indeed, of his servants—greetings and continual success according to your wishes.

Love is strong as death [Note: Song 8.]. For though death breaks the union of limbs and the friendly covenant of soul and body, love, on the contrary, fuses diverse wills into one and strengthens the union of different souls in the bond of charity. Love does not feel the losses of absence; and though most things are accustomed to grow weak through the length of time, love gains strength both through the passage of time and through local distance.

I know this through experience in your case: you have at last looked with a more gracious eye upon me, the least and almost an untimely birth among the rest, within the kindred of your magnificence. You commanded—if I remember the command faithfully [Col. 0111B]—that I should come to you more quickly, intending to remain with you as one of your household and at your table. At the word of your kindness my spirit rejoiced in a welcome exultation; and I had already determined to hasten to you, already I eagerly longed for the preparation of the journey, when that lord whom you know, approaching and ensnaring me, less cautious as I was, with immense promises and certain deceptions of flattery, recalled my purpose.

I waited patiently, and meanwhile many opportunities for benefits presented themselves. I offered petitions; my own need also pleaded on my behalf; in nothing did I find his hand generous. I still conceive hopes of a kinder outcome, and perhaps I await Arthur coming with the Britons [Note: Arthur was a most powerful king of the Britons in England. Though he assumed the kingdom when only fifteen years old and reigned for a short time, he nevertheless fought many battles in which he defeated very fierce peoples, especially the Saxons, his most hostile enemies. When Mordred, Arthur’s nephew and a deserter, joined the Saxons, they were slain and routed in battle; Arthur himself was mortally wounded, was carried to the island of Avalon to heal his wounds, and died there. He was buried in the cemetery of the monks in A.D. 542. “When dying, he had withdrawn himself from battle,” says the Westminster chronicler, “lest enemies should insult so great a calamity and friends be grieved.” Since his death and burial were then known to few, the British people, through the greatness of their love, maintain that he still survives. Hence the proverb.

He was buried, with few persons aware of it, in a very small tomb at the monastery of Glastonbury—commonly Glastingebury—of the Order of St. Benedict, in Somerset [Col. 0111D]. This is on the island of Avalon, blessed and most fortunate, so called from *aval*, which means “apple” in the British language, because the place abounds in apples and orchards. Someone has elegantly said of it:

> The island of apples, called fortunate,  
> Takes its name from its nature, because it produces everything of itself.  
> It has no need of farmers ploughing its fields.  
> All cultivation is absent except what nature supplies.  
> Of itself it produces fertile crops and grapes;  
> And apples, born from their own precious seed in its woods.  
> The whole earth brings forth all things, freely overflowing in place of grass.  
> There people live for a hundred years and more.  
> This was the new Jerusalem; this also the polishing-stone of faith.  
> This is the tomb of saints; this alone is celebrated by heaven.  
> He who is buried here scarcely pays the penalties of hell.

This island was called the tomb of saints because innumerable bodies of saints are buried there. Hoel [variant: Coel], king of the Armorican Britons [Col. 0112C], Arthur’s nephew through his sister and father of St. Helena, mother of Constantine the Great, also rests there.

Moreover, after 648 years Arthur’s body was found, and, placed in a tomb of magnificent workmanship, was transferred to the greater church, as may be seen in William of Malmesbury, Book I, *On the Deeds of the English*. The Chronicle of Ralph of Coggeshall, a Cistercian monk in England, preserved in manuscript in the library of St. Victor at Paris, says of him:

> “In the year 1191—that is, under Philip Augustus—the bones of the most famous Arthur, once king of Britain, were found at Glastonbury, deposited in a very ancient sarcophagus. Near it stood two upright ancient pyramids, on which certain letters had been inscribed; but because of their extreme barbarity and defacement they could not be read. They were found on this occasion. While they were digging the earth there in order to bury a monk who, in his lifetime, had earnestly desired this spot as a place of burial [Col. 0112D], they found a sarcophagus upon which had been placed a leaden cross, inscribed thus: ‘Here lies the renowned King Arthur, buried in the island of Avalon.’ That place, once enclosed by marshes, was called the island of Avalon, that is, the island of apples.”

John Bromton says much the same in his *Chronicle*, p. 1152; he also lucidly refutes many of the fabulous things Geoffrey of Monmouth assembled concerning Arthur.

Likewise Henry of Knighton, canon of Leicester, Book II of *The Events of England*, where one may see that what is said concerning Arthur, his deeds, and his burial is not fiction; rather, the fictions are British claims that Arthur is still to come. Henry himself is to be believed as an eyewitness (*ἀυτόπτῃ*), since he attended such a translation and touched with his own hands Arthur’s body and all the things mentioned above.]

—and I await the Messiah with the Jews. It befits noble and magnificent persons to promise nothing, but, as if foreknowing people’s desires, to anticipate their petitions with gifts. It still serves me to lose a little time, so that his will may be explored most exactly: namely, why he has promised so much, and why he keeps me suspended in longer expectation. And would that he might consider the jeopardy to his reputation, and, concerned not about my advancement but about his own standing, frequently heed Solomon’s saying: “Wind and clouds and rain that do not follow: a boastful man who does not fulfill promises” [Note: Prov. 25.].

If within a very few days [Col. 0112B] his generosity does not smile upon me more kindly, “I will cast my care upon you, Lord, and you will nourish me.” Trusting especially in your compassion, I expect no assistance from elsewhere. “Remember your word to your servant, in which you gave me hope” [Note: Ps. 118.]. If affection for his pious liberality and for my summons remains in you, let it be your pleasure to express your will to me by a speedier message.

For the lot of mortality has removed my father and mother from the company of humankind; and bitter death at the first onset has plundered those whom I considered most necessary to me [Col. 0113A], making me an example of extreme calamity and a plaything of fortune. Therefore, since I place singular trust in you, make it possible for me to draw breath under the hand of your magnificence after the long tempest of misfortune. Farewell.

## LETTER XXXV. TO ANSELMA, A NUN

**SUMMARY.**—He highly praises Anselma, a most noble virgin, for having embraced the monastic rule, and exhorts her, after conquering every temptation of flesh and world, steadfastly to guard the treasure of chastity.

To Anselma, beloved in Christ, P. of Blois, archdeacon of Bath, greetings in him whom to serve is to reign.

Holy Church exults, and with one voice gives thanks to the common Giver of grace, because God has regarded you, his humble handmaid [Col. 0113B]; because, though reared among the seductive pleasures of courtly rank, he has encouraged you by the spirit of counsel and fortitude toward the purpose of religious life and the desire for a poor life. Therefore, “Hear, daughter, and see, and incline your ear” [Note: Ps. 44]; and lest the favor of popular applause entice you amid the first beginnings of your initiated holiness, forget your people and your father’s house.

Many indeed offer you the poisons of treacherous flattery from the cup of Babylon. Rehearsing your beauty and the distinction of your birth, they murmur as though grieving and lamenting that you are lowly in the house of the Lord and do not dwell in the tents of sinners. But you must remember that you have dedicated your nobility and beauty [Col. 0113C] to him who is fairer than the children of men [Note: [Col. 0113] Ibid.]; whose beauty sun and moon admire; whose nobility the prophet, unable sufficiently to disclose it, declares: “Who shall recount his generation?” [Note: [Col. 0113] Isa. 53.] To him you consecrated the undefiled flower of your youth among the lilies of chastity—him whom the young maidens loved exceedingly, who says of himself: “I am the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys” [Note: [Col. 0113] Song 2.]. [Note: [Col. 0113] Ambrose, Sermon 90, On Saint Agnes.] Entrust therefore your thoughts and the outcome of the life you have begun to the judgment of him who invited you to the marriage of an undefiled bed and to desirable embraces: in serving him you are free; in loving him, chaste; in touching him, undefiled.

I know indeed that your parents’ wish generally tended toward joining you in marriage to the nephew of the Duke of Burgundy, so that the kinship thus contracted with him might become both an occasion of mutual affection and an increase of power. Certainly, as regards bodily endowments, that young man surpassed all the magnates of that province. By prowess in arms and elegance of form, he became in men’s eyes an object of astonishment and wonder; and—what might have bewitched a maiden’s mind—none was more polished in speech, none more generous in gifts, none more lavish in every liberality. Yet, with wiser prudence and a stricter guard, imposing on yourself the observance of chastity, you triumphed more gloriously over lust where a graver conflict and a more perilous battle threatened. Now you sail in harbour [Note: [Col. 0113] Terence, *Andria*]; yet even now the wind of temptation, breaking forth from the land of unlikeness, secretly whistles at you.

“If you were now in the world, the arms of illustrious men would support you among ranks of matrons. If you were now in the world, you would proceed conspicuous through abundance of wealth and variety of furnishings, glorious in numerous relatives and in the fruitfulness of offspring. If you were now in the world, everything would now overflow for you according to your desire. But now you are enslaved to cloistered narrowness, where every liberty of wandering is barred; where every laugh, every frivolity, all worldly pleasures [Col. 0114B] and desires of the world are banished; where there are funeral garments, unbroken vigils, drinking water and wine mixed together, and food consisting of vegetables and rather austere bread.”

Thus the enemy of the human race artfully suggests these things to you, most dear one, cleverly disguising the disadvantages of worldly life. I pass over how barren and uncertain human pleasure is: although it often pleases, it brings repentance; and although it delights for a little while, over a longer period it will displease. Wealth and honours are inseparably accompanied by anxiety. The world’s splendour and popular favour are smoke and a breeze suddenly vanishing. Add that a woman gives birth in pain and very great danger; and that, most frequently, a bitterer misfortune interrupts the glory of children—now by sickness, now by captivity, now by death. Therefore guard your heart with all vigilance [Note: [Col. 0113] Prov. 4.], that you may possess your vessel in sanctification. For the treasure of chastity is beyond comparison. Chastity alone follows the Lamb wherever he goes [Note: [Col. 0113] Rev. 14.]; chastity alone refashions life into an angelic one. Foolish virgins suppose that pleasure lies in the loss of chastity, though it cannot be lost without shame and grief; its loss admits of no valuation. And though we heal every sin through repentance, the fall of virgins alone does not deserve a remedy of restoration. Farewell.

## LETTER XXXVI. TO CHRISTIANA, A NUN

**Subject.**—He praises the nun because she has preserved the chastity consecrated to God in religion; he exhorts her [Col. 0114D] to join charity, humility, and perseverance to virginity.

To his dearest sister CHRISTIANA, P. of Blois, Archdeacon of Bath, her own, greeting in him without whom there is no salvation.

“My soul magnifies the Lord, and my spirit has rejoiced in God my saviour” [Note: [Col. 0113] Luke 1.], because, walking in the saving Spirit, you preserve your vessel in sanctification and in the fragrance of sweetness. Hence too, “your name is as ointment poured out” [Note: [Col. 0113] Ps. 47]. It is publicly said, [Col. 0115A] and you have earned very great praise before God and men, because from the time when you professed the life of a nun, you have not ceased from observance of chastity and holiness. Hence, “as is your name, so is your praise unto the ends of the earth” [Note: [Col. 0115] Hos. 2.].

When you were destined for the marriage of mortals, the Son of the Most High deigned to betroth you to himself, as he himself speaks through the prophet: “I will betroth you,” he says, “in mercy and compassions, and I will betroth you to me in faith” [Note: [Col. 0115] II Cor. 12.] For virgins are betrothed to Christ in order that they may offer him their chastity. “I have betrothed you,” says the Apostle, “to one husband, to present you as a chaste virgin to Christ.” For God most willingly binds to himself in the love of betrothal those whom the world has not defiled. He is the lover and zealous guardian of virginity, who chose beforehand to be born of a Virgin. Therefore [Col. 0115B] he especially wished to be born of a virgin, so that other virgins might follow his virgin mother’s example of chastity and humility and become participants and companions in the glory of eternal dwelling. “Virgins shall be brought after her; her companions shall be brought to you. They shall be brought in gladness and rejoicing; they shall be led into the temple of the king” [Note: [Col. 0115] Ps. 44.].

See therefore, dearest sister, that you have not received the grace of God in vain [Note: [Col. 0115] II Cor. 12.]. For you have received Christ’s grace in vain and carry an empty lamp if you do not possess the oil of charity—that is, if you do not love Christ with your whole heart. Chastity is then beautiful and pleasing to Christ when charity is its companion, according to the saying: “O how beautiful is a chaste generation with charity” [Note: [Col. 0115D] All copies read thus, although the Vulgate version has always read “with brightness.” But Blesensis reads it thus because he was speaking of charity. The passage in the Septuagint reads: **Κρείσσων ἀτεκνία μετὰ ἀρετῆς**, that is, “Better is childlessness with virtue.”]. Have therefore charity, sister, and humility, which [Col. 0115C] is most acceptable to him who dwells in heaven and looks upon the lowly in heaven and on earth [Note: [Col. 0115] Ps. 112.]. “Upon whom,” he says, “shall my spirit rest, except upon the humble and gentle person who trembles at my words?” [Note: [Col. 0115] Isa. 66.] The Lord looked upon the Virgin Mary not because she was beautiful, noble, or wise, but because she was humble. “He has regarded,” she says, “the humility of his handmaid” [Note: [Col. 0115] Luke 1.].

Therefore be humble, you who for Christ humbled yourself and chose to be lowly in the house of God rather than to dwell in the tents of sinners [Note: [Col. 0115] Ps. 83.]. Humility is of no benefit unless it perseveres to the end. For, although all virtues run toward the prize, perseverance alone is crowned. “All the glory of the king’s daughter is within,” says the Prophet, “in golden fringes” [Note: [Col. 0115] Ps. 41.]. Fringes are the extremities of a garment. Thus the glory of a nun lies in the fringes: [Col. 0115D] for the glory of good conduct at its beginning avails nothing unless the end too is glorious [Col. 0116A]. Hope of harvest relieves the farmer from labour, and hope of a crown makes the brave boxer despise the pain of blows. May expectation of jubilee likewise steal away from you the burdens of the cloister and the service of welcome bondage. Then the dove, sent out from the ark on the seventh day, will not return again [Note: [Col. 0115] Gen. 8]; and, according to Job’s word [Note: [Col. 0115] Job 39.], the young of hinds, going out to pasture, will by no means return again to their mothers. For you and those like you, going into the glory of the children of God, will be in the place of pasture and will not return to the troubles of this life.

These brief exhortations and entreaties, dearest sister, I have resolved to address to you, not because you need my admonition, but that you may run more courageously toward the palm and the prize; because, according to the pagan poet,

> It does no harm to put the spur to a horse already set in motion.  
> [Note: [Col. 0115] Ovid, *Pontic Letters*, II.6.]

## LETTER XXXVII. TO ALEXANDER, PRIOR OF JUMIÈGES

[Col. 0116B]

**Subject.** He explains why he did not return, at the appointed time, the book which he had promised to restore.

To his dearest companion and friend, Master ALEXANDER, Prior of Jumièges, P. of Blois, Archdeacon of Bath, his own, greeting in the true Saviour.

I had promised to return your book on the Saturday which has now passed; this I did not do. Yet the Apostle too promised that he would go into Spain, and, the Lord disposing otherwise, did not fulfil his promise [Note: [Col. 0115] Rom. 15.]. I had thought that I should read through the whole book before the appointed day; afterward, however, I did not have even a moment’s opportunity to read. [Col. 0116C] Therefore, trusting in your affection, I presume to retain the book still. And though presumption ordinarily makes one liable to accusation, here presumption itself makes the matter excusable [Note: [Col. 0115] Digest, book XIII, title 6, law 5]. For in civil law, if anyone takes a horse lent to him beyond the time and place assigned to him, he is liable to an action for theft; nevertheless, if he has done this through confidence in affection, he is excused from theft and fraud. May my friend prosper, and pray for me.

## LETTER XXXVIII. TO ALBERT

[Note: [Col. 0115D]

This was Albert of Morra, a native of Benevento. Adrian IV first created him cardinal deacon of Saint Adrian, and later cardinal priest of Saint Lawrence in Lucina, in 1158. Alexander III then made him chancellor of the Holy Roman Church and sent him as legate to England to investigate the murder of Saint Thomas. There, after carefully examining the matter, he absolved King Henry and declared him free from that killing, drawing up a public instrument on the matter and writing letters to the bishop of Ravenna; these are found in Baronius, vol. XII of the *Annals*, under the year 1172. Finally, on Urban III’s death, he was elected supreme pontiff and called Gregory VIII. Although his pontificate was exceedingly brief—about two months—he nevertheless left great monuments of his piety. For, when he first received at Ferrara news of his elevation, he immediately directed his mind to securing aid for the Holy Land. Having learned that Saladin, Sultan of Egypt, had captured the city of Jerusalem, together with the Lord’s sepulchre and cross, after a great slaughter of Christians, and that his predecessor Urban III had died from grief at so great a disaster, this most pious pontiff, successor alike to his see and to his grief, immediately sounded the call to arms and sent letters throughout the world to stir the hearts of all princes and Christians, so that they might devote all their resources to repelling Christ’s enemies. And because, as commonly happens, such great and numerous evils had occurred through the sins of Christians themselves, he imposed a five-year fast on the entire Christian world, while prescribing for himself and the cardinals an even harsher form of penance.

I think this letter was written about the year 1175.]

TO A CARDINAL OF THE ROMAN CHURCH. [A.D. 1176.]

**Subject.** He describes the merits of the Archbishop of Canterbury and defends him against the charges brought against him: that he is ignorant of law, avaricious, and excessively devoted to advancing his own relatives.

[Col. 0116D] To his beloved lord ALBERT, by God’s grace priest-cardinal and chancellor of the Roman Church, [Col. 0117A] P. of Blois, the humble chancellor of the Lord of Canterbury, his own, greeting in the true Saviour.

“If I speak to my lord, though I am dust and ashes” [Note: [Col. 0117] Gen. 18.], I do so as though leave had been obtained by edict. I ask that participation in the same office may, just as it compels me to boldness, so incline you to indulgence. I give thanks to God and to you because, in a spirit of gentleness, you have, according to your custom, touched mildly and almost fraternally upon the matters which appeared noteworthy in my lord. I know that “the spiritual person judges all things, but is himself judged by no one” [Note: [Col. 0117] I Cor. 2.]. Therefore I receive your rebuke, whether it concerns me or my lord, with thanksgiving. For it is written: “Those whom I love, I rebuke and chastise” [Note: [Col. 0117] Rev. 3.]. And would that “the righteous man may correct me in mercy and rebuke me, but that the oil [Col. 0117B] of the sinner may not anoint my head” [Note: [Col. 0117] Ps. 140].

I do not say that my lord [Note: [Col. 0118D]

Richard, successor of Saint Thomas in the archbishopric of Canterbury, at whose table and as whose chancellor Peter served.

Written about 1176, when Peter was a member of Richard’s household.]

is such a one as “committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth”; for I should lie. For “if we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” [Note: [Col. 0117] I John 1.]. Nor ought you to be moved with severity if human frailty sometimes falls under a violent impulse of temptation. Behold, those who serve God are not steadfast, and he finds perversity in his angels [Note: [Col. 0117] Job 4.]. Nevertheless, since it pleased him who “calls those things which are not as though they were” [Note: [Col. 0117] Rom. 4.] to set apart my lord to minister to him in the priesthood within the patriarchal church—for he did not take the honour to himself, but was called by the Lord [Col. 0117C] as Aaron was [Note: [Col. 0117] Heb. 5.]—he did not put off the monk, becoming “Ephraim, a trained heifer loving to tread the grain” [Note: [Col. 0117] Hos. 10.]; nor was he a lord over the clergy, but an example to the flock among the people, preserving his vessel in sanctification and not loosening consecrated lips for idle talk. He held his food, dress, and every action under the restraint of a stricter rule, so that one who had served God in the camp of monastic religion from the first movements of youth might now be acknowledged not as a monk but as an angel in human form.

If you consider his humility, no one is lower in his own eyes; and, as is written of Moses [Note: [Col. 0117] Num. 12.], he is the meekest of all who dwell upon earth, gladly attentive to the needy and poor, making the afflictions of the poor his own in the depths of mercy. As if he foresaw [Col. 0118A] the necessities of widow and orphan, he anticipates the preparation of their hearts with benefactions. Since it is written of Job [Note: [Col. 0117] chap. 1] that he was simple, upright, and God-fearing, my lord’s simplicity is counted against him as a fault, though he is just and God-fearing. Yet we read that Christ Jesus chose Peter, Andrew, and the others through whom he wrought salvation in the midst of the earth, not from Justinian’s law-court but from the simplicity of fishing. For the wisdom of this world puffs up [Note: [Col. 0117] I Cor. 8.], as does the windy loquacity of laws; one should not think more highly than one ought to think, but think soberly. If my lord thinks humbly, if he does not aspire to high things, if he does not walk in great and wonderful matters above himself, if he is ignorant of the tricks of crafty law, he is nevertheless instructed in the law of the Lord and in wisdom from above, and walks [Col. 0118B] in the paths of justice, determining nothing in the decisions of cases which he would not bring before a common hearing and the public knowledge of men. For he brings forth his righteousness as the light and his judgment as the noonday [Note: [Col. 0117] Ps. 36.].

I know, however, certain people whose mouth is full of cursing and bitterness, who have assailed my lord’s innocence with slanders, branding him with the mark of avarice because he does not lavish the goods of the poor and the patrimony of the Crucified One upon hunters. He does not seek the favour of such men, whose praise he accounts blame; nor does he beg for glory through the service of another’s voice, since this is his glory: the testimony of his conscience [Note: [Col. 0117] II Cor. 1.]. I have often advised him to be more indulgent toward his reputation and [Col. 0118C] to stop the mouths of those speaking evil with gifts. His reply was: “If I pleased such people, I should not be Christ’s servant” [Note: [Col. 0117] Gal. 1.]. If it is expedient to please people, let my praise be in the Lord among the gentle and just; as though he said with the Prophet: “My soul shall be praised in the Lord; let the meek hear and rejoice” [Note: [Col. 0117] Ps. 33.]. For it is not the person who commends himself, or whom men commend, who is approved, but the one whom God commends [Note: [Col. 0117] II Cor. 10.].

Others charge him with being excessively anxious over the advancement of his relatives, and say that it is not the Spirit of the Father but flesh and blood that reveals this to him. But if he bestows the affection of piety upon his relations, this is not outside the order of charity, since the Apostle says: “Anyone who does not care for his own, especially members of his household, has denied the faith [Col. 0119A] and is worse than an unbeliever” [Note: [Col. 0119] I Tim. 5.]. Nevertheless, he does not indulge blood relationship so greatly that he fails to provide generously and magnificently also for strangers, if they are honourable, preferring them even to nearer blood-relations. The slanderers have proceeded in their malice, as the Apostle says, “hateful to God” [Note: [Col. 0119] Rom. 1], and have disturbed the serenity of your favour toward my lord, alienating friend and neighbour from him. I grieve, I grieve; and since you have set him against yourselves, I have become burdensome to myself [Note: [Col. 0119] Job 7]. For I know that, apart from any deficiency in his merits, you have withdrawn your favour from him. Yet, Lord, “you will add, that you may be more well pleased still” [Note: [Col. 0119] Ps. 76], and in anger you will remember mercy. For the Lord will reveal the marks of virtue and the gifts of grace which he has planted in him; he will confound lying lips and show to be liars [Col. 0119B] those who have stained the innocent [Note: [Col. 0119] Wis. 10.].

It will belong to your holiness, moreover, to cherish in the bowels of Christ my lord, who loves you with all truth and sincerity, and, supplying for my inadequacy, kindly and effectively to present and promote his affairs, in which equity and reason stand beside him. Farewell.

## LETTER XXXIX. TO A CERTAIN FRIEND

PETER of Blois, Archdeacon of Bath, to E., his friend and companion: greeting and progress toward better things.

Sincere affection has no need of colourful prefaces or the painted pomp of words. Therefore, being entirely certain of the mutual union of affection between us, I employ a brief [Col. 0119C] discourse; and from this letter I cut away both the hunting blandishments of flattery and every weariness of prolixity. I give you thanks because your servants did not allow us to remain ignorant of what was in your stores. Know this: the Roman Curia has, according to its custom, bound me in many debts; but if I escape Scylla once, by God’s grace I shall not fall back into Charybdis.

## LETTER XL. TO A CERTAIN PRELATE, HIS FRIEND

**Subject.**—He inveighs against H., a prelate who slanders princes.

To his dearest friend H., P. of Blois, Archdeacon of Bath, his own, greeting and a guard upon the lips.

[Col. 0119D] I should rejoice greatly if your speech were more restrained and corrected, if your tongue did not sit upon slippery ground. For you provoke the hatred of many against yourself while you do not restrain your spirit, while you unlawfully loose your uncircumcised lips for whispering and slander. But, to say nothing of other matters, what madness is it to slander the lord king and assail his reputation with poisonous words? Certainly all filthy speech is unbecoming in a prelate and is often harmful. Since no one bears patiently the injuries of slander, princes—who are owed [Col. 0120A] greater reverence—bear them more impatiently and are often stirred to destroy their slanderers.

The apostle John, rebuking his slanderer who babbled against him, says: “Diotrephes, who loves to hold the first place, babbling against us, does not receive us; therefore, if I come, I shall call to mind his deeds” [Note: [Col. 0119] III John 9–10.]. From this it is clear that an itching tongue displeases even saints and those perfect in the Lord. Such people are gnats, biting and stinging in secret; and, while they corrode and spoil the good qualities of others by slanders, they are compared to rust and to the serpent. Therefore Solomon says: “If a serpent bites in silence, the secret slanderer has nothing less” [Note: [Col. 0119] Eccl. 10.]. And again: “The whisperer and double-tongued person is cursed, for he disturbs those at peace” [Note: [Col. 0119] Sir. 28.]. “The teeth of the children of men are weapons and arrows” [Note: [Col. 0119] Ps. 56.]. “Their mouth [Col. 0120B] is full of bitterness and deceit” [Note: [Col. 0119] Ps. 13.]; and their slanders stink before God and men, because “their throat is an open and stinking tomb; the poison of asps is under their lips” [Note: [Col. 0119] Ps. 5].

Therefore the Apostle, writing to the Corinthians, says: “We command and exhort in the Lord those who are such, that, working without complaint and without rumours, they may have peace among themselves” [Note: [Col. 0119] I Cor. 7; II Thess. 3.]. Words by which the lives of princes are disparaged cannot be concealed; once brought into public, they arouse the indignation of magnates and turn to evil upon their authors. Solomon says: “Do not slander a ruler in secret, for the birds of heaven will carry the word, and that which has wings will report the matter” [Note: [Col. 0119] Eccl. 10]. And, speaking also of the indignation of princes, he says: “The anger [Col. 0120C] of a king is a messenger of death” [Note: [Col. 0119] Prov. 16.]. Likewise in the law of God, one who curses a ruler is a child of death [Note: [Col. 0119] Exod. 22.].

Certainly it is excessively absurd for a prelate to devote himself to buffoonery and to pollute lips consecrated to Christ’s Gospel with the unclean and damnable impertinence of words. But if you have so great and unbridled a desire for slander, let it at least suffice to exercise the malice of your itching tongue against persons of middling rank. “Do not set your mouth in heaven, nor let your tongue pass over the earth” [Note: [Col. 0119] Ps. 72.]; for, according to the Apostle, reverence is owed “to the king as supreme” [Note: [Col. 0119] I Pet. 2.]. Since you have also bound yourselves to him by the bond of fealty, I beg you to look more cautiously to yourselves: do not have your spirit in your nostrils, or your tongue on slippery ground; but, as befits the order of your profession, set a guard upon your tongue, so that it may not loosen itself into the liberty of malice. For, as James testifies: “If anyone thinks himself religious and does not restrain his tongue, that person’s religion is vain” [Note: [Col. 0119] Jas. 1.]. “A man of tongue shall not be established upon the earth” [Note: [Col. 0119] Ps. 139.]. For the tongue is a small member, yet it often pollutes the grace of the whole body [Note: [Col. 0119] Jas. 3.]. Nor should one hope that a person who does not restrain the uncleanness of his tongue will restrain himself from any disgrace. For, in Solomon’s testimony: “Like a city lying open and without the circuit of walls is the person who cannot restrain his spirit in speaking” [Note: [Col. 0119] Prov. 25.]. [Col. 0121A] So too, in the law of God [Note: [Col. 0121] Num. 19.], a vessel without a cover is reckoned unclean.

## LETTER XLI. TO HENRY II, KING OF ENGLAND [A.D. 1177]

**Subject.**—He complains that the King of England wanders among uncertain residences; reports that his envoys sent to Rome have returned; and mentions the arrival of envoys of the kings of Spain.

To the lord King of England, PETER of Blois, Archdeacon of Bath, his own, greeting in him who gives salvation to kings.

For a long time I sought and did not find him whom my soul desires; for a long time I pursued you but did not overtake you. For the unreliable reports of the people, differing variously about your routes, while my foot stood upon the straight path, turned me aside [Col. 0121B] into trackless country. Solomon indeed says that there are three things beyond investigation, and a fourth which cannot be discovered at all: the way of an eagle in the sky, the way of a ship at sea, the way of a serpent upon the earth, and the way of a man in his youth [Note: [Col. 0121] Prov. 30.]. I can add a fifth: the way of the King in England. Thus far, lord, I have run at random; and still I do not know where I should come or where I should go.

Worn out by the journey, and moreover seized at Newport [Note: [Col. 0121C] Newport is in Flanders, a very strongly fortified maritime town, three miles from Ostend.] by severe dysentery, I sent ahead in every direction various couriers of yours, scouts of the road. Therefore, most gracious prince, command where and on what day you may be found, so that I may run in the way of your commands and “your word may be a lamp to my feet.” Since it concerns the commonwealth that the business entrusted to me by you should be completed more promptly, I shall spare neither my wretched nor afflicted body until I behold your most desired face; “but do you direct my way before you, O Lord” [Note: [Col. 0121] Ps. 5.].

Your envoys have returned from the Roman Curia, relieved of silver but burdened with lead; not greatly honoured with clothing or mounts. [Col. 0122A] Moreover, the envoys of the kings of Spain have arrived in a great company [Note: [Col. 0121C]

These kings were Alfonso of Castile and Sancho of Navarre, his uncle. Being violently at variance with one another and on the point of moving from plundering and raiding to open arms, they at last, with difficulty and upon their friends’ advice, referred the matter to the arbitration of Henry, King of England. Henry accordingly summoned archbishops, bishops, and magnates of his realm to London; after mature deliberation, he pronounced a solemn judgment which was most agreeable to both kings and brought their peoples the longed-for peace and tranquillity. Ralph, Brompton, and Gervase relate the whole affair at length, together with Henry’s judgment, in their chronicles.

This letter was written in the year of Christ 1177, when these events occurred.]

, bringing before you that ancient—and would that it were now obsolete—controversy between kingdoms, which has drawn the peoples of so many cities into destruction and ruin. But blessed be God: for, as the Queen of the South came from the ends of the earth to hear Solomon’s wisdom [Note: [Col. 0121] III Kings 10.], so today the most distant kings submit themselves to your judgment in this grave and insoluble dispute, earnestly requesting that so knotty a question be resolved under the examination of your discernment. May my most dear lord prosper, and may he live and reign long and happily.

## LETTER XLII. TO ROBERT, ELECT OF CAMBRAI

[Note: [Col. 0121D] This is Robert whom Philip, Count of Flanders, made provost of Saint Donatian at Bruges and Saint Peter at Aire, and chancellor of Flanders, as well as administrator of the vacant bishoprics of Tournai and Arras. Later, after Peter, the count’s brother, renounced the bishopric of Cambrai, Robert was elected bishop of Cambrai; and, as he was proceeding to Cambrai, he was killed in 1174 by James of Avesnes, whom he had formerly gravely offended. Alberic says of him in a manuscript chronicle: “Robert, provost of Aire in Flanders, governed two bishoprics, Arras and Cambrai; he was the son of a rustic smith of Chartres and, as they say, employed a familiar demon through whom he had attained such high honours.” The *Annals of Flanders*, book VI, under the year [Col. 0122D] 1174, speak of him as follows: “At Cambrai Robert, +bishop of Aire [Note: [Col. 0121D] He was only provost.], was chosen in Peter’s place, a man thoroughly full of simony and excessively notorious for ambition, and very dear to Philip, Count of Flanders. He was engaged in a serious quarrel with James of Avesnes, a most powerful knight, and did not dare to set out for Cambrai. Accordingly he was rebuked in a letter by Peter of Blois, a man most learned in letters as letters then were, because he had delayed so long in undertaking a bishop’s duties. At length, after receiving a public guarantee and the noble knight Louis of Fraisnes as guide from Baldwin, Count of Hainaut, he made for Cambrai; but the man of Avesnes laid an ambush for him and, as he was coming to Condé, killed him on the bridge over the Scheldt through certain of his retainers.”]. A.D. 1173?]

[Col. 0122B]

**Subject.**—He reproves R., provost of Aire, because, though elected bishop of Cambrai, he does not perform a bishop’s office, entangles himself in secular affairs, handles cases of bloodshed, tyrannically despoils his subjects, and permits no one to move him.

To the reverend father and lord R., Provost of Aire and Elect of Cambrai, P. of Blois, Archdeacon of Bath, his own, greeting and remembrance of eternal salvation.

In the letter which I send you, “provost” precedes “elect,” because at the courts of earthly kings, and especially in common speech, the title “Provost of Aire” is more celebrated than that of “Elect of Cambrai”; nor is this surprising. For the divine calling has become so cheap in your eyes that you shrink both from the name and office of bishop and, ungrateful to the Most High, blush at the grace offered to you. The Church of Cambrai chose you as shepherd and bishop of souls; [Col. 0122C] but you, while receiving the emoluments of the bishopric, still place provost before elect, and, disdainfully refusing the pastoral ministry, strive to divert episcopal revenues to extraordinary uses.

I grieve indeed that so long and perilous a delay has suspended the grace of your consecration. Episcopal [Col. 0123A] advancement always imparts honour together with burden. But you, impatient of burden and labour, seek your chief pleasure in laborious work. It is written that a person who is ashamed of Christ’s ministry makes himself unworthy of Christ. “Whoever,” says the Lord, “shall confess me before men, him will I also confess before my Father” [Note: [Col. 0123] Matt. 10.]. Would that you were less concerned with the wisdom of this world, which is hostile to God [Note: [Col. 0123] Jas. 4], and diligently sought instead the knowledge of the Lord’s ways and of his discipline.

I fear that in the near future it may be said to you by the Lord: “Because you have rejected knowledge, behold, I reject you from ministering to me as priest” [Note: [Col. 0123] Hos. 4.]. The sentence of your condemnation is already becoming common talk in everyone’s mouth. “He would not have blessing,” they say, “and it shall be far from him” [Note: [Col. 0123] Ps. 108]. [Col. 0123B] What gravely damages the reputation of your name is that you conduct cases involving bloodshed, and that, casting aside concern for the churches, you wholly occupy and entangle yourself in secular business. Yet the profession of your order permits neither the base concerns of the world nor the violence of the material sword. The Apostle says: “If you have secular disputes, appoint as judges those who are of least account among you” [Note: [Col. 0123] 1 Cor. 6.]. It does not befit the order you profess to play any longer at the hazard of so great a peril, and, despising the soul’s salvation, thus damnably to entangle yourself in secular affairs and to circle Mount Seir with a giddy spirit. See what the Prophet imprecates upon such persons: “My God, make them like a wheel, and like chaff before the face of the wind” [Note: [Col. 0123] Ps. 82]. The Lord struck these in their hinder parts: their end is destruction; they sow [Col. 0123C] seed upon the earth; they turn manna and the *gomor* into decay [Note: [Col. 0123] Exod. 16]; their rivers are changed into blood [Note: [Col. 0123] Exod. 7], knowledge into error, their glory passes into confusion, and their life is perpetuated into death. Solomon says in Proverbs: “A wise king winnows the wicked and brings the wheel of evils over them” [Note: [Col. 0123] Prov. 20]. This is the wheel upon which you shall roll without ceasing, while ambitiously thrusting yourself into public and lay affairs and profaning Christ’s sacraments. Chosen as a pontiff, you exercise the power of the sword with a bloodstained conscience. Let him exercise the material sword who has received authority over the sword: for authorities are established by God [Note: [Col. 0123] Rom. 13], that they may take up the sword for the punishment of evildoers and the praise of the good [Note: [Col. 0123] 1 Pet. 2]. But concerning those who usurp the use of the sword for themselves it is written: “[Col. 0123D] Every one who takes up the sword shall perish by the sword” [Note: [Col. 0123] Matt. 26].

For even those who received authority over the sword by virtue of office nevertheless perished by the sword, because they abused the power entrusted to them. Certainly, if you consider in order the fates of Roman rulers, you will find none among them who shed blood whose own blood was not shed. Julius Caesar [Note: [Col. 0123] Dio] was slain by Brutus and Cassius; Antony killed himself; Claudius Caesar was killed by Gaius Caligula; Gaius was killed by the praetorian soldiers; Nero, murderer of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul [Col. 0124A], became his own killer; Galba succeeded Nero, and Otho killed him; Otho too afterwards killed himself. Vitellius succeeded him; slain by a most shameful death, he lacked human burial. Next came Domitian, who banished the blessed John the Evangelist to the island of Patmos; he was condemned by the senate and killed in the palace. Aurelius Commodus, Helvius Pertinax, Julianus, the killer of Helvius, Aurelius Antoninus also, Macer, Macrinus, Marcus Antoninus, Alexander the Roman, Maximinus Julius, Gordian, Philip and Decius, moreover Gallus and his son Volusianus, Quintillus, Aurelian, Probus—all these, and others whom we enumerate elsewhere, both from the Gentiles and from the Jews, because they presumptuously and unjustly exercised the office of the sword, fell by the edge [Col. 0124B] of the sword [Note: [Col. 0123] Dio]. For, as the poet recalls:

> Few kings descend to Ceres’ son-in-law  
> without slaughter and wounds, and tyrants by a dry death.  
> [Note: [Col. 0123] *Tract on the Journey to Jerusalem*.]

For the Prophet’s word is: “Men of blood and deceit shall not live out half their days” [Note: [Col. 0123] Juv. Sat. 10]. Yet among those whom we have just noted as having breathed out their souls by the sword were very many who used the sword only for the furtherance of justice or for overcoming the rebellion of a barbarian people; and these, when they had completed life’s due course, paid the debt of the human condition through the natural dissolution of the body. For Nerva [Note: [Col. 0123] Ps. 54], who recalled blessed John from exile; Aelius Hadrian [Note: [Col. 0123] Dio], who rebuilt Jerusalem and named it Aelia after himself; likewise Antoninus Pius [Note: [Col. 0123] Eusebius, *Hist.* III.15 and *Chron.*; Victor; Theodoret, *Hist.* III.20] and Antoninus the philosopher escaped the savagery of swords. But Aurelius [Col. 0124C] and Julian the Apostate, most wicked persecutors of the Christian name, were struck by Christ himself through heavenly judgment. I fear that you may wish to follow Julian’s footsteps: though called to the Lord’s lot, to become emperor, he made himself excluded from the Christian profession.

What advantage does ambition for great renown among the nations confer upon you? Recall Christ’s words, if you profess yourself his disciple: “The rulers of the Gentiles lord it over them, and those who have power over them are called benefactors. But it shall not be so among you; rather, whoever wishes to become greater among you shall be your servant” [Note: [Col. 0123] Matt. 20]. If you have accepted Christ’s ministry, if you do not reject Christ’s yoke, remain in the calling in which you were called [Note: [Col. 0123] 1 Cor. 7], and leave the government of the people to laymen. Certainly Philip of Merleac, a canon of Chartres, throwing off the Lord’s yoke, as you know, took himself [Col. 0124D] to arms; and, having recently commanded great forces, he was struck by an arrow and died in battle. For it is the heavenly law and the rule of divine judgment that one who abandons Christ’s service under the pretext of worldly rule will meet an unhappy end to this life. Philip’s death, and that of very many others, ought to deter you. In them the Lord has given you a sign, that you may flee from the face of the bow. For it is written: “When the pestilent man is punished, the wise man becomes wiser” [Note: [Col. 0123] Prov. 21], and “the righteous man shall wash his hands in the blood of the sinner” [Note: [Col. 0125] Ps. 57].

Yet it is said that you are so carried away by vanities and false insanities, and, having cast aside the grace of your divine calling, so ardently seek power, that you despoil those subject to you and, by tyrannical oppression, heap up for yourself from the spoils of the poor the wrath and indignation of the Lord. For it is written: “The mighty shall suffer mighty torments” [Note: [Col. 0125] Wis. 6]. Plainly, the exactions which you frequently make under the pretext of being a count have stirred up against you the hatred of many whom you think to be your friends and household, so that, as it is written, “the enemies of a man are those of his own household” [Note: [Col. 0125] Matt. 10]. Robbery in a cleric is indeed detestable: “Do not covet robberies,” says the Prophet [Note: [Col. 0125] Ps. 61]. Certainly he prohibited the act of plundering who cast avarice out of extortion when he forbade the desire for robbery. The griffin-vulture, [Col. 0125B] osprey, hawk, kite, and vulture, because they are birds of prey, are rejected in the Lord’s law and excluded from sacrifice [Note: [Col. 0125] Lev. 11]. If, therefore, you wish to offer yourself as a sacrifice acceptable to God, neither hunger after plunder nor seek power nor accept a gift [Note: [Col. 0125] Isa. 33]. For, in the Prophet’s testimony: “In whose hands are iniquities, their right hand is full of gifts” [Note: [Col. 0125] Ps. 25]. Job too says that fire shall devour the bodies of those who willingly accept gifts [Note: [Col. 0125] Job 15]. I wonder indeed—and cannot sufficiently wonder—whence this accursed ambition has so ardently crept into you. What you usurp for yourself alone from the patrimony of the Crucified would abundantly suffice for three bishops. But I fear that the Lord has rejected you and cast you away from his face, because you have been ashamed of [Col. 0125C] his ministry and obstinately cast off his yoke. Therefore come to your senses, and forestall the Lord’s anger in good time. For if he whets his sword like lightning [Note: [Col. 0125] Deut. 32], if his hand takes hold of judgment, I fear that then you will desire to repent when you cannot do so. For when his anger has blazed up shortly [Note: [Col. 0125] Ps. 2], unquenchable flames will be kindled—flames which, by timely correction and a few penitential tears, you might have extinguished.

That I write to you more harshly than usual, and do not flatter you with the adulation of the plural number, is caused by your obstinacy. For you burned the letters of exhortation which I had recently sent you through the abbot of Clairmarais before reading them; and you assailed with insults the man of God who brought words of life. When he was turning you, [Col. 0125D] so far as he could, away from the path of death, you compared his most holy exhortation, as they say, to the barking of a dog. May the Lord remove the heart of stone from within you and establish you in the keeping of his commandments, so that you may desire to be the minister of him who came to minister for us.

## LETTER XLIII. TO PETER, A FRIEND AND PHYSICIAN

[Col. 0126A]

**SUMMARY.**—He tells Peter, skilled in medicine, that while travelling he visited a nobleman who was ill and treated him. He explains the nature of the illness and of the treatment, and henceforth entrusts the patient to Peter’s care.

To his dearest friend PETER, Master Peter of Blois, greeting in him who is truly salvation.

Recently I was passing through Amboise [Note: [Col. 0125D] I have restored this reading from all our manuscripts. Amboise, or Ambasia—Ambocia in Gregory of Tours—is a town in the province of Touraine on the Loire, so delightfully situated that it might dare to compete with all other places [Col. 0126D] in this kingdom; hence, says Merula in his *Cosmography*, it is no wonder that kings often resided there. I add that it is fortified by an impregnable castle set on an exceedingly high rock.], where the nobleman Geldewin was gravely ill. The lord of the castle met me and humbly and urgently begged me to turn aside to the sick man.

He maintained that, even if I did not apply the hand of treatment, he would nevertheless receive some consolation from my visit. At the urging of the magnates, who most devoutly petitioned on behalf of the sick man, [Col. 0126B] I stayed there three days. Since, owing to my occupations, which you yourselves know, I could not remain longer, I advised that they summon you and encourage your diligence toward the patient with generous payment. Although you are observant in these matters, as one frequently experienced in similar cases, nevertheless, since experience, according to Hippocrates’ testimony, is deceptive, and the Lord sometimes reveals to one person what he conceals from others, do not be reluctant to hear the character of this illness, its symptoms—which will instruct you more fully—and the remedies to be employed in it. It is indeed a common fault of physicians always to differ concerning illnesses; thus, if three or four come to a patient, they never agree either in assigning [Col. 0126C] the cause or in prescribing treatment. But as the two of us are united in purpose, so it is fitting that our works and words should be the same. I have applied the first measures of treatment; and I am certain that he will easily recover, if there is someone who prudently continues his hand.

You should know with certainty that he suffers from a middle *hemitritaeus* fever. For although he suffers continuously every third day, he is afflicted more severely. You know that, if it were the lesser *hemitritaeus*, since it is generated from putrefied phlegm within and outside the vessels, its attacks would never recur on the third day. If it were the greater *hemitritaeus*, because of the putrefaction of black bile within and outside, in the movement of the internal matter, the patient would also lose movement and the use of his limbs [Col. 0126D]; moreover, his teeth would close against one another. Since none of these things occurs at all in this fever, it is clear that this is a middle *hemitritaeus*, arising from yellow bile putrefied in the vessels and stomach. For if the putrefaction were in the liver—which can sometimes occur—red and thin urine [Col. 0127A] would threaten combustion and tend toward blackness. Since this does not occur, you see that the matter remains in the vessels and stomach.

Accordingly, when I arrived, because the fever had seized him that very day, I had the hepatic vein opened. And because, while the disease is increasing—as is apparent from the fact that the urine is still red and thin—purging must not yet be used, I employed astringent remedies and applied violet oil over the heart and liver and to his forehead. It remains, therefore, that when thicker urine announces the time of complete digestion, you give him cold *cahonis* [uncertain medicinal preparation], which is safer to give than oxymel or anything else; for in it all the harmful quality of scammony has disappeared through the effect of cooking. A decoction of cassia fistula, yellow myrobalans, maidenhair, and the seeds of citron, gourd, and melon would also be excellent for him, provided you judge the patient’s strength able to bear these things. His diet, as you know, must be very thin: namely, ptisan, and bread-crumb washed three or four times in water. Nor should fomentations of mallow, violets, and poppy be lacking around his feet, for there the heat is especially intense. But if violent heat should seize the summit of the head, as often happens, let the head be shaved, and let the head, forehead, and [Col. 0128A] temples be soothed by cloths dipped in rosewater and the juice of nightshade, houseleek, *crassula*, *vermicularis*, and plantain. Because of the onset of thirst, let the tongue be washed, as you know, with parsley, and scraped with wood. For sleeplessness, apply to the feet a decoction of black poppy, mallow, violet, and henbane, and apply the boiled herbs to the head. Against constipation, make a suppository or administer clysters. I write this to you not because you need instruction, but so that the treatment which proceeds from our common deliberation may be safer for you and more acceptable to the patient. For often, through a physician’s gracious aptitude and through a certain confidence which the patient thereby conceives, nature, already failing, recovers strength. You must therefore be watchful and energetic in attending this man; from his recovery both a great title of honour will accrue to you and profit will answer your desire.

## LETTER XLIV. TO ARNULF, BISHOP OF LISIEUX

[Note: [Col. 0127C]

This Arnulf was liberally but Christianly educated from his earliest boyhood, apparently among the regular canons whom his brother John, bishop of Séez, had brought from the celebrated house of Saint Victor at Paris into his cathedral. He was archdeacon of that church for some time, until, upon the death of his uncle John, bishop of Lisieux, he was elected bishop of the same place by the common vote of all. Although the count of Anjou tried to oppose this election, it was confirmed by Innocent II, supreme pontiff, through the intervention of Peter the Venerable, abbot of Cluny. He was intensely devoted to the Holy Apostolic See. Thus, standing among the foremost against the schismatics on behalf of Pope Alexander III, he also induced Henry II, king of the English, to support Alexander’s cause. When he wrote to the supreme pontiff about this matter, Alexander publicly ordered Arnulf’s letter to be read in the assembly of cardinals, in order openly to testify how welcome it was to him; so Alexander himself wrote back to Arnulf [Col. 0127D]. How highly Alexander afterwards valued him is evident from the fact that he very often wrote to him familiarly and used his services in various ecclesiastical affairs. Nor is this surprising, since he was numbered among the most learned and wisest men of his age, as his works, handled by all learned people, bear witness.

He lived forty years in the episcopate. Having sought advice from his friends, especially from Peter of Blois—as is clear from this present letter—he resigned it for the sake of solitude and withdrew to the monastery of Saint Victor at Paris, a dwelling-place of holiness and innocence. There he died after a year, that is, in 1181, and was buried in the old basilica which he had founded; in 1550 he was transferred to the larger church, where he rests.

Concerning the cause of his retirement, Baronius, following Roger, speaks rather unfavourably when he says that Arnulf left his bishopric because of the hatred of the king of England which he had incurred. First, what that hatred was and why Arnulf incurred it, no writer of that age except Roger alone [Col. 0128C] has said a word; yet several wrote about Henry II’s affairs, and quite freely—Matthew Paris, William of Malmesbury, Polydore Vergil, Gervase, Ralph, Brompton, the canon of Leicester, and others.
