Among all of them there is a remarkable silence about this hatred, although some have spoken of his voluntary retirement and resignation of the episcopate. Certainly Robert of Torigni, a writer of those times earlier than Roger, or at least his contemporary, offers no other cause; indeed, he writes without qualification that Arnulf, bishop of Lisieux, after governing the same church for forty years, resigned the bishopric and went to Paris, there to spend the rest of his days at Saint Victor, in the very beautiful dwellings he had built there for his own use.

Add also the necrology of the same Saint Victor, which reads: “The solemn anniversary of our father of pious memory, Arnulf, bishop of Lisieux, who, because of the great devotion which he had had toward our church for many years previously, came to us from his bishopric, became our canon, and chose this church above all others as the place of his repose and burial. By many great benefactions he left to posterity a worthy and perpetual memorial of his name and love,” etc. [Col. 0128D] I pass over the fact that in the letter of Peter of Blois there is not even a word of this matter; indeed, it silently suggests another cause, without, however, asserting it. Further, so far was he from incurring Henry’s hatred that all writers agree that Arnulf always possessed very great authority and favour with King Henry: first, when he inclined Henry to the side of Alexander, the lawful pontiff, as is clear from what Alexander himself wrote to Arnulf in testimony of his own feeling:

> “We render thanks to the Creator of all things, offering proclamations of praise, because we have heard that that magnificent and most serene prince of the world, Henry, king of the English, remains firm and steadfast in the unity of the Catholic Church, and that, especially through your influence, he has strengthened his mind in this holy purpose. We ask, indeed, that you continue always watchful and solicitous concerning him,” [Col. 0129D] etc.

Further, he was very frequently sent by Henry to Thomas, archbishop of Canterbury, to prevent the excommunication which Thomas proposed to thunder against him. Finally, when Henry was in distress because of the dreadful rebellion and conspiracy of his sons against him, he sent Arnulf, together with Rotrou, archbishop of Rouen, as envoy to the king of the French for reconciliation, as is clear from Letter [Col. 0130D] 153 in Peter of Blois, which both envoys wrote to Henry.

Moreover, this letter appears to have been written about the year 1108, when, or a little after when, Arnulf resigned the episcopate.]

. [c. A.D. 1108.]

[Col. 0128B]

**SUMMARY.**—He advises A., bishop of Lisieux, not to resign his bishopric because of troubles unjustly inflicted by the prince, the chapter, or others, but only if he attained it through the support of human ambition.

To the reverend father and lord ARNULF, by God’s grace bishop of Lisieux, P. of Blois: greeting, and the spirit of counsel and fortitude.

Since you are a man of lofty counsel and tested prudence, [Col. 0129A] I wonder that you seek counsel from me and from other lesser men in a dangerous and arduous matter, unless because it is itself an act of prudence to examine the counsel of lesser men in difficult affairs. For the Lord often reveals to a lesser person what he conceals from the greater. You desire to resign episcopal administration and transfer yourself to holy leisure, if you have the counsel and assent of your friends in this matter. It would be rash for me to pronounce upon a matter so dangerous and difficult unless I first knew all the circumstances of your condition. I know that you are already declining into old age and senility, and that your body, broken by labours and years, foretells its own end. The institution of the holy Fathers provides that an assistant be added for bishops who are infirm and elderly [Col. 0129B]. Thus Augustine was joined to Valerius, bishop of Hippo [Note: [Col. 0129] Possidius, *Life of Augustine*, ch. 8]. Thus an assistant was given, by Gregory’s authority, to the bishop of Rimini; and, by Pope Zachary’s authority, to Boniface, archbishop of Mainz, when they suffered bodily infirmity.

But if you fear your prince’s displeasure, the harassments of your chapter, or other troubles of this life, and therefore choose peace and quiet, such conduct befits a man of base and faint-hearted spirit, not you, whom all know to have possessed beyond others a great and generous heart. Certainly in this repose you would not find rest; and behold, in your peace there would be most bitter bitterness [Note: [Col. 0129] Isa. 38], while you remembered with groaning and anguish of spirit that you had failed there [Col. 0129C] where you ought to have stood most firmly; and, having cast aside the spirit of counsel and fortitude, you would see that you had been overthrown by faintness of spirit and a slight storm. If you believe me, no vexation ought to lead you to resign the episcopate. Perhaps the Lord works all these things in order that vexation may give you understanding. Grain is threshed that it may be stored in the granary; a stone is squared that it may be placed in the temple’s building without the sound of a hammer; the whirlwind is stirred that Elijah may be carried to heaven [Note: [Col. 0129] 4 Kings 2].

If, however, you seek your prince’s favour, you can obtain it very easily, provided you conduct yourself toward him humbly and devotedly. He is a man who detests rebellion and contumacy in bishops above all things. He is one who conquers and is conquered by humility alone. Yet another legitimate [Col. 0129D] ground for resignation may be present. Since it is written [Note: [Col. 0129] Gen. 3] that the human inclinations are prone to evil from youth, it is said that from youth you began to scent ecclesiastical honours, and that you aspired to this [Col. 0130A] dignity, which now burdens you, through acts of service, intercessions, and other supports of human ambition. Run, therefore, to the testimony of your conscience; and if you find that your entrance was less than canonical, be concerned about your departure. For here resignation has a place. For, as blessed Gregory attests [Note: [Col. 0129] Book IX, Letter 40], one who climbs into the sheepfold not through the door but by another way vainly exhausts himself for the prize of eternal salvation unless he entirely abandons the dignity in which he sinned. Thus it is a holy and salutary thought, after resigning the episcopate, to choose a private life, if you recall that your conscience was wounded even slightly in pursuit of the promotion just mentioned. If you accept the counsel of my lowliness, retain for yourself absolutely nothing [Col. 0130B] that you acquired through sin.

Evening is now drawing on for you, and the days of your life have declined. The enemy also watches your heel and waits for your final struggle. Break the bonds of iniquity and cast off the oppressor’s yoke. Lay down the burdens of ambitious possessions, lest the hidden wrestler find you laden. A naked athlete fights more strongly. A swimmer strips himself to cross a river. A traveller is relieved of his burdens so that he may run more freely. On this road you are soon to swim the torrent of death and to fight with him against whom the contest is always uncertain, the fall dangerous, restoration difficult, and victory rare and never secure. Let him find nothing in you that is his own. Rather, let him who once defeated you in your stronger years find you victorious, even though decrepit [Col. 0130C] and infirm. Farewell.

## LETTER XLV. TO A CERTAIN ANONYMOUS PERSON [c. A.D. 1174]

**SUMMARY.**—He denies that Reginald, bishop-elect of Bath, was either a persecutor or killer of Saint Thomas, archbishop of Canterbury; but if in word or deed he offended against him in any way, this happened through ignorance, or was in any case expiated through alms, tears, and voluntarily undertaken penances.

You accuse and condemn R., bishop-elect of Bath [Note: [Col. 0130D] Because Reginald had been charged with the persecution and killing of Saint Thomas, certain people were trying to impede his consecration to the bishopric of Bath. Peter accordingly endeavours in this letter to clear him of so great a crime.], as though he were the persecutor and killer of the blessed martyr Thomas. You surely know how dangerous it is to brand an innocent person with the mark of so great a crime and to raise a detestable infamy against one who has done no wrong. Even should you wish to erase it, you will be unable to restrain its spread [Col. 0130D]. I know that he loved the martyr from his heart, and that among the desirable things of this world he had once especially wished to attach himself to the martyr’s friendship and service. For the blessed [Col. 0131A] martyr had suspended his father, the bishop of Salisbury [Note: [Col. 0131D]

That is, Jocelin, whom Thomas, archbishop of Canterbury, had excommunicated because he was present at the coronation of the Young King, performed contrary to the right of the Church of Canterbury [Col. 0132D].

This letter was written about the year 1174, when Reginald was elected.]

. It is no wonder if at that time the son, compassionating his afflicted father, sometimes spoke too harshly or less prudently concerning the holy martyr. For we too, being foolish, thought his life madness and his end without honour; but he has been counted among the sons of God, and his lot is among the chosen [Note: [Col. 0131] Wis. 5]. Whatever he did under the pretext of charity and zeal for justice was turned into a charge of hatred and envy. Conversely, whatever human malice contrived for his disgrace, the Lord turned to his crown.

Of our own head, Jesus Christ, Isaiah says: “We thought him a leper, struck by God and humbled” [Note: [Col. 0131] Isa. 53]. We likewise regarded Christ’s most precious member as [Col. 0131B] leprous and rejected. This is the leprosy that spreads itself over the saints of the Lord. Concerning this leprosy I remember reading in Leviticus [Note: [Col. 0131] ch. 3]: “If the spreading leprosy has blossomed over the skin, the priest shall judge the leprosy entirely clean.” Although every leprosy is unclean, the leprosy of infamy which afflicts the innocence of saints is clean; for when adverse opinion spreads abroad and iniquity outwardly lies against itself, the souls of the saints are in God’s hand [Note: [Col. 0131] Wis. 3], and the righteous, scorning the words of outward reproach, are secure through the treasure of conscience.

Observe in Christ the traces of this leprosy, which pass from head to members, from father to children. The Lord healed the sick and was called a violator of the Sabbath. “This man,” they said, “is not from God, because he does not keep the Sabbath” [Note: [Col. 0131] John 9]. He cast out demons, and they attributed this [Col. 0131C] to sorcery: “He casts out demons,” they said, “by Beelzebub, prince of demons” [Note: [Col. 0131] Matt. 19]. At one time they called him a Samaritan, at another a carpenter’s son [Note: [Col. 0131] Matt. 13]. Therefore Zechariah portrays him clothed in filthy garments [Note: [Col. 0131] Zech. 3], because it is fitting for him and his imitators that in a filthy garment there should be beauty of mind, in leprous skin purity of heart, and amid detractors’ reproaches a pure and clean conscience in the saints. Therefore the bride says in the Song of Songs [Note: [Col. 0131] ch. 1]: “I am black, but beautiful.” If, therefore, the bishop-elect of Bath, like all of us, sometimes held the martyr’s life in derision, and sought to obtain the benefit of release for his father, this ought not to be imputed to him as a crime. But even if he offended against him in any respect, ignorance makes him excusable [Col. 0131D]. “I persecuted the Church of God,” says the Apostle, “but I obtained mercy, because I acted ignorantly” [Note: [Col. 0131] 1 Tim. 1].

I believe that if Abel’s blood cries from the earth for vengeance [Note: [Col. 0131] Gen. 4], the blood of the most gentle martyr cries for the remission of sins, especially in those [Col. 0132A] who perform humble and devout repentance. So far as human frailty can judge by outward signs, I know that if the aforesaid bishop-elect attempted anything to the martyr’s dishonour, he expiated it by the harshness of haircloth, more generous alms, more abundant tears, and stricter disciplines. It is a matter full of danger to suspect evil of an innocent man. Therefore the Apostle, writing to the Romans, says: “Receive him who is weak in faith, not for disputes over opinions” [Note: [Col. 0131] Rom. 14]. There are none today, or few, who inspect other people’s consciences, who can say with Elisha to Gehazi: “Was not my heart present when you received silver and garments” [Note: [Col. 0131] 4 Kings 5] from Naaman? It is rash for you to conceal your own fault and judge another’s. The Satirist says [Col. 0132B]:

> Thus no one tries to descend into himself; no one  
> looks at the wallet hanging from his own back.  
> [Note: [Col. 0131] Persius, *Satires* 4.]

Therefore do not accuse a man criminally; do not judge the Lord’s servant, for he stands or falls to his own lord. Judgment belongs to him who searches hearts and kidneys [Note: [Col. 0131] Rom. 8], who searches Jerusalem with lamps [Note: [Col. 0131] Zeph. 1], to whom human thought confesses [Note: [Col. 0131] Ps. 75]. “It is a very small thing to me,” says the Apostle, “that I should be judged by a human being or by a human day” [Note: [Col. 0131] 1 Cor. 4]. In agreement with this is what the Lord says through Isaiah: “Do not fear the reproach of men, and do not fear their blasphemies” [Note: [Col. 0131] Isa. 51]. Let judgment be left to him alone to whom the Father has given all judgment [Note: [Col. 0131] John 5]. Although he now patiently endures many things, he will nevertheless judge in his own time. “When I receive,” he says, [Col. 0132C] “the appointed time, I shall judge with equity” [Note: [Col. 0131] Ps. 74]. Then the good shall be distinguished from the evil [Note: [Col. 0131] Matt. 25]. For the God of gods, the Lord, shall speak and summon the earth [Note: [Col. 0131] Ps. 49]; and, having the winnowing-fan in his hand [Note: [Col. 0131] Matt. 3], he shall come to distinguish his people [Note: [Col. 0131] Ps. 49].

Meanwhile the Jebusite dwells with the Jerusalemites [Note: [Col. 0131] Josh. 15]. Meanwhile, in the master’s garden are alike mountain nard (*saliunca*) and fir, nettle and myrtle [Note: [Col. 0131] Isa. 55]. In Jacob’s flock are white and black animals, lambs and kids [Note: [Col. 0131] Gen. 30]. In Peter’s net are good and bad fish [Note: [Col. 0131] Matt. 13]. In Noah’s ark are clean and unclean animals [Note: [Col. 0131] Gen. 7]. In the Lord’s field are lilies among thorns [Note: [Col. 0131] Song 2], and tares among ears of grain [Note: [Col. 0131] Matt. 13]. In the Lord’s ark is grain with chaff. In Christ’s cellar are wine with grapes [Note: [Col. 0131] Num. 6], oil with dregs. It is not ours to judge anyone [Note: [Col. 0131] Matt. 7]; for the Lord knows who are [Col. 0132D] his [Note: [Col. 0131] 2 Tim. 2]. I therefore advise and exhort you, brother, in Christ, that we cease even from words irrelevant to the matter. Since the first shall be last and the last first [Note: [Col. 0131] Matt. 20], I believe that the man whom you regard as last will go before you into life.

## LETTER XLVI. TO RICHARD, BISHOP OF SYRACUSE

[Note: [Col. 0133C]

This Richard was an Englishman, distinguished by noble birth, experience, learning, eloquence, and other virtues. He was accordingly intimate with both William, father and son, kings of Sicily, and indeed one of the chief administrators of the kingdom. When William I was at the point of death, he appointed his wife Margaret as administrator of the kingdom and Richard as participant in its counsels, until his son, still a child, should be fit by age to govern the realm. Afterwards, when William II was administering the kingdom, Richard was admitted to his most intimate counsels and became the kingdom’s great chancellor. As is customary, the king’s continual intimacy stirred envy against him among everyone, so much so that when Cardinal John exercised a legation in Sicily, at the prompting of the kingdom’s leading men, he compelled Richard to accept consecration. At last he was consecrated in the year 1169.

He was also joined in friendship with Thomas, archbishop of Canterbury, who sent many of his kinsmen, exiled on his account, into Sicily under the protection of Queen Margaret and Bishop Richard. This is clear from Saint Thomas’s letters, in which he expresses his gratitude to Richard; Baronius, vol. XII, under the year 1164 [Col. 0133D].]

. [A.D. 1173?]

[Col. 0133A]

**SUMMARY.**—He gives Bishop Richard the reason why he does not wish to return to Sicily, namely the unhealthfulness of the climate; then he digresses into praises of the blessed martyr Thomas of Canterbury; finally, he urges the bishop to spend the remainder of his life in England, his native land.

To the dearest father and lord RICHARD, by God’s grace bishop of Syracuse, P. of Blois: greeting in him who is truly salvation.

That you wish me to return to Sicily and are concerned for my recall, I thank you as much as I can; yet I am not so [Col. 0133B] prodigal of my life as to wish to exchange rest for toil, safety for dangers, health for sickness, homeland for exile, life for death, and delights for hardship. For your land devours its inhabitants: it spares neither age nor defers to sex, considers neither person nor accepts the favour of condition or the grace of rank. Thirty-seven souls entered Sicily with Lord Stephen [Note: [Col. 0133D] He was the son of the count of Perche and cousin of Margaret, queen of Sicily and mother of the boy William. Having summoned him from France, although he was still young, she made him chancellor of the kingdom. The canons of Palermo also, having received from the queen free authority to choose a pastor for themselves, unanimously bestowed the votes for the archbishopric upon this same Stephen, with the people and Cardinal William of Pavia approving the act. Thus, having obtained the two greatest dignities of the kingdom, he assumed, after the queen, the burden and honour of the whole court, says Falcandus. But scarcely a year had passed when, because of the Sicilians’ innate hatred of the French, a sedition was stirred against him by the nobles [Col. 0134C]; he was compelled to relinquish his dignities and quickly abandon Sicily. He crossed to Syria, where he died shortly afterward. For more, see Fazellus.], and all were shut up in death except myself and Master Roger the Norman [Note: [Col. 0134C] After returning from Sicily with Peter of Blois, this Roger devoted himself to theology at Paris. When, after the death of St Thomas, archbishop of Canterbury, many debated on both sides concerning his sanctity, Roger vigorously opposed Master Peter the Chanter—then one of the most celebrated theologians—who maintained that Thomas ought to be called a saint. Caesarius of Heisterbach, an author nearly contemporary with these events, relates the matter more fully in Book VIII, chapter 69, of his *Dialogues*. Roger later became dean of Rouen in the year of Christ 1198. Accordingly, he is mentioned in 1199 in the cartulary of the chapter and in the old obituary of the Church of Rouen; he is also named in the cartulary of the priory of Bellilocus in 1200, and in a donation of Margaret, wife of Henry the Younger, in the cartulary [Col. 0134D] of the chapter of Rouen.], a learned, industrious, and modest man. By His mercy the Lord brought only us two out from the midst of the shadow of death [Col. 0134A] in the strength of His hand [Note: [Col. 0133] Ps. 106.]. And since departure is scarcely, if ever, permitted to those who have entered once, I do not wish to enter:

> For the tracks alarm me—  
> all look toward you as they face you; none turn backward.  
> [Note: [Col. 0133] Horace, Book I, Epistle 1.]

Sicily has acquired from its climate [Note: [Col. 0134D] Nearly all geographers and historians testify that Sicily is exceptionally fertile, rich, and pleasant, especially Fazellus, a native of that region. Therefore one must say that Peter of Blois here vents himself somewhat harshly against Sicily—unless perhaps we say that he attacks rather the manners of the Sicilians than their sky and soil, since he had been forced to leave Sicily, where he had spent a year in the highest honour, because of the sedition raised against the French, in which a very great multitude of them was overwhelmed with unheard-of cruelty. For a fuller account see Fazellus, Decade 2, Book VII, chapter 5.], and also from the wickedness of those inhabiting it, such a character that I judge it hateful to me and almost uninhabitable. The disorder of its climate and the frequent spreading of poison make it abhorrent to me; by that poison’s most savage cruelty the unwary simplicity of our countrymen is continually endangered there. Who, I ask, can dwell there safely, where, besides other afflictions, mountains continually vomit forth infernal fire and exhale a sulphurous stench? For there beyond doubt is the gate of hell [Col. 0134B] of which it was said: “Deliver my soul, O Lord, from the gate of hell.” The gates, I say, of death and hell are the mountains of Trinacria [Note: [Col. 0134D] Fazellus explains why Sicily is called Trinacria in Decade 1, Book I, chapter 2, on the authority of Greek writers: it is from the three headlands which give it its form.], where men are swallowed up by the earth and descend alive into hell. Your soul has rejected the sweetness of your native English air and every food of our land, and has drawn near even to the gates of death. Every kind of food or drink among us is wholesome and agreeable. Your people err in their meagre diets: though they live only on celery and fennel, which make up almost your entire fare, yet from these there is generated a humour which decays into the cause of a most acute illness and the material of death.

I add this, which is constantly read in the book of experience: since it is written [Note: [Col. 0135] Read Fazellus, Book VII, Second Decade, chapter 5.] that all island peoples are generally faithless, the inhabitants of Sicily are friends of sophistry and secret, utterly depraved traitors. I would not write these things to you unless I knew that you yourself had learned the same things by sure and frequent experience. Hence it is that, whereas the Lord chastises other peoples faithful to Himself in a spirit of mercy and gentleness, He chastises the people of Sicily now with the judgement of Sodom and Gomorrah [Note: [Col. 0135] Gen. 19.], now with the plague of Dathan and Abiram [Note: [Col. 0135] Num. 16.], now with a spirit of judgement and burning.

You know that Mount Etna [Note: [Col. 0135C] From Gervase of Tilbury: “Mount Etna is full of sulphur produced from moist nutritive matter; from its opening flames are vomited forth, driven by the violence of winds—by night a dreadful spectacle, by day a dim light—which can no more be tempered by any cold than the cold can in any way disperse it.” On Etna and its fires, see Fazellus at length, Decade I, Book II, chapter 4.] frequently spreads its fires immeasurably in every direction; and even now, for the distance of a day’s journey, the whole face of the district has been burned and disfigured on every side [Col. 0135B]. The stormy abyss of the raging flame either drove out or burned up all the inhabitants. The inheritance of the wretched was given over to burning and as food for fire; and, to speak more expressly, “fire and sulphur and a stormy blast are the portion of their cup” [Note: [Col. 0135] Isa. 4.]. That plague by which the people of Catania in Sicily were recently struck, on the vigil of Blessed Agatha, has now gone forth into every land and to the ends of the earth, when that most accursed bishop [Note: [Col. 0135C]

John of Agello, the twenty-first bishop of the Church of Catania in Sicily, was brother of Matthew the notary, chancellor of the king of Sicily. He had first been intruded by secular power—namely, by King William of Sicily—contrary to the canons; afterward, however, he was consecrated by Alexander III and, in the manner of archbishops, honoured with the sacred pall in 1168, as Rocchus Pyrrhus records in volume II of the *Notitiae of Sicily*, Notitia I, “Church of Catania.” Pyrrhus also relates from an ancient copy that celebrated diploma by which that supreme pontiff, following in the footsteps of his predecessors, decreed that the same bishop and abbot of Catania, canonically elected by the monks, should be blessed and consecrated by the Roman pontiff [Col. 0135D] and should be subject to him alone. He also granted him the use of the pallium as to archbishops, etc.

Concerning that immense disaster and enormous earthquake by which Peter of Blois says that the city of Catania was overthrown, Nangius writes briefly under the year of Christ 1169: “In Sicily the city of Catania was overthrown by an earthquake, in which the bishop, clergy, and abbot of Mileto, with forty monks and nearly fifteen thousand people, perished.” But the Sicilian author Hugh Falcandus, who saw with his own eyes the entire event as it occurred, tells the story somewhat more fully; so too after him Thomas Fazellus, likewise a native, and Baronius, drawing on both, in volume XII under the year 1169. Rocchus Pyrrhus, in the place cited, further states that a manuscript found among the people of Catania describes the event in these verses:

> Why does man grow proud? He is ash, flesh as food for worms,  
> a flower of hay: father, son, mother, offspring.  
> I grieve for Catania; the grief is pitiful to tell.  
> Bright, mighty, ancient in people, soldiers, and clergy,  
> in wealth, gold, beauty, valour, and triumphs she had been.  
> Alas! that power of things fell in an earthquake.  
> The young man fell in death; man dies, bride and husband die.  
> Why does man grow proud? In a single hour God destroyed  
> towers, ornaments, garments, and every preparation.  
> Who could restrain groans, tears, and heart-felt sighs  
> amid such lamentation? The greater part of the people perished—  
> alas for grief!—and forty-four monks and more;  
> and the shepherd of the fatherland perished, Father John himself.  
> Thus perished the pontifical dignity, the light of the kingdom.  
> May rest be granted to all; may the eternal light shine  
> upon the bishop and his monks, now and for ever.

This occurred on 4 February, indiction I.

], brother of Matthew the notary [Note: [Col. 0136D]

This man was a royal notary, extremely powerful in the court of the kings of Sicily. Under William II he was first vice-chancellor of the kingdom; then King Tancred made him great chancellor, says Rocchus Pyrrhus in the *Chronology of the Kings of Sicily*. Pyrrhus further adds that he left many memorials of his piety not only in his native Salerno but also at Palermo, and built churches and monasteries. For more on him see Falcandus and Fazellus.

I think this letter was written about the year 1173, namely shortly after the death of St Thomas of Canterbury.]

—who, as you know, took honour upon himself without being called by the Lord as Aaron was, and entered that see not by canonical election but by the venality of Gehazi—was offering the incense of abomination. Then the Lord thundered from heaven, and behold, a great earthquake occurred. For the angel of the Lord [Col. 0136A], striking the bishop in the Lord’s wrath, overthrew him together with the people and the whole city. It is therefore clear that, through sins demanding it, they had incurred the offence of most blessed Agatha.

May our most gracious martyr, Blessed Thomas, not be angry with us in this way, I pray. If his anger should blaze forth swiftly [Note: [Col. 0135] Ps. 2.], may he not unlearn the patience which he always possessed, and in anger may he remember mercy. Indeed, my hope is that whenever the Lord threatens us with the scourge of His indignation, the martyr stands in the breach for us and, with unutterable groanings, pleads for the Judge’s mercy. Rejoice, England; rejoice, West, because “the dayspring from on high has visited us” [Note: [Col. 0135] Luke 1.]. India and the Eastern region boasted of Thomas the Apostle; but He who dwells in heaven and looks upon the lowly [Col. 0136B] regarded the Western Church [Note: [Col. 0135] Ps. 112.]. The Lord gave England our Thomas; we do not envy India her Thomas. Let Thomas the Apostle be in India; let Thomas our martyr be in England, so that through these two witnesses of Christ the name of the Lord may be praised from the rising of the sun to its setting. Let whoever wishes go to India for the intercession of the blessed Apostle: such a long pilgrimage is too burdensome for me; my Thomas is sufficient for me. That one touched the Lord’s side and the wounds of the nails; because he saw, he believed. Blessed is he who did not see and believed and did not doubt, and who offered himself as a whole burnt-offering to Christ and for Christ. I do not labour to compare a martyr with an apostle, since an apostle is greater than a martyr. But it is glorious for us to have a martyr who bears an apostle’s name and [Col. 0137A] either imitates or surpasses an apostle in miracles. The Apostle is not offended—for neither is the Lord of apostles and martyrs offended—if at times the Holy Spirit more fully and more famously pours Himself into someone in the working of miracles. “And these things,” says the Lord, “you shall do, and greater things than these you shall do” [Note: [Col. 0137] John 14.].

Love for the martyr has drawn me a little from my purpose; I return to it. Yet, most loving Father, I shall not return to you in Sicily. England now cherishes me in old age, as she cherished you in infancy. Would that you, Father, might leave that mountainous and monstrous land and return to the sweetness of your native air. You ought to be moved to this by long life and its safety, love of your native land, the law of nature, the condition of your upbringing, and above all—and before all—love for the lord king [Col. 0137B] of England, who embraces you in the arms of sincere charity. Unless you reject the favour offered you in the land of your birth, he has prepared incomparable glory and honour for you. I beg that burial may answer to your birth: choose to be laid with your fathers, and let England, which brought you forth, receive your ashes. It is sweet to die in the embraces of friends, to be received by the tears of those dear to one, and to be buried with one’s own forebears. As you read, the holy patriarchs were exceedingly careful to observe this. Flee, Father, from the flame-vomiting mountains; let Etna’s vicinity be suspect to you, and let not that infernal land see you die.

## LETTER XLVII. TO HENRY III, KING OF THE ENGLISH. [A.D. 1174.]

[Col. 0137C]

**SUMMARY.**—Richard, archbishop of Canterbury, urges Henry, son of Henry II, king of the English, to desist from the war which he had raised against his father; and threatens him with excommunication if he does not do so.

To HENRY the Third, by God’s grace king of England and son of the lord king, RICHARD, humble minister of the Church of Canterbury: the spirit of counsel with salvation.

[Col. 0138A] If we are about to say anything harsh to you, most illustrious prince, bear it patiently; for the mouth speaks from the abundance of the heart and the violence of grief. Do not take it ill if we ask for the things that make for peace, if we labour that the hearts of sons may be turned toward their father. We grieve, and cannot conceal our grief, because you persecute your father and yourself give over to plunder and spoil his land, which you ought to have defended even to the shedding of blood. How has it come about that you have become leader of the Brabançons [Note: [Col. 0137C]

The Brebantiones, Brebensones, or Brabantians were so called because they derived their origin from Brabant. They were utterly wicked men who, either of their own accord or hired for others’ wages, ravaged everything far and wide. They were also called Cotarelli and Ruptarii; this name then denoted the entire mob of public robbers and brigands. The Chronicle of Auxerre calls them “an accursed race”; Matthew Paris, “most filthy and ignoble”; Alexander III, in Letter 45, “an unrighteous race”; and Peter here, “an excommunicated and utterly lost race”—because both they and those who hired them were struck with anathema at the Lateran Council under Alexander III in 1179. The words of the council, chapter 27, are:

> “Concerning the Brabançons and Cotarelli, and those who exercise such savagery against Christians that they spare neither churches nor monasteries, nor widows and orphans, nor old men and children, nor any age or sex, but after the fashion of pagans ruin and lay waste everything: we likewise decree that those who hire, retain, or support them in the regions where they thus rage shall be publicly denounced on the Lord’s Days and other solemn days.”

William the Breton aptly describes their depraved habits and savage fury in Book I of the *Philippide*, speaking of them under the name Cotarelli:

> Without delay the army went toward the shores of Bourges  
> [Col. 0138D] to break the force and savagery of the Cotarelli.  
> For sacred persons, sacred possessions, or sacred places,  
> no honour was shown, no reverence at all;  
> valour counted for nothing in a young man, nor feeble age in a child.

When King Henry the father had been placed in distress, he appealed by letter to Pope Alexander that he might wield Peter’s sword against his rebellious sons. This he did, and ordered Richard, archbishop of Canterbury, to bind with the bond of excommunication, all appeal removed, whoever disturbed the peace of the lord king, says our Peter of Blois in Letter 69 to the bishop of Angers. He adds: “Relying on this authority, the lord of Canterbury recently excommunicated at Caen all opponents of the lord king, granting no exception either to the Young King or to anyone else.”

This letter was written in the year of Christ 1174, when the events related above took place, according to Roger’s *English Annals*.]

and attached yourself to an excommunicated and utterly lost people, in order to destroy a people most devoted to you? In what has your father offended you? In what has he forfeited your favour? Never has he presented himself to you as lord or king, but rather as steward of your kingdom and a most faithful servant in the administration of your affairs [Col. 0138B]. He lives for you, not for himself. Whatever he can do, knows, does, gathers, or possesses is yours. Where is filial affection? Where reverence for a father? Where the law of nature? Where the fear of God? Where are those oaths which you personally made to your father in our presence? Where is the intercession by which you bound us and the other bishops of the realm to your father with the bond of surety on your behalf? Do you suppose that God can be mocked thus? He is King of kings, terrible among the kings of the earth, and He takes away the spirit of princes. Love and honour your father, dearest son, so that, in return for the honour shown your father, you may have length of days. “Honour your father and your mother,” says the Lord, “that you may live long upon the earth” [Note: [Col. 0137] Deut. 5; Exod. 21.]. “The son who curses father or [Col. 0138C] mother” is stoned in the law of the Lord [Note: [Col. 0137] Matt. 15.]. Since, therefore, doing evil is much graver than cursing, the man who wounds father or mother with insults and harasses them with injuries deservedly lies under a heavier punishment. Solomon testifies [Note: [Col. 0137] Prov. 17.]: “A wise son is his father’s glory”; but he who dishonours his father is abominable to God. By many examples we are taught how grateful, favourable, sweet, lovable, and acceptable to God is filial affection toward parents [Col. 0139A]; and, conversely, how execrable, condemned, and fit to be destroyed by penal punishments is irreverence toward parents. We read many things that effectively exhort you and others to observe reverence toward a father.

Philip was the first among Roman rulers to profess the Christian faith. He had a son, Philip, who, while his father still lived and assented, was raised to the imperial height. He counted it his highest glory that his father survived, and the emperor obeyed his father’s authority no less humbly than a devoted soldier, surrendering to his father in all he possessed—not as emperor, but as son. Hermes, son of King Agathocles, when his father was at the point of death and the people called upon him to become king, replied that he ought not assume the office of kingship so long as there remained hope that his father would live, whose prudence in administering the commonwealth had been approved. When the emperor Decius proposed to adorn his son Decius with the imperial diadem, the younger Decius declined, saying: “I fear that, if I become emperor, I shall unlearn how to be a son. I would rather not be emperor and be a humble son than be emperor and an undevoted son. Let my father rule; let my empire be to obey humbly one who commands.” The emperor Volusian, son of the emperor Gallus, although he ruled with his father, claimed nothing in common with his father except this: when his father was killed by enemies, he allowed himself to be killed for him and with him. The emperor Valerian [Note: [Col. 0139] Aurelius Victor, *On Valerian*], under whose tyranny the blessed martyrs Sixtus and Lawrence triumphantly won the happy crown of martyrdom, because he once cruelly beat his father, was captured by Sapor, king of the Persians, and grew old in such ignominious slavery under him that, whenever the king was about to mount a horse, Valerian, lying prone upon the ground, lifted him into the saddle with his back, not his hands; and he ended his life in this shameful servitude.

I pass over Absalom [Note: [Col. 0139] II Kings 18.], because the history is known to all. Adrammelech and Sharezer, sons of Sennacherib [Note: [Col. 0139] IV Kings 19.], because they persecuted their father, were expelled from the kingdom and delivered over to captivity, reproach, and death [Note: [Col. 0139] Isa. 37.]. Demetrius, son of King Demetrius, having most cruelly persecuted his father, ended a miserable life as a wanderer and fugitive upon the earth, in exile and dishonour. Aristobulus [Note: [Col. 0139] Josephus, Book XIII, chapter 18.], because [Col. 0139D] he consigned his pregnant mother to prison chains, miserably expired amid the death and blood of his brother Antigonus, whom he loved above all things. From these and countless other examples, dearest son, you can understand how commendable before God and men is reverence shown to a father, and how execrable and condemned to calamitous outcomes is injury inflicted upon parents.

Moreover, it seems to me that the son degenerates whose will differs from his father’s will. For he is his father’s flesh and blood, and has borrowed his own being from his father’s being. [Col. 0140A] Remove the sunbeam from the sun and it does not shine; the stream from its spring and it dries up; the branch from the tree and it withers; the limb from the body and it decays. Separate the son from devotion to his father, and he is no longer a son, but a brother and companion of those to whom it is said: “You are of your father the devil” [Note: [Col. 0139] John 8.]. At the beginning of Isaiah we read [Note: [Col. 0139] Chapter 1.]: “I have nourished and exalted sons, but they have despised me.” The final utterance of the same prophet is: “Their worm shall not die, and their fire shall not be quenched” [Note: [Col. 0139] Isa. 66.]. The whole world proclaims your uprightness, prudence, generosity, constancy, beauty, and the other gifts of grace with which nature has richly endowed you. Yet if you do not show true humility and love toward your father, the more celebrated your praise, the more it will be turned into [Col. 0140B] greater and more general reproach.

You know that your father is a man who is softened by humility shown to him alone. Therefore be subject to him, and he will subject his whole will to you in all things. Show yourself a son to your father in true humility, and he will show himself to you not merely as father but as servant. You shall be king of a king and lord of your lord, who lives for you and dies to himself for this purpose: that after his death you may live splendidly. With many labours and expenses he strengthens and confirms your kingdom and throne, so that the persecution of barbarian hostility may not overthrow it in times to come. You are heir of your father and successor in the kingdom. Secure and certain of hereditary succession, wait; do not hasten. For Solomon testifies [Col. 0140C]: “An inheritance hastily acquired at the beginning will lack blessing at the end” [Note: [Col. 0139] Prov. 20.]. The prompting of flatterers leads you most damnably astray: they whisper and urge that you assert for yourself a definite share in the kingdom. But they desire not so much honour for you as the distribution of offices and goods for themselves, so that they may exercise dominion over their wretched fellow people. Would it not be wiser for you, through the prudence of your most faithful father, to preserve the people in peace than, through unfaithful flatterers, to disturb the tranquillity and peace of the people entrusted to you? Certainly that great sum of money could not be extorted from the kingdom of France without many acts of violence and sins, whereas your father’s generosity now bestows it upon you without labour or guilt on your part. Would that you knew how sweet and [Col. 0140D] pleasant it is to have parents and to honour those whom one has. This most sweet joy is often unknown while parents live, and is learned only from their loss.

Still, most loving son, we beseech you devoutly and humbly to make and speak peace to your people; to abandon the company of that excommunicated and lost race, which draws you into the path of wickedness; and to return to your father. We shall endeavour to provide for your honour and advantage in such a way that by the benefit of peace you will obtain more than you could extort by fire and sword. But if [Col. 0141A] you refuse to acquiesce in and consent to the counsel of ourselves and our suffragans, who write to you jointly on this matter, know that we have received orders from the supreme pontiff to bind you and all who disturb the peace of your lord with the bond of excommunication, with the remedy of appeal removed. Though unwilling and sorrowful, we shall carry out the command laid upon us fully, with prompt effect and due reverence, unless you repent within fifteen days.

## LETTER XLVIII. TO WILLIAM OF PAVIA, CARDINAL. [A.D. 1178.]

[Note: [Col. 0141C] He was called thus from the city of Pavia, where he was born. Taken from the Cistercian order, he was first made archdeacon of Pavia, then by Adrian IV cardinal deacon, and finally cardinal priest. With three other cardinals he was also sent by Adrian to Emperor Frederick, to settle the dispute which had arisen between them concerning the rights of the supreme pontiff; Baronius treats this matter fully under the year of Christ 1159. After Adrian’s death, when a serious schism arose over the election of the supreme pontiff, he took Alexander’s side against Octavian, though at first he had behaved somewhat coolly, according to Baronius under the year 1160. For when Emperor Frederick, who favoured Octavian, had summoned at Pavia—where William happened then to be among his own people—a council of certain cardinals and bishops, William himself, though present at that schismatic conventicle, did not oppose the emperor openly as was proper; nor did he resist the bishops who were present, but remained entirely silent. Hence he was not free from suspicion of tacit connivance, which branded him with no slight mark of infamy. Thus, when Alexander III sent him to England in the case of St Thomas, St Thomas himself refused to accept as judge a man marked by such infamy, as is clear from Thomas’s letters preserved in Baronius at the place cited above. Baronius adds: “Since William was a most eloquent man, he was then thought to be suffering from the sore throat of Demosthenes. But afterward he declaimed where no fear pressed him.” For in 1167, sent by Alexander to the kings of France and England, he so plainly refuted the objections of the envoys of the antipope Victor that both princes, rejecting Victor, received Alexander as supreme pontiff of the Catholic Church [Col. 0142C]. The same Alexander also sent him as legate to Frederick when peace was first discussed; and he prevailed so greatly by his eloquence that Frederick, casting aside the antipopes whom he had set up against the legitimate pontiff, fell at Alexander’s feet and swore him perpetual obedience.]

**SUMMARY.**—He congratulates William, cardinal of Pavia, that the long-standing schism raised against Alexander III has at last been extinguished before Emperor Frederick through William’s prudence and eloquence. He then sharply censures Octavian, author of the schism, and those who elected him.

To the reverend father and lord WILLIAM of Pavia, cardinal priest of the most holy Roman Church, PETER of Blois, his most devoted son: greeting and the affection of sincere love.

Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who at last, looking upon the face of His covenant, chose and singled you out beforehand, so that through the grace of prudence and eloquence divinely granted to you the tear of schism might be sewn up into unity, and the Church of God might breathe again into peace after her various labours. For Peter’s little boat had long been tossed by stormy waves; and though the surges of the sea were wondrous, [Col. 0141C] more wondrous is the Lord on high, who made the storm become a gentle breeze. For, after contempt had been poured upon princes [Col. 0142A] as they wandered in a trackless place and not in the way, He who commands winds and sea commanded the emperor. He who recently raged against the Church of God with brutish fury now, through Christ’s grace, lays aside severity, and his anger is softened into favour. Today, by the grace of the Redeemer—who had especially made you gracious in speech for this task—the persecutor of the Church has become a son; the wolf has become a lamb; the enemy a friend; the proud man devout. He who is before the ages has humbled him; He humbles every height that exalts itself against the knowledge of God [Note: [Col. 0141] II Cor. 10.]. Secular men had grievously oppressed and trampled down Christ’s Church; but today she has been raised up into the everlasting pride, and henceforth she shall tread upon the necks of the proud and lofty, as the Lord says through [Col. 0142B] the prophet: “I shall make you an everlasting excellency; you shall no longer be called Forsaken, but the Holy City” [Note: [Col. 0141] Isa. 60.].

That Octavian, author of the schism [Note: [Col. 0142C] He was a Roman, descended from the noble family of the counts of Tusculum. He was first created cardinal deacon by Innocent II, then cardinal priest of St Cecilia by Eugenius III. Baronius briefly describes his perverse character under the year 1155: “He was another Judas, since he always sought, whenever he could, to devise something against the pontiff, the Roman Church itself, and the college of cardinals.” First he attempted to disturb the peace between Pope Adrian and Emperor Frederick. Then, after Adrian’s death, although Alexander III had been canonically elected supreme pontiff by the assembly of cardinals according to the customary rite [Col. 0142D], Octavian, elected by only two cardinals—John, priest of St Martin’s, and Guy, priest of St Callistus’s—was violently intruded and called Victor IV. This happened in the year of Christ 1159. He lived tyrannically in his antipapacy for about five years and died in 1164. Baronius states under that year what kind of illness caused his death: “Fifteen days before he died, Octavian became continuously delirious and fell into such madness that he remembered neither God nor himself.”], had gathered wealth and riches throughout his life in order to disturb the peace of the Church. By his gifts he had so bewitched the wise of this world that he had gained the favour and goodwill of great men and drawn a great part of the curia with him into error. But, according to the word of Jeremiah [Note: [Col. 0141] Chapter 17] the prophet: “The partridge brooded over what she did not lay; he amassed riches, and not by judgement; in the latter part of his days they shall leave him, and in his end he shall appear a fool.” Octavian had been raised up as an insult to Christ’s Church, and he fell. For Satan cast out Satan, and the firstborn of death took him away, as Job says [Note: [Col. 0141] Chapter 18]; for pride is the primal offspring of death. After him Guy of Crema was exalted [Note: [Col. 0142D]

He was called thus because he came from the Lombard city of Crema [Col. 0143C]. He was made cardinal by Adrian IV; with Emperor Frederick he held secret discussions against him. Then, upon Adrian’s death, he was foremost in the election of the pseudo-pontiff Octavian; after Octavian’s death he himself was intruded into the apostolic see and called Paschal III. But after six years in his pseudo-pontificate he died a miserable death, consumed in 1170 by a cancer appearing in his kidneys.

After the death of the antipope Paschal, the schismatics no longer had any cardinal whom they could put in the place of the last two leaders of their faction. They therefore chose to set over themselves a certain John, abbot of Struma. Ciaconius calls him a Strumian from Pannonia; Baronius calls him an apostate, slippery, voracious, and wandering. He was called Callistus III, but possessed that false and imaginary prelateship for only a few days. For, despised by all good men as he deserved, and seeing himself deposed from his rank at the council held at Venice and rejected by Emperor Frederick, who had gone over to the side of Alexander, the legitimate pontiff, he was at last led by repentance to fall at Alexander’s feet. He humbly acknowledged his guilt and publicly confessed before the cardinals and many others that he had sinned grievously. Alexander, in his native humility and gentleness, not only received him kindly but afterward kept him honourably in his court and at his table, says Romuald of Salerno, a contemporary author (*syngchronos*), in Baronius. Such was the end of this long and grievous schism, and peace was restored to the Church. In this letter, written in 1178 when these things occurred, our Peter congratulates his friend William of Pavia on it [Col. 0144C].

Busaeus’s error here should be noted: he says that Guy of Crema was called Callistus II and John of Struma Paschal III. Yet in Otto of St Blasien, Brompton, and the author of the appendix to Radevicus, a writer of this age; likewise in Platina, Ciaconius, Onuphrius, and the other writers of the lives of the supreme pontiffs; and in Baronius himself, a most trustworthy witness in this matter, Guy is called Paschal III, while John of Struma is called Callistus III.]

…and fell. After him John of Struma was raised up, and cast down and shattered, vanished away. Behold the idol Dagon, which had first been set up beside the ark of the Lord, fell prostrate [Note: [Col. 0143] 1 Sam. 5.]. Raised up a second time, it fell, broken in large part. But when raised up a third time, it was at last found wholly shattered and scattered in every part of its body. Thus Octavian, in pride and usurpation, had arrogated to himself the supreme priesthood, and for this reason had disturbed cities by a violent schism and shaken kingdoms, destined to share the lot of Korah, Dathan, and Abiram, whose imitator he had made himself. Behold what Isaiah had foretold concerning him and men like him [Note: [Col. 0143] Ch. 14.]: “Is not this the man who troubled the earth, who shook kingdoms, who made the world a wilderness and destroyed its cities? His pride shall be brought down to hell; [Col. 0143B] his corpse has fallen; the moth shall be spread beneath him, and the worm shall be his covering.” I still recall how glorious he was in his own eyes, how pompous in speech. I was present when he caused himself to be adored as though he were a statue. For I too, with others, while travelling to the Roman curia, was seized by his executioners, stripped, and beaten. And when my companions had been thrown into chains and remained in fetters, I, through the prior mercy of Christ, neither bent my knees before Baal nor fixed my foot in fetters; but, leaving behind my cloak and losing everything, I was let down through the wall in a basket and thus escaped his hands. God knows that I do not lie; and from that day I have continually [Col. 0144A] prayed the Most High to cast down his pride, for He humbles the proud. At length the saying of Job concerning the king of pride was fulfilled in him: “Though his pride ascend to heaven and his head touch the clouds, he shall perish at the end like dung; and those who saw him shall say, ‘Where is he?’ Like a flying dream he shall not be found; he shall pass away like a vision of the night” [Note: [Col. 0143] Job 20.]. The memory of him and all his accomplices is damned for ever. These are the Philistines who, when they presumed to rush upon and seize the ark of the Lord, were struck by the Lord in their hind parts, and He gave them an everlasting reproach [Note: [Col. 0143] Ps. 77]. Were not these struck in their hind parts—men whose end is destruction, whose posterity is condemned, so that their successor may never again arise in the Church of God? [Col. 0144B] “The iniquity of the fathers shall always return to remembrance, and the sin of Octavian shall not be blotted out for ever” [Note: [Col. 0143] Ps. 108]. For he was the one who more cruelly than the rest afflicted clerics, persecuting poor and needy men and putting to death those contrite in heart. O how blind and clouded is the eye of envy! Where, I ask, were the hearts of the cardinals when they raised the son of pride and the idol of abomination to the summit of the apostolate? To say nothing of you, lest I seem to flatter, how did they pass by with closed eyes Lord Bernard of Porto [Note: [Col. 0144C] Formerly a regular canon and prior of the Lateran monastery, he was first made cardinal-priest by Eugenius III, then bishop of Porto by Adrian IV. After Adrian’s death, when the most dreadful schism arose, he worked to have Alexander III created supreme pontiff and adhered to him with the utmost constancy. A man of exceptional prudence, he discharged many great legations under Eugenius III, Adrian IV, and Alexander III.], Henry of Pisa [Note: [Col. 0144D] He was so called because he was born at Pisa of a noble family. Already a subdeacon of the Roman Church, he had entered the Cistercian order; thence he was chosen and made cardinal-priest of Saints Nereus and Achilleus by Eugenius III. Adrian IV sent him as legate to Sicily in the dispute between himself and William, king of Sicily; then to Emperor Frederick; afterwards Alexander III sent him to England to King Henry II, that he might induce Thomas, chancellor of the realm, to accept the archbishopric of Canterbury. A man of great holiness, he died under Alexander III about A.D. 1178.], Lord Hyacinth [Note: [Col. 0144D] He was a Roman, surnamed Bobo, made cardinal-deacon by Celestine II. During Octavian’s schism he stood firmly for Alexander III as legitimate pontiff. Having prudently and most honourably conducted various legations, he was eventually elected supreme pontiff after the death of Clement III, was called Celestine III, sat for approximately six years, and died in 1198. From Baronius, at the end of volume XII.], Lord [Col. 0145A] Humbald, bishop of Ostia? [Note: [Col. 0145D] His surname was Allucingolus; he was Tuscan by birth. He was first made cardinal-priest of St Praxedes by Innocent II, then bishop of Ostia by Adrian IV. He performed many legations with distinction, but his prudence shone especially when he recalled Emperor Frederick, supporter of Octavian’s schism, to obedience to the legitimate pontiff. At length, after Alexander III, he was elevated to the supreme pontificate and called Lucius III, in which office he sat four and a half years.] They rejected men of peace and raised up a man of dissension and scandal. Here we may indeed observe Jotham’s parable concerning the sons of Gideon: when the sons of Israel wished to choose a ruler for themselves, despising the legitimate sons, they chose Abimelech, a bastard and cruel judge. In accordance with his saying, the trees of the forest chose for their king neither the olive nor the fig tree nor the vine, but the bramble; and fire came forth from the bramble and devoured the cedars of Lebanon [Note: [Col. 0145] Judg. 9]. From Octavian there issued wickedness which violently shook the whole world in tumult; but at last the hand of the Lord, through the ministry of your tongue, beyond hope and beyond the wishes of all, calmed everything by ineffable power. I am yours; and would that an opportunity might present itself for you to prove [Col. 0145B] by experience that I am yours. I still remember how devoutly and mercifully you received me, returning from exile as a wanderer and fugitive; you clothed me naked, fed me hungry, and—to include much in little—fulfilled in my case the whole sixfold work of mercy [Note: [Col. 0145] Matt. 25]. May He repay you for me who rewards good works and stands surety for the poor.

## LETTER XLIX. TO THE DEAN OF CHARTRES AND THE ARCHDEACON OF BLOIS

**Subject.**—In many words he laments the wickedness of certain canons of Chartres, his friends and colleagues, because, in order to deprive him of the dignity of the provostship of Chartres, they even attempted to defame his father; whose innocence he here defends [Col. 0145C].

To his dearest friends and associates G., dean of Chartres, and G., archdeacon of Blois, P. of Blois, archdeacon of Bath: greeting, and the putting on of the bowels of compassion.

I suffer, I suffer grievously, and there is no one to share my suffering, none to pity the afflicted man. “Have pity on me, have pity on me, at least you, my friends, for the hand of the Lord has touched me” [Note: [Col. 0145] Job 19]. Long have I laboured in my groaning; but now I bring the cause of my groaning into public, and therefore my words are full of sorrow. “Streams of waters run down from my eyes” [Note: [Col. 0145] Ps. 118], and torrents of tears flow forth. For the arrows of the Lord are in me, whose indignation drains my spirit [Note: [Col. 0145] Job 6]; and the torrents [Col. 0146A] of another’s iniquity have troubled me. Would that the floodgates of my miserable head might be opened and that I might wholly flow away in tears; for tears are a consolation to many and, to a very great extent, lessen the magnitude of grief. Grief indeed bears the character of fire, because the more it is concealed, the more it burns. If the Lord had scourged me by loss of temporal goods, by the death of friends, or by affliction of my own body, I should endure it all with composure. But I feel a wound penetrating into the innermost part of my heart; nor am I less distressed than if someone were violently tearing my entrails from me. Are not my friends my entrails—those whom I cherish, and who cherish me, in the sweet interchange of services and identity of affections? Without them every thought would be weariness to me, every action toil, [Col. 0146B] every land exile, every life torment. For whom do I live, if not for my friends? Without their consolation, to live would be to die.

These, my dearest friends, are the crosses by which your friend is afflicted. These are the distresses that he laments, because his friends have “been turned into a crooked bow,” so as to become “a man’s enemies of his own household” [Note: [Col. 0145] Matt. 10]. Those in whose affection he had trusted most confidently, and upon loving whom he had poured out his whole soul, have become his chief enemies. The lords of Chartres, whose brother and fellow-canon I was, whom I loved from my whole inward self, have spoken an unjust word against me. They have rendered me evil for good, and hatred for my love [Note: [Col. 0145] Ps. 108]. For in the case which I had [Col. 0146C] against R. of Salisbury [Note: [Col. 0146D] Who this R. of Salisbury was is uncertain. That he was Reginald of Salisbury, as Busaeus conjectures, is not probable, since he was a most intimate friend of Peter of Blois, as appears from the letters, and also because he advanced from archdeacon of Salisbury to the bishopric of Bath. Nor is there a word in historians that he was provost of Chartres. Neither can he be Robert, nephew of John of Salisbury, with whom Peter was closely connected and whom he had so earnestly commended to his uncle, then bishop of Chartres, in Letter 70.], concerning the provostship of Chartres—which I still claim as mine—they submitted infamous letters to our judges and, most wickedly maligning my father’s life, attempted thus to blacken my name. Unjust witnesses rose up against the dead man and against the innocent man in my person, and iniquity lied to itself [Note: [Col. 0145] Ps. 26]. I call God and the innocence of Christ to witness that my father lived innocently and holily; for he was a simple and upright man, fearing God [Note: [Col. 0145] Job 1], without complaint or deceit, gentle, mild, and humble. I would not affirm this with such confidence, had not you yourselves and the whole province known it. [Col. 0147A] You know without doubt that, if my father had been trained in letters, his prudence and holy manner of life would have abundantly qualified him to govern a dignity of the highest rank. I confidently extol and praise my father, whose son I would rather have been than the son of that noble traitor from whom our rival, as you know, boasts that he was descended. I am conscious of nothing against myself [Note: [Col. 0147] 1 Cor. 4], nor could you yourselves find anything for which my father could be marked, except that he was not among the wealthier men of the region. Certainly virtue does not consist in riches; for behold, sinners, abounding in the world, have obtained wealth [Note: [Col. 0147] Ps. 72]. Yet I judge him to have been sufficiently rich, since his resources abundantly sufficed for himself, his household, and Christ’s poor, whose most devoted servant he always showed himself to be [Col. 0147B]. He was commendably rich enough, being well provided with buildings, lands, meadows, and vineyards. Indeed, even had he been very poor, poverty would not deprive him of the titles of nobility. As is publicly known, my father and mother derived their origin from the leading families of Lesser Brittany. I say this not in boastfulness, but that the mouths of those who speak iniquity may be stopped—those who, in a manner wholly unworthy of their own nobility, presume to slander others. I deem that nobility true and praiseworthy which joins virtue to distinction of birth; and those who reproach my father with the poverty of his exile are utterly devoid of it. Was not Brutus an exile? Was not Aeneas an exile? Yet Trojan nobility did not degenerate in their exile. [Col. 0147C] This I have learned with certainty: if our rival had known any disgrace either in me or in my father, he would most gladly have brought it into public. But I, conscious of my own innocence and suspecting nothing of the kind,

> I received a wound without waiting for one from an enemy.  
> [Note: [Col. 0147] Ovid, *Heroides*, “Hypsipyle.”]

In the house of God, in the church of the Blessed Virgin of Chartres, of which I was a canon, I was thought to be the friend of one whose every thought concerning me was evil, who beneath a flattering tongue nourished an asp’s venom. If an enemy had cursed me, I should surely have endured it; but you were a man of one mind with me, my guide and acquaintance, who took sweet food with me and walked together in the house of God in harmony [Note: [Col. 0147] Ps. 54]. You loved me with your mouth, but with your tongue [Col. 0147D] you lied to me, magnifying your treachery against me and staining an innocent man by treacherous devices. Look, Lord, and consider; hear the voices of my adversaries and judge my cause. You know all things; You know my innocence [Col. 0148A] and that they hated me without cause. You know my reproach, my confusion, and my reverence. Before You are all who afflict my soul [Note: [Col. 0147] Ps. 68]. Let them, I pray, be turned back and ashamed, who persecuted me, a poor and needy man, and filled my afflicted soul with reproaches. I had certainly intended both to remain and to die in the church and service of the Blessed Virgin. I desired to take upon myself the needs of the church and to fight for her at my own expense, to live for all, and by the labour and inconvenience of my own body to procure advantages for all. Is evil returned for good? For my friends dug a pit of destruction for me, and in my necessity my neighbours stood against me. [Col. 0148B] “I have become a stranger to my brethren and an alien to the sons of my mother” [Note: [Col. 0147] Ps. 63]. The home of my birth, in the words of another prophet, has become to me like a lion’s den and like the dwelling-place of ostriches [Note: [Col. 0147] Job 30]. Since “no prophet is accepted in his own country” [Note: [Col. 0147] Jer. 50], may the Lord make exile a homeland for me; and may He who led me like Joseph’s sheep lead me, in the place of my pilgrimage, by the paths of His mercy. “You are good, O Lord, to those who hope in You, to the soul that seeks You” [Note: [Col. 0147] Luke 4]. My domestic enemies plotted to overthrow me and wholly remove me from the provostship of Chartres. But lest I, humbled and confounded, should be cast down, You redeemed my rejection and reproach with a greater and richer benefice [Note: [Col. 0147D] He seems to speak of the archdeaconry of Bath, for he is known to have held no richer benefice.]. Thus Leah, the more fruitful, was given to Jacob in place of Rachel [Note: [Col. 0147] Gen. 29]. Thus David received [Col. 0148C] the more beloved Michal in place of Merab, who was given to Hadriel the Meholathite [Note: [Col. 0147] 1 Sam. 18]. But I gratefully accept the gift of God Most High, and whatever He has graciously ordered concerning me, deeming my wishes fully satisfied if He humbles those whose pride always rises and shows to be liars those who have stained an innocent man. But you, dearest lords and friends, if you cannot avenge our injuries, at least bestow with patient mind the affection of compassion.

## LETTER L. TO H., BISHOP OF BAYEUX

[Note: [Col. 0147D] He was first dean of Salisbury, from which I infer that he was English. Indeed, from Letter 201 of John of Salisbury, congratulating Henry on his promotion to the bishopric of Bayeux, in these words: “I hear, Father, and rejoice that all things succeed you according to your merit; and you who, while it was permitted, honoured the name and rank of deans, now by the splendour of your virtues illuminate the office of bishop in a foreign land, to the envy of many,” etc., it is apparent what a great man is praised by what a great man. He was certainly prudent, an exceedingly watchful guardian of his flock, and most zealous in renewing and enlarging the possessions of his church, [Col. 0149C] as appears from many grants, examples of which are preserved in the archives of the chapter of Bayeux; some of them will be appended at the end of the notes. He was indeed present at the coronation of the younger Henry, but by command of the king his father, who, “under the pretext of arranging the realm, had summoned the magnates of England and Normandy to London,” says the *Processus*, book II, chapter 29. Henry died, however, according to the Chronicle of Caen, in 1205, after governing the Church of Bayeux for almost forty years with the highest praise.]  
[A.D. 1170.]

**Subject.**—He endeavours to persuade Henry, bishop of Bayeux, to forgive G., the abbot’s chamberlain, who had committed a killing in self-defence and was offering satisfaction: first because Christ receives the penitent, and secondly because the command to love one’s neighbour demands it [Col. 0148D].

To the reverend father and lord H., by God’s grace bishop of Bayeux, from his own P. of Blois, archdeacon of Bath: greeting, and an abundance of the bowels of compassion.

[Col. 0149A] Today we hear what has not been heard from the ages: cruelty rages in the lamb, while ferocity grows gentle in the wolf. Almost the whole world knows that, beyond all mortals, you abound especially and singularly in the grace of compassion and the spirit of gentleness; and therefore all are astonished why you show yourself so hard and inexorable toward G., chamberlain of the abbot of Caen, who, in great contrition of heart and humility of penitence, offers himself for every satisfaction.

He does not deny that he killed a man; but because he did this when provoked by enemies, in defence of his own body, and in vengeance for his father’s death, the gravity of the crime is greatly diminished. For the lord king, who punishes transgressions of this sort more strictly and terribly than all [Col. 0149B] men, restored him to his favour and to his native soil. Moreover, where the material sword is merciful, the sword of the Church ought not to be inhumane; and the authority of the saints declares that it is safer for us to be judged for the humanity of mercy than for stricter justice. Receive, I pray, into penitence the humbled and contrite man, lest, if the bosom of mercy should perhaps be closed against him, he fall into the abyss of despair. For God more gladly [Col. 0150A] accepts the repentance of a humble and contrite sinner [Note: [Col. 0149] Ps. 50] than the innocence of a lukewarm and negligent righteous man. And there is greater joy among the angels of God over one sinner doing penance than over ninety-nine righteous persons who need no repentance [Note: [Col. 0149] Luke 15]. Since in sacred speech the sheep signifies the innocence of a simple life, while the goat signifies the impurity of a sinner, the sheep is nevertheless commanded under the law of the Lord to be offered far from the door of the tabernacle [Note: [Col. 0149] Lev. 3]. But the goat, which is a peace-offering, is sacrificed at the very door from which the sheep is removed. For Sacred Scripture everywhere invites and receives sinners to repentance. Those, however, who practise empty and sluggish innocence are kept away from the sanctuary; while those who have vigorously cleansed away wickedness through repentance are more familiarly admitted to the bosom of Mother Church. You see the Lord eating and drinking with sinners and publicly declaring: “I came not to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance” [Note: [Col. 0149] Matt. 9]. You have David, Peter, the publican, and Paul, who surpassed the first grace of merit by fruitful repentance. Christ, rising from the dead, deigned first to appear not to His blessed Virgin Mother but to Mary the sinner, from whom He had cast out seven demons [Note: [Col. 0149] Mark 16], [Note: [Col. 0149C]

The author states this truly, in accordance with Scripture and the Fathers. Mark 16: “Now when He had risen early on the first day of the week, He appeared first to Mary Magdalene.” Ambrose, Sermon 54: “Mary Magdalene, because she loved Jesus more ardently, since she persevered beside the tomb, saw the Lord before all others and announced Him to the apostles.” Augustine, Homily 2 on the second part of Psalm 68: “The disciples were so distressed that Mary Magdalene, who saw Him first, joyfully announced to the mourners what she had seen.” Cyril of Alexandria, book XII on John, chapter 1, on the words, “But go to my brethren,” etc. That is:

> He does not permit Mary to touch His flesh, although in her love of God she most ardently longed to obtain this. Yet He rewards her attendance upon Him, and grants a double reward for such strenuous faith and love, showing that devotion toward Him is not fruitless for those who practise it. And what is more glorious still? In her—in Mary herself, I mean—the whole female sex is, as it were, crowned with a twofold honour and freed from ancient infirmities. For she, being the first thus to mourn and to find occasion for tears, has Christ change her mourning into joy.

Gregory, Homily 35 on the Gospels: “Inflamed by the fire of her love, she burned with desire for Him whom she believed taken away. Thus it happened that she alone then saw Him who had remained behind to seek Him, because perseverance is indeed the power of a good work.” And below: “Behold, the fault of the human race is hidden where it arose. For because in paradise a woman offered death to a man, from the tomb a woman announces life to men; and she who had told the words of the deadly serpent tells the words of her Life-giver. It is as though the Lord says to humankind, not in words but in deeds: ‘From the hand from which the draught of death was brought to you, receive the cup of life.’” Had the Blessed Virgin first seen her risen Son at the tomb, she, as a second Eve, would have announced life to men. Bede, on Mark 16: “She who was healed of seven demons—that is, freed from every crime—first saw the Lord rising from the dead, lest any worthy penitent despair of pardon for sins committed, seeing that she who had formerly been subject to so many and such great vices was suddenly advanced, by the merit of faith and love, to such a height that she first proclaimed to the very evangelists and apostles of Christ the miracle of the accomplished resurrection.” Alcuin, book VII on John, chapter 41, and Anselm—or whatever other author wrote the *Expositions on Matthew*—say the same thing in the same words as Gregory just cited. The martyrologies of Bede, Notker, and the Roman Martyrology support our view. Cajetan follows the Fathers cited on Mark 16:9: “God’s great grace toward sinners is signified by His having wished first to appear to a sinner, and such a sinner—that is, one who had been subject to all sins signified by [Col. 0151A] the seven demons.” If Busaeus had taken a little more care to consider these matters, he would surely have understood upon what foundation our author wrote that Christ appeared first to Mary Magdalene rather than to Mary His blessed Mother. But upon what foundation Busaeus himself, following certain modern writers, writes that Christ appeared first to Mary His Mother rather than to Mary Magdalene, I do not sufficiently understand. The Evangelist absolutely asserts [Col. 0151B] that Christ appeared first to Mary Magdalene. What does Busaeus say to this? “The intention of the Evangelists,” he says, “was to relate not every appearance, but only those that served to confirm the unbelieving and doubtful, among whom the Blessed Virgin was not to be counted.” But I ask upon what foundation he asserts this. Certainly a weak one. But grant that the Evangelists did not relate every appearance of Christ. Grant that Christ the Lord appeared to His Mother. Does it follow that He appeared to her first, contrary to Scripture, which teaches that He appeared first to Mary Magdalene? Let us now hear Busaeus bring forward the arguments by which he supports his opinion. “But if,” he says, “we consult the tradition of the ancients and truth itself, we must say that Christ appeared first to His blessed Mother rather than to Mary the sinner. Thus teaches Rupert, abbot of Deutz, book VIII [he should have written VII] of *On the Divine Offices*, chapter 25; Blessed Ildefonsus, Sermon 5 [Col. 0151C] on the Assumption of the Blessed Virgin; Symeon Metaphrastes, in the oration on the life and dormition of the Blessed Virgin; Blessed Anselm, book *On the Excellence of the Virgin*, chapter 6; Blessed Bridget, *Revelations*, book VI, chapter 94; and in the angelic sermon on the excellence of the Blessed Virgin, chapter 19.” What a splendid tradition of the ancient Fathers, what well-grounded truth, that conflicts with the word of God, with the authority and words of the holy Fathers Ambrose, Augustine, Cyril of Alexandria, and others; which in fact is said to originate only in the ninth century, and yet is rashly and falsely claimed to begin in that century. Ildefonsus, in Sermon 5 on the Assumption, does not say that Christ appeared to His Mother before Mary Magdalene. He says only: “Concerning the Lord’s burial, some say that she was much more solicitous than those holy women; and, unless I am mistaken, the evangelic poet Sedulius, an eloquent orator and Catholic writer, seems to support their opinion.” Ildefonsus reports the view of others, not his own. Nor does the view he mentions establish that Christ [Col. 0151D] was seen by His Mother before the other women. Sedulius explains it thus in Book V of his poem:

> At this dawn of light,  
> The Virgin Mother and the other mothers together, bringing the gift  
> Of aromatic harvest, came mourning  
> To the familiar tomb.

From these words only this may be inferred—even Busaeus himself admitting it—that the most holy Mother saw her Son not first, but together with the other women. Add that Sedulius joined Mary with the other women through the error by which he thought her to be the “other Mary” of Matthew 28. Finally, his words,

> They came mourning  
> To the tomb,

[Col. 0152A] do not sufficiently accord with the faith which the Mother of God had in the Lord’s resurrection.

Metaphrastes, as Bellarmine rightly observes in his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, added many things from his own invention when writing histories or lives of saints—not as they occurred, but as they could have occurred. It is as true that he writes that the Virgin Mary first saw her risen Son as that, immediately before, he had written that she sat continually beside [Col. 0152B] the tomb and thereby came to see Him first.

The authority of Anselm is alleged from the book *On the Excellence of the Virgin*. But this book, Bellarmine himself concurring, is not Anselm’s: “That little work,” he says, “*On the Excellence of the Blessed Virgin*, does not seem to be Anselm’s, not only because Eadmer does not mention it, but also because it lacks Anselm’s style and gravity.”

Rupert speaks conjecturally, not assertively, as they say: “When the risen Son perhaps announced His victory to her before all mortals, not depriving the Virgin of maternal honour,” etc. We may conjecture that this happened, lest the Son seem to dishonour His Mother if He did not appear to her immediately upon rising; but this reason is certainly very slight. For He who died for our offences and rose for our justification ought, risen to life, first to have appeared to those [Col. 0152C] whose faith was wavering and who were to be fitting witnesses of the resurrection. But the Virgin Mother of God possessed most steadfast and unshaken faith and, owing to her maternal dignity, would have been an insufficiently suitable witness of her Son’s resurrection before unbelievers. Christ had to be concerned with the things of His Father, putting aside consideration of His Mother.
