And if the angel instructed the women to announce specifically to Peter that Christ had risen from the dead, one should not suppose this was done merely for honour, because he was to receive primacy, but from necessity, because he had denied the Lord three times. Hence Gregory, Homily 21 on the Gospels, and after him Bede on Mark 16: “We must ask why Peter, the disciple, is designated by name. But unless the angel had expressly named him, he who had denied his Master would not have dared to come among the disciples. Therefore he is called by name, lest he despair because of his denial.” And Cajetan: “Peter had denied Jesus; and therefore the angel names no one except Peter, both to commend God’s great grace toward sinners [Col. 0152D] and so that Peter, hearing the angelic message from the women’s mouths, might become more confident.” Far be it from us, against Scripture and tradition protesting, to say that Christ did whatever the human mind, led by feeble little arguments, persuades itself it would have been fitting for Him to do for honour’s sake. Concerning the revelation made to Blessed Bridget, nothing more apt can be said than what Cajetan says in his treatise *On the Conception of the Blessed Virgin*, chapter 5: “New revelations, opposed to so many holy and ancient doctors, seem to suggest to the wise either an angel of light transformed into an angel of Satan, or fantasies, or even fictions,” etc.

Moreover, it should be noted that in his edition Busaeus added after the words “but to Mary the sinner” these two words, “I think,” supposedly to strengthen his own [Col. 0153C] opinion about Christ’s appearance to the Blessed Virgin, seizing, that is, upon the occasion of one defective manuscript codex from Würzburg. But we have rightly deleted them, since they are absent from all our printed and manuscript codices alike—at least sixteen of which we examined—as also from the six others used by Busaeus himself.]

Therefore let not the goat be rejected from the door of the tabernacle as [Col. 0151A] the sheep is, because the conversion of a sinner is more pleasing to God and His angels than the lukewarm simplicity of innocence. If the bosom of mercy is shut against the penitent man, I fear that the latter end of the man may become worse than the former [Note: [Col. 0151] Matt. 12], and that his soul, because of your hardness, may be demanded from you more harshly. Every day we ask that our sins be forgiven us, as we forgive our debtors. [Col. 0152A] The Lord’s Prayer is dangerous for the person who does not forgive his neighbour’s sins. “Forgive,” says the Lord, “and you shall be forgiven” [Note: [Col. 0151] Luke 6]. “With the measure with which you have measured,” He says, “it shall be measured back to you” [Note: [Col. 0151] Matt. 7]. The theological poet Prosper teaches the same, saying:

> Let a sinner grant pardon to a sinner, that on equal terms  
> He may reconcile the Lord to himself.

[Col. 0153A] But if you have conceived any bitterness or hatred against the aforesaid G., the chamberlain, forgive it, I beseech you, kindly and charitably. For “charity is kind” [Note: [Col. 0153] 1 Cor. 13]. Nor is there any place for charity in you if bitterness or hatred is retained against your neighbour. Nor do we rightly love God unless our neighbour is loved for His sake. Love divides itself into a twofold affection, beginning with one’s neighbour and extending to God, uniting in Him the diverse affections and establishing Him, both as principal cause and in Himself, as the ground of all love. Yet although the Lord wills that He be loved for one’s neighbour, not for Himself—for He has no need of our goods—we nevertheless do not depart from His will if we love our neighbour for His sake. Indeed, we resist the divine will if we do not love our neighbour for God’s sake, [Col. 0153B] since the Lord asks to be loved in him, and that neighbour, in the matter of being loved, stands as Christ’s vicar. From love of neighbour God measures our affections. For how do we love God, whom we do not see, if we do not love our neighbour, if we do not have compassion on our neighbour whom we see? [Note: [Col. 0153] 1 John 4.] Thus God admits one’s neighbour to participation and fellowship in love, so that He will have neither the neighbour loved without Himself, nor Himself loved without the neighbour. For love profits nothing unless it is joined together and removes every reproach of exclusiveness. Hence the scarlet material which was to be placed in the priestly garment was commanded to be dyed twice [Note: [Col. 0153] Exod. 27]. Hence Elisha asked that his master’s spirit be doubled in him [Note: [Col. 0153] 2 Kgs. 2]. Hence also a portion of the fine flour that is offered is burnt to the Lord upon [Col. 0153C] the altar, while another portion is reserved for the use of Aaron and his sons. In these the twofold love is marked: that neither neighbour be loved without God nor God without neighbour. Therefore, if you love—indeed, because you love God—turn the hatred you have conceived against the aforesaid G. into love and goodwill for God’s sake.

[Col. 0154A] You who both walk in and teach the way of perfection ought not to cherish hatred, except that of which the prophet speaks: “With perfect hatred I hated them.” Perfect hatred, or the hatred of the perfect, exists if we hate sin in the person, not the person in sin. It is publicly said—and perhaps you yourselves are ignorant of it—that some of your people have cast their eyes upon his hereditary possessions and for that reason stir up your mind against him. For the common saying is [Note: [Col. 0153] See *Adagia*, manuscript, p. 1139]: “Troubled water is better for fishing”; and they themselves expect the profit of succession from your disturbance. Yet, since neither God nor the Church judges twice for the same thing, many consider it absurd that G., after satisfaction through penance, should be punished in his patrimonial goods.

## LETTER LI. TO JO. [Note: [Col. 0153C] Jocelin, a Lombard by birth, was made bishop of Salisbury in A.D. 1139, having previously been archdeacon of Winchester, according to Simeon of Durham in his *History of England* [Col. 0153D]. At the beginning of the persecution raised against St Thomas, he stood firmly for him. Hence Harpsfield, in his *History of the English Church*, and Baronius, from the *Four-Part History*, report the following concerning him: “Bartholomew, bishop of Exeter, falling at the feet of the lord of Canterbury, said: ‘My father, have mercy on yourself and on us. For today we all perish because of hatred directed at your head. For an edict has gone forth from the king that whoever should continue to stand with the archbishop of Canterbury should be judged a public enemy and punished capitally. It has also been said that Jocelin, bishop of Salisbury, and William, bishop of Norwich, because they still resisted, should immediately be dragged off for punishment by mutilation of their limbs’; and they too were begging the archbishop of Canterbury on behalf of their safety.”

Yet afterwards he gravely incurred St Thomas’s displeasure because he attended the coronation of the younger Henry [Col. 0154C], performed contrary to the right of the Church of Canterbury, and for this reason was excommunicated by Thomas himself. After St Thomas’s death, however, through the intervention of King Henry, he was released from excommunication. Alexander III wrote letters on the matter to the bishops of Bourges and Nevers; these are reported by Brompton and by Baronius from Roger, under the year 1172. Arnulf, bishop of Lisieux, also wrote to Alexander III on his behalf [Col. 0154D], clearing him of the accusations made against him in connection with St Thomas. He declared him to be an honourable, prudent, and devout man, “who, at the beginning of the storm, had among his fellow bishops adhered with particular zeal to that target—namely, St Thomas—and had endured many injuries for the liberty of the Church and out of regard for him.”

Moreover, the dissension between them seems to have arisen not so much from the coronation of the younger king as from the fact that Reginald the archdeacon, Jocelin’s own son, had been sent by King Henry the father to the supreme pontiff against St Thomas. The holy man was consequently vehemently angered against Reginald, as appears from his own letter in Baronius, vol. XII, under the year 1168.] BISHOP OF SALISBURY. [A.D. 1170?]

[Col. 0154B]

**SUMMARY.**—He admonishes the bishop to honour his promise by paying the money, if he wishes to safeguard his reputation; then, not to treat his nephews with excessive indulgence.

To his venerable father and lord Jo., by God’s grace bishop of Salisbury, P., archdeacon of Bath, sends greeting and truth.

Your kindness most certainly promised me that before the coming Christmas you would send your nephews to Paris for instruction, and that through them you would pay the annual debt which you owe me. “I waited and waited for my lord,” and he did not attend to me [Note: [Col. 0153] Ps. 39.]. I still await the promised favour—perhaps as Britain awaits Arthur [Note: [Col. 0154D] On him see what we have said on Letter 34.], as Judaea awaits the Messiah.

Your grant was indeed at first free and generous; but because the bond of a written promise intervened, so that the gift became annual, you have turned favour into the necessity of a debt. Would that this money had never existed—its expectation has so long tormented my mind. In hope of it, I incurred debts at usury by making expenses more lavish than I could afford. Had a simple promise preceded, I should have spent more cautiously and would have treated a light word lightly. But now, in the book of experience, I read how holy and effective is the teaching of evangelical truth: “Let your speech be, Yes, yes; No, no; for what is more than this is from evil” [Note: [Col. 0155] Matt. 5.].

I now feel this evil, for which the bishop’s document and his emphatic assurance have given cause. Yet the words of bishops, who are sons and heirs of the apostles, contain the force of an oath: among them, what is a simple statement in others is an oath; and what in others is a simple lie is in them perjury or sacrilege. Consider what the Doctor of the Church says: “Did I use fickleness, or do I make my plans according to the flesh, so that with me there should be Yes and No?” [Note: [Col. 0155] 2 Cor. 1.] The prophet Isaiah’s saying is appropriate to those who promise and do not pay: “Behold, you are from nothing, and your work is from that which is not” [Note: [Col. 0155] Isa. 41.].

Great discernment is required in making a promise; for an empty promise often makes enemies for itself out of close friends. But if you intend to stand by your promises, this delay is neither welcome to me nor honourable to you, as the poet testifies:

[Col. 0156A]

> Great delay is ruin;  
> and delay in giving carries no slight blame.

“Do not say to your friend,” says Solomon, “Go, and return tomorrow, and I will give to you,” when you can give at once [Note: [Col. 0155] Prov. 3.]. “Tomorrow, tomorrow” is the raven’s cry; the frequent repetition of a promise is pleasing neither to God nor to men. I believe Solomon meant this too when he says: “My son, do not repeat a word in your mouth” [Note: [Col. 0155] Ecclus. 7.]. Therefore, reverend Father, give to your word the voice of action, and let generous intentions be fulfilled in deeds, lest a document conceived as testimony to truth be able to charge with falsehood lips consecrated to the Gospel.

But I most strongly condemn the fact that you indulge your nephews—who ought to be exercising themselves in the camp of learning—in luxury and caress them with flatteries. Know that all this is the emptying-out of virtues and the overthrow of honourableness. Their life is still uncertain, because they have not yet passed the fork of Pythagoras’s letter [Note: [Col. 0155C]

Pythagoras said that human life was like the Greek letter Y, and that the first stage of life was indeterminate, since it has not yet devoted itself either to vices or to virtues; this was signified by the lower stem of the letter. The fork of the letter, however, begins with youth, when people follow either vices—that is, the left-hand branch—or virtues—that is, the right-hand branch. Virgil, or another author, rightly says in the little work *On the Letter Y*:

> Pythagoras’s letter, divided by its two-horned distinction,  
> seems to display the image of human life:  
> for the path of virtue seeks the steep right-hand track  
> and at first offers a difficult entrance to those who look upon it.  
> But at its highest summit it grants rest to the weary.  
> The broad way displays a soft path, but at its final goal  
> hurls down those it has caught and rolls them over jagged rocks.

Hence mythographers invented the story that Hercules, when childhood was completed and he had reached the years of puberty, saw two roads, one of pleasure and the other of virtue, and for a long time greatly hesitated which to enter; finally, rejecting pleasure, he entered the steep and rough road of virtue. Xenophon, Book II of the *Memorabilia* (*Hypomnēmata*), should be read, as also Cicero, Book III of *On Duties*, drawn from him. Persius too alludes to this, *Satires* 3:

> And the letter which divided for you the Samian branches  
> will show the path that rises by the right-hand boundary.

Likewise *Satires* 5:

> When the way is uncertain, and error ignorant of life  
> divides trembling minds at branching crossroads.

See Casaubon and the other commentators on these passages of Persius.].

Therefore it would be more expedient to correct them than to caress them. It is written: “He who spares the rod hates his son” [Note: [Col. 0155] Prov. 13.]. Eli was struck by the Lord together with his sons because he had in no way corrected them: “You have loved your sons more than me,” said the Lord [Note: [Col. 0155] 1 Sam. 4.]. Today, in place of the sons whom God has taken away from prelates of the Church, they are permitted to have nephews, to the dissipation of Christ’s patrimony and the loss of their own salvation [Note: [Col. 0155D]

The sacred canons forbid clerics and bishops to enrich their blood-relations from the goods of the Church: Canon 40 of the Apostles; Canon 25 of the Council of Antioch; Paris VI, canon 16; *Capitularies*, Book V, canon 171. Finally, the Council of Trent, session 25, *On Reform*, canon 1, absolutely forbids them to seek to enrich relatives or household members from Church revenues, since the canons of the apostles also prohibit them from giving ecclesiastical goods, which are God’s, to relatives. If relatives are poor, they are to distribute to them as to poor persons and not squander such goods for their sake. Indeed, the holy synod most strongly exhorts them, as far as possible, utterly to cast off every merely human affection of the flesh toward brothers, nephews, and relatives, from which a seedbed of many evils has arisen in the Church.

Ambrose, Book I of *On Duties*, chapter 30: “You did not dedicate yourself to God in order to make your people rich, but that you might acquire eternal life through the fruit of good work and redeem your sins by the price of mercy. Do they think they ask too little? They seek your price; they endeavour to take away the fruit of your life, and they think themselves right in doing so. He accuses you because you have not made him rich, while he wishes to deprive you of the reward of eternal life.”

Bernard, treatise *On the Life and Conduct of Clerics*, chapter 7: “Let him not exalt his relatives through the resources of the Church, nor give his nieces—lest I say daughters—in marriage. To give the property of the poor to those who are not poor is recognized as a crime equal to sacrilege. Certainly, the resources of churches are the patrimonies of the poor; and whatever ministers and stewards, who are assuredly not lords or possessors, receive beyond food and clothing is taken from them with sacrilegious cruelty” [Col. 0156D].

Peter the Chanter, *Abridgement of the Word*, chapter 47: “Give to nature, because he is a human being—if, that is, he is in need. Yet by ‘nature’ we sometimes mean carnality and blood: give to blood-relations from what is your own, from your patrimony, not from that purchased by Christ’s blood, whose administration has been entrusted to ecclesiastical persons so that they may distribute it to the poor. For this reason the Lord commanded in the Law that such a priest and Levite should be chosen as could say to father and mother, ‘I do not know you.’ But shall I not give from the patrimony of the Crucified One to my good and upright kinsman? No: you are not to set him up as a pillar in the Church, because of the harmful example. For people do not consider that you have given to a good man, but that you have given to a kinsman, so that they may draw it into precedent. Give to grace, and especially from the patrimony of the Crucified One; for it is bestowed freely [*gratis*]. Therefore it ought rather to be bestowed on grace—indeed, on grace alone—not on nature, that is, carnality.

“Thus in the *Lives of the Fathers*: ‘My abba, should I give alms to a parent, child, or blood-relation?’ The abba replied, ‘No.’ ‘Why, my abba?’ ‘Because a little blood draws you.’ And afterwards: ‘In giving from these same goods either to a relative, an outsider, or anyone at all, let us consider need, so as to give nothing beyond it. But shall I put a relative before an outsider? No, if both are equally in need, because of the harmful example—just as the seven deacons would not have put their own blood-relations before others for this purpose. If you object that the time is different now: indeed it is. Yet we, like them, are stewards, not lords, of the goods cast down at the apostles’ feet. Therefore give to need, not to blood’” [Col. 0157D].

We read of Benedict XII in Bernard Gui that, when a merchant of Toulouse went to Avignon with his wife, Benedict’s niece, and they were admitted to an audience with him, they heard him say that, as Jacques Fournier, he indeed recognized them, but that, having been made pope, he had neither relatives nor connections. They obtained nothing from him except the expenses incurred on the journey and what was necessary for their return home.

Note that in Maz. I, after the words “they are permitted to have [them] to the loss of their salvation,” the following two verses are added:

> When the Creator of things had deprived the clergy of offspring,  
> a throng of nephews succeeded in fulfilment of Satan’s wish.

]. The indulgent laxity of elders is ruinous to the young. Therefore the Wise Man says [Note: [Col. 0157] Ecclus. 17.]: “You have daughters: do not show them a cheerful face.” Your kindness has loosened for them the restraining bridle against every allurement. I therefore fear that their life may degenerate in its first bloom, as is written in Job [Note: [Col. 0157] ch. 15.]: “Its cluster will be damaged like a vine in first flower, and like an olive casting away its blossom.”

Moreover, one sins enormously and makes himself answerable for another’s life when he softens boys in their tender age through excessive familiarity and sweet words. Cyrus the Persian—of whom Isaiah had prophesied two hundred and ten years beforehand, “To Cyrus, my anointed, whose right hand I have grasped, that I may subject nations before his face” [Note: [Col. 0157] Isa. 45.]—defeated Croesus beside the river Halys. Yet although many victories had made him glorious, because he made the Lydian nation, formerly most warlike, devote itself to feasting, games, and embraces, thus emasculating a most valiant people, he was defeated and killed by Tomyris, queen of the Massagetae. She put his head into a skin filled with blood and said: “Drink the blood for which you thirsted.”

“Lay hold of discipline,” says the prophet David, “lest at any time the Lord be angry” [Note: [Col. 0157] Ps. 2.]. Rebuke and instruct your nephews more diligently, lest an excessively indulgent and familiar affection furnish them an occasion of insolence. I beg that they be formed for honourable works, so that they may not learn by experience what sin is and that every occasion of shamefulness may be cut off. As the book of Judges relates, Judah and Simeon cut off the extremities of the hands of King Bezek, or Adoni-bezek, who attacked them [Note: [Col. 0157] Judg. 1.]; so we too must forestall the impulses of puberty and cut away the first beginnings of wicked deeds. These are the little ones of Babylon, whom one must dash against the rock which is Christ. “Blessed is he who shall seize and dash your little ones”—those, namely, of Babylon—“against the rock” [Note: [Col. 0157] Ps. 136.]. For it is written that the inclinations of humankind are prone to evil from youth [Note: [Col. 0157] Gen. 8.]. Therefore cut away the itching evil in its tender age, for seedlings of thorns are more easily uprooted before they grow together.

## LETTER LII. TO R. [Note: [Col. 0158D] Richard. See Letter 5 concerning him.] ARCHBISHOP OF CANTERBURY. [A.D. 1178.]

**SUMMARY.**—He explains to the archbishop of Canterbury, who had sent him to the king, how great a storm he suffered at sea; he declares that, because of benefits received from him, he refuses no labour. Finally, he asks for prayers that he may successfully transact the entrusted business with the king.

To his dearest lord R., by God’s grace archbishop of Canterbury, primate of all England and legate of the apostolic see, P. of Blois, archdeacon of Bath, greeting in him without whom there is no salvation.

I had lately girded myself to obey your command, and, having taken leave and received the favour of your blessing, was departing, when you recalled me because of certain matters which then happened to arise, and firmly enjoined me to keep you informed by frequent messengers concerning my condition and what happened to me on the journey.

I had gone down to the sea and boarded a ship. When we had already spread the sails to the winds and exposed our lives to danger, behold, snow, hail, rain, and storm-winds covered the heavens with darkness and transformed the sea’s flat surface into dreadful mountains of water. “The upliftings of the sea were wondrous” [Note: [Col. 0157] Ps. 92.]: the waves ascended to heaven and descended to the deeps, and my soul melted away within them. All who were in the ship were shaken and staggered like a drunken man, and all their wisdom was swallowed up [Note: [Col. 0157] Ps. 106.].

The man in charge of the helm, seated in the stern, cast aside his skill and abandoned his station, committing the ship to chance. Everyone suffered the spirit of dizziness, the spirit of loathing and nausea. There was no one to lift hands or eyes to heaven; no one to offer prayers to God, or to devote himself to satisfaction [penance] or repentance. All lay deprived of the use of their limbs or crushed in spirit, and became like dead men.

Although at that time the summer solstice had greatly cut back the night’s duration in order to lengthen the day, never did any night seem so long to me. For this night began at noon; by a kind of stormy tyranny it seized a time not its own and turned daylight into its darkness. O most accursed night, not to be counted in the whole circuit of the year: night of whirlwind, night of wrath, night of horror and death! All that dreadful night we were in the heart of the sea and, as it were, in the belly of hell, until the most desired rising of the sun announced to us the favour of a gentler breeze. He who commands winds and sea calmed the sea [Col. 0159A], “made its storm a breeze, and its waves were still” [Note: [Col. 0159] Ps. 106.]. We rejoiced because they were still, and because the Lord had led us to the harbour of our desire.

But I, as though risen from the dead, ate no food that day; my soul abhorred all food. I therefore remained over until the following day, since, disordered by the confused sound of sea and waves, I could not easily recover my breath completely. You ought to ponder anxiously these and similar hardships which I suffer greatly on your account, and show compassionate concern for those who endure the harshest labours for your peace. Yet, as is commonly said, those who languish in idleness with you, and spend their days in desires and pleasures, find with you more abundant fruit of favour and enter into the labours of those who bore the burden and heat of the day for your necessities.

But whether absent or present, I have always found your generosity magnificent; as though you anticipated my desires, you have continually anticipated me in your favours, without any request on my part and beyond all my deserving. Therefore, whenever some pressing necessity of yours calls for my service, I do not refuse the labour, being wholly ready to go to prison and to death for your honour. The lord king is heading for Gascony, and I, travelling by *duploma* [at double pace], follow him immediately [Note: [Col. 0159D]

A similar expression occurs in Letter 59: “He returned to you amid the same madness of storm, travelling by *diploma*”; read *duplomate*, on the evidence of all our manuscripts. What, then, is *duploma* here? A double journey, or speed in travelling, when two stages are completed each day. Ralph of Diceto, *Images of History*, under the year 1172: “He came to Porchester as though at double pace [*duplomate*].” The same author, under 1179: “Henry, father and king of the English, foreknowing a sudden claim and a sudden arrival, and setting out at double pace, hastened to meet the king of the French as he disembarked from a ship at Dover.” And under 1184: “The king, proceeding under pressure of time, came almost at double pace to Canterbury.” The word is understood in this sense in the law *Continuus*, *On Obligations of Words*: “One who promised to give at Ephesus is not bound to continue his journey at double pace, day and night, disregarding every kind of weather.” And later: “But if, travelling at double pace or by fortunate navigation, he arrived earlier than anyone…” The gloss: *duplomate*: “I go twice as fast as another”; or “by a doubled journey”; or “with speed.”

This letter seems to have been written about the year 1178.].

Would that I may so run as to attain! But do you, Father, pray to the Most High [Col. 0159C] that, finding favour in his eyes and having successfully and swiftly completed your business, I may return to you rejoicing.

May our great rustics be well—Master G. [Note: [Col. 0160D] Perhaps Gerard Puella, who was a member of the household of the archbishop of Canterbury along with Peter of Blois. We shall speak more suitably of him elsewhere.] and the archdeacon of Bayeux. May our other companions also be well; I belong wholly to each one of them and to them all.

## LETTER LIII. TO THE BISHOPS OF ENGLAND. [A.D. 1178?]

**SUMMARY.**—Richard, archbishop of Canterbury, commands his fellow bishops not to permit foreign bishops of uncertain ordination to discharge episcopal functions, and to proclaim excommunicated those who forge the pope’s bull or bishops’ seals.

RICHARD, by God’s grace archbishop of Canterbury, primate of all England, to his venerable brothers and fellow bishops established in the province of Canterbury, greeting in the true Saviour.

Although we cannot entirely avoid scandals to come—for, as it is written, “scandals must come” [Note: [Col. 0159] Matt. 18.]—yet the office of administration entrusted to us and to you obliges us, so far as we can, to cut off the material of scandals and, by more timely counsel, to meet dangers that threaten us. Long has the angel of Satan known how to transform himself into an angel of light; and beneath sheep’s clothing and a feigned simplicity, the wolf’s ancient rapacity rages.

In these days, moreover, certain pseudo-bishops from Ireland—or men feigning the barbarous speech of the Scots—although they have received the laying-on of hands from no one, administer episcopal functions to the people. The Apostle testifies: “No one takes this honour upon himself, but he who is called by God, as Aaron was” [Note: [Col. 0159] 2 Cor. 11.]. Yet they enter not through the door but by another way; they defile Christ’s Church and, so that our ministry may be maligned, by sacrilegious presumption dishonour the sacrament of episcopal dignity. Though they have never received the grace of sacred anointing, they confer orders, dedicate churches, consecrate altars, bless abbots, and thus, miserably begging food and clothing [Col. 0160C], turn the sacraments of our redemption into a pitiful and lamentable source of gain.

Since manifold occasion for scandal has already arisen in the English Church from the ministrations of such men [Note: [Col. 0159] Heb. 5.], and since the sacred canons do not admit those whose ordination is doubtful [Note: [Col. 0159] Distinction 92, canon “If any bishops”], we command and enjoin upon all of you that throughout your dioceses you take care generally to prohibit such persons—of barbarian nation and uncertain ordination—from being permitted to perform episcopal offices [Note: [Col. 0160D]

A similar prohibition is found in the Council of Verneuil, canon 13: “Concerning wandering bishops who have no parishes and whose ordination we do not know: according to the institutions of the holy Fathers, it has been resolved that they must not minister in another’s parish or perform any ordination without the command of the bishop whose parish it is. If they presume to do this, let them be suspended from office until they come concerning this matter to the synod, and there receive sentence according to canonical institution, except only for the sake of travel,” etc.

And in the Council of Vermerie, canon 14: “Let no ordination of priests be performed by bishops travelling through the lands. If those priests are good men, let them be consecrated again” [Col. 0161B].

Earlier, in the Council of Soissons, chapter 5: “Let bishops or priests arriving from other regions not be received into the ministry of the Church unless they have first been examined by the bishop whose parish it is.”

And a little earlier, in the Council of Lestines, canon 4: “According to canonical precaution, let all unknown bishops or priests arriving from anywhere not be admitted to ecclesiastical ministry before synodal examination.”

And in the third supplementary capitulary, canon 37: “In some places there are Scots who say that they are bishops and who ordain many negligent persons as priests and deacons without the permission of their lords or masters. Since their ordination commonly falls into the heresy of simony and is subject to many errors, we have unanimously decreed that it must in every way be deemed invalid” [Col. 0161C].

The Council of Celchyth, held in the English Church in the ninth century, likewise decreed against the Scots, canon 5: “Let no one of the Scottish race be permitted to usurp sacred ministry in anyone’s diocese; nor may anyone consent that he touch anything belonging to sacred order, or receive from them in baptism or in the celebration of masses, or even administer the Eucharist to the people, because it is uncertain to us from where, or whether by anyone, they are ordained.”

Nor was it enough for Richard of Canterbury to prohibit these bishops of barbarian nation and uncertain ordination from being allowed to carry out episcopal functions throughout the province [Col. 0161D]; it was also necessary to prohibit persons seeking ordination from resorting to them. Canon 5 of the Council of Westminster, held under the same Richard in 1175: “Because certain clerics, despairing of receiving ordination from their bishops—whether because of ignorance, sexual incontinence, condition of birth, lack of a title, or insufficient age—are ordained outside their own province, sometimes even by bishops from beyond the sea, or falsely claim to have been ordained, bringing unknown seals to bishops, we decree that the ordinations of such persons are to be deemed invalid,” etc. See Council of Trent, session 6, *On Reform*, canon 5, and session 14, canon 2.].

For just as dedication or baptism is not understood to have preceded where there is doubt concerning persons of this kind [Note: [Col. 0161D] Thus Council of Carthage V, canon 6; the African Council, canon 39; Felix IV, Letter 2, canon 2; and, specifically concerning baptism, Leo the Great, Letter 37, canon 1, and Letter 92, canon 16; Gregory I, Book XII, Letter 31; Trojanus, bishop of Saintes, in a letter to Eumerius of Nantes; Gregory II, Letter 9; Gregory III, Letter 1.], so neither do we account as bishops those whose consecration is unknown.

Furthermore, because in these regions the public pest of forgers has crept in—men who, with counterfeit bulls and letters, bring false charges against innocent people and attempt to overthrow the status of rightful possessors—we strictly command your prudence to have excommunicated solemnly proclaimed on every feast day those who presume to forge the bull of the lord pope or our seals and yours [Note: [Col. 0162B]

On forgers of apostolic bulls, see canon 30 of the Council of Tribur: “If indeed—which is unfitting—any person, whether priest or deacon, is convicted of having brought a false letter from the Apostolic See by devising some disturbance and plotting against our ministry, or anything else that did not suitably come from it, then, with faith preserved and full humility toward the Apostolic See, the bishop has authority either to commit him to prison or to another custody, until he appeals through letter or suitable delegates of his party to the apostolic highness, so that it may deign, by its holy legation, to decree most especially what the Roman law determines ought justly to be decided concerning such persons; thus both he may be corrected and a limit imposed upon others” [Col. 0162C].

And in the chapter *Ad falsarios*, *On the Crime of Forgery*, which belongs to Innocent III, and in the chapter *Licet*, which belongs to the same pope, nine ways in which forgery may be committed are set forth. Baronius, vol. XII, under the year 1195, should also be consulted.], as well as those who support them; so that those whom the judgment of their own conscience does not restrain from wickedness may at least be deterred by the frequent repetition of this proclamation. Fare well in Christ.

## LETTER LIV. TO L., ARCHDEACON OF POITIERS.

[Col. 0161B]

**SUMMARY.**—He urges the archdeacon of Poitiers not to compel his niece Adelitia, against her will, into monastic life, since the states both of marriage and of monasticism require free choice of mind.

To his dearest friend L., archdeacon of Poitiers, P. of Blois, archdeacon of Bath [Col. 0162A], greeting and the affection of deepest love.

Your niece Adelitia complains and laments that you wish to force her into a monastery and enslave her, unwilling and resisting, to cloistered confinement. She had indeed envisaged marital embraces and expected the fruit of offspring from works of the flesh; but now, as she says, she is compelled to renounce a mother’s office and, bidding farewell at life’s very threshold to its pleasures and this world’s desirable things, laments that she is incurring the reproach of perpetual barrenness.

Truly, I greatly wonder at your prudence and moderation. For since the said Adelitia has now reached an age of discretion, she ought not, as it seems to me, to be violently compelled toward the religious life—especially since Scripture testifies that forced service is not pleasing to God. The authority of the canons also declares that one becomes monk or nun by personal profession or parental dedication [Note: [Col. 0162C]

Council of Orléans I, canon 19; Toledo IV, canons 49 and 55; Toledo X, canon 6; Gregory II, Letter 9. It was customary for parents to offer their children to God in a monastery while they were under age, by a fixed and prescribed rite. St Benedict describes this in chapter 59 of his Rule:

“If perhaps one of the nobility offers his son to God in a monastery, and the boy himself is under age, his parents shall make the petition of which we have spoken above, and, with the offering, wrap that petition and the boy’s hand in the altar-cloth, and thus offer him. Concerning their property, they shall either promise under oath in the present petition that they will never, either personally, through an intermediary, or in any way, at any time, give him anything or provide him with an opportunity to possess anything; or, if they are unwilling to do this and wish to offer something to the monastery as alms for their own spiritual reward, they shall make a donation to the monastery from the property which they wish to give, reserving for themselves, if they wish, a usufruct. Thus every avenue shall be closed, so that no hope remains for the boy by which he might be deceived and perish—God forbid—as we have learned by experience. Poorer persons shall do likewise. But those who have absolutely nothing shall simply make the petition and, with the offering, offer their son before witnesses.”

In Gratian, 20, question 3, canon *Praesens*, said to be by Nicholas I, where the monastic status of Lambert is disputed: “Nor did I, his father, offer him clothed in the altar-cloth.”

Lanfranc, *Decrees*, chapter 17: “A boy to be offered, after first receiving the tonsure, shall be presented by his parents after the Gospel to the priest celebrating Mass, carrying in his hands the host and the chalice with wine, as is customary. When the priest has received this offering, the aforesaid parents shall wrap the boy’s hand in the cloth covering the altar, a portion of which hangs down in front; then the abbot shall receive him. Once this has been done, the parents shall immediately promise before God and his saints that neither they themselves nor anyone set up by them shall ever cause the boy to leave the order he has received, and that they will knowingly give him nothing from which he might perish—God forbid. They shall first declare this written promise there before witnesses, and afterwards place it upon the altar” [Col. 0163A].

Bernard, Letter 1, speaking of his kinsman Robert, who among other reasons for his defection from the Cistercians to the Cluniacs alleged that his parents had offered him to the monastery of Cluny: “Although there is no doubt that he was promised, not given; for the petition required by the Rule was not made for him by his parents, nor was his hand wrapped with that petition in the altar-cloth, so that he might thus be offered before witnesses.”

And in Letter 324, where he teaches that Thomas of Saint-Omer, wishing to transfer from the Benedictines to Clairvaux, should not be prevented: “The parents’ vow remains intact, and their offering has not been rendered void, but increased.”]

Under the old law, minors offered to God in a monastery by their parents could not leave it, either before or after puberty. This is inferred from canon 49 of the Fourth Council of Toledo:

> “Either paternal devotion or personal profession makes a monk. Whichever of these it may be, it will hold him bound. Accordingly, we forbid such persons to return to the world, and prohibit them every entrance into secular life.”

The canon concerns minors, whom paternal devotion, not personal profession, makes monks, and adults, whom personal profession alone makes monks; and it declares both to be bound and to have no liberty to return to secular life. Canon 55:

> “Whoever, having received penance while still laymen, have had themselves tonsured, and then, by transgressing, have become laymen again, when apprehended by their bishop, are to be recalled to the penance from which they withdrew. But if any are irrevocable through penance and, when admonished, will not return, they are truly to be condemned before the Church by a sentence of anathema as apostates. The same applies to those who were tonsured by their parents, or who, having lost their parents, devoted themselves of their own accord to religion, and afterwards assumed secular dress,” etc.

The canon requires those tonsured by their parents who subsequently assumed secular dress to be subjected to anathema. It therefore establishes that paternal devotion binds a person permanently to monastic life. Toledo X, canon 6:

> “If, at any lesser age, either one or both parents have given their children, of either sex, either the tonsure of religion or the garment due to religion, and, though the children themselves were unwilling or unaware, they have not immediately repudiated what was received and seen in their children, but have permitted those children, before themselves or before the Church and openly in the assembly, to possess such things, it shall never thereafter be permissible for the children themselves to return to secular dress. Rather, once it has been established that they formerly had the tonsure or religious clothing, they shall immediately be recalled to the worship and habit of religion, and compelled to serve under the perpetual strictness of this observance.”

That canon says that children offered to a monastery by their parents while under age cannot return to secular life. Gregory II, writing to Boniface:

> “You further added the question whether, if a father or mother has entrusted a son or daughter within the enclosure of a monastery, during the years of infancy, to regular discipline, it is lawful for them, once they have reached the years of puberty, to depart and contract marriage. We wholly reject this, because it is sinful for the reins of pleasure to be loosened for children offered to God by their parents.”

What could be clearer? In the chapter *Praesens* in Gratian, Lambert is said not to be a monk because his father did not offer him clad in the monastic cloak. This reasoning would be pointless if a child offered by his father could abandon the monastery. Bernard too, unless he assumed this, ought to have answered the objection of the Cluniacs and the monks of Saint-Bertin differently from the way he did. In a word, he should have objected that Robert, while under age, had indeed been offered to the monastery of Cluny, and Thomas to that of Saint-Bertin, but that both had gone over to Clairvaux because those made monks by paternal devotion are not so bound that, when adults, they may not reject this manner of life—and may therefore all the more transfer to another order in which regular observance flourishes.

Besides, if a boy, once he has reached puberty, is free to remain or depart, why, according to the Rule and Lanfranc’s decrees, is the father commanded to dispose of all his possessions, removing from his son every share whatsoever in the inheritance? Why does he promise this? Why does he confirm his promise by an oath? What is this removal of paternal inheritance but an obstacle set up and a kind of force applied to a man supposedly free, lest he exercise his natural liberty—confirmed for him by the canons—to abandon the monastery? But if the son cannot return to secular dress, what is this same stripping of inheritance except an act of extraordinary piety, by which the father harms his son’s liberty in no respect and employs no force?

I say further: why is the father commanded in the same Rule and decrees to do this, so that every avenue may be blocked and no occasion remain for the boy by which, deceived, he might perish? Is he to perish because he rejected a manner of life to which he was bound by no obligation to adhere? Not at all. But he will undoubtedly perish if he has been permanently bound by the offering made by his father.

Finally, the contrary opinion is supported by no foundation. [Col. 0164C] It rests on chapter *Illud*, 20, question 1, which is said to be Pope Marcellus’s, but falsely. In Marcellus’s time infants were not offered to God in monasteries. It rests on chapter *Sicut* in the same place, and chapter *Puellae*, likewise. But those passages deal with girls at puberty; they do not concern minors offered to God in a monastery by their parents.

The defenders of that opinion say that it seems harsh for one who does not wish it to become a monk. But the Fathers did not judge it harsh that a boy should be devoted to God by another’s will—he who by another’s will was made a son of God in baptism. If a father could give away, if he could sell, his underage son, why could he not consecrate him to the Lord? “But,” they say, “the new law is opposed to this, as we shall presently state.” What follows from that?

Under the new law, they may leave the monastery, upon reaching years of discretion, if they do not wish to ratify the paternal offering. So Clement III, chapter *Cum virum*, *De regularibus*, and Celestine III, chapter *Cum simus*, under the same title, in these words:

> “If the said boy has reached years of discretion and does not wish to retain the monastic habit, then, if he cannot be persuaded to do so, he is by no means to be compelled; for then it shall be free for him to leave it and to claim the paternal goods that come to him by succession.”

. [Col. 0163A] But she is not bound by the bond of her own profession [Note: [Col. 0164D] Leo the Great, Letter 92, chapter 13. Council of Mainz under Leo III, chapter 33: “Let no one be tonsured without the lawful age and spontaneous will.” Nicholas I, in response to the questions of the Bulgarians, chapter 87: “To put on the monastic habit and lead a secluded life is required only of one who pledges himself to God. Therefore whoever uses force against another so that he assumes a monastic habit and a more secluded life which he neither desired nor chose cannot escape sin as one who commits violence. And since that which is done without the recipient’s wish does not count, neither does one receiving the religious habit thereby earn a reward, nor will the one inflicting it escape judgment for his cruelty.” In Gratian, 20, question 3, chapter *Praesens*, a certain Lambert is declared not to be a monk, and thus not to be deprived of his paternal and maternal inheritance, because, not having been offered by his father in tender age, he put on the monastic habit unwillingly. See the Council of Trent, session 25, *On Regulars*, chapters 17, 18, and 19.], [Col. 0164A] because she resists and protests against this profession to the extent that she can. Nor does paternal devotion bind her [Note: [Col. 0165C]

There are two reasons why Adelitia could not be bound to the monastic life. The first is drawn from her age, the second from her emancipation. Blesensis touches on the first a little earlier when he writes:

> “For since the aforesaid Adelitia is now of age and has reached years of discretion, she ought not, as it seems to me, to be forced violently into a religious purpose.”

If you ask at what age someone is reckoned, in this respect, to be beyond paternal authority by reason of age, I answer with Toledo X, canon 6:

> “Parents shall have permission to commit their children to religion no longer than until their tenth year of age. Thereafter, whether it be with the will of their parents or through a solitary vow of their own devotion, it shall be lawful for the children themselves to assume the observance of religion.”

Accordingly correct Ivo of Chartres, who in part VII of his *Decree*, chapter 27, reads “twelfth” instead of “tenth”; and Gratian, who in 20, question 2, chapter *Si in qualibet*, wrote “fourteenth”—perhaps because each wished to adapt the canon to the practice of his own age. In the seventh century, when the council was held, children could be offered only up to their tenth year; in the twelfth century, when Ivo flourished, they remained under paternal authority up to their twelfth year; and in the following century, when Gratian lived, up to their fourteenth.

Our Peter explains the second reason in this way:

> “Nor does paternal devotion bind her, because she is not in her father’s household, but is, as it were, emancipated by her father’s death [Col. 0166C] and does not fall back into another’s power,” etc.

From this it follows that guardians, relatives by marriage, and blood-relatives may not commit permanently to a monastery minors orphaned of father and mother who are unwilling. The Fifth Council of Orléans, Toledo IX and X, and Saints Benedict, Lanfranc, and Bernard themselves use the word *parents* because it properly signifies father and mother, not relatives by marriage, blood-relatives, or guardians. And what Toledo IV expresses by the phrase “paternal devotion,” Toledo X explains by “father and mother,” or “either one or both parents have given.”

But what if the father wishes to offer a son or daughter while the mother objects? He may offer the child alone. What if the mother wishes to do so against the father’s will? She may not; but after the father’s death, this will lie within her discretion. Gregory II sufficiently indicates that by “parents” here father and mother, not others, are meant: “If a father or mother [offers] a son or daughter,” etc. But if a minor were made a monk or nun while the parents were unwilling or [Col. 0166D] unaware, and thus did not consent at all? According to Toledo X, the child should be recalled as soon as possible by the parents; or else, according to the council called Triburiense, they would entirely forfeit their right. But according to chapter *Puella*, 20, question 2, the parents could annul the act within a year and a day; after that period, just as the person who had entered in this manner could no longer depart, so neither could they reclaim that person.

What right, then, do guardians have over minors? Although they could not offer minors unwilling to be offered, they could nevertheless remove them from the monastery, even against their will, within a year and a day after they had entered it of their own accord. The Council of Tribur, chapter 24, teaches this clearly, without any mention of parents—though Gratian seems to have wished to extend the canon to them in the cited chapter *Puella*.]

, because she is not in her father’s household, but, as though emancipated by her father’s death and not falling again under another’s authority, she has acquired free disposal of her own will. By the benefit of both laws, marriages are free. Therefore, if carnal marriage enjoys granted liberty, spiritual marriage is privileged by a fuller grace of liberty; for where the Spirit is, there is liberty. [Note: [Col. 0165] II Corinthians 3.]

If you intend to betroth your niece to the Son of the Most High, you know that the bridegroom desires to be presented with a holy, voluntary, not compelled mind. For in Genesis [Note: [Col. 0165] Chapter 24.] you read concerning Rebecca’s betrothal that her will was commanded to be carefully sought. Joshua also [Note: [Col. 0165] Ibid.] places before the people of Israel the choice of serving the gods of Mesopotamia, or the gods of the [Col. 0165B] Amorites, or the Lord God, indicating that service is not meritorious before God when it is compelled apart from the free goodwill of choice.

Moreover, your niece publicly declares that you weary her to no purpose and labor in vain for her conversion. For, as she asserts, she would become more perverse through that very conversion; and even if she were shut up in cloisters a thousand times, she would nevertheless procure for herself a timely departure, to your disgrace and contempt. Thus, as it seems to me, you are occupied by useless labor and superfluous concern; and I fear that someone may apply to you that saying of the Lord: “Woe to you, who compass sea and land to make one proselyte, and when he has been found, you make him [Note: [Col. 0165] Matthew 23.] twice as much a son of Gehenna.” [Col. 0166A]

Cease, therefore, from what you have begun. If your niece recoils from the yoke of religion and refuses to be betrothed to the immortal God, let her be betrothed to a mortal man; and she who cannot be saved on the mountain may at least be saved in Zoar, [Note: [Col. 0165] Genesis 19.] a small city. Yet because she is very learned, I shall still approach her both by letters and in person, wishing to test in her case what human eloquence can accomplish in such matters after the grace of God. For human persuasion without God’s grace is nothing but sounding bronze or a clanging cymbal. [Note: [Col. 0165] I Corinthians 13.] He alone gives mouth and wisdom who says: “Without me you can do nothing.” [Note: [Col. 0165] John 15.] Therefore, gracious Lord, breathe upon her; you who raise up children to Abraham from stones, take away from her the heart of stone and instill in her, in the spirit of the fear of the Lord, the desire for conversion [Col. 0166B] and holy conduct.

## LETTER LV. TO ADELITIA, A NUN

**Subject.**—He congratulates Adelitia on aspiring to the monastic life and on having secretly bound herself by a vow to enter a monastery. He praises virginity, urges her to persevere, and to renounce the world completely.

To beloved and most beloved ADELITIA in Christ, Master P. of Blois: greeting in the Lord God, our salvation.

All who love you rejoice, and there is joy also among the angels of God, because you hold in your desires the purpose of a holier [Col. 0167A] life. For, as is said, you have renounced—though secretly—this deceitful world, and wisely resolved to leave the world before it leaves you. Blessed are you, who, despising the sons of men, have chosen for yourself as bridegroom the Son of the Most High. He is King of kings and Lord of lords; he is the one who has desired your beauty, and the Prophet invites you to union with him: “Hear, O daughter, and see; incline your ear, and forget your people and your father’s house.” [Note: [Col. 0167] Psalm 44.] Your beauty lies not in the body but in the mind: “For all the glory of the king’s daughter is within.” [Note: [Col. 0167] Ibid.]

You will be more pleasing to Christ your bridegroom to the extent that your clothing is humbler, your bodily adornment more lowly, your speech rarer, your expression more downcast, your gaze more modest, and your bearing more mature. “There is none holy as the Lord,” [Col. 0167B] [Note: [Col. 0167] I Samuel 2.] because he is the Holy of holies, who asks of you nothing except the holiness of chastity. For it is written: “Grace upon grace is a holy and modest woman.” [Note: [Col. 0167] Ecclesiasticus 26.]

Would that you might say to him who calls you daughter through the prophet, as it is written, “You are the father of my virginity,” [Note: [Col. 0167] Jeremiah 3.] and that he might answer you with what is read elsewhere: “You will call me Father,” [Note: [Col. 0167] Ibid.] “and you will not cease to follow after me”—following after the virgin mother of the bridegroom. For she is the virgin of virgins who goes before: “Virgins shall be brought to the king after her; her companions shall be brought to you, and they shall be brought into the temple of the king.” [Note: [Col. 0167] Psalm 44.]

The daughters of this world are daughters of Babylon. They appoint successors for themselves through the uncleanness of the flesh; they conceive in sin, give birth in pain, rear their children in fear, are always anxious about the living, and are inconsolably afflicted over the dead. [Col. 0167C] If you wish to give birth, you wish to perish; for childbirth, like that of a viper, burdens and tears apart the mother’s limbs, and it is astonishing that the fetus itself is not torn and broken. But once it comes forth into this valley of weeping and misery, it begins with weeping and, to the end of this brief and wretched life, continues its days in sorrows.

As blessed Job [Note: [Col. 0167] Chapter 14.] observes, saying: “Man born of woman, living for a short time, is filled with many miseries.” How much happier is the condition of those men and women [Col. 0168A] who have made themselves eunuchs for the kingdom of heaven, whose praise is in the Gospel, and to whom the love of Christ is sweeter than a multitude of children! [Note: [Col. 0167] Matthew 19.] Hear what Isaiah says of such persons: [Note: [Col. 0167] Chapter 56.] “Let not the eunuch say, ‘Behold, I am a dry tree’; for thus says the Lord to the eunuchs: ‘I will give them in my house and within my walls a place and a name better than sons and daughters.’” [Note: [Col. 0167] Ibid.]

Both prophetic and evangelical speech call those persons eunuchs who have bound themselves by a vow of chastity for Christ’s love. Of old it was said: “Increase and multiply, and fill the earth”; [Note: [Col. 0167] Genesis 1.] and, “Cursed is he who has not left seed upon the earth.” [Note: [Col. 0167] Exodus 23.] Therefore Jephthah’s daughter, as subject to the curse of the law, lamented her chastity, deprived of posterity. [Note: [Col. 0167] Judges 10.] Nevertheless, since the Lord came, fulfilling the law and not abolishing it; [Col. 0168B] since the voice of the turtledove was heard [Note: [Col. 0167] Song of Songs 2.], and Paul, the herald of chastity, gave counsel concerning virginity, marriage has filled the earth and chastity paradise.

You have acted wisely, because for Christ’s love you have abandoned the deceitful riches and treacherous wealth of this life. He himself, the zealous guardian and keeper of a chaste heart and body, will preserve you holy, undefiled, and a companion of angelic purity. [Note: [Col. 0167] I Corinthians 7.] You have begun excellently; nevertheless, he who judges the ends of the earth attends not to the beginning but to the end. Therefore run in such a way that you may attain the prize. For the glory of virgins is in golden fringes, [Note: [Col. 0167] Psalm 44.] and the oil of blessing pours itself down to the hem of the garment.

I beg you, let nothing secular remain in your heart; rather, offer yourself wholly, that you may be an acceptable burnt offering before the Lord. Ananias and Sapphira were delivered to destruction [Note: [Col. 0167] Acts 5.] because they wished to withhold some part of what had been offered to the Lord. [Col. 0168C] Renounce the world altogether and enter the cloister. Wear the habit which you have familiarly assumed and whose assumption you can no longer conceal. The wishes of all now predestine you to an abbacy, [Note: [Col. 0167D] Perhaps because she was highly learned, to use the words of our Peter in the preceding letter. Yet the office of abbess requires far different and holier qualities—qualities lacking not only in one aspiring to the monastic life, but even in many learned and upright nuns, and which will continue to be lacking. Indeed, even if there were hope that she would someday be endowed with these gifts of mind and this holiness of conduct, she ought not to be given hope of an abbacy, lest the prospect of honors and riches incite her to undertake religious life or furnish an occasion for pride and self-exaltation to one bound by a religious vow. Thus Blesensis let this fall unthinkingly. And indeed, one must first be a daughter before being a mother, a disciple before becoming a teacher. Hear what the Sixth Council of Paris, chapter 34, thought about widows who, as soon as they bid farewell to the world—the same reasoning applies to virgins—become abbesses:

> “Contrary to what divine authority and the Christian religion teach, women who, having lost their husbands, had lived carnally until then are suddenly, without examination of probation, drawn into the governance of souls and set over nuns as spiritual mothers, though they have never been disciples of the same calling. The result is that those who perhaps had been progressing happily fall miserably through their wicked examples.”

Therefore, while the honor of such preeminence is conferred on these women—or at least because of worldly riches—it must be feared that a pit of ruin is being prepared for their souls.], and temporal riches are added to eternal happiness. Complete, then, more promptly what you have begun. For if you mock Christ and make void your first faith, you will share the lot of Babylon’s daughters, and your disgrace shall not be erased for ever.

## LETTER LVI. TO WALTER, [Note: [Col. 0169C] Walter, or Gualter, brother of Theobald, Archbishop of Canterbury, was elected Bishop of Rochester by the monks of the Church of Rochester in the chapter-house of Canterbury, according to ancient custom. This was done by Theobald’s concession, for he restored to the monks that right which his predecessors, the Archbishops of Canterbury, had usurped. He held the episcopate for thirty-five years, that is, until the year of Christ 1182.] BISHOP OF ROCHESTER

[Col. 0169A]

**Subject.**—He strongly dissuades Walter, an eighty-year-old bishop, from the pursuit of hunting, with many arguments; and urges him to imitate the spiritual hunting practised by the apostles.

To the reverend Father and lord WALTER, by God’s grace Bishop of Rochester, P. of Blois: greeting and patience.

Placed amid difficulties, I do not know where to turn. If I tell you what ought to be said, I fear incurring the offense of your indignation; but if I keep silent, to use Job’s words, [Note: [Col. 0169] Chapter 9.] “my mouth will condemn me,” especially since my silence is matter for your shame and an occasion of ruin. Yet I prefer to offend you by consulting for your reputation than to keep damnable silence toward you and conceal your disgrace by silence. You may know with absolute certainty that it has been reported to the lord pope that, neglecting the care of the people entrusted to you and entirely casting off the gravity proper to a bishop, you devote your whole life to hunting with dogs; nor does your more advanced old age restrain in you the delicate itch of frivolity. The lord pope and the cardinals would already have pronounced upon you a sentence of the gravest censure, but they have entrusted both inquiry into the matter and execution of the sentence to the legate who will shortly arrive.

It does not become, most beloved Father, an eighty-year-old man to occupy himself with such things—much less a bishop; not even youth would excuse him from them. [Note: [Col. 0169C]

The author speaks not of hunting oppressive to people, or of hunting in the arena, but of woodland hunting, of which John of Salisbury also speaks in *Polycraticus*, book I, chapter 4. Certain persons are permanently excluded not only from this pursuit but also from certain others regarded as lighter and pleasurable, such as those constituted in holy orders and those holding the highest offices. This kind of hunting is forbidden to bishops and other clergy in the German councils: at Liptines, chapter 2:

> “We have forbidden all servants of God to engage in those hunts and woodland wanderings with dogs, and to keep hawks and falcons.”

At Mainz, chapter 14:

> “Let it be permitted to all others whatsoever to follow dogs and birds in hunting,” etc.

At Regensburg, chapter 4:

> “And let him not personally conduct hunts with dogs, hawks, or *capis*, which the common people call falcons.”

In the councils of Gaul: at Tours III, chapter 8:

> “Let them by no means pursue the hunting of wild beasts or birds.”

And in the *Capitularies*, book V, chapter 12:

> “Let priests, [Col. 0170C] deacons, and subdeacons not presume to carry arms or to undertake any hunting.”

In the councils of England: at Westminster, under Alberic of Ostia, legate of Innocent II, chapter 8:

> “We decree that clerics who hunt, pursue shameful gain, and manage public secular business are nevertheless to be removed from ecclesiastical office and benefice.”

It is recorded in book I of the *Life* of Boniface of Mainz that he reproached Bishop Gervilio, saying that he had seen him with his own eyes playing with birds and dogs, which was not lawful for a bishop. The Lateran Council under Innocent III, chapter 15:

> “We forbid hunting and fowling to all clerics; accordingly, they are not to presume to keep dogs or birds for fowling.”

And finally, the Council of Trent, session 24, *On Reform*, chapter 12. Let learned persons consider what judgment should be passed on the opinion of some who contend that noisy hunting is indeed forbidden to clerics, but not that undertaken without great shouting. Or let them consider what they will say of another opinion, which asserts that even non-noisy hunting is prohibited if done, albeit very rarely, for recreation—or indeed for pleasure; for, not to say more, they make distinctions where the law makes none. On the same subject, our Peter, Letter 61.

This letter appears to have been written about the year 1176, when Peter of Blois was at Rome on the business of the Archbishop of Canterbury, of which his *Life* speaks.]

We read that Pope Nicholas judged a sentence of suspension and excommunication ought to be pronounced against Bishop Lanfred because he practised the art of hunting, although he was more excusable by reason of youth. Survey, from the beginning of the world, the succession of holy Fathers. Come to the patriarchs, [Col. 0170A] approach the leaders, descend to the judges; examine the lives of holy kings, prophets, and priests, and you will find none of them devoted to hunting. “I have read of a holy fisherman,” says Jerome, “but I have not read of a hunter.” For if Saint Eustace is sometimes recorded to have been a hunter, Matthew too was once a tax collector, [Note: [Col. 0169] Matthew 9.] and Paul a persecutor of the Church. [Note: [Col. 0169] Acts 9.]

Nimrod, the mighty hunter, is the very one who built Babel in the land of Shinar, where there occurred the schism of languages and confusion of speech. [Note: [Col. 0169] Genesis 10.] Esau, while carrying out the office of hunting, was deprived of the grace of the birthright and his father’s blessing. [Note: [Col. 0169] Genesis 27.] If one traces the invention and beginnings of the hunting art, it will appear condemnable from its very origin. For the Theban people are recorded as the inventors of this craft—or rather, [Col. 0170B] this evil art: a people foul with parricides, detestable for incest, distinguished by fraud, notorious for perjuries. The Athenians ridiculed them, inventing a tale that Dardanus, a hunter, was carried away under some covering to drinking-bouts and from drinking-bouts to unlawful and shameful embraces. To say nothing of the holy Fathers, scarcely among the number of illustrious men can one find anyone who practised hunting for pleasure.

> “Although victorious Alcides  
>  Pierced the bronze-footed hind, or tamed the woods  
>  Of Erymanthus,” [Note: [Col. 0169] Virgil, *Aeneid* VI.]

if the founder of the Roman race slaughtered the bodies of stags, if Meleager struck down the devastator boar of Calydon, these men served thereby not private pleasure but public usefulness. Yet what comparison is there between pagans and a priest of Christ, who ought to have chosen the torments of death before he could be compelled to such things?

Certainly, another sort of hunting was incumbent upon you by virtue of your office: one in which lies the salvation of those subject to you and the glory of the one who presides. For the Lord says through the prophet: [Note: [Col. 0171] Jeremiah 16.] “Behold, I will send hunters, and they shall hunt upon every mountain.” The prelates of the Church hunt on every mountain when, on the heights of knowledge and teaching, they seize wandering souls as prey for Christ’s service. The apostles, sent into the whole world, rebuked the beasts of the reeds [Note: [Col. 0171] Psalm 67.] when, following the example of their Master, rejecting the hypocrisy of the Pharisees and the figurative observance of ceremonial rites, they hunted many thousands of people in one day into the faith.

Would that you might be willing to devote yourself to this hunting and compensate by the fruit of a better life and the instruction of your people for the waste of so long a time that has vanished into vanities. I beg you, act so that a more disciplined life in you may precede the coming of the legate. For he will come in a mighty spirit [Note: [Col. 0171] Acts 2.], [Col. 0171B] not to build or plant, but to destroy and uproot. [Note: [Col. 0171] Jeremiah 1.]

Know, moreover, that on Palm Sunday I received leave from the lord pope and his brethren, and on the following day I set out to come. The legate, meanwhile, was making every urgent provision for what was necessary to his journey and legation. After the perils and labors of this journey, I hasten to the lord king, expecting great exertions in his service. Fare well.

## LETTER LVII. TO HIS FRIEND G. OF ALNET [Note: [Col. 0171D]

Alnet, commonly Aulnay, is a Cistercian abbey in Normandy, situated in the diocese of Bayeux. It was founded in 1131 by Aichard, constable of France, later a monk of that house. Thus Jongelinus in his Cistercian notice, and Manriquez, volume II of the *History of the Cistercians*. The latter speaks of this letter as follows:

> “There survives a letter of Peter of Blois to a monk of Alnet, recently converted, who believed that after entering a monastery he would be freed from temptations. Peter, on the contrary, shows at length that monks are more exposed to temptations than secular persons, but nevertheless resist them more strongly.”

This letter was written in the year of Christ 1193, shortly after Richard, King of England, was captured by the Duke of Austria.]

.

**Subject.**—To his friend, who believed that after entering a monastery he would be free from temptations, he shows that monks are more subject to temptations than secular persons, but must contend against them bravely. [Col. 0171C] Then he sends him a little song vividly expressing the struggle of flesh and spirit, to relieve his tedium.

To his dearest companion and friend G. of Alnet, PETER of Blois, Archdeacon of Bath: greeting, and strength in the Lord.

From youth there has grown between us an affection of love which neither blood in kindred relationships could overcome nor nature surpass. I have often experienced this amid great reversals of fortune. If I suffered bodily sickness or other troubles of this life, you stood by me as a most faithful helper and most attentive comforter. I likewise always made your misfortunes my own, and amid the changing events of life I joined my lot to yours in a reciprocal friendship, united to you by a most welcome sharing. [Col. 0171D]

You say that you chose the purpose of a holier life especially in order to escape the temptations of this world; yet now, with mournful complaint, [Col. 0172A] you lament that, at the very entrance to religious life, you are encompassed by temptations far more miserably than before, and that your flesh, through its very subjection, resists the spiritual law more stubbornly. Had you not read that human life is temptation and warfare upon earth? [Note: [Col. 0171] Job 7.] Wisdom says: “My son, when you approach the service of God, stand in justice and fear, and prepare your soul for temptation.” [Note: [Col. 0171] Ecclesiasticus 2.]

The world fights more fiercely against those who desert it, and a harsher contest awaits those leaving the allurements of secular life. For Pharaoh rages more violently when Israel departs from Egypt; [Note: [Col. 0171] Exodus 14.] and Satan, leaving the man whom he had held from childhood, tears him apart by afflicting him more grievously. [Note: [Col. 0171] Mark 9.] A whirlwind arises so that Elijah may be taken up to heaven; [Note: [Col. 0171] IV Kings 2.] nor does Israel prevail against Benjamin [Col. 0172B] until it is purified by the slaughter of many thousands. The common course of the present life is to be assailed by temptations. For the Jebusite was left among the Jerusalemites for the exercise of virtue; [Note: [Col. 0171] Joshua 15.] and a spirit of Satan was given to the Apostle lest he be exalted by revelations. [Note: [Col. 0171] II Corinthians 12.]

You have entered the arena of a twofold contest, in which you will not gain the prize unless you run, nor be crowned unless you fight. [Note: [Col. 0171] II Timothy 2.] But may the Lord, the strength of his people, the Lord of hosts, the Lord strong and mighty in battle, [Note: [Col. 0171] Psalm 23.] teach your hands for battle and your fingers for war. If he permits you to be tempted, he will also make an issue with the temptation; [Note: [Col. 0171] I Corinthians 10.] you will not remember your affliction, as waters that have passed away; and when you think yourself consumed, you will rise like the morning star. [Note: [Col. 0171] Job 11.] [Col. 0172C] From weakness you will advance to a crown, and from faintness of spirit to triumph.

But as for your request for the amorous playthings of your youth and adolescence as consolation for your weariness, I do not think that counsel advisable, since such things customarily arouse and nourish temptations. Setting aside, therefore, more wanton songs, I send you a few pieces that I composed in a more serious style, in case they might perhaps relieve your tedium and edify you unto salvation.

### A LITTLE SONG ON THE STRUGGLE OF FLESH AND SPIRIT

“I once served as a soldier,” etc. [See among the poems of Peter of Blois, below.]

“He who has ears, let him hear,” etc. [See the same place.]

## LETTER LVIII. TO REGINALD, [Note: [Col. 0172D] On this Reginald see what we said on Letter 30.] BISHOP OF BATH. [A.D. 1180.]

[Col. 0172D]

**Subject.**—He vehemently remonstrates with the Bishop of Bath because, contrary to legal procedure, he suspended his vice-archdeacon from office; and because he seeks every [Col. 0173A] opportunity to injure him over an unpaid debt.

To his beloved and most beloved lord and Father R., by God’s grace Bishop of Bath, P. of Blois, his Archdeacon of Bath: with greeting, most devoted obedience.

Your letters of indignation—indeed, of thunder—I have read; and my soul was exceedingly troubled, and my heart failed me. Yet, to use the prophet’s words, “your servant found his heart to pray to you” [Note: [Col. 0173] 1 Chron. 17]. I therefore beg that, as though I had obtained leave by edict, you allow me first to swallow my spittle and to mourn my grief a little: not reproaching proudly, but answering dutifully, though sometimes, in the vehemence of pain, inserting some sharper word.

[Col. 0173B] Therefore, if from the abundance of my heart my words have at times exceeded the course of devoted humility, let your generosity pardon me; for, as the wise man says [Note: [Col. 0173] Seneca, *On Anger*, bk. I, chs. 7–8], “the heat of anger and the onset of indignation are not within a man’s control.” Mercifully forgive one who acknowledges his fault, since among the first cradles of the laws you learned that holiness leaves to a bishop the glory of forgiving.

I know that you seek occasions against me, and, induced by treacherous insinuation, stir up matter for contention. Most beloved Father, to use Job’s words, “Do not contend with me in great strength, nor crush me beneath the weight of your greatness” [Note: [Col. 0173] Job 23]. Set equity against me; let my iniquity and the evil that I suffer be weighed in the balance. If [Col. 0173C] you opened your eyes to justice in dealing with him whose offence you accuse, you would grieve that you had offended gravely, according to Solomon’s testimony: “A friend is not to be dishonoured in litigation” [Note: [Col. 0173] Prov. 25]; for his dishonour cannot easily be repaired.

You have often read in the book of experience how many dangers and labours I have borne for you, and how solicitous and effective was the service I rendered toward your advancement [Note: [Col. 0173] What our Peter did for Reginald is plainly apparent from Epistles 24 and 30]. If you recall our more secret counsels, you know with complete certainty that neither death nor sword, nor any occasion of disturbance, ought to have separated me from your affection. Yet, although love is strong as death [Note: [Col. 0173] Song 8], flattery, stronger than love, has taken you from me—if indeed one could take from me [Col. 0173D] him whom, as the present event proves, I never possessed at any time.

During my absence, without any legal solemnity, you issued against me your rather unsynodal prohibitions in a synod. They troubled me only insofar as they displayed the violence of your anger and the intemperance of episcopal eminence. You suspended my vice-archdeacon, though he offered himself for every satisfaction and for justice, to the dishonour of my name. Consider [Col. 0174A] whether you judged justly, you who judge the world, remembering that he who judges the ends of the earth will also judge judges.

You did not learn such things at the Lateran Council, where, before every sentence of excommunication or suspension was pronounced, a first, second, and third admonition had to be given. Nor should that privileged protection of the Roman Church, which I obtained beneath the shelter of your wings, and which was confirmed for me much more fully and solemnly at the time of the Lateran Council [Note: [Col. 0173] Lateran Council under Alexander III, pt. I, ch. 6], have slipped from the memory of your kindness. It specifically grants me that neither archbishop nor bishop may excommunicate or suspend me or my people, unless publicly convicted or confessing in law.

Yet, to use Job’s words: “Even if I have anything of justice, I will not answer, [Col. 0174B] but will entreat the Lord and judge” [Note: [Col. 0173] Job 9]; “though he slay me, I shall hope in him” [Note: [Col. 0173] Job 13]. This adds to the fullness of my grief: this dissension has been raised over the twenty shillings that I owed you—although, by God’s grace, I was able to pay, even had I owed two hundred marks or more. I ask: could this money have been what separated from me a friend and neighbour? Rather, I accuse the malice of flatterers, whose poisonous suggestion was able to turn my lord’s favour toward me into hatred and rancour.

But know this for certain: I have instructed Arnold of Bath and Azo of Paterne—upon whose advancement I congratulate with all my heart—to answer you in my stead concerning the debt. Indeed, if [Col. 0174C] I had bound myself concerning this debt by a bond of faith or by a written obligation, what I had done would have sufficed. For, by the authority of the Council of Chalcedon, of Pope Gelasius, and of Augustine, one does not imperil his good faith or promise who has secured release from what he owed.

Nevertheless, to use the words of the king of Samaria, “you seek occasions against me” [Note: [Col. 0173] 4 Kings 5]. Occasions, however, are readily available. I, who gave up—lest I offend you—that which was more precious and glorious than everything else that kinder fortune had bestowed upon me, am prepared, before you are more seriously offended with me, to leave England and all English benefices, and to break every tie of ambition—which I wish reigned neither in me nor in you. I do not shrink from poverty, [Col. 0174D] in which I was richer and happier than amid accursed wealth. If you lose me once, perhaps you will grieve that you have lost me, and will more heavily bear the absence of one whose present service you now either disdain to use or do not know how to use.

With you everything turns to the contrary for me. While I wholly labour and wholly wear myself out for your honour and advancement, you do not cease to add to the pain of my wounds. But I shall bear everything with equanimity; [Col. 0175A] I shall not set my mouth against heaven, nor speak against my Lord or against his Christ.
