But, to conclude all things in Job’s humility [Note: [Col. 0175] Ch. 9]: let him who scourges kill me at once; let him who began it himself crush me; let him loose his hand and cut me down; and let this be my consolation—that in afflicting me with pain he does not spare me. Farewell.

## EPISTLE LIX. TO R., ELECT OF BATH

**Subject.**—By many arguments and examples he tries to persuade R., elect of Bath, to restore to favour Master Henry, who had formerly deserved exceedingly well of him but had fallen from favour; and to exclude from his society Simon, a most wicked flatterer and slanderer.

To the reverend lord and friend R., elect of Bath, his own P. of Blois: greeting and moderation.

[Col. 0175B] Being asked, I am compelled to ask you. Yet even if a thousand entreaties had anticipated my intervention, I am bound humbly to plead with you for my friend. If you remembered his services, he ought not to have had to beg the aid either of my intercession or of another’s. He is the man who so often exposed himself to dangers of the sea for your needs; who once, when the Cyllenian mountains were closed, when harsh weather had fixed our feet at the boundary of the sky, and the mountain roads were full of the corpses of the dead, did not fear to cross the Alps into Italy on our business, “free as among the dead” [Note: [Col. 0175] Ps. 87]. Having completed your affairs with the count of Maurienne, he returned to you through the same madness of storm, using a passport.

[Col. 0175C] The memory of such great service ought not to have been effaced either by length of time or by the enormity of a grave offence—still less by the treacherous suggestion of your Simon, whose chief purpose is to claim you wholly and exclusively for himself, and to take you away from everyone else. I wonder how, at the word of a contemptible flatterer, you could be so inflamed against a man of most acceptable reputation and proven loyalty—unless because a flatterer’s tongue can throw everything into turmoil: its contagion is always evil, and “the words of his mouth are iniquity and deceit” [Note: [Col. 0175] Ps. 35].

That seller of oil, who fattens and soothes your head with flatteries, accused Master Henry, no less shamelessly than foolishly, of having deceitfully divulged your counsels. Master Henry, rebuking him for falsehood, would have confirmed his words with his fist in his [Col. 0175D] teeth, had he not deferred to the reverence due to you, who were personally present. Moreover, provoked by zeal for justice rather than anger, he spoke to you certain bitter words, because you cherished, to the disgrace of your household and the common injury of all, a man of discredited reputation. Therefore you cast him from your presence, and a momentary offence destroyed the long-standing merits and the fruit of reward due to him.

It was not fitting to treat thus a man whom God chose as priest for himself, and who is bound by the duty of his office to promise patience and mercy. [Col. 0176A] If Master Henry, in an emotional impulse, spoke perhaps less cautiously or too sharply, you know that emotional impulses are not under a man’s control; and that what is done or said in the heat of anger should not be recalled to mind before you have established that it proceeded from deliberate judgment.

Suppose a man of approved reputation said something too intemperately, whether through a slip of the tongue, imprudence of counsel, heat of anger, or any other emotional impulse: it was your concern to overlook and endure everything with equanimity. For thus, according to the Apostle’s teaching, “we surround with more abundant honour those members of the body which we think less honourable” [Note: [Col. 0175] 1 Cor. 12]. Thus a mother loves her weaker son more tenderly. Thus the householder received the prodigal son more kindly [Note: [Col. 0175] Luke 15]. Thus the oil of charity, thus the love [Col. 0176B] of God, pours itself more fully and abundantly into vessels of mercy.

The sacred constitution of the emperors lays down nothing harsh or severe in such cases: for if this proceeded from frivolity, it should be disregarded; if from madness, it is most worthy of compassion; if from injury, it should be forgiven. Julius Caesar [Note: [Col. 0175] Read John of Salisbury, *Polycraticus*, bk. III, ch. 14], the first and most powerful emperor, greatly resented his baldness, and used to draw the thinning hair from the back of his head over his forehead. An angry soldier said to him: “It is easier, Caesar, for you not to be bald than for me to have acted, or to act, in any way more cowardly in battle.” The emperor received this patiently [Note: [Col. 0175] Cicero, in the letter to Octavius].

When Augustus Caesar was reproached with having earned adoption by his maternal uncle Julius Caesar through the shameful prostitution of his body, he turned his emotional response into laughter [Note: [Col. 0175] Suetonius, *Augustus*]. When someone reproached the same emperor for his short stature, calling him a dwarf, he calmly replied that he ought to wear somewhat larger shoes. [Note: [Col. 0175] Diogenes Laertius, bk. II.] Aristippus, withdrawing from someone who abused him, said: “As you are master of your tongue, so I am master of my ears.” Antisthenes likewise, despising a man’s insults, said: “Hearing ought to be stronger than the tongue, since every person has one tongue but two ears.”

Therefore, if your most faithful servant spoke to you with greater freedom from confidence of friendship, or perhaps with a view to correction, bear it all, I beg you, with equanimity, remembering, as the wise man testifies [Note: [Col. 0175] John of Salisbury, cited work]: “A slip of the tongue is not easily to be dragged into punishment.”

[Col. 0176D] And who in Greece was more powerful or eminent than Alexander? Yet Antigonus broke his lyre and threw it away, saying: “At your age it is now fitting to reign; be ashamed that the pleasure of luxury should rule in a royal body.” Scipio [Note: [Col. 0175] Sextus Julius Frontinus, bk. IV, ch. 7] Africanus, mightiest in arms, when someone accused him of being insufficiently combative, said: “My mother bore me to be a commander, not a fighter.”

Was not Master Henry most justly stirred against that infamous man when he branded him with the mark of treachery? I could scarcely believe that a man of such sound judgment had fallen [Col. 0177A] into such folly as to disclose secrets entrusted to him, as Ovid testifies [Note: [Col. 0177] *Art of Love*, bk. I]:

> It is an exceptional virtue to keep silence about matters;
>
> but, conversely, it is a serious fault to speak of what ought to be kept silent.

Yet rich men’s secrets cannot be concealed. For “a bird of the air,” as Solomon says, “will carry the word, and that which has wings will report the matter” [Note: [Col. 0177] Eccles. 10]. For that reason it is dangerous for the rich to share their counsels. If anything escapes through carelessness, blame will be laid upon the confidant; and what you believed known to yourself alone will become common talk in marketplaces and taverns everywhere. Hear the testimony of the Aquinian poet:

> O Corydon, Corydon, do you suppose that any rich man’s secret  
> [Col. 0177B] can exist? If slaves are silent, the beasts of burden will speak—  
> and the dog, the doorposts, and the marble. Shut the windows;  
> let curtains cover the cracks; bar the doors; remove  
> the lamp from the room; let everyone cry out; let almost no one recline nearby.  
> Yet what that man does at the crowing of the second cock,  
> the innkeeper next door will know before daylight.  
> [Note: [Col. 0177] Juvenal, Satire 9.]

If Midas’s barber secretly buried his master’s secret in the ground, a reed would grow up, which by singing would bring it into public: “King Midas has ass’s ears” [Note: [Col. 0177] Persius, Satire 1]. Pallas could not conceal her Erichthonius [Note: [Col. 0177] On Erichthonius, see Natalis Comes, *Mythology*, bk. IX, ch. 6], without the chatter of a crow making him public.

Why then, on the insinuation of a detractor hateful to God, do you presume against an innocent man, whose loyalty and [Col. 0177C] diligence you have so often learned in the book of experience? It is more probable that your informer maliciously divulged the counsel, so as to fasten the charge upon Master Henry, who knew the secret, and to sow tares and matter for scandal between you.

Lay aside, therefore, all rancour and restore Master Henry to your favour. You know that his company is pleasant, his life commendable, and his intimacy fruitful. By now he would have attached himself to another lord, who would more promptly and more generously have rewarded his services; but I have kept him back by gentle speech, until I see whether, rejecting the companionship of those who “call evil good, and good evil” [Note: [Col. 0177] Isa. 5], you wish to admit more closely those whose loyal faith does not waver.

For it is written: “He who touches pitch shall be defiled by it” [Col. 0177D] [Note: [Col. 0177] Ecclus. 13]; and “evil associations corrupt good morals” [Note: [Col. 0177] 1 Cor. 16]. Jehoshaphat, who is commended with many praises for his past life, is severely rebuked by the Lord for association with the wicked king Ahab: “You give help,” says the prophet [Note: [Col. 0177] 2 Chron. 19], “to the ungodly, and join yourself in friendship with the wicked; therefore you have deserved the Lord’s wrath. Yet good works were found in you, because you cut down the groves from the land of Judah.”

The same charge is laid against you, who have admitted into the sanctuary of your familiarity a man whose mouth is full of cursing and bitterness, and who by the poison and malice of his tongue [Col. 0178A] has already driven many people away from you; and who, as is publicly said, has procured for certain persons not merely their departure, but their ruin. Certainly his fabrications ought not to have moved you. But through some distortion of nature, refined ears of the rich receive more pleasantly the flatteries of a false and prostituted tongue than the open testimony of truth. For according to the Satirist, the perverse flatterer,

> when he has gently distilled into the ear  
> a small drop of the poison of one’s nature and country,  
> immediately drives out all who speak the truth.  
> [Note: [Col. 0177] Juvenal, Satire 3.]

“The sons of men—their teeth are weapons and arrows, and their tongues a sharp sword” [Note: [Col. 0177] Ps. 56]; “they dealt deceitfully with their tongues; judge them, O God” [Note: [Col. 0177] Ps. 5]. These are “the frogs in the inner chambers of their kings” [Note: [Col. 0177] Ps. 104], that is, the chattering and talkative persons [Col. 0178B] in the houses of great men. These are the dog-flies and gnats that sting secretly.

I see that a deceitful tongue has most badly corrupted your heart. But would that “sharp arrows of the mighty” [Note: [Col. 0177] Ps. 119], that is, the judgments of the Lord, might be applied to the deceitful tongue, so that you may restrain the tongues of your people from evil and their lips from speaking deceit [Note: [Col. 0177] Ps. 33]. For it was God’s most just judgment that the first man was exiled from paradise because, despising the divine command, he consented to an enemy who flattered him.

Remembering, therefore, dearest lord and friend, that, according to Solomon’s testimony, “the blows of a loving friend are better than the flattering words or blows of a flatterer” [Note: [Col. 0177] Prov. 27], restore Master Henry to favour; and, according to the pattern of evangelical instruction, so “possess your souls in patience” [Note: [Col. 0177] Luke 21] [Col. 0178C] that you cherish no offence in your mind from the past.

> Virtue is a widow unless patience makes her steadfast.

I promise you that in Master Henry you will find faithful service, unblemished friendship, ready obedience, and wholesome counsel. May my lord fare well, and all who love him with affection and in truth!

## EPISTLE LX. TO MASTER R., FRIEND AND COMPANION

**Subject.**—To a friend complaining that bishops enrich their nephews from Christ’s patrimony rather than poor scholars devoted to virtue, he declares that this is an ancient complaint, but that poverty is greatly preferable to wealth.

[Col. 0178D] To his dearest companion and friend Master R., P. of Blois: greeting and a stronger spirit.

You complain of and accuse the wickedness of bishops, who are so exclusively occupied with promoting their relatives that they desire or dream of nothing else, and do not relieve the need of scholars even by a modest visitation. The kindred of pontiffs walks in purple; exalted from the patrimony of the Crucified, it pours itself out in pride and abuse [Note: [Col. 0177] Ps. 30] toward every allurement of secular life. They do not consider what is fitting, provided they obtain what pleases them. Since all things succeed according to their desire, and all things turn adversely for those who are the only soldiers of honour, you complain that divine providence in temporal matters is senseless or asleep.

Friend, this is an ancient complaint; it once shook the mind of King and Prophet David. When he saw the oppression of the just and the more unrestrained wandering of the wicked through every desire of this life, he asked whether there was indeed fruit for the righteous, and whether there was a God judging the wicked on earth [Note: [Col. 0179] Ps. 57]. At first he doubts and wavers; then, resorting to God’s hidden judgments, he at last carefully unravels the knot of his difficult question.

“My feet,” he says, “were almost moved; my steps had almost slipped, because I was jealous of the wicked when I saw the peace of sinners. They are not in the labour of men, nor will they be scourged with men. [Col. 0179B] Therefore pride has seized them. For behold, these sinners, abounding in this world, have obtained riches. And I said: Have I therefore purified my heart in vain and washed my hands among the innocent? And I was scourged all the day, and my chastisement came in the mornings. I thought to understand this; it was labour before me, until I entered into the sanctuary of God and understood their latter end. Yet because of deceit you set them up; you cast them down when they were lifted up. For they were brought to desolation; suddenly they failed and perished because of their iniquity” [Note: [Col. 0179] Ps. 72].

We could pursue each point in a fuller discussion, but the text explains itself through public exposition. It shows how treacherous and deceitful riches deceive their lovers: they [Col. 0179C] deceitfully raise them up in order to cast them down with pain. These are those who extend their boundaries to infinity, whose end is destruction without end.

Blessed Job, moved by the same doubt, enumerates the varied successes of the rich; and, assigning in these the judgment of lofty counsel and the justice of divine dispensation, he frees every scruple of doubt from its snare. “Why,” he says, “do the wicked live, are raised up, and strengthened with riches? Their seed remains before them; the crowd of their kinsfolk and of their nephews is in their sight; their houses are secure and peaceful, and the rod of God is not upon them. Their bull has conceived and has not miscarried; their cow has calved and has not been deprived of its offspring. Their little ones go forth like flocks, and their children leap in play. They take up the tambourine and lyre, and rejoice at the sound of the instrument” [Note: [Col. 0179] Job 21]. They spend [Col. 0179D] their days in good things, and in a moment descend to hell. Behold how they were brought to desolation, and the counsel of the Most High cast them down as they were lifted up. Riches were given them as a snare, and pleasures as a trap.

It is exceedingly dangerous commerce: transitory pleasure exchanged for eternal death, as the pagan poet testifies:

> Pleasure bought with pain is harmful.  
> [Note: [Col. 0179] Horace, bk. I, Epistle to Lollius.]

Yet it is more than harmful to perpetuate life in death and death in eternal sufferings. You hear [Col. 0180A] David and Job recounting the manifold glory of the rich and the most unhappy end of momentary happiness. Hence the poor person in his misery must be deemed happier than the rich person amid deceptive wealth and seductive glory. For an accumulation of pleasures will pass into an accumulation of miseries; and that person will endure their torments more impatiently who has been accustomed longer and more delicately to this life’s desirable things.

To that rich man in the Gospel, who asked Lazarus for a finger to cool his burning tongue, it was said: “Remember, son, that you received good things in your life, and Lazarus likewise evil things” [Note: [Col. 0179] Luke 16]. Do you not think that he then wished he had endured many hardships, so that the fire of Gehenna might have been somewhat less severe for him? Yet after departure from this life, eternal pain [Col. 0180B] does not pass away along with temporal punishment; for in hell there is no redemption. Since that place bars the way to merit, it does not admit even the benefit of recompense.

Do not, I beg, desire riches that flee from you and, where they abound, “have more aloes than honey” [Note: [Col. 0179] Juvenal, Satire 6], and at last lead to immeasurable death. Let poverty itself be your consolation: it makes one both most free while living and most secure in dying. Few rich men die without desiring at the end of this life that they had been very poor. Thus many direct the eye of providence toward the future, maintaining spiritual poverty amid riches.

David, seated upon the royal throne, says: “Lord, incline your ear and hear me, for I am needy and poor” [Note: [Col. 0179] Ps. 85]. And elsewhere: “I am poor [Col. 0180C] and in labours from my youth” [Note: [Col. 0179] Ps. 87]. Poverty is an elegant and illustrious gift of God, if impatient and ambitious rashness deigns to count it among God’s gifts. Lucan, Seneca’s nephew, understood the grace of this gift, recounting a poor man’s security of spirit amid civil wars:

> O secure resource of life,  
> the poor man’s narrow home; O gifts of the gods not yet  
> understood! Within what walls  
> or temples could it happen that no one trembled  
> when Caesar’s hand struck?

Nebuzaradan, when Jerusalem was overthrown, left all the poor in peace and carried only the rich into captivity [Note: [Col. 0179] Jer. 52]. Christ, when invited, refused to enter the house of the royal official [Col. 0180D] lest he seem to honour riches [Note: [Col. 0179] John 4].

You who now rail against bishops will soon, God granting it, become a bishop yourself; and, if I know you well, you will furnish the scholars of that time with occasion for public criticism. For those also who have already gained the sweet wood, while they were once campaigning as scholars, sharpened their impudent tongues against bishops and wove over a long time the web that you now begin.

But I know most certainly that, once you are snatched up to the episcopal chair, the memory of scholarly life will be snatched from your heart; affection for [Col. 0181A] your nephews will suddenly spring up [Note: [Col. 0181B] Our Peter censures the carnal affection of prelates toward their relatives, through which they put ahead of men who have deserved well and would be most useful to the Church relatives who may be altogether unworthy. On this matter, the Tenth Council of Toledo, ch. 3: “We have learned that certain pontiffs are so forgetful of the command of the prince of the apostles, who says, ‘Feed the flock which is among you,’ etc. (1 Pet. 5), that they often unlawfully appoint as prelates in certain monasteries and parish churches either persons of their own kindred or partners in their favour, etc. Therefore it fittingly pleases all both to rescind such an act in the present case and to forbid its being done hereafter. For whichever pontiff henceforth attempts, in the audacity of wicked presumption, to grant such favours first to relatives by blood or to any persons bound to him by favour, both what has been done shall be declared void and the man who ordained shall suffer the penalty of a year’s excommunication.”

Bernard, *On the Life and Morals of Clerics*, ch. 3, listing the crooked ways by which persons enter the clergy: “That man,” he says, “is worthy of an archdeaconry because he is the son of a prince—or still more because he is the bishop’s cousin: in him, assuredly, lies the whole episcopal progeny.” And in *On the Morals and Office of Bishops*: “When they have earned the first ranks of honour in the Church—and have earned them either by merit of life, or by money, or even by the prerogative of their own flesh and blood, which shall not possess the kingdom of God,” etc.

Peter the Chanter, *The Abbreviated Word*, ch. 43: “Where it is said of those entering the Church through the door, ‘Who were born not of bloods, nor of the will of the flesh, but of God’ (John 1), it may be said of those entering through flesh and blood, in receiving ecclesiastical orders and benefices, that they were born of bloods and of the will of the flesh, not of God.”

Clement IV ordered his clerical nephew, who held three canonries, to relinquish two and retain whichever single one he preferred, judging that Peter’s successor ought not to be one who gave more to kinship than to piety and Christ. Albert of Strasbourg reports [Col. 0181D] that Benedict XII pretended not to know his agnates and blood-relatives, and declared that the Roman pontiff had no relatives. When many pressed him to promote them, he added that Davidic verse, which was his motto: “If my own people have not ruled me, then I shall be undefiled” (Ps. 18). Except for his one nephew, whom he wished to make archbishop of Arles, he acknowledged no relative by blood or agnation.

It is written of Adrian VI that, when a cardinal conferred a priestly benefice with an annual income of seventy gold pieces upon Adrian’s nephew, and another vacant benefice had somewhat richer revenues, he could scarcely be induced to give him the latter. He used to say that he wished to give people to benefices, not benefices to people. Baronius, under the year 1187, no. 20, praises Leo XI because, though ill, he could not be induced by the exhortations of cardinals and royal envoys to enroll in the sacred college of cardinals his exceptionally modest young nephew, whom he had reared with him and loved uniquely. The eminent annalist also observes that Leo expelled his confessor for repeatedly urging this upon him, and forbade him to come near him thereafter, since he recognized that the man advised him to indulge the affection he bore his relatives rather than to care for the salvation of his soul.], and you will anxiously devise marriages for your nieces. Neither in benefices will you attend to merit, nor in marriages to equality [Note: [Col. 0182B] Not so Clement IV. Scarcely after being proclaimed pontiff, he wrote in these words to his nephew Peter Grossus:

> “We wish you to know that you ought to be more humble than usual. What greatly humbles us ought not to exalt our own people, especially since the honour of this world is momentary and passes like morning dew. We do not wish you, or your brother, or any other of our people, to come to us without our special command; for if, disappointed in his hope, anyone should presume to come otherwise, he would have to return in confusion. Nor should you seek a higher rank for your sister in marriage because of us; for you would not have us favourable, nor helpful in any respect. Yet if you betroth her to the son of an ordinary knight, we offer to assist you with three hundred Tours pounds. If you seek loftier things, do not expect a single penny from us.”

Concerning the two daughters whom he had had in lawful marriage, he adds:

> “Know also that we do not wish any man or woman of our blood to press claims under the pretext of our elevation; rather, we wish both Nobilia and Caecilia to have those husbands whom they would have had if we were an ordinary cleric.”

Master Anselm had the same attitude toward his nephews, as Peter the Chanter reports in *The Abbreviated Word*, ch. 47. When Stephen, seneschal of France, wished to advance Anselm’s nephews by making them knights and marrying them to noble [Col. 0182D] girls, Anselm said: “Far be it, lord, that you should do this. Rather, let them remain in the same condition and calling in which the Lord called them, lest they be lifted up in pride. They were born of poor and rustic men; therefore, I beg you, let them remain such. I would rather never have read Holy Scripture than have them, thus promoted, abandon humility.”], and in this madness you will singularly reckon the fullness of your desire to lie in staining the titles of another nobility with the baseness of degenerate little women, and defiling the house of God with infamous persons. Farewell.

## EPISTLE LXI. TO R., ARCHDEACON OF SALISBURY

[Note: [Col. 0182D] On this Reginald, who later became bishop of Bath, see the notes to Epistle 30.]

**Subject.**—He dissuades Archdeacon R. from the vanity of bird-hunting; first, because by reason of his office he has undertaken care not of birds but of sheep; and secondly, because he will soon be raised to the dignity of the episcopate.

To his dearest lord R., archdeacon of Salisbury, P. of Blois: greeting in God our salvation.

[Col. 0181B] Because, as Jerome testifies [Note: [Col. 0181] Epistle 3 to Paulinus], the living voice possesses I know not what hidden efficacy, I first warned you in person, and with earnest [Col. 0182A] entreaty, and afterwards by letter, that you should indulge more sparingly the vanity of courtly birds. I know that, as the Apostle testifies, every creature is subjected to vanity unwillingly [Note: [Col. 0181] Rom. 8.]. Hence the Prophet too cries in complaint: “Sons of men, how long will you be heavy of heart? Why do you love vanity and seek falsehood?” [Note: [Col. 0181] Ps. 4.] Yet you, who have already put on the arms of penitence and embraced a purpose of holiness, ought not to pursue vanities and false madnesses [Note: [Col. 0181] Ps. 39.]. Haircloth and a hawk do not go well together: bodily affliction and the practice of pleasure.

The kings of the nations, and those who rule over them, because they either do not know, or cannot, avail themselves of the consolation of literary learning, sometimes steal for themselves some respite from the burden of their monstrous cares through the diversion of birds; for, in the Prophet’s testimony [Note: [Col. 0181] Baruch 3.], [Col. 0182B] these are they who play with the birds of heaven. According to ancient histories, Ulysses introduced armed birds into Greece for the solace of those whose parents had fallen in the Trojan battle; yet the prudent man would not have his son Telemachus occupied by this vanity. With what audacity, then, will a disciple and professor of Christ presume in his own case what a pagan abhorred in his son? [Note: [Col. 0183] John of Salisbury, *Polycraticus*, bk. I, ch. 4.]

Some say that the Maccabee domesticated hawks for catching birds; but, having wholly cast aside this vanity, he exposed himself to wars and to death in order to uphold the ancestral laws, renew the rites, cleanse the holy places, restore due honour to the Temple and dignity to his nation, and recover its lost liberty. This kind of hawking is certainly most laborious, and the expenses it requires are not repaid by the advantage gained by those who pursue it [Note: [Col. 0183] Ibid.].

When Marcellus, Augustus’s nephew, [Col. 0183B] was diligently occupied in catching birds, Virgil asked him whether he would rather have a bird equipped for the plundering of birds, or a fly for the extermination of flies. When the question was reported to his uncle, he preferred a fly which would drive away every fly from Naples; and the result fulfilled his request. I would rather you possessed Virgil’s fly than these costly birds, which are forbidden in the Law of the Lord as sacrifices to Him [Note: [Col. 0183] Lev. 11.], and which, through a certain corruption of degenerate nature, are such that among them the female sex is stronger than the male [Note: [Col. 0183D] This is known to all who have investigated the nature of birds: among hawks the female is stronger than the males, something not found among other kinds.].

If, therefore, you are Christ’s disciple and professor, cease, I beg you, from running and shouting after pleasurable birds. Run and cry after Him who directs those who run well, [Col. 0183C] who hears those who cry devoutly; without whose grace a religious purpose, however grave and austere its manner of life, will possess no merit. I see some whose minds the delight of birds consumes by wholly occupying them. Do these not bear the image of Tityus, whose liver, the poets [Note: [Col. 0183] Tibullus, bk. I and 13 [uncertain citation]; Virgil, *Aeneid* VI] report, is continually devoured by birds? For those who are tormented by this excessive concern with birds are indeed devoured enough by birds.

Certainly, with the ecclesiastical benefices by which the Lord has greatly enriched you, you have undertaken the care not of birds but of sheep. On the dreadful [Col. 0184A] day you will be counted on the left with the goats and cast outside the Lord’s flock if you do not prefer sheep to birds. Although you have not yet ascended to the seat of episcopal eminence—which, God granting, will happen shortly—you nevertheless owe the pastoral office to the souls for whose peril you have assumed responsibility. The most exacting Judge will demand their care from you, and will exact the talent entrusted to you, even with interest, setting you over many things if you have been faithful over few.

Therefore, casting aside the vanity of birds, turn your zeal toward books, lest the Lord find you ignorant of His law; for “he who is ignorant shall be ignored” [Note: [Col. 0183] Isa. 56.]. “They were shepherds,” says the Lord, “and did not know understanding.” No one can more stubbornly repel from himself the knowledge of God than by the preoccupation [Col. 0184B] of unlawful love or by the pleasure of hawking. Therefore, either you will desist from this rashness, or I fear that the Lord may one day say to you: “Because you have rejected my knowledge, behold, I reject you, that you may not exercise the priesthood for me” [Note: [Col. 0183] Hos. 4.].

The birds of heaven, like the fish of the sea, have been granted to man not for pleasure but for use—if, indeed, these predatory and rapacious birds deserve to be reckoned among the birds of heaven; by their pursuit heaven is shut and hell opened. Since, therefore, according to the common judgment of clergy and people, the day of your visitation is near at hand, prepare yourselves to receive and bear the Lord’s yoke, and turn the rashness of birds and the wickedness of this life into Christ’s warfare and the exercise of honourable conduct.

## LETTER LXII. TO MASTER R. BLOND

[Col. 0184C]

**SUMMARY.**—Geoffrey, bishop-elect of Lincoln, reproves one of his clerks for disobedience because, abandoning him, he has attached himself to a certain abbot; and he warns him not to set himself against the Archbishop of Canterbury under the abbot’s name.

G. [Note: [Col. 0183D] Geoffrey—or, as others have it, Galfrid, which is the same name—the natural son of Henry II, king of England, was first archdeacon of Lincoln and then, after a vacancy of seventeen years, bishop-elect of that same church, namely in 1180. He nevertheless postponed his consecration for seven years, content with the very ample revenues of that church so that he might give himself more freely to vice, as William of Newburgh says, bk. II, ch. 22. At length Pope Alexander III informed him by letter that he must either renounce the election or receive holy orders. He renounced the bishopric, with the consent, of course, of his father Henry, who considered the delicate young man insufficiently fit for the summit—or rather the burden—of so great an honour. He therefore made him his chancellor, an office which he administered, not without praise for fairness and prudence [Col. 0184D], until his father’s death—that is, for eight years. When his father and brother had died, he was raised to the metropolitan see of York by King Richard, who later regretted it.

Perhaps Richard feared that some dissension might arise between him and William, bishop of Ely and chancellor of the kingdom. This did occur. For when Richard, about to depart upon the Jerusalem expedition, had forbidden Geoffrey, then staying in Normandy, to proceed to his see before three years had elapsed, Geoffrey nevertheless, having received consecration from the Archbishop of Tours at the command of the supreme pontiff, wished to cross to England. But he was treacherously seized by the chancellor, then governing the kingdom in the king’s absence, and shamefully cast into prison. He was afterwards released through the intervention of John, King Richard’s brother and his own, and the chancellor was expelled.

Thomas Stubbs, in his *Acts of the Archbishops of York*, praises him as a man of great abstinence and purity; Godwin as [Col. 0185D] of upright character and modest. He was also a most vigorous defender of the Church’s rights. Accordingly, when King John, his brother, attempted to harass the Church with many exactions, he firmly resisted and, secretly leaving England, underwent voluntary exile, having first bound all invaders of ecclesiastical property under a sentence of anathema. After seven years’ exile in lands overseas, he died, namely in the year of Christ 1209, or, as others prefer, 1213, in about the twenty-first year of his archiepiscopate. Newburgh, Ralph, Matthew Paris, and other English writers treat him more fully [Col. 0186D].], by God’s grace bishop-elect of Lincoln and son of the lord king of England, to Master R. BLOND: greetings, and a disposition to think more humbly.

[Col. 0185A] Since you state in your letter that you wish to dispute with me as an equal, you overstep the limits of our agreement; and would that you contended with me merely as an equal, rather than as a superior! For you have made yourself my superior, or my opponent, in this: that, setting aside my summons, you have resolved to remain in England at the command of a certain abbot. Disputation in contradiction and opposition of deeds is indeed stronger than that of words.

Since you ought to come to me and be with me, and will not, you are against me; because, according to the testimony of Truth, “he who is not with me is against me,” and “he who does not gather with me scatters” [Note: [Col. 0185] Matt. 12.]. As for the passages from Tibullus and the monasteries of Egypt which you appended to your letter in condemnation of idleness: that was the act of an idle man. For I was calling you to labour, not to idleness. [Col. 0185B] You would not have been idle if you had worked diligently at my affairs, to which you ought to have devoted yourself of your own accord, without any summons whatsoever.

Yet you are rendered excusable by the fact that you have always had me as a companion, never as a master; and so you know how to write to a companion, not how to write to a master. Had you had a master, you would have become accustomed to the obedience which you reject. Nevertheless, fiercely stubborn in your untamed self-will, after the letter of my summons you now plan and arrange to plead cases at Paris, now to return to Bologna, now to proceed to Lincoln, now to stay at Oxford. Yet in this ordering there is great confusion, where your mind seethes with contrary desires and you are wholly at variance with yourself. If you had accepted the good of obedience, devout fear would have bound to the judgment of a single will [Col. 0185C] those wandering and unbridled desires which compel you to fluctuate in different directions.

But now Lady Ambition, who promises you a new benefice from the bounty of the aforesaid abbot, drives you through disobedience into the crime of divination and idolatry; for, according to the testimony of Holy Scripture, “to resist is the sin of divination, and not to submit is like the crime of idolatry” [Note: [Col. 0185] 1 Sam. 15.]. Would that you behaved more humbly toward me and, by a more ready service, moved me to benefit you through the fuller grace of your merits! For the world lies in wickedness [Note: [Col. 0185] 1 John 5:7]; and, as you know very well, the benefice which you hold from our generosity could readily be revoked on account of ingratitude and disobedience. For ingratitude is a scorching wind, drying up the fountain of liberality, [Col. 0185D] the dew of friendship, and the streams of favour.

I earnestly [Col. 0186A] warn you not, as is said, to oppose yourself in the affairs of the lord of Canterbury on behalf of a beggarly and lying abbot. Since you are enrolled among my own followers, he would seem to be attacked through you. Therefore, if you cannot—or perhaps dare not—take part in his affairs and assist him, nevertheless, as you love me, do not attempt in any respect to harm him. I know that he loves me with sincere affection, and in my difficulties I have proved by experience the utter sincerity of his loyalty. Therefore, desiring to embrace and foster his friendship, I could not patiently endure, or pass over, injuries done to him.

## LETTER LXIII. TO PETER, BISHOP OF ARRAS

[Note: [Col. 0186D]

This Peter was abbot of Cîteaux, then elected bishop by the unanimous votes of all the clergy of Arras on account of his outstanding probity of character and learning, and consecrated at Verona in Italy by William of Blois, cardinal and Archbishop of Reims, in 1184. He attended the marriage of Ingeborg, wife of Philip Augustus, in 1193, and died in 1203.

This letter was written about the year of Christ 1190.]

[A.D. 1190.]

[Col. 0186B] **SUMMARY.**—He thanks the Bishop of Arras for a gift sent to him.

To the reverend father and lord PETER, bishop of Arras, PETER of Blois, archdeacon of Bath: greetings, and that affection of charity which is in Christ.

I offer your generosity such thanks as I can for the cup which you sent me through a brother of your order. In it, excluding all features pertaining to ornament and common use, you have portrayed to the eye an image of sincere charity. I see there two metals fused into one and two pieces of wood fashioned into a single little vessel. The metals by themselves, and the woods separately, each would make one vessel and each, when separated, would suffice for itself; but combined, they represent the condition of [Col. 0186C] true charity. Charity desires to be joined together; and, uniting one’s neighbour to oneself in the embrace of love, it removes every reproach of separateness.

The dye is combined in scarlet [Note: [Col. 0185] Exod. 25.]; and Elisha asked that his master’s spirit be doubled in him [Note: [Col. 0185] 2 Kings 2.]. Thus everything in this vessel is double, so that no one may find in its form anything double-dealing. For charity, whose type it most plainly bears, is so one in God that it admits one’s neighbour together with itself; and just as the Lord is loved through Himself and for Himself, so the servant is regarded as the representative of the Lord’s charity. The Lord speaks through Ezekiel concerning the union of the faithful with God and with one another: “I will make them all one piece of wood, and they shall be one in his hand” [Note: [Col. 0185] Ezek. 37.]. Therefore I venerate this gift as a symbol of charity, and devoutly embrace in the gift the friendship of its giver.

## LETTER LXIV. TO CELESTINE, ROMAN PONTIFF

[A.D. 1193.]

[Col. 0187A]

**SUMMARY.**—The Archbishop of Rouen, together with his suffragans, asks the supreme pontiff to secure the release of Richard, king of England, imprisoned by the Archduke of Austria on his return from the Jerusalem pilgrimage.

[Note: [Col. 0187A] Richard, son of Henry II, king of England, a vigorous man distinguished by military glory, succeeded to the kingdom upon his father’s death in 1189. Since he had taken the cross before his father died, he set the affairs of his kingdom in order and departed for Syria with many other Christian princes. There he performed marvellous deeds of war for God, which may be read in the authors of that period. But when urgent affairs of his kingdom obliged him to return, he suffered shipwreck, was captured by Leopold, duke of Austria, and delivered up to Emperor Henry VI, as Gervase, John Brompton, Henry Knyghton, and Matthew Paris record under the year 1192, as does the author of the *Life of Celestine III*, to whom this letter was written in the name of the bishops of the province of Rouen.

But was he held unjustly? Gervase reports the matter as follows: “When the Christians stormed the city of Acre and different men took different lodgings in the city, the duke’s standard was raised over the noblest palace in the city. Seeing it and envying it, the king, with a strong force of soldiers, cast down the banner and deprived the duke of this highly desirable lodging. Therefore the duke and all the Germans left in indignation; and they laid many ambushes for the king as he returned, and at length, as I have said, he was captured.”

John Brompton tells the matter differently. He says that, while Richard was engaged in rebuilding the walls [Col. 0187C] of Ascalon, he proposed to the duke that he should arrange for a certain portion to be repaired by his own men. The duke replied that his father had never been a mason or carpenter. Angered by this response, the king struck the duke with his foot and forbade his banner thereafter to be raised among his company. “For this reason,” says Brompton, “the said duke, withdrawing from the king and the Christian army toward his own territories, said that, should he ever find a suitable opportunity, he would avenge himself on the king for this affront.”

Knyghton relates it differently again: “Whether by chance or by the king’s will, the banner of the duke of Austria was trampled in mud. The duke himself, moved by this, returned home, intending afterwards to take a most severe revenge upon King Richard.”

Matthew Paris says: “When the marshals sent ahead by Leopold of Austria had taken lodging for him and were preparing necessities, a certain knight of King Richard’s household suddenly arrived—a native [Col. 0187D] of Neustria, boiling over in the foolish boastfulness customary to his nation—and asserted that he had a greater right to that lodging than anyone else, since he had arrived there first and assigned it to himself and his companions. As abuse was multiplied on both sides, the clamour reached the king’s ears. The king, excessively favourable and credulous toward the Northman’s cause, flared up in anger against the duke’s household. Without considering the Lord’s measured procedure in judgment, namely, ‘I will go down and see,’ he precipitately and improperly ordered that the banner fixed in that lodging as a sign be thrown into a privy. When the duke, deprived of his lodging and disgracefully provoked by the chattering Northmen, learned what had happened, he approached the king with his complaint; but he received only derision. Thus, scorned by the king, the duke turned to the King of kings and called upon the Lord God with tears for vengeance, that He who breaks the proud might console one who had suffered so great an injury,” [Col. 0188A] etc.

The author of the *Life of Celestine III* says: “He was captured because he had ordered his banner, hung in the lodging as a sign, to be thrown into a privy.”

That Richard was held unjustly is affirmed, together with our Peter of Blois, by Nicholas Trivet in his *Chronicle*, in these words: “On the feast-day of St Dionysius, King Richard embarked; and about the feast of St Martin, having at last emerged from the long tossing of the stormy sea, he reached land in the empire of Constantinople. But, suspecting the guile of the emperor and his Greeks and unwilling to be seen there, he happened upon pirates and made an agreement with them. Having paid the fare they demanded, he secured from them a swifter conveyance to a more convenient land. Accordingly, leaving the royal fleet behind and changing his dress so as to conceal that he was king, he crossed with only four companions into Slavonia, then passed through Aquileia, and, having entered the territory of Leopold, duke of Austria, was captured in the city of Vienna on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of January. Duke Leopold, hating him because of the death of the marquis, of which he suspected the king, committed him to prison.”

That marquis was Conrad, marquis of Montferrat, who had gone to Syria with Philip Augustus. Because some discord had arisen between him and Richard, Richard was accused of his cruel murder, but falsely. For after Conrad had carried off the wife of the prince of Toron, that prince arranged, through two hired soldiers of a certain chief of the Assassins, for the marquis to be killed, as became known from that chief’s letter to Leopold, which we shall report later. Trivet says of this marquis: “A certain French marquis had married the daughter of Amalric, king of Jerusalem. He therefore wished to deprive King Guy of the kingdom, because the wife through whom Guy had obtained the kingdom had died. Philip of France supported the marquis; Richard of England, Guy. The matter having been submitted to arbitration among the magnates, it was determined that Guy should retain royal dignity for life, while the marquis, who had married the heiress of the kingdom, should possess the counties of Tyre, Sidon, and Baruch; and that, upon Guy’s death, he should be invested with the royal crown,” etc.

He then tells how the marquis was killed: “When Richard, before his departure, summoned through envoys the marquis whom they had elected king of Jerusalem, before he could come to the king, after dining one day with the bishop of Beauvais, he was killed on his return by two Assassins.” Then, declaring that Richard was unjustly accused of this murder, he says: “Yet from this death the prince of the Assassins, by whom, as has appeared above, the marquis was killed, exculpated King Richard in a letter of this kind: ‘To Leopold, duke of Austria, the Old Man of the Mountain sends greetings. Since many kings,’” etc. Since these words occur in precisely the same form in Walsingham, we omit them for brevity’s sake.

Leopold nevertheless kept King Richard for some time under close guard, then handed him over to Emperor Henry VI, who held him in chains for almost two years. Although the supreme pontiff repeatedly threatened him with the thunderbolts of excommunication, he would not permit Richard to depart free until a large sum of money had been paid.]

To the reverend father and lord CELESTINE, by God’s grace [Col. 0188A] supreme pontiff, G., by that same permission humble minister of the Church of Rouen, and his suffragans—the bishops of Bayeux, Évreux, Séez, and Avranches—greetings, and the affection of most devoted service.

It is commonly said that new and unusual kinds of illnesses require new remedies. We indeed believe it wholly foreign to the practice of our times [Col. 0189A] that anyone pursuing the Jerusalem pilgrimage should be captured or in any way compelled to ransom himself, either on his outward journey or his return. We remember that the Roman Church received under its guardianship and protection those who professed that journey and the holy sign. Nor is there any doubt that whatever is attempted against her children contrary to the authority of that Church rebounds upon the head of the whole Church.

Our most Christian prince, the most illustrious lord king of England, and most devoted son of the Roman Church, whom it had especially received into its protection during his pilgrimage, was captured and unjustly detained upon his return, after labours and dangers, after distresses and perils of life, which he had long endured for the love and honour of God. [Col. 0189B] We lament our griefs and distresses. Would that you might share them with us in the fatherly affection of compassion, and show by experience amid our afflictions how great is the filial affection owed to you! The public book of experience teaches that the affection of charity is fuller in parents toward their children than in children toward their parents. Therefore, considering the devotion which the kings of England have hitherto shown toward the Roman Church, we hope in Him who is our hope that, in this our distress, that abundant and inexhaustible fullness of grace will not fail—the grace which gives itself to the afflicted, raises the fallen, and restores the injured; and, to enclose much in little, communicates itself to all: He who is wholly present to all [Col. 0189C] and to each, and who publicly calls himself the servant of the servants [of God].

[Note: [Col. 0189C]

Gregory the Great prefixed some of his letters in this form: “Gregory, servant of the servants of God,” as appears from Letter 1, bk. IX, to Innocent, prefect of Africa; Letter 1, bk. X, to Dominic, bishop of Carthage; Letter 1, bk. XII, to Marinianus of Ravenna; and Letter 31, to Felix, bishop of Sicily. Later pontiffs retained this formula, beginning with Boniface V, who sat in 618. John the Deacon says of this in bk. II, ch. 12, of the *Life of Gregory*: “He was the first of all humbly to determine that, at the beginning of his letters, he should write himself ‘servant of the servants of God’; and he left to all his successors as an inheritance an example of his humility, both in this matter and in the modest pontifical vestments—which are still preserved in the holy Roman Church.”

Very many bishops adopted this same title after Gregory’s example: Desiderius of Cahors, Letters 4, 5, 10, and 12; Eligius of Noyon, Letter 6 among the letters of various pontiffs addressed to Desiderius [Col. 0189D]; Boniface of Mainz, Letters 2, 3, 8, 9, etc.; Daniel, Letter 33 among the letters of Boniface; Torthelm, Letter 43; Guthbert, Letter 70; another unnamed bishop, Letters 87 and 94; Coena, Letter 99; Bergonoinus, Letter 103; Lull, Letters 109 and 111; Hincmar, Letter 45; Diederic of Metz in Gerbert, Letter 31.

Augustine had already used the same form of expression: in Letter 107, “A servant of Christ and through Him a servant of His servants”; in Letter 121, “A servant of Christ and of Christ’s servants”; and at the beginning of the book *On the Good of Widowhood*, “Servant of Christ’s servants.” The same formula was also used by [Col. 0190C] priests, as is clear from Letter 53 to abbots; Letters 83 and 84 to abbesses; and Letter 38 to kings among the letters of Boniface: “Sigebald, king, unworthy servant and lowest servant of the servants of God.” Similar also are these formulas in Augustine: “Servant of Christ and of His Church,” Letter 89; “Servant of the people of God,” in Bishop Daniel, Letters 66 and 67 among the letters of Boniface; and in Hincmar, Letters 15, 17, 23, 25, 29, 32, 38, 39, 40, 50, 52, and 53.

For Richard’s death and his remarkable penitence, see the writers on English affairs.

This letter was written in 1193, shortly after Richard’s capture; for he was captured on 2 December 1192.] What will he do for so great a son, for so great a prince, whose utterly unjust capture provinces lament, peoples grieve, churches weep over, and every law, both modern [Col. 0190A] and ancient, condemns?

Let your hand draw the sword of blessed Peter, most merciful father. Show in deed what, and how much, you owe to so great a son, so that lesser and inferior sons may learn through experience how much help they ought to expect from you in their necessities. Farewell.

## LETTER LXV. TO A COMPANION AND FRIEND

**SUMMARY.**—He teaches his friend that it is not lawful to investigate foreknowledge of the future through auguries, dreams, visions, chance occurrences, or other forbidden means.

To Peter, his dearest companion and friend, his own Peter of Blois: greetings, and whatever is better than health.

When Master G. Pulcher had recently left his lodging, my brother Master William of Blois, a monk, [Col. 0190B] met him as he was going out. He warned him to turn back, urgently forbade him to proceed, and declared that great danger threatened him that day if he presumed to continue his journey. But Master G., perfect in Christ, judging to be empty talk whatever was not founded in the root of faith, set out safely upon his way. He joined the retinue of the lord of Canterbury, of whose household he was reckoned a member.

Having gone a little way, he fell with his horse, through insufficient caution, into an exceedingly deep ditch overflowing with converging waters. Horse and rider were submerged and struggling in the rushing waters, and at last Master William, with many people gathering and helping, barely [Col. 0190C] escaped. You saw this, as did all who at that time were attached to the archbishop’s company. You therefore began scrupulously to inquire, and especially to ask me, whether I gave credence to such things and what I thought concerning omens of this kind [Note: [Col. 0190C] The word *omen*, from which *ominous* is derived, is not ecclesiastical but pagan. Augustine, *Retractations*, bk. I, ch. 1: “I do not recall having read the word *omen* either in our sacred writings or in the discourse of any ecclesiastical disputant, although *abominatio* [‘abomination’] is said to derive from it and is constantly found in the divine writings.”

Concerning such encounters Chrysostom says, *Homily 32 on the Epistle to the Ephesians*: “Ὁ δεῖνά μοι πρῶτος ἐνέτυχεν, φησὶν, ἐξίοντι τῆς οἰκίας, πάντως μυρία δεῖ κακὰ συμπεσεῖν”—that is: “Such-and-such a man met me first as I was leaving my house; surely countless evils must happen.”

And in Homily 21 to the people of Antioch: “Πομπὴ δὲ σατανική ἐστι θέατρα, καὶ ἱπποδρομίαι, καὶ πᾶσα ἁμαρτία, καὶ παρατήρησις ἡμερῶν, καὶ κλήδονες, καὶ σύμβολα· καὶ τί ποτε ἐστι σύμβολα; φησί. Πολλάκι ἐξελθών τις τὴν οἰκίαν τὴν ἑαυτοῦ εἶδεν ἄνθρωπον ἑτερόφθαλμον ἢ χωλεύοντα, καὶ οἰωνίσατο· τοῦτο πομπὴ [Col. 0191B] σατανική· οὐ γὰρ ἡ ἀπάντησις τοῦ ἀνθρώπου πονηρὰν ποιεῖ τὴν ἡμέραν γενέσθαι, ἀλλὰ τὸ ἐν ἁμαρτίαις ζῆν.” That is: “The procession of Satan consists in theatres, racetracks, every sin, the observance of days, prognostications, and omens. And what, after all, are omens? Often a man leaving his own house sees a one-eyed or lame man and takes an omen from it. This is Satan’s procession; for it is not meeting a person that makes the day evil, but living in sins.”

And afterwards: “Εἴπω καὶ ἕτερον καταγελαστότερον. αἰσχύνομαι μὲν καὶ ἐρυθριῶ, ἀναγκάζομαι δὲ ὅμως διὰ τὴν ὑμετέραν σωτηρίαν εἰπεῖν. Ἐὰν ἀπαντήσῃ παρθένος, φησίν, ἄπρακτος [Col. 0191C] ἡ ἡμέρα γίνεται· ἐὰν ἀπαντήσῃ πόρνη, δεξιὰ καὶ χρηστὴ, καὶ πολλῆς ἐμπορίας γέμουσα.” That is: “Shall I mention something even more ridiculous? I am ashamed and blush, but for your salvation I am nevertheless compelled to say it. ‘If,’ he says, ‘a virgin meets one, the day will be unproductive; but if a prostitute meets one, it will be favourable and good, and full of much trade.’”

Augustine, *On Christian Doctrine*, bk. II, ch. 20: “To these are added thousands of utterly empty observances: if some bodily member twitches; if, while friends walk together, a stone, dog, or child passes between them. Of these, the fact that they tread upon the stone as though it severed friendship is less troublesome than that they strike an innocent child with a slap if it runs between people walking together. Yet it is war when children are sometimes avenged by dogs; for certain persons are so superstitious that they dare even strike the dog that passes between them—not with impunity, since from the vain remedy it sometimes quickly sends its striker to the true [Col. 0191D] physician. Such also are these practices: treading upon the threshold while passing in front of one’s own house; returning to bed if one sneezes while putting on one’s shoes; returning home if one stumbles while setting out; and, when a garment is gnawed by mice, fearing the sign of coming evil more than grieving over the present damage. Hence the elegant saying of Cato, who, when consulted by a man claiming that his shoes had been gnawed by mice, replied that this was no portent; it would truly have been a portent if the mice had been gnawed by the shoes.”

Eligius, bishop of Noyon, in his exhortation to his people: “Let no one, going out of or entering a house, observe what meets him, [Col. 0192B] or whether there is any cry of protest, or what kind of bird sings or chatters, or what he sees anyone carrying; for whoever observes these things is shown to be pagan in part.”], concerning dreams, [Col. 0191A] ghosts (*lemures*), [Note: [Col. 0192B]

*Lemures* properly are nocturnal spectres and terrifying appearances of images and beasts, according to Nonius. Horace, bk. II, Epistle 2:

> “He laughs at nocturnal Lemures and Thessalian prodigies.”

Persius, *Satires* 5, calls them “black Lemures.” Augustine, *City of God*, bk. IX, ch. 11, reporting Plotinus’s opinion, says: “He says indeed that the souls of men are demons, and that men become Lares if their merits are good; Lemures or Larvae if bad; while they are called Manes, or gods, when it is uncertain whether their merits are good or bad.” And later: “For he calls Larvae harmful demons made from men.”]

concerning birds in flight, [Note: [Col. 0192C] That is, birds from whose flight, song, or feeding future events are foreshadowed; such signs are called auguries or auspices. In the manuscripts of Fulda, Bec, and Hautmont, the reading is *volatibus*.] and concerning sneezes. [Note: [Col. 0192C] Omens were taken from these, whence sneezes were called fortunate or unfortunate. Ambrose, Sermon 33: “Those who consult augurs, sacrilegious diviners, haruspices, diviners and enchanters, and those who trust in amulets and magical characters, or in sneezes, singing birds, divinations, mathematicians [astrologers], or any other evil arts, shall be damned.” Chrysostom, Homily 12 on Ephesians: “Κἂν ὄνος ἀνακράξῃ, κἂν ἀλεκτρυών, κἂν πτάρῃ τις”—that is: “Even if a donkey brays, or a cock, or someone sneezes,” [Col. 0192D] etc. Augustine, *On Christian Doctrine*, bk. II, ch. 21: “If someone sneezes while putting on his shoes.” Eligius of Noyon, exhortation to the people: “Do not observe sneezes.” John of Salisbury, *Polycraticus*, bk. XIX, ch. 1: “For what difference does it make to the course of events if someone sneezes once or more often?”]

On that occasion I would have answered according to the capacity of my understanding, had I not then, as you yourself recall, been sent to the lord king and been anxiously considering what was necessary for my journey. Yet what I could not then explain orally, I shall now set forth in writing; a more careful exposition in writing will make up for the defect of speech.

Since you read in the sacred word that “this is the victory which conquers the world, our faith” [Note: [Col. 0191] 1 John 5.], the enemy of humankind, in order to overthrow our faith, directs his malice toward manifold deceits. For his deceits are many, as the Apostle testifies: “We are not ignorant,” he says, “of Satan’s devices” [Note: [Col. 0191] 2 Cor. 2.]. Therefore, introducing fantastic [Col. 0191B] illusions into human minds, he now promises knowledge of the future through birds’ flight, now through meetings with people, now with beasts, dreams, and other means; and so he announces events as fortunate or unfortunate that he may disturb the quiet of hearts by vain curiosity and gradually encrust something upon the purity of faith.

[Col. 0192A] At the devil’s suggestion certain women form waxen or clay images [Note: [Col. 0192D] Practitioners of this frivolous or harmful superstition are called *vultivoli*. John of Salisbury, *Polycraticus*, bk. I, ch. 12: “*Vultivoli* are those who, in a soft material—perhaps wax or clay—fashion images of persons whom they try to corrupt, in order to change their affections.”], in order thus to torment and inflame enemies or lovers, in accordance with Virgil’s line:

> “As this clay hardens, and as this wax melts,” [Note: [Col. 0191] Virgil, *Eclogues* 8.]

etc.

Some possess bewitching eyes, according to Virgil’s line:

> “I do not know what eye bewitches my tender lambs.” [Note: [Col. 0191] Id., *Eclogues* 3.]

Some infer future events from the flight of birds, whence this passage:

> “Had not a crow, from the hollow ilex,
>
> Warned me on the left against whatever new quarrels might arise,
>
> Neither your Moeris here nor Menalcas himself would still be alive.” [Note: [Col. 0191] Id., *Eclogues* 9.]

It is also read [Note: [Col. 0191] Justin, Book XXIII] that, on the shield of Hiero as he was setting out [Col. 0192B] for war, an eagle alighted, signifying that he would become victor and king. Some consult natal astrologers, some mathematicians, some soothsayers, some Pythonic diviners. And because the outcome sometimes corresponds to their divination, the rash place faith in them. For the father of lies frequently presents a shadowy semblance of truth [Col. 0193A] [Note: [Col. 0193D] This is what Augustine, in the passage cited, chapter 23, expressed in these words: “For this reason it happens that, by a certain hidden judgment of God, people desirous of evil things are handed over, in accordance with the deserts of their evil wills, to be mocked and deceived by transgressing angels who mock and deceive them, and to whom this lowest part of the world is subjected by the law of divine providence according to the most beautiful order of things. By these mockeries and deceptions it comes about that many past and future things are foretold through these superstitious and pernicious kinds of divination, and happen exactly as foretold; and many things happen to those who observe such practices in accordance with their observances, so that, entangled thereby, they become more inquisitive and insert themselves ever more deeply into the many snares of most pernicious error.”], until he hurls the children of unbelief with himself into Gehenna. Thus Saul, while consulting the Pythoness, deserved to be slain with his sons on the mountains of Gilboa [Note: [Col. 0193] 1 Kings 28.]. Thus Ahaziah, who had fallen through the lattice, while inquiring how long he would live, had the thread of his life cut short as though it were to be woven [Note: [Col. 0193] 2 Kings 1.]. Alexander was deceived by Apollo’s oracle [Note: [Col. 0193] Justin, Book XI; Cicero, Book II, *On Divination*.]. Croesus, having crossed the Halys in reliance on an equivocation concerning destruction, was struck by the worse outcome. Let the Christian’s settled conviction, then, be to inquire nothing concerning future things, but humbly to obey the disposition of Him who orders all things sweetly, whose counsellor no one has been. For we cannot say to Him, “Why do you act thus?” [Note: [Col. 0193] Romans 11.] He is Lord: let Him do what is good in His own eyes. Let us not labour to know the times or moments [Col. 0193B] which the Father has placed in His own power [Note: [Col. 0193] Acts 1.]. For to seek knowledge of future things by auguries or other unlawful means is a diabolical temptation and an occasion of eternal condemnation.

For the mouth of the Lord has spoken, instructing the people of Israel: “When you have entered,” He says, “the land which the Lord your God will give you, beware lest you imitate the abominations of the nations. Let there not be found among you one who purifies his son or daughter by leading them through fire; let there not be one who consults soothsayers and observes dreams and auguries; let there not be a sorcerer or enchanter; let no one seek truth from the dead through Pythons or diviners: the Lord abominates all these things” [Note: [Col. 0193] Deuteronomy 18.]. “If,” He says, “a prophet arises in your midst, or one who says that he has seen a dream, and foretells [Col. 0193C] a sign and wonder, and what he has spoken comes to pass, do not listen to the words of the dreamer or prophet” [Note: [Col. 0193] Deuteronomy 13.].

And it frequently happens, dearest friend, that prodigies of events attain their predicted outcomes; nevertheless, no faith should be put in them. Although they often announce true things, they lie more often and more dangerously. Nor should it trouble you that persons worthy of esteem are sometimes read to have accepted such things by divine dispensation. For Saint Daniel caused King Nebuchadnezzar, troubled by a vision of an image, to redeem his sins by alms and for a time to avert the sentence of divine punishment [Note: [Col. 0193] Daniel 4.]. The interpretation of dreams made Joseph great in Egypt [Note: [Col. 0193] Genesis 41.]. The elegance of visions made Ezekiel and John the Evangelist admirable in sacred speech [Col. 0194A]. Yet to place one’s hope in visions is superstitious and contrary to salvation; nevertheless, most persons accustomed to such things cannot be torn away from them.

Thus, some people who are about to set out on business turn back if you ask them where they are going—perhaps recalling the saying of Judith, who, when she departed from the city of Bethulia, which Holofernes had besieged, hoping for deliverance of her country and victory over the tyrant through the hand of the Lord, forbade anyone to ask her where she was going [Note: [Col. 0193] Judith 8.]. They infer, therefore, that the question possessed some omen capable of hindering the success of their journey. Blessed Mark the Evangelist also, as he was travelling by ship to Alexandria for the purpose of preaching the Gospel, broke his shoe as he left the vessel and, giving thanks to God, declared [Col. 0194B] that his journey would be successful. Whatever others may believe, I firmly believe that the holy Evangelist did not say this from superstitious curiosity: even if his shoe had never broken, the Lord would nevertheless have revealed to him by the Holy Spirit the unimpeded course and success of his journey.

Certainly, prognostications of this deceptive kind generally shape themselves into varied, or perhaps opposite, outcomes. Thus Julius Caesar, whom no superstition or augury could ever deter from his undertakings, as he set out for Africa slipped when leaving the ship; but, changing the omen into a better sense, he said: “Africa, I hold you,” and he did indeed possess it [Note: [Col. 0193] Suetonius, *Caesar*.]. King William too, conqueror of England, on his first [Col. 0194C] arrival in the land spurred the horse he had mounted to a gallop, fell with the horse, and was thrown to the ground [Note: [Col. 0193] Polydore, Book VIII, *English History*]: “The land,” he said, “is mine”; and the outcome fulfilled it [Note: [Col. 0194D] Matthew Paris thus relates this story under the year 1066: “Duke William, while disembarking, slipped with his foot. A knight standing nearby interpreted the fall favourably, saying: ‘O duke, you hold England; you will be king.’” Knyghton, Book II, *On the Events of England*, chapter 1, gives a fuller account: “After the feast of St Michael in the year of grace 1066, when William leapt from the small vessel in haste to land, he stumbled on one foot and fell into the sand, so that his mouth was filled with sand. ‘God,’ said William, ‘is my helper; the land is mine.’ At once a knight likewise cried out to him: ‘My lord count, you now hold the land of England; shortly you will be king.’”].

Concerning visions and dreams the prophet testifies and says: “Your old men shall dream dreams, and your young men shall see visions” [Note: [Col. 0193] Joel 2.]. If I were to recount the visions and dreams of the ancients, I would burden this letter with examples. Joseph, the husband of the blessed Virgin, was repeatedly instructed by an angel in dreams [Note: [Col. 0193] Matthew 1.]. The Magi are forbidden to return to Herod [Note: [Col. 0193] Matthew 2.]. Peter is taught, in the sheet filled with creeping things, that the fullness of the nations is to be gathered in [Note: [Col. 0193] Acts 10.]. Constantine was visited by the apostles, and the majesty of the world publicly professed that the kingdom and empire belong to Christ [Note: [Col. 0193] In the Acts of St Silvester.]. The vision of Africanus [Note: [Col. 0193] Cicero, *The Dream of Scipio*], the Apocalypse of the apostle [Col. 0195A], the oracles of Daniel and Ezekiel, and the dreams of Pharaoh and Joseph frequently occur to readers [Note: [Col. 0195] Genesis 41.]. By these and other means the Lord reveals His will to His own, as He wills.

Nevertheless, no dreams will induce me to place faith in dreams. I do not deny that the soul frequently prefigures certain images of future things from residues of thought or from an inborn faculty of discernment; but it is often deceived. For, as I have learned by experience, from a vision that had at times foretold joy to me, I afterwards received the opposite result. Therefore, dearest friend, do not heed dreams, nor entangle yourself in the error of those who fear meeting a hare; who detest meeting a woman with loosened hair, a man deprived of his eyes, a man maimed in the foot, or a hooded man [Col. 0195B]; who boast of a pleasant lodging if they meet a wolf or a dove; if the bird of Saint Martin flies from their left to their right; if, as they set out, they hear distant thunder; or if they meet a hunchbacked or leprous person [Note: [Col. 0195] John of Salisbury, *Policraticus*, Books I and II.]. My own opinion, however, is that Master G. incurred the danger of that drowning even if no monk had met him.

## LETTER LXVI. TO WALTER [Note: [Col. 0195C]

This Walter was an Englishman by nationality, according to Pitseus, a man of distinguished learning and especially conversant with humane letters. But where the same Pitseus obtained his assertion that Walter was sent beforehand to Sicily by Henry II, king of the English, to instruct King William, still a youth, in better disciplines, since he had intended to give him his daughter Joanna in marriage—I do not know; for this is read in none of the writers of that time, and indeed it conflicts with Fazellus, a Sicilian writer, who makes Walter tutor to the royal children even while William the Elder, father of this William, was alive. [Col. 0195D] Add that Falcandus writes that the mother-queen of William the Younger asked her uncle Rotrou, archbishop of Rouen, to send her one of his kinsmen, and that Stephen, son of the count of Perche, arrived; with him thirty-six others travelled from France to Sicily, says Baronius. Among them was Peter of Blois, who would become tutor to the younger king, whom Walter had until then instructed in humane letters, as Blois himself testifies in the present letter in these words: “You know that the lord king of Sicily was my pupil for a year, and that he had received from you the first elements of poetic and literary art.”

Walter was first, while William the Elder lived, archdeacon of Cefalù; then dean of Agrigento; afterwards, under William the Younger, archbishop of Palermo, after Stephen of Perche. Stephen, when a conspiracy against him arose, [Col. 0196C] had been compelled to flee secretly and surrender both ecclesiastical and secular dignities. “After a few days,” says Falcandus, “Walter of Agrigento, having enlisted a crowd of the people and compelled the canons by fear, with the court consenting, assumed governance of the Church of Palermo—not so much elected as violently imposed.” Although the queen and others who were still labouring to restore Stephen hoped that such an election would not be confirmed by the supreme pontiff, since Stephen appeared not so much to have relinquished his dignity as to have been despoiled of it by force and threats, nevertheless, [Col. 0196D] when King William urged the matter with Alexander III, whose favour he had earned by very many benefits, the pope issued a diploma for Walter. Indeed, in order to comply with the king’s wish that Walter should not be obliged to go to Rome for consecration, he granted this also in the diploma. Walter was likewise chancellor of the kingdom of Sicily; and, being one of the leading ministers, he was employed in every major affair of the state.

Moreover, he governed the Church of Palermo for twenty-five years with the highest praise, and bestowed many benefits upon it, as may be seen in Rocco Pirro, first *Notice of the Church of Palermo*.

He wrote certain minor works which have not come down to our memory, or which perished while their author lived among foreigners, so that not even their titles can be found, except for one book on the rudiments of the Latin language, says Pitseus.]

## TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF PALERMO. (A.D. 1077.)

### SUMMARY.—He congratulates the Archbishop of Palermo upon having been raised from a humble station to so great a dignity. He briefly describes the figure and character of King Henry II of England, and demonstrates that he was by no means the author of the killing of Saint Thomas, Archbishop and Martyr of Canterbury [Col. 0195C].

To WALTER, formerly companion, now lord, and dearest friend in Christ, by God’s grace Archbishop of Palermo: P. of Blois sends greeting and continual successes according to your wishes.

Blessed is the Lord God of Israel, who has visited you and shown you His mercy, raising you, needy man, from the dust, that you may sit with princes and hold the throne of glory. The Lord is terrible in His judgments; in His mercies He is great and exceedingly praiseworthy, for His mercies are over all His works [Note: [Col. 0195] Psalm 144]. Therefore keep an unceasing and steadfast remembrance of the mercies He has magnified in you; nor let that Jewish reproach be marked in you: “They were not,” he says, “mindful of His benefits and the wonders which He showed them” [Note: [Col. 0195] Psalm 77]. Nothing provokes the indignation of the Most High so greatly as ingratitude: it is the provocation of evils, the emptying of benefits, [Col. 0196B] the destruction of merits.

Out of reverence for Him who raised you from contemptible poverty, show a fuller office of humanity toward the poor from this side of the Alps. You can afflict in many ways those who go to or return from the land in which the Lord’s feet stood; and you can also, as your predecessors did, relieve their necessities with the consolation of more humane favour. Know this: He who exalts the humble and humbles the mighty is Himself the father of orphans and the poor. For the sake of His poor who travel as pilgrims, He calls upon you, so that they may find with you the aid of your customary kindness. You should therefore fear lest their cry and complaint ascend to the ears of Him who is terrible among the kings of the earth, who judges the cause of the poor [Col. 0196C] and pleads for the meek of the earth.

For the golden belt, the silk girdle, the samite, and the other gifts which I received from your generosity through the bearer of this letter, I render you thanks—not as great as I wish, but as great as I am able. [Col. 0197A] For this proves the ancient constancy of your liberality, which neither intervals of time nor distances of place, nor the assumption of honour, nor the other destroyers of friendship have been able to overthrow.

As for what you most earnestly requested of me—that I should send you a definite description of the person and character of the lord king of England [Note: [Col. 0197D] A description of Henry II, king of England, similar to this one is found in the contemporary author Gerald of Wales, Book I of *The Conquest of Ireland*, chapter 45, and in William of Jumièges.]—it exceeds my powers; for even the vein of Mantuan genius would seem quite insufficient for the task. Yet what I know, I communicate to you without envy or detraction. David is said [Note: [Col. 0197] 1 Samuel 16.] to have been ruddy, in praise of his beauty. Know, then, that the lord king has hitherto been reddish in complexion, save that venerable old age and advancing grey hair have somewhat altered this colour.

[Col. 0197B] His stature is moderate, so that he appears neither tall among short men nor very small among taller men. His head is spherical, as though a seat of great wisdom and a special sanctuary of profound counsel. Its size is such that it corresponds in proportional balance to his neck and whole body. His eyes are round: when his mind is calm, they are dovelike and guileless; but in anger and disturbance of heart they seem to flash fire and, in their vehemence, to blaze like lightning. His hair does not fear the losses of baldness, though supplemented by the skill of a barber’s cutting. His leonine face expands almost into a square. The prominence of his nose is inclined, in natural proportion, to the beauty of his whole body. His arched feet, horseman’s shins, broad chest, and wrestler’s arms proclaim a man strong, [Col. 0197C] active, and bold. Yet on one joint of his foot, a part of the nail grows into the flesh and increases greatly, to the disfigurement of the whole foot. His hands, by a certain coarseness, display a man’s neglectfulness: he wholly disregards their grooming, and never uses gloves except when carrying birds.

Every day at Mass, in councils, and in other public business of the kingdom, he stands from morning until evening. Although his shins are terribly wounded and bruised by the frequent blows of kicking horses, he never sits unless he is riding or eating. In a single day, if necessary, he rides four or five day-stages, and thus, forestalling his enemies’ plots, frequently deceives their designs by unlooked-for speed. [Col. 0198A] He uses uncreased boots, unpretentious caps, and practical clothes. He is an ardent lover of woodland; when he ceases from war, he exercises himself with birds and dogs. Indeed, his flesh would have burdened him excessively with the mass of fat, had he not subdued the insolence of his stomach by fasts and exercise. In mounting a horse and riding out, retaining the agility of youth, he tires even the strongest by travelling almost every day. For, unlike other kings, he does not lie about in his palace, but runs through the provinces, investigating everyone’s actions, and especially judging those whom he has appointed judges of others.

No one is shrewder in counsel, more forceful in speech, more confident in dangers, more apprehensive in prosperity, or more steadfast in adversity. One whom he has once loved he scarcely ceases to love; but one whom he has once hated he scarcely admits into the favour of intimacy. Bows, swords, hunting-spears, and arrows are always in his hands, unless he is in council or among books. Whenever he can take breath from cares and anxieties, he occupies himself with private reading or labours to unravel some knotty question among a circle of clerics. For though your king knows letters well, our king is far more learned. I have known the capacities of both in literary learning. You know that the lord king of Sicily was my pupil for one year, and that, having received from you the first elements of poetic and literary art, through my diligence and care he acquired the benefit of fuller learning. But as soon as I left [Col. 0198C] the kingdom, he put aside books and gave himself over to palatial idleness.
