By contrast, with the lord king of England his daily school is the constant company of most learned men and the continual discussion of questions.

No one is more gracious than our king in speech, more polished in eating, or more temperate in drinking; no one is more magnificent in gifts or more generous in alms. Therefore his name is as ointment poured out, and every church of the saints recounts his almsgiving [Note: [Col. 0197D]

Newburgh, Book III, chapter 26, briefly says this of Henry’s kindness and alms: “In his commands he took great care for orphans, widows, and the poor, and in many places he expended notable alms with a lavish hand.”

The greatness of his alms is attested by his innumerable gifts, foundations, and confirmations, with which England, Normandy, Anjou, Maine, Aquitaine, Poitou, and the other provinces then obedient to his rule are full. Some of these have been printed in various books, especially in the *Monasticon Anglicanum*; others, still unpublished, we have printed at the end of this work.].

Our king is peaceable, victorious in wars, glorious in peace. Beyond all desirable things of this world, he is zealous for and secures the peace of his people [Note: [Col. 0198D] Newburgh, in the same place: “At the height of royal power, he was most zealous to guard and cherish the public peace.” A little later: “Horrified by the shedding of blood and the deaths of men, he strove to seek peace by arms when he could not otherwise do so, but more willingly by money when he could.”]. Whatever he thinks, says, [Col. 0199A] or does pertains to the peace of his people; that his people may rest, he unceasingly undertakes anxious and enormous labours. It pertains to the peace of his people that he summons councils, confirms treaties, makes alliances, humbles the proud, threatens wars, and instils fear in princes. The immense sums of money which he gives, receives, gathers, and disperses also pertain to his people’s peace. [Col. 0200A] In walls, defensive works, fortifications, ditches, enclosures for wild beasts and fish, and the construction of palaces, none is more skilful or more magnificent.

[Note: [Col. 0198D] These words occur somewhat differently in our manuscripts. In Ful., Bec., and Laon. the reading is the same; but these words are added afterwards: “It pertains to the peace of the people that he summons councils, confirms [Col. 0199A] treaties, makes alliances, humbles the proud, threatens wars, and instils fear in princes.” But in Dom. the reading is: “Whatever he thinks, says, or does pertains to the peace of his people. That his people may rest, he unceasingly undertakes anxious and enormous labours.” Nicholas Trivet likewise has this in his manuscript chronicle [Col. 0199B] under the year 1154, where he reproduces this letter of Blois.]

His most powerful and noble father, the count [Note: [Col. 0199B]

That is, Geoffrey, surnamed Plantagenet, Count of Anjou, descended from the most illustrious and powerful stock of the counts, or consuls, of Anjou. John, monk of Marmoutier, wrote their history for the benefit of his king. Since it has not yet appeared in print, we shall insert here, from the manuscript codex of the most illustrious and celebrated Lord de Marolles, abbot of Villeloin, certain matters relevant to our subject:

“To Lord Henry, king of the English, duke of the Normans, count of the Angevins, Touraine, and Maine, prince of Aquitaine, duke of Gascony, Auvergne, and also of Berry: John, brother of Marmoutier, the humblest of monks and least of clerics, wishes peace with every joy, life, health, and soundness from Him who gives health to kings.

[Col. 0199C] “From many writings of learned men I have taken the history, or deeds, of the Angevin counts, your ancestors, and wished to compile it into one body [ [Col. 0199D] This is Thomas Pacius.]. Although someone before me wrote a short chronicle and prefaced its prologue with words of this kind, ‘Concerning the counts of Anjou,’” etc.

Thereafter he set out a brief history of those counts. Since it does not concern our subject and we aim at brevity, we omit it here; having only listed the names of the earlier counts, we shall set forth what he wrote concerning Geoffrey, Henry’s father.

The counts of Anjou begin in the year 853: Torquatus, or Tortulus; Tertullus, prefect of the district of Gastinais, appointed by Charles the Bald; Ingelger, made Count of Anjou by the king; Fulk the Red; Fulk the Pious; Geoffrey Grey-Tunic; Maurice; Geoffrey Martel; Geoffrey the Bearded; Fulk Rechin; [Col. 0199D] Geoffrey Martel the Second; Fulk Nerra.

“Geoffrey Plantagenet was admirable for piety, distinguished for justice, devoted to military arts, excellently learned, most eloquent among clerics and laymen, prudent in counsel, tall in stature, handsome in face, endowed with almost every good quality; and although he suffered many tribulations from his own people, he was nevertheless loved by all. Once, when heat pressed upon him, he bathed in a certain river and was seized by a sharp fever at Château-du-Loir; there he died, not without the grief of his people. What wonder? If death came upon the young Geoffrey while nature resisted and fought against it, when, as Cicero testifies, young men are often seen to die as the force of flame is smothered by a mass of water; and just as unripe apples are violently torn from trees, while ripe and cooked ones fall of themselves, so force takes life from young men, [Col. 0200A] maturity from old men. By his wife Matilda he begot three sons: you, my lord king; Geoffrey; and William—handsome boys, not degenerating from the worthiness of their forefathers.

“Henry, you are fourteenth among your ancestors, namely the counts of Anjou, [Col. 0200B] whose possessions you hold after your brothers’ deaths and will, with God’s help, happily leave to your sons. Those who love you can say with me: ‘May you have health and soundness from Him who gives health to kings.’ You alone keep your father’s counsellors permanently in intimacy and companionship. For you are constant in adversity, faithful in uncertainty, and modest in prosperity; simple in dress, unassuming in speech, pre-eminent in counsel. You earnestly fulfil proven friendships, preserve them steadfastly, and practise them honourably. You are slow to believe, and quick to reject, the words of flatterers. You are comparable to stern fathers, who consider not so much the lives of their young sons as their advantage. You prefer to benefit your people rather than please them. In integrity of life you are altogether like Cato; by giving little except what is good, you have attained glory. You are the ruin of evildoers. Your steadfastness is greatly praised. You know how to spare the subject and subdue the rebel. In you are devotion to moderation, dignity, and the greatest severity. You do not contend with the wealthy by wealth [Col. 0200C] nor with the factious by faction, but with the energetic by virtue, with the modest by modesty, with the innocent by abstinence. You prefer to be good rather than merely seem good. Farewell, my lord king; and may you, with your sons growing up, flourish in prosperity according to your wishes.

> I pray you, live—but live for God; for to live for the world  
> is death, while to live for God is true life.”

Moreover, Geoffrey Plantagenet was proclaimed Count of Anjou while his father was still alive. For when his father Fulk had been summoned by Baldwin, king of Jerusalem, to marry Baldwin’s daughter with the prospect of the kingdom, he gave the county to his son before setting out. Then he went to Jerusalem and married Baldwin’s daughter; after Baldwin’s death he was elevated to be king of Jerusalem. This is Matthew Paris, under the year 1129. He adds that Henry I, king of the English, at the same time joined his daughter Matilda, widow of Emperor Henry V, in marriage to Geoffrey, count of [Col. 0200D] Anjou.

But after the death of Henry I, who died without male offspring, Stephen of Blois, Henry’s nephew through his sister, seized his inheritance. Geoffrey therefore declared war on Stephen in order to recover for his wife the inheritance due to her; after capturing Normandy and already being called duke of the Normans, he was hastening to cross into England with forces. Yet death overtook him, and he left this prize to his son. He died in the year of Christ 1151 and was buried at Le Mans, having two years earlier restored the duchy of Normandy to his son Henry. John of Hexham, continuator of Symeon of Durham, writes thus of him under the year 1125: “Geoffrey, count of Anjou, a prince powerful and exceedingly prudent in ordering his state, died, leaving his son Henry, duke of Normandy, heir to his valour and honour.” You may read the same in Gervase’s *Chronicle* under the year 1151.]

greatly extended his dominions; but this son, [Col. 0201A] adding to his father’s resources by the strength of his own hand the duchy of Normandy [Note: [Col. 0201B] From what has been said above it is apparent that Henry did not wholly subdue Normandy by his own arms, since all Normandy had already been occupied by his father Geoffrey, as we said above, and Geoffrey himself was called duke of Normandy. Unless we say that Henry, though still young, accompanied his father in this war. How vigorously Henry defended and enlarged the duchy of Normandy is recorded in the Norman Chronicles under the years 1151, 1153, 1157, 1159, and 1166; in Ralph de Diceto under 1151 and 1175; and in Matthew Paris under 1151.], the duchy of Aquitaine [Note: [Col. 0201B] Because Henry married Eleanor, or Alienor, daughter of William, duke of Aquitaine, he possessed Aquitaine and Poitou through his wife. See the Norman Chronicles under 1153; Ralph under 1159; Brompton under 1160; Matthew Paris [Col. 0201C] under 1159.], the duchy of Brittany [Note: [Col. 0201C] Certainly Henry was never duke of Brittany, but his son Geoffrey was, according to Newburgh, Book II, *English Affairs*, chapter 5: “Henry acquired Brittany not by arms, but by joining the daughter and heiress of Conan, duke of Brittany, to his son Geoffrey.” See the Norman Chronicles under 1157, 1163, 1165, 1166, and 1167, and Brompton under 1163.], the kingdom of England [Note: [Col. 0201C] Stephen of Blois, nephew through his sister of Henry I, king of the English, seized Henry’s kingdom as though due to him by hereditary right because Henry left no male offspring, while Matilda, Henry’s daughter and legitimate heir, could not resist him, and her son Henry was still under age. But when Henry had grown up and had entered England with an armed force, capturing certain cities and castles by force, Stephen made peace with him through mediating friends, although unwilling and greatly resisting it: “For,” says Gervase, “he grieved that such great preparations for war must vanish entirely, and could not quickly moderate the fervour of a youthful heart raging for war.” The condition of peace was that Stephen should possess the kingdom while he lived, but that after his death it should revert to Henry, the legitimate heir. This took place accordingly: when Stephen died about two years later, Henry obtained possession of the kingdom in the year of Christ 1155. Consult the Norman Chronicles under 1150, 1152, 1153, and 1154; Ralph under 1152, 1153, and 1175; Brompton under 1153; Gervase under 1152, 1153, 1154, and 1155; Knyghton under 1154; Matthew Paris under 1152 and 1154; Roger of Howden under 1152, 1153, 1155, and 1156.], the kingdom of Scotland [Note: [Col. 0202B] Having captured William, king of Scotland, and almost all the great men of the kingdom, as will be said below, Henry could have claimed the kingdom of Scotland by right of war. Yet, through his singular humanity and greatness of spirit, he released William on the sole condition that he render homage for the kingdom of Scotland to Henry and his successors. Thus he was never possessor of the kingdom of Scotland. On this matter see the Norman Chronicles under 1156 and 1162; Ralph under 1157; Brompton under 1155, 1174, 1175, and 1176; Matthew Paris under 1157 and 1173.], the kingdom of Ireland [Note: [Col. 0202B] The writers of this age—Gervase, Brompton, Newburgh, Matthew Paris, Ralph, Knyghton, Howden, and especially the native Gerald, who was present at all these events—relate the means by which Henry acquired Ireland.], and the kingdom of Wales [Note: [Col. 0202C] Henry invaded Wales in the first year of his reign. The Welsh are the remnant of the Britons, who were the first inhabitants of this island, now called England but formerly Britain; they are of the same nation and language as the Britons across the sea. When the British people were expelled by the invading English, those who could escape took refuge in Wales, protected by nature against the inroads of enemies, etc., says Newburgh, Book II, chapter 5. Naturally hostile to the English people and rejecting Henry’s yoke, they resisted for some time; but, after assembling a great army, Henry finally forced them to surrender. These matters are narrated in the Norman Chronicles under 1156 and 1162; in John Brompton under 1158 and 1165; and in Matthew Paris under 1157.], immeasurably enlarged the titles of his paternal magnificence.

No one is gentler to the afflicted, more approachable to the poor, or more unbearable to the proud. In a certain image of divinity, he has always sought to crush the arrogant, raise up the oppressed, and stir up continual persecutions and destructive troubles against the swelling of pride. Although, according to the custom of the realm, he has the foremost and most powerful part in making elections, he has always kept his hands innocent and free from every kind of venality. I touch only lightly upon these and other gifts, [Col. 0201B] both of his mind and body, by which nature remarkably distinguished him above others; [Col. 0202A] I do not describe them. For I confess my inadequacy and believe that Cicero or Virgil would sweat over such a subject. Yet this small portion which, at your request, I have briefly sampled concerning his person and character will be ascribed by many to my rashness. For I shall seem either to have undertaken an unbearable burden or, through envy, to have cut away too much from the magnificence of so great a man. Yet, serving your affection, I do what I can; and what I know I communicate with the readiest will, without envy or detraction, in answer to your request. Among the other illustrious men who write the praises of my lord, I, together with the poor widow, cast my small coin of devotion into the treasury.

But concerning the death of the blessed martyr Thomas, [Col. 0202B] which you ask about [Note: [Col. 0202C]

Peter of Blois, and with him all the writers of that age, as well as the Apostolic See itself—whose office it is to pronounce judgment in matters of this kind—openly and solemnly declared that King Henry was innocent of the impious and criminal murder of St Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury. We shall dispose briefly of a matter that has been described at great length by everyone, and only insofar as the subject requires.

William of Newburgh, who saw all these things either with his own eyes or those of others, or at least received them from trustworthy men, says in Book II, chapter 25, of *The History of English Affairs* that the cardinals Albert and Theodinus were sent from the Apostolic See as legates to investigate the death of St Thomas:

> “When, in the land of the king of England, an eminent assembly of churchmen and nobles had been convened, and that prince himself appeared there humbly and firmly asserted that what had burdened his reputation had occurred neither by his will nor by his command, and that he had never grieved more deeply over anything, they solemnly received his purgation. He certainly did not deny that those murderers had perhaps taken occasion and boldness for so great a frenzy from certain words of his uttered too incautiously, when, on hearing of the suspension of the bishops, he had spoken less soberly. ‘For this reason,’ he said, ‘I do not refuse Christian discipline. Determine what you please: I shall devoutly embrace and carry out your decree.’ Having said this, and having cast aside his clothing, according to the custom of public penitents, he submitted his naked body to ecclesiastical discipline. Delighted by the humility of so great a prince and weeping for joy, while many others also wept and praised God, the cardinals strengthened that prince’s conscience and relieved his damaged reputation, and dismissed the assembly.”

Ralph of Diceto, in the *Images of Histories*, under the year 1172, p. 560:

> “After the king of England had landed in Normandy, he immediately hastened to Lord Albert and Theodinus, cardinals and legates of the Apostolic See, sent by the lord pope into those parts. At length, after long and extensive negotiations, first conducted at Savigny and afterwards at Avranches, in the presence of the legates the lord king swore that the death of the most glorious martyr Thomas had been committed neither by his will nor with his knowledge, nor procured by his contrivance. But because evildoers had taken from words which, heated by anger, he had uttered less cautiously an occasion to kill the holy man, he humbly requested absolution from them; he requested it and obtained it. Thus, solemnly absolved in the face of the Church, according to the will and command of the cardinals he promised,” etc.

Gervase, Brompton, and Matthew Paris in his *English History* under the same year, 1172, relate the matter in almost the same way. Whoever wishes for more may consult the other contemporary writers, among whom he will also read the diploma of the supreme pontiff and the letters of the legates of the Apostolic See concerning King Henry’s absolution.

But although Henry had been judged innocent by the Church and solemnly absolved, since an immense scandal had arisen over the matter throughout the whole Christian world, he resolved to perform public penance for this crime, though it was not wholly his own. That most Christian prince knew that it was written: “After sin has been forgiven, do not be without fear” (Ecclesiasticus 3). Following therefore the example of the most holy King David, who, although he had heard from the mouth of the prophet sent by God that his sin was forgiven, nevertheless watered his bed with tears each night.

Certainly remarkable are the things historians relate concerning Henry’s penance—indeed, even those who appear to have been most hostile to him. I suppress their names; let the reader judge them. The first witness, concerning whom no one can doubt, is the *Process of St Thomas*, or the *Four-Part History*, compiled from four historians who were not merely of that period but companions and intimates of St Thomas. Thus Book IV, chapter 5, reads:

> “When news of so deadly a deed had been published everywhere and at once reached the king of England, he was afflicted with great affliction; and for forty days he sat grieving, and throughout that penitential number of days he mourned far more bitterly than men mourn the dead. He ate the food of mourners; he did not mount a horse; no lawsuit of disputants, no consultation concerning business, no complaint of petitioners came before him; no cause involving the government of so many lands was proposed to him, as he in his grief put all things aside. For he withdrew into solitude, continually groaning and grieving over what had happened, and often repeating again and again: ‘Alas! Alas! that it should have happened thus.’”

And chapter 7, concerning the king’s solemn penance after the sentence of absolution given by the legates, says:

> “Before the king entered the city and that metropolitan church in which the martyr rests, he at once humbled and devotedly emptied himself beyond belief. Such power assumed the form of a poor servant: barefoot, with his entire body stripped except for a certain coarse tunic worn upon his nakedness, he entered the city openly before the eyes of all; and through the streets and muddy lanes of the city he went humbly, like one of the meanest common people. Behold another David: as the first David left the city with bare soles because his dearly beloved son, as it were another Absalom, was pursuing him on account of his sin, so this second David enters it. Thus, with sighs and groans, he who had formerly been feared by so many peoples and nations, himself fearful and trembling, approached the martyr’s tomb. There he spent the entire day of his arrival and the following night fasting and wakeful before the martyr. Unless I am mistaken—for I do not doubt it—he poured forth sorrowing and devout prayers before the martyr whom he had loved so deeply and by whom he had been so deeply loved, affectionately commending himself to the martyr’s prayers and patronage—without doubt through his merits—as the issue of events soon afterwards proved. There also, before the martyr’s tomb, as though before the martyr himself, having summoned that holy and venerable assembly of brethren, he received from each brother one stroke of the disciplinary rod: as it were a second apostolic forty lashes, indeed royal dues, and, as I think, something unheard of until then,” etc.

All the historians of this period—Newburgh, Ralph, Gervase, Brompton, Edward in the *Life of St Thomas* in Surius, the manuscript chronicle of Ralph, monk of Coggeshall in England, preserved at Saint-Victor in Paris, likewise the manuscript chronicle there of John Frasquet, and others everywhere—relate this extraordinary penance of King Henry in the same manner.

I shall add, in praise of that most devout king, what St Ambrose said concerning the penance of the Emperor Theodosius in the discourse which he delivered upon Theodosius’s death:

> “He laid aside every royal insignia which he used. Publicly in church he bewailed his sin, which had stolen upon him through the deceit of others. With groans and tears he prayed for pardon. What private persons are ashamed of, the emperor was not ashamed to do publicly in penance.”

And I too shall say with the same holy teacher, in the *Apology for David*:

> “David sinned, as kings commonly do; he did penance, wept, and groaned, as kings do not commonly do. He confessed his fault, implored forgiveness, and, prostrate upon the ground, mourned his misery. He fasted and prayed, and through public sorrow transmitted the witness of his confession to all future ages. What private persons are ashamed to do, the king was not ashamed to confess.”

What will those who have called Henry a most unjust king reply to this? If the question concerns those laws which St Thomas opposed so vehemently, it is certain that they were not enacted by Henry; they were ancestral customs which he had received, as it were, from his elders and predecessor kings, and which all the bishops, the magnates of the realm, and indeed all England, Thomas alone excepted, had accepted. If the matter concerns piety toward God: all who have read the histories of this time know him as a most devout prince, most observant of the divine majesty, and a most severe enforcer and avenger against blasphemers and ungodly persons. If it concerns zeal and reverence for the Church: who can doubt that he was always a most devoted son of the Church? He was the first, after the king of France, to acknowledge and support Pope Alexander III, and he set himself as a wall against schismatics for the legitimate shepherd of the Church. Alexander himself publicly and repeatedly testified to this, calling Henry now a devout prince, now Catholic, now most Christian.

I pass over the great and timely aid Henry gave to Pope Lucius III against the rebellious Romans, as Baronius reports from Roger under the year 1183. If I were silent about his munificence and profound generosity towards the Church, churchmen, and the poor, the almost innumerable churches, monasteries, and hospitals which he founded, and which still remain and flourish, would speak; so that scarcely any other man can be found who bestowed so many and such great benefits upon the Church. Moreover, he always honoured ecclesiastics and religious so highly that he kept them familiarly with him and arranged for distinguished men, eminent in piety, to be placed over the various churches of his kingdom.

To omit the rest, concerning St Hugh Nicholas Trivet says in the manuscript history held by the distinguished Mr Bigot:

> “The renown of the religious holiness of Hugh, a Carthusian monk, having reached the ears of King Henry II, kindled him vehemently with love for him. With much difficulty, by many prayers, he obtained that Hugh should accept the office of governor in a house of the same order in England, founded by that king in the diocese of Bath and richly endowed with many estates and privileges. When the king frequently visited him, delighting in his words and virtues, and when the see of Lincoln fell vacant, he persuaded the canons of that church to elect Hugh, the prior of his house, as bishop and establish him as their shepherd,” etc.

What shall I say of his singular humanity and kindly affection toward his subjects, when almost all historians speak of it? “He never imposed,” says Newburgh, Book III, chapter 26, “any grievous burden upon the kingdom of England or his overseas territories, until that final tithe for the Jerusalem expedition—a tithe, of course, which was likewise levied in other regions.” But Newburgh in the same place especially bears witness to how kind and merciful he was toward the poor, the sick, and the afflicted:

> “At the very beginning of his reign, with exceptional piety he corrected the ancient inhuman custom concerning shipwrecked persons; ordering that an act of humanity be shown to people delivered from danger at sea, he decreed severe penalties against anyone who might presume to trouble them in any way or seize anything of their goods.”

Even when his own sons, supported and aided by the forces of the king of France and the count of Flanders, attacked him in war and widely devastated everything, “he,” as Ralph says, “judging it worthy of royal majesty to restrain his subjects as much as possible from roaming through the country, popular conflagration, plundering of the poor, wrongs against widows, oppression of orphans, imprisonment of captives, rape of virgins, and likewise bloodshed, always turned both his eyes and mind away from tyranny.” Finally, was he unjust towards St Thomas, whom he cherished and loved so deeply both in life and after death, as we shall show below?

“In the word of the Lord and in the order of a deacon, I tell you that I have by no means in my conscience that he was guilty of this deed; and Lord Theodinus, Bishop of Porto, and Lord Albert, the chancellor, will give you the fullest assurance of this. While serving as legates in our regions for this purpose, they investigated and discovered the man’s innocence; and [they found] that this had been attempted by certain persons under his shadow, and that this whole iniquity had proceeded from the sanctuary.”

[Note: He means Roger, Archbishop of York; Jocelin, Bishop of Salisbury; and Gilbert, Bishop of London, who inflamed Henry against Thomas. Henry had in fact made peace with Thomas and had granted the holy man everything he requested: that he might return to his church; that everything taken from him and his people should be restored; and that he should pronounce the excommunication imposed by the supreme pontiff upon the bishops because of the coronation of Henry’s son. Thomas had, in short, entirely returned to the king’s favour. Henry declared this by letter to his son the king, and Thomas to the supreme pontiff. But when the bishops could not obtain absolution from Thomas, they again stirred up the king against the holy man; hence he uttered harsh words, from which arose the occasion of Thomas’s death. See the *Four-Part Legendary History*, Book III, chapter 8; Ralph and others.]

“After they had received his canonical purgation, they, by command of the supreme pontiff, publicly pronounced him innocent of this crime before God and men; and they turned the mark of infamy upon certain magnates, whose malice in this matter they had plainly exposed.”

[Note: This instrument of the king’s absolution is reported by Roger of Hoveden, in which Henry’s protestation is inserted in these words: “Because those evildoers,” etc.]

“You should also know that the lord king has the glorious martyr as his chief patron in all his troubles.”

[Note: So Ralph under the years 1174, 1175, and 1181; Gervase under 1274 [probably 1174]; Knyghton and Paris under 1174, 1176, and 1179; and Hoveden under 1174.]

“For on the very day on which he first visited the martyr’s tomb, he consigned to prison in chains the king of Scotland, a persecutor and most vigorous assailant of the king. Thereafter, through the martyr’s aid, with a continuing favour of success he triumphed most gloriously over all his enemies.”

[Note: Historians relate remarkable things concerning the effects of Henry II’s penance: namely, on the very day when the king approached St Thomas’s tomb and publicly performed so humble and hitherto unheard-of a penance, at the very hour when, prostrate before the martyr, he heard Mass of the Martyr, he gained, gloriously and against everyone’s expectation, through divine favour and the prayers of the most holy archbishop, a notable victory over his rebellious sons and other enemies—among whom William, king of the Scots, his most bitter enemy, was captured. All writers of this period who relate the whole matter at length under the years 1174 and 1175 should be read. I shall cite only what Ralph of Coggeshall says briefly in his unpublished chronicle:

> “Henry II, king of England, as is read in the chronicles of England, humbly cleared himself by oath of the murder of St Thomas of Canterbury. Yet, lest he might have been in some way an occasion of that killing, and it might harm his soul, he zealously endeavoured, as best he could, to fulfil penitential satisfaction. Coming to the church of Canterbury, he willingly received from each brother of the church a single stroke of discipline; after making satisfaction, he obtained glorious triumph over his sons who were persecuting him and over others.”]

“You should therefore know most certainly that the love with which king and martyr once loved one another mutually was not abolished either by death or by the sword. For love is strong as death” (Song of Songs 8); “and though all things pass away, love never fails” (1 Corinthians 13). “This is the beautiful gate which remained whole and untouched in the destruction of Jerusalem”; and although all things are emptied in death, love does not die in death, for death yields to its strength.

[Note: That Henry loved St Thomas greatly both in life and after death is clear from the fact that he raised him from a rather humble condition to such great dignities, made him his chancellor, enriched him with wealth, entrusted to him greater and more confidential affairs of the kingdom, went into France to be reconciled with him and establish a firm peace, twice performed the groom’s office by holding his stirrup as he mounted his horse, returned him peaceably to his church, graciously restored whatever had been taken from him during exile, and wrote to his son the king concerning the peace made with him. When he heard of Thomas’s wicked murder, he grieved intensely; as a penitent he approached the tomb, adorned it with distinguished ornaments and many gifts, restored property and freedom to Thomas’s parents, and finally appointed the saint’s sister Mary as abbess of Barking monastery.

How great was St Thomas’s love for Henry is evident from the fact that during life he faithfully adhered to him and diligently watched over his safety. After death he obtained for him a glorious triumph over his enemies and was his constant helper in all troubles, as all historians unanimously report and the king himself very often confessed.

Why then, you will ask, did so bitter a dispute break out between them? Why did they contend with one another so vigorously? Because each defended his own rights: Henry those of the kingdom, Thomas those of his Church. Henry wanted ancestral customs—established, that is, by his grandfather Henry and his other predecessors—to be observed; Thomas complained that they were contrary to God and the Church. Yet after their long dispute and the archbishop’s seven-year exile, Henry, for the sake of peace, had been reconciled with the archbishop through the mediation of Pope Alexander III and Louis the Younger, king of the French. Henry wrote to his son the younger king and Thomas to Alexander III about that reconciliation. Copies of their letters are found in Ralph under the years 1170 and 1172; Brompton under 1171 and 1172; Gervase under 1172; and Matthew Paris under 1170, 1171, and 1174.

But behold: a new occasion of discord suddenly arose. Thomas complained that the younger king had been crowned by the archbishop of York contrary to the rights of the Church of Canterbury. Having secretly obtained from the supreme pontiff, without the king’s knowledge, a sentence of excommunication, he publicly declared excommunicated the archbishop of York and the other bishops who had been present at the coronation. The bishops, however, unable to obtain absolution from Thomas, at once fled to the king and, by this new and unexpected news, inflamed his mind—already repeatedly provoked and by nature somewhat more prone to anger—to such a degree that he burst into harsher words which furnished the occasion of Thomas’s death.

Certainly the holy man appears to have been able to act somewhat more mildly and to overlook for a time the injury inflicted upon his Church; or at least to obtain from Henry that the younger king should again be crowned by himself. This was afterwards done by Rotrou, Archbishop of Rouen, who, at the request of Louis, king of the French, again crowned that younger Henry with his wife Margaret, daughter of the same Louis, as Brompton relates. In this matter too he might have imitated St Anselm, his predecessor in that see. Although Henry I, during Anselm’s exile, had been crowned by the bishop of London at the command of King William II, Anselm, after returning from exile, did not protest, but confirmed the coronation for the sake of peace, as Ralph, Gervase, and Knyghton report.

But what reason there was for such severity in a bishop so kind and gentle is for God’s judgment alone. We can neither ought nor dare to form any rash opinion upon it. William of Newburgh, Book II, chapter 25, says:

> “While the king was therefore overseas, the archbishop, with royal permission and favour, was returning to his own church. Unknown to the king, he had secured letters from the lord pope against the archbishop of York and the other bishops who had been present at that most disastrous coronation—letters which would disturb the peace already made and provoke greater wrath. Having sent them ahead into England for the suspension of the bishops, he followed, fervent with zeal for justice—whether fully according to knowledge, God knows. For to our littleness it is not granted to judge rashly the acts of so great a man. Yet I think that the most blessed Pope Gregory, while the king’s reconciliation was still soft and tender, would have acted more mildly and would have judged that matters which could be endured without danger to the Christian faith should be overlooked in view of the time and the settlement of peace, according to the prophetic saying: ‘The prudent man will keep silence in that time’ (Proverbs 11), because it is an evil time. Therefore I judge neither that what was then done by the venerable pontiff should be praised, nor do I presume to blame it; but I say that, if the holy man went even a little too far in such matters through a somewhat excessive impulse of commendable zeal, that very excess was refined by the sacred fire of the Passion which followed.”

Yet I would not for that reason call King Henry free from sin. Although he did not in fact kill St Thomas, he seems to have killed him with the sword of the tongue, since, uttering harsher words against the holy man in the heat of anger, he furnished the occasion for his killing. Thus he sinned; he himself confessed that he had sinned; and in a letter to Pope Alexander III—no. 136 among the letters of Blesensis—he wrote that God had punished him for his sins. Nor was this without cause. Although his sin was forgiven because he groaned and did penance, following David’s example, yet because he had caused the enemies of God to blaspheme, the sword did not depart from his house. His firstborn son Henry, already crowned king, was taken away by an untimely death. Richard, the second son, and heir to the kingdom for no long time, died unhappily. His third son, John, likewise a king, lost Normandy, Aquitaine, Poitou, Anjou, other provinces, and almost the whole kingdom of England. Henry himself, attacked by his wife, sons, and magnates of his kingdom, wasted away in grief and died.

All historians of this period, especially those who wrote of English affairs, agree as to how Henry died. They say this: when Henry saw that he was attacked in war by the king of France and abandoned by his sons Richard and John with the greater part of his army, he initially tried to resist. But, recognizing that many cities had already been captured and that he was unequal to battle, he was compelled to make peace with the Frenchman on inequitable terms. Soon afterwards, overwhelmed by excessive grief, especially at his sons’ treachery, he fell into a fever and died at Chinon. He made a will ordering that his body be buried in the monastery of Fontevraud,

> “which in his lifetime he had especially cherished as renowned for its distinguished religious character and had anticipated with such great benefactions that, in it above all, according to merit and his own wish, his body ought to receive a place of rest while awaiting the future resurrection.”

This is from Newburgh, a contemporary witness (*συνχρόνος*), Book III of *The History of English Affairs*, chapter 25. You may read similar accounts in Roger of Hoveden, Matthew Paris, Ralph, the Westminster chronicler, Walsingham, Giraldus, Brompton, Nangis, and others. It is therefore clear how absurdly some anonymous Flemish chronicle, supported by no witness or authority, reported that, when Henry was pressed more severely by the French army, he fled into an inner chamber, where “the soldiers pursuing him found him, it is said, strangled with a horse’s rein.” I wonder that a recent, though celebrated, writer wished to repeat this fable in a French history and gave it more credence than countless other historians beyond every exception.

The eulogy found in the necrology of the nuns of Fontevraud will place the crown upon the praises of this most devout prince. The most distinguished and learned Monsieur Pavillon, with his great kindness, recently sent it to me; he is shortly to publish a history of that most celebrated monastery, from which the reader may draw many further facts bearing upon the munificence and piety of our Henry, besides those cited above. The eulogy is as follows.

## HENRY II, KING OF ENGLAND

> “On the Nones of July, 1189, Henry, a man of good memory, illustrious king of the English, duke of the Normans and Aquitanians, count of the Angevins, devout father, vigorous defender, and magnificent benefactor of the Church of Fontevraud, happily departed from this world. Therefore the supreme and eternal Creator of all things enriched this our most beloved father beyond other princes and kings of the earth with the gift of uprightness and the noble treasure of learning, so that he was thought a second Alexander in integrity and another Solomon in wisdom. In governing his subjects he was prudent; a foremost defender against injuries, and, according to the divine sentence, he confounded the stubbornness and arrogance of the proud. He cherished the poor and humble, orphans and widows, in the bosom of his mercy. So prudent was this our most devout father in honourable conduct that, harshening no one by hard words, he showed himself lovable to all.
>
> “From the days of his youth, through love of God and the intercession of his maternal aunt Matilda, of blessed memory, the venerable abbess of our house, he undertook most generously to sustain, protect, cherish, and enlarge our church, which had been oppressed by extreme poverty. He was always its sole provider and patron. His benefits are in truth unutterable and unspeakable: they can neither be comprehended by the mind nor explained by the tongue. Nor have we judged it right to be silent that we were accustomed to experience not only the compassion of his mercy toward ourselves, but that he also enriched by the abundance of his benefits and gifts our convents scattered among other nations.
>
> “Meanwhile he took care greatly to enlarge our very confined workshops; moreover, he restored the buildings of St Lazarus and rebuilt the decaying structures of Blessed Mary Magdalene. Nor should this be omitted: how he assisted us in a time of overwhelming famine. Hardly any of us would have remained at Fontevraud, had God, in his customary mercy, not supplied us aid through Henry’s hand. Finally—what cannot be said without sorrow of heart and an overflowing outpouring of tears—just as Christ loved his own, so at the end he especially loved us. That is, to show us the truth of the sincere love which he bore us, he granted and allowed us this: leaving aside his own churches situated throughout the various regions of his land, although they possess greater dignity and authority, his body, as he had arranged, was committed for burial in our church among Christ’s poor virgins and handmaids. Therefore with many sighs we entreat the immeasurable mercy of the supreme God that, through the intercession of the most blessed Virgin Mary, our sweet and singular mediatrix, in whose church his body rests, he may cause the soul of this our most beloved father to rest with all his saints and chosen ones,” etc.

The kingdom of England, which he had gained by strenuous military labours against King Stephen—

[Note: From what has been said above, it is clear that the kingdom of England was acquired not by Henry’s arms—he was very young and a novice in warfare—but by the exertions of his father Geoffrey and his mother Matilda.]

—although he was still young and despised, his sons had disturbed by a grave rebellion, through the counsel and assistance of the neighbouring kings and princes.

[Note: So Ralph under 1174 and 1175; Brompton under 1174; Gervase and Matthew Paris under that and the following year; and Hoveden, in whom the instrument of peace is found. Read also what he writes under 1183. This letter appears to have been written about 1177, after the sons of King Henry had returned to their father’s favour.]

But he, abandoned by his own people and attacked by foreigners, prevailed over all through the help of him by whose power one man puts ten thousand to flight. The Lord delivered his enemies into his hands, “to bind their kings with chains and their nobles with fetters of iron” [Note: Luke 2.] Therefore may he who turns the hearts of sons toward their father raise up and send filial and devoted dispositions in the sons of our king; may he establish their father’s throne for long ages and make peace. For I know that, if they again stir up wars against their parent, the Lord will cut them off. For it has been ordained by God’s judgment and a fatal law that whoever of his kindred has presumed to attack him in war shall not live out half his days. We have already read this concerning many persons in the book of experience and have recognized it by eyewitness faith.

## LETTER LXVII. TO HENRY, KING OF ENGLAND. [c. A.D. 1161.]

### Argument

The Archbishop of Rouen attempts, by many arguments and examples of both secular and sacred kings, to persuade Henry II, king of England, that his son Henry, heir to the kingdom, should be educated in letters.

To his most beloved lord HENRY, illustrious king of the English, duke of Normandy and Aquitaine, and count of Anjou: his own ROTHROU, by divine permission Archbishop of Rouen, greeting in him through whom kings reign.

[Note: We have said much concerning him in the note to Letter 28.]

Although your prudence is sufficient for itself and does not beg the aid of another’s learning, nevertheless we can neither conceal nor ought to conceal what we believe will contribute to your advantage and honour. For experience has taught us how much benefit accrued to your land because you steeped the first years of your youth in the liberal disciplines. While other kings possess an unformed and uncultivated intellect, yours, trained in letters, is provident in administering great affairs, subtle in judgments, cautious in commands, and circumspect in counsel.

Therefore the unanimous wishes of all your bishops concur in this: that your son and heir Henry should apply himself to letters, so that we may have, in him whom we expect as your heir, a successor alike to your kingdom and your wisdom. You know that the sum of all prudence is contained in books. If a commonwealth must be governed; if battles must be joined; if camps must be laid out; if engines must be raised; if embankments must be renewed; if defensive works must be made; finally, if the peace of liberty, the cultivation of justice, reverence for the laws, and friendship with neighbouring peoples must be secured—books perfectly teach all these things.

A king without letters is a ship without a helmsman and a bird without wings. Histories relate how much Julius Caesar benefited from learning letters.

[Note: Plutarch, *Life of Caesar*.]

He was so great in literary study that he could dictate four letters at once. The laws of the Romans show how great he was in knowledge of civil law. The refinement of the leap-year calculation proclaims the power of his mighty intellect, which he constantly exercised in philosophy. Aristotle’s teaching and the continuous exercise of virtue under him made Alexander great, magnified, and exalted him.

[Note: Plutarch, *Life of Alexander*.]

Add that faithfully learning the liberal arts

> Softens manners and does not allow them to be savage.

[Note: These two verses are drawn from Ovid. This letter was written about the year 1161, when Henry, the king’s son, was approximately seven years old.]

Solomon testifies: “Wisdom is better than all precious riches, and nothing desirable can be compared with her.” [Note: [Col. 0211] Wisdom 7.] The same peaceful king confesses that he loved her above health and every form of beauty, and boasts that with her all good things came to him together. How shall a king, to whom all judgment among the people has been entrusted, judge his people according to the law of the Lord if he has not known the law of the Lord? It is written of the king in the law of the Lord as follows: “After the king has sat upon the throne of his kingdom, he shall write out for himself the Deuteronomy of the law in a book.” [Note: [Col. 0211] Deut. 17.] From this it is most plainly clear [Col. 0211D] that knowledge of letters is required in a king, so that his delight may be in the law of the Lord and he may meditate upon it day and night. His meditation and whole exercise were in the law of the Lord, in its righteous ordinances and commandments. “I have meditated on your law,” he says, “and your law is my meditation. I was exercised in your righteous ordinances, and I was exercised in your commandments.” [Note: [Col. 0211] Ps. 118 [119].] [Col. 0212A] And there are very many such passages.

Let other kings come forward with David: Hezekiah, Josiah, and the other most holy kings, who kept the covenant of the Lord and the commandment which he gave them. Of King Josiah we read [Note: [Col. 0211] 2 Kings 22] that, when Deuteronomy had been read in his presence, he humbled himself and wept before the Lord because he had not kept the law of the Lord; and he made a covenant with the Lord that thereafter he would walk in His ways—which indeed he did. Let Constantine, Theodosius, Justinian, Leo, and other most Christian rulers also come forward from the school of the Gospel: men who governed the people according to the law of the Lord, by strength of arms and no less by the soldiery of letters. I do not see how a ruler can remain secure in his kingdom or judge peoples with equity unless he is fortified by the counsel of literary [Col. 0212B] wisdom. For Wisdom says: “A wise judge shall judge his people, and the rule of one who has understanding shall be stable.” [Note: [Col. 0211] Ecclesiasticus 10.] And in the same place: “The king who judges the poor in equity, his throne shall endure for ever.” [Note: [Col. 0211] Prov. 29.]

Because David asks the Lord to be taught wisdom and knowledge, the Lord therefore testifies that He found in him a man after His own heart. [Note: [Col. 0211] 1 Sam. 13.] And after He had subsequently raised him to the royal throne, He promises him an everlasting kingdom through the uninterrupted succession of times. “Of the fruit of your womb,” He says, “I will set one upon your throne.” [Note: [Col. 0211] Ps. 131 [132].] Again: “I will establish his seed for ever and ever, and his throne as the days of heaven. If your sons keep my commandments and these testimonies [Col. 0212C] of mine which I shall teach them, they and their sons also shall sit upon your throne. But if his sons forsake my law,” etc., “I will visit their iniquities with a rod, and their sins with scourges.” [Note: [Col. 0211] Ps. 88 [89].]

From the foregoing I plainly infer that, through the imprudence of sons, the kingdoms of the mighty are transferred to foreigners. For, according to the saying of Wisdom: “A kingdom is transferred from nation to nation because of injustices, wrongs, insults, and various deceits.” [Note: [Col. 0211] Ecclesiasticus 10.] Review the history from the first king in Israel, and see how the life of Saul and Jonathan, and of all their successors, was cut short like a spider’s web in a little while; and how, the more they swelled in pride against the knowledge of God, the more grievously He cast them down when they had been lifted up. There is no counsel against the wisdom of God. In vain does one run [Col. 0212D] to fortifications and formations of armed men. It is the Lord who judges the kings of the earth, who takes away the spirit of princes, [Note: [Col. 0211] Ps. 75 [76].] and there is none who can rescue from His hand. The Lord speaks through the Prophet: “Be instructed, you who judge the earth.” [Note: [Col. 0211] Ps. 2.] This is the voice by whose hearing blessed Job [Note: [Col. 0211] Ch. 36] summons kings with a threat: “If,” he says, “kings hear the voice of the Lord, they shall complete [Col. 0213A] their days in prosperity and their years in glory. But if they do not hear, they shall pass by the sword and be consumed in folly.”

Behold how terrible is the end of kings who do not admit the Lord’s instruction. Behold how the folly, or illiteracy, of kings turns to their destruction; and how the rashness of rulers themselves frequently hurls their subjects into ruin. David’s rash presumption [Note: [Col. 0213] 2 Sam. 24] in numbering the people was the occasion of that great plague which killed seventy thousand of the people. Because of Saul’s sin the people fell on Mount Gilboa. [Note: [Col. 0213] 1 Sam. 31.] Jeroboam’s fault recoiled upon the people. [Note: [Col. 0213] 3 Kings 14.] It is the common opinion of religious men that no son from your loins shall sit upon the throne unless he is first instructed in letters and more diligently taught the law [Col. 0213B] of the Lord. The power of the Lord is no less in transferring a most mighty kingdom than in overthrowing a poor man’s hut.

Who in Greece was more powerful than Alexander? [Note: [Col. 0213] Quintus Curtius, final book.] Yet we read that he was succeeded not by his own son but by the son of a dancing-girl. Adoption, not nature, made the successor of Julius Caesar. [Note: [Col. 0213] Suetonius, *Augustus*.] Read again and review the whole course of the imperial house, and you will find that in a short time their memory perished and they descended to the underworld, because they cast away from themselves the knowledge of God and were themselves cast away; and enemies, or unknown and foreign men, succeeded them. Therefore take pains, most beloved prince, that your son may devote the course of his boyhood to literary studies, so that by the benefit of letters he may unlearn [Col. 0213C] his inborn malice and become accustomed to the examples of praiseworthy deeds. Farewell.

## LETTER LXVIII. TO POPE ALEXANDER III. [A.D. 1180?]

**SUMMARY.**—R., Archbishop of Canterbury, accuses the Abbot of Malmesbury of withdrawing himself from obedience to his bishop. He then at length deplores the great evils which followed from exemptions of abbots, granted by Roman pontiffs on account of the tyranny of certain bishops.

To the most holy Father and lord ALEXANDER, by the grace of God supreme pontiff: R., humble servant of the Church of Canterbury, most devoted obedience of submission.

“Since the eminence of the apostolic see,” etc. See among the various letters to Alexander, after his *Registers*, *Patrologia*, vol. CC. [Col. 0213D]

## LETTER LXIX. TO RADULPH [Note: [Col. 0213D]

This Radulph was descended from the distinguished family of the Counts of Beaumont, being the son of Richard by a natural daughter of Henry I, king of the English. He was raised to the bishopric about the year 1178, and shortly afterwards, namely in 1179, attended the Lateran council presided over by Alexander III.

The year in which this letter was written is uncertain. For Baronius’s assigning it to 1173 [Col. 0214D] does not agree with the chronology of the bishops of Angers, since from what has been stated above it is evident that in that year he was not yet bishop, but only in 1178—or, according to Sigebert, 1179. But because the sons often waged wars against Henry, this letter may be understood to have been written during the war waged between Henry and his sons shortly before the death of Henry the Younger, who died in 1183.]

## BISHOP OF ANGERS. [A.D. 1182?]

[Col. 0214A]

**SUMMARY.**—He deplores the defection of the people of Anjou, who had shamefully abandoned by flight Henry II, king of the English, while he was waging war against his rebellious son Henry; and he exhorts the bishop either to bring them back to loyalty to their ruler or to restrain them with the spiritual sword.

To the reverend Father and lord RADULPH, by the grace of God Bishop of Angers: his own PETER of Blois, Archdeacon of Bath, greetings of soul and health of body.

As my soul was troubled by your illness, so it rejoices still more vehemently at your recovery. Blessed, moreover, be the Lord, who chastened you indeed but did not deliver you to death, mercifully [Col. 0214B] preserving you to give the knowledge of salvation to His people. It is surely time to gird on the sword and take up judgment, “to execute vengeance upon the nations and chastisements upon the peoples.” Your people have sinned outrageously; unless you crush their malice by a punishment worthy and timely, it is to be feared that the Lord will be angry with you and the people, and that another’s transgression will be poured back upon your own head.

Whence comes this wickedness of treacherous faction: that the army of Anjou, like deserters and fugitives, by flight exposed its lord in battle to the hostile formations? Their flight would have been more excusable if provisions had been lacking, arms had failed, a stronger enemy had pressed them, or their ruler had been led captive or fallen in battle. But now, without fear, wound, [Col. 0214C] danger, or enemy, the army fled, seeking the favour of enemies through the abandonment of its own ruler. Indeed, because the kindness of royal majesty had always governed and treated them gently, “their iniquity came forth as from fatness”; abusing the benefit of indulgent mildness, they insolently and stubbornly raised themselves up.

I know that they maliciously desire the rule of the son, so greatly that, to use the poet’s words, [Note: [Col. 0213] Lucan, Book VIII:]

> The common people  
> Break with their prince, and love the custom that is to come to peoples.

And, as their common opinion has it:

> Under a new king, the lot of kingdoms is most gentle.

The soldiers also, who in a secret conspiracy passed over to the son’s party contrary to the oath they had sworn to the father, [Col. 0214D] ought to be punished no less than the people, because:

> Those whom a crime defiles it makes equal.

Because in the son a longer life and a more terrible dominion are anticipated,

> Degenerate spirits tremble and devise worse things.

Nevertheless, just as Moses, inflamed with zeal over the molten calf, burned with anger and, by killing twenty-three thousand men, avenged the fault of many in a few, [Note: [Col. 0215] Exod. 32; Augustine, *Questions on the Old and New Testaments*, ch. 102.] and just as Julius Caesar restrained by the punishment of a few a military mutiny which many had raised against him, [Note: [Col. 0215] Julius Frontinus, Book IV, ch. 5.] so it would be fitting for the lord king neither to dissemble nor neglect this offense, but to cut off with the sword of vengeance the insolence of a few in such a way that, terror being passed on to posterity, the crime may not return as a precedent.

The Lord speaks through the prophet: “If I am Lord, where is my fear? If I am father, where is [Col. 0215B] my love?” [Note: [Col. 0215] Mal. 1.] For the most noble king, who had tempered the rigor of dominion with paternal gentleness, found among a faithless people neither love nor fear. In the *Stratagems* of Julius [Frontinus], Clearchus, commander of the Lacedaemonians, is recorded as saying that a commander ought to be more feared by an army than the enemy. [Note: [Col. 0215] J. Frontinus, *Stratagems*, Book IV, ch. 1.] Let fear, I beg you, make humble those whom the ruler’s gentleness made swollen with pride and rebellious.

Imperial laws have prescribed the ordinary punishment, namely the gallows or the beasts, for one who is a deserter, fugitive, or absent without leave. Appius Claudius, we read, killed with a club every tenth soldier, chosen by lot, of those who had abandoned their military post. [Note: [Col. 0215] J. Frontinus, ibid., ch. 1.] Fabius [Col. 0216A] Rullus, the consul, from two legions which had given ground, struck down with an axe twenty men selected by lot in the sight of all. [Note: [Col. 0215] Ibid.] Q. Fabius Maximus cut off the right hands of deserters. [Note: [Col. 0215] Ibid.] Marcus Cato did the same to comrades caught in theft. Nothing is more detestable in a soldier than the mark of a traitor. Although Joab did all things bravely, he is nevertheless not counted in the catalogue of David’s mighty men, because his treachery against Abner and Amasa blackened his courage. [Note: [Col. 0215] 2 Sam. 3.]

I do not say that, by your advice or exhortation, the lord king should exercise the severity of the material sword against your people; for I know that in this respect he will discharge the office of an exacting judge. But do what belongs to you. Strengthen feeble hands, weak knees, and trembling minds; and either recall faithless spirits to loyalty [Col. 0216B] to their ruler or restrain them with the spiritual sword. For you should know that a new command has issued from the lord pope: that whoever disturbs the peace of the lord king shall, all appeal being set aside, be bound by the bond of excommunication. [Note: [Col. 0215C] That is what Peter of Blois had written in Letter 47 to Henry, king, son of Henry II, in the name of Richard of Canterbury, in these words: “Know that we have received commands from the holy pontiff that we bind all who disturb the peace of your lord, with recourse to appeal removed, by the bond of excommunication.”]

Relying on this authority, the lord of Canterbury recently excommunicated at Caen all opponents of the lord king; he made no exception in favour either of the younger king or of anyone else. [Note: [Col. 0215C] Roger of Howden, under the year 1183: “Meanwhile Richard, Archbishop of Canterbury, Henry of Bayeux, John of Évreux, Radulph of Lisieux, Frogerius of Séez, and Waleran, Bishop of Rochester, together with the abbots of Normandy, clergy, and a great multitude of people, came to Caen; and there, in the monastery of St Stephen, solemnly pronounced in the common hearing of the people a sentence of excommunication against all who should hinder the making of peace and concord between the lord king and his sons, excepting the person of the king’s son alone.” Our Peter declares that the younger king was not excepted from this sentence of excommunication; Roger, on the contrary, maintains that he was excepted. [Col. 0215D] These two statements appear contradictory, unless one reconciles them by saying that Henry the Younger was not expressly excepted by name in the sentence of excommunication—and this is what Peter of Blois meant—yet he was not included in it, and thus in a certain sense was excepted: namely, so that the magnates of England might not be excommunicated without consultation with the king. For, according to Eadmer, William I would not permit any of his bishops publicly, without his command, to accuse, excommunicate, or bind with any penalty of ecclesiastical rigor any of his barons or officials charged with incest, adultery, or another capital crime.

And Radulf de Diceto, under the year 1163, speaking of a certain excommunication pronounced by Blessed Thomas of Canterbury without the king’s knowledge against William, lord of Aineford, says: “The archbishop excommunicated him. Because he had done this without sufficiently informing the king, he incurred the king’s greatest indignation. For the king maintains, in accordance with the dignity of the realm, that no captain, no knight of the realm, no official of the king—in ordinary speech, no one holding in chief from the king a castle, town, or estate—may be excommunicated by anyone without the king’s knowledge, lest, through ignorance if the king has not been informed, he communicate with an excommunicate person by kissing a captain who comes to him, inviting him to a kiss, or receiving him into council.”

Matthew Paris gives the same account; and in the Council of Clarendon held in the following year, chapter 7: “No one who holds in chief from the king, nor any official of his household, shall be excommunicated; nor shall any of their lands be placed under interdict, unless the lord king, if he is in the kingdom, is first approached—or his justiciar, if he is outside the kingdom—so that he may do justice concerning him. Thus whatever belongs to the king’s court shall be determined there; and what pertains to the ecclesiastical court shall be sent to that same court and determined there.” [Col. 0216D] The decrees of this synod are extant in Gervase under the year 1164. They are also extant in Matthew Paris, but corrupted. Indeed, none of the historians wrote that Henry the Younger was struck with anathema, nor did our Peter himself in Letter 2, in which, while consoling Henry II—who was grieving exceedingly over his death—he recalls the errors of his former life and his final repentance.]

But hold this for certain: he never excommunicated anyone who either did not die shortly afterward or whose face was not covered by sudden and shameful confusion. [Note: [Col. 0216D] If Henry the Younger was not excepted from the number of those whom Richard of Canterbury struck with anathema, it follows that he too must be counted among those who died soon after the sentence of excommunication had been pronounced by that pontiff; for he departed this life in the same year, namely 1183, as the historians note: Howden, [Col. 0217D] Diceto, Brompton, Gervase, Matthew Paris, etc.]

Therefore wield the sword of Peter, so that those who ought willingly to have exposed themselves to death and imprisonment for the salvation of their ruler may be compelled against their will to observe [Col. 0217A] the loyalty due. Loyalty alone enlarges a people’s glory, establishes peace, and inspires terror in enemies. Faithful peoples are still recorded in the annals, and their names shall live for ever. Frontinus relates [Note: [Col. 0217] *Stratagems*, Book IV, ch. 5] that, when Hannibal besieged the people of Casilinum, they preserved such loyalty to the Romans that neither hunger nor sword bent them to surrender; and they were so afflicted by famine that a mouse sold for one hundred denarii. The seller of the mouse died of hunger, while the buyer escaped the danger of death. [Note: [Col. 0217] Ibid.]

When the Petelini were besieged by the Carthaginians, they drove out their parents and children because of scarcity; but they themselves, sustaining life on hides soaked and dried by fire and on the leaves [Col. 0217B] of trees, defied the siege for eleven months. Mithridates besieged Cyzicus in insult to the Romans, brought forth captives from the city, and showed them to the besieged, thinking that pity for their own people would compel the townsmen to surrender. [Note: [Col. 0217] Frontinus, Book IV, ch. 5.] But they exhorted the captives to meet death bravely and kept faith with the Romans.

Your people of Anjou, however, whose fame in deeds of war had been more renowned than that of other peoples, “like the sons of Ephraim, bending and shooting the bow, turned back on the day of battle”; [Note: [Col. 0217] Ps. 77 [78].] and, like degenerate and unwarlike men, where they ought to have stood more bravely and faithfully by their ruler, they turned to a most shameful flight. Nevertheless, we hope in Him who is [Col. 0217C] our hope, who turned the sea into dry land, that He will shortly turn the hearts of sons toward the father and sweeten this bitterness of dissension. He likewise who judges the ends of the earth will give victory to our king and exalt the horns of His Christ. Farewell.

## LETTER LXX. TO JOHN, BISHOP OF CHARTRES [Note: [Col. 0218D] This is John of Salisbury; see Letter 22.] [A.D. 1175?]

**SUMMARY.**—He tries to persuade the Bishop of Chartres that he would act more rightly if he promoted his nephews—though poor, yet respectable—rather than outsiders to ecclesiastical benefices.

To his beloved lord, beloved above all others, John, by the grace of God Bishop of Chartres: his own canon PETER of Blois, greetings, and remembrance of mercy in wrath. [Col. 0217D]

We have hoped in you and concerning you for such a grace of maturity and prudence that deceitful flattery will not easily mislead you. For it is proverbially said:

> It is foolish to encrust a sound vessel.  
> [Note: [Col. 0217] Horace, *Satires*, I, satire 3.]

And Solomon testifies: “In vain is a net cast before the eyes of winged creatures.” [Note: [Col. 0217] Prov. 1.] You know that Robert Salebere is your flesh and blood. Yet those whose mouth is full of bitterness and deceit, who [Col. 0218A] call good evil and evil good, estrange from you your friend and kinsman; relying on the poison of their tongue, they strive to tear him from your inmost affections, destroying through seductive flattery the law of nature, the bond of blood, and the benefit of nurture.

I beg you, while your nephew is honorable and fit for ecclesiastical benefices, do not prefer to him an outsider less fit or worse, nor turn away from him the favour of your generosity, in whom these two things concur: nature and merit. Certainly, in every capacity, what proceeds from nature is stronger than what is added from without; and a nephew’s affection, following nature, will always be more sincere toward you than an affection arising from fortune’s inconstancy. You remember Aristotle’s statement [Note: [Col. 0217] Book III, *Topics*, ch. 1] that everything which is such by nature is more such than what is not such by nature.

Why is it that in civil law an agreement nullifies a stipulation, while it is not nullified by a stipulation? Is it not because an agreement is a natural bond, whereas a stipulation is a civil obligation? Civil law cannot destroy natural law, though civil law is sometimes set aside by natural law. It is hard indeed, and excessively harsh, for you not to be gracious to those whom nature commends to you. For, according to the Apostle’s testimony, one who does not provide for his own, and especially for members of his household, has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever. [Note: [Col. 0217] 1 Tim. 5.] Brute animals nourish their young and, when they have grown somewhat larger, abandon them. This does not become a human being, whom reason and intelligence make pre-eminent over other creatures.

Beware, I beg you, of those who seek to please men: they are confounded who say everything [Col. 0218C] for pleasure and nothing for truth. Flattery is indeed a most wicked pest: though immediately detected by a poor man, it steals secretly upon the rich and may deceive even the watchful and prudent. For monstrous flattery disguises itself under the image of love, the pretext of devotion, or the simulation of some service, so that it may be received more welcome; poisons are not administered unless they are coated with honey.

“It brings you glory,” says the crafty flatterer, “that in granting benefices you prefer honorable poor men to your nephews. This is God’s work; flesh and blood have not revealed it to you.” Who would not detect malice in this exhortation? Thus the deceitful Pharisee and Herodian once approached Him in whom there was no guile: “Master, we know that you are truthful and teach the way of God in truth; you care for no one and do not regard persons. Is it lawful to give tribute to Caesar or not?” [Note: [Col. 0217] Matt. 22.] Blandishments come first, but poison lies in the speech. Yet all snares of malice are loosed when the tribute coin is produced and what belongs to God is assigned to God, and what belongs to Caesar to Caesar.

Your discernment also does not fail to recognize [Col. 0219A] that honorable outsiders should be admitted and granted benefices, but they should never be preferred to honorable nephews. [Note: [Col. 0219D] Three things are certain. First, a worthy nephew ought to be preferred to an unworthy outsider. Thus Peter of Blois rightly says here: “While your nephew is honorable and fit for ecclesiastical benefices, I beg you not to prefer to him an outsider less fit or worse.” Second, a worthy outsider ought to be preferred to an unworthy nephew. Third, a worthier nephew should be preferred to a less worthy outsider, and a worthier outsider to a less worthy nephew. But what in an equal case? Let the nephew be preferred if it does not plainly appear that anything is being granted to carnal affection in promoting him; let the outsider be preferred if the nephew’s promotion seems inseparably joined, in the eyes of reputable men, with a certain scandal. For nothing is more necessary for a bishop to avoid than staining his reputation, in the judgment of fair evaluators, through suspicion of carnal affection toward nephews.

Peter the Chanter, chapter 43, aptly says: “Do not, therefore, raise your nephew to a position of harm to the Church; yet you may assign him an ecclesiastical benefice by which he may be supported. But what if he is as honorable and worthy as an outsider? Even this is dangerous unless his integrity demands it and excludes every reproach, scandal, and bad example—which does not happen easily. For an example is not taken from the good conduct of our actions, but from their outer bark, appearance, and surface, not from their truth. If I gave to my nephew because of favour, others will use my example to give to theirs for kinship rather than merit, saying: ‘Shall I not give to my own as he gives to his? I give to Merit; he gives to Nature.’”]

It is the greatest wrong against nature to reject a poor and honorable nephew and expose one’s own flesh and blood to the reproach of public beggary. The she-bear and lioness love their own offspring, and even the offspring of others if they have received from them the benefit of nurture. Even sea-monsters (lamiae), according to the prophet, uncover their breasts and suckle their young. [Note: [Col. 0219] Lam. 4.] Shall a man, then, be so savagely inhuman as to neglect the one whom he has taught and reject the one whom he has nourished? Those who suggest this to you, reverend Father, build a wall and whitewash it. Yet the Lord has given you heart and wisdom, so that spirits of falsehood may not deceive you under the appearance of flattery, so that you may catch flatterers in their craftiness [Col. 0219B] and another’s deceit may not extinguish in you the debt of nature.

Moreover John the Evangelist, although a kinsman of the Lord, was nevertheless loved by the Lord above the rest; and the other son of Zebedee, James the Less, Joseph the Just, Jude, and Simon were not cut off from Christ’s fellowship by the line of kinship. If your nephew is honorable and prudent, love nature in a prudent man and honorableness in a kinsman. If the benefit of nature does not suffice for him with you, let at least his honorableness and learning suffice, so that he may find you kindly and approachable—one before whom, every line of kinship set aside, he claims favour and grace on account of the demands of his own merits.

## LETTER LXXI. TO MASTER ERNALD OF BLOIS

[Col. 0219C]

**SUMMARY.**—Peter of Blois had bought law books at Paris and paid the price, but had not taken them away; another man, having paid a higher price, took them away. Peter therefore contends that those books, though not delivered to him, could not be bought by another.

To his dearest companion and friend, Master ERNALD of Blois: PETER of Blois, Archdeacon of Bath, greetings.

When the lord king of the English had recently sent me as an envoy to the lord king of the French, books of law were offered for sale to me at Paris by that B., a public bookseller. Since they appeared suitable for the use of one of my nephews, I agreed [Col. 0220A] with him concerning the price, left them with the seller, and paid him the price. But C., Provost of Saxeburg, afterward came, as I have heard, offered more, outbid me, and carried the books violently out of the seller’s house. Therefore, because I must return promptly to the man who sent me, while you will remain in Paris, I entrust the management of the aforesaid affair entirely to your discretion. Or, if some necessity prevents your remaining in Paris, entrust it, under the authority of my letters, to Master Hugh of Genoa.

For since under civil law the most exact diligence is owed to the affairs of others, I know that, if you diligently perform the office of agent in this present case, in which equity is strongly on my side, your efforts will attain their purpose with honour and advantage. For although ownership of a thing sold, given, or owed under the terms of a legacy is not usually transferred without delivery, I nevertheless have here a useful real action by which I claim that the books be produced and delivered to me. Supporting this are that law in the *Digest* “To a Municipal Corporation,” concerning the law of all inhabitants, and the third law of the *Digest* “On Producing Children.”

I likewise claim my freedman, whose possession I have never had; and likewise my son, once the ground has been stated, under the law of the Quirites. Likewise a citizen or a city claims its own decurion, as in the *Institutes*, “On Actions,” under “prejudicial actions”; and in the *Digest*, “On Vindication of a Thing,” first law, paragraph “By This”; in the *Code*, “On Farmers and Registered Taxpayers,” the laws *Quisquis* and *Omnes*; the *[uncertain corrupt citation]* concerning Palestinian coloni; and the *Code* “On Thracian Coloni,” the *Code* “On Fugitive Coloni,” and also “On Farmers and Slaves,” the second and third laws. [Col. 0220C] In all these cases I vindicate a thing whose possession I have never obtained. Yet in none of them is delivery or possession mentioned. For I may claim a freedman who has neither been delivered nor possessed. Otherwise, what will happen if immediately after manumission he asserts that he is freeborn? Or if I have bought the right of patronage from a patron, I still bring an action even though I have not possessed it. Indeed, if my father assigned a freedman to me, I claim him after my father’s death without any delivery or possession.

Likewise, if a debtor was ready to pay but subsequently agreed to retain the money as a loan, a loan is contracted, because the creditor is understood to have received it and given it back to him; as in the *Digest*, “On Things Lent,” law *Singularia*. By an explicit analogy, I appear to have received the books from the buyer and left them as a deposit. Moreover, one kind of delivery is real, occurring through a physical act; hence it is said: “By deliveries and usucapions ownership of things is acquired,” as in the *Code*, “On Pacts,” law *Traditionibus*. Another delivery occurs through a fiction of law, which is threefold. It occurs by constitutum, as in the *Code*, “On Donations,” law *Quisquis*, and the *Digest*, “On Sale of a Thing,” law *Mulier*, and the *Digest*, “On Acquiring Possession,” law *Interdum*. Another occurs through the completion of one act which conceals another, as in the *Digest*, “On Gifts between Husband and [Col. 0221B] Wife,” law *Haec ratio*, § *Sciendum*, in the middle of the paragraph. Another occurs by the appointment of a custodian, as in the *Digest*, “On Acquiring Possession,” law *Quarundam*.

I have used this brief consideration not to instruct you, who are eminent in civil law, but to stimulate you toward subtler points. An unformed beginning will lead you toward the best conclusions; for it is written: “Give occasion to a wise man, and he will be wiser still.” [Note: [Col. 0221] Prov. 9.] A small stream, by continuous flow, often overflows into a great pool; and a spark of fire, aided by winds, spreads itself without limit. Farewell.

## LETTER LXXII. TO A FRIEND AND COMPANION

**SUMMARY.**—He vehemently attacks a certain former companion and friend who, out of envy, had caused [Col. 0221C] Peter of Blois not to be admitted into the household of the Archbishop of Sens and to lose other ecclesiastical benefices. The letter is learned and abounds in verses of poets.

Master PETER of Blois to G., once his friend and companion: the greeting he has deserved.

When the lord of Sens [Note: [Col. 0221] This is William, to whom Peter of Blois wrote Letter 128 on this subject.] summoned me from the scholarly militia and enrolled me in his household with a definite expectation of a timely benefice, at your repeated prompting he withdrew his intention; and, as you publicly boasted, after deceiving me as to my hope, he introduced another in my place. But blessed be God, who took away my hope and gave me the reality, and afterward did not cease to afflict your conscience with the torment of remorse. For according to the moral poet:

> Whatever is committed as an evil example displeases  
> Its very author: this is the first punishment, that no guilty person  
> Is acquitted when he is his own judge.  
> [Note: [Col. 0221D] Juvenal, *Satires*, 13.]
