This, moreover, comes gratefully to my wish: it is publicly known that this proceeded not from my fault but from your envy; and the torment of your conscience is a consolation to me.

> The Sicilian tyrants devised  
> No greater torment than envy.  
> [Note: [Col. 0221] Horace, Book I, Epistle to Lollius.]

[Col. 0222A]

> It is indeed a violent punishment, far more cruel than those  
> Which grim Caedicius or Rhadamanthus devised:  
> To carry one’s own witness in one’s breast night and day.  
> [Note: [Col. 0221] Juvenal, *Satires*, 13.]

It was envy that incited Cain to commit fratricide, Joab to kill Amasa, Saul to persecute David, the Jews to hand Christ over to Pilate, and Jacob’s sons to sell Joseph to the Ishmaelites. Certainly you would never have envied a poor man if any nobility of birth or mind had been in you, because, in the poet’s testimony:

> Envy, an idle vice, does not rise to noble characters,  
> But, like a hidden viper, crawls upon the lowest ground.  
> [Note: [Col. 0221] Ovid, Book III, *Pontic Epistles*, elegy 3.]

I shall no longer regard myself as wretched, since another can envy me. For it is commonly said that misery alone is free from envy. Until the day of my death I shall not judge myself liberated and immune from the bite of envy. For, according to [Col. 0222B] the moral poet, he who tamed and escaped monsters

> Found that envy is subdued only at life’s final end.  
> [Note: [Col. 0221] Plautus, *Truculentus*.]

Certainly, if my enemy had cursed or harmed me, I should indeed have endured it; but now:

> I received a wound not expected from an enemy.  
> [Note: [Col. 0221] Horace, Book II, Epistle 1.]

And therefore I bear it more impatiently. For, according to Naso:

> Whatever you suffer deservedly must be borne gently;  
> Punishment that comes undeservedly comes to be lamented.  
> [Note: [Col. 0221] Ovid, *Hypsipyle* [citation uncertain].]

What especially increased the injury and kindled the fire of indignation was that you rendered my innocence hateful to so great a majesty, which by a mere nod can condemn and crush my insignificance. We read [Note: [Col. 0221] Macrobius, *Saturnalia*, Book II, ch. 4] [Col. 0222C] that Augustus wrote abusive verses against Pollio; when Pollio was urged to answer Augustus, he said: “But I keep silent. It is no light matter to write against one who can proscribe for a trifling cause.”

May the lord archbishop, I beg, keep his hand far from me, and may his power not terrify me.

> He who is struck by Jupiter does not receive a slight wound.  
> Though Achilles himself restrained his strength,  
> The Pelian spear, once hurled, dealt grievous blows.  
> [Note: [Col. 0221] Ovid, Book I, *Pontic Epistles*, elegy 8.]

May he not oppress me, I beg, by the weight of his greatness. For I bear with sufficient equanimity the loss which my hidden enemy procured for me.

> A man’s grief ought not to be more blazing than is right,  
> Nor greater than the wound.  
> [Note: [Col. 0221] Juvenal, *Satires*, 13.]

I still retain the consolation of great hope:

[Col. 0222D] Yet my fortunes are not so oppressed

that I cannot raise my head: an impartial fate regards those who deserve it. [Note: [Col. 0221] Lucan, book VIII.] Above all my desires, my chief wish was to obtain some benefice in the land of my birth, because

I know not by what sweetness one’s native soil touches all alike  
and does not allow them to forget it. [Note: [Col. 0221] Ovid, *Letters from Pontus*, elegy 4.]

[Col. 0223A] But now, my sins demanding it, wandering and fugitive upon the earth,

Wherever the storm carries me, I am borne as a stranger. [Note: [Col. 0223] Horace, book I, epistle 1.]

Yet because my innocence has been overthrown by malice, I have consolation in Christ: that wisdom may conquer malice and order sweetly all the things which I am compelled grievously to endure while awaiting his mercy.

Every land is a homeland to the brave, as the sea is to fishes;  
as whatever lies open in the world is to the bird in empty air. [Note: [Col. 0223] Ovid, *Fasti*, book II.]

If fortune had cast me into the narrow lane, so to speak, of more constricted hardship, I would not be afraid. For, in the poet’s testimony,

The most wretched fortune is secure:

[Col. 0223B] for fear of a worse outcome is absent. [Note: [Col. 0223] Ovid, *Letters from Pontus*, book II, elegy 2.]

But now I cannot complain of poverty:

For he is not poor who has the use of things at hand.  
Let him to whom enough falls desire nothing further.  
If your belly, your side, and your feet are well supplied,  
royal riches will be able to add nothing greater. [Note: [Col. 0223] Horace, book I, epistles 12 and 2.]

Behold, those who are in kings’ houses wear soft clothing. Yet I would use neither healthier food nor more splendid garments, even if I lived in royal palaces.

Let me have what I have now—nay, even less—so that I may live for myself  
through whatever remains of my years, if any life remains to me.  
For joys do not fall to the rich alone,  
nor has he lived badly who passed unnoticed both in birth and death. [Note: [Col. 0223] Horace, book I, epistles 19 and 18.]

I have absolutely nothing besides my patrimony, [Col. 0223C] and I bestow and distribute all of it among my relatives; perhaps I should become more miserly, or more generous, if fortune smiled more kindly upon me. Indeed, by the Lord’s grant, it will smile; and what you have poured upon me will be shamefully poured back upon your own head, because, a courtier skilled in guile, you tripped up one who was simple. I would already have repaid you with the requital of vengeance due to you; but I count it a very small thing, though you are great in your own eyes, to seek vengeance against one vile and contemptible.

For vengeance is always the pleasure  
of a petty and feeble mind. [Note: [Col. 0223] Juvenal, *Satires*, 13.]

[Col. 0224A] For my vengeance it is enough that, as time proceeds, through the mercy of the Most High advancing me,

you may see it, and waste away at the sight.

Indeed, without any action on my part, your overthrow is ready at hand, because, in the poet’s testimony,

All human things hang by a slender thread,  
and things that have been strong suddenly fall by chance.  
You too, then, should take care to fear, and think that the things which seem pleasing to you  
may, while you are speaking, become sad. [Note: [Col. 0223] Ovid, *Letters from Pontus*, book IV, elegy 3.]

You think that you have harmed me ruinously because, employing the counsel of Jannes and Mambres, and the counsel of Ahithophel—whose heirs still besiege nearly every court—you have estranged from me my lord, friend, and neighbour. I recall how many plots of rivals I once experienced at the court of William II, king of Sicily [Note: [Col. 0223D] Our Peter was tutor of William II, king of Sicily, after Walter, archbishop of Palermo, as he himself testifies in letter 66: “You know that the lord king of Sicily was my pupil for a year, and he who had received from you the first elements of versification and literary art obtained, through my industry and care, the benefit of fuller learning.” Thereafter he was royal keeper of the seal and participant in all the kingdom’s counsels, and he had rivals. On this matter he says in letter 131: “When I was in Sicily, keeper of the seal and teacher of King William II, then of the boy and afterwards of the queen,” etc. “Since the government of the kingdom, with the election of the archbishop of Palermo, depended greatly upon my decision, certain rivals of mine, plotting to exclude me from the king’s familiarity, arranged for the Church of Naples [Col. 0224D] to elect me archbishop and, through the leading members of the chapter, to request my ordination by a common decree and unanimous vote. But when called I did not go; though repeatedly asked and urged, I did not consent. The bishopric of Rochester was also offered to me twice, and I declined it when offered; measuring honour by its burden, I confined ambitious impulses within the sober bounds of moderation.” At length, however, he left Sicily, as appears from letter 90.]—[Col. 0224B] when, after they had repeatedly endeavoured to remove me from the king’s side and could not do so, they caused me first to be nominated and then solemnly elected to one bishopric and another, and finally to the metropolitan see of Naples. But no artifice of fraud could incline me to this; for I knew that all their cunning turned upon this and around this: that, once I had been removed from courtly society, they might crush me by open persecution. You, on the contrary, after one benefice and another, by which you had fraudulently drained me, also tripped me up in the provostship. Moreover, God, terrible in judgments, judged terribly between me and the Sicilian traitors. May he spare you; for I expect no vengeance from you.

## LETTER LXXIII. TO THREE BISHOPS OF ENGLAND

[Col. 0224C]

**Subject.**—R., archbishop of Canterbury, urges the bishops to remove an abuse that had grown prevalent in England: namely, that murderers of lay persons were punished capitally, while murderers of clerics and bishops were punished only by excommunication.

RICHARD, by the grace of God archbishop of Canterbury, primate of all England, and legate of the Apostolic See, to his venerable and beloved brothers in Christ, R., bishop of Winchester, G., bishop of Ely, and Jo., bishop of Norwich [Note: [Col. 0224D] These three bishops were very powerful with King Henry II. Hence the archbishop of Canterbury asks them to procure from the king the abolition of that damnable custom which had become prevalent in England and had grown into an enormous detriment to the clergy: that if anyone killed a priest, etc. These matters are treated fully in this letter.], greetings and salutary counsel.

[Col. 0225A] In the English Church a custom harmful to all, and wholly deserving condemnation, has grown prevalent [Note: [Col. 0225C] Murderers of clerics are clerics or laymen. Bishops deposed clerics from office, but did not wish to surrender those so deposed to the secular judge for punishment on account of that crime, lest they be punished twice for the same thing. On this matter R. de Diceto, under the year 1164: “The king of the English, wishing, as he said, to punish due offences in every case with severity, and considering it improper that the dignity of an order should be turned to an unjust advantage, had decreed that clerics caught by his justices in a public crime should be handed over to the bishop of the place, so that those whom the bishop found guilty should, in the presence of the king’s justice, be deposed from office and afterward delivered to the court for punishment. The bishops held the contrary view: those whom they deposed from office, they maintained, should be protected from the lay hand, otherwise they would be judged twice for the same thing,” etc. Matthew Paris says the same under the same year, as do John Brompton and Gervase under the preceding year. But when a layman killed a cleric, the bishops excommunicated the murderer according to the canons, and wished the force of that excommunication to make murderers immune from the severity of civil laws enacted against them, lest they be punished twice for the same thing. Thus clerics were in some manner killed with impunity, since ecclesiastical censures were despised by such men. Hence Richard says there: “But because our sins demand it, Peter’s sword has become covered with rust. And because it cannot cut, it has been given over to contempt,” etc. The bishops usurped royal jurisdiction; hence the same Richard says: “We rashly usurp, through ambition, a jurisdiction belonging to another and wholly not due to us.”], and unless it is wholly removed from our midst through your diligence, it will grow violently into an enormous detriment to the entire clergy. If a Jew or the most insignificant of laymen is killed, the murderer is immediately sentenced to death; but if anyone kills a priest or a cleric of lower or higher rank, the Church, content—or, more truthfully, treated with contempt—with excommunication alone, will not seek the aid of the material sword. [Note: [Col. 0226D] That is, it prevents the sword from being drawn, as is gathered from what follows.] You know indeed that the Lord said to Moses: “You shall not suffer sorcerers to live.” [Note: [Col. 0225] Exodus 31.] And, in the Apostle’s testimony: “The ruler bears the sword for the punishment of evildoers and the praise of the good.” [Note: [Col. 0225] Romans 11.] Moreover, the Lord says: “Whoever touches you touches me.” [Note: [Col. 0225] Zechariah 2.] And through prophecy: [Col. 0225B] “Do not touch,” he says, “my anointed ones.” [Note: [Col. 0225] Psalm 104.]

Where, then, could a crime more monstrous and execrable be found than to rage against the Lord’s anointed and, with the boldness of free impunity, wield the sword against the people of his possession? A sentence of excommunication in such cases would be acceptable to me if it struck fear into murderers. But because our sins demand it, Peter’s sword has become covered with rust; and because it cannot cut, it has been given over to contempt. If a goat or a little sheep is stolen or killed, a sentence of excommunication is issued against the perpetrator of the act if he is unknown; if he is convicted or confesses, he is assigned to the gallows. Yet clerics or bishops who are murderers are sent to Rome [Note: [Col. 0226D] For the sake of absolution, according to chapter *Si quis, suadente diabolo*, 17, question 4, which is the council of Innocent II held at London in 1143 under Roger, bishop of Winchester, legate of the same Roman pontiff, according to R. de Hoveden and John Brompton under that year.]; and they go in luxury and return with the fullness of apostolic grace and with greater boldness in wrongdoing. [Col. 0225C] The lord king claims for himself the punishment of such excesses, but we damnably reserve it to ourselves; and by providing free occasion for impunity, we provoke the swords of laymen against our own throats. It is disgraceful that a heavier penalty is imposed for a goat or a little sheep, and a lighter one for a murdered priest. But we deserve these things and worse, we who rashly usurp through ambitious pride a jurisdiction belonging to another and [Col. 0226A] wholly not due to us.

For we remember having read these words both in the body of decrees and in the Epistle to the Romans [Note: [Col. 0225] Chapter 13.]: “There are certain enormous crimes which are judged rather by the judges of the world than by the rulers and judges of the Churches. For example, when someone kills an apostolic pontiff, a priest, or a deacon, the kings and princes of the world condemn persons guilty of this sort.” Indeed, every administration of justice exists in order that innocence may enjoy due peace and the recklessness of the wicked may be restrained. Yet in this cursed jurisdiction, which we arrogantly and proudly presume to exercise, we offend God and the lord king, and open to laymen a very safe path for maligning clerics.

Recently at Winchester a priest commendable for learning [Col. 0226B] and upright conduct was maliciously killed by William Frechet and his wife [Note: [Col. 0226D] From this it appears that English bishops wished lay murderers of clerics, even after they had been excommunicated, to enjoy the same immunity as murderer-clerics who had been deposed from office.]; nor do they deny the crime. Therefore they are ready to approach the Roman court. For her husband’s heart trusts in her, and he intends to proceed successfully by means of her appearance and beauty; and from his wife’s prostitution on the journey he expects to bring back, beyond the benefit of absolution, sheaves of richer profit. Therefore, most beloved brothers, strive to meet this public plague with more timely counsel while it is still in its course. For if it escapes a little more freely and licentiously, the danger which now moves among the poor will soon threaten our own necks. Let the Church first exercise her jurisdiction; and if that does not suffice, let the secular sword supply what it lacks.

[Col. 0226C] The authority for this has issued from the synod of Pope Urban, the decree of Gregory, the letter of Nicholas to the bishops of Gaul, likewise the council of Pope Martin, the Third Council of Carthage, and many ordinances of the holy Fathers. Nor should it be said that anyone is thereby punished twice for the same thing; for that does not appear repeated which one authority begins and another completes. There are two swords which borrow mutual aid from one another and reciprocally impart their strength: the priesthood to kings, and royal power to priests. [Col. 0227A] Therefore, if the insufficiency of one is supplied by the other, there is not a double crushing or a combined punishment.

For even those who are condemned to the gallows, according to the Council of Mainz, are spiritually punished through contrition of heart and penance before they are led to torture; this does not introduce a double contrition, but the penance and satisfaction which precede are a certain preparation for death. Therefore, rendering to God what belongs to God and to Caesar what belongs to Caesar, let us, according to the lord king’s request, leave to him the punishment of such great crimes. But, when the guilty stand at the point of death, since they have incurred the sentence of the [Col. 0227B] established canon, if they request absolution, let us mercifully offer, in this and in other matters, so far as we can without scandal or danger to the Church, the counsel of humanity. For it is publicly expedient that those who neither fear God nor defer to the Church nor reverence the censure of the canons should be restrained by the material sword. Fare well.

## LETTER LXXIV. TO G., ARCHDEACON

**Subject.**—He advises the archdeacon not to punish a second time his guest Guy, who has relapsed into the crime of adultery and is therefore incorrigible, but rather his father, who accustomed him from his earliest age to the game of dice, the seedbed of all evils.

To his beloved friend G., archdeacon, P. of Blois, archdeacon of Bath, [Col. 0227C] greetings and continual success according to your wishes.

I would offer you affectionate prayers for Guy, my guest, but I find neither the desire to pray nor do the prayers offered deserve effect. I do not excuse before you a man who publicly accuses himself by the enormous dishonour of his life; for, to use Naso’s words,

The case of an accused man who confesses is not to be defended. [Note: [Col. 0227] Ovid, *Letters from Pontus*, book II, elegy 2.]

I hoped that he had become more corrected by the scourge of your most recent punishment [Note: [Col. 0227D] From this passage it is inferred that adultery at that time belonged to the ecclesiastical forum, although committed by a layman.], and that vexation had given him understanding; but now too he has returned to his vomit, and forgetful of the penalty he endured, he has recalled to illicit embraces the adulteress whom he had rejected.

The wounded gladiator, says the poet, avoids battles, yet he himself  
takes up arms again, forgetful of his old wound.

[Col. 0228A] He who after shipwreck had lately feared pools and lakes  
again ventures upon the sea’s waters with an oar. [Note: [Col. 0227] Ovid, *Letters from Pontus*, book I.]

I utterly despair of his correction; perhaps he will be more capable of amendment if he is left to his own will until he is sated.

We see certain wounds made worse by treatment,  
which it had been better not to touch.  
This is a kind of wound which, since it cannot be healed,  
I think it safer not to handle. [Note: [Col. 0227] Ovid, *Letters from Pontus*, book II, elegy 2.]

His father, however, seems to me far more blameworthy in this respect. For whereas he ought in his son’s childhood to have formed him in holy and honourable conduct, he trained his natural disposition in gambling and corrupted it with the varied shamefulness of seductions. [Note: [Col. 0227D] As though he ought to be subject only to the laws of dice, like the Huns of whom Ambrose says in book *On Tobit*, chapter 2: “Though they live without laws, they are accustomed to obey the laws of dice alone.” John Gerson inveighs against parents who bring up their children so perversely, in his work *On Leading Little Children to Christ*, in these words: “Many parents and teachers take either no care at all, or only the last care, for the character of their little children and their disciplined protection. What wonder, then, if, set without a guide upon a slippery and dark road [Col. 0228D]—whom an evil angel of the Lord pursues—they fall easily? Would that they merely neglected them. Before their eyes are placed examples of such wicked deeds and leaders; indeed, images of shameful pictures and wanton writings, at which they look—what do they then do except act perversely? Listen to the Satirist.”

> Domestic examples corrupt us more swiftly and sooner  
> when great authorities enter our minds.]

Then indeed he ought to have been instructed and made fit to receive every form, like

[Col. 0228B] moist and soft clay, which must now, now be hurried  
and shaped without end upon the swift wheel. [Note: [Col. 0227] Persius, *Satires*, 3.]

For

The trainer fashions a horse, docile in its tender neck,  
to follow the path shown by its rider. [Note: [Col. 0227] Horace, book I, epistle 2.]

But if he has grown into an age of harder fibre, he cannot be trained to the gentleness of a walking pace. For character is shaped by companionship: “He who touches pitch shall be defiled by it,” [Note: [Col. 0227] Ecclesiasticus 13.] and bad associations corrupt good morals, as the satirist testifies:

Domestic examples of vices corrupt us more swiftly and sooner  
when great authorities enter our minds. [Note: [Col. 0227] Juvenal, *Satires*, 14.]

[Col. 0228C] What will a son do except what he sees his father doing? [Note: [Col. 0228D] To this is proverbially applied that saying of pastoral verse:

> A man’s offspring follows its father.]

If ruinous gambling delights the old man, the heir too, still wearing his childhood bulla, plays  
and shakes the same weapons in his little dice-box. [Note: [Col. 0227] Ibid.]

I do not wonder that the young man is vicious when his father devoted his childhood to gambling. Gambling is indeed the mother of lying, perjury, theft, and sacrilege. Therefore Cato, instructing his son, says: “Flee gambling.” Attalus the Asiatic is said to have invented dice-playing and gambling, [Note: [Col. 0227] John of Salisbury, book I.] which it is much better not to know than to know. Chilon of Sparta, sent to Corinth to form an alliance and friendship, found the leaders and elders of the people playing at dice. [Note: [Col. 0227] *Policraticus*, chapter 5; P. Gregory, book 39, *Syntagma*, chapter 4.] Therefore he returned without accomplishing his business, saying that the glory of the Spartans, whose valour was then resplendent at newly-founded Byzantium, ought not to be [Col. 0229A] stained by this disgrace, so that they might be said to have contracted an alliance with gamblers. King Demetrius too received such golden dice from the king of the Parthians, that his childish frivolity was reproached: he who, in royal majesty, devoted himself to trifles.

Since, therefore, the son has been corrupted in his father, he should be corrected in his father also, so that the father’s punishment may teach the son to abstain from shameful things. It is written: “When the pestilent man is punished, the wise man will become wiser,” [Note: [Col. 0229] Proverbs 19.] and “the righteous shall wash his hands in the blood of the sinner.” [Note: [Col. 0229] Psalm 57.] It often happens that we heal one member through another. The ears ache, and cups are applied to the shoulders; the eye’s weeping cleanses the heart’s offence. The hand has sinned, and the breast is beaten. The sexual organs have done wrong, and the back is exposed to lashes. Certainly, the father does not fear a sentence of suspension or the bond [Col. 0229B] of excommunication. [Note: [Col. 0229D] From this I infer that Guy’s father was a cleric.] All these are merely verbal things, and he will not desist from ingrained disgrace unless he is restrained by loss of money. [Note: [Col. 0229D] The author of Blois advises the archdeacon to whom he writes to punish the adultery of the incorrigible son by imposing a monetary fine upon his father. It follows: first, that the Church can punish parents for their children’s crimes when they neglected to form them in holy and honourable conduct in childhood; secondly, that an ecclesiastical judge may impose a monetary fine on clerics. Indeed, formerly the same judges imposed such fines on laymen.]

I promise you the father’s most certain amendment through the taking away of his money. That sentence is felt, not merely verbal, and therefore causes greater pain and fear. For, according to the moralist,

Lost money is mourned with real tears.  
Sacred words do not restrain the hand; with greater tumult  
coins are lamented than funerals. [Note: [Col. 0229] Juvenal, *Satires*, 13.]

Therefore make them both a gain in one matter; and, by the father’s loss, recalling the son to the benefit of honour, restrain in the father’s grief the wandering and unbridled wantonness of the son. For to correct his son on this occasion would be nothing other than to spur on a madman, to apply oil [Col. 0229C] to a furnace, and to stir up fires with winds.

## LETTER LXXV. TO ROGER, DEAN

**Subject.**—He advises Dean Roger, since he had certain harsh matters to announce to the king, to wait for an appropriate time, when the king’s mind would be calmer. He then adds that the pope has postponed for three years the consecration of the elected bishop of Lincoln.

PETER of Blois, archdeacon of Bath, to ROGER, dean: greetings and salutary counsel.

No teacher is more faithful or effective than one who has learned by experience what he imparts to others by instruction. Recently, sent to the lord king to manage the affairs of the Church of Canterbury, I approached as cheerfully as usual. Yet, reading and understanding from his face the disturbance of his mind, [Col. 0230A] I immediately suppressed my lips and restrained my tongue, fearing that if I spoke his anger would be more vehemently aroused, as his face, the faithful interpreter of the mind, informed me. I therefore deferred the business until a happier hour should favour it and a calmer countenance smile upon me.

For I consider approaching an offended prince concerning business to be nothing other than spreading nets for capture upon a stormy sea. He hastens to destroy both himself and his nets who thrusts himself into a tempest and does not await a calmer face of the sea. I know that you have been sent to announce harsh things to the lord king; hence you must also be more cautious in this matter.

For even things pleasant in themselves sometimes displease when reported without judgment, and harsh things are sometimes reported with such skill that they please. Take care [Col. 0230B] not to approach the lord king to lay out your business until an approach has first been tested by me or by another who knows his character. For he is a lamb while his mind is calm; but when he burns more fiercely, he is a lion, or more savage than a lion. It is no game to incur the indignation of one in whose hand are honour and disgrace, inheritance and exile, life and death. In Solomon’s testimony, “The indignation of a king is a messenger of death.” [Note: [Col. 0229] Proverbs 16.]

When Aristotle sent his pupil Callisthenes to Alexander, he urged him either never to speak with him, or to speak most agreeably, so that at royal ears he might be safer either in silence or more welcome in speech. [Note: [Col. 0229] Valerius Maximus, book IV, chapter 2.] But Callisthenes, while reproving Alexander as he exulted in a Persian salutation, [Col. 0230C] while correcting and regulating his life, was deprived of life. [Note: [Col. 0229] Plutarch, *Life of Alexander*; Justin, book XV.]

I know what you are bringing, and I have already accomplished for you the greater part of the task entrusted to you. Therefore take more circumspect care lest, through an untimely approach or unconsidered speech, a matter which is proceeding according to wish should fall into danger or failure. For you can overturn the whole business in a few words, though I have endeavoured to advance it by pressing vigilance and more earnest caution.

You know that the bishopric of Lincoln, for which we were specially sent, has now been vacant fifteen years or more. [Note: [Col. 0229D] This was from the death of Robert, a man of great humility, who, according to R. de Diceto, passed to the Lord in 1167. Although Geoffrey, the illegitimate son of Henry, was elected bishop of that church in 1173, of which he was archdeacon, and under cover of this election received the revenues of the bishopric for seven years, Peter wrote that the see of Lincoln had been vacant fifteen years or more because Geoffrey refused to be consecrated bishop throughout that period.] The lord of Canterbury has received commands from the supreme pontiff to compel the elect to accept consecration and the episcopal office, or else, after removing every occasion and appeal, to ordain another there without delay. [Note: [Col. 0230D] Roger of Hoveden records the same under the year 1181: “The lord pope gave strict commands [Col. 0231C] to Richard, archbishop of Canterbury, that, setting aside every occasion and excuse, he should compel by ecclesiastical censure Geoffrey, elected to the Church of Lincoln and son of the lord king of England, to renounce his election, or, without delay, [Col. 0231D] receive the order of priest and the dignity of the episcopal office.”]

But matters have turned to the contrary: for now the Roman Church has anew postponed the elect’s consecration for three years. [Col. 0231A] Therefore it would be rash for you to employ a strictness which another’s dispensation annuls. Moreover, whatever the Roman pontiff may postpone, I am utterly certain that it is the lord king’s earnest desire and fixed purpose that within four months the Church of Lincoln shall have a consecrated bishop. [Note: [Col. 0231D] The king’s will was fulfilled: by his command and in his presence Geoffrey renounced the election made of him in 1182. His letter of renunciation to Richard of Canterbury is extant in Roger of Hoveden at the place cited: “On the Sunday on which *Jubilate* is sung, Walter of Coutances was elected by the chapter and afterward consecrated at Angers, in the Church of Saint Laud, by the archbishop of Canterbury.” Radulfus de Diceto.] This desire of his would already have attained its desired fulfilment, had not those persons impeded the common good of the people; from whose hands the destruction of the people shall be more strictly required. I have certain things to explain to you in person which would make you better informed, things which I would not entrust to a messenger or to writing. Farewell.

## LETTER LXXVI. TO MASTER PETER OF BLOIS

[Note: [Col. 0231D] He was a canon of Chartres; see below at letter 114.]

[Col. 0231B]

**Subject.**—He earnestly and learnedly admonishes his companion, who had spent almost his whole life in the study of civil law and poetic fables, and still devoted himself to composing and singing love verses, at last to apply himself to the study of theology and to attend more diligently to the care and salvation of his soul.

To his dearest companion, Master PETER of Blois, P. of Blois, archdeacon of Bath, greetings in the author of salvation.

Often by letters, often by word of mouth, I have warned and begged you to abstain from frivolous and buffoonish things; and, to use the Apostle’s words, I have not shrunk from declaring to you the counsel of the Lord. [Note: [Col. 0231] Acts 20.] And because the correction previously offered has found no place with you, according to Paul’s counsel it is not burdensome to me to write the same things again. [Note: [Col. 0231] Philippians 3.] Indeed, in the testimony of a certain wise man, that is never said too often which is never sufficiently learned. [Note: [Col. 0231] Seneca, *Letters* 27.] Although various occupations begrudge me the leisure or ability to write, nevertheless, inflamed by the zeal of charity, I shall take up the page of sudden correction. The zeal of Phinehas killed those who were coupling together. [Note: [Col. 0231] Numbers 25.] Moses, led by zeal, killed idolaters; [Note: [Col. 0231] Exodus 32.] Samuel killed the king of Amalek; [Note: [Col. 0231] 1 Kings 15.] Elijah, the captains of fifty; [Note: [Col. 0231] 4 Kings 1.] Mattathias, a Jew who was sacrificing; [Note: [Col. 0231] 1 Maccabees 2.] and Peter killed Ananias [Col. 0232A] and Sapphira. [Note: [Col. 0231] Acts 5.] Zeal for the Lord drove from the Temple those who sold and bought. “Zeal for thy house hath eaten me up.” [Note: [Col. 0231] John 2.] Woe is me because I have kept silent, because for so long a time I have been mute and have held my peace from good things. I fear lest my brother’s blood cry to the Lord from the ground against me. [Note: [Col. 0231] Genesis 4.] I call him brother whom the adoption of divine regeneration has made with me a son of Christ. [Note: [Col. 0231] John 2.] It is the prophet’s word: “Cursed is he who restrains his sword from blood,” [Note: [Col. 0231] Jeremiah 48.] that is, [he who withholds] the word of exhortation from the mortification of sin. For the sword is beneath the tongue of one who rebukes; but honey and milk are beneath the tongue of a flattering harlot. I do not spare you, so that God may spare both me and you. King Ahab spared King Ben-hadad, as you read in the third book of Kings, [Note: [Col. 0231] Chapter 20.] and the Lord spoke to him through Micaiah, saying: “Because thou hast let go out of thy hand a man [Col. 0232B] worthy of death, thy life shall be for his life.” Because Saul spared the king of Amalek, his kingdom was taken away from him. [Note: [Col. 0231] 1 Kings 15.] I grieve that duty and custom require me to speak more harshly; accordingly my words are full of sorrow.

Your scholarly learning had indeed raised you to the highest ranks of distinction; and whereas you ought to have been for others a pattern of virtues and a mirror of integrity, through buffoonish trifles and fabulous inventions of the heathen you have become to many a snare unto ruin. [Note: [Col. 0231D] Augustine, *Confessions*, book I, ch. 16: “Do I not then read in you of Jupiter thundering and committing adultery? Certainly he cannot do both; but it was so contrived that he might have authority for imitating real adultery, the false thunder acting as a procurer.” And below: “Thus indeed we should not know such words as ‘golden shower,’ ‘lap,’ ‘deception,’ ‘the temples of heaven,’ and the words written in that passage, unless Terence introduced a wicked young man who set Jupiter before himself as an example for debauchery, while he looks at a painting on a wall, where there was this picture: Jupiter, who, they say, once sent a golden shower into Danaë’s lap, having played a trick upon the woman. And see how he incites himself to lust, as though by heavenly instruction: ‘But what god?’ he says, ‘the one who shakes the temples of heaven with supreme sound. Could I, a little man, not do it? Indeed I did it, and gladly.’ It is not at all through this indecency that such words are learned more conveniently; rather, through these words that indecency is committed more boldly.”]

What have you to do with false vanities and insanities? What have you to do with the fabulous loves of heathen gods, when you ought to be an instrument of truth? O good Jesus, O true Truth, how truths have been diminished among the children of men! “Lord, the beginning of thy words is truth”; [Note: [Col. 0231] Psalm 118.] truth is round about thee; and all [Col. 0232C] thy commandments are truth. [Note: [Col. 0231] Ibid.] And what madness it is to sing fables of Hercules and Jupiter, and to depart from God, who is the way, the truth, and the life! [Note: [Col. 0231] John 14.] “The wicked have related fables to me,” he says, “but not as thy law.” [Note: [Col. 0231] Psalm 118.] For thy law, O Lord, is an immaculate law, [Note: [Col. 0231] Psalm 18.] converting souls; and it converts souls because it does not permit them to be tripped up. For it is written of the just man: “The law of God is in his heart, and his steps are not tripped up.” [Note: [Col. 0231] Psalm 36.] “Sinners,” he says, [Col. 0233A] “have set a snare for me, and I have not wandered from thy commandments.” [Note: [Col. 0233] Psalm 118.] How have you not wandered? Because “I have acquired thy testimonies as an inheritance,” [Note: [Col. 0233] Ibid.] so that I may not sin against thee. “Sinners,” he says, “waited for me, that they might destroy me; but they did not prevail, because I understood thy testimonies.” [Note: [Col. 0233] Ibid.]

In the fables of pagans, in philosophical studies [Note: [Col. 0233D] That is, those which St Augustine, *Letter* 131, called “the chattering subtleties of philosophers, vanities, lying insanities, windy trifles, and proud errors.”], and finally in civil law [Note: [Col. 0233D] See Letters 26 and 140, in which he shows that a cleric ought not to spend his days, even to old age, on civil law, but ought wholly to give himself to the study of theology and to the reading of divinely inspired writings.], you have spent your days even to old age; and, contrary to the wish of all who love you, you have culpably recoiled from the sacred page of theology. Hear the prophet: “You looked for much, and behold it came to little; you brought in your labour, and you said, ‘Behold, from my labour’; and I blew it away, saith the Lord of hosts.” [Note: [Col. 0233] Haggai 1.] You are already sprinkled with grey hairs, yet you still devote yourself to childish things. Wisdom cries aloud in the streets: “How long, little ones, [Col. 0233B] will you love childhood, and fools embrace things harmful to themselves?” [Note: [Col. 0233] Proverbs 1.] I fear lest that saying of the wise man applies to you: “Strangers have devoured his strength, and he knew it not; yea, grey hairs are spread upon him, and he knew it not”—you who ought to think of the Lord in goodness and, in the life-giving Scriptures, to taste the glory of the magnificence of his sweetness, yet write love-songs [Note: [Col. 0233D] On love-songs of this sort Augustine, *On the Ten Strings of the Heart*, ch. 4: “By such indecencies of songs human minds are enticed, enfeebled, and fall away from virtue, flowing down into shamefulness; and afterwards, because of those very shameful acts, they feel pains and digest with great bitterness what they drank with temporal sweetness.”] and, by profane inventions, arousing passions of desire both in yourself and in others, provoke the Creator’s indignation. You make your shame public, so that blood may touch blood, and he who is in filth may become filthier still. [Note: [Col. 0233] Apocalypse 22.] “They have proclaimed their sin,” says the prophet, “as Sodom did.” [Note: [Col. 0233] Isaiah 3.] But, on the contrary, the prophetic discourse cries: “Do not go up to Beth-aven or Gilgal,” [Note: [Col. 0233] Hosea 4.] that is, do not publicly [Col. 0233C] proclaim your disgrace. It is the mark of a mad mind to sing of illicit loves and boast of oneself as a corrupter of virgins. Hear what Job says: “I made a covenant with my eyes, that I would not even think upon a virgin.” [Note: [Col. 0233] Chapter 31.] It is a wise man’s saying [Note: [Col. 0233] Herodotus.]: “Do not speak shameful things; for shame gradually slips away through words.” “Let not even shamefulness,” says the Apostle, “be named among you.” [Note: [Col. 0233] Ephesians 5.] And he himself, speaking of buffoonish and meddlesome persons in the Second Epistle to the Thessalonians, says: “We denounce to you, brethren, and command you through Jesus the Son of God, that you have no fellowship with them.” [Note: [Col. 0234D] This is cited from the Apostle in sense, not in his exact words.]

What profit, I ask you, is there in speaking words into the wind and expending the talent of learning entrusted to you by the Lord upon fabulous inventions? He will demand back his talent [Col. 0233D] with interest. [Col. 0234A] He is a hard man: he reaps where he has not sown. [Note: [Col. 0233] Matthew 25.] For the treasure which you possess, you have thus far placed in an earthen vessel as though at the hazard of dice. See whether that word of the Lord through the prophet touches you: “Thy silver is turned into dross”; [Note: [Col. 0233] Isaiah 1.] and again: “I gave them my gold and silver, but they made Baal from my gold and silver.” [Note: [Col. 0233] Hosea 2.] What have you to do with Jupiter and Hercules? Against the prohibition of the law, you presume to plant a grove of idolatry beside the altar of the Lord. Alas, alas! The prince of this world had been cast out; [Note: [Col. 0233] John 12.] and we bring him back by sirens’ songs and the ravings of rhythms.

By your introduction the nations have entered into the Lord’s inheritance. The nations have entered—that is, heathen customs—into God’s sanctuary, of whom he had commanded that they should not [Col. 0234B] enter his Church. I too once gave my attention to trifles and erotic songs; [Note: [Col. 0234D] Here the author accuses his own sin and commends God’s mercy toward himself.] but through the grace of him who separated me from my mother’s womb, I rejected all these things at the very threshold of youth. The dragon of Moses devoured Pharaoh’s dragons within me, [Note: [Col. 0233] Exodus 7.] when the charm of theological sweetness emptied out the knowledge of vanity. This is the water of Jericho, whose barrenness Elisha healed by adding salt; and he went out to the springs and said: “There shall be no more death or barrenness in them.” [Note: [Col. 0233] 4 Kings 2.] The wisdom which is from above, James testifies, [Note: [Col. 0233] Chapter 3.] is first chaste, then peaceable. Therefore, having repudiated the adulterous embraces of worldly learning, you who are greater than the world, embrace the study of saving knowledge, and endeavour to present it as a chaste virgin to Christ. The Wise Man chose her as his bride and [Col. 0234C] companion when he said: “I sought her out from my youth; I took her to myself as a bride, and I became a lover of her beauty.” [Note: [Col. 0233] Wisdom 8.]

Indeed, in the law of Moses the Lord commanded the people of Israel [Note: [Col. 0233] Exodus 34.] that no one should take a wife from the race of Canaan. Moreover Jacob’s mother said: “I am weary of living because of the daughters of Heth. If my son takes a wife from the stock of Canaan, I do not wish to live.” [Note: [Col. 0233] Genesis 27.] I too, if not with a mother’s, at least with a brother’s affection, say that my soul is weary of my life unless you abandon this vanity more promptly. Furthermore, you compose everything you write with wonderful artistry and with the most exquisite elegance of thought and expression. But the Apostle condemns [Note: [Col. 0233] Colossians 2.] [Col. 0234D] things which indeed have an appearance of wisdom [Col. 0235A] according to human teachings, but do not build up unto salvation.

I once drew back from that destructive vanity, by salutary admonitions, the noble talent of my brother Master William, which was degenerating through a kind of servile occupation into the writing of comedies and tragedies. [Note: [Col. 0235D] On these, Letter 93: “Your tragedy concerning Flaura and Marcus, your verses on the flea and fly, your comedy concerning Alda, your sermons, and the other works of theological learning, render your name worthy of commendation by a more lasting remembrance,” etc. On his learning also see Letter 77. That he was a monk is clear from Letter 65; that he was abbot, from Letter 90, of the monastery of Maniace in Sicily; there he resigned that office on the counsel of our Peter: cf. Letter 93.] In a short time, pre-eminent in the practice of heavenly doctrine, he most fully repaired the loss of wasted time by the earnestness of fruitful preaching. Therefore let old things depart from your mouth, for God is the Lord of knowledges, and thoughts are prepared for him. He knows your thoughts, that they are vain. Those whose gatekeeper you strive to be, when they had known God, did not glorify him as Lord, but became vain in their thoughts, and their foolish heart was [Col. 0235B] darkened. For, professing themselves wise, they became fools. [Note: [Col. 0235] Romans 1.] But the wisdom of God has been justified by her children, [Note: [Col. 0235] Matthew 11.] who reject the wisdom of this world. The children of this age, however, are wiser in their generation than the children of light, regarding as foolishness the wisdom of preaching through which God ordained to save believers. You cannot possess at the same time the wisdom of this world, which is hostile to God and the death of souls, and the wisdom of God. You cannot walk in two ways or serve two masters; [Note: [Col. 0235] Matthew 6.] a short cloak cannot cover two persons. [Note: [Col. 0235] Isaiah 28.] How long, then, do you halt between two sides?

I ask only that, as you have presented your heart and tongue to serve uncleanness and iniquity unto iniquity, so now present the same members [Col. 0235C] to serve righteousness unto sanctification. It is already your sixth hour: why do you stand idle all day when the Lord invites you to work? It is the Wise Man’s saying: “Whatever thy hand is able to do, do earnestly; for there is neither reason, nor knowledge, nor counsel in hell, whither thou art hastening.” [Note: [Col. 0235] Ecclesiasticus 9.] The Sabbath will soon be at hand, when it will no longer be lawful for you to gather a *gomor*, or to do other work. [Note: [Col. 0235] Exodus 16.] In lost study and labour you exercise yourself subtly indeed, but uselessly. Would that you had devoted to God’s service what you have laboured to gain in human favour and grace! Paul, who considered that he knew nothing save Jesus Christ, and him crucified, said: [Note: [Col. 0235] 1 Corinthians 1.] “Whether we are beside ourselves, it is for God; whether we are sober, it is for you.” [Note: [Col. 0235] 2 Corinthians 5.] He attributed all his study to God; he never ceased to take every understanding captive into his service.

And you, venerable [Col. 0236A] master, have hitherto flourished beyond all your contemporaries in secular learning; but today the prophet’s saying has become a proverb among the people and a reproach against you: “Before the harvest it has altogether blossomed, and immature perfection shall bring forth useless unripe grapes.” [Note: [Col. 0235] Isaiah 18.] Indeed, not only the tree which bears bad fruit, but also that which bears no good fruit, awaits the sentence of cutting down; therefore the axe and fire hang over you as over a useless tree. [Note: [Col. 0235] Matthew 3.] But if you transplant yourself beside waters of refreshment—that is, into the study of sacred reading—you will flourish in the courts of the Lord’s house and bear desirable and abiding fruit. “Blessed is the man,” says one, [Note: [Col. 0235] Psalm 1.] “who meditates in the law of the Lord day and night: he shall give his fruit in its season.” The spiritual fruits, moreover, according to the Apostle, [Note: [Col. 0235] Galatians 5.] [Col. 0236B] are charity, peace, patience, long-suffering, and so forth. And what fruit do you now have in those things of which you would now be ashamed and grieved, if you tasted the delights of theological sweetness? Come out, I beg you, from the foulness of swine, so that you may be fed on the delights of God’s house; for the table of sacred Scripture is prepared for you against all spiritual wickednesses. Therefore the table of the tabernacle is said to have been placed toward the north. [Note: [Col. 0235] Exodus 26.] For this reason it is written: “Thou hast prepared before me a table against those who trouble me.” [Note: [Col. 0235] Psalm 22.]

Furthermore, that conclusion of your letter greatly troubled me in which you call the Gospel discourse harsh, tasteless, and childish. [Note: [Col. 0235D] Because, evidently, he did not comprehend it. “For there is no Scripture,” says Augustine, *On Genesis against the Manicheans*, book I, ch. 1, “which cannot easily be criticized by those who do not understand it.” And the same holy doctor says, *On the Morals of the Catholic Church*, ch. 25: “Only those who do not understand criticize, and only those who criticize are unable to understand.”] I answer each of the three charges briefly. The Lord’s [Col. 0236C] discourse is not harsh; rather, you are harsh: an earthly man, carnal, animal. Earthly and carnal persons are blind. The animal man, in the Apostle’s judgment, [Note: [Col. 0235] 1 Corinthians 2.] does not perceive the things which are of God’s Spirit, because they are foolishness to him, and he cannot understand them. When the Lord spoke of the sacrament of his body and blood, some went back in apostasy, saying: “This saying is hard.” [Note: [Col. 0235] John 6.] In calling the Lord’s discourse hard, you disgracefully conform yourself to their apostasy. The diamond and hyacinth, and other gems, are indeed hard stones, yet are no less precious. [Note: [Col. 0235] Deuteronomy 28.] It is not the Lord’s discourse [Note: [Col. 0236D] Augustine, *Exposition on Psalm* 54: “For certain things in the Scriptures seemed hard when they were obscure; once expounded, they became softened. Indeed the first heresy among Christ’s disciples arose, as it were, from the hardness of his discourse,” etc. And below: “Therefore, if the discourse is hard and is not yet understood, let it be hard to the impious; but for you let it be softened by piety, because it will someday be explained and will become oil for you, penetrating even to the bones.”] but rather you who are hard; according to the prophet’s word, the angry Lord seems to have sent upon you a bronze earth and an iron heaven—that is, hardness of reason and understanding.

And in calling the Gospel word tasteless, you differ greatly from him who says: [Col. 0237A] “How sweet are thy utterances to my palate, more than honey to my mouth!” [Note: [Col. 0237] Psalm 118.] “They are more desirable than gold and much precious stone, and sweeter than honey and the honeycomb.” [Note: [Col. 0237] Psalm 18.] I do not deny that the words of truth are childish and simple; for simplicity is always the friend of truth. [Note: [Col. 0237D] Such was Augustine’s judgment concerning the holy Scriptures, as he testifies concerning himself in *Confessions*, book III, ch. 5: “And behold, I see something not discovered by the proud nor laid bare to children, but lowly in its entrance, lofty in its progress, and veiled in mysteries; and I was not such that I could enter into it or bend my neck to its steps. For when I attended to that Scripture, I did not think as I now speak; it seemed to me unworthy to compare with Tully’s dignity. For my pride shrank from its manner, and my acuity did not penetrate its inward parts. Yet it was such as would grow with little ones; but I disdained to be a little one, and, swollen with arrogance, seemed great to myself.”] This is Shamgar’s ploughshare, by which he slew six hundred Philistines. [Note: [Col. 0237] Judges 3.] These are the droolings running down David’s beard. [Note: [Col. 0237] 1 Kings 21.] For what is more foolish in God is wiser than men. [Note: [Col. 0237] 1 Corinthians 1.] And the Apostle’s word is: “If you wish to be wise in this age, become foolish, that you may be wise.” [Note: [Col. 0237] 1 Corinthians 3.] For through the foolishness of preaching the Lord wrought salvation in the midst of the earth. Therefore be renewed in the spirit of your mind, so that, as you have borne the image of the earthly man, you may bear the image of the heavenly. Entirely abandon useless songs, [Col. 0237B] old wives’ tales, and childish ditties. [Note: [Col. 0238D] Augustine, *On True Religion*, ch. 81: “Therefore, abandoning and rejecting theatrical and poetic trifles, let us feed and give drink to the mind through consideration and treatment of the divine Scriptures—a mind weary and fevered by the hunger and thirst of vain curiosity, vainly wishing to be refreshed and satisfied by empty phantasms as though by painted banquets.”]

This especially fills me with astonishment: from where can material for singing burst forth for you, when I see you beset by innumerable anxieties? The arrows of the Lord are in you, whose indignation drinks up your spirit; [Note: [Col. 0237] Job 6.] how, then, can you devote yourself to jests when the force of grief wholly occupies your spirit? There is a time for laughing and a time for mourning. [Note: [Col. 0237] Ecclesiastes 3.] That cruel wound and recent death of John, your first-born brother, ought not to have fallen from your heart. Yet the death of Gerard renews the memory of a greater grief; though he was younger in years, he had claimed greater affections within your heart. I pass over your nephew Nicholas, of glorious promise, who was entering upon the first fruits of life, and whom bitter death suddenly snatched from your hands. I pass over in [Col. 0237C] silence the prison hardships of your brother Ammon, which he desired with the greatest longing to end swiftly through death. How did you find material for singing amid such griefs? “Music in mourning is an untimely tale.” [Note: [Col. 0237] Ecclesiasticus 22.] This one thing I ask: leaving aside empty songs, write things that savour of theological gravity, that bear fruit for integrity and build up unto salvation.

## LETTER LXXVII. TO MASTER PETER OF BLOIS

**ARGUMENT.**—He congratulates Master Peter of Blois on the sharing of their name, since he is now known throughout the whole world through his writings; then he shows that human beings are made immortal by writings. He attacks courtly flatterers and submits his book *On the Deceptions of Fortune* to Peter’s criticism.

[Col. 0237D] To his most beloved master PETER of Blois, P. of Blois, [Col. 0238A] Archdeacon of Bath, greetings and steadfastness in the sincerity of friendship.

I congratulate you with my whole heart upon our identity of name; nor do I think this happened without divine dispensation, so that we whose identity of wills had made us alike from childhood might have uniformity of names as well. If a man of more sluggish life or humbler reputation shared this name, he would be obliged to add as much honour to it as he detracted from the common titles. But now, by acquiring revenues, by intimacy with magnates, by popular favour, or by writings, I add as much praise to the shared name as you, on your part, extend knowledge of it by the same means, or perhaps by more elegant ones. Already that name has gone forth into all the earth and to the ends of the world. [Note: [Col. 0237] Psalm 18.] Our writings too, which spread and make themselves public everywhere, neither flood, fire, ruin, nor the manifold passage of ages will be able to erase. Writings alone perpetuate mortals in a kind of immortality of fame and permit no old age to steal upon the deeds of the ancients which they convey to posterity.

> “I shall be read by the lips of the people; and through every age, by fame—  
> if the prophecies of poets contain any truth—I shall live,”

says Ovid. [Note: [Col. 0237] *Metamorphoses*, book XV, at the end.] When Antony cut out Cicero’s tongue, which had dictated invectives against him, Cicero is said to have replied:

> “You achieve nothing, Antony: eloquent writings remain.”  
> [Note: [Col. 0237] Euphorbius, in the epitaph of Cicero.]

Who today would have known Lucilius unless Seneca had made him famous through his letters? The writings of Virgil and Lucan added more to Caesar’s praises [Col. 0238C] than all the riches he amassed from the world’s various provinces. The prudence of the Ithacan and the valour of Peleus’ son would to this day have lain hidden in the darkness of ignorance, unless the divine mind of Homer had made them public in verse. [Note: [Col. 0237] In the *Odyssey* and *Iliad*.] Therefore, among the rulers of the earth and those who seek or perform the world’s arduous undertakings, nothing could be found more advantageous for acquiring renown than to have as intimates and friends persons who knew and were able, by writing, to transmit deeds done to posterity.

Yet, as you recently sang most elegantly, flattery banishes truth from palaces. Only those are admitted into the favour of magnates who stroke them with blandishments and make fame-thirsty ears drunk on Babylon’s cup. They enrich with [Col. 0238D] benefits those whom they ought to torment, and deter by punishments from the presumption [Col. 0239A] of flattering. We read [Note: [Col. 0239] Valerius Maximus, book VI, ch. 3.] that the Athenians punished Timagoras with death because, in the offices of greeting, he flattered Darius. The senate of the Lacedaemonians likewise ordered Caristolus to be put to death, because he preferred secretly to disparage men rather than publicly and steadfastly rebuke them; and they imposed silence upon both flatterers and detractors.

But today the sinner is praised in the desires of his soul, and the wicked man is blessed. [Note: [Col. 0239] Psalm 10.] The most biting detractor in a man’s absence proposes nothing in his presence except what he thinks will please: “The words of his mouth are iniquity and deceit.” [Note: [Col. 0239] Psalm 35.] For he has bound himself to Gnatho’s maxim, whose words in the comic poet are these:

> “Does someone say no? I say no. Does he say yes? I say yes. In short,  
> I myself have commanded myself to agree with everything.”  
> [Note: [Col. 0239] Terence, *Eunuch*.]

> “The nation is a comic actor: you laugh? With louder guffaws  
> [Col. 0239B] he is convulsed. He weeps if he sees the tears of a friend,  
> but does not grieve. If you ask for a little fire in winter,  
> he puts on an *endromis* (a heavy cloak); if you say, ‘I am hot,’ he sweats.  
> We therefore are not equals,” says Umbricius: “the better man is he who always,  
> night and day, can assume another’s expression,  
> fling up his hands before a face, ever ready to praise  
> if his friend has belched well or done the other things.”  
> [Note: [Col. 0239] Juvenal, *Satires* 3.]

> “As those hired to weep at a funeral say  
> and do almost more than persons grieving sincerely, so  
> a mocker, however, will please more than a flatterer.”  
> [Note: [Col. 0239] Horace, *Art of Poetry*.]

Things would go well with magnates if they knew how to distinguish flattery from praise. But blind ambition for praise, believing others about itself more than itself, receives both without distinction. This too greatly advances the fortune of the flattering condition among courtiers: although not everyone may seek praise, no one rejects or despises it when offered. I do not know whether you have chosen any of our princes as matter for praise. In my book *On the Deceptions of Fortune*—which I entrust to your critical examination for correction—I magnify, according to my small ability, the deeds of my lord King Henry II of England, trusting in the Lord that the reader, if he is not envious, will receive this little work gratefully. For my desire is that my lord the king may not die in dying, but may live after death through praise; and that, when all flattering tongues have vanished, the glory of his memorial may be made eternal by the benefit of writing. I ask you always to write something that instructs readers and pours out your name into the memory of the saints and a fragrance of sweetness. [Col. 0239D] The first part of my book was corrected by Master William, my brother; but, because I fear that he may be too indulgent toward me if he finds anything faulty in it, I ask you to review the whole from the beginning with more careful attention, so that nothing may remain in it which offends the reader, induces error, does not exercise virtue, does not build up faith, does not instruct life, or does not savour of integrity.

## LETTER LXXVIII. TO R., DEAN, AND THE CHAPTER OF THE SAVIOUR

[Col. 0240A]

**ARGUMENT.**—He congratulates the dean and chapter of Blois on the restoration of their church through a certain nobleman, Geoffrey; and he exhorts them to unity and harmony of mind, and to the daily celebration of the divine office.

To his beloved lords and friends, Master R., dean, and the chapter of Saint Saviour at Blois, P. of Blois, Archdeacon of Bath, greetings, and, together with an increase of temporal goods, growth in virtues.

Thanks to the Giver of grace, because, according to the multitude of sorrows in your heart, His consolations have made our souls glad. For when, our sins demanding it, our countrymen, wandering and fugitives upon the earth, had nowhere to lay their heads [Col. 0240B], He who dwells in heaven and looks upon the lowly—the Father of orphans and Consoler of mourners—gathered together from various regions those scattered among the nations. We read that, when the children of Israel were paying tribute under the kings Chushan-rishathaim, Eglon, Moab, and Amalek, the Lord raised up Othniel and Ehud to remove the oppressor’s yoke. [Note: [Col. 0239] Judges 3.]

In a vivid image of His mercy, the Lord sent my lord John, bishop of Chartres, for our salvation, so that the walls of our earthly Jerusalem might be rebuilt and the Church of Blois, disfigured by its ancient ruins, might return to its desired renewal. The whole world had spat you out and cast you away from before its face; your pitiable captivity did not move bishops or abbots [Col. 0240C] to compassionate feeling, so as to admit you into some little church—whatever kind it might be—even under however great a burden of servitude. But Geoffrey, a knight, indeed slight in resources but distinguished by nobility both of blood and spirit, a most faithful imitator of the evangelical Samaritan, [Note: [Col. 0239] Luke 10.] showed mercy to the clergy of Blois, whose sufferings priest and Levite had despised as they passed by. Therefore his name shall be remembered from generation to generation, and his house shall inherit an everlasting blessing.

We draw confirmation of this from an example. For in the Book of Kings we read that the Lord blessed the house of Obed-edom because he received the ark of the Lord into his home. [Note: [Col. 0239] 2 Samuel 6.] Fittingly, the ark of the Lord is understood to be with him [Col. 0240D] in whose care a secure dwelling is provided for Christ’s poor, scattered abroad. My spirit has revived in this compassion of the Most High, after long being consumed by pain and sorrow. It seems to me that the times of the prophets have returned.

That common and celebrated rejoicing of the peoples comes to mind: when, under King Darius, the Temple was rebuilt through Zerubbabel; [Note: [Col. 0239] Ezra 5.] when, under Artaxerxes, Ezra restored the library, Nehemiah rebuilt the walls, and, uncovering and digging out the hidden fire after [Col. 0241A] seventy years from the thickness of the water, accomplished the burnt offering. [Note: [Col. 0241] 2 Esdras 2.] My mind gladly portrays within itself, as it were, how the Maccabees recalled their scattered brethren, restored the fallen laws, renewed the ceremonies, cleansed the holy things, adorned the Temple with golden crowns, and by a compendious act of extraordinary courage made good the losses of long desolation. [Note: [Col. 0241] 2 Maccabees 1.]

You well remember that formerly there were several clerical and prebendal churches at Blois; but our predecessors were cast down because of the enormity of their lives, and drew countless churches of the land into the share of their precipice and ruin. “Our fathers ate a sour grape, and the teeth of their sons are set on edge.” [Note: [Col. 0241] Ezekiel 18.] But this proverb shall no longer be in Israel, nor among you. For Christ, the first-fruits of those who sleep, [Col. 0241B] has appointed in your case the first fruits of resurrection after that public ruin of the clergy: raising the fallen, strengthening the broken, freeing slaves, enriching the poor, exalting the humble, gathering wanderers, and recalling those who have strayed.

And since your Church is still a rather newly planted one, more vigilant provision must be made for your peace and quiet. For plants not yet rooted deeply in the earth must fear the tyranny of the north wind and the stronger assaults of the winds. You have rivals who have tried to hinder your rising, who, corrupting Christ’s grace, waste away at your advancement. Yet this new congregation is Christ’s work, as He Himself spoke through the prophet: “The work of my hands, my inheritance, Israel.” [Note: [Col. 0241] Isaiah 19.] Therefore [Col. 0241C] the malice of the envious is not raging against you but against Christ, just as Moses says to the unbelieving and rebellious people: “What indeed are we? Your murmuring is not against us, but against the Lord.” [Note: [Col. 0241] Exodus 16.] Thus Israel is afflicted by the Jebusite, Abel by Cain, Jacob by Esau, the just by the unjust, the innocent by the guilty.

Yet the lily flourishes among thorns; and while sinners build upon the back of the righteous, the Church spreads. The iniquity of the proud is now arming every sort of malice against you. But toward those who disturb your peace, keep peaceful hearts, as the Prophet says of himself: “With those who hate peace, I was peaceable.” [Note: [Col. 0241] Psalm 119.] Conquer evil with good. For wisdom too conquers malice; and the Lord shall break the cedars of Lebanon, [Col. 0241D] shall lift His hands against their pride, and shall humble every height that exalts itself against the knowledge of God.

You are still few, and a multitude attacks you. Yet do not fear, little flock. For the Lord of Hosts comes not in a multitude, but in a few. You indeed must grow, but they must diminish; and already they are most evidently declining toward failure. He who calls things that are not as though they were, who chooses the weak in order to confound the strong, [Note: [Col. 0241] 1 Corinthians 1.] has gathered you together in His blessed name in order to repress the pride of Moab. For His word is: “Where [Col. 0242A] two or three are gathered together in my name, there am I in the midst of them.” [Note: [Col. 0241] Matthew 18.]

According to the Prophet’s testimony, “It is good and pleasant for brethren to dwell together in unity.” [Note: [Col. 0241] Psalm 132.] But your dwelling is not “together in one” unless there is among you a common union of wills. You whose single and chief desire is to see the newly founded Church prosper must know with certainty that it will grow only through unity. Let us recall the infancy of the Church at its birth, and we shall see how it had both origin and progress from unity; and in unity it shall also be completed. For the ark was made complete in one cubit; [Note: [Col. 0241] Genesis 6.] one Spirit, one faith, one baptism—these three founded the Church in Him of whom it is written: “Hear, Israel: thy God is one.” [Note: [Col. 0241] Deuteronomy 6.]

It also prospered through the benefit of unity. [Col. 0242B] For we read that “the multitude of believers was of one heart and one soul, and they had all things in common.” [Note: [Col. 0241] Acts 4.] Paul fostered this grace of unity in himself and others: “I became all things to all men, that I might gain all in Christ.” [Note: [Col. 0241] 1 Corinthians 9.] And again: “I beseech you, brethren, that you all think the same thing, and that there be no schisms among you.” [Note: [Col. 0241] 1 Corinthians 10.] The Apostle Peter, moved by the same affection and concern, says: “Before all things, have mutual charity among yourselves.” [Note: [Col. 0241] 1 Peter 4.] “Have peace among yourselves,” says Paul, “and holiness, without which no one shall see God.” [Note: [Col. 0241] Hebrews 12.] Therefore have unity of spirit in the bond of peace. For no more vivid form of angelic life can be found than social unity.

I also add this to my devout prayers: that in your church the service of due worship may be celebrated daily and solemnly [Col. 0242C]. Let observance be unceasing in chant and psalms; for this is the sacrifice of praise by which the Lord demands to be honoured. “The sacrifice of praise,” He says, “shall honour me.” [Note: [Col. 0241] Psalm 49.] Angels gladly attend psalmody if it is orderly and proceeds from devotion. “The princes went before,” says the Prophet, “joined with those singing psalms, amid maidens playing timbrels.” [Note: [Col. 0241] Psalm 67.] And again: “In the sight of angels I will sing psalms to thee, O my God.” [Note: [Col. 0241] Psalm 137.]

But if you murmur in choir; if you hiss serpent-like counsels to one another; if dishes withdraw and steal the mind from devotion; if unclean thoughts steal in while you sing psalms—then this is no pleasant and fitting psalm, no delightful and seemly praise. The hostile angel [Col. 0242D] stands beside such psalmody, while the friendly and neighbouring angel withdraws. Thus let your devotion be exercised in psalms, hymns, the sacrament of the altar, and almsgiving, so that people may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven. [Note: [Col. 0241] Matthew 5.] Thus very many will be kindled with desire for your fellowship, and the resources of the newly founded Church will receive continual increase in revenues.

Therefore, as one of the foremost among those who restored the Church of Blois, I should believe my desire fully satisfied if I saw the structure of your church rise to completion; the cloister buildings [Col. 0243A] laid out and erected; its vessels and ornaments multiplied; the number of canons increased to eighty; and service conducted in the church in good order. May my eyes see these things before I die, so that my soul may magnify the Lord, and I may close my last day in exultation and with the Song of Simeon: “Now dismiss thy servant, O Lord, according to thy word in peace.” [Note: [Col. 0243] Luke 2.] Fare well, each and all.

## LETTER LXXIX. TO R., HIS FRIEND

**Argument.**—He ridicules R., a deacon, because, although from early youth he had been a foremost enemy of the female sex, he has allowed himself, through love of women, to be drawn even into sacrilegious marriage. He greatly amplifies the inconveniences of marriage, from Book VIII, chapter 11 of John of Salisbury’s *Polycraticus*. [Col. 0243B]

M. Peter of Blois, archdeacon of Bath, to his beloved friend R., greeting, and more prudent conduct of business.

Who would not mingle heaven with earth and sea with heaven? Must we believe that anything may easily come to pass which common usage abhors and nature has forbidden? He who from boyhood detested the female sex, who always armed a slanderous tongue for its disgrace, has now fallen into the pit which he had always avoided; and he who once, in pride and derision, insulted women has of his own accord bound his neck in women’s snares. Let women then rejoice, because they have happily triumphed over their persecutor. The wolf has been captured by sheep, and the fox’s cunning has been caught out by a simple hen. [Col. 0243C]

Most wretched of men, what Hecate bewitched you? What Erinys drove your brain from its place, so that you should cast an inextricable noose about your throat, throw away most delightful liberty, and choose disgraceful slavery? In the very thing in which you sinned, God has most justly punished you. For women today stop the mouths of those who speak iniquity—women who so often endured from you the injuries of a shameless tongue, to use the words of blessed Augustine. You sailed; you took a wife. It would have been better for you to be led into exile than to lead her thus; for this very “leading” is nothing other than exile farther from good repute and tranquillity of mind.

The marital bond is not without very many inconveniences, and peace of mind with a wife is scarcely thought attainable. Valerius Maximus reports [Col. 0243D] [Note: [Col. 0243] Laertius, *Lives*.] that Socrates, when a young man asked him whether he ought to take a wife or abstain from marriage, answered that whichever he did he would regret it:

> “On this side await you solitude, childlessness, extinction of your line, and a stranger as heir; on that, perpetual anxiety, a woven web of complaints, reproach concerning her dowry, the importunity of in-laws, a mother-in-law’s chattering tongue, an angry wife because of another’s marriage, and uncertainty as to the outcome of children.”

That most renowned king Phoroneus, who was famous for distributing rather than keeping treasures, on the day he died is said to have told his brother Leontius that nothing had been lacking for his complete happiness—if only [Col. 0244A] he had lacked a wife. When Leontius asked the reason, he replied: “All husbands know it.”

According to Jerome’s testimony, [Note: [Col. 0243] Book I against Jovinian.] Aurelius Theophrastus in his book *On Marriage* asks whether a wise man ought to take a wife; and, having decided that a wise man may do so if she is beautiful, well behaved, of honourable parents, and if he himself is healthy and wealthy, immediately adds:

> “But all these circumstances very rarely concur in marriages. There are many things necessary to women’s uses: costly clothing, gold, jewels, expenditures, maidservants, varied furnishings, litters, and gilded carriages. Then come chattering complaints throughout entire nights: ‘That woman appears in public better dressed; this one is honoured by everyone; I, poor creature, am despised in the gathering of women. Why did you look at the neighbour? Why did you speak with that little maidservant? What did you bring home from [Col. 0244B] the forum?’”

We cannot have a friend or companion: she suspects that another person’s affection is her own hatred. It is difficult to support a poor wife and torture to endure a rich one. When Marius offered his daughter—rich in dowry, noble in beauty, famous in reputation, illustrious in ancestry—to Metellus in marriage, Metellus answered: “I would rather be mine than hers.” Marius replied: “Indeed, she herself will be yours.” “A wife,” said Metellus, “ought to belong to her husband.” For, in the logical rule, subjects are such as their predicates permit them to be. [Note: [Col. 0243] Jerome, Book I against Jovinian.] Thus, by a witticism, he turned his back from burdens. [Note: [Col. 0243] Psalm 80.]

Add that there is no choosing a wife: whatever sort comes along must be accepted, whether she is bad-tempered, foul-smelling, proud, foolish, or ugly. A horse, ass, ox, dog, even the cheapest slaves, a wooden chair, jugs, and pots are inspected first and then bought; a wife alone is not shown, lest she displease before she is taken. Whoever she loves, though they may be objectionable, must nevertheless be loved and honoured by you. If you entrust the whole household to her management, you must be her servant. If you reserve anything for your own control, she will think you do not trust her; this will turn into hatred, and, if she can, she will devise your destruction by poison.

If you admit old women, soothsayers, diviners, dealers in gems and silken garments, chastity is in danger; if you forbid them, you are guilty of the offence of suspicion. Livia killed her husband, whom she hated exceedingly; Lucilia killed hers, whom she loved most passionately—this one with a love-potion, that one with poison. [Note: [Col. 0243] Jovinian; Dio, *Augustus*; Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations* 2.] [Col. 0244D] Deianira subdued the tamer of monsters with monstrous poison while, in the blood of Nessus, whom Hercules had killed, she sought the blood and life of the slayer [Hercules]. [Note: [Col. 0243] Ovid, *Metamorphoses* IX.]

For this reason the Emperor Valentinian, choosing a higher life, vowed chastity and never relaxed his flesh to unlawful impulses. [Note: [Col. 0243] Bruzon, Book I, *On Abstinence*.] Hence, when he was dying as an octogenarian and heard recalled the praises of his triumphs, by which he was exceedingly famous, he said that he gloried in one victory alone. Asked about that victory, he replied: “I have always subdued and conquered my worst enemy, my own flesh.”

But to take a wife for children’s sake—so that [Col. 0245A] our name may not perish, that we may have supports in old age, and may enjoy certain heirs—is utterly foolish. What are these supports of old age? What madness is it to nourish at home one who may perhaps die before you, or prove corrupt in character, or, once you have reached mature age, think that you live too long for him? Better and more certain heirs are friends and relatives whom you choose by your own judgment than those whom you are compelled unwillingly to have.

A woman, however honourable and chaste she may be, is accustomed, as quickly as she can lay aside her clothing, to cast off modesty. Thus Herodotus writes: “A woman lays aside shame along with her garment.” [Note: [Col. 0245] Book I; Jerome, Book I against Jovinian.] If you had read and reread more often that satire of Juvenal, [Note: [Col. 0245] Satire 6.] “I believe in chastity,” and so forth, no treacherous malignity of women would have cast you down into this misery.

Canius, a poet [Note: [Col. 0245] Book III, Epistle 20.] of gentle and pleasing eloquence, was rebuked by Livius the Carthaginian, a grave married man, because he delighted in the love of many women. “You cannot,” said Livius, “share in our philosophy while you are shared by so many. For Tityus does not love Juno with that liver which many vultures tear into many pieces.” Canius replied: [Note: [Col. 0245] Book III, Epistle 20.]

> “Whenever I suffer, I rise more cautious; whenever I am crushed, I recover my breath more cheerfully. The alternation of days makes the nights pleasant; but unending darkness is like hell.”

I do not condemn marriage, in which there is a great sacrament of Christ and the Church, [Note: [Col. 0245] Ephesians 5.] but I am beyond measure astonished that you have contracted marriage—and, more astonishing still, that you are now married—especially because you were most ardent [Col. 0246A] in study and a most celebrated professor of philosophy.

We read that when Cicero was urged, after repudiating Terentia, to marry Hirtius’s sister, he rejected marriage altogether, saying that he could not devote himself equally to philosophy and to a wife. Blessed Jerome writes [Note: [Col. 0245] Book I against Jovinian.] that all Euripides’ tragedies are denunciations of women; and that Epicurus, when his disciple Metrodorus married Leontion, said: “The wise man should very rarely enter into marriage, because many and most serious inconveniences are mingled with the brief delights of marriage.”

Pacuvius, weeping, said to his neighbour: [Note: [Col. 0245] Valerius, in the Epistle to Ruffinus.] “Friend, I have in my garden a most unfortunate tree.
