My first wife, whom I had, hanged herself from it; my second wife chose to hang herself from the same tree; and my third [Col. 0246B] wife also hanged herself from it.” His friend replied: “I wonder that in so many successes you have found tears.” And again: “Good gods, from how many losses that tree has suspended you! Give me shoots from your tree, that it may come to life and grow for the death of my wife.” Such a tree would have been necessary for you.

But know that this cohabitation—lest I call it marriage—will have an unhappy outcome. For everything done in it has been undertaken against God and against apostolic enactments. You had indeed been chosen for the Lord’s portion and had risen to the order of deacon. [Note: [Col. 0245C]

For it was very recently forbidden for a deacon to pass into marriage at the Council of Westminster, under Richard, archbishop of Canterbury, in the year 1175, canon 1:

> “But if those established below the subdiaconate contract marriages, they are by no means to be separated from their wives, unless by common consent they wish to enter religious life and there remain diligently in God’s service. Yet, while living with their wives, they are in no way to receive ecclesiastical benefices. But those who, being in the subdiaconate or above, have entered into marriages are to leave their women even unwilling and resistant.”

And earlier, in 1127, at a council held in the same place under William, apostolic legate:

> “We utterly forbid priests, deacons, subdeacons, and all canons the cohabitation of illicit women. If, which God forbid, they cling to concubines or wives, let them be deprived of ecclesiastical order, honour, and benefice alike.”

The canons are extant in the continuator of Florence of Worcester. And in 1125, at another council convened there under John of Crema, apostolic legate:

> “By apostolic authority we forbid priests, deacons, subdeacons, and canons the cohabitation of wives, concubines, and indeed of all women,” etc.

Continuator of Florence.

After the death of Anselm of Canterbury, the clergy of England were compelled by royal edict to obey the statutes of the London councils held under that same pontiff. On this matter Eadmer, *Historia Novorum*, Book IV, says:

> “At the same time the cause of the priests of England was handled, and they were more strictly restrained from the society of women during the time of Father Anselm. For very many of them, greatly rejoicing at Father Anselm’s death, promised themselves that, he being removed, what they had lamented as unlawful while he lived would become lawful.” [Col. 0246C]

But the affair turned out otherwise. For the king, who was feared by many more than God, bound them by his law so that, willing or unwilling, they became at least executors in the sight of men of the London council which we noted above.

And at another council in the same place, under Anselm, in 1108:

> “It was decreed that priests, deacons, and subdeacons should live chastely, and should not have women in their houses except those joined to them by close kinship, according to the determination of the holy synod of Nicaea. But those priests, deacons, and subdeacons who, after the prohibition of the London council, kept their women or took others, if they wished thereafter to celebrate Masses, must make them altogether strangers to themselves, so that neither may the women enter their houses nor the men enter the women’s houses,” etc.

The decrees are extant in Roger of Hoveden under this year.

[Col. 0246D] And Eadmer, Book IV of the *Historia Novorum*, observes that this synod was held at the urging and request of King Henry I, because priests, despising the statutes of the earlier London council, retained their women or took women whom they had not previously had; and the king wished to suppress this crime of incontinence. This London council was held in 1102. The statute under discussion is as follows:

> “Let no archdeacon, priest, deacon, or canon take a wife or retain one already taken,” etc.

It is extant in William of Malmesbury, Book I, *On the Deeds of the Bishops of England*, under Anselm, [Col. 0247C] and in Eadmer, Book III of the *Historia Novorum*. Concerning it, Anselm, Book III, Letter 62.

And before Anselm, the Council of Enham, drawn from all England, under Ælfheah of Canterbury, chapter 2:

> “We especially beseech and instruct all ministers of God, and priests in particular, that, obedient to God, they cultivate chastity and thus fortify and defend themselves against the wrath of the Lord. For let them know with certainty that they ought not, for any reason of sexual intercourse, to have the society of a wife,” etc.

And earlier Lanfranc of Canterbury, Letter 17 to John of Rouen:

> “Moved by your example and that of the venerable Fathers, throughout the whole land of England I have, by pastoral authority, forbidden any canon of whatever order to take a wife, and have decreed that anyone who had previously taken one, if he is a priest or deacon, may no longer keep her unless he wishes to be without his prebend.”

Again Lanfranc himself, in Letter 21 to Herfast, speaking of a deacon ordained irregularly:

> “When I asked him whether he had a wife, he replied that he had one and did not wish [Col. 0247D] to put her away. Therefore, supported by divine authority, I decree that provision be made for him on these terms: the diaconate is to be taken from him, and he is to be promoted to the other lower orders at suitable intervals. But he is never to receive the order of deacon unless he lives chastely and promises by canonical attestation that he will live chastely from then on. If, however, he has lived a celibate life and is willing to promise that he will do so always, you shall not ordain him again to the order of deacon, but shall restore the office itself to him through the book of the Holy Gospel, either in synod or in an assembly of many clergy.”

A general English council under Dunstan of Canterbury in 969 decreed that all canons, [Col. 0248C] priests, deacons, and subdeacons should either live chastely or leave the churches which they held. So says Osbern, precentor of Canterbury, in the *Life of St Dunstan* in Surius, 19 May, and the *Acts of St Oswald* in the same author, 15 October. If the Magdeburg Centuriators are to be believed, in the eighth century, chapter 9, a London council was held in the year of the Lord 712 under Boniface, apostolic legate, and Berhtwald of Canterbury, which issued a decree concerning the repudiation of priests’ wives.

Finally, in the year of Christ 601, Gregory the Great, answering Augustine’s question whether clerics unable to remain continent might marry, and, if they married, whether they ought to return to secular life, replied thus:

> “But if there are clerics outside the sacred orders who cannot contain themselves, they ought to take wives.”

The same discipline also prevailed in Gaul, as is clear from Innocent I to Victoricius of Rouen, chapter 9; Leo the Great to Rusticus of Narbonne, [Col. 0248D] chapter 92, response to inquiry 9; the Council of Tours, chapter 2; Agde, chapter 9; Auvergne, chapter 13; Orléans IV, chapter 17; Lyons III, chapter 1; and Pope Zachary, Letter 9.

The discipline was the same in the Churches of Spain, as clearly appears from the Council of Elvira, chapter 37; Siricius, as cited by Innocent I to Exuperius of Toledo; Toledo I, chapter 1; Toledo II, chapter 3; Toledo III, chapter 5; and Toledo VIII, chapter 5.

The same held in the African Church, according to Siricius, Letter 4, *To the Africans*, chapter 9; the Second Council of Carthage, chapter 2; and so forth.

The same held in the Eastern Church, according to Ancyra, canon 10; Epiphanius, *Heresy* 59. Read Jerome, *Against Vigilantius*, chapter 1.]

—and perhaps under that pretext you rushed into marital vows, intending, once you had satisfied the appetite of new lust, to obtain a divorce by reason of the unlawful union. Moreover, apart from the danger to your soul, it is dangerous for you thus to mock your wife’s parents, who have often complained that they debased the rank of their family too greatly by admitting you to a share in their kindred. I see you hemmed in by unavoidable straits: whether you remain in marriage or separate from your wife, you will not escape danger to life or reputation. Farewell, and conduct your affairs more wisely.

## LETTER LXXX. TO G., HIS FRIEND

**Argument.**—He advises his friend G. not to leave the monastery because of the envy or ill will of false brethren; such envy has benefited many by advancing them in virtue. Then he warns him not to cloak his own wickedness under the pretext of another’s ill will.

Peter of Blois, archdeacon of Bath, to his most dear friend [Col. 0247B] G., greeting and the unfading fruits of patience.

It is reported that you wish to issue a prohibition against leaving, and, after greeting from the very threshold the congregation of saints, say that you cannot endure the envy within your house and the danger from false brethren. The occasion for your departure is either nonexistent or futile; for it ought to have redounded to your glory that you possess something which a rival might envy. Envy ignores only the wretched. Yet the sting of another’s malice rouses a strong man to exercise virtue, nor does the envy of detractors allow the eyes of the mind to grow dull.

Jacob, [Note: [Col. 0247] Genesis 32.] who crossed the Jordan with his staff, would not have returned with two companies unless Esau’s envy had stirred him. [Col. 0248A] Joseph would not have ruled Egypt [Note: [Col. 0247] Genesis 37.] unless his brothers’ envy had sold him. For it is written: there can be no Abel whom Cain’s envy does not test. Perhaps someone envied you, but you had your avenger. He who raised the instruments of envy against your innocence bore his own torturer in his mind. For, according to the saying of the moralist:

> Nothing is more just than envy, which immediately  
> Torments its own author, racking his mind.

Are they not torments—to wither, languish, and perish because of the good things of others? Hear the poet: [Note: [Col. 0247] Horace, Book I, Epistle 2.]

> The envious man grows lean at another’s prosperity.

Hear another, defining the character of envy:

> To exult over misfortunes and grieve at prosperity. [Note: [Col. 0247] Statius, *Thebaid* II.]

Hear Job also: [Note: [Col. 0247] Chapter 5.] “Anger kills the fool,” he says, [Col. 0248B] “and envy slays the little one”; for faint-heartedness produces envy. In judging himself inferior and lesser than another, malice kindles in him the fire of jealousy. Therefore endure it while your envious rivals kill themselves, so that their sword may enter into their own hearts. Thus Goliath was killed with the sword with which he threatened David’s destruction. [Note: [Col. 0247] 1 Samuel 17.] Haman was hanged on the gallows upon which he had destined Mordecai for punishment. [Note: [Col. 0247] Esther 7.] Solomon’s saying is: “He who casts a stone upward, it shall fall upon his own head.” [Note: [Col. 0247] Ecclesiasticus 27.]

> Nor is there any law more just  
> Than that contrivers of death should perish by their own contrivance.

Since this plague is more tolerable to the envied person than to the envious, you are excessively delicate if you cannot endure the suffering of your rival. Detractors, hateful to God, as the Apostle says, [Note: [Col. 0249] Romans 1.] the more maliciously they corrupt your innocence, the more they prove themselves inferior and the more splendidly exalt the titles of your virtue, as the poet testifies: [Note: [Col. 0249] Ovid, Book I, *Remedies for Love*.]

> Envy aims at the highest; winds blow upon the loftiest heights.

Those whose lives are more favourable to glory feel sharper bites of envy.

> He who surpasses the arts  
> Set beneath him burns with his own brilliance. [Note: [Col. 0249] Horace, Book II, Epistle 1.]

We read that, when Plato’s companions envied him, he asked his teacher Socrates how he might avoid their envy. Socrates replied: “Become like Thersites.” In this he plainly showed that envy is absent where the grace of virtues is absent. [Col. 0249B]

Christ’s innocence did not escape the stings of envy. Thus Pilate at one point recognized that they had delivered Him through envy. [Note: [Col. 0249] Matthew 27.] “Is this not the carpenter’s son?” [Note: [Col. 0249] Matthew 13.] they said. “This man is not from God, because he does not keep the Sabbath.” [Note: [Col. 0249] John 9.] “He casts out demons by Beelzebub, prince of demons.” [Note: [Col. 0249] Luke 11.] Whom would not such words burn, proceeding as they did from the furnace of envy? As the old man in the *Andria* teaches:

> If you wished to serve humility and patience, you would find praise  
> Without envy, and friends as equals. [Note: [Col. 0249] Terence, Act I, Scene I.]

We read [Note: [Col. 0249] Plutarch, *Apophthegmata*.] that Julius Caesar, upon hearing of Cato’s death, grieved for it and lamented that an outstanding citizen had been removed and taken from the commonwealth. Yet he confessed that Cato had envied his actions, and that he himself had envied Cato’s glory. [Col. 0249C] I see nothing more glorious in you than that you have envious people: that you afflict and burn those who hate you, and torment your enemies amid your pleasures.

Yet I fear that something other than the envy of brethren is shutting you out from the cloister. For I know the fickleness of your mind; and, if public report is to be believed, you do not flee the envy of those in the cloister but pursue worldly pleasure. Take care not to wish, under the pretext of another’s ill will, to cloak your own wickedness, and, by leaving the cloister, prepare for yourself an entrance into hell.

## LETTER LXXXI. TO SIMON, CANON OF CHARTRES

**Argument.**—He urges Simon, a canon who has abandoned the study of letters in order to gather wealth, to pursue literary study, cutting off the desire for riches, after the example of many philosophers.

M. Peter of Blois, archdeacon of Bath, to Simon, canon of Chartres: health of mind and body, and a desire for virtue.

My soul, which your illness had greatly saddened, has been gladdened by your recovery. Now, however, you would restore me to complete exultation of spirit if, leaving childish things behind, you applied yourself to more mature pursuits, since you have now passed the bounds of childhood. The farmer’s hope is more keenly delighted if he sees the plant he cultivates bloom and promise timely fruit. Conversely, he is deeply dismayed if the plant never swells into flower, but merely spreads itself into branches and luxuriates in a degenerate abundance of leaves. Certainly it is time for you to devote yourself to more honorable studies, and to restrain the first stirrings of a prurient puberty beneath a tighter bond of guardianship and a more watchful prudence. Desires of the flesh indeed creep in; they secretly destroy the grace of study and, under a certain indulgence granted to one’s age, make war to the detriment of virtue. If you had tasted even a little of the love of wisdom and the sweetness of learning, the hope I entertain for your virtue would smile upon me more securely.

[Col. 0250B] For until now you have been under the rod of discipline and the master’s yoke; the urgency of your teacher has shaped your character like the forcible impression of a seal. But you would display the surest signs of virtue if you changed fear into love and necessity into desire. Since study is an intense application of the mind to doing or considering something, no one can be studious whose mind is not kindled by a voluntary desire to learn. But one who is negligent or slack in such matters is not very unlike a person who, with appetite languishing and palate dull, takes food and forcibly thrusts incompatible dishes into a stomach disgusted by its fastidious throat. If you had once tasted the sweetness of wisdom, everything apart from [Col. 0250C] it would turn to distaste for you. For it possesses incomparable treasures of delight and grants in fullness the favor of every good; and perhaps Solomon’s words refer to this: “I loved wisdom above health and every beauty, and I resolved to have her in place of light. All good things,” he says, “came to me together with her.” [Note: [Col. 0249] Wisdom 7.]

Once admitted, the love of learning is with difficulty lost; passing into longing, it perpetuates itself by its own delight and lasts as long as a human life. We read [Note: [Col. 0249] Valerius Maximus, book VII, chapter 7; Plato, *Republic*, book VII] that Solon, pre-eminent in his own time among the Athenians for the glory of wisdom, when he was in his last illness, raised his head as his friends sat beside him and conversed with one another; and, when asked why he had done so, replied: “So that, when I have understood this—whatever it is that you are discussing—I may [Col. 0250D] die.” Carneades the philosopher [Note: [Col. 0249] Cicero, *Academics*, I], a laborious soldier of wisdom, spent and completed ninety years in study. Yet you have scarcely completed four years in the schools, and, casting aside your studies, you plunge yourself into the anxieties of temporal affairs. You seek to set your estate in order—an estate that will doubtless be endangered in your hands—and, moreover, whatever you have learned thus far will fly away into the winds. I know that, as a son of this world, you thirstily seek riches; but you would act more wisely and more bravely if, with Solomon, you preferred wisdom to riches. You cannot attend equally to learning and riches. Nor does wisdom deign to dwell in a soul which it sees infected by desires and entangled in temporal cares. It is written [Note: [Col. 0251] Wisdom 1] that “wisdom will not enter a malevolent soul, nor dwell in a body subject to sins.”

Formerly, professors of philosophy execrated riches, and did not think that wisdom could be gained amid anxiety for them, or that one could serve worthily in the camp of learning. The poet says [Note: [Col. 0251] Juvenal, *Satires*, 7]:

> What place is there for genius, unless, when they vex themselves  
> with song alone and are carried to the lords of Cirrha and Nysa,  
> our hearts admit not two concerns?  
> It is the work of a great mind, not one stunned by having to provide a blanket,  
> to behold chariots and horses and the faces of gods,  
> and the Fury that confounds the Rutulian.

[Col. 0251B] Therefore, when Demetrius’s father [Note: [Col. 0251] Valerius Maximus, book VIII, chapter 7] had left his son such great wealth that he could have maintained King Xerxes’ army for one day, Democritus gave his patrimony to his native city; and, spending his days at Athens in learning and teaching, he completed the arduous business of study in golden poverty. Crates of Thebes, having thrown no small weight of gold into the sea, said: “Go to the bottom, most evil riches! I shall drown you, lest I be drowned by you.” When Anaxagoras, after long years of study, returned to his country and found that his own estates had been enormously squandered during his long absence, he said: “I should not be safe, unless these had perished.” Socrates is said to have declared [Note: [Col. 0251] Cicero, *To Paetus*] that no one becomes studious unless he considers himself moderately poor. For just as superfluous wealth is to be rejected, so poverty, unless it is bearable and clean, does not permit study. For riches inflame the mind, and poverty overthrows it, as the moral poet says [Note: [Col. 0251] Horace, book I, epistle 10]:

> A man whose circumstances do not fit him, like a shoe long ago:  
> if it is larger than his foot, it will trip him; if smaller, it will hurt him.

Since, therefore, God has abundantly provided you with the means to continue your scholarly service, I ask, advise, and counsel you to pursue with fuller study the praiseworthy beginning of your natural gifts; for a time suspend the acquisition of riches, and devote your whole self to the love of wisdom. According to Solomon’s testimony [Note: [Col. 0251] Wisdom 7], temporal and eternal goods alike will follow it as accessories and consequences. Farewell.

## LETTER LXXXII. TO THE ABBOT AND CONVENT OF CÎTEAUX

[Col. 0252A]

**SUMMARY.—**Richard, Archbishop of Canterbury, after great praise of the Cistercian order, shows that it is gravely tarnished by this single blemish: that they withhold customary tithes from clerics and monks. He then threatens excommunication and the force of the secular arm unless they pay them.

RICHARD, by God’s grace Archbishop of Canterbury, Primate of all England, and legate of the Apostolic See, to his beloved brothers and friends in Christ, the abbot and convent of Cîteaux: greeting and salutary counsel.

Although we love you in the bowels of Christ and with unfeigned charity, we are nevertheless compelled to bring to you, and concerning you, a grave and public complaint. For although, by God’s grace, your house is most renowned [Col. 0252B] for observance of the order and perseverance in holiness [Note: [Col. 0251D] The same occurs in praise of Cîteaux in letters 8 and 96. Stephen of Tournai, letter 1: “Fulfilling the Gospel, they observe the monastic rule which Benedict, the faithful innkeeper of the Samaritan, added as a work beyond obligation, so that they seem not to let one iota of it pass by.” John of Salisbury, *Polycraticus*, book VII, chapter 21: “The Cistercians follow to the letter the precepts and footsteps of blessed Benedict, who is known to have been full of the spirit of all the righteous.” Philip, Abbot of Bonne-Espérance, *On the Continence of Clerics*, chapter 125: “They adhere so closely to the Rule of Benedict under which they live that they persevere in everything which it either commands literally or urges; believing that they could not otherwise observe it to the letter unless they exercised the utmost diligence in small matters as well as great. Concerning that monastery called Cîteaux, in which, in our times, the Benedictine Rule is restored to the truth of its letter,” etc. William of Malmesbury, book IV, *Deeds of the Kings of the English*: “They are so intent upon the Rule that they think not one iota or stroke ought to be passed over.”], it is dangerous, for the sake of a trifling matter, to lose the title and glory of so great a reputation and exchange them for a temporal advantage at the cost of one’s good name.

Among all the varieties of orders by which Christ’s bride is adorned, no order is more fragrant in virtue, none sweeter in the odor of its holy name in Christ, than yours—if you remove the single matter through which the enemy of humankind presumes to assail your integrity. You know that avarice is the root of all evils [Note: [Col. 0251] 1 Timothy 6]; yet it is publicly said—and we repeat it ourselves with tears—that this mother of transgression, teacher of wrongdoing, chief captain of iniquity and charioteer of malice, murderer of virtues, [Col. 0252C] origin of sedition, pit of scandals, has dared to force its way even into your congregations. You renounced the world and its desires, and with Joshua you overthrew within yourselves your spiritual Jericho. He who rebuilds Jericho incurs the sentence of a curse; and, with Achan son of Carmi, he is buried beneath stones who is convicted of taking something from the accursed things of Jericho [Note: [Col. 0251] Joshua 7]. Tobit says [Note: [Col. 0251] Chapter 2]: “See that it is not stolen.” For theft is committed whenever another’s property is handled against its owner’s will. Indeed, in civil law the crime of robbery is defined as a more wicked kind of theft [Note: [Col. 0251] *Digest*, “On acts done through fear,” § “He who uses force”]. We do not call anyone robber or thief; but we fear that your reputation will be blemished if you covet or seize another’s property.

All speak with one voice: professors of the Cistercian order bear the triumphant titles of holiness in so much greater distinction [Col. 0253A] than others as they cling more expressly to the footsteps of apostolic religion. In scantiness of food, roughness of clothing, vigils, confessions, disciplines, psalms, humility, hospitality, obedience, charity, and all else by which the fruit of life is sown on earth, you abase the flesh and raise up the spirit. Everywhere people would compare you to the purity of angelic life, since universal human praise attends you with the fullest favor—were it not for one “unless,” which cries out to the contrary and discolors the fair countenance of your glorious reputation. And what is this cursed conjunction, “unless,” if not that which separates you from Christ’s grace and from human favor? We say this unwillingly and with grief, but universal murmuring and common complaint compel us to say it. The wishes and tongues of all would be freely loosed in praise of your holiness, unless you seized what belongs to another, unless you took tithes from monks and clerics. This is indeed a conjunction, and a very small word, but one which gravely dishonors your life.

By the testimony of Holy Scripture, tithes are revenues belonging to needy souls. What is this injurious exemption, that you should be exempt from paying tithes upon lands which were liable for them before they became yours, and which have hitherto been paid to churches—not on account of the persons holding them, but by reason of the territory? If lands have passed into your possession, why should another’s right be endangered in this respect? For, in common opinion, the lands passed to you [Col. 0253C] with their burden. Why do you procure privileges for your lands and provisions, to another’s injury, in order to take what is another’s? Did not Abel have regard to the Lord from his own provisions? [Note: [Col. 0253] Genesis 4.] Are you more righteous than the first of all righteous men, that you should raise yourselves against God’s justice? Through the prophet [Note: [Col. 0253] Malachi 3], the Lord commanded tithes to be brought into His storehouse; you command them to be taken from His storehouse. It is the justice of the divine law that tithes should fall to the lot of the Levites [Note: [Col. 0253] Leviticus 27]; therefore he plainly resists God’s justice who strives to remove from the ministers of the Church the right of tithe-taking.

Indeed, from these matters and similar ones it is sufficiently clear that, if the virtue of obedience consists in payment of rents, rendering of tithes, or recognition of another’s right, you would readily cast off the yoke of obedience. The knights of France claim for themselves the right of levying tithes [Col. 0253D] and, paying no respect to your privileges, forcibly exact them from you. You ought to rise against them, not against clerics or the churches of clerics; you ought to recall that you yourselves were once clerics and received the sacraments of salvation in their churches. Yet both the bond of Christian profession and the devotion of filial affection have put on the character of stepchildren and, under the pretext of religion, have passed into contempt.

We do not set our mouth against heaven, nor do we dispute the act of the supreme pontiff. But if the lord pope at some time granted you a special indulgence, when your order rejoiced in poverty and liberally poured out the resources of its slender means for the use of the needy, it could temporarily be tolerated—though it issued in a common injury—that what necessity had introduced should continue. Now, however, when your possessions have multiplied even beyond measure, these privileges are judged instruments of ambition rather than of religion. Whatever privileges of the Roman Church may grant, I do not believe it expedient for you to usurp, against your conscience, what belongs to another.

What if that See had issued a public edict that, wherever you found clerics or monks of another habit riding, you might dismount them from their mounts and keep their horses for your own use? What difference is there whether [Col. 0254B] you seize horses or tithes, except that a tithe is a spiritual thing and therefore sacrilege committed in tithes is more monstrous than that committed in horses? Since the Lord commands that tithes be paid [Note: [Col. 0253] Ibid.], who could dispense against His command? Where divine and human command contradict one another [Note: [Col. 0253] Matthew 22], God must be obeyed rather than men [Note: [Col. 0253] Acts 5]. And since there are two laws, external and internal, the internal always prevails: what the purity of conscience dictates to me is stronger than an external command and renders void every indulgence of another’s dispensation.

If the children of Israel, by the Lord’s command and in recompense for the long service they had rendered to the Egyptians, took from them vessels of silver and gold [Note: [Col. 0253] Exodus 12], it does not serve your purpose to draw this as a consequence unless it is established that the Lord commanded it and that you have rendered us, as Egyptians, the service of long slavery. Therefore act more wisely and modestly: take care that the mark of the aforesaid ambition, which dishonors the titles of your holiness, be cut away from you; and do not provoke universal scandal against yourselves for perishable things. “Woe to those through whom scandal comes!” [Note: [Col. 0253] Matthew 18.] Do not believe that your conscience will be harmed in any respect by restoring another’s property; for if anything is lost to your advantages in this matter, the devotion of the people, now greatly disturbed toward you, will restore all of it with more abundant generosity.

But if you show yourselves stubborn and unyielding, we shall bind with the bond of anathema all who give or sell you anything from which a right to tithes may arise [Col. 0254D]; and we shall cry to heaven and appeal to the throne of the supreme Judge that no one may absolve this bond of excommunication. We shall also obtain the favor of princes most fully in this matter, so that the civil hand may stand beside the spiritual sword, and whatever has been sold or given to you against the principal ordinance may be confiscated. Therefore, before the matter turns to a worse outcome, provide more promptly for your reputation: be willing to accustom yourselves to paying tithes, especially those which you usurp with the greatest rancor and hatred of all, and which clerics [Col. 0255A] or monks have hitherto received. For if you retain tithes only from newly cultivated lands, as Pope Adrian of blessed memory established, our loss in that matter will be more tolerable, since we have not experienced its advantages. But, in the philosopher’s judgment, what is possessed pleasantly and conveniently is not lost without pain. Farewell.

## LETTER LXXXIII. TO B., BISHOP OF EXETER

[Note: [Col. 0255B] Bartholomew, Bishop of Exeter, was a man distinguished for learning and literary eminence, a friend of John of Salisbury, from whom several letters to him survive. He was consecrated in 1167 and died in 1175.] [A.D. 1167–1175.]

**SUMMARY.—**Walter, archdeacon, urges the Bishop of Exeter, acting as an ecclesiastical judge, to dissolve, by command of the Roman pontiff, a marriage unlawfully contracted between blood relatives.

To his dearest lord and friend B., by God’s grace Bishop of Exeter, [Col. 0256A] WALTER OF COUTANCES, Archdeacon of Oxford [Note: [Col. 0255B] He became Bishop of Lincoln and afterwards Archbishop of Rouen; elsewhere we shall speak more suitably of him.], greeting in Him who judges the ends of the earth.

Since extensive learning, together with practice and experience in affairs, has made you prudent and circumspect in deciding cases, I wonder—and others who are learned in both laws also wonder—why you have delayed so long to pronounce a divorce between Robert and his kinswoman Ismene [Note: [Col. 0255B]

The degree of consanguinity between Robert and Ismene is not clear from the text. It is nevertheless certain that the marriage contracted by them was null if they were related within the seventh degree inclusive. For this was the discipline of the British churches at that time, as is made clear from these words of the Council of London held in 1125: “We forbid marriages to be contracted between persons related by blood or affinity up to the seventh generation; if any have been thus joined, they shall be separated.” See also the council of the same place in 1102; the Council of Ænham, [Col. 0255C] chapter 8; the ecclesiastical law of King Cnut; the fifty-second law of the priests of Northumbria; constitution 7 of Odo of Canterbury; and so forth; chapter 15 of the Council of Clovesho. From these passages you may also infer that in earlier centuries marriages within seven degrees of consanguinity were forbidden in England.

It was not so at the beginning of the seventh century. For Gregory the Great, answering Augustine’s seventh question, permits marriages in the third and fourth degree: “A certain earthly law,” he says, “in the Roman commonwealth permits either a brother and sister, or the son and daughter of two full brothers, or of two sisters, to unite. But we have learned by experience that offspring cannot arise from such a union, and the sacred law forbids the uncovering of the shame of kindred. Hence it is necessary that the third or even fourth generation of the faithful may lawfully be joined to one another; but the second generation, of which we have spoken, must in every way abstain from itself.”

If anyone asks why Gregory did not forbid marriages between kindred in the third and fourth degree, although they were forbidden at Rome at that time, let him hear what the same pontiff answered Bishop Felix of Sicily, who asked him about this, in letter 31, book XII: “What I wrote, as you remember, to Augustine, bishop of the English people—your fosterling—regarding unions of kindred, you should understand to have been written specially for him and the English people, who had recently come to the faith, and not generally for others, lest, through fear of harsher requirements, they should withdraw from the good which they had begun. Therefore the entire Roman city was witness for me. Nor did I commit these things to writing for them with the intention that, after they had been established with a firm root in the faith, if they were found within their own kinship, they should not be separated, or that they might unite within the line of affinity—that is, up to seven generations. Rather, while they were still neophytes, they should first very often be taught to avoid unlawful acts, by words and examples, and what they subsequently did in such matters ought reasonably and faithfully to be excluded.” And later: “Certainly, know that in these matters we did something otherwise than we ought, not on account of itself, but as an act of compassion.” And again: “For if I were to destroy what our predecessors established, I should justly be proved not a builder but a destroyer.” These latter words show that marriages between kindred in the third and fourth degree had been prohibited not first by Gregory but by Gregory’s predecessors. But did he first prohibit them in the fifth, sixth, and seventh degrees? This seems probable. It is certain and unquestionable, however, that neither during Gregory’s pontificate nor long after his death were such unions forbidden in Gaul.

But, to begin the matter from its origin: marriages in the first degree of consanguinity in the collateral line were prohibited from the time when people had the possibility of marrying persons other than their own kin, once the human race had multiplied sufficiently. Augustine, *City of God*, book XV, chapter 16: “Since the human race, after the first union of the man made from dust, required the union of males and females in order that it might multiply by begetting, and since there were no human beings except those born second from those first persons, men took their sisters as wives. Certainly, the more ancient this was, being compelled by necessity, the more blameworthy it became afterwards when religion forbade it.” And later: “When the human race had increased and multiplied, we see that this is observed even among the impious worshipers of many false gods: although brother-and-sister marriages are permitted by perverse laws, yet a better custom has preferred to shrink from this very permission. And although in the earliest times of the human race it was altogether lawful to take sisters in marriage, this is now so abhorred as though it could never have been lawful.”

[Col. 0256D] Subsequently, marriage between first cousins was disapproved by human custom before it was disapproved by human laws. Thus Augustine, in the same place: “We have experienced, even in our own times, how rarely marriage between first cousins occurred in practice, on account of the degree of closeness next to the fraternal degree, although it was lawful; for divine law did not forbid it, nor had human law yet forbidden it. Nevertheless, though lawful, the deed was abhorred because of its proximity to what was unlawful; and what was done with a first cousin seemed almost to be done with a sister, because they themselves, owing to so close a blood relationship, are called brothers and are almost siblings.”

From Ambrose, letter 48, we learn that Theodosius enacted a law condemning marriages between first cousins: “The Emperor Theodosius,” he says, “forbade paternal cousins and first cousins to enter into marriage with one another.” This law is found in the Theodosian Code, *On Incestuous Marriages*. Yet the prohibition was either not universal or was promptly amended. For marriages of first cousins are permitted by the law *Celebrandis*, which is that of Arcadius and Honorius, chapter *On Marriages*. Justinian also permits the same in the *Institutes*, *On Marriages*. The Church nevertheless thought that it ought not depart from Theodosius’s law.

Nor did it forbid only the marriage of first cousins, but also that of second cousins, that is, those born from first cousins; French synods made this kind of prohibition. I do not cite canon 61 of the Council of Agde, for it speaks indefinitely: “Or one who [marries] someone from his own consanguinity.” But I cite Epaone, chapter 30: “If anyone joins himself to a first cousin or second cousin”; Auvergne, chapter 12: “A first cousin or second cousin”; Orléans IV, chapter 27; Tours II, chapter 21; and Lyons III, chapter 4, because they embrace the determinations of the synods mentioned above. I cite Auxerre, chapter 31: “It is not lawful to take in marriage a first cousin—that is, one descended from two brothers or two sisters—nor may those born from them be joined in marriage.” [Col. 0257C] Finally, Paris V, chapter 14: “A first cousin, a second cousin.”

At that time Gregory the Great’s ruling that seven degrees of consanguinity invalidate marriage had not yet been received in practice among the Gauls. If this were not sufficiently evident from those passages in which, when such degrees are enumerated, the enumeration stops at the third, it would become altogether clear from chapter 1 of the Council of Verberie, where the third degree is treated as an invalidating impediment and the fourth as non-invalidating: “Those joined in the third degree are separated; and, after doing penance, if they so wish, they have permission to join themselves to others. But if they are found in a union of the fourth degree, we do not separate them, but impose penance upon them; nevertheless, if the act has not occurred, we grant no permission to contract a union in the fourth generation.”

Shortly afterwards, the fourth degree began in some fashion to be considered invalidating, insofar as it was desired that spouses joined by a mixed third and fourth degree should be separated. For, according to the rule found in the chapter *Quod dilectio* and the chapter *Viri*, *On Consanguinity*, in the transverse or collateral line, when persons stand at unequal distances from their common ancestor, they are related to one another in the degree in which the more remote of them stands from the common ancestor. I said “in some fashion,” because the fathers of the Council of Compiègne did not wish those who were four degrees distant from the common ancestor to be separated. Its chapter reads: “If persons are found joined in the fourth generation, we do not separate them; but if they are found in the third, they shall be separated. And those related to one another, one in the fourth and the other in the third degree, who are found joined, we separate.”

But the Council of Mainz, assembled under Charlemagne in 813, most explicitly counts the fourth degree among invalidating impediments, chapter 54: “We also prohibit anyone henceforth from being joined in marriage in the fourth generation; wherever such a union is found after the prohibition has been made, let it be separated.” It is reported in the capitularies, book V, chapter 99.

There is deep silence in Gaul concerning more remote degrees before Leo IV. But after he decreed to the bishops of Brittany, chapter 5: “As the Fathers have determined, no one may dare to join himself to one of his own kindred; otherwise let him be anathema.” Whence the decrees of blessed Gregory the Younger are most particularly to be observed: then the invalidating prohibition began to be extended as far as the seventh degree. Thus we read in the capitularies of Herard of Tours, chapter 36: “Let no one be joined in marriage in the fifth or sixth generation, and let descent be observed as far as the seventh generation.” And in chapter 7, chapter 335.

The cited decrees were promulgated in 721 at the first Roman council under Gregory II. Its chapter 9 reads: “If anyone takes as wife a woman of his own kin, or one whom his kinsman has had, let him be anathema.” This is elucidated by Gregory’s answer to Boniface’s first question, framed thus: “In what generation of relatives may marriage be contracted?” Gregory says in letter 9: “We say that, so long as people recognize themselves as related by affinity, they ought not to enter into the fellowship of this union. But since moderation rather than severity of censure is more pleasing, especially among so barbarous a people, it must be granted that they may marry after the fourth generation.” Lest anyone hesitate over the words “so long as they recognize themselves as related by affinity”—which also occur in Zacharias’s letter 7 to King Pippin and the bishops of France, chapter 22, “while one generation recognizes itself”—he should remember that Gregory III, successor of Gregory II and predecessor of Zacharias, declared in letter 1 to that same Boniface that this degree does not extend beyond seven. For thus, in answer to Boniface’s fifth question: “We have decreed that every person shall observe his own lineage to the seventh generation.” Nicholas I likewise replied to the inquiries of the Bulgarians, title 19, number 6: “Let no one take a wife from his own consanguinity until after the seventh generation, or for as long as the kinship can be recognized.”

This was the practice not only of Gaul but of the whole Church: marriages contracted within the seventh degree of consanguinity were dissolved. [Col. 0258D] It remained in force until the Lateran Council under Innocent III, chapter 50, which decreed: “Henceforth the prohibition of marital union shall not extend beyond the fourth degree of consanguinity and affinity.”

Observe three points. First, Roman pontiffs formerly dispensed persons related by blood so that they might lawfully marry. Thus Gregory II dispensed in the fifth degree and in two lower degrees with siblings through Boniface, and Gregory the Great in the third and fourth degree.

Second, the bishops of Gaul dispensed in the second and third degree for persons who had entered marriage through ignorance. Thus the Council of Orléans III, chapter 10, and Orléans IV, chapter 27, and others.

Finally, the Councils of Agde and Epaone, in the passages cited, decreed that marriages contracted before the determinations of those councils by second cousins, first cousins, and the other persons there mentioned were not to be dissolved.]

—especially since you have an express mandate of the lord pope on this matter, and since the sacred canons judge it detestable to permit such persons to live together. Lawful witnesses, liable to no exception, have indeed been produced. If in this case they have not fully persuaded you, then, according to that clause in the lord pope’s letters [Col. 0257A] which says, “and many others,” the authority also of Fabian and Celestine, together with that of other holy Fathers who lived after them and give nearer and more reliable testimony, should be admitted, so that diligent inquiry into the truth may be a lamp to your feet in turning justice into judgment. For the more shameful and monstrous the sin of incest is, the more scrupulously certainty of consanguinity must be sought, so that the judge’s sentence may not waver when pronouncing divorce.

A judge may do nothing here evasively, where the danger of souls is at stake. Therefore spare the friends further trouble and expense. They ought already to have received one judgment or the other; moreover, they gladly waive a second and third production of witnesses, if you are willing to expedite the case upon the testimony of others. If a further production is required for fuller knowledge of the matter, they offer themselves for the hearing and the second production. Choose whichever course you wish, [Col. 0259A] provided only that you do not wish further to contrive dilatory delays to their injury.

There is one matter in this case that especially troubles us. Since Robert is the firstborn son of my firstborn brother, and the whole line of our kindred depends upon him, as it were upon its head, by reason of his father, we fear that the stain of an incestuous union may be transmitted to posterity. For the entire succession will receive corruption if the limbs do not lawfully proceed from the head, the streams from the fountain, and the branches from the stock. As Holy Scripture testifies [Note: [Col. 0259] Leviticus 18], the children of incestuous persons are abominable to God. And, as blessed Gregory states [Note: [Col. 0259] Book XII, *Register*, letter 31], legitimate offspring does not arise from incestuous intercourse. Therefore, most prudent father, act decisively, and bring into effect without delaying postponement the lord pope’s mandate which you have hitherto suspended; or, by return letter, be willing to inform us why you cannot proceed in this case. Farewell.

## LETTER LXXXIV. TO ALEXANDER, POPE OF ROME

**SUMMARY.—**R., Archbishop of Canterbury, defends the reputation of bishops residing at the royal court against slanders, and shows from examples of the ancients how profitably they serve there for the kingdom.

To ALEXANDER, by God’s grace Supreme Pontiff, RICHARD, humble servant of the Church of Canterbury: devoted service of humility and obedience.

“Detractors hateful to God” [Note: [Col. 0259] Romans 1], etc. See among the various letters to Alexander, after his *Registers*, *Patrologia*, vol. CC.

## LETTER LXXXV. TO R. OF SALISBURY

**SUMMARY.—**He severely rebukes R. of Salisbury for the gluttony of his belly, explains how many evils arise from it, and shows by ancient examples how highly sobriety should be valued.

MASTER PETER OF BLOIS, Archdeacon of Bath, to R. of Salisbury: greeting in God our Savior.

If I lay before you rebukes harsher than usual, your insolence causes it, and the iniquity that proceeds from fatness. Though this has been amiably and gently urged by my many exhortations, it has not accepted the benefit of correction. If you thought of the salvation of your soul, or at least the soundness of your body, you would serve your soul more and your body less, your belly less and your spirit more. You have conspired toward the destruction of your soul, and summon the belly’s assistance to oppress it. While its gluttony seeks life by devouring everything, it kills the soul by its voracity and darkens the light of the inward person.

I should bear the monstrous growth of your belly more patiently, if from it there did not threaten very grave loss to your estates. Moreover, your possession imitates and follows its possessor: while you make a belly, your houses make bellies. Wretched man, do you not perceive the ruin of noble buildings [Col. 0260A] which the greatness of soul of your predecessor constructed? So long as you build your belly:

> You trifle with yourself, bald man;  
> a fat paunch projects by a sloping foot and a half.  
> [Note: [Col. 0259] Persius, *Satires*, 1.]

But pot-bellied walls are forbidden to project [Note: [Col. 0259] *Digest*, book 18]; their height and strength are humbled by the free course of winds and the assault of rain. In these ruined houses everyone blames not age but your idleness, seeing you dissolved in fleshly pleasures and more solicitous than is right in tending your skin:

> And all laugh at the hog from Epicurus’s herd.  
> [Note: [Col. 0259] Horace, book I, epistle 4.]

This fleshly fastidiousness entirely empties and perverts whatever was spiritual in you. It will neither permit you to halve your days nor allow you to pass with enjoyment that little of life [Col. 0260B] which remains to you. For in such a mass of body the soul, as though besieged by prison-darkness, cannot breathe into spiritual light. The limbs, moreover, abandoned by their proper functions through long idleness and torpor, await grievous disorders. Many fall ill from excessive gluttony and remedy their drunken surfeit by vomiting, shamefully casting out what they shamefully took in.

Galen, indeed, the most faithful interpreter of Hippocrates, as Jerome testifies [Note: [Col. 0259] Book II against Jovinian], reports that athletes, whose life and art consist in fattening themselves, cannot either live long or remain healthy; and that their souls, wrapped as it were in mud by excessive blood and fat, have no taste for anything refined or heavenly, but always think of belching and gluttony. On Hippocrates’ testimony [Note: [Col. 0259] In the *Aphorisms*], thick and corpulent [Col. 0260C] bodies require frequent bloodletting and other means of reduction; otherwise paralysis, gout, and other deadly diseases will break out. Hence Galen is said always to have imposed abstinence upon himself every tenth day as a medicinal aid to life; nor does one who fasts frequently, or observes the rule of a more moderate diet, easily fall ill. We read that certain persons suffering from joint disease [Note: [Col. 0259] Jerome, Book II against Jovinian] or gout were restored to the use of their limbs by the confiscation of their possessions and a simpler table. Pompeius Trogus relates [Note: [Col. 0259] Justin, Book II] that Dionysius, that utterly foul tyrant of Sicily, while devoting himself to greed and voracity, lost the sight of his eyes. For nothing preys more upon the eyes than the glut of the belly; and, as Pontinianus says, gluttony breaks down food and devours eyes. Therefore [Col. 0260D] Lucius Sulla, the consul Lepidus, and very many others are recorded [Note: [Col. 0259] Plutarch, *Life of Sulla*] to have enacted food laws, which Cato the Censor elsewhere calls sumptuary laws [Note: [Col. 0259] Aulus Gellius, Book II, ch. 24], in which the proper measure of living and nature’s sufficiency are set forth. For whatever is consumed in feasts beyond necessary use is not a debt owed to nature, but the vice of pleasure. Paul had bound himself by sumptuary laws when he said: “Having food and covering, with these we are content” [Note: [Col. 0259] 1 Tim. 6]. Scipio Aemilianus, while walking with his friends, used to eat bread so as not to lose any portion of the day [Col. 0261A] in idleness; Alexander the Great too is said to have adopted this practice [Note: [Col. 0261] Frontinus, Book IV, ch. 3]. Augustus ate ordinary and modest food; among his delicacies he counted second-quality bread, little fishes, and cow’s-milk cheese pressed by hand; he was especially fond of green figs which bore twice yearly [Note: [Col. 0261] Suetonius, *Augustus*]. Socrates said that some people live in order to eat and drink, whereas he ate and drank in order to satisfy nature and sustain the course of frail life [Note: [Col. 0261] Diogenes Laertius, Book II, *Lives of the Philosophers*]. The moralist says:

> Believe it the greatest crime to prefer life to honour,  
> And, for the sake of living, to lose the reasons for living.  
> [Note: [Col. 0261] Juvenal, *Satire* 8]

“The kingdom of God is not food and drink” [Note: [Col. 0261] Rom. 14]. “Food is for the belly, and the belly for foods; but God will destroy both it and them” [Note: [Col. 0261] 1 Cor. 6]. Yet some are wholly in their throat, [Col. 0261B] rightly comparable to gurguliones—gluttons—whose entire thought is about the belly, in the belly, and beneath the belly. They cannot be satisfied at all, until, when the belly foams over, the delight of the throat stirs up the pleasure of the loins toward sexual indulgence. Having cast aside reverence and fear of the dreadful judgment, they give themselves up to every enticement and wallow in every extraordinary pleasure.

> But when stony gout in the hands  
> Has broken the branches of the old beech—its joints—  
> Then they groaned that their fat days had passed away,  
> And the marshy light, and that life was now left to them too late.  
> [Note: [Col. 0261] Persius, *Satire* 5]

Thus sweetness will turn into bitterness, pleasantness into harshness, delight into pain; and there will be something like hell, or the beginning of infernal punishment: a continuation of pains [Col. 0261C] and a longing for death. This too is added to the height of the pain: through intemperance in eating some hunt for an empty reputation and fruitless glory, imagining that by gluttony and drunkenness they acquire from men titles of glorious renown. Yet they see honourable men, who keep their own bellies closed, exposed to every deprivation of human life and publicly begging. They consider liberality especially displayed in such persons: yet there is freedom to sin, but slavery of the soul to bodily pleasure. Certainly, as Cicero [Note: [Col. 0261] *On Duties*], Apuleius, and, what is greater, Augustine [Note: [Col. 0261] On Psalm 145] and Jerome testify, the soul is greater than the body [Note: [Col. 0261] Matt. 6]. But these men, heedless of the soul’s loss, devote the most eager [Col. 0261D] service to miserable flesh, as it is written: “He fed the barren woman, and did not treat the widow well.” But blessed Job [Note: [Col. 0261] ch. 24] most fully fulfilled the name and office of liberality: granting nothing to drunkenness or gluttony, and not following the false vanities and insanities of this life, he devoted himself wholly to the necessities of the poor. He did not feed lions, bears, or monkeys. Actors, confectioners, and singers of tales or empty trifles did not flock to him. Rather, from the consciousness of pure liberality, from a sincere heart, [Col. 0262A] and from unfeigned charity, he said:

> “Let my shoulder fall from its joint, and let my arm be torn away with its bones, if I denied the poor what they wanted; if I made the eyes of the widow wait; if I ate my morsel alone and the orphan did not eat of it; if my door was not open to the traveller; if I despised a passer-by because he had no clothing, or a poor man without a covering; if his sides did not bless me, and if he was not warmed with the fleeces of my sheep.”  
> [Note: [Col. 0261] Job 31]

Oh, how much better and in every respect more commendable is this modest and sober liberality, which bears fruit unto eternal life, than that which overturns the mind, dulls reason, destroys the body, and builds for Gehenna! If you afflicted yourself with fasts, if you relieved the fasts and afflictions of the poor, you would have provided [Col. 0262B] more wisely for yourself, and neither the abyss of the belly nor the Scyllaean whirlpool of the throat would have cast your houses headlong into ruin. But now, after the loss of your soul, I especially lament that they admit winds and rains on every side; that they are open to bats; that they have been reduced to the horror of desolation; that they hang over a precipice; that there are neither seats nor other furnishings there, neither bolts, doors, nor windows. Yet the ancient glory of the buildings would rise again if you restrained the gulf of gluttony and the destructive surfeit of your belly.

## LETTER LXXXVI TO MASTER ALEXANDER, A MONK

**Subject.**—By many arguments he seeks to persuade Alexander, a Carthusian monk, not to abandon his order—then exceedingly renowned—either because he cannot celebrate the divine service in it daily, [Col. 0262C] or for other reasons, and pass to a less strict one.

M. Peter of Blois, Archdeacon of Bath, to Master Alexander, monk: greetings, and steadfastness in the saving desire.

If I could conceal in silence the spirit of indignation conceived within me, I would rather be silent than write. But, to use Job’s words: “I am full of words, and the spirit of my belly constrains me; I am like new wine without a vent, which bursts new bottles” [Note: [Col. 0261] Job 32]. Though unwilling, I am invited and compelled by your rashness to write an invective. For, as the deer longs for shade and the hired labourer for the end of his work [Note: [Col. 0261] Job 7], so it was my particular wish to abstain from words by which [Col. 0262D] friendship is wounded. Nevertheless, I cannot bear with equanimity the ruin of your reputation. You have become a byword among clergy and people, a mockery; the shameless insolence of itching tongues rages against you, and those who consume you do not sleep [Note: [Col. 0261] Job 30]. Though you wash yourself with nitre and multiply for yourself the herb borith [soapwort], the stain of your transgression will not be taken away from you [Note: [Col. 0261] Jer. 2]. Yet you do not count the loss of reputation an injury, you who drink mockery like water; and, to use the prophet’s words, the forehead of a harlot has become yours: you refused [Col. 0263A] to be ashamed [Note: [Col. 0263] Jer. 3]. You have forsaken the fountain of living water and dug for yourself a broken cistern, unable to hold water [Note: [Col. 0263] Jer. 2]. And now what do you seek for yourself on Egypt’s way, and what on the way of the Assyrians, that you may drink troubled water? You are considering migration and are girding yourself for departure, to the confusion and scandal of your brethren. You are very unlike him who wished himself to be anathema from Christ for his brethren [Note: [Col. 0263] Rom. 9]. You began in the Spirit and are to be consummated in the flesh [Note: [Col. 0263] Gal. 3]; and, as Isaiah says, you conceived burning heat and brought forth stubble [Note: [Col. 0263] Isa. 33]. In another wise man’s words, the wind has carried away [Col. 0263B] your desire, and your faith has passed like a cloud [Note: [Col. 0263] Job 30]. For, making void your first pledge of faith, despising the newness of holy conduct by which you ought to have renewed the old man in yourself, you seek riches under some appearance of religion and sow among thorns, though it is written: “Break up your fallow ground, and do not sow among thorns” [Note: [Col. 0263] Jer. 4]. You have already grown old, and your wrinkles bear witness against you. How then has this instability crept upon you in advanced age, so that with you there is always “yes” and “no,” and you are always at variance with yourself? But by God’s judgment, he who does not agree with Christ cannot agree with himself. “You have set me,” he says, “as one opposed to you, and I have become burdensome to myself” [Note: [Col. 0263] Job 7]. The state of your mind is like the uncertainty of a breeze, like the swell of the sea, and like passing smoke. Indeed, the Lord desires to be praised among a weighty people [Note: [Col. 0263] Ps. 34]. Therefore the prophet, rebuking your life and that of those like you under the figure of Jerusalem, says: “Jerusalem sinned a sin; therefore she became unstable” [Note: [Col. 0263] Lam. 1]. In the Book of Wisdom it is written that a fool changes like the moon [Note: [Col. 0263] Ecclus. 27; Ecclus. 33]. And in the same book you read that the inward parts of a fool are like a cartwheel, and his thought like a turning axle [Note: [Col. 0263] Jer. 13]. More advanced age ought to have established your mind in some maturity. But if the Ethiopian can change his skin, or the leopard its spots, then your mind will be able to put on the gravity of a more mature life [Note: [Col. 0263] Jer. 8]. Thus my words too are full of grief. Why do you, by transgressing, [Col. 0264B] debase the holy Carthusian order, famed for its glory? “Is there no balm in Gilead, or is there no physician there?” [Note: [Col. 0263] Lam. 3] There you had found a place of penitence, the secrecy of solitude, peace of soul, the hidden joy of contemplation in the Holy Spirit, the gift of salvation, and the efficacious benefit of medicine. But, disdaining heavenly manna and sighing for the pots of flesh, you seek that house which will satisfy your desire and serve you more delicately and indulgently. Therefore you prefer the anxiety of the tumultuous crowd to silence and solitude, although you know it is written that he who takes the Lord’s yoke ought to sit alone and be silent [Note: [Col. 0263] Ecclus. 19]. This is what you find fault with and condemn in the Carthusian order: that they do not celebrate Masses on every day [Col. 0263C]

Just as I would not excuse from blame those who, out of excessive zeal for antiquity, immediately condemn and reject whatever the conditions of this age have introduced into the Church’s rites and discipline, however slight and harmless it may be; so neither can those be tolerated who measure everything by present custom, maintaining that what is now done must always have been done, and who do not hesitate to disdain and despise practices most holily and wisely established and observed by the ancients, if they have now fallen into disuse. And yet how many such people there are! Custom, now almost the sole rule, prevails. Let the author of a certain Ethiopian history serve as an example: in enumerating the errors of the Abyssinians, he counts among them the practice of prolonging fasting until evening, although this manner of fasting, most holy, handed down by the holy Fathers and observed for many centuries in the Church, was once in force; whereas the practice now received by custom, which that author alone acknowledges as if received by the Church, plainly displays a relaxation and weakening of ancient rigour. [Col. 0263D]

From the same source comes the view that, since it is now customary for those who profess Christian devotion with greater zeal to partake more frequently of the dread mysteries of the altar, it seems contrary to devotion to follow another path. That this is Busaeus’s opinion is beyond doubt to anyone who reads his words, in which he seems to criticize the ancient Carthusian custom: “The common opinion of theologians,” he says, “is that devout priests who, out of love for God, celebrate the sacred rites of Mass daily do more rightly and praiseworthily than those who refrain from them out of reverence,” etc. Before this question is weighed, one must observe that this author does not present the matter in question in good faith. For no one doubts that a man stands at a higher degree of virtue if he approaches the Eucharist daily with a supreme ardour of charity than if, led by fear alone rather than love—or by only a slight measure of love—he presents himself rarely at the divine table. But the question is whether, of two men equal in charity, the humble reverence of one, deterring him from more frequent communion, ought to be ranked beneath the zeal of the other who communicates often. The solution of this question need not be sought far off; for it is supplied fully and completely by Saint Augustine in the very passage cited by Busaeus.

Augustine, who denies that Zacchaeus, although he received Christ in his house, is to be preferred to the centurion who declared himself unworthy of so divine a guest, says: “Both honouring the Saviour in a different and almost opposite manner, both miserable through sins, both received mercy. This also bears upon the comparison: in the first people manna tasted in every person’s mouth according to his own will; so it must be judged in the mouth of every Christian how it is received. For one man, in honouring it, does not dare to receive daily; another, in honouring it, does not dare to omit it on any day. That food wills no contempt, just as manna wills no loathing.” [Col. 0264D] The certain and fixed rule, therefore, is that the degree of perfection must be judged from love, fear, and reverence toward Christ. If men are equal in these virtues, they ought not to be preferred one to another; nor can one be said to arrive at perfection more readily than another, whether he approaches the sacred table more frequently or more rarely, provided that loathing for that divine food is absent. Indeed, no one can doubt that the Church has been so minded, since she never reproved the many holy monks who communicated very rarely on that account; nor did it occur to her to prefer to their piety the custom of the populace who attend the altar’s mysteries more frequently. Nor would anyone judge the Carthusians of the present age, however great their devotion, holier than the ancient Fathers of the same order, who offered less frequently. [Col. 0265A]

I know that communion in Christ’s body is a necessary remedy, by which our weakness is aided and sustained and the heart kindled with the fire of charity. For what are we without it but earth without water? But if we receive it with the devout disposition of soul that is fitting, one communion will be equivalent to many. For we must not think that our perfection lies in frequent participation in this mystery. A surer road to it is to live according to the laws and guidance of that Spirit by whom the Church is governed; for from him the whole fruit of our communions must be expected, and he, even though we communicate rarely, can abundantly bestow upon us whatever grace we may hope for from it. It is indeed true that a religious person whom his community’s common rule and law impel toward more frequent communion would be at fault if he refused to follow the custom observed by the others; for that, unless some particular and weighty reason prevents it, is a sign of a mind wishing to live by its own direction and desiring another path than that which it could usefully follow together with others.

But by the same reasoning, others would not be praiseworthy who, finding with difficulty the contrary custom of another monastery tolerable, wished to receive the Eucharist more often than the rest. This could proceed only from misplaced zeal, deceptive devotion, or hidden pride, and would show a rashness deserving punishment. Therefore Paul wrote on another matter: “He who eats, let him not despise him who does not eat; and he who does not eat, let him not judge him who eats” (Rom. XIV) [Col. 0265C].

We are commanded by Christ under such a solemn law to approach communion that whoever does not obey is undoubtedly guilty of violating the commandment and is proved to despise the immeasurable charity which prepared that divine food. Yet the question whether these most holy mysteries are to be received more often or more rarely must be determined from the Church’s usage and discipline, which prescribes this with a view to the greater benefit of her children. It is ours to obey and to fulfil whatever she commands. If we faithfully observe what the profession of the Christian name requires, if our one concern is to follow Christ, and therefore to be prepared with the holiness fitting for daily reception of the altar’s mysteries, we need take no further care except to follow the Church’s rule and leave the frequency of our communions to depend on the rule of religious life which we profess, or on the judgment of prelates who know our soul’s inward disposition. [Col. 0265D]

I know that it may happen that one who postpones communion neglects to make himself such as he ought to be for worthy reception of the divine mysteries. For it is scarcely possible for one who approaches Christ rarely to have the disposition toward Christ that he ought. Hence come less watchfulness over oneself and a freer, less cautious manner of life, because no necessity of communicating impels us to the vigilance without which conscience would not permit us to receive such holy mysteries. This is especially what those who approach the altar less frequently must guard against. I readily grant that the Church’s laws do not require you to communicate daily; but, if you wish to take thought for your salvation, Christ commands you to live daily in such a way as to be worthy to communicate daily. If, therefore, you defer communion with the intention of making yourself more ready in the meantime through good works, you must order your life so that whatever you do, whatever you pray, whatever occurs in the whole course of life, may make you worthier day by day. [Col. 0266A]

Conversely, those who approach the Eucharist more frequently must take dreadful care lest familiarity make them careless, and lest they partake in these most holy mysteries perfunctorily and without the attention of soul that is fitting; lest they labour more to communicate than to communicate worthily; finally, lest, being less holy, they perform the holiest thing of all. Let them remember that, however frequently one approaches God, one must always approach in spirit and truth and with perpetual newness of heart. [Col. 0266B]

But if both strive, as far as they can, to advance on the path prepared for them by Christ, though differing in their manner of action they will obtain the same Spirit in Christ, the same grace, and the same mercy. But I leave these matters to be discussed by wiser persons; let each abound in his own judgment.

As for history, it is certain that the Carthusians, whom John of Salisbury in the *Polycraticus* calls “an exact model of perfect religion,” sacrificed less frequently. That this was the custom at the beginnings of the order is shown by its very statutes; and Busaeus himself admits it.

Guibert, abbot of Nogent, who flourished in Saint Bruno’s time, in Book I of his *Life*, chapter 11, where he describes Carthusian morals and institutions, writes among other things: “Unless I am mistaken, they hear Mass on Sundays [Col. 0266C] and solemn feasts.”

Peter of Cluny, somewhat later than Saint Bruno, in Book I of *Miracles*, chapter 28, where he launches into praise of the most holy order, speaks thus: “Only on feast days, in emulation of the ancient hermits, lest they be impeded from other sacred works, though inferior in dignity, do they offer to almighty God the saving sacrifice for their own salvation and that of the world.” And afterwards: “On sacred days, called the Lord’s Days by the singular privilege of the Lord or by his resurrection, and on the solemnities of himself or his saints, they celebrate Masses.” Peter the Chanter, who wrote nearly a hundred years after Saint Bruno, says almost the same in chapter 28 of the *Verbum abbreviatum*: “If the holy Carthusian order—here also an offering made to God as a holocaust, purified from the stain of the world through abstinence and mortification of the flesh, and now flying upon the wings of the winds—does not dare to consecrate except on feasts and on weekdays designated for spiritual office, how do you, a sinful priest, dare,” etc.

[Col. 0266D] Nor is there any reason why Busaeus should maintain that this custom is no longer observed among the Carthusians, since even now among them only one Mass is celebrated on more solemn feasts, and at it all the priests also communicate.

Moreover, it is known to all that this same custom of offering sacrifice less frequently prevailed not only among the Carthusians, but among almost all religious persons flourishing in the Church four hundred years ago. I shall offer a single example from Saint Francis, taken from the letter which he himself wrote to the priests of his order, commonly called the *Testament of Saint Francis*, found in volume XIII of the Cologne edition of the *Library of the Holy Fathers*. He speaks thus: “I warn and exhort in the Lord that in the places [Col. 0267D] where the brethren dwell only one Mass be celebrated in a day, according to the form of the holy Roman Church. But if there are several priests in a place, then, through the love of charity, let one be content to hear the celebration [Col. 0268D] of another priest, because our Lord Jesus Christ fills those absent and present who are worthy of him,” etc.]

—and under the pretext of this religion, or rather superstition, [Col. 0265A] you contrive your departure. Your letters make you mad. But in the words of Wisdom: “Better is a man diminished in wisdom and lacking understanding, yet possessing fear, than one who abounds in understanding and transgresses the law of the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0265] Saint Benedict]. You know that the Father of monks and founder of the sacred order did not even attain the rank of priesthood; and, deprived of Masses for a long time, he did not know, even on Easter Day, whether it was the Paschal solemnity. Paul the first hermit, Antony, the apostles Peter and Paul, and the rest whose praise is in the Gospel, are not recorded to have offered the sacrifice of salvation every day [Note: [Col. 0267] Gregory, *Dialogues*, Book II, ch. 1]. Frequency breeds contempt, and reverence for the sacrament increases from its very rarity. We sin continually, indeed, and where sins are continuous the remedy for sin ought to be continuous. Yet the priceless price of the world and common sacrifice for human salvation may not be offered except in a spirit of humility and a contrite heart. “There is death in the pot” [Note: [Col. 0267] 2 Kings 4], unless Elisha’s little meal is added as seasoning. Formerly the soul that was not afflicted at appointed times was cut off from its people [Note: [Col. 0267] Lev. 23]; nor [Col. 0267B] was the sacrifice of the Paschal lamb celebrated except amid the bitterness of wild lettuces [Note: [Col. 0267] Exod. 12]. It is a great sacrament, and must never be celebrated except with a contrite and humble heart. “Great,” says the Apostle, “is this mystery of godliness: manifested indeed in the flesh, justified in the Spirit, appeared to angels, preached among the nations, believed in the world, taken up in glory” [Note: [Col. 0267] 1 Tim. 3]. According to Ambrose’s testimony [Note: [Col. 0267] In the prayer before Mass], the sacrifice in which lies the salvation of the world must never be offered except with a pure heart, clean hands, and devout contrition. Your view, however, is that you should incorporate Christ into yourself every day, without discerning the body of the Lord [Note: [Col. 0267] 1 Cor. 11]. “For this reason many are weak and many sleep in sins” [Note: [Col. 0267] ibid.]. The wise man says: “When you sit at the table of a rich man, put a knife to your throat” [Note: [Col. 0267] Prov. 23], so that you may distinguish, with devout reverence, between heavenly food and lay or common food. Take care lest the Lord say of you: “Behold, the hand of him who betrays me is with me at the table” [Note: [Col. 0267] Luke 22]; and: “They gave gall for my food” [Note: [Col. 0267] Ps. 68]. For the Lord forbids a stranger or an unclean person to eat of the Paschal lamb [Note: [Col. 0267] Exod. 12]. Nor may Christ be laid except in a clean shroud and a new tomb [Note: [Col. 0267] Matt. 27], because the bread of life must not be received except with a clean conscience and sincere heart. For a sacrifice received unworthily condemns its recipient; it does not save him, pollutes him and does not cleanse him. The prophet says: “What is this, that my beloved has committed many crimes in my house? Will holy flesh take away his evils, in which he gloried?” [Note: [Col. 0267] Jer. 11] And elsewhere: “You who believe yourself cleansed [Col. 0267D] by sacrifices, know that you will not be cleansed, but will be polluted more greatly.” Nevertheless, lest you become in your house a cause of general scandal, and the mouth of those speaking iniquity be stopped [Note: [Col. 0267] Ps. 62], brotherly charity granted you the concession of offering the sacrifice each day with special devotion. Knowing and prudent as you are, therefore, you turn aside from life and hasten into death; and, in making excuses for sins [Note: [Col. 0267] Ps. 140], you will henceforth be able to allege no reason. If you attend to the Carthusian house which you desire to leave, consider whence you come and where you are going. You abandon Jerusalem for Babylon, the land of promise for Egypt, your homeland for exile, heaven for hell, rest and peace for labour and misery. For the Carthusian house and site of its dwelling lie among mountains, crags, and rocks, so that it is rather a habitation of angels than of men, to give the Most High a voice of confession and praise, as it is written: “Above it the birds of heaven will dwell, and from the midst of the rocks they will give their voices” [Note: [Col. 0267] Ps. 103]. The dove too nests in the clefts [Col. 0268B] of the rock [Note: [Col. 0267] Song 2]; and the prudent man builds his house upon a rock, where neither the waves of the sea, nor the wind of the storm, nor the flood of rains, nor overflowing water is feared [Note: [Col. 0267] Matt. 7]. “Truly this place is dreadful; this is none other than the house of God and the gate of heaven” [Note: [Col. 0267] Gen. 28]. And though that house is in a land of horror and vast solitude [Note: [Col. 0267] Deut. 32], it is nevertheless most renowned for observance of religion and order. Through God’s grace its fame has gone out into all the earth, and it has poured out the fragrance of its sweetness to the ends of the world [Note: [Col. 0267] Ps. 18]. For it is God’s planting and the vineyard of the Lord of Hosts. Thus it has already grown beyond measure and has produced manifold fruits. See whether its shade has not now covered the mountains, and whether it has not extended its branches as far as the sea and its shoots as far as England [Note: [Col. 0267] Ps. 79]. But you [Col. 0268C] have taught your tongue falsehood, that you might act wickedly and corrupt the order of the holy house. It is written that “the spiritual man judges all things, and is himself judged by no one” [Note: [Col. 0267] 1 Cor. 2]. But you, since you are a carnal man, sold under sin, judge spiritual men and, to your soul’s loss, bring scandal upon a most holy house. For after the pattern of that house of which it is written, “In my Father’s house are many dwelling places” [Note: [Col. 0267] John 14], each person here has his own cell and little dwelling, that he may devote himself more freely to contemplation and prayer. Thus Truth instructs us in the evangelical school, saying: “But when you pray, enter into your chamber; and, having shut the door, pray to your Father” [Note: [Col. 0267] Matt. 6].
