The Prophet had chosen the solitude of this cell, who, as he himself recalls, [Col. 0268D] “became like a pelican of the wilderness and like a solitary sparrow on the roof” [Note: [Col. 0267] Ps. 101]. “I fled afar off,” he says, “and remained in solitude” [Note: [Col. 0267] Ps. 54]. He who desires Rachel’s embraces and the delights of contemplation, in Job’s words, despises the multitude of the city and does not hear the voice of the taskmaster [Col. 0269A] [Note: [Col. 0269] Job 3]. Hence Jeremiah also: “Who will give me a place in the wilderness? Or a travellers’ lodging?” [Note: [Col. 0269] Jer. 9] If you desired leisure for yourself and wished to write, pray, read, meditate, and sing psalms, you would never have preferred the city to the wilderness, or anxiety to solitude. Now it is very plainly clear what you have nursed in your heart for many days. You dissembled for a long time, and beneath suspect silence conceived pain and brought forth iniquity [Note: [Col. 0269] Ps. 7]. In the Prophet’s words: “They have hatched eggs of asps; whoever eats of the eggs will die; and that which is brooded over will burst out into a basilisk.” It harmed your prior that he treated you too familiarly and gently; from his humility you conceived pride. He would have acted more prudently had he burdened your insolent neck and shown himself more severe toward you in many matters. [Col. 0269B] It is written in the Book of Wisdom that idleness teaches wickedness [Note: [Col. 0269] Isa. 59], and continual labours bend a servant [Note: [Col. 0269] Ecclus. 33]. And again: “A malevolent servant deserves fetters and torture, lest he be idle” [Note: [Col. 0269] ibid.]. I repeat further that knowingly and prudently you are plunging yourself into the destruction of your soul and danger to your reputation. For it is written: “He who loves danger will perish in it” [Note: [Col. 0269] Ecclus. 3]. The wisdom of religious persons is not found where you hunt and seek it; for it is not found in the land of those living pleasantly. You entered upon the path of a more perfect life, but your religion quickly withered, like a vine in its first blossom, and like a cluster casting off its flowers [Note: [Col. 0269] Job 15]. You had scarcely yet been must when you were spoiled into vinegar.

Had you learned through long experience the sweetness of that order, you would have thought more wisely. For, according to Wisdom’s testimony, [Col. 0269C] “a man experienced in many things will consider prudence, and he who has learned much will bring forth understanding” [Note: [Col. 0269] Ecclus. 34]. I can say to you what the Apostle said to Timothy: “From childhood you have known the sacred letters, which could instruct you unto salvation” [Note: [Col. 0269] 1 Tim. 3]. But, as he says to the Hebrews: “Though by this time you ought to be teachers, you again need to be taught; and you have become such as need milk, not solid food” [Note: [Col. 0269] Heb. 5]. In laws and decrees I once had you as a fellow student, but he has made you foolish who, in Job’s words, “brings counsellors to a foolish end and judges to bewilderment” [Note: [Col. 0269] Job 12]. And why is it in you to withdraw from the place to which you bound yourself by a vow of religion and the bond of stability? Learn, I beg you, to conduct your affairs more cautiously, lest you begin to repent when there will be no place for repentance. [Col. 0269D] You ought to have deliberated this before subjecting your will to another’s decision. For earlier it was in your power to decline the Lord’s service. You were in the hand of your own counsel; discernment between good and evil, fire and water, life and death was offered to you. But now you are bound by the necessity of your vow; and he who did not demand the offering now requires what has been offered. What, I ask, did you lack while you were with [Col. 0270A] the Carthusians? What is sufficient does not seek increase; sufficiency does not beg for external aid; and fullness has no need of addition. “Does the wild ass bray when it has grass, or does the ox low” (for “I do not will the death of the sinner, but that he should turn and live” [Note: [Col. 0269] Ezek. 33]) “when it stands before a full manger?” [Note: [Col. 0269] Job 6] The nature of brute animals condemns you, because, when their common fodder suffices, they rest. Your iniquity proceeded from abundance; after the labours of study and the constraints of student life, idleness made you unstable and sufficiency made you defiant. For, in the poet’s testimony:

> Minds commonly run to excess in prosperous circumstances.

“Nor is it easy to endure prosperity with an even mind.” [Note: [Col. 0269] Ovid, *Art of Love*.] I should bear it more patiently if you were transferring yourself to the observance of the Cistercian order. [Col. 0270B] For if your purpose is religious life, there is there a most approved school of religion; there the highest practice of moderation, regularity of conduct, brotherly affection, peace of mind, community of all things, mutual service, the strength of discipline, love of obedience, the bond of charity, subjection of the flesh, the exercise of hospitality, freedom for mourning, nocturnal vigils, the repose of meditation, and devotion in psalmody. What sweetness or devotion, I ask, will you find among those for whom the grumbling and confused repetition and stuffing-out of the psalms has become nauseating? Paul says: “Let us sing psalms with the spirit; let us sing psalms also with the understanding.” [Note: [Col. 0269] 1 Cor. 14.] If devotion is absent from those who sing, even though they repeat the same psalm a thousand times, this is not the psalm, the pleasant and comely praise. [Note: [Col. 0269] Ps. 146.] Solomon’s teaching [Col. 0270C] is: “My son, do not repeat a word in your mouth.” [Note: [Col. 0269] Ecclus. 7.] And since elsewhere he says, “Every labor of man is in his mouth,” [Note: [Col. 0269] Ecclus. 6.] I fear that this may be applied to them too dangerously: “The labor of their lips shall cover them.” [Note: [Col. 0269] Ps. 139.] “Ephraim is a delicate child”; [Note: [Col. 0269] Jer. 31.] and you will know that the pleasures of the flesh have withdrawn you from spiritual study. Perhaps, at the beginning of your manner of life, you were frightened by the untried harshness of life, the rigor of the order, the law of obedience, the terror of solitude, and, above all, the austerity of discipline. Yet discipline alone is the key to innocence, the anchor of religious life, the guardian of order; through it especially the motions of the mind are recalled from evil and established in good, since the Prophet warns us to “lay hold of discipline.” [Note: [Col. 0269] Ps. 2.] The Apostle echoes and agrees with the Prophet: “If you are,” he says, “without discipline, then [Col. 0270D] you are illegitimate children.” [Note: [Col. 0269] Heb. 12.]

You are certain that your departure will cause scandal to many. But it is written universally, and no one is excepted: “Woe to the man through whom scandal comes.” [Note: [Col. 0269] Matt. 18.] You would be excusable if you sinned through simplicity; but you do this deliberately, so that “your iniquity may be found unto hatred.” [Note: [Col. 0269] Ps. 35.] In Exodus the firstborn of an ass is either killed or redeemed by a sheep; [Note: [Col. 0269] Exod. 13.] by this we are given to understand that divine punishment threatens every religious man [Col. 0271A] if he does not redeem slothfulness or a failure of good work by simplicity of heart. What is expedient for you, you must see. But, to adapt the Apostle’s words to our exhortation: if there is in you any consolation in Christ, any comfort of charity, any fellowship of the Spirit, any bowels of compassion, [Note: [Col. 0271] Phil. 2.] fulfill my joy; fulfill the promise you made, lest you give your soul to destruction and your reputation to reproach.

We have long contracted a covenant of friendship, and I zealously and thirstingly desire the salvation of your soul in the bowels of Christ and in unfeigned charity. [Note: [Col. 0271] 1 Cor. 6.] Therefore I advise you what I judge expedient and honorable. I know that newcomers have lately arrived who urge you to depart. But I fear that, in your counsels, will may prevail over reason, and [Col. 0271B] in friendship novelty over long-standing attachment. Wisdom says—if indeed you deign to hear Wisdom’s word: “Do not forsake an old friend, for a new one will not be like him. New wine, a new friend: it will grow old, and you will drink it with sweetness.” [Note: [Col. 0271] Ecclus. 9.] Consider, I pray, according to the Prophet’s word, [Note: [Col. 0271] Job 6.] the paths of Tema and the roads of Sheba; and wait a little, lest, after more mature deliberation, the unstable relaxation of life, amid the overflowing turbulence of your mind, seize you for earthly things with the bonds of impiety. Be at rest within yourself; and in that calling in which you were called [Note: [Col. 0271] 2 Thess. 1.] apply yourself steadfastly to the business of your salvation.

Thus the Apostle, writing to the Philippians, [Col. 0272A] says: “Make it your endeavor to be quiet and to conduct your own business.” [Note: [Col. 0271] Phil. 9.] And in the First Epistle to the Corinthians: “My beloved brethren, be steadfast and immovable, abounding in the work of God.” [Note: [Col. 0271] 1 Cor. 15.] Always accustom yourself, I pray, to the Lord’s yoke: as you have begun, put your foot into His fetters, and do not grow weary of His bonds. [Note: [Col. 0271] Ecclus. 6.] If there is anything burdensome or bitter in the Carthusian order, love will make it all light, charity will make it all sweet. “Charity bears all things, endures all things.” [Note: [Col. 0271] 1 Cor. 13.] Nothing is difficult to one who loves.

You see that every creature is subject to vanity. [Note: [Col. 0271] Rom. 7.] “Man passes away in an image.” [Note: [Col. 0271] Ps. 38.] “His days pass like a shadow”; [Note: [Col. 0271] Ps. 143.] and all that you desire will quickly come to nothing, like running water. [Note: [Col. 0271] Ps. 57.] Therefore turn aside from the wandering excursions you desire and from the freedom of your former custom, [Col. 0272B] lest in the house of a more lax life, with immense loss of reputation, you build yourself a house of hell.

## LETTER LXXXVII. TO WILLIAM, BISHOP OF ELY

[Note: [Col. 0271C]

This William was called William Longchamp. After the death of King Henry, his father, he was appointed chancellor of the realm by Richard the king, and was then consecrated bishop of Ely. Since he possessed very great influence and favor with the king, Richard, when setting out on the Jerusalem expedition, left him as supreme administrator of the kingdom. He was indeed a great man, but not approved by all. William of Newburgh, Book IV of the *History of England*, chapter 11, calls him “a man of fierce spirit and desirous of glory.” For, in order that he might become supreme governor of the kingdom as well as of the Church, “being,” as the same author says in chapter 14, “singular in boldness and cunning, he sent a large sum to Rome and sought also the powers of the apostolic see; and through such intercession easily obtained them.”

Matthew Paris, under the year 1190, speaks of him thus: “This same chancellor was great among all westerners, king and priest in England. He regarded everything as nothing, since, not content with episcopal dignity alone, [Col. 0271D] he showed that he hoped for things too lofty. For at the very head of his letters he expressed vanity and pride when he said: ‘William, by the grace of God bishop of Ely, lord king’s chancellor, justiciar of all England, and legate of the apostolic see, greeting,’” etc. “These dignities, however, which he had obtained at a price, he exercised with immoderate excess, wishing to refill the coffers which he had emptied in obtaining them. He distributed his money at table, intending, when it returned, certainly to extort it again with interest. For he performed the office of legate, which he had acquired by paying out a thousand pounds of silver, so excessively that he became burdensome to all the churches of England, both conventual and cathedral.” [Col. 0272C] etc.

Ralph de Diceto and John Brompton, under the years 1190 and 1191, state nearly the same. All of them recount how the chancellor caused Geoffrey, archbishop of York, who was attempting to enter England against the king’s prohibition, to be thrown into prison, and how he himself was later disgracefully expelled from the kingdom by hostile parties. Yet that this was plainly attempted by envious persons is clear, since William himself, after King Richard’s return—whose deeds could not have been unknown to him—returned to his former intimacy with the king, was restored to his dignity, and was made a participant in all the king’s counsels until his last breath. We should rather believe our Peter of Blois, who knew the man especially well, in Letter 89 to Bishop Hugh, who was insufficiently fair to William, not to say envious and malicious, where he calls William “a bishop beloved of God and men; a man wise, lovable, generous, kind, gentle, and lavish in every [Col. 0272D] liberality,” etc.

Nor should it be passed over that Celestine III, the supreme pontiff, having heard of his innocence and the very grave wrongs which his adversaries had inflicted upon him, wrote letters in his favor to all the bishops of England; these are found in Baronius under the year 1191.

Moreover, having been sent by Richard as legate to the supreme pontiff together with the bishop of Durham, he was seized by illness in the region of Poitou, died, and was buried in the Cistercian monastery of Pinu, not far from the city of Poitiers, in the year 1197.]

### TO THE BISHOP. [A.D. 1191.]

**Subject.—**He consoles G., bishop of Ely, shamefully driven from the administration of the kingdom of England by the treachery of certain persons, and inveighs vehemently against the faithless counselors of kings.

To the reverend Father and lord WILLIAM, by God’s grace bishop of Ely, chancellor of the king of England and legate of the apostolic see, PETER of Blois, archdeacon of Bath, greeting, and constancy in adversity.

[Col. 0273A] I was lying sick upon my bed of pain when the frequent report of passers-by, adding pains to pains, announced how treacherously and maliciously the factional conspiracy of the envious had overthrown your innocence. From that day the arrows of the Lord have been in me, and their indignation drinks up my spirit. [Note: [Col. 0273] Job 6.] Therefore, as I groan and my eye pours forth water, the affection of one who suffers with you finds no rest. For, to use blessed Job’s words: “If I sleep, I say, ‘When shall I arise?’ and again I await the evening, and am filled with sorrows until darkness.” [Note: [Col. 0273] Job 7.]

Indeed, before you left England with the lord king, I was present and foretold to you how your rivals were already forging against you the weapons of iniquity in the furnace of envy. Envy is what delivered Christ [Col. 0273B] to death. Envy armed Cain against his brother, Saul against David, Joab against Abner and Amasa. “Through envy,” says Solomon, “death entered into the world.” [Note: [Col. 0273] Wisd. 2.] This is the beast of the forest that devoured Absalom’s army. [Note: [Col. 0273] 2 Sam. 18.] Of it the Wise Man says: “Do not walk or eat with an envious man. ‘Eat and drink,’ he will say to you, but his heart will not be with you.” [Note: [Col. 0273] Prov. 23.] “Before your eyes,” says Ecclesiasticus, “he will weep, and, as though helping you, will undermine your feet.” [Note: [Col. 0273] Ecclus. 12.]

That son of perdition [Note: [Col. 0273D] He appears to be Hugh, bishop of Coventry, to whom Letter 89 is addressed: namely, the man who, against the chancellor, supported the party of Count Mortain, who was disturbing affairs in England during the absence of his brother the king. On him more fully below, at Letter 89.]—who never made God his helper, but trusted in lying words—had honey and milk in his mouth, but concealed a scorpion’s tail in his heart. He and his accomplices, whose mouth was full of bitterness, who always taught their mouth [Col. 0273C] to speak falsehood, dealt deceitfully with their tongues. Sirens, sweet even unto destruction: your prudence could have detected their most wicked feigned friendship, but prosperity does not distinguish between friend and foe.

I saw, I saw, most reverend bishop, when those detractors hateful to God, those sellers of oil, said to you, “Well done, well done,” wickedly humbling themselves and keeping watch for your ruin. For, says Ecclesiasticus, “There is one who humbles himself wickedly, and his inward parts are full of deceit.” [Note: [Col. 0273] Ecclus. 19.] The cunning of their whorish tongue had indeed made them your household members and of one mind with you; but now “there is a sword in their lips.” [Note: [Col. 0273] Ps. 58.] And in the book of experience you read that “a man’s enemies are those of his own household”; [Note: [Col. 0273] Mic. 7.] as fire in the bosom, a serpent in the lap, and a mouse in the purse repay [Col. 0273D] their hosts.

How quickly the occasion for malice presented itself! To use Isaiah’s words: “They hatched the eggs of asps, and what was warmed among them broke forth into a basilisk.” [Note: [Col. 0273] Isa. 59.] If your enemy had cursed you, you would certainly have borne it; but now “the man of your peace, who ate your bread and walked with you in agreement,” [Note: [Col. 0273] Ps. 59.] “has greatly [Col. 0274A] increased his treachery against you.” [Note: [Col. 0273] Ps. 40.] As a man first sets out good wine, and then, when they have become drunk, that which is inferior, [Note: [Col. 0273] John 27.] so those impious deceivers, after the wine of flattering gentleness, gave you to drink wine from the suburbs of Gomorrah, the incurable poison of asps.

And I had believed, Father, that through use and familiarity you had come to know that seed of Canaan, that brood of vipers. For it is a crooked and provoking generation, which never directed its heart, and whose spirit is not right with God. [Note: [Col. 0273] Ps. 77.] If the Ethiopian can change his skin or the leopard his spots, [Note: [Col. 0273] Jer. 13.] then these men also, who have drunk iniquity like water from their youth, will be able to forget the wickedness they contracted from their parents. Solomon’s word is: “Though you pound a wicked man in a mortar like [Col. 0274B] barley, striking him from above with a pestle, his wickedness will not depart from him.” [Note: [Col. 0273] Prov. 27.]

Alas, alas! Where is the fear of God? Where is the remembrance of death? Where is the terror of hell, and that dreadful expectation of the fearful judgment? How did the bond of faith, the memory of so many benefits, so great a promise of covenant and obligation of oath, not turn back that son of eternal lamentation from so great a crime? Indeed, according to Jeremiah’s word, “the forehead of a harlot was made his; he refused to be ashamed.” [Note: [Col. 0273] Jer. 3.] His heart hardened in wickedness, and his hand is still stretched out.

Lord Jesus Christ, who are the lover of truth—or rather love and truth—how have truths failed among the children of men? [Note: [Col. 0273] Ps. 11.] “Truth and justice,” says Isaiah, “have fallen in the streets.” [Note: [Col. 0273] Isa. 49.] And Hosea: “There is no truth, there is no [Col. 0274C] mercy in the land. Cursing and falsehood have overflowed, and blood has touched blood.” [Note: [Col. 0273] Hos. 4.] Therefore cursed is the man who trusts in man; [Note: [Col. 0273] Jer. 17.] for the heart of man is perverse and inscrutable—who can know it?

Your rival displayed before you the appearance of sophistical affection, while from the foulest pit of his conscience there were already bubbling up the exhalations of hell: a burning wind, pestilential air, and corrupting breath. But, in Job’s testimony, though the pride of the wicked rises to heaven, [Note: [Col. 0273] Job 20.] in the end he shall perish like dung; for he shall pass away like a vision of the night, and the evils he has done shall find him. Solomon’s word is: “A perverse man always seeks quarrels, but an evil angel shall be sent against him.” [Note: [Col. 0273] Prov. 17.]

Therefore, Father, be patient and gird yourself for the work of strength. For if in a spirit of gentleness [Col. 0274D] you endure these things, He who pleads for the meek of the earth and leads the meek unto salvation will, because of your gentleness and justice, deliver and exalt you. “He who is afflicted and humbled,” says Job, “shall be in glory.” [Note: [Col. 0273] Job 22.] And you too should sing more often and say: “It is good for me, Lord, that you have humbled me.” [Note: [Col. 0273] Ps. 118.] The Lord has tested you as gold [Col. 0275A] in the furnace. [Note: [Col. 0275] Wisd. 3.]

There is no Jacob whom Esau does not persecute; no Abel whom Cain’s malice does not attack. “The just man falls seven times in the day and rises stronger.” [Note: [Col. 0275] Prov. 24.] For “many are the tribulations of the just.” [Note: [Col. 0275] Ps. 33.] “In six tribulations,” says Job, “the Lord will deliver you, and in the seventh evil shall not touch you.” [Note: [Col. 0275] Job 5.] Do not, I pray, abandon patience; for “the patience of the just shall not perish forever.” [Note: [Col. 0275] Ps. 9.] Let not the reproaches of those who reproach you disturb you, [Note: [Col. 0275] Ps. 68.] because, in Scripture’s testimony, “whatever happens to him shall not make the just man sorrowful.” [Note: [Col. 0275] Prov. 12.]

The examples of the great teach us that the courage of magnanimous men grows when provoked by graver injuries. Nothing arduous, nothing great, is great to a great man; nor should he fear that anything is difficult, since difficulty is accustomed to arise from fear alone. [Col. 0275B] If you endure with difficulty losses to your household and the loss and oppression of your own people, recall the Apostle’s word to the Hebrews: “Having been made a spectacle by reproaches and tribulations,” [Note: [Col. 0275] Heb. 10.] “we received with joy the plundering of our goods, knowing that we have a better and enduring possession.”

There will be a time, a time when “it will be pleasant to remember these things.” There will be a time when you will answer those who reproach you with a word. There will be a time when, with thanksgiving, you will sing and say: “You have shown me, Lord, many and grievous tribulations, and, turning, you have given us life.” [Note: [Col. 0275] Ps. 70.] “According to the multitude of my sorrows in my heart, your consolations have made my soul glad.” [Note: [Col. 0275] Ps. 93.] “A lamp,” says Job, “despised in the thoughts of the rich, shall be ready at the appointed time.” [Col. 0275C] [Note: [Col. 0275] Ch. 12.] “The sinner shall see all these things and be angry.” [Note: [Col. 0275] Ps. 111.] For you must increase, but he must decrease.

A prince will indeed think thoughts worthy of a prince, and from your restoration there shall follow a fuller and more overflowing glory. Then you shall see and abound, because you shall be repaid in the measure in which they measured to you. “I have taken,” says the Lord through Isaiah, “the cup of my indignation from your hand; you shall not add to drink it any more. And I shall put it into the hand of those who humbled you.” [Note: [Col. 0275] Isa. 51.] For God, says Job, does not cast away the mighty, since He Himself is mighty; [Note: [Col. 0275] Job 35.] but He considers the causes of each person. [Note: [Col. 0275] Job 36.] I know that the Lord will render judgment on those who persecute you; [Note: [Col. 0275] Ps. 118.] this hope is laid up in my bosom. [Note: [Col. 0275] Job 19.] I await the slaying of Goliath by the sword he prepared for David’s death, [Note: [Col. 0275] 1 Sam. 17.] and the punishment of Haman upon the gallows he prepared for Mordecai. [Col. 0275D] [Note: [Col. 0275] Esther 7.]

But let your circumspection, Father, henceforward examine more carefully the loyalty of each person whom you determine to admit into the sanctuary of your familiarity. For, as you read in Ecclesiasticus, [Note: [Col. 0275] Ch. 6.] “There is no price for a faithful friend, and the weight of silver and gold is not comparable [Col. 0276A] to him.” “Conduct your cause,” says Solomon, “with your friend, and do not reveal your counsel to a stranger.” [Note: [Col. 0275] Prov. 25.] And Ecclesiasticus says: [Note: [Col. 0275] Ecclus. 12.] “Never trust your enemy, for as bronze always rusts, so his wickedness does.”

Fare well, most gracious Father, and for a long time. And may the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, guard your heart and understanding, [Note: [Col. 0275] Phil. 4.] that you may serve Him in holiness and justice before Him all your days. But I have gone to the lady queen [Note: [Col. 0275D]

Eleanor, Richard’s mother, whom he had left as administrator of his kingdom together with the chancellor.

This letter was written in the year 1191, when William of Ely was compelled to leave England by the faction of the envious.]

until I see vengeance upon your enemies and your return to your former position with glory and honor.

## LETTER LXXXVIII. TO THE ABBOT OF TEWKESBURY

[Note: [Col. 0275D] The monastery of Tewkesbury is situated in England, in [Col. 0276D] the province of Worcester, according to William of Malmesbury, Book IV, *On the Deeds of the Bishops of England*, who also adds: “Tewkesbury is said to be, as it were, *Theotocosbiria*, that is, ‘the court of the Mother of God,’ a name composed of Greek and English.”]

**Subject.—**R., archbishop of Canterbury, asks, urges, and by many arguments impels [Col. 0276B] the abbot of Tewkesbury to receive back into the order a monk who had deserted it but has now come to his senses.

R., by God’s grace archbishop of Canterbury, primate of all England and legate of the apostolic see, to his beloved son the abbot of TEWKESBURY: greeting in the bowels of mercy and the spirit of compassion.

The pitiable and lamentable complaint of P., bearer of this letter, moved our bowels and effectively induced us to be concerned for his salvation and henceforth to reckon his perdition against ourselves unless we procure his salvation with exact diligence. It is true, and he neither wishes nor can deny it, that after taking the religious habit in your church he eventually made the vow of profession. Yet, recoiling with damnable fickleness from the stability which he had promised, he flew back from food to vomit, from heaven to mire, from paradise to hell, from cloister to the world.

The wandering sheep was to be sought and by pastoral care reconciled to the fold, if it fled, if it rejected the congregation of saints, the rod of discipline, and the Lord’s yoke. But he who departed through the fault of fickleness returns in devout humility, and by the lowliness of a more abject habit and more abundant tears redeems and compensates for the crime of his departure. Therefore do not close against him the bosom of mercy, lest he despair. You know that there is greater joy among the angels of God over one sinner doing penance than over ninety-nine righteous persons who have no need of repentance. [Note: [Col. 0275] Luke 15.]

For the goat, which bears the image of the sinner, is sacrificed at the entrance [Col. 0276D] of the tabernacle, whereas the sheep is commanded to be offered far from the tabernacle. [Note: [Col. 0275] Lev. 3.] “I desire mercy,” says the Lord, “and not sacrifice.” [Note: [Col. 0275] Hos. 6.] “For I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he should be converted and live.” [Note: [Col. 0275] Ezek. 18.] From the throne and equality with the Father the Son of the Most High descended [Col. 0277A] into this vale of tears and the misery of human condition, in order to bring back the hundredth sheep to the folds.

Although the poor customarily go to the rich and powerful in their necessities, the Almighty came to the weak, the rich to the poor, the blessed to the wretched. He did not wait for us to come to Him; He anticipated us in the blessings of His sweetness. If you were His imitator or His son, you ought not to have waited for the return and repentance of the wandering sheep, but to seek it with pastoral concern and by saving admonitions to recall it from error and the pathless way to the path of life. For its salvation and death will be required from your hands by the strict and terrible Judge.

Thus what would have cost you labor has fallen to your advantage: he has returned, he knocks at the door, [Col. 0277B] he confesses his transgression, he devoutly and humbly asks mercy, he offers himself to every satisfaction according to the usage and Rule of Blessed Benedict, [Note: [Col. 0277] Rule, ch. 24.] and he does not exclude judgment from mercy. The mercy which the founder of the monastic order restricted to the number three, the gentleness of evangelical grace has extended to seventy times seven. Therefore, by the testimony of the saints, it is better that we be judged for overflowing mercy than for exact rigor of justice.

If he has fallen, by the Lord’s gift he will add the power to rise. If he has sinned, we too have all sinned and need God’s grace. “I was a blasphemer,” says the Apostle, “but I obtained mercy; where sin abounded, grace superabounded.” [Note: [Col. 0277] 1 Tim. 1.] Who sinned more monstrously in the world than Paul? Who more grievously in religious life than [Col. 0277C] Peter? Yet through repentance they deserved to attain not only pardon for sins, not only the ministry of faith, but also the teaching office of holiness.

The Lord says in the Gospel: “Wicked servant, I forgave you all the debt because you asked me; ought you not also to have mercy on your fellow servant, as I had mercy on you?” [Note: [Col. 0277] Matt. 18.] Where is the bond—or rather the obligation—of the Lord’s Prayer, by which we say: “Forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors”? [Note: [Col. 0277] Matt. 6.] “Forgive,” He says, “and you shall be forgiven”; [Col. 0278A] but if you do not forgive from the heart, neither will my heavenly Father forgive you. [Note: [Col. 0277] Ibid.] Paul, writing to the Ephesians, says: “Let all bitterness and indignation be taken away from you, that you may be merciful, forgiving one another the offenses committed.” [Note: [Col. 0277] Eph. 4.] Solomon’s word is: “Man reserves anger against man and does not preserve mercy toward one like himself.” [Note: [Col. 0277] Ecclus. 28.] But James [Note: [Col. 0277] Ch. 2.] says: “Judgment without mercy shall be for him who has not shown mercy.”

The Lord says through the prophet: “I desire mercy and not sacrifice.” [Note: [Col. 0277] Hos. 6.] Read of Joseph’s mercy toward his brothers, [Note: [Col. 0277] Gen. 42.] of Moses toward an unbelieving and rebellious people, of David toward Saul, [Note: [Col. 0277] 1 Sam. 24.] Absalom, and Shimei, and of others who were merciful men; and you will find that none of them, nor any others who showed mercy, perished. [Note: [Col. 0277] 2 Sam. 16.]

If [Col. 0278B] your monk has sinned, it is human to sin; but it is inhuman and devilish neither to depart from sin nor mercifully to pardon one who repents. It is a fault to pursue a fault to the uttermost. “Blush, O Sidon,” says the sea. [Note: [Col. 0277] Isa. 23.] Hear and blush, Christian, at the deeds of the pagans, who were most renowned in the exercise of mercy. Hear also the poet: [Note: [Col. 0277] Ovid, *Letters from Pontus*, Elegy 3.]

> Slow to punish, O prince, swift to reward,  
> And grieving whenever you are compelled to be harsh.

Remember the mercy which the evangelical father is read to have shown to the prodigal son on his return; [Note: [Col. 0277] Luke 15.] willingly receive the returning son in the bowels of compassion. For if—God forbid!—you show yourself hard and inexorable in this matter, we shall turn justice into judgment and mercy into necessity, perhaps not [Col. 0278C] without loss to you. Farewell.

## LETTER LXXXIX. TO HUGH

[Note: [Col. 0277D]

Hugh de Nonant was born of an illustrious Norman family. Hence it is apparent that Baronius errs under the year 1171, where he calls him Roman rather than Norman. Hugh was first a member of the University of Oxford, then archdeacon of the church of that place—though Roger of Howden calls him archdeacon of Lisieux, an error for Oxford—if we believe the *Four-Part History of St. Thomas*, which, counting him among the household of St. Thomas, archbishop of Canterbury, says:

“After Girard, Hugh, surnamed Datinant [a corruption for *de Nunant*], a Norman by nation and then archdeacon of Oxford, discreet in counsel beyond what might be expected from his youthful years, prudent in action and vigorous in execution, was elevated to the episcopal see of Coventry when Girard had entered upon the path decreed for all flesh.”

But the outcome showed how poorly [Col. 0278D] he imitated the character of his holy master. Peter of Blois is not alone in attacking his thoroughly bad character; others who wrote the English history of this period do so as well. Gervase of Canterbury, under the year 1187, says of him: “He was keen of mind in conducting affairs, crafty in speech, ready to utter curses in order to frighten the timid, using blandishments to overthrow the steadfast.” Henry of Knighton, Book II, *On the Events of England*, under the year 1189: “Hugh, a cunning and shameless man, bold in reckless undertakings, equipped with learning and audacity, expelled the monks of Coventry by armed force.” The same account, in exactly the same words, is found in John Brompton under the year 1191.

All also report that, while King Richard was held in the emperor’s chains, Hugh attached himself to the schemes of the king’s brother John, who was stirring up troubles in England and attempting to seize the kingdom; and that by his counsel and [Col. 0279C] machinations the bishop of Ely, chancellor of the realm, was deposed and expelled from England. In Roger of Howden is read Hugh’s letter on the chancellor’s deposition, beginning, “What is recorded by the characters of letters,” etc.; in it he describes the entire tragedy of that deposition at length and with sufficient malice. In the same Howden there is also this apologetic letter of Peter of Blois on behalf of the chancellor.

How perversely Hugh behaved is evident from the fact that, when Richard returned to England, he was driven into exile; though shortly afterward he redeemed this by payment of money. For thus Howden has it under the year 1195: “The king remitted his anger and ill will toward Hugh, bishop of Coventry, and restored to him his bishopric for five thousand marks of silver, which he gave him.”

William of Newburgh says nearly the same, Book V, *On English Affairs*, chapter 5: “Hugh of Nonant, bishop of Chester, a man unstable in all his ways, who had fled to France from the face of the king of England because his bad conscience pricked him, appeased the same king with no small sum; and, having recovered his bishopric, thereafter took care to serve royal affairs rather than the offices [Col. 0280C] of pastoral care.”

It is, moreover, known from authorities that Hugh ended a life perversely spent with a praiseworthy end. For when, travelling to Rome, he was seized by a serious illness in Normandy, he summoned such bishops, abbots, and religious men from Normandy as he could; shedding abundant tears, he asked them to impose penance upon him. When they, out of reverence toward him, declined to command it, he asked them to enjoin upon him, in place [Col. 0280D] of penance and for the remission of his sins, the pains of purgatory until the last day of judgment. And because he grieved that he had sinned grievously against the monks of Coventry, whom he had expelled from his church, he found no other form of correction to make satisfaction for this crime than to end his life in their habit. Then he distributed to churches and the poor all that he possessed in gold, silver, gems, and precious vessels, and so came to rest with a holy end in the monastery of Bec in the year 1198. Matthew Paris gives this account more fully under that year, though Baronius reports it from Roger. See also Gervase under the year 1197 and Knighton under the year 1189.]

### TO THE BISHOP. [A.D. 1192.]

He inveighs sharply against Bishop H., because he was the chief author of the disgraceful deprivation of William, bishop of Ely, from the office of administering the kingdom of England.

To the sometime lord and friend H., called bishop of Coventry and Chester: the remembrance and fear of God.

[Col. 0279A] The monstrousness of a treacherous faction has today disclosed the goal of its malice and the direction of its envy. The bishop of Ely, beloved by God and men—a wise, lovable, noble, kindly, gentle man, lavish in every liberality—had, according to the dispensation of divine grace and the measure of his merits, attained the administration of the commonwealth and the supreme direction of affairs. You saw and envied; from that moment came your wrath. There envy conceived sorrow and gave birth to iniquity. Yet he, walking in simplicity, summoned you into the sanctuary of his confidence, into unity of friendship and the bond of alliance. His whole spirit rested upon you, while all your thoughts toward him were evil. “Woe,” says Ecclesiasticus, “to the double-hearted, and to wicked lips, [Col. 0279B] and to the sinner who walks by two ways” [Note: [Col. 0279] Ch. 2.].

Formerly the hypocritical face of friendship veiled the evil of your inward conscience as a pretext, while secretly you practised upon an innocent man the injuries of a seditious and insolent tongue. “Cursed,” says Solomon, “is the whisperer and double-tongued man among peoples; for he disturbs the peaceable” [Note: [Col. 0279] Ecclus. 28.]. He poured out all his conscience into your bosom, for he regarded you as another self; but you drove him toward an occasion of ruin by treacherous flatteries. O detestable treachery! Judas betrayed the Son of Man with a kiss [Note: [Col. 0279] Luke 22]; and you outwardly performed the office of one who loves, while your tongue fashioned deceits. “Sitting, you spoke against your brother, and against the son of your mother you set a stumbling-block.” “Woe to that man through whom the stumbling-block comes” [Note: [Col. 0279] Matt. 18].

Indeed, this [Col. 0279C] crime branded you with an endless stain of evil repute; and whatever commendable quality you had received from nature’s beneficence, guilt has permanently blotted it out. Joab, certainly, had done many brave deeds; but his treachery against Amasa and Abner blackened every title of virtue in him [Note: [Col. 0279] II Kings 3, 20]. O slanderous lips, O malicious and deceitful tongue! What shall be added, Lord, against [Col. 0280A] this deceitful tongue? Would that arrows might be added to pierce it, and desolating coals to set it ablaze! Would that you, Seraph, who cleansed the prophet’s lips with a heavenly coal, might, by cleansing, destroy his entire mouth and tongue with the flame of Gehenna [Note: [Col. 0279] Isa. 6], so that we might sing and say: “You have destroyed him from cleansing” [Note: [Col. 0279] Ps. 88].

Lips consecrated to the Gospel never cease pouring forth wind into words of falsehood. Everything that was owed to truth is given over to vanity. Moreover, “a man of tongue shall not be established upon the earth” [Note: [Col. 0279] Ps. 139]. Therefore, let him who stands take heed lest he fall. “For the heart is lifted up before ruin” [Note: [Col. 0279] Prov. 16]. Unhappy man, you exult and boast that you have supplanted an innocent man; but assuredly he has been set for the fall and resurrection of many—that is, for his own restoration and that of his followers. But for your [Col. 0280B] downfall and that of your accomplices, this bean will be beaten back upon your head. For every fraud, returning upon itself, is shattered. From deceit you shall gather only the fruit of sorrow; and you have woven a web in order that you may be clothed in a double garment. It is the saying of Isaiah [Note: [Col. 0279] Ch. 30]: “You who weave a web and trust in Egypt’s shadow, await the day of bitterness.”

You publicly glory and boast that you have stirred up this mob, that you have deceived and led on an unwary populace, so that with arms and ambushes they might attack an unarmed innocent man. “Why do you glory in malice, you who are mighty in iniquity?” [Note: [Col. 0279] Ps. 51]. Why do you proclaim your malice, which, as your infamy runs through many provinces, has now become common talk? But of you and your like it may be said: “They rejoice when they have done evil, and exult in the worst deeds” [Note: [Col. 0279] Prov. 2]. Moreover, the saying of the Wise Man is: “He who [Col. 0280C] rejoices in another’s ruin shall be punished” [Note: [Col. 0279] Prov. 17]. Solomon also says elsewhere: “When your enemy falls, do not rejoice, lest God see it and turn His anger upon you” [Note: [Col. 0279] Prov. 24].

Certainly it has always been familiar and characteristic of your lineage to sow the seed of dissension; and the pestilent branch has drawn its malice from the root of an evil tree. O perverse generation, O exasperating house, O brood of vipers! Who taught you to flee from the wrath to come? Do you suppose that the Lord does not see and investigate these things? “Therefore the wicked man has provoked God; for he has said in his heart, ‘He will not investigate’” [Note: [Col. 0281] Ps. 9]. But the Lord certainly will investigate. He also, in whose present straits you glory, will at some time, God granting it, breathe freely again. For Wisdom will not abandon the righteous man who has been sold, and in due time there shall be regard for him [Note: [Col. 0281] Wis. 10].

The gravity of your order required you to reconcile peace among peoples and quiet seditions, especially in England, which, receiving you poor enough, enlarged you with splendid honours. Jeremiah, speaking to those in the Babylonian captivity, says: “Seek the peace of the city to which the Lord has caused you to migrate, for in its peace [Col. 0281B] shall be your peace” [Note: [Col. 0281] Jer. 29]. On another occasion I wrote to you and earnestly entreated you, with salutary admonitions, to desist from such conduct. Yet David’s harp never entirely calmed Saul’s madness [Note: [Col. 0281] II Kings 16]; and still his hand is stretched out.

Remember, therefore, man—if indeed you are a man—remember, I say, your condition; remember the brevity of this life. Remember the strict and dreadful Judge. Remember the terrible, horrible, intolerable, endless punishment prepared for you for eternity if you do not cease from such wrongdoing.

## LETTER XC. TO MASTER WILLIAM OF BLOIS, ABBOT [c. A.D. 1169]

First he explains why, with the Sicilian king’s consent, he left Sicily. Then he strives by every means to persuade his brother, the abbot, either to surrender the pontifical insignia—[Col. 0281C] the mitre, ring, and sandals—which he received from the pope, or to resign the administration of the abbey.

To his dearest brother, Master WILLIAM of Blois, abbot [Col. 0282A] of Mathin (Mathinensis): PETER of Blois, greeting and salutary Trinacria.

[Note: [Col. 0281C] Busaeus reads “of Maniace,” although he found it written so in no manuscript, but rather either “Mathirensis” or “Mathinensis.” This is likewise what occurs in all our manuscripts, namely either “Mathinensis,” or, more often, “Mathin” by abbreviation, which signifies the same thing; but in none at all is “Maniacensis” read. Busaeus drew his conjecture from Fazellus, in whom a monastery of Maniace in Sicily is said to exist. But if we believe the most learned Bulaeus, formerly rector of the University of Paris, in volume II of his History, William of Blois became abbot in Sicily at the time when his brother Peter of Blois was seal-bearer and instructor to the king of Sicily: namely, in 1167, according to Rocco Pirro after [Col. 0281D] Baronius. Yet the monastery of Maniace was built by Queen Margaret, William’s mother, only in 1174, according to the same Rocco Pirro, who in his third account of the Church of Monreale writes:

> “In 1174 Queen Margaret, mother of William II, began to build in the town of Maniace, in the diocese of Messina, a monastery of the Order of St Benedict. But the queen wished it to be subject to the monastery of Monreale. William summoned monks and Abbot Theobald from the monastery of Cava, gave them this house, and by a diploma issued in 1176 granted them numerous lands and estates. In 1177 the same Theobald, bishop of Monreale, granted the monastery of Maniace the power to choose its own abbot, in a diploma addressed to Timothy, abbot of St Mary of Maniace.”

From this it is evident that there was no abbot of the monastery of Maniace in 1168 or 1169, when William of Blois bade Sicily farewell; for in the same Rocco Pirro Timothy is said to have been the first abbot of Maniace in 1178. Anyone who reads this letter and Letter 93 attentively will plainly discover that William of Blois did not remain in Sicily long after his brother Peter, who left it in 1168.]

How fiercely the Sicilian traitors conspired for the destruction of Lord Stephen, the elected archbishop of Palermo [Note: [Col. 0281] Read Fazellus, *On Sicilian Affairs*, book VII, ch. 5], and royal chancellor of Sicily, needs no report.

[Note: [Col. 0282C] Nearly all writers of this age recount this disastrous history of the Franks—or rather, this accursed perfidy of the Sicilians—especially Hugh Falcandus, who saw the event with his own eyes, and Fazellus after him. William of Nangis, too, in his as yet unpublished history, summarizes it briefly under the year 1168:

> “There was then in Sicily a certain Frenchman, Stephen, son of the Count of Perche, chancellor of King William. Some powerful Sicilians, hating him, sent letters throughout Apulia and Calabria directing that all Franks found there should be put to death; and this was done. But when the king of Sicily learned of it, he condemned the authors of that sedition to the same sentence.”

This letter was written about the year 1169.]

. For by these and other harsher things, which you have often heard, your ears have rung. But I, when in that disturbance and in the departure of my lord I was suffering from a hemitertian fever, was, by command of the lord king, entrusted to the care and protection of the archbishop of Salerno, who showed no less concern for me than if I had been his lord or his son. When I had recovered, I approached the lord king, asking him and the magnates of the court for leave to depart. The king, however, through the lord of Salerno and through R., bishop-elect of Syracuse [Col. 0282B], repeatedly caused me to be urged to remain at his court and in the office of the seal; but neither prayers, promises, nor gifts could bend me to this.

For that land devours its inhabitants; and, fearing the malice of those dwelling in it, I had reduced the sum of all my desires to this: that I might have leave and a safe departure. Since, therefore, to leave Sicily on horseback and travel through Calabria seemed extremely hazardous to me and to all who were with me, the lord king there gave me a certain Genoese ship, which Sicilian pirates had captured, together with its men and merchandise, equipped with every kind of provision—with mats, mattresses, and tapestries. After the Genoese had sworn to furnish me loyalty and protection for my person [Col. 0282C] and for those with me, who might be reckoned at about forty, in order to escape death on land I exposed myself to death at sea.

Then, under the beguiling mildness of spring [Col. 0283A] and with the winds dying away, our ship lay motionless; and for a whole month we could not complete a voyage which, by the favour of a better wind, we ought to have traversed in five days. Arriving at Genoa, I was received with honour by the great men of the land, especially by those who had seen me among the Sicilians in royal magnificence; how much service and honour they bestowed upon me I could scarcely explain in words.

[Note: [Col. 0283A] In the manuscripts kept in the British Museum [Royal 14 C. iv and Arundel 227], this letter is divided into two. What follows here is a separate letter, prefaced with the heading: “To his dearest brother, Master W., abbot of Matina: P. of Blois, greeting.”]

One of your messengers told me that the lord pope had invested you with the mitre from his own head and with other [Col. 0283B] episcopal ornaments. I rejoice in the blessing; but episcopal insignia in an abbot I neither approve nor accept. For a mitre, ring, and sandals in anyone other than a bishop constitute a certain proud exaltation [Note: [Col. 0283D] Bernard, Letter 42 to Henry of Sens, ch. 9: “Indeed, if the dignity of things is considered, the monastic profession shrinks from this; if the monastery is considered, it is clear that it belongs only to bishops.”

Certainly noteworthy is the deed of the blessed Peter, abbot of Cava, in Surius, volume II, in his *Life*:

> “When, according to his custom, he was sitting in a synod bareheaded, Pope Urban of holy memory sent him a pontifical mitre. The man of God received it reverently out of respect for the supreme pontiff, and greeted it with every fitting mark of honour; nevertheless, even at the pope’s request, he declined to use that priestly mitre. He is believed to have done this for no other reason than to condemn by the example of humility the arrogance of certain persons who, while vainly exalting themselves, do not fear to usurp for themselves undeserved honours of the holy Church.” [Col. 0284D]

The same Urban allowed Hugh of Cluny and his successors the use of a mitre, dalmatic, gloves, and sandals; see the Library of Cluny, col. 514 and following. Alexander II had granted the same favour to Egelsin, abbot of St Augustine’s, Canterbury; abbots judged that its use should be avoided until Roger, who, as Ralph de Diceto records under 1179, “having been made abbot by Pope Alexander III, received at Tusculum, on 28 January, consecration and, as a sign of the emancipation granted to him, a mitre, ring, and gloves.” In later centuries this was granted almost everywhere, when requested, to abbots of monasteries, especially of the Benedictine order. Read the chapter *Ut apostolicae*, *On Privileges*, in the Sixth Book.]

—and a presumptuous display of independence. Their use belongs to the dedication of churches, the consecration of virgins, and the celebration of ordinations. Why, then, does one use—or rather misuse—these things, when he is forbidden to use them? To a man who possesses them but does not use them, they are more a burden and a mockery than an honour. Androgynes do not reproduce, according to Hippocrates [Note: [Col. 0283] Book I, *On Regimen*]; therefore, what genitals do on a mule, sandals do on an abbot. Has this misuse of episcopal things issued from the Rule of St Benedict [Note: [Col. 0283] Albert the Great, book XVIII, *On the Soul*, treatise 2, ch. 3]? Are such emancipations prescribed in the Gospel and the prophets?

Do not, [Col. 0283C] I beg you, dearest brother, reject the yoke of obedience; for death entered through disobedience, which still does not cease to sow among bishops and abbots the tinder of disputes and matter for scandals. Adam perished through disobedience; Saul lost his kingdom through disobedience [Note: [Col. 0283] I Kings 15]. Nor should anyone flatter himself that by a privilege of the Roman Church he is excused from disobedience. For God, with whom obedience is better than sacrifices, detests disobedience whatever man may emancipate or privilege. If God commands one thing and man permits or commands another, God must be obeyed rather than man [Note: [Col. 0283] Acts 5].

You know that Abdon, sent by the Lord to Jeroboam [Note: [Col. 0283] III Kings 13], [Col. 0284A] was forbidden by Him to eat on the way. At another prophet’s suggestion that he should eat, who said that he himself had been sent by the Lord for this purpose, he ate. But although he had done it on the authority of another prophet, he nevertheless perished, devoured by a lion, because of disobedience. When he had received the Lord’s particular command, no dispensation from the Lord’s injunction was admissible at a man’s suggestion.

If the Roman pontiff has exempted you from the jurisdiction of your bishop, do not, I beg you, use a privilege that introduces matter for rebellion. Uzzah was struck by the Lord because he rashly put forth his hand toward the ark of the Lord [Note: [Col. 0283] II Kings 16]. Miriam was struck with leprosy because she reproached Moses [Note: [Col. 0283] Num. 12]. The earth swallowed Dathan and Abiram alive because they raised themselves in pride against Moses and Aaron [Col. 0284B] [Note: [Col. 0283] Num. 16]. Their accomplices, too, punitive flame consumed; “for fire blazed in their assembly, and flame consumed sinners.”

Although pride is detestable everywhere, it is more detestable in one who professes humility. What rust is in iron, what a moth is in cloth, what gall is in milk, what poison is in honey—such is pride in monastic habit. You think that in accepting the mitre, sandals, and ring you have greatly advanced your monastery’s dignity; yet in them I see nothing but the evil of disobedience, a seedbed of hatred, swelling self-exaltation, and the wind of pride. Pride is heavenly by origin; it always strives upward in order to fall more heavily.

Now the first son of pride, that Lucifer—or rather, bearer of darkness—finds imitators and followers in cloisters: [Col. 0284C] he who was assigning himself a seat on the sides of the north and arrogating to himself likeness to the Most High [Note: [Col. 0283] Isa. 14]. Where, and at what, had that wretch laboured, who was already planning to sit and rest? All others were sent forth for service, devoted and humble at their Creator’s command. “Thousands of thousands,” according to Scripture’s testimony, “stood before Him, and ten thousand times a hundred thousand ministered to Him” [Note: [Col. 0283] Dan. 7]. But this one was setting up a seat for himself before he had laboured. “I shall set my throne in the north,” he says, “and shall be like the Most High” [Note: [Col. 0283] Isa. 14]. He sought equality with the Most High, something not his own. The Son of God alone did not think equality with God a thing to be seized [Note: [Col. 0283] Phil. 2]; by nature it belongs to Him [Col. 0285A] to sit not beneath His feet but at His right hand.

Let that son of pride, then, be cast down, and let the chair of pestilence be overthrown. Let the robe of delight, with which the Creator’s hand had clothed him, be taken away; stripped of gratuitous gifts, let him be thrust into outer darkness and unending flames, to which likewise are assigned those who, through pride and abuse, reject obedience to prelates. For what else is the setting of a seat in the north and the usurpation of likeness to the Most High, but the acquisition for an abbot of independence and episcopal insignia?

Therefore, by the welfare of the Father who begot us and by the breasts which we sucked from the same mother, unique brother, I adjure and beseech you to surrender the pontifical insignia into the bosom of complete humility; or, if this cannot be done without scandal, to resign [Col. 0285B] the administration of the monastery into the lord pope’s hand, and, after an appropriate pastor has been appointed there at your request, to turn yourself toward cloistered leisure and healthful warfare. Farewell.

## LETTER XCI. TO RALPH, BISHOP OF LISIEUX [A.D. 1181–93]

[Note: [Col. 0285D] He is called here by Robert of Torigni Ralph of Vanneville, by others of Varneville; he succeeded Arnulf in 1181. He had previously been archdeacon of Rouen and chancellor of the king of England. Robert writes under 1181: “Ralph of Vanneville, archdeacon of Rouen, who had been chancellor of the king, was elected to the aforesaid bishopric”—that is, Lisieux. He had earlier resigned the chancellorship, “for which the king had given him lands of great revenues,” says the same Robert of Mont-Saint-Michel. Roger of Howden names him under 1183 among the bishops present at Caen for the excommunication pronounced against all who hindered the making of peace and concord between King Henry and his sons. Ralph died about the year of the Lord 1193.]

### Argument

He vehemently attacks the bishop of Lisieux for avarice and devotion to lending at interest, especially because, in a time of dearth, he did not open his granaries to the poor.

To his dearest lord and friend RALPH, bishop of Lisieux: his own PETER of Blois, archdeacon of Bath, true greeting in Christ’s resurrection.

If you confidently and without doubt expected the glory of eternal resurrection, you would not now do what you are doing, nor so immerse yourself in the dregs of earthly things—you who wholly entangle and envelop yourself in the unclean bonds of avarice and ambition. For it is written that “their glory is in their shame, who mind earthly things” [Note: [Col. 0285] Phil. 3]; and you wish to know or love nothing but what is earthly. “He who is of the earth speaks of the earth” [Note: [Col. 0285] John 3]. You see the earth, you love the earth; and like a mole deprived of sight, you do not admit the benefit of freer air.

You ought to have been the light of the world; but if your light has become darkness, how great will your darkness be? You cannot see heaven’s light because you are fixed in the mire of the deep [Note: [Col. 0285] Ps. 68], and “your belly has been glued to the earth” [Note: [Col. 0285] Ps. 43]. It is written that “the eyes of the wise are always in his head” [Note: [Col. 0285] Eccles. 2], but the eyes [Col. 0285D] of the fool are at the ends of the earth [Note: [Col. 0285] Prov. 17]. You savour earth, speak earth, lick earth. You cannot be stripped of this dross of earthly things until a pit is dug for the sinner, until, [Col. 0286A] being earth, you return to earth [Note: [Col. 0285] Gen. 3].

Lift up your eyes, I beg you, see and look upon heaven’s light; consider that the friends of God have been taken away from earth, and that their commonwealth is in heaven [Note: [Col. 0285] Phil. 3]. In this earthly dwelling there is nothing but labour and pain, and a certain image of infernal misery. In your life and works almost the entire countenance of hell is painted. You lack neither the water of Tantalus, the liver of Tityus, the wheel of Ixion, the jar of the Danaids (Belides), nor the stone of Sisyphus [Note: [Col. 0285] Ovid, *Metamorphoses*, book IV], while you hunger amid riches, agonize amid cares, are tortured by desire, are snatched toward unlawful things, gather into a perforated bag [Note: [Col. 0285] Hag. 1], and afflict yourself by continual and needless labour in gathering riches.

Because you listen unwillingly to histories, I insert fables; yet from the moral teaching of pagan fables a pattern [Col. 0286B] of instruction is sometimes drawn [Note: [Col. 0286D] See what we said on Letter 8 concerning the usefulness of reading pagan books], since it is lawful to be taught even by an enemy. The Apostle does not fear to borrow truth from the pagans, since, by whomever it is spoken, it is from the Holy Spirit; and when we take it from the books of the ungodly, we do not seize what belongs to another, but reclaim for ourselves what is ours from unjust possessors. The Lord also willed that His peculiar people should be honoured and adorned with the gold, silver, and every possession of the Egyptians [Note: [Col. 0285] Exod. 12].

The Lord has placed you to be salt of the earth; I fear lest you become salt that has lost its savour, since you are already trampled underfoot by enemies. You grievously dishonour the condition of bishops and expose Christ’s ministry to reproach and contempt. Would that this money had not existed, which draws you away from the path of honour and salvation [Col. 0286C]! For in the course of this mortal life you will never attain the prize of life without contempt for riches and the provision of charity.

You know that Hippodamia [Note: [Col. 0285] Ovid, *Metamorphoses*, book IV], as long as she slowed the course of her competing suitors by throwing down gold, ran ahead to the prize; and, though the maiden had won many triumphs, at last the despiser of gold triumphed over the maiden. The Lord has indeed opened for you a most ready path of salvation; for severe famine rages among the poor, in whom the Lord has set His kingdom out for sale to you. The kingdom of God is worth as much as you bestow upon His poor out of compassionate affection. The poor man is Christ’s vicar; and just as Christ grieves to be rejected in him and is ashamed to be despised in him, so He delights to be received in him. “As long as you did it to one of these,” He says, [Col. 0286D] “you did it to Me” [Note: [Col. 0285] Matt. 25].

Open, therefore, your heart and granaries publicly to beggars, lest you incur the sentence of that condemnation: “Cursed is he who hides grain [Col. 0287A] from the peoples” [Note: [Col. 0287D] This curse is directed against those who close their granaries to the poor in a time of high grain prices. In the Septuagint this saying appears somewhat more obscurely: *Ho synechōn siton, hypoleipoito auton tois ethnesin*—“He who holds back grain, let him leave it to the nations.” In some manuscripts, instead of *synechōn* (“holding back”), there is *timioulkōn ton siton*, “seeking the price of grain.” Ambrose follows this reading in book III of *On Duties*. Cyprian has nearly the same words in book III of the *Testimonies to Quirinus*, ch. 61: “He who seeks advantage from a scarcity is cursed among the people.” Symmachus and Theodotion read, instead of *synechōn*, *ho kōlyōn*, “he who prevents.” The original Hebrew has the same sense: “one preventing” or “one not sharing.”].

Sow in blessings, so that you may also reap blessings [Note: [Col. 0287] II Cor. 9]. Pour out generously what you greedily gathered. For he who sows sparingly shall reap sparingly; “for God loves a cheerful giver” [Note: [Col. 0287] ibid.]. Do not, I beg you, continue to embrace temporal usury, which He most gravely detests—the One who lent you everything you possess and now asks that it be lent to Him in His poor. “Blessed is the man who has mercy and lends” [Note: [Col. 0287] Ps. 111]; for he does not show mercy who pursues temporal gain. But “he who has mercy on the poor lends to the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0287] Prov. 19]. He closes to himself the gate of mercy before God who does not open his compassionate heart to a begging neighbour.

Among those whom you succeeded in Christ’s ministry, all things were held in common, and they distributed to every person according to his need [Note: [Col. 0287] Acts 2]. [Col. 0287B] Under one head we are all one body, and in one body we are members one of another. If hands, feet, eyes, or members of this kind suffer sympathetically for another member’s injury, when will you begin to extend to the poor and widows a compassionate heart and the affection of pity? Countless thousands of poor people have already died through hunger and want, and you have not yet extended the hand of mercy to a single one of them. Know this one thing: the most strict Judge will require from you the deaths of all those whose lives you could have redeemed by the benefit of grain.

Certainly the fields are already whitening for harvest, yet in this disaster of famine you have not refreshed a single poor person. Even now you first propose to open your granaries, not to relieve the misery of the afflicted, but to sell at a higher price [Col. 0287C] and lend at interest. Most unhappy man, the money and grain which you lend are God’s, not yours; therefore conduct your business more cautiously. For He is a stern man: He reaps where He did not sow [Note: [Col. 0287] Luke 19]. But another lender, stronger and more exacting than you, shall come upon you and seize your labours, and what is written shall happen to you: “Let the usurer search out all his substance, and let strangers plunder his labours” [Note: [Col. 0287] Ps. 119].

It is the saying of Isaiah: “Woe to you who plunder, for you also shall be plundered” [Note: [Col. 0287] Isa. 33]. And according to the testimony of blessed Job, “the treasures which you swallowed you shall vomit up, and God shall draw them from your belly” [Note: [Col. 0287] Job 20]. You shall expiate all that you have done and yet not be consumed. For you shall not be able to escape the pains of eternal death. As sheep, once shorn, are allowed to grow their wool again so as to be shorn anew, [Col. 0287D] so by dying you shall live, in order never to cease dying. It is the prophet’s saying: “Like sheep they are set in hell; death shall feed upon them” [Note: [Col. 0287] Ps. 48].

> Thus the liver of Tityus, unconsumed and ever renewed,  
> Does not perish, so that it may be able often to perish.  
> [Note: [Col. 0287] Ovid, *Letters from Pontus*, elegy 2.]

The Lord says through the prophet Amos: “You cause the needy of the land to fail, saying: ‘When will abundance pass, so that we may sell grain, possess the needy for silver, and sell the sweepings of the grain?’ But I shall make you dark at midday and turn your festivals into mourning,” says the Lord; “the hinges and the lights above shall be shaken” [Note: [Col. 0287] Amos 8:9]. For avarice is at their head, and “I shall strike them with the sword even to the last.” The two-edged sword of the Lord awaits you, bishop, to cut you in two without mercy, since you have shown no mercy to Christ and His poor [Col. 0288B].

Why are you not ashamed, most ruined of men, that your name stinks among the people, that provinces condemn your avarice, that no one hears your Mass, that you disgrace the pastoral office while men proclaim you a most oppressive exacter and a public usurer? Other bishops now borrow from elsewhere to relieve the poor’s need; they sow temporal things so that they may reap eternal ones. You, occupied with temporal things, do not think of eternal ones. It is enough for you to place a coin where it may produce many children and return to you with abundant offspring.

Coins return multiplied to the Lord; and because they have gained much from little, they enter into the joy of their Lord. For the avaricious man’s joy is his treasure. “Where your treasure is,” He says, [Col. 0288C] “there is your heart also” [Note: [Col. 0287] Matt. 6]. Therefore, whenever it is asked, “Where is the heart of the avaricious man?” the just answer is: “In the chest.”

> “The people,” says the miser, “hiss at me; but I applaud myself  
> at home whenever I gaze upon the coins in my chest.”  
> [Note: [Col. 0287] Horace, *Satires* 1.]

These, miser, are your gods; these are those whose image you have preferred to the image of your Creator. I have sometimes heard from your own mouth that, as though to “excuse excuses in sins” [Note: [Col. 0287] Ps. 140], you boasted of your generosity and claimed to give more in one instance than all the bishops of the region. Certainly what you give to the lord king is, like the payment made by other lenders or Jews, a burden of tributary service and a certain image of Jewish servitude. If you give to the great men of the land, that generosity does not proceed from liberality; it is cast out like a snare [Col. 0288D] while it expects a return of abundant recompense.

[Col. 0289A] Hear what the poet sings about you and your like:

> Because you send huge gifts to old men and widows,  
> do you wish to be called generous, Gargilianus?  
> Nothing is more sordid, nothing fouler than you,  
> who can call your snares gifts.  
> Thus the deceitful hook indulges greedy fish;  
> thus cunning bait deceives foolish beasts.  
> I shall teach you what it is to give freely, what it is to make a gift:  
> if you do not know, Gargilianus, give nothing.  
> [Note: [Col. 0289] Martial, book I, epigram 136.]

Your predecessor [Note: [Col. 0289] He means Arnulf; see what we said on Letter 44.] acquired the most celebrated titles of renown by the grace of lavish hospitality and the magnificence of unstinting liberality; but as much as his memory rises into glory, so much has your utterly condemned name cast you down into shame and reproach.

## LETTER XCII. TO REGINALD, BISHOP OF BATH

[Col. 0289B]

### Argument

He attacks Zoilus, the detractor of his writings.

To his lord R., bishop of Bath: his own P., archdeacon, greeting and the affection of devoted submission.

I hear that in your presence a secret detractor presumes to assail my little works by covert distortion. In this I regard myself as so much the happier, as my envious opponent is more severely tormented and more miserably wastes away. I have founded all my works upon the rock of help, in which “the mouth of those speaking iniquity shall be stopped” [Note: [Col. 0289] Ps. 62], and the teeth of biting envy shall be broken.

My rival calls me a compiler because I support everything that I write in my letters or sermons with examples from histories or authorities of Holy Scripture. I have borrowed this practice from the holy Fathers, who frequently insert words of the New and Old Testaments throughout all their works so that their artistic joining may add strength and ornament to their own sayings. And what envy is it if what I have gleaned from manifold reading of books, through the ordering of more ardent study, grows together into material for virtue and an exercise of prudence?

For, as we read in the *Saturnalia* and in Seneca’s books to Lucilius [Note: [Col. 0289] Macrobius, book I, at the beginning; Seneca, Letter 35], we ought to imitate bees: they gather flowers, and, after separating and arranging them in a honeycomb, by skilled blending transfer their various juices into one flavour bearing a certain property of their own spirit. My rival criticizes and ascribes to presumption my collecting into one body letters scattered far and wide in diverse places; [Col. 0289D] my prescribing a form of composition for beginners; my devoting to public benefit the gift of devoted labour and the office of charity.

Let my rival cease from verbal injuries. For if he continues to say what he wishes, he will hear what he does not wish.

> I am full of cracks;  
> I leak through here and there.  
> [Note: [Col. 0289] Terence, *Eunuchus* 1.2.]

> Whoever stirs me, I cry that it is better not to touch me;  
> he shall weep, and his name shall be sung throughout the whole city.  
> [Note: [Col. 0289] Horace, *Satires* II.1.]

[Col. 0290A] Would that my envious opponent might test the strength of his own talent and compose a similar little work from the gathered blossoms of sacred eloquence! Yet if he attempts what he now considers very easy, I fear that he will sweat greatly and labour in vain:

> Unhappy at the climax of the work, because to set forth the whole…

He will not know. [Note: [Col. 0289] Horace, *On the Art of Poetry*.] He may indeed be able to begin, but if I know the capacity of this upstart, he will finish shamefully and disastrously. Whatever the dogs may bark, whatever the swine may grunt, I shall always be an admirer of the writings of the ancients: they will be my occupation; nor, if I can help it, will the sun ever find me idle. We are like dwarfs standing upon the shoulders of giants; through their benefit we see farther than they do, while, clinging to the treatises of the ancients, we restore to a kind of newness of being their more elegant thoughts, which antiquity or human neglect had obliterated and left, as it were, already dead. [Col. 0290B]

We read in the *Saturnalia* [Note: [Col. 0289] Macrobius, book VI.] that Afranius, a writer of Roman-dress comedies, replying in the comedy entitled *Compitalia* to his rivals, who said that he had taken much by plucking from the book of Menander, declared: “I admit that I took things, but things which I did not believe I could discover better myself.” And in the same work: “Who would charge Virgil with wrongdoing if, for the embellishment of his poem, he borrowed certain things from Homer or from others? Rather, gratitude is due to him because he transferred into a work destined to endure forever the sayings of men whom we had already consigned to neglect and ridicule.” And shortly afterwards: “Finally, he achieved such judgment in transferring and such moderation in imitating that, when we read something borrowed in him, we marvel that it sounds better there than where it was born.” [Col. 0290C]

We know that the apostles drew from the prophets, the doctors from the apostles, and other doctors from doctors: Jerome from the books of Origen; Augustine and Bede from the books of Ambrose; Ambrose himself from the writings of Cicero and Seneca; and Gregory also from the writings of Augustine and Jerome. They accepted for the purpose of borrowing not merely thoughts but the very words themselves.

I say confidently, and with many witnesses, that I have always been accustomed to dictate letters more quickly than anyone could write them down. That very speed certainly excludes both the fault and the suspicion of compilation. I say this for truth, not for boasting. The lord of Canterbury once saw—and you yourself with him, together with many others—me dictate on different subjects to three scribes and keep pace with the hurried pen of each; indeed, as is written of Julius Caesar alone [Note: [Col. 0289] Pliny, book VII, chapter 25; Plutarch, in his *Life* from Oppius.], I dictated and wrote a fourth letter. [Col. 0290D] If this should seem doubtful to anyone, I ask that the experience of the deed establish the credibility of the assertion.

I know whence he has conceived this spirit of arrogance and why your Cornificius swells. But as a bladder full of wind collapses when pierced by a small needle, so with one little word I shall drive the windy verbosity out of the bellows of his unskilled throat. [Col. 0291A] “I shall fill his face with disgrace”; for he has an abundance of material for shameful confusion:

> Since his anus is very well known among Socratic catamites.  
> [Note: [Col. 0291] Juvenal, *Satires* 2.]

If my little works should at some time fall into the hand of my rival through an unfavorable chance, he will say: “These would be good, if the authorities which he himself applies were more suitably placed or answered the subject matter.” Thus envy and the venomous malice of detractors are very often described in the writings of the ancients:

> Peleus was happy in his son, happy in his wife,  
> And all things had befallen him—if you remove  
> The crime of slaughtered Phocus.  
> [Note: [Col. 0291] Ovid, *Metamorphoses*, book II.]

[Col. 0291B] And this: “I admit that Julius Fortunatus was a brave man; yet I wonder how he escaped a prosecution for extortion. Publius Antonius would plead most elegantly, were it not that he acted deceitfully in the case of Lucilius.” Behold how envy poisons honey; tormented by another’s merit, it maliciously corrupts the good which it cannot find in itself. For it reckons another’s loss of reputation as gain for its own fame, and believes that everything is taken away from itself which accrues to the distinctions of a neighboring merit.

Moreover, what Martial [Note: [Col. 0291] Book I, epigram 79.] imprecates against his own envier, I imprecate against mine:

> You who make faces and do not read these things gladly,  
> Envy everyone, envier; no one envies you.

## LETTER XCIII. TO MASTER WILLIAM, ABBOT. [A.D. 1170.]

[Col. 0291C]

**SUMMARY.**—He congratulates his brother the abbot because, following his advice, he resigned the abbey into the hands of the supreme pontiff, preferring submission to a superior over the dignity of office, and France over Sicily.

To his dearest brother, Master WILLIAM, abbot of Matines, P. of Blois: greetings, and perseverance in virtue.

I congratulate your magnanimity because, in accordance with the counsel of my insignificance, you rejected the insignia which the more lavish favor of the lord pope had granted you and voluntarily resigned the care of the monastery of Matines into his hands. It belongs to a noble and magnanimous heart to relinquish the dignity of so great an advantage, for whose acquisition the anxious ambition of many had striven. [Col. 0291D] Your contempt for honor is more honorable than its attainment; for its acquisition was Fortune’s work, but its contempt was the work of courage.

To hunt honors, to gather riches, and to seek pleasure in them is a common vice and the public road of ambition. But it is a distinguished title of virtues to triumph over worldly pomp and, trampling down the riches of the world, to consider oneself rich in poverty alone. The Lord of the ages taught us to flee worldly dignities. For after he had fed five thousand persons from a few loaves, the crowds, perceiving the Lord’s majesty in the miracle, wished, according to the Evangelist’s testimony, to make him king; but he fled to the mountain. [Note: [Col. 0291] John 6.] When the Lord had delivered Israel through the hand of Gideon, they said to him: “Rule over us, you and your son and your son’s sons, for you have delivered us from the hand of the Midianites.” But he replied: “I shall not rule over you, nor shall my son rule over you; the Lord shall rule.” [Note: [Col. 0291] Judges 8.]

Valerius Maximus reports [Note: [Col. 0291] Book VII, chapter 2.] that when an imperial robe with a diadem was offered to a man of proven virtue, he looked at the robe and said: “O cloth more noble than fortunate! If anyone considered how full it is of anxieties, dangers, and miseries, he would not pick it up even as it lay in the mud!” [Col. 0292B] This man had recognized the anxious and hidden torments of the rich. For unless riches and honors pierced people with the various stings of anxiety, the Lord would never have compared them to thorns. [Note: [Col. 0291] Matthew 13.]

The wisdom of this world is wonderfully deceived: for the children of this age, their riches are continually turned into misery and torment; but the children of light continually discover that lacking riches makes one free and blessed. “I confess to you, Father of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and revealed them to little ones.” [Note: [Col. 0291] Matthew 11.] The poor and righteous person despises riches and lacks nothing, because God suffices him. But the rich man—the son of avarice, worshipper of Mammon, servant of money—finds greater anxiety, fear, and misery in that in which he had established for himself fuller pleasure.

If you wish to spend your days in holy religious life and golden poverty, the glory of kings cannot be compared with your happiness. “A little is better than the many riches of sinners.” [Note: [Col. 0291] Psalm 36.] You have lost the days which you spent in worldly works. Henceforth, “one day in the courts of the Lord will be better than thousands.” [Note: [Col. 0291] Psalm 83.] [Col. 0292C] While you were in Sicily, you were like a lost vessel. For that infernal region, which devours its inhabitants, made your return seem hopeless; but now, by God’s grace, you drink your native air and the wines of Blois. Had Sicily held you longer, it would, in its own fashion, have offered you the wine of asps.
