By now, brother, you would be lying in a marble tomb, perhaps with this inscription written upon it as a profit of empty glory: “WILLIAM OF BLOIS, ABBOT OF MATINES, LIES HERE.” Brother, in the poet’s testimony:

> The loss of a tomb is slight.  
> [Note: [Col. 0291] Virgil, *Aeneid* II.]

Your tragedy about Flaura and Marcus, your verses on the flea and the fly, your comedy about the *alda* [uncertain title], your sermons, and your other works in theology—which I wish had been published more widely and more famously—will make your name commendable in a more enduring memory. Your writings have added more honor to you than four abbeys.

The appearance of gold had indeed deceived you; hence some of our countrymen have exchanged Sicilian wealth for the loss of life. [Col. 0293A] The lord chancellor also—so the Jerusalemites report—has gone to his fate. For when the ulcer called *estiomenus*, commonly “the wolf,” had grievously seized his thigh, all the instruments of the physicians proved useless; at last, in the holy city of God, in the arms of the king and amid a company of princes standing about and weeping, he breathed out his spirit.

[Note: [Col. 0293D] This is Stephen, son of the Count of Perche, whom Margaret, mother of William II, king of Sicily, summoned from France to govern the kingdom with her during her son’s minority; she made him chancellor of the kingdom and arranged for his election to the archbishopric of Palermo. But shortly afterwards, compelled by the hostility of certain nobles to leave Sicily, he set out for Jerusalem, where he died soon after.

We have spoken at length about the destruction of the city of Catania in connection with Letter 46.

I infer that this letter was written about the year 1170, namely shortly after the destruction of Catania, which occurred in 1169. Peter was in France, as he himself says near the end of this letter: “We are, brother, in sweet France.” For he was not yet in England.]

I also learned through the trustworthy report of travellers that, in vengeance for Lord Stephen, the city of Catania was shaken and overthrown by an earthquake; in it that son of pride, the brother of Matthew the notary, who had fraudulently supplanted you in the bishopric and raised a treacherous faction against innocent persons, was caught and buried, and belched forth his soul—the handmaid of iniquity and slave of Satan. [Col. 0293B]

We are, brother, in sweet France, which alone, according to Jerome’s testimony, has no monsters. [Note: [Col. 0293] *Against Vigilantius*.] “It is good for us to be here.” [Note: [Col. 0293] Matthew 17.] Let those live in Sicily who procure treacheries and poisons—the officials of flattery—and who soothe the itching ears of great men, itching for the wind of empty glory, with poisonous sweetness.

> Let Arthur live there,  
> And Catulus; let those remain who turn black things white.  
> [Note: [Col. 0293] Juvenal, *Satires* 3.]

It is enough for me if I may live and die there where I was born and reared. A circular life pleases me: let the course of my life be bounded by its beginning in birth. Farewell.

## LETTER XCIV. TO J., ARCHDEACON

[Col. 0293C]

**SUMMARY.**—He complains to the archdeacon about the insolence of his nephews, knights, because they impiously attack the sacred order of clerics, pursue idleness, and have departed very far—as have others of their age—from the virtue of former knights, whose praises he depicts.

To his dearest lord, JOHN, archdeacon, PETER OF BLOIS sends greetings in the author of salvation.

I cannot endure the arrogant glory of your nephews, the knights, who boast of the preeminence of military life while corrupting the estate of clerics with manifold detraction, treating their life and works with reproach and contempt. Certainly, their distinction is not greatly advanced by the corruption of our order. If they were knights, or knew what the profession of knights is, they would show deference to clerics and restrain themselves from the buffoonery of words by a certain maidenly modesty. [Col. 0294A]

For the order of knights now consists in observing no order. Whoever pollutes his mouth with greater filthiness of language, swears more abominably, fears God less, despises God’s ministers, and does not stand in awe of the Church—he is now reckoned stronger and more renowned in the company of knights. I should bear it more tolerably if men other than your nephews had burst forth into this audacity of pride and misconduct, especially since from the cradles of childhood they have known in you only modesty and learned from you only uprightness.

Yet, since every age is inclined toward evil from youth onward, after they attached themselves to their fellow-soldiers, they contracted ruined morals from them. Rhetoricians too draw an argument from association: “He who touches pitch will be defiled by it.” [Note: [Col. 0293] Ecclesiasticus 13.]

> And a grape takes its purple hue from seeing another grape.  
> [Note: [Col. 0293] Juvenal, *Satires* 2.]

[Col. 0294B] The military discipline which Vegetius Renatus and very many others taught has now utterly vanished and has deformed itself into a kind of freedom to do wrong and a form of buffoonery. Formerly knights bound themselves by the bond of an oath: that they would stand for the stability of the commonwealth; that they would not flee in battle; and that they would put the public good before the advantage of their own lives.

Even today novices receive their swords from the altar, so that they may profess that they have received the sword as sons of the Church, for the honor of the priesthood, the protection of the poor, the punishment of evildoers, and the liberation of their country. But the matter has been turned to its opposite. For as soon as they are adorned with the military belt, they rise up against the anointed of the Lord and rage against the patrimony of the Crucified. [Col. 0294C] They despoil and plunder Christ’s poor subjects; they afflict the wretched miserably and without mercy, so that in others’ sufferings they may fulfill unlawful desires and extraordinary pleasures.

Luke relates that soldiers came to John the Baptist and asked him: “Master, what are we also to do?” He said: “Do violence to no one, make no false accusation, and be content with your wages.” [Note: [Col. 0293] Luke 3.] Those who ought to exercise their strength against the enemies of Christ’s cross instead battle with drinking and drunkenness; they devote themselves to idleness, grow sluggish through gluttony, spend a degraded life in uncleanness, and dishonor the name and office of knighthood.

Nothing is more blameworthy in a knight than idleness. [Col. 0294D] Through it the use of arms is unlearned, cowardice is nourished, strength decays, lethargy creeps in, and the mind is occupied with unclean acts. Therefore P. Nasica, when commanding an army in winter quarters, although he had no need of the use of fleets, nevertheless ordered ships to be built, lest the soldiers be corrupted by idleness or gluttony, or grow arrogant through freedom from occupation. [Note: [Col. 0293] Frontinus, *Stratagems*, book IV.]

We read that the emperor Trajan, whenever his soldiers were free from battles, exercised them in running, jumping, swimming, the practice of striking with cuts or thrusts, throwing stones by hand or sling, and hurling missiles; he trained them in every method by which war must be sustained or waged. [Note: [Col. 0295] Dio, *Life*.] Sallust reports of the great Pompey that he competed in jumping with the agile, in running with the swift, and in lifting a bar with the strong. [Note: [Col. 0295] Vegetius, book I, *On Military Affairs*, chapter 9.]

Yet after he, the senate, and the Roman people began to devote themselves to idleness and ease, those who had once repelled hostile attacks among the most remote nations with a small force abandoned the defenses of their most powerful city when Caesar arrived with a small army, [Col. 0295B] and placed their confidence in flight alone. Moreover, what especially stirred Caesar’s boldness was that he had to deal with an idle army and a worn-out general who had, through a long peace, unlearned generalship.

Trogus Pompeius reports [Note: [Col. 0295] Justin, book I.] that Sardanapalus, the last king of the Assyrians, was shamefully cast down from his royal throne because of idleness and softness of life. What raised the Romans up? Whence did they obtain supremacy over all peoples? The practice of arms and exercise in battle won them their name and glory.

According to Vegetius Renatus [Note: [Col. 0295] Book I, *On Military Affairs*, chapter 3.], a man reared tenderly and accustomed to luxuries is wholly useless for military service. He judges more fit for battle the man reared under the open sky and sun, patient of labor, indifferent to shade, unfamiliar with baths, bearing alike the assaults of cold and heat, inexperienced in lawsuits, simple in conduct, content with moderate food; one who is not ashamed to dig a ditch, repair ramparts, carry stones and mortar, and bring together supplies of timber. [Col. 0295C]

Therefore, according to the same author [Note: [Col. 0295] Ovid, *Metamorphoses* 15.], Roman youth once washed in the Tiber the sweat gathered by running or exercise in the field; nor did it shrink less from baths than from the effeminizing waters of Salmacis. Even in the time of the Judges, Jerubbaal, or Gideon—leaving aside the mysteries of figurative interpretation—was, by the Lord’s command, forbidden to confront the Midianites with a multitude that was soft, untrained, and cowardly. When Gideon cried aloud, so that all heard: “Whoever is fearful and timid, let him return,” [Note: [Col. 0295] Judges 7.] twenty-two thousand departed from him, and only ten thousand remained. [Col. 0295D]

From these too he selected as fit for war only those who, in their thirst, lapped like dogs and hastily brought water to their mouths; he entirely rejected those who bent the knee and stooped down to drink. Thus deliverance of the people came through three hundred men; I do not think that they learned to lap water amid delicate feasts and exquisite banquets. The Lord chose them beforehand because they met necessity within the humility of nature.

Today our *philosymbola* [reading uncertain], excessively occupied with care for the skin, is reared in luxury and wholly abandons itself to fleshly delights:

> Youth excessively industrious in caring for its skin.  
> [Note: [Col. 0295] Horace, book I, epistle 2.]

[Col. 0296A] If our knights must ever go on campaign, their packhorses are loaded not with iron but wine, not with lances but cheeses, not with swords but wineskins, not with spears but roasting-spits. You would think they were going to a banquet-hall, not to war. They carry shields excellently gilded, desiring the enemy’s booty rather than combat with the enemy; and, so to speak, they bring them back virginal and untouched. Yet they have battles and cavalry engagements painted on their saddles and shields, so that they may delight in a kind of imaginary vision of combats which they do not dare actually to enter or even see. [Col. 0296B]

Scipio Africanus, as Julius Frontinus relates elegantly in the *Stratagems* [Note: [Col. 0295] Book IV, chapter 1.], when he saw a certain man’s shield decorated in many ways with gold and jewels, said that he did not wonder that the man had adorned so carefully that in which he had more protection than in his sword. We read that Aeneas transferred gems from his fingers to his sword, Birro from his fingers to drinking-cups. Pericles says that not painting, nor gold and stones, but a shield split apart, a broken helmet, a blunted sword, and a wounded face furnish a soldier’s adornment.

But when our knights return from a campaign, by God’s grace, without wound or scar and with their arms also sound and whole, they rush into a conflict of drinking:

> Therefore joyfully they set out bowls and crown the wines,  
> [Note: [Col. 0295] Virgil, *Aeneid* VII.]
>
> And sing of battles, after draining Mars in heavy measure.
>
> [Col. 0296C] Here Achilles, here Ulysses was straining;  
> And they paint all Troy in flowing wine.  
> [Note: [Col. 0295] Ovid, *Pentel.*]

They chatter, then, and let loose their insolent tongues in detraction against innocent people; they rage against the anointed of the Lord and compare and contrast their own labors with the leisure of priests. Thus a resolution is passed among them and sanctioned by common law: that they should take away tithes; that they should not show deference to the Church and clergy; that they should not fear excommunication; that they should not revere God; that they should inflict injuries upon priests; and that they should empty out whatever has accrued to the uses of the Church from the generosity of their ancestors or fathers.

Nevertheless, the Lord is great and exceedingly terrible: he humbles every height exalting itself against the knowledge of God; he will save the children of the poor and humble the slanderer; and, taking away the rod of sinners from above the lot of the righteous, he will plead for the meek of the earth, [Col. 0296D] stop the mouths of those speaking iniquity, and cast down every exaltation of the proud. [Note: [Col. 0295] Isaiah 11.]

Since the Lord says to his priests, “He who despises you despises me,” [Note: [Col. 0295] Luke 10.] and, “He who touches you touches the pupil of my eye,” [Note: [Col. 0295] Zechariah 2.], if you love your nephews and are zealous for their life, lest they perish with Uzzah while he stretches out a rash hand toward the ark of the Lord, [Note: [Col. 0295] 2 Samuel 6.], instruct them by salutary admonitions in reverence for the Church [Col. 0297A] and Christ’s officers. For, since you have received them into the lot of your household and the fellowship of your table, you are not altogether free from fault if you allow your table-companions to chatter everywhere against clerics and to behave insolently toward the Church.

It is true that your nephew S., through the arm and valor of the advocate of Béthune, once—perhaps only once—won the celebrated distinctions of knighthood. But for this reason he ought not to have conceived a wind of pride against the Church of God. Nothing diminishes the value of praise more than incessantly boasting of one’s successes and hawking one single day throughout every day of the year.

We read of Marius [Note: [Col. 0297] Plutarch, *Life of Gaius Marius*.] that, although he performed very many things splendidly, he lost the glory of his reputation through a single act of self-praise; and because he presumed to ascribe to himself what he ought to have sought from another’s mouth, he forfeited the rewards of public commendation. [Col. 0297B]

To come to examples of boasting and display from our own household: King Hezekiah, [Note: [Col. 0297] Isaiah 39; 2 Kings 20.] whom the Lord had honored above all kings through the shadow on the sundial, the addition of years, and the flight of Sennacherib, showed to the messengers of Merodach, son of Baladan, king of Babylon, his spices, ointments, house of vessels, storerooms of aromatic substances, and everything in his treasures, for display and boasting. Therefore, according to the word of Isaiah son of Amoz, his treasures were taken away and transported to Babylon; and his sons were carried captive and made eunuchs in the palace of the king of Babylon.

A threefold choice of divine punishment was likewise offered to David because he numbered the people of God for vainglory. [Note: [Col. 0297] 2 Samuel 24.] But Nebuchadnezzar, [Note: [Col. 0297] Daniel 4.] because he magnified himself in the strength, splendor, and glory of his kingdom, was humbled: he was likened to a brute animal, joined to senseless beasts, and made like them. [Note: [Col. 0297] Psalm 48.] [Col. 0297C]

Would that they did not swell with pride against Christ and his anointed, but humbly and devoutly recalled how, by the grace of God—or rather by yours—they were raised from the dust of poverty and from dung! Abraham too, though chosen and called by the Lord, nevertheless remembered his condition: “I shall speak to the Lord, though I am dust and ashes.” [Note: [Col. 0297] Genesis 18.] In Leviticus also, [Note: [Col. 0297] Chapter 1.] concerning the sacrifice of birds, it is commanded that the feathers and the little bladder of the lung be laid down in the dust, so that one whom the Lord exalts may be humbled and, amid the magnificences of divine grace, recognize himself as dust. [Col. 0297D] Fare well.

## LETTER XCV. TO H., KING OF THE ENGLISH

**SUMMARY.**—Since the king of England could not be aware of everything done in his very extensive provinces, he warns him about various abuses by sheriffs and other subordinate officials, and explains how they may be corrected.

To his dearest lord H., by God’s grace most illustrious [Col. 0298A] king of the English, duke of the Normans and Aquitanians, count of the Angevins: his own P. of Blois, archdeacon of Bath, greetings; and, amid a temporal kingdom, remembrance and love of the heavenly kingdom.

I fear to speak, but it is not expedient to be silent. It would nevertheless seem safer to me to conceal in silence the agitation of my boiling mind; but great danger to my soul hangs over me from my silence. Therefore I shall speak, because, to use Job’s words, “If I keep silent, my mouth will condemn me.” [Note: [Col. 0297] Job 9.] I shall speak what ought to serve your honor and safety, and the peace of your subjects.

Although beyond all kings of the earth you know the character of your subjects and the condition of your kingdom, yet because it exceeds human capacity to know everything that happens in provinces so many and so extensive, [Col. 0298B] hear a few things which neither I can keep silent without sin nor you can remain ignorant of without danger. For many things are sometimes hidden from the lord which are known to his subjects. In the Aquinate’s testimony:

> He will be the last to know the disgrace of his household.  
> [Note: [Col. 0297] Juvenal, *Satires* 10.]

Since many things happen in private households which escape their masters’ knowledge, it should not be imputed to your negligence or lack of care if, in regions so broad and widespread, over which the Lord has set you, you do not fully know the offenses of every individual. For even those justices whom we commonly call errant or itinerant frequently happen to err while diligently investigating human errors. People’s offenses are concealed, whether through affection, fear, the law of kinship, the duty of compassion, or redeemed by secret gifts. [Col. 0298C] For the voice of purchased pity is admitted, and abolition is obtained contrary to the senatorial decree of Turpilius. [Note: [Col. 0297] *Code*, book X, title 45, law “Is demum.”]

The countless officers of foresters and sheriffs, while striving to satisfy their own avarice and greed, despoil the poor, lay snares for the simple, foster the wicked, oppress the innocent, exult in the worst deeds, rejoice when they have done evil, [Note: [Col. 0297] Proverbs 2.] feed upon the sins of the people, and luxuriate in widows’ tears, orphans’ hunger, the nakedness of the poor, and the affliction of the simple.

It is written in the book of Wisdom that the prey of the lion is the wild ass in the wilderness. [Note: [Col. 0297] Ecclesiasticus 13.] So the poor are the food and drink of sheriffs, forest judges, and other subordinate officers, and the public occasion of plunder. [Col. 0298D] The wicked devours the righteous; the courtier, the peasant; the tax collector, the innocent; the fraudulent man, the simple.

The multitude of officials is as great as that of locusts: when these depart, others succeed them; and what has been partly devoured, others devour ruinously and consume. Thus is fulfilled in them that prophetic saying: “What the caterpillar left the locust has eaten; what the locust left the beetle has eaten; and what the beetle left the mildew has eaten.” [Note: [Col. 0299] Joel 1.] [Col. 0299A]

These are the cormorants, driving their greed by the plunder of fish; Saint Martin, when driving them away, used to say: “This is the form of demons.” These are the leeches of princes, continually thirsting and drinking another’s blood. [Note: [Col. 0299] Sulpicius, Letter 2 to Bassula.]

Of Samuel it is written that he judged the people Israel, going around Bethel, Gilgal, and Mizpah, and returning to Ramah, where were his birthplace and dwelling. [Note: [Col. 0299] 1 Samuel 7.] From this it is most clearly inferred that he sought neither food nor drink from his jurisdiction. Hence, speaking to all the children of Israel, he said with a free and confident conscience: “I have lived among you from my youth. Speak concerning me before the Lord and before his anointed: whether I have taken anyone’s ox or donkey; whether I have falsely accused anyone; whether I have oppressed anyone; whether I have received a gift from anyone’s hand. I shall despise it today, and restore it to you.” [Note: [Col. 0299] 1 Samuel 12.] [Col. 0299B]

Similar is what blessed Job says: “If my land cries out against me”—as though to say: “No subject of mine cries out against me because of some burden or oppression.” [Note: [Col. 0299] Chapter 31.] Today the simple and innocent person is accused of having cut wood in the forest, consented to the taking of game, concealed the rights of the crown, failed to pay the tribute of public service, failed to appear at the hundred-court and the hallmoot, [Note: [Col. 0299D] *Hundred* or *hundredus* is understood in three ways. First, it means a part of a county or province containing one hundred villages, or in which lived one hundred sureties for the king’s peace; it was otherwise called a *cantred*, that is, a “hundred,” namely from the number of one hundred sureties. Hence the lord of a hundred was the same as a *centenarius*. A *hundred* was also called a *wapentake*, from *wapen*, “arms,” because whenever there was a new lord of a hundred, those subject to him were required to render arms as a sign of subjection.

Second, it means the court or pleas—what we call assizes—summoned by the authority of the lord of the hundred; all hundred-men were required to attend them. [Col. 0300D]

Finally, it means the payments or tributes owed to the lord of the hundred. A *halimot* is the assembly of the court of a lord’s manor or barony in villages and domains, or of tribes, wards, and associations in boroughs and cities. Thus *hundred* is here used in the second sense: failure to attend the hundred and halimot means nothing other than absence from the pleas or court which hundred-men—that is, those subject to the lord of the hundred—were obliged to attend. See much discussion of these terms in the glossaries of Spelman, Somner, and William Wats, and in Vossius, *On the Faults of Speech*.] or failed to entertain the king’s officials honorably, although he had nothing with which to provide for himself, his wife, and his children. [Col. 0299C]

Even this would be more tolerable if he were allowed to answer them and plead his poverty. But with such men the words of the poor are lighter than wind, and however firm their oaths, they are held cheap, because, in the words of the pagan:

> The poor man is believed to despise thunderbolts  
> And the gods themselves, with the gods’ own permission.  
> As much money as each keeps in his chest,  
> So much credit does he possess.  
> [Note: [Col. 0299] Juvenal, *Satires* 3.]

Although it is written: “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness,” [Note: [Col. 0299] Matthew 5.] these men who judge your poor, ignorant of justice and prudence, hunger and thirst for money alone. For your greater officials appoint as their substitutes only such persons as the expectation of profit, kinship, natural relation, or upbringing commends to them. Hence Wisdom laments in miserable complaint: “Those who held the law did not know me”; [Note: [Col. 0299] Jeremiah 2.] “they became judges, and I did not know it.” [Note: [Col. 0299] Hosea 8.] [Col. 0300A]

Judicial power and the ministry of equity ought indeed to proceed not from affection of the flesh but solely from love of human beings or of God, through a sure dispensation. Certainly, when Moses had doubts concerning the daughters of Zelophehad, they were admitted by the Lord’s judgment to the benefit of their paternal inheritance. [Note: [Col. 0299] Numbers 27.] Succession of blood makes an heir; election makes a judge.

Those, indeed, ought to be appointed judges of peoples whose purer life and outstanding prudence have distinguished them above the rest. For the vices of subjects are restrained by the reverence and authority of those who preside. Scipio Africanus was commended by such gravity of character and stern maturity of chastity that, by the example of his chastity alone, he established among the people a public resolve toward continence.

As Titus Livy reports, [Note: [Col. 0299] Decade 3; Gellius 6, chapter 8; Valerius 4, chapter 5.] after Scipio had subdued the provinces from the Pyrenees to the Pillars of Hercules and the Ocean, defeating Hannibal and the other enemies of Rome, he restored to the barbarians captive boys and girls of exceptional beauty, and did not allow them to come into his sight, lest even his eye take anything away from the integrity of chastity. [Col. 0300B]

We read that Fronto displayed such gravity of life in his deeds and countenance that he restrained in people not only unlawful actions but unlawful inclinations as well. Job says of himself: “When I went out to the city gate, they prepared a seat for me in the square. Young men saw me and hid themselves; old men rose and stood. Princes ceased speaking and put a finger upon their mouths.” [Note: [Col. 0299] Job 29.]

Noble and discerning men are indignant because those whom they know to be commoners, and who display no titles of prudence or virtue, are set over them in jurisdiction—except that they have attached themselves to your household officers through kinship or affinity, service or gifts. [Col. 0300C]

These things, most gracious prince, cannot readily come to your notice. For although you may wish kindly and mercifully to hear the cries of the poor, the poor man nevertheless fears to disclose the malice of the exactors, lest they devise harsher measures against him and his latter condition become worse than his former. But if anyone, moved by compassion and mercy, should venture to reveal to you the oppressions of the poor and the tyrannical exactions of your officials, their masters will be deeply stirred, [Col. 0301A] and, in hatred of him who has brought the cause of the poor before you, will rouse all the other courtiers against him. Although enmities and jealousies reign especially among most courtiers, yet whenever anyone is defamed on such a pretext, he finds even his enemies become his defenders. And although in almost everything their pleasures conflict, nevertheless, in mutual excuse and defence they preserve the bond of social favour and the spirit of unity. For these are the scales of Behemoth, of which it is read in Job that one is joined to another, and that no breath of life passes through them. [Note: [Col. 0301] Job 41.]

If legal affairs are argued in the hearing of your Highness, or before your princely justice, there neither the breeze of gifts nor respect of persons finds a place. There all matters proceed [Col. 0301B] in judgment and justice, and do not overstep your established bounds of equity even in the slightest degree. But if the affairs of the poor are referred down to inferior and lesser judges, the wicked man is justified for gifts; and, for the overthrow of justice and the ensnaring of the poor, pedantic quibbles over syllables and snares of words are set forth. There are some who do not grant letters concerning the granting or execution of justice except upon a definite promise of money. But whoever has sold letters of this sort should know that he puts up for sale the justice of God, of which he is a debtor and which he is bound to render freely. For, by the authority of the holy Fathers, whoever sells one thing without which the rest cannot be obtained leaves neither unsold.

Certainly justice is more acceptable to God than a prebend; [Col. 0301C] and therefore, although simony can be committed in either case, every act of venality in rendering justice is nevertheless more damnable in His sight than the sale of a tithe or a prebend. These matters, most just prince, you must investigate diligently and, when investigated, correct, lest the excesses of lesser men be required from your hands by the Lord. For often the fault of the people rebounds upon the ruler, as though the errors of the lesser arose from the negligence of the greater.

It is read in the Book of Numbers [Note: [Col. 0301] ch. 25.] that, while the people of Israel were committing fornication with the Midianites, Phinehas pierced with a dagger Zimri and the Midianite woman as they coupled together; the wrath of the Lord ceased, and the word of the Lord came to Moses: “Take,” He said, “all the princes of the people and [Col. 0301D] hang them up in gibbets before the sun.” The princes had not sinned, but the people; nevertheless the princes are punished for the people’s sin. Eli was punished for the sin of his sons. [Note: [Col. 0301] I Kings 4.]

Bear patiently, most invincible prince, what I lay before you out of sincere devotion. For with the most ardent affection of charity I zealously thirst for your salvation. There is no trifling in the oppressions of the poor: they are not expiated by gifts, nor redeemed by alms. For he who offers sacrifice from the substance of a poor man, Solomon testifies, acts like one who sacrifices a son before the eyes [Col. 0302A] of his father. [Note: [Col. 0301] Ecclus. 34.] “Do not say,” says the Wise Man, “God will regard the multitude of my gifts, and when I offer gifts the Most High will be appeased.” [Note: [Col. 0301] Ecclus. 7.] Certainly God has no need of our goods. And He who gives the kings of the earth their riches does not demand from them gold or silver, but that they hear the cause of the widow and orphan, and that they plead for the meek of the earth. [Note: [Col. 0301] Isa. 11.]

It is fitting, most illustrious prince, that you attend carefully to these matters, and appoint such ministers of public law as fear God through the example of yourself and your princely justice; who do not pursue recompense, show no favouritism, and derive neither confidence of impunity nor boldness in cruelty from kinship with your household officers. Among the ancients, Cicero testifies, [Note: [Col. 0301] Book III, *On Duties*] it was said proverbially: “Whoever puts on the person of a friend puts off [Col. 0302B] the person of a judge.” For equity, to which a judge owes obedience, knows neither the left hand of hatred nor the right hand of love. Such ought the minister of law to be, that in his hand the balance of justice neither totters nor wavers through regard for any person. [Note: [Col. 0301] See John of Salisbury, Book V of the *Polycraticus*, ch. 12.]

In a military court the case of mighty Alexander was condemned, notwithstanding the fear inspired by his fellow-soldiers. Pythagoras, the most renowned teacher of eloquence, pressed insistently for judgment in a case which he had against his disciple, yet his petition was not heard. Neither Alexander’s terror nor Pythagoras’s authority could turn the scale of justice away from equity. Nothing shines so gloriously in a prince as to love and dispense justice without any respect of persons. [Col. 0302C]

Zaleucus, [Note: [Col. 0301] Aelian, *Various History*] when his son in the city of the Locrians had been caught in adultery and, according to the law of the city which he himself had established, was to be deprived of both eyes, while the whole people, out of regard for his father’s honour, remitted the punishment due to him—resisted for some time. At length, overcome by the people’s prayers and insistence, he first put out one of his own eyes and then the other eye of his son; and so, leaving to each the use of sight, by a remarkable tempering of equity he preserved justice in the father and mercy in the ruler.

But if you wish to bear sheaves of justice before the great and strict Judge, you must judge the judges of your realm with the utmost strictness, so that the terror and reverence of royal majesty may stir to saving conduct those whom the fire of Gehenna and the endless punishment assigned to wicked [Col. 0302D] judges do not deter. Farewell.

## LETTER XCVI

**SUMMARY.**—Richard, raised from a Cistercian monk to the archbishopric of Canterbury, commends himself to the prayers of the Fathers assembled at Cîteaux.

To the venerable and holy Fathers assembled in the chapter of Cîteaux, R., by God’s permission minister of the Church of Canterbury: greeting in the Author of salvation.

[Col. 0303A] Among the desirable things of this world, it held first place among my wishes to be personally present at the assembly of your holiness. But the demands of a new calling and the pressing length of my business deprive me of the fruit of the joy I desire, and do not permit me for the present to be among those blessed camps.

O camps to be desired! O venerable congregation! O Cîteaux, how great is thy household, how fruitful in sons, how splendid in tongues, how glorious among peoples! “Lift up thine eyes and see: all these are gathered together; they have come to thee.” The diversity of tongues among you is signified by the profession of one life; and religion gathered from every nation represents the miracle of Pentecost in the sending forth of the Holy Spirit. Thus, to use the Apostle’s words, [Note: [Col. 0303] Rom. 1.]: “God is my witness [Col. 0303B] how I long for you in the bowels of Jesus Christ,” cherishing mutual affection in the bowels of charity; not forsaking your assembly, which I embrace in Christ through the presence of the spirit, mindful of your fellowship, which I cannot forget. For you are my glory and joy, the honour of my head and my crown.

He who, according to Job’s word, [Note: [Col. 0303] ch. 5.] “sets the lowly on high”; He who “calls those things which are,” [Note: [Col. 0303] Rom. 4.] has Himself called me to a burden too heavy for me to bear. [Note: [Col. 0303] Matt. 23.] But I, a man who sees my poverty [Note: [Col. 0303] Lam. 3.] and my insufficiency, reflecting also how for a like cause the giants groan beneath the waters [Note: [Col. 0303] Job 26.] and those who bear the world bend beneath it, would be overthrown by faintness of spirit and tempest unless I had conceived confidence in the stone of help and in the aid [Col. 0303C] of your prayers. For, according to Job’s word, [Note: [Col. 0303] ch. 6.] “What is my strength, that I should endure?” Behold, there is no help in me, but weakness and deficiency.

I fear that the Lord, offended with me, has imposed upon me this care for many, when I was not sufficient even to manage the business of my own salvation. But the Lord has placed in you for me the word of reconciliation, so that, if He is offended with me, He may through your prayer show Himself propitious to me and supply what is imperfect in me. For He is able to do all things exceeding abundantly beyond what we ask or understand. Therefore, “if there be any consolation in Christ, if any comfort of charity, if any fellowship of spirit, if any bowels of compassion, fulfil my joy.” [Note: [Col. 0303] Phil. 2.]

For after God I place the fullness of my joy [Col. 0303D] in your prayers: that, through the benefit of your petitions, the mercy of the Lord may be pleased to sustain my deficiency in this administration entrusted to me. For although the Apostle was made a chosen vessel and clothed with power from on high, he nevertheless deemed the prayers of the saints necessary to him for the teaching of the Gentiles: [Col. 0304A] “I beseech you,” he says, “by the Lord Jesus Christ and by the charity of the Holy Spirit, that you help me with your prayers to the Lord.” [Note: [Col. 0303] Rom. 15.]

We therefore, weak and frail, devoutly and humbly entreat that the bond of our fraternal profession, the communion of charity, the obligation of subjects, and the need and devotion of the petitioner may, through your holy affection toward us, be stirred up on our behalf.

## LETTER XCVII. TO THE ABBOT OF EVESHAM

[Note: [Col. 0303D] From William of Malmesbury, Book IV of *The Deeds of the Bishops of England*: the monastery of Evesham, of the Order of St Benedict, situated in the province of Worcester, was founded by St Egwin, third bishop of Worcester. The same account occurs in the *Monasticon Anglicanum*, vol. I, p. 144.]

**SUMMARY.**—He shows that the variety of monastic orders deserves praise, and that one ought not readily pass from one to another; but that manual labour in them is neither to be praised nor censured.

To the reverend Father and lord, the abbot of Evesham, M. PETER of Blois, archdeacon of Bath: greeting in the Author [Col. 0304B] of salvation.

It is characteristic of envy to regard another’s praise as one’s own injury. But the religion proved in you, and the pleasant sweetness of manners, interpreter of your native kindness, will not count it an insult that I seemed to commend the Cistercian or Carthusian order above the rest. I took nothing from you in praising them. I approve them and praise you; I did not set up their distinctions to the prejudice of your reputation.

Christ is not divided. Whether in a white or a dark habit, in every profession and order, among every people, whoever does the will of the Lord is acceptable to Him. [Note: [Col. 0303] Acts 10.] He with whom there is no [Col. 0304C] distinction of Jew and Greek [Note: [Col. 0303] ibid.] does not distinguish between a white and a black habit. The Lord considers the mind, not the garment; merits, not colour. On Monte Cassino the monastic form of dress used by St Benedict remains, it is said, to this day. Who would dare to revile in his sons the habit of so great a father? For if the firstfruits are holy, so is the mass; and if the root is holy, so are the branches.

Whether someone is whiter than snow with the Nazarites, [Note: [Col. 0303] Lam. 4.] or whether, with blessed Job, his skin has been blackened upon the ash-heap, [Note: [Col. 0303] Job 30.] each works out salvation in the house of the Lord. Indeed, in Jacob’s sheepfold there are white and black lambs. [Note: [Col. 0303] Gen. 30.] In the vineyard of Sorec there are white and black grapes. [Note: [Col. 0303] Isa. 5.] And the bride who is made exceedingly white by the lilies of the valleys herself says: “I am black, but beautiful.” [Note: [Col. 0303] Song 1.] In the bride of Christ variety is not unfitting, since she herself is described as clothed about with varieties [Col. 0304D] [Note: [Col. 0303] Ps. 44.]. Variety itself is the cause of unity. For on the harp, from the diversity of strings comes a single modulation in harmony.

Moreover, according to the Apostle, [Note: [Col. 0303] I Cor. 12.] there are diversities of gifts, diversities of ministries, and diversities of operations; but it is the same God who works all things in all. It is read [Col. 0305A] in the Book of Numbers [Note: [Col. 0305] ch. 3.] how the Lord willed different offices to be established for the ministry of the tabernacle: some Levites, some Merarites, some Kohathites, some Gershonites, some Aaronites. And, the Apostle testifying, the Lord gave some as apostles, others as prophets, others as evangelists, others as pastors and teachers. [Note: [Col. 0305] Eph. 4.] For all members of the body do not have the same activity, [Note: [Col. 0305] Rom. 12.] so that through many persons and forms the graces of God may be given thanks for by many, according to the gift that is in us.

You may see the bride’s beauty in diversity of actions, professions, manners, opinions, and orders. Therefore in sacred speech she is described as a cedar, a cypress, a palm, a planting of roses, an olive, a plane-tree, cinnamon and balm, choice myrrh, storax and galbanum, [Col. 0305B] onycha, a terebinth, and uncut Lebanon. [Note: [Col. 0305] Ecclus. 24.] Pointing to this diversity through Isaiah, the Lord says: “Behold, I will lay thy stones in order; I will found thee upon sapphires, jasper, and sculpted stones.” [Note: [Col. 0305] Isa. 54.] The Apostle testifies that in the house of the Lord there are vessels of gold and silver, wood and clay, fit for ministry; [Note: [Col. 0305] II Tim. 2.] and that all the members of the body, though many, are one body. [Note: [Col. 0305] I Cor. 12.] For all works, studies, and counsels are brought to one end. For Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes. [Note: [Col. 0305] Rom. 10.]

The order of Cluny is holy, and so is that of Cîteaux; and in each the Lord has placed the ministry of reconciliation and the work of salvation. Let no one take the diversity of orders among men amiss; for there is order also [Col. 0305C] among the stars. The moon also, Habakkuk testifies, stood in its order; and the different orders of angels are distinguished. [Note: [Col. 0305] Hab. 3.] “See then your calling.” [Note: [Col. 0305] I Cor. 1.] Let each remain in the calling in which he was called.

Some, through reckless levity of mind, leave religious houses with enormous scandal, glory in an alien rule, and hold in contempt the rule to which they bound themselves by the bond of profession. Nor do they heed that saying of the Apostle: “not glorying in another’s rule.” [Note: [Col. 0305] II Cor. 10.] For this reason I lately became angry with Master Alexander in a certain letter [Note: [Col. 0305] 86.] and allowed words specifically concerning him to range more freely than they should have done, to the offence of some. [Col. 0306A]

I confess that lengthiness of psalmody, if it proceeds from devotion, is most healthful; if it has sloth as its companion, it is nevertheless an honourable occupation; and if it does not wholly restrain the wandering excursions of the mind, at least by it a man becomes accustomed to more honourable pursuits. But as for manual labours in a monk, I presume neither to censure nor praise them. For although the Apostle says to the Corinthians, “We labour with our hands,” [Note: [Col. 0305] I Cor. 10.] and to the Ephesians, “Rather let him labour with his hands,” [Note: [Col. 0305] Eph. 4.] and to the Thessalonians, “Labouring night and day, lest we burden any of you,” [Note: [Col. 0305] II Thess. 3.]; yet, writing to Timothy, he says: “Exercise thyself unto godliness; for bodily exercise is profitable for little.” [Note: [Col. 0305] I Tim. 4.]

Of the former the Apostle says: “He who does not work shall not eat.” [Note: [Col. 0305] II Thess. 10.] But to the latter the Lord gives this command through Isaiah: “Strangers shall stand [Col. 0306B] and feed your flocks; their sons shall be your farmers and vinedressers. But you shall be called the holy ones of the Lord, ministers of God.” [Note: [Col. 0305] ch. 61.] To the former, through Ecclesiasticus, it is said: “Do not hate laborious works and farming created by God.” [Note: [Col. 0305] Ecclus. 7.] But to the latter, conversely, it is said: “Write wisdom in leisure; and he who is diminished in action shall find it.” [Note: [Col. 0305] Ecclus. 38.]

In this diversity the Lord knows those who are His. [Note: [Col. 0305] II Tim. 2.] Moreover, according to Job’s word, God “has put a sign in the hand of every human being, that each may know his own works”; [Note: [Col. 0305] Job 37.] and, by the same witness, “a book of remembrance was written before Him for those who fear God and think upon His name.” [Note: [Col. 0305] Mal. 3.] Likewise, among diverse orders, in my judgment that man alone wisely and happily orders his way of life whose service of obedience the Lord graciously accepts from his heart and hand. [Col. 0306C]

## LETTER XCVIII. TO THE SUFFRAGANS OF THE CHURCH OF CANTERBURY. [A.D. 1185]

**SUMMARY.**—The Archbishop of Canterbury declares to his suffragan bishops how necessary it is to aid the land of Jerusalem, and urges them diligently to collect money from their subjects for that purpose according to the prescribed formula.

B. [Note: [Col. 0305D] Baldwin, first abbot of Ford, of the Cistercian Order in England, was then made bishop of Worcester in 1181; afterwards, upon Richard’s death, he was elected Archbishop of Canterbury by the Canterbury monks in 1183. He had first indeed been elected by the suffragan bishops of the Church of Canterbury; but when the monks resolved to appeal to the Apostolic See against this election, made contrary to their right, King Henry II, who loved Baldwin, intervened with entreaties and, leaving the monks free power to elect whom they wished, urged them to elect Baldwin. This they did, though they took it ill that no one from the Cistercian Order had yet presided over the English Church, says Gervase of Canterbury, treatise *On the Disputes between the Canterbury Monks and Archbishop Baldwin*. For some time Baldwin dealt peaceably with them. But a serious quarrel arose between them over a certain church which Baldwin was endeavouring to build to the detriment of the Church of Canterbury. For this dispute, consult the historians, especially Gervase, who recounts the whole matter at great length. In the war against Saladin, together with many other bishops and magnates, he took the cross; and he died in 1191, during the siege of the city of Acre in the Holy Land.]

By the grace of God Archbishop of Canterbury, Primate of England, to the venerable and beloved in Christ suffragans of the Church of Canterbury: greeting in the Author of salvation.

Where there is public loss and common damage, [Col. 0307A] just as grief spreads through the whole body, so common counsel and assistance must be employed. To use Jeremiah’s words: “A voice of lamentation has been heard from Zion, and weeping from Jerusalem.” [Note: [Col. 0307] Jer. 9.] “Her enemies have become the head; her foes have prospered.” For, our sins demanding it, the enemies of Christ’s cross have grown so strong [Note: [Col. 0307D] On this invasion of the Holy Land, all the historians of this period should be read, and among them Baronius under the year 1185 and following years.] that they attempt, in pride and abuse, to destroy the Holy Land, in which the Lord’s feet stood—the inheritance and patrimony of the Crucified One. And, according to the complaint of the same prophet of lamentation, [Note: [Col. 0307] Isa. 51.] “there is none to sustain her of all the sons whom she has borne, and none to take her by the hand of all the sons whom she has nourished.”

[Col. 0307B] Jerusalem, our mother, therefore cries out to you; she lays her distresses before us and seeks filial devotion as a remedy for her pain. Since, then, you are sons, take upon yourselves your mother’s sorrows, and, as Isaiah says, [Note: [Col. 0307] Isa. 66.] “mourn with Jerusalem and grieve with her, all you who love her.” For the nations come into the inheritance of the Lord in order to defile His temple. Those who hate the Lord have lifted up their head and have boasted; [Note: [Col. 0307] Ps. 73.] all who hate Zion [Note: [Col. 0307] Ps. 128.] have said together in their heart: “Let us cause the name of Christ to cease from the earth; let us take away the place and the nation. Come, and let us destroy, with a mighty multitude, the small number of the Christian people.”

Yet we hope in Him who is our hope, because He will look upon the face of His covenant. For Zion is the city of our strength: the Saviour will be placed in her as wall and rampart. [Note: [Col. 0307] Isa. 26.] Although the enemy devises much evil [Col. 0307C] against the holy place, the hand of the Lord is not shortened, that it cannot save. Rather, He tests us, that it may appear whether we love the house of Jacob and the place where His glory dwells, which He acquired by His blood and made illustrious in many ways by His birth, life, preaching, death, and resurrection.

According to the public principle of civil law, we shall be guilty of treason against the Son of God if an apostate nation violently rushes into the land which He holds by His Father’s eternal gift and by His mother’s hereditary succession, while the people redeemed by Him do not devote themselves to the defence of the Lord’s inheritance. For since the Father has given the nations as an inheritance and the bounds of the earth as a possession, His mother—who drew her origin in direct line from the tribe of Judah and [Col. 0308A] the stock of David—demands from our hands the kingdom of herself and of her Son, and requires without evasion that the faithfulness which we promised in baptism be rendered for its defence.

For this reason the Patriarch of Jerusalem [Note: [Col. 0307D] Heraclius, who, together with the grand masters of the Hospital and the Temple, was sent by the Christian inhabitants of the Holy Land to Christian kings and princes for war against Christ’s enemies. They first came to Rome to Pope Lucius III, from whom they received letters to the Christian kings, foremost to King Henry of England; together with the letters they offered him the royal banner, the keys of the Lord’s sepulchre, and also the keys of the Tower of David and of the city of Jerusalem. Roger of Howden records this under the year 1185, and also gives Lucius’s letter to Henry. Ralph de Diceto, in *Images of Histories*, Gervase in his *Chronicles*, and Knighton, *On the Events of England*, for the same year 1185, say the same.] and other magnates were sent to our most illustrious king—men whom nothing but the vast and most urgent necessity of the land could have induced to undertake so laborious a journey.

But our most gracious prince [Note: [Col. 0308D]

All the historians relate how graciously Henry received the envoys of the Holy Land. Henry himself also promised a considerable sum of money for the aid of the Holy Land, and ordered that the tithe called the Saladin tithe be collected throughout all the provinces of his dominion.

From the foregoing it is evident that this letter was written about the end of 1185 or the beginning of 1186, because the envoys of the Holy Land arrived at Canterbury on the Kalends of February.]

considered matters worthy of a prince. Seeing the grievous peril threatening the holy city, he laid a splendid and generous hand upon his private treasures and, with the common counsel of the bishops, earls, and barons of the realm, established a levy. In accordance with the form appended below, [Col. 0308B] you are to see that it is diligently and effectively observed throughout every parish of your dioceses, so that our mother Jerusalem, overcome by most grievous mourning, may draw breath under the dutiful visitation of her sons. Farewell.

## LETTER XCIX. TO POPE URBAN OF ROME. [A.D. 1185–86]

**SUMMARY.**—Baldwin, Archbishop of Canterbury, congratulates Pope Urban on having been chosen, by the unanimous agreement of the electors, to succeed Lucius III as pope, and gives him thanks for receiving the pallium.

To the most holy Father URBAN, by God’s grace supreme pontiff, BALDWIN, humble minister of the Church of Canterbury: greeting and the service of due devotion.

“The house of God,” etc. See among the various letters to Pope Urban [Col. 0308C] after his *Registers*, in volume CCII of the *Patrologia*.

## LETTER C. TO R., HIS FRIEND. [A.D. 1176]

**SUMMARY.**—He defends the reputation of a certain new archbishop, accused of excessive mildness, and explains at length what mildness in a bishop deserves praise and what deserves blame.

To his dearest lord and friend R., his P. of Blois, archdeacon of Bath: greeting and the fruit of patience.

You accuse an innocent man and call a strong man lukewarm and remiss; and, using that word of Leviticus, [Note: [Col. 0307] ch. 2.] “you shall burn no honey in sacrifice to the Lord,” you declare a man of proven religion to be estranged from divine sacrifices. [Col. 0309A] Certainly, since the Spirit of God bears witness to his spirit, it matters little to him that he should be judged by a human being or by a human day. And who are you, to judge another’s servant? He stands or falls to his own master; but he shall stand. [Note: [Col. 0309] Rom. 14.]

For if you consider more attentively the settled disposition of his mind, you will find in him nothing changeable or uncertain; rather, whatever he determines in his mind by antecedent reason, you will find supported by the firmest constancy. “Honey,” you say, “is not accepted in the sacrifice of the Lord; nor is the gentle and lax mildness of prelates, signified by honey, accepted by the Lord.” Friend, there is mildness and there is mildness. There is necessary mildness and lax mildness. For although honey, as you incessantly reproachfully allege, is forbidden in sacrifice, nevertheless the firstfruits of honey are offered; and where the sacrifice of honey is forbidden, [Col. 0309B] there the firstfruits of honey are commanded to be offered.

You would wish—and all who share your folly would wish—that my lord [Note: [Col. 0309D] He means Richard, Archbishop of Canterbury, of whom Peter of Blois was a familiar associate and chancellor. See what I have said on Letter 5.] should, at every emotional impulse, dissolve the alliance and peace between kingdom and priesthood, and should not offer the firstfruits of honey in the oblation of peace first extended. By every law and according to the customs of all peoples, peace must first be offered even to enemies, especially in the faith of Christ, in which nothing ought to be done precipitately and no one becomes supreme at once.

Consider carefully, therefore, that there is a certain cautious and necessary forbearance which is shown to the powers of this world, and especially to the king as pre-eminent. For all power is from the Lord God. [Note: [Col. 0309] Rom. 13.] This mildness makes kingdom and priesthood one; and by this kindness he obtains what [Col. 0309C] he would never extort from princes by threats or violence. [Note: [Col. 0309D]

That rulers should not be exasperated or reproached too sharply is shown by our Peter in Letter 10.

This letter was written about the year 1176, namely, shortly after Richard’s consecration as Archbishop of Canterbury.]

In this mildness neither God nor man is offended, since by it the prelate keeps faith both with God and with man. Of this mildness and this faith it is written: “In faith and in his mildness He made him holy.” [Note: [Col. 0309] Ecclus. 45.]

It is indeed shameful and absurd for a prelate to rebuke with anger and harshness. As the Apostle says in writing to Timothy: “The servant of the Lord must not quarrel, but must be gentle and patient toward all, correcting with mildness those who resist the truth.” [Note: [Col. 0309] II Tim. 2.] It is read [Note: [Col. 0309] Isa. 8.] that the waters of Siloam run quietly, whereas the waters of Rezin pass with tumult. And when the bride says in the Song of Songs [Note: [Col. 0309] ch. 5.], “My beloved drinks wine with milk”—that is, he exercises strictness with gentleness—he, turning to the bride and preferring gentleness to severity, says: “Thy breasts are better than wine.” [Note: [Col. 0309] Song 1.]

When [Col. 0310A] the prophet said: “Behold, a great wind breaking rocks, and the Lord was not in the wind; and after the wind an earthquake, and the Lord was not in the earthquake; and after the earthquake a fire, and the Lord was not in the fire,” he adds: “and after the fire a whisper of a gentle breeze; and the Lord was in it.” [Note: [Col. 0309] III Kings 19.] For while the spirit of anger and agitation, and the fire of wrath, displease God, gentle and mild correction is itself accepted.

Yet in this mildness—or rather in this honey—the gall of fruitful correction lies hidden. For in his mildness he possesses zeal, and in his gentleness, stings; and behold, “in peace his bitterness is most bitter” [Note: [Col. 0309] Isa. 38.] against those who are ignorant and in error. Where he loves more truly, he corrects more sternly, yet secretly; and dove-like gentleness is more effective for the amendment of princes [Col. 0310B] than outward severity and angry countenance. Thus it is noted in Jeremiah: [Note: [Col. 0309] ch. 25.] “The land of the wicked,” he says, “has become a desolation before the wrath of the dove.”

This mildness possesses the spirit of strength. And, to use Job’s words, [Note: [Col. 0309] ch. 34.] it is this which says to the king, “Apostate,” and calls rulers impious; it does not respect the persons of princes, nor recognize a tyrant when it pleads against a poor man. Consider, therefore, that gentle and severe correction admit distinction and beneficially, wisely alternate their respective turns.

For of both it is written in Ezekiel: [Note: [Col. 0309] ch. 1.] “There was fire in the midst, and from the midst of the fire as it were the appearance of electrum”; and because electrum is a most tempered kind of metal, it signifies the gentlest soothing of correction. But of severity it is written there: “There was fire in [Col. 0310C] the midst of the living creatures, and lightning went forth from the fire.” [Note: [Col. 0309] ibid.]

Severity, therefore, must sometimes become gentle. For also in the work of the Temple, where lions are carved and straps painted, this signifies that the severity of discipline must needs be restrained and tempered by the strap of gentleness. Yet the laxity which closes the prelate’s mouth, casts down his mind, and makes him a flatterer and seller of oil, while he hunts for ease and honour in the favour of princes—this casts the wretched into the pit of scandals. In this pit, as the prophet says, [Note: [Col. 0309] Isa. 34.] the *lamia* lies down and finds rest for herself. In it, blessed Job testifies, [Note: [Col. 0309] ch. 37.] the beast enters its hiding-place and remains in its den.

This is the laxity by which one builds a wall [Col. 0310D] and another plasters it; by which “the sinner is praised in the desires of his soul, and the wicked man is blessed.” [Note: [Col. 0309] Ps. 10.] By it dumb dogs, unable—indeed unwilling—to bark, [Col. 0311A] [Note: [Col. 0311] Isa. 56.] through uniformity of agreement take on the face and likeness of the sinner, as it is written: “How long will you judge iniquity and accept the face of the sinner?” [Note: [Col. 0311] Ps. 81.] By it wretched prelates nullify the good of penitence which they see in rulers, by stroking them and promising them Christ’s more abundant mercy even unto grey hairs.

Against such men the prophet, angered under the figure of Ephraim, says: “Strangers have consumed his strength, and he did not know it; grey hairs also are scattered upon him, and he did not know it.” [Note: [Col. 0311] Hos. 7.] This is the wind of flattery: a most evil, burning wind, raising many into pride and tearing them away from the purpose and desire of holiness. Thus Job says in their person: [Note: [Col. 0311] ch. 30.] “Thou hast taken away my desire like the wind; Thou hast lifted me up, and, setting me upon the wind, hast dashed me down.”

Certainly you know that no suspicion of flattery or lax indulgence falls upon my lord, [Col. 0311B] whose life is above every objection; whose words, to use Jeremiah’s testimony, [Note: [Col. 0311] ch. 23.] are “like fire and like a hammer breaking a rock.” Yet there is a reason why for a time he does not have rebukes in his mouth. He is still new and inexperienced in the office of administration laid upon him; and you know that one does not plough with the firstborn of an ox, nor do green ears of grain come for an offering until they are scorched by fire. [Note: [Col. 0311] Lev. 2.]

His whole intention now, therefore, is to establish bishops, so that he may have help like himself; for “woe to him who is alone.” [Note: [Col. 0311] Eccl. 4.] For he alone is not sufficient for the burden beneath which those who bear the world bend. If meanwhile he is rebuked by some under the pretext of [Col. 0311C] love, as they say, he, secure in his intention before God, will answer and say with blessed Job: [Note: [Col. 0311] ch. 16.] “My friends are full of words; my eye drops tears to God.”

Indeed, it is customary for itching tongues to exercise themselves against prelates; and prelates were appointed for this purpose, that they might bear modestly and patiently the injuries of a whorish tongue. As Paul says among blasphemers: “You know that we are appointed for this.” [Note: [Col. 0311] I Thess. 3.] If you look to Christ our head, no one’s innocence was more bitterly assailed by the malicious or the detractor. Jewish superstition called Him now a carpenter’s son, [Note: [Col. 0311] Matt. 13.] now a wine-drinker, now a glutton, [Note: [Col. 0311] Matt. 11.] now a servant of Beelzebub, [Note: [Col. 0311] Matt. 12.] now an associate of heathens, now a destroyer of the Sabbath, [Note: [Col. 0311] John 9.] and in many ways poured out against Him the poison of its malice. [Col. 0311D]

## LETTER CI. TO R., ARCHDEACON OF NANTES
**SUMMARY.**—He sets out for the archdeacon his judgment regarding the abilities of two nephews entrusted to his instruction, and at the same time teaches that one should not leap to higher studies until the foundations of grammar have been properly laid.

To his dearest lord and friend R., Archdeacon of Nantes, P. of Blois, greetings, and whatever is better than health.

[Col. 0312A] The day before yesterday you entrusted to me two of your nephews to be educated: one still in the years of childhood, the other fully grown into adolescence. Yet now, in your letter, you highly exalt and commend the talent of the elder, asserting that you have never found a man of subtler natural ability. Therefore you beg and urge that the vigilance of a master should be directed to him more promptly; for you consider that it will be easy to put the finishing hand of highest perfection to a structure whose growth another’s care has advanced.

Yet the matter has turned out the other way. For I have better hope of the education of the one who came to me raw and unformed than of the other, whose natural disposition has already in part hardened and, as it were, received in itself the imprint of another teacher. Clay, wax, and things of that sort, which offer themselves to receive form and impression, are shaped more easily and more faithfully according to the will of the one impressing them if they have previously received no outlines of forms within themselves.

Quintilian indeed relates in his book *On the Education of the Orator* [Note: [Col. 0311] Book II, chapter 3.] that a certain Timotheus, celebrated in the art of flute-playing, used to demand double fees from those whom others had taught before him. For in such cases the labour is twofold: first, to wash away the less commendable teaching with which they had been imbued; secondly, to impart knowledge that would bring both profit and reputation. For what tender age has learned is unlearned with difficulty, because:

> The jar long retains the scent  
> With which, when fresh, it was once imbued.

[Note: [Col. 0311] Horace, Book I, Epistle 1.]

In civil law too, under the aedilian edict, seasoned slaves [Col. 0312C] who have been trained into other habits are rejected; and it was at times doubtful whether they were subject to an action for rescission of sale. New slaves, indeed, were regarded more favourably, because they are more receptive of discipline and fitter for service.

You commend William as a man of subtler vein and sharper intellect because, passing over the study of grammar and authors, he flew to the sophistries of logicians. There he learned dialectic not in books, as is usual, but in loose sheets and notebooks. Such people possess no foundation of literary learning, and this subtlety which you extol is harmful to many. Seneca says [Note: [Col. 0311] Epistle 88.]: “Nothing is more detestable than subtlety where it is mere subtlety.” For what advantage is it to spend their days upon matters useful neither at home, nor in military service, nor in the law-court, nor in the cloister, nor in the court, nor in church, nor anywhere to anyone, except merely in the schools?

Seneca, writing to Lucilius, says: “What is sharper than an ear of grain, and for what is it useful? Such,” he says, “is an intellect that sports in mere subtlety, with no weightiness abiding in it.” Icarus [Note: [Col. 0311] Ovid, Book I, *Tristia*, Elegy 1.], while he is borne aloft toward heaven in youthful lightness, is plunged into the waves of the sea. So too such persons, while rashly raising themselves in the arts, are dashed down.

Before some people are imbued with elementary disciplines, they are taught to inquire about the point, [Col. 0313A] line, surface, the quantity of the soul, fate, the natural inclination of nature, chance and free choice, matter and motion, the principles of bodies, the progression of multitude, and the division of magnitude; what time is, what void is, what place is; sameness and difference; what is divided, divisible, and indivisible; the substance and form of speech; the essence of universals; the origin, use, and end of virtues; the causes of things; the ebbing of the ocean; the source of the Nile; the various secrets of hidden nature; the different forms of causes arising in contracts or quasi-contracts, wrongs or quasi-wrongs; the first beginnings of things; and countless other matters which demand the foundation of fuller learning and more eminent understanding.

The earliest stage of tender age was spent on the rules of the grammatical art: analogies, barbarisms, solecisms, tropes, and figures. Donatus, Servius, Priscian, Isidore, Bede, and Cassiodorus devoted very great diligence to teaching all these matters; and they would surely not have done so if a foundation of learning could be acquired without them. For Quintilian too [Note: [Col. 0313] Book I, *Education of the Orator*, chapter 7.], who teaches and declares that this discipline must be taught, raises it with such praise that he publicly affirms that the name of learning cannot subsist without it.

Gaius Caesar published books *On Analogy*, knowing that without this knowledge neither prudence, in which he was most accomplished, nor eloquence, in which he was most powerful, could easily be attained by anyone. Marcus Tullius, as is evident from his frequent letters, diligently urges upon his son, whom he loved most tenderly, the study of grammar.

And what benefit is there in turning over loose sheets, establishing propositions by word of mouth, and twisting about the subtleties of sophisms; in condemning the writings of the ancients and rejecting everything not found in the notebooks of their own masters? It is written [Note: [Col. 0313] Job 12.] that “with the ancients is wisdom.” Nor is Jeremiah [Note: [Col. 0313] chapter 38.] drawn out of the pit until old and worn garments are lowered to him on ropes. For one does not ascend from the darkness of ignorance to the light of knowledge unless the writings of the ancients are reread with more earnest study.

Jerome boasts [Note: [Col. 0313] Jerome, to Pammachius and Oceanus, *On Error*.] that he devoted especially laborious attention to the writings of Origen. Horace likewise [Note: [Col. 0313] Book I, Epistle 2.] boasts [Col. 0314A] that he reread Homer,

> Who tells, more fully and more well than Chrysippus and Crantor,  
> What is noble, what base, what useful, and what is not.

I know that it greatly benefited me that, when I was being instructed as a small boy in the art of versification, I used, at my master’s command, to take my subject matter not from fables but from the truth of histories. It benefited me that, while still young, I was compelled to memorize and recite exactly the letters of Hildebert, Bishop of Le Mans, distinguished by elegance of style and pleasing urbanity.

Beyond the other books famous in the schools, it benefited me frequently to consult Trogus Pompeius, Josephus, Suetonius, Hegesippus, Quintus Curtius, Cornelius Tacitus, and Titus Livy, all of whom insert into the histories which they recount many things for the edification of conduct and the advancement of liberal learning. I have also read countless others who deal with no histories. In all of these, as though in gardens of spices, the diligence of moderns can gather flowers and make honey for itself through the graceful sweetness of speech.

Therefore do not further allege the subtle talent of your nephew William; and let it not be counted a fault in me if, within a short time, he does not advance to perfection. For the sick man is purged before he is healed; and, according to the judgment of Timotheus, who demanded double payment for his labour on the pupils of others, useless things must first be uprooted so that useful things may be planted.

For in the *Marriage of Mercury and Philology*, Philology vomits out the books of useless learning before she deserves to be raised to the eminence of her desired dignity. Indeed, I fear that Timotheus’s assertion may be all too true. John already precedes William by a certain shortcut in learning; the head is turned into the tail; and, if John perseveres in his purpose, the younger will supplant the firstborn, and Jacob Esau.

## LETTER CII. TO H.

[Note: [Col. 0313D]

This solitary letter H perhaps denotes Hugh. A certain charter of his is found in the *Monasticon Anglicanum* for his monastery of Reading, where mention is made of H. Walter, namely Hubert Walter, Bishop of Salisbury, in whose diocese the monastery of Reading was situated.

That monastery of Reading was founded by Henry I, King of the English, in honour of the Blessed Virgin Mary; hence it is commonly called the monastery or church of St Mary of Reading. William of Malmesbury speaks of it thus in Book II of *The Deeds of the Bishops of the English*: “In the district of Berkshire are two monasteries, Abingdon and Reading,” etc. “Reading was once a convent of nuns, but has now for many years been destroyed. King Henry, intending to restore it as a penance imposed upon him, attached to it two monasteries formerly ruined, Leominster and Cholsey; and he established it between the two rivers Kennet and Thames, in honour of the Mother of the Lord and John the Evangelist, in a place where it might serve as a lodging-place for almost all travellers going to the most populous city of England; and he placed there Cluniac monks, a distinguished proof of unwearied holiness.”

A manuscript in the Cottonian Library, cited in the *Monasticon Anglicanum*, volume I, also says: “In the year 1126, Henry, King of England, out of joy at the hand of the blessed apostle James, founded the noble abbey of Reading, endowed it with many goods, and placed in it the hand of the blessed apostle James.” In the same place: “In the year 1135, King Henry I died at the Castle of Lions, and was buried at Reading, where he had founded a monastery of two hundred monks.” There too is found the charter of foundation of this monastery issued by the same Henry I, and its confirmation by Henry II.

Concerning this matter Robert of Torigni also writes: “In the year 1165, about the octave of Easter, King Henry caused the church of the Blessed Mary of Reading to be built, and for three days royally supplied the community of monks and their guests, granting also no small endowment to that church.” That Henry I wished to be buried in the same monastery, founded by himself and endowed with immense revenues through royal generosity, is reported by Malmesbury, John of Hexham, and Richard of Newburgh, both priors, under the year 1135.]

### TO THE ABBOT OF READING.

**SUMMARY.**—He recounts at length the complaint of the Abbot of Reading, who wishes, because of grave dangers, to resign the dignity he has assumed. He then answers the complaint and advises him carefully to consider whether resignation is expedient.

To the reverend Father and lord H., by God’s grace Abbot of Reading [Col. 0315A], his own Peter of Blois, Archdeacon of Bath, greetings and happy success in accordance with your wishes.

Whenever I recall the words of that conversation which we recently held between us, my heart grows warm within me, and in my meditation a fire is kindled [Note: [Col. 0315] Ecclesiasticus 24.]. For your speech was intensely aflame, and there was a spirit of life in your words—or rather, those words are spirit and life—for it was not you who spoke, but the Spirit of the Father who was in you. I know indeed that those words, conceived in the person of another, especially touched you; and therefore, like burning sparks, they came forth from the abundance of your heart.

Most beloved Father, although by God’s grace you stand pre-eminent in exceptional holiness among the perfect men of this age, I am nevertheless certain that you aspire to a fuller measure [Col. 0315B] of perfection, as a vigorous imitator of the Apostle [Note: [Col. 0315] Philippians 3.], who, while advancing, does not consider himself perfect: “Not that I have already attained,” he says, “or am already perfect; but, forgetting all that lies behind and stretching forward to what lies before, I pursue the prize of the heavenly calling in Christ.”

And he adds: “Let all of us, therefore, who are perfect, think this way” [Note: [Col. 0315] Ibid.]. Most reverend Father, I neither draw you back nor discourage you from so blessed a purpose; for whoever is hastening from earth to heaven is greatly harmed by anyone who detains him even a little.

You seek to relinquish an honour desirable to many, because you have enlarged it in many ways, so that, having withdrawn, you may, like a locust, be free to rejoice in the joy of the people whom Christ has inherited, so that He may be praised with His inheritance. Certainly no worldly occasion invites you to this, but Christ’s love alone [Note: [Col. 0315] 1 Timothy 1.]. For the law is not laid down for the just man; nor have you received again the spirit of slavery in fear, but the Spirit of adoption as sons.

Yet Truth says: “Take my yoke upon yourselves” [Note: [Col. 0315] Matthew 11.]. As though He said: “I do not impose it; you impose it upon yourselves. Take it up, if you wish to find rest for your souls.” You gave your hand to the evangelical profession; and it seems alien to you from the way of God’s ordinances to follow the deceits of this world.

In the bitterness of your soul, with anxious weeping and lamenting groans, you bewailed your present circumstances. Although I do not recall the exact sequence of that complaint word for word, I do not depart from its meaning. Sighing, you said:

[Col. 0315D] “Wretched man that I am, carnal and sold under sin: what have I to do with riches and honours? Why have I arrogated to myself mastery and a chair over others? [Col. 0316A] Was my own iniquity not enough for me, unless I should sin among a multitude and bind double sins upon myself? I had entered God’s camp as a professor of evangelical poverty and had bound myself to spiritual warfare; now, however, by assuming this accursed honour, like a fugitive and deserter I have cast aside the arms of regular innocence.

“Alas, alas! They made me a keeper of vineyards, though I cannot keep myself. I who am insufficient to govern myself have been appointed to govern others: an unlearned teacher, and a blind man serving as guide. I had conformed myself to the likeness of Christ’s death and, fleeing, had withdrawn from the paths of men, so that I might abstain from defilements. But now I dwell in the midst of a people with unclean lips; I have mingled with the nations and learned their works.

[Col. 0316B] “The Lord has mixed within me a spirit of dizziness and made me wander as one who wanders drunk and vomiting—and truly vomiting. For what the Lord threatens the wicked through blessed Job has happened to me: ‘The riches which he swallowed he shall vomit up, and God shall draw them out of his belly’ [Note: [Col. 0315] Job 20.].

“Indeed, by the judgment of those who love God, I may await His terrible judgment, since I read in the Book of Wisdom [Note: [Col. 0315] chapter 6.] that the Lord shall appear dreadfully and swiftly, and that the harshest judgment shall be for those who rule. I, a spirit that goes and does not return—how have I looked back, after putting my hand to the plough? Having vomited out the world, how have I returned to my vomit? Having put off the garment of the old Adam, how have I put it on again? Having washed my feet, how have I defiled them once more?

[Col. 0316C] “How have I been brought back to the gates of hell, though I had already set one foot in paradise? Who has so sought his soul as to lose it? Who has so impiously thought to reject his reward and that splendid inheritance, of which I had already received the earnest and pledge? Yet, by the just judgment of God, he who has no peace toward Christ cannot have peace toward himself. ‘You have set me against Yourself, and I have become burdensome to myself’ [Note: [Col. 0315] Job 7.].

“I have placed my soul as though under the throw of dice, when, for the uncertain prospect of riches, I committed myself to the sure peril of eternal death. And what does it profit a man if he gains the whole world yet suffers loss of his own soul [Note: [Col. 0315] Matthew 16.]? No price can be put upon the loss of a soul. I knew that every honour of this age was a grave impediment [Col. 0316D] and, as it were, a death-dealing obstacle to eternal salvation. For whom do we read of as having passed from worldly delights to eternal delights?

“O how deceitful and empty is [Col. 0317A] the glory which people seek and receive from one another, while they do not seek the glory that is from God alone. Truly it is empty, because the sons of men are empty. If a monk wishes to be preferred above others, is he not the companion of him who says: ‘I shall set my throne toward the north, and I shall be like the Most High’ [Note: [Col. 0317] Isaiah 14.]? But he who mounts that man’s chair should fear his precipice and fall.

“Many, through transitory honours, have withdrawn from Christ, saying: ‘Anathema to Jesus’ [Note: [Col. 0317] 1 Corinthians 12.]. Certainly the hearts of those who wish to preside over others are vain, when empty of virtue they swell with the spirit of self-exaltation and the wind of fleeting glory. I had chosen to be lowly in the house of God [Note: [Col. 0317] Psalm 83.], and lowliness and contempt were to me the highest honour. But now, raised in God’s wrath to the pastoral chair—whose assumption I did not procure, though I accepted it not without an ambitious will—

[Col. 0317B] “my poverty was enough for me. It was enough for me to rule only my own body, so that sin might not reign in me. It was enough for me to preserve the Lord’s treasure in this earthen vessel—I mean my soul, for which that great merchant shed His blood.

“I see in cloisters heavenly men, or rather earthly angels, whose citizenship is in heaven [Note: [Col. 0317] Philippians 3.], who, with a certain noble pride, despise the honours and riches of this world. But we sinners, flourishing in the world, have gained riches which Truth condemns in the Gospel [Note: [Col. 0317] Matthew 13.]. With these, the wise king, the winnower of the wicked, has set the wheel of evils upon me.
