“These are waters from the well of Samaria, which, the more they are drunk, the more they inflame the thirst of desire [Note: [Col. 0317] John 4.]. But blessed is the man whose hope is the Lord, who lacks nothing because Christ is sufficient for him. These are flies that destroy the sweetness of ointment [Note: [Col. 0317] Ecclesiasticus 10.]; the birds which Abraham drove away [Note: [Col. 0317] Genesis 15.]; mice that boil up from the earth—that is, from earthly affection—and gnaw their inward parts; that set the ark of the Lord beside Dagon, that is, confuse the knowledge of Holy Scripture [Note: [Col. 0317] 1 Samuel 5.] through the misuse of worldly care.

[Col. 0317C] “Therefore the Lord says [Note: [Col. 0317] Ezekiel 16.]: ‘I gave them my gold and my silver; but they made Baal out of my gold and my silver.’ Before heavenly indignation laid this honour—or rather, this burden—upon me (for I was called to it in God’s wrath), I felt the Lord in the goodness and simplicity of my heart, and continually rejoiced in the remembrance of human sweetness.

“Frequently, in my prayers, amid burning compunctions, secret jubilations, pious sighs, and devout whispers, the affections of my devotion were borne toward God with a certain vehemence of longing. Where now are those ardours of divine inspiration, those experiences of heavenly sweetness, and those foretastes of eternal enjoyment? My ruined, unhappy soul now no longer feels those movements of heavenly grace which, in the Lord’s good day and in the hour of His favour, it gathered from the love of Christ, as from the tree [Col. 0318A] of life, fruits of salvation and the delights of paradise.

“But now my soul has abhorred every food and has drawn near even to the gates of death. My flesh has failed [Note: [Col. 0317] Psalm 72.], and my heart is troubled [Note: [Col. 0317] Psalm 54.]. The joy of my heart has failed. My heart is troubled: my strength has forsaken me, and the light of my eyes—even that is not with me [Note: [Col. 0317] Psalm 37.]. Lord, my soul has become before You like land without water [Note: [Col. 0317] Psalm 142.].

“For it is either hardened against tears, or, in the whirlwind of rushing cares, scattered as though into winds toward vain and false insanities. I beg You: let the floodgates of my head be opened and the abysses of my heart burst forth, so that a flood of many waters may overflow the face of this earth. Lord, You have given me an iron heaven and a bronze earth, so that upon this [Col. 0318B] Mount Gilboa, swollen through the pride of office, neither dew nor rain may fall.

“I have therefore lost my time. My days have failed in vanity and my years in haste. I became rich in order to become wretched. I attained honours in order to lose God, for loss is the consequence of honour. Certainly honours and riches have attached to themselves security of life, wine and rich food, leisure and satiety, contempt of God and loss of self. The Gospel plainly distinguishes between honour and poverty when it blesses Lazarus in Abraham’s bosom and buries the rich man in hell [Note: [Col. 0317] Luke 16.].

“I, who ought to mourn the days I have lost because I lived ruinously, have become a hunter after favourable breezes: I follow the court, attend the counsels of magnates, judge my inferiors, and reverence and adore my superiors more than the author of my salvation. [Col. 0318C] In these things, squandering and wasting Christ’s patrimony under the pretence of false generosity, I expend my entire self upon the capture of empty glory and the magnificence of secular display.

“For what does that superfluous multitude of mounts which I lead around accomplish, or that multiplicity of retainers? What shall I say of hospitality, which with good reason is reckoned hostility rather than hospitality? For Christ does not furnish its cause, but the pretext of empty glory. When rich men are received as guests with honour and reverence, every luxurious delight is set before them from the patrimony of the Crucified. But Christ, once crucified long ago upon the wood, is crucified and tormented outside, in His poor, in the mud.

[Col. 0318D] “Among them, either wholly naked or wasting away in scant garments, famished and trembling with cold, He seeks some relief for His distress from what is given within to dogs; and there is no one moved over Joseph’s affliction. Behold present-day hospitality: the rich feast splendidly for the glory of demons, while Christ, who is charity, is afflicted by contempt, hunger, and nakedness. And I, forgetting God’s terrible judgments and unmindful of my own soul, sit like Belshazzar among revelers, misusing the Lord’s vessels and the patrimony of the poor [Col. 0319A] to Christ’s insult.

“Meanwhile, from the houses of hosts, serving-boys go out, laden and drunk with food, so that the surplus of the guests may add a fuller store of pain and torment to the poor. Under the pretext of this false hospitality, we render every service of courtesy to sheriffs, foresters, and other officials—or rather, men who ruin offices—as though to lords and masters. Yet a complaint about lack of hospitality will be raised, and ingratitude will overturn the whole grace of hospitality, unless the master of the feast keeps up drinking battles with his guests until nausea and dizziness of the head.

“He whose judgments are hidden, and therefore more to be feared, will judge all this. Such detestable and excessive expenses are not made from our labour or patrimony, but from the alms of the faithful, [Col. 0319B] from offerings and tithes, from the tributes of needy souls, from the exactions and oppressions of the poor, and even from the proceeds of lawsuits. Though we ought to eat our bread in the sweat of our brow, we appropriate the labours of the wretched for our pleasures and in gluttony and drunkenness drink another’s sweat.

“It is written: ‘His judgments are a great deep’ [Note: [Col. 0319] Psalm 35.]. He who beholds the depths and sits upon the cherubim, terrible in His counsels over the children of men, will judge the cause of the poor when they stand with great steadfastness against those who oppressed them [Note: [Col. 0319] Wisdom 5.]. The Father of orphans and Judge of widows will avenge all these things; the patience of the poor will not perish forever.

[Col. 0319C] “Where then, I ask, is the saying of the Prophet: ‘He has scattered; he has given to the poor’ [Note: [Col. 0319] Psalm 111.]? We ought neither to give to the rich, nor to carry wood into a forest, nor to pour water into the sea. It is Jerome’s saying [Note: [Col. 0319] Epistle 26 to Pammachius, *On the Death of Paulina*, chapter 4.] that it is sacrilege not to give the goods of the poor to the poor. And again: ‘To give to sinners and to sacrifice to demons are alike; nor is it less shameful to give things to shameful people than to give them for shameful purposes.’

“Ecclesiasticus says [Note: [Col. 0319] chapter 12.]: ‘Do good to the humble, and do not give to the ungodly; give to the good, and do not receive a sinner.’ Jerome likewise [Note: [Col. 0319] Epistle 2 to Nepotian.]: ‘A cleric who can be supported from his own goods, if he takes what belongs to the poor, certainly commits sacrilege; and through abuses of this kind he eats and drinks judgment upon himself.’

“If this is decreed concerning a cleric, what will become of a monk, who, if he possesses anything as his own, has [Col. 0319D] nothing in common with Christ? It is full of danger to maintain a proud household from the spoils of the poor; it would be safer for me to be humbled with the meek than to divide spoils with the proud [Note: [Col. 0319] Proverbs 16.].

“Are not offerings and tithes the spoils of the poor, when, by fear of ecclesiastical sentence, I violently extort them from the poor? It is written: ‘Take the psalm and give the timbrel’ [Note: [Col. 0319] Psalm 80.]. With what face do I receive temporal things when I do not dispense spiritual things? What shall I say about tallages and exactions, the proceeds of lawsuits, [Col. 0320A] and the other wicked extortions?

“I hear the Lord complaining mournfully through Isaiah [Note: [Col. 0319] chapter 3.]: ‘The exactors of my people have despoiled them. Why do you crush my people and confound the faces of the needy? For you rule with severity and power; in your houses is found the plunder of the poor.’ It is indeed detestable in a monk, under any appearance of honour or title of authority, to possess fiefs, male and female slaves, homages, fealties, and bonds of service; to impose upon people forced labour, carriage-service, and the other burdens of public obligation; and thus to squander and waste Christ’s patrimony on extraordinary uses—or rather abuses—as you elegantly proposed.

“It is damnable that he should be a plunderer of the poor, a wicked exactor, and a grim [Col. 0320B] Procrustes. Hear Jerome [Note: [Col. 0319] Homily on Psalm 145.]: ‘Monk, if you are needy and receive, you give rather than receive; but if you are not needy and receive, you rob.’ Moreover, a monk is not needy if he has what nature requires, and the Apostle prescribes this sufficiency by a definite rule: ‘Having food and covering, let us be content with these’ [Note: [Col. 0319] 1 Timothy 6.].

“What madness, then, is it to heap up treasure from the labours of the poor and provide pleasures for myself and mine from another’s blood? Will the support of relatives, the reputation of false hospitality, the number of my mounts, and the multitude of my retainers be able to excuse me before the strict Judge? Was I obliged on that account to seize the goods of the poor? For I seize them, even if not by my own hand but by another’s, [Col. 0320C] as though by a long hand. Yet it is written: ‘Hand in hand, the evil man shall not be innocent’ [Note: [Col. 0319] Proverbs 11.].

“Saul is not excused from David’s death, nor the Jews from Christ’s death, although they strove to accomplish their malice through another’s hand. And though the hand with which I rob is long, the Lord’s hand is not shortened, so that He cannot judge the poor in righteousness and reprove with equity for the meek of the earth.

“Blessed Job says: ‘If my land cries out against me’ [Note: [Col. 0319] Job 31.], by which he indicates the dangerous cry of the poor against their oppressive lords. Let those do these and like things whose God remembers them no more, who have been cast out from His hand, whose death is not regarded, and whose condition in their affliction is secure. But what agreement have I with robbery, I who have renounced everything [Col. 0320D] that I possessed as my own?

“Certainly neither kite, nor hawk, nor vulture, nor heron, nor any other bird of prey is accepted in God’s sacrifice [Note: [Col. 0319] Isaiah 33.]. For the Lord detests covetousness acquired through fraud and an offering made from robbery [Note: [Col. 0319] Leviticus 11.]. It is contrary to the edict of the heavenly Emperor not only to desire or seize another’s property, but even to reclaim one’s own through litigation. The Apostle says to Timothy: ‘The servant of God must not quarrel.’ And likewise: ‘This itself is a fault among you, that you have lawsuits; why do you not rather suffer wrong?’ [Note: [Col. 0319] 1 Corinthians 6.]

“Did I receive these damnable riches so that I might indulge [Col. 0321A] my flesh more lavishly? I knew well how terribly the Apostle threatens those who make provision for the flesh in its desires. According to Christ’s testimony, the flesh profits nothing [Note: [Col. 0321] John 6.]. Nor, as the Apostle testifies, shall flesh possess God’s kingdom [Note: [Col. 0321] 1 Corinthians 15.]. This is barren land and near to a curse, producing only thorns and thistles; the Lord will come to strike it with the breath of His mouth.

“If I feed the barren woman and do not do good to the widow, then, by Job’s testimony, I incur the sentence of divine judgment [Note: [Col. 0321] Job 24.]. Against the soul that pours itself out into worldly pleasures the Lord burns with grave anger, saying to the executors of His judgment: ‘As much as she glorified herself and lived in delights, give her so much torment and mourning’ [Note: [Col. 0321] Revelation 18.].

“Certainly wisdom does not dwell in the land of those who live pleasantly; nor is the kingdom of God food [Col. 0321B] and drink, but righteousness, peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit [Note: [Col. 0321] Romans 14.]. We were bought at a great price, that we might glorify and bear Christ in our body, lest, being too indulgent in care for the body, we hear what the Lord reproaches the self-indulgent with through the prophet: ‘You have cast me behind your body’ [Note: [Col. 0321] Ezekiel 23.].

“Shall I sacrifice my flesh to the table of demons, though I ought to offer it as a living, holy sacrifice pleasing to God—my rational service? If I received riches in order to relieve the need of my relatives, blessed Jerome frightens me [Note: [Col. 0321] Epistle 128, to Fabiola.] by saying that, when we regard kinship of bodies, we offend the Creator of body and soul. He adds: ‘Many lose their souls while showing compassion to their parents.’ These are those who, in my judgment, cruelly and damnably lay down their souls for their friends.

[Col. 0321C] “I read Jerome’s letter to Heliodorus and found with what severe and rigorous sternness every attachment to kindred must be cut away in those who turn to God. The cows that had calved, which bore the ark of the Lord to Beth-shemesh, did not turn their necks back toward their calves. Nor is a priest or Levite chosen in the house of the Lord unless he says to father and mother: ‘I do not know you.’

“I was dead to the world, and the world to me. But the love of the age, which had withered in my heart, grows green again under the pretext of a certain false piety through attachments of blood. Wretched are those who spend upon their parents that from which they rejoice after those parents’ death, since the vain joys of the living often pass [Col. 0321D] into the punishments of the dead.

“Therefore may the Lord destroy in me every height that exalts itself against the knowledge of God, and bring every understanding of mine captive into the obedience of Christ. Now at last I perceive how fruitful for a person and how glorious before God is the title of poverty. A person does not know its value. For poverty alone is the safe and direct road to life; the other roads are full of wicked robbers. For the world lies [Col. 0322A] in evil [Note: [Col. 0321] 1 John 5.], full of dangers, full of snares, full of stumbling-blocks, full of corrupt conversations and evil examples, treacherous words, and unjust counsels.

“But why do I delay? Why do I wait? Perhaps this very night they will demand my soul. Any loss of time, however small, is a loss of salvation. It is utter madness to postpone the business of the soul until a moment of necessity, until the thunderbolt of divine indignation frightens one whose idleness is nourished by false expectation. ‘Woe,’ He says, ‘to those who are pregnant and nursing in that day’ [Note: [Col. 0321] Matthew 24.]. Alas for me, because my sojourn has been prolonged [Note: [Col. 0321] Psalm 119.]. Who then will give me wings like a dove’s, that I may fly away and be at rest [Note: [Col. 0321] Psalm 54.]?

“But You, Lord God of hosts, Father of mercies and God of all consolation, when will You console me? When will You fill [Col. 0322B] my desire with good things? To You I have said: my heart and my groaning are not hidden from You [Note: [Col. 0321] Psalm 37.]. For what have I in heaven, and what have I desired upon earth besides You? God of my heart, and God my portion forever [Note: [Col. 0321] Psalm 72.]. Your eyes have seen my imperfection [Note: [Col. 0321] Psalm 138.]; and, You who inspire the desire, grant the accomplishment, You who can do all things, because without You we can do nothing.”

## RESPONSE.

I have gathered, Father, as I think, the sequence of your complaint in faithful recollection, and have reviewed what I gathered. But since you seek counsel, hear with equanimity what filial affection and friendly frankness, in unfeigned charity, advise you. I see that you have the countenance of one going to Jerusalem; but beware lest you receive your soul in vain, and lest he deceive you who [Col. 0322C] often transforms himself into an angel of light [Note: [Col. 0321] 2 Cor. 11.]. Many, according to the Apostle’s testimony, are Satan’s wiles [Note: [Col. 0321] 2 Cor. 2.]; take care that he does not supplant you from the counsel and assembly of the righteous. But if the spirit having authority over you should rush upon you, do not abandon your place [Note: [Col. 0321] Eccles. 10.]. A change of places is dangerous, and a sign of a sick soul. He who changes his place is like one fleeing the shadow of his own body: in fleeing himself, he carries himself about.

The kingdom of God is within you [Note: [Col. 0321] Luke 17.]: within yourself is that by which you may please the Most High. It is a matter of more abundant grace to be religious among secular persons, righteous among the ungodly. David was peaceable among those who hated peace [Note: [Col. 0321] Ps. 119]; righteous Lot lived in Sodom [Note: [Col. 0321] Gen. 29]; Joseph in Egypt with Pharaoh [Note: [Col. 0321] Gen. 41]; Daniel in Babylon with Nebuchadnezzar [Col. 0322D] [Note: [Col. 0321] Dan. 2]; Tobias in Nineveh [Note: [Col. 0321] Tobit 1]; Hushai amid Absalom’s counsels [Note: [Col. 0321] 2 Kings 16]; Obadiah with Ahab and Jezebel [Note: [Col. 0321] 3 Kings 18]. Yet the wickedness of others diminished nothing of their merit; indeed, the company of the ungodly increased their merit.

That you desire to leave everything for Christ is a perfect gift of God, descending from the Father of lights. For to those who leave everything for Christ a judicial seat at the regeneration is promised [Note: [Col. 0321] Matt. 19]; nor will those sit as judges with Christ who do not leave everything for him. Yet it is good to preside over brethren; for to those who rule well a double crown is promised, according to the Apostle’s testimony [Note: [Col. 0323] 1 Tim. 5]. There are, indeed, diverse paths to salvation and diversities of graces; but to each is given the manifestation of the Spirit for usefulness [Note: [Col. 0323] 1 Cor. 12]. Noah, Daniel, and Job earned the denarius of eternal life through different vocations of life.

If you expose yourself to labours for the advantage of the brethren and burden yourself with cares, it is good; but perhaps it is better, in accordance with the Apostle’s counsel, that you exercise yourself in godliness [Note: [Col. 0323] 1 Tim. 4]. For by his own testimony bodily exercise profits little, but godliness profits in all things, having the promise both of the life that now is and of that which is to come. It is good to be anxious with Martha, but more peaceful to sit at the Lord’s feet with [Col. 0323B] Mary [Note: [Col. 0323] Luke 10]. It is sweeter to set the Lord always before one’s eyes, to be still and see how sweet the Lord is.

Many place their brethren’s salvation before their own; I do not think with these. For no one is more closely akin to me than I myself. For my brethren I gladly expose my body to dangers, but not my soul—unless by “soul” you mean life. For although Moses, standing in the breach before the Lord, prays either that he forgive the people’s sin or blot him from the book which he wrote [Note: [Col. 0323] Exod. 31]; although Job, rooted in charity, does not hesitate to be brother of dragons and companion of ostriches [Note: [Col. 0323] Job 30]; although Paul wishes to be anathema from Christ for his brethren [Note: [Col. 0323] Rom. 9]: they indeed abounded in oil and grain, whereas I, poor little man, have nothing but [Col. 0323C] a little oil with which my wounds may be anointed.

They were anointed above their fellows; for in wine, grain, and oil [Note: [Col. 0323] Ps. 4]—that is, spiritual riches—they abounded above others. Would you hear their riches? Hear the Lord speaking of Moses and saying: “If I speak to my servants the prophets, I speak to them in a vision or through a dream; but not so to my servant Moses, who is faithful in all my house: for I speak to him face to face” [Note: [Col. 0323] Num. 12]. Of blessed Job he says to Satan: “Have you considered my servant Job, that there is none like him upon earth, a simple and upright man, fearing God and departing from evil?” [Note: [Col. 0323] Job 1.] The Apostle, moreover, overflowed wholly with the oil of mercy when he said: “I am certain that neither death, nor sword, nor life, nor angels, nor principalities, nor height, nor depth, [Col. 0323D] nor things present, nor things to come, nor any other creature shall be able to separate me from the charity which is in Christ Jesus” [Note: [Col. 0323] Rom. 8].

He who, caught up to the third heaven, had learned among the other mysteries of God that he could not be separated from Christ, out of great confidence and certainty wishes for his brethren’s salvation to be, for a time, anathema from Christ [Note: [Col. 0323] Rom. 9]. But I, a man seeing my own poverty, always have my soul in my hands, entrusting it to him who is able to keep my deposit unto that day. Although I am [Col. 0324A] animal, earthly, and carnal, I nevertheless speak to you, insofar as I am able in the teaching of the Spirit, comparing spiritual things with spiritual. But you who are spiritual know what is the good, well-pleasing, and perfect will of God [Note: [Col. 0323] 1 Cor. 2]. Nor does my speech prejudice you. The spiritual man indeed judges all things, but is himself judged by no one [Note: [Col. 0323] 2 Cor. 3]. For where the Spirit of God is, there is liberty [Note: [Col. 0323] 1 Cor. 11]. But those who are led by the Spirit of God are sons of God.

I indeed prefer spiritual exercise to bodily, just as spirit to flesh. For man was not made for woman, but woman for man [Note: [Col. 0323] Gen. 3 according to the LXX]; she is the one to whom the Lord says: “And toward your husband shall be your turning” [Note: [Col. 0323] Gen. 28], so that animality may presume nothing whatever from itself, but, subject to the spirit as to a husband, may obey without murmuring [Col. 0324B].

You have before your eyes, most holy Father, the ascending steps of charity, Jacob’s ladder [Note: [Col. 0323] Ezek. 40], and the pattern shown to Ezekiel upon the mountain of God’s visions [Note: [Col. 0323] Job 12]. I no longer urge you to run in the way of God’s commandments: you need a bridle rather than spurs. I exhort you only to hold so to the rule of moderation in vigils, fasts, disciplines, and other spiritual exercises that your body does not languish to the detriment of the service owed to God, your strength fail, your desire be withdrawn from the spirit, the effect from the work; lest the glory of your conscience be taken from you, lest you become a murderer of your own household.

But I, good Jesus, from whom is every grace, render thanks to you because you affect and inspire so great and venerable a man in this manner. Yet I know that this change [Col. 0324C]—which is undoubtedly a change wrought by the right hand of the Most High—will displease many, especially the great men of the earth, and will be an occasion of general scandal. Their love will pass into hatred, familiarity into contempt. But, in blessed Job’s testimony, “a lamp despised in the thoughts of the rich is prepared for the appointed time” [Note: [Col. 0323] Gal. 1]. It is better to please God than man. “If I pleased men,” says the Apostle, “I should not be Christ’s servant.” Those who please men are confounded, because God has rejected them [Note: [Col. 0323] Ps. 52].

If your countenance is confounded for a time, this confusion will bring glory; and in exchange for this confusion and shame you shall possess double things in your land. I know that princes will take offence; but I pray, let not their offence scandalize you. Certainly, when Christ’s disciples said: “Do you know that the Pharisees have taken offence at this saying?” he answered: “Let them alone: they are blind leaders of the blind” [Note: [Col. 0323] Matt. 15]. He therefore who forbids the causing of offence to one of the little ones believing in him gently bears the offence of Pharisees and chief priests.

It is glorious before the Lord of glory to deny oneself, and rather to be subject to the judgment of another’s will than to preside; and it is of greater merit to render obedience to one’s inferior or equal than to one’s superior. For charity forms the former obedience, whereas imperious necessity extorts the latter. Yet it is true that in the administration of office full perfection can scarcely ever be found. Certainly blessed Martin [Note: [Col. 0325] Sulpicius, *Dialogue* 2, “On the Virtues of St Martin,” ch. 7] was more renowned for miracles before he ascended the chair of pastoral eminence.

We read that Geoffrey of Perronne, prior of Clairvaux, when elected bishop of Tournai, did not assent to the election at all. Afterward, when he had died and appeared to a certain brother who asked how he fared, he replied: “The holy Trinity revealed to me that, had I accepted the episcopate, I should have been among the reprobate.” What then will unhappy men do, who willingly and gladly plunge themselves into the waves of temporal cares; who, feasting splendidly, sleeping, drinking, sitting at the revenue-office, [Col. 0325B] managing fiscal accounts, seeking what is their own—or rather what belongs to Caesar and not to God [Note: [Col. 0325] Phil. 2]—spend their lives in vanities, yet consider themselves perfect because they commit neither thefts, robberies, nor murders? “By their fruits you shall know them” [Note: [Col. 0325] Matt. 7].

While these men boil over in the incitement of covetousness and are drawn by the desire of empty glory, every misery which they endure is changed for them into delight. Of such persons Job says [Note: [Col. 0325] ch. 30]: “They reckoned it a delight to be under thorns.” These are the giants of whom the same Job says [Note: [Col. 0325] ch. 26]: “The giants who bear the world groan beneath the waters, and those who are with them.” At those for whom covetousness makes torments pleasurable the prophet Hosea [Note: [Col. 0325] ch. 10], under the figure of Ephraim, scoffs and says: “Ephraim is a heifer taught to love threshing.”

For either covetousness lightens their anxieties, or the profit of empty glory does so; and consequently they do not wish to cease from such things even when they may. Doubtless they have been made drunk by Babylon’s cup, and do not attend to the terrible and sudden judgments of God which are threatening them at hand. Therefore the Lord says in the Gospel: “Take heed to yourselves, lest your bodies be weighed down with gluttony, drunkenness, and the cares of this life, and that day come upon you suddenly” [Note: [Col. 0325] Luke 21]. “For when they say, ‘Peace and security,’ then sudden destruction shall come upon them, and pain like that of a woman with child, and they shall not escape” [Note: [Col. 0325] 1 Thess. 5]; for the prosperity of fools shall destroy them [Note: [Col. 0325] Prov. 1]. And when they have spent their days in temporal goods, according to Job’s testimony [Note: [Col. 0325] ch. 21], in a moment they shall descend to hell.

Great trees, indeed, grow for a long time, [Col. 0325D] and are cut down in a short time. Thus these wretches scorn to possess what might give them spiritual joy, and through temporal straits acquire matter for temporal and eternal groaning. Therefore, understanding their latter end, let us pity those who are ignorant and erring. For the axe is laid at their root, and, like fruitless trees, they await the sentence of cutting down and burning [Note: [Col. 0325] Matt. 3].

I had determined to write this little exhortation of mine in a more compressed style; but love, which knows no end—for charity [Col. 0326A] never fails [Note: [Col. 0325] 1 Cor. 13]—could scarcely find an end to writing. Thus brevity has escaped into immensity, the little sheet has grown into a skin, and the letter has passed into a book. Farewell.

## LETTER CIII. TO H., ABBOT OF READING

**Subject.**—He excuses himself for the length of the preceding letter.

To the reverend Father and lord H., by God’s grace abbot of Reading, his own Peter of Blois, archdeacon of Bath, wishes the spirit of counsel, with health.

I had begun to write briefly to you; but the brief grew long. For, as the material for composition overflowed, my pen wandered more freely than it should into immensity.

[Col. 0326B]

> Orestes is written even on the back, and is not yet finished.  
> [Note: [Col. 0325] Juvenal, *Satires* 1.]

Indeed, in dictating and writing I seemed to myself to speak with you in person; and thus prolixity was diminished by affection, while devotion stole from me all the labour of writing. If, therefore, my rather extended discourse burdens your ears while they are occupied with heavenly exercises, let the love which draws me into fault intercede for pardon. When, however, in reading you have passed over the first face of the preceding roll, turn it over to the back, and then proceed from the first roll to the second. You would have received this little exhortation of mine long ago, had not a throng of continually pressing affairs delayed me in many ways.

## LETTER CIV. TO THE DEAN AND CHAPTER OF THE CHURCH OF SALISBURY

[Col. 0326C]

**Subject.**—He congratulates the canons of Salisbury because they intend to bring their church down from the hill to the plain.

To his beloved lords and friends, the dean and chapter of the Church of Salisbury, Peter of Blois, archdeacon of Bath, wishes health in him who is true health.

“I rejoiced at the things said to me” [Note: [Col. 0325] Ps. 121], namely, that you intend to transfer the seat of the Church of Salisbury. I wholeheartedly congratulate you on this purpose. For that place was exposed to winds, barren, dry, deserted, and cramped. There was there a tower like that in Siloam [Note: [Col. 0325] Luke 13], which oppressed the inhabitants of the place with the burden of long servitude. But he who raised up the spirit of Othniel [Note: [Col. 0325] Judg. 3] to shake from God’s people the yoke of tyrannical oppression has himself stirred your bishop’s desire for a work of remembrance.

Thus long ago, on Elisha’s advice [Note: [Col. 0325] 4 Kings 6], the sons of the prophets came down from a cramped and barren place to the streams of the Jordan, so that there they might build more spaciously and make more suitable dwellings for themselves. The Church of Salisbury was captive upon that hill; and long ago the ark of the Lord was captured and held captive by the Philistines on Mount Gilboa [Note: [Col. 0325] 1 Kings 1], beside which that tower was erected, like another Dagon, in pride and misuse. Would that it had received, together with the aforesaid idol, the sentence of breaking and overthrow! Certainly [Col. 0327A] Noah’s ark [Note: [Col. 0327] Gen. 8], which had once saved the remnant of the human race, after it came to rest among the mountains of Armenia, was fit for no use.

Let us therefore descend under a happy omen to the level ground, where valleys will abound in grain, fields will grow rich in splendid fertility, each man will eat beneath his own vine and fig tree, and one day in those courts will be better than thousands [Note: [Col. 0327] Ps. 83]. When I thoughtfully consider and weigh your bishop’s prudent heart and magnificent hand, his honour, the peace also of the clergy, the memory of future time, and the enduring memorial, my soul fails and melts from longing for this time.

For with a certain pleasing imagination my mind depicts to me what was done in ancient days, when the Most High divided [Col. 0327B] the nations, when he separated the sons of Adam, establishing the boundaries of their dwellings according to the number of the sons of Israel; how, under Joshua [Note: [Col. 0327] ch. 13] and Caleb, the land of Canaan was assigned by lot to the twelve tribes by the measuring-line of distribution. Thus my spirit has revived, and my flesh seems to me to have blossomed again, because in our days I see the times of the prophets return.

There comes to my mind that common and celebrated rejoicing of peoples when, under King Darius, the Temple was built; when under Artaxerxes Nehemiah repaired the walls [Note: [Col. 0327] 2 Macc. 1], and, digging up and drawing forth the fire hidden for many years in a well, accomplished the burnt offering by means of the thick substance of the water. I recall the man in Ezekiel [Note: [Col. 0327] ch. 40], whose appearance was like the appearance of bronze, with a linen cord in his hand and a measuring rod [Col. 0327C] in his hand; and he measured the length, breadth, and height of the building, its walls, gates, vestibules, thresholds, altars, tables, Holy of Holies, treasuries, and windows.

I seem to see Solomon eagerly intent on the building of the Temple; Hiram supplying timber; stonecutters, masons, *biblii* [uncertain: perhaps a class of workmen], and bearers of burdens labouring diligently at the construction. Since, therefore, our Darius, the lord king, has readily assented to this change—which is beyond doubt a change wrought by the right hand of the Most High—I beg that your hand work all the more earnestly whatever it can. For we do not know what [Col. 0328A] the coming day may bring forth. The world lies in wickedness [Note: [Col. 0327] 1 John 5], and the devil, foreseeing the incalculable fruit of this translation, applies all his cunning arts to hinder it.

Therefore let no delay frustrate a work which ought to be pressed more urgently and promptly, lest there happen to you what the prophet says in reproaching the faithless people: “This people says: ‘The time has not yet come to build the house of the Lord’” [Note: [Col. 0327] Hag. 1]. I myself had chiefly wished to be personally present at this distribution of dwellings; but the command of one greater than I and the law of obedience draw me back from my purpose, unwilling and reluctant.

## LETTER CV. TO THE PRIOR AND CONVENT OF FOUNTAINS

[Note: [Col. 0327D] From Neubrigensis we learn that the monastery of Fountains, also called *Fontanense*, “of Fountains,” or “of the Springs,” was founded in the district of York by monks from the York monastery of the Cistercian order, whom Archbishop Thurstan brought there. Thus it was named, according to Jongelinus, *Notitia Cisterciensis*, book VIII: “Because it abounded in springs, it drew its name under a happy omen; for waters of every living piety and heavenly desire flowed abundantly, springing up into eternal life. From it, indeed, came many bishops,” etc. Manriquez, vol. [lacuna] of the *Cistercian Annals*, under this year, states that the subsequent shortage of crops, by which Fountains monastery was afflicted beyond measure and concerning which our Peter consoles the monks in this letter, occurred in the year 1163 [Col. 0328D]. If this is so, the title calling Peter archdeacon of Bath must be corrected: for he had not yet gone to England in that year, but only about 1170, after his return from Sicily. Nor is this consistent with what the same Manriquez says, namely that Peter of Blois wrote this consolatory letter when, sent to England by Pope Alexander and his business already completed, he was returning. For nowhere is it read that Peter of Blois was sent to England by Alexander; rather, he was summoned by Henry II, as he himself says somewhere and as we have elsewhere demonstrated.]

**Subject.**—He consoles monks distressed by the failure of the harvest [Col. 0328B].

To the venerable lords and friends, the prior and convent of Fountains, Master Peter of Blois, archdeacon of Bath, wishes health, and whatever is better or more fruitful than health.

With your permission and blessing I depart from the province of York and go to him who sent me. My absence from you in acts of service and visits was due to the absence of the lord abbot, continual occupation concerning our Church, diligent reading—which does not patiently allow the loss of idle time—and, above all, the desolation of your house. Over this I am wholly distressed by an affection of compassion, indeed of dying with you. Although [Col. 0328C] for a time I do not see you bodily, I nevertheless carry you about in my inward parts, present in spirit. For as the soul surpasses the body, so much nearer am I to you in the bowels of Christ; and the soul, far richer in its affections, repays the loss of bodily absence.

Indeed, beyond human hope, provisions have failed you at this time, and this is the cause of the aforesaid desolation. But he who in the desert fed five thousand men from a few loaves [Note: [Col. 0327] Matt. 14], who in time of drought entrusted Elijah’s sustenance to a widow and a raven [Note: [Col. 0327] 3 Kings 7], is able to show a more abundant mercy from heaven. And if, from the little which you possess, you show mercy to the needy, neither [Col. 0329A] the jar of flour nor the flask of oil will be diminished by the gift.

May the fountain of mercy, the fountain of wisdom, the fountain and abyss of eternal exultation, pour more abundant streams of his compassion upon me and the brethren of Fountains, that we may be made drunk from the torrent of his delight and draw water with joy from the fountains of the Saviour.

## LETTER CVI. TO R., SUBDEAN OF SALISBURY

**Subject.**—He teaches that calamities are sent by God not only because of princes’ sins, as that subdean thought, but also because of the people’s sins.

Master Peter of Blois, archdeacon of Bath, to his beloved companion and friend R., subdean of Salisbury: health in him who is true health.

You assert confidently, as though you possessed the spirit of prophecy and knew beforehand God’s secrets, that it was through our [Col. 0329B] prince’s offence that so great a tempest of hostility has shaken the provinces entrusted to him. He who takes away the spirit of princes, as he is terrible in his judgments, so he is inscrutable in his counsels concerning the children of men. “For who has known the mind of the Lord, or who has been his counsellor?” [Note: [Col. 0329] Rom. 11.] I think that the sins of the peoples no less than those of the prince supplied the matter of the present evils.

We read [Note: [Col. 0329] Jer. 31] that peoples and kings have often incurred the sentence of divine punishment, now for others and now for themselves. The prince eats a sour grape and the people’s teeth are numbed. Fire comes forth from the bramble, and the cedars of Lebanon are devoured. David sinned in numbering the people, and seventy thousand men of the people were struck by divine [Col. 0329C] indignation. Frequently the head is afflicted because of the members’ excess, and punishment is imposed upon princes because of the people’s iniquity.

For the whole community is often afflicted because of the sin of one or a few; for when Achan sinned, the people incurred the anathema [Note: [Col. 0329] Josh. 7]. Because Gad, Reuben, and half the tribe of Manasseh built a sacrilegious altar in the land of Canaan, God’s wrath raged universally against the people [Note: [Col. 0329] Josh. 22]. The Lord often begins his vengeance at the sanctuary [Note: [Col. 0329] Ezek. 9]; and he who punishes the powerful powerfully often burns more harshly against those in authority. Israel commits fornication with the Midianites, and its princes are hung on gibbets facing the sun [Note: [Col. 0329] Num. 25]. Moses and Aaron, who excelled among God’s people in merit and office, through the multitude’s impetuosity [Col. 0329D] forfeited entrance into the land of promise at the waters of contradiction [Note: [Col. 0329] Num. 20]. For the sin of his sons Eli fell from his seat and, his neck broken, expired [Note: [Col. 0329] 1 Kings 4].

Who has supplied the cause of this evil, I do not know. Would that both prince and people considered themselves guilty of so great a danger! Would that our king, with King David, humbled himself and said to the destroying angel: “Turn the sword upon me, for I am he who has sinned” [Note: [Col. 0329] 2 Kings 24]! Would that subjects, with the people of Nineveh, proclaimed that they had sinned, and turned aside the vengeance of heavenly wrath by [Col. 0330A] weeping, groaning, and the harshness of sackcloth [Note: [Col. 0329] Jonah 3]! Would that priests wept between porch and altar, saying: “Spare, Lord, spare your people” [Note: [Col. 0329] Joel 2]! Would that someone supplied Moses’ office, so that God’s people might prevail against Amalek through the raising of their hands [Note: [Col. 0329] Exod. 17]!

Moreover, it is no longer only Amalekites who must be feared, nor does every evil now come forth only from the north [Note: [Col. 0329] Jer. 1]; but the two tails of smoking firebrands, breaking forth from Africa, ravage Spain [Note: [Col. 0329] Isa. 7]. May the Lord look upon the face of his covenant and stir up the faith of our princes—for “faith is the victory that conquers the world” [Note: [Col. 0329] 1 John 5]. If they deal faithlessly or negligently with Christ’s cause, may Christ himself plead his own cause against those who blaspheme the Holy One of Israel; may he choose from [Col. 0330B] his people one who is humble, that in humility he may overcome pride. For it is he by whose good pleasure infantrymen defeated the most powerful king of Syria [Note: [Col. 0329] 3 Kings 20], a widow defeated Holofernes [Note: [Col. 0329] Judith 13], and gnats defeated Pharaoh [Note: [Col. 0329] Exod. 8]. Farewell.

## LETTER CVII. TO B., A MONK AND FRIEND

**Subject.**—He rebukes the monk B. because he pursues courtly life and its vices, detraction and flattery.

Master P. of Blois, archdeacon of Bath, to his beloved friend B., a monk: health, and departure from the midst of Babylon.

You gave your hand to the apostolic profession and assigned yourself especially to the service of him whom to serve is to reign. But now, having shaken off the yoke of that service which led you into the liberty of God’s children, you have immersed yourself in courtly waves, incurring the reproach of shameful servitude through the very liberty of sinning. For according to the Apostle’s testimony, he who commits sin is the slave of sin [Note: [Col. 0329] John 8].

Character is acquired from companionship, and the corruption of life is transmitted through intercourse with the wicked. You have become one of the locusts [Note: [Col. 0329] Rev. 9], whose whole power lies in their tongues and tails; a companion of those whose mouth is full of bitterness and deceit. Their tails also are foxes’ tails, to which Samson bound fire [Note: [Col. 0329] Judg. 7]; their end is destruction, their punishment fire and worm. You who had consecrated your mouth to the Gospel now dishonour it with the poisons of detraction and the filth [Col. 0330D] of flatteries.

Doubtless you have chosen to dwell with the frogs that are in the chambers of kings; and, among courtiers, while displaying the image of an affected piety, you hunt the favour of magnates at great danger to your soul and affliction of your own body. As for your complaint that tears of devotion once wholly habitual to you have dried up, do not wonder if the Lord has shut his heaven against you, given you a brazen earth, and withheld rain from Mount Gilboa. For, since you are eager for favourable breezes and a seeker after courtly favour, this appetite, like a scorching wind, [Col. 0331A] has dried up the dew of heavenly mercy and the streams of grace.

Yet what if you abound in tears? In many people tears flow easily and dry up with equal ease. There are fornicators, adulterers, ambitious men, the avaricious, and other persons of most wicked life who, when God offers them his grace, overflow with torrents of tears. Nevertheless, “in a flood of many waters they shall not draw near to God” [Note: [Col. 0331] Ps. 31]. They are pierced with compunction for a time, and in the time of temptation they fall away. Of such it is written: “Their mercy is like a morning cloud, and like the dew that passes away in the morning” [Note: [Col. 0331] Hos. 6]. They weep for sins committed and continue to commit things that should be wept for.

Moreover, although Achsah, daughter of Caleb, possessed both the upper and the lower watering-place [Note: [Col. 0331] Judg. 1], such tears are lost unless they repent of evil works [Col. 0331B]. They are therefore grievously deceived who think themselves something when they are nothing, and, presuming upon grace offered to them, say with Manoah’s wife: “If the Lord had wished to kill us, he would not have received a sacrifice from our hands” [Note: [Col. 0331] Judg. 15].

Accordingly, let not the servant grow proud if he is admitted by God’s grace to the table of sons. For of persons like these it is written: “He fed them with the fat of wheat, and satisfied them with honey from the rock” [Note: [Col. 0331] Ps. 80]. Yet they falsely reckoned themselves among God’s friends, as is indicated by the verse preceding: “The enemies of the Lord lied to him, and their time shall endure for ages.” But I fear that, just as you have cast away from yourself fear of God and of his terrible judgments, God may cast you away. “With the holy man he is holy, and with the perverse he is perverted” [Col. 0331C] [Note: [Col. 0331] Ps. 17].

Above all, I beg you to fear that saying of Solomon—or rather the thunderbolt of divine judgment: “Consider the works of God, because there is no one able to set right him whom he has cast away” [Note: [Col. 0331] Eccles. 7]. Cain heard the Lord’s voice; but because God had cast him away, he did not receive the grace of correction [Note: [Col. 0331] Gen. 4]. And, that the letter may close with the poet’s verse:

> Live with yourself, and you will know how scant is your household stuff.  
> [Note: [Col. 0331] Persius, *Satires* 4.]

Farewell.

## LETTER CVIII. TO G., BISHOP OF ELY

[Note: [Col. 0331D] Concerning this William, see what has been said on Letter 87.]

**Subject.**—He implores the royal chancellor’s aid against the tyranny of a sheriff.

To the reverend Father and lord W., by God’s grace bishop of Ely [Col. 0331D], legate of the Apostolic See, and chancellor of the lord king [Col. 0332A] of England, Peter of Blois, archdeacon of Bath, wishes health and the wholesome exercise of the royal priesthood.

Because your name is as poured-out oil, and the generosity native to you has spread itself throughout the world in the display of magnificent liberality, I run with the rest to this oil, to this inexhaustible fountain of kindness and munificence. I too offer, with the rest, an empty vessel [Note: [Col. 0331] 4 Kings 4], that it may be filled with your oil. For the oil will stand still unless vessels are offered frequently; and you lose nothing through expenditure. For as charity is stronger from weakness, so when emptied it increases the more: it does not feel loss from distribution; it receives strength from giving; and its emptying passes into increase.

I ask from you not gold, not money, but the favour of intercession with [Col. 0332B] the king. For the Lord has placed you among the pillars of the realm, among the hinges of heaven, among the giants who bear the world, so that with the gentle shoulder of compassion you may support the burdens of those oppressed by wrongful accusation, and, in accordance with your promise, restrain by royal power the tyranny of the sheriff of Stafford, by which he cruelly oppresses my men.

I beg you, consider the justice of the poor who cry to you, so that he who judges the ends of the earth may turn his judgment for us into mercy. The aforesaid men have been oppressed, contrary to the ancient privileges of our church of Wolverhampton, by the yoke of a most grievous servitude. But, according to Isaiah’s word, may that yoke rot away before the oil [Note: [Col. 0331] Isa. 10]; and may judgment proceeding from your countenance turn from the oppressed poor the rod of the exactor [Col. 0332C]. Farewell.

## LETTER CIX. TO H., ARCHBISHOP OF CANTERBURY

**Subject.**—He states that illness prevents him from returning to court.

To the reverend Father and lord H., by God’s grace archbishop of Canterbury [Note: [Col. 0331D] This Hubert, formerly dean of York, was made bishop of Salisbury in the first year of King Richard. With Richard he undertook the Jerusalem expedition, and there conducted himself so bravely that he earned the king’s favour. Accordingly, after Baldwin died on the Jerusalem expedition in 1191, Richard caused him to be elected archbishop of Canterbury [Col. 0332D], appointed him chancellor and chief justiciar of England. Moreover, a lawsuit long continued between him and the monks of Canterbury concerning a church which Baldwin had earlier begun, to the prejudice of the Church of Canterbury. But after prolonged litigation, first at Celestine III’s command and then at Innocent III’s, that church was demolished and peace between Hubert and the monks was confirmed; thereafter he lived peacefully with them. He died in 1205.], primate of all England and legate of the Apostolic See, his own P. of Blois, archdeacon of Bath, wishes health and the sincere affection of filial obedience.

After the journey which I made, I had intended to come to you and obediently embrace your command, whatever filial affection could endure. Yet I have already felt the preliminary heats of an approaching and threatening quartan fever; and, because I have experienced its malignity continuously for two years, [Col. 0333A] I fear that its malignity may recur in me if I undertake courtly commotions, violate the regimen, or expose myself to labour or cold air.

Therefore let not fear of the illness I suffer, but rather fear of death, excuse my delay before your favour. Yet if, God forbid, grave danger should threaten the Church of Canterbury or your person, and necessity should require my presence, let your eye spare neither a dying man nor one who is sick. In respect to danger to you or to the Church’s condition, it is publicly incumbent upon me to obey without all dissimulation and evasion. Whoever in such matters hesitates or draws distinctions concerning obedience presumptuously tastes, to his own ruin, of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. May it please God that, as we suffer the loss caused by the first disobedience, obedience may likewise close the course of my life for me. Farewell.

## LETTER CX. TO THE ABBOT AND CONVENT OF LA CHARITÉ

[Note: [Col. 0333D] The abbey of La Charité, situated in the district of Chartres, was founded in 1121 by Theobald the Great, count of Champagne, as Manriquez, vol. I of the *Annals*, under that year, and Jongelinus in the *Notitia Cisterciensis* report.]

**Subject.**—Being ill, he implores the aid of the monks’ prayers.

To the venerable lords and friends, the abbot and convent of La Charité, Master Peter of Blois, archdeacon of Bath, wishes health in him who commands Jacob’s deliverances.

As your house, in accordance with its name, is pre-eminent among others for the fragrance of its holy reputation, so its praise has proved equal to that name. From that time I have poured out my soul in every affection of love toward you; and I have resolved to visit that place, so desirable to me, more frequently [Col. 0333C], to take comfort with you, and to rejoice in mutual edification. Certainly, I have not been well since I departed from you. First I suffered in my eyes; afterward I fell into an acute fever. A tertian followed the acute fever, which, after various deceptive changes by which it tormented me for a very long time, passed into a quartan. Since, therefore, my wretched body is pitiably afflicted by the fire and chill of fever—or rather of hell—and bodily medicine gives me no assurance of recovery, I devoutly implore the aid of your prayers. For how much another person’s faith or prayer avails, I have learned not only by experience but also from the Gospel narrative. For in Matthew’s Gospel [Note: [Col. 0333] Chapter 9.], when certain persons carried a paralytic on a bed and presented him to Christ; when the centurion pleaded for his servant [Note: [Col. 0333] Matt. 8.]; when the Canaanite woman [Col. 0333D] pleaded for her daughter [Note: [Col. 0333] Matt. 15.]; and when Mary and Martha pleaded for Lazarus [Note: [Col. 0333] John 11.], he who is life for the dying, or even for those already dead, annulled the claims of death and showed by his deeds how great is the benefit of another’s prayer. I often pass through the fire and water of fever; but if, for my sake, the water of devotion is poured out even once between you and [Col. 0334A] God, I shall pass into refreshment, and shall soon come to you to repay the debt of thanks. Let the condition of human fellowship move you, most beloved friends; let the obligation of communion which we mutually undertook with you in chapter, the bond of charity, the distress of one suffering, and the devotion of one pleading move you. Farewell.

## LETTER CXI. TO G., A CANON AND HIS FRIEND

**SUBJECT.**—He exhorts G., a canon, to read the sacred writings diligently if he wishes to resist the temptations of the flesh.

To his dearest companion and friend, G., canon, M. Peter of Blois, archdeacon of Bath, greetings, and consolation in desolation.

By a certain law of nature it belongs to the covenant of friendship [Col. 0334B] that friends should anticipate one another with mutual consolation, and should bear more patiently, through the benefit of shared charity, the burdens of temptations that press too heavily upon each. You had left the vain manner of life of this world, in order that you might sacrifice abominations to the Lord in the desert. The Egyptians, indeed, abominate sheep; but among evil spirits every simplicity is detestable. You therefore believed that you had wholly escaped fleshly desires; yet Pharaoh’s malice has not yet cooled, and his hand is still stretched out. For in the desert you found the labours of Egyptian servitude; in solitude, tumult; in peace, war; in harbour, shipwreck. For, as you lament in complaint, the desires of the flesh and earthly affections, which had wholly withered in your heart, [Col. 0334C] are growing green again through a kind of relapse of poisonous growth.

The incentive and cause of this evil is that, having abandoned the study of sacred Scripture and the exercise of spiritual warfare, you disdain the food of the soul and the heavenly manna. For the soul which, degenerating from spiritual life, does not aspire to heavenly things must necessarily be cast down toward carnal and earthly things. Therefore the Lord sent you quails [Note: [Col. 0333] Num. 11.], and rained flesh around you like dust. Quails rise only a little above the ground: these are earthly affections and desires of the flesh, which wage war against the soul. Take care not to savour earthly things, lest you set aside the bread of angels for the flesh which heavenly indignation has rained down—that is, for fleshly affections.

The Lord has set before you sacred Scripture, consolation in every temptation. This is the table that refreshes, [Col. 0334D] according to the saying: “You have prepared a table before me against those who afflict me” [Note: [Col. 0333] Ps. 22.]. This is David’s harp, while he sings upon it, through which the wicked spirit departs from Saul [Note: [Col. 0333] 1 Sam. 16.]; when it is silent, the same spirit again torments him. Apply yourself, therefore, vigilantly to reading and prayer, lest hostile temptation overthrow you. Farewell.

## LETTER CXII. TO R. [Note: [Col. 0335D] This letter is addressed to “R.” in our manuscripts Sorbonne 1, Mazarin 1, Saint-Victor 1 and 2, as also in Merlin’s edition. In the others, namely Vall., Saint-Victor 3, and Hard., in which this letter occurs—for it is absent from the rest—there is no heading. Some suppose, however, that this is a scribal error, the copyists having written R. instead of P., because at that time there was a certain Peter, bishop of Orléans. I agree that there is an error, but think that H., rather than P., should be written, since it more closely resembles the letter R. This is how it is written in the ancient manuscripts. It denotes Henry, son of Robert, count of Dreux; Robert was nephew of Louis the Fat, king of the Franks, and that Henry was therefore a blood relative of Philip Augustus. Hence it appears that this letter was written to him. [Col. 0336D] Further, it mentions the Jerusalem expedition, which occurred under this bishop, namely in the year 1190. These details are drawn from the antiquities of Orléans, published in French in the history *On the Lives of the Bishops of Orléans*, by François Le Maire of Orléans. That Henry is also named by Demochare in his book *On the Sacrifice of the Mass*. Moreover, in 1198 Henry set out for Rome to secure the release of his brother Philip, bishop of Beauvais, whom the king of England held in chains; he died on the journey, as the chronicle of the canon of Laon records, and was buried at Siena in Tuscany.] TO THE BISHOP OF ORLÉANS. [A.D. 1199.]

[Col. 0335A]

**SUBJECT.**—He argues vigorously for ecclesiastical immunity: that the king of France, for the war against the Saracens in Jerusalem, should exact from clerics not money but prayers alone.

To the most reverend father and lord R., by God’s grace bishop of Orléans, M. Peter of Blois, archdeacon of Bath, greetings and the affection of sincere love.

It is written [Note: [Col. 0335] Eccles. 3.]: “There is a time to keep silence, and a time to speak.” Long have I been mute and kept silence even from good things; but now I cannot conceal by silence the injury done to the Christian faith. Already savage barbarism rages fiercely near the borders of your land [Note: [Col. 0336D] He means Saladin’s incursion into the Holy Land and the slaughter of many Christians; the historians of this period should be consulted concerning it.], and the monstrous cruelty of the nations ranges abroad for the destruction of the Christian [Col. 0335B] name. Why then do you stand here idle all day? The enemy’s sword is brandished against your necks, and there is no one to mount up in opposition, no one to set the zeal of faith against those who reproach the name of the God of the hosts of Israel.

You therefore, most reverend Father, since you hold a pre-eminent place of greater dignity among the other pillars of the Church, bear witness to your faith, and do not linger further in Christ’s cause. Let not the word of the Lord be bound in you; but, as the Lord has magnified you in the sight of kings, so exercise the office of pontifical magnificence. Through Jeremiah, the instrument of his Spirit, the Lord cries to you [Note: [Col. 0335] Chapter 26.]: “Stand,” he says, “in the court of the house of the Lord, and speak to all the cities of Judah the words which [Col. 0335C] I have spoken to you.” And, expressing those words, he adds: “Go and cry: ‘Return, rebellious Israel,’ says the Lord, ‘and I will not turn my face from you’” [Note: [Col. 0335] Jer. 3.]. In the same Spirit Ezekiel cries [Note: [Col. 0335] Chapter 33.], saying: “If the watchman sees the sword coming and does not sound the trumpet, and the enemy comes and takes one soul from the people, I will require his blood at the watchman’s hand.”

Do not, then, be idle with the Lord’s talent; rather practise the Lord’s evangelical commerce, so that the Lord may receive back with interest the talent entrusted to you. Be urgent therefore in season and out of season [Note: [Col. 0335] 2 Tim. 4.]; do the work of an evangelist; fulfil your ministry. Do not emulate evildoers [Note: [Col. 0335] Ps. 36.]—I mean bishops—who flatter [Col. 0336A] your king with smooth adulation, dumb dogs unable to bark [Note: [Col. 0335] Isa. 56.]. In bishops, indeed, the profession of truth is most acceptable to God. Do not fear to lay down your life for truth, that you may see good days; for the Lord will demand the blood of the perishing person from the hand of the silent priest. For the ark of God is captured and the people fall by the sword while the priest grows sluggish in correcting his sons [Note: [Col. 0335] 1 Sam. 4.].

Do not fear the king’s agitation or displeasure; but address him with saving counsels in all freedom, because “where the Spirit of God is, there is freedom” [Note: [Col. 0335] 2 Cor. 3.]. John the Baptist [Note: [Col. 0335] Matt. 14.] preferred to incur danger with the king rather than to conceal the Lord’s law; he discharged the office of an envoy to Herod and Herodias, as Elijah had done to Ahab and Jezebel. Therefore remember God, and do not be silent; do not give [Col. 0336B] silence to your mouths [Note: [Col. 0335] Isa. 62.]. John used the sword of zeal against Herod; Phinehas against the Jew and the Midianite woman [Note: [Col. 0335] Num. 25.]; Samuel against King Agag [Note: [Col. 0335] 1 Sam. 15.]; Peter against Ananias and Sapphira [Note: [Col. 0335] Acts 5.]; Paul against Elymas the magician [Note: [Col. 0335] Acts 13.]. Their lives set before you an example of correction.

The law of God and faith in Christ must be valued above every worldly possession, even above honour, reputation, and one’s own safety. When King Ahab [Note: [Col. 0335] 1 Kings 20.] had offered to the king of Syria, who was grievously oppressing him, his servants and maidservants, sons and daughters, wife, and all his possessions, once it came to violating God’s law, although he was wicked in other respects, he nevertheless did not fear to enter upon the hazard of battle for God’s law. It is better to fall into human hands than to abandon [Col. 0336C] God’s law.

If you stand in awe of the face of the king of the Franks, bring in some of your fellow bishops who are led by God’s Spirit, so that you may use such moderation in speech that, if your language is strong, it may nonetheless be gentle. For wisdom, which “reaches mightily from end to end, orders all things sweetly” [Note: [Col. 0335] Wis. 8.]. Above all, I beg you, avoid the mark of a flatterer and the role of a fawner. For the honey of flattery is excluded from the Lord’s sacrifice [Note: [Col. 0335] Lev. 2.].

There are often men at courts who ingratiate themselves by smooth applause even in shameful matters to the soft and delicate ears of princes, placing cushions beneath the head and pillows beneath every elbow. Hardly anyone is found in courts who does not sell oil, who [Col. 0337A] does not make the sinner’s head fat with oil [Note: [Col. 0337] Ps. 140.]. For “the sinner is praised in the desires of his soul, and the wicked is blessed” [Note: [Col. 0337] Ps. 10.]. But let him fear what is said to Zedekiah through Jeremiah [Note: [Col. 0337] Chapter 38.]: “O Zedekiah, your peaceful men have deceived you.”

[Note: [Col. 0337] Justin, book II; Herodotus, book VII of the *Histories*.] When Xerxes’ army had an innumerable multitude of ships and chariots, and courtly flatterers told him that neither the sea would suffice for so great a fleet, nor the air for the missiles of so many peoples, nor the earth in its vastness contain so many chariots, there was one man in that immense army, Demaratus, who dared, in a spirit of freedom, to say to Xerxes: “You will be conquered by yourself, and the multitude of your army will overwhelm you.”

Do not cease, I beg you, from exhortation, even though, following the counsel of his attendant advisers, he hardens himself against your urgency. For I know that Jannes and Mambres still resist Moses at Pharaoh’s court [Col. 0337B] [Note: [Col. 0337] 2 Tim. 3.], and that successors of Ahithophel maliciously pervert the counsels of the righteous. The broadest field of discourse lies open concerning the malice of prostituted tongues; but, hastening to other matters, we pass over all these things in silence. You may judge what is expedient for your reputation.

But apply diligent care, so that your kinsman, as the Church’s chief standard-bearer, may carry the banner of faith before the kings and princes of the earth; so that, as he has been more vigilant in military affairs, he may now not prove backward in the defence of the Christian faith. If, moreover, he has resolved again to undertake the journey of this pilgrimage, let him furnish travel provisions for himself and his men not from the spoils of churches nor from the sweat of the poor, but from his own revenues; or let him wage Christ’s wars from enemy plunder. For the Lord’s hand has not been shortened [Col. 0337C], so that he who did great things in Israel cannot also exalt the arm of his magnificence among the people of his own acquisition.

Certainly, when Israel departed from Egypt, the Lord enriched the Hebrews from the spoils of the Egyptians [Note: [Col. 0337] Exod. 12.]. When the people entered the land of Canaan, they gathered for themselves countless riches from the plunder of their enemies. Indeed, it is a public law of war that princely liberality should bestow pay from military proceeds upon its fellow soldiers. What reason is there that those who fight for the Church should despoil the Church, which they ought to have enlarged by the spoils of its enemies and by triumphal gifts? Do the foolish and wretched suppose that Christ, who is supreme justice, wishes a sacrifice to be offered to him out of injury and sacrilege, or that he will permit [Col. 0337D] plunder acquired by such means to prosper? For if, by the witness of truth, the person who did not give his own goods to the poor is sent into eternal fire, where, I ask, should one be sent who has seized or defrauded the goods of the poor or of the Church?

On account of these and similar matters, “the sons of Ephraim, who bend and shoot the bow, turned back on the day of battle” [Note: [Col. 0337] Ps. 77.]. Never have the spoils of the poor or of the Church [Col. 0338A] had the auspice of a successful outcome. Therefore, in the last pilgrimage, contempt was poured out upon princes, and the Lord caused them to wander in a pathless waste and not on a road [Note: [Col. 0337] Ps. 106.]. Destruction and unhappiness were in their ways, because they did not know the way of peace [Note: [Col. 0337] Ps. 13.]. The patrimony of Christ and of his Church is today turned into an occasion of scandal and material for servitude.

Certainly, under Pharaoh [Note: [Col. 0337] Gen. 47.], when by royal decree all were generally compelled to pay a fifth part, the priests were nevertheless exempt from the observance and burden of that ordinance. Likewise, in the book of Numbers [Note: [Col. 0337] Chapter 18.], as a figure of perpetual freedom, the Lord commands that the Levitical tribe be free from every public obligation and subject only to the judgment of the high priest. What else can or ought a ruler demand from bishops [Col. 0338B] or clergy, except that the Church should pray to God for him without ceasing? Every priest taken from among men is appointed for men in matters pertaining to God, that he may offer gifts and sacrifices for king and people [Note: [Col. 0337] Heb. 5.]; and, if the Lord is angry with them, the priest should intercede in the middle and become a reconciler in the time of wrath.

The angry Lord had determined to destroy his people Israel [Note: [Col. 0337] Ps. 105.]; and Moses stood in the breach before him and appeased the movement of divine indignation by prayer. The flame of divine judgment was raging against the people; Aaron, taking up the censer, placed himself in the middle between the living and the dead before the flame, and the devastation ceased [Note: [Col. 0337] Num. 16.]. Likewise, Israel prevailed against Amalek while Moses prayed and [Col. 0338C] raised his hands to the Lord [Note: [Col. 0337] Exod. 17.]. Later, in the days of Joshua [Note: [Col. 0337] Chapter 6.], while the priests ministered, the walls of Jericho fell.

I know that if your king resolves to burden the Church with forced services, transport requisitions, exactions, poll taxes, and other base and extraordinary imposts, he will find very many bishops who support this measure [Note: [Col. 0337D]

He speaks of Philip Augustus, who, in order to carry out the holy war against Saladin, invader of the Holy Land, exacted tithes from all his subjects, lay and ecclesiastical alike.

[Col. 0338D] This letter was written about the year 1190, in which the Jerusalem expedition against Saladin was undertaken.]

. For, forgetting evangelical freedom, which makes not only sons of God but friends, they will permit their ear to be pierced with an awl in disgraceful perpetual servitude [Note: [Col. 0337] Exod. 21.]. Thus formerly, when King Antiochus [Note: [Col. 0337] 1 Macc. 2.] overthrew the rights of the Temple and priesthood, many Israelites came forth who, out of regard for flattery alone or empty fear, consented to that tyranny.

But you, most reverend [Col. 0338D] Father, go up in opposition for the house of Israel, and set yourself as an impregnable wall for God’s covenant. For you will incur an enormous danger to your reputation and soul if you conceal this injury to Christ through silence or neglect. By your teaching and exhortation, let the lord king remember that he received from the Church the power of the sword not to oppress the poor but to protect the Church [Col. 0339A]. And he who, while living, continually experiences the Church’s aid will need its benefits much more abundantly after death. For he shall die; and would that he considered the uncertain issue of death, and, remembering his last things, might compensate for future misery through present wealth! Ecclesiasticus says [Note: [Col. 0339] Chapter 10.]: “A king is today, and tomorrow he shall die; and when he is dead, he shall inherit serpents, beasts, and worms.” “His spirit shall pass through him, and shall not remain; and he shall know his place no more” [Note: [Col. 0339] Ps. 102.].

Let him therefore recognise the place and office in which the Lord has set him; and let him wage the Lord’s wars not from the treasures of the Church, which are owed to the poor alone, but from the royal treasury. Let him not trust in the strength or multitude of armed men, but in the Lord [Col. 0339B]. For, according to Solomon’s testimony, “the name of the Lord is very great strength” [Note: [Col. 0339] Prov. 15.]. “The Lord is the strength of his people” [Note: [Col. 0339] Ps. 66.]. This is most clearly apparent in the battles of old. How did one pursue a thousand, and two put ten thousand to flight [Note: [Col. 0339] Deut. 33.]? Was it not because God sold them and the Lord shut them up? “For they did not possess the land by their sword, nor did their arm save them; but your right hand and your arm, O Lord, and the light of your countenance, because you were pleased with them” [Note: [Col. 0339] Ps. 43.]. But the Lord will be pleased with those who are faithful in his covenant. “Without faith it is impossible to please the Most High” [Note: [Col. 0339] Heb. 1.]. For “this is the victory that conquers the world: our faith” [Note: [Col. 0339] 1 John 5.].

And because I see nearly all the magnates of the realm [Col. 0339C] becoming slack in the Lord’s way through a certain weariness of labour and faint-heartedness, I beg you by the persistent urgency of preaching to strengthen the feeble hands and weak knees. Clearly, because the previous pilgrimage did not succeed according to their desire, they think the Lord’s hand has been shortened and the inexhaustible fountain of heavenly grace has dried up. Yet they departed then in pride and misuse, and measure their judgment not by the failure of their faith but solely by the outcome of divine dispensation. Their faith was indeed tested once and found deficient. The Lord will test it still further; for the issue of victory depends on their faith and humility, and from these especially the triumphal outcome of battles must be expected.

The tribe of Benjamin had sinned in the matter of the Levite’s wife, and the remaining tribes armed themselves for vengeance upon the crime [Note: [Col. 0339] Judg. 20.]. Their cause was more just, and their army far more numerous and stronger. Yet when the Lord had assigned them a leader for battle, and they had gone down to fight at his command, God, terrible in counsel over the sons of men [Col. 0340A] [Note: [Col. 0339] Ps. 65.], permitted the righteous to be defeated by the wicked, the many by the few; and twenty-two thousand Israelites fell that day. Again they came to battle by the Lord’s command and were defeated, and eighteen thousand Israelites were slain. Surely because they relied upon their own strength and multitude, they were defeated and humbled the first and second time, so that they who had been defeated through pride might conquer again through humility.

Their faith, however, did not languish after the first and second reverses; rather, increasing through this double calamity, they again girded themselves for battle—more humbly, and therefore more strongly. On the third encounter, purified by so great an effusion of blood, they almost annihilated the whole tribe of Benjamin. Know that we shall reap the outcome of the second pilgrimage according to the faith of the people [Col. 0340B]. Therefore instruct both people and their leader in faith and the fear of God; and, to include much in few words, most reverend and beloved Father, I entrust to your judgment the peace of religious persons, the tranquillity of the simple, the cause of Christ, and the Church’s liberty.

## LETTER CXIII. TO G., ARCHBISHOP OF YORK [Note: [Col. 0339D] This is Geoffrey, natural son of Henry II, king of England; see Letter 62.]

**SUBJECT.**—He exhorts the archbishop to resist heretics and, by the clergy’s common consent, punish them so severely that others may be deterred from heresy.

To the reverend father and lord G., by God’s grace archbishop of York, his own P. of Blois, archdeacon of Bath: may you think of the Lord in goodness and defeat the assailants [Col. 0340C] of the Catholic faith.

While your father was engaged in human affairs, while the deceptive glory of the world and the treacherous prosperity of this life smiled upon him, you long remained uncertain what it was expedient or fitting for you to do: whether to pursue clerical office or to prefer military honours to scholarly pursuits. We saw and were present when the kingdom of Palestine [Note: [Col. 0339D] In 1185, when Saladin had occupied the Holy Land, Heraclius, patriarch of Jerusalem, went to the Christian princes to seek [Col. 0340D] aid against the unbelievers. On reaching England, he offered King Henry, on behalf of the Christians dwelling in the Holy Land, the kingdom of Jerusalem, as Ralph de Diceto, Knighton, and Matthew Paris relate under that year.]—and also the kingdom of Italy—was offered by the magnates and peoples of both kingdoms to your father, or to one of his sons whom he might choose for this purpose. Some, moreover, observing your virtue and ability, destined for you, by common desire, the eminence of manifold honours.

But when the young king and the duke of Brittany, your brothers, who in their times attained triumphant military glory above other mortals, had been taken away, and at last your father, King Henry of blessed memory, had paid nature the tribute of death, [Col. 0341A] you saw that every living human being is altogether vanity. For “man passes away in an image” [Note: [Col. 0341] Ps. 38.]. Therefore you abandoned vain and false insanities, and, using more mature counsel, chose the service of him whose service is to reign.

Since, therefore, the harvest entrusted to you is great, and the vineyard of the Lord of Hosts, of which he himself appointed you guardian, extends its branches more widely, you must provide and act more circumspectly, lest the vine’s shoots degenerate into wild vines, wheat into tares, gold into dross, and oil into lees. For in your time preachers of false doctrines have arisen: teachers of falsehood, enemies of truth, and overthrowers of faith. They are gentle and simple as lambs, but cunning as foxes and ravenous as wolves. These are the heretics who come [Col. 0341B] in sheep’s clothing. These are the wolves from whom the hireling flees [Note: [Col. 0341] John 10.]. These are the foxes that destroy vineyards.

Since, therefore, you are Peter’s successor and vicar [Note: [Col. 0341D] A similar manner of speaking occurs in St Hilary’s *Fragments*, where he calls bishops “successors of Peter and Paul”; in Lucifer of Cagliari, book I, *On Not Sparing Those Who Sin against God*, where he writes of “those who are found to have been successors of blessed Peter”; and in Gaudentius of Brescia, sermon on the day of his ordination, where he calls Ambrose “the successor of the apostle Peter.” Cyprian gives the reason for this in his book *On the Unity of the Church*: namely, that the episcopate is one and the chair is one, whose unity began from Peter, to whom Christ granted primacy. “In order,” he says, “to make unity manifest, he established one chair, and by his authority ordained that the origin of that same unity should begin from one. Certainly the other apostles were what Peter was, endowed with an equal fellowship of honour and power; but the beginning proceeds from unity. Primacy is given to Peter, and the one Church and one chair of Christ are shown; and all are shepherds, but one flock is shown, which is fed by all the apostles in unanimous agreement.” So too Hincmar, in the capitularies of the year 874, the first of which is: “Blessed Peter the apostle, in whose place bishops serve in the Church,” etc.], who has received the Lord’s sheep to guard and feed, it is greatly your concern to foresee and guard against the cunning devices of those who secretly transgress the Lord’s law, who spread snares and traps to capture the simple, and who hurl themselves with others into the abyss of eternal damnation.

Let zeal for the Lord’s house, therefore, be kindled in you. Go up in opposition; set yourselves as a wall against the enemies of Christ’s cross; bear witness to your faith; and stand manfully and effectively for God’s covenant. Summon the clergy; assemble the people [Col. 0341C], so that by the common deliberation of those who possess the Spirit of God, a formidable decree may be promulgated in your province, whereby those afflicted with this plague may be punished with so severe a penalty that others may be terrified by their punishment. Farewell.

## LETTER CXIV. TO J. [Note: [Col. 0342D] This is John of Salisbury, who, through the efforts of Louis the Younger, was elected bishop by the unanimous consent of the canons of Chartres. See what has been said of him at Letter 22.] BISHOP OF CHARTRES. [A.D. 1179.]

**SUBJECT.**—He congratulates John of Salisbury on his elevation to the episcopate, on his promotion of his namesake Peter of Blois, and on his elegant composition of the *Life* of St Thomas the Martyr.

To his dearest lord and father J., by God’s grace bishop of Chartres, P. of Blois, archdeacon of Bath, greetings, and whatever may be better than health.

Blessed be the Lord who has raised you as a title and glory of his praise, planting you like a fruitful olive tree in the house of the Lord, to give his people knowledge of salvation; to redeem, according to the prophet’s word [Note: [Col. 0341] Jer. 30.], those scattered among the nations, and to bring back children from afar.
