The clergy of Blois, proscribed by the dispensation of heavenly judgment, had wandered as fugitives over the earth until a bishop of their souls was given them, one who could sympathise with sufferers [Col. 0342B] and knew from long experience of exile how humane it is to pity exiles.

Called by the Lord as Aaron was, you did not immediately yield to flesh and blood; you did not begin the grace of episcopal generosity with your relatives; you did not build Zion in blood; but you consecrated the first-fruits of your benefactions in the person [Note: [Col. 0342D] The person spoken of here is the other Peter of Blois, to whom our Peter writes Letters 76 and 77, and whom an old manuscript of the venerable lord Hoyau, canon of Chartres, describes as chancellor of the Church of Chartres in these words: “Peter, chancellor of the Church of Chartres, wrote on the Psalms in the time of this bishop, John of Salisbury,” etc.] whom I perceive to be another myself, who bears me wholly in mind, appearance, name, surname, and stature. According to the measure of his merits, whether you look to his life, character, or learning, he deserves that the oil of fuller grace should be poured upon him. Your hands first distilled myrrh; I hope that hereafter they will overflow with the balm of more abundant grace [Note: [Col. 0341] Song 5.].

Remember, moreover, what that mouth consecrated to truth and the Gospel whispered more privately into my ears concerning the advancement of our own man [Col. 0342C]: “My secret is mine; my secret is mine” [Note: [Col. 0341] Isa. 24.]. You will give to your voice a voice of strength; nor will “yes and no” be found in you. Instead, in the fields of Gath and at the crossroads of Ascalon the glory of your name shall be proclaimed—where recently the shame of your exile was constantly before the eyes of public disgrace. Fare well.

You should know, however, that I would have ventured, by the command of my lord the archbishop, to write the triumph of blessed Thomas the Martyr, had not chance provided me with another work [Col. 0343A] in which the elegance of its style displayed the genius and tongue of Master John of Salisbury [Note: [Col. 0343C]

This indicates the book *On the Life of St Thomas the Martyr*, written by John of Salisbury and included in the *Quadrilogy*, or four-part history, composed by four of St Thomas’s intimates. [See *Patrology*, vol. 190, editor.]

I judge that this letter was written about the year 1180, shortly after John of Salisbury’s advancement; for he was elected bishop of Chartres in 1177.]

. Admiring, therefore, the grace poured out upon your lips, I stopped, lest I should disfigure with unlearned words of human wisdom and a degenerate style the praises dictated by an educated tongue, and should wrong the martyr by diminishing through the inadequacy of a crude intellect praises of so great a majesty. Farewell.

## LETTER CXV. TO H., ABBOT OF MESSENDER

**SUBJECT.**—He explains the proposed question concerning degrees of affinity and when they invalidate marriage.

To his dearest lord and friend H., by God’s grace [Col. 0343B] abbot of Messender, Peter of Blois, archdeacon of Bath, greetings in the author of salvation.

You are rightly concerned and press the question whether the marriage contracted between Robert and Adelitia can stand, since they are connected by a certain kind of affinity. As I faithfully recall it, you set out the course of that affinity in the following sequence and calculation. John, brother of Mary, Andrew’s wife, married Agnes. After John’s death Agnes married Elias; from them came Robert, who betrothed Andrew’s daughter Adelitia. If I rightly recall what the judgment of the canons determines on this question, John, brother of Mary, Andrew’s wife, and Andrew stood in the first kind of affinity. Agnes, however, wife of John, Mary’s brother, and Andrew contracted affinity of the second kind. For it is a rule of law that a person joined to a person by carnal union changes the kind, not the degree.

[Note: [Col. 0343C] Cujacius rightly observes on title 14, “On Consanguinity and Affinity”: “It should be noted that the canons themselves make a distinction between degrees of affinity and kinds of affinity, as I demonstrate thus. Marriages are now forbidden as far as the fourth degree of affinity and kinship, the fourth degree itself included, as I shall explain more fully in the penultimate chapter. Nor are marriages now forbidden except in the first kind of affinity; in the second and third kinds they are permitted, as stated in the penultimate chapter. Therefore there is a difference between degrees and kinds of affinity. In the first kind of affinity, a husband is related by affinity to his wife’s blood-relatives, and conversely a wife to her husband’s blood-relatives; these are properly called relatives by affinity, etc. In the second kind, however, a husband is related by affinity to his wife’s relatives by affinity from a previous marriage, and conversely a wife to her husband’s relatives by affinity from another marriage. Yet these are not properly relatives by affinity, but hold the place of such relatives. Thus, in Book V, *On the Rite of Marriage*, the wife’s daughter-in-law is in the place of a daughter-in-law to the husband, and the husband’s son-in-law is in the place of a son-in-law to the wife, etc. But now, by the aforesaid penultimate chapter, or by the Lateran Council held under Innocent III, marriages in the second kind of affinity are not forbidden, and the aforesaid Law 15 has been repealed [Col. 0344C]. Still less are they forbidden in the third kind of affinity, which consists, to explain this also, between myself and the second wife of one who was formerly the son-in-law of my wife.”

The same Cujacius, on that penultimate chapter: “In this chapter the kinds of affinity are separated from the degrees of affinity. In the first kind of affinity marriage is forbidden as far as the fourth degree; in the second and third kinds of affinity it is not. This Peter of Blois also explains and confirms in Letter 115. The daughter of my wife by another husband—that is, my stepdaughter—is related to me by affinity in the first degree. Her husband, who is my wife’s son-in-law, is related by affinity to my wife in the first kind, but to me only in the second kind. The second wife of that same son-in-law of my wife is related to me by affinity in the third kind, as I remember explaining above in the preface to this title. Thus my wife’s sister is related to me by affinity in the first kind; her husband, who is my wife’s brother-in-law, is related to me by affinity in the third kind; and the second wife of that same brother-in-law of my wife is related to me by affinity in the third kind. Likewise, the wife of my brother, who is called a sister-in-law, is related to me by affinity in the first kind; but his second wife in the third.” For he evidently held that the canons which forbid marriages between persons related by affinity in the second and third kinds were not to be interpreted as meaning that a marriage so contracted was void, but only that those contracting it sinned, although the marriage remained valid and binding.]

By virtue of this definition, the marriage contracted by John’s widow with Elias plainly produced a third kind of affinity. Robert, therefore, son of Elias, and Adelitia, daughter of Andrew, are joined in the second degree of the third kind of affinity. For among persons related by affinity we customarily calculate degrees not by the marriage bond, but by degrees of consanguinity, in accordance with the wording of that instructional rule: “A person joined to a person by propagation of flesh changes the degree, not the kind.”

But, to answer your inquiry briefly: if I found persons so married in so disparate and remote a kind of affinity, I would not dissolve their marriage bond. These rules are disciplinary, introduced by a certain exercise of scholastic discipline as a safeguard for stricter observance. Certainly the Lord, in the law of Moses,

[Note: [Col. 0343] Lev. 18.]

excepted only about twelve persons, among whom marriage with one’s own close flesh and the unlawful uncovering of nakedness are forbidden. But in the Old Testament narrative, or in the Gospel, beyond the exceptions of those twelve persons, I do not remember reading anything about the second or third kind of affinity. When John the Baptist said to Herod, “It is not lawful for you to have your brother’s wife,”

[Note: [Col. 0343] Matt. 14.]

understand: while his brother was living; he indicated the first kind of affinity. For by the public ordinance of the Law,

[Note: [Col. 0343] Josephus, *Antiquities*, Book XVIII, ch. 9.]

a brother was commanded to raise up offspring for his brother—not while he lived, but after his death—if he had died without children.

[Note: [Col. 0343] Deut. 25.]

We, however, understand and observe this article of the Law spiritually. For Christ, who is the firstborn among many brethren, who died for our salvation, and is the firstborn of the dead, who says to Mary, “Go to my brethren,”

[Note: [Col. 0345] John 20.]

we raise up the seed of faith by the word of preaching; and nonetheless we observe generally the oracle of the divine Law, concerning not taking the wife of one’s brother, whether that brother be living or dead. There are indeed canons from whose interpretation scholastic ingenuity has expounded the threefold kind of affinity and the distinction of differing degrees within them. Yet, in the judgment of my conscience, this new invention and teaching of the masters does not prejudice marriage, for which the divine Law, as we have noted, prescribes fixed limits.

Indeed, in the marriage of the first parents only two persons, because mankind was then few, namely father and mother, were excepted from the marriage law, where it is said: “Therefore [Col. 0345B] a man shall leave father and mother and shall cleave to his wife”:

[Note: [Col. 0345] Gen. 2.]

that is, neither a daughter shall cleave matrimonially to her father nor a son to his mother. In the course of time the Lawgiver excepted mother, stepmother, sister, granddaughter, paternal aunt, maternal aunt, uncle’s wife, daughter-in-law, brother’s wife—understand, of a living brother—the stepdaughter of a stepson, the daughter of a stepdaughter, and one’s wife’s sister.

[Note: [Col. 0345] Lev. 18.]

But since the voice of the turtledove was heard in our land, and blessedness was promised to those who made themselves eunuchs for the kingdom of God,

[Note: [Col. 0345] Matt. 19.]

public decency has beneficially introduced many regulations for the observance of continence, which I have enclosed in the brevity of verses:

> A vow, a condition, violence, spiritual  
> kinship, error, and difference of faith;  
> age, shameful crime, blood, union, time—  
> if you wish to conform to canonical strictness,  
> these laws forbid you by right to enter the marriage-bed.

Farewell.

## LETTER CXVI. TO H., ABBOT OF SAINT-DENIS.

[Note: [Col. 0345D] This letter has the single initial “H.” in all copies except Maz. 1, where it reads “Henry.” But wrongly: for the succession of the abbots of Saint-Denis shows that Hugh Fulcald was elected in 1185 and died in 1197. He was the man who, with his community, received Philip Augustus when he was returning from the expedition to Jerusalem and came to visit the bodies of the holy martyrs in prayer, in 1191, as Rigord testifies in *On the Deeds of Philip Augustus*.]

**Subject.—He sends Abbot H. a book composed by himself for examination, and at the same time consoles him in the affliction inflicted upon him by the king.**

To his dearest lord and friend H., by God’s grace abbot of Saint-Denis, Master Peter of Blois, archdeacon of Bath, greeting and the first-fruits of a new work.

I send you a new work, but an unfinished and wholly uncorrected one. May it please you, therefore, when you have read it, to return it, once read, to its author’s file, so that, if your dignity approves it, it may return to you more corrected [Col. 0346A] together with my other little works, among which a more elegant style, more pleasing matter, and sweeter and more abundant fruit may be found. I ask, moreover, that you share with me, if possible, the treatise which you wrote in Sicily concerning your condition—or rather your downfall—so that curtain may draw curtain, one cherub may look upon another, and, among old friends, the mutual sending of writings may pass back and forth in a welcome exchange.

I know your distresses; I know your crosses; I know the plundering of your goods; I have heard the thunder of the royal threat. I was even personally present when he stirred your own household against you to tumult. You have been placed in the Lord’s furnace; but your greatness of soul, which has often exercised itself in such severe circumstances, will be shown by perseverance to the end. For immense sums of money, he promises you peace and the kiss of a fox-like reconciliation—he who had stubbornly stopped his ears against the prayers of the supreme pontiff, the entreaty of the bishops and abbots of his province, the cry of sacred virgins, and the tears of monks. This mercenary confederacy is shameful, and this purchased favor is unwelcome to God and men. May he provide you a more honorable peace who takes away the spirit of princes and tramples the necks of the exalted by his own power. For many, open persecution has indeed been better than feigned peace. The king of Israel once made peace with Ben-hadad,

[Note: [Col. 0345] III Kings 15.]

but it turned to his scandal and the people’s ruin. Therefore let your eyes be always toward the Lord. Set [Col. 0346C] your heart upon your ways, so that the Lord may approve them and make peace. For it is written in Proverbs: “When a man’s ways please the Lord, he will turn even his enemies to peace”; and: “May the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, guard your heart and mind”—

[Note: [Col. 0345] Phil. 4.]

—and bring this contest to its completion for you in glory and triumph. Farewell.

## LETTER CXVII. TO G., ABBOT OF MARMOUTIER.

[Note: [Col. 0346D] This was Geoffrey, a Breton by nationality, of noble birth, educated in clerical learning, handsome in stature and countenance, according to the anonymous author in *Gallia Christiana*, vol. IV. He was elected in 1187 and held office until 1202, when he voluntarily resigned the administration.]

**Subject.—He rebukes Abbot G. for having drawn the prior of Saint-Cosmas into litigation over certain land and pastures.**

To his most beloved lord and friend G., by God’s grace abbot of Marmoutier, Master Peter of Blois, archdeacon of Bath, peace of mind unto salvation.

The prior of Saint-Cosmas mournfully complains and laments [Col. 0347A] that, on account of certain land and pastures which, as he asserts, belong to his church by a long prescriptive title, you are drawing him into litigation and presumptuously harassing him by every means in your power. Yet if you attentively considered the vow of the profession by which you are bound, you would pursue with more eager zeal the things above, not those upon the earth, according to the Apostle’s teaching: “The servant of God ought not to contend”;

[Note: [Col. 0347] II Tim. 2.]

when elsewhere he says: “It is already a fault in you that you have lawsuits; why do you not rather suffer wrong?”

[Note: [Col. 0347] I Cor. 6.]

He himself endures the plundering of his goods with joy, inviting you by word and deed to like equanimity. It did not become a man of so great an order to litigate over land, whose manner of life, as common opinion held, was already in heaven. Far, far be it that a spiritual man should so covet land as to incur loss of reputation or danger to his soul. But this is what that triple Geryon—that three-formed and monstrous man, earthly, carnal, animal—suggests to you; all his thoughts against you are for evil. Would that he might be so crucified in you that the body of sin may be destroyed and we may no longer be slaves to sin.

And you, earthborn ones and sons of men, why do you litigate over land, when it is near at hand that the Lord may destroy you from the earth, that the earth may swallow and consume you? Of you it is written: “You shall destroy their fruit from the earth, and their seed from among the sons of men.”

[Note: [Col. 0347] Ps. 20.]

Sons of men, how long will you be heavy of heart? Why do you love vanity and seek falsehood?

[Note: [Col. 0347] Ps. 4.]

For the possession of this world is false and passing, wherein there is nothing but the lust of the eyes, the lust of the flesh, and the pride of life. It is the Prophet’s word: “O earth, earth, earth, hear my words.”

[Note: [Col. 0347] Jer. 22.]

Man is earth, because he is taken from earth, lives upon earth, and returns to earth: he savors earth, licks earth, thirsts for earth. “His belly cleaves to the ground.”

[Note: [Col. 0347] Ps. 43.]

He descends to the lower regions of the earth, forgetful of heavenly things; he litigates for land, he fights for land, nor will he cease from such things until he who is of earth returns to earth. Then seven or eight feet of earth will suffice him for whom now the breadth of fields and the vastness of regions do not suffice. There, O man, the clod of your body—which is earth—will be returned from earth to that whence it was taken.

[Col. 0347D] This is your allotment of inheritance, you who now litigate for land, as though you possessed the land by inheritance, though soon you will be a little draught of earth, the possession of serpents and food for worms. Recently, in the court of the archbishop of Tours, I saw you litigating over this land and pasture; and I grieve that I saw you so forgetful of all religion and decency that you, who ought by face, gesture, and habit to have displayed monastic gravity, turned everything to abuse and made yourself a mockery to all. You flung your hands about, sprang [Col. 0348A] into the middle, rolled your eyes, distorted your lips, and, assailing the poor prior with a certain arrogant and insulting expression, thundered in a fevered spirit and with a sailor’s shout.

But he who dwells in heaven and looks upon lowly things himself delivered the poor man from the powerful and the needy man from those who despoiled him; for, owing to the hostility provoked by your disordered and utterly restless conduct, the prior was that day released from the prosecution of the suit, and, as regards the present point in that controversy, you carried away the adverse judgment. Yet a graver judgment and a more perilous day hangs over you: it will put an end to your lawsuits, which now, notorious in every court, you pursue to the injury and scandal of the monastic profession. Since, therefore, against a poor and needy man you have exercised such unbridling of your limbs and such an insult of a shameless tongue, the day of death, which hangs over your grey head, will exact due vengeance for these things. The flesh will stiffen, the legs grow rigid, hands and arms fall, the breast gasp, the neck fail, the lips foam, the eyes grow dark, the face turn pale as a potsherd. Thus in a little earth a pit shall be dug for the sinner,

[Note: [Col. 0347] Ps. 93.]

and his tomb shall be his house forever,

[Note: [Col. 0347] Ps. 48.]

until that dreadful day comes which shall repay every man according to the demands of his deserts. Therefore cease—or rather let all religious cease—from such deeds, by which the consciences of holy persons are wounded, good reputation blackened, the order scandalized, and souls slaughtered. For those who litigate for land or pastures are unworthy of the land of the living [Col. 0348C] or of being placed in a place of pasture. Farewell.

## LETTER CXVIII. TO G., ARCHDEACON OF YORK.

**Subject.—He rebukes an archdeacon who boasts of his innocence, although there was much in him deserving rebuke.**

To his dearest companion and friend G., archdeacon of York, Peter of Blois, archdeacon of Bath, greeting and restraint of the lips.

I recently heard you, among abbots, archdeacons, and other men of great respectability, boasting of the purity of your conscience; and I began to wonder whence such confidence in great innocence had come to you. Blessed Job fears all his works,

[Note: [Col. 0347] Job 9.]

and the prophet Isaiah compares all his acts of righteousness to a menstrual cloth.

[Note: [Col. 0347] Isa. 64.]

If you glory in your infirmities, you will not be foolish.

[Note: [Col. 0347] II Cor. 12.]

If you commend yourself, such commendation is not secure; for it is not he who commends himself who is approved, but he whom God commends. That perfect and consummate commendation must be judged to be when each shall have praise from God.

[Note: [Col. 0347] II Cor. 10.]

Would that you thought more humbly of yourself,

[Note: [Col. 0347] I Cor. 4.]

and believed that whatever good you possess, you do not possess of yourself! No man knows what is in a man except the spirit of the man that is in him,

[Note: [Col. 0347] I Cor. 2.]

yet even he has not fully known his own inward parts. For the human heart is perverse and unsearchable.

[Note: [Col. 0349] Jer. 17.]

Job, whom the Lord commended above others, saying that there was none like him on earth, a man simple, upright, and fearing God, could himself say: “My heart has not reproached me in all my life.”

[Note: [Col. 0349] Job 1.]

And Paul, whom Christ made a chosen vessel for himself,

[Note: [Col. 0349] Acts 9.]

though he said, “I am conscious of nothing against myself,”

[Note: [Col. 0349] I Cor. 4.]

did not therefore reckon himself justified. And who can trust that he has a clean heart, who was conceived of unclean seed and lives in a world full of the filth of sins? Let him who stands take heed lest he fall—or rather, lest he have already fallen. Peter, presumptuously confident of his firmness, fell more weakly at the very point where he trusted most firmly to stand.

[Note: [Col. 0349] Matt. 26.]

“If we say that sin is not in us,” John says, “we deceive ourselves and the truth is not in us.”

[Note: [Col. 0349] I John 1.]

This very thing [Col. 0349B] is a grave sin and a mark of an obstinate mind: that you understand yourself to be burdened by no sin. For a limb so numb that it cannot feel is far from health. You have become wholly insensible if you do not consider the fear of God, if expectation of the coming judgment does not exercise you in serious reflections.

Indeed, we scarcely pass one day in which we do not offend God or neighbor: by anger, detraction, murmuring, envy, giving scandal, coveting, idle talk, following the belly, serving the flesh, resisting the spirit, desiring the things of the world, despising the things of God, forgetting how monstrous are our deeds, how harsh the punishments we have deserved, how mercifully God waits for us in forbearance unto repentance, how terrible are his threats, how uncertain death is, and how intolerable and unending the punishment that hangs over us. Yet the Lord knows those who are his,

[Note: [Col. 0349] II Tim. 2.]

and the Apostle defines them in a fixed formula, saying: “Those who belong to Christ have crucified their flesh with its vices and lusts.”

[Note: [Col. 0349] Gal. 5.]

Consider what kind of cross you bear, keeping hard ways because of the words of his lips. I judge no one; but, as many assert, Mammon’s yoke is sweeter to you than Christ’s yoke. Some think themselves most righteous because they commit none of the more condemnable crimes; but their heart is vain, for “no living person shall be justified in his sight.”

[Note: [Col. 0349] Ps. 142.]

Take care that you do not dissolve Jesus. He dissolves Jesus who confesses him in words but denies him in deeds. John’s saying is: “Every spirit that dissolves [Col. 0349D] Jesus is not from God.”

[Note: [Col. 0349] I John 4.]

I see you prudent and anxious in worldly affairs, but sluggish and lax concerning the salvation of your soul. In your own estimation you are holy, innocent, undefiled; yet varied furnishings, more delicate food, finer clothing, abundant revenues, ambition for higher things, spacious buildings, numerous retainers, and a more lavish care for the desires of the flesh, contradict your opinion in many ways.

But “the fire will test each person’s work”;

[Note: [Col. 0349] I Cor. 3.]

when the Lord sits as a refiner’s fire and purifier of silver,

[Note: [Col. 0349] Mal. 3.]

when the Lord washes away the filth of the daughters of Zion and the blood of Jerusalem [Col. 0350A] from her midst in a spirit of judgment and a spirit of burning.

[Note: [Col. 0349] Isa. 4.]

“If you observe iniquities, O Lord, Lord, who shall stand?”

[Note: [Col. 0349] Ps. 129.]

Oh, how dangerous it is to fall into the hands of the living God!

[Note: [Col. 0349] Heb. 10.]

When his wrath has been kindled in a little while,

[Note: [Col. 0349] Ps. 2.]

blessed is he whose work shall not burn. Happy is he who has built gold and silver and precious stones. It is enough for me, an unprofitable servant, if, when the wood, hay, and stubble which I have piled up for myself for Gehenna have been burned, I escape from that fire half-scorched. It is already the eleventh hour for me, and the day is declining; yet the Lord still invites me to work. Delicate, weak, impatient, I have until now postponed perfect repentance. It is expedient for me that the fruit of repentance required from me compensate for the loss of time I have squandered.

Therefore I shall humble myself under the mighty [Col. 0350B] hand of God; I shall keep myself from my iniquity; I shall put my mouth in the dust, if perhaps there may be hope. Why should I fear in the evil day? Is it not better to fear in the good day? Behold, now is the acceptable time in which I can work and flee from the midst of Babylon, lest my flight occur at the dreadful crisis, in winter or on the Sabbath. You, who walk in things great and marvelous beyond yourself, are confident about the secret of divine predestination, certain that neither death nor sword nor anything else can separate you from Christ. You have fought the good fight and completed the course—you who have attained the kingdom of God through luxuries. But consider what answer you will make to him who will demand an account of every idle word,

[Note: [Col. 0349] Matt. 12.]

who will judge not only sins but also righteous deeds. I see [Col. 0350C] that you are blind and do not see yourself; you are lame and do not walk in the straight way.

[Note: [Col. 0349] Ps. 9.]

I beg you, fear that old proverb: “The blind and the lame shall not enter the temple.”

[Note: [Col. 0349] II Kings 5.]

## LETTER CXIX. TO R., A CANON.

**Subject.—He reproves Canon R. because he insulted those to whom he had been sent; he interprets their alleged detractions favorably, showing by many examples that this is the proper course.**

Master Peter of Blois, archdeacon of Bath, to R., canon, greeting and due regard for circumstances in speech.

Because I had a high opinion of your eloquence and discretion, I entrusted you with carrying out my business before the prince. I had for the most part brought these matters to completion, [Col. 0350D] but you grievously impeded them. When my hopes were already sailing into harbor, by your rashness you threw me back into the deep. You exceeded the limits of your commission, because, stirred by one man’s slight word and carried away by the heat of anger, you loosened the bridle of moderation into insulting language. You offended all who were present; and, as a man of brazen brow and prodigal of shame, you spared neither your own order, nor showed regard for the bishops sitting there, nor even for the prince himself.

Even if one of them had uttered, as you assert, some bitter word against you, or even against me, you still ought not to have become so inflamed as to turn the violence of your mind into their public insult. In the second book of Valerius Maximus we read

[Note: [Col. 0351] Val. 2, ch. 2; Livy, Book XII; Florus, Book I, ch. 2.]

that ambassadors of the Roman republic, sent by the senate to Tarentum, received grievous injuries, so that one of them was splashed with urine; yet, continuing their embassy, they made no complaint about the injuries done them, lest they speak beyond what had been entrusted to them.

Now those whom you say publicly disparaged me, and for whose sake you were therefore angered against them, are my friends. I have no suspicion that they said this with the purpose of disparagement; for by repeated proof of experience I have found that they love me affectionately. Nor ought I, nor can I, think that their words or deeds should turn to my disadvantage. [Col. 0351B] Love, therefore, which has often been proved by reciprocal exchange, admits no mark of suspicion. Someone alleged to Plato, as Valerius Maximus writes,

[Note: [Col. 0351] Book IV, ch. 2.]

that Xenocrates, his pupil, had disparaged him in many ways; and when he offered to confirm this very thing by oath, Plato replied: “It is not credible that he does not love me faithfully, whom I love so effectually.” When the accuser persisted, Plato added: “Even if he said this, he knew that this very thing was beneficial to me.”

[Note: [Col. 0351] Id., Book III, ch. 8.]

When Alexander was ill, Philip, his physician and friend, prepared a medicine with his own hands and, by the common judgment of the physicians, offered it to him. A letter from Parmenio arrived, urging the king to beware of Philip’s plot, since Darius had bribed him with money. Having read it, Alexander drank without hesitation; then he handed the letter to Philip to read. He entrusted himself confidently to his friend, and the strength of love banished fear of death in the very messenger of death.

But suppose they had spoken of me with a malicious purpose. I answer you that Suetonius reports

[Note: [Col. 0351] Suetonius, *Augustus*, ch. 4.]

that Caesar Augustus replied in a letter to his grandson Tiberius, who complained that many persons spoke ill of him. He wrote thus: “My Tiberius, it is no great matter if men speak ill of us, provided that they do not do us harm.” Would that you had set a guard upon your mouth and that unconsidered talk had not put my business at risk! It is written: “A man of tongue shall not be established on earth.”

[Note: [Col. 0351] Ps. 139.]

Therefore Blessed Serapion used to say: “There is no member in my body which I fear as I fear the tongue.” Over a slight and trivial word you rushed into blasphemous insults, sparing neither your reputation nor your soul, showing no respect for the assembly of bishops or magnates, nor even for royal majesty.

[Note: [Col. 0351] Plato, *On Alexander*; Q. Curtius, Book VIII; Justin, 15; Valerius, Book V, ch. 2.]

Thus formerly Callisthenes, Aristotle’s pupil, sent to Alexander, because he did not observe the limits of obedience prescribed to him, lost both the fruit of his assigned embassy and himself. Deeply offended by your embassy, I close this letter, recalling that the word of Blessed James is true: “If anyone thinks himself religious, while not restraining his tongue from evil but deceiving his own heart, that man’s religion is vain.”

[Note: [Col. 0351] Jas. 1.]

You therefore, who profess the habit of religion, conduct yourself more religiously: speak more sparingly, and behave more modestly. But I, who rebuke you, ought rather to be rebuked. The cup I now drink I mixed for myself, because I would not listen to Solomon, who says: “He is lame in his feet who sends words by an imprudent messenger.”

[Note: [Col. 0351] Prov. 26.]

## LETTER CXX. TO R., DEAN OF TOURS.

**Subject.—He asks the dean to correct his nephew, who buys up many ecclesiastical benefices simoniacally and is bound by very great debts.**

To his dearest lord and friend R., dean of Tours, Master Peter of Blois, archdeacon of Bath, greeting in the author of salvation.

[Col. 0352B] I would gladly address your nephew P. in the office of living speech, were it not that distance denied me both his presence and yours. It is not expedient for me to send him a letter, since he is almost illiterate: he would either not read the letter or, not understanding it, neglect it. For, as the wise man testifies, “To read and not understand is to neglect.”

[Note: [Col. 0351] Cato.]

I beg you earnestly to restrain his rashness, which is all too public and notorious, and which no little blackens the glory of your reputation, lest he sin openly before common knowledge. Either let him cease from the traffic of simony, or cut him off from your society as a rotten member from the body. In the streets of Gath and at the crossroads of Ashkelon it is publicly [Col. 0352C] proclaimed how, by manifold purchase, he hunts after dignities in different churches, and how obstinate he is in his ambition, fearing neither Simon’s destruction nor Gehazi’s leprosy.

[Note: [Col. 0351] IV Kings 5.]

Very recently he became the object of popular hissing and universal mockery, because in the morning he bought an archdeaconry and lost it again in the evening. For the seller discovered that he was bound by enormous debts and consequently insolvent. One may jest about his archdeaconry as Cicero, in the *Tusculan Disputations*, is said to have mocked Vatinius, consul for a single day:

[Note: [Col. 0351] Macrobius, *Saturnalia*, Book II, ch. 2; Cicero, Book VIII, letter to Curio.]

“A great portent occurred in the year of Vatinius: under that consul there was neither winter, nor spring, nor summer, nor autumn.” When Vatinius afterwards asked why Cicero had not come to him, he answered: “I wished to come during your consulship, but [Col. 0352D] night overtook me.”

Your nephew has obtained diverse *personae*—ecclesiastical benefices or offices—in diverse churches by disgraceful traffic. He did not enter through the door, and will one day hear that dreadful word: “How did you come in here not having a wedding garment?”

[Note: [Col. 0351] Matt. 22.]

You know that the wedding garment is charity, humility, and integrity. But he is advanced not by integrity but by greed; not by moral character but by purchase; not by learning but by money; not by election but by ambition; not by merit but by price; not by virtue or holiness but by contract. It is the prophet’s word:

[Note: [Col. 0351] Mic. 3; Hab. 2.]

“Woe to those [Col. 0353A] who build Zion with blood! Woe to those who gather what is not their own—how long do they heap up against themselves thick mud!” Though he is one *persona*, or rather a many-headed beast, he nevertheless surpasses Hydra and Briareus and the other monstrous prodigies with many faces in the number—or rather the multiplicity—of his ecclesiastical offices. It is indeed detestable presumption that he does not consider his own inadequacy and does not weigh his strength against the burdens of the dignities he usurps.

When the Lord sent Moses into Egypt for the liberation of the people, Moses said: “Who am I, that I should go to Pharaoh and deliver the people from Egypt?”

[Note: [Col. 0353] Exod. 3.]

Although the Lord had chosen him as worthy, he nevertheless humbly judged himself unworthy of so great an embassy. With what face, I ask, does he presume to preside who does not know how to benefit others? According to Jerome’s testimony,

[Note: [Col. 0353] On Ezekiel, ch. XXXIV.]

it is not the degenerate bull, but the one surpassing the rest in strength, that leads the herd.

[Note: [Col. 0353] Seneca, Letter 90.]

Likewise, among a herd of elephants, the one taller than all the rest goes before and leads. Does not a man seem mad to you if, wholly ignorant of navigation, he despised the most skilled sailors amid the peril of a storm, yet rashly usurped the mastership of the ship, to his own destruction and that of others?

It is written in Matthew:

[Note: [Col. 0353] Ch. 24.]

“When you see the abomination of desolation sitting in the temple, then woe to the pregnant and nursing women!” As though he said: When you see in the Church an ambitious and foolish man set above better men, woe to those who, through the skill of a prudent prelate, had conceived from the spirit of the fear [Col. 0353C] of the Lord; and when they had begun to produce the fruit of life, their fruitfulness is turned into miscarriage by the wickedness of his successor. Therefore Ecclesiastes complains and says:

[Note: [Col. 0353] Ch. 10.]

“I saw an evil under the sun: a fool set in high dignity, and wise men sitting below.” O detestable commerce: to lose one’s soul for transient honor, and to pay out so much money for a revenue that its returns could not produce within five years the amount paid. I say nothing of the ruin or salvation of his soul; for the soul is his last concern. The wretched man does not consider what God, terrible in counsels over the sons of men,

[Note: [Col. 0353] Ps. 65.]

is devising concerning him. Who knows whether sudden death may seize him today or tomorrow, and there be none to deliver him? Has ambition so maddened him that by right and wrong alike [Col. 0353D] he acquires ecclesiastical offices, sets not [Col. 0354A] God before his eyes, fears not God’s judgments, and does not even heed that thunderbolt of divine indignation: “Fool, this night they shall demand your soul from you; and the things you have prepared, whose shall they be?”

[Note: [Col. 0353] Luke 12.]

Unhappy man: for the wind of empty glory he slays his own soul and, in addition, never ceases to bind himself with infinite and unpayable debts. Certainly, in the public estimation of everyone, all the revenues of the archbishopric of Tours would scarcely suffice to free him from debt. I marvel—and cannot marvel enough—whether sleep can steal upon him even for half an hour beneath so great a burden of debts, amid so many torments of usury by which Jews torment him, amid the many and urgent vexations of creditors.

Cicero relates in the *Tusculan Disputations*

[Note: [Col. 0353] Macrobius, *Saturnalia*, Book II, ch. 4.]

that Augustus Caesar, on hearing that a certain Roman knight had died who had concealed in his lifetime two hundred thousand sesterces of debt, requested the two-cubit mattress found among the dead man’s possessions. When people asked why he did so, he said: “This mattress ought to be used for sleeping, since a man whom so great a mass of debt ought continually to have made anxious was able to sleep upon it.” But I believe your nephew consoles and lightens the distresses of his debts with that epigram of Martial:

[Note: [Col. 0353] Book II, epigram 3, ch. 5.]

> Sextus, you owe nothing; I admit, Sextus, you owe nothing.  
> For whatever Sextus can pay, Sextus owes.

His debts are surely like those apples in Sodom which, as Blessed Augustine relates in Book XXI of *The City of God*, are at times beautiful and ripe, but when tested by a bite suddenly vanish into smoke and ashes [Col. 0354C]. Indeed, the creditors’ action against him is vain and empty, for the debtor’s poverty nullifies it.

## LETTER CXXI. TO J.

[Note: [Col. 0353D]

This was John of Coutances, nephew of Walter, Archbishop of Rouen. According to Roger of Hoveden, he was first Archdeacon of Oxford, then Dean of Rouen, and was finally elected Bishop of Worcester in 1196.

Concerning his election, King Richard of England writes thus to Hubert, Archbishop of Canterbury, in Ralph of Diceto’s *Images of History*, under the year 1196: “Know that our beloved Dean of Rouen, a gracious, modest, prudent man, walking according to God, was solemnly and canonically elected Bishop of Worcester, in our presence [Col. 0354D] and that of your clerics, by those whose business it was. We have therefore thought fit to request that you hold that election valid and acceptable, and be pleased to confirm it,” etc. John died in the year of Christ 1198. Moreover, he is the man for whose sake our Peter wrote the treatise *On the Institution of a Bishop*, or *Episcopal Rule*, as is apparent from its title and entire course: there he sets Walter before John himself as the model of a perfect bishop to be imitated.]

### TO THE DEAN OF ROUEN.

**SUBJECT.**—He urges the Dean of Rouen not to allow churches, on the pretext of the Jerusalem expedition, to be crushed by exactions; and not to permit the departure, as on other occasions, to be postponed longer.

To his dearest lord and friend J., Dean of Rouen, M. PETER of Blois, Archdeacon, greetings and the affection of sincere love.

Since the most exact diligence is required in a compact of good faith, I ask you, by that social bond and friendship which we formed long ago, that in the business of our Lord, concerning which I wrote to you on another occasion, [Col. 0354D] your vigilance may keep such watch that your prudence in this matter may provide not only for the body’s welfare but also for the salvation of the soul [Col. 0355A]. The Lord has magnified you in the king’s sight, and, after your uncle, has set you above the rest in his duchy.

[Note: [Col. 0355C] For he was vicar-general of the archbishopric of Rouen during the absence of Archbishop Walter, who had set out in the company of King Richard of England [Col. 0355D] upon the Jerusalem pilgrimage.]

Therefore perform the office of the most valiant judge of Israel, the ambidextrous Ehud [Aioth] [Note: [Col. 0355] Judges 3], who was equally ready with right hand and left. And so guide him through temporal matters that he may not lose eternal things. Solomon’s saying is: “Give portions to seven, and also to eight.”

[Note: [Col. 0355D] Among the Septuagint it is read thus: “δὸς μερίδα τοῖς ἑπτά, καὶ γε τοῖς ὀκτώ” (*dos merida tois hepta, kai ge tois oktō*), that is, “Give a portion to the seven, and indeed to the eight.” Interpreters understand this reading in two ways: either in reference to time or to persons. In reference to time, it signifies that one must always give; as though he said: “Kindness should be shown for seven days; when these have passed and the eighth approaches, it must begin again, and no end should be set to giving.” So Clarius. In reference to persons, it means that all, or very many, should receive; this being signified by seven and eight, namely a definite number used for an indefinite one. The sense, says Pagninus, is: “Bestow liberally upon all who are in need.” The expression was taken from the banquets of the ancients, at which [Col. 0356C] portions were given to each guest and were sent to the poor. This letter was written about the year 1191, when Walter, John’s uncle, had gone [Col. 0356D] with King Richard of England on the Jerusalem expedition.]

For not only must those things be done which are expedient for the present life of this sevenfold period, but also those which look toward the eighth. Press him, therefore, and urge him more insistently to subject himself in every respect, in fear and humility, to the divine will; for “in his will is life” [Note: [Col. 0355] Psalm 24]. Let it be your concern [Col. 0355B] that he may not follow his heart’s inclination, nor pursue the desires of the world; lest, receiving his soul in vain, he take his will for reason and, abandoning the counsel of venerable maturity, acquiesce in men less prudent. Certainly, the kingdom of Rehoboam, Solomon’s son, was divided because, rejecting the elders, he preferred the counsel of the young [Note: [Col. 0355] 3 Kings 12].

Above all, stand courageously for the house of the Lord, lest through your neglect the condition of ecclesiastical dignity be humbled. The Church has indeed been free from ancient days, and her children are free with that freedom by which Christ set us free, saying in the Gospel [Note: [Col. 0355] Matthew 17] that “the children are free.” But if she is oppressed by the exactions and oppressions of the powerful, she is compelled into servitude: she has now become Hagar, who is in bondage with her children [Col. 0355C]. But what does Scripture say? “Cast out the bondwoman and her son” [Note: [Col. 0355] Galatians 4]. If your princes, under the pretext of a new pilgrimage, wish to register the world and brand the Church of Christ with the mark of servitude by tributary duties, let whoever is a son of the Church rise up in opposition; let him choose rather to die than to serve.

Seneca reproaches Catiline and Lucius Sulla because their peace was worse than war [Note: [Col. 0355] Book V, *On Benefits*, ch. 16], and because they afflicted the people subject to them more by tyrannical exactions than enemies did by battles. Therefore, in imposing levies and leading an army, let your prince not follow [Col. 0356A] his own judgment; rather, let the careful deliberation of wise men always go before his mind and order all his acts in advance. Panaetius, in the *Tusculan Disputations*, asserts that neither a commander in war nor a ruler at home can beneficially conduct great affairs if he follows the impulse of his own heart, if, before an event arises, he does not sketch out all his business for the sake of more mature counsel.

I ask and advise one thing: that God’s work not be prolonged by frustrating delays, as it was on another occasion. It is written: “Cursed is he who does the work of God negligently” [Note: [Col. 0355] Jeremiah 48]. Caesar [Note: [Col. 0355] Suetonius, *Life*, ch. 37], on hearing of the rebellion of the Pontic region, immediately directed armed ranks there; and his victory was achieved with such speed that in his triumphal procession he uttered these three words: “I came, I saw, I conquered” [Note: [Col. 0355] Plutarch, *Life*; Polyaenus, Book VIII].

Semiramis, queen of the Assyrians, was occupied with arranging her hair [Col. 0356B] when she was informed that Babylon had revolted. With one part of her hair still unbound, she ran to war; nor did she arrange the neglected part of her head before she had reduced the city and its citizens to her power [Note: [Col. 0355] In the year 1188; see the *Treatise on the Journey to Jerusalem*]. We could produce examples of many persons, but let that two-year enterprise of the latest pilgrimage suffice as an example—a venture that turned into a cause of groaning for all Christendom. So too, they began their journey with exactions and made their travelling funds from the plunder of the poor and the spoils of churches. Therefore that journey was a stumbling-block to them.

Solomon’s saying is: “To begin a good way is to do what is just” [Note: [Col. 0355] Proverbs 7]. But divine judgment distinguishes between the ways of the righteous and of the wicked: “For [Col. 0356C] the Lord knows the way of the righteous, and the way of the wicked shall perish” [Note: [Col. 0355] Psalm 1]. Farewell.

## LETTER CXXII. TO WILLIAM, ARCHBISHOP OF RHEIMS

[Note: [Col. 0356D] We have already spoken elsewhere about him, especially in the note to Letter 15.]

**SUBJECT.**—Hubert, Archbishop of Canterbury, praises the Archbishop of Rheims for the charity he showed to St Thomas the Martyr during his exile; he asks him not readily to believe those who disparage Hubert’s reputation and to preserve his former affection toward him.

To the venerable father and lord WILLIAM, by God’s grace Archbishop of Rheims and legate of the Apostolic See, HUBERT, by divine mercy Archbishop of Canterbury [Note: [Col. 0356D] He was first Dean of York and then Bishop of Salisbury in 1189. Subsequently, after Baldwin died on the Jerusalem expedition and Reginald, Bishop of Bath, had been elected Archbishop of Canterbury—who himself also died shortly afterward—Hubert was elected by the monks of Canterbury in 1193, at the request of King Richard, who was then still held in the emperor’s captivity. Dear to kings and honored by all, he lived praiseworthily in the pontificate for more than eleven years. He died in 1205.], [Col. 0357A] Primate of all England and legate of the Apostolic See, greetings in the Author of salvation.

To the King of glory and Giver of grace we render thanksgivings, because, according to Job’s saying [Note: [Col. 0357] ch. 25], he who “makes peace in his high places” has also restored our princes on earth to peace through your labor and your intervening diligence [Note: [Col. 0357D] Nearly all writers testify that William, Archbishop of Rheims, acted as mediator of peace between Philip Augustus and Richard of England.]. Therefore you enjoy among men the favor of public esteem, and in the land of the saints you confidently await “the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding” [Note: [Col. 0357] Philippians 4].

From that day on which you received me into the bosom of your affection and favor, sincere devotion toward you has continually taken root in my heart. We have regarded it as foremost among our desires that, should an opportunity be offered, we might demonstrate by our deeds what we hold in our wishes. Yet we are more strongly bound to every duty of affection and service toward your eminence because divine providence entrusted to us—though we are insufficient—the office of our friend, Blessed Thomas the Martyr [Col. 0357B]. It has not fallen from the common memory with how many and how devout offices of humanity your inborn generosity relieved his exile [Note: [Col. 0357D] On the benefits bestowed by William of Rheims upon St Thomas during his exile, those who wrote the Life of St Thomas should especially be read.]; and all the Church of the saints still recounts your alms. He had intended to repay you in accordance with your merit, but untimely death cut short both his life and his purpose.

We profess ourselves, as his successors, to be forever debtors for the favor shown to the martyr; and would that we might be heirs of the affection which you had for him! Yet we have heard that that brother of yours, concerning whom you once wrote to me, has suggested certain unfavorable things about us to your eminence, to the disparagement of our reputation [Col. 0357C]. Nevertheless, one must not believe every spirit, but test the spirits whether they are from God [Note: [Col. 0357] John 4].

A principle of natural law also enters into the compact of friendship: no mark of suspicion should arise against a friend on the accusations of informers until the evidence of the deed proves him guilty. You well know that, from ancient times, his predecessors have acted contentiously against our Church with an almost hereditary hatred. This man likewise, from the beginning of his advancement, has exerted all his efforts in affronting us. But if he detracts from us, if he judges us before men, then, to use the Apostle’s words, it is a very small thing [Col. 0358A] that we should be judged by that man [Note: [Col. 0357] 1 Corinthians 4].

We know the impulse of his mind, and in time you too will know him by his fruits. God, the Searcher of hearts, knows that we compassionately share, with fraternal charity, the afflictions which he presently endures. He would have found with us ready consolation in his distress, if he allowed himself to be guided, if he permitted counsel to be given him, if he prescribed moderation to his actions, and, finally, if affliction had given him any understanding.

We shall close the letter; and, to reduce its length to brevity, in the bowels of Christ, in memory of the martyr, and in that charity with which you have mutually loved us, we devoutly and humbly commend ourselves and our Church to your favor.

## LETTER CXXIII. TO R., BISHOP OF LONDON

[Note: [Col. 0357D] This letter is addressed to R. in all copies, both manuscripts and printed editions. It denotes Richard of Ely, natural son of Nigel, Bishop of Ely. While he was a canon of London, Dean of the Church of Lincoln, and Archdeacon of Ely, he was elected Bishop of London [Col. 0358D] shortly after the death of Henry II, King of England, whose treasurer he had been. A dispensation concerning the defect of his birth had previously been obtained from Alexander III; its charter is extant in Ralph of Diceto’s *Images of History*, under the year 1189. “He spent much money,” says Godwin, “on the construction of his church and of the buildings belonging to his see.” He died in 1198. Ralph writes thus concerning his death under that year: “Richard, Bishop of London, of blessed memory, the third, after sitting eight years, eight months, and ten days, closed his final day.”]

[Col. 0358B]

**SUBJECT.**—He declares that he does not wish to advance from the diaconate to the rank of priestly eminence, not out of contempt but reverence. He then shows that no one ought to be compelled to the priesthood.

To the reverend father and lord, by God’s grace Bishop of London, his own PETER of Blois, Archdeacon of Bath, greetings in him without whom there is no salvation.

I know that what you wish and ask—namely, that I be induced, or, if need be, drawn and compelled, to advance to the further rank of the divine mystery—proceeds from deepest affection and unfeigned charity. First of all, I desire Your Holiness to know beyond doubt that the rank of the priestly eminence terrifies me beyond measure; and that reverence, not contempt, causes me to defer or decline it. Great and surpassing is the heavenly dignity of the sacrament [Col. 0358C]; and who can attain to it?

I know that this sacrifice uniquely saves souls from eternal destruction, since it represents the saving mystery of the death of God’s Only-Begotten Son. Certainly Christ, who rose from the dead, dies no more: death shall have no further dominion over him [Note: [Col. 0357] Rom. 6.]; and yet, though he lives in himself immortally and incorruptibly, he is daily sacrificed for us in the mystery of the altar. I know also, and openly profess, that at the time of the offering, at the very hour of incense, the heavens are opened at the priest’s voice; angels stand by in attendance; visible and invisible things become one and the same; and, through the working of the Holy Spirit, earthly things are joined to heavenly [Note: [Col. 0357] Gregory, *Dialogues*, IV.58.].

Therefore this sacrament is great beyond all estimation, beyond all understanding, [Col. 0359A] beyond every eminence: in it are the salvation of the world, the price of the age, a price without price, a priceless price. Speaking of it, the Apostle says: “Great is this mystery of godliness: manifested in the flesh, justified in the spirit, appeared to angels, preached among the nations, believed in by the world, taken up in glory” [Note: [Col. 0359] I Tim. 3.]. The prophet’s word is: “Be cleansed, you who bear the vessels of the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0359] Isa. 52.]; how much cleaner ought those to be who bear Christ in their hands and in their bodies? To them the Apostle says: “You were bought at a great price: glorify and bear Christ in your body” [Note: [Col. 0359] I Cor. 6.].

A priest must have the same mind that was in Christ Jesus: not only that he may empty himself through humility, but that, representing the Lord’s crucifixion, he may bear his wounds in his own body [Col. 0359B] and crucify himself to the Lord upon the altar of his heart. Solomon’s saying is: “Have you sat at a rich man’s table? Know that you must prepare the same things” [Note: [Col. 0359] Eccli. 31.]. For in Leviticus the priest retains the skin of the victim [Note: [Col. 0359] Lev. 7.], because the priestly order requires that, while he sacrifices the saving victim at the altar-table, he should conform himself to the victim by a certain cross of contrition.

Formerly the paschal lamb was not eaten except with wild and bitter lettuces; the loins too were girded: in this are signified both the bitterness of penitence and the purity of continence. The lamb’s blood was also put upon both doorposts, so that the priest may look upon the sacrament of the Lord’s Passion not only with his mouth for redemption, but with his heart for imitation. For only then will the sacrifice benefit him, if, making himself a sacrifice, [Col. 0359C] he is willing humbly and effectually to imitate what he performs. The Apostle’s word is: “Let a person test himself, and so eat of that bread and drink of that cup” [Note: [Col. 0359] I Cor. 11.]. O how blessed is the person found approved! “Test me, O Lord, and try me; burn my inward parts and my heart” [Note: [Col. 0359] Ps. 25.], that I may be found worthy of so great a sacrament.

For terrible is what follows: “Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself” [Note: [Col. 0359] I Cor. 11.]. Lord Jesus Christ, you left the sacrament of your body and blood as a pledge and surety of heavenly grace, and in it you established for us not death but life, not judgment but salvation. How ruined, then, is one who turns redemption into destruction, sacrifice [Col. 0359D] into sacrilege, mystery into parricide, and life into death.

In the law of Moses the Lord forbids a stranger, a sojourner, or an unclean person to eat of the paschal lamb. With what great and damnable rashness, then, does an unworthy priest presume to minister—he who, to use the Apostle’s phrase, tramples underfoot the Son of God, regards as unclean the blood of the covenant [Col. 0360A] by which we were sanctified, and insults the Spirit of grace [Note: [Col. 0359] Exod. 12.]. To priests it is said through the prophet: “You shall be called the holy ones of the Lord; you shall be called ministers of the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0359] Heb. 10.]. And he adds: “All who see them shall know them, because they are the seed whom the Lord has blessed” [Note: [Col. 0359] Isa. 61.].

But today I see—and say it weeping—that innumerable unlettered men, or rather ignoramuses, nevertheless living carnally, usurp the rank of so great an office. Thus the dignity of the sacrament is cheapened by an unworthy multitude, and there comes to pass what the prophet Hosea laments and says: “The people multiplied altars for sinning; altars were made for them unto transgression” [Note: [Col. 0359] Hos. 8.]. For this reason the Carthusian order celebrates Mass rarely.

[Note: [Col. 0359D] According to the ancient statutes of Guigo, chapter 14, paragraph 5: “For Mass is rarely sung here. For our chief study and purpose is to devote ourselves to the silence and attentiveness of the cell, according to that saying of Jeremiah: ‘He shall sit alone and keep silence’ (Lam. III).” See what I have said on this matter in connection with Epistle 86.]

For, just as contempt is wont to arise from frequency, devotion is kindled by rarity itself [Col. 0360B]. Certainly those who serve the tabernacle of the flesh have no authority to eat from the heavenly altar [Note: [Col. 0359] Heb. 13.]. For to those consumed by carnal desires the Lord’s cup is turned into dragons’ gall; the bread of angels is taken away, heavenly manna rots for them, and the Lord rains flesh upon them like dust [Note: [Col. 0359] Ps. 77.].

It should be noted that under the same sun flesh hardens and manna melts, because, according to the differing demands of their merits, God permits some to be hardened in their wickedness, while he dissolves others into saving tears by devout affection. And while the former, with a sickly and fastidious stomach, receives the sacrament as though it were bran and husk, the latter’s soul grows fat from heavenly richness, from the kernel of divine wheat. The former’s spirit is like Mount Gilboa, upon which [Col. 0360C] neither dew nor rain falls; but for the latter God has set apart voluntary rain, as for his inheritance [Note: [Col. 0359] II Sam. 1.].

Through the disordered and undisciplined multitude of priests, the venerable sacrament of our redemption is now exposed to mockery. For those who ought to have been vicars of the Apostles and sons of Peter have become companions of Judas and forerunners of Antichrist. Gregory’s saying is: “He who consecrates Christ’s body unworthily betrays Christ, so that, when Christ is betrayed, he may say: ‘Behold, the hand of the one betraying me is with me at the table’” [Note: [Col. 0359] Luke 22.].

Augustine, on the verse, “They gave me gall for food” [Note: [Col. 0359] Ps. 68.], says: “They sin more gravely who offer Christ, reigning in heaven, unworthily than those who crucified him while he walked on earth.” And again: [Col. 0360D] “Those sin more who betray Christ with sinful members than Judas, who betrayed him to the Jews who crucified him.” He applies to wicked priests that lamentable saying of Christ: “They gave me gall for food, and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink” [Note: [Col. 0359] Ibid.].

Indeed, the Lord hungers and thirsts for our salvation; and therefore the person who approaches his body with the gall of an evil conscience and the vinegar of iniquity sins damnably. Blessed Jerome’s saying is:

> “The faithless Jew, the faithless Christian: the former sheds Christ’s blood from his side, the latter from the chalice. Joseph bore Christ’s body with pious hands; but this man does so with polluted hands, hands which shortly before touched a prostitute’s shameful parts. He touches the salvation of humankind and receives it with the mouth with which he shortly before pressed kisses upon a harlot. He who had been a member of Christ takes away Christ’s member, says the Apostle, and makes it a member of a harlot. For whoever is joined to a harlot becomes one body and one member with her [Note: [Col. 0361] I Cor. 6.]. Christ’s body is placed abominably and detestably in this member.
>
> “That most precious body was laid in a clean shroud and in a new tomb [Note: [Col. 0361] Matt. 27.]; [Col. 0361B] but this man plunges him, whom angels desire to behold and from beholding whom they receive eternal delights, into a mouth still foul-smelling from yesterday’s drink and into the bilge of a belly still hot with the previous debauch. Should he not rather be judged Antichristian than Christian, who, so far as lies in him, treats Christ—now made incapable of suffering—so unworthily, heaps such insults upon him, so cruelly kills him, and buries him dishonourably?
>
> “But because they do not experience the judgment of heavenly punishment, as Dathan and Abiram [Note: [Col. 0361] Ps. 105.] did in the very act of usurping sacrifice, they think they have escaped divine judgment, saying with Manoah’s wife: ‘If the Lord had wished to kill us, he would not have received the sacrifice from our hand’ [Note: [Col. 0361] Judg. 13.]. Certainly Mary, whom Christ’s love had ardently inflamed, [Col. 0361C] is forbidden to touch the Lord [Note: [Col. 0361] John 20.]. John the Baptist also—than whom, by Christ’s testimony, no greater has arisen among those born of women—fears to lay his hand upon the head of the Saviour, at which angelic powers tremble [Note: [Col. 0361] Matt. 3.]; yet a son of eternal lamentation, with sacrilegious hand and polluted mouth, receives the sacrament in which is eternal life, and presumes damnably to incorporate it into himself—or rather to imprison it within himself.”

Every iniquity first had to be purged by penitence and long practice before one might come to the horn of the altar—that is, to the grace of so great a sacrament. The Prophet says: “I will wash my hands,” [Col. 0362A] that is, my works, “and so will compass your altar, O Lord” [Note: [Col. 0361] Ps. 25.]. And again: “Send forth your light and your truth; they have led me and brought me to your holy mountain and to your tabernacles; and so I will enter your altar, O Lord” [Note: [Col. 0361] Ps. 42.].

All inward affections, indeed, must be washed. For in Leviticus, before the victim is offered, all its entrails are carefully washed [Note: [Col. 0361] Lev. 1.]. The Lord appeared to Moses [Note: [Col. 0361] Exod. 3] and also to Joshua [Note: [Col. 0361] Josh. 5], commanding each to remove the sandals from his feet; for sandals are made from the skins of dead animals. But terrible is the place in which the Only-Begotten Son is sacrificed to God the Father. Therefore whoever approaches the ministry of so great a sanctification must first put off every uncleanness of dead works.

It is a difficult [Col. 0362B] and arduous thing to minister in the priesthood, to govern souls, and, in Solomon’s phrase, to cast oneself into the crowd of the people and bind double sins to oneself [Note: [Col. 0361] Eccli. 7.]. For the Lord’s word is: “If my anointed priest sins, he shall cause my people to sin” [Note: [Col. 0361] Lev. 4.]. On this passage Blessed Gregory says: “Priests ought to know that, if they commit perverse acts, they deserve as many deaths as the subjects whom they lead onward by examples of their own destruction” [Note: [Col. 0361] *Pastoral Rule*, 5.].

And who knows his own works? Who knows whether he is worthy of love or hatred [Note: [Col. 0361] Eccl. 9]? Who understands his offences? The human heart is perverse and resistant to healing [Note: [Col. 0361] Ps. 18]; the sinner’s conscience is a deep, dark, and unsearchable abyss. For, to say nothing of other things, if I examine and sweep [Col. 0362C] my spirit, if I wash myself with natron and multiply for myself the herb *borith* [Note: [Col. 0361] Jer. 17.], the Lord plunges me into filth.

[Note: [Col. 0361C] This reading differs from the original text of Holy Scripture. The Vulgate reads: “You are stained in your iniquity before me, says the Lord God.” The Septuagint translators likewise read this, except that, in place of “in your iniquity,” they read “in your iniquities”: ἐν ἀδικίαις σου, “in your injustices.” But in the Hebrew it is: “Your iniquity is marked before me,” etc., as Pagninus renders it. The Hebrews explain it thus: “Your iniquity is written down, or impressed.” And, as one learned among them explains: “It is so manifest that you cannot deny it.” As if he said: “Even if you try to conceal your idolatry, you will not deceive me.” Thus Vatablus. The Chaldee paraphrase: “For if you think that you are cleansed from your sins, just as people cleanse with natron and whiten with soap, behold: as the mark of a stain which is not cleansed, so your sins have become multiplied before me, says the Lord God.”

[Col. 0362C] The Syriac version reads: “Even if you whiten yourself with natron and apply very much sulphur to yourself, nevertheless your sins have impressed scars upon you before me, [Col. 0362D] says the Lord God.” The Arabic: “Although you wipe yourself with natron and apply much cleansing substance to yourself, nonetheless I shall defile you before me with your perversities, says the Lord your God.” Lyra on this passage: “Natron is a kind of earth used by those who cleanse garments; it is derived from *niteo*, ‘I shine,’ because it makes garments bright. *Borith* signifies soap, which likewise has cleansing power. By these is understood the multiplication of the sacrifices of the Old Law for expiating sins; these are of no avail for this purpose without due penitence.” Jerome should be read on that passage.]

Thus washing is lost upon a dead person; thus I wash a brick; and, while I shake off more filth, finding more transgressions that I have not yet fully bewailed as I ought, I am defiled by the very recollection of my crimes. Therefore, frightened by the majesty of so great a sacrament, I anxiously plead the insufficiency of the holiness which that rank requires.

Certainly Moses, though already chosen to lead the people and sent to Pharaoh, and Jeremiah [Note: [Col. 0361] Ch. 2.], likewise called by the Lord to instruct a rebellious people, humbly excuse themselves. And there is no doubt that [Col. 0363A] the priestly dignity surpasses the office of the fathers of old as greatly as the reality surpasses the hope, substance the shadow, and the fulfilment of truth the promises. Isaiah, when the Lord asked whom he should send, offered himself for the ministry of preaching, but was first cleansed by a coal from the altar [Note: [Col. 0363] Isa. 6.]. For no one is fit for spiritual ministries until purified by the fire of the Holy Spirit.

Out of reverence for the eminence of this ministry, Blessed Mark, whose heart and tongue the Lord had cleansed with the fire of the Holy Spirit, nevertheless feeling himself still imperfect, cut off his own thumb lest he be compelled to enter the priesthood. We read that, when Blessed Ammonius was unwillingly dragged toward the governance of the people, he cut off his left ear at the root with a knife, saying: “The divine law permits no one with a severed ear to become a priest.” [Col. 0363B] The clergy and people therefore returned to Timothy, then patriarch, who judged that Ammonius ought to be promoted because of his holiness, not merely if his ears were mutilated but even if his nose had been cut off. When they returned and again dragged and compelled the man of God, he said: “If you compel me further, I shall cut off with my own teeth the tongue for which I please you.” Thus at last he was left alone.

Moreover, Paul the Hermit, Antony, Apollonius, Mutius, Hilarion, Paphnutius, both Macarii, Arsenius, the blessed Benedict also, and other men of the most celebrated religious life, whose memory is in blessing, never attained the rank of priesthood; yet in their [Col. 0363C] simplicity they were saved. For, as Blessed Odilo, abbot of Cluny, writes in his exhortations [Note: [Col. 0363] Trithemius, *On Illustrious Men*], each of them, during one hour of the day, devoutly and faithfully gathered together, as it were into a bundle of memory, the benefits of the Lord’s Passion and of our redemption; and thus, in fear and humility, storing these in their conscience in order to enjoy them sweetly and securely, they ate the body of the Lord spiritually.

Thus the Lord commands the Apostles, saying: “Do this in remembrance of me” [Note: [Col. 0363] Luke 18.]. And the abbot adds: “For just as an unworthy person sometimes does not receive the sacrament, so no one receives the thing signified by the sacrament unless worthy.” It cannot be expressed in human speech with how great devotion Christ’s body ought to be consecrated, with how great caution dispensed, and with how great reverence received. I fear to consecrate what I desire to receive; for although a pure conscience is required in both cases, a more perfect life and more eminent conduct are required of a priest because of the various circumstances of that order.

Would that [Col. 0364A] the holiness of modern men were such that, by the example of virtue worthy of imitation, it might inspire in us a desirable longing for the priestly rank. Moreover, the Levitical order is not altogether free from burden, for it is strictly bound to the most exact observance of honourableness. Hence the Apostle, in the Epistle to Timothy, says: “Deacons must be chaste, as bishops are; not double-tongued, not given to much wine, not pursuing shameful gain” [Note: [Col. 0363] I Tim. 3.]. From this it is plainly gathered that continence, sobriety, and the watchful guard of life are enjoined upon deacons; that every ambition must be cut off from them, and everything in which the shamefulness of temporal profit is involved.

The Lord speaks to Moses, saying: “Let no priest or Levite be chosen unless he has said to his father and mother: ‘I do not know [Col. 0364B] you’” [Note: [Col. 0363] Exod. 33.]. In this not only the occasion of sin but attachment to kindred is cut away. Therefore I too “fled far away” [Note: [Col. 0363] Ps. 54.] from my parents; yet in this my pilgrimage I cannot wholly forget my people and my father’s house.

Since, according to the apostolic institution [Note: [Col. 0363] Acts 6.], it belongs to the Levitical order to serve tables and nevertheless to proclaim God’s word, it is a great task for me, beyond my powers, to fulfil the office of deacon adequately. From my youth onward my lords, the archbishops of Canterbury, have repeatedly urged me to consent to promotion to the priesthood. But I waited anxiously for a suitable occasion of exile or martyrdom to present itself, so that, after the example of Blessed Thomas, I might stand as a devoted assistant to those fighting in the arena of this world; [Col. 0364C] and, humbly venerating the footsteps of Blessed Lawrence, might publicly profess the duty of my Levitical rank and say to my lord and father, should he perhaps hasten to the struggle without me: “Where are you going without your son, Father? Where do you hasten, priest, without your minister? You shall surely discover whether you chose a fit minister, to whom you entrusted the consecration of the Lord’s body and blood.”

[Note: [Col. 0363D] Thus also Maz. 1; Vall.; Vict. 2 and 3; Dom. and Merl. read. Sorb. 1 alone has *ministrationem*, “ministration”; but incorrectly, because of what follows in this epistle: “For to us deacons is entrusted the consecration of that saving sacrifice, not that we may consecrate it, but that we may humbly assist those who consecrate it.” The same reading occurs in the manuscripts of St Ambrose, *On Duties*, I.41, from which this passage was drawn, [Col. 0364D] especially in the four very ancient and excellent manuscripts of St Ambrose which we examined: two are in the library of Saint-Germain-des-Prés and the other two in the Victorine library. It was likewise the reading in the earliest editions of St Ambrose’s works, as may be seen in the Basle edition published by Johann Amerbach in the year of the Lord 1492.]

For to us deacons is entrusted the consecration of that saving sacrifice, not that we may consecrate it, but that we may humbly assist those who do. And what absurdity is there if deacons, especially archdeacons, remain in their own order? For canonical authority prescribes this order of archdeaconship; and just as the priesthood is annexed to the episcopate, so the order of deaconhood is joined to archdeacons by a certain inseparable consequence [Col. 0364D].

Accordingly, simple deacons can, under the pressure of necessity or utility, be compelled to higher orders in accordance with the Council of Carthage [Col. 0365A]; but I have never read that an archdeacon may by law be forced to this. On the contrary, Blessed Gregory [Note: [Col. 0365] *Register*, II.15.] decreed, by way of punishment, that Natalis, bishop of the Church of Salona, should be deprived both of the use and honour of the pallium because he had caused Honoratus, archdeacon of the same Church, against his will to be ordained priest.

Among other things which Pope Simplicius writes to John, archbishop of Ravenna, concerning a similar case, these words are found [Note: [Col. 0365] Dist. 74, ch. *Ubi ista*]:

> “He deserves to lose the privilege of rank who abuses the authority granted him. Therefore we declare that, if henceforth you presume anything of this kind and believe that you can make anyone—whether bishop, priest, or deacon—against his will, you are to know that the ordinations of the Church of Ravenna and of Emilia will be taken away from you.”

With due peace [Col. 0365B] and reverence toward Pope Gelasius, those whose faculties have been trained in sacred eloquence either do not approve, or excuse themselves with filial reverence, for what he wrote: namely, that persons who defer priesthood or excuse themselves from receiving that order should be passed over in honours and stipends for lesser persons, so that they may endeavour to seek the honour and profit which they had fled. Certainly neither honour nor profit ought to be the occasion for entering the order, but the love of Christ and the salvation of the soul.

In the *Register*, Gregory [Note: [Col. 0365] II.19; Dist. 74, ch. *Gesta*.] rebukes a certain bishop with threats because he had promoted his protesting archdeacon to the priesthood. He inserts in that letter the following:

> “Just as it is right that no one should be compelled against his will to rise [*crescere*, not OCR *credere*], so [Col. 0365C] I think it must be decided that no one should be compelled to withdraw from the rank of his own order.”

[Note: [Col. 0365D] There is an error here: for *credere* one must read *crescere*, “to rise.” Thus it is found in all copies of Gregory, both printed and manuscript; likewise in Ivo of Chartres, part VI, chapter 279. So too in our manuscripts Vall., Dom., and Maz. 1; Sorb. 1 reads *conscendere*, “to ascend.”

[Col. 0366D] The precise year in which this letter was written cannot be determined. Yet Celestine III, the Supreme Pontiff mentioned here, was elected in 1191, while Richard, bishop of London, died in 1198; it may therefore be conjectured that it was written between these two dates.]

Moreover, with the order of ranks disturbed, archdeacons today take precedence over priests and exercise over them the force and authority of their jurisdiction. Therefore promoting an archdeacon to the priesthood is not an increase but a diminution of his honour. For although, as we have noted, compulsion may in some instances have place in the attainment of a higher rank, we know that compelling anyone to descend from a higher status expressly contradicts a decree.

This is most clearly evident from the letter of Pope Gregory [Note: [Col. 0365] XI.34; Dist. 74, ch. *Quorumdam*.] to John, bishop of Syracuse, which begins: “It has come to us by the report of certain persons.” It is also evident from that well-known and solemn chapter of Augustine [Note: [Col. 0365] 23 q. 4, ch. 34; Augustine, Ep. 204]: “It displeases you.” How, then, can anyone be removed from a rank [Col. 0365D] which he has canonically attained, especially when removal itself reduces him? For the Council of Chalon decreed by common law that no one should lose what he has legitimately [Col. 0366A] obtained unless grave fault intervenes.

Here, however, there is a certain loss of honour. For if the pre-eminence of archdeacons and the subordination of ordinary priests are considered more carefully, this promotion is, in the case of archdeacons, a kind of degradation. But, to introduce some parallel instances from civil law relevant to the matter, Ulpian [Note: [Col. 0365] Law IV, ch. 7, law 2.], disputing about appointing a guardian over property, reports Cassius as writing that no one should be compelled against his will to become a guardian; and adds: “Therefore a willing person must be sought.”

I believe that priests are guardians of souls. Hence Ambrose says: “The priest’s hand which tends the soul’s salvation must be clean.” And Solomon: “Care will put an end to very great sins” [Note: [Col. 0365] Eccl. 10.]. Likewise, Justinian [Note: [Col. 0365] Digest XLIX.16.4.] counts compelling anyone into military service among causes of disgrace; for this itself entails the crime of extortion. What reason, then, is there that an archdeacon should be forced, at such peril to his soul, thus to ascend—or rather to descend?

The Apostle indeed admonishes each person to remain in his own calling [Note: [Col. 0365] I Cor. 7.]. And, writing to the Ephesians [Note: [Col. 0365] ch. 4.], according to the distribution of the Holy Spirit, he assigns in the Church of God offices of diverse profession, so that the queen standing at the Bridegroom’s right hand may be adorned with the manifold variety of orders. As a figure of this, the Lord in the Book of Numbers [Note: [Col. 0365] ch. 3.] distinguishes diverse offices concerning the service of the tabernacle: some are Levites, some Merarites, some Gershonites, some Kohathites, and others Aaronites. Nor was there an alteration of ranks there, so that one order should pass into another, unless the most urgent reason of dispensation required it.

Finally, no one takes honour to himself, but only one who is called by the Lord, as Aaron was [Note: [Col. 0365] Heb. 5; Luke 14.].
