Therefore perhaps your lot and condition would still have been among the Levites rather than among the Aaronites, had not the Lord said to you: “Friend, go up higher” [Note: [Col. 0365] Luke 14.], and so clothed you in pontifical mitres. Blessed be the Lord, who chose you as his priest, sufficient and fit to give his people knowledge of salvation; to preach the acceptable year of the Lord; to bless the peoples on Mount Gerizim; effectually to convert unbelievers to the wisdom of the righteous; and to prepare for the Lord a perfect people.

We have seen very many in the Roman Church minister in the order of deaconhood until [Col. 0366D] decrepit old age and their final breath. Certainly Lord Celestine, who sits today, as I have frequently learned from his own mouth, had completed sixty-five years in the office [Col. 0367A] of Levite before the Lord raised him to the summit of the supreme pontificate.

Why, against our will, are we invited to priesthood? Certainly Joshua [Note: [Col. 0367] ch. 24.] leaves it to the choice of the people of Israel whether to serve the gods of Mesopotamia or God. And we too are free; for we have not received a spirit of slavery, but the Spirit who is from God, in whom we cry, “Abba, Father” [Note: [Col. 0367] Rom. 8.]. “Where the Spirit of God is, there is freedom” [Note: [Col. 0367] II Cor. 3.]. If God is Father in this Spirit, then we also are sons. But if we are sons, free by Christ’s testimony and called through Christ into the liberty of the glory of the children of God, so that we may be sons and heirs [Note: [Col. 0367] Rom. 8.], then we are indeed sons of God through Christ, but heirs of Christ through God.

Therefore, I beg, let no one presume to ordain archdeacons against their will; for the Lord does not accept forced service. [Col. 0367B] Assuredly, the services which we render to God are weighed not by the deed but rather by the will. I know who said: “I will sacrifice to you willingly” [Note: [Col. 0367] Ps. 53.]. I too am a human being, not an ass: I should be invited voluntarily to burdens, not compelled against my will. The profane and savage cruelty of pagan tyrants indeed customarily imposes upon Christians by force the necessity of sacrifice. But I, a Christian, may perhaps be compelled to priesthood; yet, apart from the judgment of free and devout will, I shall never sacrifice at any altars. Farewell.

## LETTER CXXIV. TO WALTER, ARCHBISHOP OF ROUEN

[Note: [Col. 0367C] This is the man whom all historians call Walter of Coutances, an Englishman by birth. He was first a canon of Rouen, then archdeacon of Oxford, afterwards bishop of Lincoln in 1183, and finally, after Rotrou, archbishop of Rouen in 1185. He was indeed a great man and for that reason greatly esteemed by both kings of England, Henry II and Richard.

First, while a canon of Rouen, he acted as vice-chancellor under Henry II, according to Ralph of Diceto in the *Images of Histories*, under the year 1173, in these words: “Adulf of Varneville, sacristan of Rouen and treasurer of York, was appointed chancellor of England. He did not change the manner of life, scarcely different from that of a private person, which he had always formerly maintained; preferring to entrust the duties at the royal court to Walter of Coutances, canon of Rouen, rather than to invite daily, for the advancement of his own name’s glory, knights attending at the prince’s side with more lavish expenditure and more sumptuous tables.”

How dear Walter was to Richard is evident from this. When Richard, in the Jerusalem expedition, had already arrived in Sicily and received letters from his mother Eleanor and the leading men of the kingdom, full of complaints against William of Ely, chancellor and administrator of the realm, he sent Archbishop Walter back to England to govern the kingdom together with the chancellor. Subsequently, after the chancellor had been expelled [Col. 0368C] by a conspiracy of the kingdom’s magnates, Walter himself was appointed chancellor and chief administrator of the realm by the queen mother and the Count of Mortain, the king’s brother. But when King Richard returned from the Jerusalem expedition and the bishop of Ely was restored to his former dignity, Walter returned to the administration of his archbishopric. Having governed it wisely for twenty-three years, he died in 1208.

It should be noted here that several copies read *Willelmus* or *Willermus* instead of Walter, corruptly; for no archbishop of Rouen named William is recorded at this time. It is an error of scribes ignorant of the histories, who were misled by the letter W, supposing it to denote William.]

[A.D. 1195.]

**ARGUMENT.**—He consoles W., archbishop of Rouen, exiled [Col. 0367C] from his church, and defends his flight as just against detractors.

To the reverend Father and lord WALTER, by God’s grace archbishop of Rouen, his own PETER of Blois, archdeacon of Bath [Col. 0368A], greeting and constancy amid adversities.

While savage hostility raged among our princes [Note: [Col. 0368D] He speaks of the war between Philip Augustus and Richard, fiercely waged in Normandy at this time, namely after each had returned from the Jerusalem expedition. All historians speak frequently of this war. That Peter of Blois here says Walter was mediator between the two kings is likewise attested by English writers, especially Roger under the year 1194, who names Walter among the arbiters appointed to reconcile the kings.], you, as mediator and angel of peace, very often made various journeys through difficult and laborious passages. At that time there was not even the faintest talk of peace or disturbance in your Church. At length you prevailed in your purpose, and through your skill you became reconciliation in a time of anger. Then for the first time rumour sounded that your Church was still being harassed by the storms of an old tempest. Others came, firmly asserting that the lord king had smoothed away every last scruple of that dispute. There were also those who said that you had departed from the province of Rouen [Col. 0368B] and migrated to Germany.

[Note: [Col. 0368D] Walter had withdrawn not to Germany but to Cambrai [Col. 0369B], because, while Philip, king of France, and Richard, king of England, were at variance with each other, he refused to accept certain terms which seemed to him insufficiently equitable. Afterwards, when those terms had been rejected by the same kings, he was peacefully recalled, and the losses inflicted upon Walter and the property of the Church of Rouen were made good.

Indeed, on the part of the king of France, who sent to Cambrai in order to recall him Anselm, dean of Thérouanne, and his chamberlain, Urson, with the following letter, reported by Ralph under the year 1196:

> “PHILIP, king of the French, to W., archbishop of Rouen.
>
> “We remember that we sent to you our beloved and faithful Anselm, dean of Thérouanne, and Urson, chamberlain, through whom our will was made known to you: namely, that you were in our love and favour, and that we had freely restored to you Andely, your other land, and the other things belonging to you [Col. 0369C]. We give you the same command, and from day to day you advance in more abundant favour and affection. We also wish you to know for certain that, if you wish to come into our land, our land is open and prepared for you and all your people, as for our most special clerics and friends.”

What Philip gave in compensation for the losses inflicted upon the Church of Rouen is not established by the writers. It is nevertheless certain that full satisfaction was made by him, as that charter of Walter indicates, which we reproduce from the royal archive kept in the royal chapel at Paris:

> “To his dearest lord PHILIP, by the grace of God illustrious king of the French, W., by divine favour minister of the Church of Rouen: greeting, grace, and the blessing of almighty God.”

> “Let Your Excellency know that full satisfaction has been made to us, to our canons, and to all the other ecclesiastical persons of our province, to the honor of God, of our Church, and of ourselves, for all the injuries inflicted upon us by you, your men, and those belonging to you. And that we and all the aforesaid persons have received full restitution both of Andely and of all our revenues and other possessions. Therefore we have relaxed the interdict under which we had placed your land in our province, and we release forever you, your men, and all who belong to you from every claim concerning those things which you took from our property and from the Church in the land of the lord king of England within our province before the vigil of St Nicholas in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1195. On this account we shall demand nothing from you or yours, nor shall we bring any action against you concerning it, nor allow you to be harassed by our subjects. We attest this by the present writing, with the attachment of the seals both of ourselves and of the chapter of our Church.”  
>
> Yet in another letter which he wrote to his friend Ralph, dean of London, preserved by that same Ralph under the year 1196, he states that, under the terms of the settlement made between the kings of France and England, the Church of Rouen “was endowed, in compensation for its losses, with a yearly and perpetual revenue of five hundred pounds.” It is nevertheless credible that these five hundred pounds of annual revenue were given by the king of France, since it is certain that at the same time the king of England gave the Church of Rouen three hundred measures of wine in compensation for those same losses, as this charter testifies, which we obtained through the kindness of the distinguished M. d’Herouval, in the following form:
>
> **“Grant of Richard, king of England, to the Church of Rouen for damages inflicted in time of war.”**
>
> “RICHARD, by the grace of God king of England, duke of Normandy [Col. 0370C] and Aquitaine, and count of Anjou, to the archbishops, bishops, etc.
>
> “Know that we have granted and given in perpetual alms to God and to the Church of Blessed Mary of Rouen, for our soul and for those of our predecessors and successors, for our anniversary, and for the restoration of the losses and damages which our lord Philip, king of France, inflicted upon the archbishop and Church of Rouen during the war between us and the aforesaid king, three hundred measures of wine, to be received every year from our wine-measure at Rouen, by whole casks, as we customarily receive them, and of such wine as we customarily receive at our wine-measure. That is: the archbishop shall have from this wine one hundred measures each year for his own use; and the canons shall have the remaining two hundred measures of wine for their own use and their common provision. But if our aforesaid wine-measure cannot suffice to make up the three hundred [Col. 0370D] measures of wine, the aforesaid archbishop and canons shall receive from us and our heirs twenty Angevin shillings for every measure of wine lacking, until the full three hundred measures of wine have been supplied. They shall receive that money from our revenue at Rouen. Given at Rouen in the sixth year of our reign.”
>
> Two seals were attached to this document; on one of them the full name Walter is inscribed. But that concord between Richard and Walter did not last long. Shortly afterward a serious disagreement arose between them concerning the town of Andely, which was the patrimony of the Church of Rouen; but I shall discuss this matter more fully below, under Letter 138.”
>
> This letter was written in 1195, when Walter had withdrawn to Cambrai.]
>
> Finally, some of your household reported to me in private that the lord king had recalled you from those regions and was most devotedly offering peace, honorable both to God and to you, on terms determined by your own will. Suspended amid so great a variety of rumors, I was anxiously agitated between uncertain outcomes. For it is written that rumors ought to be believed—and that they ought not to be believed. Whatever heavenly providence decreed concerning your exile, my wishes would have been complete had I afforded you consolation on this journey of your desolation. I know how meritorious and commendable before God and men it is to provide companionship to afflicted friends, especially to lords: that we may sympathize in adversity with those whose prosperity we have shared.
>
> When Naomi was travelling abroad, Ruth the Moabite did not leave her side. [Note: [Col. 0367] Ruth 1.] Jerome asks [Note: [Col. 0367] Letter 25 to Paula.] what God gave her in return for this, and adds: [Col. 0369A] “Christ was born from her.” The messengers of our Church, frequently sent to the lady queen, with whom I was then staying, learned by experience how often and with what zeal and industry I thwarted the schemes of your rivals. Peter, her chaplain and our fellow canon, bears witness that, because I defended you and your cause in many ways, she sometimes became so inflamed against me that, forgetting feminine modesty, she thundered at me with insults and abuse in the spirit of Hecate or Tisiphone.
>
> Even now the lord of Canterbury feels my absence keenly, gladly accepts my company, and considers my association with him honorable and useful. Whether I am with him, with the lord king, or with another, my soul is with you. Jonathan, indeed, was bodily with his father Saul, but his soul was with David. [Note: [Col. 0369] 1 Kings 16.] When Hushai the Archite wished to give the comfort of companionship to David as he fled from Absalom, [Note: [Col. 0369] 2 Kings 15.] David sent him back to remain with the priests Zadok and Abiathar, knowing that their staying near Absalom would be more advantageous to him—as the event afterward showed.
>
> Let your prudence judge what is expedient for you and for me. I am in the evening of my life. It is my desire to offer my final days to the Most High, whose earlier days I squandered because I lived wastefully. Would that you may run in such a way, not as toward an uncertain goal; fight in such a way, not as one beating the air; and establish your heart [Col. 0371A] so firmly in the Lord that you may be among the sons of the shaken. [Note: [Col. 0371] Phil. 3.] Deliberate carefully with yourselves; and, sitting down, according to the Gospel parable, [Note: [Col. 0371] Luke 14.] first calculate the cost, and see whether you can meet with ten thousand the one who comes against you with twenty thousand.
>
> Therefore, since you have taken up a work of courage, ground your purpose upon the stone of help, establish yourselves upon the foundations of Zion, and square your mind firmly against every persecution and injury. See that Christ alone, who is supreme justice, is in the cause of so great an undertaking. For the saying of blessed Peter is: “If you suffer for Christ, you are blessed.” [Note: [Col. 0371] 1 Peter 3.] And he adds: “Let none of you suffer as a thief or as a coveter of what belongs to others.” [Note: [Col. 0371] Ibid., 4.] In confessors, life makes death precious; in martyrs, the cause does so. In all things, therefore, display the banner of Christ and the title of innocence.
>
> I know your greatness of spirit, and I know that nothing is great, burdensome, or difficult to your great heart. The Church, which is our mother, is free; but today she is compelled to serve as a slave with Hagar. [Note: [Col. 0371] Gal. 4.] Therefore you depart, lest you see the evils of your Church, as the prophet laments [Note: [Col. 0371] Lam. 1.] and says: “Judah has gone into exile because of affliction and the multitude of her servitude.” But when the popular mobs of Dathan and Abiram are swallowed by the earth [Note: [Col. 0371] Num. 16.] and go down alive into hell—those who dare to provoke Aaron, the Lord’s holy one, who rise up against the Lord and against his Christ—then through them Antichrist is already working the mystery of iniquity.
>
> But act manfully [Col. 0371C] and be strengthened, remembering what is read in Proverbs: “The name of the Lord is the greatest strength.” [Note: [Col. 0371] Prov. 15.] “The righteous man shall be delivered from distress, and the wicked shall be given up in his place.” [Note: [Col. 0371] Prov. 11.] They now boast that they have prevailed in their emptiness; their joy, to use Job’s phrase, is like a point; [Note: [Col. 0371] Job 20.] their end is destruction; [Note: [Col. 0371] Phil. 3.] their burial is the burial of an ass; [Note: [Col. 0371] Jer. 22.] their recompense is fire and the worm. It is unheard of that persecutors of the Church have escaped her avenging hand: the hand of him who punishes the mighty mightily, who has always trampled the necks of the proud and exalted by his own power. For if he permits sinners for a time to build upon the back of the righteous, he fashions for that righteous person a crown of glory out of the very hammering of the wicked.
>
> But concerning those who rebel against the Lord’s priests, Amos [Col. 0371D] the prophet writes [Note: [Col. 0371] ch. 7.] and says: “Your wife shall prostitute herself in the city; your sons and daughters shall fall by the sword; your land shall be measured out by the line. You shall die in an unclean land, and your people shall go into captivity away from their land.” Some members of our prince’s household maliciously condemn your flight and attribute to arrogance of mind what love of justice dictates to you. May they rejoice in the soundness of their teeth to precisely the extent that they utter these things from filial affection. Certainly no wise person blames your [Col. 0372A] departure; for the Lord teaches us to flee from one city to another. [Note: [Col. 0371] Matt. 10.] He himself sometimes hid from the face of the Jews, [Note: [Col. 0371] John 6.] and the Apostle, his imitator, escaped his persecutors by being lowered in a basket. [Note: [Col. 0371] Acts 9.]
>
> Yet it is holy and acceptable to God to disdain, for justice’s sake, the malice of pride, riches and honors, and intimacy with princes. It is a noble pride; noblest of all is to disdain even disgrace without being confounded, for Christ’s sake—Christ who, as the Apostle writes, [Note: [Col. 0371] Heb. 12.] endured the cross, despising shame, for the joy set before him. To the Apostles and apostolic men the Lord said: “You shall consume the strength of the nations, and you shall take pride in their glory.” [Note: [Col. 0371] Isa. 61.] Wisdom also says in the book bearing her name: “With me are proud riches and glory.” [Note: [Col. 0371] Prov. 8.]
>
> I have publicly answered certain persons that you possess this pride; and because they were hurrying away, I pursued them with a letter, still extant, in which I plainly described the gifts of your character: how, when the height of dignity flattered you in former times and the breeze of prosperity blew, the swelling of windy praise could not move the steadfastness of your conscience. Rather, as the Apostle Peter teaches, [Note: [Col. 0371] 1 Peter 5.] you were “an example to the flock” among the people; and you could safely say to your subjects with Paul: “Not that we lord it over your faith, but we are helpers of your joy.” [Note: [Col. 0371] 2 Cor. 1.] You did not walk amid things too great and wonderful for you. By a certain graceful art of service, you remained humble amid riches and honors, and restrained every impulse to glory in power.
>
> If, then, detractors—as the Apostle says—who are hateful to God malign you, [Note: [Col. 0371] Rom. 1.] remember the word of Isaiah, [Note: [Col. 0371] ch. 51.] who says: “Do not fear their reproaches and blasphemies; the time is near when the mouth of those speaking iniquity shall be stopped.” You may further answer those who reproach you with the saying: “The servant is not greater than his master.” [Note: [Col. 0371] John 13.] Christ was not ashamed of reproaches for us; neither should you be ashamed of them for Christ.
>
> If perverse malice intends to overthrow the dignity of the Church, God, on the contrary, intends to raise it into a better condition; and there is no doubt that the divine purpose will prevail. For the Lord of hosts has sworn, saying: “Surely, as I have thought, so shall it be; and as I have planned, so shall it come to pass.” [Note: [Col. 0371] Isa. 14.] Even if the whole sea of this age, boiling and surging, should rush against the Church, Christ [Col. 0372D] walks upon the waters, and winds and sea obey him. [Note: [Col. 0371] Matt. 8.] And if Christ sleeps in the ship, let him be awakened by the prayers of those crying out: “Arise, why do you sleep, O Lord?” In the time of the Flood, the ark, shaken by the inundations, was raised on high. Its shaking is itself its raising; for, as blessed Hilary says, [Note: [Col. 0371] Book VII, *On the Trinity*] it is characteristic of the Church to conquer when she is wounded; to understand when she is rebuked; to be secure when she is abandoned; and to prevail when she seems defeated.
>
> The ark of the covenant, [Note: [Col. 0373] 1 Kings 5.] once captured by the Philistines and set beside Dagon, did not cease to display its power; at last it was brought back to Jerusalem with great rejoicing. I therefore ask that the condition of your noble conscience may not fail, but that you set your heart upon your ways. If you hear of the pride of Moab, [Note: [Col. 0373] Jer. 48.] know that its pride is greater than its strength. Indeed, by whatever judgment a person judges, he shall be judged; and he shall receive measure for measure. It is the Spirit of Wisdom who says: “By the things through which a man has sinned, by these he shall also be punished.” [Note: [Col. 0373] Wis. 11.] Pharaoh was drowned, because he had drowned the Hebrew infants; [Note: [Col. 0373] Exod. 14.] Goliath was killed by the sword with which he had attacked David; [Note: [Col. 0373] 1 Kings 15.] Haman was hanged on the gallows which he had prepared for Mordecai. [Note: [Col. 0373] Esther 7.] If your hope is rooted in Christ, it will grow strong toward [Col. 0373B] victory and bear fruit unto glory. May God, who girded you with strength for battle by standing by you, instructing and strengthening you, lead you onward to triumph. Farewell.

## LETTER CXXV. TO THE SAME PERSON

**Summary.**—He advises the same man diligently to avoid idleness in his exile and to devote himself to reading the divine Scriptures and to prayer, whose benefits he here describes.

To the reverend father and lord WALTER, by God’s grace archbishop of Rouen, his PETER of Blois, archdeacon of Bath: greeting, and consolation in desolation.

[Col. 0373C] In frequent letters I had urged you to withdraw from courtly business and redeem the time, because the days are evil; [Note: [Col. 0373] Eph. 5.] yet I do not know whether you received those admonitory letters, for you answered me only once, and briefly. But blessed be the Lord, because necessity has at last wrung from you what the devout humility of one who entreated you could not obtain. Administration of your office, intimacy with the king, and the other impediments of this world, as the Apostle calls them, held you fast. Like golden fetters, though they are less displeasing, they are more harmful.
>
> The Lord does not allow the time owed to repentance to be further given over to restless curiosity; and the one whom divine gentleness advised to devote himself to reading and prayer, his forceful compulsion has brought thereto. Thus the Lord speaks through the prophet: “As I live, says the Lord, with a mighty hand, an outstretched arm, and in my wrath I shall reign over you; I shall subject you to my sceptre and bring you into the bonds of my covenant.” [Note: [Col. 0373] Ezek. 20.] It is indeed a perfect gift of God, descending from the Father of lights, [Note: [Col. 0373] Jas. 2.] to be free—whatever the reason—and to see how sweet the Lord is. [Note: [Col. 0373] Ps. 45.]
>
> Therefore, since you have an understanding trained in sacred discourse, possess in the tribulation and pain of evils the consolation of Holy Scripture. Scripture is David’s harp, [Col. 0374A] by which Saul’s madness is moderated. [Note: [Col. 0373] 1 Kings 16.] Scripture is Shamgar’s ploughshare, [Note: [Col. 0373] Judg. 3.] by which the soil of our heart is tilled, by which six hundred Philistines are laid low and the rest put to flight. It is the jawbone of an ass by which the thirsty Samson is refreshed and a thousand Philistines are slain. [Note: [Col. 0373] Judg. 15.]
>
> Let sacred reading, therefore, be for you food, sword, medicine, and rest. Food, because man lives not by bread alone but by every word proceeding from the mouth of God; [Note: [Col. 0373] Matt. 4.] and not only food, but life and spirit, as Truth says: “The words that I speak to you are spirit and life.” [Note: [Col. 0373] John 6.] It is the table of the tabernacle set on the north side, [Note: [Col. 0373] Exod. 26.] so that each person may safely receive upon it all temptations, as it is written: “You have set before me a table against those who trouble me.” [Note: [Col. 0373] Ps. 22.]
>
> But if armies take their stand against you, [Col. 0374B] if battle rises against you, let the sword of the Holy Spirit, which is the word of God, be in your hands. If your knees are weak, if your hands hang down, if your feet are shaken, if your steps are poured out, trust that the heavens were established by the word of the Lord. If the soul is hardened against tears and God has made heaven bronze, so that no spiritual dew or rain descends, the Lord will send out his word and melt them; he will send forth his spirit in his word, and waters shall flow—indeed, his spices shall flow—that your manner of life, and that of those belonging to you, may pour forth the fragrance of sweetness.
>
> Do not be idle in exile, unless you count the business of the soul as idleness. For idleness without letters, Jerome testifies, is death and the burial of a living person. [Col. 0374C] Freedom from the cares of this world is the leisure of which Solomon says: “Wisdom is written in leisure, and those who are less occupied with action receive it.” [Note: [Col. 0373] Ecclus. 38.] Therefore the Lord’s disciples, passing through the grainfields on the Sabbath—that is, on the day of rest—rubbed the ears of grain and ate them. [Note: [Col. 0373] Matt. 12.] For subtler insights concerning hidden matters are drawn forth in a time of cessation, and souls are nourished by them. The gate in Ezekiel [Note: [Col. 0373] ch. 46.] which faced east was opened only on the Sabbath. For when the soul keeps Sabbath from worldly desires, the Wisdom of God more freely opens itself to the one who seeks it; contemplation and prayer then converse with one another more intimately.
>
> When the pressure of urgent necessity comes, one must run manfully to the weapons of prayer. For when a mass of miseries threatened Israel, it hastened to the tabernacle of the covenant. The efficacy of prayer [Col. 0374D] is great. The Lord was angry with his people; [Note: [Col. 0373] Ps. 105.] Moses stood in the breach, and the Lord was appeased. Israel fought against Amalek; while Moses raised his hands, Israel prevailed, but when he lowered them Amalek prevailed. [Note: [Col. 0373] Exod. 17.] A certain righteous man, believing that he would be delivered from the malice of his detractors by prayers, said: “In return for my love, they slandered me; but I gave myself to prayer.” [Note: [Col. 0373] Ps. 108.]
>
> How powerful is the prayer of the righteous is shown by Elijah’s prayer, [Col. 0375A] by which he closes and opens heaven for rain at his will. [Note: [Col. 0375] Jas. 5.] Prayer constantly made by the Church for Peter freed him from his chains. And Christ says to the Apostles: “Watch and pray.” [Note: [Col. 0375] Matt. 26.] By persistent prayer, a widow obtained from a certain judge vengeance against her adversary. The friend in the Gospel obtained three loaves by importunity. [Note: [Col. 0375] Luke 11.] In Ecclesiasticus it is written concerning prayer: “The prayer of the humble pierces the clouds and will not depart until it has looked upon the Most High.” [Note: [Col. 0375] Ecclus. 35.]
>
> Prayer, however, has its proper accompanying conditions: persistence, humility, fasting, and the other defenses of virtues. Therefore the prophet says: “Like the young of the swallow I shall cry; I shall meditate like a dove.” [Note: [Col. 0375] Isa. 38.] Know one thing: the demon by which we are afflicted is cast out only by prayer. [Note: [Col. 0375] Matt. 17.] Therefore, as the Apostle says, [Col. 0375B] “Pray without ceasing,” [Note: [Col. 0375] 1 Thess. 5.] so long as persecution does not cease. For as prayer grows strong, the shaking will cease; the publican shall go down justified, the sinful woman shall be absolved, and the Canaanite woman shall be told: “Let it be done to you as you wish.” [Note: [Col. 0375] Matt. 15.] And in all the churches with which I am bound by the ties of brotherhood or friendship, I devoutly seek for you the aid of prayers.

## LETTER CXXVI. TO R., ABBOT OF GLOUCESTER

[Note: [Col. 0375C] This monastery is in the city of the same name, in the diocese of Worcester, and is situated on the River Severn. Spelman and Godwin say that it was first founded by Osric, king of the Northumbrians, around A.D. 700. But William of Malmesbury, earlier than these, writes in Book IV of *The Deeds of the Bishops of England* that the daughter of the same king—whom he calls Ælfred—named Ælfred, together with her husband Æthelred, king of the Mercians, built this monastery. John Brompton says the same under the year 908. But after it had shortly afterward been ravaged and destroyed by the Danes, it lay deserted until the time of Aldred, archbishop of York, formerly bishop of Worcester. Simeon of Durham says concerning this:
>
> “In the year 1058, Aldred, bishop of Worcester, honorably dedicated in honor of Peter, prince of the Apostles, the church which he had built from the foundations in the city of Glaworna—that is, Gloucester—and afterward, by the king’s permission, appointed Wulfstan, a Worcester monk whom he had ordained, as abbot there.”
>
> Ralph of Diceto has these same details in his *Abbreviations of Chronicles* under the year 1058.]

**Summary.**—At Abbot R.’s request, he describes the life and character of Odo, a most noble man, elected bishop of Paris from the office of cantor of Bourges.

To the reverend father and lord R., by God’s grace abbot of Gloucester, PETER of Blois, archdeacon of Bath: greeting in [Col. 0375C] him without whom there is no salvation.

You ask in writing whether I know this new bishop of Paris, what I think of his life and character, and what I have heard about his election. It is the part of a curious man to inquire into these matters; but I know that love and devotion for your lord Henry, of blessed memory, lately bishop of Worcester, compel you to make this inquiry. For you know how peacefully and devoutly his whole spirit rested upon Odo, cantor of the Church of Bourges; and how much he desired and delighted, whenever an opportunity offered, to celebrate him and his brother, the archbishop of Bourges, with abundant praise.
>
> Of Odo’s life I shall relate what I know; of his election, what I have heard. When Maurice, of pious memory, was removed from this body of death, [Note: [Col. 0375D] Maurice succeeded Peter Lombard, the foremost theologian of his age. Born of humble station at Soliac, a town on the Loire, he was raised to this dignity by learning and virtue. Thus the monk of Auxerre says of him in his *Chronicle*: “Maurice, bishop of Paris, flourishes. Through outstanding industry, learning, and eloquence, he rose from the lowest depths of great poverty to the summit of pontifical dignity. Among his notable works, he built from the foundations the church over which he presided, and constructed two stone bridges, one over the Seine, the other over the Marne.”
>
> For his election to the episcopate and the events occurring at his death, see the authors of this period, including Caesarius, monk of Heisterbach, *Dialogues*, Book VI, chapter 19, and Book IX, chapter 43; James of Vitry, *Western History*, Book II, chapter 38; and Rigord, *Deeds of Philip Augustus*. He governed the Church of Paris with the highest distinction for thirty-two years and died in A.D. 1196 at St Victor’s, whither, shortly before death, he had withdrawn with the canons in order to devote himself more freely to God and to prepare more earnestly to render account of his stewardship. He lies in the middle of the choir of that same Church of St Victor.
>
> The manuscript *Chronicle* of John of St Victor also says of his death, under the year 1196: “Then died Maurice, bishop of Paris, of good memory. He founded many monasteries in the diocese of Paris: namely, Hérivaux, of the Order of St Victor of Paris; and Hermières, near Lagny, of the Premonstratensian Order; likewise the convent of nuns at Hierres and that of nuns at Gif. He gave much to other abbeys and religious houses. He was buried at St Victor’s in the choir, and at his death was made a canon of that place. By his command this was written upon his breast: ‘I believe that my Redeemer lives’ [Job 19], etc.”], the chapter of Paris was considering the appointment of another.
>
> [Col. 0376B] There were certain sons and heirs of Simon Magus who, though professed religious and men of many years, had nonetheless, with the money they had accumulated, from ancient days girded themselves for the market of that election; through certain successors of Gehazi they repeatedly proposed terms for concluding a purchase. But in so chosen an assembly of prudent men, mercenary cunning was foiled; and those who hoped to prevail by bidding alone were rejected as though decayed and barren stocks. Led by the fragrance of Odo—as of a full field which the Lord has blessed—they carried him off by common consent to be their bishop, amid the rejoicing of the whole land.
>
> I rejoice in his glory—if any glory can truly be ascribed to one whom public favor and common devotion drew unwillingly to the episcopal chair. For he was elected by the wishes of all, but not by his own; and by a certain commendable intrusion he attained the dignity which pursued him all the more urgently as he humbly fled from it.
>
> I knew and devotedly loved him at Paris during the beginnings of his studies and the still weak and rudimentary apprenticeship of his scholarly soldiery. There, as a boy, he eagerly grasped learning more through spiritual anointing than through a master’s instruction. For amid the exercises of the liberal arts, heavenly teaching poured richer gifts upon him. Thus, being wiser than the aged, he made the days of childhood old through his character, anticipated his years by his merits, and made up by virtues what his age lacked.
>
> Peter of Vern, his tutor—a disciple and friend of mine—often told me privately how diligently and devoutly, yet secretly and swiftly, Odo, still a little boy, exercised himself in works of piety. He often seasoned his almsgiving with tears and enriched the burnt offerings of mercy with the fat of compassion. He had passed through childhood, and while the down of budding youth was already flourishing upon his face, he visited the Apostolic See, at the time when Gregory VIII succeeded Urban.
>
> I was then at the curia and saw—without envy—that the honor shown him by the supreme pontiff and the assembled Fathers seemed scarcely inferior to the reverence accorded bishops. The Holy Spirit, the instructor of good minds, continually multiplied in him the seedlings of virtues until he became a perfect man. Seeing the things given him by God, he began to add works beyond what he had received. Though from childhood he had possessed his vessel in sanctification and honor, he nevertheless restrained the unruly impulses of the flesh by an authority of pre-eminent mastery, and compelled the flesh itself to serve as a handmaid through vigils, fasts, and disciplines. He knew that continence is an excellent kind of balm, preserving the flesh from corruption.
>
> While others run to seize the spoils of this world and regard godliness as gain, he wisely distributed the ample income he possessed in England: he scattered it, gave to the poor, and, by impoverishing himself, enriched three students who were needy but industrious and honorable. But God, the guarantor of the poor, repaid him another timely benefit, not without a great increase of interest; and because he had been faithful over a little, [Col. 0377D] he set him over much.
>
> Therefore he who, like a tree [Col. 0378A] sending its roots toward moisture, had begun to bear fruit in the Church of Bourges, is now transplanted by the Lord to Paris in order to bear more fruit, so that, set upon a lampstand, his lamp may shine more gloriously upon all—he who anxiously hid its light beneath the bushel of humility from the eyes of public notice. Finally, having been consecrated bishop, [Note: [Col. 0377D] For Odo’s life and deeds, see the volumes of the *Patrologia* shortly to be published, under the year 1208. EDITOR OF THE *PATR. LAT.*] he does not cease, as is publicly said, to interpret his name through his deeds. As a faithful mediator between God and men, he offers the people’s vows to God and brings God’s grace back to the people, continually restoring to the way of justice those whom the crafty impostor had led away from it.
>
> He is the brother of the archbishop of Bourges [Note: [Col. 0377D] This is Henry of Sully, first a monk and abbot of La Charité, of the Cistercian Order, and later, after Guarin, elected archbishop and patriarch of Bourges in 1183. There he was consecrated by Lambert, cardinal and archbishop of Milan, formerly archdeacon of the Church of Bourges, who afterward became Pope Urban III. In a certain diploma he calls Henry prudent and discerning, similar to himself in character and birth. He therefore made him a cardinal of the Holy Roman Church and legate of the Apostolic See through the province of Bourges. According to Rigord and the anonymous author of the *History of the Archbishops of Bourges*, he died in 1199; the latter adds: “He flourished from 1183 to 1199, while Lucius III, Urban III, Gregory VIII, Clement III, Celestine III, and Innocent III presided at Rome; while Frederick I and Henry VI ruled as emperors; and while Philip Augustus, the second king of that name, governed the realm of the Franks vigorously and successfully.”], and, though descended from the most illustrious princes—on one side kinsman to the king of England, and on the other related by a closer line of descent to the king of France—he disdains the eminence of his lineage through a nobler greatness of spirit. By that very disdain, in the judgment of those who think more rightly, he adds greatly to the distinction of his birth. Farewell.

## LETTER CXXVII. TO ODO, BISHOP OF PARIS. [A.D. 1197]

**Summary.**—He asks that the friendship formed with Odo in their youth be confirmed, and urges him to fulfill his episcopal office.

To the reverend father and lord Odo, by God’s grace bishop of Paris, his PETER of Blois, archdeacon of Bath: greeting, and whatever is sweeter or more desirable than greeting.

Among the desirable things of this world, it is my special and heartfelt wish to go and see your face, most dear to me. For I believe that, with a conscience secure, you can sing to God with the prophet David: “Those who fear you shall see me and rejoice.” [Note: [Col. 0377] Ps. 118.] But the intervening distance, the closure of the sea, and the prohibition of superiors confine the purpose of my ardent affection within the limits of my ability.
>
> As the Apostle testifies, charity never fails. Therefore I ask more confidently that the affection which my tenderer years first formed in you toward me [Note: [Col. 0378D] The preceding letter explains more clearly the intimacy which our Peter had with Odo.] may not limp away from the integrity of its origin, but, with the aid of your gracious favor, may grow stronger in mutual love and in the bond of friendship. I ask that you become the successor and continuator of that favor which your nearest and closest relatives customarily showed me beyond all my deserving.
>
> Henry II, king of England and your kinsman, first drew me into England. Having often experienced his generous and magnificent hand, I learned from his loss how great an advantage would have come to me had he lived long. But a new Pharaoh arose who did not know Joseph; and would that, in my long exile, no human being had known me! Once, overwhelmed in spirit and consumed with grief at the death of that most illustrious king, I would have left England behind and migrated elsewhere because of my soul’s weariness, had not the welcome and cherished friendship of the lord of Worcester [Note: [Col. 0379C] Namely Henry, formerly abbot of Glastonbury, who became bishop of Worcester in 1192 and died in 1195.] and the lord of Durham [Note: [Col. 0379C]
>
> This was Hugh, surnamed Pudsey or de Puiset, nephew through his sister of Stephen, king of England, and therefore Odo’s kinsman. While treasurer of the Church of York and archdeacon of Winchester, he was elected bishop of Durham in 1152, though Henry, archbishop of York, protested and objected, says William of Newburgh. He was consequently compelled to go to Rome to receive consecration and was consecrated by Pope Anastasius in 1153. He governed the Church of Durham for a full forty-two years and accomplished many notable things there. For a fuller account, see William of Newburgh, *History of English Affairs*, Book V, chapter 10. He died in 1194.
>
> This letter was written in 1197, that is, near the beginning of Odo’s episcopate.]
>
> and of his archdeacons, then still living, relieved me of that burden and of the distress of every desolation.

[Col. 0379B] For what pressure could be so heavy and unbearable that it would not be lightened by the conversation, aid, counsel, and consolation of such great men? They calmed every agitation of misfortune for me and made a homeland for me in the land of my pilgrimage. But their life has been cut off as by a weaver, and cruel, murderous death believed that it had slain me by snatching from me, in them, the consolation of living. Yet I give thanks to God, who graciously provides for the afflicted against the pressing necessities of inevitable fate, raising up, according to the word of Amos, prophets from among sons and Nazirites from among young men. [Note: [Col. 0379] Amos 2.] In place of fathers sons are born, [Note: [Col. 0379] Ps. 44.] and anew there springs up a glorious crop [Col. 0380A] of descendants; as old friends vanish, a generation of new friends grows together, bearing the riper and sweeter fruits of friendship.

Since, then, God has magnified his mercy toward you, according to the name of the great who are in the earth—since you have been great in small things, may you be greater in great ones. May your nobility never decline from ancestral greatness of soul. To a great heart nothing is great. Seek not a gift, but its fruit; and think not of living for yourselves, but for all. In Paul’s witness, “Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today, and for ever.” [Note: [Col. 0379] Heb. 13.] He who has advanced you to great things has preserved you for greater ones. Yet it is fitting that you prove untiring in rendering thanks, so that ingratitude, hateful to God, may not presume to assail you even in a small matter; rather, always offer yourselves as indebted to him [Col. 0380B] whose benefits even angels acknowledge themselves unable to equal. Farewell.

## LETTER CXXVIII. TO WILLIAM, ARCHBISHOP OF SENS

[Note: [Col. 0379C] On him, see Letter 15.]

**Subject.**—He complains that promises made by the Archbishop of Sens are fulfilled more slowly than is fair. The archbishop had promised to receive him into his household and to endow him with an ecclesiastical benefice.

To the venerable Father and lord WILLIAM, by God’s grace Archbishop of Sens, PETER OF BLOIS sends greetings, and himself wholly at his feet.

“I waited and waited for my lord,” yet he gave me no heed. I hoped that he would put his word into effect and actually confer upon me the favour which Master Gerard [Note: [Col. 0379D] This is Gerard surnamed Puella (“the Boy”), an Englishman, very intimate with Peter of Blois, since both had taught at Paris and afterward had attached themselves in England to Richard, Archbishop of Canterbury, and had been admitted to his household. Yet I read in the *Quadrilogue* of St Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury, that he is numbered among that holy man’s household in these words: “Gerard surnamed Puella, distinguished in name and reputation, an Englishman by nation. After long draughts of the muddy waters of Siloam, he at last drank the purest water from the springs of Siloam. Before the saint [Thomas] went into exile, he was the first to advance him to the clerical order and the first to confer upon him an ecclesiastical benefice. After the passing of his lord, through the merits of his good, gentle, honourable conduct and learning, he was promoted to the bishopric of Coventry.” He was also a friend of John of Salisbury, several of whose letters to Gerard survive, exhorting him to use the influence he possessed with Henry, king of England, to assist the exiled and afflicted Archbishop Thomas.

After Thomas’s death he attached himself, together with Peter of Blois, to Richard, Archbishop of Canterbury; both were enrolled in that archbishop’s household. Richard accordingly sent them together to Rome, to Alexander III, concerning the case between himself and Roger, Abbot of St Augustine’s, Canterbury, who refused to make the profession of obedience owed to his prelate. On this matter see what I have said in the *Life of Peter of Blois*, from William Thorn, in the *Chronicles* under the year 1179, p. 1821, where the entire history of this dispute is related.

Moreover, Gerard Puella became Bishop of Coventry and was consecrated by Richard, Archbishop of Canterbury, whose clerk he was, as Gervase says. He administered that bishopric for only seven months. Thus Nicholas Trivet, under the year 1183: “Master Gerard called Puella was elected and consecrated Bishop of Coventry.” And below: “In the year 1184 Gerard of Coventry, having sat for eighteen weeks, passed to his fate.” Concerning his death Gervase writes under the same year, 1183, p. 1465: “Soon after he was enthroned, stricken by a severe illness, he took to his bed and died, in the fourth month of his ordination, on the Ides of January; and he was buried at Coventry.”] had announced to me on his behalf [Col. 0381A] would be shown in deeds. I was in great bitterness; but Master G. reported to me things welcome and sweet, so that, according to the multitude of sorrows in my heart, his consolations made my soul glad.

The tardy and uncertain fulfilment of my hope was, indeed, as though it were cooking me in a frying-pan. If I were dealt with thus much longer, and if the life of my spirit remained in such a state, it would be far sweeter for me to die than to be tortured by living in a continual death. Nevertheless, if you have not forgotten to show mercy, if you intend still to be more favourably disposed, assign what remains of my old age to your service. Remember that “the time to show mercy has come, for the time has come.” It is now drawing toward evening for me, and the days of my life have declined. [Note: [Col. 0381] Luke 24.] To use Job’s words, “my wrinkles bear witness [Col. 0381B] against me, and my grey hair proclaims old age.” [Note: [Col. 0381] Job 16.]

Very many great men entice me into their service by promises and gifts; but your promise and the sweetness of my native air draw me more powerfully, especially the desire for the prebend at Chartres, for which you gave me hope. For that reason I have set more abundant and certain revenues below your bare promise. For, to use Gideon’s phrase, “One cluster of Ephraim is better for me than the vintage of Abiezer.” [Note: [Col. 0381] Judg. 8.] “One day in your courts is better for me than thousands.” [Note: [Col. 0381] Ps. 83.] Moderation in your company is better and more welcome to me than an unbounded abundance of riches among others.

Since, therefore, you have hitherto kept my soul in suspense, and through my messenger I have brought back no certainty about your intention, lest my heart continue to toss in uncertainty, I shall go [Col. 0381C] and visit him whom my soul loves. May the Lord who has fed me from my youth make my journey prosperous and fill me with joy in your presence, for “I shall seek your face, O lord.” Farewell.

## LETTER CXXIX. TO R., ARCHDEACON OF ORLÉANS

**Subject.**—He vehemently attacks R., Archdeacon of Orléans, because he has introduced the plague of simony into the Church, and shows by many examples that it is execrable.

To his dearest lord and friend R., Archdeacon of Orléans, Master PETER OF BLOIS sends greeting in the author of salvation.

While you were still young, I admired the first fruits of your noble disposition. Yet in the field which [Col. 0381D] I had cultivated with most painstaking care, an enemy has sown tares over the crop. Thus the seeds of learned diligence that I had sown, from which I confidently expected the growth of the fruits of righteousness, are degenerating into darnel and thorns.

Dearest friend, I beg you to endure this little exhortation of mine with equanimity. I admonish you, in case perhaps you will listen, in case perhaps you will be willing to uproot the wicked plants and viperous roots which my heavenly Father did not plant and which therefore must be plucked out all the more forcefully because they have been planted so monstrously. I shall not spare you, so that [Col. 0382A] God may spare you. Though you are greater than I and higher in rank, you are nevertheless my brother. I do not wish the voice of a brother’s blood to cry to the Lord against me.

In the Third Book of Kings the Lord says to the son of the prophet: “Because you have let go a man deserving death, your life shall be for his life.” [Note: [Col. 0381] Chapter 20.] The saying of Jeremiah also extends to all: “Cursed is he who withholds his sword from blood,” [Note: [Col. 0381] Ibid., ch. 48.] that is, from the killing of sin. You were accustomed to sew yourself loincloths out of leaves—that is, to allege the gentleness of your youth and the slipperiness of your age in order to make excuses for sins. But now you have reached the full stature of manhood. The leaves that covered the shamefulness of your life have withered; indeed, what is worse, you publicly and openly display your outrageous deeds upon the eyelids of common fame, [Col. 0382B] so that the text applies to you: “They proclaim their sin like Sodom.” [Note: [Col. 0381] Isa. 3.]

But the prophet’s word is: “Do not go up to Gilgal, and do not go up to Beth-aven.” [Note: [Col. 0381] Hos. 4.] By this we are forbidden to make our sin public, lest we become an occasion of ruin to others and an example of destruction. Under the figure of Israel the prophet Hosea addresses the soul that sins publicly: “If you have sinned, Israel, at least let Judah not sin.” [Note: [Col. 0381] Ibid.]

Would that you accustomed yourself to reading! Constant reading would remove uncultivated manners and bring in the rule of due correction. Certainly King Josiah of Judah, when Deuteronomy was read in his presence, although he was a boy, was struck with fear on hearing the threats of the law; he tore his garments, sat down, and wept before the Lord because he had not kept [Col. 0382C] his commands. [Note: [Col. 0381] IV Kings 22.] He therefore made a covenant before the Lord that he would walk in all his commandments; he cast every unclean vessel out of the house of the Lord and also destroyed the altars and groves.

But you do not cast the filth of avarice and the uncleanness of simony out of God’s Church; you bring them in. You know that the Lord burned fiercely against transactions of this sort and drove them out with whips as loathsome abominations among living creatures. And now he sharpens his sword like lightning, that his sword may devour flesh and fire consume even to the lowest depths of hell. He has bent his bow and prepared upon it instruments of death against those whom he has placed as heads and hinges of others.

The prophet Amos says: “I saw the Lord [Col. 0382D] standing upon the altar, and he said: Strike the hinge, and let its threshold be moved.” Avarice is at the head of them all: “and I will slay them with the sword.” [Note: [Col. 0381] Amos 9.] This simoniacal avarice is itself the worm and the destroyer: a most destructive grub, the rust and moth of the heart, which rusts and consumes every good thing.

> The once venerable name of a noble Church  
> is put up for sale, and sits in the marketplace like a prostitute.

[Note: [Col. 0381] Ovid has: “That of friendship.”]

And how, dearest friend, did this plague steal upon you? Who made you Simon’s disciple and Gehazi’s successor? Who made you a buyer of leprosy and a seller of spiritual [Col. 0383A] oil? Could canonically acquired revenues and ecclesiastical resources not suffice you, unless you built Zion with blood and amassed riches through execrable sale and damnable gain?

By daily use and experience we have learned that sellers of spiritual things,

> The more wealth they pile up, the greater is the want in which they are always confounded.

Filthy plunder has no good outcome. And therefore at times,

> Whatever avarice has wickedly drawn in, it pours out again in worse extravagance.

[Note: [Col. 0383] Ovid, *Ex Ponto* II.3.19.]

Achan took from the accursed things of Jericho and was stoned. [Note: [Col. 0383] Claudian, *On the Gildonic War*.] Korah usurped a spiritual office and was consumed by fire sent from heaven. [Note: [Col. 0383] Num. 16.] Jason bought the priesthood from Antiochus, [Col. 0383B] [Note: [Col. 0383] II Macc. 4.] and the fire kindled by Jeremiah was extinguished. [Note: [Col. 0383] II Macc. 1.] Saul brought gifts to the prophet and came under God’s wrath. [Note: [Col. 0383] I Kings 15.] Jeroboam conferred the priesthood upon all who filled his hand, and his house was overthrown. [Note: [Col. 0383] III Kings 13.] Belshazzar, because he misused the vessels of the tabernacle, was captured and killed. [Note: [Col. 0383] Dan. 5.] Dathan and Abiram were swallowed up by the earth because they abused a spiritual office. [Note: [Col. 0383] Num. 18.]

I beg you, let the stoning of Achan, the burning of Korah, the leprosy of Gehazi, [Note: [Col. 0383] IV Kings 5.] Simon’s money, [Note: [Col. 0383] Acts 8.] Saul’s rejection, [Note: [Col. 0383] I Kings 15.] the overthrow of Jeroboam’s house, the ruin of Dathan and Abiram, and the extinction of the fire under Jason deter you. That fire is the Holy Spirit, who is extinguished in you through wickedness; and therefore it is written: “Do not quench the Spirit.” [Note: [Col. 0383] I Thess. 5.] Let another’s peril serve as your warning, not your own. [Col. 0383C] Let the punishment of others instruct you, lest you be punished likewise. “When the pestilent man is punished, the wise man becomes wiser”; [Note: [Col. 0383] Prov. 21.] and “the righteous shall wash his hands in the blood of the sinner.”

## LETTER CXXX. TO JOHN, BISHOP OF CHARTRES

**Subject.**—He clears himself of the slander of certain persons who had spread abroad that, concerning the provostship of Chartres, he had sought the assistance of kings, counts, and the pope against John, Bishop of Chartres. He rejoices that the bishop’s nephew has been restored to favour, and declares himself wholly devoted to him because of benefits received.

To his most beloved Father and sole redeemer after God, JOHN, by God’s grace Bishop of Chartres, PETER OF BLOIS, chancellor of the Archbishop of Canterbury, sends greeting in the true Saviour.

[Col. 0383D] I have heard, and I have been grievously disturbed, because certain detractors hateful to God, as the Apostle says, [Note: [Col. 0383] Rom. 1.] have tried to cloud for me the serenity of your favour, taking from your goodness an occasion for malice. Thus, because the mercy of the Most High has sometimes made you accommodating and kind toward my requests, they might with a like—indeed, a very unlike—readiness incline you to hatred against me.

[Note: [Col. 0383] In place of “A whisperer has dared,” down to “and a neighbour,” the Paris edition has the following: “A whisperer and double-tongued man has dared to inform your discretion that I have sought, against you, the assistance of kings and counts in order to obtain the provostship of the Church of Chartres. I believe that, if I sought their aid, they would willingly support my petition. But confident in the justice of my cause and the purity of your conscience, I do not seek the begged-for support of men. It pleases me—if it is also pleasing in your sight—that my case be brought to the hazard of controversy and the outcome of judgment. But if you intend mercy rather than judgment toward me, I commit myself to your written instrument, authenticated, which you made for me concerning the provostship, to the abbots also who were present, and to your conscience.” GILES.]

A whisperer and double-tongued man has dared to charge me with the shamefulness of trafficking, wickedly thinking me like himself. For if I have known trafficking in ecclesiastical matters, may I not enter into the powers of the Lord; may he remember my injustice alone and not his mercy. In heaven I have Christ, and on earth the consciousness of my innocence, as witnesses, that every word may stand by the mouth of two or three witnesses. Most carefully inquire into the truth from the provost, Lord Robert, your nephew, without whose knowledge nothing was done. I call upon his testimony against me, because, as is publicly said, [Col. 0384B] though not in proportion to my deserts, he is most seriously offended with me. For his deceitful tongue has assailed my name in many ways and has estranged friend and neighbour from me.

Nevertheless, the Lord will save the son of the poor man, humble the slanderer, and expose as liars those who have stained the innocent. This amazes me and, above all, pains me: that human craftiness could persuade your most prudent wisdom that I either entered into some transaction contrary to honour or obtained letters from the Roman court against you. “Shall an axe boast against him who cuts with it? Or shall a rod exalt itself against him who lifts it? It is, after all, wood.” [Note: [Col. 0383] Isa. 10.] It would be so if I, carnal and sold under sin, rose up against [Col. 0384C] God, against his Christ, and against him who redeemed me from reproach and exile.

I know and continually recall what great things you have done for me. Hence your mercies are and always will be my song in the land of my pilgrimage. For you did not love me because I first loved you; rather, I loved you because you loved me and anticipated me with your blessings. I know what good you have done me; I know what you have done for the whole land; I know what you have done for your domestic enemies and mine. Concerning you I can most confidently say with the prophet: “Unless the Lord of Hosts had left us a holy seed, we would have become like Sodom and been made like Gomorrah.” [Note: [Col. 0383] Isa. 1.]

Meanwhile I bear patiently until the Lord blows away and disperses the counsels of those who call good evil and evil good; for he will overthrow the wicked, and they shall be no more. But may your wisdom overcome malice; [Col. 0385A] and if your anger has briefly blazed up at the words of my adversaries, resolve to be more favourably disposed still, and do not cut off your mercies from me, your servant. For I offer myself to every censure and correction from you, if I have offended you in anything. “Let the righteous man correct me in mercy and rebuke me!” Even if in correcting me you should exceed the bounds of equity, I would judge that very thing sufficiently desirable; for, in Job’s words, “Even if you kill me, I shall hope in you.” [Note: [Col. 0385] Job 13.]

For, in Wisdom’s testimony: “The injustice of a man is better than a woman who does good.” [Note: [Col. 0385] Sirach 42.] Your blows are certainly sweeter to me than the breasts of those who feed you with the milk of lamiae (witches), and who have sometimes given me to drink from the cup of Babylon. But I receive it most sweetly, and I count it among my prayers, if you have received your nephew into favour, provided that my own position is not harmed. For your favour toward your nephew is demanded both by the condition of nature and by the order of charity, as the Apostle says: “Whoever does not provide for his own, and especially for members of his household, has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever.” [Note: [Col. 0385] I Tim. 5.]

Indeed, I add most earnest prayers—if you deign to accept the prayers of your servant—that you do not call to mind your nephew’s former offences. For where he displeased you, he will please you; and where the offence abounded, grace will abound more abundantly. [Note: [Col. 0385] Rom. 5.] I conclude the sum of my prayers and wishes in this brief form of words: count me as yours—indeed, as most wholly yours. For soon, God [Col. 0385C] granting, I shall dedicate myself wholly to the service of the blessed Virgin and to yours, being like Ephraim, a heifer trained to love threshing. I shall place my treasure and glory in him who is able to keep my deposit until that day, and in you, whose life, manner of life, and words are most precious to me.

For what treasure can be more precious than to hear the prudent words and discourses of one who always builds toward life in word and deed, whose words are spirit and life? As Wisdom says: “Desirable treasure rests in the mouth of the wise.” [Note: [Col. 0385] Prov. 2.] I thirst and long for this treasure as a deer for springs of water. I shall come to it, and in it I shall live and die, whatever the most unclean swine may snarl or grunt, whatever poisonous fabrications the most wicked [Col. 0385D] detractors may devise.

Soon, with Christ Jesus as my guide, I shall conquer cunning by simplicity, impatience by gentleness, fraud by truth, pride by humility, [Col. 0386A] and malice by goodness. I beg you to read this letter a second or third time: it was written from the inkwell of sorrow and flowed from distress of spirit. May my dearest lord fare well, and all who love him affectionately. Farewell.

## LETTER CXXXI. TO E., PRIOR OF MONASTERIOLUM

**Subject.**—He reproves his nephew, a monk, because, neglecting the study of sacred letters and solitude, he seeks the friendship of princes and of the world.

M. PETER OF BLOIS, Archdeacon of Bath, to his beloved and most dearly beloved nephew E., Prior of Monasteriolum, [Note: [Col. 0385D] This letter E. seems to designate Ernald, who, as the following letter shows, became abbot of Saint-Laumer from prior of the church of Monasteriolum. That Monasteriolum is a priory dependent on the Abbey of Saint-Laumer of Blois; it lies in the district of Perche, in the diocese of Chartres, and is called Saint-Laumer of Moutiers, commonly *Moustiers*. Ernald, abbot of Saint-Laumer, is named under the year 1202 in a charter of the priory of Fonte-Mellaud of Marmoutier, as I read in a parchment from the Abbey of Saint-Laumer preserved in the library of Saint-Germain-des-Prés.

But where a charter of the *Grand Pastoral* of Paris has R., Abbot of Saint-Laumer, under the year 1203, this is a copyist’s error, who wrote R. for E. This error entered the *Gallia Christiana*, in its catalogue of the abbots of Saint-Laumer.] greeting in the author of salvation.

If what I write seems harsh and hard to you, nevertheless bear it with equanimity; for all this [Col. 0386B] is dictated by the overflowing affection of love, and out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks. In the inward parts of Christ I zealously thirst for your salvation. Hence this entire course of exhortation flows from the marrow of my soul and from the richness of charity. Long have I been mute and kept silence even from good things. For with you I was like a vessel lost, as one dead to your heart, since you disdained to greet your uncle by letter or messenger. Would that you were dead to your heart, and that your life were hidden with Christ in God! You understand more than the elders, and, as the Apostle writes to Timothy [Note: [Col. 0385] 1 Tim. 3], you have known the sacred Scriptures from childhood, by which you can instruct both yourself and others unto salvation. Yet, having entirely cast aside the exercise of the literary warfare, you hunt after the friendships of great men; and, that you may please princes, you entangle yourself in the surging waters of ambitious courts. [Col. 0386C]

Moreover, a learned man who does not exercise himself in constant reading is like a deserted house, in which, according to the prophet’s word [Note: [Col. 0385] Isa. 34], hairy demons cry one to another and demons encounter onocentaurs. The unclean spirit also finds the house vacant and often takes seven spirits more wicked than himself to dwell in it [Note: [Col. 0385] Matt. 12]. For this reason you seek honours, worship the breeze of popular favour, and officiously thrust yourself into the counsels of the great; and all these things the Gentiles seek. It displeases me if, in order to please the world, you do not fear to displease God. Those who please men are confounded, because God has rejected them [Note: [Col. 0385] Ps. 52]. “If I still pleased men,” says the Apostle, “I should not be Christ’s servant.” You cannot please God and the world. Whoever wishes to be a friend of [Col. 0386D] this world makes himself an enemy of God [Note: [Col. 0385] Jas. 4]. For what fellowship has the Spirit of God with the spirit of the world? As light with darkness; as Christ with Belial. If you seek glory [Col. 0387A] that comes from man, you lose the glory of Him who gives grace and glory. It is Christ’s word: “You seek glory from one another, and do not desire the glory that comes from God alone” [Note: [Col. 0387] John 5]. The Lord of glory Himself says: “If I seek my own glory, my glory is nothing” [Note: [Col. 0387] John 8]. Let your glory be the testimony of a good conscience, with which he can never share who, borne in the chariot of pride, races across the field of self-exaltation.

I fear, moreover, that flattering words may foster you in your error. For there are those who stroke you, saying, “Well done! well done!” [Note: [Col. 0387] Ps. 34], and add horns to the sinner. These are they who greet you hypocritically, bearing a kiss upon their lips, a dart in their heart, and poison in their concealed affection. It was once said to King Zedekiah: “Your men of peace have deceived you” [Note: [Col. 0387] Jer. 38]; and those who glorified you lead you into error. [Col. 0387B] Would that the righteous man might correct you mercifully and rebuke you, and that the oil of the sinner might not make your head fat [Note: [Col. 0387] Ps. 140]!

You gave your hand to the monastic profession; I beg you, consider the course of your manner of life. See how much of your life you have lost, and what fruit you have in things of which perhaps you are now ashamed. Jeremiah’s word is: “It is good for a man when he has borne the Lord’s yoke from his youth; he shall sit alone and keep silence, because he shall lift himself above himself” [Note: [Col. 0387] Lam. 3]. I fear that, in a contrary and perverse sense, you have lifted yourself above yourself: not thinking humbly, but exalting yourself, walking in great matters and wonders beyond yourself. For from the first movements of youth you shook from your neck the Lord’s yoke which you had received; and, leaving the way that led to the city of habitation, you followed [Col. 0387C] the byways of youthful levity. The unrestrained freedom of life and impunity in sinning added incentives to the itching wantonness of extraordinary impulses; and since human senses are inclined to evil from youth, the violence of a certain habit and a more licentious urge carried you away, darkening and overwhelming your understanding, so that you consented to wickedness without perceiving it. By a certain persistence in sinning, you even wished, through rash rivalry, to surpass evildoers. Thus they gradually overthrew your heart into negligence. For the mind gradually flows away, and by continual practice the soul slips into worse things. Indeed, a ship, as water drips little by little into its bilge, is secretly and suddenly submerged.

We know, moreover, that in your country there are many corrupters of the simple; [Col. 0387D] hence, from the wickedness of those dwelling there, you contracted a manifold dross of morals. Yet it would have been more tolerable not to have undertaken the purpose of repentance than to go back after repentance. It is a matter of great peril to carry the disgrace of the age beneath a religious habit, impiety beneath the covering of piety, and to conceal Antichrist under Christ’s garments. Would that you had tasted how sweet the Lord is, and learned His mercies by experience! For if Truth—or rather, because Truth—speaks truth, His yoke [Col. 0388A] is sweet and His burden light [Note: [Col. 0387] Matt. 11]. But for whom? Not for slaves, but for sons: namely, those who are led by God’s Spirit. These are those who by the Spirit mortify the deeds of the flesh, whose members are the temple of the Holy Spirit. They were bought at a great price—that is, Christ’s precious blood—bearing Him and glorifying Him in their flesh.

There are, however, some who had resolved to bear in their body the mortification of Jesus, but, driven by a torrent of invading wickedness, have become a crooked bow, making their members weapons of iniquity for sin; and, having expelled God’s Spirit from themselves, they have received within themselves the spirit of this world, saying, “Jesus be accursed” [Note: [Col. 0387] 1 Cor. 12]. At one time it was in your power not to receive the Lord’s yoke; but once received, you were not permitted to cast it off. God therefore now exacts what has been offered, though He did not exact [Col. 0388B] its offering. Will has been transformed into necessity; and you are bound by the bond of profession to pay the vows which your lips pronounced.

I would therefore earnestly desire you to remain in that calling in which you were called, according to the measure of the rule by which God measured you. If you cannot keep it, inability excuses you; if you can fulfil it and do not will to do so, pride condemns you. But if you allege that your abbot has released you from observing the monastic law, know that, though dispensation has been entrusted to an abbot, he is nevertheless not permitted to establish or tolerate things that hinder the profit of charity. No superior or subject is permitted to follow his own will [Note: [Col. 0387] St Benedict, Rule, ch. 3]. For the legislator of monks, as though by a general edict, commands that all follow the mistress Rule; [Col. 0388C] and neither abbot nor prior is excepted from this law.

Where is the safeguard of obedience which you promised? Where is the profession to which you gave your hand? Where is that which your Rule says: that the monk should subject himself to his superior in all obedience? It is the word of the apostle Peter: “Purifying your hearts in the obedience of charity” [Note: [Col. 0387] 1 Pet. 2]; that is, one subject by vow to another should obey, and filial affection, always keeping paternal reverence before its eyes, should pour itself out, unconfined by any limits, into the breadth of charity as it runs in desire. But if a superior commands things contrary to the soul’s salvation and opposed to the Lord’s command, the counsel is plain: the sentence of blessed Peter must be observed: “We must obey God rather than men” [Note: [Col. 0387] Acts 5]. This is also drawn from Samuel’s saying: “If a man sins against a man, [Col. 0388D] God may be propitious to him; but if anyone sins against God, who shall pray for him?” [Note: [Col. 0387] 1 Sam. 2].

Whatever, therefore, your superior commands you that does not oppose the soul’s salvation, you ought to embrace as though God Himself had commanded it. For even if impossible things are commanded, according to the tenor of the Rule, trust in God’s help and obey in charity [Note: [Col. 0387] St Benedict, Rule, ch. 68]. Speaking to superiors, the Lord says: “He who despises you despises me; and he who hears you hears me” [Note: [Col. 0387] Luke 10]. Blessed Benedict also [Note: [Col. 0387] Rule, ch. 5] declares that the obedience shown to superiors is rendered to God. [Col. 0389A]

It is ruinous in any way to scandalize one’s superior. For if God established a dreadful punishment for scandalizing the little ones, what will become of scandalizing superiors? Certainly, in all things commanded by a superior, contempt is universally damnable. And as charity commends the merit of obedience, so rebellion increases the evil of disobedience. It is a form of contumacy to inquire into the manner of a command, to hesitate, distinguish, or delay. For in the covenant of obedience disputation or argument has no place. If you submit the things commanded to you to examination or suspicion, you stretch out the hand of transgression to the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. This obedience, which passes into the deliberative kind of question, is excessively refined. [Col. 0389B] This is not to obey at the hearing of the ear. It is not regular obedience without delay, but evasive cunning and manifest pride.

But if the abbot is of a wicked life, nevertheless he must be obeyed in charity. For it is written: “Do what they say, but do not do what they do” [Note: [Col. 0389] Matt. 23]. Therefore avoid contempt above all things. For although the Lord at times, according to the prophet’s testimony, prayed for sinners and transgressors [Note: [Col. 0389] Isa. 52], lest they perish; although He prayed for His own crucifiers [Note: [Col. 0389] Luke 23]; although the Church prays for schismatics and Jews: yet you will never find either God or the Church to have interceded for despisers. Nevertheless, concerning contumacy and contempt, the prudence of the holy Fathers made provision, and a remedy was set before transgressors against the evil of disobedience.

I give thanks to God, however, because, as I heard from the report of certain persons, you bade farewell at the first threshold of maturer life to the sins of your youth and the trafficking of ambitious honour, and redeemed the waste of a long time by the fruitful shortening of repentance. But now let not that word of the Wise Man fall from the bosom of your memory: “My son, concerning sin forgiven and propitiated, be always watchful” [Note: [Col. 0389] Ecclus. 5]. For many think it sufficient for the advance of repentance that they have ceased from their shamefulness, and do not recall former excesses. As though these had vanished with the passage of time, they believe that by forgetfulness alone they have fully settled their iniquities with the Lord. Job, speaking to the Lord in the person of such a penitent, says: “You have sealed up my sins as in a bag” [Note: [Col. 0389] Job 14]. And Moses in Deuteronomy: [Col. 0389D] “Are not these things stored up with you and sealed in your treasuries?” [Note: [Col. 0389] Deut. 31]. Things that have grown together in the marrow of the heart are not so easily healed without tears, groaning, and bitter pain of heart; nor is guilt lightly remitted unless humility [Col. 0390A] in repentance corresponds to the magnitude of sin.

Therefore I count it towards the fulfilment of your vows that you have restrained the arrogance of self-exaltation and the gaping appetite of ambition beneath the rule of modesty. For I recall that once you complained and accused God because He raised no one of our tribe to the chair of the elders. Whatever you may now desire, may God humble and bring every understanding of mine and yours into captivity for the service of His own lordship. You have often been able to learn, moreover, from the testimony of the very pope now seated, of many of his cardinals who have exercised legatine office in my time, of my brother, of the abbot of Saint-Denis, and of other great men in the land, that when I was chancellor in Sicily and tutor of King William II, then a boy, and, after the queen and the elected Archbishop of Palermo, [Col. 0390B] the administration of the kingdom depended considerably on my judgment, certain rivals of mine, plotting to exclude me from the king’s intimacy, procured that the Church of Naples should elect me archbishop and that the leading members of the chapter should demand my appointment by a common decree and unanimous vote. Yet, though summoned, I did not go; though repeatedly entreated and pressed, I did not consent.

The bishopric of Rochester was also twice offered to me [Note: [Col. 0389D] This is an error. Since in Epistle 72 he says that while he was in Sicily he was twice called to a bishopric, that bishopric must have been in Sicily, or at least in the lands of the Sicilian king, and not in England, where the bishopric of Rochester is situated. He may, however, be speaking of the archbishopric of Rossano, in Upper Calabria, that is, in the part of the Kingdom of Naples [Col. 0390D]; since it has no suffragans, perhaps at that time it was a bishopric and within the dominion of the Sicilian king. Thus it is written in certain manuscripts, such as Maz. 1 and another manuscript in Busaeus.] and I refused what was offered, measuring honour by its burden and restricting ambitious impulses within the sober bounds of moderation. Most beloved nephew, “Let your modesty be known to all men; the Lord is near” [Note: [Col. 0389] Phil. 4]. He is near, for your day is coming. And, to use Solomon’s testimony: “Judgment will be swiftly and terribly executed upon those who rule” [Note: [Col. 0389] Wis. 6]. For it is dreadful [Col. 0390C] to fall into the hands of the living God [Note: [Col. 0389] Heb. 10], to heap up double sins for oneself, and to incur the flames of Gehenna for the iniquities of others.

Therefore I judge it safer to lie hidden and smoke beneath a bushel than to ascend a lampstand and force my darkness upon the eyes of others. For in riches my light would be darkness, and my illumination would lie in my pleasures. The shamefulness of many, indeed, remained hidden until their assumption of honour, opening the eyelids of public report, brought into public knowledge what their humbler condition had concealed; for dignity reveals the unworthy. Add also that the dominion of many is their damnation. As many as poverty advances to heaven, so many hell swallows up with their dignities. Beware, therefore, lest [Col. 0390D] the deep swallow you and the pit press its mouth over you.

The day of your death is uncertain, and bitter death enfolds old and young alike. What will you do when the condition of human dissolution separates you from the company of those dear to you?
