Therefore, when the eternal night begins to grow black and dreadful, when [Col. 0391A] the importunate and cruel exactor has drawn you beyond the day through the paths of darkness from which there is no return, to hurl you into that monstrous and terrible chaos, into the region of eternal death—how will it be with you when, cut off from the Church of the saints by perpetual excommunication, you see the Son of God lavish the rewards of glory upon His soldiers, while for you, to complete your misery, another’s fulness of pleasure gives way? O how mournful it will be to see and lose God, and to perish before the face of one’s Saviour! Where then will be your high spirits and delights, of which only remembrance remains to accuse you and obligation remains to torment you? The entire substance of the wretched human being will be devoured by unquenchable flames, and there will be no measure, interruption, or end of punishments. For there the end will always begin; [Col. 0391B] death will not die, nor will failing fail, so that the condition of the condemned person may ever recur as material for pain and fuel for eternal death.

Beloved, remember these things, speak them, and exhort others; and, showing yourself lovable and worthy of imitation to your brethren, I go before them toward the prize of life before God in righteousness and holiness. I have cooked a stew for you and for those with you, the sons of the prophets; but if this less gentle exhortation tastes of colocynths, let Elisha add the flour of patience and devotion [Note: [Col. 0391] 4 Kings 4]. Since I have not visited you with any greeting for a long time, affection has poured itself more broadly into the field of prayer, so that a longer letter may compensate for the rarity of letters passing between us. Fare well.

## LETTER CXXXII. TO E., ABBOT OF SAINT LAUNOMAR. [A.D. 1202.]

[Col. 0391C]

**SUMMARY.—** He offers outstanding counsels to a newly appointed abbot, to be carefully noted by all other superiors.

To his beloved nephew E., by God’s grace Abbot of Launomar [Note: [Col. 0391] On him see what we said on the preceding letter], Master Peter of Blois, Archdeacon of Bath, greeting.

Although, in Jerome’s testimony [Note: [Col. 0391] Epistle 103, to Paulinus], I know not what hidden efficacy belongs to the living voice, and the living voice is more effective than writing, nevertheless those who experience the power of charity know that the presence of the spirit is more excellent than that of the body; and, since the spirit is the better part of the lover, so much the worthier is its presence than bodily presence. For if the union of flesh makes two one flesh [Note: [Col. 0391] Gen. 2], how much more strongly does the bond of love and the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace unite two persons? The soul is the better part of me. If your soul does not disagree, nothing impairs the unity of two souls willing the same thing. Yet in this union not only souls but bodies are joined, since I can say of my nephew: “My bone and my flesh.” I glory in your glory and rejoice in the joy of your people. Whether, however, it is expedient for you to rejoice, you must consider. I beseech you by the inward parts of Christ’s mercy to heed the peril of this seat, remembering Solomon’s saying: “Judgment shall be made swiftly and terribly upon those who [Col. 0392A] rule” [Note: [Col. 0391] Wis. 6]. Have mercy on your own soul by pleasing God [Note: [Col. 0391] Ecclus. 30]. Make your ways and pursuits good. Let those who love you rejoice that you are the faithful and prudent servant whom the Lord has set over His household [Note: [Col. 0391] Luke 12]. “The greater you are, humble yourself in all things” [Note: [Col. 0391] Ecclus. 3]. Hear humble and awe-inspiring Christ: “He who is greatest among you, let him become as the younger” [Note: [Col. 0391] Matt. 23]. Your brethren have appointed you their ruler: be as one of them [Note: [Col. 0391] Ecclus. 32].

Benedict, Basil, Arsenius, the two Macarii, and many other masters of religious life hold this same view: namely, that a vow of religious profession, once undertaken, must never afterward be annulled upon any pretext. If the monks’ election, and not ambition, as you wrote to me, made you leader of your brethren, it nevertheless did not take away your being a brother. If you have borne the Lord’s yoke [Col. 0392B] until now, henceforth bear it more patiently, and live regularly among those whom you instruct in the pattern of regular life; otherwise you will be marked by those Gospel words: “They bind heavy and unbearable burdens and lay them on men’s shoulders, but they are unwilling to move them with their finger” [Note: [Col. 0391] Matt. 23]. For the legislator’s ordinance confirms [Note: [Col. 0391] Rule of Benedict, ch. 2] that you should show by your deeds that the things which you teach your disciples to be contrary should not be done—leaving aside the great and greatest commandments. If, according to the constitution of the Gospel [Note: [Col. 0391] Matt. 5], you break even one of the least commandments of the Law and so teach men, you shall be least in the kingdom of heaven.

No election, as I have already touched upon, no prelacy releases you from that vowed promise; nor does the authority entrusted to you annul the vows of promise which [Col. 0392C] your lips pronounced. In your laws [Note: [Col. 0391] Digest, bk. XXXII, title I, law 23], of which you were once a student, the emperor’s statement is: “Although we are released from the laws, yet we wish to live by the laws.” And that of the Code [Note: [Col. 0391] vol. XIV, law 4]: “It is a voice worthy of the majesty of a ruler for the prince to profess himself bound by the laws.” The honour you have assumed has not exempted you from your profession, but has bound you more tightly to observe it. You, already sufficiently burdened with your own transgressions, have, according to Solomon’s word, bound double sins upon yourself [Note: [Col. 0391] Ecclus. 7]. Your subjects honour you, but burden you more heavily. Therefore guard yourself first, that you may more safely procure the guardianship of others.

A weighty stewardship has been entrusted to you. God, terrible in His judgments, will require an exact account of this stewardship. Gregory bears witness that a superior multiplies for himself as many crowns as he gains souls for God. [Col. 0392D] Superiors must also know that, if they commit perverse deeds, they deserve as many deaths as they transmit examples of their own ruin to their subjects. Therefore strive first from yourself and then from those subject to you to root out the deep-rooted shoots of laxity, which long impunity—the mother of insolence—has allowed to take root. With all diligence guard your heart, so that you may be an example to others and may more freely remove scandals from the kingdom of God, which is within you. Do not reserve this office, to the peril of your soul, for the angel-reapers, to whom this ministry is due by heavenly ordinance on the dreadful day [Col. 0393A] [Note: [Col. 0393] Matt. 13].

Set it in your mind that you approach as a new founder of your monastery, knowing that it is more praiseworthy to reform what is corrupted than to give form to what is unformed; therefore do not think upon the looser reins of your predecessors. In everything you must employ riper counsel and more watchful caution. Let their simplicity—or rather their negligence—and the downfall of some make you more circumspect. Put your hand to strong things, and know that every house in which discipline does not rule is disordered. In blessed Gregory’s testimony, “The governance of souls is the art of arts” [Note: [Col. 0393] *Pastoral Rule*, Part I, ch. 1]. Yet you cannot govern souls except through discipline, so that justice and judgment may be the preparation of your throne. Correct your sons with the rod, and, in the Wise Man’s testimony, you will save their souls [Note: [Col. 0393] Prov. 23].

Nevertheless, in every [Col. 0393B] exercise of discipline let mercy hold the first place, so that what severity has embittered by word or blow, devout gentleness may soothe. Be not prone to anger, impetuous in reproach, hasty in judgment, or vehement in vengeance. Let charity prescribe and affection shape your words and deeds; and attend not to what is useful to yourself, but to what is useful to many. For charity does not seek its own things [Note: [Col. 0393] 1 Cor. 13]; nor will you more effectively provide for your own advantage than if your care is devoted to your brethren’s benefit and salvation. Be not haughty in countenance, grim-faced in speech, harsh in threats, excessive in diet, more splendid in horses or household, or conspicuous in dress. You will be beloved by God and men if you preserve your conscience and acts with every caution.

[Col. 0393C] Seek the better gifts, not the familiarity of princes, not the favour of the popular breeze, not the rewards of another’s praise, but the treasure of a good conscience founded in self-abasement and Christ’s charity. Yet you cannot truly be humble if you believe flatterers, if you do not despise your own excellence. But if you desire to be higher rather than better, you will expect not a reward but a precipice. “May the Lord destroy all deceitful lips, and the tongue of those who speak great things,” who say to you, “Well done! Well done!” [Note: [Col. 0393] Ps. 11]. Take counsel with yourself concerning yourself; reject blandishments and close your ears to flatteries. Those who call you blessed lead you into error. If you know yourself to be such as another’s praise depicts, ascribe it not to yourself but to God, saying with the Apostle: “By the grace of God I am what I am” [Note: [Col. 0393] 1 Cor. 15]. “For what have you that you did not receive? And if you received it, why do you glory as though you had not received it?” [Note: [Col. 0393] 1 Cor. 4]. It is as though the Apostle said: all that you have, you received from God. Therefore glory in these things, not in yourself, but in the Lord. But by the counsel of that same Apostle, test your own work, and thus you will have glory in yourself and not in another [Note: [Col. 0393] Gal. 6]—or, what is safer, neither in yourself nor in another, but in God.

It is indeed exceedingly dangerous to entrust one’s glory [Col. 0394A] to another’s tongue and to gain or lose praise at the discretion of one who flatters or cajoles. “Let your soul glory in the Lord; let the meek hear and rejoice” [Note: [Col. 0393] Ps. 33]. Let your praise be at your departure, so that your works may praise you in the gates, when each shall have praise from God [Note: [Col. 0393] 1 Cor. 4]. Do everything with counsel. For Wisdom, the mother of chaste counsels, says in the book bearing her name: “I dwell in counsels and am present among learned thoughts” [Note: [Col. 0393] Prov. 8]. Keep with you in counsel, service, and companionship men tested in religious life, guardians and witnesses of your integrity. As you excel others in rank, so surpass them in the merits of life.

And because perhaps my exhortation carries less weight with you concerning the office of instructing an abbot, I set down the very words of blessed Gregory [Note: [Col. 0393] *Pastoral Rule*, Part II, ch. 2]: “The conduct of a superior ought to surpass the deeds of his subjects as far as the shepherd’s life is normally removed from the flock.” And he adds: “Let him therefore be pure in thought, pre-eminent in action, discreet in counsel, fruitful in speech, near to each individual in compassion, raised above all in contemplation; through humility a companion of those who do well, but through zeal for justice erect against offenders; not diminishing the care of inward things through concern for outward things, nor neglecting the administration of outward things through care for inward things.”

Finally, the abbot, says Gregory, should strive in all things to imitate Christ’s life. For the Apostle testifies: “He who says that he abides in Christ ought himself also to walk as Christ walked” [Note: [Col. 0393] 1 John 2]. Therefore the same Apostle says of himself: “Be imitators of me, as I also am of Christ” [Col. 0394C] [Note: [Col. 0393] 1 Cor. 4]. And, that the pattern of the spiritual rule may be expressed, let him keep continually in his heart the Apostle’s saying: “The grace of God our Saviour has appeared to all men, instructing us that, denying impiety and worldly desires, we should live soberly, piously, and justly in this world” [Note: [Col. 0393] Titus 2].

Let denial of impiety and worldly desire go before, so that you may live piously, soberly, and justly: piously toward God, justly toward your neighbour, soberly toward yourself. Piety, indeed, according to blessed Augustine’s testimony, consists in faith, hope, and charity. Natural justice is this: that you should not wish to do to others what you would not wish done to yourself, and should do to others what you would wish done to yourself. Moderation in temporal things belongs to sober living: a restrained use that satisfies necessity rather than serving pleasure.

[Col. 0394D] The honour you have assumed has obliged you to the guardianship of your subjects. Hear Solomon: “My son, you have pledged yourself for your friend; you have struck hands with a stranger. You are ensnared by the words of your mouth and caught by your own sayings. Do therefore what I tell you, my son: run, hasten, rouse your friend; do not give sleep to your eyes, nor let your eyelids slumber” [Note: [Col. 0393] Prov. 6]. According to Gregory’s exposition [Note: [Col. 0393] *Pastoral Rule*, Part III, admonition 5], to strike one’s hand with a stranger is to take upon oneself, at the peril of one’s own conduct, the care of another soul which one did not previously have.

[Col. 0395A] You are therefore commanded to awaken those entrusted to you with saving admonitions, so that, rising from the torpor of sin and keeping watch in holy thoughts and works, they may bring back from their brief and passing labour sheaves of eternal rejoicing. May He who permitted you to be called to this office so call you that He does not reject you; so honour you that He does not humble you; so exalt you that He does not put you to shame, cast you down, or dash you to pieces. Farewell.

## LETTER CXXXIII. TO R., DEAN, AND THE CHAPTER OF THE CHURCH OF SALISBURY

**SUMMARY.—** He argues that, because of the smallness of his benefice, he ought not rightly to be compelled to reside at Salisbury church.

[Col. 0395B] To his beloved lords, brethren, and friends, R., dean, and the chapter of Salisbury Church: Peter of Blois, Archdeacon of Bath, greeting, and prudence in judgment.

I am astonished that for a prebend of five marks [Note: [Col. 0395C] “A mark is an English monetary unit of thirteen shillings and four sterling pence, or, reckoning each mark in denarii,” says Matthew Paris under the year 1135; likewise William Thorn, p. 2107. Spelman says in his *Glossary*: “A mark is a reckoning of money which today among us contains twelve shillings and four pence.” There is also a gold mark and a silver mark: a gold mark contains fifteen silver marks.] you press me to undertake residence, although you know that my entire prebend would not suffice for travelling expenses as far as Salisbury. If it is insufficient for the journey, much more is it insufficient for residence. But you seek profit from my absence rather than benefit from my presence. Everywhere, in every church, allowance is made for the weak and infirm, or for those who otherwise lack the means of residing; but you impose a penalty upon [Col. 0395C] those whom impossibility itself releases from penal [Col. 0396A] obligation. For punishment is introduced not by inability or failure, but solely by hatred of contumacy.

The constitution of our bishops Osmund and Jocelin is directed against those who hold wealthy prebends [Note: [Col. 0395C]

I have not found among English authors what constitution of these bishops this was. It nevertheless appears to have concerned the residence of Salisbury canons. Osmund, a Norman by birth and governor of the city of Sées, crossed into England with William I, king of the English. Made Earl of Dorset by him, and, because of his supreme prudence, made chancellor and one of the kingdom’s chief counsellors. Of him William of Malmesbury, a contemporary author, writes thus in Book II of *On the Deeds of the Bishops of the English*. Having spoken of Herman, Bishop of Salisbury, who, prevented by death, could not complete his church which had already been begun, he continues:

“On the succession of Osmund, a most excellent man, the church was brought to completion and the other necessary additions were supplied. Clerics distinguished in letters came from every quarter; they were not merely willingly retained, but liberally compelled to remain. There shone out, more than elsewhere, the distinction of the canons in chant and learning, in keeping with the abundance of noble books which had been gathered, while the bishop himself did not disdain either to write or to bind written books. He was outstanding in chastity. The fickleness of report would blush to lie about his virtue; hence it happened that he seemed harsher than was fair to penitents, since he punished more severely in others what he did not find in himself. Free from ambition, he was too wise to squander his own goods or seek others’, and did not oppress the abbeys situated within his diocese with any heavy payment.”

Henry of Knighton, Book II of *The Events of England*, writes of him thus: “In the year 1072 Herman, the first bishop of Salisbury, died. He was succeeded for twenty-four years by Osmund, the king’s chancellor, who built a new church there and gathered clerics distinguished both in learning and in chant, so that the bishop himself did not disdain to write, bind, and illuminate books. He also composed the book of the order of ecclesiastical office, called the *Customary*, by which nearly all England, Wales, and Ireland now make use.” Bromton has the same account under the year 1076, except that he says Osmund was consecrated in the year of Christ 1075, which is more probable. For according to Matthew Paris, Osmund died in 1099.

Concerning Jocelin, Bishop of Salisbury, I spoke at Letter 51. According to Matthew Paris, he died in the year 1184 [Col. 0396D].]

—those whose revenues enable them to build houses in Salisbury [Note: [Col. 0396D] Namely, because the episcopal see—formerly at Sherborne—had recently been transferred to Salisbury, where houses for the canons and others had to be built.] and easily procure what is necessary for residence. Yet, just as contrary practice abolished the decree of Pope Telesphorus concerning the addition of a seventh week [Note: [Col. 0396D] The canonists take this view, together with the archdeacon and Torquemada, on the passage cited, Distinction IV, chapter *Statuimus*. In it they say: “This word *Statuimus* is today merely advisory.” Thus one reads in the first chapter of Telesphorus’s letter to all the faithful without exception: “Know from us and from all the bishops assembled in this holy and apostolic see that it has been ordained that all clerics shall fast from flesh for seven full weeks before holy Easter. For as the life of clerics ought to differ from the conduct of laypeople, so distinction ought also to be made in fasting.”], so—or rather, more strongly—the custom of those who practise the opposite has altogether abrogated the constitution of the aforesaid bishops.

Since, therefore, the means of residing have been cut off from me, what fault of mine brings this penalty upon me—that, because I do not do what is impossible for me, I ought to lose a fifth part of my prebend? [Col. 0396B] Pharaoh’s rule is more tolerable than this constitution. For when all Egypt was compelled, by the king’s public edict, to assign a fifth part of its possessions to the treasury, the priests and Levites did not feel the burdens of that law. Do you wish me to spend here the revenues of other churches? The Council of Gangra forbids this to me: by its authority, my residence ought to be more frequent where I receive the better benefices, as ought my daily support of the poor. Therefore spare your brother, my lords and friends, whom impossibility itself exempts from the necessity of residence. For what I cannot do, I am not bound to do; what is not owed is unjustly demanded of me. Therefore I appeal to the legate against this unjust [Col. 0396C] exaction. Farewell.

## LETTER CXXXIV. TO WILLIAM, ELECT OF SAINT MARY’S. (A.D. 1196.)

[Col. 0397A]

**SUMMARY.—** He excellently instructs V., recently elected abbot, in all matters pertaining to his office.

To the reverend Father and lord WILLIAM, by God’s grace elect of St Mary’s at Blois [Note: [Col. 0397D] It is today called Bourg-Moyen, commonly Bourgmoyen, and is a monastery of Regular Canons of St Augustine. For an eloquent commendation of them, especially of their four communities of canons, among which the community of St Mary’s at Blois is listed, see James of Vitry, *History of the West*, book II, chapter 21 [Col. 0398D]. In *Gallia Christiana*, moreover, that William is recorded as abbot of Bourg-Moyen in the year 1196; and thus this letter seems to have been written in that year, namely the year in which William was elected.], his own PETER of Blois, archdeacon of Bath, greeting in him who sends forth roots among his chosen ones.

You have been chosen abbot by your brethren. Therefore I magnify in you the mercy of the Saviour—if indeed it is mercy, rather than a certain trial, so that the gain of honour may someday turn into lamentation. It was far safer to be subject than to preside; yet it is greatly meritorious if you preside in such a manner as to be of benefit. My dearest Father, while you served in a lesser office, you were often a stumbling-block to yourself, frequently a burden to yourself, and always in danger; but now, set upon the lampstand, you have entered the arena of an uncertain issue.

For if you consider the anxieties of possessions and the perils of souls, “without are conflicts, within fears.” According to Solomon’s saying [Note: [Col. 0397] Ecclesiasticus 7], you have thrust yourself into a multitude and bound double sins upon yourself. Hence many wish to lie hidden under a bushel, and, cherishing in the bosom of memory the good of inward glory, shut themselves within the bounds of conscience, recalling that prophetic word: “My secret is mine; my secret is mine” [Note: [Col. 0397] Isaiah 24]. And now, most loving Father, you must be drawn in diverse directions, toil for others, be anxious with Martha, set aside that one thing necessary [Col. 0397C], and pass from Mary’s repose into a kind of labyrinth of the soul [Note: [Col. 0397] Luke 10].

Yet do not let outward care so carry you away that the abyss of worldly anxieties swallows up your soul, for which Christ died. Always bear about with you a certain inner solitude, so that a mind gathered into itself may not flow away into external things, nor heed what appears outside or what sounds outwardly. Amid many people you will be alone with yourself, becoming one of those whom blessed Job describes when he says: “These are they who build solitudes for themselves, that they may not hear the voice of the taskmaster” [Note: [Col. 0397] Chapter 3]. Minister, then, in such a way that your ministry is not blamed; reckon yourself the servant of every individual, though you are lord of all. Let the contemplative and active lives alternate their turns in you, so that you have no idle time [Col. 0397D]. The spirit is better than the body, and bodily exercise profits little; but godliness is profitable for all things, having promise of the life which now is and also of that which is to come [Note: [Col. 0397] 1 Timothy 4]. Therefore desire the better gifts [Note: [Col. 0397] 1 Corinthians 12]. For flesh and blood shall not possess the kingdom of God [Note: [Col. 0397] 1 Corinthians 15]. The flesh profits nothing [Note: [Col. 0397] John 6].

But the fruits [Col. 0398A] of the Spirit are charity, joy, peace, patience, long-suffering, faith, modesty, gentleness, self-control, chastity [Note: [Col. 0397] Galatians 5]. It is good to be anxious with Martha, but it is more tranquil to sit at Jesus’ feet with Mary: to set the Lord always before one’s sight, to be still and see how sweet the Lord is [Note: [Col. 0397] Psalm 45]. Therefore, after you have arranged what the brethren’s need demands, descend into the gardens of spices, that you may feed upon spiritual delights and gather the most pleasing lilies of joys. When you have released your soul to rest, let no one, I beg, awaken the beloved until she herself wills it. Nor permit anyone to tear you away prematurely from Rachel’s embraces and from the breasts of holy delight.

You know that those who profess the holy Rule, if they entangle themselves inquisitively in secular affairs, suffer great losses in spiritual exercise [Col. 0398B]. A ship, though it may not at once perish amid stormy whirlpools, nevertheless sustains the loss of its cargo, so that it reaches harbour empty and void.

Your brethren have chosen you: be among them as one of them [Note: [Col. 0397] Ecclesiasticus 32]. Build them up by word, deed, countenance, dress, and bearing. Show yourself so lovable and imitable that your whole conduct builds others up unto salvation. Do what benefits not only yourself but many people. Never live separately. Have neither, like foxes, a den; nor, like birds, a nest; nor purses like Judas.

From the first stirrings of my youth I have known, venerable Father, your character, fragrant with gentleness, sociable in companionship, seasoned with humility [Col. 0398C], and fashioned for every propriety. It is commonly said that honours change character—or rather reveal it. I pray that your present administration may never fall away from that nobility of character; let no prompting of self-exaltation or glory steal upon you because of your promotion. If you must glory, glory in your infirmities, so that Christ’s power may dwell in you. For if you judge yourself weak for the burden, less competent and less worthy, that very self-abasement will grow strong unto grace, abound unto fruit, and be accumulated unto a crown.

The Lord of glory himself says: “If I seek my own glory, my glory is nothing” [Note: [Col. 0397] John 8]. “You seek glory from one another,” he says, “and do not desire the glory which is from God alone” [Note: [Col. 0397] John 5]. “Not unto us, O Lord, not unto us, but give glory unto thy name” [Note: [Col. 0397] Psalm 113]. But you, Father, if you glory in God, will not [Col. 0398D] be foolish: “Let him that glories, glory in the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0397] 2 Corinthians 10]. And as for that glory which is the testimony of your conscience [Note: [Col. 0397] 2 Corinthians 1], ascribe it to God and not to yourself. For, to use the Apostle’s words: “What have you that you did not receive?” [Note: [Col. 0397] 1 Corinthians 4]. Therefore, if a favourable breeze blows upon your ears at the voice of flatterers, let that saying of the Apostle be in your mouth and heart [Col. 0399A]: “By the grace of God I am what I am” [Note: [Col. 0399] 1 Corinthians 15].

Nothing stands nearer to, or with greater confidence before, divine majesty—and nothing is more pleasing—than true humility. The Author of the universe confesses himself meek and humble of heart [Note: [Col. 0399] Matthew 11]. Therefore let not the foot of pride come upon you; but the greater you are, humble yourself in all things [Note: [Col. 0399] Ecclesiasticus 3]. Account this administration a burden, not an honour; and root out every stirring of itching pride with Solomon’s saying: “The mighty shall suffer mighty torments, and swift and terrible judgment shall be made upon those who rule” [Note: [Col. 0399] Wisdom 6].

Always consider that the Lord will demand from you a most exact account of his sheep. “For this reason the wicked man has provoked God: for he has said in his heart, ‘He will not require it’” [Note: [Col. 0399] Psalm 9]. But God says through Ezekiel [Note: [Col. 0399] Chapter 34]: “Behold, I will require my sheep from the hand [Col. 0399B] of the shepherd.” The Lord says, “I will require”; the wicked man says, “He will not require.” Whose assertion do you think will prevail? It is the word of the prophet Isaiah [Note: [Col. 0399] Chapter 14]: “The Lord of hosts has sworn, saying: Surely, as I have thought, so shall it be; and as I have purposed in my mind, so shall it come to pass.”

Do not, I beg, emulate evildoers [Note: [Col. 0399] Psalm 36]. For there are abbots who seek rather what is their own than what belongs to Jesus Christ [Note: [Col. 0399] Philippians 2]. “By their fruits you shall know them” [Note: [Col. 0399] Matthew 7]. These, having entirely set aside the care of souls, judge that they have fulfilled the highest duty of their office if, to their own destruction and that of their dependants, they magnificently cultivate and enlarge their church’s possessions by right and wrong, with tillage and buildings. But the care of souls, which had conceived the fruit of salvation from the spirit of fear, they perniciously procure as an abortion; so that the prophet’s saying is rightly applied to them [Note: [Col. 0399] Amos 1]: “They cut open the pregnant women [Col. 0399C] of Gilead, to enlarge their borders.” These are those driven by the spirit of this world, the spirit of dizziness and error.

It is better for you to increase your household in morals than in possessions. It is better to fill heaven than a granary; and you can do this without omitting the other. But cut down promptly the lingering shoots of vices which have sprung up through the negligence of certain of your predecessors, lest suckers that never bear fruit impede the growth of their own cut branches. Do everything with counsel going before; yet do not believe every spirit, but first test whether it is from God [Note: [Col. 0399] 1 John 4]. Always put your confidence more in prayer than in your own prudence; in God alone, not in familiarity with princes, for “cursed is he who trusts in man” [Col. 0399D; Note: [Col. 0399] Jeremiah 29], and according to the Wise Man’s sentence, “The name of the Lord is exceeding strength” [Note: [Col. 0399] Proverbs 18].

You write that, through the continual cunning of the crafty enemy, you suffer grievous troubles; and that you therefore need the aid of Holy Scripture, whose frequent reading may frustrate hostile efforts and calm, by a certain serenity of grace, the storms of boiling temptations. For this reason you urgently ask back your book [Col. 0400A], which you call one of four. I know that scarcely half an hour of cloistered life passes without temptations. Hence regular warfare requires spiritual arms, of which the Apostle, writing to the Corinthians, says: “The weapons of our warfare are not carnal, but mighty through God for the destruction of strongholds, destroying every height that exalts itself against the knowledge of God, bringing every understanding captive into the obedience of Christ” [Note: [Col. 0399] 2 Corinthians 10].

Sacred reading is therefore necessary for you. It is the table of the tabernacle, placed to the north [Note: [Col. 0399] Jeremiah 1], whence every evil is opened. The Psalmist signifies this when he says: “You have prepared before me a table against those who trouble me” [Note: [Col. 0399] Psalm 22]. Isaiah speaks of this table and of spiritual weapons [Note: [Col. 0399] Chapter 21]: “Set the table,” he says, “keep watch in the watchtower; arise, princes, and take up the shield.” Sacred reading is food, because, as Truth testifies: “Man does not live by bread alone, but by every word which proceeds from the mouth of God” [Note: [Col. 0399] Deuteronomy 8; Matthew 4]. Through this food we breathe and live. “The words,” says the Lord, “which I speak to you are spirit and life” [Note: [Col. 0399] John 8]. Certainly Christ in the wilderness used the testimony of sacred utterance alone against all the devil’s temptations. Therefore, if armies stand against you, arm yourselves with the shield of good will and with the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God. The field of my exhortation indeed extends very widely; but the pressing necessity of my occupations, girding this letter down to brevity, turns me to other matters.

[I beseech the sons of your obedience, my brethren and lords, in the bowels of Christ and in unfeigned charity [Col. 0400C], to have this mind in themselves which was also in Christ Jesus: that, as for us he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant [Note: [Col. 0399] Philippians 2], so they may humble themselves for Christ in the service of servitude. Let them present their body as a living, holy sacrifice pleasing to God, so that their whole faculty of sense, absorbed by reason, may be subjected to the spirit in the service of the living God. Sensuality is the woman to whom it is said: “Your turning shall be toward your husband” [Note: [Col. 0399] Genesis 3]. Therefore let all reason be humbled and all understanding be led captive into the obedience of Christ.

You have declared war upon your own flesh, striving not to be what you are and courageously recovering what you lost in your first origin, so that you may seize the kingdom of heaven by force and violently press yourselves into the inheritance of the saints. With the Samaritan woman [Col. 0400D] you have left behind the water-jar of desire [Note: [Col. 0399] John 4], and you have destroyed your spiritual Jericho within yourselves [Note: [Col. 0399] Joshua 6]. But it is written: “Cursed is he who rebuilds Jericho.” Therefore you, dearest brother, who have given your hand to the apostolic law, who have put your hand to mighty deeds, use the counsel of the Wise Man: put your foot into the fetters of obedience, and do not grow weary of its bonds [Note: [Col. 0399] Ecclesiasticus 6].

Remember that the obedient man, in Wisdom’s testimony, “speaks victories” [Col. 0401A], while through the good of obedience he triumphs in Christ over the devil, the world, and himself. Without any choosing, without any exception, let the professor of the Rule do what is commanded him. Let him not distinguish what, of what kind, or how great the thing commanded is; otherwise he presumes to eat of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. For the judgment of discernment belongs to the spiritual Father, “who judges all things, while he himself is judged by no one” [Note: [Col. 0401] 1 Corinthians 3]. Therefore let him distinguish nothing. Let him be undiscerning, that he may understand; let him be foolish, that he may be wise. Let him not judge it an injury if he is at times grieved by correction or a blow, when he recalls that he has often exceeded measure through empty joy. All discipline is bitter in the present, but in the future it produces the most peaceful fruit of righteousness [Note: [Col. 0401] Hebrews 12].

Let one who slackens on the way [Col. 0401B] of the Lord endure stern rebuke from his shepherd; for the sluggard must be pelted with ox-dung [Note: [Col. 0401] Ecclesiasticus 22]. Therefore, whoever is led by the Spirit of God should bear an admonishing master with equanimity; and, if what he hears is harsh, let him judge himself worthy of harsher things.

And you, beloved, God has set apart as an inheritance for himself, that he may rejoice in the goodness of his chosen ones with his inheritance—provided that you have not received again the spirit of this world. Therefore set your hearts upon your ways, lest you become land near to a curse, which the Lord will strike with the spirit of his mouth. Remember that not only the tree that bears bad fruit, but also the tree that bears no good fruit, shall be cut down and cast into the fire. The axe [Col. 0401C] is indeed laid to the root [Note: [Col. 0401] Matthew 3]; and whether a tree falls to the south or to the north, there it shall be [Note: [Col. 0401] Ecclesiastes 11]. For the Lord shall judge the ends of the earth and shall catch man in his deeds.

While you were in the world, the ancient enemy exercised no envy against you; for he does not attack those whom he considers his own from the testimony of their works. But now, because he sees his idols changed into Christ’s temples, after losing his prey he goes about like a roaring lion, and, anxiously seeking every art of harm, he turns his wiles in every direction. The person whom he cannot suddenly cast down from the state of a good conscience, he gradually troubles by certain fantastical imaginations that secretly creep in. For, according to blessed Job’s words, waters hollow out stones; the falling mountain slides away; the rock [Col. 0401D] is moved from its place; and by alluvial washing the earth is gradually consumed [Note: [Col. 0401] Job 14]: so hidden temptations soften and overthrow the strength of the mind. But the soul torn from the foundation of virtue falls into sin.

Adding iniquity upon iniquity, he multiplies assaults through evil angels, and thus, after he has brought it down from its citadel as from a higher place, he rises in combat and wins an ignoble triumph over the wretched and deceived soul. Thus, through the enticements of this life, wretched people are removed far from God, saying, “Anathema to Jesus”; and at last, turned into a crooked bow and given over to a reprobate mind, they reap evils in destruction [Col. 0402A]. You know that human life is temptation and warfare upon earth [Note: [Col. 0401] Job 7]. Some temptations are above us, some beneath us, some beside us, some within, some without; and all are against us.

Walk therefore cautiously. The world is full of snares, full of ambushes, full of dangers and unavoidable stumbling-blocks, and of innumerable deaths. You have entered the cloister: it is good for you to be here and not depart from the counsel and assembly of the righteous. Friend, if you leave the cloister, you transgress, and as though under the cast of a die you put your soul at hazard. The lion is at the doors to seize you, and there will be none to rescue you. The burning wind rushes from the wilderness, if perhaps it may find chaff to snatch away and scatter for its sport. By manifold devices of refined fraud [Col. 0402B], the apostate angel strives to change the congregation of saints into a theatre, the people of acquisition into a worldly spectacle, and the school of innocence into derision.

Brother, I beg, let your soul always be in your own hands [Note: [Col. 0401] Psalm 118]. You possess an incomparable treasure in an earthen vessel; and when you leave the cloister, you expose to the danger of a hazardous throw the drachma for which that great merchant gave his life. Let Dinah’s departure and her violation terrify you, brother [Note: [Col. 0401] Genesis 34]. Remember that Jacob, remaining at home, inherited his father’s blessing [Note: [Col. 0401] Genesis 27]. But Esau, wandering and hunting abroad, was deprived of his birthright, his father’s blessing, and his inheritance [Note: [Col. 0401] Genesis 25].

Never enter the houses [Col. 0402C] of secular people; for wickedness is in their dwellings, nor will God be known in their houses. Therefore say with the Prophet: “I have hated the assembly of evildoers, and I will not sit with the ungodly” [Note: [Col. 0401] Psalm 25]. You dwell among scorpions; therefore, according to Jerome’s teaching [Note: [Col. 0401] Jerome, letter to Eustochium, *On the Guarding of Virginity*, ch. 11], be honourable at home and seldom seen among people or in public. Should one of your relatives fall ill or die, let neither their illness nor death be an occasion for your departure. “Let the dead bury their dead.” Family affection is deceitful and treacherous. Carnal love, apart from God’s love, will swiftly take hold of you; and affection for the world, which had already withered in you, will grow green again to the soul’s destruction. You are dead to the world and to your relatives; you have been planted together in the likeness of Christ’s death, and your life is hidden with Christ in God. Do not again [Col. 0402D] live in the world and surrender the weapons of victory to the enemy.

Jerome says [Note: [Col. 0401] Letter 1 to Heliodorus]: “The enemy holds a sword to kill me, and shall I think of my parents’ tears? Shall I concern myself with my parents’ burial, when I ought to be concerned lest I be buried in hell?” Do not, I beg, go out, because death is in the going out and waits for you at the threshold. As soon as you leave the door, death enters through the windows of your eyes. I pray that you have no dealings at all with a secular person. For “he who touches pitch shall be defiled by it” [Note: [Col. 0401] Ecclesiasticus 13]; evil conversations corrupt good morals, and a depraved life [Col. 0403A] is drawn from companionship.

Seneca, writing to Lucilius, says [Note: [Col. 0403] Letter 7]: “Frequent association with the base, and a multitude unlike themselves, could shake the good character even of Socrates, Laelius, and Cato.” The Apostle says: “We are not ignorant of Satan’s devices” [Note: [Col. 0403] 2 Corinthians 2]. From this very circumstance the devil is given an apt and manifold opportunity for malice: the uncircumcised have surrounded you, and you dwell as though in the midst of Canaanites. A small interval of walls stretches between your cloister and the marketplace. You dwell as though in the midst of Babylon; and it is strange—indeed miraculous—if the uproar of the populace does not disturb the sabbath of your rest.

You are so besieged by the importunity of secular people that you can lament with the mourning prophet: “The enemy has built round about me and surrounded me with gall and labour. He has enclosed my ways with squared stones; he has become to me a bear lying in wait, a lion in hiding; he has turned aside my paths and made me desolate” [Col. 0403B; Note: [Col. 0403] Lamentations 3]. You dwell in the midst of a people with polluted lips, who frequently apply to you in mockery the saying: “They mingled among the nations and learned their works” [Note: [Col. 0403] Psalm 105]. Would that one of the seraphim might fly to you and, taking a coal from the altar, cleanse in them the rust of their hearts and the dross of their lips [Note: [Col. 0403] Isaiah 6].

But act prudently, providing what is good not only before God but also before men [Note: [Col. 0403] Romans 12], and apply yourselves more watchfully to the business of your salvation. Let the fear of God, the fire of Gehenna, the remembrance of Christ’s sufferings, the memory of your own transgressions, the day of death, and the expectation [Col. 0403C] of the dreadful judgment be continually before the eyes of your heart. Hear Jerome saying: “Let the people praise, let men indulge themselves, let rumours spread abroad; and say: ‘It is good for me to cleave to God and to place my hope in the Lord my God. For what have I in heaven, and what have I desired upon earth besides you? God is the God of my heart and my portion for ever’” [Note: [Col. 0403] Psalm 72].

The time is near when lovers of the world and transgressors of the holy order, cut off from the root of eternal life, will be driven into outer darkness and excluded from the Church of the saints by perpetual excommunication; then, amid intolerable anguish of pain, they will measure how perniciously the appetite for transient pleasure deceived them. Therefore let the fear of God not permit you to slacken in the Lord’s way, but let it continually stir your hearts toward better things: life is short, the end uncertain, the Judge terrible [Col. 0403D], the flame unquenchable, the worm undying, and the punishment has neither respite nor end. Farewell.]

## LETTER CXXXV. [FROM HUBERT, ARCHBISHOP OF CANTERBURY, TO THE DEAN AND CHAPTER OF SALISBURY.] [A.D. 1189–1200.]

**ARGUMENT.—**The Archbishop of Canterbury exempts a certain canon from the law of residence and teaches that clerics may for many reasons be exempted from it.

H., by God’s grace Archbishop of Canterbury, primate of all England [Col. 0404A], and legate of the Apostolic See, to his beloved sons in Christ, the dean and chapter of the Church of Salisbury: greeting, grace, and blessing.

Since greater reverence is due everywhere to superiors, and especially to the king as pre-eminent, fiscal administration or public necessity exempts from the common law those who transact the business of the king or kingdom, because one who devotes himself to the advantage of all sufficiently performs his function in every man’s condition, though absent. Therefore, because Master Thomas of Esseben’s fidelity and industry have been proved in many ways in the public affairs of the kingdom, we do not wish you to compel him to residence so long as he is occupied in such affairs. You know moreover that from each of the kingdom’s cathedral churches we may, at our discretion, call into a share of the charge laid upon us those whom we know to be more suitable for this purpose [Col. 0404B]. Nor does it seem improper that the canons of our suffragan bishops should be at our service, if members obey the head.

It is certain that some are necessary to the lord king, some to us; some are ill, some are engaged in studies, some are on pilgrimage; and some persons’ prebends do not suffice for residence [Note: [Col. 0403D] This seems to have been said on account of Peter of Blois, who had excused himself from residence at the Church of Salisbury, of which he was a canon, because of the smallness of its income, as he writes in Letter 133 [Col. 0404D].]. In all these cases judgment marked by discernment and caution must be exercised, so that, in individual cases, consideration may be given to each person’s particular means in observing residence. Therefore, if we write or have written to you on behalf of any such person, let our requests obtain such effective place with you [Col. 0404C] that your own petitions may in due time obtain a desirable result with us. For we bear toward you such an affection of fatherly kindness that we wish neither to command nor request anything of you that ought to result in prejudice to your honour.

## LETTER CXXXVI. TO POPE ALEXANDER. [A.D. 1177?]

**ARGUMENT.—**Henry II, King of England, complains of the rebellion against him of Henry and his other sons, and implores the aid of Pope Alexander III.

To his most holy lord ALEXANDER, by God’s grace supreme pontiff of the Catholic Church: H., King of England, Duke of Normandy and Aquitaine, Count of Anjou [Col. 0404D] and Maine, greeting and the service of devoted submission.

“In the straits of great dangers,” etc. See among the various letters to Alexander after his *Regesta*, in volume CC of the *Patrologia*.

## LETTER CXXXVII. TO MASTER ALEXANDER OF ST ALBANS

**ARGUMENT.—**He congratulates Master Alexander, now a novice, on entering religious life; exhorts him courageously to bear the new yoke of obedience and the unfamiliar rigour of discipline; and to die perfectly to the world and to himself.

To his beloved and most beloved companion and friend, Master ALEXANDER [Col. 0405A] of St Albans, Master PETER of Blois, archdeacon of Bath, greeting, and triumph over the world.

With all the marrow of my soul I rejoice at your conversion and religious life. From my first knowledge of you I loved you—not for appearance, not for profit, but for your virtues in the Lord of hosts. Your learning, indeed, and the widely renowned fragrance of your most commendable reputation have gained many friends for you, notwithstanding Cicero’s judgment, who writes in his book *On Friendship* that scarcely four pairs of friends had existed over many centuries. But today friends have multiplied beyond number. For charity has been poured out in our hearts, and it alone is the seasoning of true friendship. Thus, from the days of the nascent Church, love began to extend the manifold shoots of affections into unity of minds, so that already then the multitude of believers had one heart and one soul [Col. 0405B; Note: [Col. 0405] Acts 4].

I therefore give thanks to God, who brought you out from the midst of a crooked and perverse generation, so that you may hate the assembly of evildoers and wash your hands among the innocent—hands which contracted many stains from the foulness of the world. I rejoice indeed because you have set before all a wondrous and imitable beginning of religious life. Long before your conversion, having cast aside a return desired by many, you chose to be lowly in the house of the Lord. You have spurned the honour of mastership, the praise of men, and the empty joy of this world, that you might rejoice in the joy of the people whom Christ has inherited, that he may be praised with his inheritance.

[Col. 0405C] You have set your foot on the straight way; indeed, dearest friend, you have cast your feet into Wisdom’s fetters [Note: [Col. 0405] Ecclesiasticus 6]. See that you do not grow weary of its bonds. You have put your hand to mighty things, that you may do violence to the kingdom of heaven and force your way into the inheritance of the saints. Assuredly, through adoption you have become God’s son and Christ’s co-heir. For “those who are led by the Spirit of God, these are sons of God” [Note: [Col. 0405] Romans 8]. You may now confidently say: “The Lord is the portion of my inheritance; you are he who will restore my inheritance to me. Therefore the measuring-lines have fallen to me in pleasant places; indeed, my inheritance is glorious” [Note: [Col. 0405] Psalm 15]. Blessed, therefore, are you whose portion and inheritance is God.

Yet while you are a novice, while you are a little child, you differ nothing from a servant, though you are lord of all, but are under guardians and stewards until the time appointed [Col. 0405D] by the Father [Note: [Col. 0405] Galatians 4], to be sent in due time into full possession of the eternal inheritance. I therefore exhort you in the bowels of Jesus Christ: do not let the first fruits of conversion, the new yoke of obedience, the unfamiliar rigour of the order, and the austerity of discipline deter you. Whatever now seems harsh, obedience will turn to gain; and what is now bitter will grow sweet through practice. For to those advancing from darkness into light, the light is troublesome at first, until the eyes become accustomed to it. Amid hard and harsh things, let that prophetic saying console you: “Because of the words of your lips, I have kept hard ways” [Col. 0406A; Note: [Col. 0405] Psalm 16].

It is advantageous to endure hard things lest harder ones come. But if you murmur, if you reject the yoke of obedience, you have received your soul in vain. Moreover, what is hard for you will not be softened either by disobedience or by murmuring. If you now endure grave things for the kingdom of heaven, know that more grievous things were lately endured for transient gain, and not without danger to your soul. Therefore, because, according to blessed Peter’s testimony, children of obedience purify their hearts [Note: [Col. 0405] 1 Peter 1], conquer through obedience the bestial motions of the passions; for, according to Solomon’s saying, “the obedient man speaks victories” [Note: [Col. 0405] Proverbs 21]. For he conquers the world, the devil, and himself. Let not obedience, which was fitting for the Son of God, be shameful to you, I beg; for “the servant is not greater than his lord” [Note: [Col. 0405] Matthew 20].

Therefore have this mind in yourself [Col. 0406B] which was also in Christ Jesus, who, though he was in the form of God, took the form of a servant and carried the course of obedience as far as the punishment and shame of the cross [Note: [Col. 0405] Philippians 2]. But you, humbled and made poor with the Lord of majesty, submit the wandering and free choice of your will, for his sake, to freely chosen servitude. If you recall how much he endured for you, even if you could give yourself a thousand times to death for him, you would still not suffice to make an equal return. He who is mighty has done great things for you, and the worth of so great a benefit admits no equivalent compensation. Therefore let your limbs be worn out by vigils, reduced by fasts, broken by labour; let your eyes melt into tears—indeed, even if your whole brain and the marrow of your body should flow out in weeping, the sufferings of this present age are still not worthy [Col. 0406C] of the glory which may indeed be attained [Note: [Col. 0405] Romans 8], but cannot be valued or repaid.

For what can dust and worm render to the Lord of glory, who enclosed his own soul in death for him, that he might enjoy a blessedness which eye has not seen nor ear heard? [Note: [Col. 0405] 1 Corinthians 2.]

Take careful heed, therefore, how much you owe your Lord; and while you are making progress, never suppose yourself perfect. “Not that I have already attained or am already perfect,” says the Apostle; “but I follow after, if perhaps I may lay hold of that for which I have been laid hold of. But one thing: forgetting what lies behind, I stretch myself toward what is before, pursuing the prize of the heavenly calling in Christ” [Note: [Col. 0405] Philippians 3]. Attend, therefore, to the beginnings of your vocation, that you may know what things have been granted [Col. 0406D] you by God.

It is God’s glorious gift to have renounced the riches and delights of this world. Who is wise and will know these things? Who will understand the Lord’s mercies: that he so mercifully converts the perverse and repays, in exchange for the little substance of this life, the riches of eternal salvation? Therefore vomit out the world in such a manner that you do not return to the vomit. Let affection for the world so die within you that it may never again revive into desire; and so fashion and plant yourself together in the likeness of Christ’s death that you may be dead to the world, dead to your own heart, and that your life may be happily hidden in Christ.

[Col. 0407A] Judge the conversion of those people damnable who leave the world for the cloister but bring worldly manners into the cloister; who despise modest means for Christ’s sake but conceive a greater hope contrary to Christ. Beneath contempt for temporal things a more intense greed lies hidden; for fire burns more fiercely when covered.

It is not enough for you to renounce riches unless you also renounce vices; for it is less dangerous to be a rich man of Christ than a poor man of Antichrist. Turn over and search out every corner of your heart, and cast away from them whatever you have contracted from the world. Let the old man be crucified in you with his deeds, so that the body of sin may be destroyed and you may be reborn into a certain infancy of newness. The Lord has given you trained senses and the grace of surpassing knowledge. I believe [Col. 0407B], moreover, that you also have the Spirit of God. Yet no one pronounces anathema upon the world except in the Spirit of God. Therefore, the better you are, the more watchfully you must beware the wiles of Satan, who does not think it much if he devours the simple; for his food is choice [Note: [Col. 0407] Habakkuk 1.], nor is he astonished if he swallows up a river, but is confident that the Jordan will flow into his mouth.

Therefore, as you approach the service of God, prepare your soul for temptation [Note: [Col. 0407] Ecclesiasticus 2.], recalling how the Lord called the people of Israel: first through the allurements of signs in Egypt; then through patient endurance of temptations in the wilderness; afterward, with nations subdued, the divine promise was fulfilled for them in peace. Thus today God offers certain sweet and gentle beginnings of holy conversion; afterward, the struggles of temptations; and at last a secure rest in Christ [Col. 0407C], and a peace surpassing every understanding [Note: [Col. 0407] Galatians 5.].

You have raised yourself above yourself, so that you may see how sweet the Lord is: so that, on the Lord’s good day, when you hear the voice of the Spirit like a whisper and the soft murmur of a gentle breeze, with an affection of heart as it were purified, you may gather spiritual fruits from the tree of life. Now the fruits, according to the Apostle’s testimony, are charity, joy, patience, long-suffering, goodness, kindness, gentleness, faith, modesty, self-control, chastity [Note: [Col. 0407] Philippians 4.]. In these fruits you have received, soldier of Christ, the pledge of heavenly glory, which contains the promise of the life that now is and of that which is to come. By tasting them you anticipate certain experiences of this world and blessed first-fruits of the eternal vision. With certain wings of desire one flies up [Col. 0407D], and, in the flights of contemplation, hastens onward even to the delights of jubilation, even to the face of the Beloved. Thus one is suddenly carried away from oneself, so as to live now not in oneself [Col. 0408A] but in Christ, being one spirit with him; and, differing from the Holy of Holies only by the barrier of this mortality, one exults in an ineffable though momentary sweetness of enjoyment, and in a drop of heavenly delights experiences how immeasurable is the blessedness of those whose desires are inundated by the torrent of eternal delight.

Since, therefore, God has called you to run after the fragrance of his ointments [Note: [Col. 0407] Song of Songs 1]: “I am the man who sees my poverty” [Note: [Col. 0407] Lamentations 3.]; I cry to you: “Draw me after you” [Note: [Col. 0407] Song of Songs 1]. I am fixed in the mire of the deep; but pray that the deep may not swallow me, that the storm may not submerge me, that the pit may not press its mouth upon me [Note: [Col. 0407] Psalm 68]. O sweetness of hearts, God of souls, delight and glory of those who love you, my hope from my youth: take from me an uncircumcised heart, a congealed heart, a heart of stone. Give [Col. 0408B] me a heart of flesh, a new heart, a humble and contrite heart. Inspire in me love of you, contempt for the world, hatred of sin, and perseverance in repentance, which neither death may interrupt nor sickness anticipate, until your mercy continues it unto progress. Farewell.

## LETTER CXXXVIII. TO WALTER, ARCHBISHOP OF ROUEN

[Note: [Col. 0407D] Concerning him, see what has been said in connection with Letter 124. To this must be added that, while Walter was in Germany on King Richard’s business, a serious conflict arose between the canons and the people of Rouen. The clergy suffered numerous injuries and losses, churches were plundered, and many houses of the canons were demolished. Accordingly, by the authority and with the consent of Walter, the citizens of Rouen were excommunicated by the bishops of three suffragan sees of the Church of Rouen. They were not absolved until the damages inflicted upon the Church had been fully repaired [Col. 0408D]. Documents concerning this excommunication issued by Pope Celestine III are found at the end of the Appendix to the notes. We have also added certain other charters of the same Walter, as well as the Council of Rouen held at the beginning of his pontificate. Since all these came into our hands too late, we were compelled to place them here, although they properly belong with Letter 124.]  
[A.D. 1197.]

### Summary

He congratulates Archbishop W. upon his return from exile and the restoration of peace to the Church of Rouen. He explains why the righteous suffer and warns him to ascribe peace to God, its author.

To his beloved and most dearly beloved lord, WALTER, by God’s grace Archbishop of Rouen, PETER of Blois, Archdeacon of Bath, his own, greeting—and whatever may be sweeter [Col. 0408C] or more desirable than salvation.

Occupied with the cares of a certain new work, I scarcely set my pen in motion to write a letter; yet obedience stirs and rouses my sluggishness, love invites me, and imperious devotion compels me. For with devoted and anxious feelings of compassion I often reflect how manfully you laid down your life for God’s covenant and exposed it to danger: your kinsmen to banishment, your household to proscription, your possessions to plunder, and your reputation to mockery. Yet certain persons who were bound to you and to your church by the bond of their profession, shrinking faint-heartedly from the loss of worldly goods, sold the title of ecclesiastical liberty for a temporal advantage [Col. 0408D], subjecting you to voluntary servitude. For though the year of release were offered them a thousand times, they would prefer to have their ears pierced with an awl [Note: [Col. 0407] Exodus 21].

Thus, when the storm of adversity broke forth [Col. 0409A], the contrived pretence of a hypocrite’s love proved to be apparent but nonexistent. Measuring a person by fortune, they became a crooked bow, together with those who built upon the back of innocence. But, in accordance with the saying of blessed Job [Note: [Col. 0409] chapter 12], “a lamp despised in the thoughts of the rich is prepared for an appointed time”; and the lamp long oppressed and darkened beneath a bushel has illuminated the whole West more serenely and gloriously.

Certainly, had they possessed the affection owed to every Christian, they ought to have rendered more earnest reverence to their afflicted pastor. The more unworthy were the things which the innocent man endured, the more he deserved abundant service and honor. Blessed Job [Note: [Col. 0409] chapters 2 and 29] was more glorious lying on the dung-heap than sitting upon a throne surrounded by an army. Those who deemed you unworthy of their subjection ought rather to have measured your dignity precisely by your persecution. For in every dignity nothing is more worthy than the casting off and contempt of honor for the sake of ecclesiastical liberty.

You alone, therefore, went up against the enemy and set yourself as a wall for the house of Israel. You cried out, and there was none to hear; you looked about, and there was none to help. Thus, as an imitator of the most valiant Ehud, the ambidextrous judge of Israel [Note: [Col. 0409] Judges 3], protected through prosperity and adversity, through dishonor and good repute, on the right hand and on the left by the shield of the Lord’s good will, you brought your labors to a fruitful completion. Truly, the name of the Lord is a most strong tower: for who has hoped in [Col. 0409C] the Lord and been confounded? Who has remained in his commandments and been forsaken? “Let those who know your name hope in you, for you do not forsake those who seek you, O Lord.” For you are a counselor in hardship, a helper at fitting times, in tribulation, a guardian in prosperity, and a comforter in adversity.

In your first exile, as I have often written to you, my mind foresaw the omen of a happier outcome, firmly holding that your perseverance would carry the work of your undertaken courage through to triumph. Thus the Lord tests the spirits of the elect with scourges; thus the Canaanite and the other nations are left by the Lord, that he may train Israel through them. For two things afflict us: vices and scourges. Through the former we learn what we are in ourselves; through the latter, what we may hope from [Col. 0409D] the world. The Lord scourges the just man, and he scourges the wicked. For of the scourge of the wicked the Lord says through the prophet: “I struck you with the wound of the wicked, with a cruel chastisement” [Note: [Col. 0409] Jeremiah 30]. And again: “Why do you cry out over your affliction? Your wound is incurable” [Note: [Col. 0409] ibid.].

But God scourges the just man, and dispenses around him both prosperity and adversity with fatherly moderation, so that a man may know himself; may correct his own faults; may deter others by his example; may make human virtue known; and so that affliction may give understanding for caution, while caution may lead to a crown and glory [Col. 0410A]. By the teaching anointing which instructed you about all things, God taught you from the first beginning of your exile; and, establishing your heart upon the stone of help, he fashioned you for the endurance of every injury. He receives insults more safely who arms himself beforehand with the shield of patience. The power of this virtue is such that, if anything harsh comes, it receives it courageously; what does not come, it counts as gain; and amid hardships it considers itself worthy of still harsher things.

There are, then, very many who attribute this peace of kingdom and Church to your merits, because of Solomon’s saying: “When a man’s ways please the Lord, he will turn even his enemies to peace” [Note: [Col. 0409] Proverbs 16]. But you must provide more cautiously and vigilantly lest ingratitude take away what grace has bestowed. Refer to God’s glory, and not to your own, all that [Col. 0410B] God has mercifully worked with you. Far be it from you to share the lot of those who once said: “Our hand is exalted, and not the Lord, made all these things!” [Note: [Col. 0409] Deuteronomy 32.] Therefore do not hope in your bow, because your sword will not save you, but God’s right hand and his arm, and the light of his countenance [Note: [Col. 0409] Psalm 89].

It is best for one set on high not to think highly, but to fear. For blessed is the person who is always afraid [Note: [Col. 0409] Proverbs 28]. Security is dangerous everywhere; therefore holy Job [Note: [Col. 0409] chapter 9] feared all his works. Though he had devoted himself to sacrifices, humility, hospitality, and almsgiving; though he was just, upright, and God-fearing; although the Lord’s scourges had fully purified him, still, mindful of his imperfection, he said: “I am troubled at the Lord’s presence, and am anxious with fear” [Note: [Col. 0409] Job 23].

Indeed, the daughters of security are negligence, ingratitude, and pride. These led King David [Note: [Col. 0409] 2 Samuel 24] to number his people; and it turned to lamentation for him and for all the people of Israel. These overthrew King Hezekiah [Note: [Col. 0409] Isaiah 38], whom the Lord had honored by the sun’s retreat and Sennacherib’s flight, so that he displayed to the messengers of Merodach-baladan, son of Baladan, king of Babylon [Note: [Col. 0409] Isaiah 39], for empty glory, the houses of spices, gold and silver, spices and ointments; and at once he heard the thunder of divine judgment. Let the example of Job’s sons [Note: [Col. 0409] chapter 1] frighten you: while feasting and rejoicing in their eldest brother’s house, Satan killed them. This is spiritually fulfilled today [Col. 0410D] in those who are set over others for the keeping of discipline, if the hidden enemy finds that they are given over to empty rejoicing.

Let no security therefore steal upon you. Rather, serve the Lord in fear, and cast your thoughts upon him, to whom it is good to cling [Note: [Col. 0409] Psalm 72], to place one’s hope in the Lord God; and abhor utterly everything belonging to worldly display. Establish your heart, then, in spiritual exercise, in the service of him who cleared the cloud of persecution by which the Church was blackened yet beautiful; who, amid pressures, forged for her from the very hammers of injuries [Col. 0411A] a crown of glory.

Certainly, as blessed Hilary testifies [Note: [Col. 0411] Book VII, *On the Trinity*], it is characteristic of the Church that she understands when rebuked, conquers when she appears conquered, and rises more free when her deliverance is despaired of. For Noah’s ark is lifted on high as the flood grows strong [Note: [Col. 0411] Genesis]; and the ark of the covenant, when humbled, shattered Dagon and struck the Philistines in their hind parts [Note: [Col. 0411] 1 Samuel 5]. Since, therefore, it belongs to the human condition to grieve with those who grieve, rejoice with those who rejoice, and bestow anxious feelings of compassion upon your persecution, I congratulate you with all the marrow of my soul on your peace.

For the town of Andely, whenever conflict broke out between kings, was the first to receive the assaults of war [Note: [Col. 0411B]

Concerning Andely—also called Andeleium or Andeliacum—I have already spoken in connection with Letter 28. As Peter of Blois notes, this place was a frequent occasion of evils while the kings of France and England waged war against one another, namely because it lay upon the boundary of those kings’ lands. Nevertheless it was under the lordship of the king of England. Hence it became the cause [Col. 0411C] of a new disagreement between King Richard and Archbishop Walter.

When Richard wished to fortify the place against the frequent incursions of the French, Walter firmly opposed him, maintaining that great loss would thereby arise for his church, of which Andely was a possession. When compelled to yield by force, he fled to the Apostolic See in order to plead his cause before Celestine III. Before doing so, however, he placed all Normandy under interdict, as Roger of Hoveden, under the year 1196, Matthew Paris, and others record.

The following account of the same interdict is found in a manuscript chronicle kindly communicated to me by the distinguished Charles Baron, priest of Paris:

> “In the year 1196 the city of Rouen and all Normandy were placed under interdict because of the castle which the illustrious King Richard built upon the rock of Andely, contrary to the dignity of the Church of Rouen, while the bishops opposed and disobeyed, in order to please the king. The archbishop, however, departed into exile for the Roman court; and the bishops of Lisieux and Évreux [Col. 0411D] went against him, in order, if they could, to reduce his cause to nothing; but they were frustrated in their hope and wish.”

[Col. 0411] A scribal error: all historians give Ely.]

Moreover, three bishops—of Ely, chancellor of the realm; of Lisieux; and the bishop-elect of Durham—were sent by Richard to the supreme pontiff to defend his cause. The first died on the journey, as I stated in connection with Letter 87. On this matter Radulfus de Diceto should be read under the year 1198; there are also found Walter’s letters to that same Radulfus, his friend, in which he sets out for him the entire reason for his exile.

William of Newburgh, Book V of *On English Affairs*, chapter 27; Hoveden, Part II of the *Annals*; and others report that Pope Celestine, having weighed the force of the arguments on both sides, urged Walter to be reconciled with his king and to reach an agreement with him concerning Andely. Walter therefore soon returned to Normandy, made peace with Richard, and advantageously exchanged the town of Andely [Col. 0412B] for other, richer possessions. The manuscript chronicle cited above says of this exchange:

> “In the year 1197, with the consent of the lord pope and the Church of Rouen, Archbishop Walter received an exchange for Andeleium. And the bishops who had formerly been disobedient and had been suspended [Col. 0412C] came prostrate to his feet in solemn procession on the feast of the Conception of the Blessed Virgin Mary, with their mitres and pastoral staffs restored into his hand; and he, moved by mercy, restored to them his favor and their office.”

What that exchange was, Trevet reports more particularly in his manuscript Chronicle under the year 1197, in these words:

> “King Richard, observing that the town of Andely and certain adjoining villages belonging by right to the Church of Rouen were exceedingly favorable to incursions by enemies, made an exchange with the archbishop and the said Church. In return for the said villages he gave his mills at Rouen, on condition that the archbishop should pay from them the alms anciently established; the town of Dieppe, and the town of Busselles, on condition that he should pay the assigned alms of three hundred and seventy-two pounds in Angevin money. He also gave them the manor of Louers [Louviers], and the forest of Alexmund [Aliermont], with its game and all other appurtenances [Col. 0412D].”

Thomas of Walsingham gives precisely the same account in the *Hypodigma Neustriae*. Roger, Matthew Paris, Brompton, and others say much the same. The form of the peace and agreement between King Richard and Archbishop Walter is given in full by Radulfus de Diceto, as is the confirmation of the same exchange made by Pope Innocent III.

Furthermore, from the possessions given to the Church of Rouen in exchange for Andely, Walter assigned a tenth to the chapter of Rouen, as the manuscript Chronicle of Normandy records:

> “In the year 1199 Archbishop Walter gave the chapter of Rouen a tenth of Dieppe.”

The instrument of this donation is printed below in the Appendix of charters.

From all the foregoing it is clear that this letter was written in the year of Christ 1197, when that exchange was made.]

—subject to the yoke of plunder and fire. But now the Lord has made your borders peace [Note: [Col. 0411] Psalm 147] and has set the whole of your affairs in safety. Moreover, your church has received no small increase in its revenues. For those who seek the Lord shall lack no good thing; and God will always make, even with temptation, a way of escape [Note: [Col. 0411] 1 Corinthians 10].

You have come [Col. 0412A] bearing peace and enlightening your homeland; and may peace indeed come in your days! But let it be true peace, the peace of God, which no one else can give—not that peace of which it is said, “Peace, peace, and there is no peace” [Note: [Col. 0411] Ezekiel 13]. For in such peace, behold, there is most bitter bitterness [Note: [Col. 0411] Isaiah 38]. What kind of peace is this, if the maidservant rests while her mistress serves beneath a harsh and degrading yoke? What benefit is it that the flesh has respite from the distress and pain of evils, if a labyrinth of anxieties sets the wheel of evils in motion against the noble soul for which Christ died?

“All who are led by the Spirit of God,” as the Apostle testifies, “are sons of God” [Note: [Col. 0411] Romans 8], and therefore sons of peace as well. For where peace is, there God is. “His place was made in peace” [Note: [Col. 0411] Psalm 75], and by his own testimony peacemakers shall be called sons of God [Note: [Col. 0411] Matthew 5]. The Lord has proclaimed to you the acceptable year; he has given you [Col. 0412B] his peace and has left you his peace: one peace outwardly, the other inwardly. Recognize what has been given you by God, and make use of the benefit of the peace granted; for there is a future for the peaceable person.

It is plainly altogether unworthy and absurd that the most noble soul, appointed [Col. 0413A] for the embraces of the heavenly Bridegroom, should, forgetting its origin and him whose image it bears [Note: [Col. 0413] Genesis 1], be carried off into mechanical affections. Go out more often, then, with Isaac into the field to meditate [Note: [Col. 0413] Genesis 24]; go down into the gardens of spices, that you may taste spiritual delights and gather the most pleasing lilies of joys. Receive from the tree of life the spiritual fruits which, according to the Apostle’s testimony, are charity, joy, peace, patience, long-suffering, goodness, kindness, gentleness, faith, modesty, self-control, and chastity [Note: [Col. 0413] Galatians 5]. To these fruits there is, as it were, an addition and sequel: reverence in one who loves God, diligence in one who seeks him, wisdom in one who finds him, devotion in one who holds him, joy in one who enjoys him.

Rest, therefore, between the two portions, amid the most loving embraces of Rachel [Note: [Col. 0413] Genesis 29]. There be still, and see how [Col. 0413B] sweet the Lord is [Note: [Col. 0413] Psalm 45]; and let no tumult of busy life tear you away from the breasts of desired repose. Hide the treasure of a good conscience more carefully, affixing to it this title, sealed with a more emphatic seal: “My secret is for me; my secret is for me” [Note: [Col. 0413] Isaiah 24]. And may the peace of God, which surpasses every understanding, guard your heart and your understanding [Note: [Col. 0413] Philippians 4], that it may be the form of beauty and seal of holiness for your soul; and may the God of your heart fill your desire with good things, and may God be your portion forever [Note: [Col. 0413] Psalm 72].

## LETTER CXXXIX. TO R., ABBOT, AND THE CONVENT OF CIRENCESTER

[Col. 0413C]

### Summary

He begs the monks’ prayers, that he may be worthily initiated into the priesthood, and gives the reasons why he has hitherto shrunk from it.

To the reverend father and lord R., by God’s grace abbot of Cirencester, and to the entire convent of the same church, PETER of Blois, Archdeacon of Bath, greeting in the author of salvation.

For a long time I have been pressed by the prayers, counsels, and admonitions of friends to pass into the lot of the priesthood and render the due service of obedience to him for whom to serve is to reign. Yet, resisting until now, I have delayed the priesthood; for I considered my works and was afraid. For who, even though most perfect, would not fear to involve himself in the divine mysteries, to present himself as minister of that ineffable sacrament which the Holy Spirit [Col. 0413D] accomplishes, at which angels stand in humble service, by which earthly things are joined with divine, and which receives them into the unity of the assumed body of the majesty of the divine presence?

John the Baptist trembled when about to lay his hand upon Christ’s venerable head [Note: [Col. 0413] Matthew 3]; the prince of the apostles was terrified by the miraculous catch of fish: “Depart from me, Lord,” he said, “for I am a sinful man” [Note: [Col. 0413] Luke 5]; and the centurion deemed himself unworthy that Christ should enter his house [Note: [Col. 0413] Matthew 8]. By what confidence in my merits, then, by what boldness of mind, shall I presume to handle the life of souls, the price [Col. 0414A] of the world, the bread of angels? The higher and more eminent the rank of this ministry, the more gravely danger hangs over it because of its very dignity. “The Lord’s mercies are many, because I am not consumed.” Why then, against the prohibition of the wise man, should I put myself among the sins of the people and add double sins to myself? [Note: [Col. 0413] Ecclesiasticus 7.]

Let one approach it innocent in hands and clean in heart, called by the Lord like Aaron, whom he himself chose. For even if unlawful acts are restrained from my body, nevertheless from my foulest heart, as from a bilge reeking with thoughts, the filth of corrupting imaginations breathes out like a pestilential vapour. Finally, I fear lest, when I ought to become reconciliation for others in the time of wrath, the imposture of my itching conscience may cloud for me and for others Christ’s most serene [Col. 0414B] face, and the bold usurpation of an office may turn sacrifice into sacrilege and life into death for us.

Therefore, glorious and ever-to-be-glorified Jesus, work in me, not according to my misery but according to your mercy, both the willing and the accomplishing of what is pleasing in your sight; and do not weigh your judgments against my offenses. For if you mark iniquities, Lord, Lord, who shall endure?
