[Note: [Col. 0413] Psalm 129.] Therefore, wishing to redeem my days, which I have lost because I have lived ruinously and in ruin, I have resolved to bow my neck beneath the Lord’s yoke, to renounce the more relaxed liberties of life, and, though free, to become in all things the servant of all.

But you, Lord, breathe graciously upon me: strengthen what trembles in me; kindle what grows cold; make firm what wavers; teach what is foolish; raise what despairs; bind what wanders; humble what is proud; rouse what is sluggish; enlighten what is darkened. You also, my beloved lords and friends, in whom God has placed the word of reconciliation, that you may order his covenant over sacrifices and offer to God sacrifices acceptable to him; you whom the very fountain of gifts has more abundantly watered, so that in you the flowers of virtues now burst forth into fruit; you whom he has made an elect race, a royal priesthood, that you may be a crown of glory in the Lord’s hand and a diadem in the hand of our God: you, I say, I beseech through Christ’s mercy, aid me with prayers, help me with vows, lest the weakness that wavers [Col. 0414D] sink beneath the mass of an unbearable burden.

A pure conscience, an unstained life, and an unblemished reputation are required of me, that I may be Christ’s good fragrance in every place. But these are not a human being’s merits; they are the gifts of him who calls things that are not as though they were [Note: [Col. 0413] Romans 4], whose generous and overflowing kindness is rich toward all who call upon him. For he gives abundantly and does not reproach, justifying the ungodly freely [Note: [Col. 0413] Romans 3], so that where sin has abounded grace may abound still more [Note: [Col. 0413] Romans 5].

For, deprived of the support of all merits, after God I have cast and placed the foundation of my confidence in you, most certainly knowing how much another’s faith or prayer can avail even in matters of merit, since the Church often proclaims its efficacy in the daughter of the Canaanite [Note: [Col. 0415] John 11], in Lazarus [Note: [Col. 0415] Matthew 8], in the servant of the centurion and of the royal official [Note: [Col. 0415] John 4], and in very many others. Certainly, in Christ we are all one; and the integrity consisting in the uniform connection of the Church’s members imposes upon all a rule of mutual fellowship and undivided affections of charity.

I therefore adjure you by the unity of faith, the communion of saints, and the confession of one baptism: let the eyes of your charity see my imperfection, and uphold with your prayers the weak man whom the greatness of the burden terrifies. With Christ, what benefits another through him never fails anyone; for grace grows by being bestowed, and the little oil-flask overflows all the more fully the more abundantly charity, the mother of virtues, pours from it into the vessels presented. Your prayer, therefore, never falls empty to the ground; for even if it does not prosper for the person for whom it is sent, at least it returns into the bosom of the one who prays.

Know, moreover, that from my earliest age I have always served either in schools or in courts. Scholarly labor, although ineffective for salvation, nevertheless has in it a certain worldly honorableness and secular innocence. But almost everything done in courts is destructive of salvation: ambitious, flattering, feigned, slanderous, deceitful, envious, cruel, and impious; and, generally, it hunts after temporal gain [Col. 0415C] and empty glory.

I remembered these things and poured out my soul within me, for I shall pass into the place of the wondrous tabernacle [Note: [Col. 0415] Psalm 41]. For behold, the tabernacle of God is with human beings, after the pattern of that shown to Moses on the mountain. Here first is the bronze altar: namely, the contrite and humbled heart, upon which bestial impulses of the mind and irrational acts are sacrificed in repentance. The second altar, free from every rust of bronze, shines with the gold of charity. Nothing carnal is offered upon it, since the conversation of its offerer is now in heaven [Note: [Col. 0415] Philippians 3]; its sacrifice is a holy mind, devout prayer, thanksgiving, and the voice of praise.

At the third altar—which is more properly a mercy-seat than [Col. 0415D] an altar, and is not merely holy but the Holy of Holies—the priest enters with the blood, in sweet affection and with pure, clarified intention, now offering the true blood of the spotless Lamb and sharing in Christ’s sufferings. Hence, often going out from himself in a certain blessed ecstasy, passing over into the Beloved, and becoming one spirit with him, he performs the office of propitiator amid certain experiences of divine sweetness; while through him, as through a mediator of God and men [Note: [Col. 0415] 1 Timothy 2], for those on whose behalf he intercedes with God, the fruit of propitiation [Col. 0416A] is obtained from that blessed yet very brief enjoyment.

Judging myself unworthy of these things, I depend wholly upon you; I lean wholly upon you. Pray to the Lord of anointing that he may anoint me with the oil of his mercy; for the anointing teaches concerning all things [Note: [Col. 0415] 1 John 2]. May it teach me to do God’s will, to bring all my understanding captive into Christ’s obedience, to exercise the priesthood, and to offer him worthy incense as a sweet fragrance.

## LETTER CXL. TO PETER, CLERK OF THE KING OF ENGLAND

### Summary

He exhorts Peter the deacon to reject the study of jurisprudence, which brings ruin to many, to devote himself wholly to sacred theology and the reading of divine writings, and to order his life suitably to his rank. Here is a notable teaching on the Holy Eucharist.

M. PETER of Blois, Archdeacon of Bath, to his beloved companion and friend Master PETER, clerk of the lord king of England: greeting in him without whom there is no salvation.

You are divided, and your heart is drawn in different directions. Carried away by the shifting waves of deliberation, you hesitate whether to turn toward knowledge of the laws or toward the practice of sacred Scripture. In this perplexity, the intention of the end makes the distinction: toward the one you tend on account of the world’s vanity; toward the other, on account of God’s truth. Therefore, following the Apostle’s counsel, seek the better gifts [Note: [Col. 0415] Romans 12], and let Moses’ dragon devour Pharaoh’s dragon in your heart [Note: [Col. 0415] Exodus 7]; that is, let knowledge of truth devour knowledge of vanity.

For he shall not ascend the mountain of the Lord nor stand in his holy place who has received his soul in vain [Note: [Col. 0415] Psalm 23]. You know that the law of the Lord is spotless, converting souls [Note: [Col. 0415] Psalm 18]. But Justinian’s law perverts many and makes them children of Gehenna. The prophet intimates this under a kind of riddle: “He called judgment to fire, and it devoured the great deep” [Note: [Col. 0415] Amos 7]. This happens when judges, presuming upon the depth of civil learning, call God’s judgment against themselves and incur the wrath of divine punishment.

You see how unsearchable an abyss, how thorny a forest, how immeasurable a sea the *Pandects* are, wherein civil law is contained: a whole human lifetime does not suffice for them, and their entire fruit consists in pride and ambition [Col. 0416D]. But the Lord has made a shortened word upon the earth, so that, for the knowledge of salvation and life, you need no longer cross the Alps or cross seas. For, as is read in Deuteronomy: “The word is near, in your mouth and in your heart” [Note: [Col. 0415] Deuteronomy 30]. And, according to the Apostle’s testimony: “The kingdom of God is within us” [Note: [Col. 0415] Luke 15]; it consists not in speech but in the power of God.

There are indeed two things which strongly impel a person toward knowledge of the laws: ambition for rank and desire for empty glory. These are Rechab and Baanah, who slew the sleeping Ish-bosheth by striking him in the groin [Note: [Col. 0415] 2 Samuel 4]. Read, therefore [Col. 0417A], what suits your order and your profession; what recalls your mind from the heat of ambition; what banishes vanities and false insanities far from the affection of your heart; so that, in the fear of the Lord, which is the beginning of wisdom, you may rise diligently and devoutly to spiritual understanding, in which lies the salvation of the soul.

I beseech you, take up spiritual weapons, which, according to the Apostle’s testimony, bring the whole human understanding captive into Christ’s obedience [Note: [Col. 0417] 2 Corinthians 10]. Take up the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God [Note: [Col. 0417] Ephesians 6]. These are David’s weapons, with which, about to overcome Goliath, he rejected Saul’s heavier arms. This is the Wisdom which, according to blessed James’s testimony [Note: [Col. 0417] chapter 3], is from above. First, indeed, it is chaste, and then peaceable. It is chaste because an incorrupt profession pledges it to present a chaste virgin to one husband, Christ; it is peaceable [Col. 0417B] because it asks for the things that make for peace and commands a person to be peaceable even with those who hate peace.

But knowledge of the laws is unchaste, because, in the manner of a prostitute, it is profit-seeking and mercenary; and whatever it has gathered by study for the fair of vanity, it puts up for sale shamelessly and commercially by a contemptible bargain. It is scarcely ever peaceable, because it always litigates over contracts, or as though concerning wrongs, or as though concerning various forms of actions, concerning suits and obligations, judgments, sentences, appeals, and other matters which ought to put lawsuits to sleep, but always stir up the ashes of lawsuits already asleep.

Against this wisdom the Lord speaks openly in the Gospel and does not use a parable: “In vain do they worship me, teaching doctrines [Col. 0417C] and commandments of men” [Note: [Col. 0417] Matthew 15]. And in the prophet: “I shall catch the wise in their own cunning, and I shall reject the prudence of the prudent” [Note: [Col. 0417] Job 5].

Finally, the laws were for the most part established by pagans; but God gave a law of life and discipline. For the God of gods, the Lord, spoke and summoned the earth [Note: [Col. 0417] Ps. 49], so that man, who was earth, might become heaven, and that by the benefit of the fiery law which the Lord brought from Seir, flesh might pass into spirit. The wisdom of the world is indeed folly with God, and the wisdom of the flesh is death. For the Apostle condemns things which have indeed an appearance of knowledge according to human teaching, if they do not build up toward salvation. Human law, therefore, puffs up; divine law builds up. Its professors are wise in doing evil, but [Col. 0417D] do not know how to do good. Its disciples are meek and humble in heart, and the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, guards them. Those are the people who continually go round Mount Seir and never enter the land of promise. These, with the Apostle, judging themselves to know nothing except Jesus Christ, and him crucified, reach the way of life by a kind of shortcut of saving knowledge, and already taste beforehand, by a certain spiritual experience, how sweet the Lord is. And what is sweeter, what more delightful for exultation, what more fruitful for salvation, than to comprehend and embrace you, O God, by [Col. 0418A] faith, hope, and love? It is written: “To know you, O God, is perfect understanding” [Note: [Col. 0417] Wis. 6]. Truth plainly indicates the surpassing character of this knowledge when it says: “And this is eternal life: that they may know you, Father, and Jesus Christ whom you sent” [Note: [Col. 0417] John 17].

They build Jerusalem with bloodshed [Note: [Col. 0417] Mic. 3], whose rivers are turned into blood; for all their learning and eloquence are converted into sin, and the complaint which God makes through the prophet is fulfilled: “I gave them my gold and my silver; but they made Baal out of my gold and silver” [Note: [Col. 0417] Ezek. 16]. Certainly, they make an idol out of the Lord’s gold and silver who reduce their wisdom and eloquence to an instrument of greed and avarice, which is the service of idols. To such persons belong these blasphemous words: “Our lips are our own; [Col. 0418B] who is lord over us?” [Note: [Col. 0417] Ps. 11]. Therefore God gives them a brazen heaven and an iron earth, so that they may be without feeling and without devotion; that they may be dry land, like the mountains of Gilboa, upon which neither dew nor rain descends [Note: [Col. 0417] II Sam. 1].

Civil jurisprudence often has elegant words, but they are leaves without fruit, tuneful trifles, and Sirens sweet unto destruction. I am lying if you have ever seen a professor of that learning attain a happy end in its practice. Blessed Jerome was scourged almost to death by an angel because, enticed by the rhetorical charm of style, he was devoting himself to vanity [Note: [Col. 0417] Jerome, Epistle 22 to Eustochium]. Yet the Lord chastened him severely and did not hand him over to death. But the law of the Lord imparts wisdom to [Col. 0418C] little ones [Note: [Col. 0417] Ps. 18]. It builds up, gives life, and illumines. For “the commandment of the Lord is bright, enlightening the eyes,” so that the soul made in God’s image may, according to the Apostle’s promise, behold with unveiled face the glory of God and be transformed into the same image from glory to glory, as by the Spirit of the Lord [Note: [Col. 0417] II Cor. 3].

Hear the power of Holy Scripture and the efficacy of God’s word; for the understanding of it I urge you to gird yourself with fear and trembling. Truth speaks in the Gospel, saying: “Blessed are those who hear the word of God and keep it” [Note: [Col. 0417] Luke 11]. The prince of the apostles also, when Jesus asked the disciples whether they too wished to depart, said: “Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life” [Note: [Col. 0417] John 6]. Again, the words by which this same man confesses Christ to be the Son of the living God [Col. 0418D] were revealed to him not by flesh and blood but by the Spirit of God the Father [Note: [Col. 0417] Matt. 16]. Finally, God’s words are so spiritual and life-giving that they are spirit and life, as he himself testifies when he says: “The words that I speak to you are spirit and life” [Note: [Col. 0417] John 6].

As the Apostle says: “The word of God is living and effective, and sharper than any two-edged sword, reaching even to the dividing of soul and spirit, and also of joints and marrow” [Note: [Col. 0417] Heb. 4]. For it has the force of the strongest medicine, by which every harmful affection is expelled from the human spirit and purged. And, [Col. 0419A] so that experience of this may convince you: if you are lukewarm, read Holy Scripture more earnestly, and know that the Lord’s utterance will kindle you; for “his word is exceedingly refined by fire” [Note: [Col. 0419] Ps. 118]. If you walk in darkness, you will hear what the Lord God speaks within you in the Gospel and the prophets: “His word shall be a lamp to your feet and a light to your paths” [Note: [Col. 0419] ibid.]. If you have contracted the stain of any uncleanness, Christ’s word will cleanse you. “Already,” he says, “you are clean because of the word which I have spoken to you” [Note: [Col. 0419] John 13]. If a temptation so grave seizes you that your feet are almost moved and your steps almost slip [Note: [Col. 0419] Ps. 72], God’s word will strengthen you so that you do not fall. For, what is more, “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and all their power by the spirit of his mouth” [Note: [Col. 0419] Ps. 32].

If you are in mortal sin, [Col. 0419B] which is the death of the soul, sacred reading will give you life, and what the Lord says in the Gospel will be fulfilled: “The hour is coming, and now is, when the dead shall hear the voice of the Son of God, and those who hear shall live” [Note: [Col. 0419] John 4]. Know this beyond doubt: the Holy Spirit both produced and expounded both Testaments, and by an ineffable artistry of wisdom fitted one to the other. Therefore to the prophet Ezekiel a wheel appeared within a wheel; the wheels rose and moved together, and the spirit of life was in the wheels [Note: [Col. 0419] Ezek. 1]. And what spirit, I ask, rules today among professors of law? The spirit of pride, the spirit of covetousness and boasting, the spirit of dizziness and error. Reject, then, the learning which draws one into destruction; lay hold upon the learning which builds up toward salvation. Learn in order that you may teach, that curtain may draw curtain; [Col. 0419C] “and let him who hears say, ‘Come’” [Note: [Col. 0419] Rev. 22]. Be an imitator of him who says: “Without deceit I learned, and without envy I share” [Note: [Col. 0419] Wis. 7]. Let every deceit be absent, because “the Holy Spirit of discipline will always flee from what is feigned” [Note: [Col. 0419] Wis. 1]. “Freely receive; freely teach” [Note: [Col. 0419] Matt. 10]. For whoever does so and teaches people accordingly shall, by Christ’s testimony, be great in the kingdom of heaven [Note: [Col. 0419] Matt. 5].

Hear, I beg you, Daniel’s testimony on this point: “Those who are learned,” he says, “shall shine like the brightness of the firmament; and those who instruct many unto righteousness, like stars for everlasting eternities” [Note: [Col. 0419] Dan. 12]. But do not search into things above you, nor devise empty speculations; do not strain yourself through the subtleties of disputation or quibbles over words. For the Apostle forbids such things, writing in the First Epistle to Timothy: “If anyone,” he says, [Col. 0419D] “teaches otherwise and does not assent to the sound words of our Lord Jesus Christ and to the teaching which accords with godliness, he is proud and sick about questions and disputes over words.” His judgment is severe [Note: [Col. 0419] I Tim. 6]. Hear, I beg you, what the Wisdom of God says concerning this in the book bearing its name: “Think of the Lord in goodness, and seek him in simplicity of heart” [Note: [Col. 0419] Wis. 1].

Today there is among many a varied contention of opinions; and the waters of Siloam, which flowed quietly [Note: [Col. 0419] Isa. 8], have become waters of contradiction, beside which Moses and Aaron forfeited entry into the land of promise [Col. 0420A] [Note: [Col. 0419] Num. 20]. Thus today, among many people, the flesh of the immaculate Lamb is boiled in water contrary to the prohibition of the law, or torn limb from limb with bestial savagery. It ought rather to have been roasted with fire; and if anything remained, it was to be burned with fire—that is, with the Holy Spirit. Therefore do not presume to prophesy from your own heart; rather, according to the teaching of sacred utterance, learn and teach everything, praying with the Prophet and saying: “According to your word, Lord, give me understanding” [Note: [Col. 0419] Ps. 118]—not above it, not outside it, not against it.

There are indeed those who rashly investigate God’s heights. But, in Solomon’s testimony, it is not good to eat too much honey, and the searcher of majesty shall be overwhelmed by glory [Note: [Col. 0419] Prov. 25]. Ecclesiastes says: “I shall become wise, and wisdom has withdrawn far from me” [Note: [Col. 0419] Eccl. 7]. For man shall approach [Col. 0420B] the deep heart, and God shall be exalted [Note: [Col. 0419] Ps. 63]. God’s knowledge has indeed become wondrous, and you shall not be able to attain it [Note: [Col. 0419] Ps. 138]. Accordingly Paul, doctor of the Church, admonishes us with entreaty: “I say, through the grace of God given to all who are among you, not to think more highly than one ought to think, but to think soberly” [Note: [Col. 0419] Rom. 12]. To think lofty thoughts, certainly, is death; and he easily falls into peril who, considering himself on a height, is struck senseless.

Finally, the angel speaking to Tobias says: “It is good to conceal the king’s secret, but honorable to reveal his works” [Note: [Col. 0419] Tob. 12]. Distinguish, therefore, between mysteries and works. For in Deuteronomy too the heavens were darkened with dew [Note: [Col. 0419] Deut. 33]. And in the Psalm: “Water is dark in the clouds of the air” [Note: [Col. 0419] Ps. 17]; that is, understanding is obscure [Col. 0420C] in heavenly mysteries and prophetic writings. But in those things through which God wrought salvation in the midst of the earth—his emptying into the form of a servant, the shining forth of miracles, the Passion, Resurrection, and Ascension; his establishing faith, teaching us to pray, and instructing us by word and example in humility, meekness, repentance, and mercy—God wills to be honored; and there is the way by which God’s salvation is shown.

But let inquiry and investigation concerning mysteries cease. Let the well be closed, lest an ox or an ass fall into it; lest the bones of the king of Edom be most dangerously reduced to ashes [Note: [Col. 0419] Amos 2], and the beast which touches the mountain be stoned [Note: [Col. 0419] Heb. 12]. Great is the eminence in mysteries, whose understanding must be pursued rather by faith than by [Col. 0420D] human invention.

And, so that by way of example you may see in one of the mysteries an abyss most profound and imperceptible to human sense: when bread and wine are transubstantiated, by the power of heavenly words, into Christ’s body and blood, the accidents which were previously there remain and appear without a subject. And although Christ’s body is flesh and not spirit, it nevertheless refreshes spirit and not body, feeding and giving life spiritually. The same body is among us in diverse places, since it is on diverse altars contrary to the nature of a body; yet that same body at the same time [Col. 0421A] is in heaven. For although by its bodily and circumscribable nature it is in one place only, nevertheless by its virtual power and in a spiritual manner it is in many places.

So great is the union of divinity and flesh—the flesh having been made wholly divine and glorious—that from the fullness of divinity, which, as the Apostle testifies, dwells bodily there [Note: [Col. 0421] Col. 2], that body, though it is bodily and naturally in one place, is nevertheless in many places by divine and spiritual power. And just as God himself, though virtually and essentially in many places—indeed in all places—is nevertheless, in a certain mode of existence, that is, personally, in one place, namely in the very man assumed by grace, so that which belongs to divinity ineffably communicates to its body: by virtue of the union, the Word is spiritually in one man, [Col. 0421B] and the incomprehensible sacrament of that body and blood is in many places.

Gregory, in his Easter homily [Note: [Col. 0421] Gregory, *Dialogues*, book 4, ch. 58]: “At the very same moment Christ’s consecrated body is borne into heaven by the ministry of angels and is seen before the priest’s eyes upon the altar.” But just as the divinity of the Word fills the whole world, so that body is consecrated in many places; and there are not many bodies, but one body and one blood. Therefore, whether someone receives more or less of it, all alike receive the whole and undivided body of Christ.

In these matters and similar ones, reason wholly fails; faith nevertheless does not fail, but reaches what reason does not presume to reach. And, more wonderfully, God’s power is strengthened by the failure of reason. [Col. 0421C] Faith apprehends by grace what reason could not grasp by itself; reason is weakened so that faith may be stronger; reason yields so that faith may deserve more abundantly. Nor does reason begrudge faith its merit, but gladly and humbly assents. For what faith merits, it does not merit for itself, but rather for reason. Faith will indeed be done away, and reason will remain. For faith exists only on the way, whereas reason will be perfect and complete in the homeland. There reason, or knowledge, will reap what faith now sows; and it is fitting that reason there receive the fruit of faith’s merit, which it assists while here, wholly renouncing itself, it fails of itself, in order that one day, by faith’s benefit, it may grow in itself. Faith, therefore, assenting without contradiction, rests wholly on God’s grace and gives glory to God, [Col. 0421D] knowing that he can do what human reason cannot comprehend.

I have touched upon these few matters for you in a rather compressed style, because you are a deacon and will soon, with the Lord’s favor, ascend to the rank of priesthood. You know, moreover, that service at table and proclamation of God’s word are attached to the diaconate. For this reason the apostles chose deacons [Note: [Col. 0421] Acts 6], that they might serve tables and nevertheless preach to the people the word of life. Hear, then, what manner of man you ought to be before ascending Mount Gerizim, there to bless the people with Aaron’s sons [Note: [Col. 0421] Deut. 27].

[Col. 0422A] Paul, in the First Epistle to Timothy, says: “Deacons must be chaste” [Note: [Col. 0421] I Tim. 3]. Understand this of mind and body: they must keep their vessel in holiness and honor; they must exercise themselves in that wisdom which is chaste and peaceable, not in that which is folly with God [Note: [Col. 0421] Jas. 3] and hostile to God, which prostitutes the human tongue—or rather, the soul for which Christ died—by the whorish venality of a sordid bargain. Therefore the Apostle immediately adds in the same place: “Not double-tongued, nor pursuing shameful gain” [Note: [Col. 0421] I Tim. 3]. Here those are openly rebuked who, with a deceitful and double tongue, betray causes entrusted to them and, by a damnable bargain, consign to the punishment of eternal condemnation souls for whose price Christ gave his most innocent blood.

Finally, the rank of the Levitical [Col. 0422B] order not only renounces extraordinary vanities but even extirpates natural affections, so that no one may presume to minister in it unless the attachment of family has first been wholly extinguished in him. For the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: “Let no priest or Levite serve me unless he has first said to his father and mother: ‘I do not know you’” [Note: [Col. 0421] Deut. 35; probably an erroneous citation]. With what conscience, then, may one who is divinely forbidden concern for carnal parents presume to plunge himself into condemnable profits and the inextricable labyrinth of anxieties?

Therefore, brother, I beseech and exhort you, through the power of the heavenly sacraments to which you will soon give the hand of profession: prepare yourself thus, read thus, [Col. 0422C] study thus, live thus, speak and exhort thus, so that you may be called by the Lord like Aaron, whom he chose to exercise the priesthood for his praise and to offer worthy incense as a sweet-smelling savor. Farewell.

## LETTER 141. TO W., ARCHBISHOP OF ROUEN. [A.D. 1197?]

**Summary.**—He complains that the revenues of his benefice have been withheld for five years by a certain Elias, and asks the archbishop, by his authority, to compel him to make restitution.

To the reverend father and lord W., by God’s grace Archbishop of Rouen: Peter of Blois, Archdeacon of Bath, his servant, greeting—and whatever may be sweeter or more desirable than health, with every humility.

Having been assured of your well-being, I give thanks to the author of all graces [Col. 0422D]. For, to use the Apostle’s words [Note: [Col. 0421] Phil. 4], “I live, if you stand firm in the Lord”; for this is my glory and joy, and the crown of my head. Yet in regard to the new work which your graciousness has requested from me, although my excuse has already preceded it, this too may suffice for my fuller excuse: that literary elegance in writing, which once flourished in the young man, now withers in the old. There is scarcely any vigor left in a tree whose root has dried up. Moreover, the human mind embittered by injuries follows in its words the onset of disturbance rather than [Col. 0423A] elegance of expression; for I speak from the abundance of my heart. A person’s heart is like a full vessel, and by its outpouring it shows what it contains within.

I had entrusted to Lord Elias the chaplain the care and keeping of my prebend, as to a faithful and truthful man. But now I am compelled to complain with the Prophet, because truthfulness has diminished among the children of men [Note: [Col. 0423] Ps. 11]. I can also ask with Christ and say: “When the Son of Man comes, do you suppose he will find faith on earth?” [Note: [Col. 0423] Luke 18]. I say nothing to his disparagement, though it seems greatly to blacken his reputation that for five years and more he has rendered me nothing from my prebend; and, forgetful of faithfulness and priestly moderation, he not only inflicts loss upon me but makes this very injury redound [Col. 0423B] to my disgrace and contempt.

I frequently send messengers there, and he always sends them back empty and unprovided for. He speaks to them well, but no deed follows his voice, because “his voice is Jacob’s voice, but his hands are Esau’s hands” [Note: [Col. 0423] Gen. 27]. Indeed, I would more easily wrench a club from Hercules’ hand than a penny from his. He does not regard it as robbery to seize what is mine and to assail me with insulting words. He colors his wrongdoing with this one excuse: that I abound in ample revenues from elsewhere, as if the wrong of an inflicted loss could not be done to the wealthy, or as if possessions held by the better-off could not be expended for honorable uses.

Certainly, many are considered rich who are truly poor; for although wealth flows to them, they do not set their heart upon flowing wealth. Finally David, established on the royal throne, says: “Incline, O Lord, your ear and hear me, for I am needy and poor” [Note: [Col. 0423] Ps. 44].

I believe that riches honorably acquired are commendable, if they are spent without luxury, to the extent that moderate necessity requires. Abraham possessed wealth for lawful uses, and many holy Fathers, lavish in distributing temporal goods, laid up treasure for themselves in heaven. Alas, alas! Since he who does not distribute his own goods to the poor is condemned by Christ [Note: [Col. 0423] Matt. 25], what will become of one who withholds his brother’s property and lives by theft? With what presumption will he offer sacrifice at the altar while his brother has something against him [Note: [Col. 0423] Matt. 5]? He cannot drink the cup of the Lord and the cup [Col. 0423D] of demons [Note: [Col. 0423] I Cor. 10]. How will he escape the common saying: “Sin is not forgiven unless what was taken is restored” [Note: [Col. 0423] Augustine, Epistle 54, 9. 6, ch. 1]? How, according to the Apostle’s teaching, will he lift pure hands to God without contention [Note: [Col. 0423] I Tim. 2], he who invites me into grounds for contention?

For I have letters of the supreme pontiff against him. Yet to me, an old man, it seems absurd to provoke an occasion of scandal against an old man and my brother. For, to use the Apostle’s words, “I am already being poured out, and I have received in myself the sentence of death” [Note: [Col. 0423] II Tim. 4]; and nonetheless death is at [Col. 0424A] the doors, as the Apostle says: “Everything that grows old and is aged is near to destruction” [Note: [Col. 0423] Heb. 12]. Both of us feel death’s forerunners: namely, the failing of the senses and the infirmities of old age. The farther we have withdrawn from the day of our birth, the nearer we have become to death’s end. For, in Solomon’s testimony, “Man does not know his end; but as fish are caught by a hook and birds by a snare, so are human beings [caught] in an evil time” [Note: [Col. 0423] Eccl. 9]. A little life remains to each of us, and even that does not stand still. Soon we shall say to the world, “Farewell,” and unwillingly leave behind what we now cling to with the greatest obstinacy.

For Lady Avarice, who is accustomed to exercise greater tyranny over old people, is, in Zechariah’s testimony, “their eye in all the earth” [Note: [Col. 0423] Zech. 4]. And according to the same witness, “from the greatest to the least, all pursue avarice” [Col. 0424B] [Note: [Col. 0423] Jer. 6]. This beyond doubt is the Samaritan woman’s water-jar: whoever drinks from it will thirst again [Note: [Col. 0423] John 4]. Whatever can be desired could not satisfy the gaping appetite of human covetousness.

How much more gloriously would old people live justly and honorably, and rest in a fruitful old age, so as to be for others an odor of life unto life, a pattern of justice, and instruction unto salvation. For it is written: “Old age is a crown of justice, found in the ways of righteousness” [Note: [Col. 0423] Prov. 16]. I see sick old men whose flesh is consumed, whose skin clings to their bones, and to whom only the grave seems to remain. Their limbs grow cold, but their covetousness burns; their flesh is oppressed by old age, but their ambition grows young. Scarcely will life’s end put an end to avarice. A kind of penal hell will burn in them [Col. 0424C] until a pit is dug for the sinner, until sinners are caught in the works of their own hands and go down alive into hell.

For suddenly the soul which had wholly seethed in the heat of temporal desires, when it departs from its union with the body, naked and miserable, burdened with sins and cut off from the Church of the blessed by perpetual excommunication, will be thrust down into the horror of eternal night and terrible chaos. On that day all his thoughts shall perish, and the Lord who executes judgments shall be known [Note: [Col. 0423] Ps. 9]—the Lord whose warnings they refused to understand. Since, therefore, “it is dreadful to fall into the hands of the living God” [Note: [Col. 0423] Heb. 10], I adjure you by that most strict Judge, who will judge even acts of justice, to turn my right into judgment [Col. 0424D] and, by your ordinary jurisdiction and the office of judge, to be willing to request what makes for peace.

For the Lord has given you a learned tongue, that you may correct those who err; moreover, your tongue has been made the key of heaven. Finally, the Lord has placed you among the angelic reapers, that you may remove from the kingdom of God—which is the Church—all scandals, so that, according to the rules of justice which render to each person what is his own, my property may be restored to me. Nothing is lost to the interests of the Church if things belonging to another are restored.

## LETTER 142. TO P., PRIOR, AND THE CONVENT OF EVESHAM

[Note: [Col. 0425D] Where this monastery of Evesham is situated, I have already said in Letter 97.]

[Col. 0425A]

**Summary.**—He consoles monks under severe affliction, exhorts them to endure it patiently, and instructs them how they ought to conduct themselves.

To his beloved brothers and friends P., prior, and the convent of Evesham: Peter of Blois, Archdeacon of London, greeting—and whatever may be sweeter or more desirable than health.

With all the inmost feelings of my soul and with earnest charity sympathizing with your affliction, I had resolved to write you a consolatory letter in some elegance of style. But because a crowd of business continually and tumultuously presses upon me, and I am almost wholly absorbed by it, [Col. 0425B] I am either not myself or am divided and distracted; and so my thoughts, which torment my heart, are scattered, so that I can scarcely write—not to say a letter—but the briefest little note.

But you who are spiritual, to each of whom manifestation of the Spirit has been given for usefulness [Note: [Col. 0425] I Cor. 12], know how you ought to conduct yourselves and struggle with the world amid the heated wickedness of this storm. For the world lies in evil [Note: [Col. 0425] I John 5], full of snares, scandals, and sins; surrounded by dangers, corrupt speech, wicked counsels, most evil examples, and countless deaths of the soul. Therefore let us redeem the time, because the days are evil [Note: [Col. 0425] Eph. 2]; and comfort cannot fail you if you will devote yourselves earnestly to prayer and Holy Scripture.

Moreover, scandals must come, human hearts must be tested, and amid the Lord’s scourges affliction must give understanding to the heedless. We are all indeed children of wrath [Note: [Col. 0425] Eph. 3]; and if the Lord appears angry with us, let us reckon this love rather than hatred and bear his scourge with equanimity. The Prophet’s word is: “I will bear the Lord’s anger, because I have sinned against him” [Note: [Col. 0425] Mic. 7]. The Lord certainly scourges the one whom he reproves, and in his blows hides from us the remembrance of the abundance of his sweetness, so that those whom he makes humble he may preserve dear to himself. For he wishes us to gather spiritual fruits and sheaves of righteousness from our patience as from a tree of life.

Now the fruits of the Spirit are, as the Apostle testifies, charity, joy, peace, patience, long-suffering, goodness, kindness, meekness, faith, modesty, continence, [Col. 0425D] chastity [Note: [Col. 0425] Gal. 5]. Whoever lacks endurance is deprived of all these. Therefore Solomon says: “Woe to those who have lost endurance” [Note: [Col. 0425] Ecclus. 2]. The scourges of the Lord God, by which he trains us unto salvation, must therefore be endured patiently. He casts down in order to raise up, wounds in order to heal, so that pressure may be turned into grace and affliction into a crown; so that one who was previously scourged may sing with the Prophet: “I will give thanks to you, Lord, because you were angry with me; your wrath has turned away, and you have comforted me” [Note: [Col. 0425] Isa. 12].

Christ, therefore, in effecting purification from sins, purifies those whom he loves by salutary admonitions, temptations, and scourges. For when the Lord permitted the Apostle to be buffeted by Satan, he made him hear: “My power is made perfect in weakness” [Note: [Col. 0425] II Cor. 12]. The Apostle also says of himself: “When I am weak, then I am strong and powerful” [Note: [Col. 0425] ibid.]. Would that he may correct us in this way, cleanse us by amendment, and not destroy us; and that late repentance may not compel us to complain and say: “You have destroyed us instead of cleansing us” [Note: [Col. 0425] Ps. 88]; and: “It was sweated over with much sweat, [Col. 0426B] yet its rust did not come out of it” [Note: [Col. 0425] Ezek. 24]; and again: “I struck them, and they did not grieve” [Note: [Col. 0425] Jer. 5].

Grieve, then, and lament at least the losses to your spiritual discipline. For through this disturbance you lose Rachel’s most tranquil embraces, experiences of divine sweetness, and transports of blessed contemplation. For how shall a human mind, perplexed and anxious and entangled in human cares, cleave to spiritual things or think on eternal things? The cause of this evil is certain perverse persons among the converted: ravens among doves, snakes among eels, whisperers and detractors hateful to God. In order to have material for riding about, they sow tares over and among the brethren, devise deceits, loathe manna, crave bloody fare, and turn the measure of a gomor into pots of flesh and into Egypt’s garlic and melons.

Thus, abhorring the delights of the cloistered paradise, they leave it, draw behind them the world which they had abandoned, thrust themselves into secular courts and, in the running about of roads and the tumults of courts, exchange whatever they had merited in the cloister by a damnable bargain for eternal destruction. Finally, having become deserters and lawless runaways from the cloister, wanderers and Sarabaites [Note: [Col. 0425D] In describing the four kinds of monks at the beginning of his Rule, St Benedict says this of the Sarabaites: “The third and most detestable kind of monks is that of the Sarabaites. They have not been tested by any rule under the experience of a master, like gold in a furnace, but, soft in nature like lead, still keep faith with the world in their works and are known to lie to God by their tonsure. Two or three together, or indeed singly, without a shepherd, enclosed not in the Lord’s sheepfolds but in their own, have the pleasure of their desires as their law: whatever they have imagined or chosen, that they call holy; and what they do not wish, they judge unlawful.”], they are given over to a reprobate mind, so that they no longer heed the peril of the soul, fear no disgrace, nor dread God’s terrible judgments, until a pit is dug for sinners and, with every opportunity for repentance wholly removed, cut off from God by perpetual excommunication, they fall into Gehenna.

In this crisis of such necessity, therefore, sing wisely, [Col. 0426D] pray fervently, persist in vigils, burning compunctions, jubilations, secret tears, groans, and disciplines. Thus the Lord will turn this storm into a breeze, and you will without doubt experience [Col. 0427A] divine help when human help is denied you. The Lord has sworn and will not repent [Note: [Col. 0427] Ps. 109]; nor will Truth lie, which confirmed under oath, saying: “Amen, amen, I say to you: whatever you ask the Father in my name, he will give you” [Note: [Col. 0427] John 15]. Who, then, neglects to seek peace unless he refuses to obtain it? Correct your ways, I beg you, and direct them toward God; for, in Solomon’s testimony, when a person’s ways please God, he will turn that person’s enemies toward peace [Note: [Col. 0427] Prov. 16].

Moreover, I entreat you by God’s mercy to maintain a faithful, sincere, and undivided affection toward your shepherd, who exposed himself to the danger of such a perilous path for the common liberty. Be also of one mind among yourselves, and of one manner in the house [Note: [Col. 0427] Ps. 67]; let there be no schisms among you [Note: [Col. 0427] I Cor. 1], but unity of spirit in the bond [Col. 0427B] of peace [Note: [Col. 0427] Eph. 4]. For where peace is, there God is; “his dwelling has been made in peace” [Note: [Col. 0427] Ps. 75].

Every congregation or convent ought indeed to be David’s harp, in which many different strings, through a certain regular moderation—as though by a plectrum—make the sweetest harmonious concord from the combination of differing minds. If there is a string which sounds harshly or makes a noise, let it be restored by every effort to harmony, lest it introduce discord.

I am astonished and complain that you have found no remedy for this disturbance with the Lord Archbishop of Canterbury, a man of great prudence and outstanding counsel [Col. 0428A]. For he is accustomed sometimes to restrain hopeless lawsuits and restore the implacable discords of magnates to favor. Yet would that you had no confidence in the Romans! For, that I may keep silent about certain matters which I have read in the book of experience, I can remind you of this: as long as the leaders of the Maccabees trusted in the Lord, they carried off trophies of triumph over their enemies; but once they made alliances with the Romans, they fell miserably in battle. But you, trust in the Lord. For whoever trusts in him shall not be confounded. His name is a most strong tower [Note: [Col. 0427] Prov. 18]; Christ is yesterday, today, and for ever [Note: [Col. 0427] Heb. 13], and his hand is not shortened so that it cannot save. Only ask in the Savior’s name; for I promise that you will suffer no [Col. 0428B] refusal from him if you request things conducive to salvation.

## LETTER 143. TO CONRAD, ARCHBISHOP OF MAINZ. [A.D. 1192]

**Summary.**—Through their old friendship begun long ago in the schools, he entreats the Archbishop of Mainz to exert every effort with the other princes of the Empire to free King Richard of England, captured by the Duke of Austria and the Emperor, from his chains.

To the reverend father and lord C., by the grace of God Archbishop of Mainz, Peter of Blois, Archdeacon of Bath, greeting in the author of salvation.

[Note: This Conrad was of Bavarian birth, a kinsman of Emperor Frederick I. After Arnold, Archbishop of Mainz, had been killed by seditious citizens, Conrad was appointed in his place in 1162, by the unanimous consent of the canons and at Frederick’s own request. But because he supported the party of Alexander, the legitimate pope, against Octavian, the antipope favoured by Emperor Frederick, two years after his election—that is, in 1164, according to Gaspar Bruschius—he fled to Rome to Pope Alexander. Dodechinus, in his Appendix to Marianus Scotus under the year 1164, says that Conrad, Archbishop-elect of Mainz, was driven from his bishopric by Emperor Frederick because he had bound himself to Pope Alexander by faith and oath.

“Then,” says Bishop Conrad in the Chronicle of Mainz, “the emperor appointed Lord Christian, indeed the chancellor of his court, in place of Lord Conrad the Bavarian—a man of remarkable prudence, most subtle in counsel and swiftest in invention amid doubtful and difficult affairs. He was also [Col. 0427D] a man of remarkable patience in adversity. No pride exalted him in prosperity; by the kindness of his countenance he was gracious to all, and he was otherwise adorned with honourable morals. Therefore, because he knew that this man enjoyed the favour both of ecclesiastical and secular persons, he made him Bishop of Mainz. This schism lasted eighteen years. At last Lord Christian interposed himself between pope and emperor and brought both back to concord. It was settled concerning the bishopric of Mainz that Lord Christian should hold the archbishopric of Mainz peaceably and quietly, while Lord Conrad, receiving the archbishopric of Salzburg, should govern it. For he had been brought up in that very church from childhood.”

He then discusses Christian’s death and, returning to Conrad, continues thus:

“After this certain princes restored Lord Conrad, Archbishop of Salzburg, to the emperor’s favour, so that the emperor himself requested that this same Archbishop Conrad return to the Church of Mainz; and Lord Conrad himself desired this most earnestly. Therefore Lord Conrad was received into the Church of Mainz as though he had been an angel of God.”

Other writers of the same age likewise relate similar things about him. Romuald, Archbishop of Salerno, in his Chronicle, in Baronius under the year 1177:

“At the time of the Council of Tours, Conrad, a noble cleric of Germany and kinsman of the emperor, who had been elected to the Church of Mainz, unwilling to agree with Octavian and the schismatic emperor, abandoned his church and, without the emperor’s knowledge, hastened to Pope Alexander in France. The pope received him very graciously and afterward brought him with himself as far as Rome; then he promoted him to be Cardinal-Bishop of Sabina, and finally raised him to be Archbishop of Mainz [Col. 0428D]. When the emperor heard this, he was moved to anger and caused his chancellor, named Christian, to be elected in the Church of Mainz and consecrated by his suffragans.”

John of Salisbury writes almost the same to St Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury, in a letter found in Baronius in the same place:

“The Archbishop-elect of Mainz, who recently withdrew from the lord pope and the curia, expelled from his territory the messenger of Guy—that is, of the antipope Callistus III—when he came to him; and he threatened him that, if he himself or any other messenger on behalf of the schismatics should come to him again, he would have his eyes torn out. He openly proclaims the lord pope’s name. The emperor knows this and grieves greatly.”

John Brompton, in his Chronicle, p. 1130, after speaking of the peace made at Venice between Emperor Frederick and Pope Alexander, continues:

“At this council Conrad, cousin-german of the aforesaid emperor, received the archbishopric of Salzburg [Salzburg or Salisburg] from the hand of the lord pope; and, with the emperor’s consent, the lord pope granted this same Conrad the legateship of the whole German kingdom for his lifetime. This Conrad, when during the time of the schism he had been elected to the archbishopric of Mainz, refused to be consecrated by Octavian the antipope; rather, he preferred soon to live in want [Hoveden reads: “to live poor”] among Catholics for Christ’s name than to abound in riches and transitory goods among schismatics. He therefore came into the regions of Gaul, to the city of Sens, and, finding there the supreme pontiff Alexander, who at that time had come beyond the mountains in order to hold a council there, he remained with him for the love of God and the peace of the Church. Being honourably received by him, he was numbered among the cardinal bishops.”

These matters are reported by Gervase of Dover and Roger of Hoveden. Ciaconius adds, under Alexander III, that Conrad, together with certain bishops and nobles of Germany, set out for Syria for the recovery of the Holy Land, having been appointed legate of the Apostolic See by Celestine III; on this journey he crowned Leo, King of Armenia. According to Bruschius, he died in 1205, though others maintain that he died in 1200.]

[Col. 0429A] Since we once served in the scholarly camp under the same master, and through long residence together in the same lodging entered into the obligations of social friendship, I write to you with greater confidence. For the passage of a short time does not prescribe limits to our love, nor does my affection acknowledge any change caused by your altered rank. Indeed, since I last saw your most desired face, divine providence has advanced you to the dignity of archiepiscopal eminence. Yet, if I rightly remember how steadfast the integrity of your faith and love has always been toward me, I am certain that your accession to honour does me no injury in respect of our friendship.

Therefore, since love on the one hand gives me boldness to speak, while on the other grieving sorrow violently presses me [Col. 0429B] into tears and groans, forgive me if in any word I exceed the restraint of modesty and the bounds of propriety: for “out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks” [Note: [Col. 0429] Matt. 12]. My soul is in bitterness, and it supplies me with the entire course of this letter from sorrow’s inkhorn.

Who, amid the common tears, can disguise his grief or suppress his lamentation, when the clergy mourns, religion laments, the people groans, and the nobility is distressed? He who is cherished and protected by common love cannot fail to be mourned amid the sorrow of all. “The crown has fallen from our head, and our dance has been turned into mourning.” Our king is in the frying-pan, and because of him the pan of this wickedness rages through very many provinces. The whole community wastes away and dies with its suffering lord [Col. 0429C]; through compassion, the affliction of the head runs down into the members.

The Duke of Austria, a man of blood and bloody conscience [Note: [Col. 0430D]

In Sorbonne MS 1, “Duke of Astutia” occurs, that is, Austria. I have spoken of the capture of King Richard in Letter 64.

This letter was written in the year of Christ 1192, namely the year in which Richard, King of England, was in chains.]

has not feared to lay sacrilegious hands upon the Lord’s anointed and to humble in iron fetters feet shod with the Gospel of peace. May God, terrible in judgments, destroy him utterly, pluck him from His tabernacle, and root him out from the land of the living, because he did not remember to show mercy but persecuted an innocent man and a pilgrim, still engaged in the service of the Crucified and entrusted with the care of the commonwealth. For after he had endured grievous labours for God’s covenant [Col. 0430A], worn out by the exertions and expenses of war, he was returning home so that, with wiser counsel and happier auspices, he might prepare the way for a second pilgrimage, in which he would render a still greater testimony of faith.

And now, O kings, understand; take heed, you who judge the earth [Note: [Col. 0429] Ps. 2], whether, from the infancy of the newborn Church onward, any peaceful, faithful, innocent, pilgrim king has ever been so treacherously captured, so maliciously detained, so cruelly sold, so unworthily afflicted, and, together with his people, burdened by so greedy and detestable an exaction. Where is the law of nature? Where is equity? Where is reverence for pilgrims—pilgrims whom even Christ’s crucifiers respected, when they transferred the price for which Christ had been sold to the potter’s field for the burial of strangers [Col. 0430B] [Note: [Col. 0429] Matt. 27]?

Moreover, when Abraham was a pilgrim in the land of Canaan, King Abimelech showed him the favour of full humanity [Note: [Col. 0429] Gen. 20]. Jacob with Laban [Note: [Col. 0429] Gen. 29], Moses with Jethro [Note: [Col. 0429] Exod. 2], David with King Achish [Note: [Col. 0429] 1 Sam. 21], and the other ancient fathers—though they had not yet received the promises, but saw them from afar and confessed that they were strangers and pilgrims upon the earth [Note: [Col. 0429] Heb. 11]—found abundant consolation in their wandering among the barbarian nations.

May both he who sold him and he who bought him be reckoned in the lot of Judas Iscariot and under the curse of Jewish treachery, so that their own money may be with them unto perdition. May the earth swallow them alive with Dathan and Abiram: successors of Judas, sons of avarice, servants of Mammon, seed of Canaan, brood of vipers, members of the devil [Col. 0430C], ministers of Satan, forerunners of Antichrist. While the tyranny of these men rages against the peoples, public mortality increases; cities are emptied by pestilence and famine, which come upon the whole world.

Nor can we disguise or keep silent that, according to the Apostle’s word, Antichrist is already working the ministry of iniquity, so that he may be revealed in his own time [Note: [Col. 0429] 2 Thess. 2]. For iniquity abounds, and the love of many grows cold [Note: [Col. 0429] Matt. 24]. The best man is he who is not excessively wicked. As a sign of the coming of that son of perdition, the world as a whole lies in evil [Note: [Col. 0429] 1 John 5]; the pestilential disease rages, and dearth increases. It is written [Col. 0431A] that death is with him and want goes before his face [Note: [Col. 0431] Job 41]. For all of us in our sister Germany these evils are springing up. Alas, alas, princes of the north! Truly, “from the north every evil is opened” [Note: [Col. 0431] Jer. 1].

Yet this evil shall be turned to good for our king, who uses it well. For God, the judge of innocence, will soon render judgment for him who suffers wrong; the Lord will show mercy to His Christ. The zeal of the Lord of hosts will do this, and all shall know that “there is a remnant for the peaceable man” [Note: [Col. 0431] Ps. 36]. “O Lord, in thy strength the king shall rejoice” [Note: [Col. 0431] Ps. 20]; “the righteous shall be delivered from his distress” [Note: [Col. 0431] Prov. 11]. But the wicked man shall fall into the snare he laid, and his iniquity shall come down upon his own head [Note: [Col. 0431] Ps. 7].

O avarice, rust of souls! O greed, moth of hearts! You have so blinded men that, forgetful of God and of His judgments [Col. 0431B], they spare neither their own souls nor their reputation. Money indeed will be consumed, but the mark of treason will not be erased. The enormity of so great a crime will pass down to posterity, and this iniquity will be written with an adamantine nail [Note: [Col. 0431] Jer. 17]. These sons of eternal lamentation obtain these things not from the fiscal treasury [Note: [Col. 0431] See William of Newburgh, *History of English Affairs*, bk. IV, ch. 35; Matthew Paris, Polydore, and others], nor from royal treasures, but from the inheritance of the Crucified, from the support of the poor, the tears of widows, the resources of religious persons, the sustenance of orphans, the dowries of maidens, the furnishings of churches; from crosses and consecrated chalices. For every shilling they gather for themselves, they heap up as many curses; they store up for themselves as many endless torments on the terrible day of wrath. Whatever the munificence of venerable antiquity expended for the adornment [Col. 0431C] of God’s house, the gaping maw of insatiable avarice now swallows, that they may possess God’s sanctuary as an inheritance and become accursed by as many sacrileges as are committed in the regions of the Western Church.

[Col. 0432A] Rise up, therefore, O man of God; let the other enrolled fathers also rise, to whom two-edged swords have been given in their hands. Come to the aid of the Church’s wound. Let your hand seize judgment, and, drawing the sword of your tongue, exercise against the public robbers of churches and sacrilegious invaders the zeal which Peter exercised against Ananias and Sapphira, defrauders of ecclesiastical property [Note: [Col. 0431] Acts 5].

The most illustrious king is tortured by prison chains and hunger; “the sword has pierced through his soul” [Note: [Col. 0431] Luke 1]. For he sits in poverty and iron, and there is none to be moved by Joseph’s ruin. His handsome face grows pale with fasting, provisions having been denied him; the strength of his body is about to pass into the strength of his soul, and the beauty of nature, which flowered in his face, withers as nature fails. If, therefore, there is any kindness in you, any consolation of charity [Col. 0432B], any regard for Christ, any bowels of compassion, any remembrance of God’s judgments, let the impulse of merciful compassion be awakened within you. Go up against them, and let pontifical authority restrain the course of so detestable a sacrilege, lest your princes rage against holy things; lest the Western peoples waste away longer in grief and tears; lest innocent blood be required at your hands. Farewell.

## LETTER CXLIV. ELEANOR, QUEEN OF ENGLAND, TO POPE CELESTINE. [A.D. 1192.]

**Argument.**—Eleanor, Queen of England, piteously implores the pope’s aid for the liberation of her son Richard, King of England.

To the reverend father and lord Celestine, by the grace of God [Col. 0432C] supreme pontiff, A. [Note: [Col. 0431C]

The letter A denotes Eleanor, called by English writers Alienor, Alienora, and Alienordis, and by French writers Eleonor or Eleonora. She was the daughter of William, the last Duke of Aquitaine and Count of Poitou. When he set out for St James in Spain as an act of penance, he died on the journey and was buried in the church of St James, as John Frasquetus reports among others in a manuscript chronicle at Saint-Victor, under the year 1135:

“The following year William, Count of Poitou, set out for St James, and on Good Friday died in the church of St James and was buried before the altar. As he was dying, he charged his nobles who were with him to give his elder daughter Alienordis to Louis, King of the Franks, together with the duchy of Aquitaine. The said Louis joined her to himself in most solemn marriage at Bordeaux, in the presence of the nobles of the realm.”

The will of Duke William himself is extant in Baronius under the year 1136. In it he declares that he wishes his elder daughter Eleanor to be given in marriage to Louis, King of the Franks, with Aquitaine and Poitou; to his other daughter, Petronilla by name, he leaves the possessions and castles which he held in Burgundy. It should incidentally be noted that Baronius in the same place refutes the story circulated concerning William’s astonishing penance, since it appears in no historian of this period; indeed, several state that he ended his life at St James during his pilgrimage, including Frasquetus cited above, Robert of Torigni in the Appendix to Sigebert, and Suger in the *Life of Louis the Younger*, whose chief minister of the realm he was.

William of Jumièges, in his Chronicle, in André du Chesne’s *History of the Normans*, bk. VIII, ch. 42:

“About this time William, Duke of the Aquitanians, died not long afterward. Louis, son of the King of the Franks, took as wife his only daughter, together with her duchy.”

The Chronicle of Limoges, vol. II of the *New Library*, ch. 48:

“William, Duke of Aquitaine, died as a pilgrim at St James and was buried there.”

Ralph de Diceto says nearly the same in his *Images of Histories*, p. 267.

The author of the *Deeds of Louis VII*, ch. 4, in André du Chesne, vol. IV of the *History of the Franks*, p. 591, relates the matter more clearly:

“In these days William, Duke of Aquitaine, undertook a journey to St James. By God’s will, before he reached the destination of his pilgrimage, he died after completing part of the journey, leaving no male heir in the duchy of Aquitaine. Nevertheless, he had two daughters: one, the elder, was named Alienordis, and the other Alaidis. Louis VII married Alienor, while he joined the second, Alaidis, in marriage to his kinsman Ralph, Count of Vermandois.”

Moreover, Eleanor was repudiated by Louis after ten years, although he had had two daughters by her. Historians give various accounts of the reason for this divorce. Alberic, monk of Trois-Fontaines, has this in his manuscript Chronicle, taken from Helinand:

“Henry, Count of Anjou and Duke of Normandy, soon to be King of England, married the wife—or, more correctly, the repudiated wife—of Louis, King of the Franks; hence war arose between them. King Louis left her because of the woman’s incontinence: she behaved not as a queen, but made herself almost common property. She was called Eleanor, daughter of William, Count of Poitou and Duke of Aquitaine. After she had borne to the King of France two daughters, Mary, Countess of Troyes, and Alice, Countess of Blois, she afterward bore to the aforesaid King Henry four sons and three daughters.”

Matthew Paris, under 1150, says of this:

“A divorce was celebrated between Louis, King of the Franks, and his Queen Eleanor, because she was defamed for adultery even with an infidel, one who was of the devil’s kindred. For they were related in the fourth degree.”

Brompton, p. 1040, says much the same; and Gervase, in his Chronicle, p. 1370:

“In 1152, after Louis, King of France, had returned from his pilgrimage to Jerusalem, a certain discord arose between him and his Queen Eleanor, perhaps because of certain matters better left unspoken which had occurred during that pilgrimage. And behold, he suddenly began to contrive the dissolution of the marriage under the pretext of consanguinity. The divorce, therefore, between King Louis and his Queen Eleanor was solemnly celebrated in the face of the Church, after much labour and artful swearing,” etc.

Paul Aemilius, bk. V of his *History of the Franks*:

“On returning from Syria to France, Louis considered nothing more pressing than to dissolve his marriage to Leonora. A council was held at Beaugency. The archbishops of Reims, Sens, Rouen, and Bordeaux sat there. Witnesses were examined; proof of kinship was established; it was determined that the marriage could not lawfully stand. Thus Leonora, whom he had held as wife for so many years and by whom he had begotten two daughters, was dismissed, not without the astonishment of the lands.”

Whatever the case, after being repudiated by King Louis, Eleanor quickly returned to Aquitaine, leaving with him their children in common; shortly afterward she married Henry, Duke of Normandy and Count of Anjou, soon to become King of England, and bore him four sons and three daughters. But when she incited the sons, who were at variance with their father the king, and, leaving her husband, followed her sons to war, the sons were reconciled with their father and she was placed by Henry in strict custody [Col. 0434B]. There she remained for twelve years, until, at the request of Baldwin, Archbishop of Canterbury, she was released, as Gervase has under 1185:

“Queen Eleanor, at the request of B., Archbishop of Canterbury, was released for a short time from her long imprisonment, in which she had been held confined for almost twelve years.”

But shortly afterward she was again thrown into prison, where she remained for four years—that is, until the death of her husband Henry. When he died, she was released by her son King Richard and made a participant in the government of the kingdom. Nicholas Trivet thus writes in his manuscript Chronicle:

“In 1179 Henry, the elder King of the English, estranged from his wife, held her in custody for many years; she was not brought out until Henry’s death, namely in 1189, by her son Richard.”

And below:

“In 1189 Queen Eleanor, after the death of King Henry, was brought out of custody by the command of her son Richard, in which she had been for about ten years.”

Ralph de Diceto, under 1189:

“Queen Eleanor, who for many years had been assigned to strict custody, received from her son authority to determine whatever she wished in the kingdom. I mean a custody continuing without interruption for sixteen years.”

Similarly Matthew Paris, under 1188:

“Richard’s mother, Queen Eleanor, who had been separated from her husband’s bed and held under strict custody for sixteen years, received from her son authority to determine whatever she wished. The princes of the realm were commanded to arrange all things according to the queen’s pleasure. On receiving this authority, she immediately released throughout England all prisoners from their jails, having learned by experience that prison custody is exceedingly burdensome to men.”

She lived fourteen years after her husband, that is, until the year of Christ 1204, in which she died, according to Thomas of Walsingham in the *Hypodigma Neustriae*:

“In the year 1204 Eleanor, Duchess of Aquitaine and mother of the King of England, departed from this life.”

That is, at the monastery of Fontevraud, to which toward the end of her life she had withdrawn for penance and where she had taken the habit of a nun, according to the records of Fontevraud. She was buried in the same church of Fontevraud near the tombs of her husband Henry and her son Richard, as is recorded in the necrology of that monastery under 30 March 1204.]

by the wrath of God Queen of England, Duchess of Normandy, and Countess of Anjou, a wretched mother, asks you to show yourself a father to her.

“I had resolved to remain silent,” etc. See among the various letters to Celestine III after his *Registers*, *Patrologia*, vol. CCVI.

## LETTER CXLV. THE SAME TO THE SAME. [A.D. 1192.]

Of the same subject.

To the most holy father and lord C., by the grace of God supreme pontiff, A., by that same grace Queen of England, Duchess of Normandy, and Countess of Anjou, greeting, and may you abound in the bowels of mercy.

“My soul is weary of my life,” etc. See the same place.

## LETTER CXLVI. THE SAME TO THE SAME. [A.D. 1192.]

Of the same subject.

[Col. 0433B] To the reverend father and lord Celestine, by the grace of God [Col. 0434A] supreme pontiff, A., wretched—and would that she were pitiable—Queen of the English, Duchess of Normandy, Countess of Anjou, a wretched mother, asks you to show yourself a father of mercy.

“Prevented by the envious distance of places,” etc. See the same place.

## LETTER CXLVII. TO ROBERT, BISHOP OF BANGOR. [c. A.D. 1197.]

**Argument.**—He reproves Bishop R., who was attempting to retain for himself an ecclesiastical benefice already conferred on another.

To his once beloved companion, but now reverend lord R., by the grace of God Bishop-elect of Bangor [Note: [Col. 0434D] This is Robert of Shrewsbury, consecrated Bishop of Bangor in 1197. In 1210 he was captured by John, King of England, in his cathedral church; for his ransom he gave the king two hundred hawks, says Matthew of Westminster. He died in 1213, and at his death commanded that his body be buried in the middle of the marketplace at Shrewsbury. From the same Matthew of Westminster], M. Peter of Blois, Archdeacon of Bath, may you be rooted in Him who sends out roots in His elect.

[Col. 0435A] On the day of your ordination you ought to have put off the old man with his deeds and put on the new man, who was created according to God. Thus David, from the day of his anointing, was changed into another man, and the Spirit of the Lord was directed upon him [Note: [Col. 0435] 1 Sam. 16]. But you, beginning with wrongs, troubled my lord the archbishop at the very time of your ordination and provoked him to anger.

Behold the good priest, who on the day of his consecration ought to have pleased God and men, and on a day of anger ought to have become an agent of reconciliation. Yet you consecrated your first-fruits to discord, and at a time of friendship became an occasion of strife and sedition. Solomon testifies [Note: [Col. 0435] Prov. 6]: “There are six things which the Lord hates, and a seventh which His soul detests.” Having enumerated the six hateful things, he makes the seventh this: sowing discord among friends.

If you have received—indeed, since you have received—not the spirit of this world but the Spirit who is from God, by whom those who are God’s children are led, even if I had grievously offended you, you ought to have been more ready to forgive than to take revenge. The sole occasion of dissension between us is that I do not confer upon you a benefice already granted to another, contrary to the form of the canons, contrary to my conscience, contrary to your soul, and contrary to God.

That parable which Nathan the prophet put before King David openly touches you: the rich man who had many sheep took from a poor man the single one which he possessed [Note: [Col. 0435] 2 Sam. 12]. That poor clerk, to whom I gave that small prebend [Note: [Col. 0435D] This prebend was in the deanery of Wolverhampton, whose dean was our Peter, as he himself says in Letter 152 to Pope Innocent. From this it appears that the conferral of these prebends belonged to him], has already appealed to the Apostolic See [Col. 0435C]. Do you believe Roman justice has degenerated so far that it will permit a poor and needy man, educated and honourable, trained in ecclesiastical and scholastic learning, to be oppressed by a powerful man?

You ought not so to shrink from the poverty of your church, which you allege all day before men in order to burden another. Poverty is a glorious title before Christ; and that which became the Son of God ought not to disgrace you. The prince of apostles and bishops says: “Silver and gold have I none” [Note: [Col. 0435] Acts 3]. Great Augustine likewise [Note: [Col. 0435] Possidius, *Life*] made no will because, being Christ’s poor man, he had nothing from which to make one [Col. 0436A].

Your office is to live by the Gospel, as the Lord has ordained for you—not to proceed pompously in sumptuous clothing, the ostentation of horses, and a multitude of retainers. It befits you, as a professor of priestly and episcopal holiness, utterly to cut off the traces of your former manner of life. What henceforth have you to do with the dwelling at Wolverhampton? I beg you, cut off every occasion of evil report, and, according to the Apostle’s counsel [Note: [Col. 0435] 1 Thess. 5], “abstain from every appearance of evil,” and provide things good not only before God but before men. It is greatly in the interest of your honour that no trace, however slight, of former levity spring up again, and that no hostile opinion taint, even with the faintest breath, the newness of the innocence you have assumed.

And, to use the Apostle’s words [Note: [Col. 0435] 2 Cor. 4], let a man regard you [Col. 0436B] as a minister of Christ. Choose to conduct yourself with such modesty that your modesty may be known to all men; and so reduce every movement of the mind to self-control that the day of your coming consecration may find you such a man as the Apostle describes to his disciple when he says: “A bishop must be blameless, as God’s steward; not quick-tempered, not quarrelsome, not pursuing shameful gain” [Note: [Col. 0435] 1 Tim. 3].

Spare, then, the poor clerk, lest he must needs undertake a journey to the Apostolic See. For if by this complaint he brings these matters to the ears of the supreme pontiff, that See will condemn without any retraction whatever has been done regarding this paltry income, or the other revenues which you have held until now. Spare yourself, dearest friend; spare me also; and you who were once mine in this small prebend [Col. 0436C] [Note: [Col. 0435D]

It is probable that Robert, before becoming bishop, was a canon in the church of which Peter of Blois was dean.

He wrote this letter about 1197, the year in which Robert was elected.]

be willing now to bind me to yourself in it in the service of everlasting affection. Farewell.

## LETTER CXLVIII. TO SAVARIC, BISHOP OF BATH. [c. A.D. 1195.]

**Argument.**—He exhorts the bishop to return to his diocese and not to abandon his church for the sake of pilgrimage.

To the reverend father and lord S., by the grace of God Bishop of Bath [Note: [Col. 0435D] This Savaric, formerly Archdeacon of Northampton, was made Bishop of Bath at the request of Richard, King of England, while the latter was on pilgrimage to Jerusalem, in the year of Christ 1192. Ralph thus writes of him in the *Images of History*, under 1192:

“While King Richard was on pilgrimage in Syria, and while the see of Canterbury was vacant, Savaric, Archdeacon of Northampton and Treasurer of Salisbury, was elected bishop by the monks of Bath, despite the objections of the clerics of Wells [Col. 0436D]. Walter, Archbishop of Rouen and justiciar of the realm, gave the king’s assent. Savaric came to Rome and, by command of the supreme pontiff, was ordained priest in the Lateran patriarchal palace. Alban, Bishop of Albano, imposed the hand of consecration on the third day before the Kalends of October.”

After King Richard had given Savaric the abbey of Glastonbury, he wished to transfer the episcopal see there, and for this reason often called himself Bishop of Glastonbury. He was a kinsman of Emperor Henry and was a hostage with him, together with Walter, Archbishop of Rouen, and others, for the release of King Richard, as Roger has under 1194. The same writer calls him Chancellor of Burgundy under 1197:

“Henry, Emperor of the Romans, began to fall ill and sent Savaric, Bishop of Bath, his kinsman and Chancellor of Burgundy [Col. 0437D], to Richard, King of England, and offered him repayment of the money which he had taken from him for his ransom.”

Savaric held office for thirteen years], Peter of Blois, his archdeacon, greeting in Him without whom there is no salvation.

[Col. 0437A] My inmost feelings are continually shaken by a devout impulse of compassion over your labours and fatigues. Who could endure with composure that your noble soul, trained in scholarly pursuits, imbued with spiritual teaching, and endowed with so many and such great graces, should so degenerate as to forget itself and be unmindful of those who are yours; and should remember neither the church espoused to you, nor the care of souls which you received to guard at no small peril, nor the terrible judgments of God?

Have mercy, most gracious father, on your soul, for which Christ laid down His own soul and which you have, as it were, put at the throw of dice. Charity compels me, reverend bishop, to share your suffering and to fear for you; would that you also feared! For “blessed is the man who is always fearful” [Note: [Col. 0437] Prov. 28]. Who indeed would not fear concerning his lord and his friend during so long a sojourn, amid so many perils of travel, amid so many wandering, varied, and uncertain journeys? What profit, honour, or necessity has compelled you into the exile of so long a pilgrimage?

Truth says to the apostles: “If they persecute you in one city, flee to another” [Note: [Col. 0437] Matt. 5]. The Saviour permitted flight to His disciples not in a time of peace but of persecution. Yet I believe your mind possesses such steadfastness that, if persecution threatened you, no slight hostile pressure could drive you into flight. But now many judge your flight far more dangerous because it is the flight of a hireling. He flees who is frightened by the attack of wolves; you flee not wolves but your own sheep, whom through the benefit of your presence [Col. 0437C] you could turn from wolves into sheep. For what could be so difficult for you in the whole kingdom that the common favour which all bear toward you, the native subtlety of your intellect, and your industry, tried in many ways, could not alter it according to your wish?

Recall, Father, that you are the vicar of blessed Peter. [Note: [Col. 0437D] See what we have said on this matter in connection with Epistle 113.] To you, in his person, it was once said: “If you love me, feed my sheep.” [Note: [Col. 0437] John 21.] What is it to feed the sheep, except to preach the Gospel to those subject to you? To render to God a people acceptable to him; by word, deed, and example to direct the ways of the Lord; and to prepare for the Lord a perfect people? Know that perpetual exile and wandering are the greatest misery; and, according to Solomon’s testimony: “To go from lodging to lodging is a most wretched life.” [Note: [Col. 0437] Ecclesiasticus 29.] If today—may God avert it—death, which lies in wait for all, [Col. 0438A] should suddenly snatch you away, what gains of souls, what increase from the spiritual talents entrusted to you, would you bring back to the Lord? May the Lord not allow you to belong to the number of those of whom he says: “I gave them my gold and my silver; but they made Baal from my gold and my silver.” [Note: [Col. 0437] Ezekiel 16.] God has bestowed abundantly upon you the gold of wisdom and the silver of eloquence. Far be it that these should henceforth be turned to the vanities and false follies of this age! Far be it that my lord should hear the thunder of that terrible sentence which heavenly indignation threatens against the useless—and therefore wicked—servant who wrapped his lord’s talent in a napkin and hid it in the earth. Even the servant who kept his lord’s talent was condemned, because he made no profit from it. [Note: [Col. 0437] Matthew 25.] [Col. 0438B] Nor shall only the tree that bears bad fruit, but also that which bears no good fruit, be cut down and cast into the fire. [Note: [Col. 0437] Matthew 3.] O how great is the shame of those who love you affectionately, when they see—and grieve—that your church has lain desolate for so long, and you, like a bird that has flown from its nest and left its young, like a traveller in the wilderness, a man exiled and wandering without cause, voluntarily roaming and fugitive upon the earth. Laypeople lament your absence; clerics groan; religious mourn; and the desires of all hang upon your return, while with all the marrow of their souls they sigh for the shepherd and bishop of their souls.

I have discussed your [Col. 0438C] Glastonbury affair with many great and wise men. [Note: [Col. 0437D] He means the transfer of the see of Bath to the Church of Glastonbury, discussed above.
