It should also be noted that, although Savaric sat there throughout his episcopate, immediately after [Col. 0438D] his death the monks of Glastonbury recovered their abbey from King John and appointed an abbot over themselves in 1205, the year in which Savaric died.] All agree that your cause approaches the impossible: kingdom and priesthood concur alike in this, that under no circumstances may a single mitre mutilate the king’s crown or the Church of Canterbury. [Note: [Col. 0438D]

For Savaric, by transferring his see of Bath to the monastery of Glastonbury, was attempting to curtail the kingdom of England and the Church of Canterbury by means of one mitre—namely, an abbatial one.

From the foregoing we may infer that this letter was written about the year of the Lord 1195.]

If, therefore, you see that your endeavours do not attain the desired result, do not be ashamed to return to what is your own. You know that there is a shame which brings sin, and a shame which brings glory. [Note: [Col. 0437] Ecclesiasticus 4.] Let my lord neither be ashamed nor blush if he cannot obtain at will what none of the other bishops could obtain. But if you attribute this to shame and embarrassment, know that in exchange for this shame and blush you will be granted to possess double portions in your own land, with honour and glory. Return, I beseech you, lest [Col. 0438D] your ministry be further reproached; and let the shortness of [Col. 0439A] this life, the dangers of wandering, the fear of God, the memory of death, grieving friends, and desolate souls invite you to return; for those who wander much are seldom sanctified. Farewell.

## EPISTLE CXLIX. TO J. AND P., FRIENDS. [c. A.D. 1200?]

**Summary.**—He complains that, now old and retired from service, he is being stripped of the honour of the archdeaconry through the false accusation of ill-wishers, and implores the assistance of two courtiers in this matter.

PETER of Blois, archdeacon of Bath, to J. and P., greetings, and may you be moved by Joseph’s affliction.

I am wholly consumed by the bitterness of my soul and the inconsolable grief of my heart; and would that all the [Col. 0439B] cataracts of my head might flow into weeping! Would that the greater part of the brain and jaws of my whole wretched body might dissolve into tears, so that I might weep and lament what I cannot see!

Summoned into England by King Henry, enriched by him and by his sons with lavish gifts, and exalted by archbishops, bishops, and all the magnates of the land with every honour until the malice of this present time: I am now, on the occasion of certain letters obtained from the lord pope both by suppressing truth and by asserting falsehood—while the whole people and clergy of so great a city, whose care and protection were entrusted to me, have been most cruelly deceived—an old man and retired servant driven out by a young man; a simple and sickly man by an ambitious man; a gentle and [Col. 0439C] innocent man by a crafty man. And, to speak more moderately, I am violently expelled from every honour of my archdeaconry, having been defamed by a disgraceful charge. The bearer of this letter will explain this tragedy to you more fully; for grief full of sobs, hindering my mouth with fainting fits and *leipothymia* (loss of consciousness), does not permit me to speak or write. By the craft of a malicious man I have been made an object of reproach and contempt, unless my misery awakens your mercy and my sufferings provoke the feeling of your compassion. “Have pity on me, at least you who are my friends.” [Note: [Col. 0439] Job 19.] Although the desert of my merits has not made you my friends, yet pious compassion—which often enters into a bond of friendship—compels you to love this wretched man. I write to no one in the court [Col. 0439D] except you two: for after God I have fixed in you the sole anchor of my hope. Nor have I forgotten the word which Truth says in the Gospel: “Whatever matter two of you agree upon on earth, it shall be done for them.” [Note: [Col. 0439] Matthew 22.] A pagan also says:

> What two men have wished is not without effect.

Farewell.

## EPISTLE CL. TO THE CLERICS OF THE ROYAL COURT

**Summary.**—He moderates what he had said more harshly about courtly life in Epistle 14, and admits that it is fitting for some clerics, and even bishops, to frequent the courts of kings, provided that they do not abandon their flock or imitate the vices of the court.

To his dearest lords and friends, the clerics of the court of [Col. 0440A] the lord king, Master PETER of Blois, archdeacon of Bath, greetings in the author of salvation.

While in bodily distress and danger of death, I wrote you a letter in which I seemed to dissuade rather vehemently from the service—lest I call it the wickedness—of courtly life. For at that time, struck by grave illness and therefore moved by grave repentance, I considered not only the court but the world, and everything belonging to the world, unclean and damnable. As you have learned by experience, illness is an express image of shipwreck: for when a ship is dashed upon rocks or shaken by the stormy fury of winds and waves, all the world’s precious things become worthless, and whatever had been an occasion of pleasure turns into repentance. Therefore, if an exhortatory letter flowed to you from a contrite and humble heart, [Col. 0440B] none of you ought to have taken offence on that account.

For I love you in the inward parts of Christ, and whatever was written in that letter for your edification proceeded not from hatred of courtiers but from sincere charity. Certainly it is dangerous to die at court, and one who has bound himself with military ties and entered the courtly labyrinth will not lightly ascend to the height of perfection. Yet I do not condemn the life of courtiers: though they do not devote themselves to prayer and contemplation, they are occupied with the interests of the commonwealth and often perform works of salvation. Nor can all take up the way of the stricter life; for the Lord’s way is narrow and steep. Yet it is a great thing if those who have not ascended to the mountain’s height accompany Lot and are saved in the little city of Zoar. [Note: [Col. 0439] Genesis 19.] I know that those admitted into the sanctuary of royal intimacy can do and say many things by which the necessity of the poor is relieved, religion fostered, justice done, and the Church enlarged. In these and like works of mercy courtiers can build up life for themselves, provided they do not slander, do not envy, shake their hands free from gifts, and do not seek to repay evil for evil. For this is a common vice of courtiers: at another’s slightest fault they blaze up violently and bear most impatiently with the error of one who has simply offended, nor do they weigh on a balance the injuries for which they demand revenge.

[Col. 0440D] I do indeed confess that it is holy to stand beside the lord king; for he is holy and the Lord’s anointed. Nor has he received in vain the sacrament of royal anointing, whose efficacy—if it is unknown or doubted—will be most fully demonstrated by the disappearance of the groin disease and the healing of scrofula. “To Cyrus, my anointed, whose right hand I have grasped, I will subject cities and kingdoms,” says the Lord through the prophet. [Note: [Col. 0439] Isaiah 45.] There the Lord calls King Cyrus his anointed. Hence David would not spare even the young man who, at Saul’s request, had killed Saul, [Note: [Col. 0439] 2 Kings 1.] because he had presumptuously laid hands upon the Lord’s anointed. It does not seem absurd to me if you render honour and service to the lord king, as to one who is [Col. 0441A] pre-eminent, according to the Apostle. [Note: [Col. 0441] 1 Peter 2.] For I judge that kings should be served with all humility and reverence, not only when they are good and moderate but also when they are harsh. [Note: [Col. 0441] Ibid.] The Hebrews too are commanded to pray for the Babylonians, [Note: [Col. 0441] Jeremiah 29.] because in the peace of rulers lies the rest of peoples. Christ himself also decreed that tribute should be paid by the faithful to Caesar. [Note: [Col. 0441] Matthew 22.] Thus the association of clerics with princes is not merely to be tolerated, but often to be desired. We read, indeed, that priests and prophets had frequent intercourse and familiarity with kings. The lives of kings are then beneficially ordered when they follow the exhortations of religious persons and are guided by the counsel of the wise. Nevertheless, although it is often advantageous for bishops and others who have undertaken the care of the Lord’s flock to attend the counsels of kings, [Col. 0441B] it concerns them to ensure that they do not render void the ministry of pastoral vigilance; rather, in the presence of kings, they must remember their own condition and not abandon Peter’s little boat, over which they preside, amid the stormy waves of the court. For the poles by which the ark of the Lord was carried, although they could be moved and drawn in different directions, could nevertheless not be drawn out or wholly torn away. [Note: [Col. 0441] Exodus 37.] This most clearly signifies that prelates of the Church, although temporarily drawn aside for the various needs of public affairs, should in no way separate themselves from the embraces of the Bride or from care for the people entrusted to them. From ancient times it has been desirable to find favour in the eyes of princes; for, as the pagan witness says:

> To have pleased princely men is no last praise.  
> [Note: [Col. 0441] Horace, Book I, Epistle 18.]

[Col. 0441C] Therefore I consider it not merely praiseworthy but glorious to stand beside the lord king, to manage the commonwealth, to forget oneself, and to belong wholly to all. Yet through me no one shall become entangled in, nor through me be released from, the bond of court life. Let each person follow and maintain the choice of his own will. For Joshua also places before the people of Israel the choice whether to serve the gods of Mesopotamia, the gods of the Amorites, or the Lord God, unwilling to impose upon anyone, apart from free will, the compulsory service of another master. [Note: [Col. 0441] Joshua 24.] Indeed, if in this letter and in the other letter which I previously sent you I should be reproved for having written varied, and perhaps contrary, things, as Didymus is said to have rejected in one of his books [Note: [Col. 0441] Epistle 18 of Jerome, *On Illustrious Men*.] a certain history which in another of his books he had most vehemently commended—certainly, since Solomon closely joins these words, “Answer a fool according to his folly,” [Note: [Col. 0441] Proverbs 26.] and “Do not answer a fool according to his folly,” [Note: [Col. 0441] Ibid.] if the words in proverbs and letters are interpreted more kindly, neither in your Ecclesiastes nor in your Peter of Blois will any sayings contradict one another.

## EPISTLE CLI. TO POPE INNOCENT III. [c. A.D. 1199]

**Summary.**—He entreats and adjures the supreme pontiff to ensure that the London archdeaconry, now offered to him in his old age, is endowed with more ample revenues.

To lord pope INNOCENT [Note: [Col. 0441D]

This man was born of the illustrious family of the counts of Hernici in Campania, Italy. He was first a canon of the Church of Anagni, then a regular canon of the Lateran Church. He afterwards went to Paris for study, where he became most expert in every kind of learning, to such a degree that he publicly taught sacred letters with the highest praise and admiration. Then Clement III made him cardinal; finally, after the death of Celestine III, he was raised to the supreme pontificate in 1198, although, according to Ciaconius, he was only thirty years old. The following should also be noted concerning his elevation: when Celestine III was dying, he summoned the cardinals and persuaded them to elect no one other than Lothair, cardinal deacon of Saints Sergius and Bacchus, distinguished in learning and character. This was done. All historians relate at length how much Innocent III accomplished in his pontificate; his own writings, especially his innumerable decretal letters, also abundantly demonstrate the man’s eminent gifts. He sat for eighteen years and six months.

This letter was written near the end of Peter of Blois’s life, that is, about the year 1199.]

PETER of Blois, archdeacon of London, greetings, and himself wholly at his feet.

If, from the abundance of my heart, I write anything too rashly with uncircumcised lips, you who are spiritual should bear with such a one in a spirit of gentleness. For the Lord has given you a learned tongue, that you may know how to sustain by a word one who is about to fall; and your tongue has been made the key of heaven, while the authority to whose fullness you have been called comes not from man but from God. Hear patiently, therefore, if I briefly lament my pain: I have been lifted above the wind in order to fall more disgracefully and become a spectacle and mockery to others. When the London archdeaconry was offered to me, I refused it, repeatedly impressing upon the bishop Isaiah’s saying: “I am not [Col. 0442C] a physician”; and also, “In my house there is neither bread nor clothing; therefore do not appoint me ruler of this people.” [Note: [Col. 0441] Isaiah 3.] The patriarch Jacob, who often held familiar converse with the Lord’s word, counted all the days of his life few and evil. [Note: [Col. 0441] Genesis 47.] But I, until receiving this archdeaconry, reckoned all my days to have been passed under a more favourable stone and a happier omen. Now, however, the arrows of the Lord are in me, and their wrath drinks up my spirit. I am at life’s evening—if indeed what I live is life. Oppressed by diseases and besieged by the diverse discomforts of old age, my chief desire is to say farewell to the world. By God’s grace I am already being consumed, and I have received the answer of death [Col. 0443A] in my limbs; its reapers strive to enter my wasting little body. O how much more quietly and safely I should always have remained hidden beneath the bushel than rashly ascended to the London archdeaconry. Truly I ascended above the wind. For that archdeaconry is a dragon, having nothing by which it may live except wind. It is an honour existing only in bare and pure conceptions. Although there are forty thousand people in that city and one hundred and twenty churches, I receive neither tithes, first-fruits, nor offerings from laypeople, though I perform priestly office; nor can I draw from those subject to me any synodals, cathedraticum, procurations, aids, lodging, or any customary dues owed to archdeacons from any of the churches. [Col. 0443B] Yet beyond my strength I devote myself, with anxious and tireless solicitude, to correcting and instructing both clergy and people. Would it be a great thing if we who sow spiritual things were to reap temporal things? Where is: “Take the psalm and give the timbrel”? [Note: [Col. 0443] Psalm 80.] Where is: “The labourer is worthy of his wages”? [Note: [Col. 0443] Luke 10.] God knows, and the whole region knows, that the archdeacon of London, unless he had support for life from elsewhere, could not maintain himself for one month out of all the revenues of that office. Therefore, because God has called you into the fullness of authority and among his angels, that you may remove scandals from his kingdom, which is the Church, I entreat and adjure the glory of your holiness to cut off this evil, this scandal, and to be pleased, before I die, to restore to the honour of proper order what has from ancient days been made disorderly. [Col. 0443C] For although I suffer from this, I have still greater compassion for my successors. They will not know how to dig; they will be ashamed to beg; and necessity will force them to beg shamefully and publicly.

I beg you, command the bishops of Ely and Winchester to come to the place and arrange this archdeaconry according to the condition of the other archdeaconries; and let them cause what they establish to be inviolably observed by the king. Most holy and most mighty Innocent, since you are the hammer of the guilty and the comforter of the innocent, either free me from this archdeaconry by apostolic kindness, or, in accordance with the grace given you by God, by your command alone arrange and order it through certain good men, [Col. 0443D] so that among posterity the memory of your favour and glory may endure above every memory.

## EPISTLE CLII. TO THE SAME

**Summary.**—He beseeches the supreme pontiff that the church of Wolverhampton, of which he was dean, may, because of the incorrigible conduct of its clergy, be converted into a monastery of the Cistercian order.

To the reverend Father and lord I., by God’s grace supreme [Col. 0444A] pontiff, PETER of Blois, archdeacon of London, greetings and the service of devoted humility.

I was dean of the Church of Wolverhampton in the diocese of Chester; nevertheless it was answerable or subject to no pontiff except the archbishop of Canterbury and the king. For by a most ancient custom, which many regard as law, the kings of England have always granted that deanery. The granting and institution of prebends belonged to the dean. But because that clergy, like the Welsh and Scots, was wholly undisciplined, such dissolution of life had crept in among them that their vice became contempt of God, destruction of souls, disgrace of the clergy, and a hissing and mockery among the whole people. And, to borrow the words of Scripture, their shameful acts were sung [Col. 0444B] in the streets of Gath and at the crossroads of Ashkelon. [Note: [Col. 0443] 2 Kings 1.] I frequently recalled to their memory Hosea’s words: “Though you, Israel, commit fornication, let Judah at least not sin.” [Note: [Col. 0443] Hosea 4.] But they publicly and openly committed fornication and proclaimed their sin like Sodom; in the very sight of popular infamy they took as wives one another’s daughter or niece. So great was the web of kinship among them that no one could dissolve the bonds of their impiety. For they were like the scales of Behemoth, [Note: [Col. 0443] Job 41.] each joined to the next, and no breath of life passes through them. Therefore the earth cried out against them and the heavens revealed their iniquities. With the most exact diligence I laboured to cut away the poisonous offshoots of their vices, but I would more easily have turned wolves into sheep and [Col. 0444C] beasts into men. “Will the Ethiopian change his skin, or the leopard his spots?” [Note: [Col. 0443] Jeremiah 13.] Whenever I could gather some of them in the church, so that I might have opportunity for speech with them, they stopped their ears after the manner of the asp, for they would not understand in order to do good; [Note: [Col. 0443] Psalm 35.] indeed, like the mountains of Gilboa, upon which neither dew nor rain falls, [Note: [Col. 0443] 2 Kings 1.] they opposed salutary admonitions and cared neither for their crimes nor their dangers. These wretches had cast away their inward parts and, given over to a reprobate mind, ran unbridled like released stallions toward every precipice of vice.

I pressed their correction with all the marrow of my soul and with the whole affection of charity, for there was continual grief in my heart; but they hated one who reproved at the gate [Col. 0444D] and abhorred one who spoke salvation. I devoted myself to prayer and placed my mouth in the dust, if perhaps there might be hope; groaning, I spoke in the bitterness of my soul. And lest the sacrifice of compassion lack the fat of an offering, I seasoned the bitterness of my contrite heart with tears. The king and archbishop wrote terrible threatening letters to them; I, however, most firmly promised that the Roman pontiff would take away their place and nation, and that they would be cast out of their dwellings. But their contumacy increased under threats, and their contempt under admonition. They were few, yet [Col. 0445A] their iniquity multiplied into a multitude; the brood of vipers increased. Eggs of asps burst forth into basilisks, and from poisonous roots spurious shoots sprang up. From the seed of Canaan there proceeded a perverse and provoking generation, sons of Belial, wicked sons. Wishing to possess God’s sanctuary as an inheritance, whenever an honourable man was substituted for a canon who had died, the dead man’s nephew or son said that what was the Crucified One’s patrimony was his own patrimony. Then, fleeing into the forest and becoming companion to thieves and to men who despoiled others with sword and flame, he raged to destroy the canon who had been appointed in the deceased man’s place. Therefore, seeing that these wretches were now approaching the gates of death, and considering my own inadequacy, I desired to be accursed from [Col. 0445B] brethren of such great wickedness, to which not even the end of life could impose an end. There was continual grief in my heart that I had rashly undertaken the care of men whose iniquities I could not break through. I understood that the strict Judge would terribly demand from my hand an account of my stewardship and their destruction, and that what I was exposing to certain danger was greater than every treasure. I hated the congregation of evildoers, and their dwelling with me became like a lioness’s den. Thus I left them according to the desires of their hearts, to go after their own lusts. For God is not before their eyes; nor is there among them anyone willing to fear or believe God’s terrible judgments, until a pit is dug for the sinner, until God is known as the one who executes judgments, and until he who rejoices and exults in the worst things suddenly descends to hell. Therefore I approached the lord of Canterbury, humbly and earnestly begging that, by his assistance and with the king’s consent, once the filth of that abomination was removed, religion of the Cistercian order might be planted there. This proposal gained great support from the fact that the place abounds in woods, pastures, flowing waters, and revenues which, through the industry of a prudent man, would quickly attain great increase. In expectation of this change—which truly is the right hand of the Most High—I solemnly resigned the deanery into his hand. He, as a foremost lover of religion, watches over and labours at the work, and has already introduced certain members of the Cistercian order [Col. 0445D] to mark out and arrange the site of the church and its workshops.

Therefore, most holy Father, whom God has placed among the reaping angels so that through you scandals may be gathered out of his kingdom, I beseech you to confirm our purpose and mercifully grant the favour and grace of apostolic kindness to the monastery which the archbishop, with the king’s consent and to the rejoicing of the whole land, intends to build. [Col. 0446A] Transform a pigsty and Satan’s brothel into a temple of God and a workshop of the Holy Spirit. Let the shamelessness and robberies of the lost be removed; and for those who seek the face of the God of Jacob let a paradise of delight be built, where they may enjoy the delights of contemplation and Rachel’s embraces; where there may be Christ’s manger, the trench of one cubit which Ezekiel saw at the altar. [Note: [Col. 0445D] Ezekiel 43.] Uproot wickedness and sow innocence, most holy Innocent. Raise up children of Abraham from the stones. I beg you, take up the zeal of Phinehas, so that this cancerous plague, which monstrously disfigures the beauty of the Lord’s house, may be cut away in these men, and that men like them may be terrified by the example of apostolic severity. Indeed, it will redound to your glory if Christ’s glory is extended through you, [Col. 0446B] and by the merit of this good work you will obtain good days eternally.

## EPISTLE CLIII. TO HENRY II, KING OF ENGLAND. [c. A.D. 1173]

**Summary.**—The archbishop of Rouen and the bishop of Lisieux freely set forth the substance of their embassy to the king of France, reveal the reasons for the war proclaimed by him for the ruin of the kingdom and king of England, and urge Henry to make God favourable to himself through his own prayers and those of others.

To HENRY, by God’s grace illustrious king of the English, etc., R., archbishop of Rouen, and ARNULF, bishop of Lisieux, greetings in him through whom kings reign.

We judged that the embassy entrusted to us should be carried out all the more promptly and diligently [Note: [Col. 0445] For this embassy of Rotrou and Arnulf, historians of this period should be consulted throughout at the years around 1173.] because [Col. 0446C] delay seemed more dangerous in so great a crisis. Therefore, equipped for the labour of the journey undertaken, we approached the king of the Franks. After first offering a most courteous greeting and thereby forestalling his displeasure, we could by no effort obtain any answer to your greeting. We explained one by one the articles of our embassy, repeatedly urging the benefits of peace and the disadvantages of dissension. He, however, patiently received all our speech except the greeting. When the course of our embassy had thus been carefully completed, after a short interval he began reproachfully to charge us with the deceits and artifices by which he complained that he had very often been outwitted. He said that you had often violated, upon the slightest pretext, the pledged faith mutually agreed between you, and that you had shown yourself so unreliable in all things [Col. 0446D] that henceforth he would place no trust in you. Most illustrious king, do not take it ill if we report what we heard. For this is the condition of messengers: that they conceal nothing, suppress nothing, and diminish nothing from the answer entrusted to them.

He further added that he had held the firmest intention of attacking you before your son [Col. 0447A] had arrived at Chartres; and he advanced these causes of dissension and hatred: that you do not permit his daughter to return to her husband; that you do not restore to her her dowry; that you have stirred up against him, out of hatred for him, peoples subject to his authority from the mountains of Auvergne as far as the Rhône; and that, to the detriment of his crown, you have received the count of Saint-Gilles as a liege man. Finally, he confirmed by oath that henceforth he would never have treaty or concord with you unless it were with the consent of your wife and your sons. Now, therefore, sounder counsel must be employed in guarding your fortifications and especially in protecting your person. For all France has conspired by common purpose for your destruction. Nor is it enough for him to devastate the face of the land with fire and sword: against your [Col. 0447B] person—God forbid!—he is devising an abominable crime. We advise, indeed, that if you have taken anything or injured anyone, you restore what has been taken and transform hostilities into favour. For this especially invites your enemies to battle: they know that you have internal enemies, and those who eat sweet food with you, when opportunity is given, will greatly exalt their treachery against you. “Cursed is the man who trusts in man and makes flesh the strength of his arm.” [Note: [Col. 0447] Jeremiah 17.] What is more beloved than children? What more intimate than a wife? Yet your wife has departed from your side, and your sons rise up against their father. Hence that man, wisest of men, did not speak without purpose when he said: “Trust not a friend. From her who sleeps in your bosom guard the doors of [Col. 0447C] your mouth. For a son dishonours his father, and a man’s enemies are those of his own household.” [Note: [Col. 0447] Micah 7; Matthew 10.] We judge that the aid of him in whose hand are the hearts of kings should certainly be implored. [Note: [Col. 0447] Proverbs 21.] In his name David’s smallness overcame Goliath’s greatness. [Note: [Col. 0447] 1 Kings 17.] In his name Samaria, so consumed by famine while Ben-hadad besieged it that a donkey’s head was sold for thirty silver pieces, [Note: [Col. 0447] 2 Kings 6.] was delivered in the twinkling of an eye and overflowed with an abundant plenty of provisions. Whoever hopes in him will not be weakened. If battle rises against you, hope in this. If camps rise against you, your heart will not fear; for he himself will teach your hands for battle. Take to your aid the prayers of the Church. If you have offended her in anything, render due satisfaction, and henceforth show her every reverence. For she is Christ’s bride, and Christ counts the injuries of his bride as his own; nor is there anything that incites your enemies to conflict more than their belief that you have been insufficiently devoted to the Church of God. May our dearest lord prosper, and against those who raise themselves against him in pride and arrogance [Col. 0448A] may he, through the might of the Most High, gain glory and triumph.

## EPISTLE CLIV. TO THE QUEEN OF ENGLAND. [A.D. 1173]

**Summary.**—Eleanor, queen of the English, is admonished to be reconciled to her husband, while she and her sons conspire against their father Henry.

To the queen of the English, [Note: [Col. 0447D]

This is Eleanor, concerning whom and the matters dealt with in this letter see what we have said above in connection with Epistle 144.

[Col. 0448D] This letter, like the preceding one, was written in 1173, the year in which Henry’s sons made war upon their father.]

the archbishop of Rouen and his suffragans, greetings, and a charge to seek the things that make for peace.

It has become public knowledge, and no Christian may be ignorant how firm and indissoluble the marriage bond is. Truth, which cannot lie, has decreed that marriages once contracted cannot be dissolved: “What God has joined together, let no man separate” [Note: [Col. 0447] Matt. 19]. Now, just as one who separates married persons makes himself a transgressor of the divine command, so too is the married woman blameworthy who separates herself from her husband and does not keep faith with the social bond. Since spouses become one flesh, the union of their bodies must be accompanied by unity of spirit and equality of consent. That woman nullifies the condition of nature, the apostle’s command, and the law of the Gospel, who is not subject to her husband. For the husband is the head of the wife [Note: [Col. 0447] Eph. 5]; she was taken from the man, is united to the man, and is subject to the man’s authority.

Therefore we all lament in a common and grievous complaint that, although you are a most prudent woman, you turn aside from your husband: side withdraws from side, member does not serve the head; indeed, what is more monstrous, you allow the entrails of the lord king—and your own—to rise against their father, so that he may rightly say with the prophet: “I have nourished and exalted sons, but they have despised me” [Note: [Col. 0447] Isa. 1]. Would that, as another prophet recalls, the last hour had overtaken our days and the earth covered our face, so that we might not see these evils!

We know that, unless you return to your husband, you will be the cause of a general ruin; and your individual wrongdoing now will turn into a common loss. Return therefore, illustrious queen, to your husband and our lord, so that through your reconciliation rest may be restored to those in distress, and through your return joy may return to all. If our prayers do not move you to this, let at least the affliction of the peoples, the impending oppression of the Church, and the desolation of the realm trouble you. For either Truth lies, or every kingdom divided against itself shall be laid waste [Note: [Col. 0447] Luke 11]. Certainly this desolation cannot fall upon the lord king, but upon his sons and their successors. Against a woman’s hand and childish counsel you provoke the anger of the lord king, before whom even the mightiest kings bow their necks.

Therefore, before the affair declines to a worse outcome, return with your sons to your husband, to whom you are bound to obey and to live with; turn yourself, and let neither you nor your sons distrust him. For we are altogether certain that he will show you every affection and the fullest assurance of security. I beg you, urge your sons to be subject and devoted to their father, for whom he has endured so many anxieties, so many dangers, so many labours. Therefore, lest unconsidered impulsiveness squander and destroy what has been acquired with such great sweat, we say these things to you, most pious queen, both from zeal for God and from the affection of sincere charity; for you are our parishioner, as is your husband. We cannot fail justice. Either you will return to your husband, or by canon law we shall be compelled and bound to exercise ecclesiastical censure upon you [Col. 0449B]. We say this unwillingly; and, unless you come to your senses, we shall do it with grief and tears. Farewell.

## LETTER CLV. TO THE PRIOR AND CONVENT OF LA CHARITÉ

[Note: [Col. 0449D] This priory, the first dependency of the abbey of Cluny, is situated on the Loire in the diocese of Auxerre. It was called La Charité because of the immense alms which the monks there gave to all who came from every quarter. It is said first to have been founded by Pepin, king of France, about the year of Christ 754. Then, after the monastery had been destroyed by the Vandals in 741, another was newly built in 1056 by Geoffrey, bishop of Auxerre, and by his father Hugh and his brother William, counts of Nevers, and was given to Saint Hugh, abbot of Cluny.] [1174?]

**Summary.** Rothrod, archbishop of Rouen, invited by the monks to repose during the war, explains that he cannot leave his flock without scandal; he asks that, if peace cannot be made between the father king, his son, and the king of France, they should commend the matter to the Lord in their prayers.

R., by God’s grace archbishop of Rouen, to his dearest friends E., prior of La Charité, and the entire convent: greeting in him who is the salvation of all.

[Col. 0449C] Although we are bound to you in many ways by the services formerly bestowed upon us, yet it adds still more abundantly to your merit that, amid our tribulation, you summon us to rest and generously offer yourselves for every service. And indeed, if no discord had disturbed Normandy, if we enjoyed full peace, our soul would yearn toward you with all its efforts—much more so in this storm, when we regard dwelling among you as blessedness and as an image of another paradise. Nothing today aggravates our distresses more severely than both the memory and the loss of that repose which we enjoyed with you, living among you as though outside the world, as though among angels.

Now it would complete our desires to do what you ask, if it could be done without very great and enormous scandal. But to leave the sheep desolate amid this public slaughter would be the act of a hireling rather than a shepherd. We do not say that we wish to meet enemies: we see no enemies; on both sides we see our lords, to whom we are bound and devoted—the eminence of the lord king of France, the lord king of England, and his son, the younger king [Col. 0450A]. If we cannot be restorers of peace, at least we shall ask God for those things that make for peace. We shall perform the part of a bishop: we shall grieve with the living, die with the dead, and, through mutual participation in compassion, make the public affliction and common danger our own.

Would that this slaughter could be redeemed by our blood and compensated by our death together with the general loss; for we alone would suffer what all are to suffer. Pray therefore, beloved brothers, to our Lord, that he may look upon the face of his covenant and calm the tumult of the present discord into peace. For if the hope of peace smiled upon us, this alone is our wish: to spend with you that little remainder of life left to our old age [Col. 0450B]. Farewell.

## LETTER CLVI. TO G., BISHOP OF ELY

**Summary.** He implores the bishop’s help to free him from debt.

To his dearest lord G., by God’s grace bishop of Ely, his P. of Blois, archdeacon of Bath: greeting, and an abundance of merciful compassion.

Driven by the most urgent necessity, I am going to Canterbury to be crucified by faithless Jews, who torture and afflict me upon the grievous gallows of debts by their interest. I expect the same cross in London unless you mercifully free me—you in whom mercy and abundant redemption are looked for. Remove therefore, dearest father and friend, this cross, and take upon yourself the six pounds which I owe Samson the Jew, so that by this deliverance of mine you may turn an obligation into service and a debt into favour [Col. 0450C]. Farewell.

## LETTER CLVII. TO G., HIS VICAR

**Summary.** He admonishes his vicar to care diligently for the flock entrusted to him and to lead by the example of his life those whom he teaches.

Master PETER of Blois, archdeacon of Bath, to G., his vicar: greeting in him who is the salvation of souls.

Although you have been fully instructed concerning the duty of ecclesiastical administration, nevertheless, because you perform my office in this matter, it greatly concerns me that you should exercise the care of souls with all the greater attentiveness, since it is more certain that negligence in this office redounds to the common loss of our salvation. The salvation of the souls whose guardianship you have undertaken will be demanded from your hands at the strict and supreme judgment; nor shall I have a lawful ground of excuse, since, even if I have not held the care of souls, I was nevertheless bound to provide a suitable shepherd for it [Col. 0451A].

Therefore, brother, I warn and exhort you in Christ: guard vigilantly and circumspectly the vineyard of the Lord of Hosts, whose protection has been entrusted to your care. For there are foxes which secretly destroy this vineyard: namely, the wiles of hidden enemies, who not only delight in the destruction of subjects, but watch the heel of the elect and greedily take prelates for food, as Scripture testifies that “Behemoth’s food is choice food.” O ruined men, who do not consider how great a peril from the care of souls threatens them, yet rush greedily into the assumption of office! And though the Apostle says, “No one takes the honour upon himself, but he who is called by God, as Aaron was” [Note: [Col. 0451] Heb. 5], they, neither chosen nor called, thrust and force themselves into dangerous administration.

The most unhappy priest is altogether insufficient for the care of his own soul, yet presumes to undertake the charge of many souls. Without doubt he is a hireling: he seeks the profit of the purse, not that of the soul. For when he feels himself burdened with sins, weighed down by the mass of this body, entangled in earthly cares, occupied by carnal desires, weak against persecutions, trembling with fears, anxious with suspicions, subject to countless necessities, wretched, prone to vices, and powerless for virtues—by what presumption does he undertake to bear a burden which he cannot sustain for an hour? [Col. 0451C]

But accursed ambition blinds the wretch: while he receives the offerings of the altar and feeds upon widows’ tears and the patrimony of the Crucified One, he does not consider that these things will be required from him with utmost exactness on the dreadful day by the Lord. “For this the wicked has provoked God; for he has said in his heart, ‘He will not require it’” [Note: [Col. 0451] Ps. 9]. Certainly the Lord will require it to the last farthing. Yet he, long-suffering and merciful toward many, endures the wickedness of priests for a time with patience; but when they say, “Peace and security,” then sudden destruction will come upon them, like labour pains upon a pregnant woman, and they shall not escape [Note: [Col. 0451] 1 Thess. 5].

I have resolved to communicate these things to you, dearest brother, so that you may order the state of your life with maturer counsel; and, if you have hitherto behaved negligently concerning the care of the Lord’s flock, that the loss of time may be redeemed and what has been wrongly done may be reformed for the better [Col. 0451D]. If you wish to rule and teach others, first rule and teach yourself: “Jesus began to do and to teach” [Note: [Col. 0451] Acts 1]; first do, and then teach. You teach badly if, while acting badly, you speak well; for the voice of action is stronger than the voice of speech.

At a priest’s ordination, his lips and hands are consecrated to the Lord. “The lips of the priest preserve justice” [Note: [Col. 0451] Mal. 2]. But the hands which handle the most pure body and blood of Christ ought to be most pure. Let your words, then, profit those subject to you; let your deeds furnish an example, as Gregory testifies [Note: [Col. 0451] Gregory, *Pastoral Rule*, III.5]: “If you act perversely, you make yourself deserving of as many deaths as the examples of destruction you pass on to your subjects.”

Examine diligently the life of each person counted among your flock. If you find anything needing correction, first rebuke it in a spirit of gentleness; if he does not listen to you, “tell it to the Church” [Note: [Col. 0451] Matt. 18]; and if an incurable wound still does not feel the remedies of exhortation, apply the knife of excision. “Reprove, press upon, exhort, in season and out of season” [Note: [Col. 0451] 2 Tim. 4]. If you have done what belongs to you, and your rebuke does not accomplish that for which it was sent but returns empty, like a dart that strikes and rebounds, it shall no longer be imputed to you as guilt [Col. 0452B]. For he excuses you who says: “They will not listen to you, because they will not listen to me” [Note: [Col. 0451] Ezek. 3]; and: “He who despises you despises me” [Note: [Col. 0451] Luke 10]. If your exhortation bears fruit, you will gain your own soul together with another’s.

I could invite you by these and similar things to the fruit of a better life; but, to gather much into few words, my counsel is that you should either free yourself altogether from the care of souls, or strive to make yourself such a person as can answer, before the terrible tribunal of the supreme Judge, for your own soul and for those of others.

## LETTER CLVIII. TO J., BISHOP OF CHARTRES [A.D. 1176]

[Col. 0452C]

**Summary.** He complains bitterly that at the Roman curia certain men, corrupted by gifts, attempted unsuccessfully to set an unlearned layman over an abbey contrary to the canons.

To his dearest father and lord J., by God’s grace bishop of Chartres, his P. of Blois, archdeacon of Bath: greeting, and remembrance of promised mercy.

Knowing that you are occupied with the care of churches, I use few words, lest I hinder ears of your holiness devoted to the public good. After the matters which my lord had particularly entrusted to me had been happily accomplished beyond all my desire [Note: [Col. 0451D] On this embassy of Peter of Blois to the Roman curia on behalf of the archbishop of Canterbury against Roger, abbot of Saint Augustine’s, see what has been said in the Life of the same Peter of Blois and in our notes], and after receiving the pope’s blessing and permission to depart and greeting the cardinals, I was joyfully preparing for my return [Col. 0452D], when, upon the arrival of the elect of Saint Augustine’s, the lord pope recalled Master G. and me from the journey we had begun.

[Note: [Col. 0452D] This is Gerard Puella, concerning whom see what I have said elsewhere.

This letter was written in 1176, when Peter of Blois was returning from Rome.]

For he was graciously received by those who, as you know, esteem men’s gifts more highly than personal merit. They hoped that his promotion would provide matter for quarrel and an occasion of greater gain [Col. 0453A]; and, swallowing a river, they trusted that the Jordan would flow into their mouth. Master G. stood firmly and wisely in opposition; and I too stood, as God in his sweetness ministers to the poor. Yet certain leading men among them regarded both the laws and the canons, and whatever we could bring forward from sacred Scripture to establish our side, as fatal and sacrilegious; and they publicly judged us enemies of the Roman Church unless we ceased from such words, by which we attempted to subject the Church of Saint Augustine’s, which they claim as their special possession, to the Church of Canterbury.

Paying no attention to the loss of souls among the monks, they allow them every unlawful thing: throwing off altogether the yoke of discipline, they run wandering and wanton toward every enticement of the flesh; and every excess which they commit during the year they redeem by an annual payment [Col. 0453B]. Therefore, when we had been publicly forbidden in this case to introduce canons or laws, but only privileges—if we happened to have any at hand, though they knew we possessed none at that time—and when they saw us in this matter deprived of every human assistance, they wished to set over the abbey an unlearned layman, but one shrewd in buying offices—an abbey which he had acquired through simoniacal trafficking, not secretly but publicly and in the marketplace. I sprang to the accusation and seized a written bill of charges against the elect.

For when I alleged matters against him that were manifest and notorious [Col. 0453C], those whom he had made friends by means of the mammon of iniquity poured wine and oil into the wounds of his reputation and infamy. Having exhausted the merchants of Flanders for silver, he finally borrowed an infinite quantity of gold from the Romans. Thus the wings of the silvered dove and its back in the brightness of gold brought it about that they would not hear even two words, or even one, concerning the liberties and dignities of the holy mother Church of Canterbury, for which the blessed martyr fought unto death, and which, dying, he confirmed by the outpouring of his brain and reddened with his own blood.

They had ordered the elect to have himself tonsured and shaved, since he was to receive blessing from the lord pope on the following Sunday. Therefore, placed amid distresses and crosses, amid countless deaths [Col. 0453D], seeing that our justice was not being turned into judgment, I turned to arguments of natural reason and brought it about, without any promise or outlay of gifts, that the blessing was deferred for him. Therefore, having commended the cause of the Church of Canterbury to God and to our martyr, I left the curia, grievously feverish, at the beginning of July. Farewell.

## LETTER CLIX. TO HENRY, BISHOP OF BAYEUX

[Col. 0454A]

**Summary.** He reminds the bishop of Bayeux of his duty, while asking pardon for having dared to do so.

To his beloved and above all beloved H. [Note: [Col. 0453D] Concerning this Henry, see the notes to Letter 50], by God’s grace bishop of Bayeux, PETER of Blois: greeting, and whatever is more precious than health.

I would very often have sent you letters, but I fear lest a detractor should ascribe it to importunity if I interrupt your care, occupied with the public interests of the Church, at an unsuitable time. Yet, setting aside every risk of detraction, I shall speak to my lord, though I am dust and ashes. For although he is above humankind, he does not deny that he is human [Col. 0454B]; and while in this land of unlikeness and among the workshops of the Chaldeans he conforms himself, in the purity of chastity, to the purity of angelic conduct, he is not shaken by the breeze of secular glory, trampling underfoot popular favour, which others hunt with labour.

Let my lord therefore offer the head and tail of the sacrifice, and what he has faithfully and happily begun let him complete with a yet happier outcome. Let him whose name is as ointment poured forth be the good odour of Christ unto life, so that what is mutable may be turned into what is firm, what is worldly into what is heavenly, and what is temporal into what is eternal. I have set my mouth in heaven and, being most foolish, teach wisdom: I, who am full of the foul worms of conscience, admonish one whose conversation is in heaven, who already dwells as a bundle of myrrh between the breasts of the bride [Col. 0454C].

For he is one who, though in the world, does not know the world; a persecutor of his own flesh, running in the fragrance of ointments, he sings: “His left hand is under my head, and his right hand shall embrace me” [Note: [Col. 0453] Song 8]. I would indeed have imposed silence upon my mouth, had I not found it written: “Admonish a wise man, and he will love you; rebuke an imprudent man, and he will hate you” [Note: [Col. 0453] Prov. 9]. Nabal is recorded to have become worse from admonition [Note: [Col. 0453] 1 Sam. 25], Pharaoh more obstinate [Note: [Col. 0453] Exod. 11]; Manasseh came to his senses through correction [Note: [Col. 0453] 2 Chron. 33]; Balaam, through the speech of the ass, abandoned his purpose of cursing [Note: [Col. 0453] Num. 22]; Moses, at Jethro’s admonition, administered the offices of public government more prudently [Note: [Col. 0453] Exod. 18].

Let my lord therefore hear the braying ass rehearsing that saying of the Apostle: “All of us who are perfect are nevertheless imperfect” [Note: [Col. 0453] Phil. 3]. And elsewhere: “When we have done all things well, let us say that we are unprofitable servants” [Note: [Col. 0453] Luke 17]. For Job testifies: “Those who serve God are not steadfast, and in his angels he finds perversity” [Note: [Col. 0453] Job 4]. Elijah, thinking himself the only righteous man, cried to the Lord: “Lord, they have overthrown your altars, killed your prophets, and I alone remain among them, and they seek my life” [Note: [Col. 0453] 3 Kings 19]. The Lord rebuked him: “There still remain,” he said, “seven thousand who have not bent their knees before Baal” [Note: [Col. 0455] 3 Kings 19]. Peter fell where he had most confidently promised to stand [Note: [Col. 0455] Matt. 26]. “Therefore let him who stands take heed lest he fall” [Note: [Col. 0455] 1 Cor. 10].

I would write to you at greater length, but I fear that the letter may seem to turn into a sermon. Put on, I beg you, dearest one, Joseph’s long robe; and, as you have done hitherto, persevere to completion; fight lawfully, that you may triumph. May God, the beginning and end of all things, fit your end to your beginning, preserve you holy for himself and safe for us. Farewell.

## LETTER CLX. TO ODO, BISHOP OF PARIS [c. A.D. 1197]

**Summary.** Since Peter of Blois had lived twenty-six years in England, he asks Bishop Odo to recall him to France, so that, if not to live, he may at least be buried in his native country.

To his lord O. [Note: [Col. 0455D] This is Odo of Sully, bishop of Paris, concerning whom we have spoken at length in the notes to Letter 126.

This letter appears to have been written about 1197, shortly after Odo’s promotion; he was consecrated bishop in 1196], his most devoted P. of Blois: greeting, and whatever is more desirable than health.

I rejoice in your glory, because, as I have learned from the many reports of travellers, the renown, praise, and honour of your fame continually increase. As your name is ointment poured forth, pour out and spread more widely its glory, so that, as Abram became Abraham, Odo may become fragrance, and you may be the good odour of Christ in every place [Note: [Col. 0455] 2 Cor. 2]. Let the ointment of noble liberality descend from Aaron’s head to the hem of his garment [Note: [Col. 0455] Ps. 132], so that we, who aspire to touch the fringe of your garment, may be drawn after you [Col. 0455C] and run in the fragrance of your ointments [Note: [Col. 0455] Song 1]. For the oil of grace grows through expenditure, nor will it cease its abundance until it stops being distributed because the vessels fail.

For twenty-six years, wandering in England, I have heard a tongue that I did not know. Alas for me, for my sojourning has been prolonged [Note: [Col. 0455] Ps. 119] for so long a time, and there is no one to pity the exile; none is moved by Joseph’s affliction! Shall I always be a wanderer and fugitive upon the earth? Will no one set an end to my pilgrimage, so that at least once, before I breathe out my final spirit, I may be permitted to breathe in my native air? Many, accustomed to prolonged wandering, prefer exile to their country; and, becoming “Ephraim, a heifer trained to love threshing” [Col. 0455D; Note: [Col. 0455] Hos. 10], compensate the weariness of exile by the solace of straw. I feel otherwise.

> My native soil touches me with a certain sweetness  
> and never allows me to forget it.
>
> [Note: [Col. 0455] Ovid, *Letters from Pontus* I, elegy 4.]

The bishops of Gaul, among whom I have become like one dead in heart, like a broken vessel, have grown too hard toward me in grace. But let the north wind arise, and let the south wind come [Col. 0456A], blowing upon your heart. Let the word of God come and melt it; and, as the spirit of mercy blows, let the spices of your favours flow forth upon me. I do not know whence it comes or where it goes, this kindly spirit which continually suggests to me that God has specially reserved to your grace the ministry of recalling me. Let those, then, who savour carnal things harden themselves against me; and let him who is led by the Spirit of God melt toward me in mercy. For Scripture testifies that in the desert, long ago, meat hardened in the sun and manna melted [Note: [Col. 0455] Exod. 16].

Therefore I shall await my salvation in silence and hear what my Lord says within me. For he often raises me when I lie fallen and cheers my waning confidence, because your great fellow-countrymen, the bishops whose memory is blessed [Col. 0456B], honoured me by a certain privilege of special favour, and, when removed from the earth, left in you shoots of their old friendship. When you were precentor of the Church of Bourges, you extended the hand of your generosity to comfort foreigners even to the furthest borders of England; nor has your hand been shortened, but through consecration it has become so much more extended as the bishop is greater than the precentor.

> Who does not know that a bishop’s hands are long?
>
> [Note: [Col. 0455] Ovid, *Heroides*, epistle 16.]

It is readily apparent how much honour and advantage will accrue to you from my recall. For I believe that, as the Apostle says, the manifestation of the Spirit has been given to you for usefulness [Note: [Col. 0455] 1 Cor. 12]. Indeed, to use the prophetic saying [Col. 0456C]: “We will eat our own bread and wear our own garments; only let your name be called upon us: take away our reproach” [Note: [Col. 0455] Isa. 4]. Let the liberality innate in you remove the disgrace of my wandering and exile, so that you may make me wholly your own, and whatever I am, whatever I can do, whatever I know, whatever I possess, and whatever I am able to accomplish may wholly serve your honour and service.

Whatever you do for me will be a small and temporary favour, and your benefaction will return to you in due season with much thanksgiving from God and men. He to whom it is not permitted to live in his own country should at least be permitted to be buried there. And, that the letter may conclude with a verse of Lucan:

> “. . . Let it be permitted Martia to have inscribed upon Cato’s tomb”:
>
> so let it be permitted me to write: “Peter of Odo.”

## LETTER CLXI

[Note: [Col. 0456D] This letter and those following are not counted by many among the letters of Peter of Blois; consequently they lack titles, at least superscriptions, and are found in few copies.]

[Col. 0456D]

**Summary.** He complains bitterly that a man whom he had thought his closest friend has become a hostile enemy and detractor. It appears to have been written to a bishop.

It is unseemly for those to contend in harsh disputes whose manner of life others ought to conform themselves by emulation. I had thought myself stored away in the sanctuary of your friendship; I judged that you alone were another self to me. Yet, cherishing the poison of guile, you veiled the device of fox-like fraud beneath a covering of pretended affection. But though I was deceived by the speech of painted generosity, experience at last taught me to discover the ambiguous likeness of love: you gnaw at me with poisonous murmuring, speak ill of me in my absence, and do not cease to assail an innocent man with curses.

Either then command silence to the foulness of your speech, or, sprinkled with satiric vinegar,

> You shall weep, and your fame shall be sung through the whole city.
>
> [Note: [Col. 0457] Horace, *Satires* II.1.]

Love degenerates from the integrity of affection when flattery compels it to limp and easy opportunity disturbs it [Col. 0457B]. For such was the identity of mind which had bound me to him that we shared, as it were, one soul, and I judged him another self. But, spurred by the sting of envious whispering, he sowed the poison of discord and, scattering those who were joined, made a friend into an enemy for me. Therefore, because it adorns the excellence of prelates to soften insults and repair discords, I fall at your knees and implore your majesty that you may be willing to recall Master G. and me—between whom flattery has sown a little cloud of hatred—to concord.

## LETTER CLXII. TO E., HIS FRIEND

**Summary.** He says that he lives in a foreign region because he is little accepted among his own countrymen at home; and he thanks his friend E., who almost alone has shown himself a friend and like a brother.

The same, to E., his intimate friend: greeting, and, would that he could send himself in person.

I frequently desire, as I wish, to revisit the land of my birth, although no affection draws me there except the desire to see you. “I am not accepted in my own country” [Note: [Col. 0457] Luke 4]; and, as the Prophet adds, “My brothers have not known me” [Note: [Col. 0457] Ps. 94]; and, as another prophet complains [Note: [Col. 0457] Jer. 7], “The house of my birth has become for me a den of asps and a dwelling of scorpions.” My native land has closed the bosom of mercy to me and to my fellow-captives, and, spurning us, has compelled us to make a homeland elsewhere.

Among friends and brothers, experience has shown you alone to be a brother and friend to me [Col. 0457D], a favour for which I could not sufficiently repay you even if I shone all over with gold and silver. For “the children of men are deceitful in balances” [Note: [Col. 0457] Ps. 61], since they gladly receive services and do not repay what they have received. May the Lord repay you for me; and may the overflowing generosity of him who distributes in many ways to all from the treasures of his grace discharge what the incapacity of my lowliness does not presume to do.

Of the devotion which I bear toward you, God in heaven and my conscience on earth are witnesses, as the Apostle says [Col. 0458A; Note: [Col. 0457] 1 Thess. 2]. It is known only to God and to my conscience; I judge it superfluous to unfold it because my words would savour of flattery and would exceed all probability beyond measure. Greet all our friends. I cannot tell you certainly when I shall arrive, because unforeseen labours of travel and the vicissitudes that beset court attendants entangle me. See that the bearer of this letter is provided an escort as far as London.

## LETTER CLXIII. TO REGINALD, ELECT OF BATH [A.D. 1177?]

**Summary.** He congratulates Reginald, from whom he had received great benefits, on having been elected bishop of Bath.

[Col. 0458B] To his dearest lord R., by God’s grace elect of Bath, P. of Blois: greeting in him who is the salvation of the elect.

“My soul magnifies the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0457] Luke 1], because he has magnificently and wondrously exalted his mercy in one who dealt mercifully with me. Since I was not sufficient to repay the benefit I had received, Christ, surety of the poor, most abundantly answered for me according to his merit, raising to a bishop’s chair the man who raised me from the pit of poverty [Note: [Col. 0457] Ps. 39]. No one could add anything to the fullness of my joys, when I see him for whom alone I feared the mockeries of uncertain fortune and chance events, for whom alone I anxiously fluctuated between hope and fear, sailing in the safest harbour.

[Col. 0458C] O how worthy of glorification are the works of the Lord, and his mercies above all his works! [Note: [Col. 0457] Ps. 144.] Since I have experienced his mercies in all my necessities, his favour now breathes far more kindly upon my desire, because he has happily brought to effect what I had unceasingly long sighed for. I call God and my conscience to witness: I do not congratulate you on your election in order now to conceive hope of my own advancement from it, but because I see my wishes fulfilled. I can now safely both die and live, because this alone I awaited with desire: that there should be someone to answer to your generosity, your magnificence, and your labours. May the Lord still grant me this little span of life, that I may see you in pastoral eminence, you whom God has chosen as priest for himself [Col. 0458D].

## LETTER CLXIV. TO MASTER PHILIP

**Summary.** A certain man is reproved for accusing the archbishop of Canterbury of excessive gentleness.

To his beloved companion and friend Master PHILIP, Master PETER of Blois: perseverance in salvation and moderation of tongue.

You harshly criticize my lord, the Archbishop of Canterbury, [Col. 0459A] by misrepresenting his counsels and judgments, and you ascribe to folly and fickleness everything that he says, establishes, or ordains. In your eyes he has become guilty of every charge, because he seems to have erred in this one matter alone. He appears less discerning in judging other men’s actions who condemns all men on the basis of one. Would that you kept silent; or, if you take up the office of judge, that you judged yourself and not another! Job, speaking to his friends, says: “Would that you kept silent, and you would appear wise!” [Note: [Col. 0459] Job 13.] Would that you too, my friend, set a guard upon your mouth, so that by silence you might at least conceal or dissemble the ill-considered—indeed, not to say brain-sick—impulses of your mind!

If my lord suspended Ralph from the office which he held, if he turned justice into judgment, this sentence proceeded, in accordance with the gravity of Ralph’s offenses, from the counsel and deliberation of prudent [Col. 0459B] men. For, having been convicted in law of usurious exaction, a lapse of the flesh, and various forms of disgraceful conduct, he would, by the example of his evil deeds and the license of unchecked impunity, have drawn many into sin, unless canonical correction had cut down the crop of rising vices and the malice bearing fruit in him. But he, returning to his senses, promptly endeavored to gird the extraordinary stirrings of the flesh with the belt of sobriety, and to redeem the loss of long time through the short course of a stricter penitence and honorable conduct. His most abject penitence stirred in my lord feelings of compassion, and it was publicly believed that it had moved the lord himself to mercy.

[Col. 0459C] And when the lord king had sent him petitions requesting that he restore the aforesaid R. to the office of his former administration and to the serenity of his favor, after deliberation with the wiser men he imitated Him who, when angry, remembers mercy, and who in the school of the Gospel teaches Peter—and in Peter teaches us—to forgive not once, nor merely seven times, but seventy times seven. [Note: [Col. 0459] Matt. 18.] You accuse my lord of fickleness because he had compassion upon a penitent man, because he showed mercy to his neighbor and old, proven friend—though you know that on the dreadful day it is safer to answer for mercy shown than for justice exacted and strict severity.

You attribute to my lord’s fickleness the fact that, after he had pronounced a sentence of suspension against him, he freely yielded to the prayers of the lord king, to whom, according to the Apostle, [Note: [Col. 0459] 1 Pet. 2.] [Col. 0459D] as preeminent, especial honor must be shown, seemingly contradicting his own sentence. You know that, out of regard for royal eminence, ecclesiastical rigor is sometimes moderated and the severity of the canons softened. We read that the great Gregory and other venerable Fathers of the Church made dispensations, in these and similar and even greater matters, in various ways—not only on account of humble penitence or the intercession of princes, but sometimes for the simple favor of friends.

Therefore do not reprehensibly accuse my lord for what ordinary kindness among men is accustomed to do every day. But if you deign to follow the conduct of modern men or to draw the common practice into your argument, listen, I beg you, and let an example of unheard-of but carefully noteworthy kindness move you. I have read in Eusebius’s *Ecclesiastical History* that, when blessed Gregory, bishop of Caesarea, being overtaken by a storm and difficulty of circumstances, had taken refuge in the Alps in a shrine of Apollo, and had been received with most attentive hospitality by the pagan and profane priest of the place, he remembered the service and hospitality rendered him. He therefore, at the priest’s request, [Col. 0460B] released Apollo—whom he had suspended from giving oracles and from deceiving souls.

The priest, then, marvelling at the majesty of Him whose humble servants could so magnificently command the gods of the gentiles, and could by a word suspend or torment them, despised and abandoned Apollo, followed Gregory, and in Gregory followed Christ. Thus Gregory afterwards had as his successor in the government of the Church of Neocaesarea the priest of Apollo whom he had had as a disciple in the faith of Christ. Since, therefore, you see that at a man’s prayers a man released the demon whom he had bound, do not wonder if my lord—who by the common judgment of all is the gentlest of all who dwell upon earth—at the request of the lord king and the magnates of the land, in the case of a man humbly and truly repentant, [Col. 0460C] fulfilled the claims of old friendship.

## LETTER CLXV. FROM GUY, ARCHBISHOP OF SENS, TO POPE GREGORY. [A.D. 1187.]

**SUBJECT.**—The bishop of Laon is cleared of the crimes alleged against him.

To the most holy Father and lord G., by the grace of God supreme pontiff: G., by divine permission the humble minister of the Church of Sens, and his suffragans, whose seals are appended to the present letter: most devoted kisses of your blessed feet.

“Since the prudence of your fatherhood,” etc. See under Pope Gregory VIII, at the year 1187, after his *Registers*.

## LETTER CLXVI. TO THE POPE.

[Col. 0460D]

**SUBJECT.**—Certain persons intercede for the abbot of Saumur.

To the Supreme Pontiff.

Since from the proximity of the places and from trustworthy report we have learned that brother M. [Note: [Col. 0459D] This denotes Mainerius, who was the eleventh abbot of St. Florentius near Saumur, and was created [Col. 0460D] in the year 1176. He governed that monastery for twenty-six years and six months.]—the venerable abbot of Saumur—both lived a praiseworthy life before his promotion and, after his promotion, caused ascents [Col. 0461A] to arise in his heart, advancing from virtue to virtue; and that he governed his abbey well and praiseworthily for fourteen years or more, in peace and observance of the order, so that this monastery excelled the other abbeys of the province of Tours in spiritual and temporal matters: we are greatly astonished to hear that certain men, led, as is said, by perverse counsel, do not fear to disturb the peaceful condition of that abbey.

Yet the abbot, both before and after their appeal, offered them what the institutions of the monastic order require: having summoned neighboring abbots and worthy men, he was prepared to abide by their counsel and to amend whatever required amendment. Therefore, for the peace and tranquility of that Church or abbey, we beseech you, most holy Father, that by repelling the wicked and approving those who are [Col. 0461B] upright in heart, you may mercifully attend to the tranquility of that Church. Fare well, and long.

## LETTER CLXVII. TO ELEANOR, QUEEN OF ENGLAND. [A.D. 1183.]

**SUBJECT.**—Christians in the Holy Land console Eleanor, queen of England, over the untimely death of the son of Henry III, king of the English, and report that they celebrated his obsequies in the presence of the legate of the Apostolic See.

A mournful and sorrowful report has lately resounded in our land, full of bitterness and not devoid of an abundance of grief, wounding the hearts of our people by the novelty of a dreadful blow. It is indeed to be lamented by all the faithful [Col. 0461C] and mourned by all Christians; but it is more grievous for us to bear, and more bitterly distressing, because, placed amid the perils of mourning and funeral anxieties, we are compelled—alas, for sorrow!—to send back to that quarter the antidote of consolation from which we expected the help of support; toward which we trust to attain a harbor of tranquility out of so many waves; from which, finally, benefits continually bestowed upon the Holy Land from its earliest times have come down through the increase of ages, and welcome remedies have flowed forth. To that place we are forced to extend the affection of compassion; to that place, finally, we are constrained to minister the ointment of mitigation and the comfort of healing.

But since we are in no way sufficient either to put an end to your griefs or to repel our own dangers, [Col. 0461D] how can we be found adequate to assuage so bitter a grief in your highness? We who have wholly failed to mitigate or heal our own wounds—how shall we apply a healing hand and a remedy of medicine to a mother’s wound?

We know indeed that your spirit is deeply grieved at the bitter removal of your son and wounded in its inmost feelings; and not without reason. For, with the order of mortality disturbed, a mother offers tears for her son which the son had reserved for his mother. She sees a youth, not yet firmly arrived at maturity, undergo the judgment of untimely death before the judgment of old age has come upon him. And he who was awaited by all as successor to so great a dignity [Col. 0462A] is now, like a flower falling before fruit, like fruit plucked while the season is still immature, rightly lamented and mourned by all who cherish the posterity of such persons and desire the undying increase of their lineage.

There is therefore abundant matter for grief on every side; yet the antidotes of consolation are not lacking, if the force of grief would admit reason and if we did not follow the will of carnal feeling. But when we consider wisdom and the examples of ancient kings, that illustrious king, filled with the Spirit of God, although he grieved bitterly during his child’s sickness and passed mournful days, nevertheless at the child’s funeral raised not only himself but others also from the sea of grief by manifold consolation. For he declared, with both prophetic spirit and the clear-sightedness of human reason, that he would go to his son, but that his son would not thereafter return to him, nor return through the aid of anyone’s tears. [Col. 0462B] [Note: [Col. 0461] 2 Sam. 12.]

Remember, noble lady, that you bore a mortal son; that you received no exemption from momentary mortality; and that you have no sufficiently lasting ground for grief in the loss of one son, when the Lord has endowed you with such numerous offspring and enriched you, finally, with such great prosperity. Who knows whether the Holy Spirit, the razor of human generation, timely cut short in the royal child the thread of life which He had not yet woven perfectly, lest thereafter the fascination of vanity should turn away his understanding and the deceitfulness of worldly illusion should deceive his soul? And therefore, because his soul was pleasing to God, he was made beloved and was transferred from darkness to light, from prison to kingdom, [Col. 0462C] from mortality to life, and finally from exile to his homeland.

But what are we to do? Shall we not expose ourselves to deserved reproach when we offer drink to the fountain, food to bread, consolation to her who consoles all? We know, illustrious lady, that through God’s grace the fame of your royal name has spread through the whole world: and although a mother’s inward affections may be stirred by natural feeling at the death of so great a son and the loss of such a child, nevertheless, through the anointing of the heavenly gift with which the Almighty has richly anointed you above all your predecessors, so great a consolation overflows in you as an example of virtue and patience that, poured forth upon others, it has furnished refreshment to some, joy to others, [Col. 0462D] and has stirred still others to emulate virtue and patience.

Furthermore, most excellent and special lady, though we desist from words of consolation as persons insufficient and unequal to the task, we make known to your greatness our sentiments of compassion and tokens of devotion, in which the whole people of Acre poured themselves out upon hearing of the death of your dearest son, as a demonstration of their complete submission and affection. For, when all prelates and rulers of churches, the barons of the kingdom of Jerusalem, and all the people had been summoned to the church of the Holy Cross, the funeral rites were celebrated according to custom. On the following day the solemnities of the Mass were celebrated by the legate of the Apostolic See, and a great indulgence was granted [Col. 0463A] on the part of the legate and other prelates. The aforesaid legate, with us standing by him, enjoined special prayers upon all the people for the repose of the dead man. He also commanded that more particularly and abundantly they pray for the preservation over a longer time of the life of the king, queen, and their children and brothers, devoutly commending the kingdom and the king with his consort and children to the Childbearing Woman of Bethlehem, as he has always been accustomed to do in his sermons.

## LETTER CLXVIII. TO N., ROMAN PONTIFF.

**SUBJECT.**—A certain king congratulates himself and the whole West because N., from his own land, has attained the supreme pontificate; and he exhorts him to promote only worthy men [Col. 0463B] to ecclesiastical dignities.

To such a pope, such a king.

A sweet breeze has breathed upon our ears, because, as we have learned, the novelty of your election, like a glowing dawn, has driven away the darkness of the desolation of the Roman Church. The Apostolic See rejoices at having obtained consolation in its widowhood. All Churches rejoice, seeing a new light arise and awaiting its growth unto the perfect day. But our West rejoices especially because, like the East, it has deserved to pour a new light upon the world, and because the West, by God’s gift, has restored the sun of Christendom, which lately set in the East.

Therefore, holy Father, greatly rejoicing in your honor and pursuing the magnificence of the divine Majesty with devout praises for this reason, we disclose our wishes more familiarly to your fatherhood, in whose filial zeal and devotion we trust. [Col. 0463C] For if a son according to the flesh confidently lays open his earthly affections to his father, how much more confidently may a spiritual son reveal his spiritual desires?

Assuredly, among our other desires, we are not a little moved that, since the divine right hand has seen fit spiritually to plant your most reverend person as a life-giving tree in the midst of paradise, and to transplant you from our land into its own orchard, you should exert yourself with the utmost earnestness so to refresh all Churches by fruitful works and teachings that all generations may call the nation of your blessedness blessed. We also thirst with sincere heart that the spirit of storms, [Col. 0463D] which is accustomed to blow most violently about the heights of dignities, may never tear you away from the pursuit of holiness, lest—God forbid!—the higher summit of dignity be followed by a more grievous precipice.

And we earnestly desire this also: since the ordering of all the Churches belongs to you, may you take care, without the loss of delay, to appoint as cardinals such men as know, are willing, and are able to bear your burden—looking not to nearness of country, quality of lineage, or extent of power, but to whether they fear God, hate avarice, thirst for justice, and burn with zeal for souls.

Nor does it move our concern but little that, since the unworthiness of ministers harms Churches beyond measure, you should be careful to keep the closest watch whenever your provision is sought in the conferring of dignities or prebends, [Col. 0464A] lest any unworthy person rush into the patrimony of the Crucified One. And since the blessed land—consecrated by the origin of blessed redemption, by the life and blood of Christ, and especially bound to be venerated by Christian devotion—is, as you know by eyewitness faith, disturbed by such incursions of peoples and defiled by abominations, we ardently desire that you gird the powers of your solicitude for its liberation.

And who ought not to desire that the formerly illustrious empire of Constantinople, now grievously desolated, should receive timely consolation through your prudent foresight? For, both out of regard for your honor and out of zeal for the common good, we ought to desire that you, who by divine promotion preside over the universal Church, [Col. 0464B] should keep continual watch over the instruction and reformation of all Churches.

But we trust and hope in the Lord that, just as, divinely raised from virtue to virtue and from honor to honor, you took care to shine according to the demands of those offices, so, summoned to the summit of apostolic eminence, you will take care to enlighten and inflame the Churches subject to you, so that none may be found who hides himself from your light and warmth. May you leave after your death such traces of holiness that the land of your birth, which rejoices in a happy origin, may with still greater happiness glory in the Lord over a happy end.

Finally, from special confidence we ask and entreat your fatherhood that you may deign to hold us, our household, and the condition of our kingdom especially commended [Col. 0464C] in your words and prayers.

## LETTER CLXIX. TO A CERTAIN QUEEN.

**SUBJECT.**—He consoles a queen mourning the death of her sons.

Health and a happy length of days, with the increase of the well-wished blessings of health and joy.

From the beginning of this present world, although the Creator of all things gave diverse natures to things themselves, He nevertheless willed all to be enclosed within this condition: that they should be subject to movement and corruption, and at last to decay; and that all things which originally proceeded from nothing should thus be brought back into nothing.
