Hence it is that darkness of night succeeds the pleasant light of day; tribulation is joined to prosperity; changeableness alters stability; adversity mocks happiness; the sting of grief wounds joy; and finally death carries off the triumph from present life. [Col. 0464D] This, indeed, is a law that admits no exception; this is the unchangeable will of the supreme Creator. It spares neither the highest dignities nor immense powers, but

> Making scepters equal with spades, equal toward all, it makes all equal in this respect.

The common law must therefore be borne with equanimity, and we must humbly obey the decree of Him who had no counselor; and who, in order to show us that this law does not spare us, did not spare even His own Son.

What then is the reason that, at the glorious passing of so many such persons, [Col. 0465A] you continually utter, as we understand, irrepressibly sobbing groans of grief, sad laments, dolorous cries, and bitter tears? Certainly, a noble spirit, the rank of nobility, and the measure of prudence neither approve nor allow such things. Therefore we beseech your highness with all the prayers we can, and entreat you in the Lord Jesus, utterly casting aside the aforesaid anxieties, daughters of faint-heartedness, to direct your bodily and mental eyes toward the Lord Himself, praising Him in all His works with the whole ardor and application of your mind.

For although you suffer in the flesh because you have lost persons so great, so exalted, so magnificent, you should rather give thanks to the Most High and praise His justice and mercy, because through His gift you deserved, as has been said, to possess such persons. Consider also [Col. 0465B] carefully that whatever we possess is a loan from God, not a gift: for He has placed on deposit, not bestowed outright, whatever benefits we hold under Him. Let us therefore give thanks for their use, and when He demands them back, let us render them without ingratitude; but recognize yourselves again as obliged to give thanks for the happy abundance of children, in whom, if you consider well, there is both matter of joy for you and, moreover, abundant restoration for what has been lost.

## LETTER CLXX. TO A CERTAIN QUEEN.

**SUBJECT.**—He exhorts a queen not to mourn beyond measure over the death of the king of Aragon.

Perhaps it benefited you until now not to know of the death of the king of Aragon, and thereby to have stolen so much time from grief; but it has plainly harmed us, because we are compelled to feel grief’s sword with you—a sword which wounded our soul at his death. The wound, too, which the very length of time had covered with a scar, now, gaping open with renewed sighs, comes again to life. For what good would it do to exhort you, wounded by so bitter a blow, not to grieve, when a fresh wound is not without pain? Or to urge you not to weep at a funeral so deserving of tears, when we ourselves, in the first freshness of grief, were entirely unable to restrain our tears, and even now can scarcely restrain them at the memory of it?

For grief, like the other emotions, has its own laws, which endure no one’s command. And just as fear suffuses any living person with pallor, and shame with blushing, so the force of grief enclosed in the inmost heart, bursting outward and delayed by no command, pours itself forth in streaming tears. [Col. 0465D] Thus the patriarch Jacob, believing that his son Joseph had been devoured by a beast, continued for many days in mourning. [Note: [Col. 0465] Gen. 37.] Thus Job, the singular example of patience, expressed the force of grief at the bitter death of his children by tearing his garments. [Note: [Col. 0465] Chapter 1.]

Now, therefore, we intend to persuade you, as though you were stronger than those mentioned above, entirely to exclude grief in such abundant cause for sorrow. We wish you rather to observe measure in grieving and to imitate Job himself, of whom mention has just been made. After he had expressed the vehemence of grief, [Col. 0466A] as stated above, he at once remembered the Creator’s benefits and humbly obeyed the divine will: “If we have received good things from the hand of the Lord,” he says, “why should we not receive evil things?” [Note: [Col. 0465] Job 2.]

And you, who have received many good things, even abundantly, from the hand of the Lord, why then are you indignant if bitterness has been sprinkled upon so many sweet things? Or do you not know that human life upon earth is a pilgrimage? And as on the long road of pilgrimage there is now dust, now mud, now fair weather, now rain, so in this life there are now hope, now fear, now sorrow, now joy. [Note: [Col. 0465] Augustine, Sermon 2, *On Consolation in Death*.] Finally, what can you gain by superfluous grief, except to afflict yourself and dismay the spirits of your subjects?

Behold, we offer you the example of King David, that you as queen may wisely imitate a king. [Col. 0466B] His servants wondered that, while his son was still living, he fasted and wept; but after he had died, David washed his face and ate, replying: “While he was still alive, I fasted and wept, in case the Lord might grant him to me. But now, since he is dead, why should I fast? Shall I be able to call him back again? I shall go to him, but he will not return to me.” And by such deed and word the king consoled both himself and his own. [Note: [Col. 0465] 1 Sam. 12.]

You therefore, dearest daughter, begin to console yourself and your own by these examples. Do not fail, but make progress, being corrected by David, lest you be so cast down by remembrance of the past that you lose the joy of the present. Rather raise in yourself confidence in things to come, considering how fleeting and perishable temporal glory is, [Col. 0466C] so that you may earnestly strive to obtain that glory which has no end.

## LETTER CLXXI.

**SUBJECT.**—He consoles someone grieving over the death of many persons.

Against the reverses of the world, as varied as they are bitter; against the destructive assaults by which the human condition is continually afflicted—whose harp is turned to mourning, whom the snares of death tear apart, whom errors constrain and do not permit to breathe—we must take up the arms of patience, gently bear so many adversities, and endure, not only patiently but with thanksgiving, the good pleasure of God, at whose mere nod the world is now shaken and all things tremble.

[Col. 0466D] Certainly, although a bitter, anxious report, full of wormwood, spread everywhere concerning the fall and likewise the death of such persons, accumulates material for weeping and pierces the inward parts of the heart, it belongs to a prudent mind to endure the Lord’s heavy hand with moderation, lest, by desiring the contrary, one be convicted of unwillingness to accept what pleased the Most High and what God’s judgment ordained.

Therefore we have thought it right to entreat the prudence of your heart—which we know to be circumspect, which we know with certainty was not lifted up in prosperity nor cast down in adversity—that you may bear with so steadfast a spirit the passing of such persons, whom the Creator’s grace transferred from the misery of this world to the kingdom, [Col. 0467A] that the gift of patience may be bestowed upon you.

## LETTER CLXXII. [A.D. 1189.]

**SUBJECT.**—He most bitterly laments the disastrous death of the emperor Frederick, called Barbarossa.

A terrible, horrible, and unspeakable report, lately impressed upon our ears and those of others, has wounded the vital parts of our heart so bitterly, so deeply to the marrow, so mortally—more penetrating than any two-edged sword—that an antidote is scarcely hoped for, confidence in living scarcely remains, and scarcely any hope of survival endures. For we have heard—and almost failed in the very hearing from grief—[Col. 0467B] that that immovable pillar of the empire and firm support of the kingdom of Apulia, that morning star more shining than every glittering star; that, I say, enormous chrysolite more precious than every jasper and precious stone—namely Frederick, our most serene emperor—has, alas, closed the final day of his fate.

At his death the sun, moon, and all the lights of heaven seem darkened for all his faithful, and especially for the inhabitants of the realm, who flourished in the quiet of unshaken peace under the defense of your protecting aid; because that most radiant light has been extinguished, which, while it shone everywhere, gave cause until now to fear no stumbling-block of error or terror. Alas! What are we to do? To whom shall we flee? Whose protection shall we await? Who henceforth will be our great safeguard? Who a gentle relief to the people of the realm? Who a secure defense for the Apulian people?

[Col. 0467C] For the strongest lion has set, whose illustrious countenance and most mighty right hand frightened the fierce beasts of the earth and, everywhere in the world, tamed the monsters of rebellion by bringing their necks beneath himself. Mourn, therefore, you faithful of the kingdom, bereft of the protection of so great a prince; howl, young men; weep, old men, brides and virgins with youths. For the guide and governance of your life, your life and salvation, your light and defense, your guardianship and strength, anchor of hope, refuge and aid—alas!—has been subjected to the dominion of death.

Alas, alas for the unbridled insolence of importunate death, and the unrestrained presumption of the three sisters who draw out the threads of human life! Their names, taken from the word for sparing, are assigned to them antiphrastically—that is, with the contrary sense. Why do they not at least take true names for themselves in the case of so great a prince, so that they might safeguard the health of that head which had already spared a thousand heads deserving condemnation? [Col. 0467D]

O wondrous condition of mortals—and, if it is permitted to say so, lamentable condition—when empires bow beneath death’s power and the necks of nobles are subjected to its yoke, though the heads of poor and rich, weak and powerful, are placed beneath their dominion. Yet this is believed to have been ordained by divine providence: that, just as the condition of birth is alike for all, so a similar end and destruction should follow all and each alike.

Therefore, because such a great and irrecoverable loss must be mourned almost inconsolably, the minds of many are so beset with uncertainty that they do not know what ought to be done hereafter regarding war and peace. For the heirs of the lord emperor have a by no means powerless adversary, who, as is believed, strives with all his strength, if he prevails, daily to heap evils upon evils against them. [Col. 0468A] Hence we entreat your affection, in which we have full confidence, that you, to whose knowledge the secrets of the court come and the counsels of certain persons are revealed, may explain to us by letter whatever you can conjecture about future events, whether it is likely to be favorable or harmful, so that, insofar as we can, we may choose a safer course amid uncertainty. For missiles cast by enemies inflict less injury if they have been foreseen. [Col. 0468B]

## LETTER CLXXIII. TO THE SUFFRAGAN BISHOPS AND ABBOTS.

**SUBJECT.**—The Archbishop of Rouen implores the aid of bishops and abbots to relieve the poverty of the Roman pontiff.

The Archbishop of Rouen, to his suffragans and abbots, greeting.

You know, and we believe it has gone forth to the ends of the earth, by how many disturbances and pressures the Roman Church has long been harassed. We believe that it has become commonly known how the lord pope, for the defense of ecclesiastical liberty, exposed himself to every danger, and, continually dying with the Church of God amid persecutions, has been worn down in his own person and weighed down by the burden of debts.

Therefore your mother Church, exhausted by burdensome expenses, cries out to you and, placing full confidence in your generosity, asks to breathe again through your consolation; for your sake she feels herself desolate and consumed with grief. Surely the storm of schismatic power has now in part subsided; a gentler breeze now promises a safer harbor to Peter’s little ship, if the services of your generosity breathe favorably upon the opportunity for peace which God has offered. [Col. 0468C] For we have learned by certain report that the lord pope’s generosity and counsel have repeatedly overcome and brought low the savage malice of the Romans and their insatiable thirst for money. Nothing is lacking for complete fullness of peace and security except that the lord pope, drained by immense expenses, should restore from your generosity a sufficient supply of provisions for himself and his people. [Col. 0468D] Fare well.

## LETTER CLXXIV. TO THE TEACHERS OF THE ACADEMY OF NAPLES.

**SUBJECT.**—He laments the death of Master Walter, professor of grammar.

To all the teachers of the Neapolitan school, sitting beside the waters of bitterness and hanging their instruments upon the willows: Master P. wishes the consolation of the Holy Spirit and [Col. 0469A] that peace of our Lord Jesus Christ which surpasses all understanding.

By the calling of Him whose dominion extends in heaven, on earth, and over every creature, our companion and brother, Master Walter—distinguished among grammarians—has lately been summoned from this wicked world and vale of misery to the schools of the flourishing homeland, where no tumult of shameless babbling is heard. He has passed from our sight like a shadow—indeed, he has vanished. At his passing, the sun of the Parthenopean school was darkened and the moon turned into eclipse.

For the art of grammar, signified by the name of the moon, bereft of the rays of its beauty, sits sorrowful in darkness; and it has reason to renew its grief, having been widowed of two husbands in so brief a time. The wounds of the preceding and recent grief [Col. 0469B] have not yet been healed, and so calamity is added to calamity, storm to storm, grief to grief, and wounds are inflicted upon wounds. Here is a wonderfully perverse and disordered sequence: for by nature the disciple follows the master; but here the master has followed the disciple. This is because death’s irregularity, in its perverse custom, overturns order: it puts after what ought to be before, and conversely puts before what ought to be after.

Alas for sorrow! How suddenly has the leafy vine, whose fruit had abounded to the full, withered! For in the multitude of children whom that tireless pedagogical womb begot, he surpassed all and grew tall like a cedar of Lebanon, to which the shrubs of the wilderness are not equal. [Col. 0469C] He was another Joseph in the land of Egypt, [Note: [Col. 0469] Gen. 37.] whom all the mighty envied, whom a savage beast devoured: namely death, which, by aphæresis, takes away the head from all mortals and divides and tears it from the limbs.

At his severing, you who flourish in chairs of learning, as heads of many and full of eyes looking behind, look back and carefully consider how thin and fragile is the glory of singular distinction: it is like a vapor lasting a little while, and like grass that flowers in the morning, falls and withers in the evening. Therefore, most illustrious teachers, for the safeguard of living well, reflect in yourselves upon the condition and passing of your departed master through that “syncope” from which no grammarian is exempt; and draw one effective argument by analogy: that you will likewise run the road [Col. 0469D] which your companion has run before you, since the same judgment applies to like cases.

## LETTER CLXXV. TO STUDENTS OF GRAMMAR.

It has the same subject as the preceding letter, for it laments the death of a professor of grammar.

To those still crying in the cradle of the art of grammar, and to disciples but newly born: may every man who follows truth have a good life and a better end.

Because the subject matter begins with bitterness, and painful things cannot be recounted without disturbance of mind, do not be surprised if, with a certain anxiety and broken speech, we announce to you scholars, who dwell throughout the world from sea to sea—especially to you sons whom mother Grammar bore in travail—news bitter and all too harsh for the present time. For we speak with a sting of grief: the lamp of grammatical art has lately been extinguished, the well-watered fountain has dried up—the fruitful Euphrates, Master N., who deserved to be derived not from the name of the positive degree but from that of the superlative, since none rose above him. Indeed, as the eagle surpasses every kind of winged creature, so was he a man mighty in deed and speech, a rare bird upon earth, worthy to be called singular without the company of a plural.

At his passing, as though the sun were setting, darkness came over the whole face of the earth. For he alone, drawing light from Priscian’s dark and confused treatises, cleared away the darkness. He restrained his old and antiquated Donatus and reformed the apostate; and, like another Moses, a lawgiver from the gloom of Mount Sinai, he brought back to humankind a grammar written for him by God and not by man—a grammar under such and so great an artificer in which not merely the first arts but the other arts also are born. What, then, will the walls do when the foundation has fallen? What will unhappy Grammar do, bereft of her parent? Of him that prophetic saying has been fulfilled: “A voice was heard in Ramah,” that is, in the heights, “weeping and much wailing: Rachel weeps for her husband, and there is none among all her dear ones to comfort her” [Note: [Col. 0469] Jer. 31; Matt. 2.].

For who was like him, that the Lord might raise up his spirit through some necromancer, so that for a time that most learned master of masters, who led others into astonishment, might speak to you? But since we all die and, like waters that do not return, pass away; and since, as the philosopher testifies, equality consoles us for the cruelty of fate [Note: [Col. 0469] Seneca, *On Consolation to Polybius*, ch. 2], lay aside grief, you who loved such and so great an author, and gather for his obsequies, praying for that wondrous teacher. From morning until evening he cried out like a young swallow and meditated like a dove; in laying down his life for his pupils, he ceased by teaching and taught by ceasing.

## LETTER 176. TO PROFESSORS OF CIVIL LAW

[Col. 0470D]

**Subject.**—It laments the death of a certain outstanding professor of civil law.

P. to all professors of civil law: greetings, and a charge to attend to the last before the first.

“Most bitter bitterness” [Note: [Col. 0469] Isa. 38] and matter compounded of human griefs have lately presented themselves to our minds. For James of the Region, that unique and singular man in whom the laws came together and lived as in their own proper home—the trumpet of eloquence, fullness of counsel, voice of the people, and, to the end and at the end, the best and most excellent persuader of all—has surrendered his life-giving spirit to Jesus Christ; and the glory of his countenance has suddenly been grievously shattered.

[Note: [Col. 0471D] This was one of the first four who restored the study of civil law at Bologna and taught there. [Col. 0472D] See Bulaeus, vol. II of the *History of the University of Paris*, p. 348.]

At his setting, not Lombardy alone, deprived of its sun, but also the greater part of the living world groans amid continual tears, and the sword of grief has pierced the entrails of many [Note: [Col. 0471] Luke 1]. Nor without reason: for, as lawgiver and supreme teacher, he gave form to the unformed meanings of the prescribed books of law; and, as though still alive, he does not cease to give them form. Though as a man he has ceased, he does not cease as a master. Being dead, he teaches how harsh and violent death’s summons is: no resistance can be made to it; by the mode of necessity it overcomes every syllogism; it admits no exceptions and regards no delays.

Yet this rule governing mortals is wondrous: it never deceives, and it deceives all—a truthful deception, which is not accepted in belief. It is the mist of joy, the begetter of sorrow, the overflowing of tears, the extermination of all flesh, and the destroyer of individuals. Therefore, prudent men, learn wisely from the dead teacher what death can do, and how much stronger it is than angels; and diligently observe that the eloquence of laws does not resist the command of death.

## LETTER 177

**Subject.**—It warns a certain person not to mourn a deceased person immoderately.

The Lord did not spare His own Son [Note: [Col. 0471] Rom. 8], lest the law of the common cause, glory, and human nature should have an exception. Human nature, having proceeded from the mortality of its first corruption, has incurred the necessity of dying; and therefore it is permitted and fitting to pay nature’s debt, because it is written: “My son, shed tears for the dead” [Note: [Col. 0471] Ecclus. 38].

But your tears ought not differ from the Saviour’s tears, if you are friends of the Saviour, who is said to have wept and mourned not for Lazarus’s death, but for his restoration to temporal miseries [Note: [Col. 0471] John 11]. Whoever assails nature beyond what is due assails not nature but nature’s Author; and it is not safe to inflict injury upon Him who knows how to inflict it upon no one. Therefore see to it and beware lest an eternal and saving affection yield to earthly affection, which will afterward perish.

Accordingly, we advise and earnestly exhort your sincerity, commanding through apostolic letters that, out of reverence for God and yourselves, laying aside all sorrow, you rejoice in Him who, in the depth of heavenly counsel, disposes and orders, calls and recalls creatures subject to His providence; who with fatherly and paternal affections corrects His children and directs them toward eternal life. Take more careful thought for that which cannot perish and is eternally alive without end, through the aid of the sacraments and other works of piety. Therefore commit to memory the consolation of the holy man Job, who, after the loss of his possessions and children, said: “The Lord gave, the Lord has taken away; as it pleased the Lord, so it has been done; blessed be the name of the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0471] Job 1].

## LETTER 178

**Subject.**—Consolation concerning death.

If all flesh is grass [Note: [Col. 0471] Ecclus. 14], and all its glory like the flower of the field [Note: [Col. 0471] Isa. 40]; if we see the moon grow pale and the sun sometimes undergo eclipse, what is man, that you groan with tears for your dead brother? Why does not the pupil of your eye cease pouring forth the bitterness of grief? Do you not know that every composite thing, as the philosopher testifies, is dissolved, and that every creature except the angels dies?

Hence that prophetic saying: “Man has become like vanity, and his days pass away like a shadow” [Note: [Col. 0471] Ps. 143, 101]; and “he shall be broken like a potter’s vessel” [Note: [Col. 0471] Ps. 2]. To weep is human, but to prolong weeping is wholly inhuman, since the Apostle says: “Do not grieve as the rest do, who have no hope of resurrection” [Note: [Col. 0471] 1 Thess. 4]. Therefore Augustine says [Note: [Col. 0471] Ep. 6, to Italica]: “We have not lost those who have departed from this world; we have sent them on before us.”

There is another consolation: no one is excepted from the rule of death:

> For it makes sceptres equal to hoes.

[Note: [Col. 0471] Augustine, sermon 2, *On Consolation in Death*.]

For by an equal judgment it envelops old and young, strong and weak, powerful and infirm, rich and poor. Everything that is born dies, and nothing beneath the sun is everlasting. Great is the Lord who kills and makes alive, and great is His power, so that He can raise what declines and heal, and so forth.

Since, therefore, your brother has passed over to the region of holy spirits, as one who had a part in the first resurrection, cease to weep, lest you provoke the Lord’s name, should you wish—though in vain—to alter His judgment. For it is the Lord who kills and makes alive, brings down to hell and brings back [Note: [Col. 0471] 1 Sam. 2]; at whose command all things are ordered, and who consoles His own in tribulations.

## LETTER 179. Of the Same Subject

“A voice was heard, weeping and much wailing” [Note: [Col. 0471] Matt. 2; Jer. 31] at the death of your distinguished brother, who left matter for so much greater sorrow as nature had privileged him with greater endowment and marked him with the preferential title of spiritual virtues. O envious death, bitter death, which cut short the thread of life in him while it was still being spun—a most beautiful vine cut off, with no branch left behind.

We know indeed that cause for grief is present; nevertheless, grief must have its measure, because “the Lord gave, the Lord has taken away” [Note: [Col. 0473] Job 1], in whose hands are death and life. He who gave origin also gave death; and thus the law is common both to life and death, nor is the law changed by power or favour. Since the Lord has made use of His own right, He has done no injury, though His hand may for the present seem full of severity.

Moreover, since it is fitting that we conform our feelings to His will, we advise and specially request that, with grief moderated and the flow of tears restrained, you now spare yourselves, becoming for kinsfolk and friends a mirror of consolation and an example of strengthening.

## LETTER 180. TO A CERTAIN QUEEN

**Subject.**—It consoles a queen mourning the death of her husband and son.

Those set upon the revolving wheel of the world, if they experience changing fortunes and suffer diverse vicissitudes from the unstable changeability of time, neither marvel nor are astonished, when they are guided by the right judgment of well-ordered reason. For they know that nothing can stand firm whose foundation is in perpetual motion. Therefore, wishing by a certain happy foresight to forestall doubtful misfortunes and to despise future contingencies, they have so established their minds in the noble disposition of virtuous constancy that, bearing all things with equanimity, they neither fear threatening fortune nor rejoice along with prosperity.

This is the praiseworthy greatness of spirit which is not exalted by prosperity nor broken by adversity, but remains the same in every event and is sufficient to itself. We believe that you have heard many reports concerning such matters, according to their variety; and among others, the welcome progress of the Christian army, grievously affected in many ways by the death—or, rather, not death but glorious passage to the things above—of your lord and consort, King of blessed memory, and of your son, Lord John.

Although we may presume that Your Serenity is endowed with the virtue of the aforesaid greatness of spirit and uses such judgment of reason that this irrevocable adversity does not break you beyond nature’s due, yet the charity with which we sincerely love you compels us to believe that the force of grief does not know virtue, and that the movements of sorrow do not permit their proper measure. O that you may not be so tossed by the waves of excessive grief, nor so swallowed by the jaws of immoderate sadness that you fail to consider carefully that death is nothing other than the end of pilgrimage, the ending of misery, the goal of labours, the boundary of exile, the gate of the homeland, the birth into life, the beginning of blessedness, and the firstfruits of rewards for all who die in the Lord.

Since, therefore, the aforesaid champions of Christ, zealots for the faith, receive, as we hope, the wages of eternal things for the struggle undertaken on behalf of their realms, one should rather rejoice at so happy an exchange, in which heavenly things are given for earthly, eternal things for transitory ones. But even if we admit temporal consolation, you cannot wholly mourn as a widow or lament, as though desolate, the hardships of desolation. The mercy of the Most High has enriched you with numerous offspring, so that the pleasant multitude of your children may make the loss of one more bearable and their remaining number may supply the absence of a husband.

O, if your mother had possessed marriage for so long a time; if she had enjoyed the desired comfort of so many children; if she had been surrounded by the companionship of so many sons, the occasion for grief would assuredly have yielded to the joys of children. Let Your Highness therefore consider these things diligently; put an end to useless tears, and do not add losses to losses by further harmful grief.

## LETTER 181. Of the Same Subject

We fully believe and hold without doubt that, upon hearing of the death of such a man, you received a cup of great sorrow and bitterness. Yet you were neither the first nor the only one; for before we were bound to know, and before that grief reached you, it passed through us, and did in us all that reason, according to God, was able to permit. Certainly, while he lived we sufficiently showed how greatly we should grieve at his death, and affection in a friend marked what sorrow would follow the loss.

Rightly, among the secular princes whom we loved, we preferred him with a certain special prerogative, because against the perfidy of the Saracen people he pursued, as a singular athlete of Christianity, the common interest proper to a Christian as though it were his own. Nor is it credible that the liberality of the supreme Giver should not answer his labours with a fitting recompense, since He is not sparing in reward, He who by the abundance of His mercy exceeds, from grace alone, the merits and prayers of His suppliants.

Certainly, He did no injury if, using the fullness of His own right, He recalled at His own time the spirit which He had entrusted to the body for a time. “What man lives and shall not see death?” [Note: [Col. 0473] Ps. 88.] Does not dust return to dust? [Note: [Col. 0473] Gen. 3.] Does not man, coming forth like a flower, wither and flee like a shadow, never remaining in the same state? [Note: [Col. 0473] Job 14.] The frailty of the human condition must indeed pay debts certainly owed to death. Thus the exaction of importunate death knows how to leave nothing of the debt owed by the human lot, violently exacting it without distinction or discrimination.

Yet do not think that he has departed from you altogether, since he has left behind a son of illustrious character, who may for a time represent his father, so that the shoot may answer for the root. It remains, therefore, that you receive in him the spirit of consolation, remembering that great King David bitterly wept for his son when he was ill, but did not mourn him when dead, lest he seem opposed to the divine will [Note: [Col. 0473] 2 Sam. 12].

Therefore, lest you embitter the Lord God, you who are placed in authority over others, console others by being yourself an example for the present and an instruction for posterity. We would also have you consider this: the more you seem deprived of the presence of your own, the greater increase divine mercy will grant you in carrying matters forward.

## LETTER 182. Of the Same Subject

Since no guest of this present life can avoid the command of bitter death, and man is corruptible and mortal, you ought, if you please, to moderate the sorrow which you have conceived in your mind over the death of your brother Nicholas. For God, unwilling that he should be further troubled in this age by the corruptions of the present life, recalled him to confess His name. Moreover, since he received the ecclesiastical and divine sacraments, he lives in the Lord: “Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0475] Rev. 14].

Accordingly, I have thought fit to advise your friendship by these present letters that, considering the prophetic saying, “You have set his bounds which cannot be passed” [Note: [Col. 0475] Job 14], and that your brother could not pass the boundary of death, you should set an end to your grief, lest you seem to disapprove what has been done by the Lord.

## LETTER 183. Of the Same Subject

Among the other mournful defects of the human condition, the uncertain and unstable state of man is above all to be lamented by mortals. When each person proceeds from the conception of mothers to birth and emerges into open light from the cramped chamber of the womb, he is offered up to countless miseries and surrounded by a constricting wall of distresses. Thus, while he lives exposed to varied chances of death, the flower which comes forth from the day of his mother’s delivery rarely puts forth leaves after blossoming, and still more rarely grows into a full tree after the beauty of its foliage.

Does man and his day indeed bloom like grass and as the flower of the field, as is written? [Note: [Col. 0475] Ps. 102.] He seems, I say, like grass that exists today and tomorrow is cast into the furnace [Note: [Col. 0475] Matt. 6], and like the flower of the field, whose delightful preciousness and lavish flowery beauty, struck by the scorching blight of wind or heat, vanishes in a brief breath.

I know that the mournful report of the recent bitter death of G., our and your kinsman, has greatly embittered the mind of us all with deep sorrow. As we consider the manner of death by which he perished, we lament in him the departure of his soul more than that of his flesh, being very uncertain and doubtful whether the death that so swiftly seized and so suddenly engulfed him took him while in a state of salvation.

But because these are the hidden judgments of almighty God, who according to His good pleasure recalls rational creatures from this wicked world when and how He wills, we beseech, admonish, and earnestly exhort your nobility in the Lord to banish from your heart the sorrow conceived at the removal of the said G. and now cease to mourn one whom mourning groans or however great an outpouring of tears cannot restore to you. Instead, receive consolation of spirit under this scourge of divine power; bless God, whose pleasure it was; and show toward him these tokens of brotherly love: love in spirit him whom you loved in the flesh, helping G.’s soul by every remedy of virtue and every aid of charity.

## LETTER 184. FROM B., DUCHESS OF GLIRIGEOT, TO COUNT THEOBALD

B., Duchess of Glirigeot, formerly wife, to her lord and brother Count Theobald, seneschal of France: greetings.

He deserves to lose the name of ruler who departs from the just path of judgment, especially since God has placed rulers on earth for this purpose: that by a right examination they may determine and decide the disputes that come before them. As I have lately heard, Guy of Bonavalle accuses my faithful man John of Alludia of homicide and intends to convict him if by any means he can. Therefore I implore your brotherhood by these letters that the aforesaid John may have you favourable in this cause, so that he may not complain that he has been improperly treated.

## LETTER 185. A Certain Executory Reply

It is no light matter to defend the accusation of a man whom the authority of common opinion defames, attacks, and accuses. I received the letters of your charity, asking me to support your faithful man John in his cause of justice, so that iniquity and injustice might not prevail against him. I granted your request insofar as I could; but the aforesaid man abandoned justice and refused to hear judgment, since he knew that he would be condemned by judgment. For he had an inner judge, and by that judge’s judgment he withdrew from the case and did not await human judgment.

## LETTER 186. Recommendation of Guardianship

The authority of equity and the principle of love compel us faithfully to preserve a friend’s deposit. When I was leaving your territories, and the patronage of many was offered to me, I chose rather to entrust the whole custody of my affairs to your charity. Therefore I beseech and exhort your love by these letters to show yourself so faithful in guarding my affairs that you may make yourself worthy of the favour and support of many.

## LETTER 187. Reply

When a promise binds us to our friends, we are rightly covered with shame if we do not bring what was promised to fulfilment. When I received the charge of your affairs, I acknowledge and remember that I promised to preserve faithfully and safely everything entrusted to me. I shall not depart from the agreement I made with you, nor, if I can prevent it, shall your affairs suffer any loss.

## LETTER 188

Those who exercise cruelty against God’s ministers and persist in their crimes sharpen the wrath of the supreme Judge and provoke His vengeance against themselves. You have offended in the supreme pontiff the protector of pontiffs and the supreme avenger; he bears human transgressions for a time, but offenses do not pass unpunished. You know that whoever presumptuously offends the minister of any lord also offends the lord; and, if you take our counsels to heart, make haste to lay aside Pharaoh.

## LETTER 189

He opens a window to every transgression who permits what he has vowed to be allowed by wrongdoing. Leniency in a king is called simplicity, whereas it is his duty to correct excess, not loosen the reins for excess. That Alexander whom you call pope committed improper acts against our person; we judged them punishable by counsel of the realm, not things to be endured in the moderation of lax simplicity. Yet you advise us henceforth to desist from such vengeance; we would believe that you wished to give a counsel greater than this.

## LETTER 190. Reply

Our justice does not regard the person of the powerful and bend itself to serve that person’s wishes. If the tyrant exercised the emperor’s rage against the Roman Church and wielded against her the sword of fury, is it necessary that harm be done to him so that he may desist from his cruelty? Is it not more fitting that one who has presumed to commit a crime should present himself as a suppliant than that the sufferer should be entreated to grant pardon for its commission? The force and rationale of equity would demand that he who presumed to assail the holy Church should himself ask forgiveness.

But, as your letters testify, the emperor has assumed a penitent and contrite spirit. Thus penitence pleads for pardon, and we forgive him his past transgressions and open to him the bosom and embrace of love.

## LETTER 191. A Friend to a Friend: Greetings, and All That He Himself Is

Elegance of speech helps little when it does not advance the petitioner toward what is sought, unless prayers are coloured by payment. Concerned for the fulfillment of your request, I laboured as much as I could; but little is permitted to a petitioner if the authority and intervention of gifts do not plead on his behalf. And what more? I suffered refusal because the hand that acted was empty, and nothing is granted to it to obtain.

## LETTER 192

When powerful men are hard pressed, the obligation of an oath commands and urges their faithful followers to aid them in repelling their adversaries—an obligation always to be observed in every matter. The audacity of the stubborn king of England has attacked our kingdom and shut up some of our men in a town, who expected anything rather than such a thing. He caught the unprepared unprepared; and, as their letter has informed us, they desire speedy provision for themselves. Intending to meet this audacity, we admonish your fidelity by these letters to gather troops and hasten to present yourself to us at Paris. To crush him will bring us great glory, and lasting disgrace will follow him if he sees himself powerless to accomplish his designs.

## LETTER 193. Reply: Greetings and Service

Those whom a common injury does not fear to provoke ought to be stirred up jointly to vengeance. From the report of certain persons I had learned—and I did not wish to give credence to the report—that the king of England had besieged one of your fortresses; but I could not believe that such audacity of presumption was possible. Had I known beforehand what I still do not dare know now, [the remainder is materially uncertain: “qui” = “who”; “ducaturus” = “about to lead”; “in tempore” = “in time”; “locus fuit” = “there was an opportunity/place”; “novum rursus in balneum introisset” = “would have entered again into a new bath”].

## LETTER 194. On Love Lightly Lost

Whoever endures being without the thing he loves, and within a brief interval joins himself to it again, makes himself unworthy of the name of love, which he falsely claims. At the beginning of our love you used to enter stormy seas, even when the waves of the sea and the excessive violence of winds thundered threateningly against you. You observe that the elements have ceased their violence; yet I perceive that you have taken on their hardness. I wonder at this: the cunning of courtesans, as I see, has deceived you; a new love has inserted its blandishments and found you all too changeable—an outcome I had believed no one could alter. I promised myself quite the contrary; but one promises oneself in vain what is set in the gamble of fate.

## LETTER 195. [A.D. 1219.] On the Capture of Damietta

To the most holy father and lord H., by God’s grace supreme pontiff: A., patriarch; John, king of Jerusalem; bucon. [uncertain abbreviation]; Nicholas, arch. p. of Albano [abbreviations uncertain]; J. of Acre; [lacuna]; bishop; the master (magr.) of the Hospital of Saint John, of the Temple, and of the Hospital of the Germans; of eeucado, commertar. [readings uncertain]; Savary of Mauléon; of Jovisvilla; E. of Castro; and the consuls of the counties: greetings, subjection, and reverent service.

The Lord heard from His holy height the voices of His servants, not permitting so many expenditures made by Christians at Damietta to be rendered useless, nor so great a slaughter of Christians to be left thus. But mercifully providing for us in these matters, He has graciously fulfilled in large part our desire. For because of her manifold defenses, the city of Damietta could plainly be taken neither by land nor by water, neither by force nor by the courage of any person. But while the right hand of God alone fought for us, and all of the army attacked except him who, as regards zeal for the common enterprise, took charge of it, the city of Damietta was taken on the Nones of February, in the silence of the night, stealthily—or rather, miraculously.

Thus none of ours was killed in that capture or even slightly wounded. But so many Saracens fell by the sword that even we were displeased to behold it. Yet other leading Saracens took refuge in a certain very strongly fortified tower until noon and would not surrender, hoping that the sultans of Babylon and Damascus would attack our camp; and that, should the Christians happen to be defeated, they themselves would recover the city through that tower, as they hoped.

But all our army, except for the few who had entered the city, ran so completely to the barriers and ditches made between us and the Saracens for the fortification of our camp that the Saracens did not dare in any way to rush upon our camp. When morning came, on Tuesday, and the sultans first learned that the city had been taken, tearing their garments and clawing at their hair, they wept most bitterly and thought no longer of relieving the city but of flight, fearing that our army would attack them.

Now, therefore, since the Lord has opened to us the gate of Egypt, we beseech and request Your Holiness on bended knees, and implore you by the shedding of Christ’s blood, to take care to send prompt assistance in both men and money. Know certainly that the Christian people will come in force to capture the city of Cairo; it will then be quite easy to obtain the remaining part of Egypt and consequently the kingdom of Jerusalem, which they presently retain through Egypt’s assistance. Thus grave danger may be avoided and the expedition into Egypt undertaken more safely. Compel the emperor to come, as you have very often promised us; and likewise compel the other cross-bearers to fulfill their vows. Let the redemption of vows cease, from which we perceive no advantage whatever; but from the redemption of persons we suffer the most evident harm.

Whether it was lawful or fitting to divert to other uses the twentieth part which, by consent of the general council, had been specially assigned to the aid of the Holy Land—when such diversion is not advantageous—see to that yourselves. Given at Damietta, the third day before the Ides of November.

## LETTER 196. CONGRATULATION ON THE CAPTURE OF DAMIETTA. [A.D. 1219.]

HONORIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all Christ’s faithful established throughout the province of Tours: greetings, etc.

[Col. 0480A] Let the multitude of His faithful rejoice in the Lord and, bursting forth joyfully into a voice of thanksgiving and praise, say with the Apostle: “Blessed be God,” etc., “who comforts us in all our tribulation” [Note: [Col. 0479] 2 Cor. 1]. He is born too much for himself alone, too intent upon his own concerns, too neglectful of the common cause of the Christian people, who in these days has not been in mental distress and tribulation: knowing that the Christian army had besieged the great and most strongly fortified city of Damietta, in what was virtually the midst of paganism, separated from the other faithful by so great an expanse of lands, sea, and valley, and surrounded on almost every side by unbelievers, so that it could be called not so much besieging as besieged.

Whose mind did not hang in doubt and fear the outcome, [Col. 0480B] anxious not so much for the safety of individuals as suspended, amid alternating hope and fear, over the whole army? Indeed, who did not forget that army—who remembered its peril, considering beneath how great a danger it stood and by how slender a thread the honour of the entire Christian people hung? Truly, matters had reached such a state that the army itself had now wholly despaired of its own strength; and, mindful of the mighty works which divine power is accustomed to perform for its faithful, it hoped in His mercy alone. Therefore He who does not abandon those hoping in His mercy, who is near to all who call upon His name in truth, who enlarges His own in tribulation, so that when they think themselves consumed they may rise like the morning star for the Church—[Col. 0480C] behold, He delivered the aforesaid city into their hands as wonderfully as mercifully, filled not only with treasures but also with provisions far beyond hope and expectation.

And in order manifestly to ascribe the glory of this event to His own name, no Christian perished in its capture, nor even received a mortal wound, as is clearly shown by letters sent to us by our venerable brethren P., bishop of Albano and legate of the Apostolic See—whose ministry God especially chose to employ in this undertaking—as well as by the patriarch of Jerusalem, the king, and the brethren of the Hospital, the Temple, and the German House at Jerusalem. And so that they might rejoice and be strengthened by a manifest sign of divine favour, when they feared that, upon their entering the city, [Col. 0480D] the surrounding army of Saracens would attack their camp, the river belonging to those same Saracens, by divine direction, suddenly overflowed so greatly that it rendered the camp itself inaccessible. It thus plainly appeared that the very elements were fighting for Christ’s worshippers against the senseless [Note: [Col. 0479] Wisdom 5]. Many other miracles were performed there, which it would be too long to recount one by one.

“Sing praises to our God, sing praises to our King, sing praises” [Note: [Col. 0479] Ps. 146]. Sing, indeed, but wisely: not swollen with pride, but devout in humility, prudently recognizing and humbly confessing that it was not a human hand but the Lord who did all these things, so that he [Col. 0481A] who glories may glory in the Lord [Note: [Col. 0481] 2 Cor. 10], solemnly rendering to Him praise and thanks by processions held in appropriate places.

Moreover, since the Lord has made with us a sign for good, since He has opened for us so great a door, shall we fail the grace that extends to us its right hand? He, mindful of the reproaches inflicted upon Him all day long by foolish Saracens, has arisen to judge His cause and to scatter His enemies terribly. Now, certainly now, is the time to rise from the sleep of the body [Note: [Col. 0481] Rom. 13]. Now it is necessary to hasten to assist our champions who are there, and, while the idolaters flee from God’s face, to press upon them with all zeal, all strength, and all the resources of possessions and persons, while they still tremble from the fresh wound; while, from the capture [Col. 0481B] of the aforesaid city, which had been the head and strength of Egypt, they are so dismayed that they consider no place safe against the power of Christians—indeed, against the power of Christ.

For never has the Christian army stood in greater need of assistance, since it is by no means sufficient both to inhabit the aforesaid city and to advance against others, without which Damietta itself cannot be held by Christians. Nothing remains, therefore, except either shamefully to abandon it, conquered with such glory, or manfully to subdue the surrounding places and, with the Christian name going before and God granting success, happily bring them into subjection. We, adapting the past to the future, undertake to look toward those times in which the Maccabees, having overthrown the nations, restored their holy places with great joy of their people [Col. 0481C] [Note: [Col. 0481] 1 Macc. 2]. Trusting in the abundance of divine mercy, we hope that in these present times this joy ought to be renewed among the Christian people.

We therefore admonish, beseech, and implore all of you by the sprinkling of the blood of Jesus Christ, that, inflamed with desire for such joy, you may apply yourselves, with renewed courage and strength, to the assistance of the oft-mentioned army at this moment of such opportunity. Besides renewing from the beginning the indulgences granted to the brethren, we grant full remission of sins—for those sins of which they have been contrite in heart and confessed with the mouth—to all who undertake this labour in person and at their own expense; likewise to those who do not go there in person but, at their own expense and according to their means, send suitable men; and likewise to those who go in person, though at another’s expense [Col. 0481D]. We also promise them an increase of the eternal reward in the recompense of the just. We further will and grant that, in proportion to the amount of their aid and the devotion of their disposition, all who suitably contribute from their goods to assist the aforesaid undertaking, or furnish timely counsel or aid, shall share in this remission.

## LETTER CXCVII. An Exhortation

We believe that it is known to Your Highness that we have remained enclosed for so long with the other cardinals [Col. 0482A] for the election of the supreme pontiff; and that we have not yet been able to agree unanimously. From what has occurred we may conjecture the future; indeed, from what we especially discuss and see each day, we may visibly fear that deliberations in the Roman Church will encounter no slight danger over a long period, and that the election of the supreme pontiff may be delayed, to the detriment of that Church, of many regions, and perhaps even, we may say, of the whole Christian religion.

Oh, how many new scandals rise up in the various quarters of the world! How many provinces are disturbed by sedition! How many regions and kingdoms are shaken by the frenzy of war! Although the Roman Church compassionates these with maternal affection, yet, because as a widow she cannot effectively provide for them, we grieve and lament for them also. But by God’s grace there remains for us very great consolation, because we know that you are devoted to the Church with ardent desire and desirable ardour, and all the more steadfast toward her as she appears to be tossed by greater storms and more swelling waves; so that your faith may thereby prove much purer than gold tried by fire. This restrains the unlawful attempts of many, and limits and checks presumptuous audacity.

We are also consoled because we know that it is in the heart of Your Serenity to come to the aid of the tribulations and dangers of the Holy Land. To this end you and your illustrious children have manfully girded yourselves by taking the sign of the divine cross. Yet, [Col. 0482C] speaking for your good, compelled by the sincere affection with which we love you with our whole heart: although we believe this undertaking useful for the Holy Land, we fear that it is less useful for your own land and for the Roman Church. For perhaps many have long conceived their wicked schemes, which they have not dared to bring forth in the province of Your Excellency; and by your absence they are permitted to carry out still more wickedly what they wickedly proposed.

Let royal highness therefore weigh these and many other considerations, and let it not be burdensome to alter its plan for the better: namely, that such a person should cross the sea with an honourable company, to whom, whenever need requires, you may send assistance both of money and troops; while you and your children—whom their still tender age does not permit [Col. 0482D] to bear the burdens of arms—should be willing to remain upon the royal throne for the tranquillity and peace of your land and of many others. Thus you will in many ways provide for the welfare of your land, of many others, and of the Roman Church. We therefore urge and believe that these advantages should be preferred to others; but, if it please you, pardon us for speaking thus. Pressing necessity, evident advantage, and, moreover, the sincere affection with which we love you in such purity of heart especially move us to this.

## LETTER CXCVIII

Your magnificence holds this judgment of our concern: that you delight to hear reports concerning the continuance of our condition [Col. 0483A] and the course of so great a matter, reports which we know you continually desire to be happy in the Lord. Therefore, lest your expectation be without the certainty it deserves—since up to now frequent reports and letters from us could have conveyed to you the truth concerning these matters—we inform Your Highness that, divine clemency attending us, the desired benefits of bodily health are sufficiently abundant for us. Yet an anxious and searching concern deprives us of peace of mind regarding the restoration of the Holy Church, a matter to which we, together with the other cardinals, continually apply ourselves.

At last we hope in the Lord, who knows not how to restrain the gifts of His mercy, that He will so prepare the way of salvation and render the minds of those in deliberation concordant in one will, that the same [Col. 0483B] Church will soon be provided with so good and useful a shepherd. This will redound to the praise of God; abundant increases of salvation will come to the Christian profession; and, concerning such a Lord, your wishes and those of your people may rejoice in tranquil sweetness.

And would that favourable reports might satisfy us regarding the course of your condition, whose prosperity we desire. We ask that Your Highness, if it please you, inform us in reply of the benefits by which the kindness of the Saviour favours you; and also, if it please you, indicate to us through the same reply whether there is anything you wish us to do that would please you.

## LETTER CXCIX

Since it is fitting that we should console such a person over the grievous death of such a man [Col. 0483C], we have thought it expedient to entrust you with the task of going personally to that person without delay and presenting the letters of credence which we shall direct to her; for the bearer of the present letter will deliver them to you. You shall therefore arrange, on our behalf, such a discourse of consolation with her as you see fit: setting forth in suitable order our compassion, which we direct toward the condition of all Christendom and of the Roman Church, as well as toward her own person and the troubled tranquillity of her mind, in consideration of the ruinous loss of such a prince; and adding the remedy of consolation, which she may find in surviving offspring so commendably provided for and supported by the strength of power, friends, and no less of divine grace [Col. 0483D], ascribing to God’s good pleasure the debt of human frailty which all flesh must necessarily undergo.

Finally, we by no means wish you to omit offering her, on our behalf, your good will and prompt concern in all her affairs and those of her people; asking and urging her confidently to entrust to us the advancement of her wishes. For she will find us faithful and willing in all things, and even more attentive than we have hitherto been, since we know that henceforth this is more expedient for her. Having carefully considered these matters and whatever else you deem suitable and worthy, go to their presence without delay.

## LETTER CC

Such a cardinal to his venerable brother, the Bishop of Paris: greeting in the Lord.

[Col. 0484A] If you consider carefully the weight of the words we write, they are not light, since they proceed from a grave matter that has brought no small astonishment to our minds and appears to display, as it were, a new kind of impropriety. The quality of the business and the novelty of the incongruous deed plainly indicate why we are compelled to wonder and be troubled concerning you and your proceedings—proceedings which the gravity of circumspection, the foresight of truth, and the rectitude of justice ought deservedly to have prevented—if matters are as they have been brought before our hearing.

For we have received word that, although you alleged that it had come to your notice that our venerable brother A., cardinal priest of the title of Saint Praxedes, had entered the way of all flesh, you acted not because you had obtained reliable information concerning the condition of such and so great a person. Rather, preferring the judgment of your own will to equity and neglecting what the debt of justice required in this matter, you sent your bailiff and certain other messengers to the house in which the care of his archdeaconry of Paris was exercised. The venerable brother R., cardinal deacon of Saint Angelo, had considered this house to belong to him and had granted it to the said A. for a time [Col. 0484B]. Through them you strictly forbade the said Cardinal A. to exercise any jurisdiction, and nevertheless ordered his seal-bearer to surrender the seals of the said court, to be broken, as is customary upon the death of the archdeacon of Paris.

Although that same seal-bearer, having taken possession of those seals and placed them in a certain bag, had confidently had recourse to you through the aforesaid bailiff and messengers; although he urgently requested you to revoke this action, asserting that his lord was alive; and although he openly showed you letters recently received from his lord concerning the matter, in which it was specifically stated that he was in good health—nevertheless, not only did you fail to desist from the injuries thus begun, but you again expressly ordered the same seal-bearer that, since you had become fully certain of the death of the aforesaid cardinal, he should completely surrender the aforesaid seals and render an account of the income received from them from the time when you said that the same archdeacon had died [Col. 0484C]. Finally, it is said that you granted the office and the position of seal-bearer as a favour—though it appears rather to be a manifest and outrageous injury—and that, for the exercise of the jurisdiction of the office, you associated a co-judge and a co-sealer with the seal-bearer, while the income arising from the seals was to be placed daily in sequestration.

Certainly, after consideration of so many improprieties, such conduct ought not fittingly to have had place in such a prelate. Even if the cardinal had held a lesser dignity or office, the truth should have been more diligently investigated before proceeding thus against him. Deference could also have been shown to the household of the aforesaid Cardinal R., lest possession of the house of the said archdeaconry be thus disturbed in his own house, and lest such a person claim a place there for himself by right. You ought also to have been solicitous for your own reputation, lest your action [Col. 0485A] injure another’s right and lest a harmful precedent be drawn from it in the future. Above all, offence against the Roman Church should have been avoided, since injuries done to its members are known to turn to its disgrace and contempt; nor was it a small matter to take account of the disturbance of the same cardinals, whose goodwill you ought more diligently to have preserved.

Therefore, since you can plainly gather from this itself that in the foregoing matters you have offended both us, that same Church, and the aforesaid cardinals, we ask and exhort your brotherhood, attentively commanding you, to take care to provide and act so wholesomely and wisely that suitable satisfaction may precede judicial examination of these matters; that nothing clouded may remain in the hearts of those whom the injury has touched; and that it may not be necessary for us or for a future supreme pontiff to apply some other counsel or remedy for correction.

## LETTER CCI. Lament for the Death of a Friend

Reviewing in bitterness of spirit our years and the matter of manifold affection which, though unworthily, we endure in ourselves and in our thoughts, never has an occasion of such great grief taken root in our feelings as when the truth was lately declared to us concerning the death of such a zealous defender of the divine law and lover of every form of religion. And, to omit those things which could readily have been observed by those present in our person immediately upon hearing so great a misfortune—external actions which sometimes reveal the hidden stirrings of a troubled mind—there came upon us, stunned by this adverse event, the cup of tribulation and distress, full not with intoxication but with madness; and, offering gall of bitterness and the horror of wormwood, it pierced our inmost parts with a double wound, without any intervening remedy of consolation. Nor is this without reason, if our tearful discourse, oppressed on every side by such anguish, begins with the head and the worthier part [Col. 0485C].

## LETTER CCII. Papal Invective against a King

Within the bounds of paternal remembrance, deserving it by the greatness of your royal devotion, we frequently direct toward you our prayers, that, sprinkled with the dew of heavenly blessing, you may flourish in the grace of well-being and may at last deserve to attain the joys of the true light. This desire has long burned in our breast, and has received the greater increase of fervour because, though unworthy, we sit in the Apostolic See and bear the burdens of the pastoral office; thus we are bound to watch more diligently for your salvation and that of all the faithful.

The chief purpose of our exhortation urgently seeks and asks that, having the eyes of earnest consideration fixed upon our Redeemer, the Lord Jesus Christ, whom you bear figured within your heart, you may delight to pursue what pleases Him; and that, considering therefore [Col. 0486A] that “the fashion of this world passes away,” and that kings and princes have departed and still depart, together with all others subject to corruption—nothing born beneath the sun possessing stable permanence—you may persevere in love of the divine name, wisely building, while regarding earthly things as transitory and perishable and despising them for their worthlessness, so that in the kingdom of heavenly glory you may establish for yourself an everlasting dwelling which shall neither fail nor perish.

Furthermore, pondering with no small compassionate feeling the oppressions and distresses inflicted upon the Holy Land, which we saw and touched, as it were, with our own hand while holding a lesser office, and desiring that swift help be provided for it lest it perish altogether, we have resolved to disclose our mind on this subject through special letters. We have thought fit to direct them through such a man, dear and most acceptable to us and to our brethren through the gifts of his virtues [Col. 0486B]. We therefore ask and earnestly exhort your royal magnificence with paternal confidence to employ your influence zealously with that same person in this matter, so that you may thereby receive an increase of eternal reward.

Moreover, that our intention may be more fully known to you, we ask you to believe without doubt that what such a person shall report to Your Excellency on our behalf concerning all the foregoing has been spoken by our own mouth. Nor should you wonder that a bull not expressing our name is attached to these letters, which are sent before the solemnities of our consecration or blessing; for those elected Roman pontiffs have always been accustomed, before receiving consecration, to observe this practice in sealing letters [Col. 0486C].

## LETTER CCIII. Reply to the Preceding

We have understood the tenor of your letter fully. Yet you should know that we judge the reasons for the death of such a person added in that letter to be insufficiently becoming and insufficiently reasonable. For these two things do not agree well: that he should exercise the office entrusted to him and should attend upon us at a time of pressing necessity. For no one can serve two masters, as we remember having read [Note: [Col. 0485D] Matt. 6]. Indeed, he might be so far removed [Col. 0486D] from our presence that, if necessity arose, we might be compelled to pay the debt of human nature, or incur other dangers of body and soul, before we could enjoy his visitation and counsel.

We therefore take it grievously—indeed, most grievously—that you have not acceded to our wishes in this matter, considering the sorrows, bitterness, and anxieties surrounding our mind. What we have been unable to obtain from you, an archbishop, a bishop, or another person inferior to you would, as we believe, have obtained from you. What more need be said? Since we cannot have him, we do not wish to share in the disadvantages; we shall have recourse to others and shall have less favour among our own people.

## LETTER CCIV. A Certain Exhortation

[Col. 0487A] From the notable proofs of affection which you have hitherto displayed toward such persons in the fullness of sincerity, we are plainly given to understand that you cherish their memory, laid up in our breast, with the more abundant munificence of benefits because you are believed to be zealous for their more prosperous condition; and that maternal concern is said diligently to urge us toward the honour and advantage of those same persons.

Moreover, since the fullness of their hope depends especially upon you, and since after God no other protection than yours appears to be available to them, by which their affairs may be advantageously directed and their undertaking happily fostered, we affectionately ask you that, since concerning the succession to such an inheritance, while such a man is in these days gravely ill, there appears already to have arisen both a danger from certain persons on behalf of certain others and an impulse toward a disputed succession—not without disturbance to such persons—which, God forbid, might bring them no small harm, you may be present, as you see expedient, to those to whom the succession of that inheritance ought rightfully to devolve, namely those who alone survive in the male line [Col. 0487B]. In this moment of uncertainty you should be of assistance, so that proper provision may be advantageously made for their rightful condition and they may not thereby incur any loss.

Concerning this, if it please you, send your messengers and letters to that same person; through them make him understand that it is expedient for the condition and tranquillity of that place that, with counsel suggesting the advantage and peace of such persons, he should so determine, order, and arrange matters that, should anything adverse happen to him—which God forbid—you may rejoice that their advantages have resulted, and your wishes may delight in their happy condition [Col. 0487C].

## LETTER CCV. Reply to the Foregoing

“My harp has been turned to mourning, and my organ into the voices of those who weep” [Note: [Col. 0487] Job 30]; “my strength has been weakened by sorrows, and my bones are troubled in groanings” [Note: [Col. 0487] Ps. 30; Lam. 1], when the tenor of your letter itself announced to me an unexpected fate and an everlasting calamity. Therefore my tears are my bread by day and by night [Note: [Col. 0487] Ps. 41]. Would that I had been consumed within my mother’s womb, so that my eye might not see such things, or that I had closed my final day, lest I should become the miserable taster of so many dangers [Col. 0487D].

Alas for me! Shall I say, “My son, why did my mother bear me, a son of bitterness and grief?” Why was I received upon the knees? Why nursed at the breasts? Why given over to sorrows? Why surrounded by tribulations? And would that I had died in my mother’s womb, and had been as though I had not been, carried from the womb to the tomb! Alas, miserable me! I have lost the indivisible son of my soul, the consolation of my life, the light of my eyes, and the staff of my old age. What more? “For Zion’s sake I will not be silent, and for Jerusalem’s sake I will not rest” [Note: [Col. 0487] Isa. 62], but I shall continue my days in tears and grief until I fail through weeping.

Yet I give you thanks, because through your letter [Col. 0488A] you have assigned me a remedy of consolation; but I cannot be comforted, because no grief is like my grief.

## LETTER CCVI. Concerning One Believed to Be Dead

A thing horrible and bitter to tell, turning my joys into sorrow, has lately reached my ears: Master Nicholas, my only brother, who was the hope of my life, my refuge and protection, has ended the life of the flesh by death, to which he will return no more. My innermost parts are so troubled concerning him, and I am filled with infinite griefs, that from the sole of my foot to the crown of my head there is no member not set in pain. And deservedly so; for I have lost without hope of recovery him who was bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh, and through whose agency I received the goods I possess; and through whom I had also hoped to obtain better things in the future.

Nevertheless, because this has reached me from no source other than common report, I am doubtful of his life and not firmly certain of his death. I have therefore thought fit to ask your friendship by these letters to inform me in your reply whether the report is true or contrary to fact, so that I may grieve for his death and my kinsmen and friends may grieve with me, as the human condition requires and demands; or so that I may rejoice concerning his life as usual, and those who are saddened by such a report may rejoice with me concerning it, as they are accustomed [Col. 0488B].

## LETTER CCVII. Consolation for the Death of a Friend

[Col. 0488C] We are bound by an exceedingly cruel fate, and tortured by no less cruel anguish of heart. For inward grief draws forth from our eyes a fountain of tears; the mind, withdrawn into the shadows of bitterness, is moved within; the wounded heart is pierced by the darts of sorrow in its deepest chambers. Thus what we conceive in our mind we can neither express in words nor contain in a written sequence. For the immensity of grief and the deep infusion of mourning exclude the ability to speak. Yet we are compelled, in a brief letter—or rather a sorrowful one—to inform you that that father of ours, the chief cornerstone of our advancement, a pre-eminent member of the universal Church, a pillar of justice, an immovable foundation, a faithful defence of friends, a secure refuge of family or nation, [Col. 0488D] a safe shield of his country, and the firm staff of paternal old age; conspicuous for prudence, distinguished by maturity, brilliant in knowledge, and supreme in constancy—G., your father and son in different respects—has, as it pleased the Lord, alas, fulfilled the due of fate on the day after the Annunciation of the Blessed Virgin.

At his death, although it befit you to mourn your father and the painful loss of paternal companionship, and to grieve while grieving, yet the judgment of sound consideration draws your grief and mourning away toward manifold consolation proportionate to the cause. For we wish to supply and assume, with whole devotion, full charity, and filial service, the burdens or place of his solicitude toward your fatherhood; and henceforth to obey your wishes with the greater devotion as we more eagerly intend to perform his part in serving your desires. Thus he should not be counted lost who is decreed to live by a vicarious substitution [Col. 0489A].

Furthermore, venerable old age and wisdom rich in years, sharing in the infirmity of age, may gratefully breathe in the Lord, with offspring surviving, under a prince whom the grace of the supreme pontiff embraces by reason of his merits and the goodwill of lords pursues. The merciful compassion of the merciful Father also moderates our weeping: He fulfilled your wishes both in our lord, this my brother, and in the son. If in His judgment He has wished to recall what He granted and remove what He created, you ought not to complain; for if we have received good things from the hand of the Lord, we should not bear adverse things with resentment [Col. 0489B].

There is another consolation also: no one is exempt from the law of death:

> For it makes sceptres equal to hoes.

For by an equal sentence it envelops old and young, strong and weak, powerful and infirm, rich and poor alike. For everything that is born dies, and nothing beneath the sun is everlasting. Great indeed is the Lord, “who kills and makes alive” [Note: [Col. 0489] 1 Sam. 2]; and great is His power, so that He can raise what He has cast down and heal what He has wounded.

We therefore earnestly exhort and ask that you extinguish utterly the flames of grief thus conceived by pouring in the dew of reason, taking in grief a remedy and in mourning a consolation which may serve as an example to others, so that you may not be able to embitter the name of the Lord [Col. 0489C]. For we write and command our brethren that in all things they obey your commands as though they were our own.

## LETTER CCVIII. On the Benefit of Writing for Preserving the Memory of Things Past

Things whose memory writing perpetuates will not be erased by advancing old age. For it is customary that matters which ought to be retained should be committed to the characters of letters, so that through the benefit of writing they may remain secure in the future from malicious disputes. Among the advantages of human invention, nothing is judged more useful than the benefit of writings, through which memory is renewed; what forgetfulness has obscured returns to freshness; and what the antiquity of time has made old is restored [Col. 0489D]. So greatly has the ardour of human ambition prevailed in our times that lawful donations and works of mercy cannot escape the cunning of litigants unless they are safeguarded for the future by documentary records and a multitude of witnesses.

## LETTER CCIX. SUBJECT.—The Archdeacon’s Complaint against Bishops’ Officials

In the Council of H. and E. it was decreed that every dignity should enjoy its own privilege, and that a bishop, who alone can confer a benefice, should not presume to diminish or take away an honour once conferred. Pope Damasus, on the counsel of blessed Jerome and with the whole senate of the Roman [Col. 0490A] order, decreed—and afterwards induced all the bishops of the world to agree—that their office and the memory of their office should be abolished for ever. For they lacked all authority, and were cast down all the more contemptibly because they presumed more ambitiously and proudly in spiritual matters concerning sacred things. He adds that in the company of Christ only two ranks of ministers were established, namely apostles and deacons, and the other disciples who served in their ministry under them; and after much else he concludes that whatever lacks reason and authority must necessarily be uprooted.

Here lies the difference: co-bishops were priests and therefore did not presume to administer the sacred offices owed to bishops; but now acolytes and even subdeacons presume, against God and the writings of the canons, to usurp the episcopal office. The title of co-bishop, judged, condemned, and eternally extirpated by the Roman See, has again secretly crept in under the contrivance of a certain borrowed name [Col. 0490B]. Ashes already asleep are revived, and the eggs of the asp, long warmed in the hidden scaffold of the basilisk, have burst forth into a king-serpent. These are the vipers, officials of iniquity, surpassing every wickedness of asp and basilisk.

Today the archdeacon goes to the synod alone or with very few companions. But the official, together with the dragon who fell from heaven, draws after him a third part of the stars; and, drawing with him the deans and priests belonging to the archdeacon, while knowing neither how to feed himself nor others, and seeking what is his own rather than what belongs to Jesus Christ [Note: [Col. 0489] Phil. 2], he is plainly not a shepherd of sheep but [Col. 0490C] of wolves. It is commonly said: “By bad guarding I feed the wolf.” How shall he guard the souls of others, who has neither morals, learning, nor order sufficient to guard his own soul?

Again, it is commonly said that archdeacons are the eyes of their bishop; but modern bishops themselves block and confound their archdeacons, their own eyes, and, newly assuming the eyes of Argus—the eyes of the Evangelists, which they ought to have before, behind, and all around them for their own salvation and that of those subject to them—they turn them to the pursuit of money, not without their own damnation. When I was a boy, I once read in Cato concerning this kind of men in the following form:

There is a kind of men called *officiperdi* [office-wreckers]. I believe that such an office exists for destruction and scandal, [Col. 0490D] since it devotes itself wholly and breathes only malice and plunder. Most innocent Innocent, I think that such men derive their name and the rationale for their name not from the noun *officium* (“office”), but from its verbal force [*perdere*, “to destroy”]. The active practice of the Church was that the archdeacon should be the official of persons, and that sins of persons investigated by the archdeacon which could not be corrected by him should be referred to the bishops. Shall this official be without duty—or a bishop, or fellow-bishop—whose name, memory, and office are to the injury of the mother Church of the whole Catholic Church?
