Perhaps an archdeacon will be assigned to a bishop, to whom all appeal from the archdeacon who have secular and sacrilegious causes. [Col. 0491A] At one time we archdeacons said to him: “Who has made you a judge over us?” [Note: [Col. 0491] Luke 12.] For all the archdeacons have divided themselves off and appeal unanimously to the throne of his Innocence. Innocent, in modern times the office and name of archdeacon have ceased in the Church: take thought that, because many abuse this office against God, this name and office may this day be abolished forever.

Certainly, I was never driven into this archdeaconry—which I would not undertake except unwillingly and under compulsion, and, after many delays which I sought from holy and religious men, as a burden rather than an honour—and it is now to your glory, Holy Father, that men should be set over our heads; that he who yesterday sat at my feet should today, without my consent and that of the other archdeacons, having assumed [Col. 0491B] new horns, toss about our whole Church, and in my presence suspend and excommunicate my priests; and that, while threatening sentence of excommunication, before these letters can reach them, he should abuse the power of darkness granted him in these and still graver acts against me. Today there is one man and tomorrow another, and so, week by week, the bishop carries off their turns.

I know, and cannot deny, that R. Eb., bishop—who in his day was neither the justiciar of the lord king in England nor in Normandy, and was utterly ignorant of letters—appointed officials for the sake of secular profit rather than priests of God. His act in this matter or in others must never be drawn into precedent or consequence [Col. 0491C] for any Catholic. Alas, alas: the oppressed man appeals to the justice and mercy of the Apostolic See. But the official, concealing the appeal, carries on his business; and by proud abuse, insults, and threats, he has violently shut the mouth of appeal. Should the rashness or rather the greed of an illiterate man—or of a layman—have had imitators?

For the extirpation of this greed it may suffice that profit was the cause why Lincoln obtained the authority for this singular institution from the Apostolic See or from ancient canons. Ely and the others maintain their own archdeacons. Either let this status be preserved, or let its name be abolished forever. But I, a priest of the Lord, an old man and a witness of Christ’s mercies, in a certain zeal for justice am indignant that this office [Col. 0491D] has become so cheapened and vulgarized in the Church of God that the honour of archdeacons—which began with blessed Stephen, and advanced gloriously in the blessed Lawrence and Vincent and the other martyrs to the perfection of holiness—has today, with the arrival of new officials, been given over to contempt, reproach, spectacle, and derision.

## LETTER CCX. [TO P., BISHOP.]

**SUBJECT.—An apology and the same writer’s complaints concerning the lying and falsification of copyists.**

To the reverend Father and lord P., by the grace of God bishop, P. B. sends greeting, and whatever may be sweeter than greeting.

[Col. 0492A] From the many reports of those who have seen you, I have learned the stature, countenance, and features of your body. I still read continually in the book of public opinion of your most honourable character, your mature speech, and certain dispositions of a well-ordered mind; and I paint in my soul, by a kind of imaginary representation, many things which eye has never seen nor ear heard. For charity, by a marvellous art, compensates for the loss caused by bodily absence: those whom we are forbidden to see in the flesh we behold and embrace more delightfully with the eyes of the soul and the arms of charity. Let therefore the love which is strong as death redeem the losses of sight and bodily absence. [Note: [Col. 0491] Song of Songs 8.] For friends who are present are separated by death, while those absent are united through undivided affections of love; [Col. 0492B] and, in the inmost parts of the soul and in the bowels of Christ, affection passes between them in a most sweet intercourse.

For love is charity which does not act—but if charity never fails [Note: [Col. 0491] I Cor. 13.], this is the communion of the Holy Spirit, which joins diverse minds and presents the absent friend to one who truly loves. No times, places, distances, or waters can extinguish charity. In that charity, therefore, which I have conceived from your most holy reputation, I offer you whatever I am, whatever I know, whatever I possess, whatever strength I have, and whatever I can do.

After your departure, certain persons on your behalf asked me to have my letters, which I had entrusted to others, entrusted to that same person. I sought for them [Col. 0492C] the most accurate exemplar; they sought a copyist; and, after everything necessary for him had been supplied, he wrote two or three quires falsely and shamefully and was removed from that task. Afterwards we could find only falsifiers and workers of iniquity. Yet, God willing, I shall endeavour with your countrymen that you may have those letters correctly copied.

Know, moreover, that whenever a suitable occasion for writing presents itself to me, I write most willingly: what ought to contribute to the edification of others should contribute to my salvation. And, to use Ovid’s expression:

> Yet I do not correct them; the labour is greater than writing.

This is plainly because among us there is a great scarcity and falseness of copyists. For the consolation of your expectation, freely and [Col. 0492D] from the inmost feeling of reverent fear, I send you certain pieces from my other little works; in time, God granting, I shall send better and more acceptable things.

## LETTER CCXI. TO S., BISHOP, AND THE ABBOTS

**SUBJECT.—An account of the reasons which induced Baldwin, Archbishop of Canterbury, to establish a church of clerics, and of certain miraculous events occurring in connection with this.**

To the reverend Fathers and friends N., bishop S., and the abbots of N. and E., P. B., their most devoted servant, sends greeting in Him without whom there is no salvation.

You anxiously ask what reason induced Baldwin, [Col. 0493A] Archbishop of Canterbury of glorious memory, to establish at Lambeth a church of clerics, in contempt of the Church of Canterbury—as some chatter—almost as though he were setting altar against altar, or rather exalting Dagon seated against the Ark. [Note: [Col. 0493] I Sam. 5.] The archdeacon, a man of most approved religious life, surpassing the other pillars of the Cistercian order in holiness, rank, and wisdom, advises us that he undertook a church of secular clerics—called by certain monks a brothel of Venus and a synagogue of Satan—in a sufficiently secular disturbance of mind; so that, whatever a baleful voice may angrily say, it is nevertheless the church of the holy martyrs Stephen and Thomas, the first martyr and the primatial martyr.

For you saw the shadow of a great name [Col. 0493B] which overthrew from its foundations this church of martyrs, still crying in the cradle of infancy. But within a very short time he died on the feast of the most blessed Stephen and was buried on the feast of Saint Thomas, as though one had slain him and the other consigned him to the tomb. We must consider what he was in his works, he who throughout his life kept his vessel in sanctification and honour, [Note: [Col. 0493] I Thess. 4.] since from the first down of puberty he held a foremost primacy of eminence among cathedral clergy. He became archdeacon of Oxford, and did not yield to flesh and blood, [Note: [Col. 0493] Gal. 1.] but, leaving all things, girded himself for Christ’s service with the belt of Cistercian warfare. Thereafter, unwilling and drawn onward, he was promoted [Col. 0493C] to be abbot, then bishop, and finally archbishop and primate.

Having been tested and proved in such great offices, this same monk and bishop knew something of them; he gathered clerics into Christ’s service. And, to explain my purpose more plainly, I shall go back a little further and briefly recount the seed-bed of dissension between him and the monks. The Lord set him “to give knowledge of salvation to His people.” [Note: [Col. 0493] Luke 1.] Accustomed to spiritual exercises, he found the province undisciplined and resolved generally to wield the hoe of correction. Accordingly he began at the sanctuary of the Lord, at the head of the kingdom, so that, as the Church of Canterbury had once been the leading column of the faith and is the metropolis of the province, so it might furnish the other churches with a pattern of discipline.

He therefore restrained his [Col. 0493D] sons from *fermae* [leases or farms], on the occasion of which some—though few—had entered into a shameful compact with their own bodies and burdened the school of cloistral innocence with an evil reputation. Possessing, then, the words of eternal life, he uprooted these shoots and those of other vices, which lax impunity, their dissolute mother, had nourished through long abuse. He declared wandering licence to go abroad to be the chief capital offence, and that under the yoke of the Lord’s service lay the complete liberty of the soul.

While he kept continual pastoral watch over the flock entrusted to him, the sheep were changed into wolves and the children of obedience were turned into a crooked bow. But the man of God, holding that the kingdom of God is not in word but [Col. 0494A] in power, [Note: [Col. 0493] I Cor. 4.] showed himself to all, continually and in his deeds no less than in words, wonderful, lovable, and unchanging; so that their transgressions might return to their hearts, and some through fear, others through love, might yield to their father’s judgment. Yet in some there remained deep in the marrow of the soul an inward wound, which dissimulation covered for a time, until an occasion of rebellion broke forth—as the subsequent event showed.

For after a short intervening time, certain of them stirred up the waters of contradiction: they changed the waters of Siloam, which flowed silently, into the waters of Rezin [Note: [Col. 0493] Isa. 8.]; and, pouring out waters, became the heads of quarrels. Thus those who longed after the pots of Egypt [Note: [Col. 0493] Exod. 16.], returning to their leases, “confirmed for themselves an evil word” [Note: [Col. 0493] Ps. 63], namely, that they should appeal to the Apostolic See, [Col. 0494B] throw from their necks the yoke of their bishop and abbot, renounce obedience, and contend with him concerning their own possessions.

Having therefore gone to the supreme pontiff, they gained little or nothing, except that they stirred him up against the Archbishop of Canterbury to implacable hatred. I testify before Him who is supreme life what I heard and saw. When Pope Urban had left Verona and was travelling to Ferrara, I rode with him and began to plead more devotedly and urgently for the archbishop. I commended to him the man of God as a vessel chosen by the Lord: a vessel firm in faith, four-square in humility, prudence, courage, and charity. But he, greatly inflamed with anger, said: “May it never please the Lord that I should dismount [Col. 0494C] from this horse and mount it or another, if within a short time I do not depose him from the archbishopric.”

He had scarcely uttered the words when the golden cross carried before his face by a subdeacon fell broken before our feet. While all were troubled and horrified, a certain Templar brother, R., his chamberlain, took the clasp of his cloak and fastened the cross as best he could to its staff. That very day we came to Sutri, where, seized by severe dysentery, he had himself carried from his boat onwards; and, never thereafter mounting another horse, he died after a short space of time. What we know we speak, and what we have seen we testify; and we invoke as witness and judge of this assertion Him whose testimonies have become most credible and whose judgments most terrible.

If you ask what occasion drew me there, [Col. 0494D] I say that it was love for both men. For I had been Urban’s companion and pupil in the schools at Malmesbury; at that time I was also the archbishop’s table-companion. Wishing therefore to help one through the other, I cast myself, not without grave danger to my life, into the labyrinth of that controversy. I knew that the master of every grace, herald of the divine word, trumpet of the Gospel, salt of the earth, light of his country, glory of religious men, delight of God, renown of good character, and school of virtues, was promoting the tranquillity of monks and the public good of the kingdom. For the instructor of good minds, the Holy Spirit, had so fitted and adapted him to Himself that, wholly cleaving to God, he was one spirit with Him; nor did he act or speak in a way in which [Col. 0495A] charity did not return, and so that a more ready understanding might run the course of this field with unimpeded foot.

For a fuller demonstration of my argument, I have decided to insert briefly certain matters which a fitting occasion offers me, established by the memory of the living and by authentic writings. When blessed Anselm was banished by William II, king of England, and lived as an exile in parts of Gaul, only his clerics remained with him in his trials; from neither his suffragans nor his monks did he receive any consolation during so long a desolation. After the death of the said king, on the very day when he was slain in England, the holy man, at Lyons, being divinely recalled, returned to his own country. Received amid the rejoicing of the whole land, he destroyed, in honour of blessed Stephen, the church of the Canterbury clerics [Col. 0495B] beside the city walls. While he was there arranging prebends from parish churches belonging to his patronage, he was called by the Lord and caught up to heaven—he of whom the world was not worthy—and his desire did not attain fulfilment.

In the course of time, moreover, the most blessed martyr, as is publicly known, throughout all seven years of his exile was to his suffragans and monks “as one dead from the heart,” [Note: [Col. 0495] Ps. 30.] except that very many of those from whom he hoped for better remedies added pain upon his pain. Only the clerics, banished with him and for his sake, stood by him faithfully and with filial devotion in his struggle. Therefore, when a feigned peace had been restored to him and he had returned to England, he turned his vows, as the public words and writings of his followers testify, with more fervent zeal to the restoration of the church of Saint Stephen which Saint Anselm had begun. But, brought to completion by martyrdom, he did not put his purpose into effect.

[Col. 0495C] We saw the martyr’s successor, Richard of good memory, who, although he had sprung from the bosom of the Church of Canterbury, burned with desire for the same project. Yet he differed from his predecessors in this: at M. he planned to transfer the site of the church, not on account of the various advantages of the place. Nevertheless, a simple, gentle, and very yielding man, he abandoned the undertaking at the most urgent insistence of his prior and convent. The work of his desire, delayed, collapsed and came to nothing.

[Col. 0495D] Baldwin, the archbishop of blessed memory, who succeeded him, endeavoured to restore the work of his predecessors, which envious death, the destroyer of good works, had cut off as though a web from its weaver. And behold, the enemy sowed tares among it, turning into material for scandal whatever charity had ordained for the common benefit. Something had almost slipped from the recesses of my memory which I could not, without a scruple of conscience, shut up in silence or pass over.

## LETTER CCXII. TO POPE INNOCENT

**SUBJECT.—P. B., Archdeacon of London, asks Pope Innocent to free him from the most wicked and crafty harassment of B., the cantor.**

To the reverend Father and lord INNOCENT, by the grace of God supreme pontiff, his own P. B. sends greeting, and wishes that amid the pressures of afflictions he may be judge and avenger.

[Col. 0496A] Formerly accustomed to write to my lords from the abundance of my heart, and to draw forth spiritual waters and draughts from the fountains of the Saviour into the streets, I am now compelled to write in the ink of grief and to break off my words with weeping, groaning, and frequent sobbing rather than utter them. For indignation has drunk up my whole spirit; amid the troubles of old age, a veteran and discharged soldier, I am called back to war, so that the floodgates of my wretched head might be opened and my brain and the marrow of my bones melt away into tears.

A certain messenger of Lord L., bishop, deceiving your Holiness, sorrowfully represented to you on his lord’s behalf [Col. 0496B] that the aforesaid bishop desired to establish a new chantry in the church of L., and requested your indulgence in this matter. At the very first word, “iniquity lied to itself.” [Note: [Col. 0495] Ps. 26.] G., of good memory, instituted as canon and cantor the third before this man—[the text reads *est*, “is”]—the son of a most distinguished man of the aforesaid Church. But this man was made cantor out of nothing.

The king gave this bishop a poor little parish church on the condition that two chaplains should be maintained from it: one to serve that little church, the other to celebrate daily in the Church of London a Mass for the dead, every day, for the soul of the lord king and of his predecessors and successors. There is no revenue there from which two [Col. 0496C] priests can be supported even most meagrely. Whence then will arise the foundation and resources of the chantry? An occasion has been given not for singing but for weeping, unless revenues and the dignity of honour are assigned to him from our former revenues, to our disgrace.

You granted the bishop the rights which other cantors possess in stalls, processions, and other English churches. Under pretext of those letters this cantor asks the Archdeacon of London for a stall and other rights—he who is the greatest person in the church after the dean—and asks that something be taken from every person of the church out of his dignity and conferred upon himself. This is expressly contrary to the clause of your letters in which you permit these things to be done without injury or loss to anyone.

Under his general and simple petition, he who is [Col. 0496D] the very last of all and as it were an untimely birth asks to have the first voice in the election of the dean, the second in the election of the bishop, and many other things which from the first foundations of the church the archdeacons of that church are known hitherto to have held peacefully and honourably. Therefore, while cruel crosses look on, may you graciously condescend with compassionate affection toward a man now old and discharged from service. For it would be utterly absurd that a youth, carried away by ambition and pride, should so cruelly despoil a man of such great name of an ancient and rightful dignity. Since, after the bishop, the clergy and people of the whole city are bound to show love to the archdeacons alone, who could behold with dry eyes the disgrace and abasement of the archdeacon, and the whole honour of the archdeaconry [Col. 0497A] so cruelly usurped before clergy and people by a youth who is not yet fully created and already chatters, who is not yet in being and already has entered upon office?

It is intolerable to good and grave men that one beloved by God and men should be so enormously assailed without judgment and without sin, and that there is none “who is moved over the affliction of Joseph.” Look providently upon his innocence, most innocent Innocent. Turn his justice into judgment. Carefully and diligently inquire whether the first letters which you granted, and the second which you sent to Bishop C., were obtained by true or false representations. Let it please you that the clause in your indulgence should have force: namely, that he should possess the dignities which he seeks without injury to another.

Indeed, since subject dioceses ought to follow the Metropolitan Church, the occasion of universal disturbance will be removed from your Church if, according to the laws and dignities belonging to a cantor, the cantor of his own church is made to restrain the madness of his ambition. [Col. 0497B] Customs differ in English churches: some have a dean, some do not; some have a treasurer, some do not. In some the cantor is lesser; in some the treasurer is greater. But far be it that the Bride of Christ, clothed in varieties—clerical, monastic, white and black, linen or woollen—should, for one man’s ambition, endure Joseph’s cloak or Christ’s tunic to be thus torn apart!

Lord L., foreseeing the disturbance secured by the letters of indulgence sent to him, suppressed [Col. 0497C] them for three years and never wished to use them. But the often-mentioned B., having acquired letters of indulgence by clandestine subreption, caused them to be recalled and sent afresh to Lord G.; we are armed with an inextricable prolixity. For we must either consent to this evil or oppose it: if we consent, we are despoiled of every right which we possess; if we oppose it, by the authority of those letters we are struck by the censure of the Church.

But, God willing, injuries shall proceed from the place whence laws are obtained. The hidden enemy has explored the weakness and decline of my body, and will not cease from persecution until he has wrung life out of me and there comes to pass what was said to the idolater Ahab concerning the life and death of Naboth: “You have killed, and moreover taken possession.” [Note: [Col. 0497] III Kings 21.] Therefore the Archdeacon of London, before and at the installation of that cantor, [Col. 0497D] solemnly appealed against him together with all the persons of the church. For he heard and still remembers that saying of Wisdom: “My son, if the spirit of one having power over you comes upon you, do not leave your place.” [Note: [Col. 0497] Eccles. 10.] In these words he commends his lot into the hands of God and of yourselves.

## LETTER CCXIII. FROM EMPEROR FREDERICK TO SALADIN

**SUBJECT.—Emperor Frederick requests from S., ruler of the Saracens, restoration of certain places; otherwise he threatens him with severe war.**

FREDERICK, by the grace of God Emperor of the Romans, ever august, magnificent triumphator over the enemies of the Empire, and ordained governor of the whole monarchy, [Col. 0498A] to S., ruler of the Saracens, once an illustrious man: flee Jerusalem after the example of Pharaoh.

We received your letters, sent to us in times long past, concerning grave affairs which indeed would have profited you had faith corresponded to your words, with the magnificence fitting the majesty of our person. We have deemed it worthy to advise your greatness through the addresses of our letters; but now, because you have profaned the Holy Land, we, who rule an empire through the Eternal King, are admonished by the solicitude of the imperial office to decree due punishment, as ruler of Judaea, Samaria, and Palestine, upon the presumptuous and punishable audacity of so great a crime.

Therefore, unless before all else you restore the occupied land, adding the satisfaction prescribed by sacred ordinances for such impious offences, lest we appear in the slightest degree to wage an unlawful war, we set you a term, beginning on the first day of the Kalends of November, when the year has run its course, to test the fortune of war at Campotaneo, in the power of the Holy Cross and in the name of the true Joseph.

[Col. 0498B] For we can scarcely believe that this is unknown to you, or that from the writings of the ancients and the ancient histories you are ignorant of the novelty of our age and deed. Do you pretend not to know both Ethiopias, Mauretania, Parthia, Syria, Persia—made the first towered possessions of our dictator Marcus Crassus—Judaea, Samaria, Mauretania, Arabia, Chaldaea, and Egypt itself? There, alas for shame, the Roman citizen Antony, a man endowed with distinguished courage, cast down from so lofty a height of affairs through a lack of self-restraint and conduct unworthy of a soldier, [Col. 0498C] too little soberly served the loves of Cleopatra. Do you likewise pretend not to know Armenia and innumerable other lands subject to our dominion? Kings know it, whose blood Roman swords have more frequently drunk.

And indeed by the very experience of events, with God as author, you shall understand what our victorious eagles and cohorts of diverse nations can accomplish; what German fury, taking up arms in peace, can do:

> What the untamed head of the Rhine can do; what the avenging Danube—  
> the Danube that has never known flight; what Bavaria, what subtle Swabia;  
> what circumspect Franconia, what Saxony that plays with the sword;  
> what Thuringia, what Westphalia, what swift Brabant; what Lorraine, [Col. 0498D] ignorant of peace;  
> what restless Burgundy, what the wanton Alpine peoples, what Frisia powerful in cattle;  
> what Bohemia rejoicing to die of its own accord, what Poland fiercer than its own wild beasts;  
> what the March of Ancona, what the Illyrian regions, what Lombardy, Tuscany, Venice,  
> and the Pisan shipmaster can do.

Finally, that day, full of reverence and the joyous triumph of Christ, shall teach you how our right hand—though you accuse it of being enfeebled by age—has learned to wield the sword.

## LETTER CCXIV. TO WALTER, ARCHBISHOP OF ROUEN

**SUBJECT.—Consolation in exile.**

To the reverend Father and lord WALTER, by the grace of God Archbishop of Rouen, P. B. sends greeting in Him without whom there is no salvation.

[Col. 0499A] I heard with grief that certain members of your household, seeking rather what is their own than what is Jesus Christ’s [Note: [Col. 0499] Phil. 2], do not cease, by the frequent importunity of letters, to urge you to return to the garlic and melons of Egypt, and, casting aside the authority of ecclesiastical liberty, to suffer your ears to be pierced with an awl as a reproach of perpetual servitude [Note: [Col. 0499] Exod. 21]. Your Church indeed, which is our mother, was free; but today she is compelled to be enslaved with Hagar [Note: [Col. 0499] Gal. 4]. Therefore you departed, lest you should behold the evils of your Church, as the prophet laments and says: “Judah has migrated because of affliction and the multitude of servitude” [Note: [Col. 0499] Lam. 1].

Would that you may run in such a way as not uncertainly, and fight not as one beating the air [Note: [Col. 0499] 1 Cor. 9], but so establish your heart in the Lord that he may at last number you among the children of the deliverer. First of all, deliberate carefully with yourselves and, according to the Gospel parable [Note: [Col. 0499] Luke 14], sit down first and count the cost, and see whether you are able with ten thousand to meet him who comes with twenty thousand. See that Christ alone, who is supreme justice, is the cause of so great a resolve; for blessed Peter says: “If you suffer for Christ, you are blessed” [Note: [Col. 0499] 1 Pet. 3]; and he adds: “Let none of you suffer as a thief or a murderer, or as one coveting what belongs to another” [Note: [Col. 0499] 1 Pet. 4]; but “if you endure for righteousness, this is grace” [Note: [Col. 0499] 1 Pet. 2].

[Col. 0499B] In confessors, their life makes a man’s death precious; in martyrs, the cause does so. Therefore, amid this oppression, bear everywhere before you the banner of Christ and the title of innocence. The wicked person is afflicted in one way and the righteous in another. Though ointment and mud are stirred alike, sweetness breathes from the one and stench rises from the other; in the same fire gold glows and straw smokes.

Many bless the Lord in prosperity, according to the saying: “He will praise thee when thou hast done well to him” [Note: [Col. 0499] Ps. 48]; but they fail in hard times and do not stand firm amid miseries. But if the Lord questions you with scourges, say in a voice of exultation, confession, and salvation with the Psalmist: “It is good for me, Lord, that thou hast humbled me; thou art righteous, Lord, and thy judgment is right” [Note: [Col. 0499] Ps. 118]. For the Apostle testifies: “The sufferings of this present age are not worthy to be compared with the future glory that shall be revealed in us” [Note: [Col. 0499] Rom. 8].

Blessed Job, struck by the death of his children, the loss of his possessions, and the affliction of his own heart, recognizing the righteousness of God in his goodness, said: “When God shall have fulfilled his will in me, many things still remain with him” [Note: [Col. 0499] Job 14]. The Apostle, placed amid distresses, cries: “Wretched man that I am, who shall deliver me from the body of this death?” [Note: [Col. 0499] Rom. 7]. And likewise: “We were burdened beyond measure, so that we were weary even of life” [Note: [Col. 0499] 2 Cor. 1].

[Col. 0499C] Considering, therefore, that this brief and momentary tribulation works in us an immense weight of glory, he says [Note: [Col. 0499] 2 Cor. 4] not only that we glory, but that we glory also in our tribulations. If therefore your rivals now boast that they have prevailed in their vanity, know that their joy, to use Job’s expression, [Col. 0500A] “is as a point” [Note: [Col. 0499] Job 20]; their end is destruction [Note: [Col. 0499] Phil. 3], their burial that of an ass [Note: [Col. 0499] Jer. 22], and their recompense fire and worm.

It has never been heard that persecutors of the Church have ever escaped unpunished the avenging hand of him who punishes the mighty mightily [Note: [Col. 0499] Wis. 6], who has always crushed by his own strength the necks of the proud and exalted. For if, for a time, the Lord permits sinners to build upon the back of the righteous, he fashions for that righteous person a crown of glory and eternal beauty from the very hammering of the wicked.

We have often read and seen that by the measure in which anyone has judged [Note: [Col. 0499] Matt. 7], he is judged, and receives measure for measure. It is the Spirit of Wisdom who says: “By the things through which a man sinned, through those same things he shall be punished” [Note: [Col. 0499] Wis. 11]. Pharaoh was drowned because he had drowned the Hebrew infants [Note: [Col. 0499] Exod. 15]. Goliath was slain by the sword with which he had attacked David [Note: [Col. 0499] 1 Sam. 17]. Haman was hanged [Col. 0500B] upon the gallows which he had prepared for Mordecai [Note: [Col. 0499] Esth. 7].

Let those, therefore, beware whose rebellion compelled you to depart from your province. For Hosea the prophet writes and says of those who are obstinately rebellious against their prelates and priests: “Your wife shall commit fornication in the city; your sons and daughters shall fall by the sword; your land shall be measured by the line; you shall die in a defiled land; and your people shall migrate in captivity from their own land” [Note: [Col. 0499] Amos 7]. God is ready to judge your cause; and I fear that he may do so more swiftly and severely than they would wish.

For I know that sorrow has never so swallowed up the magnanimity of your heart that paternal affection toward your children should degenerate. It is written in the book of Job [Note: [Col. 0499] ch. 36]: “Let not anger so oppress you that you oppress anyone.” Certainly a pious shepherd threatens his subjects with severe things, but nevertheless devoutly endeavors to avert them from them; and although he rages against offenders with the zeal of charity, he yet desires, if need be, to die for them.

[Col. 0500C] The fine flour offered on the griddle or in the oven is first sprinkled with oil according to the teaching of Leviticus, lest it be burned by the violence of the fire. In like manner, pour upon your conscience the oil of charity and mercy, lest the fire of anger turn into injury to the soul what heavenly dispensation has appointed in you for salvation. I would rather that your subjects should return to you with filial devotion than that, turned into a crooked bow and obstinate in wickedness, they should incur the punishment of the heavenly sentence.

Some derive consolation from the destruction of their enemies. I beg you, let not your soul consent to be consoled by such consolation. Rather set before the eyes of your heart David, who, when temptation rushed upon him, persecution raged, a rival afflicted him, one of his own cursed him, and his son sought his life, did not repay evil to those repaying him evil. For, concerned for the salvation of his persecutor and grieved at the death of his enemy, he was willing to be reproached and would not endure to be avenged.

[Col. 0500D] Surely charity is patient and kind [Note: [Col. 0499] 1 Cor. 13]. In David then, and today in his imitators, it humbly bears the malice of persecutors and diligently seeks their salvation. But you, most loving Father, “keep innocence and behold equity, because there is a remnant for the peaceable man.” Make from the necessity an occasion of salvation and virtue; turn sin into merit; and let your peace attain that peace which surpasses all understanding [Note: [Col. 0501] Phil. 4].

Your peace is at the gates. For, as is read in Proverbs: “When a man’s ways please the Lord, he will turn even his enemies to peace” [Note: [Col. 0501] Prov. 16]. By the requirement of strict justice, it belongs to your adversaries humbly to beg peace from you. Let your humility bend those whom your steadfastness has found proud and incorrigible. Let your moderation therefore be known to all men; let the meek hear of your gentleness and rejoice. Under the pretext of meekness, do not wait to be asked, but ask for the things that make for peace.

[Col. 0501A] Receive with meekness the implanted word, so that you neither inflict nor return an injury. For this is your meekness: neither to become an enemy nor an avenger. By this way the Lord directs the meek to salvation: if your mercy triumphs over judgment; if you are more ready to forgive than to avenge; and if zeal for justice toward his children so moves a father that he never forsakes saving charity.

Among your subjects, indeed, there are many difficult and perverse persons who, like restless beasts of burden, do not draw in the yoke. It is difficult to bring them to the unity of the Spirit, without which every joining is a tearing apart. Let something therefore be taken from severity, where the ruin of many lies, until you proclaim the year acceptable to the Lord, until enemies are changed into sons and wrath into favor.

Above all I ask one thing: when it comes to securities for peace, let the divine law prescribe their form. Let your purpose so proceed that the honor of God and the observance of ecclesiastical liberty suffer no prejudice; let the priests of the Lord be invested with full authority and justice, so that no unpunished presumption may recoil upon Christ or his Church.

[Col. 0501B] For the insult was not inflicted upon you but upon Christ. Moses, speaking to unbelievers and rebels, says: “Your murmuring is not against us, but against the Lord. For what are we?” [Note: [Col. 0501] Exod. 16]. Let your peace therefore yield to God for glory and to the honor of the Church, and to clergy and people for quiet, so that in this respect, as the angel most wisely distinguishes: “Glory be to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” [Note: [Col. 0501] Luke 2].

If you make peace otherwise, your bitterness in peace will be most bitter, and it will be said: “Peace, peace, and there is no peace” [Note: [Col. 0501] Jer. 6]. We may also complain with Lucan:

> Liberty perishes together with peace.

Recall, I pray, Father, what peace Ahab king of Israel made with King Ben-hadad, which afterward was turned for Ahab himself by his people into groaning. To gather much into a brief conclusion: let your peace, I beg, include the benefit of full restoration, together with the honor of God and the integrity of ecclesiastical liberty. But concerning the satisfaction of penitents, let mercy greatly abate [Col. 0502A] severity; let vengeance pass into favor, and discipline into gentleness.

## EPISTLE CCXV

The glory of a judge falls into the disrepute of public opinion when, despising the poor, he exposes himself for gifts eagerly sought from the rich. I confess that the fulfilment of my wishes has been increased by the fact that the favor of your generosity requested from me a poem suited to my own capacity. The composition now before us, however, asks to be revised because of the narrowness of time and the hurried haste of writing.

For it fears the examination of so great a judge, since it is neither adorned with the attractive embellishments of rhetorical persuasion nor armed with forceful sentiments, but disfigured by the meagerness of a starving reason. If therefore your discernment finds anything weak or superfluous, let a more careful file correct it. Nor shall I judge it burdensome if the examination of so great a person corrects the fault of my ignorance.

[Col. 0502B] A man of such name, a man of so widely proclaimed discernment, who neither begs for the loss of reputation nor pleads on the basis of another’s blood:

> Tell, man, what is man, who is like unto vanity,  
> whose days pass away as a shadow [Note: [Col. 0501] Ps. 143].  
> First investigate your origin; begin with the source of your generation;  
> and then applaud, if you will, the births of kings.

The first man was the original seed-bed both of all kings and of the whole multitude of humankind. Therefore trace back his beginnings. In what blood does he boast, or by what birth does he ennoble the progeny yet to be born? Earth indeed was his mother, the ancient and long-lived nurse of the human race. When he had been formed from mud into a fragile body of clay, God’s beneficence breathed into him the breath of heavenly life.

[Col. 0502C] Behold the nobility of the human race; behold the loftiness of human boasting; behold the glory of ancestry! But how will one clothed in purple endure to descend? How will the attendant of royal majesty be humbled? How will the festivity of royal glory become kindly toward common people and be leveled with plebeian servitude, so that the dominion of the same blood is common with the people, so that the generation of servants and king is alike, so that royal offspring and the crowd consist of the same elements?

Let the king descend from the throne of his glory, clothed in sackcloth instead of purple; let him sprinkle with ashes and haircloth the head crowned with royal majesty; let him tread the earth with bare feet; and, tracing back his ancestors, let him confess that he is descended from a poor farmer. The first father of humankind, man, was made from the mud of the earth; from the dregs of that mud man has been propagated into posterity.

The origin of the perverse generation conceived neglect of the Creator’s first command; and it immediately received the punishment of retaliation as recompense and stumbling-block. It received, as the reproach of its posterity, death for the fall of disobedience, servitude for its negligence; finally, it was given as a provision appropriate to its condition that, from the sweat of unceasing labor, it should sustain the wretched wage of mortal and perishing life.

[Col. 0502D] Why then do you recall your forefathers, when, if you trace their origin, it would be safer [Col. 0503A] to have been silent than to have boasted of your beginning? A plea is to be avoided which contains more harm than benefit, more shame than honor, especially before wise persons, from whom it cannot conceal its disadvantages to salvation or strip honor of its due dignity.

It is fitting for human conduct to be altered in accordance with the times and manners of people, especially in these times in which expediency outweighs honor. Blessed be the Lord God of Israel, who in our times has restored peace to the poor and ancient dignity to the Church. We confess that a divine gift, to be proclaimed by the good among all good things, has given us a judge to correct vices and a founder of morals. The throne of justice has been exalted, and under a most merciful king its proper order is restored to affairs, for he knows how to render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s [Col. 0503B] and to God the things that are God’s.

Moreover, he has attained the glory of a more favorable fortune who judges a day lost in which he has not been able to act against corrupted morals. In his court military service is so learned that honor is not unlearned. In his camp neither service is deprived of reward nor virtue of reverence; he does not attend to merits, but surpasses all men in merits.

## EPISTLE CCXVI. TO THE ABBOT AND CONVENT OF CROWLAND

**ARGUMENT.—Peter the orator implores the prayers of all.**

PETER, to his beloved lords and friends in Christ, H., by the grace of God abbot, and the convent of Crowland: greeting [Col. 0503C] in him without whom there is no salvation.

Summoned and drawn by the lord of Canterbury, I have decided to cross promptly into Normandy, perhaps to proceed farther. For a man’s way is not in himself; and although a man orders his own paths, it belongs to God alone to direct his steps [Note: [Col. 0503] Prov. 16]. I therefore most devoutly entreat you, in a spirit of humility and affection, to commend my journey to the Lord by your devoted prayers.

May your eyes look upon my imperfection and the infirmity of my body with pious compassion, so that through the strength of your prayers weakness may be made strong for labor, and labor may bear fruit unto salvation. The book of experience teaches you how greatly another’s faith or prayer benefits those who despair of themselves and hope in others, who distrust their own merits and trust in the holiness of others.

The Church continually proclaims the power of another’s intercession in the daughter of the Canaanite woman [Note: [Col. 0503] Matt. 15], in Lazarus [Note: [Col. 0503] John 11], in the centurion’s servant [Note: [Col. 0503] Matt. 8], in the royal official’s son [Note: [Col. 0503] John 4], and in very many others. The apostle Peter escaped from the hands of Herod and from all the expectation of the Jews, delivered by the prayer of the Church [Note: [Col. 0503] Acts 12].

[Col. 0503D] Finally, the Teacher of the Gentiles, amid the imminent perils of temptations, humbly implored the prayers of the saints: “I beseech you,” he says, “through the Lord Jesus Christ, that you help me by your prayers to God” [Note: [Col. 0503] Rom. 15]. But I, dust and ashes and a worm in comparison with blessed Paul, and more miserable than all people, have a still greater need for the urgency of holy prayers; and with eager and hungry longing I beg for the crumbs that fall from the table of my lords who offer acceptable sacrifices to God.

You know that we are all one in Christ; and the wholeness of the Church, consisting in the harmonious joining of its members, commands you to follow a rule of mercy and compassion toward your neighbor’s need, so that with undivided affections and, as it were, the shoulders of one heart, you may bear my burden. Therefore I adjure you in the unity of faith, in the communion of saints, and in the confession of one baptism, that the bond of charity, the law of nature, ready compassion, the bond of brotherhood, the spiritual obligation of the promise formerly made in your chapter, the demonstration of love, the weakness of my [Col. 0504A] body, the danger of the journey, and the devotion of the suppliant may stir your pious affections toward me.

Charity never fails; nor can prayer, or anything whatever expended for Christ from charity, fail. Your prayer shall return into your own bosom. For what benefits another through someone never fails that person; indeed, grace increases through expenditure, and the flask of oil overflows all the more fully as charity, the mother of virtues, pours more abundantly from it into the vessels presented.

Fare well, all and each of you; and, I beseech you, pour the oil of mercy upon the wounds of mine before the merciful God.

## EPISTLE CCXVII

**ARGUMENT.—Commendation of a certain abbot after his death.**

Perhaps there will be someone who will disdain the lean and bloodless nakedness of this present letter. But just as it is contrary to propriety to shine in a splendid display of clothing amid the tearful funeral rites of a beloved deceased person, so in a matter so mournful and full of sobs it was not fitting that speech should play with elaborate little flowers of words.

For if the eloquent sweetness of discourse were to flatter readers, enticing their minds, fascinated by its sweetness, to linger upon itself, it would steal from those who read the feeling of compassion that ought to be shown. Therefore, since we send you not something to be read but something to be mourned, attend in this letter not to ornament but to lamentation, not to the beauty of words but to the abundance of tears.

For we have not written to you what relentless grief has long polished away; rather, drawing from an inkhorn full of tears and bitterness, we have written what grief itself dictated—grief, I say, which, by the peculiar character of an irreparable loss, outweighing every other sorrow, has driven us to such a degree of calamity that it seems to add much dignity and consolation to our grief if we appear more miserable than others.

[Col. 0504D] Therefore, most beloved brethren and lords, we ask and entreat you in Christ Jesus that you may grieve with our misery—not so that the mass, as it were, of sorrow may diminish in you, but so that it may flow by fellow-sufferers’ compassion even to the afflicted. Yet it will supply a measure of consolation if we know that the bitterness of our misfortune is held in such esteem among you that it can draw from all a feeling of pity.

Why we claim preeminence in sorrow over other mourners, no one who knows the cause of our tears will wonder; rather, he will blame the niggardly and almost insensible hardness of your heart, should you not yield sufficiently to tears. For he has died—he has died—and has been freed from this body of death: our father and shepherd of good memory, Lord G., abbot of Blois.

If we were to recount fully the merit of his life through the service of the pen, we should be little removed from flatterers and could not avoid the reproach of falsehood. For just as his life was almost more than human, so it surpasses belief how infinite was the abundance of virtues in him while he lived.

[Col. 0505B] Yet if we touch upon his manners, fashioned to perfection, only lightly and coolly, a slackness in praise will incur the appearance of detraction. It is not to avoid derogating from his qualities to touch upon only a few of his virtues while the finer part of them is passed over, buried in silence, though it seems to be breaking into the light of public knowledge.

We judged it sounder counsel to proceed more cautiously and restrain his titles below the truth of his merit, so that the reader may find us sparing of truth and miserly in genuine praise rather than lavish with falsehood. For he was one who so presided that, desiring more to benefit than to rule, he never ceased to serve; considering not the singularity of office but the common condition, he showed himself companion or servant to all.

[Col. 0505C] For he had read: “Let him that is greater among you become as the younger, and he that goes before as one who serves” [Note: [Col. 0505] Luke 22]. Thus no one experienced him as a master except one whose perversity had to be restrained by the rod of authority. Indeed, the mother of virtues, discernment, had blended in him a certain sweet and delightful mixture of piety and justice, so that he neither denied the master in the father nor failed to recognize the father in the master.

He thus preserved each in the other: paternal kindness never abandoned the indignation of the prelate, nor did the masterly severity of discipline sleep amid paternal affections. Thus, in the ark of his discerning heart, he preserved both rod and manna; thus he mixed the oil of mercy with the wine of strictness, so as to reproduce in healing the wounds of vices the diligence of our Samaritan.

And because he knew the written saying, “A lying mouth kills the soul” [Note: [Col. 0505] Wis. 1], he abhorred falsehood no less than murder. He so overflowed with the bowels of mercy that, by a kind of fellowship in compassion, he counted as belonging to his own troubles whatever afflicted his neighbor. For he felt with the Apostle, who says: “Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is scandalized, and I do not burn?” [Note: [Col. 0505] 2 Cor. 11].

[Col. 0505D] Moreover, he shone with so great a virtue of generosity that he thought a service shamefully sold if a friend had extracted it by entreaties. With generous hand he anticipated the request of a friend, as though foreseeing the need for which he would be asked. The unceasing cries of the poor testify how freely he opened all his affections in the distribution of alms; they, like ourselves, lament inconsolably the removal of their shepherd.

How solicitous he was in receiving guests, how generous and devoted he showed himself toward them once received, experience itself bears better witness than our speech could adequately express, even if in us the grace of Tullian eloquence should bloom again twofold. For he was not querulous but diligent; not suspicious, but obliging as a steward. He brightened every act of kindness he bestowed by a pleasing and habitual cheerfulness of face, more precious than every service.

[Col. 0506A] For he knew that Christ is received in the guest, and that at the end he will say: “I was a stranger and you took me in” [Note: [Col. 0505] Matt. 25]. The abundant provision of food in his house, known by sight, bears witness to the watchful diligence with which he attended to matters committed to him.

In required building works, he devoted himself perceptively and effectively to restoring what had fallen down, as both the construction of new buildings and the repair of those which the devouring envy of age had consumed most fittingly attest. And, what more especially completes his reformation, he so confined his monks within the bounds of a stricter life that the relaxed liberty of conduct more indulgently allowed to other abbots gave the more strictly regulated life of his subjects no cause to murmur.

[Col. 0506B] But, to conclude the extensive matter of his praise in a shorter compass, his life was nothing other than a gathering of good qualities and a mass of virtues; it provided to all a model of conduct and an example for living. Although by such manifold excellence of virtues he raised for himself a ladder to things eternal, nevertheless, knowing that he had here no abiding city but sought the one to come, and because the course of this present life cannot exist wholly without some stain of earthly conduct, we beseech in Christ the favor of your brotherhood, that the persistence of your prayers may supply what was lacking in our aforesaid father.

We also entreat your charity that the benefits of your generosity may so assist the bearer of this letter that the duty entrusted to him may not be delayed through want of travelling provisions.

## EPISTLE CCXVIII

[Col. 0506D]

**ARGUMENT.—Congratulations for the bishop-elect of Chartres, and a reply to those hindering him.**

To his dearest lord and Father, bishop-elect of Chartres by the grace of God, his own P. B. sends greeting in the author of salvation.

Long before we saw your countenance, so greatly desired by us, your name was like poured-out ointment. For a lamp destined to be raised upon the Church’s lampstand could not be hidden under a bushel [Note: [Col. 0505] Matt. 5]. But when it pleased him who set you apart that you should offer to him in the church of the Blessed Virgin, his Mother, the remainder of your life as an evening sacrifice, [Col. 0507A] we came, like the queen of the South, to see the wisdom and uprightness which public report proclaimed in you [Note: [Col. 0507] 3 Kings 10; OCR reads “20”].

Coming, we saw as we had heard, except that report was less than truth; for the course of report, either through envy or through insufficiency, is delayed by leaving much of the substance of a matter unspoken. I give thanks to the maker of graces, who has granted us as shepherd and bishop of our souls one such as the need of our Church required: one needed by us to call back what had been alienated, to make firm what was broken, to raise what had fallen, to gather what was scattered, to punish what had gone astray, to forbid what was unlawful, to set in order what was disordered, to strengthen what was weak, [Col. 0507B] and to restore what was lost.

There is nothing which a rival can find to censure in you except the plainness of your clothing. Yet Jesus the high priest appeared to Zechariah in filthy garments. Some, moreover, murmur about the inadequacy of your age. Nevertheless, as I often say, if you pay the tribute of old age according to the course ordained by fate, the inward man, who was created according to God, is nonetheless renewed day by day in you.

And I remember reading in Job [Note: [Col. 0507] ch. 12] that “wisdom is with the aged, and understanding in length of days.” There are perhaps some still dwelling in a spirit of division who murmur against the election; they plotted in the removal of the royal rights, but at the third stage—that is, at the consecration—they will be unable to do harm. Goliath was brought down by the third stone, and the magicians failed at the third sign [Note: [Col. 0507] 1 Sam. 17].

[Col. 0507C] What is more intolerable is that those who today hand you a bill of repudiation boast that hereafter they will possess your favor more fully because they have taken away the royal right and your crops from you. These men may cite the deed of Absalom as an example: in order that Joab might gain for him the favor of his father, he is said to have burned Joab’s fields [Note: [Col. 0507] 2 Sam. 14]. Yet “woe to the man through whom scandal comes” [Note: [Col. 0507] Matt. 18].

But if anyone hisses against you with the spirit of his rashness, endure it patiently. For “in your patience you shall possess your souls.” I know that, according to the prophet’s word [Note: [Col. 0507] Isa. 50], the Lord has opened your ear so that you know how to bear the injuries of one who speaks against you. He has also given you a learned tongue [Col. 0507D] so that you know when it is fitting to speak.

Therefore dissemble, because you have in the Lord an example of such dissimulation, as Isaiah says [Note: [Col. 0507] ch. 57]: “You have lied, and have not remembered me, nor considered in your heart, because I am silent and as though not seeing.” Following also the example of him who gave his back to the scourges, endure it while sinners build upon the back of the righteous. The slander of your rivals ought to be so much the less valued by you as they are regarded as more worthless than others.

Indeed, the greater and better persons, at the urging of those who love you sincerely, have returned to a better mind. The storm has been turned into a breeze; a gentler and wiser speech has moderated those turbulent and ill-considered movements. I hasten to the bishop of Bath, who, as he has informed me in his letters, longs greatly to see you. I was yours while I was with you; now I am more yours; and when I return I shall be yours most entirely.

[Col. 0508A] I ask you, in that humility in which one can pray to the Lord, to give your voice a voice of power, and to be willing to restore me wholly, from half of myself, to the service of the glorious Virgin. “One thing have I asked of the Lord; this will I seek: that I may dwell in the house of my Lady” [Note: [Col. 0507] Ps. 26]. For in all things I sought rest, and I shall abide in her inheritance; and I have resolved to lead and end my life in her house, in which I received all the sacraments of the Christian faith.

And although greater riches might be offered me elsewhere, I nevertheless say with Gideon that “the grape-cluster of Ephraim is better than the harvest of Abiezer”; and one day in these courts is better for me than thousands [Note: [Col. 0507] Ps. 83]. Since therefore it lies in the hands of God and yours whether I find rest or wander as a fugitive over the earth [Note: [Col. 0507] Gen. 4], and since by my migration your bounty toward others loses nothing, but you may claim me altogether as your own, I place my lot in the hands of God and yours.

May my dearest lord fare well, and all who love him sincerely.

## EPISTLE CCXIX. TO HENRY, KING OF ENGLAND

We have heard how Jerusalem has been destroyed [Col. 0508C] and how the cross upon which Christ redeemed us has been captured. The king of Jerusalem has been led into Babylon; all the cities and fortresses, except Ascalon and Tripoli, have been captured; and it is still uncertain whether Jerusalem can resist the unclean dogs.

The lord king of Sicily, when he heard these reports, immediately clothed himself in haircloth; and, mourning for four days and hiding himself from people’s sight, he promised with anxious and steadfast devotion to assist that land to the best of his ability. The cardinals, moreover, with the assent of the lord pope, firmly promised among themselves that, casting aside all riches and luxuries, they would preach the cross of Christ not only in word but in deed and example; that they would go begging, take up Christ’s cross, preach, [Col. 0508D] and precede others into the land of Jerusalem.

They also decreed, with the lord pope’s assent, a most binding truce among all Christian princes for seven years, so that whoever should wage war against a Christian during that period would be subject to the curse of God and the lord pope, and to excommunication by all the prelates of the universal Church.

They likewise firmly promised among themselves that henceforth they would receive no gifts from anyone who had a case in the court, but might receive only those given or sent for their necessities; and that they would not mount a horse so long as [Col. 0509A] the land upon which the Lord’s feet stood remained under the feet of the enemy.

Farewell.

## EPISTLE CCXX
The onward course of the age, unceasingly hastening toward its end, has entangled the misery of the human condition in the snares of so many errors and stained it with the contagions of so many adversities that many, despising the beacons of Zion and climbing the heights of Samaria, smear their prayers with the pitch of the doctrines of heretical perversity. Veiling the exaltation of their souls under a certain appearance of humility—though inwardly they are excessively inflated by its swellings—they do not fear to scorn the inhabitants of Jerusalem; enclosing their own fatness within themselves, they do not shrink from incurring that curse upon those who despise Zion and trust in the mountain of Samaria, saying: [Col. 0509B] “We have no portion in David, nor inheritance in the son of Jesse” [Note: [Col. 0509] 2 Chron. 10.]. To them the Lord might deservedly threaten: “I will send a famine into the land—not a famine of bread nor a thirst for water, but rather for hearing the word of God” [Note: [Col. 0509] Amos 8.]. Yet he wills that no one should perish; indeed, he runs to embrace returning sons.

He still entrusts the work of the heavenly seed to his faithful stewards for distribution. But although the word of God has resounded through all the earth, while the heavens declared his glory, and although the rain of evangelical truth is still poured out through the bishops of places, who have been called by the Apostolic See to share in its solicitude, nevertheless, as the outstanding Doctor confesses concerning the Church in its rising: “There must be heresies, so that those who are approved may become manifest” [Note: [Col. 0509] 1 Cor. 11.].

At present [Col. 0509C] very many are weighed down by the burden of sins, and their foolish heart is darkened, so that they do not turn back from the crooked paths which they follow to uprightness, nor cry with the Prophet: “Deliver me from blood-guiltiness, O God, God of my salvation” [Note: [Col. 0509] Ps. 50]! Rather, like a house that provokes and transgresses the law of Christ, they recklessly leap toward the bitterness of doctrine, despising the food of heavenly speech and ensnaring the souls of the simple by hidden traps.

Indeed, among others, as has been reported to our ears, so great a multitude of unbelievers has grown in the province of Narbonne that, material sword being lacking, the spiritual sword is held in contempt; and the corruption of wild vines creeps into Catholic offshoots, while no one sets himself as a wall for the house of the Lord or dares to go up against the enemy, either to defend those who have not yet been sunk like lead in the sea of pestilence [Col. 0509D] [Note: [Col. 0509] Exod. 15.], or, if possible, to raise those lying in the hiding places of blindness.

Although the report of such foolish fig-trees has reached the hearing of certain religious persons and stirred their minds to lead forth the streams of their learning against them and divide the waters with zeal in the public squares, yet, since they were not sent, they have not dared on their own authority to undertake the office of preaching, lest they receive the portion of Dathan and Abiram, whom the earth swallowed alive [Note: [Col. 0509] Ps. 105.]. There is no one [Col. 0510A] to plead the cause of God before the erring people. But zeal for his house has consumed us [Note: [Col. 0509] Ps. 68], he who, though we are unworthy, has granted us to sit in an exalted watchtower. We desire to be weak with the weak and to apply fatherly counsels by which medicine may be brought to wounds; and, so far as lies in us, that even the swollen wound may receive care.

Therefore, may the swelling wound also receive care, so far as lies in us. [The following words are materially corrupt in the supplied text; they appear to direct that this be enjoined upon persons found suitable and legally approved to carry it out:] imitating the poverty of the poor Christ, they must not fear, in despised dress and fervent spirit, to approach the despised. Strive to impose this upon them for the remission of sins, so that, hastening to those same heretics, by the example of their conduct and the teaching of their speech, they may, with the Lord’s grant, so call them back from error that—unless the frequent shamelessness of guilt hardens their brow [Col. 0510B], and it may deservedly be said of them, “You have acquired the brow of a harlot; you refused to be ashamed” [Note: [Col. 0509] Jer. 3.]—they may rejoice in having attained, through hope, that Gospel saying: “Fear not, little flock, for it has pleased my Father to give you [the kingdom]” [Note: [Col. 0509] Luke 12.].

And let those religious obtain that saying of Solomon—namely, that one who rebukes a man finds greater favor than one who speaks pleasing words [reading uncertain: *g. mag. quam his qui loquitur q. delectant*]—so that, returning with rejoicing, they may be able to bring back sheaves from the seed they have scattered.

## LETTER 221

**To the Bishop of Vaison: the spirit of sounder counsel.**

You are said to be salt that has become tasteless, lacking the seasoning of wisdom. But we ask you whether the study of reading has ever brought you to that passage in Leviticus [Col. 0510C] where salt is commanded to be put upon every sacrifice [Note: [Col. 0509] Lev. 2.]. If you answer affirmatively, you may be accused of contempt, since your deeds are not seasoned with discernment.

But, in order to evade this objection, you will take refuge in the shadow of excuse: you will allege that the wandering eye passed over that command, or that your hasty tongue did not wait; that a sluggish intellect, or at least an unfaithful memory, promptly scattered whatever imagination had commended to it on such a subject. And lest you complain that you lack evidence on these matters, the action to which necessity bears witness, and that wicked proceeding against the beloved son, the provost of Vaison, clearly show that jurisdiction must have in you the same effect that a two-edged sword has in the hands of a madman.

You had requested [Col. 0510D] from that same man the benefit of absolution because, as you said, a priest formerly not subject to your jurisdiction had wronged you while you held the office of provost in the Church of Albi. You had caused him, naked and at your pleasure, to be scourged in your presence, to use the words of certain of your letters. When the provost excused himself by letter, maintaining that he could not do this without a mandate from the Apostolic See, you—having at hand sentences of excommunication ready for every assault—rashly pronounced against him words sufficiently expressive of an intention to excommunicate [Col. 0511A]. And, as though this were insufficient offense, you stripped him of the provostship of the Church of Vaison, although he had been appointed to carry out the business of the Cross not by just anyone but by the Apostolic See.

From this matter, therefore, draw for yourself the following questions. First, whether you ought to have carried into your episcopate the hatred conceived during your provostship, retaining resentment so that delay, contrary to custom, added more indignation, and, having become more powerful, you might take more powerful revenge for what perhaps you had passed over in a lesser office because the means were lacking. Second, whether the priestly order—or at least reverence for him who through priestly ministry is offered upon the altar to God the Father for the salvation of humankind—ought to have mattered so much to you that you would not expose a naked priest to mockery, indulging your will in his insults and beatings. [The third question is absent from the supplied text.] Fourth, whether you ought to have had such regard for Christ and the Apostolic See that you would not excommunicate a man of such honorable testimony before he had carried out the business of the Cross entrusted to him, nor despoil him contrary to justice of his provostship and other goods.

Draw the conclusion of these questions: from the first, that you may be called a diligent keeper of hatred; from the second, an affectionate sacrilegious man; from the third, sufficiently foolish; from the fourth, excessively presumptuous and an enemy of justice. Open your eyes, therefore, and see whether, in these matters, your eyelids went before your steps and whether the deed waited for the judgment of deliberation.

But because the Apostolic See ought to be both the bridle of oppressors and the refuge of the oppressed, having carefully heard both your letters and those of the chapter of the Church of Vaison, we decree that the sentence of excommunication which you pronounced against the same provost on the aforesaid ground—if indeed it deserves to be called a sentence—is utterly null. We restore to him the provostship thus taken away, whether you still retain it in your hands or have intruded another into it. We command them to put him into bodily possession of that provostship and protect him once installed. If anyone should appear as a holder after their mandate and does not provide full restitution to him within ten days, we deprive that person of every ecclesiastical benefice and of the exercise of office; and let them restrain other opponents through ecclesiastical censure. Moreover [Col. 0511D], let them make suitable satisfaction to him concerning the other property.

We also strictly command you not only to raise no obstacle in these matters against the aforesaid provost, but also to restore all expenses and property taken, and to present yourself before us, so that, concerning the matters promised and also concerning your abandonment, as we have heard, of the sign of the Cross, you may learn at the Apostolic See what befits pastoral moderation. Furthermore, since you can well recognize for yourself the character of your sentences, unless you bind reason against impulse, so that you may be punished in that in which you are known to have sinned, by authority of these presents we decree that henceforth you shall presume to pronounce no sentence against the often-mentioned provost, nor even with the common counsel of the whole chapter of Vaison; otherwise it shall have no force of validity.

## LETTER 222. FROM THE CHAPTER OF WORCESTER TO POPE INNOCENT

[Col. 0512A]

**To Pope Innocent, from the chapter of Worcester.**

The Gospel net entrusted to Your Holiness, with the Lord’s favor, will prosper most greatly in your hands for its catch if it is cast more carefully by the nail of discernment into those waves where a more abundant multitude of fish flows together for capture. This will come about more readily on the right side of the vessel at the Lord’s command when the eminence of your apostolate, in its customary gentleness, receives the prayers of suppliants and promotes to favor that which advances the growth of the universal Church.

In ancient days Bishop Wulfstan sat in the episcopal chair of Worcester. Guided by the Lord, he governed it, enlarged its religious life, enriched it with endowments, and consecrated it to the Virgin of virgins. What a simple, upright, and God-fearing man he was in life; how conscious of heavenly things and intimate with God at death; how venerable he was in life and glorious in death—the testimonies of miracles which antiquity has left us prove by clear evidence. Their credibility rests the more firmly because he does not yet cease to work miracles among us: magnificently, indeed, because they are for our glory; beneficially, because they occur in our own times; and for the benefit of those subject to us, so that, as new signs arrive, the old may be renewed and the cold warmed again, and those who did not believe the word of the earlier sign may believe at least the word of the following sign.

That it may be clear to your holy fatherhood what wonders God performs among us upon earth, we have sent from the bosom of our Church [Col. 0512C] trustworthy men, who may faithfully establish the truth of what they have seen, in whatever manner the prudence of your discernment shall prescribe as suitable for belief. Therefore, prostrate at your fatherhood’s feet, we ask and beseech you in the Lord that the authority of the Apostolic See may support the devotion of its children and grant the petition: that he whom, as we believe, God has enrolled among the number of his citizens in heaven may be numbered in the catalogue of saints on earth. For we trust that in this the welfare of your See will prosper in the Lord, if the prayers of the faithful are advanced and the honor of the saints is increased in your days. May the Most High preserve for long ages the well-being of Your Holiness, which, as is fitting, we desire in the Lord both devoutly and dutifully.

## LETTER 223. FROM THE BROTHERS OF MARMOUTIER TO THE BISHOP OF NANTES

[Col. 0512D]

**To the Bishop of Nantes, from the brothers of Marmoutier.**

Since Lord Matthew of Lire has incurred a sentence of excommunication for a dreadful and horrible deed which he committed to the injury of our house and of the whole Church, those who hear are astonished that, on the pretext of an apostolic mandate received by you in general form, you intend—God forbid!—to proceed to his absolution, omitting or wholly reducing whatever satisfaction he had promised us for that offense before obtaining that same mandate.

Although that which cannot truly be called satisfaction ought not to suffice for the gravity of the offense [Col. 0513A], nevertheless, seeking the things that make for peace, we are ready to accept what was proposed at Matthew’s own petition by the counsel of good men and granted by both parties. We therefore entreat and request your fatherhood that, lest the ease of punishment invite others to a similar act, you may, out of regard for God and love of blessed Martin, deal with us and our Church in this matter in such a way that our Church—which shows itself devoted to you in the sharing of spiritual and temporal goods—may not feel itself burdened by a reduction of that paltry satisfaction. Rather, set yourself as a wall for the house of the God of Israel, so that others may be held back from a similar excess through fear of punishment, and that we may be bound to render you the fullest thanks.

## LETTER 224

[Col. 0513B]

Within the enclosure of our fatherly memory abides [a passage corrupt in the supplied text], stirred by the greatness of royal devotion, [so] that, bedewed by the dew of heavenly blessing, you may flourish in the grace of salvation and at length merit to attain the joys of blessed light. This desire had long burned in our breast; and it has gained all the greater increase of ardor inasmuch as, although unworthy, we sit in the Apostolic See and bear the burdens of pastoral office, being bound to watch more diligently for your salvation and that of all.

Therefore my chief exhortation earnestly seeks and asks that you keep the eyes of attentive consideration fixed upon Christ Jesus our Lord, the Redeemer, bearing his image within your heart; that you delight in pursuing what pleases him; and that, considering that the fashion of this world passes away, and that kings, princes, and all others subject to corruption have departed and are departing, and that nothing born under the sun possesses a stable foundation, you persevere in the love of the divine name. Build prudently in the things above, despising lower things as transient and perishable in their worthlessness, so that you may establish for yourself an abiding dwelling in the kingdom of heavenly glory, which will neither fail nor perish.

Furthermore, reflecting with no slight feeling of compassion on the reported oppressions and distresses of the Holy Land, which we saw and touched with our own hand while holding a lesser office, and desiring henceforth that it should not utterly perish if such assistance can be provided, we have resolved to disclose our mind on this subject [Col. 0513D] in special letters. We have judged it appropriate to send them to you and your brothers through such persons as [the corrupt supplied text describes as] acceptable to him through the gift and manifold abundance of their virtues. Therefore we ask and earnestly exhort your royal magnificence with fatherly confidence that you apply your prayers to the same end with effective effort, so that you may thereby receive an increase of eternal reward.

That our intention may be more fully known to you, we believe that what has thus been spoken from our mouth concerning all those who have suffered such things on our behalf ought to be reported to your excellence. Nor should you wonder that our bull, not expressing our name, is attached to these letters [Col. 0514A], which are sent before the solemnities of our consecration or blessing. C. [lacuna] those who have been elected Roman pontiffs have been accustomed, in letters sealed with bulls, to observe this practice before the conferral of their consecration.

## LETTER 225. TO THE ARCHDEACON OF SALISBURY

**Subject.—A petition.**

To his reverend lord . . . ., archdeacon of Salisbury, Peter, his own B., greeting, and may compassion abound in you toward me.

I shall speak to my lord, though I am dust and ashes. Trusting in his natural kindness, I address him the more confidently, although he is occupied with ecclesiastical affairs. For if I should say anything insufficiently circumspect that could draw the generous brow of my lord into a frown, I know nevertheless that he has read that prophetic saying: “The Lord has given me a learned tongue, that I may know how to sustain the weary with a word” [Note: [Col. 0513] Isa. 50.].

Your reverence, most gracious Father, may recall how devoutly and how long I have served in the ministry of your Church, and what meager fruits I have brought back from my labor. For, according to the Apostle, the laboring farmer ought to receive from his fruits. “Who ever serves as a soldier at his own expense?” [Note: [Col. 0513] 1 Cor. 9.] Or who is not a transgressor of the law if he has decreed to retain with himself his hired worker’s denarius until night [Col. 0514C]?

Blessed are you, daughter of Zion, as Isaiah testifies, in your rewards, because lambs feed in you according to their order [Note: [Col. 0513] Isa. 5.]. And, as Gregory testifies, those who toil for ecclesiastical interests deserve to enjoy ecclesiastical remuneration. After various and enormous pressures of fortune, at last breathing again from the storm into harbor through the grace of Jesus Christ, I implore your mercy: out of regard for mercy and in honor of the Lord, turn more compassionate eyes upon me and extend to me, your servant, the hand of generosity in the assignment of the first prebend that falls vacant.

What I request is little for your highness but very great for my lowliness. Yet by it you gain for yourself both the mercy of God, the favor of the Roman Curia [Col. 0514D], and human goodwill. For, to use the Apostle’s words, “what is momentary in the present works in us a weight of glory for eternal life, while we look not at things seen but at things unseen” [Note: [Col. 0513] 2 Cor. 4.]. And, as Augustine testifies, God repays beyond telling what is mercifully bestowed.

I could indeed procure compulsory letters from the lord king of England and a more urgent mandate on the part of the lord pope; but toward my lord I proceed humbly and modestly, preferring to obtain this through mercy rather than extort it through force. For would an axe boast against him who cuts with it [Col. 0515A], or a saw exalt itself against him by whom it is drawn?

I offer and give myself wholly to you. Whatever I am, whatever I am worth, whatever I can do, is yours.

## LETTER 226. POPE ADRIAN TO HENRY II, KING OF ENGLAND

Adrian, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest son in Christ, Henry, illustrious king of the English: greeting and apostolic blessing.

“Praiseworthily and very fruitfully,” etc. See under Pope Adrian, after his *Regesta*, *Patrologia*, vol. CLXXXVIII.

## LETTER 227

**Subject.—A letter of consolation to his bishop.**

Compassionating your desolation with filial devotion, [Col. 0515B] I had endeavored, so far as I knew and could, to persuade you by salutary admonitions that, shaking off the little burdens of this world, you might run like a grasshopper in the way of the Lord’s commandments. And whereas many others, by the wealth of friends, breathe again from similar injuries and pressures and recover the peaceful tranquility of their minds, you, as though swallowed up by an abyss of despair through the tribulation of evils and sorrows, harden your spirit against every consolation. You regard the plundering of your goods—which others reckon the Lord’s sweet yoke and light burden [Note: [Col. 0515] Matt. 11.]—as the Lord’s cruel and inexorable wrath.
