Thus, what is an odor of death to others, and likewise what is a cause of joy to others, turns to punishment for you. So indeed, under the same sun flesh hardens and manna melts [Col. 0515C].

But may the Lord God of hosts, who opens and no one shuts [Note: [Col. 0515] Rev. 3]; who opens his hand and fills every living thing with blessing [Note: [Col. 0515] Ps. 144]; who is rich toward all who call upon him [Note: [Col. 0515] Rom. 10]; who gives to all abundantly and does not reproach [Note: [Col. 0515] Jas. 1]; he who makes the deaf hear and the mute speak [Note: [Col. 0515] Mark 7]—may he now inspire in me the grace of heavenly teaching and soften your heart, so that this little exhortation of mine may be capable of bringing consolation and comprehensible instruction.

What is this that has become common talk among men? That you bewail inconsolably your own losses and those of your parents, though you ought to endure both these and those steadfastly and with equanimity. The compassion you have for your parents ought to have been directed not toward an offering of money but toward correction of their conduct [Col. 0515D]. For they were wealthy before you conferred any income upon them. Yet the bishops of this age, rejecting prudent and honorable men, pour out with mad prodigality upon parents who ought to be rejected their hearts and whatever they possess together with their hearts. They do not fill empty vessels, but heap an overflowing, pressed-down, and shaken measure upon vessels already full and brimming to the utmost.

It is indeed pious to have compassion on one’s neighbor lest he be in need; but greater mercy is to have compassion on one’s neighbor lest he perish. It is good to grieve over evils which one’s neighbor suffers; but it is more pleasing to God to grieve over evils which one’s neighbor commits. [Col. 0516A] It is written: “A man’s enemies are those of his own household” [Note: [Col. 0515] Matt. 10]. Affection for one’s kin is harmful to many, for frequently, while one strives to be kind to one’s parents, one becomes cruel to oneself.

Christ mercifully laid down his life for his friends. The anxious love of parents cruelly sacrifices its own soul for its friends, now worried and wholly inflamed with promoting its parents. But when it has closed its final day, there is no consolation for its soul in the prosperity of the living. Indeed, I fear that the sins which they committed on the occasion of their riches may result for the dead in everlasting groaning and punishment. From the very resources by which he provided his parents with material for sin, he could have relieved the needs of many and made more salutary provision for his own soul hereafter.

But affection for parents is a most flattering seductress. “No one ever hated his own flesh” [Note: [Col. 0515] Eph. 3]. Yet these words require a careful understanding. For, when the same Apostle says elsewhere, “Whoever does not provide for his own, and especially for members of his household, has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever” [Note: [Col. 0515] 1 Tim. 5], he seems to disagree with himself.

But one must know that nature prescribes both the origin and the measure of the love by which people love themselves or their parents. Nature causes a hen to grow weak over her chicks, and a she-bear or lioness to murmur tenderly over her young. Even the *lamia* bares her breasts to feed her cubs. In these and in all living creatures nature produces certain sweet impulses of love. A human being naturally loves himself and loves his parents [Col. 0516C]. But just as it is impossible not to admit either of these affections, so it is a very great virtue not to follow it.

Therefore, since this natural affection is more prone and indulgent, and since it must be advantageous both to one’s own people and to the salvation of one’s soul, it must have the bridle of reason, by whose moderation it is guided. The Apostle therefore wills that, under the management of reason, the love of one’s household should seek either their need or the estimation of their deserts.

How natural affection sometimes oversteps the lawful limits of reason and makes us forgetful of God and of ourselves, we are constantly taught by the instruction of experience, when a certain soft and sweet affection for our flesh inclines us through its enticements toward pleasant and unlawful things. Writing to Timothy, the Apostle portrays these indiscriminate impulses of love, by which people love themselves or their own, as disordered, saying: “Know that in the last days perilous times will come, and people will be lovers of themselves, greedy, proud, without peace, slanderers, incontinent, swollen with pride, violent, lovers of pleasures more than of God” [Note: [Col. 0515] 2 Tim. 3].

Christ distinguishes the two movements of love according to reason and according to their effect in a brief saying: “He who loves,” he says, “his soul will lose it” [Note: [Col. 0515] John 12]. He denotes love that proceeds from irrational affection. Again: “He who hates his soul in this world keeps it unto eternal life” [Note: [Col. 0515] ibid.]. For hatred of the present life, which is here signified by “soul,” follows [Col. 0517A] reason and is therefore preserved eternally. Explaining this, Augustine says: “If you have loved badly—that is, from affection and not from reason—you have hated; if you have loved well—that is, for Christ and thus from reason—if you have hated your life, then you have loved.”

Certainly, “he who loves iniquity hates his own soul” [Note: [Col. 0517] Ps. 10]. The love by which we love pleasant and sweet things is irregular and unjust. But the love by which we love hard and harsh things for Christ’s sake leads the soul onward to salvation. Therefore, if from enriching our parents we see danger to our souls or scandal to our reputation threatening us, it is pious and holy to cut them off from the excessive affection of our love.

Thus the author of piety and Holy of Holies instructs us under a certain image of our members: “If your eye,” he says, [Col. 0517B] “or your foot causes you to stumble, tear it out and cut it off from you” [Note: [Col. 0517] Wis. 5; Matt. 18]. Neither father nor mother, whom we were bound by legal decree to honor more carefully, is excepted from this sentence of cutting-off or hatred. Therefore it is far better for me to withdraw from father, mother, and my life the love that comes from affection rather than reason—though this bears an appearance of hatred—than to love myself and them so irrationally that I am unworthy of Christ and deserve the fire of Gehenna.

What are we doing? Why do we cast words into the wind? We are washing brick and beating the air in vain. For we see those who had long wept for the loss of their possessions:

> For lost money is wept over with genuine tears.

We see, I say, that, buried in their griefs, they have as it were risen from the dead. And though their love for themselves and their parents had been extinguished in them, the old impulse of love, now rekindled, boils again amid ashes where it had lain asleep. Drawn by affection for their own interests and their parents, they creep again on hands and feet toward riches and honors. Now the spirit of this world—a spirit of dizziness and error—drives them more madly; they seek from men more ambitiously than before the glory of this world, and not the glory that comes from God. “But they were confounded, because God despised them” [Note: [Col. 0517] Ps. 52].

For daily events show that the fame and memory of those who seek the wind of worldly glory pass away sooner than the wind; their praise, which they believed would endure forever, is buried in shameful oblivion; and their sins [Col. 0517D], which they imagined had been revealed to no one, publicly return as a stain of infamy and common reproach. It now appears that they had oil, but oil tainted with dregs; learning, but learning that puffed up; understanding, but understanding deceptively perverted; memory, but memory of injuries; eloquence, but eloquence for evil. In short, all the things they attributed to themselves for magnificence and glory now turn for them into disgraceful reproach and, what is more serious, into Gehenna.

O *doxa*, *doxa*—O deceitful glory! O scorching wind, pestilential air, corrupting breeze, swelling of ears, bladder puffed up [Col. 0518A] as full of wind as of nothing: how you play with and mock great men, whom, by flatteringly calling them blessed, you lead into error!

The Apostle thought otherwise when he said: “Not commending ourselves, beloved” [Note: [Col. 0517] 2 Cor. 3]; and of himself: “By the grace of God I am what I am” [Note: [Col. 0517] 1 Cor. 15]. He reckons himself the least of the apostles and as one untimely born. But the inadequate and useless usurper of ecclesiastical honor magnifies and exalts himself. He has compliant flatterers who stroke his little ears with treacherous praise and persuade him to believe many great things of himself, of which the poor man’s conscience is wholly unaware. They praise the fool with their mouths and condemn him in their hearts; and sometimes, turning their faces backward, they represent in mockery of him the tongue of an Apulian dog, the beak of a stork, or the ears of an ass with moving hands.

If you remember the comic Terence, you can there clearly recognize the character and race of Thraso. Although a priest of the Lord ought to have testimony from those outside, his glory nevertheless ought to be this: the testimony of his conscience [Note: [Col. 0517] 2 Cor. 1]. True praise is that of which it is said: “My soul shall be praised in the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0517] Ps. 33]. And, as blessed Peter the Apostle says: “The inquiry of a good conscience toward God” [Note: [Col. 0517] 1 Pet. 3].

The field of this subject is very broad; but, to bring the discourse into brief compass, all that ought to have been spent on the worship of God and the need of souls is given over to worldly curiosity. To Peter and to all prelates it was said: “Feed [Col. 0518C] my sheep” [Note: [Col. 0517] John 21]. He did not command them to shut up and feed fish in a pond or beasts in an enclosure.

My itching tongue eagerly desired to pursue this topic, but lest I seem burdensome to those who hate one who rebukes at the gate, I shall restrain my lips with a finger. I saw, Father—and am grieved to have seen—when you were the heart and soul of a prince, foremost among courtiers, god and lord of Pharaoh. Yet that intimacy could not long endure, for courtly affection is perishable and does not belong to that charity which never fails [Note: [Col. 0517] 1 Cor. 13].

Did you think to fill with your gifts the abyss of greed in those who pursue gifts and rewards? But among them the hunger for gold and silver is more insatiable than hell. Therefore the gifts by which you wished to escape the forced exactions of the fisc you sent into a pierced sack [Col. 0518D] [Note: [Col. 0517] Hag. 1]. For you lost everything:

> Thus, that he may not lose, the gambler never ceases to lose,  
> And the enticing dice call back his greedy hands.

Christ, crushed and afflicted, begged in his poor, and there was no one moved by Joseph’s affliction. But, as Augustine reproaches certain persons: “The treasury takes what Christ did not receive; finally, the venom of a slanderous tongue—the malice of vipers—poured itself out against you before the king, and envy, more cruel than every serpent, secretly disturbed your peace.”

Certainly Ahithophel has left many heirs in nearly all the courts of great men. [Col. 0519A] There are still Jannes and Mambres there, who resist Moses and contradict the Holy Spirit [Note: [Col. 0519] 2 Tim. 3]. Since, therefore, you have learned by experience how great is the bitterness of the riches and honors of this age, and how deceitful and sophistical is the glory of this world, “taste and see how sweet the Lord is” [Note: [Col. 0519] Ps. 33]. From the very great proceeds of income which you have, store up in heaven through the hands of the poor whatever remains after daily needs.

For God is faithful because he is truth [Note: [Col. 0519] 2 Cor. 1], and no deceit has been found in his mouth or heart [Note: [Col. 0519] John 1]. No thief will be able to steal anything from you, no robber carry it off, nor the violence of powerful persons extort it. Then at last, with the Apostle and with the full security of conscience, you will be able to say and sing: “I know whom I have believed, and I am certain that the just judge is able to keep my deposit [Col. 0519B] until that day” [Note: [Col. 0519] 2 Tim. 1].

## LETTER 228

**Subject.—A supplication for the Church of Rouen.**

Affliction inflicted upon a flock turns to the shame of a negligent shepherd, and injury to subjects rebounds as reproach upon their ruler. It belongs to the exercise of royal office to cherish Christ’s poor and to provide them with the safeguard of unremitting protection.

Most just king, singular remedy for our oppression, saving help of our little vessel: our Church, afflicted by many insults, cries to you. It will suffer shipwreck through prolonged adversity unless your mercy extends the healing support required by our distress. For presumptuous malice intensifies our innocence from day [Col. 0519C] to day and, having torn away our possessions, compels our community to beg.

We therefore flee to the aid of your protection, that you may cause satisfaction to be made to us for the injury inflicted and fitting restoration for the plunder. For it is right that you should strive to protect the alms bestowed upon us through your benefit from the wolves [lacuna] surrounding us.

## LETTER 229. TO THE DEAN AND CHAPTER OF CHARTRES

To the venerable men, Lord G., dean, and the chapter of Chartres: Peter of Blois, their own, archdeacon of London, greeting in him without whom there is no salvation.

I had intended especially to come to your Church before the day of the Lord’s Ascension, [Col. 0519D] but certain persons reporting the timely arrival of the lord of Canterbury called me back from that desired purpose. I therefore write to you so that, through the service of writing and the devotion of the writer, the loss of bodily absence may in some manner be made good between us.

The love of God, by which we cleave to him, is a certain ineffable bond of union. For the Apostle testifies: “He who cleaves to God is one spirit with him” [Note: [Col. 0519] 1 Cor. 6], preserving unity of spirit with God and neighbor in the bond of peace [Note: [Col. 0519] Eph. 4]. The Apostle rebukes people who love themselves. For if there is charity, it disdains to be solitary. [Col. 0520A] Therefore it reaches beyond itself; unwilling to possess anything as private, it brings even its own good into common possession. More wonderfully still, by a certain ineffable artifice of charity, a person often loves in another what he does not possess in himself; and by the service of compassion he makes his own not only another’s goods, but also another’s needs and distresses.

Certainly, just as he rejoices with one who rejoices, so he weeps with one who weeps; and, bearing another’s scandals or burdens upon a shared shoulder, although he does not love separateness, nevertheless, so that the affliction of his neighbor may be relieved, he chooses to suffer alone.

Two things the Apostle Peter notes in charity: that it is mutual and continuous. “Before all things,” he says, “having among yourselves mutual, unceasing charity” [Note: [Col. 0519] I Pet. 4.]. [Col. 0520B] It is mutual when it passes from me to you and from you to me; it loves not in word and tongue, but in deed and truth. It is continuous when it is broken by no suspicions and obscured by no pretences. We read likewise in the book of experience that the law of mutual love is written in my members. If one hand is injured, the other hand compassionately and gently serves the suffering one. The head or eye does not disdain to bend humbly toward a foot or shin in pain; and a certain kindness of nature has bound the joints of veins and sinews together in such a union of love that this whole inward operation may grow also in us, by the example of imitation, into the fruit of social friendship.

The Father of mercies and God of all consolation is the father of the wretched. [Col. 0520C] Therefore, although I may seem to need consolations, yet my soul refuses to be comforted. For, to use Job’s words [Note: [Col. 0519] Ch. 13.]: “Though God should kill me, I shall hope in him.” I bear with equanimity the seizure of my goods, nor do I lament the loss of earthly household possessions. For what have I besides you, O God? And what have I desired from you upon earth? As the Apostle testifies: the riches of this world are hindrances to salvation, making men wretched; nor are they merely hindrances, but as it were golden fetters and chains—except that gold is more burdensome than iron and harder to bear. “The Lord gave; the Lord has taken away” [Note: [Col. 0519] Job 1.]. If I look to what was given, I am less than all his mercies; if I consider what was taken away, I have been shaken off like a locust [Note: [Col. 0519] Ps. 108], and, having cast off a heavy burden, have become readier to run in the way of the Lord. [Col. 0520D]

Let that man confess himself wretched whose inward conscience teems with worms, who makes a covenant with death and a pact with hell. There indeed is misery; there is no consolation; there the rich man asks for a drop of water from the finger of a leper and does not deserve to receive it. Woe to those who are frightened neither by another’s example nor by the expectation of their own condemnation; who must be admonished by the terrible horror of Gehenna’s punishment, and in whom is fulfilled what is written: “Being terrified, they shall be purified” [Note: [Col. 0519] Job 41.].

Indeed, the Lord cast out our parents—or rather, our destroyers—from the place of delight [Col. 0521A] into the valley of weeping, where afterward no one was born except amid wailing and lamentation, save Zoroaster alone, who is read to have laughed at his birth—an portentous and detestable omen. For he is said to have been the first to discover and teach the art of magic. Yet the Lord did not take paradise from us so that we might make for ourselves a temporal paradise in this world. It is a matter of great peril that the human spirit, going and not returning, should be so led by the resounding wind of glory and by ambition that it never casts away its inner self; that, running and feverishly striving to plunder this world’s little loads, it forgets itself and God’s judgments, and falls asleep not in Christ, who is life, but in death. Woe to the wretch whose faith is dead, whose work is death, whose inheritance is the worm, whose dwelling is Gehenna!

O [Col. 0521B] how dreadful it is to fall into the hands of the living God [Note: [Col. 0521] Heb. 10.], before whose tribunal we must all stand, so that each may receive according to what he has done in the body, whether good or evil [Note: [Col. 0521] II Cor. 5.]. There all things will be naked and open; there no evasion will avail; there no exception will find a place. Rather, as the Lord distinguishes between Lazarus and the rich feaster, he who suffers evil here with Lazarus will receive good [Note: [Col. 0521] Luke 16]; but he who spends his days here in prosperity shall in a moment descend into that endless evil, where it shall be said of the pleasure-loving man: “As much as he glorified himself in delights, so much give him torment and mourning” [Note: [Col. 0521] Rev. 18.]. The moth shall be spread beneath him, and the worm shall be his covering.

But good is the transaction by which transitory things [Col. 0521C] are taken away and eternal things bestowed: thus one emancipated from the slavery of sin is sent into the full possession of the eternal inheritance. Truly wretched are those who shrink from the title of holy poverty and, in order to heap up wealth that damns them, stake their souls as though on the throw of dice. O how great is the multitude of your sweetness, O God [Note: [Col. 0521] Ps. 30], while you dispense adversity and prosperity to your servants in wholesome measure: now as a wise physician using cautery, now poultices! In Solomon’s testimony, God “will give medicine to men, and fools despise it” [Note: [Col. 0521] Ecclus. 38]. The Lord’s scourge is medicine: it restrains human insolence and heals vice; through it a person’s virtue becomes known and grows strong unto the fruit of glory. Usefully, therefore, is he corrected by adversity [Col. 0521D] who is corrupted by prosperity.

It is the Prophet’s word: “I will bear the rebukes of the Lord, because I have sinned” [Note: [Col. 0521] Mic. 7.]. This mirror is like a broad sea, where, as in a flooding deluge, the swellings of the sea rise up, fierce whirlwinds rage, torrents of anger flow around, and abysses of desire and avarice boil over; the swellings of pride, the assaults of lust, and the voracity of gluttony clash with one another. For those struggling patiently in the shipwreck of this storm, poverty is a harbor and the gate of life. For if we wish to wrestle or swim vigorously, or to become unencumbered travelers, let us throw off our garments [Col. 0522A], even if they are not burdensome.

The adulteress held holy Joseph by a fold of his cloak; but, leaving the cloak in the adulteress’s hands, he escaped free [Note: [Col. 0521] Gen. 39.]. Adulterous desire has held you for a long time. Blessed are those who leave the cloak and display Christ’s nakedness in place of great or small household possessions. One never comes from the riches and delights of this world to the delights of heaven; nor does any saint seek to flourish in the world and reign eternally with Christ. Let those who have riches have them, I pray, as Abraham did: from just causes, for lawful uses, for the grace of hospitality—not for hoarding, but for distributing to the poor. For the sustenance of the poor is the wealth and redemption of the rich.

Finally, poverty is assessed rather from humility of mind than from [Col. 0522B] a small estate. And it should be observed that the rich man is anxious for himself, whereas God is anxious for the poor, according to the words: “But I am needy and poor; the Lord is mindful of me” [Note: [Col. 0521] Ps. 39]; “God the Father will spare the needy and poor and save the souls of the poor” [Note: [Col. 0521] Ps. 71]. Yet he says to the rich: “Woe to you rich, who have your consolation here” [Note: [Col. 0521] Luke 6]!

Indeed, the title of poverty, although contemptible among men, is nevertheless lovable and honorable with God. The kingdom of heaven belongs to the poor, not merely for their own possession, but also to share with others, so that they may receive them into eternal dwellings. Already tasting beforehand the first fruits of heavenly life, they are given drink not from a torrent but from a little stream of inward delight. They know that [Col. 0522C] whatever flows in within this world flows away; therefore they disdain its abundance. Of and concerning such persons the Apostle says: “As sorrowful, yet always rejoicing; as having nothing, and possessing all things; as needy, yet enriching many; as dying, and behold, we live” [Note: [Col. 0521] II Cor. 6.].

Certain others, abounding in riches and vices, imitate Naaman, rich but leprous. Are not those rich people deservedly reckoned leprous who are sprinkled, as with a variety of leprosy, by the diversity and multitude of their crimes? At the prompting of their passions, they think it better to support the poor from the overflow of this world than to follow Christ in poverty. Naaman preferred the rivers of Damascus, Abana and Pharpar, to the Jordan [Note: [Col. 0521] IV Kings 5], which is interpreted “humility” or “descent,” and which works the healing of spiritual [Col. 0522D] leprosy more sweetly and effectively.

Moreover, the humility of beneficence is not to be shown to the poor alone. For although it is written, “He has scattered abroad; he has given to the poor” [Note: [Col. 0521] Ps. 111], nevertheless experience and practice teach us that some rich persons need the supports of nature, according to the saying, “The rich have lacked and hungered” [Note: [Col. 0521] Ps. 33], and again: “Those who possess much need much.” Thus the net of charity encloses both just and unjust. For although we read, “Let almsgiving sweat in your hand until you find a righteous man to whom you may give,” and likewise, “Give to the merciful man and do not regard the sinner” [Note: [Col. 0521] Ecclus. 12], nevertheless we must show an affection of mercy even to [Col. 0523A] the unjust and sinners if they are in need. Hence Augustine:

> “There are those who think that alms should be bestowed only upon the righteous, and nothing upon sinners. But in evildoers we ought to pursue their iniquity, while in those same persons assisting their common human condition.”

Likewise John Chrysostom:

> “Let us cease from this absurd, devilish, and destructive inquisitiveness. If anyone says that he is chosen into the clergy, yet asks for food, do not examine him in these matters. If Abraham had scrutinized those who came to him, he would perhaps never have received angels into his lodging. But because he received everyone, he received angels also, as blessed Ambrose testifies.”

The order of charity is that the affection of kindly compassion should first be bestowed upon parents, associates, and brothers, if they are good, whether they have fallen from their own wealth or are carnal or spiritual [Col. 0523B]. In this matter the will, not necessity, distinguishes and directs benefits; it is counsel, not command, for no one is liberal in cases of necessity. Hence the Apostle writes to the Corinthians in these words: “I do not say this as commanding, but through the earnestness of others, also proving the genuineness of your charity. For you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ: that for your sakes he became poor, though he was rich, so that by his poverty you might become rich; and in this I give counsel, for this is useful to you” [Note: [Col. 0523] II Cor. 8.]. Behold, he does not command but approves; he gives counsel, not a precept; he calls it useful, not necessary. This usefulness, moreover, is measured by the will.

Hence the same Apostle [Col. 0523C] says to the Corinthians: “If the will is ready, it is acceptable to the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0523] Ibid.]. For he seeks not the seed but the fruit, not gain but godliness. But, to use the Prophet’s words: “I am a man seeing my poverty” [Note: [Col. 0523] Lam. 3.]; I shall await the Lord’s mercy in silence, because silence is the guardian of righteousness, and in silence and hope shall be my consolation.

Why then are you sad, O my soul, and why do you trouble me [Note: [Col. 0523] Ps. 41]? Why are my thoughts scattered, tormenting my heart? Is there no balm in Gilead, or is there no physician there [Note: [Col. 0523] Jer. 3]? Has the Lord’s hand been shortened, so that he cannot save you and place you in safety and in the beauty of peace? And you, O Lord, are the form of beauty and the seal of holiness. Seal my heart with your love, O God of my heart, and God my portion [Col. 0523D] for ever.

And you also, O good Jesus, O gracious one, O beloved, O sweet one, O sweet love! O God, O charity! Deign to answer, according to his merit, for me to the dean of Chartres, who, though I neither wished nor asked it, freely offered me half of his income; and by the example of his liberality induced certain others present to show mercy. I am no less bound by his promise than by the gift; and although I have a fixed and certain purpose of receiving nothing in this persecution either from him or from another, nevertheless I confess that, if I am anything, if I have anything, or can have anything in the future, it is his.

The Virgin of virgins prescribes to all who [Col. 0524A] devoutly serve and humbly venerate her the pattern of loving God and neighbor in the ordering of her charity. For the King who brought her into the wine-cellar [Note: [Col. 0523] Song 2], intoxicating her with the cup of love, set his charity in order within her. O fairest of women, who, wounded by charity, once said: “Daughters of Jerusalem, tell my beloved that I languish with love” [Note: [Col. 0523] Song 2]. Do you still languish? Is charity a languor? Surely it ought rather to be considered a medicine. For charity covers a multitude of sins, as is plainly clear in the case of the one of whom Truth says: “Many sins are forgiven her, because she loved much” [Note: [Col. 0523] Luke 7]. For sin is a sickness of the soul, and charity is its medicine.

Yet charity is sometimes a languor, when the soul [Col. 0524B] burns and sighs with anxious affection, when what it desires is further delayed. Thus love is one thing in the desire for enjoyment and another in the enjoyment of what is desired. The former desires and does not yet enjoy; the latter enjoys the desired object, and yet the desire is not diminished. As it is written: “Those who eat me shall still hunger, and those who drink me shall still thirst” [Note: [Col. 0523] Ecclus. 24]. The traveler has a desire to enjoy; the possessor has the enjoyment of desire. The one belongs to the way, the other to the homeland; the one expresses the labor of Leah and Martha, the other the enjoyment and repose of Rachel and Mary.

But what need have you, O beloved, of the daughters of Jerusalem—that is, the angelic powers—to report anything to him concerning your languor, when he calls you his only dove, his sister, and his bride [Note: [Col. 0523] Song 3]? Is he not the one [Col. 0524C] whose left hand is under your head and whose right hand embraces you [Note: [Col. 0523] Song 2]? Who can speak to him more intimately concerning you than you yourself, who are his mother and who, by a special prerogative, can say: “I am my beloved’s and my beloved is mine” [Note: [Col. 0523] Song 8], and who by privileged favor ask and obtain that he kiss you with the kiss of his mouth [Note: [Col. 0523] Song 1]?

What does it mean, O blessed one, that in complaint or rejoicing you say that the watchmen of the city took away your cloak? What is this cloak but your body, which clothed three natures in Christ—namely, divinity, flesh, and soul? This is that aromatic substance from which the Holy Spirit prepared that incense (*thymiama*) from three kinds—that is, the three aforesaid natures. Christ, standing as high priest, offered it to God the Father as an evening sacrifice [Note: [Col. 0523] Ps. 140]. The watchmen of the city—that is, [Col. 0524D] the angels—carried this cloak, that is, your body, perfumed with every balm of virtues, into heaven.

Yet, however they carried away your cloak, we know that they did not carry away your shift: you left it to us as an earnest and pledge of that charity which you had in your Passion. Christ came to us and you to Christ, compassionating the suffering one and dying with the dying one. Some believe that, according to the Savior’s charity, ordered charity was in him. The hands and feet of your son were pierced with iron nails; your soul too was pierced—and more bitterly—when the side of him, already dead, was perforated by the lance [Col. 0525A] [Note: [Col. 0525] John 19]. He felt nothing, but the sword passed through your own soul [Note: [Col. 0525] Luke 1].

O truly your soul was his—not merely in the sense in which your son says, “All souls are mine,” and in Job [Note: [Col. 0525] Ch. 34], “I made every breath,” that is, every soul; but your very own soul, concerning which holy Simeon says: “Because in every sanctification and glory he preferred her to all creatures.” Let us return, therefore, to the Virgin’s shift, beneath whose protection we take refuge in every need—O garment made divine!

## LETTER CCXXX. To his lord, wholly devoted.

By living speech, and now also by the entreaty of a letter, I exhort you: since you have received pontifical honor, be willing diligently to weigh the burdens of that honor. The souls [Col. 0525B] for whom the Son of God offered himself to death have been entrusted to your care; weigh, I beseech you, your danger. For Gregory testifies: “The government of souls is the art of arts.” Nor should you attend any less to the fruit of your office. For the prince of the apostles and witness of Christ’s sufferings writes thus to his fellow bishops:

> “When the Prince of Shepherds appears, you shall receive the unfading crown of eternal glory.”

It is a most grave peril to the soul when a man presides but does not benefit, when he ascends the teacher’s chair and does not teach those subject to him. When you stand before the tribunal of the supreme Judge to render an account of your stewardship, it will be sweeter and more glorious for you to have converted several [Col. 0525C] souls from their iniquities to salvation by the word of edification than to have possessed all the riches and triumphs of Alexander the Great and Julius Caesar.

Jerome’s teaching, exhorting you to diligence in reading, says: “The life of a man without sacred reading is the burial of a living man.” Paul says to Timothy, his disciple: “I testify to you before God and Christ Jesus, by his coming and kingdom: preach the word; be urgent in season and out of season; do the work of an evangelist; fulfil your ministry” [Note: [Col. 0525] II Tim. 4.]. The same Apostle also writes concerning himself: “Woe to me if I do not preach the Gospel! But if I do it diligently, I shall receive the reward of salvation” [Note: [Col. 0525] I Cor. 9.].

It is blessed Gregory’s saying: “A shepherd ignorant of preaching is a mute herald.” “The Lord most strictly requires that the bread of life—that is, the word [Col. 0525D] of God—be distributed to the simple with unwearied diligence. Accordingly, the lamenting prophet complains, saying: ‘The little children asked for bread, and there was no one to break it for them’” [Note: [Col. 0525] Lam. 4]. Certainly no ignorance can excuse a prelate in this matter, especially if he has trained senses. Those who are of duller intellect, slippery memory, and more impeded speech have plunged themselves into graver condemnation, because, though insufficient, they presumed to lay upon their shoulders an unbearable burden, to the destruction of themselves and their people [Note: [Col. 0525] Matt. 23].

But no pretext of excuse can free you [Col. 0526A] from this danger. For God has bestowed upon you a clear and subtle intellect, a capacious and retentive memory, a ready tongue, and a searching understanding of heavenly matters. Therefore act so that you may say with the Apostle: “By the grace of God I am what I am, and his grace in me shall not be empty” [Note: [Col. 0525] I Cor. 15]. For heavenly grace will be emptied in you unless you return to the Lord the talent of divine grace with the increments earned among bankers.

Indeed, the Lord complains mournfully through the prophet: “I have not lent at interest,” he says, “nor has anyone lent to me at interest, and all curse me” [Note: [Col. 0525] Jer. 15]. The Lord regards a prelate’s silence as a curse: he ought to have put the Lord’s money out as a loan and exercised spiritual usury. For he has buried the Lord’s talent in the earth or hidden it in a napkin [Note: [Col. 0525] Luke 19], [Col. 0526B] and shuts under a measure the light which ought to shine for all [Note: [Col. 0525] Mark 4].

God is generous; God now tests you in a few things, so that, once proved, he may set you over many. Concerning those who possess wisdom and eloquence yet do not employ them for the edification of their neighbor, but permit them to be prostituted for base uses of the world, the Lord complained grievously through the prophet, saying [Note: [Col. 0525] Hos. 2]: “I gave them my gold and my silver; but they made Baal from my gold and silver.” By gold and silver he signifies wisdom and eloquence; by Baal he denotes the filth of this world.

Long ago the Philistines craftily arranged that no smith should be found in all Israel to make weapons or sharpen them [Note: [Col. 0525] I Kings 13]. [Col. 0526C] This parable is quite suitable to the prelates of the present time, because among all your colleagues scarcely anyone today is found who is not a mute herald—or, if it may be said, a mute dog unable to bark [Note: [Col. 0525] Isa. 56]. Therefore, because the days are evil, redeem the time [Note: [Col. 0525] Eph. 5]; or, for love of God and for the salvation of yourselves and of the people entrusted to you, be willing on any day to devote at least one little hour to reading Holy Scripture. Commit your undertakings to the Holy Spirit, and there shall be given you the manifestation of the Spirit for usefulness. What will advance others through you will never fail you, as Solomon [Note: [Col. 0525] Wisdom 7] affirms that he did: “Learn without pretence and communicate without envy.” For God’s gift overflows more abundantly through giving, and all knowledge grows through expenditure.

Day by day your memory [Col. 0526D] will become more capacious and your speech more learned; for the Holy Spirit gladly rests upon a lover of wisdom and graciously breathes himself into that person’s desires [Note: [Col. 0525] Ecclus. 1]. For the Wisdom of God says of itself in the book bearing its name: “Son, desire wisdom, and the Lord will give it to you.” A most fitting opportunity for this is offered you. You can have various writings which antiquity excerpted from great volumes, gathering flowers as it were from very broad meadows to make honey, so that it might have each thing ready to hand when wanted; it has compacted them, by careful study and [Col. 0527A] useful labor, into some sermon or other short treatise.

Moreover, you know how to write, which can especially assist you: placing now this authority, now that one, afterward or before; and according as one must speak in the vernacular or in Latin, arranging each word more carefully and discreetly in its proper place. Know this for certain: although beginnings may seem difficult to you, brief practice will smooth everything, and you shall read in the book of experience how abundant a harvest comes from the labor of your study when, through the gaining of souls, you offer sheaves of righteousness.

Far from you, I pray, be that reproach of the slothful shepherd: “He would not understand so as to do good” [Note: [Col. 0527] Ps. 35]. He who is ignorant shall be ignored; and he who would not shine for others shall be driven into outer darkness. But I, perhaps better absent than present, shall gladly devote wholly to your honor and [Col. 0527B] usefulness whatever I am, know, can do, possess, or am able to accomplish.

## LETTER CCXXXI

To the cardinal bishops of the Apostolic See, P., a sinful monk: greeting in the Lord.

As words are indications of thoughts for those present, so letters are instruments of words among those absent. The skill of warfare is learned in war in order to be taught afterward in peace; so too, when it is taught in leisure, it is exercised more cautiously in war. In the conflict concerning the Apostolic See, in which you still toil unanimously, I too fought as a combatant. But since I have been released from the military belt and settled in the peace of a municipality, [Col. 0527C] I now wish to teach what I have learned.

Therefore, amid all the battle-lines of vices roaring around you, amid the thickest storms of falling missiles like hail, you must keep especially alert against avarice and oppose the shield of faith to its arrows. It hastens headlong to inflict a deadly wound upon the wretched, especially when it extinguishes the sight of the forehead rather than that of the heart. Hence the wise man says: “Dedications and gifts blind the eyes of judges, and, like a mute thing in the mouth, turn away their rebukes” [Note: [Col. 0527] Ecclus. 20]. For it arms those who approach with gifts, and through them besieges and blinds hearts which hold the chief place for making suggestions at the ears.

Concerning these the Lord complains through Isaiah [Note: [Col. 0527] Ch. 1], saying: “Your princes are faithless, companions of thieves; all love gifts, [Col. 0527D] and follow rewards.” Someone may say: “For my part, I seek nothing; but if something is freely offered, I do not refuse to receive it.” Observe: here not those who seek gifts are condemned, but those who merely love them [Note: [Col. 0527] Isa. 1]. They are not undeservedly called companions of thieves, because while they receive stolen gifts, they fear being caught by fellow servants and associates as though guilty of theft. And note that it says: “They follow rewards.” For though they grant to their benefactors the assistance they request, they nevertheless do not escape the stains of guilt. For while they receive requital for their service, [Col. 0528A] they lose the fruit of eternal reward.

Of these he says a little later: “Alas, I shall take consolation over my enemies and take vengeance on my foes” [Note: [Col. 0527] Ibid.]. The sons of Samuel are known to have had no crime other than that they loved gifts. Because they did not follow the example of their father’s purity, they irretrievably lost leadership over the Israelite people. And note that when Scripture says of them, “They turned aside after avarice and accepted gifts,” it immediately adds: “They perverted judgment” [Note: [Col. 0527] I Kings 8]. It is indeed near and closely connected: after a gift has been accepted, judgment is perverted even by a corrupted judge.

O how clean was Samuel’s face from gifts when he said: “I have conducted myself before you from my youth until this day. Behold, I stand ready: [Col. 0528B] speak concerning me before the Lord and before his Christ, whether I have taken anyone’s ox or ass; whether I have slandered anyone; whether I have oppressed anyone; whether I have accepted a gift from anyone’s hand. I shall despise it today and restore it to you” [Note: [Col. 0527] I Kings 12]. Hence the Law commands: “Do not accept gifts, which blind even the prudent and overturn the words of the just” [Note: [Col. 0527] Exod. 23]. And Deuteronomy [Note: [Col. 0527] Ch. 16] says similarly: “You shall not accept a person or gifts, because gifts blind the eyes of the wise and alter the words of the just.”

How opposed Abraham was to receiving gifts when he withstood Melchizedek, king of the Sodomites, saying: “I lift up my hand to my Lord Most High, possessor of heaven and earth, that from a thread of the weft [Col. 0528C] to a sandal-strap I shall receive nothing from all that is yours” [Note: [Col. 0527] Gen. 14]. How unstained by received gifts was Moses, who called the Lord, knowing all things, as witness: “You know,” he said, “that I have never accepted even an ass from them, nor afflicted any one of them” [Note: [Col. 0527] Num. 16].

For where gifts are coveted, it follows that, as the judge justifies one person upon receiving payment, so he afflicts another who gave nothing. Hence it is said through Isaiah: “Woe to you who justify the wicked for gifts and take away from the just person his justice” [Note: [Col. 0527] Isa. 5]. He immediately threatens them with the vengeance due to them, adding: “Therefore, as the tongue of fire devours stubble and the heat of flame burns it up, so their root shall be as ashes, and their shoot shall rise as dust” [Note: [Col. 0527] Ibid.]. The same prophet elsewhere complains concerning them, saying: [Col. 0528D] “All have turned aside into their own way, every one to his own avarice, from the greatest to the least” [Note: [Col. 0527] Isa. 56].

Avarice plainly provokes Almighty God’s anger against itself and continually vexes the heart it possesses with various thoughts. Hence the prophet complains of the avaricious man: “Because of the iniquity of his avarice, I was angry and struck him; I hid myself and was indignant, and he went wandering in the way of his heart” [Note: [Col. 0527] Isa. 57]. Certainly no wound’s corruption stinks more intolerably in God’s nostrils than the dung of avarice. And every greedy man, while he amasses profit from filthy money, [Col. 0529A] turns his chair into a latrine, as though he were heaping up a mass of dung.

Hence it is said through Ezekiel: “Their silver shall be cast out, and their gold shall be in the dung-heap. Their silver and gold shall not be able to deliver them in the day of the Lord’s wrath” [Note: [Col. 0529] Ezek. 7]. Elsewhere it is written: “Woe to him who multiplies what is not his—how long?—and loads upon himself thick mud” [Note: [Col. 0529] Hab. 2]. For the avaricious man to load thick mud upon himself is to pile up earthly profit together with the weight of sin. Habakkuk the prophet also says: “Woe to him who gathers evil greed for his house, so that his nest may be on high, and thinks himself safe in the day of evil” [Note: [Col. 0529] Ibid.].

But as wood does not satisfy fire, so amassed money does not soothe the heat of avarice. Rather, as a flame is raised by fuel, so avarice likewise increases as profits are accumulated. [Col. 0529B] “The avaricious man,” he says, “shall not be filled with money, and he who loves riches shall not receive fruit from them” [Note: [Col. 0529] Eccl. 5]. He would indeed receive fruit from them if he were willing to scatter them generously rather than love them; but because he loves them by retaining them, he leaves them here without fruit. The passage continues: “Where there are many riches, there are many who consume them; and what benefit is there to their owner, except that he sees his riches with his eyes?” [Note: [Col. 0529] Ibid.]. Of these same riches Solomon says: “Riches kept for the harm of their owner perish, and in most grievous affliction he shall beget a son who will be in utter poverty” [Note: [Col. 0529] Ibid.]. And to show how unfaithful riches are to their possessor, he immediately adds: “As he came naked from his mother’s womb, so shall he return, and he shall take nothing with him from his labor” [Note: [Col. 0529] Ibid.].

## LETTER CCXXXII

[Col. 0529C]

### SUBJECT.—An exhortation to those who neither take up nor preach the cross.

Speak, faint-hearted men; speak, fearful and weak men: why do you fear momentary death, which opens the way of life and has become the gatekeeper into the kingdom of the children of God? Why do you fear, you of little faith [Note: [Col. 0529] Matt. 8]? You ought rather to fear eternal death, with which, as I see, you have made a covenant and pact; so that what is spoken through the prophet rightly applies to you: “We have struck a covenant with death and made a pact with hell” [Note: [Col. 0529] Isa. 28]. Without doubt you are going to die, and you cannot escape temporal death; moreover, it is written: “Remember that death does not delay” [Note: [Col. 0529] Ecclus. 14]. For every creature is subject to vanity [Col. 0529D]; and we are all debtors to nature: we are all bound to pay it the tribute of death.

Who, moreover, is secure about the present day? Who knows whether a shameful, disgraceful, sudden death may seize him unprepared, with no one to rescue him? When a person’s life is sweetest and most pleasant, then bitter death separates him from it: “When they say, ‘Peace and security,’” he says, “then sudden destruction and anguish will come upon them, like that of women with child, and they shall not escape” [Note: [Col. 0529] I Thess. 5.]. For, as Job testifies [Note: [Col. 0529] Chap. 21.], “They spend their days in prosperity and in a moment descend to hell”; a limit is appointed to all flesh, and, willing or unwilling, all are drawn toward it. “My days,” says Job [Note: [Col. 0529] Chap. 16.], “pass away, and by the path upon which I go I shall not return.” “The human eye shall not return to see good things” [Note: [Col. 0529] Job 7.]. “The spirit shall pass through him and shall not remain, nor shall he know his place any longer” [Note: [Col. 0529] Ps. 102]. Death “with impartial foot knocks at the hovels of the poor” [Note: [Col. 0529] Horace, *Odes* 3.] and at the thrones of kings; for, as Ecclesiasticus says, “A king is today, and tomorrow he shall die. But when a man dies, he shall inherit serpents, beasts, and worms” [Note: [Col. 0529] Ecclus. 12].

Holy and salutary, therefore, is the thought of always keeping one’s last things before the eyes of the heart: to use death almost as a certain benefit, and to turn its unavoidable necessities into virtue. The counsel is to hide one’s life in him who is able [Col. 0530B] to preserve the entrusted deposit until that day. For he himself is a faithful and wise guardian, a mighty defender, an abundant rewarder. Securely cast upon him your thought and your anxiety: his wisdom cannot be deceived, his power overcome, nor his goodwill wearied. Those who have girded themselves for this pilgrimage in Christ’s name are already written in the book of life. For, according to Malachi’s testimony [Note: [Col. 0529] Chap. 3.], “The Lord heard and gave heed, and a book of remembrance was written before the Lord for those who fear God and think upon his name.”

But I judge those to be written down—and proscribed—in the book of death who grow slack in every part of their holy purpose, and, though they possess heavenly manna, choose, in contempt of it, to remain and sit beside the flesh-pots, turning the Lord’s business into idleness and the measure of a gomor into [Col. 0530C] a moderation of pleasures [Note: [Col. 0529] Exod. 16.]. Certainly they ought to have gone there, not lukewarmly but fervently and with all the heart’s exultation, where Mount Zion is founded from living stones, “the joy of the whole earth” [Note: [Col. 0529] Ps. 47]. These men, then, who so reject the Lord’s yoke and sow the scandal of the cross, perhaps suppose that they will escape by removing the Lord’s scourge. Isaiah speaks in their person: “When the overflowing scourge shall pass through, it shall not come upon us; we are protected by falsehood” [Note: [Col. 0529] Isa. 28.].

Do they believe that the cities in which they dwell are immune from divine indignation, when they see the Lord raging so terribly against the holy city and the land consecrated by his presence? How will he spare foreign cities when he did not spare his own? [Col. 0530D] The Lord began at his sanctuary; and, unless his wrath is turned away, he will offer the cup of his anger to those who are far off, and will envelop in the same—or a still heavier—whirlwind of storm those who make sloth their refuge. Concerning the cup of his indignation, Jeremiah reads thus [Note: [Col. 0529] Chap. 25.]:

> Thus says the Lord: “You shall surely drink; for behold, in the city in which my name is invoked I begin to afflict them; and shall you be innocent and exempt? Know that you shall not be exempt.”

When in former times the Lord was offended by the ancient fathers, those who sought to escape swords frequently perished through hunger or plague. Hence Jeremiah says: “Those slain by the sword were better off than those killed by hunger” [Note: [Col. 0531] Lam. 4.]. Now those who have confessed faith in Christ should fear not merely, I pray, sword or plague, but hell. Let unbelievers consider the dreadful day of judgment, the terrible tribunal, the angry judge, the burning river, the worms that do not die, the unquenchable flames [Note: [Col. 0531] Isa. 66.], the death-dealing stench, the gnashing of teeth, the shadow of death, and pain to which no similar or equal pain can be imagined. All these things are stored up for themselves by those who stir up the scandal of the cross, building the high places of Tophet [Note: [Col. 0531] Jer. 7.], and paying no heed that Christ, in accomplishing the cleansing of sins, established for us the ministry of the cross as repentance unto salvation.

Why, I ask, do these unhappy men so shrink from, so fear [Col. 0531B] taking up Christ’s cross? If they were not robbers, they would not fear the cross. Do you wish to see robbers? Christ, speaking of the Church, says: “You have made it a den of robbers” [Note: [Col. 0531] Mark 11.]; but today it has become a hedgehog’s pit and a hyena’s den. Yet you answer and say: “What could I, an unarmed cleric, do among soldiers—unwarlike among armed and warlike men?” You are a soldier of Christ; nor should you count yourself unarmed when you hear the Apostle writing to the Corinthians and saying: “The weapons of our warfare are not carnal, but mighty through God for the destruction of strongholds, destroying every height that exalts itself against the knowledge of God, bringing every thought into captivity to the obedience of Christ” [Note: [Col. 0531] II Cor. 10.].

Certainly you will be idle among [Col. 0531C] soldiers unless you have leisure and the word of God bound upon your mouth. Hear what the Apostle writes to Timothy: “From childhood you have known the sacred Scriptures, which are able to instruct you unto salvation” [Note: [Col. 0531] II Tim. 3.]. “For all Scripture inspired by God is useful for teaching, for reproof, for training in righteousness.” The book of experience teaches that bronze trumpets and cymbals are necessary in war. For they stir not only human hearts but also the hearts of horses to battle and conflict. Jericho was overthrown by the blast of trumpets [Note: [Col. 0531] Judg. 7.]; how much, I ask, can a living voice accomplish where sounding bronze and ringing cymbal can do so much [Note: [Col. 0531] I Cor. 13.]? It is Jerome’s saying: “I do not know what hidden power a living voice possesses.” If the sound of a trumpet raises slack hands and feeble knees to a posture of courage and strength, what [Col. 0531D] will the living and effective word of the Lord do, sharper than every two-edged sword, reaching even to the division of soul and spirit [Note: [Col. 0531] Heb. 4.]?

Nothing serves Christ’s soldiers more strongly for the exercise of virtue and consolation amid their labours than that the trumpet of salutary exhortation should continually sound. This trumpet, “in the dreadful day, in an instant, at the last trumpet,” will free its hearers from evil report [Note: [Col. 0531] Ps. 111.] and from the harsh word [Note: [Col. 0531] Ps. 90.]. The Apostle entrusted this trumpet to his disciple when he said: “Preach the word; be urgent in season and out of season; rebuke, entreat, reprove; and, in all patience and teaching, [Col. 0532A] do the work of an evangelist; fulfil your ministry” [Note: [Col. 0531] II Tim. 4.]. The Lord has made you a watchman for the house of Israel. Hear, therefore, what the Lord threatens concerning you and your like through Ezekiel [Note: [Col. 0531] Chap. 33.]: “If the watchman sees the sword coming and does not sound the trumpet, and the sword comes and takes one life from among the people, I shall require his blood at the watchman’s hand.”

The Lord has established for us in the cross the sacrament of reconciliation and the confidence of salvation. Therefore, venerable Father, consider whether you are consulting for your reputation while you neither take up nor preach the cross, and conceal Christ’s wrongs by shameful silence and perilous neglect. If you escape now amid the troubles and labours of this most salutary pilgrimage, know that you will not escape God’s judgment. If you do not believe me, believe the Apostle writing to the Hebrews: “How,” he says, [Col. 0532B] “shall we escape if we neglect so great a salvation?” [Note: [Col. 0531] Heb. 2.]

Know, most beloved Father, that the Lord himself called and chose you as a priest for himself, that you might be among his people a teacher and leader, an example of repentance, a model of holiness, giving his people knowledge of salvation; that you might strive to make the people acceptable to the Lord, followers of good works, loving the way of Christ and preparing for the Lord a perfect people. God gave you wisdom so that you might expend it for public benefit; and, leading others through the understandings of your hands, you might say: “Without guile I learned, and without envy I share” [Note: [Col. 0531] Wisd. 7.]. Do not doubt that the grace bestowed upon you by God will harm you yourself if you do not strive through it to benefit others.

[Col. 0532C] But you say: “It is enough for me to benefit those over whom the Lord has chosen to set me.” Is the word of the Lord so bound—or rather so curtailed—that it is confined within the narrow limits of a single parish? The Apostle was debtor to wise and foolish, Greeks and barbarians [Note: [Col. 0531] Rom. 1.]. And though formerly God was known only in Judaea, he at last willed that all nations should come to the knowledge of his name. For this reason Abraham’s name is enlarged; for this reason he goes out from his land and kindred, that he may increase among the nations. He also who “was not sent except to the lost sheep of the house of Israel” [Note: [Col. 0531] Matt. 15.] commands that all nations be baptized in invocation of the holy Trinity [Note: [Col. 0531] Matt. 28.]. By his own testimony, “the harvest indeed is plentiful, but the labourers are few” [Note: [Col. 0531] Matt. 9.]. If you withdraw yourself from this small number, you may be accused of negligence or unbelief, because, [Col. 0532D] so far as you are concerned, you diminish the yield of the Lord’s harvest. They have appointed you a guardian in the vineyard.

It is therefore your concern that the vineyard of the Lord of hosts should spread its branches more widely, that the olive-tree should be grafted upon wild olives and that the wild vine should be propagated into the vineyard. It is your concern that those who are ignorant and erring should leave error through your saving admonitions, and that those who scorn to come to the heavenly wedding should, by your ministry, be compelled to enter.

But you say: “Whoever kills unbelievers is a murderer. I do not wish to incur the charge of homicide by killing men, for the Lord abominates the man of blood; hence David is excluded from [Col. 0533A] building the Temple.” Friend, it makes a great difference how a person kills. For if he does these things by the command of law, the law excuses him from the charge of homicide. And what greater law excuses him than the common constitution of the Church, the command of the supreme pontiff, zeal for the Lord, and love of Christ? Indeed, it counts to Christians as merit if, inflamed by zeal of charity, they manfully attack those who blaspheme Christ, defile the Lord’s sanctuary, and in their pride and abuse humiliate the glory of our Redeemer. It is the word of the Lord: “You shall kill blasphemers, and you shall not suffer sorcerers to live” [Note: [Col. 0533] Exod. 22.]. I believe it most acceptable to God if those most unclean dogs are driven from the Holy Land; the ministry of this matter belongs to men, but authority and power belong to the Lord.

[Col. 0533B] “For the zeal of the Lord of hosts shall accomplish this.” Do you count yourself holier than Moses, Samuel, Phinehas, Elijah, or Peter? Did not Moses, killing twenty-three thousand of his people, expiate the sin of their idolatry by their deaths [Note: [Col. 0533] Exod. 32.]? Samuel cut King Agag into pieces [Note: [Col. 0533] I Sam. 15.]; Phinehas pierced with a dagger a Jew having intercourse with a Midianite woman [Note: [Col. 0533] Num. 25.]. Elijah consumed two companies of fifty men, with their hundred men, by sending down heavenly fire [Note: [Col. 0533] III Kings 18.]. Peter terribly put Ananias and Sapphira to death [Note: [Col. 0533] Acts 5.], not to mention the battles of Joshua and the other judges, David also and the other ancient kings. The Maccabees live because they fought for their ancestral laws; they received everlasting names in heaven; the entire Church of the saints recounts their triumphal crowns and praises.

But now, through the example of your faint-heartedness, many hearts have been weakened, and they have fallen even into the pit of distrust. In Ecclesiasticus you read: “Woe to those weak in heart, who do not believe the Lord! Woe to those who have lost endurance, who have forsaken the straight way” [Note: [Col. 0533] Ecclus. 2.]. “They profess to know God, but deny him by their deeds” [Note: [Col. 0533] Titus 1.]. Beyond doubt, those who do not expend themselves upon the labour of this way for the necessity of Christian faith are unbelieving toward the Lord and appear to deny him. For Paul, writing to Timothy, says: “If we endure for Christ, we shall also reign with him.

> If we deny him, he also will deny us” [Note: [Col. 0533] 2 Tim. 2.].

Already [Col. 0533D] I hear some murmuring—men whom I should certainly not hesitate to call enemies of Christ’s cross, “whose end is destruction” [Note: [Col. 0533] Phil. 3.]. They have not yet entered the way and already complain and murmur about its dangers, though it is written of such persons: “They murmured and perished by serpents.” For the charity of many grows cold and iniquity abounds [Note: [Col. 0533] I Cor. 10.]. Thus I seem already to hear the blasphemies of that ancient unbelieving people whenever they provoked the Lord in the desert and, provoking the Holy One of Israel, said: “Perhaps there were no graves in Egypt; therefore the Lord brought us [Col. 0534A] out to die in the wilderness” [Note: [Col. 0533] Matt. 24.].

Thus that unbelieving people once lamented at Marah because of lack of water [Note: [Col. 0533] Exod. 14.]. Thus they murmured at Elim because bread failed [Note: [Col. 0533] Exod. 15.]. Thus at Rephidim, where there was no water, they quarrelled with Moses [Note: [Col. 0533] Ibid.]. Their imitators have arisen today, either scorning Christ’s cross or carrying it as a forced burden, and distancing God’s grace from themselves through murmurings. Therefore I fear that the Lord may say what he is recorded once to have said of the murmuring people: “My soul is not with this people” [Note: [Col. 0533] Exod. 17.]. And Jeremiah: “Shall I not visit for these things, says the Lord, and shall not my soul most strongly avenge itself upon such a nation?” [Note: [Col. 0533] Jer. 5.]

Great and mighty Lord of hosts is your name: you are able to do all things far more abundantly than we ask or understand. Make the voluntary offerings [Col. 0534B] of my mouth pleasing in the ears of those to whom I speak, and soften the hardness of their heart. For, as the prophet testifies, “My words are like fire and like a hammer breaking the rock” [Note: [Col. 0533] Jer. 23.]. You who open my mouth, let my speech open the door of their will; for men tender and delicate, bound by the habit of pleasures, are converted to their heart—not by loftiness of speech nor by persuasive words of human wisdom, but by God’s power [Note: [Col. 0533] I Cor. 2.]—so that they forsake vanities and false madness, and, renouncing life’s delights, “because of the words of your lips keep hard ways” [Note: [Col. 0533] Ps. 16.].

O way, truth, and life! O wisdom, “reaching mightily from end to end” [Note: [Col. 0533] Wisd. 8.]! My God, my mercy! My heart has said to you: “You know all my desire, and my groaning [Col. 0534C] is not hidden from you” [Note: [Col. 0533] Ps. 37.]. According to the ineffable abundance of your sweetness and in the strength of your hand, O God of hosts, gather, guard, and direct the Christian armies. But I trust in your great mercies that I shall not see death until the land of promise, freed from the oppression of unbelievers, breathes again; until I see my Joseph—or rather my Jesus—reigning in the land of Egypt, ruling Jacob and the ends of the earth.

## LETTER CCXXXIII. TO THE CONVENT OF CANTERBURY

To his dearest lord and friend Geoffrey, prior of Christ Church, Canterbury, his own Peter of Blois, archdeacon of Bath, greeting, and himself most ready for true service and honour.

The king, who always wished Baldwin, archbishop of Canterbury, to have grave and inexorable disputes and continual anxieties, so that he might always keep him humbled and dependent upon himself, compelled and forced me, on his behalf—against you, indeed against God and against myself—to labour for eight months in the Roman curia, at my own expense and in continual danger to my life. But I lost both labour and expense; and, as my sins required, the Lord permitted me to be ruinously deceived on that archbishop’s account, he who “permits a hypocrite to reign because of the sins of the people.” Yet blessed be God that I gained no fruit from unlawful labour.

May the Lord grant and add this to me: that I may redeem the things I have committed, and recompense by the rendering of honour and service the insults which, under another’s prompting, I inflicted upon my lords. I promise and testify before God and in him who is my hope and life that no living person shall see me as an adversary either of you, or of your Church, or of your honour. I understand the Lord’s scourge: for as I stood against you for eight months, so the Lord afflicted me for eight months with the punishment of a most severe illness. Therefore forgive me and pray for your penitent son, who promises satisfaction and humbly offers himself, from the whole depths of his heart, to devote every service to the defence of your dignities and liberties [Col. 0535B]. Fare well; and may every lord, all and each, fare well.

## LETTER CCXXXIV

### ARGUMENT.—He exhorts nuns to holiness and chastity.

I beseech you through the mercy of God, dearest daughters and sisters, that you present your bodies as “a living sacrifice, holy, pleasing to God” [Note: [Col. 0535] Rom. 12.]. The Apostle Paul exhorts you to observe the continence which you have vowed. For it is dangerous to vow and not to fulfil. “Vow,” says the Prophet, “and render” [Note: [Col. 0535] Ps. 75.]. Christ most strictly demands the chastity once offered, though he did not require it to be offered. Today you have become [Col. 0535C] brides of Christ. A bride is so called from *spondere*, “to pledge,” because today you have pledged a vow of continence; today, through his mercy, the Son of the Most High has deigned to betroth you to himself. As the prophet says: “I will betroth you in mercy and compassions, and I will betroth you to myself in faith” [Note: [Col. 0535] Hos. 2.]. This is what the Apostle says: “I have betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a chaste virgin to Christ” [Note: [Col. 0535] II Cor. 11.].

Christ binds in the love of espousal only those whom the world has not defiled. For he is a lover of virginity and chastity. Thus the Virgin of virgins went first, a virgin into the bridal chamber of the supreme King, so that afterward other virgins might be brought in. “Virgins shall be brought to the king after her; her companions shall be offered in joy and exultation; they shall be brought into the temple of the king” [Note: [Col. 0535] Ps. 44.]. This is the temple of which the Apostle says: [Col. 0535D] “If anyone violates the temple of the Lord, the Lord will destroy him” [Note: [Col. 0535] I Cor. 3.].

Today, dearest daughters, the Lord has given you grace and glory: grace, because he led you out from the filth of this age; glory, because today he mercifully betrothed you. Therefore see, as the Apostle says, that you do not receive God’s grace in vain [Note: [Col. 0535] II Cor. 6.]. For you have received grace in vain and carry empty lamps if you do not have the oil of charity, if you do not love Christ, your bridegroom, from the whole depths of your soul. For chastity without charity neither pleases the Lord nor is beautiful to him. As the Wise Man declares: “O how beautiful is a chaste generation [Col. 0536A] with charity!” [Note: [Col. 0535] Wisd. 4.]

Marital fruitfulness is indeed acceptable to Christ, but virginity is more acceptable to him: marriage fills the earth, virginity paradise; and through the benefit of virginity, the life and manner of angels are renewed in humankind. Conjugal fruitfulness is good, according to Scripture’s testimony; but widowed continence is better; virginal integrity is best; yet better and most surpassingly excellent of all is virginal fruitfulness. Nevertheless, this has been found in no woman except her who alone is without example:

> Possessing a mother’s joys with virgin honour.

She was seen to have no like predecessor and to have no successor. By her humility she acquired from Christ this prerogative, this privilege—this privilege, I say, which shall never be taken away. See how greatly the Virgin’s humility pleased him who dwells in heaven and regards the humble in heaven and on earth. He regarded neither her wisdom, beauty, nor nobility, but the humility of his handmaid [Note: [Col. 0535] Luke 1.].

You, therefore, who have seized the way of humility, who have cast aside the world and chosen to be lowly in the house of the Lord rather than dwell in the tents of sinners [Note: [Col. 0535] Ps. 83.], trust in Christ, who will visit you and rest in you. Thus he himself declares through the prophet: “Upon whom does my spirit rest, except upon the humble, gentle, and trembling at my words? [Note: [Col. 0535] Isa. 66.] This is my rest for ever; here shall I dwell, because [Col. 0536C] I have chosen her” [Note: [Col. 0535] Ps. 131.]. At judgment he will say terribly: “Come, my chosen one and my friend; I will set you upon a throne.”

The Lord reserves this glory and honour for those virgins who continually offer to God a holy mind devoted to him and a pure conscience, and who persevere to the end in this devotion. For “all the glory of the king’s daughter is within, in golden fringes” [Note: [Col. 0535] Ps. 44.], because our glory within is the testimony of our conscience, as the Apostle says; and fittingly it is in golden fringes, in which perseverance and the end are signified, for fringes are the extremities of a garment. Hence the Prophet, indicating the final charity of the righteous man, says: “And his latter parts are in the paleness of gold” [Note: [Col. 0535] Ibid.].

Let the virgins, then, whom the most high Son of the Most High has betrothed to himself, rejoice: he will place them in the ethereal bridal chamber [Col. 0536D] with his most blessed mother, with the Lady of angels. But let widows and other women who have been sinners rejoice, if they cannot attain the dignity of virginity, that they have nevertheless escaped this world’s sea. Let the widow of Zarephath be a consolation to widows, she who deserved to receive the prophet Elijah [Note: [Col. 0535] III Kings 47]. Let blessed Anna the widow be their consolation, she who not only prophesied concerning Christ, but deserved to see and hold the very Saviour of the world [Note: [Col. 0535] Luke 2.].

Let the devotion of the Canaanite woman, the repentance of the Egyptian woman, and the love of Magdalene raise sinners to hope and stir them to confidence. By her tears, Magdalene deserved not only to be cleansed of all [Col. 0537A] her iniquities but to raise up her brother, already dead three days [Note: [Col. 0537] John 11.]. Without doubt, the tears that compelled Christ to weep proceeded from great devotion. Therefore she who had been a sinner in the city deserved, by love and tears, not only to be freed from sins, but to become an apostle and evangelist—or rather, what is greater, the apostle of the apostles—hastening to announce the Lord’s resurrection to the apostles and running in the fragrance of his ointments.

O immeasurable, unfailing, inexhaustible mercy of the Saviour! He draws virgins to himself and after himself, regards widows, and receives sinners. In the sinner he establishes for himself a living sacrifice; in the widow, a holy sacrifice; in the virgin, a sacrifice pleasing to God. To the sinner he gives mercy, to the widow grace, to the virgin [Col. 0537B] glory. Thus, in sinner, widow, and virgin, he invites us to that joy of the heavenly homeland which the Lord has promised to those who love him, he who is blessed for ages of ages. Amen.

## LETTER CCXXXV

To the reverend father and lord A., abbot of Gloucester, P. of Blois, archdeacon of London, greeting; and, with observance of gentleness, forgetfulness of anger.

I am astonished, and very many are astonished with me, that although Master Alexander of Gloucester, a man of honourable reputation and commendable learning, has served you and your house faithfully, usefully, and honourably from the first bloom of his youth, you now intend to trouble him, as though disowning and tearing him away from the bosom of your favour [Col. 0537C], and are showing yourself toward him harsh, inexorable, and ungrateful, as is publicly said.

Certainly, among all the evils which we have inherited, as if by a right of succession, from our first parents—or rather, our first destroyers—nothing is more gravely condemned before God and men than ingratitude. For ingratitude is the nurse of baseness and the stepmother of honour. In the testimony of sacred speech, it is a scorching wind, drying up the fountain of affection, blocking the rivulets of love, and drying out the streams of grace and the blessing of human satisfaction. If he has sinned or offended you in any respect, it is human to sin; but it is inhuman stubbornly to harden oneself against one who asks forgiveness. He is prepared to make satisfaction at the counsel of good men, and humbly to restrain the fault of his negligence or ignorance by the more abundant interest of his services [Col. 0537D].

Therefore let not your anger be more vehement in vengeance than his failure was culpable. There are indeed faults in which it is itself a fault to pursue the entire fault; and your religious profession especially befits you in restraining and checking, by the bridle of moderation, the onset of conceived revenge. If he has fallen, the Lord will grant that he rise again. Perhaps at some time the insinuation of a detractor has disturbed you and embittered the sweetness of your affection into hatred. But far be it that the bitterness of any rancour should rule in a prelate. Rather let what the Apostle, writing to the Ephesians, says be done: “Let all bitterness and indignation be removed [Col. 0538A] from you, that you may be merciful to one another, forgiving offences” [Note: [Col. 0537] Eph. 4.].

Father, if you do not hear the Apostle, attend to what the poet says of a pagan ruler:

> Slow to punish, a prince swift to reward,  
> And grieving whenever you are compelled to be fierce.

The Lord’s Prayer—indeed, nearly the entire text of the Gospel—binds us to the duty of mercy. You will not be forgiven, Father, if you do not forgive. If you do not show mercy, you will be punished without mercy. Therefore use the counsel of Christ and the apostles, and do not think Prosper’s saying contemptible:

> Let a sinner grant pardon to a sinner, that on equal terms  
> He may reconcile the Lord to himself.

I beg you, most innocent Father, look more promptly to the reputation, honour, and advantage of your house. Master [Col. 0538B] Alexander, known and beloved by many, a man of extensive learning and fragrant reputation, can in many ways advance or hinder your affairs, whether personally or through others. These things, dearest Father, I have decided briefly to set before you in sincere affection, so that you may generously spare one brought up by you and faithful to you:

> And if you do not wish to spare him, spare yourself.

## LETTER CCXXXVI

I fear that before the magnificent majesty of the Apostolic See I shall be judged rash—or rather shameless—for putting forward certain ravings, since, smoking beneath a bushel, I am compelled to bring my darkness to a lamp set on a lampstand—indeed, to that most serene luminary which shines before the whole Church. For all [Col. 0538C] my inward parts burn to write; and, to use Job’s words, “my spirit is like new wine bursting new wineskins” [Note: [Col. 0537] Job 32.]. Since “out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks” [Note: [Col. 0537] Matt. 12.], if I write too slowly or incautiously, you who are spiritual should correct this in a spirit of gentleness [Note: [Col. 0537] Gal. 6.]. “The Lord has given us a learned tongue, that you may know how to sustain him who is weary with a word” [Note: [Col. 0537] Isa. 50.].

Perhaps it would be more prudent for me if the conceived presumption to write lay concealed in the bosom of my learning and were shut within the hinges of silence. Forgive an old man, you who understand more than the old. For evening is now drawing on for me, and I hasten toward the setting of my passing life. This is plainly shown to me by failing memory, dimming eye, a duller gaze of reason, and a talent once of keener vein, now blunted by the infirmity [Col. 0538D] of old age. The grace of greenness rarely proceeds from an aged stem whose root has dried up. But I am already being consumed and have received in my limbs the answer of death. Little of my lifetime remains, and even that does not stand still.

Yet before I say a final farewell to worldly intercourse, I should most earnestly wish to consult the wisdom given us by God and, with the sickle of Apostolic authority, remove a scruple of perilous doubt which has taken deep root in many minds and has drunk up my whole spirit. Great indeed is the astonishment and horror inflicted upon those ministering at the altar when, amid the words of life and the sacraments [Col. 0539A] of eternal salvation, words alien to Christ are ascribed to him—words which make the truth suspect, which do not cohere with one another, which are neither Christ’s nor read in the Gospel. For in the consecration of Christ’s blood it is written thus: “Likewise, after he had supped,” etc.

## LETTER CCXXXVII

### ARGUMENT.—The case of a slave with respect to receiving an inheritance.

In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.

A certain man, in his testament, had made his slave both free and heir, provided, however, that he should deserve this from the four daughters whom he had. Two of these daughters gladly give their assent, both that he should obtain freedom and that he should receive the inheritance. [Col. 0539B] The other two utterly oppose it. These four daughters, dearest brothers, are the daughters of the great King: namely mercy, truth, justice, and peace.

The testator is the Lord, who first established the Old Testament in the blood of sacrifices, and afterward confirmed the New Testament in his own blood. The slave is man, who, though created in full freedom of will, sold himself under sin and became a slave of punishment. Mercy and peace wished to bestow upon him the benefit of freedom and inheritance; but justice and truth, on the contrary, maintain that he is wholly unworthy of either.

There was a great dispute among the sisters, and the contention grew beyond measure, except that peace intervened with her offices and asked for the things that make for peace. “Let us dispute, sisters,” she said, “not with reproaches or contentions, but by reason and laws. Let us approach the judge, and let our law plead its case before him. Let us seek the judgment of Solomon, the peaceful man who makes both one—that is, Christ. For the Father has given all judgment to the Son” [Note: [Col. 0539] John 5.], as it is written: “O God, give your judgment to the king, and your justice to the king’s son” [Note: [Col. 0539] Ps. 71.].

The counsel pleased them jointly.
