They come before the judge, and mercy, having recovered her breath a little so that she may be drawn by greater affection, takes the office of assessor; for at that time, perhaps, that constitution concerning removal of the *assertio* had not yet been promulgated. First, then, she alleges much concerning human misery, in order to incline the judge toward compassion. “Man,” she says, “did not fall by himself, as the devil did; rather, he was impelled and overthrown so that he might fall, and is therefore most worthy of compassion. Have mercy, therefore, Father, because the time has come to have mercy on him, because the time has come” [Note: [Col. 0539] Ps. 101.].

Then, turning to justice: “Why, sister,” she says, “do you wish to add to the pain of this wretch’s wounds? Why do you provoke our Father to anger against him? You display your power against a leaf carried away by the wind, and pursue dry stubble. For you write and inscribe bitter charges against him, and wish to consume the mercies of our Father, which remain for ever [Note: [Col. 0539] Ps. 60.] and unto age after age.”

Can you set fixed bounds to mercy, whose mercy has no end, whose loving-kindness has as its measure [Col. 0540A] boundlessness? Our Father and Lord is himself the Father of mercies and the Lord of all consolation, sweet, gentle, mild, and abounding over malice; for whom it is proper to have mercy and to spare. “Will God cast off for ever, and will he no longer be favourable? Will God forget to have mercy, or will he in anger withhold his mercies?” You will not take from him what is his own, since even when angry he remembers mercy.

I confess indeed—for I cannot deny it—that man sold himself under sin. But neither did the sale hold good in law, nor could it redound to man’s prejudice; and this we shall demonstrate most clearly both by arguments and by laws. For we have very substantial grounds even in civil law, and we very often temper its severity. Man [Col. 0540B] either fell through the deceit and craft of his adversary, or through the slipperiness and facility of his own judgment. Whichever of these ways he fell, the benefit of restitution is granted him.

Yet if he was injured by his adversary’s craft, even if he is over twenty years of age, that law of the Code *On Fraud*, “If he is over age,” grants him restitution. More fully, the law of the Digest *On Purchase*, in Celsus, called “If he is over age,” grants it, where it is said that, if anyone, induced by the deceit of his wife, repudiates an inheritance, although he is over twenty-five years old, he may nevertheless bring an action for fraud against his wife. To this also the law of the Code *On Rescinding a Sale*, “If through Deceit,” and the law *Deceit*, lend most effective support, where it is said: “But if anyone has been induced by the deceits of his adversary [Col. 0540C] to sell, the governor of the province shall revoke the sale.” For deceit is assessed by the character of the act, not by the amount of money.

If the contract is one of good faith—which is required in these contracts in abundant measure—then, to prove the same point, he has produced the legal maxim, the law *Counsel* and the law *Agreement*, where it is said that no obligation arises from fraudulent counsel, nor does that deserve effect which began in fraud. But if he fell through the facility of misleading counsel, the aid of restitution is not denied him, by the argument of the Code *On the Restoration of Minors to Their Former Position*, law *For Minors*, where it is said that persons under twenty-five are restored in matters in which they consider themselves deceived, even though the adversary’s fraud cannot be proved; and from the Code *On Free Status*, law *Not for That Reason*, where it is said [Col. 0540D] that a woman above twenty years of age, even if sold by the fisc, is not prejudiced against herself unless she allowed herself to be sold for the sake of sharing in the price. And in the Digest *On Free Status*, law *For Children*: “If anyone knowingly [lacuna] who alleges fraud, let him prove the fraud by clear indications.”

For through his wife man was induced by deceit to sell himself under sin; and he pleads that law of the Digest *On Fraud*, “For he who,” and the law *Whoever*. Moreover, he excuses man’s act on account of ignorance and error, as in the *Institutes*, *On the Capacity of Heirs*, section “It Must Be Known,” and in the Digest *On the Jurisdiction of All Judges*, law *On Error*, where it is said that restitution is given, just as to [Col. 0541A] those who approached one praetor supposing him to be another; for they are understood to have done nothing, since those who are mistaken do not consent in any way.

“We proceed still further,” says Mercy. “It is a settled and regular rule that no one’s own fraud ought to profit him,” as in the Digest *On Partnership*, law *It Is True*, section “Time”; and it is the judgment of the law that no one is aided by his own fraud.

## LETTER CCXXXVIII

Who would give to my head a fountain, so that my mind, overwhelmed by the darkness of grief and stirred by the whirlwind of sighs because of the monstrous atrocity inflicted upon a king, might unceasingly pour forth streams of tears in confused lamentation like rain? Who would embitter my words of denunciation with the wormwood of cursing, or poison them with the gall-like sharpness of reproaches? Who would arm invectives unequal to so dreadful a subject [Col. 0541B] with the sting of ironical ferocity? Who would sharpen the point of my tongue for blows of detestation like lightning, so that, as a fit assailant, I might powerfully transfix the wicked crime recently perpetrated, by abominable means, against the lord Andrew, King of Jerusalem and Sicily, of lamentable memory?

I do not undertake this boldly enough, for I reasonably fear lest the magnitude of so grave and atrocious a wickedness—perhaps to be spread among peoples remote throughout the regions of the world—should exceed the endurance of its hearers, weigh down the measure of my talent, and surpass the power of my weak speech. For my inward sight impatiently recoils from this fatal monster and monstrous spectacle; the stunned ear shuns it; and the trembling [Col. 0541C] mind shudders.

But how can it, however carefully, be restrained by the bridle of moderation? How can the onset of grief, arising from a public injury damnably inflicted upon one person, but upon all the faithful and especially upon one endowed with royal eminence, endure to be shut fast in the chamber of silence? Alas, how greatly the condition of Mother Church is diminished! How greatly her honour is impaired, when her uniquely beloved son and foster-child alike is slaughtered as it were in her arms! Alas, with how filthy brands of disgrace, with how notorious stains of infamy, this new crime bespatters the age and shakes the present times—savage with unprecedented frenzy, unknown to barbarians and unheard of in former ages!

Tell me, I pray, you whom diligent concern for ancient books occupies: where [Col. 0541D] do long-lived ravens report, or ancient tragedies declaim; where does any history record, or where do the monuments of old annals recall, that a prince gentle in the sweetness of clemency, resplendent in the brilliance of ancestry, shining in the pure brightness of innocence, and flourishing in the first bloom of youth—whose character, in his tender age, promised magnificent deeds and, while he was still under youthful years, displayed the most well-ordered government—was so mercilessly crushed, basely suppressed, treacherously overthrown, and cut down before his time, not by open bands of enemies, not by ranks of declared or public rebels, but by companies of courtiers—indeed, of buffoons—and crafty throngs of subjects, fortified with deceitful frauds and suborned by deceptive abuse?

These men, indeed, against whom the arrow of divine [Col. 0542A] indignation is aimed, were stirred by no injury received in wars, provoked by no losses of possessions, nor goaded by any insult of words. While the solemnities of the coronation were at hand, so that they might anticipate the festival with an ill-starred funeral and forestall the instruments of joy with the mourning of good men, conspiring in a most foul compact against the royal majesty entrusted to their keeping with too little caution, in the hostile city—whose unhappy name attests its misfortune—they treacherously led him, in the untimely silence of night, which provident nature has appointed for living creatures’ rest, from the secrecy of the bedchamber, the safest refuge of human safety, to become a victim of death.

For the abominable completion of this criminal service, as the report spread by rumour, privy to secrets, suggests, [Col. 0542B] after a noose had secretly and murderously been cast about the innocent man’s neck—a noose which legal severity devised for punishing robbers, not for strangling kings—and, what I cannot recount without shame, one of them shamelessly laid impious hands upon the vessels of the invaded Lord’s seed, cruelly mangling them: thus, under the intolerable agony of tortures, life yielded up its vital strength to deadly torments.

After this, not content with the limit of canine ferocity—which does not know how to harass prey once killed with the annoyance of superfluous disturbance—they cast down from a precipice the lifeless body which, a little before, a high-spirited soul full of great hope had animated. Furthermore, driven by the madness of some excessively raging fury, as the report of a friend disclosed, they treacherously withheld from the funeral of that prince all attendance of magnates, every following of nobles; thereby violating those duties of piety toward a lord which antiquity often preserved, worthy of imitation even toward capital enemies: so that, if one adversary, prevailing over another in the final outcome of combat, had become the author of his death, then after his destruction, not taking vengeance upon his private person from hatred’s bitterness, but rendering to all his nature the office of humanity, he would freely permit his funeral rites.

O radiance of union! O shining star, which clearly shed light upon Hungary, to establish the wretched soil of troubled Italy, to illumine it with the throne of justice and the ray of peace: with how many reproaches you have been darkened, and with what punishments eclipsed, I can neither discuss in the style of Scripture [Col. 0542D] nor adequately set forth in the course of a prolonged lament!

For now, to pursue this mournful disaster more seriously in all its particulars, would that divine consideration for his fellow-countryman might, without detriment to his glory, call back from the bosom of the tomb the eminent teacher Jerome, overflowing with the fullness of eloquent wisdom and wise eloquence, who also drew his origin from the regions of Hungary! What if, now suitably equipped by the eloquence of an articulate orator according to the merits of the cause, the once most renowned Minos, illustrious king of Crete, restored to life by the life-giving Lord, should pronounce a just sentence against the detestable authors of the crime on behalf of the most afflicted mother of fallen Andrew and his most illustrious consort, so pitiably widowed? Minos, the avenger and grandfather of Androgeus, as is read, enclosed the Athenian murderers of that same Androgeus within the dreadful labyrinth, while the censure of the law remained in force, and the devouring Minotaur swallowed them.

What if the Hungarian Attila, emerging again to the vital air, were allowed the scourge by which he crushed the wickedness of his own time, and now, at the command of the author of mercy, should mercifully rage in vengeance for one who shared his nation but not its cruelty? O intensity of anxious grief, which the slowness of those in authority—moving with impeded steps toward the goal of rendering justice, and, if it may be said, never ceasing almost timidly to petition even at the very beginning of proceedings—forces us to turn toward invoking the aid of the dead! Yet the mourner’s feeling is refreshed by this consolation at least: that, even if the ministers cease, the vigilance of the heavenly prince will not cease; and, however heavily they may be burdened, God, zealous and ready, will gird himself, and the God of vengeances will act freely.

## LETTER CCXXXIX

**Subject.—An anxious complaint against a prelate.**

For a very long time I have been tortured by this, and still this grievous affliction rages in the depths of my heart [lacuna] “This God, terrible in judgments, long suffering in concealing your evils, will destroy him utterly because he persecuted men” [lacuna] and, magnifying the devout in heart, he wholly gapes after plunder, that he may amass limitless money: a son of avarice, an idolater of money, a servant of Mammon. There he reads where he studies; there is his heart, because there is his treasure. And since he bears Peter’s sword, he seeks to blunt it, to dash justice to pieces, to soften it, to make void the Lord’s bow and the rigour of justice. You have always called the inquiry that was made “your business”; far be it that he should degenerate into [lacuna] and into a disgrace in commerce. The clergy cry out, the people cry out; writings cry out, and the voices of those who, murmuring about his insufficiency and uselessness, have testified against us. Will he now spare the Church—he who has profaned the whole Church?

Almost every day I must fight with the beast; yet I fight him as though beating the air: I am not resisted when I attack, but, in the witness of the pagan poet,

> “There is no fight where you strike and I alone receive the blows.”  
> [Note: [Col. 0543] Juvenal, 3.]

He carried off the crops and burned the houses. He inflicts upon me punishments and [Col. 0543D] losses; he mocked the afflicted man himself and the magnates all the more, insulted me more grievously, and displayed my loss and my humiliation as a spectacle for public derision. “In all these things his anger has not turned away, but his hand is still stretched out” [Note: [Col. 0543] Isa. 5.]. He will never grant me a favour or do me good in anything; but read continually in the book of experience the evils he has done from the time of his promotion onward. How long, Lord Jesus, will this iniquity last? [lacuna] why does useless toil occupy the ground? The axe is laid to the root, and there is none willing to cut it down; but whoever does not correct the evildoer when he can, does all his evil deeds.

On another occasion, he ordered crops violently taken away to be trampled in mud rather than threshed, so that he might afflict me with a double loss, because I humbly asked that restitution be made to me. Though I was neither summoned nor called by him or by another, he first declared me an appellant and, without any cause or judicial procedure, suspended me. Yet amid all these things it is not enough that your little sheep, [lacuna] most [uncertain] pastor, when snatched away, is more cruelly afflicted and tortured. For when he has spread himself abroad among bishops and all other powerful persons of his own party, they neither suffice for themselves nor need another’s support. Look upon an old man, weak and continually afflicted; for he seeks nothing other than to bring down my grey hairs in sorrow to death [Note: [Col. 0543] Gen. 44.].

Therefore, lest your Naboth be killed for his vineyard—or rather for his Church—hard, he says, but late is the complaint addressed to Ahab: “You have killed and moreover taken possession” [Note: [Col. 0543] III Kings 21]. Roman [Col. 0544B] princes of old, by a word alone, emancipated those whom their masters maliciously harassed. Emancipate this wretched man, oppressed by intolerable servitude, O bishop of the city of Rome, who alone possesses over all bishops the fullness of power. But if it is beyond your greatness to emancipate him outright, exempt him at least for five years. For already I have received the answer in my limbs; and I am certain that, when the skin of this wretched life has been shaken off, God will add some vital grace beyond [uncertain: “he will carry one soul beyond the boundary”].

Can Innocent be so cruel as to overlook the enormous peril of his little sheep and not rescue her from the jaws of the rushing lion or wolf? Either provide peace for me, or I promise and, without [Col. 0544C] any contradiction, resign into your hands whatever I possess. You ordered E., bishop, and I., dean, to render me justice concerning what had been taken from me. But I, compelled by the counsel of friends, restrain with my finger my lips against his terrible threats and certain dangers to my life; and he makes a child, compelled by his masters, swallow back with his eye the tear which has burst forth from it. It is commonly said that he is unhappily flogged who does not dare complain of the flogging.

Hear, O heavens, and give ear, O earth, to the great evils that I suffer and the still graver ones I fear and expect. If [lacuna] with him who, beyond all his predecessors, “is terrible among the kings of the earth” [Note: [Col. 0543] Ps. 75], be witnesses for me that he can free me and rescue me from the jaws of the cruel beast with a single word. O single word, be mine! O consolation, be honour; O glory [Col. 0544D] of him “who rescues the poor from the mighty, and the old and weak man who has no helper” [Note: [Col. 0543] Ps. 71]. “Wretched man that I am, who will free me from the prison of this death?” [Note: [Col. 0543] Rom. 7.] Under what unlucky omen was I transferred from sweet France, where I had been born, nourished, and educated, into this barbarous servitude? But I shall speak to Innocent, and I am certain that Innocence can drive out his wickedness.

## LETTER CCXL

**Subject.—An exhortation against the bonds of the court.**

To his beloved and most dearly beloved lord and friend G., dean of St Martin’s and archdeacon of Norwich, P. B., archdeacon of London, [Col. 0545A] sends greetings, and whatever is sweeter or more desirable than greeting.

I give abundant thanks to the magnificent and generous Giver of gifts, who has called you back from the furnace of courtly cares, as from a burdensome labyrinth—or rather from the belly of hell—into the tranquil freedom of the soul. For where the Spirit is, there is freedom: so that the human soul, drawing breath from manifold turmoil, may dwell with itself, attend to itself, and see how sweet the Lord is, and with what freedom Christ has endowed you.

For when worldly glory and the favour of great men smiled more sweetly upon you, you fled from the ambition of the court—which flattered you with manifold allurements of goods—like Joseph, who left his cloak when the adulteress had seized it [Note: [Col. 0545] Gen. 39.]. Truly, nothing is great to a great heart; [Col. 0545B] and therefore what others pursue through hazards of body and soul, you have despised with a certain noble disdain of soul. Indeed, it is noble pride to prefer wisdom to riches and integrity to honours. For wisdom too has her riches and delights, as she herself says in the Book bearing her name: “With me are proud riches and glory” [Note: [Col. 0545] Prov. 8.].

Therefore I congratulate you with all the marrow of my soul on this matter. For all things which we think accrue to friends for honour, peace of heart, and salvation of soul are contrary to true friendship. Let others run to plunder the baggage of this age, staking their souls—for whom Christ died—as though upon a throw of dice, while they are agitated around ambitious honours by a demonic spirit, not without danger [Col. 0545C] of eternal perdition. These are those driven by the spirit of this world, the spirit of giddiness and error: they are lifted up upon the wind in order to fall more heavily; they throw themselves into the crowd of people and heap double sins upon themselves.

Saint Eusebius writes that, just as a gem is in mud, so episcopal authority is when conferred upon an unworthy man. We continue with Solomon’s saying: “He who gives honour to a fool is like one who casts a stone into Mercury’s heap.” Jerome too does not keep silence on this point; these are his words to Pammachius: “A splendid honour becomes vile in a base man.” And, that human ambition may be put to shame by the example of beasts, he adds: “Among animals, a bull not degenerate precedes the herd, but one superior in bulk and strength; among elephants too, the more robust and handsome leads all the others by a certain prerogative of stature. Today, however, men creep on feet and hands after honour who, according to the measure of their merits, ought to hold the lowest place in the Church.”

O how far their heart is from the purpose of blessed Ammonius, of whom Saint Jerome reports that, when because of his learning and honourable character he was being seized by clergy and people to become a bishop, he long resisted, and, prevailing over himself so that he might not be promoted, cut off one of his ears at the root. When this was reported to the metropolitan, he wrote back that Ammonius was now worthy of the episcopate. But when he was again dragged toward the episcopal chair, he said: “Unless you let me go, [Col. 0546A] I shall cut off with my teeth the tongue for whose glory and resonant speech you are dragging me”; and thus he escaped the honour whose dangers he truly feared.

Geoffrey of Péronne, whom I saw in the schools at Paris, was afterwards elected, when prior of Clairvaux, to be bishop of Tournai. He refused the bishopric; and although he was compelled in many ways by the abbots of that order, he nevertheless never consented to receive the episcopate. Afterwards, when he had died, he appeared to a certain companion and intimate of his; and, asked how he fared, answered him: “Excellently; and know that I have been assured by the Lord that, if I had accepted the episcopate, I would have been among the reprobate.”

Without doubt, men ought first to be tested. For not even to Peter the apostle were the keys of the kingdom [Col. 0546B] of heaven entrusted [Note: [Col. 0545] Matt. 16] until, questioned three times, he had been tested in his confession of love and faith. Ecclesiastes complains on this matter, saying: “See the evil that is under the sun: a fool placed in lofty dignity and wise men sitting below” [Note: [Col. 0545] ch. 10]. Woe to the man who presides and does not benefit, who presides over men and is not himself presided over by the Lord!

Formerly, divine aid was invoked in elections. Today, with no prayer first offered, no preceding inquiry into the life and learning of the man to be ordained and the other circumstances of his merits—which the Apostle knowingly wove into a long catalogue—men follow, against the judgment of their own conscience, the favour of great men and the uncertainty of shifting opinion. Moses, prince of the people [Col. 0546C] of Israel, in the book of Numbers [Note: [Col. 0545] ch. 27], prays to the Lord that a successor be appointed to him. “Let the Lord,” he says, “provide a man who may be over this multitude”; and he deserves to hear the reply: “Take Joshua, son of Nun, a man in whom is the Spirit of the Lord, and lay your hand upon him, that he may go in and go out before my people.”

Accordingly, when Moses is sent to free the people of Israel from Egypt, he declares that he has been slow of speech from yesterday and the day before yesterday [Note: [Col. 0545] Exod.]. Jeremiah likewise, though sanctified from the womb, when the Lord imposed on him the office of messenger and teacher, fearing his own insufficiency, excused himself as though he were an elementary child, saying: “Ah, ah, ah, Lord God, I do not know how to speak, for I am a child” [Note: [Col. 0545] ch. 1]. Who today alleges his own imperfection? Who reveals [Col. 0546D] his ignorance? Who considers himself unworthy? Who resists? Who protests? Who flees? Who today does as most of the saints did, who hid themselves in caves and pits so that they might not be made bishops?

The unworthy prelacy of such men causes the Church, which was once free, in this age to be shamefully compelled to serve as a handmaid with Hagar [Note: [Col. 0545] Gal. 4]. And the saying formerly uttered is a parable of the present time [Note: [Col. 0545] Ps. 77]: “The Lord rejected the tabernacle of Shiloh, his tabernacle, where he dwelt with men.” Of old God said to the Church: “I will make you the pride of ages, the joy from generation to generation. [Col. 0547A] You shall suck the milk of nations and be nursed at the breasts of kings” [Note: [Col. 0547] Isa. 60]. But now she is not merely weaned, but disowned and cast aside, and there is none to comfort her among all her beloved ones. “Her enemies have become the head” [Note: [Col. 0547] Lam. 1]; and her sons have turned away and have not kept the covenant; they “have turned into a crooked bow” [Note: [Col. 0547] Ps. 77].

For those who sit in Moses’ chair [Note: [Col. 0547] Matt. 23] allow the Church to be oppressed by exactions, and, to the prejudice of ecclesiastical liberty and as a sign of perpetual servitude, willingly permit their ears to be pierced with an awl [Note: [Col. 0547] Exod. 11]. Yet they think they have fulfilled a bishop’s office if they build palaces from the patrimony of the Crucified One, from the sweat of the poor, from the extortions of their subjects; if they surround themselves with fishponds and vast preserves for wild beasts; and, forgetting the promises which they uttered with their lips at their consecration, take no care for the souls entrusted to them.

They might lawfully build fishponds and the rest from lawfully acquired goods, and nonetheless keep more watchful and diligent vigil for the salvation of souls. “These they ought to do, and not omit the others” [Note: [Col. 0547] Matt. 23]. Would that they were wise and understood and provided for their latter end [Note: [Col. 0547] Deut. 32]! For although they now appear to escape human judgment, by the testimony of Holy Scripture, “a swift and dreadful judgment shall be upon those who rule, and the powerful shall suffer powerful torments” [Note: [Col. 0547] Wis. 6].

That terrible Judge says: “I myself will seek my sheep” [Note: [Col. 0547] Ezek. 34]. From whom will he seek his sheep except from those to whom they were entrusted, who, abusing their milk, wool, and flesh, perform rather [Col. 0547C] the office of hireling than of shepherd? “Therefore the shepherd provoked God; for he said in his heart, ‘He will not seek’” [Note: [Col. 0547] Ps. 10]. Which assertion of these men will prevail? “The Lord of hosts has sworn, saying: Surely, as I have thought, so shall it be; and as I have purposed, so shall it come to pass” [Note: [Col. 0547] Isa. 14].

Certainly I judge no one: “there is one who seeks and judges” [Note: [Col. 0547] Josh. 22]. Nor should anyone be angry with me because I set my mouth against heaven, or because I, a sheep, accuse shepherds. It is enough for me if, with the other sheep, I may bleat and weep and lament the negligence of shepherds, which turns into a common peril. The wolf goes about to seize the sheep, and there is none to rescue them. For it is supremely important to rouse the shepherd, that, having pity on the wandering sheep, he may gather them into the fold and stir up pastoral care for his flock.

For the highest glory of rulers [Col. 0547D] is to turn unbelievers to the wisdom of the just and to prepare for the Lord a perfect people. Would that, according to the word of the Gospel [Note: [Col. 0547] John 5], they sought the glory which is from God and not that which is from men! For that glory is a scorching wind, a pestilential and corrupting air. O *doxa*, *doxa*—O glory, deceitful! O inflation of ears! O swelling bladder, as empty though full of wind as though full of nothing!

Therefore, as you have begun, establish your heart in the Lord and in the stone of help. Strengthen your purpose, so that [Col. 0548A] you may not return to false vanities and madnesses, but that your soul, imbued with so many and such refined disciplines, may serve him whom to serve is to reign. Devote yourselves, I pray, to reading; and let the contemplative mind often descend into the gardens of spices, that there it may feed upon spiritual delights and gather lilies of joys most pleasing to itself.

Jerome’s saying indeed is: “Leisure without literature is death and the burial of a living man.” But according to Solomon’s testimony: “Leisure is a friend to the soul.” Yet there is a leisure that builds toward salvation. For freedom from the cares and anxieties of this world, along with reading and study, is indeed busy leisure and leisurely business. Of this leisure Solomon says: “Write wisdom in leisure, and he who is diminished in activity shall receive it” [Note: [Col. 0547] Ecclus. 38]. In a figure of this, the disciples of the Lord, [Col. 0548B] passing through the fields on the Sabbath—that is, the day of leisure—rubbed ears of grain and ate them [Note: [Col. 0547] Matt. 12]. For in time of freedom we draw from hidden things subtler meanings by which souls are refreshed. Finally, in Ezekiel [Note: [Col. 0547] ch. 40], the gate facing east was not opened except on the Sabbath, that is, in holy leisure.

Therefore seek for yourselves solitude from the noise of this world. For concerning those who wish to be still and see how sweet the Lord is [Note: [Col. 0547] Ps. 45], blessed Job says [Note: [Col. 0547] ch. 3]: “These are they who build solitudes for themselves, lest they hear the voice of the exactor.” The exactor is the wicked spirit, who, as if through instruments of voices, disturbs the favour of princes with the poison of insolent tongues. Are not his voices or tongues the deceitful flatterers [Col. 0548C] and detractors, as the apostle Paul says [Note: [Col. 0547] Rom. 1]: “These are hateful to God,” frogs in the inner chambers of kings themselves?

Nor are Jannes and Mambres lacking today in courts, men who oppose Moses before Pharaoh [Note: [Col. 0547] II Tim.]. Ahithophel too has left many heirs in courts, who make foolish the counsels of great men. There are many Hamans today who incite King Ahasuerus to hatred and destruction of the innocent Mordecai [Note: [Col. 0547] Esther 5].

The fulfillment of my desire and the sum of my exhortation is this: gird yourselves for the work of strength, lest the noble first-fruits of the Spirit in you degenerate, but through love of Christ and contempt for the world grow into sheaves of righteousness and eternal salvation. I urge upon you no observance of an order; rather, I entreat you to live in the world in such a way that you are higher than the world, [Col. 0548D] that you have the world beneath your feet, and that, according to the Apostle’s word, by seeking and setting your mind on the things above [Note: [Col. 0547] Col. 3], your citizenship may be in heaven [Note: [Col. 0547] Phil. 3].

## LETTER CCXLI

**Subject.—A consolatory letter sent by P. B. to his bishop, severely afflicted by adversity.**

To the reverend father and lord H., by God’s grace bishop of Salisbury, P. B., archdeacon of London, sends greeting and steadfastness in adversities.

I who formerly gloried in your glory am now afflicted by your [Col. 0549A] affliction. For he is no faithful friend who conceals the distresses of his friend, who does not make them his own by the feeling of compassion, who does not support the blows of that friend’s adversity by the shared shoulder of compassion. Therefore I have resolved to do what I can and ought: namely, to render you the service of devoted duty as to my lord, and faithful and filial affection as to my father, so that, amid this wisdom of your blessings, a mind unaccustomed to such things may not be swallowed up in sorrow and, softened by salutary admonitions, may recognize in the present scourge the grace of divine love.

Would that the righteous man correct me and my lords in mercy [Note: [Col. 0549] Ps. 140], not in his wrath, lest the force of his words break the patience of our hearts! The heavenly physician, the Dayspring from on high, visits his elect [Note: [Col. 0549] Luke 1]: now by visions, now by writings, now by benefits, [Col. 0549B] now by scourges; now using the cautery, now soothing applications; now dispensing adversities, now prosperities, around us with most healthful moderation.

Therefore divine correction is to be embraced in a spirit of humility, even if its sending is accomplished through evil angels. For unless Satan had buffeted the Apostle [Note: [Col. 0549] II Cor. 12], he would not have heard from the Lord: “My grace is sufficient for you, for power is perfected in weakness.” For a passing punishment is done with in order that an eternal one may be avoided; and a merciful judge, having put the question by means of rods, severely flogs a thief so that he may escape decapitation or the peril of the gallows.

Accordingly, the judgments of God, by which he tests us, must be carefully considered. For he visits early and suddenly proves the man whom he loves; he kills and makes alive, brings down to hell [Col. 0549C] and brings back; he makes poor and makes rich, humbles and exalts [Note: [Col. 0549] I Kings 2], and mercifully promotes man’s salvation amid so great a variety of reversals.

But if God turns aside the danger of an impending storm into a breeze, men immediately run together to plunder the booty of this world. They stake their souls as though upon a throw of dice, and, giving no heed to God’s judgments or to the dangers of this life, immerse themselves in worldly cares and suppose that they can possess both God and the world. But woe to the man walking by two ways, because “no one can serve two masters” [Note: [Col. 0549] Matt. 6]. For he is divided: the love of God has no share with worldly love. Hear the poet:

> [Uncertain: “Serta”:] when the mind ranges in two directions, divided between them,
[Col. 0549D] “One love diminishes the strength of another” [Note: [Col. 0549] Ovid, *Remedies for Love* 443]. Finally, upon those whom greed has blinded, God sends a wheel of evils. For while they whirl about and burn with unbearable cares in the labyrinth of avarice, they reproduce Samson’s misery: deprived of his eyes and bound to the millstone. Daily experience indeed teaches us that whatever a man labours at under the sun [Note: [Col. 0549] Eccl. 1], whatever he undertakes, pursues, and gathers in the world, whatever he prepares or preserves for his own use through anxieties and dangers to the soul, all will come to nothing, like running water [Note: [Col. 0549] Ps. 57]; it will pass like a vision of the night [Col. 0550A] [Note: [Col. 0549] Job 20], vanish like smoke, and fly away like a dream. For when the rich man dies, he will not take all things with him, nor will the glory of his house go down with him [Note: [Col. 0549] Ps. 48]. “They have slept their sleep,” he says, “and all men of wealth have found nothing in their hands” [Note: [Col. 0549] Ps. 75]. Therefore men of high rank, set in the eminent watchtower of the episcopal office, ought to shun riches as they would the feminizing waters of Salmacis. For the Apostle calls them the impediments of this age, because they obstruct our salvation, weaken courageous minds, soften even the most steadfast affections of charity, draw us away from divine benefits—indeed, take the Lord from us. And what does it profit a man if he possesses Croesus’ riches, Solomon’s splendours, everything that Julius Caesar or great Alexander and the other powerful men of the earth possessed in [Col. 0550B] treasures and delights, if he suffers loss to his own soul? [Note: [Col. 0549] Matt. 16.]

Moreover, some amass riches so that through them they may ransom themselves from terrible damnation. But Eliphaz says in the Book of Job [Note: [Col. 0549] ch. 15]: “Let no one, deceived by error, believe that he can be redeemed for any price.” For a human being cannot redeem himself by perishable gold or silver, but by contempt for the world, self-abasement, humility, faith, hope, love and compassion for one’s neighbour, by Christ’s death, and by that charity through which we are bound to love God. Love of riches so often engulfs a man that he has no freedom either to meditate on, hear, or proclaim God’s word. In the figure offered for our instruction, the Samaritan woman first left behind her water-jar [Note: [Col. 0549] John 4], by which the greed of this [Col. 0550C] world is signified, and ran to preach God’s word to the people.

Let us follow, I pray, the counsel of the Prophet: “If riches abound, do not set your heart upon them” [Note: [Col. 0549] Ps. 61]. It is not riches, but the heart’s covetousness, that is forbidden. Hence the Apostle says: not those who have riches, but those who wish to have riches, fall into temptation and the devil’s snare [Note: [Col. 0549] 1 Tim. 6]. Riches may therefore be possessed, as Abraham possessed them for just causes: for lawful uses, for the grace of hospitality, and for the support of the poor, so that they may receive us into their dwellings. For theirs is the kingdom of heaven [Note: [Col. 0549] Matt. 5], in such a way that they are able not merely to possess it for themselves but also to share it with others.

Take comfort, children of the poor Crucified One, disciples of Peter, who have neither silver nor gold, yet are redeemed without [Col. 0550D] silver. Hasten, buy, and eat: for those who possess nothing gain this kingdom more easily than those who possess everything. In holy poverty lies the purchase of so precious a thing; poverty bestows what riches cannot bestow. See how profitable it is to have no share in the ruin of this world, so that you may have a share in Christ’s resurrection, and receive in exchange for transient things goods which will remain yours without end. For it is written: “The rich have lacked and suffered hunger” [Note: [Col. 0549] Ps. 13]. Therefore the rich man, not believing himself needy, is always anxious about himself. But blessed is he [Col. 0551A] who can say: “But I am needy and poor; the Lord is mindful of me” [Note: [Col. 0551] Ps. 39]. Thus the rich man is concerned for himself, but the Lord takes thought for the poor; the Lord spares the poor and needy and will save the souls of the poor.

David, knowing how precious and noble before God is the title of poverty, though it is contemptible in the world, amid royal riches and sitting upon a royal throne, because he was poor in spirit, confidently said: “Incline thy ear, O Lord, and hear me, for I am poor and needy” [Note: [Col. 0551] Ps. 85]. Poverty is measured before God more by humility of mind than by slenderness of estate. Accordingly Solomon says: “A man’s substance is according to his heart.” Hear the benefits of poverty. It drives away from itself all gnawing anxieties,

[Col. 0551B] [lacuna] and, purified in its own furnace, does not fear the purgatorial fire. The poor man has within himself a sure pledge of future joy; already he tastes the first fruits of eternal salvation and, as though gathering desirable fruits from the tree of life, receives what, according to the Apostle’s testimony, are righteousness, joy, and peace in the Holy Spirit [Note: [Col. 0551] Rom. 14]. His is the promise that the Lord will soon introduce him into full possession of the everlasting inheritance, and he will sing exultantly: “The Lord is the portion of my inheritance and of my cup; thou art he who wilt restore my inheritance to me” [Note: [Col. 0551] Ps. 15].

The rich man, dying, grieves that his riches are separated from him. The poor man, trampling underfoot the heights of this world, disdains to lower his eyes toward the desire for worthless spoil. For he counts riches [Col. 0551C] as dung. Since he confidently aspires toward heaven, he abhors even the name of riches while the joyous host of heaven awaits him for heavenly delights. The rich man, bidding farewell to the world’s abundance, departs poor. For whatever flows abundantly in the world flows away, and causes its lover to flow away with it.

Hear, I pray, the Apostle speaking of his fellow-poor: “As sorrowful, yet always rejoicing; as having nothing, yet possessing all things; as dying, and behold, we live” [Note: [Col. 0551] 2 Cor. 6]. By the adverb “as,” the Apostle indicates that the evils which the poor endure in this world are not real evils, just as the goods of the rich are not real goods. How can goods be real goods if they pass away in a moment? “They spend their days in prosperity,” he says, “but in a moment they go down into hell” [Col. 0551D] [Note: [Col. 0551] Job 21]. Amid his riches and pleasures the rich man imagines himself equal to heaven. But “when he says, ‘Peace and security,’ then sudden destruction will come upon him” [Note: [Col. 0551] 1 Thess. 5], and hell will suddenly swallow him up along with the rich man clothed in purple.

Marking this in the Gospel, Truth says: “And thou, Capernaum, shalt thou be exalted to heaven? Thou shalt be cast down to hell” [Note: [Col. 0551] Luke 10]. Thus passes away the form of this world [Note: [Col. 0551] 1 Cor. 7]. Thus the feasting rich man is most bitterly tormented, while Lazarus rests in Abraham’s bosom [Note: [Col. 0551] Luke 16]. Thus Jacob crosses his hands over [Col. 0552A] Joseph’s sons, so that his left hand is laid upon the one who expected the right [Note: [Col. 0551] Gen. 48]. By the left hand adversity is signified; by the right, prosperity.

Recall, therefore, amid prosperity and adversity, Job’s endurance and Christ’s patience, and the constancy of those who joyfully endured the plundering of their goods. Accordingly, let no movement of distrust steal into your fatherhood. The Lord’s hand has not been shortened, so that he cannot restore what has been taken away. “The Lord gave; the Lord himself has taken away; as it pleased him, so it has been done” [Note: [Col. 0551] Job 1]. And, blessing his name, say with the Prophet: “I will bear the wrath of the Lord, because I have sinned” [Note: [Col. 0551] Mic. 7]. I was a child of wrath and deserved the Lord’s anger. Yet I know, Lord, that when you are angry you will remember mercy [Note: [Col. 0551] Hab. 3]; and with Isaiah I shall sing: “I will give thanks to thee, O Lord, because [Col. 0552B] thou wast angry with me; thy wrath has turned away, and thou hast comforted me” [Note: [Col. 0551] Isa. 12].

Far be it, sweetest Father, that there should be any murmuring against God or neighbour, because, in the Prophet’s testimony, “It is good to wait in silence for the saving help of God” [Note: [Col. 0551] Lam. 3]. For your strength shall be in silence. I pray that the Lord’s scourges, which seem bitter to you, may become sweet in his love. “For all things work together for good to those who love [God]” [Note: [Col. 0551] Rom. 8]; nor will he allow you to be tempted beyond what you can bear, but will make with the temptation also the way of escape [Note: [Col. 0551] 1 Cor. 10].

## LETTER CCXLII. TO G., ELECT OF ST MARY’S

To the reverend father and lord G., by God’s grace elect of St Mary’s, PETER, etc., greetings in him who sends forth a root in [Col. 0552C] his chosen ones.

When the abbot of blessed memory, named Philip, paid the tribute of death—for, in the Prophet’s testimony, all of us have made a covenant with death, because we have within ourselves the sentence of death [Note: [Col. 0551] 2 Cor. 1]—you, dearest Father, were chosen by your brethren as abbot. For from ancient days sons have been born to the Church in place of fathers; and according to Hosea’s word, “The Lord raises up prophets from among the sons, and Nazarites from among the young men” [Note: [Col. 0551] Amos 2]. Thus, when old friends vanish, new shoots grow together for the later and sweeter fruits of friendship.

I rejoice in your glory, because great men in the Lord’s name dwell in your land. The Lord has magnified his mercy toward you—if indeed it is mercy and not [Col. 0552D] rather some trial, so that the gain of honour may one day turn into lamentation. Yet it is a late lamentation to say, “Having raised me up, thou hast dashed me down” [Note: [Col. 0551] Ps. 101]. It was far safer to live alongside others than to preside over them; nevertheless, it is highly meritorious if you preside in such a way as to benefit them.

Father dear to me, while you served in a lesser office, you were often a stumbling-block to yourself, frequently a burden to yourself, and always in danger. But now, set upon a lampstand, you have entered the arena of a doubtful outcome. For if you weigh the possession of responsibilities and the danger to souls, “without are fightings, within are fears” [Col. 0553A]; according to Solomon’s saying: “You have entered into a crowd and bound upon yourself double sins” [Note: [Col. 0553] Ecclus. 7]. Many have preferred to lie hidden beneath a bushel and to shut up the good of inward glory within the bounds of conscience, cherishing in the bosom of memory that prophetic word: “My secret is for me, my secret is for me” [Note: [Col. 0553] Isa. 24].

Most loving Father, you must be drawn away into vain affairs, labour for others, be anxious with Martha, postpone that one thing necessary, and pass from Mary’s leisure into a certain labyrinth of the soul. Yet let not outward concern so seize you that the abyss of worldly cares swallows your soul, for which Christ died. Therefore always bear within yourself a certain inward vigilance directed against yourself, so that a mind gathered into itself may not flow away to external things, and may not [Col. 0553B] attend to what appears outside or sounds outwardly. Among many, you will be alone with yourself, becoming one of those whom blessed Job describes when he says: “These are they who build solitudes for themselves, so that they may not hear the voice of exaction.”

Minister, then, so that your ministry may not be blamed; regard yourself as the servant of each individual, and be lord of all. Let the contemplative and active life alternate their offices in you in such a way that you have no idle time. The spirit is better than the body, and bodily exercise profits little; but godliness is profitable for all things, having promise of the life that now is and of that which is to come [Note: [Col. 0553] 1 Tim. 4]. Therefore strive after the better gifts [Note: [Col. 0553] 1 Cor. 12]. For flesh and blood shall not possess the kingdom of God: “The flesh profits nothing” [Note: [Col. 0553] John 6]; [Col. 0553C] but the fruits of the spirit are charity, joy, peace, patience, long-suffering, faith, modesty, gentleness, self-control, and chastity [Note: [Col. 0553] Gal. 5].

It is good to be anxious with Martha, but it is more peaceful to sit at the Lord’s feet with Mary [Note: [Col. 0553] Luke 10], to set the Lord always before your eyes, to be ever at leisure for him, and to see how sweet the Lord is. Therefore, after you have arranged what brotherly necessity requires, descend into the gardens of spices, that you may feed upon spiritual delights and gather the most welcome lilies of joys. For when you have released your soul into rest, let no one, I pray, awaken it until it so desires; nor fear lest anyone too hastily empty you of embraces and draw you away from the breasts of holy delight.

You know that those who profess the holy Rule, if they diligently involve themselves in secular [Col. 0553D] affairs, suffer great losses in spiritual exercise. A ship, though it does not immediately perish amid stormy whirlwinds, nevertheless loses its cargo, and thus reaches port empty and bare. Your brethren have chosen you: be among them as one of them. Build them up by brevity in action, by countenance, dress, and gesture. Show yourself so lovable and adaptable that your whole manner of life may build others up unto salvation. Do what is expedient not only for yourself but for many.

Never live apart, so that you have a fox’s den; [Col. 0554A] nor a nest like the birds, nor money-bags like Judas. From my earliest impulses I have been moved, venerable Father, by your dispositions, breathing forth gentle fellowship, seasoned with humility toward companions, and shaped toward every kind of propriety. It is a common saying that honours either change men, or rather reveal them. I pray that your present administration may never decline from that nobility of character. Let no title of self-exaltation or glory insinuate itself because of your office. If you must glory, glory in your weaknesses, so that Christ’s power may dwell in you. For if you reckon yourself weak for this burden, less fit and less worthy, that very objection you make against yourself will grow strong unto grace, abound unto fruit, and be increased unto a crown. The Lord of glory himself says: “If I seek my own glory, [Col. 0554B] my glory is nothing” [Note: [Col. 0553] John 8]. “You seek glory from one another,” he says, “and do not desire the glory which comes from God alone” [Note: [Col. 0553] John 5]. “Not unto us, O Lord, not unto us, but unto thy name give glory” [Note: [Col. 0553] Ps. 113].

But you, Father, if you wish to glory in God, know that you are foolish unless those who glory glory in the Lord. Ascribe to the Lord, not to yourself, that glory which is the testimony of your conscience; for, to use the Apostle’s words, “What hast thou that thou hast not received?” [Note: [Col. 0553] 1 Cor. 4]. If, therefore, at the voices of flatterers the breeze of favour blows upon your ears, let that apostolic saying be in your heart and on your lips: “By the grace of God I am what I am” [Note: [Col. 0553] 1 Cor. 15]. Nothing is more familiar or more confidently admitted into the presence of divine majesty, nor more pleasing, than true humility. The very author of humility daily confesses himself [Col. 0554C] humble and gentle. Let not the foot of pride come upon you; but, the greater you are, humble yourself in all things, and regard this administration as a burden, not an honour. Uproot every stirring of itching pride by Solomon’s saying: “The mighty shall suffer mighty torments, and judgment shall quickly and terribly be made upon those who rule” [Note: [Col. 0553] Wisd. 6].

Always consider that God will require of you a most exact account of all that is his. “The wicked has provoked God,” for he has said in his heart, “He will not require it” [Note: [Col. 0553] Ps. 10]. But God says through Malachi: “Behold, I will require my sheep at the hand of the shepherd” [Note: [Col. 0553] Ezek. 34]. The Lord says, “I will require”; the wicked says, “He will not require.” Whose assertion do you think will prevail? It is the word of Isaiah the Prophet: “The Lord of hosts has sworn, saying: Surely, as I have thought, so shall it be; and as I have purposed, so shall it come to pass” [Note: [Col. 0553] Isa. 14].

Do not, [Col. 0554D] I pray, emulate those who do evil [Note: [Col. 0553] Ps. 36]. There are abbots who seek their own interests, not those of Jesus Christ [Note: [Col. 0553] Phil. 2]: “By their fruits you shall know them” [Note: [Col. 0553] Matt. 7]. They entirely neglect the care of souls, and count it the chief object of their office to enlarge and embellish the property of their church through tillage and buildings, by right and wrong alike, to their own ruin and that of those belonging to them. Yet the souls which had conceived the fruit of salvation through the spirit of fear, they ruinously procure as an abortion, so that the Prophet’s saving word may fittingly be applied to them: “They ripped open the pregnant women of Gilead, that they might enlarge [Col. 0555A] their borders” [Note: [Col. 0555] Amos 1]. These are the men driven by the spirit of this world, the spirit of dizziness and error.

It is better for you to enlarge your household in morals than in possessions; better to fill heaven than a granary. You can do this without omitting the other [Note: [Col. 0555] Luke 11]. But cut down early the lethargic shoots of vices which have sprouted from the negligence of certain of your predecessors, lest fruitless suckers, which never bear fruit, proclaim their new growth by the forked branches of their mistletoe. Do everything with counsel as your companion. Yet do not believe every spirit, but first test whether it is from God [Note: [Col. 0555] 1 John 4].

Always, however, be more concerned about your sheep than about your estates; put your trust in God alone, not in the familiarity of princes. For “Cursed is he who trusts in man” [Note: [Col. 0555] Jer. 17]; and according to the Wise Man’s sentence: “The name of the Lord is exceeding strength” [Col. 0555B] [Note: [Col. 0555] Prov. 15]. But knowing that you endure grievous troubles through the continual assault of the crafty enemy, and that the help of sacred Scripture is therefore necessary to us—its frequent reading frustrates hostile attacks and calms the tempests of boiling temptations with a kind of serenity of soul—you repeatedly request with earnestness the book of Origen, whom you call one of the four.

I know that scarcely half an hour of cloistered life passes without temptation. Therefore the regular warfare requires spiritual weapons, concerning which the Apostle, writing to the Corinthians, says: “The weapons of your warfare are not carnal, but powerful through God for the destruction of strongholds, destroying every height that exalts itself against the knowledge of God, bringing every understanding captive [Col. 0555C] into obedience to Christ” [Note: [Col. 0555] 2 Cor. 10].

Sacred reading is therefore necessary for you. It is the table of the tabernacle, placed on the north, whence every evil is opened up; the Psalmist indicates this when he says: “Thou hast prepared before me a table against those who trouble me” [Note: [Col. 0555] Ps. 22]. Isaiah speaks of this table and of spiritual arms [Note: [Col. 0555] ch. 21]: “You contemplate the table with discernment from the watchtower; arise, princes, and seize the shield.” Sacred reading is food, because Truth testifies: “Man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God” [Note: [Col. 0555] Matt. 4]. By this food we hope and live. “The words which I speak to you,” says the Lord, “are spirit and life” [Note: [Col. 0555] John 8]. Christ himself, in the wilderness, used the sole certain testimony of sacred utterance against all the devil’s temptations [Note: [Col. 0555] Matt. 4].

If therefore camps stand against you, [Col. 0555D] arm yourselves with the shield of good will and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God. If your knees are weakened, your hands slackened, your feet shaken, or your steps poured out, trust that “the heavens were established by the word of the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0555] Ps. 32]. If, under burning compunctions and the hidden clouds of the heart, the soul grows cold or numb; if it hardens against tears; if heaven has become bronze to it, so that spiritual dew or rain does not descend upon Mount Gilboa—devote yourselves to sacred Scripture. For the Lord will send forth his word and melt them; he will send forth his spirit and waters will flow—indeed [Col. 0556A] his spices will flow—that the repute of your holiness may pour forth the fragrance of aromatic sweetness. The field of my exhortation is very broad; but the pressing necessity of occupations constrains this letter into brevity and compels me toward other matters.

## LETTER CCXLIII

To the venerable man and friend in Christ S., prior of C., PETER of Blois, archdeacon of London, greetings.

You asked me to set down in writing what those antiphons mean which, as Christ’s Nativity approaches, are sung with a special prerogative at the *Magnificat*: “O Wisdom,” “O Adonai,” and the like. I answered you orally that I had learned from great teachers that the aforesaid antiphons were, as it were, the voices of patriarchs and prophets [Col. 0556B] desiring and asking God to hasten his coming and rescue them from the enemy’s power and the distress of their prison. Yet I could not satisfy your request unless I confirmed by the authorities of the holy Fathers the answer I had given you verbally. What I learned without pretence, I share with you without envy.

The tearful voice of one longing for the Lord’s coming was: “Do you think I shall endure? Do you think I shall see? Do you think that Nativity will find me here?” Hence, concerning the verse, “With expectation I waited for the Lord, and he inclined unto me and heard my prayers” [Note: [Col. 0555] Ps. 39], it is read that the ancient Fathers obtained Christ’s incarnation through their prayers. Isaiah says [Note: [Col. 0555] ch. 64], “O Lord, would that thou wouldst rend the heavens and come down!” and adds: [Col. 0556C] “Thou didst rend them and come down.” And David says: “Bow the heavens and come down” [Note: [Col. 0555] Ps. 143]. Authority also says that the merits of the holy Fathers drew the Lord down from heaven.

The Lord had indeed delayed his Christ because of the hardness and unbelief of certain people; for God resists the proud and graciously hears the humble [Note: [Col. 0555] Jas. 4]. Further, on the verse, “He hath regarded the prayer of the poor and hath not despised their petitions” [Note: [Col. 0555] Ps. 101], the expositor’s words are these: here he speaks in the person of the faithful, who, filled with the spirit of humility, prayed that Christ might come. Likewise, concerning the verse, “How long, O Lord, wilt thou forget me unto the end?” [Note: [Col. 0555] Ps. 12], it is said that here it is first expounded in the person of the ancient Fathers awaiting and desiring Christ’s coming.

Finally, as we read in the Book of Kings [Note: [Col. 0555] 3 Kings 10], [Col. 0556D] King Solomon gave the Queen of Sheba whatever she asked, and other things which she did not ask, because Christ grants his Church not only those things which it asks, but also those which it does not dare to ask. Likewise Origen, speaking in the person of the Church in his commentary on the *Song of Songs*, says: “While the Bridegroom sends me kisses through Moses and the prophets, let him come himself; let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth” [Note: [Col. 0555] Song 1]. And the Father heard the bride and sent her his Son. Likewise, concerning Isaiah’s verse [Note: [Col. 0555] ch. 12], “I will give thanks to thee, O Lord, because thou hast heard me,” we read that the righteous of old devoutly implored Christ’s help.

Therefore it was not without reason, but by God’s deep counsel, established that the desires of the ancients concerning Christ’s first coming—which they awaited and sought with pure affections, frequent groans, burning devotions, and sighs—should be recited in the Church with such solemn chant and privileged acclamation. Thus, strengthened by the support and instructed by the examples of the ancient Fathers, we may receive him as he comes into us in his second coming, so that in his third coming we may not fear him coming against us. For in his first coming he came humble; in the second he comes into us, desirable and most sweet, as Truth testifies of him in the Gospel: “He who loves the words of God, my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our dwelling with him” [Note: [Col. 0557] John 14].

He comes into many who, once they have received him, cast him out through the foulness of their iniquity [Col. 0557B]. For it is written that three things drive a guest from his house: a quarrelsome woman, which is the concupiscence of the flesh; a dripping which falls from above to below, that is, pride which fell from heaven; and smoke, which is the concupiscence of the eyes, blinding the eyes of the flesh. We also read that a guest is more shamefully cast out than not admitted. This concerns the first and second comings; but of the third it is written: “He is a man, and who shall see him? Who can stand with devouring fire, or who shall stand amid everlasting burnings? For fire shall go before him and burn up his enemies round about; their worm shall not die, and their fire shall not be quenched” [Note: [Col. 0557] Isa. 66].

Through [Col. 0557C] the plaintive voices of the ancient Fathers, and through their prayers and merits, they are said to have first obtained Christ’s coming. Yet very many hold that the incarnation of the Redeemer must be ascribed not to human merits but to God’s grace alone. Hence, in the Epistle to the Romans [Note: [Col. 0557] ch. 1], on the passage, “who was made to him of the seed of David,” Authority says that the Apostle preferred to say that Christ was made of the seed of David, who had been circumcised, rather than of the seed of righteous Abraham, so that he might be believed to have been born of the Virgin not by merit but through God’s grace. Haimo says: God can do many things which no one could ask or understand, such as that God should become man or suffer death for man. Likewise, on Isaiah’s words [Note: [Col. 0557] ch. 9], “A son is given to us,” Authority adds: “He was given to us [Col. 0557D] by God’s grace alone.”

The scrupulous question is often raised whether the Blessed Virgin merited the incarnation of Christ, since through her we merited to receive the Lord Jesus Christ, the author of life. This must be understood thus: “through whom we merited to receive” means “through whose merit we received the author of life.” For, in consenting to the angelic annunciation, she appears to have merited to become the Lord’s mother; moreover, she prayed that the Lord might be born and that the angel’s promise might be fulfilled, saying: “Be it done to me according to thy word” [Note: [Col. 0557] Luke 1]. She prayed devoutly, for herself, for salvation, and perseveringly, that what she had conceived in herself might be fulfilled.

There is, moreover, in theology [Col. 0558A] a general rule and irrefutable argument: if a righteous person asks something of God devoutly, for himself or herself, for salvation, and perseveringly, that person deserves to be heard. We may therefore safely say that she merited that the Lord should be born from her. Yet “merit” is used in three senses: first, for a cause—merit in justice is the reason why a person is saved; it is also used for requirement, for our misery required that the merciful God, who considers labour and pain, should blot out our guilt by his Passion. Hence it is written: “O happy fault of Adam, which merited to have such and so great a Redeemer” [Note: [Col. 0557] Office of the Church, in the chant *Exsultet*]. Merit is also used for worthiness, as when the Virgin is said to have merited to bear from her own flesh God’s Son. For this reason she was prefigured by the signs and oracles of the patriarchs, desired beforehand [Col. 0558B] and foretold by the prophets, most dutifully greeted by the angel, consecrated by the power of the Holy Spirit, and in his visitation most abundantly endowed beforehand with divine gifts.

Certainly the Virgin who was to bear the Holy of Holies had to be holy. For just as, among the other members, the eye alone is capable of receiving light, so among all women the Virgin alone was found able to enclose in her body the magnificence of divine majesty; for, by the Apostle’s testimony, “in him dwelt bodily all the fullness of divinity” [Note: [Col. 0557] Col. 2]. Accordingly, the last of the eight antiphons most fittingly belongs to the Blessed Virgin: “O Virgin of virgins!” Thus, speaking to the daughters of Jerusalem—that is, the angelic powers and holy souls—she says: “Daughters [Col. 0558C] of Jerusalem, what do you marvel at? What you behold is a divine ministry, truly a divine ministry hidden from the ages, which God revealed at the fitting time: that is, when the fullness of time came, in which God sent his Son.”

Speaking of this mystery or sacrament, the Apostle says: “Great is this sacrament of godliness, hidden from the ages, manifested in the flesh, justified in the spirit, revealed to angels, believed in the world, taken up in glory” [Note: [Col. 0557] 1 Tim. 3]. Therefore the chant of these antiphons is like a voice of proclamation and an awakening of our minds, so that we may sing beforehand, as it were, an invitatory for the Lord’s Nativity; and so that, according to the multitude of sorrows in our hearts, God’s consolations may gladden the souls of the afflicted, and we who were in darkness [Col. 0558D] may meet our Saviour, saying: “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord; the Lord is God, and he has shone upon us” [Note: [Col. 0557] Ps. 117].

Accordingly, in the first antiphon, “O Wisdom,” the devotion of the ancients asks that God’s wisdom may come to them and teach them the way of prudence. In the second, they call upon Adonai—that is, our Lord—the fire who appeared to Moses in the fire [Note: [Col. 0557] Exod. 3] and was to send Moses for Israel’s redemption, asking that he himself may now come and redeem them. In the third, they invoke him who is the Root of Jesse—that is, Christ—of whom the promise was made in the figure of Isaac to his father Abraham, and in the figure of Solomon to his father David, son of Jesse. In the fourth, they humbly [Col. 0559A] pray that Christ, who opens and no one shuts, who saves and no one condemns, may come and lead them out from the outer prison of hell. In the fifth, they cry to the Son of God, who is the splendour of eternal light and the Sun of righteousness, that he may come and illuminate those sitting in inner darkness and in the shadow of death. In the sixth, in the person of the Gentile people, they cry out and beg with affection that he may deign to join the two peoples, as two walls, in the one corner-stone and save them. In the seventh, with humble rejoicing they entreat that he who was called by God the Father through Isaiah Emmanuel, that is, “the Lord with us,” may come as our king and lawgiver, sent to us by God, and save us. Finally, because many of them, by God’s inspiration, had known beforehand that the mystery of human salvation would be fulfilled through the son of a Virgin, [Col. 0559B] they direct the eighth antiphon—which, for a definite reason, we mentioned incidentally beforehand—to the Virgin of virgins, that she may proclaim to the powers of heaven and holy souls the saving mystery of divine wisdom.

I have run briefly through these songs of the ancients and the evening antiphons that precede the Lord’s Nativity. Yet for this reason I have neither omitted nor delayed writing and singing what I believed to concern the honour of God and the Church and the edification of Christ’s people. I know that it is far sweeter and more fruitful to think and write of things which work toward the salvation of the soul than of those by which we pursue worldly splendour and secular glory. Yet there is a middle course between these two: that in writing we reverently [Col. 0559C] keep God before our eyes, and instruct the Christian people in the building up of the soul by wholesome counsels. Therefore, according to sacred Scripture, we must do these things without omitting the others. For although I have neither golden nor silver vessels nor precious stones to offer for the work of the tabernacle, I nevertheless offer, with the poor widow, two small coins: honour to God and edification to the Christian people.

Nor do I presume to appear empty before God with a song. The ancients sang with the moderns a new song, though their song was then old: namely, Christ yet to be incarnate. We too sing the same song, but new; for him whom they sang as to be incarnate, we sing as incarnate [Col. 0560A]. For it is written: “Those who went before and those who followed sang: Hosanna in the highest!” [Note: [Col. 0559] Mark 11]. The shadow of the ancients has been changed for us into light, the figure into truth, hope into certainty, and promise into the full possession of the inheritance.

If I am to be blamed—indeed, since I am blameworthy in many ways—and acknowledge the fault of my frivolity in songs and rhythms, I rebuke myself. But you who are spiritual, I ask, correct such frivolity in a spirit of gentleness. Nevertheless the prophets used human voices and musical instruments, and wrote in metre. For metres and songs move human hearts more powerfully; and where ordinary speech is ineffective, an elegant thought clothed in refined words sometimes effectively builds up toward salvation.

Out of love for you I had wished to take up the eight burdens which Isaiah sets forth and arranges, and to fit the same eight, by a certain proportion, as reciprocal opposites to the eight Beatitudes. Going further, I had resolved in my mind that the eight antiphons beginning with “O!” should correspond, as it were with a most sweet kiss and agreement, to eight paths leading to the eight Beatitudes, and through Christ should offer the rod of the oppressor and the yoke of his burden, as in the day of Midian. For Christ is that ash-baked bread which, in the figure of Gideon, overthrew the camp of Midian [Note: [Col. 0559] Judg. 16]. He himself was tormented and baked beneath the ashes of our mortality in the oven of the cross; but that bread which came down from heaven was preserved through the glory of the resurrection, by which he shook from his flesh the ashes of passibility [Col. 0560C].

But while this intention was burning more fervently in my heart, a certain very great and prudent man told me that he had seen and read a treatise by Master Achard of Saint-Victor on Isaiah’s eight burdens, in which the burdens were removed through the prayers and desires of the ancients and the eight Beatitudes succeeded them. I, however, yield to Master Achard with the reverence and deference which Statius, at the end of the *Thebaid*, pays to Virgil, saying to my soul:

> Do not attempt to equal the divine *Aeneid*;
>
> But follow far behind, and ever venerate its footsteps.

[Col. 0559]

## SERMONS OF PETER OF BLOIS

*(Works, edited by J. A. Gilles, Oxford and London, 1846, octavo, vol. IV.)*

## SERMON I: ON THE ADVENT OF THE LORD

“While all things held the midst of silence, and night in its course had passed the middle of its journey, the almighty Word came from the royal thrones.” [Note: [Col. 0559D] Wisdom 18.]

[Col. 0560D]

From ancient days, after the Lord had cried [Col. 0561A] to the first transgressor, “Adam, where are you?” [Note: [Col. 0561] Gen. 3], and after Abel’s blood had cried from the earth, the human race was silent, because death had entered into it through sin. Humanity was silent: dead in respect of gratuitous gifts, wounded in natural powers. So injured and weakened was man that there was in him neither voice nor feeling. And I understand this to have been the first silence.

Moses came, and the Law was given. The Law indeed showed the measure of weakness, but did not show its remedy. “I did not know,” says the Apostle, “what sin was, except through the Law.” [Note: [Col. 0561] Rom. 7.] Therefore, once people recognized their wounds, they began to cry out and seek medicine; and thus the first silence was broken. But when the sick considered that salvation was not in the Law—for the Law justified no one and led no one to perfection—[Col. 0561B] they at last, worn out by long expectation and weariness after their cry, fell silent. This is the middle silence.

This silence, moreover, was broken in three ways: by a voice, by a word, and by a song. By a voice: through him who says, “I am the voice of one crying in the wilderness: Prepare the way of the Lord,” and so forth. [Note: [Col. 0561] Matt. 3.] By a word: for “the almighty Word came from the royal thrones.” By a song: for at the birth of the incarnate Word the angels sang, “Glory to God in the highest.” [Note: [Col. 0561] Luke 2.] Moses had delivered many words, but none of them was almighty. For they failed in their promise and could not accomplish what they declared. But “by the Word of the Lord the heavens were established”; and the almighty Word not only promised or spoke, but did whatever he willed. [Col. 0561C]

The third silence will be in the regeneration, when the Son of Man sits upon the throne of his majesty. [Note: [Col. 0561] Matt. 19.] Then the Lord will wipe tears from the eyes of his saints, and there will no longer be crying or pain. [Note: [Col. 0561] Rev. 21.] Then the righteous person will obtain rest from his labours, [Note: [Col. 0561] Rev. 14.] and “his place will be made in peace.” [Note: [Col. 0561] Ps. 75.] And for those whose strength, according to Isaiah’s word, lay in silence and hope, [Note: [Col. 0561] Isa. 30.] there will be joy and peace in eternal silence.

Therefore, as Solomon says, “There is a time for silence and a time for speaking”: [Note: [Col. 0561] Eccl. 3.] a time for silence, while all things held the midst of silence; a time for speaking, when John cries in the wilderness, “Prepare the way of the Lord; make straight the paths of our God.” [Note: [Col. 0561] Matt. 3.] John had withdrawn and fled into the solitude. He preferred solitude to anxious care, peace to disturbance, quiet to tumult, [Col. 0561D] and the wilderness to the city. He cries in the wilderness, knowing that the farther he was from the throng of people, the freer he would be from the contagion of sins.

Observe, brothers, that from the times of Elijah and the other prophets the wilderness was consecrated to holiness, so that it might be, as it were, God’s more secluded bridal chamber on earth and the familiar audience-chamber of the Holy Spirit. John, a prophet and more than a prophet, succeeded the prophets; through his dwelling there, great reverence and honour accrued to the wilderness.

Jesus came also, and dedicated to penitence the wilderness which he had consecrated by a fast of forty [Col. 0562A] days. There, when tempted, he refuted the malice of the tempter, so that whoever flees into solitude need no longer fear the enemy’s ambushes, but may have, in a place of terror, a place of safety, and may find in solitude a city to dwell in. He who fasted in the wilderness fed the crowds in the wilderness and there bestowed abundantly manna—that is, the bread of angels—so that they might confess the Lord’s mercies and that those who follow Christ in the wilderness might no longer despair and say, “What shall we eat or what shall we drink?”

He who satisfies the empty soul and the hungry soul with good things, who gives their food to the beasts and to the young ravens that call upon him, [Note: [Col. 0561] Ps. 146,] will [Col. 0562B] not abandon in the wilderness the soul that is deserted there—the soul which has betrothed itself to Christ through the obligation of a vow and the bond of profession. Rather, in the abundance of his mercy, he will minister to it and say: “I remember you, in pity for your youth and the love of your betrothal, when you followed me in the wilderness.” [Note: [Col. 0561] Jer. 2.] Therefore, in a land of salt, in a land of terror and vast solitude, in a land which hitherto has produced nothing but thorns and thistles, the Lord will cause grace and blessing to spring forth. Those souls, the beauty of the wilderness, will grow rich; the Lord will make the wilderness for it like delights and solitude like a watered garden.

In this wilderness, in this solitude, some sit alone, yet are not silent: a crowd of worldly cares clamours around them, although it is written of the religious person, “He shall sit solitary and raise [Col. 0562C] himself above himself.” [Note: [Col. 0561] Lam. 3.] He raises himself above himself who prepares within himself the way for the Lord. Therefore, brothers, in this wilderness the voice of one crying is heard: “Prepare the way of the Lord; make straight the paths of our God.” [Note: [Col. 0561] Luke 3.]

Would that, in the wilderness of my heart, this voice might be heard and the silence in which I lie like one wounded and sleeping among the tombs might be broken! Would that I might hear not only the voice preaching repentance, but the Word himself; and might hear what the Lord God says within me! Would that he himself might speak in my heart, and that I might speak to my Lord! Long have I been silent, humbled, and silent even from good things. [Note: [Col. 0561] Ps. 38.] Would that I had been silent from evil things! But I am not one who can say, “That I might not sin with my tongue.” [Note: [Col. 0561] Ibid.] I have often received reproach against my neighbours; and when I ought to have ordered [Col. 0562D] my words in judgment according to the observance of justice, my speech, suborned by the trickery of a crafty man, became an instrument of calumny and the overthrow of justice, and, like a sharp sword, of the killing of my soul; and my tongue fashioned deceits.

But now I am silent toward God, toward the world, and toward myself: toward God, whose praise I do not have in heart and mouth; toward the world, whose malice I condemn neither by word nor deed; toward myself, because I do not accuse my sins by confession, redeem them by satisfaction, or make recompense through good works. This is the silence in which I more willingly hear the wisdom of this world, which is foolishness with God, [Note: [Col. 0563] 1 Cor. 3,] than the word of God and the Law of the Most High. Perhaps this is what Solomon indicates when he says: “The words of the wise are heard in silence more than the cry of a ruler among fools.” [Note: [Col. 0563] Eccl. 9.]

Cry out, I pray, you who are the voice of one crying. Cry; do not cease. Like a trumpet lift up your voice; [Note: [Col. 0563] Isa. 58.] cry out, thunder, flash, and blaze, perhaps he who sleeps may rise, perhaps he who has become almost wholly deaf to the Lord may bestir himself to rise. Many also are weak, and many sleep; and, to use Jeremiah’s words, “Their ears are uncircumcised, and they cannot hear.” [Note: [Col. 0563] Jer. 6.] Cry out, I pray, herald of the Lord, that they may prepare the way of the Lord and make straight the paths of our God. [Note: [Col. 0563] Matt. 3.]

And what is this, brothers? Is it not from eternity [Col. 0563B] that John admonishes us to prepare the Lord’s ways and make straight the paths of our God? Are not his ways straight from age to age? Concerning the straightness of his ways, the Lord disputes with the ungodly; for, as the prophet testifies, “The ungodly said in his heart: ‘The Lord’s way is not straight.’” [Note: [Col. 0563] Ezek. 18.] But the Lord most firmly rebukes and refutes him: “Are my ways not straight? Are not rather your ways crooked?” says the Lord.

We know indeed, and cannot deny, that the Lord’s ways are beautiful and all his paths peaceable. [Note: [Col. 0563] Prov. 3.] He who says, “The way of the Lord my God is undefiled; his path unstained,” confessed this with us. [Note: [Col. 0563] Ps. 17.] The Lord’s way is so straight, as the prophet testifies, that even fools do not go astray upon it. [Note: [Col. 0563] Isa. 35.] Certainly I have seen many wise people wandering in this life. For since the wisdom [Col. 0563C] of this world is earthly, animal, and demonic, [Note: [Col. 0563] Jas. 3,] it is not surprising if those who are wise in that manner wander and do not know the way to the eternal city.

But that folly by which it pleased God to save believers [Note: [Col. 0563] 1 Cor. 21]—that is what does not wander; that is what knows the way which God has hidden from the wise and prudent of this age and revealed to the foolish and little ones. [Note: [Col. 0563] Matt. 11.] O Lord, you have prepared the straight paths of the way of your commandments: direct my way in your sight. And what is it to straighten the Lord’s path except to correct one’s own life?
