He prepares a way for the Lord who humbles his heart before God and purges by penitence the sins in which he has offended.

We must therefore consider with all diligence that nothing crooked may be found in [Col. 0563D] our wills; nothing rough in our conduct; nothing dark, slippery, or distorted: crooked through malice, rough through impatience, dark through ignorance, slippery through inconstancy, distorted through discord and the unevenness of life. Some are always rough, slippery, and distorted; among their brothers they are like snakes among eels, ravens among doves, thorns among lilies, and briars among roses. “Ruin and misery are in their ways, because they have not known the way of peace.” [Note: [Col. 0563] Ps. 13.] The way of such people is darkness and slipperiness, with the angel of the Lord pursuing [Col. 0564A] them. [Note: [Col. 0563] Ps. 34.] I have very often seen people of this sort—restless and quarrelsome—severely scourged by the Lord. For against their malice the Lord sends assaults through evil angels. [Note: [Col. 0563] Ps. 77.] Why was he contrary and insulting to God and his brother? Let him be handed over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh; and let him who made himself burdensome and intolerable to others become burdensome to himself. This is what is read in Proverbs: “An evil man always seeks quarrels; but a cruel angel shall be sent against him.” [Note: [Col. 0563] Prov. 17.]

Therefore, if anything in us is dark, let it be enlightened through confession; if slippery, let it be made firm in Christ’s love; if distorted, let it be directed to the equity of the divine rule; if rough, let it be made smooth by the gentleness of spiritual grace. Thus the Lord will [Col. 0564B] direct the meek and teach the gentle his ways. [Note: [Col. 0563] Ps. 24.]

If the Lord’s ways seem narrow to anyone, let him not wonder. The Lord’s ways require travellers who are slender and unencumbered, not weighed down by the mass of earthly care. They are narrow because of the constraint of poverty; yet they seem exceedingly broad to those who love the Lord and look, according to the Apostle’s word, to the rewarder of eternal salvation. [Note: [Col. 0563] Heb. 11.] Such was Moses, of whom the Apostle writes that “he considered the reproach of Christ greater riches than the treasures of Egypt; for,” says the Apostle, “he looked to the rewarder.” [Note: [Col. 0563] Ibid.] This is also what is read in Ezekiel: that the two cherubim looked, with each face, toward the palm tree. [Note: [Col. 0563] Ezek. 41.]

For in everything we do, whether temporal or spiritual, we ought to direct the eyes of our intention toward the rewarder of life. [Col. 0564C] If the righteous person, who lives by faith, considers how great are the things which the Lord prepares for those who love him; if he considers the end of every completion, he will cry and say, “You have enlarged my steps, O Lord,” [Note: [Col. 0563] Ps. 17.] and, “Your commandment is exceedingly broad.” [Note: [Col. 0563] Ps. 118.] For the Lord’s way is widened when the soul delights in the greatness of the reward and the shortness of the labour.

Let a person therefore go to the ends of the roads; for there those are taken up who are commanded to be brought to the wedding feast. [Note: [Col. 0563] Matt. 22.] At the limits and ends of the ways he will receive heavenly things for worldly things, eternal things for transitory things, and rest and endless glory for temporal labour. Therefore rejoice, brothers, and sing in the Lord’s ways: “For great is the glory of the Lord.” [Note: [Col. 0563] Ps. 137.] Rejoice while awaiting the blessed [Col. 0564D] hope and the appearing of the glory of the great God. [Note: [Col. 0563] Titus 2.] For the Lord is near, to render you the reward for your labours; and you who have kept hard paths for Christ will receive from Christ unfading and eternal crowns. May Christ Jesus deign to grant these to you—he who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit, God through all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON II: ON THE SAME ADVENT

“I looked in a vision of the night, and behold, one like a Son of Man came in the clouds of heaven and came as far as the Ancient of Days; and they presented him before him. And he gave him power and honour and a kingdom; and his power is an eternal power, and his kingdom shall not be destroyed.” [Note: [Col. 0565] Dan. 7.]

[Col. 0565A]

Daniel, inflamed by desire for the Lord’s advent—whence he was called by the angel “a man of desires” [Note: [Col. 0565] Dan. 9.]—poured out his soul, that he might pass into the place of wondrous mystery and see the sacrament of the Lord’s Incarnation, hidden from the saints, as the Apostle says. [Note: [Col. 0565] Eph. 3.] Hence he looked in a vision of the night.

There is a vision of night, a vision of day, and a vision of light: the nocturnal vision is before grace; the vision of day, under grace; the vision of light, in glory. The prophets and patriarchs saw in a vision of night. Thus it is written: [Col. 0565B] “You spoke in a vision to your holy ones and said: ‘I have set help,’” and so forth. [Note: [Col. 0565] Ps. 88.] Of the second vision, which occurred in the apostles in the time of grace, Paul says: “Beholding the glory of the Lord, we are transformed into the same image from glory to glory, as by the Spirit of the Lord.” [Note: [Col. 0565] 2 Cor. 3.]

Now we see spiritually as though in a mirror, in an enigma; but when the vision of light comes, the righteous will shine like the sun in the sight of God. Then they will see light in light, and, with purified eyes, will behold the light which a mortal eye could not endure.

“And behold, one like a Son of Man came in the clouds of heaven.” There are three clouds: obscurity in the prophets; depth in the divine counsels; and the hidden, unheard-of fruitfulness [Col. 0565C] of virginity. Of the cloud of the prophets it is written: “Dark water in the clouds of the air.” [Note: [Col. 0565] Ps. 17.] Of the cloud of God’s counsels we read: “Drop down dew, heavens, from above, and let the clouds rain down the Just One.” [Note: [Col. 0565] Isa. 45.] Of the cloud of virginity and hidden fruitfulness the prophet says: “The Lord shall enter Egypt upon a light and white cloud.” [Note: [Col. 0565] Isa. 49.]

In these clouds he came as though a Son of Man. He fittingly says, “as though a Son of Man,” because he who was the Son of God from eternity was only temporally the Son of Man. He was not yet the Son of Man; but he who was soon to become the Son of Man was already regarded as though he were a Son of Man. If anyone attends carefully to Daniel’s words, he will discover most plainly in them Christ’s Incarnation, in that the Son of Man came; Christ’s Passion, in that they presented him; Christ’s Resurrection, in that [Col. 0565D] eternal honour and power and an incorruptible kingdom were given him; and his Ascension, in that he came to the Ancient of Days—for this was his return to the Father.

Yet, because the other mysteries have their own times, let us say something about the advent now before us. Not Daniel alone, but all the other prophets with him, cry unanimously concerning the Lord: “For he comes.” [Note: [Col. 0565] Ps. 95.] What then remains except that we should go out to meet him, as the Apostle testifies? [Note: [Col. 0565] 1 Thess. 4.] He is the one who enters in order to save the nations. Let us [Col. 0566A] therefore meet our Saviour. Let us greet from afar him who sends salvation to Jacob and gives salvation to kings. For he did not wish to greet us from so great a distance, but to save us nearby.

I know that, when he comes, the lawgiver will give blessing; he will prosper in the things for which he was sent, and whatever he does will prosper. [Note: [Col. 0565] Ps. 1.] Let us therefore go and come before his face in confession. [Note: [Col. 0565] Ps. 94.] If any brother is weak, let him raise himself above himself; forgetting what is behind, let him stretch himself out toward what is before, eagerly awaiting the coming Lord. Thus, as we all meet him with one mind, let us say: “O Lord, grant good success!” [Note: [Col. 0565] Ps. 117.] “Give heed, proceed prosperously, and reign.” [Note: [Col. 0565] Ps. 44.] “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord, the king of Israel, the Saviour.” [Note: [Col. 0565] Ps. 117; Matt. 21.]

Certainly the sick usually come to physicians, [Col. 0566B] the needy to the rich, and servants to their masters. What then, O Lord, Ruler of rulers? “What is man, that you are mindful of him, or the son of man, that you visit him?” [Note: [Col. 0565] Ps. 8.] “What is man, that you magnify him, or that you set your heart upon him?”

Brothers, human misery moved God’s mercy. For the pious and merciful God, seeing that the enemy had deceitfully overthrown man, conceived thoughts of peace toward him. Man was cast down by the prompting of another, that he might fall. But because the enemy fell through his own malice, his iniquity was found worthy of hatred.

The troubles of imprisoned humanity moved the Father of mercies: humanity bewailed its misery [Col. 0566C] and implored mercy, saying continually, “Bring my soul out of prison”; [Note: [Col. 0565] Ps. 141.] “May it please you, O Lord, to deliver me”; [Note: [Col. 0565] Ps. 39.] “for I was secretly carried away from my land, and here I was cast innocent into the pit.” [Note: [Col. 0565] Gen. 40.] I confess that I am guilty; yet I am innocent in comparison with him whose fraud deceived me. May your grace help me, whom another’s malice harmed; may your mercy and truth come to my aid, for another’s impiety and falsehood overthrew me.

O Lord Christ Jesus, I who have now wholly rotted away in this prison: when shall I see your face? When will you come, O salvation of my countenance and my God? [Note: [Col. 0565] Ps. 41.] O Lord, God of my salvation, do swiftly, I beg you, that for which you come. Come, Lord, and do not delay; come, show your face, and we shall be saved. [Note: [Col. 0565] Ps. 79.] For we await you: be our arm in the time of tribulation; [Note: [Col. 0565] Isa. 33.] surely tribulation is near, and there is none to help.

[Col. 0566D]

Solomon’s word is: “Remember that death does not delay.” [Note: [Col. 0565] Ecclus. 14.] What are we doing, brothers? Why do we not meet the Lord with steps of devotion and humility? Let us go, greet him, and invite him to dwell in our lodging. Otherwise the prophet will lament over the cities of the south, shut up with no one entering. [Note: [Col. 0565] Jer. 13.]

Such is he who, in the abundance of his goodness, offers himself before he is invited. He is good to the soul that seeks him, and he comes gladly and swiftly to meet it before being invited. Isaiah knew this, speaking of such a meeting: “You met,” he says, [Col. 0567A] “him who rejoices and does righteousness; in your ways he will remember you.” [Note: [Col. 0567] Isa. 64.] Yet, just as he spontaneously offers himself to one inviting him, so, when invited, he often appears to decline entering the lodging of one who asks. He must therefore be drawn by the force of prayers and the service of devout humility.

As he walked with the two disciples, although he wished to be received in the lodging with them and by them, he nevertheless pretended to be going farther. [Note: [Col. 0567] Luke 24.] Likewise, when Lot worshipped and begged the two angels to enter his house, they held back and said, “Not so; we shall remain in the street.” [Note: [Col. 0567] Gen. 19.] But of the disciples it is written, “They compelled him”; [Note: [Col. 0567] Luke 24.] and of Lot it is written that he strongly compelled the angels [Col. 0567B] to enter. [Note: [Col. 0567] Gen. 19.] O holy compulsion! O praiseworthy force which makes Christ and the angels guests!

Therefore, brothers, if he uses some appearance of hesitation in response to our supplication, as though he wishes to go farther and to avoid our lodging, let us persist forcefully. For no greater force can be brought to bear than if we invite him by confessions, vigils, disciplines, secret jubilations, burning compunctions, groans, and sighs. In this manner he will be overcome; and whatever he first appeared to withhold, he will at last grant to our desires.

Those who have experienced it know how, when the soul of one contemplating or praying is suspended, drawn by a certain blessed amazement amid the delights of sweetness and glory [Col. 0567C] and by desire for heaven, all the inward parts of the person rise up to meet God as he comes. Thus, according to the Apostle’s teaching, it is caught up in the clouds to meet Christ, and thus is with the Lord. [Note: [Col. 0567] 1 Thess. 4.] But this lasts only a short time, not even half an hour. For when it thinks it has grasped him, as secretly as he came, so secretly he slips away. “The Spirit breathes where it wills, and you do not know whence it comes or where it goes.” [Note: [Col. 0567] John 3.] Hence Solomon says, “How do you not know the way of the spirit?” [Note: [Col. 0567] Eccl. 11.] And Job says, “The bird did not know its path.” [Note: [Col. 0567] Job 28.]

The Bride expressly declares these very delays of his in the Song of Love, when the Bridegroom knocks at the door of the soul: “The voice,” she says, “of my beloved knocking: ‘Open to me, my sister, my friend, my dove, for my head is full of dew,’” and so forth. “I arose,” she says, “to open to my beloved. But he had turned aside and passed on; [Col. 0567D] I sought him and did not find him; I called, and he did not answer me.” [Note: [Col. 0567] Song 5.] And blessed Job says, “If he comes to me, I shall not see him.” [Note: [Col. 0567] Job 9.]

Therefore, when the Canaanite woman had called to him for a long time, he did not answer her; but at last he gave her the desired and salutary reply: [Note: [Col. 0567] Matt. 15.] indicating that he is to be called upon with love and persistence, and drawn powerfully into the lodging of the soul by humble devotion. Thus the merciful guest will answer the pleading host, the praying Canaanite woman: “Woman, great is your faith; let it be done for you as you have asked.” [Note: [Col. 0567] Ibid.]

Therefore, brothers, with every precaution [Col. 0568A] the lodging of our body must be prepared, lest he find in it anything offensive to the eyes of his majesty. Let there be in it no quarrelsome wife, smoke, or dripping; for these three drive a guest from the house: namely, the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life.

Why, brothers, would he disdain to turn aside to you, if he is drawn devoutly and humbly, when he entered the house of Zacchaeus uninvited? If Zacchaeus gave half his goods to the poor and, if he defrauds, makes fourfold restitution, [Note: [Col. 0567] Luke 19,] certainly I see here many Zacchaeuses who not only restored fourfold, not only gave half their goods for Christ, but left all temporal goods behind. He will not disdain to dwell with human beings, because he is the Son of Man. May he himself come [Col. 0568B] to us and make his dwelling with us, so that from this dwelling he may bring us forth to the dwelling of eternal blessedness, in which there is peace that does not fail, light that is not extinguished, and glory that does not pass away. May he deign to grant this to us—he who lives and reigns as God with the Father and the Holy Spirit through all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON III: ON THE SAME ADVENT

“We await the Saviour, our Lord Jesus Christ, who will refashion the body of our lowliness, conformed to the body of his glory.” [Note: [Col. 0567] Phil. 3.]

It is written: “The expectation of the righteous is joy.” [Note: [Col. 0567] Prov. 10.] Hence the righteous man, sustained by expectation of divine mercy, said: “And now what is my expectation? Is it not the Lord?” [Col. 0568C] [Note: [Col. 0567] Ps. 38.] O expectation of the nations: all who await you shall not be put to shame. [Note: [Col. 0567] Ps. 44.] “Our fathers awaited you; they hoped in you and were not put to shame.” [Note: [Col. 0567] Ps. 21.]

Among the ancients there were those who, disbelieving the prophetic oracles, mocked Isaiah and the other prophets with sarcastic derision, saying: “Command, command again; command, command again; await, await again; a little here, a little there.” [Note: [Col. 0567] Isa. 28.] To such people the same prophet makes a most severe threat: “It shall be for them,” he says, “that they may go and fall backward, be ensnared, and be taken.” [Note: [Col. 0567] Ibid.] For these and others like them fall into the temptations and snares of the devil.

He has nooses, traps, and snares. “Sinners have hidden a snare for me,” he says. [Note: [Col. 0567] Ps. 141.] And Job says: “His trap is hidden [Col. 0568D] in the earth, and his snare upon the path.” [Note: [Col. 0567] Job 18.] Of this capture Solomon says: “Man does not know his end; but as fish are caught by a hook and birds by a snare, so people are caught in an evil time.” [Note: [Col. 0567] Eccl. 9.]

Therefore, brothers, let us await the Saviour’s advent with confidence. “I am certain,” he says, “that he will appear at the end and will not lie. If he delays, I shall await him.” [Note: [Col. 0567] Hab. 2.] And he who sends salvation to Jacob greets through the prophet Hosea his beloved, the Church, whom he has betrothed to himself in faith. He consoles her [Col. 0569A] and, so that her husband’s heart may have confidence in her, teaches how she ought to await him: “For many days,” he says, “you shall await me; you shall not commit fornication, and you shall not be with another lover.” [Note: [Col. 0569] Hos. 3.]

These things, brothers, were spoken from ancient days. Thus Isaiah says: “Does not the Lord come from afar?” [Note: [Col. 0569] Isa. 30.] But we are those upon whom the ends of the ages have come. [Note: [Col. 0569] 1 Cor. 10.] Therefore he is near to come: the Bridegroom, our king and our lawgiver, is near to come. For he will come quickly and will not delay.

Let us then, like people awaiting their master, do what he commands: let us not commit fornication; let us not follow other lovers. The world is a deceitful lover; it mocks souls with treacherous deception. It is Shechem son of Hamor, who soothes Dinah, Jacob’s daughter, whom he has abducted and violated, with blandishments. [Note: [Col. 0569] Gen. 34.] For the wretched [Col. 0569B] soul, drawn away and enticed by its own desires, when it agrees with the world and the devil and thus prostitutes itself from the Lord, makes void its first faith and, in the passion of desires and destructive pleasure, denies itself to God. It follows deceitful lovers because they offer themselves in the present; and it does not await justly, devoutly, and soberly Christ Jesus, the Lord of glory, its bridegroom and Saviour.

Therefore, following the Apostle’s counsel, let us live soberly, justly, and devoutly in this age, awaiting the blessed hope and the appearing of the glory of the great God. [Note: [Col. 0569] Titus 2.] Piety concerns a person’s relation to the Lord, justice that person’s relation to a neighbour, and sobriety that person’s relation to self. The Lord’s Advent is harmful to us unless we await it with piety, sobriety, [Col. 0569C] and justice.

There are three advents of the Lord: the first into the flesh, the second to the soul, and the third for judgment. The first was at midnight, the second in the morning, and the third at noon. To pursue the words of evangelical truth concerning the first advent: “At midnight a cry was made: ‘Behold, the bridegroom comes!’” [Note: [Col. 0569] Matt. 25.] I understand it to have been midnight when, in the midst of silence, night was running its course. It was night among the Jews, whose eyes malice had darkened lest they should see. Likewise, the people of the Gentiles walked in darkness. The Bridegroom came, and a cry was made.

The silence of night was broken. For he came who enlightens the hidden things of darkness; he took away the night and made day. “The night,” says the Apostle, “has gone before; but the day has drawn near.” [Col. 0569D] [Note: [Col. 0569] Rom. 13.] What does it mean that a cry was made at midnight except that, in the midst of the silence of all things, while night ran its course and the almighty Word had determined to descend from the royal thrones, the prophets, recognizing Christ’s advent, burst forth into a cry of joy and broke the middle silence?

For it was a great cry when the prophets cried, each separately and all together. David cried: “Bow down your heavens and descend.” [Note: [Col. 0569] Ps. 143.] Isaiah cried: “Would that, O Lord, you would rend the heavens! Send forth the Lamb, O Lord, [Col. 0570A] ruler of the earth.” [Note: [Col. 0569] Isa. 16.] And, more forcefully, he cried out for the consolation of the people: “Hope in the Lord; my Just One is near; my Saviour has gone forth; my salvation shall not be far off, and it shall delay no longer than an hour.” [Note: [Col. 0569] Isa. 51.] And in the Lord’s person: “I shall give my salvation in Zion and my glory in Jerusalem.” [Note: [Col. 0569] Isa. 46.]

Jeremiah too cried from the pit of misery and from the chain: “Behold, days are coming, and the Lord shall raise up for David a righteous seed.” [Note: [Col. 0569] Jer. 23.] “He will make a new thing upon the earth: a woman will encompass a man.” [Note: [Col. 0569] Jer. 31.] Joel likewise, breaking forth into a cry of joy and exultation, says: “Daughters of Zion, rejoice and be glad, for the Lord has given you a teacher of righteousness.” [Note: [Col. 0569] Joel 2.] Micah no less, with exultation of heart and uplifted voice, said: “The Lord will come, and his going forth is from the days of eternity.” [Note: [Col. 0569] Mic. 5.]

If we wished to bring forward [Col. 0570B] the various voices, oracles, and prayers of the prophets—clamorous with sorrowful desire and devotion—the time for recounting would fail before the material to be recounted. Yet one thing is necessary. If we wish Christ’s advent to be a remedy for us, let us prepare ourselves for his advent. For, as the prophet teaches us in the person of Israel: “Be ready, Israel, to meet the Lord, for he comes.” [Note: [Col. 0569] Amos 4.] And you, brothers, be ready, for at an hour when you do not expect him, the Son of Man will come. [Note: [Col. 0569] Luke 12.]

The first advent has already passed. For Christ was seen among human beings and lived with them. [Note: [Col. 0569] Baruch 3.] Christ came to fulfil in himself the Law for us; and, since, according to the Apostle, a testament is completed in death, [Note: [Col. 0569] Heb. 9,] he completed the testament of our redemption [Col. 0570C] on the cross in word, spirit, and deed.

We are in the second advent, provided that we are such persons as he deigns to visit; assured that, if we love him, he will come to us and make his abode with us. This advent is uncertain to us. For who knows what is in God except the Spirit of God? Those who are sometimes caught up in ecstasy by heavenly desire know when he comes; yet they do not know whence he comes or where he goes, as Job says: “If he comes to me, I shall not see him; and if he goes away, I shall not understand him.” [Note: [Col. 0569] Job 9.]

Of the third advent it is most certain that it will come; yet it is most uncertain when it will come. What is more certain than death? Yet nothing is more uncertain than the hour of death. The Wise Man says: “When they say, ‘Peace and security,’ then [Col. 0570D] sudden destruction and pain will come upon them, as upon a woman with child, and they shall not escape.” [Note: [Col. 0569] Prov. 29.] Was not the Lord’s advent fearfully impending over that man in the Gospel to whom the Lord said: “Fool, this night they shall demand your soul from you; and whose will be the things you have prepared?” [Note: [Col. 0569] Luke 12.]

In this life we can be secure only of this: that we are not secure. Now we are healthy; now we fall ill. Now prosperity flatters us; now adversities afflict us. Now we are; now we are not. For death spares neither age nor sex. Whatever we gather, say, think, or do will all [Col. 0571A] come to nothing like running water.

Whoever, therefore, is the true Israel, let him prepare to meet the Lord: “Prepare yourself, Israel, to meet your God, for he comes” [Note: [Col. 0571] Amos 4.]. We must be prepared, so that we may forestall death rather than be forestalled by death. He prepares himself wisely who guards himself from the contagion of iniquity. The prophet, who could not guard himself from death, at least guarded himself from iniquity: “I will keep myself,” he says, “from iniquity” [Note: [Col. 0571] Ps. 17.]. Oh, how blessed is he who can safely say: “My heart is ready, O God; my heart is ready” [Note: [Col. 0571] Ps. 107.]; and again: “I am prepared, and I have not been disturbed” [Note: [Col. 0571] Ps. 118.]. Such a person receives the fruit of grace from the first coming, and will receive the fruit of salvation and glory from the second coming. For the first is ancillary to the second [Col. 0571B]; the second is preparatory for the last.

The first coming was hidden and humble; the second is secret and lovable; the third will be manifest and terrible. In the first he came to us, that in the second he might come into us; in the second he comes into us, lest in the third he come against us. In the first coming he showed mercy; in the second he gives grace; in the third he will give glory, because “the Lord will give grace and glory” [Note: [Col. 0571] Ps. 85]. In the first he appeared contemptible, lowly, and frail: for Herod despised him, the Jew spat upon him, and the Gentile killed him. Speaking of the second, the Apostle says: “Beholding the glory of the Lord, we are transformed into the same image from glory to glory, as by the Spirit of the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0571] II Cor. 3.]. In the first he was judged unjustly; in the second [Col. 0571C] he justifies us by grace, and in the last he will judge justly. A lamb in the first, he will be a lion in the last, and a friend in the middle.

Of the first, he says through Isaiah: “I was silent and did not open my mouth” [Note: [Col. 0571] Isa. 42.]; of the last: “Like a woman in labor, he will speak” [Note: [Col. 0571] Ibid.]; of the second: “We shall come to him and make our dwelling with him” [Note: [Col. 0571] John 14.]. He who first came gentle and meek will come as an awe-inspiring and terrible judge. He who came in a spirit of humility will come in a spirit of judgment and a spirit of burning. It is dangerous, brothers, to fall into the hands of the living God; for “as wax melts before fire, so sinners shall perish before the face of God” [Note: [Col. 0571] Ps. 67.]. “Their fire shall not be quenched, and their worm shall not die” [Note: [Col. 0571] Isa. 66.]. For their death will not die: they will live only in order to be tormented eternally.

But the righteous shall feast in the sight of God and [Col. 0571D] delight in the abundance of peace, having, in Isaiah’s testimony, “a crown instead of ashes, oil of gladness instead of mourning, a garment of praise instead of a spirit of sorrow” [Note: [Col. 0571] Isa. 61.]. For the Lord will render to the saints the reward of their labors; but he will condemn the wicked by the sentence pronounced upon Babylon: “As much as she glorified herself in luxury, give her so much torment and mourning” [Note: [Col. 0571] Rev. 18.]. Of this coming he himself says: “Behold, I come quickly, and my reward is with me, to render to each according to his works” [Note: [Col. 0571] Rev. 22.]. May Christ Jesus, whom we have received as Savior and await as judge, save us not according to our evil works which we have done, but according to his great mercy. To him be honor and glory for ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON IV. ON THE FEAST OF ST. ANDREW

“Hail, precious cross; receive the disciple of him who hung upon you—my master, Christ.”

Man is like vanity; and therefore he seeks vanities and false madnesses. Thus, through a certain corruption of nature, given over to a reprobate mind, he despises things earthly and heavenly, follows bodily pleasures, and entangles himself in the snares of eternal destruction. Whence, then, can unhappy man, sold under sin, obtain the power to lift his head, restrain the flesh, and command the waves violently surging within his heart [Col. 0572B]?

This is not man’s doing, but that of him who works in us both the willing and the accomplishing according to his good will [Note: [Col. 0571] Phil. 2.]. Yet Andrew was a man, subject to suffering like ourselves. Forgetting, as it were, his own condition, he preached most earnestly the sweetness and pleasantness of the cross. A most devoted imitator of Christ, he so loved Christ’s cross in Christ that he placed the sum of all his desires and affections in pains and torments. The fire which the Lord came to cast upon the earth burned fiercely within him, so that he exulted amid punishments and counted the torture of a most shameful death as an addition to the height of his joy.

To me, wretched and weak as I am, it seems terrible and horrifying to seek—or, having sought, to find—delights upon so dreadful a gibbet [Col. 0572C] or cross. Who seeks rest in torments, life in death, health in sickness, pleasure in pain? Yet Andrew, through the exceeding ardor of faith and love, greets the cross and says: “I come to you secure and rejoicing” [Note: [Col. 0571] In Vit. ap. Boll.]. Andrew considers it a supreme pleasure if he may be left upon the gibbet until he is consumed there; and, surpassing all the strength of human capacity, as though already absent from the body, he does not feel the agony upon the cross. For he loves Christ thus, and thus longs for fellowship with him: it seems long to him that the gibbet is not hastened, that he does not already hang there, that death is not brought upon him, that life is prolonged, that punishment is deferred.

Therefore we ought now rather to rejoice with him in his passion than to suffer with him. Why should we not rejoice with one who suffers, when he has turned suffering into joy? O blessed wood! O fruitful wood! O most precious tree! From the price of the world which you bore, you still, even in death, put forth the most peaceable fruit of life; you pour forth the oil of gladness; and you cause those who grasp the tree of life, amid the straits of a most cruel death, to taste the first-fruits of eternal sweetness.

The cross, which once had been an instrument of condemnation and an exquisitely shameful death, today repays its lovers [Col. 0573A] with life instead of death, security instead of fear, and glory instead of shame. Truly, “what is foolish in God is wiser than men” [Note: [Col. 0573] I Cor. 1.]. For while human wisdom found in the cross nothing but the bitterness of death, disgrace, and horror, Peter and Andrew discovered hidden manna in the cross and found a treasure of supreme delight.

Christ Jesus himself, the firstborn from the dead, not forgetful of these delights of the cross—now having suffered, been buried, and been glorified—meets Peter and goes to Rome to be crucified again. Was it not enough for the reproach of the cross to have been satisfied once, unless he still hungered and, in hungering, desired the cross for his nobler members? I do not wonder that Christ loved the cross, on which, when lifted up, he drew all things to himself [Col. 0573B] [Note: [Col. 0573] John 12.]: to himself, I say, to love, to imitation, to fellowship. Through it all power in heaven and on earth was given to that man [Note: [Col. 0573] Matt. 28.]. Through it was given to him the name above every name [Note: [Col. 0573] Phil. 2.]. Through it his rule was placed upon his shoulder [Note: [Col. 0573] Isa. 9.].

But how did Andrew, a weak and frail man, come to glory thus in the cross, exult thus in torments, and overflow with joy? Certainly Elijah, frightened in spirit by the threat of one little woman, threw himself beneath the shade of a juniper tree and asked that his soul might die. “It is enough for me,” he says; “take away my soul” [Note: [Col. 0573] III Kings 19.]. The apostle Paul, hemmed in amid the pressures of temptations, is compelled to cry out and by his cry bears witness to his grief: “Unhappy man that I am! Who shall deliver me from this body of death?” [Col. 0573C] [Note: [Col. 0573] Rom. 7.] That Job, whose endurance is so solemnly celebrated, considering his weakness and failure, says: “What is my strength, that I should endure? My strength is not the strength of stones, nor is my flesh bronze” [Note: [Col. 0573] Job 6.]. Jonah likewise, fleeing from the face of the Lord and disturbed by the withering of the ivy, says: “I am angry unto death” [Note: [Col. 0573] Jonah 4.].

Why wonder at Jonah? Christ himself was afraid. “Behold, more than Jonah is here” [Note: [Col. 0573] Luke 11.]: that is, Christ, who began to be weary and troubled unto death. Christ says: “My soul is troubled” [Note: [Col. 0573] John 12.]; and: “Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me” [Note: [Col. 0573] Matt. 26.]. Andrew cries: “Hail, beautiful cross! I come to you secure and rejoicing; receive the disciple of him who hung upon you—my master, Christ” [Note: [Col. 0573] In Vita ap. Boll.]. Is the disciple [Col. 0573D] greater than his master, or the servant than his lord?

Consider, brothers, the ineffable and immeasurable abundance of sweetness and overflowing charity in Christ. The physician suffers with and shares the weakness of the sick person; the hen grows weak with her chicks. Thus the whole burnt offering might be complete, and the work of perfected mercy fulfilled in Christ: as he suffered for us in the flesh, so he chose to endure the sufferings of the soul. For my sake he trembles, for my sake he is troubled, for my sake he is weary; he suffers wholly for me and wholly suffers with me. Therefore, by suffering with me, he suffers so that his trembling may become my strength, his sadness my joy, his weariness my cheerfulness, his desolation my consolation, and his trouble my rest.

The servant suffers, providing for himself and serving his Lord. The Lord suffers, emptying himself and suffering with the servant. “Receive,” he says, “the disciple of him who hung upon you” [Note: [Col. 0573] Ibid.]. Andrew most ardently longs to ascend the cross, that from there he may despise the world and the prince of the world, and that from there, as from the loftiest tower, he may safely receive the enemy’s missiles. For what is the cross but the watchtower of Zion, the tower of David, the tower of strength against the enemy [Note: [Col. 0573] Ps. 60], from which, as from a high and elevated place, every malice of the enemy is confounded? “You have placed your refuge on high, O Lord” [Note: [Col. 0573] Ps. 90.]. He who ascends the watchtower of the cross—the enemy shall gain nothing against him, and the son of iniquity [Col. 0574B] shall not add to harm him [Note: [Col. 0573] Ps. 88.].

“The horn of the cross,” says the prophet, “is in his hands” [Note: [Col. 0573] Hab. 3.]. In whose hands? In Christ’s, surely: with the horns of the cross he scatters the enemy and defeats the powers of the air, saying: “I have conquered the world” [Note: [Col. 0573] John 16.]. The cross has not lost the office or effect of its power. It still exalts the horns of the righteous and breaks the horns of sinners. If you love the Crucified One, brothers, love Christ’s cross, to which you have fastened yourselves with the nails of humility and obedience.

Three things make the cross lovable: fear, hope, and charity. Fear begins, hope advances, charity perfects; for “charity is the fulfillment of the law” [Note: [Col. 0573] Rom. 13.]. He who begins in fear endures Christ’s cross patiently. He who advances in hope carries it willingly. He who is perfected in charity embraces it ardently. Such a one can say with blessed Andrew: “I have always been your lover, and I have desired to embrace you, O good cross!” [Col. 0574C] [Note: [Col. 0573] In Vit. ap. Boll.]

The cross in which blessed Andrew found such sweetness is bitter and burdensome to some who are lost. They carry it under compulsion, more wretched than all human beings, because from the present cross they are about to pass into eternal torments. So foolish are they, and so given over to a reprobate mind, that they do not perceive the sweetness of the tree of life. “The natural man does not receive the things of the Spirit of God, for they are foolishness to him, and he cannot understand them” [Note: [Col. 0573] I Cor. 2.].

But if anyone humbly and devoutly gathers this wood in his heart, like a bundle of myrrh, he will have the fruit of refreshment, the balm of sweetness, and the oil of anointing. Two pieces of wood make a cross. From the time when the widow gathered these two pieces of wood, neither oil nor flour failed in her house or among her people [Col. 0574D] [Note: [Col. 0573] III Kings 17.]. These are the two pieces of wood by which bitter waters under Moses [Note: [Col. 0573] Exod. 15.], and salty waters under Eliezer [Note: [Col. 0573] read: Elisha. IV Kings 2.], were sweetened.

And what is saltier, what more bitter, than Christ’s tears at the raising of Lazarus and over the future destruction of Jerusalem? What is more bitter than the water which flowed from the side of the Crucified One? I spoke as one less wise, judging that bitterness was there where the height of love, the sweetness of grace, and the fullness of incomprehensible goodwill reside. For what is sweeter or more lovable [Col. 0575A] than those waters which flow from his side and eyes, as from the fountains of the Savior? These are the waters in Ezekiel which healed the waters of the Dead Sea [Note: [Col. 0575] Ezek. 47.]. This water splits the hardness of stones. Therefore, one whose heart is not split by devotion and compassion at the remembrance of Christ’s cross is more than stony.

On the cross the Lord placed the mystery of reconciliation. He first commended it in himself, then in the apostles and martyrs. He set it before us as the propitiatory of mercy, the ascent of virtues, and the ladder by virtues to the joy of heavenly gladness. May he deign to grant this to us, he who lives and reigns as God with the Father and the Holy Spirit through all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON V. ON THE NATIVITY OF THE LORD

“A child is born to us, and a son is given to us” [Note: [Col. 0575] Isa. 9.]. [Col. 0575B]

Do not wonder, brothers, that Christ is designated by Isaiah with the name of child. For the Father too, speaking of him, says: “This is my child whom I have chosen” [Note: [Col. 0575] Isa. 42; Matt. 12.]. Why should he not be called a child, who in his goodness and because of our need took upon himself the weaknesses and miseries of childish helplessness? “A child,” says the prophet, “is born to us.” He who, setting a little child before his disciples, commended innocence in childhood, preferred to appear as a lovable child rather than as a terrible one, wishing to invite love rather than instill fear. For filial affection is more pleasing to him than servile affection, voluntary love than compelled love.

If we wish him to reform us and conform us to himself, let us be conformed to the infant, that we may be as newly [Col. 0575C] born infants: humble, rational, and without guile [Note: [Col. 0575] I Pet. 2.]. No one enters his kingdom unless he humbles himself like this little child. “I,” he says, “am the door. If anyone enters through me, he shall be saved” [Note: [Col. 0575] John 10.]. Woe to those who are not humbled, who do not lay aside the gigantic magnitude of proud exaltation: how will they enter without striking their heads? Therefore the Lord “shall strike the heads of many upon the earth” [Note: [Col. 0575] Ps. 109.]. Rather, let us humble ourselves beneath his mighty hand. Especially while he is a child, let us use the benefit of his childhood. The child Jesus rarely grows angry, and, when angered, is easily appeased. Let us seek and preserve for ourselves the grace of the child, and we shall not fear in the future the wrath and fury of the judge, terrible and awe-inspiring.

“A child is born to us” from the Jews: he is born to us, not to them. He was born to us so that we, who had been born unto condemnation, might be happily reborn through him. For “to as many as received him, he gave power to become children of God through grace” [Note: [Col. 0575] John 1.]. Through that grace, as the Apostle testifies, “we stand and glory in the hope of the glory of the children of God” [Note: [Col. 0575] Rom. 5.]. He who teaches man knowledge, who instructs and forms the tongues of angels—the Word of God, the Power of God, and the Wisdom of God—chose simple and speechless infancy. It was too little that he had been made lower than the angels, unless he also became lower [Col. 0576A] than men; and, to reform us unto the glory of immortality, he conforms himself not merely to a mortal body but to the frail age of a little child. See, brothers: the immeasurable Lord, the redemption of the righteous, the downfall of the proud, the judgment of the wicked—a tender and weak infant.

“A child is born to us.” It would not have been enough that he was born, unless he had also been given. In that he was given to us, all things were also given to us with him, as the Apostle says: “The Father who gave him—how did he not also give us all things with him?” [Note: [Col. 0575] Rom. 8.] This is the child who, according to the word of Isaiah, before he knew how to call his father or mother, the strength of Damascus and the spoils of Samaria would be carried away [Note: [Col. 0575] Isa. 8.]. This is the child of whom Ecclesiastes says: “A poor and wise child is better than an old and [Col. 0576B] foolish king who does not know how to provide for himself in the future” [Note: [Col. 0575] Eccl. 4.].

Christ is the poor child: for he made himself poor in order to enrich us; he emptied himself in order to fill us. Therefore his name is as poured-out oil, that from his poured-out fullness we might all receive. And what greater emptying is there than that the splendor of glory, the figure of God’s substance, the image of divine majesty, the Only-begotten of God, should appear in the form of a servant, having neither form nor beauty? Great—indeed more than great—is the emptying that makes wisdom foolish, weakens power, humbles majesty, and makes him utterly rejected and lowly both in birth and in passion.

Yet this child, so lowly and poor, is incomparably better than the old and foolish king. Who is this old and foolish king but the ancient enemy, grown old in evil days? [Col. 0576C] He is “king over all the children of pride” [Note: [Col. 0575] Job 41.]; claiming for himself a throne on the sides of the north, he provided badly for himself and his own future. This poor and wise child defeated him—the one whom the Apostle calls the Power of God and the Wisdom of God [Note: [Col. 0575] I Cor. 1.]: “He stripped principalities and powers,” he says, “confidently triumphing over them openly in himself” [Note: [Col. 0575] Col. 2.]. In his childhood the great Herod sought him to kill him; in his adulthood a second Herod, when he was brought before him, despised him. At the voice of this one, who cries in the cradle, angelic powers tremble.

Accordingly Isaiah and all the prophets who bear witness cry out: “This is our God, and no other shall be reckoned beside him” [Note: [Col. 0575] Baruch 3.]. “This is our God for ever and ever; he [Col. 0576D] shall govern us for ages” [Note: [Col. 0575] Ps. 47.]. All kings shall adore our little child. All nations shall serve him; every kingdom that will not serve him shall perish.

Some inquire more curiously than earnestly what necessity there was for Christ to assume the necessities of our misery, not attending to the ineffable mystery of the dispensation in Christ, without which it was neither necessary nor fitting for us to be saved. To answer such people in a more concise word: God became man so that man might become God; so that he to whom it was once said, “You are earth, [Col. 0577A] and into earth you shall go” [Note: [Col. 0577] Gen. 3.], may henceforth hear: “You are heaven, and into heaven you shall go.” O wonderful exchange! He took humanity in order to confer divinity; he took misery in order to give glory. Thus “the kindness and humanity of God our Savior appeared” [Note: [Col. 0577] Titus 3.]; his humanity appeared to us because we were unworthy for his divinity to appear to us. And he who was one with the Father by an ineffable unity became one with man by an inconceivable unity.

Therefore, that man might be taken up into God, God our receiver, the God of Jacob, took up man; for “our taking up belongs to the Lord, and to the Holy One of Israel, our King” [Note: [Col. 0577] Ps. 88.]. Thus from our misery he devised the remedy for our misery. For as, by a certain craftsmanship of heavenly love, God and man together tempered in himself our riches and needs, so he tempered his blessedness and our misery in himself: rich and poor united in one. Thus, through the working of the ineffable mystery of the dispensation, blessedness might absorb misery, life swallow death, and the whole man rise through the benefit of resurrection into the glory of heavenly life.

He who said, “I fill heaven and earth” [Note: [Col. 0577] Jer. 23.], is wholly enclosed in the virginal womb, wholly in swaddling-clothes, wholly in a manger. He was the true light; therefore, in order to illumine our darkness, he is born at night and amid miseries, that the illumination of his birth may be in our delights. The guardian of Israel is born by night, our Samaritan—whose name means “guardian”—to whom the prophet long ago cried: “Guardian, what of the night? Guardian, what of the night?” [Note: [Col. 0577] Isa. 21.] And observe carefully that the most high Son of the Most High, who has times in [Col. 0577C] his own power, chose for his birth a time that could have been more burdensome for a tender little child and for the son of a poor woman, who scarcely possessed swaddling-clothes in which to wrap her child.

But he is that little child of whom Isaiah foretold that he would reject evil and choose good [Note: [Col. 0577] Isa. 7.], thereby confounding the judgment of the world and the prudence of the flesh, which is hostile to God. It is the flesh that calls evil good and good evil, embracing the pleasures of this age and reckoning in them the highest good. But our little child, from the very beginning of his birth, in cold and nakedness, in a lodging-place, in a manger, deigned in himself to inaugurate and consecrate the harshness, lowliness, and rejection of life, and every form of humility and religious devotion.

He who is terrible among the kings of the earth, invisible and inaccessible, clothed in light as with a garment amid the splendors of the saints—the Power of God and the Wisdom of God—was born a little child in order that he might make us great. He was born in a lodging-place, that we might know ourselves to be strangers and pilgrims upon the earth. He was laid in a manger, that by his example we might learn to choose the lowest place. He was fed with milk and wrapped in swaddling-clothes, that, having food and coverings, we might be content with these. He chose to be poor and clothed in rags, [Col. 0578A] that he might receive the poor and ragged into a share and inheritance of the glory of his kingdom.

Hear, O heavens, and give ear, O earth, how greatly the Lord has magnified his mercy toward us: the almighty Word descended for us from royal seats into a stable. The Word that was spirit became flesh [Note: [Col. 0577] John 1.]; the Word that was invisible became visible and tangible. Hence some could say: “Our hands have handled the Word of life” [Note: [Col. 0577] I John 1.]. He became able to be tasted, smelled, and heard, so that, just as death had infected and corrupted all our senses, so Christ, our life, might reform all our senses, becoming all things in us.

He is wrapped in swaddling-clothes; the new Adam is not, like the old Adam, clothed in skins. I see Jesus the high priest clothed in filthy garments, as Zechariah foretold [Note: [Col. 0577] Zech. 3.]. Therefore, speaking to the shepherds, the angel gave the swaddling-clothes as a sign: “And this,” he says, “shall be a sign to you: you shall find the child wrapped in swaddling-clothes” [Note: [Col. 0577] Luke 2.]. Your swaddling-clothes, Jesus, were set as a sign from your infancy; but as a sign that was contradicted, and is continually contradicted.

Although the apostle Peter says, “Not in costly clothing” [Note: [Col. 0577] I Tim. 2.], although Elijah and John are praised for the roughness of their clothing, and on the testimony of him who lies in the manger, those in kings’ houses are clothed in soft garments [Note: [Col. 0577] Matt. 11.], yet soft and delicate clothing is still sought by many. Do we contradict Christ in clothing alone? Indeed, for many other reasons he is “set for the fall and rising again of many, and for a sign that shall be contradicted” [Note: [Col. 0577] Luke 2.]. Do we not contradict [Col. 0578C] him in almost everything? For he desired humility, while we desire exaltation; he desired misery, while we desire glory. His food was to do the will of his Father; our food is to fulfill the desires of our flesh. He was obedient to the Father in all things; some, rejecting the yoke of obedience, almost every hour break the bond of their vow, the rule of the cloister, and the law of silence.

The child Jesus was silent; the almighty utterance, the Word of the Most High, was silent, and could say: “There is no speech on my tongue” [Note: [Col. 0577] Ps. 138.]. Therefore he was silent, in order to commend to us the virtue of silence. Some often gather together and break silence: when they ought to speak of God’s law and the matter of their salvation, they tell tales and fabrications of rumors. “The wicked have told me fables, but not according to your law” [Note: [Col. 0577] Ps. 118.]. Let them know that they cannot speak long without loss to their salvation; for, according to Scripture, “sin will not be absent in much speaking” [Note: [Col. 0577] Prov. 10.]. “Life and death are in the power of the tongue” [Note: [Col. 0577] Prov. 18.].

A light, careless, and incautious word flies out. Yet that very light word makes you a murderer when it kills the charity wounded in your brother. Your brother has been gravely harmed, and perhaps you do not reckon it so because of the cheapness and triviality of the word. But what is more trivial than a dead fly? Yet it spoils sweet ointment [Note: [Col. 0577] Eccl. 10.]. See [Col. 0579A] how he invites you to the humility of obedience: though he was the Son of God, he was obedient to a craftsman and a woman.

“And,” says the evangelist, “he was subject to them” [Note: [Col. 0579] Luke 2.]. Consider carefully all that concurs in Christ’s charity; and unless you stubbornly choose to contradict, you will see in all things a sign and pattern of obedience, an example of humility, and a law of life and discipline. The Apostle says of Christ that he “was made for us by God righteousness and sanctification and redemption” [Note: [Col. 0579] I Cor. 1.]. Already the flowers of righteousness and sanctification appear in him; already in Christ is fulfilled what he would one day say of his apostles: “For their sakes I sanctify myself” [Note: [Col. 0579] John 17.]. Beyond doubt our sanctification has already blossomed upon him, because in every way the Savior’s infancy prescribes for us a rule of holiness [Col. 0579B].

Let us love him, brothers, who was born and given to us, from whom come “every good gift and every perfect gift” [Note: [Col. 0579] Jas. 1.]. He is the beloved and only-begotten Son of the Father, of whom he says: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” [Note: [Col. 0579] Matt. 17.]. And he says of the Father: “I always do the things that please him” [Note: [Col. 0579] John 8.]. Whoever does not love him—it would be better for that man if he had not been born, especially since the Apostle says: “If anyone does not love our Lord Jesus Christ, let him be anathema, maranatha” [Note: [Col. 0579] I Cor. 16.]. Let us love him who loved us and washed us in his blood, Jesus Christ, who has preceded us in his love and blessing. To him be blessing for ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON VI. ON THE SAME NATIVITY OF THE LORD

“In the sun he placed his tabernacle, and he himself is like a bridegroom coming forth from his chamber” [Note: [Col. 0579] Ps. 18.].

[Col. 0579C]

From the days of eternity the Word of the Father had lain hidden and concealed, as it is written: “He made darkness his hiding-place” [Note: [Col. 0579] Ps. 17.]. And another prophet says: “Truly you are a hidden God, the Savior, King of Israel” [Note: [Col. 0579] Isa. 43.]. And another prophet says: “To whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?” [Note: [Col. 0579] Isa. 53.] For he came from the dense and shadowy mountain. For this mystery, as the Apostle says, “was not made known to other generations” [Note: [Col. 0579] Eph. 3.]. Therefore it seemed to the ancient fathers that Christ was exceedingly distant from them. Thus, when Isaiah spoke of the incarnation of the Word, he said: “The Word shall come from afar” [Col. 0579D] [Note: [Col. 0579] Isa. 30.]. And this is what is read in Numbers: “A hearer of my words: I shall see him, but not now; I shall behold him, but not near” [Note: [Col. 0579] Num. 24.].

The Lord had shut up all things under sin, that he might have mercy on all [Note: [Col. 0579] Rom. 11.]. All had sinned and needed the grace of God [Note: [Col. 0579] Rom. 3.]. Therefore the Lord was distant from them, because “salvation is far from sinners” [Note: [Col. 0579] Ps. 118.]. But our true Isaac went out to meditate in the field, as he himself says: “I came forth from [Col. 0580A] the Father and came into the world” [Note: [Col. 0579] John 16.]. Begotten from the Father’s womb before Lucifer, he came into the womb of the Virgin Mother. “His going forth is indeed from the height of heaven” [Note: [Col. 0579] Ps. 18.]. And in the testimony of the prophet Micah: “His going forth is from the beginning, from the days of eternity” [Note: [Col. 0579] Mic. 5.].

Bearing witness to his going forth and return, the evangelist says: “He came from God and goes to God” [Note: [Col. 0579] John 13.]. Isaac goes out into the field to meditate [Note: [Col. 0579] Gen. 24.]. What is this field but the Virgin’s womb, which produces the Lord’s shoot in magnificence and glory? This is the field which the Lord blessed and of which it is written: “The beauty of the field is with me” [Note: [Col. 0579] Ps. 49.]. And what does the Lord think? “I have thought thoughts of peace,” he says [Note: [Col. 0579] Jer. 29.]. This is the true Joseph, sent by his father to see his brothers and their flocks. Was not he sent who says: [Col. 0580B] “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me; he has sent me to preach good news to the poor” [Note: [Col. 0579] Isa. 61; Luke 4.]? He is the one who says: “The Lord has sent me and his Spirit” [Note: [Col. 0579] Isa. 48.].

Joseph was sent to his brothers. All who receive Christ’s faith are Christ’s brothers. For “as many as received him, he gave power to become children of God, to those who believe in his name” [Note: [Col. 0579] John 1.]. If they are children of God, then they are also brothers of Christ: indeed heirs of God and co-heirs of Christ. That he might be the firstborn among many brothers, the blessed Virgin gave us this brother. Of this brother Solomon says: “Who will give you to me as my brother, nursing at my mother’s breasts?” [Note: [Col. 0579] Song 8.]

Nor does our Joseph visit brothers only; he visits the flocks as well, for “the Lord shall save men and beasts.” He is the one who says: “I shall visit my sheep as a shepherd visits his flock” [Col. 0580C] [Note: [Col. 0579] Ezek. 34.]. See, brothers, a wheel within a wheel, a wing within a wing. Observe that the two cherubim look upon one another with reciprocal faces. Shepherds were those to whom the figurative Joseph was sent; and today our true Joseph, our Jesus, is revealed to shepherds. Jesus, I say, not Joseph; Savior, not dreamer; Lord of heaven, not of Egypt.

Once the name Jesus has been spoken, I do not care to hear Joseph; all the names of antiquity become wearisome to me. Most sweetly does the name Jesus taste: the new name, the name of him who says, “Behold, I make all things new” [Note: [Col. 0579] Rev. 21.]. That is the name of necessity which Rachel imposed; this is the new name which the mouth of the Lord named. New things have come, and therefore old things have passed away. “You shall eat the very oldest of old things,” says the Lord through Moses, “and when new things come, you shall cast out the old” [Col. 0580D] [Note: [Col. 0579] Lev. 26.].

And what are the old things, the most ancient things, or the new things? Teach us, Lord—you who teach man knowledge; you have known all things, the latest and the ancient. I believe the most ancient things to be these: that in the beginning was the Word; that Christ was begotten by the Father; that he is coequal, coeternal, and consubstantial with the Father. Most ancient too are those things which existed before the Law, [Col. 0581A] such as the offering of bread and wine made by Melchizedek. The old things are the rites of sacrifices, the observances of ceremonies, and the oracles of the prophets. The new things are that God united humanity to himself in unity of person; that a woman encompassed a man in her womb; that a Virgin conceived and gave birth. “The Lord,” says Jeremiah, “will make a new thing upon the earth: a woman shall encompass a man” [Note: [Col. 0581] Jer. 31.]. Let the old things therefore be cast away, because new things have come; let the figure cease, because truth has come; let the promises cease, because fulfilment of the promises has been made.

“The men of old wandered in the wilderness, in a trackless and waterless place” [Note: [Col. 0581] Ps. 106]; but, according to Isaiah’s testimony, the old error has departed [Note: [Col. 0581] Isa. 26]. Truth and error cannot exist together. Error has therefore departed, because “truth has sprung up from the earth” [Note: [Col. 0581] Ps. 84]. The Apostle testifies that the old things have passed away: “If anyone has been made a new creation in Christ,” he says, “the old things have passed away; behold, all things have become new for him” [Note: [Col. 0581] 2 Cor. 5].

Let us eat the most ancient things, so that, while we worship the little child in the cradle, we may believe him to be coeternal and coequal with the Father, and worship him as Creator of the universe and Lord of majesty. Let us eat Melchizedek’s loaves; for they are the most ancient and therefore the sweetest. And let us cast away the loaves of presentation, which are old, since the new bread that descended from heaven has come. This bread the woman of the Gospel mixed from three measures of flour [Note: [Col. 0581] Matt. 13]. For the most blessed Virgin conceived in the unity of one human person three substances: namely divinity, flesh, and soul. This is Joseph’s many-coloured garment, resplendent with the wondrous diversity of its natures, [Col. 0581C] a long robe because it “reaches from end to end, mightily and sweetly ordering all things” [Note: [Col. 0581] Wis. 8].

This bread which the Virgin prepared was baked in the oven of the cross and divided in the resurrection. For what use are hidden wisdom, an unseen treasure, and bread neither divided nor broken [Note: [Col. 0581] Ecclus. 20]? But the bread was broken, the book opened, the sack torn open; and the Spirit of Christ, descending into hell as one free among the dead, led forth the captives from the prison-house, those sitting in darkness and the shadow of death [Note: [Col. 0581] Isa. 42]. Yet the dying flesh destroys death, and with it the life of humankind rises again, regenerated into the hope of life through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead. Thus our daily and supersubstantial bread was formed from three measures of flour in the conception, [Col. 0581D] baked in the Passion, and broken in the resurrection. This is the barley-cake which overthrew the camp of Midian [Note: [Col. 0581] Judg. 7].

Blessed be God in his gifts, who satisfies the empty soul and the hungry soul with good things: the Lord gave us bread and flesh. For the Son of God became bread, and “the Word became flesh” [Note: [Col. 0581] John 1]. We have bread and flesh: bread, which he gives to the world; flesh, which whoever eats, by the testimony of Truth, has eternal life [Note: [Col. 0581] John 6].

Therefore let the poor eat and rejoice; and let those who in the sweat of [Col. 0582A] their face ate the bread of sorrow now eat the bread of life and gladness. We read that in the time of the Law a raven brought Elijah bread in the morning and flesh in the evening [Note: [Col. 0581] 3 Kgs. 17]. Moses likewise says: “In the morning you shall eat bread, and in the evening you shall be filled with flesh” [Note: [Col. 0581] Exod. 16]. This distribution of foods seems rather unsuitable—and truly raven-like—unless flesh is eaten without bread and bread without flesh. If anything from those loaves and flesh pertains to us, let it be cast away. For these observances are old and now stink. Had they been seasoned with our salt, perhaps they would never have decayed. But now some are rancid and some fetid. The loaves too are hard and mouldy, so that they might break the eater’s tooth. Is not that bread, “eye for eye, [Col. 0582B] tooth for tooth,” mouldy and hard?

But let us eat the flesh of the new Lamb: the flesh of the spotless Lamb, whose blood frees Israel from Egypt; who was foretold in the Law and the prophets; who, by John’s testimony, takes away the sins of the world [Note: [Col. 0581] John 1]. This is he whose coming Isaiah desired: “Send forth,” he says, “God the Father, the Lamb, ruler of the earth, from the rock of the wilderness” [Note: [Col. 0581] Isa. 16]. The wilderness is the Gentile world, hardened in its error, and therefore the rock of the wilderness. But the Lord turned the wilderness into delights and the solitude into the garden of the Lord, because from the rock of the wilderness the Lamb, ruler of the earth, was sent forth.

You who were cut from the rock, do you wish to see the rock of the wilderness? Look at Ruth the Moabite. For Boaz the Jew begot Obed by Ruth the Gentile, the father of Jesse, [Col. 0582C] the father of David. But Christ is David’s son according to the flesh. Therefore Christ, who came to seek what had perished, chose to be born from believers and unbelievers, from righteous persons and sinners. For the lamb sacrificed under the Law was, according to the Septuagint version, taken from sheep and goats. But let us return to the child whom we left crying in the cradle; let us go, and with the shepherds hastening there, see “this thing which has happened, which the Lord has made known to us” [Note: [Col. 0581] Luke 2].

O unhappy rich people of this world, since you have your consolation here, that in the world to come there may be for you gnashing of teeth and weeping, when you receive torments and mourning in return for your pleasures!

At the hour when Christ was born, many rich persons were sleeping; many too were indulging themselves in [Col. 0582D] luxurious, soft beds. But those who are not in the labour of humankind do not deserve consolation from an angelic visitation. Perhaps there were some awake and occupied with the wisdom of this world. But Christ, who made worldly wisdom foolish and chose through the foolishness of preaching to save believers [Note: [Col. 0581] 1 Cor. 1], revealed the sight of angels, the song of glory and praise, and the manifold glory of his birth, not to wise men or philosophers but to shepherds—rustic, simple, humble people. [Col. 0583A] “I confess to you, Father of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and prudent, and revealed them to little ones” [Note: [Col. 0583] Matt. 11].

Brothers, even if you are not shepherds, today you shall nevertheless see in the manger of the altar that little one of ours whom many kings and prophets desired to see: not in the form of glory, but wrapped in swaddling-clothes. As at the time of his birth his true power was present but concealed beneath that covering, so even now his majesty is concealed in the sacrament. But there will be a time when he shall appear no longer covered in swaddling-clothes, but “clothed with light as with a garment”; as the Only-Begotten from the Father; as the king in his beauty, having his tabernacle in the sun; amid the splendours of the saints; in light that does not fail; in glory that does not pass away. May our little one, who is blessed for ages of ages, deign to grant this to us. Amen.

## SERMON VII. ON THE DAY OF THE CIRCUMCISION

“Every male whose foreskin is not circumcised, that soul shall perish from among his people” [Note: [Col. 0583] Gen. 17].

The Word of the Lord had been sufficiently shortened upon the earth, made a little lower than the angels. Yet today the law of circumcision further diminishes him in that littleness. Something is cut from the flesh which Christ had assumed in the form of a human being, so that he may bear, as it were, the mark of a thief and the cautery-mark of a transgressor. For what is the cutting off of a foot, ear, or other member except a clear indication that someone has been caught [Col. 0583C] in an offence?

O good Jesus! O wisdom of God! O our righteousness and sanctification! Are you not he in whom no deceit was found, nor iniquity found in your heart, nor falsehood found in your mouth? Are you not true God from God the true Father? Are you not innocent and undefiled, born from an undefiled and Virgin mother? And what are you doing, most blessed among women, you who know your own virginity and his innocence? What are you doing, Joseph, who learned through the angel that what Mary conceived is of the Holy Spirit? Christ, who is without sin, ought not to be marked with the cautery-mark of sins. For he is the one whom the Father sealed and sent into the world. Do you, Mary and Joseph, really think that by this sign he will be made more evident to his Father? [Col. 0583D] Indeed, certainly, if the Father could forget his Son or fail to know him who is his wisdom; or if any doubt could fall upon him—by inspection of this sign, which belongs only to sinners—the Father could doubt his Son.

You who wish to circumcise the child, cease, I beg you, from such things. Let nothing, I beg, be cut from that flesh which is entirely owed to the work of our redemption, which must be entirely preserved for the fullness of the sacrifice. For although the Law of Moses says, “The soul whose foreskin is not circumcised shall perish from among his people,” a sentence issued against sin does not make liable to itself one who is free from sin. That he did not contract sin is proved by the Father’s divinity; his mother’s integrity bears witness that he did not commit sin; his very age and divine nature confirm it.

As it seems to me, O Jew, you hasten too quickly and prematurely. For it is written: “You shall not boil a kid in its mother’s milk” [Note: [Col. 0583] Exod. 23]. But you are already boiling by circumcision’s fire of pain the suckling kid, who will become the scapegoat. For by circumcising you are already cooking him. That circumcision inflicts pain is proved by Hamor, Shechem his son, and the people of their city: on the third day, when the pain of wounds is usually most severe, Levi and Simeon killed them [Note: [Col. 0583] Gen. 34].

Lord, what is man that you regard him, or why do you set [Col. 0584B] your heart upon him, that for sinful man you endure so many and such great things? O how great was the wound of our iniquity, for which it was necessary that you should suffer such things. Could you not have kept your flesh whole and unharmed by circumcision—you who kept your mother’s womb unharmed and whole, and who, after you had died, kept your body altogether incorrupt?

Moreover, two things, brothers, must be noted in this act: just as the Lord of majesty subjected himself obediently and humbly to man and woman, so the Lord of the Law, who came to fulfil the Law rather than abolish it, did not shrink from subjecting himself to the Law. He is therefore circumcised in order to be for us an example of humility. He is circumcised also so that he, who was to work salvation in the midst of [Col. 0584C] the earth for thirty years, might begin the work of our salvation from the very cradle, at his mother’s breasts, tasting the first fruits of the Passion.

For this reason he shed his blood in many ways, both in infancy and in old age, for us: he who had determined to add an evening sacrifice to the morning sacrifice, so that those who had been born of blood and had stained the robe of innocence by sin might wash their robe in the blood of the Lamb. Christ Jesus, the head of the Church, is therefore circumcised—not for himself but for his members. For it often happens to us that we treat one suffering member through another. The sides hurt, and blood is drawn from the arm. The eyes hurt, and the shoulders are tormented with tow and incision. Thus, for the corruption of our whole body, our head was cauterized today; nor does he disdain to receive the sign [Col. 0584D] of Circumcision who was appointed “as a sign of contradiction” [Note: [Col. 0583] Luke 2], “as a target for the arrow” [Note: [Col. 0583] Lam. 3]. And as he chose to be circumcised for us, so for us he decreed to be scourged, crucified, and to die.

Thus today he who made the Law was made subject to the Law. For, the Apostle says, “God sent his Son into the world, born of a woman, made subject to the Law” [Note: [Col. 0583] Gal. 4]. He accepted a binding who had no wound; medicine is not needed by the healthy, but by those who are ill. But you, Lord, came for the unrighteous to fulfil all righteousness: perfect righteousness is to subject oneself to one who is lesser. You fulfil this: when you were [Col. 0585A] eight days old, you subjected yourself to the observance of the Law, so that when you were thirty years old, coming to baptism, you might place yourself under your servant’s hands.

The things which you have deigned to suffer for us are enough for us, Lord. The times have changed; let the sacraments too, I beg, be changed with the time. Formerly you sent Abraham, then Moses with the knife of circumcision, that they might mark your sheep by cauterizing them and heal them by marking them. Yet because you, Lord, are gentle and mild, remove, I beseech you, this hard, cruel, stony knife of circumcision. A stone knife and the harshness of the Law were fittingly imposed upon a stiff-necked and stony people; but upon us, to whom you have promised to give a heart of flesh, bestow the water of regeneration.

Does it not seem harsh to you that so great an inhumanity should be inflicted upon a tender infant newly born, so that, when he has come into the valley of weeping and pain, pain should be added to pain? Remove, remove, I beg, the knife, and employ another means of purification. Why should the corruption of the original wound be scraped or cut away with a knife, when it can be washed more fully and gently by baptismal water and healed by the anointing of grace? Lord, not circumcision alone, but also your word sanctifies for cleansing. You yourself bear witness concerning your word, saying: “You are already clean because of the word which I have spoken to you” [Note: [Col. 0585] John 15]. Your Apostle Paul says concerning baptism: “God has cleansed our hearts from an evil conscience and washed our bodies with pure water” [Note: [Col. 0585] Heb. 22].

Brothers, the Lord has not defrauded us of [Col. 0585C] our heart’s desire. He who first commanded through his servant, saying, “Every soul whose foreskin is not circumcised shall perish from among the people,” afterwards says through himself: “Unless anyone is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he shall have no part in the kingdom of heaven” [Note: [Col. 0585] John 3]. Yet he himself received in himself the sacraments of both laws; and, making the two one, joined in himself, the cornerstone, the two walls. As lawgiver he gave blessing in both, not abolishing the Law but fulfilling it; and in each Law acquiring for us the inheritance of blessing. To him be blessing and glory and thanksgiving for ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON VIII. ON THE SAME CIRCUMCISION

“And his name was called Jesus, as it had been called by the angel before he was conceived in the womb” [Note: [Col. 0585] Luke 2].

[Col. 0585D]

We must speak of this name, because, although all other names are imposed by human choice, this is the name “which the mouth of the Lord has named” [Note: [Col. 0585] Isa. 62]. “There is no other name under heaven in which we must be saved” [Note: [Col. 0585] Acts 4]. Let whoever wishes write characters, barbarous names, even names which, as most people maintain, may not lawfully be uttered. May your name, Jesus, always be in my heart and mouth, in my memory and on my tongue; for it is no less beneficial than authoritative.

Gabriel says to Mary: “You shall call his name Jesus” [Note: [Col. 0585] Luke 1]. He also says to Joseph: “You shall call his name Jesus”; and, adding the cause and effect of the name, he says: “For he shall save his people from their sins” [Note: [Col. 0585] Matt. 1]. Speaking also to the shepherds: “I announce to you great joy, because today a Saviour has been born, who is Christ the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0585] Luke 2].

The name of Jesus—so desirable, lovable, sweet, and health-giving—is a source of great confidence. If it were said, “God has come,” this name would be terrifying to the kings of the earth. Conscious of my iniquity and wickedness, I would flee at the terror of this name from his face, as Adam fled and did not escape. He who looks upon the earth and makes it tremble; who touches the mountains and [Col. 0586B] they smoke; who takes away the spirit of princes; who is terrible among the kings of the earth—he would seem unbearable and intolerable to me and to those like me, whom conscience accuses and iniquity burdens, unless he had tempered the terror of his majesty not only in the form of a human being, but also in the saving name.

What, then, should we now fear? Jesus has come; the Saviour has come to seek and save what had perished. He came not to judge but to save, not to destroy but to redeem. As it is written: “The Son of Man came not to judge the world, but that the world might be saved through him” [Note: [Col. 0585] John 3]. Jesus, therefore, is he who saves; Christ, he who heals. For he heals with the oil of mercy, and makes the yoke decay because of the oil. Neither is Jesus without salvation, nor Christ without anointing. Let those who are lost rejoice that Jesus came to seek [Col. 0586C] and save what had perished; let the sick take heart, because Jesus came, because he heals the broken-hearted with the anointing of his mercy. The prophet briefly embraces both, saying: “Heal me, Lord, and I shall be healed; save me, and I shall be saved” [Note: [Col. 0585] Jer. 17]. In that he is Christ, he heals; in that he is Jesus, he saves.

I see two things together in Christ: circumcision of the flesh and the giving of the name. In the circumcision of the flesh he is shown to be the son of Abraham; in the giving of the name, the Son of God and Saviour of humankind. Before the birth the angel calls him Saviour; after the birth, a human being calls him Saviour. For he who had saved angels from the beginning saves humankind from the time of the Incarnation. We have an angel and a human being as witnesses to our salvation. “Every word stands by the mouth of two witnesses” [Note: [Col. 0585] Matt. 18].

Circumcision and the receiving of the name of salvation coincide, so that we may be circumcised not in flesh but in spirit, after Christ’s example, since Christ’s circumcision has been prescribed to us as a pattern of life. The Jew is circumcised in one bodily member only, where the seat of desire lies. Yet, because we have become corrupt and abominable, and from the sole of the foot to the crown there is no soundness in us, we must be circumcised throughout the whole body [Col. 0587A]. Christ, making purification of sins and working salvation in the midst of the earth for thirty years, was first circumcised in the small part of a slight member; afterward, when he was thirty years old, he was washed in baptism, which is a second circumcision; finally, stretched out over the whole body upon the cross, he fulfilled the sacrament of the third circumcision, no longer merely circumcised but slain.

## SERMON IX. ON THE DAY OF THE LORD’S EPIPHANY

“Having opened their treasures, they offered the Lord gold, frankincense, and myrrh” [Note: [Col. 0587] Matt. 2].

Blessed are those who have treasures from which they can bring forth offerings to the Lord. But do only the rich of this age possess treasures, so as to make an offering to the Lord? Behold, sinners and those who abound in this world have acquired riches [Note: [Col. 0587] Ps. 72]. Are those who lay up treasure upon earth more acceptable to the Lord? What then shall Christ’s poor and ragged disciples do—the sons of Peter, whose voice is: “Gold and silver I do not have” [Note: [Col. 0587] Acts 3]?

Indeed, they count their poverty the highest riches: having nothing and possessing all things, they followed the naked Christ while naked themselves. They and their followers, though beggars and needy, though the reproach and outcast of the people, were nevertheless honoured and rich before the Lord and his saints. For the Apostle says of them: “I give thanks to my God that in all things you have become rich in righteousness, [Col. 0587C] and in every word, and in holiness, so that you lack nothing in any glory” [Note: [Col. 0587] 1 Cor. 1].

There is one who boasts and considers himself rich; he is also considered rich by others because of an abundance of temporal property. But the prophet adds and corrects this, saying: “Blessed is the people whose Lord is their God” [Note: [Col. 0587] Ps. 143]. In the Apocalypse an angel speaks to one who trusted in the treasures of money; reproving him, he rejects his riches, saying: “You say, ‘I am rich and need nothing’; and you are wretched, miserable, poor, and naked” [Note: [Col. 0587] Rev. 3]. And who, I ask, is more wretched or miserable than one who is now strong, now sick; now lives, now dies; now prospers, now suffers adversity; now is, now is not?

O rich poverty, O honourable nakedness, which hides in heaven inestimable treasures, from which [Col. 0587D] you can continually take and yet nevertheless offer abundantly! This is the treasure which whoever finds goes and sells all that he has. By it they go; through these treasures those ten Israelites whom Ishmael had shut up at the point of death escaped the murderer’s sword.

The kings offered gold, frankincense, and myrrh. The Evangelist puts gold first, as more worthy than frankincense and myrrh; frankincense, however, above myrrh. But when the significance of the gifts is weighed in relation to the progress of virtues and holy works, myrrh is offered first, frankincense second, gold third.
