By myrrh—which is most bitter, medicinal, and destructive of worms—is signified repentance, when someone in the bitterness of his soul recalls his years and grieves most bitterly for his sins, accusing himself and withdrawing his plea against himself through confession. Such a one offers myrrh to the Lord. Myrrh kills worms and preserves flesh from decay.

Is not lust a worm, creeping in smoothly, biting sweetly, piercing pleasantly, and killing voluptuously? Sloth too is a worm, secretly corrupting the human heart as a moth gnaws. For it is a saying of the wise: “As a worm harms wood, so sadness harms the heart” [Note: [Col. 0587] Prov. 20]. Worldly desires also are worms. Hence, according to Solomon’s testimony, “Desires [Col. 0588B] gnaw the slothful” [Note: [Col. 0587] Prov. 21]. There is no idleness without desires. We read that every idle person lives amid desires; moreover, it is commonly known and said that idleness is the enemy of the soul.

Would you see the power and efficacy of myrrh? Suppose there is a religious man who has recently subjected himself to the yoke of the Rule: for him, myrrh—or the bitterness of myrrh—is frequent fasting, daily labour, scanty food, brief sleep, the restraint of silence, and the severity of discipline. From all these he makes for himself not myrrh—that is, bitterness—but a bundle of myrrh, for love of him of whom the bride says in the Song of Songs: “My beloved shall dwell between my breasts like a bundle of myrrh” [Note: [Col. 0587] Song 1]. Bitter indeed are the things he endures; but in comparison with the bitterness which he feels [Col. 0588C] in remembering and grieving over his own sins and transgressions, they become sweet.

Thus the bitterness of wormwood or aloe purges the bitterness of bile and the humours that have increased through indulgence. The dreadful horror of medicine and the pain of burning cautery most often heal. Myrrh belongs to beginners, frankincense to those making progress, and gold to the perfect. That myrrh precedes frankincense is found where it is said: “Like a column of smoke from the spices of myrrh and frankincense” [Note: [Col. 0587] Song 3]; and: “I will go to the mountain of myrrh and to the hill of frankincense” [Note: [Col. 0587] Song 4]. In both passages frankincense follows and myrrh precedes.

After someone has made satisfaction through contrition and repentance for his transgressions, he is thereafter concerned for the progress of virtues and asks for perseverance. When he sees himself freed from death’s snare, the remnant of his thought keeps a feast [Col. 0588D]; and then he offers frankincense, an offering which is indeed festive. Those who experience this frequently know how the offering of devout prayer solemnly produces joy in the soul, while it ascends, like incense, like a column of smoke from spices, before the sight of the divine majesty. He who previously offered the sacrifice of a contrite and humbled heart now offers the frankincense of devotion; he who was formerly pierced by compunction can now, rejoicing with his Redeemer, say: “You have turned my mourning into joy for me, and have surrounded me [Col. 0589A] with gladness, that I may sing glory to you and not be pierced by compunction” [Note: [Col. 0589] Ps. 29].

Thus the Lord gives to Zion’s mourners, according to Isaiah’s word, a crown instead of ashes, oil of gladness instead of mourning, and a garment of praise instead of a spirit of sorrow [Note: [Col. 0589] Isa. 61]. Then he can sing and chant: “Rejoicing, I will rejoice in the Lord, and my soul shall exult in my God, because he has clothed me with the garment of salvation and surrounded me with the robe of righteousness” [Note: [Col. 0589] Ibid.].

Gold is charity, which, when perfect, has no pallor in itself; which has cast fear outside, so that its latter parts are no longer in the paleness of gold, but in the brilliance of purest gold. John too saw the angel who spoke to him girded at the breasts with a golden belt [Note: [Col. 0589] Rev. 1], because charity restrains the shifting flow of temporal thoughts. Therefore he offers gold who loves Christ with his whole heart. He offers gold who recognizes divinity in Christ the man. As it is read in the Song of Songs: “His head is the finest gold” [Note: [Col. 0589] Song 5]; for the head of Christ is God. But gold is also wisdom. Hence he offers gold to Christ who confesses Christ as the power of God and the wisdom of God.

The Magi, with the star shining before and leading them, come from the East to that true East whose name is *Oriens*, “the Rising One.” The star bears witness to the Sun, light to Light; and the kings, in the brightness of its rising, recognize eternal splendour amid the dark and obscure poverty of the infant. The star goes before them not as a star, but as a rational creature: it stops where they were to stop, and with its ray, as with a finger, points to where the little child lay. I thank you, God, who said [Col. 0589C] that light should shine out of darkness, and who have shone in our hearts for the enlightenment of knowledge in the face of Christ Jesus [Note: [Col. 0589] 2 Cor. 4]. Do not wonder that they followed the star’s guidance, for in their hearts had shone the star from Jacob and that morning star which knows no setting.

Good Jesus, my salvation, my mercy, and my portion forever: with what joy the Magi exult today in your heavenly inheritance, before your Father, amid the splendours of the saints, while they worship you in the palace of heaven, upon the throne of majesty, as the Only-Begotten of the Father, crowned with glory and honour, with your Father’s diadem! They who once saw you in Bethlehem, in an inn, in a manger—little, poor, crying in a cradle.

“And entering the house,” etc. O Magi, I speak to you: you have come from a far country to see the King [Col. 0589D] of kings and Lord of the universe. What, I ask, have you found? What are you doing? Whom do you worship? You worship a nursing child, the son of a poor woman, in a lowly shelter and in cheap swaddling-clothes. Is he to whom you now render honour God? Surely “the Lord is in his holy temple; the Lord, his seat is in heaven” [Note: [Col. 0589] Ps. 10]. Yet you seek in a stable and hay the one whom you worship prostrate. Why do you offer gold and precious gifts? You seek the King of kings: therefore he himself is king. Where is the royal court, where the throng of courtiers, where the pomp of nobles? I see nothing but a stable, a manger, and Mary with [Col. 0590A] Joseph. The kingdom which you seek is not of this world.

Surely I see clearly that the wisdom of the Chaldeans has become foolish—for these too were Chaldeans. Indeed, wise men became foolish in order to worship a child contemptible both in his age and poverty. Yet they became foolish in order to become wise: what the Holy Spirit then taught them, the Apostle later preached, saying: “Whoever wishes to be wise, let him become foolish that he may be wise” [Note: [Col. 0589] 1 Cor. 1]. Since the world could not know the Lord through wisdom, it pleased God through foolishness to save believers.

Do not, I ask, be scandalized, O Magi. He who weeps in the cradle is he who thunders in heaven; he is the one to whom all the prophets bear testimony, because he is the Lord our God [Note: [Col. 0589] Bar. 3], and “no other shall be accounted in comparison with him” [Col. 0590B]—he himself almighty and saviour. All say: “For this is God, our God, forever and ever; he himself will rule us for ages” [Note: [Col. 0589] Ps. 47].

But why do I admonish them? They come against Jerusalem, led by the Holy One, led by the star to Bethlehem, a very small town, a tiny village; and, finding the little child wrapped in swaddling-clothes, they do not recoil from the stable, but fall down, venerate the nursing king, and worship him as Lord. And let us too, brothers, worship and fall down before God; let us worship God in spirit and truth. For he himself seeks such people to worship him in spirit and truth [Note: [Col. 0589] John 4]. Let true worshippers now at least come! Let us worship and weep with them before the Lord who made us, because he who is mighty has done [Col. 0590C] great things for us, and holy is his name. To him be honour and glory for ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON X. SUNDAY WITHIN THE OCTAVE OF EPIPHANY

“Jesus came from Galilee to the Jordan to John, to be baptized by him” [Note: [Col. 0589] Matt. 3].

The Bridegroom comes to the bridegroom’s friend; the Word to the voice; the Teacher to the disciple; the Lord to the servant. The sick usually come to the physician; but behold, he who makes all things new renews the signs, changes the wonders, and in all things presents us with examples of the highest humility. The fountain seeks water from the stream: for rivers go out from the sea and return to the sea, that they may flow again [Note: [Col. 0589] Eccl. 1].

This is the fountain of which Zechariah bears witness: a fountain went out from the house of David for [Col. 0590D] the cleansing of the sinner and of the menstruating woman [Note: [Col. 0589] Zech. 13]. From this fountain springs rise for us—springs of mercy, waters leaping up into eternal life—so that we may draw water from the fountains of the Saviour [Note: [Col. 0589] Isa. 12]. The Lord of circumcision and baptism comes, so that he who deigned to be circumcised might, as a demonstration of complete humility, endure baptism. “Thus,” he says, “it is fitting for us to fulfil all righteousness,” indicating humility by “righteousness,” since humility is the fullness of righteousness.

He comes to the waters of the Jordan, not because he needs to be washed by water, since he is wholly clean; not to be washed, but to wash the waters, and powerfully infuse into the element the power of cleansing and regeneration through the virtue of his name and the washing of his body. Although we are regenerated by the Spirit into the hope of life, the head of the ancient serpent is crushed in the waters through baptism. But its venomous head, the root of bitterness and sin, sprouts again.

Wretched man that I am! I was washed once in baptism, and there the wounds of the first transgression were fully washed and healed. But because I rendered my first faith void, “my scars have putrefied because of my foolishness” [Note: [Col. 0591] Ps. 37]. Therefore my soul is troubled within me [Note: [Col. 0591] Ps. 41], and in the bitterness of my soul I recall my days; nor is there remedy or consolation for me. Yet remembering, good Jesus, that you descended into the Jordan for us and not for yourself, and mindful of your humility, I shall humble myself and descend. [Col. 0591B] For *Jordan* is interpreted “descending”: “Therefore I shall remember you from the land of Jordan,” descending from the little mountain [Note: [Col. 0591] Ibid.], from the pride of life, which is short, passing, and momentary.

Naaman descended from the chariot of pride into the waters of the Jordan and was healed. The proud person descends to the waters of humility and repentance and is cleansed. Naaman washed himself seven times in the Jordan [Note: [Col. 0591] 4 Kgs. 5]; but I, wretched and more than leprous, have been permitted to be baptized only once, because there is “one Spirit, one faith, one baptism” [Note: [Col. 0591] Eph. 4]. I was washed once in baptism; but after I defiled my garments—to use blessed Job’s expression—“though I wash myself with snow-water” [Note: [Col. 0591] Job 9], though I cleanse myself with nitre or with the herb *borith* [Note: [Col. 0591] Jer. 2], you, Lord, dip me in filth; [Col. 0591C] for “all our righteousnesses are before you like a menstrual cloth” [Note: [Col. 0591] Isa. 64]. And who can make clean one conceived from unclean seed? Is it not you alone [Note: [Col. 0591] Job 14]?

But if I should somehow be cleansed, I would easily relapse and would not guard myself against my iniquity. For two things drag me into the abyss: on the one hand, corrupt condition; on the other, weak will. Therefore, since baptism’s power has once discharged its office in me and cannot be repeated, the washing of repentance alone remains to me as a remedy.

For repentance too is a baptism—not because baptism is repeated in it, but because it buries sins and, burying us with Christ in humility, conforming us to his death, regenerates us in the hope of eternal life, so that we may be like infants newly born. [Col. 0591D] Thus Naaman’s flesh, whose washing was set before us as a sign of wisdom, was restored to the purity of childhood. Some, once immersed in penitential waters, immediately think themselves cleansed of all sins; but this is insufficient unless, with Naaman, they wash seven times in the Jordan. Fast until your breath stinks; scourge, bruise, burn your body until it burns: you accomplish nothing unless the sevenfold Spirit of repentance is present. Do not the rich of this world, who spend their days amid comforts and pleasures, who despise repentance, seem to say that the rivers of Damascus, Abana [Col. 0592A] [Note: [Col. 0591] 4 Kings 5.] and Pharpar, are better than all the waters of Israel, so that they may wash in them? This is the one remedy after baptism. “God created medicine for human beings,” says Solomon, “and fools despise it.” [Note: [Col. 0591] Sirach 38.] This is the second plank after shipwreck. Christ needed neither repentance nor baptism; yet, in order that we might be cleansed, he chose to be baptized; and, in order to take away our sins, he fasted and wept in the manner of penitents. After fasting he came to the Jordan, to John, to be baptized by him. In Christ’s baptism the whole Trinity is made known: the Father is heard in the voice, the Son in the flesh, the Spirit in the form of a dove. “And,” he says, “a voice came from heaven: ‘This is my beloved Son, in whom I am pleased,’” etc.—“The voice of the Lord is over the waters; the God of majesty has thundered.” [Note: [Col. 0591] Psalm 28.] But today the Son too makes himself known to his [Col. 0592B] disciples. Thus a threefold appearance, or revelation, is celebrated in the Church today. He appears to the Chaldeans by the sign of a new star, and through them the firstfruits of our faith among the Gentiles are consecrated today. He appears to the Jews through the testimony not only of John but also of the Father and the Holy Spirit; beginning his regenerative power from the waters, he openly displays his divine power to his disciples today by changing water into wine. As the Gospel says: “This is the beginning of his signs, and he manifested himself.” [Note: [Col. 0591] John 2.] He had been born, but was not known: “He was in the world, and the world was made through him, and the world did not know him.” [Note: [Col. 0591] John 1.] And it should be noted that, by a wonderful design of divine wisdom, the star bears witness to him alone who is the Sun of righteousness, [Col. 0592C] the voice to the Word, the dove to the Lamb. As the lamb is the gentler among animals, so the dove is the simpler among birds; and dove and lamb suit one another perfectly. By the prophet’s testimony, he is “a gentle Lamb led to the sacrifice.” [Note: [Col. 0591] Jeremiah 11.] He is the dove, as it is written: “The earth was laid waste before the wrath of the dove.” [Note: [Col. 0591] Jeremiah 25.] “This,” he says, “is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; hear him.” [Note: [Col. 0591] Matthew 17.] Truly he pleases the Father in saying: “I always do what is pleasing to my Father.” [Note: [Col. 0591] John 8.] Hear him. The Son of God, God’s Word, the almighty utterance, who had long kept silence under a woman, having received permission from the Father, at last speaks—putting our pride to shame by the example of his humility. For we are slow to hear and quick to speak, wishing first [Col. 0592D] to teach rather than to be taught; first to be masters rather than disciples; first to exist rather than to exist together. Let us therefore descend with Naaman from the chariot of pride into the Jordan, that we may be washed seven times in penitential waters. For “the righteous person falls seven times in a day.” [Note: [Col. 0591] Proverbs 24.]

## SERMON XI. II. ON THE DAY OF THE PURIFICATION OF BLESSED MARY

Today the Lord of the Temple is brought to the Temple; today the mother offers her Son to his Father. This is the first procession, and no small one, for our child is still little. Here are Mary, righteous Simeon, [Col. 0593A] and Anna the prophetess, with Christ in the midst: he is offered, received, and prophesied of. All are righteous; there is no sinner. Does God, then, reject all sinners? “Do not fear, little flock, for it has pleased the Lord concerning you.” [Note: [Col. 0593] Luke 12.] And why is it that she who is holy, she who is immaculate, as though she had suffered something womanly either in conception or childbirth, seeks remedies for feminine weakness and submits herself to the Law? But the Son answers for the mother: “Thus it is fitting for us to fulfil all righteousness.” [Note: [Col. 0593] Matthew 3.] The first woman, mother of all—and of sins—when she sought excuses for her sin, turned her own blame upon another. The Mother of God, the mother of mercy, after the example of her Son, pays what she did not seize. And although she stood outside the necessity of the Law, since she had borne a son without receiving seed, [Col. 0593B] she submits herself to the Law’s requirement. Both had come to fulfil the Law, not to abolish it. Today the lofty fruit of the earth is presented to the Creator. Christ, accomplishing the purification of sins, permits his virgin Mother to undergo the law governing other women, in order to instruct us by an example of humility. Today he is offered in the Temple by maternal and virgin hands; he is to be offered on the cross by Jewish and sacrilegious hands. Today the arms of righteous Simeon receive him; a time will come when the terrible arms of the cross will receive him, and then there will be a second procession. This sacrifice is morning sacrifice; that will be evening sacrifice. In both he was offered, because he himself willed it. “Whatever he willed, he did.” How blessed may one judge himself to be who has completed the day of his purification! [Col. 0593C] Simeon fulfilled not only the days of purification but also of expectation, so that he might now deserve to see Christ the Lord, and, dismissed in peace, sleep in one and the same peace and rest in that peace which surpasses all understanding.

Our purification is in water and blood, in spirit and fire. By water and blood, as John testifies: “This is he who came through water and blood.” [Note: [Col. 0593] 1 John 5.] And likewise: “He himself will baptize in spirit and fire.” [Note: [Col. 0593] Matthew 3.] There is another, more terrible purification, in “the spirit of judgment and the spirit of burning.” [Note: [Col. 0593] Isaiah 4.] Do you wish to hear of water? He baptized in water; in waters he washed feet; he poured out waters from his eyes. Of blood there is no doubt: he shed it in many ways, so that we might wash our robes in the blood of the Lamb. Of the Spirit I read that “the grace of God has been poured into our hearts through [Col. 0593D] the Holy Spirit who has been given to us.” [Note: [Col. 0593] Romans 5.] Fire too was given for purification, namely the Holy Spirit in tongues of fire. [Note: [Col. 0593] Acts 1.] Thus the Lord purifies by the water of washing, the blood of passion, the Spirit of sanctification, the fire of perfection, and also the fire of tribulation. “We passed through fire and water, and you brought us out into refreshment.” [Note: [Col. 0593] Psalm 65.] This is the taper; this is the lamp to be set upon the lampstand—yet still placed under a bushel—sufficient for the illumination of the Jews, for the revelation of the Gentiles, for the salvation of all peoples. To this taper the mother contributed wax; [Col. 0594A] but the Father of lights supplied the light. This is he “who enlightens every person coming into this world.” [Note: [Col. 0593] John 1.] Come to him and be enlightened, [Note: [Col. 0593] Psalm 33.] that you may see form in image, appearance in radiance, light in light. He himself is the radiance, form, and substance of God. He brought us from darkness into his wonderful light, that we might be children of light, though we had been children of darkness. Light bears witness to Light, the star to the Sun. Thanks be to you, God, who said that light should shine out of darkness, and who shone in our hearts for the illumination of knowledge in the face of Christ Jesus. [Note: [Col. 0593] 2 Corinthians 4.]

With how much joy, with what exultation, do you think that the souls of the Magi rejoice today in God’s presence, amid the splendours of the saints, when they see in the palace of heaven [Col. 0594B] and adore upon the throne of majesty him whom they once saw at Bethlehem, a little city, in a lodging-house, a little child crying in a manger, in a cradle? Him whom they first saw little and weak they now see perfect in all majesty and power, crowned with glory and honour in his Father’s diadem, as the Father’s Only-begotten. Observe in these stages the progress and order of advancement. They go on from the vision of a star to the vision of the morning light, and from there to see the sun at the noon of its strength. Thus they advance from the sight of the child to the sight of God. This is the advancement of the righteous and the growth of the Church at its birth. As Solomon says: “The path of the righteous, like a shining light, goes forward and grows unto the perfect day.” [Note: [Col. 0593] Proverbs 4.] What [Col. 0594C] wonder, then, that they came to that very Light-bearer? For the star rising out of Jacob shone in their hearts, and that Light-bearer knows no setting.

Today not one star only, but many, lead us to the recognition of this child. For as many as are instructors in righteousness, so many are stars, according to Daniel’s testimony: “Those who instruct many unto righteousness shall be like stars for everlasting ages.” [Note: [Col. 0593] Daniel 12.] Therefore Paul too calls them lights that shine in the midst of a crooked and perverse nation. [Note: [Col. 0593] Philippians 2.] The Lord of lights also, when he set the moon and stars in authority over the night, said: “You are the light of the world.” [Note: [Col. 0593] Matthew 5.] And again: “Let your good works so shine before people that they may glorify your Father who is in heaven.” [Note: [Col. 0593] ibid.] Solomon testifies: “It is sweet and delightful for the eyes to see the sun.” [Note: [Col. 0593] Ecclesiastes 11.] But I [Col. 0594D] believe that no desirable things, no delights that can be imagined, can surpass the Sun of righteousness; yet it is not granted to bleary eyes to gaze upon that wonderful light. If we cannot fix the eye of the mind upon the disk of the sun, or upon that luminous body of righteousness—for “the seeker into majesty will be overwhelmed by glory”—and if we ought not to seek things higher and stronger than ourselves, let our eye at least be directed to the light of the faithful and take delight in the splendours of the saints. For the saints are mountains, from which God enlightens us, according to the testimony [Col. 0595A] of the Prophet: “You enlighten wonderfully from the everlasting mountains.” [Note: [Col. 0595] Psalm 75.] And you, brother, lift your eyes to the mountains, whence help may come to you. You who are in darkness, approach that great mountain and be enlightened, and your faces shall not be put to shame. [Note: [Col. 0595] Psalm 33.] Among the other mountains through which he enlightens us, I regard righteous old Simeon as a great mountain, who not only enlightens us in the faith of Christ but strengthens us by enlightening us. O faithful old man, whose praise is in the Gospel, whose old age is in the mercy of the Word: when you carry the Only-begotten, who bears all things by the word of his power, reveal to us how wholesomely he imparted himself to your inward parts, how delightfully he poured himself into your soul and breathed his Spirit into your breast—he whom you carried in your arms. Could Simeon not answer and say: “I had received an answer from the Holy Spirit that I should not [Col. 0595B] see death until I had seen the Christ of the Lord. I had waited long; my eyes had already failed for your word, saying: ‘When will you comfort me?’ I had become like a wineskin in frost” [Note: [Col. 0595] Psalm 118.]: cold, dry, withered, and despised. But at last, Lord, you remembered your word to your servant, in which you gave me hope. [Note: [Col. 0595] ibid.] Now in my flesh I see the Lord my Saviour; and I do not merely see him, but hold and embrace him. Now I feel myself grow warm, from diseased old age into salvation.

“My youth has been renewed like the eagle’s.” [Note: [Col. 0595] Psalm 102.] Now with unblunted sight I contemplate the Sun of righteousness. “The Lord is faithful in all his words.” [Note: [Col. 0595] Psalm 144.] “My eyes have seen my salvation.” I see you in my own countenance, in [Col. 0595C] my flesh; I shall see you in your countenance and your glory, where there will be full joy and full satiety in joy, because, Lord, I shall seek your face; I shall be satisfied when your glory appears. [Note: [Col. 0595] Psalm 16.] I have seen the Lord, and my soul has been saved. I have seen and see; nor will I let you go until you dismiss me in peace. “In peace I shall sleep and rest in one and the same state.” [Note: [Col. 0595] Psalm 4.] It was not given to Simeon alone to see, carry, and embrace the Lord, but to all those who truly love the Spirit: those who hold, embrace, and cherish Christ in the desire of their souls, in holy, devout, and desirable service; who can say with the Bride: “My beloved will dwell between my breasts like a bundle of myrrh.” [Note: [Col. 0595] Song of Songs 1.] This is he of whom Malachi foretold: “Behold, the sovereign Lord and the Angel of the covenant whom you desire will come to his holy Temple.” [Col. 0595D] [Note: [Col. 0595] Malachi 3.] You Jews seek and do not seek; you desire and do not desire. If you seek, seek; turn back and come. You seek one who will free you from the slavery of human beings, not of demons; who will grant earthly things, not eternal things. Behold, this is he whom you seek, to whom all the prophets bear witness: “This is our God, and no other shall be reckoned beside him”; [Note: [Col. 0595] Baruch 3.] “he himself will rule us forever.” [Note: [Col. 0595] Psalm 47.] “Today, O God, we have received your mercy in the midst of your Temple.” [Note: [Col. 0595] ibid.] The Temple [Col. 0596A] of God is the dwelling-place of his glory; the Temple is the virginal womb; the Temple is Christ’s body; the Temple is that building of Solomon which Christ once foretold would be destroyed, because it deserved to be destroyed. For it had become far too narrow and small, and therefore unworthy of the worship of so great a majesty. May a people of possession, from the rising of the sun to its setting, build for you, Lord Jesus, a Temple of more abundant grace; may it build a palace for your majesty, Redeemer of the Church, so that “as your name, O God, so also your praise reaches to the ends of the earth.” [Note: [Col. 0595] ibid.] But you, Christ Jesus, who are offered in the Temple today, who are the Lord of the Temple, my illumination and my salvation, who enlighten my lamp by faith and the knowledge of your truth, enlighten my darkness. For I neither see nor understand all my transgressions: “Who understands sins?” [Col. 0596B] Evils beyond number have surrounded me, and I could not see. Enlighten us, Lord, that we may be free of this world’s darkness and attain the homeland of eternal brightness. Hear us, Father of lights and enlightener of hearts; illumine our darkness, that we may please you in the light of the living—you who are the image and radiance of the substance of God the Father, Jesus Christ, to whom be honour and glory for ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XII. ON THE SAME PURIFICATION

“We have received your mercy, O God, in the midst of your Temple.” [Note: [Col. 0595] Psalm 47.]

Today, beloved brothers, the Lord was received [Col. 0596C] and offered in the Temple; today the most pure Mother of Christ fulfilled the obligation of her purification. For Moses had commanded in the Law that, if a woman who had conceived seed bore a son, she should be unclean for seven days, and on the eighth day the boy should be circumcised; thereafter for thirty-three days the woman should abstain from entering the Temple, and on the fortieth day she should offer the child in the Temple with sacrifices. [Note: [Col. 0595] Leviticus 12.] Mark the words, and the mysteries in the words. See how much care and circumspection Moses employed in these words. If he had said, “A woman who gives birth to a male shall be unclean for seven days,” then he would have declared the most blessed woman, who was to bear a male, unclean. Therefore he prefaced it: “A woman who, having received seed, bears a male.” [Col. 0596D] He therefore plainly excepted the blessed Virgin. For she alone is the virgin who gave birth, who conceived not from seed but from grace and sanctification. Could not the most holy Virgin therefore have said, when she was being led to the Temple: “What need have I of sanctification, when I was neither defiled by seed nor made unclean by childbirth? What need have I to enter the Temple, when I have become the Temple of the Holy Spirit? What need have either I or my Son of these offerings, he who is to offer himself upon the altar of the cross in order to redeem all?” Do not [Col. 0597A] say these things, holy mother: be among women as one of them. Remember that your Son too, though without sin, chose to be circumcised. For he came to fulfil the Law, not to abolish it. Enter the Temple, blessed Virgin; offer the blessed fruit of your womb; offer the firstfruits of our blessing; offer the lofty fruit of the earth, the holy sacrifice pleasing to God, our reconciliation. There will be a time when he will not be offered in the Temple or in Jerusalem, but outside Jerusalem. There will be a time when he will not be offered in Simeon’s arms, but in the arms of the cross. The day will come when he will not be redeemed with birds, as today, but will himself redeem us in his blood, because “the Lord sent redemption to his people.” That will be evening sacrifice; this is [Col. 0597B] morning sacrifice. Rejoice, mother, in the morning sacrifice, because in the evening sacrifice you will grieve, and a sword will pierce your own soul. [Note: [Col. 0597] Luke 2.] “Weeping will remain at evening, and joy at morning.” [Note: [Col. 0597] Psalm 29.] In this sacrifice and in that he was offered, because he himself willed it. Rejoice, mother, and exult greatly, daughter of Zion; rejoice and sing the nuptial song of virginity’s newness. Listen, Virgin, and incline your ear, for Anna and Simeon sing with you: righteous Simeon sings the song of righteousness, “Now dismiss your servant, Lord,” etc.; [Note: [Col. 0597] Luke 2.] Anna, the song of continence. You too sing the song of chastity, the new song, the unheard-of song, the song of virginity and fruitfulness, the song of humility, glory, and blessedness. [Col. 0597C] “Behold,” she says, “from this time all generations shall call me blessed.” [Note: [Col. 0597] ibid.] Truly all generations, because “your name is like ointment poured out,” [Note: [Col. 0597] Song of Songs 1.] and your memorial is in every generation and generation.

Brothers, today there is no day of salvation except through the Virgin. For she is our sole mediatrix and intercessor with the Son. We were sinners and feared to approach the Father. For he is terrible over the kings of the earth, who takes away the spirit of princes; [Note: [Col. 0597] Psalm 75.] he looks upon the earth and makes it tremble; he touches the mountains and they smoke. [Note: [Col. 0597] Psalm 103.] He gave us Christ, his Son. What would such a Son not obtain from the Father? He will be heard because of his reverence; but, since he himself is God, intercession is needed with him. Yet we have the blessed Virgin, in whom there is nothing terrible; [Col. 0597D] for in her are the fullness of grace and the purity of human life. The Son will hear his mother for us; the mother will offer our prayers to her Son—to her Son, I say, whom she offered in the Temple today, so that we too may receive his mercy in the midst of his Temple.

What, brothers, is this mercy that we have received today? For his mercies are many, and there is no number to his compassions. If I recall the general course of our redemption, I find seven mercies. If I consider the daily and individual redemption of each person, [Col. 0598A] I find seven compassions. It was a work of mercy that God created humanity in order to make it a participant and sharer in his glory. Humanity sinned and made itself deserving of eternal death; indeed, its iniquity was found deserving of hatred; yet God did not condemn it eternally. This is the second mercy. The third mercy was that, though we were under a curse, he promised us blessing in the seed of Abraham. The fourth mercy was that, as we wandered without law, he gave us the Law through Moses for instruction and correction. The fifth was that, when we were in great desolation and hung beneath uncertainty of hope, he strengthened us by diverse consolations through his prophets. The sixth was that he chose not angelic nature but conformity with [Col. 0598B] our misery and our deformity. The seventh is that we have received the incarnate one in the midst of his Temple. This is that great mercy of which it is said: “Have mercy upon me, O God, according to your great mercy,” [Note: [Col. 0597] Psalm 50.] because it is the completion of all the others. For the fact that Christ thirsted, hungered, endured reproaches, nails, the lance, and death on the cross: all these proceed from his birth; all these are additions and consequences of this mercy.

According to the individual state of each person, I find another seven compassions. The first is that when demons offer an opportunity for sin, the Lord prevents the evil will from [Col. 0598C] reaching its effect; and the Lord removes the rod of sinners from above the lot of the righteous, lest the righteous stretch out their hands to iniquity. [Note: [Col. 0597] Psalm 124.] The second mercy is that we continually sin and offend the Lord, adding sins to sins, and yet the Lord patiently endures and waits for us to repent. According to David: “You did these things, and he was silent.” [Note: [Col. 0597] Psalm 49.] And in Isaiah: “You did not consider in your heart that I am a silent man, and as though not hearing.” [Note: [Col. 0597] Isaiah 57.] The third mercy was that the Lord moved our heart to repentance, so that in repenting we recall our days in bitterness, as it is written: “You shook the earth and troubled it; heal its breaches, for it has been shaken.” [Note: [Col. 0597] Psalm 59.] The fourth mercy is that we may desire, long for, and will [Col. 0598D] what through human weakness we are unable to desire. The Psalmist says: “I have longed to desire your ordinances at all times.” [Note: [Col. 0597] Psalm 118.] The fifth is to establish us in a resolution of holiness, according to the saying: “You set my feet upon a rock.” [Note: [Col. 0597] Psalm 39.] The sixth mercy is to forget all worldly things, to advance and set out in obedience and observance of God’s commandments. As the Apostle says: “Forgetting those things which are behind, I stretch out toward those before me.” [Note: [Col. 0597] Philippians 3.] The seventh is when we receive Christ in the midst of his Temple—or rather, when he receives us in the midst of his Temple; then we become Christ’s Temple. As the Apostle says: [Col. 0599A] “God’s Temple is holy, and you are that Temple.” [Note: [Col. 0599] 1 Corinthians 3.] For if we thus receive him in our heart, in the midst of our Temple, we are secure: when the Judge of the living and the dead comes, he himself will receive us in the midst of his Temple, amid the splendours of the saints, in joy that does not fail, in glory that does not pass away. May he deign to grant this to us, he who lives and reigns as God with the Father and the Holy Spirit through all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XIII. ON SEPTUAGESIMA

“The kingdom of heaven is like a householder who went out early in the morning to hire labourers for his vineyard.” [Note: [Col. 0599] Matthew 20.]

[Col. 0599B] “The things we have heard and known, our fathers have declared to us.” [Note: [Col. 0599] Psalm 77.] The things which God commanded our fathers to make known to their children. The vineyard of the Lord of Hosts is the people of God, who often provoked God to anger because of their various iniquities. He therefore gave his vineyard over to trampling; and thus in divine reading we frequently encounter those by whom the Lord’s vineyard was laid waste. At one time the people of Israel are oppressed beneath Pharaoh by the yoke of most grievous slavery; but the Lord’s mercies are many. The people cry to the Lord and are freed through Moses. Again the people began to depart from the Lord’s ways, and the Lord gave them into the hands of Chushan-rishathaim; they cried to the Lord and were delivered through Othniel, the brother of Caleb. [Note: [Col. 0599] Judges 3.] Again, departing [Col. 0599C] from the Lord’s ways, they were given into the hands of Eglon king of Moab and of the Ammonites; and they cried to the Lord, and he raised up for them Ehud, son of Gera, son of Benjamin, who delivered them. [Note: [Col. 0599] ibid.] Again they were oppressed by Jabin king of Canaan, and he delivered them through Deborah, the wife of Barak. [Note: [Col. 0599] Judges 4.] Again they went astray before the Lord, and the Lord handed them over to Midian and Amalek; but when they returned in repentance, they were delivered by the Lord through Gideon, by lamps, trumpets, and jars. [Note: [Col. 0599] Judges 7.] Why should I speak of Jephthah, Samson, David, and the rest, through whom the Lord magnified his mercy toward the people and his vineyard whenever the people chose to return to their heart and repent of what they had committed? Nothing so softens and mitigates the indignation of almighty God as [Col. 0599D] the humility of the penitent. For what will the supreme Judge do when he sees the sinner exercise judgment upon himself and punish his own sin in himself? The Judge’s role has been rendered void; he will no longer exercise the part of a judge, but the office of an advocate. He who threatened punishment to the sinner will immediately heap grace upon the penitent.

Therefore today the Lord sends labourers into his vineyard, that his people may be taught to bring forth worthy fruits of repentance and thus avert the Lord’s scourges. Thus, in the Gospel, dung is ordered to be placed around the barren fig tree [Col. 0600A] and cultivation is permitted, so that it may bear fruit through the lowliness of repentance and the hoe of discipline. [Note: [Col. 0599] Luke 13.] The Apostle says: “If we judged ourselves, we would certainly not be judged; but when we are judged, we are corrected by the Lord.” [Note: [Col. 0599] 1 Corinthians 10.] Therefore, in order to correct his people and summon them to the humility of repentance, the Lord permitted them to be held for seventy years in grievous bondage under the king of the Assyrians. This season plainly signifies that seventy-year captivity; for this whole life, which is governed by the number seven, scarcely exceeds seventy years: “if [it is] eighty years, its excess is labour and sorrow.” [Note: [Col. 0599] Psalm 89.] This whole life, he says, is reckoned as slavery. As Job, having been delivered, says: “O how heavy a yoke of slavery lies upon the children of Adam from the day they come out of [Col. 0600B] their mother’s womb until the day of their return to the mother of all.” [Note: [Col. 0599] Sirach 40.]

Let us therefore too be mindful of our slavery, humbling ourselves beneath the mighty hand of God, making every thought captive in obedience to Christ. The children of Israel hung their instruments upon the willows; for it was not fitting to sing the Lord’s song in a foreign land. [Note: [Col. 0599] Psalm 136.] During these seventy days we too keep silence concerning “Glory to God in the highest,” “Alleluia,” and the other songs of newness. For, when the seventy years were completed, they returned to Jerusalem under Jesus the high priest; and after those seventy days we await the resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ, and in his resurrection the grace of our liberation. Then the songs of newness will return, because, with the oldness of sin laid aside through repentance, we shall rise in the hope of eternal life. Then from the vineyard of the Lord of Hosts new wine will be given to us, to be put into new wineskins, not old ones, lest they burst. We are invited to the Lord’s vineyard and commanded to labour in it. He who ordains labour in a command establishes a reward for labour. No age is excepted; the Lord is no respecter of persons. He receives both those who come in the morning and those who arrive late. For the denarius—that is, eternal life—is rendered to every labourer. [Note: [Col. 0599] Matthew 20.] This is the reward of the saints which the Lord promised to his faithful from of old. May he deign to grant it to us and to you, to whom be honour and glory for ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XIV. ON LENT

“Return to me with all your heart, in fasting and weeping; and rend your hearts, not your garments.” [Note: [Col. 0599] Joel 2.] [Col. 0600D]

He who admonishes us to return to him knows that we have turned away from him. But where shall we turn? Wherever I turn—whether to the right or left, whether I ascend to heaven or descend to hell—Lord, you are everywhere, filling all things; but we are commanded to turn [Col. 0601A] in heart, not body. Hosea speaks of this conversion, saying: “Return, Israel, to the Lord your God, for you have fallen through your iniquity; take away iniquity and receive good.” [Note: [Col. 0601] Hosea 14.] Since we have been turned away and perverted, we are commanded to turn and return. As the soul is told in the person of the bridegroom: “Return, return, Shulamite; return, return, that we may gaze upon you.” [Note: [Col. 0601] Song of Songs 6.] It is good to turn from malice to innocence, from destructive joy to wholesome grief, from pride and wind-swollen arrogance to a gentle and humble spirit. “Return,” he says, “with all your heart.” For one entering upon the way of repentance, the first necessity is the devotion of a contrite and humbled heart. And because abundance of food has raised our flesh into pride and wantonness, it is necessary that we return in fasting. Whoever fasts for Christ will be refreshed by Christ at that heavenly table which God has prepared for those who love him. Conversion must also be made in weeping, so that the face disfigured by sins may be washed in penitential waters. For how great the power and efficacy of a penitent’s tears are is shown by Peter’s reconciliation, Lazarus’s resurrection, and the sanctification of that most famous sinful woman.

We must also turn in mourning, suspend ourselves from joy, and in bitterness of soul recall our days, redeeming by repentance the time we have lost in sinning. For in these three—fasting, weeping, and mourning—are marked contrition of heart, confession, and satisfaction. Of the first it is said: “A troubled spirit is a sacrifice to God,” [Col. 0601C] etc. [Note: [Col. 0601] Psalm 1.] Of the second: “I said, ‘I will confess to the Lord,’ and you forgave.” [Note: [Col. 0601] Psalm 31.] Of the third: “I have laboured in my groaning.” [Note: [Col. 0601] Psalm 6.] By fasting the wantonness of the flesh is restrained; by weeping and mourning the soul is purified, mortifying itself in them and, as it were, conformed to the likeness of Christ’s death. It turns in its affliction, and its affliction is turned into grace and glory, because “the Lord will give grace and glory.” [Note: [Col. 0601] Psalm 83.] By these means we can sanctify the fast, as the Lord admonishes through the prophet: “Sanctify the fast.” [Note: [Col. 0601] Joel 1.] To sanctify the fast is to fast in holiness and righteousness before God, not before human beings, like the gloomy hypocrites. [Note: [Col. 0601] Matthew 6.] The Lord discloses to us the form and manner of fasting, saying: “This is the fast [Col. 0601D] that I have chosen: loosen the bonds of impiety”—by humbly confessing—“untie the burdens that oppress”—by devoutly making satisfaction—“set free those who are broken”—by mercifully pardoning—“break your bread for the hungry, and bring the needy and wandering into your house,” etc.—redeeming sins by almsgiving. [Note: [Col. 0601] Isaiah 58.] Give earthly bread to the poor, that you may have heavenly bread; lend earth, that you may possess heaven. By saying, “Untie, loosen, break,” he calls some sins light, some grave, some most grave: [Col. 0602A] for some are raised outside the gate, some on a bed, some in the tomb—in will, in act, in habit. In the last case the Lord groans in spirit, troubles himself, weeps, and cries: “Lazarus, come forth.” [Note: [Col. 0601] John 11.]

“Do not,” he says, “become like gloomy hypocrites.” [Note: [Col. 0601] Matthew 6.] The Lord does not condemn sadness of heart but of face; not penitential sadness, but hypocritical and superficial sadness. For, according to Solomon’s saying, “The heart of the wise is where there is sadness.” [Note: [Col. 0601] Ecclesiastes 7.] Since he invites us through confession, fasting, weeping, and mourning, lest we be swallowed up by sadness and lest, through superficial sorrow, we lose the merit of fasting like the hypocrites, he exhorts us to spiritual joy: “God loves a cheerful giver”; [Note: [Col. 0601] 2 Corinthians 9.] and “all fat belongs to the Lord by perpetual right.” [Col. 0602B] [Note: [Col. 0601] Leviticus 3.] This indicates that no sacrifice is acceptable to God unless it proceeds from cheerful devotion. Hence we are commanded to anoint our head. [Note: [Col. 0601] Matthew 6.] Our head is Christ. Although this head had been anointed by the Father with the oil of gladness above his companions, [Note: [Col. 0601] Psalm 44.] Mary Magdalene added her ointment to that anointing. When the disciples murmured, he who today commands the head to be anointed excused and commended the ointment. [Note: [Col. 0601] Matthew 26.] In the head is the fullness of the spiritual ointment descending not only upon the beard but also to the hem of the garment; [Note: [Col. 0601] Psalm 32.] for “from his fullness we have all received.” [Note: [Col. 0601] John 1.] Therefore to anoint the head is to pour all our affections back upon him with thanksgiving. For that person fasts and anoints his head who delights in bodily affliction for Christ’s sake. [Col. 0602C] But the person who anoints himself rather than his head seeks the favour of worldly applause from his works; while fasting and hunting popular praise through his fasting, he fattens his own head with the oil of the sinner. The prophet goes further and says:

“Rend your hearts, and not your garments.” In the rending of garments is signified the hardness of Jewish superstition: for those who could not rend their hearts rent their garments. But we ought to rend—that is, divide—our hearts, so that, according to the divisions of graces, they may be capable of receiving divine gifts. Let each preserve, and not rend, his garment, lest he walk naked on the road. Preserve, I beseech you, that garment which covers a multitude of sins—charity, I mean—through which iniquities are forgiven and the sins of many are covered. [Col. 0602D] Let us rend our hearts through mercy, by suffering with the afflicted; for, according to the Apostle’s word, unless we suffer with them, we shall not reign with them [Note: [Col. 0601] Rom. 8.]. Let them be rent through repentance and confession, so that corruption may run from the wound of the heart, and renewing grace, coming upon it, may remove the festering decay of its former state. As often as we grieve with our neighbour through compassion, as often as we give alms from the heart, we rend our hearts.

[Col. 0603A] Almsgiving is both spiritual and bodily. Spiritual almsgiving corrects the neighbour who sins, loves one who hates, and forgives the person who sins against it. Bodily almsgiving consists in the six works of mercy. These works are the six wedding-jars, the six sons of Leah, the six brothers of David, the six steps of Solomon’s bed, by which Solomon—the true Peaceful One—ascends into us, while he makes us, converted from our perversity and returned to himself, ascend to his love and contemplation. To him be honour and glory for ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XV. IN THE SAME LENT—ON PERFORMING REPENTANCE

[Col. 0603B] Today Christ, in the school of evangelical instruction, most aptly sets before us, through the prodigal son [Note: [Col. 0603] Luke 15], an example of repentance and humility. When he was afflicted by a most grievous famine, he resolved to return to his father and to be one among the hired servants. Who squanders all his goods in luxurious living except any sinner who corrupts and loses, by sinning, both gratuitous and natural goods? But, returning to himself and beginning to hunger for righteousness, he humbles himself in his own sight and, with devout humility, descends from the rank of son to the lot of a hired servant.

Blessed indeed are those who hunger for righteousness, for they shall be satisfied [Note: [Col. 0603] Matt. 5]. “He has filled the hungry with good things” [Note: [Col. 0603] Luke 1]. For those who seek temporal riches will not be satisfied by them. [Col. 0603C] This is the water from the well of Samaria: whoever drinks of it will thirst again [Note: [Col. 0603] John 4]. This water does not refresh, because it does not suffice. “The rich have lacked and suffered hunger; but those who seek the Lord shall lack no good thing” [Note: [Col. 0603] Ps. 33]. But the more the food of righteousness is desired, the sweeter it becomes. Hence he who “has become for us wisdom and righteousness from God” says: “Those who eat me shall yet hunger, and those who drink me shall yet thirst” [Note: [Col. 0603] Ecclus. 24].

Yet the desire for righteousness is not insatiable as is the love of money: in the latter there is desire without satisfaction; in the former, satisfaction without weariness. Hence the Prophet: “In righteousness I shall appear before your face; I shall be satisfied when your glory appears” [Note: [Col. 0603] Ps. 16]. Therefore, whoever hungers in the present shall be satisfied in the future. But do all who wish to be righteous hunger for righteousness? By no means.

[Col. 0603D] There are many wicked people who wish to be righteous; yet, conquered and bound by the habit of sinning, they still feed swine and do not return to the Father. They desire and sigh not to love what they love; pierced toward righteousness, they embrace the delight of sin and do not depart from evil, though they burn with desire for good. Their compunction toward good is a kind of grace of calling, not of justification. For righteousness is to be judged not by feeling but by effect and consent. “What participation,” says the Apostle, “has righteousness with iniquity? Or what agreement has the temple [Col. 0604A] of God with idols?” [Note: [Col. 0603] 2 Cor. 6].

If someone mourns the life that he has ruined and consents to righteousness, he already hungers for righteousness; he already resolves to return to the Father; he has already placed his foot upon the straight path; and, longing for better things, says: “Would that my ways might be directed to keep your ordinances” [Note: [Col. 0603] Ps. 118]. And although he desires, he yet seeks more earnestly, saying: “My soul has longed to desire your ordinances at all times” [Note: [Col. 0603] ibid.]. He labours toward progress in order to attain perfection. For his Father sees him from afar, since “salvation is far from sinners” [Note: [Col. 0603] Ps. 118:155]; yet he hastens to meet the one who comes and approaches joyfully. Isaiah speaks of such a course: “You met,” he says, “the one rejoicing and doing righteousness; in your ways he shall remember you” [Note: [Col. 0603] Isa. 64].

If the merciful Father responded according to merit, he would turn his eyes away from him, be deaf to his prayers, [Col. 0604B] reproach him with the disgrace of his former conduct, and sharply rebuke him. But overcome and won by the son’s humility, he lays aside severity, puts on mercy, and changes into grace the rigour which the son had deserved. It is slower for a father to bestow mercy on his son than for a son to obtain his father’s mercy. He forestalls and anticipates the prayers of his returning son; he hastens and meets him, falls upon the son’s neck, kisses him, and says:

> “Quickly bring out the first robe and put it on him; put a ring on his hand and shoes on his feet; bring the fattened calf, kill it, and let us eat and feast, because this my son was dead and has come to life again” [Note: [Col. 0603] Luke 15].

The robe is sanctification [Col. 0604C] of the Spirit; the ring, faith; the shoes, the teachings of doctrine. The calf is the sacrifice of the altar; the solemn feast, the joy of angels at the sinner’s conversion. The father kisses and embraces his son, intimating by the kiss and embrace that he receives him into the depths of paternal compassion, that he opens himself wholly to him and pours out his whole self through inspiration, so that he may be one spirit with him who, in luxurious living, had been one member with harlots. He joins and grafts him into his own members who had been a member of a harlot.

What, I ask, were the feelings of that wretched man—or rather, that blessed and supremely blessed penitent—amid the embraces and kisses of the gracious Father, when the heart of the afflicted and almost despairing man grew warm again and breathed freely; when the Father poured into him a clean heart, a right spirit, and the joy of salvation? [Col. 0604D] The human heart is narrow, and the human soul is unable fully to contain heavenly joy. Therefore his soul melts and his heart is rent within itself by contrition and groaning; conceiving burning compunctions from the remembrance of its former misery and its unexpected joy, and unable to contain them inwardly, the soul—its joy mingled with pain—in a flood of many waters cannot contain itself, and, melted by the gift of such great grace, pours itself out.

The sinner, then, or son, drawn in different directions by shame on one side and sorrow on the other, by joy on one side and not love on the other, is unequal to the joy [Col. 0605A] offered to him, and compels his father not only to pity him but also to rejoice in pitying him. O good Jesus! O gracious one! O lovable one! O God who is love! O God who is charity! If your consolations for penitents are so great, how great will your joys be for those who reign?

The son’s humility awakens this life-giving affection of the Father; it alone reconciles the son to his Father. For, according to the saying of the Wise Man, humility is the guardian of peace [Note: [Col. 0605] Prov. 11]. Do not be proud, O man, for God resists the proud, and his converse is with the humble. Humble yourself, therefore, under the mighty hand of God, so that with the penitent son you may say to the Father: “Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you. Father, I am no longer worthy to be called your son; make me as one of your hired servants” [Note: [Col. 0605] Luke 13]. Nothing makes you so worthy of the Father’s grace as judging yourself [Col. 0605B] unworthy of his grace.

Therefore let your sin always be before you. And, as the Wise Man says, “Concerning a sin forgiven and pardoned, do not be without fear” [Note: [Col. 0605] Ecclus. 5]. When you have received the grace of sonship, and when you have done all things well, judge yourself an unprofitable servant. For humility alone is the foundation of innocence; it is the protection and discipline of progress and profession in the virtues. It is the seasoning of all righteousness; without it all my righteous deeds are like a menstrual cloth. If in a person there is any deficiency of virtues, humility supplies everything; if there is anything displeasing, humility redeems and excuses everything. It alone passes through the snares displayed to Antony; it alone reconciles and commends us to him. Christ Jesus, who for us [Col. 0605C] became meek and humble of heart, invites us to humility and repentance; to him be honour and glory for ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XVI. IN THE SAME LENT—ON MOURNING

> “The sorrow of a man shall humble him, and he shall be gladdened by a good word” [Note: [Col. 0605] Prov. 12].

The Wise Man indicates the fruit and effect of sorrow; but we also have within ourselves a most abundant grace for meriting and matter for mourning. We can and ought to mourn the good things we have lost and the evils we have committed: here is the first testimony; the dangers we feel, here is the second; the tribulations by which we are pressed, here is the third; the terror of the future judgment, here is the [Col. 0605D] fourth. The Psalmist distinguishes this fourfold matter for mourning, saying: “The sorrows of death surrounded me, and torrents of iniquity troubled me. The sorrows of hell surrounded me; the snares of death overtook me” [Note: [Col. 0605] Ps. 22].

The sorrows of death are persecutions and pressures which we suffer; they are certain preliminaries of death. For we have the answer of death within ourselves. The torrents of iniquity are the assaults of sins; the sorrows of hell are self-evident; [Col. 0606A] the snares of death are the temptations and nets of the enemy. The Prophet mourns for evils committed: “My iniquities,” he says, “have multiplied beyond the hairs of my head” [Note: [Col. 0605] Ps. 39]. He admonishes us concerning goods omitted: “My days have failed in vanity, and my years in groanings” [Note: [Col. 0605] Ps. 30].

If the floodgates of my head were opened and poured forth into tears; if springs of water burst forth, so that from the abyss of my heart a flood of many waters might overflow through tears, I could not fully mourn the evils I have done, the days I have wasted—I who from my youth drank iniquity like water. Yet because of evils threatening me and importunate temptations, there is mourning for me and continual pain in my heart [Note: [Col. 0605] Rom. 9], for “my soul is filled with evils” [Note: [Col. 0605] Ps. 87], and “evils without number have surrounded me” [Note: [Col. 0605] Ps. 39]. [Col. 0606B] “I am sunk in deep mire” [Note: [Col. 0605] Ps. 68], because my iniquities have passed over my head; “like a heavy burden, they have weighed heavily upon me” [Note: [Col. 0605] Ps. 37]. But you, Lord God of hosts, deliver me from my iniquity and cleanse me from my sin [Note: [Col. 0605] Ps. 50]. “Let streams of water flow down from my eyes” [Note: [Col. 0605] Ps. 118]. Grant me Peter’s mourning and tears, by which his apostasy was blotted out. Grant me the tears of Mary the sinner, by which she was cleansed and Lazarus raised. I mean tears which compelled the Author of life himself to weep.

The second matter for mourning is the pressure of temptations, which hem us in on every side: some are above us, others beneath us, others around us, and all are against us. In all that we think, do, say, acquire, or lose; in all that [Col. 0606C] pleases or displeases, helps or harms us—in all these things we are tempted and afflicted. In short, all that we are and all that we live is temptation. As it is written: “The life of man upon earth is temptation” [Note: [Col. 0605] Job 7, according to the Septuagint]. And this is what blessed Job says: “Man, born of woman and living for a short time, is filled with many miseries” [Note: [Col. 0605] Job 14]. Truly, many are human miseries: a person is born in misery, nourished in misery, and spent in misery. We are filled inwardly with misery and surrounded outwardly by misery.

Amid these straits of temptation Paul is compelled to cry: “Wretched man that I am! Who shall deliver me from this body of death?” [Note: [Col. 0605] Rom. 7]. And elsewhere: “We were burdened beyond measure, so that we even grew weary of living” [Note: [Col. 0605] 2 Cor. 1]. Jonah also says: “I am angry even unto death” [Note: [Col. 0605] Jonah 4]. Elijah [Col. 0606D] likewise, amid diverse temptations and pressures, asked that his soul might die: “It is enough for me,” he says; “take my life” [Note: [Col. 0605] 3 Kings 19]. David too declared the weight of temptations with tears, saying: “With rebukes for iniquity you have corrected man. Hear my prayer, O Lord; give ear to my tears” [Note: [Col. 0605] Ps. 38].

The expectation of future judgment may terrify us, where there will be severe justice in the Judge, fierce and unheard-of cruelty in the torturers, and in the punishments [Col. 0607A] intolerable and eternal anguish. “Who shall be able to endure the day of his coming? Or who shall stand to see him?” [Note: [Col. 0607] Mal. 3]. For who can dwell with devouring fire? Or who shall inhabit everlasting burnings? [Note: [Col. 0607] Isa. 33]. The righteous man says: “Your wrath has passed over me, O Lord, and your terrors have troubled me” [Note: [Col. 0607] Ps. 87]. This last refers to eternal punishment. Job also says: “The arrows of the Lord are in me; their indignation drinks up my spirit, and terrors wage war against me” [Note: [Col. 0607] Job 6]. When he says, “The arrows of the Lord are in me,” this is: “Your wrath has passed over me.” When he says, “Terrors wage war against me,” this is: “Your terrors have troubled me.”

Yet there are pleasant and sweet tears which proceed from expectation of future joy. Hence the Prophet: “You have placed my tears in your sight, as also in your promise” [Note: [Col. 0607] Ps. 55]. “When shall I come and appear before the face of the Lord? My tears became my bread day and night” [Note: [Col. 0607] Ps. 41]. This is the wine of gladness of which it is said: “Give wine to the sorrowful and strong drink to those of bitter spirit” [Note: [Col. 0607] Prov. 31]. This wine is necessary to us because of frequent infirmities. Yet it must be tempered, lest it bring about drunkenness and the spirit of dizziness which the Lord mixed in the midst of Egypt [Note: [Col. 0607] Isa. 19]. Therefore it is fitting that our cup be mixed with weeping, so that the sorrow of a man may humble him. Even patience, when worn down, grows greater, and strength is perfected in weakness.

There are tears drawn from charity, as it were from the springs of the Saviour, when the mind, dissolved by a certain spiritual joy through desire for heavenly things, [Col. 0607C] flows and melts into tears, and wonderfully pours itself forth inwardly in the recollection of its beloved things, so that it may say: “I remembered these things and poured out my soul within me, for I shall pass to the place of the tabernacle, even to the house of God” [Note: [Col. 0607] Ps. 41]. He had known by experience the sweetness of these tears who, in languishing love, said: “My soul melted when my beloved spoke” [Note: [Col. 0607] Song 5]. For it is written: “He shall send forth his word and melt them; his spirit shall blow and the waters shall flow” [Note: [Col. 0607] Ps. 147].

Therefore, while the Beloved speaks and the Holy Spirit blows, waters flow by which the garden of delights is watered, so that its spices may flow forth. These are honey-flowing waters by which the field blessed by the Lord is made fruitful; for the heavens have distilled drops upon the earth, by which it shall rejoice in sprouting; [Col. 0607D] and God shall set apart voluntary rain for his inheritance, so that we may go forth weeping and sow our seed. But we shall come again with exultation, bearing our sheaves, receiving consolation from sorrow and fullness of joys from pain, through the gift of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom be honour and glory for ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XVII. IN THE SAME LENT: ON OBEDIENCE, THE CROSS, AND THE PASSION OF CHRIST

> “Christ became obedient to the Father for us unto death” [Note: [Col. 0607] Phil. 2].

[Col. 0608A] First the Most High declares the greatness of obedience’s power in all things created by him; afterwards, in himself, who is the Creator of the universe. Heaven and earth, the sea and all things in them hear him and obey his voice. At his command the earth brought forth green grass and fruit-bearing trees according to their kind, and so forth—things which would take long to recount. The heavens divided the waters from the waters and received the luminaries; and the luminaries, being called, said, according to the Prophet’s word, “Here we are” [Note: [Col. 0607] Baruch 3], and shone for him with gladness. Sea and winds obey him [Note: [Col. 0607] Matt. 8]. Fire, snow, ice, and stormy winds fulfil his word [Note: [Col. 0607] Ps. 148]. His word accomplishes all things, because all things were made by his word. All things obey and serve the Most High. As it is written: “By your ordinance [Col. 0608B] the day endures, because all things serve you” [Note: [Col. 0607] Ps. 118].

Man alone—created spiritually for this purpose, that he might serve his Creator—scorns to serve. Therefore all creation would rightly rise up on the Lord’s behalf to accuse and condemn man, according to that saying of Wisdom: “The whole world shall fight for him against the senseless” [Note: [Col. 0607] Wis. 5]. And Ecclesiasticus: “Every creature serving you, its Maker, is inflamed into torment against the unrighteous” [Note: [Col. 0607] Wis. 16]. But the Son of God, conquering malice by wisdom and pride by humility, says: “If man refuses to serve me, I shall serve him; and, in order to redeem him from slavery, I shall make myself a servant for him, so that I may bear his burdens; I shall make myself a beast of burden.” And speaking to the Father: “My heart,” he says, “is ready; [Col. 0608C] my heart is ready” [Note: [Col. 0607] Ps. 56]. If you will that man suffer anything, my heart is ready to suffer. If you will that man be scourged, behold, I am ready to undergo scourging for him.

Alas for me! Who would not fear, who would not tremble, considering the weight of our iniquity, whose redemption required so great a price? Truly, incurable was the wound and dreadful the condemnation of man, for which the Son of God had to die! O how condemnable was our iniquity, for which Christ shed his blood so often! He shed it in circumcision; he shed it when he was in agony, when his sweat became like drops of blood running down to the ground; he shed it when, bound to the post, he offered his back to the scourges; he shed it when nailed to the cross through feet and hands; he shed it, pierced many times by thorns upon his head; [Col. 0608D] and he shed it when pierced by the lance.

Christ indeed shed his blood in many ways so that those born “of bloods,” who had defiled the robe of innocence by sin, might wash their robes in the blood of the Lamb. For otherwise they could not be cleansed, as the Apostle says: “Whom God set forth as a propitiation through faith, in his blood” [Note: [Col. 0607] Rom. 3]. Thus the Paschal Lamb was sacrificed in the evening of the fourteenth moon [Note: [Col. 0607] Exod. 12]. The phrase “fourteenth moon” signifies the full moon; “at evening” signifies the setting of the sun. Christ is the sun of righteousness; the Church is the moon. The sun—that is, Christ—moves toward the setting of death; the moon—that [Col. 0609A] is, the Church—illumined by the sun of righteousness rises toward its dawn.

He became obedient not only unto the Father’s good pleasure but unto death’s anguish and the shame of the cross. For in order that man might ascend from hell, Christ descended from heaven and ascended the cross. This is what he had once foretold in the Song of Songs in the person of the Bride: “I shall climb the palm tree and seize its fruits” [Note: [Col. 0609] Song 7]. The cross of Christ is faith, and the palm of the cross is victory. “This is the victory which conquers the world” [Note: [Col. 0609] 1 John 5], which triumphs over the prince of this world. Clearly death has been destroyed, and he who possessed the empire of death has been conquered and cast out.

He who hung upon the cross, Christ Jesus, climbed this palm, of whom the prophet Ezra had foretold: “He had anointed me, not like the Father who delivered us [Col. 0609B] from the land of Egypt, standing before the judgment-seat of the judge; you humbled me, hanging upon the wood, and handed me over to death.” Of this same matter Moses the lawgiver says: “Your life shall hang before your eyes” [Note: [Col. 0609] Deut. 28].

Although the cross was once the gallows of the condemned, its fruits were fear, horror, disgrace, and death. But since Christ climbed the palm, since the innocent Lamb ascended the cross victoriously, its fruits have changed. Where formerly were fear, horror, pain, disgrace, and death, there may today be found peace, honour, delight, life, and glory. The cross, which once had been an instrument of most extreme contempt and a punishment of refined condemnation, is today raised in magnificence and glory. From being the torment of thieves [Col. 0609C] it has been transferred to the foreheads of emperors and kings, and to the heads of the highest pontiffs.

The fruits of the cross are many and wonderful. “Come to it, all who labour and are burdened” [Note: [Col. 0609] Matt. 11], who have fallen, been broken, and been crushed. What else so restores those who have fallen? What so strengthens the broken? What so preserves the holiness and devotion of human conduct? What is so merciful, so trustworthy, so health-giving, or medicinal as remembrance of Christ’s cross? What so kills sin? What so empties the enemy’s power? What so crucifies every evil in a human being? Nothing is sweeter, more welcome, more lovable, or more pleasant to those, O Christ, who love you and who bear in their flesh the mortification of the cross for love of you.

O depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! By what incomprehensible and ineffable artistry of charity Christ, tormented upon the cross, extinguished eternal torments! [Col. 0609D] From human death and misery he fashioned the antidote of life and salvation, so that misery may swallow misery, death may devour death, and the whole person may rise through the benefit of Christ’s passion into the grace and glory of impassibility. These are the mysteries; these are the benefits of the cross. This is what brought the children of Israel out of Egypt, what redeemed us from eternal captivity. This is the rod that devoured Pharaoh’s dragons; this is what drew waters from the rock and makes penitential tears flow from a stony heart; this is what sweetened the waters [Col. 0610A] of Marah, because the remembrance of the Lord’s passion makes every sorrow exceedingly sweet.

The cross is indeed for us the ark of the covenant. It is for us the mercy-seat of being heard, the standard of salvation, the title of holiness: the hope of victory, the covenant and ark of divine grace, the mark of Christian soldiery, the foundation of faith, the overthrow of the enemy, the despoiling of hell, the ladder of heaven, the gate of paradise, the raising of those who have fallen, the opening of those shut in, the consolation of the afflicted, the protection of bodies, the armour of spirits, the salvation of the living, the life of the dead, the liberation of captives, the consolation of the humble and the casting down of the proud, the tower of David, the watchtower of Zion, the universal salvation of all, the one and common refuge of all.

Above all, Christ Jesus, the passion of your cross makes you lovable to us; here you showed how greatly [Col. 0610B] you loved us. For “no one has greater love than this: that someone lay down his life for his friends” [Note: [Col. 0609] John 15]. Your passion, cancelling every suffering, has made propitiation for all our iniquities. Nothing, brothers, is so deadly that Christ’s death does not heal it. He himself redeemed Israel in his mercy from all its iniquities. “For with the Lord is mercy, and with him abundant redemption” [Note: [Col. 0609] Ps. 129].

But what shall Christ do amid the tears of his mother, and of grieving and sighing disciples; amid the reproaches of those reproaching and saying, “He saved others; he cannot save himself. If he is the Son of God, let him now come down from the cross, and we believe him” [Note: [Col. 0609] Matt. 27]? Peter says: “May it be merciful to you, Lord” [Note: [Col. 0609] Matt. 16]. [Col. 0610C] And the disciples: “We were hoping that he was the one to redeem Israel” [Note: [Col. 0609] Luke 24]. The Jew rejoices and mocks him; while the other disciples flee, Peter despairs and denies him. “How long, O Lord, shall sinners—how long shall sinners glory?” [Note: [Col. 0609] Ps. 93]. You who look upon the earth and make it tremble, show your power, so that the nations may know that your name is the Lord, that you alone are Most High over all the earth.

Yet while he is sold and handed over, bound, scourged, spat upon, condemned, and fastened to the cross—forgetful of his own pains and miseries but mindful of mercies—he says: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” [Note: [Col. 0609] Luke 23]. Jesus, Jesus! Your irrevocable word flies forth; it shall not return to you empty, but shall accomplish that for which you sent [Col. 0610D] it. O how abundant are you in forgiveness, O Lord! The Jews cry, “Crucify!” [Note: [Col. 0609] John 19]; you cry, “Forgive.” O how great is the abundance of your sweetness, O Lord! [Note: [Col. 0609] Ps. 30]. O how your mercy has been strengthened over us, O Lord! [Note: [Col. 0609] Ps. 116]. O good Jesus, O gracious, lovable, desirable, pleasant, sweet one; O God who is love, O God who is charity! With what sweet, desirable torrent of delight will you give drink to those who love you, since you anoint with the oil of mercy those who hear you thus and crucify you!

Certainly no prayer has ever been made so fitting, so measured, so suited to the time and need. For in that lifting [Col. 0611A] of your hands, Jesus, when the morning sacrifice passed into the evening sacrifice, in the very power of incense which ascended to heaven, covered the earth, and sprinkled the lower regions, you cry—as one heard because of your reverence—“Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing.” In the wrath of the raging Jewish people, the Lord turned away his own wrath and poured out grace.

This word of grace, this word of mercy, must always be held in the heart and always kept on the lips: “Father, forgive them,” and so forth. “My soul melted when my beloved spoke” [Note: [Col. 0611] Song 5]. “Shall not my soul be subject to God? For from him comes my salvation” [Note: [Col. 0611] Ps. 61]. Now, understanding and wisely knowing the mercies of the Lord, I am secure, because I have as advocate him whom I had as judge. “Father,” he says, “forgive.”

Why, my soul, are you consumed with grief? [Col. 0611B] “Why are you sad, my soul, and why do you trouble me?” [Note: [Col. 0611] Ps. 41]. Have you no counsellor? Is there no balm in Gilead and no physician for you—you who spoke so peacefully to your crucifiers? “Speak, Lord, for your servant hears” [Note: [Col. 0611] 1 Kings 3]. Speak peace to your people. Give to your voice a voice of power. Heal my soul, for I have sinned against you [Note: [Col. 0611] Ps. 40]. Say to my soul: “I am your salvation” [Note: [Col. 0611] Ps. 34]—you who are supremely good, without whom no one is good; who are, as the Apostle says, the image of the Father, the form of beauty, the seal of holiness [Note: [Col. 0611] Heb. 1]. Seal my heart under your protection, O God of my heart and my portion for ever. Seal all who adore the sign of the cross and, in adoring you, honour you, who are the honour, power, and wisdom [Col. 0611C] of God, our righteousness, redemption, and sanctification [Note: [Col. 0611] 1 Cor. 4], Jesus Christ, who are blessed for ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XVIII. ON THE LORD’S SUPPER

> “When Jesus rose from supper, he poured water into a basin,” etc. [Note: [Col. 0611] John 13].

At the beginning of Lent the Lord commanded us to wash our faces by fasting [Note: [Col. 0611] Matt. 6]. Today the same Lord, in the school of evangelical discipline, teaches us both by word and example to wash one another’s feet. For although the Creator made us in his image, through the first transgression the heavenly image in us was deformed. Therefore it must be washed with tears of repentance, so that, as through the sin [Col. 0611D] of the earthly man we bore the image of the earthly, so through repentance we may be re-formed into the image of the heavenly.

The Apostle says: “The first man is earthly, from the earth; the second man heavenly, from heaven. And as we have borne the image of the earthly, let us bear the image of the heavenly” [Note: [Col. 0611] 1 Cor. 15]. Describing the image of the earthly man, the Psalmist says: “Man has been made like vanity” [Note: [Col. 0611] Ps. 143]. Truth is the image of the first; vanity the image of the second. For his days pass in vanity and perish like a shadow. [Col. 0612A] Nothing in us is so deformed that repentance does not wash and restore it.

Peter had apostatized, but tears blotted out his apostasy. That blessed sinful woman, possessed by seven demons, is freed through the benefit of tears [Note: [Col. 0611] Luke 7]. Samuel’s tears obtained pardon. Tears opened Tobit’s eyes and drove the demon away from his daughter-in-law. Tears compelled the Creator of the universe to weep and merited Lazarus’s resurrection. These are the warm waters which Anah, son of Zibeon, found while he was tending his father’s asses. Of them the Prophet says: “Streams of water ran down from my eyes, because they did not keep your law” [Note: [Col. 0611] Ps. 118].

But because we cannot avoid contracting something from the dust of human conduct, we are commanded to wash our feet, [Col. 0612B] so that, after the time of repentance has now been completed, the end and completion of our life—which is signified by the feet—may be wholly cleansed not only from mortal but also from venial sins. Thus the prophet recalls: “There was filth upon her feet, and she did not remember her end” [Note: [Col. 0611] Lam. 1].

Jesus therefore, performing purification, after he had already cleansed his disciples by grace and word—as he himself says, “You are clean because of the word which I have spoken to you” [Note: [Col. 0611] John 15]—said elsewhere, because Judas was still among them: “You are clean, but not all” [Note: [Col. 0611] John 13]. Rising therefore from supper and girding himself with a towel, he poured water into a basin, and so forth.

This supper is the Lord’s table, which is set before us for protection and defence against the enemy’s evils. “You have set a table before me against those who afflict me” [Note: [Col. 0611] Ps. 22]. There are three tables. The first is Moses’ table in the wilderness, of which it was said: “You shall make for me a table of shittim wood, and overlay it with pure gold” [Note: [Col. 0611] Exod. 25].
