For if we render honour to the saints, we ought to honour the sanctification of all with greater diligence and devotion. The Holy Spirit is a certain sweet nature in God: God’s kindness, God’s love, and God himself. “Love,” says the Apostle, “has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us” [Note: [Col. 0637] Rom. 3]. The Holy Spirit gives himself to us; nor does he disdain to bestow the author of the gift—himself—in his own gift.

Certainly, our vessels must be cleansed and emptied of sin; otherwise the oil must necessarily remain. “Wisdom shall not enter into a malicious soul” [Note: [Col. 0637] Wis. 1]; nor does the Holy Spirit receive any falsehood into himself. There is no [Col. 0637B] fellowship of light with darkness, of heaven with mud, of balm with poison, or of the Holy Spirit with sin. The Holy Spirit is wine which gladdens the heart of man [Note: [Col. 0637] Ps. 103], and this wine is not put into old wineskins. The Holy Spirit is water: “Whoever thirsts,” he says, “let him come and drink. Rivers of living water shall flow from his belly” [Note: [Col. 0637] John 2]. The Holy Spirit is sweeter than honey. Let us therefore pray, in a spirit of humility, to the Holy Spirit, by whom today the heavens were established, by whom today the heavens distilled before the God of Sinai; that today he may send into our hearts the dew of blessing, the drops of spiritual gifts, and voluntary rain to wash our consciences; and may Jesus Christ pour the oil of gladness and the fire of his love into our hearts—he whom the Father anointed, in whom he placed the fullness of anointing and [Col. 0637C] blessing, that we might receive of his fullness. To him be honour and glory for ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XXVI. ON TRINITY SUNDAY

“He who is has sent me to you” [Note: [Col. 0637] Exod. 3].

These are the words of Moses speaking to the people. Nothing belongs more fittingly to God than being, since he alone truly is, and through him alone whatever is, is. Yet what he is cannot be thought. Therefore I believe it rash to speak of the ineffable, to think of the unthinkable. In Solomon’s testimony: “He who searches majesty shall be overwhelmed by glory” [Note: [Col. 0637] Prov. 25]. However greatly you strive and labour [Col. 0637D] to comprehend what God is, so much the more do you fail within yourself. “Man shall ascend to the deep heart, and God shall be exalted” [Note: [Col. 0637] Ps. 63]: the human condition always desires to know lofty things. So did those of whom the Apostle says: “They became vain in their thoughts” [Note: [Col. 0637] Rom. 1]. For flesh and blood cannot reveal this knowledge; only the Son of God can reveal it to whomsoever he wills.

Let us therefore seek it from him, saying: “Rabbi, where do you dwell?” “Lord, show us the Father” [Note: [Col. 0637] John 1]. But he, while he is at his table, will answer and say: “Come and see: [Col. 0638A] do you not know that I am in the Father and the Father is in me?” [Note: [Col. 0637] John 14.] It is advantageous for us to implore knowledge of God, not through ourselves, but through him who is the power of God and the wisdom of God, lest in wandering and rash freedom we meditate on vain things.

God is simple, pure, whole, and perfect; constant to himself; drawing nothing to himself from times or places; possessing nothing that passes into number, and nothing that departs from eternal immutability. He is great, and “there is no end of his greatness” [Note: [Col. 0637] Ps. 144]. He is beyond estimation, incomprehensible, and unthinkable: for eternity has no beginning, infinity no end, and immensity no measure. If we think of him, we think of him not as he is, but in part, as far as we are sufficient to think—though we fail in thought. He must be understood without visible form, without [Col. 0638B] bodily appearance, without composition of parts, and without differentiation of limbs: wholly free from the law of time, from every changeability, and from every condition of rest.

Through creatures we can find the Creator in whatever way we can. For all the works of God are to be carefully observed, as though they were certain words and signs, certain sure proofs which declare his glory to us and announce, in the ordering of things, the power of divine sovereignty. Thus one comes through the knowledge of the creature to knowledge of the Creator, as the Apostle says in speaking to the Romans: “What is known of God is manifest to them. For his invisible things, understood through those things which have been made from the creation of the world, are clearly seen—his eternal power and divinity also” [Note: [Col. 0637] Rom. 1]. For the human mind, considering the course and [Col. 0638C] order of things, discovers that there is one ruler of all and one principle of all. It strives also to comprehend that principle, although it is itself incomprehensible; and it finds its own deficiency before it reaches perfection.

Human reason, therefore, considering its own imperfection and being unable to comprehend that principle, understands that there is something above itself which it cannot grasp; and it most certainly comprehends that this very thing is incomprehensible. It is a kind of knowledge of God to know that he cannot be known, that knowledge of God cannot altogether be comprehended. A clear likeness of this is a person standing on the shore of the sea: seeing its breadth, but unable to see the end of that breadth. [Col. 0638D] For the sea extends itself farther in breadth than sight can extend in length. Thus from the failure of his own sight, that person knows that there is something of the sea beyond and above what he can see, to whose comprehension he is unequal.

Accordingly, although the greatness of the sea appears from what is seen and is in part comprehended, its immensity becomes known more fully from that which cannot be seen at all. It is indeed beyond humankind, and exceeds every power of human [Col. 0639A] intellect, to comprehend the nature of the Godhead. But the best gift, the perfect gift, descends from the Father of lights [Note: [Col. 0639] Jas. 1]: to understand the Son in the Father, and the Holy Spirit in both. No one can know these things or teach another except he alone “who teaches man knowledge” [Note: [Col. 0639] Ps. 93], whose anointing teaches concerning all things [Note: [Col. 0639] I John 2].

Plato, foremost among philosophers in knowledge and opinion, having devoted much diligence to the books of Moses, boasted that he had found the one who works all things; but he confesses that he could not find the third. Yet those who have been instructed in Christ’s school venerate and proclaim the Trinity in God and the unity of essence which the philosopher indeed dreamed of; but, because he became vain in his thoughts, he could not find it. Therefore that disciple [Col. 0639B] who had drunk more intimately and fully the streams of heavenly knowledge from Christ’s breast most clearly declared the mysteries of Trinity and unity in God, when he said: “There are three who bear witness in heaven: the Father, the Word, and the Holy Spirit; and these three are one” [Note: [Col. 0639] I John 5]. “I confess to thee, Father of heaven and earth, because thou hast hidden these things from the wise and prudent and revealed them to little ones” [Note: [Col. 0639] Luke 10]. For eternal life is to know you, God the Father, and Jesus Christ whom you sent [Note: [Col. 0639] John 17].

The sacred writings, however, plainly declare both the generation of the Son and the procession of the Holy Spirit. For concerning the generation of the Son it is written: “His going forth is from the beginning, from the days of eternity” [Note: [Col. 0639] Mic. 5]. The Son of God himself, being the power of God and [Col. 0639C] the wisdom of God, speaks sufficiently plainly of his ineffable birth, saying: “The depths did not yet exist, and I was already conceived; the springs of waters had not yet burst forth; the mountains had not yet stood with their heavy mass; before all the hills I was brought forth. When he prepared the heavens, I was present; when he set the foundations of the earth in balance, I was with him, ordering all things” [Note: [Col. 0639] Prov. 8]. Isaiah said of the Son’s generation: “Who shall recount his generation?” [Note: [Col. 0639] Isa. 53.] And blessed Job says: “To whom has the root of wisdom been revealed?” [Note: [Col. 0639] Ecclus. 1.] For it is hidden from human eyes and concealed from the birds of heaven—that is, from the angels of God.

Of the Holy Spirit it is written: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me; he has sent me to bring good news to the poor” [Note: [Col. 0639] Isa. 61]. And blessed Job says: “The Spirit of the Lord made me, and the breath of the Almighty gave [Col. 0639D] me life” [Note: [Col. 0639] Job 33]; and, to show that this Spirit is the maker of all, he adds: “Behold, God made me as he made you.”

Frequently, therefore, in sacred speech you find plurality in the persons, as in: “Let us make man in our image and likeness” [Note: [Col. 0639] Gen. 1]. You also find unity in the essence, when it adds: “And God created man in his image; in the image of God he created him.” In Genesis the plurality of persons is marked where it says that “the Lord rained fire and sulphur from the Lord upon Sodom and Gomorrah” [Note: [Col. 0639] Gen. 29]. Who is that Lord who rained from the Lord, if not [Col. 0640A] the Son from the Father? Of him the Psalmist says: “The Lord said unto my Lord,” etc. [Note: [Col. 0639] Ps. 109].

Do you wish to see the whole Trinity most plainly declared in the sacred writings? The Psalmist says: “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the spirit of his mouth all their power” [Note: [Col. 0639] Ps. 32]. Likewise, in Isaiah the Son of God speaks, saying: “I am the first and the last; my hand founded the earth, and my right hand measured the heavens. Before they came to be, I was there; and now the Lord God has sent me, and his Spirit” [Note: [Col. 0639] Isa. 48]. Behold the river flowing from the place of delight to water the face of the earth: namely, knowledge of the Trinity, by which God leads us out of the darkness of ignorance into his marvellous light [Note: [Col. 0639] I Pet. 2]. For the highest light—indeed, eternal life—is to know one’s Creator: to know the Trinity in three persons, [Col. 0640B] and in the Trinity to worship unity.

But you ask: How shall I find the Trinity where there is only unity, where there is only simple and utterly single identity, if I may so speak? Since the Trinity cannot exist without number, and unity does not admit number, how is there number? Is there number without number, or a numerical unity? Does unity pass into number, or is number swallowed up by unity, so that what are three are one? Yet we number three persons in one substance, and in three persons we worship one substance. We proclaim one and triune Lord, so that there is no confusion in the Trinity; and thus we confess the Trinity in the persons, that no injury may be done to unity.

[Col. 0640C] For the unity in God is so great that you find nothing in him except one. If you say that the Lord is good, blessed, wise, almighty, or anything similar, although you multiply such predicates, you add nothing. He is all things, as the Apostle says [Note: [Col. 0639] Rom. 11], “from whom are all things, through whom are all things, and in whom are all things.” From whom are all things by creation, not materially or seminally. Through whom are all things, so that you may understand him as the author of all things. In whom are all things, not as in a place, but in power and might. For as he is who is not in a place, so he must be conceived as nowhere, since he is not enclosed by place, and as not absent anywhere, since he is not excluded by place. But in a certain sublime and ineffable way, as all things are in him, so he is in all things.

When Christ has refashioned the body of [Col. 0640D] our lowliness, conformed to the body of his love; when he has opened the eyes of our heart, we shall know him as we are known: not through bodily vision, as Moses on Sinai; not through imaginative vision, as John in the Apocalypse; not in a riddle, as Ezekiel in [uncertain *Lumbari*, perhaps “brick”], the razor, and the frying-pan; but we shall see light in light, the Son in the Father, and the Holy Spirit in both. And this is eternal life. This is endless blessedness, unfailing glory, and consummate joy. May the Son of God, Jesus Christ, deign to grant this to us: to whom [Col. 0641A] are honour, glory, and blessing for ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XXVII. ON THE FEAST OF ST JOHN THE BAPTIST

“Among those born of women none has arisen greater than John the Baptist” [Note: [Col. 0641] Matt. 11].

Solomon’s saying is: “Let the lips of your neighbour praise you, and not your own” [Note: [Col. 0641] Prov. 27]. If praise is to be sought, it must not be sought from oneself, but from the mouth of one’s neighbour. Yet more glorious is praise proceeding from the mouth of the Most High: “For it is not he who commends himself who is approved, but he whom God commends” [Note: [Col. 0641] II Cor. 10]. Even if we spoke with the tongues of human beings and angels, we could not fully explain [Col. 0641B] John’s merits, or Christ’s encomia of John. John’s praise is celebrated in the Gospel because, wherever mention of John occurs, he is commended by Christ. Therefore he does not beg for the assistance of human praise, who is praised by God and can say: “My soul shall be praised in the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0641] Ps. 33].

The Lord commends Noah, saying: “I have seen you righteous before me” [Note: [Col. 0641] Gen. 7]. He commends Abraham by making promises to him of blessing in future generations [Note: [Col. 0641] Gen. 22]. Speaking also to Satan of blessed Job, he magnifies him because none upon earth is like him: “A man simple, upright, and fearing the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0641] Job 2]. He says likewise of Moses: “If there be a prophet among you, I shall speak to him in a vision or through a dream. But my servant Moses is not such, who is most faithful in all [Col. 0641C] my house: mouth to mouth I shall speak to him” [Note: [Col. 0641] Num. 12]. And although David himself says, “O God, do not be silent concerning my praise” [Note: [Col. 0641] Ps. 108], he is praised by the Lord, who says: “I have found a man according to my heart” [Note: [Col. 0641] I Sam. 13].

These and many others were great by God’s testimony [Note: [Col. 0641] Acts 13]. Yet by that same testimony, “among those born of women none has arisen greater than John the Baptist.” They amassed riches of praises and acclamations; he surpassed them all. His birth was announced by the archangel Gabriel, as Christ’s birth was; his name was called by an angel before he was conceived in the womb; he was foretold within the Holy of Holies and sanctified in the womb, so that he could say: “Holiness grew with me from infancy, and came forth with me from my mother’s womb.” Thus he was made before he was [Col. 0641D] born, and therefore in the course of time more than holy.

John is magnified and exalted before God and human beings by the miracle of his conception, the joy at his birth, holiness in his manner of life, humility amid eminence, truth in preaching, zeal in rebuke, and constancy in suffering. John was still tender in age, yet austere in life. Although by succession in dignity and hereditary right the pontifical mitres were owed him, he preferred sackcloth to gold-woven robes, and restrained his tender limbs with a leather girdle, the roughness of hair, [Col. 0642A] and austerity of food. Though sanctified from the womb, he chastised, weakened, and afflicted his most innocent body in many ways. In all things John offered us a model of holy conduct, as a certain boundary between the New and Old Testaments. As it is written: “The law was until John.”

He was sent by God before Christ: as the shadow before the light; the voice before the Word; the servant before the Lord; the angel before God; the friend before the bridegroom; the herald before the judge; the soldier before the king; the forerunner before the redeemer; the dawn before the day; the morning star before the sun; and the lamp before noon. He was sent in the spirit and power of Elijah, to turn the hearts of fathers toward children [Note: [Col. 0641] Luke 1]. He is the angel of God of whom it is written: “Behold, I send my angel, who [Col. 0642B] shall prepare the way before you” [Note: [Col. 0641] Matt. 11]. The Lord prepared him as a lamp for his Christ, so that, enlightening others, he might prepare for the Lord a perfect people. “And you,” it says, “shall be called the prophet of the Most High; for you shall go before the face of the Lord to prepare his ways” [Note: [Col. 0641] Luke 1]. And it adds: “To give knowledge of salvation to his people” [Note: [Col. 0641] Ibid.].

Let us therefore speak of the magnificence of the glory of holiness in John. If we cannot imitate it, let us nevertheless strive to admire it with joy. If we cannot shine like the lamp which the Lord prepared for his Christ, at least let us walk in the splendours of this lamp. That John is a lamp is testified by him whose testimonies have been made exceedingly credible [Note: [Col. 0641] Ps. 92]—namely, Christ speaking in the Gospel: “John,” he says, “was a burning and shining lamp” [Note: [Col. 0641] John 5].

John was like a lamp under [Col. 0642C] a bushel while, still enclosed in his mother’s womb, he burned with desire for his Lord who was coming, and leapt joyfully to meet him [Note: [Col. 0641] Luke 1]. But the lamp which was then beneath a bushel had to be set on a lampstand, that it might give light to all who are in the house [Note: [Col. 0641] Luke 11]; and the one that then illuminated only its bushel was to irradiate the whole world with new splendours. Did he not illuminate his own bushel when, through the Holy Spirit, he revealed to his mother knowledge of so great a mystery? “And whence is this to me,” Elizabeth said, “that the Mother of my Lord should come to me?” [Note: [Col. 0641] Luke 1.] Who told you, holy woman, that the Mother of your Lord was coming to you? “As soon as,” she says, “the voice of your greeting came to my ears, the infant leapt for joy in my womb” [Note: [Col. 0641] Ibid.].

John therefore burned, because fire had been sent from on high through Gabriel’s mouth [Col. 0642D] into the Virgin’s womb, so that the Holy Spirit, coming through the Virgin’s mouth to the little child, might infuse ardour and prepare him as a lamp for the Lord. John’s soul melted when Mary spoke. The Holy Spirit, who dwelt most fully in the Virgin, proceeds from the Virgin into John, and from John into Elizabeth and Zacharias. As Mary’s spirit rejoiced in God her Saviour [Note: [Col. 0641] Ibid.], John immediately leapt in the womb at her coming; his mother also leapt. Father and mother prophesied; all were filled with the Holy [Col. 0643A] Spirit. Rivers flow from Mary’s womb, for she was “a fountain of living water springing up into eternal life” [Note: [Col. 0643] John 4]. The fire of the Holy Spirit powerfully kindled all who were in the house; and among them there is none who can hide himself from his heat [Note: [Col. 0643] Ps. 18]. All burn; all shine.

Do you wish to see John burning? He burned and leapt to meet the Lord before he had been born. It has not been heard from the ages that anyone should leap in the womb. After his birth, indeed, he burned with the purpose and zeal of holiness. He burned against the ungodly with zeal and the constancy of free rebuke. Behold how he burned; but he shone by the merit of his life, he shone in word, and he shone in example. Was he not light, being promised by an angelic oracle, named by an angel, conceived miraculously, and sanctified in the womb? [Col. 0643B] Did he not shine, leading upon earth an angelic life, living in the flesh for the sake of the flesh, and never ceasing from the ministry of human salvation: now instructing the Church as a catechist, now proclaiming repentance, now correcting through preaching, now cleansing through baptizing, and in all things preparing a perfect people for the Lord?

“John,” he says, “was a burning and shining lamp” [Note: [Col. 0643] John 3]. Some desire to shine but do not care to burn. Yet it is better to burn than to shine. “I came to cast fire upon the earth,” he says, “and what do I desire but that it burn?” [Note: [Col. 0643] Luke 12.] Both are good, but burning is more beneficial. He who burns and does not shine benefits himself and not another. He who shines and does not burn benefits others and not himself. But he who both shines and burns accomplishes in himself at once what he owes to God [Col. 0643C] and to humankind.

Because the moon receives its light from elsewhere, it is now great, now small, now nothing. But because the sun both shines and burns from itself, it always remains in the fullness of its own light. The fool is therefore rightly compared to the moon, because he places his own conscience and reputation in other people’s lips. Thus Solomon says: “The wise man remains like the sun, but the fool changes like the moon” [Note: [Col. 0643] Ecclus. 27]. One who shines by the favour of another’s praise, like the moon, is now raised up, now brought low; now great, now moderate or nothing, according as flattering adulation or biting detraction varies around him. Not so the Apostle, who, glorying in the testimony of his conscience, said: “It is a very small thing to me that I should be judged by a human being or by a human day” [Note: [Col. 0643] I Cor. 4].

Once that son of wrath, that son [Col. 0643D] of perdition, who fell from heaven, shone; hence he was called Lucifer, but now Night-bearer or Darkness-bearer. If he had burned, he would never at any time have fallen. Those follow in his footsteps who choose rather to shine than to burn, to appear religious rather than to be so. But they shall burn in that fire prepared for the devil and his angels [Note: [Col. 0643] Matt. 25], whose flame shall not be extinguished, whose stench kills, whose heat mortifies, yet does not permit the sufferer to die. May that Holy One of holy ones turn us away from it—he who today made his holy one Jesus Christ wonderful and great upon earth, [Col. 0644A] to whom are honour and glory for ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XXVIII. ON SS PETER AND PAUL

“I saw men joined together, and the angel of the Lord spoke, saying: These are holy men made friends of God.”

Who are these men joined together, if not Peter and Paul, the venerable princes of the earth and of the Church? The same faith joined them; the same city, the same manner of life, and the same day of suffering in martyrdom under the same tyrant made them equal. Yet, since they are joined together in many ways, it is fitting that their feast also be united, so that, although each is worthy of honour in himself, the title of honour may be doubled for their glory. [Col. 0644B] It is indeed fitting for us to pursue with praise those whose patronage we need—if only we are worthy to offer praise or honour to such highly honoured princes. “Your friends, O God, are exceedingly honoured; their dominion is exceedingly strengthened” [Note: [Col. 0643] Ps. 138]. Christ changed Saul into Paul, and Cephas into Peter; for of them the prophet had once foretold: “And he shall call his servants by another name” [Note: [Col. 0643] Isa. 65]. “You are Peter,” he says, “and upon this rock I will build my Church” [Note: [Col. 0643] Matt. 16]. For Christ was the rock [Note: [Col. 0643] I Cor. 10], and he shares his own name with Peter, so that Peter may be a rock. For as water flowed from the rock in the wilderness for the thirsty people, so from Peter there flowed the confession of saving faith for others who were parched in faith.

[Col. 0644C] As Christ was about to ascend into heaven, he entrusted his sheep and lambs to Peter to pasture; and after the governance of a small boat, he committed to him the helm of a great ship—that is, the teaching office of the whole Church. To Peter, as the best steward, he handed over the keys of his house. Peter’s righteousness obtained such authority to judge that the judgment of heaven depends upon his decision; nor may even an angel presume to appeal from Peter’s sentence. When the Lord asked Peter whom men said that he was, Peter, in the brief compass of a confession, declared the hidden mystery of the divine majesty in Christ. “Flesh and blood, Peter, has not revealed this to you”; for flesh and blood shall not possess the kingdom of God, but the Spirit of God the Father, who is in heaven [Note: [Col. 0643] Matt. 16]. A wondrous fisherman: he who once searched the depths of the sea faithfully confesses the [Col. 0644D] unsearchable mystery of divinity in Christ.

When the Lord asked, “Peter, do you love me?” [Note: [Col. 0643] John 21], Peter erased his threefold denial by a threefold confession in the transaction. When Christ spoke concerning the sacrament of his flesh and blood, certain persons turned back; for many walk with Christ until the point comes of eating his flesh and blood. When the Lord asked whether the rest also wished to depart, Peter, as the rock of faith and defender of public truth, answered for all: “Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life” [Note: [Col. 0643] John 6]. As if he said: “Man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God” [Note: [Col. 0645] Matt. 4]. “How sweet are your utterances to my palate, sweeter than honey to my mouth” [Note: [Col. 0645] Ps. 118]. “What have I in heaven, O Lord? And apart from you, what have I desired upon earth?” [Note: [Col. 0645] Ps. 72].

[Col. 0645A] Heaven and earth, air and sea obey Peter. He casts Simon Magus down from the air; he raises Tabitha from the earth; he walks upon the waters; like the Lord of life and death, he strikes down Ananias and Sapphira while living; and he closes and opens heaven with authority. We have heard of Peter; do you wish to hear of Paul? We have heard how many evils this man did in Jerusalem—he who was carried in frenzy not only through Jerusalem but throughout all Judaea, in order to tear Christ’s members to pieces upon the earth. Yet, breathing threats and slaughter against the disciples of the Lord, he is adopted by the Lord as a disciple. Exhaling poison from his whole breast and blaspheming the name of the Lord, from a vessel of blasphemy he became a vessel of election, to bear the Lord’s name before kings.

[Col. 0645B] “Where sin abounded, grace abounded still more” [Note: [Col. 0645] Rom. 5]. Therefore, changed into another man, he said: “The saying is faithful and worthy of every acceptance: that the Lord Jesus came to save sinners, of whom I am the first” [Note: [Col. 0645] I Tim. 1]. While Paul still lived on earth, he was caught up into the third heaven; in the school of the Holy Trinity he learned what he was not permitted to communicate to others. If, then, he disclosed to us things that the human mind cannot comprehend, how great are those things which he was forbidden to disclose to us! Since the heavenly school had instructed Paul, the Lord entrusted to him, as a fit teacher, the office of ecclesiastical instruction.

[Col. 0645C] That he struck Elymas [Note: [Col. 0645] Acts 13]; that he snatched Eutychus from death [Note: [Col. 0645] Acts 20]; that he endured for Christ hunger, nakedness, thirst, and almost every danger belonging to the human condition; and the rest that is read in the Acts of the Apostles—all these contribute to Paul’s abundance of glory and honour. There will be no excuse for Peter if, after recognizing the truth, he turned back, looked behind him after putting his hand to the plough, and, ungrateful for grace received, committed the crime of apostasy. Paul, even after his fall, says: “I was a blasphemer, but I obtained mercy because I acted ignorantly” [Note: [Col. 0645] I Tim. 1]. Ignorance excuses Paul; and ignorance made it so that this blasphemy in Paul was not against the Holy Spirit, which is unforgivable.

[Col. 0645D] The one fell, the other was cast down; both were weakened, so that each might rise stronger and perfected. “God set apart a willing rain for his inheritance; it was weakened, but you made it perfect” [Note: [Col. 0645] Ps. 67]; for “strength is made perfect in weakness” [Note: [Col. 0645] II Cor. 12]. Truly these are men of mercy, having obtained so great and inestimable a mercy. Peter, presuming upon his own steadfastness, fell more grievously where he had promised to stand more firmly; nevertheless, after the detestable guilt of apostasy, he obtained the primacy of teacher of the faith and of ecclesiastical dignity.

[Col. 0646A] Paul, struck with blindness and cast down to the ground, is raised up to the third heaven, so that with a more purified eye of the mind he may behold the ineffable glory of the heavenly court. I believe, brethren, that while we recall the glorious death of these men, we advance the glory of all apostles and martyrs; for we venerate them as martyrs and as apostles of the apostles. O blessed martyrdom! O glorious death, which makes immortal those who die with Christ, and causes those planted together in the likeness of his death now to reign with him! “They seemed to the eyes of the foolish to die, and their end was judged an affliction” [Note: [Col. 0645] Wis. 5]; but “blessed are those who die in the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0645] Rev. 14]. They fell asleep in Christ so as to become Christ’s fellow-heirs. “When he gives sleep to his beloved, behold, the inheritance of the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0645] Ps. 126]. “In peace, in the selfsame place, I shall sleep and rest” [Note: [Col. 0645] Ps. 4].

[Col. 0646B] They laboured manfully, even unto death, in the vineyard of the Lord of Hosts. “Henceforth,” says the Spirit, “that they may rest from their labours, for their works follow them” [Note: [Col. 0645] Rev. 14]. What does it mean that their works follow them? The Lord explains it: “Give them of the fruit of their works, and let their works praise them in the gates” [Note: [Col. 0645] Prov. 31]. The gate is the departure from life.

And what is the departure from life for a righteous person but the gate of death and the gate of life? It is written: “The righteous man shall not fear when he speaks with his enemies in the gate” [Note: [Col. 0645] Ps. 126]. Blessed Martin did not fear when he spoke to the enemy standing at the gate: “Why do you stand here, bloodthirsty beast? You will find nothing deadly in me.” Securely he could sing and say with the Prophet: “Return, my soul, to your rest, for the Lord has dealt kindly with you; for he has delivered my soul from death, my eyes from tears, my feet from stumbling” [Note: [Col. 0645] Ps. 114]. Let our apostles also say: “Our soul, like a sparrow, has been delivered from the snare of hunters. Blessed be the Lord, who did not give us as prey to their teeth” [Note: [Col. 0645] Ps. 123]. O most wicked dragon, whom the Lord formed to be mocked [Note: [Col. 0645] Ps. 103], you plotted destruction against the blessed apostles, but destruction was turned for them into triumph. They made strength for themselves out of necessity; they changed the desert of sin into a reward. Thus the Lord pays the wage for the labours of his saints; and the Lord, mighty, generous, and rich, recompenses according to their merits in abundance. “Amen, I say to you: he shall set them over all his goods”—

[Col. 0646D] namely, those goods “which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor have entered into the heart of man, which God has prepared for those who love him” [Note: [Col. 0645] I Cor. 2]. This is the measure full, shaken together, and overflowing: namely, the peace of God which surpasses every understanding [Note: [Col. 0645] Phil. 4]. Behold, men of mercy, whose righteous deeds have not been consigned to oblivion, while good things endure with their seed [Note: [Col. 0645] Ecclus. 44].

Oblivion destroys a person’s righteousness for three reasons. If you are lukewarm in righteousness, the Lord vomits you from his mouth, and thus forgets your [Col. 0647A] righteousness. If you turn away from your righteousness, he remembers none of all the righteous deeds which you have done, and thus your righteousness is left under oblivion. In the hypocrisy of your righteousness you have received your reward, and this righteousness merits no remembrance with God. “Good things endure with their seed,” he says. Christ went out to sow his seed. Christ’s seed is the generation of the righteous in faith, as it is written: “His seed shall be mighty upon earth; the generation of the upright shall be blessed” [Note: [Col. 0647] Ps. 111]. This generation shall be blessed, because these are the seed whom the Lord has blessed. Speaking again of the seed of the upright, he said: “The seed of your servants shall possess the land, and those who love his name shall dwell in it” [Note: [Col. 0647] Ps. 68].

[Col. 0647B] Indeed Christ, since he was the firstborn among many brothers [Note: [Col. 0647] Rom. 8], spoke as though he were about to die without seed: “I am alone until I pass over” [Note: [Col. 0647] Ps. 140]. He spoke thus according to the observance of the Law, so that brothers might raise up seed for a dead brother [Note: [Col. 0647] Deut. 45]. Those, then, whom the Lord calls brothers and of whom he says, “Go and tell my brothers,” etc. [Note: [Col. 0647] John 20]; and, stretching out his hands toward the disciples, “These,” he says, “are my brothers” [Note: [Col. 0647] Matt. 12]—these men begot us through grace for Christ as for their brother, not for themselves. For no one says, “I belong to Paul; I belong to Cephas; I belong to Apollos” [Note: [Col. 0647] I Cor. 1], because we all belong to Christ: Christ’s seed and heirs by adoption; the sons and grandsons of the apostles through preaching.

But we are degenerate children and wholly unworthy of the inheritance: like women and helpless children, we praise the battles and triumphs of our fathers, while we shrink from receiving the cup of the saving word; even in slight temptations we are overwhelmed by faintness of spirit and in the storm. These men, indeed, bore witness to faith in their own blood. Would that we might be able to bear witness to salvation in water and Spirit! Moses indeed came in water only; these came in water and blood—in the water of repentance and the blood of suffering. Nor was the Holy Spirit, their third witness, lacking to them; for “the Spirit is he who bears witness” [Note: [Col. 0647] I John 5]. But it is written: “Whoever does not have the Spirit of Christ does not belong to him” [Note: [Col. 0647] Rom. 8].

[Col. 0647C] Christ Jesus is the Wisdom of God. He himself says: “My Spirit is sweeter than honey” [Note: [Col. 0647] Ecclus. 24]. Truly he is sweet magnificently and in many ways. “O God, how great is the abundance of your sweetness” [Note: [Col. 0647] Ps. 30], through which even the bitterness of death itself is sweetened for apostles and martyrs. What are we doing, brethren? We see that the apostles passed through suffering into glory; but we, lukewarm and slack, pursue vain things and false insanities, hoping to obtain forgiveness without repentance, reward without labour, and a crown without tribulation. I ask one thing. If we wish to understand Christ’s patience, through which he mercifully waits for us unto repentance, let us at least feel his scourges, by which he instructs us and compels us to consent to his most salutary will.

[Col. 0648A] And may what he himself says through the prophet come to pass: “With a strong hand and an outstretched arm, and with my scourge, I will reign over you; I will subject you to my sceptre, and bring you into the bonds of my covenant” [Note: [Col. 0647] Ezek. 20]. May Christ Jesus deign to fulfil this in those who delay repentance—he to whom be honour and glory for ever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON XXIX. ON THE SAME FEAST

“Your two breasts are like twin fawns of a gazelle, [Col. 0648B] feeding among the lilies” [Note: [Col. 0647] Song 4].

In the Song of Love the bridegroom addresses the bride, comparing her two breasts to two twin fawns of a gazelle, etc. These two breasts are the two apostles whose feast is celebrated today, on which we drink from the breasts of their consolation. These are the kings and princes of the earth, of whom it is written: “You shall appoint them princes over all the earth” [Note: [Col. 0647] Ps. 44]. And although they are kings, they are nevertheless breasts, because they nourish us with the milk of doctrine, as is read in the prophet: “Your princes shall be your foster-fathers, and at the breasts of kings you shall suck” [Note: [Col. 0647] Isa. 49]. Does not Peter seem to nurse novices and those almost infants in faith when he says: “Like newborn infants, desire the rational milk without deceit” [Note: [Col. 0647] I Pet. 2]? And Paul: “I gave you milk to drink, not solid food” [Note: [Col. 0647] I Cor. 13]. And again: “I became in your midst like a nurse sitting and nourishing her little children” [Note: [Col. 0647] I Thess. 2].

[Col. 0648C] He gave the breast to little ones, and he also gave his soul; the Son, full of the milk of mercy, desired not only to milk out the mercy of the Holy Spirit, but to expend his whole self. He abounded in a breast full of the milk of mercy; at his beheading milk was shed in place of blood. Before these men had been clothed with power from on high, before there came suddenly a sound from heaven, before these breasts were full of the milk of grace, the Church of blessed spirits had compassion upon the Church still little. It said, as is read in the Song: “Our little sister has no breasts” [Note: [Col. 0647] Song 8]. Christ indeed, in the days of his flesh, had begotten many children through the Word of truth, but they were still infants and, as it were, some first-fruits of his creation [Note: [Col. 0647] Jas. 1]. Therefore it fell to the apostles to instruct them diligently until they were brought

[Col. 0648D] to perfection and Christ was formed in them. In the advancement of these men the Church glories that she has become not only mature, but also a city. “I am a wall,” she says, “and my breasts are towers” [Note: [Col. 0647] Song 8]. These are the twin pillars in the tabernacle of the Lord, the two bronze mountains, the two silver trumpets which Moses made to sound at new moons and in wars. These are the two ears of grain, as is read in Zechariah, and the two sons of shining oil, who stand before the ruler of the whole earth [Note: [Col. 0647] Zech. 4].

Are they not rightly called sons of oil, who, founded and begotten in Christ’s love,

[Col. 0649A] flourish and bear fruit both in themselves and in others, like a fruitful olive tree in the house of the Lord [Note: [Col. 0649] Ps. 51]? Jeremiah says of the Church of the righteous: “The Lord called your name a luxuriant olive tree, beautiful, fruitful, fair” [Note: [Col. 0649] Jer. 11]. Truly they are sons of oil, whom the anointing teaches about all things [Note: [Col. 0649] I John 2]. To one of them, that is, Peter, sterile Judaea was committed—barren and unfruitful, of which it is said through the prophet: “The work of the olive tree shall fail” [Note: [Col. 0649] Hab. 3]. To Paul was entrusted the wild olive, that is, the Gentile people, to be grafted into rich olive trees.

These are men of mercy, both because they obtained mercy and because they are full of mercy. “I was a blasphemer,” Paul says, “but I obtained mercy” [Note: [Col. 0649] I Tim. 1]. “Where sin abounded, grace abounded still more” [Note: [Col. 0649] Rom. 5]. The same man, mourning for those who had sinned and had not repented, was he not a man of mercy? “Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is scandalized, and I do not burn?” [Note: [Col. 0649] II Cor. 1]. These men of mercy are concerned for our salvation, so that we may be perfected with them unto life. As the Apostle says: “God provides for us, lest they should be perfected without us” [Note: [Col. 0649] Heb. 11].

[Col. 0649B] These are two martyrs, and more than martyrs, because they are leaders of martyrs; like two eyes in the body of the Church, like two lights in the firmament of heaven. Since, even to this day, they have instructed many unto righteousness, they have been raised into everlasting eternities [Note: [Col. 0649] Dan. 12]. Let us rejoice in their honour and glorification—if, indeed, we can honour them or are worthy to do so—for “your friends, O God, are exceedingly honoured” [Note: [Col. 0649] Ps. 138]. The feast of one would have sufficed for the joy of the whole Church, but the united feast of both is joined for an increase of joys.

[Col. 0649C] The twin fawns of the gazelle are now no longer fawns but stags leaping upon the mountains; no longer disciples but teachers and princes of shepherds. Yet they are twins, because, as glorious princes of the earth, just as they loved one another in their life, so neither were they separated in death. On one and the same day, without the year having turned, as the iniquity of certain persons falsely alleged to itself [Note: [Col. 0649] Ps. 26], Peter was crucified by Nero in the Vatican, and Paul in the Catacombs was brought to his end by the sword, as though by a more worthy death, since he was a Roman citizen.

These men taught us your law, O Lord: not to invert Plato’s invisible riddles, nor to discuss Aristotle’s sophistries, nor to expound the contradictions of deceptive law, but they taught us how to live. He lives well who lives in an ordered, social, and humble manner: orderly toward himself, socially toward his neighbour, humbly toward God. We hold them, brethren, in memory and reverence, because they are most powerful to help us before God. If they had power as mortals, they have become more powerful as immortals.

[Col. 0649D] And who is more powerful than Peter, to whom the earth returned its dead, to whom the sea offered itself to be trodden underfoot, who dashed down Simon Magus when he had been raised into the air, who received the keys of heaven with such authority that his sentence precedes

[Col. 0650A] the sentence of heaven? Who is wiser than Peter, to whom not flesh and blood but the Spirit of the highest Father revealed this [Note: [Col. 0649] Matt. 16]? What of Paul, who struck Elymas the magician with blindness, raised a young man who had fallen from a window, was caught up to the third heaven, learned the mysteries of the heavenly school, and brought us the knowledge of life? If we wished to recount the miracles which God performed through them, a whole day would not suffice. Truly they are men of mercy, through whom the Lord magnified and made wonderful his mercy in us. And who sinned more grievously than Peter within religion? Who more grievously than Paul outside religion? Yet both attained not only holiness, but also the ministry of faith and the teaching office of holiness.

O how precious is the death of the saints, through which the inheritance of eternal salvation is given! “They seemed to the eyes of the foolish to die” [Note: [Col. 0649] Wis. 3], but they sleep in peace; for Lazarus too, who is a friend, sleeps [Note: [Col. 0649] John 11]. “When the Lord gives sleep to his beloved, behold, the inheritance of the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0649] Ps. 126]. These are sons of oil, men of mercy, twin fawns of a gazelle, two olive trees, two ears of grain, the bride’s two breasts. From their teaching we often desire milk, so that we may grow unto salvation, until Christ is perfected in us and we are perfected with his saints unto life, he himself granting it, to whom are honour and glory for ever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON XXX. ON SAINT MARY MAGDALENE

“There is joy among the angels of God over one sinner doing penance, more than over ninety-nine righteous persons who have no need of repentance” [Note: [Col. 0649] Luke 15].

[Col. 0650C] Let sinners rejoice, and especially penitents, because today a public sinner and blessed penitent has set herself before us as an example of repentance and has shown how great the Saviour’s mercy is toward penitents. Let anyone who feels himself to be a sinner devoutly approach the remembrance of the sinner. Not to mention the blessed Virgin, who was filled beyond measure and overflowing with the Holy Spirit, Elijah, Jeremiah, and John the Baptist, who were sanctified from the womb, did not suffer our weaknesses. She who has at some time suffered our miseries knows better how to have compassion on them; and she has experienced in another the benefit which she sees being sought from her.

[Col. 0650D] I believe that she became the chief standard-bearer and teacher of all penitents in the business of acquiring heavenly grace. The confession of the thief upon the cross, the supplication of the Canaanite woman, the devotion of the Publican, the tears of Peter, and the conversion of Paul took their cause and beginning from her example and imitation. Cain groaned after his sin, Esau wept, Judas repented; but because none of them possessed Mary’s contrition, none bore the fruit of repentance. Many wished to placate God by pouring out an abundance of tears; nevertheless, “in the flood of many waters they shall not come near him” [Note: [Col. 0649] Ps. 31].

[Col. 0651A] For what use are tears unless they proceed from a contrite and humbled heart? In Mary’s soul there was indeed a great agitation, which, pouring itself out through contrition of heart and penitential tears, wonderfully manifested the inward movements of the soul. The Lord summoned the earth, and it heard him with trembling. When he made judgment heard from heaven, the earth trembled; but, purified by trembling and repentance, it became still. She who had formerly been a cesspool of vices became a sanctuary of the Holy Spirit; she who had been an abyss of crimes became a storehouse of spiritual graces. She for whom the axe had been laid at the root and the fire prepared for burning now became fruitful in the house of the Lord, so that she might say: “Listen to me, you divine fruits, for like a rose planted beside streams of water I have borne fruit.”

[Col. 0651B] Recalling her sins and God’s terrible judgments, Mary was shaken by vehement sorrow. “Deep calls to deep” [Note: [Col. 0651] Ps. 41]. For there is an abyss of God’s judgments, as it is written: “The judgments of God are a great abyss” [Note: [Col. 0651] Ps. 18]. There is an abyss of sins, of which it is written: “When a sinner comes into the depth, or abyss, of vices, he despises” [Note: [Col. 0651] Prov. 35]. Thus the abyss of judgments calls to the abyss of sins: when she is shaken by fear of divine judgment, she is disturbed by the remembrance of sins. Therefore the earth was moved and trembled. “It is dreadful to fall into the hands of the living God” [Note: [Col. 0651] Heb. 10]. “At the presence of the Lord the earth was moved, at the presence of the God of Jacob, who turns the rock into pools of water” [Note: [Col. 0651] Ps. 113]—that is, he melted into an abundance of tears her who had hardened herself in wickedness.

[Col. 0651C] These are the waters of which the Prophet speaks, saying: “Streams of waters flowed from my eyes, because they did not keep your law” [Note: [Col. 0651] Ps. 118]. These waters are drawn from fear and humility, as though from the fountains of the Saviour. Mary loved Jesus, and, hearing from him words of life and the terrible judgment of eternal death for those who do not seize the way of repentance, she wasted away through fear of judgment and longing for the heavenly homeland, and could say: “My soul melted away when my beloved spoke” [Note: [Col. 0651] Song 5]. At the words of the beloved she melts and dissolves into a flood of waters. For it is written: “He will send forth his word and melt them; his Spirit will blow, and the waters will flow” [Note: [Col. 0651] Ps. 147]. For the word of the Lord is living, effective, and more piercing than every two-edged sword [Note: [Col. 0651] Heb. 4]. Although the Lord’s words are sweeter than honey and the honeycomb, according to Jeremiah’s testimony they are like fire and like a hammer crushing rock [Note: [Col. 0651] Jer. 23]. Hence the Psalmist also says: “His words are softer than oil, yet they are darts” [Note: [Col. 0651] Ps. 54].

[Col. 0651D] Therefore, while the beloved speaks and the Holy Spirit blows, she who loves melts, and waters flow by which the garden of delights is watered—the garden upon which the south wind blows, so that its spices may flow. These tears are indeed honey-sweet; for heaven distilled drops upon the earth, by which it shall rejoice as it germinates, and “God will set apart a willing rain for his inheritance” [Note: [Col. 0651] Ps. 67].

[Col. 0652A] This woman obtained both kinds of watering [Note: [Col. 0651] Judg. 1]: the lower watering, which gives her life and fruitfulness, and also the upper watering, which sprinkles her with the dew of divine contemplation. Therefore, if she who had been planted in a salty land was, through Christ’s grace, transplanted beside the water of refreshment, truly this change is “the change of the right hand of the Most High.” There are persons who delay and despise conversion to repentance and change for the better through repentance; to them that utterance does not apply: “This is the change of the right hand of the Most High” [Note: [Col. 0651] Ps. 76]. For there is no change in them, and they did not fear God, so as to be wise and understand, and through fear and repentance to provide for their latter end. Yet it is certain that “the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” [Note: [Col. 0651] Ps. 110]. The beginning of wisdom is the same as the beginning of the good way. And according to Solomon’s testimony: “The beginning of the good way is to do what is just” [Note: [Col. 0651] Prov. 10].

[Col. 0652B] Righteousness is acquired through repentance and confession. For what is righteousness but the forgiveness of sins? “I said, ‘I will confess,’ and you forgave” [Note: [Col. 0651] Ps. 31]. This is the righteousness that walks before God, as it is written: “Righteousness shall walk before him and shall set his footsteps in the way” [Note: [Col. 0651] Ps. 48]. In this blessed sinner, righteousness and peace meet and kiss one another [Note: [Col. 0651] Ps. 84]: namely, the righteousness of the sinner punishing herself, and the peace of God granting pardon. In this kiss the covenant of reconciliation is confirmed. For what will the godly and merciful judge do when he sees a contrite and humbled heart, a broken spirit, and a sinful woman repenting and weeping and watering his feet with tears?

Great is the fruit of humility. Nothing is greater than it among God’s gifts, nothing more precious among the treasures of the Most High, nothing holier among the charisms of divine generosity. Truly, Christ Jesus, with you are the fountain of life, the hope of pardon, the expectation of forgiveness, the fullness of mercy: you who so suddenly make the daughter of Babylon a daughter of Zion; the daughter of perdition, a daughter of grace and salvation; and not merely a daughter, but the bride and friend of the Most High.

[Col. 0652C] A figure of this is the prodigal son, who, after living dissolutely, returns to his father and is received with paternal gentleness [Note: [Col. 0651] Luke 15]. The hundredth sheep that had perished is sought and brought back to the folds [Note: [Col. 0651] Ibid.]. The woman sweeps her house and, after lighting a lamp, finds the drachma which had been lost [Note: [Col. 0651] Ibid.]. Was there not a lamp lit in Mary’s heart, by which she shone with examples of repentance and burned with longing for divine love? [Col. 0652D] Because she loved ardently, she escaped everlasting flames. O how much better it is to burn with delightful love than to burn in the fire of horror and death! Amid penitential tears the fire of Gehenna is extinguished, and the Babylonian furnace becomes a wind of dew.

Alas for me, if the Lord washes away the filth of the daughters of Zion and washes the blood from the midst of Jerusalem “in a spirit of judgment and a spirit of burning” [Note: [Col. 0651] Isa. 4]! Wretched that I am, who will be able to dwell with devouring fire and with everlasting burnings [Note: [Col. 0651] Isa. 33]?

[Col. 0653A] It would be good to be purified with Mary through repentance and thus escape the dreadful and unending punishment. It would be good to burn with Mary through love and thus escape everlasting burning. For what is love but a kind of fiery ardour? “I came to cast fire upon the earth, and what do I desire but that it should burn?” [Note: [Col. 0653] Luke 12]. May your love be kindled in us, Jesus Christ, so that we may be sincere and without offence on the day of the Lord, made participants through repentance with those to whom the Lord promised the glory of his kingdom—to whom are honour and glory for ever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON XXXI. ON THE FEAST OF SAINT PETER IN CHAINS
[Col. 0653B] Histories relate that the second Herod, Herod Antipas, who beheaded blessed John, was deported by Gaius Caesar to Lyons with Herodias, and that they died there. Herod Agrippa, son of Aristobulus, grandson of Herod the Great, and brother of Herodias, was appointed in his place by Gaius not only tetrarch but also king of all Judaea. Wishing to ingratiate himself with and please the Jews, after he had killed James, the brother of John the Evangelist, with the sword, he arranged to seize Peter, so that after Passover he might make him a spectacle and laughing-stock for the people, and finally put him to a shameful death. But, freed from his chains by an angel, he escaped the malice of Herod and the Jews, though he lay between two soldiers and was guarded by four squads of four soldiers [Note: [Col. 0653] Acts 12.].

In the course of time, when the daughter of a certain Roman prince suffered from a throat-swelling (a disease of Campania), by the counsel of blessed Pope Alexander—whom the girl’s father held in chains—she sought the chains with which blessed Peter had formerly been bound in prison, and was healed by touching them. Therefore blessed Alexander, released from his chains, instituted this feast and built a church in Rome, which he called St Peter ad Vincula [St Peter in Chains].

Jeremiah and other prophets are recorded to have been in chains; so too were Paul, John, who was banished to the island of Patmos, James, and almost all the others. Yet no one’s chains have been held in so great reverence as Peter’s. This perhaps occurred because of the aforesaid miracle, or rather—as I think more truly—his chains ought to be held in honour because he himself is lord of chains. For to him, by a singular privilege, was given the power of binding and loosing [Note: [Col. 0653] Matt. 16.].

Let us therefore say something about Peter’s chains, and see in what manner and by whom he was held in chains. He had indeed been handed over to four squads of soldiers and lay in a dark prison between two soldiers, bound with two chains. Each of us may contemplate this actual imprisonment of Peter spiritually within himself. For “the invisible things of God, understood through the things that have been made, are perceived from the creation of the world” [Note: [Col. 0653] Rom. 1.].

[Col. 0654A] We have our Herod, our prison, and our squads of four. For *quaternio* is the name of an office, not a number, like centurion, commander of fifty, decurion, duumvir, and triumvir. We have our soldiers, our chains, and our angel.

“Herod” is interpreted “skin-clad,” that is, “deceiver,” because he is crafty and two-faced. Hence the Apostle says: “We are not ignorant of Satan’s devices” [Note: [Col. 0653] 2 Cor. 2.]. Herod, so long as we are away from the Lord, afflicts us as though in a certain prison—indeed, in the prison of this death, the prison of the body. Hence the Psalmist says: “He has placed me in darkness like those long dead” [Note: [Col. 0653] Ps. 142]. And Jeremiah, shut in this prison, is compelled to cry: “He has built around me on every side, so that I cannot go out; he has made his fetter heavy upon me” [Note: [Col. 0653] Lam. 3.]. And the same writer says: “He has set me in dark places like those eternally dead” [Note: [Col. 0653] Ibid.]. The Apostle, feeling the straits of this same flesh, cries out in complaint: “Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from this body of death?” [Note: [Col. 0653] Rom. 7.]

There are four squads of soldiers, each having four soldiers under it. The first squad is pride; the second malice; the third lust; the fourth avarice. Pride has under it vainglory, arrogance, presumption, and singularity.

Vainglory is when someone swells up because of the good that is in him, and is oppressed by that very empty glory, thinking himself better than he is. Of this the prophet says: “Moab is proud, and his exaltation is greater than his strength” [Note: [Col. 0653] Isa. 16.], as is read of Eleazar: when he had killed the elephant, he was crushed by it [Col. 0654C] [Note: [Col. 0653] 1 Macc. 6.].

Arrogance is when someone boasts of the honour and riches of this age, as Nebuchadnezzar says: “Is not this great Babylon, which I have built by the strength of my power and for the glory of my majesty?” [Note: [Col. 0653] Dan. 4.]

Presumption is when someone ascribes to himself rather than to God the gifts he has from God, like the pagan philosophers who say: “Our lips are our own; who is lord over us?” [Note: [Col. 0653] Ps. 11.] Though they knew the Lord of glory, they did not glorify him as God.

Singularity is when someone, while acknowledging that he has spiritual gifts from God, nevertheless despises others in the exaltation of his own conscience, like that Pharisee: “I give thee thanks, O God, that I am not like other men—sinners, robbers, adulterers—or even like this publican” [Note: [Col. 0653] Luke 18.]. You have an example in Elijah, but a more familiar one in the Pharisee.

[Col. 0654D] Malice has four soldiers under it: cruelty, impatience, audacity, and shamelessness. Under lust are four others: gluttony of the belly, softness of clothing, impurity of the flesh, and the laxity of idleness and sleep. Under avarice are faint-heartedness, inhumanity, contempt of God, and forgetfulness of death.

The two soldiers between whom the wretched prisoner lies are ignorance of the good and desire for evil. The two chains are the titillation of the flesh and love of the world. And who is this angel who leads Peter out of prison? He is the one “who brings out prisoners in strength, and those who dwell in tombs” [Note: [Col. 0653] Ps. 67.].

[Col. 0655A] For our bodies are the tombs of souls: he who “broke the bronze gates and shattered the iron bars” [Note: [Col. 0655] Ps. 106], who sets the humble on high, raising mourners into safety. This angel is steadfast obedience. This is what the Lord sends ahead of his face as an angel and prepares the way of life. Thus it fittingly leads out Simon Peter: Simon means “obedient,” Peter “steadfast.” For the person steadfast in observing obedience is freed from prison through obedience, so that prison is no longer a confinement for him but a bridal chamber of rest and a paradise of delight.

He passes the first and second guard-posts. The first guard-post is habit in sins; the second, the forcefulness of temptation. These guard-posts are difficult to pass: it is difficult to abandon what one is accustomed to, and difficult, after the pleasures of this age, to embrace the hardship and strictness of a more abstinent life. Moreover, it is difficult to escape the temptations that continually arise, by which demons attack the soul—as they have attacked it from its youth—unless the humility of obedience goes before; for it makes the obedient person pass through everything without difficulty.

This humility passes through every snare of the devil. For the devil has snares, concerning which it is written: “In this way in which I walked, they hid a snare for me” [Note: [Col. 0655] Ps. 141.]. And Job says: “His trap is hidden in the ground, and his snare upon the path” [Note: [Col. 0655] Job 18.]. It is recorded that blessed Antony, caught up by the Lord in ecstasy, saw all the snares of the enemy; and they were exceedingly tangled and intricate, because, as Job says, “the sinews of Leviathan’s testicles are intertwined” [Col. 0655C] [Note: [Col. 0655] Job 40.]. Seeing these impassable and inextricable snares, the saint cried: “Lord, who will pass through these snares?” And a voice came, saying: “Humility.”

Humility passes where, brothers, pride is dashed against the threshold; humility escapes where malice is caught in its own cunning. The iron gate is charity; because of its strength it is elsewhere called the Beautiful Gate. This is the gate of which it is written: “This is the gate of the Lord; the righteous shall enter through it” [Note: [Col. 0655] Ps. 117.]. This is the Beautiful Gate which alone remained in the destruction of Jerusalem. For whether faith or knowledge shall be brought to an end, charity never fails [Note: [Col. 0655] 1 Cor. 13]; and therefore, because of its permanence, it is called iron. It leads to the city of habitation. “For we have here no continuing city, but seek the one that is to come” [Note: [Col. 0655] Heb. 13], [Col. 0655D] where there is day without night, rest without labour, and glory without end. May the immeasurable charity of Christ bring us there—to whom be honour and glory for ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XXXII. ON THE FEAST OF ST LAWRENCE

Moses set apart beyond the Jordan, on the eastern side, three cities of refuge: Bezer in the wilderness, in [Col. 0656A] the plain-country from the tribe of Reuben; Ramoth-gilead from the tribe of Gad; and Golan and Gaulon in Bashan from the tribe of Manasseh [Note: [Col. 0655] Deut. 4.].

There are three refuges, or remedies. The first is contrition for our own and others’ sins; the second is suffering for Christ; the third is being suspended in contemplation upon the desire for heavenly things. Let the names of the places of refuge and the meanings of those names be noted, and there will be complete harmony and correspondence. The first place belongs to penitents, the second to martyrs, the third to contemplatives.

Bezer is interpreted “tribulation” or “contrition,” because contrition and humility suit the heart well. Therefore this city is situated in the wilderness, the place of the penitent, in the tribe of Reuben, which is interpreted “vision of the son.” For who can see the Son—whom only the pure in heart see—unless he has cleansed [Col. 0656B] the eyes of his heart through penitence?

Ramoth is interpreted “vision of death,” or “high sign.” And what sign is higher than the sign of martyrs, the sign of the cross? Of this Isaiah says: “Raise up a sign among the nations” [Note: [Col. 0655] Isa. 5.]. And Christ says: “Whoever wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me” [Note: [Col. 0655] Matt. 16.].

Gilead means “heap of testimony,” which pertains to the whole company of martyrs. For *martyr* means “witness.” It is from the tribe of Gad, which is interpreted “girded.” And what is more girded than one who has girded his loins with strength, being girded by the Lord with power for battle? If the ungirded man boasts, then let the girded man boast as well.

The ungirded person is one who, withdrawn from the storm of spiritual conflicts, [Col. 0656C] devotes himself, with Mary at Jesus’ feet, to the peace and repose of the soul. He dwells in Golan, the third city of refuge; he is in Bashan and in the tribe of Manasseh. Golan is interpreted “migration,” which concerns those who migrate from love of this age to love of heavenly things, and, as though in ecstasy, spiritually ascend the mountain of the Lord—the mountain of divine sweetness and delightful refreshment—so that they may say: “In a place of pasture he has set me” [Note: [Col. 0655] Ps. 22.].

Therefore this city is in Bashan, which is interpreted “fatness,” and from the tribe of Manasseh, which is interpreted “forgetful.” For this appears spiritually fitting for the contemplative, who, forgetting his people and his father’s house, forgetting the things behind, stretches himself upward towards those before him. His soul, as though filled with fatness and richness, rests in Rachel’s bosom and in the shadow of desire.

[Col. 0656D] Each of these has his own zeal. The first has zeal in grief over his own and others’ sins; the second in enduring sufferings; the third in the desire for eternal things. The Apostle displays the first when, reckoning himself carnal and sold under sin, he says: “I endure all things for the elect, so that they too may obtain salvation” [Note: [Col. 0655] 1 Tim. 2.]. He expresses the second when, declaring himself ready to be bound in Jerusalem, he says: “I do not count my life more precious than myself” [Note: [Col. 0655] Acts 20.]. The third [Col. 0657A] is plainly declared when, caught up to the third heaven and inflamed by the desire for things above, he says: “I desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ” [Note: [Col. 0657] Phil. 1.].

By this threefold zeal a person sacrifices his soul; this is the threefold sacrifice of fine flour. It is offered as fine flour in an oven, on a griddle, and in a frying-pan. What is baked in an oven is hidden; likewise, contrition of heart is open only to him to whom every thought makes full confession. What is cooked on a griddle lies openly before all: in this the persecution of martyrs is clearly signified. What is fried in a pan sometimes appears and sometimes is concealed, according to the motions of boiling oil; likewise, the devotion of the mind now lies hidden within, now appears outwardly through the intensity of desire and love.

For though blessed Martin and Mary Magdalene burn inwardly with the oil of charity, their desires nevertheless emerge outwardly through the display of their deeds: he, looking toward heaven and sighing, desires to be with Christ; she, loving Christ above all things, kisses his feet and waters them with tears. Thus Paul speaks in the oven, Lawrence on the griddle, Mary or Martin in the frying-pan. Since blessed Lawrence’s griddle claims this entire day particularly as its own, let us proceed to speak of blessed Lawrence and his griddle.

When fine flour is to be offered on the griddle, it must afterwards be sprinkled with oil, lest it be burned by the violence of the fire. Three things are required in this sacrifice: that the fine flour be without leaven; that it be cooked on the griddle; and that it be sprinkled with oil. Fine flour is purity of conscience. Unless it is sprinkled [Col. 0657C] with the oil of charity, it is consumed by the fire of persecution; for human weakness cannot stand without the grace of the Holy Spirit. This is illustrated as follows.

Before the outpouring of the Holy Spirit, Peter had denied Christ at a servant-girl’s voice. But, clothed with power from on high, when forbidden by the chief priests to speak in Jesus’ name, he said: “We must obey God rather than men” [Note: [Col. 0657] Acts 5.]. And Christ indicated at the time of the Passion: “Where I am going, you cannot follow me now; but you will follow afterwards” [Note: [Col. 0657] John 13.]. Likewise all the disciples were told: “Remain in the city until you are clothed with power from on high” [Note: [Col. 0657] Luke 24.].

Fine flour is without leaven when one suffers for Christ and his righteousness, and not for one’s own wickedness. As it is written: “If you suffer for Christ, you are blessed” [Note: [Col. 0657] 1 Pet. 3.]. “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake” [Col. 0657D] [Note: [Col. 0657] Matt. 5.]. Peter says: “Let none of you suffer as a murderer, thief, evildoer, or coveter of others’ goods” [Note: [Col. 0657] 1 Pet. 4.].

It must be sprinkled with oil, for whatever you offer without charity will have no merit of life. These are Paul’s words: “If I hand over my body so that I burn, but do not have charity, it profits me nothing. Charity bears all things, endures all things, because charity is patient” [Note: [Col. 0657] 1 Cor. 13.]. Therefore the glory of the martyrs was that they were tortured for Christ’s name. “In this,” says the Apostle, “we labour and are reviled, because we hope [Col. 0658A] in the living God” [Note: [Col. 0657] 2 Tim. 4.].

Oh, how happy we should judge him who was so purified by material fire that he did not feel the fire of purgatory! Terrible is the expectation of that time when the Lord will sit, refining and cleansing silver. “He shall cleanse,” it says, “the sons of Levi in the spirit of judgment and the spirit of burning” [Note: [Col. 0657] Mal. 3.]. Happy is he whose work will not burn; happy is he who has built with gold, silver, and precious stones [Note: [Col. 0657] 1 Cor. 3.]. “When his wrath has flared up in a little while,” it says, “blessed are all who trust in him” [Note: [Col. 0657] Ps. 2]. We must pass through fire: fire will test all our works.

I fear that our gold will there be turned into dross. For “all our righteousnesses are like a menstrual cloth” [Note: [Col. 0657] Isa. 64.]. And what shall we wretches do when he purifies our iniquities, who will even judge our righteous deeds? [Col. 0658B] Whatever we now overlook, whatever in ourselves or others we flatter by overlooking it, the avenging fire and torturing flame will consume.

I, most wretched, who cannot endure a tiny drop from a burning candle if it falls upon my hand—what shall I do if I see myself encircled and laden with burning chains, pressing, scorching, and not consuming? How shall I await the Lord of majesty, judge of the universe, coming in a spirit of wrath and the whirlwind of tempest, in the fire of sulphur and everlasting burning? For “fire shall blaze before him, and a mighty tempest round about him” [Note: [Col. 0657] Ps. 49.].

Against this most fragile straw and leaf carried away by the wind, consuming [Col. 0658C] and devouring fire will be kindled, even to the lowest depths of hell. O how blessed is Lawrence’s griddle, through which both that penal fire is escaped and the repose of eternal refreshment and the joy of eternal glory are obtained!

Could not we too endure some fire? We could indeed, and very often we endure a most grievous fire. Is not envy fire? Is not greed fire? Yet this is alien fire, and it kills the sons of Aaron. This fire does not warm but devours; it does not enlighten but blinds, so that we do not see the sun of righteousness. “The fire of malice fell upon them, and they did not see the sun of righteousness” [materially uncertain OCR reading; cf. supplied wording]. Abimelech kindles this fire to burn the town of Thebez [Note: [Col. 0657] Judg. 9.]. The Amalekites kindle it to burn Ziklag [Note: [Col. 0657] 1 Sam. 30.].

And the enemy kindles straw within us, extinguishing in us that fire which the Lord sent into the earth and ardently wished to be kindled. Do you think that blessed Lawrence could have endured the burning of material fire so patiently unless he burned with another fire which consumed and removed every wickedness of that other fire? It is natural and physical that heat drives out heat. Thus the fire of charity burned upon the altar of his heart, and through it the outward fire was conquered. This is the fire of which Moses says: “Fire shall always burn upon the altar; the priest shall put wood upon it” [Note: [Col. 0657] Lev. 6.].

Perhaps [Col. 0659A] he had placed wood upon this fire and had long nourished it—that supreme blessed priest Sixtus, or, through the ministry of blessed Sixtus, the supreme priest of supreme priests. Of him it is written: “The Lord sent fire into my bones and instructed me” [Note: [Col. 0659] Lam. 1.]. And the ministers of Satan press on. With insult and torment they interrogate Christ’s martyr; the martyr stands—afflicted indeed, but unconquered. They heap on coals and stir up flames; with iron forks, burning hot, they handle his limbs. He, mindful of Christ’s sufferings and delighting in those sufferings, forgets his own pains and pays no attention to his body’s torture, because he is away from the body. This must not be attributed to stupor but to love; not to insensibility but to charity. For the awareness of pain is not lost but subdued; and whatever human malice can inflict is despised for love of Christ.

[Col. 0659B] See how blessed Lawrence’s fine flour was sprinkled—indeed, abundantly sprinkled—with oil. Unless there had been oil, it would undoubtedly have been entirely burned and wholly failed. But anointed with the oil of exultation, he not only rejoices in torture but taunts the torturer: “It is roasted,” he says, “turn it now and eat.” See how great is the faith of the saints; see how great is the power in faith, victory in power. “The saints,” it says, “through faith conquered kingdoms” [Note: [Col. 0659] Heb. 11.]. Through faith, it says. For “this is the victory that conquers the world: our faith” [Note: [Col. 0659] 1 John 5.].

The world attacks faith in three ways: by prudence, by power, and by obstinacy. Faith, however, conquers the world in three ways: by folly, by patience, and by the grace of works. By folly it conquers prudence. For though “the children of this age are wiser than the children of light in their generation” [Note: [Col. 0659] Luke 16], “it pleased God through the folly of preaching to save those who believe” [Note: [Col. 0659] 1 Cor. 1.]. The Apostle says: “We preach Christ crucified: a stumbling-block to the Jews and folly to the Gentiles” [Note: [Col. 0659] Ibid.].

By patience it conquers power. “In your patience,” he says, “you shall possess your souls” [Col. 0659C] [Note: [Col. 0659] Luke 11]. Again: “Do not fear those who kill the body; they have nothing that they can do to the soul” [Note: [Col. 0659] Matt. 10.]. Obstinacy is conquered by the grace of works. For who is so obstinate that holy and miraculous works would not lead him to the love of Christ?

This is Gideon’s battle with trumpets, jars, and lamps [Note: [Col. 0659] Judg. 7.]: in the trumpet, preaching; in the jar that is broken, the martyrdom of the body; in the lamp, the display of miracles. And what earthen vessel or glass is more fragile than our flesh? Thus, rightly, our flesh is also a jar.

If we cannot ascend the mountain of martyrdom, because not all can receive the word of that perfection of life, let us at least be saved in Zoar, the little city [Note: [Col. 0659] Gen. 19]. Let us fight, with Gideon, against the Midianites by trumpets, jars, and lamps. Let our trumpet be [Col. 0660A] in hymns, psalms, and spiritual songs; let us break these earthen vessels by vigils, fasts, and disciplines. “Let your lamps burn before men, that they may see your works and glorify your Father who is in heaven” [Note: [Col. 0659] Matt. 5.]. Let the Midianites also see and flee—those who hate the Lord—from before his face.

Behold the three cities of refuge: the contrition of penitence, the affliction of the flesh, and the longing for heavenly life. Behold the three sacrifices: fine flour in the oven through hidden contrition of heart; on the griddle through affliction of the body; in the frying-pan through the will of a bubbling and burning desire. Therefore, because “we have here no continuing city, but seek the one that is to come” [Note: [Col. 0659] Heb. 13], let us flee, brothers, to the cities of refuge, so that through them we may return to that city from which we are now exiled, whose dwelling is in glory and honour, [Col. 0660B] in peace and repose, in eternal blessedness and unending joy. May Jesus Christ lead and bring us into it—to whom be honour and glory for ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XXXIII. ON THE ASSUMPTION OF BLESSED MARY

“Let us all rejoice in the Lord as we celebrate the feast day,” etc. [Note: [Col. 0659] Office of the Church in the Mass.]

The angels rejoice because Christ’s Mother is today assumed into heaven. Since human beings, who are always in sorrow and mourning, rejoice, how should not the angels rejoice, whose nature is to rejoice and whose condition admits no sorrow? They rejoice over one sinner who repents; how should they not rejoice over the Mother of God ascending to heaven? Why should the angels not rejoice when the Lord of angels rejoices?

Christ rejoices and today hastens to meet his Mother; nor does he disdain to fulfil his own law, by which he commands that parents be honoured. David, who bore the figurative image of Christ, rejoiced and sang psalms before the ark of the old covenant [Note: [Col. 0659] 2 Kings]. Do you think that Christ does not rejoice before the ark of the new covenant, before the chamber of spices, before the mercy-seat of hearing, before the sanctuary of the Holy Spirit?

Let the angels rejoice and meet their Lady, the Queen of angels, the mediatrix of God and humankind. Consider what John once did while he was still in his mother’s womb [Col. 0660D]. Though enclosed and not yet brought forth into the light, he nevertheless leapt joyfully to meet Mary [Note: [Col. 0659] Luke 1.]. The child’s soul melted when Mary spoke. Let the angels melt, both to hear Mary’s voice and to enjoy Mary’s presence. Let them rejoice for themselves and for us: for themselves, because they receive in heaven their advocate.

Let no one, I beg you, my brothers, be troubled because I call Mary queen and lady of the angels.

[Col. 0661A] The angels glory that they have as their Lady the one whom the Lord of angels chose as his Mother. Inasmuch as she more gloriously and ineffably bore the Son and heir of God, so she inherited a name different from, and more glorious than, all others. It is great and glorious for an angel to have been made God’s minister. Without doubt it is greater and more glorious for Mary to have been made God’s Mother.

As the Apostle says: “Eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the human heart, what things God has prepared for those who love him” [Note: [Col. 0661] 1 Cor. 2.]. If God prepares such precious things for one who loves him, what do you think he prepares for one who bears him? To which of the angels was it said: “The Holy Spirit shall come upon thee,” etc. [Note: [Col. 0661] Luke 1.]?

I will show you a still more eminent prerogative. “Come, my chosen one, and I will place my throne in thee.” To which of the angels was such a venerable, lovable, intimate word ever spoken: “Come,” he says, “my chosen one, come” [Note: [Col. 0661] Song 2.]? This is a calling to a supereminent dwelling-place of glory. “Many indeed are called, but few chosen” [Note: [Col. 0661] Matt. 22.]. She is called and chosen—not merely chosen, but chosen beforehand. God chose her and chose her beforehand.

“Blessed, O Lord, is she whom thou hast chosen; she shall dwell in thy courts.” Indeed, if we attend to the Lord’s words, he shall dwell in her and place his throne in her, because he chose her as his dwelling: “This is my rest for age upon age; here will I dwell, because I have chosen her” [Note: [Col. 0661] Ps. 131.].

O Virgin of virgins! O glory of virgins! You seemed forsaken at the time when the fruit of your womb—the fruit of the exalted earth—ascended into heaven; but [Col. 0661C] you shall no longer be called Forsaken, and your land shall no longer be called Desolate; rather, it shall be called “God’s will is in her,” and your land shall be inhabited.
