But the wicked were in pains and torments, as is evident from the Gospel story of the rich man and Lazarus [Note: [Col. 0685] Luke 16].

But Christ, “having accomplished purification from sins” [Note: [Col. 0685] Heb. 1], abolished in his blood the handwriting of our condemnation, descended to hell, shattered the bronze gates, and broke the iron bars [Note: [Col. 0685] Ps. 106], bringing out the bound from the prison-house, those sitting in darkness and the shadow of death. Therefore he placed them beneath God’s altar, hiding them in his tabernacle in the day of evils and sheltering them in the secrecy of his tabernacle. There they rest and delight in beholding Christ’s [Col. 0686B] glorified body, awaiting until the number of their brethren is fulfilled [Note: [Col. 0685] Apoc. 6], until Christ clothes them over, reforming the body of our lowliness to be conformed to the body of his glory [Note: [Col. 0685] Phil. 3].

Therefore they are not in Abraham’s bosom but under the altar; no longer in hell but in heaven—except that the Church is accustomed also to call the paradise of heaven Abraham’s bosom. Moreover, although the soul’s robe is thirstily desired by the righteous in this life, the robe of flesh is desired still more. Hence one says: “My soul has thirsted for you; how greatly also my flesh has longed for you” [Note: [Col. 0685] Ps. 62].

From these things a threefold state of the holy soul is understood: in warfare, in rest, and in glory. The first is in tents, the second in courts, the third in the house of the Lord. You hear the first when it is said: “How beloved are your tents, O Lord of hosts” [Note: [Col. 0685] Ps. 83]. The end [Col. 0686C] of the same verse expresses the following, more desirable state: “My soul longs and fails for the courts of the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0685] Ibid.]. But because you have not yet found blessedness, proceed further, to the house of God. “Blessed are those who dwell in your house, O Lord” [Note: [Col. 0685] Ibid.].

He knew this progress who said: “I remembered these things and poured out my soul within me, for I shall pass into the place of the wonderful tabernacle, even to the house of God” [Note: [Col. 0685] Ps. 41]. And because perhaps you fear that one comes to the house but not into the house, hear the voice of joy and exultation: “I rejoiced at those things which were said to me: ‘We shall go into the house of the Lord’” [Note: [Col. 0685] Ps. 121]. For those who conquered the world, led out from the prison of the body, now stand in the Lord’s courts and await the time when they will receive their bodies [Col. 0686D] again. They rejoice because, when the number of their brethren has been fulfilled, they will enter the house of the Lord.

Nor will they enter the house of the Lord, whether planted ones or others, without the people. “This has been done by the Lord, and it is marvellous in our eyes” [Note: [Col. 0685] Ps. 127]. For although the soul is the image of the Most High while the body is stench and carrion, the soul nevertheless awaits the body with unspeakable longing, for a share in its glory: that it may fully receive eternal delights with that body with which it shared temporal miseries.

Then they will enter Jerusalem, [Col. 0687A] which truly is the vision of peace. For there is the peace of God surpassing every understanding [Note: [Col. 0687] Phil. 4], which eye has not seen, ear has not heard, nor has entered into the human heart—which God has prepared for those who love him [Note: [Col. 0687] I Cor. 2]. There, moreover, there will be nothing but thanksgiving and the voice of praise. Then, O Lord, we shall offer the calves of our lips; then we shall place calves upon your altar. For those who are now beneath the altar will then be upon the altar. They will then delight not merely in the sight of glorified flesh in Christ, but, enjoying the sight of the divine majesty, will see and know the true God the Father and Jesus Christ whom he sent—which is eternal life.

They will see not in a mirror or in an enigma, but face to face; and, passing by, he will minister to them the inestimable riches [Col. 0687B] of his glory, so that they may see and know Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, equal in glory and undivided in majesty, where they will see Christ as the Only-begotten from the Father. Without doubt you will see him there, as he said to you: “O how great is the multitude of your sweetness, O Lord!” [Note: [Col. 0687] Ps. 30].

For the soul that has been stripped of the body and rests at the point of its perfected blessedness is meanwhile, as it were, hidden; but a time will come when, having resumed the body, it will sit upon thrones as a judge of the children of men. As it is written: “You have perfected [your goodness] for those who hope in you, O Lord, in the sight of the children of men” [Note: [Col. 0687] Ibid.]. Nor indeed has he yet dealt kindly; but now he will bring it to completion; nor will the righteous person say to his soul: “Return to your rest, because God has dealt well with you” [Note: [Col. 0687] Ps. 114].

[Col. 0687C] Meanwhile, since the former things have passed away, the soul is no longer between hope and fear as it had previously been, but exists uniquely in hope and expectation of glory, so that it may confidently say: “In peace, in the selfsame place, I shall sleep and rest; for you, O Lord, have established me uniquely in hope” [Note: [Col. 0687] Ps. 4]. In this state, indeed, the bridegroom’s left hand is under that part of the bride, and then she will pass to the endless delight of his right hand. For “delights are at his right hand unto the end” [Note: [Col. 0687] Ps. 15].

And as Christ’s soul and flesh are now glorified, so in him we shall obtain perfect, full, and consummate glory both of soul and body. Do not, I beg you, doubt; rather, hear the disciple whom Jesus loved, and whom, as he lay in his bosom, he gave drink from the torrent of heavenly knowledge. “Now,” he says, “we are children of God, [Col. 0687D] but it does not yet appear what we shall be. Yet we know that, when he appears, we shall be like him” [Note: [Col. 0687] I John 3].

It should be noted that, just as the soul has a threefold faculty—rational, concupiscible, and irascible—so its glorification will be threefold. With respect to reason, knowledge and ignorance are opposites. Ignorance will be removed, but knowledge perfected. Likewise, two opposites attach to the concupiscible faculty: desire and contempt. Contempt will cease, while desire will be perfectly fulfilled. Similarly, in the irascible faculty, [Col. 0688A] joy and sadness move in a certain opposition. Sadness will be removed, and there will be everlasting gladness and completed joy.

Thus the soul’s blessedness will be true wisdom, desire for the things that ought to be desired, and full joy never interrupted. But the body is weak and has more needs. Therefore its blessedness consists in four things. Because it has once died, it shall not fear dying again: “Rising from the dead, it dies no more; death shall have no more dominion over it” [Note: [Col. 0687] Rom. 6]. But because it might live eternally in order to suffer eternally, it is given the glory of impassibility; and this is the second glorification of the body.

Our body today is an earthly and burdensome mass; agility will be added to it, so that the subtlety, lightness, and agility of bodies will be as great as [Col. 0688B] our thoughts are today. Moreover, so that glory may dwell in our land, and the whole earth—which is to be assumed into the rebuilding of the heavenly Jerusalem and into the fullness of Christ’s body—may be filled with the Lord’s majesty, brightness follows. In it the Lord will reform us, conforming us, glorifying us with him, and making us bright with the brightness of his body.

For the righteous will shine before the Lord, possessing in both soul and body, among angels and archangels, agility, immortality, impassibility, and bodily brightness; and, in the soul, eternal wisdom, unending delight, desire in joy, and joy in desire without end. Amen.

## SERMON XLII. ON THE SAME FEAST

[Col. 0688C]

“Seeing the crowds, Jesus went up onto the mountain” [Note: [Col. 0687] Matt. 5], and so forth.

“Whatever was written,” says the Apostle, “was written for our instruction, that through the consolation of the Scriptures we might have hope” [Note: [Col. 0687] Rom. 15]. Thus Christ’s ascent of the mountain, raising us to hope for life, teaches us more clearly that, leaving behind the disturbances of this world, we should ascend the Lord’s mountain, to the height of virtues.

For Christ also, who in all his works is set before us as an example, that we may follow in his footsteps—he, in accordance with what the prophet long ago foretold of him, “Go up upon a high mountain, you who bring good news to Zion, you who bring good news to Jerusalem” [Note: [Col. 0687] Isa. 40]—when he was about to speak the word of preaching, [Col. 0688D] first ascended the mountain of action. As Luke the evangelist says: “Jesus began first to do and then to teach” [Note: [Col. 0687] Acts 1]. In this he teaches us first to ascend to the height of good works before assuming the office of teacher. Whoever seeks the name and honour of master must first do the things to be taught before teaching what is to be done.

Formerly Moses had gone up the mountain to receive the law, while the people remained below [Note: [Col. 0687] Exod. 19]; today the lawgiver, about to give the blessing, ascends the mountain while the crowds remain behind. The disciples also go up with him, [Col. 0689A] that he may make them eternal mountains for the illumination of his people Israel, as it is written: “You shine wondrously from the eternal mountains” [Note: [Col. 0689] Ps. 75]. Since by humility they had been valleys, let them grow like mountains into greatness of dignity. They go up, therefore, “that the mountains may receive peace for the people and the hills righteousness” [Note: [Col. 0689] Ps. 71].

“And opening his mouth,” and so forth [Note: [Col. 0689] Matt. 5; Isa. 1]. He who formerly opened the mouths of prophets and who then often opened the mouths of the mute opened his own mouth—that mouth of which the prophets had often foretold, “the mouth of the Lord has spoken” [Note: [Col. 0689] Matt. 5]. “Blessed,” he says, “are the poor in spirit” [Note: [Col. 0689] Luke 7]. Now John’s disciples can safely return to him and say that “the poor are evangelized” [Note: [Col. 0689] Isa. 1].

In Christ is most plainly fulfilled, as he himself testifies, that prophetic saying of Isaiah: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, [Col. 0689B] because he has anointed me; he has sent me to proclaim the good news to the poor” [Note: [Col. 0689] Luke 6]. He proclaims good news to the poor and begins the law of his Gospel with the blessedness of poverty—he who compares riches with thorns and condemns the rich. “Woe to you rich, who have your consolation here! Blessed are the poor in spirit” [Note: [Col. 0689] Matt. 5].

Let the poor hear and rejoice at what their portion and inheritance are: “for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” [Note: [Col. 0689] Ibid.]. It is theirs not merely to possess but also to share with others whom they have made friends. As it is written: “Make friends for yourselves from the mammon of iniquity, so that when you fail, they may receive you into eternal dwellings” [Note: [Col. 0689] Luke 16]. Behold here again the honour of the poor.

The poor who here are received by the rich receive the rich in [Col. 0689C] their kingdom. Since they were faithful over little, they have been set over much; and therefore, in a happy exchange, they will be able to repay their benefactors more fully and abundantly according to their merit. It would have been more tolerable and better for that rich man in the Gospel if he had looked upon Lazarus and thereby deserved relief for his burning tongue; but he received no consolation from Lazarus, since he had given Lazarus no consolation [Note: [Col. 0689] Ibid.].

“The Lord is righteous and loves righteous deeds; his face has seen equity” [Note: [Col. 0689] Ps. 10]. Since that Lucifer—or rather, night-bearer—was impatient amid those riches of honour and glory, it is God’s just judgment that the person who patiently bears poverty should gloriously possess the kingdom from which the impatient and proud one was disgracefully cast down.

[Col. 0689D] “Blessed,” he says, “are the poor in spirit”: not all poor people, but those who embrace voluntary poverty—not forced or necessary poverty, but freely chosen poverty. For only that which proceeds from the will is acceptable to God. “I will sacrifice to you willingly,” says the Prophet [Note: [Col. 0689] Ps. 53].

Moreover, Socrates of Thebes and many other philosophers despised riches and loved poverty; but “they became vain in their thoughts and were given over to a reprobate mind” [Note: [Col. 0689] Rom. 1]. They were removed from the kingdom [Col. 0690A] of heaven because they were not poor in spirit.

I do not know, brethren, whether you fully understand what it is to be poor in spirit. This expression has sometimes introduced a scruple of doubt among many. Some abound both in understanding [Note: [Col. 0689] Ecclus. 19] and in spirit, like the children of this age, who are wiser in their generation than the children of light [Note: [Col. 0689] Luke 16]. I do not venture to call these either poor or rich in spirit. Who then will be poor in spirit? Is it someone disturbed and shaken by faintness of spirit and tempest? Certainly, it is not fitting to call such a person poor in spirit.

Let us run to the Apostle. For he is a circumspect man and experienced in many things. “We have not received,” says the Apostle, “the spirit of this world, but the Spirit who is from [Col. 0690B] God” [Note: [Col. 0689] I Cor. 2]. Now the spirit of this world is the spirit that puffs up, the spirit of pride, of which the same Apostle says: “You walked according to the prince of the power of this air, the spirit which now works in the children of unbelief” [Note: [Col. 0689] Eph. 2]. I think that if anyone were freed from this spirit, he would be poor in spirit. But this would not suffice unless the Spirit of God bore witness to his spirit.

Let us proceed further, if perhaps we can understand what it is to be poor in spirit. I think that poor in spirit is the person who, failing from himself and denying his whole self for Christ, has nothing in thought or memory, nothing in delight or desire, except Christ. Such a person can say: “I remembered God and was delighted, and my spirit failed” [Note: [Col. 0689] Ps. 76].

He who said, “Answer me swiftly, O Lord, for my spirit has failed” [Note: [Col. 0689] Ps. 142], and, “When my spirit failed within me, you knew my paths” [Note: [Col. 0689] Ps. 141], seemed to possess this renunciation of self, this poverty, and this failure of spirit. [Col. 0690C] Therefore the one who renounces the world, rejects himself, humbles himself under God’s mighty hand and beneath the observance of rule: this is the poor and humble person in spirit. Of such persons it was said: “The Lord is near to those who are troubled in heart, and he will save the humble in spirit” [Note: [Col. 0689] Ps. 33]. These are led by the Spirit of God, “not thinking high things, but consenting to the humble.”

“Blessed are the poor in spirit.” Are they not already in part made blessed, those who delight in their poverty and count temporal riches as their own misery? And perhaps this is what Solomon says concerning the Church of spiritual [Col. 0690D] poor: “Many daughters have gathered riches; this one has surpassed them all” [Note: [Col. 0689] Prov. 31]. Many gather riches and do not find in them the fruit of riches [Note: [Col. 0689] Eccl. 5]. Should not the fruit of riches be sufficiency? Yet I find written: “The rich have lacked and suffered hunger, but those who seek the Lord shall lack no good thing” [Note: [Col. 0689] Ps. 33].

The wisdom of this world has been wonderfully deceived. The children of this world, wise in their own eyes, experience daily [Col. 0691A] that possessing riches turns to anxiety and torment for them; but the children of light, who seek spiritual wisdom, have found that leaving riches makes one free and blessed. “I confess to you, Father of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and prudent and revealed them to little ones” [Note: [Col. 0691] Matt. 11].

See how just the Lord is: the poor in spirit despise riches, detest money, and lack nothing, because God suffices for them, and besides this the kingdom of heaven is wholly theirs. But the rich follower of greed, worshipper of mammon, slave of money, apostate for a coin, idolater in a coin—who has made money his god—sins more grievously. In that in which he had established his greater pleasure, he has greater fear, greater anxiety, and in every respect greater bitterness [Col. 0691B].

But you poor in spirit, though you have nothing, yet possess all things; for Christ is your portion. The voice of one poor person is: “God is the God of my heart, and God is my portion for ever” [Note: [Col. 0691] Ps. 72]. Do you not possess everything if you have him who possesses all things? To the one who has God, nothing is absent; to the one for whom Christ suffices, nothing is lacking. “Those who fear God lack nothing” [Note: [Col. 0691] Ps. 33].

The rich, burdened with the useless yet heavy loads of this world, hasten to hell under the devil’s leadership. For, according to Truth’s testimony, “it would be easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich person to enter the kingdom of heaven” [Note: [Col. 0691] Matt. 19]. Do not those whose citizenship is in heaven [Note: [Col. 0691] Phil. 3] already taste the first fruits of the heavenly kingdom? Having despised earthly [Col. 0691C] possessions, they desire nothing but Christ, with whom they have placed their treasure. Thus in vow and desire they are in heaven. For “where your treasure is, there will your heart be also” [Note: [Col. 0691] Matt. 6].

Are not the forms of virtues, the fragrance of good action, security of conscience, a certain natural affinity for the good, certain spiritual delights of delight, heavenly desires in Christ, the widening of love toward all, joy, and peace in the Holy Spirit, like a paradise and garden of delights in the righteous soul? Although these do not constitute that blessedness which eye has not seen nor ear heard [Note: [Col. 0691] I Cor. 2], they nevertheless belong to that hundredfold promised to those who despise earthly things for Christ’s sake.

Because they know in whom they have believed and are certain, they already pluck certain first fruits of eternal exultation, according to the saying of the Wise Man: “The expectation of the righteous is joy” [Note: [Col. 0691] Prov. 10]. He who said, “I delighted in the way of your testimonies, as in all riches” [Note: [Col. 0691] Ps. 118], was conscious of this treasure. This is a foretaste of future sweetness, the soul’s food in the present; it was this food that he who said, “I have forgotten to eat my bread,” had forgotten [Note: [Col. 0691] Ps. 101].

O how precious, how glorious in the Son of God’s sight is the title of poverty! For though he was rich beyond all, [Col. 0692A] he became poor beyond all, in order to transfer the poor into the riches of his glory. And who would dare say to him, “Have mercy on me, Lord” [Note: [Col. 0691] Ps. 6], “Help me, Lord” [Note: [Col. 0691] Ps. 108], because I am rich? This would rather provoke anger than obtain mercy.

Therefore David, knowing that God was a lover of the poor, although he ruled upon a royal throne, was nevertheless poor in spirit. Hence he confidently said: “Incline your ear, O Lord, and hear me, for I am needy and poor” [Note: [Col. 0691] Ps. 85]. And elsewhere: “I am poor and in labours from my youth” [Note: [Col. 0691] Ps. 87]. “I,” he says, “am a beggar and poor; the Lord is concerned for me” [Note: [Col. 0691] Ps. 39]. Why did he say this? For he knew that “the Lord will spare the poor and needy and will save the souls of the poor” [Note: [Col. 0691] Ps. 71].

But what is written about the rich and powerful? “The powerful shall suffer powerful torments” [Note: [Col. 0691] Wis. 6]; and again: “They spend their days in prosperity and in a moment descend to hell” [Note: [Col. 0691] Job 21]. [Col. 0692B] Therefore let the poor rejoice, because theirs is the kingdom of heaven. To the other saints a promise is made concerning the future.

“Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the earth. Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called children of God. Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” [Note: [Col. 0691] Matt. 5.]. The reward of all is deferred to the future. Only the poor in spirit and those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake—that is, martyrs—have the fruit of eternal recompense immediately at hand. Thus the poor and martyrs are judged equal; for, from the equality of their rewards, as it seems to me, an equality of merits is inferred. [Col. 0692C] Why should the reward of the poor and of martyrs not be equal, when poverty is martyrdom, and to be poor is to be a martyr? For one martyrdom is in the flesh, another in the spirit. What is the difference between them, except that the affliction of the poor is prolonged gradually over a longer period, whereas the suffering of martyrs is completed by a certain brief course of death and pain? What the one endures with delay, the other endures swiftly; what the one endures little by little, the other all at once. Yet in this they are equal: the anguish of suffering which the former endures in passing, the latter compensates for by the long weariness of torment. To both the one and the other a promise is made in the present: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.” Here it should be noted that, whereas all the other meek—namely, the peacemakers, the merciful, and the rest who are enumerated [Col. 0692D] in this catalogue of the blessed—have contracted something of the dust of human life and often carry with them wood, hay, and stubble, these two, purified respectively in their own blood and in the furnace of poverty, and tried in the frying-pan of a contrite spirit, carry with them nothing that needs to pass through fire. Therefore they immediately fly to the place of blessedness; the others attain blessedness, as it were, through fire.

Of God’s martyrs it is said that “they washed their robes [Col. 0693A] in the blood of the Lamb” [Note: [Col. 0693] Rev. 22.]; of the poor, because they judged themselves, because in contrition of heart and the burning of devotion they burned out every rust of sin within themselves, it is said: “And he shall cleanse the sons of Levi” [Note: [Col. 0693] Mal. 3.] “with the spirit of judgment and the spirit of burning” [Note: [Col. 0693] Isa. 4.].

Brothers, you have set your hands to mighty things; you have laid hold of the kingdom of heaven. The kingdom of God is within you, close at hand, as the reward of your labours. Since the days of man are short, the day of death is near: terrible for the rich of this age, but desirable for the poor, to whom that same day of judgment will give riches of honour and glory, the kingdom of heaven, and blessedness and glory without end. May Jesus Christ deign to grant this to us, to whom be honour and glory for ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XLIII. ON THE SAME FEAST

[Col. 0693B]

“Blessed are the poor in spirit,” etc. [Note: [Col. 0693] Matt. 5.].

The poor receive the Gospel today. Let the poor therefore hear and rejoice, for the King and Lord of heaven gives them the kingdom of heaven today. For the Lord loves the poor; for their sake he made himself poor, and in a manner divested himself of his kingdom and royal majesty, so as to make the poor lords and heirs of his kingdom. He compares riches to thorns and condemns the rich. “Woe to you rich,” he says, “who have your consolation here!” [Note: [Col. 0693] Luke 6.]. Hence, when asked, he would not enter the house of the ruler, lest he seem to have honoured riches. Thus God condemns the rich man and spares [Col. 0693C] the poor and needy. He humbles the one and exalts the other: the rich and the poor alike in one whole. He humbles the rich man, for whom honour turns to disgrace, exaltation to abasement, riches to misery, pleasures to torment. He exalts the poor man, “raising the needy from the dust and lifting the poor from the dung-heap, that he may sit with princes and hold the throne of glory” [Note: [Col. 0693] 1 Sam. 2.].

The title of poverty is renowned and glorious before God. Thus, placing perfection of life in poverty, he says: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell all that you possess, and give to the poor” [Note: [Col. 0693] Matt. 19.]. When Peter had said beforehand, “Lord, behold, we have left all things and followed you; what then shall there be for us?” he received this answer: “At the renewal, when the Son of Man shall sit upon the throne of his majesty, you too shall sit, judging the twelve tribes [Col. 0693D] of Israel” [Note: [Col. 0693] Ibid.]. Therefore those who are regarded as lowly and contemptible shall judge. The rich man shall be judged; the poor man shall glory. This is displayed most clearly in Lazarus and the rich man [Note: [Col. 0693] Luke 16.].

As a sign of this, Nebuzaradan, at the destruction of Jerusalem, left the poor in peace and carried the rich away captive [Note: [Col. 0693] 4 Kings 25.]. “Behold, we have left all things,” says Peter [Note: [Col. 0693] Matt. 19.], and judgment of the world was given to him. Joseph left his cloak to the Egyptian woman [Note: [Col. 0693] Gen. 38.], and became lord of Egypt. The Samaritan woman left her water-jar [Col. 0694A] [Note: [Col. 0693] John 4.], and was saved. John left his linen cloth [Note: [Col. 0693] Mark 14.], and was given as guardian to the blessed Virgin and delivered from the tribute of death.

Truly, blessed are the poor in spirit. “Because of the misery of the needy and the groaning of the poor, now I shall arise,” says the Lord [Note: [Col. 0693] Ps. 11.]. “He shall save the souls of the poor, and their name shall be honoured before him” [Note: [Col. 0693] Ps. 71.]. Yet this poverty must be assessed by humility and meekness of soul, not by the amount of one’s property. Poverty is not meritorious if it lacks meekness, if it makes one bitter and impatient of discipline. Therefore it is added: “Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the earth” [Note: [Col. 0693] Matt. 5.].

Do not the fierce and tyrants possess the earth today? But the meek are blessed because they shall possess the earth; are wicked tyrants therefore more blessed, because they already possess the earth? Yet I know [Col. 0694B] that it is written of them: “The Lord shall destroy their memory from the earth” [Note: [Col. 0693] Ps. 33.]. “You shall destroy their fruit from the earth, and their seed from among the children of men” [Note: [Col. 0693] Ps. 26.]. “But the meek shall inherit the earth, and shall delight in the abundance of peace” [Note: [Col. 0693] Ps. 36.].

The fierce and cruel, who savour earthly things, shall be consumed by the earth; for they are nothing other than earth: earth made from earth, destined to return again to earth. It is the prophet’s word: “Hear, earth, earth, earth” [Note: [Col. 0693] Jer. 22.]. You earth-born and sons of men [Note: [Col. 0693] Ps. 48.], who desire earth, lick earth, and contend for earth, know that you have no, nor shall have any, share in the earth which the Lord promised to the meek.

And what is this earth promised by the Lord? Without doubt, the land of promise. Is it that land extending from Dan [Col. 0694C] to Beersheba, and from the great river Euphrates to the river of Egypt, which is Rhinocorura, from sea to sea, and from the river to the bounds of the world? This is the land of Canaan—that is, the land of our heart. This is the land promised to Abraham and his seed, to whom, while he dwelt among the Chaldeans, the Lord said: “Go out from your land, and come into the land which I shall show you” [Note: [Col. 0693] Gen. 12.]. Therefore the land of Canaan was given to him by the measuring-line of distribution, and the Canaanites were uprooted. By this the Lord instructs us notably to depart from the house of iniquities. Let us fight against Canaan, against vices and spiritual wickednesses—for “our life is warfare upon earth” [Note: [Col. 0693] Job 7.]—so that we may possess the land of our heart.

“Subject my soul to yourself, Lord, that I may subject to you the land [Col. 0694D] of my body.” “Shall not my soul be subject to God?” [Note: [Col. 0693] Ps. 61.], so that I may possess my body in peace—not resisting, not wanton, but obedient and subject to reason. Lord, if I cannot entirely exterminate unlawful impulses, at least add this grace to me: that I may subject them to slavery. For Israel could not destroy the Jebusite, but made him tributary. He subjected him as a slave who said, “I chastise my body and bring it into slavery” [Note: [Col. 0693] 2 Cor. 9.].

Meekness pacifies the disorderly [Col. 0695A] motions of the flesh, so that what the Prophet prays for may come about: “Let peace be in your strength” [Note: [Col. 0695] Ps. 121.], that is, in meekness. For although all Christ’s virtues are from Christ, this one is spiritually said to be Christ’s own. For he himself says: “Learn from me, because I am meek and humble of heart” [Note: [Col. 0695] Matt. 11.]. “And upon whom shall my spirit rest, except upon the humble and meek man, and upon him who trembles at my words?” [Note: [Col. 0695] Isa. 66.].

The time will come when the entire seed of Canaan shall be exterminated from our land, when creation itself shall be delivered from the slavery of corruption into the liberty of the glory of the children of God [Note: [Col. 0695] Rom. 8.]. Then “the meek shall inherit the earth and delight in the abundance of peace” [Note: [Col. 0695] Ps. 36.]. “Because of meekness and righteousness,” says the Prophet, “your right hand shall guide you marvellously” [Note: [Col. 0695] Ps. 44.]. “The Lord shall rebuke on behalf of the meek of the earth” [Note: [Col. 0695] Isa. 11.]. “Let the meek hear and rejoice” [Col. 0695B] [Note: [Col. 0695] Ps. 33.]. “For the Lord shall exalt the meek unto salvation” [Note: [Col. 0695] Ps. 149.], because the meek shall inherit the earth; and therefore, “Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the earth” [Note: [Col. 0695] Matt. 5.]: the land of our body, which to behold in its glorification is the highest glory and the supreme good.

Certainly that ancient father of men—or rather, of crimes—infused into his posterity the poison of the ancient transgression. Therefore I still feel in my members a contrary law, resisting the law of my mind [Note: [Col. 0695] Rom. 7.]. I see that I have wasted my days, as one drinking water, that is, committing iniquity from my youth. Therefore the arrows of the Lord are in me, whose indignation drinks up my spirit [Note: [Col. 0695] Job 6.]. I see below me, above me, beside me, and against me countless perils of death and pains of hell, so that I may lament with the Prophet and say: “Your wrath, Lord, [Col. 0695C] has passed over me, and your terrors have troubled me” [Note: [Col. 0695] Ps. 87.]. “The pains of death surrounded me, and the perils of hell found me” [Note: [Col. 0695] Ps. 114.].

Therefore I shall mourn and humble myself beneath the mighty hand of God; I shall put my mouth in the dust, if perhaps there may be hope. I shall mourn because I have lost the days of old; I shall mourn in order to gain the days of eternal consolation. For I know who said: “Blessed are they that mourn, for they shall be comforted.”

## SERMON XLIV. ON THE SAME SUBJECT

“Blessed are they that mourn, for they shall be comforted” [Note: [Col. 0695] Matt. 5.].

“It is indeed better to go to the house of mourning than to the house of feasting” [Note: [Col. 0695] Eccles. 7.]. There is mourning of repentance, of which the Prophet says: “Streams of water flowed from my eyes, [Col. 0695D] because they have not kept your law, O Lord” [Note: [Col. 0695] Ps. 118.]. And: “Every night I shall wash my bed; with my tears I shall drench my couch” [Note: [Col. 0695] Ps. 6.].

There is mourning of affection, which David showed over Absalom [Note: [Col. 0695] 2 Sam. 19.] and Jacob over Joseph [Note: [Col. 0695] Gen. 27.]. God does not greatly approve such mourning. Hence Samuel was told: “How long will you mourn Saul?” [Note: [Col. 0695] 1 Sam. 16.]. There is mourning of avarice, according to this saying:

> Lost money is mourned with genuine tears;

and this the Lord detests. There is mourning of despair—the mourning, that is, of Esau and the mourning of Cain—and this the Lord abominates. There is mourning of devotion and affliction, and this the Lord embraces. Of this it is written: “You have placed my tears in your sight, as also in your promise” [Note: [Col. 0695] Ps. 55.]. “Hear my prayer, O Lord; give ear to my tears before you” [Note: [Col. 0695] Ps. 38.]. This is the mourning that makes people blessed. For “blessed are they that mourn, for they shall be comforted.”

Of this mourning or sorrow the Prophet says: “The sorrow of a man shall humble him, and he shall be made glad by a good word” [Note: [Col. 0695] Prov. 12.]. And another Prophet: “They went forth, going and weeping, scattering their seed. But they shall come again with rejoicing, carrying their sheaves” [Note: [Col. 0695] Ps. 125.]. “Amen, amen, I say to you, you shall weep and mourn, but the world shall rejoice.” What does “the sorrow of a man shall humble him” mean? “You shall [Col. 0696B] weep and mourn, but the world shall rejoice.” What does “he shall be made glad by a good word” mean? “Your sorrow shall be turned into joy.” And, “They shall come again with rejoicing” [Note: [Col. 0695] John 16.].

Wretched man that I am, who will give water to my head? Who will open for me the floodgates of my most miserable head, that I may mourn the goods I have lost and the evils I have committed; that I may mourn public necessities; that I may grieve and lament domestic distresses? For the whole life of man is temptation upon earth [Note: [Col. 0695] Job 7 according to the LXX.]. We are inwardly full of most miserable temptations and outwardly surrounded by them. What I see, what I hear, what I will, what I do not will, what pleases me, what displeases me, what I ponder, what I speak, what I keep silent about, what I labour at, what I rest from—in short, my whole life is temptation and affliction of spirit.

Let my eyes pour forth tears and give a flood of many waters, so that [Col. 0696C] I may wash away the stains that I have contracted from my youth. For my senses have inclined to evil from youth [Note: [Col. 0695] Gen. 8.]. I made a covenant with hell and struck a pact with death [Note: [Col. 0695] Isa. 28.]. And behold, my days have failed in vanity, and my years in haste [Note: [Col. 0695] Ps. 77.]. I am fixed in the mire of the deep, and there is no firm ground [Note: [Col. 0695] Ps. 68.]. And now, what is my expectation? Is it not you, O Lord? For my substance is with you [Note: [Col. 0695] Ps. 38.].

Give me, Lord, Peter’s tears, the tears of the Canaanite woman, the tears of the sinful woman. Give me the lower watering-place, for my soul is like waterless land before you [Note: [Col. 0695] Ps. 142.]. Give me, O fount of mercy, a fountain of waters with which I may wash the stains of my heart, so that I may utter my speech against myself: mourning, lamenting, accusing, and condemning [Col. 0696D] my utterly ruined life.

There is indeed the upper watering-place, which I do not yet presume to ask for: namely, a stream of heavenly waters proceeding from the heat of love and devotion. For a soul melted by pious devotion and desire into love for Christ flows down in tears and melts away. Therefore she who languished with love said: “My soul melted when my beloved spoke” [Note: [Col. 0695] Song 5.]. These are the hot springs found by Anah, son of Zibeon [Note: [Col. 0695] Gen. 36.]. This water is now no longer [Col. 0697A] water; it has been changed into wine, to make glad the heart of man. As it is written: “Give wine to those who mourn, and strong drink to those bitter in soul” [Note: [Col. 0697] Prov. 31.].

This wine is necessary to us because of our frequent infirmities. This is wine from the vineyard of Sorek [Note: [Col. 0697] Judg. 16.], namely the longing for holiness and the desire for God’s ordinances. He did not yet desire these ordinances, but desired to desire them, who said: “At all times I have longed to desire your ordinances” [Note: [Col. 0697] Ps. 118.]. Indeed, from righteousness itself grows a desire for righteousness, and the fervour of devotion arouses the spur of love. Thus, as the food of righteousness refreshes more, it becomes sweeter; as it is received more abundantly, it is hungered for more intensely. For vehement desire is hunger. Therefore he who is supreme righteousness says: “Those who eat me shall still hunger, and those who [Col. 0697B] drink me shall still thirst” [Note: [Col. 0697] Sir. 24.].

This is not like those who ate the bread of Moses in the desert or drank from the Samaritan woman’s jar; rather, the hunger of the present life is the satisfaction of the life to come. Then there shall be satisfaction without anxiety, desire without weariness, continual affection without failure. There shall be desire in satisfaction, and satisfaction in desire. “That you may eat,” he says, “and drink at the table in my Father’s house” [Note: [Col. 0697] Luke 22.]. Then vessels of mercy shall be filled from the abundance of God’s house and the torrent of delight. Now grace hungers for righteousness; interminable satisfaction in glory shall follow. This was suggested by one who said: “But I shall appear before you in righteousness; I shall be satisfied when your glory appears.” Hunger and thirst for righteousness [Col. 0697C] are the cause of blessedness [Note: [Col. 0697] Ps. 16.]. For “blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be satisfied.”

## SERMON XLV. ON THE SAME FEAST

“Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be satisfied” [Note: [Col. 0697] Matt. 5.].

Do I hunger for righteousness if I desire to be righteous? And who is there who does not desire this? Balaam the diviner desired not only the life of the righteous but also their end: “Let my soul die the death of the righteous, and let my last things be like theirs” [Note: [Col. 0697] Num. 23.]. I wish to be righteous, and I do not wish to be righteous, because, while desiring righteousness, I consent to iniquity. “What participation has righteousness with iniquity? Or what agreement has God with idols?” [Note: [Col. 0697] 2 Cor. 6.] No one can serve two masters [Note: [Col. 0697] Matt. 6.]; no one can [Col. 0697D] consent to iniquity and righteousness.

If you feel the motion of sin and consent to it, you do not hunger for righteousness; indeed, you are unjust and wicked. But if you feel it and, by resisting, refuse consent, your foot is on the straight path, and I believe that you hunger for righteousness, so that you may safely say with the Prophet: “Would that my ways were directed to keeping your ordinances!” [Note: [Col. 0697] Ps. 118.] There is indeed a great struggle [Col. 0698A] between sensation and consent, between flesh and spirit. Therefore the Apostle, feeling but not consenting, says that he does evil but does not perform it. “The evil which I do not will, I do,” he says—that is, I do it through concupiscence—and, “Now it is no longer I who perform it, but sin that dwells in me” [Note: [Col. 0697] Rom. 7.].

Bound by this inextricable perplexity, the Apostle is compelled to cry: “Wretched man that I am! Who shall deliver me from this body of death?” [Note: [Col. 0697] Ibid.] The same Apostle consoles us and says: “If Christ shall set you free, you shall be truly free” [Note: [Col. 0697] John 8.]. O Lord, merciful and righteous, deliver my soul [Note: [Col. 0697] Ps. 114.]. You are our righteousness, redemption, and salvation. Say to my soul: “I am your salvation” [Note: [Col. 0697] Ps. 34.]. Heal my soul, Lord, for I have sinned against you [Note: [Col. 0697] Ps. 40.]. “If you should mark iniquities, O Lord, Lord, who shall endure?” [Note: [Col. 0697] Ps. 129.] For all [Col. 0698B] our righteousnesses are like the cloth of a menstruous woman [Note: [Col. 0697] Isa. 64.].

Therefore my eye has been troubled by anger. My soul is greatly troubled, and my words are filled with pain. “Why are you sad, my soul, and why do you trouble me?” [Note: [Col. 0697] Ps. 41.] “Is there no balm in Gilead, or no physician for you?” [Note: [Col. 0697] Jer. 8.] And you, man, have mercy on yourself; have mercy on your soul by pleasing God. If you wish to have mercy on yourself, you have escaped all miseries. The compassionate and merciful Lord will also show himself to you as you wish to show yourself to yourself and to your neighbour. Have mercy on your soul, lest it be said of you: “He fed the barren woman and did not do good to the widow.” For everyone acting wickedly is cruel and impious toward his own soul. For “he who loves iniquity [Col. 0698C] hates his own soul” [Note: [Col. 0697] Ps. 10.]. Practise mercy and attain blessedness before God. For “blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy.”

## SERMON XLVI. ON THE SAME SUBJECT

“Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy” [Note: [Col. 0697] Matt. 5.].

James’s word [Note: [Col. 0697] ch. 2.] is: “Judgment without mercy shall be for him who has not shown mercy.” Yet God’s mercy triumphs over judgment. The Bride’s word is: “Your breasts are better than wine” [Note: [Col. 0697] Song 1.]; “I desire mercy and not sacrifice” [Note: [Col. 0697] Matt. 9.]. “Forgive, and you shall be forgiven” [Note: [Col. 0697] Luke 6.]. “If you do not forgive from the heart, your heavenly Father shall not forgive you” [Note: [Col. 0697] Matt. 18.].

Solomon’s word is [Note: [Col. 0697] Sir. 28.]: “A man keeps anger against a man, and does not keep mercy toward a man [Col. 0698D] like himself.” “Wicked servant,” says the Lord, “I forgave you all the debt because you begged me. Ought you not also to have had mercy on your fellow-servant, as I had mercy on you?” [Note: [Col. 0697] Matt. 18.] Paul to the Ephesians: “Let all bitterness and indignation be removed from you, so that you may be merciful, forgiving one another’s offences” [Note: [Col. 0697] Eph. 4.].

Recall Joseph’s mercy toward [Col. 0699A] his brothers [Note: [Col. 0699] Gen. 45.]; Moses’ mercy toward a contentious, unbelieving, rebellious people; David’s mercy toward Saul [Note: [Col. 0699] 1 Sam. 24.], Absalom, and Shimei [Note: [Col. 0699] 2 Sam. 16.]; and the mercy of others who were men of mercy. You will find no one who showed mercy to have perished.

There is mercy of intercession, as in Samuel for Saul, in Daniel, and in Moses for the people of Israel. “He said that he would destroy them, had not Moses stood in the breach before him, to turn away his wrath lest he destroy them” [Note: [Col. 0699] Ps. 105.]. There is mercy of consolation, as Job says [Note: [Col. 0699] ch. 29.]: “I was the comforter of those who mourned; I was an eye to the blind, a foot to the lame. I was father to the poor, because compassion grew with me from my infancy and came forth with me from my mother’s womb.” There is also mercy of correction, as he writes to the Galatians [Col. 0699B] [Note: [Col. 0699] ch. 6.], saying: “If a man is overtaken in any fault, you who are spiritual should instruct such a one in a spirit of gentleness, considering yourself lest you too be tempted.”

Mercy extends even to an enemy, as it is written: “Love your enemies; do good to those who hate you” [Note: [Col. 0699] Matt. 5.]. Paul to the Romans [Note: [Col. 0699] ch. 12.]: “Bless those who persecute you, and do not curse; rendering to no one curse for curse.” And again: “If your enemy is hungry, feed him; if he thirsts, give him drink” [Note: [Col. 0699] Ibid.]. For Christ also prayed for those who crucified him.

While there are two sons of Rachel—that is, two works of charity—there are six sons of Leah, that is, six works of mercy, which the Lord enumerates in the Gospel: “I was hungry and you gave me to eat; [Col. 0699C] I was thirsty and you gave me to drink” [Note: [Col. 0699] Matt. 25.]. Almsgiving encompasses these six works of mercy. For almsgiving is whatever a person, moved by compassionate feeling, bestows upon another’s needs. Ecclesiasticus says: “Hide almsgiving in the bosom of the poor man, and it shall pray for you and deliver you from every evil” [Note: [Col. 0699] Sir. 29.]. “Water extinguishes fire; almsgiving, sin” [Note: [Col. 0699] Sir. 3.].

In Luke [Note: [Col. 0699] ch. 3.] it is written: “He who has two tunics, let him give to him who has none; and he who has food, likewise.” Martin [Note: [Col. 0699] Sulpicius, in his *Life*.] did more than was required when he divided his cloak with a poor man. He even gave his whole and only tunic to a poor man, for whom his archdeacon bought another for five denarii. Whatever is given to a poor man is lent to the Lord, for he himself is the surety for the poor. “Blessed is the man who has mercy and lends” [Note: [Col. 0699] Ps. 111.].

[Col. 0699D] If you scatter your goods and pour them out upon the poor, you establish for yourself righteousness for eternity and the fruit of righteousness. For it is written: “He has scattered; he has given to the poor; his righteousness remains for age upon age” [Note: [Col. 0699] Ibid.]. An hermit, stripped by robbers and walking half-naked in a short undergarment, was asked who had stripped him. He answered: “This heavenly book, teaching that all things must be given to the poor.” When he was told that he still had something, [Col. 0700A] he gave that very undergarment to a poor man.

Paulinus, bishop of Nola, not only gave his possessions, but also gave and handed over himself into slavery for the son of a poor widow. “And I,” says the Apostle, “will be spent beyond measure for your souls” [Note: [Col. 0699] 2 Cor. 12.]. If you do not lay down your life for a life, at least lay down your temporal goods for yourself. “Make friends for yourselves from the mammon of iniquity” [Note: [Col. 0699] Luke 16.]. “Honour the Lord from your substance” [Note: [Col. 0699] Prov. 3.]. “Give to everyone who asks of you” [Note: [Col. 0699] Luke 6.]. Do not wait for alms to be given on your behalf after your death, which you ought to have given while alive.

The almsgiving of the living is a light before the face of one walking; but almsgiving after death is like a lamp behind one’s back. Almsgiving is the soul’s light, provided it is done with cheerfulness of heart; for “God loves a cheerful giver” [Note: [Col. 0699] 2 Cor. 9.]. Hence the Apostle to the Corinthians: [Col. 0700B] “Each one according as he has determined in his heart, not from sorrow or necessity” [Note: [Col. 0699] Ibid.], but willingly. “Willingly,” he says, “I shall sacrifice to you” [Note: [Col. 0699] Ps. 53.]. Willingly, not by compulsion; for one who gives alms under the compulsion of duty, reputation, or temporal advantage has neither lot nor share in the fruit of almsgiving. Perhaps he is equal to the raven that fed Elijah and the widow.

Paul’s word is: “I do not seek the gift, but I seek the fruit” [Note: [Col. 0699] Phil. 4.]. Do you wish to hear the fruit of almsgiving? “Blessed is he who understands concerning the needy and poor; in the evil day the Lord shall deliver him. May the Lord preserve him, give him life, make him blessed on earth, and not hand him over to the will of his enemies” [Note: [Col. 0699] Ps. 40.]. He delivers and preserves, gives life and makes blessed, [Col. 0700C] according to the word of the son of Sirach: “The almsgiving of a man is like a purse with him, and it shall preserve favour for him” [Note: [Col. 0699] Sir. 17.].

Almsgiving cleanses and purifies the eyes of the heart. Luke says [Note: [Col. 0699] ch. 11.]: “Give alms, and all things are clean for you.” Purity of heart indeed consists in holiness, without which no one shall see God [Note: [Col. 0699] Heb. 12.]. But almsgiving cleanses the eyes of the heart and opens them for seeing. “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God.”

## SERMON XLVII. ON THE SAME FEAST

“Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” [Note: [Col. 0699] Matt. 5.].

There are six works of mercy, as we have said, which [Col. 0700D] purify and cleanse a person. Are not these works the six water-jars placed in Galilee for the purification of the Jews? Water cleanses; almsgiving cleanses; faith cleanses: “By faith,” he says, “cleansing their hearts” [Note: [Col. 0699] Acts 15.]. “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God.”

Is not eternal life to see you, God, and Jesus Christ whom you sent? Blessed, Lord, are those who have seen you and believed in you—in hope, [Col. 0701A] not in reality. For even now the pure in heart see you, yet they are not blessed; they see, but “through a mirror and in an enigma” [Note: [Col. 0701] 1 Cor. 13.], and as though beneath a cloud. The time shall come when they see you face to face in the splendours of the saints [Note: [Col. 0701] Ps. 109.], crowned with glory and honour [Note: [Col. 0701] Ps. 8.], not in the diadem of your majesty, but as the only-begotten from the Father, full of grace and majesty. Then we shall exult and our heart shall rejoice [Note: [Col. 0701] Prov. 23.]; then there shall be Sabbath after Sabbath; then there shall be a new song in the mouths of men [Note: [Col. 0701] Ps. 39.] and a voice like that of all who rejoice. There, just as Christ is the brightness and figure of God’s substance, so he shall appear in the figure of God and the glory of majesty.

O guardian of men and our redeemer, to you I have lifted my eyes [Note: [Col. 0701] Ps. 122.], the eyes, that is, of my heart. For as the eyes of servants are upon the hands of their masters, so [Col. 0701B] are our eyes upon you, O Lord, until you have mercy upon us [Note: [Col. 0701] Ibid.]. Yet “my eye has been troubled by anger” [Note: [Col. 0701] Ps. 6.]; “my strength has failed me, and the light of my eyes itself is not with me” [Note: [Col. 0701] Ps. 37.]. I cannot see your face except with the eye of a pure heart. “My mother conceived me in impurities” [Note: [Col. 0701] Ps. 50.]; and: “Who can make clean that which is conceived from unclean seed? Is it not you who alone are able?” [Note: [Col. 0701] Job 14.]

“Create in me a clean heart, O God” [Note: [Col. 0701] Ps. 50.], God of my heart, and God my portion for ever [Note: [Col. 0701] Ps. 72.]. My heart said to you; my face has sought you: “Your face, Lord, I shall seek” [Note: [Col. 0701] Ps. 26.]. “For what is there for me in heaven, and what have I desired upon earth apart from you?” [Note: [Col. 0701] Ps. 72.] “The Lord is my illumination and my salvation; whom shall I fear?” [Note: [Col. 0701] Ps. 26.] Enlighten my eyes, lest I ever sleep in [Col. 0701C] death, lest my enemy say: “I have prevailed against him” [Note: [Col. 0701] Ps. 12.].

You are the measuring-line of my inheritance [Note: [Col. 0701] Ps. 104.], my portion in the land of the living [Note: [Col. 0701] Ps. 141.]: in the land promised to the meek; in the land of consolation offered to those who mourn; in the kingdom of heaven given to the suffering and poor; in the inheritance of the saints and peace of the children of God; in the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding [Note: [Col. 0701] Phil. 4.] and makes God’s children sharers in blessedness. For “blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called children of God.”

## SERMON XLVIII. ON THE SAME SUBJECT

“Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called children of God” [Note: [Col. 0701] Matt. 5.].

God is not a God of dissension but of peace. He made peace [Col. 0701D] through the blood of his only-begotten Son, between the things in heaven and the things on earth [Note: [Col. 0701] Col. 3.]. Those who pacify their inward motions into slavery and obedience to Christ, who have peace with their neighbour, and who reconcile brothers to peace—upon these rests the Lord’s peace, and they are to be called God’s repose. For peacemakers shall be called children of God.

“Seek peace and pursue it” [Note: [Col. 0701] Ps. 33.]; “there is a remnant for the peaceable man” [Note: [Col. 0701] Ps. 36.]. Do you wish to see the remnant [Col. 0702A] of this peace? Eternal peace follows this peace, and the Lord gives both kinds of peace. As it is written: “The Lord shall give peace upon peace.” He clearly indicates both kinds when he says: “Peace I leave with you; my peace I give to you” [Note: [Col. 0701] John 14.].

Let the world press you, let the body press you, let the devil attack you. If you have peace with your neighbour toward God, and with God toward your neighbour; if you do what the Apostle exhorts the Hebrews, saying, “Pursue peace with all men” [Note: [Col. 0701] Heb. 12.], know that “the Lord has made your borders peace” [Note: [Col. 0701] Ps. 147.]. “Your dwelling is made in peace,” and you may say confidently: “In peace, in the selfsame, I shall sleep and rest” [Note: [Col. 0701] Ps. 4.]. “Great peace have those who love your name, O Lord, and for them there is no stumbling-block” [Note: [Col. 0701] Ps. 118.].

We owe two things to God and neighbour: glory to God and peace to neighbour. Therefore the angel [Col. 0702B] most wisely distinguished between God and man, saying: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to men of good will” [Note: [Col. 0701] Luke 2.]. For the highest wisdom is to love absolutely nothing except God or for God’s sake. This is God’s chaste wisdom, as James says [Note: [Col. 0701] ch. 3.]: “The wisdom of God is first indeed chaste, then peaceable.” It is chaste when it exercises itself in virtues, so as to keep itself unstained from this world, and thus acquires the fruit of eternal peace and blessedness. For “the Lord shall give strength to his people, and the Lord shall bless his people in peace” [Note: [Col. 0701] Ps. 28.].

For, according to James’s testimony, “the fruit of righteousness is sown in peace” [Note: [Col. 0701] Jas. 3.]; and therefore “righteousness and peace have kissed” [Note: [Col. 0701] Ps. 84.]. Paul joins righteousness and peace together as though [Col. 0702C] in one kiss: “Being justified by faith,” he says, “let us have peace with God” [Note: [Col. 0701] Rom. 5.]. The Lord gives righteousness as strength, but peace as reward and blessing, according to the saying: “The Lord shall give strength to his people; the Lord shall bless his people in peace” [Note: [Col. 0701] Ps. 28.].

Yet there is a peace which is neither merit nor reward: the peace of earthly pleasure, which the Lord hates. Of it the Lord says: “I came not to bring peace upon earth, but a sword” [Note: [Col. 0701] Matt. 10.]. For peace pursued amid the delights of the flesh is most evil, as the Prophet testifies when he says: “I was jealous of the wicked, when I saw the peace of sinners” [Note: [Col. 0701] Ps. 72.]. “Peace, peace, and there is no peace” [Note: [Col. 0701] Jer. 6.]. For this momentary peace is followed by everlasting bitterness. “Behold,” he says, “in my peace is most bitter bitterness” [Note: [Col. 0701] Isa. 38.]. For when they shall say, “Peace and security,” etc., [Col. 0702D] sudden destruction shall come upon them, and pain as upon a woman with child, and they shall not escape [Note: [Col. 0701] I Thess. 5.]. There is a treacherous peace, of which it is written: “The man of my peace, in whom I trusted, who ate my bread, has magnified his treachery against me” [Note: [Col. 0701] Ps. 40.]. Joab practised this against Abner and Amasa; therefore he is not written in the catalogue of the mighty. There is a deceptive peace, of which Jeremiah says: “O Zedekiah, your peaceable men have deceived you” [Note: [Col. 0701] Jer. 38.]. Leave us your peace, O Lord; give us your peace. Give peace, O Lord, in our days, for there is none other who fights for us. The world attacks us, the flesh attacks us, the evil spirit attacks us: conquer, O Lord, those who attack us. Speak peace to your people. Give peace, O Lord, to those who wait for you; we have waited and looked for peace, and behold, disturbance. The pains of death surrounded me, and the perils of hell found me. “I found tribulation and sorrow” [Note: [Col. 0703] Ps. 17.]. For whatever is under the sun is tribulation and affliction of spirit [Note: [Col. 0703] Ecclus. 1.]. I am a wayfarer and a guest in this land of our pilgrimage. But three things drive me from the house: smoke, dripping water, and a quarrelsome wife. That is, love of the world, the lust of the eyes, and the flesh, a most evil wife [Col. 0703B]. I would truly be a son of God if I patiently and peacefully endured these things, and could say with the Prophet: “With those who hate peace, I was peaceable” [Note: [Col. 0703] Ps. 119.]. But one does not stand firm amid miseries. For what is my strength, that I should endure? If you give me, O Lord, the grace to endure my infirmities, your grace is sufficient for me. “Have mercy on me, O Lord, for I am weak” [Note: [Col. 0703] Ps. 6.]. I am weak and feeble, and mighty wicked men have rushed upon me. My enemies surrounded me, saying: “God has forsaken him; pursue and seize him, for there is none to deliver him” [Note: [Col. 0703] Ps. 70.]. “O Lord, I suffer violence; answer for me” [Note: [Col. 0703] Isa. 38.]. For what shall I answer, when I myself have done it? Truly, I am with you: I have done it. For the prophet also says: “Your ways and your iniquities have done these things to you” [Note: [Col. 0703] Jer. 4.]. And who is more iniquitous [Col. 0703C] toward me than I myself? Who is so ingenious in bringing about my death? Who, as I do, thus seeks my soul for destruction? Who thus contrives to take from me my splendid inheritance and drive away my reward? I suffer—and would that it were for righteousness, rather than for my own sins! But if I bear punishment for my sins, I suffer for myself, not for Christ. The prince of the apostles says: “Let none of you suffer as a thief, or a murderer, or one who covets what belongs to others; but if, while doing good and patiently enduring, you suffer, blessed are you” [Note: [Col. 0703] I Pet. 4.]. For blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.

## SERMON XLIX. ON THE SAME FEAST

[Col. 0703D]

“Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” [Note: [Col. 0703] Matt. 5.].

All the virtues which we have enumerated in the construction of the heavenly ladder are strengthened through patience.

For the virtue which patience does not make firm is a widow—that is, bereft.

For patience is placed eighth upon Jacob’s ladder, and the eighth returns to the beginning. Therefore the first and the last, [Col. 0704A] that is, voluntary poverty and patience amid persecutions, receive the kingdom of heaven not as a promise, like the other virtues, but as a possession and property. The meek shall possess the earth; those who mourn shall be comforted; those who hunger shall be filled; the merciful shall obtain mercy; the pure in heart and the peacemakers shall see God and shall be called sons of God. But blessed are the poor in spirit, and those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven. The others are admitted into expectation; these are immediately sent into possession of the eternal inheritance. Patience and poverty fittingly and elegantly correspond to one another in both merit and reward. For true poverty for Christ’s sake, and true patience, belong to Christ’s poor. Yet the spiritual poor person differs from the martyr in this: the torments and pains which the poor endure for a very long time in the furnace and frying-pan of poverty are recompensed in the martyr by the brief span of momentary suffering. In either case, however, patience makes the martyr. To martyrs it is said: “In your patience you shall possess your souls” [Note: [Col. 0703] Luke 21.]. Of the poor it is written: “The patience of the poor shall not perish forever” [Note: [Col. 0703] Ps. 9.]. This is the good seed which fell into good ground and bears fruit in patience [Note: [Col. 0703] Luke 8.]. In the Second Epistle to the Corinthians, the Apostle exhorts us to present ourselves as ministers of God “in much patience” [Note: [Col. 0703] II Cor. 6.]. Great is the virtue of patience. A patient man, Solomon testifies, is better than a strong man [Note: [Col. 0703] Prov. 16.]. For incomparably better is he who patiently endures one who tortures him than [Col. 0704C] he who cruelly tortures one who endures. A certain hermit, struck by a possessed man, patiently offered him the other cheek; and the demon went out crying: “Patience alone conquered me; patience alone cast me out.” Where, brothers, is our patience? At a trifling word we grow angry and seek vengeance in our anger, and amid quite contemptible annoyances we lose endurance. But woe to those who have lost endurance. I myself am witness against myself that I can bear no annoyance whatsoever. Yet if I were wise, delicate as I am, accustomed to pleasures, weak and impatient of such things, I would punish myself for a time. O if I either do not wish, or cannot, or shrink from punishing and correcting myself, you, O Lord, rebuke me; you correct me. For blessed is the man whom the Lord corrects. These are [Col. 0704D] your words: “Those whom I love, I rebuke and chastise” [Note: [Col. 0703] Prov. 3.]. Would that the righteous man might correct me in mercy [Note: [Col. 0703] Ps. 140.], not in anger, not in fury! O Lord, rebuke me not in your fury, nor correct me in your anger [Note: [Col. 0703] Ps. 6.]. Anger is in purgatory; fury is in hell. Correct me thus, that you may not destroy me; amend me thus, that you may not ruin me, and that it may not be said of me: “You destroyed him from purification” [Note: [Col. 0703] Ps. 88.]. That terrible fire will be destructive rather than purgative to me if I wait for it. [Col. 0705A] How did the Lord purify the sons of Levi? “For he shall sit as a refining fire, and purifying silver” [Note: [Col. 0705] Mal. 3.]. “Then every violent plundering with tumult, and garment mingled with blood, shall be for burning and fuel for the fire” [Note: [Col. 0705] Isa. 9.]. He is the one who says through Joel: “I shall cleanse their blood, which I had not cleansed” [Note: [Col. 0705] Joel 3.]. And who among us can dwell with devouring fire? Or who shall stand with everlasting burnings [Note: [Col. 0705] Isa. 53]? It is better to burn here with the love of God than there to be tormented by terrible burning. Here you can temper the fire of Gehenna with penitential tears, just as the furnace of Babylon became a dew-bearing wind for the three boys [Note: [Col. 0705] Dan. 3.]. She of whom it was said, “Her many sins are forgiven, because she loved much” [Note: [Col. 0705] Luke 7.], burned with the fire of love. With this fire the [Col. 0705B] patriarchs, prophets, apostles, martyrs, confessors, virgins, and all others who, running in the course of this life, obtained the prize and gained rest without end in exchange for temporal affliction, burned intensely.

And what are we doing, brothers? Why do we not hasten to enter into that rest? The Apostle testifies that we have been called to possess blessings as an inheritance [Note: [Col. 0705] I Pet. 3.]. But we see our homeland from afar and salute it from afar; indeed, as far as we can, we flee from it and remove ourselves from it, and we have regarded the desirable land as nothing. Lord Jesus Christ, we know that in the house of your Father there are many dwelling-places, where you have prepared most radiant dwellings for your saints. For each person shall have, in eternal [Col. 0705C] glory, a place according to the measure of his merits. And where shall we unhappy people be? Certainly, if you mark iniquities, O Lord [Note: [Col. 0705] Ps. 129], if you deal with us according to our wickedness, I know that we have neither part nor lot in the inheritance of the saints. Shall we be with the virgins, we who have rotted in our own dung, drinking the urine of our sins? And what communion has light with darkness, chastity with enticements, purity with impurity? He shall have no place among the virgins who has defiled his body with countless stains of lust, either in body or in the desire of concupiscence. And what fellowship can we have with confessors, martyrs, and apostles? For neither the punishment of martyrdom has tested us, nor the rigour of penitence exercised us, nor holiness of life marked us. [Col. 0705D] Therefore scarcely anyone shall see God. We ought not expect any fellowship with the angels; for they abhor us, since our whole manner of life stinks in the angels’ nostrils. It remains, then, that we should be with him whom we served: that we should go with the curse into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his ministers. The saints shall exult in glory; we shall be tormented in Gehenna. For it is the just judgment of God, as the Apostle testifies in his Epistle to the Romans, that those whom God’s kindness and patience have not led to repentance, according to their hardness and unrepentant heart, store up [Col. 0706A] wrath for themselves on the day of God’s dreadful judgment [Note: [Col. 0705] Rom. 2.]. Therefore the wicked shall be sent into outer darkness, where there is the shadow of death and no order. The Lord in his anger shall trouble them, and fire shall devour them. “He shall make them as a fiery furnace in the time of his countenance” [Note: [Col. 0705] Ps. 20], that is, at the time of his indignation and wrath. “Their fire shall not be quenched, and their worm shall not die” [Note: [Col. 0705] Isa. 66]. “A fire has been kindled in his fury, and shall burn unto the lowest depths of hell” [Note: [Col. 0705] Deut. 32]. “Fire and brimstone, and a blast of storms” [Note: [Col. 0705] Ps. 10]; there death shall feed upon them [Note: [Col. 0705] Ps. 48]; there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth [Note: [Col. 0705] Matt. 8]; there shall be the grinding of burning chains, pressing, constraining, and not consuming; there, as Zephaniah says, shall be a cry from the first gate and a howling from the second [Note: [Col. 0705] Zeph. 1.]. For as the saints shall receive the twofold robe of glorification in soul and body, so they shall be condemned with *diploide*, that is, a twofold shame of soul and body. [Col. 0706B] Let us repent, brothers, while it is permitted; for time is short, the end uncertain, the judge terrible, and the punishment unimaginable, endless, and unbearable. May Jesus Christ, who is glorious in his saints, deign to deliver us from it through the merits of all the saints. Amen.

## SERMON L. ON A SINGLE CONFESSOR

“Blessed Moses, beloved of God and of men, whose memory is in blessing” [Note: [Col. 0705] Ecclus. 45.].

If we consider the fruit of divine love, it is the fruit of eternal salvation and the tree of life for those who lay hold of it. For this is charity, from whose root [Col. 0706C] every good proceeds; among its fruits are numbered joy and peace in the Holy Spirit [Note: [Col. 0705] Gal. 5.]. This tree is most fruitful; therefore, if anyone expends himself in cultivating it, it repays that very effort with fruit at multiplied interest. For if we love God, we are loved more by him. “A good measure, pressed down, shaken together, and running over, shall he give into your bosom” [Note: [Col. 0705] Luke 6.]. For your love is as a tiny spark in comparison with that poured-out and most abundant divine charity. If we wish to anticipate Christ in love, he himself goes before the paths of our desires and outruns us by the grace of his love. For it is from him that we love him, and in order that we may love him he forestalls us with his love; not because we loved him first, John says, but because [Col. 0706D] he first loved us [Note: [Col. 0705] I John 4.]. He loves us first, who everywhere precedes us in his blessings; but we seek an irrefutable proof of divine love. God, the Son of God, laid down his life for us: “No one has greater love than this, that a man lay down his life for his friends” [Note: [Col. 0705] John 15.]. This love was stronger than life, because it took life away; it was stronger than death, for he who had the power of death also destroyed it, and wholly swallowed up and abolished death. Besides this general and common love, in which and through which the Lord wills all [Col. 0707A] people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of his name [Note: [Col. 0707] I Tim. 2], there is another love: namely, the infusion of grace and the conduct flowing from that infusion. This is what makes a man beloved of God. It is altogether certain, moreover, that he is loved by God who loves God; and because the proof of love is the performance of a work [Note: [Col. 0707] St Gregory, Homily 30 on the Gospels], it is likewise certain that he loves God who keeps God’s commandments. “If anyone loves me,” says the Lord, “he will keep my words” [Note: [Col. 0707] John 14.]. “Let us love,” says the Apostle, “not in word or tongue, but in deed and truth” [Note: [Col. 0707] I John 3.]. Therefore, beyond doubt, he loves God who hates what God hates: namely, iniquity, vanity, and things of that sort. As it is written: “You hate all who work iniquity” [Note: [Col. 0707] Ps. 5]. And again: “You hate those who heed useless vanity” [Note: [Col. 0707] Ps. 30]. Led and drawn by this love, [Col. 0707B] the Apostle counted all the gains he had possessed in the world as losses for Christ’s sake [Note: [Col. 0707] Phil. 3]. Rooted, therefore, in charity, he said: “Who shall separate me from the charity of Christ? Tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or danger, or the sword?” [Note: [Col. 0707] Rom. 8]. The first thing in the love of God is to hate evil and love good. Moreover, no one loves God unless he first hates evil. “You who love God,” says the Prophet, “hate evil” [Note: [Col. 0707] Ps. 96]. But this is not enough; one is required to love his words and commandments and, by loving them, to keep them. Hence the Prophet: “I shall meditate upon your commandments, which I have loved; and I lifted up my hands to your commandments, which I loved exceedingly” [Note: [Col. 0707] Ps. 118]. Many people certainly know whether they love God; but whether they are loved by [Col. 0707C] God they do not know. For “who has known the mind of the Lord, or who has been his counsellor?” [Note: [Col. 0707] Rom. 8]. “Who knows of himself whether he is worthy of love or hatred?” [Note: [Col. 0707] Eccles. 9]. Although the Apostle Paul says most confidently, “I am certain that nothing shall separate me from the charity of God” [Note: [Col. 0707] Rom. 8], he nevertheless begs, as it were, for the suffrages of others’ intercession: “I beseech you,” he says, “through the Lord Jesus Christ and through the charity of the Holy Spirit, that you assist me with your prayers” [Note: [Col. 0707] Rom. 15]. “The judgments of God are a great deep” [Note: [Col. 0707] Ps. 35]. He is merciful to some whom he hates, while he loves others toward whom he seems angry. “Let mercy be shown to the wicked man, and he will not learn to do righteousness” [Note: [Col. 0707] Isa. 26]. He has mercy upon the wicked so that they may not be chastised with men, and he lets them go according to the desires of their heart, so that they may walk in their own inventions [Note: [Col. 0707] Ps. 80], adding iniquity to [Col. 0707D] iniquity, so that he who is filthy may become filthier still [Note: [Col. 0707] Rev. 22]. Yet, O Lord, “because of their deceits you have set them up; you cast them down while they were lifted up” [Note: [Col. 0707] Ps. 72]. In these present miseries foolish and unhappy people prepare for themselves the sentence of endless wrath and the judgment of eternal death. Therefore the Wise Man says: “The prosperity of fools shall destroy them” [Note: [Col. 0707] Prov. 1]. Truly foolish are those who do not discern God’s mercies and do not attend to the wrath of the future Judge. Of wrath the Prophet says: “Who knows [Col. 0708A] the power of your anger?” [Note: [Col. 0707] Ps. 89]. Of miseries also he says: “Who is wise, and will keep these things, and understand the mercies of the Lord?” [Note: [Col. 0707] Ps. 106]. He who truly loves God—for he is the one loved by God—distinguishes more keenly between God’s wrath and mercy; he knows that God scourges every son whom he loves [Note: [Col. 0707] Heb. 12]. Thus, not setting his heart upon delights or riches, if they abound, he counts it all joy when he falls into various temptations. Such a man is beyond doubt both chosen and beloved of God. But when he is called beloved of God, why is “and of men” added? What does this conjunction of divine and human love mean? What communion has light with darkness [Note: [Col. 0707] II Cor. 6], life with death, salvation with confusion? Are not those who please men put to shame, [Col. 0708B] because God has rejected them [Note: [Col. 0707] Ps. 52]? What is human favour but a scorching wind, pestilential air, and a corrupting breeze? What is the love of men but God’s hidden hatred? A thief lying in wait, a serpent in the road, a horned viper on the path, biting the horse’s hooves so that its rider falls backward [Note: [Col. 0707] Gen. 49]. For the man who seeks human favour, according to Job’s saying, is set above the wind [Note: [Col. 0707] Job 30], and so the vain man is lifted up into pride [Note: [Col. 0707] Job 11]; but all his merits are scattered into nothing by a slight breath of favourable breeze. He himself, too, as a rider of pride, is hurled down into a precipice and ruin. But just as faith working through love makes a man beloved of God, so gentleness or mildness makes a man pleasing to men, so that by love he may be sanctified by God [Col. 0708C] and by men, on account of his gentleness and mildness, may be loved as a saint of the Lord. As it is written: “The Lord made him holy in faith and gentleness” [Note: [Col. 0707] Ecclus. 45]. The love of God, then, must be sought in every way. The love of men, however, is not to be sought; but if offered, it ought not to be disdainfully rejected or despised, since Truth himself says: “Let your works so shine before men that they may glorify your Father who is in heaven” [Note: [Col. 0707] Matt. 5], so that what he says concerning the only-begotten Son of God may also be said of the adopted son: “Father, glorify your Son, that your Son also may glorify you” [Note: [Col. 0707] John 17]. The Apostle seems to give and urge the same counsel: “Provide things good,” he says, “not only before God, but also before men” [Note: [Col. 0707] Rom. 12]. I do not think that God is displeased if someone pleases men [Col. 0708D] under the guise, or with the prospect, of gentleness. For he himself, who is maker and redeemer of men, so brightens certain persons’ countenances with a certain graciousness and favourable cheerfulness, and so endows their words and deeds with a certain heavenly gift, that by their very appearance they win human hearts to themselves, and reverence of human favour is bestowed upon them as though upon angels. Therefore we owe faith to God and gentleness to men: faith whose seasoning is love, so that by loving God we may be loved by him; [Col. 0709A] and in mildness and gentleness, that we may be an example and pattern of life to others. Yet gentleness in a man is remarkable only if it is seasoned with some salt of firmness. Thus gentleness was condemned in Eli. And therefore, when the Teacher of truth said: “Learn from me, for I am meek and humble of heart” [Note: [Col. 0709] Matt. 11], he had first enjoined that we have salt in ourselves, so that humility might be seasoned with salt. We say this concerning faith: although the righteous lives by faith [Note: [Col. 0709] Heb. 2], faith does not give life, just as it brings death, unless it has love as its companion. For many believe, but their faith is rather unto death. Since demons believe and tremble, these people, worse than unbelievers and demons, believe but do not love; they believe and utterly despise. Therefore, on the day of wrath they store up for themselves a dreadful judgment; and those who now do not fear [Col. 0709B] etc., “shall not fear an evil report” [Note: [Col. 0709] Ps. 111], having, in place of the abyss of their wickedness, an abyss of fire as cause for fear and horror, and, in place of contempt for damnation, the punishment of eternal condemnation. May he deign to avert this from us, to whom be honour and glory for ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON LI. ON THE SAME FEAST

“My soul was troubled because of the chariots of Aminadab” [Note: [Col. 0709] Song 6.].

The bride in the Song of Love, namely the Church, complains to the Redeemer concerning the chariots of Aminadab, that in her there are not the reverence and honours that ought to be. Aminadab is interpreted “willing,” that is, Christ, who of his own will offered himself to death for us. For he was offered [Col. 0709C] because he himself willed it [Note: [Col. 0709] Isa. 53]. His four charioteers are understood as the four Evangelists, who formerly bore the word of salvation publicly through the four quarters of the world, producing abundant fruit and gathering from the seed of God’s word many sheaves of righteousness. Therefore the Church complains that today the word of the Lord is bound in the mouths of preachers, the book is folded up, and those entrusted with the provision of the Lord’s word conceal the grain from the people; and thus the saying of the prophet of Lamentations comes to pass: “The little children asked for bread, and there was no one to break it for them” [Note: [Col. 0709] Lam. 4]. Of these chariots and their wheels it is said in Ezekiel [Note: [Col. 0709] ch. 10] that their likeness was one, as though there were a wheel in the midst of a wheel; by this is signified that one Testament is like and corresponds to the other Testament. For [Col. 0709D] as in the Old Testament there were commandments, judgments, and promises, so also in the New. As there was there one Lawgiver and many ministers; as there were there twelve prophets on one side and four on the other; so in the time of grace under Christ seventy-two disciples were appointed, twelve apostles, and four Evangelists, by whose testimony the preaching of both the seventy-two and the twelve was confirmed and publicly proclaimed in writings for all. These four are designated in Ezekiel and in the Apocalypse of John by the four living creatures. Matthew is prefigured by the man, because his concern in the Gospel is with Christ’s humanity; whence [Col. 0710A] he begins the Gospel narrative from Christ’s temporal generation. Mark is compared with the lion because he deals especially with Christ’s resurrection; therefore his Gospel is read in the Church on the day of the Resurrection. Luke is signified by the calf because he especially attends to the narrative of the Passion. For a heifer is a priestly victim; hence he begins from sacrifice. John is designated by the eagle because, like the trumpet of incomprehensible theology, he sounds forth the divine generation.
