While the others walk on earth with Christ, he, like an eagle—indeed, more than an eagle—flies higher than all the rest. And although each has special and proper concerns regarding Christ, the concern of each is nevertheless fourfold, since they speak of Christ’s Nativity, Passion, [Col. 0710B] Resurrection, and Ascension. Therefore these living creatures too appear to have four faces. “There were,” he says, “four faces to each one” [Note: [Col. 0709] ch. 1]. Or they are said to have four faces because they treat of and proclaim him who fulfilled in himself those four faces. For he is man in being born, calf in suffering, lion in rising again, eagle in ascending.

Therefore the bride was troubled because of the chariots of Aminadab. There is no one who fulfils the Evangelist’s word, no one who announces peace to the people, who preaches good things, who instructs by word and example toward eternal things [Note: [Col. 0709] Rom. 1]. O how beautiful are the feet of those who preach peace, who preach good things! But not all obey the Gospel; [Col. 0710C] indeed, perhaps few or none. For whereas the Gospel teaches us to despise the world, love poverty, hate the present life, and seek only heavenly and eternal things, we set aside the Gospel and abandon the chariots of Aminadab which lead to life, and run in Pharaoh’s chariots toward death. Pharaoh’s chariots are many; in this region of ours we can often find and see them. There is the chariot of malice, the chariot of lust, the chariot of avarice, the chariot of pride, the chariot of envy. Let us speak of some, so that examples of the others may be formed from their pattern. The chariot of malice has four wheels: cruelty, impatience, audacity, and shamelessness. These wheels are swift toward evil; this chariot is swift to shed [Col. 0710D] blood. The chariot of lust has four wheels: the gluttony of the belly, the desire of impurity, softness of clothing, and the dissolution of sleep and idleness. The wheels by which avarice is drawn are stinginess and rapacity, anxiety to acquire and fear of losing. In all these chariots the shafts are contempt for God and forgetfulness of death. The diligence of individuals can fashion for itself, at will, other chariots from Pharaoh’s army. Isaiah says [Note: [Col. 0709] ch. 2]: “His horses are many and his chariots innumerable.” Yet because it is written: “Some trust in chariots and some in horses, but we in the name of the Lord our God” [Note: [Col. 0709] Ps. 19], let us leave Pharaoh’s chariots, in which lies the destruction of souls, and return to the chariots [Col. 0711A] of Aminadab, in which is salvation, as the prophet says: “You shall ride upon your horses, and your chariots are salvation” [Note: [Col. 0711] Hab. 3]. As Pharaoh has his chariots, so your Aminadab has his horses and chariots. Do not justice, prudence, temperance, and fortitude make a four-horse chariot? Is this not the chariot and four-horse chariot of Elijah? This chariot is drawn not only by the four Evangelists but also by the four states of religious persons: beginners, those making progress, those running, and those arriving. Do you wish to see the chariots of our Aminadab, going toward eternal life, as numerous as the chariots at a fair? One four-horse chariot consists of devotion, prayer, reading, and meditation. Another consists of contrition of heart, confession of mouth, satisfaction for sin, and avoidance of wrongdoing. There is another chariot: hatred of the world, [Col. 0711B] contempt of self, compassion for Christ, and love of God. Likewise, faith in the Incarnation, Passion, Resurrection, and Ascension makes one most ample chariot for you. Another, perhaps more venerable, consists of purity of conscience, harshness of life, humility of obedience, and austerity of discipline. If the volumes of sacred Scripture were diligently turned over in inquiry into such things, the tongue would fail before the words did. But what is meant by the saying that “the spirit of life was in the wheels,” except that eternal life is in the writings of the Evangelists? Therefore the living creatures went and did not return, because, despising temporal things and longing for heavenly things, they never return again to earthly things. For he who has once put his hand to the plough, if he looks back, judges himself unworthy [Col. 0711C] of the kingdom of God [Note: [Col. 0711] Luke 9]. Therefore, forgetting what is behind, the Apostle says [Note: [Col. 0711] Phil. 3], “I stretch forward to those things which are before.” Today blessed Matthew teaches and instructs us in this by the example of the chariot and charioteer of true Israel: once called by the Lord and taken from the tax office, he did not return again to taxes and worldly occupations [Note: [Col. 0711] Matt. 9]. And although Peter, after conversion, returned to the practice of fishing, Matthew did not return to the constraints of worldly occupation or to the vomit of his former life; in perseverance in holiness he offered us an example and pattern of conversion. “The living creatures went,” he says, “and did not return” [Note: [Col. 0711] Ezek. 1]. Certainly you have no share with these living creatures if, after leaving the Egypt of this world, you again long for Egypt’s garlic and melons. Moreover, many, though they are [Col. 0711D] dead to the world, are drawn back by affection for their relatives and return to the age, if not with their feet, then with their affections. That most harmful seductress and most flattering flatterer, affection for relatives, draws many into the pit of eternal destruction, when a love that had been mortified in them comes to life again on account of kinship. Thus, making their first faith void, they love in others what they hate in themselves; and, disguising the love of the flesh beneath the image of charity, they foolishly and credulously risk their souls for their friends and household members. I say for friends and household members; but “a man’s enemies are those of his own household” [Col. 0712A; Note: [Col. 0711] Matt. 10]. For that friend and household member would wish you to take from them support for yourself and something as your own, seeking only to satisfy his own desire and not considering the eternal loss of your soul. I tell you one thing: if you possess anything as your own, you no longer have anything in common with Christ. Remember that you are dead to the world and to your parents, and have been planted together into the likeness of Christ’s death. Therefore do not lose for them your life, which is hidden with Christ in God, because they do not care about your destruction, provided only that they obtain from you, in whatever way, what they want. The Lord called you out of the Egypt of this age, from the sea of this world, from the midst of a crooked and perverse generation. Do not run back to it; for this return is a return to hell. The Lord called you out of [Col. 0712B] the midst of Babylon, from Ur of the Chaldeans, from Matthew’s tax office. Recognize your calling and persevere in it. Let neither Matthew return to the tax office nor you, brothers, return to Egypt, whether in deed or desire. I know that gnats, frogs, and the exceedingly grievous fly of Egypt often come from those regions. I beseech you: let neither these things nor the eating of meat overthrow you. Remember your calling. “I came,” says the Lord, “to call sinners to repentance” [Note: [Col. 0711] Matt. 9]. Matthew supplied the occasion for this saying—or rather, this decree. For all have sinned and need the grace of God [Note: [Col. 0711] Rom. 3]. “If we say that sin is not in us, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” [Note: [Col. 0711] I John 1]. And who can trust that he has a clean heart? When we have done all things well, the Apostle says, we ought to say that we are unprofitable servants [Note: [Col. 0711] Luke 17]. For, according to the Prophet, all our righteousnesses are as the cloth of a menstruating woman [Note: [Col. 0711] Isa. 64]. But what shall I say of us secular people, who constantly hear and see the conversions of saints and are neither contrite nor moved in any way? “Today,” says the Lord, “if you hear my voice, do not harden your hearts” [Note: [Col. 0711] Ps. 94]. But we, like the deaf asp that stops its ears, make ourselves deaf to Christ’s voice [Note: [Col. 0711] Ps. 57], and close our ears lest we hear what is good. We cannot allege that God’s grace is lacking to us; but he can allege that we are lacking to his grace, and whenever he calls us to salvation, we shut the eyes of the heart and turn our shoulder to him as we depart. Yet I often desire to have left everything [Col. 0712D] for Christ; I wish I had done everything; I long for the bridle of obedience and the yoke of voluntary poverty. I have it in my vow that I should be converted wholly; but here companion timidity, here affection for the flesh as a friend, here divine ambition distract me, and by turning me away from the resolve of conversion and holy manner of life, pervert me. Thus I knowingly act without wisdom, and deliberately perish; for it is perverse to defer the resolve of salvation and postpone repentance until the final moment of life, and into the danger of eternal death.

I know that the Lord is terrible in His judgments upon the children of men [Note: [Col. 0713] Ps. 65.], and yet I either do not fear His strict and sudden judgments, or pretend to fear them. Does not one pretend who, wounded unto death, rejects the healing medicine? Repentance is the medicine for sins. Of this Solomon says: “The Most High created medicine, and fools despise it” [Note: [Col. 0713] Ecclus. 38.]. Are not our kinsmen and friends almost daily snatched suddenly away to death? The Lord bends His bow against them, and has prepared in it instruments of death [Note: [Col. 0713] Ps. 7.], thereby giving us warning to flee from before the bow. Yet we nonetheless follow vanities and false madnesses: we quarrel, build, and gather possessions, paying no heed to that voice of dreadful thunder and of the judicial trumpet: “Fool, this night they shall demand thy soul of thee. And the things which thou hast prepared, whose shall they be?” [Note: [Col. 0713] Luke 12.]

O fountain of mercy, [Col. 0713B] O mercy, O goodness, O loving-kindness—God, do not abandon me; draw me after You. I cannot move a foot, because I am stuck fast in the mire of the deep [Note: [Col. 0713] Ps. 68.]; I am burdened too, because my iniquities have risen above my head [Note: [Col. 0713] Ps. 37.]. Yet I trust that, if You draw me, I shall run after the fragrance of Your ointments [Note: [Col. 0713] Song 1.]. If I am unwilling or unable to enter the wedding-feast that is prepared, do You, most gracious Jesus, compel me to enter [Note: [Col. 0713] Luke 14.], for unless I enter through You, I cannot enter. You who live and reign as God through all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON LII. ON THE DEDICATION OF A CHURCH

“Jerusalem, which is built as a city, whose fellowship is in the same” [Note: [Col. 0713] Ps. 121.].

[Col. 0713C] Jerusalem is understood in three ways: first, that bloodthirsty city which kills the prophets, of which it is said, “It is not fitting that a prophet should perish outside Jerusalem” [Note: [Col. 0713] Luke 13.]; the Lord made it a sign and portent to all cities, an evidence of His wrath and indignation, a burdensome stone and a stone of stumbling among the nations. There is also Jerusalem, the Church militant, which has its tent beneath the sun and fights upon earth. Of this it is said: “Arise, be enlightened, O Jerusalem” [Note: [Col. 0713] Isa. 60.]. There is likewise Jerusalem, the Church triumphant, gathered from angels and the spirits of the blessed. Of this Scripture says: “Jerusalem which is above is free, and she is our mother” [Note: [Col. 0713] Gal. 4.].

There is also a fourth Jerusalem, small and slight, which, although it is not a city, is nevertheless like a city. Therefore I understand this too when it is written: [Col. 0713D] “Jerusalem, which is built as a city.” For that which is like a city is not truly a city; nor is that which is ordered like an army in battle array truly an army in battle array [Note: [Col. 0713] Song 6.]. It is rather a house than a city—and truly a house, because it is the house of God and the gate of heaven [Note: [Col. 0713] Gen. 28.]. But if it is God’s house, take care that no uncircumcised or unclean person passes through it. “Holiness befits Your house, O Lord” [Note: [Col. 0713] Ps. 92.].

This house, this place, has been dedicated and sanctified to God for the purpose that propitiatory sacrifices may be offered to God within it. “In the time of propitiation this place was made a safeguard [Col. 0714A] of grace, and an offering of devotion was accepted; and in the time of wrath it became reconciliation” [Note: [Col. 0713] Ecclus. 44.]. To those willing to dwell in it, this place is a house of prayer, a house of refreshment, and a house of rest. It is a house of prayer, as it is written: “My house shall be called a house of prayer” [Note: [Col. 0713] Matt. 21.]; a house of refreshment, whence it is said: “Let my soul be filled as with marrow and fatness” [Note: [Col. 0713] Ps. 62.]. Those who dwell here are refreshed not by bread alone but by every word which proceeds from the mouth of God [Note: [Col. 0713] Matt. 4.].

It is a place of rest, for the Spirit of the Lord rests upon those who dwell in that place. “Upon whom,” He says, “shall My Spirit rest, except upon the humble and meek man, who trembles at My words?” [Note: [Col. 0713] Isa. 66.] This is Jacob’s place of rest. We read in Genesis that, when Jacob had departed from Beersheba and was going to Haran, [Col. 0714B] desiring to rest at night, he placed a stone beneath his head; and in sleep he saw a ladder, angels ascending and descending, and the Lord leaning upon the ladder. When he awoke, he said: “Truly the Lord is in this place” [Note: [Col. 0713] Gen. 28.].

Jacob means “supplanter”; Beersheba, “the well of the abyss and of despair.” Departing from Beersheba, he was going toward Haran, which is interpreted “lofty”; but again he rests and sleeps in the place called Bethel, that is, “house of God.” This is the pattern of our way and life: we who have gone forth from the pit of destruction, the pit of iniquity and despair, concerning which the righteous man prays that the pit may not press its mouth down upon him [Note: [Col. 0713] Ps. 68.]. Thus Abraham too once departed from Ur of the Chaldeans [Note: [Col. 0713] Gen. 11.], from the power of demons and the burning of vices.

[Col. 0714C] You sleep while passing through this life, “among the midst of the lots” [Note: [Col. 0713] Ps. 67.], between two portions: the worldly life which you flee, and the heavenly life which you seek. There is among you one who sleeps and rests. But earthly wisdom gives no heed to the rewards of eternal recompense. Of this man’s rest it was said: “His enemies saw him and mocked at his Sabbaths” [Note: [Col. 0713] Lam. 1.]. Yet he who places his head not upon earth but upon the stone of help sees angels. He who sleeps on earth, who is buried in earthly things, sees neither with heart nor with eye. But he who rests upon Christ the stone, though asleep in body, is awake in heart and deserves to see angels. “I sleep,” he says, “but my heart watches” [Note: [Col. 0713] Song 5.].

But he who sleeps upon earth, because he is occupied with earthly things, has his eyes shut, as it is written in Ezekiel: [Col. 0714D] “Let the ground be up to the windows, and the windows closed” [Note: [Col. 0713] Ezek. 41.]. You, dearest brothers, who have departed from Beersheba, from the well of worldly wickedness, in order to come to Haran, that is, to the heights, are in the place where Jacob wrestled. You too must fight and wrestle, not only against the aerial powers of wickedness in the heavens, but also against the angel of God. For it is written of Jacob, whose imitators you are, that he was strong against God. He held God fast in wrestling, saying: “I will not let You go unless You bless [Col. 0715A] me” [Note: [Col. 0715] Gen. 32.].

That he wrestled with the Lord and not with an angel is evident from the Lord’s words: “Why do you ask My name, which is wonderful?” And Jacob said: “I have seen the Lord face to face” [Note: [Col. 0715] ibid.]. O blessed wrestling! O desirable contest, which wrested forth the fruit of blessing! If the sinew of the thigh is touched, there is no cause for concern. Would that not only the sinew of the thigh, from which the offspring of generation issues, but the whole body might be so dried up and mortified that the mass of the body may not weigh down the mind with its many thoughts, but that the spirit, free from earthly and carnal things, may ascend to Haran—that is, to the height!

God glories in the wrestling of man. It is no wrestling when a man prays and pours out his heart like water, yet God rejects his prayer for a time, so that he may be more deeply pierced. [Col. 0715B] He then assails the Lord again with importunity and, laying hold more firmly, says: “I will not let You go until You have blessed me.” Moses stood in the breach against the Lord and held back His hand so that He might not destroy Israel [Note: [Col. 0715] Ps. 105.]. Therefore Jeremiah, lamenting that there was no one like Moses, says: “You were stronger, O Lord, and prevailed” [Note: [Col. 0715] Jer. 20.]. And elsewhere: “The Lord was distressed because there was no man, and no one to meet Him” [Note: [Col. 0715] Isa. 59.]. The Lord also says through Ezekiel: “I sought a man who would set a hedge in the way and stand opposed before Me for the land, lest I should destroy it; and I found none” [Note: [Col. 0715] Ezek. 22.]. And elsewhere: “There is none who rises up and holds Me fast” [Note: [Col. 0715] Isa. 64.].

Gird yourselves, therefore, with strength and be sons of might; seize the kingdom of heaven by force, for from the time [Col. 0715C] of John the kingdom of heaven suffers violence [Note: [Col. 0715] Matt. 11.]. If you contend bravely in the contest you have begun, you will seize not only the kingdom of heaven but the very King of heaven. He was pierced with so many wounds, afflicted with so many scourges, and shed so much blood through sweat, through words, through the lance, and through nails, because though He was “beautiful in form above the sons of men” [Note: [Col. 0715] Ps. 44.], now He has neither beauty nor comeliness. Yet that charity still endures which overcame Him and emptied Him even unto death. He will not be able to resist you if you imitate that charity. If you love Christ as He loved you, He will permit Himself to be overcome and will rejoice that He and His kingdom are taken.

You too shall rejoice, like those who rejoice at harvest, like victors dividing spoils after taking the prey [Note: [Col. 0715] Isa. 9.], receiving the reward [Col. 0715D] of your labours in the heavenly Jerusalem: the vision of the peace above; the vision, apprehension, and blessing of Him who is eternal life, Jesus Christ, who is blessed for ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON LIII. ON MANIFOLD WISDOM

“Blessed is the man who shall abide in his wisdom, who shall meditate upon justice, and in understanding shall consider the watchfulness of God” [Note: [Col. 0715] Ecclus. 14.].

Many have sought wisdom and have not found it; [Col. 0716A] many have found it and have not held fast to it. But blessed is he who abides in wisdom. Solomon found wisdom but did not abide in it, for, estranged from wisdom through foreign women, he became foolish. Philosophers too found wisdom, but did not in understanding consider the watchfulness of God. Although they knew the God of glory, they did not glorify Him as Lord; instead they became vain in their thoughts, their foolish heart was darkened, and they were given over to a reprobate mind, serving the creature rather than the Creator [Note: [Col. 0715] Rom. 1.].

The highest wisdom is that which this world considers folly: the wisdom of Christ—or rather, Christ is wisdom. According to the Apostle, He was made for us by God not only wisdom but also righteousness, sanctification, and redemption [Note: [Col. 0715] 1 Cor. 2.]. Therefore Paul, [Col. 0716B] devoted to the school of this wisdom, said: “I judged that I knew nothing except Jesus Christ, and Him crucified” [Note: [Col. 0715] Cor. 2.]. It is good to seek and hold this wisdom, which is sanctification and redemption. Since every other wisdom is pride and destruction, you cannot be a disciple of this school unless you renounce all that you possess. “He who does not renounce all that he possesses cannot be My disciple”; indeed, “he who does not hate father and mother and his own soul is not worthy of Me” [Note: [Col. 0715] Luke 14.].

Good Jesus, what have You done to us in this manner? [Note: [Col. 0715] Luke 2.] Moses had brought a burden which neither we nor our fathers were able to bear [Note: [Col. 0715] Acts 15.]. We hoped that, when You came, You would lighten our burdens, and now You make Your hand heavier. Were the hands of Moses not heavy enough? Have You come to strike [Col. 0716C] us with scorpions? Do You seek grounds to be angry with us and to destroy us? Are You not Jesus the Saviour, rather than the destroyer? Why do You command what I cannot do—namely, to hate father and mother and my own soul, and to love an enemy? “This saying is hard; and who can hear it?” [Note: [Col. 0715] John 6.] I would go to other schools and choose another teacher for myself; but I hear Peter answering, both for himself and for others: “Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life” [Note: [Col. 0715] ibid.]. Though You fashion toil in the commandment and harshness in the saying, I nevertheless know that great is the multitude of Your sweetness, which You have hidden for those who fear You [Note: [Col. 0715] Ps. 30.].

Therefore I shall hope in You, whose wisdom cannot be deceived, whose power cannot be overcome, whose goodwill cannot be wearied, and whose charity cannot diminish. If You scourge me, burn me, cut me, [Col. 0716D] or kill me, I shall hope in You, O Lord—provided that You help me and teach me to do Your will. Only do this, Lord: give a sign for good, that I may seek You and hope in You. For You are good to those who hope in You, to the soul that seeks You [Note: [Col. 0715] Lam. 3.].

I know that those who serve You are not burdened but honoured, because “Your friends, O God, are exceedingly honoured.” I know that every yoke of servitude is made welcome in remembrance of Your sweetness, according to the saying of Isaiah: “The yoke shall rot away because of the oil” [Note: [Col. 0715] Isa. 10.]. Brothers, this saint whose memory is blessed today [Col. 0717A] sought wisdom neither in the school of philosophers nor in Justinian’s law library; yet he found it, and, abiding in wisdom, taught it by word and example. Like a star in the firmament of heaven, he shone before all the teachers of our time in glory and honour.

Thus, Lord, You promised through Daniel, and thus You fulfilled it in this man: “Those who are learned shall shine like the brightness of the firmament, and those who instruct many unto righteousness, like stars for everlasting eternities” [Note: [Col. 0717] Dan. 12.]. For his speech, living, effective, and more penetrating than any two-edged sword [Note: [Col. 0717] Heb. 4.], shone with such charming sweetness, such grace of cultivation and pleasantness, that while he spoke it seemed not that a man but an angel was speaking. All his writings also surpass the capacity of human invention and ought rather to be believed to have been dictated and written by the finger of God than by human genius.

From childhood he sought wisdom; abounding in prudence, he shone through circumspection and miracles. As a vigorous husbandman of the Lord’s vineyard, walking in holiness and righteousness before Him all the days of his life [Note: [Col. 0717] Luke 1.], he allowed no hour of the day to remain idle. Ascending from virtue to virtue and from degree to degree of perfection, he most fully brought the day of sanctification to completion in himself. As Solomon writes in Proverbs concerning him and those like him: “The path of the righteous proceeds like shining light and grows unto the perfect day” [Note: [Col. 0717] Prov. 4.].

Let us therefore, brothers, loosen and unbind our tongues in praise of the Lord, who [Col. 0717C] has made His saint wondrous today. We know that he has attained the prize of his course and, sailing happily, has entered the powers of the Lord, the abysses of eternal light. Therefore we ought to rejoice with him, who has passed from labour to reward and from the sorrow of this age to the joy of angels.

Although, while seeking wisdom, his soul was accustomed in devout meditation, during the exile of this pilgrimage, to penetrate the heavens, enter the dwellings above, survey their diverse delights, greet the fathers, and join, by the vehicle of contemplation, the prophets, apostles, choirs of martyrs, and confessors, nevertheless at that time he saw all things through a mirror and in an enigma. But now, with unveiled face, amid the splendours [Col. 0717D] of the saints, he sees Him whom angels desire; and in the wisdom which he had sought and longed for while confined in this prison-house of the body, now freed from the bonds of flesh, he abides in contemplation according to his soul’s desire. “Blessed is he,” Scripture says, “who shall abide in wisdom” [Note: [Col. 0717] Ecclus. 14.].

We can now safely call him blessed; while he was a pilgrim away from the Lord, it was uncertain what end he would have. And who in this land of unlikeness can be secure concerning the reward of eternal life? Who knows whether he is worthy of love or hatred? Who knows what tomorrow’s day will bring? For with wonderful art and yet more wonderful charity the Most High so dispenses [Col. 0718A] His grace that He always leaves those whom He loves uncertain of His love, so that the more uncertain they are, the humbler they may be. “Blessed is the man who is always afraid” [Note: [Col. 0717] Prov. 28.].

Now He sends hard and bitter things; now He grants gentle and prosperous things. He visits in the morning and suddenly tests; now He kills, now He leads down to hell, now He brings back; now He makes poor, now He enriches; now He humbles, now He raises up. And through all these things He works the increase of His grace. Yet Paul says: “I have fought the good fight, I have finished the course, I have kept the faith. A crown of righteousness is laid up for me, which the Lord, the righteous Judge, shall render to me on that day” [Note: [Col. 0717] 2 Tim. 4.]. Therefore he also says: “I am certain that nothing shall separate me from the charity of God” [Note: [Col. 0717] Rom. 8.].

But Paul was indeed Paul, and had been caught up to the third heaven, when he spoke so [Col. 0718B] confidently; he was permitted to say: “I live—yet no longer I, but Christ lives in me” [Note: [Col. 0717] Gal. 2.]. He had clung so closely to Christ as to be one spirit with Him. Yet, as though he feared being rejected by the Lord, he says elsewhere: “I chastise my body and bring it into slavery, lest, after preaching to others, I myself should become a reprobate” [Note: [Col. 0717] 1 Cor. 9.].

Job, whom his heart had not reproved during his life, secure concerning eternal life, yet speaking of this uncertainty, says: “I know that in my flesh I shall see God my Saviour” [Note: [Col. 0717] Job 19.]. He also says: “What manner of man am I, that I should answer God?” [Note: [Col. 0717] Job 9.] “If I have anything righteous, I shall not answer, but shall entreat my Judge. And when He has heard me calling upon Him, I do not believe that He has heard my voice. For in the whirlwind [Col. 0718C] He shall crush me, and without cause will not permit my spirit to rest.”

You clearly see that the certainty which prevails for a time in Paul and Job vanishes in those same persons for a time. Therefore let him who stands take heed lest he presume and fall [Note: [Col. 0717] 1 Cor. 10.]. And who would presume to have a clean heart? “All our righteousnesses are like the cloth of a menstruous woman” [Note: [Col. 0717] Isa. 4.]. When we have done all things well, we ought to say that we are useless servants [Note: [Col. 0717] Luke 17.]. The days of man are short; shall the small number of my days quickly come to an end? The Lord alone knows those who are His [Note: [Col. 0717] 2 Tim. 2.]; but the day is near when the hidden things of hearts shall be illuminated, and each person shall see whether he is worthy of love or hatred.

May the Lord find you abiding in wisdom. The highest wisdom is not to read Plato, nor to turn over the subtleties of Aristotle, [Col. 0718D] but to love Christ, serve Christ, and willingly, effectively, faithfully, and to the end remain in this most welcome and fruitful service. So Paul acted and taught; so Bernard acted and taught. Be their imitators, if you wish to share their blessedness. May Jesus Christ, who is blessed for ages of ages, deign to grant this to us. Amen.

## SERMON LIV. ON THE SACRIFICE OF THE ALTAR

As the Apostle testifies, those who offer gifts according to the law [Col. 0719A] offer them to the pattern and shadow of heavenly things [Note: [Col. 0719] Heb. 8.]. But Christ is the mediator of a better covenant—better, I say, as is shown by the testimony drawn by the same Apostle from the prophet Jeremiah: “Behold, the days are coming, says the Lord, and I shall complete over the house of Israel and over the house of Judah a new covenant, not according to the covenant which I made with their fathers on the day when I took their hand to lead them out of the land of Egypt” [Note: [Col. 0719] ibid.].

“Covenant” is understood in various ways in sacred discourse: as the will and ordinance of a testator. Thus the Apostle says: “No one rejects or adds to a man’s covenant” [Note: [Col. 0719] Gal. 3.]. And elsewhere: “A covenant is confirmed in death” [Note: [Col. 0719] Heb. 9.]. “Covenant” is also called the confederacy of the wicked, according to the saying: “Against You the tents of [Col. 0719B] Edomites and Ishmaelites have made a covenant” [Note: [Col. 0719] Ps. 82.]. “Covenant” also means God’s promise, as in: “I have established a covenant with My chosen ones,” etc. [Note: [Col. 0719] Ps. 88.]; and: “He has remembered His covenant forever, which He commanded for a thousand generations” [Note: [Col. 0719] Ps. 104.]. “Covenant” also means eternal death, as it is written in Ecclesiasticus: “Remember that death will not delay” [Note: [Col. 0719] Ecclus. 14.]; and “the covenant of those below which has been shown to you.”

But Christ established a covenant of peace in His blood, and through this covenant erased the covenant of hell. As Isaiah says: “Your covenant with death shall be erased, and your pact with hell shall not stand” [Note: [Col. 0719] Isa. 28]. In the Old Testament there were four principal elements: promises, judgments, commandments, and sacraments. [Col. 0719C] All these have been changed.

The promises have been changed. There, abundance of grain, wine, and oil was promised, as it is written: “He gave them the possessions of the nations, and they took possession of the labours of peoples” [Note: [Col. 0719] Ps. 104.]. Here, no earthly substance or glory is promised, but an eternal inheritance. For by Christ, who was poor, the poor are evangelized: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” [Note: [Col. 0719] Matt. 3.]; and: “Woe to you rich, who have your consolation here” [Note: [Col. 0719] Luke 6.]. Those to whom the promises were spoken died without receiving the things promised, but beholding and greeting them from afar upon earth, and confessing that they were pilgrims and strangers [Note: [Col. 0719] Heb. 11.].

The judgments have been changed, for in the Old Testament temporal punishments were threatened against transgressors. But now it is said: [Col. 0719D] “Those who have done evil shall go into eternal fire” [Note: [Col. 0719] John 5.]. The commandments too have been changed; for, since the law brought no one to perfection, the moral commandments remain, such as “Honour your father,” etc., while the ceremonial observances, which, when observed, possessed only a figure of truth, have been spiritually abolished as to the letter.

A change was made in the sacraments because, as the Apostle testifies, they could not make the worshipper perfect according to the conscience through foods, drinks, and various washings [Note: [Col. 0719] Heb. 9.], the Holy Spirit signifying that the way into the holy places had not yet been made manifest [Col. 0720A]. Therefore there had to be such sacraments as contained both the signification of truth and the truth of the signification. In promises love is suggested; in judgments fear is incurred; in commandments life is conducted; in sacraments Christ’s grace is figured and given. “The law indeed was given through Moses, but truth came through Jesus Christ” [Note: [Col. 0719] John 1.].

Therefore if Christ is truth—indeed, because He Himself is truth—if we believe in Christ, let us also believe Christ. For He is the one who says: “I am the living bread who came down from heaven” [Note: [Col. 0719] John 6.]. He is the manna that refreshes; He is the lamb that was sacrificed and eaten under the law. For He offered Himself to us as food and ransom: He refreshes our fathers in manna, refreshes us in bread, and fulfills in Himself that which is written: “When new things come, you shall cast out the old, and shall eat the very oldest [Col. 0720B] of the old” [Note: [Col. 0719] Lev. 26.].

The old things are the sacrifices of the old law, offered by Aaron and his sons as they slaughtered the young of rams and poured out the blood of calves and goats. But the very oldest of the old were the bread and wine offered by Melchizedek, prefiguring Christ’s sacrament, concerning whom the Father swore: “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek” [Note: [Col. 0719] Ps. 109.]. When the new things came, therefore, the legal observances had to be cast away and the very oldest of the old eaten, so that man might eat the bread of angels, as God from ancient days prepared it in His sweetness for the poor.

The assumption of our nature is the bread by which we are fed. For Christ transformed the hay of our flesh into grain, that He might feed us with the fatness of wheat. [Col. 0720C] He became bread for us, because He became a grain of wheat to be sown and multiplied in the good ground of the human heart. Bread strengthens for the consolation of this wretched life and the support of the toil of the journey: bread in the word of doctrine, bread in the example of life, bread of spiritual grace, bread of unending glory.

“This,” He says, “is the new covenant in My blood” [Note: [Col. 0719] Luke 22.]. This covenant was confirmed for us in Christ’s death, so that we too might be planted together in the likeness of His death, die to the world, and have our life hidden with Christ in my God. Sacrifices must be ordered upon this covenant, so that the whole person, offering himself as a living sacrifice pleasing to God, may first offer the sacrifice of repentance. “A contrite spirit is a sacrifice to God; a contrite and humbled heart, O God, You will not despise” [Note: [Col. 0719] Ps. 50.].

The second sacrifice is the performance of mercy, which, because of its surpassing excellence, is called by the Lord not sacrifice but righteousness. “I desire mercy,” He says, “and not sacrifice” [Note: [Col. 0719] Matt. 9.]. That this sacrifice is righteousness is clear from the saying: “He has scattered and given to the poor; his righteousness remains for age upon age” [Note: [Col. 0719] Ps. 112.]. And when He spoke of the sacrifice of alms, He said: “Take heed not to do your righteousness before men” [Note: [Col. 0719] Matt. 6.]. Of this sacrifice it is [Col. 0721A] written: “Offer the sacrifice of righteousness” [Note: [Col. 0721] Ps. 4.].

There is a third sacrifice, wholly in fat and richness, proceeding entirely from the marrow of the soul and the inward parts of the heart. This is the sacrifice of praise, honouring the moon. Desiring to bring this sacrifice, from the richness of the heart and abundance of charity, the prophet says: “Let my soul be filled as with fat and richness” [Note: [Col. 0721] Ps. 62.]. The first relates to myself, the second to my neighbour, the third to God. Yet I refer all things to God and offer them for God’s sake.

But if we wish to offer sacrifices upon Christ’s covenant, there is one rule and proclamation; its order is this: just as we are commanded to cast our thoughts upon Him, so we should cast the faith of sacrifices upon His word. Let a man believe Christ rather than himself, so that his spirit may be believed with God; let him deny himself and follow Christ in hope and faith, for He is the way, the truth, and the life [Note: [Col. 0721] John 14.]. “I know,” says the Apostle, “whom I have believed, and I am certain” [Note: [Col. 0721] 1 Tim. 2.].

And these are the words of that same Apostle: “Whoever eats this bread and receives this cup unworthily eats and drinks judgment to himself, not discerning the body of Christ” [Note: [Col. 0721] 1 Cor. 11.]. In the words both of the Master and of the disciple, you hear and understand the body of Christ. Therefore do not hesitate concerning this or any other sacrament; but establish your heart and faith firmly in the word of Him by whose word the heavens were established, to whom be honour and glory for ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON LV. TO PRIESTS

[Col. 0721C] “He who is of God hears the words of God” [Note: [Col. 0721] John 8.].

Words must be received with effect. It is not enough to hear and not to do. For he who hears and does not do is a deaf hearer. “He who hears Me,” says Wisdom, “shall not be confounded” [Note: [Col. 0721] Prov. 24.]. And James says: “Be doers of the word, and not hearers only” [Note: [Col. 0721] Jas.]. For to hear and not understand, or to understand and not do, is negligence. “Good understanding belongs to all who do these things” [Note: [Col. 0721] Ps. 110.]. Neither understanding nor memory profits anything unless it leads to doing. “They remembered His commandments in order to do them” [Note: [Col. 0721] Ps. 102.]. Hearing through action is better than hearing through the ear.

The word must indeed be heard, so that faith or another work of virtue may come from hearing. “Faith comes by hearing, and hearing through the word of God” [Note: [Col. 0721] Rom. 10.]. But some [Col. 0721D] have ears and do not hear [Note: [Col. 0721] Ps. 134.]; for they do not have ears for hearing, but for neglect.

Therefore the Lord frequently says in the Gospel: “He who has ears to hear, let him hear” [Note: [Col. 0721] Matt. 11.]. “He who is of God,” and so forth. Let each of you consult his conscience whether he is of God; for if he is not of God, he cannot hear the words of God. Some are of God, some of the world, some of the devil. “I came forth from God and came into the world,” says the Lord [Note: [Col. 0721] John 16.]. And to the disciples: “If you had been of the world, the world would certainly love what was its own” [Col. 0722A] [Note: [Col. 0721] John 15.]. And to the Jews: “You are of your father the devil” [Note: [Col. 0721] John 8.].

He is of God who clings to God. “He who clings to God,” it says, “is one spirit with Him” [Note: [Col. 0721] 1 Cor. 6.]. But because the world and the devil have entered into partnership, whoever is of the world is of the father, the devil. These two burden the ears of the soul, so that it cannot hear. Thus the Prophet, speaking to the soul which had already become somewhat deaf, says: “Hear, O daughter, and see, and incline your ear; forget your people and your father’s house” [Note: [Col. 0721] Ps. 44.]. For those who savour earthly things have burdened ears and cannot hear the word of God.

Therefore you, who are now no longer of the world, who have renounced the devil and his pomps, and who, because you are of God, hear His words—do so provided that you fulfill God’s words in deeds. Take care, however, because God is not [Col. 0722B] mocked [Note: [Col. 0721] Gal. 6.]. Recall what you promised God in your manner of life. Take care not to build the high places of Topheth and Jerusalem in blood [Note: [Col. 0721] Jer. 7.].

He who once departed from Egypt, if he longs for Egypt’s garlic and melons; if he returns to the world which he has vomited out, rebuilds his own Jericho, and his firstborn dies, because the merit of his first conversion is extinguished. Of such people the Lord says: “My Spirit shall not remain in man forever” [Note: [Col. 0721] Gen. 6.]. Thus spirit is turned into flesh, heaven into earth, gold into dross, oil into lees. He who had been angelic and heavenly becomes earthly, carnal, and animal.

Behold our most wicked Jebusite, our assailant: the inward man who is earthly, animal, and carnal. He is earthly [Col. 0722C] who is of earth and speaks of earth: he savours earth, licks earth, and cannot be torn away from earthly things until a pit is dug for the sinner [Note: [Col. 0721] Ps. 93.], until he who is earth returns to earth [Note: [Col. 0721] Eccl. 12]. Of this earthly man the Apostle says: “The first man is of earth, earthly; the second is from heaven, heavenly” [Note: [Col. 0721] 1 Cor. 15]. And again: “Therefore, as we have borne the image of the earthly man, let us also bear the image of the heavenly man” [Note: [Col. 0721] ibid.].

The image of the earthly man is Adam’s transgression, through which we have become like vanity, seeking vanities and false madnesses [Note: [Col. 0721] Ps. 39.]. Thus man has become like vanity [Note: [Col. 0721] Ps. 143.]; thus man passes away in an image, and is vainly troubled besides [Note: [Col. 0721] Ps. 38.]. This earthly man is foolish, unable to see heaven. “The eyes of the wise are always in his head” [Note: [Col. 0721] Eccl. 2.]; “the eyes of the fool are at the ends of the earth” [Note: [Col. 0721] Prov. 17.]. Forgetting his God, he pours out his whole self upon earthly things [Col. 0722D]. Speaking in the person of this man, that lamenting prophet says: “My inward parts have been poured out upon the earth” [Note: [Col. 0721] Lam. 2.].

The carnal man derives his name elsewhere: not from earth, but from flesh. He served Chushan-rishathaim, Eglon, Jabin, Midian, and the other oppressors of God’s people for a long time under tribute, because he sold himself under sin [Note: [Col. 0721] Rom. 7.]. “It is of little account to me that I should be judged by a man or by a human day.” Once that son of wrath, that son of perdition, who fell from heaven, shone brightly. Hence he was called Lucifer, but now [Col. 0723A] *noctifer*, or “bearer of darkness.” Had he burned, he would never at any time have fallen.

Those follow in his footsteps who choose rather to shine than to burn, to appear religious rather than to be so. But they shall burn in the fire prepared for the devil and his angels [Note: [Col. 0723] Matt. 25.], whose flame shall not be quenched, whose stench kills, whose heat causes death, yet does not permit the sufferer to die. May that Holy One of holy ones turn us away from it—Jesus Christ, whose mercies today have made His saint wonderful and great upon earth [Note: [Col. 0723] Ps. 4.]. Some keep concubines; some misuse other men’s wives; thus [lacuna].

“Each man is drawn by his own pleasure” [Note: [Col. 0723] Virgil.].

But what is worst is that they do not conceal their wickedness; rather, they proclaim and display their incontinence in public drinking-bouts and banquets [Col. 0723B]. Although it is written: “Do not go up to Gilgal, nor enter Beth-aven” [Note: [Col. 0723] Hos. 4]—that is, do not disclose the shamefulness of your sin. The body of Christ is the price of the soul: an unfailing, inestimable, unstained, unconsumed, incorruptible treasure. With this treasure are purchased heavenly riches, possession of glory, an unending kingdom, peace without end, unshaken security, and eternity of life. This is the living bread which came down from heaven [Note: [Col. 0723] John 6] and gives life to the world. Those who serve the tabernacle have no authority to eat of it, as the Apostle says to the Hebrews [Note: [Col. 0723] ch. 13]—that is, those who serve the body and make provision for the flesh in its desires. Woe, then, to those to whom the dispensing of Christ’s body [Col. 0723C] has been entrusted, if their umbilical cord has not been cut, if they do not discern the body of Christ, if they do not honour Jesus, Mediator of the New Testament, and the sprinkled blood speaking better things than Abel’s. Christ Jesus, judge of the living and the dead, will not endure patiently being treated so irreverently and disgracefully. But because the Father loves his only Son with inestimable and ineffable charity, he will avenge the contempt and injury done to his only-begotten Son with dreadful indignation and zeal.

Behold two leavens: the leaven of avarice and of lust—the one by which evil is done against one’s neighbour, the other by which wickedness is done against God; and this is the leaven of malice and wickedness. Next comes the matter of honey, which is rejected in sacrifice. Honey in sacrifice is the excessively gentle and lax [Col. 0723D] indulgence of prelates. Yet there is a cautious and circumspect indulgence, and there is a foolish and lax indulgence. Cautious indulgence is fruitful: by it proper deference is prudently given to the powers of this world, and especially to the king as supreme. For every authority is from the Lord God [Note: [Col. 0723] Rom. 13]. It fosters the peace of the Church. It makes kingdom and priesthood one. By its kindness and gentleness it obtains what it could not extort either by threats or by judicial sentences. This is the indulgence, or gentleness, in which neither God nor man is offended, and in which the due faithfulness owed to God and man is shown. Of this faithfulness and this gentleness [Col. 0724A] it is written: “In faithfulness and gentleness he made him holy” [Note: [Col. 0723] Ecclus. 54]. In this indulgence—or rather, in this honey—the bitter gall of correction is concealed. For this indulgence has zeal beneath its gentleness, and a sting beneath its blandishments. At the fitting time it rises up against the adversary and sets itself as a wall for the house of Israel; and where it loves more truly, there it corrects more severely those who are ignorant and erring [Note: [Col. 0723] Job 34]. It is this that calls the king an apostate, calls rulers ungodly, does not respect the persons of princes, and does not recognize the tyrant when he has contended against the poor.

Therefore, brothers, whose office it is to offer pleasing victims to the Most High, keep far from yourselves the leaven of malice and wickedness. Cast away the honey of flattery or lax indulgence, the honey of worldly affection and deceptive pleasure. Let each one [Col. 0724B] keep his own vessel in holiness and honour, so that your ministry may not be reproached, and so that by word and example you may render the people entrusted to you acceptable to the Lord, zealous for good works [Note: [Col. 0723] Titus 2]. For on the day of dreadful judgment you will render an account of the souls of the people: for their destruction, you will incur the sentence of shame and eternal death; but for their salvation, you will obtain an unfading crown and eternal, ineffable glory. May he deign to grant this to you, he who lives and reigns through all ages of ages. Amen.

## Sermon LVI. To the Same Persons

“Fire shall always burn upon the altar; the priest shall feed it [Col. 0724C] day by day, laying wood upon it” [Note: [Col. 0723] Lev. 6].

Among all the acts of service which human devotion can render to God, nothing can be more acceptable to God than that he himself, who is truth and loves us in truth, should be loved by us. Rightly, and in accordance with his great mercy and gentleness, he wishes to be loved in truth: he who anticipates us in his love and blessings, as John the Evangelist recalls: “Not because,” he says, “we loved him, but because he first loved us” [Note: [Col. 0723] 1 John 4]. This is why, among the first-fruits of legal observance, he established as the first and greatest commandment of love: “You shall love the Lord your God with your whole heart and all your strength” [Note: [Col. 0723] Matt. 22]. He kept, taught, and displayed this love—the one who laid down his life for us [Col. 0724D] [Note: [Col. 0723] John 10]. “No one,” he says, “has greater love than this: that someone lay down his life for his friends” [Note: [Col. 0723] John 15]. He preserved and observed this love to the end: “Having loved his own, he loved them unto the end” [Note: [Col. 0723] John 13].

The Lord saw that the fire of this love, which had been kindled in the ancient fathers and extinguished in us, had left behind only desolated coals; he came to kindle this fire on the altar of our heart. Therefore the coals were rekindled by him who says: “I came to cast fire upon the earth; and what do I will, but that it burn?” [Note: [Col. 0723] Luke 13]. Upon the altar [Col. 0725A] of the heart a contrite spirit is sacrificed, according to the words: “A sacrifice to God is a broken spirit; a contrite and humbled heart God will not despise” [Note: [Col. 0725] Ps. 50]. This is the fire that must continually be fed upon the altar of the heart by the priest; this is the fire of which the prophet says: “His fire is in Zion, and his furnace in Jerusalem” [Note: [Col. 0725] Isa. 31]. And Jeremiah: “From heaven the Lord sent fire into my bones, and instructed me” [Note: [Col. 0725] Lam. 1].

Nehemiah dug up this fire, which Jeremiah had buried. We read in the Book of Kings [Note: [Col. 0725] 4 Kings 25] that, when the people of Israel had been carried away into Babylonian captivity and a small remnant remained under Gedaliah, Jeremiah too remained; in the valley of Jehoshaphat he hid fire in a pit. After a long course of time Nehemiah sought and dug it up, but [Col. 0725B] found, as it is written, only burnt logs and thick water [Note: [Col. 0725] 2 Macc. 1–2]. He poured that water upon the altar, and fire was kindled. This is the water of love, which rouses fire from desolated coals; and it is so thick that the priest’s sacrifice becomes rich. The day was called Nephar, that is, “purification.” Priests are bound to approach and nourish this fire for the purification of souls. Yet three kinds of wood are necessary to feed it, drawn, together with the water of thick love, from the well of a good conscience.

The three pieces of wood are: the example of holy conduct; the word of diligent preaching; and the office of devout administration. For a priest ought to be holy in conduct, diligent in preaching, and devout in administration. He must be holy, for it is written: “Be holy, because I am holy” [Note: [Col. 0725] Lev. 11, 19]. How could he cleanse the impurities of others unless he himself were holy? The Apostle says that the hand which undertakes to wash away filth must be clean. Today we see priests, with the sons of Eli, holding flesh-hooks [Note: [Col. 0725] 1 Kings 2], keeping watch with women in the court of the tabernacle, and becoming stallions let loose, as the prophet says [Note: [Col. 0725] Jer. 5]: each neighing after his neighbour’s wife. Today we see priests sitting with Belshazzar at banquets with wives and concubines, abusing vessels consecrated to the Lord God. But surely that last hand is near, and the dreadful writing: *Mane, Thecel, Phares*—“numbered, weighed, divided” [Note: [Col. 0725] Dan. 5]. For he numbers [Col. 0725D] the priest’s days; all his deeds are gathered together and sealed as though in a bag; he weighs the grace he has bestowed; and he destroys and confounds the hope and confidence which the priest has in a longer life. “When they say, ‘Peace and security,’ then sudden destruction will come upon them, and anguish like that of a woman in labour, and they shall not escape” [Note: [Col. 0725] 1 Thess. 5], because, according to Solomon, “the prosperity of fools will destroy them” [Note: [Col. 0725] Prov. 1].

Those who ought to have placed Jeremiah’s fire upon the altar with the sons of Aaron place strange fire there: that fire of which the Psalmist says, “Fire fell upon them, and they did not see the sun of righteousness” [Col. 0726A] [Note: [Col. 0725] Ps. 57]. Their eyes are fixed upon gifts; they give no heed to orphan and widow; they do not heed that accursed sentence: “Woe to those who justify the ungodly for gifts, and take away from him the justice of the just” [Note: [Col. 0725] Isa. 5]. For they drag weak women and other pitiable persons into court without cause; they defame women of unimpaired reputation, judge those already cleared, acquit the wicked, and condemn the innocent: “Entering the houses of widows, taking captive weak women laden with sins” [Note: [Col. 0725] 1 Tim. 3]. Certainly such men do not see the sun of righteousness, for they have only the left eye, through which they cannot see that sun.

A human being has two eyes, the left and the right. The left is occupied with temporal matters; the right, with eternal things. The left is sensuality; the right is consideration of eternal realities. With the left eye we see most sharply, prudent and astute in acquiring temporal goods, but having no prudence in eternal things. “They are wise,” he says, “to do evil, but they do not know how to do good.” These are those whose right eye Nahash the Ammonite removed, as is read in the Book of Kings [Note: [Col. 0725] 1 Kings 11]. *Nahash* means “serpent”: namely, the enemy of the human race, who so blinds the souls of priests that they are blind guides of the blind. With their left eye they see only avarice. For the prophet says of avarice: “This is their eye throughout all the earth” [Note: [Col. 0725] Zech. 3]. In your chapters, where corrupted by gifts you overthrow the justice of the just, acquit, as we have said, the ungodly, and defame the innocent, you do not see the sun of righteousness.

“When you come [Col. 0726C] together in this way, it is no longer to eat the Lord’s supper” [Note: [Col. 0725] 1 Cor. 11]. For he approaches the most holy body of Christ far too dangerously who, in judgment, does not heed the sun of righteousness; who either judges his neighbour unjustly or defames him wrongly. Therefore, brothers, whenever you meet in your assemblies to judge others, remember that it is said: judgment awaits you. Consider that this life is fleeting and short; your stewardship is burdensome and weighty, its administration difficult, its end dreadful, its punishment endless.

We do not say these things, dearest brothers, on your account. For among you are many who excel in the merit of holiness and upright conduct. Yet among you, as the Apostle says, there are [Col. 0726D] many who are weak, and many sleep [Note: [Col. 0725] 2 Cor. 11]. For the Lord’s threshing-floor has not yet been winnowed: the lily is still among thorns, and tares among ears of grain.

These things concern the first wood which the priest adds to the fire for its fuel. The second wood is the word of sacred preaching, which especially belongs to the priestly office: the priest must be “mighty in sound doctrine,” as the Apostle says to Titus [Note: [Col. 0725] ch. 1], able to contradict evil men, rebuke the perverse, and refuse assent to those who err. Here the Apostle very aptly calls assent a springing shoot [*verna*; reading uncertain], assigning the most certain rationale for this matter. “Therefore you do not rebuke others, because you yourselves repeatedly do the same things” [Col. 0727A]. Although priests’ lips are consecrated to the Gospel, they spend the whole day in idle talk and withhold the bread of life from Christ’s hungry faithful. One must never grow weary or cease from salutary exhortation. Thus rightly, “day by day”—that is, assiduously and without interruption.

In sacred speech, days are virtues. “Every day,” says the prophet, “I shall bless you” [Note: [Col. 0727] Ps. 114]. And in Job: “Times are not hidden from the Almighty; but those who know him do not know his days” [Note: [Col. 0727] Job 24]. Conversely, sins are nights, as in the Psalm: “Every night I shall wash”—that is, by confessing each sin, “I shall wash my bed,” namely, my conscience [Note: [Col. 0727] Ps. 6]. The priest therefore lays wood upon the fire day by day when, by the example of holy conduct [Col. 0727B] and the word of sacred preaching, he exhorts those subject to him toward every virtue, and thus kindles in the hearts of the faithful the fire of charity.

There follows the third wood: namely, the office of devout administration. Although priests’ administration is exercised in many things—in confessions, baptisms, anointings, and exorcisms—it consists especially in two: psalmody and the celebration of Masses. In these, humble and ready devotion is always required. What does a psalm profit unless devotion accompanies it? To sing psalms without devotion is like sounding brass and a tinkling cymbal [Note: [Col. 0727] 1 Cor. 13]. “Let all who seek you and love your salvation exult and rejoice” [Note: [Col. 0727] Ps. 39]. But such persons do not love your salvation when there are disorderly apocopations and syncopations, nor are such *synaloephae*—elisions—acceptable to God [Col. 0727C]. Jerome warns concerning psalmody that prayer should be made word by word. Therefore two things are necessary in psalmody: understanding and the devotion of an unstained heart. Then not only angels, but the Lord of angels, comes and most willingly places himself among them; and what the Prophet says comes to pass: “I shall sing psalms and understand in the blameless way: when will you come to me?” [Note: [Col. 0727] Ps. 103]. “I desire,” says the Apostle, “to speak five words with my understanding rather than ten thousand words in a tongue” [Note: [Col. 0727] 1 Cor. 14].

In the sacrifices of the altar, a great fire of devotion and love is required, for there is our whole salvation. Certainly the priest is utterly without devotion if he is not broken there, where the Son of the Most High is sacrificed before the Father’s eyes. Indeed, the devout and prudent priest, while he stands at the divine table, thinks of nothing except Christ Jesus, and him crucified [Col. 0727D]. Before the eyes of his heart he sets Christ’s humility and patience, his distresses and pains; he devoutly and diligently recalls Christ’s reproaches, spittle, scourges, lance, cross, and death; and in this very remembrance of the Lord’s passion he crucifies himself.

If sacrifice is offered specially to him and for him who bodily offered himself for us, how grave, how perilous, my brothers, is the office of administration! For on the day of dreadful judgment you are bound to answer not only for your own souls but for those entrusted to you. And how will he keep another’s conscience [Col. 0728A] who cannot keep his own? Conscience is indeed an unfathomable abyss, a deepest night; yet to the wretched priest who has undertaken this night, and is challenged concerning it, the cry is made: “Watchman, what of the day? Watchman, what of the night?” [Note: [Col. 0727] Isa. 21].

What shall that most wretched priest do who feels himself burdened with sins, entangled in cares, defiled by the dregs of carnal desires, blind, bent, weak, hemmed in by a thousand difficulties, anxious through a thousand necessities, afflicted by a thousand disturbances, prone to vices, and feeble for virtues? What shall the son of sorrow, the son of eternal weeping, do—he who kindles the fire of charity neither in himself nor in others? Certainly he is prepared as food and fuel for fire. “A fire has been kindled in the Lord’s wrath, and it shall burn unto the lowest depths of hell” [Note: [Col. 0727] Deut. 32]. A place among everlasting burnings is assigned to him; the worm that does not die is prepared; smoke, vapour, and storm-winds; horror and dark gloom; the burdens of chains that punish, constrict, burn, and do not consume.

May that fire deliver us from these things: the fire which does not consume but perfects, which does not devour but enlightens every person coming into this world. May he himself enlighten us, to give the knowledge of salvation to his people. May he deign to grant this to us—he who, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, lives and reigns as God through all ages of ages. Amen.

## Sermon LVII. To the Same Persons

It is written in Leviticus [Note: [Col. 0727] ch. 2]: “Every offering offered to the Lord shall be without leaven; neither [Col. 0728C] shall any leaven or honey be burned in sacrifice to the Lord. Whatever sacrifice you offer, you shall season with salt; in every offering you shall offer salt.”

My lords, we speak to you concerning sacrifice, because the care of the sacrifices of which we speak has been entrusted to you by God: you administer sacred things and offer sacrifices; therefore you hold the name and office of priests. Yet, because evangelical purity has now removed the bloody filth of legal slaughter, those nevertheless offer spiritual sacrifices today who devote themselves and all that is theirs to Christ with their whole heart. They offer peace-offerings who are careful to have peace with God and not to offend Christ by any criminal offence. He offers an ox who undertakes works of perfection; a sheep, he who seeks to please God in his simplicity [Col. 0728D]; a goat, he who takes up the way of the penitent; birds, he who ascends the way of charity or the watchtower of contemplation.

From all these and the many other sacrifices, leaven and honey are kept far away and damnably excluded. Salt, however, is everywhere favourably admitted. Leaven, by whose admixture the whole mass is corrupted, is the avarice and incontinence of churchmen, which corrupts subjects by perverse imitation. For what will a simple layperson do except what he sees his spiritual father doing? Priests’ avarice is conspicuous in many ways: especially when they get themselves ordained for temporal profit; when, in hope of a most paltry offering, they perform the sacraments; when they litigate over corpses and sell burial and baptism; when they give nothing freely but pursue their own avarice in everything. Thus Malachi says: “Who among you will shut my doors and put incense upon my altar without payment? I have no pleasure in you, and I will not receive a gift from your hand, says the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0729] Mal. 1].

And this is, according to Zechariah, the jar (*amphora*) going forth; it is “their eyes throughout all the earth” [Note: [Col. 0729] Zech. 5]. Isaiah also says of them: “The shepherds themselves have each turned aside to his own avarice” [Note: [Col. 0729] Isa. 56]. And Jeremiah: “From the least even to the greatest, all pursue avarice; and from prophet even to priest, all practise deceit” [Note: [Col. 0729] Jer. 6]. They are concerned with the sheep’s wool, not its salvation. What is weak [Col. 0729B] they do not strengthen; what is sick they do not heal; what is broken they do not bind up; what has perished they do not seek; what has been cast away they do not bring back [Note: [Col. 0729] Ezek. 34]. Instead, providing for their own avarice, they eat the sins of the people and, by the example of their wicked conduct, invite them to worse things. As Hosea says: “They eat the sins of the people and raise up their ways to iniquity” [Note: [Col. 0729] Hos. 4].

These men, in Job’s words, “eat the fruits of the earth without payment” [Note: [Col. 0729] Job 31]: receiving temporal things, they dispense spiritual ones. Though they should savour nothing but heavenly things, they savour earthly things, seeking not what is above but what is upon the earth. Though they were appointed by God, according to the testimony of the Apostle speaking to the Philippians, as lights in the world, holding the word of life [Note: [Col. 0729] Phil. 2], they have despised it and are bound to the earthly houses of iniquities [Col. 0729C]; their spiritual eyes have been clouded and darkened by the dregs of earthly things, as is said in Ezekiel’s vision [Note: [Col. 0729] ch. 41]: “The ground was up to the windows, and the windows were shut.”

Jeremiah, lamenting in the person of these men the inward person dissolved by desire for earthly things, says: “My inward parts have been poured out upon the earth” [Note: [Col. 0729] Lam. 2]. But how greatly avarice harms priests! Speaking of clerical avarice, the Apostle says to the Hebrews [Note: [Col. 0729] ch. 13]: “Let your conduct be without avarice, content with what is at hand.” The avarice of clerics is shown by the fact that they hold chapters or councils almost daily, seeking not the correction of morals but the extortion of money. “Let not my soul be in the judgments” of certain men, in whose courts justice and equity are scattered, and judgment does not return, as Habakkuk says: “The law has been rent, and judgment does not reach its end” [Note: [Col. 0729] Hab. 1].

But if they speak of administering justice or restoring peace, the proceeding will not be without a new exaction: something is demanded from either side, and woe to the party that has given nothing! Micah says of such men [Note: [Col. 0729] ch. 3]: “They bite with their teeth and proclaim peace; but if anyone does not put something into their mouths, they raise war against him” [Note: [Col. 0729] Mic. 3]. First the archdeacon receives something, and then the official receives something. The dean too, and the rest, make some matter profitable to themselves [Col. 0730A], so that we may say: “What the caterpillar left, the locust ate; what the locust left, the grub ate; what the grub left, the mildew ate” [Note: [Col. 0729] Joel 1]. These men most plainly build the high places of Topheth [Note: [Col. 0729] Jer. 7] and prepare for themselves a road to Gehenna. For, in Job’s testimony [Note: [Col. 0729] ch. 15], “Fire shall consume the bodies of those who gladly accept gifts”—especially where justice, owed freely to all and each, is put up for sale.

Woe to the prelates of the Church if they do not correct these things! Hence Amos says [Note: [Col. 0729] ch. 6]: “Woe to you who are wealthy, chief men of Samaria!” The heads of the people, who ought to be examples of uprightness and humility, judge in pride and abuse, command harshly, and lord it over the clergy, not becoming examples to the flock among the people. These things concern clerical avarice.

There follows the other part of the leaven prohibited from the sacrament: namely, incontinence. Among all the plagues of vices, this is the foremost, and attacks us most vigorously. Against it we must gird our loins and put on spiritual armour, so that each may chastise and reduce his body to slavery [Note: [Col. 0729] 1 Cor. 9]. Thus the Apostle writes to the Corinthians: “The weapons of our warfare are not carnal, but powerful through God for the destruction of strongholds, bringing every understanding into captivity to the obedience of Christ” [Note: [Col. 0729] 2 Cor. 10]. Worldly priests, whatever they may do for others, do not administer the sacraments to themselves; rather, they blind themselves. They do not sanctify themselves, but subject themselves to a curse.

Let us consider our deeds and iniquities, by which we frequently offend the Lord’s mercy, so that with Jeremiah [Col. 0730C] we may say: “The mercies of the Lord are many, because we have not been consumed, and because his compassions have not failed” [Note: [Col. 0729] Lam. 3]. Some keep concubines, etc. Verbatim as in Sermon LV, to the end.

## Sermon LVIII. To the Same Persons

“N., beloved by God and by men, whose memory is in blessing.” If we consider the fruit of the love spoken of, it is the fruit of eternal salvation and a tree of life to those who grasp it. For this is called charity, from whose root all good things proceed; among its fruits are numbered joy and peace in the Holy Spirit. This ardour is most fruitful: therefore, if anything is bestowed upon it for cultivation, it repays that very thing with a multiplied increase of fruits. And if we now love the Lord, we are loved more by him; for “he will give into your bosom a good measure, pressed down, shaken together, and overflowing” [Note: [Col. 0729] Luke 6].

For your love is as a little spark in comparison with that poured-out and most abundant divine charity. If we desire to attain Christ’s love, he himself anticipates the paths of our desires, and by the grace of his love runs before us. For it is from him that we love him; and, in order that we may love him, he anticipates us by his own love. “Not,” says John [Col. 0731A], “because we first loved him, but because he first loved us” [Note: [Col. 0731] 1 John 4]. He loves us who everywhere anticipates us in his blessings.

But if we seek an irrefutable proof of the divine love just mentioned, God the Son of God laid down his life for us, although no one has greater love than to lay down his life for his friends [Note: [Col. 0731] John 15]. This love was stronger than life, because it took life away; stronger than death, because he who possessed the dominion of death destroyed it and utterly swallowed up and abolished death. Besides this general and common love, in which and through which the Lord wills all to be saved and to come to knowledge of his name [Note: [Col. 0731] 1 Tim. 2], there is another love: namely, the infusion of grace and the preservation of what has been infused. This is what makes a person beloved by God [Col. 0731B].

It is entirely certain that one who loves the Lord, and in whom he reveals his Son, is loved by God. Paul says of this revelation: “He who set me apart from my mother’s womb and called me through his grace, that he might reveal his Son in me” [Note: [Col. 0731] Gal. 1]. Speaking of this same revelation, the Lord says to Peter: “Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jonah, because flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven” [Note: [Col. 0731] Matt. 16].

The Father bears witness when, after Jesus was baptized and came up from the water, the heavens were opened and a voice was heard from heaven, saying: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” [Note: [Col. 0731] Matt. 3]. Of this voice Peter says in his Catholic Epistle: “Such a voice came down to him from the magnificent glory: ‘This is my beloved Son, in whom I am pleased; hear him.’ And we ourselves heard this voice brought from heaven, when we were with him on the holy mountain” [Note: [Col. 0731] 2 Pet. 1].

In John’s Gospel Christ says of the Father’s testimony: “The Father who sent me himself will bear witness concerning me” [Note: [Col. 0731] John 5]. And John says in his Catholic Epistle: “If,” he says, “we receive the testimony of men, the testimony of God is greater” [Note: [Col. 0731] 1 John 5]. And this is God’s greater testimony: that he has testified concerning his Son. The Son gives testimony when he shows by his blood and works who he is. Thus, when he said, “I am the light of the world,” and the Pharisees said, “You bear testimony about yourself; your testimony is not true,” he answered: “Even if I bear testimony concerning myself, my testimony is true, because I know whence I came and where [Col. 0731D] I am going” [Note: [Col. 0731] John 8]. Again: “It is written in your law that the testimony of two is true. I am one who bears testimony concerning myself, and the Father who sent me bears testimony concerning me” [Note: [Col. 0731] ibid.]. Again: “My Father is he who glorifies me, whom you say is your God; and you have not known him” [Note: [Col. 0731] ibid.].

When he says, “If I bear testimony concerning myself, my testimony is not true,” understand: without the Father’s testimony. Hence he immediately adds: “And there is another who bears testimony concerning me” [Note: [Col. 0731] John 5]. The Son gives testimony on the mountain by not denying the truth. Therefore Paul says in the First Epistle to Timothy [Col. 0732A] [Note: [Col. 0731] ch. 6]: “I command you before God, who gives life to all things, and Christ, who under Pontius Pilate gave testimony by the good confession, that you keep the commandment spotless and blameless.” The Son gives testimony by rising again and, after the resurrection, manifesting himself by many proofs. He bore testimony by ascending before the sight of those with whom he had lived, as it is written: “While they watched, he was lifted up” [Note: [Col. 0731] Acts 1].

The Holy Spirit gave his testimony from ancient days, when he was borne over the waters [Note: [Col. 0731] Gen. 1], sanctifying them then in order to sanctify us later. In them he bore testimony by inspiring the prophets, foretelling future things, and showing the way of the saints that had not yet been made known. He also gave testimony at the time of our visitation, when he came upon the blessed Virgin, visited her, and made her fruitful [Note: [Col. 0731] Luke 1]; when he apportioned tongues of fire [Note: [Col. 0731] Acts 1]; when, in the unity of faith and the proclamation of one God, he united languages.

Therefore the Father, the Word, and the Holy Spirit give testimony, and these three are one: one in unity of essence, in the agreement of the nature of each testimony. But there are three that give testimony on earth: the Spirit, water, and blood [Note: [Col. 0731] 1 John 5]. According to the view of those who see more keenly, everyone who lives spiritually is called “spirit,” as Paul says in the First Epistle to the Corinthians [the citation prints “2 Cor. 6”]: “He who cleaves to God is one spirit with him.” And John says in his Epistle: “Do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits to see whether [Col. 0732C] they are from God; for many false prophets have gone out into the world. By this the Spirit of God is known: everyone who confesses that Jesus has come in the flesh is from God; and every spirit that dissolves Jesus is not from God” [Note: [Col. 0731] 1 John 4]. He “dissolves” Jesus who confesses Christ in words and denies him by deeds.

Water gives testimony when someone, living spiritually after baptism, preserves the innocence received in regeneration; or, having fallen after baptism, washes himself in penitential water. Such a person bears witness and is sanctified, because Christ is truth. The blood of martyrs also publicly confesses Christ. Thus the spirit of the righteous, the water of penitents, and the blood of martyrs testify that Jesus Christ is truth, crying out with one voice and one confession.

The demons themselves too, whether willing or unwilling, bear testimony to Christ. For in Matthew [Note: [Col. 0731] ch. 8] they cry and say: “What have we to do with you, Jesus, Son of God? Have you come before the time to torment us?” And in Mark [Note: [Col. 0731] ch. 1] the unclean spirit cries: “What have we to do with you, Jesus of Nazareth? Have you come to destroy us? I know who you are: the Holy One of God.” And he sternly commanded them not to make him known. Again, in the same Gospel another demon says: “What have I to do with you, Son of the Most High God? I adjure you by the Most High God, do not torment me” [Note: [Col. 0731] Mark 5]. And in Luke [Note: [Col. 0731] ch. 4], demons went out from many [Col. 0733A], crying and saying: “You are the Son of God”; and rebuking them, he did not allow them to speak, because they knew that he was Christ.

In the Acts of the Apostles [Note: [Col. 0733] ch. 19], when certain Jews attempted to invoke Jesus’ name over demoniacs, each saying, “I adjure you by Jesus whom Paul preaches,” the unclean spirit said to them: “Jesus I know, and Paul I know; but who are you?” Behold: in bearing testimony to Christ, the demons profess not only that they know Paul, but that they know Christ.

But we, professing the Christian name, deny by our deeds the faith we profess in words. We who ought through faith to overcome the world are overcome by the world through unbelief. What, do you suppose, will that dreadful judge do on the day of dreadful judgment when he sees that we, who have been born of God through baptism, have [Col. 0733B] degenerated from our Father? Will he not say: “You are of your father the devil” [Note: [Col. 0733] John 8]? Will he not say: “Go, accursed ones, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his children” [Note: [Col. 0733] Matt. 25]?

Therefore, brothers, let us beware of this evil hearing. Let us overcome the world, lest we be overcome by it. Let us return to Christ through repentance in faith and truth, so that Jesus Christ, who adopted us as sons, may make us sharers and heirs of eternal life. To him be honour and glory for ages of ages. Amen.

## Sermon LIX. To the Same Persons

“Hear this, O priest; give heed, house of Judah; listen, house of the king, because judgment is for you. For you have become a snare for the lookout, and like a net spread upon Mount Tabor; and you have turned aside your victims into the deep” [Col. 0733C] [Note: [Col. 0733] Hos. 5].

The words are those, dearest brethren, of the prophet Hosea, who wonderfully magnifies and exalts the dignity of the priestly order. “Hear these things, priests; house of Judah, house of the king, listen.” As though he said: Hear, holy nation, people of possession, chosen race, royal priesthood. For the higher the dignity of priests, the graver their fall and the more perilous their ruin. The same prophet adds: “For judgment is for you”: you who surpass all men in the dignity of your order, take heed, for judgment is for you. And this is what is written elsewhere [Col. 0733D]: “Judgment shall begin from the house of the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0733] I Pet. 4.]. And the Lord, speaking to His angels, says: “Go, and begin from my sanctuary” [Note: [Col. 0733] Ezek. 9.]. Although you are promised, in the apostles, that you shall sit upon twelve thrones and judge the twelve tribes of Israel, it is shameful if judgment begins with you, and if you are judged first, though you ought to have judged others. It is shameful if shepherds are to be numbered with the goats at the left hand; if fishers are to be cast out with the bad fish; if the workers in the vineyard of the Lord of hosts are kindled with the branches and unfruitful shoots. Near is the time [Col. 0734A] when the Lord’s judgment shall begin with you, and the great and terrible day of the Lord shall come upon you: “For you have become a snare for those who watch, and like a net,” etc.

You know that laypeople and the unlearned multitude observe the conduct and life of priests, in order to conform themselves to their morals, as we read in Job: “The oxen were ploughing, and the she-asses feeding beside them” [Note: [Col. 0733] Job 1.]. The oxen are the teachers of the Church, whose concern it is to labour continually in the field of the Lord’s harvest. The she-asses are the simple, who place their hope and salvation in the teaching of their prelates. Thus the priest becomes a snare to the watchfulness of the humble when, by the example of his depraved conduct, he draws the people subject to him into a snare and ruin.
