For, as is read in Solomon: “A wicked priest is the ruin of the people.” And in Leviticus [Note: [Col. 0733] ch. 4.] we read: [Col. 0734B] “The anointed priest, if he sins, shall make his people sin.” So too St Gregory testifies: “Prelates ought to know that, if they perpetrate wicked deeds, they deserve as many deaths as the examples of their own perdition which they pass on to their subjects.” Therefore let the lamps of good works be in your hands, that your good works may shine before men and they may glorify your Father who is in heaven [Note: [Col. 0733] Matt. 5.]. For as you excel in dignity, so it is fitting that you should excel in holiness of works. Thus in Leviticus [Note: [Col. 0733] ch. 7.] it is also commanded that the right shoulder, set apart from the sacrifices, be taken, so that a priest’s activity may be not merely useful and honourable, but singular and pre-eminent; so that those whom he surpasses by the prerogative of dignity and order, he may [Col. 0734C] transcend by the practice of virtues.

But today, according to the word of Isaiah: “As the master, so the servant; as the people, so the priest” [Note: [Col. 0733] Isa. 24.]. Hence the same prophet, crying out elsewhere in indignation: “Be ashamed, Sidon,” he says; “the sea has spoken” [Note: [Col. 0733] Isa. 23.]. Let priests be ashamed if laypeople, immersed in the waves of this world, are found to lead a more consecrated life. Truly the plough is set before the oxen, and the back rises above the head; and a house tends to ruin when a subject is found equal or superior to his prelate.

The Lord called you to give knowledge to His people, to feed the Lord’s flock, and to be a pattern for the flock among the people. Yet I fear lest that saying of Isaiah be fulfilled in you: “These shepherds have not known understanding” [Note: [Col. 0733] Isa. 36.]; and that Gospel saying: “They are blind leaders of the blind” [Note: [Col. 0733] Matt. 15.]. You ought to have been guides of peoples [Col. 0734D] unto life; see that you do not lead both yourselves and them unto death. Be their guides to repentance, continence, and prayer, as the Psalmist recounts: “The princes of Judah, their leaders; the princes of Zebulun, the princes of Naphtali” [Note: [Col. 0733] Ps. 67]. Judah is interpreted “confession,” which pertains to repentance; Zebulun, “strength,” which pertains to continence; Naphtali, “a hind sent forth,” in which is marked the swiftness of prayer, which, proceeding from a devout heart, penetrates heaven.

Therefore let each one of you, dearest brethren, recognize the burden of his calling. “Feed the Lord’s flock which is among you” [Col. 0735A] [Note: [Col. 0735] I Pet. 5.], so that “your ministry may not be blamed” [Note: [Col. 0735] II Cor. 6.]. Your ministry is comprised in a few things: singing psalms, offering, and teaching. If you sing psalms, sing wisely. “Let us sing,” says the Apostle, “with the mouth; let us sing also with the mind” [Note: [Col. 0735] I Cor. 14.]. Offer to the Lord with the apostles a honeycomb. What is a honeycomb but honey in wax? And what is honey in wax but devotion in the letter? There are some who, from the moment they begin a verse, find it exceedingly long until they reach its end; and they rush headlong through every word so that neither honey nor wax remains in the Lord’s honeycomb. They swallow one verse beneath one cadence, race through the song of the Lord, and cut it in half with perfunctory *synaloephae* [elisions]. At times, while we sing psalms, we build castles in the mind and imagine false vanities and follies. [Col. 0735B] The lips are in the songs; the mind is in the dishes. What remains except that the Lord should say: “This people honours me with their lips, but their heart is far from me” [Note: [Col. 0735] Matt. 15.]? This is not a psalm, “a pleasant and fitting praise” [Note: [Col. 0735] Ps. 146.]. Angels gladly attend psalmody, as the Psalmist recounts: “They went before, joined with those singing psalms in the midst of maidens playing timbrels” [Note: [Col. 0735] Ps. 67.]. And elsewhere: “In the sight of angels I shall sing psalms to you, my God” [Note: [Col. 0735] Ps. 137.].

So much concerning psalm-singing. It remains now to say what sort of offering one ought to make, or what sort of teaching to give. He whose body and blood you offer to God the Father is His Son. See that you do not offend the Father in the Son, lest you regard the blood of the Son as polluted. For He is “holy, innocent, undefiled, made higher than the heavens” [Note: [Col. 0735] Heb. 7.]. If you approach uncleanly [Col. 0735C], you receive not the food of salvation but the judgment of eternal condemnation. Your teaching consists in words and deeds. A priest’s words without works are vain and fruitless. But, I pray, let your good works shine before men [Note: [Col. 0735] Matt. 5.], and the words of your exhortation will have, in the hearts of those subject to you, the efficacy of most health-giving medicine. Thus, on the day of terrible judgment, for your care of the flock entrusted to you, an aureole will be given to you; and because you have taught many unto righteousness, you shall be as stars for everlasting eternities [Note: [Col. 0735] Dan. 12]. May He deign to grant this to us, He who lives and reigns as God with the Father through all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON LX. TO THE SAME PERSONS IN SYNOD

[Col. 0735D] “Hear these things, priests; attend, house of the Lord; house of the king, listen, for judgment is for you” [Note: [Col. 0735] Hos. 5.].

“For you have become a snare for those who watch, and like a net spread upon Mount Tabor.” Great and manifold, dearest brethren, is the praise of priests in sacred Scripture. For even the Lord’s words give them precedence above others: “You,” He says, “are the light of the world; you are the salt of the earth” [Note: [Col. 0735] Matt. 5.]; you are angels; you are gods. Angels, as it is written: “The lips of priests preserve knowledge” [Note: [Col. 0735] Mal. 2.]. You are gods, as the Prophet recounts: [Col. 0736A] “God stood in the assembly of gods; but in the midst He judges gods” [Note: [Col. 0735] Ps. 81.]. And Moses commanded that the leper be brought to the gods, that is, presented to the priests; and, to use an elegant and concise phrase, priests possess Abel’s primacy, Abraham’s patriarchate, Noah’s helm, Melchizedek’s order, Aaron’s dignity, Moses’ authority, Samuel’s power, Peter’s poverty, Christ’s anointing. “You are kings,” etc. He who says, “All power in heaven and on earth has been given to me” [Note: [Col. 0735] Matt. 28.], gave you the power of binding and loosing. To you it was given by God to sit upon thrones and judge the twelve tribes of Israel [Note: [Col. 0735] Matt. 19.].

Yet I fear that matters may turn to the contrary, and that it may someday be said of you: “You cast them down when they were lifted up” [Note: [Col. 0735] Ps. 72.]. Too late is the complaint, “By lifting me up, you dashed me down” [Col. 0736B] [Note: [Col. 0735] Ps. 101.]. Zechariah’s word is: “My wrath is angry against the shepherds” [Note: [Col. 0735] Zech. 10.]. The Lord is angry because you are undisciplined, because you do not keep the Lord’s law and commandment, as Jeremiah complains: “This is the nation which has not heard the voice of the Lord, nor received discipline” [Note: [Col. 0735] Jer. 7.]. And in the same place: “The priests said, ‘Where is the Lord?’ Those who held the law,” says the same Prophet, “did not know me, and the shepherds transgressed against me” [Note: [Col. 0735] Jer. 2.].

Because of our sins, Christ’s holy Church is trampled upon and made a reproach. Because of our sins, Peter’s sword is today cheap and covered with rust. Everywhere today, for these reasons, the Lord’s name is taken in vain with impunity; Peter’s sentence is despised; with impunity today [Col. 0736C] Pashhur stretches out sacrilegious hands against Jeremiah, Malchus against Christ, Jason against the sacred offerings, Belshazzar against the vessels of the Lord. That prophet laments, bewails, and mourns this cheapening and abasement of priests, saying: “The illustrious sons of Zion, clothed in finest gold—how have they been reckoned as earthen vessels, the work of a potter?” [Note: [Col. 0735] Lam. 4.] Those who ought to have been vessels of contemplation and strength have become earthen vessels. For they are frail in flesh, weak in spirit, prone to sin, slow toward virtue, burdened in rising to high things, precipitous in falling to low things.

The Lord has been offended by us. Therefore, as the Apostle says to the Corinthians: “We act as ambassadors for Christ, as though God were exhorting through us. We entreat you for Christ: be reconciled to God” [Note: [Col. 0735] II Cor. 5.]. Our iniquity separates us from God, and the cloud of sin hinders [Col. 0736D] our prayer from rising to God. “Lord,” says the prophet, “you have interposed a cloud, so that prayer should not pass through” [Note: [Col. 0735] Lam. 3.]. Yet, says Isaiah, “the hand of the Lord is not shortened, that it cannot save; nor is His ear weighed down, that it cannot hear: but our sins divide between us and God” [Note: [Col. 0735] Isa. 59.]. Cease from sins, and God will be reconciled.

Who today obtains an ecclesiastical benefice without payment? Who ministers in it without payment? Have not all the Church’s sacraments been reduced to merchandise and profit? [Col. 0737A] That great sacrament of piety, that inestimable and ineffable price of the world, given without price—the priceless price—is today sold and offered at the valuation of a paltry coin. Adam first sold himself; Esau gave his birthright for a dish of lentils. Many are sons of Esau; many are sons of Adam, who sell their heavenly and eternal inheritance for a small pleasure.

Beyond other sins, and before other crimes, the pest of lust disgracefully dishonours the priesthood today. Whether lust is exercised in refined manner, costly dress, or worldly conduct, all of it turns to the clergy’s reproach and to the peril of eternal death. This is Athaliah, who almost exterminated the entire royal line [Note: [Col. 0737] Kings 11.]; this is she who slew one of the virtues; this is the beast of the forest that [Col. 0737B] slew Absalom’s army. The Apostle, writing to the Hebrews, says: “There remains a certain fearful expectation of judgment, and a jealous fire which shall consume the adversaries. Anyone who makes void the law of Moses dies without any mercy on the testimony of two or three witnesses. How much worse punishments, do you think, does he deserve who has trampled the Son of God underfoot, regarded as polluted the blood of the covenant by which he was sanctified, and insulted the Spirit of grace?” [Note: [Col. 0737] Heb. 10.] The prophet’s word is: “If an enchanter is bitten by a serpent, who will heal him?” [Note: [Col. 0737] Ecclus. 12.] “Physician, heal yourself” [Note: [Col. 0737] Luke 4.]. For such ought to be a priest: one who has made his people imitators of his own works, acceptable to God and followers of good works [Note: [Col. 0737] Titus 2.].

Yet it frequently happens that the priest is regarded as worse than the whole body of his people, so that Micah’s saying fittingly applies to priests: “The best among them is like a bramble, and the upright like a thorn hedge” [Note: [Col. 0737] Mic. 7.]. Those who ought to have been the lights of heaven and the splendour of the firmament have become filth and a stain in the moon: the sun has been darkened, and the air by the smoke of the pit. The salt of the earth has lost its savour, and the light of the world has been turned into darkness. Therefore, according to Jeremiah’s word, “the Lord has rejected His altar; He has cursed His sanctuary” [Note: [Col. 0737] Lam. 2.]. “What,” says the Lord through Jeremiah, “has my beloved done, committing many crimes in my house? Shall holy flesh take away his wickedness, in which he has gloried?” [Note: [Col. 0737] Jer. 15.] And in Malachi: You who believe that you are cleansed by sacrifices, know that you [Col. 0737D] shall not be cleansed but shall be further defiled [Note: [Col. 0737] Mal. 2.]. And there follow the words of the same prophet: “And now this commandment is for you, O priests. If you will not hear, and if you will not lay it to heart, to give glory to my name, says the Lord of hosts, I will send poverty upon you, and I will curse your blessings” [Note: [Col. 0737] Mal. 2.].

We see that both these things have occurred. For you, whom the Lord appointed over His household to give it food in due season, afflict it with hunger and famine: “The little ones asked for bread, and there was none to break it for them” [Note: [Col. 0737] Lam. 3.]. The word of the Lord has been bound in [Col. 0738A] your mouth, and you are unwilling to minister the bread of life to the hungry, though it is written: “Cursed is he who hides grain from the peoples” [Note: [Col. 0737] Prov. 11.]. “God is not mocked” [Note: [Col. 0737] Gal. 6.]: He has sealed up your sins as if in a bag [Note: [Col. 0737] Job 14.]. When Gideon was pursuing Zebah and Zalmunna, he passed through Succoth and asked the elders of the city for bread for himself and the men who were with him. Since they refused food to him and his men, after returning victorious from battle he crushed them with thorns and briars [Note: [Col. 0737] Judg. 8.]. Thorns and briars are the torments and eternal tribulations.

Because of priests’ negligence, innumerable and destructive heresies have sprung up today; and some now hold damnable opinions concerning the sacrament of the altar, marriage, and the other sacraments of the Church. Consequently, the holy Church has been most grievously wounded almost throughout the whole world; “there is no balm in [Col. 0738B] Gilead, and there is no physician there” [Note: [Col. 0737] Jer. 8.]. Yet, as the Apostle writes to the Thessalonians: “God has not appointed you for wrath, but for obtaining salvation” [Note: [Col. 0737] I Thess. 5.]. And to the Corinthians: “The Lord has placed in you the word and ministry of reconciliation” [Note: [Col. 0737] II Cor. 5.], and He gave you authority for building up and not for destruction. But you despise and adulterate the Church of God, so that the heart of her husband no longer trusts in her. Therefore the Lord has rejected His altar and spurned His inheritance [Note: [Col. 0737] Ps. 77]. And when there is a cry from distress and tribulation, He turns away His ear and does not look upon the face of His covenant. These are your works; this is the service you have rendered to Christ.

I see that you have made a covenant with hell and have within you the answer of death [Col. 0738C]. What remains except that the Lord should require at your hand the blood of those [Note: [Col. 0737] Ezek. 3.] whom you ought to have led by word and deed into the way of life, but whom, by the example of your depraved conduct, you have led into the way of eternal death? If someone were appointed a chief centurion and leader in war, what ought to be done with him if he delivered the people committed to him into the enemy’s hands? The people of God, whom Christ had redeemed from the devil’s power by His precious blood—you, by nullifying the benefit of Christ’s Passion, have cast them back again into the devil’s power.

Take heed, I pray, brethren, to your ministry and to your peril; and attend henceforth more watchfully and diligently to what you have hitherto performed negligently. Consider that He is terrible over the children of men, to whom you must render an account of the souls [Col. 0738D] entrusted to you. If you keep them to reproach, eternal fire and worm shall be your expectation and recompense. But if you instruct and govern them wisely, you shall have not only a crown but an aureole of eternal joy, promised to those who instruct many unto righteousness [Note: [Col. 0737] Dan. 12]. This is the double honour which Paul promises to presbyters in writing to Timothy: “The presbyters who rule well,” he says, “shall be considered worthy of double honour” [Note: [Col. 0737] I Tim. 5.]—especially the everlasting glory of singular eminence. May He deign to grant it to us, who [Col. 0739A] lives and reigns through all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON LXI. TO THE SAME PERSONS

“Let a man so regard us as ministers of Christ and stewards of the mysteries of God” [Note: [Col. 0739] I Cor. 4.].

Brethren, these are Paul’s words addressed to us. If a ministry has been entrusted to us by God, do as he himself exhorts and teaches us, so that our ministry may not be blamed. See, brethren, your calling, the eminence and dignity of your order, to whom the dispensation of the Lord’s body and blood has been entrusted. See that the Son is not trampled underfoot in the Father’s eyes. For in the Father’s honour is the Son’s honour, and in the Son’s honour is the Father’s honour. You are not ignorant [Col. 0739B] concerning the body and blood of the Lord: with what reverence it must be consecrated, with what fear received, and with what caution dispensed. This sacrament is great beyond all estimation, beyond all eminence, beyond all understanding: namely, that under the visible species the whole Christ is received.

For angels are satisfied from the fatness of wheat [Note: [Col. 0739] Ps. 147.], sit at the rich man’s table, and feed upon the delights of God’s house; but we receive the truth in a mirror and enigma [Note: [Col. 0739] I Cor. 13.]. For if we saw Christ and enjoyed Him as He is, our faith would no longer be meritorious, nor indeed would it be faith but knowledge. He shall come and shall not be silent, to summon the earth and judge it in the spirit of judgment and the spirit of burning. “The God of gods,” says the Prophet, “has spoken and called the earth. [Col. 0739C] He summoned heaven from above, and the earth, to distinguish His people” [Note: [Col. 0739] Ps. 49.]. And what does He say? “Gather to Him His saints, who have ordered His covenant over sacrifices” [Note: [Col. 0739] Ibid.]. This saying concerns you, to whom it is enjoined to order the Lord’s covenant over sacrifices. You are to be gathered, you who, though you were living stones, have been scattered abroad, drawn away toward vices, and everywhere going after the desires of your flesh: “The stones of the sanctuary have been scattered at the head of every street” [Note: [Col. 0739] Lam. 4.]. “Gather to Him His saints,” He says [Note: [Col. 0739] Ps. 49.]. Who are the saints? Priests, of whom it was said: “Let your priests be clothed with righteousness, and let your saints rejoice” [Note: [Col. 0739] Ps. 131.]. Those who serve and minister to the Holy of Holies ought to be holy. [Col. 0739D] “Be holy,” He says, “for I am holy” [Note: [Col. 0739] Lev. 11.]. And the prophet says: “You shall be called the holy ones of the Lord, ministers of God” [Note: [Col. 0739] Isa. 61.].

It will be said of you today: “The conduct of priests is the overthrow of the people.” Iniquity has also gone forth from the elders of the people [Note: [Col. 0739] Dan. 13.]. For those who ought to have corrected errors for the amendment of life themselves mix wine with water and show favour to sinners. As the Lord says through the prophet: “My tavern-keepers mix water with wine” [Note: [Col. 0739] Isa. 1.]; and through another: “How long do you judge iniquities and show favour to sinners?” [Col. 0740A] [Note: [Col. 0739] Ps. 31.] To mix water with wine and to show favour to sinners is to consent to sinners’ errors. Today there is no one to admonish, teach, or exhort to good. All priests are mute dogs, unable—or rather unwilling—to bark [Note: [Col. 0739] Isa. 56.]. They have bound up the word of the Lord entrusted to them, wrapped it in a napkin, and buried it in the earth, not considering the word of the evangelical householder who says: “Wicked servant, ought you not to have given my money to the bankers, so that, when I came, I might receive it with interest?” [Note: [Col. 0739] Matt. 25.]

The Philistines contrived that no blacksmith should be found in all Israel [Note: [Col. 0739] I Sam. 13.]: there is no one to make spiritual weapons, or sharpen those already made. Therefore new Amorites and new Philistines attack us; new and recent heretics overthrow the whole world: [Col. 0740B] they are called *publicani* or *patinui*. These are those who admit neither baptism for infants, nor the reality of the body and blood upon the altar, nor the grace of the Holy Spirit in priests, nor the fellowship of marriage among faithful laypeople. These have today increased beyond number [Note: [Col. 0739] Ps. 39.]. And if this heresy is extinguished in one place, elsewhere it returns in multiplied fashion like the heads of the Hydra. All this evil proceeds from your silence.

Was it not commanded to us in Timothy: “Insist in season and out of season” [Note: [Col. 0739] II Tim. 4.]? Is it not commanded in Leviticus that a sound be heard when the priest enters and leaves the tabernacle [Note: [Col. 0739] Exod. 28.]? Does not the prophet say: “Cry aloud; do not cease; lift up your voice” [Note: [Col. 0739] Isa. 58.]? “Upon your walls, Jerusalem, I have appointed watchmen; all day and all night they shall not [Col. 0740C] be silent” [Note: [Col. 0739] Isa. 62.].

How much time has passed since you bound yourselves by the vow of continence? Was it not publicly decreed and solemnly enacted, and confirmed by the apostolic see, that your fornications should be removed from you and the material of a shameful life cut off in you? What profit do you now have in all your pleasures and impurities, which you have hitherto practised, as the Apostle says: “What fruit had we in those things of which we are now ashamed?” [Note: [Col. 0739] Rom. 6.] In the work of lust, what is delightful passes quickly, while what torments remains without end. Nothing remains from that most evil pleasure except the shame of confusion and the sting of fear: a foul and fetid conscience, testimony to sin and torment of the soul. It is supreme madness to give joy that does not fail in exchange for a small and passing pleasure. The end of all lust is a heap of death and eternal misery.

The Apostle says: “Abstain from fleshly desires, which wage war against the soul” [Note: [Col. 0739] I Pet. 2.]. “For if you live according to the flesh, you shall die” [Note: [Col. 0739] Rom. 8.]—that is, the death which neither dies nor ends. If you wished to return to the weapons of innocence, the Lord would destroy every height lifting itself against the Church of God; and, in the prophet’s testimony, the whole multitude of nations that fought against Ariel would be “like the dream of a night vision” [Col. 0741A] [Note: [Col. 0741] Isa. 29.]. Whatever is attempted against you would all come to nothing, like running water [Note: [Col. 0741] Ps. 57.].

Therefore, brethren, cast aside the works of darkness and the works of the flesh [Note: [Col. 0741] Rom. 13.], and let not sin reign in your mortal body [Note: [Col. 0741] Rom. 6.]. Notice: “Let it not reign.” Sin reigns when it reaches consent or action. Therefore, so that it may not reign in its first stirrings, the will to sin must be cut off. “Pierce my flesh with your fear” [Note: [Col. 0741] Ps. 118.]. And this is what is signified by Simeon, whose name is interpreted “bringing sadness,” that is, contrition of heart, and Judah, whose name is interpreted “confession”: these two tribes invaded Bezek and captured Adoni-bezek, that is, “lord of the city,” and cut off the extremities of his hands [Note: [Col. 0741] Judg. 1.]. This happens whenever, through [Col. 0741B] contrition and confession, we cut off the first beginnings of evil deeds.

Therefore amend and correct your actions, dearest brethren, and do not wait for correction from another. Each of you knows himself more fully; let him examine himself and lift up his conscience, that he may gather in it the fruit of life. “He who clings to a harlot becomes one body with her. Shall I,” he says, “take a member of Christ and make it a member of a harlot?” [Note: [Col. 0741] I Cor. 6.] What was a priest but a member of Christ? What has the priest become but a member of a harlot? He from whom and in whom the body of Christ is received has become, in and through himself, a member of a harlot. Therefore, through our uncleanness, the body [Col. 0741C] of Christ is taken and received by a member of a harlot. See where you have placed the body of the only-begotten Son of God. See what you have done. You have incurred the Apostle’s curse after the curses of other imprecations: “Whoever violates this temple, the Lord shall destroy him” [Note: [Col. 0741] I Cor. 3.]. May He who is blessed for ever and ever free us from this curse and confer His blessing upon us. Amen.

## SERMON LXII. TO CLOISTERED RELIGIOUS

“Cursed is he who rebuilds Jericho” [Note: [Col. 0741] Josh. 6.].

This is Joshua’s interpretation. Those who, abandoning the frailty and instability of secular life, afterwards return to the love of worldly things—these, by rendering their first [profession] void, hold the bond of their profession [Col. 0741D] in mockery and indulge in wantonness against Christ. Certainly Achan son of Carmi, because he took something from the accursed things of Jericho, was stoned [Note: [Col. 0741] Josh. 7.]. They bear an exact likeness to Achan: having renounced worldly things, they immerse themselves in worldly things, if not in deed, yet in affection and desire. Such persons have already been judged and condemned by that stone laid in the foundation of Zion [Note: [Col. 0741] Isa. 28.], and by that stone of which it is said: “Whoever falls upon it shall be broken; but upon whomever it falls, it shall crush him” [Note: [Col. 0741] Matt. 21.].

Once a monk has put on the new man, who is created according to God [Note: [Col. 0741] Col. 3.], no traces of the old life ought to remain. The plantings of the old manner of life must be rooted out entirely, [Col. 0742A] so that they may not be like those whose beards Hanun, David’s enemy, shaved halfway, and whom he then dismissed with reproach and shame [Note: [Col. 0741] II Sam. 10.]. Hanun shaves half the beard of a religious when a religious person renounces the world but, like Ananias and Sapphira [Note: [Col. 0741] Acts 5.], does not entirely relinquish worldly desires.

We read that Israel, because it was unwilling to kill the Canaanite, was given into the hands of Chushan-rishathaim and served him for a long time and in affliction [Note: [Col. 0741] Judg. 3.]. However religious you may become in the cloister, you lose everything if you have retained anything of the world. “A little leaven corrupts the whole lump” [Note: [Col. 0741] Gal. 5.]; one sin overwhelms and subverts a multitude of virtues. Thus Abimelech, Gideon’s son, kills those born of the wives, because worldly desire destroys the virtues which a religious person [Col. 0742B] acquires in the cloister.

“Cursed,” he says, “is he who rebuilds Jericho.” We read that Hiel of Bethel rebuilt Jericho; but during the building of its first gate his firstborn died, and at its last gate the last of his sons died [Note: [Col. 0741] III Kings 16.], because once someone returns to worldly affections, whatever good he had done either in the world or in the cloister perishes and is nullified. Of those gates the prophet says: “From the first gate there shall be a cry, and from the second a howling” [Note: [Col. 0741] Zeph. 10.].

Once you have gone out from Jericho, my brethren, you have ascended from Jericho to Jerusalem, from Babylon to Zion, from Egypt to the land of promise, from darkness to light, from the place of unlikeness, from the place of horror to the house of joy [Col. 0742C] and salvation. You have come from the land of saltiness to an inhabitable land, from Ur of the Chaldeans to refreshment, from spiritual hunger to nourishment, from transgression to grace, from worldly anxieties to rest. Truly these are the camps of God, which are none other than the house of God and gate of heaven [Note: [Col. 0741] Gen. 28.].

Nevertheless, not everyone understands the glory and sweetness of this house. “It is a tree of life to those who lay hold of it” [Note: [Col. 0741] Prov. 3.]. For many are called, but few are chosen [Note: [Col. 0741] Matt. 22.]. “You have multiplied the nation,” he says, “but not increased the joy” [Note: [Col. 0741] Isa. 9.]: the Lord’s yoke is not bearable by all; His burden is not sweet to all. The Jebusite, who cannot be exterminated, still dwells among you. There is still a lily among thorns, and tares among ears of grain. In the householder’s garden there are together [Col. 0742D] *saliunca* [a salt-loving plant] and fir, nettle and myrtle. Jacob’s sheepfold still contains white and black animals, lambs and goats; Peter’s net, good and bad fish; Solomon’s temple, Satan at the right hand of Jesus the high priest; Noah’s ark, clean and unclean animals; the Lord’s cellar, wines and grapes, oil and olive dregs.

How hateful and dreadful it is for one cloistered to become secular again, and for him who has vomited the world to return to the world. “I fear,” says the Apostle, “lest, having begun in the Spirit, you be perfected in the flesh” [Note: [Col. 0741] Gal. 3.]. Does not a cloistered person become secular if he even thinks about [Col. 0743A] or concerns himself with the things of the world? “If you have secular matters,” he says, “appoint to judge them those who are held in least esteem among you” [Note: [Col. 0743] I Cor. 6.]. The Apostle defines secular or temporal things, saying: “The things which are seen are temporal; but those which are not seen are eternal” [Note: [Col. 0743] II Cor. 4.].

Since “covetousness is the root of all evils” [Note: [Col. 0743] I Tim. 6.], we grieve—and cannot but grieve—if in this house, most renowned for observance of religion and rule, that mother of transgression, mistress of doing harm, chief captain of iniquity, and charioteer of malice has dared to set even one foot. Let not the monk who covets another’s goods flatter himself by saying: “The occasion of sin belongs to secular people. Whatever they have, if I take it away, if I seize it, if by the violence of princes or through purchase I acquire something for the use of our Church, I am pursuing not my own business but the common good.” Wretched man: if covetousness accuses you with respect to private possessions, does it not accuse you with respect to common ones? For since every person of our life is his own neighbour, more damnable is he who makes himself deserving of Gehenna for another’s sake than he who does so for his own; and, as authority declares, he shall burn no less who burns for many or with many.

Most beloved brethren, why do you need riches, you who chose voluntary poverty for Christ, who was poor? Do you wish to become rich again and return to the worldly things you abandoned? In them, as is publicly known, there is fleeting consolation, brief use, deceptive joy, an unknown end, a heavy judgment, and, in exchange for the transient acquisition of temporal things, [Col. 0743C] misery without end. If your sufficiency is from God [Note: [Col. 0743] II Cor. 3]—indeed, if it is God, in whom the rich person lacks and the poor person abounds—
Sufficiency from God was possessed by him who said: “Having food and coverings, let us be content with these.” For those who wish to become rich fall into a snare and into the temptations of the devil. [Note: [Col. 0743] 1 Tim. 6.] With God you lack nothing; without God nothing suffices. Alas for the children of Adam, who still seek temporal riches, although poverty is commended by God! Enduring riches have been prepared for you and set ready at hand; necessities are readily available, yet you labour for superfluities. The apostate angel lost the kingdom of heaven through the abundance of his riches. Your profession is to acquire through poverty the kingdom that he lost. Certainly it is more expedient for you to go hungry—which, nevertheless, through God’s grace ought not to be necessary—than to do anything from which even a slight taint of avarice may arise. “I know,” says the Apostle, “both how to be filled and how to be hungry, both to abound and to suffer want.” [Note: [Col. 0743] Phil. 4.] If you seek provisions for yourselves by the labour of your hands, you are no greater than the Apostle. The Apostle did this. If you labour in order to refresh Christ’s poor, the poor cannot be exhausted, according to the testimony of Scripture: “God will render a reward for the labours of his saints.” [Note: [Col. 0743] Wis. 10.] It is holy, devout, and meritorious to feed the poor; but it is not good for you to become rich under the pretext of the poor.

The supreme merit of a true profession is voluntary poverty: whoever abandons this, as it seems to me, wholly departs from his own profession. [Col. 0744A] “It is good,” someone says, “to refresh the poor.” It is good, I reply, to refresh them—but in such a way that you do not fall away from your saving purpose. I counsel caution; I do not cut off mercy. Having despised riches, by means of which you might have supported many poor persons, you chose a place where you might be one poor person among many. I consider it great if, in the poverty you profess, you are not in want; greater if you are frequently in want. Certainly, if you abound in necessities, you are not poor; nor are you poor if you distribute to the poor from what is superfluous to you. Perhaps you are equal to the rich who put into the treasury from what overflowed for them, but you do not attain to the merit of the poor widow. If you can employ your riches for some excuse other than the support of the poor, I would gladly hear it. One thing [Col. 0744B] I know: the poorer a person is, the more copiously and abundantly he possesses that by which he can please the Most High. Do not, I beg you, speak of refreshing the poor: for when you speak of such matters, you place yourselves outside the flock of the poor. Brothers, you did not leave either possessions or the hope of riches in order to minister to the poor, but in order that you yourselves, as poor persons, might be ministered to.

These things I admonish and say, dearest brothers, so that you may persevere in the purpose of poverty. This is our crown: through it the kingdom of heaven is yours. Yet the Lord and ruler of the kingdom of heaven says: “Give what remains as alms,” [Note: [Col. 0743] Luke 11.] indicating that whatever necessity does not confine within the narrow limits of poverty is superfluous. I ask and counsel two things, most beloved [Col. 0744C] brothers. Be less anxious, I pray, in acquiring lands, because our portion is in the land of the living; and you will provide both for your soul and for your reputation. Strive rather to please God in your own poverty than in another’s, and you will acquire in the kingdom of heaven riches without end. May he deign to grant this to you who became poor for our sake, Jesus Christ, to whom be honour and glory for ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON LXIII. TO NUNS

We read that Moses [Note: [Col. 0743] Exod. 30.] made a bronze basin, so that those entering the tabernacle might wash; and he made it from the mirrors of the women who kept watch at the entrance of the tabernacle. I believe that these are the prudent virgins [Col. 0744D] who, with their lamps kindled, joyfully await the bridegroom’s coming through good works. [Note: [Col. 0743] Matt. 25.] For it is written: “The expectation of the righteous is joy.” [Note: [Col. 0743] Prov. 10.] From the mirrors of these women a washing-place is made for others, when from their manner of life an example of purity and sanctification is drawn.

Women who in the world expect from their flesh the fruit of posterity serve their flesh; while they make provision for the flesh in its desires, they lose eternal life for momentary pleasure. To cloistered women who have declared war upon their flesh an inestimable crown is due. For they strive not to be what they are, and courageously recover what they lost in their first [Col. 0745A] origin. For who can make clean one conceived from unclean seed? [Note: [Col. 0745] Job 14.] But these women, while ruling their flesh, are not only cleansed but conformed to angelic purity. Yet in the judgment of many, virginity is stronger than angelic purity, since a virgin is pure by virtue, while an angel is so only by nature. It is more than angelic to preserve these corruptible vessels in righteousness and sanctification; to experience in the flesh the glory of the heavenly Jerusalem, where “they neither marry nor are given in marriage.” [Note: [Col. 0745] Matt. 22.] For the exercise of chastity on earth is in some measure a fruit of heavenly eminence. From the virginal flower an unfading crown is woven, and an immortal bridegroom is acquired in heaven, while earthly marriages are [Col. 0745B] despised.

For these are those to whom the Apostle speaks, saying: “I have betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a chaste virgin to Christ.” [Note: [Col. 0745] 2 Cor. 11.] See how great was the effect of virginity. Virginity, penetrating beyond the clouds, beyond the heavens, beyond and above the angels, sought and found in the bosom of the Father the Word through whom all things were made: from there, through virginity, that author of salvation descended to us. We would still be walking in darkness had not the light of life shone upon us from the lamp of the blessed Virgin. Virginity is a balm by which corpses are preserved from decay. For it keeps the human senses and limbs from corruption; the rest, like beasts, rot in their own dung. Virgins alone, and the continent, preserve these vessels of corruption in incorruption.

But Wisdom says in [Col. 0745C] the person of virgins: “I am like uncut Lebanon, and my fragrance like unmixed balm, like a terebinth spreading branches of grace and salvation.” [Note: [Col. 0745] Ecclus. 24.] Chastity surpasses the eminence of all virtues, provided that it has charity as its companion; for without charity chastity is a lamp without oil. A lamp does not shine without the benefit of oil; neither does chastity please God without charity. Therefore Wisdom says: “O how beautiful is a chaste generation with charity!” [Note: [Col. 0745] Wis. 4.] But this is detestable—and may it be far from us!—if any stain of pride is mingled with chastity. For devout and lowly humility is far better than proud virginity. If chastity is considered in itself, it is more splendid than humility; yet humility is better in every respect. The former belongs to counsel, the latter to command. For the Apostle [Col. 0745D] says: “Concerning virginity I have no commandment, but I give counsel.” [Note: [Col. 0745] 1 Cor. 7.] And the Lord, speaking in the Gospel of virginity: “He who can receive it,” he says, “let him receive it.” [Note: [Col. 0745] Matt. 19.] But concerning humility: “Learn from me,” he says, “for I am meek and humble in heart”; [Note: [Col. 0745] Matt. 11.] and: “Unless you become like this little child, you shall not enter the kingdom of heaven.” [Note: [Col. 0745] Matt. 18.] Since the Holy Spirit rests only upon the humble and meek, you see that humility is more acceptable to God than virginity: without the former no one can be saved, whereas without the latter many can. The word of the blessed Virgin is: “He has regarded the humility [Col. 0746A] of his handmaid.” [Note: [Col. 0745] Luke 1.] She says “humility,” not “virginity,” indicating that not even her virginity would have pleased God without humility.

If, therefore, a virgin is proud, she must be reckoned among the foolish. For what is pride in virginity but poison in milk? Nothing can be given that is more abominable or that more completely blackens the lily of chastity than pride. Isaiah inveighs against the pride of virgins: “The daughters of Zion,” he says, “have been lifted up, and have walked with stretched-out necks and gone with beckoning eyes.” [Note: [Col. 0745] Isa. 3.] And the same chapter continues: “The Lord will make bare the crown of the head of the daughters of Zion, and uncover their hair.” [Note: [Col. 0745] Ibid.] And the Lord says in the same place: “For curled hair I will give baldness.” [Note: [Col. 0745] Ibid.] And what are you proud of, most wretched flesh, when you are both ash and dust? [Note: [Col. 0745] Gen. 18.] You are proud of your noble [Col. 0746B] lineage; know that nature did not make worldly nobility, but ambition invented it. Wisdom says: “No king had any other than a poor beginning at birth. There is one entrance into life for all human beings, and one exit.” [Note: [Col. 0745] Wis. 7.] Is a poor person born more foully than a rich person? David laments that he was conceived in sins; [Note: [Col. 0745] Ps. 50.] yet he too, though a king, begot his sons in sins. If you consider the power of rebirth, birth ennobles all alike, rich and poor; and adoptive nobility makes all one.

Virginity joined with noble character is a glorious title of nobility. As Wisdom says: “She glorifies her noble birth, having fellowship with God; because the Lord of all loved her.” [Note: [Col. 0745] Wis. 8.] According to the word of the Apostle: [Col. 0746C] “The prudent virgin considers the things of the Lord, that she may be holy in body and spirit.” [Note: [Col. 0745] 1 Cor.] In body, that she may be chaste; in spirit, that she may think humbly and not be exalted by praise of her chastity. For it is written: “Let him who boasts boast in the Lord; for it is not he who commends himself who is approved, but he whom God commends.” [Note: [Col. 0745] 2 Cor. 10.] It is most wretched to put the merit of one’s virginity or continence up for sale for empty glory. For when the bridegroom comes on the day of judgment, the oil of sinners—that is, the flattery of others—will not help the foolish virgins. Then the foolish virgins will say: “Our lamps are going out”; [Note: [Col. 0745] Matt. 23.] the prudent virgin will bear an inextinguishable light. As Wisdom says of her: “Her lamp shall not be extinguished in the night.” [Note: [Col. 0745] Prov. 31.]

You boast of your beauty: beauty is deceptive glory and vanity. [Col. 0746D] Job says of proud beauty: [Note: [Col. 0745] ch. 18.] “Let the firstborn of death devour her beauty”—that is, pride, which is the first deadly sin. What is vain beauty but beautiful rottenness? “I said to corruption: You are my father; and to the worms: My mother and my sister.” [Note: [Col. 0745] Job 17.] Indeed, beauty is deceptive unless it is a pleasing deception: while we are deceived by a false appearance, hidden ugliness lies beneath thin skin—things which, if they could be seen, would be horrible in appearance, and now are unworthy even of thought. “All flesh is grass, and all its glory is like the flower of grass.” [Note: [Col. 0745] Isa. 40.] As grass quickly withers, so [Col. 0747A] a beautiful face fades when fever comes on; but when death rushes upon it, it becomes foul through decay.

Virtue, however, which is the beauty of the soul, will bloom eternally before the Lord like a lily, like a palm, like a cedar of Lebanon in the house of the Lord. [Note: [Col. 0747] Ps. 91.] Therefore he who is “beautiful in form beyond the children of men,” [Note: [Col. 0747] Ps. 34.] the flower of the field and lily of the valleys, [Note: [Col. 0747] Song 2.] speaking of the righteous, says: “Upon him my sanctification shall blossom.” [Note: [Col. 0747] Ps. 131.] It is not your outward face but your inward conscience that will make you beautiful. “All the glory of the king’s daughter is within, in golden fringes.” [Note: [Col. 0747] Ps. 44.] For this is our glory: the testimony of our conscience. [Note: [Col. 0747] 2 Cor. 1.] This beauty, this adornment, the bridegroom desires in his bride. O virgin, “the king has desired your beauty”; [Note: [Col. 0747] Ps. 44.] therefore, if you wish every ugliness of soul to be taken away from you and to love Christ in humility, [Col. 0747B] you have become beautiful and sweet, and the Lord will present you to himself “without spot or wrinkle.” [Note: [Col. 0747] Eph. 5.] You will hear the voice of joy and exultation: “You are wholly beautiful, my friend, and there is no spot in you.” [Note: [Col. 0747] Song 4.] “Come, my chosen one; I shall set my throne in you, so that the Lord may rest in you and you may rest in him; so that the bridegroom may rejoice over the bride, and your God may rejoice over you.”

Set before your mind’s eyes as an example that nun who, because of the extreme lowliness and contemptibility of her body, was thought foolish and unclean by her sisters, but through a revelation of the Holy Spirit was found by the bishop of the province to be holier than the entire community and more acceptable to Christ. Certainly, if you are proud, if you desire the world, if you assent to your flesh, [Col. 0747C] if you murmur, if you envy your sisters, if you slander, if you cast off the yoke of obedience, you are no longer a daughter of Zion but a daughter of Babylon. You are excluded from the company of virgins who enter with the Lord, their lamps kindled, into the bridal joy. You may weep uselessly with Jephthah’s daughter over your virginity, for the Lord does not accept you as a sacrifice to himself. You will see tax collectors and prostitutes going before you into the kingdom of God; for you have turned your virginity, which was God’s most splendid gift, into reproach and insult. See where pride has hurled you: from heaven into filth, from paradise into hell, from angelic purity into the abyss of eternal horror and burning.

What, then, must you do? [Col. 0747D] Return to your heart; recall your days in the bitterness of your soul. Seize firmly the weapons of penitence, and do not postpone the fruit of repentance. For you do not know what the coming day will bring forth:

> One who is not ready today will be less fit tomorrow.  
> [Note: [Col. 0747] Ovid.]

Whoever does not act when able will not be able to do penance when willing. “It is dreadful to fall into the hands of the living God.” [Note: [Col. 0747] Heb. 10.] It is dreadful to come to the place of torments, where neither fire is extinguished nor worm dies, [Note: [Col. 0747] Isa. 66.] and where no end or measure is imposed upon stench, burning, or pain. May Christ Jesus, the bridegroom of holy [Col. 0748A] virgins, deign to deliver us from these things—to whom be honour and glory for ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON LXIV. TO THE SAME WOMEN

> “Hear, daughter, and see; incline your ear, and forget your people and your father’s house.”  
> [Note: [Col. 0747] Ps. 44.]

Dearest sisters, you are those to whom the Apostle Paul speaks, saying: “I have betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a chaste virgin to Christ.” [Note: [Col. 0747] 1 Cor. 11.] For according to the testimony of Truth: “Blessed are those who have made themselves eunuchs for the kingdom of heaven.” [Note: [Col. 0747] Matt. 19.] The Apostle says: “Though we walk in the flesh, we do not wage war according to the flesh”; [Note: [Col. 0747] 2 Cor. 10.] and, “He who gives his virgin in marriage does well, and he who does not give her does better.” [Note: [Col. 0747] 1 Cor. 7.] And, speaking of his own virginity: “I wish,” he says, “that all of you were as I myself am.” [Col. 0748B] [Note: [Col. 0747] Ibid.] And would that each might remain according to my counsel! “For concerning virgins I have no commandment, but I give counsel.” [Note: [Col. 0747] Ibid.]

Great is the prerogative of virgins. To virgins alone has God granted the singing of the new song, which no one else sings, and the following of the Lamb wherever he goes. [Note: [Col. 0747] Rev. 14.] It is written: “Grace upon grace is a modest and holy woman.” [Note: [Col. 0747] Ecclus. 26.] God is born into the world; in order to redeem the world, he chose a virgin as his mother. No mother but a virgin was fitting for God; nor was any son but God fitting for a virgin.

There are some among you whose virginal integrity has been violated, whether by a good marriage or by a slippery course and the ease of counsel. These follow the Lamb, but limp on one foot. They possess the foot [Col. 0748C] of humility, but not that of virginity. Therefore they do not follow the Lamb wherever he goes. For some are no longer virgins, and yet, although they have lost virginity, nevertheless seek to please the Lord through humility. They have broken the seal of virginity, but strive to repair what has been broken. For, just as they presented their members to serve impurity unto impurity and iniquity unto iniquity, so they present their members to serve righteousness unto sanctification. She who had been the slave of flesh, for the delights of the world and to Christ’s dishonour, has become the slave of the spirit, for contempt and hatred of the world and for love and glory of God. The daughter of Edom, the daughter of Babylon, made drunk with the Holy Spirit, has become daughter and bride, sister and beloved of the King Most High.

[Col. 0748D] And this is perhaps what Jeremiah says: “Rejoice and be glad, daughter of Edom; to you also shall come the intoxicating cup.” [Note: [Col. 0747] Lam. 4.] This is the cup of love, the love-potion by which she was intoxicated who entered the wine-cellar and said: “Tell my beloved that I languish with love.” [Note: [Col. 0747] Song 5.] Thus, through charity, she recompenses the loss of virginity and repairs by repentance the damage of corrupted flesh. With Rachel she hides her father’s idols beneath dung, and with Jacob the fragments of Laban’s idols beneath the terebinth; while through the humility of penitence and remembrance of the Lord’s Passion she turns away her iniquities from the face of the supreme exactor. [Col. 0749A]

Both widows and virgins have confidence in Christ’s promise, for God is no respecter of persons. [Note: [Col. 0749] Acts 10.] A humble virgin is the companion of angels. But if she has experienced womanly things, then either she sits with Mary at Jesus’ feet or, with Martha, occupies herself in devout works. [Note: [Col. 0749] Luke 10.] The Prophet urges both virgin and defiled woman to perseverance in holiness when he says: “Hear, daughter, and see; incline your ear,” and so forth.

You have gone forth from this wicked world, you have gone out of Egypt, and have come into this wilderness to sacrifice to the Lord your God. Do not return to Egypt’s garlic and melons, to bloody foods; let heavenly manna and the bread of angels suffice you. For death is in Egypt’s pot. With the Samaritan woman you left the water-jar of worldly desire; you have destroyed both spiritual Jerichos. [Col. 0749B] He who rebuilds Jericho incurs Joshua’s curse. [Note: [Col. 0749] ch. 6.] I know that Egypt’s music often hisses to you, and that the enemy’s hidden temptation invites you to return to the world. Draw yourself back from the people whom you left and from the house of your Amorite father.

“Hear, daughter, and see; incline your ear, and forget your people and your father’s house.” What have you to do with your kin? Are you not dead both to your parents and planted together in the likeness of Christ’s death? But you say: “One of my close relatives is sick or dying; I must go out to him.” Hear, daughter, and see: do not go out. “Let the dead bury their dead.” [Note: [Col. 0749] Matt. 8.] See that you are not buried in [Col. 0749C] hell for their sake. We frequently read in the book of experience that attachment to kindred has drawn many into weakness. Whenever you leave the cloister, you stake your soul, placing it, as it were, under a throw of the dice; and that which you expose to certain danger is greater than every treasure. Therefore feel with the Prophet and say: “My soul is always in my hands.” [Note: [Col. 0749] Ps. 118.]

I beg you, have no commerce with secular persons: for “he who touches pitch will be defiled by it,” [Note: [Col. 0749] Ecclus. 13.] and “evil conversations corrupt good morals.” [Note: [Col. 0749] 1 Cor. 15.] Fire in the bosom, a serpent in the lap, and a mouse in the purse ill reward their hosts. Do not be among those of whom it is written: “They mingled among the nations and learned their works.” [Note: [Col. 0749] Ps. 101.] Do not, daughter, go out in public; for the world is full of snares, full of dangers, [Col. 0749D] full of deaths.

You have been betrothed to Christ. If flesh and blood, if love of parents, or anything else reveals or suggests something to you, look to Christ and say: “I will not depart from the counsel of the righteous, from the congregation of the saints.” The Prophet teaches you and says: “I shall confess to you, O Lord, with my whole heart, in the counsel of the righteous and in the congregation.” [Note: [Col. 0749] Ps. 110.] If anyone of your kindred calls you, or sends for you, it is Satan’s temptation. Do not look back with Lot’s wife. [Note: [Col. 0749] Gen. 19.] The wild cows that carried the ark of the Lord to Beth-shemesh did not turn their necks [Col. 0750A] back toward their calves; [Note: [Col. 0749] 1 Sam. 6.] nor should you turn neck or feet back toward your blood relatives. You have given the hand of obedience and placed its yoke upon your head. Hear Wisdom, which says: “Put your foot into her fetters, and do not be weary of her bonds.” [Note: [Col. 0749] Ecclus. 6.]

If you leave the cloister, you transgress. Dinah, Jacob’s daughter, went out to see the entertainments of foreigners, and was violated by Shechem, son of Hamor. [Note: [Col. 0749] Gen. 34.] For chastity is not where the world is; therefore there is no chastity outside the cloister. Sarah, daughter of Raguel and wife of the younger Tobias, said: “You know, Lord, that I have never mingled with those at play, nor with women who walk in frivolity.” [Note: [Col. 0749] Tob. 3.] Jeremiah too says: “I did not sit in the assembly of those at play; I sat alone because you filled me with bitterness.” [Note: [Col. 0749] Jer. 15.] Let Sarah be your example; [Col. 0750B] and Jacob also, who remained at home and inherited the blessing. [Note: [Col. 0749] Gen. 27.] Esau, however, wandering outside, lost his birthright along with his father’s blessing.

The Lord is near to render to each person according to his works. [Note: [Col. 0749] Rev. 22.] The Queen of virgins will go before; her companions shall be brought, and with her shall be led into the king’s temple. [Note: [Col. 0749] Ps. 44.] Then the heavenly Jerusalem will be like a bride adorned for her husband. Then the bridegroom will rejoice over the bride and say: “Come, my chosen one, and I will set my throne in you, so that I may sit and rest in you, and you may be my seat for age upon age.” [Note: [Col. 0749] Ibid.] On that day the glorious things spoken of you will appear, when “the dwelling-place of all who rejoice shall be in you”; [Note: [Col. 0749] Ps. 86.] when the blessed Virgin with her virginity shall enter into the delights of everlasting brightness and joy, [Col. 0750C] Sarah with married women, Anna with widows, and Magdalene with her penitents. Then will come to pass what God promised through Isaiah: “Behold, I create Jerusalem rejoicing, and her people joy; and I shall rejoice in Jerusalem and be glad with my people; and there shall no longer be heard in her the sound of crying and weeping; and month shall follow month, and Sabbath Sabbath.” [Note: [Col. 0749] Isa. 65.] There we shall be satisfied with the good things of the Lord’s house and be given drink from the torrent of his delight. [Note: [Col. 0749] Ps. 35.] There we shall see the Son in the Father, the Father in the Son, and the Holy Spirit in both: this is eternal life and consummate glory. May he deign to grant it to us, he who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit through all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON LXV. TO THE PEOPLE

[Col. 0750D]

On two verses of Psalm 93: “Who will rise up for me against evildoers, or who will stand with me against workers of iniquity?” and: “Unless the Lord had helped me,” etc.

You ask me, dearest brother, to communicate to you in writing a sermon delivered to the people, and to try to render into Latin speech what I set before laypeople rather crudely and insipidly, as their capacity required. You hope, no doubt, that the subject may acquire brilliance not only through elegance of expression but through the fluency [Col. 0751A] of Latin diction, because, by a certain prerogative of this idiom, words add very great honour and force to thoughts, and discourse thus runs more conveniently to its end. But if you think the subject of any importance, why do you ask me to pursue it rather than excuse, against the insistence of your request, either the inextricable cares in which I am wholly entangled or my own foolishness?

Yet you do not so much obtain this from me, importunate as you are, as extort it. You will repay the favour if you either keep this little work to yourself or, after reading it once and then setting it aside, destroy it by fire or tear and shred it with the smallest cutting. Nor should you wonder if the brevity of daily speech is exceeded, because the dignity of Latin eloquence itself demands that the thoughts which I passed over in the compactness of the vernacular should be enriched somewhat with fuller grace. This, then, was the beginning of that discourse: “Who will rise up,” and so forth, as above.

“Unless the Lord had helped me, my soul would almost have dwelt in hell.” These are the words of the Psalmist, my brothers, considering, in the person of each one of us, the frailty of our condition, the cunning of the enemy who drives us on, and finally the power of resistance. “Who,” he says, “will rise up for me?” For me, I say: a mortal, sinful, and frail person, against evildoers—that is, the threefold enemy, flesh, world, and devil. Because, as though they did not suffice to drive us on by strength, they add cunning as well in order to overthrow us. What then shall I, a wretched human being, do—driven by the enemy’s strength, [Col. 0751C] and overthrown by cunning also, so that I fall—unless the Lord receives me, unless he rises against evildoers, unless he takes hold of weapons and shield and rises to help me? [Note: [Col. 0751] Ps. 34.]

This righteous man meditated by night with his heart; he exercised himself and searched his spirit. He exercised himself, I say, in the law of his God, in fear of his Judge, and in love of his Deliverer. This exercise is not of little use, because it leads to godliness, which is profitable for all things. Hence he says: “I exercised myself,” and through exercise he saw: “I searched my spirit.” [Note: [Col. 0751] Ps. 76.] For in what better order can the spirit be cleansed than through saving exercise: once we have grasped what the law commands, and also considered how greatly our life contradicts the law—which produces fear of the Judge—we finally breathe again in love [Col. 0751D] of the Deliverer?

We must therefore consider more carefully what the law says: “Consult the mouth of the Lord,” [Note: [Col. 0751] Josh. 9.] that is, investigate Holy Scripture. For this was why the children of Israel sinned: they did not consult the mouth of the Lord. Hence it is commanded in Deuteronomy: “Let not this book of the law depart from your heart or from your mouth, so that you may direct your way and understand all that you do.” [Note: [Col. 0751] Josh. 7.] Next, we must fit the course of our lives to the divine commands and frequently refresh past acts in tenacious memory, so that either the testimony of conscience may produce glory, or the blush of saving shame may arise—of which it is said: “Fill [Col. 0752A] their faces with dishonour, and they shall seek your name, O Lord.” [Note: [Col. 0751] Ps. 82.] Thus, according to Solomon’s wisdom, our life will be as though hanging before us, [Note: [Col. 0751] Deut. 28.] so that from good things may come thanksgiving, or from evil things the salutary lament of penitence.

When, then, our life is applied to the Scriptures, who among us, I ask, fulfils even one of the Law’s commandments—of which not one iota will pass away without being fulfilled? [Note: [Col. 0751] Matt. 5.] This application therefore instils fear of the Judge; but lest a person be cast down beyond measure and consequently fall through sloth into the pit of despair, from this useful fear he breathes again in the mercy of the loving Father, in love of the Deliverer, who, when angry, is accustomed to remember mercy.

Thus charity is indeed introduced through fear, and godliness through exercise. But for us worldly people, who are not only in the world but are of the world, who are established amid a crooked and perverse nation, crooked and perverse ourselves, who are frequently made drunk to nausea from Babylon’s cup—for us, I say, I believe that exercise which instils fear of the Judge to be exceedingly useful and fruitful: the Judge who will judge the world by fire; by which the saints will judge the nations; by which the wretched daughter of Babylon will receive her requital, [Note: [Col. 0751] Ps. 136.] that is, a miserable requital, an eternal requital.

O happy souls of the saints, who, still placed in the flesh, live outside the flesh and exhibit an angelic life in human form! O truly happy ones, to whom it is granted to gather the sweetest [Col. 0752C] fruits of contemplation; to whom, in this great and wide sea, a kind of harbour of tranquillity has been given; whom neither a wind rushing upon them from the opposite quarter shakes with fear nor the commotion of the stormy sea can unsettle! O blessed three and four times over, before whose eyes there is always love of the Deliverer, love of father and homeland, while fear of the Judge and hell are viewed as if from a most distant region! These indeed, forgetting what lies behind, stretch themselves toward what is before. They now not only disdain to fear but do not know how to fear; and, once the introductory fear of charity has been expelled, they are now in a sense unable not to love, since once they have sweetly burned with love.

Let them indeed be anointed with the Samaritan’s oil; let us use the wine of compunction. Let them draw waters with joy from the fountains of the Saviour [Note: [Col. 0751] Isa. 12.] and [Col. 0752D] be made drunk from the abundance of his house; [Note: [Col. 0751] Ps. 35.] let them drink the water of saving wisdom. Let us temper our drink with weeping, be fed with the bread of tears, and receive in measure the drink which the Lord gives in tears. [Note: [Col. 0751] Ps. 79.] Let them always have a feast before the Father, who is merciful and gentle, the giver of gifts with blessings; let us more often turn our eyes to the Judge, who is severe and jealous, the strict examiner not only of deeds but of every idle word. No way is readier for us to reach their blessed state; no entrance more fitting; no progress more useful. This way is arduous at its entrance, more tolerable in its progress, more fruitful at its end. This is the first way to the homeland: for “the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom.” [Note: [Col. 0753] Ps. 110; Ecclus. 1.]

The first path is steep, and it requires sure moderation—sure indeed, lest we turn to the right by presuming too much upon the sweetness of mercy, or to the left by despairing of mercy. Fear is a narrow bridge; unless you cross it with the greatest diligence and caution, you cannot reach the pleasant places of contemplation. By this narrow bridge entrance is made into the breadth of charity; while crossing this bridge, beware equally of the precipice on both the right and the left. Therefore, to return to what we began: we especially who are of this world, in whom the world also loves what is its own, whenever we return to our heart, let fear meet us first—fear, I say, of the Judge; fear of that dreadful examination, in which each will receive according to what he has done in the body [Note: [Col. 0753] 1 Cor. 5.]; or in which that great householder who had gone abroad will settle accounts with his servants [Note: [Col. 0753] Matt. 21]. That is, when all the books shall be opened, and each person shall be his own counsellor, advocate, and judge; for all the books shall be opened to all.

Now I observe three books in the judgment: the book of the way, the book of conscience, and the book of life. By the book of the way I mean the book given on the way and for the way; and this is a threefold book: namely, that of Mosaic instruction, prophetic preaching, and Gospel preaching. But who does not know that the book of conscience is the knowledge of good works unto glory, or of evil works unto shame and disgrace? [Col. 0753C] The book of life is the book of eternal predestination. Two of these books are opened to us in particular; the third is sealed and closed universally.

The book of legal instruction has now been opened to us by the Lamb who was slain, who alone was found worthy to open the book and loose its seals. For the Lion of the tribe of Judah, who conquered [Note: [Col. 0753] Rev. 5], opened for us the book of the law, formerly closed both to the lettered Jew and to the unlettered philosopher—the key of David, who opens and no one shuts [Note: [Col. 0753] Rev. 3]. This book was opened when the Lord made his word brief upon the earth, and enclosed and fulfilled all things in one word, namely in his Christ, who is the gloss and exposition of the whole Old Testament.

Hence, in the Passion the rocks were split and the veil of the Temple from top to bottom; then the tombs were opened, and many letters of the saints who had slept in the tomb rose again [Note: [Col. 0753] Matt. 27]. Then the heart of God became like melting wax [Note: [Col. 0753] Ps. 21]; then the declaration of the Lord’s words illuminated the dark water in the clouds of the air and gave understanding to little ones [Note: [Col. 0753] Ps. 118]. Thus Philip, running up, joins the chariot and says, “Do you think that you understand what you are reading?” [Note: [Col. 0753] Acts 8]. And, mounting the chariot, he shows that the book closed in the letter is opened to one who reads but does not understand; and, naming Christ, [Col. 0754A] he makes Gospel from prophecy: “He was offered, because he willed it,” etc. [Note: [Col. 0753] Isa. 53].

Therefore the book of the way is also open to us in the present, as regards its two divisions; its third division, consisting of the New Testament, is open to us by faith, and will be opened in the future by sight. Hence Jerome says that a veil has been placed in part over the apostles and evangelists; but at the judgment the eyes of the blind shall be opened and the ears of the deaf shall be unsealed [Note: [Col. 0753] Isa. 35], and all flesh shall see that the mouth of the Lord has spoken [Note: [Col. 0753] Isa. 40]. Thus the book of the way will then be wholly open.

The book of conscience too is now closed; hence: “The heart of man is deep and inscrutable; and who shall know it?” [Note: [Col. 0753] Jer. 17]. And elsewhere: “For who among men knows the things of a man except the spirit of the man which is in him?” [Note: [Col. 0753] 1 Cor. 2]. [Col. 0754B] That book, I say, shall then be opened, when the hidden things of our heart shall be made manifest. Then a man shall appear naked, bearing the bundle of his works, when it shall be said: “Behold the man, and his works with him.” The Lord will also open the book of life in the judgment, when he shall place the sheep on the right and the goats on the left [Note: [Col. 0753] Matt. 25]; when the angels shall go forth and separate the wicked from the midst of the righteous [Note: [Col. 0753] Matt. 13]; when all who have been foreordained to eternal life shall be brought into glory [Note: [Col. 0753] Acts 13]; and then everyone found written in the book of life shall be saved [Note: [Col. 0753] Rev. 20].

Perhaps someone will add the book of experience, in which those who read negligently in the book of life, who were unwilling to understand in order to do good [Note: [Col. 0753] Ps. 35], shall read most bitter histories. Then their thorns shall understand the buckthorn [Note: [Col. 0753] Ps. 57]; and those who refused to become skilled in punishment will become wise in punishment. It would therefore be very fruitful and useful for us to place before our eyes the manner and form of that judgment—indeed, to hold daily in our mind as it were a new judgment—and to consider the Lord reproving us, setting [our sins] before our face, and judging us from our works. For, as the Apostle says: “If we judged ourselves, we should certainly not be judged” [Note: [Col. 0753] 1 Cor. 11].

Would that you might bear with a little of my folly [Note: [Col. 0753] 2 Cor. 11], and, patiently hearing the form of this daily judgment which I conceive, prudently turn what you have heard to the forming of your conduct and to the fear of God. That householder could indeed settle accounts with us daily; and, just as on the last day he will judge the course of our whole life, so he could daily discuss our daily actions with us and say: “What you did or did not do today to one of the least of mine, you did or did not do to me” [Note: [Col. 0753] Matt. 25]. Let us therefore set the Lord as the judge seated, the devil as accuser, some man—even one of ourselves—as defendant; and let us reduce these to the customary form of judgment [lacuna].

Nor should anyone wonder that I have said the devil stands before God in order to accuse a man, since it is plainly read in Job [Note: [Col. 0753] ch. 1]: “On a certain day, when they stood by,” etc., [Col. 0755A] “Satan too was present among them.” That he accused holy Job is shown not only by the following text, but also by Job’s manifold affliction. In the Apocalypse [Note: [Col. 0755] ch. 12] he is also called the accuser of the brethren. Now, in the time of grace, he strives to accuse with greater cunning, in proportion as a man more cautiously sets against his fiery darts the pledge of his faith for his own defense and the fortifications of the Church’s sacraments.

For before the time of grace, when through the fault of the first parent man had been sold as a slave to the devil, he did not endure such cunning assaults by the tempter; but he was like a horse and mule, which have no understanding [Note: [Col. 0755] Ps. 31]. Thus there was not such savage violence in raging against men, since no power of resistance was granted them. [Col. 0755B] But when Christ, the stronger one, came upon him, entered the house of the strong devil, and carried off his goods [Note: [Col. 0755] Matt. 12], the devil began more sharply to pursue those who resisted more eagerly; and he set forth snares of more cunning deceit, the more ways of human deliverance he saw. Then, according to blessed Job [Note: [Col. 0755] ch. 20], he began to crave choice foods; hence he even sought power to sift the apostles.

But now let us return to what we began. Employing, in some fashion, the words of accusers before the householder seated as judge, let us endeavor to defame the man set in the midst, as though he had squandered that householder’s goods.

“This man stands here, Lord: wholly man, wholly earth, wholly flesh. His faults are manifest; his offenses against your majesty are infinite. It is no slight guilt of his that obtains pardon, but the persistence of monstrous sins provokes wrath and vengeance. If henceforth you persist in sparing one who is stubborn; if you still wait for one so obstinate and ungrateful, though repentance has been offered and rejected so often, you are no longer performing the office of a judge, but that of one negligent and lax. Remember, I pray, your righteous judgments, and repay those who hate you. Your mercy, Lord, has nothing to object if justice now punishes one whom the ruin wrought by his deeds and their unbroken succession plainly declare wholly incorrigible.

“If at last you now render to him according to the works of his hands, if you repay him according to the wickedness of his devices [Note: [Col. 0755] Ps. 27], you will nevertheless not be said to have forgotten your mercy [Note: [Col. 0755] Ps. 97]; for, even against my will, you will punish one condemned far short of what his deserts require. Here mercy will triumph over judgment, while penal affliction rages far short of the measure demanded by his merits.

“But lest I seem to adhere only to general methods and lay no particular accusation against him—passing over the rest, which exceed both measure and number—I attack him especially on the charge of three crimes, and confidently press against him the accusation of a threefold transgression. First, I plainly declare him a liar and perjurer; second, a double and perverse traitor; third, I lay upon him the crime and vice of a robber. In all these matters the sufficient answer is evident, and the presentation of manifest proof is ready at hand. [Col. 0756A]

“For who would deny that he is a liar and perjurer, when, by drawing it up with me, he cancelled the bond of sin which he had publicly made and promised under the attestation of lawful witnesses; and when he broke the baptismal covenant, so solemnly made and approved by so many witnesses, through violation of his pledged faith? There, good Judge, deceit was being practiced against you, when this deceitful promise, veiled in a cloud of words, obtained remission of original sin. Yet, unless I am mistaken, God understands a promise or oath according to the intention of him to whom it is made or sworn. Did you intend, good Judge, that deceit was being practiced against you there—and did you keep silent? Or did you not intend it? Were you deceived—you to whom every heart lies open, every will speaks, and from whom no secret is hidden?

“But if you perceived the deceit, why did you grant remission? Or why, at least, did you not remit in deceit, so that art might deceive art, and the false promisor and discovered deceiver might fall into the pit which he had made [Note: [Col. 0755] Ps. 7]? Yet, lest I seem to rebuke your mercy too importunately when I demand judgment—though mercy, whether I wish it or not, will be the companion of judgment—suppose you were merciful or lenient at baptism and perhaps excused the promisor’s age: who will answer me concerning the second and third promise, or indeed those repeatedly renewed many times? I am not bringing the judge to court with the defendant; rather, I offer the defendant to the judge to be judged—or indeed, if justice is now done, as already judged.

“You established, Lord, a second plank after shipwreck, restoration after a fall, repentance after a lapse. I pass over in silence [Col. 0756C] the fact that this institution was made to my disadvantage; and because I cannot destroy it, let it stand—let it be valid, I endure it.

“This defendant renounced Satan and all his works and all his pomps in baptism; and, forgetful of his promise, as quickly as he could he gave himself back to the one he had renounced, entangled himself in his works, and mingled himself with his pomps. But, having recognized what he had done, he changed his resolve for the better. Let it be so: he returned to his heart, converted so as to hate his own people and his father’s house. Let it be so: the wicked man forsook his way and the man of iniquity his thoughts, returned to the Lord, and the Lord had mercy upon him [Note: [Col. 0755] Isa. 55]. Let it be so, provided that this too is equally established: he again changed his resolve for the worse, and the last state of that man became worse than the first [Note: [Col. 0755] Matt. 12]. I shall show this briefly.

[Col. 0756D] “Remember, I pray, that before your vicar, before your Christ—that is, before your priest—he renewed the baptismal covenant and bound himself by the obligation of a renewed promise. Certainly he cannot there excuse his age, plead compulsion, or allege incapacity. He came before your priest as an adult and capable of discernment; he promised voluntarily and not under compulsion, and fearlessly took upon himself of his own accord a burden not unequal to his shoulders. What more need be said? In one and the same moment he departed from the priest and recoiled from his purpose. He deceived the priest, he deceived you, he deceived himself. He cast aside the easy yoke and the light burden; and, under the yoke of sin, embraced again his former slavery. He cast aside the garment of innocence and put on a garment clotted with blood. He cast aside the short cloak that cannot cover both, and again seized the cloak which he had left with the Egyptian mistress. To state it more briefly: the more freely he returned to sins already committed and undertook sins not yet attempted, the more guilty he had been of greater crimes before confession, so that he might draw a long rope, and sin like a cart-rope.

“Therefore, as though the bundle of former sins were insufficient for condemnation, he added the transgression of promise and of faith. Nor did he come deceitfully to the priest only once; rather, following the custom of confession at the appointed time rather than purity of conscience, once each year he added this to his preceding sins: that in the sight of your Christ he lied to you and deceitfully carried away from the priest a shadowy remission. If he has assumed holy orders, with which a promise of continence is joined, and has behaved in holy orders so disorderly that the latter error was worse than the former [Note: [Col. 0757] Matt. 27], time would fail me if I were to enumerate the violations of promises which he made to you and the frustrations of vows.

“I say nothing of the lies with which his daily speech has always been sprinkled. I say nothing of his frequent, incidental oaths and perjuries, by which he repeatedly cast up against you the frailty assumed on his behalf; by which he shamefully reproached you with death, the cross, the Passion, and the other humiliations of your humanity. Indeed, in some sense surpassing the raging cruelty of the Jews, he ground your mouth to pieces—indeed, counted your bones and in some fashion tore you apart into the smallest bones. [Col. 0757C] If you judge these things light, Lord, you greatly derogate from the benefit of assumed humanity; nor do you truly acknowledge as yours those limbs or wounds which you so easily endure to be torn by such great insults. Therefore either avenge the injuries of your limbs and the insults to your wounds, or concede that you were a phantom, as your disciples thought.

“Therefore, good Judge, if the beginning of your words is truth [Note: [Col. 0757] Ps. 118]—indeed, if you yourself are truth—since the word of truth has utterly been taken from this defendant’s mouth [Note: [Col. 0757] ibid.], judge in truth, I pray, and destroy for truth’s sake the soul whose mouth has lied so often; exclude the perjurer from the eyes of truth. I believe enough has been argued concerning the first charge, especially before you, to whom neither verbal subtleties nor skill in rhetorical training establishes the credibility of what is said; rather, judgment proceeds from your countenance—that is, from your knowledge.

“What has been said could therefore suffice for the purpose; but, so that the discourse may follow its enumeration, let him be shown plainly to be both traitor and robber. First I demonstrate plainly that he is a traitor. Do you grant, good Judge, that he is a traitor who eats your bread and magnifies treachery against you? [Note: [Col. 0757] Ps. 40].
