Is not the hand of him who betrays you with you at table, [Col. 0758A] when man eats the bread of angels [Note: [Col. 0757] Ps. 77], the bread which came down from heaven and gives life to the world [Note: [Col. 0757] John 6]? Yet nonetheless he has fellowship with your enemies, walks in the counsel of the ungodly, stands in the way of sinners, and—what is more wicked, indeed most wicked—glories in sitting in the seat of pestilence [Note: [Col. 0757] Ps. 1].

“Either concede that such a man is a traitor, or wholly reject your Augustine, who says plainly that a person sins as greatly by betraying Christ through sinful members as does one who betrayed him to the Jewish crucifiers. In your disciple, the betrayal displeased you—a betrayal punished not only by a temporal noose but expiated without remedy by eternal fire. Why then does vengeance and retribution cease in the like case? Why is it delayed, when in this successor of Judas the crime of a traitor appears?

“You communicated to him, Lord, from your table, from your holy altar, not just any bread but the bread of angels; not just any drink but your precious blood. You fed him with true food and gave him true drink. Hence you said: ‘My flesh is truly food, and my blood is truly drink’ [Note: [Col. 0757] John 6]. He sat at the great table, and though he ought to prepare similar things, he instead resolved to offer you gall and vinegar, crucifying the Son of God again in himself and holding him up to contempt [Note: [Col. 0757] Heb. 6].

“What if you appointed him as a faithful and prudent servant over your household, that he might give them their measure of wheat in due season? [Note: [Col. 0757] Matt. 24]. What if you placed him over the very angels in making the bread of angels, granting him the consecration of the Lord’s body and [Col. 0758C] blood, to which the purity of angelic nature does not attain? Angels behold that bread, at which they rejoice with trembling, but do not dare to make it; for what you granted sinful human beings was not granted to the most pure angels. You found perversity in your angels [Note: [Col. 0757] Job 4], yet overlook the sins of men. You seem to honor and love more the lost human being, redeemed with a certain violence and difficulty, than your angel, never lost and therefore never to be redeemed.

“You cause yourself to be called ‘fairer in form than the sons of men’ [Note: [Col. 0757] Ps. 44], as though surpassing men were glorious to you—though by the brightness of your vision you nourish and sustain the purity of angels. Truly your delights are with the children of men [Note: [Col. 0757] Prov. 8], to whom you assigned not only angelic guardianship but also undertook to exalt human nature above angels.

“Thus Paul, as though placed outside humanity, dares, by glorying over angels, to prefer himself to them as though their judge: ‘Do you not know,’ he says, ‘that we shall judge angels?’ [Note: [Col. 0757] 1 Cor. 6]. But I leave these things to you, good Judge, and am silent. Let your eyes see whether it is just for human nature to ascend in order to judge angels, or whether it is rather worthy to descend, judged together with us. Humble your angels as much as you please; bow your heavens however greatly you wish; raise and exalt man. Let the prodigal son find favor in his father’s sight, and let the tenth drachma, lost and found, surpass the nine drachmas; let the hundredth sheep, with the ninety-nine left in the wilderness, be dearer [Note: [Col. 0759] Luke 15]. I endure it—behold, I am silent. I can grieve; I can envy; I cannot hinder it. Yet I would have you so love man that you hate the traitor. I do not wish you to persecute nature, but vice. Let human nature retain its titles; let it retain the prerogative of its dignity, provided only that guilt receives what it has deserved, that guilt does not go unpunished, and that man, however much he may glory in the dignity of his state, may glory in punishment. Receive the man, if you please, but despise the traitor.

“If you overlook the betrayal of this liar and perjurer, and according to your custom seek occasions to spare him, you now wrong your justice, which demands vengeance from him even if I say nothing. [Col. 0759B] For the betrayal that I allege is evident: this table-companion of yours joined himself to your enemies; he opened to them when they knocked, went out to meet them when they entered, welcomed them gladly, and served them familiarly in hospitality with whatever diligence and solicitude he could. This new Judas abandoned the counsel of peace and took counsel with the wicked.

“Are not pride, covetousness, gluttony, lust, and such things what you hate, Lord? Consider briefly, if you please, how much familiarity he showed them and how devotedly he gave himself to their service. Who placed pride, celestial by origin, more highly in the citadel of his heart? Who bestowed more diligent care upon serving Mammon? Who was more enticed by the greedy excess of gluttony? Who was more stained by the filth of lust? Whom, I ask, did covetousness more inflame, avarice spur, pride inflate, ambition suspend, wantonness effeminate, lust defile? It is easy to show that he opened to the devil and closed to Christ.

“For he who receives pride excludes not only humility but also Christ, the teacher of humility, who says: ‘Learn from me, because I am meek and humble of heart’ [Note: [Col. 0759] Matt. 11]. He who introduces covetousness not only banishes generosity, but also the giver of gifts, who, to establish the liberality of his generosity, forbids thought for the morrow. He who is skilled in gluttony not only despises the saving fast, but also shuts out him who, after fasting forty days, afterward hungered [Col. 0759D] [Note: [Col. 0759] Matt. 4]. He who lodges lust in his chamber not only expels holiness, without which no one shall see the Lord [Note: [Col. 0759] Heb. 12], but also at the same time repels him who consecrated the glory of virginity in his mother and began to fill heaven through virginity’s fruitfulness.

“At other times my leech bears daughters for me; but I have especially selected the aforesaid four, who more often bring me the victories I desire and more frequently yield greater gain. Therefore, that we may first deal with the firstborn—pride—which brought me triumph over this man, I shall explain briefly. First, whenever he performed a work of the kind called good—for example, [Col. 0760A] if he gave alms, fasted, or prayed; if, by meditating on the law of the Lord, he was able to write something which he believed worthy of remembrance; or if he acted prudently in some matter—pride, which desires to be the companion of virtues, knocked, entered, reclined at table, and finally took possession of the entire work for itself.

“It knocked through consideration of the deed; entered through approval; reclined through a certain exalting and admiration of the deed; took possession through the praise sought from human favor and glory. It knocked, I say, as prudent and discerning; entered caressingly and deceitfully; reclined lofty and glorious; took possession rewarded with human praises. Thus it knocked cautiously, entered secretly, reclined openly, and took possession securely.

“Therefore, though he ought to have been ambidextrous with Ehud [Aioth], he became with the devil ‘ambisinister’: he made the right hand into the left, when he corrupted a good work by the infection of left-handed formation. Thus he inclined his right hand to the left—indeed, so confused left and right—that, by doing good, he refused to be crucified with you, and preferred to be crucified among those on the left by giving the good deed itself a sinister formation. But if you judge a man by his works, he will be on the left in judgment who was crucified on the left in the world.

“His right hand was full of gifts [Note: [Col. 0759] Ps. 25], and the devil stood at his right hand [Note: [Col. 0759] Ps. 108], while even the good that he did he did for the reward of human praise. Thus, by yielding himself from the right side to the left, he rendered useless to himself the water coming out of the Temple from the right side; and he did not allow the streams of the Lord’s blood flowing from the right side, because with the Lord there is abundant redemption, to benefit him. [Col. 0760C]

“Nor did victorious pride merely begrudge goodness to his good works; it also arranged that his evils themselves should be done proudly and with the bearing of one who despises. He dared to glory, mighty in wickedness, in iniquity [Note: [Col. 0759] Ps. 51]. He sinned not by fleeing beneath God and before his face, but by resisting the Lord and confronting him, daring to provoke the vengeance of the Lord’s wrath. For nothing is read to displease God so much as a raised neck after sin. Therefore, Lord, break the sinner’s neck; crush the obstinacy of one who resists you to your face, who has risen from offending you into pride, and from contempt of your commandments—indeed, of yourself—into the haughtiness and exaltation of his eyes.

“For his heart exulted as though he had won a victory over you; and, with all fear of you removed, he now seemed to ignore, or not to know, that he who sleeps should add something whereby he may rise [Note: [Col. 0759] Ps. 40]. Thus pride infected his good things and completed his evil things: it took seasoning from the good and supplied completion to the evil. Things that seemed divine it made human; things belonging to human frailty it rendered diabolical. For he expected from man the recompense of good deeds, and in his evil deeds displayed in man an example of diabolical exaltation. Thus pride, gloriously crowned, returned to me from a double battle, as has been said, having gained triumph over the enemy.

“Through pride, therefore, he opened to the devil and closed to Christ. Covetousness, her mistress, did the same in him, as is shown both by the condition of poverty and by the luxury of riches. [Col. 0761A] For if poverty was given him by God as a pious gift, he was unwilling to follow Christ poor, but chose the rich world. Nor did he choose the second harbor of the golden mean, but hoped in uncertain riches and placed his hope in gold, in which men trust. Therefore condemned covetousness knocked, entered, reclined at table, and took possession at the little door of the poor man’s heart.

“It knocked by setting out the glory of riches; entered by promising it; reclined by establishing hope in it; took possession by making it the end of blessedness. It knocked by displaying the things to be promised; entered by promising what it displayed; reclined by fixing hope in the promises; took possession by establishing the end in what was hoped for. It knocked when it showed all the kingdoms of the world; entered as though saying, ‘All these things will I give you if, falling down, you worship me’ [Note: [Col. 0761] Matt. 4]; reclined when it taught him to hope in money-treasures; took possession when, excluding the other master, it caused him, deliberately, willingly, and with settled resolve, to serve Mammon alone.

“Thus men went into the bowels of the earth; riches were sought by right and wrong; treasures wishing to lie hidden were dragged out against their will; and, once dragged out, were thrust again into other darknesses, lest gracious generosity scatter what wicked covetousness had gathered. Thus the itching scab of thirsty covetousness defiled the blessed condition of poverty, turned medicine into disease, and through the various windings of desires distorted the shortcuts granted for the homeland. [Col. 0761C]

“But what shall I say of the state of the rich man, whom slavery to idols has wholly claimed for itself, and who necessarily either commits injustice or is heir to one who does? For every rich man is either unjust or the heir of an unjust man. Since ingenious covetousness enters the poor man little by little, it multiplies its continuing strength from the increase of riches; for the more the miser acquires, the more he learns to desire greater things:

> Love of money increases in proportion as money itself increases.  
> [Note: [Col. 0761] Juvenal, *Satires* 14.139.]

As in the sickness of the dropsical man:

As the more water they drink, the more they thirst for water. [Note: [Col. 0761] Ovid, *Fasti*, book I, v. 215.] Thus greed, which flatters the poor while enticing them, tortures and wrings out those pursuing riches; but once a person has become rich, it wholly claims and swallows him up. This is what blinds the eyes of the wise and bends the strength of authority. This is what drives kings into harsh tyranny, overturns the statutes of laws, allies prelates of the Church with Judas the traitor, and weakens the sanctions of decrees. This is what withdraws patronage from truth, justice from the poor, and equity from judgments. Therefore, as has been shown, this defendant opened himself to the devil through greed and closed himself to Christ. And greed accomplished this powerfully—the same greed which, through the tasting of the forbidden fruit, expelled the first man from Paradise. [Note: [Col. 0761] Gen. 3.]

This is gluttony (*gastrimargia*), which likewise knocked when it offered the labours of the kitchen and delicate foods; entered when it invited the belly not by hunger but by price; reclined at table when it taught him to feast splendidly every day; and took possession when the belly began to be God in place of Christ. It knocked through the sweetness of appetite; entered through the pleasure of taste; reclined through the absorbing force of habit; and possessed through the unlawful dominion of the belly. Hence blind drunkenness deformed the image and likeness of God which shines in man, and irrational sensuality lowered man into a brute animal. Then he is betrayed into the desire of the heart; iniquity comes forth from fatness; and Jerusalem is taken captive by Nebuzaradan, chief of the cooks. [Note: [Col. 0761] IV Kings 25.] Thus iniquity, sitting upon a talent of lead, descends from the belly’s gluttony to the ignoble members, the belly’s companions.

For, once the belly has been fattened and stuffed, the frenzied pageantry of lusts ranges through the whole person; with a kind of unbridled roar and dreadful agitation it powerfully bends even the other members toward the consent of the genitals. The moistened humours of the body indeed produce the thorns of pleasures, and, as though reason were lulled asleep, sensuality alone holds dominion over the human body. And certainly, through feasting and drunkenness, every organ of the human constitution goes mad, and the nature of all the members readily degenerates into vice. At banquets the wanton eye breaks into a lustful gaze; whence it is written: “Luxurious at banquets, having eyes full of adulteries and of sin that never ceases.” [Note: [Col. 0761] II Pet. 2.] At banquets the tongue stammers in quarrelling and confuses half-formed words with superfluous chatter; hence the rich man in Gehenna especially asks for refreshment of his tongue. At banquets the right hand rages in blows, and words frequently give way to strikes; whence it is also written: “Whose are quarrels? whose is woe? whose are wounds without cause? whose is redness of eyes? Is it not those who linger over wine and devote themselves to draining cups?” [Note: [Col. 0761] Prov. 23.]

What more, good Judge? What will you say concerning your Christ, concerning your holy priest? Or rather, if one proceeds rightly, what will you say of him who pursues Egypt’s melons, garlic, and pots of meat, and repeatedly belches yesterday’s drunken excess into the chalice? For, though he has passed the whole night in sleep and either omitted the morning watches altogether or hurried through them in a broken and interrupted fashion, he gives among the holy things convulsive belches from yesterday’s wine, caused by indigestion. The apostle Paul had foretold: “We have an altar from which those who serve the tabernacle have no authority to eat,” [Note: [Col. 0761] Heb. 13.] that is, those who serve bodily pleasure and an abundance of food. Blessed Augustine says: “If you gorge yourself with wine, however much your tongue may sound God’s praises, your life blasphemes.”

Having briefly passed over these matters, it remains to show how this defendant opened himself to the devil and closed himself to Christ through lust, since lust likewise knocked, entered, reclined, and took possession. It knocked when, through its first movements, it sought consent; it entered when, with the sweet heat of the marrow, it flooded the consenting person’s limbs; it reclined when it bent its captive to the accomplishment of the unlawful deed; it possessed when it pressed down the person so bent beneath the stone of habit. Thus it knocked through appetite, entered through consent, reclined through the completed act, and possessed through the bond of habit. It knocked by putting forward nature as a pretext; entered by conceiving guilt; reclined by committing the conceived act; and possessed by repeatedly committing what had become customary.

Therefore, if lust tickled his senses, if natural weakness enticed him toward unlawful desires, this defendant did not crush wickedness by the force of knowledge, did not dash the little ones against the rock, [Note: [Col. 0763] Ps. 136.] and did not catch the little foxes which destroy the vineyard of the Lord of Hosts. [Note: [Col. 0763] Song 2.] Rather, he at once willingly burst forth as far as consent and bent himself to the unlawful deed; he threw himself headlong into the pit of shame; and, pressed down and buried beneath the stone of habit, he fell asleep against the Lord. “The pit closed its mouth over him, and waters entered even to his soul.” [Note: [Col. 0763] Ps. 68.] In this respect he not merely failed to resist an approaching temptation, but often went before it; and by provoking his own concupiscence he performed the office of the most wicked spirits, whose business it is to lead into temptation and to revive the sleeping sparks of kindling by heaping thorns and straw all around, until it burns “like fire among thorns.” [Note: [Col. 0763] Ps. 117.]

He therefore opened himself to the devil through lust and closed himself to Christ, because he not only received the devil knocking at his door as a guest, but, as though the devil were resisting, dragged and enticed him in against his will. And if he set the ark of the Lord beside Dagon—as is now the custom of many priests, who set the Son of the Virgin beside the son of Venus—then, unclean as they are, neither with loins girded nor with hearts consumed by zeal, they presume to handle the most pure sacraments. They receive that most sacred body not wrapped in a clean shroud but with a blood-stained conscience; not in a new tomb cut from rock, [Note: [Col. 0763] Matt. 27.] but in a whitewashed sepulchre, inwardly full of every filth and of dead men’s bones. [Note: [Col. 0763] Matt. 23.]

Understand, Lord, more from these matters than is said here, lest the concision adopted for the case produce loss, and curtailed brevity bring detriment. For the speech would extend without limit if I wished to set out, by number, times, and modes, the intercourse which this your table-companion has had with your enemies—intercourse which is plainly marked and tainted by the proposed treachery. We must not linger longer in proving him a robber when he is not doubted to be a traitor and perjurer, lest a speech prolonged at length delay the deserved punishment which I demand.

Now consider briefly the robber. Who can deny that it is manifest robbery when another’s property is handled against its owner’s will, and, taken away from its proper owner, is transferred to another’s dominion? This defendant is convicted of having done this: he alienated from God’s service a soul not given to him but lent to him by God, and subjected it instead to my dominion. From a handmaid of divinity he made a handmaid of iniquity. “For whoever commits sin is the slave of sin.” [Note: [Col. 0763] Matt. 23.] If he denies that he is a robber, then let him equally avoid the robber’s name and crime—he who is accustomed to borrow and not repay, an ungrateful debtor concerning a loan, faithless concerning a deposit.

Moreover, if the faithful keeper of that Gospel talent is reproved because he hid his master’s money, though prepared to return what had been entrusted to him together with interest, [Note: [Col. 0763] Matt. 25.] who would allow to go unpunished one who did not multiply talents entrusted and lent freely into grace, but perverted them into guilt? For the sake of gain, God distributed talents at interest: yet this man did not refer the gifts of nature and gratuitous gifts back to the Author of nature and Giver of grace, but turned them toward shameful passions, taking from your goods the opportunity and material for sinning. He became more prone to guilt in proportion as he had been raised higher by natural gifts and the abundance of graces. Thus, good Judge, he took your soul and your gifts away from you, subjected them to my dominion against your good pleasure, made gain for me from what was yours against your will, and gave your share out at interest for my profit.

I pass over the manifest robberies by which not only are the burdens of neighbours taken away through violence, but even the possessions of the poor are unjustly retained. For your Scripture plainly calls a robber the person who does not distribute goods entrusted to him to the poor, and it declares that there is not much difference between failing to give one’s own goods and plundering another’s. Therefore, to conclude briefly with what has been said: this evil speech appears to have attained its end, since it has most plainly shown the man to be a perjurer, convicted him of treachery by irrefutable argument, and established him as a robber by manifest reasoning.

I therefore demand, good Judge, the punishments he has deserved, now calling upon your justice as a right, lest he hereafter promise that mercy is negligent or lax; rather, let it fulfil the reality of its name, and, repaying one openly convicted according to his works, let it render what is just with rigorous severity.

You have heard, dearest brethren, with what subtleties the enemy of the human race attacks this man, with what persuasions he proceeds, with what arguments he provokes the Judge’s wrath and demands punishment for the sinner. Which of us, I ask, for whom this discourse has been written especially, when reviewing the acts of his past life, would not fear beneath the rigour of this accusation? Who could endure these fiery darts of speech? Who would not tremble in his inmost being at the decisive verdict in this perilous case? Indeed, who could sufficiently excuse himself from the crimes laid to his charge? Or who could conceal and deny the truth in this examination, especially when all is conducted before the gaze of the Judge who sees everything?

Yet not so much does the construction of the foregoing accusation terrify us as the subtlety of the accuser, which is known to have been acquired not only from the keenness of his nature but also from the very long experience of things and times. For we must believe that he can introduce stronger arguments into his accusation in proportion as he is known to possess a more tenacious memory, more penetrating malice, and more savage envy. Moreover, what human senses would not be dulled by fear so instilled? What inmost parts would not be shaken by terrible dread, when he appears to stand before a Judge both true and severe for the truth of the case, and to pour out the poisons of his iniquity not so much in accusing as in protesting against injury done to truth?

I confess: when I recall my years in the bitterness of my soul, [Note: [Col. 0765] Isa. 15.] when I place the sequence of my crimes before the Judge’s eyes in accordance with the justice of this accusation, fear and dread rush upon me; terror and trembling come over me; and certain darknesses, as it were, enfold my heart in a murky wrapping. “I was grieved in my meditation, and troubled at the voice of the enemy and the oppression of the sinner.” [Note: [Col. 0765] Ps. 54.] Yet let us breathe a little from this fear and make some effort to answer the charges. It would certainly be well provided for if, by some slight objection to what seems to confront us, we could excuse the force of this accusation.

[Col. 0765B] Let us say, without prejudice to better counsel—or rather, let the defendant standing in judgment say: “Lord, it has been established by the equity of laws, to be avoided, that an enemy may not be received as accuser of an enemy; for truth would very often suffer malicious, calculated slander, while biting envy, intending to pursue not the fault but the person, did so. It is clear, however, that the ancient enemy not only of me but of the human race has composed this accusation against me. For this reason, good Judge, I humbly ask to be absolved from it, so that the curses which he has heaped upon me from his ancient envy may not be able to harm me.”

The accuser says: “This device will profit you nothing, whatever evasive objection you may raise; for you do not escape the entirely true arguments of the accusation that has been set forth. Grant, I say, that I am your enemy and therefore am not admitted to accuse you—provided only that she does not keep silence, at whose judgment no guilty person is acquitted, whom every guilty person is compelled

> Night and day to bear in his breast as his own witness.

Speak, conscience: speak, you who customarily accuse the guilty, who pierce and torment them with biting stings, and before the punishments of hell mercilessly wring and tear the souls of the wretched. Speak, I beg you, speak, conscience; bring hidden secrets into the light, and proclaim upon the housetops what was done in darkness. Cry aloud, I beg you; do not cease.” [Note: [Col. 0765] Isa. 58.]

“What,” says conscience, “what shall I cry? Where shall I begin? In what speech shall I describe this man’s deeds? Do you want me again to construct the arguments of a very long accusation? Indeed, whose ears would not ring at what they heard if I attempted to disclose what I have held back in summary? Yet, so that I may discharge myself briefly, I plainly agree with your speech and affirm that everything you have alleged is true. Rather, your curtailed speech has omitted very much which truth deserves to have remembered, and its studied brevity has set forth the course of events less clearly. For speech certainly fails me if I must recount and enumerate my reproaches and the biting stings of my retaliations, with which, an insatiate avenger, I gnawed the wretched man for each individual offence; for speech is insufficient, since in these matters language cannot match their extent, nor can sand equal their number.

“But from a few things your Judge knows how to gather many; before him, beyond Simon’s services, every heart lies open, every will speaks, and one cries out to him even by silence.”

“What now,” says the accuser, “what do you, wretched man, answer to these things? By what objection can you now quibble? By what intervention will you strive to delay the punishment you have earned? Will you call even this your enemy because she bears witness to the truth?” [Note: [Col. 0765] John 5.] “Has truth produced such hatred in you that in this case you fear nothing except what is true? Do you make your conscience, conscious of your truth, into a familiar enemy, and one more effective in harming you, under the pretext of truth? If you judge even her to be your enemy, I summon and bring forward as witnesses for truth the angels themselves, followers of truth—provided they are willing to speak what they know and testify to what they have seen. Indeed, let them speak of you as they wish; let them testify as they please; let them lie, if they can; and through angels of lies and evasions of falsehood let them, if possible, depart from the plain paths of truth.

“Let that angel speak, I beg you, Lord, especially he who was assigned uselessly to guard this man, yet so often yielded, defeated, to Satan’s angel, and, repulsed and scorned in all his counsels, often departed, as it were, more sorrowful and confounded. One thing only, good Judge, I finally ask: let truth furnish the advocacy of my case, and let justice, truth’s sister, unwillingly determine the issue for truth by hastening the judgment.”

Would that, my brethren, even at this point of constriction an objection might devise a place which would repel conscience from the importunity of this accusation and free this man from the impending decisive verdict! Must an objection be made that a woman is not admitted in an accusation unless her own injury or that of her people is in question? It is clear that conscience is grammatically classed under a feminine name; therefore the grammatical form seems to exclude her from the right of accusation, and the very nature of the matter is distinctly expressed by a feminine noun.

“But,” says conscience, “my own injury is plainly at issue. I was created clean by God; clean, I was given to you, wretched man, by God; I was commanded to be kept clean. And lest any shoot of the stain of original filth should remain in me, neither the instruction of faith or of the sacraments, nor the reason implanted in me by God, nor guardianship availed to prevent you from dragging me, though resisting and reproaching you, toward unlawful desires; from polluting me, though resisting and unwilling; and from making me stink before our Creator and the holy angels, while the unextinguished spark of reason continually resisted. Mine, then, mine is the injury; mine is the case at issue; mine especially are the accusation and complaint.”

What now, dearest brethren, can be brought against the subtleties of this reply? Must we still persist in useless objections? Certainly we cannot evade the accusation; we do not dare deny truth in the presence of so great a Judge. As has been said, objections accomplish nothing, because, if you repel the enemy from the right of accusation, conscience springs forward and proclaims her own injuries. And if you reject even her, the angels—most true witnesses—are summoned.

Who then will be called as our advocate in this court, so just, so true, and so severe? For if we have offended either the Judge himself or any one, however humble, of his assessors, we must necessarily have offended them all alike, because they all have one will, brotherly love for one another, mutual affection among all, and an equal and sincere bond of charity. Since, then, we are not sufficient in ourselves, but “our sufficiency is from God,” [Note: [Col. 0767] II Cor. 3.] we must seek from him an advocate and counsel in our case, and say: “Who will rise up for me against evildoers, or who…?” [Note: [Col. 0767] Ps. 94.] From whom should we seek an advocate more fittingly than from him who is himself our advocate with the Lord and Father? And from whom should we seek more useful counsel than from him whose name is Counsellor, from the Angel of Great Counsel, from whom comes right counsel?

In this royal court stand three daughters of the King, whose authority carries no small weight in the entire court; through them alone sinners approach pardon and the righteous draw near to the palm of victory.

They stand, as befits daughters of so great a King, “in honoured apparel, in clothing of gold, surrounded by variety.” [Note: [Col. 0767] Ps. 44.] By gold I understand wisdom—indeed, that wisdom which made foolish the wisdom of this world, of which it is said: “I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and I will reject the prudence of the prudent.” [Note: [Col. 0767] I Cor. 1.] Their variety consists in the diversity of gifts; hence divided tongues appeared to the apostles. [Note: [Col. 0767] Acts 3.] These three daughters of the highest King are the three catholic virtues: faith, hope, and charity. Wisdom delights graciously in their variety, playing before God in the circle of the earth. What sport upon earth is more pleasing? What variety more delightful? What delight more savoury than to meditate, with the sweetest foretaste of eternal life, upon their affections, and to feel their most sweet movements in alternating changes?

For now, in a natural order, we rise from faith’s movement to hope, and thence, raised to the heights of charity, delight in their breadth. Now, pleased rather by an artificial order, we put charity first: it otherwise precedes in dignity as the form that gives shape, and, by the prerogative of its affection, makes the other virtues to be virtues.

The first order, which we called natural, is indicated when it is said:

> First, Faith, ready to fight, enters the field  
> Under the doubtful lot of battle.

The second is expounded where it is said: “But the greatest of these is charity.” [Note: [Col. 0767] I Cor. 13.] Each of them also has her own gold; each has her own varieties, of which this present matter is not the place to speak. Yet we could not introduce these virgins, so venerable, gracious, and beautiful, without rising a little in their praise and inserting, as it were, some brief songs of love.

Let us therefore ask the Judge for their advocacy. Without their prior guidance we have no access to the mercy of the loving Father; without their assistance no mortal can see the Judge in safety. Let the three sisters therefore come forward, I pray—or rather, because of the abundant mercy in which they excel, let them offer themselves unasked. Let them not wait, I pray, until the defendant, standing in judgment and trembling and pale in so great a crisis, calls them either by merits going before or draws them by prayers of carefully composed appeal. For the course and record of his past life manifestly renders him undeserving of their advocacy; the greatness of his congealed fear excludes the boldness to speak, constricting, as it were, the arteries of the voice and scarcely permitting sounds to emerge between deep sighs broken by frequent sobs.

Thus, springing into the midst,

> Ever bold and shameless,

Faith is first to enter the field, ready to fight under the doubtful lot of battle. And so that she may lawfully be able to assist by aid and counsel a man burdened in so many ways together with her sisters, she reverently implores the gentleness of the loving Father.

But the cruel enemy, as is always his custom, strives to hinder this pious work and hurls the poisons of his ancient envy even against her. “What then, kindly Faith, do you detract from your own purity? Why do you either dissemble or blind your own knowledge? Do you not know that I have undertaken this trial on account of injuries done to you—injuries concerning which, had I remained silent, you ought to have made the same complaint? Yet now, by so overturning and perverting the order of things, you prepare harm for your champion and advocacy for your adversary. And if you now love your enemies and those who hate you, cherish those who persecute you, and nurture those hostile to you, why do you henceforth cry in the streets, preach in churches, and announce and set forth your miracles with promises of rewards? For now, as I see, it is pleasing to despise you, useful to persecute you, and safe to put you to death.

“But if your customary shamelessness drives you to set yourself steadfastly against me while I labour for you and your sisters, your sister Hope—more mature in counsel, firmer in resolve, and, as befits her, stricter in severity—will never assent to your unprecedented undertaking. And although you dissemble the Apostle’s words, ‘Faith without works is dead,’ [Note: [Col. 0767] Jas. 2.] and pass by your own death with a deaf ear, she will nevertheless demand vengeance for her own injuries: she who promulgated punishments for transgressions of herself under an edict of curse: ‘Cursed is the man who sins in hope.’ Charity, too, will be much less inclined to your shameless purpose: she is higher in dignity, more enduring in constancy, and is said to be greater than the others because she is known to be nearer to supreme justice and equity. This is charity, which declares the injuries of all virtues to be her own, and maintains that by a single transgression against herself all virtues alike are violated and proscribed. Therefore, to state it briefly, this defendant has rendered himself undeserving of your advocacy alike: for he has often put you, Faith, to death through unlawful deeds; by frequently sinning in hope he has put on the curse as a garment; and by sinning more often in the one thing—that is, charity—he has made himself guilty before all.”

To this Faith replies: “O ancient serpent, O persecutor and rival of every virtue, do you lay snares for my heel and attempt to undermine the uprightness of my sisters by the subtleties of your words? You accomplish nothing, most wicked one, by your exhortations; your venomous words gain nothing, for we neither are ignorant of your devices nor depart, once we know the will of our most loving Father, from the undefiled path of implanted gentleness. We know, utterly depraved one, we know what pleases the divine will, what accords with justice, and what belongs to equity. For we always stand in the divine presence; and what we have seen and heard of the mysteries of divinity in his presence, we speak and testify to humankind for human salvation.

“It belongs to our institution, therefore, not to believe your exhortations or yield to your arguments and persuasions, but to administer against the poisons of your wickedness the antidote of saving treatment. Yet you take the Testament of God into your mouth and strive to twist Scripture’s resisting rectitude in order to establish your perverse purpose. You assert that I have been put to death by works, pronounce sin in hope, and accuse an offence in the one thing, charity.

“But, most wicked serpent, I shall appear the greener in the sight of the Most High to the extent that, through the death inflicted by the works of most wicked men, I have for a time become drier; for my triumph in rising again will be more glorious in proportion as the fall in human sin has been lower. ‘Where sin abounded, grace abounded still more.’ [Note: [Col. 0769] Rom. 5.] My sister Hope, who does not confound, who always delights in good things, and who, however often people have gone astray, calls them away from their evil path and brings them back by the promise of rewards, rejects your calumnies against herself. She directs the curse only finally against those who sin in her and fall asleep in death, and declares that no one should be despaired of while he remains in mortal life.

“And what worn-down impudence has urged you to summon our most excellent sister, Charity—singularly marked with the light and impress of the divine countenance—by accusation, when you do not doubt that it is her proper character to love enemies, pray for persecutors, and overcome evil with good? [Note: [Col. 0770A]] Since she patiently bears all things, and does this alone with a certain loving violence, she does what she forcefully grants. She will not abandon her character for your sake or leave her customary way; however injured, however despised, she will humbly bend herself to help the fallen and offer herself as patroness of the afflicted.

“Finally, we are daughters of the King, whose property it is always to have mercy and spare, who reveals his omnipotence most especially by sparing, whose mercies extend over all his works. We desire to imitate him; we are not permitted to oppose him. Therefore we do not abandon the mercy we learned from our loving Father, nor condemn misery, lest we seem to prescribe limits to the grace of mercy. Nor are we much moved if your eye is evil, because we are good.”

Having obtained permission from the Father of mercies, the three aforementioned sisters, while the demon still protests—or is confounded—undertake the man’s advocacy on his behalf. They draw him aside in private and endeavour to direct him toward sound counsel; and Faith thus addresses the man:

“You see, man, how great are the charges against you. You hear how weighty are the testimonies spoken against you. What, then, do you answer to what these men testify against you? Every way of denial is closed to you; you must either confess or be convicted by silence. For not only to the Judge, but also to his assessors, to the holy multitude standing by, and even to us who are present in the council, the truth of your conduct lies bare; the course of your life is known without concealment; the deeds of your misery are manifest without concealment. Yet do you not consider for how great a matter you have undergone the danger of this case, and what punishment must await one who is convicted?

“Do you know that, if you lose the case, eternal fire is prepared for you, ‘which is prepared for the devil and his angels’? [Note: [Col. 0769] Matt. 25.] Do you know that a bed is made for you in the outer darkness, where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth? [Note: [Col. 0769] Matt. 8.] This is certainly not a dispute conducted in any fashion over a small sum of money; rather, the accounting is so much stricter because of the talents entrusted by the Lord. The contest is not over a temporal and contemptible inheritance, nor over clothing that wears out, nor food that is cast into the privy, but over the soul—which is more than food—and the body—which is more than clothing: whether they shall possess forever, as though by hereditary right, the splendour of the Lord’s house or the horror of that prison.

“If, in this crisis of such necessity and danger of such a dispute, you have counsel, declare it, I beg; hasten and speak. Judgment summons us; no free delay remains to us while this most reverent assembly awaits your answer. Yet we see you trembling and pale, and because of the greatness of your horror we perceive every avenue of counsel to be closed to your stunned mind. But lest fear wholly swallow you up and hurl you with a most dreadful shock into the pit of despair hateful to God, we shall no longer press harsher matters or threaten severe things. Instead, we open for you an easy and useful path to deliverance. If you rely on our counsels, cast your care upon us, and do not refuse to comply with saving admonitions, behold: we are here to offer you ready aid and advocacy. For we bestow on you pardon for past crimes and forbearance from the Judge, so that you may prepare yourself for better things.

“We can indeed postpone the impending judgment, but we cannot wholly frustrate it, because at an hour you do not know you must stand before the Judge’s tribunal, to receive according to what you have done in the body, whether good or evil. But unless you withdraw yourself from our counsel, we will free you from imminent dangers and teach you not to dread the day of judgment, so that you may depart free from this place and thereafter be able to see the Judge’s face with greater confidence.”

“We agree,” say the sisters, “and what our sister promises you on our behalf, we too firmly promise you.”

“Very well,” says Faith: “either yield to our counsel and be freed, or withdraw from us and be judged according to your own deserts.” Who, brethren, in so great a crisis would not choose deliverance? Who would neglect and reject useful counsel? Indeed, who could be of so rash a mind as not to accept advice so salutary?

“I believe,” says the sinner, “I believe you, Lady Faith. Help my unbelief, and bring to completion in your paths my insufficiency which comes from myself. Illuminate, I beg you, my darknesses; pour over me the light of saving doctrine; and enlighten me with the splendour of your brightness. Lady, there will be no one lacking to fulfil what you command; nor will anyone ever read anything else in the deed than what you now see me setting forth in promise.”

“Everything will turn out as you desire,” says Faith. “Return confidently to judgment, to receive pardon for your sins and forbearance from the Judge. But first you must take up the light burden and sweet yoke, and then safely approach the Judge with us. Henceforth it is fitting that, in right faith, firm hope, and unfeigned charity, you continually carry remembrance of your sins, continual contrition, and fruitful repentance. Moreover, lest you suffer relapse in any way, you must employ the caution of Christian discernment.

“Regard as very slight—or rather, I call it almost playful—the temporal satisfaction which, after confession, shall be imposed upon you at the discretion of the priest. For it will not only deliver you from eternal death, but also from that purgatorial punishment which no Sicilian tyrant could equal; indeed, in comparison with it every worldly punishment may be called honeyed sweetness, ice may be reckoned a bath, and a furnace refreshment.”

“My lady,” he says, “what you say seems light, what you command sweet; only hasten to free me, by however long a postponement, from the terror of the judgment that threatens me.”

“Let us make haste,” say the sisters, “let us bring the case before the judge and briefly plead for the advantage of a postponement.” Thus, having somewhat comforted the man, who now hopes for his deliverance, they again set him before the judge’s tribunal; and, as befits royal virgins, they seem together to request a hearing from the judge with modest countenances, and silence from the crowd. Faith, the first, as she had begun, assumes for herself the authority of patronage and rebuts the very long series of accusations with a most brief speech.

“Good judge,” she says, “the cruel, envious serpent has sufficiently—more than sufficiently—unfolded the poisons of his inward malice and, as befitted a devilish ingenuity, has most craftily woven together the arguments of his accusation. For from ancient times the serpent has been craftier than all the living creatures that are upon the earth [Note: Col. 0771D, Gen. 3]. Yet we do not repel each of his darts with a separate defence [Col. 0772B], nor do we deem each argument worthy of a separate response; rather, by a most ready, brief, and clear principle, we refute all the charges together.

“For the most narrow law of this most holy court is confined to only two words: ‘You have sinned: cease.’ To this law, most merciful Father, we firmly adhere, and on the authority of this law we seek a postponement of judgment; for postponement alone can show whether he who does not deny that he has sinned ought henceforth to cease from sinning. Come then, that we may seem in some measure to favor the opposing side: he has sinned beyond the number of the sand of the sea, and his sins have multiplied. Granted; but his iniquity is not greater than can deserve pardon. Since divine mercy exceeds misery, Lord, you will remember none of [Col. 0772C] his iniquities, provided that he ceases to act perversely and learns to do good.

“Finally, he does not come to be instructed anew; he does not now for the first time seek the rudiments of saving doctrine. Rather, supported by the mysteries of Christian faith and the protection of the sacraments, he turns more readily to the holy records of a reformed way of life. Therefore, that he may hereafter be bound to you by a stricter promise, hear, Lord, if it please you, from his own mouth how, established in faith, strengthened in hope, he now begins to take root in charity; and how he proposes to amend for the better whatever vices he has contracted through the devil’s deception, and whatever sins he committed in ignorance.

“Say, then: O man, do you believe in God the almighty Father? Do you believe also in [Col. 0772D] his Son, born and suffering? Do you believe also in the Holy Spirit? Finally, to put it briefly: Do you believe all that the orthodox Fathers declare to be so necessary to salvation that without faith in these things salvation cannot exist?”

“I believe,” he says, “my lady; I believe most firmly. For, washed from infancy in holy baptism, always nurtured in the Catholic faith, I have never wavered from its firmness through any hesitation, nor ever departed from it when sins pressed upon me. I confess that the enemy prevailed against me, when he took from my faith the form of its power; but he could not shake the substance of faith. He could not bring it about that faith was wholly absent from me; rather, he caused me not to taste the character of its power.”

[Col. 0773A] “You hear,” says Faith, “good judge, what he confesses with his mouth; and you consider no less what he believes in his heart. He has laid an immovable foundation for his house and established his dwelling-place upon a most firm support. For the foundation has been laid, other than which no one can lay: the man Christ Jesus.

“O kindly Hope, O dearest sister, why do you not make clear what you possess in this man? Let him at least answer openly when questioned what he thinks concerning the resurrection of bodies, concerning the glory of the saints in both robes, and concerning immortality with Christ.”

“Openly,” says the man, “before this sacred assembly I confess whatever is preached in churches concerning the Catholic faith, whatever is asserted concerning the certainty of sacred hope, whatever is maintained by holy teachers concerning the surpassing efficacy of charity. [Col. 0773B] But there should not even be an examination concerning these matters, had not the iniquity that I committed too often deprived me of the grace of the virtues and their saving efficacy.”

“But indeed,” says Faith, “do you promise that, whatever offenses you have committed against the Lord up to this hour, you will henceforth remain in right faith, firm hope, and unfeigned charity; that you will have repentance for past sins and caution against future ones?”

“I promise, my lady,” he says, “nor shall vigorous sensual desire, the passing luxury of the world, or the assaults of devilish fury ever make me will anything else.”

“What then,” says Faith, “good judge, what remains except that this man depart free, since he repeats before you such Christian promises? For he no longer seems [Col. 0773C] to need an advocate who thus pleads for himself, who thus both renounces sins and proposes to adhere to your commandments. It remains, therefore, that you stretch forth your right hand to the work of your hands and, having cast out the prince of this world, retain for yourself alone sovereignty over your creature. For a son of your adoption is not lightly to be abandoned to Satan; nor is the servant, for whom you gave up your Son, to be driven away without mercy.”

As sacred Faith thus prays, the holy choir of those sitting by rises, and, in order to obtain from the judge the postponement of judgment and the pardon requested for the accused, they reverently implore him not so much with vocal outcry as with faces humbly bowed. Here the glorious Mother of the Mediator between God and men is to be believed to intervene all the more effectively because she shares more intimately in the judge’s throne and, crowned on the right hand of Majesty on high, rejoices and triumphs in exaltation [Col. 0773D].

What could he either be able or obliged to deny her there? If she shows him the breasts at which he was nursed; if in supplication she recalls the weakness of the sacred infancy which she bore and cherished with maternal devotion; if she attributes to sinners this very dignity as an occasion of mercy—that she is at once virgin and mother—and therefore ought specially to sustain their miseries. Here she also offers prayers especially for sinners. Likewise, if any saint has been honored by him with special service and, among others, anticipated with more frequent devotion and more fervent prayer [Col. 0774A].

For although some saints are believed to surpass others in more frequent devotion, merits, and rewards, yet the greater are believed very often to show deference to the lesser and to honor them first, so that the intercession of the lesser more frequently grants human beings what the greater’s ampler grace and glory has deferred to bestow. If this were not true, blessed Peter, apostle and prince of the apostles, would never have left to the virgin Chrodeberta the task of restoring sight to a blind person; for this is more fully explained in the Life of that virgin.

Thus, moved by multiplied intercessors, the judge seems both to grant pardon to the accused and to defer sentence, under the following terms:

“Go,” he says, “O man, and show yourself to your priest; reveal your wounds to the physician, if you wish to be cleansed from the filth of your wounds. Otherwise wounds do not attain health, but, as their matter boils up more and more in its stench, they rot away even unto destruction [Col. 0774B]. Take courage, son: your sins are forgiven you [Note: Col. 0773, Matt. 9], provided that you also desire to embrace salutary shame and fruitful repentance. Go, therefore, and sin no more. You will undergo more grievous dangers of judgment if, having cast aside the terror of this now fearsome examination, you choose to relapse and return, like a dog, to your vomit [Note: Col. 0773, Prov. 26].

“Nor is it expedient now to instruct you further at length, or to review the order of commandments in a longer discourse. You have Moses and the prophets; indeed, you have apostles and evangelists; you have doctors and shepherds sent for the ministry of faith: ‘Whoever hears them hears me’ [Note: Col. 0773, Luke 10]. You also have the brief word, if gracious brevity [Col. 0774C] pleases you: ‘Have charity, and do whatever you will.’

“Beyond all this you have my grace, unless you fail grace; and unless you shamefully repel it, as though with violent importunity, it will always be at hand to supply your deficiencies and confer saving advances. I therefore exhort you to live by these things, meditate on them, and, through meditation and life, continually await a little longer until the inescapable day of judgment comes upon you. On that day you will plead not with words but with deeds; you will argue not with quibbles, nor proceed by delaying exceptions; but, ‘in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye’ [Note: Col. 0773, 1 Cor. 15], you will be repaid according to the fruit of your hands, and will receive good or evil according to what you have done in the body.

“Let that day be feared by you all the more certainly because its coming is known all the more uncertainly [Col. 0774D]. Always believe that the judge is at the doors, concerning whom it has precisely been ordained that he will come unexpectedly. For ‘the day of the Lord will come like a thief’ [Note: Col. 0773, Luke 12]. You do not know whether it will be in the evening, at midnight, at cockcrow, or in the morning [Note: Col. 0773, Mark 13]. Yet you will repeatedly receive summonses from this so unexpected judge: losses, dangers, illnesses, deaths of people, and all the other things which interrupt the sweetness of temporal things with the manifold gall of bitterness, and season the deadly enticements of the flesh with much salt so that they may not become sweet.”

[Col. 0775A] “Consider all these things as the judge’s heralds sent in advance, and reckon them all final summonses. They will indeed be so frequent for you that no temporal pleasure will wrest you away from diligence, nor ruinous drowsiness corrupt your watchfulness. ‘Do this, and you shall live’ [Note: Col. 0775, Luke 10]. Otherwise the postponement you have obtained will become an accumulation of condemnation for you; for the longer one’s persistence in sins, the greater will be one’s affliction in torments.

“Yet if you fall, the path of rising again is not closed to you, since the pattern of forgiving up to seventy times seven has been handed down in vain otherwise.”

Therefore, as has been said, having obtained a postponement of judgment, the judge restored the accused to the freedom of his will, while the suspended axe was raised higher and higher: that it might strike more forcefully if iniquity continued; deliver more wonderfully [Col. 0775B] if righteousness and equity were chosen; and crown more gloriously if the long-suffering of perseverance followed. Thus, delivered from the danger of impending condemnation, the man may say: “Unless the Lord had helped me, my soul would almost have dwelt in hell” [Note: Col. 0775, Ps. 93].

But, as was indicated at the beginning of this little work [Col. 0776A], for us who are placed in the world, whose actions necessarily take place amid tumult, who must daily either perish or conquer, who walk in the midst of snares, who, wherever we turn, see the enemy assaulting us—for us, I say, it will, I think, be no useless thing if we repeatedly turn this examination over in our minds, or believe that it has already taken place for us or is past; and if, for each individual action, we attend to the interval of an undetermined postponement granted us by the judge, and consider ourselves always moved, living, and existing under the peril of impending judgment.

Thus fear will make us begin to turn away from evil; and thereafter, as we advance by God’s grace, love will make us do good, until we attain to a perfect man, to the measure of the fullness of Christ. May the God [Col. 0776B] of peace, who brought again from the dead the great shepherd, our Lord Jesus Christ, by the blood of the eternal covenant, fit us for every good work, that he may do in us what is pleasing before him, through Jesus Christ, to whom be honor and glory for ages of ages. Amen.

## FRAGMENT

[Note: This fragment is badly and most ineptly placed at the end of Homily 62 in the Paris edition. Where it ought to be placed, I truly do not know. GILES.]

[Col. 0775]

[Col. 0775C] … was saying: “For whoever commits sin is the slave of sin” [Note: Col. 0775, John 8]; and whoever is a slave is not wholly free. Hence he does the evil that he does not wish, and does not do the good that he wishes [Note: Col. 0775, Rom. 7]. Therefore Paul too, drawn away and enticed by his own desire, said: “I am a carnal man, sold under sin” [Note: Col. 0775, ibid.].

This carnal man savors nothing but flesh. Hence he entangles himself in carnal desires and pours himself out toward every onrush of pleasure. But this pleasure will be turned into nausea, and the accumulation of delights will be turned into an accumulation of torments. As the Lord says concerning Babylon: “As much as she exalted herself in delights, so much give her torment and mourning” [Note: Col. 0775, Rev. 18].

The Apostle says concerning the natural man: “The natural man does not receive the things of the Spirit of God; for they are foolishness [Col. 0775D] to him, and he cannot understand them, because they are spiritually discerned. But the spiritual man judges all things, and is judged by no one” [Note: Col. 0775, 1 Cor. 2]. The earthly man savors earth; the carnal man, the desires of flesh. But the natural man walks in darkness; he accounts the knowledge of God’s ways foolishness; he calls good evil and evil good, and makes light darkness and darkness light [Note: Col. 0775, Isa. 5]. He is sluggish in the divine office; he hates, neglects, and disdains the exercise of spiritual warfare. Others gladly hear the word of edification; this man, because he is not of God, does not hear God’s words [Col. 0776C] [Note: Col. 0775, 1 John 4].

This is the threefold man we have identified: earthly, carnal, natural. “Our old man has been crucified with him,” says the Apostle: “Our old man has been crucified with him, that the body of sin may be destroyed, so that we may no longer serve sin” [Note: Col. 0775, Rom. 6]. Let the earthly man be crucified through contempt for earthly things and voluntary poverty. Let the carnal man be crucified on the cross of obedience and in the exercise of discipline. Let the natural man be crucified in contrition of heart and love of Christ.

If we cannot crucify this Jebusite, or wholly destroy him, let us at least compel him to serve under tribute, bringing every understanding into captivity to the obedience of Christ. “I chastise my body,” says the Apostle, “and reduce it to slavery” [Note: Col. 0775, 1 Cor. 9]. If we reduce this generation, this threefold man, to slavery [Col. 0776D], we shall no longer be of the devil our father, no longer of the world, but of God; and, safe from evil hearing, we shall hear the word of mercy, the word of grace, the word of glory: “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” [Note: Col. 0775, Matt. 25]. May he deign to grant this to you, he who lives and reigns as God with the Father and the Holy Spirit through all ages of ages. Amen.

## THE SHORTER WORKS OF PETER OF BLOIS

[Col. 0777]

## ON THE TRANSFIGURATION OF THE LORD

[Col. 0777A] To his reverend father and lord FRENALD, by God’s grace bishop of Arras, his own PETER OF BLOIS sends greeting in him who is true salvation.

The frequent urging of Master Sigerius and the authority of your command compel me to write something concerning the Lord’s Transfiguration which may publicly edify hearers and shine forth for the common good. Yet, conscious of my imperfection and unequal to so great a command, I would most willingly decline the burden laid upon me, unless the Lord’s threat frightened me: “Cursed is he who hides grain among the peoples” [Note: Col. 0777, Prov. 11].

Therefore, lest I be judged a wicked servant if I either wrap the talent entrusted to me in a cloth or bury it in the earth [Note: Col. 0777, Luke 19], I shall minister to others from my own poverty, as God was pleased in his goodness to provide for the poor. For I have placed my hope [Col. 0777B] in him who is our hope; in him who hides from the wise and prudent what he reveals to little ones [Note: Col. 0777, Luke 10]; in him who chose Peter and Andrew, and the sons of Zebedee [Note: Col. 0777, Matt. 11], as ministers of the Word of the Lord, not from the loudness of logicians, not from the elegance of rhetoricians, not from Justinian’s school, but from simple roughness—and yet through them wrought salvation in the midst of the earth.

I shall therefore speak; for, if I am silent, to use Job’s words [Note: Col. 0777, ch. 16], “my mouth will condemn me” [Note: Col. 0777, ch. 9]. I am bound to speak by the bond of covenant, the fear of the Lord, and brotherly charity. Would that the Lord may make acceptable the free offerings of my mouth, and that I may bear fruit in others, though I bear either no fruit or rare fruit myself. For swords are sharpened by the service of a whetstone which cannot cut [Col. 0777C]; and though the native power of germination cannot grow strong in channels, it nevertheless passes through the channels to the flower-beds.

Receive, therefore, the work of one day, and do not seek in it Ulpian’s charm or Tully’s flowers. For I seek not the profit of fame but of souls; and it is enough for me if the hasty composition of this little work, dashed off amid the tumult of courtly anxieties, deserves not praise, I say, but pardon.

That Teacher who teaches man knowledge, in [Col. 0778A] whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge [Note: Col. 0777, Col. 2], instructs us in conduct in the school of evangelical discipline, kindles us in charity, raises us in hope, and confirms us in faith. By his own example first of all he warns us that we must entrust our secrets especially to those whom a more certain affection of devotion binds to us.

For Christ, because “every word stands by the mouth of two or three witnesses” [Note: Col. 0777, Matt. 18], chose three from among the twelve disciples, to whom he might more secretly reveal the glory of his Transfiguration: Peter, James, and John [Note: Col. 0777, Matt. 17]. Their most devoted charity deserved the privilege of sincere love and familiarity. To the others, who were carnal and still thought carnally, he displayed himself only in the form of passible flesh. But to these, who had already conceived on the mountain of contemplation the hope of the future resurrection [Col. 0778B] and the glory of blessed expectation, he showed the reality of glorified flesh: offering himself to their carnal eyes as he knew that they already recognized with spiritual eyes that he would rise from the dead.

Many are troubled, however, as to how the reality of glorification could appear in flesh subject to suffering and death; and, if glorification was truly present there, how flesh, once made impassible, could afterward be subject to death and decay. Did God wholly lay aside the misery of human nature, and, in order to put on the robe of glory for a time, cast off the sackcloth of our captivity [Note: Col. 0777: See St Thomas, *Summa Theologiae*, III, question 4, article 1]?

Far be it that the man who has once been assumed through grace should ever be cast aside because of the assumption of some honor and glory. Human nature, once assumed by divinity, neither suffered divorce nor received a bill of repudiation: the sacrament of that blessed marriage remains. And those whom God joined together, no subsequent occasion of honor or necessity separated.

Let no one, therefore, be astonished or introduce the scruple of doubt concerning this change wrought by the right hand of the Most High. For he who, while the glory of his divinity remained whole, truly bore the misery of our mortality [Col. 0779A], could in his mortal flesh display the glory of true immortality. And he who after the resurrection showed the scars of wounds in a glorified body, by that same power displayed the glory of the resurrection in passible flesh. Thus in that very glorification he remained passible, though amid the failings of our mortality he was most truly immortal.

This is the rod turned into a serpent; when Moses was terrified by it, he took its tail, and it was turned into a rod [Note: Col. 0779, Exod. 4]. For when the disciples were terrified by the dreadful glory of divine wisdom, the serpent is in some manner turned back into a rod—that is, the divine appearance returns to the human.

By this vision Christ wonderfully confirmed in these three disciples the first principles of their new faith. For they who still believed with doubt that Christ was true [Col. 0779B] man and true God now recognize this same thing by visible appearance and seeing faith. Nor should it be passed over in silence that the future glorification of the body was made known in this Transfiguration not wholly but in part. Since the glorification of the body consists in four things—brightness, agility, subtlety, and immortality—here he appeared glorified in brightness alone. He demonstrated the future subtlety of bodies when he entered among the disciples while the doors were shut [Note: Col. 0779, John 20]; agility, when he walked over the waters with dry feet [Note: Col. 0779, Matt. 14].

“And his face shone like the sun, and his garments like snow” [Note: Col. 0779, Matt. 17]: he showed in himself the brightness that he was to confer upon the righteous. “The righteous,” he says, “will shine like the sun in the kingdom of my Father” [Note: Col. 0779, Matt. 13]. This indeed will happen when he reforms the body of [Col. 0779C] our lowliness, conformed to the body of his glory [Note: Col. 0779, Phil. 3].

The Evangelist compares the sun of righteousness to the worldly sun because, among the works of nature, there was no creature whose likeness to Christ could be more express. Christ surpasses sun and moon by the splendor of his glory as much as the Creator must more gloriously exceed the creature. For if Christ’s throne is compared to the sun, as the Father speaks through the prophet: “And his throne shall be as the sun before me” [Note: Col. 0779, Ps. 88], how much more splendid than the sun will be the face of him seated upon the throne?

This is the sun of which the prophet says: “You shall no longer have the sun to shine by day, nor shall the splendor of the moon give you light; but the Lord your God shall be for you an everlasting light” [Note: Col. 0779, Isa. 60]. Above every beauty [Col. 0780A] and splendor is your splendor; you are “beautiful in form beyond the children of men” [Note: Col. 0779, Ps. 44]. For you are he into whom angels desire to look; who, begotten before Lucifer [Note: Col. 0779, Ps. 109], dwell in inaccessible light [Note: Col. 0779, 1 Tim. 6], in the splendors of the saints [Note: Col. 0779, Ps. 109]; the radiance and image of the Father’s substance [Note: Col. 0779, Heb. 1], and a certain brightness of eternal life [Note: Col. 0779, Wis. 7].

Therefore all my bones shall say: “Lord, who is like you?” [Note: Col. 0779, Ps. 34]. “There is none like you among the gods, O Lord, and there are no works according to your works” [Note: Col. 0779, Ps. 85]. If, then, that Lucifer who rose in the morning [Note: Col. 0779, Isa. 14], now no longer light-bearer (*Lucifer*) but darkness-bearer (*tenebrifer*), presumes to usurp the likeness of your glory, let the son of pride be cast down and the chair of pestilence overthrown. For “there is no God like the Lord, and there is no God like our God” [Note: Col. 0779, 1 Sam. 2].

Christ alone is God; he “did not consider equality with God to be robbery” [Note: Col. 0779, Phil. 2], the Most High [Col. 0780B] Son of the Most High, seated not beneath his feet but at his right hand. He rightly shines like the sun, who “set his tabernacle in the sun” [Note: Col. 0779, Ps. 18]. Nor is he glorified without sacramental significance on Mount Tabor, which is interpreted “coming light”: the light prepared for the revelation of the Gentiles and the glory of the people Israel [Note: Col. 0779, Luke 2]; he who formerly gave light from the everlasting mountains; he who today enlightens every person coming into this world [Note: Col. 0779, John 1].

Certainly, if the heavenly bodies possessed the grace of human understanding but did not recognize Christ as God and man, the moon would blush that it yielded to so great a brightness, and the sun would be ashamed because it could not surpass the light proceeding from a human body. This is what we read Isaiah to have prophesied in the Holy Spirit: “The moon shall blush and the sun be ashamed, when the Lord reigns in Zion and is glorified in the sight of his saints” [Col. 0780C] [Note: Col. 0779, Isa. 24].

Christ’s garments are his faithful, who both put on Christ and are clothed by Christ, as the Apostle says: “As many of you as were baptized into Christ have put on Christ” [Note: Col. 0779, Gal. 3]. Washed by Christ through the washing of regeneration [Note: Col. 0779, Titus 3], they shall be made whiter than snow, as the Prophet says: “You shall wash me, and I shall be made whiter than snow” [Note: Col. 0779, Ps. 50].

Yet, because sins often dead in baptism relapse, and that which had been made whiter than snow grows black again in us, another washing is granted us: namely, the second plank after shipwreck, the remedy of repentance. But many also use this washing negligently.

[Note: Rightly Peter of Blois writes in his little work *On Sacramental Confession*: “For whatever you have not cleansed in the present life, God will cleanse in the fire of purgatory, as he himself says through Joel (3:21): ‘I will cleanse the blood which they did not cleanse.’ Isaiah also says (3:3): ‘And he will cleanse the sons of Levi in a spirit of judgment and a spirit of burning.’ But Christ, effecting the cleansing of sins not in judgment but in desire, not in burning but in love, mercifully assigned us three purgatories: contrition of heart [Col. 0780D], confession of the mouth, and affliction of the flesh. Those use the remedy of repentance negligently in this life who do not take care to make satisfaction to God through affliction of the flesh and other works of that kind to the degree to which they are bound to make satisfaction.”

Peter Lombard, *Sentences*, book IV, distinction 20, letter B: “For if contrition of heart and reproach for the offense are so great that they suffice to punish sin, such persons pass free from other penalties to life, even if their penance has not been completed [Col. 0781A], because they have repented and groaned perfectly in heart. But those who are not so thoroughly contrite in heart and do not groan for sin, if they depart before completing their penance, will experience purgatorial fire and be punished more severely than if they had completed their penance here. For it is dreadful to fall into the hands of the living God (Heb. 10:31).

“For because God is merciful and just, in mercy he forgives the penitent, not reserving sin for eternal punishment; but in justice he does not leave an offense unpunished. Either a human being punishes it, or God. A human being punishes it by repenting; God, by exacting punishment. And punishment is inward and outward. Therefore, if inward repentance [Col. 0781B] is so great that it is sufficient vengeance for sin, God, who knows this, does not further exact punishment from the person who thus repents. But if inward repentance is not sufficient for the punishment of sin and outward penance is not fulfilled, God, who knows the kinds and measures of sins and punishments, adds sufficient punishment.

“Therefore let each person strive to correct offenses in such a way that after death punishment need not be endured. For certain mortal sins become venial in repentance, yet are not immediately healed. A sick person would often die if not treated, but even when treated is not immediately healed. He remains ill though he will live, who previously was about to die.”]

They wait [Col. 0781A] until whatever defilement or rust in them confession has not cleansed is washed away by purgatorial fire.

[Note: [Col. 0781B] An outstanding passage on purgatory. It is certainly an article of faith that purgatory exists, by the Florentine canon in the decree on union, session 23; by Trent, session 25, in the decree on purgatory; and by the profession of Catholic faith. To these must be added the councils which establish that prayer should be made and sacrifice offered for departed believers, and the universal custom of the Church, concerning which Augustine writes in *On Care for the Dead*, book 1, chapter 1:

“We read in the books of Maccabees that sacrifice was offered for the dead. But even if this were read nowhere in the older Scriptures, the authority of the universal Church, which is evident in this custom, is nonetheless not slight; for in the prayers of the priest, which are poured out to the Lord God at his altar, the commemoration of the dead also has its proper place.”

And in Sermon 32, *On the Words of the Apostle*, chapter 2:

“By the prayers of the holy Church, the saving sacrifice, and alms which are distributed for their spirits, there can be no doubt that the dead are helped, so that the Lord may deal with them more mercifully than their sins deserved. For the universal Church observes what has been handed down by the Fathers: that prayer is made for those who died in the communion of Christ’s body and blood, when they are commemorated in their proper place at the sacrifice itself, and that the offering is also mentioned as being made for them [Col. 0781D]. When works of mercy are performed for the sake of commending them, who can doubt that these help those for whom prayers are not vainly presented to God?” etc.

And in chapter 109 of the *Enchiridion*:

“Nor is it to be denied that the souls of the dead are relieved by the piety of their living relatives, when the sacrifice of the Mediator is offered for them or alms are given in the Church. But these things benefit those who, while living, deserved that they might benefit them afterward. For there is a manner of life neither so good that it does not require these things after death, nor so bad that they are of no benefit after death. There is indeed a state so good that it does not require them; and again one so bad that, after leaving this life, it cannot be helped even by these.”

And later:

“Therefore, when sacrifices, whether of the altar or of any alms, are offered for all baptized dead [Col. 0782A], they are thanksgivings for the very good; they are propitiations for those not very bad; and for the very bad, even if they are no help to the dead, they are consolations of whatever kind for the living. Those whom they benefit are benefited either so that there may be full remission, or at least that the condemnation itself may become more tolerable.”

When, however, in speaking of purgatory he mentions fire, he employs a manner of speech common among Latins after Augustine, *City of God*, book XXI, chapter 10, who writes:

“Though by wonderful yet true modes even incorporeal spirits may be afflicted by the punishment of bodily fire, if the spirits of human beings—though certainly incorporeal—could now be enclosed in bodily members, and may then be inseparably bound by the bonds of their bodies.”

Gregory the Great subscribes to this in *Dialogues*, book IV, chapter 29. The Greeks, however, believe that purgatory exists, but do not believe that souls are cleansed or tormented by fire in purgatory, as is clear from the following words of the private synod convened at Ferrara on 4 June 1438, prefixed to session 1 of the Council of Florence.

The Greeks maintain only a future fire and a temporary punishment of souls: namely, that the souls liable for sins go to a dark place, a place of sorrow, where for a time they remain in sorrow and punishments, deprived of divine light. But they are cleansed—that is, freed and absolved from that dark place and affliction—by the prayers and sacrifices of priests and by alms, but not by fire. For the Greeks do not admit the action of fire as the Italians do; rather, prayer, supplication, and almsgiving alone operate [Col. 0782C].

This, then, is the difference between them: the Greeks affirm punishment, its force, and a place of punishment, but not by fire; the Italians, punishment and purification by fire. The same Greeks, as is recorded in the Council of Florence, session 25, when questioned by Eugenius IV about purgatorial fire, answered in these words:

“Concerning purgatorial fire, this has been determined: that the souls of the saints have obtained a perfect crown in heaven, insofar as they are souls; but that the souls of sinners perfectly pay their punishments. Between these are souls in a place of torments; but whether it is fire, or darkness and storm, or something else, we do not contend.”

Hence there is no mention of fire in the definition of the dogma concerning purgatory. Bellarmine aptly writes in *On Purgatory*, book II, chapter 11:

“The common opinion of theologians is that it is a true and proper fire, of the same species as our elemental fire. This opinion is not, indeed, of faith, since it has nowhere been defined in the Church. Indeed, at the Council of Florence the Greeks openly professed that they did not posit fire in purgatory; nevertheless, in the definition made at the final session, purgatory is defined to exist, without any mention of fire. Yet it is a most probable opinion” [Col. 0782D].

Bellarmine might have added that the same was also defined at the Council of Trent, likewise with no mention of fire, and that the same silence is profound in the profession of faith.]
