“O [Col. 0782A] foolish [Note: Col. 0781D, Gal. 3] and blind ones! If the Lord shall wash away the filth of the daughters of Zion in a spirit of judgment and a spirit of burning” [Note: Col. 0782D].

He calls the contrition of the heart brief in comparison with the fire of purgatory; yet, absolutely speaking, it ought not to be brief, but prolonged and persevering, so that a person may obtain mercy and not fall back into sins. For our author explains himself thus in the work already cited:

> “Some think it sufficient for them that for a while they have abstained from their foulness; and, presumptuously relying on the first fruits of the continence they have seized upon, they do not recall their former transgressions. They suppose that their offences have vanished, as it were, through the passage of time, or that God has forgotten them or sleeps, and imagine that they have settled all their debts by a brief and easy reckoning.” [Col. 0783A]

And later:

> “Things which have become ingrained through long practice and fixed in the inmost marrow of souls are not healed without the bitterest pain of heart and anxious affliction of heart; nor can those for which eternal death is due be redeemed by an hourly and light contrition.”

And below:

> “Therefore let perseverance accompany the purpose of repentance.” [Col. 0783B]

And again:

> “Let no one, therefore, presume upon momentary contrition or an abundance of tears. For very many are irreligious—or rather, swallowed up in the abyss of iniquities—rejoicing when they have done evil and exulting in the worst deeds; yet we see them, through fear of punishment or remembrance of sins, pierced even to tears, melting with wondrous devotion into love of Jesus, and embracing him with all the marrow of their soul and with the arms of devout affection.”

And later:

> “If therefore you feel in yourself the grace of compunction and an abundance of tears, do not on that account immediately judge yourself reconciled to the Lord; nor should the servant suppose himself to be a son, even though he is sometimes fed with the bread of sons.”

And again:

> “Does not this very compunction blind the eyes and stop up the ears of the heart in those who, believing themselves to be something when they are nothing, think that with a few tears they have washed away the abominable stains of crimes without fruits of repentance? For true repentance does not consist in momentary tears or hourly compunction.” [Col. 0783C]

And finally:

> “You surely see how pleasing to God is the sacrifice of tears, and how sufficient a burnt offering it is for every offence. But for whom? For those confessing, repenting, not returning to their vomit, but fleeing in a spirit of humility and a contrite heart to the merciful bosom of Jesus, and continually producing fruits worthy of repentance.”

Busaeus thought that our Peter, by these words—“Would it not have been more advisable for you to be purified by a brief contrition and confession of heart than to await that conflagration?”—seemed to imply that a person who is contrite and has confessed is not bound to make satisfaction to God for sins in this life, but may without penalty postpone satisfaction to be rendered in the other life, in purgatory. Yet he rashly attributes this opinion to the man of Blois.

Indeed, if he had any basis for his view, it would be this alone: that when the author says, “to be purified by a brief contrition and confession of heart,” [Col. 0783D] he mentions contrition and confession, but is silent about satisfaction. But this has no force whatever. First, because just before this he had likewise mentioned confession while suppressing the name of contrition: “so that whatever filth or rust confession has not cleansed in them,” etc. Yet one could not correctly infer that contrition is unnecessary because the man of Blois here enumerates confession alone.

Moreover, he also mentions satisfaction as necessary in the work cited: both where he says that Christ has mercifully assigned us three purgatories, namely contrition of heart, confession of mouth, and affliction of the flesh; and where he writes:

> “If, therefore, repentance seems burdensome to you, consider that Gehenna is incomparably more burdensome. Exercise yourself in tears, vigils, fasts, and disciplines; nor let it seem absurd to you if your head sometimes aches because of repentance, when it has more often ached from drunkenness; if your belly growls, though frequent gluttony has choked it. Thus the pus of sin must not merely be wiped away but scraped off by the harshness of pain. Then indeed you scrape away the pus with a potsherd, like blessed Job, if by stricter repentance you wipe away filthy pleasures.” [Col. 0785B]

[Col. 0785C] He also refutes those who think that they have washed away the abominable stains of crimes with a few tears and without fruits of repentance; and, finally, he requires perseverance in fruits worthy of repentance.

Certainly penitents are bound to fulfil their penance in this life by ecclesiastical command: Lateran Council, canon *Omnis utriusque sexus*, etc.: “Let him endeavour, according to his strength, to fulfil the penance imposed.” Indeed, that they are bound to this very thing by force of divine command is plainly inferred from the Council of Trent, session 14, chapter 8, which declares that priests ought, insofar as spirit and prudence suggest, according to the character of the crimes and the capacity of the penitents, to impose salutary and suitable satisfactions; and that they must keep before their eyes that the satisfaction they impose is not only for the preservation of a new life, but also for the avenging and chastisement of past sins.

The Council adds:

> “For the ancient Fathers also believed and taught that the keys of priests were granted not only for loosing, but also for binding.” [Col. 0785D]

But if priests are commanded, by reason of their office—because the keys were given them for binding as well as loosing—to impose penance upon those confessing, it follows that those confessing are also commanded to accept it. Yet they would be bound in vain to accept it if, once accepted, they were free either to fulfil it or not to fulfil it.

This truth is confirmed by the other matters contained in the same chapter. The Synod teaches that satisfaction to God, perpetually commended by our Fathers to the Christian people, is required because the principle of divine justice seems to demand that those who sinned through ignorance before baptism should be received into grace in one manner, but those in another who, once delivered from the slavery of sin and the devil and having received the gift of the Holy Spirit, have not feared knowingly to violate the temple of God and grieve the Holy Spirit. How otherwise, if penitents are received into grace by God even though they intend not to fulfil satisfaction [Col. 0786B] in this life, but to defer it for performance in the other life, in purgatory?

The Synod teaches that it befits divine clemency not to forgive us sins without any satisfaction in such a way that, taking occasion from this and regarding sins as lighter, we should, as persons injurious and insulting to the Holy Spirit, fall into more grievous sins, [Col. 0786C] storing up wrath for ourselves on the day of wrath. But if a penitent is permitted to postpone satisfaction to the other life, will he not, taking occasion from this and regarding sins as lighter, fall, as one injurious and insulting to the Holy Spirit, into more grievous sins and store up wrath for himself on the day of wrath?

The Synod teaches that these satisfactive punishments greatly recall persons from sin and restrain them, as it were, with a bridle; they make penitents more cautious and watchful for the future. They also heal the remnants of sins and remove vicious habits acquired by evil living through contrary actions of the virtues. Those who refuse to fulfil penance here voluntarily deprive themselves of so many and such great aids and remedies.

The Synod teaches that no safer path has ever been considered in the Church of God for removing punishment impending from the Lord than that people should frequently practise these works of repentance with true sorrow of heart. Therefore, those who defer works of repentance to the other life are pleased [Col. 0786D] not to remove from themselves the punishment impending from God.

The Synod teaches that, while we suffer for sins in making satisfaction, we are made conformable to Christ Jesus, who made satisfaction for our sins; and that from this we also have the most certain pledge that, if we suffer with him, we shall also be glorified with him. Therefore those who refuse to make satisfaction here do not care to be made conformable to Christ Jesus; they do not wish to suffer with him and be glorified with him.

Such, then, is their condition, to compress much into little: they approach repentance with the same ease with which they would approach baptism. They themselves give themselves occasion to commit more grievous sins. They cast away the bridles by which they might be restrained from sin. They disdain to use the means by which they might become more watchful and cautious in the future. Finally, they make little account of healing the remnants of their offences, removing vicious habits, fleeing the impending wrath of God, suffering with Christ, and therefore being glorified with Christ.

[Note: [Col. 0781D] Isaiah 4.] Would it not have been more advisable for you to be purified by a brief contrition and confession of heart than to await that conflagration [Note: [Col. 0784A]

The author holds that souls in purgatory are burned by corporeal fire, following Gregory the Great, in the passage cited, in these words:

> “We say that a spirit is held by fire so that, in the torment of fire, it may be punished by seeing and feeling. For it suffers fire precisely because it sees it; and because it sees itself being burned, it is burned. Thus it comes about that a corporeal thing burns an incorporeal one, when from visible fire an invisible burning and pain are drawn, so that even an incorporeal mind may be tortured by a corporeal flame,” etc.

Yet this doctrine concerning burning fire is not certain and indubitable among all theologians. For first, some freely confess that the manner in which souls suffer from corporeal fire in purgatory is unknown to them. Hugh of St Victor, *On the Sacraments*, book II, part XVI, chapter 3, proposes to himself this question: “How can souls without bodies suffer from bodily things?” He answers thus:

> “Let us say this: we do not know how this can happen. Does it therefore cease to be true because we do not know how it is?”

And below:

> “Yet because all these things of which we have spoken cannot be investigated by human reasoning, we establish our minds firmly upon those things which undoubting faith proves: namely, that sinful souls which did not correct their fault in this life have punishment after this life. Although we do not understand how it is felt by them, what does it matter, since it is no less felt by them even though it is not understood by us?”

Albert the Great, on book IV, distinction 20, article 5:

> “What kind of fire the fire of purgatory is, I do not think anyone knows, unless it has been revealed to him by God.” [Col. 0784C]

Finally, the same opinion is expressed in those words by Dionysius the Carthusian, on book IV, distinction 20, question 1.

Others think that souls in purgatory do not suffer from fire in reality, but only through a certain resemblance and accommodation: namely, because their spiritual affliction, arising from the beatific vision’s being delayed to them, and their supreme spiritual pain, are said by resemblance and accommodation to arise from fire, since supreme sensible pain arises in reality from fire, which is supremely active. Thus Durandus, on book IV, distinction 44, question 11, §13.

Before him, several others held the same view, of whom St Bonaventure speaks in book IV, distinction 44, article 3, question 2, and Richard of Mediavilla in the same distinction, article 38, question 9.

St Thomas, *Against the Gentiles*, book IV, chapter 90, explains the punishment of fire endured by the separated soul through its binding to corporeal fire:

> “Incorporeal substances,” he says, “suffer from corporeal fire by way of a certain binding.” [Col. 0784D]

And below:

> “And this itself is an affliction to them: that they know themselves to be bound as a punishment to lower things. The punishment which a nobler substance suffers precisely because it is bound to a lower substance is not properly called burning.”

But to suffer from fire by way of binding is not properly to be burned by fire. Hence Dominic Soto, on book IV, distinction 19, question 3, article 2, says that souls suffer not only in this way, as though shut up in a prison, but also through sorrow, as though they were being burned in bodies.

Third, those who explained this punishment as a torture properly inflicted by fire proposed this opinion only as probable. So Bonaventure, Richard of Mediavilla, Soto, and others.]

, although it is not eternal, surely exceeds all [Col. 0784A] the pains of the present life and all the distresses of our sensuous nature [Note: [Col. 0784D] The same is found in Peter the Chanter, *Verbi abbreviati*, chapter 146.]?

And behold, Moses and Elijah appeared with him [Note: [Col. 0783D] Matthew 17]. [Col. 0785A] Since Christ is Lord of the Law and the Prophets, rightly the greatest prophet and the most renowned lawgiver are said to appear with him [Note: [Col. 0785] Numbers 12]: each an inhabitant of Christ’s glory, each privy to the secrets of God, each a forty-day faster. Thus Elijah appears with him, most severe; and Moses, the meekest of all who dwell upon earth.

Moses repeatedly endured with patience the reproaches and threats of the Jewish people, and sometimes fled to the tabernacle in order to avoid the people as they rushed upon him. Yet when the Lord said, “Let me alone, that my wrath may be kindled against them and I may destroy them, and I will make you into a great nation,” he answered: “If you are willing to forgive, forgive; but if not, blot me out of your book” [Note: [Col. 0785] Exodus 32]. Behold a meekness which exceeds every measure of meekness and every abundance [Col. 0785B] of kindness.

Elijah, by contrast, because of the wickedness of the idolatrous king, shut up heaven for three years and six months and withheld the benefit of rainwater [Note: [Col. 0785] 3 Kings 17; James 5]. He killed four hundred prophets of Baal [Col. 0786A] together with another three hundred at the torrent Kishon [Note: [Col. 0785] Judges 4]. He consumed two captains of fifty with their hundred men by the sending of heavenly fire [Note: [Col. 0785] 3 Kings 18; 4 Kings 1]. Behold manifest and just severity. They therefore appear with him: on the one hand merciful and meek, on the other severe and just [Note: [Col. 0785] Psalm 144].

For while the Lord is merciful and compassionate [Note: [Col. 0785] Psalm 144], he is just and loves righteousness [Note: [Col. 0785] Psalm 10]. All the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth [Note: [Col. 0785] Psalm 24]. And it should be noted that Moses comes from the lower world, Elijah from heaven, and Peter, James, and John from the earth, so that heavenly, earthly, and infernal beings may bear witness to the glorification of him to whom every knee bends, of beings in heaven, on earth, and under the earth [Note: [Col. 0785] Philippians 2].

They spoke, moreover, as another Evangelist [Note: [Col. 0785] Luke 9] relates, about the departure—that is, Christ’s death—which may deservedly be called a departure because it exceeds every kind of humility. Surely we must believe that those speak with Christ whose intention, whose glory, whose desire is to be with Christ, who know and relish nothing but [Col. 0787A] Christ. “This,” says the Apostle, “is eternal life: that they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent” [Note: [Col. 0787] John 17].

Peter then answered and said to Jesus, etc. [Note: [Col. 0787] Matthew 17]. As the desires of the saints speak with Christ and in Christ, so saints sometimes answer their own desires, supposing it to be as though there had been a word expressing the vehemence of their wish which had preceded. Thus Mary Magdalene, when she does not find Christ in the tomb, when she runs about in anxious concern, when she expends all her affections in seeking him, says: “If you have taken him away, tell me” [Note: [Col. 0787] John 20]. “Him,” she says, as though something had preceded to which the meaning of the pronoun could refer.

For holy souls, inflamed by love of Christ and desire [Col. 0787B] for the heavenly homeland, become foolish through a kind of blessed error; wholly forgetful of themselves, they answer not the words which have preceded but the thoughts of their own mind. “Lord, it is good for us to be here; if you wish, let us make three tabernacles here” [Note: [Col. 0787] Matthew 17].

Peter asks that three tabernacles be made for Christ, Moses, and Elijah, entirely forgetful of himself; as though a pilgrim away from the body and rapt into the delights of the heavenly vision, he makes no mention of a tabernacle for himself or his fellow disciples. Contemplation of the divine majesty yielded to him the fulfilment of his desires; for he had found a place of rest, the secrecy of solitude, the serenity of light, a dwelling of peace, a shelter from the heat of day [Note: [Col. 0787] Isaiah 25], and a hiding-place from whirlwind and rain [Note: [Col. 0787] Isaiah 4].

What are you doing, Peter? Do you wish to make a tabernacle on earth for him [Col. 0787C] who dwells in heaven, who chose to live on earth in such a way that he had nowhere to lay his head [Note: [Col. 0787] Luke 9]? You were recalling, Peter, paradise—the first fruits of ancient happiness, the delights of human creation—how the first man, a fellow citizen and companion of angels, surrounded and supported by flowers [Note: [Col. 0787] Song of Songs 2], crowned with glory and honour [Note: [Col. 0787] Hebrews 2], felt neither want nor trouble; and so, from desire, you said to the Lord: “Lord, it is good for us to be here.”

The Prophet, anxiously panting for the glory of this vision and desiring a free departure to heaven, mournfully lamented the bonds of the flesh and the prison of this body, saying: “Bring my soul out of prison, O Lord” [Note: [Col. 0787] Psalm 141]. Paul too had found in the third heaven the treasure of this blessed contemplation; and so, drawn by the affection of the same desire, [Col. 0787D] he said: “I desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ” [Note: [Col. 0787] Philippians 1]. And: “Wretched man that I am, who shall deliver me from the body of this death?” [Note: [Col. 0787] Romans 7].

Jacob had ascended here, and therefore, glorying and exulting, said: “I have seen the Lord, and my soul has been saved” [Note: [Col. 0787] Genesis 32]. O happy ones who have deserved to ascend to the citadel of this contemplation! O blessed condition of the angels, who continually behold the most desired face of Christ! They sit at the rich man’s table and are fed [Col. 0788A] in delights from the fat of wheat [Note: [Col. 0787] Psalm 80].

But while we are in the body, while we are away from the Lord, we are fed only with a certain husk and bran of the sacrament. Grain with chaff is set before us—that is, truth beneath the veil of faith. And this is what we believe the Prophet foresaw when he said: “The foals of asses that till the ground shall eat a mixed mash” [Note: [Col. 0787] Isaiah 30], that is, barley with chaff. For Christ sets before us the sacraments of the Church as a consolation during expectation, that we may be sustained by them until he appears glorious in his saints.

Then hope will pass into possession, image into truth, remembrance into presence, time into eternity, the husk of bran into flour. Then we shall be satisfied with the glory of his face. “I shall be satisfied,” says the Prophet, “when your glory shall appear” [Note: [Col. 0787] Psalm 16]. [Col. 0788B] And the Apostle: “When Christ, our life, shall appear, then we too shall appear with him in glory” [Note: [Col. 0787] Colossians 3].

While he was still speaking, behold, a bright cloud overshadowed them [Note: [Col. 0787] Matthew 17]. As the Apostle relates, from the creation of the world the invisible things of God are clearly seen, being understood through the things that are made [Note: [Col. 0787] Romans 1]. Hence, if these things which were seen in the sacred Transfiguration are carefully considered, the whole Trinity will be most plainly known to have been present.

Since Christ is God from God, light from light, he rightly appeared in light, according to the saying: “Lord, in your light we shall see light” [Note: [Col. 0787] Psalm 35]. The Holy Spirit was in the cloud; formerly he led the children of Israel out of Egypt in a pillar of cloud and baptized them in the cloud and in the sea [Note: [Col. 0787] Exodus 14; 1 Corinthians 10]. Thus the Son shines forth in light, [Col. 0788C] and the Holy Spirit overshadows in a cloud.

And lest you doubt that the whole Trinity is present, the Father is heard in the voice. For a voice came from heaven: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; he in whom I was displeased in Adam—hear him” [Note: [Col. 0787] Matthew 17; Luke 9]. This is the word which Moses formerly used, saying: “God will raise up a prophet from among your brethren; hear him as you would me. Whoever does not hear him shall be exterminated from his people” [Note: [Col. 0787] Deuteronomy 18; Acts 2].

The Father confirms Moses’ word concerning the Son, so that Scripture may agree and all may understand that Moses foresaw this concerning Christ and not another. For Christ discloses what Moses wrote concerning him when he says: “If you believed Moses, you would believe me also, for he wrote of me” [Note: [Col. 0787] John 5].

Rightly, “my Son”: not by adoption, but by nature; not temporal, but eternal; not from another, [Col. 0788D] but consubstantial; beloved eternally and uniquely most beloved. Of him it was said through the Prophet: “Behold my servant whom I have chosen, my elect one; my soul has taken pleasure in him” [Note: [Col. 0787] Isaiah 42; Matthew 12]. He is rightly called beloved whom, above all things, one must love before all others. Truly beloved, of whom the bride says in the Song of Songs: “I am my beloved’s, and my beloved is mine” [Note: [Col. 0787] Song of Songs 6]. Thousands of thousands and hundreds of thousands [Note: [Col. 0787] Daniel 7] are with the beloved. And I come to the beloved.

It is no wonder that he is loved [Col. 0789A] by the Father, since he is the Only-begotten from the Father. The Father loves the Son [Note: [Col. 0789] John 5]: the eternal loves the coeternal, the highest the equal, the loving one the one who loves. For as the Son is loved by the Father, so Christ also loves the Father. This is what is said in the Gospel: the Father glorifies the Son, and that same Father is glorified by the Son [Note: [Col. 0789] John 17]. The evangelical history therefore recounts the reciprocal glorification between Father and Son, lest the Son seem lesser than the Father, and lest he be thought, as one without glory, not to possess his glory from himself.

The Son asks to be glorified with the glory which he had before the world was made. Certainly the Son’s glory is not later than the Father’s glory; for as he is equal to the Father in the substance of divinity, so he is coeternal with him in the glory of splendour.

And the disciples fell on their faces and were exceedingly afraid [Col. 0789B] [Note: [Col. 0789] Matthew 17]. If Peter, prince of the Apostles, and James and John, who were the strongest pillars of the Church, could not endure the majesty of the divine presence, what shall we miserable people do on that day of dreadful judgment? In that judgment equity will be so great, the judge’s severity so great, the majesty’s sublimity so great, and in the very countenance there will be such terrible and unheard-of novelty, that, as the Prophet testifies: “The day of his coming cannot be imagined. And he is a man—who shall stand to see him?” [Note: [Col. 0789] Malachi 3].

What do you think will happen when that consuming fire [Note: [Col. 0789] Hebrews 12]—that is, the judge of the living and the dead—comes in the greatness, strength, wrath, and truth of his divinity against a leaf carried by the wind, to show his power and pursue dry stubble [Col. 0789C] [Note: [Col. 0789] Job 13]? Angels and archangels will fear; and who shall free us from everlasting terrors?

Therefore I am troubled by faintness of spirit and tempest. I fear the wrath of the Mighty One, the face of fury, the crashing of the world, the conflagration of the elements, the voice of the archangel, the harsh word, the belly of hell, those roaring creatures prepared for food. Do not remember, Lord, my iniquities; do not weigh in the balance my sins, by which I have deserved wrath [Note: [Col. 0789] Daniel 6]. “If you observe iniquities, O Lord, Lord, who shall endure?” [Note: [Col. 0789] Psalm 129].

Who, I say, shall endure the heats of fires, the coldness of snows, the pressure of chains that weigh down, bind tight, burn, and do not consume? “Where are your ancient mercies, O Lord?” [Note: [Col. 0789] Psalm 88]. Certainly, considering my iniquities and recalling my years in the bitterness of my soul, I should have fallen into [Col. 0789D] the pit of despair, unless that dreadful Judge had as his own special property always to pity and spare.

For I know that he will not hide his mercy forever, nor will God forget to have mercy; but in wrath he will remember mercy. The Son of Man will have mercy upon human beings. And when his wrath has blazed forth briefly, as he will be terrible to the lost, so he will be gentle to those who hope in him. He will therefore free those who fear him from evil tidings; his mercy will be upon his saints, and his regard upon his chosen ones.

To signify this, after the terrible vision Christ approaches the disciples as a kindly comforter and says: “Rise, and do not be afraid.” But when they lifted their eyes, they saw no one except Jesus alone [Note: [Col. 0789] Matthew 17]. Moses and Elijah vanished from the eyes of the Apostles, and they saw only Jesus, because, once the veil in the figures of the Law and the Prophets had been removed, the grace of evangelical truth appeared in the things previously set forth.

Moreover, in the phrase “lifting,” it should be noted that the higher anyone raises the eyes of his reflection, the less he comprehends of the nature of the divine essence. For a person approaches a deep heart, and God shall be exalted [Note: [Col. 0789] Psalm 63]. Therefore David did not walk in things great and wonderful beyond himself, but thought humbly [Note: [Col. 0789] Proverbs 25]. Therefore Paul, lest, as an investigator of majesty, he should be overwhelmed [Col. 0790B] by glory, since the Wise Man says, “Do not seek things higher than yourself, and do not investigate things stronger than yourself” [Note: [Col. 0789] Ecclesiasticus 3], proposed to know nothing else except Christ Jesus, and him crucified [Note: [Col. 0789] 1 Corinthians 2].

For he did not wish heavenly secrets to be concealed. Hence, having been caught up into the third heaven, he testifies that he saw things which it is not permitted for a human being to speak [Note: [Col. 0789] 2 Corinthians 12]. Hence Moses, coming forth from God’s secret presence, veils his face [Note: [Col. 0789] Exodus 34].

And as they were coming down from the mountain, Jesus commanded them, saying: “Tell the vision to no one until the Son of Man rises from the dead” [Note: [Col. 0789] Matthew 17]. For what is holy must not be given to dogs, nor pearls cast before swine [Note: [Col. 0789] Matthew 7]. This would indeed have happened if Christ’s mysteries had been made public either unwisely or untimely before the confirmation of our faith, which Christ’s resurrection strengthened.

For by that very publication [Col. 0790C] they would have become cheap, and would have hindered the new plantations of faith and the first fruits of the nascent Church, if the disciples had proclaimed the glory of Christ which they had seen when they were soon to see him vile and rejected, hanging shamefully on the cross. They would have greatly detracted from the authority of their preaching and generated scandal for the weak.

Therefore, dearest brothers, let us celebrate the memory of this glorious vision with most devout affection. For if that day is recalled with veneration, on which Christ, descending from the right hand of God the Father, appeared to us without glory and in weakness, we must believe that day should be recalled with honour and reverence on which Christ appeared to us glorious in this our weakness. This is the day on which the disciples behold Christ [Col. 0790D] as the Only-begotten from the Father, as a king in his beauty.

Moreover, since there are different kinds of visions, this one is to be preferred to all. Some occurred before grace, some under grace; this one is in glory. Some occurred in night, some in day; this one is in light. “I saw,” says Ezekiel, “in a vision of the night” [Note: [Col. 0789] Daniel 7]. Paul was caught up into the third heaven. “The night has passed,” he says; “the day has drawn near” [Note: [Col. 0789] Romans 13]. Behold a vision of night; behold a vision of day.

In this present vision, therefore, the certainty of the future resurrection is expressed. [Col. 0791A] In it there is set before us a pledge and earnest of that most blessed vision, in which there is day without night, rest without labour, and glory without end. May he who reigns and rules as God with the Father and the Holy Spirit mercifully deign to prepare and grant it to us through all ages of ages. Amen. [Col. 0792A]

[Col. 0791]

## ON THE CONVERSION OF ST PAUL

[Col. 0791A] The conversion of blessed Paul ought to be commemorated with rejoicing, dearest brothers. For if there is joy among God’s angels over one sinner doing repentance [Note: [Col. 0791] Luke 15], we too ought to rejoice with more eager gladness in one in whom we have a mirror of teaching, a pattern of repentance, [Col. 0791B] and an example of conversion and manner of life. Though he had been a vessel of blasphemy, a vessel of insult and wrath, he became a vessel of honour, a vessel of election and grace.

“I was a blasphemer,” he says, “but I obtained mercy” [Note: [Col. 0791] 1 Timothy 1]. For from a wolf he became a lamb; from an enemy, a member of the household; from a persecutor, a son; from a torturer, a teacher; from one who corrupted, a disciple; from an assailant, a defender; from the most unbelieving, the holiest preacher of the faith. Truly great and unutterable are the works of God [Note: [Col. 0791] Psalm 110], and his mercies are over all his works [Note: [Col. 0791] Psalm 144].

For Saul, still breathing threats and slaughter against the disciples of the Lord, is adopted by Christ as a disciple [Note: [Col. 0791] Acts 9]; and he who, in the unbridled cruelty of his spirit, panted for the destruction of the Church is established as the Church’s firmest pillar. For the Father [Col. 0791C] of mercies chastens every son whom he receives [Note: [Col. 0791] Hebrews 12]. He chastens Saul that he may receive him, blinds him that he may enlighten him, casts him down that he may raise him, afflicts him that he may heal him, weakens him that he may strengthen him.

Saul had received letters for a most cruel mission, that if he found any men or women belonging to this Way, he might bring them to Jerusalem. Yet the just Judge, who humbles every height that exalts itself against the knowledge of God, who does not permit his own to be tempted beyond what they can bear, but with the temptation also provides the outcome, so that they may be able to endure it [Note: [Col. 0791] 1 Corinthians 10], will judge on behalf of the meek of the earth [Note: [Col. 0791] Isaiah 11] and will save *p. v. ca.* [reading uncertain].

As Saul was therefore travelling, it happened that he approached Damascus, and suddenly a light from heaven shone around him [Note: [Col. 0791] Acts 9]. For outward light shines around one who was covered by the inward darkness of ignorance. And falling to the ground he heard a voice [Note: [Col. 0791] ibid.], which he had not deserved to hear while he stood in the way of sinners. Light alone does not suffice for faith, and therefore the hearing of a voice is added: [Col. 0792A] “Faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of God” [Note: [Col. 0791] Romans 10; Acts 9].

“Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?” He who says in the Gospel, “As long as you did it to one of the least of mine, you did it to me” [Note: [Col. 0791] Matthew 25], counts the injury done to his own as done to himself. Nor in these words does he confess himself [Col. 0792B] subject to death or persecution, since he is immortal and incapable of suffering; rather, the affection of his love for the disciples is expressed: having loved them before, he loved them to the end.

The same is confirmed by the story of Peter, who, when fleeing from Rome, asked the Saviour whom he encountered: “Lord, where are you going?” He heard: “I am going to Rome to be crucified again” [Note: [Col. 0791D] “Pope Innocent III, almost a contemporary of our man of Blois, recounts this event once and again in his sermons. Then blessed Gregory, on the fourth penitential psalm; Hesychius, *On the Destruction of Jerusalem*, book III; St Ambrose, *Against Auxentius, on the Handing Over of the Basilicas*; St Athanasius, in the book *On His Flight*; Linus, in the *History of the Death of the Apostles Peter and Paul*. Read Onuphrius Panvinius, *On the Seven Churches of the City*, and Caesar Baronius, volume I of the *Annals of the Church*.”].

Here Christ is described as in some sense to be crucified in the person whom he adopted as a member of himself. Thus, sympathizing with his members, Christ is angry at Saul as he rages against his disciples; but because it is always his special property to pity and spare, in anger he remembers mercy [Note: [Col. 0791] Habakkuk 3]. Therefore he restrains him, as one maddened, lest he tumble headlong into the precipice of eternal death; and he checks him as he kicks against the goad, lest he be wounded.

[Col. 0792C] “It is hard for you,” he says, “to kick against the goad.” And he: “Who are you, Lord?” “I,” he says, “am Jesus of Nazareth, whom you are persecuting” [Note: [Col. 0791] Acts 9.]. He could have declared who he was in majestic and terrifying words, saying: “I am the Lord, God of vengeance” [Note: [Col. 0791] Ps. 93], “who look upon the earth and make it tremble; I touch the mountains and they smoke” [Note: [Col. 0791] Ps. 103]. But he answers gently, in order to awaken him to hope and invite him to faith. “Lord,” Saul adds, “what do you want me to do?” [Note: [Col. 0791] Acts 9.] At the voice of divine correction, the persecutor’s pride is humbled; severity melts away in Saul, and unbridled fury is gentled into grace. The wild olive is cut down so that a fruitful olive may be planted in the house of the Lord; the wolf is changed into a sheep, the buckthorn into a vine, [Col. 0792D] the heron into a dove, the assassin into an apostle, the blasphemer into a saint, Saul into Paul. He who changes Saul’s life changes his name also, according to the word of Isaiah [Note: [Col. 0791] Ch. 65]: “And he shall call his servants by another name.” Truly, this conversion and change is the right hand of the Most High [Note: [Col. 0791] Ps. 76].

In [Col. 0793A] the right hand of the Most High are two things: power and mercy, as it is written: “These two things have I heard: that power belongs to God, and to you, O Lord, belongs mercy” [Note: [Col. 0793] Ps. 61]. Power humbles Saul; mercy lifts him up. Power reproves and converts the perverse man; mercy consoles and raises up the convert. Power instils fear and trembling; mercy supplies consolation and exultation, so that Saul may both rejoice and fear with the Prophet, and say to the Lord: “Let my heart rejoice, that it may fear your name” [Note: [Col. 0793] Ps. 85].

There are many who, when reproved by the Lord, harden themselves in their obstinacy after the manner of Pharaoh and do not feel the merciful lashes of discipline that should bring amendment. Of such people the Lord complains through Jeremiah, saying: “I have slain and destroyed my people, and yet [Col. 0793B] they have not turned back from their ways” [Note: [Col. 0793] Jer. 15]. And elsewhere: “We have treated Babylon, and she has not been healed” [Note: [Col. 0793] Jer. 51].

But Saul carefully recalled the saying of Wisdom: “Agree with your adversary while you are with him on the way, lest he hand you over to the judge, and the judge to the torturer” [Note: [Col. 0793] Matt. 5]. Therefore, struck by the rod of paternal correction, he humbly submits himself to obedience; and, as though offering himself in satisfaction, he asks the will of the one who lashes him: “Lord, what do you want me to do?” “Rise,” he says, “and enter the city, and there you will be told what you must do” [Note: [Col. 0793] Acts 9].

Cast down on the road, he is sent into the city to be instructed. For the most kindly teacher of justice and mercy wished him to be taught gently and companionably by a human being, since he knew that he could not endure the thunder of the divine [Col. 0793C] voice. Thus Moses spoke between God and the people of Israel. For they said: “Speak to us yourself, lest the Lord speak to us and we die” [Note: [Col. 0793] Exod. 20].

Now Saul rose from the ground, and, though his eyes were open, he saw nothing [Note: [Col. 0793] Acts 9]. A light from heaven had shone around him, but that light which enlightens every human being coming into this world had not yet fully shone upon him [Note: [Col. 0793] John 1]. Those leading him by the hands brought him into Damascus [Note: [Col. 0793] Acts 9]. He was being led outwardly by the hands, while inwardly the Lord was drawing him from the filth of this life, that he might run after the fragrance of his ointments [Note: [Col. 0793] Song 1]. For unless he were drawn, he could not come to him who says: “No one comes to me unless my Father draws him” [Note: [Col. 0793] John 6].

O most gracious recompense of the Saviour: he is drawn by Christ into life who used to drag Christ’s disciples to death. The confession of the thief on the cross, the repentance of the sinful woman Magdalene, the devotion of the tax collector, the entreaty of the Canaanite woman, and Peter’s tears had established for us a most firm foundation of hope and confidence; but Saul’s conversion raises still more abundantly and fully the overflowing mercy of God, for it so utterly changes the persecutor’s life that afterward he declares that not he lives in himself, but Christ lives in him. “I live,” [Col. 0794A] he says, “yet no longer I; rather Christ lives in me” [Note: [Col. 0793] Gal. 2].

“And he was there three days without sight, and neither ate nor drank” [Note: [Col. 0793] Acts 9]. For three days he did not see, though he was being prepared as a light for the revelation of the Gentiles [Note: [Col. 0793] Luke 2]. For three days he did not eat—he for whom the bread of life and the refreshment of angels were being prepared.

Now there was a disciple in Damascus named Ananias, and the Lord said to him in a vision: “Ananias.” And he said: “Here I am, Lord.” And the Lord said to him: “Rise and go into the street” [Note: [Col. 0793] Acts 9], etc. He goes to Saul in order to give light to the blind, loose the bound man, bring back the wanderer, reconcile the guilty, console the afflicted, strengthen the weak in faith, feed the fasting man, and cleanse the unclean by baptism. But Ananias had hidden himself in secret, fearing the persecutor’s presence. [Col. 0794B] For there was a boiling pot from the north; nevertheless there was a watchful rod [Note: [Col. 0793] Jer. 1], an iron rod that breaks the potter’s vessel [Note: [Col. 0793] Ps. 2], so that from hardened clay a golden vessel might be fashioned.

But Ananias answered: “Lord, I have heard from many about this man, how many evils he has done to your saints in Jerusalem,” etc. And the Lord said to him: “Go, for this man is a vessel of election to me, to bear my name before Gentiles and kings and the children of Israel. For I shall show him how much he must suffer for my name” [Note: [Col. 0793] Acts 9]. “Your testimonies, Lord, have become exceedingly trustworthy” [Note: [Col. 0793] Ps. 92]. For the Church frequently recounts the Apostle’s afflictions: how for a very long time he was in abundant labours, in stripes beyond measure, frequently in deaths; how five times he received from the Jews forty lashes [Col. 0794C] less one, and three times was beaten with rods [Note: [Col. 0793] 2 Cor. 11], etc.

By these and other means, fighting in the arena of this world, he completed his triumph by his sword and offered his blood, in the name of Jesus Christ, to God the Father as an evening sacrifice. This is Benjamin, the young man in ecstasy of mind. This is Benjamin, the ravening wolf, devouring prey in the morning and dividing spoils in the evening [Note: [Col. 0793] Ps. 67]. Saul is especially signified by Benjamin because he derived his origin from the tribe of Benjamin [Note: [Col. 0793] Gen. 48], as he himself testifies in the Epistle to the Romans [Note: [Col. 0793] Ch. 11]: “I too,” he says, “am an Israelite, of the seed of Abraham, of the tribe of Benjamin.”

And just as Benjamin was the last-born among Jacob’s sons, so Paul was the latest among Christ’s disciples in conversion and calling [Col. 0794D] [Note: [Col. 0793] 1 Cor. 15]. While the others had advanced, through growth in virtues, toward the mature state of mind upon Christ’s teaching, he was still new in faith and, as it were, a youth. Hence he calls himself an untimely birth among the rest. But, caught up to the third heaven in ecstasy of mind, he contemplated God’s ineffable mysteries [Note: [Col. 0793] 2 Cor. 12], and he redeemed and made up for the delay of his calling and the loss of time through the greatness of his revelations and the multiplied fruit of his preaching.

The [Col. 0795A] ravening wolf, devouring prey in the morning, divides the spoils in the evening: in the early age, as it were the morning of his life, he persecuted the Lord’s flock; in the evening of his conversion he distributes to the Lord the spoils taken from the devil, and, apportioning diverse offices in the Church of God, adorned Christ’s bride with varieties. It follows:

“And Ananias went and entered the house, and, laying his hands upon him, said,” etc. “And immediately there fell from his eyes as it were scales, and he received sight” [Note: [Col. 0795] Acts 9]. These are the scales of Behemoth, of which we read in Job [Note: [Col. 0795] Ch. 41], that one is joined to another and no breath of life passes through them. These are worldly enticements and the bonds of impiety, dissolved through the laying on of hands by the breath of the Holy Spirit.

Thus [Col. 0795B] he received sight, who a little before had been walking in darkness; and he is refreshed by heavenly bread, being destined to give the bread of life to the hungry, moreover to scatter among the Gentiles the seed of the divine word and gather the most abundant sheaves of faith. “And rising up, he was baptized” [Note: [Col. 0795] Acts 9]. Rising from the dust of vanity and the mire of sin, in the sanctified waters he puts off the old man; and, according to the word of the prophet, the Ethiopian lays aside his blackness and the leopard his spots [Col. 0796A] in baptism [Note: [Col. 0795] Jer. 13].

“And immediately, entering the synagogues, he preached Jesus, that he is the Son of God” [Note: [Col. 0795] Acts 9]. The finger of God, who wrote the law of life in human hearts, does not know how to delay. Hence a sound from heaven suddenly came upon the apostles [Note: [Col. 0795] Acts 2], and Saul, the vessel of election, immediately poured forth the sweetness of fragrance. “But Saul increased still more in strength and confounded the Jews living at Damascus, affirming that this is the Christ.” He steadfastly affirms concerning the Son of God that this is the Christ—he who a little before had stubbornly denied that Jesus was God’s Son.

Thus the Lord turns back from Bashan into the depths of the sea [Note: [Col. 0795] Ps. 67]; thus he raises up children of Abraham from stones [Note: [Col. 0795] Matt. 3]; and he sends forth his ice like morsels [Note: [Col. 0795] Ps. 147], when those frozen by the cold of dispersion and unbelief, hardened in their obstinacy, [Col. 0796B] are not only called to faith but are made ministers of God’s word. Thus the Lord not only calls Paul, once a persecutor, to faith, but makes him an apostle and teacher of the Gentiles, to give his people knowledge of salvation and to reveal the glory of our Lord, to whom belong honour and glory for ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 0795]

## A COMPENDIUM ON JOB. TO HENRY II, MOST ILLUSTRIOUS KING OF THE ENGLISH

[Col. 0795C] To HENRY, by the grace of God most illustrious king of the English, duke of Normandy and Aquitaine, and count of Anjou: his own PETER OF BLOIS, archdeacon of Bath, greeting in him who is true salvation.

I give thanks to the giver of grace, because you gladly hear what builds up unto salvation; and because, escaping the frying-pans of courtly anxieties and the intricate labyrinths of business, you willingly meditate upon the law of the Lord and, after your daily labours, take breath in the reading of the sacred page. For it is glorious in a prince to begin his daily actions with, and end them in, him who is the beginning and the end [Note: [Col. 0795] Rev. 1]; who is the beginning without a beginning and judges the ends of the earth.

You commanded me, after the likeness of those treatises which I had composed on the Transfiguration of the Lord and [Col. 0795D] the conversion of blessed Paul, to treat briefly and in a kind of compendium the life of holy Job, inserting only those matters which might more fully instruct you in patience and the other virtues [Note: [Col. 0795] Prov. 21]. Indeed, I consider this to have been divinely instilled into your heart—for the king’s heart is in God’s hand, and he turns it wherever he wills [Note: [Col. 0795] Ps. 2]—that you should wish willingly to set the life of holy Job and of the other ancient Fathers before the eyes of [Col. 0796C] your mind, so that you may be instructed by them, according to the Lord’s command through the Prophet: “Be instructed, you who judge the earth” [Note: [Col. 0795] Ibid.].

For by examples such as these faith is strengthened, hope raised up, charity nourished, pride cast down, humility preserved, devotion increased, and the desire to do good awakened. Thus the Lord caused the names of the sons of Israel to be written upon the breastplate of judgment, that they might be visible to all [Note: [Col. 0795] Exod. 28], and that others might take the life and conduct of the holy Fathers for their own following and example.

Therefore I undertake an arduous work and a burden of great weight: not because we are sufficient, as the Apostle says, to think anything of ourselves as from ourselves; but our sufficiency is from God [Note: [Col. 0795] 2 Cor. 3], from him who says: “Open your mouth, and I will fill [Col. 0796D] it” [Note: [Col. 0795] Ps. 80]. And again: “When you stand before kings and governors, do not consider what or how you shall answer; for in that hour there shall be given to you what you shall say” [Note: [Col. 0795] Matt. 10].

I shall begin, then, in the blessed name of him who is blessed for ever, humbly and earnestly entreating your magnificence to be willing patiently to endure the exhortation of your most devoted servant, [Col. 0797A] remembering that, when Moses was prince among God’s people, he gladly accepted Jethro’s counsel [Note: [Col. 0797] Exod. 18]; Peter, the prince of the apostles, did not reject Paul’s correction [Note: [Col. 0797] Gal. 2]; Balaam yielded to the voice of the she-ass [Note: [Col. 0797] Num. 22]; David, king and prophet, humbly endured the rebuke of Nathan, a lesser prophet [Note: [Col. 0797] 2 Sam. 12].

Jesus too, when he had remained at Jerusalem and said that he must be occupied with the things of his Father, although his parents did not assent to him, followed them to Nazareth: the king followed servants, the teacher disciples, God human beings, the Word of God and Wisdom a craftsman and a woman; and he was subject to them, as the Gospel narrative adds [Note: [Col. 0797] Luke 2].

I also ask the reader not to look here for the polish of a finished work. The roughness of a spare and unpolished style is excused both by lack [Col. 0797B] of time and by the pressures of court. For the business of the Church of Canterbury has made me, for a time, serve in the camp and follow the court. There I have neither bodily rest nor peace of mind, neither abundance of books nor leisure for writing, neither opportunity for study nor an unencumbered judgment of mind nor full freedom of choice. Therefore I compose this present work only from what God in his sweetness provides for the poor man, and from what I recall either having heard or read at some time.

## CHAPTER I. “There was a man in the land of Uz,” etc.

Three qualities are placed here: simple, upright, and fearing God. And because fear of God is the reason why we turn away from evil, there is added, “departing from evil,” [Col. 0797C] Scripture bearing witness when it says: “He who fears God will do good” [Note: [Col. 0797] Sir. 15]. And again: “Those who do evil have no fear of God before their eyes” [Note: [Col. 0797] Ps. 13].

Job is commended in three things: simplicity, uprightness, and fear. Now there is discerning simplicity and undiscerning simplicity; there is a simplicity akin to foolishness, and there is a simplicity commended in the Gospel: “Be,” he says, “wise as serpents and simple as doves” [Note: [Col. 0797] Matt. 10]. Job was simple in innocence, upright in justice, fearful in caution: simple toward himself, upright toward his neighbour, fearing toward God.

No one is upright unless he divides rightly. Cain offered well, but did not divide rightly [Note: [Col. 0797] Gen. 4]; indeed, he divided most wickedly, offering sacrifices to God while persecuting his innocent brother. [Col. 0797D] He is not upright who offers his tongue to God and his soul to the devil. He is not upright whose iniquities have passed over his head and have weighed heavily upon him like a heavy burden [Note: [Col. 0797] Ps. 37]. He is not upright whom avarice contracts, ambition torments, or pleasure bends; but upright is he who gives his voice the voice of virtue, speaking well and acting better. For the voice of action is better than the voice of the mouth. Job was therefore rightly upright: his deeds answered to his words. Rightly upright, whom pride did not puff up, [Col. 0798A] whom iniquity did not weigh down, whom adversity did not break. It follows:

“And fearing God.” He did not fear those who kill the body and afterward, as the Gospel says, have nothing more that they can do; but he feared him who can kill the body and destroy the soul in Gehenna [Note: [Col. 0797] Luke 12]. He feared not slavishly, on account of punishment, but with filial affection, on account of grace.

Four kinds of fear are distinguished in sacred discourse: worldly, servile, initial, and filial or chaste. Worldly fear is when we dread the danger of death or losses of temporal things. Servile fear is when we fear eternal pains and the torments of Gehenna. Initial fear is when someone begins to delight in keeping God’s commandments, when things that had seemed harsher [Col. 0798B] and more austere to him become sweet. Of this fear the Apostle says that charity casts out fear, because fear is not in charity [Note: [Col. 0797] 1 John 4]. Filial, or chaste, fear is when a wife fears to offend her husband, whom she loves above all things, or when a son fears to do something displeasing in the eyes of his most loving father. This fear arises not from dread but from love; this fear, in the testimony of the Prophet, remains for age upon age [Note: [Col. 0797] Ps. 18].

Thus Job feared God: “Blessed is the man who fears God” [Note: [Col. 0797] Ps. 111]. I have frequently experienced this in truth: nothing is more effective for meriting, retaining, and recovering grace than that a person should be found before God at all times not to think lofty things, but to fear. Therefore the Wise Man says: “Blessed is the man who is always fearful” [Note: [Col. 0797] Prov. 28].

Thus [Col. 0798C] Job—whose name means “sorrowing”—was in the land of Uz, which means “counsel”; simple, upright, and fearing God, because amid anxious sorrows and unbearable pressures he was comforted by divine counsel, and overcame the shrewd, impious, and proud enemy of the human race through simplicity, justice, and fear.

“And seven sons were born to him,” etc. In a multitude of children and an abundance of possessions, the happiness of this world is commonly thought to consist. Yet there is no happiness in this world, for the world and its desire pass away [Note: [Col. 0797] 1 John 2]. “I have seen all things that are under the sun,” says the Wise Man, “and all are vanity and affliction of spirit” [Note: [Col. 0797] Eccl. 1].

This most valiant soldier considered all these worldly things utterly worthless. His abundance [Col. 0798D] of offspring and enlargement in temporal goods are recounted in order to show how great was his constancy, since neither the death of so many children could shake him nor the loss of so many possessions disturb him. Thus God tests his gold in the furnace of justice; thus he proves his saint in adversities, in order to advance him to a crown and make him an example of patience, constancy, and humility both to princes of the world and to prelates of the Church.

“Unhappy man that I am, who will give water to my head and a fountain of tears to my eyes?” [Note: [Col. 0797] Jer. 9.] For those who [Col. 0799A] should have been imitators and followers of blessed Job’s constancy have reed-like minds: they yield to every breath, believe every spirit, are carried about by every wind; in judgments they melt under favour, in counsel they fail from fear; they are disturbed by sadness, contracted by avarice, drawn out by ambition, troubled by suspicions, seethe with anxieties, waste away with hatred, are gnawed by envy, burn with anger, swell with honours. They have eyes for gifts and give no heed to orphan or widow.

Indeed—what is far more grievous, and what I cannot set forth without a sorrowful groan—prelates melt together in the furnace of avarice Christ’s reproaches, spittle, scourges, nails, lance, cross, and death; enclosing in their money-bags the price of the whole world, they either distribute the crucified one’s patrimony to their nephews, [Col. 0799B] retain it damnably, or dissipate and squander it for extraordinary uses.

Do these wretches not consider that they will die? Do they not reflect that the Lord will demand from each person an account of his stewardship, or the honour due to his office of rule? “Therefore the wicked man has provoked God, for he has said in his heart, ‘He will not demand it’” [Note: [Col. 0799] Ps. 10]. But certainly he will demand it with the utmost exactness, to the last farthing, and will richly repay those who act proudly [Note: [Col. 0799] Ps. 30]. Therefore he will miserably destroy the wicked and lease his vineyard to other cultivators [Note: [Col. 0799] Matt. 21].

Woe to the workers in the vineyard of the Lord of hosts if they are cut off with the branches! Woe to shepherds if they are numbered on the left with the goats! Woe to fishers if they are cast out with the bad fish! Woe [Col. 0799C] to cultivators of the Lord’s harvest if they are burned with the chaff! These are the shepherds whom Isaiah reproaches, saying: “They were shepherds, and they did not understand understanding” [Note: [Col. 0799] Isa. 56]. And Jeremiah says [Note: [Col. 0799] Ch. 2]: “Those who held the law did not know me.”

Perhaps they are shepherds in that they feed themselves. As regards the care of the sheep, they are rather shearers than shepherds: they seek milk and wool in sheep, not salvation. Indeed, Leviticus commands [Note: [Col. 0799] Ch. 7] that priests should have in the sacrifices the right shoulder, set apart; so that a prelate’s action may not merely be holy, signified by the right side, but may be foremost in example and singular in merit, so that he may surpass his subjects in conduct as greatly as he surpasses them in rank.

Let each person, then, acknowledge the honour of his calling. Let him know that he is an angel of the Lord [Col. 0799D] of hosts [Note: [Col. 0799] Mal. 2]; let him know that he is the salt of the earth and the light of the world [Note: [Col. 0799] Matt. 5]. Let the prelate, I say, remember [Note: [Col. 0799] Bernard, Book 2, *On Consideration*] what predecessors he has had and whose dignity he retains. For he has Abel’s primacy, Abraham’s patriarchate, Noah’s governance, Melchizedek’s order, Aaron’s dignity, Moses’ authority, Samuel’s virtue, Peter’s power, and Christ’s anointing. He who does not exercise the office of administration entrusted to him must be accused and judged before God by all these.

What then is to be thought of clerics who take upon themselves the care of countless souls and do not care for their [Col. 0800A] salvation? There are many who have scarcely learned even the number of their churches, much less the souls for which they are bound to answer on the day of dreadful judgment. They join church to church, prebend to prebend, house to house, field to field. Of such people Isaiah says [Note: [Col. 0799] Ch. 5]: “Woe to you who join house to house and couple field to field, even to the boundary of the place!” And Habakkuk [Note: [Col. 0799] Ch. 2]: “Woe to him who multiplies what is not his without end, and heaps up against himself thick mud!”

Clerics, who ought to possess nothing, presume to possess everything. They do not labour, plough, sow, build, sail, or fight [Note: [Col. 0799] Exod. 32]; and, to use the Psalmist’s words: “They are not in the labour of human beings, nor shall they be scourged with human beings; therefore pride has taken hold of them” [Col. 0800B] [Note: [Col. 0799] Ps. 72].

O unhappy men, if only they were wise and understood and foresaw their latter end! If only the wretched understood what this phrase portends: “nor shall they be scourged with human beings”! Certainly, those who are not scourged with human beings in time will suffer eternal scourges with demons.

Monks and regular canons who have chosen the way of stricter life and holy leisure are indeed simple as doves [Note: [Col. 0799] Matt. 10], but in appearance, not deed; in dress, not disposition. “They will come to you,” says the Lord, “in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly they are ravening wolves” [Note: [Col. 0799] Matt. 7]. Today there is no law court or marketplace into which religious men do not intrude and upon which they do not most importunately press themselves. For, deceiving the world with a kind of counterfeit religion, [Col. 0800C] they are themselves most grievously deceived: though dead to the world, they conduct business and hunt after worldly things.

But if the Church is the kingdom of God, as we read, “The kingdom of God is within you” [Note: [Col. 0799] Luke 17], then, when they seize churches by force or purchase, I safely infer that the kingdom of God suffers violence, and the violent seize it [Note: [Col. 0799] Matt. 11].

Of kings and princes, who ought to imitate Job’s uprightness and justice, the Apostle says that they do not bear the sword without cause [Note: [Col. 0799] Rom. 13], for the punishment of evildoers and the praise of the good. Therefore they have been established as fathers of orphans, judges of widows, punishers of offences, advocates of religion, and defenders of the Church. Hear what Job says [Note: [Col. 0799] Ch. 29]: “I was a father to the poor; I broke the jaws of the wicked and snatched prey from the teeth of the unjust. I did not deny the poor [Col. 0800D] what they wanted, nor make the eyes of petitioners wait.”

The last clause of this statement especially concerns those princes who, although they can easily settle the business of the poor, continually put it off and hold the hopes of those waiting in suspense by constant delay. “Do not say,” Solomon says, “Go, and return tomorrow, and I shall give to you,” when you are able to give at once [Note: [Col. 0799] Prov. 3]. For, as my master says most elegantly [Note: [Col. 0799] John of Salisbury, bishop of Chartres]:

> Mere delay blackens the merit of the giver;  
> gifts given promptly win greater praise and greater favour.

[Col. 0801A] “Whatever your hand is able to do,” says Wisdom, “do at once” [Note: [Col. 0801] Eccl. 9], for we do not know what a coming day will bring forth. We are entirely certain of death, yet nothing is more uncertain to us than the hour of death. We have already come to grey hairs and received the forewarnings of hastening death. Thus the Apostle says to the Hebrews [Note: [Col. 0801] Ch. 8]: “What is becoming obsolete and growing old is near destruction.”

For we do not know at what hour the Lord will come, because, like a thief, he will come in the night. “When they say, ‘Peace and security,’ then sudden destruction shall come upon them, as pain upon a woman with child, and they shall not escape” [Note: [Col. 0801] 1 Thess. 5], because, according to Solomon, “the prosperity of fools will destroy them” [Note: [Col. 0801] Prov. 1]. Hence the Apostle, writing to Timothy, says: “Command the rich of this age not to think proudly, nor to hope in the uncertainty [Col. 0801B] of riches” [Note: [Col. 0801] 1 Tim. 6]. Truly they are uncertain; for the Psalm says: “They have slept their sleep, and all men of riches found nothing in their hands” [Note: [Col. 0801] Ps. 75]. It follows:

“And his sons went and made feasts,” etc. Since jealousy and rivalry commonly arise among brothers over the division of an inheritance, Job’s prudence is evident: he had so ordered his children’s lives that they should love one another with mutual charity and invite one another in turn to friendly feasts. “For it is good and pleasant for brothers to dwell together” [Note: [Col. 0801] Ps. 132]. For the more pleasing brotherly love is in the sight of God and human beings, the more monstrous it is if dissensions and schisms are fostered among them. Therefore the Apostle says: “I beseech you, brothers, through the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that you all think the same thing [Col. 0801C] and that there be no schisms among you” [Note: [Col. 0801] 1 Cor. 1].

Thus there was full concord among the sons and daughters toward their father, so that, according to the Apostle, they might preserve one another in the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace [Note: [Col. 0801] Eph. 4]. For if children differed from their father, there would no longer be charity among them, because they would not preserve the charity owed to their father. Remove a ray from the sun and it does not shine; cut a stream from its spring and it dries up; sever a branch from a tree and it withers; sever a limb from the body and it decays. Separate a son from filial devotion and he is no longer a son, but a brother and companion of those to whom it is said: “You are of your father, the devil” [Note: [Col. 0801] John 8].

At the beginning of Isaiah we read: “I have nourished and exalted sons, but they have despised me” [Note: [Col. 0801] Ch. 1]. But the final word of the same prophet is: “Their worm shall not die, and their fire [Col. 0801D] shall not be extinguished” [Note: [Col. 0801] Isa. 66]. In the Old Testament [Note: [Col. 0801] Exod. 12], the paschal lamb was commanded to be eaten in one house, so that harmony of conduct and sameness of affection among those dwelling there might be signified, as it is written: “He makes those of one manner dwell in a house” [Note: [Col. 0801] Ps. 67].

Therefore, in addition to Job’s other virtues, this too accrued to blessed Job: that he had reared his children in love and restrained the wandering impulses of youth under the rule of discipline. For Eli, although just in other respects, was judged rejected by the Lord; and the chair on which he sat [Col. 0802A] overturned, he fell with his neck broken because he did not correct his sons. “You have loved,” the Lord says to him, “your sons more than me” [Note: [Col. 0801] 1 Sam. 4]. Therefore he perished because he was negligent concerning the correction of his sons. His wife too died in childbirth, and his sons Hophni and Phinehas were killed.

Let spiritual fathers who sit in chairs beware, lest through their negligence their sons be killed, the Church be destroyed, and the chairs be overthrown to their own confusion and ruin.

“And when the days had gone round,” etc. Job had seven sons; therefore they used seven feasts, and when the seven days had been completed, Job sent for them and sanctified them. The number seven signifies the condition of the present life, because the present time runs [Col. 0802B] and is divided according to the course of seven days. Therefore, after seven days have elapsed, Job sanctified his children, because after the course of this present life we await that utterance of sanctification and grace by which the Lord says to his children: “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” [Note: [Col. 0801] Matt. 25].

Rising early, he offered, etc. “Perhaps,” he says—for it would be rash to pronounce judgment upon another’s heart. For man sees what is before his eyes; but He judges hearts, to whom every heart lies open, who alone searches hearts and reins [Note: [Col. 0801] Ps. 7]. Therefore the Apostle says: “It is a very small thing to me that I should be judged by a human being, or by man’s day” [Note: [Col. 0801] 1 Cor. 2]. Job offered burnt offerings for each of his sons [Col. 0802C], fearing that at their feasts they might have spoken disparagingly of the Lord. For talkativeness commonly arises from feasting. “Unless,” says Gregory [Note: [Col. 0801] Book I of the *Moralia*, ch. 4], “immoderate speech carried away those devoted to gluttony, that rich man who feasted splendidly would not have burned more grievously in his tongue, saying: ‘Father Abraham, have mercy upon me, and send Lazarus, that he may dip the tip of his finger in water and cool my tongue, for I am tormented in this flame’” [Note: [Col. 0801] Luke 16].

The tongue, indeed, is a small and mobile member, and sometimes defiles the other members with manifold wickedness. There is a loose tongue, an indecent tongue, and a boastful tongue. The loose tongue is found in idle speech; the indecent tongue, in shameful words; the boastful tongue, in pride and arrogance. The first serves buffoonery, [Col. 0802D] the second licentiousness, the third arrogance. And what is more detestable than the tongue of that king of Babylon, with which he said: “Is not this great Babylon, which I have built as the house of my kingdom, by my own strength and for the glory of my majesty?” [Note: [Col. 0801] Dan. 4]. For this cause the presumptuous exaltation of that ruler deserved to be humbled into the degradation of a brute animal. For when man was in honour, he did not understand; and therefore he was compared to senseless beasts and made like them [Note: [Col. 0801] Ps. 48]. Certainly, if oxen and asses could speak, they could [Col. 0803A] say: “Behold, Nebuchadnezzar has become like one of us” [Note: [Col. 0803] Gen. 3].

Job therefore feared lest the slipperiness of the tongue should draw his sons into sin, so that in their hearts they might “bless”—that is, curse—the Lord. He curses in his heart who performs good works without a right intention. He curses God in his heart who attributes to himself, and not to God, what he has from God. Most corrupt dust, destined to be scattered by a breath of wind, what have you from yourself for which you can or ought to boast? “Let him who boasts boast in the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0803] 1 Cor. 1]. If in any respect you claim glory for yourself, you are a thief: for you steal and rob it from God. “If I have kissed my hand,” says Job [Note: [Col. 0803] ch. 31], “that also is the highest iniquity and denial of God.” To kiss one’s own hand is to glory in one’s works. Therefore let glory be referred to Him alone, [Col. 0803B] who alone is glorious for ever [Note: [Col. 0803] Dan. 3]. “Not unto us, O Lord, not unto us, but give glory unto thy name” [Note: [Col. 0803] Ps. 113]. May you alone possess glory, who alone fought, who alone triumphed on the cross. “I have trodden the winepress alone, and of the nations there was no man with me” [Note: [Col. 0803] Isa. 63]. “Give us peace, O Lord, and it is enough for us”; “speak peace, O Lord, to thy people” [Note: [Col. 0803] Ps. 84], “and let peace be in thy strength” [Note: [Col. 0803] Ps. 121]. For we know that the angel distinguished most wisely when he said: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to men of good will” [Note: [Col. 0803] Luke 2].

Job therefore offered burnt offerings for his sons. For he knew that drunkenness frequently arises from feasting, and rashness from drunkenness. Feasting disturbs the state of the soul; drunkenness [Col. 0803C] confuses the judgment of reason; rashness hurls one into guilt. Therefore the Apostle repeatedly forbids feastings and drunkenness [Note: [Col. 0803] Gal. 5; Rom. 13]. “Their god is their belly, and their glory is in their shame” [Note: [Col. 0803] Phil. 3]. “Food,” says the Apostle, “is for the belly, and the belly for foods; but God shall destroy both it and them” [Note: [Col. 0803] 1 Cor. 6]. It is read [Note: [Col. 0803] Jer. 52] that Nebuzaradan, captain of the guard, destroyed the walls of Jerusalem, because it often happens that the vice of gluttony destroys the merits of those who have chosen the way of religion and the purpose of holy peace.

What brings me material for grief above all else is that today religious men and professed members of holy orders dispute over the number of dishes. If a religious man finds in himself either a rapid pulse, highly coloured urine, or a dull appetite, he consults physicians, [Col. 0803D] examines spices, prepares electuaries, and uses no seasonings not compounded with cinnamon, clove, and nutmeg. O how hateful it is in a man that he who ought always to speak of the heavenly hierarchy [Col. 0804A] learns to discourse about *hiera picra* and *hiera Logadii*.

[Note: [Col. 0803D] *Hiera* is a Greek word and means “sacred.” In medical usage it signifies either the *hieran noson* (ἱερὰν νόσον), the “sacred disease” or epilepsy; or, as it is used here by Blesensis, a medicinal compound. Scribonius Largus explains the reason for the name in Book *On Medicinal Compositions*, ch. 99. It is called *hiera*, now *picra* (πικρά), because it is bitter—for it is composed chiefly of aloes; now *Logadion* (λογάδιον), from its author, because it varied and was described differently by different persons. One formula belonged to Antipater, another to Andromachus, another to Galen, another to Rufus, another to Logadius. See the lexicographers under ἱερός.]

“This is harmful to the head,” he says [Note: [Col. 0803] Bernard, Sermon 30 on the Song of Songs], “this to the eyes, this to the stomach, this to the liver. Butter is of a changeable nature; beer produces wind; cabbages are melancholic; leeks inflame bile; peas cause gout; beans constipate; lentils blind; cheese is universally most harmful. Standing long at prayer weakens the sinews; fasting disturbs the brain; keeping vigil dries one out.” Are such distinctions found in the Gospel or the Prophets? Certainly the Rule of blessed Benedict does not contain them; rather, flesh and blood reveal them to wretched men.

This is enough concerning feasting. But concerning drunkenness, which is a portion and consequence of feasting, I shall touch briefly upon this: just as Adam was subject to gluttony, so Noah and Lot were subject to drunkenness. Certainly, says Ambrose [Note: [Col. 0803] Book *On Elijah*, ch. 5, §§13–16], slavery would never have existed if drunkenness had not existed. What, moreover, shall we say of those men of ruined mind who contend in drinking, who judge victory to consist in drinking more? who drink more abundantly when they thirst less? who consider themselves fortunate when they see either themselves or their companions staggering in tongue and feet? who then hate a man who does not pursue drunkenness, and cannot sleep unless they are drunk? Let them hear what the Lord says through Isaiah, the instrument of the Holy Spirit: “Woe to you who are mighty at drinking and strong at mixing drunkenness” [Note: [Col. 0803] Isa. 5]. Solomon sums up the miseries of drunkenness [Col. 0804C] in concise and polished brevity, saying: “Who has woe? Whose father has woe? Who has wounds? Who has quarrels? Who has dimness of eyes? Is it not those who linger over wine and study emptied cups?” [Note: [Col. 0803] Prov. 3]. It follows:

**Thus Job did all those days.** In this is signified perseverance in good work. Perseverance has this prerogative: although all virtues run toward the prize, perseverance alone is crowned. For the persistent prayer of a righteous man has great power [Note: [Col. 0803] Jas. 5], as is most plainly evident in Moses’ prayer. While he prayed and raised his hands, the people of God prevailed; but when he lowered his hands or ceased praying, Amalek prevailed [Note: [Col. 0803] Exod. 17]. Therefore Job offered burnt offerings for his sons every day, because the daily feasts presented him with matter for sinning [Col. 0804D]; and the remedy had to be continual where the occasion and inclination to sin were continual.

**Now on a certain day, when the sons of God had come to stand before the Lord, Satan also was present among them** [Col. 0805A]. There are many courts, and in every one some Satan is always found. He is the accuser of the brethren and corrupter of the good, the hidden adversary of all, and, as it were, a serpent among eels. Embassies are more frequently laid upon him; and perhaps what he claims for himself as glory is imposed upon him by God’s judgment as labour. Good angels are sometimes sent by the Lord, sent in ministry for those who shall inherit salvation [Note: [Col. 0805] Heb. 1]. Evil angels too are sent for the vexation of the wicked, so that there may be, as the Prophet says, “missions by evil angels” [Note: [Col. 0805] Ps. 77]. They are also sent for the testing of the good, for the exercise of virtue, for the increase of grace in them, and for growth in glory. But with what face, with what audacity, does that son of pride, that apostate angel, presume [Col. 0805B] to appear among the sons of God?

But because he fell through pride, he ascends by being proud. “The pride,” he says, “of those who hate thee rises continually” [Note: [Col. 0805] Ps. 72]. For pride is heavenly by origin: in heaven it conceived sorrow and gave birth to iniquity, and it tends most willingly toward the place from which it fell. Satan does not therefore appear among God’s angels in order to see His face—the face into which angels long to look, and which angels always behold [Note: [Col. 0805] Matt. 18]—for man shall not see God and live [Note: [Col. 0805] Exod. 34]. “The sinner is removed, lest he see the glory of God.” Satan therefore appears before the Lord in order that he may be seen by Him whom he cannot see: like a blind man who stands in the sun’s ray, does not enjoy the benefit of the sun, and is permitted to see only [Col. 0805C] that which is reckoned to him as torment. For he is tortured by envy, pines away at the felicity of angels, and wastes away at the prosperity of the faithful, according to the words: “The sinner shall see and be angry; he shall gnash his teeth and waste away” [Note: [Col. 0805] Ps. 111].

**And the Lord said to him: “Whence do you come, Satan?”** The Lord asks Satan, as though ignorant whence he comes; because, as it is said, the righteous man appears not to know how to lie because he does not wish to lie and does not attempt falsehood. Thus the Lord knows the way of the righteous but does not know the way of the sinner [Note: [Col. 0805] Ps. 1].

**And he answered and said, etc.** He rightly says, “I have gone around,” for “the wicked walk around in a circle” [Note: [Col. 0805] Ps. 11]. For our adversary, like a roaring lion, prowls about seeking whom he may devour [Note: [Col. 0805] 1 Pet. 5], and he attempts most eagerly to devour those [Col. 0805D] whom he has recognized as of holier life, because it is written: “His food is choice” [Note: [Col. 0805] Hab. 1].

**And the Lord said to him: “Have you considered, etc.?”** He begins with a commendation of the righteous man. “For it is not he who commends himself who is approved, but he whom God commends” [Note: [Col. 0805] III Cor. 10]. He sets before Satan those virtues which Satan especially hated, in order more violently to torture the enemy and provoke him to test Job. For the Lord wishes his servants to be strongly tested, so that with the temptation he may also make a way out [Note: [Col. 0805] 1 Cor. 10]. A commander rejoices if he sees his soldier fighting bravely [Col. 0806A] against a strong adversary. Christ exults when he sees his martyr now scourged, now stretched upon the rack, now torn by iron claws, now exposed to arrows, now mutilated in limb, now placed upon fires. The martyr stands afflicted indeed, yet unconquered; and, seeing his blood bubble forth from different parts of his body, he attends not to his own wounds but to those of the Redeemer. Thus, dancing and triumphing amid the sharpest agonies, he does not feel the pains of his lacerated body, because he is away from the body. This is not caused by numbness but by love; pain is not absent, but it is despised for Christ’s sake. Thus the Lord exposes both the possessions and the person of his servant Job to the malice of the tempter, so that, afflicted inwardly and outwardly, yet guarded by the Lord on right and left, he may grow [Col. 0806B] in grace and advance toward the crown.

**And Satan answered and said: “Does Job fear God for nothing, etc.?”** Because Satan finds no evil in the holy man to accuse, he falsely and maliciously converts his good into evil, wishing to charge him with the vice of ingratitude, since he could not otherwise corrupt him. It is as if he said: “He does not fear you—being ungrateful; nor is there any reason for him to fear you, because you have hedged in him and his house, and have cut off every cause of fear and reverence in him.” For the adversary knew that ingratitude was the vice by which a man could most grievously displease God [Note: [Col. 0805] Bernard, Sermon 51 on the Song of Songs]. Ingratitude is a scorching wind, drying up the fountain of piety, the dew of mercy, and the streams of grace. Ingratitude is the scattering of virtues, betrayal of benefits, and emptying-out of merits.
