For man [Col. 0806C], before Christ’s Passion, suffered from the disease of ingratitude; for created but not yet redeemed man said: “I am no more bound to God than the other creatures. He spoke, and I was made; he laboured no more upon me than upon any brute animal.” Thus human impiety took an occasion for ingratitude from the matter of God’s gifts. But today the mouth of those who speak iniquity has been stopped, and therefore there is no place for ingratitude. For God laboured more in the redemption of man alone than in the entire construction of the world. For from Lord he became servant; from rich, poor; from immortal, mortal; from Word, flesh; from Son of God, son of man. He bore the reproaches of those who reproached him; he suffered [Col. 0806D] plotters in deeds, opponents in words, mockers in distress, the needs of the flesh, the horror of death, and the shame of the cross.

Most beloved prince, I ask and, in asking, counsel your excellence to hold continually in mind how great are the things the Lord has done for you. He raised you from count to duke, from duke to king. Afterwards, by force, he subjected many and very great kings, with their provinces, to your dominion. And because “his mercies are over all his works” [Note: [Col. 0805] Ps. 144], I beg you each day to render special praises and thanks to the Most High for [Col. 0807A] the mercy which he showed you in the dissension of your sons. Your flesh had departed from you; your own bowels had been torn from you. All those around you—princes and peoples—and almost all your own men thirsted for your destruction; and, as the prophet says, “a man’s enemies are those of his own household” [Note: [Col. 0807] Mic. 7; Matt. 10]. But He who is before the ages humbled them, and gave your enemies into your hands, “to bind their princes in fetters and their nobles in chains of iron” [Note: [Col. 0807] Ps. 149]. He also turned the hearts of sons toward their father [Note: [Col. 0807] Luke 1], and bowed them in submission and humility at your feet so that they now do not hesitate to undertake every labour for you and offer themselves to death for your honour.

Do not therefore attribute this to yourselves, but to the Lord; nor let that Jewish reproach [Col. 0807B] be marked upon you: “They did not remember his benefits and the wonders which he showed them” [Note: [Col. 0807] Ps. 77]. Let that pestilential saying, hateful in the ears of the Most High, be far from your mouth and heart: “Our hand is high, and not the Lord has done all these things” [Note: [Col. 0807] Deut. 32]. Hear what the Wise Man says: “The greater you are, humble yourself in all things” [Note: [Col. 0807] Ecclus. 3]. And the Apostle: “Humble yourselves under the mighty hand” [Note: [Col. 0807] 1 Pet. 5] “of God,” under him through whom kings reign [Note: [Col. 0807] Prov. 8], whom to know is life, whom to serve is to reign; without whose grace neither has the prince honour, nor the people peace, nor religion quiet, nor the Church liberty.

**“Touch all that he possesses, etc.”** The face of the Lord is his mercy. “Show thy face, O Lord,” says the Psalmist, “and we shall be saved” [Note: [Col. 0807] Ps. 79]. And [Col. 0807C] elsewhere: “Let my judgment come forth from thy countenance, O Lord” [Note: [Col. 0807] Ps. 16]. Again: “Thy face, O Lord, will I seek” [Note: [Col. 0807] Ps. 26]. Therefore he curses God to his face who despises his grace—grace which he kept in prosperity—when temporal goods are taken away or his body is afflicted.

**Then the Lord said to Satan: “Behold, all things, etc.”** The Lord is not moved by the devil’s favour or entreaty to expose his servant to Satan’s testing; rather, he provides for his servant’s advantage and honour, sending his soldier to battle, whom he knows will bring back glory and triumph from the battle. It is indeed a most just judgment of God that this most evil hammerer of the humble, while he presses the righteous between hammer and anvil, should fashion eternal crowns for them; that he who attempts to overcome all should be overcome by all; and that what is multiplied for the glory of the saints should be turned back upon him much more abundantly unto shame and confusion.

“Only do not stretch out your hand against him.” God exposes Job’s possessions to the enemy but protects his body, though he will later give up his body also. In this he acts by the highest [Col. 0808A] dispensation. For he knew that Job would resist one temptation more strongly than two, and that from victory in the first struggle Job’s mind would be more steadfastly strengthened for endurance of the other temptation. For, as the Apostle says, God does not permit his own to be tested beyond what they are able to bear, but makes with the temptation also a way out, that they may be able to endure [Note: [Col. 0807] 1 Cor. 10]. And the Lord removes the rod of sinners from over the lot of the righteous, lest the righteous stretch out their hands unto iniquity [Note: [Col. 0807] Ps. 124].

**And Satan went out from the presence of the Lord.** Truly he went out—he who did not stand in the truth [Note: [Col. 0807] John 8], who fell in his pride, who did not remain in grace.

**Now on a certain day, while his sons and daughters, etc.** He chose a most opportune time for testing: namely, when he found Job’s [Col. 0808B] sons eating and drinking. “Their food,” he says, “was still in their mouths, and the wrath of God rose against them” [Note: [Col. 0807] Ps. 77]. Since feastings can scarcely occur without sin, the enemy gladly insinuates himself into feastings; but he always hates prayer and fasting, because there is also a kind of demons which is cast out only by prayer and fasting [Note: [Col. 0807] Matt. 17]. It should be noted that the sin lies not in taking food but in delighting in food. For sometimes one man is no less gluttonous amid the meanest food than another amid luxurious banquets. Jonathan is recorded as having sinned in tasting honey [Note: [Col. 0807] 1 Sam. 14]; Esau, in a dish of lentils [Note: [Col. 0807] Gen. 26]; the Sodomites, in fullness of bread [Note: [Col. 0807] Ezek. 16]. Therefore, as Jerome testifies [Note: [Col. 0807] Book II against Jovinian], it is not food but appetite that is at fault.

Three things are considered [Col. 0808C] in taking food: time, measure, and quality. Time: that the hour not be anticipated. Measure: that food be taken with blameless moderation. Quality: that foods not be excessively refined or excessively costly. To eat after satiety is superfluous; before hunger, idle; in hunger, lawful; after hunger, meritorious. Certainly, I do not believe that fasting in a healthy person has any merit when hunger does not precede it.

[Note: [Col. 0807D] Although such fasting, insofar as it customarily afflicts, may seem to have no merit, it can nevertheless be joined with merit on other grounds: if undertaken because it has been commanded by an ecclesiastical precept; to avoid giving offence to one’s neighbour; to provide others with a good example; to preserve the custom of the Christian people; or to show one’s willingness to afflict oneself.]

To fast without being afflicted by fasting has neither the force nor the merit of fasting. If the vigils of the apostles or other times indicating the necessity of fasting are imminent, on the preceding day we fill and gorge ourselves with a variety of dishes, cramming into our bellies, in fraud of the coming fast, as much as a sober steward could sufficiently dispense for three days [Col. 0808D]. “This,” says the Lord through the prophet, “is not the fast which I have chosen” [Note: [Col. 0807] Isa. 58]. For there are fasts which God has rejected, and fasts which he has chosen. Some fast because of nature’s weakness, others because of avarice, others for display, others for eternal life, others for bodily health. [Col. 0809A] The sick man fasts in order to recover; the hypocrite, in order to be seen; the sated man, in order to regain appetite; the miser, in order to save money. In all things, your intention gives your work its name. In all things discretion must be observed: it is the charioteer of virtues and works, and the best moderatrix of thoughts. It follows:

**And while he was still speaking, etc.** Satan employs his cunning in manifold arts of temptation and in various devices for doing harm. For his wiles are many, as the Apostle says: “We are not ignorant,” he says, “of Satan’s wiles” [Note: [Col. 0809] 2 Cor. 2]. He therefore causes unexpected and sudden losses to be reported, so that Job may be more violently dismayed by the unbroken succession of disasters. He adds wounds to the pain of wounds, so that, as evil after evil arrives, the memory of former evils [Col. 0809B] may be reopened, and so that his iniquity may be found unto hatred. He brings forth fire from heaven, winds from the air, and a hostile assault from the earth, so that this son of pride may seem to possess some power in heaven, air, and earth. Yet he is permitted, not by his own power but by God’s, to move the elements against Job for the exercise of his malice, so that Job, under the pressure of blows, may burn more fiercely like mustard as he is more thoroughly crushed, and that while the adversary tries every kind of harm, he may be overcome in all things.

**Then Job rose and tore his garments.** Behold, he felt the blow; accordingly, he immediately displayed signs of grief in the tearing of his garments.

[Col. 0809C] **And having shaved his head, he fell down, etc.** The vessel of perfume was shaken and gave forth the sweetness of fragrance; the spices were crushed and emitted their scent. Job was afflicted, and he turned himself to the praises of the Lord. So long as he was in the day of his prosperity, he offered daily burnt offerings; but in the night of adversity he does not cease to offer a song of praise, according to the Psalmist’s words: “By day the Lord commanded his blessing, and by night his song” [Note: [Col. 0809] Ps. 41]. It should be noted that, having shaved his head and fallen to the ground, he worshipped. In shaving his head, falling to the ground, and worshipping, humility is shown—a humility especially commendable in Job: in appearance, in deed, and in affection.

It is not new that clerics are shaved, that they are crowned on the head. We have an example of the tonsure in Job; [Col. 0809D] an example of the crown in Christ, who wore a crown of thorns on his head as a sign of humility [Note: [Col. 0809] Bede, Book V of the *History*, ch. 22]. Some pagans are also said to have shaved the head of the Apostle Peter in reproach and contempt of Christ; yet he, mindful of Christ’s crown of thorns, endured it patiently and willingly. In remembrance of this humility Priscilla and Aquila shaved themselves, as is read in the Acts of the Apostles [Note: [Col. 0809] chs. 18 and 21]. Paul also shaved himself at Cenchreae. Thus Job shaves himself as a sign of humility. Considering that he was being crushed and humbled by blows, [Col. 0810A] he humbles himself still more and assists the hand of him who strikes: “Naked,” he says, “I came forth from my mother’s womb, and naked I shall return there.”

Job recalls the misery of the human condition, so that it may afford him consolation that he once possessed nothing; and so that he may know that one should not grieve at the loss of temporal things, which are quickly acquired and vanish still more quickly. Man, formed from earth, returns to earth, as was said in Genesis to the first man: “You are ashes, and to ashes you shall return” [Note: [Col. 0809] Gen. 3]. We believe this was said so that, so long as man serves as a soldier in this mortal life—indeed, in this living death—he may remember his origin and keep firmly in mind whence he comes and whither he goes. “Earth, earth, earth, hear my words,” says the prophet [Note: [Col. 0809] Jer. 22].

The prophet calls man “earth” three times [Col. 0810B], because man is earth in three ways. He is earth because he was created from earth. He is earth because he lives upon the earth. He is earth because he will return to earth. He is earth in creation, earth in manner of life, earth in death. He is earth by nature, life, and burial. And because “earth” is here repeated three times, the Bridegroom repeats “Return” to the Shulammite three times, so that she may return from the land of unlikeness to the land of the living: “Return, return, O Shulammite; return, return, that we may look upon thee” [Note: [Col. 0809] Song 6]. Return from the land of unlikeness; return from the land of sin; return from the land of misery to the land of freedom; return to the land of grace and to the land of glory.

Wretched man that I am, what occasion for pride can creep upon a miserable man [Col. 0810C] who was conceived from unclean seed and will again become most unclean dust? [Note: [Col. 0809] Bernard, *Meditations*, ch. 2]. To someone who asked a philosopher, “What was I, what am I, what shall I be?” the philosopher is said to have answered: “Vile semen, a sack of dung, food for worms.” Let soldiers who glory in their strength or beauty hear this, I beg, and hold firmly to the saying. Certainly, we could not believe the misery of our body to be so great unless the book of experience, with eyewitness faith, taught us this continually.

For we see men most valiant in arms, women most elegant in form, princes terrible in power, dying throughout the day and being buried in the earth, so that what was earth may return to earth. He beneath whom the world now trembles, whom peoples fear, and whom foreign provinces [Col. 0810D] dread, if he dies today, will within a short time be reduced to most worthless dust and may be blown away by the slightest breath. Where now is Julius Caesar? Where Alexander the Great? Where Charlemagne?—except that Charles chose the better part, which shall not be taken away from him. Others are condemned to everlasting torments, as it is written: “The mighty shall mightily endure torments” [Note: [Col. 0809] Wis. 6].

Nevertheless, because Charles believed in Christ, although he sinned grievously in his youth, he washed away the sins of his youth by confession and repentance; and in [Col. 0811A] the evening of his life, turning to the Lord, he offered himself to God as an evening sacrifice. Most prudent prince, observe that evening is now drawing on for you: for you have already passed half your life, or more. King Hezekiah considered that he had lived very long in sins and was hastening by the straight road toward hell; therefore he said: “I said, in the middle of my days I shall go to the gates of hell” [Note: [Col. 0811] Isa. 38]. And he added: “I shall recount to thee all my years in the bitterness of my soul” [Note: [Col. 0811] Ibid.]. Go and do likewise.

Let the evil reputation of certain princes deter you, of whom it is said that, the older they grew, the more they indulged the vanities and enticements of this world and the licentiousness of the flesh. May that prophecy of Merlin be fulfilled in you: “His steps were wandering at the beginning, [Col. 0811B] but his end shall fly up to the heavens.” If you have sinned, cease; for the best way of repenting is to cease from sin. Perhaps in your mind you arrange and plan: “I shall still play; I shall still wait and delay, until I am of more mature age and less able to sin.” Tell me, I beg, what grace is due you from the Lord if you cease from sin only when you are unable to sin? Hasten, I beg, to do good; do not delay; do not wait.

It is the prophet’s word concerning an obstinate people: “This people says: The time has not yet come to build the house of God” [Note: [Col. 0811] Hag. 1]. And elsewhere: “I shall be satisfied in my iniquities, and when my soul has been filled with evils, I shall consider my ways.” What I wish and counsel is that you should always have this boast before God and always be able to allege to him [Col. 0811C] that for love of him you have each day omitted some sin.

There are two things which preserve a man marvellously from sin: frequent confession and still more frequent discipline [Col. 0812A] [Note: [Col. 0811C] From this passage and many others it appears that discipline—that is, the scourging of one’s own body, a practice also received in this age throughout Rome and Italy, Spain, the Indies, and elsewhere—was common in Gaul and England more than four hundred years ago, not only among those devoted to monastic life but also among clerics and laymen, bishops, princes, and kings, as is clear from many letters.

For, when in Letter 82 and in the *Invective* he had praised the Cistercian monks because they surpassed all clerics and laymen in chastising the flesh with disciplines, he immediately added a defence of clerics: “Do you think that all of them”—the clerics—“are so far removed from God that neither fear of the misery of hell nor the blessedness of heavenly glory stirs them? Are they wholly ignorant of discipline and penitence and the other things [Col. 0811D] belonging to spiritual exercise? Is there no balm in Gilead?”

Then, in Letter 16, writing to a certain aged bishop, he says that by reason of his profession the bishop is bound to cleanse the flesh with fasts and disciplines, and that this will be required of him by God with the utmost exactness on the Day of Judgment. In Letter 46, defending Reginald, bishop of Bath, who was thought to have been hostile to St Thomas the martyr during his lifetime: “I know,” he says, “that if the aforesaid elect attempted anything in insult to the martyr, he expiated it by the harshness of haircloth, more generous alms, more abundant tears, and more austere disciplines.”

But in Letter 126, describing the youth of Odo, bishop of Paris and kinsman of the kings of France and England: “Although,” he says, “he had possessed his vessel in sanctification and honour from childhood, nevertheless, restraining the insolence of the flesh and its irregular movements by a certain authority of superiority, he compelled it to serve as a handmaid through vigils, fasts, and disciplines.” Likewise, in the *Episcopal Instruction*, instructing a certain bishop: “Always,” he says, “impose upon yourself in secret, either for discipline, or tears, or other things which you can perform alone without human witness, the yoke of the Lord’s service.”

Moreover, Letter 27 says that St Thomas the martyr, who became archbishop of Canterbury from chancellor of the kingdom of England, restrained from his earliest youth the impulses of fleshly insolence by vigils, fasts, disciplines, haircloth, and the girdle of continual continence. How securely the bishop later raged daily with scourges against his domestic enemy may be seen in his *Life*. [Col. 0812D] Blesensis mentions the same discipline in many other places: Letters 11, 58, 74, 142, and 205; Book I *On Penance*; the treatise *On the Institution of a Bishop*; and Sermon 6, *On the Nativity of the Lord*. Since this custom was widely received in Blesensis’s age, it is not likely that it arose in that very age, but rather that it had been handed down from ancient times. For St Peter Damian, cardinal of the Roman Church, who lived one century before our Blesensis, having described in the *Life of St Dominic Loricatus* the custom of daily scourging both of that saint and of his own monastery, adds that the custom of chastising the body prevailed in his regions not only among monks but also among secular persons, both men and women, however noble in birth.]

Yet some are so weak and delicate, and so bound by the habit of sinning, that they shrink from a priest no less than a thief from a judge. “Why do you doubt, O you of little faith?” [Note: [Col. 0811] Matt. 14]. Do you fear that the Lord will not forgive your sins? Did he not nail them to the cross with his own hands? He suffered for sinners, not for the righteous. Hear what the Prophet says to the Lord: “I said, ‘I will confess,’ and thou hast forgiven the impiety of my sin” [Note: [Col. 0811] Ps. 31]. “If you uncover your sin,” says the Lord, “I cover it; if you acknowledge it, I forgive it; if you accuse it, I excuse it; if you judge and condemn yourself, I neither judge nor condemn you.” “But if you judged yourselves,” says the Apostle, “you would certainly not be judged” [Col. 0812B] [Note: [Col. 0811] 1 Cor. 11].

David—an adulterer, murderer, and traitor—when Nathan the prophet rebuked him, because he humbly acknowledged his sin, deserved to hear: “The Lord has removed your sin from you” [Note: [Col. 0811] 1 Sam. 12]. But Saul, because he answered Samuel rebuking him proudly, heard: “The Lord has removed your kingdom from you” [Note: [Col. 0811] 3 Kings 15]. From one, sin was removed; from the other, the kingdom was removed. I offer this warning and counsel so that, after the example of blessed Job, you may remember your condition. For you entered naked and shall depart naked, because when the rich man dies, he shall not take all things, nor shall his glory descend with him [Note: [Col. 0811] Ps. 48]. You will carry back with you only that which you have sent ahead into heavenly treasures through the hands of the poor. It follows:

[Col. 0812C] **“The Lord gave, and the Lord took away,” etc.** Job mixes honey with wormwood: grace and blessing with persecution, [Col. 0813A] so that in thanksgiving the bitterness of persecution may be sweetened, and there may be not merely drink mingled with tears in due measure, but the wormwood of affliction and the honey of thanksgiving may season it into an acceptable nectar. “You have given us to drink,” says the Prophet, “the wine of compunction” [Note: [Col. 0813] Ps. 59], or of tribulation; but to this wine Job adds that which comes “from the torrent of delight”; and he seems to employ the Apostle’s words: “Most gladly therefore will I glory in my infirmities” [Note: [Col. 0813] II Cor. 12]; and, “When I am weak, then I am stronger” [Note: [Col. 0813] Ibid.]. He strengthens his spirit for the endurance of every evil and glories in his distresses. We read that Ehud, son of Gera, was ambidextrous, fighting with either hand [Note: [Col. 0813] Judg. 3]; Job presents his exact likeness, since his left hand fought no less than his right: strong in prosperity, stronger in adversity. Such was the Apostle, knowing [Col. 0813B] how to abound and how to endure want [Note: [Col. 0813] Phil. 4], glorying in his infirmities, proceeding midway through ill repute and good repute, through glory and dishonour [Note: [Col. 0813] I Cor. 6], enduring adversities without murmuring, and in all things making virtue out of necessity. It follows:

**“In all these things he did not sin,” etc.** He speaks foolishly against God who says that the Lord scourges him without any due claim arising from his merits, and who, as though pleading his own innocence, proudly accuses the justice of the One who scourges him.

## CHAPTER II. “And it came to pass, when on a certain day the sons of God had come,” etc.

Satan is silent concerning the losses he had inflicted upon the holy man and concerning the steadfastness he found in him. For he counts himself [Col. 0813C] defeated and confounded when he sees that the man whom he was urging, through losses and pains, to curse God, gives blessing to God instead and offers Him a sacrifice of praise.

**“And the Lord said to Satan,” etc.** The Lord recounts the virtues of His soldier, adding, beyond all his praise and to the tempter’s reproach and shame, a covert reminder to Satan of his own wickedness, as if to say: “The innocence which you lost while you were in heavenly blessedness, amid the splendours of the saints and the dignity of angels, man—even though of fragile nature and wretched condition—has preserved even in affliction.” Thus the Lord wisely and fittingly mocks the devil: “This dragon, O Lord, is he whom Thou hast made to be mocked by him” [Note: [Col. 0813] Ps. 103]. He is mocked by You, by man, and by the angel: by [Col. 0813D] You, when You permit him to harm man, so that in harming him he may advance him; by man, because the more he weakens him, the stronger he finds him; and by the angels, because, as he beholds them exalted in glory, abounding in grace, shining in heavenly brightness, and resounding with divine praises, he remembers whence he fell and, groaning at the joys of others, wastes away in wrath and envy. It follows:

**“But thou hast moved Me,” etc.**—that is, without cause: namely, since no preceding sins existed in Job that demanded the scourge of so great an adversity; or, “in vain,” [Col. 0814A] with regard to your purpose: for in the very matter in which you intend to harm him, you are useful to him. “But thou hast moved Me.” It must not be believed that Satan moved God, with whom there is neither change nor shadow of turning [Note: [Col. 0813] Jas. 1]. And as Malachi says: “I am God, and I change not” [Note: [Col. 0813] Mal. 3]. But God’s change is His scourge. The Lord scourges in fury, in wrath, and in mercy. In fury He scourged the devil; in wrath, man; for both meditated iniquity, and both desired exaltation—the former of power, the latter of knowledge. The Lord scourged the devil in fury, casting him down without hope of restoration from the throne of pestilence which he had raised in the north. “I saw,” He says, “Satan falling like lightning from heaven” [Note: [Col. 0813] Luke 10]. Therefore the Lord will not have mercy on him, [Col. 0814B] because “his iniquity has been found unto hatred” [Note: [Col. 0813] Ps. 35]. He scourged man in wrath when He expelled him from the delights of Paradise; nevertheless, because man did not fall by himself but at another’s instigation—because he was driven and overthrown—the Lord appointed him a time for mercy; and although He scourged him in wrath, He nevertheless chose, in His anger, to remember mercy. The scourge of fury and the scourge of wrath are greatly to be feared, because each is most grievous. “I have trodden them,” says the Prophet, “in My fury, and I have trodden them in My wrath” [Note: [Col. 0813] Isa. 63]. And the Psalmist, dreading and recoiling from both, said: “O Lord, rebuke me not in Thy fury, nor chasten me in Thy wrath” [Note: [Col. 0813] Ps. 6].

The third scourge is that of mercy: when the human body is afflicted, or temporal goods are withdrawn, for the testing of life, the advancement of virtues, and the [Col. 0814C] increase of the crown. With this scourge the Lord scourges every son whom He receives. “I,” He says, “rebuke and chasten those whom I love” [Note: [Col. 0813] Heb. 12; Rev. 3]. With this scourge the Lord struck the children of Israel when they sinned in their inventions, yet even amid the scourges He was gracious to them. “O God,” says the Psalmist, “Thou wast gracious to them, and taking vengeance upon all their inventions” [Note: [Col. 0813] Ps. 98]. The wounds of one who loves are sweeter than the flatteries of an adulator. “Let the righteous man rebuke me in mercy and reprove me; but let not the oil of the sinner fatten my head” [Note: [Col. 0813] Ps. 140]. The sinner’s oil is the softness of flatterers. “Their words,” he says, “were softer than oil, and yet they are darts” [Note: [Col. 0813] Ps. 54]. I see those who ought at least to exercise the rod of gentle and private rebuke [Col. 0814D] becoming flatterers and sellers of oil. “The sinner is praised in the desires of his soul, and the wicked man is blessed” [Note: [Col. 0813] Ps. 10], and by their agreement he is stirred to worse things. Therefore I groan, and my eye pours forth water. O most shameless dogs, unable to bark: how long will you judge iniquity and accept the persons of sinners? [Note: [Col. 0813] Ps. 81]. To accept the person of a sinner is to conform oneself to those who sin by permission and consent. Do you know why you do not correct human sins? The Apostle gives a most certain and natural cause: “Therefore,” he says, [Col. 0815A] “you do not rebuke, because you yourselves do the same things repeatedly” [Note: [Col. 0815] Rom. 2].

**“And Satan answered and said,” etc.** He gives skin for skin who exposes one limb to injury in place of another, more important limb: as when someone offers his left arm to an approaching sword lest he be wounded in the head. Satan’s meaning is: Job bears all outward losses patiently and calmly because he fears being scourged more grievously within. He prefers to suffer outward losses rather than be scourged in his body at the peril of his life. For this reason a man will give not only the skins of animals but even his children for his soul—that is, for his life. At times we call the soul the nobler part of man, which after the Day of Judgment will either be glorified with the body or eternally put to death with the body. Of this soul it is said: “Bless the Lord, O my soul” [Note: [Col. 0815] Ps. 102]; and: [Col. 0815B] “My soul has cleaved after Thee” [Note: [Col. 0815] Ps. 62]; and the like. At other times we call the soul the life of the body, as the Gospel says: “He who hates his soul in this world for My sake shall find it”—that is, shall preserve it—“and he who loves his soul in this world shall lose it” [Note: [Col. 0815] John 12]. Certainly it is good for everyone to lose his soul here, lest it be lost. I prefer to lose my soul in order to preserve it, rather than preserve it in order to lose it. The master of this judgment was that most excellent appraiser of things, the Apostle Paul, who, being ready not only to be bound in Jerusalem but also to die for the name of Jesus, said: “I do not make my soul more precious than myself” [Note: [Col. 0815] Acts 21].

The day before yesterday I saw a certain disciple of this school, a brother of the Carthusian Order named Gerard. [Col. 0815C] For seven years he had desired, above all his desirable things, to die, longing to leave the prison and chains of this flesh, as the Prophet says: “Bring my soul, O Lord, out of prison” [Note: [Col. 0815] Ps. 141]. Trusting, therefore, in his merits, but more fully in the mercy of the Redeemer, he desired to be dissolved and to be with Christ [Note: [Col. 0815] Phil. 17]. Certainly he held this present life no less hateful than we wretches hold death; he recoiled from living no less than we recoil from dying. Every night, at the beginning of the watches—indeed, before the night watches—he arose. I and certain others who were with him gave rest to our temples and slumber to our eyes [Note: [Col. 0815] Ps. 131], but he spent the night in prayer, always with weeping and groaning. Hardly ever did he eat [Col. 0815D] bread for an hour without tears; he mingled even his drink with weeping [Note: [Col. 0815] Ps. 101]. In every work he sighed for Christ, looking down upon earth and looking up to heaven; using the world as though not using it; and, by a certain inward taste, distinguishing between things to be used and things to be enjoyed, he used transient things transiently and embraced eternal things, in some measure, with an eternal affection. Truly, “in some measure eternal,” because a steadfast, firm, and unshaken equality in the face of death is a kind of image of eternity.

Although he was a layman and knew no letters, he nevertheless had written upon his heart, by the finger of God, the knowledge of life and [Col. 0816A] discipline. Indeed, He who teaches man knowledge had taught him [Note: [Col. 0815] Ps. 93]; and would that all learned men were thus teachable by God, and that grace might pour into them what instruction did not confer. I call God to witness: he answered concerning the articles of the Christian faith no less judiciously and soundly than if he had spent the greater part of his life in the schools of Paris. For he had been trained in the school of Him who taught and inflamed the Apostles, of whom it is written: “His fire is in Zion, and His furnace in Jerusalem” [Note: [Col. 0815] Isa. 33]. He was therefore a fellow-pupil of the Apostles and of him who says: “From on high the Lord sent fire into my bones, and taught me” [Note: [Col. 0815] Lam. 1]. He spoke as though uttering the words of God, for he always had at hand words of life.

Let our jurists learn, I pray, what that civil [Col. 0816B] and ornate manner of speech, that Babylonian cup by which the sinners of the earth are made drunk, those laws of princes in whose service I myself once unhappily laboured, contribute to the salvation of their souls. Yet their use would be most beneficial to human life, if human malice did not abuse their goodness. There is one King, and His law alone is true: “The law without blemish, converting souls and giving wisdom to little ones” [Note: [Col. 0815] Ps. 18]. It accommodates itself to little ones, great persons, and those of middling station; it stoops to the needs of the poor, the anxieties of the oppressed, the disturbances of the sorrowful, and the faults of offenders. It is most sweet to the perfect, compassionate toward the imperfect, gentle to those of middling station, bearable to the delicate, sufficient to the stronger, moderate to the weak, kindly to the humble, merciful to penitents, severe to the perverse, [Col. 0816C] and best to the good. This law instructs and forms one for life. But the wisdom of this world is foolishness before God. And what did the windy loquacity of worldly philosophy profit Aristotle and his followers? Swollen with secular knowledge, they did not know the God of Sabaoth. They were from Him, but not with Him; through Him they lived, but not for Him; from Him they had wisdom, but not Him Himself. Therefore let my wisdom and philosophy be the philosophy of Brother Gerard, who had nothing else in mouth and heart but Jesus Christ. Let my philosophy be the philosophy of Paul, who most steadfastly declared that he knew nothing else but Jesus Christ, and Him crucified [Note: [Col. 0815] I Cor. 2]. It follows:

**“Otherwise, stretch out Thy hand,” etc.** As if he said: Job bears all things patiently and blesses God in all [Col. 0816D] things, so long as he is not harmed in his body. “Otherwise”—as though he said—“if You do not believe this, experience itself will teach You.” Stretch out Your hand, therefore, and touch his bone and his flesh—that is, scourge and afflict him in his body—and You will see that he will bless You to Your face. Observe how malicious, how shameless, how rash that apostate angel is. See how maliciously he contrives man’s overthrow, how shamelessly iniquity lies to itself, and how rashly he promises the Lord that what the Lord has ordained otherwise will happen.

[Col. 0817A] **Then the Lord said to Satan: “Behold, he is in,” etc.** The Lord permits the enemy to rage against an innocent man, so that, defeated a second time, he may be confounded with greater disgrace, while repeated victory may accrue more abundantly to the glory of the afflicted man. The Lord therefore says: “Behold, he is in thy hand; nevertheless, preserve his soul.” Although Job was one of the sheep of whom the Lord says, “No one shall snatch them from My hand” [Note: [Col. 0817] Job 10], He nevertheless places him in the adversary’s hand, but does not abandon him once placed there. Thus He abandons His soldier while preserving him by abandoning him. He abandons him that he may be tempted; He preserves him that he may not be overcome by temptation. “Behold,” He says, “he is in thy hand; nevertheless, preserve his soul”—that is, preserve it, lest you presume to attempt anything against his soul. Although “many are the tribulations of the righteous” [Col. 0817B] [Note: [Col. 0817] Ps. 33], “through many tribulations we must enter into the kingdom of God” [Note: [Col. 0817] Acts 14]. The bodies of saints are tormented, but their souls are not disturbed. The shining lantern is shaken, but its lamp is not extinguished; the chaff is threshed, but the grain is not harmed. The treasure which we carry in an earthen vessel [Note: [Col. 0817] I Cor. 4] is not lost when the vessel is broken. Thus, though Job’s body is placed in the hostile hand and exposed to torments, his soul is preserved unharmed: “The souls of the righteous are in the hand of God, and the torment of malice shall not touch them” [Note: [Col. 0817] Wis. 3]. It follows:

**“So Satan went out,” etc.** The proud enemy wounds the holy man; but You, good Jesus, turn back upon him the wounds he inflicts. “Thou shalt humble the proud man as one wounded, in the arm of Thy strength” [Note: [Col. 0817] Ps. 88], and [Col. 0817C] “let his iniquity return into his own bosom.” The time will yet come when You shall break his bow, shatter his weapons and shield, and burn them with fire [Note: [Col. 0817] Ps. 45]. Satan wounds the righteous man in the body, whom he would rather wound in the soul. Would, O Lord, that I had in the flesh the wounds which I have in my soul, and that my soul were healed! Grant, O Lord, in Thy good will, that Thou mayest heal my soul of its wounds. “Heal my soul, O Lord, for I have sinned against Thee” [Note: [Col. 0817] Isa. 40]. At times I have applied the medicine of penitence to the wounds of my soul, and through the benefit of confession and satisfaction the wounds were covered over into scars. But afterwards, when through my own folly I relapsed into the same thing and returned to the vomit, the pain grew raw again, and the infirmity returned more dangerously than before. [Col. 0817D] Then I could say with the Prophet: “My scars have become putrid and corrupt through my folly” [Note: [Col. 0817] Ps. 37]. But I needed to return to the aid of the familiar medicine, to Him who heals all the broken in heart and binds up their wounds [Note: [Col. 0817] Ps. 46]. For He is the Father of mercies, and His mercy has no end. I know that He is more ready for mercy than for malice [Note: [Col. 0817] Joel 2], and that His mercy is greater than my iniquity. No one has been wounded by so many wounds in the soul, no one so afflicted by so many sores, whom our bronze serpent will not heal, if the eye [Col. 0818A] of our mind is turned toward Him.

Suppose that someone labours under manifold vice: puffed up with pride, vainly glorious, pinched by avarice, boiling with ambition, hasty to anger, stubborn in hatred, defiled by lusts, wasting away with envy, devoted to detraction, shameless of face, unbridled in mind, prodigal of tongue, deceitful, indulgent in gluttony; suppose that he disturbs peace, is suspicious, incites hatred, dissembles, is double in speech, dishonourable in works, sows disputes, troubles his companions, burdens his neighbours, accuses the brethren, betrays, flatters, despises the Church, forgets God, neglects his own soul, and is given over to a reprobate mind. Suppose that one so afflicted by wounds adds wounds to wounds and iniquity to iniquity, like an imprudent debtor [Col. 0818B] who continually burdens himself with borrowed money until he is overwhelmed by interest, as it is written: “The sinner shall borrow and shall not repay” [Note: [Col. 0817] Ps. 36]. Yet if he returns with tears to his Redeemer, the Lord “shall redeem his soul from iniquities and usuries” [Note: [Col. 0817] Ps. 71], since with the Lord is mercy, and with Him abundant redemption [Note: [Col. 0817] Ps. 129]. For He is the One who says: “At whatever hour the sinner groans over his sin, he shall live the life and shall not die” [Note: [Col. 0817] Ezek. 21]. He is the One “wounded for our wounds” [Note: [Col. 0817] Isa. 53], who wills, is able, and knows how to heal all our wounds. He did not shrink from the thief hanging on the cross, from the weeping sinful woman, from the supplicating Canaanite woman, from the woman caught in adultery, from the [Col. 0818C] disciple who denied Him, from the man sitting at the tax-office, from the publican, from the persecutor of His disciples, or even from His own crucifiers. It follows:

**“Who scraped the discharge with a potsherd,” etc.** To scrape the discharge with a potsherd is to wipe away one’s iniquities by penitence and discipline. The potsherd, because it is rough, signifies the harshness of penitence and the austerity of discipline. Indeed, a potsherd, which is earth without moisture, figures the sinful soul, neither sprinkled with heavenly dew nor soaked with the moisture of charity, as the Prophet says: “My soul is as earth without water before Thee” [Note: [Col. 0817] Ps. 142]. Likewise: “My strength has dried up like a potsherd” [Note: [Col. 0817] Ps. 21]. Therefore he who, sitting on the dung-hill, scrapes his discharge with a potsherd remembers his wretched and unclean origin; he recalls that he was conceived from unclean seed, born from corruption, [Col. 0818D] given as food to worms, and that corruption will return to corruption, as our athlete says concerning himself: “I am to be consumed as rottenness, and as a garment that is eaten by a moth” [Note: [Col. 0817] Job 13]. By the frequent remembrance of our most wretched condition, the discharge of the inward wound is scraped away and the will to do evil is cut off.

**“Then his wife said to him,” etc.** The adversary, who had taken from blessed Job both his children and all his possessions, left him his wife, not for the man’s consolation [Col. 0819A] but for the completion of his own wickedness: that he might conquer through a woman the man whom he had not conquered by persecution, and accomplish through the words of a woman what he could not accomplish by blows. He saw no freer or more convenient opportunity of doing harm than through a familiar enemy and a domestic traitor. For it is written: “From her who sleeps in thy bosom, guard the doors of thy mouth” [Note: [Col. 0819] Mic. 7]. He knew that a woman’s nature, the more fragile it is, is the more pliable toward fault and, through a certain innate corruption, more inclined to harm. Frequent experience of events and a multitude of examples furnished him with fullest proof of this. Through a woman Joseph was imprisoned [Note: [Col. 0819] Gen. 39], Naboth killed [Note: [Col. 0819] III Kings 21], Samson bound [Note: [Col. 0819] Judg. 16], Ish-bosheth slain [Note: [Col. 0819] II Kings 4], Solomon made an apostate [Note: [Col. 0819] III Kings 11], David made a murderer [Col. 0819B] and traitor [Note: [Col. 0819] II Kings 11], Sisera pierced with a nail [Note: [Col. 0819] Judg. 4], and the Forerunner and Baptist of the Lord beheaded [Note: [Col. 0819] Matt. 14]. Solomon, expressing a woman’s wickedness more vehemently, says: “Better is the iniquity of a man than a woman doing good” [Note: [Col. 0819] Ecclus. 41]. Through a woman death entered; and when our redemption had been ordained through the Son of God, the enemy, foreseeing that in Christ’s death the dispensation of our redemption was being fulfilled, contrived to hinder the salvation of the whole human race through a woman. Thus he sent deceptive visions and phantasmal illusions into Pilate’s wife, so that, seeking to dissuade Pilate from Christ’s death, she sent him this message: “Have nothing to do with that righteous man; for today I have suffered many things in a dream because of him” [Note: [Col. 0819] Matt. 17]. It follows:

**“Who said to him,” etc.** Now the enemy applies the kindling [Col. 0819C] of temptations, that he may set the house of God ablaze with flames of anger; now he sends a southern blast, now a wind of whirlwind and vexation. But the Lord strengthens the righteous and sends roots into His elect, so that they may safely receive the wind of temptation and not be uprooted. Job therefore takes weapons away from the enemy, that they may become weapons of virtue for himself. Hence he rebukes his wife, in order that he may instruct her in salvation when she has been brought into subjection and corrected. “If we have received good things from the hand of the Lord,” he says, “why should we not endure evil things?” As though he said: The correction of the Creator must be borne with an even mind, for according to His good pleasure He both grants prosperity and sends adversity. I cannot justly complain of His justice, whose mercy I await and whose mercy has gone before me. “My God,” says [Col. 0819D] the Psalmist, “His mercy shall go before me, and His mercy shall follow me all the days of my life” [Note: [Col. 0819] Ps. 58]. He has taken away no good thing except what He Himself bestowed. If we have been emptied and made poor, we hope in Him who is our hope, because we shall be filled with the good things of His house. Foolish woman, what do you know whether God may turn, forgive, and leave a blessing behind Him? [Note: [Col. 0819] Joel 2]. The Lord stores up delight and exultation for those whom He afflicts; and as He is severe in scourges, so He is gentle in remedies. Thus the bride says in the Song of Songs: “My beloved drinks wine [Col. 0820A] with milk” [Note: [Col. 0819] Song 5], that is, He exercises severity together with gentleness. It follows:

**“In all these things Job did not sin with his lips.”** We sin with our lips in two ways: either when we say what ought to be silent, or when we keep silent about what ought to be said. But Job replied with nothing proud against the Lord, because in correcting and instructing his wife, as she offered perverse counsel, he restrained her. Satan therefore, seeing that Job was not conquered by the loss of temporal things, by bereavement of children, or by his wife’s suggestion, stirred up his three friends to afflict him with reproaches, so that, provoked to anger, he might burst forth into words of malice and, offended himself, offend the Lord of all.

**“Therefore, when the three friends heard,” etc.** Blessed are you, O Lord, whose help is from You. For such a person is not disturbed [Col. 0820B] by insults, not broken by injuries, not conquered by losses, not led away by flatteries, not deceived by frauds, nor overcome by distresses. He despises all adversities that occur in this world, placing himself in safety and acting confidently therein. It should be noted that, although Job’s friends insulted him with reproachful words, they should nevertheless be thought to have done this from ignorance rather than malice. For it would be blameworthy in a man so prudent and holy to have wicked and insulting friends, since every honourable man ought to abhor the companionship of the wicked. “He who touches pitch shall be defiled by it” [Note: [Col. 0819] Ecclus. 13]. In the Book of Chronicles Jehoshaphat, who is extolled by many praises for his former life, is rebuked for his friendship with King Ahab: “Thou givest help to the ungodly, and art joined in friendship with those who [Col. 0820C] hate the Lord; therefore thou didst deserve the Lord’s wrath, unless good works had been found in thee, because thou didst remove the groves from the land of Judah” [Note: [Col. 0819] II Chron. 19].

Many hand down [Note: [Col. 0819] LXX interpreters] that Eliphaz was a prince of the Temanites, descended from the sons of Esau; Bildad, a tyrant of the Shuhites; and Zophar, king of the Minaeans. When the friends came to console him, they lifted up their eyes, cried aloud and wept, scattered dust over their heads toward heaven, and, sitting with him seven days and seven nights, spoke not a word to him, displaying in all things the countenance of grief and the affection of compassion. For, if consolation is to lighten the sorrow of the afflicted, one must weep with those who weep and grieve with those who grieve. For seven days they are continually silent, but afterwards overflow with much talk. This indicates that those who are slower to speak generally do not know how, once they have begun, to set an end to their words. For, as a certain wise man says: “The discipline of silence is the nourisher of speech.”

Some wish to understand by Job’s friends, who incite him to sin, our vain thoughts, the desires of the flesh, and the enticements of this world. These too attend us familiarly and flatter us in many ways. Vain thoughts scatter and confound the state of the soul that watches and contemplates God; hence one of these friends [Col. 0821A] is aptly called Zophar, that is, “scattering of the watchtower.” The desires of the flesh, which war against the soul, utterly mortify the new man, who has been created according to God, so that the soul, forgetting all newness, may relish oldness alone. Hence the second friend is called Bildad, which is interpreted “oldness alone.” Thus, when the judgment of reason has been scattered and troubled within it and the desires of the flesh have grown strong, the soul begins to despise God. “For when the sinner has come into the depth of vices, he despises” [Note: [Col. 0821] Prov. 18]. Hence the third friend is called Eliphaz, which is interpreted “contempt of God.” Religious persons, and those who have undertaken the life of stricter observance, frequently experience these friends—or rather, these domestic enemies. It happens sometimes that, while one devotes oneself more fervently to contemplation, “dying flies spoil the sweetness of ointment” [Col. 0821B] [Note: [Col. 0821] Eccl. 10], because vain thoughts creep in, disturbing the peace of contemplation, and through the desires of the flesh awaken love of the world and contempt of God.

Thus a religious man who shortly before was panting with desire for heaven, whom charity inflamed, whom observance of the holy Order delighted, gradually begins to forget heavenly things, to think of worldly things, and to despise the things of God. The judgment of reason is troubled within him; the paths of counsel are occupied; the light of the heart is obscured; devotion grows cold; freedom of spirit vanishes; vigour of soul slackens; reason is lulled to sleep; understanding is confounded; the fervour of the Order cools. Fear of poverty harasses the wretch; [Col. 0821C] vain hope deceives him; ambition draws him; his spirit contracts; grace is withdrawn; expectation of a longer life is prolonged; pleasure flatters; the world allures; security deceives; old habit is recalled; the law is disregarded; right is rejected; what is lawful is proscribed; fear of God is abandoned; hands are given to shamelessness; and that apostate leap is attempted—that shameful and foul leap from the height into the abyss, from the throne to the dung-hill, from heaven to mire, from Paradise to hell, from cloister to the world. I say this not to disparage the monastic Order, which I hold most holy; but let the religious person, I pray, blush to be worse in the cloister than he was in the world. Let him not take up again what he has vomited, nor seek again the world which he left. “Blush, Sidon,” says the sea—these are Isaiah’s words [Note: [Col. 0821] ch. 23]—that is, let the man of [Col. 0821D] cloistered life blush to be worse in the cloister than when he moved among the waves of this world. It follows:

## CHAPTER III. “After these things Job opened his mouth,” etc.

There are two kinds of cursing: the first arises from consideration of justice; the second, from the rancour of vengeance. The first kind is permitted; the second is forbidden. In the first sense the Lord says to Adam: “Cursed is the earth in thy work” [Note: [Col. 0821] Gen. 3]; and to Abraham: “I will curse those who curse thee” [Note: [Col. 0821] Gen. 12]. Of the second mode of cursing the Apostle says: “Do not curse” [Note: [Col. 0821] Rom. 12]; and, “Those who curse shall not possess the kingdom of God” [Note: [Col. 0821] I Cor. 6]. Job therefore curses the day [Col. 0822A] of his birth by the prompting of reason and the motion of justice, not out of zeal for vengeance or a desire to injure another.

For there is a condemned birth of man, a justified birth, and a blessed birth. The first birth of man belongs to nature, the second to grace, the third to glory. In the first is sin, in the second merit, in the third reward. The first is that one may live; the second, that one may live justly; the third, that one may live blessedly. Job therefore curses his first birth, in which man is conceived through fault, begotten for misery, and born for punishment. Following the ancient judgment of divine retribution, he condemns in himself the condition of human nature, condemned from the beginning of the world—not in order to curse God’s creature or the day, which no longer existed in the order of things, but in order that he might acknowledge himself as deservedly afflicted [Col. 0822B] according to the equity of the divine sentence.

And because it is your pleasure, most unconquered prince, that I should set forth the life of holy Job in brief and compact brevity, I pass over his words, the replies of his friends, and the hidden mysteries enfolded in them, fearing that I might offend the delicate ears of Your Excellency with too lengthy a discourse if I undertook that boundless sea. Most blessed Pope Gregory, indeed, explains everything to the smallest detail in his *Moralia*; and it must not be doubted that the finger of God wrote that treatise in his heart—the man who published it openly in a manner of speech somehow angelic, with a dove foretelling it. It remains, therefore, to compress the length of this extensive work into a summary and, in a more curtailed course of words, to recount the mercy of the Most High that He displayed in many ways toward His servant Job: forgiving through Job’s prayer the sin which his friends had committed against him; healing wounds; easing pains; removing temptations; multiplying temporal goods; prolonging life; restoring the loss of his children; and giving him fairer and better daughters in recompense. This is what, near the end of the book, the text of the history declares in few words.

## CHAPTER XLII. “And the Lord blessed the latter end of Job,” etc.

Job had advanced in his days and fallen into the most miserable poverty. Yet he shall still be multiplied in fruitful old age, because, according to the multitude [Col. 0822D] of the sorrows in his heart, Thy consolations, O God, made his soul glad. For Thou shalt add days upon days to him; Thou shalt add riches to poverty and length of days to old age. You earthborn and children of men, hear how greatly the mercy of the Lord has been magnified over us. For if the Lord doubled temporal goods for Job and for His other servants, we should hope in Him who is our hope that, in the time of grace, He will bestow His grace upon us in a fuller measure. “A full measure,” He says, “pressed down, shaken together, and overflowing, shall He give into your bosom” [Note: [Col. 0821] Luke 6]. The Lord’s measure is without measure, and [Col. 0823A] His bushel without limit. With this measure He will measure out to His disciples, saying: “Whoever shall leave father, or mother, or wife, or children, or house, or fields for My sake, shall receive a hundredfold and shall possess eternal life” [Note: [Col. 0823] Matt. 19]. Do you wish to see how this measure overflows and runs over? “His mercy has no end, and His mercy endures for ever” [Note: [Col. 0823] Ps. 117]—and beyond. It follows:

Job lived after these things, etc. The Father of mercies and God of all consolation supports with his left hand and embraces with his right the son—indeed, the servant—returning from the exile of misery; sustaining him in temporal things and advancing him toward eternal things, so that he may sing with the bride: “His left hand is under my head, and his right hand will embrace me” [Note: [Col. 0823] Song 2]. By the right hand, indeed, eternal life is signified, as the Prophet recalls: “Delights are at your right hand unto the end” [Note: [Col. 0823] Ps. 15]. Thus with one hand the Lord heaps riches and honors upon his servant Job, while with the other he adds length of days, because, as it is written: “In her left hand are riches and honor, and in her right hand length of days” [Note: [Col. 0823] Prov. 3].

And note that it says: “After these scourges.” By a great dispensation of divine grace, affliction came first, so that after sorrow joy, after shipwreck harbor, after labor rest, sweetness after bitterness, and prosperity after persecutions might smile more graciously. Indeed, sinners, by divine permission, work upon the back of the righteous man, set between hammer and anvil, so that after the evil days in which he was afflicted and humbled, fuller gladness may follow, as the Prophet says: “We rejoiced for the days in which you humbled us, for the years in which we saw evils” [Note: [Col. 0823] Ps. 89]. According to the saying of the Wise Man: “Before ruin the heart is lifted up” [Note: [Col. 0823] Prov. 16]; and, conversely, humility precedes glory. For humility is the way to exaltation, pain to joy, persecution to blessedness, groaning to laughter, death to life.

Therefore the Lord scourges his own, lest they be scourged hereafter; he punishes them temporally, lest they be punished eternally. We read in the Book of Kings [Note: [Col. 0823] III Kings 6] that, when Solomon was building the Lord’s temple, all the stones were hewn outside, so that they might be set in the construction of the temple without the sound of a hammer. The saints are struck by scourges in time, so that in the building of the heavenly Jerusalem, which “is built as a city” [Col. 0823D] [Note: [Col. 0823] Ps. 121], they may be joined by the bond of charity, without the scourge of discipline and without the groaning of repentance. For in the other life, amid everlasting fires, there is no place to earn pardon, because in hell there is no redemption; nor is a sacrifice for sin left to a person dead in sins. Christ died once and dies no more [Note: [Col. 0823] Rom. 6]; he is not crucified again, and the blood which he once shed for the remission of sins will not be shed again. Nor will all the sinners of the earth drink from it, because once they have been removed from the earth, if they have carried mortal guilt with them, neither death nor Christ’s blood will benefit them for salvation [Col. 0824A].

It follows:

“And he saw his sons,” etc. Death concludes all human felicities. For when you have proclaimed Abraham’s faith, Joseph’s piety, Moses’ charity, Samson’s strength, Phinehas’s zeal, David’s virtue, Elisha’s miracles, Solomon’s prudence and riches, still “the end of joy is occupied by grief” [Note: [Col. 0823] Prov. 14]; and the end of a human life makes the end of the story, while for all there is one conclusion: “And he died.” But in the fact that Job died old and full of days, it should be noted that some die empty of days and others full. A person empty of days dies when, serving the vanities of this world during life, he carries with him in death no merits of eternal life. But one full of days departs from the world who devoted himself to virtues, fulfilled his desire from them, and so brought his transitory days to completion that he finds the days of eternity in the life to come [Col. 0824B].

It is good, indeed, to live well, but far better to die well. Yet no one dies well who has not lived well. Some desire to die rather than turn to the virtues; “their end is destruction” [Note: [Col. 0823] Phil. 3]. Samson prefigured their end by setting the foxes’ tails on fire [Note: [Col. 0823] Judg. 5]. Their end has been assigned to that fire prepared for the devil and his angels [Note: [Col. 0823] Matt. 25]. Very many people, unwilling to live well, desire to die well. They know that “precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints” [Note: [Col. 0823] Ps. 115]; they know that, “when he gives sleep to his beloved, behold, the inheritance of the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0823] Ps. 126]; they know that “blessed are the dead who die in him” [Col. 0824C] [Note: [Col. 0823] Rev. 14]. Yet they do not wish to share the labors of those to whom the Lord says: “You are those who have remained with me in my temptations” [Note: [Col. 0823] Luke 22]. They wish to reign with Christ, but they do not wish to die with him [Note: [Col. 0823] Rom. 8].

Such was Balaam the diviner. Considering the camp of the children of Israel and understanding the promise of eternal blessedness made to them by the Lord, he said: “May my soul die the death of the righteous, and may my last things be like theirs” [Note: [Col. 0823] Num. 23]. He desired their glorious end, but shrank from the labors by which they earned glory. Yet you will not reap unless you sow [Note: [Col. 0823] Luke 12]; you will not attain the prize unless you run [Note: [Col. 0823] I Cor. 9]; you will not reign unless you serve as a soldier; you will not rejoice unless you suffer; you will not be crowned unless you fight [Col. 0824D] [Note: [Col. 0823] II Tim. 2].

Do you suppose that someone rejoices both in the present life and in the future—if, indeed, that can be called joy which is continually disturbed and sprinkled with bitterness? You are far too delicate if you presume upon both: to make use of the world and enjoy Christ; to possess the delights of the present world and nonetheless obtain the riches of heavenly glory. Hear what was said in the Gospel to that rich man who was tormented in flame and sought relief for his burning tongue: “Son, remember that you received good things in your life, and Lazarus likewise evil things” [Note: [Col. 0823] Luke 16].

Oh, how utterly different in merit may we judge those most holy kings and prophets, apostles and martyrs, confessors, and even tender and most delicate virgins to be from madmen, if all of them, having despised riches and trampled underfoot the delights of this world, offered themselves to tribulation and death for Christ, while they could have obtained in riches and pleasures the glory which they won amid straits and pain! Therefore, most beloved prince, withdraw and steal for yourself something each day from this world’s pleasures. Enter upon the way of repentance; and do not think it harsh if you wisely renounce what pleased you vainly. Nothing can be endured with distress in this life-giving death which could sufficiently correspond in worth to heavenly joys. “For the sufferings of this present age are not worthy to be compared with the future glory which shall be revealed in us” [Col. 0825B] [Note: [Col. 0825D] Rom. 8].

We have sacrificed the flower of our youth to the world; let us at least sacrifice the dregs of old age to the Most High, and with what remains of our short and wretched life purchase the eternal kingdom. For the kingdom of God is worth as much as you offer for it from the desire of your heart. And according to the Apostle’s saying: “What is light and momentary in our tribulation works in us an immeasurable weight of glory” [Note: [Col. 0825D] II Cor. 4].

For this, moreover, I give most abundant thanks to the King of kings: because you love learned men; because you gladly devote yourselves to Holy Scripture; because, in a certain image of divinity, you humble the proud and exalt the humble; because you zealously seek salvation and peace for the peoples entrusted to you by the Lord; because you show yourselves gracious and gentle toward widows and orphans; because you kindly receive religious persons and the poor—indeed, your ear has heard the preparation of their heart, and, as though foreknowing their needs, you anticipate them with your blessings [Col. 0826A]. Today, for this very reason, the whole church of the saints recounts your alms even among the most distant nations. Therefore act while there is time: scatter abroad; give to the poor; and do not entrust the management of this matter to your heirs. The examples of many may deter you. By alms from your own hand, raise for yourselves a ladder and ascent to that dwelling of the citizens above, where there is eternal peace, unchangeable rest, joy that does not fail, light that is not extinguished, and glory that does not pass away. May the Son of the Most High, Jesus Christ, who triumphs and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit through all ages of ages, deign to prepare and grant this to us and to you. Amen.

[Col. 0825]

# AGAINST THE PERFIDY OF THE JEWS

## CHAPTER I. Preface, in which he shows that disputation with Jews and heretics is difficult and dangerous

[Col. 0825C]

In your letter you have woven a long and anxious complaint: that, surrounded by Jews and heretics, you are continually attacked by them, and that you do not have at hand the authorities of Holy Scripture by which you may refute their calumnies and answer their deceptive wiles. Indeed, as the Apostle testifies, “there must be heresies and schisms, so that those who are approved may become manifest” [Note: [Col. 0825] I Cor. 11]. Therefore life is still granted even to the Jews today, because they are our book-carriers: they carry about the prophets and the Mosaic Law in support of our faith. Not only in their books, but also in their faces, we read Christ’s passion. Therefore Truth speaks concerning the Father in the Psalm, saying: “God has shown [Col. 0825D] me” [Note: [Col. 0825] Ps. 58], etc.

Would that no one lacking trained faculties should dispute with a heretic or a Jew! For because of unlawful and incautious disputations, the poisonous crop of heresies grows wild everywhere. While those who are ignorant and in error wish to stop the mouths of those speaking iniquity, they “make light darkness and darkness light” [Note: [Col. 0825] Isa. 5]; and while they wish to relieve others of their errors, they hurl themselves into worse ones. It is absurd to dispute concerning the Trinity in the streets, and to thrust the eternal generation of the Son into material for scandal and into the arena of public contention [Col. 0826C]. Therefore Justinian, the most Christian emperor, established by a general enactment that the supreme Trinity and the Catholic faith should not be disputed about. In the Law of the Lord likewise, the beast that touches the mountain is stoned; a pit must be covered [Note: [Col. 0825] Exod. 19; Heb. 12]; pearls are forbidden to be scattered before swine and what is holy to be given to dogs [Note: [Col. 0825] Matt. 7].

The angel’s word to Tobit is: “The king’s secret,” etc. [Note: [Col. 0825] Tob. 12]. For disputation concerning the sacrament of Christ’s body and blood, and concerning the other articles of our faith, is full of danger. But to speak of hope and charity and the other spiritual gifts, and also of the creation and governance of things, and in these matters to recount God’s mighty works, is permitted and lawful for anyone. Solomon’s judgment, too, is that we should think of the Lord in goodness and seek him in simplicity of heart [Col. 0826D] [Note: [Col. 0825] Wis. 1]. Therefore one must not dispute with those who, plotting the overthrow of faith, always run to denial and turn the waters of Siloam, which flowed quietly, into waters of contradiction [Note: [Col. 0825] Isa. 8].

Speaking of such persons, the Apostle says in the First Epistle to Timothy [Note: [Col. 0825] Chap. 5]: “If anyone does not assent to the sound words of the Lord,” etc. Therefore do not dispute with a Jew or a heretic. For a time be like one who does not hear and has no reproofs in his mouth [Note: [Col. 0825] Ps. 37]. For if you enter alone and unarmed into the theatre of a common fight, danger threatens you if you are overcome. But if you conquer the enemy of Christ’s cross, he will not therefore be converted in heart; rather, for that very reason he will seek evasions more obstinately, corrupt the Scriptures, and refuse to understand in order to do good [Col. 0827A] [Note: [Col. 0827] Ps. 35], because “wisdom will not enter into a malicious soul” [Note: [Col. 0827] Wis. 1].

The mouth of the heretic is full of cursing, bitterness, and deceit; and, “walking in things great and wonderful beyond himself” [Note: [Col. 0827] Ps. 130], he searches out the deep things of God and by a ruinous inquiry investigates the reason of things that are above reason. Yet Blessed Gregory says [Note: [Col. 0827] Homily 26 on the Gospels] that faith has no merit when human reason furnishes proof. Thus he spills over into much verbosity; abandoning the straight paths of sacred speech and overstepping the boundaries set by our fathers, he runs into his own inventions and, contrary to the prohibition of Deuteronomy [Note: [Col. 0827] Chap. 12], plants a forest of opinions and words beside the altar of the Lord our God [Col. 0827B]. Thus the maker of lies and cultivator of perverse doctrines thinks unthinkable things, utters what cannot be uttered, and speaks what it is not lawful for a human being to speak [Note: [Col. 0827] II Cor. 12].

Among such people the paschal lamb is boiled in water [Note: [Col. 0827] Exod. 12], and what remains of it is not burned with fire; its bones are broken, though it is written: “You shall not break a bone of it” [Note: [Col. 0827] John 19]. An outrage is done to the Spirit of grace; the blood of the covenant is shamefully trampled underfoot; and the bones of the king of Edom are reduced to ashes [Note: [Col. 0827] Amos 2; IV Kings 3].

But your desire to dispute with Jews, in order to convict and convert them to the faith, wins my approval all the less for that very reason, because you are beating the air and wearing yourself out in foolish and vain effort [Col. 0827C]. God has indeed set them a boundary which they cannot pass. Their hour has not yet come; rather, he has blinded them for a time, until the Gentile world is converted to the faith. Hence he speaks through Isaiah, saying: “Go, and blind the heart of this people,” etc. [Note: [Col. 0827] Isa. 6]. And in the same prophet: “Who is blind,” etc. [Note: [Col. 0827] Isa. 48]. He calls the prophets and apostles messengers. But, as the Apostle testifies: “Blindness has now happened in part to Israel” [Note: [Col. 0827] Rom. 11]. For although some of them have received the faith, the rest still persist in their obstinacy. It remains, then, for the fullness of the Gentiles to enter into the faith [Note: [Col. 0827] Isa. 10]; and then the remnant of Israel will be saved [Note: [Col. 0827] Exod. 32].

It would seem more prudent to me to overlook for a time the injury done to our faith than to enter into a contest with a people stiff-necked and of truly beastly obstinacy [Col. 0827D], and, with no hope whatever of a future result, cast oneself into danger to one’s soul and faith. Yet because in your lamentable complaint you bewail being besieged by heretics and Jews, and having no means at hand to overthrow their devices: what I know, I do not begrudge you. For, since according to Blessed Peter’s command each person must give an account of the faith and hope that is in him [Note: [Col. 0827] I Pet. 3], it is useful for you to have ready material on every article of faith by which the obstinacy of Jewish deceit may be blunted and the defense of your side be wholly strengthened by testimonies of the Law and the Prophets [Col. 0828A]. How you, or any Catholic, ought to oppose the wiles and blasphemies of heretics, I believe I have explained more fully in the book which I entitled *On Faith*.

## CHAPTER II. Testimonies of the Law and the Prophets concerning the Trinity and unity in God

It is not our purpose to weave a treatise on the holy Trinity and indivisible unity, but only to bring forward those sayings and authorities of the Law and the Prophets by which the adversaries of orthodox faith may be refuted, the tower of David built, and the strongholds of salvation raised [Note: [Col. 0827] Song 4]. Since, therefore, the Trinity in one God and unity in three persons strike Jews with scandal and horror—that God is one and three—we shall, with the Lord’s help, prove this by an irrefutable argument.

The lawgiver of the Jews speaks and says: “Hear, Israel: the Lord your God is one God” [Note: [Col. 0827] Deut. 4]. And the Lord, speaking in his own person: “I am the Lord, establishing the heavens. God alone stretched out the heaven and established the earth” [Note: [Col. 0827] Isa. 42]. And in Isaiah: “I am the Lord, establishing the heavens, alone making the earth firm, and no one is with me” [Col. 0828B] [Note: [Col. 0827] Isa. 44]. Likewise Moses in Deuteronomy: “Know today, and consider,” etc. [Note: [Col. 0827] Deut. 4]. And in the same book: “You alone were his leader, and no foreign god was with him” [Note: [Col. 0827] Deut. 22].

Yet, according to the testimony of Blessed Hilary, God is one in such a way as not to be solitary. For unity does not annul Trinity, nor does any solitude prejudice Trinity. Clearly, in sacred speech God is said to exist, to speak, or to create something in such a way that now one person, now two, now indeed three are most clearly designated. Hear one: “I am the Lord God, who fill heaven and earth and all things that are in them” [Note: [Col. 0827] Jer. 23]. Hear the Father in Jeremiah speaking of the Son: “If they had stood,” he says, “in my substance,” etc. [Note: [Col. 0827] Ibid.]. And he adds: “Who will stand in my substance and see my Word?” Concerning this Word the prophet David testifies: “My heart has poured forth a good Word” [Note: [Col. 0827] Ps. 44]. And John the Evangelist: “In the beginning was the Word” [Note: [Col. 0827] John 1].

For God, speaking and acting are the same, as it is written: “He spoke and they were made; he commanded and all things were created” [Note: [Col. 0827] Ps. 148]. Therefore the Son of God is God’s Word, God’s power, and God’s wisdom. In him, as in his wisdom and as in the beginning of all things, God made all things, as it is written: “In the beginning God created heaven and earth” [Note: [Col. 0827] Gen. 1]. This is God’s Wisdom which, in the book bearing its name, declares its eternal generation and says: “I came forth from the mouth of the Most High, first-born before every creature” [Col. 0828D] [Note: [Col. 0827] Sir. 24]. And likewise: “The Lord possessed me,” etc. [Note: [Col. 0827] Prov. 8].

Since before the creation of the world there was nothing that was not God, how was this Wisdom already begotten? How were all things created through her? Either the Jew will confess that that Wisdom is God and was begotten from God, and thus is the Son; or, lying, he will say that Holy Scripture contains a falsehood. But let the Christian recognize that God’s Wisdom, through whom he himself makes all things, is the same as the Son of God [Col. 0829A]. Nor is it absurd that God the Son should be begotten from God the Father, just as splendor is begotten from the sun; indeed, anyone who does not believe the Son’s eternal generation from the Father and temporal generation from his mother incurs the judgment of prophetic malediction. For the prophet’s word is: “Woe to him who says to the father, ‘What do you beget?’ and to the mother, ‘What do you bring forth?’” [Note: [Col. 0829] Isa. 45]. And, that you may understand this of the Son’s generation, hear God the Father speaking in the same Isaiah.

## CHAPTER III. Testimonies of the Law and the Prophets concerning the Father and the Son

Concerning the Son’s eternal generation, God the Father speaks through Isaiah [Col. 0829B]: “Shall I, who make others give birth, not myself give birth, says the Lord? Shall I, who grant generation to others, be barren?” [Note: [Col. 0829] Isa. 66]. And in the Psalm the Son speaks, saying: “The Lord said to me: You are my Son; today I have begotten you” [Note: [Col. 0829] Ps. 2]. The Lord’s day is eternity; hence “today” also signifies from eternity. Likewise: “In the splendors of the saints, from the womb, before the morning star, I have begotten you” [Note: [Col. 0829] Ps. 109]. For he who was the splendor and illumination of the saints who were to be was today—that is, eternally—begotten from the womb, from the hidden substance of the Father.

Isaiah speaks concerning the Son’s generation, saying: “Who shall declare his generation?” [Note: [Col. 0829] Isa. 53]. Therefore, as light is from light, so the Son is from the Father. Hence the Psalmist also says: “For with you is the fountain of life, and in your light we shall see light” [Note: [Col. 0829] Ps. 35]. Because God has a Son, certain psalms are entitled “For the hidden things of the Son”; their words can apply to no one but the Son of God—as in Psalm Nine, “I will give thanks,” and in “My heart has poured forth,” “A song for the beloved” [Col. 0829C] [Note: [Col. 0829] Ps. 44]; and in the Psalm “God is our refuge and strength,” “For secrets” [Note: [Col. 0829] Ps. 45].

Hear the Father in Hosea speaking of the Son and saying: “I will save them in the Lord their God” [Note: [Col. 0829] Hos. 1]. Let the Jew tell me: who is that God whom God calls the God and Lord of the Hebrews [Note: [Col. 0829] Exod. 9]? And in Genesis: “The Lord rained sulphur and fire from the Lord and overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah” [Note: [Col. 0829] Gen. 19]. Who is the God who rained from the Lord, except the Son from the Father? Or is there another God who rained from God? Show, Jew, or acknowledge with us, that the Son does and orders all things with the Father.

And in the Psalm: “The Lord said to my Lord” [Col. 0829D] [Note: [Col. 0829] Ps. 109]. And in Genesis: “The Lord said to Jacob: Arise and go up to Bethel; make there an altar to that God who appeared to you when you fled from the face of your brother” [Note: [Col. 0829] Gen. 30]. And in Exodus: “The Lord said to Moses: How long will you refuse to hear my commandments? Has not the Lord God given you this Sabbath day?” [Note: [Col. 0829] Exod. 16]. The Lord speaks and says that the Sabbath day was given by God. Stiff-necked man, tell me who that Lord is of whom God commands the patriarch Jacob to make an altar.

That he who speaks with Jacob and wrestles with him is God, not an angel, I prove to you. When Jacob asks his name, he answers: “Why do you ask my name, which is Wonderful?” [Col. 0830A] [Note: [Col. 0829] Gen. 32]. This cannot apply to an angel. Again, in Hosea the Lord says: “Jacob spoke with us in Aram” [Note: [Col. 0829] Hos. 12]. These are God’s words, not an angel’s. Again, in the Psalm: “Your throne, O God, is for ever and ever. You loved righteousness and hated iniquity; therefore God anointed you with the oil of gladness” [Note: [Col. 0829] Ps. 44]. This God whose throne is for ever and ever, the very same one, according to the prophet’s testimony, God anointed above his companions. And what God anointed God except the Father the Son?

He who was anointed by God is either God or man. If God, then God was anointed by God; if man, then his throne is for ever and ever. Consider whether there is or has been any man besides Christ to whom this could apply. The prophet joins these two points: that he himself is God and that his throne is for ever and ever [Col. 0830B]. Hear in Hosea the Father speaking of the Son: “I will save them in the Lord their God” [Note: [Col. 0829] Hos. 1]. He who speaks is God, yet he saves in the Lord God. Who is the God who saves in God, except the Father in the Son? O Jew, did God create without his Wisdom, whom we call the Son of God? “God founded the earth by wisdom.” Why then do you shrink from the name when you cannot deny God’s Wisdom?

## CHAPTER IV. Testimonies of the Law and the Prophets concerning the Holy Spirit

All Holy Scripture proclaims the Spirit of God. Hear Isaiah: “Woe, rebellious children, says the Lord: you have formed a plan, and it is not mine, nor through my spirit” [Col. 0830C] [Note: [Col. 0829] Isa. 30]. And likewise: “The Spirit came down from God,” he says, etc. [Note: [Col. 0829] Isa. 63]. David: “And they provoked the Spirit of the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0829] Ps. 105]. Haggai: “Therefore I am with you, says the Lord,” etc. [Note: [Col. 0829] Hag. 2]. Isaiah: “And the hinds met,” etc. [Note: [Col. 0829] Isa. 35]. Zechariah: “My words,” etc. [Note: [Col. 0829] Zech. 2]. David: “Where shall I go from your spirit?” [Note: [Col. 0829] Ps. 138].
