And the Lord in Zechariah: “I will put my spirit upon your seed” [Note: [Col. 0829] Zech. 4]. And likewise: “This is the word of the Lord by the hand of Zerubbabel,” etc. [Note: [Col. 0829] Ibid.]. David: “You will send forth your spirit and they shall be created” [Note: [Col. 0829] Ps. 103]. Isaiah: “Not an angel, nor a messenger,” etc. [Note: [Col. 0829] Isa. 63]. And in the Book of Wisdom: “The Spirit is he who made me” [Note: [Col. 0829] Wis. 7].

## CHAPTER V. Testimonies of the Law and the Prophets concerning the Trinity
[Col. 0830D] But that the whole Trinity may be made known, hear Moses saying in Genesis: “In the beginning God made heaven and earth” [Note: [Col. 0829] Gen. 1.]. The expression “made” indicates unity of substance. But when it is said, “in the beginning God,” it is to be understood that the Father created in the Son. For that beginning was not something other than God. When there is added, “And the Spirit of the Lord was borne over the waters,” the whole Trinity is plainly expressed. Note also that God first uttered this word: “Let us make man in our image and likeness” [Note: [Col. 0829] Ibid.]. When “let us make” is said, plurality of persons is shown.

[Col. 0831A] For God did not say “Let us make” to the angels, since they themselves are not makers and creators, nor was man to be made in the likeness of an angel. Therefore he says “Let us make” of him, so as to intimate the Trinity. Of him Moses says “made,” “said,” and “saw,” so as to express, in three, the unity of the same substance. Likewise, in Genesis we read that Abraham saw three and worshipped one, saying: “If I have found favor in your sight, do not pass by your servant” [Note: [Col. 0831] Gen. 18]. He first stated that there were three; and he speaks to the three as though to one, when he says: “Lord, do not pass by your servant.” And in the same place: “Let water be brought and let your feet be washed.” Behold, several persons. And: “He set a table before them, and they ate.” In these words he intimates plurality of persons. But when he adds, “Returning I shall come to you at this time, with life accompanying,” he declares that they are one.

[Col. 0831B] It follows: “Rising from there, they went,” etc. Behold, still three. And he adds: “But the Lord said: Shall I conceal from my servant Abraham what I am about to do to Sodom?” In all these passages, both three speak to Abraham and one speaks; and Abraham speaks both to three and to one. In all of them you have the mystery of Trinity and unity explicitly expressed.

Since the finger of God in sacred speech is the power of God, the three are designated by the name and number of three fingers. Thus Isaiah says: “Who has weighed the mass of the earth with three fingers?” [Note: [Col. 0831] Isa. 40.] What can be designated by three fingers except the Trinity of persons? For in Exodus too the finger of God is called the power of God. Pharaoh’s magicians say: “This is the finger of God” [Note: [Col. 0831] Exod. 8.]. Therefore let the Jews say with us—or at least with Pharaoh’s magicians—that the Holy Spirit is

[Col. 0831C] the finger of God. Indeed, our Messiah says in the Gospel: “If I cast out demons by the finger of God, then the kingdom of God has surely come upon you” [Note: [Col. 0831] Luc. 71.]. We confess that the three fingers are the three persons in God.

Thus, in the prophet Haggai, the words of the Lord plainly express the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, when he says: “I am with you” [Note: [Col. 0831] Agg. 2], etc. Behold the Father, his Word, and his Spirit. Likewise the Psalmist: “He shall send forth his word and melt them; his Spirit shall blow, and the waters shall flow” [Note: [Col. 0831] Psal. 147.]. And: “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the spirit of his mouth all their power” [Note: [Col. 0831] Psal. 32.]. And in Isaiah: “The man to whom it was appointed concerning the Christ of God said,” etc. Behold three: the Lord, the Word, and the Spirit—that is, the Father, the Word, and the Holy Spirit.

Hence in Jeremiah: “I said: Ah, ah, ah, Lord God. They say to me: ‘Does this man speak in parables?’” [Note: [Col. 0831] Jerem. 4.]. He sighs three times and invokes the Trinity. But by adding in the singular, “Lord God,” he indicates the one substance of the three persons. Similar is what is heard in Isaiah: the voice of angels praising God and saying, “Holy, holy, holy” [Note: [Col. 0831] Isai. 6.]. That threefold repetition signifies the Trinity. But by adding “Lord God of Sabaoth,” it intimates unity. And in the Psalm: “May God bless us, our God; may God bless us” [Note: [Col. 0831] Psal. 66.]. This threefold repetition of the name would be pointless

[Col. 0832A] unless the mystery of the Trinity were contained in its reason.

The prophet Haggai also declares the Trinity quite openly, when God the Father speaks in him of the Spirit and of his Son: “My Spirit is in your midst” [Note: [Col. 0831] Agg. 2.]. Behold the Father and his Spirit. And he adds: “For behold, I shall shake heaven and earth, and the Desired One of all nations shall come.” And behold the Son. In the Psalm: “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord; the Lord is God, and he has shone upon us” [Note: [Col. 0831] Psal. 117.]. Here it is most plainly evident that God comes in the name of the Lord.

These too are the words of the man: “He sent from on high and received me” [Note: [Col. 0831] Psal. 17.]. And: “Blessed is he whom you have chosen and taken up” [Note: [Col. 0831] Psal. 64.]. Isaiah, plainly declaring both the Trinity in God and humanity in the Son, speaks in the person of God the Father, saying: “Behold,” he says, “my Servant; I shall receive him,” etc.

[Col. 0832B] [Note: [Col. 0831] Isai. 42.]. Isaiah, in the person of the Son: “I am the first and I am the last,” etc. [Note: [Col. 0831] Isai. 47.]. Who could ever say this truthfully except God—yet he is sent by the Spirit of God? And in the same prophet: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me,” etc. [Note: [Col. 0831] Isai. 61.]. Here you have the Spirit; him whose Spirit it is; and him who is anointed with the Holy Spirit. Christ, reading in the book of Wisdom, testifies that this prophecy was fulfilled in himself on that day [Note: [Col. 0831] Luc. 4.].

In all these matters the nature of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit is most plainly declared, so that you may have more explicitly the plurality of persons and unity in God. Know that in Hebrew God is sometimes called *El* and *Adon*, which signify “God” or “Lord” in the singular, because of the unity of the divine substance. But sometimes *Eloi* and *Adonai* are used in the plural, and indicate plurality of persons

[Col. 0832C] [Note: [Col. 0831] Exod. 6.]. The singular is used in the example from Genesis cited above, where it is said: “The Lord spoke to Jacob: Rise” [Note: [Col. 0831] Gen. 35.], etc. Here both the name of God and his action are expressed in the singular in Hebrew. But when it is said, “He built an altar there and called the name of the place ‘House of God’” [Note: [Col. 0831] Ibid.], “God appeared to him” is there expressed in Hebrew with both “God” and “appeared” in the plural. For there *Eloim* is said, and *inglu* is said, which signifies “they appeared” in the plural. For if he had spoken in the singular, he would have used *El* and *ingla*, which are singular.

In the book of Samuel too, David, praising God, says: “For what nation is there on earth like your people?” [Note: [Col. 0831] II Reg. 7.], etc. Here “God” and “went” are said in Hebrew in the plural, *Eloim* and *alon*, which are plural forms and signify

[Col. 0832D] plurality of persons; for *ala* is singular. But “redeemed” and “for himself” are expressed in the singular because of unity of substance. Likewise Jeremiah [Note: [Col. 0831] Cap. 10.]: “But the Lord is the true God, the living God, and the everlasting King”: these are put in the singular, by which unity of substance is indicated.

Likewise Moses in Deuteronomy: “Know today and consider that the Lord himself is God, and there is no other” [Note: [Col. 0831] Cap. 4.]. There “Lord,” as in Latin, is used in the singular in Hebrew. But where “God” is said here, there is *Eloim*, which is expressed in Hebrew with plural force. And lest several substances might be understood from the plural designation,

[Col. 0833A] there is added, “and there is no other.” What necessity or reason induced the Hebrews to introduce together this association of singularity and plurality, unless it was because God wished both to conceal for a time and to reveal in its own time the mystery of the Trinity?

Moreover, that name of God which is ineffable among the Jews in the secret of secrets, and is called the Tetragrammaton, although it has four written figures, has only three elements: *Io, he, vaf, he*; for *he* occurs twice. Therefore, if you examine this name carefully, in Hebrew it is threefold and one. For if you join only the first and second letters, namely *Io* and *he*, one name of God is formed in Hebrew. If you place the second and third together, that is, *he* and *vaf*, you have another name of God. But if

[Col. 0833B] you join the third letter and the fourth, that is, *vaf* and *he*, you have a third. Again, if you join them all together in their order, you find only one name. He who arranged that there should be three names intended you to understand, in the unity of three persons of the same substance, one name.

Likewise, in Numbers [Note: [Col. 0833] Cap. 6.], the Lord says to Moses: “Speak to Aaron and his sons,” etc. With these blessings the priest, while blessing others, held both palms extended before his face. But when he said “Lord”—which they expressed by that Hebrew name mentioned above, threefold and one—he raised upright and higher the first three fingers, namely thumb, forefinger, and middle finger, of each hand; and, having thus said “Lord,” he lowered his fingers as before.

[Col. 0833C] What can be understood more fittingly in a mystical sense by the raising of the three fingers than the exaltation of the Trinity? Note also that in this most solemn blessing the form of the cross, without which Christians perform no blessing, is distinctly expressed. With these three fingers, as has been stated above, the mass of the earth is weighed; and Pharaoh’s magicians confessed the finger of God—that is, the Holy Spirit—whom the Jews stubbornly deny.

Three solemn observances in Exodus express the mystery of the Holy Trinity [Note: [Col. 0833] Exod. 8.]: the feast of unleavened bread, the feast of firstfruits, and the feast of gathered fruits. In Deuteronomy also [Note: [Col. 0833] Cap. 16.] the same observances are commanded: the first feast of unleavened bread, the second of weeks, and the third of tabernacles. At Passover sacrifice is offered. At Pentecost the Holy Spirit is given. At the Feast of Tabernacles the power of paternal majesty is declared.

Therefore ask the Jew more closely how he understands those words of the prophet Jeremiah [Note: [Col. 0833] Cap. 23.]: “You have perverted the words of the living God, the Lord of hosts, your God.” For, lest he be compelled openly to confess the Trinity, he there perverts the words of God. Jerome says in the Prologue on Genesis that these words read there in Jeremiah are not found in the Latin and Greek codices. Yet the Hebrews read these words against themselves in their own books and, willing or unwilling, proclaim the sacrament of the Trinity.

There are very many other testimonies concerning

[Col. 0834A] the Trinity of persons which the Seventy Interpreters did not translate, although they existed in the Hebrew truth. For, as blessed Jerome says in the Prologue on Genesis, they either kept silent about much—or everything—concerning the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, or translated it differently. They are said to have acted prudently, lest Ptolemy, a worshipper of one God, at whose request they were translating, should suppose that there were several gods. They were also unwilling to publish the hidden things of the faith. Thus, when the Seventy Interpreters found in Isaiah concerning the child born and given to us that he would be called “Wonderful, Counselor, Mighty God, Father of the age to come, Prince of Peace” [Note: [Col. 0833] Isa. 9.], frightened by the majesty of these names, they did not dare to call this child God, but “Angel of Great Counsel,” which is not found in Hebrew.

## CHAPTER VI. Arguments and authorities concerning faith in the Holy Trinity

[Col. 0834B]

We have introduced some points for the refutation and confounding of the Jew; let us now introduce some concerning the Trinity for the edification and consolation of the Christian. These are the words of John the Evangelist, who drank streams of heavenly wisdom upon the Savior’s breast [Note: [Col. 0833] Joan. 13.]: “There are three who bear witness in heaven: the Father, the Word, and the Holy Spirit; and these three are one” [Note: [Col. 0833] I Joan. 5.].

These too are Christ’s words in the Gospel: “The Spirit who proceeds from the Father … he shall receive of mine,” by which he teaches most plainly that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son [Note: [Col. 0833] Joan. 15.]. Again, the Doctor of the Gentiles, intimating the Trinity, says: “For from him, and through him, and in him

[Col. 0834C] are all things” [Note: [Col. 0833] Rom. 11.]. The Father, from whom are all things; the Son, through whom are all things; the Holy Spirit, in whom are all things. The same Apostle: “We speak from God, before God, in Christ” [Note: [Col. 0833] II Cor. 12.]. He also who is Truth itself says in the Gospel: “Go, baptize all nations in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” [Note: [Col. 0833] Matth. 28.].

If, then, the Jew cannot deny that the wisdom and goodness of God have always been with him, and that he himself has never been without them, who can doubt concerning the Trinity, when the wisdom of God is called his Son and the goodness of God is called his Spirit?

You understand that in the human mind there are reason, memory, and will, and these three are one mind. Yet none of them is the other: for reason is not memory or will; memory is not will or reason; and will is not reason or memory. In the same milk there are three distinct properties: whey, cheese, and butter. In the sun there are three distinct things: that spherical body, heat, and brightness. Those three are one sun, and none of them is the other.

[Col. 0834D] A simple hermit is said to have deceived a certain Jew who was disputing with him and arguing: “The Father is God, the Son is God, the Holy Spirit is God; but the Father is not the Son, nor is the Holy Spirit the Son; therefore the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are not the same God.” Making three folds in his cloak, he said: “This fold is cloth, and this one, and the third; none of these folds is another;

[Col. 0835A] therefore these three folds are three cloths.” But rather, one cloth.

Yet the Holy Trinity is not to be scrutinized by analogies or arguments, but embraced by faith. It surpasses the capacity of all human reason. Let us simply think of it what the sacred Scriptures teach us, so that with the Psalmist we may say: “According to your word, give me understanding” [Note: [Col. 0835] Psal. 118.]. Lord: not beyond it, not short of it, not above it, not against it, but according to it.

## CHAPTER VII. Prophetic testimonies that the Son was sent by the Father

That he who was sent by God the Father for our salvation is the Son, God from God, is most plainly evident from those things continually read in both our codices and those of the Jews. For in that authority previously cited,

[Col. 0835B] where the Wisdom of God declares herself begotten before all things, she concludes at the end of the passage: “My delights were to be with the children of men” [Note: [Col. 0835] Prov. 8.]. For she takes special delight in that love which she showed us, in becoming man in order to redeem man.

Concerning him the prophet Jeremiah says: “This is our God, and no other shall be accounted beside him; he discovered every way of knowledge and instruction” [Note: [Col. 0835] Baruch. 3.]. And he adds: “After this he was seen upon earth and lived among men” [Note: [Col. 0835] Ibid.].

## CHAPTER VIII. Testimonies that Christ came in the flesh

That Christ would be born from Abraham’s seed, the Lord makes clear in Genesis, saying and speaking to Abraham: “In your seed all nations shall be blessed”

[Col. 0835C] [Note: [Col. 0835] Gen. 21.]. What nations were blessed in Isaac? The Jews? Are they not, above all peoples, cursed and condemned by the Lord? Seek, therefore, another from Abraham’s seed in whom all nations are blessed, and you will find none but Christ. The Lord gave him the blessing of all nations [Note: [Col. 0835] Eccli. 44.], and all are blessed in him by the Lord who made heaven and earth [Note: [Col. 0835] Psal. 120.].

Of this seed Isaiah says: “Unless the Lord of Sabaoth had left us a seed, we should have been as Sodom and become like Gomorrah” [Note: [Col. 0835] Isa. 1.]. This cannot at all be understood of Isaac. By what power, knowledge, or strength could Isaac free us from any sin?

As a sign that Christ would be born from Abraham’s line, Abraham made his servant swear upon his thigh [Note: [Col. 0835] Gen. 24.] that he would carry out his command

[Col. 0835D] concerning the seeking of a wife for Isaac. For one swearing upon Abraham’s thigh was understood to swear not by Abraham or Isaac, but by him who was to be born from Abraham’s thigh. In reverence for the same faith, Abraham himself, Isaac, and Jacob [Note: [Col. 0835] Gen. 17 and 21.], together with their descendants, received spiritually the sign of circumcision, so that the people from whom he in whom the blessing was deposited would be born might be distinguished from other peoples.

Therefore Balaam says in the book of Numbers [Note: [Col. 0835] Cap. 24.]: “A star shall arise from Jacob,” etc. That Christ also would be born from Abraham’s descendants is found in Deuteronomy

[Col. 0836A] [Note: [Col. 0835] Cap. 18.], in the words of Moses speaking to the people: “The Lord shall raise up a prophet from your nation and from your brethren,” etc. The Jews understood this of Joshua, not of Christ. But that you may know it was said of Christ, not Joshua, examine the sequence of the history and you will have no doubt.

For a little earlier, on Mount Horeb, the children of Israel requested [Note: [Col. 0835] Exod. 19 and 20.] that they might not again hear the Lord’s dreadful voice or see the fire, lest they die. Therefore the Lord says to Moses: “I shall raise up for them a prophet from among their brethren” [Note: [Col. 0835] Deut. 18.], that is, from the tribe of Judah. For that tribe was situated in the midst of the other tribes. That he calls him a prophet suits Christ. For I do not read that Joshua ever prophesied. But Christ says of himself: “A prophet is not without honor except in his own country”

[Col. 0836B] [Note: [Col. 0835] Matth. 13.]. For he prophesied concerning his own passion, resurrection, and ascension; concerning the calling of the Gentiles and the spreading of faith in the Gospel [Note: [Col. 0835] Matth. 16, 18, 20.]; concerning the destruction of Jerusalem; and concerning many other things certainly known to have happened [Note: [Col. 0835] Luc. 19.].

Moreover, the addition “like Moses” intimates that Christ, like Moses and not Joshua, gave the law. Again, when the Lord says to Moses concerning Joshua: “Lay your hand upon him, and give him commands in the sight of all” [Note: [Col. 0835] Num. 27.], it is plainly shown that Joshua was inferior to Moses, since Moses laid his hand upon him. And when there is added: “If anything must be done, Eleazar the priest shall consult the Lord,” etc. [Note: [Col. 0835] Gen. 20.], Joshua is shown to be inferior even to Eleazar.

It is evident, then, since all the tribes of the earth are to be blessed in the Messiah and he cannot be inferior to Moses or Eleazar, that these words do not refer to Joshua but to Christ: “I shall raise up for them a prophet from among their brethren, like himself”

[Col. 0836C] [Note: [Col. 0835] Deut. 18.]. It follows: “And I shall put,” etc. [Note: [Col. 0835] Ibid.]. No one of sound judgment can doubt that these refer to Christ, especially since his words are spirit and life.

You have a more explicit parallel in the case where David, considering building a house for the Lord, is addressed by the prophet Nathan in the person of the Lord: “When your days are fulfilled,” etc. [Note: [Col. 0835] II Reg. 7.]. It is certain that Solomon reigned while his father was still alive. How, then, can these words apply to Solomon: “When your days are fulfilled and you sleep with your fathers, I shall raise up your seed” [Note: [Col. 0835] Ibid.]—that is, Solomon your son? Nor does the following suit Solomon: “I shall establish his throne forever” [Note: [Col. 0835] Ibid.], because his kingdom soon came to an end. This too is far from Solomon: “I shall not take my mercy from him” [Note: [Col. 0835] Ibid.]. For these words are read in Third Kings: “When Solomon was old, his heart was corrupted by women, so that he followed foreign gods. Solomon worshipped Astarte, goddess of the Sidonians; Chemosh, god of the Moabites; and Moloch, idol of the Ammonites. Therefore the Lord was angry with Solomon, because his mind had turned away

[Col. 0837A] from the Lord God of Israel” [Note: [Col. 0837] III Reg. 11.]. Therefore the Lord says: “Because you have not kept my covenant, I shall tear your kingdom asunder” [Note: [Col. 0837] Ibid.]. Was not God’s mercy therefore taken from him, when he allowed him to apostatize, tore apart his kingdom, and, taking it from his son, gave it to a servant?

## CHAPTER IX. Testimonies that Christ would be born from David

That Christ would be born from David is found in the testimony of Jeremiah, who says: “Behold, days are coming, says the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0837] Jer. 32.], etc. In Jeremiah’s time David, Solomon, Hezekiah, and all the holy and righteous kings were already dead. Find, O Jew, another to whom this can apply besides Christ. When he says, “Behold, days are coming,” this cannot refer to your Messiah, whom you imagine is yet to come. For the time which the prophet fixed for the Messiah’s coming has already passed.

Likewise David: “I have sworn to David my servant” [Note: [Col. 0837] Psal. 88.], that is, I have promised immutably and without condition: “Forever I shall establish your seed and your throne from generation to generation.” These words cannot apply to Solomon, but to Christ, who shall reign forever.

## CHAPTER X. Testimonies that Christ would be born from the Gentiles

That Christ would be born from the Gentiles may be gathered from Isaiah’s words: “Send forth, O Lord, the lamb, ruler of the earth, from the rock of the wilderness to the mount of the daughter of Zion” [Note: [Col. 0837] Isa. 10.]. The wilderness is the Gentile world;

[Col. 0837C] Ruth is the rock of the wilderness [Note: [Col. 0837] Ruth. 1.], because she was a Moabite—as though he said: “From you shall come forth the lamb who shall take away the sins of the world and rule the whole earth.” Ruth bore Obed to Boaz; Obed begot Jesse; Jesse, David; and from David came Christ [Note: [Col. 0837] Matth. 1.].

Hear Isaiah again, more plainly declaring that Christ would call Jews and Gentiles alike to the end: “It is too small a thing for you to be my servant, to raise up the tribes of Jacob,” etc. [Note: [Col. 0837] Isa. 49.]. Again Isaiah intimates simultaneously Christ’s divinity and humanity, speaking in the person of God the Father: “Behold, I shall lay in the foundations of Zion,” etc. [Note: [Col. 0837] Isa. 28.]. By the name “stone,” of course, is designated the most innocent humanity of Christ, a firm and stable creature. But in what he says, “He who believes in him shall not be confounded”

[Col. 0837D] [Note: [Col. 0837] I Petr. 2.], his true divinity is expressed. For if Christ were man and not God, believing in him would be idolatry. But if the Jew understands or believes this literally, he will believe in a stone and be condemned as an idolater; or he will not believe this stone, and by the prophet’s testimony will be confounded.

Christ, the cornerstone rejected by the Jews, joined together the two peoples—Jew and Gentile—as two separate walls, as the Psalmist relates: “The stone which the builders rejected has become the head of the corner” [Note: [Col. 0837] Psal. 117.]. Isaiah plainly declares Christ’s divinity:

[Col. 0838A] “The labor of Egypt and the merchandise of Ethiopia,” he says [Note: [Col. 0837] Isa. 45.], etc. Since these things can be adapted neither to a mere man nor to a mere God, let the Jew either show to whom they apply, accuse the prophet of falsehood, or acknowledge that he is both God and man.

“Savior” is the same as Christ, whom the prophet therefore calls “a hidden God.” For he was first hidden in the Father’s bosom, afterward in his mother’s womb, in the manger, in the tomb, and also in the sacrament of the altar. Let not the Jew ascribe these words to King Cyrus: for neither Cyrus nor any king other than Christ is hidden God or manifest God.

Others judge according to sight or hearing; but Christ, who is supreme justice and supreme wisdom, judges in himself, as Isaiah testifies when he says: “He shall not judge according to the sight of his eyes

[Col. 0838B] nor reprove according to the hearing of his ears; but he shall judge the poor in justice and reprove with equity for the meek of the earth” [Note: [Col. 0837] Isa. 11.]. And to declare that his power surpasses every human power, he adds: “He shall strike the earth with the rod of his mouth, and with the spirit of his lips he shall slay the wicked.” It belongs to God alone to destroy Antichrist and to judge human beings according not to their words, but to their hearts and merits.

## CHAPTER XI. That Christ came in his own person

That Christ, as he had been desired by the patriarchs and foretold by the prophets, came in his own person, the Lord plainly intimates through Isaiah, saying: “Therefore my people shall know my name on that day, because I myself who spoke—behold, I am present” [Note: [Col. 0837] Isa. 52.]. It is as though he said: “I who spoke in the prophets take flesh and come.” Hence, at his coming, the same prophet summons us and says: “Prepare, Israel, to meet the Lord your God, for he comes” [Note: [Col. 0837] Amos 4.].

Thus, for those dwelling in the region of the shadow of death, a light arose for them [Note: [Col. 0837] Isa. 9.]. He is the one, O Christian, who says to you of himself in the Gospel: “I am the light of the world” [Note: [Col. 0837] Joan. 8.]. This is the child who, according to Isaiah’s testimony, “has been born to us, and a son has been given to us: Wonderful, Counselor, Mighty God”

[Col. 0838C] [Note: [Col. 0837] Isa. 9.]. And he adds: “His dominion shall be multiplied, and there shall be no end of peace.” And, to accumulate honor more fully: “From now,” he says, “and forever.” Tell me, O Jew, who is that child born to us, or son given to us, whom Isaiah affirms to be God and whose dominion is everlasting?

Likewise the prophet, revealing both Christ’s power and the shame of his passion: “Behold,” he says, “my servant shall be lifted up and exalted” [Note: [Col. 0837] Isa. 52.], etc. Jerome explains this to mean that the kings and wise men of this age will restrain their mouths—that is, they will not speak against, but will assent to Christ’s law—who shall sprinkle the nations with his blood and baptism. And those to whom no report concerning him was made shall see and understand, as Truth himself says in the Gospel: “Blessed are those who have not seen and have believed” [Note: [Col. 0837] Joan. 20.].

## CHAPTER XII. That Christ was God and man, from Abraham’s seed

[Col. 0839A]

In sacred speech Christ is frequently called Abraham’s seed [Note: [Col. 0839] Joan. 8.], or the Lord’s shoot, or fruit. Hence Isaiah: “On that day the shoot of the Lord shall be in magnificence and glory, and the fruit of the earth sublime” [Note: [Col. 0839] Isa. 4.]. Of this fruit the Psalmist says: “The Lord shall give goodness, and our land shall give its fruit” [Note: [Col. 0839] Psal. 84.]. And, intimating the glory of the fruit, he adds: “Justice shall walk before him and shall set his steps in the way.—In his days justice and abundance of peace shall arise, until the moon is taken away” [Note: [Col. 0839] Psal. 71.]. Who is this fruit, whose justice and peace are given for as long as the moon shall endure?

The Psalmist marvels that anyone could be persuaded that Christ was born in the city—or Synagogue—which he made. For he says: “Will

[Col. 0839B] any man say?” [Note: [Col. 0839] Psal. 86.]—that is, persuade the Synagogue—this utterly astounding miracle: that in that city of God, of which glorious things have been said, one and the same person was both born as man and founded it as God [Note: [Col. 0839] Ibid.]? It is as though he said: This cannot be persuaded to the Jew except by divine power.

Therefore Isaiah cries out and says: “Lord, who has believed our report?” [Note: [Col. 0839] Isa. 53.]. Truly it can be divinely persuaded, because the Lord recounts in the writings of the peoples and princes, those who were in her [Note: [Col. 0839] Psal. 85.]—that is, in the Synagogue—to whom the prophecies were given and to whom Christ was especially promised. O city of God, in you is dwelling as of all who rejoice! For whoever dwells and perseveres in the faith of Christ shall rejoice eternally.

[Col. 0839C] Again Jeremiah: “This is our God” [Note: [Col. 0839] Baruch. 3.], etc. After this—that is, after he had given the law—he was seen on earth and lived among human beings [Note: [Col. 0839] Ibid.]. And if he finds no one besides Christ, let the lost man, lest he perish, confess him with us.

Nor should the Jew murmur that these words are Baruch’s and not Jeremiah’s. For Baruch received these words from Jeremiah’s mouth, as his secretary, and wrote them down. Hence it is read in the same Jeremiah [Note: [Col. 0839] Jer. 36.]: “Jeremiah called Baruch son of Neriah, and Baruch wrote in a book-scroll from Jeremiah’s mouth all the words of the Lord which the Lord had spoken to him.”

Daniel wrote thus concerning Christ’s coming, his offering unto death, his ascension, and glorification: “I saw in a vision, and behold, one like a son of man came in the clouds of heaven” [Note: [Col. 0839] Dan. 7.]. Behold his coming. “And he was offered to the Ancient of Days”

[Col. 0839D] [Note: [Col. 0839] Isa. 53.]. Behold the passion. For he was offered because he willed it [Note: [Col. 0839] Ibid.]. “And everlasting power was given to him” [Note: [Col. 0839] Dan. 7.]. Behold the resurrection. For, having risen, he says to his disciples: “All power in heaven and on earth has been given to me” [Note: [Col. 0839] Matth. 28.].

See, therefore, O Jew, whether these words apply to anyone among human beings other than Christ: that he should come in the clouds of heaven like a son of man and be offered to the Ancient of Days, that is, the eternal Father; that his power should be everlasting and his kingdom incorruptible. The same Daniel relates concerning the three boys in

[Col. 0840A] the furnace that a fourth among them was like a son of man [Note: [Col. 0839] Dan. 7.]: “This is the stone cut out without hands” [Note: [Col. 0839] Dan. 2.], that is, conceived from a virginal womb without intercourse and human seed; and, after crushing all kingdoms, it became a great mountain and filled the whole earth.

O Jew, understand how plainly Daniel foretells Christ’s coming and birth in the third vision. Nebuchadnezzar had seen a statue whose head was gold, the next part of its body silver, the third part bronze, and the fourth partly clay and partly iron. Daniel explains Nebuchadnezzar’s kingdom, namely the Babylonian kingdom, as gold; the kingdom of the Medes and Persians as silver; the third kingdom, namely that of Alexander of Macedon, as bronze, both because of the resonance of its fame and the eloquence of the Greek

[Col. 0840B] language. He calls the fourth kingdom, namely that of the Romans, iron, because that kingdom subdued and oppressed all nations. The feet and toes of the statue he describes were partly iron and partly clay, because the stronger that kingdom was at its beginning, the more shamefully it has now declined from its original strength and become base through a certain broken weakness.

At the end of these kingdoms of gold and silver, bronze and iron, a stone was cut out without hands, that is, without human work. This stone grew into a great mountain and broke and crushed the statue. See, O Jew, how gloriously Christ has been magnified, that stone which you rejected; how he filled the world, and the earth was filled with his majesty [Note: [Col. 0839] Isa. 6.]. Take care lest you stumble

[Col. 0840C] over this stone [Note: [Col. 0839] Isa. 28.]; for whoever stumbles over it shall be broken [Note: [Col. 0839] I Petr. 2.], but the one on whom it falls it shall crush.

Behold, in Daniel [Note: [Col. 0839] Cap. 2.] the stone cut out without hands; in Isaiah [Note: [Col. 0839] Cap. 8.] Emmanuel conceived of a virgin; in the Psalm, God descending into the virgin like rain upon fleece [Note: [Col. 0839] Psal. 71.]. She herself is the gate always shut, and yet the prince enters and goes out through it, as Ezekiel testifies, saying [Note: [Col. 0839] Cap. 44.]: “He turned me to the outer gate of the sanctuary,” etc.

On this passage Isidore says: “The female genitals are called gates, because they are closed and opened for childbirth.” Hence Job [Note: [Col. 0839] Cap. 3.]: “He who did not close the gates of the womb that bore me.” He shall sit in the gate—that is, in the virgin’s womb—and eat bread—that is, do God’s will—according to: “I have bread to eat which you do not know”

[Col. 0840D] [Note: [Col. 0839] Joan. 4.], and: “My food is to do the will of my Father” [Note: [Col. 0839] Ibid.].

Likewise, the virginity of the Mother of God is plainly declared in Isaiah when it is said: “Therefore the Lord himself shall give you a sign” [Note: [Col. 0839] Isa. 8.], etc. What does this phrase, “God with us” [Note: [Col. 0839] Ibid.], mean, O Jew, except God-man, since he himself was conceived and born in order that he might be with us and might be God? Show us someone conceived by any woman and born, whether from a virgin or another, who is God with us; and since you find no other, believe in this one.

Moreover, what sign or miracle would there be if

[Col. 0841A] a woman other than a virgin conceived and bore a child? Therefore God gave this sign, because a virgin gave birth. On this passage Jerome says: “When it is said, O Jew,” etc.

If, then, a young woman or girl, as you falsely assert, and not a virgin, gives birth, what sign or miracle will there be? In Hebrew a virgin is called *betulah*, which is not written in the present passage; but in place of that word stands *alma*, which all the interpreters except the Seventy translated “young woman.” Yet *alma* is ambiguous among them: for it signifies both “young woman” and “hidden,” that is, *apocryphos*. In Genesis [Note: [Col. 0841] ch. 20], where Rebecca is called an *alma*, Aquila translated it “hidden.” An *alma* is not merely a girl, a virgin fit for marriage, but a virgin concealed, more carefully guarded, and never exposed to men’s gaze.

Jerome further adds [Col. 0841B] that he had never read *alma* of a married woman, but of one who is a virgin, young in age, and intact in virginity. It follows: “He shall eat butter and honey” [Note: [Col. 0841] Isa. 7], namely, foods for infants, so that he may be known as a true human being, not a phantom.

Likewise Isaiah speaks of the Saviour’s infancy and the power of the child: “I approached the prophetess, and she conceived and bore a son” [Note: [Col. 0841] Isa. 8], etc. The “stylus of a man” is that with which men ordinarily write. Isaiah wrote, moreover, in this book which we now read. And for what purpose? That the child when born might no longer endure the kingdom of the devil, but might himself plunder the spoils of the strong man armed. By “prophetess” is here understood the spirit of prophecy; and “spirit” in Hebrew, *ruach*, is regarded as feminine in gender. Isaiah approached the spirit of prophecy, according to the prophecy of Isaiah that Christ is conceived of the Holy Spirit.

But because certain Jews profess the learning of astrologers, and perhaps believe them more readily than their own prophets, they read in the book of Albumasar, published long before Christ’s birth, and there expressly find these words: “The mother of the virgin’s first decan is born,” etc. Hence you have what our Virgin is; for you will not be able to find another to whom these things apply. You have, I say, both that she was to be born under the sign of Virgo and that she was to have a husband who would not touch her, and that the Virgin would suckle the Father. Notice too that Christians, ignorant of astrology, still celebrate annually the Nativity of the Virgin while the sun is in Virgo.

Likewise, the sanctification of the assumed humanity is described [Col. 0841D] in the same prophet when he says: “A rod shall come forth from the root of Jesse” [Note: [Col. 0841] Isa. 11], etc. The last gift is referred to speech, and the remaining gifts to the head. Nor should that saying trouble you: “I, the Lord, created her” [Note: [Col. 0841] Isa. 45]. Him who calls himself a worm, who made himself created flesh, whom the earth brought forth, I do not shrink from calling a creature. “Let the earth be opened,” says the prophet, “and let it bring forth a Saviour” [Note: [Col. 0841] ibid.]; “truth sprang up from the earth, and righteousness looked down from heaven” [Note: [Col. 0841] Ps. 84].

And what is read in the Psalm, “He shall descend like rain” [Note: [Col. 0841] Ps. 71], etc., denotes Christ’s conception through the sanctification of the Holy Spirit, who did not take away virginity but consecrated it. This is the Son of Man of whom it is said [Col. 0842A] in the Psalm: “Let your hand be upon the man of your right hand, and upon the Son of Man whom you have strengthened for yourself” [Note: [Col. 0841] Ps. 79]. He is rightly called the Son of God’s right hand, who sits at God’s right hand [Note: [Col. 0841] Heb. 1].

## Chapter XIII. Testimonies concerning the place and time of Christ’s birth

That Christ was to be born at Bethlehem Micah [Note: [Col. 0841] ch. 5] once foretold: “And you, Bethlehem Ephrathah,” etc. Let the Jew tell me who he is whom the prophet foretold would be born in Bethlehem and whose going forth is, as he himself says: “I came forth from the Father and came into the world” [Note: [Col. 0841] John 16]. And the Psalmist says of the same: “His going forth is from the highest heaven” [Note: [Col. 0841] Ps. 18].

Jacob reveals the time of Christ’s birth in Genesis when he says: “The sceptre shall not be taken away from Judah” [Note: [Col. 0841] Gen. 49], etc. Review the histories and you will find [Col. 0842B] that Zedekiah was the last king from the tribe of Judah [Note: [Col. 0841] 4 Kings 26]; afterwards there were leaders from that tribe until Herod, son of Antipater. Tell me, then, most lost Jew: from the time of Saul until Herod, did anyone rule the people of Israel, whether king or leader, who was not a Jew? Herod himself was a Gentile and therefore a foreigner. No one doubts that Christ was born under him [Note: [Col. 0841] Matt. 1]. Therefore either charge Jacob with falsehood, or agree with his prophecy and confess that Christ has come, whom your patriarch foretold as the expectation of the nations.

Again, Christ’s coming was not only prophesied by Daniel, but was announced and promised to him by Gabriel the archangel in Daniel’s tenth vision. Gabriel’s words [Col. 0842C] are these: “Daniel, I have now come forth to teach you; therefore pay attention” [Note: [Col. 0841] Dan. 9], etc. Gabriel assigns a third period in which the Holy of Holies is to be anointed and the prophecies fulfilled, which we see fulfilled in Christ. For all the prophets spoke of him, and that sin might be blotted out—namely, by Christ’s death, which he immediately mentions. Therefore those who await the Messiah while requiring all these things to be fulfilled in Christ do so damnably.

And the Angel adds: “Know therefore and consider, from the issuing of the word” [Note: [Col. 0841] ibid.], etc. Let the Jew hear of Christ’s killing and see Christ’s people ready for every punishment of death before they deny Christ; let him see his desolation, let him see the anointing of the Jews cease, and know that the Messiah has come. It follows: “The Lord shall destroy the city and the sanctuary” [Note: [Col. 0841] ibid.], etc. Consider, [Col. 0842D] foolish Jew, willingly miserable, that the time fixed by the angel has long since elapsed. Everything he foretold has happened to your city; do not dream falsely any longer of times of divine visitation. For your desolation began long ago, the appointed times have passed, and your captivity will have no further end until you are converted to Christ.

You see the tabernacle removed, the Temple overthrown, the ceremonies ended; and what Hosea [Note: [Col. 0841] ch. 3] foretold has been fulfilled in your people: “For many days,” he says, “the children of Israel shall sit without a prince, [Col. 0843A] without an altar, without an ephod, and without teraphim.” We read in the history [Note: [Col. 0843] 2 Chron. 15] that Azariah, son of Ebeth, when the Spirit of God came upon him in the presence of King Asa and his army, prophesied, among other things: “Many days shall pass in Israel,” etc.

According to Bede’s testimony, these seventy weeks, reckoned by seven years each, signify four hundred and ninety years. From the issuing of this word to Cyrus were seven weeks. The sixty-two, however, extended from Cyrus to Titus; and in the one week of the siege—that is, within the completed seven-year period during which the city was besieged by Titus—offering and sacrifice ceased, and the abomination of desolation was seen in the Temple, because an image of Caesar was set up in the Temple, in revenge for that saying: “We have no king but Caesar” [Note: [Col. 0843] John 19]; so that they might be compelled to have as [Col. 0843B] God him whom they had preferred to their Saviour.

Let no one be disturbed that he first sets down seven weeks and afterwards seventy; for this is a Hebrew idiom. For when a Latin speaker says that Abraham lived one hundred and seventy-five years [Note: [Col. 0843] Gen. 25], the Hebrew conversely says five and seventy and one hundred. Since, then, it is certain that the number of these weeks has already been completed, and that no greater weeks are found in sacred speech, it is certain that the Jews’ anointing has ceased and that the Messiah has come.

It should also be noted that, since two other captivities preceded this captivity, the Jews should be asked what cause there is for this captivity so long and without end. For idolatry was the cause of the two preceding captivities. [Col. 0843C] The prophets testify to this; nor can the Jews deny it, since they are recorded to have worshipped idols during those captivities. Since, therefore, after their return from Babylon they are not found to have worshipped idols, neither Jew nor anyone else can discover another cause for such a grave offence, such dispersion, and such prolonged captivity than the iniquity, prompted by envy, committed against Jesus Christ the Son of God.

For just as it is certain that God judges rightly, and this captivity is greater and longer than the Babylonian one, a greater offence must be assigned by them. Jerome raises this question in his commentary on Hosea and can find no cause other than Christ’s crucifixion. Josephus, however, wrote in the eighteenth book of the *Antiquities* that Jerusalem was destroyed because of the killing [Col. 0843D] of James; but all of this redounds to the Saviour’s glory. For James was thrown by the Jews from the pinnacle of the Temple and had his brains dashed out with a fuller’s club because he bore witness to Christ’s truth. Yet it is still asked what was the cause of so desperate a captivity, because Josephus does not resolve this.

## Chapter XIV. That the prophets’ desires concerning Christ have been fulfilled

If you consider the prophets’ desires regarding Christ’s [Col. 0844A] coming and God’s certain promises, you cannot doubt that the Messiah has come. Isaiah says: “Oh, that you would rend the heavens and come down, that the mountains might melt away before your face!” [Note: [Col. 0843] Isa. 9]. And shortly thereafter he adds: “You came down, and the mountains melted before your face” [Note: [Col. 0843] ibid.]. Jerome says this because the prophet had prayed to God and, understanding himself to have been heard and that the prophets’ desires were soon to be fulfilled, adds: “You came down,” because “the Word was made flesh and dwelt among us” [Note: [Col. 0843] John 1]. Thus the unbelieving and proud melted away, because, failing in themselves, they ran into the path of faith.

Likewise the Lord says in Zechariah [Note: [Col. 0843] ch. 2]: “Rejoice and be glad, daughter Zion,” etc. Here the Jew will not answer, because he cannot answer. And Isaiah: “Awake, awake, put on strength, arm of the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0843] Isa. 51], [Col. 0844B] etc. As though he said: As you delivered through the Red Sea, so now deliver through baptism.

God the Father himself speaks in the same prophet: “Listen to me, you hard of heart, and you who are far off” [Note: [Col. 0843] Isa. 46], etc. Twelve hundred years have now passed since Christ our salvation was born, yet you, Jew, still wait. Where, then, is what God foretold—that his salvation would not delay, and that it would soon take place in Zion and Jerusalem? Whom should one believe more, God or you? God said that salvation would not delay, and what he said he has now fulfilled: a thousand years have passed. But you, who have already waited a thousand years after God’s promise, how long will you wait?

To the prophet David Christ’s delay was grievous, when he said: “Lord, bend [Col. 0844C] your heavens and come down; touch the mountains and they shall smoke” [Note: [Col. 0843] Ps. 143]. And: “You who sit upon the cherubim, manifest yourself before Ephraim, Benjamin, and Manasseh” [Note: [Col. 0843] Ps. 79], that is, make yourself known to all. And: “Stir up your power and come, that you may save us” [Note: [Col. 0843] ibid.]. And: “O God, give your judgment to the king” [Note: [Col. 0843] Ps. 71].

And as though he had heard David’s prayer, he says: “I have placed help upon one who is mighty, and exalted one chosen from my people” [Note: [Col. 0843] Ps. 88]. And again: “I will make him my firstborn, higher than the kings of the earth” [Note: [Col. 0843] ibid.]. You cannot understand these words of David. Many kings in his time were more powerful and more eminent on earth; nor was he God’s firstborn. That belongs to Christ alone, who was firstborn among many brothers and made us, by adoption, his brothers and sons of God, heirs of God and his fellow-heirs [Note: [Col. 0843] Rom. 8; Gal. 4].

## Chapter XV. Testimonies of the Law and Prophets that Christ would come in humility

[Col. 0844D]

Humanity fell through pride [Note: [Col. 0843] Gen. 5]; Christ came humble in order to redeem humanity, born of a humble Virgin. He chose humble and simple apostles [Note: [Col. 0843] Matt. 4], through whom he might confound the wisdom and pride of this world [Note: [Col. 0843] 1 Cor. 1]. Therefore Zechariah says [Note: [Col. 0843] ch. 4]: “Who are you, great mountain, before Zerubbabel?” etc. Mountain is humbled by mountain—that is, the devil by Christ—and grace is matched with grace, while the things promised in the Old Testament [Col. 0845A] are fulfilled in the New.

Likewise the prophet Zechariah speaks of Christ’s humility [Note: [Col. 0845] ch. 9], saying: “Rejoice greatly, daughter Zion,” etc. In all the Law which you read without understanding, O Jew, you will not find any king who sat upon a she-ass and the foal of a she-ass in Jerusalem, whose dominion extended from sea to sea.

The ancients prophesied not only of Christ’s coming, but also of John the Baptist, the Forerunner of that coming—namely Malachi [Note: [Col. 0845] ch. 3]: “Behold, I send my Angel,” etc. The prophet does not say “he will come later,” but “immediately”; from the fact that you know John the Baptist has come, know that Christ followed without delay. “Behold, he comes,” says the Lord of hosts, “and who can contemplate the day of his coming?” [Note: [Col. 0845] ibid.]

## Chapter XVI. That Christ would cast out demons and perform miracles

[Col. 0845B]

Zechariah bears witness to the expulsion of demons and says: “On that day I shall destroy the names of idols” [Note: [Col. 0845] Zech. 9], etc. Isaiah foretold that Christ would perform miracles [Note: [Col. 0845] ch. 55]: “Then the eyes of the blind shall be opened,” etc. This is what the Christian reads in the Gospel, when Christ says to John the Baptist’s disciples, sent to him: “Go and report to John what you have heard” [Note: [Col. 0845] Matt. 11], etc.

Likewise Isaiah says of his miracles: “Behold, a king shall reign in righteousness” [Note: [Col. 0845] Isa. 32], etc. From these things it is clear how welcome and secure Christ’s protection is. Jeremiah speaks of Christ’s power and says: “Who shall raise up the righteous one? Who [shall give] him the nations?” [Note: [Col. 0845] Isa. 41], etc. [Col. 0845C] Habakkuk, foreseeing that Christ would come quickly, announces him as though present: “Your going forth is for the salvation of your people, with your Christ” [Note: [Col. 0845] Hab. 3].

## Chapter XVII. Testimonies of the prophets concerning the rejection of legal sacrifices

The Lord speaks in Isaiah [Note: [Col. 0845] ch. 43]: “I did not make you serve, Jacob,” etc. Amos says of the same [Note: [Col. 0845] ch. 5]: “Did you offer sacrifices?” etc. Likewise Isaiah [Note: [Col. 0845] ch. 1]: “What is the multitude of your victims to me?” etc. And in the Psalm: “I shall not take calves from your house” [Note: [Col. 0845] Ps. 49], etc. Likewise: “Your new moons” [Note: [Col. 0845] Isa. 1], etc. David in the Psalm: “A sacrifice to God is a spirit” [Note: [Col. 0845] Ps. 50], etc. Isaiah says of the same [Note: [Col. 0845] ch. 66]: “To whom shall I look, says the Lord,” etc. In the prophet Amos [Note: [Col. 0845] ch. 3]: “I hate,” etc. Micah says of the same [Note: [Col. 0845] ch. 6]: “Shall I offer to God?” etc. Malachi says of the same [Note: [Col. 0845] ch. 1]: “I have no pleasure in you,” [Col. 0845D] etc.

Here is declared not only the rejection and repudiation of the legal observances of the Jews, but also the calling of the Gentiles. Isaiah says [Note: [Col. 0845] ch. 66]: “He who sacrifices an ox is as though,” etc. The Psalmist, in Christ’s person: “Sacrifice and offering you did not desire, but you perfected ears for me” [Note: [Col. 0845] Ps. 53]. Or, according to another translation: “But you prepared a body for me,” so that from it I might offer you an immaculate sacrifice.

It is read in the Book of Kings that Samuel said: “Does God desire burnt offerings?” [Note: [Col. 0845] 1 Kings 15], etc. By [Col. 0846A] obedience one’s own will is slain; by a victim another’s flesh is slain. Likewise David: “For if you had desired sacrifice” [Note: [Col. 0845] Ps. 50], etc. And: “I shall not reprove you for sacrifices” [Note: [Col. 0845] Ps. 49]. And, after first saying, “I shall not take calves from your house,” etc., he adds: “Offer to God a sacrifice of praise” [Note: [Col. 0845] ibid.].

## Chapter XVIII. Testimonies of the Law and Prophets concerning Christ’s Passion

Christ’s Passion is prefigured in many ways in the Law and Prophets; the sacrifice of the paschal lamb most openly foreshadowed it. Carefully consider the month, the moon’s phase in the month, the hour of day in which the lamb was sacrificed, and the other things done with the lamb [Note: [Col. 0845] Exod. 12], and you will see the same things fulfilled in Christ.

Isaiah says [Note: [Col. 0845] Isa. 53]: “Like a sheep led to slaughter,” etc.—understand, in order that he might prevent [Col. 0846B] his own Passion. Habakkuk says [Note: [Col. 0845] ch. 3]: “Horns are in his hands.” They are the horns of the cross: “There his strength was hidden” [Note: [Col. 0845] ibid.]. For who then would have believed the almighty God to be a man enduring such cruelties so patiently and humbly?

Likewise Isaiah: “Woe to the soul, because they devised,” etc. The soul of Christ is sometimes called the people Israel, according to the saying: “Your soul has sinned, O God” [Note: [Col. 0845] Hab. 3]. Likewise Isaiah says [Note: [Col. 0845] ch. 53]: “He had neither form nor beauty,” etc. Since the Jew finds no prophet to whom he can rightly adapt Isaiah’s words, and sees Christ’s cross glorious among the rulers and peoples of the earth, let him at last return to Christ, who redeemed us through the narrow straits of the cross.

He himself says in the Psalm: “They pierced my hands and my feet” [Note: [Col. 0845] Ps. 21]. And in order to free us from the curse, he became accursed. For it is written: “Cursed is everyone who hangs upon a tree” [Note: [Col. 0845] Deut. 21]. Zechariah says [Note: [Col. 0845] ch. 13]: “When someone prophesies,” etc. And shortly afterwards he adds: “What are these wounds?” [Note: [Col. 0845] ibid.], etc. From this it is quite evident that the Jews, from whose people Christ was born, crucified him.

They still kick against the goad and falsely pervert the power of Christ’s Passion, so that David’s word spoken to Christ may be fulfilled in them: “In the multitude of your power your enemies shall lie to you” [Note: [Col. 0845] Ps. 65]. Let the wretched hear what is read in Isaiah [Note: [Col. 0845] ch. 28]: “That he may do his work,” etc. Likewise: “The government has been made upon his shoulder” [Note: [Col. 0845] Isa. 9], because he carried the cross upon his shoulders [Note: [Col. 0845] John 19]. Isaac [Note: [Col. 0845] Gen. 21] openly prefigured this, for while he was being led to be sacrificed, he himself carried the wood of his Passion.

Zechariah says [Note: [Col. 0845] ch. 13] of the Passion [Col. 0846D]: “Awake, sword, against my shepherd,” etc. Who is the man joined to the God of hosts, except Christ, God and man, whom God the Father offered for us when he raised up the sword—that is, persecution—against him and scattered the sheep, that is, dispersed the apostles? Hear the Lord say in Jeremiah [Note: [Col. 0845] ch. 11]: “You have shown me their designs,” etc. And in the same place: “Let us put wood in his bread” [Note: [Col. 0845] ibid.], etc. Hear, Jew, from what source your captivity proceeded.

The Psalmist also declares [Col. 0847A] Judas’s destruction: “The man of my peace,” he says, “in whom I trusted, who ate my bread”—that is, my apostle and table-companion—“has magnified betrayal against me” [Note: [Col. 0847] Ps. 40]. Christ expressed this very thing at supper through the morsel [Note: [Col. 0847] John 13]. Indeed, if you carefully examine the prophets’ testimonies concerning Christ’s Passion, you now read not only the prophets but the Gospel as well. For everything done in the Lord’s Passion—the words, plans, and deeds of the Jews, Judas’s betrayal, the piercing of feet and hands—is openly proclaimed both by the Evangelists and by the prophets. The Jews’ obstinacy is therefore all the more damnable: they feel the punishment for their crime and yet harden themselves in their malice.

In the Psalm: “Hear, O [Col. 0847B] God, my prayer when I make supplication” [Note: [Col. 0847] Ps. 63]. And in the Psalm: “O Lord God of my salvation” [Note: [Col. 0847] Ps. 87]. In these and many other passages not only Christ’s Passion but also its manner is described sufficiently plainly. Isaiah also did not keep silent about Christ’s tomb.

## Chapter XIX. Testimonies concerning the Lord’s tomb

Isaiah says: “There shall be a root of Jesse” [Note: [Col. 0847] Isa. 11], etc. The sign for the peoples is Christ’s cross, which, though once the most cruel punishment of a condemned man, has today become the peoples’ security and protection. See how, according to the prophet, this sign has been raised up: it has been transferred from the deaths of criminals to the brows of emperors and rulers, to the foreheads and heads of the supreme pontiffs. Without this sign nothing is secure, nothing holy. In this sign, according to the prophet [Col. 0847C] Habakkuk [Note: [Col. 0847] ch. 3], the Saviour’s hidden strength lay.

Where we say, “as a sign for the peoples” [Note: [Col. 0847] Isa. 11], etc., the Seventy translated: “He shall rise from the dead, where he is to be ruler of all nations, and all peoples shall hope in him.” Likewise, in Isaiah, the Father’s words concerning the Son: “I shall give the wicked for his burial” [Note: [Col. 0847] Isa. 53], etc.; that is, I shall give my Son the Gentiles, wicked through idolatry, and the Jews, rich in Law and Prophets, so that he who suffered for Jews and Gentiles may be the Lord and Saviour of all. According to the saying: “Ask of me,” etc. [Note: [Col. 0847] Ps. 2].

## Chapter XX. Testimonies concerning Christ’s resurrection

Zechariah bears witness to Christ’s resurrection [Note: [Col. 0847] ch. 9] and says: “You indeed, in your blood, have sent forth your prisoners from the pit in which there is no water,” clearly indicating [Col. 0847D] that by rising and descending into hell he led from the pit of death those who were in darkness.

Likewise the Lord speaks through Hosea of the resurrection and the despoiling of hell [Note: [Col. 0847] ch. 13]: “From the hand of death I shall deliver them,” etc. Isaiah speaks of this redemption [Note: [Col. 0847] ch. 52]: “You were sold for nothing, and without silver you shall be redeemed.” Truly without silver, because by Christ’s precious blood alone. Isaiah again says of this same redemption [Note: [Col. 0847] ch. 53]: “If he shall lay down his soul for sin,” etc. Because Christ [Col. 0848A] laboured, he shall see a long-lived seed, that seed of which he himself says: “The sower went out to sow his seed” [Note: [Col. 0847] Luke 8].

Likewise Hosea [Note: [Col. 0847] ch. 6]: “He is prepared as the dawn,” etc. Because of the morning resurrection, the twentieth Psalm is entitled “For the morning taking-up”; yet in it Christ is like the early and the latter rain, because at the time of recompense and in the evening of this life he will be our life and resurrection. Likewise Hosea says of the same [Note: [Col. 0847] ibid.]: “Come, and let us return to the Lord,” etc. Likewise the Psalmist: “But you, Lord, have mercy on me” [Note: [Col. 0847] Ps. 40], etc. Christ as man asks what, as God, he possessed with the Father.

Likewise: “Awake, my glory; awake, psaltery” [Note: [Col. 0847] Ps. 107], etc. His flesh is the psaltery in the angels’ joy; like a lyre yielding sound, it has become the joy and [Col. 0848B] resurrection of the dead. Isaiah indicates Christ’s resurrection [Note: [Col. 0847] ch. 63], saying: “Who is this who comes from Edom?” etc. The angelic powers, marveling at the glory of Christ’s resurrection, say to the other angels: “Lift up your gates, O princes” [Note: [Col. 0847] Ps. 23], etc. When they ask, “Who is this King of glory?” [Note: [Col. 0847] ibid.], others answer: “The Lord strong,” [Note: [Col. 0847] ibid.], etc. And again: “The Lord of hosts, he is the King of glory” [Note: [Col. 0847] ibid.].

That he is called beautiful in his robe, and with dyed garments from Bozrah [Note: [Col. 0847] Isa. 63], accords with what the bridegroom says in the Song of Songs [Note: [Col. 0847] ch. 5]: “My cousin is white and ruddy.” Ruddy in the Passion, white in the resurrection. Likewise in Isaiah [Note: [Col. 0847] ch. 63]: “Why then is your garment red?” etc. Jerome, on this passage, says that where “red” is now written, the Hebrew reads *Edom*: it is not the name [Col. 0848C] of a place but of blood. “I have trodden the winepress alone,” he says [Note: [Col. 0847] ibid.], etc. A winepress, moreover, in sacred speech, Jerome testifies, signifies torture. Hence Jeremiah says in his Lamentations: “The Lord has trodden the winepress” [Note: [Col. 0847] Lam. 2], etc.

The sun’s rising makes other days. This day was made by the Sun of righteousness rising from the dead. Formerly he rose as the Dayspring from on high [Note: [Col. 0847] Luke 1]; now, coming forth from the setting of death, God the Lord has risen in his splendours and has shone upon us.

Likewise in Genesis [Note: [Col. 0847] ch. 49], Jacob, having summoned his sons, says: “Gather together, that I may tell you,” etc. Since Christ was born from Judah, this prophecy plainly foretold that Christ would be worshipped by the other Jacobs—that is, by the Jews; that, rising from death, he would ascend into heaven and lead captivity captive [Note: [Col. 0847] Eph. 4]. For the things [Col. 0848D] foretold cannot apply to Judah. Where is it written that his hands were upon his enemies’ necks? Or where did his brothers worship him?

Just as a lion’s cub is revived by its father’s voice, so by the Father’s power the Son of God rose from death on the third day. Who shall raise him? No one, understand, except he himself who says: “Destroy this temple, and in three days” [Note: [Col. 0847] John 2], etc. All this denotes the shedding of blood and the mystery of the Passion.

## Chapter XXI. Testimonies of the prophets concerning the Lord’s ascension

[Col. 0849A]

You have, O Jew, Christ’s Passion, his glorious tomb, and his resurrection. What then do you await? All that was written of him through the prophets has been fulfilled. Do you wish to hear of his ascension? Hear him himself say in Hosea [Note: [Col. 0849] ch. 5]: “I shall take,” etc.—that is, from hell and earth into heaven. Isaiah says of the Lord’s ascension [Note: [Col. 0849] ch. 4]: “On that day the branch of the Lord shall be in magnificence,” etc. And again: “Now I shall arise, and I shall be exalted into heaven” [Note: [Col. 0849] Isa. 33]. Habakkuk likewise says of the same [Note: [Col. 0849] ch. 3]: “The sun was lifted up, and the moon stood in its order.” In all these passages Christ’s ascension is evident.

The Psalmist says of the same: “Be exalted above the heavens, O God, and let your glory be over all the earth” [Note: [Col. 0849] Ps. 107]. Observe, O Jew, that [Col. 0849B] after Christ’s ascension his name was immediately glorified throughout all the earth by the apostles. David, speaking to the angels, says: “Make a way for him who ascends above the west; the Lord is his name” [Note: [Col. 0849] Ps. 67]. Tell me, Jew: who but God is this Lord, whose name is Lord, who ascends above the west? How, moreover, would he ascend unless he had first descended? I therefore believe that he who ascended and he who descended first bent the heavens and descended in order to become man; now, however, he ascends above clouds and above winds, God and man together.

For the same prophet bears witness thus: “He makes the cloud his ascent; he walks upon the wings of the winds” [Note: [Col. 0849] Ps. 17]. Believe, therefore, unhappy one, that just as he ascended as a true man into heaven with the ineffable [Col. 0849C] joy of the angels, so he will come terribly in judgment against the other unbelievers. For the same Psalmist testifies: “God ascended with jubilation, and the Lord with the sound of the trumpet” [Note: [Col. 0849] Ps. 46]. With the jubilation, that is, of angels, apostles, and prophets; and with the trumpet, that is, with the clear threat of judgment, the angels saying: “He will come in judgment in the same way as you saw him going into heaven” [Note: [Col. 0849] Acts 1].

Likewise in the same Psalm: “Ascending on high, he led captivity captive” [Note: [Col. 0849] Ps. 67; Eph. 4], etc. Open your ears, you deaf man, and understand that Christ, ascending into heaven, led captives out with him and made hell captive; and he gave gifts to men, so that some might be apostles, others evangelists, others teachers, others pastors of the Church. Do you wish to hear, unhappy one, that Christ, stronger than the strong devil, bound him and snatched away the spoil which he had seized, namely the human race? You who read and do not understand because you neglect what you have read, hear how Isaiah [Note: [Col. 0849] Isa. 50] rebukes your hardness: “Can spoil be taken from the strong man, or what has been captured,” etc. Depart, wretch, from those who are to be judged because they judged the Son of God, so that you may be adopted among God’s children [Note: [Col. 0849] Gal. 4].

## Chapter XXII. Testimonies of the prophets concerning the sending of the Holy Spirit

The sending of the Holy Spirit was openly foretold: “Who shall investigate the things that are in heaven?” [Note: [Col. 0849] Wis. 9], etc. That the rush of the river—that is, the torrent of the Holy Spirit—would gladden [Col. 0850A] the city and sanctify God’s temple is affirmed by the Psalmist: “The rush of the river makes glad the city of God” [Note: [Col. 0849] Ps. 45], etc. Isaiah bears witness that he would come like a river [Note: [Col. 0849] ch. 59], saying: “And those who are from the west shall fear the name,” etc.

In this twofold gift the Holy Spirit is indicated: the Holy Spirit is given generally in baptism and afterwards in confirmation. Likewise the Lord says in Isaiah [Note: [Col. 0849] ch. 44]: “I shall pour water upon,” etc. The Psalmist says of the same: “Send forth your spirit” [Note: [Col. 0849] Ps. 67], etc. Christ’s apostles, his heirs, were made weak and scattered at the time of the Passion [Note: [Col. 0849] Matt. 26], and afterwards strengthened [Note: [Col. 0849] Acts 2]. Likewise: “There are no speeches” [Note: [Col. 0849] Ps. 18], etc.

## Chapter XXIII. Testimonies of Jewish and Gentile histories concerning the resurrection

The things which we have said concerning Christ’s Passion, resurrection, and ascension [Col. 0850B] are established not only by the greatness of the miracles and by the testimonies of the apostles and others who saw all these things and were present, but are also confirmed by the manifold authority of Jewish and Gentile histories. Thus our profession of faith is stronger against the Jews precisely because even enemies bear witness to its truth.

For in the *Chronicles*, where Tiberius Caesar is discussed and the things done in his time are reported, there is read a letter sent to Tiberius by Pontius Pilate, whose contents are as follows:

> “Pontius Pilate sends greetings to his Claudius.”
>
> “Recently there occurred something which I myself verified: through envy the Jews cast themselves and their descendants into cruel condemnation. For, although their fathers had received the promise that God would send them from heaven his Holy One, who would rightly be called their king, when he came and they saw him enlightening the blind, cleansing lepers, healing paralytics, driving demons from people, and even raising the dead, the chief priests became envious of him. They handed him over to me and, lying one thing for another, said that he was a magician and acted contrary to their Law. But I believed this to be so, and after scourging him I handed him over to their will. But they crucified him; and, after he had died and been buried, those same men posted guards. Yet, while my soldiers guarded him, he rose on the third day. Their wickedness, however, so blazed forth that they gave the soldiers money, saying: ‘Say that [Col. 0850D] his disciples stole his body by night.’ Nevertheless, after receiving the money, the soldiers could not keep silent about what had occurred. For they testified both that he had risen and that they had received money from the Jews. I have written this so that no one, reporting otherwise, may lie and suppose that the Jews’ lies ought to be believed.”

This letter was occasioned by the ancient Roman custom, as the Ecclesiastical History relates, that provincial governors, if any new event occurred in the provinces under their rule, should report it to the emperor or the senate, lest they appear ignorant of anything taking place in the world. Tiberius Caesar, then, with a strongly favourable vote, brought this letter before the senate, requesting that Christ be acknowledged as God. For from ancient times there had been a public law that no one should be held to be a god among the Romans unless confirmed by decree and judgment of the senate. But the senate refused to receive Christ, indignant that the letter had not first been presented to it according to custom; public opinion had anticipated its authority, and by an edict it decreed that Christians should be expelled from the city—Sejanus, prefect of the city, resisting this most obstinately as he supported the Christian religion. Tiberius nevertheless, as is read in the Ecclesiastical History, maintained his opinion and attempted nothing against Christ’s teaching. This, beyond doubt, was divinely ordered, lest divine power be thought to need human endorsements.

[Col. 0851B] Tertullian, most expert in Roman institutions and laws, likewise says concerning this matter in his *Apology against the Gentiles*, omitting a few words:

> “Tiberius, in whose time the Christian name entered the world, having received from Syria Palestine reports that had disclosed to him the truth of this divinity, referred the matter to the senate. The senate rejected it and remained in its decision, threatening danger to the accusers of Christians.”

So Tertullian. We, adhering to the foregoing, believe that its rejection by decree of the senate occurred through the hidden counsel of divine providence: so that, for laying the first foundations of Christian faith, God did not choose the powerful or wise of this world, but, as the Apostle says [Note: [Col. 0851] 1 Cor. 1], chose the weak in order to confound the strong, lest the catholic faith appear to have been approved by human beings through worldly wisdom or power. At the beginning of the Church’s birth, the world boiled over with public malice, as the Prophet says: “The kings of the earth stood forth” [Note: [Col. 0851] Ps. 8], etc.

## CHAPTER XXIV. Testimonies of Josephus the Jew concerning Christ

Josephus too, the distinguished writer on the Jewish captivity and antiquities, wrote very plainly concerning Christ: that he was crucified through the envy of the priests and rose again on the third day. Thus Jerome says in his Prologue on Josephus [Note: [Col. 0851] *In the Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers*]:

> “Josephus, son of Mattathias, a priest from Jerusalem, was captured by Vespasian and set free by his son Titus. Coming to Rome, he presented to the emperors, father and son, seven books on the Jewish captivity; these were placed also in the public library, and through the renown of his talent he deserved a statue at Rome as well.”

He also wrote twenty other books of *Antiquities*, from the beginning of the world down to the fourteenth year of the Emperor Domitian. In the eighteenth book of the *Antiquities*, he states very plainly that Christ was put to death by the Pharisees because of the greatness of his signs; that John the Baptist was truly a prophet; and that Jerusalem was destroyed because of the killing of the apostle James. He wrote of the Lord in this manner:

[Col. 0852A]

> “At the same time there was Jesus, a wise man, if indeed it is lawful to call him a man. For he was a worker of wondrous deeds and a teacher of people who gladly hear what is true. He won over many Jews, and also many Gentiles. He was the Christ. When Pilate, at the accusation of the leading men of our nation, had decided that he should be crucified, those who had loved him from the beginning did not abandon him. For on the third day he appeared alive again, in accordance with what divinely inspired prophets had foretold—both these things and countless other miracles concerning him. And to the present day both the name and the race of Christians, so called from him, endure.”

Christian faith, therefore, is so much the stronger because it is confirmed harmoniously and irrefutably not only by the oracles of the prophets, but also by the ancient histories of Jews and Gentiles, enemies of Christ. It itself, like the mustard seed, which was formerly the least among seeds, has grown into a great tree.

The Ecclesiastical History further relates that after Tiberius Gaius assumed the empire. He condemned Herod, the killer of John the Baptist, to perpetual exile after he had been tortured by many punishments, as Josephus writes. In his time Philo, a most distinguished writer, flourished pre-eminently not only in Latin learning but also in Greek philosophy. He recounts very plainly what grievous and terrible vengeance the Jews endured for the crimes committed against Christ.

[Col. 0852C] The aforementioned man sets out in the second book of his work *On Virtues* how Pilate, who had consented to Christ’s death, was cruelly afflicted; how Gaius also polluted the temple of the holy city—which alone then remained—by turning it into a temple bearing his own name, so that it was called the shrine of Jupiter, of Gaius, the most renowned new god; and innumerable other disasters surpassing every tragic grief. Josephus, answering him in a harmonious voice, writes that Pilate, sent by Tiberius into Judaea, publicly set up images of Caesar in Jerusalem, so that swift vengeance followed that saying which the Jews had uttered beforehand: “We have no king but Caesar” [Note: [Col. 0851] John 19].

The same Pilate, Josephus testifies, violently seized the common treasury of the temple, which in the native language they called *Corbona*, to insult the Jews, and spent it on building an aqueduct. Pilate himself, afflicted by exile and deadly torments, unable to endure such pain, ran himself through with a sword and breathed out his accursed soul.

Herod, persecutor of the apostolic order and murderer of blessed James, when he had gone down to Caesarea, as Luke testifies in the Acts of the Apostles [Note: [Col. 0851] ch. 12], and was addressing the people, while the people cried out that it was the voice of a god and not of a man, was struck by God and died swarming with worms. They were continually afflicted by these and other punishments, and the Lord’s harshest scourges never ceased from them until the overthrow of their city. [Col. 0853A] For forty-three years God mercifully invited them to repentance; but they were moved neither by threats nor by scourges, being instead hardened still more obstinately.

Accordingly, when Jerusalem was besieged by Titus, son of Vespasian, the siege began at the solemnity of Passover, when the multitude of Jews had assembled. By God’s just judgment vengeance was then exacted from them: those who on the days of Passover had killed our Saviour with bloody hands and sacrilegious cries were, on those same days, as though shut together in one prison, to undergo the deadly destruction of punishment which they had deserved. The city was burned, its wall razed to the ground, and throughout the siege countless thousands of Jews were killed. The captives carried away numbered ninety-seven thousand [Col. 0853B]. The noble and stronger captives were reserved for the triumphal procession. In each city through which Titus returned, certain prisoners were thrown to wild beasts or put to death by other punishments, so that everywhere the desolation of the city and God’s manifest indignation against them might become known.

The Romans were weary of much killing; and because few buyers could be found, thirty Jews were sold for one coin. This was the final destruction of the temple, occurring in the year 1102 from the time when it had been built; and Christ had plainly foretold it in the Gospel [Note: [Col. 0853] Luke 19; Matt. 24]. Yet before the temple was burned, for a whole year a comet appeared above it, bearing the likeness of a sword and signifying that the city would be laid waste by fire and sword. [Col. 0853C] During the very solemnity of Pentecost, at night, priests entering the inner parts of the temple to offer sacrifices declared that they first felt a certain movement, and then heard the voices of angels crying, “Let us depart from here.”

The Jews ought more often to recall these events and bewail the Creator’s inexorable offence and the incomprehensible destruction of their people. Yet even now they boast of their lineage in pride and error; they call themselves God’s peculiar people, and so magnify the law of Moses that, in comparison with it, they despise every law and every kind of wisdom. But in what follows, by giving them most abundant matter for reading, we cut off forever every ground on which they might pride themselves.

## CHAPTER XXV. Testimonies that the new law was to be preferred to the old

[Col. 0853D]

That the Mosaic law having been rejected, the evangelical law ought to prevail, is most plainly clear from many declarations of the prophets. Thus Jeremiah says [Note: [Col. 0853] ch. 31], “Behold, days are coming, says the Lord,” etc. Here it is declared most plainly that after the first covenant another was to be given—not such as was given to the ancient fathers—because the former was carnal and the latter spiritual. Ezekiel says the same [Note: [Col. 0853] ch. 6]: “I will establish for you an everlasting covenant,” etc. Likewise Zechariah says [Note: [Col. 0853] ch. 2], “Many nations,” he says, “will flee to the Lord.”

For the law of Moses had already been given; and lest anyone suppose that he who promised had delayed long in coming, he immediately adds: “My righteous one is near” [Note: [Col. 0853] Isa. 51]. And again: “The son of the stranger shall not say” [Note: [Col. 0853] Isa. 56], etc. As though he said: The law of Moses, given from Sinai, is practical for the Jew; the law given me, a Christian, from Zion is spiritual, so that there may be one law and one people. And he adds: “The Lord will not cause [them] to fly away” [Note: [Col. 0853] Isa. 30], etc.

The law itself is corrected in certain respects by the prophets. Though it is read in the beginning, “Interest shall be taken from brothers,” usury is nevertheless prohibited generally in the Psalms: “He has not given his money at interest” [Note: [Col. 0853] Ps. 14]. In the Gospel an increase of virtue is expressed. There Truth says: “Lend to those from whom you do not hope to receive” [Note: [Col. 0853] Luke 6], etc. Here both the new law is indicated [Col. 0854B] and the coming of the new lawgiver is declared.

Indeed, in the commandment of charity the whole virtue of the Mosaic law is fulfilled, according to the saying: “I have seen an end of every perfection; your commandment is exceedingly broad” [Note: [Col. 0853] Ps. 118]. For charity, or the breadth of the Gospel, displays its affection not only toward neighbours but also toward enemies. Isaiah says of this [Note: [Col. 0853] ch. 10]: “A shortened consummation will cleanse righteousness.” For the Lord God of hosts will bring about consummation and abbreviation in the midst of the earth, because “the law shall go forth from Zion, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem” [Note: [Col. 0853] ch. 2].
