Jerusalem is, as it were, the navel of the earth, as Ezekiel writes [Note: [Col. 0853] ch. 5], saying: “Thus says God: This is Jerusalem,” etc. For Asia lies to its east; Europe to its west; Libya and Africa to its south and southward; Armenia, Persia, and Pontus to its north. Amos says the same [Note: [Col. 0853] ch. 1]: “The Lord will roar from Zion and give forth his voice from Jerusalem.” And the Psalmist: “Appoint, O Lord, a lawgiver” [Note: [Col. 0853] Ps. 9], etc.

Isaiah says [Note: [Col. 0853] ch. 55]: “All you who thirst, come to the waters,” etc. As though he said: Come to the law of the Gospel, that you may draw waters with joy from the fountains of the Saviour. But if you do not possess the wisdom or eloquence of this world, signified by gold and silver, nevertheless buy that water of which Christ says in the Gospel: “Whoever drinks the water which I …” [Note: [Col. 0853] John 7], etc., signifying the Holy Spirit whom believers were to receive. Wisdom or eloquence was not required of Paul; rather it was said to him: “My grace is sufficient for you” [Note: [Col. 0853] 2 Cor. 12]. He himself says: “By grace we have been saved” [Note: [Col. 0853] Eph. 2]. And the Lord says to the disciples: “Freely you have received; freely give” [Note: [Col. 0853] Matt. 10].

[Col. 0854D] Wine and milk signify righteousness and the innocence of little children. Thus Isaiah indicates that wisdom must be pursued—not wisdom in the leaves of words, but in the marrow and fruits of meanings. Nor need you cross seas in order to know the Lord’s law; rather, as is read in Deuteronomy [Note: [Col. 0853] ch. 18], “The word is near in your mouth.” No writing teaches a person so fully how wretched the human condition is as does the evangelical law.

The rejection of the old law and institution of a better one, then, appears not only from the prophecies we have offered [Col. 0855A], but also from Moses’ own deed. When Moses came down from the mountain, though the people of Israel were worshipping one God, he threw from his hand and broke the tablets written by the finger of God [Note: [Col. 0855] Exod. 32]. Again, at the Lord’s command he went up the mountain, and God gave him the law anew on other tablets cut to the likeness of the former ones [Note: [Col. 0855] Exod. 34].

Thus, in the fact that the first tablets were immediately broken while the second tablets of the law remained whole, it was very plainly prefigured that God had ordained two laws and established two Testaments, New and Old: the Old, which would shortly cease; the New, which would remain firm. Therefore the Ten Commandments were written on the second tablets: this number is signified by the tenth letter, in which the figure of the cross is expressed. The Prophet sought this new law when he said: “Set a law before me, O Lord” [Note: [Col. 0855] Ps. 118], etc.

The old law, indeed, does not justify a human being. For it led no one to perfection. “But give me understanding” [Note: [Col. 0855] ibid.], until the new law is given, so that I may understand the law already set forth and search it—that is, the old law—to discover what in it is moral and what mystical. For if the old law is to be understood only literally and not spiritually, why should it be searched so diligently, since its literal sense is evident to simple and unlearned people, unless hidden and mystical meanings were in it? Why would the Prophet ask that the eyes of his heart be unveiled in order to contemplate the wonders of the law? Why say, “Give me understanding, that I may learn your commandments” [Note: [Col. 0855] ibid.]?

[Col. 0855C] He therefore understood that the law’s commandments, spiritually understood, give life; and for this reason he says, “I shall never forget for ever” [Note: [Col. 0855] ibid.], etc. Again, he indicates the effectiveness and power of the spiritual law, saying: “I have understood above all my teachers” [Note: [Col. 0855] ibid.], etc.

Let the Jew answer me, I pray: what wisdom or benefit is there today in distinguishing in the law what is to be done with the breast, what with the shoulder, and what with the entrails? Where the blood of goats or rams is to be poured out; where the fat is to be burned; where the carcass with its hide is to be carried; where the ashes are to be deposited; whether the victim has a tail, ears, or testicles cut off or crushed. O how profound and necessary is the teaching that instructs us not to eat crocodiles, bats, and moles!

Since it is therefore manifest that knowledge of the law according to the letter neither makes one wise [Col. 0855D] nor gives life to the soul, it is clear that the Prophet longs for another law, hidden in the old one. Thus Ezekiel saw “a wheel within a wheel” [Note: [Col. 0855] ch. 1], because the New Testament lies concealed in the Old. This law makes clear what that one promised, and the new law is an exposition of the Old Testament. Therefore, when figurative matters ceased, moral ones remained and were transferred into the teaching of the Gospel with an increase of grace.

Accordingly Pope Leo says, *On Moral Precepts*:

> “No decrees of the former Testament have been rejected; rather, they have been enlarged for the better by Gospel teaching. For those which give salvation are more perfect than those which promise the Saviour.”

Therefore attend to both senses of the law, O Jew, and you will see plainly that spiritual understanding possesses the delights of wisdom. The literal sense, however, is like an outer bark: dry and bloodless. You think that Sabbath observance consists solely in bodily rest; but the Christian judges the true Sabbath to be rest from every servile work—that is, from every mortal sin. “For whoever commits sin is the slave of sin” [Note: [Col. 0855] John 1].

The Jew understands the entire sanctity and observance of circumcision to lie in the cutting away of the fleshly prepuce of one member—that is, the genitals. The Christian understands circumcision as the voluntary chastening of all carnal senses and shameful pleasures. Both the prophet and the law itself frequently indicate this spiritual understanding in figurative commandments. At times, impossibility occurs in matters which the Lord commands strictly, and then one must come to the spiritual sense. For when Sabbath and circumcision are strictly commanded by the Lord, if the eighth day of an infant falls on the Sabbath, necessity pressing, one commandment of the law overrides another on the Sabbath; and the very impossibility of observance proves that the law is not to be understood in this way.

[Col. 0856B] For how can anyone understand literally that Moses commanded circumcision of the heart in Deuteronomy [Note: [Col. 0855] chs. 9 and 30]? For he says: “Circumcise the foreskin of your heart” [Note: [Col. 0855] Jer. 4]. Ezekiel agrees with him, saying: “Every foreigner uncircumcised …” [Note: [Col. 0855] Ezek. 44], etc.; and: “All nations are uncircumcised …” [Note: [Col. 0855] ibid.], etc.

Nor should the Jew excuse himself by impossibility, saying that he does not observe circumcision of the heart because it cannot be accomplished in a living person. Let him then perform it upon the other members, in which circumcision can be carried out. Let them hear the prophet Jeremiah [Note: [Col. 0855] ch. 6]: “Behold, this people is uncircumcised in ears.” On this passage Origen says:

> “Why,” he says, “do those who hear this not cut off their ears? I want them to be circumcised in their ears; for I do not allow them to flee to our allegories.”

Likewise Moses, in Exodus [Note: [Col. 0855] ch. 6], excusing himself as unworthy to be sent by the Lord, says: “I am uncircumcised in lips.” According to Moses’ testimony, one uncircumcised in lips is less worthy. Therefore one circumcised in lips is worthier. Let them then circumcise [Col. 0856D] ears and lips with iron. This is not impossible, although it is shameful.

Let the Christian therefore hear what Paul the Apostle, most learned in both laws, says concerning circumcision: “We are the circumcision,” he says, “because we serve God in the Spirit and have no confidence in the flesh” [Note: [Col. 0855] Phil. 3]. And likewise: “For he is not a Jew who is one outwardly” [Note: [Col. 0855] Rom. 2], etc.

Therefore that person is spiritually and fully circumcised who stops his ears lest he hear bloodshed; who closes his eyes lest he see evil; who sets a guard over his mouth lest he sin with his tongue; who for Christ’s sake [Col. 0857A] abstains, lest his heart be weighed down with drunkenness or dissipation [Note: [Col. 0857] Luke 21]; who washes his hands among the innocent; who restrains his feet from every evil way; who chastens his body and brings it into slavery [Note: [Col. 0857] 1 Cor. 9]; and who keeps his heart with all vigilance, because life proceeds from it.

Do not wonder, O Jew, if we, for whom truth has sprung up from the earth, omit literally some things found in your law, since even your fathers destroyed certain things instituted by God himself. Circumcision, which God had commanded most strictly through Moses, was discontinued for a long time. Thus it is read in Joshua [Note: [Col. 0857] ch. 5]: “The people who were born in the wilderness …” The observance of the Sabbath, one of the greatest commandments, was likewise violated and abandoned by everyone in the time of the Maccabees [Note: [Col. 0857] 1 Macc. 1]. The altar of burnt offering [Col. 0857B], made at the Lord’s command, was also destroyed by the Jews at the same time. Likewise holy King Hezekiah broke the bronze serpent [Note: [Col. 0857] 4 Kings 18] which Moses had set up in the wilderness at the Lord’s command.

After the Jews’ evident rejection and the calling of the Gentiles; after the abolition of legal ceremonies; after the destruction of their city; after the eradication of the temple and sacrifices; after their dispersion; after God’s wrath manifestly implacable against them—still the Jews boast in pride and error, exalt themselves above every people, and say that the Lord calls them his son and his firstborn, that he miraculously brought them out of Egypt [Note: [Col. 0857] Exod. 4], that he gave them the land of the nations [Col. 0857C] [Note: [Col. 0857] Luke 13], and the like.

But that their glory consists in error is clear from their own testimonies. The Lord says in Isaiah [Note: [Col. 0857] ch. 1]: “I have nourished and exalted sons, but they have despised me.” God complains about the very thing in which the wretched boast. Consider that this people is not called the only-begotten, which would exclude all other brothers, but the firstborn, to show that others would follow. Let the Jew also know that, according to the mystery of the Scriptures, not firstborn sons but second sons receive the inheritance. Cain was firstborn, but Abel’s gifts pleased God [Note: [Col. 0857] Gen. 4]. Ishmael was firstborn, but Isaac received the inheritance [Note: [Col. 0857] Gen. 16 and 21]. Esau was firstborn, but Jacob the supplanter seized his father’s blessing [Note: [Col. 0857] Gen. 27]. Reuben was firstborn, yet the blessing of the seed was transferred to Judah [Note: [Col. 0857] Gen. 49].

Thus they were first according to the order of calling [Col. 0857D] and were called the head. We, the second, who were called the tail, have been made the head and are called children of God. “But as many as received him, he gave them power to become children of God, to those who believe in his name” [Note: [Col. 0857] John 1].

As for their boasting that the Lord brought them out of Egypt [Note: [Col. 0857] Exod. 4], drove out nations for love of them, and gave them the nations’ lands: let them know that they lie against the prophet Amos—indeed, against Moses himself. For just as the Lord moved the Jews, so he moved many other peoples from their regions [Col. 0858A]; and he introduced them into the land of promise not because of their merits but because of the sins of the nations. Let them therefore hear the Lord speaking in the prophet Amos [Note: [Col. 0857] ch. 9]: “Are you not like the children of the Ethiopians …?” And Moses in Deuteronomy [Note: [Col. 0857] ch. 9]: “Do not say in your heart, when he has destroyed …” These are Moses’ words; let them answer him, not me.

## CHAPTER XXVI. Testimonies concerning baptism

In the old law, the sum of all figurative commandments pertains to abstaining from vices and preserving virtues. In the new law the two principal sacraments for sanctification of souls are baptism and the eucharist; and these are prefigured in many ways in the Old Testament.

Zechariah says concerning baptism [Note: [Col. 0857] ch. 14]: “On that day living waters shall flow out of Jerusalem,” etc. By the East is signified the people of circumcision; by the West, the Gentile people, concerning whom the Lord says in the Gospel: “They shall come from the East” [Note: [Col. 0857] Matt. 8], etc. Summer and winter are prosperity and adversity, in which the solemnity of baptism does not cease. When did these waters go forth from Jerusalem, or when shall they flow out? Though he gives no definite answer, he understands that the baptismal waters went forth from Jerusalem. For from those regions the grace of baptism flowed out to us.

Isaiah says [Note: [Col. 0857] ch. 1]: “Wash yourselves; be clean.” And again: “When the Lord has washed away the filth of the daughters of Zion” [Note: [Col. 0857] Isa. 4], etc. He calls “the blood of Jerusalem” the pride and contempt of the Jews crying, “His blood be upon us [Col. 0858C] and upon our children” [Note: [Col. 0857] Matt. 27]. What is light is washed away; what is heavy is burned up. Thus John the Baptist says in the Gospel: “I baptize you in water” [Note: [Col. 0857] Luke 3], etc.

Zechariah says the same [Note: [Col. 0857] ch. 13]: “On that day there shall be a fountain,” etc. Jerome says concerning this fountain which goes forth from the house of David:

> “It is written in the prophet Ezekiel [Note: [Col. 0857] ch. 47] that a fountain bursts forth from the house of the Lord and grows into a river, called the river of remission and forgiveness; it goes to the wilderness and to the sea now called the Dead Sea, and gives life to all fishes.”

From all this it is clear that baptism began from the house of David—that is, from the land of Jerusalem. What is the water that goes to the Dead Sea and gives life to all fishes, unless it is the water of baptism, in which those dead in sin are made alive? [Col. 0858D] John the Baptist gave instruction on the mountain “of the one who is to come” or “who comes” [Note: [Col. 0857] Luke 3; the Latin reading is uncertain: *futuri vel venturi*]. When the man came, he baptized, and his followers baptized also.

This house is called the house of the Lord God in Ezekiel [Note: [Col. 0857] ch. 43], and the house of David in Zechariah [Note: [Col. 0857] ch. 13]. It is the Church of Christ. Ezekiel says [Note: [Col. 0857] ch. 47]: “When I had turned, behold, on the bank …” These are the trees which, beside the courses of waters, bear fruit in their season [Note: [Col. 0857] Ps. 1]. It is certain that sins are most fully remitted in baptism.

The same Psalmist says: “The rushing of the river makes glad the city of God” [Note: [Col. 0857] Ps. 45], etc.—that is, his Church through baptism. And again: “The God of majesty thundered over many waters” [Note: [Col. 0859] Ps. 28]. He thundered when, over Christ after his baptism, the Father’s voice was heard: “This is my beloved Son” [Note: [Col. 0859] Matt. 17].

The world was cleansed in the flood [Note: [Col. 0859] Gen. 7], and baptism was prefigured in it. At the crossing of the Red Sea charity was increased, faith confirmed in God’s people, and the multitude of persecutors overthrown [Note: [Col. 0859] Exod. 13]; in this the remission of sins through grace in baptism is evident. Under the old law [Note: [Col. 0859] Lev. 15], by means of water the fidelity of a marriage maintained or violated was tested. Moses cast the dust of the golden calf into the water and, by means of that drink, exposed the leaders of idolatry [Note: [Col. 0859] Exod. 32]. At Jerusalem there was the Sheep Pool: whoever first entered it after the water was stirred was healed [Note: [Col. 0859] John 5].

The Jews also believed—and still believe—that their sins are forgiven through cold water. Therefore they too customarily engage in many washings. Nor without a wondrous sacrament did God set waters above the firmament [Note: [Col. 0859] Gen. 1], judging from that time that at some point something of heavenly grace ought to be poured upon the world.

## CHAPTER XXVII. On the sacrament of the altar

By the dispensation of heavenly providence, it came about wonderfully that the common opinion of humankind should place confidence in the power of sacrifices and should serve the religion to come. The chief sacrifice in the law of the Lord was the paschal lamb [Note: [Col. 0859] Exod. 12], which was commanded not only to be slain but also eaten, signifying that he was to give himself to us both as ransom and as food [Col. 0859C], and prefiguring also the grace of the deliverer and the mercy of the redeemer, who by his death freed lost humanity from sin and from the debt of death.

But in the sacrament of the altar is eternal life, so that it is impossible for those who partake worthily to die eternally. The bread and wine offered by Melchizedek, king and priest, were, as it were, sacraments of this sacrament [Note: [Col. 0859] Gen. 14]; and this sacrifice is celebrated in bread and wine, Christ having instituted it—he who is priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek [Note: [Col. 0859] Ps. 109]. Although this sacrament was prefigured in Isaac’s sacrifice and in the sacrifices of other righteous persons, Melchizedek’s offering prefigured it more expressly.

But if the Jew grumbles, saying that Melchizedek gave bread and wine to Abraham for his refreshment, not in order to offer a sacrifice to God, let him hear the reading of Genesis: after Melchizedek’s offering of bread, it immediately adds, “For he was priest of God Most High” [Note: [Col. 0859] Gen. 14]. He could have brought these things for refreshment even if he were not a priest. But in this, the office of a priest is shown: it belongs to him to sacrifice, bless, and receive tithes [Note: [Col. 0859] Exod. 12 and 16].

The law prefigured the sacrament in bread, the lamb, and manna. Bread grows from the earth, according to the saying: “That you may bring forth bread from the earth” [Note: [Col. 0859] Ps. 103]. And: “Truth—Christ—has sprung from the earth” [Note: [Col. 0859] Ps. 84]. Christ was the lamb sacrificed, as Isaiah testifies [Note: [Col. 0859] ch. 53]: “Like a lamb he was led to slaughter.” Manna came down from heaven [Note: [Col. 0859] Exod. 16]. And Christ says: “I came down from the Father and came into the world” [Note: [Col. 0859] John 16]. Manna was not received by the Jews with the reverence it deserved [Note: [Col. 0859] Num. 11]. Christ also came into his own, and his own did not receive him [Note: [Col. 0859] John 1].

## CHAPTER XXVIII. On the transfer of the law to the Gentiles and the rejection of the Jews
How great the blindness of the Jews is we touched on above in part; but why they harden themselves more obstinately, so that their iniquity may be found unto hatred, we shall return to certain matters already mentioned, in order to set forth their wretched blindness more fully. The Lord speaks to Isaiah, saying: “Make the heart of this people blind” [Note: [Col. 0859] Isa. 6], etc. Isaiah says of the same matter [Note: [Col. 0859] Ch. 29]: “The Lord has mingled for you a spirit of stupor” [Col. 0860B], etc. For, as Christ says in the Gospel: “I came for judgment” [Note: [Col. 0859] Mark 4; John 9], etc.; that is, that the Jews might incur blindness, and that the people of the nations might be called to the light.

Therefore the book was sealed to the Jews; its seals are opened in the Apocalypse by the lion from the tribe of Judah [Note: [Col. 0859] Ch. 5]. By this book the whole body of sacred Scripture is signified. This is the book which, in Ezekiel [Note: [Col. 0859] Ch. 2], was written within and without—that is, spiritually and literally. Of it we read in the Psalm: “At the head of the book it is written of me” [Note: [Col. 0859] Ps. 39]. You see most plainly, O Jew, that the Law has been taken from you, though you were learned in letters, and given to the people of the nations, who did not know the Law because they were ignorant of it.

The Lord indicates the curse and rejection of the Jews through Jeremiah, saying: “I have forsaken my house, [Col. 0860C] I have abandoned my inheritance” [Note: [Col. 0859] Jer. 12], etc. That he calls the people of Israel his beloved soul is the same as what is said elsewhere: “Your soul has sinned, O God” [Note: [Col. 0859] Hab. 2]. Elsewhere the Lord says: “Israel is my inheritance” [Note: [Col. 0859] Isa. 19]. Here he says that he has abandoned this inheritance and hated it, because it raised its voice against him when it cried: “Crucify him, crucify him” [Note: [Col. 0859] John 19].

The same prophet says of the same matter: “The Lord said to me: Though Moses should stand” [Note: [Col. 0859] Jer. 15], etc. Observe that God’s wrath and aversion against the Jews is so great that Moses and Samuel, God’s familiar friends, cannot reconcile them. Let them therefore tell me whom they will have as reconcilers. Perhaps their gods, whom Moses reproaches in Deuteronomy [Note: [Col. 0859] Ch. 32], saying: “Where are your gods?” etc. Amos says of the same matter [Note: [Col. 0859] Ch. 5]: “Hear this word,” etc. This sentence of God is final and admits no hope of any recompense [Col. 0860D].

Moses in Deuteronomy [Note: [Col. 0859] Ch. 9] declares both the rejection of the Jewish nation and the cause of its rejection, saying: “Remember,” etc. In the same book: “You have seen all that the Lord did” [Note: [Col. 0859] Deut. 29], etc. If you understand, they had no understanding when Moses was with them. Let the Jew tell me under what leader, or when, understanding of the Law was given to them.

Isaiah, indicating their incurable wound, says [Note: [Col. 0859] Ch. 1]: “It has not been bound up, nor treated with medicine, nor softened with oil.” The same prophet also metaphorically describes the perpetual desolation [Col. 0861A] of the Jewish nation through the vineyard which ought to have produced grapes but produced wild grapes, whose hedge God removed so that it might put forth thorns and briars [Note: [Col. 0861] Isa. 5]. He therefore commanded the clouds above [Note: [Col. 0861] Ps. 77]—that is, the prophets—not to rain upon it. God withdrew from them the voluntary rain [Note: [Col. 0861] Ps. 65], namely, the grace of good will and the dew of his mercy, that they might be like Mount Gilboa, upon which neither dew nor rain falls [Note: [Col. 0861] 2 Sam. 1].

The same prophet says concerning the rejection of the Jews and the conversion of the nations: “Bind up the testimony; seal the Law among my disciples” [Note: [Col. 0861] Isa. 8], etc. Bind and seal the testimonies of the Law away from the Jews, that they may not understand them; and entrust it to Christ’s disciples. Jeremiah says of the irreparable desolation of the Jews [Note: [Col. 0861] Ch. 19]: “You shall break the flask before the eyes of the men,” etc. Behold a wound [Col. 0861B] without remedy. Again: “Therefore, behold, I will take you away, bearing you off” [Note: [Col. 0861] Jer. 23], etc. Not only by Christians but also by pagans, the Jews are reproached for having killed their Lord God. The Psalm says of the same matter: “Let their habitation become desolate” [Note: [Col. 0861] Ps. 11]. The prophet Amos says of the same: “In that day the beautiful virgins shall fail,” etc. [Note: [Col. 0861] Ch. 8].

The same Isaiah says of the cause of the Jews’ rejection: “Where is the bill of divorce of your mother?” [Note: [Col. 0861] Isa. 49], etc. Earlier he had said: “Zion has forsaken me; the Lord has forgotten me” [Note: [Col. 0861] Ibid.]. But the Lord makes clear that she was abandoned through her own fault: namely, because she would not follow and hear him, and turned from him a departing shoulder. Hence he speaks to her, saying: “Your apostasy shall instruct you” [Note: [Col. 0861] Jer. 2], etc. Likewise: “Hear, house of Jacob, who are called by the name of Israel” [Note: [Col. 0861] Isa. 48], etc. [Col. 0861C] Behold: Israelites in the flesh, not in the spirit. Again, of the same: “Are you not wicked children, a lying seed?” [Note: [Col. 0861] Isa. 57], etc. This is the most grievous charge on account of which the Jews are accused, repeatedly arraigned, and even condemned: that they abduct Christian children and crucify them in secret.

## Chapter XXIX. On the Calling of the Nations to Faith

Isaiah had prophesied that, after the Jews were rejected, the nations would be converted to Christ, saying [Note: [Col. 0861] Ch. 54]: “Rejoice, barren woman, who do not bear,” etc. The Gentile world was barren, while the Synagogue was fruitful in offspring. Thus Isaiah also says [Note: [Col. 0861] Ch. 35]: “The wilderness shall rejoice,” etc. And, to show openly that Christ’s coming would bring this about, he adds: “They themselves shall see the glory of the Lord and the beauty of our God” [Note: [Col. 0861] Ibid.].

Jerome says that Lebanon is understood as the Temple [Col. 0861D]. Thus Zechariah also says [Note: [Col. 0861] Ch. 11]: “Open your gates, O Lebanon.” And in Ezekiel [Note: [Col. 0861] Ch. 17]: “A great eagle with great wings, full,” etc.—Nebuchadnezzar [took] the treasures of the Temple. Carmel is a most fertile mountain; in it is signified the fruitfulness of the Synagogue. Sharon is interpreted “plains” or “deserts,” and signifies the barrenness of the Gentile world. Again Isaiah says [Note: [Col. 0861] Ch. 19]: “In that day there shall be an altar,” etc. Here you plainly have it prophesied that Christ’s name was to be invoked among the nations.

Malachi says [Note: [Col. 0861] Ch. 1]: “I have no pleasure in you, says the Lord Almighty,” etc. [Col. 0862A] Isaiah says of the same matter [Note: [Col. 0861] Ch. 54]: “Behold, a stranger shall come,” etc. In Malachi the rejection of the Jewish nation and its sacrifices is plain; in Zechariah the calling of the nations is evident. Isaiah says [Note: [Col. 0861] Ch. 40]: “The voice of one crying in the wilderness,” etc. That is, he openly declares the Word of God and God’s incarnation, as if saying: “All flesh shall see the salvation of our God” [Note: [Col. 0861] Isa. 52].

Furthermore, as a figure of this matter, the Lord adds in the same prophet: “Do not remember the former things” [Note: [Col. 0861] Isa. 43], etc. By these are signified the nations, living in a certain beastly cruelty; and, as if explaining this, he adds: “I have formed this people for myself; they shall declare my praise” [Note: [Col. 0861] Ibid.]. Again in Isaiah [Note: [Col. 0861] Ch. 49]: “In an acceptable time I have heard you,” etc. These are the plain words of the Father to the Son who was sent; as elsewhere in the same prophet [Col. 0862B] it is said [Note: [Col. 0861] Ch. 42] that he gives opening to those shut up, release to captives, and illumination to the blind. The Apostle refers these things to Christ’s first coming, and let us likewise refer them with him to it.

The Father gave the nations to his Son as an inheritance, and the Son won them by his death. Therefore in Isaiah [Note: [Col. 0861] Ch. 53] the Father speaks, saying: “Therefore I shall divide many to him,” etc. That Christ would be the leader and teacher of the nations is shown more openly, when the Father says concerning the Son: “Behold, I have given him as a witness to the people” [Note: [Col. 0861] Ibid.], etc. And in the same place: “They sought me who before,” etc. [Note: [Col. 0861] Isa. 65]. The Gentile centurion was not seeking God, yet deserved to hear from the Lord: “I have not found such great faith in Israel” [Note: [Col. 0861] Matt. 8].

Again, concerning their swift and sudden multiplication, behold Isaiah speaking and marveling [Note: [Col. 0861] Ch. 66]: “For before [Col. 0862C] she travailed, she brought forth,” etc. Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and the other patriarchs increased in their descendants over long intervals of time. But Christ’s people was multiplied beyond estimation suddenly and in a short time. The apostles began without delay to preach Jesus Christ. “Their sound went out into all the earth” [Note: [Col. 0861] Ps. 18], etc. On almost every day many thousands were baptized, and peoples were born into the adoption of God’s children through the grace of innocence, their mother [Note: [Col. 0861] Rom. 10].

Isaiah says [Note: [Col. 0861] Ch. 52]: “The Lord has made ready his arm,” etc. And in the same prophet: “Turn to me from the ends of the earth” [Note: [Col. 0861] Ch. 45]. And the Psalmist: “They shall remember and turn” [Note: [Col. 0861] Ps. 21], etc. Isaiah says [Note: [Col. 0861] Ch. 19]: “The Lord shall strike Egypt,” etc. Again Isaiah says [Note: [Col. 0861] Ibid.]: “In that day Israel shall be,” etc. Behold, God’s blessing has been transferred from Israel [Col. 0862D] to Assyria and Egypt. Again: “Will it not yet be in a little while?” [Note: [Col. 0861] Isa. 29], etc.

“Let the Jews answer,” says Jerome [Note: [Col. 0861] Book 9, Commentary on Isaiah], “how Lebanon, a mountain facing Phoenicia, has been turned into Mount Carmel, which in Hebrew is called *Chermel*, and lies on the border of Palestine and Phoenicia, overlooking Ptolemais; and how Carmel is reckoned as a forest. Since they cannot say this, [Col. 0863A] let them hear that Lebanon, which means ‘whitening,’ signifies the people of the nations, who, washed in baptism, are made white in Christ.” Therefore the Psalmist says: “All nations, clap your hands” [Note: [Col. 0863] Ps. 40], etc. And again: “I shall give thanks to you among the peoples, O Lord” [Note: [Col. 0863] Ps. 32]. In these and many similar passages, the prophets offer the Lord manifold thanksgiving for the conversion of the nations.

The prophets foretold that the firstfruits of Israel would be converted to the Lord [Note: [Col. 0863] Isa. 10; Jer. 3], and for this Christ came especially. The Lord bears witness to this in Zechariah [Note: [Col. 0863] Ch. 2], saying: “Sing praise and rejoice, O Zion,” etc. Who can be understood by the Lord God who sends and the God who is sent, except the Father and the Son? Isaiah says [Note: [Col. 0863] Ch. 60]: “Who are these who fly like clouds?” etc. Again, concerning the Church gathered together and the nations: “Instead of your having been forsaken” [Note: [Col. 0863] Ibid.], [Col. 0863B] etc. Again Isaiah says [Note: [Col. 0863] Ch. 66]: “They shall proclaim my glory among the nations,” etc. Again Zechariah says [Note: [Col. 0863] Ch. 8]: “Behold, I shall save my people from the land of the east,” etc.

Isaiah, indicating this, says to the Jews [Note: [Col. 0863] Ch. 65]: “You shall leave your name as an oath to my chosen ones,” etc. Jerome on this passage:

> “Paul says: ‘Not all those who are from Israelites are Israel, nor are all who are Abraham’s seed children’ [Note: [Col. 0863] Rom. 9]. To this Christ says in the Gospel: ‘If you were Abraham’s children, you would do his works’ [Note: [Col. 0863] John 8]. Therefore one is no longer called a Jew from Judah, but a Christian from Christ. Nor is an oath now sworn by idols, but by God. And this statement is confirmed, as by a seal, through ‘Amen.’”

## Chapter XXX. Testimonies of the Prophets That the Remnant of Israel Will Be Converted and Saved

[Col. 0863C]

Isaiah says [Note: [Col. 0863] Ch. 10]: “In truth the remnant shall be converted,” etc. This is what the Apostle says to the Romans [Note: [Col. 0863] Rom. 10 and 11], that full salvation shall come under Christ. Again Isaiah says to the same remnant [Note: [Col. 0863] Ch. 8]: “Sanctify the Lord of hosts himself,” etc. Jesus was first sent to the lost sheep of the house of Israel [Note: [Col. 0863] Matt. 15]; but, when they rejected the preaching of salvation, the apostles passed over to the nations, though certain firstfruits of the Jews had gone before [Note: [Col. 0863] Acts 13].

It remains, then, that the fullness of the nations enter at the end, and afterward the remnant of the Jews; and the last shall be first and the first last [Note: [Col. 0863] Matt. 20]. Again Isaiah more fully makes clear that a remnant is to be saved [Note: [Col. 0863] Ch. 17], saying: “In that day the glory of Jacob,” etc. Jerome says: “For ‘the valley [Col. 0863D] of Ephraim,’ the Septuagint translated ‘the hard valley,’ in order to express the hardness of the Jewish heart; yet from among them a few humble persons will be chosen.”

Again, he plainly reveals the confusion of the rejected Jews through the sanctification and glory of those who are to be converted to faith. “Jacob shall no longer,” he says, “be ashamed” [Note: [Col. 0863] Isa. 29], etc. We continually see this fulfilled: Jews are converted to the faith, while others waste away in grief and despise and reject the converts. But Isaiah consoles them, saying: “Hear [Col. 0864A] the word of the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0863] Isa. 66], etc.

Isaiah again consoles Israel’s remnant, as though lamenting that God had abandoned them. Thus these are the remnant’s words: “The Lord has forsaken me, and the Lord has forgotten me” [Note: [Col. 0863] Isa. 49]. The Lord replies: “Can a mother forget the child of her womb?” [Note: [Col. 0863] Isa. 63], etc. Similar is that passage in Isaiah: “The voice of those who turn to repentance: ‘Abraham did not know us’” [Note: [Col. 0863] Ibid.], etc. As if to say: Abraham and Jacob, who knew God, do not acknowledge us as children, because we displease God.

Again, concerning the remnant to be saved at the end, we read in Deuteronomy [Note: [Col. 0863] Ch. 4]: “Moses said to the people of Israel,” etc. It should be noted that, because they are not yet converted to the Lord, they are not yet acceptable to him. Again Isaiah says [Note: [Col. 0863] Ch. 52]: “Arise, arise, put on strength,” etc. The prophet speaks not only to Jerusalem [Col. 0864B] but to Jews scattered everywhere. Jeremiah says of the same matter [Note: [Col. 0863] Ch. 3]: “Return, children,” etc. In these words you have most plainly that the ark of the covenant, in which the Law was deposited, would be abolished, and that new teachers would teach the Law otherwise than the old teachers had taught it.

Again, of the same matter: “I shall gather the remnant of my flock” [Note: [Col. 0863] Jer. 23], etc. Hosea plainly distinguishes which tribes God has rejected and whose remnant he will save. For the same prophet says: “And she conceived again and bore a daughter” [Note: [Col. 0863] Hos. 1], etc. Indeed, the ten tribes to this day serve the kings of Persia, and their captivity will never at any time be ended. But to the house of Judah he promises mercy, and says that he will save them in the Lord their God.

Again [Col. 0864C] Isaiah says of the same matter [Note: [Col. 0863] Ch. 11]: “In that day the Lord shall set his hand again a second time,” etc. Ezekiel says of the same matter [Note: [Col. 0863] Ch. 33]: “I shall save my flock,” etc. Jerome says: “This is he who says of himself in the Gospel: ‘I am the good shepherd’ [Note: [Col. 0863] John 10], born from David’s stock. For David was dead when the prophet said these things.” The Psalmist: “They shall return at evening” [Note: [Col. 0863] Ps. 58], etc. For the Jews, converted at the evening of the world and hungering for God’s word, shall bark against the faithless and go around the city—that is, the Church—to fortify and defend it.

Again Isaiah says of the same matter [Note: [Col. 0863] Ch. 65]: “Thus says the Lord,” etc. For we believe that many are to be saved from tribes other than Judah also. For the Apostle Paul says: “Has the Lord cast away his people?” [Note: [Col. 0863] Rom. 11], etc.

## Chapter XXXI. Testimonies of the Prophets Concerning the Glorious State of the Church

[Col. 0864D]

It should be noted that the prophets foretold many things concerning the state of the Church which cannot suitably be applied to the first, second, or third Temple which the Jews imagine and expect. Solomon declares in Third Kings [Note: [Col. 0863] Ch. 48] that the Temple he built is not God’s dwelling-place, saying: “Is it then to be supposed that the true God,” etc. That a handmade temple [Col. 0865A] is not a dwelling worthy of God, the Lord shows, as if indignantly, through Isaiah [Note: [Col. 0865] Ch. 66], saying: “What is this house that,” etc. As though he said: I dwell not in buildings but in pure consciences and holy congregations.

He who, according to the prophet [Note: [Col. 0865] Isa. 40], holds heaven in a measure and earth in his fist, whose throne is heaven and whose footstool is the earth, is not confined to a place. Rather, he dwells in the soul of the righteous and rests upon the humble, gentle person who trembles at his words. Isaiah says to the primitive Church concerning its builders: “Lift up your eyes and see” [Note: [Col. 0865] Isa. 60], etc. For when the Holy Spirit descended, the Church of God began to be built. And, as we read in Acts of the Apostles [Note: [Col. 0865] Ch. 2], persons from the whole world were gathered in Jerusalem, and they first received the word of God through the apostles [Col. 0865B].

Isaiah says in the person of the Church [Note: [Col. 0865] Ch. 61]: “Rejoicing, I shall rejoice in the Lord,” etc. Again Isaiah says [Note: [Col. 0865] Ch. 58]: “And in it they shall be called strong ones of righteousness,” etc. This building is built from faith in Christ. Isaiah says concerning the Church of God [Note: [Col. 0865] Ch. 5]: “A vineyard was made for my beloved on a horn of oil,” that is, in the kingdom of God’s mercy. For throughout almost all sacred speech, a horn signifies a kingdom or power, as in the Psalm: “With a horn we shall scatter our enemies” [Note: [Col. 0865] Ps. 43], etc., and many other passages in the same manner.

Isaiah, speaking of the building of the Church and preferring it to the Temple, shows by comparison with metals and stones that the Church’s shepherds are better than the Temple’s magistrates and teachers. He continues, saying: “And the children of foreigners shall build” [Note: [Col. 0865] Isa. 60], etc. These things, O Jew, cannot apply to your Temple and city [Col. 0865C]. But today we see kings of the earth, and emperors themselves, submitting their necks to Christ’s yoke, building churches at public expense, and promulgating laws against heretics and persecutors of the Church. No one is repelled from the faith, and no one who wishes to believe is barred from the bosom of Mother Church.

Again Isaiah says [Note: [Col. 0865] Ibid.]: “Instead of bronze I shall bring gold,” etc. Again Isaiah says [Note: [Col. 0865] Isa. 50] to the Church gathered through the apostles: “Behold, I have inscribed you on my hands,” etc. The Septuagint provides another reading, namely: “You shall swiftly be built by those by whom you had been destroyed.” It was built because of the Jews’ fault and rebuilt by the Jewish apostles.

Again Isaiah says to the Church from the nations, that it may not be ashamed of the errors of its former idolatry, because its Lord has redeemed it: “Do not,” he says, “fear, because not” [Note: [Col. 0865] Isa. 64], etc. And because [Col. 0865D] the primitive Church was to be oppressed by many pressures of persecutions, Isaiah consoles it [Note: [Col. 0865] Ch. 54], saying: “Poor little one, tossed by the tempest, without any consolation,” etc.

Observe, O Jew, how plainly the prophet removes you from the literal sense. For after first saying that the city would be founded in sapphires, he immediately explains the stones he means—namely, virtues—by saying that its children would be taught not by man but by God, and that that city would be founded in righteousness. Again, to the primitive Church: “Arise, be enlightened, Jerusalem” [Note: [Col. 0865] Isa. 60], etc. The Church which had fallen in the Synagogue [Col. 0866A] then arose when he who built it was born in that city, of which glorious things were spoken, and the Most High himself founded it [Note: [Col. 0865] Ps. 85].

## Chapter XXXII. Plain Authorities Showing That the Scriptures Cannot Be Understood Literally

Among all the gifts and goods which we have from God, faith working through love is more pleasing and acceptable to him. He loved us so greatly that he gave his own life to death for us [Note: [Col. 0865] 2 John 3]. Mutual love, therefore, or charity between a human being and God, holds the highest and foremost dignity above all virtues.

Solomon treats in his Song of Songs of this intimate charity between God and humanity, between Christ and the Church. Therefore, because of the surpassing excellence of love, he called that book the *Song of Songs*. [Col. 0866B] Since the Christian draws from the words which the bridegroom uses to the bride—Christ to the Church, or conversely the Church herself to him—the sweetest fruits of grace from the marrow of spiritual understanding and certain delights of holy love, let the Jew, who follows the literal sense, tell me what he understands here, when literally he finds nothing but the enticements of lovers, words, and senses of extraordinary sensual pleasure.

And so that, O Christian, the words of that book may be readily at hand, I bring forward certain passages from it by which you may convict the Jew of the most evident rashness, as he studies such things, and may thereby demolish with him the literal—or rather, the harlot’s—understanding: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth, for your breasts are better than wine, fragrant [Col. 0866C] with the finest ointments” [Note: [Col. 0865] Song 1], etc.

O truly foolish description of a woman: that her eyes should be like doves’ eyes, or like a pool in Heshbon; her hair like a flock of goats; her teeth like a flock of shorn sheep; her cheeks like a turtledove and like fragments of a pomegranate; her neck like the tower of David; her nose like a tower in Lebanon; her lips like a scarlet ribbon; and her belly and breasts like a bowl and young goats [Note: [Col. 0865] Song 7], with many similar things of this sort. Here at least let the Jew be ashamed of his own writings, and know that “the letter kills, but the spirit gives life” [Note: [Col. 0865] 2 Cor. 3].

It must therefore be understood that, as the Apostle Paul testifies concerning the ancient Fathers: “All things happened to them in figure” [Note: [Col. 0865] 1 Cor. 10]. Hence their actions, words, and journeys, consolations and scourges, ceremonies and sacrifices, even the miracles performed, and likewise the names of all the patriarchs and prophets serve our benefit today. Likewise Ezra the prophet, drawing us toward spiritual understanding, by revelation of the Holy Spirit attached the titles to the Psalms in such a way that frequently, although the history is sometimes touched upon in the title, it is not the history but the meaning of the history that is discussed—something your examination will discover in very many Psalms [Col. 0866D].

## Chapter XXIII. Testimonies Concerning the Coming of Antichrist

Moreover, this is added to complete Jewish condemnation: those who refused to receive Christ for their salvation will receive Antichrist at the peril of their own death. Thus the Lord prophesied to them in the Gospel, saying: “I came in the name of my Father” [Note: [Col. 0867] John 5], etc., thereby indicating Antichrist.

Zechariah prophesies concerning Antichrist’s coming, in whom the Jews expect the Messiah, and says [Note: [Col. 0867] Ch. 11]: “And the Lord said to me: Again take for yourself,” etc. In the prophet Daniel [Note: [Col. 0867] Ch. 7], in the Gospel [Note: [Col. 0867] Matt. 24], and in Paul’s Epistle to the Thessalonians [Note: [Col. 0867] 2 Thess. 2], Antichrist is prophesied as the abomination of desolation, who will sit in the Temple of the Lord and present himself as God.

The Psalmist foretold both his power and his destruction: “He shall fall when he has ruled over the poor” [Note: [Col. 0867] Ps. 10], etc. Daniel says of the same matter [Note: [Col. 0867] Ch. 7]: “The judgment [Col. 0867B] shall sit, so that power may be taken away, and be broken and perish.”

## Chapter XXXIV. Testimonies of the Prophets Concerning Christ’s Final Coming in the General Resurrection

The Old and New Testaments bring forward many true testimonies concerning Christ’s final coming and the common resurrection of humankind. Thus blessed Job says [Note: [Col. 0867] Ch. 19]: “I know that my Redeemer lives,” etc. Whoever therefore denies the power of the resurrection should be ashamed at the words of a faithful man, though still a Gentile, and consider how terrible the heavenly punishment must be if he still does not believe in his own resurrection, though Job hoped that the resurrection of the Lord Jesus was still to come.

It must therefore be believed that a human being will not rise in an airy body or in a substance of another nature; for it would not be a true resurrection unless true flesh rose again [Col. 0867C]. Blessed Job affirms this, saying: “And again I shall be clothed with my skin” [Note: [Col. 0867] Ibid.], etc. The resurrection is proved again, as Ambrose says, by reason, by the example of the universe, and by the testimony of events: for very many have risen.

Reason requires that the body rise. How indeed shall a person be summoned to judgment without the body, concerning himself and his companion, for which he must answer? You see risings and settings, the succession of day and night, in which there is a daily setting and a renewed return. The fruits of the earth seem to die when they fall, and rise again when they grow green. What is sown dies and, rising again, is restored to the same species. The grain is clothed with a husk, and its vital warmth, as though beginning to animate it, forms in a heap the youthful stage of the growing ear; then it clothes its maturing state with certain coverings and gradually supplies the crop, as though emerging from its first cradle, with what the necessity of nature requires [Col. 0867D].

But our flesh, now corruptible, shall put on incorruption, and what is mortal, immortality [Note: [Col. 0867] 1 Cor. 15]. Why then do you marvel if the earth restores the humans entrusted to it, when it thus gives life, clothing, and growth to the bodies of seeds? Does God care for restoring crops and trees, and have no concern for human beings? Why should humanity, substantially made from earth, not return to earth? Does the earth fail only in human beings, while regenerating everything entrusted to it [Col. 0868A]? You see that it is natural to rise again, and contrary to nature to perish.

Suppose that human limbs are torn apart, scattered, burned, reduced to ashes, and given to the winds: can he who created all things from nothing not restore that body from such scant and frail material? The pagans indeed falsely claimed that souls pass from certain bodies into others; but which is more difficult: that souls return to their own bodies or enter bodies not their own?

What follows in Job [Note: [Col. 0867] Ch. 19], “And in my flesh I shall see God my Savior, whom I myself, and not another, shall see,” is to be understood thus: it will be the same flesh and not another, but altered in the same person—altered, namely, by glory. It will be subtle because incorruptible; it will be tangible because it will not change the essence [Col. 0868B] of true flesh. “This hope has been laid up in my bosom” [Note: [Col. 0867] Job 20]. We believe that we possess nothing more certainly than what we hold in our bosom.

Of the same matter in the book of Tobit: “As kings insulted blessed Job, so [they insulted] holy Tobit” [Note: [Col. 0867] Tob. 2], etc. Of the same matter in the book of Maccabees: “The most valiant man Judas, having made a collection” [Note: [Col. 0867] 2 Macc. 12], etc. Again Ezekiel says of the same matter [Note: [Col. 0867] Ch. 37]: “The hand of the Lord was upon me,” etc.

If the Jew barks that this figures not the resurrection but the restoration of the Israelite people, and that the liberation of the captive people is shown through the likeness of resurrection, that is enough for me. For the likeness of things is proved not by unreal or merely similar things, but by true ones. When we say, “Just as it is true that I sit here, so it is true that I hear,” the sitting must be true in order for the hearing to be proved. The Lord, by the explicit form of a comparison, proves resurrection through the resurrection of his people. As though he said: “Do you think the liberation of my captives impossible? Just as the resurrection of the dead is possible to me, so their liberation is possible to me.”

Whether, therefore, the preceding words are referred to the general resurrection, or whether the liberation from captivity is understood through the likeness of resurrection, it has an irrefutable argument for both resurrections [Col. 0868C]. Note also that the Lord could have employed other, much more suitable comparisons. But by teaching the manner of rising and his own power in raising, he more fully disclosed to us faith in the resurrection.

## Chapter XXXV. Testimonies of the Prophets Concerning the Day of Judgment

[Col. 0868D]

Isaiah says [Note: [Col. 0867] Ch. 13]: “Behold, the merciless day of the Lord comes, of wrath,” etc. And David sings in the Psalm: “In the beginning you, O Lord, founded the earth” [Note: [Col. 0867] Ps. 105], etc.

## Chapter XXXVI. Testimonies of the Prophets Concerning the Glorification of the Saints

Isaiah says [Note: [Col. 0867] Ch. 30]: “The light of the moon shall be as the light of the sun,” etc. Again of the same matter: “The Lord of hosts shall make for all peoples” [Note: [Col. 0867] Isa. 25], etc. Again: “You shall have no sun to give you light” [Note: [Col. 0867] Isa. 60], etc. Note that he does not say that the light of the sun [Col. 0869A] or moon will fail or cease, or that it will not be necessary to those being saved; for the Lord himself will be their light. “For as the new heavens which I make shall stand” [Note: [Col. 0869] Isa. 66], etc. Zephaniah says [Note: [Col. 0869] Ch. 1]: “Be silent before the face of the Lord God,” etc.

## Chapter XXXVII. Testimonies of the Prophets Concerning the Condemnation of the Wicked

Isaiah says [Note: [Col. 0869] Ch. 24]: “And it shall be in that day: the Lord shall visit,” etc. Jerome says concerning this passage that this visitation will be for their evil. Again: “Behold, the Lord shall come in fire” [Note: [Col. 0869] Isa. 66], etc. Nahum says of the same matter [Note: [Col. 0869] Ch. 1]: “The mountains were shaken by him and the hills were laid waste.” Zephaniah says [Note: [Col. 0869] Ch. 1]: “The voice of the Lord God is bitter; the mighty man shall be distressed. That day, that day is a day of wrath,” etc. The Psalm: “Our God shall come openly; our God [Note: [Col. 0869] Ps. 49] [Col. 0869B] …,” etc.

## Chapter XXXVIII. Testimonies of the Gentiles Concerning the Faith

We believe that the materials we have brought forward from the Mosaic Law and the prophets sufficiently refute the faithless hardness of the Jews. But we might bring forward, in support of our faith, certain testimonies of Jews: John the Baptist; his parents Zechariah and Elizabeth; the aged Simeon; Anna the prophetess; and also Christ’s disciples and apostles, who were personally present at Christ’s Passion and Ascension, and who bore testimony to Christ both faithful and plain, and consonant with the prophets. Yet the Jews, out of hatred for the Christian name, abhor not only their words but even their names [Col. 0869C].

But lest the nations should seem altogether alien to divine grace, some among them were granted prophecy concerning Christ, in order that they might convict the Jews of manifest unbelief—Jews who would not believe the prophets whom they accepted. First Balaam, signifying by a star that Christ himself would be born from Jacob, prophesied more unwillingly than willingly, by the inspiration of God’s grace, and prophesied that the kingdom of Moab would be devastated by Christ’s power.

Maro of Mantua also, describing and announcing Christ’s first coming, says:

> Now comes the final age of the Cumaean song.  
> [Note: [Col. 0869] Vergil, *Eclogue* IV, v. 4.]
>
> Now a new offspring is sent down from high heaven.  
> [Note: [Col. 0869] Ibid., v. 7.]

Zechariah agrees with him when he says: “The Dayspring from on high has visited us” [Note: [Col. 0869] Luke 1]. “For his going forth is from the height of the heavens” [Col. 0869D] [Note: [Col. 0869] Ps. 18].

The Cumaean Sibyl also, a prophetess, prophesied so plainly and in such agreement with the holy prophets concerning both comings of Christ and certain articles of our faith that it is most manifest to everyone that the calling of the nations is figured in her. Blessed Augustine introduces her verses for the confusion [Col. 0870A] of the Jews in that sermon which begins: “I address you, O Jews” [Note: [Col. 0869] Book XVIII, *City of God*, ch. 23; and in the oration *Against the Jews*, ch. 16].

### Verses of the Sibylline Prophetess

>

>

>

>

>

>

>

>

>
> Of the sea shall cease; the broken earth shall perish.

>
> World, groaning over wretched sin and its manifold labors;
>

These things concerning Christ’s birth, Passion, resurrection, [Col. 0870C] and second coming are said in such a manner that, if anyone wishes to examine the initial letters of these verses in Greek, he will find: **Ἰησοῦς Χριστὸς Θεοῦ Υἱὸς Σωτήρ**—“Jesus Christ, Son of God, Savior.” This may also be written and pronounced in Latin: *Jesus Christus Dei Filius, Salvator*. Apart from this, the particular character of the Greek letters cannot be preserved so fully in Latin.

### Conclusion of the Work
Use the weapons sent to you for the defense of faith; employ them cautiously. For the Jew is always inconstant and changeable. Now he affirms, now he denies; now he falsifies the letter, now he refers it all to the times of his own Messiah, that is, Antichrist; and, after the manner of his father the devil, he frequently transforms himself into monstrous shapes. [Col. 0870D] Therefore, if you wish fully to detect and destroy his wiles, set the library of the Spirit before him in the midst, so that he may have no opportunity either to flee or equivocate, but that Goliath may be slain with his own sword. [Note: [Col. 0869] 1 Sam. 17.]

[Col. 0871]

## A DOUBLE TREATISE ON CHRISTIAN FRIENDSHIP AND ON LOVE OF GOD AND NEIGHBOUR

### PROLOGUE TO BOTH TREATISES

[Col. 0871A] Since truths have diminished among the children of men [Note: [Col. 0871] Ps. 11], and since, as the charity of many grows cold [Note: [Col. 0871] Matt. 24], scarcely anyone finds in another integrity of faith, and scarcely is a love found which is not mercenary and for sale, I grieved over this common evil and resolved to write something more privately for the instruction and practice of loving. Thus I dug for myself a private spring, in which no stranger might share. For, gathering as it were flowers from diverse writers in order to make honey for myself, I compressed into a single compendium of brief reading the opinions of many, both ancient and modern, concerning friendship and the love of God and neighbour. Rejoicing in the testimony of my conscience concerning this, I prefixed to the treasure which I keep hidden a title stamped with this more emphatic seal: “My secret is for myself, my secret is for myself.” [Col. 0871B] [Note: [Col. 0871] Isa. 24.]

It is certainly safer for me to keep this present little work shut up in my bosom, as under a bushel, than to expose it to the eyes of the envious and transfer into the theatre and into derision the little bundle which I delight to keep more secretly between my breasts. [Note: [Col. 0871] Song 1.] For I know that, if this little book should ever reach the public, the envious man will immediately grunt and, muttering with venomous lips, charge it with compilation: namely, that I endeavour to bring to clarity the opinions of the ancients, already obscured by age or perplexed by the intricacy of an ambiguous meaning; and that matters which had become obsolete through the decay and neglect of antiquity may, when arranged with more ardent care, be worked into material for virtue and coalesce into a treatise of richer grace.

For, as is often read in the book of the *Saturnalia* and in Seneca’s *Letters to Lucilius*, we ought to imitate bees, which, after the flowers have been transformed by the wonderful craftsmanship of nature into various juices, impart to them a new flavour and great potency by a certain distinctive quality of their own spirit. As Valerius Maximus relates, Curius Albinus used to say that this was the fruit of reading: that the reader should emulate the talents [Col. 0872A] of the ancients and eventually make his own what he admires as well said by others.

Likewise, in the book of the *Saturnalia*, Afranius, a writer of Roman comedies, replies to his detractors in the comedy entitled *Compitalia*, who said that he had taken over from a book of Menander not only thoughts but whole words:

> “I have taken them over,” he says, “but those which I did not believe I could discover better myself.”

And in the same place:

> “Who would charge Virgil with wrongdoing if he borrowed much from Homer—things which neglect and the long passage of time had already caused to disappear?”

And shortly afterwards:

> “Finally, he is to be commended in this very respect: we marvel that what is foreign in his work sounds better there than where it was born.”

What envy, then, is there if, from among barren shoots planted from an old vine, those are selected [Col. 0872B] which, when planted together in order, may propagate the succession of a more fruitful vineyard? It is the poet’s saying:

> You will speak strikingly if a skilful arrangement  
> makes a familiar word new.  
> [Note: [Col. 0871] Horace, *Art of Poetry*, v. 47.]

Why then does the envious man disparage and bark, if modern diligence explains more clearly thoughts lying in a barren heap and grimy from older neglect; and if the fastidious reader, who lately disdained them, now desires them eagerly when they have been brought forth in more elegant dress?

Accordingly, let not the tongue of the ancient serpent hiss any longer through my enemy against this present little work; let the mouth of the unjust detractor be stopped; let the ears of the asp be stopped; and let the sight of innocence anticipate the eyes of the basilisk. For the gomor [measure] which I gather for myself I do not share with him, but only with those to whom manifestation of the Spirit has been given for usefulness, [Note: [Col. 0871] 1 Cor. 12] so that, in simplicity of heart, they may, if they wish, examine this little book more familiarly; and if they find anything knotty in it, I ask that they smooth it out with a more careful file.

## TREATISE I: ON CHRISTIAN FRIENDSHIP

[Col. 0871]

### CHAPTER I. What True Friendship Is

[Col. 0871D]

Someone will mock and accuse me, an old man, of playing at love, [Col. 0872D] when I am already being consumed and have received in my limbs the answer of death. But let Michal mock the nakedness [Col. 0873A] of dancing David; [Note: [Col. 0873] 2 Sam. 6] for my part, would that I might play with David and become more contemptible in my own eyes, so that with him I might bring the ark of the covenant into Zion.

Yet it would be a great thing to me if, through this little work, even a few from the whole mass of those who have been drawn away and swallowed up by worldly love, and who, with eyes gouged out and hair shorn, labour at the mill with Samson, [Note: [Col. 0873] Judg. 16] might enter into Jonathan’s covenant with David, [Note: [Col. 0873] 1 Sam. 18] so that in the most sweet love of Christ they might breathe again after the tribulation and sorrow caused by evils.

Indeed, from the time when Caleb obtained Hebron through Joshua, [Note: [Col. 0873] ch. 13] the people rest from battles. For the conflicts of temptations cease after the contemplation of the heart begins to exercise itself in the course of love. The field of love, indeed, [Col. 0873B] lies more broadly open and spreads wider expanses of the soul than the other affections. For love is a certain appetitive power toward the things which we choose and embrace out of desire in order to enjoy them.

Moreover, love frequently exercises its appetites even in brute animals, which are strangers to reason. And although “to enjoy” is said to belong spiritually to those things which concern God, Paul nevertheless uses the word *frui* (“to enjoy”) differently. For, writing to Philemon, he says: “Yes, brother, let me enjoy you in the Lord; refresh my heart in God.” [Note: [Col. 0873] Philem. v. 20.]

Affectionate love (*dilectio*), to be sure, gains strength from a definite judgment of the mind; friendship, however, proceeds from a certain practice of loving, together with the choice of the thing to be loved and deliberation concerning it. According to Cicero, friendship is “a complete agreement concerning things human and divine, joined with goodwill and charity”; [Col. 0873C] by *charity* perhaps meaning the affection of the mind, and by *goodwill* the effect of mutual service.

It does not seem likely that this pagan understood by the name *charity* that love which is the mother and root of all virtues; rather, he meant that affection of mind on account of which we customarily call our friends dear. Some philosophers are said to have placed friendship among the highest and enduring virtues, whom Solomon seems to imitate in Proverbs when he says: “A friend loves at all times.” [Note: [Col. 0873] Prov. 17.] Hence blessed Jerome says: “Friendship which can cease was never true friendship. Therefore, one who, being offended, ceases to love the person whom he loved was not truly a friend.” [Note: [Col. 0873] Ep. 41 to Rufinus.]

Far removed from the law of friendship is the person who loves today in such a way as to hate tomorrow; who is every person’s friend but faithful to no one; who praises today and censures tomorrow; flatters today and bites tomorrow; is ready for kisses today and reproaches tomorrow; whose friendship is lightly formed and is blown away by a slight offence. True friendship, finally, is solid in itself; and, adapting itself in all the friend’s needs to every compassion and endurance, it is more severely afflicted by sympathy for a friend than the friend is by suffering. See how the Apostle [Note: [Col. 0873] Rom. 9] strengthens the weak, runs alongside those who are scandalized, and has great sorrow for his brethren and continual pain in [Col. 0874A] his heart. Truly he was a friend: now rebuking them as a teacher, now fearing that their minds might be corrupted, now summoning them with sorrow to tears and repentance, now mourning those who had not repented.

### CHAPTER II. That Friendships Were Once Rare

Cicero relates [Note: [Col. 0873] Cicero, *On Friendship*, bk. I] that scarcely three or four pairs of friends existed throughout all the centuries before his time. But no one should wonder that professed practitioners of true friendship were rare among unbelieving peoples. For they did not know him who is charity, who is love, whose charity has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who was given to us. [Note: [Col. 0873] Rom. 5.]

But once the voice of the turtledove was heard in our land, [Note: [Col. 0873] Song 2] the voice announcing peace, announcing the truth of friendship, and saying, “This is my commandment: that you love one another,” [Col. 0874B] [Note: [Col. 0873] John 15] many thousands of people formed true friendships, loving each other more honourably, truly, surely, wisely, and strongly than Pylades and Orestes.

Was there not among those of whom it is written, “The multitude of believers had one heart and one soul, and no one said that anything belonging to him was his own, but all things were common to them,” [Note: [Col. 0873] Acts 4] a complete agreement about divine and human matters joined with charity and goodwill? Moreover, after Truth declared that no one has greater love than to lay down his life for his friends, [Note: [Col. 0873] John 15] pairs of friends were multiplied beyond number. For how many not only endured the loss of household property for their brethren in Christ, [Col. 0874C] but also, gladly embracing bodily torments, laid down their lives for their friends?

### CHAPTER III. How Sweet and Fruitful Friendship Is

Among human things nothing is found sweeter than friendship, nothing is sought more holy, nothing is preserved more fruitfully; for it bears fruit for the life which now is and that which is to come. By its own sweetness it seasons the other virtues, moderates adversities, orders prosperities, and makes sorrows pleasant.

A person without a friend has no one with whom to share life and affections, no one to whom to open the bosom of conscience, no one to whom to pour out, for consolation, something of troubling anxieties. One without a friend is alone. He is rightly called alone, because if he falls, he has no one to lift him up. [Col. 0874D] [Note: [Col. 0873] Eccl. 4.]

Conversely, how great the delight, how great the security, to have someone with whom you may speak as with yourself; someone to whom you dare entrust the secrets of your heart; someone whom you possess in your most private concerns as yourself; someone to whom, in full confidence, you may reveal how far you have fallen short or advanced before God in spiritual pursuits. Finally, what is more desirable or sweet than such a union of two minds that, when one is rebuked or praised by the other, no anger intervenes, no discord, no fear of accusation between them, no suspicion of flattery?

“The friend,” says the Wise Man, “is a medicine of [Col. 0875A] life.” [Note: [Col. 0875] Sirach 6.] [Note: [Col. 0875] Augustine, *On Friendship*, ch. 5.] For the best medicine for one person is another person: one who remedies his adversities, enters into his disadvantages, lightens heavy things, and carries the burdens of a friend as though with shoulder joined to shoulder. A true friend does not endure his own injury more impatiently than his friend’s.

It is the philosopher’s saying: “We do not use water, fire, or air more often than a friend.” [Note: [Col. 0875] Cicero, *On Friendship*.] In every action, every pursuit, matters certain and doubtful, every outcome, in private and in public, in every deliberation, at home and abroad—and, to include much in few words—in all that concerns divine and human affairs, the mutual favour of those who love one another proves useful.

Hear Cicero: “So great,” he says, “is the power of friendship that, by its benefit, absent friends stand present to one another, the needy abound, the weak are strong, and, what is more wonderful, the dead live.” Friendship, finally, serves the rich as glory, the poor as wealth, exiles as a homeland, the weak as strength, the sick as medicine, and the dead as life. And, as the same Cicero said: “They seem to take the sun from the world who take friendship from human life.” And again: “Friendship is a kind of life for human beings, without which there is no consolation in human life.”

Friendship is a certain step for human beings toward God. Through love, a person approaches God, while from being a person’s friend he becomes God’s friend. Hear God speaking to people whom he had established in love of neighbour and saying: “I will no longer call you servants, because the servant does not know what his lord does. [Col. 0875C] But I have called you friends, because all things whatsoever I heard from my Father I have made known to you.” [Note: [Col. 0875] John 15.] All these things, as most saints maintain, consist in love of God and neighbour.

### CHAPTER IV. That in True Friendship There Is Nothing Greedy or Dishonourable

It must be understood that in true friendship there is nothing dishonourable, nothing pretended, nothing seeking temporal gain or empty glory. For that love is not worthy of the name or honour of friendship which is formed under the pretext of some worldly advantage. Friendship exists for its own sake; it is its own reward. And far below the bounds of friendship remains the love which ambitious expectation or hope of profit precedes.

Love is indeed the source and origin of friendship and stands to it as genus to species. For although love often exists without friendship, friendship never exists without love. Love, then, sometimes has its cause in natural instinct, sometimes in carnal impulse, sometimes in duty, sometimes in reason alone, and very often proceeds from both reason and affection. [Col. 0875D]

### CHAPTER V. On Natural Love

Nature prescribes both the origin and the measure of friendship. By nature a mother loves her son; by it a hen gathers her chicks and shares the weakness of the weak, [Note: [Col. 0875] Matt. 23] a bear even growls over [Col. 0876A] her cubs, [Note: [Col. 0875] Prov. 7] and an eagle flies over her young, carrying them upon her shoulders. [Note: [Col. 0875] Deut. 32.] Even sea-monsters (*lamiae*) have bared their breasts and suckled their young. [Note: [Col. 0875] Lam. 4.]

Love led Jacob to mourn his son Joseph. Moved by natural love, David mourned his parricidal son and said: “Absalom, my son, my son Absalom! Who would grant that I might die for you, my son Absalom?” [Note: [Col. 0875] 2 Sam. 18.]

Natural friendship, however, often transgresses the law of moderation, forgetting God and one’s own salvation because of the excessive tenderness and affection of parents. Friendship is formed from duty when, through the rationale of giving and receiving, mutual gratitude grows between friends. But whoever professes true friendship should take care lest, under the pretext of generosity, the poison of mercenary friendship creep in.

Pure reason alone provides the ground for friendship when we love certain persons more because of divine authority than through our own affection. Thus we embrace in Christ, with the arms of sincere love, not only the peaceful but also the difficult and perverse, who are a burden and labour to us, for Christ says: “Love your enemies; do good to those who hate you.” [Col. 0876B] [Note: [Col. 0875] Matt. 22.] Without any pretence, we care for them, share the suffering of the afflicted, and bear their burdens on the shoulder of compassion.

Friendship is generated from reason and affection together when someone whom reason tells us to love makes himself lovable to us by his own virtue, so that love which is chaste through reason may be sweet through affection. The ordering of divine moderation introduced this love, commanding [Col. 0876C] a person to love his neighbour as he loved himself. Since human will was unbridled and headlong in this regard, God placed a bridle upon it; and lest it be free to wander outside the limits of moderation, he restricted it to the love which it had for itself and proportioned the affection itself to love of neighbour by a commensurable measure: “Love your neighbour,” he says, “as yourself.” [Note: [Col. 0875] Ibid.]

I believe that you love yourself, provided that you love God. Consider, then, whether you think any reward should be demanded for the love by which you love yourself. Certainly not. For everyone is dear to himself in and through himself; he needs neither external nor inward assistance in order to be stirred more intensely to love himself. Therefore, in order to love another equally as yourself, you must pour into him the affection of love which you have for yourself, [Col. 0876D] so that he may be to you as another self.

No external fruit should be sought from friendship of this sort, since it is charity itself, which never fails, [Note: [Col. 0875] 1 Cor. 13] and whose fruit is joy and peace in the Holy Spirit. Indicating this fruit, Truth says in the Gospel: “I appointed you to go and bear fruit, and that your fruit may remain.” [Note: [Col. 0875] John 15.]

### CHAPTER VI. On Carnal Love

Love arising from the flesh follows its ears and eyes as they commit fornication in various ways, and through their entrances introduces even into the mind the image of things to be desired. Thus, in the manner of a harlot, [Col. 0877A] it spreads its legs and exposes itself to the filth of every unclean spirit, promising itself a longer span of life. It despises the terrible judgments of God and attributes to its life only this: that it indulges extraordinary pleasure.

And so the mind, enticed and drawn by shameless looks, words, gestures, and services, is miserably taken captive. While two minds are fused in one will by a certain foul pact, doing what is more hateful to God and more destructive to the soul, the wretches imagine that whatever they do is done according to the law of friendship.

This friendship is neither entered upon through deliberation, nor tested by judgment, nor ruled by reason; rather, following the impulse of wandering affection, it is indiscriminately carried away through unlawful things. It observes neither measure nor honour; it distinguishes neither what is beneficial from what is ruinous. It is led by a spirit of dizziness and, boiling with the flames of unbridled desire, is driven as by certain inward furies. This bastard and degenerate friendship, polluted by lust or defiled by the guilt of some other plague, experiences feelings that are pleasurable for a time but perpetually destructive. For what gives pleasure quickly passes, while what torments remains without end. Let friendship therefore be contracted honourably and chastely; in it all things are secure, sweet, peaceful, pleasant, and delightful. [Col. 0877B]

### CHAPTER VII. That Friendship Is Not True If It Is Mercenary

Friendship introduced by unclean greed [Col. 0877C] is deceitful: it has nothing certain, secure, or stable. It loves a person’s goods, not the person; it measures love by profit. It embraces fortune with its wishes, not the individual, in accordance with the saying:

> He is not the friend of the person but of prosperity,  
> whom sweet fortune holds and bitter fortune drives away.

Sacred Scripture testifies: “There is a friend according to the occasion, and he will not remain in the day of tribulation.” [Note: [Col. 0877] Sirach 6.] This is a mercenary friendship which, the more closely it conforms to greed, is the more remotely banished from the palace of friendship.

Although many advantages commonly come to cultivators of friendship from friendship itself, true friendship establishes its fruits within itself and, with sheer generosity, precedes every hope of future return. No one believes that the friendship of Barzillai the Gileadite with David had its beginning in the benefits by which he kindly received, supported, and numbered David among his chief friends when he fled from Absalom. [Col. 0877D] [Note: [Col. 0877] 2 Sam. 17.] Rather, the affection of friendship, which preceded his generosity, furnished the cause for the humaneness he bestowed. It is well known that the king did not need that man’s assistance; and, since the man was extremely wealthy, he expected no recompense from the king for it. Hence, when David offered him the wealth and delights of the whole city, he consented to accept nothing.

Likewise, the venerable covenant between David and Jonathan [Note: [Col. 0877] 1 Sam. 18] was consecrated not by expectation of earthly advantage but by contemplation of proven virtue. Yet in each case benefit to the other arose: the diligence of one preserved the life of the other, and by one’s benefit the posterity of the other was not destroyed. Friendship, then, does not consist in profit or flattery, but in truth and fidelity.

Hear blessed Ambrose: “Friendship,” he says, “is not tributary but generous. For it is a virtue, not gain; it is acquired not by money but by favour; it is neither produced nor fostered by bidding prices, but by the mutual striving of goodwill.” [Note: [Col. 0877] Book III, *On Duties*.] The sweetest kindling of friendship is sincerity of affection, mutual helpfulness, frequent sharing of honourable matters, equality of wills, and continual, inviolable fidelity.

Certainly Hushai the Archite [Note: [Col. 0877] 2 Sam. 15] sought to exalt and sustain David’s friendship with such fidelity that he preferred anxiety [Col. 0878A] to safety, and the dangers and labours of death to joy and rest, choosing to share the pains of his friend rather than the honours of a murderer. The words of Ittai the Gittite were these [Note: [Col. 0877] Ibid.]—when David fled barefoot from Jerusalem before Absalom, and David told him to return—“As the Lord lives, I will not abandon you, either in life or in death.”

### CHAPTER VIII. That One Kind of Friendship Is Commended and Another Reproved

Closely akin to the love which takes its cause and origin from the lust of the flesh or the pride of life is the love of the world, which rests wholly upon vanity alone, according to the saying: “Children of men, how long will you be heavy of heart? Why do you love vanity and seek falsehood?” [Col. 0878B–C] [Note: [Col. 0877] Ps. 4.]

There are also loves which, if ordered, are approved: social, fraternal, and conjugal love. Social love is exemplified by David and Jonathan. The affection of this love pressed David to mourning, so that he said: “I grieve for you, my brother Jonathan, most beautiful and lovable beyond the love of women. As a mother loves her only son, so I loved you.” [Note: [Col. 0877] 2 Sam. 1.]

Brother and sister possess within themselves the interchange of sweetest love and nurture mutual and undivided affections by the agreement of reciprocal will. Bridegroom and bride, by domestic affections and an indissoluble bond, preserve the chastity of marital fidelity.

It should further be noted that there is an incipient friendship, concerning which blessed Augustine writes and which he describes as follows: conversing and laughing with a friend; rendering kindly service; reading and discussing together; disagreeing with each other without hatred, as one disagrees with oneself; longing for the absent with distress; receiving those who come with joy; returning the love of one who loves; defending those present; excusing the absent; blunting the tooth of detraction; and in every way faithfully displaying the ardour of inward love. [Col. 0878D] [Note: [Col. 0877] *On Friendship*.]

Blessed Augustine here indicates certain properties of tender affection which good and bad people commonly share. But the friendship of which we speak ordinarily arises only among the good, advances among the better, and is brought to completion among the best.

### CHAPTER IX. On the Origin of Friendship

[Col. 0879A]

Finally, if we consider friendship’s origin, it drew its essence from the supreme nature, which is God. God indeed impressed the first affections of friendship upon human minds; practice and experience increased it; finally, the authority of law ordered it.

For God, supremely good, supremely merciful, powerful, self-sufficient in his own blessedness—which he himself is—and in his ineffable glory, had need neither of heaven nor earth, angel nor human being.
