Every creature declares his sufficiency and says: “You are my God, because you have no need of my goods.” [Note: [Col. 0879] Ps. 15.] He, the cause of all existing things, the life of sentient beings, the wisdom of intelligent beings, [Col. 0879B] the love and glory of angels, deigned to draw humanity to love himself and, through these invisible things, to invite it to desire his invisible things.

Thus he prescribed by eternal reason a certain bond of friendship not only to the four elements but also to all creatures. For they would not be good unless, by a certain mutual and friendly covenant, they agreed with one another. For we read that God saw all the things he had made, and they were very good. [Note: [Col. 0879] Gen. 1.] They are good insofar as they are from God; beautiful insofar as every part agrees with its whole; and ordered insofar as each thing in this universe receives a fitting place, time, and measure.

A place: because angels obtained heaven, irrational creatures the earth, and human beings the better place, paradise. [Col. 0879C] A time: because angels were made at one and the same time; human beings were created at different times and, in respect of the soul, will exist forever; whereas irrational creatures were neither made simultaneously nor will exist forever. God set this measure for rational creatures: if they are just, they become participants in blessedness; if unjust, they are subject to eternal condemnation. For irrational and sentient creatures, God prescribed this measure: because they can be neither blessed nor miserable, they either serve the salvation of the predestined or add to the misery of those foreknown for damnation.

Therefore the Wise Man rightly says: “Fire and iron, milk and bread, honey, a cluster of grapes, oil and clothing: as all these turn to good for the holy, so they turn to evil for the ungodly.” [Note: [Col. 0879] Sirach 39.] Thus God, whose supreme good is to be immutable and whose being is always the same—as the Prophet says, “You are always the same” [Note: [Col. 0879] Ps. 101]—orders creatures so that each has a nature by which it is good, a form by which it is beautiful, and a use through which it benefits the rational creature by being well ordered.

In this the Creator’s wisdom is especially to be admired and praised: though he made nothing evil, he nevertheless orders and disposes our evils so that things capable of harming us do not harm us, but, being set before us for correction or punishment, work toward salvation—especially for those who love God. For “all things work together for good for those who love God.” [Col. 0879D] [Note: [Col. 0879] Rom. 8.]

Therefore he who is unchangeably good and blessed provided for the rational creature alone and willed it to be capable of his blessedness, so that it might be fit to cleave to him in love and hope, whose image it is, and to cast all its desirable things into his knowledge and service; for to know him is life, and to serve him is to reign. [Col. 0880A]

### CHAPTER X. How Love, First Deformed by Sin, Was Afterwards Reformed

Finally, when charity grew cold through their transgression, greed entered in. Preferring private goods to common ones, it introduced suspicions, rivalries, quarrels, and hatreds. Yet the image of the Creator, although corrupted in humanity, has not been altogether abolished. Therefore humanity possesses memory, though liable to forgetfulness; knowledge, though exposed to error; and love, [Col. 0880B] though inclined toward greed.

For it was fitting to heavenly justice that, because humanity had abused free will and turned its love away from the true and immutable good toward a deceptive and transitory good, arrogating to itself God’s likeness by robbery, it should be added to the likeness of beasts. Thus, “Man, though he was in honour, did not understand; he was compared with senseless beasts and became like them.” [Note: [Col. 0879] Ps. 48.] So, insolently seeking advancement, he fell into deficiency; presuming to become more like God, he became unlike him and lost both God and himself.

Yet no transgression could so abolish the image of God that humanity would not in some fashion retain within itself an image of the blessed Trinity. For the human soul remembers itself, knows itself, [Col. 0880C] and loves itself. It also remembers its knowledge, knows it, and loves it; and it loves and remembers its own love and memory, and knows them both. Thus you may see, as it were, unity in the one substance of the soul, and an image of the Trinity in the three—namely knowledge, memory, and love—in which the soul’s substance resides.

For this reason we believe the Psalmist said: “Surely man passes in an image, yet he is troubled in vain,” [Note: [Col. 0879] Ps. 38] indicating that the image of God is not lacking by nature, but corruption is present through fault. Forgetfulness corrupts memory, error darkens knowledge, and love degenerates into greed.

But once the debt of the ancient transgression had been discharged through Jesus Christ our Saviour, once the handwriting of death whose obligation held us bound had been blotted out, and once the principalities and powers to whom the divine sentence had delivered us had been triumphed over, human memory began to be repaired by sacred discourse, knowledge restored through the sacrament of faith, and love to grow fervent again through the example of that charity which Christ displayed to us upon the cross. [Col. 0880D]

The reformation of this image will be complete where forgetfulness does not interrupt memory, error does not darken knowledge, and greed for another thing does not corrupt love of God. These things will be in the homeland, where there will be no place for forgetfulness among those living in eternity, no prick of greed among those absorbed in charity. There will be supreme peace, [Col. 0881A] full rest, eternal happiness, a happy, pleasant, and unfailing tranquillity.

Meanwhile, returning to friendship, we say that friendship arises, is preserved, and is perfected only among those who live soberly, justly, and devoutly in this world; [Note: [Col. 0881] Titus 2] who wish neither to seek nor grant anything dishonourable, and neither do, think, nor consent to anything which they perceive may displease God, endanger the soul, or result in common harm.

In this respect the opinion of certain persons is to be rejected: those who think friendship should be formed against faith, honour, the commonwealth, or the common good. Certainly the servants of King Saul commendably kept faith with their lord in refusing to obey his cruelty in shedding the blood of the priests, unlike Doeg the Edomite, [Note: [Col. 0881] 1 Sam. 22] who, by the wickedness of that same sacrilege, likewise defiled himself in obeying his lord’s command. [Col. 0881B]

Jonadab, Amnon’s friend, by advising and arranging his incest, cruelly violated the law of friendship when he rendered service for shameful conduct. [Note: [Col. 0881] 2 Sam. 13.] It is evident that Absalom’s friends were wicked transgressors of friendship: by stirring up war against their king and kingdom, they incurred with Absalom the crime of treason. [Note: [Col. 0881] 2 Sam. 15 and 16.]

Let those, then, be ashamed to profess the name of true friendship who defile it by consenting to or cooperating in vices; who, abusing the word “honour,” presumptuously claim for themselves, with sacrilegious presumption, the glory of mutual friendship. For one who does not love is not a friend. But one who loves iniquity does not love; indeed, beyond doubt, he hates that soul [Col. 0881C] whose iniquity he loves, [Note: [Col. 0881] Ps. 10] and therefore loves neither another’s soul nor his own.

### CHAPTER XI. That All the Virtues of the Soul Are Made Sweet Through Love

There are three things by which we cleave spiritually to God: memory, knowledge, and will. Memory is in a certain way capable of eternity, knowledge of knowing, and will of love. In these three the first human being held God in memory without forgetfulness, knew him in knowledge without error, and desired him in love without desire for another thing. And although humanity was blessed in these three, yet in the third—that is, in love—he cleaved to his Creator more intimately in proportion as he tasted more sweetly how sweet God is. [Note: [Col. 0881] Ps. 33.]

For the greater the love of the highest good, the sweeter the delight in it and the fuller the blessedness. Though memory retains many past things, and though knowledge comprehends things most profound, still there is no delight there unless the sweetness of love pours itself in. Therefore, in rational beings God orders memory, knowledge, and love, so that love may grow strong through memory and knowledge, and those two may be sweetened in love. [Col. 0881D]

From these, in certain persons, there is formed and established an affection toward God and a gentle, friendly communion of wills among themselves. Finally, in the creation of humanity a social covenant and bond is specially commended. God says: “It is not good for the human being to be alone; let us make for him a helper like himself.” [Note: [Col. 0881] Gen. 2.] And, as a greater and clearer sign of union, he propagated the substance of one from the substance of the other. Thus the companion was taken from Adam’s side, so that those who were side by side in substance might be equal also in life and conduct. [Col. 0882A]

Thus nature inscribed the first impulses of love in human hearts; later, the inner sense increased them by a certain practice of loving, as by a taste of sweetest sweetness.

### CHAPTER XII. On Love for a Friend, and What Hinders It
In entering into friendship, many elements are involved by which friendship is formed, strengthened, and continually enlarged [Note: [Col. 0881] Augustine, *On Friendship*, ch. 12.]. Since a friend ought to be one to whom you entrust your heart and all the hidden things of your heart [Col. 0882B], he must first be chosen, then tested, then admitted, and finally treated with the highest reverence and cultivated with constant devotion. That all things in friendship may proceed in due order, they should first be consecrated in God, as in the foundation of the first fruits of love; afterwards friendship should be nurtured by choice, testing, consent, and unbroken familiarity, with love’s first fruits consecrated in God as its foundation, so that it may contain an image not only of stability but even of a kind of eternity.

Thus you should belong to him and he to you, so that no discord of minds, judgments, affections, or words may creep in between you, whether in spiritual or bodily matters. For friendship is strengthened and perfected by choice, testing, admission, and a complete harmony in divine and human things, joined with goodwill and charity [Col. 0882C]. Choice requires that no one be selected for friendship whose reputation is burdened by the enormity of some crime. Yet a person may be chosen and admitted if he is otherwise commendable in life and can readily be cured of the vice whose blemish disfigures his commendable character.

There are four vices by which the noble honor of friendship is frequently obscured: anger, instability, suspicion, and talkativeness. Sacred Scripture says of the angry person: “Do not be a friend to an angry man” [Note: [Col. 0881] Prov. 22.]. For anger is brief madness. Hence the same Scripture adds: “Do not walk with a furious man” [Note: [Col. 0881] Ibid.]. Likewise Solomon says: “Anger rests in the bosom of a fool” [Note: [Col. 0881] Eccles. 7.]. And in Ecclesiasticus: “There is a friend who will expose hatred, quarrelling, and insults” [Note: [Col. 0881] Ecclus. 6.].

But some are angry by the natural condition of their own temperament, while nevertheless not allowing the agitation of their mind to advance to those things which, according to the testimony of Scripture, dissolve friendship [Col. 0882D]. So long as their affection is assured, such persons should patiently be endured; the excess of their speech and conduct should be gently corrected and kindly instructed, or patiently overlooked, or pardoned in a friendly way. From the vice of anger five vices commonly spring up like the five heads of a hydra, each of which often dissolves friendship: insult, reproach, pride, disclosure of a secret, and a treacherous blow [Note: [Col. 0881] Ecclus. 22.].

Hear not my words, but those of Sacred Scripture, which says [Col. 0883A]: “He who insults a friend dissolves friendship” [Note: [Col. 0883] Ecclus.]. Yet if a friend, forestalled by some sudden impulse, speaks a harsh word, or prefers his own counsel to yours, friendship ought not to be dissolved on account of these and similar things. For, as the same Wise Man says, friendship still remains, except in the case of insult, reproach, pride, revelation of a mystery, and a treacherous blow [Note: [Col. 0883] Ibid.].

Insult wounds charity, because whatever someone says against a friend under the prompting of anger is believed true by others, since it has been uttered by one privy to his secrets. Reproach is indeed detestable when someone, by bringing false accusations, covers the face of an innocent person with shameful blushes, outwardly burdening his reputation and inwardly wounding charity. Pride is the enemy of humility [Col. 0883B], and especially to be detested because, excluding the remedy of repentance or the humility of confession, it makes a person bold in committing injuries and obstinate against correction and counsel.

Finally, the disclosure of a mystery or secret is execrable. It shamelessly empties out whatever love or favor existed between friends and sprinkles everything with the gall of bitterness, hatred, and indignation. Therefore the Wise Man says: “He who reveals the secrets of a friend loses trust” [Note: [Col. 0883] Ecclus. 27.]. And a little later: “To disclose the mysteries of friends is the despair of an unhappy soul” [Note: [Col. 0883] Ibid.]. For restoration of friendship must be despaired of in one who has made void the original trust and, by revealing what was entrusted to him as though to God, has thrown everything into disorder.

A treacherous blow is the bite of a serpent and asp [Col. 0883C]. For Solomon says: “If a serpent bites in silence, he who secretly slanders is no better” [Note: [Col. 0883] Eccles. 10.].

## CHAPTER XIII. Examples of the things that hinder friendship.

And, to add examples concerning insult, reproach, and the rest: let us recall that when Shimei pursued David, fleeing from Absalom, with insults [Note: [Col. 0883] 2 Kings 16.], David, among his testamentary words, consigned Shimei by a heavenly sentence to the punishment of death. You have an example of the punishment of reproach in Nabal of Carmel: when he reproached holy David as a servant and fugitive, this same Nabal was struck by the Lord and perished [Note: [Col. 0883] 1 Kings 25.].

We have an example of the punishment of pride in Ammon, son of Nahash, king of the Ammonites [Col. 0883D] [Note: [Col. 0883] 2 Kings 10.]. King David had long maintained friendship with King Nahash; after Nahash’s death, David offered his son Ammon a covenant of friendship. But Ammon, proud and ungrateful, added insult to contempt for his friend. In vengeance for that crime David devastated him, his people, and even his cities with fire and sword [Note: [Col. 0883] Ibid.].

We have an example of disclosure of a secret in Ahithophel. Joining the son of the parricide, he betrayed to him the counsel of his father David; then, giving himself an end worthy of the crime of treachery, he hanged himself with a noose [Note: [Col. 0883] 2 Kings 17.]. We have an example of the poison of slander [Col. 0884A] in Miriam, the sister of Moses. When she presumptuously disparaged her brother while rebuking him, God struck her with leprosy, expelled her from the camp, and cut her off from fellowship with the people for seven days [Note: [Col. 0883] Num. 11].

Not only the angry, but also the unstable and suspicious, must be excluded from the choice of friendship. Since security is a great fruit of friendship, by which you trust and entrust yourself to a friend, how can you be secure of the love of one who is carried about by every wind, who assumes Proteus’ faces all day long, and does not remain in the same purpose even for a little while? The suspicious likewise must be banished far from the choice of friendship. Nothing is more fitting to friendship than a certain peace and the quiet tranquility of the heart; but curiosity continually disturbs the suspicious person, suggests the stings of fear [Col. 0884B], and supplies abundant material for disturbance.

If he sees his friend speaking more privately with another, he imagines treachery; if he sees his friend showing himself kind and pleasant to another, he thinks himself despised. He interprets a friend’s correction as hatred and praise as mockery. Thus he is perverse in everything, perverting all things.

I do not think that talkative persons should be chosen for the secrets of friendship. “A talkative man shall not be established on the earth” [Note: [Col. 0883] Ps. 139.]. And according to the testimony of the Wise Man [Note: [Col. 0883] Prov. 26.], if you see a man ready to speak, you can hope no more from him than from a fool. Therefore choose as your friend one who accords with your character and your integrity. For, as blessed Ambrose testifies [Note: [Col. 0883] *On Duties*, book III, ch. 16.], friendship cannot exist between unlike characters.

Although anger, instability, suspicion, and verbosity often hinder the choice of friendship [Col. 0884C], it seems to me that those should nevertheless not be excluded from this choice of friendship [Note: [Col. 0883] Augustine, *On Friendship*, ch. 15.] who restrain anger by patience, check frivolity by due seriousness, and dispel suspicions by true love. I should judge these the more approved and the more worthy to be chosen for friendship, and to be embraced with all the greater devotion because they restrain vices more strongly by virtues and, fighting against themselves, rule their own wills.

## CHAPTER XIV. The fidelity of friendship, and what should be loved in a friend.

Friendship is tested by fidelity, intention, discernment, and patience [Col. 0884D]. By fidelity, through which you entrust yourself and all that is yours to the one whom you love without any suspicion [Note: [Col. 0883] Ibid., ch. 18.]. By intention, so that nothing is expected from friendship except God and the natural good of which He Himself is the author. By discernment, so that with careful caution and exact examination you investigate what must be rendered to a friend; in what matters one ought to grieve for a friend or rejoice with him; and in what he must be corrected, or in what and how he must be endured. Patience too has a very great place in friendship, for it is friendship’s guardian and nurse.

In prosperous and adverse circumstances [Col. 0885A], and in every condition of life, patience remains the same, looking with the same eye on a friend whether rich or poor, strong or weak, healthy or sick, lowly or exalted. Yet it gives more eager attention to those things concerning the soul of a friend; it does not greatly consider those things outside the friend’s soul. If they are present, it does not value them highly; if absent, it does not seek them. The things concerning a person’s soul are character, grace, and virtues; those outside the soul are reputation, riches, and honors.

And it should be noted that, as gold is tested in the furnace [Note: [Col. 0885] Prov. 27.], so fidelity is tested in necessity. For it is written: “A friend is tested in necessity.” And again: “Many are the friends of a rich man, but in riches the fidelity of friendship lies hidden. He who loves deceptively in prosperity will be an adversary in adversity” [Col. 0885B]. Let love lay aside its mask: in the storm of the whirlwind the hypocrite will uncover the paint of his counterfeit intimacy—the man who flatters you with smooth service and sophistically measures himself by the rule of true friendship.

Solomon says: “A friend loves at all times, and a brother is proved in distress” [Note: [Col. 0885] Ibid. 17.]. And, reproving the faithless person, he says: “A rotten tooth and a weary foot is one who trusts in the unfaithful in a day of distress” [Note: [Col. 0885] Ibid. 25.].

The fidelity of friendship is tested not only by adversity but also by silence regarding secrets. The Gospel saying is this: “He who is faithful in a little thing will also be faithful in much” [Note: [Col. 0885] Luke 16.]. If, therefore, you wish to test a friend’s fidelity, do not first entrust to him the hidden things of your heart, but rather some outward and small matters, from the disclosure of which no great loss would arise [Col. 0885C]. Nevertheless, entrust even these under such caution and fearful adjuration as though their betrayal would harm and their concealment would help. Having proved him in smaller matters, you may more securely test him in greater ones.

Finally, if rumor has spread some malicious report about you, or a slanderer has charged you, in your absence, with some disgraceful deed, and that friend cannot at all be moved to believe it, stirred by no suspicion or wavering in no doubt, then his fidelity is sure and stable and you ought to have no hesitation concerning him.

We read in the book of Valerius Maximus [Note: [Col. 0885] book IV, ch. 2.] that someone informed Plato that Xenocrates had repeatedly slandered him, and the informer offered to confirm this by oath. Plato replied: “It is not believable that one whom I faithfully love does not faithfully love me” [Col. 0885D]. When the accuser persisted, Plato added: “And if he has said these things about me, he judged these very things to be beneficial to me.”

Alexander was ill [Note: [Col. 0885] Valerius Maximus, book III, ch. 8.], and, by the common judgment of the physicians, his physician and friend Philip offered him a medicine prepared by his own hands. A letter from Parmenio arrived, urging the king to beware of Philip’s treachery, since Darius had allegedly bribed him with money. After reading it, Alexander drank without hesitation; then he handed it to Philip to read, weighing the affection of his friend by his own love, and in the very announcement of death he drove out the vice of suspicion [Col. 0886A].

Flaccus briefly includes certain matters especially important in testing a friend [Note: [Col. 0885] *Satires*, book I, satire 4, line 1.], saying:

> He who tears apart an absent friend,  
> who does not defend him when another blames him;  
> who hunts for unrestrained laughter and the reputation of a wit;  
> who can invent what he has not seen,  
> who cannot keep entrusted things silent—  
> he is a liar; he is an unfaithful friend.

## CHAPTER XV. By what means the intention of one who loves is tested.

It remains to consider how intention is to be tested. There are those who intend or hope for nothing in friendship except gain. Such people love their friends as they love their ox or ass: they expect profit from them and seek not favor or peace of mind, but gain. Therefore the intention of the person whom you propose to admit to the sanctuary of your intimacy must be tested [Col. 0886B], lest he wish to enter friendship with you in hope of temporal advantage. Such an intention is mercenary, not gratuitous.

For this reason the friendships of the poor are generally found to be firmer than those of the great. Many seek favor from the rich by flattery. But no one behaves deceitfully toward a poor person; and the affection of charity toward the poor is purer insofar as there is no occasion for flattery or pretense in his case. Therefore, if you see a person anxiously desiring something which you can provide, either personally or through another, but in the obtaining of such a thing someone else is preferred to him, you will easily discover the intention with which he has attached himself to you. For in such a case the distress of an ambitious mind may be detected now in downcast eyes, now in a turned-away face, now in a somewhat sorrowful word, now [Col. 0886C] in a forced laugh, now in more negligent respect and service.

## CHAPTER XVI. That indiscretion is harmful in friendship.

Discernment is exceedingly necessary among friends. For just as a ship without a helmsman, so the spirit of friends without discernment is carried about by an irrational and unstable motion. Such people bear their friends’ slight faults impatiently and rebuke them harshly; in their own conduct they are rash, neglect great matters, grow inflamed over trifles, and, confusing everything, attend neither to person, place, time, nor to the contingency of ignorance or necessity. A person of this sort, through an undiscerning movement of mind, does not know to whom or when he should disclose a matter or conceal it [Col. 0886D].

## CHAPTER XVII. That friendship is tested by patience.

Test a friend’s patience, if you see fit, by rebuking him somewhat sternly, so that his endurance may be exercised and tested. If at some time he gives offense by an incautious disclosure of a secret or some slight transgression, do not therefore withdraw from choosing or loving him, so long as some hope of correction remains. Nor should you weary of exercising the most exact deliberation in choosing and testing friends, since from such care you receive a desirable fruit: namely, a remedy of life [Col. 0887A] and the firmest foundation of lasting joy.

Take care, however, that, as often happens, some impulse of love does not outrun the interval of testing and anticipate the judgment of trial. Therefore a prudent person should gradually check and restrain this impulse, so that, setting out the measure of goodwill, he may pass by rule and discernment into affection, and at last, after testing has gone before, entrust himself to his friend.

Testing is necessary among people who are not very good, or where good and bad persons are mixed. But those whom God has tested require no examination: those whose citizenship is already in heaven [Note: [Col. 0887] Phil. 3.], whom a regular rule of life makes of one character in one house, whom a faithful equality of wills and a sure communion of charity unite. Among them each loves the other as himself, and by mutual affection the exultation of all becomes the individual possession of each [Col. 0887B]. There, the joy of the whole community, drawn inwardly from the testimony of a good conscience, is made his own by every person through the communion of charity and the benefit of friendship.

## CHAPTER XVIII. By what means friendship should be fostered.

Friendship must be fostered with the most exact care and caution. Above all, every suspicion must be banished from it, for suspicion is the poison of friendship. Therefore let our minds be strengthened, as it were, with a firmer impulse, so that we may neither think ill of a friend, nor believe one who speaks ill of him, nor consent even a little to such speech.

If you saw someone who regarded everyone else with suspicion, suspecting in every person plots of treachery, loving no one and thinking that he was loved by no one [Col. 0887C], would you not consider him wretched in a condemnable way? Conversely, judge that person most blessed who loves everyone in such a way as to deserve to be loved by everyone, and whose tranquility of mind is stirred by no scruple of fear or suspicion.

Friendship must therefore be fostered so that our speech has pleasantness, our face cheerfulness, our conduct sweetness, and even our very look a certain gracious and welcome delight of the eyes. Let there be frequent conversation about honorable matters, communication of secrets, and mutual compliance with one another’s wishes. For Truth has given us a pattern to follow, that we may reveal our secrets to one another and mutually fulfill the will of friends, when He says: “I will no longer call you servants; but I have called you friends, because I have made known to you the things that I heard from my Father” [Col. 0887D] [Note: [Col. 0887] John 15.]. And again: “You are my friends, if you do what I command you” [Note: [Col. 0887] Ibid.].

In these words, as blessed Ambrose says [Note: [Col. 0887] *On Duties*, book III, ch. 13.], He gave us a pattern of friendship to follow: that we should reveal our secrets to one another and mutually fulfill the will of friends. Friendship, then, is nourished by reciprocal rejoicing; and if a friend’s more severe face sometimes displays a mature gravity, that gravity will be all the more commendable insofar as it more kindly descends to a social effect. Indeed, the law of friendship humbles the superior together with the inferior, so that those who excel in rank, dignity, or knowledge [Col. 0888A] may, in a full spirit of humility, condescend to those beneath them.

## CHAPTER XIX. That God’s or nature’s gifts, and not other things, are to be loved in a person.

[Note: [Col. 0887] Augustine, *On Friendship*, ch. 24.] A person should judge the gifts of God and the endowments of nature to be what must especially be valued in a friend, and should consider as nothing all things outside these. Friendship is not adorned with jewels or silks; it is not fattened with luxuries, puffed up with honors, or expanded by extensive possessions. In a friend, therefore, let equality of nature be considered; do not seek the trappings or accidents of fortune.

But let equality of minds so order all things between friends that the lofty descends and the lowly rises, the poor becomes rich and the rich suffers need, and equality results from equal affection and fellowship [Col. 0888B], as it is written: “He who had much did not abound, and he who had little did not lack” [Note: [Col. 0887] 2 Cor. 8; Exod. 16.]. The law of friendship is to receive a friend with proportionately greater reverence as one understands that he labors under greater need.

Jonathan, David’s friend, gave no thought to succession in the kingdom or to his father’s threats. He preferred to the glory of the kingdom the servant of his father, whom he had received into friendship—the man driven into flight by his father, condemned to death, and hidden in the wilderness. “You,” he said, “will be king, and I shall be second after you” [Note: [Col. 0887] 1 Kings 23.].

Let people hear this venerable and most worthy-of-imitation word of friendship. Saul sought David’s death and, accusing the priests of treachery, slaughtered them upon suspicion alone. He besieged rocks, mountains [Col. 0888C], valleys, and groves with soldiers, and compelled all the princes to swear to David’s destruction. Jonathan alone—who could have envied or resented David as his rival and disinheritor—resisted his father, showed honor to his friend, brought consolation to the afflicted man, and, preferring friendship to a kingdom, said: “You will be king, and I shall be second after you.”

Saul pressed Jonathan with insults and dreadful threats, seeking to provoke his friend David into Jonathan’s hatred. When Saul pronounced sentence of death upon David, Jonathan, as though appealing from the sentence of his father’s inhumanity, said: “Why should David die? What has he done [Note: [Col. 0887] 1 Kings 20.]? He put his life at risk for your life and struck the Philistine, and you rejoiced; why then should he die?” But Saul, turned to madness, tried to pierce him through the side with a spear [Col. 0888D]; and, adding reproaches to Jonathan, called him “the son of a woman who seizes men of her own accord.”

He added that Jonathan loved David to the shame of Jonathan and of his dishonored mother; and, vomiting out the whole poison of envy and seeking to arouse an incentive to ambition and hatred, he said: “As long as the son of Jesse lives, your kingdom will not be established” [Note: [Col. 0887] Ibid.]. Whom would these words not move? Whose friendship would they not corrupt into hatred? Who would not prefer himself and his own descendants to another? Who would not break the pledge of fidelity in this matter?

But the strong and true friend, patient under insults and threats, preferring his friend to his sons and the friend’s honor to his own honor, in all things mindful of kindness and forgetful of glory, said [Col. 0889A]: “You will be king, and I shall be second after you.” Cicero testifies [Note: [Col. 0889] Cicero, *On Friendship*.] that some are mistaken in thinking it base to prefer money to friendship. But he says it was impossible to find those who did not prefer honors, magistracies, commands, and powers to friendship. For human nature is weak and maimed when it comes to despising power offered to it. Yet Jonathan was found victorious over nature and, against nature, a despiser of power and glory.

This is true, stable, and eternal friendship: when so tested, so battered by rams and siege engines, it does not waver; it is not moved by suspicion; nor, when assailed by envy, ambition, injuries, threats, or reproaches, does it falter [Col. 0889B]. Thus friendship is fostered by equality. Hence blessed Ambrose says [Note: [Col. 0889] *On Duties*, book III, ch. 16.]: “Show deference to your friend as to an equal, and do not be ashamed to take the lead in rendering service to a friend.”

## CHAPTER XX. What kind and degree of generosity friendship requires.

The law of friendship, as the authority of writers declares, is that we ask nothing dishonorable from those whom we receive into the bosom of friendship; and, when they ask something, that we grant them ready consent and suitable assistance without difficulty or delay, as it is written: “Lose money for the sake of a friend” [Note: [Col. 0889] Ecclus. 29.]. If money is to be lost for a friend, then it ought still more readily to be supplied for his advantages and needs.

Yet not everyone is richer or poorer than everyone else in every respect; some are richer in certain things and poorer in others [Col. 0889C], and thus we cannot all do everything. One abounds in money, another in lands, another in honors; one has greater power in counsel, another in familiarity with the powerful. Whatever you spend upon a friend, never reproach him for it; recall the words of James: “If anyone,” he says, “lacks wisdom, let him ask it from God, who gives to all abundantly and does not reproach” [Note: [Col. 0889] Jas. 1.].

Whenever, then, you give to a friend [Note: [Col. 0889] Augustine, *On Friendship*, ch. 25.], do not turn away your face, draw down your brow, lower your eyes, expect recompense, delay, or postpone. Rather, seek to season your generosity with a cheerful expression or serene face and pleasant speech. Anticipate, as though foreknowing, the wish of the petitioner, and outstrip his desire by liberality [Col. 0889D], so that you may seem to grant without being asked what you give. Nothing makes a noble spirit blush more than asking. Since you and your friend ought to have one soul and one heart, it is absurd that you should not have one purse with your friend. Let us take care to forestall the person who is about to ask us with benefits, so that the recipient may seem rather to confer a favor than the giver.

Boaz, observing the poverty of Ruth the Moabite while she gathered ears after his reapers, spoke to her, comforted her, and invited her to the meal of his servants [Note: [Col. 0889] Ruth 2.]. Sparing her modesty, he also ordered the reapers deliberately to leave ears behind, which she could gather without shame [Col. 0890A].

Certainly, in this generosity poverty excuses no one. If only all were poor in spirit, a richer yield of mutual kindness in beneficence would stand forth! The Wise Man says [Note: [Col. 0889] Plato, *Republic*; Chrysostom, *On Acts*] that all would live the happiest life if two words were removed from among us: “mine” and “yours.” Seneca testifies in *On Benefits* [Note: [Col. 0889] book I, ch. 8.] that, when many people had offered many things to Socrates, their teacher, according to their means, Aeschines, his poor pupil, said: “I find nothing worthy of you that I can give you, and in this one respect I feel myself poor. This alone which I have—that is, myself—I give to you. Others have given you many things and retained very much for themselves; I give entirely what I am and what I have.” Socrates replied: “You have given me a great gift, unless you think yourself small. I accept the gift gratefully [Col. 0890B], and I shall return it to you better.”

Thus one gave from his own resources who had nothing from the goods of fortune to give; and in the narrow confines of poverty generosity found material for bounty. Therefore, if you are a son of Christ or a disciple of Peter, so that you can say, “Gold and silver I do not have” [Note: [Col. 0889] Acts 3.], you nevertheless possess something more precious than gold and silver. You can pray for friends, console the afflicted, raise up the fallen, sympathize with those who suffer, and rejoice with those who rejoice. You can teach the ignorant, regard another’s desolation as your own, bear with the difficult, and strengthen the fainthearted.

## CHAPTER XXI. With what discernment and caution friends should be helped.

Among the precepts of friendship, this too must be carefully arranged with provident discretion [Col. 0890C]: although you love all your friends, you should not advance all equally by generosity to benefits or honors when opportunity is offered. There are indeed many who complain that they are not loved and protest that they are regarded with contempt if they see others, and not themselves, involved in offices and responsibilities.

But from the beginning you should carefully consider not merely what you can bestow, but what and how much the person to whom you intend to give can bear and adequately fulfill. We receive and cherish many into the bosom of true friendship whom we cannot raise to the eminence that they seek without damage to our reputation, danger to themselves, or public scandal. We must therefore measure a person’s virtue and prudence, so that in the distribution of goods reason, not affection, may prevail [Col. 0890D]. Yet generous affection should retain its place in such matters where equality of virtues is found. Nevertheless, no one should think himself despised if a better person is preferred to him.

Certainly, when the Lord preferred Peter to John, He did not withdraw His affection from the disciple whom He loved while conferring primacy upon Peter. He gave Peter the keys of the kingdom of heaven, so that he might open and shut heaven [Note: [Col. 0889] Matt. 16.]; but to John He revealed the secrets of His breast, to be opened for us. To Peter He entrusted the care and rule of His Church; to John, the care and guardianship of His Mother. Peter, then, was more exalted, but John more secure [Col. 0891A]. Peter is assigned to action, John to affection. To Peter the Lord foretells His own passion, predicting that another would gird him and lead him where he did not wish to go; but of John He says: “Thus I will that he remain until I come” [Note: [Col. 0891] John 21.].

Peter does not dare ask the Lord who would betray Him; but John, at Peter’s signal, confidently asks what the Prince of the Apostles feared to inquire. Therefore let duties among friends be distributed with such modesty and such provident consideration that reason, not affection, governs all; and let it be discerned, according to the capacity of each, what each person can bear or what will benefit him.

Yet equal affection ought not to be bestowed upon everyone, because a definite pattern for loving is prescribed to us according to people’s characters, intercourse, and merits [Col. 0891B]. John was loved more intimately by Christ [Note: [Col. 0891] John 13.], but it may be questioned whether he was loved more fervently. Paul writes of Timothy that he has no one else so closely in his soul; speaking also of Titus, he says: “When I came to Troas, I had no rest in my spirit, because I did not find Titus my brother” [Note: [Col. 0891] 2 Cor. 2.]. And again: “When we came into Macedonia, our flesh had no rest; but God, who consoles the lowly, consoled us by the coming of Titus” [Note: [Col. 0891] 2 Cor. 7.].

Let there therefore be among friends a reasonable mutual exchange, arising from a measured distribution of benefits. Let one be the other’s hand, eye, staff of support, mutual rest of their spirits, and place of refreshment in distress. Finally, let them conduct themselves in friendship so as to deserve to ascend to that love by which Christ is loved with the whole heart [Col. 0891C], and to reap in it the greatest fruit of friendship, when, fear and anxiety removed, they enjoy in full and eternal security the mutual care which they now render one another.

## CHAPTER XXII. On the reverence to be shown between friends, and on their mutual correction.

Moreover, let a friend so reverence the countenance of his friend that he does not offend his ears or eyes by word, gesture, or deed. Modesty is the best companion of friendship and its most precious ornament. Conversely, shamelessness is its ruin, together with the folly of a hardened brow. It often happens that, when the fire of anger conceived in someone’s heart was already breaking forth in public, or when a word of insult had already risen to his throat, the sight of a friend who came upon him calmed the agitation of his boiling mind, and suddenly made serene the disturbed face of his mind by a certain gentleness of expression and venerable authority.

Here also the great power of friendship appears: it has much force in persuasion or dissuasion, since its loyalty is not doubtful and its gentle admonition is not suspected. Therefore openly, freely, and confidently urge upon a friend what is honourable; and, if his welfare requires it, do not fear to rebuke him. But because truth is usually unwelcome, and friendship is sometimes consequently disturbed, according to the comic poet’s saying: “Compliance produces friends; truth produces hatred” [Note: [Col. 0891] Terence, *Andria*], that compliance is certainly blameworthy which makes a friend more indulgent toward vices. Let admonition therefore not be bitter, rebuke not insulting; let honourable and gracious friendliness be present. Let all flattery be far removed, as alien to the character of friendship.

It is a saying of blessed Ambrose [Note: [Col. 0891] Book *On Friendship*, ch. 27, book III; *On Duties*, ch. 16]: “If you discover something faulty in a friend, first correct him privately; if he does not listen to you, correct him openly; but if he thinks himself injured, nevertheless correct him; and if bitter correction wounds his mind, nevertheless correct him. For the wounds of a friend are more tolerable than the kisses of flatterers” [Note: [Col. 0891] Prov. 27].

As the Roman master of eloquence writes, rebukes are sometimes necessary; they must be made with greater force of voice and sharper seriousness of words, [Col. 0892B] so that we may appear angry. Yet, as in cauterizing and cutting, we should come to this kind of chastisement reluctantly and very seldom—especially if no other remedy remains. But anger itself must be far away, since with it nothing can be done thoughtfully or rightly. Let correction, then, be tempered with seriousness and gentleness, so that insult may be excluded, and the rebuked person may recognize himself as the cause of this severity.

In all things, therefore, let the restraint of moderation be observed, lest anyone seem to be satisfying his own anger more than love. For there are those who boil within and cloak and colour the heat of madness with the name of zeal; but those who follow the impulse of their own mind rather than reason scarcely, or never, make progress in correcting others. Therefore, I beg you, let one’s speech in correction be sadder, one’s expression subdued; let sobs and tears interrupt one’s words, so that the person rebuked may feel that all this proceeds from love, not resentment. If perhaps he rejects the first correction, he will accept the second. Meanwhile pray, weep, sigh, and let the voice be broken by groaning. Let a friend act in truth by whatever means he can soften the other’s mind; yet let nothing in word, lamentation, or sobbing be contrived by any simulation.

For simulation and flattery are two most poisonous plagues, which should always be banished far from friendship. It is a saying of the wise man: “The dissembler and the crafty man provoke the anger of God” [Note: [Col. 0891] Job 36]. By “crafty” he means the cunning of the flatterer, as the comic poet expresses it in the *Eunuch*: “Does someone deny? I deny. Does he affirm? I affirm. In short, I have commanded myself to agree with everything” [Note: [Col. 0891] Terence].

It is written through the prophet: “My people, those who call you blessed lead you into error and destroy the way of your steps” [Note: [Col. 0891] Isa. 3]. Likewise, the prophet speaks of flatterers in the person of the unbelieving people: “See empty things for us; speak pleasing things” [Note: [Col. 0891] Isa. 30]. And again: “The prophets prophesied falsehood, and the priests applauded with their hands, and my people loved such things” [Note: [Col. 0891] Jer. 5]. Again Solomon says of the dissembler: “A dissembler deceives his friend with his mouth” [Note: [Col. 0891] Prov. 21], “and in the time of turning away he devises deceit.”

Therefore let the correction of a friend proceed wholly from the marrow of the soul and from deepest compassion, so that one may act for the friend’s amendment as the Prophet desires to be treated himself, saying: “May the righteous man correct me in mercy and rebuke me; but let not the oil of the sinner anoint my head” [Note: [Col. 0893] Ps. 140].

But as simulation and flattery poison the purity of friendship, so dissimulation among friends sometimes produces and nourishes purity of affection. There is, indeed, a dissembling—but prudent—postponement of correction, according to place, time, and person. For if a friend must be rebuked publicly, then, as far as may be done without violating the law of friendship, it is fitting for us to conceal or excuse his fault, seek a suitable time for his correction, and choose familiar privacy. For while the sick mind is still more unsettled by recent disturbance, great concealment is needed until, when the cloud of the mind has cleared, it will more calmly admit the words of one gently warning it.

Certainly, when King David had added treachery and murder to adultery [Note: [Col. 0893] II Sam. 11–12], the prophet Nathan, although intending to rebuke him, nevertheless deferred to royal majesty. He did not suddenly, while David’s mind was disturbed, charge him with the crime of so great a wickedness; but, first employing fitting concealment and proposing an appropriate riddle, he drew from him a judgment against himself.

## Chapter XXIII. How long a friend is to be endured if he persists incorrigibly in some enormous vice

It is often found that some persons, not merely admitted but already established in friendship, suffer from an evil reputation, so that their sins recoil to the loss or disgrace of their friends [Col. 0893C]. Such persons must be treated with salutary warnings. If they show themselves incorrigible, friendship is not to be broken off at once, but gradually unstitched, as a certain wise man elegantly teaches [Note: [Col. 0893] Cicero, *On Friendship*, *Cato*].

Yet this itself admits an exception. Friendship must be broken off if the friend’s crime is so enormous that it cannot be endured without loss of reputation: namely, if he has presumptuously undertaken something damnable against the faith of Christ, against the public good, or the like. Friendship should be unstitched in such a way that one does not rush into quarrels, seditions, or insulting words. For it is dishonourable to wage war against one whom you had as the confidant of your intimacy.

When friendship has been dissolved, let no one heap curses upon friends, whisper in darkness, slander in corners, or falsely excuse himself in order to dishonour others. Finally, when friendship has been ended, this honour must always be shown to the person whom you had regarded as a friend: the blame must lie with the one who inflicts, not the one who suffers, injury.

Therefore let friendship never degenerate from its own permanence. “Whoever is a friend loves always” [Note: [Col. 0893] Prov. 17]. Therefore always love the one who has loved you; and though friendship be withdrawn, let love nevertheless continue. Have regard for his reputation, his welfare, and his peace; never betray the secrets of friendship, even though he himself has betrayed them.

Yet in all these matters walk so cautiously [Col. 0894A] that, in advising him or speaking otherwise, you do not contaminate the good fragrance of your reputation by accusing another. Rather, order the condition of your mind so that no love may prejudice religion, faith, the peace of many, or your own welfare.

King Ahasuerus, although he had admitted proud Haman above the rest to the innermost circle of his familiarity, hanged him on the gallows [Note: [Col. 0893] Esth. 7], preferring fidelity to his marriage and the welfare of the multitude to a friendship which Haman had stained with fraudulent counsels. Jael, the wife of Heber the Kenite, although peace had been established between Sisera and her husband’s house, nevertheless preferred the peace of the people to him and pierced Sisera’s head with peg and hammer [Note: [Col. 0893] Judg. 4]. King David, though by the right of his former friendship he ought to have spared Jonathan’s descendants, nevertheless, hearing that because of Saul and his house, and because of the blood of the Gibeonites whom Saul had killed, the people had been afflicted by the Lord with a most grievous famine for three years, handed over seven men of Saul’s and Jonathan’s kindred to the Gibeonites for punishment [Note: [Col. 0893] II Sam. 21].

## Chapter XXIV. How friendship should be dissolved, and with what moderation

This should be noted in the dissolution of friendship: so far as the person who is truly a friend is concerned, the dissolution of friendship never occurs. For one who is injured does not cease to be a friend to the injurer: he loves one who does not love him, blesses one who curses him, honours one who despises him, and shows himself beneficent to one who plots evil against him.

It is shameful, especially for an orthodox man, to rub up injuries again and revive anew the sleeping ashes of hatreds [Col. 0894C]. It is written in the Law of Moses: “You shall not seek vengeance, nor remember the injury done by your fellow citizens” [Note: [Col. 0893] Lev. 19]. Cicero, writing of Caesar’s praises, says: “He is accustomed to forget nothing except injuries.” And in Ecclesiasticus: “He who seeks vengeance will find vengeance from God” [Note: [Col. 0893] Ecclus. 28]. And the Apostle: “Rendering evil to no one for evil, nor curse for curse” [Note: [Col. 0893] Rom. 12]. In the Gospel [Note: [Col. 0893] Matt. 18] we read that the man who would not show mercy to his servant was handed over to the torturers until he had paid the whole debt.

Therefore let gratitude for former intimacy always remain in memory, and let no later malice ever be able to abolish it.

## Chapter XXV. On the grounds and in the respects in which friendship should be dissolved rather than broken

There are four respects in which the severance of friendship has a place: love, affection, confidence, and pleasant companionship [Col. 0894D]. Love consists in advising, providing for, and conferring benefits on a friend. Affection includes a certain delightful and most sweet enjoyment. Confidence consists in sharing all kinds of secrets without any fear or suspicion. Pleasant companionship, moreover, consists in kindly, familiar, sweet, and gentle conversation about prosperity and adversity, useful and harmful things, and everything by which the human mind is affected.

In these respects friendship suffers a cutting-away; for although love remains in some degree [Col. 0895A], that inward and most sweet affection of love is withdrawn, confidence—by which secrets were disclosed—is lost, and the pleasantness once made serene by gentle conversation is disturbed. Love therefore remains [Col. 0896A], but the favour of intimacy is removed; nevertheless, some reverence must always be shown to the traces of former friendship, unless the enormity of the offence abolishes it.

# Treatise II. On the Charity of God and of One’s Neighbour

[Col. 0895]

## Chapter I. That charity is the most excellent of all virtues

[Col. 0895B]

As the preceding matters have taught, true friendship does not exist unless it has its foundation in God. Therefore, since friendship is a gift of God, it is right that whoever loves from God’s gift should love nothing apart from God, or except for God’s sake; so that the rivers may flow back to the place from which they flow, lest the stream that issues from the fullness of overflowing grace degenerate from its source.

For we profess that friendship to be uniquely, singularly, truly, and supremely real, by which God has deigned to call us his friends, if we do his commandments. “You are my friends,” he says, “if you do what I command you” [Note: [Col. 0895] John 15]. This is the friendship and charity of God, by which he loved us before the foundation of the world and chose us in [Col. 0895C] his beloved Son [Note: [Col. 0895] Eph. 1].

It is the source of all good things that come to us from heavenly munificence. From it every lawful love receives its order and form; nor can any affection of the mind be ordered unless it derives from this charity its cause, measure, and order. Of this most orderly charity, Wisdom says in the book bearing her name: “From eternity I was ordained” [Note: [Col. 0895] Prov. 8]. Ordained by God, this charity orders angels in their ministries. It orders the pursuits and exercises of the righteous in their vocations; through it the law was ordained through angels by the hand of the mediator.

Without it friendship among human beings cannot be ordered. For since the Apostle says, “Let all things be done among you according to order” [Note: [Col. 0895] I Cor. 14], and again, “Let all your things be done in charity” [Note: [Col. 0895] I Cor. 16], it is clear that things done outside charity have no order.

Charity is the way and life of the virtues. It is the more excellent way, and the path upon which the saving help of God is shown. Hence the Apostle says in the First Epistle to the Corinthians: “I show you a still more excellent way” [Note: [Col. 0895] I Cor. 12]. And again: “To know also the charity of God that surpasses knowledge” [Note: [Col. 0895] Eph. 3]. This is the way of which Isaiah said: “Those whom the Lord has freed and redeemed shall walk on this way, and shall come to Zion with praise; sorrow and groaning shall flee; everlasting gladness shall be upon their heads; they shall obtain joy and gladness” [Note: [Col. 0895] Isa. 35].

Charity is the Lord’s clear commandment, enlightening the eyes [Note: [Col. 0895] Ps. 18]. For it is the light of the heart, clarifying and making serene all a person’s senses and affections, so that one may learn and [Col. 0896B] know where the light of the eyes and peace are. Charity is oil, which floats above every liquid, heals, illuminates, and softens every harshness by its own sweetness. Anointed with this oil, the apostles and martyrs considered the bitterness of death and the savagery of dreadful torments most sweet. For Christ, anointed by God with this oil above his companions, anoints his own with it [Note: [Col. 0895] Heb. 1], and makes the yoke of the oppressor decay before the oil. “The Spirit of the Lord,” he says, “is upon me, because he has anointed me.”

Charity not only sweetens the bitterness of death and punishments, but by its most powerful virtue destroys death itself. Was not Christ’s charity the destroyer of death, when he himself, the leader of life and destroyer of death, threatened and said: “I will be your death, O death” [Note: [Col. 0895] Hos. 13]? For love is strong as death [Note: [Col. 0895] Song 8], indeed stronger than death. For death takes away temporal life; charity introduces us to eternal life. Death cast us down from transitory life; charity restores us to life and glory without end.

Charity is the Beautiful Gate, which, at the destruction of Jerusalem, remained whole and untouched when all the other gates had been completely destroyed. “Charity never fails” [Note: [Col. 0895] I Cor. 13]. This is the most beautiful Shunammite woman, who warmed David in his virginity, because he could not be warmed by the skins of dead animals [Note: [Col. 0895] III Kings 1]. For those who dwell in dead works, when charity has grown cold, are warmed again by contemplating Christ’s Passion.

This is the little cloud which, at Elijah’s prayers, grew into great rain [Note: [Col. 0895] III Kings 18]. When someone begins to love God with his whole heart, he immediately pours out not only upon neighbours but even upon enemies the drops of goodwill and streams of grace [Col. 0896D].

Certainly charity is the widow’s oil, which receives continual increase through its distribution. The woman—the wife of one of the prophets, Obadiah’s wife—cried to Elisha, saying: “My husband has died, and behold, the creditors are taking my two sons to serve them” [Note: [Col. 0895] IV Kings 4]. At the prophet’s word she filled vessels with the oil with which she was to be anointed. The sons are fear and love, who bring not a few vessels, into which their mother, grace, pours the oil of goodwill and devotion; yet she closes the door of conscience against the favour of human praise, lest she be counted among the foolish virgins without oil.

The creditors are the most importunate exacters, evil spirits, who demand eternal punishments in return for transitory pleasure [Col. 0897A]. The neighbours, from whom vessels are borrowed, are the angelic powers and the souls of the saints, who teach us by their counsels and examples to pour the oil of mercy upon our neighbours. and we know that, so long as vessels of this kind remain, the oil will not stop, and charity bestowed on more people will receive a more abundant increase.

The tongues of angels, the tongues of men, support of the poor, and martyrdom are nothing without charity; prophecy foretells, knowledge comprehends, faith believes. But neither prophecy, nor knowledge, nor faith—even if it moves mountains—has any value without charity; without charity it can profit nothing [Note: [Col. 0897] I Cor. 13], while with charity nothing can harm. When charity’s benefit intervenes, sins do no harm: charity covers a multitude of sins [Note: [Col. 0897] Jas. 3].

Charity is the law of life, the discipline of morals, the peace of those living together, the glory of those in concord, the abolition of crimes, the fulfillment of the law, the compendium of sacred Scripture, the completion of God’s commandments, the virtue of virtues, and the perfection of good merits. All commandments of life and all works of righteousness are referred to it. From it the commendation of works and devout prayers receive their efficacy; and from it, as fruit from a tree and a branch from a vine, hang the whole law and the prophets. For as fruit receives its nourishment from the shoot until it comes to maturity, so the fruit of good work, holy devotion, and everything piously done receives from charity its beginning and progress [Col. 0897C].

## Chapter II. That charity is the fulfillment and life of faith

In order that what charity is may be understood more clearly and effectively by a definite definition, let us hear how the Apostle defines or describes it. Writing to Timothy, he says: “The end of the commandment is charity from a pure heart, a good conscience, and unfeigned faith” [Note: [Col. 0897] I Tim. 1].

A commandment is called law, and human life is formed by its precepts. There is a positive law: namely, the law of Moses and of earthly rulers. Of this the Apostle Paul says: “The law is not laid down for the righteous, but for the unrighteous” [Note: [Col. 0897] ibid.]. And there is another law, which the Psalmist asks for when he says: “Set before me a law, O Lord, the way of your justifications” [Note: [Col. 0897] Ps. 118]. The latter law is spiritual; the former, carnal. One who professes the latter fears nothing before rulers or among swords; the former terrifies the unjust and evil-doers. The former is established for the unrighteous, whom it commands not to kill; the latter is not established for the righteous, because the law of rulers finds nothing in righteous people to punish.

Hear what the Apostle says: “Do you wish not to fear authority? Do good, and you will have praise from it” [Note: [Col. 0897] Rom. 13]. And he adds: “But if you do evil, fear” [Note: [Col. 0897] ibid.]. Charity from a pure heart exempts the righteous from this fear. Therefore it is the end of that law which inspires fear; and hence it is also the end of death. Charity is likewise the end of the law established for the righteous [Col. 0898A], since it is the completion of good works and abolition of evil works. Thus it is the end of both laws: of the law of evils, which it abolishes, and of the other law, which it fulfills.

Certainly their end is feigned, of whom it is said: “They loved him with their mouth, and lied to him with their tongue” [Note: [Col. 0897] Ps. 77]. Warning us against this evil, the Apostle John says: “Do not love in word or tongue, but in deed and truth” [Note: [Col. 0897] I John 3]. Truth in deed is action with a right intention; truth in the mouth is simplicity in speech. And just as a pure heart does not dissemble, so a pure intention does not err. Where there is neither error nor simulation nor pretence, there is pure and simple intention, and charity rests in it.

But feigning of faith is banished far from charity. The faith of those is called feigned [Col. 0898B] who devise from their own heart the form of their faith and do not hesitate to oppose sound doctrine. A certain wise man also calls feigned faith *fictilis*, “earthenware,” because, like a fragile clay vessel, it quickly departs from truth in the time of temptation.

It is written in praise and commendation of charity: “If a man gives the substance of his house for love, he will despise it as though it were nothing” [Note: [Col. 0897] Song 8]. The Apostle Peter invites us to it thus: “Before all things, have mutual charity among yourselves” [Note: [Col. 0897] I Pet. 4]. And Paul: “Above all these things, have charity” [Note: [Col. 0897] Col. 3]. And again: “Pursue charity” [Note: [Col. 0897] I Cor. 14]. And again: “Be zealous for the better gifts” [Note: [Col. 0897] I Cor. 12]—meaning charity, for whose sake he says that he reckoned all things which he had regarded as gains to be loss, and counted them as dung, that he might gain Christ [Note: [Col. 0897] Phil. 3].

Paul, firmly established in the charity that is the end of the commandment, from a pure heart and unfeigned faith [Note: [Col. 0897] I Tim. 1], says: “Who shall separate us from the charity of Christ? Tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or the sword? I am certain that neither death nor life, neither angels nor powers nor principalities, neither height nor depth, neither things present nor things to come, nor any creature, will be able to separate us from the charity of God which is in Christ Jesus” [Note: [Col. 0897] Rom. 8].

Truly charity from a pure heart and unfeigned faith burned in Paul like a sparkling fire. Thus his fiery speech still does not cease to set many ablaze. Charity itself says through this faith that Christ dwells in us; and while Christ lives in us, he lives through faith [Col. 0898D]. The righteous person, moreover, is said to live through this faith, as is proved by the testimony of the prophet Habakkuk and the Apostle Paul, who plainly declare that “the righteous lives by faith” [Note: [Col. 0897] Rom. 1; Hab. 2].

The faith by which, or through which, we must live must certainly be living faith. It should therefore be noted that, as we recognize the life of the body by motion, so we establish the life of faith by good works. That faith lives which works through love. Charity, then, is the life of faith; when it grows cold, faith dies, just as the body dies when the spirit departs. But it is the Spirit of God, [Col. 0899A] through whom charity is poured out into our hearts [Note: [Col. 0899] Rom. 5]. Yet there are those who, having begun in the Spirit, are completed in the flesh; and to them applies the saying: “My Spirit shall not remain in man forever, because he is flesh” [Note: [Col. 0899] Gen. 6].

## Chapter III. How God, who is charity, should be conceived

It must be known that, by as much as earth lies beneath the height of heaven, so much more excellent, sublime, and inestimably sweeter is the love of God than love of one’s neighbour. And so that, as we speak of the love of God, the field of our intended theme may open itself more desirably and freely to understanding, we shall touch briefly upon a few matters concerning God, as though tasting them, so that it may appear with what ineffable grace and incomparable condescension the God of glory stoops down to humanity through the benefit of charity [Col. 0899B].

God, I say, must be believed and conceived as living in himself with a certain perpetual life and giving life to all things; immutable, and making all changeable things unchangeably; understanding all things and creating every intelligence. He is wise, and Wisdom itself; fixed Truth; unbending Justice; highest Power; perfect Goodness; divinity, eternity, greatness, immensity, highest essence—from which comes all being—supreme and eternal substance, not subject to the categories of words or things conceivable, but the causal, efficient, and superessential principle of all things.

God must be conceived as simple, pure, whole, and perfect: possessing nothing subject to number; deriving nothing from time or place; yet in every place, without being enclosed or excluded by place. God must be conceived without visible form, without bodily spirit, without composition of parts, without distinction of members; from whom all things are caused, not materially; in whom all things exist not in place but in power; good without quality, great without quantity, presiding without position, containing and disposing all things without a habit or external condition.

For he disposes as Wisdom, works as Power, loves as Charity, reveals as Light, has mercy as Piety, knows as Truth, sees as Equity, and presides as Majesty. You do not comprehend his greatness unless you become little in your own eyes, submitting yourself to every human creature for his sake.

“God is charity” [Note: [Col. 0899] I John 4]; yet the Spirit is especially signified by the name of charity. For he is the love of Father and Son, their sweetness, unity, kiss, embrace, and whatever can be common to both. When, through the grace of the Holy Spirit, the human soul is wonderfully and miraculously united to God, one must know that this same Spirit is both giver and gift in that union. Hence the Apostle Paul includes the Holy Spirit in his catalogue of God’s ministries, saying: “In chastity, in knowledge, in long-suffering, in kindness, in the Holy Spirit, in unfeigned charity, in the word of truth, in the power of God” [Note: [Col. 0899] II Cor. 6].

He places the Holy Spirit in the middle as the maker who forms all affections into good will toward God, directs [Col. 0900A] actions, and disposes all things strongly and all things sweetly [Note: [Col. 0899] Wis. 8]. For it is the Spirit who gives life to the human spirit and teaches and forms it to love God, seek him and find him, hold him and enjoy him. He is the concern of those who seek God in humility, the piety of one exhorting in spirit and truth. He is the wisdom of the one who finds, the love of the one who possesses, and the joy of the one who fully enjoys.

## Chapter IV. That covetous desire causes human beings to err in many ways from the true good that is in charity

Some choose for their own enjoyment things destructive of salvation. For, infected with the poison of covetous desire and swallowed up by the evil of this world—that is, deceptive riches, transitory honours, pleasures of the flesh, and worldly favour—they set the end of their intention in such things and, as if dreaming, paint their happiness in false imagination in what is an occasion of eternal condemnation.

In order to reach the goal of their intention, they choose the losses of various paths; and behold, made mad by the many deceits of covetous desire, they proceed toward the end they desire through detours and winding ways. One aims at the prize of his course through military service; another through trade; another through practicing some craft; another through thefts or robberies. But what each person especially loves is that to which the whole of his intention is finally directed. The rest—military service, trade, and the like—are merely aids through which one tries to obtain what he has chosen to enjoy.

Meanwhile the deceived mind, which uselessly foretold for itself an image of happiness, when after obtaining the desired thing it feels itself oppressed by still greater need, begins to loathe what it had preferred and is again kindled with desire for another thing—yet never to be satisfied, but to be deceived by the image of another false happiness [Col. 0900C]. This is the circuit of the wicked. This is the reproach of the many who dwell in a circuit. This is Samson’s mill [Note: [Col. 0899] Judg. 16], which the ensuing circuit of covetous desire turns round after the hair of virtues has been cut off and the eyes of prudence gouged out, the short path of charity having been abandoned. “The head of the circle around them: the labour of their lips shall cover them” [Note: [Col. 0899] Ps. 139].

A person is not satisfied by this labour, unless perhaps that satiation is brought about by the husks of swine [Note: [Col. 0899] Luke 15] which does not allow the rich man to sleep. For where abundance of riches overflows more greatly, there the heavier trouble of cares, disturbing all repose, intrudes itself [Col. 0900D].

The rational soul, then, although it longs eagerly for the highest blessedness, is drawn away by other things; an image of false happiness deceives it, or a likeness of real misery frightens it. For who would not reckon poverty, persecution, and sickness a great share of misery? Yet through these both true misery is avoided and true blessedness obtained. Certainly poverty acquires the kingdom of heaven: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven. Blessed are those who mourn, [Col. 0901A] hunger, and endure persecution, for they shall be filled” [Note: [Col. 0901] Matt. 5]; those shall receive consolation, while these have already obtained the heavenly kingdom, not merely to possess it for themselves but to confer it also upon others.

## Chapter V. How great are the evils in riches

To give, by way of example, some account of the shadowy and destructive happiness of temporal riches and delights, and to make clear that it is altogether alien to the blessedness that comes from charity, consider first how great a throng of troubles surrounds money. Money is acquired with labour, kept with fear once acquired, and finally lost with grief. From money’s increase one may estimate the growth of misery; for, like a dropsical person who thirsts more the more he drinks, the covetous desire for money grows through multiplication [Col. 0901B].

At first one fears a powerful person lest he take it away, a servant lest he steal it secretly. And the saying of the wise man is frequently fulfilled: riches are kept to the harm of their owner [Note: [Col. 0901] Eccl. 5]. Therefore it is better to be poor, because one neither fears the powerful nor dreads a traitor or thief. The poor man sings; the rich man weeps. For, according to the critic:

> Money lost is mourned with genuine tears.  
> [Note: [Col. 0901] Juvenal, *Satires* 13.]

Nothing is lacking to the poor person for whom Christ suffices. But the rich person, the more he possesses, the more he needs; nor does he ever find in riches the abundance he seeks. Solomon’s saying is: “The miser will not be satisfied with money, and he who loves riches will not obtain fruit from them” [Note: [Col. 0901] Eccl. 5].

It is carefully said, “he who loves riches”; for a person may so love riches that there is no circumstance in which, if they abound, he would not set his heart upon them. Therefore the Apostle commands that the rich be taught not to think proudly, not to hope in the increase of riches, but to give readily and share, and to store up for themselves a good foundation, that they may lay hold of true life. For he testifies: “Not those who are rich, but those who wish to be rich, fall into temptation and the snare of the devil” [Note: [Col. 0901] I Tim. 6], and store up wrath for themselves on the day of wrath.

Indicating this, Habakkuk says: “Woe to him who gathers what is not his! How long? And who heaps up thick mud against himself?” [Note: [Col. 0901] Hab. 2]. Even amid riches, the saints are troubled neither by anxiety in keeping them nor by fear of losing them.

For the Lord forbids this anxiety, saying: “Do not be anxious, saying, ‘What shall we eat [Col. 0901D] or what shall we drink?’” [Note: [Col. 0901] Matt. 6]. And shortly afterward: “Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things shall be added to you” [Note: [Col. 0901] ibid.]. As such persons never glory in riches, so neither do they grumble at their loss; indeed, they receive the plundering of their goods with joy, knowing that they possess a better and enduring substance.

For the perverse, finally, everything turns to the opposite. Since they suppose that the appetite of the rational soul, which God alone can satisfy, can be sated by the cheap abundance of worldly things, they make no progress by however great an accumulation of things; they do not remove their thirst, unhappy as they are; they do not rest from labour; and, what is more miserable, they swell with vain delight in such things [Col. 0902A]. I speak of those whose “glory is in their shame” and “whose end is destruction” [Note: [Col. 0901] Phil. 3], whose life is continual labour and whose outcome is misery without end. Thus, deceived by the trifling and deceptive happiness of temporal riches, they turn the fruit of their past life into material for tears.

## Chapter VI. The lamentable complaint of those who depart from charity through covetous desire

Sacred Scripture plainly expresses and describes the misery of such persons:

> “They say within themselves, repenting and groaning in anguish of spirit: ‘We are wearied in the way of iniquity and destruction; we have walked difficult paths, but the way of the Lord [Col. 0902B] we have not known. What has pride profited us, and what has boasting of riches brought us? All things have passed away like a shadow, and like a messenger running ahead; like a ship passing through the surging waters, whose track cannot be found after it has passed. So we, having been born, immediately ceased to be; we were unable to show any sign of virtue, but were consumed in our wickedness.’ Thus spoke in hell those who sinned, because the hope of the ungodly is like down carried away by the wind; like thin foam scattered by a storm; like smoke dispersed by the wind; and like the memory of a guest who passes by for one day.”  
> [Note: [Col. 0901] Wis. 5.]

## Chapter VII. How many evils are in the pleasure of the flesh
[Col. 0902C] The book of experience continually teaches how deceitful and delusive is that destructive happiness which most people locate in fleshly pleasure: in the work of unchastity, what delights passes quickly, while what torments remains without end. From the act of impurity nothing remains but the foul and fetid recollection of sin, for the torment of the soul and the expectation of hell. Therefore I judge that such persons should rather be lamented than discussed. We see those who were created in God’s image degenerating into bestial impulses and brutish drives, seeking what belongs to the belly and beneath the belly, and shamelessly giving themselves over to unchastity, without heeding the fearful judgments of God that hang over them. For what is more unworthy than to subject one’s soul, for which Christ died, to the baser part of one’s body [Col. 0902D] and to make oneself like irrational beasts?

Moreover, this pleasure is attended by many pains. First, the power of sight is blinded in the person who exceeds the natural limits of its capacity. Thus habitual indulgence in this vice, and frequent indulgence in any pleasures whatever, seems to bring not only peril to the soul but destruction also to the body. Therefore nothing is more foul, more restless, or further removed from natural tranquillity than these pleasures. This most sordid pestilence pollutes the flesh and makes the mind effeminate. Whatever is honourable and manly in a human being, it wholly overwhelms and enfeebles.

And whereas other vices [Col. 0903A] cloak themselves in certain coverings of virtues, and often swell with a self-exalting boastfulness before human eyes, the mind conscious of this shamefulness displays, at the very outset, such horror at its own deed that not only at the hour when its flesh is seized by destructive pleasure, but even when it hears others speaking of its shamefulness, it is suffused with blushes, seeks seclusion, and is tormented by the recollection of its unclean deed. Therefore it always seeks hiding places, and because it does evil, it hates the light. Yet, hidden in secret places, it will not be able to escape the fearful Judge who sees the secrets not only of bodies but also of hearts.

Nor should it pass in silence that the Creator of all condemned the generative members with such shamefulness that paternal [Col. 0903B] cursing and perpetual servitude were inflicted upon him who scorned reverently to cover them in his father. [Note: [Col. 0903] Gen. 9.] Certainly, when today the cross of Christ triumphs everywhere, the most powerful conqueror of lust, it is utterly absurd that very many professed sons of the Blessed Virgin rot like beasts in their own dung. [Note: [Col. 0903] Joel 1.] They drink the urine of their sins, wallow in their abominations, and until they experience God’s sudden wrath, they neither consider nor fear the fire already kindled in his fury.

Moreover, before the sinner is caught in his own desires, let the wretched man understand that the impurity of the flesh—in which he dreamed his blessedness lay—has been inflicted by God upon some as a most grievous punishment, since he wills them to be punished in this [Col. 0903C] way: that he has abandoned them to their own pleasure. For these are the words of the Lord in the Psalmist: “But my people did not hear my voice, and Israel gave no heed to me.
