So I gave them up according to the desire of their heart; they shall walk in their own devices.” [Note: [Col. 0903] Ps. 80.] The Apostle also, speaking fearfully of those who exchanged the glory of God for the worship of idolatry, says: “God gave them over to the desires of their hearts, to impurity, so that they might dishonour their bodies among themselves.” [Note: [Col. 0903] Rom. 1.] This is not because God incites evil, but because, abandoned by grace, they experience assaults sent through evil angels.

Concerning incestuous persons and those whose sins God bodily condemned at Sodom by fire and sulphur [Note: [Col. 0903] Gen. 19.], so that the abomination of iniquity might be made known from the stench and horror of the punishment, it is proper to pass over the matter in silence, lest [Col. 0903D] abhorrent speech disgrace this present little work, in which we are treating of charity, the soul’s inward rest. From what has been said it is most clearly evident how destructive is the love of flesh and lusts. In detestation of these, God said to the angels who execute judgment concerning the scarlet-clad harlot: “As much as she glorified herself in delights, give her so much torment and mourning.” [Note: [Col. 0903] Apoc. 18.]

## CHAPTER VIII. Solomon shows how great is the vanity of this world.

It remains to pursue the point that blessedness or rest lies neither in the pleasure of the eyes [Col. 0904A] or ears and of the other senses, nor in the ambitious honour or dominion of power belonging to the luxuries of this life. Let then the richest, most powerful, most pleasure-loving, and yet wisest king come forward—Solomon, that is—and let us see what judgment he makes about the end of such things.

“I said in my heart: I will go and abound in delights, and enjoy good things.” [Note: [Col. 0903] Eccl. 2.] And below: “I built houses and planted vineyards; I made gardens and orchards, and planted them with trees of every kind.” [Note: [Col. 0903] Ibid.] Continuing, he added many similar things: “I possessed male and female servants, and a very great household; I amassed for myself silver and gold, the wealth of kings and provinces.” [Note: [Col. 0903] Ibid.] And, adding the pleasure of hearing: “I acquired for myself male and female singers.” [Note: [Col. 0903] Ibid.] Shortly afterwards he adds: “Whatever [Col. 0904B] my eyes desired, I did not deny them; nor did I prevent my heart from enjoying every pleasure and delighting itself in the things I had prepared for myself.” [Note: [Col. 0903] Ibid.]

What, I ask, could be more luxurious or more pleasant? Yet observe that nothing is emptier, nothing more changeable. Solomon continues and adds: “When I turned,” he says, “to all my works in which I had laboured in vain, I saw vanity and affliction of spirit in them all, and that nothing endures under the sun.” [Note: [Col. 0903] Ibid.] He had first set forth the general judgment, saying: “I saw all things done under the sun, and behold, all is vanity and affliction of spirit.” [Note: [Col. 0903] Ibid.]

## CHAPTER IX. Rest and peace are in charity alone.

From Solomon’s words you have vanity and affliction of spirit. Truth adds a third thing: namely, slavery. [Col. 0904C] “Everyone,” he says, “who commits sin is the slave of sin.” [Note: [Col. 0903] John 8.] Let these three, therefore, be joined together: vanity, slavery, and affliction of spirit. [Note: [Col. 0903] Eccl. 2.] Where rest is, there is Sabbath. Is this not the word of the Law: “You shall do no servile work on it”? [Note: [Col. 0903] Lev. 32.] Who is there that has not sinned? Who then is not the slave of sin? King David says: “Behold, I was conceived in iniquities, and in sins my mother conceived me.” [Note: [Col. 0903] Ps. 50.] John says: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us.” [Note: [Col. 0903] 1 John 1.]

Who then will free us from the old yoke and slavery of sin? He of whom Truth says in the Gospel: “If the Son sets you free, you shall truly be free.” [Note: [Col. 0903] John 8.] He himself invites us to the Sabbath: “Come to me,” he says, “all you who labour and are burdened, and I will refresh you.” [Note: [Col. 0903] Matt. 11.] Behold refreshment, [Col. 0904D] as it were the preparation for Sabbath. Let us hear also the Sabbath: “Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, because I am meek and humble of heart; and you will find rest for your souls.” [Note: [Col. 0903] Ibid.] Behold the Sabbath; behold quiet tranquillity. “For my yoke is sweet, and my burden light.” [Note: [Col. 0903] Ibid.]

This yoke does not press down, but lifts up. It has wings by which it raises one up, not wings by which it weighs anyone down. That yoke is charity: love of God and of neighbour. Here one rests; here one keeps Sabbath; here one is free from every servile work. For charity “does not act unbecomingly” and “does not think evil”; [Note: [Col. 0903] 1 Cor. 13.] moreover, the love [Col. 0905A] of one’s neighbour “does not work evil.” You see, O Jew, where Sabbath is. Even if some stealthy incursion of sin occurs there from weakness, still the Sabbath observance is not lost, because “charity covers a multitude of sins.” [Note: [Col. 0905] Jas. 5.]

## CHAPTER X. Worldly desire is why the Lord’s yoke seems burdensome.

Yet we see some who, though they ought to breathe freely beneath so sweet and light a yoke and burden, labour and murmur under both. Addicted and accustomed to Babylonian slavery, they cannot unlearn the vice of ingrained habit; therefore they do not understand that this arises from their own sickness, but suppose it comes from the Lord’s yoke or burden.

Let all who complain about the Lord’s yoke or burden while wearing a religious habit know [Col. 0905B] that they submit the shoulders of their minds to the pressure of worldly affairs, and attribute to the Lord’s yoke their impatience with the labours they endure for the world. These are like unclean dogs returning to their own vomit; [Note: [Col. 0905] 2 Pet. 2.] under the guise of abstinence they serve their belly; beneath penitential haircloth they seek worldly glory; under the sacred garb of chastity and purity they campaign; beneath sheep’s fleece they conceal a wolf; and, burning with insatiable greed, they join house to house and field to field. They arm themselves for lawsuits and disputes; they spare neither poor person, widow, nor orphan; nor are they moved by Joseph’s affliction.

It belongs, indeed, to the yoke of the world that they boil with anxieties, burn with hatreds, and are tortured by envy; this is the yoke [Col. 0905C] of cupidity and the heavy burden of the age. For the Lord’s yoke is sweet and his burden light. [Note: [Col. 0905] Matt. 11.]

And, I ask, what is sweeter or more delightful for a human being than to despise the world and count oneself higher than the world; standing upon the summit of a good and secure conscience, to have the world beneath one’s feet; to see in it nothing to desire, no one to envy or fear; to find no evil that another can inflict upon oneself and no good that another can take away; and, fixing one’s eyes upon the incorruptible, undefiled, and unfading inheritance reserved in heaven, to trample deceptive riches, destructive honours, and condemnable luxuries underfoot?

What, I ask, is more desirable or more tranquil than to establish one’s soul so firmly [Col. 0905D] that it is shaken by no movements of fleshly desire, feels no extraordinary incentives of appetite, recoils from seductive sights, and compels the flesh, made gentle by the dew of chastity, to serve the spirit; so that it has the flesh no longer as a most ready helper enticing it toward fleshly allurements, but toward the exercise of spiritual warfare?

Further, what bears the image of divine tranquillity so fully as the soul which so fortifies itself for the endurance of all injuries that insults offered to it do not move it, no devices of threats or injuries cast its mind down from its condition, and it preserves the same constancy in prosperity and adversity, looking upon friend and enemy with the same eye? Is it not like [Col. 0906A] him who “makes his sun rise upon the good and evil, and rains upon the just and unjust,” [Note: [Col. 0905] Matt. 5.] and draws and embraces all in the net of charity in Christ? Although these things happen around it in changeable ways, there is nevertheless no change of heart in it.

## CHAPTER XI. All virtues are from charity.

Truly, in charity is Sabbath. Since the other virtues serve as a vehicle or provisions for obtaining rest, all rest in charity. Indeed, this is worthy of admiration: without charity no virtue is anything, and charity itself makes each virtue to be a virtue.

Faith, which here works unto life, will no longer be faith in the vision of God, but truth. For faith will be swallowed up when that which is loved above all things is seen. Nor will it be necessary to believe what we shall be allowed to grasp with full knowledge. Neither will hope henceforth have a place there, where, burning with love for God, we shall have nothing further to hope for. Here temperance fights against lusts, prudence against errors, fortitude against adversities, justice against inequalities. But in charity there is always perfect chastity; therefore there is no lust there for temperance to oppose. In charity is perfect knowledge; therefore there is no error for prudence to remove. In charity is true blessedness; therefore there is no adversity for fortitude to overcome. In charity all things are tranquil and equal; therefore there is no inequality there requiring correction.

Finally, faith is not a virtue unless it works through love. [Col. 0906C] Nor is hope a virtue unless what is hoped for is loved. Again, if you wish to assess the nature of the virtues more precisely, what is temperance except love which no pleasure entices? What is prudence except love which error does not deceive? What is fortitude except love which yields to no adversity? And finally, what is justice except love which distributes to each person what is his own?

## CHAPTER XII. Charity is Sabbath, and the six virtues are like six days before Sabbath.

Just as charity is the true rest of the human mind and the perfect Sabbath, so also the six virtues mentioned above—faith, hope, temperance, prudence, fortitude, and justice—are like certain days of work. Charity, however, is a certain most radiant day [Col. 0906D] of rest, tranquillity, and peace.

“And now, what is my expectation, unless it is you, Lord?” If perhaps your ear hears the desire of the poor, may I rest for a little while with kings and consuls, who build solitary places for themselves and fill their houses with silver? Yet scarcely for a moment am I permitted rest from Pharaoh’s taskmasters. Nevertheless, let me keep Sabbath even for half an hour. Would that I might be granted leisure to be still and know that Jesus Christ is God: he is the Sabbath of the soul that seeks him, preparing for those who love him a tranquil and unchangeable Sabbath-rest.

O how blessed are those who enter the place of the wonderful tabernacle, even to the house of God, [Col. 0907A] and dance and exult with the sound of rejoicing and praise, mindful of your words, Jesus, and singing with the prophet Habakkuk: “But I will rejoice in the Lord, and exult in God, my Jesus.” [Note: [Col. 0907] Hab. 3.]

The Jew keeps Sabbath because he reads that God worked for six days and, as though wearied by the labour of work, rested on the seventh day. [Note: [Col. 0907] Gen. 2.] Certainly the Creator did not labour in creating, but spoke, and all things were made according to his good pleasure; he commanded, and all things were created. God, supreme and eternal being, needing nothing and fully sufficient to himself, remaining unbendingly and unchangeably in his most tranquil charity while making mutable things, rests alive in himself: the peace and unfailing rest of the blessed.

Therefore, just as the mutability of creation is signified by mornings and evenings alternating in the succession of days, [Col. 0907B] so in God—to whom nothing comes, nothing passes away, and nothing succeeds—his eternal tranquillity and peaceful eternity are indicated.

It should be noted that the number six is assigned to God’s works, and the number seven to divine rest. For six is a perfect number, consisting of its own parts. If you join one, two, and three, you have the perfect number six, which is especially assigned to God’s works, so that in the totality of these works you find nothing superfluous and nothing imperfect.

Great indeed is the excellence of the day on which the first light shone forth at God’s command; nor is the day of mediocre prerogative on which God divided the upper waters from the lower by means of the firmament. Nor do I judge inferior in dignity the day [Col. 0907C] on which, the waters having been gathered into one place, the dry land was clothed by God with herbs, adorned with trees, beautified with flowers, and made fruitful with fruits. [Note: [Col. 0907] Gen. 1 passim.] Nor should that day be deemed inferior on which God adorned heaven with its luminaries and arranged the course of the entire year according to the succession of times and the cycles of the signs. But neither is that day devoid of praise on which God placed one portion of living creatures in the waters and another in the air. The sixth day does not fall away from the eminence and privilege of these days, for on it God fashioned man in his own image and, breathing life into him, set him over the whole multitude of living creatures.

But the pre-eminence of the seventh day surpasses them all. On it is commended no creation of any thing, but the perfection of all creatures and the rest of the day. Of each individual day it is written: “There was evening and there was morning, one day,” or “a second day,” and so forth. [Note: [Col. 0907] Ibid.] But to the seventh day neither morning nor evening, neither beginning nor end, is assigned. For the day of Christ’s rest is immutable and eternal.

For the mutual love of Father and Son—their sweetest embrace, that is, the charity of both, by which the Father is in the Son and the Son in the Father—is itself their most delightful rest, indivisible unity, undisturbed peace, eternal tranquillity: the Holy Spirit, who proceeds from both. Indicating this, the Son of God says: “I have kept my Father’s commandments, and I abide in his love.” [Note: [Col. 0907] John 15.] And again: “I and the Father are one.” [Col. 0908A] [Note: [Col. 0907] John 10.] And the Father says of the Son: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.” [Note: [Col. 0907] Matt. 3.]

## CHAPTER XIII. Comparison of the six virtues with the six days.

Having thus presented the image of an apt comparison, as we labour during six days, so we exercise ourselves in six virtues in works of pious intention, so that after the alternations of holy actions we may breathe freely in the tranquillity of charity, as in the mind’s true Sabbath.

Therefore, let us place faith on the first day, on which believers are separated from unbelievers as light from darkness. Let hope also hold the place of the second day, by which those “whose citizenship is in heaven” [Note: [Col. 0907] Phil. 3.] are distinguished from others who savour earthly things and, melting within themselves, sink and dissolve away. Let temperance shine forth as the third day, [Col. 0908B] on which, mortifying our members upon earth, we restrain the flux of fleshly desire—like most bitter waters—within the fixed bounds of continence, so that the earth of our heart may appear and, thirsting for the fountain of life, bring forth the flowers and fruits of virtues.

Let prudence, as the fourth day, cause the light of knowledge to break forth, so that, discerning between things to be done and not to be done, it may divide day from night, and the light of wisdom may shine like the brilliance of the sun. Yet the light of spiritual knowledge increases in some and decreases in others, as the lesser light of the moon appears. The example of the Fathers who went before also distinguishes, like stars, among days, years, and months: namely, what difference exists between those who advanced before the Law, [Col. 0908C] those under the Law, and those under grace; and under what understanding the ceremonies, commandments, judgments, and promises serve our salvation.

Let fortitude be the fifth day, by which in this great and spacious sea we may endure, like spiritual fishes, the stormy surges of waves; restrain the slipperiness of the tongue under the discipline of silence; and, like winged birds, now rise to heavenly things, and now, stooping to works of mercy, render the fruits of good works beneath God’s blessing.

Finally, let justice be established as the sixth day, by which, renewed according to the divine image and ruling over beastly desires and creeping vices, we subject body to spirit and spirit to God, and thus give to each what is its own. And it should be noted [Col. 0908D] that the Lord blesses not beasts, cattle, or creeping things, but human beings, birds, and fishes; and cattle and beasts are subjected to man. For to those who bear God’s image in themselves are subjected cattle—that is, our bodies—and beasts—that is, spiritual wickednesses, concerning which the Prophet prays: “Do not hand over to the beasts the souls of those who confess you.” [Note: [Col. 0907] Ps. 73.] And the Lord says through another prophet: “I will take away evil beasts from your land, and I will make you sleep in confidence.” [Note: [Col. 0907] Lev. 26.] This sleep is the most tranquil day of the seventh day.

For the seventh day is charity: the day of Sabbath, the day of rest, [Col. 0909A] gladness, and peace, through which a man says in fullest security: “In peace, in the selfsame place, I will sleep and rest.” [Note: [Col. 0909] Ps. 4.] It is the consummation of all virtues, the sweet refreshment of holy souls, the mind’s most tranquil holiday. It is the seventh day on which heavenly manna refreshes us; it is the seventh month, in which, after the flood of rushing temptations, the ark of the heart rests most sweetly; it is that Sabbath which the prophet Isaiah describes: “And there shall be Sabbath after Sabbath, month after month,” [Note: [Col. 0909] Isa. 66.] so that after the seventh times seventh year the year of jubilee may begin, the year acceptable to the Lord, in which each person’s inheritance is restored to him: an ancient possession and eternal freedom, full of gladness.

Here we are refreshed with milk from the breasts of her consolation. When we have been torn away from the milk, we shall feast upon entry into her glory, and what the Lord promises in Isaiah will be fulfilled: “Behold, I create Jerusalem rejoicing, and her people joy; and I will rejoice in Jerusalem and delight in my people, and the voice of weeping and the voice of crying shall no longer be heard in her.” [Note: [Col. 0909] Isa. 65.]

Lord God, how long will the jubilee be delayed? When will your mercy come before me? Meanwhile I shall eat my bread in the sweat of my face [Note: [Col. 0909] Gen. 3.] and my tears by measure, until wine is given to those who mourn and strong drink to those bitter in spirit, [Note: [Col. 0909] Prov. 31.] and may my whole soul be absorbed in those delights of which I already taste the first fruits.

## CHAPTER XIV. A human being has a threefold Sabbath in the love of God, neighbour, and self.

[Col. 0909C]

“There shall be month after month, Sabbath after Sabbath.” [Note: [Col. 0909] Isa. 65.] In the Old Testament, indeed, a threefold distinction of Sabbaths is assigned. The first Sabbath is called the seventh day; the second, the seventh year; the third, the year following seven times seven years, that is, the fiftieth year. Thus there is a first Sabbath of days, a second of years, and a third, the Sabbath of Sabbaths; so that the number seven is contained in unity, proceeding from unity and completed in unity.

For every work takes its beginning from faith in the one God; receiving increase through the sevenfold gift of the Holy Spirit, it returns to him who is truly one—indeed, who is true unity. As a figure of this, the construction of the ark is completed in one cubit.

[Col. 0909D] It should be noted that in this charity a threefold Sabbath is found, if you observe more carefully. In the Law two commandments of love are expressly given: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, all your soul, and all your mind; and your neighbour as yourself.” [Note: [Col. 0909] Deut. 6; Matt. 22.] These two commandments indicate three things that are to be loved. No one can love his neighbour as himself unless he loves himself. Therefore a human being is bound to love God and his neighbour as himself. For “no one ever hated his own flesh.” [Note: [Col. 0909] Eph. 5.] But if one loves the flesh, one is still more bound to love the mind. For I believe that every [Col. 0910A] human being desires rather to be sound in mind than in body.

Therefore let the first Sabbath of a human being be self-love; the second, love of neighbour; and the Sabbath of Sabbaths, love of God. In their extension or distinction there is a remarkable interconnection, such that each is found in all and all in each: all are contained in one, and no one is possessed without all the others. For no one loves himself unless he loves God and neighbour; nor can he love his neighbour as himself unless he loves himself. Likewise, one is clearly shown not to love God at all if one does not love one’s neighbour. For “whoever does not love his brother whom he sees, how can he love God whom he does not see?” [Note: [Col. 0909] 1 John 3.]

Therefore, because God is loved for his own sake, if a human being loves himself or his neighbour for God’s sake, it is evident that love of God is a certain living essence of the other loves: it lives in itself and supplies the other two with their cause of life. Some love themselves for their own sake, and this is not to love oneself but to hate oneself. “He who loves iniquity hates his own soul.” [Note: [Col. 0909] Ps. 10.] Of such people the Apostle says: “In the last days people will be lovers of themselves, greedy, proud, disobedient, unrestrained,” [Note: [Col. 0909] 2 Tim. 3.] and the like. From these things it is plainly shown that they are not loved by themselves for Christ’s sake, but for the vanity of the world.

## CHAPTER XV. On a human being’s Sabbath in self-love.

Therefore, when a human being loves himself, love of God begins in him; [Col. 0910C] when he loves his neighbour, a certain more capacious fold of affection is opened. But when that divine fire grows warm from the marrow and draws the other loves, as certain sparks of itself, into its own fullness, it absorbs every movement of the soul in desire for that lofty and ineffable good. Thus neither the person himself nor his neighbour is loved except insofar as each affection, failing away from itself, is wholly transferred into God.

Yet by an ineffable artistry of providence it comes about that, although these three loves are always together, they are not always felt equally. At one time the mind’s pleasant sweetness proceeds from the purity of one’s own conscience; at another it receives the effect of shared joy from a neighbour’s good; at another, contemplating, it aspires [Col. 0910D] toward God in desire and exultation. As someone entering various chambers of spices is now delighted by the fragrance of one kind, now of another, so the soul of one who loves is now suffused with an inestimable sweetness by consideration of itself, now by consideration of God or neighbour.

Therefore, one who formerly recalled the days wasted in the bitterness of his soul, after giving worldly desire a writ of divorce and, having obtained remission of sins, recognizing that he has received the pledge and earnest of heavenly grace—when he reads in the book of his conscience nothing that accuses him or ought to displease God—will find that “the remnant of thoughts keeps a feast” for him.

[Col. 0911A] For when, free from outward tumult, he has withdrawn within the secret places of contemplation; when he has shut the door of his mind against crowds of clamouring cares; when he has examined the inward treasures of conscience and finds nothing disordered, unsuitable, or contrary to reason, but all things peaceful and pleasant; when, like a most disciplined household, he sees the multitude of his thoughts, words, and works obeying him as a certain master of the house, and all his inward parts rising up to him in a certain humility—then from all these things there bursts forth a wonderful security, from security a wonderful tranquillity, and from this an ineffable jubilation of heart. It is all the more devout in Christ’s praise as he understands more clearly that it all proceeds from Christ’s grace.

This is the festive solemnity of the seventh day, which six days precede: that is, the six works of mercy. For the righteous person proves himself in their exercise, and, breathing freely in the bosom of holy conscience and in the testimony of good works, faithfully keeps Sabbath in the grace given him by God. This is the filial gladness of the first Sabbath, in which servile works—that is, sins which make slaves—are forbidden; in which the fire of desire is not kindled; and in which burdens—that is, bonds of impiety—are not borne without transgression of the Law.

## CHAPTER XVI. On the second Sabbath: love of neighbour.

Certainly, if he leaves that more inward bedchamber of the heart, which he dedicated in the first Sabbath, and moves to that lodging [Col. 0911C] where he is accustomed to rejoice with those who rejoice, to become weak with the weak, and to burn with those who are scandalized; if he feels his soul joined to his brothers by the indissoluble glue of charity, so that neither sinister suspicion, nor the bite of envy, nor the heat of anger or sadness can creep in on any occasion; but, embracing and cherishing them with the arms of most sincere love, bearing alike and with one and the same shoulder the circumstances of others, whether joyful or adverse—then, with every noise of vices and tumult of anxieties stilled, he is dissolved into an inestimable joy amid the delights of so great a sweetness, and in the sweetness of his love becomes inwardly free, released from every harmful occupation of mind.

For that brotherly charity permits absolutely no vice to remain in the rest of this Sabbath is witnessed by the Apostle, the continual keeper [Col. 0911D] of this second Sabbath, saying: “You shall not commit adultery, you shall not steal, you shall not bear false witness”; [Note: [Col. 0911] Exod. 20; Rom. 13.] and if there is any other commandment, it is summed up in this saying: “You shall love your neighbour as yourself.” [Note: [Col. 0911] Ibid.]

David, affected by the sweetness of this delight and bursting into a cry of jubilation from so great a union of minds, says: “Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together in unity!” [Note: [Col. 0911] Ps. 132.]

It should be noted that, just as only one day is dedicated to the first Sabbath—because it is singular, consisting in the tranquillity of each person’s own conscience—so not without reason a whole year is consecrated here. For just as a year is made up of many days, so from many souls one heart and one soul are fused by the fire of charity. The six years preceding this Sabbath may be understood as six kinds of people, in whose love we exercise ourselves according to the obligation imposed by their nature or by command. Just as a year comprises many days, so in each of those kinds of people many are joined to us in the union of hearts.

First, then, let our love extend by a natural order to those of our own blood: as we are bound to love them by the necessity of nature, so it is exceedingly inhuman to exclude them from the sanctuary of our love. For, as the Apostle testifies: “Whoever does not care for his own, and especially for members of his household, has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever.” [Note: [Col. 0911] 1 Tim. 5.] Hence this love that proceeds from nature is first established by God’s command among the commandments that concern love of neighbour: “Honour your father and your mother.” [Note: [Col. 0911] Exod. 20.]

From there, extending to those specially joined to us by reciprocal friendship or duty, our love is broadened in a more expansive embrace. Yet this love does not surpass the righteousness of the Pharisees, to whom it was said: “You shall love your friend and hate your enemy.” [Note: [Col. 0911] Matt. 5.] Although affection for parents and friends, when preserved, gains little reward—since natural law prompts us to the former and mutual services urge us to the latter—nevertheless, if either is neglected, it brings an increase of condemnation.

Truth says in the Gospel: “If you love those who love you, what reward will you have? Do not the Gentiles do the same? And if you greet your brothers, what more do you do?” [Note: [Col. 0911] Ibid.] Therefore, that our love may extend into a greater breadth, let it embrace also those who serve God with us and are joined to us in the profession of the same life, in the bond of peace and unity of the Spirit.

God is indeed the efficient cause of this love, since spiritual anointing flows from the head down upon Aaron’s beard and to the hem of his garment, [Note: [Col. 0911] Ps. 132.] so that those anointed by the Anointed One, called Christians from Christ, may all embrace one another in participation in Jesus’ name through the common bond of mutual charity.

There remain two kinds of people; if we gather them into the net of our love, nothing remains but to enjoy [Col. 0912D] the rest of that true Sabbath. For concerning those who are outside—namely Gentiles and Jews, schismatics and even heretics—we must grieve over their ignorance, have compassion on their weakness, and lament their hardness; through compassionate feeling we must help them with the assistance of prayers, so that they too may run after the fragrance of our ointments in Christ Jesus our Lord.

Charity extends its tent still further and broadens and stretches the cloak that in the time of the old Law was short, so that it suffices to cover two, as it joins one’s enemy to one’s soul through the new union of the Holy Spirit. By this love a human being [Col. 0913A] becomes a son of God, and the image of divine goodness is most fully restored. The Lord says: “Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you, and pray for those who slander you, that you may be sons of your Father who is in heaven.” [Note: [Col. 0913] Matt. 5.]

This love, looking upon an enemy with a single eye, can say in fullest security: “Forgive us, as we also forgive.” [Note: [Col. 0913] Matt. 6.] Thus the one who forgives is forgiven. Thus one becomes a son of God, an heir of God and co-heir with Christ. Consider, O man, how secure, sweet, and delightful it is to have compassion on enemies, not to be moved by injuries, to love for Christ’s sake the person by whom I feel myself unloved, and to have toward him the affection that a most indulgent father has toward a dearly beloved son suffering from frenzy: so that, the greater the injuries he inflicts, the more fervently [Col. 0913B] charity burns toward him.

## CHAPTER XVII. On the third Sabbath in the love of God.

Yet every Sabbath has six preparatory days, on which we gather heavenly manna, so that in that splendid festival which is to be celebrated in the love of God, we may suck milk from the breasts of his consolation and rest most blessedly between the two lots, between the bridegroom’s breasts, between left and right, through the tender mercies of our God. These six days are Christ’s conception, birth, preaching, passion, resurrection, and ascension. On these six days the Lord wrought salvation in the midst of the earth; and, resting from all the work that he had accomplished [Note: [Col. 0913] Gen. 2.], and seated in the glory of God the Father, he mercifully invites us to that Sabbath which is most glorious in his love.

[Col. 0913C] O good Jesus, O gracious, lovable, pleasant, sweet God—O God who is love. What is sweeter, more pleasant, or more lovable than to be at leisure and see how greatly you have loved us: how devoutly and mercifully, in your conception and birth, you deigned to empty yourself even to the weaknesses of infant nature; how graciously and carefully you taught us the way of life by word and example; with what condescension you offered yourself to death for us; how, rising into your glory, you restored human nature; and how, ascending into heaven, you placed it gloriously upon the throne of your majesty.

What could be happier or more delightful for that soul’s Sabbath which, embracing the Lord by contemplation and love and forming within itself certain experiences of divine sweetness, is moved by the immeasurable joy of holy enjoyment, while, becoming a stranger to itself, it now dwells in heaven and exults and rejoices in remembrance of the abundance of God’s sweetness? O peaceful rest, O delightful Sabbath, O sweetness of love, which raises the soul that loves God to his highest mighty works, and, once raised, makes it rest amid eternal delights. Through the repose of this Sabbath the whole inner person is made joyful; its understanding is made serene, its affections become sweet, and its holy desires are dissolved in God in a most blessed kind of fruition.

O [Col. 0914A] morning, O day, better than thousands in the courts of the Lord. O brightness of light and ardour of love, which inflames the angels and illuminates the inner being of the saints. O splendid festival, O pleasant pause and delightful Sabbath—O glorious Sabbath! And what glory can be more delightful or desirable than to cling to God from the marrow of one’s being, to cast upon him all one’s thoughts and affections, and from love of him to gather fruits of such certainty that one need not hesitate at all concerning the salvation of one’s soul, fellowship with the angels, and that endless exultation prepared for those who love God?

Therefore the apostles went rejoicing from the presence of the council [Note: [Col. 0913] Acts 5.]. Andrew, glorying and exulting, ran to the cross. Paul likewise, flooded with the sweetness of so great a joy, [Col. 0914B] said: “Far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ” [Note: [Col. 0913] Gal. 6.]. Secure concerning Christ’s recompense, he said: “I know whom I have believed, and I am certain that the just Judge is able to keep my deposit until that day” [Note: [Col. 0913] 2 Tim. 2.]. Having experienced that the love of God is the cause that produces so pleasant a security, he said: “I know and am certain that neither death, nor life, nor sword, nor angel, nor powers, nor any other creature will be able to separate me from the love which is in Christ Jesus” [Note: [Col. 0913] Rom. 8.].

Moses, relying on so firm a love, chose rather to be blotted out of the book written by the Lord [Note: [Col. 0913] Exod. 32.] than to endure the destruction, by divine indignation, of the people entrusted to him. Fortified by this impregnable citadel, Ezekiel [Note: [Col. 0913] Ch. 1.] went down into Chaldea, and Jeremiah [Note: [Col. 0913] Ch. 47.] into Egypt, trusting in its protection. [Col. 0914C] Through it Job [Note: [Col. 0913] Ch. 30.] became the brother of dragons without fear of danger, and companion of ostriches. Under so sure a security Paul did not fear to become an anathema from Christ for his brothers [Note: [Col. 0913] Rom. 9.]. Secure beneath its shadow, David did not fear to walk through the shadow of death [Note: [Col. 0913] 1 Reg. 27.]. For since God is love [Note: [Col. 0913] 1 John 4.], he knows that where love is, there God is. “Though I walk in the midst of the shadow of death,” he says, “I shall fear no evils, because you are with me” [Note: [Col. 0913] Ps. 22.].

Wretched I, until now I have loved the world and put your love, O God, after worldly love. Now, on the contrary, according to the riches of your mercy, make me love you and despise, in comparison with your love, the world and everything in it. May my soul, in desire for you, O God, disdain heaven and [Col. 0914D] earth and all that is in them. “For what have I in heaven, and what have I desired from you upon earth? God of my heart and my portion, God for ever” [Note: [Col. 0913] Ps. 72.]. May my soul fail and melt away in your love, so that, failing from myself, I may sing and chant with my spirit [Note: [Col. 0913] Ps. 141.] the delights of your love and the riches of that charity through which those are made to drink from torrents of eternal delight whose affection is wholly absorbed by your love.

For just as heated iron passes into a certain essence of fire; as a drop of water, poured into a full cask of wine, lays aside its own tastelessness and takes on the essence of the better substance; and as air, flooded with the brightness of the sun, is wholly brightness: so the human spirit, affected by divine love, is wholly love. Therefore, whoever loves God, dead to self and living to God alone, in a certain manner—if one may say so—becomes consubstantial with the beloved. For if Jonathan’s soul was joined to David’s soul [Note: [Col. 0915] 1 Reg. 18.], or if one who clings to God becomes one spirit with him [Note: [Col. 0915] 1 Cor. 6.], then, by a not dissimilar principle of union, the whole affection passes into God by a kind of co-essence; all gathered into itself, without exception for any other desire, it is transferred into God, the fullness of all things desirable.

Yet the soul will love more perfectly when it is brought into the joy of its Lord [Note: [Col. 0915] Matt. 25.], into the bridegroom’s embrace, and makes the blessedness of all the righteous its own through the communion of love. By the benefit of this communion, [Col. 0915B] God will be all in all [Note: [Col. 0915] Eph. 4.].

## CHAPTER XVIII. An apostrophe, or exhortation, that God may be loved.

Hear, O heavens, and give ear, O earth [Note: [Col. 0915] Isa. 1.], how greatly God has magnified his mercy toward us. And who has considered the abyss of such ineffable grace? Who has tasted from the source of so great a sweetness and not loved? “Will you not be subject to God, O my soul?” [Note: [Col. 0915] Ps. 61.] Why do you not pour out all your affections upon God—affections which you direct toward false vanities and madnesses? [Note: [Col. 0915] Ps. 39.] “Why are you sad, O my soul, and why do you trouble me?” [Note: [Col. 0915] Ps. 41.] Do you have no counsellor or saviour? Is there no balm in Gilead, or no physician there? [Note: [Col. 0915] Jer. 8.] “Return, return, O Shulamite” [Note: [Col. 0915] Cant. 6.]; return to [Col. 0915C] the Lord your God [Note: [Col. 0915] Ecclus. 17.], O my divided, torn, and lost self—yet raised by Christ and redeemed by Christ’s passion. Why, I ask, do you love anything other than him who so graciously and mercifully redeemed you from so many miseries?

By constant examination and continual meditation, consider how the only-begotten Son of God the Father, though he was “the brightness of his glory and the figure of his substance” [Note: [Col. 0915] Heb. 1.], after emptying himself even to the form of a servant [Note: [Col. 0915] Phil. 2.], after hunger, thirst, weariness, tears, bonds, scourges, gall, vinegar, a crown of thorns, nails, and even a spear, once hung upon the cross between two thieves for your salvation [Note: [Col. 0915] Matt. 27.]. Indeed, the horns of the cross were in his hands, and from them that merciful Samaritan poured wine and oil into your wounds [Note: [Col. 0915] Luke 10.]. Yet [Col. 0915D] there his strength was hidden, and in the bitterness of death was his sweetness. “O how great is the multitude of your sweetness, O Lord, which you have hidden for those who fear you” [Note: [Col. 0915] Ps. 30.]. In Isaiah’s testimony: “Truly you are a hidden God, King of Israel, Saviour” [Note: [Col. 0915] Isa. 45.].

Your Saviour was dying, O my soul, in order to give you life. He was fastened to the cross in order to fasten your iniquities to the cross with his own hands. He raised his hands to the Father in the evening sacrifice in order to invite you to friendly embraces. He offered his life, which was subject to death in no respect, to death for you, so that, when the just one is unjustly slain by the prince of darkness, the latter—being convicted of having usurped what was not his own—might be deprived of the power which he possessed by right.

[Col. 0916A] In so overflowing a benefit, in so great a heap of graces, by which divine generosity almost overwhelms and confounds you, take care that you are not ungrateful. Ingratitude destroys salvation: it is the breath of the asp, the poison of the soul, the scorching of virtues, a pestilential wind and corrupting breeze, drying up the drops of piety, the dew of grace, and the streams of mercy.

## CHAPTER XIX. The soul is further reproached with God’s benefits, that it may be grateful to God.

I say further: nothing is sufficiently said which must always be said and repeated in continual remembrance. You were bound to that most grievous creditor, the angel Satan, like some most savage exactor, by a bond of debt as numerous as your sins, [Col. 0916B] and you were unable to pay. But the Son of God paid for you, not what he had taken, but what you had taken; and, what was an act of fuller condescension and more abundant grace, he did not appoint another debtor, but gave his own soul as the means of payment.

When that renegade and fugitive angel sought to claim you for detestable slavery, Christ made his own the suit brought against you. After the various productions of witnesses from the law, the oracles, the prophets, and the signs, he finally pleaded his own blood; and that plea won the judgment of your freedom. Upon the judgment-tablet the letters were written on the parchment of the crucified body and confirmed by the kiss of mercy and truth, justice and [Col. 0916C] peace meeting one another. Finally, the seal was impressed: namely, the wound in his side, which he continually presents before the Father’s eyes as the price of our redemption and perpetual propitiation. There still remains the title of the case, inscribed in memory of such great love.

Know that, if he finds you ungrateful and unwilling to make use of so great a benefit, he will most strictly demand his death from you; and I fear that one day, in greatest indignation, he may say to you: “Put forth your hand and place it in my right side; put your fingers into the nail-marks, and see how much I have suffered for you.” O ungrateful and cruel impiety! Do you not think that God will regret the riches bestowed upon you if he sees that they have perished through ingratitude?

Therefore our prayer is often rejected, and I think this itself is done by a merciful dispensation, [Col. 0916D] lest we who have been ungrateful for benefits previously received should, by a new bestowal of heavenly gifts, be burdened with the graver guilt of ingratitude. For, since God regards as lost a benefit which is not followed by an act of thanksgiving, it is better for us not to be heard than, to the increase of our condemnation, to obtain what we ask and thereby gain matter for ingratitude.

With what presumption, then, will you fail to love him who loved you when you did not love him, who did not despise you when you were a sinner? Consider, I ask, by what recompense and what merit you can answer the supreme and eternal Trinity. [Col. 0917A] For your sake the Father gave his only-begotten Son over to death. The Son likewise gave himself over to death for your salvation. Finally, the Holy Spirit was given to you; for the Apostle testifies that “the love of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” [Note: [Col. 0917] Rom. 5.]. Thus the Father loves us, the Son loves us, the Holy Spirit loves us: the whole Trinity, God, loves us.

The eternal, almighty, and immeasurable God loves us—he whose greatness has no end [Note: [Col. 0917] Ps. 144.], whose wisdom has no number [Note: [Col. 0917] Ps. 146.], whose peace surpasses all understanding [Note: [Col. 0917] Phil. 4.], from whom and in whom are all visible and invisible things, heavenly and earthly [Note: [Col. 0917] Col. 1.]. Certainly, when you love, you do so from obligation; if he loves you, he does so freely. Consider the height of heaven, the magnitude of the firmament, and a little mud in marshy places: even so, the disparity between you and God is beyond measure, as that between mud and heaven. [Col. 0917B] What comparison is there between you and the ineffable, incomprehensible, incomparable One? You could repay him nothing commensurate with his merit, even if, in return for what he endured for you, you tortured yourself for a thousand thousand years in the fire of Gehenna.

## CHAPTER XX. That God loves us more excellently and fully than we love him.

Everything which is in God is immeasurably more excellent than what is in us. He loves as love itself; judges as justice; disposes as wisdom; reveals as light; has mercy as piety; knows as truth; acts as power; presides as majesty.

[Col. 0917C] Setting aside all matters pertaining to the dispensation of his Incarnation, consider carefully that the whole universe obeys you at his command. All nature serves your needs: heaven, air, earth, sea, and the things in them all alike minister to your necessities and pleasures. The yearly cycle of the seasons fashions flowers and fruits of trees and plants through a renewed revival; and, while shoots wither and the natures of seedlings grow old, the revolving course of time supplies you with the continual gifts of God.

Recognize, O soul, that once you did not exist, and that you were made by him. You gave him nothing in order that he might make you, for you could give nothing, because you did not exist. But since it was better to exist than not to exist, he freely granted you existence, preferring you to all those things [Col. 0917D] which he could have brought forth from non-being into being, but did not. He added form to you; and, though your essence had come forth from nothing, through the grace of the Saviour he marked you with his own image and likeness. Along with beauty he bestowed life.

Whence came such great, gratuitous, and unheard-of condescension—that you should be made in his image and likeness—unless it was so that you might love your like, and be conformed by reciprocal love to him who preceded you in free love? Indeed, you fittingly give yourself to him by loving. Therefore offer to love him your heart and the inward parts of your very marrow—him who deigned to love you while finding nothing in you worthy of love. Love [Col. 0918A] your seal and your image; and, so that the more distinct form of your Creator may appear in you, conform yourself by faith and love to him who is love. Make his benefit an occasion for thanksgiving by continual meditation.

Your lover invited you to this by prophetic exhortation: “Set me as your memorial upon your heart and arm” [Note: [Col. 0917] Cant. 8.], that is, upon heart and body, so that, laying aside the image of the earthly man, you may bear the image of the heavenly one. Consider the proofs of divine love, which cannot be refuted: “Set me upon your heart, as a seal of faith, as an example of love” [Note: [Col. 0917] Ibid.].

Before his transgression, the apostate angel represented such a seal in himself, according to Ezekiel’s testimony: “You are the seal of likeness, full of wisdom and perfect in beauty” [Note: [Col. 0917] Ezek. 28.]. For in his creation the angel was joined to God in such conformity [Col. 0918B] that he was rather a seal of likeness than something similar or sealed. From a seal there is expressed imaginally such a likeness as is held essentially in the seal itself; and this belongs to the human being. But the angel, by reason of the subtlety of his nature, clung to God in a more express likeness, because he was wholly and only spirit.

But love restores us, enclosed in a prison of clay and cast down in an earthly dwelling, to the state of angelic dignity. And although the corruptible body weighs down the soul and the earthly habitation depresses the mind that thinks upon many things, nevertheless the new commandment of love reforms us, disfigured by sin, into God’s likeness.

The Lord multiplied his gifts to you: he added [Col. 0918C] to your beauty the powers of living, sensing, and discerning. In all that his generosity bestowed, your need received; his grace preceded, rather than any claim of your merit. He espoused you by faith, adorned you outwardly with the senses as though with certain radiant jewels, and marked you inwardly with wisdom as with a natural beauty. He knew what adornment suited you better; therefore he gave what became you, and gave it so fully that he might even love you on account of this very gift which he gave.

Indeed, you are mad if you love only moderately him who preceded you with so great a love; who, bestowing such great and precious gifts, also promises greater things to one who loves him—things which eye has not seen, ear has not heard, nor has their estimate entered into the human heart [Note: [Col. 0917] 1 Cor. 2.]. By his gift you are bound to weigh how greatly he ought to be loved, who loves so greatly that you must now judge it not merely rash but even wicked not only to fail to love one who loves you, but not to embrace with all your entrails and all your inmost heart the love of one so great, so powerful, and so excellent.

[Col. 0918D] O bridegroom most beautiful in form above the sons of men [Note: [Col. 0917] Ps. 44.], love the bridegroom; love the king in his beauty, the King of virtues, full of grace and truth, the Lord of majesty crowned with glory and honour [Note: [Col. 0917] Ps. 8.]. The king indeed desired your beauty and your gifts [Note: [Col. 0917] Ps. 44.], with which he deigned to adorn you; they inclined his affection toward you for your honour. He loves you in [Col. 0919A] his own gifts. For if you have any good, you have it as his gift, understand this. It is the Apostle’s word: “What do you have that you have not received? And if you have received it, why do you glory as though you had not received it?” [Note: [Col. 0919] 1 Cor. 4.]

If you glory in something as though you had received it from yourself and not from God, you steal from God what is his, seize another’s honour for yourself, and, presumptuously intruding yourself into another’s glory, you indeed have glory—but not before God, because you wickedly usurp another’s glory against God. Take care, therefore, that the mark of ingratitude never steals upon you. Remember without ceasing that you were lost by your own iniquity and restored by his mercy.

## CHAPTER XXI. How great is the soul’s prerogative above other creatures.

[Col. 0919B] Endeavour in every way you can to please him who deigned to make you such that you might please him. Would that you knew yourself and, by contemplating your own beauty, tested the grace of your Creator in you. But the eye that sees all things does not see itself; therefore sometimes look upon the face of your heart in the mirror of your own reason, lest you do injury to your dignity. You do so if you wish to set things lower than yourself above yourself and to make equal with yourself—who are most beautiful in truth—those things which have merely an imaginary and shadowy beauty.

You cast yourself down from your dignity most monstrously and shamefully if you desire or admire the transient and empty beauties of things. The world was made for you; therefore do not love the world, because the world is not worthy of you, since you are far [Col. 0919C] more worthy than it, and than the sun, moon, and all creatures. For all temporal things acknowledge the failing of their beauty; but you do not fail through labour, grow pale from sickness, wither through old age, or waste away in death.

Accordingly, if you love anything else in this world, which is wholly subject to you, it is the height of rashness, when you ought to love such things only as things serving you—as gifts of the bridegroom, presents of friends, benefits of the Lord. Do not love these things along with him, but for his sake; love him through them, and, loving him, above them. You degenerate into the love of prostitutes if you love the giver’s gifts more than the affection of the lover. You do injury to the giver; indeed, you dishonour yourself with prostituted shame if you receive gifts and do not return love in exchange.

[Col. 0919D] Therefore love him for his own sake, and love his gifts for his sake. Love yourself for him and him for yourself. Love him in order that you may enjoy him; set your affections in him, and, when you love more fervently, you will be loved more affectionately. This love is holy, having nothing sordid or impure; in the remembrance of God it is most sweet, surpassing all the delights of the world, and in a certain way eternal by the nature of its own steadfastness.

But keep continually in memory that, by as much as his essence surpasses human frailty more excellently, so much more sweetly, incomparably more delightfully, and more desirably does he love and is loved than an angel, a human being, gold, silver, a precious stone, health, freedom, [Col. 0920A] or any other things by which human hearts are divided. Do not believe that you are loved less by him because, together with certain animals of the earth, he shares with you the benefit of sun and moon and the other gifts of his grace. Do not doubt that whatever has been given to them has been given for your sake; for, that all things may serve you, they have received from divine goodness the gifts necessary to them, without which they cannot exist or serve.

Does his love for you seem greater if he had given everything to you alone? Would you be happier if you alone inherited the world and possessed everything in it without any consolation of social life? And even if you complain of the company of wicked people, know beyond doubt that, just as other things serve you and wicked people, so divine providence makes the life of wicked people serve your progress in spiritual warfare.

[Col. 0920B] Through the company of the wicked, those who are good are exercised toward better things. They are also taught to desire the virtues and other gifts of God which the wicked themselves lack and which are far better than all things possessed together with unjust people. Finally, when they see the wicked rushing toward destruction, their affection for God increases in expectation of their own salvation; and a more devout offering of thanks follows for divine gifts in which there is no sharing with the impious.

Therefore, since all things work together for your good, so that the wicked become an exercise to you and the good a consolation, do not judge yourself less loved because he does not love you alone. Yet he loves you with a certain singularity of love, in that he bends both good and evil people to the service and benefit of your life. And since, by the very law and obligation of love, you desire all others together with yourself to be partakers in eternal blessedness, your good will makes another’s good your own; and, through the communion of the Holy Spirit, your blessedness increases by the blessedness of all.

[Col. 0920C] Thus love becomes singular through this very communion, since nothing is diminished by the participation of many, and though diffused among all it is found whole in each. Therefore he loves you singularly who, loving nothing without you, loves other things for your sake. Although love is diffused among many, it is nevertheless whole in each, so that, loving all uniquely, he is uniquely loved by all. Therefore this love is unique, not private; solitary, not isolated; common, not [Col. 0920D] divided; neither failing through use nor diminishing through time or participation.

Store up, therefore, in the treasury of memory and recall without ceasing what has been given you by God, so that you neither presume concerning what has not been given nor grow slack in thanksgiving for benefits received from him.

## CHAPTER XXII. How much sweeter is the love by which God loves us than the love by which we love him.

By as much as divinity surpasses humanity, by so much is Christ’s love for us sweeter, firmer, deeper, more forceful, more penetrating, more inward, more compassionate, more fervent [Col. 0921A] and more pleasant than that love which we have for him or for our neighbour. The immeasurable charity which he has for us surpasses every maternal affection and every agreement of brothers and spouses.

Expressing in himself the grace of fatherly gentleness, he speaks to the faithful soul: “From now on call me: You are my Father, and you are God, the guide of my virginity” [Note: [Col. 0921] Jer. 3.]. And: “You shall call me Father, and you shall not cease to follow after me” [Note: [Col. 0921] Jer. 3.]. Anticipating us with maternal kindness, he says: “As a mother comforts her children, so I will comfort you” [Note: [Col. 0921] Isa. 66.]. And again: “Can a mother forget her infant, so as not to have compassion on the child of her womb? Even if a mother should forget, yet I will not forget you” [Note: [Col. 0921] Isa. 49.].

Taking upon himself the mode of brotherly love, he thus speaks to the faithful soul: “A garden enclosed, my sister” [Note: [Col. 0921] Cant. 4.]. And again: [Col. 0921B] “You have wounded my heart, my sister, bride” [Note: [Col. 0921] Ibid.]. He is a friend when he says to the faithful soul: “You are beautiful, my friend” [Note: [Col. 0921] Ibid.]. And the soul says of him: “Such is my beloved, and he is my friend” [Note: [Col. 0921] Cant. 5.]. He is a bridegroom when it is said of him: “As the bridegroom rejoices over the bride, so your God will rejoice over you” [Note: [Col. 0921] Isa. 62.].

Let us therefore have in ourselves the same mind that was also in Christ Jesus, who, stretching out his hands toward his disciples, calls them brothers, and, what is more, father and mother and sister [Note: [Col. 0921] Mark 3.]—namely, everyone who does his will, or that of a neighbour, in a holy, humble, chaste, and sociable manner.

## CHAPTER XXIII. Repetition of God’s benefits for a greater affection of love.

[Col. 0921C] If you carefully recount the abundant and unwearied magnificence and generosity of God’s grace toward you, although he is the universal dispenser to all, you will nevertheless see it as though wholly and singularly occupied with your advantages. Wherever you turn, a provident attendant, solicitous and loving for your sake, stands by you. In your intentions, meditations, words, counsels, works, adversities, prosperity, outwardly and inwardly, his grace follows and precedes you. In every tribulation he offers you a remedy. He heals you when sick, brings you back when wandering, corrects you when sinning, consoles you when afflicted, raises you when fallen, makes you joyful when sad, and does not permit you to waver long when failing.

This, O soul, I counsel you as though you were my own soul. As I remember having admonished you elsewhere, consider the first beginnings [Col. 0921D] of your creation, turning them over by continual examination and careful meditation: that he made you beautiful; that he added manifold endowments of grace; that when later, through your own action, you had become foul and fetid, he, mercifully pitying your turning away in his free kindness, loved you while you did not exist so as to create you, and restored you by his grace when you had been created but lost.

The Lord, the fountain of mercy, speaks in Jeremiah: “It is commonly said: If a woman sleeps with an adulterous man, will she return to her husband? But you have committed fornication with many lovers. Return to me, and I will receive you, says the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0921] Jer. 3.]. [Col. 0922A] He who had created you whole and undefiled had bestowed upon you, with bridal generosity, gifts of manifold grace. But you, clinging to alien lovers, gave your bridegroom a bill of divorce; you exposed your integrity to corrupters, and, desiring illicit embraces, spread your legs for unclean spirits.

At last, above all prostitutes, a brazen face came upon you. You would not blush, but, rushing headlong toward unlawful things with an unbridled mind, you cast yourself into the abyss of eternal condemnation. Yet he—so exalted, admirable, mighty, and glorious—after your so damnable fall looked upon you with the eye of mercy. To raise you from the mire of foulness, he descended from the majesty of his glory; to abolish the shame of your corruption, he endured dreadful and shameful things for you. [Col. 0922B] And, to include much in few words, in order to free you from death, he offered himself to a most accursed death. Nor could he more expressly, faithfully, sweetly, or graciously show the love with which he loves you.

Even now, forgetting your transgression, he restores the grace you lost, renews the love you corrupted, and reproaches you neither with his benefits nor with your offenses. Rather, if you deign to cling to him humbly and faithfully, he will heap grace upon grace, so that you may become more beautiful and purer than ever before; and from the restoration after your fall you may know how great is his love toward you. You know how fruitful it is to love him who is so ineffably good and incomparably gentle—something which perhaps you would never have known unless you had learned it through the experience of so great a danger—knowing yourself to be strong from weakness, stable from falling, cautious from danger, and happy from unhappiness.

[Col. 0922C] Therefore I urge you still, and again I shall repeat it to you to the point of weariness: think continually how much one so great endured for you, so small and so lost, setting his blood and death as your price, though his blood is beyond price and his death admits no measure of valuation. Above all, you must guard against arrogantly presuming upon his outpoured generosity. Instead, continually remember how he washed you with his blood, loved you, and restored you to integrity when you had prostituted yourself in brothels to shameful uncleannesses. For his love is accustomed to restore violated integrity, not to violate integrity that is whole.

Although [Col. 0922D] you do not see his face, do not doubt that he is always present to you. See, therefore, that by any indecency you do not offend the eyes of him who is present. Know without doubt that he who loved you when you were ugly will love you more fully when you are beautiful. Put on, therefore, I pray, the garment of innocence. Adorn yourself, as with an embroidered garment, with the variety of virtues; and let him who has betrothed you by the ring of faith rejoice to smell in you the fragrances of graces.

I pray you, love wholly your Lord and bridegroom—your life, consolation, counsel, help, and refuge. Finally, love him who is for you whatever can be desirable or lovable. [Col. 0923A] Love him chastely, devoutly, and holy, not in word or tongue but in deed and truth. In your love seek not what is your own, but what belongs to Jesus Christ [Note: [Col. 0923] Phil. 2.]. For thus the Prophet taught us to love when he said: “Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good, for his mercy endures for ever” [Note: [Col. 0923] Ps. 104.]. But of one who seeks what is his own it is written: “He will praise you when you have done him good” [Note: [Col. 0923] Ps. 48.].

Cast your whole self upon him, then; by loving, pass wholly into the beloved, so that, forgetting yourself and becoming to yourself like a lost vessel, you may live in him and fail from yourself, so that you can say with the Prophet: “My heart and my flesh have failed; God is the God of my heart and my portion for ever” [Note: [Col. 0923] Ps. 72.]. “My heart said to you, O Lord my God: My face has sought you” [Note: [Col. 0923] Ps. 26.]; but when will this be, [Col. 0923B] O God? When will you come, O my soul, and appear before the face of God? When will the left be changed into the right? When will the bridegroom present you without spot or wrinkle [Note: [Col. 0923] Eph. 5.]? When will the rush of the river make glad the city of God? When will the holy temple, which you are, be adorned with golden crowns? When will all the earth be filled with majesty? When, exulting in God’s presence and delighting in joy, will he minister to you, passing—as I say—from that bodily appearance which he displayed to his apostles to that glory, to the form in which he is coequal, eternal, and almighty with God the Father?

Exercise yourself continually, therefore, in hope and expectation of future things, with prayers and desires; and let thanksgiving and the voice of praise always be with you for the reception of present blessings.

## CHAPTER XXIV. God’s benefits are again repeated, that the soul may thereby be more humble.

How long will you sleep, my soul? How long will you slumber, so that even a brief idle hour may steal upon you in which you do not remember the Son of God, crucified for your mercy? Anyone would judge it most grievous if he had rendered great service to his companion and found that person ungrateful for the benefit bestowed. What then will the Lord of majesty do if he finds us, who are dust and ashes [Note: [Col. 0923] Gen. 18.], ungrateful for so great a mercy? As a father has compassion on his children, so he has had compassion on us. For if he hardens, judges, and condemns anyone, this is not from him but from us; although he has mercy on whom he wills and hardens whom he wills [Col. 0923D], yet he, whose proper work it is always to have mercy and to spare, crowns his mercies in us and punishes our wickedness. Indeed, the Father of mercies speaks through the prophet, saying: “Is the death of the wicked my will,” says the Lord, “and not rather that he should turn and live?” [Note: [Col. 0923] Ezek. 18.]

Recall that the only-begotten God of God, for your salvation, bowed the heavens and came down [Note: [Col. 0923] Ps. 17]; and, by an ineffable artistry, while remaining what he was, he laid aside his majesty even to the crying of infancy, even to the bruises and wounds of the Passion, in order to raise you from the mire of filth. [Col. 0924A] Moses indeed took an Ethiopian woman, but did not change the blackness of her skin in her [Note: [Col. 0923] Exod. 2]. The Son of God found you blackened by the manifold foulness of sins; at last he washed you with his tears, his baptism, and the wave of his blood, and presented you to himself glorious. You know, nor can you doubt, how far beneath your bridegroom you are in birth, appearance, and dignity. Whence, then, comes to you so great and inestimable an honor: that God has deigned to choose you as his bride—he through whom all things were made; who has power over life and death; king of heaven and earth; splendor and image of the Father’s substance [Note: [Col. 0923] Heb. 1]; into whom angels desire to look [Note: [Col. 0923] 1 Heb. 1]; whose beauty the sun and moon admire; creator and ruler of the universe; desire of angels and archangels; God of glory and Lord of majesty? [Col. 0924B]

Whence comes this to you: that he has received you as a companion of glory, a fellow heir of the kingdom, a participant in the bridal chamber—he whom, when you touch him, you are chaste; when you know him, learned; when you see him, blessed; and when you can enjoy him, glorious, even for a moment? The angel of the Lord stands ready to cut you in two if you admit a foreign lover, if your love toward him grows cold, if you show yourself at all undevout or ungrateful. Recall how great things God has done for you: how he has drawn you to the throne of his grace, and will again advance you to the throne of glory—you who did not dare even to think of his footstool or of pardon.

## CHAPTER XXV. That the commandment concerning love is frequently impressed upon us, yet is not more deeply fixed in our hearts.

[Col. 0924C]

How affectionately, sincerely, sweetly, and delightfully you are bound to love God, the Lord teaches through Moses, saying: “You shall love the Lord your God with your whole heart, with your whole soul, and with your whole mind” [Note: [Col. 0923] Deut. 30]. This commandment of God carries within itself the most exacting necessity of observance. Someone may indeed excuse himself on the ground that he is unable to keep vigil, fast, or work; but no one can excuse himself on the ground that he cannot love. Virginity is advised, not commanded. “He who can receive it, let him receive it,” says the Lord [Note: [Col. 0923] Matt. 19]. And the Apostle: “Concerning virgins I have no commandment, but I give counsel” [Note: [Col. 0923] 1 Cor. 7]. But charity is commanded by God; and his command is imposed upon human hearts strongly, urgently, and under threat [Col. 0924D] of punishment.

The Lord has indeed commanded that this commandment be kept most carefully; and, so that he might drive it into our hearts more deeply than a nail, he repeatedly impressed it upon us as with frequent blows: first, that we should love with the whole heart; next he adds, with the whole soul; finally, he adds, with all our strength. See that this commandment is a nail or goad. For as Solomon says: “The words of wisdom are goads, and like nails driven deeply” [Note: [Col. 0923] Eccl. 12]. Is not the living and effective word of God more than a goad or a nail, and sharper [Col. 0925A] than every two-edged sword? [Note: [Col. 0925] Heb. 4.]

Certainly, the hardness of our heart required this insistent repetition, so that this commandment might pass into our hearts’ inward parts, just as a nail is driven into a hard block by repeated blows until it is forced inward. It was also fitting for us, whose hearts worldly love had infected and whose soul’s inner recesses it occupied, that this love should be cast out, exiled from our hearts, so that the heart might remain in God and God in it. Who can be confident that he possesses his whole heart, when the Prophet complains of his heart and says: “They have multiplied beyond the hairs of my head, and my heart has forsaken me” [Note: [Col. 0925] Ps. 39]? And again, rejoicing at the recovery of his heart: “Your servant,” he says, “has found his heart, to pray this prayer to you” [Note: [Col. 0925] 2 Sam. 7].

We often read in the book of experience how we are [Col. 0925B] forsaken by our heart: now it is with us, now elsewhere; now it flies away, now returns; and, abiding only in slipperiness, it never stands fast in any stability of its own. How, then, shall I love with my whole heart, when I am cut off from my whole heart? Or how can I possess my heart whole unless God makes it mine? Indeed, I shall possess nothing of my heart unless God makes it mine. But if, with God’s help, I directed all the affections, intentions, and movements of my heart toward him, and held it fixed in him with immovable devotion; if, moreover, that heavenly fire kindled even the marrow of my soul, of which the prophet speaks: “The Lord sent fire into my bones and instructed me” [Note: [Col. 0925] Lam. 1], then perhaps it would be possible for me to love with my whole heart.

But now [Col. 0925C] may your eyes, O God, see my imperfection, so that, if we are not granted to love as much as we ought, at least we may love as much as we can. Let us recall God’s benefits—not only those in which the Dayspring from on high visited us through the dispensation of the flesh [Note: [Col. 0925] Luke 1], but also the daily and almost continual benefits by which the Father of mercies unceasingly consoles us when we are set amid distress and affliction of spirit. Who could answer or repay him one thing for a thousand—him who, heaping mercy upon mercy and pressing it upon us, doing great things with us in all things, overwhelms and confounds us with gifts so frequent? Therefore, in order to draw our whole heart into the grace of his love, and wholly to tear us away from love of the world—for whoever is a friend of the world is his enemy, and sacred [Col. 0925D] teaching instructs us in this—he invites our heart to his love with fatherly gentleness. For when we are commanded to love God with our whole heart, whole soul, and whole mind, it is as though God were instructing us to love him sweetly, wisely, and strongly.

## CHAPTER XXVI. God is loved sweetly through remembrance of the Passion.

And what is sweeter than continual remembrance of that dispensation through which the kindness and humanity of God our Savior appeared? Above all things, Christ Jesus, your Passion makes you lovable to us; it has made atonement for all our iniquities. For when your guiltless blood was shed, the bonds recording all our sins were erased. Thanks be to your cross, Jesus. For it empties all our torments of their force; thanks be to the nails that opened to us the inner depths of the mercy of our God, in which the Dayspring from on high visited us [Note: [Col. 0925] Ibid.].

Oh, how dreadful and incurable is the wound of our transgression, for which the Son of God had to endure so many harsh reproaches, so many terrible wounds! Abel’s blood cried from the earth for vengeance [Note: [Col. 0925] Gen. 4]; Naboth’s blood cried out [Note: [Col. 0925] 3 Kings 20]; the blood of all the righteous, shed upon the earth, cried out: “Avenge, Lord, our blood, which has been shed upon the earth” [Note: [Col. 0925] Rev. 26]. Christ’s blood alone cried out for the reconciliation and redemption of his people; his death cried out to the dead for life, to sinners [Col. 0926B] for pardon, to captives for deliverance, and to the lost for salvation. He continually pleads with the Father that the price of his blood and the reward of the obedience which he rendered to the Father may be turned, for sinners, into the redemption of those who repent.

For, as the Apostle testifies, “God appointed his Son for us as a propitiator through faith in his blood” [Note: [Col. 0925] Rom. 3]. The Apostle placed this clause, “through faith,” most carefully. For if you cast your faith and confidence upon the bruises and wounds of the Crucified One, and turn the remembrance of the Lord’s Passion to the use of your salvation, his blood will be the price of your redemption. His death will turn into life for you, his pain into your joy, his distresses into your delights, [Col. 0926C] his reproaches into your honor; and, so that you may obtain salvation by the multiplied interest of grace—the salvation which he wrought in the midst of the earth—his temporal suffering will yield you eternal delights.

O fountain of mercy, Jesus, what would not move one to love you: that amid the reproach of insults, amid the agonies of death, forgetful of your own miseries but mindful of your mercies, you intercede so devoutly and so opportunely with the Father for your crucifiers? For when your body was stretched out and pierced, when in that very hour of incense the figurative middle was already being overthrown, when the power of the burnt offering was already opening heaven, shaking earth, and despoiling hell, and when you, the high priest, were about to enter with blood into the Holy of Holies [Note: [Col. 0925] Heb. 9], to be heard because of your reverence, you cry: [Col. 0926D] “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” [Note: [Col. 0925] Luke 23]. How sweet will he be to those who love him, when he forestalls even those who hate and kill him with kindness so great, so undeserved, so freely given, and so astonishing!

## CHAPTER XXVII. What it is to love wisely.

Yet because the whole love of the heart lies in affection, lest it be too rash it ought to be governed by wisdom and discernment. We are therefore commanded to love God with the whole soul—that is, wisely. For the soul is the seat of wisdom. Peter loved the Lord sweetly indeed, but not wisely, because he loved carnally; for the heart’s love follows the tendencies of carnal affection. [Col. 0927A] Therefore he tried to prevent him from dying, since he loved not wisely but sweetly, not discerningly but rashly. Because the disciples too loved sweetly indeed, but unwisely, it was said to them: “If you loved me, you would surely rejoice because I go to the Father, for the Father is greater than I” [Note: [Col. 0927] John 14]. As if he said: If you loved me wisely, my ascent to the Father would be desirable to you, since I bear with me your human nature to be placed in the Father’s glory.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. What it is to love God strongly.

The third love is strengthened by zeal of faith and a certain fervor of affection; it establishes a person’s mind in loving God with all inward strength, and firmly and strongly prepares that person, in desire for heavenly things and contempt for temporal things, to endure hard and dreadful things for Christ. [Col. 0927B] But because Peter did not love as wisely as was fitting, although he loved affectionately, he was rebuked by the Lord and called Satan, because he opposed the redemption of all, which Christ was arranging in the Passion of his body [Note: [Col. 0927] Matt. 16]. In this too it is evident that he then loved unwisely, when, led only by carnal affection, he impeded his own salvation and Christ’s glory. Yet he loved neither sweetly, nor wisely, nor strongly when, at a servant-girl’s voice, he denied him whom he had promised never to deny, even to avoid the danger of death [Note: [Col. 0927] Luke 22].

Accordingly, so that this threefold love might be purified and strengthened in Peter, he was, as we believe, questioned three times by Christ: “Peter, do you love me?” Thus he who had been found deficient in [Col. 0927C] this threefold love might redeem and supply his imperfection by a threefold confession. Thus, in the ministry of the dispensation, he must be loved sweetly; and, lest we presume too much upon the benefit of our redemption or lose confidence in any respect, he must be loved wisely. But, considering the power and glory of the resurrection, by which he mightily delivered us from the power of darkness and opened for us the gates of glory, he must be loved strongly and steadfastly.

## CHAPTER XXIX. That, as God must be loved sweetly in his benefits, so he must be loved wisely in his promises.

Finally, since God must be loved with the whole heart in his benefits, as we have touched upon in the preceding discussion, so we are bound to love him with the whole soul in his promises. [Col. 0927D] He who is Truth, who wishes, knows, and is able to save us, promises us rest from labor, security from fear, joy instead of sorrow, resurrection from death, eternal life after the passing of this life; he promises the kingdom of heaven, refreshment at the Father’s table; he promises what eye has not seen, ear has not heard, nor has entered into the human heart—the things he has prepared for those who love him [Note: [Col. 0927] 1 Cor. 2]. Moreover, he promises us himself, as he promised to Abraham our father that he would give himself to us [Note: [Col. 0927] Luke 1].

In all his promises he stirs our desire, so that [Col. 0928A] we may run with the full capacity of the soul toward his promises, which surpass every desire.
