Although human desire for this ought to be without measure, nevertheless it receives measure from human deficiency itself. This desire concerning God’s promises has no limit to its excess beyond measure. And this is a praiseworthy impatience: when delayed hope afflicts the soul [Note: [Col. 0927] Prov. 13], and love receives continual increase from desire. David, bearing this delay with the greatest impatience, says: “As the deer longs for springs of water, so my soul longs for you, O God” [Note: [Col. 0927] Ps. 44]. The Apostle too, impatient of patience, says: “I am constrained by two things: having a desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ, for that is much better; but to remain in the flesh is necessary for your sake” [Note: [Col. 0927] Phil. 1].

[Col. 0928B] The Bride also, ardently and impatiently burning with desire for the Bridegroom, and commending her affections to the heavenly powers and to the prayers of the saints, says: “I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, if you find my beloved, tell him that I am sick with love” [Note: [Col. 0927] Song 5]. And it should be noted that the love which proceeds from longing for what is promised belongs first to the soul. For in the desires of the saints it is frequently expounded as an affection of the soul, as in: “My soul longs for and fails in the courts of the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0927] Ps. 83]. And again: “My soul thirsted for you, O God” [Note: [Col. 0927] Ps. 62]. And in another prophet: “Your name, O Lord, and your remembrance are the desire of the soul. My soul desired you in the night; indeed, my spirit within my inmost parts [desired you]” [Note: [Col. 0927] Isa. 26].

## CHAPTER XXX. That God must be loved strongly in his judgments.

[Col. 0928C]

But just as affection, by which we love God with our whole heart, proceeds from God’s benefits, and desire, through which we seek God with our whole soul, arises from God’s promises, so love, by which we love God with all strength and all powers—that is, strongly and steadfastly—has its cause and beginning in God’s judgments. Now there is a desirable judgment of God, as in: “Look upon me, O God, and have mercy on me, according to the judgment of those who love your name” [Note: [Col. 0927] Ps. 118]. And there is a terrible judgment, of which it is said: “Do not enter into judgment with your servant, O Lord” [Note: [Col. 0927] Ps. 112]. Because of this dreadful judgment, no one loves God before himself.

God, I say, in his most just judgment has mercy here upon some on whom he will not have mercy [Col. 0928D] in the future. Others he scourges as though angry, so that his wrath and scourges may be turned into glory for those afflicted. He abandons them to the desires of their hearts, that they may walk in their own devices, adding iniquity to iniquity. “And let those who are filthy become more filthy still” [Note: [Col. 0927] Rev. 22]. Of this mercy and wrath the Prophet speaks, saying: “Who is wise and will observe these things, and understand the mercies of the Lord?” [Note: [Col. 0927] Ps. 106]. And likewise: “Who knows the power of your anger, and can reckon your wrath according to your fear?” [Note: [Col. 0927] Ps. 89]. “O God, how greatly your works have been magnified; your thoughts have become exceedingly deep. [Col. 0929A] A senseless man will not know, nor will a fool understand these things” [Note: [Col. 0929] Ps. 103; Ps. 91]. Therefore the prosperity of fools will destroy them [Note: [Col. 0929] Prov. 1].

Even if they are corrected by the Lord, they are neither cleansed nor amended; rather, their cleansing becomes an occasion of destruction to them. As in: “He destroyed them by cleansing” [Note: [Col. 0929] Ps. 88]. These persons murmur and blaspheme amid God’s scourges, piling the punishments of Gehenna upon present punishments. But the saints, while amid scourges—and loving his scourges for God’s sake—also give thanks to God, accuse themselves regarding his judgments, and say with the prophet: “All that you have done to us, O Lord, you have done in true judgment [Note: [Col. 0929] Dan. 3], because we have sinned against you; but give glory to your name” [Note: [Col. 0929] Ps. 110]. To such persons applies that prophetic saying: “The daughters of Judah rejoiced because of your judgments, O Lord” [Note: [Col. 0929] Ps. 96].

There are some who not only endure God’s judgments [Col. 0929B] patiently, but themselves judge themselves and assist the hand that scourges them: they accuse themselves, bear witness against themselves, judge themselves, and execute their own sentence. God’s judgment produces patience in the afflicted. “For tribulation produces patience; patience, testing; testing, hope; and hope does not disappoint” [Note: [Col. 0929] Rom. 5]. For how could there be disappointment where there is that which surpasses every hope and confidence—namely, the certainty of eternal glory? Under this expectation the Prophet said: “Lord, in your judgments I have hoped beyond hope” [Note: [Col. 0929] Ps. 118]. And likewise: “The judgments of the Lord are true, more desirable than much gold and precious stone, and sweeter than honey and the honeycomb” [Note: [Col. 0929] Ps. 18].

Why then should I fear in the evil day? It is wiser to be punished here, burned here, and [Col. 0929C] torment ourselves here by accusation and judgment, than to fall into the hands of the living God [Note: [Col. 0929] Heb. 10] and, on the dreadful day of eternal condemnation, await punishment from the terrible and inexorable Judge.

## CHAPTER XXXI. That charity is proved by obedience to the commandments of God.

God must be loved with the whole mind in his commandments. God also wills that the whole human mind should bend itself to obedience, spending all its senses and affections in observing the heavenly commandments. To obey God is to consent in every respect to his will, and by thus obeying to live, “for life is in his will” [Note: [Col. 0929] Ps. 29]. But since God’s will is expressed in his commandments, no one can love God unless he loves his commandments. Finally, [Col. 0929D] love is proved by God’s commandments: if we meditate upon them, act according to them, and exercise ourselves in them.

The Prophet indicates this: “I will meditate,” he says, “upon your commandments, which I have loved” [Note: [Col. 0929] Ps. 118]: behold, diligent meditation. “And I lifted up my hands to your commandments, which I have loved” [Note: [Col. 0929] Ibid.]: behold, loving action. “And I will exercise myself in your justifications” [Note: [Col. 0929] Ibid.]: behold, a justifying exercise. Of meditation it is written: “What God has commanded you, ponder always” [Note: [Col. 0929] Sir. 3]. Let God’s commandments indeed be considered: how holy, [Col. 0930A] honorable, sweet, health-giving, delightful, faithful, and confirmed for ever and ever [Note: [Col. 0929] Ps. 110].

In the lifting of hands holy action is signified, to which the righteous person gladly applies himself. For he is certain that eternal recompense will answer his merits most abundantly. Continual exertion, however, has struggle and unceasing labor joined to it. But the righteous fight in order to be crowned, receiving from him rest for labor who “fashions labor in the commandment” [Note: [Col. 0929] Ps. 93]. Therefore, charity is proved to be genuine if a person loves the commandments and keeps them by meditation, action, and the performance of works—him whom to serve is to reign. Obedience to the commandments has no merit unless it proceeds from charity; for since obedience and charity are joined together, one who does not [Col. 0930B] love does not keep the commandments.

Hear what Truth says: “If anyone loves me, he will keep my word” [Note: [Col. 0929] John 14]. And he adds: “He who does not love me does not keep my word” [Note: [Col. 0929] Ibid.], plainly indicating that whoever loves obeys, while whoever does not obey does not love. True obedience is true observance of God’s commandments; therefore obedience always clings inseparably to charity. For this reason it is written: “Whoever offends in one point is guilty of all” [Note: [Col. 0929] Jas. 2]. This may be briefly explained by one commandment, so that like judgment may be formed concerning similar cases.

Concerning this commandment, “You shall not kill” [Note: [Col. 0929] Exod. 20]: the person who loves and does not kill obeys in love; but the person who does not love, though he does not kill, indeed observes the commandment according to the letter, yet does not observe it according to the meaning of the commandment, because he does not love. [Col. 0930C] For to fulfill the law is not to follow its words outwardly, but obediently to fulfill its sense and intention. Therefore, because obedience that does not arise from true love is not sincere, one who does not love is not said to obey, even though he does not kill, since he keeps the law only in deed and not with pure intention.

For charity is patient and kind [Note: [Col. 0929] 1 Cor. 13], qualities in which obedience is commended. It does nothing wrongly, because it does nothing against its conscience; it is not puffed up by God’s benefits; it is not ambitious, because it rejects every dominion; it does not seek what is its own, but what belongs to Christ or its neighbor—indeed, it does not even reclaim what has been taken away; it is not provoked—understand, to anger; it does not think evil, so as to repay evil for evil; it does not rejoice over [Col. 0930D] iniquity—understand, another’s iniquity, for it has none of its own; it bears all things patiently, believes all things, hopes all things said or promised by God, and endures all things [Note: [Col. 0929] Ibid.] in humble obedience.

Therefore, one who obeys from charity fulfills the law of God’s commandments, which otherwise he cannot fulfill at all without charity. Thus charity itself is the end of the law, the fulfillment of the commandments, and the limit of perfect consummation, according to: “I have seen an end of every consummation; your commandment is exceedingly broad” [Note: [Col. 0929] Ps. 118]. This is the testimony of our conscience [Note: [Col. 0929] 2 Cor. 1]; [Col. 0931A] this is the glory that comes to us from the Spirit of truth. For the Spirit of truth bears witness to our spirit [Note: [Col. 0931] John 1] that we are children of God, regenerated in the hope of life through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead.

The Evangelist John indicates this regeneration when he says: “We know that one born of God does not sin” [Note: [Col. 0931] 1 John 3], because heavenly generation—that is, the renewal of charity—preserves him: namely, charity, through which God foreknew that he would be made conformed to the image of his Son. For although David added adultery and murder to treachery [Note: [Col. 0931] 2 Sam. 11], although Magdalene was afflicted by seven demons [Note: [Col. 0931] Luke 8], and although Peter incurred the sin of apostasy [Note: [Col. 0931] Matt. 26], yet there was none who could snatch them from the Lord’s hand. Charity is the renewal of life, through which the old [Col. 0931B] person—the earthly, carnal, and animal person—is crucified and destroyed in us. Thus ambitions and lusts, evil works and depraved desires, vanish when charity makes all things new; but now, if there is any new creature, old things pass into it.

## CHAPTER XXXII. Again, concerning love of neighbor and its progress.

Charity is never idle; it always extends itself toward another, either toward one’s neighbor or toward God. For it is the nature of charity both to love and to wish to be loved. As it cannot fail to burn, so charity cannot fail to love. For love is fire, and to love is to burn. “I came,” says the Lord, “to cast fire upon the earth” [Note: [Col. 0931] Luke 12]. Fire always extends itself outward, and, as it kindles other things, grows inwardly in itself.

There are indeed people who love themselves and serve their own desires; these are dead while living. As the Apostle writes [Note: [Col. 0931] 2 Tim. 3] concerning the widow who, living in pleasures, is dead. Rebuking self-love, or self-precedence, the Apostle says: “People will be lovers of themselves” [Note: [Col. 0931] 2 Tim. 3], so occupied with their own care that they have no concern for their neighbor’s need. [Col. 0931C] But love pours itself into another, because it disdains to be solitary and therefore wishes to be communicated to another, lest it be alone.

Since, when we attain that highest and most blessed gift, each person will enjoy it according to his capacity, while all together will be more capacious than individual persons considered separately, that happiness will beyond doubt be more abundant. For no one can possess it fully unless he can possess it in another. But he will be unable truly to possess, or make his own, another’s good unless he loves another’s goods in that person. Nor will he love the good in another unless he loves the other person himself. Accordingly, the authority of the divine law fittingly instructs us in the second commandment: “You shall love your neighbor” [Note: [Col. 0931] Matt. 22].

Moreover, because God, our highest blessedness, is the object of enjoyment in himself, in us, and in our neighbor, he himself must be loved wholly by you, so that you love him with your whole heart, whole soul, and all your strength [Note: [Col. 0931] Mark 12]. Therefore, [Col. 0932A] because you will rejoice in your neighbor’s blessedness as much as in your own, it is rightly added: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself” [Note: [Col. 0931] Ibid.]. Two things, then, must be loved by us for enjoyment: God and neighbor, though in different ways. God, so that we may enjoy him in himself and for his own sake; neighbor, so that we may enjoy that person in God and for God’s sake. Properly speaking, we are said to enjoy God; improperly, our neighbor, although the Apostle says to his disciple: “Yes, brother, let me enjoy you in the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0931] Philem. 20].

Now although it is written, “No one has ever seen God” [Note: [Col. 0931] 2 John 4], and although God, who dwells in inaccessible light [Note: [Col. 0931] 1 Tim. 6], often graciously pours some small portion of his light into our hearts; and although it is written of him: “Lord, with you is the fountain of life, and in your light we shall see light” [Note: [Col. 0931] Ps. 35]; nevertheless he himself [Col. 0932B] is the river “whose rush gladdens the city of God” [Note: [Col. 0931] Ps. 45]. He himself says through Isaiah: “Behold, I turn toward you like a river of peace, and like an overflowing torrent of the glory of the nations” [Note: [Col. 0931] Isa. 66]. And what is this city, gladdened by the river’s rush [Note: [Col. 0931] Ps. 45] and watered by the torrent of delight and glory, if not the fellowship of those whom God makes one heart and one soul [Note: [Col. 0931] Acts 4] in the bond of charity?

“You shall love your neighbor as yourself” [Note: [Col. 0931] Matt. 22]. It is as though he said: Love the companion of your nature, who is to become a companion of my glory. Love yourself in another; recognize yourself in my image; and, for my sake, act mercifully toward your neighbor, lest you shut against yourself the entrance of mercy with me. Therefore God, who has no need of our goods, entrusted to us [Col. 0932C] our brothers and neighbors in his place, that we might confer benefits upon them as though they were his representatives—benefits which, if he were in need, we would wish to bestow upon him. How can anyone show mercy to God, who needs nothing and cannot be seen, if he does not show compassionate affection to a needy brother whom he sees?

At first, a person loved himself for his own sake, and this was carnal love. “First is that which is animal; afterward, that which is spiritual” [Note: [Col. 0931] 1 Cor. 15]. This love is carnal because “no one has ever hated his own flesh” [Note: [Col. 0931] Eph. 5]. But lest this love should henceforth wander more widely into evil, the bridle of temperance is put upon it, and it is commanded to love the companion of its nature as itself. Therefore, let a person love himself as much as he wishes, provided that he admits his neighbor to the measure of that same love [Col. 0932D]. Love of neighbor requires willing the same things and refusing the same things; likewise, loving God, seeking God, and consenting in all things, by mutual wills, according to God.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. When, in regard to one’s neighbor, there ought to be complete community of all things.

There is indeed full community in true love of neighbor. For whether a person has or does not have anything which is fitting to share, charity makes it shared by the one who has it and the one who lacks it. [Col. 0933A] What a person has, he makes common to others; and he loves in others what he does not have. In adversities too, a community of wills has a particular place, through which each becomes a participant in one necessity: so that, when one suffers, another suffers with him. For the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, the love of God, and the communion of the Holy Spirit [Note: [Col. 0933] 2 Cor. 13] work these affections of mutual fellowship in us. For charity does not exist without communion, nor the Holy Spirit without communion. And charity is poured into the hearts of the elect through the Holy Spirit given to them [Note: [Col. 0933] Rom. 5].

## CHAPTER XXXIV. That the highest communion is in the Holy Trinity.

The highest communion—or rather union—is in the Holy Trinity; and from it, as from a fountain of light, [Col. 0933B] the gift of communion flows forth to human beings. God is certainly not singular or solitary, because he is three and one; nor was it fitting that he should be solitary or have no companion in his blessedness. Therefore, since Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one life and one essence, their life, essence, and nature are common. There is life from life, essence from essence, nature from nature: the Son from the Father, and the Holy Spirit from both.

The Son is life, who says: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” [Note: [Col. 0933] John 14]. And since he himself is life, he has life in himself from the Father. “As,” he says, “the Father has life in himself, so he gave the Son also to have life in himself.” In the Holy Trinity there is communion so great that wisdom, power, eternity, and [Col. 0933C] everything belonging to the essence of the Trinity are one; nor does the distinction of persons impair that unity. Therefore, whatever the Son has from the Father, he has all of it with the Father. For he is the splendor of glory, the figure of God’s substance [Note: [Col. 0933] Heb. 1], and his image.

As the Son is life from the Father, so the Holy Spirit is life from both: their love, the bond of the two, and eternal communion. Because of this ineffable communion, through which Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are the same life and the same essence, the Son says to the Father: “Father, all that is mine is yours, and all that is yours is mine” [Note: [Col. 0933] John 17]. Likewise John says: “The Father loves the Son and has given all things into his hand” [Note: [Col. 0933] John 3]. Again Truth says: “The Father loves the Son and shows him all things which he himself does” [Note: [Col. 0933] John 5].

## CHAPTER XXXV. That holy communion flows from God into angels and human beings.

[Col. 0933D]

From that ineffable union, of which the Son says, “I and the Father are one” [Note: [Col. 0933] John 10], there flowed forth a certain communion of love into the angels. By the Son and the Holy Spirit they were made steadfast, as it is written: “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the spirit of his mouth all their host” [Note: [Col. 0933] Ps. 32]. Therefore in them there is the same willing and the same unwillingness; thus each is loved by each, and all by each. In imitation of the angelic communion, God’s charity has been poured into human hearts [Col. 0934A] through the Holy Spirit [Note: [Col. 0933] Rom. 5]. For thus the Lord once promised through Joel: “I will pour out,” he says, “of my Spirit upon all flesh” [Note: [Col. 0933] Joel 2].

The sharing of this Spirit enters human hearts so that what belongs properly to one may, through charity, become common to others. Blessed Peter indicates this when he says: “As each of you has received grace, ministering it to one another” [Note: [Col. 0933] 1 Pet. 4]; “if anyone speaks, [let him speak] as the utterances of God; if anyone ministers, [let him do so] from the strength which God supplies, so that God may be honoured in all things.” This communion derives from that ineffable fountain of the supreme and undivided Trinity; and in the unity of Spirit, faith, and baptism the primitive Church was founded, as the Apostle briefly says: “One Spirit, one faith, one soul, one baptism” [Note: [Col. 0933] Eph. 4].

[Col. 0934B] In this sharing of Spirit, faith, and baptism, the multitude of believers had one heart and one soul. Behold the inward union of hearts and identity of wills: no one called anything which he possessed his own, but all things were common among them; and they were distributed to each according as each had need [Note: [Col. 0933] Acts 4]. But what is meant by this communion and this distribution? Distribution makes the thing distributed the property of the person to whom it is given; communion, however, rejects possessing anything as one’s own. Yet charity, abhorring the vice of private possession, does not wish what is distributed to be private, but to pass, though distributed, into common use.

For, according to the Apostle’s testimony, “There are divisions of gifts, and divisions of ministries, [Col. 0934C] and divisions of workings. To each is given the manifestation of the Spirit for usefulness” [Note: [Col. 0933] 1 Cor. 12]; “each has his own gift from God, one indeed in this way and another in that” [Note: [Col. 0933] 1 Cor. 7]. But charity causes each person to receive his particular gift not for himself, but for God and for his neighbour: that he may seek, from God’s gift, not his own glory but God’s, not his own advantage but his neighbour’s. For charity “does not seek its own things” [Note: [Col. 0933] 1 Cor. 13], but those of Jesus Christ, or those of its neighbour in Jesus Christ.

With the eye of faith you see that in that most holy Trinity there is one power and one essence, common to the three persons. For person is distinguished from person by its proper designation; and the benefit of communion—or rather, of union—is shown in this: that the Father alone is Father, and the Son alone is Son. [Col. 0934D] For the Father is Father not for himself but for the Son, to whom, begotten from his substance, he gave to have life in himself. Charity, therefore, makes all things common among neighbours; yet individual assistance must be bestowed on each according to his particular need. For what each receives in this way does not depart from the benefit of communion. Others too have what they have for themselves—indeed, some have less and others more for themselves.

Let people therefore understand that whatever they receive by the gift of heavenly grace belongs not to themselves but to all. Let them fear that what God has bestowed upon them may harm them unless they make it [Col. 0935A] beneficial in common. For grace harms them if it does not benefit others through them. But if they share grace, they transfer it into the glory of God. Therefore whoever shares God’s gift, “to him shall be given, and he shall abound.” And he truly possesses what he has; but from one who does not possess in this way, even what he seems to have shall be taken away from him.

For God’s grace is given to a human being on credit, and becomes a matter of loan: it binds the recipient to God and to the neighbour—to God, to render glory; to the neighbour, to communicate grace. Such a person is “the righteous man who has compassion and lends” [Note: [Col. 0935] Ps. 36]. But a person sins if he presumes to violate the agreement of gift and reception, or of credit and loan. For it is written: “The sinner shall borrow and shall not repay” [Note: [Col. 0935] Ibid.].

## CHAPTER XXXVI. That there is no communion of good things with the wicked

[Col. 0935B]

A stranger has no share in this fountain, this holy communion. For the greedy or covetous person, or whoever is opposed to the Christian faith, is divided off. But one who communicates God’s gifts preserves undivided affections toward his neighbour. Such a one, like the dove and turtledove, receives no division: when Abraham, at the Lord’s command, divided the heifer, the she-goat, and the ram, and placed each half opposite the other [Note: [Col. 0935] Gen. 15].

Let the affection of communion from neighbour to neighbour therefore be undivided, yet never let there be consent in evil. Let one’s neighbour be loved in such a way that he is not praised in the desires of his own soul [Note: [Col. 0935] Ps. 10]. Whoever loves the sinner in this respect truly hates his neighbour. For, as we have said, love of neighbour is not genuine unless it is founded and [Col. 0935C] made firm in Christ. Christ himself is indeed the bond of our communion, strengthening among us the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace [Note: [Col. 0935] Eph. 4]. And he who, according to the saying of Job [Note: [Col. 0935] ch. 25], “makes peace in his high places,” is himself our peace, “who made both one” [Note: [Col. 0935] Eph. 4].

Therefore, following the counsel of Blessed Peter [Note: [Col. 0935] 1 Pet. 4], let us strive to have mutual charity among ourselves—charity fostered by sincere goodwill, not darkened by pretence or interrupted by suspicion. Christ impresses this upon human hearts and confirms it by example: “This,” he says, “is my commandment: that you love one another as I have loved you” [Note: [Col. 0935] John 15].

## CHAPTER XXXVII. That we are trained in love of neighbour by the mutual service of our members

Let this also be noted more carefully concerning the love of neighbour: [Col. 0935D] the very nature of our body teaches us the observance of mutual charity. For “we, though many, are one body, and each is a member of another” [Note: [Col. 0935] Rom. 12]. One Spirit gives life to all the members and joins their structure together by mutual services and reciprocal compassion.

The eye sees not merely for itself, but directs the steps of the feet. The mouth does not eat merely for itself, nor does the stomach digest for itself alone; rather, each serves the common benefit of the members. If any member is injured, the tongue, making that member’s suffering its own compassion, rebukes the injurer, saying, “Why do you hurt me?” The heart, solicitous for the common good, [Col. 0936A] arranges plans advantageous to all the members. The hands, which are not ashamed at times to serve even the lowliest members, exert themselves for the use of the common good.

If, by some chance, one hand wounds the other, the injured hand does not strike back or rise up in vengeance. Rather, the hand that inflicted the injury, as though accusing itself, applies to its wounded sister the best remedies it can; and, in humility and concern, asks that it be forgiven, removing every suspicion of malice by its diligent compassion. If, through the service of the eyes, the hand perceives a drawn sword threatening another member, it pays no attention to its own danger. Fearing more for the other than for itself, it receives the sword; and, that the other may be spared, it does not spare itself.

Let that law of communion, [Col. 0936B] written in our members, therefore be in us: that one Spirit may give life to us all as to one body; that through a true union of hearts we may abide in God and God in us; so that the whole body, through the bonds, joints, and connections of the members, may grow into the measure of the age of Christ’s fullness.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. That by God’s command we are bound to love our enemies

We are commanded to love an enemy among our neighbours, although the preceding statement seems contrary to it: “You shall hate your enemy” [Note: [Col. 0935] Matt. 5]. Divine ordering, by the wonderful art of charity, decreed this so that the human will, which is prompt to hate an enemy, might be restrained by the command of the love enjoined; and that will, which was too headlong in loving a friend, might be moderated by the judgment of the divine law [Col. 0936C] that directs hatred toward an enemy.

Concerning virginity, almsgiving, humility, surrendering possessions and giving them to the poor, visiting the sick, and other works of mercy, we have counsel from the Lord; and although these do not always carry an imposed necessity, we expect eternal recompense for them. Yet concerning love of an enemy, the Lord binds us in the Gospel by a certain and express decree of judgment, so that whoever does not love an enemy is found to be a transgressor of the divine law. “Love,” he says, “your enemies, and do good to those who hate you, and pray for those who persecute and slander you”; and, adding the measure of reward: “That you may be,” he says, “sons of your Father who is in heaven” [Note: [Col. 0935] Ibid.].

[Col. 0936D] God is supreme goodness, for love of whom you must compel your own will, so that, as he “makes his sun rise on the good and the evil” [Note: [Col. 0935] Ibid.], you may look with the same eye of grace upon friend and enemy for Christ’s sake. If you love a friend because he loves you, the law of friendship requires this; if you love a friend for Christ’s sake, this adds to your merit. But you earn God’s grace in a far more distinguished and eminent way if, mastering your own will for Christ’s sake, you love an enemy for God’s sake.

Hear what Truth says in the Gospel: “If you love those who love you, what reward shall you have? Do not even the tax collectors do this?” [Note: [Col. 0935] Ibid.]; indeed bears, lions, and lamiae (monsters) too obey nature in loving their own [Col. 0937A] [Note: [Col. 0937] Lam. 4]. But if you are Christ’s disciple or professed follower, you must do good to evildoers, bless those who curse you, and pray for those who persecute you. For the order of heavenly justice and the divine rule of equity require that those already illuminated by the sun of righteousness should pray for their adversaries’ illumination, so that those who are darkness may become light in the Lord, in accordance with the Prophet’s prayer: “For you light my lamp, O Lord; enlighten my darkness” [Note: [Col. 0937] Ps. 17].

Paul says: “Rendering evil for evil to no one” [Note: [Col. 0937] Rom. 12], “nor curse for curse” [Note: [Col. 0937] 1 Pet. 3]. Christ, as Blessed Peter testifies, suffered for us and left us an example that we might follow his footsteps [Note: [Col. 0937] 1 Pet. 2]. He prayed for those who crucified him: “Father,” he said, “forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” [Note: [Col. 0937] Luke 23]. James and Stephen [Col. 0937B] followed these footsteps [Note: [Col. 0937] Acts 7], as did very many others who, amid death’s straits, embraced their murderers with the inmost charity of their whole souls [Note: [Col. 0937] Heb. 11].

The person whom you regard as your enemy is an enemy to himself, not to you. He harms himself, not you; you suppose that he injures you, while he advances you toward innocence. For it is written [Note: [Col. 0937] Gregory, *Morals*, bk. IX, ch. 39]: “There can be no Abel whom Cain’s malice does not test.” If you repay evil for evil and curse for curse, you assert legal right in your own cause and make yourself judge in your own affair; so far as lies in you, you strip of the power of judging and repaying him to whom God the Father gave all judgment [Note: [Col. 0937] John 5], and who says, “Vengeance is mine, and I will repay” [Note: [Col. 0937] Rom. 12].

Show your enemies for Christ’s sake, therefore, [Col. 0937C] the love that you would show to those who love you. Though this may at first appear burdensome, you will gather from this love the sweetest fruits of life. It is indeed a new commandment from which this love flows. For whereas the decree of the old law commands us to love a friend and hate an enemy [Note: [Col. 0937] Matt. 5], the judgment of the new law binds us to love an enemy, not in shadow or pretence, but in deed and truth [Note: [Col. 0937] 1 John 3]. Therefore the Lawgiver, not content to say, “Love your enemies,” but plainly declaring that they are to be loved in will and deed, added: “Do good to those who hate you” [Note: [Col. 0937] Matt. 5].

And again: “If your enemy is hungry, feed him; and if he thirsts, give him drink. For by doing this you shall heap coals upon his head” [Note: [Col. 0937] Rom. 12]. The head of the inward person is reason; and, as [Col. 0937D] I think, no one is so cruel that he is not softened by benefits bestowed, that he does not come to hate hatred in response to a neighbour’s goodwill, and that he does not kindle thoughts of charity, like fiery coals, once the heat of anger has been removed.

Therefore, in the person who most grievously troubles you, love the image of God, a sharer in your nature; and hate his sin in such a way that you love the sinner. For this is the hatred of the perfect: “With perfect hatred I hated them” [Note: [Col. 0937] Ps. 138]. Recall Joseph’s charity toward his wicked brothers [Note: [Col. 0937] Gen. 45], Moses’ toward a rebellious people [Note: [Col. 0937] Exod. 32], and David’s mourning for his most grievous persecutors, Saul [Col. 0938A] and his parricidal son [Note: [Col. 0937] 2 Sam. 15 and 18]. And although Christ, the legislator of the Gospel, first promulgated the decree of this love, many of the ancient Fathers, inspired by his grace, had nevertheless humbly practised its observance.

## CHAPTER XXXIX. That, according to people’s differing conditions, there are different degrees in love

We judge this also worthy of notice: that in love of neighbour the order and rank of those who are loved or who love are often different. For it is evident that some rule over others, some are subject, and others are equal; some moreover are helpful, while others are harmful. In all these cases the judgment of discernment must be present.

A superior ought indeed to correct an inferior and, if necessary, strictly compel him to works of virtue; yet let love be present in correction and compassion be shown in compulsion. But if an inferior conducts himself lawfully in his station, he may be moved to rise to better things, but not compelled, except by salutary counsels and examples—especially if the superior knows that the inferior himself ardently desires this. [Col. 0938B] It belongs to an inferior to seek counsel from a superior in doubtful matters, to stand by respectfully, petition devoutly, and obey humbly. An equal ought to offer honourable counsel to an equal; in joy or sorrow, to show the affection of congratulation or compassion; to assist his benefit or need; mutually to foster one another by holy conversation; and to outdo one another in honour. A friend is bound to embrace in the depths of his soul and bowels of charity one who is helpful—that is, a friend.

But one who is harmful—that is, an enemy—he should endure patiently, forgive his faults mercifully, love him, and furnish him with what is necessary for God’s sake. One’s neighbour, however, must be loved in such a way that account is taken of the charity by which you love God above yourself. For if you do not love God, you love neither your neighbour nor yourself. Since therefore you are bound to love your neighbour as yourself, know that by the measure of love with which you love God you may judge how much you love your neighbour or yourself. For one who does not love God does not love himself; and if he does not love himself, neither does he love his neighbour as himself. Hence, from your love of God, you may measure with certainty the love which you have for yourself and your neighbour.

## CHAPTER XL. Whether love is lawful when, for another’s benefit, it suffers harm to the soul

[Col. 0938D]

Those greatly err who suppose that every person ought to love a neighbour in such a way that he is bound to love two people more than one, and that the quantity of love should be reckoned by the number of neighbours to be loved. Certainly it is not said, “You shall love your neighbour as much as yourself,” but “as yourself”; nor should charity’s affection be multiplied according to the multiplicity of neighbours. Otherwise I should be bound to love a hundred persons, or all humanity, more than myself—which is wholly contrary [Col. 0939A] to reason and human well-being. “For what valuation shall a person give for his soul? Or what does it profit him if he should gain the whole world, even for eternal salvation, yet suffer loss to his own soul?” [Note: [Col. 0939] Mark 8].

Nor does this judgment seem opposed by Moses’ plea for the people of Israel: “Lord, either forgive them, or blot me out of your book” [Note: [Col. 0939] Exod. 32]. Nor by the Apostle’s statement: “I once wished to be accursed from Christ for my brethren according to the flesh” [Note: [Col. 0939] Rom. 9]. For Moses loved the people with a kind of maternal affection. If a poor mother could not otherwise be admitted to food she desired unless she left her son outside, what would she say except, “Either admit my son with me, or forbid entrance to us both”? Moses indeed disclosed [Col. 0939B] the affection which he had for the people, but did not state a considered judgment. Thus the Apostle’s words too should be judged as proceeding from affection rather than from deliberative judgment.

Some understand this saying thus: that the Apostle wished to be *anathema*—separated—from Christ for his brethren, that is, from the secret place of meditation, from perseverance in prayer, and from the hidden place of contemplation. For in a sense he was separated from Christ for his brethren’s salvation: while he gave himself to prayer and contemplation and saw how sweet the Lord is [Note: [Col. 0939] Ps. 45], returning to the world’s tumult and to secular labours, he was in a sense torn away from Christ.

Certainly no command or reasoning binds anyone to procure a neighbour’s soul’s salvation by the destruction of his own soul, or the deliverance of another’s body, without hope [Col. 0939C] of eternal salvation, by the death of his own body. For the command that we lay down our lives for our brethren pertains to contempt for bodily life, not to loss of the soul for which Christ died. Thus to lay down one’s life for one’s brethren is not to lose one’s soul, but to save it.

Accordingly, those who by their own temporal death redeem their masters from death do rightly, provided that they place in question the salvation of their own souls rather than the deliverance of another’s body. Since their conscience tells them that they owe fidelity to their masters, it seems also consonant with reason that they ought to prefer their masters’ lives to their own bodily lives. But if they expose themselves to such danger in pursuit of glory rather than to preserve fidelity, they act rashly, because they have placed the reward of their blood in popular reputation alone.

For the sake of love, and especially for the salvation of many, anyone may beneficially expose his body to death. But neither reason nor the rule of love can tolerate that he should suffer the loss of his soul for the salvation of the whole world. To lose one’s soul is to depart from the love of God, to lack the vision of him, and to incur the sentence of everlasting condemnation.

## CHAPTER XLI. That the fruit of the ordered exercise of these affections is delightful and necessary

Thus one’s neighbour is to be loved so that, according to the demands of his merit or dignity, one person may be preferred to another, [Col. 0940A] and a determinate measure of order may be preserved in showing love. Therefore, according to the rank, mode, and state of orders, let the rule of love distribute to each what we owe him.

To make this clear, let us set forth an image in the loving soul, as in Noah’s ark built of incorruptible woods—that is, constructed of holy virtues—with three storeys and chambers; so that enemies and friends, strangers and intimates, may be placed in the bosom of the heart according to each one’s dignity and rank. Let us assign to the lowest receptacles the beasts—that is, persecutors raging with beastly cruelty. Since there are exterior chambers for them, we allot outward places to this class of people, who are outside.

But those who are counted with us in the profession of the same faith we by no means repel from the inner chamber; we assign them a place higher than reptiles and beasts of burden—namely, those who savour earthly things [Note: [Col. 0939] Phil. 3], or who, serving the belly or lust, rot in filth like cattle [Note: [Col. 0939] Joel 1]. To such we offer the counsel of exhortation and the whip of correction, and we give them precedence over the lower beings. Yet after those above them we extend means of life to them. To those who touch us by closeness of nature, by the humanity of duty, or by the benefit of nurture, [Col. 0940B] we entrust the inner places; the rest do not deserve the interior.

There are some who imitate neither beasts in ferocity, nor cattle in savagery, nor reptiles in the desire for earthly things, but who also do not transcend the condition of human steadiness by any virtue. Among these, the more closely someone is joined to us either by flesh or by a favour graciously received, the more inwardly should he be received into the depths of our soul and the bosom of charity.

Certainly, a place higher than those already named belongs to birds. These, rising above humankind on the wings of virtues, are higher in kind within Noah’s ark insofar as we believe them to cling more familiarly to God. Among them, those whom affection has more closely united to us in the glue of charity should be more secretly and sweetly stored in the ark of our breast, and cherished by the most exact goodwill of the heart.

Above all these rises a certain more glorious place, over which presides the builder and ruler of this ark, “fair in beauty above the children of men” [Note: [Col. 0939] Ps. 44], the “splendour and image of the substance” [Note: [Col. 0939] Heb. 1] of God the Father. Illuminating all other ranks with ineffable brightness, he “reaches from end to end mightily and orders all things sweetly” [Note: [Col. 0939] Wis. 8]. He draws the breadth of this [Col. 0940D] spiritual ark, by linear measurement, to the one cubit of his love. Before all and in all, he directs our affections into himself; claiming in the dwelling-place of our heart both the highest and the lowest place, he offers us in himself the riches of his glory with tireless and unfailing goodness.

## CHAPTER XLII. On the variety of affections, by which both the use and the fruit of love are assessed

According to this variety of ranks and degrees, diverse affections are formed, from which love derives its movement and exercise. For a clearer understanding of the affections [Col. 0941A] from which love is born, grows, and is exercised, we must see what love is; how it passes into charity or degenerates from it; or how it remains in the shapelessness of its birth.

In the judgment and estimation of some, love is a certain appetitive power of the rational soul toward things which a person chooses for enjoyment. Although this power of the soul is naturally in itself a certain good, yet by freedom of choice a person either uses this good well, aided by grace, or misuses it, abandoned by justice. Its good use, therefore, makes good love and a praiseworthy person.

Use operates in three things: choice, movement, and state. Choice arises from deliberation; movement, from desire and action; fruit is weighed from usefulness and end. It belongs to deliberation [Col. 0941B] to distinguish bitter from sweet, pleasant from harsh, Creator from creature, temporal from eternal. Thus the choice of a thing which one desires for enjoyment comes first; from that choice the soul is moved to desire, so that, when it has attained what it chose, it may enjoy it—that is, use it with delight. Thus choice is love’s beginning; the movement of desire, its act; and the end or usefulness, its fruit.

If, therefore, the mind chooses for enjoyment what it ought, is moved to desire it as it should, and enjoys it as it ought, then such a beloved choice, such a fitting movement, and such a healthful and desirable fruit are rightly called charity. Thus charity begins in choice, is exercised in movement, and is perfected in enjoyment. But if the mind chooses imprudently, is moved improperly, and misuses shamefully, from these arises, grows strong, and is perfected covetousness.

You have, then, two springs: two origins or roots of good and evil. For charity is the root of all good things, [Col. 0941C] and covetousness the root of all evil things [Note: [Col. 0939] 1 Tim. 6]. Further, one whose deliberation is more circumspect, understanding purer, and eye of reason keener, considers how greatly a human being surpasses every other creature; how everything desirable in the world entangles a human being more intricately in miseries than it advances him toward the state of blessedness; and measures in every respect the privileges of his dignity. Such a person sees how beneficially the divine law commands a person to serve him alone, “whom to serve is to reign,” and to desire that alone in which alone supreme blessedness lies.

Therefore, rejecting temporal riches and pleasures, avarice, idolatry, and money, he renders devoted service solely to him concerning whom sacred Scripture commands: “You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve” [Note: [Col. 0939] Deut. 6; Matt. 4]. Since, therefore, a human being understands that the divine nature is so great, so holy, so sublime, and so pre-eminent that it alone can make a human being blessed, he chooses God especially for enjoyment, seeing rightly that singular service is owed to him. Thus love of God begins; thus it advances through the exercise of desire, until at last it is converted into the enjoyment of desire. Therefore the divine law establishes and writes in the human heart the first commandment concerning love: “You shall love,” it says, “the Lord your God” [Note: [Col. 0939] Deut. 30].

## CHAPTER XLIII. On movement toward desire

[Col. 0942A]

We have already touched upon how, in choosing things that hold out a shadowy image of happiness, a spirit of dizziness and error agitates some people. It remains to explain more carefully how and by what aids the mind is moved toward the choice of things to be desired. For movement occurs either inwardly toward desire or outwardly toward action: toward desire, when we are moved and attracted to enjoyment by a certain inward appetite; toward action, when we are compelled to outward action by a certain affection of love.

It should be observed that love is more strongly stirred by certain things, either toward desire or toward action; these direct love’s course and prescribe for it a whole diversity of forms according to their varied character. There are chiefly two things which move and excite the soul toward desire and action, and imprint diverse forms upon it: affection and reason. For sometimes affection alone stimulates love, sometimes reason stimulates it either to outward action or to inward appetite.

Affection is a spontaneous, sweet, and pleasant inclination of the mind toward something. One affection is spiritual, another rational, another irrational, another arising from service, and another natural.

## CHAPTER XLIV. On spiritual movement, which is twofold

Spiritual movement occurs when God, by a hidden infusion of grace and inspiration, or by someone’s word, [Col. 0942C] example, or the fatherly scourge of correction, invites someone to love what is honourable and beneficial and inspires the desire to reform one’s life. Spiritual movement occurs also in the contrary direction, when God permits impulses to be made upon one whom he rejects through evil angels. Thus a wretched person sinks into unlawful acts. As the prophet says concerning some: “A spirit of fornication deceived them” [Note: [Col. 0939] Hos. 4].

Unless I am mistaken, Amnon, David’s son, loosened by an evil spirit’s prompting into an affection for harmful pleasure [Note: [Col. 0939] 2 Sam. 13], burned with desire for the embrace of his own sister; and, defiling the house of so great a father by incest, he provoked his brother’s sword against himself and finally sowed the occasion and material for the future parricide by which the unhappy Absalom, desiring the kingdom, was to assail his father.

## CHAPTER XLV. On rational movement

[Col. 0942D]

A rational affection is one which proceeds from consideration of another’s virtue. This affection, upon hearing at times of the triumphant suffering of martyrs, floods the hearers’ hearts with a most sweet devotion. For who, hearing in the memory of Blessed Paul of “dangers from rivers, dangers from robbers,” and the other things too lengthy to recount [Note: [Col. 0939] 2 Cor. 11]; and, beyond this, the voice of a strong athlete, the voice of virtue—of a man trained in all things, in all things ready through him who strengthens him to be satisfied and hungry, to abound and suffer need, ready to be bound at Jerusalem, to lay down his life for his brethren, and desiring [Col. 0943A] “to be dissolved and to be with Christ” [Note: [Col. 0943] Phil. 17]—who, I say, can set these things down in earnest recollection within the soul without being moved by a certain grateful and sweet affection?

Who, recalling the words of constancy in Blessed Lawrence, blessed Vincent, and the other martyrs, as though sparkling from an enkindled heart, is not inflamed toward them with the sweetest love and ready devotion? This affection consecrated the first fruits of most sweet love between David and Jonathan, and bound the bond of social grace in the weightiest covenant of mutual charity, never to be dissolved by paternal change. For the sight in the young man of steadfast, unchangeable integrity—by which an unarmed boy overthrew an armoured giant [Note: [Col. 0943] 1 Sam. 17]—was in Jonathan an increase of virtue, though in others it might have been the seed of envy.

[Col. 0943B] Therefore, according to Scripture’s testimony, Jonathan’s soul was bound to David’s soul, and Jonathan loved him as his own soul [Note: [Col. 0943] 1 Sam. 18]. Jesus himself mercifully transformed this affection in himself when, looking upon the young man who had declared his virtues to him, as the Evangelist says [Note: [Col. 0943] Matt. 19], he loved him.

Contrary to this affection is the irrational affection, which, upon learning of someone’s vice, shameful skill, utterly vain philosophy, or foolish boldness in military matters, inclines others to an undue love of him. More remarkably still, it gives abundant favour and applause to many because they are profligate, or talkative, or detractors hateful to God, or followers of buffoonery or worldly folly.

## CHAPTER XLVI. On affection arising from service

[Col. 0943C]

We call that affection “official” which is won by service or gifts. Moses, indeed, when he fled from Pharaoh’s wickedness, by a memorable service won the affection of the priest of Midian [Note: [Col. 0943] Exod. 2]: although a foreigner, he had manfully protected the priest’s virgin daughters from the insolence of the shepherds. Admiring the young man’s goodwill, the priest desired him to become not only his friend but also his son-in-law.

Moreover, when King David fled from Absalom [Note: [Col. 0943] 2 Sam. 17], Barzillai the Gileadite received him with most dutiful devotion and won his affection also by gifts. This attachment remained so steadfastly in David’s mind that, when about to depart this life, the king immediately directed his son Solomon, among his testamentary commands, to recompense such generosity [Col. 0943D] [Note: [Col. 0943] 1 Kgs. 2].

## CHAPTER XLVII. On natural affection
### CHAPTER XLVII. On Natural Affection

There is also a natural affection of a husband for his wife, of a mother for her son, and of a person for one of his own household and blood. “No one ever hated his own flesh” [Note: [Col. 0943] Eph. 5.]; and a mother cannot forget her infant so as not to have compassion on the son of her womb [Note: [Col. 0943] Isa. 49.]; and whoever does not provide for his own, especially for members of his household, has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever [Note: [Col. 0943] 1 Tim. 5.]. Led by this affection, the ancient fathers are said to have bound their descendants by solemn charges to bury their bodies, not among strangers, but in the tombs of their fathers [Col. 0944A] [Note: [Col. 0943] Gen. 49.], so that those whose souls had been united by the bond of charity might have their bodies also united by the benefit of burial.

Wise Solomon judged that a mother’s affection should be tested in the dispute between the two prostitutes by means of the sword. When, upon the sword being brought, the king’s wisdom had decreed the division of the child, natural affection disclosed the mother. Thus she yielded to affection, though she had not yielded to wickedness; and she who had striven not to be deprived in vain of her own child pleaded that he should rather be handed over to her enemy. “I beseech you,” she said, “give her the living child, and let him not be killed” [Note: [Col. 0943] 3 Kings 3.]. Conversely, she who, devoid of maternal compassion, had hardened herself to the loss of the other’s child said: “Let him be neither mine nor yours, but divided” [Note: [Col. 0943] Ibid.].

Moreover, natural affection in the breast of holy Joseph outweighed the fratricidal [Col. 0944B] wrong. When [Note: [Col. 0943] Gen. 42.] he charged his brothers, with the sternness of a steward, with the crime of spying, he saw them tortured by their belated repentance for betraying their brother. Following his affection, he turned away from them for a while and burst into tears.

Not even the savagery of David’s persecuting son erased this affection from David’s devout heart. Though he himself was being sought for death by him, David forgot the injury and remembered nature: he sent men to meet his son’s madness, showing himself a father in all things and overlooking the persecution of his murderous son. “Preserve for me the young man Absalom,” he said [Note: [Col. 0943] 2 Kings 18.].

The Savior himself transferred this affection into himself in pitiful compassion. Seeing the city which was his own metropolis, and from which the fathers were his according to [Col. 0944C] the flesh, he was moved by natural pity and lamented its future destruction [Note: [Col. 0943] Luke 19.]. I also think that Paul, pierced by natural affection, at one time wished himself to be accursed from Christ for the sake of his brothers according to the flesh [Note: [Col. 0943] Rom. 9.].

### CHAPTER XLVIII. On Carnal Affection

Very closely related to natural affection is carnal affection, which is divided in two ways. For often a person’s virtue or vice is not weighed; rather, the mind of the observer, moved by some outward bearing of the person, is inclined to love someone. For example, if there is greater elegance of appearance, greater polish of speech, more suitable dress, or a dignified gait.

Such grace shone in Moses while he was still a child [Note: [Col. 0943] Exod. 2.] to such a degree that, despite Pharaoh’s tyrannical decree [Col. 0944D] ordering the Hebrew males to be killed, he was preserved by his parents for three months, as the Apostle says, because they saw that the infant was beautiful [Note: [Col. 0943] Heb. 11.]. Finally, when he was exposed to the danger of death, the beauty of his form drew forth the compassion of Pharaoh’s daughter. Having been adopted as a son, he became great before all Pharaoh’s servants.

There is another carnal affection, which softens the human mind toward the desire for harmful pleasure. It caught David off guard as he walked on the roof of his house, before the sight of Bathsheba [Col. 0945A] [Note: [Col. 0945] 2 Kings 11.]; having caught him, it weakened him; having weakened him, it overwhelmed him; and the man whom it emboldened for the condemnable embrace of another’s wife, it armed, by a contrary impulse, for the cruel death of his own soldier. This affection swallowed up Solomon’s wisdom [Note: [Col. 0945] Ibid.], and, having dissolved him in carnal lust, the detestable worship of idols cast him down into the abyss of spiritual fornication.

### CHAPTER XLIX. That Affection without Consent Is Neither Greatly Beneficial nor Harmful

In all these affections one must proceed with prudent moderation. Since they are certain origins or roots of love excited by them, we judge that they are neither greatly beneficial if good nor ruinous if evil. For affection is not love, but the origin of love.

For many frequently misuse to their destruction that spiritual affection which we placed first [Col. 0945B] among the affections of the soul; while by this final affection, namely the carnal one, although it is considered more suspect than the others, even very righteous people are stirred toward the merit of testing. Therefore, we do not judge it beneficial or harmful simply to be moved by these affections. For when these affections move the mind, there is either a visitation or a temptation, provided that, without the mind’s consent, they still remain in their unformed state. But if the mind is moved in accordance with its affections as one desiring, then the will has already fully consented.

Consent is either hidden and occupies the interior, or manifest and is exercised outwardly even to action. Whether the human mind ought to be moved to love in accordance with the aforesaid affections, in what manner, and [Col. 0945C] with how much moderation, will be declared more fully in what follows.

But since we have set down two, as it were, incentives and courses of love—affection and reason—it is fitting, for greater clarity, to say something concerning the movement of reason. For reason often moves a mind which no affection stirs to the love of God and neighbor; and it does so with greater holiness, safety, and purity, inasmuch as nothing is more excellent than rational love.

### CHAPTER L. That Rational Affection Is Aroused in Three Ways

To stir a languishing mind toward the desire of its Creator, reason relies on three arguments: our necessity, our advantage, and God’s worthiness. Reason counsels that God must be loved because this is necessary for us, profitable for us, [Col. 0945D] and worthy of him: necessary, lest we be condemned; profitable, that we may be saved; and worthy, because he himself first loved us and requires from us the return of this love.

Since God is the highest good, without whom nothing is good, he must be desired: he does not need our goods, while we continually need his benefits. Therefore, if reason has begun to move the mind toward love of God, it pursues its task, knowing that it cannot attain what it desires unless it obeys his commandments as proof of true love.

And since reason considers how greatly it is bound to love one who shares our nature, not only by its own judgment but by divine command, [Col. 0946A] it directs its purpose toward providing for its neighbor; and, bestowing upon him the benefit it would wish bestowed upon itself, it recognizes in him the image of its Creator. Since every neighbor is either our friend, not our enemy, or even our enemy: a friend is served by help or counsel; one who is not an enemy, by not harming him; an enemy, by doing him service. You see that a friend is such by blood or grace; one who is not an enemy, by innocence; and an enemy, by injury.

Therefore, for a person to devote himself to a friend, reason proposes three grounds; to assist one who is not an enemy, two; to aid an enemy, one. Benefit is owed to a neighbor for three reasons: by nature, by service, and by command. By nature, because he is a human being, or perhaps a member of one’s household. By service, because he is beneficent and a friend. By command, because he is a neighbor, even if an enemy. [Col. 0946B] For reason embraces God’s command by which he commanded that an enemy be loved. One who loves on this rational basis does not lose the merit of charity, even if he has no affection in that love.

### CHAPTER LI. That Rational Affection Is Aroused in Three Ways

Since the order of charity and the rule of loving require that a person neither love what ought not to be loved nor fail to love what ought to be loved, and that he not love equally or in the same manner things which ought to be loved unequally or differently, I judge that a subtle and careful distinction must be made between the two loves which proceed from affection and reason.

Let two persons be proposed. One is calm, agreeable, cheerful, wise, and polished, and by the attractiveness of his human character wins everyone’s [Col. 0946C] love. The other is more serious in character, more mature and advanced, but sterner in face, sadder in expression, and harsher in speech. The observer’s affection moves him to love the former; reason and the consideration of charity compel him to love the latter.

Knowing therefore that his mind is steeped in a certain sweetness of love at the sight of the first, while his own heart inclines at the sight of the second, a person is perplexed and fears that the spirit may be required to exceed the bounds of charity. Yet when I have begun to love someone because I believed him conspicuous for holy and moral sweetness, and discover him to be vicious in some respect, a certain regret begins to consume the affection of my incipient love; and because of the vice he becomes contemptible to me, though the reputation of virtue had made him pleasing.

### CHAPTER LII. Comparisons between the Affection of Love and the Appetite for Food or Desire for Speech

[Col. 0946D]

Let us suppose that there are two kinds of food for the soul, namely virtue and vice, one food beneficial and the other harmful. Let a person’s exterior austerity or kindness be like two vessels, one rustic and the other refined, in which the two foods are served. Beneficial food is knowingly taken even in vessels that are often unattractive; harmful food is admitted not even in precious vessels. It also happens that inferior food is sometimes received more pleasantly because of the beauty of the vessels, while the most precious food, because of the forbidding aspect of the vessels, is either not accepted or is taken only with difficulty.

[Col. 0947A] Thus in a stern and grave person, a harsher manner may sometimes please because it proceeds from his virtue; while in another person, who is polished in manner, his refined pleasantness displeases because of his vice, although it had formerly been an occasion of love.

Suppose again that truth, virtue, and pleasantness are considered as the strength of speech; that excessive severity of manners is like unpolished and rustic speech; and that a person’s outward benevolence is seasoned with a certain charm like speech more eloquent and more effective in moving its hearer. You see that, just as sweetness is not to be admitted in pleasant conversation when it lacks truth, so truth is not to be despised in harsh and rustic speech. To state the comparison plainly: vice does not please in a person outwardly gentle and agreeable; nor does virtue please in a hard and severe person when it turns into weariness.

[Col. 0947B] But if each is known to commend what is true and salutary, the former’s speech, even when crude and unpolished, is received unwillingly, while in the latter’s prudent and polished presentation the salutary judgment is received with pleasure. Speech may indeed be so disconnected, disjointed, and inept that, although it contains very great usefulness, what is heard nevertheless burdens the listener with weariness.

Finally, just as eloquence in youth is usually livelier, more cheerful, and readier, so in old age it is weightier, more cautious, and altogether more mature. Neither does the cheerfulness of the former pass into the vice of dissipation, nor does the mature gravity of the latter incur the vice of excessive harshness.

A person, therefore, is loved from affection alone when we judge him lovable from his outward bearing; but where virtue alone is the cause of loving, we love from reason alone. [Col. 0947C] If reason and affection meet in one will, this is a third love, distinguished above the others by a certain pre-eminent privilege. The first affection is sweet but dangerous; the second harsh but fruitful; the third, arising from affection and reason, is secure. In the first, sense draws the mind by sweetness; in the second, manifest reason compels it; in the third, reason itself is sweetened by affection.

### CHAPTER LIII. Affections Are Discerned from Love

From the sequence of what has preceded, you may infer that if there is a perverse choice in the things we choose for enjoyment, then what follows from that choice will be perverse, so that such love is rightly called not charity but cupidity. Moreover, the choice itself may be sound while the inward and outward movement is perverse. [Col. 0947D] Finally, both the choice and the movement belonging to desire may proceed from reason, while the movement in action may corrupt by its own corruption both the choice and the inward movement.

Suppose, for instance, that someone chooses God as the object of enjoyment but places something carnal in the enjoyment itself, as Jewish tales imagine: that in the future life they will abound in banquets and pleasures of the flesh, and that the flesh of Behemoth will never fail in that abundance of delights. The choice was indeed commendable, but the pernicious expectation of desire contaminates its goodness.

Just as this inward movement of desire makes the choice blameworthy, so sometimes does outward action—for example, if a person strives to attain the fruit of life by the sacrifices [Col. 0948A] of the Gentiles, Jewish ceremonies, or some superstition. But if the choice is sound, the desire fitting, and the action commendable, then regulated love follows and has not strayed beyond the boundary of charity.

Such love will therefore be affectionate, discerning, and strong: it clings sweetly, wisely, and perseveringly to the thing loved; through its sweetness it overcomes whatever is sweet or desirable in this life; against Satan’s wiles and hidden temptations it sets the counsel of discernment; and through its strength it rises against persecutions.

### CHAPTER LIV. As in Love of God, So Also in Love of Neighbor Choice Has a Place

Nearly the same points must be noted concerning the love of neighbor. For if some shameful desire [Col. 0948B] or blameworthy action follows the choice belonging to that love, the integrity of the choice itself is thereby violated.

And this must be considered: in loving God, we provide for ourselves, not for God. God does not need our goods. But in love of neighbor, because we need mutual help, it is fitting that we provide for one another in matters pertaining to bodily necessity and the salvation of the soul. The more fervent anyone is in these matters, the more perfect he is in charity.

This love too is sometimes moved by affection and sometimes by reason. Therefore, careful consideration must be given to which affection, and to what extent, a person ought to follow. Certainly, spiritual affection arising from diabolical suggestion, as well as irrational and carnal affection, which no one doubts are vicious, must not [Col. 0948C] only not be followed but must be uprooted entirely from our hearts. Accordingly, spiritual affection which is from God must in every way be aroused and beneficially fostered.

### CHAPTER LV. What Action of Ours Is Not to Be Performed Following Spiritual Affection

By this affection, our desire ought to be stirred more fervently. Our action too must be stirred by the same affection, but cannot be ordered according to it. The more fervent the will to do good, the more fruitful it will always be. But if this affection directs our activity, the activity will be disordered, because it exceeds the limits of bodily capacity.

Since this body is of an earthly nature and, by its frailty, liable to diverse sufferings, [Col. 0948D] it cannot bear the force of fervent affection. Therefore, unless outward action is tempered by some moderation, it will fail or collapse before the undertaking it has assumed is completed. Affection surely knows no measure, does not gauge the body’s strength, and, rushing with a kind of force toward the beloved, thinks only of what it desires. Enticed by the sweetest delight, it does not perceive what is burdensome, arduous, painful, impossible, or, finally, destructive of the present life.

Accordingly, certain persons, ignorant of all moderation in this affection and rashly and importunately following the impulse of their own desire, are weaker rather than holier, since the will itself, oppressed by excessive affection, grows lukewarm. A person who ought to have adjusted his mind, in accordance with the dispensation of his [Col. 0949A] strength, to withstand every assault of suffering, turns back on the day of battle; and where victory depended upon virtue, there he succumbs through his rashness.

### CHAPTER LVI. That Our Action Must Sometimes Be Directed according to Rational Affection, but Not Always

Rational affection, arising from contemplation of another’s virtue, is more perfect than the other affections by which we are stirred to love our neighbor. Love of virtue itself is no slight indication of virtue, and emulation of the better gifts results in great merit. I do not think that our desire, or inward movement, ought to be criticized if directed according to this affection; rather, it is considered commendable.

If someone [Col. 0949B] desires the presence of one by whose word he is instructed, whose gesture and bearing educate him, and whose example forms him, nevertheless, I pray, that movement should not pass into action in such a way that he is physically troubled for a long and unbroken period on this account. Those whom we cannot visit bodily, let us behold with the eye of the heart and embrace with the arms of holy affections. For as heaven is more worthy than earth, so spiritual sight is more excellent than bodily sight.

Indeed, in civil law, possession in the mind is superior to natural possession—that is, to bodily occupation—for it is not so easily lost, nor is ownership acquired through it by prescription. Finally, Christ requires from Mary a spiritual touch of faith when he forbids her bodily touch [Note: [Col. 0949] John 20.]. Of this touch or sight of faith [Col. 0949C] Paul says: “Even if we have known Christ according to the flesh, yet now we know him so no longer” [Note: [Col. 0949] 2 Cor. 5.].

Thomas, in unbelief, puts his hand into Christ’s right side and the wounds of the nails; but he touches more excellently and fruitfully through faith when he says: “My Lord and my God” [Note: [Col. 0949] John 20]. It is as though he said: It is more glorious now to see Christ by faith than it was to have seen him mortal in the flesh.

That presence, however, which we await in heavenly dwelling is especially to be considered. If we desire the eternal presence of the saints, it is fitting that we live holily, justly, and devoutly in this age. This bodily presence of the saints is indeed usefully desired, but is not always usefully sought. Therefore not affection but reason should regulate this action.

[Col. 0949D] The bodily presence of Paul and Barnabas was most welcome to the Antiochenes, who were strengthened in faith by their teaching, conference, and disputation. Yet when they heard from the Holy Spirit, “Set apart for me Barnabas and Paul for the work to which I have called them,” although affection resisted, reason prevailed; and, laying hands upon them, they sent them away [Note: [Col. 0949] Acts 13.].

### CHAPTER LVII. That Official Affection, Though Dangerous, Is Sometimes Commendable

Official affection follows. Although it may be admitted, it is admitted dangerously. It is fitting indeed, and consonant with reason, that we return a service [Col. 0950A] to a serving hand and thanks to one who gives. Yet one must take the greatest care not to favor a vicious person in his vice because one has been enticed by service or softened by gifts.

I am not speaking of those who love gifts and pursue recompense, who make justice a thing for sale and favor not persons but gifts. We speak of those who loved the person before his gifts: who did not love the person because of the gifts, but loved the gifts because of the person. Yet even here there is room for suspicion: lest, fearing to be ungrateful for his services, one become complicit in his vices.

Therefore, the condition of the person loved must be carefully examined, so that, if he has sufficient merit to be worthy of affectionate love, official affection may pass into rational affection. The person whom we loved because of benefits rendered, [Col. 0950B] we may begin to love because of virtue. Thus, just as we sometimes loved reasonably but not sweetly a stern and grave person, if he shows himself generous and kind, he who formerly pleased but did not delight now pours himself, as it were, into our desire with sweet affection.

### CHAPTER LVIII. What Measure Ought to Be Kept in Natural Affection

Let us now proceed to ask what measure ought to be kept in natural affection. As it is impossible not to admit this affection, so it is the highest virtue not to follow it. The family affection of parents is restrained when a chosen disciple, recalled from his parent’s [Col. 0950C] burial, hears the Lord say: “Let the dead bury their dead; but go and proclaim the kingdom of God” [Note: [Col. 0949] Matt. 8.].

Love of oneself is a certain portion of natural affection. “No one ever hated himself” [Note: [Col. 0949] Eph. 5.]; yet Truth says: “Whoever comes to me and does not hate his own life cannot be my disciple” [Note: [Col. 0949] Luke 14.]. And again: “Whoever comes to me and does not hate father and mother cannot be my disciple” [Note: [Col. 0949] Ibid.].

But since the Apostle seems to say the opposite—namely, that one who does not provide for his own, especially for members of his household, is to be judged an unbeliever and transgressor against the faith [Note: [Col. 0949] 1 Tim. 5.]—what shall we say in so great a contradiction? A distinction must be made between these loves. Though a person is moved toward himself and his own by natural affection, he must nevertheless [Col. 0950D] regulate that affection by reason.

That this affection arises from the flesh, the Apostle testifies when he says: “No one ever hated his own flesh” [Note: [Col. 0949] Eph. 5.]. Yet the Lord prohibits this affection toward oneself, one’s parents, and one’s own life, where it is usually more inclined: “Whoever does not hate father and mother, and even his own life, cannot be my disciple” [Note: [Col. 0949] Luke 14.].

But the measure of love according to reason is prescribed by apostolic authority: “Whoever does not provide for his own, especially for members of his household, has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever” [Note: [Col. 0949] 1 Tim. 5.]. For this love follows reason rather than affection, so that in one’s household member one considers nature, necessity, or the estimation of merits.

That affection toward oneself and one’s parents suggests the movement of unlawful love may be gathered from the Apostle’s words. Writing to Timothy, he says: “Know this: in the last days dangerous times will come, and people will be lovers of themselves, covetous, puffed up, without peace, slanderers, incontinent, swollen with pride and insolent, [Col. 0951A] lovers of pleasures more than of God” [Note: [Col. 0951] 2 Tim. 3.]. For this affection suggests what is soft and most pleasant, delicate, tender, and enjoyable; but it flees and abhors what is arduous, harsh, useful, and honorable.

The Savior distinguishes both movements of love, according to affection and according to reason, in a short saying: “Whoever loves his life [Col. 0951B] will lose it. Whoever hates his life in this world will keep it for eternal life” [Note: [Col. 0951] John 12.]. This love is that of affection; this hatred, that of reason. Therefore a holy man says [Note: [Col. 0951] Augustine, *Tractates on John*, 51]: “If you love badly, then you hate; if you hate well, then you love.” For one who loves according to affection surely hates, because one who loves his belly hates his soul. But one who hates according to affection loves according to reason.

The words “in this world” are added in order that the affection may be expressed more strongly. For everything in this world, according to the testimony of blessed John, is either the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eyes, or the pride of life [Note: [Col. 0951] 1 John 2.]. Whoever therefore loves his life according to affection certainly loves it in this world, because he loves it in the desire [Col. 0951C] of the flesh, the desire of the eyes, or the pride of life—all of which proceed from affection.

### CHAPTER LIX. On the Diverse Causes of Affections

It should be noted that one kind of love is love in God, another is love for God’s sake. Someone is loved for his own sake when his virtues stir a person to love him; and such a person is loved neither for God’s sake nor in God. Yet if this love regards the divine goodness with thanksgiving, then the cause of this love is no longer affection but reason. And although he is not loved particularly for God’s sake, that love is nevertheless beneficially exercised by God.

But an enemy, whom reason and the authority of the divine command teach us to love, does not deserve to be loved for his own sake; he is loved for God’s sake. Thus we are bound by sound reason to love some for their own sake, as the righteous; others [Col. 0951D] in God, as friends; and others for God’s sake, as enemies.

It is fitting, therefore, that this natural affection in all things and through all things be guided by the moderation of reason, so that, if it is at first soft and sweet, it may be made somewhat harder by reason’s assistance. The patriarch Joseph first showed his natural affection for his brothers by tears; then, so that they might be purified from the crime of betrayal, he charged them with espionage [Note: [Col. 0951] Gen. 42.]. The Savior likewise first lamented the city of Jerusalem with deepest compassion and, after this outpouring of natural affection, foretold the calamities which it had deserved for its iniquities [Note: [Col. 0951] Luke 19.].

We [Col. 0952A] therefore embrace our neighbors beneficially with natural affection if they are honorable; but if we know that they suffer from some vice, let us persist in correcting them, so that, as we distinguished in official affection, careful discernment may prevent us from being stained by any consent to another’s vice.

### CHAPTER LX. That One Affection Is Sometimes Changed into Another

It often happens that one affection ends or is changed into another, and that one which began from virtue frequently has a vicious outcome.
