There was in our region a virgin renowned for abstinences, persistence in prayer, tears, vigils, and disciplines. A holy man began to love her because of her virtue and the high reputation she possessed. He began to visit her through messengers, honor her with gifts, and refresh her with [Col. 0952B] conversations. Mutual love began to burn between them through mutual services. Thus love, whose cause had been uprightness, began to flourish through mutual generosity and suddenly passed into official affection, though it had proceeded from reason alone.

Finally, as this affection stretched itself more familiarly toward certain caresses, that carnal affection—more ruinous than the rest—began secretly to creep in from natural and official affection.

We have heard of certain people of the highest perfection and most proven reputation who admitted chaste young persons, conspicuous for every virtue, to greater familiarity through love of virtue and the consideration of reason. Because services were diligently rendered to them, rational affection began to degenerate into another: first into official affection, [Col. 0952C] then into carnal affection. A person who had formerly ordered the measure of his love according to reason’s judgment, being captivated by his own eyes, was thereafter stirred by unlawful desire whenever he looked upon such a person, even for a reason or in passing.

It is therefore more prudent, considering age or sex, to close the recesses of one’s own mind with watchful circumspection, lest it be allowed to flow into familiar words or empty caresses. For even in persons however perfect and holy, one affection is secretly, suddenly, imperceptibly, and as ruinously as astonishingly changed into another.

### CHAPTER LXI. That Affections Are Often Opposed and Fight One Another

We must consider that affections themselves often become estranged from one another and fight each other. [Col. 0952D] Each tries to drive the other from the human heart, so that a person, divided and perplexed among various desires, may fluctuate within himself amid uncertainties, not knowing which of two contrary things he ought rather to choose.

Therefore the greatest care must be taken lest the lower affection expel the higher and more excellent. Abraham, commanded by the Lord to sacrifice his son, did not harden himself against natural affection [Note: [Col. 0951] Gen. 21.]. Natural affection suggested mercy toward his son, but spiritual affection stirred him to obedience toward God. These two affections fought in the holy man’s breast; nevertheless, he preferred God to his son and set natural affection after spiritual affection.

[Col. 0953A] The excellent youth Jonathan [Note: [Col. 0953] 1 Kings 18.], whose soul rational affection had united to David’s soul by the bond of charity, did not betray David to his father’s hostile purpose, by which Saul had condemned David to death; but he discreetly preferred rational affection to natural affection. Nor is it surprising that he preferred the favor of his friend to his father’s cruelty [Note: [Col. 0953] 1 Kings 19 and 20.], since, as was publicly believed, he had despised his own injury on behalf of his friend with unchanging virtue.

David himself, when the people had won victory over his parricidal son, having first displayed natural affection, preferred official affection to natural affection. Setting aside his grief, he went out rejoicing to meet the victorious people who had made peace in Israel [Note: [Col. 0953] 2 Kings 18 and 19.].

The Savior also, in view of natural affection—by which no one ever hated his own flesh [Note: [Col. 0953] Eph. 5.]—when he cried to the Father that the cup of death might pass from [Col. 0953B] him, if possible, submitted that same affection to spiritual affection, through which he was obedient to the Father, for his own grace and for our salvation, saying: “Nevertheless, not as I will, but as you will” [Note: [Col. 0953] Matt. 26.].

Accordingly, this general rule should be observed in these affections: the affection by which the human mind is stirred toward God must be preferred to all the rest; then rational affection to official, official to natural, and natural to carnal.

### CHAPTER LXII. That the Fruit in the Ordered Exercise of These Affections Is Delightful and Necessary

Let the rational soul therefore exercise itself in these affections with prudent circumspection, and let it think of the Lord in goodness and simplicity of heart. Let it strive to make itself, with such vigilance, a wine-cellar and receptacle of divine fire that, on the Lord’s favorable day and in the hour of his good pleasure, when it hears the voice of the Spirit and the holy whisper like the sound of a gentle breeze, it may offer a pure affection and faithful understanding, and may deserve to gather spiritual fruits as from the tree of life.

The fruits, according to the Apostle’s testimony, are charity, [Col. 0953C] joy, peace, patience, long-suffering, goodness, kindness, gentleness, faith, modesty, and chastity [Note: [Col. 0953] Gal. 5.]. O happy soul, if you are permitted to experience by sure indications his good will, the inspiration of heavenly grace, and his presence with you! For at the recollection of him a certain sweetness will touch you; you will be affected by a new and untried delight, so that, as though carried away and wholly alienated from yourself, you may exult in a certain heavenly loveliness.

The proof of his presence immediately appears in this: [Col. 0953D] all your senses grow cheerful, your understanding is made serene, your desires grow warm, and you breathe toward the embrace of him whom you feel yourself holding and fear may slip away. Therefore, as much as you can, though not as much as you wish, you bind him with a delightful bond of inward charity.

This, O soul, is your beloved, invisibly, mercifully, and graciously approaching: to awaken you; to breathe himself into the bosom of your love; to make himself known to you; to kindle your desire; to enlighten your inward eyes; to inflame your affection. He offers you the first-fruits [Col. 0954A] of his sweetness, not its fullness—not unto satiety, but unto tasting—so that by whatever experience you may prove how sweet, pleasant, joyful, and delightful he will show himself to you when his glory appears, when you see him, his face unveiled, crowned with the diadem of his Father, whom you now adore in the diadem of his mother.

This is sobriety—sober, nevertheless. Hence the Apostle: “Whether we live or whether we die” [Note: [Col. 0953] Rom. 14.], “we are sober unto God” [Note: [Col. 0953] 2 Cor. 5.]. This intoxication alone is produced by the wine of charity, as the Bridegroom intimates in the Song of Love, saying: “Eat, friends, drink, and be intoxicated” [Note: [Col. 0953] Song 5.].

In the present life, the soul doing battle for God eats the bread of tears in the sweat of its face [Note: [Col. 0953] Gen. 3.]. After departing this life, it will not be fed with the bread of sorrow, because sorrow and labor will no longer exist, because the former [Col. 0954B] things have passed away [Note: [Col. 0953] John 21.]. Instead, it will be refreshed and intoxicated by the cup of love, according to the words: “My intoxicating cup—how splendid it is!” [Note: [Col. 0953] Ps. 22.].

I believe Isaiah also spoke of this cup when he said: “To you also, daughter of Edom, the cup has come, and you shall be intoxicated” [Note: [Col. 0953] Lam. 4.]. The soul, then, will be intoxicated by the abundance of God’s house, drinking pure and new wine in the kingdom of Christ’s Father. Meanwhile, it drinks its wine with tears and in measure, until the king brings it into the wine-cellar, or makes it itself a cellar for himself [Note: [Col. 0953] Song 2.], and orders charity within it.

For now it loves, but does not yet receive the fruit of love; and, exercising itself only in affections, it does not say, “I am wounded by charity.” Rather, it speaks to the angels and souls of the saints, saying: “I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, if you find my beloved, tell him that [Col. 0954C] I languish with love” [Note: [Col. 0953] Song 5.].

### CHAPTER LXIII. That Charity, While It Exists in Desire, Is Languor
Yet it is remarkable how love or charity can be the languor of the bride or of the soul, when charity covers a multitude of sins [Note: [Col. 0953] Jas. 5]; and when Mary Magdalene, because she loved much, was healed from the assault of seven demons and from the sickness of seven capital sins [Note: [Col. 0953] Luke 7; Mark 16]. Indeed, love is languor while the lover is tormented by the postponement of desire, while she longs for the Bridegroom’s embraces. But you who heal all your infirmities, O my soul, will cure your languor by fruition, when he offers himself to you to possess, to behold, and to enjoy with unveiled face; and henceforth you shall never be separated from his [Col. 0954D] sight or embrace. Truly the Bridegroom shall rejoice over the bride; your God shall rejoice over you. Then the fruit of love shall exclude the anguish of languor; for languor will pass away, but love will not, because charity never fails [Note: [Col. 0953] 1 Cor. 13].

Therefore love is now languor while it is tortured by the desire for enjoyment; but it will be health when it delights in the enjoyment it has desired. For the desire of enjoyment differs from its enjoyment as hunger from satiety, as appetite from the fulfilment of desire. Meanwhile [Col. 0955A] she is grievously sick and consumed by languor, while he supports her upon the bed of her pain. The voice of one languishing and weeping is: “Sustain me with apples; strengthen me with flowers, for I languish with love” [Note: [Col. 0955] Song 2].

The beginnings of virtues are flowers, and their fruits are honour and uprightness. The riper apples, however, are exercises and examples of patience. Thus the soul is sustained with apples when it receives the fruits of time past, turning to its own benefit Christ’s scourges, reproaches, and sufferings, and all else that he endured even to the shame of the cross; and all these things have passed away. For Christ now dies no more [Note: [Col. 0955] Rom. 6], yet every day we gather fruit from his Passion. The bride is strengthened with the flowers which the renewal of human nature brought forth from Christ’s resurrection. For winter has passed, the rain [Col. 0955B] has gone and departed, and flowers have appeared in our land. This is he who says: “I am the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys” [Note: [Col. 0955] Song 2]. Rising from the dead, he caused the earth of our flesh—which under the ancient curse brought forth thorns and thistles [Note: [Col. 0955] Gen. 3]—to bloom again, and restored us to the infancy of a new regeneration.

With these apples and these flowers she must be sustained and strengthened, lest the affection she has toward God grow dull, until, received into the Bridegroom’s embraces, she says: “His left hand is beneath my head, and his right hand shall embrace me” [Note: [Col. 0955] Song 2]. Whatever she now receives from the Bridegroom’s left hand in his first coming, she will deem little in comparison with the glory she is to receive in the embrace of his right hand, as it is written: “In his left hand are riches and glory, and in his right hand length of life” [Note: [Col. 0955] Prov. 3].

## CHAPTER LXIV. On the dimensions of charity and the communion of saints

[Col. 0955C]

Certainly, just as God is now known imperfectly and in part, so also he is loved imperfectly. For the knowledge which we presently have of God is as nothing compared with the knowledge of the homeland, when with unveiled face we shall see God; when he shall be seen in his glory; when he shall show his face, and we shall be saved [Note: [Col. 0955] 1 Cor. 13]. And as the entrance of morning light through the narrowest crevice compares with the noon-day splendour when the sun shines in its strength, so the love of God possessed in this pilgrimage is like a tiny spark of fire compared with that great fire of love in which the righteous, with the seraphim, shall burn with the fire of charity in the heavenly Jerusalem [Col. 0955D]. For now there is fire in Zion, but then there shall be a furnace in Jerusalem [Note: [Col. 0955] Isa. 31].

But since, according to the Apostle’s testimony, there are in God’s love toward us length, breadth, height, and depth [Note: [Col. 0955] Eph. 3], human love adapts itself to divine charity in the measure of its insufficiency. God did not love us superficially or moderately, but fully, sincerely, and from the depths of his being. Would that we too might comprehend with all the saints the height, length, breadth, and depth of so great a love!

Its height is the excellence of the glory which [Col. 0956A] God has prepared for those who love him, which eye has not seen nor ear heard [Note: [Col. 0955] 1 Cor. 2]. Its depth is the descent of divine majesty from equality with the Father to the form of a servant, and the Son’s emptying of himself even to death and the disgrace of crucifixion. Its length is without beginning and without end. For his love neither begins nor ceases—the love by which he chose us before the foundation of the world in his beloved Son [Note: [Col. 0955] Eph. 1]. And, as it is written, “His mercy is from eternity and unto eternity upon those who fear him” [Note: [Col. 0955] Ps. 102].

Its breadth is wide, extended, and diffused in every manner of goodwill. For he wills all people to be saved [Note: [Col. 0955] 1 Tim. 2]. By this love he did not spare his own Son, but delivered him up for us all; and, in giving him to us, he gave us all things in him, as the Apostle testifies [Note: [Col. 0955] Rom. 8]. Thus, in corresponding reciprocity, human [Col. 0956B] charity also conforms itself to divine charity by a like dimension. It is high when it contemplates eternal and heavenly things. It is deep when, for God’s sake, a person seeks lowliness and abasement. It is long because it perseveres to the end: for faith, hope, knowledge, and the rest shall be abolished, but charity never fails [Note: [Col. 0955] 1 Cor. 13]. It is broad because it is joyful, when the human heart is enlarged in delight in righteousness. It is broad when it extends itself not only toward God and neighbour, but also embraces an enemy with devout love. It is broad, whose commandment is broad, as the Prophet says: “I have seen an end of every perfection; your commandment is exceedingly broad” [Note: [Col. 0955] Ps. 118].

O broad and enlarging charity, how great is your house and how vast the place of your possession, whose [Col. 0956C] length, breadth, height, and depth the saints comprehend! Would that we too might be comprehended together with them in the same net of charity! Charity therefore spreads its tent among the saints, so that, if we have loved God and neighbour, we may be received into the common exultation of the saints. Therefore let us not be straitened in our own hearts, nor confined within the bounds of however small a righteousness of our own. Let us believe in the Holy Spirit, the holy Catholic Church, and the communion of saints, so that your eyes, Jesus, may see our imperfection and, in your good pleasure, our insufficiency may be supplied by the communion of the saints.

For if we love God in the saints, they too, according to the measure of their merits, will communicate their blessedness with us before God [Col. 0956D]. For if God shall be all in all in the midst of those who love him [Note: [Col. 0955] 1 Cor. 12], shared affections must necessarily be accompanied by a communion of joys. Therefore not only the blessedness of our neighbour, but the entire blessedness of Christ, shall be ours through the communion of love and exultation and through participation in another’s joy. Whatever blessedness I shall possess in lesser measure, I shall supply from another’s blessedness. For the good which I love in God or in my neighbour I shall make my own by loving it, so that the perfection of another’s joy may supply what is imperfect in mine.

Would you have me establish this matter for you by a familiar example? [Col. 0957A] A mother sees her son, whom she loves above all things, distinguished by royal anointing, an imperial diadem, sceptre, and imperial fillets: as great as the mother’s love is, so great is her exultation in her son’s honour; and the affection of joy accompanies the ardour of her own love. Therefore, just as a mother makes her own her son’s joy, the people’s applause, and everyone’s congratulations, so in the land of the living each person, through the benefit of charity, rejoices together in the blessedness of all.

O communion! O sweetness of love! O security, O rest, O delightful Sabbath! O entrance into eternal blessedness, which charity from a pure heart and unfeigned faith [Col. 0958A] makes more precious than all treasures, more desirable than all riches, more splendid than all kingdoms [Note: [Col. 0957] 2 Cor. 6]! Who will grant me to be made drunk with this draught of love, to be put to sleep by this lethargy, so that, wholly dead to my own heart and wholly transported into the love of God and neighbour, I may sleep and rest in peace, in one and the same state, between these two lots [Note: [Col. 0957] Ps. 4]? Who will enroll me in that holy communion, where the joy of the angels will be poured into all and by all returned to God, and God will be all in all [Note: [Col. 0957] 1 Cor. 12], so that he himself may be for all who love him love, joy, peace, life, rest, brightness, security, jubilation, the satisfaction of all desires, and the eternal and complete fullness of glory! Amen.

[Col. 0957]

## THE PASSION OF REGINALD, FORMER PRINCE OF ANTIOCH

[Col. 0957B] “Before I eat, I sigh; and my groaning is like flooding water, because the fear which I feared has come upon me, and that which I dreaded has happened.” I had hoped in him who is our hope, who makes peace in his high places, that, once the contention poured out upon the princes had been calmed, those who had bound themselves by vow to that pilgrimage would render the promised aid to the land of promise. But now the word of the cross, which had kindled the minds of the faithful with an unheard-of fervour of charity, has grown so cold, has been daily so buried in torpor, that God seems to have sent upon the children of men a spirit of sleep and forgetfulness of death.

Where is the devotion of those who once said, with sobbing sighs and in an unceasing flood of tears: “If I forget you, Jerusalem, let my right hand be forgotten” [Col. 0957C; Note: [Col. 0957] Ps. 136]? Those whom Christ’s love had inflamed for service, degenerating from the faith and charity that are in Christ, have turned God’s warfare into wickedness. Those who ought to have shone before others by the flame and example of virtues, I see smoking like desolating coals rather than blazing. They ought to have gone there not lukewarmly, but fervently and with all the exultation of their hearts—to the place where Mount Zion, the joy of the whole earth, is founded from living stones [Note: [Col. 0957] Ps. 47].

The Lord had opened and levelled for them the way of life, that they might enter that rest to which the Apostle invites us. But because they dealt deceitfully in his sight, the Lord sends upon them the wheel of evils; concerning them he says: “I swore in my wrath: they shall not enter into my rest” [Note: [Col. 0957] Ps. 94]. To the magnates who had received the sign of the cross [Col. 0957D], it will seem too little to serve the Lord by raising up the tribes of Jacob and taking possession of the land of promise, so that they might become a light to the nations and bear [Col. 0958B] the Lord’s name to the end of the earth.

But, tossed by the wind of boastfulness like unbridled sons, they who bend and shoot the bow turned back on the day of battle [Note: [Col. 0957] Ps. 77], so that Solomon’s saying may fittingly be applied to them: “Wind and clouds and rain that do not follow: a boastful man who does not fulfil promises” [Note: [Col. 0957] Prov. 25]. Therefore the land of promise, in which the Lord’s feet stood [Note: [Col. 0957] Ps. 131], has, to use Job’s words, been given into the hand of the wicked [Note: [Col. 0957] Job 9]; and the few faithful who remained from this lamentable slaughter are slain all day long and reckoned as sheep for slaughter [Note: [Col. 0957] Ps. 43].

Moreover, that noble marquis, harassed by the long siege of Tyre and by continual assaults of enemies, and exhausted by hunger, awaited for a very long time the arrival and aid of the western princes. In this hope he bore everything courageously, awaiting the arrival of a warlike people; [Col. 0958C] but I fear that he awaits it as the Britons await Arthur and the Jews the Messiah. It is written: “Cursed is the man who trusts in man and makes flesh his arm”; therefore let that blessed man trust in the Lord, and the Lord shall be his confidence [Note: [Col. 0957] Jer. 17]. Let him act manfully and let his heart be strengthened [Note: [Col. 0957] Ps. 26]; dwelling in the aid of the Most High and abiding under the protection of the God of heaven [Note: [Col. 0957] Ps. 90], let him await him who is the expectation of Israel [Note: [Col. 0957] Jer. 14], that he may be his arm in the time of tribulation and work salvation through him in the midst of the earth [Note: [Col. 0957] Ps. 73].

For, having rejected the magnates who have until now delayed to avenge Christ’s wrongs and the blood of the faithful, he has reserved this man especially for himself, to execute vengeance among the nations [Note: [Col. 0957] Ps. 149]; and let it be sung of him what is written concerning Solomon: “By one wise man a country shall be inhabited, and by three faithless men it shall be deserted” [Col. 0958D; Note: [Col. 0957] Ecclus. 16].

For the liberation of the kingdom of Jerusalem, the Lord offered us the kingdom of heaven. Nor is it because he found us less worthy of his offer that he himself, disdaining human aid, will, by whatever means he wills, in his displeasure—or rather his indignation—scatter the strength of the nations, and will say: “My arm shall save me, and my indignation itself shall help me” [Col. 0959A; Note: [Col. 0959] Isa. 63]. Since they do not suffer with his injuries and take no care to remedy the loss of divine glory, through which they were to gain glory, he himself will not fail himself. As Isaiah speaks through him: “For my own sake,” he says, “I will act, that I may not be blasphemed; and I will not give my glory to another” [Note: [Col. 0959] Isa. 48]. “Vengeance is mine, and I will repay; I will strike, and I will heal” [Note: [Col. 0959] Deut. 32].

We know, Lord, that affliction and consolation, life and death, are in your hand. Isaiah says: “Who gave Jacob over to plunder, and Israel to ravagers? Was it not the Lord himself, against whom we sinned?” [Note: [Col. 0959] Isa. 42]. Truly, Lord, everything you have done [Col. 0959B] to us, you have done in true judgment [Note: [Col. 0959] Dan. 3], because we have sinned against you and have not obeyed your commandments. But give glory to your name [Note: [Col. 0959] Ps. 113], and deal with us according to the multitude of your mercies [Note: [Col. 0959] Ps. 105], because we have sinned against you. Save us, O Saviour of Israel, because our iniquities have answered against us and our apostasies are many. For they have humbled your people, Lord, and vexed your inheritance [Note: [Col. 0959] Ps. 95]. Our glory has been transferred to strangers; your cross, most gracious Jesus, has been removed far from us.

This was for us the ark of the New Testament; this was the propitiatory of heard prayer, the banner of salvation, the title of holiness, the hope of victory, the covenant and ark of divine grace, the mark of Christian knighthood, the foundation of faith, [Col. 0959C] the overthrow of the enemy, the spoiling of hell, the ladder of heaven, the gate of paradise, the raising of the fallen, the opening of those shut in, the consolation of the afflicted, the protection of bodies, the armour of spirits, the salvation of the living, the life of the dead, the liberation of captives, the exaltation of the humble, and the casting down of the proud.

That you permitted the ark of the Old Testament to be captured by the Philistines, Lord, was a harsh blow, a grave punishment, and a sign of fierce indignation. But in the capture of your cross you have poured out your wrath, Lord, all the more grievously and intolerably because the cross was more acceptable to you than the ark, the New Testament than the Old, light than shadow, truth than figure. What comparison is there between light and darkness, between the life-giving cross and the old ark, a dead piece of wood? What, I ask, good Jesus, was nearer or more closely joined to you than your cross [Col. 0959D]?

Look, Lord, upon the nail-marks not only in your hands and feet, but also in the arms of the cross, upon which you were once affixed, reconciling the world to yourself. It alone remained as a victorious ensign or title of triumph from the battle in which you conquered the world, left as a testimony of faith and example of virtue, as a memorial of ineffable grace and precious love. Recognize in it, Lord, the signs of your warfare, and do not delay to redeem from captivity that by which you redeemed the world [Col. 0960A]. For when Saul had been conquered and slain, the Philistines are said to have placed his weapons in the temple of Dagon. I beseech you, Lord, let not your weapons, by which you defeated the aerial powers, be humiliated in Dagon’s temple, but glorified in your holy temple, which is in Jerusalem. See that the cross, reddened by that blood which split rocks, darkened the sun, shook the earth, opened tombs, and raised the dead, is not defiled by impious hands.

O God of inexhaustible and ineffable mercy, why do you humble and confound the heart of your people, and permit the horns of your enemies to be exalted to the injury of your name and the reproach of the Christian faith? Jeremiah’s complaint is: “Why does the way of the wicked prosper?” [Note: [Col. 0959] Jer. 12]. For those who hate you glory [Note: [Col. 0959] Ps. 73], while those who [Col. 0960B] love your name are scattered upon desolate paths. Job also complains and says: “Why do the wicked live? They are exalted and strengthened; their houses are secure and peaceful, and the rod of God is not upon them” [Note: [Col. 0959] Job 21]. “This,” says Solomon, “is the worst of all things under heaven: that the same things happen to everyone, to the righteous and to the wicked” [Note: [Col. 0959] Eccl. 9].

David was once so troubled and shaken by this question that he said: “My feet were almost moved; my steps nearly slipped; for I was jealous of the wicked when I saw the peace of sinners” [Note: [Col. 0959] Ps. 72]. Having argued the present question in many ways, he finally cut away every scruple of doubt by a certain conclusion, when he added: “Yet because of their deceits you have set them up; you have cast them down while they were being lifted up” [Note: [Col. 0959] ibid.]. Their prosperity, indeed, [Col. 0960C] has been set for them as a snare and a ruin, as it is written: “The prosperity of fools shall destroy them” [Note: [Col. 0959] Prov. 1]. For by his hidden judgment God permits some to prosper and gives them over to the desires of their heart, that they may go after their own inventions [Note: [Col. 0959] Ps. 80]. “Let us have mercy on the wicked,” he says, “and he will not learn to do righteousness” [Note: [Col. 0959] Isa. 26]. But those whom he hates, honouring and exalting them for a time, he heaps iniquity upon their iniquity [Note: [Col. 0959] Ps. 68], so that he who is filthy may become still more filthy [Note: [Col. 0959] Rev. 22], and may pour himself out into every desire of his heart until his wickedness is complete.

Thus the sinner rejoices in the desires of his soul [Note: [Col. 0959] Ps. 10], not understanding what he who is terrible in counsel toward the children of men intends concerning him [Note: [Col. 0959] Ps. 65]. For the heap of these brief pleasures suddenly turns into a heap of intolerable and endless [Col. 0960D] pains. For, according to Job’s testimony, the wicked man is reserved for the day of destruction and led to the day of wrath [Note: [Col. 0959] Ps. 21].

But the righteous of the Lord are scourged by the Lord; for he chastens every son whom he receives [Note: [Col. 0959] Heb. 12]. Or, patient amid tribulations, they gratefully accept God’s judgments. For although, in afflicting them bodily and temporally, the Lord may seem angry with them, they nevertheless exult with a voice of praise and consolation because of the Lord’s judgments, whose mercy they wisely recognize in scourges [Col. 0961A]. “The daughters of Judah rejoiced because of your judgments, Lord” [Note: [Col. 0961] Ps. 96].

But those who are not in the labour of men and are not scourged with other people [Note: [Col. 0961] Ps. 72] rush toward their own death, because, not understanding their latter end and blinded by prosperity, they do not distinguish between the Lord’s wrath and mercy. For in showing mercy the Lord is angry with Israel, and in being angry he shows mercy. Therefore the wise man says: “Who knows the power of your wrath?” [Note: [Col. 0961] Ps. 89]. And of mercies he says likewise: “Who is wise and will keep these things, and understand the mercies of God?” [Note: [Col. 0961] Ps. 106].

A merciful judge sometimes scourges an accused person in order to save him from hanging, and a physician cuts open an abscess in order to heal more thoroughly and completely. So too the physician of all physicians cleanses a person from sin better [Col. 0961B] and more effectively when he seems not to hear the cry and complaint of the sick person. The Apostle cries out against Satan’s thorn and asks the Lord three times, yet is not heard [Note: [Col. 0961] 2 Cor. 12]. It is also recorded that, when blessed Antony was harassed by evil spirits, after very severe blows, once those apparitions had vanished and he had at last been refreshed by heavenly light, he said: “Good Jesus, where were you until now?” And a voice said to him: “Antony, I was here, and I was awaiting your patience.”

Therefore the Prophet says: “My God, I shall cry by day and you will not hear; and by night, and not unto foolishness for me” [Note: [Col. 0961] Ps. 21], indicating that, although God sometimes does not answer a person according to that person’s wish, by not answering he nevertheless provides for that person’s salvation. For who knows what is expedient for himself? Who knows whether he is worthy of wrath or [Col. 0961C] of hatred? [Note: [Col. 0961] Eccl. 9]. Therefore blessed Job, unaware that the Lord’s scourges had cleansed him effectively and fully, says: “When the Lord shall have fulfilled his will in me, many other things are still before him” [Note: [Col. 0961] Job 23].

Thus God exalts the children of perdition so that they may be dashed down more grievously, while he casts down the righteous for a time so that they may be exalted more gloriously. But the righteous await with joy the reward of their labours [Note: [Col. 0961] Wis. 10]; for the expectation of the righteous is more joyful, and the hope of eternal delight makes them unashamed. “Tribulation produces patience; patience, proof; proof, hope; and hope does not confound” [Note: [Col. 0961] Rom. 5]. Therefore let those who know your name trust and hope in you, because you do not forsake those who hope in you, Lord [Note: [Col. 0961] Ps. 9].

Having the pledge of this hope, the Apostles [Col. 0961D] considered it the height of blessedness in this life to suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake [Note: [Col. 0961] Matt. 5]. For it is a heavenly gift, a best gift descending from the Father of lights [Note: [Col. 0961] Jas. 1], to endure reproaches for Christ. Hence the Apostle says: “To you, brothers, it has been granted not only to believe in him, but also to suffer for him” [Note: [Col. 0961] Phil. 1]. For, according to the testimony of sacred speech, just as Christ suffered in the head—that is, in himself—so he must suffer in his members, so that, to complete his holocaust, each person may pay his allotted portion [Col. 0962A] as the obligation of a public service. Therefore Paul, one outstanding member among the other members of Christ, says: “I fill up in my flesh what is lacking to Christ’s Passion” [Note: [Col. 0961] 2 Cor. 9].

The righteous therefore account it gain and esteem it joy whenever they encounter various tribulations for Christ, as the apostolic voice admonishes: “Brothers, count it all joy when you fall into various temptations” [Note: [Col. 0961] Jas. 1]. For we know that all who desire to live devoutly in Christ, as is written to Timothy, suffer persecution. But evil persons and deceivers advance in punishments, going astray and sending others astray [Note: [Col. 0961] 2 Tim. 3].

Not only the righteous, but also the perverse and wicked, are sometimes burned in the fire of tribulation. For the Lord sends frequent visitations upon them through evil angels [Note: [Col. 0961] Ps. 77]. But [Col. 0962B] glowing gold in a furnace and smoking straw are very different things; and although ointment and mud may be stirred by the same motion, fragrance issues from the one while stench rises from the other. So amid pressures the righteous are proved, but the wicked rejected. And while the righteous possess their souls in patience [Note: [Col. 0961] Luke 21], the wicked, having no patience in adversity, bless the Lord in prosperity, as it is written: “He will praise you when you have done him good” [Note: [Col. 0961] Ps. 48]; but they fail in hard circumstances and do not endure miseries. It is written of those who have lost endurance [Note: [Col. 0961] Ecclus. 2].

Therefore, in that lamentable slaughter and inconsolable blow which the wrath of the Lord recently inflicted in the land of promise, many saints and many wicked persons miserably fell by the sword, so that in that crushing the grain might be separated from the chaff, vessels [Col. 0962C] of dishonour might be shattered, and the Lord might reveal his mercy in vessels of grace. For, as the Apostle says: “Wishing to show his wrath and make known his patience, God endured with much patience vessels of wrath fitted for destruction, that he might show the riches of his glory in vessels which he has prepared for glory and called” [Note: [Col. 0961] Rom. 9]. Thus he struck the wicked and the righteous together, in order to consume the one and to perfect the other. “The death of sinners is most evil” [Note: [Col. 0961] Ps. 33], but “precious in the sight of God is the death of his saints” [Note: [Col. 0961] Ps. 115].

## TRANSITION TO WHAT FOLLOWS

That Babylonian dog, that son of perdition, had gathered together nearly all the princes of the nations. “All the kings of the earth assembled against the Lord and against his Christ” [Col. 0962D; Note: [Col. 0961] Ps. 2]. When, on the other side, the small number of Christians advanced to battle, the Saracens, spread abroad everywhere beyond count and number, covering the face of the earth from every side, surrounded Christ’s soldiers on all sides.

The brother of the king of Jerusalem, who was captured with the cross, told us; the brothers of the Hospital and Temple also reported that all those who, weak and degenerate, had made flight their refuge [Note: [Col. 0963] Lam. 3; Note: [Col. 0963] Ecclus. 45], were killed and crushed as it were in the twinkling of an eye [Col. 0963A]. But the others, who, founded in Christ’s charity, had girded their loins with strength, confidently awaiting the unfading crown and the incorruptible, undefiled inheritance in heaven [Note: [Col. 0963] 1 Pet. 1], though few and weary from a long journey, nevertheless resisted that immeasurable multitude for a very long time, not without a very great slaughter of enemies; and, rather driven and overwhelmed than captured, were brought before that Antichrist.

For the cruel beast sat at the entrance of his tent, and in his mouth was the death of Christ’s soldiers. They stood there too, stripped of their arms like sheep for sacrifice, indeed strong and altogether fearless. For, above everything desirable in this life, they had as their one chief wish to endure for Christ whatever hostile malice could devise [Col. 0963B]. They held Christ’s Passion and the reward of eternal life before the eyes of their hearts; in remembrance of them they strengthened themselves to endure every evil. They looked, as the Apostle speaks concerning them and others in the Epistle to the Hebrews [Note: [Col. 0963] ch. 12], to Jesus, the author and finisher of faith, who, for the joy set before him, endured the cross, despising shame.

Among them was Reginald of glorious memory, once prince of Antioch, lord of Mont-Royal, an eminent and most steadfast confessor of Christ, soon to be crowned with the blessed martyrdom for Christ. I would commit to writing, perhaps for the edification of the simple, a few things that I have learned concerning his triumph from an entirely trustworthy report. Yet [Col. 0963C] I, a man who sees my own poverty [Note: [Col. 0963] Lam. 3], fear to make the glory of so great a man material for a narrative, since it requires a greater pen of wisdom and eloquence.

Yet, to use Job’s words [Note: [Col. 0963] ch. 9], “If I keep silent, my mouth will condemn me,” and by my silence itself I shall seem to have slighted Christ’s martyr. It is enough for me if, through the leaves of words, however inadequately, I reveal in him the fruit of most proven virtue, so that the name of him whose memory is in blessing may be commended to memory. Would that I might begin so great a journey that another’s more elegant eloquence ought to complete! For I am a man of unclean lips, dwelling among a people of unclean lips [Note: [Col. 0963] Isa. 6]. Would that a coal might be brought to me from the heavenly altar, so that by its touch, in speaking worthily of so great a martyr, the dross of my most unclean [Col. 0963D] mouth might be burned away.

## ON THE LIFE AND VIRTUES OF PRINCE REGINALD
He was, by hereditary right, lord of Chastelion, Sanciti Bourbon, and other Castles of great renown. When the Duke of Burgundy offered him his daughter in marriage, though still a boy he nevertheless, with the gravity of old age, mocked the world as it smiled upon him, contemptuously trampled underfoot both the world’s bloom and that of his own body, and began to glory in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ. Longing with all his heart for the land in which the Lord’s feet had stood, he took the sign of the cross and hastened to Jerusalem, [Col. 0964A] thus satisfying his desire. For the Lord of our salvation had granted him a prosperous journey, having set him apart from his mother’s womb for a work of virtue and as an example of fortitude.

Who would judge this boy’s faith inferior to that of Moses? Commending Moses’ faith, the Apostle says: “By faith Moses, when he had grown great, refused to be called the son of Pharaoh’s daughter, choosing rather to be afflicted with the people of God than to enjoy for a time the pleasure of sin; for he considered the reproach of Christ greater riches than the treasures of Egypt” [Note: [Col. 0963] Isa. 6.]. O how good it is for a man when he has borne the Lord’s yoke from his youth [Note: [Col. 0963] Hebr. 11.]. For while he was still a youth and despised, nevertheless, beneath the Lord’s yoke he restrained with holy maturity the impulses of the lusting flesh; and the Lord magnified him in the sight of [Col. 0964B] kings and established him for an everlasting kingdom. Indeed, in the Lord’s left hand are riches and glory, and his right hand gives love unto the end [Note: [Col. 0963] Psal. 11.].

Thus wisdom and grace abounded in him before God and men [Note: [Col. 0963] Luc. 2.]. He was most valiant in arms, most steadfast in faith in Christ, serene in countenance, reverent in deeds, long-suffering in hope, lavish in charity, merciful, provident, gentle and humble; moreover, pleasant yet prudent in speech. Truly, honey and milk were beneath his tongue; and the Lord had given him a learned tongue, so that he knew when he ought to utter a word.

Therefore, although he had made the whole province illustrious with such vigorous and glorious deeds of war that it could fittingly be said of him that there had been given him “the glory of Lebanon, [Col. 0964C] the beauty of Carmel and Sharon” [Note: [Col. 0963] Isa. 35.], no boastful word ever proceeded from his mouth, nor did any sign or movement of pride appear in his face. And when he had become Prince of Antioch, he concealed from human praise, by reserve and silence insofar as he could, the triumphant successes by which he magnificently extended Christ’s glory to the confusion of the nations.

Does Isaiah not seem to have foretold concerning him what he says: “He was a man concealing his words, and he shall appear in the land of Zion like a glorious river in a thirsty land”? Moreover, during his pilgrimage, he begot a daughter by his devout and holy wife, whom he had received together with the principality; and, having given her in marriage to the illustrious king of Hungary, he steadfastly resolved in his heart to contend for the law of his Lord unto death. [Col. 0964D] For he saw that in this pilgrimage he had no abiding city, but that the city to come must be sought [Note: [Col. 0963] Hebr. 13.].

Thus the Apostle, speaking of Abraham, says: “By faith he sojourned in the land of promise, dwelling as in a strange land; he awaited the promise, having as the foundation of hope a city whose maker and creator is God” [Note: [Col. 0963] Hebr. 11.]. He brought every thought and every bodily exertion into the obedient service of him whom to serve is to reign.

But one day, when he had triumphed more gloriously than usual over the sons of dissension, the heavenly Potter, wishing to test the vessel which he had made for honour and glory, [Col. 0965A] allowed him to be captured by enemies through the treachery of certain false brethren and carried into exile. Captive in the land of unlikeness, he was like another Ezekiel, serving by fasts and prayers day and night [Note: [Col. 0965] Luc. 2.]. Therefore, while sinners built upon his back with injuries and insults, he set the shield of patience against every assault of hostile malice, overcoming evil in every respect with good. And he was, as is written of the remnant of Jacob [Note: [Col. 0965] Mich. 5.], among the peoples like dew from the Lord and like a drop upon a tree, which does not wait for a man nor look for the sons of men.

Having his life in his hands and trained in all things, as the Apostle says, he knew both how to be full and how to hunger, to abound and to endure want; he could do all things in him who strengthened him [Note: [Col. 0965] Phil. 4.]. Truly, he who [Col. 0965B] says to his faithful ones, “I will not leave you orphans” [Note: [Col. 0965] Joan. 14.], who does not permit his own to be tested beyond what they can bear [Note: [Col. 0965] I Cor. 10.], but removes the rod of sinners from over the lot of the righteous, lest the righteous stretch out their hands unto iniquity [Note: [Col. 0965] Psal. 124.], determined to test him in exile, not to exhaust him.

Accordingly, when the fifteen years of his exile had passed, he brought him out of the furnace of captivity like most refined silver, like pure gold. At his most eagerly desired liberation, not only the kingdom of Jerusalem but all Christian kingdoms were filled with inexpressible joy. Though he was young, premature old age—arising from captivity rather than years—had sprinkled his whole head with untimely grey hair. [Col. 0965C] Now it is written: “Old age is a crown of dignity, found in the ways of righteousness” [Note: [Col. 0965] Prov. 16.].

A venerable old age, not long-lasting nor reckoned by the number of years, turned to his glory. For when a man’s understanding had grown grey with the hair of his head, and since the Apostle says, “Everything that grows old and ages is near to destruction” [Note: [Col. 0965] Hebr. 8.], his grey hair therefore compelled him to be mindful of his last things. The man of God, whose manner of life was already in heaven [Note: [Col. 0965] Phil. 3.], began to dwell at Mont-Royal, of which he was lord. There, to use Isaiah’s words [Note: [Col. 0965] Cap. 32.], as a prince “thinking things worthy of a prince,” he continually devoted himself to vigils, fasts, disciplines, prayers, and almsgiving. And as he surpassed the rest in the distinctions of Christian knighthood, so he excelled every religious person in the land in the grace of holiness. [Col. 0965D]

Very great and ambitious honours, even the kingdom of Jerusalem, were at times offered to him; but for Christ’s love, content with an honourable smallness of possessions, he retained for himself only those things which seemed sufficient for the use of the poor and the exercise of arms against the enemies of Christ’s cross. Does he not seem to you another Jonathan, of whom it is written that “the soul of Jonathan was knit to the soul of David” [Note: [Col. 0965] I Reg. 18.]? For “he who is joined to the Lord is one spirit with him” [Note: [Col. 0965] I Cor. 6.]; and Jonathan stripped himself of the tunic in which he was clothed and gave [Col. 0966A] it to David, with the rest of his garments, even to his sword, bow, and belt [Note: [Col. 0965] I Reg. 18.]. But that Jonathan, when the ark of the Lord was captured, was put to flight and died; this man, captured together with the Lord’s cross, completed the course of this life in glorious combat.

## THE LENGTH AND BREADTH OF PALESTINE ACCORDING TO JEROME

Moreover, that son of perdition, Saladin—whose baleful and accursed name I unwillingly and sorrowfully defile this letter by writing—had for two years not ceased, by rewards, entreaties, and promises, to gather almost all the princes and peoples of the nations. Such was the multitude of the dogs who came upon them that it could neither be contained by number nor estimated by human reasoning.

For the purpose of counsel the patriarch of Jerusalem [Col. 0966B] had gone to the western regions; but, shameful as it is to say, so few or none followed him that they did not even constitute a number. The holy and prudent man said that such a small force could not resist so infinite a multitude, knowing that the Lord was angered with his own land, in whose faith and strength one pursued a thousand and two put ten thousand to flight [Note: [Col. 0965] Deut. 32.]. Indeed, if anyone carefully considers the narrowness of the promised land and the immeasurable vastness of the surrounding provinces and regions which assail it, he will clearly see that God is set within it as a wall and outer defence, and that he never permits that multitude to prevail unless he is offended.

From Dan to Beersheba, where scarcely forty miles lie between, [Col. 0966C] its length extends; but its breadth is from Joppa to Bethlehem, a distance of ten miles, for a very extensive wilderness borders upon it. But if, according to the Book of Numbers [Note: [Col. 0965] Cap. 34.], you wish to measure the circumference of the promised land on every side, begin in the south from the Salt Sea, through Syria and Kadesh-barnea, as far as the torrent of Egypt, which flows into the Great Sea near Rhinocorura; and on the west, the sea itself which stretches along Palestine, Phoenicia, Coele-Syria, and Cilicia; on the north, Mount Taurus and Zephyr as far as Hamath, which is called Ephraim of Syria; and on the east, through Antioch and Lake Ceremth, which is called Tiberias, and the Jordan, which flows into the Salt Sea, now called the Dead Sea.

Beyond the Jordan, moreover, lies the possession of the two and a half [Col. 0966D] tribes: Reuben, Gad, and the half-tribe of Manasseh. Such things were promised, indeed, not possessed; for neither David, the mightiest king, nor Solomon in all his glory, nor their successors, are read to have held one palm’s breadth beyond the first division which we have made. Nor did Abraham himself, to whom the promise was made, possess a foot of that land, as the blessed Stephen, the protomartyr, testifies in the Acts of the Apostles. And the Apostle, speaking of the holy fathers, says: “These men died without receiving the promises, but seeing them from afar, greeting them, and confessing that they were strangers and pilgrims upon the earth” [Note: [Col. 0967] Hebr. 11.].

To Jews who think earthly thoughts, the land of Canaan was promised; but to those who think heavenly thoughts, the kingdom of heaven is promised. From this it is most certainly clear that there is another land of promise, in which is the heavenly Jerusalem, of which this one is a figure. Hence, even when David reigned in it, he said, as though journeying toward another land: “I am a stranger and a pilgrim, as all my fathers were” [Note: [Col. 0967] Psal. 38.]; and: “Alas for me, for my sojourn has been prolonged” [Note: [Col. 0967] Psal. 119.]; and, awaiting its blessedness: “I believe,” he says, “that I shall see the goodness of the Lord in the land of the living” [Note: [Col. 0967] Psal. 26.].

It pleases him who formed the hearts of men one by one to transfer his beloved from the earthly Jerusalem to the heavenly. Therefore, in that city through which we received the foundation of our faith, [Col. 0967B] a free way and ascent to heaven is prepared and offered to us. For this reason the earthly Ilium is frequently destroyed by hostile attack, so that, according to the prophet’s word [Note: [Col. 0967] Isa. 60.], “the sons of strangers may rebuild it,” and may build for themselves in heaven a city not made by hands. For, as Isaiah says, the Lord set it as “a burdensome stone for all nations,” while, in its devastation, each of the surrounding princes tests his strength [Note: [Col. 0967] Zach. 12.].

We indeed read that, when Moab and the Philistines attacked, later Syria harassed it, and finally Babylon ravaged it, the Temple remained in desolation for seventy years. At last, under Cyrus king of the Persians, as Ezra and the prophet Nehemiah report most fully, the Temple [Col. 0967C] was rebuilt; and under Darius king of the Persians and Medes, by Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel and Joshua son of Jozadak, the high priest.

The city endured intolerable pressures, as Egyptians, Medes, and Macedonians attacked in turn. Why should I speak of the tyranny of the most cruel Antiochus Epiphanes, of the oppressive Pompey, Gabinius, and Scaurus alone, each of whom brought about the ruin of that city and land? I pass over Titus and Vespasian: when they attacked, the city was given over to lamentable desolation, solitude, and wilderness. Why should I speak of certain of its own people—Manasseh, Haman, Jehoiakim, Zedekiah—who all, destroyed by a condemnable end, were made for all kings a subject of horror and an example of fear? In these things the Lord gives those who fear him [Col. 0967D] a sign, that they may flee from before the bow [Note: [Col. 0967] Psal. 59.].

Therefore, whenever that people grow deaf in their wickedness against the Lord’s merciful scourges, he pours upon the inhabitants of the land a spirit of indignation and contempt, as blessed Job speaks in the spirit of prophecy: “He pours contempt upon princes; he loosens the belt of kings and girds their loins with a cord. He brings counsellors to a foolish end and judges to astonishment; he leads priests into glory and overthrows nobles” [Note: [Col. 0967] Job 12.]. Thus in anger he humbles those whom, when appeased, he exalts; for “wrath is in his indignation, and life in [Col. 0968A] his will” [Note: [Col. 0967] Psal. 29.].

We have learned that all these things recently happened in that land. For, to take up the prophet’s words, the Lord could no longer endure because of the wickedness of evil men; for their sins had reached heaven, and the Lord remembered the iniquities of the people and poured upon them the wrath of his indignation [Note: [Col. 0967] Thren. 4.]. But why should I make so long and tedious a digression? Why do I not return to our prince?

Saladin had ordered this man and certain other fellow-captives, more distinguished than the rest in reputation and birth, to be brought before him. That son of unbelief had first intended to employ enticements, in order thus to gain Mont-Royal and the other strongest fortresses by treacherous persuasions. But “the net is cast in vain before the eyes of winged creatures” [Note: [Col. 0967] Prov. 1.]. For faithful [Col. 0968B] Naboth neither exchanges nor sells the inheritance of his fathers; he accepts no price or other exchange for Mont-Royal except the mountain of the Lord, that he may dwell upon it for length of days [Note: [Col. 0967] Psal. 22.].

From the years of his childhood he had vowed his life to the Lord, and had given it as the price of his redemption, at a fixed valuation. Speaking of this price, the Apostle, the best assessor of things, and setting life, or soul, as the price of his redemption, says: “I do not make my life more precious than myself” [Note: [Col. 0967] Act. 20.].

But so that that most crafty tyrant might bend the hearts of Christ’s soldiers more firmly and effectively to his will, as though he were about to restore to them the Lord’s cross, which he held captive because of our sins, he ordered it to be shown to the captives. [Col. 0968C] Yet the wisdom of God turns all things to good for those who are called saints according to his purpose [Note: [Col. 0967] Rom. 8.]. Thus, at the presence of the life-giving cross, so great a love of Christ and such strength of grace grew warm in our prince that he could fittingly say with the prophet: “From on high the Lord sent fire into my bones, and instructed me” [Note: [Col. 0967] Thren. 1.].

Accordingly, taking up a word of exhortation, he said: “Behold, brothers, behold the wood upon which the Son of God hung and redeemed us. Suffering death upon it for us, he opened heaven; and, having destroyed death, on it he gave us eternal blessedness. It was captured with us, that it might free us from eternal captivity; and because we left our native lands for its sake, it will lead us back into our homeland. Rejoice, brothers, because the Lord has looked upon us. [Col. 0968D] He purposely allowed his cross to be captured with us, that our redemption might become our fellow-captive and be consolation to us in our present death. For I know that death is prepared for us, and I consider it the highest glory to die where I see the banner of Christianity’s glory and human salvation.

“He follows the leader and prince of this banner who laid down his life for us and demands that we lay down our lives for him. It is safe to entrust one’s life to him who is the leader of life and the Lord of glory. Show by your deeds, if you love Christ, for whom you have laboured so [Col. 0969A] long. Behold the reward of our labours! For love of him, let us love death and despise this present toilsome and miserable life, because today the Lord will place us in the kingdom of his glory among the holy martyrs.”

I alter absolutely nothing of the prince’s words, but commit them to memory and writing in the same simplicity in which they were reported and written to the lord pope and to many who were then present, and were afterward more clearly explained in spoken testimony by the brother of the king of Jerusalem, who was captured there, to the Archbishop of Canterbury and to us who were likewise present.

But that prince of unbelief and treachery, understanding that he could make no progress with the holy prince by flattery, raged in body and gnashed his teeth. “Your Christ,” he said in Arabic, “will teach you; nor will he himself be able today to free you from my hand unless you deny him.” [Col. 0969B]

Truly, he whom the favour of a flattering breeze had not moved was not bent by a stormy tempest. For that noble cedar had fixed its root in heaven, and feared the violence of no tempest; for, as the Apostle writes to Timothy: “The firm foundation of God stands, having this seal” [Note: [Col. 0969] II Tim. 2.]. The prince, having been captured in his youth, heard the Arabic language which he knew; but after long practice and the instruction of necessity, he had learned it fully. Replying in Arabic, he said: “Christ deceives no one; but he is deceived who does not believe in him. I worship him, I confess him, and I proclaim his name to you. If you believed in him, you might escape the punishments of eternal damnation, which you should not doubt are prepared for you. But why delay what you are going to do? I know that you thirst for nothing except Christian blood.”

Accordingly, the bloody beast ordered armed soldiers, prepared for the slaughter of the saints, to be brought in. But when the stormy tempest rushed upon the prince, it became evident what was in the man. His face did not grow pale; his blood did not freeze; [Col. 0969C] his hair did not stand on end; his voice did not stick in his throat; his body did not tremble, nor was his mind disturbed; his understanding and memory did not grow numb. Rather, fearless and far more secure than usual, he lost nothing at all of the condition of his customary dignity.

It is written in praise of Moses that he did not fear the king’s wrath. But this man, now exalted above the world and trampling down the conquered world—for, in John’s testimony, “This is the victory which conquers the world: our faith” [Note: [Col. 0969] Joan. 5.]—tasted nothing except what was divine and heavenly, and therefore despised the tyrant’s terrible threats and the surrounding swords. Yet the mustard seed was still whole; but once it began to be crushed, it would gain greater power from the crushing [Note: [Col. 0969] Matth. 13.].

That hammerer [Col. 0970A] of Christ’s faithful ones thundered and uttered terrible threats; but the most valiant athlete of the Lord, sending forth burning words like sparks of inward charity—for “out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks” [Note: [Col. 0969] Matth. 12.]—set against the weapons of wickedness and the onset of death nothing except Christ’s name and the shield of faith. For charity in him was strong as death—indeed, stronger than death—and tempered the very bitterness of death into sweetness.

O God, how great is the abundance of your sweetness, which you have hidden for those who fear you [Note: [Col. 0969] Psal. 30.]! How sweet and pleasant you are to those of holy heart, for whom the anointing of your charity makes death itself sweet and most desirable. Captivated by this sweetness, the most renowned prince, though a pilgrim away from the body and conformed to [Col. 0970B] the likeness of Christ’s death, desired to be dissolved and to be with Christ [Note: [Col. 0969] Phil. 1.].

With the highest desire he sought the end of life—or rather, to speak more truly, the beginning of living. For, as Solomon says: “When a man has finished, then he begins” [Note: [Col. 0969] Eccli. 18.]. For his departure from this passing life is into that life which neither passes away nor fails. The unconquered prince knows in whom he has believed, and is certain that the righteous Judge is able to keep his deposit until that day [Note: [Col. 0969] II Tim. 1.]. According to God’s counsel, it seems safer to him to lose his life in order to keep it than to keep it in order to lose it [Note: [Col. 0969] Marc. 8.]. For who will keep his life more faithfully than its Creator and Redeemer? He will multiply strength in his soul [Note: [Col. 0969] Psal. 137.], so that the soul which earthly dwelling weighed down may be restored free, without spot, without wrinkle, and crowned with the glory of eternal light. [Col. 0970C]

The prince’s constancy had wonderfully strengthened his brothers to endure every torment. And now the thoughts of many hearts were revealed, so that with loud voice they cried out, unanimously confessing Christ. The prince rejoiced with them and, scarcely able to contain himself for joy, said: “Take courage, brothers, for the kingdom of glory is prepared for you; and know that our blood will most exactly be demanded shortly from that impious man and his people.”

The Lord will yet, most illustrious prince, give to your voice a voice of power [Note: [Col. 0969] Psal. 67.]. Your blood will be required from the hands of the empire; and the avenging sword will answer this slaughter with a multiplied offering of the slain. Thus will be fulfilled both your word and the saying of the prophet: “The Lord has a sacrifice in Bozrah and a great slaughter in the land of Edom” [Note: [Col. 0969] Isa. 34.].

I desire and await that day, Lord God, when your enemies shall perish [Note: [Col. 0969] Psal. 91.], when you shall pass judgment on those who persecute you [Note: [Col. 0969] Psal. 118.]. I know that you will do this and will not delay. This hope of mine is laid up in my bosom [Note: [Col. 0969] Job 19.]. And although that dog glories in the victory which has now befallen him because of our sins, I nevertheless know, to use Job’s words, that from the beginning, since man was born upon the earth, their praise is brief [Note: [Col. 0969] Job. 20.]. Therefore, with heart attentive and ear alert, I knowingly await reports [Col. 0971A] of a happier outcome; for, in Solomon’s testimony: “Cold water to a thirsty soul is good news from a far country” [Note: [Col. 0971] Prov. 25.].

Avenge, Lord, the blood of your saints, which the Synagogue of Satan, the assembly of the lost, has shed in insult to your name, Jesus Christ. This is that woman of whom we read in the Apocalypse: “I saw a woman drunk with the blood of the martyrs of Jesus Christ” [Note: [Col. 0971] Apoc. 17.]; and: “Her sins have reached unto heaven, and the Lord has remembered her iniquities. Render to her,” he says, “as she herself rendered to you; in the cup in which she mixed, mix for her double; as much as she exalted herself in delights, give her so much torment and mourning” [Note: [Col. 0971] Apoc. 18.].

But the Lord, turning toward Jerusalem and changing judgment into mercy in the words of Isaiah, says: “Behold, I have taken from your hand the cup of drowsiness, [Col. 0971B] the dregs of the cup of my indignation; you shall not add to drink it any more, and I will put it into the hand of those who humbled you” [Note: [Col. 0971] Isa. 51.]. Indeed, sinners shall perish from the face of the earth, and the sons of unbelief shall suddenly be exterminated; and in your strength, Lord, all nations shall come to knowledge of your name.

But do you suppose, Lord Jesus, that we shall endure? Do you suppose that we shall see it? Has he yet come through whom you have poured out your indignation? Has he yet been born through whom you will seize the blessing? I know that you will give blessing to the lawgiver. Hasten, Lord, and make your prophets prove true. You will subject nations and kingdoms to yourself, so that you may be established as the head of nations.

It is Jeremiah’s word: “The Lord is my strength and my might; [Col. 0971C] to you they shall come from the ends of the earth and say: Truly our fathers wrought falsehood and vanity, which did them no good” [Note: [Col. 0971] Jer. 16.]. Through Zephaniah likewise he promises that he will restore to the people a chosen speech, so that all may call upon the Lord’s name and serve him with one shoulder; for “beyond the rivers of Ethiopia are my suppliants,” says the Lord, “and the children of my dispersed ones shall bring me an offering” [Note: [Col. 0971] Sophon. 3.].

Hear Zechariah also: “My peoples shall come,” he says, “saying: Let us go and entreat the face of the Lord, and let us seek the face of the Lord of hosts” [Note: [Col. 0971] Zach. 8.]; and shortly afterward: “He will judge peoples and take hold of strong nations afar off” [Note: [Col. 0971] Mich. 4.]. For although they reject the service of the Lord with malicious will, nevertheless, willing or unwilling, they must be compelled to serve the living God. For I judge such compulsion highly acceptable to God, so that [Col. 0971D] the salvation of men may be procured and, as far as lies in us, the Lord’s will advanced; for “we are God’s fellow-workers” [Note: [Col. 0971] 1 Cor. 3.].

Therefore, as we pray that the kingdom of God may come, so let us actively strive that his dominion may be multiplied, that nations may be subjected to him with an iron rod, and that those who willingly wish to enter may be violently drawn into the kingdom. The Lord speaks through the prophets of this violence: “With a strong hand,” he says, “and an outstretched arm and in my wrath I will reign over [Col. 0972A] you, and I will subject you to my sceptre, that they may bring you into the bonds of my covenant” [Note: [Col. 0971] Ezech. 20.].

There were among the barbarian people and that perverse and adulterous generation men who sharply reproached their tyrant because he had endured for so long the pride of the condemned. O how commendable and pleasing to God is that pride, without doubt, to those who are merely natural and do not receive the things of the Spirit of God [Note: [Col. 0971] I Cor. 2.]! Holy men seem proud when they despise the world, mock their torturers, and disdain honours and riches. The liberty of a noble conscience and the free nobility of Christian faith are reckoned pride.

Of this pride we read: “I will make you the pride of ages” [Note: [Col. 0971] Isa. 60.]; and: “You shall eat the strength of the nations, and you shall take pride in their glory” [Note: [Col. 0971] Isa. 61.]. Again, speaking of this glory, [Col. 0972B] Wisdom says: “With me are riches and glory, proud and righteous wealth” [Note: [Col. 0971] Prov. 8.].

The impious men hastened and used every means to ensure that innocent blood should be shed without delay. Yet to the holy prince and his other fellow-martyrs it seemed exceedingly long that their sufferings were delayed; every moment they counted a loss to their glory.

But you, profane, impious, and cruel Antichrist, why do you protract and prolong the martyrs’ desire? What thoughts rise in your heart? Do you perhaps seek kinds of punishments by which to tear the minds of the faithful from Christ’s charity? It is the saying of your predecessor, Agag, the unbelieving and fat king: “Does bitter death thus separate?” [Note: [Col. 0971] I Reg. 15.]. Know that that death does not separate, but unites in Christ. Therefore that death is sweeter than life to those for whom one day in the courts of the Lord is more welcome than thousands [Note: [Col. 0971] Psal. 83.].

Consider and deliberate; exhaust all human inventions in punishments. Then neither death, nor sword, nor life, nor angels, nor principalities, nor powers, nor height, nor depth, nor things present, nor things to come, nor any other creature will be able to separate me from the charity of God which is in Jesus Christ [Note: [Col. 0971] Rom. 8.]. They know that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with that future glory which shall be revealed in us [Note: [Col. 0971] Ibid.]. They know that for double shame and disgrace, they shall possess double things in their land; that the light and momentary burden of our tribulation works in us an immense weight of glory [Note: [Col. 0971] II Cor. 14.].

The martyr sows in tears and [Col. 0972D] pain, but his seed shall be mighty upon the earth [Note: [Col. 0971] Psal. 111.]. For pain will generate joy, oppression liberty, affliction delight, and bitterness sweetness. Is it not a profitable and sweet exchange to sow a mortal, animal, ignoble body, that it may rise immortal and spiritual [Note: [Col. 0971] I Cor. 15.], crowned in the splendours of the saints [Note: [Col. 0971] Psal. 109.] with glory and honour [Note: [Col. 0971] Hebr. 2.]?

But if the righteous man is overtaken by death, he shall be in refreshment [Note: [Col. 0971] Sap. 14.]; and, to use blessed Job’s words: “He shall forget his misery and shall not remember it as waters that have passed away; at evening he shall rise like the noonday brightness, and when he thinks himself consumed, he shall arise as the morning star” [Note: [Col. 0973] Job 11.].

Rush upon the righteous man, most inhuman tyrant; burn, crush, kill, cut, hew down: you accomplish nothing. For you cannot uproot those rooted in Christ’s charity. This is the tree which sends its roots toward honour and shall not be anxious in time of drought. Of this tree Job says: “A tree has hope [Vulgate: *spem*], if it is cut down [Vulgate: *praecisum*], that it will grow green again and its branches will sprout anew” [Note: [Col. 0973] Job 14.].

The Christian, for whom to live is Christ and to die gain [Note: [Col. 0973] Phil. 1.], finds life in dying; and though he seems in the eyes of the foolish to die [Note: [Col. 0973] Sap. 3.], his place is made in peace [Note: [Col. 0973] Psal. 75.] and he is set in a place of pasture [Note: [Col. 0973] Psal. 22.], because his life is kept with Christ in the Lord.

## CONCERNING THE SAME MAN

[Col. 0973B]

The ministers of Satan hung upon the tyrant’s mouth, swift to shed blood; and behold, the son of eternal death was about to pronounce a sentence of death upon the sons and heirs of heavenly life. “The hand of mine,” he said, “shall kill this man who dared blaspheme the glory of my majesty; but let the others be removed from here, and let all who have not denied Christ be punished capitally.”

By the dispensation of heavenly counsel the Lord set him apart from others, and gave him a mighty contest, that he might conquer and know that Wisdom is the protector of all. The most illustrious prince is thrown to the ground; and while he lay upon his back, with his eyes raised and fixed upon heaven, the tyrant, placing his right foot upon his holy breast, drove a sword into his very throat. The sword cut short the name of Christ, which was ever in his heart and on his lips. That excellent martyr of Christ moved no part of his body: he was plucking the fruit of life from the tree of the cross. For the remembrance of Christ’s cross turned his torment into delight. This is that tree of which the Bride says in the Song of Songs: “I sat in its shadow, and its fruit was sweet to my throat” [Note: [Col. 0973] Song 2.]. The renowned prince had the fruit of the cross in his throat; reckoning the sword sweeter than every food, amid the straits of death he tasted and saw how sweet the Lord is [Note: [Col. 0973] Ps. 33.]. To him this sword was what fire was to blessed Lawrence, who laughed at his executioners and mocked his judge [Col. 0973D], since the Apostle says: “Far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ” [Note: [Col. 0973] Gal. 6.]. Since blessed Andrew found in the instrument of the cross inestimable treasures of delights, it is clear that in the suffering of the saints some fruit of heavenly life and some hidden foretaste of eternity is tasted beforehand. Otherwise the Prophet would not say: “Surely there is fruit for the righteous; surely there is a God judging them on earth” [Note: [Col. 0973] Ps. 57.]. And why should sweetness not be hidden in Christ’s passion? For there [Col. 0974A] his strength is hidden [Note: [Col. 0973] Hab. 4]; there heavenly manna is hidden for those who have laid hold of the tree of life.

As elephants are roused to battle by the sight of blood, so the sight of the life-giving cross and the remembrance of the Lord’s passion had roused Christ’s soldiers still more strongly. For that saving tree, namely, soaked in the Saviour’s blood, thereafter did not cease to pour out the oil of gladness, to exude the balm of graces, to drip the ointment of strength, and to bring forth the fruit of life. In that by which Christ triumphed, he also causes his soldiers to triumph, as the Apostle writes to Timothy [Note: [Col. 0973] Rather, to Heb. 2]: “We see Christ, crowned with glory and honour because of the suffering of death, having been tried.” And, “In that he himself suffered and was tried, he helps those who are tried” [Note: [Col. 0973] Heb. 2.]. For the cross of Christ is [Col. 0974B] folly to those who perish, but to those who are being saved it is the power of God and the wisdom of God. And, writing to the Corinthians, he says: “As the sufferings of Christ abound in us, so through him our consolation also abounds” [Note: [Col. 0973] II Cor. 1.].

It contributed to the prince not merely consolation but fullness of joys, that the remembrance of Christ’s wounds banished every pain of his own body, together with the certain and swift recompense of rewards. He knows that the threshing-floor will soon overtake the vintage, and that the disgrace inflicted upon his bruised body will turn for him into joy and a crown. Behold, most noble prince, behold the end of your journey and the completion of your pilgrimage. You drank from the torrent on the way; therefore your head shall be lifted up in your homeland [Note: [Col. 0973] Ps. 109.]. You may now safely say: “You are my protector, [Col. 0974C] my glory, and the lifter up of my head” [Note: [Col. 0973] Ps. 3.]. Beyond doubt you shall be crowned, because you have contended lawfully [Note: [Col. 0973] II Tim. 2.]. For, according to Job’s testimony: “He who has been afflicted shall be in glory” [Note: [Col. 0973] Job 22.]. Thus the wicked man, in humiliating you, fashioned for you a crown of glory. Blessed are you, because you have deserved today to enter, with your companions, into possession of the glory which Adam lost with his offspring.

You directed your ways most well; you may say: “Without iniquity I ran and set things straight” [Note: [Col. 0973] Ps. 58]. You fought the good contest; you established the course [Note: [Col. 0973] II Tim. 4]. Blessed are those who believed your counsels; and as the Wise Man says of blessed Elijah: “Blessed are those who saw you and who delighted in your friendship” [Note: [Col. 0973] Ecclus. 48]. Yet I believe that, if you did not wish for certain persons according to the flesh, perhaps now you know them, since you have entered into the powers of the Lord and gone into the abysses of light and eternal [Col. 0974D] delight.

You see that the tyrant has withdrawn his sword from his throat, and that the blessed soul, freed from its corruptible coverings and released from the tribute of death, has flown freely into heaven. It was received by him who says: “I will [Note: [Col. 0973] Vulgate: I go] prepare a place for you” [Note: [Col. 0973] John 14]; and again: “I will come to you, that I may take you to myself”; and: “Father, I will that where I am, there may my servant also be” [Note: [Col. 0973] John 12]. From his childhood onward, at every age, as though in every hour of the day, he laboured like a vigorous cultivator in the vineyard of the Lord of Hosts; and at the consummation [Col. 0975A] of the saints he closed his day in most perfect virtue, as it is written in Solomon: “The path of the righteous, like a shining light, goes onward and increases unto the perfect day” [Note: [Col. 0975] Prov. 4].

The prince’s death moved many to tears, but here I see no cause for tears. That death, through which the Lord made his saint wonderful [Note: [Col. 0975] Ps. 4], is not death but sleep: the gates of death are the gate of life. He was called to heaven, of which the world was not worthy. This lamp has not been extinguished, but struck by a passing blast, so that it can no longer be extinguished, and so that, lighted from heaven, it may shine upon all who are in the house. “You granted him the desire of his heart, O Lord, and did not defraud him of the request of his lips” [Note: [Col. 0975] Ps. 20]. Let us therefore rejoice, brethren; for he too rejoices and exults, [Col. 0975B] having been brought into the joy of his Lord.

## On the Same Subject

Those glorious soldiers also, companions in the sufferings, went rejoicing from the presence of the council, because they were counted worthy to suffer death for Christ’s name [Note: [Col. 0975] Acts 6]. In accordance with the counsel of the Wise Man, it seemed better to them to go to the house of mourning than to the house of feasting [Note: [Col. 0975] Eccles. 7]. All these were found approved by the testimony of faith; and therefore they rejoiced, as the Apostle, speaking to the Hebrews, says: “Looking unto Jesus, the author and finisher of faith” [Note: [Col. 0975] Heb. 12]. They know that if the earthly house of this dwelling is dissolved, they have a building from God, a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens [Note: [Col. 0975] II Cor. 5]. They know that, he says, the temporal sleep [Col. 0975C] is exceedingly brief. “When he gives sleep to his beloved, behold, the inheritance of the Lord!” [Note: [Col. 0975] Ps. 126]. Then the meek shall inherit the earth and delight in abundance of peace [Note: [Col. 0975] Ps. 36].

For as they have been planted together in the likeness of Christ’s death, so also they shall be in that of his resurrection: reborn into the hope of life, they shall rise in the glory of the sons of God. “For the righteous shall shine as the sun” [Note: [Col. 0975] Matt. 13] in the presence of God, when Christ has transformed the body of our lowliness to be conformed to the body of his glory [Note: [Col. 0975] Phil. 3], so that he who is the radiance and image of God’s substance [Note: [Col. 0975] Heb. 1] may not disdain to conform the sons of his adoption to his image. Thus blessed John speaks [Col. 0976A] in his Epistle: “Now we are sons of God; but it has not yet appeared what we shall be. Yet we know that when he appears, we shall be like him” [Note: [Col. 0975] I John 3].

They came to the place of martyrdom and gladly exposed their bodies to torments. Woe to the sinful nation, evil seed, criminal children [Note: [Col. 0975] Isa. 1]! It does not suffice the ministers of Satan to cut off the martyrs’ heads; with swords they gouge out their eyes and search with blades the inner hiding places of their souls. Inhuman cruelty can rage against bodies; but the souls of the righteous are in God’s hand, and the torment of malice shall not touch them [Note: [Col. 0975] Wis. 3]. Thus, being perfected in a short time, they fulfilled many years [Note: [Col. 0975] Wis. 4]. O how precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints [Note: [Col. 0975] Ps. 115]—truly precious! For by this price they were purchased from the earth; by this price [Col. 0976B] are given them possession of glory, the kingdom of heaven, an unfading crown, and the peace of life. They seemed, in the eyes of the foolish, to die; but they are in peace [Note: [Col. 0975] Wis. 3]. Therefore I do not think these should be mourned.

They turned their mourning into joy [Note: [Col. 0975] Jer. 31]. The Lord shall wipe tears from their eyes, and there shall now be no mourning, nor any pain, because the former things have passed away [Note: [Col. 0975] Rev. 21]. Unrighteous death bit, but did not swallow up, the men of God. It appeared to have conquered and consumed them, but death was swallowed up in victory. “Where, O death, is your victory?” [Note: [Col. 0975] I Cor. 15]. Surely he who holds the power of life and death will destroy your power, so that you may henceforth become the cause of life and the entrance to salvation.

## Transition to Other Matters
