[Col. 0976C] These aforesaid martyrs so glorified the Lord in their bodies and received the cup of salvation. “What shall we render to the Lord for all that he has rendered to us?” [Note: [Col. 0975] Ps. 115]. We are marked with the same image, redeemed by the same blood, initiated into the same sacraments; and yet we cannot, or will not, suffer anything for Christ. Someone may say: “I would gladly suffer for Christ if the occasion presented itself.” The Lord knows our fashioning [Note: [Col. 0975] Ps. 102]; for the choice which we display in small matters plainly declares what we would do in great ones.

[Col. 0975]

## Dialogue between King Henry II and the Abbot of Bonneval

[Col. 0975D] **KING.** “I have nourished and exalted sons, but they have despised me” [Note: [Col. 0975] Isa. 1]. “My friends and my neighbours have stood against me” [Note: [Col. 0975] Ps. 36]. Those whom I had as household members and intimates I have found to be cruel and wicked enemies and traitors. [Col. 0976D] Yet the God of vengeances, the Lord God [Note: [Col. 0975] Ps. 93], shall take vengeance for me upon my enemies; may he destroy and confound those who desire my confusion. They have set evil against me for good, and hatred for my love [Col. 0977A]. May the Lord appoint over them a destroying angel, and may the devil stand at their right hand. When they are judged, may they go forth condemned; may their days be few; may their children become orphans and their wives widows; may their offspring perish; may none pity their fatherless children; and may their memory perish from the earth [Note: [Col. 0977] Ps. 108]. May their ways be dark and slippery, with the angel of the Lord pursuing them [Note: [Col. 0977] Ps. 34]. May they be ashamed and troubled forever and ever; may they be confounded and perish [Note: [Col. 0977] Ps. 82]. May death come upon them, and may they go down alive into hell [Note: [Col. 0977] Ps. 54], where their fire shall not be quenched and their worm shall not die [Note: [Col. 0977] Isa. 66]. May their delights be turned into bitterness and sorrow; and with Dathan and Abiram, with Cain and Judas the traitor, may they have their portion without end.

[Col. 0977B] **ABBOT.** What is this, most prudent prince? What agitation of mind is this, that you curse God’s creatures, and especially man, who is the form of God and the image of the Most High? It neither becomes you nor is lawful for you to seek vengeance for what he himself does. The evils which you endure are wrought by the Lord. If you do not believe me, believe Isaiah, who says: “There is no evil in a city which God does not do”; and in the same prophet: “Who gave Jacob over to plunder and Israel to ravagers? Was it not the Lord, against whom we sinned?” [Note: [Col. 0977] Isa. 42]. If a man hates or persecutes you, it is God’s judgment; it comes not from man but from God.

When David went out from Jerusalem because of the blow dealt by his son Absalom, barefoot and in ashes and sackcloth, Shimei cursed him, saying: “Go out, man of Belial; go out, man of blood” [Col. 0977C] [Note: [Col. 0977] II Sam. 16]. When Abishai, Joab’s brother, wished to kill the man who thus cursed the king, David forbade him, saying: “Do not kill him, because the Lord himself sent him to curse me” [Note: [Col. 0977] Ibid.]. If you wish, O king, to be an imitator of David, confess and say: “The Lord sent these men to curse me.”

**KING.** If these men were sent to curse me, why was I not sent to curse my evildoers? If I cannot harm them as much as I wish, still I shall curse them as much as I can; for a curse itself is in some way a kind of vengeance for me, and a welcome consolation in adversity.

**ABBOT.** Most illustrious prince, from the moment you cursed your enemy, you have already judged him and already taken [Col. 0977D] vengeance upon him. Thus you have deprived God, the supreme Judge, of the opportunity to render judgment or vengeance for you against your enemy. Did not he who is the avenger of evils and judge of all men know better and have greater power to avenge you? For he himself says through the prophet: “Vengeance is mine, and I will repay” [Note: [Col. 0977] Rom. 12]. You have done what he should have done; for, as it is written: “The Lord will not punish twice for the same thing” [Note: [Col. 0977] Nah. 1]. He finds nothing to punish in your enemy, because you have already punished him—the man whom God ought to have punished [Col. 0978A]. For God does not punish things already judged—that is, he does not judge them—and he does not punish things already punished.

If we wish to escape Christ’s judgment, let us judge ourselves and not others. For if we are judged by ourselves, judgment is already, as it were, justice. For the Apostle Paul says: “If we judged ourselves, surely we would not be judged” [Note: [Col. 0977] II Cor. 11].

**KING.** In the Old Testament I read that leaders, kings, and even prophets often took the most severe vengeance upon their enemies. Yet, to use the words of Elijah the prophet: “I am not better than my fathers” [Note: [Col. 0977] III Kings 19]. The Lord says to Moses: “You shall not suffer sorcerers to live” [Note: [Col. 0977] Exod. 22]; and, “Cursed be he who does not fulfil the words of this law.” Hence six tribes were stationed on one mountain to curse transgressors of the law. Abraham also was told: “Whoever [Col. 0978B] curses you, let him be cursed” [Note: [Col. 0977] Gen. 27]. These things would neither be read in sacred speech nor written unless it were lawful to curse or harm enemies.

**ABBOT.** Consider, king, that you are not of the people of the Jews or a disciple of Moses, but of the people of acquisition, and a disciple and professor of Christ. That Jewish people was stiff-necked, as it is written: “You are hard, and your neck is exceedingly iron” [Note: [Col. 0977] Isa. 48]. Therefore it delighted in the repayment of evils; accordingly, without any mercy it exercised the hardness of vengeance, taking hand for hand, tooth for tooth, eye for eye [Note: [Col. 0977] Deut. 19]. Because of this hardness the Lord commanded them: “You shall love your friend and hate your enemy” [Note: [Col. 0977] Matt. 5].

Moreover, although the commandments of the Old Testament—that is, of the Law—concerned the preservation of bodies, they did not bring salvation of the soul. The Lord plainly shows this through his prophet, saying: “I gave them a law not good and precepts not good, commandments by which they should not live” [Note: [Col. 0977] Ezek. 20]. Therefore the Lord, coming compassionate and merciful—as he himself says [Note: [Col. 0977] John 12]—to be judged and not to judge, teaches us not merely to pardon our enemies and persecutors, but to love enemies and pray for them. “Love,” he says, “your enemies; do good to those who hate you; pray for those who slander and persecute you” [Note: [Col. 0977] Matt. 5]. For mercy exalts itself above judgment, and he who does not practise mercy [Note: [Col. 0977] Jas. 2] shall be condemned without mercy for ever.

**KING.** Whatever you may find in Gospel or other Scripture [Col. 0978D], I cannot find it in my heart to do good to my persecutor or love my enemy. That belongs to a more perfect life. I see that at times a lamb grows angry with a lamb and a dove with a dove; the one striking with horns, the other with wings, they express their anger as they can. But shall it not be permitted to me to be angry, since anger is a certain power of the soul and a natural faculty? What nature permits me does not seem unlawful. By nature [Col. 0979A] I am a son of wrath; how then shall I not be angry? God himself grows angry, in whom, as it is written, “there is no change nor shadow of turning” [Note: [Col. 0979] Jas. 1]. How then shall I establish my heart so as not to grow angry—especially against those whose every deed, every word, and every thought toward me is evil? To use the words of Job, a most prudent and patient man: “Is my strength the strength of stones, or is my flesh of bronze, that I should endure these things?” [Note: [Col. 0979] Job 6].

**ABBOT.** Yet through Christ you must endure these and like things, if you do not wish to endure endless and intolerable pains in hell. It is therefore expedient that you use force upon your heart, turning hatred into favour and enmities into love. If you impose this force on your heart for Christ’s love, through this force [Col. 0979B] you will obtain the heavenly kingdom. “For the kingdom of heaven suffers violence” [Note: [Col. 0979] Matt. 11]. The Lord says in the Gospel: “Forgive, and you shall be forgiven”; and, “If you do not forgive others from your heart, neither will my heavenly Father forgive you” [Note: [Col. 0979] Matt. 6]. He who does not show mercy shall perish without mercy.

And again the Lord says in the Gospel: “With what measure you have measured, it shall be measured back to you” [Note: [Col. 0979] Matt. 7]. Therefore show mercy to your neighbour if you wish to find mercy with God. Hear Solomon’s word—or rather, his Gospel: “One man keeps anger against another and seeks healing from God; yet he has no mercy toward a man like himself” [Note: [Col. 0979] Ecclus. 28]. Man is flesh and preserves anger: how, then, shall he seek propitiation from God? You have heard Solomon; and behold, one greater than [Col. 0979C] Solomon is here. For Christ, our Creator and Saviour, is the one who says: “If your enemy is hungry, feed him; if he thirsts, give him drink” [Note: [Col. 0979] Rom. 12]. And in the Gospel [Note: [Col. 0979] Matt. 18], the servant who refused to have mercy on his fellow-servant was delivered to the torturers until he paid the entire debt. In the Lord’s Prayer we say: “Forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors” [Note: [Col. 0979] Matt. 6].

We make a pact and agreement with God, that “he may forgive us our debts and sins as we pardon and forgive others, our enemies and evildoers.” Speaking falsely and deceptively, we deceive ourselves and knowingly incur the judgment of eternal condemnation. God is not mocked [Note: [Col. 0979] Gal. 6]; he searches the secrets of hearts and can neither deceive nor be deceived. As [Col. 0979D] you behave toward your enemy, so will he behave toward you—the one who, by his blood, made you from a servant and enemy into a son and friend. If you wish to repay evil for evil, you provoke God to anger; and I fear that he who is terrible over the children of men [Note: [Col. 0979] Ps. 65] may devise and bring upon you a greater evil.

Indeed Solomon says: “When your enemy falls, do not rejoice, lest God see it, turn his anger away from him, and turn it upon your head” [Note: [Col. 0979] Prov. 24]. For it is written: “He who rejoices in another’s ruin shall not go unpunished” [Col. 0980A] [Note: [Col. 0979] Prov. 17]. Another will rejoice in that man’s ruin. Therefore, with a secure conscience, Job said: “If I rejoiced at the ruin of my enemy and exulted when evil found him” [Note: [Col. 0979] Job 31], etc.; and David: “If I repaid those who repaid me” [Note: [Col. 0979] Ps. 7], etc. A prudent and holy man would not utter such grave imprecations or prayers if he knew that he repaid evils with evils. Certainly he had many persecutors; but amid all his anger he did not depart from mercy and gentleness. Therefore, in the glad security of his conscience, he sang: “Remember, O Lord, David, and all …” [Note: [Col. 0979] Ps. 131].

**KING.** Would that I could repay my enemies in accordance with the impulse and desire of my anger! I can be angry beyond my wish, but repayment is not [Col. 0980B] in my power. May he who can do all things repay abundantly those who act proudly against me [Note: [Col. 0979] Ps. 30], and may my soul take joy in their confusion.

**ABBOT.** Most illustrious king, it belongs to man sometimes to be angry; but one must beware lest anger turn into hatred and sin, as it is written: “Be angry, and do not sin” [Note: [Col. 0979] Eph. 4]. God forbids the sun to set upon your anger [Note: [Col. 0979] Ibid.]; and, to explain this simply, he forbids our anger to grow hard from morning until evening. Let us therefore have patience in all things. If anyone offends us, let us hate the person’s sin, not the person. This is the hatred of the perfect, or perfect hatred, as it is written [Col. 0980C]: “With perfect hatred I hated them,” etc. [Note: [Col. 0979] Ps. 138]. Therefore, putting curses aside, let us render good for evil to those who curse and harm us. Let us take as our example blessed Stephen, who prayed for his persecutors and fell asleep in the Lord [Note: [Col. 0979] Acts 7].

He also who teaches man knowledge [Note: [Col. 0979] Ps. 93] teaches and instructs us by his own example, when praying for those who crucified him: “Father,” he says, “forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” [Note: [Col. 0979] Luke 23]. If we curse men, the curse will return into our bosom, and the anger which we bear toward him who is God’s image will make everyone angry with us. If a father had many sons and one of them beat another before the father’s eyes, I believe that the father would not be angry with the beaten son, but rather with the one beating him. Let us therefore reserve all judgment for the heavenly Father [Col. 0980D], and neither do evil to nor pray for evil against our evildoers, lest our prayer become sin for us.

He who curses another entangles and envelops himself in a curse, and through his curse wins for his enemy the fruit of divine blessing. For the Lord says: “I will curse your blessings and bless your curses” [Note: [Col. 0979] Mal. 2; Deut. 28]. Therefore you cannot help your enemy better than by cursing him. Do him no harm; for thus you bring it about that he receives mercy and blessing from the Lord, while you who curse another alone lie under the curse. Therefore the Apostle says: “When we are cursed, we bless, repaying no one evil for evil; bless those who curse you, and do not curse” [Note: [Col. 0981] Rom. 12].

**KING.** My enemies grow stronger against me daily [Note: [Col. 0981] Lam. 1], and the pride of those who hate me rises continually [Note: [Col. 0981] Ps. 73]. How, then, can I humble my heart to mercy when I see my enemies exalted against me in anger?

**ABBOT.** He whom you regard as your enemy is not your enemy but his own. For in hating you he kills himself. Of this occasion—or rather, this homicide—the Evangelist John says: “He who hates his brother [Col. 0981B] is a murderer” [Note: [Col. 0981] I John 3]. While he hates you, he kills himself; and, when he unjustly persecutes you, whether he wishes it or not, he gives you life in Christ. Therefore, if you wish to obtain vengeance upon your enemy, commit everything to the Most High and trust in him. He will turn your evils into good, losses into gain, sorrow into joy, tribulations into peace, troubles into delights, and dishonour into honour.

**KING.** I could have mercy on my persecutors for a time; but if they persist in their wickedness, I cannot endure their injuries, because it would seem the utmost sloth, faintheartedness, and failure of spirit. Since, then, they do not desist from their wickedness, I cannot have mercy upon their wickedness.

[Col. 0981C] **ABBOT.** May Christ’s love, the work of mercy, fear of the divine judgment, and the examples of the ancient fathers move you to mercy, I pray, excellent prince. When the hard and stony people wished to stone Moses [Note: [Col. 0981] Exod. 17], he fled to the tabernacle and stood in anguish before God, laying down his own life for them. Upon a wicked and perverse generation he bestowed a father’s affection and the gracious compassion of a mother. David graciously forgave the wrongdoing of Nabal, a foolish man [Note: [Col. 0981] I Sam. 25]. He likewise had compassion upon Saul his persecutor [Note: [Col. 0981] I Sam. 24], and mourned the death of his mortal enemy, Absalom [Note: [Col. 0981] II Sam. 19]. Elisha, sought by the king of Samaria for death, delivered both him and his people from death [Note: [Col. 0981] IV Kings 6]. Joseph also, sold by his brothers, graciously received and honoured those same brothers [Note: [Col. 0981] Gen. 45]. If you will have patience together with humility [Col. 0981D], in humility you shall conquer all your adversaries, and in your patience you shall possess your soul [Note: [Col. 0981] Luke 21].

**KING.** Since I cannot find this patience and humility in my heart, as has been said, you speak and labour in vain, unless you wish to show me by what means I ought to obtain and preserve those virtues.

**ABBOT.** Friend and revered lord, if you desire to possess patience and humility, reflect how unclean and worthless is that from which man is conceived; in [Col. 0982A] how much pain he is born by his mother; amid how many miseries and impurities he is born and nourished; how brief his life is; through how many pains and labours it is led; to how many snares and dangers it is subject; and how horrible his end is. Consider attentively the terrible day of judgment, the dreadful tribunal, the angry Judge, the burning river, the worms that do not die, the unquenchable flames, the deadly stench, the gnashing of teeth, the shadow of death, and pain to which none is like or equal. Although all these things are not present, nevertheless know beyond doubt that they will not delay. Moreover, devout prayer greatly helps, that humility and the strength of patience may be granted to a person by the Lord God.

**KING.** Why do you speak of prayer, Father? Do you not see [Col. 0982B] that my occupations and anxieties are so unbearable that I can scarcely say the Lord’s Prayer at Mass, and can scarcely find one hour of day or night in which to breathe?

**ABBOT.** You yourself, king, make these occupations for yourself. You could possess the most tranquil peace and rest of soul, but you entangle and involve yourself in endless agitations and disturbances. Thousands of men follow you constantly: you have heard their affairs, and all are deferred to the future, though they could be settled by brief deliberation.

**KING.** Only those, as I think, Father, follow me whose petitions are unjust; because they despair of their own right, they follow the court in order to overcome me by their [Col. 0982C] shamelessness and importunity.

**ABBOT.** Do not deceive yourself, excellent prince; do not advance useless reasons to excuse excuses in sins [Note: [Col. 0981] Ps. 140]. For God is not mocked [Note: [Col. 0981] Eph. 4]. We know that you are swift and energetic in your own affairs, but slow in others’ affairs. Yet it is a great habit of many—almost another nature—to glory in the fullness of their court and a great crowd. I ask you to attend patiently and willingly to what Holy Scripture says terribly, and as it were in a voice of thunder, concerning such persons: “O you who take pleasure in crowds: power was given you by God, who will examine your works and thoughts; because, when you were ministers of his kingdom, you did not judge rightly nor walk according to God’s will. [Col. 0982D] He will appear terribly and swiftly to you, because a most severe judgment is for those who rule” [Note: [Col. 0981] Wis. 6]. For mercy is granted to the lowly, but a stronger torment presses upon the powerful.

**KING.** This Scripture is dreadful and terrifying to all rulers. Yet with a secure conscience I can say that my will and desire have always been to be in solitude and in fewness rather than in a multitude. But it has not been granted me from above ever to be able to live more privately and enjoy the tranquility of even one briefest moment. [Col. 0983A] Even at Mass not only laypeople but also clerics, men, and religious persons trouble me; as though reverence for the supreme sacrament had been set aside, they do not cease to offer me their petitions.

**ABBOT.** See, my dearest king, lest you yourself have introduced this custom. You can easily remove it if you feel that your conscience is injured by it. For it is exceedingly dangerous that, at the hour when the Son of God is sacrificed before men’s eyes, they should turn away from prayer and occupy themselves with idle talk. We know that if some very powerful prince had invited persons to his table, he would take it very ill if his guests despised his food.

**KING.** If you advise it, Father, I shall defer everyone’s petitions [Col. 0983B], and while I am in church I shall hear no one’s requests.

**ABBOT.** Preserving due reverence for Mass and the canonical hours of the day, you may hear the needs of your brethren in church no less than in your chamber; and where you ask for mercy, there show mercy to others. Indeed, whether someone asks for an honour, demands restoration of what is his, or asks that justice be rendered him, give orders accordingly. In all these matters you are debtor to all, and it is not without peril to your soul that such things are deferred. You have received the sword of justice for the punishment of evildoers and the praise of the good. Therefore, if justice is sought, administer it freely and without payment, and do not allow your most excellent office to be corrupted by any venality. If the need of the poor and religious persons [Col. 0983C] asks that the hand of your mercy and generosity be extended, do not defer it. Solomon’s word is: “Do not say to your friend, ‘Go and return tomorrow,’ when you can give at once” [Note: [Col. 0983] Prov. 3]. For you do not know what the coming day will bring forth; you do not know whether their need can endure delay and postponement. You live today and do not know whether you will live tomorrow. A man is king today and will die tomorrow; and when he has died, serpents and worms shall inherit him [Note: [Col. 0983] Ecclus. 10].

King, king, you shall have these heirs, because they will be born from your flesh. But those who have already been born from your flesh—if they do not love you while you live, how shall they love you when dead? Behold, you have sons and heirs for whom you have strained your soul and mortified your flesh. They will no more benefit your soul than they have benefited your flesh. Whatever you have placed in them is [Col. 0983D] vanity, a carnal falsehood, transient, lost; there is nothing of God in it. If you wish to have heirs, make Christ’s poor your heirs. For when your sons fail, the poor shall stand with great confidence against those who distressed you [Note: [Col. 0983] Wis. 5]. If your sons afflict you over an earthly and momentary inheritance, the poor will make you an heir of the heavenly kingdom. For by Christ’s testimony: “Theirs is the kingdom of heaven” [Note: [Col. 0983] Matt. 5].

**KING.** I cannot, will not, and ought not disinherit my sons. Although decrees and laws [Col. 0984A] exclude from paternal inheritance those who have taken up arms against their fathers, I nevertheless do not wish to exclude my sons from inheritance. Even if I could disinherit them, my heart could not bear such harshness.

**ABBOT.** You speak of your sons’ inheritance: why do you make no mention at all of the inheritance of the poor?

**KING.** My purpose and desire are to devote the greater part of my goods to the liberation of that land upon which the Lord’s feet stood, in which he redeemed us by being born and dying; to distribute a portion to the poor; and to expend the remainder mercifully for the use of orphans and other needy persons.

[Col. 0984B] **ABBOT.** Most powerful king, patiently endure what I am about to say to you. Where the salvation of your soul is concerned, I shall not spare royal power. God, maker of all things, made you from nothing. Had it pleased him, your father might have begotten you by a lowly and humble slave-woman, and you would not be among kings today; you came naked from your mother’s womb [Note: [Col. 0983] Eccles. 5]. God entrusted to you everything that you have. If you cannot repay as much as you owe, repay as much as you can. Take care lest the world turn you away from Christ. We read of a certain great man who, when at the point of death and urged by his friends to give his goods generously to the needy, answered—possessed by a spirit as malignant as his illness—“I would gladly do this, but Lady Avarice does not permit me.”

[Col. 0984C] **KING.** God knows how much I have done for churches; nor would you rebuke me so harshly if you knew how greatly the honour of the Church has increased in my time.

**ABBOT.** I know that you have given magnificently and generously to churches and churchmen, and the whole Church of the saints recounts your alms. But the Lord considers not how much is given, but from how much; not where, but whence. For if you despoil one altar in order to cover another; if you take from one poor person in order to give to another, then, according to Scripture’s testimony, God does not accept a sacrifice from robbery [Note: [Col. 0983] Isa. 61]. For whatever civil power usurps in ecclesiastical property is robbery—indeed, sacrilege.

REX. What if the Roman Church has granted and privileged my predecessors and me with great authority in ecclesiastical affairs? We ought to follow her in all things [Col. 0984D]; she is our mother and teacher, nor should it seem absurd to you if I wish to make use of her privileges.

ABBOT. It is written that one must consider not what is done at Rome, but what ought to be done at Rome. Therefore, most prudent king, carefully attend to what is fitting, not to what is permitted; to what pertains to unending salvation and ineffable glory, not to false and transitory rank. Many privileges can be bought; but there is one thing necessary which cannot be taken away [Note: [Col. 0983] Luke 10.]. The highest privilege is to obtain the freedom of the children of God and, through a temporal kingdom full of miseries and pains, to acquire the kingdom of heaven, whose glory does not fail, whose honour is not interrupted, whose blessedness does not pass away. What is more glorious or desirable in this world than to reign and exercise power over others? Yet you have learned by experience whether these sayings are true: that the happiness of a temporal kingdom—in which he who has more power fears more, he who has more possesses more needs, he who labours for every kind of rest never rests, and he who rules all serves all—is never at peace.

REX. I know, I know; nor could I conceive in my heart or express in speech how much I have laboured for my people. And this is the recompense the Lord gives me: that among my people I find neither faithfulness, nor among my sons love.

[Col. 0985B] ABBOT. King, attend, I beseech you, and reflect how much God has done for you in great necessities. I have seen you in the gravest necessities [Note: [Col. 0985] Something is missing.], and I believe that God delivered you through the prayers of your people. What you have once obtained by the grace and mercy of God, you may count most miserable if you remove it from yourself, if you do not preserve and retain it for the future.

REX. I have often experienced, both in my prayers and in my necessities, that I possess God’s grace; but I have never known how to retain or preserve what I have received. Father, I would gladly hear from your holiness how I might do this.

ABBOT. There are two things: one acquires grace, the other retains grace once acquired—pure confession of the mouth, and satisfaction in deed. For when a sinner approaches [Col. 0985C] the priest, God’s vicar, and pours out his heart like water before the face of the Most High, like a sheep before its shepherd, like a sick man before his physician, like an accused person before his judge, then, from the moment he begins to accuse and condemn himself through confession, the Judge of all receives into his grace the sinner judging himself; he embraces him, kisses him, and marks him with the ring of his love. For this is that prodigal son who had squandered his portion in extravagant living; and when he returned to his father from the husks of swine, of which he could not obtain enough, you see that while he was still far off, his father ran to his son, embraced him, and fell upon his head [Note: [Col. 0985] Psalm 13.].

What do you suppose that poor hungry son thought, when, naked and afflicted, [Col. 0985D] he felt about himself such tender compassion of fatherly sweetness? All who return to the Father of mercies in true contrition of heart experience this sweetness. Yet there are some who are ashamed to confess their sins; of these the Lord will be ashamed in his kingdom. Perhaps they fear that priests will reveal their iniquities, or that priests will think them more contemptible in their hearts because of confession. Truly, “they trembled where there was no fear” [Note: [Col. 0985] Luke 15.]: they entrust all their secrets throughout the day to talkative and unfaithful people, yet are ashamed before those whom office and sacrament make vicars of Christ. This shame does not heal but defiles; [Col. 0986A] it does not justify but condemns. You have the right to be justified in your own power: speak your iniquities, that you may be justified. It is the prophet’s word: “I said, ‘I will confess’” [Note: [Col. 0985] Psalm 31.], and you refused.

REX. I sometimes see someone make confession and receive penance; afterward he falls more grievously, and the last state of that man is worse than the former [Note: [Col. 0985] Matthew 12.].

ABBOT. Son, in this case and in similar ones you may detect false confession and simulated penitence. But, that you may understand more fully the good fruit of penitence, I beseech you, lend to my words not only the ears of your body but also the hearing of your heart.

REX. I listen gladly; and although great and arduous affairs await me, I will nevertheless set them aside for your admonitions [Col. 0986B].

ABBOT. Noble king, you know that we were all wounded in our first parents. Those wounds were healed in baptism; but through our foolishness the scars of those wounds have been renewed, with the decay and corruption of sin coming upon them. As the prophet David says: “My scars have putrefied and become corrupt because of my foolishness” [Note: [Col. 0985] Psalm 37.]. The first medicine was baptism; the second is penitence. Of this medicine Solomon says: “God has provided medicine for men, and fools despise it.” The medicine of baptism is most gentle, because it requires neither groaning nor weeping. For baptism is like a light washing of garments. But just as the rust of iron is removed only by fire and a certain hammering, [Col. 0986C] so grave sin is abolished only by grave penitence. The violation of penitence is like this: a leg or another limb, once broken, is first set and healed, and therefore is more dangerously broken again a second or third time after it has once been restored.

REX. Many people of this age, and especially knights, are ashamed to do penance before others; for some think that this proceeds from a kind of hypocrisy, or from weakness and faint-heartedness.

ABBOT. Alas for me! How ruinous and wicked is this shame for them, through which the medicine of the soul is lost and destroyed! It is the height of madness not to be ashamed of wounds but to be ashamed of binding up wounds. Our wounds are idle words, slanders, deceitful speech, false promises, perjuries, curses, anger, envy, hatred, greed, gluttony, avarice, lust, pride. Our wounds also are that we offend good men; that we sometimes grievously provoke the powerful against us; that we sell justice, admit false accusers, and support oppressors of the poor; that we frequently heed unjust petitions; that we honour neither the ecclesiastical order nor the religious life with the reverence due and fitting; that we [Col. 0987A] squander the wills of the dying, the rights of the living, and the marriages of virgins; that we desire people’s deaths; that we sow discord among friends; that we usurp ecclesiastical goods or other illicit things. Therefore let medicine be applied to our wounds, lest, if they are allowed to fester, they must be burned away or cut out with the utmost pain.

REX. Many conceal the wounds of their sins, whether from shame, negligence, or daily occupations, until they have leisure for this; but they incur the gravest danger of necessity.

ABBOT. Know, most beloved prince, that delaying penitence is most dangerous. Many believed that they would live a long time, whom sudden death carried off. How does a man delay repentance when he has not one day—indeed, not even one very brief hour—in his own power? Some wait to repent until the time of old age. What grace is owed them if they cease to sin then, when they cannot sin? If your servant served your enemy throughout all his youth, then, broken by old age, finally came to you, would you receive his service with good will? Do you wish to do to the Lord your God what you would not allow a servant to do to you? I have seen some who wished with all their heart to repent, yet delayed doing their penance; struck by apoplexy or some other sudden calamity, they departed without penitence. For the supreme Judge often allows a dying person to forget himself, since he has forgotten the one God; and he who does not [Col. 0987C] wish to do penance when he can, when he wishes to do it, cannot, because God’s wrath has come upon him. Therefore, I beseech you, let no one wait for divine judgment, but heed that saying of the Wise Man: “Remember that death does not delay” [Note: [Col. 0987] Ecclesiasticus 14.].

REX. Most merciful Father, I have sinned beyond measure. The whole life of soldiers is in sin; and, considering the time of sins and of penitence, unless the merciful Lord look upon me, I cannot do worthy penance.

ABBOT. Illustrious king, attend: Christ, the Son of God, suffering on the cross, nailed our sins to the cross with his own hands. Therefore let no one despair that the Lord will not blot out his sins through penitence; for he is so gracious that he wishes to grant forgiveness of sins. It is to be hoped that he is able to do so. Ahab was so impious that Sacred Scripture says of him that he “sold himself to do evil in the sight of the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0987] 3 Kings 21.]. But when he turned himself to the humility of penitence, immediately the word of the Lord came to Elijah, saying: “Because Ahab has humbled himself before me, I will not bring evil in his days” [Note: [Col. 0987] Ibid.]. Manasseh, who, [Col. 0988A] according to the testimony of Sacred Scripture, had filled all Jerusalem with sacrilege and iniquity, afterward, led into captivity and purified by adversity, is reckoned not least among God’s friends. You have the example of penitence in David; you have the publican, the Canaanite woman, and Saul; you have that most famous sinful woman who, as soon as she heard that Christ Jesus, the supreme physician of souls, had come, did not wait to be summoned, but, just as she had been shameless in sin, so she hurried boldly and confidently and approached the physician.

REX. Most reverend Father, I have often undertaken penitence with a contrite and humbled heart; nevertheless, I have never wholly and completely kept before God any penance imposed upon me.

[Col. 0988B] ABBOT. My dearest king in Christ, true penitence is to weep for sins committed and not to commit again what must be wept for. For it is not penitence but mockery to leave one’s sin for a time and fall back into the same thing. For Sacred Scripture says: “He who is baptized for a dead man” [Note: [Col. 0987] 1 Corinthians 15.], and it happens to him again—what profit is his cleansing? In the testimony of the apostle Peter: “A dog returns to its vomit, and a washed sow to wallowing in mud” [Note: [Col. 0987] 2 Peter 2.]. To the sinner who returns to sin, Solomon’s saying applies: “Son, have you sinned? Do not add again; but pray concerning your former sins, that they may be forgiven you” [Note: [Col. 0987] Ecclesiasticus 21.]. Therefore the Lord says in the Gospel: “Behold, you have been made whole; sin no more, lest something worse happen to you” [Note: [Col. 0987] John 5.].

[Col. 0988C] REX. Could not the journey to Jerusalem avail, for those truly confessed and penitent, toward salvation as full satisfaction?

ABBOT. Certainly it could; and this was especially my hope in Christ: that by the labour of this journey those who neglected to make satisfaction in another way might make satisfaction to God. But, because our sins demanded it, the way of the Lord which led to life has been abandoned. I see people walking on the devil’s way, hastening to death. The cross which redeemed us has been captured, and there is no one to redeem it. The Sepulchre, the Temple, and the other places which the Lord consecrated by his bodily presence are held and profaned by the impious; hence my words are full of sorrow. Therefore send me away, most gracious king, that I may weep a little for my grief. [Col. 0988D] To express more freely the constricted anguish of my sobbing sorrow, I shall take up the words of the prophet of Lamentations.

Here ends the Dialogue of Master Peter of Blois, Archdeacon of Bath, between King Henry II and the Abbot of Bonneval.

[Col. 0989]

ON THE TWELVE BENEFITS OF TRIBULATION.

[Col. 0989A] The order and method of instruction which tribulations serve is that you should endure them not only patiently but even willingly, and should be inwardly comforted because you are outwardly desolated. For, as Seneca says, “There is no greater consolation than that which is drawn from desolation.” No one can have that consolation unless he first knows the effect of tribulation: namely, how God, who sends tribulations, orders them for the advancement and benefit of those who endure them, unless by the perversity of rebellion they set themselves against the ordering of their Creator. Those, therefore, who recognize their failings on the one hand and consider the usefulness of tribulation on the other, if in their firm purpose they ask God in tribulation to uproot tribulations from them, perhaps ask against themselves—as Paul did, who [Col. 0989B] asked that the thorn of the flesh be removed. To him God replied: “My grace is sufficient for you, for strength is made perfect in weakness” [Note: [Col. 0989] 2 Corinthians 12.].

There are many fruits of tribulations; but for the present we shall touch on twelve, which contain many others as well. Whoever reads this treatise carefully, or listens more attentively, will easily understand them. For as food poorly chewed is digested with difficulty and gives little benefit, so too the teaching of Sacred Scripture when read hastily or heard without attention.

The FIRST benefit wrought by tribulation is this: tribulation is a faithful aid sent by the Lord to snatch the soul from the hands of all its enemies. These enemies are the false [Col. 0989C] joys and deceptive prosperity of this world, which seduce an undisciplined heart more perilously the more sweetly they flatter it. These are the enemies of whom the common proverb says: “The fool does not fear these.” They are to be feared all the more because they entice more pleasantly and deceive in the end. These are enemies who kill by flattering and flatter by killing. They are signified by Joab, who, taking Amasa by the chin as though he wished to kiss him, killed him [Note: [Col. 0989] 2 Kings 20.]. Hence Gregory says: “Although every fortune is to be feared, prosperity is more to be feared than adversity.” This is plainly apparent because an enemy who attacks secretly is more to be feared than one who attacks openly.

Notice that this aid of tribulation is not merely sent by God: God himself is its commander and marshal, ordering it for the deliverance of his friends. Thus God promises through the prophet David: “I am with him in tribulation” [Note: [Col. 0989] Psalm 90.], that is, when he is afflicted and tempted. And it follows: “I will deliver him and glorify him” [Note: [Col. 0989] Ibid.]. [Col. 0990A] Since, then, God is with us in tribulation, it must be endured patiently and willingly; for in proportion as tribulation weighs more heavily, God draws nearer to the afflicted person. Hence the Psalmist says: “The Lord is near to those who are troubled in heart” [Note: [Col. 0989] Psalm 33.]. Therefore, while the presence of tribulation troubles you, the presence of the Saviour, who stands with you in tribulation, gives you inward consolation.

But perhaps someone says: “I feel present tribulations well enough, but I do not feel God’s companionship in my tribulation. For if he revealed the sweetness of his presence as clearly as he reveals the bitterness of tribulation, I would endure tribulation patiently and gladly.” Perhaps you add that before tribulation you felt God’s sweetness more than when you are placed in tribulation. To this [Col. 0990B] one may reply that God’s presence in tribulation can, as is now clear, be considered or understood in two ways. First, in the bestowal of strength and grace: for as tribulation increases, so God multiplies strength and grace, according to the Apostle’s saying: “God is faithful, who will not permit you to be tempted beyond what you are able, but will make with the temptation a way out, so that you may be able to endure it” [Note: [Col. 0989] 1 Corinthians 10.]; that is, he will give an increase of grace and strength to endure tribulation patiently. For just as the lords of fortresses customarily send a garrison and relief to those besieged in their strongholds, so God customarily pours an increase of grace into the afflicted soul.

Second, God’s presence in tribulation can be considered or understood in the bestowal of inward consolation which he infuses into the afflicted person. Hence the Apostle says: [Col. 0990C] “As the sufferings of Christ abound in us, so consolation abounds through Christ” [Note: [Col. 0989] 2 Corinthians 1.]. Christ’s sufferings are said to abound in us because they are sent by him; and therefore they must be endured patiently for sin, and in conformity with Christ—and this without guilt, so that we do not suffer as a thief or murderer, who have well deserved what they suffer.

But observe that the increase of grace granted in tribulation is not always given to be felt by the afflicted person; this happens for his testing, fear, and deliverance. Moreover, consolation should not come until a place has been prepared for it; tribulation prepares that place, according to the saying: “After a storm you make calm, and after lamentation and weeping you pour in rejoicing” [Note: [Col. 0989] Tobit 3.]. Hence David says: “According to the multitude [Col. 0990D] of my sorrows in my heart, your consolations have gladdened my soul” [Note: [Col. 0989] Psalm 93.]. The consolations of one hour, moreover, exceed the tribulations of many years. For God himself, who first comes to aid you, will remain with you after tribulation [Col. 0991A] and strengthen you, as Bernard says.

And if perhaps you complain, saying that this consolation delays too long—as lovers complain—Cassiodorus replies that its very swiftness seems delay to the heart that considers and loves. But if you ask about the righteous who have never committed mortal sin, how it can be said that they have been delivered from the hands of their enemies, one may say that although the good did not fall into the hands of their enemies by consenting to mortal sin, they could have fallen; but, with God’s help, they did not fall and escaped their hands. Augustine touches on this when speaking of the righteous person whom God preserved from sin: “And you,” he says, “held him, lest he should fall into sin.”

From what has been said it may be concluded [Col. 0991B] that the afflicted soul ought not to consider itself attacked when it suffers tribulations, but rather freed and rescued from the deceiving prosperity of the world and from desolating carnal consolation. Since tribulations free the soul from enemies, therefore, though they are sometimes burdensome, they must nevertheless be endured gladly for the Lord and without murmuring. For if by murmurings a person rises up against tribulations, then he attacks his helpers and helps his enemies.

The SECOND benefit of tribulation is that it shuts the devil’s mouth, so that he does not dare address the soul in tribulation by tempting it. For he fears being repulsed and defeated. This is figured in Job [Note: [Col. 0991] Chapter 2.], where it is said that no one spoke a word to him, for they saw that [Col. 0991C] his grief was very great. Scripture speaks there of Job’s false friends, who signify demons attacking the soul. They do not dare approach an afflicted soul when they see its grace in tribulation, for they fear to be conquered by such a soul.

But note that the devil’s temptation is not dangerous or harmful to a person except through the answer that follows—that is, through delight and consent—just as speech with an excommunicated person does not harm you unless you answer him. This is signified in Isaiah [Note: [Col. 0991] Chapter 37.], where Hezekiah commanded the people not to answer the blasphemies of Rabshakeh, commander of the army of the king of the Assyrians. Rabshakeh signifies the devil, and his blasphemies signify evil thoughts [Col. 0991D] which he suggests. But they do no harm if they are not answered through delight or consent. For although wicked suggestions and insulting words brought against a person greatly afflict his heart, they neither harm nor stain it so long as no answer is made to them, as was said. On the contrary, those who bring such things against people are greatly tormented when they see that those whom they blaspheme give absolutely no answer.

The THIRD benefit of tribulation is that it purifies the afflicted soul. In this connection, one should know that there are five kinds of material purification. The first is the purging of the human body, which occurs in two ways: by a potion and by bloodletting. The second is that of metals: gold is purified by fire, iron by the file. The third purification is that of trees, by the cutting away of branches or the digging around of shoots. The fourth is that of grain, by the flail. The fifth purification is that of the vintage or wine, by the winepress. Tribulation purifies in all these ways.

First, then, the human body is purged by a potion. When tribulation seizes you, therefore, consider the medicine sent you by the Lord to cleanse you of superfluous humours and disordered affection. For as harmful humours are purged by a bitter potion, so evil habits are purged from souls through tribulations. For, according to Gregory, “Evil habits are evil humours.” Receive humbly, then, the medicine sent you by the Lord, who [Col. 0992B] is the supreme physician and knows the innermost constitution of your heart; for he knows how much you can endure, and will give you nothing except what is useful to you. For the Son of God himself drank the tribulation of death, not for his own sake but for your salvation and cleansing. Hence it is said: “Drink, my friends, and be intoxicated, my beloved” [Note: [Col. 0991] Song of Songs 5.]. And to the sons of Zebedee it was said: “Can you drink the cup which I am about to drink?” [Note: [Col. 0991] Matthew 20.] This is the saving drink which the Lord received with thanksgiving, saying: “I will take the cup of salvation” [Note: [Col. 0991] Psalm 115.]. And if because of its bitterness it seems difficult for you to swallow it, call upon the Lord for help, as David says; hence it follows: “And I will call upon the name of the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0991] Ibid.].

Note that, just as bodily medicine [Col. 0992C] ought not to be tasted or kept long upon the tongue, but swallowed quickly, so tribulation ought not to be delayed by the course of rebellion. But just as the effect of medicine is sometimes hindered, not through a defect in itself but through the ill disposition of the recipient, so the effect of tribulation is hindered by the ill disposition of a hard heart and the obstinacy of a rebellious mind. This is apparent in Pharaoh, whose heart became harder the more he was afflicted [Note: [Col. 0991] Exodus 10.]. Hence Solomon says: “A hard heart will fare badly in the end” [Note: [Col. 0991] Ecclesiasticus 3.].

Second, the human body is purged by bloodletting; this occurs in two ways, namely by opening a vein and by phlebotomy. Opening a vein is compared to confession; phlebotomy, to tribulation. Note that just as superfluous bodily [Col. 0992D] blood corrupts the veins and chambers of the heart, so sin, which in Scripture is called blood, corrupts and stains the soul. The vein through which this blood—that is, sin—is cast out is the mouth. Hence the Book of Proverbs: “The mouth of the righteous is a vein of life” [Note: [Col. 0991] Proverbs 10.], because “the righteous is the first accuser of himself” [Note: [Col. 0991] Proverbs 18.], namely in confession.

And note that, just as in bloodletting a person ought to release bad blood and retain good blood for the nourishment of his heart, so in confession one ought to declare one’s sins, that they may be cast out, and keep silent about the good one has done, lest it be lost. For good deeds spoken of in confession are lost through boasting and vain [Col. 0993A] glory. This is evident in the Pharisee, who recounted his good deeds in boasting, saying: “I fast twice in the Sabbath; I give tithes of all that I possess” [Note: [Col. 0993] Luke 18.]. But the publican did not dare lift his eyes to heaven, but struck his breast, saying: “God, be merciful to me, a sinner” [Note: [Col. 0993] Ibid.]. And it follows that “this publican went down justified to his house” [Note: [Col. 0993] Ibid.], namely through humble confession, unlike that Pharisee, who remained in his sins because of boasting. For sins that are disclosed in true and humble confession are erased. Hence the Psalmist says: “I said, ‘I will confess my injustice against myself to the Lord,’ and you forgave the impiety of my sin” [Note: [Col. 0993] Psalm 31.].

The bloodletting of phlebotomy, however, is compared to tribulation. For as many tribulations as God sends into the [Col. 0993B] heart, so many blows of phlebotomy he gives it for its purification. But note that, just as before purging and the cutting stroke of bloodletting the flesh must be warmed, so that the blows may be borne more easily, so the human heart must be kindled with the fire of love, that it may readily endure tribulations. Hence Augustine says [Note: [Col. 0993] Sermon 10, On the Words of the Lord.]: “Love makes all things savage and immense easy and almost nothing.” In figure of this, the Holy Spirit descended upon the apostles in tongues of fire [Note: [Col. 0993] Acts 2.]. Strengthened by God from that point, after receiving him they went rejoicing from the council because they had been considered worthy to suffer dishonour for Christ’s name [Note: [Col. 0993] Acts 5.]; whereas before receiving him they had been very fearful. This was evident in Peter, who denied the Lord [Col. 0993C] at the voice of a single questioning maidservant [Note: [Col. 0993] Matthew 26.], yet after receiving the Holy Spirit willingly endured crucifixion for the Lord.

The second manner of purification is that by which metals are purified: gold by fire and iron by the file. First, therefore, tribulation purifies the soul and makes it clean, as fire does gold. Hence Augustine says: What the flail does to grain, fire to gold, and the file to iron, tribulation does to the righteous. That is to say: as fire separates gold from other metals and makes it clean from dross, so tribulation makes the soul clean. Hence it is said of the martyrs in Wisdom: “He tested them as gold in a furnace” [Note: [Col. 0993] Wisdom 3.]. Job was tested by this fire of tribulation [Note: [Col. 0993] Chapter 23.], and said: “He has tested me like gold which passes through fire.”

[Col. 0993D] Note that among all metals none is more precious than gold and none baser than lead; yet gold is not tested without lead. For lead draws the dross of gold along with itself in the furnace. And the good, who are signified by gold, are frequently purified through the bad, signified by lead. Thus, if one asks in what way the wicked serve the good, the answer may be: in the way lead serves gold. Hence Solomon says [Note: [Col. 0993] Proverbs 11.]: “The fool shall serve the wise,” namely by purifying him. Thus Esau served Jacob, namely by persecuting him, of whom it is said: “The elder shall serve the younger” [Note: [Col. 0993] Genesis 25.].

[Col. 0994A] Second, tribulation purifies the soul as a file purifies iron, namely by filing and brightening it. As a sword which never leaves its scabbard, and a knife which never cuts, gather rust, so the human heart without the exercise of tribulation gathers spiritual rust. Hence Jeremiah says [Note: [Col. 0993] Vulgate: “fertilis”]: “Moab was undisturbed from his youth and rested upon his dregs” [Note: [Col. 0993] Jeremiah 48.]. Do not complain, therefore, if God files your heart with a file, that it may shine, be made bright, and appear glorious; for otherwise you cannot see God, according to Matthew’s saying: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” [Note: [Col. 0993] Matthew 5.].

The third kind of purification appropriate to tribulation is the pruning of trees. Just as a vine is pruned of superfluous branches, concerning which Christ says: [Col. 0994B] “Every branch in me that does not bear fruit, he will take away; and every one that bears fruit, he will cleanse, that it may bear more fruit” [Note: [Col. 0993] John 15.]. The vine signifies the human heart, whose moisture, causing it to bear fruit, is love. Thus, as much love as it has, so much moisture it has. For insofar as moisture is diverted through the superfluous branches of a vine or another tree, that vine bears less fruit. So too, the more the heart’s love is diffused among carnal friends or temporal things, the less fitted its heart is to bear spiritual fruit.

If a wise gardener prunes and cuts away the superfluous branches of a vine or another tree, so that the vine or tree may bear more fruit, it is not surprising if God, who is the cultivator [Col. 0994C] of the human heart, according to John’s saying, “My Father is the husbandman” [Note: [Col. 0993] Ibid.], cuts away from your heart superfluous love—namely, parents and carnal friends—with the hoe of death which he holds in his hand; or temporal goods, so that the love and desire of your heart may not exceed their proper bounds. For the Lord himself says: “Those whom I love, I rebuke and chasten” [Note: [Col. 0993] Revelation 3.]. And the Apostle says: “He scourges every son whom he receives” [Note: [Col. 0993] Hebrews 12.]. God does all this lest your heart’s love depart from him and diffuse itself among temporal things, where one must invest much and obtain from them no good end, indeed a bad one, according to Gregory’s saying: “He who leans upon what is falling must necessarily fall with the falling thing.”

The fourth kind of purification appropriate to tribulation [Col. 0994D] is the purification of grain, which occurs by the flail, so that the grain may come out and be separated from the chaff. Hence Augustine says: what the flail does to grain, as above. For example: as the flail forces the grain out of the chaff, so tribulation forces the human heart to be separated from human love, because the world displeases an afflicted heart. Therefore David, knowing the usefulness of the flail of tribulation, said: “Behold, I am ready for scourges” [Note: [Col. 0993] Psalm 37.], to endure them, so that my heart may be purified. Hence Augustine says: Do not complain about the flail of tribulation if you wish to have the bread of the great and desire to be stored [Col. 0995A] in heaven, where only pure grain will be stored.

But just as immature, undried grain is not shaken out of its chaff by the flail’s blow but clings to it more closely, so a heart possessing carnal moisture and affection is not separated from the world by the flail of tribulation but clings to it more closely through love and delight, from which, however, it receives nothing but torment and labour. For “man is born for labour and the bird for flying” [Note: [Col. 0995] Job 5.], as it is said: “Do not love the world, nor the things that are in the world. If anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him, because everything that is in the world” [Note: [Col. 0995] 1 John 2.], etc.

The fifth kind of purification appropriate to tribulation is the purification of wine in the winepress. For as the winepress presses grapes so that the precious juice may be separated from the dregs, [Col. 0995B] so God places the soul in the winepress of tribulation—by bodily illness, persecution, grief at the death of friends, or loss of temporal goods—in order to cleanse it of the dregs of evil affections and sins. Therefore do not reject the winepress of tribulation, if you wish to be stored in Christ’s wine-cellar, according to the saying: “The king brought me into the wine-cellar” [Note: [Col. 0995] Song of Songs 1.].

Hence Augustine says that in this present life the martyrs were so pressed that the gross material of their bodies remained in the winepress, while their precious souls, like precious wine, were placed in the cellar of eternal life. Do not complain, therefore, if God places you in the winepress of tribulation, since he himself first trod the winepress, as it is said: “I have trodden the winepress [Col. 0995C] alone, and of the nations there was no man with me” [Note: [Col. 0995] Isaiah 63.]. It says “man,” not “woman,” because all the apostles, leaving him at his Passion, fled; but the blessed Virgin Mary did not depart from him through unbelief, but suffered with him through compassion. Hence Simeon had promised her, saying: “And a sword shall pierce your own soul also” [Note: [Col. 0995] Luke 2.].

The fourth benefit of tribulation is that it enlightens the human heart to the knowledge of itself, wherein the perfection of the human condition consists. Hence Augustine, who had read and heard so much, asked for nothing more, saying in the book of *Soliloquies*: “May I know you.” And he says in the book of Wisdom: “To know you is consummate understanding” [Note: [Col. 0995] Wis. 6.]. For just as we see that the blow of a rod compels a pupil to bow his head, look into his book, and repeat his lesson, so tribulation is sent to you by the Lord, that through tribulation you may learn to recognize your Creator. Hence blessed Bernard says: “God made himself known by striking, when he had been forgotten; and by sparing, he remained unknown.”

We have an example of this in Nebuchadnezzar, the proud king, whom God cast out from his kingdom: his dwelling was with wild creatures and beasts, and he ate grass like an ox. But at the end of his days—that is, of his tribulation and penitence—he lifted his eyes to heaven, and his understanding was restored to him [Note: [Col. 0995] Dan. 4.]. He lifts his eyes to heaven who directs his understanding toward his Creator. In this lifting of his eyes, understanding was restored to him who had lost it by inclining toward lower things. Nebuchadnezzar, therefore, before tribulation had closed himself off from his Creator by looking toward earthly things; after tribulation, he lifted his eyes to heaven, where was he who had struck him. For God wills that the afflicted turn their faces toward him.

Consider, then, O soul, that it is the custom of lovers to send letters to one another, to call pleasant and mutual benefits to remembrance, and to fear lest they be consigned to forgetfulness. Therefore Jesus Christ, your lover, sends tribulations to you, since perhaps you had wholly forgotten him while living in prosperity, just as Pharaoh’s cupbearer, once established in prosperity, forgot Joseph, his interpreter [Note: [Col. 0995] Gen. 40.]. Consider, therefore, that Jesus himself retained, in remembrance of you, the scars of the wounds which he endured for you—as though a knot were made in a strap to retain the memory of some matter. Hence he himself says: “I shall not forget you; I have inscribed you upon my hands” [Note: [Col. 0995] Isa. 49.], namely, when I was stretched out upon the cross for love of you. Therefore, if Christ retained the scars of his wounds as a remembrance, do not be angry if he sends you tribulations to preserve his memory; for as many tribulations as you have, so many messengers does he send you, recalling you to remembrance of him.

Do not, therefore, reject good admonishers, for it is said that a good admonisher is of great worth in a city. But you might say that tribulations are unnecessary for effecting this remembrance of him, since God sufficiently admonishes by giving benefits, as Augustine says: God’s benefits are nothing other than admonitions to come to him. Let it suffice him, then, to give admonitions by bestowing benefits, since such admonition better befits God than another kind, effected by blows. To this it may be answered that, although benefits recall you to the knowledge of him, nevertheless disordered love sometimes clings to those temporal benefits, and the Creator—who is the supreme and immutable good, giving eternal goods—is forgotten. Hence God complains of such people, saying: “I stretched out my hands,” namely by lavishly bestowing benefits, “and there was none who looked” [Note: [Col. 0995] Prov. 1.]. He does not say, “There was none who received,” because many willingly receive, but few look back; for from the greater to the lesser, all love gifts and pursue recompense.

But you might say that, although it is fitting that God call back through tribulations hard and undisciplined hearts which do not turn to him through benefits, it is not fitting to call back in this manner good people, who recognize their giver through benefits. To this it may be said that, although a good heart recognizes its giver in benefits through natural delight, nevertheless it will not attain the perfect knowledge of God without the testing of tribulation. Hence it is said: “What does a man know who has not been tested? One experienced in many things recognizes many things” [Note: [Col. 0997] Sirach 34.].

But observe that God recalled Solomon to knowledge of himself by lavish gifts, whereas he recalled Job by granting him his goods and bringing adversity upon him. Yet tribulations led Job to perfection, while gifts led Solomon to folly and destruction. Therefore, if Solomon, endowed with such great wisdom, lost the knowledge of God amid the enticements of prosperity, do not be confident that you can long retain the knowledge of God therein. Endure tribulation, then, patiently and willingly, so that you may come to the knowledge of God. And if you are desolated by the greatness of tribulation, be consoled by this: greater tribulation will bring you to a greater crown.

Having said how tribulations recall the heart to knowledge of the Creator, we must now say how they recall it to knowledge of itself. For the heart which worldly joy has removed from itself cannot recognize itself. Hence David, speaking in the person of such people, says: “Even the light of my eyes is not with me” [Note: [Col. 0997] Ps. 37]. Woe to him who expends the lamp of self-knowledge upon the knowledge of external things and keeps nothing for self-knowledge! But how could one know oneself who is not with oneself? For worldly prosperity removes the soul from itself all the more as it pursues and loves it more.

But just as one besieged or struck by the violence of enemies is compelled to return to oneself, so the more adversities you have, the more effective means you have for departing from yourself. Blessed, therefore, is adversity which restores you to yourself and makes you return to your own dwelling. Hence in Exodus [Note: [Col. 0997] ch. 16.]: “Let each one remain with himself”: that is, let each know himself, attend to himself, and not depart from himself through disordered love. For a house in which no one lives is quickly destroyed; so too a heart which is not inhabited virtuously is brought to desolation and nothingness.

Woe to the heart which, like a minstrel, swallows wandering and shameful morsels outside its own house, and which, the more it sings in another’s lodging, finds all the more in its own lodging to weep over! Thus, the more the heart delights in worldly things, the less it finds in itself from which to receive consolation. Therefore tribulation is sent to the heart in order to compel it to return from worldly joys to itself, just as the minstrel is at last compelled to return to his own house and, having returned, to remain there. And as the dove, when it found nowhere for its foot to rest, returned to Noah in the ark [Note: [Col. 0997] Gen. 8.].

Noah signifies Christ; Noah’s ark is understood as the repose of the mind. For when the human heart finds nothing outwardly in which its love may rest, it then returns to itself. By the dove’s foot is understood the heart’s love. The dove finds nowhere for its foot to rest when the human heart places its love in no earthly thing; and then it returns to itself and says with the Psalmist: “Return, O my soul, to your rest” [Note: [Col. 0997] Ps. 114]. And in the Song of Songs the Lord says to the sinful soul which has permitted its heart to wander among worldly things: “Return, return, Shulammite; return, return, that we may behold you” [Note: [Col. 0997] Song 6]—that is, I and you: you may behold yourself with the eye of conscience, while I behold you with the eye of mercy.

Endure, O Christian soul, being recalled through tribulations to yourself and to God, from both of whom worldly prosperity had removed you; especially since tribulations bind and constrain you to your Creator, whereas the evil liberty of the world had loosened you and made you fly away through insolence. Hence Job [Note: [Col. 0997] ch. 36], who had experience in such matters, said: “If I am girded with the goad of poverty, he will declare to them their works.” Note that here he calls poverty not the lack of temporal possessions, but the deprivation of temporal consolation, which consists in temporal riches. Hence there is the saying in Ecclesiasticus: “There is one poor though lacking in many things.”

All tribulations sent by God to restrain the heart from worldly consolations are called the fetters of poverty. These are the fetters, or cords, of Adam, our first parent, which belong to us by hereditary right, by which God draws many people to himself almost forcibly. Of this it is said in Hosea [Note: [Col. 0997] ch. 11]: “With the cords of Adam,” that is, with tribulations, “I will draw you with the bonds of charity,” that is, bonds sent in charity. Hence Bernard says [Note: [Col. 0997] Sermon 21 on the Song of Songs]: “We are drawn when we are exercised by tribulations.”

Do not, therefore, O soul bound in fetters, think yourself made alive; nor suppose that those who are not constrained are in true liberty, namely those to whom everything they desire is granted. For you would not think a sick man in a good condition, or with good hope of recovery, if a physician granted him everything he desired, because, despairing of his health, the physician says: “Let him be given whatever he wants.” This is indeed the surest sign of his death. Hence it is clear that worldly liberty is only an argument and sign of destruction. Therefore, the more freely miserable people fulfill their wishes without tribulation, the more swiftly they descend to hell.

If, then, you wish God to be favorable to you, endure being bound by the fetters of tribulation, which come from God and draw toward God. Hence the Lord says to Ezekiel: “Behold, I have placed my bonds upon you” [Note: [Col. 0997] Ezek. 3.]. By this it is understood that the bonds of tribulation are gifts of God. From what has been said, it is clear that tribulations are bonds binding the soul to Christ; and the more vehement the tribulation, the more strongly it binds the soul to God.

The fifth benefit of tribulation is that it hastens your journey to God. Thus, for every tribulation you have undergone, God has sent you a messenger, so that you might hasten to him and not linger on the way. See how perverse are the things that delay the perverse heart from hastening toward God. Since, then, tribulation removes delight and love in transitory things, which delay a person from going swiftly to God—whence Gregory says: “The evils which oppress us here compel us to go to God”—do not regard as small the benefit of tribulation, which has freed you from a grievous prison and hastens your journey to the kingdom of heaven. According to that saying of Ecclesiastes: “Who is brought from prison and chains into a kingdom?” [Note: [Col. 0999] Eccl. 4.]

Here prison is called whatever the heart loves inordinately in this world. The bonds by which it is bound are evil affections. The greater the love, the deeper the prison. God leads you out of this prison through tribulation when he takes from you something loved inordinately, or which you would thereafter love, or makes it contrary to you. This was signified where it is said that Peter was kept in Herod’s prison; and it follows that an angel of the Lord stood by him and, striking Peter’s side, roused him, saying: “Rise quickly” [Note: [Col. 0999] Acts 12].

By the side is understood your brother, who came from the same side from which you came, or generally all those joined to you by kinship or affinity. Therefore, when one who by natural right ought to be your friend becomes hostile, or is taken away by death, understand that you have been struck in the side in order that you may leave prison and place your heart in God alone, who cannot fail. But consider that Peter does not complain of the blow to his side by which he was liberated from prison. So you ought not complain of tribulation, which heals and liberates you from evil or false worldly love. And if the blow of tribulation is perhaps difficult for you to endure, look to Christ, who was wounded in the side for you, and you will endure it more easily. Just as a good soldier, when he sees his lord’s wounds, does not feel his own.

Do not, therefore, reject the Lord’s messengers, who recall you to the Lord and compel you to hasten; for whoever rejects the messenger rejects the Lord. A messenger is rejected when the heart resists tribulation through impatience. Note that tribulation does two things: it afflicts the soul by purifying it, and purifies it by afflicting it. But when the heart receives tribulation rebelliously, the afflicted person receives no purification from the affliction. Such a person receives the bitterness of tribulation and loses its benefit, yet, whether willing or unwilling, must endure the tribulation.

The sixth benefit of tribulation is that it is given for the discharge of debts by which you are bound to God, debts from which you cannot escape and from which you can neither subtract nor conceal anything. These debts are the punishments owed for sins that you have committed. Although eternal punishment is owed for mortal sins, through contrition and confession that eternal punishment is changed into temporal punishment; and these temporal punishments are diminished through fasts and tribulations, and are sometimes wholly remitted, especially through tribulations. Thus, whatever you endure for God is counted by God toward payment of your debt.

Just as the king’s steward, when rendering an account of what he has received from his lord, reckons and enters among the monies received lead or copper coins; and at the end of his reckoning a single lead or copper coin—of little value in itself—may be worth or represent a hundred marks of gold or silver: so one hour’s tribulation in the present life, received patiently, frees one from the tribulation of hell, which is most grievous and eternal.

An example is found in the thief who was crucified at Christ’s right hand. While enduring the torment of the cross for his evil deeds and liable to another punishment in hell, he nevertheless had contrition for his sins and in that hour turned to the Lord, saying: “Remember me when you come into your kingdom.” At once he was absolved and freed from every offense and debt, because he deserved to hear that sweetest voice: “Amen, I say to you: today you shall be with me in paradise” [Note: [Col. 0999] Luke 23].

Woe to him who pays nothing in this life but adds sin upon sin, of whom it is said in the Psalm: “The sinner shall borrow and shall not repay” [Note: [Col. 0999] Ps. 36]! Woe to him who, after lavish and prodigal expenditures, is compelled to come to a most exact accounting! For one who has always lived without accounting deserves to pay penalties forever in hell, without the remission of any debt.

There many merchants will weep who now laugh and rejoice in the variety of temporal consolations. This is signified in the Apocalypse [Note: [Col. 0999] ch. 18], where it is said: “The merchants of the earth shall weep.” By the merchants of the earth are understood those who have set their thought and love upon earthly things; they shall weep bitterly because God will show all their evil commerce. But the merchants of heaven will rejoice when they see that they have attained the glory of paradise for a small tribulation. This is signified where it is said: “There is one who redeems much at a small price” [Note: [Col. 0999] Sirach 20].

This small price is the endurance of the tribulation of the present life, which God accepts for a great debt. For, according to the common proverb: “From a bad debtor, hay or oats are accepted.” And even if you are not held in any debt for mortal or venial sin, from which tribulation might free you, it nevertheless preserves you from contracting or committing offense; for according to Gregory: “There are many innocents who would quickly lose their innocence unless tribulations preserved them,” etc.

Therefore, O soul, you who feel yourself bound by debts or fear the future payment, patiently endure this world’s tribulation while you have time to make payment for the debts in which you are bound to God. For all the tribulations of the present life can scarcely be compared to the tribulation of one hour in the future. Likewise, if all the world’s tribulations were brought together, they would not be worthy to attain the glory of paradise, as the Apostle says: “The sufferings of this time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory which shall be revealed in us” [Note: [Col. 0999] Rom. 8.].

The seventh benefit of tribulation is that it enlarges the human heart for the reception of God’s glory and grace. For just as a goldsmith’s hammer, by frequent striking, spreads out gold or silver in order to make a precious vessel, so God, the maker of all creation, has ordained tribulation to enlarge the heart for receiving gifts of grace. Of this tribulation the Psalmist says: “In tribulation you enlarged my heart” [Note: [Col. 1001] Ps. 4].

Endure, therefore, the blows of tribulation; for the more your heart is enlarged by enduring more, the more spiritual gifts God will place in you. Consider that the more precious a metal is, the more ductile it is and the more obedient to the hammer’s blows. So too a precious and gentle heart has greater patience in tribulation. And although the hammer’s blows—that is, tribulation’s blows—afflict you harshly, be consoled by this: God the goldsmith holds in his hand the hammer of tribulation and knows well how to moderate his blow according to the capacity of the material receiving it.

Do not, therefore, be like unextended metal in a lump, as are hard and undisciplined hearts in which tribulation or discipline finds no place. Likewise, do not be like an old frying-pan which, because of age, breaks under a blow and, for one old fracture, receives many new ones. So the hard and impatient heart increases its own loss in tribulation. Endure tribulation gladly, as it enlarges your heart.

The Wise Man invites you to this, saying: “Endure the supports of God, joining yourself to God; and endure, that your life may increase at the end” [Note: [Col. 1001] Sirach 2.]. It is as though he said: Patiently and willingly endure the tribulations of this world for God, who endured much for you; render him a return for this service. Join yourself to God and endure—as though he said: Associate yourself with God, endure whatever he imposes upon you, and know that he will not burden you beyond your capacity. Hence the Apostle says: “God is faithful, who will not permit you to be tempted beyond what you are able to bear” [Note: [Col. 1001] 1 Cor. 10.]. Endure, then, willingly in the ways stated above, that your life may increase in the end, because through this you shall live eternally in glory.

The eighth benefit of tribulation is that God, by shutting out earthly consolations below, compels one to seek heavenly consolations above. Just as an earthly lord who wishes to sell his wine forbids anyone to dare open his tavern until he has sold his wine, so God sometimes excludes earthly consolations in order to confer heavenly ones, which are his own. This is signified in Joel, where it is said: “The beasts of the field have looked to you as a thirsty field, because the springs of waters are dried up” [Note: [Col. 1001] Joel 1].

He calls the beasts of the field carnal affections and desires. He calls the springs of waters worldly consolations. Therefore, when the springs of waters dry up—that is, when worldly consolations fail in adversities—the heart is compelled to look above and seek the giver of heavenly consolations and rewards. Thus, the more bitterness the heart finds in outward things, the more kindly disposed toward the heart is the Lord.

But you might say: I do not grieve because the tavern of worldly consolations is not open to me; rather, I grieve because the tavern of heavenly consolations is closed to me, since I find consolation neither below nor above. The answer is that, because worldly consolations are forbidden to you, you will not have heavenly ones unless you first return to your heart, desiring and seeking God and heavenly things. For God wills this because greater merit consists in desiring and seeking the Lord than in being wholly delighted in him and for his sake.

Likewise, the more fervently you desire and seek him, the greater consolation will be granted you and the greater sweetness you will find in him, just as food tastes better to a hungry person than to one who is not hungry. Know, too, that heavenly consolations will not be deferred long if earthly ones have been excluded through tribulation, provided that you ask and seek ardently, even though they seem delayed, as Solomon says: “He shall grant the righteous his desire” [Note: [Col. 1001] Prov. 10.].

The ninth benefit of tribulation is that it brings you to God’s remembrance. For through tribulations he himself recalls you to memory of him. And the greater the tribulation, the more deeply you are impressed upon God’s remembrance. This is not because God forgets anyone—he sees all things—but because Scripture says that God forgets the person to whom he gives no aid, by spiritually consoling that afflicted person and increasing grace.

Therefore, O soul, if you wish to be placed in God’s remembrance, in whose remembrance is your salvation and in whose forgetfulness consists your damnation, learn patiently to endure adversities.
