And, while enduring them, think inwardly of God; and he in turn will think of you, as a friend thinks more frequently of an afflicted friend than if that friend were free from affliction.

If, therefore, O soul, you feel yourself desolated by tribulation, be consoled, because tribulation itself places you in God’s remembrance; and God’s remembrance benefits you more than tribulation could take from you. As a figure of this, the Lord says: “I have seen the affliction of my people who are in Egypt, and I have come down to deliver them from the hands of the Egyptians” [Note: [Col. 1001] Exod. 3].

Two points must be considered in these words. First, God looks with the eye of mercy upon the afflicted people. Second, through affliction God fulfills his covenant which he had made with that same afflicted people. God’s very regard signifies a special gift by which God is moved to pity his afflicted friend.

Therefore, although the Egyptians persecuting you afflict you, nevertheless be consoled in this: God’s regard for you is of great value in affliction. Thus it is said of David, fleeing from the face of his son Absalom, that Shimei, seeing him, cursed him and said: “Get out, man of blood and man of Belial,” etc. Seeing this, Abishai said to the king: “Why does this dog curse my lord the king? Let me go and cut off his head.” David answered: “Let him alone, that he may curse me, according to the Lord’s word: perhaps the Lord will look upon my affliction and repay me good for this curse today” [Note: [Col. 1001] 2 Sam. 16].

Consider in this that David wished to endure his adversary’s curse so that he might have God’s blessing. Therefore, the more you desire God’s blessing, the more patiently you ought to endure your adversary’s curse; for endurance of the curses of the wicked calls forth God’s blessing and deliverance from evil. This is signified in Daniel 3 [Note: [Col. 1003] v. 49], where it is said that the angel of the Lord descended with Azariah and his companions into the furnace, made the middle of the furnace as though a breeze blowing with dew, and drove the flame out upon the king’s servants who were kindling it.

Observe that the fire of the furnace not only drove out the unjust, but also gave refreshment to the boys. By this is understood that Christ is present with the afflicted person. Therefore, if you wish refreshment to be given you in tribulation and your enemies, who procure tribulations for you, to be burned, endure tribulations patiently; for in tribulation God is with you, will deliver you from it, and will render to you great merit for it. Of these three things the Psalm says: “I am with him in tribulation”—behold God’s companionship; “I will deliver him”—behold deliverance; “and I will glorify him” [Note: [Col. 1003] Ps. 90]—behold the reward. Thus tribulation places you in God’s remembrance, which grants you more than tribulation could take away.

The tenth benefit of tribulation is that it causes your prayers to be heard and offered before God; for it is not God’s custom to reject the prayer of an afflicted person, but rather to hear it. Hence Solomon says: “The Lord will hear the supplication of the injured” [Note: [Col. 1003] Sirach 35]. God often strikes people and sends them tribulations in order to compel them to ask for mercy, to open their mouths in tribulation to ask him, since they had kept them shut in prosperity.

Hence Augustine says: God sends tribulations to certain people so that they may be stirred up in tribulation and ask God for what he himself wishes to grant them. The Psalmist speaks in the person of such people: “To the Lord, when I was troubled, I cried, and he heard me” [Note: [Col. 1003] Ps. 119].

And although you may call upon God in prosperity, lest prosperity make you sleep entirely, it nevertheless sometimes makes you drowsy; thus your cry in prosperity is not as effective as in adversity. And even if adversity should so occupy your heart that you are not as attentive to prayer in adversity as in prosperity, adversity itself makes prayer more precious. If tribulation oppresses you so greatly that you cannot open your mouth to cry to the Lord, nevertheless tribulation prays for you while you have patience. For Master Peter Lombard says of Lazarus that, as many wounds as he had, so many mouths he had crying to God; because when Lazarus was silent with his mouth, his wounds cried out for him.

Hence the Lord says to Cain concerning Abel, his brother whom he had killed: “The voice of your brother’s blood cries to me from the ground” [Note: [Col. 1003] Gen. 4]. Thus it is clear that tribulation makes prayer more precious and more acceptable. Tribulations are, as it were, payment for a sealed letter of one’s deliverance.

Therefore Job says [Note: [Col. 1003] ch. 6]: “Who will grant that my petition may come to me, and that God may give me what I expect? Let him who has begun, himself crush me; let him loose his hand and cut me off; and let this be my consolation: that, afflicting me with pain, he does not spare.” Note that Job, who had lost his possessions, sons, and daughters; who had been struck with a terrible wound from the sole of his foot to the crown of his head; afflicted by friends and reproached by his wife—nevertheless thought that God afflicted him too little and sought consolation in nothing other than God’s not sparing him.

But if you ask how this pertains to the deliverance from his affliction, the answer may be that his affliction is payment for his letters, just as when a poor man drinks wine in a tavern and has nothing with which to pay his reckoning, he asks to be beaten and thus dismissed. But if you ask wherein Job’s consolation lay when he asked to be afflicted, the answer may be that God does not spare certain people in the present so that he may spare them in the future.

Job’s consolation was that in present tribulation he knew he would escape future tribulation. Therefore be consoled: if you are afflicted in the present and endure patiently, God will spare you in the future. For it is said that God will not judge the same thing twice [Note: [Col. 1003] Nahum 1]. Hence Job, who asked God not to spare him in the present, elsewhere asks that the Lord spare him in the future, saying: “Spare me, Lord, for my days are nothing” [Note: [Col. 1003] Job 7].

Therefore, in order that God may spare you in the future, endure tribulation in the present; for tribulation heals the soul, as Job says: “He himself wounds and heals” [Note: [Col. 1003] Job 5]. For he wounds the body by sending tribulation, but heals the soul.

The eleventh benefit of tribulation is that it guards and nourishes the heart. Just as fire is guarded and nourished in ashes, so the heart of God’s friend is guarded in tribulation. Therefore God commanded that the tabernacle be covered with coverings of haircloth [Note: [Col. 1003] Exod. 26]. The haircloth coverings protected the precious curtains and all the vessels of gold and silver from wind and rain, signifying that in the adversity of tribulation the precious virtues of the saints—and above all humility—are preserved. For tribulation compels a person to be humbled, whom human prosperity perhaps carried beyond the limits of his weakness into excess.

Moreover, tribulation nourishes the heart, as a nurse nourishes a child. For just as a mother chews hard food which the little child cannot chew and draws it into her stomach, so that there the food is converted into milk for the child’s nourishment, so Christ is called our mother in Scripture because of the intensity of charity which he has for us, and because of the bitter things he endured on the cross, where he chewed for us punishments, harsh blows, and reproaches, in order to nourish and strengthen us spiritually to endure, after his example, the tribulations of this world.

For as wine strained through a bag full of spices, so a person enduring tribulations ought to strain them through the Lord’s body, considering the tribulation and passion which he endured for that person; and thus they will be sweetened and made tolerable, though they previously seemed intolerable.

The twelfth benefit of tribulation is that it gives a person certain testimony that God loves that person. Hence the Apostle says: “Those whom I love, I rebuke and chastise” [Note: [Col. 1005] Rev. 3], etc. And in Ecclesiasticus: “He who loves his son is frequent with his scourges” [Note: [Col. 1005] Sirach 30]—that is, he continually sends him one scourge after another.

Jesus Christ, the supreme Father, always keeps his children under some scourge and rod. Thus, when they are delivered from one, they are taken up by another. He does not send all at once, but one after another, just as a person shoots another arrow after the first. But the wicked, who in the present life live without God’s scourge and discipline, and whom no correction draws back from error—all the tribulations which he sends individually to good people in the present life, one after another, for their purification—he will shoot upon them together in the future. For all the torments which are divided throughout the whole world in the present life will in the future rest, as it were, in their own place. As the Lord says: “I will gather evils upon them, and I will expend my arrows upon them” [Note: [Col. 1005] Deut. 32].

Therefore, O soul, if you wish to be loved by God, do not reject tribulations, which show you testimony of divine love. But if you say that children receive good and evil things from God’s hand, why then is the reception of evils a greater indication of God’s love than the reception of good things? The answer is this: certainly God confers better goods upon his spiritual friends and upon those whom he loves more; but he loved Christ incomparably more than the whole world, and yet bestowed upon him many evils and few temporal goods in this world.

Indeed, according to Bernard, from his entrance into the virgin’s womb until the scaffold of the cross, he had nothing but poverty and tribulations. Therefore the consolation of tribulation and adversity is a greater indication of God’s love than the consolation of temporal prosperity. Furthermore, Jesus Christ, the Son of God, who lived in this world like a merchant at a fair, choosing good wares and rejecting bad ones, chose tribulations and fled prosperities, as is clear in the Gospel. For he fled into the desert when the Jews wished to seize him and make him king; yet he did not flee when they sought him in order to destroy and kill him. Indeed, he said to them: “I am he” [Note: [Col. 1005] John 6].

Since Christ was most wise in choosing, it is evident that those are foolish who, despising tribulations and adversities, choose worldly prosperity, which in the future will not be able to free them from the hands of their enemies, namely the demons. Endure tribulation in the present with Christ, therefore, so that at last you may receive the crown in the kingdom of heaven. Otherwise you shall not enter the kingdom of heaven, according to the Apostle’s saying that “through many tribulations we must enter into the kingdom of heaven” [Note: [Col. 1005] Acts 14]. May he who lives and reigns, God almighty, grant this to us for ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 1005]

## WHAT TRACTATES ARE. (G)*

## PROLOGUE.

[Col. 1005C] Would that it were granted to the bishops of Saintes and Limoges to live soberly, justly, and devoutly [Note: [Col. 1005] Titus 2.]. Piety and necessity—piety persuading, necessity compelling—have forced me to write to my lord, the illustrious king of the English, duke of the Normans and Aquitanians. That, in accomplishing this, the expenditure should have exceeded by far what I had calculated while sitting down beforehand, mindful of the evangelical counsel [Note: [Col. 1005] Luke 14.], I myself could not have wondered at, had I not read that much had increased out of little, and very much out of very little [Note: [Col. 1005] Luke 21.]. Yet one is compelled to marvel at these things who hears small things declared greater than great ones; who hears the wealth of the rich surpassed by the poverty of a widow—when they offered little out of much, while she offered much out of little. Likewise the widow of Zarephath, when she did not conceal the little that she possessed [Note: [Col. 1005] III Kings 17.], when she fed the prophet from her small store: the praiseworthy thrift of a poor woman had reserved it for herself and her son, but a still more praiseworthy generosity obtained that this very little should not fail.

[Col. 1005D] Thus I, being a small man, had proposed to write a small work, lest, by holding the king’s eyes—already devoted to many things—with the length of my page, I should sin against the public good. Nor would the completed work have departed from the intention with which it began, had I not been bound to satisfy digressions bordering upon my purpose. For there were certain byways around the subject, to which the importunity of the theme itself often compelled me to go out, as though to stroll through grassy places, when I was wearied by sorrowful complaint, until health-giving breezes refreshed my mind. Hence, more cheerful on my return, after I had caught my breath for a while by looking upon pleasant things, I did not know how to return home without flowers. The subject itself also, after receiving me shipwrecked into its channel, again cast me forth from itself. But because the height of the banks denied a harbour to one setting out, the sea of tenacious iniquities, which I had begun to unroll, often held me back against my will.

[Col. 1006D] From this, it seems, it happened that, although in writing I did not at all expect to exceed the measure of an epistle, I first gave the work I had begun the name of an epistle. As my pen gradually ranged farther than I had hoped, what I had begun as an epistle, judged to be brief in scope, finally emerged unexpectedly as a book. To it—unless perhaps another title may seem more fitting for the king—I have assigned a title sufficiently suited to its subject: *What Sort They Are*. For although *What Sort They Have* indicates almost the whole work that follows, because in the kinds of things they possess the fathers in question are seen, as in a mirror, to be of such a kind, the little book takes its title, without qualification, from this first part of itself.

I confess that I have exceeded due bounds not a little in this: while writing upon so lofty a subject, I could not restrain the laughter conceived from seeing their deeds, often being compelled by the tragic jokes of these men to add jokes of my own. Indeed, I remember that I often laughed, whether I wished to or not—yet with that laughter alone which pains can move in one who is alone.

[Col. 1008A] Therefore, although in many places, especially in the second and fourth parts, the little book offers the king humorous words to read, let him nevertheless suppose that the truth is no less firmly established there. Things appear playful when read superficially which, when understood, are found not to be playful.

Let the king, then, receive and read this little book. For, unless I am mistaken, neither the king will regret having read it nor I having composed it; for there, if it is read entire and with integrity, the king will find things useful to himself, I to myself, and many persons many useful things. Let his wisdom recognize that it has been divided into parts and subdivisions, so that, since both the necessary length of the writing and the king’s varied affairs prevent his reading it all at once, whenever the king may choose to interrupt it in order to turn to another reading, he may find stopping-points ready to hand, when and where he wishes.

[Col. 1007] END OF THE PROLOGUE.

THE CHAPTERS OF THE FIRST PART BEGIN.

[Col. 1007]

[Col. 1007B] This little book, then, has four parts. The first part shows what sort the fathers in question are; and from this first part the entire work is called *What Sort They Are*. The three following parts show *What Sort They Have*. The first of these three treats of bishops’ nephews—the first, second, third, and so on without end. The second treats of flatterers, who, together with the pontiffs’ nephews, hold the chief places in the greater churches. The third concerns purchasers of orders and churches, who preside over the lesser churches. At its end is briefly contained the expulsion of honourable men, and the Church’s mournful complaint, crying to the king on behalf of her sons. Each part is divided into chapters.

[Col. 1007C] Chapter 2. That it is not the writer’s wish to make crimes already sufficiently evident still more evident. Yet he reveals them, in order that these men may cease and may not begin other similar acts.

2. That opposing thoughts thrust themselves upon him as he begins this work.  
3. Explanation of the first chapter.  
4. That the usefulness of the work, the king’s piety, and charity casting out fear give him boldness to write.  
5. That it ought not to be said that he has set his mouth in heaven.  
6. That, while his eye remains single, he does not care what his rivals may say.  
7. Mention of the good and the bad shepherds, in order that these men may be separated from the former.  
8. Their separation from the others, because they do not possess the faith that joins the others to Christ.  
9. He asks whether they entered through the door, in order later to show that they did not, and why they did not.  
10. That they did not enter through the door, because they came proudly.  
11. That each is the worst of all, though one is worse than the other worst man.  
12. How utterly they differ in every respect from good shepherds.  
[Col. 1008C] 13. He asks and discovers what sort of men to call them; but he does not discover what names to call them by.  
14. That they ought not to be called pontiffs.  
15. That they are not overseers.  
16. That they are not prelates.  
17. That they are not bishops.  
18. That they are not shepherds.  
19. That they are not superiors.

THE FIRST PART BEGINS.

[Col. 1007]

## CHAPTER I

[Col. 1007D]

As I am about to signify to the king what sort of men the aforesaid fathers are, I would indeed prefer to be silent and conceal it; for on this matter my shame and tears plead with me. But I am compelled to speak things too harsh because I fear things still harsher. Nor can I cover up their crimes—crimes which heaven reveals even if I keep silent, which the world irreverently beholds laid bare. Nor would they be concealed more or less through me if I alone, a worthless little man, kept silent about the country’s tale and the cities’ whispering; nor should I be lacking in any truth that could be kept silent before heaven and earth as witnesses.

For public infamy proclaims these men with all the greater plainness because, sunk more deeply in the abyss of greedy desire, buried in the cavern of blindness, and crushed beneath the heap accumulated over them by obstinacy, ignominy, fearing to name them, conceals them.

[Col. 1008D] I do not speak of the other prelates, because I do not know the others. Especially since the worthy pre-eminence of these men, bishops in name only, furnishes sufficient matter for speech not to me but to the whole world. Yet if—God forbid—any men like these should be found in the world, whom a similar infamy associates with the infamous, it is not ours to exclude from this number those included in it; just as it is not ours to include among the infamous those whom uprightness separates from the infamous society of these men.

Therefore, lest the other bishops of Aquitaine become like these men, who have recently begun to lean upon the staff of sweet and dangerous support, they must take no little care. For unless they keep watch diligently and provide for themselves, the same scab that has baldly stripped their neighbouring heads will, to my grief, lay them bare more completely. And I fear that, refreshed as if by the same pasture, this entire flock will perish from this pestilence or pestiferous disease—may God avert it!—and that sees as yet immune from this contagion will be overthrown.

## CHAPTER II

Thus, in what I am about to say, the multitude of thoughts that suddenly confronts me makes me excessively hesitant and uncertain; and the anchor of deliberation can scarcely find where to fasten in the depth of my wavering mind, as I consider for a long time how I shall approach the unexpected Charybdis into which I have suddenly fallen. For I have entered into myself as into a certain abyss, God knows how I shall emerge.

## CHAPTER III

I had proposed to write something which I should write more fully and more safely to another, if it is presumption for me to write to the king. For who am I, that I should write to a king? Or how shall I conceal damage to the king and to the Church? With what face shall I speak? With what mind shall I remain silent? The former is above me; the latter against me.

[Col. 1009B] This too greatly distresses me: if I seem to speak against fathers, the streets will proclaim that I have set my mouth in heaven. Danger threatens on either side. For in speaking, others will find me truly humble; in remaining silent, I myself shall find myself useless to others. Neither path appears safe. Yet one of them is reasonably chosen as the one I must take. For I judge public harm through silence to be the more dangerous, when that saying of the grieving prophet presses itself upon my deliberating reason: “Woe is me, because I kept silent!” [Note: [Col. 1009] Isaiah 5.] And I determine that I ought to be more ashamed of having kept silent so long than of being called a superfluous and presumptuous writer by rivals and detractors.

## CHAPTER IV

Hence I have a noble, though not insolent, boldness to write to my lord the king. My ignorance does not indeed forbid me to write to him; but the king’s reported humility and reported mercy give me courage. The most humble King—he who came not to be served but to serve [Note: [Col. 1009] Mark 10.]—has made him not only a hearer of heavenly teaching but a doer of what he has heard [Note: [Col. 1009] James 1.]. It was not without effect that he heard from Him: “The greater you are, humble yourself in all things” [Note: [Col. 1009] Ecclesiasticus 3.].

Charity also makes me bold, though bold, casting out fear [Note: [Col. 1009] I John 4.]; it commands me to write not for myself but for the common benefit of the oppressed. In Aquitaine, as in another Egypt, they have long been afflicted by the labours of mud and brick; obedient under the pretext of reverence, groaning under the aforesaid fathers as under so many Pharaohs, they are—an unheard-of thing—exiles in their own homes and dispossessed in their own inheritances.

[Col. 1009D] May this charity, which has begun to provide for this undertaking, be present, increase, and remain increased; and may truth attend charity, so that I may have zeal for God according to knowledge, and that the serpent’s prudence may not be absent from the dove’s simplicity; so that there may be discernment in choosing, just as there is love in imitating.

## CHAPTER V

[Col. 1010A]

I, one man, call all men to witness, so far as the fathers of impiety may accuse me freely and innocently. For Ham’s laughter would have remained excusable and without fault if, among other brothers, Noah had disdained that man as his father [Note: [Col. 1009] Genesis 9.]. But because the kindly father did not exclude from paternal love the one whom a birth-order mystically arranged between the outer two enclosed in the middle, he deserved to be cursed because he did not cover his father’s nakedness but revealed it to the others by looking upon it.

Nor let anyone maintain that I have set my mouth in heaven. That would indeed be true if those called fathers were fathers. But they have no children, since they themselves are fathers of no one. Like others, I once thought that they were fathers and a refuge of the poor; afterward, like others, I more certainly ceased to think so. For why should they be accounted fathers—men who do not wish to have children, and who, if by chance they learn that children have been born somewhere, immediately order them killed? Are they to be called fathers because of the women whom they preserve, while they kill the males? Thus Pharaoh could be called father of the Israelites, though he ought rather to be called their murderer.

[Col. 1010B] And who would suppose them a refuge of the poor? A poor man experienced in the matter teaches an ignorant poor man to flee from them, lest the poor man’s flight to them occur on a Sabbath or in winter [Note: [Col. 1009] Matthew 24.]. “Seek,” He says, “and you shall find; ask, and it shall be given you” [Note: [Col. 1009] Matthew 7.]. But why should anyone seek or ask, if in seeking he finds what is contrary to what he sought, and if one who asks is given nothing except what displeases him? Often needy men, not yet experienced, ask these men for help; but in place of bread they give them a stone, in place of fish a serpent, and in place of an egg offer a scorpion [Note: [Col. 1009] Luke 11.].

For necessity so discredits these men in the eyes of those who test them that, after the shameful rebuff of those who have experienced them, the entirely fortunate opinion formerly celebrated among all first withers away. In their case, wicked suspicion first tarnished a good opinion; then what was feared, suddenly arriving from the left, brought it to an unhappy end by its fulfilment.

## CHAPTER VI

I know, I know, and the gnawing abuse of rivals does not permit me to be unaware that there are some who will attack me over this undertaking as though it were an idle and unnecessary little work, and will say openly and secretly that I am a man who ought not even to mutter about such matters, and that my mouth deserves to be broken with hard stones for such speech. It will be better to hear them patiently than to give sounding words in exchange for trifles and windy, soundless talk.

[Col. 1010D] Whatever mute whisperers may mutter into the ears of the crowd, whatever they may bark out among courtly dogs, innocence will gradually remain unharmed, and justice will suffice for defence—provided only that the whole body be full of light while the eye remains single [Note: [Col. 1009] Matthew 6.]. He who began to make it single will make it single; and He will make single the eye of one who does not wish to deceive and cannot be deceived, since He who began to make it single does not wish to deceive.

May He make it unwilling to deceive, lest, lacking good zeal, it lose compassion; may He make it refuse to be deceived, lest, lacking caution, it be without true judgment. For the eye that is not easily deceived but easily deceives is commanded to be plucked out, because it is evil [Note: [Col. 1009] Ibid.]. The eye that does not easily deceive but is easily deceived does not lead the blind man, because it is blind [Note: [Col. 1011] Matthew 15.].

[Col. 1011A] Therefore let simplicity attend prudence, lest ignorance be born from malice. Let prudence attend simplicity, lest the malice that ought to be exposed be covered through ignorance.

## CHAPTER VII

I recall that supreme Shepherd who said, “I am the good shepherd” [Note: [Col. 1011] John 10.]. He added “good,” because it was not hidden from Him that there are bad shepherds. Since all things were present to Him, He saw them all as He spoke. He saw good and bad shepherds alike—He from whose sight those who were past had not passed away, and for whom those who did not yet exist were not future.

Thus He saw all the wicked, from all of whom He separated Himself when He said, “I am the good shepherd.” But are evil shepherds shepherds? Are they not rather thieves and robbers, or useless hirelings? “All,” He says, “who came are thieves and robbers” [Note: [Col. 1011] Ibid.]. He said this of all who came apart from Him and who were to come apart from Him. He did not say it of the good shepherds of old who preceded Him, but of the good men who succeeded Him, who came not apart from Him but with Him.

[Col. 1011B] They came with Him because “in the beginning was the Word” [Note: [Col. 1011] John 15.], and they came with the Word of God. They came with Him because He is truth, and they were truthful; and good men before and after Him possessed the same faith.

## CHAPTER VIII

But what shall we say about the shepherds mentioned above and men like them? Does the same faith join them to the good, so that they may be said to have come not apart from Christ but with Him? Why should it? What has their faith accomplished? Is it not dead? And because it is without works: “Faith,” he says, “without works is dead” [Note: [Col. 1011] James 2.]. It is dead because the vitality of action does not flourish in it. It is dead because it neither moves nor directs the soul toward the joys of the heavenly homeland.

Demons are marked by faith of this kind. They believe, and nevertheless eternal fire is prepared for them. For faith without work is a flower without fruit, a sheaf without grain, a coin without silver. If their faith accomplishes nothing in them, it does not join them to those who came with Christ; they did not enter the sheepfold through the door. “He who does not enter,” He says, “through the door into the sheepfold, but climbs in by another way, is a thief and a robber” [Note: [Col. 1011] John 10.].

## CHAPTER IX

Did the two men whom we have put forward enter through the door? Those who know them deny it; those who saw them enter deny it.

[Col. 1011D] I say, and know, that this door is lowly. A person coming to this door must walk with level foot lest he stumble; he must humble himself in order to enter with his head uninjured. For Christ is a humble door; the humble keeper of this door is the same Person. He is the door because people enter through Him; He is the doorkeeper because He Himself opens the door. Let no one doubt that He is door and doorkeeper, gate and gatekeeper, who hears Him saying, “I am the door of the sheep” [Note: [Col. 1011] Ibid.].

For by this saying Christ indicates Himself not only as the door but also as the doorkeeper, since He Himself opens in this way; He opens by making what was formerly unknown known. “For whatever,” He says, “I have heard from my Father, I have made known to you” [Note: [Col. 1011] John 15.].

[Col. 1012A] Having become, therefore, door and doorkeeper, He became at once shepherd, sheep, and lamb: that He, the innocent sheep and spotless lamb, might cleanse stains and destroy the death of shepherds and sheep. The Gospel is read, and the shepherd is found: “I am,” He says, “the good shepherd” [Note: [Col. 1011] John 10.]. The prophet is read, and the sheep is found: “Like a sheep He was led to slaughter” [Note: [Col. 1011] Isaiah 53.]. The bridegroom’s friend is questioned, and the Lamb Himself is heard: “Behold,” he says, “the Lamb of God; behold, He who takes away the sins of the world” [Note: [Col. 1011] John 1.].

Did the merciful Shepherd, sheep, lamb, humble doorkeeper, and door ever open to these two men whom we have proposed, when they never proposed to enter humbly, when they presumed to approach the humble door defiantly and proudly? Far be it!

## CHAPTER X

[Col. 1012B]

How did they not come proudly? One came quite openly, raised too high against the very door; the other came far more secretly, raised more highly against the doorkeeper—who is himself also the door—and less inclined than he ought to be. Each presumed too much; each climbed too high. But he climbed higher beyond measure who descended lower beyond measure, for excessive humiliation is excessive exaltation.

Therefore I said that one came against the door and the other against the doorkeeper, although door and doorkeeper are the same, because among men an offence against the doorkeeper would be greater than one against the door. For in houses the doorkeeper is greater than the door: he who is set over another is greater than he over whom he is set.

Each was wicked; each was most wicked. But he was more wicked than the most wicked man who provoked God’s wrath. For worse is the man who provokes God’s wrath than the man who deserves it. The one who sins openly and corrupts others deserves it; the one who, though ugly and incestuous within, desires to appear beautiful and chaste provokes it.

[Col. 1012C] Each set himself above others whenever and insofar as he could. And each, thus made superior, proved proud and exalted. Yet the more proud of the proud was he who compressed the swelling of pride with the poultice of humility.

## CHAPTER XI

Whenever I recall this man, worse than the worst, I wish to dismiss the other altogether, because this man’s greater iniquity compels me to speak against him. Yet I think one thing about both. Whatever qualities can be attributed, with proper distinctions, to any pseudo-pontiffs as peculiar to each individual are all attributed to these two together, and everything fits them, though less suitably.

For whereas some among others are thieves, or robbers, or hirelings, these two are the whole of it, and they are still striving to be wolves. They are thieves, making another’s property their own; they are robbers, destroying what they have stolen. They are hirelings, seeking what is their own rather than what belongs to Jesus Christ [Note: [Col. 1011] Philippians 2.], and fleeing when they see the wolf coming. They also make themselves wolves, for they not only abandon the sheep but scatter and tear them apart [Note: [Col. 1011] John 10.].

## CHAPTER XII

O how utterly this wickedly altered posterity differs in every respect from the first shepherds, who honoured their ministry wherever they were, who were the sweet savour of Christ in every place [Note: [Col. 1013] II Corinthians 2.], whose fame was most renowned and whose life most continent!

[Col. 1013A] But our light, the pontiffs in question, does not drive darkness away with light, but light away with darkness. It does not shine upon us with splendour but troubles us with black smoke; it darkens the stars, overshadows the ground, clouds the sky, and brings night upon the earth. I would not grieve so much that it does not shine if it allowed the lesser lights, which it utterly extinguishes, to shine. I would mourn these wickedly changed men less if the house of God remained firm in its former state. But, themselves wickedly overthrown, they always contrive its overthrow and ruin.

I believe that the prophet spoke precisely of these men and their like: “Your builders have come, destroying you” [Note: [Col. 1013] Isaiah 49.]. For they endeavour to overthrow it from its foundations; and these altered architects are read to change the building together with its foundation: “A foundation has been laid,” he says, “besides which no one can lay another” [Note: [Col. 1013] I Corinthians 3.].

[Col. 1013B] How, then, will simplicity not believe that another foundation has been laid where not merely the foundation but everything founded upon it appears to have been overthrown? For what remains to be changed? There, as some have thought, hypocrisy lays the foundation, flattery raises the walls, avarice completes the roof, and deceit and falsehood adorn the completed building.

I have read of good men, the best and better men, who build gold, silver, and precious stones upon the solid rock, Christ. But perhaps these great men read differently, for we see them build nothing upon it except iron, bronze, and lead. Men who build in this way we more fittingly call destroyers than builders.

## CHAPTER XIII

I can state sufficiently worthily what sort of men they are: men whom avarice long ago compelled to bend their knees before Baal, to make a covenant with death, and to enter an agreement with hell. Among them gold commands and silver judges; laws and canons are silent; reason and equity have no place.

Where is virtue? Where is law? Where the authority of the sacred canons? Where the strictness of discipline, the gravity of morals, the maturity of counsels, the distinguished weight of authority, the reverence of majesty? Where is the light of our eyes, where our breast, where the tongue that teaches, where the untiring hand—the light of the single eye, the breast of counsel, the tongue teaching judgment, the hand not sluggish in good work?

[Col. 1013D] In these men none of these things is found, but rather their opposites. I find sufficiently worthy words to say what sort of men they are: they are what they have unworthily made themselves. But I cannot fittingly find what names to give them. Yet usage has taught us to call them pontiffs, prelates, shepherds, bishops, and by names of that sort. But if these are truly names of pontiffs, they do not belong to men whom we know to be opposed in all things and in every respect to true pontiffs. Names of one meaning do not at all suit contrary things. Nor ought those who lack the reality of a name to be called by its name.

## CHAPTER XIV

Why, then, should we call pontiffs men who do not make themselves bridges for others? For a pontiff is called one who has become a bridge across the sea of this world, extending as far as God and neighbour. He extends to God through the confidence that seeks not his own glory but God’s; to his neighbour through the compassion by which he desires to benefit not himself alone, but the neighbour himself. But are these men such? Who but a fool calls a bridge something unsupported by any foundations, which the sea receives as it falls and wraps in yet deeper depths?

## CHAPTER XV

We might call them overseers (*antistites*) because they stand against those subject to them; but because they do not stand against the demons whom they see raised up against themselves, we cannot fittingly call them overseers.

## CHAPTER XVI

Why, moreover, should they be called prelates (*praesules*), when they have given their dignity and glory to another? How can men be believed to exercise prelatial office when, having become idolaters, avarice, their chief prelate, rules them?

## CHAPTER XVII

For what reason ought those to be called bishops (*episcopi*) who do not raise toward heavenly things the lofty mouth divinely given them, who do not seek the things that are above, but bend down more lowly than cattle toward the senses of the body, cleave to what is lowest, and gape after earthly things?

## CHAPTER XVIII

Who but a fool judges those to be shepherds who feed themselves rather than their sheep, who consume the sheep’s milk and clothe themselves in their wool? The Holy Spirit denies that these are shepherds when He says: “You consume the milk of the sheep and cover yourselves with their wool; you have not strengthened what was weak, you have not restored what was sick, you have not sought what had perished, you have broken what was strong; and my sheep have been scattered because there is no shepherd” [Note: [Col. 1013] John 7.].

[Col. 1014C] He says that the sheep are scattered because there is no shepherd, though they have evil shepherds. Shall I call men shepherds who are not? Shall I assert what God denies? Far be it!

## CHAPTER XIX

Or are they to be called superiors (*praelati*) who, when necessary, do not set themselves before others? Who do not oppose themselves to the adversary roaring like a lion? Who, on seeing the wolf, flee, forgetful of the scattered sheep? Who do not place themselves before us in order to offer themselves for us, but rather, by sharing their own things with no one, take our things from us?

Are they not rather to be called exalted (*elati*) than prelates (*praelati*)? They are not pressed down by our burden, but are raised up over and against us by our honour. What, then, shall we call them? I know, and say, that many men are truly pontiffs; but men of this kind are not to be called pontiffs, but pseudo-pontiffs. Yet if, following usage, we call them by these names, we believe it pardonable for us to do so. For it is no wonder that men who say and do not do are said to be what they are not.

[Col. 1013] END OF THE FIRST PART.

THE CHAPTERS OF THE SECOND PART BEGIN.

[Col. 1013]

CHAPTER I. What sort of men they have in the greater churches. [Col. 1015A]  
2. That they give their nephews everything they can.  
3. That canonries are obtained from them by hereditary right.  
4. That there are persons who advise the election of an unknown man without parents, on account of evils of this sort.  
5. That such counsel must not be trusted.  
6. That the humility in the lowly person whom they chose was not humility but deceptive abasement.  
7. That he now retains nothing of his former state except sideways glances.  
8. That men did for him whatever he said.  
9. That all were deceived by his outward simplicity.  
10. That he is now known to others, he who has ceased to know himself and others.  
[Col. 1016A] 11. That he has remained in no good thing since he fell from humility.  
12. That the man thought to have no parent had countless relatives once raised on high.  
13. That such a man ought not to be chosen, as is inferred from what precedes and follows.  
14. That Fortune gives birth again, most excellently, to men whom the earth had first brought forth in whatever fashion.  
15. That old men must first be put off, and new men immediately put on.  
16. That in a single moment Fortune makes them courtiers, discerning, and crafty.  
17. How celebrated their repeated birth is; and how men who until then had lived harder than stones suddenly become dignified, refined, and delicate.

# SECOND PART

[Col. 1015]

## CHAPTER I

[Col. 1015B] Who does not know what sort of men they keep with them and set over churches? Men like themselves. In those regions there are greater and lesser churches. In the greater churches, bishops’ first nephews hold first place; the second nephews, second place; and so on until there are no places left. Every offspring marries a position suitable to itself, and fruitfulness, bound as though by certain marital bonds, is wedded to barrenness.

By “nephews” I mean any persons related to them by flesh, character, and way of life: those whom they favour, upon whom they heap up treasure, and whom our prelates prepare as their successors. They cannot have peace until they see their nephews and great-nephews, or the sons of their sons, “tribulation and wrath upon Israel.” Men of this kind are joined to such fathers: sons to fathers, disciples to masters, a household suitable to its lords.

## CHAPTER II

For these men the fathers acquire, preserve, seize, and guard. They acquire anxiously, preserve more anxiously, seize painfully, and guard more painfully. They run about, torment themselves, and groan, desiring to increase what they may leave to their adopted heirs. The wretches are not even permitted to touch the goods that they strive to preserve after themselves for future possessors. For they regard as entrusted goods those that they transfer to their successors even during their own lives.

[Col. 1015C] Would that it were enough for them to transfer gold, silver, and the wealth of the marketplace to ill-fated heirs, so that the Church would not also be compelled to nourish strangers for her own people and foster stepchildren in place of sons—stepchildren whose fists continually beat her breast and whose teeth tear her breasts. Would that the Ishmaels might be cast out, so that the sons of the slave-woman would not inherit with the sons of the free woman! But the reality is far otherwise. For from these men and others we hear of offices of dignity, though no merits are ever heard that might justify them. Gifts are reported, but no grounds for the gifts are discussed. Promotions are heard of, but the business underlying the promotions is not heard.

## CHAPTER III

The sons, degenerating from their fathers in no respect, or only in the slightest, demolish and even uproot the house of God, though it is established upon the firm rock. They strive for this one thing: to desolate its place, devour Jacob, and ensure that the name of Israel is remembered no more. Certain already that they will succeed as heirs, they say to one another: “Let us take possession of the sanctuary of God as an inheritance” [Note: [Col. 1015] Psalm 82.].

[Col. 1016B] Hence this brood of vipers, this nation uncircumcised in heart and ear, obtains canonries by hereditary right—alas, this ruinous inheritance which disinherits! A spiritual grace is possessed by the right of carnal custom; yet a testament does not make the heir a recipient of the wage of grace. For grace perishes where inheritance rules. Thus, to become a canon is to leave the Church, not to enter it. Those who enter in this way are not heirs of God, nor co-heirs of Jesus Christ.

When our pontiffs call such men to themselves, if perhaps they see a few present who are unlike them, they neither call nor love them, though they honour them under compulsion. They have forgotten too greatly that supreme Pontiff who, although He had apostles as kinsmen, set none of them above the others but granted primacy over them to another.

## CHAPTER IV

Perhaps someone advises that an unknown man, not suspect by reason of the nobility of parents or friends, should be chosen; and says that, in the election of a pontiff, prudence can equip electors with counsel, and useful caution can be employed through foresight. Thus a lowly man, modest in learning, wholly without reputation, known to himself but unknown to the world, abhorring eminence, should suddenly be made eminent and appointed bishop. If such a man is not in the city, such a man will not be absent from the countryside. If he is not found in a town, he will be found in the wilderness.

[Col. 1016D] The wilderness has many such poor hermits of poverty. Though daily want forced them into it, they have nevertheless more happily transferred themselves from compelled poverty into voluntary poverty. Necessity that compels toward something better is indeed happy. These men despise the world and flee the world while in the world; though they still live on earth, their manner of life is in heaven [Note: [Col. 1017] Philippians 3.]. Though earth still detains them as pilgrims in tents, heaven already receives them as inhabitants in houses.

[Col. 1017A] They take up wings, fly, and do not grow weary. For they fly upon the wings of the winds until they bring the spaces of heaven beneath themselves and almost settle altogether in heaven. Even the tiny part that scarcely remains upon earth hates and detests the earth; wholly it breathes heaven, wholly it longs for heaven. They do not care for superfluities; they halve even necessities for themselves; they discipline the flesh and strive to enrich the spirit. Their faces display something divine and transcend everything human; they make one admire, stand amazed, and tremble, because they show that a human being has fellowship with angels. These men do not know that they have parents or whence they came. I believe that men such as these may be elevated without harm. Do not trust the wicked man.

## CHAPTER V

I said, “Do not trust”: for not every spirit is to be believed. I know a hermit who became a pontiff. Before becoming what he now is, he wholly savoured of an angel—indeed, he surpassed an angel. But once the pontiff’s garment was put over him, the tunic-clad hermit lay hidden; enthroned upon the shoulders of the eminent, he saw the shadow of his horned head stretching far ahead through the city.

[Col. 1017B] At once he gave himself over, defected from himself, and entirely forgot who he had been. Suddenly lapsing into lethargy, he boasted in his heart that, through the misfortune of this sickness, he was supremely fortunate. And if among the other thoughts that freely presented themselves the memory of the wilderness later escaped him, fear, dread, and shuddering were immediately at hand.

Because, above all things that pleased him, he delighted in forgetting the wilderness, he wholly left, though he did not put off, both the wilderness and the hermit. Forgetting himself, therefore, he forsook both himself and the others—he who until then had deemed neither himself nor anyone else worthy of notice. Those who had until then condemned him gradually began to recognize him; would that they had known him thus from the beginning! For if the evasiveness of this still-uncultivated man had been apparent to townsmen, if they had understood his many-coloured deceptions, he would still be cultivating woodland clearings and groves.

[Col. 1017C] If the *rudentini* [reading uncertain] had known him well at first, that Egyptian, as though buried by Moses, would still be sleeping in the sand and would never have come forth from the grove into the light. But men who had learned to beware of the proud and noble did not know how to beware of the unknown and humble. Those whom pride, suspect to every person, could not deceive were easily deceived by a man’s humility, visible to all.

## CHAPTER VI
Yet it was not humility, but deceptive abasement; not virtue, but an action resembling the exercise of virtue. For humility is a glorious thing, with which even pride seeks to cloak itself, lest it become contemptible. He displayed humility in his countenance, though he intended to persecute humility. He showed a simple sheep upon his face, while concealing in his mind a ravening wolf. Then he was preparing the leaven by which he might corrupt the whole lump of clergy and people. Then he placed himself far behind all the rest, so that he might be far before them; so that, returning from a greater distance, he might spring forward more violently and farther. [Col. 1018A] That he might be preferred to the clergy and the people, he prepared for himself a fertile place in barren sand; so that the sand—which refuses the entrusted seed to its creditor—might bear him a fertile bishopric. Our countrymen were also prompted to esteem the place itself highly, because, being remote from places of public sinners, they believed it imparted holiness. If that were so, neither would Satan have fallen from heaven, nor Adam in Paradise, nor Lot have sinned on the mountain—he who had proved holy in Sodom. Yet this place, because it was sandy and barren, suited better than others this dry and barren man, to whom nothing rich, nothing fleshly, was pleasing. To him sweet refreshment was continual hunger unto satiety; delightful drink, unceasing thirst. For he was wholly in spirit, whose flesh had almost wholly melted away in tears. Of him [Col. 1018B] no human being can say how devout, how holy, he appeared to the eyes of the world—how far this man was from being a man.

## CHAPTER VII

Now indeed he retains nothing in himself of his former habit, except one thing only which he had practised from childhood: namely, he turns one eye upward all the more highly as he bends the other downward toward the lowest things. Thus whenever he speaks, one eye seems to see only those hearers whom it looks upon on earth, while the other, seeing those attentive to the same discourse, portends that the whole word of the pontiff is addressed to sheep in the air. This was taken as evidence of his uprightness and loftiness, and stirred many to seek his advancement. For, seeing him when speaking to them freely and [Col. 1018C] readily search the heavens with one eye, and with the other most willingly and laboriously provide on earth for the necessary needs of human beings, they gave thanks to God that they had found one head adorned with both the light of Rachel and that of Leah.

Many also, examining the matter more subtly in their opinion, said that those sinned not a little who withheld one eye from the contemplation of the other. It seemed more fitting to them that, in the same man, Peter passing over into John and Martha into Mary, the man wholly transformed into spirit should be allowed freely to enter heaven.

## CHAPTER VIII

But what did these considerations avail against him? All spoke for him; all acted for him, when they proclaimed exalted things concerning him. All strove to bring the affair of his promotion to its desired conclusion. For who [Col. 1018D] would withdraw himself from the cause of that man's holiness? Among all there was concerning the unknown man a holy and wonderful opinion, which abandoned the fact that he was unknown. Some thought well of him, others very well, all favourably; none unfavourably. For the holiness seen in the man removed every suspicion; the wondrously ordered character of religion visible in him did so. There was one will in all, one harmony of hearts, one affection of minds; the same judgment among old men, young men, and boys. For the appearance of a contemptible man united everyone in one admiration for one person: cheap clothing, humble gait, humble countenance, modest lowering of the eyes, restrained gesture, a gentle delivery of voice, [Col. 1019A] modesty in his face, pallor in his mouth, leanness throughout his body, trembling in exultation, joy in fear, fear in service.

## CHAPTER IX

Nor was it surprising that people should admire signs of rectitude in the man, when those present declared that things opposed to rectitude were even more worthy of admiration. For the supposedly simple religion apparent outwardly so dulled eyes that had once seen and minds that had once been the minds of worthy people, that among other deformed limbs which nature itself had been pleased to fashion in him, they praised most highly those that were twisted and crooked; and they asserted that he, to whom nature denied the ordinary sight of others, saw more clearly than the rest. Their folly persuaded them to believe that whatever he had received less fully, through nature's alteration, as an excellent endowment, the generous hand of grace that loved him beforehand restored to him more abundantly as a perfect gift. Yet one ought rather to have believed that the outward appearance was a sign of inward deformity: that one who saw crookedly would judge crookedly; that one who saw askew would devise askew what ought to be arranged, and would arrange askew what he had conceived beforehand. No deference ought to have been shown to eyes which, though they opened their eyelids more than others, had pupils covered with white films. Such films not only darken outward sight, but indicate darkened inward sight. For unless the film and the scab signified an inward corruption of the soul, persons possessing them would not be refused holy administration, nor would such persons be forbidden promotion in the Law. But the signs remained hidden from us until [Col. 1019C] the things signified were at hand.

## CHAPTER X

Now he is known by man, he who has ceased to know himself as a man. He is known in his public character, not in the man himself—he who had remained unknown in the man, not in his public character. He began little by little to be recognized by a few; as he proceeded further, all came to know him more and more. Now he is known outside himself, he who remained unknown so long as he remained within himself. Now he cannot feign humility without revealing it by the very attempt at concealment. He mutters, gnashes his teeth, grows angry; made brazen and shameless, he speaks readily, threatens most readily, burns with anger, is carried aloft by madness, glows with fury. Nor does the antiquity of his days weaken his strength for villainies; old age itself seems to animate him for crimes. Nor is this surprising: it is the nature of crimes that, when they are not cut off, they increase; [Col. 1019D] and one leaps into greater crimes whenever one sins secure in impunity. Hence his rage is neither diminished nor restrained: it burns, and is more inflamed by punishments.

He conceives crimes, but hastens to accomplish those conceived. He plans wicked deeds, but perpetrates them with the greatest urgency. Nor do his riches permit him to practise his own wickedness alone. For, made rich by his chest, not by merit; by possession, not by lineage; by name, not by honour, he compels many thousands to share his madness through both threats and gifts. One madman makes many mad, so that it rightly seems possible to say of him: “He runs against the humble with uplifted neck, armed with a very stiff neck” [Note: [Col. 1019] Job 15]; he walks erect and thinks himself born free like a wild ass. Thus he is proved to have fallen from the humility in which he seemed to stand into pride. [Col. 1020A]

## CHAPTER XI

But in falling from humility into pride, from what good did he not fall into what evil? From none, if he had none. But if he had possessed what he seemed to have possessed and to possess, he would have fallen from charity into hatred; from humiliation into self-exaltation; from generosity into plunder; from inward progress into outward glory; from piety into cruelty; from faith into faithlessness; from hope of the joy to come into despair; from patience into anger; from peace into quarrels; from tears into laughter; from consideration of mortal life into pleasure.

Nevertheless, all his fraud—indeed, his whole self, which is nothing but fraud; indeed, the very fraud itself—now leaves him wholly deceived. For he is now detected as the man he was before; he is exposed [Col. 1020B] when he is recognized outwardly and inwardly; he is marked by all, denounced by all, because all the more vehemently resent seeing false everything that they had formerly thought concerning him. They chose a man of peace, and have him as an enemy of peace. Under what tyrant, indeed, were ever heard so many massacres, so many ruinous disasters, so many schisms in the Church, so many scandals? What shall I say of simony and the other things to which idol-serving avarice devotes itself? Which of these crimes is this apostate angel without? What occurs in the marketplace that he himself does not do in the holy house?

## CHAPTER XII

Certainly, just as no parents had preceded him, so no successors were suspected for him. But when his name was heard, barren mountains laboured to give birth, [Col. 1020C] and ridiculous mice were born to him. When these were newly born, the entire pontifical court boiled over on the first day; on the second, fraudulent foxes were found. For, in the interval of a night, that fox—more foxy than every fox—made foxes from mice. By deforming them she conformed them to herself. By unteaching them she taught them. Having instructed them badly, she thrust them in more badly, excluding the sons of the Church. She broke off the natural branches in order to graft in the wild olive and make it a partner in the root and richness of the olive tree. And it not only became a partner: once the olive had been cut off, the wild olive, usurping dominion, claimed the root for itself.

Yet when the mercy of the Dayspring from on high looked upon it, the north wind began to rise and the south wind to come; and as it blew, the sweet fragrance of spices immediately perfumed the garden of the bridegroom. As its wondrous sweetness touched neighbouring places, a more serene breeze than usual began to blow everywhere; serenity returned with a mild and kindly countenance; and the face of the Church began joyfully to put on once more its own sun. [Col. 1020D] The spring mildness rejoices after winter; the breeze of fair weather is welcome after cloud; renewal by rest after labour is sweet; after passing through fire and water, deliverance into refreshment brings delight. Though the wild olive protested, the olive was grafted in again. For God is able to uproot the wild olive; and the olive hopes for this in long-suffering hope, whose fruit will be the more welcome the longer its hope is prolonged. Nor will it be useless even to the deceived—whom a false image long deluded—to have shaken the bad tree among the others, so that henceforth those whom the unknown deceived may beware of it once it is recognized. Formerly [Col. 1021A] they supposed it an olive by its leaves; at last they recognized it as a wild olive by its fruit.

## CHAPTER XIII

Be silent, therefore, you who advised that such a man be chosen. No longer believe that he is bloodless, without blood; spirit without flesh, a lamb without deceit, a sheep without a wolf, a man of no family without parents, or a descendant of no one without successors. A multitude is indeed the true sister of high station, and kinship clings to it more inseparably than blackness to an Ethiopian. High station without kindred is unheard of. For in one day the sand gives him as many parents as it itself contains. The earth opens its bosom and gives birth without pain; and a common people, which had grown old before it was yet stirred, rises all at once. At its birth the whole world is seen everywhere to teem with a contemptible [Col. 1021B] rabble. Whoever sees it is amazed at the fertility of the mother that gives birth, the capacity of her womb, the manner of birth, and the bearing and appearance of those born.

For such an innumerable multitude of uncultivated persons arises in a single moment that the prophecies now seem for the first time to be fulfilled: “The desert and the solitary places of the land shall be too narrow because of the inhabitants, and those who inhabited it shall be driven far away; and then the children of barrenness shall say: ‘The place is too narrow; make room for us, that we may dwell’” [Note: [Col. 1021] Isa. 49]. But what has an anxious mother-earth to say to this, having nowhere to nourish so many? Unless she speaks in the language of the same prophet and says: “Who has begotten these for me? I was formerly barren and not bearing, carried away and captive; and who would have brought these forth? I was left destitute and desolate; and where were these?” [Note: [Col. 1021] Ibid.]

## CHAPTER XIV

Therefore, when these persons have been born without a father, the anxious earth, like another mother, supplies their necessities. When she finds within herself nothing sufficient to feed so great a multitude, she takes thought for her own and makes another's children her own; and those whom nature, impoverishing them more and more from day to day, had allowed to beg from door to door—these hungry, misshapen, half-human beings fickle Fortune receives into her lap, in order that she may conceive them again, give them birth, nourish them, enrich them, and ennoble them. For she delights to exercise right and power upon such people; she who always, by her inborn habit, both makes poor and enriches, humbles and raises up, “raises the needy from the dust and lifts the poor from the dunghill” [Note: [Col. 1021] 1 Sam. 2].

Therefore she can answer the anxious mother-earth, certainly with a mournful voice, in the voice of the prophet: “Behold, I lift up my hand to the nations, and I shall raise my standard to the peoples; and they shall bring your sons in their arms, and [Col. 1021D] carry your daughters upon their shoulders; and kings shall be your foster-fathers, and queens your nurses” [Note: [Col. 1021] Isa. 49].

## CHAPTER XV

In the education of these uncultivated people, Fortune's first concern is to take them out of their ragged garments, patched and mended in many ways, with one piece of cloth sewn upon another and then another. In these garments the material was uncertain, upon which a motley diversity of colours was impressed. For if I devoted greater attention to this matter, as to this work, the mad torturer would wish to argue about the law; the needle's workmanship would greatly prejudice the case, a workmanship surpassed not by the number of people who know how to sew, but by the frequency of sewing.

For innumerable citizens and cities took great pains to entrust to fullers raw wools still needing dye, so that the plain material, made sport of by deceptive appearances, might deceive the eyes of observers no less than it had itself been deceived. And, with artfully altered fleeces, city-dwellers were pleased to compose fabrics worthy of admiration; after the passage of many years, a single cheap garment of this sort is made from them. In it a new piece of cloth—“one or another that shines”—is sewn onto an old piece, producing a greater tear. Therefore, because in such a ragged covering, joined incongruously from innumerable remnants which venerable antiquity had judged worthy of rejection, the daily necessity of the poor mender's needle finds relief, the crude workmanship of one person rightly surpasses the polished skill of many. Although a thousand hands which first sweated no little over the labour of this work have now died, a thousand remain alive. [Col. 1022B] Thus, when we newcomers arrive, Fortune destroys every trace of antiquity among her foster-children. And those whom she everywhere proclaims to be nephews of high station, she duly entrusts to high station for upbringing.

## CHAPTER XVI

Thus Fortune fully begets and gives birth to those scarcely and somehow born, whom obscurity had long hidden beneath thin cloth, so that high station may not live barren. At the very moment in which they are born, their spirited mother breathes into them lofty thoughts, exalted designs, and discriminating speech. Immediately, stripping away every trace of rusticity, she rains them into the palace like mushrooms. In the same little hour she conceives, carries, bears, adorns, and instructs them. At one time they are born and ride through [Col. 1022C] the city; they are borne about and give commands; they enter the court and arrange households. They are carried by the hand to churches, where they raise up and cast down; drawn into lawsuits by prices and prayers, where they are established alone, heard simultaneously as advocates and judges. By a moment's judgment they are made eloquent, though they had long lived unskilled and wordless: yesterday they were old men who had not yet spoken; today, newly born, they declaim and argue marvellously.

## CHAPTER XVII

Their second birth, now known, is celebrated by many, though their first birth, unknown, had deceived everyone. Those whom nature had begotten from nothing, even more insignificant than nothing, kinder Fortune makes splendidly reborn amid pomp and proclamation. Alas for shame! Formerly they were not ashamed that, naked, their private parts lay exposed to all; only recently they had come to the city barefoot. Now, suddenly clothed in soft garments, they imprison feet once free—and hostile to this honour—in padded slippers; the feet resist and kick back, as though a camel were being forced with goads to enter a silver casket. Yet their protesting, struggling heels are compelled to shine with gilded spurs. Suddenly made weighty with sudden majesty, they lean on sceptres, mount tribunals, sit softly upon silken cushions, and purple lies spread beneath their tender feet—feet which innate hardness formerly protected from the pricking of thorns and the injury of sharp stones. And those who once used to inflate pipes with their cheeks behind the flocks, transferred [Col. 1023A] from sheepfolds to lawsuits, alas, are heard boldly commanding magnates. Does this finest race of high station flourish and [Col. 1024A] bloom, aggravating perversity with perversities?

[Col. 1023] **HERE ENDS THE SECOND PART.**

**THE CHAPTER-HEADINGS OF THE THIRD PART BEGIN.**

[Col. 1023]

[Col. 1023A] 1. That those called fathers have flatterers in the same rank as their nephews. 2. Examples of prophets are adduced, showing how greatly they must be guarded against. 3. The prophet's authority concerning how these three things, especially flattery, must be avoided. [Col. 1023B] 4. That they must not only be repelled, but immediately put to shame. 5. That they bring shameful things upon those whom they flatter. 6. That these are first in everything, even when uninvited. 7. The true are asked whether the false should be believed. 8. The false are asked why they rage so against themselves. 9. That through excessive concern for others they do not know themselves, like Dinah. 10. That Joseph's seed is an example to others that they should guard themselves. 11. That they bury and are buried; and first, how hearers bury those whom they have heard. 12. How those heard bury their hearers. [Col. 1024A] 13. That they are not with themselves, since they were handed over to a reprobate mind. 14. An address to true pontiffs, lest by hearing vain men they become like them. 15. Astonishment at the false, that they are so deceived. 16. Taking occasion from the words of holy Job, a discussion of when it is good and when evil to show reverence to lords and to receive them. [Col. 1024B] 17. With the wicked excluded, an exhortation fitting for the good is made. 18. How much humility benefits the humble. 19. That they ought to imitate these two; and first it is shown that kings should imitate the King. 20. That pontiffs should imitate the Pontiff. 21. A turn from the true to the false, showing them that, even if they were such as they are proclaimed to be, praise itself would take away the good which they formerly had. 22. Another division of the members: namely, if they are not such. 23. More hardened than Pharaoh.

# THIRD PART

[Col. 1023]

## CHAPTER I

[Col. 1023C]

To those previously mentioned are added, in the same rank, the sons of deceit, who have learned to sell the oil of vainglory abundantly. Flattery, the mistress of such men, trains them to be most ready for two things: always to speak well of evil with evil intent, and to speak ill while deceitfully praising. These alike prove themselves tireless, generous judges of all the words they hear from their masters. If, because of their masters' excessive concern for a fingernail, they happen to find one cut by a rough pair of shears; if they observe a hair in the beard longer than the others; if they see a misplaced hair upon the head turning aside, they rage, gnash their teeth, and are indignant—at last scarcely to be calmed even by their masters themselves. Their whole aim is to make themselves beloved by their masters, seeking out grounds on which to curry favour. Hence, in words and deeds, they allow nothing [Col. 1023D] to pass without praise. Whatever their masters say and do, they proclaim worthy not of any number of human beings, but of angels alone. Even if their deeds are plainly most wicked, in the prejudgment of such arbiters they excel good deeds.

They favour the sayings of others, approve their deeds, refuse nothing, reject nothing. What their masters wish, they wish; what is desired from them, they desire; what is wanted, they too want. According to their masters' heart they think, do, conceive, and accomplish. They join hearts to hearts, but not with their heart; they attach mind to minds, but without mind. For flattery produces this effect in its adherents: they say yes when those whom they flatter say yes, and no when they say no; they seek to displease others and please only those from whom they mean to extort something. For flattery never comes alone; it has arrogance and detraction as inseparable companions. Thus it does not merely do what is its own office—to cajole and favour—but, by the convenient character it draws from its companions, causes them also to detract and to grow arrogant. Therefore they first anoint the heads of their masters with oil; secondly, they themselves arrogantly arrogate things to themselves and deceitfully disparage others.

The Apostle calls them “hateful to God” [Note: [Col. 1023] Rom. 1]. The Prophet likewise condemns them, saying: “May the Lord destroy all deceitful lips and the tongue that speaks great things” [Note: [Col. 1023] Ps. 11]. He directed “deceitful lips” to detraction and “the tongue that speaks great things” to arrogance. For the arrogant [Col. 1024D] exalt and boast of themselves, speak about themselves, multiply their speaking, and walk in great and marvellous things above themselves. By detraction they continually whisper, sow discord among brothers, and deny or distort the good qualities of others. In order to deceive others and not be deceived by others, they always walk by two paths. “Woe,” he says, “to sinners entering the land by two paths” [Note: [Col. 1023] Ecclus. 2]. Those enter the land by two paths who speak with heart and heart; who “speak good things with their neighbour, but evil things in their hearts” [Note: [Col. 1023] Ps. 27].

## CHAPTER II

[Col. 1025A]

Although he guarded against them not a little, the Prophet says that he was besieged and surrounded by them: “They surrounded me like bees” [Note: [Col. 1025] Ps. 117]. Those are rightly called bees who flatter with the tongue but secretly strike from malice. For in speaking they offer the sweetness of honey, but secretly inflict a wound by striking. Because of their stings another prophet calls them scorpions; to him it was said: “Unbelievers and subverters are with you, and you dwell among scorpions” [Note: [Col. 1025] Ezek. 2]. For these are unbelievers toward God, subverters of weak men, and scorpions to the strong and robust. Though they do not dare openly to contradict the latter to their face, nevertheless from concealment they inflict the wound of detraction.

They are rightly called scorpions because they appear gentle and harmless in front, but pour poison from behind; they display peace [Col. 1025B] and foster hatreds; they say friendly things and do hostile things; they arouse settled anger, compete, envy, and devour one another with sidelong bites. They disguise vices, saying, “Peace, peace,” when there is no peace [Note: [Col. 1025] Jer. 6]. Of such people it is rightly said: “The sound of terror is always in their ears, and even when there is peace, they suspect snares” [Note: [Col. 1025] Job 15]. For, acting deceitfully, they do not suppose that others deal simply with them. Their minds are always in labour, because they either devise evils to inflict or fear that others will inflict them upon themselves. Since they never cease to harass others, they have no rest within themselves. This alone is their occupation, their leisure and their labour, their rest. “For they rejoice when they have done evil, and delight in most wicked things” [Note: [Col. 1025] Prov. 2]; [Col. 1025C] but grief takes possession of the end of their joy, “and their laughter shall be mingled with sorrow” [Note: [Col. 1025] Prov. 14]. “They teach their tongues to speak lies,” and make “their mouth abound in malice” [Note: [Col. 1025] Jer. 9]; but “the labour of their lips shall cover them” [Note: [Col. 1025] Ps. 139].

## CHAPTER III

Because these three vices are deadly, the prophet shows, in three verses, that he pursues them with all his strength, where he says: “He who speaks iniquity did not walk straight before my eyes. Him who secretly detracts from his neighbour, I pursued; one of proud eye and insatiable heart, with him I did not eat” [Note: [Col. 1025] Ps. 100]. What did he say of the arrogant person? “With him,” he says, “I did not eat.” What against the detractor? “Him,” he says, “I pursued.” What against the flatterer? “He was not set right before my eyes.” Who was not set right? “He who speaks iniquity.” For flatterers are said to speak iniquitous things, and especially to speak iniquitously; because whenever these crafty robbers flatter anyone, unless he takes care, they seize and steal him from himself.

Although these three vices are together in one person and are linked almost everywhere they occur, they do not, among all those whom they harm, exercise their offices together. For when one person strikes with these three darts, not everyone whom he strikes is struck by all of them. Flattery wounds many whom detraction spares; and arrogance harms no one except the person from whom it arises. Thus it often happens that one accustomed to serve such crimes seems, whenever he changes one vice for another, [Col. 1026A] also to change his person. For the gentle flattering praiser, when he becomes a harsh detractor from a trivial supporter, differs from his former self; and the arrogant offspring of contrivance differs from both, when, while arrogating honour to himself alone, he strives to deprive everyone else of what he heaps upon the one.

Therefore, though these three are very evil, flattery is more effectively a worse evil, because it teaches its own devotees the proclamations of empty praise, then instructs those thus taught in the opposite of praise. For an immoderate praiser has never been heard of who would not know how, at any time and to whatever extent he pleased, to unsing the praises which he had sung at full voice either to the very person whom he was then praising or to anyone else. Whatever praises he lavishes today upon a hungry person, tomorrow, if he wishes, he can take away with worthier blame. Arrogance kills only those it infects; and from detraction heard patiently, virtue usually increases in the hearer. But from flattery, the more patiently it is heard, the more deeply the sweet poison is poured into its hearers. And if the wretched hearer once of his own accord tastes, drinks, and swallows it, then the servers applaud, then pour it out more lavishly, and, crying “Good, good!” again, say, “We shall devour him” [Note: [Col. 1025] Ps. 34].

## CHAPTER IV

Hence the Prophet, who was not unaware of the poison of asps hidden beneath their lips, asked the Lord not only that these people be driven away from him, but that they do so swiftly, confounded and ashamed. “Let those who say to me, ‘Good, good!’ turn back at once in shame” [Note: [Col. 1025] Ps. 69]. And elsewhere: “Let those who say to me, ‘Good, good!’ immediately bear their confusion” [Note: [Col. 1025] Ps. 39]. “At once,” he says, “let them turn back,” lest reproof against such people be delayed—although reproof is often prudently deferred, that it may later be kindly received. Thus the wise woman, seeing Nabal drunk, did not wish to rebuke him; after the wine had been digested, she rebuked him not without effect [Note: [Col. 1025] 1 Sam. 23]. But flattery, if it is patiently received even for a time, increases; it gradually caresses the mind and softens it from the firmness of its rectitude into delight in speech. To prevent it from growing, it must be struck at once. It did not grow before the eyes of him who said: “He did not walk straight before my eyes” [Note: [Col. 1025] Ps. 100].

## CHAPTER V

I recall reading [Note: [Col. 1025] 2 Sam. 10] that the sons of Ammon shaved half the beards of David's envoys, who had come to console them over their father's death, and cut their garments in the middle as far as the buttocks. For turbulent and worthless flatterers, whom David's envoys came to console over the death of their father, when ministers of Christ undertake pastoral care for them as persons bereft of their spiritual Father, turn themselves to shaving beards when they soften their vigour and severity with the oil of wicked flattery. They also cut their garments as far as the buttocks when, by evil conversation and wretched blandishments, they drag them as though soft and effeminate into uncleannesses and disgraceful acts, stripping them of the dignity of chastity. This is the sole thing which these enemies of integrity, foes of modesty, thieves of purity, and plunderers of chastity contrive, fabricate, begin, and bring to completion.
