As holy Job testifies, [Note: [Col. 1027] ch. 18] “they hide their snare in the earth, and their trap upon the path.” They hide the snare in the earth when they conceal guilt beneath earthly advantages, so that a person may see what he desires but not see in what snare of sin he sets his foot. “And their trap upon the path.” For they observe the habits of each person, to discover what vice he is prone to; and they place before his eyes those things toward which they know his mind is more easily inclined. It is impossible to be cherished by their counsels and smeared with their flatteries without losing one or both kinds of a person's chastity. Often both; always one. For chastity of mind is always lost whenever chastity trusts its enemies. When the mind does not remain whole, bodily integrity remains worthless before God. Hence Moses is commanded to circumcise the foreskin of the heart [Note: [Col. 1027] Deut. 10], and Job [Note: [Col. 1027] ch. 16] to gird his loins like a man. For he does not circumcise the foreskin of his heart, nor gird his loins like a man, who subdues the lustfulness of the flesh while the chastity of the mind is lost; since a chaste generation is in no way beautiful to God unless it is with charity [Note: [Col. 1027] Wis. 4].

Therefore David's envoys ought, against the insipid speeches of flatterers and conversations seasoned without salt, to ask God for protection, lest perhaps, after they have tasted the sweet poison of the inveterate disease, they may scarcely, or never, be able to find a curative remedy. Against people of this kind, the Prophet, finding no help for himself in himself, sought help from the Lord who made heaven and earth [Note: [Col. 1027] Ps. 120]: “Lord,” he says, “deliver my soul from wicked lips and from a deceitful tongue” [Note: [Col. 1027] Ps. 119]—from those too who openly urge me to act perversely; from those too who obscure with the leaves of words the evils they suggest. Likewise, lest he injure himself or another by speaking, he asked that every vice of the tongue be removed from him, saying: “Set, O Lord, a guard upon my mouth, and a door of restraint around my lips” [Note: [Col. 1027] Ps. 140].

## CHAPTER VI

But these empty-talkers, ill-wishers, and criminals do not want a door placed upon their lips. They treat what pleases them indiscriminately as lawful; they do not restrain mind, hand, or foot from thinking, committing, and investigating unlawful things. Rather, whatever comes into heart, mouth, or hand, they contrive, chatter, and perform wherever they walk, stand, or sit. Tongue, hand, head, [Col. 1027D] ears, eyes, fingers, and feet do not pause; no smallest part of the body is free from tumult. All their limbs move altogether and wholly, so that the inward person can be known from the movements of the outward.

In an assembly, theirs are the first seats; in deliberations, the first answers. They come uninvited; they introduce themselves unasked. They impose silence on speakers, boldly oppose everyone, choke off those answering, and blind one speech with another. When they bark thus, it is better to be silent than to reply. For it is enough for an answer to move the lips in silence whenever these men, through their own clamour, hear neither themselves nor [Col. 1028A] the person answering. For, deafening themselves, they believe that others likewise shout approval and answer in response to their snarling cries, if they merely observe the others' lips move. Their lords permit them to disarrange what has been arranged and remake what has been done. Whatever they have not done or arranged, they believe neither rightly done, nor finely said, nor properly ordered. It is their role, after judgments have been heard, to correct the judges; to judge beforehand those who are going to judge.

Their perpetual thirst and hunger is to have hearers whom they may deceive by empty boasting, draw in with vain words, pour poisonous honey upon, make aware of what and how great they are, and finally—once an opportunity to speak has been found—bring forth old and new things from the treasuries of wickedness. Their words resound, swollen and bombastic. No one asks, and they answer. No one [Col. 1028B] inquires, and they decide. They themselves ask; they themselves solve; and often they hear from one who is silent what he himself has not even considered. Nor do they know how to impose a limit upon their words, until they burst out into Elihu's words: “Behold, our bellies are like wine without a vent, which bursts wineskins” [Note: [Col. 1027] Job 32]; either we shall speak, therefore, or we shall burst. “For we are full of words, and the spirit of our belly constrains us.”

## CHAPTER VII

Let those who are pontiffs say, then, what seems to them concerning our men who are called bishops. Should those who hear such men, consult such men, and delight to give their ears to such men be believed? These prelates regard these people as their secure support. These lords cherish them tenderly. For if they perversely favour their lords, their presence is welcome to them, their companionship sweet, their conversation pleasant, their rest delightful, their speech effective, and their affection most fervent. When these are glad, the lords rejoice; when they are present, everything is at hand. When they are removed—and everything departs with them—delights and joys depart together; cares rush in, troubles assail from every side, straits are everywhere. The lords remain alone, labour alone under the burden of honour, groan alone beneath the load of high station—which they must either lay down or be crushed by, if these men withdraw their shoulders.

## CHAPTER VIII

Let those themselves who act so shamelessly, who rage so cruelly against themselves, say: whence comes this madness? Why do they not believe themselves concerning themselves, but believe their most deceitful supporters? And although in other matters they believe themselves more than others, why, concerning themselves alone, do they believe others more than themselves? They believe what they hear and applaud their praisers, but they do not consider what the praiser is attending to. They forget his intention while embracing his opinion; and whatever praise of themselves they recognize, they ascribe not to the praiser's ignorance or good will, but to their own merits. Whence comes such obstinacy? Whence this blindness? They do not know themselves, I think; they have wholly forgotten themselves and are far removed from themselves. Heaven is far removed from them; yet they themselves are far more removed from themselves than from heaven, and are nearer to Mount Caucasus than to themselves. The farther [Col. 1029A] they are from themselves, the more neglect of themselves makes them curious about other things.

## CHAPTER IX
To look about at other things Dinah turned herself [Note: [Col. 1029] Gen. 34.]; but within herself she remained sluggish and did not look about herself. She wished to appear wicked, but appeared still more wicked. She wished to know wickedly, but was known more wickedly. Leaving the guide of her youth, she went out alike from herself and from her father’s house, in order to see the women of that land. Having gone out, she saw the others; she herself was hidden from herself. She recognized many others; she did not know the one that was herself. What did she gain abroad by busy activity that she did not possess at home in repose? Corruption for herself, grief for her father, insult for her brothers, disgrace for her family. The daughter did not consult her father; she ought to be called daughter not of her father but of her uncle—of the uncle whom she imitated by leaving the house and wandering abroad, not of the father whom she refused to imitate by simply remaining at home. “Esau,” it says, “was skilled in hunting, a man of the field; but Jacob, a simple man, dwelt in tents” [Note: [Col. 1029] Gen. 25.]. While the former wandered abroad, hunting through the woods, having utterly forgotten the lentils sold by his brother, the latter prepared food at home and, when it was ready, invited his father, on the counsel of a prudent woman [Note: [Col. 1029] Gen. 27.]. Prudent was the woman who gave counsel; prudent was the man who trusted the counsel of the prudent woman. Dinah was the imprudent daughter of this prudent man [Note: [Col. 1029] Gen. 34.], but Dinah was not worthy to be called the daughter of a prudent man, nor to be called Jacob’s daughter, though Jacob was her father. For just as not all who are descended from Israel are Israelites, and not all who are Abraham’s seed are sons [Note: [Col. 1029] Rom. 9.], so neither did she deserve to be called Jacob’s daughter, since she did not wish to supplant sins, but succumbed, herself overthrown by sins. For no wise person would call a daughter who has ceased to resemble her father his daughter, just as he would not call Joseph’s sister the sister of a brother from whom she had degenerated. For he, after despising the blandishments, jests, embraces, and kisses of the shameless woman; after taking no notice of her manifold assaults; after various windings and turnings, leaving behind the garment by which he was held, escaped by flight [Note: [Col. 1029] Gen. 39.]. But he who heard the cry of Moses and Susanna when they were silent, hearing the silence of the crying modest youth, did not permit him to flee naked, but immediately covered him with a mantle far more excellent: innocence, modesty, chastity. As these triumphed in this struggle over the enemy of virginity, integrity obtained the palm it deserved; this other Jonah was not allowed to suffer shipwreck in the [Col. 1029D] whale. This boy did not feel the burning of the fire among boys, whom, so far as lay in her power, that woman—a most savage beast—devoured; yet the ravenous hunger of the devouring monster marvelled that the young man remained whole and unharmed in that very maw. Hence the patriarch Jacob, touched in part by the spirit of prophecy, weeping and lamenting, foretold: “A most evil beast has devoured my son Joseph” [Note: [Col. 1029] Gen. 37.].

## CHAPTER X

Therefore the most holy Joseph is set forth, a wonderful example to the rest, that they may beware of robbers of chastity, guard themselves, not depart from themselves, and [Col. 1030A] not forget themselves. By failing to imitate him, Dinah lost her virginity, Esau his inheritance, and the fathers mentioned above still lose their holiness. For while they neglect to know themselves, disdain to see themselves, and are sluggish in looking about themselves, they neither stretch themselves forward with the Apostle [Note: [Col. 1029] Phil. 3.], nor walk before their own face or in the presence of their own face with the holy living creatures [Note: [Col. 1029] Ezek. 1.]. They do not walk before their own face because they do not seek what lies ahead; nor in the presence of their own face, because they are not present to themselves. Those who are not concerned to seek out and know themselves are absent from themselves. While they are intent on something else, meanwhile the flattering serpent glides secretly into their heart. Its persuasion is gladly heard and its deception voluntarily embraced; its poisonous conversations please them, [Col. 1030B] and, while these are received, salutary warnings are despised. This serpent, suave in deceit, addresses those thirsty for blandishments with excessive sweetness; by flattery it restrains reason, by lies fear. And, as though they had again heard, “You shall by no means die” [Note: [Col. 1029] Gen. 3.], and, with the end of its counsel veiled, as though it were repeated, “You shall be like gods” [Note: [Col. 1029] Ibid.], they drink poison unto destruction, offered by one who is himself to perish while dispensing poison. For he does not know how to lie who says to the man wishing to bury his dead father: “Let the dead bury their own dead” [Note: [Col. 1029] Luke 9.].

## CHAPTER XI

“Let flatterers,” he says, “bury one another, together with those who listen to them, when the unworthy are praised by the unworthy and the guilty approved by the testimony of the guilty: they receive and return, obtain and repay; at one and the same time he who had given receives, and [Col. 1030C] he who had received repays.” Truth itself likewise says that fathers and sons, lovers of vain praise, should bury themselves, being dead. For they have become graves for one another—fathers for sons and sons for fathers—alike in fault, though foully conformed, and to be punished with a like punishment; yet the punishment is graver for those who corrupt those whom they ought to correct. For if failing to correct corrupt sons makes fathers worthy of a difficult punishment, corrupting still more those who are corrupt makes them liable to the most severe punishment. Eli did not correct his sons [Note: [Col. 1029] 1 Sam. 2.]; therefore his sons were killed by enemies, the ark of the Lord was captured, the woman died in childbirth, and he himself, his neck broken, fell backward from his seat. Korah, Dathan, and Abiram corrupted many [Note: [Col. 1029] Num. 16.], and perished with many. Fire was sent from heaven and consumed those offering strange fire. [Col. 1030D] Others, as the joints of the earth burst open, hell swallowed alive. What then will become of those who made no effort to correct, whose whole and entire concern is to kill those by whom they are killed, and to bury those by whom they are buried? Hearers are rightly said to bury those whom they listen to, because by listening attentively they foster them in wickedness and become flatterers. For if they turned away their ears and drew in their faces, they would teach evil speakers even by silence; such speakers would learn not to speak gladly what they had learned was not gladly heard. This is surely what one does who remembers the saying addressed to him: “Fence your ears with thorns, and do not listen to a tongue” [Note: [Col. 1031] Ecclus. 28.].

## CHAPTER XII

The dead hearer of the dead is buried by the dead when sinners, through flattery, soothe one sinning with unworthy rages and false praises, and hide him as though extinguished beneath the mound of their words. Against them Wisdom counsels every one of her sons: “My son, if sinners entice you, do not consent to them” [Note: [Col. 1031] Prov. 1.]. But those who disdain to believe Wisdom she herself rebukes as little children and fools, saying: “How long, little children, will you love childhood, and you fools desire things that are harmful?” [Note: [Col. 1031] Ibid.] Rightly indeed, though they are old and decrepit, they are called little children: disdaining the bread of adults, they are still nourished on the milk of flatterers. [Col. 1031B] In the fourth man whom he heard to be dead and did not wish to raise, after he had already raised three dead persons [Note: [Col. 1031] John 11.], the Lord fittingly signified those who are scarcely or never to be raised from sins. For those who gladly assent to wicked lips and deceitful tongues scarcely or never rise from vices. Such persons, with heads enriched by the oil of sinners [Note: [Col. 1031] Ps. 140], despise Wisdom’s counsel and, their judgment rejected, are miserably dragged into the abyss of evils and handed over captive to the tyranny of vices; so that, swallowed by the gulf of carnal desires, forgetting their own reason and the fear of God, they are compelled, foolishly, to say: “There is no God” [Note: [Col. 1031] Ps. 13.].

## CHAPTER XIII

O how terrible, deep, and unsearchable is God’s judgment! After the first crimes, iniquity follows; pleasure once experienced is gladly repeated, and when repeated it flatters; sin rules, vice stupefies, habit binds. It is indeed unworthy that a human being should be filthy; but it is most fitting that one who is in filth should become still filthier [Note: [Col. 1031] Rev. 22.]. Those who are wise in their own eyes have often read that saying of the Wise Man: “With all watchfulness guard your heart” [Note: [Col. 1031] Prov. 4]. Whence then do they depart from the heart? To whom do they meanwhile entrust themselves? Departing from the heart, they depart from God, from themselves likewise, and from us. Though they have heard a thousand times, “Return, transgressors, to your heart,” they do not return, but despise it more and more. For, when minds are scattered abroad, it is difficult to return to themselves, because crooked paths, once they have captured a person, hold him so delightfully in proportion as whatever he desires is permitted him. Since the wall of discipline offers no resistance to injuries, no punishment of retribution is foreseen to frighten them. Instead, with the eyes of their hearts shut, souls rush headlong, and they commit temporal evils all the more securely as they despair more harshly of eternal goods. Hence they do not listen, but still remain in the region of unlikeness; there, by remaining, they die, and when dead are buried. There they are not ashamed to have fed swine for a long time and to have attached themselves, not only to one of that country’s citizens, but to as many citizens of that whole region as there are flattering babblers. Shame does not call them back, reason does not restrain them, compassion does not soften them, authority does not terrify them, justice does not bend them. Captive Israel is compelled to [Col. 1032A] pay tribute to the ruling Canaanite—the one whom, by a mighty hand and outstretched arm, it had subdued and compelled, once subdued, to pay it tribute. Shamefully conquered, it arms its enemy, whom as a distinguished victor it had nobly disarmed. Nor is it said that sin, which dwells within him, sins now against the will of the one in whom it dwells. Where the soul is not ashamed to follow the traces of fleshly itchings, tickling it together with the flesh, each person most wretchedly drags and is dragged. Thus, through the unrecognized strength of the flesh, pride hurls him down, where humility, through recognizing its weakness, had raised him high. With the mouth of the pit pressing upon him, and no one bringing aid upon the bed of his pain, he lies, languishes, grows numb—blind, lame, withered—and does not deserve to hear the physician say: “Rise, take up your pallet [Col. 1032B] and walk” [Note: [Col. 1031] John 5.].

## CHAPTER XIV

Let them therefore beware of the leaven of vainglorious persons, which is flattery. Let all who have hitherto watched vigilantly beware still more vigilantly—those who have not been pleased to suggest wicked words, to whom such a stain has not clung, whom this infection has not corrupted. Let them beware lest they be deceived by empty words [Note: [Col. 1031] Eph. 5.], but resist, strong in faith [Note: [Col. 1031] 1 Pet. 5.]. For a little of this leaven corrupts the whole mass of all good things [Note: [Col. 1031] Gal. 5.]. Let no one listen; let no one believe. For once one has most miserably given one’s ears, one is enticed by blandishments; having believed at the same time, one is bound in harsh chains. For from the moment vain speech is believed, flattery undertakes to govern the believer; thereafter he must obey the habits of his mistress. He scarcely triumphs over her, over whom she once triumphed. For she binds by laws, violates every right, scrapes away divine ordinances, claims the entire person for herself, and leads him into the destruction of error, forgetting what dignity he possesses with God and from God. Let shepherds hear the Shepherd and Bishop of their souls, commanding the healed man to tell no one. Let successors of the Apostles hear Peter, who, though Cornelius was acting well, refused to be venerated beyond measure and acknowledged himself to be like him: “Rise,” he says, “do not do it; I myself also am a human being” [Note: [Col. 1031] Acts 10.]. Let them hear the angel of God answering the angel John: “See that you do not do it; for I am your fellow servant and that of your brothers” [Note: [Col. 1031] Rev. 19.]. Likewise the Apostle could not bear those who boasted of the merits of their baptizers and said: “I belong to Paul, I to Cephas, I to [Col. 1032D] Apollos” [Note: [Col. 1031] 1 Cor. 1.]; but, as though astonished on hearing Paul’s name, said: “Was Paul crucified for you? Or were you baptized in Paul’s name?” [Note: [Col. 1031] Ibid.] What answer, then, shall we give to these flatterers, who never attend to the one praised with a good intention, but with deceitful temptation? Let holy pontiffs recall what the most holy Pontiff answered the tempter: “Get behind me, Satan” [Note: [Col. 1031] Matt. 4.].

## CHAPTER XV

But what seems fine to our anti-bishops in temptations of this kind I greatly wonder. For whether they are pleased to make their own good deeds public themselves or through others, once conscience—the sound vessel fit for keeping secrets—is either broken or emptied by laying aside what it guarded, and, unwilling to remain hidden, is scattered abroad through excellent ears and empty breezes; the more reputation seeks to grow, the more, reduced to infamy, it perishes. For fame that enters and exits the throats of the infamous cannot fail to be devoured. And a treasure whose sole and entire permanence lies in being concealed is annulled when every conflict of winds scatters it abroad. The Apostle did not seek praise either from himself or from another when he said: “It is a very small thing to me that I should be judged by you or by a human day”; and added: “But neither do I judge myself” [Note: [Col. 1033] 1 Cor. 4.]. For he could not pronounce judgment even upon himself, since he did not wholly trust even his own conscience: “But the one who judges me is the Lord” [Note: [Col. 1033] Ibid.]—the Lord who cannot be deceived, because [Col. 1033B] he himself knows human thoughts [Note: [Col. 1033] 1 Chron. 28], which the eyes of him alone behold: “Take away,” he says, “the evil of your thoughts from before my eyes” [Note: [Col. 1033] Isa. 1]. He sees those who do not appear; he hears those who do not speak; he also hears in the heart of one thinking what even the thinker himself does not hear, whose ear is not silenced by rest, whose silence does not cease. “Why do you think evil in your hearts?” he says [Note: [Col. 1033] Matt. 9]. He alone judges, he who looks upon the heart [Note: [Col. 1033] 1 Sam. 16]; no word flies past him and no thought slips beneath him. He knows the deceiver and the deceived; he brings counsellors to a foolish end and judges to astonishment [Note: [Col. 1033] Job 12]. He who could fittingly commend Job as worthy of commendation—yet Job himself recoiled from commending himself, lest, though unworthy, he should be made worthy by being unworthily commended by himself. God most worthily commended him when [Col. 1033C] he said: “Have you considered my servant Job, that there is none like him upon the earth, a simple and upright man, fearing God and departing from evil?” [Note: [Col. 1033] Job 2.] But holy Job said of himself: “If I have kissed my hand with my mouth, which is the greatest iniquity and a denial against God Most High” [Note: [Col. 1033] Job 31.]; “who would grant me a helper?” He kisses his hand with his mouth who praises what he does. This is the greatest iniquity and a denial against God Most High, because whoever attributes to himself what he accomplishes is convicted of denying his Creator’s grace.

## CHAPTER XVI

That is, he did not wish his hand to be praised either by himself or by another. But when he said that he had not kissed his own hand, I believe he denied more what he understood than what he literally said. [Col. 1033D] For it is not customary for anyone to kiss his own hand. If this should happen by chance and convey no meaning, I neither praise nor blame it. Yet I both praise and blame—praise greatly, blame still more—when one person kisses another’s hand or foot, inclines his head to another’s head, or, according to the various customs of lands, renders other acts of veneration to superiors, according to the various intentions of both parties. Great is the commendation of this good, but greater is the condemnation of this evil. It is praiseworthy indeed that subjects render the honor due to authorities. For every [Col. 1034A] authority is from the Lord God; whoever resists authority resists God’s ordinance [Note: [Col. 1033] Rom. 13]. Thus whoever honors authority honors God’s ordinance—indeed, God himself. For one who renders such due reverences ought to believe that through the spiritual or secular authorities established as intermediaries between himself and God, he may ascend, as it were by ordered steps, to the highest authority of all. For it is certain that in rendering honor to kings and the other authorities of this order, the King of kings and Lord of lords is honored; and in bishops and their superiors, the same one who is honored in kings, the Shepherd and Bishop of our souls. Yet in this matter one must take special care that the person approaching to render due honor does not approach falsely or deceitfully. [Col. 1034B] Care must likewise be taken lest the sweetness of empty glory caress those who receive it, or the swelling of pride exalt them. Otherwise each side would at once become the other’s prey and plunderers, spoil and robbers; together they would swallow and be swallowed, devour and be devoured, so that what is commanded to be done in God and for God would be shamelessly done against God. That foregoing praiseworthy practice would collapse from a praiseworthy, divinely ordered use into an execrable and disorderly abuse. I have known lords’ retainers to be their enemies: they have such access to lords like themselves, and the same offense makes those who render and receive such acts unworthy. I have known people who venerate lords in order to be put in authority by them; they approach lords more familiarly in order to become lords more quickly. They kiss the [Col. 1034C] hand in order to steal the mind; they kiss the foot in order to seize the judgment; they humbly lower their heads beneath others and make their faces and eyes keen, in order that they may steal and seize for themselves those very persons to whom they do these things. For I have known men whom common people call bishops, though the heavenly court does not know them, who smile, applaud, swell, and exalt themselves when they see such conduct. Hence, as their pride continually rises [Note: [Col. 1033] Ps. 73], and their iniquity issues from this fatness of crime, believing that through these services they are being made gods, “the mighty gods of the earth have been greatly exalted” [Note: [Col. 1033] Ps. 46]. If they were disciples of the Master who is meek and humble of heart, they would have learned to be humbled rather than proud at reverences offered them. For every superiority granted by God makes its possessor lesser [Col. 1034D] if it is usurped—a superiority which the highest power of all refused to usurp. He made himself a little lower than the angels [Note: [Col. 1033] Heb. 2]; emptied in the form of a servant and made man, he did not deny that a profane human being possessed authority over him, but affirmed that it was given him from above: “You would have no authority,” he says, “unless it had been given you from above” [Note: [Col. 1033] Ibid. 2].

## CHAPTER XVII

Therefore, setting aside those mentioned above who have already come into the depth of vices and despise [Note: [Col. 1033] Prov. 18], let the other great ones, whom God concerns, learn. Let them learn from the great humble One and from the least, most lowly One to make themselves [Col. 1035A] lowly among their inferiors and humble among the humble. For that great Lord, whose greatness has no end [Note: [Col. 1035] Ps. 144], in order that the inheritance might inherit authorities anew, became a little heir and did not differ from a servant, although he was Lord of all [Note: [Col. 1035] Gal. 4]. He did not differ from a servant by setting himself above him—he who perhaps differed from his servant by subjecting himself to him. “He was subject to them,” says the Evangelist [Note: [Col. 1035] Luke 2]. Who to whom? The Lord to servants, the greater to lesser persons, God to human beings; for he possessed humility in its perfection. Some possess sufficient humility, some abundant humility; he possessed perfect humility. Sufficient humility belongs to one who is subject to a superior and does not place himself above an equal; abundant humility, to one who is subject to an equal and does not place himself above an inferior. But he possessed perfect humility, who was set above no one and subjected himself to everyone. And [Col. 1035B] being thus humble, he taught others to be humble in this way: “Learn from me,” he says, “because I am meek and humble of heart” [Note: [Col. 1035] Matt. 11]. Therefore let kings and pontiffs learn from this most humble King and Pontiff to be humble. For any authority not founded in humility is neither king nor pontiff but tyrant. One devoid of humility denies his humanity and degenerates from God. One who is humble acknowledges his humanity and binds himself in covenant with God.

## CHAPTER XVIII

Humility is the safeguard of salvation, the ornament of faith, the propitiation for sins; it proves the righteous, strengthens the holy, and displays worshippers of God. Humility is the king’s breastplate, whose shield is patience. For humility preserves the inward parts, where human life resides. And if perhaps the shield of patience is pierced by the devil’s darts, the person at whom they are aimed escapes if the breastplate of humility is opposed. Humility not only keeps what is healthy safe, but strengthens the weak and restores what has been shattered. For it is accustomed to restore and mend what is broken down and badly torn, fully returning and healing what impatience takes away and wounds. God is angry with the king of the Ninevites [Note: [Col. 1035] Jonah 3], but he immediately forgets that he is king. He throws away the purple, lays aside the diadem, and becomes more devout than the rest, though he was more powerful than the rest. Accustomed to triumph over enemies with weapons of war, he learned to conquer God with the weapons of righteousness: them by strength, him by humility. Humble King David says humbly, “I have sinned,” and hears, “The Lord has taken away your sin” [Note: [Col. 1035] 2 Sam. 12]. Magdalene renders humble service, and God answers: “Her many sins are forgiven, because she loved much” [Note: [Col. 1035] Luke 22]. Peter, prince of the Apostles, who had denied [Col. 1035D] his master, weeps humbly and is mercifully looked upon by his master [Note: [Col. 1035] Matt. 26]. The thief humbly accuses himself and is promised: “Today you will be with me in Paradise” [Note: [Col. 1035] Luke 23].

## CHAPTER XIX

What evil does humility not remove? What good does it not confer? Humility offers the kingdom to the humble, which pride takes from the proud. God chose humble David and struck down proud Saul. The one whom the people had not recognized is approved; he who had reigned over the people is despised. The former is taken from behind ewes giving suck to the kingdom; the latter is sent from the kingdom to punishment. [Col. 1036A] David was humble before kingship and remained humble in kingship. He was a most powerful king, and all called him king and lord. He called himself dust, a flea, ashes, and a dead dog. He had subdued the territories of peoples to himself—but to whom did he ascribe it? To whom did he attribute it? Nothing to himself, all to God. “I have hoped in God,” he says, “who has subjected my people beneath me” [Note: [Col. 1035] Ps. 143]. And lest he seem proud because God had subjected the people to him, he immediately added: “Lord, what is man, that you have made yourself known to him? Man has become like vanity; his days pass like a shadow” [Note: [Col. 1035] Ibid.]. Let kings consider these royal words: humble and noble. The more humbly they are uttered, the more notably humility ennobles them. Let kings consider the words of a king; let pontiffs consider [Col. 1036B] the similar words of a pontiff, who, after saying that he had labored more than all the rest, immediately added, lest he appear to have attributed what he did to his own strength: “Yet not I, but the grace of God with me” [Note: [Col. 1035] 1 Cor. 15]. But what does he mean when he says, “Yet not I, but the grace of God with me”? How did not he himself act, but God’s grace with him? Or how did God’s grace act with him if he did not act? It is as though he said: “Not I, but I.” For because he was anticipated solely by God’s grace, he says, “Not I”; but because he followed God’s grace by cooperating with it, he could also say, “I.” That king had said: “Man has become like vanity” [Note: [Col. 1035] Ps. 143]. This pontiff says: “Every creature has been subjected to vanity” [Note: [Col. 1035] Rom. 8]; and likewise: “Every creature groans and labors in childbirth even now” [Note: [Col. 1035] Ibid.]. And lest pontifical rank [Col. 1036C] seem to preserve him exempt from this vanity, he adds: “And not only it, but we ourselves also, who have the firstfruits of the Spirit, groan within ourselves.” Thus anxious and groaning, and seeking release from this vanity, he bursts from groaning into a cry: “Wretched man that I am, who will deliver me from the body of this death?” [Note: [Col. 1035] Rom. 7]. Having experienced the one and only person willing and able to deliver him, secure concerning the crown of righteousness laid up for him, he answers himself: “The grace of God through Jesus Christ my Lord” [Note: [Col. 1035] Ibid.]. Let kings and pontiffs therefore imitate these two patrons of kings and pontiffs: kings, the king, so that the broader the realms subjected to them, the more they are enlarged from day to day, and the more honor is bestowed upon them, the humbler they become and the more they give thanks to the giver. To the giver, I say, not the speaker: to the giver [Col. 1036D] who gave, so that they may thereby humble themselves more, not to the speaker who speaks, so that they may thereby boast more. For when gifts increase, one should not so much rejoice as fear concerning the reckoning for the gifts. Thus kings ought to rejoice with the aforesaid king in such a way that they fear. He who provides grounds for kings to rejoice also provides grounds for kings to tremble. For he is the one through whom kings reign [Note: [Col. 1035] Prov. 8]. He is the one who gives salvation to kings [Note: [Col. 1035] Ps. 143]. He is the one who subjects peoples to them; he is the same one who takes away the spirit of princes, terrible among all the kings of the earth [Note: [Col. 1035] Ps. 75]. He is the one [Col. 1037A] who makes the mighty suffer mighty torments [Note: [Col. 1037] Wis. 6]. Therefore it is worthwhile that, when kings bring a kingdom under their rule or triumph over enemies, they should feel themselves to be human beings, though human beings regard them as kings. Let them remember with the most faithful centurion that they are persons placed under authority who have soldiers under them [Note: [Col. 1037] Luke 7]; and let them frequently—indeed always—say with the most holy king: “What shall we render to the Lord for all that he has rendered to us?” [Note: [Col. 1037] Ps. 115].

## CHAPTER XX

Let pontiffs also imitate that pontiff who called himself one untimely born and the least of the Apostles. Thus, when they receive the reverences already mentioned, hear greetings in the marketplace, are called Rabbi by people, and have the first reclining places at banquets prepared for them, let them not rejoice in these things, [Col. 1037B] nor be exalted, nor on that account broaden their phylacteries or magnify their fringes [Note: [Col. 1037] Matt. 23]. Rather, in hearing, seeing, and receiving these things, let them fear, tremble, and be afraid more and more. Let them reckon all these things as pains, not pleasures; as poverty, not riches. In all these things, let them see burdens, not honors. For what is more ruinous to a righteous person than wishing to appear righteous, becoming cheerful and exultant at greetings in the marketplace, and being caressed by the favor of flattery? In such matters, a human being denying that he is human measures and misrepresents himself as equal to the heavenly beings. He measures himself equal to the heavenly beings when he supposes himself the maker of the few good things which he scarcely administers; and, seeking praise for them, he forgets the author of all good things, whose grace has heaped up for him titles that ought to be proclaimed. This belongs to his [Col. 1037C] pride. For after the faithful soul, rising out of the abyss of vices, has ascended to the saving summit of virtues, pride leaps out as though from an ambush and meets it; it shakes the whole building of the house of the Lord and crushes it into ruin, though it had already risen toward completion. But the two aforementioned king and pontiff did not seek empty reverences of this sort—indeed, huntings; nor did they wish to usurp glory even from good things. I recall the words of the most holy king and hear the humble king saying to the highest King: “Not to us, O Lord, not to us, but give glory to your name” [Note: [Col. 1037] Ps. 113]. I turn over the writings of the holy pontiff and find it written: “By the grace of God I am what I am” [Note: [Col. 1037] 1 Cor. 15].

## CHAPTER XXI

A moment ago my discourse was addressed to pontiffs who are [Col. 1037D] ... But discourse runs swiftly from others to others. Therefore let the pontiffs mentioned say what glory, this glory, is. For if they are such as their domestic enemies proclaim them to be, what grounds have they for glory in themselves rather than in the Lord? What do they perceive in themselves, from themselves, as commendable? What have they that they did not receive? Why do they glory as though they had not received it [Note: [Col. 1037] 1 Cor. 4]? Why do they not fear to hear: “You seek glory from one another, and do not desire the glory that is from God alone” [Note: [Col. 1037] John 5]? Or rather: “You have received your reward” [Note: [Col. 1037] Matt. 5]. Or, while they linger so long with those selling oil, do they not fear the bridegroom’s heart may be shut to them [Note: [Col. 1037] Matt. 25]? I believe they do not trust [Col. 1038A] their conscience, to which they entrust no good thing, which they empty of every good thing, whose treasure they expose to pirates and public robbers. They would not care to shine by public acclaim if they were content with the testimony of their own conscience, as he was content who said: “This is our glory: the testimony of our conscience” [Note: [Col. 1037] 2 Cor. 1]. But no good remains in a conscience of this kind. If they have perhaps conceived anything there, their souls, bringing forth violently, are compelled to give birth to an abortion; tongues that bind them in the sins of flatterers extinguish and reduce to ashes what the righteous person had begun to make shine like a spark.

## CHAPTER XXII

But if they do not perceive in themselves the good things which they hear proclaimed about them, why do they, more wretched than miserable tongues, offer their miserable ears to those tongues? Alas, alas! [Col. 1038B] While they glory wickedly and presume to be what they are not, they are cast down in confusion and lose what they are. O blind prudence of human beings! O foolish wisdom! With great care they guard against thieves, lest one sheep be stolen from them; with greater care, lest an ox be stolen; with least or no care, lest their mind be stolen. They carefully guard against those who steal human possessions, not against those who steal the masters of possessions—human beings. They guard their wealth, but neglect to guard their understanding. They are greedy in wealth, prodigal in understanding, generous in neither. They guard their things from thieves; they expose themselves to thieves. How much more precious is gold than an ear! Gold is guarded from thieves; an ear is exposed to thieves. What is more precious in a human being than the mind? What is more worthless in a human being than a lie? A lie [Col. 1038C] is heard, and the mind is bought by a lie. O, if things may be called so, what a commerce of unequal things! Here something so dear is purchased so cheaply; here what is most precious in the world, the best thing among things, is so foolishly bought with what is most contemptible in the world, what is not a thing—indeed, what is nothing. What is the mind? What is a lie? The mind is something holy, something most pure; a lie is something most filthy. The mind is something great; a lie is a great nothing. Of every sin, nothing is more nothing than a lie. O unhappy merchants of this kind, who sell themselves and receive nothing itself as the price of themselves! They read, but disregard, that the children of men are vain in the balances, so that they may deceive together from vanity [Note: [Col. 1037] Ps. 61]. [Col. 1038D] They read but do not understand that those who call blessed persons blessed are led into error. “There shall be those who deceive by pronouncing others blessed, and those pronounced blessed who are cast down headlong,” he says [Note: [Col. 1037] Isa. 9]. If they understood this rightly, they would not choose such people, but would drive them away and flee from them. The King of kings and prophets arms his king and prophet to drive them far away from himself. First he asks him what weapons avail against persons of this kind: “What shall be given to you, or what shall be added to you, against a deceitful tongue?” [Note: [Col. 1037] Ps. 119]. Then he instructs and equips him: “The sharp arrows of the mighty, with desolating coals” [Note: [Col. 1037] Ibid.]. He gives arrows and adds coals: arrows [Col. 1039A] for defense and flight, coals for consolation. The arrows of the Mighty are the Savior’s words, which inflict a wound not of resentment but of love, and overcome the tongues of flatterers, if desolating coals are added—that is, the examples of saints converted from iniquity. They are rightly called coals because they revive from the dead and, applied to others, set others on fire; and “desolating” because, while consoling the spirit, they lay waste fleshly affections. Thereafter, fortified by the arrows of divine utterances and the patterns of the saints, the prophet who had mourned became joyful, and he who had been afraid became confident. For he was afraid concerning the Almighty’s secrets, whereas Belial’s envoys do not fear [Note: [Col. 1039] 2 Sam. 32]. He guarded against those against whom they themselves do not guard—though they rejoice with vehement joy whenever they find them [Col. 1039B] to be a tomb for themselves.

## CHAPTER XXIII
Pharaoh’s heart was hardened; but these men are more hardened than Pharaoh. How Pharaoh had endured the seven preceding plagues, yet could not endure the succeeding eighth plague of locusts. “A scorching wind,” it says, “carried up the locusts, and they covered the whole face of the land and devoured every herb, and whatever fruit was on the trees” [Note: [Col. 1039] Exod. 10]. Roused by this, Pharaoh no longer sat still, but hastily rose and cried out to Moses and Aaron. What did he understand by the locusts, which have no leader, except flatterers, who neither respect man nor fear God? What then? As they approach, the grass is devoured [Col. 1040A], because they destroy by their words the words of those whose supporters they are; and they devour the fruits of the trees when they enfeeble even the deeds of those who seem strongest.

At this sudden sight Pharaoh was immediately roused: he no longer sits, but rises in haste. What was visible, terrible though it was, frightened Pharaoh; what was understood, more terrible still, does not frighten these men. The image of a future plague frightened him; the plague itself, fulfilling what had been foretold, does not frighten them. He feared the wind threatening from afar; they do not fear the hailstorm, they do not fear it when it kills the tender crops of minds, they do not fear the strokes of lightning as they strike. He feared an arrow still hidden in the quiver; they do not fear it when it leaps from the bow. “He no longer sat,” it says, “but Pharaoh rose in haste and cried to Moses and Aaron: ‘I have sinned against the Lord your God and against you’” [Col. 1040B; Note: [Col. 1039] Ibid.]. When will our Pharaohs say, “We have sinned”? Their every business is commonly fashioned, before it is done, by the deceitful pre-chewing of persons so honourable, so suitable, as they are so often called. When will they say, “We have sinned”—they who have entrusted the government of greater churches to their own Parmenios with keys; and have made themselves glorious Thrasos by means of them? For such men, the more fraudulent one is than another, the more criminal he is thought by prelates to be, the higher places they grant him in the greater churches; and the lesser place in office is held by him who is heard to be the lesser in crime.

[Col. 1039] HERE ENDS THE THIRD PART.

HERE BEGIN THE CHAPTERS OF THE FOURTH AND FINAL PART.

[Col. 1039]

[Col. 1039C] CHAPTER 1. That their being examined for three days by archdeacons neither harms nor benefits them. 2. That those who do not come with empty hands do not depart empty from ordination. 3. That those who come in this manner come confidently. 4. Who answers at the altar for such a man, and what is imposed upon him. 5. That a church is entrusted to him by the same law under which he was ordained. 6. That those unjust in every other respect are equitable only in iniquity. 7. What Simon’s decrees are. 8. That they hear and smell from afar those who possess such things. 9. That he has so far described what they are and what they possess, not what kind of men they reject. [Col. 1040C] 10. That in these things they understand nothing except the oppression of the people of the children of Israel. 11. That the cry of the Church is still extended, on behalf of the king and of her children. 12. That the King of kings entered the Temple twice, not without cause. 13. Nor, without cause, did he hastily drive out those who sold and bought. 14. That the king ought not to endure so great an injury to the Church. 15. What the writer’s intention concerning these matters is; and that he has written only from charity, and said less than he ought. 16. Another reason: that he wrote not from hatred, and that the work ought neither to be burned nor considered excessively long.

## FOURTH PART

[Col. 1039]

## CHAPTER I

[Col. 1039D]

I can scarcely say without shame what sort of men are introduced into lesser churches. Men are sought, as is fitting, who are worthy; but there is one thing that makes them worthy: the worthiness of possessing. Only those who possess are judged worthy, in the eyes of the bishops mentioned, of orders and of churches. [Col. 1040D] Before the celebration of ordinations, it is customary to make an examination from Wednesday onward, canonically appointed, through letters, so that it may be apparent who are worthy to be ordained. Now we see something done much more worthily: throughout the whole year tireless examiners do not cease to examine those who are worthy [Col. 1041A]. But books are not turned over for examining these men, but scales. The question is not how much they have read, but how much they have collected; not how much they have learned, but how much they have given. The question is not what they know, but what they possess; not what they possess in the soul, but what they possess in the chest; not what they possess in the mind, but what they possess in the granary. For with such examiners storehouses more readily obtain their requests than libraries; the support and gifts of the cellarer rather than the goods of the sacristy. No concern is shown whether they approach honourably, but how heavily laden they are.

Honours themselves raise up those who are laden—provided that they have first been relieved of their precious burdens, lest the weightiness of honour find them burdened by another load and compel them, pressed under a double weight, to go headlong downward. No concern is shown about parents or lineage, provided that they possess. [Col. 1041B] For possessions, possessed equally by all, make all equally noble and permit none of their household to live in degeneration. Courtly decurions often murmur against those to be ordained; but in the end all murmuring ceases. In short, everything is pacified, everything restored, from the sole of the foot to the crown of the head; the whole court is calmed: the holy Fathers by marks, the Fathers’ nephews by pounds, counsellors by solidi, doorkeepers by gifts. Nor are geese and fattened fowl, meat, fish, and birds of diverse kinds lacking, so that the hungry greed of both belly and purse may be satisfied.

## CHAPTER II

If, after being thus examined throughout the entire year by the Fathers—or rather, anti-fathers—they are again examined for the preceding three days by archdeacons, it neither [Col. 1041C] harms nor benefits. For the very archdeacons conducting the examination are astonished that those whom the book condemns are approved, and those whom it approves are rejected. If they venture, being doubtful about this, to ask why, they hear this answer: “It is not for you to know the times which the Fathers have placed in their own power.” Unless, that is, the archdeacons are themselves also nephews; unless they belong to those fortunate men whom blood or flattery makes Nazarites among the purple-robed choirs of courtiers, and to whom it has been given to know the mysteries of this kingdom of the world. For to the rest everything is done in parables.

## CHAPTER III

Thus, examined throughout the whole year, and most perfectly approved by men perfectly approved, they approach the bishops for ordination confidently four times a year, according to the fourfold succession of the Ember seasons. If they honour the Fathers lavishly with things appropriate to each season, the Fathers rise to greet them as they arrive and congratulate those who approach. In this fashion they embrace and kiss their sons. The book, in which nothing difficult for these men is written, receives them closed. And, because of their service through the fourfold season, they are found to have read the whole quadrivium and retained it by heart. Since whatever gifts they offer that are fitting for bishops come from the three lower elements, they are found, because of this threefold variety, to have learned the trivium perfectly.

For these bishops have no concern for the goods of the higher element. Heavenly good is not devoured by the belly, enclosed by the purse, or imprisoned in a chest. [Col. 1042A] They despise and abhor that good itself, being devoted to ease, luxury, and sleep—something scarcely attained by the sober except through labour. Their delicate nature, the Lord’s nature, denies labour to these masters; for whom even the fear of falling ill is itself an incurable disease. “For,” they say, “that is not good which is wholesome for no one; nor is that wholesome which harms breast or head.” Excessive meditation on invisible goods is highly harmful to them. For continual contemplation dries the breast, tears the mind, befools the brain, and emaciates the whole human being. Unless physicians offer help at the first onset of this fever, consumption is easily contracted.

Or, if a person is stout and seems to have escaped consumption, he must no less beware of prayers and vigils. For the excessive thirst contracted by these practices, since it cannot be quenched by superfluous and immoderate drinking, produces swelling, bloating, thirsty dropsy. From this they infer that contemplation with labour is not good, whereas their accustomed activity gives them pleasant rest without labour. Let us therefore seek goods that nourish, not goods that destroy what has been nourished. On hearing this, those who are to be ordained come confidently. Before they are ordained, men assure them so completely about the future on the basis of the past that others who know the matter call them ordained even before their ordination; and, on account of the various services of the three or four persons mentioned, call them thrice and four times blessed.

If, after being examined in the matters described above, they wish to be further examined in other matters, so that their distinguished wisdom may be more plainly displayed, let them show themselves learned in buying things for sale [Col. 1042C] and reselling what has been bought, and in returning profit multiplied by whatever means to their lord. Once this is done, because of their twofold knowledge of trade, they are found not only learned but teachers in both Testaments. Their lord praises them abundantly; the whole court pronounces them blessed; the rest judge them by the words: “These are they who bring forth from their treasures things new and old.”

As for the matters commonly investigated before ordination—namely, the character and life of those to be ordained, and whether they were legitimately born—the most prudent dispensation advises that nothing further be asked. For there is no need to ask concerning marriage where such perfection of learning prevails. Character and life are not investigated, since they are not doubted to conform to wisdom. For if perversity of life or character were attributed to these men, their wisdom would plainly appear either dull or feeble, or wholly nonexistent.

## CHAPTER IV

After this, nothing remains except entering the church. There many questions are asked, but answers are at hand. When the bishop asks whether the approaching man wishes to be ordained, money replies: “I do.” When he asks whether he is worthy, silver answers: “Worthy.” When he asks whether he is just, gold murmurs: “Most just.” Having heard this, the Father weeps, kisses his son, and blesses him, saying: “May God give you abundance from the richness of the earth—of grain, wine, and oil—and may peoples serve you.” The dew of heaven [Note: [Col. 1041] Gen. 27] is passed over, because their belly does not seek heavenly dew.

Then, although he is learned in his own right, the bishop’s authority nevertheless reminds him of certain things from the Law and the Prophets that he must keep in memory. He says: “Son, remember us in your favour, and visit us” [Col. 1043A; Note: [Col. 1043] Ps. 105]. Again: “Come, make haste, and do not delay.” And that line from the song of love: “Return, return, that we may look upon you” [Note: [Col. 1043] Song 6]. Finally, among other matters that he desires to entrust to his most retentive memory, he pours this final precept of the Law into his ears: “You shall not appear empty before the presence of your Lord” [Note: [Col. 1043] Exod. 2]. At last this most holy son withdraws, most holily cursed by his most holy father.

## CHAPTER V

Once, then, the reverent celebration of his ministry has been irreverently performed, he perhaps sees near at hand a simple or decrepit man, whose displacement from his church is the one concern both of himself [Col. 1043B] and of his relatives. Having conceived this crime, he hastens back with his friends to the bishop, so that they may together pour into the shepherd’s bosom the poisonous offspring with which they have together become pregnant. When the man has been entirely despoiled alike of possessions and of understanding, the ecclesiastical priest returns under the same canon under which he had been ordained.

For this Rule is kept by these bishops with such strictness that, if they recall ever having distinguished themselves by failing to exact the revenues of simony, they believe that they have sinned more unforgivably than against the Holy Spirit. Unless from day to day they advance by acting in their accustomed manner more deceitfully and dishonourably, they fear incurring a crime of virtue—something hateful to them above all things. Hence, if scarcity and a shortage of purchasers at some time force them to act against the majesty of Simony, heralds are scattered far and wide who never cease crying day and night: “The harvest indeed is plentiful, but the labourers are few” [Col. 1043C; Note: [Col. 1043] Matt. 9]. “All who thirst, come; and you who have silver, hurry and buy. Come,” they say, “confidently; for to everyone who has, more shall be given, and from him who does not have, it shall be taken away” [Note: [Col. 1043] Matt. 13]. Therefore those who possess are compelled to come from far away, while the local men who possess nothing are cast out and banished.

## CHAPTER VI

And so that amount may answer amount with exact justice, more secret scales are prepared in chambers to weigh gifts arriving from afar: so that the man who gives more gold may receive more God, and he who bestows more money may receive more grace, without fraud. For fraud itself causes the whole affair in such cases to proceed without fraud: since, by conducting everything fraudulently, one proceeds rightly only along the path of fraud, and in no respect departs from fraud. Thus the travellers on this road fear only this error of deviation: that, whenever they carry out the business of deceit and the force of falsehood, they may be deceived by the seduction of some virtue and turn from deceit to truth, from the crooked way to the straight. Never to depart from their own way is never to return to the way.

They would indeed deviate far too much from their road if those who confidently entrusted their gold to the just scales of bishops did not receive the equivalent in accordance with the price and value of weighed silver. Accordingly, they are looked after carefully, and they take care with circumspection, so that exchange [Col. 1044A] may suffer no fraud in the business of fraud; but that the entire commerce of both parties may conform mutually and equally to equity alone. In this deed it is wonderfully seen that men who are unjust in every matter are found most equitable in iniquity alone. We believe that they devote such effort to this most wicked equity that they obey their master Simon’s commands in all things and through all things. For in the decrees of Simon the covetous they read that to one who gives many carnal things, many spiritual things must be given.

## CHAPTER VII

“He who gives Simon many marks of gold or silver,” it says, “deserves to have many churches of great name. He who gives precious stones must be regarded as precious above the peoples. For him who gives many pounds of solidi, pounds will be weighed out from this solid church. He who gives many mares receives a suitable—not equal—gift. He who gives many cows will not be idle, but will possess many souls. He who gives many sheep will triumph, having become shepherd of many spiritual sheep.”

The bishops mentioned take such care not to violate these and similar decrees that they would consider it a lighter thing to be drowned in the depths of the sea with a millstone tied round their neck [Col. 1044B; Note: [Col. 1043] Matt. 18] than that one iota or one stroke should perish from these and similar assertions of their master Simon. Yet my tears have made so many and such great blots in my writing over these jokes that the page itself, which I wrote with my own hands, almost obliterated, bears witness. I know, and it does not escape me, that I shall appear to have written these and other matters of this kind, according to my habit, in jest. For, seeing—as the Apostle says—a time for laughing and a time for weeping [Note: [Col. 1043] Eccl. 3], a time for entreating [Col. 1044C], rebuking, and insisting in season and out of season [Note: [Col. 1043] II Tim. 4], I recall that I often inserted, after harsh rebukes, exhortations that were at once light and mournful in many places in this work.

It was fitting also that I should use the words of one playing, since I have, so far as I could, filled in the sequence here narrated the place of the Church both weeping and laughing, and shall preserve the same manner in what remains to be narrated. For Jerusalem which is above, our free mother, mourns continually here with her aforesaid sons, whom simple people call bishops: an exile and anxious woman. Yet she likewise mocks them from above—where raging folly has no right to aspire—because here below they are more devoutly occupied with trifles. For the heavenly court judges worthy of mockery those whom avarice, worshipping idols, has long bowed down; whom it long ago compelled to play before its own carved images; whose new moons it hates; and in whom it has no hope of sin being propitiated, since its very propitiation is turned for them into guilt.

For this reason the aforesaid unworthy Fathers are mocked, as they deserve to be, by sons who would be worthy if they had Fathers. For this reason too I recall that I have often interrupted grief with necessary play. I knew that a teaching was not useless in which play interrupts grief and grief interrupts play. For, while these two things alternately guard one another, grief in grief permits no opening through which lying hypocrisy may creep in; nor does play, restrained by grief, permit licentious joy, or exclude truth. Nor do I suppose that joy is either licentious or foolish when it occurs in playful syllables where the majesty and reverence of truth are preserved intact [Col. 1045A].

What truths, and how beautiful they are, lie hidden beneath the jest throughout this work wherever jesting has been commanded, I leave for ingenious readers to unfold. That they may understand the truth with me and examine it once understood; that the sluggish may be aroused and the studious exercised, I assign them continual labour. For I am compelled to pass over these matters and proceed to what the aforesaid bishops do according to the tenor of their master’s commands previously described—commands of which they are either no transgressors at all, or only slight ones.

## CHAPTER VIII

The bishops have ears for hearing and nostrils for smelling: from afar they detect those whose storehouses are full, whose sheep are fertile, and whose oxen fat [Note: [Col. 1045] Ps. 143]. Though they find many sons or daughters in their houses [Col. 1045B], well formed and like a temple adorned, they do not mock or recoil; rather, they bless the people to whom these things belong, and judge us alone worthy to serve at the altar. Yet they do not judge until secure concerning the price. No one is given permission to enter until, all his wealth having been rendered to the bishop, the animal stalls stand empty. The homes of the lords remain empty of much and varied household equipment. Their storehouses no longer pour forth from one abundance into another as before. All these things intercede for their masters with the bishops. Because they make continual intercession, no tracks are open for return.

Yet their masters are not defrauded of their desired reward: once these possessions have been worthily received, the Church receives the masters worthily. These holy anti-fathers say that such men celebrate worthily in the house [Col. 1045C] of God and sing worthily and clearly; though to me they seem rather to bellow. For although outwardly they modulate the sweet voice of a song through a human mouth, inwardly grinding with an animal mouth, men who are animals bellow more madly than any bull.

## CHAPTER IX

Behold what they are, and what sort of people they possess. But what is more grievous is what kind of men they reject—those whom they do not wish either to see or to be seen by. No prudent person, I think, can be unaware that, just as they choose the men described above as wholly like themselves, so they neglect in a different manner men unlike both them and those men. In the former nothing pleases them except evils; in the latter, only good things fail to please them—indeed, they displease them. In those men they take pleasure in uncultivated incompetence, foolish simplicity, dull ignorance, stubborn perversity, useless concerns, unlawful desires, sacrilegious habits or errors [Col. 1045D], vain fear, harmful love, shameful joys, ruined faith, abandoned hope, neglected charity, rejected understanding, and captive will.

All these together the prince of this world has made his kingdom; the armed strong man, his courtyard; the father of darkness, his dark dwelling. If perhaps there are a few in whom they see goods opposed to the evils they have named—whose days are sober, nights chaste, vigils holy, sleep pure, actions upright, conduct honourable, and life consistent with itself in every respect; whose life is precious in itself and fruitful in others; which, by helping, drives away sickness, lethargy, error, and weakness of spirit; by exhorting, negligence; by teaching, ignorance—if, I say, they find such men, they make them as few as possible [Col. 1046A] and annihilate them. They reject the honourable, dishonour the upright, drive away the simple, flee the prudent, embitter the gentle, and persecute the humble.

If one asks what crime they find that causes them to avenge themselves with such hostility upon the innocent, the answer is this: honourable conduct is nevertheless found in them, and found detestably. Nor is this surprising: from the first day until today, innocence provokes the envy it suffers, and holy life incites rivals against itself. When they hear of others’ illnesses, they waste away within themselves; when they hear of others’ good conduct, they burn with fever. Another’s wisdom is to them another kind of paralysis; and knowledge that helps others harms these men when possessed by someone else—not only in its possession by the possessor, but even when heard of by those who do not possess it. For because of the wise whom they hate, even the false [Col. 1046B] title and reputation of “wise” displeases them in others.

If anyone devotes himself more freely and readily to prayer, withdraws his hand from worldly things, and recalls his mind, they judge him excessively simple and an ignoramus. If anyone keeps watch over books, applies himself to reading, and listens to wise people, they call him sluggish and inept, pursuing foolishness and idleness, inferior to others through weakness of heart. Those who discuss and investigate together so that truth may shine out in doubtful matters, they call verbose and chattering, and attribute all their reasoning to frenzy or melancholy—though they themselves ought rather to lament, weakened by the disease of sins and afflicted by the frenzy of crimes. They call observers of the commandments and avengers of vices demoniacs, and proclaim through the streets that they must be avoided.

## CHAPTER X

[Col. 1046C]

What are we to perceive in these matters except the oppression of the children of Israel, while Joseph is unknown, lest they should perhaps multiply? Do they not set taskmasters over them, who afflict them with the harsh labour of mud and brick, when they subject them to be trampled under their own vainglories, lies, and parasites? These are their helpers, more prudent in their generation than the children of light, who never cease through continual plundering to increase their own rapacious greed and that of their masters. They lie in wait in order to seize; they seize in order to devour; and, having seized, they are tortured by a stronger hunger. Riches abound for both them and their masters, yet they are tormented by want. Poverty empties their purses, hunger has exhausted their granaries, thirst drains their storehouses. No book is read by them except the book of extortion, which they turn over a thousand times a day.

While they plunder on every side, Pharaoh is enriched and walks adorned with a diadem; but Israel, burdened with a basket, crushed by the load, deprived of honour, wearied by labour, afflicted by miseries, and harassed by injuries, groans, mourns, beats upon heaven with cries, moistens with tears the feet of the Father of orphans [Col. 1046D], and cries, groans, and sighs also to its protector, the king of England, duke of Aquitaine, that he may be pleased to behold the affliction of his Church, harshly oppressed by Egyptians.

It cries for itself; it cries for its children—indeed, many churches cry out, over which fraud rules and deceit holds sway. The Church cries for her children, for whom she is compelled to deny milk as infants and bread as adults. The mother is astonished that she cherishes in her bosom stepsons whom she hates; but she is more astonished that she acts as a stepmother to her beloved children, serving strangers instead of her own, enemies instead of friends, parricides instead of fathers, adulterers instead of spouses, Simon Magus instead of Simon Peter, and Mammon and the devil instead of God. The bride grieves when she sees [Col. 1047A] her necklaces, by which she once pleased her heavenly bridegroom, polluted by the snouts of swine.

She dwells amid ruins, where, through manifold and open damage from collapses, there remains a trace of the Judge’s lofty spiritual hall and an image of the royal house. She is exiled with her children within her own walls. Hence, with one sigh of many, one lamentation of the grieving, one tear for herself and her children, she asks counsel and implores help from the king given her by God—help from one who is powerful, counsel from one who is wise. May the house of God move the king; may he set himself as a wall for the house of Israel, which the exalted King, the humble King, chose for himself as a temple [Col. 1047B]—in which he was born a man, and which the Most High King himself founded [Note: [Col. 1047] Ps. 83].

In this house there is poor and rich; in it he who is a traveller labours, and he who is a resident rests; in it he himself seeks temporal provision for the journey and bestows eternal bread; he journeys and he reigns. But where he journeys, he requests help from kings; where he reigns, he grants kings wondrous rewards. May the king be pleased to look upon the house of the great King—yet to see it ashamed, to see it afraid. Why should it not be ashamed? Why should it not fear? The house of prayer is ashamed to have become a den of robbers [Note: [Col. 1047] Jer. 7; Matt. 21]. It is ashamed because its princes have become companions of thieves, loving gifts and pursuing rewards [Note: [Col. 1047] Isa. 1]. It fears, because it is not secure even from its own people. [Col. 1047C] The men of its peace, who eat its bread, magnify their treacherous attack against it. It fears and grieves because it feels itself harmed and violated by those entering by another way, not through the door. But it fears still more because, unless help comes soon, it sees total overthrow near at hand.

## CHAPTER XI

May the King therefore be pleased to help the queen, the bride of the supreme King. May he be pleased to examine diligently what manner of men preside over, rule, and administer the churches in Aquitaine under the Fathers mentioned above, and what manner of men there beg and live in exile. May the duke and ruler given by God deign to do so—not only for the rest, but also for the clergy. Then may the aforesaid king of the aforesaid nation deign to summon the clergy before his presence; let him see, question, and hear them himself as they stand before him. Then [Col. 1047D] my lord king will believe his own eyes and ears; he will believe himself, not me, a contemptible man who entreats and supplicates from afar.

I plead more for others than for myself: for me, exile provides riches and banishment furnishes delights; for me, pilgrimage is happy, residence fruitful, forgetfulness of former happiness happy, austerity gentle, cruelty mild, bitterness sweet, and the change from the land of my fathers pleasing. Cheerful grace has given Transalpine Italy to me as a companion:

> There I pleased all, and all pleased me.  
> The Italian laughed, the Apulian applauded,  
> the Sicilian complied, and the Roman increased my honours.

I therefore plead for the others, whom a homeland sweet in itself but bitter in its Fathers compels to live in exile among themselves [Col. 1048A], not for myself, who live happily in exile. May the king be moved by the miserable tears of compassion, the lamentation of innocence, the suffering of charity, the groans of humility, the cries of justice, the silences of kindness, the wounds of patience, the fellow-feeling of charity, the sighs of prudence, the scandals suffered by simplicity, the violence done to modesty, and the injuries to integrity.

May he be pleased to see how great is the multitude in those regions of upright and honourable persons, of prudent and simple life and excellent conduct, whose virtue silently grows old because it lacks material for action. Under the Fathers often mentioned, mother Church neither dares nor has the power to provide for them. Then he himself will know for what honourable uses—or rather, for what wretched and profane abuses—all ecclesiastical goods are, alas, expended together [Col. 1048B], reduced to smoke and ashes, and utterly consumed. When he has seen, known, and certainly learned this, the king himself will know, consider, undertake, and accomplish what he will thereafter do, what he ought to do in these matters. He will take counsel for his own sake and that of his people; he will consult his people and himself.

## CHAPTER XII

Yet one thing I know—and I say it without prejudging the matter: that great King, most powerful of all kings, who entrusted to his kings the execution of his offices and rights, entered this Temple twice in order to drive out buyers and sellers, and twice drove out those who were to be expelled. In this action, not only the expulsion but the manner of expulsion must be considered. I have read the Gospel which teaches that buyers and sellers were driven from the Temple [Col. 1048C] both by word and by lash [Note: [Col. 1047] John 2]. I have read the Gospel which relates the expulsion and is silent about the lashes [Note: [Col. 1047] Matt. 21]. I believe this was done not by chance but by deliberate providence.

For that King, whose actions are instructions for royal life, while he was still seen on earth and still conversed with men [Note: [Col. 1047] Baruch 3], since he was both king and priest, taught his later kings and priests through this action what they should do, and gave them courage to do the same. He entered the Temple; he entered once; he entered again. The king entered; the priest entered. The king drove out those to be expelled; the priest drove out those to be expelled. He drove them out with the king’s sword; he drove them out with the priest’s sword. He drove them out with tongue; he drove them out with hand; with word; with lash.

That one man exercised both swords when he pleased. So long as he pleased, he kept both hidden; for a time he humbly concealed both in the sheath of humility; at the fitting place and time he wondrously drew both from their sheaths. With both he armed his co-heirs, kings and priests: with one, kings; with the other, priests. He did not will that they should always be held in their sheaths, but that they should be drawn, in their proper place and time, as persons and causes required. He willed them to be drawn so that the ignorant might be instructed, the weak sustained, rebels struck, and the proud repelled.

He alone armed himself with both swords; he alone, I believe, drew both swords from their sheaths: he alone fights the battles of God and men, battles hell, and triumphs over demons. When both were mentioned, they said: “Lord, behold, here are two swords” [Note: [Col. 1047] Luke 22]. [Col. 1049A] And he answered: “It is enough” [Note: [Col. 1049] Luke 22]. For two were enough for the head, and two likewise suffice for the members. In God’s house the authority of the royal court and the strictness of pontifical discipline are sufficient.

## CHAPTER XIII

Nor do I believe it meaningless that the universal King had often entered the Temple, where he perhaps found many fornicators, adulterers, and murderers, whom he endured in the Temple for a time, but hastily drove out those who bought and sold [Note: [Col. 1049] John 2]. Other sinners must be gently warned and patiently awaited; finally, they must be removed only by their own bishops or vicars, so that their spirits may be saved. But sellers and buyers of doves—that is, of spiritual graces—wherever they are first found in the Temple by any king or bishop, must without delay be driven out and expelled by tongue and hand, words and lashes [Col. 1049B].

How vigorously the Lord, mighty and powerful, expelled them was shown when, having driven out buyers and sellers, he drove out the sheep and oxen, poured out the money-changers’ coins, overturned the chairs and tables of the sellers, and said to those selling doves: “Take these things away from here, and do not make my Father’s house a house of trade” [Note: [Col. 1049] Ibid.].

## CHAPTER XIV

What more shall I say? What further shall I recount? If bishops indulge the vices of bishops, if they cloak what they have indulged, if they hide crimes crying to heaven; if the lights of the world hide their eyes from seeing known crimes and peer with little eyes; if noble physicians pass by with half-deaf ears the wounds they hear reported in the illustrious and chosen race [Col. 1049C], will whoever sees dissemble, and will whoever hears be a deaf hearer? If the clergy is afflicted by superficial clergy, will there be no one to help the clergy? Will there be no hearer for the fatherless orphan? If one sword is blunt, will both be blunt? If the bishop’s sword now fails, will the king’s sword fail too—especially in this time, when bad fish break Peter’s net; when schisms rend the unity of the Church; when Roman covetousness and ambition have set Dagon beside the ark of the Lord and raised altar against altar? At such a time, sufficient unto which is its own evil [Note: [Col. 1049] Matt. 6], will the king of England, ruler of Aquitaine, slumber or sleep? Far be it!

## CHAPTER XV

I wish my entire intention in these matters to be plain; I shall not conceal it. Would that there were someone to free the house of God, someone who would with strong hand drive out all buyers and sellers [Col. 1049D]! Would that there were someone who would lay hands not upon bishops but upon Simoniacs; not upon the household of faith but the household of perfidy; not upon lawgivers or clergy, but upon corrupters of the clergy! And let not my lord king believe anyone who whispers this to him, anyone who lies to his mind, that I have written these things against bishops either in anger or in hatred. For there is no bishop in the world whose man, subject, and servant I am not; and, unless it is presumptuous to call myself a friend, whose faithful friend I am.

I am a friend of prelates, not of the exalted; of bishops, not “wealth-bishops” (*opiscopi*); not of those who look toward riches, but of those who look upward. Even in what I have thus far composed, not against the majesty of pastors but against the heresy of Simoniacs, according to the weakness of my exceedingly slight understanding, I know that I have sinned by saying not too much, but less than I ought [Col. 1050A]. Nor do I remember having said in the foregoing about Simony what even one woman might have said, had she known how to say it.
