For even an old woman may accuse men, however exalted, of Simony known to her; since in this one crime alone holy decrees aid and strengthen the accusation of the weaker sex, so that, although the weak party of accusers cannot convict the accused, the accused are nevertheless bound canonically to clear themselves.

## CHAPTER XVI
I likewise neither hate, nor ought to hate, the persons just named, concerning whom this seems to be said. For, though I might have been richer, they did not bestow; though I might have been poorer, [Col. 1050B] they did not impose. And if perhaps I hated anything in them, it was with a perfect hatred: so that I hated not what they have become, but what they do. Hence I have grieved, and always grieve. But among the rest there is one grief, the accumulation of my griefs: that, as they are accustomed, I hear that they still give the children’s bread to dogs. When I see these and the other crimes of the said fathers, I grieve; for I can grieve over evils, but cannot grieve evil. Yet I shall do—and do—not what I wish, but what I can. I behold indeed the whole world, and it is full of flatterers. Many are in the world who corrupt; scarcely one who rebukes. Oil abounds everywhere, with which the heads of the healthy are made fat; wine is found almost nowhere, with which the wounds of the injured may be washed. I know what I must do; I have found what course I should take. Henceforth I shall begin to displease, that I may please one—[Col. 1050C] men and God. At least my rebuke against the pretenders shall not cease until the pretenders themselves cease to play the pretender. I have entreated once and rebuked repeatedly; rebuke shall now be made without entreaties. I have felt the rotten place; access to the living flesh lies open. I compiled a little book, but I have now conceived books. I finish a little book, but I now begin books. Either they will cease, or I shall not cease. This I can do; this is within my power. I can expose evils, not wipe them away; report them, not remove them; grieve over them, not destroy them. Let him who can remove and destroy them; let him who has power be willing; let the king hasten and perform deeds worthy of a prince. Let him see and judge, so that, when it is heard throughout the world that the king’s honour loves judgment, and that justice and judgment are the restoration of his thrones, they may glorify the King who is in heaven. Let [Col. 1050D] the poor see these things and rejoice. [Note: [Col. 1049] Psalm 68.] Let the king see, and consider what has been written to him, not who has written it to him. Nor should anyone tell the king that this work ought to be burned; rather, let him believe those worthy of burning who have said that it deserves to be burned. Nor, because brevity is usually a friend to kings, should this writing along with its writer therefore suffer one single charge of prolixity. For what has been begun concerning two and understood concerning many will make its very length useful to some; an attentive reader will nowhere accuse it of superfluity. Length also makes a letter defective, but a book is free from this defect. Here even that which appears to have overflowed beyond the subject-matter is without doubt a feature of God’s abundant generosity, which, by the bond of indissoluble harmony, [Col. 1051A] joins diverse things to one beginning. For she who produces many sources of silver from her veins has appointed one place for gold to be smelted; and from among sounding stones she rejoices to have sent forth one voice, she who even increases wonderfully when her least gifts, wisely stored in the mind for a time, are afterwards bestowed more openly. For the other gifts of God have this property: that they enrich even their possessors more abundantly precisely when they distribute them more lavishly; and, divided, they are [Col. 1052A] multiplied more within themselves. Thus we read that the Lord Jesus himself had five loaves in one place and seven in another before they were distributed; but, when they began to be given, after thousands of people had been fed, we read that baskets and hampers were filled.

[Col. 1051] Here ends the book entitled **WHAT SORT THEY ARE**, composed by the venerable Peter of Blois.

[Col. 1051]

## ON THE DIVISION AND AUTHORS OF THE SACRED BOOKS. (G)*

[Col. 1051B] The Old Testament is so called because, when the New came, it ceased; and the Apostle also mentions it, saying: “The former things have passed away, and behold, new things have been made.” [Note: [Col. 1051] 2 Cor. 5.] It is called the New Testament because it renews. For none speak of it except persons recalled from oldness by grace and now belonging to the New Testament, which is the kingdom of heaven. The Hebrews, however, receive the Old Testament, with God as its author, as twenty-two books according to the number of their letters, dividing them into three orders: namely, the Law, the Prophets, and the Hagiographa.

The first order is that of the Law, which they receive in five books. The first of these is *Beresith*, that is, Genesis; the second, *Vellesemoth*, that is, Exodus; the third, *Vaiecra*, that is, Leviticus; the fourth, *Vagedaber*, that is, Numbers; the fifth, [Col. 1051C] *Elleaddebarim*, that is, Deuteronomy. These are the five books of Moses, which the Hebrews call *Thorah* and the Latins call the Law. Strictly speaking, however, the Law is that which was given through Moses.

The second order is that of the Prophets, in which eight books are contained. The first is *Josue Ben Nun*, which in Latin is called Jesus son of Nave; the second, *Sophethim*, that is, Judges; the third, Samuel, which is the First Book of Kings; the fourth, *Malachim*, which is the Third and Fourth Books of Kings; the fifth, Isaiah; the sixth, Jeremiah; the seventh, Ezekiel; the eighth, *There-asar*, called the Twelve Prophets. Since these books are joined together because of their brevity, they are treated as one.

The third order is that of the Hagiographa, that is, “those who write sacred things,” in which there are nine books. The first is Job; the second, the Psalter; the third, [Col. 1051D] *Massot*, that is, the Proverbs of Solomon; the fourth, *Coheleth*, that is, Ecclesiastes; the fifth, *Sir-assirim*, that is, the Song of Songs; the sixth, Daniel; the seventh, *Dibrehajamin*, that is, “words of the days,” namely Chronicles; the eighth, Ezra; the ninth, Esther. These, five and eight and nine together, make twenty-two, as stated above. Some, however, add Ruth and *Cinoth*, which is called in Latin [Col. 1052B] the Lamentations of Jeremiah, to the Hagiographa. They make twenty-four volumes of the Old Testament, corresponding to the twenty-four elders who stand before the presence of God. [Note: [Col. 1051] Rev. 4.]

Among us there is a fourth order of the Old Testament: those books which are not in the Hebrew canon. The first of these is the Book of Wisdom; the second, Ecclesiasticus; the third, Tobit; the fourth, Judith; the fifth and sixth, Maccabees. Although the Jews separate these among the apocrypha, the Church of Christ nevertheless honours and proclaims them among the divine books.

In the New Testament there are two orders. The first is evangelical, containing Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John; the second apostolic, containing Paul in fourteen Epistles, Peter in two, John in three, James and Jude in one each, the Acts [Col. 1052C] of the Apostles, and the Apocalypse. The total content of both Testaments is divided in three ways: into history, morals, and allegory. Again, these three are divided in many ways: what was done by God, by angels, and finally by human beings; what was announced by the prophets concerning Christ and his body; what concerning the devil and his members; what concerning the old and new people; and what concerning the present and future age, kingdom, and judgment.

According to the tradition of the Hebrews, these are reported as the authors of the Old Testament. First, Moses, who set forth in five volumes a cosmography of sacred history—that is, an account of the world—and is surnamed the Pentateuch. “Pentateuch” means five volumes: for *penta* is Greek for “five,” and *teuchus* means “volume.” The book of Genesis is called *Beresith*, because it contains the beginning of the world and the generation of the age. Exodus, however, recounts the departure from Egypt, or the going forth of the people of Israel, and from this has received its name. Leviticus is so called because it sets out the ministries of the Levites and the variety of sacrifices, and the whole Levitical order is recorded in it. The Book of Numbers is so called because it [Col. 1053A] numbers the tribes which departed from Egypt; and it contains a description of the forty-two encampments through the wilderness. *Deuteronomium* is Greek for what is interpreted in Latin as “the second law,” that is, a repetition of the evangelical law; it is a prefiguration that contains the earlier things in such a way that all the things repeated in it are then new.

The Book of Joshua received its name from Joshua son of Nave, whose history it contains. The Hebrews maintain that Joshua himself was its author. In its text, after the crossing of the Jordan, the kingdoms of the enemies are overthrown; the land is divided among the people; and the individual cities, villages, mountains, and water-boundaries are prefigured as the spiritual kingdoms and boundaries of the Church and the heavenly Jerusalem. Judges is named from the leaders of the people who presided over Israel after Moses and [Col. 1053B] Joshua, before David and the other kings arose. Samuel is believed to have produced this book and Ruth. The Book of Samuel describes the birth, priesthood, and deeds of that same Samuel. It therefore took its name from him; and, although this book contains the history of Saul and David, both are nevertheless referred to Samuel, because he anointed Saul and David as future kings. Samuel himself wrote the first part of this book; David wrote the remainder of it to the end.

It is accordingly called *Malachim* because it recounts, in chronological order, the deeds of the kings of Judah and of the Israelite nation. *Malach* is Hebrew, interpreted in Latin as “kingdom.” Jeremiah was the first to gather this book into one volume; for previously it was scattered [Col. 1053C] through the individual histories of the kings. It is called *Paralipomenon* in Greek, which we may call “things omitted” or “things left over,” because matters omitted or not fully related in the Law or the Books of Kings are explained in it summarily and briefly.

Some believe that Moses wrote the Book of Job; others, one of the prophets; while some think Job himself was its author after the ordeal of his suffering, supposing that he who endured the contest of spiritual warfare narrated the victories which he achieved. The beginning and end of the Book of Job are, among the Hebrews, certainly in prose; but its middle part, from the passage where he says, “Let the day perish on which I was born” [Note: [Col. 1053] Job 3.] to the passage, “Therefore I reprehend myself and do penance” [Note: [Col. 1053] Job 42.], runs throughout in heroic metre.

[Col. 1053D] The Book of Psalms is called in Greek the Psalter, in Hebrew *Nablat*, and in Latin an instrument. It is called the Book of Psalms because, while one prophet sang to the psaltery, the choir responded in harmony. The Hebrew title of the Psalms is *Ysopocalim*, interpreted as “volume of hymns.” The authors of the Psalms given in their titles are Moses, David and Solomon, Asaph, Ethan, Idithun, the sons of Korah, the Hezekiahites, and the others, all of whom Ezra gathered into one volume. All the Psalms among the Hebrews are composed in metrical song. For, in the metres of the Roman Flaccus and the Greek Pindar, some run now in iambics, now sound in Alcaic verse, [Col. 1054A] now shine in Sapphic verse, proceeding with trimeter or tetrameter feet.

Solomon son of King David produced three volumes according to the number of his titles. The first is *Massot*, called by the Greeks *Parables* and by the Latins *Proverbs*, because in it he displays figures of speech and images of truth under comparative likenesses, while reserving the truth itself for readers to understand. He called the second book *Coheleth*, which is called in Greek *Ecclesiastes*, in Latin “the preacher,” because its discourse is not directed specifically to one person, as in Proverbs, but is addressed generally to all, teaching that everything which we see in the world is transient and brief and therefore not at all to be desired. He entitled the third book *Sir-assirim*, which is translated into Latin as [Col. 1054B] *Song of Songs*, where he mystically sings, in an epithalamic poem, the union of Christ and the Church. It is called the *Song of Songs* because it is preferred above all that is contained in the Holy Scriptures, just as some things in the Law are called holy, while those which are greater are called the Holy of Holies. The poems of this third book are said by two authorities—Josephus and Jerome—to have been composed in hexameter and pentameter verses.

Isaiah produced his book in a form more evangelical than prophetic. Its whole text proceeds in eloquent prose; its song, however, runs in hexameter and pentameter verses. Jeremiah likewise produced his book together with the *Threni*, which we call lamentations because they are used in more sorrowful circumstances [Col. 1054C] and at funerals; in them he composed a fourfold alphabet in diverse metres. The first two are written in Sapphic metre, because a raised comma concludes three verses that are joined together and begin with one and the same letter. The third alphabet is written in trimeter, and the *threni* begin in groups of three verses. The fourth alphabet is similar to the first and second.

Ezekiel and Daniel are said to have been written by certain wise men. Ezekiel has beginnings and endings veiled in many obscurities. Daniel, however, foretells the kingdoms of the world in clear language and marks the time of Christ’s coming in the most manifest proclamation. These are the four prophets called Major because they produced lengthy volumes. The Book of the Twelve Prophets is designated by the names of [Col. 1054D] its authors. They are called Minor because their discourses are brief, and thus are joined together and contained in one volume. Their names are Hosea, Joel, Amos, Obadiah, Jonah, Micah, Nahum, Habakkuk, Zephaniah, Haggai, Zechariah, and Malachi.

The Book of Ezra is designated by its author’s title. Its text contains together the discourses of Ezra and Nehemiah. Nor should anyone be troubled that it is called one book of Ezra, for the second, third, and fourth books are not found among the Hebrews but are reckoned among the apocrypha. Ezra is believed to have written the Book of Esther, in which that queen, under the figure of the Church, is believed to have delivered God’s people from slavery and death; and, after Haman—whose name means “iniquity”—was killed, an annual festival is handed down to posterity.

The Book of Wisdom is nowhere among the Hebrews; hence its very style has more of Greek than Hebrew eloquence. The Jews maintain that it is by a Babylonian; and they therefore call it Wisdom because it plainly sets forth the coming of Christ, who is the wisdom of the Father, and his Passion.

Jesus son of Sirach, grandson of Jesus the high priest, most certainly composed the Book of Ecclesiasticus; Zechariah also mentions him [Note: [Col. 1055] chap. 3.]. Among the Latins the book is designated by Solomon’s title because of its similarity of style. It is called Ecclesiasticus [Col. 1055B] because it was produced with great care and method concerning the discipline of religious life for the whole Church. It is found among the Hebrews, but is now considered apocryphal. It is by no means clear by what authors the books of Judith, Tobit, or Maccabees were written. They take their names from those whose deeds they record.

The four evangelists separately wrote the four books of the Gospels. Matthew first wrote his Gospel in Hebrew letters in Judaea, announcing through his Gospel the human birth of Christ, son of David, saying: “The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, son of David, son of Abraham”; signifying that Christ bodily descended from the seed of the patriarchs, [Col. 1055C] as had been promised in the prophets through the Holy Spirit. Mark second, filled with the Holy Spirit, wrote the Gospel of Christ in Greek speech in Italy, following Peter as a disciple. He made a beginning from John in a prophetic spirit, saying: “A voice crying in the wilderness: Prepare the way of the Lord,” to show that Christ, after assuming flesh, preached the Gospel in the world. For Christ himself was also called a prophet, as it is written: “And I gave thee as a prophet among the nations.” [Note: [Col. 1055] Jer. 1.]

Luke was, among all the evangelists, the most learned in Greek speech. As a physician, he wrote the Gospel in Greece for Bishop Theophilus, beginning from the priestly spirit, saying: “In the days of Herod, king of Judaea, there was a priest, Zacharias” [Note: [Col. 1055] Luke 1.], in order to show [Col. 1055D] that Christ, after his bodily birth and the preaching of the Gospel, became a sacrifice for the salvation of the world. For he is the priest of whom it is said in the Psalms: “Thou art a priest for ever according to the order of Melchizedek.” [Note: [Col. 1055] Psalm 109.] For where Christ came, the priesthood fell silent, and law and prophecy ceased.

John fourth wrote the last Gospel in Asia, beginning from the Word, to show that he, the Saviour, who deigned to be born and suffer for us, was the Word of God before the ages, came from heaven, and returned again to heaven after death. These are the four evangelists whom the Holy Spirit, through Ezekiel [Note: [Col. 1055] chap. 1.], [Col. 1056A] signified by four living creatures. There are four living creatures because through the four regions of the world the faith of the Christian religion has been disseminated by their preaching. They are called living creatures because the Gospel of Christ is preached for the human soul. They were full of eyes within and without because the Gospels foresee what was spoken by the prophets and what they had promised earlier. Their legs were straight because there is nothing crooked in the Gospels. They had six wings, covering their legs and faces; but at Christ’s coming the things that were covered were revealed. “Gospel” means “good announcement”: for *eu* means “good,” and *angelium*, “announcement.” Hence *apostle* and *angel* mean “messenger.”

[Col. 1056B] The Apostle Paul wrote his fourteen Epistles in Greek. Of these, he wrote nine to seven Churches, and the remainder to his disciples Timothy, Titus, and Philemon. The Epistle to the Hebrews, however, is held by many Latins to be of uncertain Pauline authorship because of the difference in style; some suspect that Barnabas wrote it, and others, Clement. Peter wrote two Epistles in his own name. James, John, and Jude wrote their Epistles; they are called canonical because they were written not merely to one people or city but generally to all nations. The Acts of the Apostles recounts the beginnings of Christian faith among the nations and the history of the Church at its birth. We read that Luke the evangelist was the author of the Acts of the Apostles; in this work the infancy of the nascent Church [Col. 1056C] is woven together and the history of the apostles preserved—hence it is called the Acts of the Apostles.

John the evangelist wrote the book of the Apocalypse when he was handed over into exile on the island of Patmos because of his preaching of the Gospel. *Apocalypse* is translated from Greek into Latin as “revelation.” It is called revelation because it is the manifestation of things that had been hidden, as John himself says: “The Apocalypse of Jesus Christ, which God gave him to make known openly to his servants.” These are the writers of the sacred books who, speaking through the Holy Spirit, wrote down for our instruction precepts for living and the rule of belief.

Besides these, other volumes are called apocryphal. They are called apocryphal, that is, secret, because they are doubtful. Their origin is hidden, and it is not evident to the Fathers from whom, by a most certain and well-known succession, the authority of the truth of the Scriptures has come down to us. Although some truth is found in these apocrypha, nevertheless, because of their many falsehoods, they possess no canonical authority. They are rightly judged by prudent persons not to be writings that should be believed to belong to those to whom they are ascribed. For many writings are put forth by heretics under the names of prophets, and more recent writings under the names of apostles; all these have, after careful examination, been removed from canonical authority under the name of apocrypha.

[Col. 1057]

## ON HASTENING THE PILGRIMAGE TO JERUSALEM

[Col. 1057A] To his dearest companions and friends, Guid. and Gol., P. of Blois, Archdeacon of Bath, greetings.

“Who will give water to my head and a fountain of tears to my eyes, that I may weep for the slain of my people?” [Note: [Col. 1057] Jer. 9.] Would that I might flow wholly into weeping, and that my grief might feed upon the solace of tears; let my eyes shed tears, let my life fail in sorrow, because “a voice of lamentation has been heard from Zion: we have been laid waste and utterly confounded.” [Note: [Col. 1057] Ibid.] “The crown of our head has fallen, and our dance has been turned into mourning.” [Note: [Col. 1057] Lam. 5.] Whatever the prophets had foretold in threats against Jerusalem and its kingdom through the courses of many ages, one mournful and unhappy day—a day dark and more shadowy than every night—has fulfilled.

[Note: [Col. 1057C] “In the year of the Lord 1189 Saladin, the most powerful king of the Saracens, having found from the discord of the Christians an opportunity for successful action, captured not only many other cities but also Jerusalem, which had been occupied by our people for a full eighty years. Struck down by this most bitter news, Pope Urban III died from grief of mind. He was followed by Gregory VIII, who held the pontificate for only two months, and Clement III; offering very great remissions, they exhorted Christian princes through their legates to undertake holy war and to assume the sign of the cross against Saladin. The first of the princes to enroll in this sacred expedition was Richard, Count of Poitou, son of Henry II, king of the English, in that same year, 1187; in the following year Frederick I Barbarossa, Emperor of the Romans, and, after a conference had been held, Philip, king of the French, and Henry II, king of England, did so as well. Yet some evil genius, renewing a most grievous war between the said kings and Richard, delayed their excellent undertakings. Peter of Blois deplores this matter at length in the present treatise, marvellously interwoven, as it were, in a vermiculate work from Scriptural testimonies; and finally, if the princes are unwilling to stand by their promises, he exhorts all the poor to set out upon the Jerusalem journey as quickly as possible and to wrest the glorious wood of Christ’s cross and the Holy Land itself, the Christians’ inheritance, from the hostile enemy of the Christian name.” Thus write Vincent of Beauvais, book XXX of the *Speculum historiale*, chapter 43 and following; Polydore, book XIII of the *English History*; Newburgh, Paris, Antoninus, Platina, and all the others.]

I believe that Ezekiel’s certain and explicit oracle [Col. 1057B] concerning this most accursed day came beforehand: “Son of man, write down for yourself the name of this day, on which the king of Babylon was strengthened against Jerusalem.” [Note: [Col. 1057] Ezek. 24.] Today, as we have heard, this has happened in the city of the Lord of hosts. She sits alone—indeed, the city once full of peoples, mistress of nations and princess of provinces, has become a desolation under tribute. All her gates have been destroyed; her priests have fallen by the sword. Their young men and their virgins have been given into captivity, and their beauty into the hand of the enemy. “The enemy has stretched out his hand over all her desirable things; the Lord has taken away all the magnificent men from the midst of the city”; [Note: [Col. 1057] Lam. 1.] “in his fury he has destroyed all the fortifications of the daughter of Judah”; [Note: [Col. 1057] Ibid. 2.] “he has rejected his altar and cursed his sanctuary.” [Note: [Col. 1057] Ibid.]

And why do I turn over Jeremiah’s Lamentations? All Jeremiah would not suffice [Col. 1057C] to express the face of the present misery. Yet, to conclude the lamentable outcome of the event in the words of the same prophet: “The Lord has completed his fury; he has poured out [Col. 1058A] the wrath of his indignation”; [Note: [Col. 1057] Lam. 4.] he has made his arrows drunk with blood. And according to the word of Isaiah: “Your wickedness is completed, Jerusalem”; [Note: [Col. 1057] Isa. 40.] “you have drunk from the hand of the Lord the cup of his wrath to the bottom; you have drunk the cup of stupor and drained it to the dregs.” [Note: [Col. 1057] Isa. 51.]

O good Jesus, O kindly one, O lovable one, O desirable one, O sweet one, O gentle God, O God of love, where are your ancient mercies? [Note: [Col. 1057] Psalm 88.] How have you forgotten your compassions? How have you turned cruel toward us? [Note: [Col. 1057] Job 30.] The multitude of your tender mercies and compassions have restrained themselves from us; the yoke of our iniquities has kept watch in your hands. You have sealed up our transgressions as in a bag; [Note: [Col. 1057] Job 14.] and when we had forgotten them, were these not laid up with you and sealed in your treasuries? Therefore [Col. 1058B] you have rejected and confounded us; you have given your servants as sheep for food and scattered us among the peoples. [Note: [Col. 1057] Psalm 43.] You who had become for us from God not only wisdom but also righteousness, sanctification, and redemption [Note: [Col. 1057] 1 Cor. 1.] have now become not sanctifier or redeemer, but slayer and destroyer. “Why, Lord, have you withdrawn far away? Why do you despise us in times of need, in tribulation?” [Note: [Col. 1057] Psalm 10.] “Have mercy on us, Lord, have mercy on us, for we are greatly filled with contempt.” [Note: [Col. 1057] Psalm 122.] “Awake—why do you sleep, Lord?” [Note: [Col. 1057] Psalm 43.] “Will you forget to show mercy, O God, or in anger restrain your mercies?” [Note: [Col. 1057] Psalm 76.] “Will you cut off your mercy, or not add further that you may yet be more favourable?” [Note: [Col. 1057] Ibid.]

“We have sinned with our fathers; we have acted wickedly.” [Note: [Col. 1057] Psalm 105.] We do not deny our wickedness and misery; nevertheless, we confess no less your [Col. 1058C] justice and mercy. Curse and falsehood, homicide and theft, and adultery have overflowed, and blood has touched blood. “Therefore those who dwell in the land mourn.” [Col. 1059A] [Note: [Col. 1059] Hos. 4.] We entreat your conquering hand to remember us in the favour shown to your people; [Note: [Col. 1059] Psalm 105.] may your mercies conquer our miseries, and not our miseries your mercies; may your wisdom conquer our wickedness. And you, Lord, compassionate and merciful, [Note: [Col. 1059] Psalm 85.] look upon the face of your covenant; [Note: [Col. 1059] Psalm 83.] look upon the inheritance which you acquired in your blood, and do not reject it utterly. [Note: [Col. 1059] Psalm 43.] Although once you rejected the tabernacle at Shiloh [Note: [Col. 1059] Psalm 77; Deut. 24.] and gave the synagogue a bill of divorce, [Note: [Col. 1059] Matt. 19.] do not nevertheless reject your Church: “The heart of her husband trusts in her.” [Note: [Col. 1059] Prov. 31.] She has followed no lover except you. This the apostles, the martyrs, the other disciples of your school, and all your brothers know—I mean, the professors of your name.

[Col. 1059B] In the person of your bride you lay claim to that land which the enemies of your cross and blasphemers of your name have now invaded; through this woman “the two were made one flesh.” [Note: [Col. 1059] Gen. 2.] Not to mention your Father, who gave you the nations as your inheritance and the ends of the earth as your possession, [Note: [Col. 1059] Psalm 2.], certainly your mother descends in direct reckoning from the stock of King David. Therefore that land is yours by maternal right—if indeed you permit it to be yours, and not rather theirs who hate you without cause. [Note: [Col. 1059] Psalm 34.] We know that you have been offended by our sins; but, I pray, do not turn your offence into a reproach against your name. Your teaching is: “Do not give your honour to another.” [Note: [Col. 1059] Prov. 5.] And “if the spirit of him who has power comes upon you, do not leave your place.” I speak as one less wise, yet perhaps not with folly toward you. To me, [Col. 1059C] though a sinner, it seems more prudent that you should wipe out all sinners from the face of the earth than tolerate the sons of perdition insolently and arrogantly insulting us in the midst of your people, to the dishonour of your name. It is a common proverb: “He badly avenges an insult done to him who cuts off his own nose.”

May the Lord, I pray, not so punish his wicked servant that, in punishing the servant, he humbles himself and magnifies the enemy. Turn therefore a little, and be entreated on behalf of your servants; [Note: [Col. 1059] Psalm 89.] consider how you may yet be more favourable. [Note: [Col. 1059] Psalm 76.] Do not give your inheritance to reproach, nor the vineyard which your right hand planted to trampling. [Note: [Col. 1059] Psalm 79.] We have sinned, but, with contrite and humble heart, after anger we implore mercy. [Col. 1059D] “Let the vengeance for the blood of your servants which has been shed come into your sight.” [Note: [Col. 1059] Psalm 78.] It is enough for your people if, in that land which has been reddened by your blood and that of your servants, the glory of your name is held in renown. “Not to us, Lord, not to us, but give glory to your name,” [Note: [Col. 1059] Psalm 113.] lest perhaps the nations should say, “Where is their God?” [Note: [Col. 1059] Psalm 78.] lest the enemies grow proud and say: “Our hand is exalted, and not the Lord has done all these things.” [Note: [Col. 1059] Deut. 32.]

Let your anger rest, Lord; and let your hand, which struck us, itself heal us. “Arise, arise [Col. 1060A] from the dust, captive daughter Zion,” [Note: [Col. 1059] Isa. 52.] who have received double from the Lord’s hand. [Note: [Col. 1059] Isa. 40.] Rise up, wretched Jerusalem, who have drunk from the Lord’s hand the cup of his wrath. [Note: [Col. 1059] Isa. 51.] “As much as you glorified yourself and lived in delights, so much torment and mourning have been given you.” [Note: [Col. 1059] Rev. 18.] “As a cistern produces its cold water, so you had made your iniquity cold.” [Note: [Col. 1059] Jer. 6.] Therefore he to whom the thought of man makes confession, of whom it is written that he searches Jerusalem with lamps, [Note: [Col. 1059] Zeph. 1.] has counted all your evils. Yet he, like a man who does not hear and has no reproofs in his mouth, [Note: [Col. 1059] Psalm 37.] long dissembled and kept silence, and according to the riches of the magnificence of his gentleness waited many years for repentance. Often, when your merits demanded it, he would have sharpened his sword like lightning and seized judgment in [Col. 1060B] his hand against you; but the angels of peace wept bitterly, [Note: [Col. 1059] Isa. 33.] and, awaiting in you worthy fruits of repentance, obtained delays of divine punishment. Yet he set before them most often the word found in Jeremiah: “Go about the streets of Jerusalem, and see, consider, and seek in her squares whether you find a man doing judgment and seeking faithfulness, and I shall be merciful to them.” [Note: [Col. 1059] Jer. 5.]

What could I say of your king except what Ecclesiasticus says: “A foolish king will destroy his people, and a kingdom will be transferred from nation to nation because of injustices and various deceits”? [Note: [Col. 1059] Ecclus. 10.] And in the same book: “As the judge of a people is, so are his ministers; and as the ruler of a city is, such are its inhabitants.” [Note: [Col. 1059] Ibid.] Return therefore to your heart, Jerusalem, and return to the Lord your God. What [Col. 1060C] do you know whether he too may turn and leave behind him a blessing? For he is sweet, merciful, and ready to relent from evil. [Note: [Col. 1059] Joel 2.] He does not will the death of the sinner, but that he should turn and live. [Note: [Col. 1059] Ezek. 33.] For he is the one who says through Zechariah: “I shall return to Jerusalem in mercies. My cities shall yet overflow with good things. The Lord shall comfort Zion and shall yet choose Jerusalem.” [Note: [Col. 1059] Zech. 1.] And through Isaiah, soothing your miseries with paternal consolation, he says: “Put on the garments of your glory, captive daughter Zion; put on the garments of your glory, Jerusalem, holy city.” [Note: [Col. 1059] Isa. 52.] And a little later he adds: “For a brief moment I abandoned you, but in my mercies I shall gather you. In a moment of indignation I hid my face a little from you, but in everlasting [Col. 1060D] mercy I have had compassion on you.” [Note: [Col. 1059] Isa. 54.] “Can a woman forget her infant, so as not to have compassion on the son of her womb? Even if she should forget, yet I shall not forget you. Behold, I have inscribed you upon my hands; your walls are always before my eyes.” [Note: [Col. 1059] Isa. 49.] Therefore follow Jeremiah’s counsel, and wash your heart from wickedness. [Note: [Col. 1059] Jer. 4.] Jerusalem, take up the arms of repentance.

For I know that if the Lord is appeased toward you, then, according to the word of Isaiah, he will comfort Zion and make her wilderness like a paradise, and her desert like the [Col. 1061A] garden of the Lord; joy and gladness shall be found in her, thanksgiving and the voice of praise [Note: [Col. 1061] Isa. 51.]. Indeed, besides the prophets’ consoling words, amid the multitude of my sorrows my heart was cheered by the longed-for hope of consolation, because the princes and great men of the earth had recently taken up the sign of the cross. For by the privilege of the apostle Peter and the authority of the universal Church, the Lord had set forth in this sign the word of reconciliation: so that undertaking the Jerusalem road might be a completed repentance and sufficient satisfaction for sins committed [Note: [Col. 1061C] Before Peter of Blois, St Bernard wrote to the same effect in Epistle 322, to the bishop, clergy, and people of Speyer, whom he strongly exhorts and urges to undertake holy war against the unbelievers harassing Palestine. “Take up,” he says, “the sign of the cross, and you shall obtain at once forgiveness for all those sins of which you have made confession with a contrite heart. The material itself, if purchased, costs little; if it is taken upon a devout shoulder, it is undoubtedly worth the kingdom of God. Those, therefore, have done well who have already received the heavenly seal.” Likewise, soon after Peter of Blois, Thomas of Cantimpré [ [Col. 1061D] Flourished in the year of the Lord 1240.] writes thus in Book II of the *Examples*, called *The Book of Bees*, chapter 2, [Col. 1061D] section 10: “Concerning the indulgence preached to those who take up the cross, no believer may be allowed to doubt that those who are wholly penitent and have confessed receive forgiveness of all sins; and that, in the intention of desire by which they long to die for the faith, should occasion offer itself, they are wholly absolved both from punishment and from guilt. Therefore my faith concerning all these matters is certain, and I have no doubt that our supreme pontiff has commanded this to be done through the legates of his authority.” Thus he. From this it is clear that Martin Chemnitz, in Part IV of his *Examination of the Council of Trent*, chapter 4, spares manifest truth when [Col. 1062C] he says that no doctrine or practice of indulgences existed in the Church before A.D. 1200. For, by the privilege of Peter—as Peter of Blois speaks here—that is, by the authority of the supreme pontiffs, and by the authority of the universal Church, that is, of councils, indulgences had long before been proposed and proclaimed to the Christian people, as Bellarmine shows in Book II, *On Indulgences*, chapter 17. And in the very year 1187 and the years following, when Peter of Blois wrote this treatise, Gregory VIII and Clement III, according to Vincent of Beauvais, in the place cited above, proclaimed a plenary indulgence for all who prepared themselves for holy war. You will say that Peter of Blois here asserts that the very undertaking of the Jerusalem journey is completed repentance and sufficient satisfaction for sins, and that consequently no place remains for an indulgence. For he is properly said to grant indulgence who remits something from complete and perfect satisfaction. I reply that it is indeed a completed repentance, but by the privilege of the apostle Peter, as Peter of Blois says—that is, by a grant or indulgence of the Apostolic See. Therefore both St Bernard and Thomas of Cantimpré expressly call it an indulgence.].

Thus the mystery of the cross had inaugurated for us, as the Apostle says, a new way into the sanctuary in the blood of Christ [Note: [Col. 1061] Heb. 10.]; and the Lord was leading us also upon the straight way, that we might go to the city of our dwelling [Note: [Col. 1061] Ps. 106]. But [Col. 1061B] refusing to walk on the paths of righteousness, we chose the winding tracks of deceitful ways. You earth-born ones and sons of men, why do you seek divergences of roads when a short way to eternal life is offered you? The Lord directs you into the way of peace and salvation, yet you choose the way of discord and death. For all the ways of the Lord are beautiful and all his paths peaceable [Note: [Col. 1061] Prov. 3]. I fear that for those who turn aside from them and stand in the way of sinners, this way may truly become a stumbling-block to them [Note: [Col. 1061] Ps. 48], and that what the Psalmist says may happen to them: “Destruction and misery are in their ways, and the way of peace they have not known” [Note: [Col. 1061] Ps. 13]. There are ways, as the Wise Man says, which seem right to a man, but their end leads down to the depths of hell [Note: [Col. 1061] Prov. 16]. [Col. 1061C] As it is written elsewhere: “The ways of sinners are level with stones, but at their end are darkness and punishments” [Note: [Col. 1061] Ecclus. 21].

[Col. 1062A] All the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth [Note: [Col. 1061] Ps. 24]. Of these he himself says: “If Israel had walked in my ways, perhaps I should quickly have humbled their enemies” [Note: [Col. 1061] Ps. 80]. We seek meekness, not wars, because he scatters the nations that desire wars, while the Lord directs the meek unto salvation [Note: [Col. 1061] Ps. 24]. May God, the God of our salvations, make our journey prosperous, so that his ordinances may be songs to us in the place of our pilgrimage [Note: [Col. 1061] Ps. 118], that we may be undefiled in the way [Note: [Col. 1061] Ibid.], and that we may praise the Lord in the ways of the Lord, because great is the glory of the Lord [Note: [Col. 1061] Ps. 137]. O how blessed is he who can say: “O God, who girded me with strength and made my way undefiled” [Note: [Col. 1061] Ps. 17].

The sons of Adam do not consider this. Rejecting the grace offered them and judging themselves unworthy of the kingdom of God, they fight for a transitory kingdom [Col. 1062B] and, casting aside the remedy of divine mercy, litigate for temporal profit. By the just judgment of God, those who would not have peace in Christ cannot have peace among themselves. “You have set me against yourself,” he says, “and I have become burdensome to myself” [Note: [Col. 1061] Job 7]. Seeing that the inestimable gain of Christ and the incomparable increase of the Christian harvest were rising, as it were, with some new power through the cross, the Enemy sowed tares over it; extending his malice into every cunning device, he strives by manifold temptation to extinguish the good of this most saving way. For it is written: “My son, when you come to the service of God, stand in justice and fear, and prepare your soul for temptation” [Note: [Col. 1061] Ecclus. 2]. Thus Pharaoh rages more savagely at Israel’s departure from [Col. 1062C] Egypt [Note: [Col. 1061] Exod. 5], and Satan, when about to depart from the man whom he had held from childhood, tears that same man more grievously as he leaves [Col. 1063A] him [Note: [Col. 1063] Mark 9].

The resemblance is plainly expressed in those who have undertaken the purpose of the holy pilgrimage: attacks rage more bitterly against them, and their latter condition is worse than the former. “We have conceived and, as it were, brought forth,” says Isaiah, “and have not wrought the spirit of salvation in the earth” [Note: [Col. 1063] Isa. 26]. They had chosen the service of him whose service is to reign; yet, returning to their vomit [Note: [Col. 1063] Prov. 26], they build their spiritual Jericho [Note: [Col. 1063] Josh. 6], which they had destroyed in professing the cross. Amid the very first fruits of their most salutary vow, they established postponements of their pilgrimage, not observing that the loss of time is a loss of salvation, and that delay is great ruin.

The Apostle says: “Jerusalem, which is our mother” [Note: [Col. 1063] Gal. 4]. If she is a mother, where are her children? Surely those who allow their mother to be dishonoured, trampled down, and prostituted [Col. 1063B] are not sons but step-sons—or rather, what is worse, they incur the mark of shameful treason if they do not defend their mother’s patrimony, the Lord’s inheritance which is their own inheritance. Christ says: “He who is not with me is against me, and he who does not gather with me scatters” [Note: [Col. 1063] Luke 11]. The field in which the Lord was slain, where not only the reading of the Scriptures but the rending of the rocks proclaims the shedding of his blood, is now possessed by those who slew him; so that that word of divine indignation rightly applies to them: “You have killed and also taken possession” [Note: [Col. 1063] 3 Kings 21].

The blood of Naboth cried out [Note: [Col. 1063] Ibid.]; the blood of Abel cried out from the earth for vengeance [Note: [Col. 1063] Gen. 4], and found an avenger. The blood of Christ cries for help and finds no helper [Note: [Col. 1063] Ps. 141]. “I looked,” he says, “to the right, [Col. 1063C] and saw, and there was none who knew me.” And through Isaiah: “I looked about, and there was no helper; I sought, and there was none to aid” [Note: [Col. 1063] Isa. 63]. Good Jesus, the scorching wind, the wind of pride, has lifted up the locusts. And though the pride of those who hate you rises continually [Note: [Col. 1063] Ps. 73], there is no one who rises against them for you, no one who takes up the zeal of Phinehas and Mattathias. Miserable men see the land in which the feet of the Lord stood occupied and destroyed by the sons of unbelief. They hear the holy things profaned, their brothers imprisoned, tortured, and killed; yet they are not moved by the affliction of Joseph, while that son of perdition—whose name I do not wish to make this present letter ill-omened by mentioning—has already besieged every fortress of that land and possessed a great part of it.

Our own cross-bearers seek out various pretexts for delaying their pilgrimage [Col. 1063D], as though conspiring in the cause of that wicked man; and they have despised the desirable land [Note: [Col. 1063] Ps. 105]. O how far from salvation is the man who hunts for postponements of his salvation! O how feebly he loves—indeed, how cruelly he hates—Christ, who obstructs his honour and renders void the undertaking of public righteousness! “Grace be with all,” says the Apostle [Note: [Col. 1063] 3 Cor. 16], “who love our Lord Jesus Christ.” And again: “If anyone does not love our Lord Jesus Christ, let him be anathema, maranatha” [Note: [Col. 1063] Ibid.]—that is, “Our Lord, come!”

Do you suppose [Col. 1064A] that the Lord will not inquire whether anyone loves the house of Jacob and the place where his glory dwells? Therefore the wicked man has provoked God, for he has said in his heart, “He will not require it” [Note: [Col. 1063] Ps. 10]. What madness, I ask, in a moment of such pressing necessity, to contrive delays, prolong one’s own salvation, disregard Christ’s injuries, allow the wolf to rage in the sheepfold, and only then prepare aid once he has devoured all the sheep! Certainly, whoever abandons opportunity is abandoned by opportunity. Sons of men, how long will your hearts be heavy [Note: [Col. 1063] Ps. 4]? How are you sluggish toward what brings salvation, yet anxious for vain and perishable things? Do vintners wait until the vintage is over? Or merchants until the fair has ended? Or harvesters [Col. 1064B] until the harvest season has passed? It is written: “Cursed is he who does the work of God negligently” [Note: [Col. 1063] Jer. 48].

I had hoped that the cross of Christ would bloom again and, as though watered and quickened once more by his blood, would bring forth in due season the fruit of salvation and grace. But now, as I say weeping, enemies of Christ’s cross—who ought to have been its sons—through their greed, under the pretext of a certain damnable levy, render void the first pledge of their vow. They luxuriate at the cross of the Lord and have turned that which the apostles once preached—“a stumbling-block to Jews, but foolishness to Gentiles” [Note: [Col. 1063] 1 Cor. 1]—into foolishness and a stumbling-block among those who profess the Crucified One. “Woe to the man through whom the stumbling-block comes” [Note: [Col. 1063] Matt. 18]. “Whoever causes one of these little ones to stumble” [Note: [Col. 1063] Ibid.]—hard is what follows: he makes himself worthy of a harsher judgment who presumes to scandalize so great and choice a multitude.

Of Judas it is written that, after receiving the morsel, Satan entered into him [Note: [Col. 1063] John 13]. I fear that the sign of the cross may result in the ruin of many souls, because perhaps they took it unworthily, for gain, display, or the favour of men. This sign was set and offered for the fall and rising again of many [Note: [Col. 1063] Luke 2]. For from it follows the casting down of the Jews and the subjection of the nations. Therefore, after the prophet had first spoken of the rejection of the Jewish people, he adds concerning the calling of the nations: “Raise up a standard among the nations” [Note: [Col. 1063] Isa. 11]. Some have been marked, but the sign is not the light of your countenance, O Lord [Note: [Col. 1063] Ps. 4]. As I see it, [Col. 1064D] this sign has been given to unbelievers, not believers. For if they had established the foundation of their vow upon the stone of help, no engines of greed would have shaken the steadfastness of their holy purpose. Thus Paul writes to Timothy: “The firm foundation of God stands, having this seal” [Note: [Col. 1063] 2 Tim. 2]. Likewise, speaking to the Ephesians: “In Christ you were sealed with the Holy Spirit, who is the pledge of your inheritance” [Note: [Col. 1063] Eph. 1]. And to the Corinthians: “You are the seal of my apostleship in Christ” [Note: [Col. 1063] 1 Cor. 9].

I say further: they have been marked, but not by him who [Col. 1065A] sealed and sent his Son Jesus. For if they had been marked by him, they would grieve and groan over their sins. For he is the one who commands that *tau* be marked upon the foreheads of those who mourn and groan [Note: [Col. 1065] Ezek. 9]. This expressly shows that this sign obtains its effect only in those who groan and mourn for their sins. And it is especially noteworthy that, although very many receive the sign of this pilgrimage, they are never marked with the sign of *tau* except by the decision of divine command and the ministry of angels. Therefore, Lord Jesus, whom the Father has sealed, make for me a sign for good [Note: [Col. 1065] Ps. 85]. You, form of beauty, image of glory, seal of life, mark my heart with the light of your countenance, O God of my heart and my portion forever [Note: [Col. 1065] Ps. 72].

I repeatedly addressed the foremost and greatest among those marked with the cross, exhorting them to be wise and understand, and, foreseeing their latter end [Col. 1065B] [Note: [Col. 1065] Deut. 32], to carry out with joyful devotion the most salutary purpose of repentance. But, to use Jeremiah’s words: “Behold, their ears are uncircumcised, and they cannot hear; behold, the word of the Lord has become a reproach, and they do not receive it” [Note: [Col. 1065] Jer. 6]. Certainly, the man who had first said to Zion, “Behold, I am here” [Note: [Col. 1065] Isa. 52], and who had promised himself to Jerusalem as evangelist—that is, herald of peace and liberator of the land—by taking up the cross, has turned into a crooked bow [Note: [Col. 1065] Ps. 77]. For neither he nor the other rich men knows the great, surpassing, glorious, heavenly, and inestimable gift of repentance. This is the second plank after shipwreck, [Col. 1065C] the ladder of heaven, the reconciliation of peace, the acquisition of life, the abolition of vices, the protection of bodies, the medicine of spirits. This is that of which Solomon writes: “God created medicine for men, and fools despise it” [Note: [Col. 1065] Ecclus. 38].

Nothing so weighs down and chokes the fruit of repentance as abundance of wealth and eminence of rank. For who has greater need of the remedy of repentance than a rich man, who is always committing acts needing repentance and, scarcely or never thinking of the salvation of souls, always pursues care of the flesh in its desires? He feeds the barren woman and does no good to the widow. And when he has loosened the reins of licence, expended his days in every impulse of his will and in good things, in a moment he descends to hell. Add that the Lord, terrible in his counsels over the children of men [Note: [Col. 1065] Ps. 65], continually tests the poor man in the purgatory of poverty; but the rich man, whom he reserves for eternal punishments, he pours out like water into every desire of this life, that he may rot in all his filth [Col. 1065D]. “Let the wicked be shown mercy,” he says, “and he will not learn to do justice” [Note: [Col. 1065] Isa. 26].

Therefore delay in repentance is more dangerous for the rich, because, besides the ordinary manner of death, the sword or poison frequently gives them occasion of death. Thus the rich man’s soul ought to be readier in proportion as a more dangerous and more varied [Col. 1066A] cause of death threatens him. A pagan says:

> Few kings, and tyrants, descend to Ceres’ son-in-law  
> Without slaughter and wounds, or by a dry death.

[Note: [Col. 1065] Juvenal, *Satires* 10.]

Read the annals again and review histories, and you will find few kings who have departed by an ordinary death. First there comes before you King Saul; King Elah, son of Baasha, whom his servant Zimri killed and reigned in his place [Note: [Col. 1065] 1 Kings 31]. But Zimri also burned himself with the royal house [Note: [Col. 1065] 3 Kings 16]. Hazael strangled King Ben-hadad and succeeded him in the kingdom [Note: [Col. 1065] 4 Kings 8]. King Joash was killed by two of his servants [Note: [Col. 1065] 4 Kings 12]. Shallum, son of Jabesh, struck down Zechariah king of Israel and reigned in his place [Note: [Col. 1065] 4 Kings 15]; Menahem, son of Gadi, struck down Shallum in Samaria and seized the helm of the kingdom [Note: [Col. 1065] Ibid.]. The son of Menahem was killed by Pekah son of Remaliah [Note: [Col. 1065] Ibid.]. Hoshea, son of [Col. 1066B] Elah, killed Pekah and reigned in his place [Note: [Col. 1065] Ibid.]. King Amon was killed by two servants; King Josiah son of Amon, by archers; and King Jehoiakim son of Josiah, by Nebuchadnezzar [Note: [Col. 1065] 2 Chron. 33, 35]. Zedekiah was blinded by the same man and finally condemned to a most disgraceful death [Note: [Col. 1065] 4 Kings 25].

If it is perhaps burdensome for you to hear of the kings of the Jews, recount the deeds of the Roman rulers. Begin with Julius Caesar, who was the first to assume the name and office of emperor, and whom Brutus and Cassius killed. Antony, wishing to succeed him, was killed by his own hand. Claudius Caesar was killed by Gaius Caligula; Gaius by his own Praetorians; Otho by his own hand; Vitellius by another’s. Domitian, who condemned blessed John [Col. 1066C] and banished him to the island of Patmos, was condemned by the senate and slain in his little palace. Aurelius Commodus, excessively lustful, died by strangulation in the house of a Vestal. Julian killed his successor Aelius Pertinax. This same Julian was killed at the Milvian Bridge. Aurelius Antoninus, his successor, fell by the sword at Edessa. Macrinus, succeeding Antoninus, breathed out his life by the sword in a military mutiny. Marcus Aurelius succeeded him and fell by the sword with his mother. Alexander succeeded Marcus, Maximus Alexander, Julian Maximus; Gordian succeeded Julian, and each of these three ended his life by the sword. Philip, the first among emperors to receive the faith of Christ, perished when treacherously slain by Decius together with his son Philip, who reigned with him [Col. 1066D]. The barbarians killed his successor Decius together with his son, who ruled with his father. Gallus and Gallus’s son Volusian succeeded him, and both fell by the sword. Valerian succeeded them, he who made blessed Sixtus and blessed Lawrence martyrs. Captured by Sapor, king of the Persians, and condemned to perpetual slavery, he ended his days in a most vile death. After him the emperor Quintillus was killed. Aurelius was struck by God; Probus was slain in a military [Col. 1067A] mutiny. Varius was killed through the treachery of his father-in-law Aper; Diocletian was removed from imperial dignity; Julian the Apostate was killed from heaven by the lance of blessed Mercurius [Note: [Col. 1067] Damas., *Oration* 1, *On Images*; Amphilochius, *Life of St Basil*; *Tripartite History*, Book 8, ch. 14.]. Valens, persecutor of blessed Ambrose, was burned by the Goths in the hut where he had hidden himself in fear.

Such are the ends of rich and great men. Hence, as Valerius Maximus testifies [Note: [Col. 1067] Book 9, ch. 12], certainty of death ought to be more desirable to a rich man than hanging in suspense amid the various and terrible contingencies of life, uncertain of impending destruction. Leaving the rich aside, therefore, because my discourse cannot enter into them, I shall turn to the poor. May the Lord accept the voluntary offerings of my mouth [Note: [Col. 1067] Ps. 118], that the Spirit of the Lord may be upon me to preach the gospel to the poor [Note: [Col. 1067] Matt. 11], and that, in his sweetness, God may prepare for the poor [Col. 1067B] whatever is expedient for salvation both for me and for them [Note: [Col. 1067] Ps. 67].

Let the poor therefore run, because theirs is the kingdom of heaven [Note: [Col. 1067] Matt. 5]. The angels await them—indeed, the Lord of angels. The house is not yet full; those by whom the wedding feast may be filled are still awaited. Let us run, brothers, but in such a way that we may attain the prize. Let us redeem the time, because the days are evil [Note: [Col. 1067] Eph. 5]. The kingdom of heaven is offered to us. Do not trust in princes [Note: [Col. 1067] Ps. 145]. Follow the counsel of the Most High, and do not let the counsels of princes mislead you. The Lord rejects the counsels of princes, but the counsel of the Lord remains forever [Note: [Col. 1067] Ps. 32]. He will work in us both willing and accomplishing according to his good pleasure [Note: [Col. 1067] Phil. 2].

Nor should the journey’s labour frighten us. For he who devises toil in commandment [Note: [Col. 1067] Ps. 93] prepares rest and eternal life for us through toil. We are sent by the Lord [Col. 1067C] to act as ambassadors for him. Let us not refuse the Lord’s command with Jonah [Note: [Col. 1067] ch. 2], lest we be plunged into the sea and swallowed by the whale. Let no one, I ask, consider undertaking this pilgrimage difficult. If he is strong, in leaving his native country in spirit he does not depart from his country:

> Every land is a homeland to the brave, as the sea is to fish,  
> And whatever lies open in the empty world is to a bird.

[Note: [Col. 1067] Ovid, *Fasti* 1.]

Abraham leaves his land and kindred so that he may grow among the nations [Note: [Col. 1067] Gen. 12]. Jacob, leaving the land of his birth and crossing the Jordan with a staff, returns with two companies [Note: [Col. 1067] Gen. 32]. Joseph, sold by his brothers, is set over Egypt [Note: [Col. 1067] Gen. 40]. Moses, exposed by his parents, is adopted as a son by Pharaoh’s daughter [Col. 1067D] [Note: [Col. 1067] Exod. 2]. Let us seize heaven by force, for from the days of John the Baptist the kingdom of heaven suffers violence [Note: [Col. 1067] Matt. 11]. And what greater force is there than to obtain by repentance what is denied us by our nature and by God’s justice?

Let others amass wealth, provided that in judgment they do not despoil widows and plunder the poor. Are not these men, I ask, sacrificing the Son before the eyes of the Father whenever, from the substance of the needy, they make an offering before the Father of the poor [Col. 1068A] and Judge of widows [Note: [Col. 1067] Matt. 25]? Certainly an offering from robbery is abominable to God, as he himself says: “I the Lord love judgment and hate robbery in a burnt offering” [Note: [Col. 1067] Isa. 61]. Hence griffins, sea-eagles, vultures, kites, and the other predatory birds are never accepted in the sacrifice of the Lord [Note: [Col. 1067] Deut. 14]. The beginning of this pilgrimage ought not to proceed from wrongs or plunder. Solomon says: “The beginning of a good way is to do justice, and it is more acceptable to God than to offer sacrifices” [Note: [Col. 1067] Prov. 16]. I fear that those who now delight in violent plunder may someday become plunder themselves. It is Isaiah’s word: “You who plunder, know that you shall be plundered” [Note: [Col. 1067] Isa. 33].

O love of money, O moth of hearts, rust of minds, most grievous sickness of souls, overthrow of virtues, offspring of vices, turning love [Col. 1068B] into hatred and God’s grace into contempt! How you blind the hearts of the rich, so that the more they have, the less they think they possess! But he for whom Christ is enough lacks nothing; for one to whom a portion in the land of the living is offered, possession of earthly things must be despised. If the rich fear want, let not the poor, I ask, be afraid. It is written: “What the wicked fears shall come upon him” [Note: [Col. 1067] Prov. 10]; and “he who fears frost, snow shall come upon him” [Note: [Col. 1067] Job 6]. Behold: sinners, abounding in this world, have obtained riches [Note: [Col. 1067] Ps. 72], and yet one frequently hears of them: “The rich have lacked and hungered, but those who seek the Lord shall lack no good thing” [Note: [Col. 1067] Ps. 33].

Certainly poverty is not an ignoble title before God. The only poverty displeasing to God [Col. 1068C] is that borne with rancour and complaint, as the Wise Man says: “The most evil poverty is in the mouth of the ungodly” [Note: [Col. 1067] Ecclus. 13]. Frequent experience teaches that victory is granted to Christ’s soldiers not through money, nor through a multitude of armed men, nor through the strength of combatants, but through the power of the Lord of hosts. For the Lord is the strength of his people [Note: [Col. 1067] Ps. 27]. The Lord is strong; the Lord is mighty in battle [Note: [Col. 1067] Ps. 23], of whom it is written: “You are the glory of their strength” [Note: [Col. 1067] Ps. 88].

Would that this money had never existed: it will have no happy outcome, and through it the salvation of a thousand souls has either been delayed or taken away. The Lord is not for sale, so as to be bought with money; but we are for sale, sold under sin. For those who are to labour for Christ’s inheritance and do not wish to receive an inheritance on earth, an eternal inheritance [Col. 1068D] is prepared in heaven. For when he gives sleep to his beloved, behold, the inheritance of the Lord [Note: [Col. 1067] Ps. 126]. They shall hear: “You are those who have remained with me in my temptations” [Note: [Col. 1067] Luke 22]; it will not be said, “You who collected money.” The Lord considers not how much, but from how much a person gives. For, as is read in Ecclesiasticus: “A man’s substance is according to his heart” [Note: [Col. 1067] Ecclus. 38]. The offering of the widow was more acceptable to the Lord than that of the great. “Each one,” says the Lord, “put into the treasury from what he had in abundance; [Col. 1069A] but she put into the treasury all that she had, her whole livelihood” [Note: [Col. 1069] Mark 12].

The Lord has no need of our goods, nor does he conquer through a multitude, but through a few. When Christ was sought for death by the chief priests and the Jewish people, and there was discussion of buying swords, he chose that the twelve should be content with two swords [Note: [Col. 1069] Luke 22]. The arms of Alexander and Caesar are today surpassed in famous renown by that single sword of Peter with which he cut off the servant’s ear [Note: [Col. 1069] John 18], as a certain wise man says: “The outcome of wars lies not in the number or boldness of the strong, but in the good pleasure of him who disposes all things according to the decision of his will.” Did the children of Israel possess the land by their own sword [Note: [Col. 1069] Ps. 42]? How did one pursue a thousand, and two put ten [Col. 1069B] thousand to flight [Note: [Col. 1069] Deut. 21]? Was it not because the Lord sold them and the Lord shut them up?

He who dwells in heaven and looks upon the lowly [Note: [Col. 1069] Ps. 112], who calls things that are not as though they were [Note: [Col. 1069] Rom. 4], who chose the despised to confound the strong [Note: [Col. 1069] 1 Cor. 1], has delivered that land at times through provincial foot-soldiers, at times through a woman’s hand, from the most grievous persecutions of oppressors. Therefore it now seems likely that, having rejected the great men of the earth to whom the Lord had offered the vows of this pilgrimage, he chose men of humbler reputation, reserving for them, to the humiliation of the powerful, the triumphant outcome of this enterprise and the glory of the whole undertaking.

If the emperor of the Romans and the king of the Franks, who at one time professed the vow of this journey [Col. 1069C], had advanced in chosen smallness and devout humility, rather than in a heavy and undisciplined multitude, they would have cast off the oppressor’s yoke and established enduring peace in the land. But if our princes, perhaps following counsel of higher prudence, had decided to postpone this journey so long, why, I ask, did they not choose prudent and energetic men to go ahead, collect provisions, test the dangers, arrange crossings, and reconnoitre the enemy’s strength? Indeed, each abounds in his own opinion; but let all, individually and together, know that whose way is acceptable to the Lord, he himself will direct that person’s steps. For of such a person it is written: “A man’s steps shall be directed by God, and he will delight in his way” [Note: [Col. 1069] Ps. 36].

May he who is the way, the truth, and the life [Note: [Col. 1069] John 14] bring back our cross-marked men from error and pathlessness into the way of truth and life. May he deliver the land which he chose as a dwelling for himself [Col. 1070A] [Note: [Col. 1069] Ps. 119], which by inhabiting it he made as it were another heaven, which he illumined by his miracles, initiated by his sacraments, established by his preaching, and finally reddened with his blood; which he made glorious by the splendour of his blessed resurrection and ascension, not merely preferring it to the whole world, but through it marvelously and mercifully acquiring the whole world for himself.

Jesus Christ, may anger pass into grace, storm into a breeze, judgment into dispensation, affliction into refreshment, and striking into healing. Though you are God, the Lord of vengeance [Note: [Col. 1069] Ps. 93], yet you are man, our brother, and the Father of mercies. These are your words: “I will kill, and I will make alive; I will strike, and I will heal” [Note: [Col. 1069] Deut. 32]. Grant, according to the riches of that most abundant love in which you redeemed us, that after the terrible scourges of your discipline the people [Col. 1070C] whom you acquired may breathe again under your mercy. May the groaning of the fettered move you [Note: [Col. 1069] Ps. 78]; or, according to the word of Moses: “Avenge the blood of your servants, and be merciful to the land of your people” [Note: [Col. 1069] Ibid.].

[Col. 1069]

## INSTRUCTION IN THE CATHOLIC FAITH SENT BY ALEXANDER III, ROMAN PONTIFF, TO THE SULTAN OF ICONIUM. (G)

[Col. 1069C] Alexander, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the Sultan of Iconium: that he may acknowledge the truth and, once acknowledged, preserve it.

[Col. 1069D] From your letters and the trustworthy report of your messengers, we have learned that you desire to be converted to Christ. Since you have already received, as we hear, the Pentateuch of Moses, the prophecy of Isaiah and Jeremiah, the Epistles of Paul, and the Gospels of John and Matthew, you request that a certain orthodox man be sent to you, through whom you may be more fully instructed in the law of Christ, as it were in our stead. We, gladly concurring in the Lord with your request, which is greatly commendable, shall arrange to send to Your Excellency such persons as may discharge among you the office of apostolic authority in sound doctrine and salutary [Col. 1070D] instruction; and whose conduct and merits may not depart from the integrity and purity of Gospel teaching.

But because you ask that the sequence and tenor of our faith be disclosed to you in writing, rejoicing in your desire, we shall set it forth to you in a certain brief summary, as if by pointing with the finger. Believe devoutly and hold faithfully, therefore, that there is one God: yet so that, in the ascription of divinity, there is unity of substance and Trinity of persons. For God is Father, God is [Col. 1071A] Son, and God is Holy Spirit; but Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one. Yet the persons are distinguished in this way: the Father is not the Son; the Son is not the Holy Spirit; and the Holy Spirit is neither Father nor Son. The matter is indeed difficult to understand and exceeds the reach of human reason; yet it has all the more excellently the merit of faith, the more difficult it is to believe.

Moreover, although we can find nothing that bears an explicit image of the unity which is in God and of the supreme Trinity, nor indeed can words be found by which we may speak worthily concerning that supreme essence, nevertheless we do what we can. Stammering, as it were, by words suited to transitory things, we disclose to you the ineffable reality. The Apostle Paul says that the invisible things of God are perceived and discerned through the things that have been made, as are also his everlasting power and divinity [Col. 1071B] [Note: [Col. 1071] Rom. 1]. Consider, then, the human mind and the body of the sun, and you will see, in some manner—although faintly and as with a half-closed eye—a certain likeness of the Trinity.

In the human mind there are understanding, memory, and will. We call memory mind; we call understanding mind; we call will mind. Memory, understanding, and will are one mind; yet memory is neither understanding nor will. In the same body of the sun I see a ray, feel heat, and recognize brightness. These three are of one essence, yet none of them is another.

So also in that ineffable and uncircumscribed [Col. 1071C] glory of the Godhead, the Son is from the Father and the Holy Spirit from both. Although the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are of the same substance, power, and glory, they are not three gods; rather, in three persons they are one substance and one power, and in one substance there are three persons. This profession of our faith derived its origin not only from Christ and his followers, but had its foundation in Moses, the patriarchs, and the prophets.

In the book of Moses the unity of the divine essence is declared, where it is said: “Hear, O Israel: the Lord your God is one God” [Note: [Col. 1071] Deut. 6.]. And again: “I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt; you shall have no strange gods besides me” [Note: [Col. 1071] Deut. 5.]. Yet the plurality of persons is plainly suggested there [Col. 1071D] where he says: “Let us make man in our image and likeness” [Note: [Col. 1071] Gen. 1.]. For since the Word is the Son of God, as John, whose Gospel you accept, declares when he says: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. This was in the beginning with God. All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made” [Note: [Col. 1071] John 1.], you see that the Father’s speech is addressed to the Son and the Holy Spirit when he uses these two plurals, “let us make” and “our.” For through the Word and the Holy Spirit [Col. 1072A] the Lord God made all things. As the prophet David recalls: “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the spirit of his mouth all their power” [Note: [Col. 1071] Ps. 32.].

The same prophet also elegantly suggests the mystery of the Trinity, where in the same verse he repeats and emphasizes this name, “God,” three times, saying: “May God bless us, our God; may God bless us, and may all the ends of the earth fear him” [Note: [Col. 1071] Ps. 66.]. The aforementioned John says in his canonical Epistle: “There are three who bear testimony in heaven: the Father, the Word, and the Holy Spirit; and these three are one” [Note: [Col. 1071] 1 John 5.]. Isaiah too, the prophet whom you accept, testifies that he heard the seraphim crying: “Holy, holy, holy, Lord God of Sabaoth” [Note: [Col. 1071] Isa. 6.]. Why does he repeat “holy” a third time, unless to suggest the Trinity of persons in the Lord God of hosts?

[Col. 1072B] Therefore, in the supreme and most blessed Trinity there is the Father, who begot the Son; the Son, who was begotten by the Father; and the Holy Spirit, who proceeds from both. Nor in that begetting or procession has the divine substance suffered any loss of fullness or diminution in the Father or the Son. For just as light is taken from light without diminishing the light from which it is taken, so the Son was begotten equal to the Father, and the Holy Spirit proceeds from both, coequal with each. Yet human reason does not attain the manner of this begetting or procession. Hence, although Isaiah knew concerning the Son’s generation, he nevertheless knew its manner to be inexpressible: “Who,” he says, “shall declare his generation?” [Note: [Col. 1071] Isa. 53.]

The prophet David speaks thus concerning this generation in [Col. 1072C] the person of the Son: “The Lord said to me: You are my Son; today I have begotten you” [Note: [Col. 1071] Ps. 2.]. Solomon too, David’s son, whom God wonderfully enlightened with knowledge and understanding, speaks in the person of Christ—who, as Paul says, is “the power of God and the wisdom of God” [Note: [Col. 1071] 1 Cor. 1.]—in the book of Wisdom, if indeed you accept it, as follows: “The Lord possessed me at the beginning of his ways, from eternity; I was established before the earth was made, before he made anything. The abysses did not yet exist, and I was conceived. When he prepared the heavens, I was present; when he laid the foundations of the earth, I was with him, ordering all things” [Note: [Col. 1071] Prov. 8.].

The Apostle Paul too bears witness to the Holy Spirit—indeed, to the whole Trinity—when he says: “God sent the spirit of his Son into our hearts” [Note: [Col. 1071] Gal. 4.]. And elsewhere: “If [Col. 1072D] the spirit of him who raised Jesus dwells in you, he shall also give life to your mortal bodies, because of his spirit dwelling in you” [Note: [Col. 1071] Rom. 8.]. If you desire Christ’s testimony concerning the unity of essence and the Trinity of persons, he himself says in the Gospel: “I and the Father are one” [Note: [Col. 1071] John 10.]. Christ also says to his disciples: “Go, baptize all nations in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” [Note: [Col. 1071] Matt. 28.].

Therefore, when man had lost paradise through disobedience and had deserved the miseries of hell forever, the Son was sent by the Father [Col. 1073A]; and it was fitting that the Son, rather than the Father, should be sent. For the Father was from no one, while the Son was from someone; therefore it was more fitting that he who had had a Father from eternity should have a mother in time. For it was written in David’s Psalm: “There is none to redeem, nor to save” [Note: [Col. 1073] Ps. 7.]; “There is none who does good, not even one” [Note: [Col. 1073] Ps. 13.]; “There is none who can give propitiation for his own soul, much less for another’s” [Note: [Col. 1073] Ps. 48.]. The Son was sent by God the Father so that man might die for man, pay as man the tribute of death for captive man, and redeem him as God by heavenly power.

The patriarchs had desired his coming; the prophets had foretold it; and, bearing his delay impatiently, they continually complained: “When will he come? [Col. 1073B] When shall we see him? Give, Lord, the reward to those who wait for you, so that your prophets may be found faithful” [Note: [Col. 1073] Sir. 36.]. “Would that,” Isaiah says, “you, Lord, would tear open the heavens and come down” [Note: [Col. 1073] Isa. 54.]. And David: “Lord, incline your heavens and come down” [Note: [Col. 1073] Ps. 143.]. Moreover, Isaiah testifies that the angels of peace wept bitterly because our salvation was delayed [Note: [Col. 1073] Isa. 33.].

The same Isaiah, speaking more plainly of Christ’s birth, says: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and his name shall be called Emmanuel” [Note: [Col. 1073] Isa. 7.]. But since Mary traced her origin from Jesse, the same prophet clearly sets forth the birth of Mary, and through Mary the birth of Christ, together with the fullness of spiritual grace in Christ, when he says: “A rod shall go forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise from his root; and the Spirit [Col. 1073C] of the Lord shall rest upon him: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and might, the spirit of knowledge and godliness; and the spirit of the fear of the Lord shall fill him” [Note: [Col. 1073] Isa. 11.].

Therefore the Son of God was born from an incorrupt Virgin, just as the first Adam was fashioned from virgin and untouched earth, while the Holy Spirit worked in her and ineffably accomplished the work of our salvation. For the sacrament of the Lord’s incarnation is an unfathomable abyss. Yet many things happened to the ancient fathers in which a figure of this birth preceded it. For the fleece of Gideon was drenched with heavenly dew while the threshing-floor all around remained dry [Note: [Col. 1073] Judg. 6.]; this signifies the dew of the Holy Spirit in the Virgin, who for this purpose was specially and uniquely chosen beforehand by the Lord because of her humility. The Psalmist agrees with this when he says: “He shall descend like rain upon fleece” [Note: [Col. 1073D] Ps. 71.].

That fire appeared to Moses in the bush [Note: [Col. 1073] Exod. 3.] and the bush was not consumed by the fire signifies the integrity of Mary’s virginity. That, while the rods of the other tribes remained dry, Aaron’s rod—of whose stock the most blessed Virgin traced her origin—put forth leaves and flowers [Note: [Col. 1073] Num. 17.] pointed to the flower from Jesse’s rod prophesied by Isaiah: namely, the offspring of the incorrupt Virgin. Though we were enemies of God, we were reconciled through Christ’s coming [Note: [Col. 1073] Rom. 5.], as the prophet foretold: [Col. 1074A] “And there shall be peace in the land when he comes” [Note: [Col. 1073] Mic. 5.]. Therefore at his birth the angels sang the song of glorious peace: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” [Note: [Col. 1073] Luke 2.].

A new star also appeared to the Magi; and, according to historical testimony, a fountain of oil flowed from the ground into the Tiber at Rome. A temple formerly built in Rome, which the idols had foretold would not fall until a virgin gave birth, collapsed utterly on that very night [Note: [Col. 1073] Euc. in Chr.; Peter Damian, in a homily, in Surius, vol. VI.]. Likewise, the pool called Probatica at Jerusalem began then to be stirred at the angel’s coming and to confer healings [Note: [Col. 1073] John 5.]. The old Adam harmed us most grievously, but the new Adam benefited us more. His humility bestowed upon us more than the other’s pride had taken away.

For, as the Apostle Paul testifies, “the gift is not [Col. 1074B] as the offence” [Note: [Col. 1073] Rom. 5.]; the greatness of the benefit surpasses the measure of the loss. Him whom we formerly had as a terrible Lord and judge, we now have as a humble brother and neighbour. Therefore Christ, passing through the course of our mortality in hunger and thirst, weariness and pain, and every misery of this life, was at last betrayed by a disciple and sold like a worthless slave; he was scourged, spat upon, crowned with thorns, mocked, nailed to the timber, and condemned to a most shameful death. What he had not seized, he paid for; and voluntarily offering himself to death, he endured all things in humility, as Isaiah had once foretold: “In humility,” he says, “his judgment was taken away. He was led as a lamb to slaughter, and as a sheep before its shearer, [Col. 1074C] so he did not open his mouth” [Note: [Col. 1073] Isa. 53; Acts 8.].

Thus he who as a little child had once been offered in the Temple by righteous Simeon [Note: [Col. 1073] Luke 2.] raised his hands to the Father on the cross, at the evening of the Law and the end of its ceremonies, for our redemption, according to David’s words: “The lifting up of my hands is an evening sacrifice” [Note: [Col. 1073] Ps. 140.]. Thus the guilt which Adam had contracted through pride in delighting in the tree was removed through Christ’s humility in the bitterness of death; and, when blood without guilt had been shed, the bonds recording all sins were erased.

Indeed, the Lord could have provided another manner of redemption, but none more fitting for his kindness and our salvation presented itself.
