Since man, according to the due consequence of his transgression, was held captive by the devil, justice required that he should not be rescued by force, but that he who had fallen through pride should rise again through his own humility if he could—or, since he could not do so by his own, at least through another’s humility. Thus Christ, the innocent one whom the paschal lamb under the Law signified, offered himself as a saving sacrifice for us. And although the Law of Moses had set a goat or sheep as the price for redeeming a person from sin [Note: [Col. 1073] Lev. 4.], Christ, through whom grace and truth came [Note: [Col. 1073] John 1.], judging that the shadowy ceremonies of the Law were insufficient for salvation and valuing man more highly than the blood of sheep, goat, or calf, [Col. 1075A] offered his own blood and death for our salvation. Thus, having obtained eternal redemption, he entered the sanctuary once for all as the supreme and true high priest [Note: [Col. 1075] Heb. 9.].

Accordingly, the mighty Lion of the tribe of Judah opened the book and loosed its seals [Note: [Col. 1075] Rev. 5.]; and what the legal sacrifices could not accomplish, he accomplished: he removed the turning sword and opened the entrance to paradise, which had been closed to all the ancients [Note: [Col. 1075] Gen. 3.]. For formerly, at the death of the high priest, those who had fled to cities of refuge were customarily granted a safe return to their own homes [Note: [Col. 1075] Exod. 35.].

Formerly man was accustomed to protest and say: “Why does the Lord demand more of me than of other creatures? What has he done for me? What has he laboured for me? He spoke, and I was made. Like beasts, trees, and all other things, he created me by a nod of his power and the mere decision of his command.” But now [Col. 1075B] “the mouth of those who speak iniquity has been stopped” [Note: [Col. 1075] Ps. 62.]. For a person may not ignore how much the Lord has done for him—the Lord who, in order to redeem a slave, did not spare his own Son [Note: [Col. 1075] Rom. 8.].

Moreover, in redeeming man he encountered labour and pain, because for our ungodliness and his mercy, for our need and his humility, he endured hunger, thirst, weariness, treachery, reproaches, scourges, the crown of thorns, nails and spear, the shame of the cross, and the agony of death. “Shall not my soul therefore be subject to God?” [Note: [Col. 1075] Ps. 61.] Shall not all my bones say: “Lord, who is like you?” [Note: [Col. 1075] Ps. 34.]—so that thanksgiving and the voice of praise may henceforth never cease from my mouth and heart? How could the wisdom of God have dealt more mercifully with me, or invited me more sweetly and effectively [Col. 1075C] to love him?

Furthermore, the souls of the righteous, which in respect of their prerogative of origin fall not far short of the dignity of heavenly spirits, all descended to hell. It was fitting that God should at length remember his image and, in accordance with the proclamations of his prophets concerning the souls of the elect, repair the loss brought about by the angelic fall. Thus, in this dispensation of our salvation, Christ’s love has been made inwardly known to us. Although in the Law of Moses he gave us love of God and neighbour as commandments, in the school of Gospel teaching he impressed the same more frequently and forcefully by words, and finally by the demonstration of his deed. “No one has greater love than this: that one lay down his life for his friends” [Note: [Col. 1075] John 15.].

Therefore he gave us grounds for loving him, since he anticipated us [Col. 1075D] in loving us; and he demands nothing else from us except that we love him from the heart. Surely he is inhuman and cruel who does not remember his mercy, who does not love from affection a Lord so merciful, and who, if need be, does not willingly expose himself to the danger of death for him.

But Christ, having died and been buried, rose from the dead on the third day, as he had foretold to his disciples while he lived. Thereafter he appeared to them frequently; conversing and eating with them, and showing the wounds of his hands, feet, and side, he removed from the hearts of some, who still wavered in faith, the wound of doubt by displaying his wounds. [Col. 1076A] Having therefore lived visibly with them for forty days [Note: [Col. 1075] Acts 1.], and with them accompanying him, he came to the Mount of Olives; and while they watched, he was lifted up and ascended to the Father. We believe that he is at the Father’s right hand, and at the common resurrection we await him as judge of the living and the dead.

Therefore, as our Lord Jesus Christ willed and had to die for a time because he was man, so he was able and had to rise after death; so that the devil, who had overcome man, might be overcome by man and, once defeated, be put to shame. Let unbelievers and transgressors blush who burst forth rashly into these mad assertions: “If Christ was God, how could he die? If he was man, how could he rise?” Certainly he was God and man: because he was man, he had to die; because he was God, he was able to rise.

[Col. 1076B] It was also beneficial for us that, though he deigned voluntarily to die under an unjust judge, he was able and willing by rising to overcome death. And just as the devil through his agents rashly and violently laid hands upon his Lord, so he justly and judicially lost forever the dominion and tyranny which he had exercised over man. In this fitting manner, he who had conquered man was conquered by man; and he who had overcome at the tree was himself powerfully and wisely overcome at the tree, that is, at the tree of the cross, by God-and-man Christ Jesus—so that he might be loved as a brother by man and feared as God.

Moreover, it was necessary that he who created us should recreate us, and that he who made us should, by redeeming us, restore [Col. 1076C] and repair us when lost; lest we be bound to worship one God as Creator and be required to venerate another as redeemer, and thus serve two masters. And it was necessary and fitting that the Son—not the Father and not the Holy Spirit—should be incarnate, because man, namely Adam, had presumed to liken himself to the Son, aspiring and wishing to know good and evil as God [Note: [Col. 1075] Gen. 2.]. The Son therefore seemed to be the cause, as Abel’s holiness was the cause of Cain’s envy and thus of Abel’s death [Note: [Col. 1075] Gen. 4.].

Therefore our Son said, as it were Jonah, when he said: “I am the one who has sinned; cast me into the sea” [Note: [Col. 1075] Jonah 1.]. A slight sacrifice and burnt offering is insufficient for expiating so great a crime as man had committed. “Behold, I come; I myself come, because at the head of the book it is written of me that I should do your will” [Note: [Col. 1075] Ps. 39; Heb. 10.]; behold, I am here [Col. 1076D] to be sacrificed.

Again, if such a work, namely the redemption of man, were entrusted solely to an angel, it would not be safe, since pride made Lucifer an angel of ill repute and suspicion. If it were entrusted to a man, it would likewise not be safe, since disobedience justly condemned the first man, Adam, as guilty. The angel was insufficient; man was defective: the one weak, the other feeble. Therefore it was fittingly arranged that man should free man from the jaws of the devil, aided by the help of divinity, lest so arduous and noble an undertaking should fail; indeed, rather, so that it might attain a more unassailable [Col. 1077A] successful conclusion, and so that the angelic order, mutilated through the fall of Lucifer and his accomplices, might happily be restored.

Great therefore, and most worthy of all praise, was the most blessed mother and Virgin Mary, who brought forth to the world so great a mediator of God and man and deserved to bear our Saviour; among all the women the world has had, she deserved to have neither a first before her, nor an equal, nor a successor after her. For she conceived without shame, gave birth without pain, and departed this life without corruption, according to the word of the angel—indeed, of God through the angel—so that she might be shown to be full, not half-full, of grace [Note: [Col. 1077] Luke 1.]; and so that God her Son might faithfully fulfil the ancient commandment which he had formerly taught, namely, to honour father and mother; and so that Christ’s virginal flesh, [Col. 1077B] assumed from the flesh of his virgin mother, might not differ from her whole being.

From the aforesaid articles of Christian faith [Col. 1078A] a venerable foundation rises to lofty heights. This is the ladder of the catholic religion, by which a person is granted ascent to the homeland of eternal brightness. Therefore, if you desire to come forth from darkness into light and embrace Christ’s most saving law, you must consecrate the first beginnings of Christian life by baptismal washing, so that, putting off in the waters of regeneration the oldness of sin, you may be reborn into a new innocence of soul and infancy of life, and may become a participant in that heavenly glory which ear has not heard, nor eye seen, nor has entered into the heart of man [Note: [Col. 1077] 1 Cor. 2.]: so abundant that it cannot be exhausted; so great that it cannot be comprehended; so manifold that it cannot be numbered; so precious that it cannot be valued; so enduring that it cannot be ended. God has promised it [Col. 1078B] to those who love him [Note: [Col. 1077] Jas. 1.] and follow his footsteps little by little. Farewell; live, and may Christ live in you.

[Col. 1077]

# BOOK ON SACRAMENTAL CONFESSION

[Col. 1077B] You asked me to set down for you, in my usual concise style and on separate sheets, something concerning the power of confession. Thus a spring asks water from a stream, a master knowledge from a disciple, a contemplative from an active person, a bishop from an archdeacon, a spiritual person from a carnal one, a saint from a sinner, a wise person from one who is ignorant. The affectionate devotion of my heart indeed gives birth in me to the desire for this work. But, [Col. 1077C] as the prophet says, “she who is in labour has no strength” [Note: [Col. 1077] 4 Kings 19.]. I do what I can; and although my desire may fall short of the limits of my ability, yet may my will, overflowing in its vows and heaped-up charity, make up for my imperfection.

I shall therefore perform the office of a whetstone, which is blunt and yet sharpens iron. And, to use the word of the Wise Man though I am less wise: “What I learned without guile I communicate without envy” to your holiness [Note: [Col. 1077] Wis. 7.]. I begin, therefore, prophesying nothing from my own spirit, but confirming by the authority of the holy Fathers those matters which the present treatise requires me to expound. For I have gathered crumbs that fell from the table of my masters [Note: [Col. 1077] Matt. 15.]; and, with Ruth the Moabitess, I have collected in the field of Boaz ears of grain that escaped the reapers’ hands [Note: [Col. 1077] Ruth 2.], in the hope that, when they are threshed, an ephah-measure may be found in them [Note: [Col. 1077] ibid.], from [Col. 1077D] which pilgrims in the valley of weeping, confessing to the Lord, may make for themselves bread of tears.

The Lord spoke to Moses, saying: “A man in whose skin a mottled discoloration appears shall come to the priest and show himself to him” [Note: [Col. 1077] Lev. 13.]. By this we are given to understand that confession of the sin signified by leprosy must be made to the priest. For Augustine says [Note: [Col. 1077] Homily 49.]: “Let no one say to himself, ‘I confess secretly and do penance [Col. 1078B] before God.’ For if this confession is sufficient, then the keys were given to Peter for no purpose. It was also said in vain: ‘Whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven’” [Note: [Col. 1077] Matt. 16.].

Certainly all things are washed in confession [Note: [Col. 1077] St Bernard, Sermon 2, *On the Resurrection*.]; and as faith of the heart is unto righteousness, so confession of the mouth is unto salvation [Note: [Col. 1077] Rom. 10.]. Great is the power of confession, because, as blessed Ambrose writes in his [Col. 1078C] book *On Paradise*: “Confession washes the soul; confession opens paradise. This is the second plank after shipwreck, and the baptism of repentance.” Devout confession is like a strong draught, searching hearts and kidneys, reaching even to the division of soul and spirit, and draining harmful affections from the marrow of the soul.

But just as sins return through ingratitude, so dead works revive through confession. Hence Augustine says in the book *On Repentance* [Note: [Col. 1077] ch. 14, distinction 3.]: “It is pious to believe that the grace of God received, which destroys former evils in a person, also rewards good works, so that, after it has destroyed what it did not find to be its own, it may love and cherish the good which it planted even in the sinner.” The Apostle says to the Hebrews: “Laying the foundation of repentance from dead works” [Note: [Col. 1077] Heb. 6.]. Dead works are those which we performed [Col. 1078D] while we were in sin [Note: [Col. 1077] St Chrysostom, Epistle 5 to Theodorus after his fall, distinction 3, chapter *Talis*.]. According to Gregory’s testimony, just as these are rendered void by sin, so they live again through repentance.

Therefore let confession precede the other remedies of our salvation, that we may “anticipate the face of the Lord in confession” [Note: [Col. 1077] Ps. 94.], as it is written: “Sing beforehand to the Lord in confession” [Note: [Col. 1077] Ps. 146.]. As an auspicious sign of this, Judah—whose name means “one confessing,” or “confession”—went before the people [Col. 1079A] of Israel in the crossing of the Red Sea, by a certain privilege of dignity [Note: [Col. 1079] Jerome, *On the Epistle to the Galatians*.]. This is the second circumcision, which occurred at Gilgal [Note: [Col. 1079] Josh. 5.], a name meaning “sanctification.” For confession is our sanctification; thus the Psalmist says: “When Israel came out, etc., Judah became his sanctification” [Note: [Col. 1079] Ps. 113.].

Such is the efficacy of confession that, if a sinner exposes his guilt by confessing it, God covers it, excuses the person accusing himself, and forgives the one who acknowledges his sin, according to Solomon’s testimony: “He who conceals his crimes shall not prosper; but he who confesses shall obtain mercy” [Note: [Col. 1079] Prov. 28.]. From concealing and suppressing sin there arises a certain stony obstinacy of heart; for such persons heaven becomes bronze and earth iron in their prayers, so that they are like the mountains of Gilboa, upon which neither dew nor rain falls [Note: [Col. 1079] 2 Kings 1.]. Their wickedness [Col. 1079B] has dried up the dew of mercy, the fountain of compassion, and the streams of grace.

Therefore, in anger, the Lord leaves them to their desires, so that they may go after their own devices [Note: [Col. 1079] Ps. 80.] and store up wrath for themselves on the day of dreadful judgment [Note: [Col. 1079] Rom. 2.]. Again, the conscience of the wretched person is like a den of hedgehog and lioness; there demons, screech-owls, and shaggy creatures encounter one another, while the apostate spirit takes seven spirits more wicked than himself to dwell there with him [Note: [Col. 1079] Luke 11.].

Unhappy man, why do you hide yourself from the Lord’s face in imitation of Adam’s transgression? Why do you disguise a deadly wound? The ulcer of a corrupt conscience which you now cover will one day be publicly disclosed amid your great shame, when you stand naked before the tribunal of the dreadful Judge in the sight of all the saints; for nothing is hidden that shall not there be revealed. Then those who suppressed their crimes will say to the mountains, “Fall upon us,” and to the hills, “Cover us” [Note: [Col. 1079] Hos. 10.]. For the secrets of hearts will be manifest; and because of shame and the terrifying sight of the divine majesty, they would wish, if permitted, to flee, even to be plunged into the dark abyss of a chasm.

Therefore the child of eternal weeping, who now despises God as he counsels, warns, and mercifully reproves, will hear him angry, avenging, judging terribly, and condemning without remedy. It is most beneficial to confess to the Lord, because he is good, because his mercy endures for ever [Note: [Col. 1079] Ps. 105.]. Therefore blessed Job says: “I will not spare my mouth; I will let loose my speech against myself. I will speak in the bitterness of my soul; [Col. 1079D] I will say to God: Do not condemn me” [Note: [Col. 1079] Job 10.]. He knew that, just as God is judge and avenger of those who hide their sins, so he is advocate of those who confess. Nor can we justify our case more effectively than by undertaking the judge’s role in accusing and punishing ourselves. “If we judged ourselves,” says the Apostle, “we should certainly not be judged” [Note: [Col. 1079] 1 Cor. 11.].

The highest counsel for salvation, therefore, is to humble oneself under God’s mighty hand, present oneself as wretched before the eyes of his mercy, and subject one’s own will in all things to his will. [Col. 1080A] For “life is in his will” [Note: [Col. 1079] Ps. 29.]. Confession is therefore salutary because, according to Jerome’s testimony [Note: [Col. 1079] On Ecclesiastes, ch. 10, and Epistle to Pammachius and Oceanus.], “No one is saved without confession.” And it should be noted that confession without repentance is in one case false, as in Esau and Saul; in another desperate, as in Cain and Judas; but it is saving in Peter and Magdalene.

Four things commonly hinder the grace of confession: shame, fear, hope, and despair. Whoever lies beneath these four stones has been four days in the tomb. For “confession perishes from the dead as from one who is not” [Note: [Col. 1079] Sir. 17.]. Therefore let merciful Jesus come and cry: “Lazarus, come forth” [Note: [Col. 1079] John 11.]. The one who comes forth is the person who opens the inner things of his heart through confession. If shame prevents confession, let him remember how the books of consciences will be opened before all on the day of judgment, when the Lord reveals [Col. 1080B] “the hidden things of darkness” [Note: [Col. 1079] 1 Cor. 4.]. And just as now no one hides from his heat [Note: [Col. 1079] Ps. 18.], so then there will be no one who can hide from his brightness. Therefore let one not be ashamed to say what one was not ashamed to do; rather, let one be humbled by useful shame, so that among the splendours of the saints one may glory in the merit of one’s humility.

Against fear of penance, which seems unbearable, set the memory of Gehenna, the fear of unquenchable fire, the worm that does not die, deadly stench, and pain without interruption or end. Let the brief remedy not seem more grievous than the punishment of Gehenna. “It is fearful to fall into the hands of the living God” [Note: [Col. 1079] Heb. 10.]. Therefore let temporal punishment settle the account with eternal punishment, and let the person patiently bear the lashes of the tormentor.

But if he hopes in length [Col. 1080C] of life and presumes upon God’s mercy, let him consider how brief and uncertain his life is; how anyone who sins against the Holy Spirit, so far as he is concerned, nullifies the justice of the supreme Judge who judges all things. “You wickedly thought that I would be like you; I will rebuke you and set you before your own face” [Note: [Col. 1079] Ps. 49.]. Those who become such persons should not presume upon God’s mercy, as though God wished to ignore their deceptions and pass them over under a kind of pious dissimulation. “For this reason the wicked man has provoked God; for he said in his heart, ‘He will not require it’” [Note: [Col. 1079] Ps. 9.]. But the Lord certainly will require it, and will repay abundantly [Note: [Col. 1079] Ps. 30.] those of whom he no longer remembers, who have themselves been cast away from his hand [Note: [Col. 1079] Ps. 87.]. For iniquity has lied to itself [Note: [Col. 1079] Ps. 26.], but Truth will condemn eternally what falsehood temporarily concealed. As it is written [Col. 1080D]: “The enemies of the Lord have lied to him, and their time shall be for ages” [Note: [Col. 1079] Ps. 80.].

Despair, moreover, ruinously hurls the miserable person into every desire, so that he despises the dreadful judgments of God; for “when the sinner has come into the depths of evils, he despises” [Note: [Col. 1079] Prov. 18.]. Against this we set, O Lord God, the memory of the abundance of your sweetness [Note: [Col. 1079] Ps. 144.], which you showed to David the murderer, adulterer, and traitor; to Mary the sinner; to Peter when he denied you; to the Canaanite woman as she cried out; to the rebellious thief hanging on the cross; even to those who crucified you. Therefore let those who know your name hope in you, for you do not abandon those who seek you, O Lord [Col. 1081A] [Note: [Col. 1081] Ps. 9.]. Let no one, I beg, be swallowed up by excessive sorrow while Christ offers himself for pardon and from the cross invites us to friendly embraces.

It is the confession of the perfected, who have already escaped the perils of temptations, among whom there is nothing but thanksgiving and the voice of praise. Different is the confession of penitents, which both appeases God when angry and invites him, once appeased, to the benefits of more abundant grace. Hence in the Song of Isaiah: “I will give thanks to you, O Lord, because you were angry with me; your wrath has turned away, and you have comforted me.” [Note: [Col. 1081] Isa. 12.] Because of the threefold condition—of the righteous, penitents, and reprobate—there were written in the book given to Ezekiel [Note: [Col. 1081] Chap. 4.] a song, lamentations, and woe: a song [Col. 1081B] for those who praise, lamentations for those who confess, and woe for those who reject repentance, whom the punishment of eternal condemnation awaits. O foolish and slow to obtain God’s mercy! You are not commanded to cross seas. “The kingdom of God is within you” [Note: [Col. 1081] Luke 17.], you for whom the word is near, “in the mouth” and “in the heart” [Note: [Col. 1081] Deut. 30.]: that is, contrition of heart and confession with the mouth; you to whom the land of the living is offered, yet who “held the desirable land as nothing.” The Lord awaits your confession, and his ear has already heard the preparation of your heart. “I said,” says the Prophet, “I will confess,” and “you forgave the ungodliness of my sin.” [Note: [Col. 1081] Ps. 31.] God mercifully anticipates not merely your confession but even your desire to confess: the father sees the prodigal son returning “from afar” [Col. 1081C] [Note: [Col. 1081] Luke 15.]; and he is readier to pardon the wretch than the wretch is to ask pardon.

Jerome, to Rusticus [Note: [Col. 1081] Ep. 46, ch. 3.]: David, rebuked by the prophet Nathan, replied, “I have sinned”; and immediately deserved to hear: “And the Lord has taken away your sin.” [Note: [Col. 1081] II Kings 12.] And the same: “Thus Ahab and Jezebel committed their crime in the death of Naboth.” [Note: [Col. 1081] II Kings 4.] By Ahab’s conversion his punishment is deferred to his descendants, while Jezebel, unrepentant, is condemned by a present judgment. [Note: [Col. 1081] III Kings 21.] Therefore do not delay confession; for “you do not know what the coming day will bring forth.” [Note: [Col. 1081] Prov. 27.] You do not know whether on this very day sudden death may snatch you away and there be none to rescue you. A frequent judgment of heavenly wrath is that one who does not wish to repent when able may be unable to repent when he wishes. Of those who defer repentance until they have satisfied their desires it is written: “Woe to those who are pregnant and nursing in that day.” [Col. 1081D] [Note: [Col. 1081] Matt. 24.] Therefore confess your iniquities, that you may be justified. For, as blessed Ambrose testifies [Note: [Col. 1081] Bk. VI on Luke, and Bk. II *On Repentance*, ch. 6.]: “Confession justifies and empties out all the filth which a careless life has accumulated.” Nor should you fear to confess to the one whom God has appointed in his own place as your counsellor, according to Job’s testimony [Note: [Col. 1081] Chap. 6.]: “He who fears frost, snow shall come upon him.” Blush for a time, lest you blush eternally. If you are now ashamed, this shame will bring glory. For in return for this shame [Col. 1082A] and embarrassment, “you shall possess double in your land.” Why should you fear on the evil day? Is it not better to hear the voice of counsel than to await the thunder of that judicial sentence: “Go, you accursed, into eternal fire”? [Note: [Col. 1081] Matt. 25.]

But confession must be made in such a way that it runs through each individual iniquity and pours, as it were, ointment from the fat of devotion upon each wound from the sacrifice of the humbled heart. In the sacrifice, indeed, every inward part of the victim is washed. [Note: [Col. 1081] Lev. 1.] Augustine, *On Repentance* [Note: [Col. 1081] *On True and False Repentance*, ch. 9; Dist. *Vide poenit.*, ch. *Sunt plures*.]: “Repent concerning all things and each particular thing. God cast out seven demons at once; he healed the deaf and mute person at once; he also cast a legion out of another at once—teaching that, even if sins are a thousand, one must nevertheless repent of them all.” The Prophet says: “Every night I will wash my bed with my tears” [Col. 1082B] [Note: [Col. 1081] Ps. 6.], that is, I will wash my conscience for every individual iniquity. Tears washed Peter’s apostasy away. And if you wish to survey the examples of the New and Old Testaments [Note: [Col. 1081] Mark 7, 16; Luke 8, etc.], human reason cannot estimate their fruit and efficacy. Therefore let confessing persons bring down tears like a torrent, tears both of anguish and of sorrow.

For if all their blood and brain, and all the marrow of their bones, should flow and be poured out into penitential waters, still in the flood of many waters they will not draw near to God unless your eyes, O good Jesus, see them and make up what is lacking. Yet this should gladden the hope of the penitent: the tears of the sinful woman compelled your eyes, O Christ, [Col. 1082C] to tears. Therefore let tears be bread to the confessor day and night [Note: [Col. 1081] Exod. 15.]; let him eat the bread of sorrow and drink the water of bitterness, in the hope that God may look upon him and that, according to the saying of the great prophet, the waters of Marah may become sweet through the placing of wood. The confessor should disclose every circumstance of his sins: the cause, place, time, manner, and whatever magnifies the measure of guilt. Thus blessed Augustine writes in the book *On Repentance* [Note: [Col. 1081] Bk. *On True and False Repentance*, ch. 14.], saying: “Let the penitent set forth the quality of his crimes—in place, time, persistence, and the variety of persons—so that consideration may be given to the dignity of his office, the baseness of the deed, whether it was done in a sacred place, or on a day consecrated to festivity, prayer, or fasting, and by how great a temptation he was impelled.” [Note: [Col. 1081] Ch. *consid.*, Dist. 5, *On Repentance*.] For there are those who voluntarily offer themselves to sin, [Col. 1082D] who do not wait for temptation but anticipate pleasure, and who do everything to regain the life of their soul that they would do to avoid bodily death.

And, to provide a clear example of this matter: he who fornicates kills not only his own soul but also that soul which he has enticed into consent and participation in his iniquity. Moreover, he is the murderer of a third soul if, at his request, someone has intervened as a mediator of that shameful act. In your cheap and brief lust you have procured eternal punishment for many [Col. 1083A], and in the fire of your own desire you have kindled for them the unquenchable fire of destruction. The Lord, speaking under the figure of Babylon concerning the sinful soul, says: “As much as she exalted herself in her delights, give her so much torment and mourning.” [Note: [Col. 1083] Rev. 18.] You who must suffer such grave things for your own personal and particular sin—how much graver things do you expect for the sins of many, whose innocence you overturned by the cunning craft of seductive desire? Some of them perhaps have already died and been placed in hell, where death feeds upon them; where the unhappy suffer amid sulphurous flames in the furnace of Gehenna’s fire, tormented by an unquenchable flame like metals made incandescent and molten. Yet you, still wholly boiling with the flame of carnal desire, despise God’s terrible judgments and attend neither to their torments [Col. 1083B] nor to the impending day of your own condemnation. By corrupting with flattering and seductive promises a simple little woman—or a child, God forbid! for it is a dreadful abomination hateful to God—you have killed, for the pleasure of your own desire, the soul for which Christ died.

This is added to the accumulation of your destruction: since you have become a prince of Sodom and Gomorrah, disciples of your impurity will sit after you in the chair of pestilence, and the cancerous plague will creep through many, so that all the blood of those whom you have corrupted by blood, deed, or example may come upon you. Certainly the devil’s guilt was therefore unforgivable and his iniquity was found worthy of hatred, because in the evil that he committed at no one’s suggestion [Col. 1083C] there was the overthrow and ruin of many. Who can adequately estimate how execrably damnable before God and men was Herodian cruelty, which killed the children [Note: [Col. 1083] Matt. 2.], and Pharaoh’s wickedness, who drowned the little Hebrew children? [Note: [Col. 1083] Exod. 1.] Yet they were murderers not of souls but of bodies. How much more detestable, then, is the act—not merely the murder but the parricide—of those who have killed the souls of so many innocent persons? Without doubt, the more excellent the soul is than the body, the more wretched than Pharaoh are these betrayers, and the more damnable than Herod. Do you suppose that God will pass it over in silence and will not require from your hand the loss of his most noble creature amid your desires and impurities? Is this not the sin which the Law of Moses condemns to death [Note: [Col. 1083] Lev. 20.], [Col. 1083D] and which imperial law pursues with an avenging sword? [Note: [Col. 1083] Likewise the Julian law, *On Adultery and Public Judgments*.] God himself, who is accustomed mercifully to await sinners’ repentance, as though forgetful of his goodness, rained sulphurous fire from heaven in vengeance for so great a crime [Note: [Col. 1083] Gen. 19.], so that the stench of punishment might reveal the stench of sin, and so that, even with temporal punishment, the sufferings of eternal condemnation might begin.

You regard it as shameful to speak of so shameful a subject; but hell is more shameful. If the discourse is foul, it is fouler to rot in sin. Will you dare to do it, while I do not dare to speak of it? [Col. 1084A] God is witness in heaven, and also the knower in the heights, that I burn with zeal and thirst for the salvation of your soul, and that this entire exhortation of mine proceeds from the marrow of my soul and from the richness of charity. Therefore let confession be made in such a way that everything which appears to be an addition or consequence of your sin is also brought forward in accusation against you. A sin is scarcely found that has no other sin attached to it. For the scales of Behemoth are bound to one another [Note: [Col. 1083] Job 41.]; one is joined to another, and the breath of life does not pass between them. You see that in murders, perjuries, betrayals and slanders, revelries, drunkenness, obscene words, wicked counsels, and nearly every kind of crime, we draw another’s innocence into guilt through the partnership of consent. Therefore examine your conscience with diligent scrutiny; explore [Col. 1084B] all its corners, and let nothing remain in it unexamined. Dig through the wall, and familiar inquiry will reveal to you the monstrous abominations of your conscience. Do not neglect venial sins. For “he who despises small things gradually falls away and slips into greater things.” [Note: [Col. 1083] Sirach 19.] What is so venial that it cannot bring fear, when we must render account even for idle words and thoughts? [Note: [Col. 1083] Matt. 12.] Take care, then, that you are not buried under sand, that light matters do not overwhelm you. For drops of water, while they gradually and secretly flow into a ship’s bilge, unexpectedly sink the ship that had previously withstood the stormy assaults of the sea with strength. Beware, then, lest from the root of the serpent there arise a basilisk, and from the practice of venial sins a deadly habit. [Col. 1084C] For Augustine testifies [Note: [Col. 1083] *On True and False Repentance*, ch. 8.] that those who carelessly accustom themselves to venial sins commit sin against the Holy Spirit through a certain contempt. For this reason blessed Job feared all his works. [Note: [Col. 1083] Job 6.] For who should presume to justify himself by the benefit of confession or repentance? The Apostle himself says of himself: “I am conscious of nothing against myself, but I am not thereby justified.” [Note: [Col. 1083] I Cor. 4.] “No living being shall be justified in your sight.” [Note: [Col. 1083] Ps. 142.] Therefore you will be merciful to my sin not because of my merit but because of your name, “for it is great.” [Note: [Col. 1083] Ps. 24.] For if “the sufferings of this present age are not worthy to be compared” with the future glory to be obtained [Note: [Col. 1083] Rom. 8.], what will become of imperfect—or rather false—repentances, when the terrible and dreadful Judge judges even acts of righteousness themselves? Therefore let your sin always be before you. [Note: [Col. 1083] Ps. 50.] [Col. 1084D] And when you have done all things well, say that you are an unprofitable servant [Note: [Col. 1083] Luke 17.]; and, according to Solomon’s saying, never be without fear concerning sin forgiven and pardoned to you. [Note: [Col. 1083] Sirach 5.] “Blessed is the man who is always fearful.” [Note: [Col. 1083] Prov. 28.]

For sins frequently present themselves to memory which the penitent thought he had wiped away with the broom of repentance. Some think it enough that they have abstained from their shameful conduct for some time; presuming upon the first fruits of their newly seized continence, they do not recall their former transgressions. They think that their faults have vanished as though by the passage of time, [Col. 1085A] or that God has forgotten them or sleeps, and imagine that they have settled all their debts by the brief expedient of repentance.

Recall what Job says to the Lord: “You have sealed my sins as if in a bag.” [Note: [Col. 1085] Job 14.] And the Lord in Deuteronomy: “Are not these things stored up with me and sealed in my treasures?” [Note: [Col. 1085] Deut. 32.] Things that have become ingrained through long practice and fixed in the innermost marrow of souls are not healed without the bitterest pain of heart and anxious affliction of heart; nor can those things for which eternal death is owed be redeemed by contrition that is momentary and slight.

“Who knows whether he is worthy of love or hatred?” [Note: [Col. 1085] Eccl. 9.] A human conscience is like a mud-brick: the more it is washed, the more it is soiled. Hence the Lord says in Jeremiah: “Though you wash yourself with nitre and multiply for yourself the herb [Col. 1085B] borith, you shall be defiled in your blood.” [Note: [Col. 1085] Jer. 2.] And blessed Job: “Though I wash myself with snow-water, yet you will plunge me in filth, and my garments will abhor me.” [Note: [Col. 1085] Job 9.] But if you weigh the severity of repentance in an equal balance against the magnitude of your transgressions, even the whole length of your life is insufficient to make satisfaction to God. The kingdom of God can be acquired, but cannot be appraised; it is acquired through pains, seized through violence [Note: [Col. 1085] Matt. 11.], and the inheritance is obtained by the pressing entry of the saints. If, then, what has been imposed upon you seems burdensome, judge yourself worthy of graver burdens. Every discipline is indeed most bitter at its beginning, but afterwards, according to the Apostle’s testimony, it produces the most peaceable fruit of righteousness. [Note: [Col. 1085] Heb. 12.] Therefore confession is feigned and altogether false [Col. 1085C] if it does not proceed from the bitterness of the heart. For Tamar, whose name is interpreted “bitterness,” is joined in marriage to Judah—that is, to one confessing, or to confession—and, according to the ordinance of the Law, no one presumes to partake of the flesh of the paschal lamb except with the bitterness of wild lettuces. [Note: [Col. 1085] Exod. 12.]

Therefore recall your years in the bitterness of your soul. Keep before the eyes of your heart Christ’s Passion, the memory of your sins, and the expectation of strict judgment. Consider the necessity of the last day, the brevity of life, the uncertain end, and the terrible bow of the Lord, which he has stretched against sinners and upon which he has prepared instruments of death [Note: [Col. 1085] Ps. 7.], giving you a sign that you should flee from before the bow. [Note: [Col. 1085] Ps. 59.] Therefore do not murmur at the length or severity of repentance. For although you owe your whole self solely for the redemption of your crimes, conversely, if you look to the straits of Christ’s cross, you owe him your whole body and your whole soul. For he laid down his soul unto death for you. If from the beginning of the world until this day you had lived soberly, devoutly, and justly, you could not make a response worthy of his grace. Whatever human nature can do, if it is compared to the Lord’s Passion, is like a drop of water beside the vastness of the sea, a spark of fire beside the sun, and as nothing beside the whole universe. [Col. 1086A] The Apostle judges the present burden of tribulation light, looking to the recompense and to the eternal and inestimable greatness of the reward [Note: [Col. 1085] II Cor. 4.]: for present tribulation flows in as though drop by drop, but recompense flows in like a torrent of delight and never flows away.

If repentance therefore seems burdensome to you, consider that Gehenna is incomparably more burdensome. Exercise yourself in tears, vigils, fasts, and disciplines. Do not think it absurd if your head sometimes aches from abstinence, when it has more often ached from drunkenness; or if the belly roars which frequent gluttony has choked. The pus of sin, therefore, must not merely be wiped away but scraped off by the harshness of grief. You indeed scrape off the pus with a potsherd alongside blessed Job [Note: [Col. 1085] Job 2.] when, by stricter repentance, you wipe away filthy pleasures. [Col. 1086B] For what you have not cleansed in the present life God will cleanse in the fire of purgatory, as he himself says through Joel: “I will cleanse the blood which they have not cleansed.” [Note: [Col. 1085] Joel 3.] Isaiah likewise says: “He will cleanse the sons of Levi in the spirit of judgment and the spirit of burning.” [Note: [Col. 1085] Isa. 4.] But Christ, who accomplishes the purification of sins [Note: [Col. 1085] Heb. 1.], has mercifully assigned to us three purgatories—not in judgment but in desire, not in burning but in love: contrition of heart, confession of mouth, and affliction of flesh. These are the well-sounding cymbals; these are the three cities of refuge.

To contrition belong fear of God and desire for the kingdom, the humility of repentance, patient long-suffering, and self-abasement. “A contrite and humbled heart God will not despise.” [Note: [Col. 1085] Ps. 50.] Therefore let the pain of repentance so crush the heart [Col. 1086C] that it crushes the ships of Tarshish in a mighty wind. [Note: [Col. 1085] Ps. 47.] Tarshish is interpreted “exploration of joy.” Our minds are ships in which we sail in this whirlpool of the world, exploring the routes by which we may be borne forward to heavenly joy. We are indeed children of Peter and are commanded to walk upon the waters [Note: [Col. 1085] Matt. 14.]—upon this great and wide sea. Yet we are always sinking unless the Spirit helps our weakness, so that we may say with the Prophet: “Had the Lord not been in us, perhaps the water would have swallowed us.” [Note: [Col. 1085] Ps. 123.] Therefore let perseverance accompany the purpose of repentance. For what good will all the things mentioned above do the penitent if he returns to his vomit? The saying of the Wise Man is: “One builds [Col. 1086D] and another destroys: what is there but labor?” [Note: [Col. 1085] Sirach 34.] So also, “he who is baptized from a dead person and again touches a dead person—what did his washing profit him?” [Note: [Col. 1085] Ibid.] Augustine says [Note: [Col. 1085] Ch. *Inanis*, Dist. 3, *On Repentance*.]: “Repentance which a subsequent fault defiles is empty.” “A wound repeated” [Note: [Col. 1085] Ibid., in the *Dialogues*] “is healed more slowly; if one mourns and sins, he does not obtain pardon. Laments avail nothing if sins are repeated; nor is it effective to ask pardon for evils and to commit evils anew.” Gregory [Note: [Col. 1085] Part III, *Pastoral Rule*, admonition 31.]: “Those who lament what they have committed but do not abandon it cleanse themselves in vain and wickedly defile themselves; they wash themselves with tears [Col. 1087A] in order that, once clean, they may return to filth.” Gregory again: “‘Wash yourselves; be clean.’ For after washing, whoever neglects to remain clean—whoever does not preserve innocence of life after tears—does so in vain.”

Therefore let no one presume upon momentary contrition or an abundance of tears. For there are many irreligious persons—or rather persons swallowed up in the abyss of iniquities—who rejoice when they have done evil and exult in the worst deeds, whom we see pierced even to tears by fear of punishment or the memory of sins, and who melt with wondrous devotion into love of Jesus and embrace him with all the marrow of their soul, with the arms of devout affection. We also see others, established in the practice of repentance and amid many defenses of virtues, dry up so completely that they cannot force even one tear [Col. 1087B] from their eyes. It should therefore be known that the grace of tears is a visitation of God: sometimes given to rouse sluggishness, sometimes to console labor, sometimes as the grace of recompense. The first is like a spur pricking the idle, the second like a staff supporting the weak, the third like a bed receiving one at rest. For just as God now by word, now by example, and sometimes by the scourge summons those who live sluggishly or lukewarmly to salvation, so by hidden inspiration he invites these same persons, through compunction or terror, to a better state of life—so that this offer of divine grace becomes judgment for the reprobate but advancement for the elect. Not only tears, but also virtues—such as wisdom, eloquence, [Col. 1087C] and many such things drawn from the treasury of heavenly mercy—are turned by abuse or pride to evil for many. God’s gifts are sometimes common to good and evil alike. For Saul too was among the prophets [Note: [Col. 1087] III Kings 10.], and Judas was numbered among the apostles [Note: [Col. 1087] Matt. 10.]. For this reason the Savior says in the Gospel: “Many will say to me on that day, ‘Lord, did we not cast out demons in your name, and perform many signs in your name?’ And then I will declare to them, ‘I never knew you; depart from me, workers of iniquity.’” [Note: [Col. 1087] Ibid. 7.]

Cain’s repentance [Note: [Col. 1087] Gen. 4.], Esau’s weeping [Note: [Col. 1087] Gen. 27.], and Judas’s confession, as he lamented that he had betrayed innocent blood [Note: [Col. 1087] Matt. 27.], resulted in judgment and torment for them. The children of Israel, often rebuked by Moses in the wilderness [Note: [Col. 1087] Num. 11.], wept before [Col. 1087D] the Lord; yet that repentance profited them nothing, since they again gave themselves over to their former desires. Likewise, after entering the promised land, when the angel spoke to them in the place which was afterward called the Place of Weepers on that account, they raised their voices and wept; nevertheless, shortly afterward they continued to do evil in the sight of the Lord. [Note: [Col. 1087] Judg. 2.] But in the elect, compunction is for consolation, for those “to whom all things work together for good.” [Note: [Col. 1087] Rom. 8.] For they are advanced toward better things when, from the very sweetness they enjoy, they gird themselves more vigorously for spiritual exercises. And while they rejoice to endure hard and harsh things [Col. 1088A] for Christ, they advance to that more excellent kind of compunction which heals the infirm, strengthens the weak, and grants consolation and rest. The Prophet experienced this when he said: “I remembered God and was delighted.” [Note: [Col. 1087] Ps. 76.] And: “How great is the abundance of your sweetness, O Lord, which you have hidden for those who fear you.” [Note: [Col. 1087] Ps. 30.]

Therefore no one should falsely claim holiness in himself on the basis of the first kind of visitation, since we know it frequently occurs to the reprobate. Nor should he presume upon the second kind of visitation: it does not sanctify, but prepares for sanctification; and it sometimes comes to those who are tempted, lest they fall, and more often to those about to be tempted, that they may bear it more lightly. But if anyone grows accustomed to the second kind of visitation, he will easily advance to the third kind, which no longer merely rouses or strengthens, but rewards the victor with more abundant grace. If, therefore, you feel within yourself the grace of compunction and an abundance of tears, do not immediately suppose yourself thereby reconciled to the Lord. Nor should the servant suppose himself a son, even if he is sometimes fed with the bread of sons. For it is written of such persons: “The enemies of the Lord lied to him, and their time shall be for ever. And he fed them with the fat of wheat and satisfied them with honey from the rock.” [Col. 1088B] [Note: [Col. 1087] Ps. 80.]

Observe in these words that some are enemies of the Lord and yet are satisfied by the Lord with the fat of wheat and spiritual honey. Because God’s patience bears with and awaits such persons for repentance, they believe that they have obtained divine forgiveness. Ascribing everything to the merits of their tears, [Col. 1088C] they say with Manoah’s wife: “If the Lord wished to kill us, he certainly would not have received a sacrifice from our hand.” [Note: [Col. 1087] Judg. 13.]

I believe that the Apostle wrote concerning such people also: “The Lord gave them a spirit of compunction: eyes so that they should not see, and ears so that they should not hear.” [Note: [Col. 1087] Rom. 11.] Does not this compunction blind their eyes and stop up the ears of their heart—those who, believing themselves something when they are nothing, suppose that they have washed away the abominable stains of their crimes with a few tears, without fruits of repentance? True repentance does not consist in momentary tears or an hour’s compunction. Nor is any devout affection meritorious for salvation unless it proceeds from love of Christ. Often in tragedies and other poems of poets, or in the songs of minstrels, [Col. 1088D] some prudent, handsome, brave, lovable, and altogether gracious man is described. The oppressions or injuries cruelly inflicted upon him are also recounted. Thus performers tell certain fables concerning Arthur, Ganganus, and Tristan; through hearing them the hearts of listeners are moved to compassion and pierced even to tears. Therefore, if you are moved to pity by the recitation of a fable, and upon hearing some devout thing read concerning the Lord you shed tears, can you for this reason pronounce [Col. 1089A] a judgment that you love God? You who sympathize with God sympathize with Arthur as well. Accordingly, you lose both kinds of tears alike if you do not love God, if you do not pour out the tears of devotion and repentance from the fountains of the Savior—that is, from hope, faith, and charity.

Certainly God, by a marvelous workmanship of mercy, works our salvation ineffably. He himself illumines as wisdom; he himself terrifies as justice; he himself gently invites as charity. It is as if you wished to entice someone inexperienced in sweetness to desire honey, and therefore placed a drop of honey upon his mouth. Thus the Savior calls to salvation, by a certain dew of mercy and a certain taste of his sweetness, those immersed in carnal allurements whom neither preaching nor fear of the strict Judge converts from their iniquities, until he places upon them the most sweet yoke of his service. [Col. 1089B] Even though, after experiencing that sweetness, a man returns to the vanities of the world, nevertheless, with God’s grace at work, he returns to himself, is ashamed in himself, and hates himself because he has so often abused God’s grace offered to him. From this he considers a stricter way of life, restrains illicit impulses, and desires to impose upon himself a law of such necessity that, though he has the will to sin, he may not have the power. In such persons their holiness is the fruit of tears. For this purpose the tears were given, and through them the Most High works this result. If, then, what they were given for has been fulfilled through them, why will they be necessary thereafter for those living soberly, devoutly, and justly? You see plainly how acceptable to God is the sacrifice [Col. 1089C] of tears, and a holocaust sufficient for every offense. But for whom? For those confessing, repenting, and not returning to vomit [Note: [Col. 1089] Prov. 26; II Pet. 2.], but fleeing in a spirit of humility and a contrite heart to the merciful bowels of Jesus, and continuing fruits worthy of repentance.

Thus, in vigils, fasts, and disciplines, let the mortification of the flesh, undertaken in every member, offer itself with the pouring out of tears, so that the holocaust of the heart, growing rich with the sweetness of most devout affections, may pour forth before the high priest from the altar of the inner spirit an odor of sweetness. It is expedient for those who return to their heart to restrain the bestial impulses of the senses by a stricter discipline, so that all sensuality may be taken captive at the command of the spirit into Christ’s obedience. For “man was not made for woman, [Col. 1089D] but woman for man” [Note: [Col. 1089] I Cor. 11.]: that is, the flesh is to serve the spirit. What benefit is there if you offer well but divide badly? [Note: [Col. 1089] Gen. 4 according to the LXX.] You say “anathema” to him who says: “You have sinned; be at rest, go, and sin no more, lest something worse happen to you.” [Note: [Col. 1089] John 5 and 8.]

Therefore, at the beginning, the flesh must be bound with the knots of abstinence, so that you may then without difficulty crucify it together with its vices and desires. Christ indeed was first bound and afterward crucified. “Let this mind be in you which was also in Christ Jesus” [Note: [Col. 1089] Phil. 2.], so that with Joshua [Note: [Col. 1089] Chap. 10.] you may fasten the five kings—that is, the five senses—to the gallows of repentance. For the flesh [Note: [Col. 1089] Ps. 118.] [Col. 1090A] is our Delilah, our domestic enemy. It is not permitted us to kill it; rather, we must carry and nourish it. Yet let it be afflicted so that it serves; let the string be stretched so that it does not break. Let the beast likewise be fed so that it suffices for labor. For in the sacrifice of birds the turtle-dove’s wing-joints are not cut off but broken. [Note: [Col. 1089] Lev. 1.] But distribute with measured moderation what natural necessity demands regarding the miseries of the flesh, and transfer the entire vigilance of your effort to guarding the heart. Solomon’s saying is: “Guard your heart with all vigilance, because from it life proceeds.” [Note: [Col. 1089] Prov. 4.] For it is not sufficient for salvation to restrain the extraordinary motions of the flesh which we have contracted from the corruption of our origin, unless we procure the soul’s progress with the utmost diligence. What [Col. 1090B] good is it if you pull up the enervating growths of thorns outside or around the vineyard, but do not root out the thorns and briars within? Nor is it fitting to be concerned about the offspring of the handmaid while feeling no grief over the reproach of barrenness in the mistress. It is of no use to cultivate the soil of the body penitentially if you do not pluck out from the soul the plants of pride, covetousness, and envy.

Nor does it matter greatly if, after the flesh has been subdued, sin gains possession of the citadel of the mind, so that one who appears conquered outwardly has lost the better part of himself. It is written: “Without, conflicts; within, fears” [Note: [Col. 1089] II Cor. 7.]. It is a situation full of peril if we wage war outside the city in such a way that we nevertheless suffer destruction within the city.

[Col. 1090C] Perhaps your feet are not swift to shed blood; but your desires run toward acquiescing in flesh and blood, which do not possess the kingdom of God. Pope Pius testifies [Note: [Col. 1089] Epist. 12, c. *Nihil prodest*, dist. 3 *De poenit.*] that works of religion profit a man nothing unless his mind fasts from wicked thought in the fear of God. Therefore, first fear God and keep his commandments [Note: [Col. 1089] Eccl. 12], so that, as the Apostle says, you may work out the business of your salvation with fear and trembling [Note: [Col. 1089] Phil. 2]. For the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom [Note: [Col. 1089] Ps. 110]. And Isaiah says: “From fear of you, O Lord, we have conceived and brought forth the spirit of salvation” [Note: [Col. 1089] Isa. 26].

It is indeed expedient for those who turn back to their heart that, in fear of God’s judgments, they strictly restrain the crowd of rushing thoughts, lest these pass into the heart’s affections. Let the outward man be, as it were, dead to the heart, [Col. 1090D] so that the inward man may freely breathe in the serenity of holy meditations. There are, certainly, wandering thoughts in which there is no great danger, provided that you have the Lord before your eyes and your soul is always in your hands [Note: [Col. 1089] Ps. 118].

There are also thoughts concerning food, clothing, drink, and similar things, which bodily necessity demands; and these cling more familiarly to our flesh. For they have grown together with us from our first origin, so that they may be reckoned, as it were, our firstborn. If therefore these thoughts, or other first movements which the law of sin writes in the flesh, [Col. 1091A] begin to rise up and defile the bed of your conscience, say with blessed Jacob: “Reuben, my firstborn, do not increase, because you went up to your father’s bed” [Note: [Col. 1091] Gen. 49]; and thus let the little ones of Babylon be dashed against the rock in the spirit of strength [Note: [Col. 1091] Ps. 136].

A third kind of thought is condemnable: that which secretly creeps in from the dung-heap of lust, pride, envy, or some other detestable wickedness. As soon as you perceive it giving off its stench, turn your mind away; think upon God, terrible in his judgments; run to tears and groans; and keep that thought at a distance by commanding authority. Death is in it; therefore permit it no occasion to draw near to you. But if it has not gained mastery over you, then you shall be undefiled [Note: [Col. 1091] Ps. 18], and your desire shall be under you, and you shall rule over it [Note: [Col. 1091] Gen. 4].

But if [Col. 1091B] some poisonous thought has infected your senses even slightly, and you have been wounded by the serpent, run to the bronze serpent; call upon Christ, to whom every thought makes confession. In a contrite and humble heart, by the wondrous art of humility, you can remove your thought from his eyes, so that he who sees all may not see it. “Remove,” he says, “the evil of your thoughts from before my eyes” [Note: [Col. 1091] Isa. 1]. O how wonderful and terrible are those eyes, past which not even a small thought flies! For God, just as he sees deeds, also beholds human affections; nor is there need for anyone to bear witness to him concerning a human being. Yet after humble confession he sees no one’s sin, because charity covers a multitude of sins [Note: [Col. 1091] I Pet. 4].

Above all, strive to appear humble and [Col. 1091C] miserable before the merciful eyes of God. Before all virtues, humility stands familiarly and confidently in God’s presence. It is kin and friend to God; it alone among virtues does not know itself to be a virtue. By its own contempt it becomes more honorable; demanding other virtues in its own abasement, and profiting from that by which it harms itself, it makes recompense for the losses of all. Humble yourself, therefore; let humility not be a disgrace to you, a son of your Father, [Col. 1092A] since it was no disgrace to the Son of God.

Naaman descended from the chariot of pride into the Jordan [Note: [Col. 1091] IV Kings 5], which is interpreted “descent” or “humility,” and was cleansed from leprosy. Descend also, and humble yourself, if you wish to be cleansed from sin. Therefore the Psalmist says: “I will remember you from the land of Jordan, and Hermonim from the little mountain” [Note: [Col. 1091] Ps. 41]. The little mountain, indeed, is the pride of this life: so brief, so miserable, so uncertain. And from what should earth and ashes be proud—the stinking worm, the frog crawling in a marsh, the rotting corpse, mud teeming with worms, and a vile carcass? “Lift up your hands, O God, against our pride, and break the horns of sinners” [Note: [Col. 1091] Ps. 74].

Let our soul be humbled in the dust, that with the lamenting prophet we may put our mouth in the dust, if perhaps there may be hope [Note: [Col. 1091] Lam. 3], if perhaps [Col. 1092B] God may turn and forgive, and may not exact according to the multitude of his wrath [Note: [Col. 1091] Ps. 10. II.]. For it is dreadful to fall into the hands of the living God [Note: [Col. 1091] Heb. 10]. “For a fire has been kindled in his wrath, and it shall burn even unto the lowest parts of hell” [Note: [Col. 1091] Deut. 32]. “O Lord, rebuke me not in your fury” [Note: [Col. 1091] Ps. 6], but bear with me, while I rebuke myself by confessing.

And what glory is it to you, O God, if you cut off from the communion of the saints by perpetual excommunication a creature fashioned in conformity with your image and sealed with the character of your faith, so that the abyss of eternal death swallows it up and the infernal pit presses its mouth over it? “What profit is there in my blood, O God, if I go down into corruption?” [Note: [Col. 1091] Ps. 29]. “Which of you can dwell with devouring fire? Or who shall stand with everlasting burnings?” [Note: [Col. 1091] Isa. 33]?

May your mercy, I beseech you, O Lord, overcome [Col. 1092C] my miseries, and your kindness my iniquities. Awaken in me the affections of true contrition and confession; and, lest I be tortured in the blaze of Gehenna’s fire, kindle within me the fire of your love. May he grant this to us who lives and reigns as God through all ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 1091]

## ON PENANCE OR SATISFACTION TO BE IMPOSED BY A PRIEST

[Col. 1091D] To the venerable Father and friend in Christ, Lord W., abbot by God’s grace: N. Peter of Blois sends greetings, and repentance concerning those who must do penance.

The excessive harshness of your rigor, which you exercise in hearing the confessions of your brethren, as is said in their common complaint, generates matter for enormous scandals. For after receiving them for the remedy of penance, you publicly dishonor them after confession. Although you do not disclose their weaknesses in words, nevertheless by a certain haughty and conspicuous contempt [Col. 1092D] you stain their reputation among others with sinister suspicion.

You know with how grave a penalty the transgression of a priest who reveals sins confessed to him is punished. Nor does it matter much whether the secrets of another’s conscience are divulged by voice, sign, some scornful expression of countenance, or other excessive severity in imposing satisfaction. Canonical censure deposes such men, and, once deposed, assigns them to perpetual and ignominious pilgrimage. As blessed Gregory writes [Note: [Col. 1091D] Cap. *Qui vult*, c. *Sacerdos de poenit.* d. 8.]: “The governance of souls is the art of arts.”

Therefore the spiritual physician [Col. 1093A] must employ great caution when receiving confession. For, as we are taught in the Roman Penitential [Note: [Col. 1093] Gregory, Part I of the *Pastoral Rule*, ch. 1], the priest ought to receive the penitent with great gentleness and kindness. First he should pray for him, nor hesitate to profess himself a sinner, so that by his own example of humility he may move the penitent’s disposition to compunction. He should despise no sinner whatsoever, because, as blessed Jerome writes: “He who came to redeem sinners despises no sinner.” And he adds: “If, after confession, the penitent is despised by his prelate, he is easily thrust into the pit of despair; and this sin is so damnable that it provokes God to anger and does not deserve pardon.”

Therefore, just as humble and [Col. 1093B] sincere devotion is necessary for the person confessing, so diligent and circumspect discernment is necessary for the penitential minister—that is, the priest—so that he may distinguish leprosy from leprosy; so that he may have within himself three things: goodness, knowledge, and discipline—goodness in holiness, knowledge in learning, discipline in correction. A certain man asked for these three when he said: “Teach me goodness, discipline, and knowledge” [Note: [Col. 1093] Ps. 118].

Let him be a Samaritan, pouring in the oil of mercy and the wine of justice [Note: [Col. 1093] Luke 10]. Let his conscience, like the ark of the covenant, contain manna and the rod [Note: [Col. 1093] Heb. 9], so that he knows how to sympathize and forgive, to rebuke and admonish. Let him rejoice in the first fruits of the penitent; like a good husbandman, let him sympathize with the weak and strengthen the wavering, recalling that saying of the Apostle: “Who is weak, and I am not weak?” [Note: [Col. 1093] II Cor. 11]. [Col. 1093C] Hearing that person’s temptations, and reflecting upon his own weakness, let him say to himself: “Had I been in so great a temptation, I would have fallen more grievously.”

Let nothing be said or done with indignation and anger, “for the anger of man does not work the righteousness of God” [Note: [Col. 1093] Jas. 1]. Let him maintain the middle course, lest there be in him either excessive leniency or excessive austerity; and let him prescribe a definite measure of penances according to the ordinances of the holy Fathers. Blessed Gregory [Note: [Col. 1093] *De poenit.*, c. *Falsa*, dist. 5, in ch. 15, bk. I *Reg.* and Homily 26 on the Gospels] calls false those penances which are imposed neither according to the authority of the saints nor in proportion to the nature of the crimes.

There are indeed men who impose light and unusual forms of penance for grave sins, sewing, according to the prophet’s word, cushions under every elbow and pillows beneath the head of every age [Note: [Col. 1093] Ezek. 13]. Jerome on Daniel: “Therefore let my counsel please you: redeem your sins by alms, if perhaps God may forgive you” [Note: [Col. 1093] Dan. 4]. Since blessed Daniel, foreknowing the future, doubts the judgment of God, those who boldly promise forgiveness to sinners do a rash thing.

Isidore, *On the Supreme Good* [Note: [Col. 1093] Bk. III, ch. 13]: “There are those who quickly promise security to penitents; of them it is rightly said through the prophet: ‘They healed the brokenness of the daughter of my people with disgrace, saying, “Peace, peace,” when there is no peace’” [Note: [Col. 1093] Jer. 6]. “With disgrace,” he says, [Col. 1094A] “they heal the brokenness” who quickly promise security to the penitent.

There are those who, by austerity, make harsh the Lord’s sweet yoke and make heavy his light burden, binding burdens impossible to bear while unwilling to move them with a finger [Note: [Col. 1093] Matt. 23]. These are they who, contrary to the commandment of the Law, lend to their weak brother at usury; for usury is whatever satisfaction you impose beyond the regular due. They exercise zeal for justice in leaven and not in unleavened bread, in order to satisfy anger rather than bear fruit for Christ. Of such men it is written: “The desire of a eunuch deflowered a young woman; so too does he who enforces judgment by violence” [Note: [Col. 1093] Ecclus. 20]. For the scandalized soul of the penitent is corrupted, and no fruit of justice is generated from such correction.

Of such men the Lord says through the prophet: “They were killing souls that do not die [Col. 1094B] and making alive souls that do not live” [Note: [Col. 1093] Ezek. 13]. To perverse shepherds the Lord says through the prophet: “You ruled them with austerity.” But, according to the word of Wisdom: “A dreadful and swift judgment shall befall those who are in authority” [Note: [Col. 1093] Wis. 6]. Therefore judgments ought to be upright and free from disturbance of mind, as Elihu says in the Book of Job [Note: [Col. 1093] Ch. 36]: “Let not anger oppress you into oppressing someone.”

The lawgiver of monks says in the Rule [Note: [Col. 1093] Benedict, Rule, ch. II]: “Let the abbot consider that he must render an account of all his judgments on the day of judgment, lest perhaps the flame of zeal or envy burn his soul.” The custom of certain men—or rather, their death—is such; for the holy Fathers judge it ruinous to the soul when men pursue their own injuries more zealously than Christ’s. Yet, as blessed Augustine writes [Note: [Col. 1093] Sermon 48, *On the Saints*]: “To sin [Col. 1094C] against us is far lighter than to sin against God. For if a man sins against a man,” says Samuel, “it can be forgiven him; but if he sins against God, who shall pray for him?” [Note: [Col. 1093] I Kings 2].

“But we,” Augustine says, “are, on the contrary, merciful and indulgent toward injuries done to God; and, as though God’s willingness or unwillingness lay in our power, we remit his offense without penitential satisfaction. But if anything insulting has been attempted against us in deed or word, we pursue it with graver punishment.” Hence Ambrose says in a homily: “What is committed against a human being can easily be forgiven, but not so what is attempted against God.” Therefore you offend grievously if you leave unpunished the faults of the Lord’s debtor which are against God, [Col. 1094D] and by your presumption discharge the debt owed to the heavenly King. The authority of a penitential minister turns many men over to a reprobate mind.

Blessed Jerome relates concerning a certain old man that he had cast a young man, troubled by the spirit of fornication and doing penance, into the pit of despair. But another old man strengthened him, so that the spirit of uncleanness, leaving the young man, attacked the first old man and grievously tormented him [Note: [Col. 1093] *Lives of the Fathers*, pt. II; Cassian, Collation 2, ch. 13].

We often see some members [Col. 1095A] of your order confessing to bishops, or to those whom bishops delegate in their place; and we know this to be contrary to the constitutions of the Fathers and opposed to propriety. But what is a soul terrified by an abbot to do when it is forbidden to confess to someone from its own monastery? What shall the deceived dove, having no heart, do [Note: [Col. 1095] Hos. 7]? Take heed, O abbots, to yourselves and to all your flock [Note: [Col. 1095] Acts 20]: not as princes, not as lords, but as examples made to the flock in your communities [Note: [Col. 1095] I Pet. 2], physicians of souls—or, to speak more truly, cleaners of bilges and purgers of dung. For what dung, what menstrual blood, what decay of corpses is more unclean than sin? It is dangerous to despise one’s brother and put to death one who is contrite of heart.

Indeed, those who despise [Col. 1095B] the penitent after confession are not very unlike Simon the Pharisee, who accused Christ in his heart because he received the repentance of Mary the sinner [Note: [Col. 1095] Luke 7]. I believe that if the man who now despises a penitent brother had then been with Simon, he would have driven Mary away with kicks. Moreover, as the Apostle says, the Lord shut up all things under sin in order that he might have mercy on all [Note: [Col. 1095] Rom. 11]. For spiritual strength would not advance unless bodily weakness lay beneath it. “For strength is made perfect in weakness” [Note: [Col. 1095] II Cor. 12].

O, if you too knew with what strict and fearful judgment you must answer! According to the counsel of John of Damascus [Note: [Col. 1095] In the prayer for the faithful departed], it would be wiser and safer for you to render an account of mercy than of the severity of justice. He exalts mercy over judgment, whom you have read to have said: [Col. 1095C] “I desire mercy, and not sacrifice” [Note: [Col. 1095] Matt. 9]. If zeal for justice is at times properly observed, nevertheless mercy should hold first place, and the shepherd, like a prudent physician, should gently touch the wound of another’s conscience. Let him not break the bruised reed or quench the smoking flax [Note: [Col. 1095] Matt. 12].

With what face, then, with what eyes, with what mind, with what conscience does one presume upon God’s mercy when a brother’s misery finds him hard and merciless? There are those who compel some persons to confess to themselves and not to others; therefore such persons hide their offenses and persist in their shameful deeds. Against them that curse is directed: “Woe to those who are pregnant and nursing in that day!” [Note: [Col. 1095] Matt. 24]. For their souls are pregnant [Col. 1095D] with sins and nourish themselves in their own filth until they are satisfied with their desires. Because of the harshness of prelates, hearts turn aside to words of malice.

As Augustine says in the book *On Penance* [Note: [Col. 1095] Chs. 15 and 20]: “They are ready to make excuses for excuses in sins” [Note: [Col. 1095] Ps. 140], or they shut them up in silence—which is pernicious hypocrisy. Such physicians treat but do not heal, according to the saying: “We have treated Babylon, and she has not been healed” [Note: [Col. 1095] Jer. 51].

[Note: [Col. 1095] Luke 6.] [Col. 1096A] Augustine says: “A priest ought to be free of the fault which he judges; otherwise, by judging another, he condemns himself.” Blessed Augustine says that such a person should consider the sinful woman of the Gospel, and the Lord’s words: “He who is without sin, let him first cast a stone at her” [Note: [Col. 1095] John 8]. By what presumption, then, does the person who knows himself worthy of stoning stone another? The Lord says: “Hypocrite, first cast the beam out of your own eye, and then you will see to cast the speck out of your brother’s eye” [Note: [Col. 1095] I Cor.]. The great beam is the exaltation of the mind, which so darkens the mind’s eye that you see not what you are, but what you imagine yourself to be. What you condemn in your brother may perhaps be more condemnable in yourself. “Who are you, to judge another’s servant? To his own master he stands or falls” [Note: [Col. 1095] Rom. 14].

How do you know concerning yourself, [Col. 1096B] whether you are worthy of love or of hatred [Note: [Col. 1095] Eccl. 9]? For who understands sins? [Note: [Col. 1095] Ps. 18]. No one knows what is in a human being except the human spirit that is in him [Note: [Col. 1095] I Cor. 2]. Yet neither does a person know himself. “The heart of man is perverse and inscrutable; who knows it?” [Note: [Col. 1095] Jer. 17]. Therefore the Apostle, though conscious of nothing against himself, nevertheless by no means presumes to judge himself: “I am conscious of nothing,” he says, “but neither do I judge myself; the Lord judges me” [Note: [Col. 1095] I Cor. 4]. The Father has given all judgment to the Son. Therefore whoever judges another usurps to his own destruction the prerogative of the Redeemer.

Accordingly, let the shepherd receive the penitent kindly, and not shame him by observances of an excessively severe penance or by a grave and tyrannical expression of countenance. But if anyone is caught in some offense, let the spiritual person instruct him in a spirit [Col. 1096C] of gentleness, considering himself lest he too be tempted [Note: [Col. 1095] Gal. 6]. The Apostle Paul speaks to the wise man who does not condescend to his less wise brother and does not fear to cause him scandal: “Your brother, for whom Christ died, will perish through your knowledge” [Note: [Col. 1095] I Cor. 8].

The weaker your brother is, the gentler and more attentive you ought to be toward him. A weaker child is loved more tenderly by its mother. And, as the Apostle says, we surround the weaker members with more abundant honor [Note: [Col. 1095] I Cor. 12]. Therefore be merciful to one who is weak, that you may obtain mercy. “For with the measure with which you measure, it shall be measured to you also” [Note: [Col. 1095] Matt. 7]. “For judgment without mercy shall be to him who has not shown mercy” [Note: [Col. 1095] Jas. 2]. But “the merciful shall obtain mercy” [Note: [Col. 1095] Matt. 5].

[Col. 1096D] Christ, the splendor and figure of God’s substance, receives the sinner kindly [Note: [Col. 1095] Heb. 1]. You, a sinner: by what presumption do you despise and reject him? Christ does not consider it a slight gain to have recovered the lost sheep, and he holds a feast-day with his angels; the heavenly court rejoices over one converted and returned to the fruit of penance [Note: [Col. 1095] Luke 15]. Yet you count neither the gain nor the loss of souls; do you wish to confine within fixed boundaries the mercy [Col. 1097A] of God, whose mercy has no end?

The master of the household is generous, and the steward is miserly. “You thought wickedly that I would be like you” [Note: [Col. 1097] Ps. 49], says the Lord: “and do you measure my mercy by your hardness?” What do you know—perhaps he has already been cleansed by tears and contrition. Perhaps he was set free by the very resolve to confess. “I said: ‘I will confess,’ and you forgave” [Note: [Col. 1097] Ps. 31]. Lazarus was raised by the Lord [Note: [Col. 1097] John 11] before his bandages were untied by the apostles. Lepers were cleansed by the Lord before they showed themselves to the priests [Note: [Col. 1097] Luke 17]. Yet Christ has forgiven the sin for which you judge the penitent and, along with the Pharisee, despise the Publican [Note: [Col. 1097] Luke 18].

The loving and merciful God offers peace to the penitent, and first sends envoys concerning peace, though he ought first to have been sought concerning peace. Assuredly, in the affair [Col. 1097B] of penance, “mercy and truth meet one another; justice and peace kiss one another” [Note: [Col. 1097] Ps. 84]: justice and truth in the person judging and punishing himself; [Col. 1098A] mercy and peace in God, who pardons freely.

O blessed hope of those confessing! This prodigal son, who had sinned so monstrously against heaven and earth and had made satisfaction in nothing, was immediately reconciled to his father [Note: [Col. 1097] Luke 12]; and the father was far readier and more eager to show mercy than the son to obtain mercy. “Do not fear, little flock” [Note: [Col. 1097] Ibid.]. Come confidently to the throne of glory, you who did not dare even to think of grace. “Come, all you who labor and are burdened” [Note: [Col. 1097] Matt. 11]. Come, all you who have rotted in your uncleannesses. Whether the Pharisee’s haughty hypocrisy wishes it or not, the baptism of repentance is offered to all. Here stands open the fountain of the house of David, for the washing of the sinner and the menstruous woman. It is not you who baptize here, you who despise the penitent; it is not John, but Christ, who, by as much as he surpasses all others more excellently, by so much more sweetly and gloriously has his mercy been confirmed over us. Farewell.

[Col. 1097]

## EPISCOPAL CANON, OR A TREATISE ON THE APPOINTMENT OF A BISHOP

[Col. 1097C] To the reverend Father and Lord JOHN [Note: [Col. 1097D] He was called John of Coutances, who, from dean of the Church of Rouen, became bishop [Col. 1098D] of Worcester in England. Concerning him see what we have said in the notes to Epistle 121], bishop of Worcester by God’s grace: his own Peter of Blois, archdeacon, sends greetings, and wishes him faithfulness in the ministry of Christ.

You earnestly request, most reverend Father, that I write something for you concerning the episcopal office, which may be a consolation to you in this new situation and may build you up unto salvation. I, indeed, lurking in obscurity and smoking beneath a bushel, am compelled to thrust my darkness upon a lamp set upon a lampstand. I, untaught, am commanded to teach one learned; I, sick, to prepare a medicinal remedy for one in health. You abound in spiritual wine and oil, and the anointing has taught you concerning all things; yet you ask an anointing from me.

But I, the servant of your holiness, have only a little oil with which to anoint myself; indeed, only a little vinegar, in which, on [Col. 1097D] summer days, I may dip a morsel of bread with the reapers of Boaz [Note: [Col. 1097] Ruth 2]. Yet that tiny amount does not admit of portions; nevertheless charity never fails [Note: [Col. 1097] I Cor. 13], and the more generously it dispenses what belongs to it, the more fully it grows; and from liberal expenditure the widow’s flour and jar of oil overflow [Note: [Col. 1097] III Kings 17].

Manna indeed rots and swarms with worms if it is stored up [Col. 1098C] [Note: [Col. 1097] Exod. 16]; but, when usefully distributed, it becomes heavenly bread and food for angels. I know that God’s grace is harmful if it does not benefit another. But he who shares God’s gift for another’s use and benefit more fully merits to possess what he has; for it shall be given to him, and he shall abound. But from him who, on the contrary, hides the Lord’s talent, even what he seems to have shall be taken away [Note: [Col. 1097] Matt. 13].

I indeed have no talent, but a small coin, which I must put into the treasury. Yet it will go out on loan, so that someone may be found to receive it as a loan, if perhaps from this small principal a more abundant increase of interest may result. I shall do what I can; affection will dare what I cannot. The vein of a languishing intellect will be revived by desire, and devotion enkindled by charity will raise the fallen pen.
