That companionate affection which has grown between us through the course of long time shall never, on my part, degenerate. Your dignity has been added to it, not taken its place; and your episcopal throne has not dissolved the bond of our old familiarity.

If you walk upon the wings of the winds, if you ascend into heaven or descend into the depths, affection recognizes no change of rank. Already my mind burns, already it boils over [Col. 1099A] to write. Already this present letter, which at the beginning was fearful, emboldened by love, seeks—no less imprudently than shamelessly—to come forth before the eyes of the public and rashly expose itself to common hearing. Yet it would lie more safely in the bosom of my conscience and be more wisely shut within the hinges of silence.

Drawn and attracted by love, therefore, I share with your Holiness, without envy, what I have learned without pretence. [Note: [Col. 1099] Wisd. 7.] May he in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge [Note: [Col. 1099] Col. 2.] himself open my mouth for the good pleasure of his grace and for public benefit; and may the Holy Spirit, instructor of good minds, through whom the willing is present to me, continue in me both to will and to accomplish.

[Col. 1099B] But if the style of this letter should seem to sound somewhat harsh to delicate ears, spare an old man—you who understand more than the aged [Note: [Col. 1099] Ps. 118.]—who from the earliest conduct of youth have endeavoured to outstrip your years by merit and to make up for the inadequacy of age by virtues; and do not measure words by deeds. You have heard, most loving Father, concerning those who sit upon the seat of Moses: “What they say, do; but what they do, do not do.” [Note: [Col. 1099] Matt. 23.] It is easier to prescribe what is to be done than to fulfil what has been prescribed. For even the book of the prophet handed over to be devoured becomes sweet in his mouth, but bitter when conveyed inwardly. [Note: [Col. 1099] Rev. 10.] As the Apostle says: “You have received from him how you ought to walk and please God in all things; so walk, that you may abound more.” [Note: [Col. 1099] 1 Thess. 4.]

[Col. 1099C] And lest you have to seek examples of honourable conduct far away, the teaching of your uncle, the Archbishop of Rouen, prescribes to you the model of episcopal office. [Note: [Col. 1099] He speaks of Walter of Coutances, Archbishop of Rouen; see what has been said on Epistle 124.] If you are willing faithfully to imitate his footsteps, you will be well ordered in morals: generous, gracious, gentle, prudent in counsel, vigorous in action, discerning in command, modest in speech, fearful in prosperity, secure in adversity, mild among the perverse [Note: [Col. 1099] 1 Pet. 2.], peaceable with those who hate peace [Note: [Col. 1099] Ps. 119.], lavish in almsgiving, restrained in zeal, fervent in mercy, neither anxious nor slack in administering household resources, watchful in all things—an imitator of those four living creatures which are described as having the eyes of providence before, behind, and round about. [Note: [Col. 1099] Rev. 4.]

You have been placed, venerable Father, among the sons of the prophets; [Col. 1099D] you have ascended Mount Gerizim [Note: [Col. 1099] Deut. 11.] to bless the people. Therefore let a man regard you as a minister of Christ and a steward of the mysteries of God. [Note: [Col. 1099] 1 Cor. 4.] Now this is required among stewards: that a man be found faithful. [Note: [Col. 1099] Ibid.] Truth describes, in a concise clause, what you ought to be: “A faithful servant,” he says, “whom the Lord has appointed over his household.” [Note: [Col. 1099] Matt. 24.]

[Col. 1100A] You are faithful if you seek the things above, not those upon earth; not your own things, but those of Jesus Christ [Note: [Col. 1099] Col. 3.]; and if you make a token of public benefit from what heavenly grace has granted you. You are faithful if you love God for his own sake and your neighbour for God’s sake. But you are unfaithful if you despise common nature in another person and fail to recognize the image of God as your own. Seek, therefore, not what is advantageous to yourself, but what is advantageous to many. Seek with the Apostle not the gift, but the fruit. [Note: [Col. 1099] Phil. 4.]

It concerns the glory of your Holiness to watch over the people entrusted to you, so that you may interpret the title of bishop through episcopal service. You are debtor to the wise and the foolish. [Note: [Col. 1099] Rom. 1.] Therefore you must act more prudently. Wisdom says in the book bearing her name: “I, Wisdom, dwell in counsels, and am present among instructed thoughts.” [Note: [Col. 1099] Prov. 8.]

[Col. 1100B] Use Solomon’s counsel: “Do everything with counsel, and you shall not repent”; [Note: [Col. 1099] Ecclus. 32.] and he adds: “Discuss your cause with your friend, and do not reveal your secret to a stranger.” [Note: [Col. 1099] Prov. 25.] If you make use of the counsel of wise men, you will not be vehement in revenge, excessively severe in correction, merciless in sparing, hasty in judgments, conspicuous in food or clothing, quick to promise, slow to perform, abrupt in replies, greedy, or prodigal in expenditure.

Teach yourself before you teach others: he is not wise who is not wise for himself. And since others draw from your breast as from a fountain, drink first from the fountain of your own well. Let your springs be poured forth abroad in such a way that you are nevertheless not [Col. 1100C] forgetful of yourself. “Cursed is he who makes his own portion worse!” But he who is evil to himself—to whom will he be good? [Note: [Col. 1099] Ecclus. 14.] In the matter of the soul and in gaining the heavenly inheritance, let no one be nearer to you than yourself. Go out often into the field with Isaac to meditate [Note: [Col. 1099] Gen. 24.]; and, according to Solomon’s saying, “If you desire wisdom, keep her commandment, and the Lord will give her to you.” [Note: [Col. 1099] Ecclus. 1.]

Keep with you men whose life and words you may revere; men who, even if you wish it, will not permit you to stray, who will restrain you when headlong, strengthen you when doubtful, and rouse you when sluggish. It is great presumption to act not according to reason but according to desire; and it is beastly to prefer appetite to counsel. It is written: “Man, though he was in honour, did not understand; he was compared to senseless beasts and made like them.” [Col. 1100D] [Note: [Col. 1099] Ps. 48.] Yet do not believe every spirit, but first test whether it is from God, [Note: [Col. 1099] 1 John 4.] lest that crafty serpent perhaps whisper something through the instruments of his malice. You will easily detect his wiles from the manner of the suggestion, from face and gesture, from the offering of prayers, and from the very quality of the advice.

And, that you may utterly crush the schemes of the apostate angel, let the fear of God, the fire of Gehenna, life’s brevity, life’s utterly uncertain end, and expectation of the dreadful judgment be, as it were, before [Col. 1101A] the face of your conscience. Do nothing, nor command anything to be done, against or apart from your salvation. For if your associates or others who use the authority of your familiarity commit an offence, you know that the blame will be imputed to you. You know that ratification is equivalent to command. That is regarded as your own act to which you give your own consent through another’s agency.

There is one who trusts himself alone—which is the worst thing—and considers only that which he has devised by hardened invention. It is the word of the Wise Man: “The ways of fools are right in their own sight, but are rejected by the Lord.” [Note: [Col. 1101] Prov. 12.] And again: “There are ways that seem right to a man, but their end leads to the depths of [Col. 1101B] hell.” [Note: [Col. 1101] Prov. 16.] Therefore arrange everything with counsel and sober deliberation. If you have proposed some arduous undertaking, deliberate first with yourself, then with many whose fidelity you have tested; and, according to the evangelical parable, first sit down and calculate your costs; and when you are about to meet a king, review your forces at home, [Note: [Col. 1101] Luke 14.] lest an unguarded undertaking of a weightier purpose turn to your shame.

But where familiar counsel does not suffice, seek the counsel, even if they are not your intimates, of those whom you do not doubt to be organs of the Holy Spirit. Yet you act better and far more safely if you trust in prayer alone. Therefore now live not by your own spirit but by the Spirit of God, by whom those who are God’s sons are led. [Note: [Col. 1101] Rom. 8.] We believe, moreover, that you too have the Spirit [Col. 1101C] of God. [Note: [Col. 1101] 1 Cor. 7.] Live not by plunder and exactions, or by perquisites and judicial proceedings, but by the Gospel, as the Lord has ordained. [Note: [Col. 1101] 1 Cor. 9.] By the “proceeds of the Gospel” I mean whatever the devotion of ancient generosity has bestowed upon your Church for the faith you preach.

Others idly eat another’s bread amid a burdensome multitude of men or horses; but you should travel with few, and carry about the bread of angels for the edification of all. Always be, insofar as you can, occupied with the Scriptures; always discuss with your household the progress of virtues. For even the Apostle, who learned the Gospel not from man but from God, [Note: [Col. 1101] Gal. 1.] nevertheless judged that it should be discussed with men. Do nothing against your conscience and, [Col. 1101D] to use the Apostle’s language, do not be moved from your own judgment, if it is sound, neither by letter, nor by spirit, nor by word. [Note: [Col. 1101] 2 Thess. 2.] Even if the spirit of one holding authority over you should come, do not abandon your place. Indeed, I say more, though with the Apostle: if an angel announces anything other than what concerns Christ’s glory, let him be anathema. [Note: [Col. 1101] Gal. 1.]

Have no holiday time, but always devote yourself either to prayer, reading, or some other honourable pursuit. Thus those who are with you may read in your works [Col. 1102A] how they ought to live, while you go before them in justice and holiness. Happy is that soul which is for others a model of holiness. Let that by which another may profit through you never fail in you: a lamp is not diminished by lighting another, nor does the multitude of those who look upon it cause loss to the sun.

The Lord has placed you to give his people the knowledge of salvation, [Note: [Col. 1101] Luke 1.] to render to the Lord a people acceptable, zealous for good works, and with all diligence to prepare for the Lord a perfect people. Since the days are evil, you must set aside something from the evil of the time for the benefit of souls: something that may form morals, govern affections, direct actions, and order and ennoble your very rank. I repeat again: always be occupied with the Scriptures, and let no time find you [Col. 1102B] idle. For idleness without letters is, as Jerome says, [Note: [Col. 1101] Seneca, Ep. 83.] the burial of a living man.

You have learned sacred letters from childhood. See that you have not received the grace of God in vain. Build others up not only by word but by deed and example, because the kingdom of God is not in speech but in power. [Note: [Col. 1101] 1 Cor. 4.] Build up your subjects in countenance, look, gesture, dress, and manner of walking. To live and not labour that life may be rightly lived is to waste life. Refer all the gains of spiritual exercise to the glory of him who is the King of glory. You are a thief and robber if you presume to appropriate any of it for yourself. Let the streams return whence the rivers go forth. The living creatures in Ezekiel [Note: [Col. 1101] Ch. 1.] went and returned: whatever grace conferred upon them, they referred back to the Lord.

[Col. 1102C] Truth says in the Gospel: “You seek glory from one another, and do not desire the glory that is from God alone.” [Note: [Col. 1101] John 5.] Far be it that the Lord should say to you: “You have received your reward.” [Note: [Col. 1101] Matt. 6.] Rather say with the Lord: “If I seek my own glory, my glory is nothing.” [Note: [Col. 1101] John 8.] He who swells with empty glory is wholly empty, as full of nothing as he is of the wind of pride. Therefore, if you have anything of which you ought to glory, glory not in yourself but in the Lord, and say: “By the grace of God I am what I am.” [Note: [Col. 1101] 1 Cor. 15.]

In all God’s gifts flee self-exaltation, remembering that word of the Lord: “I saw Satan falling from heaven.” [Note: [Col. 1101] Luke 10.] “If I must glory,” says the Apostle, “I will glory in my infirmities.” [Note: [Col. 1101] 2 Cor. 12.] For the glory of a prelate is that he judges himself wretched and weak, unequal to the burden and unworthy of the honour. There are those who [Col. 1102D] regard honours as virtues and ascribe to their own merits the degree of eminence which perhaps they have obtained in God’s wrath. Assumption of office has become for many a temptation and an occasion of ruin. Therefore preside in such a way that you are of benefit. Woe to those who preside over men unless God presides over them!

Always secretly impose upon yourself the yoke of the Lord’s service, whether through disciplines, tears, or other acts that you alone can perform without human witness. For the highest kind of captivity is when the licence of freedom wanders according to its own will without the bond [Col. 1103A] of any vow. Therefore, though seated on high, do not think high things; in all things think humbly and agree with the humble. “Do not walk in great things, nor in things too wonderful for you.” [Note: [Col. 1103] Ps. 130.]

But if you glory in the good of your conscience, say with blessed Job: “Though I were righteous, I would not lift up my head.” [Note: [Col. 1103] Job 10.] “For no living person shall be justified in your sight, O Lord.” [Note: [Col. 1103] Ps. 142.] Paul, who was conscious of nothing against himself, nevertheless denied that he was justified. “I do not consider,” he says, “that I have attained.” [Note: [Col. 1103] Phil. 3.] And again: “Not,” he says, “that I have received, or am already perfect; but, forgetting those things which are behind, I stretch myself toward those which are before.” [Note: [Col. 1103] Ibid.]

He himself glories not in dominion but in service. “Are they ministers of Christ?” he says. “I am also. I speak as one less wise: I more so—in far more labours, more abundantly in prisons, beyond measure in stripes, often in deaths.” [Col. 1103B] [Note: [Col. 1103] 2 Cor. 11.]

In these things a pattern of glorying is set before you—not in costly clothing, not in abundant furnishings, not in the accumulation of money, not in buildings or estates, not in enlarging possessions, not in a multitude of horses, not in pompous adornment, nor in a numerous retinue. For all these things the Gentiles seek. [Note: [Col. 1103] Gal. 6.] But, as the Doctor of the Gentiles glories, [Note: [Col. 1103] 2 Cor. 11.] glory in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, in your infirmities, in deaths, labours, prisons, and stripes.

The Lord has given you knowledge of the saints. He who adds knowledge adds also sorrow, not glory, as it is written: “He who adds knowledge [Col. 1103C] adds also sorrow”; [Note: [Col. 1103] Eccles. 1.] concerning which a certain penitent says: “And my sorrow is always before me.” [Note: [Col. 1103] Ps. 37.] It is not human glory, which is a scorching wind drying up the streams of heavenly grace. Far from you be that grace by which you become more glorious in your own eyes and thereby more hateful in the eyes of God! It is wrath, not grace, when someone is set upon the wind, having no roots in the solidity of virtues.

You are bound to the service of him whom to serve is to reign; in regard to that service, he who holds the primacy of the Church counts himself the servant of servants. Therefore have this mind in yourself which was in Christ Jesus: as he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, [Note: [Col. 1103] Phil. 2.] so account yourself the humble and lowly servant of those subject to you. Let not the humility which befitted the Son of God be disgraceful to you. From pre-eminence you may [Col. 1103D] gain glory, but not before God; but if you glory in humility, you will not be foolish.

“The kings of the Gentiles lord it over them, but it shall not be so among you.” [Note: [Col. 1103] Mark 10.] Do not, then, present yourself as a lord, but as a minister. The apostle Peter says: “Not lording it over the clergy, but made a pattern for the flock among the people.” [Note: [Col. 1103] 1 Pet. 5; printed “50”.] What has wretched man to glory in—conceived from unclean seed, begotten and born in sin, living for a brief time, [Note: [Col. 1103] Job 14.] fleeing like a shadow and never remaining in the same state?

If then a favourable breeze should puff you up with some movement of pride, [Col. 1104A] recall what was said to Zedekiah: “Your men of peace have deceived you.” [Note: [Col. 1103] Jer. 38.] If a sinner flatters you, do not consent; nor let flattering praise—or rather, fraud—deceive you. [Note: [Col. 1103] Prov. 1.] It is ruinous for a prelate willingly to hear about himself things above what he feels within himself. “But I spare you,” says the Apostle, [Note: [Col. 1103] 2 Cor. 12.] “lest anyone think of me above what he sees in me or hears from me.” But he does not spare himself nor pity his soul who boasts of his deeds, wishing to be judged what he is not and not to be known as what he is.

Let your soul always be in your hands, and the Lord before your eyes, [Note: [Col. 1103] Ps. 118.] so that, when the flatterer begins to applaud, you may say: “The wicked have told me fables, but not according to your law.” [Note: [Col. 1103] Ibid.] And this: “Do not call me Naomi, but Mara, for I am full of bitterness.” [Col. 1104B] [Note: [Col. 1103] Ruth 1.] As wind scatters clouds, so let the severity of your countenance drive away the wind of flattery and the poison of detraction. Interrupt malicious conversations and introduce something concerning God’s law, the songs of Zion, the judgments of heavenly wrath, the merits of the saints, or the torrent of eternal delight.

There is one who puts more trust in another’s tongue concerning his own condition than in his own conscience. Such a dull and weak member, sick and not feeling himself sick, is far from salvation; precisely thereby incurable, because insensible. I see very many who, after receiving the gift of heavenly grace, give themselves up to the passions of desire, like the Gentiles who do not know God. You have long possessed your vessel in sanctification. Bring happily to completion what you have done hitherto, acting every day [Col. 1104C] as though you were always beginning.

It is common among bishops to find one who devotes the first year of his promotion to holiness; and when in his newness he has become a lamb, after a few days of growing old he becomes a most ravenous wolf. Of such a man it is written: “Before the harvest he has wholly flowered, and immature perfection shall bud forth.” [Note: [Col. 1103] Isa. 18.] And concerning the same: “If he bears fruit, others shall eat it.” [Note: [Col. 1103] Isa. 65.]

In every distress cast all your hope upon the Lord, since the name of the Lord is abundant strength. Do not trust those accustomed to give mere words, whose friendship is mercenary and whose intimacy is costly. You understand what I say; and you recall the Maccabees, who, whenever they sought the Romans’ support, found their friendship turned into sobbing for the leaders and [Col. 1104D] people of Israel.

I beg you, examine closely and frequently; consider what you are by God’s gift and what you are from yourself; render to yourself what is yours, and to God what is God’s. [Note: [Col. 1103] Matt. 22.] Recall how miserable and weak nature brought you forth from your mother’s womb. You came naked from your mother’s womb; naked you were born for labour, not for honour. If heavenly dispensation has added anything to you, always fear that saying of the Psalmist: “Yet because of deceits you have set them up; you cast them down while they were being raised.” [Note: [Col. 1103] Ps. 72.]

Some bishops abusively call the gifts of kings and the alms of earlier men “baronies” and “regalia”; and on the occasion of most disgraceful servitude call themselves barons. I fear that the Lord may complain of them and say: “They have reigned, and not through me; they have become princes, and I did not know.” [Col. 1105A] [Note: [Col. 1105] Hos. 8.] Know that you have undertaken the office of shepherd, not of baron. Certainly Joseph in Egypt instructed his father and brothers to say to Pharaoh: “We are shepherds.” [Note: [Col. 1105] Gen. 46.] He preferred them to profess the office of shepherd rather than that of prince or baron. Christ says: “I am the good shepherd”; [Note: [Col. 1105] John 10.] but you have been established by him as shepherd or steward. A stewardship has been committed to you; know that you must render an account of the stewardship.

God’s husbandry has been committed to you: you need a hoe as a husbandman, a staff [Col. 1105B] as a shepherd. Use the hoe, as a son of the prophet, to pluck up and destroy, build and plant; [Note: [Col. 1105] Jer. 1.] use the staff to restrain wolves from the sheepfold, sustain weak sheep, raise those who have fallen, and bring back those who wander. But among the fruits of episcopal office always prefer eternal things to temporal. Whenever troubling activity concerning the care of possessions makes demands upon you, let contemplative repose nevertheless never decline within you. Have another grind for you; yourself attend diligently to the salvation of souls.

The mind consecrated to the obedience of divine service ought to be free from secular concerns. You are committed to great matters: do not be occupied with little ones. Little and contemptible are all things that pertain to the gains of the world rather than to the profit of souls. “If you have secular disputes,” says the Apostle, “appoint those who are despised [Col. 1105C] among you to judge.” [Note: [Col. 1105] 1 Cor. 6.] But if the cause of a poor person, an orphan, or a widow comes before you, judge the poor in justice and rebuke with equity for the meek of the earth. [Note: [Col. 1105] Isa. 11.] Do justice for those suffering injury, [Note: [Col. 1105] Ps. 145.] procure peace for the humble, obedience for rebels, quiet for cloisters, order for monasteries, and discipline for clerics.

In judgments never be moved by rumours, nor let stealthy suspicion creep upon you. The Lord does not condemn Judas, whom he knew to be a traitor, because he was not convicted. He spares the woman caught in adultery because no accuser appears. [Note: [Col. 1105] John 8.] He does not overthrow Sodom until he descends and sees whether they have fulfilled the outcry in deed. [Note: [Col. 1105] Gen. 18.] “As I hear, so I judge”—he whose hearing [Col. 1105D] is knowing. But you should judge that sentences are to be given only upon the parties’ assertions and the reasonable movement of the mind.

There are indeed two things that make the eye of the heart grow dim in judgment: anger and greed. These two punish what should be forgiven and forgive what should be punished. Anger does not work the justice of God; greed, while seeking its own interests, despises the dreadful judgments of God. But shake your hands free from every gift, [Note: [Col. 1105] Isa. 33.] and give freely what you have received freely. [Note: [Col. 1105] Matt. 10.]

Do not be among those who pursue recompense [Col. 1106A] or sell the freedom of your conscience. Let no one be able to say to you: “We have enriched Abraham.” [Note: [Col. 1105] Gen. 14.] Rather, say confidently with Samuel: “Speak before the Lord and his Christ whether I have taken anyone’s ox or horse; whether I have falsely accused anyone; whether I have oppressed anyone; whether I have received a gift from anyone’s hand. I will despise it today and restore it to you.” [Note: [Col. 1105] 1 Sam. 12.]

If desire for gifts should tickle your mind, let it die where that most wicked shoot arises, and be smothered in its mother’s womb. Turn over in your mind how much you have advanced by assuming honour, and measure by daily comparison the spiritual progress of virtues: whether you are more presumptuous or humbler, more affable or sterner, gentler or harsher, more generous or greedier. For by a certain obligation joined to your office a fuller measure of spiritual fruits is required from you: that you be more devout in prayer, more diligent in reading, more cautious in chastity, more sparing in sobriety, more patient in hardship, rarer in laughter, more gracious in conduct, more grave in countenance, gesture, and dress, more moderate in speech, more lavish in tears, and more fervent in charity. [Col. 1106B]

Give your conscience an account of daily actions. See whether you have passed day and night without the stain of any sin; whether you have read or prayed too little; whether in speech, food, drink, or sleep you have exceeded the measure of temperance. Know that no small loss is incurred by the time spent in idleness or idle tales.

Other rich men are in their hiding places, as a lioness in her den, a hedgehog in its burrow, [Col. 1106C] a lion in its cave. But make yourself available to all, thinking yourself the servant of all; believe that you live not for yourself but as one born for all: given as a teacher to the unlearned, comforter of the poor, consolation of the oppressed, father of orphans, defender of widows, and debtor to all.

Again I repeat: exercise yourself in sacred Scripture for the instruction of many, so that what courtly life has at some time taken away from you, you may recover under grace as teacher. Idleness is the enemy of the soul. If you do not read and study, your soul will slumber from weariness, [Note: [Col. 1105] Ps. 118.] and the enemies of your soul will mock your sabbaths. [Note: [Col. 1105] Lam. 1.] Therefore, most excellent prelate, put everything after the salvation of souls. For souls are worthier than bodies and all that human ambition [Col. 1106D] desires, by as much as heaven surpasses earth in dignity.

And, to use the Apostle’s words in writing to Timothy: “Let no one despise your youth, but be an example to believers in word and conduct.” [Note: [Col. 1105] 1 Tim. 1.] Sow upon all waters, among good and bad alike, publicly and privately. By every means beware of becoming entangled in secular affairs. For there is no harmony between the Spirit of God and the spirit of this world; remain in your calling. “The world lies in wickedness.” [Note: [Col. 1105] 1 John 5.] “Do not emulate evildoers,” [Note: [Col. 1105] Ps. 36.]

[Col. 1107A] but remain in your calling, according to the measure of the rule which God has measured out to you. Today, among some, episcopal authority consists solely in this: that a field for sowing may be enriched with clay or dung, that fishponds may be multiplied, and that enclosures for game and the boundaries of estates may be enlarged. All the zeal of pontiffs burns in building palaces, mills, and ovens, and increasing revenues. Is this the Saviour’s voice to the Prince of the Apostles and of prelates: “If you love me, cultivate lands, build lofty houses”? We read that he said to Peter: “If you love me, feed my sheep.” [Note: [Col. 1107] John 21.]

You are Peter’s heir and vicar: feed my sheep by preaching the Gospel; do the work of an evangelist and a shepherd. Do not be ashamed of the Gospel, if you do not judge the shepherd’s office shameful. [Col. 1107B] Urge insistently, in season and out of season; [Note: [Col. 1107] 2 Tim. 4.] fulfil your ministry. Your ministry has more burden than honour. If you seek honour, you are a hireling; if you embrace the burden, the Lord is able to increase his grace, so that gain may be added to gain and progress to progress.

But if you recoil from the burden and consider yourself inadequate, your complaint is late: you ought first to have sat down and assessed the work, weighed the little burden, calculated the expense of virtues, and compared merit with dignity. Yet if labour beyond the ordinary measure should deter you, let hope of reward invite you: “For each shall receive reward according to his labour.” [Note: [Col. 1107] 1 Cor. 3.]

If you become immersed in the labyrinths of courtiers, and especially of the Exchequer, [Note: [Col. 1107D] “Exchequer” is used for the royal treasury, or for the royal court or tribunal in the hall at Westminster, where four barons determine matters and revenues of the fisc, from the Glossary of Matthew Paris. See William Somner in his Glossary, and Vossius, *On the Faults of Speech*, book II, chapter 17, and book III, chapter 44.] you will suffer great losses in spiritual exercise. No one [Col. 1107C] can serve two masters, God and mammon. [Note: [Col. 1107] Matt. 6.]

Let it not escape you how, at the tonsure of your head, when you were chosen into the Lord’s portion, you renounced lay disgrace. On the day of your consecration, moreover, upon renouncing secular things you uttered vows distinguished by your lips. You are bound by the words of your mouth, when, in answer to the consecrator’s question, you promised without any exception that henceforth you would separate yourself from earthly business and shameful gains, and would always devote your care to divine concerns.

What have you to do with the Exchequer? What have you to do with fiscal revenues, that for even a brief hour you should set aside care for souls? Did Christ choose you for the tax office? Matthew, once taken from it, did not return to it again. Do not, therefore, be among the crowd of those who [Col. 1107D] put secular things before spiritual, swallowing the camel and straining out the gnat. [Note: [Col. 1107] Matt. 23.]

We read [Note: [Col. 1107] Rufinus, book X, *History*, ch. 2; Gregory, book IV, ep. 75.] that in Constantine’s days certain bishops, flattering the emperor, showed greater reverence for royal edicts than for evangelical ordinances. [Col. 1108A] There are today also those to whom the dispensation of God’s word was entrusted, who “are silent concerning good things,” [Note: [Col. 1107] Ps. 38.] mute dogs, unable—or rather unwilling—to bark, [Note: [Col. 1107] Isa. 56.] unless perhaps they growl and bark at evangelical freedom. For they have been “turned into a crooked bow,” [Note: [Col. 1107] Ps. 77.] offering themselves as instruments of iniquity to sin.

“Judge justly, you who judge the world”; [Note: [Col. 1107] Ps. 9.] for he who is terrible over the children of men [Note: [Col. 1107] Ps. 65.] will also judge acts of justice. [Note: [Col. 1107] Ps. 74.] It is the prophet’s word: “Woe to you who make unjust laws and take away the justice of the righteous from him.” [Note: [Col. 1107] Isa. 5.] Do you wish that some law be proposed to you as an example?

A very poor man shudders from nakedness and hunger and sees his wife and household wasting away from deadly starvation. Certainly death threatens them unless he plunders or steals. He therefore steals some small thing, choosing an uncertain peril to life so that the certain danger of death and unbearable extremity of hunger may be avoided. The miserable man is caught in theft and condemned to death. Yet the judges weigh neither the poor man’s misery nor the pressure of necessity that compelled him to steal.

[Col. 1108B] Are they more just than God, who decreed in the law which he gave to Moses that thieves should be punished by a monetary fine? Are their laws more equitable than imperial law, which equity enacted with vigilant care and most exact deliberation? That law carefully distinguishes between a manifest and a non-manifest thief, and punishes the latter twofold but the former fourfold. Yet, as Jeremiah laments, [Note: [Col. 1107] Chs. 5 and 9.] the land is full of adulteries, and everywhere married and unmarried persons neigh after the wives of others. A poor man who steals another’s little sheep is hanged; an adulterer who steals another’s wife is endured with the utmost patience.

[Col. 1108C] This is that detestable tolerance which the Apostle puts forward ironically: “You gladly endure fools, since you yourselves are wise.” [Note: [Col. 1107] 1 Cor. 11.] Therefore let our kings hear what the wisest king Solomon says in his Proverbs: “It is not a great fault when someone has stolen; for he steals to fill his hungry soul. Yet, if caught, he shall restore sevenfold. But the adulterer, because of lack of heart, destroys his own soul; he gathers shame and disgrace to himself, and his reproach shall not be wiped away.” [Note: [Col. 1107] Prov. 6.]

The Mosaic law [Note: [Col. 1107] Lev. 20.] and imperial enactments condemn adulterers [Note: [Col. 1107] Institutes, § “Likewise the Julian law concerning adulteries,” *On Public Judgments*] and those who by an unspeakable sexual intercourse violate the law of nature [Col. 1108D] to death. For this reason the sword was also given to rulers for the punishment of evildoers. [Note: [Col. 1107] Suetonius, *On Octavius*, ch. 65.] Yet they overlook such persons’ abominations—or rather foster them by impunity.

Seeing a thief, they run with him; they place their share with [Col. 1109A] adulterers; they sin by participation in polluted speech; and they do not correct them, so that the Apostle’s saying suits them: “For this reason you do not rebuke others, because you yourselves frequently do the same things.” [Note: [Col. 1109] Rom. 13.] All unlawful acts are committed with impunity, and no one is condemned for transgressing the divine law; [Note: [Col. 1109] Rom. 2.] indeed, the sinner is praised in the desires of his soul, and the wicked man is blessed. [Note: [Col. 1109] Ps. 10.]

Impunity is indeed the daughter of negligence, the mother of obstinacy, the root of sin, the nurse of adultery and incest, the forerunner of eternal death, the preparer of hell. Through the impunity of the wicked, malice gathers strength; through it the wretched rot away in their own filth; drinking the urine of their sins, they glory when they have done evil and exult in the vilest deeds. They do not know how great a good innocence is, [Col. 1109B] who have always known how to do harm; and, all the more freely because all the more desperately, they loosen the whole reins of desire amid sins, and with the full force of their appetites rush headlong into contempt, as it is written: “When the sinner has come into the depths of evils, he will despise” [Note: [Col. 1109] Prov. 18.]. They regard God’s holy commandments and His dreadful judgments as mere words, and do not fear the punishments of eternal death, until through a most ruinous experience, amid unending torments, they learn what they refused to believe or fear.

For when Christ at the Judgment has displayed that body which He assumed for our salvation, condemned for our acquittal, pierced by nails and lance for the healing of our wounds, what will happen when, [Col. 1109C] set against our uncleannesses, its bruises and scars are produced as an accusation and condemnation of our obstinacy? This especially provokes the heavenly wrath and heaps upon many the peril of eternal damnation: that the chief priests and elders of the people, although they do not pronounce judgments of blood, nevertheless handle the same matters by debating and disputing them, and therefore count themselves free from guilt because, when they decree a sentence of death or mutilation, they merely absent themselves from the pronouncement and execution of the penal sentence. But what is more ruinous than this pretense? Is it lawful to investigate and decide what it is not lawful to pronounce?

Certainly Saul pursued David’s death by many stratagems; and, in order to cloak his malice under the shadow of innocence, [Col. 1109D] he said: “Let not my hand be upon him, but let the hand of the Philistines be upon him” [Note: [Col. 1109] I Sam. 18.]. Indeed, insofar as this dissimulation excused him before men, so much the more damnably did it accuse him before God. A clear pattern of the same thing appears in that council in which Christ was condemned to death: the Pharisees and scribes said, “It is not lawful for us to kill anyone” [Note: [Col. 1109] John 18.]. Yet when they cried out, saying, “Crucify him” [Note: [Col. 1109] Luke 23.], they dictated a sentence of death against Him in bloody malice. Him whom they killed with the sword of the tongue, they publicly declared themselves [Col. 1110A] unable to kill; and their iniquity was all the more detestable precisely because the pretense of innocence concealed it so that they might escape human judgment.

You have been set over souls, not bodies; a prelate has nothing in common with Pilate. You are Christ’s steward and Peter’s vicar; you ought to answer not to Caesar for the jurisdiction entrusted to you, but to Christ. Yet some, by usurping secular administrations, bind themselves by the obligation of the court and, as though they had renounced the privilege of their rank, await the reckoning of a harsher outcome. For on account of such a case certain bishops are today confined in Sicily in prison chains, and they expect no consolation from the Roman Church, since the supreme pontiff reproaches them, telling them to drink from the cup which they rashly mixed for themselves.

[Col. 1110B] It belongs to the shadowy justice of this age that, if a bishop or priest is killed, the punishment for so great a crime is passed over through dissimulation; but for the killing of a Jew judicial severity is exercised with the most exact rigor. Of all that multitude who lent the hand of counsel and aid to the killing of blessed Thomas, archbishop and primate, not one lost an ear. But when Aaron the Jew’s wife was killed, the whole land raged against the perpetrators and counselors of that deed with elaborate kinds of punishment.

Nevertheless, this is called an absurdity and an abomination: that, with the immunity of churches violated and the dignity of the sacred order trampled down, certain princes of the land think only of the immunity of wild beasts; [Col. 1110C] and while men groan beneath servile exactions, stags, roe-deer, fallow deer, and hares rejoice in the privilege of the highest liberty. They graze with impunity upon the crops and gardens of the poor, and no one dares drive them away; for a baneful law today condemns men not merely for taking game but for the bare suspicion of having taken it. The members which nature created for the propagation of humankind are cut off, eyes are gouged out, feet and hands are severed; and the human being created in the image and likeness of God is horribly disfigured to the dishonor of his Creator.

The lord king, indeed, did not establish these laws hateful to God, and others like them, but found them already established. Just as they turned to eternal punishment for their founders, so they would turn to the lord king’s reward of eternal salvation, [Col. 1110D] if, at your urging, he endeavored either to abolish them altogether or to moderate them in some respect. God made beasts for humankind; and, as you read in Genesis [Note: [Col. 1109] Ch. 1.], the Lord willed and commanded that man should rule over the fish of the sea, birds of the sky, beasts of the earth, and every living creature. I pass over marriages contracted through violence; the guardianships and tutorships of orphans, dictated by ambition alone; and innumerable other enormities which the common abuse introduced when the charity of many had grown cold [Col. 1111A].

Let this at least arouse your zeal: with ecclesiastical dignity trampled down, “the boar from the forest has laid waste the vineyard of the Lord, which His right hand planted” [Note: [Col. 1111] Ps. 79.]. May the Lord have mercy upon His vineyard; and, by His inspiration, may someone arise from among the sons of the shaken [Note: [Col. 1111] Ps. 126.], who will strive to replant in his own blood its torn-off shoots. You have been placed among the princes of the people, among the enrolled fathers, to whom swords have been given in their hands “to execute vengeance among the nations” [Note: [Col. 1111] Ps. 149.]. Arise, then, man of God; climb up against the foe, girding yourself for the work of strength. Bring aid to the wound of the Church. With the apostles sell your tunic, that you may buy a sword: fiery speech and a vehement spirit [Note: [Col. 1111] Ps. 118.]; weapons mighty through God for convicting all disobedience [Note: [Col. 1111] Luke 22], for taking every thought [Col. 1111B] captive into obedience to Christ. You are a chosen vessel, that you may bear the name of the Lord before nations and kings.

Draw the sword of your tongue. In the execution of episcopal justice, go about according to the form attached to your office; let your countenance be against those who do evil [Note: [Col. 1111] Ps. 33.]. Cry to the wicked: “Do not act wickedly”; and to sinners: “Do not exalt the horn.” The Lord speaks to you in Jeremiah, and through Jeremiah, saying: “Stand in the court of the house of the Lord, and speak to all, if perhaps they may hear and repent and turn from their evil way” [Note: [Col. 1111] Jer. 26.]. Go and cry these words: “Return, apostate Israel, says the Lord, and I will not turn My face away from you; return, returning children of Israel” [Note: [Col. 1111] Jer. 3.].

[Col. 1111C] There are two things, justice and liberty, for which every faithful person ought to stand even to blood. Therefore, if circumstances require it, do not hesitate, for the justice and liberty of the Church, to expose your possessions to plunderers, your reputation to mockery, your fortune to dangers, and your head to hostile swords. It is a delightful spectacle to the angels if a man, for justice’s sake, becomes “a reproach to the prosperous and a contempt to the proud” [Note: [Col. 1111] Ps. 122.]. The Apostle was not ashamed to expose his life to dangers for those subject to him: “And I,” he says, “will be spent for your souls” [Note: [Col. 1111] II Cor. 12.].

Since even angels confess themselves unequal to God’s benefits, what can you repay Him for all that His grace has bestowed upon you [Note: [Col. 1111] Ps. 115]? He laid down His life to death for you: why then do you fear to lay down for Him a brief, fragile, uncertain life, which the law of death will exact [Col. 1111D] shortly, and which devotion could now offer more healthfully? Would that willingness gave what necessity will extort, and that what will then be paid [Col. 1112A] as a debt might now be offered as a vow. By the testimony of Truth [Note: [Col. 1111] Matt. 10.], he who loses his life will preserve it, and he who preserves it will lose it; it is far wiser to lose it in order to preserve it than to preserve it in order to lose it.

If, therefore, you are a disciple of Christ, let your zeal forgive; let episcopal authority rise up; and do not prove least in great matters when you have been great in the least. If the king’s hand is long, the bishop’s hand ought to be longer. Let your hand seize judgment. If you say, “The wound is great and cannot be healed,” know that divine mercy is greater than human misery. Hope and trust in Him who “has placed help upon the mighty one” [Note: [Col. 1111] Ps. 88.], to whom no word shall be impossible. It was said to the innkeeper: “Take care of him” [Note: [Col. 1111] Luke 10.]. You are commanded to take care, not necessarily to cure.

[Col. 1112B] Therefore take care and labor. For if you have not cured the sick man, you have nevertheless fulfilled the physician’s office if you have omitted nothing that lay within your power. The Apostle does not say, “I benefited more,” but, “I labored more than all” [Note: [Col. 1111] I Cor. 15.]. God measures the reward of the labors of the saints not by the outcome of their labor but by their labor itself. Thus Paul glories not in the abundant result of his labors, but in his many labors [Note: [Col. 1111] II Cor. 11.]. Proclaim their crimes to the people. If they are hard of brow, harden your brow in return; blunt a hard brow with a harder brow, so that the Lord may say to you what He is recorded once to have said to the prophet [Note: [Col. 1111] Baruch 8.]: “I have made your brow harder than their brows.” It is enough if with the Apostle you deserve to say with a clear conscience: “I call you to witness this day [Col. 1112C] that I am clean from the blood of you all. For I did not shrink from declaring to you the whole counsel of God” [Note: [Col. 1111] Acts 20.].

As blessed Jerome writes [Note: [Col. 1111] On Matt. ch. 11.]: “John preferred to be endangered by the king rather than to keep silent about the justice of God’s law. Elijah was sent against Ahab and Jezebel, and John against Herod and Herodias. See whether you too have been sent by God to rebuke the great men of the earth, worse than Ahab and Herod.” For it is agreed that Ahab was a Jew and Herod a proselyte; but any crime is more damnable in a Christian than in a proselyte or a Jew. Thus strive to fulfill the office of bishop, that you may live in the Lord and die in the Lord. It is the Apostle’s word: “Whether we live or whether we die, we are the Lord’s” [Note: [Col. 1111] Rom. 14.]. Life makes the confessor; the cause makes the martyr [Col. 1112D]; but where the occasion of persecution is not at hand, holy severity toward oneself and the desire to suffer should make recompense for the place of martyrdom. Farewell.

[Col. 1113]

## INVECTIVE AGAINST THE CORRUPTER OF THE WORKS OF BLESENSIS

[Col. 1113A] I should have received your little exhortation with abundant thanksgiving, had not the deceptive gentleness of flattering sweet speech turned into the injury of an evident insult. It is written that every man first sets out good wine [Note: [Col. 1113] John 2.]; nor are poisons served except when seasoned with honey. If you had examined more carefully the prologue of my little work on Job, those things which wholly denied me free discretion in writing would have made me sufficiently excusable. Before that work, I had not yet undertaken this kind of writing; and you attacked with elaborate contrivances the simple first-fruits of my labor, which I dedicated to Christ’s service, and the still newborn infancy of my spiritual study.

You ought to have spared simplicity, and not made matter for mockery of the saliva [Col. 1113B] running down David’s beard [Note: [Col. 1113] I Sam. 21], or of Jeremiah’s childish words [Note: [Col. 1113] Jer. 1.]. I am indeed a carnal man, sold under sin [Note: [Col. 1113] Rom. 7]; but you are a regular canon and a spiritual man, and ought to have remembered what is read in the canonical Epistle: “If a person has been overtaken in any fault, you who are spiritual should instruct such a one in a spirit of gentleness” [Note: [Col. 1113] Gal. 6.]. “Would that the righteous might correct me in mercy and rebuke me” [Note: [Col. 1113] Ps. 140.]. For correction proceeding from charity is kindly; indeed charity is kindly [Note: [Col. 1113] I Cor. 13.].

But your mouth has spoken from the abundance of your heart and the fatness of iniquity. Therefore, with a tongue that cuts down your neighbor, you wound; you break the bruised reed and extinguish the smoking flax [Note: [Col. 1113] Matt. 12.]; in a violent spirit you shatter the ships of Tarshish [Note: [Col. 1113] Ps. 47.]. You are a pretentious smatterer, and a little learning [Col. 1113C] makes you mad. Desiring, therefore, to establish your own righteousness, you have turned to words of malice; judging and defaming others, you hunt favor for yourself from another’s corruption. Yet it is a very small thing to me that I should be judged by you or by a human day; for the Lord is He who judges me [Note: [Col. 1113] I Cor. 4.]. Who appointed you judge over us? Who are you, judging another’s servant? He stands or falls to his own Lord; but he shall stand [Note: [Col. 1113] Rom. 14.].

But I, whom you rebuke with excessive boldness and imprudence, shall rebuke you and set you before your own face, that you may learn not to blaspheme. I shall therefore bring sharp arrows of the mighty against a deceitful tongue [Note: [Col. 1113] Ps. 119]: a cursing, boastful, scurrilous, unrestrained tongue. I shall speak against the hissing of the ancient serpent; for he who once spoke in the serpent now speaks in [Col. 1114A] your tongue [Note: [Col. 1113] Gen. 3.]. For a slanderous tongue is a viper: it passes gently and strikes grievously. A member small in substance but great in malice; and, to use the words of blessed James: “The tongue is a small member, but full of deadly poison” [Note: [Col. 1113] Jas. 3.]. “If anyone thinks himself religious while not restraining his tongue, that man’s religion is vain” [Note: [Col. 1113] Jas. 1.]. You think yourself religious because you wear the habit of religion; but holiness and a viper’s tongue cannot coexist. Indeed, “a man of tongue shall not be established on the earth” [Note: [Col. 1113] Ps. 139]; for uncircumcised lips gather much filth to themselves, and every vessel which has no covering is accounted unclean in the Lord’s law [Note: [Col. 1113] Num. 19.]. Isaiah’s saying is: “The cultivation of righteousness is silence” [Note: [Col. 1113] Isa. 32.]. Would that you had set a door of restraint around your lips [Note: [Col. 1113] Ps. 140], and [Col. 1114B] had not rushed forth as far as cursing! For revilers shall not inherit the kingdom of God [Note: [Col. 1113] I Cor. 6.].

You invite me unwillingly to quarrels. Solomon testifies: “He who lets out water is the beginning of strife” [Note: [Col. 1113] Prov. 17]; and the tongue is an occasion of scandal whenever it pours itself out in a flood of detraction.

> “He who rouses me—I cry that he had better not touch me—  
> Shall weep, and be sung of throughout the whole famous city.”  
> [Note: [Col. 1113] Horace, *Satires*, II.1, vv. 46–47.]

Would that you had kept silent, that you might appear wiser. But how do you know me?

> “I received a wound from an enemy I did not expect.”  
> [Note: [Col. 1113] Ovid, *Heroides*, Epistle 6, v. 82.]

Yet although I have not seen your face,

> “. . . . . I know you within and under the skin.”  
> [Note: [Col. 1113] Persius, *Satires* 3, v. 30.]

You unjustly supposed that I was like you [Note: [Col. 1113] Ps. 49.]. I [Col. 1114C] walked simply in my work; you acted deceitfully with your tongue. I was sowing wheat, and you, an enemy man, were sowing tares over it [Note: [Col. 1113] Matt. 13.]. Do not, I beg you, boast by speaking lofty things; do not think more highly than you ought [Note: [Col. 1113] Rom. 12.]. For to think lofty things is death. And he who gazes upon himself in a high place and is astonished easily falls into danger.

You say and write that you have not seen me. I am indeed glad that you do not see me. Already I have sensed in you the spirit of an asp. May the eye of a basilisk not see me. Envious man and slanderer hateful to God, why do you bite me? For, Ecclesiastes says [Note: [Col. 1113] Ch. 10], he who slanders is like a serpent which bites secretly. “If you bite and devour one another,” Paul says, “will you not be consumed by one another?” [Note: [Col. 1113] Gal. 5.] If debate and conflict between us [Col. 1115A] were face to face, I would endure it more patiently. It is easy for you to attack one who is absent; and, according to Jerome’s witness, it is a delicate kind of learning to direct a battle from a wall. Would that you might experience in me both the word of the mouth and the word of action! Yet I do not judge it safe to pull a contentious rope with a mad-brained man, or, contrary to Solomon’s counsel, to answer a fool according to his folly [Note: [Col. 1115] Prov. 26.].

I would therefore pass over my injuries in silence; but I fear that wandering and unbridled impunity may arouse incentives to still worse presumption in you. I had begun to write a letter, but the abundant matter for speech does not permit itself to be compressed into the brevity of a letter. Therefore the letter grows into a book, and Solomon’s saying comes true: “There will be no end to the making of books” [Note: [Col. 1115] Ecclus. 12]. Your order ought to write things that would benefit the public good, refresh the mind, and reduce every thought into Christ’s servitude and obedience. But you, forgetting the apostolic profession to which you had pledged your hand, and the doctrine that accords with godliness, are, to use the Apostle’s words, proud, knowing nothing, sickly about questions and disputes of words [Note: [Col. 1115] I Tim. 6.]. Along with those who devote themselves to detraction and scurrility, you adulterate the matronly integrity of Holy Scripture, while Jeremiah laments and says: “My heart is broken within me before the Lord and His holy words, because the land is full of adulterers” [Note: [Col. 1115] Jer. 23.].

[Col. 1115C] Speaking of you and your like, the Apostle says: “We have heard that some among you walk disorderly and meddle with trifles. To such persons we announce and exhort in the Lord that they eat their own bread in silence” [Note: [Col. 1115] I Thess. 3.]. You call a man whom you do not know a flatterer of the prince and an informer against the holy order; but you have taught your tongue to speak falsehood, and in this matter iniquity has lied to itself [Note: [Col. 1115] Ps. 26.]. The Spirit of God bears witness to my spirit that I have never been a seller of oil, nor am I accustomed to stroke great men in their vices or praise the sinner in the desires of his soul [Note: [Col. 1115] Ps. 10.].

In my *Compendium on Job*, my *Letters*, my book of *Exhortations*, my *Dialogue to King Henry*, my treatise *On the Jerusalem Pilgrimage*, my book *On the Deceptions of Fortune*, my recent work *On the Affirmation of Faith*, my book *Against the Perfidy of the Jews*, [Col. 1115D] my book *On Confession and Penance*, the work entitled *Episcopal Canon*, and very many other writings of mine, I rebuke our king and the other great men of the land, whenever the subject arises, with complete freedom, [Col. 1116A] carefully suggesting whatever human devotion can offer for their edification without the injury of invective.

With my whole heart’s devotion I venerate the life of religious persons, whose kinds are diverse—for Joseph’s tunic is multicolored [Note: [Col. 1115] Gen. 37], and Christ’s bride is “clothed round about with varieties” [Note: [Col. 1115] Ps. 44]—and I embrace their feet with the arms of most devoted humility. For I know that, above all secular persons, clergy and laity alike, they bear the titles of virtues all the more distinctly in proportion as they have clung more closely, by deeper footprints, to the rules of the apostles. They exercise themselves with tireless diligence in humility, hospitality, obedience, charity, and the other things by which the kingdom of God is seized and possessed. They humble the flesh and raise the spirit; while leading an angelic life on earth, they serve Christ in spareness [Col. 1116B] of food, roughness of clothing, vigils kept as watch, psalms, hymns and spiritual songs, confessions, disciplines and tears, longings for heaven, burning compunctions and secret jubilations, ecstasies of mind and sweet whispers, certain experiences of heavenly glory, and embraces of the Bridegroom.

Yet I could by no means pass over this: while the rest pour out the balm of glorious reputation in a fragrance of sweetness, you and those like you have become “an odor of death unto death” [Note: [Col. 1115] II Cor. 2.]. If the fabric of haircloth and skins, as you plead them in excuses to excuse sins [Note: [Col. 1115] Ps. 140], is exposed outside to dust and labor, would that they were Solomon’s skins [Note: [Col. 1115] Song 1] and not the skins of the land of Midian. [Col. 1116C] Would that those who go out on their households’ business might grind for those who remain in bed, and not relax themselves more freely into unlawful acts.

We read, however, in the book of daily occurrences that among those who have vomited up the world, love of the world frequently returns; rebuilding their own Jericho, which they had overthrown in their first mode of life, they stir up the fire and ashes of ambition already lulled to sleep [Note: [Col. 1115] Josh. 4.]. And what is the love of the world in you but hatred of God? What is that heat of desire, which turns your gold into dross, but the death of the soul, mother of transgression, teacher of wrongdoing, chief officer of iniquity, charioteer of malice, assassin of virtues, source of sedition, and pit of scandals?

I say this not in boasting, but in order to blunt your shamelessness—for “the brow of a harlot” has become [Col. 1116D] yours [Note: [Col. 1115] Jer. 3.]—by the testimony and affirmation of very many English magnates. King Henry of good memory had at one time become inexorably and irreconcilably [Col. 1117A] angry with the two leading men of your order over Saint Peter’s Penny.

[Note: [Col. 1115D] That penny of Saint Peter was an alms instituted by the kings of England for poor English scholars who were educated at Rome in the English school. It was paid from every household in England and sent to Rome on the feast of Saint Peter in Chains; hence it was called Saint Peter’s Penny, in English [Col. 1116D] *Romescot*. Some attribute its establishment to Ina, king of the Mercians; others to Offa, likewise king of the Mercians. Matthew of Westminster, in the *Flowers of England*, under the year 727, writes:

> “In the year of grace 727, Ina, a happy and powerful king, leaving his kingdom to his kinsman Aethelard, went to Rome in order to exchange a temporal kingdom [Col. 1117B] for an eternal one. When he had arrived there, with the consent and approval of Pope Gregory he built a house in the city, which he caused to be called the School of the English. To it the kings of England and the royal family, together with bishops, priests, and clerics, were to come to be instructed in Christian doctrine and faith, lest anything perverse or contrary to Catholic unity be taught in the English Church [Col. 1117C]; and, thus strengthened in a firm faith, they might return to their own country. For teaching and schools of the English had been prohibited by the Roman pontiffs from the time of Saint Augustine, on account of the continual heresies which had arisen in Britain at the coming of the English, while pagans mingled with Christians had corrupted the grace of holy conduct and of the Christian faith. He therefore caused a church to be built beside the aforesaid house in honor of the Blessed Virgin Mary, in which the divine mysteries might be celebrated for English people arriving at Rome, and in which they might be buried if any English person should happen to die at Rome. And that all these things might obtain the strength of perpetual stability, it was established by a general decree throughout the kingdom of the West Saxons, over which the aforesaid Ina ruled, that every year one penny from every household, called in English *Romescot*, should be sent to Saint Peter and the Roman Church, so that the English residing there [Col. 1117D] might receive from it the support necessary for life.”

The same author, under the year of Christ 794, when he had spoken of King Offa’s Roman pilgrimage and of the favors bestowed upon him by Pope Adrian, continues:

> “King Offa considered with himself what he might worthily repay for so great a generosity. At last, divine grace inspiring the king, a salutary plan came to him. On the following day he entered the School of the English, which was then flourishing at Rome, and there gave, for the support of the people of his kingdom coming there, one silver coin from each household, to be paid every year thereafter for all future days—namely, from those whose property outside their houses in pasture amounted to as much as, but did not exceed, the value of thirty silver coins.”

And a little later:

> “The great King Offa ruled over twenty-three provinces, which the English call *shires*, etc. From [Col. 1118B] all these provinces the aforesaid king gave Saint Peter’s Penny, as stated above, which in English is called *Romescot*.”

Matthew Paris reports this in exactly the same words in his *Life of Offa, Second King of the Mercians*, and adds:

> “It is therefore called Saint Peter’s Penny because the aforesaid King Offa, on the feast of Saint Peter called [Col. 1118C] in Chains, deserved by heavenly favor to discover the martyr himself, Saint Alban, on that very day; and on that very day he granted that annual revenue to the Roman Church for the redemption of his soul, namely for the support of the aforesaid school, for the instruction of unlearned English people and those making pilgrimage there.”

Roger of Hoveden, Part II of the *Annals*, under 1180, has the following:

> “In the same year Henry, king and father of England, appointed Ranulf de Glanville chief justiciar of all England, by whose wisdom the laws appended below were composed, which we call English.”

Here is indicated what William, king of the English, established with his princes after the conquest of England. Many laws are then listed, among which is this:

> “Concerning Saint Peter’s Penny, called *Romescot* in English. Everyone who has in his house thirty pence-worth of living property of his own shall, by the law of the English, give Saint Peter’s Penny, and, by the law of the Danes, half a mark. This penny must be summoned for on the feast [Col. 1118D] of Saints Peter and Paul, and collected before the feast called Saint Peter in Chains, so that it is not withheld beyond the following day. If anyone withholds it, complaint shall be carried to the king’s custody, because this penny is the king’s alms. Justice shall cause the penny to be rendered, together with the bishop’s and king’s fine. And if anyone has several houses, he shall pay the penny from that in which he resides, on the feast of the apostles Peter and Paul.”

Nearly the same things concerning Saint Peter’s Penny are found in John Brompton, pp. 754 and 776; Ralph de Diceto, under 793; Henry of Huntingdon, *Histories*, book IV, under 768. For more, see Polydore Vergil, *History of the English*, book II, ch. 11, and Spelman, *Glossary*, under “Romescot.”]

No one dared oppose the king; I stood in the breach for them, and in the time of wrath became reconciliation [Note: [Col. 1117] Ecclus. 44.]. At my entreaty, God inspiring, the royal hand frequently poured itself out liberally and magnificently in almsgiving, and the Church of the saints still recounts those alms [Note: [Col. 1117] Ecclus. 31.]. As the courtly multitude can attest, on one occasion, at the urging of my insignificance, with the help of Him in whose hand are the hearts of kings [Note: [Col. 1117] Prov. 21.], the king forgave great debts to ecclesiastical persons, released those in chains, and lightened the punishments of the condemned.

But I cannot bear calmly that, rejecting counsel and the congregation of the righteous, you who were formerly a regular canon have become an island canon. It is a sign of a sick [Col. 1117B] mind that you have left the common life, preferred solitude to the community, and an island to the cloister. You have made yourself an anathema to your brethren: you forsake the promised land for Egypt, Jerusalem for Babylon, and heaven for hell. What have you to do with solitude? “Woe to the one who is alone” [Note: [Col. 1117] Eccl. 4.]. Solitude has cast many into peril of soul. Some wandered in the wilderness and perished [Col. 1118A] from serpents [Note: [Col. 1117] Judith 8; I Cor. 10.]. I regard the serpents as viperous thoughts which have besieged you in solitude. There the crowd of temptations clamors around you; there the manifold army of vices attacks you. Although you seem to have escaped the roar of the world, the world, in this singularity of yours, assails you with many phantasms.

You could sit alone and silent in the cloister and rise above yourself. There are, as Job testifies, those who build solitudes for themselves [Note: [Col. 1117] Job 3]; there, though among many, you could be with yourself. But now you are alone and yet amid crowds of passions. In the cloister you had the secret of solitude, a place of penance, peace of soul, the mystery of contemplation, joy in the Holy Spirit, counsel in uncertainty, remedy in temptation, and in all things the effective benefit of medicine. There is the school of virtues, [Col. 1118B] the practice of highest moderation, regularity of conduct, freedom for reading, fraternal affection, the sharing of all things, the vigor of discipline, the law of obedience, the bond of charity, and mutual service.

But the labor of penance is burdensome to you, abstinence oppressive, and the austerity of discipline intolerable—[Col. 1119A] discipline which alone is the key of innocence, the anchor of religion, the guard of the heart, and altogether the destroyer of unlawful desire. Therefore the Prophet [Note: [Col. 1119] Ps. 2.] warns us to embrace discipline. And the Apostle says: “If you are outside discipline, then you are adulterous children” [Note: [Col. 1119] Heb. 12.]. I fear that, having begun in the spirit, you may be consummated in the flesh [Note: [Col. 1119] Gal. 3.], and that Isaiah’s word may strike you: “You have conceived burning heat and brought forth stubble” [Note: [Col. 1119] Isa. 33.]. For, making your first faith void, under a certain color of religion you overthrow the foundation of the religious life you began; casting your soul as though upon the throw of dice, you plunge yourself into danger to your salvation and reputation. It is written: “He who loves danger shall perish in it” [Note: [Col. 1119] Ecclus. 3.].

And now what do you want on the way of Egypt? What have you to do with the way of the Assyrians, that you may drink muddy water? You have rejected the water of Siloam and [Col. 1119B] chosen the waters of Rezin [Note: [Col. 1119] Isa. 8.]; you have forsaken the fountain of living water and dug for yourself old cisterns which cannot hold water [Note: [Col. 1119] Jer. 2.]. For, in order that you may devote yourself to extraordinary and scurrilous speeches, you live singly like a wild beast from the forest; and though, if you were a true anchorite, you ought to be sustained by roots and herbs [Note: [Col. 1119] Ps. 79], you appropriate your brothers’ clothing and food for yourself and your boy.

Moreover, although there are two laws, inner and outer, and your singularity may please you and those who flatter you, nevertheless the Spirit of truth, who flatters no one—and He Himself is the inner law—accuses and condemns you. Therefore accustom yourself to the Lord’s yoke, brother unknown to me; for I have not seen you. As Solomon said, put your foot in His fetters, and do not fall [Col. 1119C] into His chains [Note: [Col. 1119] Ecclus. 6.]. You see that every creature is subject to vanity [Note: [Col. 1119] Rom. 8], and that man passes away in an image [Note: [Col. 1119] Ps. 38.]. Do not, therefore, under any pretext of singularity abandon your house, lest elsewhere you build yourself a house for Gehenna. Persevere to the end in the calling in which you were called.

For the Apostle, writing to the Thessalonians, says: “Make it your effort to be quiet and to conduct your own business” [Note: [Col. 1119] I Thess. 4], thereby indicating the business of salvation. Writing also to the Corinthians, he says: “My beloved brethren, be always steadfast and immovable in the work of God” [Note: [Col. 1119] I Cor. 15.]. Once you entered the cloister, you shut yourself in and bound yourself with Christ’s bonds. You are enclosed and bound by the censure of your order, the observance of discipline, the promise of stability, the enclosure of reverence and fear, and the bond [Col. 1119D] of obedience.

That enclosure was cast aside by the man of whom Solomon speaks in reproach: “I passed by the field of the slothful man and by the vineyard of the fool; its stone wall was destroyed, and nettles and thorns had filled it all” [Note: [Col. 1119] Prov. 24.]. As though you knew something loftier and more heavenly than others, you claim for yourself the freedom of a certain familiarity. But know that in departing from the cloister you withdraw from God; nor can you make yourself freer than by loving and fulfilling cloistered servitude. Indeed, your learning makes you mad and a transgressor of the rules of observance. But, according to Wisdom’s saying, “Better [Col. 1120A] is a man diminished in wisdom and deficient in understanding, with fear, than one abundant in understanding who transgresses the law of God” [Note: [Col. 1119] Ecclus. 19.]. You withdrew into solitude in order that you might more freely devise scurrilous nonsense and wander more freely to the peril of another’s reputation.

Therefore I no longer number you among the ravening wolves who come in sheep’s clothing [Note: [Col. 1119] Matt. 7], as you accuse me of having charged certain religious men; rather, I place you among biting fleas, destructive moths, dog-flies and gnats, and the exceedingly grievous flies of Egypt. Why do you accuse us over farthings, when you live on the offerings of the poor and the farthings of widows? Does not your prior add church to church, income to income, and heap possession upon possession [Col. 1120B]? But if, to colour the shamefulness of your fault, you plead the title of public utility, know that neither their number defends him nor the size of the community excuses him. For he who burns with many or for many will burn no less. Since, moreover, the Apostle says that this very thing is a fault among you, that you reclaim what is yours rather than suffer wrong [Note: [Col. 1119] I Cor. 6], you, a most impoverished lawyer, prattle about laws and, contrary to the Council of Tours, contrary to God’s law, and to the ruin of your own soul, usurp the office of plaintiff.

What have you to do with the profession of men in gowns, you who were dead to the world and conformed to the likeness of Christ’s death? Having cast aside the law of the Lord, which is spotless and converts souls, you busy yourself with abridged and corrupted laws [Col. 1120C] in the book of the poor, so that in legal cases you cite not from the original text but from an abridged and corrupted one. Certainly, as the Tripartite History reports [Note: [Col. 1119] Book X, ch. 3], John Chrysostom, though eminent in knowledge of civil law, nevertheless, when his friends asked him to plead their cases, always recoiled from the name of advocate. For in a religious man the office of advocate is base and contemptible; as the Apostle sufficiently implies when he says: “If you have secular disputes, appoint as judges those who are most despised among you” [Note: [Col. 1119] I Cor. 6]. These are the hair-shirts and skins of which you speak, who go out into the dust and labour; and would that they were stretched out like the tents of Kedar [Note: [Col. 1119] Song 1], so that they might not loosen themselves for unlawful things! You accuse clerical pleasures, which I judge, among most spiritual men in Christ, to be spiritual rather than carnal [Col. 1120D]. I know very many for whom their own chamber would be more suspect as an occasion of indecency than perhaps a church is for you; perhaps you glory more in your half-girdles than a cleric does in purple and fine linen. Humility in purple is better than pride in rags. Piety itself is the worship of God. Take care that you have the appearance of piety but not its worship, lest you be counted among those of whom the Apostle says: “Having an appearance indeed of piety, but denying its power” [Note: [Col. 1119] II Tim. 3]. Which, do you suppose, is more unjust: the public profession of sin, or the pretence of holiness? [Col. 1121A] Garments and tonsure do not remove the worm of conscience: “the kingdom of God is within you” [Note: [Col. 1121] Luke 17], not in outward clothing. I have known certain clerics who, as possessing nothing, possess much; for they possess nothing for themselves, but whatever they have is for all. They are sustained by temporal help as a traveller uses a bed at an inn. He rests and hastens to depart, knowing that he is a stranger and pilgrim upon the earth. Do you think them all so far removed from God, so forgetful of their salvation, and given over to a reprobate mind that neither fear of hellish misery nor the blessedness of heavenly glory stirs them? Are they wholly ignorant of discipline, penance, and the rest that belongs to spiritual exercise? Is there no balm in Gilead, or no physician there [Note: [Col. 1121] Jer. 8]? If Gilead means “heap of testimony,” or “martyrdom,” which is the same thing, lift up your eyes and recall whether you have ever seen a professor of any Rule triumph over the world through the contest of martyrdom. For if you cite someone who triumphed in that fashion, episcopal prerogative had exempted him from observance of the order. Not all ought to enlist in the regular soldiery. I believe it is no less meritorious, without the bond of profession and the compulsory service of an assumed obligation, simply to walk with God, to keep one’s vessel in holiness and grace, and to shake one’s hands free from the filth of bribes, than to reject an imposed burden and struggle against the yoke of obedience. For pure and undefiled religion [Note: [Col. 1121] Jas. 1] is this: to keep oneself unstained [Col. 1121C] from this world and continually to exercise oneself in works of mercy. If you consider Jacob’s sheepfold, Peter’s net, and the house of the heavenly Father, you will find different sheep, different fish, and different and many dwelling-places. Noah, Daniel, and Job followed different paths of meritorious life. And although Christ commended the leisure of Mary, he did not dislike Martha’s activity [Note: [Col. 1121] Luke 10].

The Lord often receives more gladly the repentance of a humble and contrite sinner than the innocence of a lukewarm and lax righteous person. The former falls heavily but rises more strongly; the latter, growing sluggish on the Lord’s way and soon to be vomited out, withers in his season and torpor. A sheep in the law of the Lord [Note: [Col. 1121] Lev. 3] is commanded to be offered far from the door of the tabernacle; but a goat, which is a peace-offering, is sacrificed [Col. 1121D] at the very door of the tabernacle, from which the sheep is removed. For those who punish extraordinary acts by the judgment of a harsher penance are admitted more familiarly into the bosom of heavenly grace than those who, sleeping in sloth along the way of life, languish with a fainting spirit. I do not prefer to religion—which is the certain and direct way to God—the uncertainty of our secular condition. I do not say with Naaman the Syrian that the rivers of Damascus, Abana and Pharpar, are better than all the waters of Israel [Note: [Col. 1121] IV Kings 5]. I do not say with Gideon [Note: [Col. 1121] Judg. 8] that the clusters of Ephraim are better than the vintage of Abiezer; nor do I prefer men to angels, nor compare earths with heavens. But, I pray, let your eyes see your own imperfection [Col. 1122A], and, judging yourself, do not judge one whom you do not know, until your judgment proceeds from the countenance of him who will reveal the secrets of hearts and make manifest the hidden things of darkness. Indeed, I love, magnify, venerate, and adore every holy order in the bowels of Christ. Therefore, from times long past, I have always had with me a man of your order, a witness of my manner of life and an angel and guardian of my body and soul. Yet I chose and preferred one, beloved of God and men, whom, in my judgment, a certain pre-eminence of most approved religion distinguishes far above many others. He was rich and honourable in the world, but for Christ’s sake he made himself poor. I glory in his friendship and set it [Col. 1122B] above every courtly and palatine intimacy. Without doubt he is a friend of God, a most vigorous imitator of canonical discipline, a cruel adversary of his own flesh but a watchful guardian of his soul, most firm in faith, patient in hope, lavish in charity, restrained in works, gentle and humble, provident in counsel, pleasant and circumspect in speech. Honey and milk are always under his tongue; for grace is poured out upon his lips. His face is so brightened by a certain festive cheerfulness and a certain angelic pallor; and a kind of heavenly favour so graces his deeds and words that his appearance and conversation almost draw everyone into the bond of spiritual friendship. I have set his memory [Col. 1122C] as a seal upon my heart [Note: [Col. 1121] Song 8]. His humility, maturity, prudence, constancy, and, to include much in few words, incomparable integrity, I carry in my inward being with continual remembrance; and, insofar as secular life permits, I mark myself after his example as after the image of a spiritual seal. And because, wrapping judgments in deceptive words, you corrupt my apprenticeship and first fruits in theological faculty by veiled iniquity, I answer the man rather than the argument. For since you are a difficult and perverse disputant, this whole answer is dictated by indignation alone.

You charge me with saying that the voice of deed is better than the voice of speech. Charge, then, him in whose mouth no falsehood was found [Note: [Col. 1121] Rev. 14]; for he himself, contradicting the Rule of your institution, says of you and men like you: “Do what they say, but do not do what they do” [Note: [Col. 1121] Matt. 23]. He too first acted and afterwards taught, as it is written: “Jesus began to do and to teach” [Note: [Col. 1121] Acts 1]. What he first did, he afterwards taught: he puts the voice of deed before the voice of speech. If you accuse me concerning the comparison I made between the voice of speech and the voice of deed, I still say, and repeat with Solomon, that “a patient man is better than a conqueror of cities” [Note: [Col. 1121] Prov. 13]; “a living dog is better than a dead lion” [Note: [Col. 1121] Eccl. 9]; “a wise and poor child is better than an old and foolish king” [Note: [Col. 1121] Eccl. 4]; [Col. 1123A] “it is better to go to the house of mourning than to the house of feasting” [Note: [Col. 1123] Eccl. 7]. I could introduce countless examples; all these vary reciprocally and answer one another according to an understanding of greater or lesser intensity, like things that exceed and are exceeded. You reproach me about incipient fear because there is no fear of God before your eyes, while you speak of perfect fear; indeed, fear has punishment [Note: [Col. 1123] I John 4]. Therefore I doubt how you understand a man to be perfect in fear. For where fear is, there is no perfection. Hear Augustine in his homily on the Epistle of John [Note: [Col. 1123] Tractate 9 on I John]: “If charity,” he says, “is perfect in a man, he no longer fears; for perfect charity makes perfect righteousness.
