He no longer fears, but desires that iniquity may pass away and the kingdom of God come.” Blessed Ambrose also [Note: [Col. 1123] On Psalm 118 and 31, v. 2] [Col. 1123B] says: “Chaste fear makes sweet what was previously most bitter; but neither worldly nor servile fear will exist in the future.” John of Damascus too, on the phrase in the Epistle to the Hebrews, “He was heard because of his reverence” [Note: [Col. 1123] Heb. 5], says: “Understand this reverence to be wholly free from every fear. For God is charity” [Note: [Col. 1123] I John 4], “and charity admits no fellowship with fear.” Still envy proceeds from the hedgehog’s pit and the lurking-place of more hidden wickedness, so that the simplicity of the innocent may be mocked. For you allege that I blasphemed because I said that Christ for our sake became poor from being rich. Hear what Blessed Basil writes in the book of Exhortation: “The omnipotent Word, from being by nature one [Col. 1123C] with the Father, became one with man; born from the Father, born from a woman; from the Almighty made weak; from the Lord emptied into a servant.” Beyond this, you attack the tower of David and, assailing the titles of truth with deceptive sophisms, corrupt with the twisted poison of interpretation things that have a common and simple meaning. When I spoke of the Lord’s Transfiguration, saying simply that after that manifestation of glory the divine form which appeared there in some manner returned into the human, you maliciously distort this word “form” in relation to God, so that you may never be brought to contemplate the form of his exaltation. Hear what Ambrose says, expounding that clause of Jeremiah: “Who has stood in the substance of the Lord, and seen his word?” [Note: [Col. 1123] Jer. 23]. “The Wisdom,” he says, [Col. 1123D] “the Word of God the Father, does not degenerate from his form, whose substance he offered us in another form for our remedy.” And Hilary: “The use shines forth in the image, in the gift.” And again: “For the prerogative of the form, in which were the splendour and figure of the substance of God, by the ministry of the pious dispensation so emptied itself into the form of a servant that it was not alien from the substance of the Father.” From the Council of Toledo you have that in Christ there are two natural forms: power [Col. 1124A] and weakness. Hence the Apostle says: “Although Christ died from weakness, yet he lives by the power of God” [Note: [Col. 1123] II Cor. 13]. Likewise Hilary: “The distinction of unbegottenness indicates form; nor does what is born or proceeds degenerate, whose union and conformity of form immutable nature preserves.” The imposture of malice advances further: in all these things its fury has not turned away, but its hand is still stretched out [Note: [Col. 1123] Isa. 9]. He will not allow King Hezekiah to have been subject to any sin, though Scripture publicly testifies that not even an infant of one day is free from sin [Note: [Col. 1123] Job 14 according to the LXX]. I do not deny that Hezekiah was righteous and holy; but Isaiah says [Note: [Col. 1123] ch. 64] that all our righteousnesses are like a menstrual cloth. Holy David, in whom the Lord found a man after his own heart [Note: [Col. 1123] Acts 13], [Col. 1124B] complained that his iniquities had risen above his head [Note: [Col. 1123] Ps. 37]; Job likewise, whose virtues the Lord so magnifies and extols [Note: [Col. 1123] Job 1]; Jeremiah also, Moses, and the rest whose praise is in the Gospel, were conceived, born, and lived in sins.

If you do not know Hezekiah’s sins, recall that as David numbered the people for glory and pomp [Note: [Col. 1123] II Kings 24], so Hezekiah, prideful over the flight of Sennacherib and the slaughter of his army [Note: [Col. 1123] IV Kings 19], did not give thanks to God, according to Augustine’s testimony [Note: [Col. 1123] Book II, *On the Miracles of Holy Scripture*, ch. 27]. You know, moreover, that the vice of ingratitude is altogether destructive of the soul and detestable before God. To crown his proud transgression, he displayed his storehouses of spices and the Lord’s treasures to the envoys of Merodach, [Col. 1124C] king of Babylon [Note: [Col. 1123] Isa. 39]. I call not only Merlin but also you a prophet; for you are a prophet of Antichrist: already through you the mystery of iniquity is at work [Note: [Col. 1123] II Thess. 2]. Certainly, I have never decreed that Merlin should be placed in the catalogue of the prophets who have existed since the beginning of the world, among the saints; but I place both you and him among the prophets of Baal, and number you among Ahab’s four hundred prophets, who prophesied falsely to him [Note: [Col. 1123] III Kings 18]. Or, because you have been admitted to the lot of the priesthood, I join you as colleague to the high priest Caiaphas, who in that cruel council in which innocent Christ was condemned to death, being high priest that year, prophesied [Note: [Col. 1123] John 11]. Read and understand the Scriptures, I beg you: not everything is found in Cato. Certainly, if I called Merlin a prophet [Col. 1124D] mockingly, you ought not to have become so violently enraged as to brand me as a flatterer. Recall that, when Saul had been chosen in God’s wrath and rejected by the Lord, it is nevertheless written that a band of prophets came down, and Saul was made among the prophets [Note: [Col. 1123] I Kings 10]. You ought to have spewed something venomous against the doctors of the Church concerning the pagan Sibyl, Balaam the diviner [Note: [Col. 1123] Num. 24], and others whose prophecies the Church receives. Concerning Jael, I answer you this: her husband Heber the Kenite had already departed with all his household [Col. 1125A] from his brothers and made a covenant with the king of Hazor. Sisera, therefore, trusting in that alliance, turned aside to Heber’s tent. He asked Jael to conceal him and give him a drink; Jael gave him milk that he might sleep more heavily; but she drove a tent-peg through the sleeping man’s temples into the ground [Note: [Col. 1125] Judg. 4]. See whether she is guilty of treachery, she who had offered the unhappy fugitive seeking aid the security of sleep. But, to use Job’s phrase, “shadow protects shadow” [Note: [Col. 1125] Job 40]: like excuses like; nor would you excuse her if you abhorred the crime of treachery. Yet although that deed was impious, it nevertheless contains a venerable sacrament. By the expressed pattern of likeness, the murder of his brother by Cain [Col. 1125B] [Note: [Col. 1125] Gen. 4], Judah’s intercourse with his daughter-in-law [Note: [Col. 1125] Gen. 38], David’s seizure of another man’s wife [Note: [Col. 1125] II Kings 11], the treacherous killing of Uriah by David himself [Note: [Col. 1125] ibid.], and of Abner [Note: [Col. 1125] II Kings 2] and Amasa [Note: [Col. 1125] II Kings 20] by Joab, could likewise be excused through the benefit of mystical signification. Nor should you understand that Holy Scripture specially exalted Jael with praises; rather, understand God, who had saved Israel through a woman, as miraculously delivering the enemy into a woman’s hand. It is also frequent in sacred discourse for good things to be taken in an evil and evil things in a good signification, so that the historical narrative may always serve beneficially the understanding of the mystery. Samson, whose name means “sun,” consecrated to the Lord and often bearing in sacred discourse the figure of Christ, nevertheless represents the figure of the sinner when he is bound by Delilah—that is, by carnal desire—with the ropes of sins [Col. 1125C]; and, when he turns back to penance and the Spirit of the Lord rushes upon him, his bonds are loosened [Note: [Col. 1125] Judg. 16]. Uriah, an innocent and righteous man, represents the type of the devil when he is killed on account of his wife [Note: [Col. 1125] II Kings 11]. Babylon, infamous in the sin of idolatry, is at times called the beloved of the Lord [Note: [Col. 1125] Isa. 21]; and through Saul, although he was disobedient, obstinate, rash, and presumptuous, Christ the Son of God is prefigured. Again, while you tear apart my little works, biting at them with the venomous tooth of envy, [Col. 1126A] you sneeringly charge me with blasphemy for mingling and confusing grace and free will. Yet I confidently affirm that free will so rests and depends upon grace that God’s goodness does not prejudice merit, and grace does not prescribe to free will. Although the Apostle says, “You have been justified freely” [Note: [Col. 1125] Rom. 3], that is, by grace, he nevertheless denies salvation through faith to no one. I say that grace has freed free will from the yoke of sin, so that the healed will may not receive God’s cooperating grace in vain but, by the benefit of its aid, may exercise itself for action: just as, if someone stuck in mud cannot free himself without another’s help, when he is released by someone, with his liberator leading and helping him, he proceeds unhindered. Thus, although [Col. 1126B] someone is said to be saved by faith, everything is nevertheless from grace, without which no one believes. Hence Augustine says in his letter to Sixtus that grace is the remission of sins; merits do not precede it, because it would not be grace if it were repaid for merits, or it would not be gratuitous. Writing to Boniface, he says that when the Apostle says, “You have been justified freely,” he says this lest faith be proud. “But if by faith, how freely? For what faith merits, why is it not repaid rather than given?” But the Apostle answers: “What have you that you did not receive?” [Note: [Col. 1125] I Cor. 4]. Faith, therefore, is increased by grace, so that, with grace as teacher, the will obeys and, obeying, acts. But you, more monstrous than Proteus, now ascribe everything to grace [Col. 1126C] and empty merit of meaning; now, emptying grace, you attribute everything to merit. In the first case you fall into the heresy of Manichaeus; in the second, into Pelagian blasphemy. Thus you revive once more the now-slumbering ashes of ancient errors and solemnly heap condemned dogmas, as material for logs, for your eternal conflagration. I had determined to pursue all these matters with the file of correction, or prosecute them with the razor of condemnation, in this work of mine; but, called back by various other occupations, I reserve the whole matter for a more leisurely time and a freer disputation.

[Col. 1125]

## FRAGMENT OF A LETTER ON KEEPING SILENCE

[Col. 1125D] Keep silence, because, according to Isidore, it is the guardian of all virtues. When you are permitted to speak, choose rather to be silent, if you wish to have peace of heart. When you ought to speak, prepare your mind in gentleness, lest you speak impetuously. Do not be hasty in speaking; rather, take great care to whom, [Col. 1126D] what, about what, how, where, and when you speak. Take every precaution that you may not be a scandal or an occasion of scandal to anyone. Beware lest in anger you reprove anyone’s words or deeds. Beware lest you despise good counsel, and never trust your own judgment too greatly. Restrain anger as far as you can, lest it ever appear [Col. 1127A] in your face, conduct, or words. Do not speak of absent persons, even good things, because evil things readily mingle with them. Reckon your knowledge and goodness as less than they are. Give no counsel before it is requested. Go to no consultation unless called. If anyone says evil of another, do not readily believe him. Do not gladly listen, because from this your charity grows. Do not have wandering eyes. Guard your head and other members against frivolous movement. Submit to your prelates; and in their ordinances, provided that they do not tend toward laxity, [Col. 1128A] do not resist them. Labour with all your strength to guard your heart. Subject your will to the wills of others. Turn over in your mind the day of judgment, the punishments of hell, Christ’s passion, and the joys of heaven. Strive to do all your works before God and refer them to him. Do not rashly discuss arrangements and dispositions which do not concern you. Drive private affection from yourself. And endeavour to show yourself kind and obedient in all things, etc.

[Col. 1127]

## LITTLE BOOK ON THE ART OF COMPOSITION

Here begins the prologue of Master Peter of Blois, archdeacon of the Church of Bath, to the little book *On the Art of Rhetorical Composition*.

[Col. 1127B]

Although Master Bernard’s book on compositions has been judiciously treated, it is nevertheless said to deserve blame for perplexing prolixity among refined and less rigorous readers. The masters of Tours too, reducing the science of composition to little summaries, maintain that he wrote nothing perfect. Hence it comes about that those who disdain fare both well prepared and insipid, while their teeth wither dry, are seated at philosophy’s table, richly supplied with dishes. Therefore, having put aside banquets of such great sparseness, we invite the eager followers of Master Bernard and of the men of Tours, as well as the notaries of the Roman chancery, to our feast, so that they may joyfully dine together upon what the others prepared separately with diligence. We intend to hand down, for the instruction of beginners and the remembrance of the advanced, a method of composition according to the aforesaid teachers who prescribe the art of composition.

### CHAPTER I. On the division of compositions

One kind of composition is metrical, another prose, of which we especially intend to treat, etc. [I omit this treatise, compiled from the works of Bernard and others and containing nothing new.]

[Col. 1127]

## THE POEMS OF PETER OF BLOIS (G)*

### I.—SONG OF THE STRUGGLE OF FLESH AND SPIRIT

[1.] [Col. 1127C]

Formerly I served  
The pomps of this age,  
To which I offered the flowers  
Of my youth.

Yet near life’s evening  
I drew back my foot,  
Now intending to devote myself  
To the warfare of virtue.

[2.]

The insolence of the flesh  
Fights against the spirit  
And does not measure the end  
Of temporal life.

But if rewards are rendered  
According to merit,  
The wretched flesh’s wages  
[Col. 1127D] will be immortal death.

[3.] I long endeavoured  
[Col. 1128C] to subject the flesh  
To the spirit,  
To make it submit to hunger, thirst, and the lash;

Nor could it be tamed.  
For, enslaved to pleasure,  
The wretched thing refuses  
To bear the yoke of servitude—  
Free only if it knew how to be a handmaid.

[4.]

Happy is that servitude  
Which takes away hellish groans  
And redeems  
From the hand of the oppressor.

The world promises freedom,  
Giving the opportunity to sin.  
Flee its fleeting delights  
And the deceits of its flatterer.

[5.] [Col. 1128D]

The world and the devil  
Have ratified mutual faith,  
[Col. 1129A] drawing foolish flesh  
Into partnership in fraud.

Thus through treacherous blandishments  
They prepare snares,  
And most wickedly conspire  
For the death of the most wretched soul.

[6.]

In the windows of the head  
They hide little nets,  
But in secret they hurl  
The darts of temptations.

The enemy keeps watch over entrances, anxiously  
Exploring exits,  
Drawing out into public view  
Her who knows not slippery sophistry.

[7.]

The rape of Dinah terrifies me [Note: [Col. 1129] Gen. 34],  
[Col. 1129B] whose beauty seized Shechem,  
When he rashly sought  
To take the violated  
First fruits of her modesty.

There is none to restrain the violence  
Or redeem  
The shame of the oppressed sister.

[8.]

Cease, flesh, from wantonness,  
For the day of wrath is at hand.  
Let not the world seize you;  
Let not the fraud of the unclean spirit  
Entangle you.

This life leaves us  
And passes like a shadow—  
The form of this world [Note: [Col. 1129] I Cor. 7].

[9.]

Break old knots  
So that you may overcome  
The enemy’s assaults,

Lest he defile the temple of God [Note: [Col. 1129] I Cor. 3]  
Or destroy  
Christ’s foundations.

### II.—AGAINST CLERICS GIVEN TO PLEASURE, OR ON THE GENERALLY REPROBATE LIFE OF CLERICS

[Col. 1129]

[1.] [Col. 1129B]

Let him who has ears hear [Note: [Col. 1129] Matt. 13]  
Under what a weight of crimes  
The clergy labour today,

While they live luxuriously in Christ [Note: [Col. 1129] I Tim. 5]  
And refuse to appease the Lord  
Through fruits of repentance.

But they defer and delay,  
And falsely dream for themselves  
[Col. 1129C] a long term of life  
In the uncertain chance of their lot.

[2.]

Because of excessive softness  
And the various filths of life,  
No order is spared.

The boundaries of churches  
Are drawn, bit by bit,  
Into ruin.

The ark has no rest:  
Malchus stretches impious hands  
Against Christ’s face [Note: [Col. 1129] John 18];  
Jason against the vessels of the Lord [Note: [Col. 1129] II Macc. 4].

[3.]

All irreverently rush  
Into holy orders, but never put off  
[Col. 1129D] the old man.

Nor do they wash away  
The foulness of their former depravity.

They turn the sweetness of the chalice  
Into bitterness  
And into an asp’s venom.

They clothe great Jesus in filthy  
Garments [Note: [Col. 1129] Zech. 3], and defile  
The blood of the testament.

[4.] [Col. 1130B]

With sobbing voices  
They preach and expound the word of salvation,  
With salutary admonitions,  
What all ought to do;

But in their hands they are Esau,  
While by their voice they proclaim Jacob [Note: [Col. 1129] Gen. 27].

While they everywhere entangle themselves  
In shameful acts  
[Col. 1130C] and monstrous examples,  
They kill souls and “build  
Zion in blood” [Note: [Col. 1129] Mic. 3].

[5.]

You who sell words for praise,  
Using the cultivator’s hoe,  
While you display trappings before the people,

You do not possess in your purse  
The holiness you profess;  
You delight in an empty title.

Using reverent words,  
You do not notice the beam in yourself [Note: [Col. 1129] Matt. 7],  
Which is visible to the whole world;

And you reprove the speck  
In your brother’s eye.

[6.] [Col. 1130D]

The people militant for Christ  
Flee the world’s price  
And seek heaven through martyrdom.

But the condition of clerics,  
Fruitful in nothing,  
Lies torpid in monstrous idleness.

O precious death of Christ,  
With you redemption has always been abundant [Note: [Col. 1129] Ps. 129].  
[Col. 1131A] But among these men  
The Redeemer’s passion becomes idle.

[7.]

Why do they not receive  
The cup of salvation  
And expose their heads  
To swords for Christ?

Instead they savour earthly things [Note: [Col. 1131] Phil. 3],  
And miserable men do not fear avenging wrath  
Or dread the terrible Judge.

For they worship a gnat  
And swallow a camel [Note: [Col. 1131] Matt. 2].

[8.]

You who suffer lethargy,  
Rise and awaken:  
It is now the hour to rise.

You do not show the physician  
The wound from which you die.

You know that a fistula has crept  
Into the ulcer of your heart;  
Yet you do not use remedies,  
Foolishly ashamed  
Of binding the wound.

[9.]

My mind is moved to belch forth  
A new complaint:  
The horrible things we commit.

We prostitute the daughter  
Of heavenly Zion for gain.

We sell Joseph to the eunuch [Note: [Col. 1131] Gen. 39]; we set up  
Dagon in honour of the ark [Note: [Col. 1131] I Kings 5];  
The finest colour of gold  
[Col. 1131C] has become dross.

[10.]

When he is about to ascend to high things,  
He deceitfully bears the cross;  
then, once the statue has been erected,  
A swarm of nephews springs up.

He assigns them titles  
In various churches;  
To these he lavishly pours superfluities.

He conceals  
That an honourable man is exiled;  
He does not fill empty vessels  
But heaps abundance upon those already full.

[11.]

Having professed the Gospel,  
He goes off on the way of the Gentiles.

[Col. 1131D] He who had chosen  
The peaceful leisure of holiness  
Returns to the fleshpots.

The royal priesthood  
Degenerates into the disgrace of the flesh.  
Damnable commerce!

He who had been a member of Christ [Note: [Col. 1131] I Cor. 6]  
Becomes a member of a prostitute.

[12.]

What are you doing here, most wretched soul?  
Death knocks at the door  
That the last things may celebrate  
The flesh’s divorce.

[Col. 1132A] It is the eleventh hour.  
The worst death of sinners [Note: [Col. 1131] Ps. 33]  
Has no end of fires,  
Worms, or ashes.

[13.]

I beg you, think with anxious mind  
That the sudden hour of death  
Is accustomed to seize the unwary.

Do not waste time:  
No one prepares himself too quickly  
For death.

While the world delights you,  
While it promises you life  
More pleasant and longer,  
Then bitter death separates you [Note: [Col. 1131] I Kings 15].

[14.]

Who will give water to your head?  
[Col. 1132B] Who will give you tears,  
That you may proclaim the praises of the illustrious king [Note: [Col. 1131] Richard, king of England]  
And the treacheries of the duke [Note: [Col. 1131] Leopold of Austria]?

May the capture of our king [Note: [Col. 1131] See Letter 143],  
Which afflicts so many souls,  
Spread in anxious lament  
Through the remotest regions, for the betrayed.

[15.]

O foul rust of minds,  
Plague of avarice,  
You have led him into an outrage  
Of damnable memory,

O impious enemy Herod,  
Invader of Christ’s glory. For you harm  
Not royal innocence,  
But Christ, but the Church.

[16.] [Col. 1132C]

The flower of kings, dukes, and nobles  
Found that road which had been free  
Made inextricable,

When he fell into Cerberus,  
Who readily revealed  
A base heart,  
A vessel detested by God,  
A vessel of crimes,

While he crucifies Christ anew  
In Christ’s champion.

[17.]

Judas had sold Christ.  
The duke sells the king of England,  
But this idolater of money  
Makes the crime worse.

[Col. 1132D] For he had wickedly feigned  
Peace with the king,  
While he reproached the king for having fled,  
Leaving the battle-line of the cross  
And yielding to the regions of Syria.

[18.]

Christ’s soldier charged  
Into hostile ranks.  
The duke, with the wicked and cowardly,  
Forged snares  
For the king’s capture.

Thus a crafty little fox  
Rages against a lion.

[Col. 1133A] Drink now, O avarice,  
While lavish England pours out  
Wells of silver.  
May your money perish with you [Note: [Col. 1133] Acts 8].

[19.]

Faithless and cruel,  
You defiled the triumphant banner  
Of Christ’s cross;  
You sold the people  
Of the land of promise,  
Son of perdition.

[20.]

Desiring to return,  
The king had, for three years,  
Turned discord into reconciliation;

[Col. 1133B] but your machination  
Confirms a Babylonian tyrant  
Upon David’s throne.

[21.]

Receive patiently  
What a friend suggests.  
Leave palaces;

For the court  
Is always subject  
To cares—indeed, to crosses  
And deaths.

The form of this world passes away [Note: [Col. 1133] I Cor. 7];  
When a man dies,  
He will not take everything with him [Note: [Col. 1133] Ps. 48].

The destroying day  
[Col. 1133C] will seize him, and his glory  
Will not descend with him.

[22.]

Whatever you may say today: “The delights of court  
Assist me;  
Their abundance provides  
What leaves me perplexed in my wishes.

In my great joy I do not know where to turn,  
While every sex,  
Age, and condition  
Yields to me for the use of my glory.

I am carried wholly into the embraces  
Of pleasure that meets me.”

[23.]

At court we are held by  
More refined clothing,  
More exquisite and more lavish food,

[Col. 1133D] by being feared while fearing no one,  
By enlarging  
The patrimonies of my parents,

By thundering out great things.

The counsels of the rich hold me,  
As do the contingencies  
Of dignities which the friendship  
Of magnates bestows.

[24.]

Break the bonds of court.  
Offer your whole self to God.

The parable of the fig tree [Note: [Col. 1133] Luke 13]  
Grants time for pardon.

[Col. 1134A] Rachel hides idols [Note: [Col. 1133] Gen. 31]  
Beneath the dung of penitence.

You waste expense and effort  
If you delay the grace offered you.

You conquer, reign, and rule  
If you touch Christ’s hem [Note: [Col. 1133] Matt. 9]  
And abandon the Samaritan woman’s water-jar [Note: [Col. 1133] John 4].

[25.]

Foolish are those who wish  
To make themselves wretched of their own accord.

Christ’s clemency is not impatient;  
Late repentance is sufficient.

You, babbling the words of David, not of Oedipus,  
Foretell for me the worst last things.  
But the soul cannot thus be intercepted,  
[Col. 1134B] nor is it the final glory  
To please a prince.

[26.]

What does it profit you to live  
If you wish to lose life?  
In the loss of the soul  
There is no valuation.

If you wish death and the infernal marsh  
To swallow you in everlasting punishments,  
Trust in princes [Note: [Col. 1133] Ps. 145]  
And in their sons,  
In whom there is no salvation.

[27.]

Religion is pleasing in old age;  
It does not suit the young.

[Col. 1134C] I consent to the desire of the flesh;  
For no one has hated  
His own flesh [Note: [Col. 1133] Eph. 5].

[28.]

We have seen no one  
Returning from the dead.  
We do not leave certainties  
For doubtful things.

Let the dreaming mind  
That rejects present realities  
Rejoice in empty things.

If you believe them,  
You may wait  
For Arcturus with the Britons.

[29.]

The riches which you acquire  
So anxiously and painfully  
[Col. 1134D] will vanish in a moment,  
Like the dream of those who awaken.

Without end, like thorns,  
They prick, oppress, and tear.  
Do you know what they bring you?

That you are the slave of slaves,  
While you torment yourself in them  
To serve  
The lusts of dependants  
And the bellies of horses.

[30.]

Why am I reproved, if I enjoy
[Col. 1135A]

With the good things which the hand of the Lord

Has given for human use?

As often as I wish,

I can be miserable;

If I live for myself alone,

I am lost to the whole world.

The gracious Spirit of God

Did not give these things from heaven

In order to mock us deceitfully

And through them cast us down

Into the pit of destruction.

[31.] [Col. 1136A] O vanity of vanities,

What security is this

Amid the spears of hostile men

Who gnash their teeth?

Death stands at the doors, and you dissolve

Into every desire;

But calamity will rush suddenly

Upon the wicked man,

And the delight of brief pleasures

Will be changed

Into eternal punishment.

## III.—TREATISE ON THE MYSTERIES OF THE MOST HOLY AND VENERABLE SACRAMENT OF THE EUCHARIST

[Note: [Col. 1135C] Concerning this treatise John Budaeus, its first editor, writes: “When the edition of this work, candid reader, had almost reached its conclusion, the present Treatise was brought to me from Alsace, copied from a very ancient manuscript codex of the Library of Tabernæ, belonging to the most serene and illustrious prince Charles, Cardinal of Lorraine and bishop of Metz and Strasbourg. Because of both its antiquity and the name of Anselm, Archbishop of Canterbury, which it bore at its head, it seemed worthy of being appended to the end of this work, lest it should perish entirely.

“But, as I carefully examine the whole treatise, I come under a strong suspicion that its author and father is not Anselm, Archbishop of Canterbury, but our Peter of Blois, chancellor of the Archbishop of Canterbury—for, owing to the similarity of their surnames, one might easily have been substituted for the other, the better known for the unknown. Four considerations lead me to this opinion.

“The first is that the author of the poem, in the Prologue [Col. 1135D], once and again openly reveals his own name and calls himself Peter. The second is the agreement of the date. For that manuscript codex called the *Garden of Delights* is attributed to Herrad of Landsberg, the most noble abbess of the convent of Hohenburg, situated among the Alsatians on Mount St. Odile. That this Herrad lived four hundred years ago and was therefore contemporary with Peter of Blois is plainly evident from the Life of St. Odile, recently printed in German at Freiburg im Breisgau, where it is written that the said Herrad built the monastery of Truttenhausen in Alsace in the year from Christ’s birth 1182. In that very year Peter of Blois was at the height of his activity in published writings and served as chancellor to the Archbishop of Canterbury.

“The third consideration is that Peter of Blois was not merely skilled in poetry, as we informed you in the other preface to this work, but also composed many poems. In Epistle 12 he asks a nephew to send him verses formerly composed by himself at Tours. And in Epistle 75 he sends to a friend a very long rhythmic poem [Col. 1136C]—the same kind in which this Treatise too is composed.

“The fourth and final consideration is that its style and phrasing do not differ. As a lion is recognized from its claw, Hercules’ stature from his footprint, and a man from his voice, so I may infer Peter of Blois also from a twofold similarity of phrase.

“First, when speaking of preparation for the Holy Eucharist, he has a particular expression of his own: he uses ‘to incorporate Christ into oneself’ to mean ‘to receive Christ,’ as in Epistle 86. ‘Your opinion,’ he says there to a certain Carthusian, ‘is that you should incorporate Christ into yourself every day, not discerning the body of the Lord.’ And in Epistle 123: ‘A son of everlasting lamentation, with sacrilegious hand and defiled mouth, receives the sacrament in which eternal life is, and presumptuously incorporates it into himself to his condemnation.’ He uses the same word in the same sense also in Sermon 25. But he employs the same phrase in the first chapter of this Treatise, in its final couplet:

> Therefore it is not enough for Christ to be born of the Virgin,  
> If the hungry man who belongs to him does not incorporate him into himself.

“Then, speaking of the same preparation, he cites that saying of the Wise Man: ‘When you sit at the table of a rich man, carefully consider what is set before you, and put a knife to your throat’ (Prov. 23; Ecclus. 31). He cites the same saying in Chapter 20 of this Treatise, in these verses:

> Solomon is added to this, framing a sacred pattern,  
> In which the mystery’s sacred enigma shines forth.  
> ‘When,’ he says, ‘you sit at the lofty feast of a mighty man,  
> Consider with discerning mind what foods you eat.’

“Nor should the grammatical faults of the poem deter me from this opinion. For they, like most barbarous words in all Peter of Blois’s minor works, must be attributed not to him but to the fault of the age. I have added nothing to this Treatise except the division into chapters and a few critical observations.”]

[Col. 1135]

## PROLOGUE. The author invokes the Most Holy Trinity—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—that he may be able worthily to write concerning the mysteries of the most holy Eucharist.

[Col. 1135B]

In every human deed, undertaking, and accomplishment,

God must be set before human reason;

By him reason is enriched and every thing created,

That he may favour our beginnings and be their author.

God is the true beginning and the end of things;

Without him, whatever is undertaken ends foolishly.

He ought to be worshipped first and called upon first.

When the Author has first been worshipped and invoked,

[Col. 1136B] He will not withdraw himself, but will help his worshipper.

Therefore let us confess him to be God, almighty,

Favouring our humble prayers and vows.

### Invocation of the Father

O eternal Father, who by ruling all things from on high,

Order all things by the power of sacred reason!

Be the guide of my poem and the way of its subject matter.

Mark out for me its matter, metre, falsehoods, good results, and Peter;

Give form, remove, grant, and set in order anew.

Give me, O God, yourself as my first subject, and add the file

By which I may polish a sublime matter with heavenly doctrine.

You are the wise craftsman, wisely fashioning each thing,

[Col. 1137A] Reforming misshapen rules and formless things.

Pour upon the fabric of our mind sacred teachings;

Make it fruitful, sustain it, direct it, cleanse it,

That it may behold the sacred mysteries of divine things.

Pressed by hunger for the Word, my mind, in the season of the Word,

Wishes to be refreshed and aided by the bread of the Word.

For God the Word is bread; the Word made flesh is bread,

By which you nourish us inwardly, for you are spiritual food.

This Word, born from you, not made or created,

Rules all things and accomplishes all things with you.

This Word thunders above the stars and is given upon altars for the people.

There he is ruler of heaven; here he is food and drink for the faithful.

Unfold to my mind, O God, this true bread

By which the fabric of creation lives, and which it desires to taste.

May Christ, long ago the victim of the cross, nourish its faith;

[Col. 1137B] Again upon the altar he wills to be sacrificed as victim.

And upon the altar he wills us to be satisfied with God as bread.

As I am about to write and sing new praises,

O boundless King, I ask: bring help and favour my undertaking.

### Invocation of the Son

Christ, Word of the Father, be my mouth; be my word.

Not a fabricated word, which, once spoken, swiftly passes away,

But that which, given from heaven and born of the Father, remains forever.

By such a Word, by so everlasting a Word,

May our mind be fed with the saving bread.

If you withdraw yourself—the bread—from the world, you leave it empty;

If you give yourself, it is immediately filled, lives, flourishes, and is sustained.

Christ, feed the mind that continually hungers for you;

When you, the living bread, are removed, it utterly fails.

[Col. 1137C] You are the rock, you are the bread, the gate closed to the profane,

The gate of heaven opened to the faithful people.

You are the way: open the way by which one proceeds to contemplation;

Surely no one can find you except through you.

O Rock, break Peter’s hardness; touch hard

Hearts with the sweetness of heavenly mysteries,

That I may clearly see whose food is upon the sacred altar,

Who is the fountain, who the blood by which life returns and the serpent perishes.

You are the gate of life: now open yourself to one who knocks.

Open what has hitherto been closed, as I ask;

The matter lies beneath a veil, but reveal to me what is hidden:

O Light, eternal God, shining from the heavenly seat,

Whose majesty and power are equal with the Father’s.

[Col. 1137D] Be present to this work, O Christ; being invoked, be present—

King at the glorious right hand of the Father, lamb upon the altar.

Unfold your divine power to me; pour your light into me,

That, under your guidance and secure, I may write following your signs.

My own light does not burn if yours delays to kindle it;

A mind lacking your light shines with no light.

Gracious Spirit of God, equal light of both alike;

Proceeding from the Father and the Son, yet not departing from them,

Breathe into our undertaking your wondrous gifts,

Which you once poured upon the athletes of the Lord and holy prophets

That they might sing Christ’s battles.

You are the fountain of life, and also the spiritual anointing;

With chrism you make fruitful the waters of holy baptism,

And by them open a path for souls to be made alive.

You make minds badly benumbed by the cold of sin

[Col. 1138A] Heavenly, kindled, and enriched by the doctrine of virtues.

### Invocation of the Holy Spirit

Gracious Spirit, come; coming, gently enter my breast,

Which the thorn-bush of my sins chokes.

The evil care of the world obstructs the inward lamp,

So that I cannot sincerely behold your lofty things.

Drive away evil cares, which will fall by your power;

And by your dew grant me love for Christ.

I hunger for Christ; I pray for this bread:

A man satisfied with this bread endures in Christ.

Indeed, I do not wish to pass over in silence that the Word made flesh long ago

Again wills, upon the altar, to be consecrated as flesh in bread.

Therefore, good Spirit, through whose supreme ordering

This thing comes to pass, give me right understanding,

That I may speak here of Christ the bread only soundly,

[Col. 1138B] In whom nothing is empty and nothing is perceived except what is sound.

The matter is obscure; but undertake to unfold

This sacrament to me through the instruction of faith.

You can untie every kind of knot in Scripture,

And when you will, you yourself reveal the things you previously conceal.

Holy Spirit, you enrich tongues changed by hunger,

And make them eloquent—eloquent for holy wars.

Nothing is known without you; without you nothing is disclosed to me.

Unlock for me the mystical gifts of your holy things,

You shining fire and guide along the straight path.

Direct this finished poem over the straight hill.

May my mind, with the thing as guide, direct its sail to heaven;

Rule the sail with the ship; guide it by starry power.

## CHAPTER I. That the flesh now consecrated from bread upon the altar is truly one and the same flesh as that believed to have been born of the Virgin and to have suffered upon the cross.

[Col. 1138C]

Bread, consecrated upon the altar by the power of the Word,

Becomes divine flesh, the remedy of our guilt.

It becomes no flesh other than that of Christ who redeemed us,

Full of sacrament, food and nourishment of the mind.

This flesh is daily sacrificed for the world,

Although it does not appear as flesh, but bears the appearance of bread.

Nature shudders; the order of things is amazed: the one once born of a Virgin

Is consecrated from a little bread.

It shudders that the Word made flesh becomes flesh again,

For the created thing changes its natural course.

And yet it is the same flesh then born of the Virgin

And now consecrated from bread by the Word of life.

[Col. 1138D] Then, for us human beings, he deigned to be born human;

Now in his mercy he desires to feed us with his body.

He is God and the bread of life, given that he might satisfy us.

God became man that he might raise up those who had fallen.

What use would the bread of life, given from heaven, have been

If the human being needing redemption had perished through suffering hunger?

Therefore it is not enough for Christ to be born of the Virgin,

If the hungry man who belongs to him does not incorporate him into himself.

## CHAPTER II. That Christ, the bread made man, came to the aid of a world endangered by hunger for the Word.

A dreadful hunger for the Word once oppressed humankind,

And hungry man had nothing to eat.

The angelic bread came down from heaven to the depths

When the final file was already about to cut down the world.

[Col. 1139A] Concealing his divinity beneath the chaff of our flesh,

He became known to the world by revealing signs of his Godhead.

Thus the merciful Creator did not wish his creature to perish,

But descended so that man might return to the stars.

The whole human race had collapsed; all was shaken.

The Lord came to meet it in its ruin, made a victim.

But a holy, living, spotless victim—

A victim sanctified in itself, which drives away stains;

A victim greater than which none could be offered,

And which was sufficient to make satisfaction for us.

## CHAPTER III. That none other than Christ could make satisfaction for Adam’s sins; and that, though immortal according to each nature, he nevertheless willingly died for us.

[Col. 1139B] No victim capable or sufficiently adequate

Could erase Adam’s guilt if Christ were absent.

For Adam owed payment for himself, and the poor man had nothing

With which to make satisfaction, being prevented by his grievous guilt.

God could do it, but ought not; therefore it was necessary

For God-man to do this, without whom it could not be done.

Since God can do all things in this matter, and man owes the debt,

Each nature supplies material for such a deed.

From two natures comes the same person,

Healing our bodies and likewise our souls.

Here is God, here also man: two, yet one Christ,

The one not improperly mingled into the person of the other.

[Note: [Col. 1139D] This is an improper expression, though true if a sound understanding is supplied to the words. The author of the poem indicates this fairly clearly when he says that Christ is one, namely in person. Therefore he did not mean that this God and this man are two except according to the natures; for shortly before he had said: “From two natures comes the same person.” Sophronius had long before used a similar formula in the letter read at Action 11 of the Sixth Synod, when he said: “We confess Christ both to be one and two: one because of the person, two because of the natures.” In the same sense must be explained what he immediately adds: “the one not improperly mingled into the person of the other.” For the person of the man was not mingled into the person of the divine Word—there would then be two persons in Christ—but human nature was mingled into the person of the Word, that is, assumed into the subsistence of the divine Word.]

[Col. 1139C] Though each nature was immortal,

[Note: [Col. 1140D] This too is an improper expression. It is established that Christ possessed a mortal and passible human nature from the first moment of his conception until the resurrection, as was defined at the Sixth Synod and as Blessed Leo teaches in Epistle 10, and Damascene in Book III, chapter 28, and in the book *On Heresies against the Aphthartodocetae*. The author of the poem calls it immortal because his mortality proceeded solely from God’s will; otherwise he could by right have been immortal, both because of the dignity of the person to which it was assumed and because he was conceived by the Holy Spirit without any sin, which in us is the cause of mortality. In this sense Blessed Damascene, Book III, chapter 15, says that Christ’s body was permitted by the divinity to do and suffer what was proper to it.]

While preserving his majesty and justice,

He willingly underwent the cross, though he would not have died had he not willed it,

And by his death was to give us life without end.

What the true God could not owe by reason of his divinity,

This blessed man, because of the weight of justice,

At last endured it; the divine will allowed it to be—

That will which orders all things by everlasting power.

Christ, the living victim of the cross, is struck upon the wood,

Through whom the divine substance became mortal.

O blessed victim, by whom the world and stars are filled!

Those who eat of her will not die eternally.

This is the true food; this is bread’s true refreshment.

Whoever does not live by it will find his hope vain.

[Col. 1140A] This is the true flesh of the true Lamb by which we are fed,

Through whom the violence of the sulphurous lake grew cool.

## CHAPTER IV. That the lamb sacrificed and roasted under the Law, and eaten by the people of Israel, prefigured Christ; and that, when true grace and the true sacrifice succeeded it—that is, when Christ appeared—the legal ceremonies ceased.

No longer is a roasted lamb given to the people through Moses:

Christ the Lamb is present, having suffered for us upon the cross.

That earlier lamb was the figure of him to come.

The shadow has withdrawn; light is present. God becomes the pure victim;

Christ, the solemn victim, is now sacrificed.

Yet death has no further dominion over him who suffered once.

Grace has succeeded; the old Law has disappeared.

[Col. 1140B] A new Law, new light, a new king has shone forth upon the world.

A sheep now propitiates nothing; the blood of calves accomplishes nothing;

Nothing do the burnt offerings of bulls: the old order of sacred rites has perished.

Now the minister ceases to slaughter beasts,

Since that merciful Master came to be slaughtered.

Thus Law drove away law; God the Lamb drove away the lamb;

What the old one prefigured, this new one accomplished.

Like one roasted by sacred fire when bitter passion cooked him,

He was offered to the Father as a living victim upon the altar of the cross.

With his blood we mark both doorposts of our house,

And keep the enemy far from our borders.

As we commemorate the sacred things of the cross with lips and heart,

We partake of his body together with his blood.

## CHAPTER V. That the Lamb, though sacrificed whole in different places, remains whole in the kingdom, and is wholly received by the faithful as the food of life.

[Col. 1140C]

Though he is sacrificed throughout the whole world,

He remains whole in the kingdom and is ever one.

And though he seems to be distributed in portions,

Here he is received whole; in heaven he is worshipped whole.

Filling stars and earth, the one Christ remains everywhere,

Never failing, and all things to all people.

For this food was once signified by the food

With which God fed Israel through trackless wilderness.

Manna was every food to every people in the mouth,

Having a varied taste according to varied dispositions.

He who took little of it took as much as he who took more,

[Col. 1141A] And was satisfied, because it was enough for all.

At last a great mystery shone forth in our own time,

And the mystical reality provides a mighty explanation.

Indeed, the Lord is created from the Virgin Mother as manna,

Whose body is consecrated upon the altar from bread.

But how unlike are this food and that food!

For this food is God; the other food is as ash in comparison with a shadow.

That food perished, and those who ate it perished—

Those who did not hunger for Christ, the bread of life.

O sacred bread and praiseworthy gift of faith!

The one is present to all as all things, and is sufficient for all.

## CHAPTER VI. That Christ’s bread and flesh are consecrated not by the merit of the consecrator, but by the word and power of the Creator; and that nothing greater is accomplished by a good person, nor less by a bad one.

[Col. 1141B]

The angel longs for this bread, hungers for it, and is refreshed by it.

While the pilgrim man still lives, he is nourished by it.

How blessed the bread, blessed the flesh, rich the victim!

It feeds human beings on earth and citizens in heaven.

The righteous receives no more from it, nor the wicked man less;

For Christ makes his portion equal for all.

If his own fault draws one who receives unworthily to death,

Glory exalts to heaven the one who receives worthily.

When this bread is blessed by the mouth of a priest,

It is not less in a bad man nor greater in a better one.

Though the one presiding over the sacred altar is unclean,

[Col. 1141C] No defilement can stain this sacred thing.

The Word’s power is equal, though the life of the consecrator is unequal;

It is not man who creates that work, but the power of the Creator of all.

## CHAPTER VII. That when the priest stands at the altar, recalling the sacrifice and imitating Christ’s passion with tears, he is Christ: crucified, sacrificing, and sacrificed.

The priest stands at the altar and prays for sacred things;

God fills the heavenly table; grace rains down.

Divine power showers down from above upon all

That the priest’s wondrous vow consecrates.

The sacrificer is nothing other than an image of Christ,

While he handles Christ’s sacred body together with the blood.

And while he fixes his eyes and heart upon heaven,

[Col. 1141D] Stretching out his hands and arms, he crucifies himself.

And while weeping he rehearses what Christ’s death was,

He slays the deeds of his flesh for the Lord as though upon the cross.

Thus a man made victim offers Christ as Christ,

And thus suffers the cross while he commemorates the acts of the cross.

[Col. 1142A] How rightly is he Christ—crucified and anointed—

Joined through the member of faith to Christ’s body.

## CHAPTER VIII. That God alone is the sanctifier and minister of the sacrifice, while the priest is only a servant; and that by the same Word flesh comes to be upon the altar by which it was created in the Virgin’s womb.

No other celebrates, although another seems to do so;

God the Word performs this sacred mystery.

For the Word made flesh teaches sacred words,

And through the sacrificer dispenses flesh from bread.

God is both the work and the worker here: he consecrates and is consecrated,

And he through whom all things were created becomes a creature.

For the thing which formerly remained the substance of bread

[Col. 1142B] Passes into Christ’s flesh by the gift of divinity.

Man does not know it, does not know it; the angel marvels that it is so done,

And trembles at the unsearchable covenant of the secret sacrament.

He does not know by what means or proof of power

The King who creates the elements comes forth as God from an element.

But such change belongs to the right hand of the Most High,

By whom everything that exists flourishes, whom world and heaven obey.

## CHAPTER IX. That the potter of heavenly vessels can change a small portion of bread upon the altar into something better, that is, into the glory of his flesh, since he was able to remake from death into life the vessel of our humanity which he assumed and baked in the fire of his passion.

It is possible for him who knows how to create all things

[Col. 1142C] To renew one thing again from another.

The potter turns soft clay when and how he wishes;

Creating new vessels, he changes and adorns them more fittingly.

The work obeys the Lord, who possesses the power

To restore the vessels which he wills to break.

Therefore the Son of God, the manifest power of the Father,

Descended to us, clothed in a fleshly vessel.

Yet this vessel, thoroughly baked in the oven of the cross,

Was taught by the potter’s skill to rise from death.

It was indeed well baked: no harmful water softens it;

It removes the world’s stains and our excesses.

A vessel exceedingly hard, which shattered mighty hell

And, redeeming man by the cross, subdued death by death.

From this vessel flows the oil of supreme goodness,

[Col. 1142D] Which drives away every harmful thing in the washing of baptism.

Blessed indeed is the vessel which, filled with the fountain of life,

Warms our bodies and also our souls with peaceful rest.

By this same vessel the divine lamp shines,

From which comes the blessing upon the feasts of the sacred table.

[The text is corrupt: because our faith has departed,] it is utterly empty

[Note: [Col. 1141D] A corrupt passage. As regards the sense, let the reader note that this chapter treats of the consecration of the Lord’s body and blood in the sacrifice of the Mass; for both the immediately preceding chapter and the following one plainly concern the sacrifice. The most approved opinion of many doctors is that consecration under both species is essentially required for the character of a true sacrifice, because an express representation of Christ’s death and passion belongs to the essence of this sacrifice. [Col. 1142D] It follows that the sacrifice of the Mass is empty—that is, it does not attain its proper effect—until consecration of both species has been completed. See Francisco Suárez, vol. III, *Disputations on Part III*; St Thomas, Disputation 75, question 83, article 1, section 6.

“If, however, you maintain that the passage should also be understood of those who participate in the sacrifice, that is, lay communicants, I reply that it may be so understood. Yet this poem establishes nothing further than that communion under both [Col. 1143C] species, though not everywhere customary at that period, [Col. 1143D] was consonant with reason, since for an explicit notion of refreshment or a meal not only food to drive away hunger but drink also to quench thirst seems required.

“This comparison nevertheless does not overthrow the practice, received throughout the whole Latin Church for nearly two hundred years, of communicating under one species. For under one species there is contained a complete and perfect refreshment, if one considers the essence of the matter; for Christ, who is given under it, is effective to drive away not merely hunger but also spiritual thirst. ‘For drinking and eating,’ says Blessed Cyprian in the sermon *On the Supper of the Lord*, ‘belong to the same order in spiritual matters.’ Therefore Holy Scripture itself sometimes represents the soul’s spiritual refreshment, which comes through grace, by the likeness of bread (Ecclus. 15), sometimes of water (John 4), sometimes of drink (1 Cor. 12), and sometimes of food (John 6).]

[Col. 1143A] To receive bread without wine at the sacred supper:

After receiving bread, let us seek wine from the Lord;

Let us discern what sacrament is in it.

It is of no benefit first to have eaten if, when we thirst,

We cannot in any way restrain our thirst.

Let there be cups after food for great desire,

Especially because we have received the roasted flesh of the Lamb.

Roasted flesh makes our mouths thirstier

Than tender meat softened by gentle boiling water.

Therefore, with God’s favour, I shall draw from the spring of my mind

Whatever I understand of the mystery of the sacred wine.

## CHAPTER X. That neither flesh without blood nor blood without flesh is rightly communicated, as was prefigured in Melchizedek, who, as a type of our Saviour, is said to have offered bread and wine together.

[Col. 1143B]

Wine is carried to the altar with bread; both gifts

Are offered to God when the new Passover is celebrated.

God rejoices in both and, praising, accepts both,

Through which Christ is plainly shown to be mortal and God:

God, because Christ makes himself present under each species;

Mortal, because through them he recalls the death of the cross.

Earth and vine bring forth those two things from themselves,

And by the priest’s hand the Son offers them to the Father.

This was formerly signified through Melchizedek,

[Note: [Col. 1143] Gen. 14; Heb. 7.]

Who offered to the Lord consecrated bread and wine.

In the histories concerning him we cannot find his father;

We know neither his mother nor the names of his forefathers.

Who is signified by him except Christ, man without a father—

[Col. 1143C] Born eternally from God the Father without a mother?

I acknowledge him as the high priest and rightly as king,

Who enters heaven and gives law from the sky.

He is bread strengthening us and the abundant vine,

Gladdening souls and cleansing them from guilt.

The flower of virginity brought forth for this world

This bread and sacred vine, fruit filled with divinity.

From the bread comes flesh; from the vine, sacred blood;

Wisdom veils them lest people see wrongly.

## CHAPTER XI. That the Lord willed to conceal the depths of heavenly secrets so that they might be hidden from unbelievers and the faithful might grow in merit through the strength of faith.

[Col. 1144A]

For a time the Lord conceals heaven’s secret,

And, when faith asks, reveals it to whom he wills and when he wills.

For this reason these things are removed from our eyes

And are not entirely known to us except by the light of the mind,

So that our faith may thus be instructed unto righteousness

And a greater reward of faith may follow.

Or God willed these mysteries to lie hidden

Lest Judaea could make sport of this.

If we ate the raw flesh of a slain man

And drank raw blood from the cup of blood,

Then let us enjoy sacred food and drink according to their true meaning.

[Col. 1144B] And through faith, not sight, let us climb upward,

Since by bodily vision and taste we cannot rightly discern

What kind of things they are; let us discern them with the mind.

Let a mind consecrated to God test with inward taste

What the eye and tongue cannot by outward sense.

Neither the manner nor appearance of the bread is to be considered;

Rather, the power of the sacrament must be held in the heart.

And let no one despair concerning the wine;

For blood adheres to the mind, wine to the sight.

But though it appears to possess the liquid of wine,

With faith’s assistance it is known to be sacred blood.

This is the blood poured from Christ’s wound,

Which through the priest’s mouth passes to the benefit of souls.

And, lest anything be lacking to the sacrament,

[Col. 1144C] A living fountain must be present in the altar’s wine.

## CHAPTER XII. Water is likewise mixed with wine, because both flowed together from the Saviour’s side upon the cross: the blood of redemption and the water of baptism by which the Church is signified.

Water is mixed with wine, by which we are signified—

We who are given life by saving nourishment.

The peoples whom grace fortifies are signified by water;

Christ’s blood joins them as members to their head.

Moreover, if wine without the fountain is offered to the Lord,

[Note: [Col. 1143D] The author of the poem appears to have held the opinion that the mixing of water in consecrating the chalice is necessary not merely, as the schools say, by a necessity [Col. 1144C] of precept, but also by a necessity [Col. 1144D] of the sacrament, so that if anyone attempts to consecrate unmixed wine, nothing is effected. Thus once taught someone mentioned by Blessed Bernard in Epistle 69, and also the Archbishop of Armagh in Book IX of the *Questions concerning the Armenians*, chapter 9.

“Blessed Cyprian seems to have supplied grounds for this opinion when, in Book II, Epistle 3, he says that it is contrary to the divine command and institution if water is not mixed with wine, and adds below that wine alone can no more be consecrated than water alone. But the common opinion now received by all is that the mixing of water is indeed necessary by a necessity of precept, but not of the sacrament. Yet there is no agreement among all whether it is necessary by divine or merely ecclesiastical precept. The latter is more probable; nor does the author of this poem dissent from it, as is clear from the following chapter. See Francisco Suárez, cited volume, Disputation 45, question 74, article 8, section 11.]

[Col. 1145A] Christ’s passion is denied to have been for the people.

For if the creature which had to be redeemed were absent,

There would have been no need for God to endure so much without cause.

Conversely, if the fountain of wine should be without mixture,

It is shown how the people remain alone without Christ.

The saving fountain is not propitiated without blood,

And without the sacred fountain the blood accomplishes nothing here.

Thus both should be presented together in the offering,

Just as both flowed together from Christ’s wound.

God is the true vine; Christ is held to be the fountain of life:

The fountain appears to come from the fountain, the blood from the vine.

Therefore neither is sacrificed without the other;

Thus the sacred passion of God is commemorated in full.

## CHAPTER XIII. In the consecration of the Lord’s blood, namely at the Supper, we do not read that water was mixed with the wine; but, lest anything be lacking to this sacrament in commemorating the Lord’s passion, the apostles and their successors decreed that this be done.

[Col. 1145B]

This was not performed at the birth of the chalice,

[Note: [Col. 1145D] That Christ consecrated only in unmixed wine was taught also shortly before the author’s age by Paschasius, *On the Body and Blood of Christ*, chapter 11; Rabanus, *On the Body and Blood of Christ*, chapter 28; and Thomas Walden, vol. III, *On the Sacraments*, chapter 32. But more probable is the opinion of those who think that Christ consecrated wine mixed with water. Thus many ancients maintain: Blessed James in the Liturgy; [Col. 1146D] Clement, Book VIII of the *Constitutions*, chapter 12; Irenaeus, Book II, chapter 2; Cyprian, Book II, Epistle 3; Jerome on Mark 14; Theodoret, Dialogue 1; Augustine, Book IV, *On the Trinity*, chapter 21.]

When the New Passover was consecrated after the Old Passover.

For we read that the Lord gave only bread and the liquid of wine

To the disciples at supper, changing them into his own flesh

And sacred blood, and taught us to do the same in remembrance of him.

Wondrous is God’s power: he who dines becomes the supper itself,

Dining daily with us, as in that event.

And because blood and water flowed together

From the wound of his side—our second washing—

[Col. 1145C] The modest judgment of the ancient Fathers decreed

That these two should be together at the Paschal rites,

So that what appears to have been done upon the altar of the cross

May now be repeated by us in honour of the cross.

Three things complete the sacred mystery: water, flesh, and blood.

These three redeem us, and through these three the serpent perishes.

Whoever removes one of these three from the sacred altar

Will not be able worthily, without fault, to sacrifice.

## CHAPTER XIV. Although wine and water are typologically mixed upon the altar before consecration, afterwards only blood is drunk, because the water is changed into blood, signifying that the people figured by it are changed for the better when they receive these things worthily.

[Col. 1145D]

[Note: [Col. 1146D] See Ambrose, Book IV, *On the Sacraments*, chapter 4; Paschasius, *On the Body and Blood of the Lord*, chapter 11; Alger, Book I, chapter 16.]

But although three gifts are set upon the Lord’s table,

After they are sacrificed there are only two.

Water is mixed in beforehand; but when it is consecrated with wine,

There is only blood, by which the spirit is inwardly nourished.

[Col. 1146A] The mystical reality gives water: Christ’s blood drinks it up.

For God transfers our dust into his members.

He transfers it when we are joined to him through his body,

And through faith are made new members of so great a head.

He also transferred it earlier, when the anointing of sacred chrism

Makes us peoples newly made in the font of washing.

But this spring of washing is prefigured by the fountain of the wound,

And through each God heals the wounds of souls.

He first makes their hearts clean in baptism;

Those who fall after washing he cleanses by the water of blood.

Therefore only two things, blood and flesh, are received;

The third is a figure of the peoples who are redeemed.

One nourishes, while the other intoxicates the mind,

And both unite the Catholic people in covenant with God.

[Col. 1146B] By these two jewels our twofold substance rises again,

Which the sentence of death imposed through old Adam.

Life glows in the blood; flesh rejoices when refreshed by flesh.

Purified old age rejoices to be refreshed by either good.

By these the human being, made old in sins, is renewed;

By these one reborn through the power of faith comes alive again.

By these human nature has regained its honour;

By these it rejoices to have overcome the serpent’s fury.

## CHAPTER XV. That before the Law and under the Law the gate of the kingdom of heaven was closed to the holy Fathers, but after grace was given it was opened to the thief and to all who repent devoutly.

Now the first inhabitant seeks the paradisal dwelling;

Now redeemed man claims heaven as his home.

[Col. 1146C] The cross accomplishes this; its gleaming brightness above all things

Strikes down the enemies of the human race in Endor.

The cross of the Lord is heaven’s throne and hell’s chain.

The cross is heaven’s key, the way of life, the restraint of death.

The cross enters heaven, fills the world, and splits the abyss.

The cross has impressed the Crucified upon our foreheads.

We no longer see the *tau* inscribed upon anyone’s forehead,

Since we bear the signs of the cross impressed upon us.

That sacred character bore the mystical signs of the cross

Which prevented the sword of death and deadly pestilence.

Now, because the grace of the life-giving wood redeems us,

The letter of the typical sign is erased beneath its sign.

The cross opened the path for those journeying to paradise,

For the fateful law that stood in the way has been cut off.

[Col. 1146D] That sword-bearing cherub of God, the entrance having been opened,

Now allows Christ’s people to enter, his sword withdrawn.

That flame-vomiting, turning sword rests,

And paradise’s joyful gate stands open to Christ’s people.

[Col. 1147A] Whoever loves enters; for from the time of John

The Baptist, this sacred gate, closed for so many years, stands open.

Heaven suffers violence, and the violent seize it,

[Note: [Col. 1147] Matt. 11.]

Since grace succeeded the Law for the people.

The king of heaven delights in being plundered above the stars,

and gives weapons to the plunderer, that by them he may approach his own camp.

Nor does he now threaten losses to one contending for the kingdom;

rather, when conquered, he grants prizes to the victor.

A useful contest, such happy violence,

when the plunderer's plundering is pardonable.

And when the conquered now renders honour to the conqueror,

while the conqueror declares himself inferior to the conquered.

## Chapter XVI. That through reception of this sacrament and through the power of the saving cross, paradise is opened to humankind and the devil is overcome.

[Col. 1147B]

The gate of rest, once shut against patriarchs and prophets,

is now made open to the thief.

To him power gave a shield, death gave life, good hope gave zeal,

faith gave arms, and confession of Christ gave heaven.

The fathers bore the burden and heat of the day;

this thief flies beforehand to the seat of rest.

The first and second hours did not bring them into heaven,

but a brief hour brought him in.

Long labour under the Law wearied Moses;

not him: yet the daily denarius makes both equal.

What the fathers and mothers could not do before the prophets,

thieves and prostitutes now enter to do.

Behold the thief, his foot fixed in Christ's footsteps,

[Col. 1147C] enters the kingdom, crucified together with the Crucified One [Note: [Col. 1147] Luke 23].

The Canaanite woman, called a dog, enters through faith [Note: [Col. 1147] Mark 15];

the Hebrew people, called God's vineyard, falls back.

Faithless one! Why do you flee from entering, and, barking backward,

never cease to turn your back upon the work of mercy?

And when God's mercy receives those who come,

do you sharpen your teeth against him, devoid of mercy?

Lay aside your rage, for the former times have passed away;

through Christ more fortunate times succeed them.

Those whom your Law is accustomed to stone and kill with the sword,

the grace of Christ now strives to call back to life.

Grace is now better than the letter which killed,

under which the sun of righteousness lay hidden, as beneath a cloud.

Grace proclaims that the Messiah has now come,

removing the harsh yokes of the Law and giving us rest.

[Col. 1147D] Yet you await another; but learn: search

the writings of the prophets, and here you may find Christ.

He whom Law, angel, and prophet foreshadowed—

Christ is present; all things are filled with Christ's praise.

The elements together proclaim that God has now come;

yet you do not heed the testimony of the elements.

For a new star declares that the King of heaven has been born [Note: [Col. 1147] John 2];

and water, producing new wine, declares him to be God.

Life blessed the dead and the sick with salvation;

beneath his feet the sea spread itself to be trodden upon [Note: [Col. 1147] Matthew 14].

[Col. 1148A] Finally, when he dies, sun and moon are darkened;

the trembling earth shook, and the buried rose [Note: [Col. 1147] Matthew 27].

Those also whom hell had long held miserably captive

he restored to the upper world, when that heavenly King returned.

The veil of the Temple and the stones are rent by the victim of the cross;

but it has not yet split the stone which you have in your breast.

Having seen so many signs, are you still not moved, Judaea?

Are you still held, miserably blinded, in the darkness of unbelief?

Behold what you await; but reconsider all these mysteries.

See the true Messiah, if only through his miracles.

And because the inner things, stripped of their veil, lie open,

enter with us and worship the divinity of the Crucified.

Remove the thick veil of your Moses from your face.

Learn new worship, now that the former worship has ceased.

## Chapter XVII. That Christ is the lawgiver of our law and our Moses; that, rescuing us from the devil's power, he was sacrificed as the paschal lamb; and that through this world's wilderness he brings us into the kingdom promised to us.

[Col. 1148B]

If you seek Moses, now behold Christ as Moses.

No burden of Pharaoh will harm you if you worship him.

That Moses was figurative; this true one redeemed us

and destroyed Pharaoh's people with the sword of the cross.

This true Moses led us through the Red Sea,

destroying the old serpent in the laver of faith.

He established the paschal rite to be celebrated more excellently,

suffering himself to be sacrificed as the lamb for us.

Your Passover was once a shadow and a figure of the truth;

God the sun has shone forth and bids the darkness be removed.

[Col. 1148C] He feeds us through the region of this worldly wilderness

and draws us toward the resting-place of milk and honey.

He feeds us in the Church whenever the words of the Gospels

and the power of the sacred rites are recounted to us.

He feeds us at the altar, when with life-giving food

he refreshes the hungry inward parts of the mind.

He surely feeds us at home, when, after spiritual food,

he abundantly grants us bodily food.

He feeds us also in heaven, when the mind, caught up above the ether,

clings wholly to God, captivated by the sweetness of the heavenly world.

Thus Christ, the bread of life, feeds us everywhere,

providing food for angelic citizens and for humankind.

Therefore, faithless people, darkened by the blindness of your fathers,

cease to be a wild vine, that you may become a fruitful grape.

[Col. 1148D] At last may Christ's grace soften you with its rain,

that you may produce a rich cluster on the vine of life.

## Chapter XVIII. That our Lord himself is called a grain of wheat; that, falling dead into the earth and rising again, he was multiplied in the seed of life; that from his grain arose many grains of the faithful, which are daily made one with him in the Church.

Because a digression concerning Judaea detained me a little,

my pen has recalled the preceding matters.

What is the use of scattering a grain of wheat upon a rock?

So too I judge it vain that Christ should be sown late upon Judaea.

[Col. 1149A] But Christ is the seed; Judaea represents the rock,

lacking fertility and remaining always stony.

This is the grain of wheat which the faithful earth

continually germinates, rendering its seed to heaven.

By this grain heaven's granaries have been multiplied;

the holy city Jerusalem grows rich, satisfied by it.

This is the grain of wheat [Note: [Col. 1149] John 12] which came from heaven,

whose rich substance nourishes our souls and bodies.

It, falling freely into the earth, was first put to death,

and through this rose again, multiplied.

From one grain abundance flowed into many grains,

from which is now made the living bread in heaven.

For whenever we are begotten in faith by Christ's increase,

from one grain we are created as very many grains.

When we taste his flesh or the draught of his blood,

[Col. 1149B] one bread is made, and this becomes one whole offering.

Thus two are read to be one in the flesh [Note: [Col. 1149] 1 Corinthians 10; Genesis 2];

thus Christ and the Church are made one.

Thus God dwells in us, and we in him,

while he is our head and we form a shadow for him.

Thus whatever member cleaves to so great a head

may hope always to live in Christ's body.

Nor, falling away from it even once, let it relapse into shameful defilement,

or let Christ's member be cut off by the sickle of a prostitute.

That cannot be called a member of Christ's body

which serves Satan and is subject also to a prostitute.

The spotless bridegroom loves a spotless bride,

joined to him from heaven in a virginal covenant.

## Chapter XIX. That no one who has become a member of the devil should presume, in Judas's manner, to approach the Lord's body; for Judas was condemned not only by awareness of his earlier fault, but because, still sinful and unclean, he did not fear presumptuously to approach the sacred table.

[Col. 1149C]

Therefore, whoever you are who are not of Christ's body,

while you are still defiled and have not yet repented,

you must not then hasten to the Lord's table,

lest, if you presume, you appear like Judas.

Judas knew in every way that he had sinned,

yet he did not withdraw himself from the sacred meal,

doubly guilty both of the crime of betrayal

and of contempt for violated religion.

Therefore, when so great evils followed the Lord's judgment,

Satan suddenly entered into him with the bread [Note: [Col. 1149] John 13].

[Col. 1149D] Therefore judgment and a double punishment punish him,

because before the sacred rite he had not become a suppliant for his sin.

Judas provides examples in the Church for those to come:

let none handle Christ's body except with pure hands.

For one who receives unworthily with Judas will be cast out;

one who receives rightly with Peter will be joined as a member to Christ the head.

## Chapter XX. That none of the faithful may be permitted to be ignorant of the sacrament of the Lord's body and blood celebrated in the Church, lest perhaps, because of what one does not know, one be judged unworthy to receive it.

Many receive sacred things; but what is received

[Col. 1150A] they wholly do not know, and a dreadful vengeance threatens them.

Everyone ignorant of this is unacknowledged, because he does not know

whence salvation arises, whence the fountain of forgiveness is opened.

A person ignorantly eating of consecrated things,

as Moses says [Note: [Col. 1149] Leviticus 22], shall bear the penalty of ignorance.

Solomon is added to this [Note: [Col. 1149] Proverbs 29], forming a sacred example

in which the enigma of the sacrament shines forth,

when he says: “When you sit down at the lofty banquet of a ruler,

consider with discernment of mind what foods you eat.”

For reason, the lover of virtue, must first know

what benefit life-giving flesh brings to the mind.

Thus the psalm of king and prophet together instructs us [Note: [Col. 1149] Psalm 33]:

“Taste and see, for the Lord is sweet.”

It is therefore evident how some priests

[Col. 1150B] wholly fail to know how great is the power of the sacraments.

If a person rightly knew what power flourishes in the sacred rites,

he would never approach the heavenly table except clean.

But now, because he has not learned the sacred things, he receives irreverently

and openly takes judgment and death to himself.

Thus Christ's flesh, which is given as medicine,

at once prepares for him a snare and ruin of death.

For although someone may lead a religious life,

so long as he does not know what he is doing, he lives to his own harm.

How can one defend the honour of the sacred mystery

who has not yet tasted its savour in the mind?

As the perfection of sacred things cannot stand without faith,

so their worship cannot stand without instruction.

Therefore, let one who does not know learn and reverence here,

[Col. 1150C] lest he someday be burdened by the punishment of a despiser.

## Chapter XXI. That every priest ought to know the Lord's sacraments, by which he may educate the people entrusted to him and instruct them in the true faith; without them he cannot worthily exercise the priesthood.

Let him first wish to know what the general sacrifice is,

what the tree of life is, what spiritual food is;

what the altar is, the chalice, the water poured into it, and the wine;

how these two are one after each is consecrated;

finally, why the cross marks the chalice and the cross adorns the altar,

made bright by the blood of the Lamb slain for us.

Let him wish to know what the Flood bore away and what the water removed—

[Col. 1150D] water indeed profound, but itself also a profound figure;

why the anointing of chrism belongs in the font of baptism;

and what the cross applied to the foreheads of those reborn confers.

But why do we penetrate the abyss of the Lord's sacred things?

Let the priest wish to know all things by which one goes to him.

One who does not know such things—what sin is and what burden it is—

cannot provide medicine either to himself or to his people.

Thus a blind guide of the blind comes badly to grief,

whom his grave ignorance harms along with the rest.

But one who has learned everything which he ought to know

is rightly a priest and rightly shows the way of light.

## Chapter XXII. That a priest, following in Christ's footsteps and announcing the word of life to the people, is called the Lord's Christ and his angel; and, while he kindles his neighbour toward knowledge of God and love of heavenly things, receives seraphic rank.

[Col. 1151A]

A priest is rightly a sacred rule of life for everyone;

to the people subject to him he becomes a pattern of good living,

when his life burns with love of true virtue

and he rightly imitates Christ in deeds and speech.

He is an angel of the Lord, and is also held to be his Christ,

since he appears to bear the cross and to represent Christ.

This one, since he is Christ—as the Father says through Isaiah—

is the highest angel, born of the mother Mary.

That angel is indeed abundantly good through himself;

this angel is made good by him from another source.

[Col. 1151B] This messenger ought to carry the faithful commands of heaven

from the Lord of heaven to the faithful people;

and, returning, like our herald, bring to the Lord

the prayers of the people and the grievous complaints of the weeping earth.

Standing in the temple, a mirror and lamp of faith,

contemplating God and meditating only on heavenly things,

he calls back to heaven the cold hearts of his flock,

blackened by the soot of sin and formerly sluggish toward the joys of life;

he makes them burn with the fire of faith

and, kindled for God, shine with life's brightness.

Such a man deservedly shines in seraphic form,

by whom his neighbour grows warm as sin's frost flees.

## Chapter XXIII. That the glowing coal is the same as the seraph. For when holy rulers in the Church rekindle God's people, extinguished in the darkness of sins, toward love of heavenly things by the word of salvation and the example of good action, they are indeed called living coals kindling others.

[Col. 1151C]

Thus the glowing coal, leading the people of faith in its footsteps,

makes them living coals.

But what ought coals to do in the Church?

I think that they should burn the incense of works and the incense of prayers;

let us burn the censer of flesh and of mind alike,

a twofold sacrifice pleasing to God and humankind.

Now, from the rich multitude of many coals,

let my tongue, weary for the rest, name at least two.

Lawrence was a burning coal, fire amid fire:

the gridiron gave him a palm, and death deservedly gave him heaven.

Nicholas, the honourable bishop, was a coal of the Lord,

[Col. 1151D] whose splendour of virtues is manifest from afar.

The former, red with blood, was a coal roasted among coals;

the latter, burning with merits, was rich with the fatness of oil.

God wished those long ago born black through ancestral error

to be kindled by fire from the heavenly fire.

Whom would not the manly struggle of the one kindle?

Whom would not even the childlike goodness of the other move?

By his example may we deserve a laurel through blood;

to the Lord we give gold through the other's purified life.

[Col. 1152A] Each was a soldier of God and faithful steward,
