who strove by speech and hand to store treasures in heaven.

I offer these exemplary teachers of faith

that through them I may teach every minister of the altar

to be devout, generous, brave, chaste, wise,

and patient for righteousness amid adverse things.

Such persons are worthy to receive from the book of life;

them the sentence of ancestral death does not exclude.

Such persons deserve to offer gifts worthy of God

and are not forbidden to attend upon the Lord's sacred rites.

## Chapter XXIV. That it is exceedingly dangerous to approach the sacrament of the Lord's body and blood, where, amid the multitude of angels and all saints, Christ himself, the supreme high priest, offers himself as food of life or death, discerning each person's merits with subtle judgment.

[Col. 1152B]

Therefore, prudent person, learn the sacraments of life,

and tremble at God's judgment when you receive them.

It is a terrifying matter, and one to be greatly feared,

to be fed with Christ's body while Christ is present.

For if you wish perhaps to give credit to the writings

which often teach us true things about Christ:

at the time when Christ, a dear victim to the Father,

is offered by the priest's hands on the lofty altar [Note: [Col. 1151] Chrysostom, *On the Priesthood*, book VI; Gregory, *Dialogues*, book IV, chapter 58],

all the heaven of saints is present; heaven here is opened,

and the troop of angels attends the present God.

Here Christ is truly present, the author of the sacred rites;

he judges the minds of righteous and wicked alike.

For he fully knows and sees who ought to use

the saving bread for harm or for salvation.

[Col. 1152C] And although a fleshly priest stands at the altar,

the supreme high priest is said to celebrate the sacred rites here.

He breaks the bread, offers it, blesses it,

and says that his body is present when he gives it with the blood.

Come then: will you, sinful person, presume, unless worthy,

to approach the Lord's table and pledge of life?

Learn at once what you are, what Christ's flesh is,

and in what vessel you wish the divine gifts to be placed.

Unless the vessel into which these things are received is clean,

they become destruction to the person who takes them wrongly.

Therefore Paul instructs each person first to examine himself [Note: [Col. 1151] 1 Corinthians 11]

and then to hasten to the sacred bread and chalice.

For whoever discerns the Lord's body—what he receives,

and how great it is when God reveals it—may nevertheless eat it safely,

if first examined,

[Col. 1152D] and not accused by a mortal charge of guilt.

But although lesser sins may blame someone,

since no one lives even for one hour without sin,

I do not think that such a person should be removed from the sacred meal;

rather, what continually harms him will thereby be redeemed.

And because we are daily weighed down by the burden of sin,

we are continually relieved by such medicines.

The providential wisdom of the Almighty foresees

how the wounds of the mind may be healed.

## Chapter XXV. That according to diversity of merits Christ is sacrificed in the Church as lamb and goat, as was prefigured in the Law; indeed, as blessed Jerome says, the more perfect are fed with the lamb's flesh, while sinners and penitents are fed with the goat.

[Col. 1153A]

Therefore let every faithful person prepare his heart for God,

that it may become a clean dwelling for him in heaven.

The Lord flees sluggish hearts full of filth,

whose grace is always in a clean heart.

And one whom virtue still compels, while poor, to lack,

and who cannot satisfy good hunger with the lamb's flesh,

should at least eat of the flesh of the sacred goat,

which is customarily slain as an offering for the people's sin.

The ancient order of sacred things does not teach that persons are equal,

nor does reason of mind, nor the differing nature of merits.

[Col. 1153B] Therefore Moses commands that a goat be sacrificed with the lamb's death [Note: [Col. 1153] Exodus 12],

and wishes Christ to be signified by either type.

Yet he is not like the goat that condemns and hates goats [Note: [Col. 1153] Matthew 25].

Rather, the distinction of the sacred rite reveals to you what each is.

We slaughter the lamb when we retain righteousness;

the goat when, seeking pardon, we weep for sins.

Nor do I think it absurd that Christ is signified in the goat,

since a he-goat or goat is often sacrificed.

Because the Law offers one in the wilderness and the old Law freely offers one,

it declares that Christ has a twofold substance.

Before the Temple doors the people sacrificed one;

upon the head of the other they heaped up their sins.

They thus sent it alive, bearing the sins of its people,

[Col. 1154A] to seek the wilderness wastes.

Christ is each goat [Note: [Col. 1153] Leviticus 16]: he is slain while hanging on the cross

and seeks the wilderness when he rises and tends toward heaven.

He who bore our evils while suspended on the tree

and brought back the sheep found among the ninety-nine [Note: [Col. 1153] Luke 15],

mighty at the right hand in the honoured divinity of the Father,

reigns and fills altars in the world with flesh and blood.

Though once slain he does not die again,

his death is nevertheless renewed for our life.

The devotion of priests daily slaughters Christ upon the altar,

and he himself is the slayer of sacred things.

Bread, the nourishment of life, and wine are consecrated;

the Saviour suspended on the cross is commemorated.

The altar is the wood of the cross, and the chalice signifies the tomb.

[Col. 1154B] Here Christ dies; here he sleeps; each gives its significance.

A lamb in the one, a strong and winged lion in the other,

he rose, seeking the stars, and draws spiritual eagles to himself.

## Chapter XXVI. That the priest and every faithful person ought to be conformed to their head, who is Christ, and daily follow him spiritually into heaven.

Therefore, whenever the good priest recounts these sacred things,

let him consider the cross of the flesh, that he may conform himself to Christ.

Let flesh, crucified with its vices, first die;

let the mind, made alive to God, rise and follow him.

Thus one dies well with him, rises with him, and lives with him also.

Thus redeemed humanity goes where its author went.

# IV.—On Penance

[Col. 1153]

[Col. 1153C]

Repent quickly, sinner, since the Judge is merciful;

and these five things must be noted by you:

hope of pardon, a contrite heart, confession of sin,

a satisfying penalty, and flight from wickedness.

That you may be forgiven, forgive others their sins,

and make satisfaction to those whom you acknowledge having injured.

Despise pleasures, games, and the world's spectacles;

abandon an evil companion and the tumult of the crowd;

love private prayers and works of mercy.

Let true contrition lament all sins,

keeping account of ages, senses, places, times, and bodily members.

Mourn what has been done; do not commit deeds to be mourned.

Lament offences committed, together with omissions;

and God's offences, because you have harmed your brother.

Let confession be true, whole, and clean;

[Col. 1153D] let it be prompt, firm, frequent, humble, voluntary, and bare;

personal, discrete, tearful, deliberate, and faithful.

Repent fully, if repentance is truly yours.

Not through an agent, not by a letter; but report it yourself.

Tell it to one who sympathizes, one who is wise, one who is better;

it is beneficial to confess to many priests.

If a priest is unavailable, disclose it to a companion.

As you reveal bodily stains, so reveal the sins of the soul.

Bodily sins are gluttony, perjuries, thefts, lust;

envy, hatred, pride, anger, and lust lie hidden in the mind.

[Col. 1154C]

Remember especially the seven capital plagues,

not only their sources but also the streams flowing from them.

The stream is sometimes more harmful than its source.

Thus Lot's incest was worse than drunkenness,

and Cain's fratricide worse than anger.

The sources of faults are pride, envy, and anger;

the blemish of sloth, greed, gluttony, and lust.

When you have separately told one person your mortal sins,

tell together all accompanying sins of whatever kind that burden you;

tell what you wished to commit, though not done.

Tell venial sins; tell what was rejected by the mind.

Tell your own offences; disclose these things generally.

For when someone guilty in many matters confesses sins,

unless he tells everything, he seems to have said nothing.

[Col. 1154D]

If someone purely confesses the final sin,

he may leave unspoken whatever returns and accompanies it.

Order, place, knowledge, time,

age, condition, number, delay, abundance, cause,

the manner of the sin, high position, and slight grief aggravate sins.

Let the sick person repent and confess sins.

Let no penalty be imposed upon him, but let it be explained to him.

Yet he will fulfil it if firm health is restored.

If he is about to die, let the priest absolve the contrite sick person;

and let the prayers, fasts, and alms of his own people relieve him.

That shame may be a penalty, that you may become lowly,

that you may become wiser, confession is enjoined upon you.

[Col. 1155A]

At the final judgment confession will cover sins,

so that neither God nor demon nor the persons who commit them may see them.

Let the confessor be gentle, gracious, and kind;

let him be wise, just, sweet, and compassionate,

so that he conceals the particular offence and the sins of the guilty;

let him be slow to impose penalties and quick to show mercy.

Let him grieve whenever sin makes the penitent fierce;

let him pour in soothing oil and chastening wine.

Let him not display the father's rod instead of the mother's breasts;

let him whistle and sing, yet spur on when necessary.

First of all, let him ask how the contrite person believes;

whether he believes soundly, let him confess it with heart and mouth.

After this let him carefully examine the wounds of the sinner.

Let him express no sin contrary to nature,

lest, if an inexperienced person be confronted about an enormity,

[Col. 1155B] concerning which he knew nothing, he should thus be moved to commit it.

Let a wife guilty of adultery so expiate what she has done before a skilled confessor

that she does not become suspect to her husband.

Let the confessor often admonish the penitent not to fall again;

or, if they relapse, to confess at once.

Let them avoid causes which entice them toward falls;

let them diligently fulfil the satisfying penalty;

let them carefully guard their senses, heart, and reins.

And as a judge in a secular court is forbidden

to bend judgment for a person, while a physician may vary remedies,

so let the judge of souls beware, through hatred or love,

of loading or lightening confessed persons with penalties.

Let him follow the custom of the Church or the writings of the Fathers,

[Col. 1156A] and let the measure of the penalty accord with the limits of the fault,

and be lighter insofar as contrition is greater.

As physicians treat the body with varied medicine,

healing fever, wound, or swelling,

so the ailments of the soul require varied remedies.

Therefore set contrary things against the soul's diseases.

Let the covetous give what is his own; let the lustful restrain himself;

envious person, lay aside envy; proud person, arrogance.

Let sobriety restrain gluttony, patience suppress anger;

let the injured remove resentment, the sorrowful their weariness;

let drinking water redeem excess in drunkenness;

let the scourging rod chastise fleshly pleasures.

For true repentance, let the robber restore what he took away.

I clothe, give drink, feed, give shelter, visit, ransom,

lend, show compassion, convert, give, forgive.

[Col. 1156B]

I bend the knee, keep vigil, fast, labour, scourge myself,

wear rough clothing, go barefoot, afflict my heart, make pilgrimage;

you repent, read, weep, pray: thus the flesh is mortified.

You will note that these are to be enjoined upon those who confess.

Let the penalty be public if the wrongdoing was public.

Though an enormous sin be hidden, let its penalty also be hidden.

That is: let one who sins secretly repent secretly,

while the confessor more prudently moderates each case,

taking account of effect, cause, fault, and person.

These are reasons why you must hasten to the Lord:

purifying fire, death, sickness, shame,

the gravity of anxiety, and the ruin of habit.

# V.—Verses in Praise of Wine

[Col. 1155]

[Col. 1155C]

Happy is the place which the lovely vine makes lovely;

blessed the house that, full of Bacchus' gift,

gives its guests wines from the rich vein of the vine.

But unhappy is the house where oats are brewed into ale.

The over-measured bottle must now be measured out.

The crop has been impaired—not by wine but indeed by poison.

For the most dreadful penalty follows its drink:

a staggering foot, disturbance of the brain, an alienated mind;

the troubled mind does not know how to put reins upon vices.

[Col. 1156C]

While drunkenness rages in waters and Venus's chain,

the flesh, hot with fermentation and lacking mind, is dragged along.

No rein restrains unlawful movements,

while the Lethean marsh is drunk and then, clear again,

is urinated out; sand hardens into a stone in the kidneys,

which Galen's art cannot expel except with iron.

Therefore wine with a poor meal is worth more to me

than ten dishes of bran for you with your drink.

# VI.—Reply to a Certain Person, Against Ale

[Col. 1155]

[Col. 1155D]

I write unwillingly; for the vine's grave invitation

invites me, a respectable man, to speak more severely and less respectably.

Wicked man, why do you condemn what sacred Scripture, custom,

utility itself, and God himself approve?

By the word of the Word, from the vine's gift the gift

of life is made by the sanctifying hand.

Therefore where Christ's blood is made, let bran-based,

sulphurous liquid be far away.

At his mother's request, the creator of waters turned waters into wine;

but he never made ale of them.

Why, then, is the ape of wine preferred to wine,

that horrible breed of degenerate water?

[Col. 1156D]

It borrows from wine what intoxicates and what turns sour,

thus imitating wine only in its evils.

O unhappy labour and accursed toil,

which strove to make a man drunk on water!

Do you object that Lot's incest came through wine? There the fault

was not wine's, but the failure to observe measure in wine.

The drinker sinned, not the drink, just as in the first father

not the fruit but gluttony alone was at fault.

Whatever you do, you sin unless you are moderate;

measure weighs and makes even justice just.

Great indeed is the disturbance of the brain, when a beer-addled man

praises ale in a beer-addled way.

It seems akin to urine and sister to dregs,

[Col. 1157A] not drink for human beings but food for swine.

To mark briefly what it is and whence it comes, look at its sign:

ale is made from straw and smeared with dregs.

[Col. 1158A]

Since I speak without bile, because I know you to be fond of jesting,

accept the jest pleasantly and without bile.

# VII.—Headless Poem

[Col. 1157]

[Col. 1157A]

You who read my writings may consider when the kings came

who brought the mystical gifts.

Led by a star, they come and return by another way;

in hurried course they hasten, giving three gifts to the Three-in-One.

For the kings, thirteen stages of the journey were completed.

If I reckon rightly, their delay in coming was short;

when the fierce king had been rejected, the Magi returned with glad step.

He is a king and rules himself rightly, whoever lives well;

every faithful people is ruled indeed by the weapons [reading uncertain].

[Col. 1157B]

If it rightly believes and obeys the ruler's commands,

grace goes before, is present, and never departs.

Each person, with the star as guide, now enjoys true light.

If any grace is given, let the grace itself which goes before be followed.

These make strong athletes join together the stages.

Let no one be concerned to live without pure faith,

through which the first stage is always completed;

hope, the second stage, follows with a clean mind;

the third comes after, found greater than the others:

these things, done with sincere hearts, are true love.

Let the mind be contrite, that heavenly life may be yours;

and know how to live devoutly with a contrite heart.

Rewards are certain if a contrite mind is found.

Let the talkative tongue of the mouth loosen the barriers of shame,

[Col. 1157C]

as you disclose what sin you previously committed as a guilty person,

so that whatever fault remains with you may quickly be cleansed.

If you wish to be cleansed, never cease from working;

thus one comes to faith by doing what is commanded,

so that what you often ask may be ready for you. Be watchful;

remember thus to hold the reins upon the beast of the flesh,

lest it be allowed to grow wanton or go too far.

You will do this by fasting and taming the flesh.

[Col. 1158A]

Without delay pray at once more devoutly than usual;

do not close your mouth and do not cease at any hour.

Let this labour be your exercise; let your exercise be becoming to you.

That the flesh may be lean, strive to visit holy places.

To despise oneself and be despised, I know, is a heavenly gift;

patience, which surpasses all else, drives away evils.

The gentle and peaceable person conquers wrongs by enduring them;

the final virtue retains and confers salvation.

This is the command: quickly complete what you have rightly begun.

[Col. 1158B]

Much praise is given you if what has been begun is completed;

such are the terms: the outcome always proves deeds.

When these stages have thus been completed, it is fitting

that gifts offered to Christ should be acceptable,

and that those who knew God should reverently worship him, who is gracious.

The three give three gifts to Christ, who first was living and small:

gold with incense . . . myrrh, when about to die.

This signifies supreme wisdom and fear of the Lord.

If you give incense, your mind is offered, though hard.

As incense rises, so a good mind tends upward;

myrrh, though rare, signifies bitter death.

Thus hasten yourself, because death is upon the altar of the heart.

Thus live equally by remembering every last thing,

so that you, my son, may always beware a base sin.

[Col. 1158C]

If you are a Catholic man, humble, devout, and chaste,

and offer these gifts, a worthy crown will be given you.

Those who have brought such gifts truly rejoice;

among their number I hope joyfully to live.

Having wiped away filth and at last cleansed the heart,

let the king devoted to Christ offer these three vows.

May the Three-and-One accept this threefold gift,

through Christ's aid, who is king and was king before.

# Appendix to the Works of Peter of Blois, Containing charters of certain bishops and kings which contribute to the elucidation of his letters and notes

(*Works of Peter of Blois*, edited by Peter de Goussainville.)

## I. Concerning Letter 44.—Letter of Henry, bishop of Bayeux, concerning a gift made to the chapter of Bayeux from the house of Conan the treasurer.

(From the archives of the chapter of Bayeux, given by the very distinguished Philip Taron, subdean and canon of Bayeux.)

[Col. 1157D]

To all sons of Holy Mother Church, present and future, to whom this present writing shall come: HENRY, by God's mercy humble minister of the Church of Bayeux, [Col. 1158D] greeting in him in whom is the salvation of all.

Since it befits a pious father's affection to be diligent and solicitous concerning the advancement of his children, especially those who in the Church of God apply themselves with more earnest care to divine praises, we, considering with what devotion and vigilance our beloved sons in Christ, the canons of Bayeux, labour day and night in the divine offices, have decreed at present to stir them by some small recompense from our generosity to more abundant vigilance in God's praises. Therefore, moved solely by divine consideration, we have given in perpetual alms to our aforesaid sons, the dean and chapter of Bayeux, the houses of Conan, formerly our treasurer, with all their appurtenances, to possess in perpetuity. It is established that William of Harcourt, formerly treasurer of Bayeux, obtained them by the gift of our predecessor Bishop Philip, a man of pious memory; and after his death our canon Simon of Scicaville obtained them by the grant of that same bishop. Accordingly, the chapter, rightly considering that its dean's dwelling in the city of Bayeux was insufficient for him and his household, gave him these same houses, to be possessed in perpetual right by him and by the deans canonically appointed to succeed him in our church. They were to render yearly, in respect of these houses, six Angevin pounds, by the unanimous consent of the brethren. It decreed that, after the death of the said dean, the money should be distributed, at the chapter's direction, among the clerks of the choir who should attend the celebration on the anniversary of his death; twenty shillings, however, taken from that sum, should be distributed in bread to the poor. For, moved by just reason, we wish him to be free and exempt during his lifetime from payment of that money. Therefore, wishing that what has been solemnly done may henceforth enjoy perpetual force, we have judged it fitting to confirm it by this present charter fortified with our seal.

## II. Confirmation of the same gift made by Richard, king of England

(From the same source.)

RICHARD, by the grace of God king of England, duke of Normandy and Aquitaine, count of Anjou, to archbishops, bishops, abbots, counts, barons, justices, seneschals, sheriffs, reeves, and all his bailiffs [Col. 1159C] and faithful subjects, greeting.

Know that we have granted and by this our present charter confirmed to Henry, bishop of Bayeux, the stone house which belonged to Conan the treasurer, with the whole household estate, and the grove of the same Conan, which lies outside the wall of Bayeux beside the aforesaid household estate, with all its appurtenances. Therefore we will and firmly command that the aforesaid bishop, or the person to whom he has given it, shall have and hold the aforesaid house and grove with all their appurtenances, according to the tenor of our father's charter, well and peaceably, wholly and honourably. Witnesses: Walter, archbishop of Rouen; H., bishop of Corinth; Count William de Mandeville; W., son of Ralph, seneschal of Normandy; Robert de Harcourt.

Given by the hand of William de Longchamp, our chancellor, on the sixteenth day of September, at Winchester, in the first year of our reign.

## III. Letter of the same bishop concerning a gift made to the chapter of Bayeux of the tithe of the Forest of Nuilly and of Racineto

(From the same source.)

[Col. 1159D]

To all sons of Holy Mother Church: HENRY, by the grace of God bishop of Bayeux, greeting in the Lord.

We wish it to be known to those present and to those to come that, considering that our brethren and canons cannot maintain the regular observance required by the service of our church without much labour and expense, we have given them, to augment their common fund, the perpetual tithe of the Forest of Nuilleio, the tithe of the wood of Racineto, and two parts of the mills of Maisnil-Bajocensis. And, in order that their peace in their estate may be preserved without any anxiety, we have committed this gift to writing, securing it by the attestation of our seal.

[Col. 1160A] Done in the year of the Incarnate Word 1181, on the second Nones of November [4 November].

### IV. Letter of Pope Urban III concerning the annual revenues of the prebends of deceased canons of Bayeux.

*(From the same source.)*

“To the just desires of petitioners,” etc. See under Urban, *Patrologia*, vol. CCII.

### V. Letter of Pope Lucius III concerning the burial of the bishop and canons of Bayeux in the cathedral church.

*(From the same source.)*

“At the report of our beloved son Master Ralph,” etc. See under Lucius III, *Patrologia*, vol. CCI.

### VI. To Epistle 66.—Charter of Henry II, King of England, for the Abbey of Vœu in Normandy.

*(From old parchments of M. d’Herouval.)*

[Col. 1160B]

HENRY, by the grace of God King of England, Duke of Normandy and Aquitaine, and Count of Anjou, to the justiciars and bailiffs of Normandy, greeting.

Know that, for the love of God and at the request of my lady the Empress Matilda, I have granted to the Abbey of St Mary of Vœu, near Cherbourg, and to the canons serving God there, whatever has been justly given or sold to them from my demesne in the borough or in the vill. Therefore I will and firmly command that the aforesaid abbey shall hold all its tenements well and in peace, freely and quietly, with all its customs and liberties, in woodland and open country, and in toll, tallage, road-dues, fair, and market; and I forbid anyone to inflict, or permit to be inflicted, any injury or burden upon them, their men, or their goods in this matter. Witness: Man. Bisech., the king’s steward, at Rouen. In testimony whereof we have caused our seal to be affixed to these present letters.

[Col. 1160C] Done at Cherbourg, in the year of the Lord 1278, in September.

### VII. Another gift of the same king to the same Abbey of Vœu.

*(From the same source.)*

HENRY, by the grace of God King of England, Duke of Normandy and Aquitaine, and Count of Anjou, to the Archbishop of Rouen, bishops, abbots, counts, barons, justiciars, sheriffs, and all ministers and faithful men of Normandy, greeting.

Know that, for the love of God, I have granted and confirmed under the protection of my seal to the Abbey of St Mary of Vœu—which my lady the Empress Matilda, my mother, founded from her own revenue—and to the canons serving God there: the Church of St Margaret of Tilly with all its appurtenances; the hermitage of St [Col. 1160D] Richard with all its appurtenances; the hermitage of St Martin in the meadow; likewise, whatever Roger de Magneville held in the manor of Otheville, as the charter of that same Roger attests; three parts of the mill of Tiolph of Accato belonging to my lady mother; the *marra* held by Robert the chaplain near Hoga; land acquired by purchase from William of Cartigny at Jorboch; and land at Prédreville granted by William de Braiose. And further, whatever lands or dwellings the said abbey and canons have acquired in Cherbourg by just gifts and acquisitions.

Therefore I will and firmly command that the aforesaid abbey—which, by reason of its foundation, belongs directly and without intermediary to my special lordship—and my canons shall hold and possess all their tenements and all their lawful possessions, ecclesiastical as well as secular, with all their liberties throughout my whole land: namely, in borough and vill, woodland and open country, roads and paths, waters and fisheries, fairs and markets, [Col. 1161A] freely, quietly, peacefully, and without any exaction of toll, hearth-tax, gablage, stallage, tallage, pannage, or any servile custom owing to me. Witnesses: Walter, Archbishop of Rouen; Count William de Magneville; William de Mera; and many others, at Caen.

### VIII. Another gift of the same king to the same abbey.

*(From the same source.)*

HENRY, by the grace of God King of England and Duke of the Normans and Aquitanians, and Count of Anjou, to archbishops, bishops, abbots, barons, sheriffs, and all his ministers and faithful men, French, English, and Normans, greeting.

Know that I have granted to my lady mother, the Empress Matilda, the chaplaincy of Valognes, with all its appurtenances, as fully, completely, and entirely as it was ever best held in the time of my grandfather King Henry. Moreover, I have also granted a certain holding of the *marrerium* of the Church of St Mary, namely the new vill, to be given in perpetual alms to the Abbey of St Mary of Vœu near Cherbourg, founded by that same lady. Likewise know that I have granted the site—namely, William’s Island, on which the abbey itself is known to stand—for the souls of my grandfather Henry and of my lord father G., Duke of Normandy and Count of Anjou, and of all our predecessors, for our salvation and the stability of our realm.

[Col. 1161B] Therefore I will and command that the aforesaid abbey shall hold the things above written as honourably, quietly, and freely, with all its customs and liberties, as any abbey in all Normandy holds its possessions more advantageously, peacefully, and freely. Witnesses: Herbert, Bishop of Avranches; Thomas, royal chancellor; Man. Bileiht, the king’s steward; Roger de Calley, at Rouen.

### IX. Charter of Henry II, King of England, for the Abbey of Baugé, commonly called Baugerais, of the Cistercian Order.

[Col. 1161C]

HENRY, King of England, Duke of Normandy and Aquitaine, and Count of Anjou, to the Archbishop of Tours, the justiciars, and all his ministers and faithful men in Touraine and Normandy, greeting.

Know that I have granted and confirmed by this present charter to the brethren of Baugé the place of Baugé in which they dwell, and whatever has been or shall reasonably be given to them. Furthermore, I grant that the aforesaid brethren may receive the order and observance of the Church of St Barbara in Normandy (Sainte-Barbe-en-Ange). Therefore I will and firmly command that the aforesaid brethren shall have and hold their aforesaid place, and whatever has been or shall be reasonably given them, in peace, quiet, integrity, and honour; and I forbid you to inflict, or permit any injury or insult to be inflicted, upon them in that regard. Witnesses: [Col. 1161D] Hugh, Abbot of Landais (Abbaye Landais); Richard de Hum, constable; Richard de Camilla; Robert de Briet; Stephen of Tours; Geoffrey Forest; at Châtillon in Berry (Châtillon-sur-l’Indre).

### IX bis. Another charter of the same king for the Abbey of Oratory, commonly called Louroux, in the Diocese of Angers.

*(From the same source.)*

HENRY, by the grace of God King of the English, Duke of Normandy and Aquitaine, and Count of Anjou, to the archbishops, bishops, abbots, counts, barons, justiciars, sheriffs, seneschals, provosts, all bailiffs, and all his faithful men throughout his whole land, greeting.

Know that I have given in free and perpetual alms, and by this my present charter confirmed to God and to the Abbey of Oratory, the place of Baugé with its appurtenances, for building there an abbey of the [Col. 1162A] Cistercian Order; and all other gifts which have reasonably been or shall be made to that place of Baugé. Therefore I will and firmly command that the aforesaid Abbey of Oratory, and that same Abbey of Baugé, shall have and hold the aforesaid place with all its appurtenances, all other gifts which have reasonably been or shall be made to them, and all their lawful acquisitions, well and in peace, freely, quietly, wholly, fully, and honourably: in woodland and open country, meadows and pastures, fields and mills, fishponds, pools and fisheries, roads and paths, and all other things belonging to them, together with all their liberties and free customs.

I also grant that the monks serving God in the Abbey of Baugé shall be quit and have firm peace throughout all my land from toll, passage-dues, and every custom owing to me, on all their goods and on the pannage of their own livestock [Col. 1162B] in my woods and forests. Witnesses: Geoffrey Dure, Prior of Loches; William, Abbot of Daurat; Brother Roger, my almoner; Stephen de Tyron, Seneschal of Anjou; William de Hostili; Henry de Montbazon, Provost of Loches. At Beaulieu near Loches.

### X. Letter showing that Hervé, Abbot of Villeloin, gave the place of Le Liget to brethren of the Carthusian Order at the request of Henry II, King of England and Count of Anjou, about the year of the Lord 1173.

*(From the cartulary of the Abbey of St Saviour of Villeloin, p. 125, given by the Lord Abbot of Villeloin.)*

The reliable memory of things done is preserved by writing, and occasion for dispute is removed. Considering this twofold usefulness, we have therefore taken care to make known by letters to posterity and to those present that Lord Henry, Abbot of St Saviour of Villeloin, with the assent of his whole [Col. 1162C] chapter, granted to the brethren of the Charterhouse that place commonly called Le Liget, with its appurtenances, to be possessed in perpetuity, out of charity and at the request of Lord Henry, King of England, Duke of Normandy, Count of Anjou, and at the request of Lord Stephen the seneschal.

On the condition, however, that the lord king, giving attentive consideration to the burden of the house of Villeloin, gave the brethren of Villeloin one hundred pounds and caused the two *Halieti*, which the men of Chepdune owed them, to be remitted. This was done into the hands of William the prior and the brethren then living with him: Brother Herbert, Brother William, and Brother Martin; and in the presence of very many persons: Maurice, Abbot of Beaulieu; Lord Geoffrey, Abbot of St Julian of Tours; and also in the presence of the king’s envoys, Stephen the seneschal, William Cloet, Archambaud of Vendôme, Hervé, Provost of Loches, Geoffrey Besoger, and a great multitude of monks—namely Denis, [Col. 1162D] Arnulf, Ralph, Haiméric—and very many other clerics and laymen, namely Rainaud de Sinapariis, John the Norman, Thomas Raier, Gaudric, Odulric, and many others.

### XI. Gift of the same king to the Church of Fontevraud of Ponts-de-Cé.

*(From an old parchment of M. d’Herouval.)*

HENRY, by the grace of God King of England, Duke of Normandy and Aquitaine, and Count of Anjou, to archbishops, bishops, abbots, counts, barons, justiciars, sheriffs, ministers, and all his faithful men, greeting.

Know that I have granted and given, and by this my present charter confirmed, to God, to the Church of Blessed Mary Mother of God at Fontevraud, and to the nuns serving God there, for the salvation of my soul and of my predecessors, Ponts-de-Cé, as freely and [Col. 1163A] quietly as any of my predecessors granted that same Pont to the said church to possess more fully and freely. I also grant and confirm to them the vicariate of that same Pont, with all liberties and free customs belonging to the Count of Anjou.

With respect to theft, shedding of blood, rape, and all other offences, I grant them jurisdiction and every profit, reserving to myself, through my bailiffs, the execution of justice in cases of life and limb. I give and grant them all profit thereof; and I have reserved it to myself only because it is not for religious women to judge matters of life and limb. These, moreover, are the customs of the said Pont, etc. Therefore I will and firmly command that the Church of Fontevraud itself and the nuns serving God therein shall have and hold all the aforesaid well and in peace, freely, quietly, wholly, fully, and honourably, with all their liberties and free customs, as I granted them and confirmed by my charter.

[Col. 1163B] Witnesses: William, Bishop of Le Mans; Geoffrey, Bishop of Angers; Robert, Bishop of Nantes; Stephen, Bishop of Rennes; Richard and Geoffrey, my sons; Count William de Mandemst. [uncertain]; Fulk de Monstach; Seneschal of Poitou; Stephen of Tours, Seneschal of Anjou; Maurice de Craon; Vegis; Geoffrey of Perche; Peter son of Guy; William de Hostili; Durand the Cupbearer; Gilbert of the Wardrobe. At Angers.

### XII. Copy of the foundation of the Abbey of Savigny in Normandy.

*(From old parchments of M. d’Herouval.)*

In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Let it be known to all present and future that I, Ralph, lord of Fougères, for the love of God and the salvation of my soul and of my predecessors and successors, together with my wife Amicia and my sons Matthew, Francis, Galo, Henry, and Robert, give and [Col. 1163C] grant to God and to Lord Vitalis the Hermit, as a possession and monastic dwelling-place, the Forest of Savigny, as it is bounded by the three waters Chamba, Chamberna, and Blackwater.

Furthermore, besides what the monks dwelling there may acquire, I give, grant, and establish by this present charter, as the dowry and inheritance of the monastic dwelling, one thousand pounds’ worth of annual revenue in my land of Fougères, wherever and from whomsoever they may choose, whether by gift or purchase; and I now confirm these to them as though they already possessed them. I will and grant that the aforesaid monks shall have, in the aforesaid holdings and in the men dwelling therein, as much right, as much high and low jurisdiction, as much dignity, franchise, and power, with every right and lordship, as I and my predecessors and successors could have in our demesne land; and that the monks themselves and their men shall have general common rights throughout all my land together with my own men.

[Col. 1163D] All the aforesaid things, my wife, my aforesaid sons, and I have rendered to God and dedicated to His service. Thus we have confirmed them to the monks to hold of God Himself, freely and quietly, with all high and low jurisdiction; and we have entirely released them from every custom, service, exaction, court, homage, corvée, claim, reversionary right, and every kind of profit, reserving to ourselves and our successors in all the aforesaid matters, as stated, absolutely nothing except ratification [reading uncertain].

Accordingly, neither we nor our successors shall thereafter be able to exercise any jurisdiction in any of the aforesaid matters, nor over men holding the said lands from the said monks. And if it should happen that any of their men is arrested by us or our successors for a present offence, we are bound, without delay, to restore him to the said monks in the condition in which he was, whenever we are requested by them; and they shall administer justice in the matter as they deem expedient. This gift was confirmed and secured by the impression of my seal, Ralph’s, [Col. 1164A] in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1112, in the fifth indiction, epact 28, on the Kalends of February [1 February].

### XIII. Confirmation of the foundation of Savigny made by Henry II, King of England.

*(From the same M. d’Herouval.)*

HENRY, by the grace of God King of England, Duke of Normandy and Aquitaine, and Count of Anjou, to archbishops, bishops, abbots, counts, barons, justiciars, bailiffs, sheriffs, and all his ministers and faithful men, greeting.

Know that I have granted and by this my present charter confirmed to the Church of the Holy Trinity of Savigny and the monks serving God there all the gifts written below which have been made to them: namely, from the gift of Ralph, lord of Fougères, the Forest of Savigny, as it is bounded by the three waters, Chamba, Chamberna, and Blackwater, etc. All [Col. 1164B] these lands, all the alms listed here, and all others which they possess, and which, God favouring, they may acquire by gift or purchase, I have granted, as stated, to the Church and monks of Savigny, free and quiet, with every high and low jurisdiction, right, and lordship, released from every service and custom.

I have taken the abbey itself, all possessions belonging to it, and all their men wherever they may be and from whosever gift they may derive, throughout all my land, into my hand, custody, and protection, as my demesne and proper alms. Therefore I will, command, and firmly establish that the same abbey, the monks, their brethren and servants, their men, and all things belonging to them, throughout all land acquired and to be acquired by me and my successors, shall have firm peace, perfect liberty, and full quittance by sea and land, in woodland and open country, from every [Col. 1164C] custom, service, and exaction, as alms dedicated to God for the remission of our sins and the redemption of our souls.

Therefore I will and firmly command that the aforesaid Abbey of Savigny and the monks serving God in it shall have and retain in perpetual alms these things and all others which they now possess, whether by gift or purchase from whomsoever, and those which they may hereafter, God favouring, reasonably acquire, with every high and low jurisdiction and every right and lordship, with all their liberties, free customs, and quittances. Thus all things belonging to the aforesaid monks and their men shall be quit throughout all my land of every toll, passage-dues, bridge-dues, pannage, *cohuage*, *pallage*, service, homage, military service, tallage, every aid customary or uncustomary, every kind of profit and claim, and every other custom, service, and exaction—in churches, [Col. 1164D] tithes, lands, and men; woodland and open country; meadows and pastures; waters and mills; fishponds, pools, warrens, fisheries, marshes, brichemins [uncertain term], paths, and all other places and things; and in towns and castles—well and peacefully, freely, quietly, and honourably, as my own demesne and as alms dedicated to God for the remission of my sins and those of all our predecessors and successors. We reserve nothing in all these matters to ourselves or our successors except divine recompense and what shall devolve by succession upon us and our successors.

And it is to be known that, out of my own gift, I have granted to the aforesaid monks of Savigny that they may grant their lands upon whatever customs they wish. They may summon their men wherever they wish and to whatever part of their land they wish, as often as seems expedient to them, notwithstanding any customs of the countries.

[Col. 1165A] This my confirmation and grant was made in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1157, namely the third year of my reign in England and the eighth of my duchy of Normandy, in the presence of these witnesses: Master Walter de Const. [uncertain], Archdeacon of Oxford; Ralph, Archdeacon of Hereford; Master Jocelin, Archdeacon of Chester; William, son of the Seneschal of Normandy; Ralph de fil. Seherio de Quincy [uncertain]; Bertrand de Verdun; William de Solatiis; Reginald de Paveillie; Uling de Mornist [uncertain]; and many others, at Domfront.

### XIV. Another confirmation by the same king for the foundation of Savigny.

*(From the same M. d’Herouval.)*

HENRY, by the grace of God King of England, Duke of Normandy and Aquitaine, and Count of Anjou, to archbishops, bishops, counts, barons, justiciars, [Col. 1165B] bailiffs, sheriffs, provosts, ministers, and all his faithful men throughout his whole land, greeting in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ.

Let it be known to you present and future that, for the love of God and the salvation of my soul, and for the souls of my father and mother, my wife, my children and sons, all my predecessors and successors, and all faithful Christians, I have granted in perpetual alms to the Church of the Holy Trinity of Savigny, and to Abbot Richard and the monks serving God there, all lands, alms, and quittances which my predecessors and their men had given and granted to that church. I have taken that church, with all things belonging to it, into my hand, custody, and defence, as my own abbey and demesne alms; and, in order that all subsequent properties belonging to that church might be firmly and [Col. 1165C] permanently confirmed without any doubt in perpetuity, and might be held and possessed freely, quietly, and securely by that church in the present and future time, I wished them to be specifically entered and confirmed in this present charter, so that, to the knowledge of our successors and for the benefit of their possessors, they might be preserved whole and unimpaired for ever.

Accordingly, I have granted the Forest of Savigny, bounded by the three waters Chamba, Chamberna, and Blackwater, with all its appurtenances. This forest is the first possession of that church, from which the place itself took its name, so that it was called Savigny; the same church holds this forest by the gift of Ralph de Fougères and his son Henry, and by the grant of Stephen, Count of Mortain, and Henry, King of England, etc. All these lands, all the alms listed here, and all others which they may acquire by every lawful means, I have granted, as stated, to the Church and monks of Savigny, [Col. 1165D] free and quiet and discharged from all service and custom. I have taken the abbey itself and all possessions belonging to it, wherever they may be and from whosever gift they may derive, throughout all my land, into my hand, custody, and protection, as my demesne and proper alms, etc.

This our ordinance and confirmation was made in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1157, namely the third year of my reign in England and the eighth of my duchy of Normandy.

### XV. Charter of foundation of the Abbey of Blanche-Lande.

*(From parchments of M. d’Herouval.)*

RICHARD de la Haye and Matilda his wife, to all their men and friends in Normandy and England, greeting and affection.

Let it be known to your affection and to the whole body of all present and future persons that, on our own inheritance, in a place called Blanche-Lande, [Col. 1166A] we establish a monastery in honour of our Lord Jesus Christ, His blessed Mother, and the most holy confessor Nicholas. There we establish a community of canons, to serve God according to the Premonstratensian Order. For their food and clothing, for the redemption of our souls and those of our successors and all our predecessors, we grant in perpetual alms from our small means the following things; and through the hand of Lord Richard, Bishop of Coutances, we dedicate them to the Lord, with the consent of William de Guono and his son Richard, and of Nicholas de la Haye, my nephew, who with us offer them with their own hands upon the altar of the aforesaid monastery: namely, the place itself in which the monastery is founded, with all its adjacent lands, etc.

Accordingly, in the presence and with the approval of clergy and people, we gave the things above written to this our monastery of St Michael of Blanche-Lande, [Col. 1166B] reserving absolutely nothing in any of these things, but offering them upon the altar through the hand of Richard, Bishop of Coutances, free and released from every right, lordship, secular custom, claim, and exaction belonging to us. Excepted are excluded works on the land of Paraner, of Bosseville, and on the land of Hugh Camri of Chatouville, which *masura* has its *costumae* free in the forest; and excepted is the *molt* of the men of Richard the clerk at Austremensura, and excluded works. Witnesses: Richard, Bishop of Coutances; William, Abbot of Montebourg; Robert de Perdot; Renaud de Maisvel; Richard Avenel; and many others. In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1154.

### XVI. Confirmation of the same foundation by Henry II, King of England.

*(From the same M. d’Herouval.)*

[Col. 1166C] HENRY, King of England, Duke of Normandy and Aquitaine, and Count of Anjou, to archbishops, bishops, abbots, counts, sheriffs, barons, all his ministers, and all his faithful men, greeting.

Know that I have granted and confirmed in perpetual alms to God, to the Church of St Nicholas of Blanche-Lande, and to the canons serving in that abbey according to the Premonstratensian Order, whatever has reasonably and lawfully been bestowed upon them: namely, the following alms, which Richard de la Haye and Matilda his wife, founders of the aforesaid church, Ralph de la Haye, Richard’s nephew, William de Varna and his son Richard, have bestowed upon that church—namely, the place called Blanche-Lande, where the church was founded, with all its adjacent lands, etc.

In order that all the things below written, and whatever may hereafter be reasonably bestowed upon the aforesaid church by anyone, may remain firm and unimpaired, I confirm them by royal [Col. 1166D] authority; and, having confirmed them, I commend them to be continually protected and confirmed in the kingdom after me. Witnesses: Rotrou, Bishop of Évreux; Arnulf, Bishop of Lisieux; Philip, Bishop of Bayeux; Richard, Bishop of Coutances; and Robert de Neubourg. In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1157.

### XVII. To Epistle 124.—Letter of Walter, Archbishop of Rouen, granting the tithe of Dieppe and Bouteilles to the Chapter of Rouen.

*(From an old slip of M. d’Herouval.)*

To all Christ’s faithful to whom this present writing shall come, WALTER, by the grace of God Archbishop of Rouen, greeting in the Lord.

It is just that those who have shared adversity should share prosperity. For those who have been companions in suffering ought not in any way to be strangers to consolation. Since, therefore, our dearly beloved sons, the canons of our Church of Rouen, while we were contending at great expense, with very grave exertions and dangers, to defend the patrimony of our church against [lacuna] and rulers, remained with us bravely and faithfully in our trials, it is fitting and just that what, with the Lord’s help, has permanently accrued to our benefit from the proceeds of our labours should not be wholly alien to them. Rather, those who grieved with us in our travail should together rejoice in the fruit and joy of our delivery.

Therefore, from every rent and revenue which we or our successors shall in future receive annually for our own use from Dieppe and Bouteilles and their appurtenances, we have granted our canons in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1198, in pure and perpetual alms, and given them a tenth part, to be received entire every year on the feast of Blessed Romanus [Col. 1167B] the Confessor, our patron, and divided among the brethren who on the day of our death shall celebrate the office for us according to the customary annual commemoration. Meanwhile, while we live, the canons who assemble for the solemnity of the aforesaid confessor shall receive that same tenth and divide it equally among themselves according to the common custom.

But because it would be difficult for the aforesaid tenth to be paid wholly at one term, especially near the beginning of the year, we have ordained, with the common consent of those same canons, that this tenth be paid in four instalments: one fourth at the Nativity of the Lord; another fourth at the Nativity of Blessed John the Baptist; another fourth at the feast of St Michael the Archangel; and, so long as we live, at the feast of the aforesaid confessor, as previously assigned, to be divided among the said canons. After we shall have departed this life, the same canons have ordained that they will celebrate the anniversary of the day of our death four times a year, and on each of those occasions divide one fourth [Col. 1167C] of the tithe equally among the canons present.

If, therefore, the aforesaid towns are let at farm, we decree that the farmers shall pay the tenth to the said canons at the aforesaid terms; and if at any term they do not pay the same tenth in full, they shall incur a penalty of ten pounds in current money, to be paid to the said canons but enforced by us or our successors. But if we retain those towns in our own hand, so that the proceeds and revenues cannot be assessed so plainly, their valuation shall be entrusted to the judgment of four lawful men of the same towns, who, being sworn, shall in good faith declare the total sum of all revenue and proceeds. The tenth so assessed shall then be paid without objection to the same canons at the established terms, under the penalty of ten pounds as aforesaid, with our seneschal or that of our successors, or a bailiff appointed to receive the said revenues and proceeds, intervening if payment has been omitted at any of the aforesaid terms, in whole or in part.

[Col. 1167D] Since after the date of the aforesaid donation new proceeds have accrued, both from mills and from other things, to the revenues of the aforesaid towns, lest anyone, through a captious interpretation of the words, should maintain that a tenth is not owing from these to the aforesaid canons, we, removing that doubt—though superfluous—have decreed that a tenth of both those proceeds and others which, God granting, shall hereafter accrue to the same towns is to be granted in full to the same canons; since it is not incongruous that one and the same substance should be assessed in a certain twofold manner by law.

And in order that this our gift may remain firm and stable for ever and cannot be overthrown by anyone’s contrivance, we have judged it fitting to strengthen it by the protection of this present writing and our seal. Trusting in God’s mercy, in the merits of Blessed Mary His Mother, and of our blessed patron Romanus, [Col. 1168A] we anathematize and curse all who attempt to violate this our gift and confirmation; may they incur the indignation of Almighty God, Blessed Mary, Blessed Romanus, and all the saints. We establish nothing new here, but renew the sentence pronounced at the time when the gift was made.

Given at Rouen by the hand of Robert of St Nicholas, our chaplain and canon of Rouen, on the sixth day before the Kalends of October [26 September]. Witnesses: our venerable brethren the bishops of Normandy—Robert of Bayeux, William of Avranches, Luke of Évreux, Silvester of Sées, Jordan of Lisieux, and Vivian of Coutances—who, at our request, affixed their seals to this charter; Richard, dean of the Church of Rouen; Roger, cantor; Master Simon, chancellor; Richard Haynim; Master Gilbert de Marleis, canons of Rouen; and many other witnesses.

### XVIII. To Epistle 126.—Letter of Odo, Bishop of Paris, for abolishing the Feast of Fools and restoring the solemnity of the Circumcision of the Lord.

*(From the cartulary of the most illustrious Lord Jean-Baptiste de Contes, Dean of the Church of Paris, Charter 156.)*

[Col. 1168B]

“Since the Lord Peter,” etc. See under Odo of Paris, for the year 1208.

### XIX. Another letter of the same Odo, Bishop of Paris, concerning the solemnity of the Circumcision of the Lord and St Stephen.

*(From the great Parisian Pastoral.)*

“Although we, unworthy as we are, [have been appointed] for this purpose,” etc. See in the same place.

### XX. Letter of Peter Cambius, by the grace of God Bishop of Paris, concerning the solemnity of the Circumcision of the Lord and St Stephen.

*(From the same Pastoral.)*

[Col. 1168C]

PETER, by the grace of God Bishop of Paris, to his beloved sons HUGH, dean, and the Chapter of Paris, in perpetuity.

Whatever is established for the benefit of the Church and the increase of divine worship deserves to be strengthened with perpetual force, lest in the course of time it be weakened by anyone’s malice. We therefore wish it to come to the knowledge of all that the lord Odo, of happy memory, formerly bishop of Paris and our predecessor, desiring to eliminate certain enormities that had sprung up in the Church of Paris under the pretext of a depraved custom, decreed that the feast of the Lord’s Circumcision and the Nativity of Saint Stephen the Protomartyr should be restored to a regular order and solemnly celebrated. To each canon and cleric serving at the high altar [Col. 1168D] who attends Matins on the Nativity of Blessed Stephen, he graciously granted and assigned six Parisian denarii; to each non-canonical cleric of the choir, four denarii; to each boy of the choir, two denarii; and to each cleric who sings the responsory or Alleluia at Mass in three- or four-part organum, six denarii—each sum to be received yearly, freely and without disturbance, in our Parisian provostship. On the feast of the Circumcision, moreover, he generously assigned in perpetuity, to be received from the revenues of the chapter, three Parisian denarii to each non-canonical cleric of the choir and two denarii to each boy.

He also gave, as a perpetual alms to the chapter of the Church of Paris, a yearly allowance of bread, wine, and pork, to be paid on the feast of Pentecost by whoever should then be bishop of Paris; and he ordained that each canon of Saint-Denis-du-Pas should receive half of the same allowance on that day. Furthermore, he granted and conceded to the chapter of Paris [Col. 1169A] sixty Parisian shillings of rent from Brunel, to be received every year on the day of his anniversary and distributed as he had ordained.

In addition, he likewise granted and released to the chapter of Paris the prebend and vicarage which the church of Sainte-Geneviève had customarily held in the Church of Paris, and which that bishop had acquired for the Parisian chapter, so that they might dispose of both the prebend and the vicarage at their will. Moreover, with the assent of the chapter he established eight matricularii in the Church of Paris, and both he and the chapter assigned fixed and perpetual provision for their support. He also granted and freely bestowed upon the chapter and Church, to possess in perpetuity freely and without disturbance, the tithes of all newly cleared lands, whether yet to be cleared or already cleared but not yet assigned to others, in every place of the diocese of Paris where the Church of Paris possessed, or would possess, the right of tithing—saving the right of another church that might possess a share of the tithe in the same territory.

Moreover, he transferred by pious donation into the right and ownership of the chapter that which he had purchased at Buc, [Col. 1169B] for distribution as Matins-money on the feast of Blessed Bernard. Furthermore, he assigned and granted to the Church and the succentor of Paris, for performing the Mandatum on Maundy Thursday, one muid of grain according to the Paris measure—half winter grain and half spring grain—at Herblay, from grain that he had acquired and held from the monks of Saint-Denis; provided that, if the abbot and monks of Saint-Denis assigned that grain to the bishop of Paris elsewhere, the aforesaid succentor should receive the said muid of grain where the bishop’s grain was assigned. He further gave to the Matins clerics that portion which he received from the offerings at the Cross made on Friday in the Lord’s Passion, namely, half of all offerings.

We therefore approve and hold valid the aforesaid gifts, grants, and institutions; by this present written instrument we confirm them and strengthen them by the protection of our seal, and decree and command that they remain perpetually inviolate.

Given at Paris, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1208, the first year of our pontificate.

## XXI. Copy of a Certain Letter Sent by the Venerable Faculty of Theology of the Parisian Studium to the Prelates and Chapters of the Churches of the Kingdom of France, for the Detestation, Condemnation, and Complete Abolition of a Certain Superstitious and Scandalous Rite Which Some Call the Feast of Fools, and Which Took Its Beginning and Origin from the Rite of Pagan and Unbelieving Idolaters

(From a manuscript codex of the Abbey of Cîteaux, sent by Master Jacques de Lannoy, master of novices of that abbey, to Dom Luc d’Achery, Benedictine, who communicated it to me.)

[Col. 1169D] To all prelates of churches and to their venerable chapters established everywhere: the humble Faculty of Sacred Theology of the nourishing University of Paris offers honour and the due service of Christian devotion.

Zeal for divine worship, the outcry of many faithful people, and the plaintive request of certain bishops induce and impel us to set forth in a brief letter how greatly we abhor and detest the rite of a certain festival which its inventors call the Feast of Fools. Although, from the testimonies of Sacred Scripture, both Old and New Testament, by which God most strictly commands that his temple and ministers be clean and sanctified from every defilement, it is very easy to condemn such a den of festivity, in which priests and clerics pollute themselves with inward and outward filth and defile God’s temple and churches; nevertheless, because the perpetrators of this practice attempt to defend themselves under [Col. 1170A] the law of custom and stubbornly resist their superiors on that ground, a greater and sharper rebuke is necessary—one severe enough for the bitterness of correction to break and overcome the obstinacy of such hardened persons. We have therefore briefly and succinctly declared our judgment in this matter, so that prelates may drive this pestilential rite from their subjects more diligently and boldly, even by the cautery of harsh punishment if necessary.

First, then, what do we judge concerning its origin? This filth came from the pagans; this festival is a remnant of paganism, though its supporters entitle it the Feast of Fools. For it is certain, as the annals of history relate, that the nations of the gentiles, ignorant of the true God, deceived by many frauds of demons and driven by the varied desires of their passions, were led into superfluous and superstitious worships of vain things. Nor is this surprising, since they had no circumcision of faith. Hence they worshipped statues dedicated to demons. Hence rulers, imagining themselves divine and deceived in the memory of humankind by diabolical fraud, established idols resembling themselves, to be worshipped so that they might be represented to the peoples as gods. Moreover, to lure the foolish populace more readily into worship of their idol and make their names last longer, they imposed upon young peoples solemn festivals in specified months and days, dedicated through games to the desires of the flesh. In these no deformity, vice, or crime was reproved; rather, each person was permitted to do whatever occurred to his fancy. Hence fornications, prostitutes, and other unspeakable monstrous crimes were committed openly and with impunity.

Indeed, at these feasts the priests of idols, in order with greater frenzy to stir up the populace more abundantly toward the raised-up idol, indulged in monstrous excesses beyond all others. Thus, poets recount, it happened at the feast of Bacchus; likewise the feast of Venus and Daphnis at the beginning of May; likewise the feast of Pluto and Proserpina in February; likewise the feast of the most filthy Janus on the Kalends of January; likewise at very many feasts of trees dedicated and planted for Diana; and at many others in which the greatest enormities were committed.

Beyond doubt, this is the origin of this wicked rite; this is the birth of that corruption which they call custom; this is the poisoned root of bitterness, which, putting forth shoots above, spread its woody branches. Beneath these, youth given over to luxury eagerly pursued and continued the enormities of the flesh—enormities which the knife of faith and of worship of the true God must undoubtedly circumcise away from Christians, since one is not truly a faithful follower of Christ who clings to such things. Thus the blessed Apostle Paul marks certain Corinthians as having fallen from the faith because, after receiving baptism, they observed festivals of this kind: “I fear,” he says, “that I may have laboured among you in vain, because you observe days” (Galatians IV). The gloss: that is, the superstitions and solemnities of the gentiles.

And blessed Augustine, in [Col. 1170D] a sermon on the Circumcision [Note: [Col. 1169] Sermon on the Kalends of January, about the middle; sermon 40, edited by Sirmond], reproaching such pagan rites and their continuance among Christian people, says:

> “Those who wish to observe anything from pagan custom ought to fear lest the Christian name be of no benefit to them. Whoever also shows any approval to foolish people engaging in such games should not doubt that he makes himself a participant in their sin. But for you, brothers, it should not suffice that you do not commit this evil; wherever you see it being done, rebuke, correct, and chastise it.”

Thus Augustine. Accordingly, very many most holy bishops proceeded against these festivals as against the abominations of Christians, and with all their power sought to drive them from the bounds of Christendom. Through their labours, with God’s help, it came about that such filth and such remnants of paganism ceased for the most part in Christian lands; or, if they are discovered to be practised in secret, their perpetrators do not escape without [Col. 1171A] severe punishment.

Yet the wicked tradition of the most filthy Janus still persists to this day on the Kalends of January. Diabolical instruction has handed it down to be observed by priests and clerics in many churches of this kingdom under the shadow of the Lord’s Nativity and the joy of his birthday days. It is all the worse because, during so great a feast of the Saviour and on days dedicated to it, when they should devote themselves to every holiness, they turn and apply themselves to filth and uncleanness. Imitating the most filthy Janus, they mock and defile God’s worship by mingling Janus’s games with divine service—games, I say, such that fanatical priests would not allow them to be performed in their temples and before their idols. Certainly, the aforesaid pagan festivals, serving the incitements of luxury, were conducted not in temples but in groves, fields, or the theatres of towns, and by secular persons. But this coagulation of abomination, called the Feast of Fools [Col. 1171B], is performed in churches, in consecrated places, and by persons consecrated to God; and, by making themselves abominable and profaning holy places, they jointly celebrate Janus’s rite.

How rightly this criminal assemblage is called the Feast of Fools! For in Sacred Scripture, calling someone a fool is equivalent to calling him a companion of evil men who rejoice in most wicked things.

What sensible Christian, I ask, would not call evil those priests and clerics whom he saw, at the time of divine office, masked, with monstrous faces, or dressed as women, pimps, or actors; leading dances in the choir; singing indecent songs; eating rich morsels on the horn of the altar beside one celebrating Mass; playing dice there; burning incense from the foul smoke of old leather shoes; running through the whole church, dancing, not blushing at their obscenity; and then being carried through the town and its theatres in filthy carts and vehicles to disgraceful spectacles, making shameful gestures with their bodies for the laughter [Col. 1171C] of those standing by and gathering around, and uttering the most indecent and scurrilous words? And so with many other abominations, which one is ashamed to recall and whose recital makes the mind recoil—yet which, as we have learned by trustworthy report, were committed this year in many places. What faithful person, understanding this, would not judge these churchmen godless and cruel toward God’s honour, the Church’s decency, and their own reputation? Certainly, no great learning is required to judge them, nor are great citations of Sacred Scripture needed to detest such a feast. For they rage against the first principles of morals and faith, against the worship of God, and persist obstinately.

“But,” they say, “we do this in play and not seriously, as has been customary from antiquity, so that the folly innate in us may flow out and evaporate once a year. Would not wineskins and casks of wine burst more often if their vents were not sometimes opened? We are old wineskins and half-burst casks; therefore the overly fermenting wine of wisdom, which we would hold in by force throughout the year while constraining ourselves in God’s service, would flow out vainly if we did not sometimes devote ourselves to games and follies. We must therefore sometimes engage in play, so that afterward we may return stronger to retain wisdom.”

These and similar things they say, as do their accomplices—aged old men of evil days—seeking an excuse for sins. Moreover, young people, always hungry for novelties and games, applaud such monstrosities that summon laughter.

But people solicitous for their salvation think very differently from them. They think, and hold firmly in mind, that reputation, faith, and the eye do not permit play. For just as no one would wish his eye to be pricked with a point in jest, so neither should faith be torn apart in play, nor God’s honour be permitted to suffer harm. This excuse concerning play is therefore vain. Likewise, custom ought not to be reckoned with in this matter. For it has already been shown above that this rite sprang from a poisoned root [Col. 1172A]—namely, from the corruption of nature together with demonic delusion—and took its beginning from the filth of pagans and unbelievers. It therefore cannot acquire the force of custom, since it tends against God and toward the destruction of souls. O wickedness! Is custom to be alleged against divine law, against the dictate of nature, against innate shame, against the sanctuary of the Church?

Again, the comparison they propose concerning wineskins and casks has no application here. Wisdom does not burden the soul as boiling wine does its vessel because of heat; rather, wisdom strengthens and steadies the soul’s powers. On the contrary, foolish and evil acts weaken and injure those powers, besides producing evil habits and bad residues which they contract. Hence we see that people accustomed to follies commonly become dull at the end of their days and depart this world without understanding. Therefore the statement that by breathing out in follies from time to time we return stronger to retain wisdom is false and craftily advanced. Sins and follies are contrary to rational nature and offend it.

We admit, however, that prolonged application to acts of wisdom tires the animal powers connected with the body. It is therefore good sometimes to engage in modest and honourable games, so that they may be refreshed and strengthened. Thus the most blessed Evangelist John, playing with a partridge in his hand, gave an example to one who mocked him for this very reason: he spoke of his own bow, which, if kept stretched too long and too tightly, loses the power to shoot an arrow forcefully unless it is relaxed. But this is virtuous recreation, utterly incompatible with the aforesaid insanities, although the unlearned populace calls them games, along with many foolish persons even invested with authority. Yet, if some of your predecessors considered these insanities to be games, as these men allege, they thereby certainly accuse those predecessors of sloth and negligence, since they tolerated such great outrages in churches. Therefore one must not look to what human beings ignore [Col. 1172C] and tolerate where the law plainly cries out wholly to the contrary; for God’s law, not human beings, must be followed, unless they themselves serve that law.

Therefore, O reverend Fathers and honoured prelates, heed the law of God and the saints whom God made wonderful upon earth, that they might be for us an example and a testimony of his will. Do not listen to the crafty voices of people who say: “Our predecessors, reputed notable men, permitted this feast; it is enough for us to live as they did.” Beyond doubt, this argument is diabolical and this persuasion infernal, for you do not know whether their end was good or evil. Follow, then, those whom God has declared worthy of imitation by miracles. Follow the saints—such as the Apostle Paul and Augustine cited above—who condemn the observers of this rite as fallen from faith. Follow the many glorious bishops, namely Martin, Hilary, Chrysostom, Nicholas, Germanus of Auxerre [Col. 1172D], and all others down to recent times, who rose most fiercely against such abominations. What, I ask, would they have done if they had seen the clergy alone, as today, occupied with these observances? Follow the sacred canons of the supreme pontiffs and general councils, which condemn these games as plagues of souls. Follow also the grave and devout persons who cannot behold these wicked spectacles without sorrow.

We beg you, O most renowned Fathers, to heed this and to stretch every sinew of your authority to disperse and destroy this compact of impiety. Let no exemption or privilege of anyone delay or divert you; for, since in these cases there is a vehement suspicion of heretical depravity, no exemption ought to avail. For we affirm to you that this observance—the Feast of Fools, with the aforesaid and customary filth, together with the circumstances of persons and places [Col. 1173A]—is a sacrilegious profanation of the decency and reverence due to divine worship, and an abomination detestable to all Christians. Therefore priests and clerics who persistently commit such acts must be proceeded against as persons suspected in the faith and holding evil views concerning the honour due to God and the sacraments.

Strive, therefore, most renowned Fathers, to remove this sacrilege from among you. Act in such a way that this very grave and abominable wrong does not redound upon your souls. Remember Eli the high priest, otherwise regarded as a good man. Because he did not rebuke his sons sufficiently severely, although by their wickedness the people were drawn away from the worship of God and from offerings, he fell backward from his seat through divine vengeance and died with his head broken, as an example to all superiors. Consider also with what zeal Moses, the meekest of men, and with what severity he raged against those who gave scandal to God’s worship, when in one day he killed three thousand idolaters [Col. 1173B]. Certainly, if rightly weighed, these wicked crimes are not far removed from idolatry. Although at present, under the spiritual law and law of love, such punishments are not to be inflicted, they nevertheless show how greatly that sin displeases God and how severely superiors or rulers of souls ought to abolish it.

Thus, bringing our letter to its close, we conclude that the continuation or abolition of this pestilential rite depends upon you, the prelates. For it is not credible that these churchmen are so mad and obstinate in this frenzy that, if they encountered a prelate’s stern face wholly unyielding in punishment, with the support of inquisitors of the faith and the aid of the secular arm, they would not at once yield or break. For they would fear prisons; they would fear losing benefices, losing reputation, and being driven from the sacred altars.

We therefore pray God the most merciful Father [Col. 1173C] to give you the Spirit of fortitude against these diabolical furies and all pestilential people. Amen.

The following conclusions were examined, approved, and qualified by the aforesaid venerable Faculty of Theology for the detestation and total destruction, or abolition, of the aforesaid condemnable and pagan Feast of Fools.

**First conclusion.**—A custom introduced long ago, according to which in certain churches—cathedral, collegiate, or others—churchmen annually hold, on the feast of the Innocents, Saint Stephen, the Lord’s Circumcision, or another feast, a festival called the Feast of Fools, in which they customarily perpetrate a thousand mockeries and follies, even against reverence for God and to the great disgrace of the clergy and the whole ecclesiastical estate, has been condemned by the holy Fathers and general councils. It should rather be called a corruption than a custom, and must not be observed under the pretext of any statute whatever.

**Second conclusion.**—It is not permissible in any church, under the pretext of the aforesaid evil and condemned custom, to elect a bishop or archbishop of fools, or derisively and mockingly to confirm one so elected. Episcopal dignity was first instituted by Christ in the New Testament and ordained for the governance of his holy Church and the salvation of souls. Those who make sport of so great a dignity and turn it into mockery and derision therefore appear to hold unsound views concerning the authority and pre-eminence of pontifical dignity, which nevertheless stands first in the Church’s hierarchy. Such persons also must be severely punished.

**Third conclusion.**—It is not permissible for bishops or archbishops of fools to use in any way the insignia of pontiffs, namely the mitre, pastoral staff, or other such things. Nor is it fitting that such archbishops [Col. 1174A] have a cross carried before them with a staff, as an archbishop customarily does when travelling on foot or horseback through his province, since such acts are a great mockery and disgrace of episcopal or archiepiscopal dignity.

**Fourth conclusion.**—Furthermore, it is not permissible for the aforesaid bishops or archbishops of fools to perform the divine office in church wearing the aforesaid insignia, to give blessings to those reading the lessons at Matins, or to bless the people. Such acts show great contempt and irreverence toward God and his service and greatly disgrace episcopal dignity—a dignity not only instituted by Christ, but used by him as the first, holy, and true pontiff, communicated by him to his apostles and to their successors.

**Qualification of the first, second, third, and fourth propositions.**

The alleged custom of the Feast of Fools in churches and ecclesiastical offices, together with the insolences and obscenities which people customarily observe to disturb divine worship and demean ecclesiastical dignity, must not be called a custom but a condemnable and pernicious corruption. Wherever it is found recorded for its condemnable perpetuation, especially in ecclesiastical books, it must by every means be erased and abolished as a pestilential occasion of evils and indecencies.

The stubborn observers of the aforesaid practices act like pagans; they are sacrilegious profaners of the Church’s sacraments and dignities, and detestable mockers of sacred things.

Those who stubbornly assert that, under the pretext of the aforesaid corruption which they call custom, it is permissible to engage in or observe insolences and obscenities around the Kalends of January, or at any other time, are vehemently suspected in the faith and must be judicially charged with heresy.

[Col. 1174C] **Fifth conclusion.**—Since the aforesaid acts are strictly forbidden both by decretals of the supreme pontiffs and by decrees of general councils, if anyone—especially after the public proclamation and explanation of these same decrees by the local prelate or under his authority—should, with stubborn and hardened intention, commit the aforesaid acts or give aid or authority to those who commit them, such persons may and must be punished as contemners and violators of sacred decrees. Since violators of decrees of this kind are regarded under canon law as heretics or persons suspected in the faith, because they seem to hold evil views concerning the Church’s authority, proceedings against them may be brought through an inquisitor of heretical depravity.

**Qualification of the fifth conclusion.**

Those acting in this manner are obstinate, contemners of the Church’s keys, and vehemently suspected in the faith; they are to be judicially corrected as stated above.

[Col. 1174D] **Sixth conclusion.**—If, according to the foregoing, it is not permissible at the aforesaid Feast of Fools to make bishops or archbishops of fools who use pontifical insignia, perform the divine office in churches, and confer a blessing upon the people, then, by an argument all the stronger, it is not permissible under the pretext of any ancient custom—or, more truly, corruption—to make in any exempt church immediately subject to the Apostolic See a pope of fools, who likewise performs divine service in papal insignia, blesses the people, or in any other way exercises the office of pope.
