Such acts greatly contemn and dishonour papal dignity.

**Qualification of the sixth conclusion.**

Such abominators of pontifical dignities are sacrilegious, profaners of ecclesiastical dignity and the hierarchical order, and insulting mockers; they are to be judicially charged, as stated above in the first articles.

[Col. 1175A] **Seventh conclusion.**—It is neither permissible nor fitting for churchmen, especially those constituted in holy orders—among whom devotion, holiness, and gravity of conduct ought to shine more conspicuously—to perform the divine office, or attend it, under the pretext or guise of the said Feast of Fools without ecclesiastical habits and vestments, as was formerly observed in certain churches. Those who act otherwise, namely by using at divine offices the garments of laypeople, fools, or other profane clothing, since this disgraces and ridicules the divine office, commit a mortal sin and must be severely punished.

**Eighth conclusion.**—It is not permissible to lead dances in church while divine service is being performed, or to eat or drink near the altar while Mass is celebrated, or to commit other similar mockeries and follies. Such acts are contrary to reverence and honour for God and constitute contempt and mockery of divine service. Those who commit them must rightly be punished according to the gravity [Col. 1175B] of their excesses; and if they are rebellious and incorrigible, the secular arm may be invoked against them, and proceedings may be brought against them as persons suspected in the faith.

**Qualification of the seventh and eighth conclusions.**

Priests and clerics, especially those constituted in holy orders, who commit the aforesaid acts apostatize from the decency of the priesthood and divine worship; they abominably pollute the temple and sanctuary of God; they damnably and execrably contemn the most holy sacrament of the Eucharist; and they are vehemently suspected of unbelief and irreverence toward the sacraments, to be judicially charged, etc., as before.

**Ninth conclusion.**—It is not permissible for churchmen, under the pretext or guise of the Feast of Fools, to lay aside and put off their clerical or ecclesiastical clothing and wear the clothing of laymen or fools, even outside church. Such things greatly derogate from clerical decency and the gravity of their conduct. Still less is it permissible for them to put on masked or painted faces, assume women’s clothing, perform theatrical games, mockeries, or displays of their bodies, or enact other character-parts, especially in public places or before a great crowd of the people. Those who do otherwise, even under the pretext or guise of the aforesaid feast, especially after publication of the aforesaid decrees, commit mortal sin; indeed, as contemners and violators of sacred decrees, they must be punished.

**Tenth conclusion.**—It is not permissible for churchmen, especially priests or others constituted in holy orders, before the people to perform character-parts in plays that move neither to devotion nor to good conduct, but rather to laughter and mockery, since such conduct is in no way suited to clerical decency or gravity.

**Eleventh conclusion.**—Laypeople performing such games, which are solely for laughter [Col. 1175D] or mockery, must not use the habits or garments of monks, nuns, or other churchmen, since this too is prohibited by civil law.

**Qualification of the ninth, tenth, and eleventh conclusions.**

Priests and clerics, especially those constituted in holy orders, who perform such shameful spectacles apostatize from the rule and decency of the priesthood, scandalize and disfigure the ecclesiastical estate, and must be corrected by their superiors as persons suspected of deforming the Church and ecclesiastical order, as in the first conclusions.

**Twelfth conclusion.**—To say and stubbornly assert that those who prevent the aforesaid Feast of Fools from being held henceforth sin and are excommunicated expresses heresy and error in the faith, since ecclesiastical censure was granted by Christ to the Church against rebels and obstinate persons, not against those acting rightly [Col. 1176A]. For to say that someone ought to be excommunicated and cast out of the Church for an act of virtue is unsound in the faith.

**Qualification of the twelfth conclusion.**

Those stubbornly asserting the contents of this article are vehemently suspected in the faith and must be judicially charged with heresy, as stated earlier in the first articles.

**Thirteenth conclusion.**—Since, according to blessed Augustine, the aforesaid Feast of Fools took its beginning and origin from pagans and gentiles, who performed similar games at the beginning of January in honour of Janus, whom they believed to be a god and for whom they made an idol, before whose presence and as though sacrificing to him they performed the aforesaid games, Christians ought especially to avoid and flee such games, lest by performing or attending them they appear to act like pagans and to wish to render reverence and honour to Janus’s idol—especially when these acts take place at the beginning of January, which received its name from Janus himself.

[Col. 1176B] **Fourteenth conclusion.**—If those accustomed to hold the aforesaid feast have been sufficiently informed, advised, indeed admonished—especially by their own prelate—of the foregoing authority of blessed Augustine, not to perform these games in future, especially at the beginning of January, lest they appear to act like pagans or idolaters; and if afterward, with hardened and stubborn intention, they do the contrary, proceedings must be brought against them as persons suspected in the faith and followers of pagan rites, through an inquisitor of heretical depravity and, if necessary, by invocation of the secular arm.

**Qualification of the thirteenth and fourteenth conclusions.**

This contains the truth; and it is to be said of those who assert and stubbornly observe these practices as was said in the first articles.

These aforesaid acts, the foregoing letter and the qualifications, were undertaken and concluded at the end of a congregation of the venerable Faculty of Theology in the University of Paris, held at Saint-Mathurin in the year of the Lord 1444, on the twelfth day of March, through the agency of the venerable, prudent, and learned Master Eustache de Mesnil, professor of sacred theology and dean of that faculty, after mature deliberation, in the presence of the venerable and prudent men, Masters Jean de Vernon, Jean Berondi, Guillaume Errard, Robert Cybole, Jean Vinet, Pierre de Vaucelles, and Jean Oliva, masters in theology, together with many others present there.

## XXX. Grant by Stephen, Bishop of Paris, of the Annual Revenues or Vacant Prebends in the Church of Paris, and Other Grants Made to the Canons of Saint Victor at Paris

(From the manuscript annals of the same abbey.)

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. Amen.

By the authority of the divine Scriptures we are instructed that, while we have time, we should do good to all, but especially to those who belong to the household of faith; and, redeeming our sins by alms, we should make for ourselves friends and receivers in eternal dwellings from the things which we possess only temporarily [Col. 1177C]. Therefore, since we have sinned in many things, let us strive to work charitably in many things, and especially to benefit and assist those whose merits we believe will support us in that very strict judgment.

Instructed by this authority and animated by this hope, I, Stephen, by the grace of God bishop of Paris, at the request and prayers of Berner, dean, and with the assent of the other canons of Blessed Mary and also of the priests of Saint John—namely William and Hugh—grant to the church of Blessed Victor and to the regular canons serving God there that henceforth they shall have the anniversaries of the aforesaid canons; so that for one year they shall have the revenues of the prebends of the canons of Blessed Mary in full, and shall discharge no obligation arising from this, whether to the church or to the deceased, whether concerning procession, visitation, or burial, except the anniversary office. For we do not wish to disturb them or, against their will or purpose, compel them to appear publicly.

[Col. 1177D] We add also that, if a canon of Blessed Mary, or of the hermits, or of the regular canons, or of the monks, or of any others, choosing such a life, leaves his prebend, the aforesaid church of Saint Victor shall possess the revenues of his prebend for one year. And, that everything may be clearly determined and the mouths of those who interpret perversely may be stopped, we make this sole exception:

> [Note: [Col. 1177D] This clause was later revoked by the same Stephen, whose charter is printed immediately afterward in the same place.]

If a canon of Blessed Mary returns his prebend into the bishop’s hand and pleads for someone, and the bishop hears him in this matter, the canons of Saint Victor shall have nothing in the prebend thus returned.

Nor do we wish to leave unmentioned that whatever we have granted, as determined above, to the regular canons of Saint Victor in the prebends of the canons of Blessed Mary, we likewise grant, with the common assent of the deans and canons of those churches, to the aforesaid canons of Saint Victor, to be held and possessed in perpetuity, in the prebends of Saint Marcellus, Saint Germanus of Auxerre, Saint Cloud, and also Saint Martin of the Fields.

[Col. 1178A] And, that this may be ratified, firm, and endure forever, we have confirmed this present charter by the authority of our seal and strengthened it by the signs of our canons.

Done publicly at Paris, in the chapter of Blessed Mary, in the year of the Incarnate Word 1124, in the sixteenth year of the reign of King Louis, in the first year of Bishop Stephen: the sign of Bishop Stephen; the sign of Berner, dean; the sign of Adam, precentor; the sign of Stephen, archdeacon; the sign of Theobald, archdeacon; the sign of Landon, priest; the sign of Theodoric, priest; the sign of Odo, priest; the sign of Daimbert, deacon; the sign of William, deacon; the sign of Gummeran, deacon; the sign of Hugh, subdeacon; the sign of Peter, subdeacon; the sign of Henry, subdeacon; the sign of Theobald, boy; the sign of Manasses, boy; the sign of Urban, boy. But if anyone should presume to act against this our [Col. 1178B] ordinance, let him be anathema.

### XXXI. Letters concerning the settlement of the boundaries of the bishoprics of Beauvais and Paris

(From the Paris cartulary.)

PHILIP, by the grace of God bishop of Beauvais, and ODO, bishop of Paris, to all who shall inspect these present letters: greeting in the Lord.

We make known that, whereas a dispute had arisen between us concerning the boundaries of the bishoprics of Beauvais and Paris at the place called Moynel, on the eastern side near the head of the church, we at last personally came to the place; and, after a careful inquiry had been made in our presence and in that of the abbots of the Valley of Blessed Mary, Saint-Just, and Hermeries, and of many other worthy men, among the neighbors of both bishoprics, we distinguished the boundaries by equal will and consent and set the boundary-marks in this manner: at the source of the Fountain of Moynel, which is in the brothers’ pond, the first stone marker; the second directly in the Calceya; the third in the more slender field; the fourth and final one directly beneath the oak which stands beside the wall enclosing the brothers’ gardens and beside a certain stream flowing from the aforesaid spring. Thus, what lies on the church’s side belongs to the bishopric of Beauvais; what lies on the other side belongs to the bishopric of Paris; all the other boundaries and limits of the aforesaid bishoprics remaining in the condition in which they were.

And, that this may remain ratified and unshaken, we have strengthened this present charter with the protection of our seals.

Done in the year of the Incarnate Word 1202, in November, on the day after Saint Martin’s Day.

### XXXVIII. Letter of Walter, archbishop of Rouen, concerning certain distributions to be made to the chapter of Rouen

(From the same source.)

To all the faithful of Christ to whom this present writing shall come, WALTER, by the grace of God archbishop of Rouen, greeting in the Lord.

Directing the eye of reason more attentively toward the path of salvation, we have remembered that at one time we withdrew from our beloved sons, namely the chapter of Rouen, certain provisions and supplies of temporal bread and wine, which by established custom were paid to the aforesaid chapter on specified days and solemnities by our predecessor of blessed [Col. 1179C] memory, R., archbishop of Rouen. Therefore, considering more earnestly the purpose of our soul’s salvation, and inspired by God, we have judged that those provisions and consolations of bread and wine ought to be restored fully and entirely to the same chapter, desiring to follow the practice of our good predecessor; so that the aforesaid brothers and our canons, restored more completely to the same fullness which they enjoyed in the time of our predecessor, may rejoice with us and devote themselves to divine service, not deprived of their due maintenance.

Accordingly, on the solemnities written below, we declare that we and our successors are bound to pay the aforesaid maintenance to the said chapter: namely, a provision or rent of one customary solidus on the Nativity of the Lord, likewise at Epiphany, likewise at the Purification of Blessed Mary, at the reception of an archbishop, at Easter, at the Ascension, at Pentecost, at the Assumption of Blessed Mary, [Col. 1179D] at her Nativity, at the Dedication, on the feast of Saint Romanus, and on the feast of All Saints. We are bound, moreover, to render offerings of bread and wine on the Annunciation of the Lord, on the Octaves of Easter, on the Octaves of Pentecost, on the feast of the Translation of Saint Romanus, on the feast of the apostles Peter and Paul, on the Transfiguration of the Lord, on the Conception of Blessed Mary, and on the day of the Circumcision.

And, that this restoration to the aforesaid chapter may not hereafter be overthrown by any malice, we have caused this testimony of our confirmation to be written and strengthened by the protection of our seal. Witnesses: Master Columba, canon of Rouen; Roger, dean; William, archdeacon; Henry, cantor; Philip, archdeacon; Ralph, archdeacon; Robert of Saint Nicholas; Master Evrard; and many others.

Given by the hand of Master I. the Breton, our clerk, at Grandmont near Rouen, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1207.

### XXXIX. Council of Rouen under Archbishop Walter

In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1189, on 11 February, when the most blessed Pope Clement III occupied the see, when the most glorious Philip reigned as king of the Franks, and the unconquered Richard, king of the English, governed Normandy, a provincial council was celebrated in the metropolitan see of Rouen, in the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. Our venerable father Walter, archbishop of Rouen, presided; all the suffragans were present, as were very many abbots and many prudent and discerning men. The following chapters were established.

(From the same source.)

[Col. 1180A]

I. Following the footsteps of venerable men of old, we have decreed first that all the suffragan churches of our province shall imitate this most holy metropolitan church in reading and chanting.

[Col. 1180B] II. Likewise, it was resolved that every church be furnished with books and priestly vestments; that the Eucharist be consecrated only in a vessel of gold or silver; and that no bishop consecrate any vessel of tin, unless evident necessity appears by the bishop’s judgment.

III. It was also resolved that the Lord’s Body shall not be carried, whether by day or night, without lights, a cross, and holy water, nor without the presence of a priest, unless an extreme necessity arising from a shortage of priests excuses this.

IV. It was also resolved that no cleric of whatever order shall presume to keep a concubine in his house.

V. Priests and clerics shall wear broad tonsures and a fitting circle of hair. Transgressors of this constitution shall be suspended from ecclesiastical benefices; those who have no benefices and nevertheless let their hair grow in this manner shall lose clerical privilege.

[Col. 1180C] VI. Establishing nothing new, but recalling the ordinances of ancient canons, we strictly forbid that the sons of priests shall henceforth be instituted as incumbents in churches where their fathers are known to have ministered, or that they shall obtain those churches by any indirect device through an intervening person.

VII. Concerning clerics who, because of their ignorance, condition of birth, perhaps uncleanness of life, or obstinate disobedience, evade examination by their bishop and receive orders from bishops outside the province or beyond the sea: although they bear those bishops’ seals as evidence of their ordination, we decree that they shall on no account be admitted by their own bishops to exercise the order thus received.

VIII. No ecclesiastical person or perpetual vicar shall set out beyond the province for study or pilgrimage without the permission of his own bishop or of that bishop’s officials.

[Col. 1180D] IX. We also decree that monks or clerics shall not engage in any trade for profit, and that monks, clerics, or laymen shall not hold churches or villages at farm.

X. We also forbid any priest to undertake the office of viscount or secular provost. If he presumes to do so, he shall be suspended from the office and deprived of every ecclesiastical benefice.

XI. A custom opposed to written and approved law shall not be defended by any claim of generality or length of time. Therefore, since, according to the nature of things, a person who denies a fact has no proof, and, if the plaintiff offers no proof, the defendant—even if he has furnished nothing—must be acquitted, especially if the plaintiff’s case is aided by no probable presumption, we decree that henceforth a plaintiff, in either a civil or criminal cause, may use both the testimony of witnesses and the authority of documents to establish his case. When these are lacking, [Col. 1181A] the burden of purging or proving himself shall then at last be imposed upon the defendant, when he is supported by a reputation equal to that of the contentious plaintiff, or otherwise by some probable presumption.

XII. As was provided at the Lateran Council, we decree and firmly command that archdeacons, while traveling through their archdeaconries, shall not be burdensome to those subject to them; that they shall not exceed six or seven horses; and that they shall receive no procuration from a cleric unless he has sufficient revenues. We also decree that they shall receive from no clerics with whom they cannot lodge honorably and without severe burden more than three customary solidi as compensation for their lodging. If they decide to lodge with poor clerics, or perhaps because the place is too small or because of the convenience of the business they are conducting, we decree that five, or at least four, of the nearest clerics possessing benefices shall share the burdens of that lodging jointly.

[Col. 1181B] XIII. We also decree that bishops or their officials shall not make themselves difficult about appeals on their court-days, but, because of the simplicity of some persons, shall offer this even when it is not requested.

XIV. Following the footsteps of the holy Fathers, we decree and firmly order that no one shall henceforth, under pretext of any custom, be excluded from entry into a church or from any other ecclesiastical sacrament, until, having been lawfully summoned, he has had a free opportunity to answer the charge; so that, only when convicted by spoken testimony or at least deemed to have confessed by interpretation of law, he may suffer from his judge, according to the nature of his offense, the appropriate sentence.

XV. We also decree that the testament of clerics shall be inviolably observed, and that the goods of clerics who die intestate shall be distributed to good uses through the hands of the bishops.

XVI. Concerning clerics who die after Easter, [Col. 1181C] we decree that they shall have free power to dispose by testament of the fruits of the following autumn.

XVII. Concerning the wives, households, and all goods of those marked with the cross, we command the observance of what was established by our fathers of happy memory, Urban and Gregory, and likewise by our most blessed father Clement.

XVIII. Since the oppressed and accused who flee to God’s church ought to enjoy complete security, it seems wholly absurd and contrary to all reason that secular causes involving bloodshed or corporal punishment should be tried in churches or in their cemeteries. Therefore, lest this happen henceforth, we forbid it under threat of anathema.

XIX. We also forbid under anathema that churches, tithes, or any [Col. 1181D] ecclesiastical benefices be leased by clerics, monks, or any ecclesiastical persons to laymen.

XX. No one shall henceforth presume to pay or receive private pensions and illicit payments or portions from churches or ecclesiastical benefices. Whoever does so shall be deprived of every ecclesiastical benefice and subject to excommunication.

XXI. Any ecclesiastical person, of whatever profession, who presumes to draw ecclesiastical persons before a secular judge in an ecclesiastical matter shall altogether lose the case, be subject to excommunication, and not be absolved by his bishop without adequate satisfaction.

XXII. We also forbid under anathema that anyone presume, without the knowledge of his bishop or officials, to pledge to anyone donations or ecclesiastical estates, or to alienate them in any manner.

[Col. 1182A] XXIII. All tithes of the land, whether of crops or fruits, belong to God and are sanctified to him. But because many are found unwilling to give tithes, we decree that, in accordance with the Lord’s command, they shall be admonished once, twice, and three times to pay their tithes in full from grain and wine, the fruits of trees, the offspring of animals, hay, flax, wool, hemp, cheeses, and everything renewed during the year. If, after admonition, they do not amend, they shall be excommunicated at the bishop’s command.

XXIV. No one shall presume, on the ground of a confession made to him concerning ecclesiastical rights, while that person lives, to harass that living person with lawsuits in order to extort a payment from him. Whoever does so shall be struck with anathema.

XXV. There are certain clerics as well as laymen who enter into such associations that henceforth, in any causes or affairs whatsoever, they furnish one another with mutual assistance, imposing a fixed penalty upon those who act contrary to such a constitution. Since canonical Scripture condemns such associations, or fraternities (*fratreiae*), among persons of either order, because observance of them leads some even to the crime of perjury, we forbid under threat of anathema that they be made henceforth, or, if they have been made, that they be observed.

XXVI. To restrain the malice of those who, putting aside the fear of God, endeavor through false swearers in a civil or ecclesiastical court to diminish God’s Church and to disinherit their neighbors, we decree that every Sunday, both in the cathedral and in every parish church, all those shall be excommunicated with lighted candles who knowingly swear falsely in an ecclesiastical or secular court to the injury of the most holy Church or to the disinheritance of any person. Likewise, all those shall be excommunicated [Col. 1182C] who have ever procured, by entreaty, price, or any pretext whatsoever, that such false oaths be sworn. No priest shall presume to absolve those guilty under this constitution or impose penance upon them, unless they are in danger of death. Rather, such perjurers and excommunicated persons shall be referred to their own bishops to be absolved, severely punished for so great an offense, and, for their greater humiliation, sent to the Apostolic See.

XXVII. Those also are to be excommunicated who, without the authority of the bishop or of the officials to whom it pertains, have rashly or by lay power intruded themselves into ecclesiastical benefices.

XXVIII. Forgers of seals are likewise excommunicated, as are those who knowingly use forged documents.

XXIX. Arsonists, poisoners, sorcerers, and those who knowingly associate with persons excommunicated by name are likewise excommunicated.

[Col. 1182D] XXX. Also to be excommunicated are obstinate clerics and rebellious priests who presume to celebrate divine offices contrary to the prohibition of the bishop or his officials.

XXXI. Furthermore, clerics and laymen alike are to be excommunicated who have fraudulently withheld from the lord archbishop of Rouen revenues due to him from the time when he obtained the dignity of the archbishopric, or who now withhold them, or who have diminished or diminish his rights and dignities, or shall diminish them in his absence, unless they make satisfaction before he sets out upon his journey of pilgrimage.

XXXII. It was resolved that any priest who knowingly celebrates while suspended shall refrain from divine office for one year; if he knowingly celebrates while excommunicated, he shall be sent to Rome.

- *Viris p. in a. p. ut f. s. s., ad e. c. p.* — “To men …” 192.
- *Viva v. v. et a. s. l. e., ut q.* — “Living …” 230.
- *Vocavit te n. e. C. de s. in p.* — “He called you …” 15.
- *Vox a. e., p. et u. m. in o. v. e.* — “A voice …” 179.
- *Vulgariter d., q. n et i. m. g. n. i. m. Ab* — “Commonly …” 64.

[Col. 1185]

# Order of the Matters Contained in This Volume

## PETER OF BLOIS

Prolegomena. IX

## LETTERS
### LETTER I.—Prologue, to Henry II.

This letter takes the place of a preface, as the author noted at the end of the letter [Col. 1186]; for in it he explains to Henry II, king of England, why he permitted this collection of letters to be published, although it is little polished and elaborated in style. 1

### LETTER II.—To the same King Henry.

He consoles King Henry the father, who is grieving more deeply than is fitting over the death of his son Henry III [Col. 1187]; and he argues that the custom of mourning those who have died is indeed pious if it is moderated, but that there is no reason to lament the son's death so bitterly, since he himself exacted from himself such great penalties for the failings of his past life that there can be no doubt that he exchanged this life for eternal life. 3

### LETTER III.—To G., a nobleman.

He sternly rebukes a man noble by birth who had reproached his chaplain for the lowliness of his family; and he shows that poverty is to be valued more highly than splendor of birth when that splendor is devoid of virtue; humility must be pursued, but pride avoided. 7

### LETTER IV.—To R., Prior of Cîteaux.

He congratulates a monk on his progress in religious life, laments his own lot as one living in the world, and commends himself to the monk's prayers and sacrifices. He then resolves a certain doubt. 11

### LETTER V.—To Richard, Archbishop of Canterbury.

He freely rebukes Richard, who, immediately after St. Thomas the martyr, had risen from a monastery to the archbishopric of Canterbury and was intent upon accumulating wealth and attending to secular rather than spiritual matters; he also sets forth the complaints against him both of the people and of King Henry II. 13

### LETTER VI.—To Ralph of Beauvais.

He replies to the invective of a certain master who bitterly attacks the lives of clerics dwelling in bishops' courts; and in turn he severely rebukes the man for spending his whole life on profane letters. He urges him at least to spend his final old age meditating on his last things. 16

### LETTER VII.—To Master A.

He attempts, by testimonies from Holy Scripture, to recall a certain master—changed from a most acute disputant into an excellent drinker—from devotion to drunkenness. 19

### LETTER VIII.—To a certain prior.

He explains that the Church of God, like the moon, has had varying conditions; and that sayings of pagan philosophers and even of jurists may rightly be used in handing down sacred doctrine. 21

### LETTER IX.—To a certain deserter from the school of letters.

He inveighs against one of his pupils who, having completed the course of the liberal arts, intended not to apply himself to theology until he had spent two years in idleness; and at length he demonstrates that every kind of idleness is harmful. 24

### LETTER X.—To G., chaplain of the King of Sicily.

He vehemently complains that a thoroughly unsuitable man has been raised by the youthful king of Sicily to the bishopric of the Church of Agrigento. At the same time, he shows that it is the duty of the chaplain to whom he writes to warn the king seriously of this error, not once only, but a second and third time as well. 27

### LETTER XI.—To R., a cleric now advanced in age.

He urges a certain cleric, who had promised God that he would enter religion, to fulfill his vow; nor should he permit himself to be recalled from his purpose—unless he wishes to be ruined—either by the severity of religious discipline or by the complaints of parents and friends. 33

### LETTER XII.—To a certain nephew of his.

He consoles a nephew grieving excessively over the death of his uncle, the burning of his house, and an injury to his foot. He proves that the afflictions of this life are signs of divine love toward us, and that the world is so vain that one who has died to the world through death ought by no means to be mourned. 36

### LETTER XIII.—To a novice monk.

He rebukes a novice monk who, before the time, seeks a priorate—that is, freedom to leave the monastery and authority to preach the word of God. He warns that it is more fitting for a novice monk to be taught than to teach; to be subject rather than to preside; to remain hidden rather than to come forward in public. 39

### LETTER XIV.—To the court chaplains of the King of England.

He confesses that, through the benefit of a serious illness, he came to know the dangers of courtly life. He describes at length its many vanities and troubles. He says that more learned clerics are inexcusable before God if they pursue courts, and he exhorts the chaplains to whom he writes to leave them by his example. 42

### LETTER XV.—To Count Renaud, elected Bishop of Chartres.

He instructs the son of Count R., elected bishop of Chartres, concerning the virtues with which a bishop ought to be endowed and the vices from which he ought to recoil. 51

### LETTER XVI.—To a certain bishop already advanced in years.

He earnestly urges a bishop distracted by many affairs and occupations to adopt a more tranquil manner of life, for the sake of securing his own salvation and that of others; and to consider that it is not enough to be conscious of no grave fault unless he joins many good works to an innocent life. 59

### LETTER XVII.—To a cleric engaged in trade.

He shows that a cleric engaged in commerce differs in no respect from a usurer, and that every pursuit of accumulated wealth is vain and harmful. 62

### LETTER XVIII.—To a certain master, his friend.

He most severely censures the habits, character, and utterly wicked life [Col. 1188] of a certain bishop, to whose court he was being invited by his friend. 65

### LETTER XIX.—To his friend R., a student of canon law.

He resolves two questions proposed to him. The first is whether a woman who, believing that her husband had died, had professed the monastic life may, upon his return, reclaim her husband on her own authority. The second is whether, after the husband subsequently dies, she is obliged to resume the monastic life. 69

### LETTER XX.—To Lord Crispin and Master Pagan.

He complains that the ill will of courtiers excludes him from the court and familiar society promised him by Renaud, bishop of Chartres. He praises Renaud’s humanity and generosity and urges him fearlessly to undertake the defense of ecclesiastical liberty against royal exactions. 72

### LETTER XXI.—To H., a canon and former friend.

He describes and attacks the remarkable haughtiness and arrogance of H., a canon and former friend. 75

### LETTER XXII.—To Master John of Salisbury.

He consoles John of Salisbury, living in exile with St. Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury, by the hope of future reward. He warns him to continue fighting bravely in defense of ecclesiastical liberty, while setting aside every desire for vengeance. He does not doubt that this struggle will finally have a glorious outcome in Thomas. 77

### LETTER XXIII.—To Octavius, cardinal of the Roman Church.

He sorrowfully complains that, everywhere, men unworthy in learning, virtue, and age alike rush through the highest ambition into bishoprics and other dignities. He beseeches Octavius, legate of the Apostolic See, to use his authority to keep all ambitious persons and Simonists from the helm of the Church. 82

### LETTER XXIV.—To the household of Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury.

Reginald, Archdeacon of Salisbury, had incurred the displeasure of the exiled Archbishop Thomas. Peter desires that Reginald, ready to make satisfaction and be reconciled, should be restored to friendship and thereby to fellowship in persecution. 86

### LETTER XXV.—To the official of the Bishop of Chartres.

He urges the official to abandon the office he has undertaken because of the grave and numerous abuses connected with it; accordingly, he describes at length the frauds and devices of officials. 88

### LETTER XXVI.—To a certain companion of his.

He writes that, having abandoned the study of civil law, he is applying himself to theology at Paris; that the study and practice of civil law do not suit clerics, because of the very great abuses of advocates. 91

### LETTER XXVII.—To the canons of Belvidere.

He teaches that the death of St. Thomas, martyr and Archbishop of Canterbury, is not to be lamented, since he exchanged earthly life for heavenly, and a miserable life for a glorious one. He carefully describes Thomas’s virtues and rebukes his cathedral monks because, secretly and in contempt of the common election by bishops and abbots, they chose a successor. Finally, he wishes that the supreme pontiff would restrain the ambition of clerics and monks alike. 92

### LETTER XXVIII.—A letter of Rotrodus to William, Archbishop of Sens.

Rotrodus, Archbishop of Rouen, implores the aid of the Archbishop of Sens, that by his efforts he may avert the impending destruction of the Church of Rouen and its most noble town of Les Andelys, arising from the war between the kings of England and France. 96

### LETTER XXIX.—To the abbot and convent of St. Albans.

He complains of the inhospitality of the prior of Wallingford and brings forward many matters in praise of hospitality, adding that ancient monks and monasteries had long ago been especially commended for it. 98

### LETTER XXX.—To R., Bishop-elect of Bath.

Peter had seen his friend, to whom he writes, once, twice, and three times in a dream adorned with episcopal insignia. He discloses this vision to him and wishes that, from whatever source it may ultimately have arisen, it may attain its effect. 100

### LETTER XXXI.—To Ralph, Abbot of Fontenay.

He gives thanks both to Abbot R., because he had taken pity on him while severely afflicted by illness, and especially to God, because He had mercifully scourged him. He copiously shows from the sacred writings that illnesses and other afflictions of this life are healthful, useful, and sweet, and are to be numbered among God’s singular gifts. 105

### LETTER XXXII.—To the Prior of Canterbury.

Trusting in the prior’s friendship and charity, he commends to him a certain matter concerning the convent of Canterbury. 108

### LETTER XXXIII.—To Henry III, King of England.

R., Archbishop of Rouen, attempts to recall Henry III, king of the English, from his undertaking of waging war against his father Henry II, and commends Les Andelys to his protection. 109

### LETTER XXXIV.—To P., Bishop of Périgueux.

He excuses himself before the Bishop of Périgueux, who was inviting him to his court: he is so won over by the promises of his former lord that he cannot now meet that bishop’s expectations. 110

### LETTER XXXV.—To Anselma, a nun.

He wonderfully praises the resolution of the most noble virgin Anselma, who has embraced the monastic life, and urges her, after conquering every temptation of flesh and world, bravely to guard the treasure of chastity. 113

### LETTER XXXVI.—To Christiana, a nun.

He praises the nun for preserving the chastity consecrated to God in religion. He urges her to join charity, humility, and perseverance to virginity. 114

### LETTER XXXVII.—To Alexander, Prior of Jumièges.

He excuses himself for failing to return, at the appointed time, a book which he had promised to restore. 116

### LETTER XXXVIII.—To Albert, Cardinal of the Roman Church.

He sets forth the praises of the Archbishop of Canterbury and defends him against the accusations made against him: that he is ignorant of law, avaricious, and excessively devoted to advancing his own family. 116

### LETTER XXXIX.—To a certain friend.

119

### LETTER XL.—To a certain prelate, his friend.

He inveighs against H., a prelate who disparages princes. 119

### LETTER XLI.—To Henry II, King of England.

He complains that the King of England is moving about among uncertain residences; he says that the king’s envoys sent to Rome have returned, and notes that envoys of the kings of Spain are also present. 121

### LETTER XLII.—To Robert, Bishop-elect of Cambrai.

He rebukes R., provost of Arras, because, although elected bishop of Cambrai, he does not perform a bishop’s office, entangles himself in secular affairs, hears capital cases, tyrannically despoils his subjects, and permits no one to move him. 122

### LETTER XLIII.—To Peter, his physician friend.

He informs Peter, skilled in medicine, that while traveling he visited a sick nobleman and administered medicine to him. He sets forth the nature of the illness and its treatment, and thereafter entrusts the sick man to Peter’s care. 126

### LETTER XLIV.—To Arnulf, Bishop of Lisieux.

He advises A., Bishop of Lisieux, not to resign his bishopric on account of troubles unjustly inflicted by the prince, the chapter, or others, but only if he attained it through the favor of human ambition. 128

### LETTER XLV.—To a certain anonymous person.

He denies that Reginald, Bishop of Bath, was either a persecutor or a killer of St. Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury; but if he committed any offense against him in word or deed, it happened through ignorance, or was certainly expiated by alms, tears, and voluntary penances. 130

### LETTER XLVI.—To Richard, Bishop of Syracuse.

He gives Bishop Richard his reason for not wishing to return to Sicily, namely the harshness of the climate. He then digresses into praises of Blessed Thomas, martyr of Canterbury, and finally urges the bishop to whom he writes to spend the remainder of his life in England, his native soil. 133

### LETTER XLVII.—To Henry III, King of the English.

Richard, Archbishop of Canterbury, urges Henry, son of Henry II, king of the English, to desist from the war he had begun against his father; if he does not, Richard threatens excommunication. 137

### LETTER XLVIII.—To William of Pavia, Cardinal.

He congratulates William of Pavia, cardinal, that the long-lasting schism raised against Alexander III was finally extinguished at Emperor Frederick’s court through William’s prudence and eloquence. He then sharply censures Octavius, author of the schism, and his electors. 141

### LETTER XLIX.—To the Dean of Chartres and the Archdeacon of Blois.

At length he laments the wickedness of certain canons of Chartres, his friends and colleagues, who, in order to strip him of the dignity of the provostship of Chartres, had attempted even to defame his father, whose innocence he defends here. 145

### LETTER L.—To H., Bishop of Bayeux.

He attempts to persuade Henry, Bishop of Bayeux, to forgive G., chamberlain of the abbot, who had committed homicide in self-defense and was offering satisfaction: both because Christ receives penitents and because the command to love one’s neighbor requires it. 148

### LETTER LI.—To John, Bishop of Salisbury.

He warns the bishop to keep his word in paying money if he wishes to safeguard his honor. Then he warns him not to treat his nephews with excessive indulgence. 154

### LETTER LII.—To R., Archbishop of Canterbury.

He tells the Archbishop of Canterbury, by whom he had been sent to the king, how great a storm he endured at sea. He states that, because of benefits received from him, he shrinks from no labor. Finally, he asks that prayers be offered for him, that he may successfully transact with the king the business entrusted to him. 157

[Col. 1190]

### LETTER LIII.—To the bishops of England.

Richard, Archbishop of Canterbury, directs his fellow bishops not to permit foreign bishops of uncertain ordination to perform episcopal functions, and to declare excommunicated those who forge the bull of the supreme pontiff or the seals of bishops. 159

### LETTER LIV.—To L., Archdeacon of Poitiers.

He advises the Archdeacon of Poitiers not to compel his niece Adelitia against her will to enter the monastic life, since both marriage and the monastic state require free power of choice. 161

### LETTER LV.—To Adelitia, a nun.

He congratulates Adelitia because she aspires to the monastic life and has secretly bound herself by vow to enter a monastery. He praises virginity. He urges her to persevere and wholly renounce the world. 166

### LETTER LVI.—To Walter, Bishop of Rochester.

He dissuades Walter, an octogenarian bishop, from the pursuit of hunting on many grounds, and urges him to imitate the spiritual hunting practiced by the apostles. 169

### LETTER LVII.—To G., his friend of Alneto.

To his friend, who thinks that after entering a monastery he will be free from temptations, he shows that monks are more subject to temptations than secular persons, but that they must fight bravely against them. He then sends him a little song vividly expressing the struggle of flesh and spirit, so that it may beguile his weariness. 171

### LETTER LVIII.—To Reginald, Bishop of Bath.

He strongly protests to the Bishop of Bath because, contrary to the order of law, he suspended his vice-archdeacon from office and seeks every occasion to harm him because a debt has not been paid. 173

### LETTER LIX.—To R., Bishop-elect of Bath.

By many arguments and examples, he attempts to persuade R., Bishop-elect of Bath, to restore to favor Master Henry, who had otherwise deserved very well of him, but had fallen from favor; and to exclude from his society Simon, a most evil flatterer and calumniator. 175

### LETTER LX.—To Master R., friend and companion.

To a friend complaining that bishops enrich their nephews from Christ’s patrimony rather than poor men devoted to virtue, he explains that this is an ancient complaint, but that poverty is far preferable to riches. 178

### LETTER LXI.—To R., Archdeacon of Salisbury.

He dissuades Archdeacon R. from the vanity of bird-catching, both because, by reason of his office, he has undertaken the care not of birds but of sheep, and because he will soon be raised to episcopal dignity. 181

### LETTER LXII.—To Master R. Blondus.

Geoffrey, Bishop-elect of Lincoln, rebukes one of his clerics for disobedience because he left him and attached himself to a certain abbot. He warns him not to set himself against the Archbishop of Canterbury under the name of an abbot. 184

### LETTER LXIII.—To Peter, Bishop of Arras.

He gives thanks to the Bishop of Arras for a gift sent to him. 186

### LETTER LXIV.—To Celestine, Roman Pontiff.

The Archbishop of Rouen, together with his suffragans, asks the supreme pontiff to procure the release of Richard, king of the English, who, while returning from his pilgrimage to Jerusalem, had been thrown into prison by the Archduke of Austria. 187

### LETTER LXV.—To a companion and friend.

He teaches his friend that it is not lawful to investigate knowledge of the future through auguries, dreams, visions, chance events, or other forbidden means. 190

### LETTER LXVI.—To Walter, Archbishop of Palermo.

He congratulates the Archbishop of Palermo because he has been raised from a humble station to so great a dignity. He briefly describes the stature and character of Henry II, king of the English, and demonstrates that he was in no way the author of the killing of St. Thomas, Archbishop and martyr of Canterbury. 195

### LETTER LXVII.—To Henry, King of England.

The Archbishop of Rouen attempts, by many arguments and by examples of kings both pagan and sacred, to persuade Henry II, king of the English, that Henry his son, heir to the kingdom, ought to be educated in letters. 210

### LETTER LXVIII.—To Pope Alexander III.

R., Archbishop of Canterbury, accuses the abbot of Malmesbury because he withdrew himself from obedience to his bishop. He then copiously laments how great the evils have been that followed from exemptions of abbots granted by Roman pontiffs on account of the tyranny of certain bishops. 213

### LETTER LXIX.—To Ralph, Bishop of Anjou.

He laments the falling away of the people of Anjou, who shamefully deserted King Henry II of England as he waged war against his rebellious son Henry. He urges the bishop either to bring them back to loyalty to their prince or to restrain them with the spiritual sword. 214

[Col. 1191]

### LETTER LXX.—To John, Bishop of Chartres.

He attempts to persuade the Bishop of Chartres that he would act more rightly if he promoted his nephews—provided they are poor and honorable—rather than outsiders to ecclesiastical benefices. 217

### LETTER LXXI.—To Master Ernald of Blois.

A man of Blois had bought law books in Paris and paid the price, but had not taken them away; another person, paying a higher price, took them away. The man of Blois therefore contends that those books, although they were not delivered to him, could not be bought by another. 219

### LETTER LXXII.—To a friend and companion.

He sharply inveighs against a man once his companion and friend who, through envy, had caused the man of Blois not to be admitted into the household of the Archbishop of Sens and to lose other ecclesiastical benefices. A learned letter, abounding in verses of poets. 221

### LETTER LXXIII.—To three bishops of England.

R., Archbishop of Canterbury, urges the bishops to remove an abuse that had become prevalent in England: namely, that killers of laypersons were punished by capital punishment, but killers of clerics and bishops only by excommunication. 224

### LETTER LXXIV.—To G., Archdeacon.

He advises the archdeacon not to punish for a second time his guest Guy, who has relapsed into the crime of adultery and is therefore incorrigible, but rather the man’s father, who had habituated him from early age to dice-playing, the seedbed of all evils. 227

### LETTER LXXV.—To Roger, Dean.

He advises Dean Roger, since he had certain harsh matters to report to the king, to wait for a suitable time, when the king’s mind would be more placid. He then adds that the consecration of the Bishop-elect of Lincoln has been postponed by the pope for three years. 229

### LETTER LXXVI.—To Master Peter of Blois.

He earnestly and learnedly admonishes his companion, who had spent almost his whole life in the study of civil law and poetic fables and was still occupied in composing and singing love verses, finally to apply himself to the study of theology and devote himself more diligently to the care of his soul’s salvation. 231

### LETTER LXXVII.—To Master Peter of Blois.

He congratulates Master Peter of Blois on sharing his name, since he is now known throughout the whole world by his writings. He then shows that men become immortal through writings. He attacks courtly flatterers and submits his book *On Deceptions* (*De praestigiis*) to his judgment. 237

### LETTER LXXVIII.—To R., Dean and Chapter of the Savior.

He congratulates the dean and chapter of Blois on their church’s restoration through a certain noble Geoffrey, and urges them to unity and concord of mind and to the daily celebration of the divine office. 240

### LETTER LXXIX.—To R., his friend.

He mocks R., a deacon, because, although from early youth he had been the greatest enemy of the female sex, he allowed love of women to draw him even into sacrilegious marriage. He greatly exaggerates the inconveniences of marriage, from Book VIII, chapter 11 of John of Salisbury’s *Polycraticus*. 243

### LETTER LXXX.—To G., his friend.

He warns his friend G. not to leave the monastery because of the envy or ill will of false brethren. He says that G. has been of great benefit to many in virtue; then he warns him not to cloak his own wickedness under the pretext of another’s ill will. 247

### LETTER LXXXI.—To Simon, Canon of Chartres.

He urges Canon Simon, who has abandoned the study of letters in order to accumulate wealth, to pursue learning after cutting off the desire for riches, following the example of many philosophers. 249

### LETTER LXXXII.—To the Abbot and Convent of Cîteaux.

Richard, Archbishop of Canterbury, after great praises of the Cistercian order, shows that it is greatly marred by this one blemish: that they withhold customary tithes from clerics and monks. He then threatens excommunication and the force of the secular arm unless they pay them. 252

### LETTER LXXXIII.—To B., Bishop of Exeter.

Walter, archdeacon, instructs the Bishop of Exeter, acting as ecclesiastical judge, to dissolve, by mandate of the Roman pontiff, a marriage unlawfully contracted between blood relatives. 255

### LETTER LXXXIV.—To Alexander, Roman Pope.

R., Archbishop of Canterbury, defends the reputation of bishops residing at the royal court against calumnies, and shows by the example of the ancients how fruitfully they serve the kingdom there. 259

### LETTER LXXXV.—To R. of Salisbury.

He severely rebukes in R. of Salisbury gluttony of the belly, shows how many evils arise from it, and demonstrates from ancient examples how highly sobriety is to be valued. 259

### LETTER LXXXVI.—To Master Alexander, a monk.

By many arguments he attempts to persuade Alexander, a Carthusian monk, not to abandon his order, at that time most celebrated, either because he cannot celebrate the divine service in it every day or for other reasons, and not to transfer to a less strict order. 262

### LETTER LXXXVII.—To William, Bishop of Ely.

He consoles G., Bishop of Ely, most shamefully removed from the administration of the kingdom of England through the treachery of certain persons, and he severely inveighs against the faithless counselors of kings. 272

### LETTER LXXXVIII.—To the Abbot of Tewkesbury.

R., Archbishop of Canterbury, asks, warns, and by many arguments urges the Abbot of Tewkesbury to receive back into the order a monk who deserted it but has now come to repentance. 276

### LETTER LXXXIX.—To Hugh, Bishop.

He sharply attacks Bishop H. because he was the chief cause why William, Bishop of Ely, was deprived, to his extreme disgrace, of the office of administering the kingdom of England. 278

### LETTER XC.—To Master William of Blois, Abbot.

First he sets forth why he left Sicily with the consent of the Sicilian king. Then he makes every effort to persuade his brother, the abbot, to surrender the pontifical insignia received from the pope—such as the mitre, ring, and sandals—or to resign the administration of the abbey. 281

### LETTER XCI.—To Ralph, Bishop of Lisieux.

He vehemently attacks the Bishop of Lisieux for avarice and the practice of lending at interest, especially because during a time of famine he did not open his granaries to the poor. 285

### LETTER XCII.—To Reginald, Bishop of Bath.

He inveighs against Zoilus, the detractor of his writings. 289

### LETTER XCIII.—To Master William, Abbot.

He congratulates his brother, the abbot, because, following his advice, he resigned the abbey into the hands of the supreme pontiff and preferred the humility of a subject to the dignity of a superior, and France to Sicily. 291

### LETTER XCIV.—To J., Archdeacon.

He complains to the archdeacon of the insolence of his nephews, knights, because they impiously assail the sacred order of clerics, pursue idleness, and, like others of their age, have departed very far from the virtue of ancient knights, whose praises he depicts. 293

### LETTER XCV.—To H., King of the English.

Since the King of England could not know all that was done in his very extensive provinces, he warns him of various abuses by sheriffs and other lower officials and reveals a method by which they may be corrected. 297

### LETTER XCVI.

Richard, raised from a Cistercian monk to the archbishopric of Canterbury, commends himself to the prayers of the assembled fathers of Cîteaux. 302

### LETTER XCVII.—To the Abbot of Evesham.

He shows that the diversity of monastic orders is praiseworthy and that one ought not lightly pass from one to another; but manual labor in them is neither to be praised nor blamed. 304

### LETTER XCVIII.—To the suffragans of the Church of Canterbury.

The Archbishop of Canterbury declares to his suffragan bishops how necessary it is to assist the land of Jerusalem, and warns them diligently to collect money from their subjects for that purpose according to the prescribed formula. 306

### LETTER XCIX.—To Urban, Roman Pope.

Baldwin, Archbishop of Canterbury, congratulates Pope Urban because, after Lucius III, he had been installed as pontiff by the unanimous consent of the electors, and gives him thanks for the pallium received. 308

### LETTER C.—To R., his friend.

He defends the reputation of a certain new archbishop accused of excessive leniency, and copiously explains what leniency in a bishop deserves praise and what deserves rebuke. 308

### LETTER CI.—To R., Archdeacon of Nantes.

He sets forth to the archdeacon his judgment of the ability of two nephews entrusted to his instruction, and teaches that one must not leap to higher studies until the foundations of grammar have been properly laid. 311

### LETTER CII.—To H., Abbot of Reading.

He recounts at length the complaint of the Abbot of Reading, who wishes to resign the dignity he has undertaken because of grave dangers. He then responds to the complaint and warns him carefully to consider whether it is expedient for him to resign. 314

### LETTER CIII.—To H., Abbot of Reading.

He excuses himself for the length of the preceding letter. 326

### LETTER CIV.—To the Dean and Chapter of the Church of Salisbury.

He congratulates the canons of Salisbury because they are considering moving their church from a hill to the plain. 326

### LETTER CV.—To the Prior and Convent of Fontenay.

He consoles monks desolated by the failure of the harvest. 328

[Col. 1193]

### LETTER CVI.—To R., Subdean of Salisbury.

He teaches that calamities are sent by God not only because of the sins of princes, as that subdean thought, but also because of the sins of the people. 329

### LETTER CVII.—To B., a monk and friend.

He rebukes the monk B. because he pursues courtly life and its vices—detraction and flattery. 330

### LETTER CVIII.—To G., Bishop of Ely.

He implores the assistance of the royal chancellor against the tyranny of a sheriff. 331

### LETTER CIX.—To H., Archbishop of Canterbury.

He states that illness prevents him from returning to court. 332

### LETTER CX.—To the Abbot and Convent of La Charité.

Being ill, he implores the assistance of the monks’ prayers. 333

### LETTER CXI.—To G., a canon and his friend.

He urges Canon G. to read the sacred writings diligently if he wishes to resist the temptations of the flesh. 334

### LETTER CXII.—To R., Bishop of Orléans.

He vigorously contends for ecclesiastical immunity: namely, that the King of France, for the war at Jerusalem against the Saracens, should exact from clerics not money but prayers alone. 335

### LETTER CXIII.—To G., Archbishop of York.

He urges the archbishop to resist heretics and, with the common consent of the clergy, punish them with so severe a penalty that others may be deterred from heresy. 340

### LETTER CXIV.—To J., Bishop of Chartres.

He congratulates John of Salisbury because he has been raised to the episcopate, because he promoted Peter of Blois, his namesake, and because he wrote the life of Lord Thomas the martyr in an elegant style. 342

### LETTER CXV.—To H., Abbot of Messender.

He explains the question proposed concerning degrees of affinity and when they invalidate marriage. 343

### LETTER CXVI.—To H., Abbot of St. Denis.

He sends Abbot H. a book composed by himself for examination, and at the same time consoles him in the affliction he was suffering from the king. 345

### LETTER CXVII.—To G., Abbot of Marmoutier.

He rebukes Abbot G. because, over a matter of land and pasture, he brought the prior of St. Cosmas to judgment. 346

### LETTER CXVIII.—To G., Archdeacon of York.

He rebukes an archdeacon who boasts of his innocence although there is much in him deserving rebuke. 348

### LETTER CXIX.—To R., a canon.

He rebukes Canon H. because he insulted those to whom he was sent, and he interprets their disparagements in a favorable sense, showing by the example of many that he does this. 350

### LETTER CXX.—To R., Dean of Tours.

He asks the dean to correct his nephew Simon, who is simoniacally hunting after many ecclesiastical benefices and is burdened with very great debt. 352

### LETTER CXXI.—To J., Dean of Rouen.

He urges the Dean of Rouen not to permit churches to be oppressed with exactions on the occasion of the war for Jerusalem, and not to allow the expedition, as on other occasions, to be delayed longer. 354

### LETTER CXXII.—To William, Archbishop of Reims.

H., Archbishop of Canterbury, praises the Archbishop of Reims for the charity he showed St. Thomas the martyr while he was in exile. He asks him not readily to believe those who disparage his reputation and to preserve his former affection toward him. 356

### LETTER CXXIII.—To R., Bishop of London.

He declares that he is unwilling to advance from the diaconate to the rank of priestly eminence, not from contempt but from reverence. He then shows that no one ought to be compelled to enter the priesthood. 358

### LETTER CXXIV.—To Walter, Archbishop of Rouen.

He consoles W., Archbishop of Rouen, exiled from his church, and defends his flight as just against detractors. 367

### LETTER CXXV.—To the same person.

He warns the same man diligently to avoid idleness in his exile and to devote himself to reading the divine writings and to prayers, whose benefits he describes here. 373

### LETTER CXXVI.—To R., Abbot of Gloucester.

At the request of Abbot R., he describes the life and character of Odo, a most noble man elected Bishop of Paris from being cantor of Bourges. 375

### LETTER CXXVII.—To Odo, Bishop of Paris.

He asks that the friendship formed with Odo, the new bishop, from childhood be confirmed, and urges him to fulfill his episcopal duty. 378

### LETTER CXXVIII.—To William, Archbishop of Sens.

He complains that promises made by the Archbishop of Sens are fulfilled too slowly. The archbishop had promised to receive him [Col. 1194] into his household and endow him with an ecclesiastical benefice. 380

### LETTER CXXIX.—To R., Archdeacon of Orléans.

He sternly inveighs against R., Archdeacon of Orléans, because he introduced the pest of simony into the Church, and by many examples shows it to be detestable. 381

### LETTER CXXX.—To John, Bishop of Chartres.

He clears himself of the calumny of certain persons who had spread abroad that, against John, Bishop of Chartres, he had implored the aid of kings, counts, and the pope concerning the provostship of Chartres. He rejoices that the bishop’s nephew has been received into favor and declares himself most devoted to him because of benefits received. 384

### LETTER CXXXI.—To E., Prior of Monasteriolum.

He rebukes his nephew, a monk, because, neglecting the study of sacred writings and solitude, he seeks the friendships of princes and the world. 386

### LETTER CXXXII.—To E., Abbot of St. Laumer.

He delivers outstanding instructions to a new abbot, to be carefully observed by all other superiors. 391

### LETTER CXXXIII.—To R., Dean and Chapter of the Church of Salisbury.

He proves that, because of the smallness of his benefice, he ought not rightly be compelled to take up residence in the Church of Salisbury. 395

### LETTER CXXXIV.—To William, Abbot-elect of St. Mary.

He excellently instructs W., an abbot recently elected, in all matters pertaining to his office. 397

### LETTER CXXXV.—Hubert, Archbishop of Canterbury, to the Dean and Chapter of Salisbury.

The Archbishop of Canterbury exempts a certain canon from the law of residence and teaches that clerics may be exempted from it for many reasons. 403

### LETTER CXXXVI.—To Pope Alexander.

Henry II, king of England, complains of the rebellion of Henry and his remaining sons against him and implores the aid of Pope Alexander II. 404

### LETTER CXXXVII.—To Master Alexander of St. Albans.

He congratulates Master Alexander, a novice, on entering religion. He urges him bravely to bear the new yoke of obedience and the unfamiliar strictness of discipline, and to die completely to the world and to himself. 404

### LETTER CXXXVIII.—To Walter, Archbishop of Rouen.

He congratulates Archbishop W. on his return from exile, and
Peace restored to the Church of Rouen. He gives the reason why the righteous are afflicted, and advises him to ascribe peace to God, its author. 408 **LETTER CXXXIX.—To R., Abbot, and the Convent of Chichester.**—He implores the monks’ prayers, that he may be worthily ordained to the priesthood, and gives the reasons why he has hitherto shrunk from it. 413 **LETTER CXL.—To Peter, clerk of the King of England.**—He urges Peter the deacon, abandoning the study of jurisprudence, which brings ruin upon many, to devote himself wholly to sacred theology and to the reading of divine writings, and to order his life suitably to his rank. Here is a lucid teaching concerning the Holy Eucharist. 416 **LETTER CXLI.—To W., Archbishop of Rouen.**—He complains that the revenues of his benefice have for five years been withheld by a certain Elias, and asks the archbishop to compel him by his authority to make restitution. 422 **LETTER CXLII.—To P., Prior, and the Convent of Evesham.**—He consoles monks who are grievously afflicted; urges them to bear affliction patiently; and instructs them how they ought to conduct themselves. 425 **LETTER CXLIII.—To Conrad, Archbishop of Mainz.**—On the strength of an old friendship formed long ago in the schools, he entreats the Archbishop of Mainz to strive with every effort, together with the other princes of the Empire, to free from the Duke of Austria and the Emperor the King of England, Richard, who has been taken captive by them. 428 **LETTER CXLIV.—Eleanor, Queen of England, to Pope Celestine.**—Eleanor, Queen of England, piteously implores the Pope’s help for the liberation of her son Richard, King of England. 432 **LETTER CXLV.—The Same to the Same.**—On the same subject. 433 **LETTER CXLVI.—The Same to the Same.**—On the same subject. 433 **LETTER CXLVII.—To Robert, Bishop of Bangor.**—He rebukes Bishop R., who was trying to retain for himself an ecclesiastical benefice already conferred upon another. 434 **LETTER CXLVIII.—To Savaric, Bishop of Bath.**—He urges the bishop to return to his diocese and not to abandon his church on account of a pilgrimage. 436 **LETTER CXLIX.—To J. and P., his friends.**—He complains that he, now old and discharged from service, is being deprived of the honour of the archdeaconry by the false accusation of ill-wishers, and implores the help of two courtiers in this matter. [Col. 1195] 439 **LETTER CL.—To the Clerks of the Royal Court.**—He softens what he had said more harshly about courtly life in Letter XIV, and acknowledges that it is fitting for some clerks, and even bishops, to serve in kings’ courts, provided they do not abandon their flock or imitate the vices of the court. 439 **LETTER CLI.—To Pope Innocent III.**—He entreats and adjures the supreme pontiff to ensure that the archdeaconry of London, now offered to him in his old age, is endowed with more ample revenues. 442 **LETTER CLII.—To the Same.**—He petitions the supreme pontiff that the church of Wolverhampton, of which he was dean, may, because of the incorrigible conduct of its clergy, be converted into a monastery of the Cistercian Order. 443 **LETTER CLIII.—To Henry II, King of England.**—The bishops of Rouen and Lisieux freely set forth the substance of their embassy to the King of France, reveal the causes of the war declared by him to the destruction of the realm and King of England, and advise him to make God favourable to him through his own prayers and those of others. 446 **LETTER CLIV.—To the Queen of the English.**—Eleanor, Queen of England, is admonished to be reconciled to her husband Henry, together with her sons who have conspired against their father. 448 **LETTER CLV.—To the Prior and Convent of La Charité.**—Rothrod, Archbishop of Rouen, invited by the monks to rest during wartime, excuses himself on the ground that he cannot be absent from his flock without scandal; and asks them, if peace cannot be arranged between the king-father and his son, and the King of France, to commend the matter to the Lord in their prayers. 449 **LETTER CLVI.—To G., Bishop of Ely.**—He implores the bishop’s aid in freeing him from debt. 450 **LETTER CLVII.—To G., his vicar.**—He instructs his vicar to take diligent care of the flock entrusted to him and, by the example of his life, to preach to those whom he teaches. 450 **LETTER CLVIII.—To John, Bishop of Chartres.**—He complains bitterly that, in the Roman curia, certain persons corrupted by gifts attempted, contrary to the canons, to appoint an unlettered layman as head of an abbey, but in vain. 452 **LETTER CLIX.—To Henry, Bishop of Bayeux.**—He reminds the Bishop of Bayeux of his duty, while nevertheless begging pardon for having dared to do so. 454 **LETTER CLX.—To Odo, Bishop of Paris.**—P. of Blois, since he had lived in England for twenty-six years, asks Bishop Odo to recall him to France, so that, if he cannot live there, he may at least be buried in his native land. 455 **LETTER CLXI.**—He complains grievously that the man whom he considered his greatest friend has become a hostile enemy and detractor. It appears to have been written to a bishop. 456 **LETTER CLXII.—To E., his friend.**—He says that he lives in a foreign land because he is little welcome among his fellow-countrymen at home; and he thanks his friend E. because, almost alone, he has shown himself a friend and as it were a brother. 457 **LETTER CLXIII.—To Reginald, Bishop-elect of Bath.**—He congratulates Reginald, from whom he had received great benefits, upon his election as Bishop of Bath. 458 **LETTER CLXIV.—To Master Philip.**—A certain person is reproved for accusing the Archbishop of Canterbury of excessive gentleness. 458 **LETTER CLXV.—Guy, Archbishop of Sens, to Pope Gregory.**—The Bishop of Laon is cleared of the crimes imputed to him. 460 **LETTER CLXVI.—To the Pope.**—Certain persons intercede for the Abbot of Saumur. 460 **LETTER CLXVII.—To Eleanor, Queen of England.**—Christians in the Holy Land console Eleanor, Queen of England, over the untimely death of her son Henry III, King of England, and report that they celebrated his funeral in the presence of the legate of the Apostolic See. 461 **LETTER CLXVIII.—To N., Roman Pontiff.**—A certain king congratulates himself and the whole West that N., from his own land, has attained the supreme pontificate; and urges him to promote only worthy persons to ecclesiastical dignities. 463 **LETTER CLXIX.—To a Certain Queen.**—He consoles a queen grieving for the death of her sons. 464 **LETTER CLXX.—To a Certain Queen.**—He urges a queen not to grieve beyond measure over the death of the King of Aragon. 465 **LETTER CLXXI.**—He consoles a certain person grieving over the death of many people. 466 **LETTER CLXXII.**—He most bitterly laments the unhappy death of the Emperor Frederick, called Barbarossa. 467 **LETTER CLXXIII.—To the Suffragan Bishops and Abbots.**—The Archbishop of Rouen implores the aid of bishops and abbots in order that they may relieve the need of the Roman pontiff. 468 **LETTER CLXXIV.—To the Teachers of the Neapolitan Academy.**—He laments the death of Master Walter, professor of grammar. **I.**—A song on the struggle of flesh and spirit. 1127

Prologue.—The author invokes the most holy Trinity—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—that he may be able worthily to write on the mysteries of the most holy Eucharist. 1135  
Invocation of the Father. 1136  
Invocation of the Son. 1137  
Invocation of the Holy Spirit. 1138  

**CHAPTER I.**—That the flesh now consecrated from bread upon the altar is truly one and the same flesh as that believed to have been born from the Virgin and to have suffered on the cross. 1138  
**CHAPTER II.**—That Christ, the bread made man, came to the aid of the world endangered by hunger for the Word. 1138  
**CHAPTER III.**—That no one but Christ could make satisfaction for Adam’s sins; and that although immortal according to both natures, he nevertheless voluntarily died for us. 1139  
**CHAPTER IV.**—That the lamb sacrificed and roasted under the Law, and eaten by the Israelite people, bore the type of Christ; and that, when true grace and the true sacrifice succeeded—that is, when Christ appeared—the legal ceremonies ceased. 1140  
**CHAPTER V.**—That, although sacrificed in different places, the Lamb remains whole, and is wholly received by the faithful as the food of life. 1140  
**CHAPTER VI.**—That Christ’s bread and flesh are consecrated not through the merit of the consecrator but through the word and power of the Creator; and that nothing greater is effected by the good person, nor anything less by the evil person. 1141  
**CHAPTER VII.**—That the priest, in consecration, commemorating the sacrifice and imitating with tears Christ’s Passion, is Christ and crucified, both sacrificer and sacrificed. 1141  
**CHAPTER VIII.**—That God alone is the sacrificer and administrator of the sacrifice, while the priest is only a minister; and that by the same word flesh is made upon the altar by which it was created in the virginal womb. 1142  
**CHAPTER IX.**—That the Potter of heavenly vessels can change upon the altar a small portion of bread into something better, namely into the glory of his flesh, since he was able to refashion unto life from death the earthen vessel of our humanity which he assumed and fired in the furnace of his Passion. 1142  
**CHAPTER X.**—That neither flesh without blood nor blood without flesh is rightly communicated, as was foreshadowed in Melchizedek, who is read to have offered bread and wine together as a type of our Saviour. 1143  
**CHAPTER XI.**—That the Lord wished the deep secrets of heavenly things to be hidden, so that they might be concealed from the faithless and the faithful might increase in the merit of the strength of faith. 1144  
**CHAPTER XII.**—Water is mixed with wine because both flowed together from the Saviour’s side on the cross: the blood of redemption, namely, and the water of baptism by which the Church is signified. 1144  
**CHAPTER XIII.**—In the consecration of the Lord’s blood, namely at the Supper, we do not read that water was first mixed with wine; but, so that nothing might be lacking in this sacrament for the commemoration of the Lord’s Passion, the apostles and their successors decreed that this should be done. 1145  
**CHAPTER XIV.**—Although wine and water are symbolically mixed upon the altar before consecration, afterward only blood is drunk, because the water is changed into blood, so that the people, represented by it, may be shown, when they worthily receive these things, to have been changed for the better. 1145  
**CHAPTER XV.**—That before the Law and under the Law the gate of the kingdom of heaven was closed to the holy Fathers; but after grace had been given it was opened to the thief and to all who repent devoutly. 1146  
[Col. 1202] **CHAPTER XVI.**—That paradise is opened to humankind through reception of this sacrament and through the power of the saving cross, and that the devil is overcome. 1147  
**CHAPTER XVII.**—That Christ is the giver of our Law and our Moses, who, having rescued us from the devil’s power, was sacrificed as the Paschal Lamb, and who leads us through this world’s wilderness to the kingdom promised to us. 1148  
**CHAPTER XVIII.**—That our Lord himself was called the grain of wheat, which, dying after falling into the earth and rising again, was multiplied into seed of life; from this grain sprang many grains of the faithful, which daily become one with him in the Church. 1148  
**CHAPTER XIX.**—That no one who has become a member of the devil should presume, in Judas’s fashion, to approach the Lord’s body; Judas was condemned not so much by consciousness of his former fault as because, still sinful and unclean, he did not fear presumptuously to approach the sacred table. 1149  
**CHAPTER XX.**—That no believer may be ignorant of the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood which is celebrated in the Church, lest perhaps, because of what he does not know, he be judged unworthy to receive it. 1149  
**CHAPTER XXI.**—That every priest ought to know the Lord’s sacraments, by which he may teach the people subject to him and instruct them in the true faith; without such knowledge he cannot worthily exercise the priesthood. 1150  
**CHAPTER XXII.**—That the priest, walking in Christ’s footsteps and proclaiming the word of life to the peoples, is called the Lord’s anointed and his angel; and, as he kindles his neighbour toward the knowledge of God and love of heavenly things, he receives seraphic dignity. 1151  
**CHAPTER XXIII.**—That the glowing coal is the same as the seraph. For when holy rulers in the Church rekindle God’s people, extinguished in the darkness of sins, toward love of heavenly things through the word of salvation and the example of good conduct, they are indeed called living coals which kindle others. 1151  
**CHAPTER XXIV.**—That it is exceedingly dangerous to approach the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood, where, amid the company of angels and all saints, Christ himself, the supreme priest, gives himself as the food of life or death, subtly discerning the merits of each person. 1152  
**CHAPTER XXV.**—That, according to the diversity of merits, Christ is sacrificed in the Church as lamb and goat, as was prefigured in the Law, so that, as blessed Jerome says, the more perfect may feed on the lamb’s flesh, while sinners and penitents feed on the goat. 1153  
**CHAPTER XXVI.**—That the priest and every believer ought to be conformed to his head, which is Christ, and spiritually follow him daily into heaven. 1154

**XXXIX.**—Council of Rouen under Archbishop Walter. In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1189, on 11 February, while the most blessed Pope Clement III held office, while Philip, most glorious King of the Franks, reigned, and while Richard, unconquered King of the English, governed Normandy, a provincial council was celebrated in the metropolitan see of Rouen, in the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. It was presided over by our venerable father Walter, Archbishop of Rouen, with all the suffragan bishops present, as well as very many abbots and many prudent and discerning men; in it the following chapters were enacted. 1180
